# Saint Marcellinus, Pope

[Col. 0009A]

## § I.—When and for How Long He Occupied the See

Eusebius relates that this pope governed the Church for nine years, and in his *Chronicle* assigns his death to the year of Christ 304. Thus, by counting eight complete years together with one begun as nine, he agrees with the Bucherian Catalogue, in which we read:

> Marcellinus held office for eight years, three months, and twenty-five days, in the times of Diocletian and Maximian, from the day before the Kalends of July, during the consulships of Diocletian for the sixth time and Constantius for the second, until the consulship of Diocletian for the ninth time and Maximian for the eighth.

It follows that the election or ordination of Marcellinus must be assigned to June 30, 296, which was accordingly a Tuesday, and his death to October 24, 304, although, on the authority of most martyrologies, his feast is celebrated on April 26.

[Col. 0009B]

## § II.—The Ancient Fable by Which It Was Commonly Reported That Marcellinus Offered Incense to Idols

1. Already in Augustine’s time there was a report that Marcellinus had offered incense to idols and surrendered the sacred books. That holy Doctor suspects the more recent Donatists of having originated it. First, in *On the One Baptism, Against Petilian*, chapter 16, no. 27, he proves the falsity of this fabrication from the fact that it is supported by no witness and by no reliable documentary evidence:

> Why, then, he says, is it necessary for us to refute the charges he brought against the bishops of the Roman Church, whom he pursued with incredible slanders? Marcellinus and his presbyters Melchiades, Marcellus, and Silvester are accused by him of surrendering the divine books and [Col. 0009C] of offering incense; but are they also convicted of it, or shown to have been convicted by any reliable documentary evidence? He says that they were wicked and sacrilegious; I reply that they were innocent. Why should I labor to prove my defense, when he has not even attempted to offer the slightest proof of his accusation?

[Col. 0010A] From these words of Augustine it is clear to everyone that the same charge was directed not only against Marcellinus but also against his presbyters Marcellus, Melchiades, and Silvester, who later succeeded him. If, therefore, they were altogether innocent and free from this crime, Marcellinus should no more be regarded as guilty. This will indeed be beyond doubt for us once we have thoroughly examined the cause and origin of this slander.

2. Augustine subsequently discloses this cause when he indicates that the fable was devised by the more recent Donatists so that they might avert the odium arising from the judgment by which they had been condemned by Melchiades. But why was it necessary for them to defame, together with Melchiades, the pontiff Marcellinus and the presbyters [Col. 0010B] Marcellus and Silvester? Clearly, so that their slander might appear more plausible. They therefore had to devise a time when the offering of incense and the surrender of the sacred books were being demanded at Rome, and at the same time to pretend that those who were then prominent among the Roman clergy had been led into the same impiety. For if they had spread this report about Melchiades alone, who would believe that so great a crime could have been left unpunished? But this impunity becomes more credible when both the very man whose duty it was to punish it and those who presided immediately after him are made participants in the same crime.

In the passage cited, however, Augustine convicts the new Donatists of falsehood by this decisive argument: their predecessors, either before or after the judgment of Melchiades, had never even thought of that charge:

> When the predecessors [Col. 0010C] of these men complained with the most importunate obstinacy to the aforementioned emperor, Constantine, about that judgment, alleging that it had not been fully or properly examined and delivered, they said nothing about Melchiades’ surrender of the Scriptures or offering of incense. [Col. 0011A] They certainly ought not even to have appeared at his hearing, but instead should first have informed the emperor—or insisted that he be informed—that they ought not to plead their case before one who had surrendered the divine books and had been polluted by sacrifices to idols. Since, therefore, they neither made such a representation beforehand nor, after judgment had been rendered against them in favor of Caecilian, thought that this charge should at least be brought forward when they were defeated and angry, why do these worthless men now, at so late a date, string together their slanders?

Who, moreover, could persuade himself that so public a crime remained unknown and buried until the time of Petilian? Or, if it did not remain hidden, that three presbyters guilty of so great a crime could, without anyone protesting, have been elevated to the foremost see of the Church and have gained for themselves the trust and favor of a most Christian prince? More worthy of credence is Theodoret, who in book I, chapter 3, of his *Ecclesiastical History* testifies that “Marcellinus distinguished himself during the persecution”: “Μαρκελλῖνον τὸν ἐν τῷ διωγμῷ διαπρέψαντα”—“Marcellinus, who distinguished himself in the persecution.” This may be interpreted as meaning that during the persecution he conducted himself worthily and commendably, or even that, having himself endured persecution courageously, he left behind a great reputation for his name.

3. Hence the Acts of the Council of Sinuessa collapse completely. Apart from their crude and unpolished language, many absurdities, certain internal contradictions, other details inconsistent with the statements of Petilian—who charged that Marcellus, Melchiades, and Silvester had offered incense—the offensive and repeated lying of the supreme pontiff, who is nevertheless represented as soon to be crowned with martyrdom, and very many other things of this kind deprive them of all authority.

Nevertheless, the Acts of this council are presented together with the spurious Acts of Silvester and Xystus in one and the same very ancient Colbertine codex written in Lombardic characters; and, insofar as one may judge from the kinship and agreement of their style, they appear to have the same author. We shall therefore reprint them below according to the evidence of the ancient manuscripts, which has by no means been preserved in the most recent editions of the councils, together with two letters falsely attributed to Marcellinus by Isidore Mercator.

## § III.—The Commonly Circulated Acts of the Council of Suessa, or Sinuessa, Concerning Pope Marcellinus

*[Note: [Col. 0011D]*

### Annotations on Text Block I

**I.—“They perceived above themselves.”** One of the manuscripts reads: “Sprinkled with the vacillation of their own minds, they lied about the origin, saying that they perceived the superstition of the gods above themselves to be free from vanity.” The corrector of these Acts attempted to emend the passage as follows: “Sprinkled with the pliability of their own minds, they lied about the origin of the gods, saying what they thought concerning their utterly vain superstition.” Could it not be read: “. . . saying that they perceived the superstition of the gods to be free from vanity”?

[Col. 0012D]

**“Let us stand.”** It should be noted that Diocletian and Maximian are chosen as arbiters of the dispute undertaken between Urbanus and Marcellinus.

**“Causes difficulty.”** That is, “It does not resist; it is disgraceful to become inflamed.” Their corrector, however, restored it as follows: “Since he presents us with no difficulty at which we might take offense.” From this one may perceive how much license he allowed himself in altering words and meanings.]*

### I. The Disputation of Urbanus and Marcellinus

1. Under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, when many people, through the wavering impulse of their minds, lied about the origin during their lives, saying [Col. 0011D] that they perceived the superstition of the gods above themselves to be free from vanity, and when at the same time many were induced by money to sacrifice and offer incense to the gods, a certain man named Urbanus, who was pontiff of the Capitol, came to Marcellinus, bishop of the city of Rome. [Col. 0012A] Filled with an abundance of malice, he began to dispute with him about offering incense to the gods. He said to Marcellinus, bishop of the city of Rome:

> If your Christ, whom you say was born of the Virgin Mary—why, at the first light of day, did the Magi sent by Herod offer him gifts? What gifts? Gold, frankincense, and myrrh, so that the priests might know by what means they were to appease this man whom you say rose again and sits above.

Bishop Marcellinus said to him:

> They did not offer these things to him in order to sacrifice to vanity, but in order to show that he whom they had denied was God and the most high Lord.

Urbanus replied to this:

> Let us stand together one night before our most invincible lords, the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, and the most merciful [Col. 0012B] princes, and I shall put to you the question of offering incense.

2. When they came on the day that they call the Vulcanalia, Urbanus said to him:

> Let us make two written documents, one from each side, as though they were amplifications of petitions, and let us bring them to the most merciful princes.

They both did together as Urbanus had proposed, and, coming to the most sacred princes, presented the documents to them. Then Marcellinus, bishop of the city of Rome, preserving the faith and preaching Christ, said to the princes:

> What have I to do with you, princes terrible to the whole world, since the superstition of offering incense is vain?

Urbanus, however, said:

> Speak to us and against the pontiffs, most merciful and invincible—most merciful and invincible—princes, since they fashion the god Jupiter and unconquered Hercules in bodily form, and Jupiter, whom we call the heaven, earth, and sea, measuring out the months together with Saturn. Why, therefore, does the pontiff Marcellinus not offer incense to their majesties, as I do?

Diocletian then said:

> Do not execrate this man, since he presents no difficulty to our clemency that should inflame it. Rather, let each of us accept his counsel, since we have not found it obscure to our serenity, nor do we deliver judgment against the immortal gods.

Romanus and Alexander then privately said to Diocletian:

> Lord and most invincible prince, if you hold this man to your purpose by blandishments, you will be able to preserve the entire populace of the city in unity and to rebuke the nations through most faithful sacrifices.

*[Note: [Col. 0013D]*

### Annotations on Text Block II

[Col. 0013D]

**II.—“The Vestian temple and Isis.”** Thus the Colbertine manuscripts, and not “of Vesta and Isis.”

**“Penus.”** Thus the Colbertine manuscript. Others, however, read *penes* or *per*. We would prefer *specturi*, “being about to behold,” as in “being about to behold an example of the truth.” In place of these words the corrector substituted: “to the temple, on account of the truth.”]*

### II. On Marcellinus’s Offering of Incense

3. Diocletian said to Marcellinus, bishop of the city of Rome: [Col. 0012D]

> I see that your prudence is great, so that our friendship may exist—a friendship that is, or perhaps “was,” hostile to the gods and to the whole world. Come, therefore, and make your eloquence an addition to our favor.

When he came [Col. 0013A] to the Vestian temple and to Isis, Diocletian brought the bishop inside. When they had entered, two deacons, Gaius and Innocentius, and three presbyters, Urbanus, Castorius, and Juvenalis, were with him. When they saw him enter—but did not yet see him cast incense and offer it—they all fled to their fellow presbyters. They found them in the Vatican area of Nero’s palace and told them what they had seen happen.

Many Christians then went there to behold an example of the truth—conjecturing *specturi* for the corrupt *penus*—and saw him casting and offering incense and becoming a friend of the princes. Those who departed from him in order to furnish testimony to the truth were: Bonosus, Maximus, Carpilio, Cyprianus, Olympius, Priscus, Hercules, Androphemus, Benenatus, Epiphanius, Crispinus, Victor, Theodolus, Alexander, Romanus, Bajulus, [Col. 0013B] Quiriacus, Theodolus, Caritosus, Omitazio, Honoratus, Crescentio, Maximus, Probinus, Urbicus, Concordius, Neapolus, Refrigerius, Sebastianus, Calpurnius, Julianus, Epiphorus, Crispianus, Habetdeum, Crescens, Rapula, Cyprianus, Abeulius, Exquiro, Orphitus, Venerius, Carpulianus, Constantius, Ursus, Valentinianus, Priscus, Severus, Probius, Faustus, Antonius, Quirillus, Albulus, Pulsanor, Homobonus, Caritto, Tespias, Marinus, Fabius, Crispinianus, Herculentius, Petrus, Nonnosus, Honestulus, Auriclianus, Impeditus, Furinus, Domitianus, Agapitus, Himulus, Capillatus, Nepotianus, Concordius, Bonifacius, Reparatus, Jugundinus, Auxentius, Cyprius, Bonushomo, Corporalis, Sallustius, Origanus, Venerosus, Abundius, Tinulus, and Major. All these were chosen [Col. 0013C] men of the western pound, who testify that they saw Marcellinus offer incense.

*[Note: [Col. 0013D]*

### Annotations on Text Block III

[Col. 0013D]

**III.—“A synod was therefore held.”** Against this synod it is customary to object: how, when a most savage persecution was raging, could three hundred bishops have assembled, and how could they have chosen a small town in which it was impossible for so many outsiders to remain concealed? One may also ask who summoned so many bishops, by whose command Marcellinus was brought to Sinuessa, and who presided over this synod. It is certainly evident from what was then said and done that the bishops who assembled at Rome in 502 in the case of Pope Symmachus knew nothing of any such synod.

**“Having lost their order.”** Why are those presbyters said to have been deprived of their dignity, “having lost their order,” [Col. 0014D] before they undergo examination? What was their crime, that they should be punished with this penalty? Nothing is charged against them except that, after abandoning Marcellinus, they refrained from offering incense to the gods. But the fabricator of these Acts—who wished it to be wholly unlawful for a cleric to accuse the man by whom he had been ordained, as we shall see in other Acts produced by his workshop—perhaps judged them deserving of this punishment because they had provided an occasion for accusing Marcellinus, their own creator.]*

### III. On the Synod at Which Marcellinus Denies That He Offered Incense

4. A synod was therefore held, although the priests were not assembled in their full number, because the course of the persecution was pressing upon them. When Bishop Marcellinus came, he denied that he had offered incense. He also said this and put forward this judgment: that those who appeared to have been with him in that place had abandoned him—namely, the presbyters Urbanus, Castorius, and Juvenalis, and the deacons Gaius and Innocentius.

The whole synod, however, said this with a unanimous judgment:

> You shall be the judge; by yourself you shall be condemned, and by yourself you shall be justified—yet in our [Col. 0014A] presence. When you come to your judgment, by yourself you shall be condemned and by yourself justified; for you are both judge and accused. As for the presbyters and deacons, because they abandoned the pontiff who created them in the dignity of the order of presbyter or deacon, deserted the threshing floor, and emptied the granary, let them, after losing their order, enter into examination to prove their case, since they emptied the granary. For the pontiff ought to have died with the five—supply “rather”—than to live condemned by his own judgment.

The entire synod entered the Crypt of Cleopatra in the city of Sessuana—the manuscript reads *Sensuana*—and, because a multitude could not be accommodated in the crypt, groups of fifty from the synod entered.

*[Note: [Col. 0014D]*

### Annotations on Text Block IV

[Col. 0014D]

**IV.—“The western pound.”** The word “western” is added here to distinguish it from the eastern pound, which consisted of seventy-four solidi. A pound containing seventy-two solidi is mentioned in the Theodosian Code, book XII, title VI, law 15.

**“He gave restoration. . . .”** The corrector attempted to emend these words as follows: “In restoration”—perhaps *in* should be removed and *reparatione*, “by restoration,” read—“the year rises again. This new thing also occurred, that one of the witnesses should enter who, although he had both a wife and children by her, nevertheless brought in an adulteress over the wife whom he had despised, and gave. . . .” Who could accept or tolerate a reading so foreign to the wording of the ancient codices? It is almost beyond doubt that it is far removed not only from the text but also from the author’s intention. The fabricator of these Acts was surely not the sort of person who, in a most serious case for which he required seventy-two [Col. 0015C] witnesses, would first produce a man whom both civil and ecclesiastical laws prohibited from giving testimony.

Anianus, the interpreter of the Theodosian Code, declares concerning book IX, title I, law 12:

> The admission of an accused person against anyone is dangerous and ought not to be permitted.

And concerning law 19:

> It has been established by right and by the laws that an accused person may not, by a voluntary confession, make another man accused, and that no credence concerning another is to be given to one who has confessed himself to be a criminal.

Augustine likewise proclaims in his second discourse on Psalm 36, no. 22:

> An accused person does not make another man accused.

The African canons also command in the *Code of the African Church*, chapter 129:

> All those whom the public laws do not admit to accuse persons of public crimes are not to be admitted as accusers.

And in chapter 8 they ordain:

> A man entangled in any crimes shall have no right to bring an accusation against one older than himself.

And in chapter 19 they require:

> If the character of the accuser is culpable, he shall not be admitted to prosecute the charge.

Nevertheless, lest anyone say that these rules concern accusers rather than witnesses, it must be remembered that chapter 131 of the same code decrees [Col. 0016C]:

> Those who are forbidden to be admitted as accusers are likewise not to be admitted as witnesses.

We, however, think that the statement that the first witness was the husband of one wife and had children was intended rather to commend his testimony, especially since we shall hear the same author say in the *Constitution of Silvester*, no. 6:

> A subdeacon, acolyte, exorcist, or lector shall not be condemned except upon the testimony of seven persons who have children and wives [Col. 0016D] and who in every respect profess Christ.

The earlier words of our text could therefore be restored more correctly in accordance with the author’s intention as follows: “These events accordingly occurred miraculously”—or “not without a miracle”—“so that among the testimonies”—or “among the witnesses”—“there should enter such a man, the husband of one wife,” and therefore fit to put to shame the man said to have stained himself with spiritual adultery.

**“To Hercules,” etc.** Baronius observes that this conflicts with the preceding account, in which Marcellinus is said to have been brought into the temple of Vesta and Isis, since it was customary in the temples of the gods to sacrifice only to the deities to whom those temples were dedicated. Accordingly, Marcellinus ought to have been said to have sacrificed to Isis and Vesta, not to Hercules, Jupiter, and Patusinus.]*

### IV. Urbanus, Castorius, and Their Companions Are Condemned

5. On the first day of the synod, those who condemned [Col. 0014B] the presbyters Urbanus, Castorius, and Juvenalis and the deacons Gaius and Innocentius entered. The following bishops entered to hear the pontiff, though not to judge him: Petrus, Castorius, Habetdeum, Castinus, Victor, Felicianus, Parterius, Majorinus, Castalius, Laurentius, Paulus, Bonosus, Felix, Firminus, Spesindeo, Tranquillinus, Anastasius, Castinus, Victor, Beneservandus, Joannes, Epiphanius, Castus, Yacinthus, Herculanus, Sabinus, Orfitus, Gaudiosus, Reparatus, Amplexus, Cyprus, Fortunatus, Quadratianus, Sebastianus, Cyprianus, Pascasius, Innocens, Valerius, Servulus, Cerasianus, Constantius, Quintilianus, Montanus, Catellus, Polycarpus, Athanasius, Hermias, Nepotianus, Petrus, and Aristonicius.

Entering the crypt for fear of the emperors, [Col. 0014C] in groups of about thirty, with one voice and in accordance with his counsel they rendered judgment on a single day and condemned the presbyters Urbanus, Castorius, and Juvenalis and the deacons Gaius and Innocentius, who had emptied the granary and left the threshing floor open so that the unclean creature might enter and eat the wheat. They condemned the men themselves as well.

6. They passed judgment, though they did not judge the pontiff, because they had unanimously confirmed this arrangement: amid these seventy-two testimonies he himself was to be the judge and the accused; in their presence he was to preserve himself as innocent and condemn himself as unfaithful, because “in seventy-two the year rises again by restoration according to the western pound” [corrupt text]. This event was therefore a miracle: there entered among the testimonies such a man, the husband of one wife and the father of children; just as this man too, who has a wife and children, committed adultery against his wife and gave his wife a bill of divorce [corrupt construction].

Then another ten and another three entered and said:

> We saw you casting and offering incense to Hercules, Jupiter, and Patusinus.

Marcellinus said:

> On what day?

One of them answered:

> On the day when you took off—or “cut away”—the purple and put on scarlet, and Diocletian rejoiced over you because shortly before you had persistently denied it, and you offered incense before his tribunal.

Bishop Athanasius said:

> Are the things to which these men testify true?

Bishop Petrus replied:

> Speak, pontiff—or perhaps, “Speak, you who are pontiff”—and judge your own case.

The fifty aforementioned bishops subscribed to the testimony of the fourteen men, who spoke with one voice out of the seventy-two, and confirmed the judgment.

### V. The Roman Presbyters Ratify the Condemnation of Castorius and His Companions; Another Fifty Bishops Examine the Case of Marcellinus

7. On another day, twenty-three presbyters of the city of Rome came. In their judgment they regarded the condemnation of the presbyters Urbanus, Castorius, and Juvenalis and the deacons Gaius and Innocentius as unimpaired. They upheld justice within their own order, saying:

> Having lost their order, let them deny that they and their companions belong to the Church.

8. On the second day after the condemnation of the presbyters Urbanus, Castorius, and Juvenalis and the deacons Gaius and Innocentius, another fifty bishops came and entered the crypt, [Col. 0015C] so that the third part of the synod might be completed. When they had entered the crypt because of the severity of the times, Marcellinus, bishop of the city, also entered, still retaining the name of bishop, since he had not yet been condemned unless the number, according to the order of the synod’s pound—the Colbertine manuscript reads *libra*, “pound”—proved the precedent.

[Col. 0016A] The following entered: Castinus, Bonus, Quiriacus, Dominicus, Alexander, Venerosus, Felix, Joannes, Crispus, Deusdedit, Honestatus, Majorianus, Vita, Carpurianus, Anastasius, Petrus, Crescentio, Domninus, Ursus, Agatho, Honestatus, Marcus, Urbanus, Valentinus, Sallustius, Crescens, Firminus, Spectator, Sebastianus, Ultius, Benenatus, Tristator, Servus, Marcus, Montanus, Asterius, Anthimus, Placentianus, Ambrosius, Quirillus, Andreas, Philippus, Magnus, Exsuperantius, Adrianus, Petrus, Gorgonius, Simplex, Victor, and Venerosus. They entered the crypt.

*[Note: [Col. 0016D]*

### Annotations on Text Block VI

[Col. 0016D]

**VI.—“Taken.”** The emender substituted “cultivated.” The reading *tultae*, “taken,” from *tollo, tuli, tultum*, must be retained, for examples of this usage are not lacking among writers of the later period. Nor is the preference of the same corrector a little earlier for “often mentioned” in place of “heated again” acceptable, since this latter verb is more suitable for tiles that are baked a second time.]*

### VI. They Leave Him to His Own Judgment and Approve the Condemnation of the Five Clerics

9. Bishops Anastasius and Anthimus answered:

> Judge the case with your own mouth, [Col. 0016B] not by our judgment; discharge the condition.

Bishop Sebastianus replied:

> Do not place it in our judgment, but gather your case into your own bosom and bring in witnesses to testify to the truth, since by yourself you will be justified and by your own mouth condemned. For our predecessors and fellow bishops rightly anticipated us and condemned—and with our own mouth we likewise ask that they be condemned by a single joint judgment—the presbyters Urbanus, Castorius, and Juvenalis and the deacons Gaius and Innocentius. For yesterday they broke—or “fled”—from the cave and left it heated again. Having lost their order, let them enter into examination, because, Bishop Petrus says, when all tiles have been taken from the furnace, though already baked, they are baked again by the sun and are tested by the rain in the same place, so that they may be placed upon the dwellings [Col. 0016C] of men.

*[Note: [Col. 0017C]*

### Annotations on Text Block VII

[Col. 0017C]

**VII.—“I did not sacrifice . . . I burned.”** This foolish and tasteless rationale for denial is unworthy of a pontiff, as though it could have been permissible for him not to know that one who burned grains of incense upon coals before idols was regarded as having sacrificed to the gods.

**“Fifty upon five.”** The printed editions, in three columns, read “fifty-five,” or “fifty and five.” The Colbertine manuscript more correctly reads “fifty,” namely bishops, “upon five testimonies.” For in the first session, first one man alone, then ten, and afterward three gave testimony on separate occasions; while in this second session another fourteen, questioned twice, gave testimony. From this five testimonies are produced.

**“Together with those previously introduced.”** One manuscript reads “those anticipating,” another “with those anticipating.” Their corrector reads “with the participants.” From the Colbertine manuscript, which has “of one anticipating,” we have restored “with those previously introduced,” that is, previously mentioned.

**“Together with these anticipating.”** One manuscript reads “with these anticipating.” The corrector reads “with these prescribed”; and shortly afterward, “all in a single examination.”

**“Which shortly.”** Supply “before.” Our author adds: “You were not wearing it sewn,” which refers to the time when Marcellinus did not know that his tunic had been torn. The corrector, however, departs from the author’s intention by presenting the passage as follows: “Therefore sew your tunic, and sew together the torn garment that you were wearing shortly before.”

**“Former pontiff of Rome.”** Thus the Colbertine manuscript, together with another noted in the printed editions. [Col. 0018C] This makes the contradiction in these Acts manifest: the bishops repeatedly declare that Marcellinus is to be condemned not by their own mouth but by his own judgment, yet here he is called “former pontiff” before he has condemned himself. One codex, however, is noted as reading simply “pontiff.”

[Col. 0018D]

**“Twenty-eight . . . witnesses.”** The corrector reads: “and of the twenty-eight aforementioned witnesses.” We would prefer: “and with the twenty-eight aforementioned witnesses,” namely, standing by. How, then, was the difficulty finally removed by which the bishops had initially been forbidden to assemble together, so that three hundred bishops, thirty presbyters, and fourteen witnesses could now all be in one place at the same time?

**“Ounces in the pound . . . meaning.”** The corrector’s reading is less objectionable: “the assessment will be proved by the ounces of the pound.”

**“And rend . . . because.”** Here too the corrector departs at considerable length from the archetypes, as follows: “And examine for yourself the wall you have demolished. For you will be condemned not by our judgment but by your own; by our testimony, however, you will be excused. Fear nothing, because. . . .” Certainly there is nothing anywhere in the Acts indicating that they wished Marcellinus to be excused.

**“In the sight . . . upon the ground.”** The Colbertine manuscript, together with another, reads: “From the mouth of the synod he fell upon the ground.” Another reads: “You recoil from the synod; you have fallen to the ground.”]*

### VII. It Is Proved That Marcellinus Offered Incense; Forty-Four New Witnesses Are Brought Forward; Marcellinus Condemns Himself

10. Since delay did not permit—perhaps, “did not endure”—these fifty bishops to subscribe to the condemnation of those under interdict, [Col. 0017A] so that, having lost their order, they might enter the synod, behold, fourteen witnesses entered and said that they had seen Marcellinus offering incense.

A bishop named Sallustius replied:

> Speak the truth openly.

Petrus responded and said to Bishop Marcellinus:

> Hear now, pontiff, and judge your own case, since by your own mouth you will be justified and by your own mouth condemned; for all the members cannot be sound if the head has been afflicted.

Marcellinus answered in a clear voice:

> I did not sacrifice to the gods; I merely burned grains of incense upon coals with uplifted hands.

All fifty episcopal prelates rose and said to the fourteen witnesses:

> What did you see this man doing, which he testifies to with his own mouth?

The witnesses answered as though with one voice. All fifty then subscribed to the five testimonies of the fourteen men, [Col. 0017B] so that together with those previously introduced the number twenty-eight was completed.

One of the bishops, named Quirinus, said:

> Pontiff, you have drenched your heart with malice, though for eighteen years you had guarded it in chastity. Prelate, you have wounded all your members. Therefore I shall not withdraw from any entrance of the synod: all your heart is purple.

11. On another day, those two hundred bishops determined that they too should enter the synod in groups of fifty. After a conference was held together with the hundred previously introduced, all three hundred sat in the same city for one examination; they bound and condemned the presbyters Urbanus, Castorius, and Juvenalis and the deacons Gaius and Innocentius.

Bishop Sebastianus replied:

> By our statement, our signature, our declaration, our assistance, our steadfastness and truth, and a settled and illustrious arrangement of the hearing, we present the binding force of this tribunal. For you will be justified neither by our mouth nor condemned by our mouth. Sew your tunic upon yourself—the tunic that shortly before you were not wearing sewn; now that it has been cut, sew it from your heart [Col. 0018A] and from your hands, so that you may be wrapped in your sin, Marcellinus, former pontiff of Rome.

Bishop Urbanus replied to Bishop Sebastianus:

> Let forty-four witnesses, men acting manfully, be brought in, so that the western pound may be completed by many, because what was fashioned by many must be established by many.

The following witnesses entered: Tranquillinus, Priscus, Bonus, Servulus, Cyprianus, Petrus, Quadratianus, Aresto, Tespius, Quadrus, Epiphorus, Maximus, Gordianus, Gaudiosus, Saturninus, Urbanus, Reparatus, Priscus, Venerosus, Romanus, Exsuperius, Crispianus, Barbarus, Leo, Forianus, Bacauda, Ambrosius, Terula, Johannes, Jubentius, Proculus, Octavianus, Romanus, Valerius, Iacinthus, Mellicianus, Petrus, Claudius, Exper, Probus, Nicorus, Probatianus, Ursinus, and Urbatianus.

12. Each of them stood in the midst of the three hundred bishops and thirty Roman presbyters, together with the twenty-eight aforementioned witnesses, so that the pound might be completed; for the meaning is proved by twelve ounces in the pound, and the prelate, weighed against seventy-two, will be condemned.

Bishop Quiriacus replied and said to Marcellinus:

> Do you not recognize the entire veil of your heart? See the *Acts Concerning the Purgation of Xystus III*, no. 4. Judge your own case and rend—torment—your own torment. You will not be judged by us, for you will be condemned by your own pontificate, and by our testimony you will unfold the boundaries. In the condemnation we offer no cause as an objection and defend nothing; rather, we condemn those who emptied the temple and abandoned the structure built over it by hand, so that wolves might enter, make dens, devour the spotless lambs, and make old those who had come from the old to the new. We do not condemn you, because by your own [Col. 0018C] mouth you will be justified, and by your own mouth you will be condemned.

Marcellinus, however, fell to the ground in the sight of the synod. While he lay there and remained there for some time, they condemned him. The synod and the thirty presbyters [Col. 0019A]—

*[Note: [Col. 0019B]*

### Annotations on the Text Block

**“They confirmed the written sentence.”** Two manuscripts read “the written sentence firm”; then one of them reads, “Urbanus, Castorius, Juvenalis, of these presbyters,” and the other, “of Urbanus, Castorius,” etc.

**“Of future time.”** The corrector added “as an example,” which is quite attractive. A learned man observes that, at least after Marcellinus had condemned himself, it was the synod’s duty to provide for the Roman Church, lest it remain any longer without a priest. Nevertheless, no action was taken to substitute another man in place of Marcellinus, and it is certain that no one was substituted for him.

**“For the condemnation.”** One manuscript reads “for the same condemnation”; [Col. 0020B] another, “for his condemnation.” The Colbertine manuscript reads “in it condemnation”; hence we judged that “for the condemnation” should be restored.

Baronius notes that the preceding words, “while he was engaged in the Persian war,” are false, since in this twentieth year of his reign Diocletian abdicated the imperial throne, and two years earlier had celebrated at Rome, together with his colleague Maximian, a triumph over the defeated Persians. He therefore thinks that these statements and those that follow do not derive from the Acts of the council but were afterward appended to them in the manner of an appendix. Yet all the codices that contain the preceding material contain this material as well. Nor is it surprising that an author who stumbles in so many other matters should err in this one too.]*

—in a clear voice confirmed the written sentence against the presbyters Urbanus, Castorius, and Juvenalis. They were: Humanus, Capuanus, Castorius, Innocentius, Audax, Homobonus, Petrus, Quiriacus, Herculanus, Serenus, Johannes, Nepotianus, Cyprianus, Corporanus, Eusebius, Castinus, Victor, Matthaeus, Spesindeo, Virus, Vincomalus, Collecticius, Valentinus, Priscillianus, Julianus, Lucianus, and Castorius; and these deacons: Hermes, Xystus, and Petrus. They subscribed to the condemnation of those five: the presbyters Urbanus, Castorius, and Juvenalis and the deacons Gaius and Innocentius.

13. Bishop Marcellinus, his head covered with ashes in the midst of the three hundred bishops, cried out in a clear voice:

> I have sinned before you, and I cannot remain in the priestly order, because a greedy man [Col. 0019B] corrupted me with gold—or, “because in my greed I corrupted myself with gold.”

They subscribed to his condemnation and condemned him outside the city. A priest named Helciades, a bishop, was the first to subscribe to his condemnation, not only for the present time, as order required, [Col. 0020A] but also for the future. He himself also said in a clear voice:

> Justly has he been condemned by his own mouth, and by his own mouth he has received the anathema *maranatha* (“Our Lord, come”), for he has been condemned by his own mouth. No one has ever judged the pontiff, nor has a prelate judged his own priest, because the first see will be judged by no one.

When Diocletian heard this while he was engaged in the Persian war, he learned that three hundred bishops, thirty presbyters, and three deacons had assembled for the condemnation. When all had subscribed, Marcellinus himself, first of all, concluded his own anathema with his own hand, subscribing to the anathema.

Diocletian, enraged, sent forces into that same city and brought many bishops to the crown of martyrdom. Nothing else occurred, once the three presbyters and two deacons had first been condemned. Bishop Marcellinus too was condemned by his own judgment on the tenth day before the Kalends of September, during the eighth consulship of Diocletian and the seventh of Maximian.

[Col. 0019]

# Saint Marcellus, Pope
§ I.—When and How Long He Occupied the See

[Col. 0019C] After Marcellinus’ death, the violence of the persecution did not permit a successor to be chosen for him. In the Bucherian Catalogue, the Roman see is said then to have been vacant for seven years, six months, and twenty-five days. But Bucherius thinks that “three years” should be read there instead of “seven years,” and this correction is necessarily required by the consuls under whom Marcellus is recorded in the same catalogue as having begun his pontificate. Indeed, the numerical sign V could easily have slipped in for the single stroke I. It follows that Marcellus was ordained in the year 308, on May 19, which fell on a Friday. The time during which this pope governed the Church is designated as follows by the aforementioned catalogue: “Marcellus, one year, seven months, twenty days, from the tenth consulship [supply: of Herculius] and Maximian [read: the seventh of Maximian], until after the tenth and seventh consulships”; that is, until [Col. 0019D] the following year, which was designated as the year after the tenth consulship of Herculius and the seventh of Maximian. But even from these data it cannot be established with certainty on what day he died.

Pagius, referring to Pope Marcellus what he finds in the Hieronymian [Col. 0020B] Martyrology under October 7—“At Rome, on the [Col. 0020C] Appian Way, the deposition of the bishops Marcellus and Marcus”—regards it as certain that Marcellus departed for heaven on October 7, 309. But it is more certain that Marcellus was deposited, or buried, “on the Salarian Way,” not “on the Appian Way.” Indeed, in the same Martyrology under January 16 there appears: “At Rome, on the Salarian Way, in the cemetery of Priscilla, the deposition of Marcellus, bishop and confessor.” The Bollandist *Liber Pontificalis*, copied from a manuscript belonging to the Queen of Sweden, agrees with this; in it the following is written of Marcellus: “He was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February.” We infer, however, from another manuscript of the same book, formerly belonging to Fossés and now to Colbert, that XVI is given there erroneously, perhaps through a copyist’s slip, in place of XVII; for in the latter we read “the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February,” not the sixteenth. Indeed, the Bucherian list of the depositions of the Roman [Col. 0020D] bishops records Marcellus’ deposition on January 15 in this form: “On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February, Marcellinus in [the cemetery] of Priscilla.” It is manifest that the name Marcellinus has slipped in here in place of Marcellus. Nor is confusion between those two names unusual. [Col. 0021A] This, indeed, appears to be why Eusebius nowhere mentions Marcellus and, in his *Chronicle*, records Pope Eusebius as though he had been Marcellinus’ immediate successor.

Accordingly, we judge that the authority of those records which assign Marcellus’ death to the month of January must be followed. The date of Marcellus’ death certainly cannot be reconciled at all with what the Bucherian Catalogue says about the period during which this pope governed the Church. But everything will fit appropriately if we read the same catalogue as follows: “Marcellus, one year, seven months, twenty-seven days, from the tenth consulship of Herculius and the seventh of Maximian, until the second [year, namely] after the tenth and seventh consulships.” That Marcellus’ pontificate must be extended to the second year after Herculius’ tenth consulship—that is, to the year of Christ 310—is necessarily required by what the same Bucherian Catalogue adds concerning this pope’s successors. [Col. 0021B]

§ II.—On Marcellus’ Constancy in Maintaining the Discipline of Penance

1. There survives a poem about St. Marcellus by Pope Damasus, published by Baronius under the year 309, no. 7, and reprinted among the other works of Damasus at Paris in 1672 by the press of Louis Billaine, with notes by M. Milesius Sarazanius, p. 173, and elsewhere. It is certainly worthy of inclusion here, especially since it makes clear what Marcellus’ position concerning penance was. It reads as follows.

### Pope Damasus’ Poem on Saint Marcellus the Martyr

Because the truthful ruler prescribed that the fallen  
Should bewail their crimes, he became a bitter enemy to all.

[Col. 0021C] Hence rage, hence hatred followed—discord, quarrels,  
Sedition, slaughter; the covenants of peace were broken.

Because of the crime of another, who in time of peace denied Christ,  
He—Marcellus—was driven from his native land by the tyrant’s—Maxentius’—savagery.

These established facts Damasus wished briefly to relate,  
So that the people might know Marcellus’ merit.

2. It is probable that the man on account of whose crime Marcellus is said to have been sent into exile was the same man through whose faction Marcellus’ successor Eusebius was also punished with the same penalty, and who is called Heraclius in the poem about that holy prelate which will shortly be transcribed below. Although the remedy of penance is necessary for the fallen, it is nevertheless harsh and bitter. It has therefore always offended some persons, who both rejected it and regarded as troublesome and hostile [Col. 0021D] enemies those pious pastors from whom they expected that nothing would be remitted to them. Long before, after Fabian’s death, the Roman clergy judged that they must by no means yield to the importunity of such people. Cyprian, who vigorously and steadfastly resisted the same men lest so necessary a discipline be undermined, had to endure many things at the hands of the factionalists. Finally, Marcellus preferred to undergo everything rather than permit so great an evil. Nor was Eusebius deterred by his exile from defending with unconquered courage the cause and discipline of penance which his predecessor had upheld. Both may deservedly be called martyrs of justice—that justice, namely, which those deny to God who, after offending him by sinning, refuse to make worthy satisfaction to him through penance.

3. Eusebius indeed relates in Book VIII, chapter 14, [Col. 0022A] that Maxentius, at the beginning of his usurpation of tyranny, pretended to profess our faith. But the banishment of the two pontiffs is in no way inconsistent with such a feigned profession. For since he pretended to profess our faith in order to please and flatter the Roman populace, he was easily induced to expel the two prelates from the City when, through Heraclius’ persuasion, he learned that this would be pleasing and acceptable to the people. Nor was faith then alleged as the reason for persecuting them; rather, the pretext was excessive severity, which was said to be the source of seditions. Hence one may conjecture that Heraclius possessed very great influence with Maxentius and belonged to that class of half-Christians with whom princely households abound: people who like to combine the Christian name with the pleasures of the world and who, although they do not fear to sin, utterly dread [Col. 0022B] the labors of penance and wish them to be banished far from themselves.

§ III.—On the Decree Ascribed to Marcellus, in Which the Practice by Which Parents Offered Children to Monasteries Is Discussed

1. In Gratian, causa 20, question 1, chapter 10, and thence in editions of the Councils, the following decree bears Marcellus’ name:

> We judge that this must be established: if children have been offered to a monastery while underage, or have received either the sacred tonsure or veils, we have judged it fitting that, upon reaching their fifteenth year, they be admonished by their superiors and questioned verbally whether they wish to remain in that state or not. If they profess that they wish to remain, they can by no means afterward obtain an opportunity for repentance—[that is, for changing their state and returning to the world]. [Col. 0022C] But if they wish to return to secular dress, permission to return must in no way be denied them, because it is altogether unprofitable for service to be rendered to the Lord under compulsion.

Labbeus, however, notes that the author of the Gloss on Gratian attributes it to Martin and that it is more appropriate to Martin’s times.

2. It is certainly evident that this decree belongs to the period when men began to derogate from the practice which had long prevailed—namely, that after children had been offered to monasteries by their parents, it was unlawful for them to abandon their purpose and return to the world. That this practice was never accepted among the Greeks may be inferred both from the following words of Theodore, Archbishop of Canterbury (*Spicilegium*, vol. IX, p. 62): “Basil judged that children were permitted [read: that it was permissible for children] to marry before the age of sixteen if they could not remain continent, even though they had been monks,” [Col. 0022D] and from Basil’s own words in the *Rules Discussed at Greater Length*, question 15, and in the *Shorter Rules*.

3. But the Rule of Benedict, chapter 59, affirms that practice in the West, and it is confirmed not only by the Rules of Isidore, the Master, and others, but also by the decrees of many councils held in Gaul, Spain, or Germany and by decrees of the supreme pontiffs. These had been preceded by a custom of the Church, established by the decrees of Siricius and Zosimus, by which it was lawful to consecrate sons from infancy to the sacred service of the clergy and assign them to the office of readers. They were likewise preceded by the practice that had constantly prevailed from the Church’s infancy: infants were baptized and thereafter bound by Christian laws in such a way “that, once grown, they could not [Col. 0023A] abandon with impunity” (these are the words of the Eighth Council of Toledo, canon 7) “what they had received as little children, either unknowingly or unwillingly.”

By this very example, the aforementioned council proves that those who “had obtained offices of ecclesiastical rank either through the occurrence of necessities or from fear of dangers” were bound by the laws of those offices, even if “when these offices were imposed upon them, they testified that they did not wish this to be done to them.”

Accordingly, the Fifth Council of Orléans, held in 549, canon 19, and the First Council of Mâcon, held in 581, canon 12, deprive of communion girls who, “whether they seek a monastery of their own will or are offered by their parents,” and who, “having either voluntarily, or at their parents’ request, professed the religious life or received the blessing, afterward” pass over to “marriage or the allurements of the world.”

In the year 633, canon 49, [Col. 0023B] the Fourth Council of Toledo decreed:

> Either paternal devotion or personal profession makes a monk. Whichever of these it may have been, it will keep him bound. We therefore close to such persons the way of returning to the world and prohibit every return to secular life.

The Tenth Council of Toledo confirmed the same decree in 656, canon 6, and explained it in these words:

> If, at any age short of majority, either one or both parents have given their children of either sex the religious tonsure or the garment owed to the religious life; or if, when it was undertaken unwillingly or unknowingly by them, the parents did not immediately repudiate it upon seeing it on their children, but permitted those children to possess such things either in their presence or before the Church and publicly in the assembly, it shall thereafter be utterly unlawful for those children ever to return to secular dress.

Gregory [Col. 0023C] II, when asked in 726 by Boniface of Mainz, “If a father or mother has delivered a son or daughter within the enclosure of a monastery during the years of infancy to be placed under regular discipline, whether, after they have completed the years of puberty, they may leave and enter into marriage,” answers without hesitation:

> We altogether reject this, because it is unlawful for the reins of sensual pleasure to be loosened for children offered to God by their parents.

From this question of Boniface, however, we learn that the law had already begun to seem harsh to at least some people. Nevertheless, it is clear from canon 22 of the Council of Mainz, held in that year at the command of Louis the Pious, that the law remained in force in Germany down to 868. It enacted:

> If a father and mother have delivered a daughter and a son [the text repeats “daughter”; corrected contextually] within the enclosure of a monastery during the years of infancy to be placed under regular discipline, they shall not be permitted, [Col. 0023D] after reaching the years of puberty, to leave and enter into marriage.

These words are entirely adapted to Boniface’s proposed question. The council then continues:

> Therefore, they shall not be permitted ever to abandon the habit they have assumed; rather, once it has been proved that they formerly possessed the tonsure or religious dress, they shall be compelled, whether willing or unwilling, to remain in the observance and habit of the religious life.

These words in turn are taken directly from canon 6 of the Tenth Council of Toledo, with only a slight alteration of the canon’s words—“they shall be recalled to the observance and habit of the religious life and compelled, under perpetual [or strict] discipline, to serve in this observance”—so that the removal of the power to change one’s state might be expressed more plainly. Then, in canon 23, the same council renews [Col. 0024A] and adopts as its own the aforementioned statute of the Fourth Council of Toledo, expressing it as follows:

> Therefore, either paternal devotion or personal devotion makes a monk. Whichever of these it may have been, it will keep him bound. We therefore close to him the way of returning to the world and prohibit every return to secular life.

4. Consequently, when the Aachen Capitulary of 817, chapter 36, ordained, “That the father and mother shall offer the boy at the altar at the time of his oblation and make a petition on his behalf before lay witnesses, which he himself shall confirm when he reaches an age of understanding,” this final clause must be regarded as added for the sake of greater security, not as though the boy, once he had reached a more mature age, were free to invalidate his parents’ oblation.

In that century, Gottschalk—as may be gathered from Rabanus’ short work published by our Mabillon, [Col. 0024B] *Annals of the Benedictines*, vol. II, pp. 726 ff.—opposed the vow of his parents, by whom he had been offered to the monastery as a boy. His argument, however, was not that the boy at that time lacked control over his own person, but that his parents had by no means performed this act before competent witnesses and, since they were Saxons, had summoned foreigners as witnesses, although under ancestral law “no one could be a witness unless he belonged to their own people.”

5. Around the same time, as is read in an epistle of Nicholas I in Gratian, causa 20, question 3, chapter 4, and in Ivo, part 6, chapter 356, a certain Lambert, clothed in the cowl by his father Atho between his eighth and eleventh year, petitioned the aforesaid pontiff both to be released from the obligation of leading the monastic life and not to be defrauded of his paternal and maternal inheritance. He did not allege [Col. 0024C] that he could not be bound by his father’s oblation, but that he had been “clothed in the monastic habit without an oblation by his father or the reception of a blessing from an abbot.” His father likewise testified:

> Neither did I, his father, offer him clothed in the altar cloth, as the Rule of Benedict prescribes, nor, after receiving a blessing from any priest or abbot, as custom requires, was he ever subjected to the Rule.

Thus he ought neither to have been called nor considered an oblate.

St. Bernard used the same argument in Epistle 1 to his nephew Robert, who, among the various reasons for his defection from the Cistercians to the Cluniacs, advanced the fact that he had been offered to the Cluniacs by his parents:

> Although there is no doubt that he was promised, not given—for the petition prescribed by the Rule was not made for him by his parents, nor was his hand, together with that petition, wrapped in the altar cloth so that he might thus be offered before witnesses.

Although Nicholas I, in the judgment delivered in Lambert’s case, wrote that he did not in any way think “that Lambert ought to be made a monk under such violence,” because “what a person has neither chosen nor desired, he certainly does not love; and what he does not love, he readily despises,” nevertheless, somewhat later, Rabanus vigorously defended the custom of such oblations in the short work published by Mabillon, as stated above. And in 895 the Council of Tribur, canon 16, established:

> A person whom his parents have delivered to a monastery, and who has begun to sing and read in the church, shall be able neither to take a wife nor to [Col. 0025A] abandon the monastery. If he departs, he shall be brought back; if he lets his tonsure grow out, he shall be tonsured again; if he has taken a wife, he shall be compelled to dismiss her.

6. It is evident both from Bernard’s Epistle 1, cited above, and from Sibert’s epistle to Rudolf, abbot of Saint-Trond, who flourished in the twelfth century, as well as from that abbot’s reply, that the same custom persisted into the twelfth century (*Decretals of Gregory IX*, book III, title 31, chapters 11 and 12). Even toward the end of that century, Alexander III and Clement III judged that it ought to be obeyed. Finally, their successor Celestine, when questioned concerning a boy whose father had made him assume the monastic habit before the years of discretion, replied (*ibid.*, chapter 14):

> If the said boy reaches the years of discretion and does not wish to retain the monastic habit, then, if he cannot be induced to do so, he is by no means to be compelled; for he will then be free to relinquish it and to claim the paternal goods that come to him by succession. [Col. 0025B]

7. Nevertheless, that law had already begun to fall into disuse in certain places. To Nicholas I, as we heard above, it had seemed too harsh and an infringement upon the freedom required for the choice of such a state. Nor was it for any other reason that Boniface of Mainz had earlier judged that Gregory II should be consulted about it. Later, however, the Cluniacs appear to have applied a certain mitigation to it. For St. Ulrich, describing their customs before the middle of the tenth century in book III, chapter 8, after recounting the oblation of boys and its rite, immediately adds: [Col. 0026A]

> Afterward the boy is clothed in the cowl, and thereafter his blessing is deferred until the lawful age—that is, if not longer, at least until the age of FIFTEEN YEARS.

Clement III also appears to allude to the same practice in the passage already cited. There, while utterly forbidding a girl delivered by her parents to a monastery before the years of discretion from returning to the world, he adds this reason for the prohibition:

> For she does not appear capable of casting off from herself the yoke of monastic profession, since it is not established that she clearly objected when she received the blessing—which those who are veiled receive only at the age of discretion—especially if, once subsequent ratification has occurred, the profession is confirmed, even if it is established that at some time she objected to it.

This argument embraces three points: first, that girls were not customarily blessed unless they had reached the age of discretion; second, that they then possessed the power to object to such a blessing; and finally, that those who objected had an opportunity to return to the world. [Col. 0026B]

8. Of all the testimonies that we have been able to collect or examine on this matter, none agrees more closely with our decree than the one we have produced from the customs of Cluny. It is therefore permissible to assign the decree to the end of the ninth century or the beginning of the tenth. Or it must be dated even later, if the blessing which the Cluniac customs prescribe at the lawful age was instituted so that the boy, now in control of his own person, might ratify and confirm his parents’ oblation, rather than so that he might be given the choice of returning to the world.

[Col. 0025]

# SAINT EUSEBIUS, POPE

[Col. 0025C] § I.—When and How Long He Occupied the See

In several manuscripts of the *Liber Pontificalis*, Eusebius is said to have occupied the see for six years, one month, and three days; in others, for two years, one month, and twenty-five days. Eusebius, Bishop of Caesarea, writes in his *Chronicle* that he governed the Church for seven months. Concerning this pope, we have only the following in the Bucherian Catalogue: “Eusebius, four months, sixteen days, from the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May to the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September.” In this the catalogue is inconsistent with itself, since only four months less one day intervene between the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May and the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September. The Bucherian catalogue of the depositions of the Roman pontiffs also differs from it, for there we read: “On the sixth day before the Kalends of October, Eusebius [Col. 0025D] in [the cemetery] of Callistus.” From this we learn that Eusebius was deposited in the cemetery of Callistus on September 26. The ancient martyrologies and several manuscripts of the *Liber Pontificalis* support this list.

There is therefore reason to suspect [Col. 0026C] that the copyist who transcribed the Bucherian Catalogue carelessly wrote “the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September” instead of “the sixth day before the Kalends of October,” adding the numerical sign X on his own and substituting “September”—the name of the neighboring month—for “October,” as sometimes happens. Consequently, the learned Tillemont judged that the authority of the aforementioned list and the other records supporting it should be followed. Retaining the four months and sixteen days assigned to Eusebius’ pontificate in the Bucherian Catalogue, he considers this pope to have been created on May 10, 310, and to have departed for the better life on September 26 of the same year.

Indeed, the more accomplished chronologists agree that Eusebius assumed the government of the Church only in 310 and died before the end of September. It follows that no December fell within this pope’s pontificate. What credence, therefore, is to be given either to the Bollandist manuscript of the *Liber Pontificalis*, in which three ordinations during the month of December are attributed to him, or to the other manuscripts, in which he is said to have held one ordination in that same month? [Col. 0026D]

[Col. 0027A] § II.—Explanation of the Poem Commonly Published Concerning St. Eusebius

### Epigram

> **Note [Col. 0027B].** In the latest Antwerp edition, under the year 357, no. 57, [Col. 0027C] Baronius—not without hesitation—refers this epigram, or epitaph, to the priest Eusebius, who ended his life during Liberius’ pontificate. Tillemont judges that it pertains instead to Pope Eusebius, and we readily subscribe to his judgment. Nor is it surprising that the worthy successor of Marcellus vigorously defended that discipline of the Church for whose defense his holy predecessor had been punished with exile, and that, for this reason, at the instigation of the same apostate from Christ, he suffered the same penalty from the same tyrant. Accordingly, it may reasonably be judged that Damasus, who composed the poem above concerning St. Marcellus, also fashioned this one.

### On St. Eusebius

Heraclius—

> **Note [Col. 0027C].** The name of that apostate whom the poem above concerning St. Marcellus records as having denied Christ in time of peace appears to be given here. At that time, the designation “the fallen” (*lapsi*) was commonly applied to those who had defiled themselves with sacrifices to idols or had incurred any crime of idolatry, as Cyprian’s work entitled simply *On the Fallen* and his epistles throughout demonstrate—

forbade the fallen to grieve for their sins;  
Eusebius taught the wretched to bewail their crimes.

The people split into factions as fury swelled:  
“Sits, places, houses” [read: “Sedition, slaughter”], war, discord, quarrels.

Likewise driven out by the tyrant’s savagery, following the example—

> **Note [Col. 0027D].** The example of Marcellus is recalled here; he too had been driven into exile by the tyrant Maxentius—

while the ruler—

> **Note [Col. 0027D].** Milesius Sarazanius demonstrates from many examples, in commenting upon the words “truthful ruler” in the preceding epigram, how customary it was for Damasus to designate the Roman pontiff by the name “ruler.” Eusebius is here said to have wished to preserve the covenants of peace intact because he refused to grant peace to the fallen except under the conditions on which Cornelius, together with the whole world, had decreed that it must be given. He is therefore said to have taught the wretched to bewail their sins and wash them away through worthy fruits of penance. Heraclius, by contrast, did not wish them to grieve for their sins, but to receive peace immediately, with the labors of penance omitted. By the same manner of speaking, the epigram concerning Marcellus laments that “the covenants of peace were broken”—

wished to preserve intact the covenants of peace,  
He endured exile wholly joyful beneath his judge;

On the Trinacrian shore—

> **Note [Col. 0027D].** That is, having been banished to Sicily, which Strabo and Pliny say was called Trinacria from its three promontories, Pelorus, Pachynus, and Lilybaeum. The author of our epigram teaches that Eusebius ended his life there and departed for heaven—

he left the world and life behind.

§ III.—On the Epistles and Decrees Ascribed to Pope Eusebius

1. Three manifestly spurious epistles, fabricated under Eusebius’ name by Isidore Mercator, we shall perhaps, God willing, publish elsewhere together with the other works forged in the same workshop.

2. In addition, editions of the Councils circulate four [Col. 0027B] decrees collected from various collections of canons, in which they bear Eusebius’ name. The first is:

> Parents are not permitted to give a betrothed girl to another man; she is permitted, however, to choose a monastery for herself.

Gratian, causa 27, question 2, chapter 27; Ivo, part 6, chapter 40; and Burchard, book VIII, chapter 4, ascribe this to Eusebius. It belongs to the *Penitential* of Theodore, Archbishop of Canterbury, in Petit, vol. I, p. 12, chapter 11, and was later inserted into book VI of the *Capitularies*, chapter 92, in these words:

> Parents are not permitted to give a betrothed girl to another man; nevertheless, she is permitted to enter a monastery if she wishes.

This final part concerning the power to seek a monastery is approved by Emperor Justinian both in the *Code*, book I, [Col. 0028A] title 3, law 56, and in *Novel* 123, chapter 39, as well as by Gregory, Indiction XV, Epistle 20, to Fortunatus and Cyprian.

3. The second decree is:

> With everyone’s counsel, we establish that no one shall presume to celebrate the sacrifice of the altar upon a cloth of silk or one that has been dyed, etc.

In Gratian, *On Consecration*, distinction 1, chapter 46, it bears the names of both Eusebius and Sylvester; in Ivo, part VII, chapter 40, and Burchard, book III, chapter 99, the name of Eusebius alone; and finally, in Anselm, book IX, chapter 2, the name of Sylvester alone. It was excerpted from the *Acts of Sylvester* inserted into the *Liber Pontificalis*, which Labbeus published in vol. I of the *Councils*, p. 1542.

4. The third decree is:

> Fasts established in the Church by priests shall not be relaxed without reasonable necessity.

[Col. 0028B] It was copied from Gratian, *On Consecration*, distinction 5, chapter 17, and is cited by Ivo, part IV, chapter 49, and Burchard, book XIII, chapter 17, as “from the sayings of Pope Eusebius, chapter 10.” It is chapter 23 in Capitulary 1, which Stephen Baluzius appended to the Capitularies of the year 813, p. 517.

5. The fourth is presented as follows from the codex of five books, chapter 41:

> A bishop ought to be content with moderate meals and not press his guests to eat and drink. Let every token of indecency be removed from his banquet: let neither theatrical entertainments, the empty chatter of performers, the foolish talk of buffoons, nor the tricks of jesters be admitted. Let foreigners, the poor, and the infirm be present, so that, blessing Christ from the priestly table, they may receive a blessing. [Col. 0028C] Let a sacred reading be recited and an exhortation by a living voice follow, so that those who dine may rejoice that they have been refreshed not only by bodily food but also by the nourishment of the spiritual word, so that in all things God may be honored through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Ivo, part XIII, chapter 75, and Burchard, book XIV, chapter 4, likewise cite this as “from the decrees of Eusebius, chapter 10.” It is certainly a most wise decree, and it prescribes nothing that would appear unworthy of Eusebius; but we do not think that what it prohibits is at all appropriate to his age. At that time there was no need for theatrical entertainments or the tricks of jesters to be removed from bishops’ tables. The Churches were then governed chiefly by those prelates whose reputation for modesty even a pagan author and adversary of our religion was unable to deny—men, namely, “whom” [Col. 0028D] “their meager diet and very sparing drinking, the cheapness of their garments, and eyes perpetually lowered toward the ground commended to the deity and his true worshipers as pure and modest.” Ammianus Marcellinus spoke thus in the age of Damasus, book XXVII, chapter 3.

Closely related to the aforesaid decree is what the Third Council of Tours established in 813, canon 5:

> A bishop ought not to indulge in lavish banquets, but should be content with spare and moderate food, lest he appear to abuse the Lord’s saying: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with surfeiting and drunkenness” (Luke 21:34). And as long as he is at table, let a sacred reading be recited before him rather than idle words resound from whisperers.

And canon 6:

> Foreigners and [Col. 0029A] the poor shall be the guests of bishops, so that with them they may be refreshed not only by bodily but also by spiritual food.

See also the Second Council of Reims, held in the same year, canons 17 and 18. From this one may also conjecture the period in which the decree attributed to Eusebius appeared.

6. A fifth decree might have been added to these:

> If a famine should occur, [Col. 0030A] etc.

Ivo, part IV, chapter 50, appends it to the preceding decree and cites it as from the same decrees of Eusebius, chapter 2. Burchard, however, book XIII, chapter 18, reports it as “from the decrees of Pope Liberius, chapter 2.” It was copied from book I of the *Capitularies*, chapter 118.

[Col. 0029]

# SAINT MELCHIADES, POPE

§ I.—When and How Long He Occupied the See

1. In the Bucherian Catalogue, in which, as in most ancient records, Melchiades is called Miltiades, he is said to have held the chair of Peter “from the sixth day before the Nones of July, [Col. 0029B] from the sole eighth consulship of Maximian—which was in the month of September under Volusianus and Rufinus—until the third day before the Ides of January, under the consulship of Volusianus and Annianus.”

For this inscription to be understood, it must be observed that Maximian Galerius held the consulship alone from the beginning of the year 311 until September, but that in this month Rufius Volusianus was made consul, Eusebius being joined to him as colleague. Antiquaries, sometimes suppressing Eusebius’ name, presented the two names of Volusianus alone as though they were the names of two consuls and substituted Rufinus for Rufius.

Our explanation is illustrated and confirmed by the following:

1. The list of prefects of the City in Bucherius, p. 238, in which we read under the year 310: “On the fifth day before the Kalends of November, Rufius Volusianus, P.U.,” that is, Prefect of the City; immediately afterward, under the year [Col. 0029C] 311, there follows: “Consuls, those whom Our Lords the Augusti shall command. From the month of September it became Rufinus and Eusebius.”

2. The fragment of the consular fasti in the same Bucherius, p. 250, in which the year 311 is designated as follows: “Maximian, for the eighth time, alone”; likewise the more complete Bucherian fasti, p. 42, which under the same year present: “Emperor Galerius Maximian, for the eighth time; Emperor Licinius Augustus”; elsewhere, “Rufinus and Eusebius”; and finally what is recorded in the Idatian fasti: “Under the eighth consulship of Maximian. Under these consuls—that is, Rufinus and Volusianus—the younger Maximian died.”

Accordingly, Miltiades, or Melchiades, must be said to have been ordained on July 2, 311, which fell on a Monday, and buried on January 2, 314. His death, however, is recorded on the tenth day of that month in the Bucherian list of the depositions of the Roman [Col. 0029D] pontiffs as follows: “On the fourth day before the Ides of January, Miltiades in [the cemetery] of Callistus.” It is likewise recorded on the same day in the Hieronymian Martyrology, although the same Martyrology again reads under July 2: “The deposition of Pope Miltiades.” Papebroch, however, thinks that the day of his ordination is commemorated here, while Pagius thinks it is the translation of his relics—a solemnity of this kind, he asserts, having often been celebrated on the very anniversary of a Roman pontiff’s heavenly birthday, or ordination. Therefore, the commemoration of Melchiades observed in the Roman Church on December 10 must be referred not to his death but to some other solemnity.

2. Hence it is evident that the Bucherian Catalogue, in which “Miltiades [Col. 0030A] occupied the see for three years, six months, and nine days,” must be corrected from the consuls listed immediately afterward in the same catalogue, and “two years” restored in place of “three years.” At the same time, one may observe how easily copyists slipped when transcribing numerical signs. [Col. 0030B] It is no less evident that Eusebius, Jerome, and Prosper, where in their *Chronicles* they assign three years of pontificate to Melchiades, are speaking of two completed years and one begun.

It follows, moreover, that from Eusebius’ death until Melchiades’ ordination the Roman episcopate was vacant not merely for “seven days,” as the commonly received Anastasius, or *Liber Pontificalis*, has it, but for nine months and several days. Finally, merely comparing the texts will make clear how corruptly what the commonly received *Liber Pontificalis* says concerning Melchiades was taken from the Bucherian Catalogue or similar records. It is expressed in that book as follows:

> Melchiades, an African by nationality, occupied the see for three years, seven months, and eight days, from the day of the Nones of July, in the ninth consulship of Maximinus, until the second of Maxentius, which was in the month of September, under the consulship of Volusianus and Rufinus. [Col. 0030C]

§ II.—On the Letters Given to Melchiades by Emperor Maxentius and the Praetorian Prefect, by Which They Ordered the Restoration to Him of the Churches That Had Been Taken Away
1. At the Conference of Carthage, as Augustine records both in the *Brief Summary of the Conference*, proceedings of the third day, ch. 18, no. 34, and in the book *To the Donatists, after the Conference*, ch. 13, the official acts were read, “in which it was recorded that MELCHIADES sent the deacons Strato and Cassian with letters from the emperor Maxentius and from the praetorian prefect to the prefect of the City, so that they might recover those things which the aforesaid emperor had ordered to be restored to the Christians after they had been taken away during the persecution.” Augustine immediately calls the things that Maxentius [Col. 0030D] ordered to be restored *ecclesiastical properties*: that is, both the places in which churches had been built and Christians had customarily assembled, and also the properties belonging to those churches themselves. The constitution of Constantine and Licinius, in Eusebius, *History*, book X, ch. 5, expressly directs this as follows:

> For the benefit of the Christians we decree that, if any persons appear to have purchased from our treasury or from anyone else their places in which they had formerly been accustomed to assemble—concerning which a different provision had previously been established in the letters formerly addressed to your Devotion—they shall restore them to the Christians without any payment, without any demand for repayment of an additional price, immediately and without any [Col. 0031A] evasion. But if any who purchased those places or received them as a gift wish to receive something from our Clemency, let them approach the prefect who administers justice in that province, so that consideration may be given to them by our Serenity.

Thus far concerning the places consecrated to Christian assemblies. Then, concerning properties belonging to the churches themselves, it adds:

> And since those same Christians are known to have possessed not only the places in which they were accustomed to assemble, but also other properties belonging not privately to individual persons among them but to the legal possession of the corporate body, you shall order all these, under the law already mentioned by us, to be restored without any hesitation to those same Christians—that is, to each corporate body and assembly of theirs—while observing, of course, the provision stated above: namely, that those who restore these places without repayment of the price, as has been stated, may expect compensation [Col. 0031B] from our Benevolence.

Accordingly, in the same passage of Eusebius, the same emperors also write to Anulinus, proconsul of Africa:

> You shall take care that whether gardens, buildings, or anything else belonged to the legal possession of those same churches, everything shall be restored to them as quickly as possible, so that we may understand that you have obeyed this command of ours with the utmost exactness.

2. The letters of Maxentius—which Melchiades very probably exerted himself to obtain—were granted in the year of Christ 311. They were followed by two constitutions of the emperors Licinius and Constantine on the same subject: the first, which has been lost, was promulgated late in 312, after the death of Maxentius himself; the second, preserved for us [Col. 0031C] by Eusebius and excerpted in part above, was composed at Milan around the beginning of the year 313. Finally, in that same year 313, after Maximinus had been defeated by Licinius, he likewise issued this edict, conforming himself to the benevolence shown toward the Church by the aforesaid emperors:

> So that our indulgence may appear more extensive, we also wish to enact that, if any houses or [Col. 0032A] places formerly belonging to the legal possession of the Christians were transferred to the treasury by order of our deified parents, or occupied by any city, or indeed sold or given to anyone as a gift, all shall be restored to the Christians’ former legal possession and ownership, so that in this matter also everyone may recognize our piety and providence.

(Eusebius, book IX, ch. 10.)

Indeed, let everyone rather recognize and revere the singular Providence of God toward the Church: when the most hostile emperors seemed everywhere to be persecuting her with the utmost savagery and conspiring to bring about her certain destruction, he suddenly restored to her an altogether unexpected peace. Yet this peace was immediately disturbed by the persistent and obstinate schism of the Donatists, whose case Constantine, after being petitioned by them, entrusted to Melchiades.

[Col. 0032B]

## § III.—The Case of the Donatists Is Entrusted by the Emperor Constantine to the Judgment of Melchiades

3. The Donatists maintained that Caecilian could not preside over the Church of Carthage (Augustine, *Epistle* 105, no. 8, formerly 16), because he had been ordained by Felix of Aptunga, whom they slanderously alleged to have been a *traditor*, one who surrendered the sacred books. Accordingly, in the year of Christ 313 they brought his case before the emperor Constantine by submitting the petition that Optatus reproduces near the end of his first book. “But because,” as Augustine says, “Constantine did not venture to judge the case of a bishop, he entrusted its examination and settlement to bishops. [Col. 0032C] This was done in the city of Rome, with Melchiades, bishop of that church, presiding together with many of his colleagues.” Eusebius inserted into his *History* the letter by which Constantine delegated the hearing of this matter to Melchiades, translated from Latin into Greek. Our undertaking seems to require that we present it here.

[Col. 0031C]

## COPY OF THE LETTER

*[Note: [Col. 0031] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]*

### OF THE EMPEROR CONSTANTINE, IN WHICH HE ORDERS A COUNCIL OF BISHOPS TO BE HELD AT ROME FOR THE UNITY AND CONCORD OF THE CHURCHES

Constantine Augustus to Miltiades, bishop of the city of Rome, and to Mark.

*[Note: [Col. 0031D] Who this Mark was is by no means agreed among scholars.
