Baronius, at the year 313, no. 33, conjectures that Eusebius’s Greek text is corrupt and thinks that καὶ Μάρκῳ (“and to Mark”) intruded in place of ἱεραρχῇ, that is, “to the Roman hierarch.” But if Constantine had used this term, he would previously have refrained from using the word “bishop.” No more satisfactory is Perron’s alternative conjecture, according to which καιρὸν μακρόν, that is, “a long life,” should be preferred. For such a prayer is not customarily placed at the beginning of a letter but added at its conclusion, where Constantine in fact places it. Valesius thinks that a presbyter [Col. 0032D] of the Roman Church is designated here, whom Constantine wished to attend this synod together with Miltiades—namely, that Mark who, after Pope Sylvester, held the episcopate of the city of Rome. Others, although they do not approve the conjectures of Baronius and Perron, nevertheless readily concede to them that the name “Mark” contains an error. Certainly Optatus, although he records the names of all who sat in the Roman council, makes no mention of any Mark. Nor can one easily persuade oneself that the man to whom alone, together with Melchiades, Constantine’s letter concerning the holding of the council was expressly addressed either did not attend that council or, if he did attend, should have been passed over in silence [Col. 0033D] by Optatus. For this reason they would more plausibly prefer “Merocles,” who was then bishop of Milan, in place of “Mark,” because Constantine, who was staying in Milan that very year, could have had Merocles’ fairness well tested and clearly known. One might nevertheless be troubled by the fact that, in the same address in which Miltiades is designated bishop of the city of Rome, the dignity of the other man joined with him is left unstated. Moreover, the word τιμιώτατε, “dearest” or “most honored,” with which the letter closes could be evidence that the letter was written to Miltiades alone, not to two men, were it not that this same manner of writing frequently occurs in the letters of the Roman pontiffs themselves that were addressed equally to several persons. I have now set out the scholars’ conjectures concerning this passage, together with the arguments that oppose or support them; let each person choose what pleases him most. The third part of the Conference of Carthage, ch. 319, in which this very letter had been inserted, would have taught us the truth of the matter more certainly, had that portion not been lost.]*

4. Since several petitions of this kind have been sent to me by the most distinguished Anulinus, proconsul of Africa, [Col. 0031D] in which it is alleged that Caecilian, bishop of the city of Carthage, [Col. 0033A] is accused of many matters by certain of his colleagues established throughout Africa; and since it appears most distressing to me that, in those provinces which divine Providence in sheer generosity has entrusted to my Devotion, and in which there is a very great multitude of people, the populace should turn toward worse things as though divided into two factions, and that the bishops should be at variance with one another: it has pleased me that Caecilian himself should sail to Rome with ten bishops who appear to accuse him, and ten others whom he himself shall judge necessary for his case, so that he may there be heard before you and also before Reticius, Maternus, and Marinus—

*[Note: [Col. 0034D] Constantine ordered those Gallic bishops to meet with the Roman bishop, thereby complying with this petition of the Donatists, in which one reads: “We ask that your Piety command judges to be assigned to us from Gaul, because,” they say, “Gaul is free from this crime and dissension.”]*

—your colleagues, whom I have ordered to hasten to Rome for the sake of this matter, in the manner that you know best accords with the most holy law. Moreover, so that you may obtain the fullest information about all these matters, [Col. 0033B] I have appended to my letter and transmitted to your aforesaid colleagues copies of the petitions—

*[Note: [Col. 0034D] Optatus copied the final part of the petitions or memorials near the end of book I. The rest are missing.]*

—sent to me by Anulinus. After reading them, your Gravity will consider in what manner the aforesaid controversy should be adjudicated with the utmost care and settled according to the rule of justice. For neither is your diligence unaware that I show such great reverence toward the most holy Catholic Church that I wish you to leave no schism or division whatsoever in any place. May the Divinity of the supreme God preserve you for many years, dearest one.

[Col. 0032C]

## COPY OF AN IMPERIAL LETTER

### In Which He Orders a Council of Bishops to Be Held at Rome for the Unity and Concord of the Churches

Constantine Augustus to Miltiades, bishop of the Romans, and to Mark.

4. Since several documents of this kind have been sent to me by the most distinguished Anulinus, proconsul of Africa, [Col. 0032D] in which it is alleged that Caecilian, bishop [Col. 0034A] of the city of the Carthaginians, is held answerable in many matters by certain of his colleagues established throughout Africa; and since this appears exceedingly grievous to me—namely, that in these provinces, which divine Providence of its own accord has entrusted to my Devotion, and where there is also a great multitude of people, the populace should be found persisting in a worse course, as though divided into factions, and that there should be disputes among the bishops—it has seemed good to me that Caecilian himself should sail to Rome with ten bishops who appear to hold him answerable, and ten others whom he himself may consider necessary for his own case. There, in your presence and also that of Reticius, Maternus, and Marinus, your colleagues whom I have ordered to hasten to Rome for this purpose, he may be heard, so that you may determine what accords with the most venerable law. Moreover, so that [Col. 0034B] you may obtain the fullest knowledge concerning all these matters, I have appended to my letters copies of the documents sent to me by Anulinus and dispatched them to your aforesaid colleagues. After reading them, your steadfastness will examine how the aforesaid case should be decided with the greatest care and settled according to justice. For neither does it escape your diligence that I show such reverence to the Catholic Church “in ordinance” (ἐν θεσμῷ, *sic*) that I wish you to leave no schism or division whatsoever in any place. May the Divinity of the great God preserve you for many years, most honored one.

## § IV.—Melchiades’ Judgment in the Case of Caecilian

5. In the same year 313, on October 2, which fell on a Friday, the judges assembled and took their seats [Col. 0033C] in the house of Fausta, Constantine’s wife, in the Lateran: Miltiades, bishop of the city of Rome; Maternus of Cologne; Reticius of Autun; Marinus of Arles; Merocles of Milan; and fourteen other Italian bishops, whose names and sees Optatus lists. “With these nineteen bishops sitting together,” says the same Optatus, “the case of Donatus and Caecilian was brought before each of them. The following judgments were delivered against Donatus”—Donatus of Casae Nigrae, as is clear from Augustine’s *Brief Summary of the Conference*, proceedings of the third day, no. 36, and his *To the Donatists, after the Conference*, no. 17—“because he confessed that he had rebaptized and had laid hands upon fallen bishops, which is foreign to the Church. The witnesses introduced by Donatus confessed that they had nothing to say against Caecilian.” [Col. 0033D]

Caecilian was pronounced innocent by the judgments of all those mentioned above, [Col. 0034B] including the judgment of Miltiades, which closed the proceedings in these words:

> Since it has been established that Caecilian is not accused by those who came with Donatus, in accordance with their own declaration, and since it has not been established that Donatus has convicted him in any respect, I judge that he must be retained in the unimpaired status of his ecclesiastical communion.

[Col. 0034C]

That Melchiades’ judgment was not reported in full by Optatus is clear from Augustine, *Epistle* 43, formerly 162, no. 16, where he extols it with praise in the following manner:

> What a final judgment Melchiades himself delivered! How innocent, how upright, how prudent and peaceable it was! He did not venture to remove from his college those colleagues against whom nothing had been established; and, while chiefly condemning Donatus alone—Donatus of Casae Nigrae—whom he had found to be the originator of the entire evil, he gave the others a free choice to recover soundness. He was prepared to send letters of communion [Col. 0034D] even to those who were known to have been ordained by Majorinus. Thus, wherever there were two bishops whom dissension had duplicated, he wished the one ordained first to be confirmed, while another congregation was to be provided for the other to govern. [Col. 0035A] O excellent man! O son of Christian peace and father of the Christian people! … In him neither did gentleness corrupt integrity, nor did integrity conflict with gentleness.

6. In this judgment one may discern a threefold moderation belonging to a provident shepherd, which thereafter proved of great use to the Church in similar cases. First, content with condemning Donatus, the originator of the entire evil, he left the rest of Donatus’s associates a free opportunity to return to their senses. Second, he did not refuse to admit to his communion even those ordained by Majorinus, whom the schismatics had placed over the Church of Carthage in Caecilian’s stead. Finally, [Col. 0035B] in those churches where there were two prelates, one ordained by Majorinus and the other by the Catholics, he awarded the church that he governed to the one who had been ordained first, while at the same time ordering that another congregation be provided for the other to govern.

7. Following the first of these measures, Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, together with the Gallic bishops, separated himself from the communion of Saturninus, Ursacius, and Valens, who were the leaders of the Arians in the West, “while granting the rest of their associates an opportunity to return to their senses, so that neither the will for peace would be absent nor the putrid members belonging to the principal diseases and advancing toward the corruption of the entire body be left uncut.” This was thereafter consistently maintained in the Church as a kind of rule.

8. The second measure was followed not only by the African Catholics [Col. 0035C] toward Donatists returning to unity, but also much later by Pope Felix II. To make the restoration of the churches divided over the case of Acacius more expeditious and easier, he says in *Epistle* 12 to Flavita, no. 4: “With God’s inspiration, we shall make reasonable provision … so that, with the Catholic confession preserved, none of those whom Acacius ordained or baptized may be lost, for the restoration of the Church’s charity.”

The African Catholics prove that this could be granted without injury to the faith, in the letter inserted into the record of the first hearing of the Conference of Carthage, ch. 16, by the following argument:

> For in them we detest not the divine sacraments of truth, but the inventions of human error; once these have been removed, we embrace as a brother one whose heart is united to us by Christian charity.

Pope Anastasius II explains and illustrates the same reasoning more fully [Col. 0035D] in writing to the emperor Anastasius, no. 8. Here we warn in advance how groundlessly that same Pope Anastasius is said, in Hincmar, vol. II, p. 278, not to agree or accord with the sacred canons and decrees of his predecessors because he did not refuse to receive in their orders those ordained by the condemned Acacius; for it is plain that in this matter he followed both his predecessors Melchiades and Felix and the decrees of the Africans.

9. The African bishops imitated the third measure in the letter inserted into the record of the first hearing of the Conference of Carthage, ch. 16, which also survives as Augustine’s *Epistle* 128. They promised the Donatists that, if convinced and returned [Col. 0036A] to unity, they would be received by them in such a way

> that they may not only find the way of salvation, but also not lose the honor of the episcopate. For each of us, they say, may join to himself a partner in his dignity and sit in the more eminent place by turns, as when a visiting bishop sits beside his colleague. When this is granted to both parties in alternating basilicas, each shows honor to the other in mutual deference. For when the commandment of charity has enlarged hearts, possession of peace does not become narrow; so that, after one of them has died, individual bishops may thereafter succeed individual bishops according to the former custom. Nor will anything new be done, for Catholic love has maintained this from the very beginning of the separation in the case of those who, after condemning the error of the impious division, came to appreciate—even if late—the sweetness of unity.

10. Tillemont, vol. VI, p. 49, thinks that this proposal to leave two bishops [Col. 0036B] simultaneously in one church was first devised through the charity and supported by the authority of the Synod of Arles. He offers no other reason for his opinion except that Melchiades and his colleagues decreed something different concerning those same bishops at the Roman council. But since their judgment has not been transmitted intact either by Optatus, Augustine, or anyone else, it cannot be affirmed with certainty that the other measure, which the Africans testify had been maintained among them “from the very beginning of the separation,” was not proposed in that judgment. For it could have happened that the Roman synod over which Melchiades presided opened more than one path for composing peace in churches where there were two bishops. We certainly read that this was done by those same Africans. [Col. 0036C] After proposing that the care of one church should be entrusted simultaneously to two bishops, they immediately add this alternative, under which both bishops were to withdraw:

> Or if perhaps the Christian people delight in having individual bishops and cannot tolerate the partnership of two because the situation appears unfamiliar, let us both withdraw from the midst; and, once the cause of the schism has been condemned in each place and the churches established in peaceful unity, let bishops be appointed for the unity achieved in the necessary places by those who are found to be sole bishops in their respective churches.

In his *Brief Summary*, proceedings of the first day, ch. 5, Augustine summarizes these words as follows, explaining that the Catholics had agreed that, “if the congregations could not endure two bishops in one church, both were to withdraw from the midst, and individual bishops were to be appointed, ordained by those bishops who were found to be the sole bishops [Col. 0036D] among their own congregations.” Indeed, if Optatus narrates the matter in chronological order, an example of this new arrangement had already appeared before the Synod of Arles, when Eunomius and Olympius were sent to Carthage to remove both bishops from there and ordain one.

11. For immediately after reporting the words with which Melchiades’ judgment was concluded, Optatus adds:

> It is therefore enough that Donatus was struck down by so many judgments and Caecilian vindicated by so weighty a trial. And yet Donatus believed that an appeal should be made from the bishops.

If an appeal from Melchiades’ judgment is being indicated here, the following passage appended by the same Optatus seems to pertain to it:

> To this appeal the emperor Constantine responded as follows: “O frenzied audacity of rage! They have lodged an appeal, as is customarily done [Col. 0037A] in the cases of pagans.” At the same time that same Donatus petitioned that he be allowed to return (thus the German manuscript), but that he not go to Carthage. Filuminus, an influential supporter, then suggested that, for the sake of peace, Caecilian should be detained at Brescia; and this was done. Two bishops, Eunomius and Olympius, were then sent to Africa, so that, after removing both men, they might ordain one. They came to Carthage and remained for forty days, so that they might pronounce where the Catholic Church was. The seditious party of Donatus did not permit this to be done. Daily disturbances arose from the zeal of the factions. The final judgment of the same bishops Eunomius and Olympius is recorded as follows: they declared that the Catholic Church was that which existed throughout the whole world, and that the judgment of the nineteen bishops—that is, [Col. 0037B] Melchiades and his colleagues—delivered long before could not be annulled.

But we are fully persuaded from the following considerations that the appeal noted by Optatus is the one that was followed by the Council of Arles, and that the rest of the narrative pertains to what occurred after that council.

First, the preceding words of Constantine—“O frenzied audacity of rage! As in the cases of pagans,” and so forth—were copied from this emperor’s letter to the bishops assembled at Arles (in Labbe, *Councils*, vol. I, p. 1431, d–c). Second, in *Epistle* 43, no. 20, Augustine briefly recounts in this order the judgment of the Council of Arles, the appeal from it, and the emperor’s just indignation:

> For the Christian emperor did not dare to receive their tumultuous and deceitful complaints in such a way that he himself would judge the judgment of the bishops [Col. 0037C] who had sat at Rome; instead, as I said, he appointed other bishops, from whom they nevertheless preferred to appeal once again to the emperor himself. You have heard how he abhorred them in this matter.

Finally, Optatus mentions the judgment of Melchiades and his colleagues against Donatus not as recent but as delivered long before.

This point also deserves observation: when Eunomius and Olympius were sent to Carthage after the Council of Arles to calm the disturbances of the Donatists, they made no mention of that council but declared that “the judgment of the nineteen bishops”—with Melchiades presiding—“delivered long before could not be annulled.” It therefore rightly appears that what they did at Carthage was done not so much on the basis of the Council of Arles as on the basis of Melchiades’ judgment.

[Col. 0037D]

12. In a word, by the judgment praised by Augustine, Melchiades pointed out in advance the path by which unity might be repaired. Thus the various methods by which the African Catholics attempted, either at the Conference or before it, to reconcile the schismatics to themselves and recall them to concord may be regarded as various approaches to the peaceful road that Melchiades had opened to them. By indulgently preserving their ranks and honors for clerics and bishops who withdrew from the schism, he removed a most serious obstacle to the restoration of peace. The Africans then sought, as circumstances required, to consolidate by various methods not departing from that road the peace begun along it. On this matter see also the *Code of Canons of the African Church*, chs. 117 and 118.

[Col. 0038A]

13. One further point illustrating ecclesiastical discipline remains to be observed concerning the judgment of Melchiades praised above by Augustine: namely, that wherever there were two bishops, “he wished the one ordained first to be confirmed,” but nevertheless “another congregation was to be entrusted to the other to govern.” In agreement with this judgment, the Africans at the Conference of Carthage, first hearing, ch. 16, decree that where not merely one but both bishops must be removed at the people’s request, an individual church must be assigned to each.

I consider this worthy of notice because from it appears to have arisen the later practice of transferring to other churches bishops who were either not received by their own congregations or expelled from them. It is thus [Col. 0038B] demonstrated that the following did nothing contrary to the ancient discipline: Sixtus III, Leo’s predecessor, in *Epistle* 8, when he arranged for Perigenes, who had been ordained bishop for the people of Patras but rejected by them, to be placed over the Corinthians; Leo’s successor Hilary, when he permitted Hermes, who said that he had been excluded by the people of Béziers, to preside over the people of Narbonne (Hilary, *Epistle* 8); and John III, when he entrusted the government of the Church of Nola to John, bishop of Alexandria, after the latter had been expelled from his own city (Liberatus, ch. 18).

For the same reason the transfer of Aprunculus is also excused. As Gregory of Tours, *Deeds of the Franks*, book II, ch. 23, and Baronius, at the year 484, relate:

> Aprunculus, bishop of the city of Langres, began to be regarded with suspicion among the Burgundians. As the hatred increased from day to day, an order was given that he should secretly be struck down with the sword. [Col. 0038C] When word of this was brought to him, he was lowered by night over the wall of the fortress of Dijon, came to Clermont, and there, in accordance with the word of the Lord … was appointed the eleventh bishop.

## § V.—The Ancient Donatists Reject Melchiades’ Judgment, and Later Donatists Falsely Accuse Him of Surrendering the Sacred Books

14. However moderate Melchiades’ judgment may have been, it did not please the Donatists. Immediately after being defeated in the bishops’ tribunal, they began to complain and to remonstrate by presenting petitions to Constantine. Whether this remonstrance of theirs should be called an appeal is disputed among scholars. They agree, however, that those schismatics did not abide by Melchiades’ judgment, that they demanded other judges from [Col. 0038D] Constantine, and that this demand was unjustly made by them.

They alleged that only a very few bishops had delivered judgment and that these had hastened to pronounce sentence without carefully examining everything that ought first to have been investigated. At that time they advanced this one reason alone for refusing the judgment of the Roman synod. Constantine mentions no other in the letter by which he ordered a great many bishops from different and almost innumerable places to assemble in the city of Arles to settle the same case (Augustine, *Epistle* 105, no. 8; Optatus, book I; Constantine, in Eusebius, book X, ch. 5). From this it is gathered that the Donatists, not only before the Roman council but also afterward, throughout the entire interval [Col. 0039A] between it and the Council of Arles, never entertained the thought of accusing Melchiades of the crime of surrendering the sacred books.

15. Afterward, however, they fabricated this charge and accused not only Melchiades but also Marcellinus, Marcellus, and Sylvester of the same crime. From this we may reasonably suspect that this slander was not devised by them before the time of Pope Sylvester. For although they said that this offense had been committed by Marcellus, Melchiades, and Sylvester while they were still presbyters of Marcellinus, everyone sees that they invented it to bring hatred and ill repute upon the Apostolic See and to evade its authority against themselves. Consequently, it was invented only after Marcellus, Melchiades, and Sylvester had already been adorned [Col. 0039B] with the dignity of that see.

16. Indeed, from Augustine’s words in the *Brief Summary of the Conference with the Donatists*, ch. 18, it is understood that the Donatists first laid this charge against Melchiades at the Conference of Carthage:

> For when the Cognitor compelled them to state whether they had anything to say against the council and judgment of Melchiades, by which Caecilian was recorded as having been vindicated and acquitted, the Donatists then began to accuse Melchiades himself of surrendering the sacred books and to say that their predecessors had for this reason refused his judgment.

It was not at all difficult to convict them of falsehood in making this assertion, since their predecessors, when refusing to abide by Melchiades’ judgment, are never found to have advanced anything of the kind in their petitions. But because they raised a matter previously unheard of [Col. 0039C] not only by the Cognitor but also by the Catholics themselves,

> the judge, becoming attentive to whether any public or ecclesiastical judgment concerning the crime of surrendering the books would be produced, while the Catholics themselves waited and demanded that it be proved, the Donatists read certain very lengthy acts before a prefect, in which neither was it apparent who the prefect himself was nor was the place where these proceedings occurred recorded. But the acts themselves resounded, in a very lengthy recitation, with many persons surrendering many ecclesiastical objects, while the name of Melchiades was never heard at all. When these had been completed,

the Cognitor expressed surprise “that one thing had been promised and another read aloud.”

They then read other acts in which Melchiades was recorded as having sent the deacons Strato and Cassian to recover, by order of the emperor, the places taken from the Christians during the persecution. [Col. 0039D]

> And when in these acts too no crime by Melchiades was apparent either to the Cognitor or to the Catholic advocates, the Donatists said that the deacon Strato, whom he had sent with others to recover the ecclesiastical properties, had been recorded in the earlier acts as a *traditor*. They therefore wished to smear Melchiades as well with the crime of surrendering the sacred books, because he employed that deacon without having degraded him.

But when they were asked “whether those acts concerning the surrender at least expressly stated that Strato was a deacon,” they could not prove even this.

The Catholics further replied that, even if Strato had been called a deacon and a *traditor*, it did not follow that he was the man whom Melchiades subsequently employed, since it was possible that, [Col. 0040A] just as there were among the apostles two men named James and two named Judas, and among the schismatics themselves two men named Donatus—one of Casae Nigrae and one of Carthage—so too there were simultaneously two Roman deacons named Strato (Augustine, *Brief Summary*, proceedings of the third day, *Conference with the Donatists*, ch. 18, no. 34).

> The Catholics also added that even if it were demonstrated—which it certainly was not—that the same deacon Strato whom Melchiades later sent with other deacons to recover the ecclesiastical properties had surrendered the sacred books, Melchiades would not thereby immediately be smeared with that crime. The persecution might have caused him to be far away, so that he knew nothing at all about it and regarded as innocent a man whom no one had shown to be guilty by accusing him.

(Ibid., no. 35.)

Finally, when the Donatists attempted to return [Col. 0040B] to their slanderous accusation of Melchiades, they were driven away from it by an interlocutory ruling of the Cognitor.

17. Yet they did not therefore remain quiet. Even after the Conference of Carthage they seized upon the fact that the name Cassian occurred both among Melchiades’ deacons and in the acts in which the surrender was recorded as an opportunity to slander him (Augustine, *Brief Summary of the Conference*, no. 36). But this obstinacy of the Donatists and their various attempts to defame Melchiades alone while sparing the other judges of the Roman council are evidence of how weighty and how inconvenient to themselves they felt his authority to be.

By so many and such unjust contrivances they accomplished nothing except to reveal Melchiades’ moderation, fairness, integrity, and innocence of life. Those who, while striving to devise slander against him from every direction, were compelled to seek an occasion for it in his deacons—or rather in the similarity of names shared with his deacons—must necessarily have lacked anything whatever to reproach in the man himself. [Col. 0040C] They revealed how great a fury had seized them when they refused to abide by a judgment in which the accusers and witnesses were heard in person together with the accused, and which was delivered by judges whom they themselves had requested and over whom presided the most equitable prelate and chief of all bishops; instead, they preferred to appeal to the emperor.

More religious than they, Constantine received their appeal with the greatest displeasure. Yet, by being somewhat more indulgent than was proper and failing to restrain their audacity, he furnished room and occasion for grave evils in the Church. Although he granted the appellants another judgment at Arles, [Col. 0040D] nevertheless, according to Augustine, *Epistle* 43, formerly 162, no. 20, he granted it “not because it was now necessary, but because he yielded to their perversities and desired by every means to restrain such great shamelessness.” Nor did an appeal of this kind prevent the bishops Eunomius and Olympius, who had been sent to Africa to settle the affairs of the Church of Carthage, from subsequently declaring, as we have already explained, that “the judgment of the nineteen bishops delivered long before could not be annulled” (Optatus, book I).

## § VI.—The Decrees Attributed to Pope Melchiades

18. Isidore Mercator falsely ascribed two letters to Melchiades: one to Leontius and the other bishops of Spain; [Col. 0041A] the other entitled *On the Primitive Church and Constantine’s Munificence toward It*. Since neither possesses any more authority than authenticity, we deliberately declined to print them here.

19. In the *Pontifical Book*, two decrees are attributed to the same pope. The first enacts:

> That under no circumstances should any of the faithful keep a fast on the Lord’s Day or on Thursday, because pagans observe those days as though they were a sacred fast.

Immediately after this decree, the same *Pontifical Book* adds:

> And the Manichaeans were discovered in the city of Rome by him.

20. That this decree is falsely ascribed to Melchiades is clear for two reasons. First, even before this pope’s time, the faithful had been forbidden to fast on the Lord’s Day. [Col. 0041B] Second, the reason for the prohibition was not that pagans or Gentiles kept that day as though it were a sacred fast, but that Christians judged fasting wholly inappropriate to the day on which Christ gladdened the Church by his resurrection. What they had learned to avoid through practice itself and through the tradition teaching that the Lord’s Day should be celebrated festively, they began to avoid with still greater religious care when the Manichaeans—not the pagans—began to keep that day as though it were a sacred fast. Lest we appear to say this without justification, both points must be demonstrated briefly.

21. Before the time of Miltiades, Tertullian wrote in *On the Crown*, chapter 3: “We consider it unlawful to fast on the Lord’s Day.” At the end of book V of the *Apostolic Constitutions* one likewise reads: “For anyone who fasts on the Lord’s Day will be guilty of sin, since it is the day of the Resurrection.” [Col. 0041C] No other reason is added here. But Augustine, shortly afterward, in letter 36 to Casulanus, chapter 12, no. 27, after saying, “To fast on the Lord’s Day is a great scandal,” added this new reason:

> Especially since the detestable heresy of the Manichaeans—utterly and most manifestly contrary to the apostolic faith and the divine Scriptures—became known. They appointed this day for their hearers to fast upon as though it were a legitimately established day. As a result, fasting on the Lord’s Day came to be regarded with still greater horror.

And in no. 29 he teaches that particular caution must be taken lest anyone observe a fast on the Lord’s Day,

> since the heretics, especially the most impious Manichaeans, began dogmatically to prescribe fasts on the Lord’s Day, not because of some necessity that had arisen, but as though they had been established as a sacred solemnity.

[Col. 0041D] Pope Leo likewise bears witness concerning these same heretics in letter 17 to Turibius, chapter 4:

> As was discovered and proved in our investigation, they require that the Lord’s Day, which the resurrection of our Savior consecrated for us, be spent in the sorrow of fasting.

Consequently, nothing would appear absurd in the *Pontifical Book* if it had said: “The Manichaeans were discovered in the city of Rome by Miltiades. Then that pope decreed that none of the faithful should fast on the Lord’s Day for any reason, because those heretics observe this day as though it were a sacred fast.” Mercator, however, does not correct the *Pontifical Book* but imitates it in his usual fashion, presenting Miltiades as decreeing:

> No one ought to observe a fast on the Lord’s Day or on Thursday, so that a true and not a false distinction may be maintained between the fasting [Col. 0042A] of Christians and that of gentiles, of those who truly believe and of unbelievers and heretics.

22. Around the time of the Council of Nicaea, a certain Eustathius practiced and taught many things akin to the doctrines of the Manichaeans. The Synod of Gangra, convened against him, ruled in canon 18, according to the translation of Dionysius Exiguus: “If anyone fasts on the Lord’s Day because of supposed continence or out of obstinacy, let him be anathema.” Here this council—and likewise the Council of Saragossa, celebrated in 381 against the Priscillianists, who were also commonly called Manichaeans—appears in a certain sense to permit fasting even on the Lord’s Day, provided that superstition is not its cause. For canon 2 of the latter council forbids “anyone to fast on the Lord’s Day because of the season, persuasion, or superstition.” [Col. 0042B] Jerome, indeed, writes in letter 28 to Lucinius:

> Would that we could fast at all times—a thing which, in the Acts of the Apostles, we read that the apostle Paul and the believers with him did during the days of Pentecost and on the Lord’s Day.

Augustine also noted this in letter 36, no. 28. Yet lest Jerome appear on this account to disapprove the Church’s custom and law, he immediately qualifies his statement by adding: “Nor do I say this because I think that one should fast on the Lord’s Days.”

23. This law, moreover, was observed with such religious care, according to Epiphanius (*Exposition of the Faith*, no. 22), that even those who, out of the highest zeal for piety, imposed perpetual fasts upon themselves excepted only the Lord’s Days and the days of Pentecost:

> For the Church has appointed all Lord’s Days to be festive and joyful, and she observes no fasts upon them. [Col. 0042C] For it is absurd to fast on the Lord’s Day. . . . Indeed, the Church is not accustomed to fast even on the Lord’s Days that fall within Lent itself.

Conversely, the same saint, in *Heresy* 75, no. 3, rightly reproves the Aerians because, in a foolish display of freedom, “they make a point of fasting on the Lord’s Day, but eat on Wednesday and Friday.”

No less foolish are the heterodox of our own age, who locate Christian freedom in despising the laws of abstinence and fasting which the Church, instructed by Christ and his Apostles, wisely established. It is the Church herself which, while urging the faithful to fast either by exhortations or by precepts, has always excepted the Lord’s Day—not in order to distinguish them from the gentiles, but to teach that the day of the Lord’s resurrection must always be celebrated festively. It is therefore falsely asserted that Miltiades decreed that no one should fast [Col. 0042D] on the Lord’s Day. No less false is the statement in the *Pontifical Book* that he established the same rule for Thursday.

24. Christians never possessed such a religious regard for Thursday as to be forbidden to fast on that day. A custom merely became prevalent whereby, while some fasted on Wednesday and Friday, and others on Friday and Saturday, most thought that on Thursday—which lies next to those days consecrated to fasting—they ought to abstain from fasting. Hence the *Apostolic Constitutions* (book V, chapter 24), warning us against the custom of hypocrites, who always affect singular practices, prescribe: “Let not our fasts be shared with those of the hypocrites, for they fast on Monday and Thursday.”

Augustine, in letter 36, refuting the writing of a certain Roman who maintained that one ought to fast on all six days of every week, says in no. 9:

> Among the Romans, apart from a very few clerics or monks, how many can be found who regularly observe daily fasts on all those six days—especially since it does not appear proper there to fast on Thursday?

[Col. 0043A] From this one may gather that at Rome a popular opinion indeed prevailed according to which it was thought that one should not fast on Thursday, but that no law existed on the matter. On the contrary, in Augustine’s age, daily fasts throughout all six days were observed there with commendation by some monks and clerics.

25. It is certain not only from Cassian, *Conference* 21, chapter 24, but also from Pope Gregory, that even at Rome fasting was not interrupted on the Thursdays of Lent. Gregory speaks as follows in homily 16 on the Gospels:

> There are six weeks, which of course comprise forty-two days; but when the six Lord’s Days are subtracted from abstinence, no more than thirty-six remain in abstinence.

[Col. 0043B] Everyone sees that the word “abstinence” is being used there for fasting, since the six Lord’s Days are subtracted not because abstinence from meat was suspended on those days, but because fasting was suspended. Gregory accordingly teaches that by fasting on these thirty-six days we offer God a tithe of our year.

This plainly refutes what Walafrid Strabo, chapter 20, and, following him, the *Micrologus*, chapter 50, wrote after being misled by the *Pontifical Book* and the spurious letter of Miltiades:

> Miltiades, while holding the episcopate at Rome, decreed that none of the faithful should fast on the Lord’s Day or on Thursday for any reason. For the pagans regularly observed these days as though they were fasts. Blessed Gregory therefore, in arranging the offices of the year, left Thursday within Lent without an office, so that, because it was festive like the Lord’s Day, it might also be celebrated with the office of the Lord’s Day. Since this Thursday subsequently began, like the other days, to be assigned to fasting, Gregory the Younger decreed that it should be solemnized with Masses and prayers.

[Col. 0043C] They say this in reliance upon the life of Gregory II, who was then commonly called “the Younger,” where we read in Anastasius:

> During Lent he instituted the observance of fasting and the celebration of Masses in the churches on Thursday, which had not previously been done.

But in this passage as well, Walafrid and the *Micrologus* are proved to have asserted from a preconceived opinion, rather than from any authority, that the Mass on Thursday had been repeated from the Lord’s Day. For from this very passage we learn that before Gregory II no Mass had customarily been celebrated on that day. [Col. 0043D] Thus one error readily begets another.

26. As regards fasting, St. Benedict knew of no law forbidding its observance on Thursday. For in chapter 41 of his Rule, when he prescribes an uninterrupted fast until holy Easter, he does not except Thursday. St. Isidore of Seville, in chapter 10 of his Rule, permits daily fasts throughout the entire year, with the Lord’s Days alone excepted, in imitation of the Fathers. The *Rule of the Master*, chapters 27, 28, and 53, later relaxed fasting on Thursdays, but intended the Thursdays of Lent to be excepted from this relaxation. Nor did it give as the reason for that relaxation the claim that [Col. 0044A] Thursday was a solemn fast among the pagans, but rather “because the Ascension of the Lord falls upon that day every year”—that is, because the Lord consecrated that day by his ascension into heaven.

The pagans were certainly far from consecrating that day to mourning and fasting, since they customarily celebrated it festively in honor of Jupiter. Caesarius, bishop of Arles, therefore vehemently rebukes certain Christians whom the devil had seduced into perversely imitating them, in the sermon found among Augustine’s works, Appendix, volume V, sermon 265, no. 5:

> Because we have heard that the devil so ensnares certain men and women that on Thursday neither do the men perform their work nor the women spin wool, we solemnly testify before God and the holy angels that whoever chooses to observe this custom, unless they amend such sacrilege through prolonged [Col. 0044B] and severe penance, etc.

The Council of Narbonne, held in 589, revealed in canon 15 how indignantly it regarded the same practice:

> It has come to our attention that certain people belonging to the Catholic faith, following an execrable rite, greatly honor Thursday—which is also called the day of Jupiter—and perform no work. Detesting this practice out of fear of God, etc.

This custom so greatly displeased the Fathers only because it had been derived from the impious superstition of the gentiles. To abolish it, therefore, fasts should have been prescribed on Thursday, as was done for the same reason at that time on the Kalends of January, rather than forbidden.

27. The second decree is expressed in the *Pontifical Book* as follows:

> He arranged for consecrated offerings to be sent through the churches from what had been consecrated by the bishop; this is designated the *fermentum*.

[Col. 0044C] Similar to this decree is the one which the same book attributes to Siricius:

> He decreed that no presbyter should celebrate Masses during the week unless he had received the consecrated element designated by the local bishop, which is called the *fermentum*.

In the Bollandist copy of the *Pontifical Book*, however, as also in the Fossatensis manuscript, now the Colbertinus, the same decree of Siricius is stated simply thus:

> He decreed that, without what had been consecrated by the bishop, the presbyters of any locality were not permitted to be consecrated.

Unless we read *consecrare* (“to consecrate”) instead of *consecrari* (“to be consecrated”), this decree would appear to refer to the consecration of presbyters, something we do not know ever to have been done. We know only that in ancient times certain churches adopted the practice [Col. 0044D] whereby presbyters, after their ordination, received from their bishop portions of the Lord’s body, from which they received communion for a fixed number of days. Hence the following is prescribed in the ancient Pontifical of Soissons, cited by our Edmond Martène, *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, volume II, page 322:

> Presbyters ought to receive from the bishop portions of the Lord’s body, from which they are to receive communion for forty days.

And in an ancient Roman *Ordo*, newly ordained presbyters are instructed to receive communion for seven days from the consecrated offering given to them.

Yet, on the authority of the fuller manuscripts of the *Pontifical Book*, the Bollandist and Fossatensis texts apparently ought to be corrected so that they read *consecrare*, not *consecrari*, [Col. 0045A] and the passage should be understood as referring to the consecration of the Eucharist, or the celebration of Masses. But it does not follow even from this that the custom of sending portions of an offering consecrated by the bishop through the churches and titular churches is falsely referred to Miltiades as its originator. For in the same book the Roman pontiffs are sometimes said to have established something not because they first instituted it, but because they merely confirmed it. To take Siricius himself as an example, according to this book, “he decreed that heretics should be received and reconciled through the imposition of hands,” because in letter 1 to Himerius, chapter 1, he confirms what Stephen had already defended on the authority of tradition.

28. Be that as it may, it is certain from what Innocent himself writes in letter 25 to Decentius, no. 8, [Col. 0045B] that the custom of sending the *fermentum* through the churches is older than Innocent:

> As for the *fermentum* which we send through the titular churches on the Lord’s Day, you needlessly wished to consult us, since all our churches are situated within the city. Because their presbyters cannot join us on that day on account of the people entrusted to them, they therefore receive through acolytes the *fermentum* prepared by us, so that they may not consider themselves separated from our communion, especially on that day. I do not think this ought to be done throughout the parishes situated outside the city, [Col. 0046A] because the sacraments ought not to be carried over long distances. Nor do we send it to the presbyters stationed in the various cemeteries.

From this it appears that the statement in the *Pontifical Book*—that “the presbyters of any locality were not permitted during the week to celebrate Masses,” or to consecrate, “unless they had received what had been consecrated by the bishop”—is by no means accurate. For this was decreed not concerning presbyters of every locality, but only those stationed within the city, and indeed only for the Lord’s Day.

Innocent furthermore openly indicates that this custom was introduced as a sign of the presbyters’ communion with their bishop. From this one can readily understand why the Eucharist sent in this manner was given the name *fermentum* (“leaven”). It performed the function of leaven insofar as it joined and united the churches to which it was sent with their bishop in the one body of Christ, just as leaven joins itself to the mass into which it is mixed. [Col. 0046B] From ancient glosses on the Decretals, cited by our Mabillon in *Analecta*, volume IV, page 60, we learn that this particle of the offering consecrated by the bishops was placed by the presbyters into the chalice when, during the Mass, they said, “May the peace of the Lord be always with you”—that is, at the very point when, even today, a smaller particle of the consecrated host is placed in the chalice by the presbyters.

[Col. 0045]

## A SAYING OF RHETICIUS, BISHOP OF AUTUN, ON BAPTISM. (C, S)

[Col. 0045B] Rheticius, bishop of Autun, says St. Augustine, was a man of great authority in the Church during his episcopate, as those ecclesiastical proceedings indicate in which, [Col. 0045C] at Rome, with Miltiades, bishop of the Apostolic See, presiding, he sat as judge with others, condemned Donatus, who was the first author of the Donatist schism, and acquitted Caecilian, [Col. 0046B] bishop of the Church of Carthage. When treating of baptism, he spoke as follows:

> No one fails to recognize, therefore, that this is the principal indulgence in the Church: in it we cast off the entire weight of ancient guilt and discharge the former crimes of our ignorance; there too we put off the old man together with his inborn offenses. [Col. 0046C]

## [POEM ON THE PRAISES OF THE LORD]

[Col. 0045]

## AN ANONYMOUS POEM ON THE PRAISES OF THE LORD. (C, S)

[Col. 0045D]

Who complains that virtue’s gift comes late to aid him?  
Who says the promises of God advance with sluggish step?  
Who measures by a mortal end the urn of the eternal Judge,  
and thinks that day too slow which ages must hasten—  
the day that will repay each person for his merits?

A noble glory bears witness through a mighty deed.  
For where the sluggish Saône glides past its banks  
in a stagnant train and scarcely unfolds  
its indolent stream after long delay,  
where an Aeduan people, brothers to the Rhine, is born,  
I recall a marriage of supreme devotion and faith. [Col. 0046D]

> **Note [Col. 0045D].** The author celebrates the marriage of St. Rheticius, who was subsequently elevated to the episcopate of Autun. On this matter see Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, book 1, chapter 72. [Col. 0046D]

Yet divine law increased the merit of their love.  
Both had vowed that one should precede the other in death  
and entrust to the survivor’s dutiful grief  
the care of the tomb;  
but the decree’s page chose the wife first.

Then the anxious husband ordered the stone  
that would receive his limbs after death  
to be hollowed with a broad opening:

“You shall receive me when I come  
and join our eternal covenant,  
so that those whom the same little bed had held in life,  
after God’s commandments had been fulfilled,  
a common tomb might bear.” [Col. 0047A]

The wife, prophetic, perceived her husband’s wishes  
and granted a great miracle to chaste times.  
For when arms are joined to the limbs of the dead  
and the restored hand binds its grip around the trunk,  
lest, after the duties of human life are fulfilled,  
a shapeless dissolution befall the sundered parts—

wondrous beyond telling!—when life had ended  
and the husband was to be joined to his companion  
in the place prepared for him,  
after the door of death was opened by the man’s demise  
and unwelcome daylight once more disclosed  
that dreadful home,  
the woman was found extending her left palm,  
inviting her companion with the gesture of living love.

Who gave affection to the tomb?  
Who loosed the bonds?  
How did the buried woman behold  
the shade of the husband yet to come? [Col. 0047B]

You accomplish these things, Christ our God;  
your signs are set in motion,  
and little by little you teach sleeping limbs to rise again.  
You are he whom the holy prophets sang would come,  
the incorrupt offspring of God,  
the ruler of him who rules,  
without whom the mighty Father deliberates nothing great.

At your command the sea stands within fixed shores  
and the measureless deep may not overrun the lands;  
level shores confine its mountainous waves.

You endowed the stable earth with varied gifts  
for our use, lavish in paternal kindness.  
With you as sponsor, mortals commit seeds to the furrows,  
and new offspring rises from the parched turf.  
You command vines to flow with welcome nectar;  
you give trees their juices, pleasing at human feasts  
and medicinal for health;  
you produce the sweetness of honey. [Col. 0047C]

You command every kind of living creature to serve humankind;  
you also make groves bend beneath their heavy fruit  
and new harvests arise from no seed.  
You make the various rivers assist our labor  
and renew with sacred waters an age made blessed.

Under your guidance the seas lay open  
to prows borne on sails,  
and the sailor traversed harbors divided by straits.

After the elements had been shaped  
into their appointed forms,  
lest the celestial fabric begin to lie inert  
with a rough and unfinished face,  
you marked the world with varied gifts;  
and whatever shines in heaven  
was fashioned by your right hand.

With these signs it pleased you  
to construct the palace of the Lord.

Then, lest the seas stretch inhospitably  
beside no lands,  
and so that the eager sailor might continually  
mark a harbor,  
many an island was planted in the swelling deep. [Col. 0047D]  
Though surrounded by the raging flood, it does not fear,  
but, resting on its little circuit amid the waters,  
stands firm, confident under your guidance.

Your venerable covenant, bound by equal law,  
makes highest and lowest correspond  
and does not allow them to transgress  
the limits imposed upon them.

And lest the earth lie too flat or bare,  
you commanded hills fit for abundant vines to rise  
and spacious groves to weave canopies of shade.  
Then, lest vast desolation rule in lifeless woods,  
you added countless offspring to the towering forests,  
so that the woodland would lack neither inhabitant  
nor prey for the hunter.

Then you made many birds, a thousand swarms of voices,  
resound in melodious groves with mortal harmony.  
Thus it pleased you to interweave the year  
with varied forms [Col. 0048A]  
and, through its delightful succession,  
to add fruitfulness for mortals:  
lest an ever-prolonged day scorch the world excessively,  
or one too brief snatch from growing things  
the fire they resent.

And lest labor shake all things with perpetual exertion,  
dew-laden night gives rest  
to the weary cares of humankind.  
So that human welfare might pass its years in safety,  
healing herbs spring voluntarily from the turf.  
The Father himself, rich without a plow,  
sows them by his command.

Even if my breast were sheathed in a wall of iron,  
if my voice were iron  
and I possessed a thousand tongues to sing,  
I could not recount all the gifts of your kindness.

But that Father of yours, dwelling in a hidden seat,  
not easily seen by anyone and terrible to all,  
sent you to earth as Lord and teacher of life.  
Whoever venerates the Son with proper honor  
may address his prayers to both  
and gain eternal life. [Col. 0048B]

You hold fast to chastity and righteousness,  
yet readily bend the laws after an offense  
if headlong madness has driven anyone away from you,  
beyond the prescribed boundary of life.

So that our eyes might endure to behold you,  
your Father clothed you in a human face  
and mortal limbs.  
For who would attempt to raise frail eyes  
if he had willed to present you to the trembling earth  
as you truly are—  
when with your mighty right hand you hurl thunderbolts  
and command immediate punishment  
to terrify its beholder;  
or when, appeased, you distribute rain  
upon thirsty fields  
and draw uncertain ears of grain from the furrows?

Yet, lest nothing should reveal your illustrious birth,  
you are conceived by a virgin.  
It was not enough that she should be chaste,  
nor that, being married, she could join a brother  
to the Lord, [Col. 0048C]  
unless the corruption of shameful contagion  
remained far from her womb.

Soon, when your blessed age ripened with its progress,  
you undertook through admonitions  
to preserve unteachable minds  
within the Father’s commands  
and offered the straight path to those who were falling.

And so that the commandments sent by God  
might be opened completely,  
you took its dominion from death;  
you released disease  
and commanded those without hope  
to take up once more the duties of life.  
You restored daylight to the blind;  
and lest anything remain entirely unattempted  
that treacherous error might resort to,  
you summoned awareness into tombs  
and commanded limbs long buried  
to rise again into the upper air;  
and the beloved corpses recognized their own names.

But after a worthy follower had absorbed the law,  
so that the heavenly spirit might strip itself  
of its mortal hall,  
you thereby taught one intent upon the law  
that all things must be endured [Col. 0048D]  
for the sake of the supreme God,  
and that each person rightly takes eternal life for himself  
through contempt of death.

Thus, bearing the completed commands of the Father,  
you returned to the hidden places of the highest heaven,  
where the bright ether forbids sluggish clouds  
to kindle within its own sky.

And so that assured release might be granted  
to the perishing multitude  
which shuts its pitiable ears against God’s commands,  
and that no new laws might hold those long dead,  
you broke open for us  
the death-bearing gates of the infernal prison  
and commanded a countless people  
to emerge from the darkness.  
Only those whom an impious life had marked  
remained shut within.

You assigned places of punishment  
to the shades yet to come—  
those who do not believe in you,  
or who pretend that they believe.

Holy God, venerable pledge of the supreme God,  
at whose name souls driven out by violent death,  
which have taken possession of alien breasts  
instead of their own, [Col. 0049A]  
cry aloud and grow pale and, when commanded, depart—  
as many earlier miracles concerning you reveal,  
when they are held suspended between earth and heaven,  
because through you nothing is permitted  
to the enemy who has been bound.

[Col. 0050A] But now prepare Constantine for me:  
a lord through his merits, a father through his devotion,  
gentle in command, a teacher through his rule of life,  
and equal to the ordinances sanctioned by the law established for you;  
victorious and joyful.

Nothing better than this offspring  
have you previously given to the earth,  
nor shall you give anything better.  
Would that his children might equal their father!

## [PREFACE ON JEWISH UNBELIEF]

[Col. 0049]

## CELSUS’ PREFACE ON JEWISH UNBELIEF TO THE *DEBATE OF JASON AND PAPISCUS*, ADDRESSED TO BISHOP VIGILIUS. (G, S)\*

[Col. 0049B]

> **Note [Col. 0049D]**
>
> **Although I know very many.** Before these words Colbertinus manuscript 1453 reads: “Cyprian to his brother Vigilius, greetings.”
>
> **Nevertheless.** All the manuscripts have *then*. Shortly before this, the editions have *hostile*.
>
> **Rejecting.** Thus all the manuscripts; and shortly afterward, *seeking*. The editions have the singular forms *one rejecting* and *one seeking*. Shortly before this, I added the conjunction *and* before *the fathers* from the Reims manuscript.
>
> **Reparation.** The Reims manuscript reads: “With complete reparation through penance.”
>
> **I think, it will endure.** We added these words from the Reims manuscript.
>
> **Madness.** Thus two manuscripts; the editions read *infamy*. Likewise, two manuscripts have *to acknowledge*; the editions read *we acknowledge*.
>
> **What reason, pray, is there?** Two ancient manuscripts instead read: “This—that is, Judaea—preferred to abandon the light divinely shown by reason, and to foster mental blindness [Col. 0050D] and choose the darkness of death,” etc.
>
> **Through a free and unlawful choice of destruction.** Thus four manuscripts; the editions have the accusative *free*, etc.
>
> **Those things that are beneficial.** One manuscript instead reads: “those things that are possible.”
>
> **God wishing to gather her.** Thus four manuscripts; the editions read: “the Lord.”
>
> **Manifestly.** Thus three manuscripts of the better class; the editions read: “manifest.”
>
> **Hence the Prophet.** On the authority of three manuscripts we corrected what had previously been corruptly printed: “Likewise another prophet, offering God’s benevolence through exhortation and suggesting it through preaching.”
>
> **Another also.** Thus three manuscripts; the editions read: “Likewise God also reveals his mercy in another way.” One manuscript reads: “through another.”
>
> **To the Lord.** I added these words from the Reims manuscript; and shortly afterward, *in any way* before *appease*.
>
> **Could have.** Thus the Reims manuscript; the editions read *were able*; one manuscript, *will be able*.

### I

Although I know, most holy Vigilius, that very many gentiles, turned away from the order and reason of truth, wander in mental blindness that prevents them from knowing the Lord, nevertheless I know that the madness of the Jewish people against the Lord’s name persists even now in stubborn hardness of heart, through an impiety innate both in themselves and in their fathers. They reject true salvation and do not seek the giver of eternal life. Thus those who, through the equal guilt of their inborn wickedness, are liable for the offenses of their ancient stock might at least believe, even though late, and, having turned to fear of the Lord, be freed from their iniquities through the full reparation of penance.

But the irreligious unbelief inherited from their fathers persists and endures still; and, I think, it will always endure, down to the generations that come after them. Strengthened by a madness of unbelief in its hatred of the Lord’s name, it can neither be corrected so as to acknowledge [Col. 0049C] the truth nor be taught and persuaded to fear God by his own admonitions.

For the Lord teaches and reveals, saying (John 8:12):

> I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.

What reason, pray, is there to abandon the light of life divinely revealed and, in mental blindness, to prefer to choose the darkness of death, thereby demonstrating one’s own voluntary condemnation through a free and unlawful choice of destruction, and even, in opposition to God, to reject those things that are beneficial?

[Col. 0050B] Accordingly, the Holy Spirit also speaks through the Lord’s voice, reproving Jerusalem because she refused to be gathered when God wished to gather her; and he makes manifest that God’s goodness continually desires to come to the aid of sinners (Matt. 23:37):

> Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you, how often I wished to gather your children, as a hen gathers her young beneath her wings, and you refused!

The obstinacy of the faithless people is so manifestly marked by God’s own voice that it is shown always to have spurned even its own salvation in opposition to the Lord’s merciful compassion.

Hence the Prophet, offering and presenting God’s benevolence through the exhortation of his proclamation, cries out and urges, saying (Mal. 3:7):

> Return to me, and I will return to you, says the Lord.

[Col. 0050C] Another likewise, demonstrating that the Lord’s mercy endures forever, added (Ezek. 33:11):

> I do not desire the death of the dying, but rather that he should return and live, says the Lord.

### II

What, then, is it to return to the Lord, other than to believe in Christ and, through him who is the way by which one comes to the Father, to be reconciled to God and thus be capable of salvation? But how can those return to God who refused to believe him through whom comes the knowledge of and return to God, when he proclaimed God’s will? Or how could they appease God through any reparation when, in sacrilegious hostility, they preferred to persecute him who is [Col. 0051A] our reparation and propitiation before the Father?

> **Note [Col. 0051D]**
>
> **Before the Father.** Thus the Reims manuscript together with another; the editions read *to the Father*; some manuscripts read “he spoke.”
>
> **Faith and belief.** I corrected this on the authority of the Reims manuscript; the editions read “by faith, belief.” Shortly afterward, from the same manuscript and several others, we adopted *we have conceived* and *let us return* in place of the editions’ *we conceive* and *let us be turned*.
>
> **Were.** I added this word from the Reims manuscript; another reads *was*.
>
> **That he had been born.** I added these words from the Reims manuscript. Shortly afterward four manuscripts have *it might be believed*; the editions, *they might believe*.
>
> **Warned by a divine oracle.** Thus the Reims manuscript; another has “warned by a divine response”; the editions, “by divine warning.”
>
> **Carried in.** Thus the Reims manuscript together with another; the editions read “brought.”
>
> **He proclaimed that it had been fulfilled.** Thus the Reims manuscript; the editions read “it is fulfilled.”
>
> **In manifest light.** Thus the Reims manuscript; the editions read “in manifestation, in light.”
>
> **Through the proclamation.** The editions read: “and by proclamation through the prophets, by a certain manifestation of himself, he proved his presence to everyone.” This passage and what follows, down to the words “and by unbelief,” I corrected on the authority of the Reims manuscript, with which the others agree for the most part. [Col. 0052D]
>
> **Minds.** Thus Pamelius; most manuscripts have the singular *mind*; the word is absent from the very accurate Reims manuscript. I therefore conjecture that this word, which is superfluous in itself, should be deleted. Shortly afterward, the same manuscript and four others have *of the people*; the editions, *to the people*.
>
> **Injustice.** Thus the Reims manuscript together with two others; the editions read *justice*. Shortly afterward we have adopted *and the blindness of heart* from the same manuscript in place of *the blindness of heart*.
>
> **Repeatedly proclaims**, etc. Thus the Reims manuscript together with most of the others; the editions read “is repeatedly proclaimed.”
>
> **By the Holy Spirit.** These words are absent from the Reims manuscript [Col. 0053D] and two others. The same manuscript has *forewarning*, and from it we have also corrected the following sentence, which was corrupt in the editions.

For if (1 John 2:1) “we have Christ as our advocate before God the Father,” we ought with vigilant fear to perform those things which he taught and admonished us to do, and which he will say before the Father.

We, therefore, whose minds are inclined toward fear of the Lord, who remain attentive to the admonitions of his commandments, and who have conceived in our devout and reverent hearts faith and belief arising from fear of him—what else ought we to follow, desire, prefer, and hold fast to, except that, once every night of our former mind has been dispelled from us and the darkness of our previous life wiped away, we should remember the Lord’s saving commandments, retain the promises of eternal life, return to his admonitions, and walk with confirmed belief in the light which he revealed? Thus we who once, ignorant [Col. 0051B] of future salvation, wandered astray, entangled in the errors and darkness of our former life, may now be illuminated by the brightness of his true light; and, with the boundary of a better life shown and opened to us, we may hold fast to the Lord’s commandments as things to be followed and carried out.

### III

This light of saving life which has arisen for us, this aid born for the restoration of humankind through the providence and compassion of God the Father, was first revealed by the Magi. Coming from the East, openly seeking the king of the Jews in a foreknowing proclamation with a star as their guide, and bringing gifts as well, they made it known to everyone through their attested inquiry.

And lest his identity remain hidden from anyone, when they had found the child, they fell upon their knees and worshiped him, as the Gospel bears witness:

> Now when Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judaea in the days [Col. 0051C] of King Herod, behold, Magi came from the East to Jerusalem, saying: “Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? For we saw his star in the East and have come to worship him” (Matt. 2:1–2).

They were, of course, bearing witness to the truth concerning him and showing that the star had been revealed to them as the sign and indication of his birth. With this star as their witness, and with the Magi proclaiming and affirming that he had been born, it was to be believed in Jerusalem.

The righteous Simeon also, who had been blind, had heard after being warned by a divine oracle that he would not die before he had seen Christ. When the mother carried the infant into the temple in the presence of all the people, and Simeon perceived in the Spirit that the child born was Christ, he received the boy into his hands and saw him. Blessing God, he said within the sight and hearing of everyone [Col. 0051D] (Luke 2:29–30):

> Now, Lord, you dismiss your servant in peace [Col. 0052A] according to your word, because my eyes have seen your salvation.

Simeon proclaimed that what he had heard while blind had been fulfilled in evident truth; and, by openly blessing God, he proclaimed to the people the truth which he had seen after receiving his sight. For he had seen in order that he might report it, reveal through his disclosure that Christ had been born, and instruct the faithless people concerning the first beginnings of their unbelief.

### IV

Nor do the true heavenly Scriptures offer only this testimony concerning him. Rather, the Holy Spirit also openly proclaimed beforehand through the prophets, with the awareness of all minds, that his advent into this world would occur. Unbelievers have no grounds for an excuse—either that they did not know Christ, the Son of God, or that they did not know the Savior’s advent would occur—[Col. 0052B] as David makes manifest, saying (Ps. 18:3–6):

> Day pours forth the word to day, and night declares knowledge to night. There are no speeches or words in which their voices are not heard. Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the earth. He has placed his tabernacle in the sun.

That is, in manifest light he openly showed that he himself had come; and through the proclamation of the prophets he in some fashion confirmed to everyone the manifestation of his presence.

Isaiah too prophesies this, through whom the Lord revealed his presence in the clear manifestation of proclamation, saying (Isa. 3:6):

> I myself, who was speaking, have come.

That is: “I who, through the prophets, had spoken beforehand that I would come before my advent, have now come in person, so that I myself, as my own witness, might reveal my presence to everyone.”

[Col. 0052C] What could be more evident? What could be brighter than this light? What could be said more truly? Accordingly, so that he might in some fashion be seen by the eyes, before he came, he who was already to come revealed that he would come; yet because unbelief obstructed the minds of the faithless people, no one recognized him when he came. As the same Isaiah cries out in his first reproof of the people (Isa. 1:3):

> The ox knew its owner, and the ass its master’s manger; but Israel did not know me, and my people did not understand me.

As he himself had foretold, he appeared openly to all; the manifest light of life shone upon those sitting in darkness; but the injustice of the faithless, having occupied their hearts and having set aside and rejected their own salvation, preferred darkness and blindness of heart.

### V

[Col. 0052D] The prophecy of all those who, by the forewarning of the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0053A] were chosen to be the surveyors who marked out the Lord’s advent repeatedly proclaims and makes this manifest everywhere. In the Psalms the Holy Spirit teaches and reveals that this light was given to the world and that the day of salvation, which has arisen for us, was appointed also to give life to those who believe in him, saying (Ps. 117:22–24):

> The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner. This was done by the Lord— [Col. 0053A]
>
> **Note [Col. 0053D].** [The supplied source breaks off here.]

Source/review notes: The supplied Latin of the eight-line epigram is corrupt or defective in lines 3–4 and 8; the translation explicitly marks this inherited textual uncertainty.

[Annotations on the text block] **“This has been made.”** Thus the Remigian manuscript and two others; the printed editions read, “This thing has been made.”

**Believing.** Thus the Remigian manuscript; the printed editions read, “of belief.”

**All things of the world.** A manuscript once belonging to Baluze and now in the Royal Library instead reads, “He embraced all ages.” What follows has been corrected on the authority of the Remigian manuscript, with which another manuscript agrees in part. Morel’s text read: “having turned to him in fear (Pamelius: therefore), let us believe in the eternity of life through hope of his future kingdom,” etc.

**Against pure.** Thus the Remigian manuscript together with two others, one of which has “against the true faith”; the printed editions read, “against into the pure,” or “into the true.”

[Col. 0054D]

**Whole.** The Remigian manuscript and another read “with the whole,” namely, “with the whole heart.” Shortly afterward, “what life is”; the Remigian manuscript reads “who it is,” another “what it is.”

**And devotion.** In this sequence of words and in those that follow, we adhere closely to the Remigian manuscript and correct many passages—for example, what was corruptly read in the printed editions as “with the whole faith of the breast, of a devoted mind”; and, not long afterward, “may behold the light of Christ, of salvation already obtained.”

**Namely.** We have added this from the Remigian manuscript. Shortly afterward, from the same manuscript, “by which we behold him,” in place of what stood in the printed editions, “by which indeed we behold his.”

**It was accepted and credited.** The Remigian manuscript reads, “By command it was reckoned.”

**Hardened.** Thus the Remigian manuscript; the printed editions read “made hard.”

**The Holy Spirit.** The Remigian manuscript instead reads: “For the Lord Christ, the Son of God, our Lord, who proceeded.”

**Deigned.** The Remigian manuscript reads, “And by his condescension.”]

This has been made, and it is wonderful in our eyes; this is the day that the Lord has made: let us walk and rejoice in it. The apostle Paul likewise commands, teaches, and forewarns us to walk in this day, saying (Rom. 13:11–13): “For now salvation is nearer to us than when we believed. The night has passed; the day, however, has drawn near. Let us therefore cast away the works of darkness and put on the armor of light; as in the day, let us walk honorably”—that is, in Christ and in his commandments. Illumined by his light and admonitions, and found in the brightness of his day, [Col. 0053B] with a mind believing in him we behold the salvation that is near us.

VI. The prophet Malachi also testifies and promises that Christ is the sun for all who fear him, saying (Mal. 4:2): “But for you who fear my name, the Sun of righteousness shall arise, and healing shall be in his wings.” He shows that salvation can be conferred upon us from no source except through the suffering of his cross, upon which, stretching out his hands to save all things of the world, he embraced them, so that, turning to him in fear, we may believe in the eternity of life and be encouraged by hope of his future kingdom. For who is so foolish and senseless, who so alienated from understanding his own salvation, that, unbelieving in so many and such great testimonies of the truth, he does not soften with understanding of the truth a heart hardened against pure faith, [Col. 0053C] and, stripped of the darkness of his formerly mortal life, walk in the light of the heavenly precepts and turn his illumined heart, with the whole believing conviction of mind and faith, toward fulfilling the divine admonitions and the Lord’s saving commandments? Thus may he know as God the one whom the prophets proclaimed; understand as Christ the one who openly showed that he had come into the world; and, because the Scriptures bear divine testimony, believe him to be the Son of God and God. As he himself reveals what eternal life is, saying (John 17:3): “Now this,” he says, “is eternal life: that they may know you, the only and true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.” He teaches and shows that to know God is nothing other than to believe and to open the eyes of the heart to the Lord with ready—indeed, with the whole—faith of the breast and devotion of mind. From this it follows that by believing [Col. 0053D] you understand, and by understanding what you believe, you behold it with an illumined [Col. 0054A] heart; just as the Lord himself also admonishes through Isaiah, saying (Isa. 7:9): “Unless you believe, you will not understand.” So ready, excellent, generous, and abundant is the mercy that proceeds from the Lord’s loving-kindness that, if anyone once turns himself to him with complete fear, he is admitted to the heavenly gift; immediately his mind lies open to nothing but divine things, and, lifting the eyes of his heart toward heaven and the things above, he beholds the light of Christ and the homeland of salvation.

VII. An example and proof of our fear and faith are shown in the faithful belief of the patriarch Abraham himself, who immediately believed God’s promise with a sincere mind and therefore, by a fitting recompense, deserved to have it credited to him as righteousness. This God loves, this he desires, this in his kindness he rewards and honors in his servants: namely, the sincerity of the pure heart [Col. 0054B] by which we behold him; the loving fear of the Lord by which we are proved; and the believing faith of mind by which we are accounted righteous. It is fitting for us to follow this faith and preserve this fear of God, for by keeping the heavenly words and hoping in the divine promises we have deserved to be called children of Abraham. This is confirmed by the testimony of the apostle Paul, who by the voice of God was called a vessel of election, when he says (Gal. 3:6–7): “Thus Abraham believed God, and it was accepted and credited to him as righteousness. Know, therefore, that those who are of faith are the children of Abraham.” The Jewish people, to whom the admonitions of the law had been spoken from the beginning, refused to preserve this because of the hardness of an unbelieving mind and the madness of a faithless heart; and therefore, as deserved by their distrust, they lost the name of children. Yet the minds of not all that unbelieving nation were hardened by hatred against the Lord’s name [Col. 0054C] so as to prevent them from understanding the truth. And so the Holy Spirit—that is, Christ our Lord, proceeding from God the Father—came to save what had perished of Israel. Greater and stronger in bringing the necks of the rebellious into fear of his name and under his power, he converted to knowledge of his brightness and glory those who, even then, persisted against the radiance of his light in the obstinate blindness of their minds, as easily as, in the providence of his divine mercy, he deigned to come so that he might save everyone.

VIII. Not to mention the minds of that hard-hearted and impious people which were then converted to fear of the Lord while the Lord himself preached the Gospel; not to dwell upon the people of believers multiplied throughout the whole world and brought back through the preaching of his apostles: there comes to mind that splendid, memorable, [Col. 0054D] and glorious debate between JASON, a Hebrew Christian, and [Col. 0055A] PAPISCUS, an Alexandrian Jew. In it the obstinate hardness of the Jewish heart was softened by a brief admonition [Col. 0055A] [Note: [Col. 0055D]

**Service.** Thus the Remigian manuscript; the printed editions read, “incitement.”

and a gentle rebuke; and Jason’s teaching, aided by the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, proved victorious in the heart of Papiscus. Through it Papiscus was admitted to understanding of the truth and, through the Lord’s own mercy, was formed in fear of the Lord; he believed that Jesus Christ is the Son of God and, desiring to receive the seal, entreated and petitioned Jason. This is established by the written account of their debate, which records in a work composed in Greek the arrangement and fullness of Christ as the two contended with one another—Papiscus opposing the truth, and Jason asserting and vindicating it. With God’s help encouraging me and the firmness of assisting faith sustaining me, I proceeded undauntedly [Col. 0055B] to translate it for Latin understanding while preserving the precise sense of the words.
