For those unfamiliar with comprehension of learned Greek, I expounded the whole through translation, disclosing both the meaning of the words and the full understanding and manifestation of the truth, and elucidating it in the form of Latin discourse. I earnestly entrust the evaluation of this labor to you, dearest brother, who are grounded in knowledge of both languages: so that, reverent as you are in your veneration of the Holy Spirit, by comparing a reading of the two works you may examine the boldness of my modest temerity; and by the judgment of your scrutiny, through the authority of the Holy Spirit who has flowed into your breast in a flood of heavenly grace, you may approve and correct whatever has perhaps been set forth by me inadequately or improperly. Let there also be entrusted to you from my humility, concerning this reading, an embassy and a first petition of love to be commended to you on my behalf: that you may unite the littleness [Col. 0055C] of my faith with the instruction and education of your disciples; and that you may admit into the intimate fellowship of your love, with the unity of brotherhood, me who, though situated in another part of this province, was not frightened by the length of the journey from coming to behold your face, nor delayed by age and the infirmity of a body now wearied and exhausted. Encouraged instead by service to the Lord and impelled by an urgent desire to hasten here—and disregarding every hardship of want and poverty—I came with whatever strength I possessed, drawn here by the celebrated fame of your holiness. May you likewise unite and attach me to that love of yours which the Lord left to his disciples as an inheritance, so that together with the brethren I may await, when you open your mouth, the splendor of the grace of Christ’s light. For in your treatises [Col. 0055D] you follow the light of life which the Lord revealed, which Christ at his coming showed himself to be: eternal life.

[Col. 0056A] IX. Surely how joyful, how desirable that day will be for me when, through the Lord’s mercy and favor, his summons is deferred and it befalls me to prolong this old age of mine, so that I may deserve to be joined to the prayers of the saints who earnestly and continually entreat the Lord; that I may see Christ’s martyr; that I may behold you bearing the crown of righteousness which is laid up for you with the Lord. Yet you should not suppose that the glory of martyrdom is being conferred upon you merely in accordance with the present desire of your faith. From that moment the dignity of this blessedness was conferred; then the Lord in his just judgment chose you as the martyr already destined for him when, unexpectedly removing you from the company of the righteous and taking you to himself, he appointed you priest at his altar. Splendid indeed and glorious was the choice of your calling; and new, unheard-of, and marvelous was the felicity that proceeded from the Lord’s condescension: though occupied by the necessities of a sojourn overseas, you suddenly arrived, ignorant and unaware, at the office destined for you. The timing of your return was so exactly balanced for this purpose that, through the inspired swiftness of your coming, you should understand and recognize that the honor of the heavenly priesthood was destined above all for you among the others, and that you had come and arrived, awaited by the Lord’s command, to receive what had been reserved for you. For, so that the Lord might provide for his Church with all the compassion of his loving-kindness, while the struggling people delayed over whom they should preferably choose as bishop, Christ suddenly and unexpectedly presented you to his people as they sought one; and by the unforeseen coincidence of your arrival, heavenly providence manifestly showed you to be pleasing to him. The evidence of this sudden and swift arrival revealed the operation of God’s will: what might have come about through a difficult undertaking was completed with ready speed at the command of the Lord who urged it, so that you should behold yourself standing as bishop in the Church of God, and marvel at it, before you were even recognized as having arrived.

X. From that moment the Lord confirmed the love he now shared with you by inaugurating this bond of charity; from that moment he consecrated with you the friendship which, under the triumph of his cross, he handed down and dedicated to his disciples, saying (John 15:14): “If you do what I command you, I no longer call you servants, but friends.” From that moment he marked out your martyrdom and your election to the priesthood. Great is the friendship through which you are admitted to the countenance of Christ and come before him as an extraordinary sacrificial victim. Thus are the righteous chosen; thus are the devout and sincere, chosen in the fear of Christ, put to the test: so that you may be destined for the recompense of faith beforehand, and accounted worthy in the Lord beforehand of the reward of a devoted mind, [Col. 0056D] so that, before the appointed hour has come, before you have received Christ’s sentence, the heavenly election may find you a tested and prepared sacrificial victim. For he who is not a lying God, who unexpectedly appointed you bishop for his people, will crown you in the fullness of his loving will. We ask and pray only that you remember us then, when you stand chastely before Christ’s tribunal as a tested and immaculate sacrificial victim [Col. 0057A] chosen by the Lord; when, in the glory of God’s grace, you have received the reward and recompense of a devoted mind. May the loving affection which you deign to bestow upon us cling to your memory and remain tenaciously in your thoughts, so that through your prayers our sins may obtain pardon, and through the merits of your righteousness the transgressions of our life may be cleansed. For I trust that it is comparable to martyrdom for a sinner to have deserved salvation through the petition of a righteous man, so that, even when the sinner himself can scarcely merit anything through your prayers, he may be delivered through the merits of a martyr. Thus the righteous Job is shown as about to pray to God for the sins of his three friends and obtain forgiveness, while the proof of his fear and faith is attested by the Lord’s own voice. Therefore, on the day of your deliverance, dearest brother, when you begin to present yourself before the countenance of Christ; when you have entered upon the blessed lot of reigning with Christ in the eternity and perpetuity of beholding him: through the Lord’s mercy, keep your servant Celsus then in your thoughts, most holy father.

[Col. 0057A] [Note:

[Annotations on the text block] **Modestly.** Thus the Remigian manuscript; another has, not inappropriately, the feminine form “modest”; the printed editions read “chastity.” On the authority of the same Remigian manuscript and several others, we read “tenaciously” in place of “that you may hold,” and “to merit” in place of “to advance,” and correct several other readings.

[Col. 0058A]

**Through the petition of a righteous man.** Thus the Remigian manuscript; the printed edition reads “of a righteous martyr”; and shortly afterward the same Remigian manuscript reads “through the prayers of a martyr.”

**Celsus.** The Remigian manuscript reads “Caecilius.”]

[LACTANTIUS.]

[Col. 0057]

PREFACE OF NICOLAS LENGLET DUFRESNOY [Note: [Col. 0057C]

We reprint his edition, since it must be regarded as taking the place of all those published up to the present and as having been corrected according to the evidence of innumerable printed and manuscript copies, though with some things changed for the better or added.]

ON LACTANTIUS

[Col. 0057B] I. Scholars have long been awaiting an edition of Lactantius’s works more correct and complete than any previously available. We now publish such an edition, and have taken care that the text should be as accurate as possible, while the notes should serve utility rather than display. Yet do not suppose, learned reader, that all this is owed solely to my own care. In 1707, to be sure, it occurred to me to undertake this work, so that I might devote to this study the leisure left me from serious duties, which detained me at Lille in Flanders, at the Bavarian-Colognian court. I had gathered almost all the editions of Lactantius and had collated certain manuscripts, both in Belgium and previously at Paris; likewise, through continual labor, I had composed a great many notes, collected them from every quarter, and accumulated them in a single body.

II. But at the time when I was considering these matters and applying my hand [Col. 0057C] to hasten the work toward completion, I was informed that Jean-Baptiste Le Brun of Rouen, then residing at Orléans on the Loire, was directing all his study and labor toward correcting Lactantius. I therefore laid aside the work I had undertaken and, through mutual friends, sent Le Brun ten choice editions and more than forty of the rarer ones, which I had collected with the greatest care. His learning and diligence were known and approved by me from his edition of the works of St. Paulinus and from other by no means unlearned compositions.

[Col. 0058B] III. But in 1731, without completing the work, that learned man departed to the world above; and some years afterward his papers were entrusted to me, and his annotations committed to my care. Yet it is scarcely possible to describe how great an astonishment came over me when I saw that this undoubtedly learned editor had expended ten years of unremitting labor merely in accumulating from every quarter—indeed, scraping together—the variant readings of manuscripts and editions of Lactantius, while omitting those observations, whether historical or critical, which were necessary both for grasping and explaining the author’s meaning. By following this method, Jean Le Brun would merely have increased the number of editions; he would not have extinguished the desire for the older ones, but would instead have inflamed it.

IV. But let our discussion now turn to Lactantius himself. It is certain that, among Latin authors, this was peculiar to him: that he was in a certain sense equipped for a variety of functions. For although among ecclesiastical writers he holds only the second or third place, he was undoubtedly a leading man in literary matters because of his varied learning, worthy of a man of letters. Indeed, with such eloquence, such polish, and such gravity he discusses and expounds loftily upon matters of the greatest necessity in religion that he is as welcome in our own times as he was in the earlier centuries of the Church.

V. People commonly ask why so learned and eloquent a writer published his *Institutions*. This, then, was his reason: just as legal authorities and arbiters of equity composed and published *Institutions of Civil Law*, through which the lawsuits and disputes of contending parties might be settled, so Lactantius published his *Divine Institutions* chiefly so that the faithful might have ready to hand, as though within a single view, all the arguments by which they might refute the errors of the pagans and maintain the unbroken truth of the Christian religion (Lactantius, *Institutions*, Book I, chapter 1, col. 116 of our edition).

VI. His *Institutions*, which are completed in seven books, proceed in this order: in the first three he refutes the insane worship of the gods; in the next three he instructs faithful Christians in the truth. For, as Lactantius himself says (Book I, chapter 23, col. 232 of our edition): “The first step of wisdom is to understand what is false; the second, to know what is true.” In the final book, at last, he treats the punishments and torments of the impious, and the immortal reward and blessedness of the pious. Yet you should not believe that throughout this entire work every argument is equally strong. Certain reasons which now seem comparatively slight and feeble were weighty and solid at that time. Thus it sometimes happens, because both of human disposition and human customs, that different courses of time also possess different methods of argument.

VII. Lactantius does not deny that certain writers of our own had already traversed the same road. But, as he himself says, although Minucius Felix could have been a capable defender of the truth, he did not write a complete or altogether comprehensive argument in defense of religion. In Tertullian—and rightly so—he finds clarity and ease of expression wanting; in Cyprian, although eloquent and ornate, although powerful in persuasion, he notes a mode of writing insufficiently suited to convincing the pagans. But Lactantius should not be blamed for passing over in silence the seven books written by his teacher Arnobius. For Arnobius seems to have embraced the Christian religion only in the twentieth year of Constantine, that is, in the year 326 of the common era [Col. 0059C] [Note: [Col. 0059C]

Eusebius indeed says the following: “In the twentieth year of Constantine, Arnobius was regarded as a celebrated rhetorician in Africa. While he was instructing young men in declamation in the city of Sicca, and, still a pagan, was being driven toward belief by dreams, yet could not obtain from the bishops the faith which he had formerly attacked, he elaborated most brilliant books against his former religion and at last obtained, as though by certain hostages, a covenant of piety.” Thus the *Chronicle* of Eusebius. On this basis we assign Arnobius’s accession to the Christian religion to the year 326, the twentieth year of Constantine, although the Reverend Father Rémi Ceillier places it in 303 in his *History of Ecclesiastical Writers*, volume III. If Arnobius had given his allegiance to Christ in the third year of the fourth century, Eusebius would undoubtedly have recorded this under the reign of Diocletian, not in the twentieth year of Constantine. Moreover, the testimony of his *Chronicle* must not be denied: that book was composed at this very time by a most learned man who had devoted all his effort to investigating the lives of learned men, especially those of his own century.

], at which time he published his arguments against pagan superstition, approximately six years after Lactantius had published his own *Institutions*. It is therefore unsurprising that Lactantius—according to the testimony of Eusebius of Caesarea, the most learned of the Christians—undertook so arduous a labor, and was unwilling to allow the invectives with which two philosophers had assailed the Christians to go unpunished, whether those philosophers were Hierocles and Porphyry or certain others.

VIII. Precisely when Lactantius wrote these books [Col. 0060A] is not altogether certain. Critics have adopted various opinions. Isaeus thinks they were composed in 302; but in that year the Christian faithful enjoyed a measure of peace, whereas at the time when Lactantius published his *Institutions* the Church was being harassed by persecution. Others believe it was in 311; Cardinal Baronius, after 315; finally, the more learned judge that they were published considerably later than 318, perhaps in 320 or 321. It is not my purpose here to examine the arguments of all these scholars through many circumlocutions, or to seek out too curiously the evidence adduced on either side. It will suffice to set forth the established, or at least the more probable, opinion.

IX. Under the emperor Diocletian, Lactantius had been summoned from Africa to Nicomedia in Bithynia to teach rhetorical letters there—that is, Latin eloquence; [Col. 0060B] and he remained there throughout the persecution, which raged against Christians for ten years and more. This did not end until the middle of June 313. Yet Eusebius, a most diligent writer on these times, informs us that Lactantius did not depart from Bithynia for Gaul until 317. But when Lactantius wrote the books of the *Institutions*, he was no longer in Bithynia. “When,” he says, “I had been summoned to teach rhetorical letters in Bithynia, and it happened that at the same time the temple of God was overthrown, two men appeared there who insulted the prostrate truth” (Book V of the *Institutions*, chapter 2). “I saw,” he says, “a governor in Bithynia” (Book V, chapter 11). These things, therefore, had already happened some time before; Lactantius was then absent from that province. Consequently, he wrote these works after 317.

Persecutions are nevertheless mentioned in the books of the *Institutions*; [Col. 0060C] but which persecutions these were may be seen from Lactantius himself. I do not think it was the persecution which Diocletian and Galerius were planning as 302 drew to its close, which began on 23 February 303 and ended on 13 June 313. For Lactantius was then at Nicomedia; accordingly, that is not the persecution to which he refers in this passage. The point becomes clearer from these words of Lactantius (Book VI, chapter 17): “Throughout the world the punishments of the worshippers of God have been seen and are still seen [Note: [Col. 0060D]

These words must certainly be understood of the famous confessors of those times whom the persecutors had mutilated in parts of their bodies and limbs. Many of them attended the Council of Nicaea. Among them were Saints Paphnutius of the Thebaid, Potamo of Heraclea, and Spiridion of Cyprus, bishops whose scars received for Christ the emperor Constantine kissed more than once, according to Eusebius in his *Life* of that prince, Book III, chapters 6–13, and, after Eusebius, many ecclesiastical writers.

]; new and unprecedented torments were devised for torturing them. For the mind shudders to recall the kinds of death employed, since the butchery of savage beasts raged even beyond death itself.” In this passage Lactantius is indeed speaking of the Diocletianic persecution, but it was not raging at that time. Examine these words [Col. 0060D] more closely: “The punishments have been seen; torments were devised; the mind shudders to recall; since it raged.” Do these expressions refer to a present state? Do they not, on the contrary, refer to the past? All these things, therefore, had already passed when Lactantius wrote. [Col. 0061A] Accordingly, it was considerably later than 315. But after the restoration of the Church there was no other persecution whatsoever against Christians except that of Licinius, the beginning of which must be assigned to 320. Who does not see that Book VI of the *Institutions*, chapter 6, concerns Licinius? There Lactantius says:

“Some men, by feigned integrity, prepare a path for themselves to power and do many things which good men are accustomed to do—and all the more readily because they do them for the sake of deceiving. Would that it were as easy to practice goodness as it is easy to simulate it! But when they have become masters of their purpose and desire and have seized”—that is, received—“the highest degree of power, then, casting aside pretense, they reveal their character, plunder, violate, and harass everything. They persecute those good men”—that is, the Christians—“whose cause they had undertaken, [Col. 0061B] and cut away the steps by which they themselves ascended, lest anyone be able to imitate them against themselves.”

Is this not Licinius himself, who, when an angel admonished him from heaven in a dream to pray to the supreme God for victory according to a prescribed formula of prayer, immediately prayed and obtained it? “The Licinian soldiers, therefore,” says our Lactantius, “lay down their shields, loosen their helmets, extend their hands toward heaven, and, with their officers leading, recite the prayer after the emperor”—Licinius. “After repeating the prayer three times, now filled with courage, they replace their helmets upon their heads, take up their shields, the trumpets sound, and the standards advance” (*On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 46, volume II); “the Licinian soldiers charge and attack their adversaries” (*ibid.*, chapter 47). Is this not that same Licinius who did many things which good men are accustomed to do, and who “ordered letters concerning the restoration of the Church to be posted . . . and verbally exhorted that the meeting places” of the Christians “be restored to their former condition”? (*On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 48, at the beginning and end.) Nevertheless, he persecutes those very good men whose cause he had previously undertaken; he plunders everything, violates everything, and harasses everyone.

That Licinian persecution, however, raged only in the East; the western parts of the empire, which had fallen to Constantine to govern, had long enjoyed an established and confirmed peace. Hence Lactantius himself, addressing the supreme emperor, says: “As for the wicked men who still rage against the righteous in other parts of the world, the longer the delay, the more vehemently will the same Almighty pay them the wages of their crime” (Book I of the *Institutions*, chapter 1, col. 117 of our edition). Lactantius therefore wrote and published his *Institutions* while this eastern persecution was raging, that is, perhaps in 320 or 321. God had not yet paid Licinius the wages of his crime.

The concluding address to Constantine, however, appears to belong to a later time, namely 324, when the Roman Empire obeyed that prince alone, Licinius having been defeated and removed from the commonwealth. “The providence,” says Lactantius, “of the supreme Divinity raised you to imperial eminence, so that through true piety you might rescind the ill-advised measures of others, correct their transgressions, provide for the salvation of humankind with paternal clemency, and finally remove the wicked themselves from the commonwealth. God cast them down from supreme power”—words that point to no one other than Licinius, reduced to submission—“and delivered them into your hands”—because Licinius, twice defeated by Constantine, was compelled to yield—“so that it might be clear to everyone what true majesty is. For those who wished to abolish the worship of the heavenly and unique God in order to defend impious religions now lie prostrate” (Book VII of the *Institutions*, chapter 26). Licinius was driven into exile in 324, but had not yet, as it seems, been put to death for the seditious designs he was pursuing in the East; that occurred only in 325. Hence Lactantius there praises Constantine’s true piety because, after granting pardon and life to a rebel and enemy, he even received him courteously at a banquet.

X. How can certain scholars labor so long over these addresses to Constantine—namely, over whether Lactantius dedicated his *Institutions* to the emperor? He certainly addresses that prince three or four times in the work. I do not deny that these addresses are often—indeed, very often—absent from the manuscript copies, including the most ancient, and likewise from certain printed editions. Some, though not all, are nevertheless found in reliable manuscripts. You will easily resolve the controversy if you suppose that Lactantius produced two editions of the *Divine Institutions*: one during the sorrowful period of the Licinian persecution, in 320 or 321; the other after Licinius had been defeated and reduced to submission, in 324. Then Constantine, having gained the victory, “rescinded the ill-advised measures of the wicked”—that is, of Licinius and Martinianus. Yet Lactantius showed himself a more restrained and prudent writer in that passage by not naming Licinius, who was connected to the emperor by a close family tie. For Constantine had given his sister Constantia to Licinius as his wife.

Indeed, everyone also acknowledges that these addresses, both at the beginning of Book I and at the end of the seventh, plainly savor of Lactantius’s style. We discuss this at the relevant places by comparing their vocabulary with Lactantius’s indisputable modes of expression. But how can it happen that one or another of these addresses, though not the final one, is often read in certain manuscripts [Note: [Col. 0062D]

Thus, in the manuscript of Lactantius belonging to the Capuchin Fathers of Saint-Honoré, the address in Book I is found, but not the one in Book VII.

]? This undoubtedly happened because the later copies were transcribed from different exemplars. When Lactantius added these addresses to his *Institutions*, Constantine alone ruled the Roman Empire. But if Lactantius produced a second edition of the *Divine Institutions* in 324, he could, for example, have included the Arians among the heretics (Book IV of the *Institutions*, chapter 30), whose name is found in a great many manuscripts, including ancient ones. For Arius had already been expelled from Alexandria by Bishop Alexander and condemned at two synods, namely in the years 319 and 324.

XI. Although Lactantius very often refuted the pagans with sound arguments, and although he cultivated religion sincerely and candidly, I nevertheless do not deny that he was bound by certain errors. Each person censures these in a different spirit, according to his own disposition. With St. Jerome (*Letter to Paulinus*), we rightly say of Lactantius: “Would that he had been as capable of confirming our own doctrines as he was readily able to destroy those of others!” Yet we do not proceed so far as to assail him with Antonio da Rho [Note: [Col. 0063D]

See Luke Wadding in his folio volume *Writers of the Order of Friars Minor*, Rome, 1650. This Raudensis also published another book, *On the Good Word*, which Lorenzo Valla attacks severely because of its style.

], a fifteenth-century theologian of the Order of Friars Minor, as though his books were everywhere filled with heresies and impiety. It is not my intention to incur the varied censures of the more learned, lest the same taunts be directed against me as that Raudensis experienced. Not only did a certain Adam, [Note: [Col. 0063D]

His epigram against Raudensis, consisting of eight verses, is found in the Roman edition of Lactantius of 1468, published by Pietro de’ Massimi; Albert Fabricius copied it from there in the *Supplement to the Latin Library*, p. 395. It has seemed appropriate to give it here:

Here Antonio [Raudensis], with foolish ventures, wrongly censured  
This author: an offense requiring expiation in many places.

It was not [wrong] to call those wandering in the darkness of an image a star,  
Or [to say] that a shining radiance lacked light.

Finally, since it is agreed that the devout luminaries of Holy Church  
Kept silence toward so great a man out of such deference,

But as for you—your tongue forbidden Latin eloquence—  
+ to bed +, for hellebore is weighing you down.

[The Latin text and sense of lines 3–4 and of the final verse are materially uncertain.]

] a Genoese monk, vehemently brand him insane, but so too did Francesco Filelfo, that devoted cultivator of humane letters. For Filelfo addresses Antonio da Rho as follows (*Letters*, Book V, under the year 1443), because he had criticized Lactantius badly and foolishly in three books:

“I should indeed have wished, excellent Father, that you had refrained from every such kind of writing, and had not wished to rave along with the raving Candido Decembrio. That would certainly have befitted both your order and your dignity. For, by the immortal God, what fanatical reasoning moved you to assail that most learned and eloquent man so arrogantly, so injuriously, and so impiously, as though inspired by some hostile and inimical spirit, that you not only deliberately misinterpret almost innumerable matters, but even strive to corrupt the man’s name, calling him *Lactensius* instead of *Lactantius*? For what am I to say of the matters themselves? While endeavoring to corrupt things known even to children, you make yourself ridiculous to every learned and serious man. I am truly ashamed to bring forward the points which you have noted and censured no less foolishly than erroneously.”

I have nowhere seen Antonio da Rho’s three books on the errors of Lactantius committed to print. We know of three manuscript copies of them in the Royal Library; only certain selected annotations from them were published.

XII. Joseph Isaeus’ censure also grew excessively extensive: in it ninety-four propositions in Lactantius are censured, although some of them, as Isaeus himself acknowledges, must be interpreted in a favorable sense, as is sometimes customary with ecclesiastical writers of the most ancient period. We more readily embrace the censorial annotations of Giovanni Maria Brasichelli, which are those of a moderate theologian. Although we have applied his observations to Lactantius wherever necessary, we shall nevertheless present them below together, as it were, in a single conspectus.

XIII. Nor should you attribute to Lactantius those impious doctrines of the Manichaeans [Col. 0064A] which are sometimes read in certain manuscript codices and printed editions of his works. For you will scarcely find them in the ancient copies; or at least they are written in the margins of some manuscripts as foreign and extraneous matter. In a word, it is evident from the silence of St. Jerome, St. Augustine, and other writers that Lactantius did not adhere to the Manichaeans. No writer ever numbered him among the Manichaean company—something those writers would undoubtedly not have omitted to do had Lactantius given them grounds for censure. Indeed, these impieties, very frequently stitched into the Lactantian text, not only disrupt the author’s discourse but are also plainly contrary to his doctrine, as we demonstrate when occasion arises.

XIV. Although Lactantius did not err in explaining the generation of the divine Word, he nevertheless spoke with less theological precision [Col. 0064B]; rather, he uses the modes of expression employed by philosophers. This sometimes occurs in authors who wrote before the Council of Nicaea, through which not only was Catholic doctrine explained more clearly and plainly than before, but terms most consonant with Christian doctrine were also fashioned and established. Moreover, the words thought to have been excerpted from chapter 9 of Book II of the *Institutions* contrary to the mind of the Church are neither read in the ancient copies nor consistent with Lactantius’ doctrine. For he declares that the Word, the Son of God, was begotten before the ages (Book IV of the *Institutions*, ch. 6), which the Arians denied. He also declares him “like the supreme Father” (Book IV, ch. 13, at the beginning); indeed, Isaiah, he says in the same place, testifies that Christ “was both God and man.” Thus, moreover, he says in chapter [Col. 0064C] 19 of Book VII: “For this is the Deliverer, Judge, Avenger, King, and God whom we call Christ.”

But our author proclaims at length the Catholic doctrine such as one finds it in the pre-Nicene Fathers and in the approved ecclesiastical writers of those times:

> When we speak of God the Father and God the Son, we do not speak of different beings, nor do we separate the two, because neither can the Father exist without the Son, nor can the Son be separated from the Father. . . . Since, therefore, the Father makes the Son, and the Son the Father, both have one mind, one spirit, one substance. . . . And the Son and Father, who with one accord inhabit the world, are one God, because the one is as though two, and the two as though one. . . . Finally, Isaiah shows that both the Father and the Son are one God.

All these are the words of a thoroughly [Col. 0064D] Catholic writer and are wholly alien to both the expressions and the thought of the Arians, and most strongly opposed to them. For the Arians never said that the Father and the Son were “of one substance.” But Lactantius had acquired such authority among the ancients, both because of his singular eloquence and because of his varied and extensive learning, that certain heretics, whether Manichaeans or Arians, corrupted his writings at their own discretion, as though those writings favored them.

XV. Yet I remain in suspense because of the authority of St. Jerome. For the holy Doctor says (*Letter to Pammachius*) that Lactantius, “through a Jewish error in his books, especially in the letters to Demetrianus, denies the substance of the Holy Spirit.” Yet not even a trace [Col. 0065A] of this error survives in the *Institutions* or in his other books. Hence we may say with Jerome himself (Book I of the *Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians*, ch. 4): “Who can forbid me to read the books of the *Institutions*, in which he wrote so powerfully against the Gentiles, merely because the foregoing opinion is detestable?” Lactantius spoke thus and erred, the same holy Doctor says, “through ignorance of the Scriptures.”

XVI. No one, however, denies that Lactantius embraced the opinion and errors of the Millenarians. For he believed, together with men then regarded as thoroughly Catholic, that when the world was drawing toward its end, Christ the Lord would reign on earth with the righteous for a thousand years. But this error has long since been removed from the Christian religion. Its father was a certain pious man, namely Papias, [Col. 0065B] bishop of Hierapolis in Phrygia, at the beginning of the second century. Lactantius earnestly strives to prove this error, which arose from a misunderstanding of chapter 20 of the Apocalypse, both from Virgilian verses and from the Sibylline books, which are believed to have been composed in the middle of that same century and which carried very great weight with him and with other ecclesiastical writers. But he should not be denied the pardon that others received for this error. Nevertheless, Pope Gelasius, at the end of the fifth century, rightly and wisely numbered the works of Lactantius together with the apocryphal writings, because not all the faithful could read them through without any injury whatsoever to Catholic doctrine.

Moreover, lest Lactantius’ words and authority deceive the reader and lead him into his errors, we not only refute those errors in the notes but also carefully warn against them, from various authors, in the prefatory admonitions [Col. 0065C] to this first volume.

XVII. Nevertheless, all the most learned men held his books in the highest esteem; and it is remarkable how many manuscript codices of Lactantius’ works are found throughout the literary world. In the city of Paris alone, thirty-seven and more have come to my knowledge. You will find many more in other libraries of our France; but anyone who traversed the other regions of Europe would surely obtain a richer harvest. The Vatican Library presents twelve, and the Royal Library of Turin nine. What might be expected from the Spanish libraries—especially the Escorial, wholly unknown to our own scholars, although filled with rarer manuscripts—or from those of Naples, Vienna, Venice, the Ambrosian Library, Florence, Monte Cassino, and Sicily? Not all, however, are equally ancient or of equally excellent quality. [Col. 0065D] Yet none should be passed over, since each may have been copied from an older exemplar. Hence the learned reader should be convinced how highly our forebears esteemed this most elegant writer. You will nevertheless find many manuscripts copied in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. For at that time literary studies began once again to blaze up, especially in Italy; and Lactantius was everywhere ordered to be copied, not only because of the brilliance of his Latin style but also because of his varied and by no means commonplace learning.

Moreover, in diligently correcting ancient authors, one manuscript codex is not sufficient; several must be employed. One may indeed present the true reading, but another confirms it; nor is it permissible to draw any certain conclusion without the testimony of several. Nevertheless, a certain measure [Col. 0066A] must be employed, lest a copyist’s error be accepted as the author’s genuine language.

We have compiled such a catalogue of them as we could, adding, so far as lay within our power, the date of writing, lest we incur the censure of scholars. Gallaeus is therefore not blamed without reason, and Isaeus himself is deservedly censured, because although he inspected twelve Vatican codices, he did not indicate their age. Bunemann therefore rightly—indeed, most rightly—says (*Preface to his edition of Lactantius*, p. 7):

> I do not doubt that after Isaeus’ time several codices were brought into the Vatican Library. Would that, with the assistance of HIS EMINENCE PASSIONEI, the foremost patron of polite letters, some benefit might even now return from there, by a kind of restoration, for the elucidation of Lactantius!

[Col. 0066B] XVIII. We must now briefly review the various editions of Lactantius. There is scarcely one or another writer among the profane authors—not to mention the ecclesiastical—whom scholars have more frequently corrected or booksellers more frequently printed. The complete author has been put to press a hundred times; individual books of his, however, have been published with notes fifteen times and more. And from the very infancy of printing, before the first year of the sixteenth century, his works appeared seventeen times—something you will scarcely find in any other writer. Sometimes three times, and more often twice, in a single year and in different cities, scholars both Catholic and alienated from Roman Catholic worship made him public property. Italians, Frenchmen, Germans, Spaniards, Dutchmen, and Englishmen illustrated him with notes to the best of their ability.

Yet not all editions are equally useful. All the more learned still desired something further—not only that the text [Col. 0066C] might be freed from every copyist’s error, but also that we might attain a thorough understanding of the author’s meaning. They acknowledge—Nicholas Le Nourry, a Benedictine of the Congregation of St. Maur, in the *Apparatus to the Library of the Holy Fathers*, vol. II, col. 658—that “none of all these editions is entirely perfect and complete in all its details and parts.”

Indeed, the oldest editions merely take the place of the manuscript codices that they reproduce. For if the exemplars from which they were printed were mutilated and corrupt, the printed work is undoubtedly defective and imperfect. Thus the extremely rare edition of 1465 is deficient in many places, since it was drawn from only one codex, and that an imperfect one. Greek passages are sometimes omitted; certain verses and clauses are also frequently absent. [Col. 0066D] Such is generally the case with the editions published in those early times. Scarcely any text corrected even to some degree is available to us before the Aldine editions, through the work and care of both Battista Egnazio and Onorato Fascitelli. But from that time until the year 1544, when the more correct Cologne edition appeared, there is scarcely any edition capable of satisfying the reader.

XIX. But because of Lactantius’ varied learning, annotations are necessary for understanding him more clearly. Xystus Betuleius was the first of all to prepare complete annotations; these were published at Basel in 1563, after his death. Erasmus had indeed already published some brief notes on the book *On the Workmanship of God* in 1529, as had Willichius in 1542. [Col. 0067A] But Betuleius scarcely took manuscript codices into account. His notes are much more prolix than is fitting and were composed to display varied learning, not for the benefit of readers.

Michael Thomasius Taxaquetus attempted something better, but made exceedingly meager use of two very ancient Bolognese copies and seven Vatican copies that he had seen. He therefore did not apply a healing hand plainly and completely to every wound in the Lactantian text. Far more complete is Isaeus’ recension, published at Cesena in Italy in 1646 and produced from twelve Vatican codices. He appended not only critical but also theological annotations.

Thysius sprinkled the Lactantian text with very few notes, and those of scarcely any importance; he also seems to me the first to have corrupted our author in Book I, chapter 15. [Col. 0067B] Gallaeus embraced this corruption and defended it in an annotation longer than was proper, contrary to good morals and evangelical truth, so as to champion usury; Sparkius and Walchius did not take pains to correct it. Gallaeus himself, as a young man in 1660, undertook a more correct and polished edition of Lactantius, illustrating it with notes gathered from every quarter, often extraneous and pertaining to theological controversies. Sparkius, although much more sparing than Gallaeus, was nevertheless more learned. The Cambridge editor admits that he reprinted the text of Thomasius. Cellarius added certain notes—neither useless nor unlearned—to his fairly well-corrected edition.

Johann Georg Walch, scarcely twenty years old, published in his correction of Lactantius a specimen of keen judgment [Col. 0067C] and of the learning for which he is now held in greater distinction in his native country; and I marvel that at such a youthful age he not only completed but even conceived the work of an old man.

Christoph August Heumann printed a truly elegant edition, both because of the correction of the Lactantian text—which, however, as he himself admits, he borrowed from Christoph Cellarius—and because of his own notes, which display singular devotion to the critical art and meticulous diligence. Yet far more often than he should, he imagines that glosses were introduced into Lactantius by men of little learning. Does anything difficult occur? Then there arises in him the suspicion, or even the complaint, that some addition has been made—though very often falsely, since it rests on the authority of no manuscript codex.

Finally, Johann Ludolph Bunemann wrested the palm from all others [Col. 0067D] in editing Lactantius. For such an abundance of varied observations, so manifold a profusion of variant readings, and so subtle an acuteness of judgment shine forth in his edition that no one before him had advanced so far. It was not enough for him to collate so many manuscript codices and so many different editions; he equally compared our writer with the foremost masters of the Latin language, so that all might be persuaded that Lactantius was the most eloquent of the ecclesiastical authors. For he corrected Lactantius against fifty-two manuscript codices and fifty-five printed editions. The most learned man therefore deservedly acquired great praise in Germany for his correction of Lactantius. Yet I marvel that, by employing historical annotations, he did not bring so excellent a work to the desired [Col. 0068A] goal, when he had already traversed a vigorous and immense course. Nothing would have been easier to accomplish: it would undoubtedly have required less labor to gather from the ancients those things suitable for explaining this author; yet it would have contributed more knowledge and more intellectual substance.

XX. We have stated what others accomplished in editing Lactantius; it is now our task to relate what we accomplish in this edition. Although Jean-Baptiste Le Brun rendered our author excellent service, I nevertheless thought that certain things should be added to his annotations. Lactantius’ autograph copy belonging to this editor had scarcely been entrusted to me when it occurred to me to combine and unite in one place the notes I had once assembled with the variant readings collected by Jean Le Brun. [Col. 0068B] In this way I thought it possible for this newest edition to reproduce the observations of all scholars and to stand in place of them all.

I sought out and selected other annotations—not all of them, but the choicer and more useful—from Erasmus, Betuleius, Thomasius, Isaeus, Gallaeus, Sparkius, Cellarius, Walch, and Heumann. But because Isaeus’ edition rarely comes onto the market, while his notes are learned and often composed according to theological principles, it seemed proper to append them entire at the end of the first volume, lest readers find anything lacking in this final edition of Lactantius, which encompasses all the others, as it were, at a single glance.

Therefore, if some historical or critical annotation is placed beneath the Lactantian text, you should not doubt that it is Lenglet’s; but if variant readings appear beneath it, you should attribute them—with certain exceptions—to Jean Le Brun. [Col. 0068C] This is the rule for distinguishing this editorial labor from the other’s work. But we have scarcely touched upon matters pertaining to grammar and to the comparison of other writers with Lactantius’ words. If anyone should require notes—or rather theological investigations—on Lactantius, Dom Nicholas Le Nourry, a Benedictine of the Congregation of St. Maur, will supply them most abundantly in volume II of the *Apparatus to the Library of the Holy Fathers*, columns 571–1172.

XXI. Nevertheless, I sought out certain manuscript codices and several editions that Jean Le Brun had never seen. One excellent codex, although only four hundred years old, was supplied by the most choice library of His Eminence Cardinal de Rohan, who can nowhere be named by theologians—or indeed by any men of letters—without praise. [Col. 0068D] Another codex, more than three hundred years old, was furnished with his customary courtesy by the Reverend Father Dom Louis Lemerault, prefect of the Royal Library of Saint-Germain. M. Claude Prévost, a canon regular, readily lent me from the library of the royal Abbey of Sainte-Geneviève the collations of certain Italian manuscripts made by Latino Latini, which are not found in Latini’s *Library*, as well as others collected by Pietro Ciacconio.

The distinguished chapter of Cambrai graciously permitted two codices to be sent to me: one from the tenth or eleventh century, but mutilated; the other complete, but only from the fifteenth century. Finally, we obtained a fifth from the library of the Capuchin fathers of the convent of Saint-Honoré in Paris, [Col. 0069A] written in approximately the same hand as the Saint-Germain codex, although somewhat more recent.

Jean Le Beuf, member of the Royal Academy of Inscriptions and Letters, possesses a manuscript codex, about four hundred years old, containing Lactantius’ books *On Anger* and *On the Workmanship of God*. He willingly sent it to me for consultation, and from it we excerpted certain readings. The distinguished and corrected edition of 1544 presents a certain Cologne manuscript. Thus, to the seventy-five codices enumerated by Jean Le Brun, I have added five, or even six, others.

The same judgment applies to several extremely rare editions that Jean Le Brun had not seen, and especially to the Subiaco edition of 1465, which is the first and earliest of all, and indeed the rarest; [Col. 0069B] for you will scarcely find five copies of it: one at Rome in the Barberini Library; another in the literary archive of the church of Mainz; a third in the excellent collection of the most illustrious and learned Claude de Boze, a member of both academies—the French Academy and the Royal Academy of Inscriptions—and keeper of the royal cabinets of medals; a fourth copy exists at Zurich in the Carolinum Library; and a fifth, finally, is preserved in the library of the school at Zwickau (*Cycnea*). The variant readings of this edition will be published here individually.

We have also collated our author against the Paris edition published in 1513, although it is less correct than the others. But we paid very close attention to the Cologne edition of 1544, Heumann’s edition of 1736, and certain others that Jean Le Brun had not inspected.

[Col. 0069C] I was already approaching the end of my labor when I was informed by two young men of great promise, the sons of that most learned man Johann Georg Walch, while they were visiting me at Paris, that the equally illustrious and learned Johann Ludolph Bunemann had published the newest edition of Lactantius’ works in Germany in 1739. I immediately procured it and excerpted from it a considerable number of annotations, including those that oppose our own recension. I placed these before the Lactantian text in both volumes of this edition.

XXII. Thus far I have spoken only of the *Divine Institutions*. Lactantius, however, published other minor works, many of which have either perished or lie concealed somewhere. Yet it will not be irrelevant to inquire in what order they are thought to have been composed. To do this more correctly, we must bring forward what St. Jerome said of this writer (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 80):

> Firmianus, also called Lactantius, a pupil of Arnobius, was summoned under the emperor Diocletian, together with Fannius the grammarian—whose books *On Medicinal Subjects*, composed in verse, survive—to teach rhetoric at Nicomedia; and because of the scarcity of pupils in that Greek city, he devoted himself to writing. We possess his *Symposium*, which he wrote as a young man in the schools of Africa; his *Ὁδοιπορικόν* (*Journey*) from Africa to Nicomedia, written in hexameter verse; another book entitled *The Grammarian*; another most excellent book *On the Anger of God*; seven books of the *Divine Institutions against the Gentiles*; and an *Ἐπιτομή* (*Epitome*) of the same work in a single *ἀκέφαλον* (“headless,” or acephalous) book; [Col. 0070A] two books addressed to Asclepiades; one book *On the Persecution*; four books of *Letters to Probus*; two books of *Letters to Severus*; two books of *Letters to Demetrianus*, his pupil; and one book addressed to the same man, *On the Workmanship of God*, or *The Formation of Man*. In extreme old age he was the tutor in Gaul of Caesar Crispus, Constantine’s son, who was afterward put to death by his father.

From these words of the holy Doctor and from other documents, it is possible to infer—not certainly, indeed, but by a not improbable conjecture—the time at which Lactantius published each book. He had already attained extreme old age when Constantine sent him into Gaul to educate his son Crispus in letters, which occurred, according to Eusebius’ *Chronicle*, around the year 318. [Col. 0070B] It is reasonable to conjecture that this extreme old age amounted to approximately seventy years. Therefore, if you subtract seventy from 318, 248 remains, the year of the Christian era in which our Lactantius was perhaps born.

But according to Jerome, Lactantius, while still a young man in the schools of Africa, wrote the *Symposium*, in the year 268, as I think. Scholars believed this work lost. But Heumann published it more than once under Lactantius’ name, and Bunemann does not dissent greatly. Nevertheless, as Albert Fabricius most aptly notes in the supplement to his *Latin Library*, p. 271, these riddles are attributed by the ancients to a certain Symposius. Even so, I arranged for it to be printed again in volume II of this edition. This *Symposium*, a youthful work indeed, contains one hundred riddles composed in verse, which had previously been published under the name of Symphosius or Symposius, an otherwise unknown poet; certain editions, however, bear the title: *Caelius Firmianus Symposius, Poet*.

[Col. 0070C] More elegant, however, is the *Poem on the Phoenix*, which Nicolaas Heinsius, a man of judgment both keen and refined, recognizes and proclaims to be the offspring of Lactantius. Peter Lambeck holds the same opinion in his most learned *Commentaries on the Imperial Library at Vienna*, Book II, ch. 8, p. 788. Certain more learned men, both before and after Lambeck, express the same opinion; and in many manuscripts it is read under Lactantius’ name. Thus the Saint-Germain codex also reads: “These poems are said to be by Lactantius.” If they are indeed the work of this writer, they were written around the year 280, when he had already advanced to a more mature age; nevertheless, Lactantius had not yet professed the name of Christ. [Col. 0070D] We have also included them in the second volume of our edition.

But since this most elegant writer was summoned from Africa to Nicomedia during Diocletian’s reign to teach rhetoric, and wrote his *Ὁδοιπορικόν*, that is, his itinerary, in hexameter verse, my opinion is that he was called to Bithynia around the year 290. For Diocletian did not obtain the imperial power until 284. After completing certain wars in Europe, however, he returned to Asia in the year 289 [printed “189”], and I think the people of Nicomedia then petitioned him to have that most eloquent man summoned to them. Only from the emperor could they request and obtain this. Perhaps at the same time Lactantius wrote *The Grammarian*. Neither book, however, has been found.

[Col. 0071A] But after he was later devoted to Christ, he embraced the true religion in Asia, perhaps in the year 295, seven or eight years before the persecution raged against the faithful. While that persecution was raging, Lactantius wrote his excellent little book *On the Workmanship of God*, around the year 310, for Demetrianus, his former pupil, so that one whom he had educated in letters that provided only linguistic instruction might not lack a teacher of a worthier subject and a better doctrine (*On the Workmanship of God*, ch. 1).

Lactantius wrote this book in so philosophical a manner that a Christian may nevertheless readily draw heavenly precepts from it. Yet by his own admission (*On the Workmanship of God*, ch. 20), he spoke more obscurely than was proper, and did so because of the exigencies of events and of the time, intending to publish more and better things if indulgence should come from heaven. [Col. 0071B] These words undoubtedly indicate the raging persecution. Lactantius was then contemplating a certain larger volume against the philosophers and concerning the matters that pertain to the state of the blessed life (*ibid.*). Here he indicates, not obscurely, the *Divine Institutions*, whose earlier books were written against the philosophers, while the last discusses the blessed life. Lactantius had therefore not yet published them, something that becomes much clearer to readers of chapter 20 of *On the Workmanship of God*.

Perhaps at the same time he wrote to Demetrianus himself two volumes of *Letters*, which, like his other letters, have perished. Hadrianus Junius, however, toward the end of the sixteenth century, had seen some of them in the library of Egmond Abbey, once extremely rich in manuscript codices (Hadrianus Junius, *History of Holland*, quarto, [Col. 0071C] Leiden, 1588, p. 311). Yet by the year 1573 these two books, which the abbot of that monastery had then shown Junius, had already been removed.

During the same persecution Lactantius perhaps wrote many letters to Asclepiades. A bond of association and familiarity certainly existed between him and our most elegant writer. For just as Asclepiades—otherwise scarcely known, but originating either from Greece or Asia, as his name indicates—had dedicated to Lactantius a book *On the Supreme Providence of God* (Book VII of the *Divine Institutions*, ch. 4, at the end), so Lactantius in turn inscribed two books to him. These, however, have certainly perished.

When the Diocletianic persecution had subsided, peace had been established, and the Christians had been restored to their former condition, Lactantius wrote the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, in the year 315, as it appears. [Col. 0071D] He wrote it not only after the battle at the Campus Serenus, described in chapter 47, in which Maximinus was defeated by Licinius on the first day of May 313; indeed, not only after the edict concerning the restoration of the Church, which Licinius ordered to be promulgated on the thirteenth day of June, as stated in chapter 48; but also after the death with which Valeria was punished in 315, as is recorded in chapter 51.

This little book, of which we shall speak again at the beginning of the second volume, had been lost for a thousand years and was discovered in the Colbert Library. Étienne Baluze first published it in 1679, at the command of the most illustrious Jean-Baptiste Colbert, the king’s secretary for the most confidential affairs and chief minister of the treasury. Claude Sallier, second prefect of the Royal Library, through his ingrained—or rather innate—love for the republic of letters, gave me access to this unique codex in the Christian world, which came into the Royal [Col. 0072A] Library together with all the other Colbert manuscripts.

I decided that this codex should once again be collated with the printed editions, and I noted certain things that, scarcely credible though it may be, had again been overlooked by many scholars. Thus I have even recorded in the notes what the copyist’s errors were. For these very often give more learned men occasion to devise a new and more useful or elegant interpretation.

But lest anything be lacking from our edition, we arranged for all the commentaries that Paul Bauldri had assembled in the Utrecht edition of 1692 to be reprinted, with nothing omitted. We did this with such fidelity and diligence that I did not omit even those censorial observations in which they attack Roman Catholic doctrine more severely than is fitting, though I nevertheless added an observation where necessary by which the error is cast back upon the annotator. [Col. 0072B] For what purpose are such untimely digressions when the subject under discussion is history, not theological matters? In this way we have brought into our edition all those things that a learned reader formerly had to seek out separately from every quarter in order to obtain the complete works of Lactantius and the various commentaries upon them.

Crispus was made Caesar by his father Constantine in 317, at the age of twenty. Both were then in Gaul, and Lactantius was summoned there to instruct the emperor’s son in humane letters. From that time, not only do I, led by many arguments, believe that the *Divine Institutions* were published, but Antonius Pagius (*Critique on Baronius’ Annals*, at the year 315, no. 6), Tillemont (*Ecclesiastical History*, vol. VI, p. 728), Nicholas Le Nourry (*Apparatus to the Library of the Holy Fathers*, vol. II, pp. 336 and 366), Remi Ceillier (*History of Ecclesiastical Authors*, vol. III, p. 392)—both of the latter Benedictines—Jean-Baptiste Le Brun, and very many others express the same opinion. [Col. 0072C] They are persuaded that Lactantius published this book after news of the Licinian persecution had spread—a persecution that did not begin to rage until the year 320.

Yet I would not deny that Lactantius had previously committed many observations concerning the Christian religion to his private tablets, so that he might not only undertake a work so arduous and difficult but also bring it to the desired conclusion; for it could scarcely have been accomplished otherwise.

[Col. 0072D] Moreover, not only Thomasius (*Notes on Book I, ch. 1 of the Institutions*), but Baluze himself (*Notes on On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, at the end of vol. II of our edition), and Heumann (*Notes on ch. 1 of the first book of the Divine Institutions*) have observed that Lactantius published two editions of the *Institutions*. In them you will read that the *Divine Institutions* were written in sorrowful times, but corrected, enlarged, and dedicated to Constantine in happier ones. Lactantius, Heumann says, published this work twice: first before Constantine’s reign, and again when Constantine had obtained power.

Perhaps from this double edition there issued—not all, indeed, but some—of the variant readings that cause no small labor both to learned editors of Lactantius and to scholars generally. For it is not inconsistent with even the most diligent writer, nor contrary [Col. 0073A] to reason, that he should himself revise his literary labors. One’s own correction is assuredly much happier and more agreeable than another’s.

But since this book is filled with varied and extensive learning, vigilant and exceptional effort must be applied to reading it if it is to be fully understood. Many, however, are deterred by sustained and rather intense study. Hence the *Epitome* appeared, at the request of Pentadius, whether he was Lactantius’ brother or some Christian friend whom Lactantius regarded as a brother.

This Pentadius was perhaps of the same family as another man of that name who served Emperor Constantius as a confidential secretary. For that name is not very common among the ancients. Our author therefore compressed his *Institutions* within narrower bounds in such a way as to instruct minds, [Col. 0073B] without prolixity producing weariness or brevity obscurity.

Although he presented there the same doctrine of the *Divine Institutions* that he gives elsewhere throughout his works, he nevertheless does not explain it in the same words. Just as he left certain matters untouched, so he sometimes adds many things for the sake of explaining the truth. In this he displays both ease in writing and a versatile talent adapted to every subject.

The greater part of this *Epitome* had already been missing since the time of St. Jerome. Yet the most learned Christoph Matthäus Pfaff, chancellor of the University of Tübingen, published it almost complete at Paris in 1712 from a manuscript codex of the Royal Library of Turin. At the request of the most learned Johann Daniel Schöpflin, public professor [Col. 0073C] of history and eloquence at the University of Strasbourg, Pfaff sent me a copy of that book, and in it I observed certain matters of no slight importance.

You should not suppose, however, that the *Epitome* was written immediately after the publication of the *Institutions*: several years elapsed between the two works. “Although,” says Lactantius (*Epitome*, in the preface), “the books of the *Divine Institutions*, which we composed long ago for the elucidation of truth and religion, etc.” Just as the words “not so long ago” signify a few years, so the expression “long ago” (*jampridem*), which Lactantius uses, signifies a longer interval of time. I would therefore readily believe that the *Epitome* was published in 325 or 326.

Meanwhile, perhaps in 324, this most eloquent writer published several other books during his leisure, especially the one entitled *On the Anger of God*, which he had given notice that he would publish [Col. 0073D] (*Divine Institutions*, Book II, ch. 17):

> Let the topic of the anger of God be set aside, both because the subject is richer and because it must be treated more fully in a work of its own.

Against the Epicureans, this work proves that God, being supremely just, imposes punishments upon the guilty because of the evil disposition of human beings and the crimes committed by them, just as he rewards those who deserve well with the gifts he has promised. St. Jerome rightly regards this book—not only exceedingly beautiful but also written in language at once learned and eloquent—as an epitome of Cicero’s dialogues. Would that it may soon appear in print, excellently and elegantly translated into French by Jean-François Dreux du Radier, counselor to the king and special magistrate in the district of Thymerais, just as he himself has given us hope.

[Col. 0074A] It seems to me that Lactantius wrote his two books of *Letters to Severus* at about the same time. That Severus was a Spaniard, and one of the ancestors of Aquilius Severus, of whom St. Jerome says (*Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*): “Aquilius Severus, in Spain, was descended from that Severus to whom Lactantius addressed two books of Letters.” But there was no intercourse between the people of Nicomedia and Bithynia on the one hand and the Spaniards on the other, whereas there was considerable intercourse between Gaul and Spain. Hence it is permissible to conjecture that these Letters were published by Lactantius while he was residing in Gaul. I would say the same, moreover, of the four books of *Letters to Probus*, whose name is not Asiatic but Roman, or perhaps Gallic. For in these Letters Lactantius makes certain splendid statements to him about the Gauls, to the honor and praise of that nation, [Col. 0074B] as St. Jerome attests (*Preface to Book II of the Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians*):

> “The Gauls,” says Lactantius, “are called *Galatae* from the whiteness of their bodies, and the Sibyl so names them. This is what the poet intended to signify when he said, ‘Then their MILKY necks are encircled with gold,’ although he could have said ‘WHITE.’ From this, certainly, came the province of Galatia, into which the Gauls once came and mingled with the Greeks; hence that region was first named Gallo-Graecia, and afterward Galatia.”

This, however, I myself do not deny, is a rather slight conjecture; but more certain and better conclusions must be awaited from others.

### XXIII

We have now spoken of all Lactantius’s books, both extant and lost, which St. Jerome enumerates; but we are little concerned with works that he promised but which perhaps never existed anywhere, such as the work *Against the Jews* (Lactantius, *Institutions*, Book VII, [Col. 0074C] ch. 1), of which none of the ancients makes mention. He had likewise promised *Disputations against All Sects of Falsehood* (Lactantius, Book IV of the *Divine Institutions*, final chapter, and *On the Anger of God*, ch. 2). Each of these undertakings was far too burdensome for that most elegant author to carry through successfully, since he was not sufficiently practiced in the sacred Scriptures or thoroughly versed in the Church’s doctrine.

Nor are we any more concerned with those little works that we call spurious. Certain learned men mention a book *On the Spectacles* (*Mémoires de Trévoux*, for the year 1705, p. 1992; *Nouvelles de la République des Lettres*, 1705, vol. II, p. 117; Buddeus’s *Universal Lexicon*, under the entry LACTANTIUS), which they say was published at Venice in 1705 from a manuscript under Lactantius’s name. I was unable either to obtain a copy of it or even to acquire reliable information about it from the letters sent to Venice by most distinguished [Col. 0074D] men and even by booksellers. We therefore rightly regard this edition as a fiction, together with the most celebrated Johann Ludolf Bünemann, in the *Leipzig Miscellanies*, vol. III, p. 136.

Already in 1570 Michael Thomasius had warned, in his Antwerp edition, that the poem *On Easter* was not by Lactantius but by Venantius Honorius Clementianus Fortunatus, an Italian priest of the sixth century, as is attested by a manuscript codex in the Vatican Library containing the poems of this Venantius Fortunatus, who later became bishop of Poitiers. The other verses, *On the Passion of the Lord*, have a wholly unknown author, but not Lactantius. Nevertheless, we have published these poems, lest perhaps certain captious [Col. 0075A] readers complain and suppose that our edition is mutilated and incomplete.

Although the more ancient Lactantian codices are written in one continuous text, without any division into sections or chapters, but only into books, we have nevertheless employed the received division into chapters and added summaries, so that everything may be clearer to readers. Manuscripts of the Middle Ages, such as that of His Eminence Cardinal de Rohan, contain many sections; none are to be found in the oldest Royal manuscripts or in the Cambrai manuscript, nor even in the Saint-Germain manuscript. But the codex belonging to the Capuchin Fathers, which is more recent, is divided according to the commonly received chapters.

I thought it needless to discuss Lactantius’s style at greater length. It is enough to have observed, with St. Jerome and other most learned men, that this most eloquent writer [Col. 0075B] reproduces the eloquence of Cicero. Nowhere is his discourse bombastic, and it rarely rises to great heights; rather, it flows evenly with a certain gentleness, though not without sinew and strength. It is so precise and so forceful that no style is better suited to persuasion, yet it is without judicial harshness and without the barbs of forensic pronouncements. He strives for diction that is pure, lucid, and elegant, and follows Cicero’s own rule: “The manner of philosophers is more peaceable, but that of orators more combative.” He pursues such sweetness in his arrangement of words that, even among masters of eloquence, he deserves to be called the Christian Cicero and altogether displays [Col. 0076A] the genius of the Roman Orator. He does, however, use certain foreign words; but these either belong to the age in which Lactantius lived or savor solely of African soil. Thus Tertullian, and likewise Saints Cyprian, Augustine, and Fulgentius, Africans just as Lactantius was, employ certain unusual and barbarous words. We have therefore arranged for these to be printed in the index of subjects in a different—that is, italic—type.

In this edition, which presents Lactantius’s text without typographical error, we did not wish to intermingle with the author’s words letters or symbols indicating notes, lest the sequence of the subject matter be disturbed or the order of the discourse altered, and lest, finally, the more frequent little notes inserted into the text impede the attentive reader’s mind and divert it elsewhere. We considered it sufficient to place at the beginning of each annotation the words that were to be explained more plainly [Col. 0076B] for the benefit of the less learned reader.

Let these observations suffice concerning our edition, in the printing of which Jean de Bure, bookseller, is performing his part so that learned purchasers may be satisfied both by the choice of paper and by the employment of more elegant typefaces.

Moreover, if anything should happen to have been said by us in the notes contrary to the decrees of the holy, catholic, apostolic, and Roman Church—to whose judgment these writings and all our works are subject—we wish it to be regarded as wholly unsaid, and we are prepared to correct it wherever necessary.

[Col. 0075]

# THE LIFE OF LACTANTIUS

[Col. 0075C] Lucius Caelius, or Caecilius, FIRMIANUS LACTANTIUS is rightly believed to have been born not in Italy but rather in Africa. For there, even as a young man, he had Arnobius as his teacher. Nor was it ever the custom of Romans or Italians to travel to Africa in order to be instructed in eloquence or the sciences; on the contrary, Africans very often migrated to Italy for the sake of learning the disciplines or arts. At that time Arnobius was teaching rhetoric at Sicca.

> **Note: [Col. 0075C]**
>
> Sicca was a city of Africa Proconsularis; it is sometimes called Sicca Veneria or Sicca Colonia. A bishop of Sicca is mentioned in Victor of Vita’s *History of the Vandal Persecution*.

Lactantius not only equaled Arnobius but even surpassed him in sweetness of expression, and was so named, as they say, from his “milky” (*lactea*) eloquence. Around the year 290, under Diocletian, he was summoned to Nicomedia to teach oratorical literature. St. Jerome therefore attests (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*) that he described his Ὁδοιπορικόν—that is, his *Itinerary*—from Africa all the way to Nicomedia in hexameter verse. That he was born of pagan parents and imbibed their errors together with his mother’s milk may be gathered from what he himself says about himself in chapter 48 of the *Epitome*, shortly before the end: “We who are from the Gentiles”; and at the beginning of chapter 2 of *On the Anger of God*: “Freed from the error in which we were held entangled, and formed [Col. 0076C] for the worship of the true God, we should learn justice.” Thus he also says in the final chapter of Book VII: “Casting aside the errors by which we were formerly held, let us be directed toward the eternal rewards of the heavenly treasure.”

At what time he embraced the Christian religion is not certainly known; perhaps, however, it was in the year 295, as we have already said. Nevertheless, it is enough for us to assert that he attained the heavenly light before the persecution under Diocletian began—that is, before the year 303. This is gathered from the following passage of the *Divine Institutions* (Book V, ch. 4, beginning): “When, in my presence and to my sorrow,” he says, “they unfolded their sacrilegious writings”—namely, two philosophers who were the bitterest adversaries of the Christians.

Lactantius was thoroughly cultivated in humane letters from his tender years. His precocious talent is attested by the *Symposium*, which he wrote as a young man in the schools of Africa. We do not, however, think it is the work that we nevertheless published after Heumann and Bünemann: a decidedly youthful, or even boyish, composition in which a hundred riddles are expounded. Perhaps before he enlisted in the Christian service he published the *Poem on the Phoenix*, which, in the judgment of Heinsius and other learned men, is sufficiently elegant to be ascribed to Lactantius, and is in fact ascribed to him in certain manuscripts.

Although he devoted himself to eloquence and taught rhetoric, [Col. 0077A] he never entered the forum; instead, as he himself admits, he trained young men in ingenious malice. Quintilian had done the same long before Lactantius, as his *Declamations* attest. In order to pass the time and lend dignity to agreeable leisure, he turned to writing because of the scarcity of pupils, even after adopting the Christian religion. From this came certain works published by him, concerning which we spoke above on p. XIV of our Preface (col. 71 of this edition).

After attaining the truth, Lactantius remained at Nicomedia until the year 317; he was therefore there throughout the entire decade during which the hateful cruelty of the emperors raged. What he did while it was raging, and how he himself, a Christian, escaped chains or bonds in so dreadful a tempest, is wholly unknown. Perhaps the emperors and governors regarded him not as a Christian [Col. 0077B] but rather as a philosopher. For he himself speaks of Christians in this manner (*On the Workmanship of God*, ch. 1, beginning): “So that in the future the philosophers of our school, which we defend, may become better instructed and more learned.”

In the meantime he wrote his most elegant book *On the Workmanship of God*, though in a purely philosophical style, as well as several other works; and at that time he formed the plan of disputing against all the philosophers, so that he might refute their empty opinions and expound and defend the truth. He had not, however, brought this undertaking to a successful conclusion at that time. At the end of the year 317, after leaving Nicomedia, he was summoned to Gaul in order to form the youthful mind of Crispus—the promising prince and eldest son of Constantine—in the nobler arts and sciences. Crispus had then only reached his twentieth year [Col. 0077C] when he was made Caesar by his father on the Kalends of March in the year 317, as the *Idatian Fasti* attest.

Lactantius nowhere in his writings mentions this splendid and distinguished office: such was the modesty of that most learned man. Crispus, moreover, although young, applied himself with moderation to literary studies; yet at the same time he was so occupied in administering [Col. 0078A] the state that he commanded armies, was chosen consul in the years 318, 321, and 324, conquered the Franks in 320, and defeated Licinius in 323. From this one may see that Lactantius’s literary office was indeed distinguished, but neither servile nor domestic, nor, finally, so unremitting as to deter him from writing. At that time, therefore, he undertook the work of the *Divine Institutions*, which he had not only pondered beforehand, but for the construction of which he had undoubtedly recorded learned observations on private papers whenever circumstances permitted.

He also published other works, which we have already discussed in the Preface. But from the time when he entered Crispus’s service, neither historians of his own period nor those of succeeding ages record anything about Lactantius. Eusebius merely observes that this man, whom he calls most eloquent and most learned, so abhorred courtly [Col. 0078B] luxuries and passed his life in such poverty that he often lacked even necessities—an argument for his unshaken constancy in the Christian religion. Such, certainly, was Lactantius’s poverty before he was attached to Crispus Caesar. It is therefore no wonder that with such spirit and such care he poured forth praises of evangelical poverty. Can anyone doubt that the Caesar’s tutor, whom Constantine the Great—a prince beneficent and generous toward all—held in such esteem, lived a most holy life: a man who trampled upon riches, offices, honors, and the other mortal goods; a man, finally, who so instructed his pupil Crispus that Eusebius of Caesarea called him an excellent prince and beloved of God?

[Col. 0078C] In what year or in what city Lactantius died is wholly uncertain. I readily agree, however, with the most learned Christophe Brouwer and Gilles Boucher, who report that at Trier he not only passed his extreme old age but also met his final day. Crispus, for whose sake our author had been summoned from Asia, resided in that city for a long time.

[Col. 0077]

# TESTIMONIES OF DISTINGUISHED MEN CONCERNING L. CAECILIUS FIRMIANUS LACTANTIUS

[Col. 0077D] **EUSEBIUS OF CAESAREA, in the *Chronicle*, fourth century:**

Lactantius instructed Crispus in Latin letters. He was the most eloquent man of all in his time, but so poor in this life that he generally lacked even necessities, much less luxuries.

**ST. JEROME, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, fifth century:**

Firmianus, who is also called Lactantius, a pupil of Arnobius, [Col. 0078D] was summoned under the emperor Diocletian, together with Flabo—

> **Note: [Col. 0077D]**
>
> **Flabo.** I have restored this reading from the manuscripts: Royal MS 1, no. 3736, nine hundred years old, and Clermont MS 1, with the approval of the distinguished Baluze, and from the manuscripts of the Capuchin Fathers. Printed editions have *Flavio*; one has *Fannio*.
>
> **Wrote in Africa.** So read Royal MS 1, the Tournesian manuscript, and Clermont MS 1; and not incorrectly, as in Cicero’s expression, “when I was in Sicily” (*Siciliae cum* [Col. 0078D] *essem*). The Greek version has ἐν τῇ Ἀφρικῇ, “in Africa.” Editors who did not understand the foregoing Latin idiom attempted to correct it: in several editions they removed *Africae*; in two, by placing *in scholis* before *scripsit Africa*; and in two others, by changing *adolescentulus* (“as a young man”) to *adolescentibus* (“for young men”), so that the text reads, “he wrote for young men of Africa.”

—the grammarian whose books *On Medicinal Subjects*, composed in verse, are extant, and taught rhetoric at Nicomedia. Because of the scarcity of pupils, owing, of course, to its being a Greek city, he turned to writing. We possess his *Symposium*, which he wrote as a young man in Africa; his Ὁδοιπορικόν (*Itinerary*) from Africa all the way to Nicomedia, written in hexameter verse; another book entitled [Col. 0079A] *The Grammarian*; another, most beautiful book *On the Anger of God*; seven books of the *Divine Institutions against the Gentiles*; and an Ἐπιτομή (*Epitome*) of the same work in one ἀκέφαλον (*acephalous*, or headless/incomplete, book); [Col. 0079A]

> **Note: [Col. 0079]**
>
> **Ἀκεφάλῳ.** Royal MS 1 has ἀκέφαλον; in the editions it is *acephalo*.
>
