> **To Demetrianus.** So read Royal MS 1, the Tournesian manuscript, and the printed editions. But in one Clermont manuscript and in Honorius of Autun it reads *to Demetrius*, [Col. 0080D] corruptly, as is evident from all the manuscripts and printed codices of Lactantius.
>
> **In extreme old age.** Three editions add the preposition *in*, which the others reject.

two books *To Asclepiades*; one book *On the Persecution*; four books of *Letters to Probus*; two books of *Letters to Severus*; two books of *Letters to Demetrianus*, his pupil; and to the same person one book *On the Workmanship of God*, or *The Formation of Man*. In extreme old age he was in Gaul as tutor to Caesar Crispus, the son of Constantine, who was later killed by his father.

**The same, *Commentary on Ecclesiastes*, ch. 10:**

Our Firmianus also, in the splendid work of his *Institutions* . . . discussed virtues and vices most fully.

**The same, on chapter 4 of Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians:**

Our Firmianus wrote a book *On the Anger of God* in a style both learned and eloquent. Whoever reads it, I think, may find it more than sufficient for understanding anger.

**The same, Letter 13, to Paulinus:**

Lactantius is like a river of Ciceronian eloquence; [Col. 0079B] would that he had been as capable of confirming our own doctrines as he was of easily demolishing those of others.

**The same, Letter 83 (elsewhere 84), to Magnus:**

Arnobius published seven books *Against the Gentiles*, and his pupil Lactantius the same number. Lactantius also published two volumes, one *On Anger* and the other *On the Workmanship of God*. If you wish to read them, you will find in them an ἐπιτομή (*epitome*) of Cicero’s *Dialogues*.

**EUCHERIUS, bishop, in his letter to Valerian, fifth century:**

And when, from that volume of harmonious prose, you have unrolled those most illustrious in eloquence—Firmianus, Minucius, Cyprian, Hilary, John, and Ambrose.

**HONORIUS, priest of Autun, *On the Luminaries of the Church*, or *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, twelfth century:**

Firmianus, who is also called Lactantius, a pupil of Arnobius, wrote in the schools of Africa an *Itinerary* in hexameter verse; another book entitled *The Grammarian*; another, most beautiful book *On the Anger of God*; and seven books of the *Divine Institutions against the Gentiles*; two books to Asclepiades; seven books of *Letters to Demetrius* (read: Demetrianus), his pupil; [Col. 0079C] one book *On the Persecution*; four books of *Letters to Probus*; two books of *Letters to Severus*; and one book to Demetrianus *On the Workmanship of God*, or *The Formation of Man*. He was tutor to Caesar Crispus, the son of Constantine.

Firmianus Lactantius, formerly a hearer and pupil of the rhetorician Arnobius, was a man abundantly learned in secular literature and nobly instructed in the divine Scriptures, so that in the art of speaking he readily obtained the first place after Cicero. Summoned by Diocletian, he gloriously taught rhetoric first at Nicomedia and then at Rome—incorrectly: at Nicomedia alone. And the rest as above.

**RAPHAEL OF VOLTERRA, *Anthropology*, Book XVI, as above, fifteenth century.**

Concerning the second matter—and indeed concerning both—although, as you see, the authorities are very great, it nevertheless does not seem irrelevant to insert here what the learned and eloquent Lactantius Firmianus thought about it, etc.

**And a little below in the same passage:**

But what if something of this kind had been said to Lactantius? What if it had been said to Augustine and believed by him? Hear, therefore, what Lactantius—a man most distinguished by his knowledge both of poets and of philosophers, by his Ciceronian eloquence, and, surpassing all these, by the Catholic religion—says in the first book of his *Institutions*.

And first of all Lactantius Firmianus, who, laying open the whole stage of the gods and the shameful hiding places of their crimes, embraces through a most elaborate discussion the entire sequence of the matter: who they were, what they did, what their morals were, what life they led, what ends they met, and what tombs they had.

**And Book II:**

Lactantius Firmianus, himself also a great man, in that book in which, after disarming the errors of the Gentiles, he armed our faith as far as he was able, uncovered this whole stage of the gods with wonderful and praiseworthy diligence, and in this same work prepared the way for Augustine and other followers, etc.

There came Ambrose, whose name is sacred; there came Jerome [Col. 0080B] and Gregory; last came John of the golden mouth, and Lactantius overflowing in a milky torrent. **The same, *Memorable Matters*, Book I, on Marcus Varro:**

Lactantius Firmianus, a man devout in faith and sacred in eloquence, etc.

Who among us does not see in him Cicero, but a Christian Cicero—that is, someone who reproduced Cicero to the line and the nail, with exact precision? For who does not perceive that Lactantius Firmianus equaled Cicero himself, and perhaps surpassed him, in eloquence?

**The same, *Letters*, Book III, Letter 10:**

Lactantius reproduced Cicero’s style or, as some hold, surpassed it. He seems to me richer in subject matter and maxims, no less pleasing in rhythm, and not inferior in the evenness and brilliance of his style. For he both emulated and attained these virtues [Col. 0080C] with the greatest power. Neither his contemporaries nor posterity found fault with him; no one accused him of being feeble and broken, Asiatic and redundant.

**LEONARDO BRUNI OF AREZZO, in his letter to Costanza Sforza, fifteenth century:**

Above all who have written about Christian truth, Lactantius Firmianus stands out and excels by far in a certain brilliance and richness. He was undoubtedly the most eloquent of all Christians. Read his books, I beg you, if you love literature.

**L. CAELIUS RHODIGINUS, *Ancient Readings*, Book VI, ch. 18, fifteenth century:**

Lactantius is especially illustrious for eloquence among the defenders of Christian truth.

**The same, Book IX, ch. 12:**

But I, Lactantius, would not call you mad, since you wrote many things with no little prudence and learning.

**And a little afterward in the same passage:**

I should prefer to believe that this was your purpose, most learned man and one who deserved exceedingly well of Christian truth, etc.

**JUAN LUIS VIVES OF VALENCIA, at the end [Col. 0080D] of Book III of *On the Transmission of the Disciplines*, sixteenth century:**

Lactantius is the most eloquent of all Christians; his tone is wholly Ciceronian.

**And Book IV:**

For an effective method of argument Aristotle will take first place; for the civic method, Cicero’s *Dialogues* and Lactantius will take first place.

[Col. 0081A] **And Book V:**

Judgment, moreover, since it is something natural within prudence, cannot be taught, but it can be sharpened and refined: first by reading those authors who possessed that excellent quality in the highest degree—Plato, Aristotle, Demosthenes, Cicero, Seneca, Quintilian, and Plutarch; and among our own writers, Origen, Chrysostom, Jerome, Lactantius, etc.

**GIOVANNI BATTISTA PIO, *Annotations*, ch. 98, sixteenth century:**

Lactantius Firmianus, the greatest defender of the true religion.

**GREGORIO GIRALDI OF VERONA, fifth *Dialogue on the History of Poets*, sixteenth century:**

Lactantius Firmianus lived at the same time as Juvencus and was one of the foremost Christian emulators of Ciceronian eloquence. Besides the many works that he wrote in prose, which are everywhere in people’s hands, he also composed verses, etc.

**FRANCESCO FLORIDO, *Subsecivae Lectiones*, Book II, ch. 4, sixteenth century:**

[Col. 0081B] Lactantius Firmianus, a hearer of Arnobius, was beyond dispute the most eloquent of all Latin writers who treated theological subjects and the most vigorous defender of our religion. During his lifetime he was held to be of the most celebrated reputation among devotees of Christian piety because of his singular excellence. He published not a few most elegant works filled with great learning, a substantial portion of which is handled by learned men, while another portion suffered the common shipwreck of the other Roman writings. He is thus on everyone’s lips as though he alone deserved commendation for overturning, with the best arguments, every philosophical doctrine diametrically opposed to Christianity, and for his weightiest maxims and the brilliance of his style.

[Col. 0082A] For this reason, although there have been men who cultivated other branches of theology more readily than he, and even with greater subtlety, nevertheless, in matters concerning the refutation of the doctrines of the Gentiles—for so were called all those who before Christ’s advent did not embrace the law delivered by Moses—no one has appeared down to the present day, so far as I am able to judge, who may be compared with Lactantius even at a great distance. This is so either because, through the weight of his matter and words and a certain effective force of nature, he performs splendidly the task he undertook against the most strongly fortified opinions of the pagans, or because he encompasses very much in few words, always pressing closely upon himself—as Marcus Tullius says of Thucydides—and dragging along with him none of the refuse that very many others do.

Had so excellent an author not written many things in which one could scarcely believe that a man so diligently versed in sacred and secular literature could have gone astray, I would judge him, alone among all Latin writers, especially worthy to be chosen and kept constantly in the hands of boys, so that from reading this one author they might learn at the same time both the rudiments of the Christian faith and the purity of Roman speech, etc.

[Col. 0082B] **WILLEM CANTER, *New Readings*, Book III, ch. 30, sixteenth century:**

One may not unreasonably judge that Firmianus Lactantius holds among the Latin theologians approximately the place occupied by Gregory Nazianzen among the Greeks.

We did not think it advantageous to proceed any further. It is enough to have observed that there is no writer of our times who does not mention our Lactantius with praise. Although learned men do not regard him as wholly beyond reproach, they nevertheless all proclaim his manifold learning, his varied erudition in secular matters, and, finally, his supreme eloquence.

[Col. 0081]

# SYNTHESIS OF LACTANTIUS’S DOCTRINE

[Col. 0081C] Because Lactantius devoted more effort to refuting falsehoods than to confirming truths, only a few articles of our faith were fully expounded by him; he merely touched upon most of them, and failed to understand very many. Among those matters that he explained somewhat more fully are the doctrines concerning the Christian religion, God in general, Providence, and the true inward worship of God.

He treated splendidly the parts, attributes, and effects of the Christian religion. He establishes that religion has two parts: the acknowledgment of God and worship (Book III, ch. 29; Book IV, ch. 4, etc.). He explains the following attributes of religion as contained in sacred Scripture: truth, clarity, antiquity, and simplicity.

He proves that the Christian religion is true from the fact that the predictions of the prophets were fulfilled and that the prophets could not have deceived (Book I, ch. 4); from the fact that the apostles not only underwent death for the faith, but also both knew and foretold that they would die (Book V, ch. 3); from the fact that Christians do not err in all the actions of their lives, from which it is probable that they do not err even in the highest matter itself—that is, in religion (Book V, ch. 9); from the fact that the number of Christians increases amid persecution itself; and from the fact that those same Christians are torn apart by various kinds of torture and preserve unconquered endurance while their executioners grow weary. From this even the common people conclude that neither the agreement of so many [Col. 0081D] nor the perseverance of the dying is vain, and that endurance itself could not bear such torments without God (Book V, chs. 13 and 22).

He asserts the clarity of written religion (Book VI, [Col. 0082C] ch. 21). “Can God, then,” he says, “the craftsman of mind, voice, and tongue, not speak clearly? Indeed, in his supreme providence he willed the things that are divine to be free from ornament, so that all might understand what he himself was saying to all.”

He derives the antiquity of Scripture, or of our religion, from the ages of the prophets (Book IV, ch. 5), where he says: “The prophets are found to be older even than the Greek writers. Let those, therefore, who attempt to denounce sacred Scripture as new and recently fabricated recognize their error, since they do not know the source from which the origin of the holy religion flowed.”

He teaches that many are offended by the simplicity of Scripture (Book V, ch. 1), but unjustly. For it was fitting that it should be delivered in no other way than plainly and briefly, so that when God spoke to humanity, he would not support his words with arguments, as though he were not to be believed, but would speak as the supreme judge of all things. It belongs to him not to argue, but to pronounce what is true (Book III, ch. 1).

He beautifully explains how great and extensive the effects of the Christian religion are (Book III, ch. 25):

> “Give me,” he says, “a man who is irascible, abusive, and unrestrained: with a very few words of God I shall render him as gentle as a sheep. Give me one who is covetous, avaricious, and grasping: I shall presently give him back to you as a generous man, dispensing his money with full hands. Give me one who fears pain and death: he will presently scorn crosses, fires, and the bull. Give me a lustful man, an adulterer, a debauchee: you will presently see him sober, chaste, and self-controlled. Give me one who is cruel and thirsts for blood: [Col. 0083A] that fury will presently be changed into true clemency. Give me one who is unjust, foolish, and sinful: immediately he will be equitable, prudent, and innocent.”

Finally, concerning the understanding of the Christian religion, he has this splendid declaration: “A human being cannot attain this knowledge by himself unless he is taught by God” (Book II, ch. 3).

He taught with sufficient purity concerning God—namely, what God is, what kind of being he is, and that he is one. For him God is “the eternal mind, possessed in every respect of perfect and consummate power” (Book I, ch. 4). He is likewise eternal and incomprehensible to human senses, for thus Lactantius writes in Book II, ch. 9:

> “God alone is he who was not made; and therefore he can destroy other things, but cannot himself be destroyed. He will always remain what he was, because he was not generated from elsewhere, nor does his origin or birth depend upon anything that, by undergoing change, might dissolve him. He exists from himself and therefore is such as he willed himself to be: incapable of suffering, immutable, incorruptible, eternal.”

And in Book II, ch. 5:

> “Since the origin of God cannot be comprehended, it ought not even to be investigated. It is enough for a human being’s full and perfect wisdom that he should understand that God exists. The force and highest point of this understanding is that he should acknowledge and honor the common parent of the human race and the maker of wondrous things.”

Moreover, he proves learnedly that God is one in Book I, from chapter 3 through chapter 8; the arguments may be seen in the *Analysis*.

Here and there he professes Christ to be the Son of this God, and affirms that he is both God and man in Book IV, ch. 13. The author writes that God employed Christ’s counsel and agency in the creation of the world (Book IV, ch. 6); that the Greeks more correctly call him Λόγος (*Logos*, “Reason/Word”) than the Latins call him *Verbum* (“Word”), Book IV, ch. 9; and that he proceeded from God’s mouth with voice and sound, in chapter 8 of the same book.

He attributes the following epithets to Christ: he calls him the envoy, messenger, and priest of the supreme Father (Book IV, chs. 25 and 29); the craftsman of things, the voice and wisdom of God, and a holy and incorruptible spirit (Book IV, chs. 6 and 9); and the first and greatest Son, whom the Father employed [Col. 0083C] as counselor and craftsman in the creation of things (Book II, ch. 9).

He also reconciles the apparent contradiction in our religion whereby we profess one God and yet call not only the Father but also the Son God:

> “When we speak,” he says in Book IV, ch. 29, “of God the Father and the Son, we do not say that they are different, nor do we separate the two, because the Father cannot exist without the Son, nor can the Son be separated from the Father; for neither can the Father be called Father without the Son, nor can the Son be begotten without the Father. Since, therefore, both the Father makes the Son and the Son makes the Father, there is one mind, one spirit, and one substance in both. But the former is as it were an overflowing fountain, the latter like a stream flowing from it; the former is like the sun, the latter like a ray extended from the sun. Since the Son is both faithful and dear to the supreme Father, he is not separated from him, just as neither the stream is separated from the fountain nor the ray from the sun, because the fountain’s water is in the stream and the sun’s light is in the ray.”

And a little afterward he illustrates this by the following example:

> “When someone has a son whom he loves uniquely, but who nevertheless remains in the house and under the authority of his father, although the father grants him the title [Col. 0083D] and power of master, still, by civil law, both the house is called one and its master one. Thus this world is the one house of God; and the Son and the Father, who dwell in the world in unanimity, are one God, because the one is as though two, and the two as though one. Nor is this remarkable, since the Son is in the Father because the Father loves the Son, and the Father is in the Son because the Son faithfully obeys the Father’s will.”

And near the end of the chapter:

> “There is one alone, free, supreme God, lacking an origin because he himself is the origin of things, and in him both the Son and all things are contained together. Therefore, since the mind and will of the one are in the other—or rather, one mind and will are in both—each is rightly called one God, because everything that is in the Father he transferred to the Son, and everything that is in the Son descended from the Father.”

He speaks here and there throughout the whole work of the *Divine Institutions* about the skill of divine Providence; nor did he write the book *On the Workmanship of God* for any other reason than to set before human eyes the providence of God shining in the human body, [Col. 0084A] and to counter the sophisms of the Epicureans who denied providence.

This author inserted into his writings notable pronouncements concerning the true inward worship of God. First:

> “That supreme and unique God,” he says, “cannot be worshiped except through the Son. Whoever thinks that he worships the Father alone, just as he does not worship the Son, likewise does not worship even the Father” (Book IV, ch. 29).

Next, he writes that the true worship of God is that in which the worshiper’s mind presents itself to God as an immaculate victim (Book VI, ch. 2). And in Book IV, ch. 28:

> It is certain that “no other hope of life has been set before humanity except that, casting aside vanities and wretched error, one should know God and serve God; except that one should renounce this temporal life and train oneself in the rudiments of justice for the worship of the true religion. For we are born on this condition: that, having been begotten for God, we should render him the just and due acts of service; that we should know him alone and follow him alone. We have been bound and tied back to God by this bond of piety, from which religion itself received its name.”

And in the final chapter of Book VI:

> “Both things offered to God must be incorporeal, for such are the things he employs: the gift is integrity of mind; the sacrifice is praise and hymn.”

Likewise, in chapter 1 of the same book:

> “That holy and unique majesty inwardly desires nothing else from a human being [Col. 0084B] but innocence alone—

> **Note: [Col. 0084D]**
>
> These statements must nevertheless be interpreted favorably.

> —and if anyone offers this to God, he has sacrificed with sufficient piety and sufficient religious devotion.”

These, then, are the four theological topics treated by Lactantius with sufficient fullness, to which the topic of creation may appropriately be added.

For he explains all the causes of creation here and there:

The efficient cause, in Book II, chapters 5 and 9, where he says: “God made something out of that which does not exist, because he is mighty through eternity, etc.”

The material cause, namely, that he created all things from nothing, Book I, chapter 3: “By the power and counsel of God, the immensity of the divine work was fashioned from nothing” (see also Book II, chapter 9).

The final cause, namely, that all things were created for the sake of man, Book VII, chapters 4, 5, and 6 (likewise in the book *On the Anger of God*, chapter 13); and the formal cause, namely, the order in which God created each thing, Book II, chapter 9. Concerning the destruction of the world [Col. 0084C], these words of his are also found in Book VII, chapter 1: “Because Plato was ignorant of the heavenly mystery, he therefore said that the world had been fashioned to last forever, whereas the truth is very different. For whatever consists of a solid and heavy body must, just as it once had a beginning, likewise come to an end.” Everywhere he affirms that the particular end for which man was created is this: that he should worship God, Book VII, chapter 5; Book VI, chapter 1, etc.

The topics that he touches upon only lightly, yet nevertheless expounds correctly, are these: the Church, the object of worship, repentance, marriage, the Law, the Fall of mankind, sin, the Last Judgment, and certain signs that will precede the end of the world.

Concerning the Church, he teaches what it is and what its marks are: “The Church is the true temple of God, which is not in walls but in the heart and faith of those who believe in him and are called the faithful” (Book IV, chapter 13). Likewise: “The Church is the eternal temple established for God by Christ, who calls all nations to the true religion of God. This is the faithful house, this the immortal temple; whoever has not offered sacrifice in it [Col. 0084D] will not possess the reward of immortality” (Book IV, chapter 14). “The apostles, dispersed throughout the provinces, laid the foundations of the Church everywhere” (Book VI, chapter 21). In chapter 30 of the same book he briefly describes the marks of the Church: “The Catholic Church alone retains true worship. Each individual assembly of heretics thinks that its own members above all are Christians and that its own church is the Catholic Church; but it must be known that the true Church is that in which there is confession and repentance, which wholesomely heals sins and wounds.”

He discusses the object of worship in Book II, chapter 18: “Let us adore nothing else and worship nothing except the sole and unique divine power of our Maker and Father, who for this reason created man upright: that we might know that we are being summoned to things above and heavenly.” And in Book V, chapter 18 he says, speaking of the gentiles: “They do not know how great [Col. 0085A] a sacrilege it is to adore anything other than God, who founded heaven and earth, fashioned the human race, breathed life into it, and endowed it with light.”

He teaches in Book VI, chapter 24 that people are brought back to God by repentance, in these words: “Let no one lose heart or despair of himself if, whether overcome by desire, driven by lust, deceived by error, or compelled by force, he has fallen into the path of injustice. For he can be brought back and delivered if he repents of what he has done and, turning to better things, makes satisfaction to God.” For God is appeased—not by incense, as he likewise writes in *On the Anger of God*, chapter 21, nor by a human victim, nor by costly gifts, all of which are corruptible—but by the reformation of conduct. And he who ceases to sin renders God’s anger mortal, that is, brings it to an end. For this reason God does not punish every guilty person immediately: so that a person may have the opportunity to come to his senses and reform himself.

For Lactantius, moreover, to repent means nothing other than to profess and affirm that one will sin no further (Book VI, chapter 13). For one who truly repents of his deed recognizes his former error; and so the Greeks speak better and more meaningfully of *metanoia* (μετάνοια, “change of mind”), which we might call “coming to one’s senses.” For he comes to his senses and, as it were, recovers his mind from madness who, first, regrets his error, then chastises himself for his folly, and strengthens his resolve to live more uprightly” (Book VI, chapter 2).

It is also clear from Book V, chapter 13 that those who had denied the truth during persecutions were at that time received back into the Church, provided that they repented: “It is possible,” he says, “to make satisfaction to God; and no worshipper of God is so wicked that, when given the opportunity to appease God, he will not return to him—and often, indeed, with greater devotion. For consciousness of sin and fear of punishment make a person more religious.”

He teaches that marriage is necessary for those who cannot restrain their passions: “Let him confine them within the prescribed bounds of the lawful marriage-bed, so that he may both obtain what he eagerly desires and yet not fall into sin,” he says in Book VI, chapter 23. And shortly afterward: “Everyone ought to set before himself the principle that the union of the two sexes was given to living beings for the purpose of procreation, and that this law was imposed upon these passions so that they might produce offspring.” In the same place you will find more concerning the duties of chastity.

He teaches that there are two principal heads of the Law, one prescribing what is owed to God, the other what is owed to man (Book VI, chapters 9 and 10).

He elegantly describes the Fall of our first parents from Moses (Book II, chapter 2): “That accuser,” he says, “envying the works of God, directed all his deceits and cunning toward beguiling man, so as to deprive him of immortality. First, by guile he enticed the woman to take the forbidden food; and through her he also persuaded the man himself to transgress the law of God, etc.”

Concerning sin, he testifies that man is unjust through his own fault (Book IV, chapter 24), and that sin is naturally present in all human beings (Book VI, chapter 13).

He discusses at length the Last Judgment and the signs that will precede it in Book VII, and names many signs in chapter 15. Yet all these things are not expressed adequately in accordance with the understanding of Catholics.

## THE BLEMISHES AND ERRORS OF LACTANTIUS

[Col. 0085D]

We have stated which articles of faith he expounded fully, and which he touched upon only lightly but nevertheless correctly. It follows that we should also warn the diligent reader about those matters that Lactantius appears not to have understood adequately, and thus disclose his blemishes and errors. His blemishes are of three kinds: some are theological, others chronological, and some philosophical.

### Theological Blemishes

That by a dangerous form of expression he says that God the Father was begotten from himself (Book I, chapter 7).

That he did not assert the eternity of the Son of God distinctly enough. For in Book IV, chapter 6, he writes: “Before God undertook the glorious work of the world, he begot a Spirit whom they called the Son.” The same statements are found in Book II, chapter 8.

That, contrary to the testimony of sacred history, he writes that Christ [Col. 0086A] never called himself God, because he would not have kept faith if, having been sent to abolish the gods and affirm one God, he had introduced another besides that one (Book IV, chapter 14).

That he denies that Pilate pronounced a sentence condemning Christ to death (Book IV, chapter 18).

That he says Christ departed into Galilee and was unwilling to show himself to the Jews, lest he lead them to repentance (Book IV, chapter 20).

That he does not even name the Holy Spirit; indeed, that in his letters to Demetrianus, according to the testimony of Saint Jerome, he denied the substance of the Holy Spirit and, in accordance with a Jewish error, said that the Spirit is referred either to the Father or to the Son, and that the sanctification of either Person is indicated under his name.

That he remained silent concerning the principal office of the incarnate Christ, namely, his priestly office, and contends that Christ assumed human nature only so that, just as the Father was without a father, the Son himself might likewise be *apatōr* and *amētōr* (ἀπάτωρ atque ἀμήτωρ, “fatherless and motherless”) (Book IV, chapter 13); so that he might transfer the holy religion of God to the gentiles (Book IV, chapter 11); so that he might reveal to all [Col. 0086B] nations under heaven the holy mystery of the one true God and proclaim that one God to them (Book IV, chapter 12); and, finally, so that he might be able to furnish man with examples of virtue (Book IV, chapter 25). Everyone can see how feeble all these claims are when the chief end of Christ’s incarnation has been omitted.

That he says angels were first appointed as guardians of mankind only when the human race began to increase to a greater number (Book II, chapter 15).

That he asserts that dominion over the earth was granted by God to the devil from the beginning, and that two kinds of demons were made, one earthly and the other heavenly (ibid.).

That he thinks that the most deceitful ruler of heaven enticed the good angels assigned to the protection of mankind into vices, defiled them through intercourse with women, and made them his attendants and ministers (Book II, chapter 15).

That he made the novel assertion that the day supplied by the first East belongs to God, whereas the night introduced by the farthest West belongs to him who rivals God, namely, the devil (Book II, chapter 9).

[Col. 0086C] That he thinks man was made by God from diverse and mutually opposed things. For he writes thus in Book II, chapter 12: “Man was made from diverse and opposed things, just as the world itself was made from light and darkness, from life and death. God commanded these two to contend with one another in man, so that if the soul, which has its origin from God, should prevail, it might be immortal and dwell in perpetual light; but if the body should conquer the soul and subject it to its dominion, it might dwell in everlasting darkness and death.”

That he affirms that man was fashioned from the earth mortal and imperfect (Book VII, chapters 5 and 14).

That he holds that the same man acquires immortality by his own powers (ibid.).

That he imagines God to have created an infinite multitude of souls, which, after first binding them to frail and feeble bodies, he placed in an intermediate position between good and evil, so that he might set virtue before beings composed of both natures, lest they attain immortality through ease and indulgence, etc. (Book VII, chapter 5. See, however, the note on chapter 18 [Col. 0086D] of Book III.)

That although, in Books V and VI, he expressly undertook a discourse on the righteousness of Christians, he nevertheless discusses only philosophical righteousness, or the righteousness of the Law, and does not mention even in a single word the righteousness of faith, which is proper to the Gospel.

That he asserts that the spirit, or soul, of man earns by works of righteousness the right to become an eternal spirit (Book IV, chapter 25); and likewise that the sins of the flesh are abolished by continual almsgiving (Book VI, chapter 13).

That he writes that only those who fall into sin through ignorance and lack of caution are forgiven, and that one who sins knowingly has no pardon (ibid.).

That he maintains contradictory opinions concerning the perfection of the regenerate person, and indeed within one and the same book, namely, the sixth. In chapter 13 he admits that no one can be without fault as long as he is burdened with the garment of the flesh. Yet in the final chapter he insists that the true worshipper of God [Col. 0087A] should pray for nothing except pardon for his sins, even though there are none.

That he thinks God permits evil to rage so that there may be a basis for virtue (Book V, chapter 7). He writes that God permits errors for this end (Book II, chapter 17); he says that for this end the devil was roused by God, in the book *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 20; and he thinks that for this end such a great multitude of water snakes and vipers was made by God (Book VII, chapter 4, and *On the Anger of God*, chapter 13).

That he does not wish us to believe that, whenever we pray, we are tested by God as to whether we are worthy to be heard (Book VI, chapter 13).

That he thinks military service is unlawful for a righteous person, as is accusing anyone of a capital crime (Book VI, chapter 20).

That he writes that after death souls are detained in one common custody until the time arrives when the supreme Judge conducts an examination of their merits (Book VII, chapter 21).

That in Book VII, chapters 14, 15, 16, 17, etc., he inserted dangerous opinions concerning the end of the age, the Last Judgment, and the thousand-year reign. From these it is clear that, contrary to Scripture, Lactantius affirmed two resurrections, one preceding the golden age of the millennium, the other preceding the destruction of the devil and the wicked; and likewise two universal judgments. It is also clear that he held that only the righteous, and not the wicked as well, would be judged.

Finally, that he indulges in remarkable trifling not only concerning Antichrist but also concerning the coming of Elijah to earth, who will convert many to the worship of God (Book VII, chapter 17).

There have been those who did not hesitate to accuse Lactantius of Manichaeism as well. But because neither Jerome nor any other ancient writer noticed this error in Lactantius, and because the ancient codices likewise do not contain those passages in the more recent editions that appeared to favor the Manichaeans, it is evident from this that the books of this author too were interpolated by some Manichaean.

### Chronological Blemishes

That he writes that Moses preceded the destruction of Troy by almost nine hundred years, whereas Eusebius counts only three hundred and fifty. But this controversy is still undecided. For many hold the same opinion as Lactantius.

That he limits the rule of the kings of Israel to four hundred and sixty years, whereas more learned chronologists count five hundred and fifteen years (Book IV, chapter 5).

### Philosophical Blemishes

That he denies the existence of antipodes (Book III, chapter 22).

That among the other conditions of the highest good he includes this one: that it belongs to the soul alone and cannot be shared with the body (Book III, chapter 9). But, I say, if the highest [Col. 0088B] good of man is being sought, and man consists not of the soul alone but of soul and body together, surely the highest good will belong not to the soul alone but to soul and body together—just as immortality, which Lactantius calls the highest good, will pertain equally to body and soul.

That he criticizes Cicero’s definition of a good man, according to which a good man is said to harm no one unless provoked by injury (Book VI, chapter 18), although Cicero is speaking not of private but of public vengeance.

[Col. 0087]

## CENSORIAL ANNOTATIONS ON CERTAIN ERRORS OF LACTANTIUS

### From Manuscript No. MDCLXXIII of the Royal Library, among the Theologians, in Folio: Book One of the *Divine Institutes Against the Gentiles*, Addressed to the Emperor Constantine, by Lucius Caelius Lactantius Firmianus

[Col. 0087C]

### Opposite This First Page the Following Is Written

This volume was corrected according to the censure of the Very Reverend Father Giovanni Maria Brisighella, Master of the Sacred Apostolic Palace, appointed by the Supreme Pontiff Paul V in 1607, elected General of the Order of Friars Preachers in 1608, and raised to the most exalted rank of the cardinalate in 1611.

### Furthermore, the Following Is Written Below in the Margin

Saint Jerome says more about Lactantius Firmianus in his *Catalogue* and in Letter 83, to Magnus, where he praises him extraordinarily for his eloquence. But lest anyone happen to stumble in reading the works of Lactantius, the reader must be forewarned how cautiously and circumspectly he must proceed in perusing this author’s writings. Saint Damasus, the Roman pontiff, says the following about him in his letter to Saint Jerome, which is Letter 124 among Jerome’s letters:

“I confess to you that I do not read with pleasure those books of Lactantius that you gave me some time ago, because many of the letters in them extend to thousands of lines and rarely discuss our doctrine. Consequently, their length produces weariness in the reader; and those that are brief are better suited to scholars than to us, since they discuss meters, the locations of regions, and philosophers.”

[Col. 0088C] Thus Saint Damasus. But Saint Jerome too says in Letter 13, to Paulinus: “Lactantius is like a kind of river of Ciceronian eloquence. Would that he had been as capable of confirming our own teachings as he was of easily destroying those of others!”

And in Book II of his commentary on the *Epistle to the Galatians*, chapter 4, he says: “Many, through ignorance of the Scriptures—as Firmianus too does in the eighth book of his letters to Demetrianus—assert that the Holy Spirit is sometimes called the Father and sometimes the Son.”

Again, in his *Apology to Pammachius and Oceanus*, he says: “Lactantius, in his books and especially in his letters to Demetrianus, wholly denies the substance of the Holy Spirit and, in accordance with a Jewish error, says that the Spirit is referred either to the Father or to the Son, and that under his name the sanctification of either Person is indicated. Who can forbid me to read the books of his *Institutes*, in which he wrote most forcefully against the gentiles, merely because the foregoing opinion is detestable?” Thus far Saint Jerome.

Saint Gelasius pronounces as follows in the Roman Council: “The works of Lactantius are apocryphal.” The holy pontiff certainly judged thus with grave and mature deliberation. For in these works of Lactantius there are manifold errors and opinions at variance with the purity of orthodox doctrine. Master Antonius Raudensis attached a list of them to the end of the books of Lactantius. Yet both Francesco Filelfo, in Book IV of his *Letters*, and many learned men thought that Raudensis’s censures were in some instances excessively severe, [Col. 0089A] in others inept, and that he omitted many other matters deserving correction.

**Book I, on chapter 7: “But because,” etc.** Read all these things cautiously, down to the end of the chapter, for they depart greatly from the theologians’ customary mode of expression. For God was not begotten or produced by himself, since nothing is more impossible than for something to generate or produce itself. Nor do Lactantius’s words appear capable of being reduced to any sound meaning except negatively: “begotten by himself,” that is, “not begotten by another.” Finally, in this matter, what could be more absurd than the statement: “It is impossible that whatever exists should not at some time have begun to exist”? See Possevino’s *Sacred Apparatus* under Gilbert Génébrard.

**Book II, on chapter 14: “Within one hundred and twenty years.”** Saint Jerome, in his *Hebrew Traditions* on Genesis 6, Saint John Chrysostom in Homily 20 on Genesis, and almost all other writers disagree with this opinion of Lactantius, which was also Josephus’s opinion. See Sixtus of Siena, Book V of the *Library*, annotation 75, and the more recent interpreters on Genesis 6.

**In the same Book II, chapter 15: “When, therefore, the number of human beings,” etc.** This chapter must be read circumspectly, for Lactantius involves himself in several errors. The first is that God from the beginning granted the devil power over the earth. The second is that angels were not sent to protect human beings until the human race had begun to increase. The third is that God commanded the good angels not to be stained by contact with the earth, lest they lose the dignity of their heavenly substance. The fourth is that the devil gradually enticed the good angels into vices and defiled them through intercourse with women. The fifth is that this was the sin on account of which the angels fell from heaven. The sixth is that from that intercourse of angels with women there was born a third race of beings who were neither heavenly angels, nor human beings, nor demons of hell, but a kind of offspring of earthly demons, who are the tempters and deceivers of human beings and the authors of magical arts and of human calamities and evils. [Col. 0089C] All these teachings are absurd, erroneous, and altogether foreign to the sound doctrine of theologians. Consult Sixtus of Siena, Book V of the *Library*, annotation 77, and other interpreters of Genesis 6.

**Book III, chapter 24: “What of those who say that there are opposites,” etc.** Lactantius’s denial of the antipodes, together with other ancient authors, is refuted by the manifest evidence of the New World and also by the authority of notable writers from antiquity, as Friar Thomas Malvenda demonstrates at length in Book III of *On Antichrist*, chapter 14. As for what he argues against the revolving spherical shape of heaven—even though some philosophers and Fathers are likewise found to have taught the same—it is nevertheless openly disproved both by the testimony of authors and by clear demonstrations of philosophy and astronomy. See the observations made in the same place in Thomas Malvenda.

**In the same Book III, chapter 25: “Now a few words from us concerning philosophy,” etc.** Read this chapter cautiously. For if Lactantius criticizes the entire philosophy of the ancient gentiles, he does so without sufficient judgment, since that philosophy contained many true and correct things useful and beneficial to human life. But if he condemns philosophy universally, he is by no means to be tolerated and contradicts the common understanding of the Fathers and the Church. See Alfonso de Castro, Book XIII of *Against Heresies*, under the heading “Knowledge.”

**Book VI, chapter 2: “They therefore slaughter the richest and fattest animals,” etc.** Receive with judgment what Lactantius argues in this chapter concerning the refusal to light candles and wax tapers in temples. For just as he rightly inveighs against the pagan and superstitious rite of the gentiles, so he appears, rather incautiously, to have given certain innovators an opportunity to criticize the pious and religious custom of lighting wax tapers and lamps in churches, at altars, and by the relics of martyrs, etc.—a holy practice that the impious Vigilantius also attacked. See Bellarmine, *On the Relics of the Saints*, chapters 3 and 4, and Baronius, volume I of the *Annals*, under the year of the Lord 58.

[Col. 0090A] **In the same Book VI, chapter 20: “For when God forbids killing,” etc.** Read these ten or eleven lines cautiously, for Lactantius teaches two things altogether at variance with sound theological reasoning. The first is that it is not lawful to kill a person by judicial sentence and public authority, nor to accuse anyone of a capital crime, which is a manifest error. See Saint Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, II-II, question 64, articles 2 and 3, and his interpreters; and Bellarmine, Book III of *On the Laity*, chapters 12 and 13. The second is that Christians are not permitted to serve as soldiers, which was a heresy of the Manichaeans and, in our age, of Erasmus and other innovators. See Saint Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, II-II, question 40, article 1, and his interpreters; Sixtus, Book VI of the *Library*, annotation 156; Bellarmine, Book III of *On the Laity*, chapter 64.

**In the same Book VI, chapter 25: “Now concerning sacrifice itself,” etc.** Lactantius does not argue sufficiently judiciously in this chapter concerning the external worship of God, temples and their adornment, votive offerings, and sacrifice; for he appears to reject all external worship of God. Certainly the Church’s principal sacrifice, the Eucharist, is also to a great extent external [Col. 0090B] and is immolated by an external rite. Furthermore, although the internal worship of mind and spirit is primary and is what God more especially requires from each of us—for external worship without internal worship does not bring salvation to a Christian—nevertheless, the external worship of God is in itself pious, holy, good, and pleasing to God. The external ornaments of churches, which consist partly in their buildings and partly in golden vessels, silken vestments, etc., by their very nature contribute to the pious and holy worship of God. To think the contrary is the heresy of the Petrobrusians, the Wycliffites, and the innovators of our own time. See Bellarmine, Book III of *On the Worship of the Saints*, chapter 6, and Baronius, volume I of the *Annals*, under the year 57.

As for Lactantius’s intention in this chapter, Thomasius rightly reduces it to a sound meaning in the notes he appended here at the end of the chapter, even though Lactantius does not speak with sufficient circumspection.

**Book VII, chapter 14: “Let the philosophers therefore know,” etc.** Not only Lactantius here but also many other Fathers confined the entire duration of the world within the span of six thousand years. How their individual opinions on this matter are to be understood is demonstrated at length by Father Thomas Malvenda, the Dominican theologian, in Book I of *On Antichrist*, chapters 28, 29, and 30. See Sixtus, Book V of the *Library*, annotation 190.

**In the same Book VII, chapter 27: “A great prophet will be sent by God,” etc.** Lactantius, not properly understanding the prophecy of Revelation 11, where the coming of the two prophets Enoch and Elijah in the time of Antichrist is foretold, here attributes these predictions to only one prophet. See Father Thomas Malvenda, the Dominican theologian, Book IX of *On Antichrist*, chapter 16, toward the end.

**In the same Book VII, chapter 19: “When the world has therefore been oppressed,” etc.** Lactantius, who was not sufficiently skilled in the sacred Scriptures, as Saint Jerome says, and who did not fully penetrate the words of Revelation 16, advances in this chapter certain claims concerning Antichrist that are not sufficiently consonant with Scripture. They are carefully examined in Thomas Malvenda’s Book X of *On Antichrist*, chapters 11 and 13.

[Col. 0090D] **In the same Book VII, chapter 21: “With eternal fire, whose nature,” etc.** Although it is not erroneous or rash to assert that the fire of hell is of a nature different from our elemental fire, provided that it is acknowledged to be true and corporeal fire, the better and more probable opinion of the theologians is that it is of the same nature and species as our fire, though distinguished by certain qualities. See Domingo Báñez on Part I, question [reading uncertain], article 2, doubt 2, conclusion 2.

**In the same chapter 21: “But when he has also judged the righteous,” etc.** This error of Lactantius concerning the bodies of the righteous being purged by fire after the universal judgment has been rejected by the theological schools. See Sixtus, Book V of the *Library*, annotations 170 and 171.

**In the same chapter 21: “Yet let no one think,” etc.** It is a manifest heresy, condemned by the Church, to assert that the souls of the righteous, once separated from the body and requiring no purification, are not immediately admitted to the clear vision of God [Col. 0091A], or essential beatitude. Lactantius likewise appears to have held this error, for his words scarcely admit of a sound interpretation. See Sixtus, Book VI of the *Library*, annotation 345; Bellarmine, Book I of *On the Beatitude of the Saints*, chapters 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6; Coccius, volume I of the *Catholic Treasury*, Book V, article 2.

**In the same Book VII, chapter 22: “This reasoning deceived them,” etc.** Add here the scholion placed below at chapter 24.

**In the same Book VII, chapter 24: “Now I shall append what remains,” etc.** Almost everything that Lactantius discusses at length in these last three chapters of this book—namely, chapters 24, 25, and 26—concerning the first resurrection of mankind, Christ’s golden thousand-year reign on earth after the first resurrection, the binding of the devil for [Col. 0092A] a thousand years and his release, and the battle of Gog and Magog, is based on a mistaken understanding of the prophecies of Revelation 20. These things are altogether foreign to the meaning of sacred Scripture and to the doctrine of the Church and the holy Fathers, and are openly erroneous, as Father Thomas Malvenda, the Dominican theologian, shows at length in Book X of *On Antichrist*, chapters 3 through 11.

**In the same Book VII, chapter 25: “I have already shown above,” etc.** See the note above on chapter 24. As for Lactantius’s further statement here that only two hundred years remained from his own time until the end of the world, it is disproved both by experience itself and by manifest reasoning. See Father Thomas Malvenda, the Dominican theologian, Book II of *On Antichrist*, chapter 30.

[Col. 0091]

## PROPOSITIONS FOUND IN LACTANTIUS THAT PERTAIN TO THE FAITH AND MUST BE READ CAUTIOUSLY BY CATHOLICS, EITHER EXPLAINED IN A PIOUS SENSE OR REFUTED IN THE NOTES, DRAWN FROM ISAEUS’S EDITION

[Col. 0091B]

They number ninety-four; but the passages scattered throughout the entire work that formerly presented dangerous reading number more than one hundred and seventy.

1. That God, apart from the angels, is alone or solitary: Book I of the *Institutes*, chapter 7; Book IV, chapter 8.

2. That God begot angels or human beings: Book I, chapter 7; Book II, chapter 13.

3. That God was begotten, made, or produced from himself: Book I, chapter 7; Book II, chapter 9.

4. That the use of temples is superfluous: Book I, chapter 20; Book II, chapter 2; Book V, chapter 8; Book VI, chapter 25; the book *On the Anger of God*, final chapter.

5. That altars should not be erected to God and sacrifices should not be performed: Book I, chapter 20; Book II, chapter 2; Book VI, chapters 1, 20, and 25; Book VII, chapter 6; *Epitome*, chapter 2; *On the Anger of God*, chapter 21.

6. That gifts should not be offered to God and temples should not be adorned: Book II, chapter 4; Book V, chapter 8; Book VI, chapters 1 and 25; *Epitome*, chapter 2; *On the Anger of God*, chapter 21.

7. That the use of images is superfluous: Book II, chapters 2, 3, 7, 18, and 19.

[Col. 0091C]

8. That the soul of a man is the man, while the man’s body is the vessel, receptacle, lodging, dwelling, garment, and clothing of the soul itself: Book II, chapters 2, 3, and 13; Book III, chapter 18; Book IV, chapters 24 and 26; Book V, chapter 22; Book VII, chapter 12; *On the Workmanship of God*, chapters 1, 4, and 20.

9. That brute animals possess reason and differ from man only in religion: Book II, chapters 3 and 9; Book III, chapter 10; Book VII, chapter 9; *On the Anger of God*, chapter 7.

10. That wisdom was given by God equally to all human beings: Book II, chapter 8; Book III, chapter 25.

11. That God is most prudent in devising: Book II, chapter 9. (See p. 143, note to line 5.)

12. That the Son of God is the spirit of God: Book II, chapter 9; Book IV, chapters 6, 8, 9, and 18.

13. That the supreme angel was created before the construction of the world: Book II, chapter 9.

14. That the supreme angel was of divine stock: Book II, chapter 9.

15. That the sin of the supreme angel was the sin of envy: Book II, chapter 9.

16. That the Son of God was approved by God the Father through perseverance: Book II, chapter 9.

17. That the Word of God is the first and greatest Son of God among the angels: Book II, chapter 9; Book IV, chapters 8, 10, and 14; according to one reading there, “the prince of the angels.”

[Col. 0092B]

18. That the human body is the enclosure, bond, snare, custody, and prison of the soul: Book II, chapter 9; Book VII, chapters 2, 5, 8, and 12. These matters have already appeared above, in proposition 8.

19. That there are two principles and two rulers of things, one of good things and the other of evil things: Book II, chapters 10, 15, and 18; Book VI, chapters 3 and 6.

20. That the matter of the soul consists in heat: Book II, chapter 10.

21. That the human soul is fire: Book II, chapter 13.

22. That the human soul is from the spirit of God or from the substance of God: Book II, chapter 13; Book VII, chapter 12.

23. That Adam was originally ignorant of good and evil, but obtained knowledge of good and evil by eating the forbidden fruit: Book II, chapter 13.

24. That the souls of the righteous will be introduced into the earthly paradise after the universal judgment: Book II, chapter 13.

25. That after the Flood God fixed the limit of human life at one hundred and twenty years: Book II, chapter 14.

26. That angels were sent by God to guard and protect the human race when the number of human beings began to increase: Book II, chapter 15.

[Col. 0092C]

27. That God commanded them above all not to be stained by contact with the earth, lest they lose the dignity of their heavenly substance: ibid.

28. That they were afterward enticed by the devil into vices and defiled through intercourse with women: ibid.

29. That because of their sins they were therefore no longer received into heaven but fell to earth: ibid.

30. That their sons, because they were neither angels nor human beings but possessed a kind of intermediate nature, were received neither into the lower regions nor into heaven: ibid.

31. That two kinds of demons were thus produced, one heavenly and the other earthly: ibid.

32. That demons obtain some consolation from the perdition of human beings: Book II, chapter 15.

33. That demons are certain subtle and imperceptible spirits: Book II, chapter 15.

34. That demons impair human health: Book II, chapter 15.

35. That demons seek no honor for themselves: Book II, chapter 17.

36. That God is truly and properly moved by certain passions: Book II, chapter 18; *On the Anger of God*, chapters 2, 15, and 16.

37. That God is truly and properly angry: Book II, chapter 18, and throughout *On the Anger of God*, especially chapters 16 and 17.

[Col. 0093A]

38. That the human soul has its origin from heaven: Book II, chapter 19; Book VII, chapters 9 and 12.

39. That heaven, earth, and, finally, the world are not of a round or spherical shape: Book III, chapter 24.

40. That the devil was not cast down to punishment immediately after his transgression but was permitted to remain in this world, etc.: Book III, chapter 29; Book VII, chapter 26.

41. That philosophers were turned away by divine providence so that they could not know the truth: Book IV, chapter 2.

42. That God the Father deigned to call his Son by the divine name: Book IV, chapter 6.

43. That Christ was the Son of God from the beginning: Book IV, chapter 8.

44. That the Son of God was begotten by God the Father: Book IV, chapter 8.

45. That the Word of God is a spirit uttered from the mouth of God with voice and tone: Book IV, chapter 8.

46. That the Son of God is an angel: Book IV, chapters 8 and 14; according to one reading there, “the prince of the angels.”

47. That the angels of God are spirits silently [Col. 0093B] uttered from God’s nostrils: Book IV, chapter 8.

48. That the spirits of human beings are dissoluble: Book IV, chapter 8.

49. That when Christ assumed human flesh, he put on and bore a man: Book IV, chapter 10.

50. That Christ suffered in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar: Book IV, chapter 10.

51. That God was unwilling to send his Son at his first advent in heavenly glory and power, so that the Jewish people, ungrateful toward God, might be led into error: Book IV, chapter 11.

52–53. That there will be two resurrections at the end of the ages. That after the first resurrection Christ will reign on earth with the righteous for a thousand years. He predicts many things that will occur during that time, which are marked as false once the thousand-year reign itself has been rejected: Book IV, chapter 12, at the end; Book VII, chapters 2, 14, 19, 20, 21, 22, 24, 25, and 26; *Epitome*, chapter 11.

54. That the Virgin’s womb was weakened, and that the Virgin was made a mother in great compassion: Book IV, chapter 12.

[Col. 0093C]

55. That Jerusalem was founded by Solomon: Book IV, chapters 13 and 18.

56. That Christ bore a substance intermediate between God and man, or is intermediate between God and man: Book IV, chapters 13 and 25.

57. That Christ was God and man, blended from both kinds: Book IV, chapter 13.

58. That Christ was baptized at the beginning of his youth: Book IV, chapter 15.

59. That Christ annulled the law of God: Book IV, chapter 17.

60. That Pilate did not pronounce sentence against Christ: Book IV, chapter 18.

61. That Christ the Lord was clothed in a scarlet-colored garment at the time of his Passion: same book, same chapter.

62. That after his Passion Christ was unwilling to show himself to the Jews, lest he lead them to repentance and heal them: Book IV, chapter 20.

63. That God in his pure divinity could not teach virtue because, being without a body, he would not have done the things he taught; and that Christ therefore assumed flesh: Book IV, chapter 23.

64. That Christ’s body was taken down from the cross untouched, lest it be rendered incapable of rising again: Book IV, chapter 26.

65. That although Christians say there is one God, they nevertheless affirm two: God the Father and God the Son: Book IV, chapter 29. (Isaëus appears to have criticized this less justly.)

[Col. 0094A]

66. That the Father is constituted by the Son, and the Son in turn by the Father: Book IV, chapter 29. (These words too are explained in a straightforward sense: for that which constitutes the father, or paternity, is the son or filiation, just as paternity constitutes filiation.)

67. That the use of lights in temples is superfluous: Book VI, chapter 2.

68. That one who sins knowingly has no pardon before God: Book VI, chapter 13.

69. That one who abstains from evil works is sufficiently righteous: Book VI, chapter 13.

70. That it is a very great crime for a person to experience even slight joy when he sees some adversity befall his enemy: Book VI, chapter 16.

71. That it is unlawful for a righteous person to serve as a soldier: Book VI, chapter 20.

72. That it is unlawful for a righteous person to accuse anyone of a capital crime: Book VI, chapter 20.

73. The commandment laid down in the Decalogue, “You shall not kill,” is to be understood simply and without any exception, so that it is in no way permissible to kill a human being, book VI, chapter 20.

[Col. 0094B] 74. That God is endowed with a body, book VII, chapter 5; *Epitome*, chapter 10; *On the Anger of God*, chapters 2 and 18; *On the Workmanship of God*, chapters 2 and 8.

75–76. That the human mind is lulled to sleep in those who are resting, is wholly extinguished in the insane, and grows sick through the contagion of bodily weakness, book VII, chapter 12; *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 18.

77. That the human soul, once released from the enclosure of the body, flies back to its own abode, book VII, chapter 12.

78. That the world will endure for six thousand years, book VII, chapters 14 and 25; *Epitome*, chapter 11.

79. That Adam lived for a thousand years, book VII, chapter 14.

80. That the Antichrist will not come before Rome perishes, book VII, chapters 15 and 25.

81. That at the end of the world an enemy will come upon ten kings and subdue them, but will soon himself be subdued and killed by the Antichrist, book VII, chapter 16; *Epitome*, chapter 11.

82. That at the end of the world a prophet will be sent by God, book VII, chapter 17.

[Col. 0094C] 83. That after the preaching of that prophet the Antichrist will arise, book VII, chapter 17.

84. That the Antichrist will be begotten by an evil spirit, book VII, chapter 17.

85. That the impious will not rise for judgment, book VII, chapter 20.

86. That the human soul is a spirit and therefore, when stripped of the body, is like the light winds, book VII, chapter 20.

87. That the flesh with which God will clothe the human being after the resurrection will not be like this earthly flesh, book VII, chapter 21.

88. That the fire of hell differs in nature from our fire, book VII, chapter 21.

89. That the fire of hell is pure and luminous, etc., book VII, chapter 21.

90. That the punishments and rewards of souls are deferred until the day of universal judgment, book VII, chapter 21.

91. That the passions sometimes compel one to sin, *Epitome*, chapter 4.

92. That God is the author of evils, *On the Anger of God*, chapter 3.

93. That God has set forth good and evil, *On the Anger of God*, chapter 15.

94. That the soul is nourished by air, the body by food, *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 11.

[Col. 0093]

## CATALOGUE OF LACTANTIUS’ MANUSCRIPT CODICES

### MANUSCRIPT CODICES

[Col. 0093C] **BALLIOL COLLEGE, Oxford, England:** a manuscript codex comprising the seven books of the *Divine Institutes* and the book [Col. 0094C] *On the Anger of God*. Thomas Sparke used it in the Oxford edition of 1684.

[Col. 0095A] **THE BALUZE CODEX**, that is, the manuscript codex belonging to the most distinguished and learned Étienne Baluze of Tulle, a good manuscript four hundred years old. It contains the book *On the Anger of God*, beginning at chapter 8, and the book *On the Workmanship of God*. This codex is now in the Royal Library, octavo format, number 2967; see below.

A manuscript codex of the *Divine Institutes* seen by **BARTHIUS**, from which, however, Barthius excerpted very few variant readings.

The manuscript codex used by **BETULEIUS** in the edition published after his death in 1563; Betuleius seems, however, to have made only sparing use of this manuscript.

**THE BODLEIAN CODEX** at Oxford, containing the books of the *Divine Institutes*, together with the *Epitome*, *On the Anger of God*, and *On the Workmanship of God*. It is an excellent codex, which Thomas Sparke used in the edition of 1614. Its variant readings begin only with the second book of the *Divine Institutes*.

Two codices from the monastery of **SAN SALVATORE IN BOLOGNA**, the older of which is said to be a thousand years old; from the specimen, however, it does not [Col. 0095B] seem to me to exceed nine hundred years in age. For its letters are neither square nor capitals; rather, they resemble those of Royal manuscript 3735, dated to nine hundred years ago. It is certainly a good manuscript; it sometimes differs from the others and contains some interpolations. Specimens of this very ancient codex have been published by Leo Allatius in *Etruscan Antiquities*; the distinguished Dom Bernard de Montfaucon in the *Italian Diary* and in *Greek Palaeography*; and also Dom Nicolas Le Nourry, volume II of the *Apparatus for the Library of the Holy Fathers*, p. 616.

The other **BOLOGNESE** copy is more recent but not inferior to the former. Both were collated and frequently cited by Thomasius, whom Isaeus follows. Jean-Baptiste Le Brun possessed many more variant readings from both these manuscript codices, noted by Latino Latini in the margin of his copy of Lactantius, through the care and scholarly diligence of **PIERRE HÉMARD** of Étampes, advocate in the Parlement of Paris. Lenglet possessed a similar copy—indeed Latini’s autograph—from the celebrated Library of Sainte-Geneviève. [Col. 0095C] Latini himself had not collated the Bolognese manuscripts; rather, he had received their variant readings in 1558 from Michele Tommaso Taxaquet, who is none other than Thomasius, the editor of Lactantius. More concerning this below, under **TAXAQUET**.

The codex of Dom Jean **LE BEUF**, member of the Royal Academy of Inscriptions, contains only the two short works *On the Anger of God* and *On the Workmanship of God*. It appears to have been written in the fourteenth century.

A manuscript codex four hundred years old belonging to Jean-Baptiste **LE BRUN** of Rouen, comprising the seven books of the *Divine Institutes* and the books *On the Anger of God* and *On the Workmanship of God*. Variant readings from another manuscript codex are written in its margin for the seven books of the *Divine Institutes*.

Two **CAMBRAI** codices on parchment: one dates from the ninth, or at least the tenth, century, but is so mutilated that it can be read only with the greatest diligence and care. It contains the seven books of the *Institutes* and almost everywhere has excellent Greek [Col. 0095D] written in square letters. The other was written at the beginning of the fifteenth century and contains the seven books of the *Institutes* and the short works *On the Anger of God* and *On the Workmanship of God*, or *On the Formation of the Human Being*. Greek is present, sometimes written fairly well and sometimes in ordinary Latin characters.

A manuscript codex in the Library of the celebrated **UNIVERSITY OF CAMBRIDGE**, written in the year of the Lord 1465 in the venerable Monastery of Subiaco, as is noted at the end of that codex. It contains the seven books of the *Divine Institutes* and the books *On the Anger of God* and *On the Workmanship of God*. Thus it was written there in the very year in which the first Subiaco edition was printed. The Cambridge editor saw it. This codex was not copied from the first Subiaco edition, from which it differs greatly, as is evident from the variant readings which the Cambridge editor adduces from it.

Variant readings from an excellent manuscript codex collected by Theodorus [Col. 0096A] **CANTER** and lent to Gallaeus.

A parchment codex produced in the middle of the fifteenth century and written fairly neatly. With his customary kindness, the Reverend Father Fulgentius, prefect of the Library of the **CAPUCHIN FATHERS OF PARIS** at the convent of Saint-Honoré, lent it to me. The Greek in it is elegantly written, though it is not present in all the books. This codex also contains the short works *On the Anger of God* and *On the Workmanship of God*.

An ancient manuscript codex of the highest quality, similar in almost every respect to the very ancient Bolognese codex, most carefully collated by **JO. CAUCI**, comprising the books of the *Divine Institutes*, *On the Anger of God*, and *On the Workmanship of God*. Gallaeus made use of this codex’s variant readings.

A manuscript codex of **CORPUS CHRISTI COLLEGE**, Oxford, containing the books of the *Divine Institutes*, *On the Anger of God*, and *On the Workmanship of God*. Thomas Sparke used it, though sparingly.

Two manuscript codices, four hundred and three hundred years old, belonging to the most learned and courteous **GODFREY CLERMONT** of Amsterdam, chaplain to the Dutch envoys in France [Col. 0096B] in 1715. When, in Paris, he heard from the distinguished Étienne Baluze that Jean-Baptiste Le Brun was preparing to publish an edition of Lactantius collated with and corrected according to the manuscript codices, he returned to Amsterdam and most kindly sent the two manuscripts, together with two printed editions, for Jean-Baptiste Le Brun’s use. For this reason our edition is greatly indebted to him.

A manuscript codex eight hundred years old from the **COLBERT LIBRARY**, no. 1297, from which that famous book of Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, was brought to light through the care of the distinguished and learned Étienne Baluze. Jean-Baptiste Le Brun again collated this manuscript with the greatest accuracy; Lenglet himself also devoted the utmost care and diligence to comparing it with the printed editions, and noticed several things omitted by others. There are other codices: one of them, apparently seven hundred years old, no. 2679, was written in Venice; another, five hundred years old, no. 5173, was written in the diocese of Le Puy; three others are three hundred years old, namely no. 3573, written at Bologna, and two more, nos. 4095 and 4495, comprising [Col. 0096C] the books of the *Divine Institutes* and the books *On the Anger of God* and *On the Workmanship of God*. One, likewise three hundred years old, written at Bologna, no. 1975, contains only the seven books of the *Divine Institutes*; another, also three hundred years old, no. 6210, written at Florence, contains the books *On the Anger of God* and *On the Workmanship of God*. There is yet another, eight hundred years old, no. 1336, which contains nothing by Lactantius, but does contain the poem *On the Phoenix* under Lactantius’ name. All these Colbert codices, however, are now in the Royal Library; we shall shortly give their catalogue and ages.

A manuscript codex of the *Divine Institutes* and of the book *On the Workmanship of God* seen by **COLOMESIUS**, which contains very few variant readings.

The **COLOGNE CODEX**, whose variant readings are very frequently presented by the Cologne editor of 1544; Lenglet used that edition.

The **COTTON CODEX** at Oxford, a manuscript comprising the books of the *Divine Institutes*, with the first apparently missing. [Col. 0096D] Sparke included some of its variant readings in his Oxford edition of 1684.

Two manuscript codices whose variant readings Jacques Cujas sent to de Tournes. De Tournes used them in the edition of 1579.

A manuscript codex in the Library of **EMMANUEL COLLEGE**, Cambridge, copied in the year of the Lord 1424, as is evident from the colophon added at the end; it is far more correct than the other Cambridge codex. It comprises the books of the *Divine Institutes*, *On the Anger of God*, and *On the Workmanship of God*. The Cambridge editor collated it and prefixed its variant readings to his edition.

An old manuscript codex once used by **DESIDERIUS ERASMUS**. Its variant readings are very few, except for the book *On the Workmanship of God*, which Erasmus elucidated with a small number of notes in the edition of this short work published in 1529, and in the others printed afterward, [Col. 0097A] both separately and within certain editions of Lactantius.

A very ancient codex used by Georg **ERHARD**, though Gallaeus extracted very few variant readings from it.

The person whose name is frequently found in the notes was Petrus **FRANCIUS**, professor of eloquence in the distinguished school of the city of Amsterdam. His library was notable not so much for the number of its volumes as for the manuscript notes with which this most learned man had sprinkled every book. He died, I believe, in 1704, and his literary collection was offered for sale at Amsterdam in 1705 by the bookseller Hendrik Wetstein. Jean-Baptiste Le Brun had received Francius’ annotations and conjectures on Lactantius from the Dutchman Monsieur de Clermont.

A three-hundred-year-old codex belonging to the metropolitan church of **SAINT GATIANUS AT TOURS**. Its variant readings, together with those of a manuscript codex of Marmoutier, were sent to Jean-Baptiste Le Brun by Jacques-Christophe Garreau, a learned and devout man born for the public good.

[Col. 0097B] The **GOTHA** manuscript codex of the Most Serene Duke of Saxony is about four hundred years old. It contains the seven books of the *Institutes* and the books *On the Anger of God* and *On the Workmanship of God*. Cellarius, Heumann, and Bunemann used it.

The manuscript codex of Claude Ménard, concerning which J. F. **GRONOVIUS** writes as follows: “Having come upon some not very old parchment leaves in the house of Claude Ménard at Angers, I began to collate them, whatever their quality might be, and found readings which I judged preferable to the commonly printed ones.” From this manuscript he corrected only a number of passages in the first two books of the *Divine Institutes*, in his book *Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers*.

Five **GUELPH**, or **WOLFENBÜTTEL**, manuscript codices, partly from the Gudian Library, whose variant readings Bunemann was unable to obtain. Perhaps someone else will have better fortune.

A manuscript codex belonging to **JANUS GUILIELMUS**, or at least collated by him, of no slight antiquity. It contains the books of the *Divine Institutes*, *On the Anger of God*, and *On the Workmanship of God*. [Col. 0097C] Gallaeus possessed some of its variant readings.

One paper codex belonging to Adriaan **JUNIUS**, head of the Amsterdam school in the city’s new quarter. This codex, written in a very ugly hand from an excellent archetype, was lent to Gallaeus by Adriaan Junius. Thomas Crenius, however, examined it more carefully.

Three paper manuscript codices belonging to the **UNIVERSITY OF LEIPZIG**, about three hundred years old. One of them is of the highest quality and agrees with the most ancient witnesses. They contain the books of the *Divine Institutes*, *On the Anger of God*, and *On the Workmanship of God*, except for one in which the final two works are lacking. Cellarius and Bunemann used them.

A **ROYAL LONDON** manuscript of *On the Anger of God*, of which Bunemann possessed a copy furnished by a friend.

A five-hundred-year-old manuscript codex of **MARMOUTIER**—in French, *Marmoutier*—of the Order of Saint Benedict, Congregation of Saint Maur, near Tours.

The **MERTON COLLEGE** manuscript codex at Oxford, whose variant readings Sparke reports, though far too sparingly, in his Oxford [Col. 0097D] edition. It begins only with the third book of the *Divine Institutes* and continues to the end of the book *On the Workmanship of God*.

A three-hundred-year-old manuscript codex from the Library of the **COLLÈGE DE NAVARRE** in Paris, comprising the books of the *Divine Institutes*, *On the Anger of God*, and *On the Workmanship of God*.

A parchment **PALATINE CODEX**, containing the books of the *Divine Institutes*, whose variant readings Isaac Vossius supplied to Gallaeus.

A manuscript codex of no slight quality belonging to the Spaniard Francisco **PEÑA**, auditor of the Roman Rota, comprising the books of the *Divine Institutes*, *On the Anger of God*, and *On the Workmanship of God*. Isaeus collated it but did not indicate its age.

Manuscript codices of the Library of **THE MOST CHRISTIAN KING**: two are nine hundred years old and of the highest quality, the first no. 3735 and the second no. 3736, formerly from the library of the distinguished Puteanus. Joannes Opsopoeus once collated the latter in several Greek passages from the Sibyls, and the remainder was collated by Jean Le Brun. One, four hundred years old, no. 3976, and another, [Col. 0098A] three hundred years old, no. 3739, are of the highest quality; one is three hundred years old, no. 3737; another, three hundred years old, no. 3741, is of the highest quality; one, three hundred years old, no. 3740, has excellent paintings and also contains the *Epitome of the Divine Institutes*; another, no. 3977, was copied at Mantua in 1428; another, about three hundred years old, no. 3738, was copied from a good archetype; another, two hundred or two hundred and fifty years old, is no. 3742. Two others, about three hundred years old, nos. 3978 and 3979, contain only Lactantius’ books *On the Anger of God* and *On the Workmanship of God*, or *On the Formation of the Human Being*.

Jean-Baptiste Le Brun collated all these codices, as well as the Colbert manuscripts. We give their catalogue here in the order in which they are now arranged, namely:

**No. 1662.** A parchment codex formerly belonging to Claude Puteanus: the seven books of Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius’ *Institutes*, the book *On the Anger of God*, the book *On the Workmanship of God*, and the *Epitome of the Divine Institutes*; a folio codex written in the ninth century.

**No. 1663.** A parchment codex: seven books *On False Religion*; but the end of the sixth book and most of the seventh book of the *Divine Institutes* are missing; written in the ninth century, folio.

[Col. 0098B] **No. 1664.** A parchment codex: the seven books of Firmianus Lactantius *On False Religion*, and the same author’s book *On the Workmanship of God*, addressed to Demetrianus; written partly in the twelfth and partly in the fourteenth century, folio.

**No. 1665.** A parchment codex: the seven books of Firmianus Lactantius’ *Divine Institutes*; written toward the end of the fourteenth century, folio.

**No. 1666.** A paper codex: the seven books of Firmianus Lactantius’ *Divine Institutes against the Nations*; the book *On the Workmanship of God*, or *On the Formation of the Human Being*; written at Mantua in 1428, folio.

**No. 1667.** A paper codex, formerly Colbert’s: the seven books of Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius’ *Divine Institutes*; written in 1463, folio.

**No. 1668.** A codex partly of parchment and partly of paper: the seven books of Firmianus Lactantius’ *Divine Institutes*; written in the fifteenth century, folio.

**No. 1669.** A parchment codex, formerly Colbert’s: the [Col. 0098C] seven books of Firmianus Lactantius’ *Divine Institutes*. Appended are an excerpt from Book XX of Saint Augustine’s *City of God*; *On the Last Judgment*; *On the Anger of God*; and *On the Workmanship of God*. Written in the fifteenth century, folio.

**No. 1670.** A parchment codex, formerly Colbert’s: the seven books of Firmianus Lactantius’ *Divine Institutes*. Appended are a fragment *On the Last Judgment*, the book *On the Anger of God*, and the book *On the Workmanship of God*. Written in the fifteenth century, folio.

**No. 1671.** A parchment codex, formerly Puteanus’: Firmianus Lactantius’ *Divine Institutes*, *On the Anger of God*, *On the Workmanship of God*, the poem *On the Phoenix*, the poem *On the Resurrection*, and the *Epitome of the Divine Institutes*. Written in the fifteenth century, folio.

**No. 1672.** A parchment codex: the seven books of Firmianus Lactantius’ *Divine Institutes*. Two poems are prefixed, one by an anonymous author *On the Day of the Last Judgment*, and the other, attributed to Lactantius, *On the Day of the Lord’s Resurrection*. Appended are a fragment *On the Last Judgment* from Book XX of Saint Augustine’s *City of [Col. 0098D] God*, the book *On the Anger of God*, and *On the Workmanship of God*. Written in the fifteenth century, folio.

**No. 1673.** A parchment codex: the seven books of Firmianus Lactantius’ *Divine Institutes*.
