Notes by the Reverend Father Giovanni Maria Brasichelli, Master of the Sacred Apostolic Palace, are added throughout in the margin. Written toward the end of the fifteenth century, folio. (But Brasichelli’s notes published below were written at the beginning of the seventeenth century.)

**No. 1674.** A parchment codex: the seven books of Firmianus Lactantius’ *Divine Institutes*, whose beginning is missing; *On the Divine Anger*; *On the Workmanship of God*, or *On the Formation of the Human Being*; the poem *On the Phoenix*; *On the Day of God’s Resurrection*. Written toward the end of the fifteenth century, folio.

**No. 1675.** A paper codex: the seven books of Lactantius Firmianus’ *Divine Institutes against the Nations*; *On the Anger of God*; *On the Workmanship of God*; the *Epitome*; and a more recent fragment of the book *On Reason*. [Col. 0099A] Written in a crude hand, folio.

**No. 1676.** A paper codex: Firmianus Lactantius’ book *On the Anger of God*. Written in the fifteenth century, folio.

**No. 1677.** A parchment codex: Firmianus Lactantius’ books *On the Anger of God* and *On the Workmanship of God*. Written in the fifteenth century, folio.

**No. 1678.** A paper codex: three books on the errors of Firmianus Lactantius, by the theologian Antonio da Rho. Written in the fifteenth century, folio.

**No. 1679.** A paper codex, formerly Colbert’s: the same book by Antonio da Rho, folio.

**No. 1680.** A paper codex, formerly Colbert’s: the same book by Antonio da Rho, folio.

**No. 2623.** A parchment codex, formerly Colbert’s: the seven books of Firmianus Lactantius’ *Divine Institutes*, *On the Anger of God*, and *On the Workmanship of God*. Written at Bologna in Italy in 1436, quarto.

**No. 2624.** A parchment codex: the seven books of Firmianus Lactantius *On False Religion*, *On the Anger of God*, and *On the [Col. 0099B] Workmanship of God*. Written in the fifteenth century, quarto.

**No. 2625.** A codex partly of parchment and partly of paper, formerly Colbert’s: the seven books of Lactantius Firmianus’ *Divine Institutes*, *On the Anger of God*, and *On the Workmanship of God*. Written in the fifteenth century, quarto.

**No. 2626.** A parchment codex, formerly Colbert’s: the seven books of Lactantius Firmianus’ *Institutes*, *On the Workmanship of God*, or *On the Formation of the Human Being*, and *On the Anger of God*. Written in the fifteenth century, quarto.

**No. 2627.** A parchment codex, formerly Colbert’s: Lycius Caecilius’ book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, together with other writings. Written partly in the twelfth and partly in the eleventh century, quarto.

**No. 2967.** A parchment codex, formerly Baluze’s: the book *On the Anger of God*—the first seven chapters are missing—and *On the Workmanship of God*, or *On the Formation of the Human Being*. Written in the fifteenth century, octavo.

**No. 2968.** A parchment codex, formerly Colbert’s: Lactantius Firmianus, *On the Anger of God*; *On the Workmanship of God*, [Col. 0099C] or *On the Formation of the Human Being*. Written in 1439, octavo.

The **REIMMANN CODEX**, on paper, readily made available to Bunemann, from the fifteenth century.

A single parchment codex of the fourteenth century, held by the excellent library of His Eminence Cardinal de Rohan, whose princely generosity made it available to us. It contains only the seven books of the *Divine Institutes*, in which no Greek is found, as was usual in those times.

The **ROSTOCK** manuscript codex, which has very few variant readings for the books of the *Divine Institutes*. Gallaeus received these from Isaac Vossius.

The **SAINT-GERMAIN CODEX**, likewise on parchment, formerly belonging to Séguier, Chancellor of France, elegantly written and nearly four hundred years old; its first two pages are missing. It contains the seven books of the *Divine Institutes*; the *Epitome*, though incomplete; the books *On the Divine Anger* and *On the Workmanship of God*; and finally the poem *On the Phoenix*, with this notice: “These poems are said to be by Lactantius.” Greek is sometimes present, [Col. 0099D] and is written fairly elegantly.

Two **SORBONNE** codices, three hundred years old, nos. 271 and 272. At the end of the former one reads: “I, Johannes of Mainz, wrote [this] . . . , in the year 1448.” Each comprises Lactantius’ seven books of the *Divine Institutes* and the books *On the Anger of God* and *On the Workmanship of God*, or *On the Formation of the Human Being*.

A thousand-year-old manuscript codex at **TURIN**, belonging to the King of Sardinia, from which, through the good offices of the most learned Christoph Matthäus Pfaff, the complete *Epitome of the Divine Institutes*—apart from a few passages—was published at Paris in 1712; its first fifty-five chapters had been lacking in previous editions. The distinguished Pfaff sent me a copy of this codex through the most learned Johann Gabriel Schoepflin. Pfaff notes that there are, in addition, nine [Col. 0100A] manuscript codices of Lactantius’ works in the Turin Library, but he does not indicate their age.

A codex belonging to the most learned Michele Tommaso **TAXAQUET**, diligently searched and examined by Isaeus, who did not indicate its age. It contains the books of the *Divine Institutes*, *On the Anger of God*, and *On the Workmanship of God*.

I am very often surprised that learned men speak of the manuscript codex of **TAXAQUET**, since Taxaquet is none other than Michele Thomasius, the editor of Lactantius, who was a Majorcan from the Balearic Islands. In the middle of the sixteenth century, while studying canon and civil law at Bologna—as he himself says in his letter to Cardinal Granvelle prefixed to the Lactantius of 1570—he saw not only the very ancient codex of Lactantius so often extolled, but also another copy in the same Library of San Salvatore in Bologna, admittedly less ancient, but not inferior to that very ancient manuscript. Nicolás Antonio, in the *Bibliotheca Hispana Nova*, vol. II, folio, Rome, 1672, p. 117, resolves this little controversy. For he writes as follows: “Michele Thomasius Taxaquet of Majorca in the Balearic Islands devoted himself to imperial and [Col. 0100B] pontifical law, both at Lérida among the Catalans and at Bologna in Italy. His writings display his distinguished learning and erudition; namely, he corrected the works of Lactantius Firmianus and added brief notes. Antwerp, from the Plantin Press, 1570.” Nicolás Antonio lists other works by him; but I suspect I know how the error arose. Latino Latini wrote the following in his own hand at the beginning of the Aldine edition of Lactantius of 1535, in which he copied the variant readings of the Bolognese manuscripts: “I began,” he says, “to correct these books of Lactantius from variant readings of two codices, one of which, from the Library of San Salvatore in Bologna, was written in Lombardic letters and is of extraordinary antiquity; the other, likewise at Bologna, was most diligently searched and examined by the learned Michele Tommaso Taxaquet, a native of the island of Majorca in the Balearics. Taxaquet supplied me with those corrections while he was at Rome and held me in remarkable affection—such is the man’s kindness.” Moreover, the following words, in Latini’s own hand, are written at the end of the *Epitome* of Lactantius: “I first put my hand to this correction [Col. 0100C] at Rome, on 30 May 1558.” From this, beyond doubt, Isaeus and other learned men seized upon an occasion to distinguish Michele Tommaso Taxaquet from Michele Thomasius, the editor of Lactantius. But an error once committed by one person easily spread to many. Heumann, therefore, ought not to have been blamed for failing to distinguish or separate Michele Thomasius from Michele Tommaso Taxaquet. If, then, learned men have occasion to criticize the errors of scholars, I should wish it to be done soberly and modestly, and never for them to assail those scholars in a juvenile fashion.

A manuscript codex of the seven books of the *Divine Institutes*, purchased by **DE TOURNES** when he was preparing his Lyon edition of 1567 and the subsequent editions. In their margins he inserted certain variant readings from the manuscript codex, but did not indicate the manuscript’s age.

Twelve **VATICAN** manuscript codices preserved at Rome in the Vatican Library; their readings are cited throughout. Thomasius testifies that he diligently collated seven of them, and Isaeus five still others, together with the preceding seven manuscript codices. [Col. 0100D] But they did not see fit to tell us their age, just as Gallaeus did not indicate the age of the manuscripts whose variant readings he collected.

A manuscript codex about four hundred years old belonging to the Abbey of the Canons Regular of **SAINT-VICTOR, PARIS**, comprising the books of the *Divine Institutes*, *On the Anger of God*, and *On the Workmanship of God*. Dom Vion d’Hérouval, a canon regular and then prefect of the Library of Saint-Victor in Paris, kindly shared it with Jean Le Brun.

A manuscript codex belonging to the Canons of the Blessed Virgin Mary at **UTRECHT**, copied from an excellent archetype and containing the books of the *Divine Institutes*, *On the Anger of God*, and *On the Workmanship of God*; Gallaeus used it.

[Col. 0101]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING CATALOGUE

[Col. 0101A] Learned men have long complained that Joseph Isaeus, in his edition of Lactantius’ works, referred to twelve Vatican manuscript codices which he had collated, without indicating their age or the period in which they were thought to have been written. As I was traversing the same course, it occurred to me not only to petition the Patron of letters and learned men, but to obtain from him the favor that, through his assistance, I might acquire information about the manuscript codices of Lactantius preserved in the Vatican Library. His Eminence Cardinal [Col. 0102A] Passionei therefore kindly undertook this task, not only because of his singular affection for all scholars, but also because of the longstanding goodwill with which he has embraced me for nearly forty years. Here, then, is that very catalogue, as it was readily supplied to His Eminence the Cardinal by the distinguished and most learned Giuseppe Simone Assemani, custodian of the Vatican Library. Learned reader, I hope you will make use of it, though not without a grateful disposition toward the Patron of learned men.

[Col. 0101]

## CATALOGUE OF THE MANUSCRIPT CODICES OF LUCIUS CAECILIUS FIRMIANUS LACTANTIUS PRESERVED AT ROME IN THE APOSTOLIC VATICAN LIBRARY

### Those Which Joseph Isaeus Testifies That He Collated

[Col. 0101B]

**I. VATICAN CODEX**, shelfmark no. 215, on parchment, containing 180 written folios. It contains the following: the seven books of Lactantius Firmianus’ *Divine Institutes*, fols. 1–148; one book by the same author, *On the Anger of God*, fols. 149–165; one book by the same author, *On the Workmanship of God*, fols. 165–180. No date is recorded, but it appears to have been written around the year 1480, so far as one may conjecture from the painting ornamented with minium prefixed to the codex.

**II. VATICAN CODEX**, shelfmark no. 216, on parchment, containing 264 written folios, completed on 24 August 1481, as is noted by the copyist on the final line of folio 264. It contains: the seven books of Lactantius’ *Divine Institutes*, fol. 1; *On the Anger of God*, fol. 216; *On the Workmanship of God*, fol. 235; the *Epitome of the Divine Institutes* in the form then current, whose opening is “For if the beginning,” or rather, “For if Justice,” fol. 254.

**III. VATICAN CODEX**, shelfmark no. 217, on parchment, containing 146 written folios. No date has been affixed [Col. 0101C], but it appears to be of the same age as the preceding two codices. It contains: the seven books of Lactantius’ *Divine Institutes*, fol. 1; *On the Anger of God*, fol. 123 verso; *On the Workmanship of God*, fol. 135 verso.

**IV. VATICAN CODEX**, no. 218, on parchment, containing 165 written folios, produced under Pope Sixtus IV, whose arms are prefixed to the codex on fol. 1. He occupied the Apostolic See of Rome from 9 August 1471 to 12 August 1484. The codex contains: the seven books of the *Divine Institutes*, fol. 1; *On the Anger of God*, fol. 134 verso; *On the Workmanship of God*, fol. 150.

**V. VATICAN CODEX**, no. 219, containing 180 written folios, produced under Pope Julius II, whose golden image is prefixed to the codex on fol. 1, with these words: “Julius II, Supreme Pontiff”; on parchment. He occupied the Apostolic See from 1 November 1503 to [Col. 0102B] 21 February 1513. The codex contains: the seven books of the *Divine Institutes*, fol. 1; *On the Anger of God*, fol. 133; *On the Workmanship of God*, fol. 166 verso.

**VI. VATICAN CODEX**, no. 220, on parchment, containing 171 written folios, produced before 1447. For on fol. 172 there is a note by a certain Valterius, who testifies that he received twelve ducats in cash as the price of this codex in the year of the Lord 1447, on 12 December. It contains: the seven books of the *Divine Institutes*, fol. 1; *On the Anger of God*, fol. 153; *On the Workmanship of God*, fol. 166 verso.

**VII. VATICAN CODEX**, no. 221, on parchment, containing 281 written folios, produced around 1450, as may be inferred from the paintings and images prefixed to it. It contains: the seven books of the *Divine Institutes*, fol. 1; *On the Anger of God*, fol. 252; an opening beginning, “Concerning the greatest necessities,” which exhorts Demetrianus to devote himself more diligently to piety and to contempt for the world—Isaeus did not publish this letter; *On the Workmanship of God*, fol. 267, as in Isaeus.

**VIII. VATICAN CODEX**, no. 222, on paper, containing 275 folios, produced on 21 December [Col. 0102C] 1462, as is noted on the final folio. It contains: the seven books of the *Divine Institutes*, fol. 1; *On the Anger of God*, fol. 225; *On the Workmanship of God*, fol. 252.

**IX. VATICAN CODEX**, no. 223, containing 217 folios, written in folio on parchment by the hand of Johann Hornsen, a member of the household of Lord Corrado of Montepulciano, as is noted on the final folio. Corrado’s arms are prefixed on fol. 1 with these words: “A. Corrado of Montepulciano.” It contains: the seven books of the *Divine Institutes*, fol. 1. At the end, on fol. 195, is this note: “Here end the seven books of the *Divine Institutes* of Firmianus Lactantius (thus), addressed to Emperor Constantine and against the Nations, by the hand of Johann Hornsen, the unworthy little servant of the distinguished Lord Corrado of Montepulciano (thus), in the Apostolic Palace, in the time of the Most Serene Lord Peter, Lord Nicholas, by Divine Providence Pope Nicholas V, in the year 1454, the seventh year of his pontificate.” *On the Anger of God*, addressed to Donatus, fol. 195 verso.

[Col. 0103A] **X. VATICAN CODEX**, no. 224, on parchment, containing 125 folios. It formerly belonged to the Monastery of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme at Rome, as is noted on fol. 1. It contains the seven books of the *Divine Institutes*, fols. 1–118.

**XI. VATICAN CODEX**, no. 225, on parchment, containing 135 folios, without a date; but from the script it is inferred that it was written around 1460. It contains the seven books of the *Divine Institutes*, fols. 1–135.

**XII. VATICAN CODEX**, no. 226, on paper, containing 187 folios. It belonged to Antonio de Pichetis, a most expert canon lawyer, as is noted on the final folio. It was produced at Pavia on 4 December 1441, as is recorded on fol. 180.

## VATICAN CODICES WHICH NEITHER JOSEPH NOR SIGISMUND ISAEUS SAW FOR THEIR EDITION OF FIRMIANUS LACTANTIUS

**1. VATICAN CODEX**, no. 2876, paper, quarto, written in a more recent hand: fol. 53, a fragment from Book VII of Lactantius’ *Divine Institutes*.

[Col. 0103B] **2. VATICAN CODEX**, no. 3152, paper, quarto. Fol. 21: verses of Lactantius *On the Festal Day of the Lord’s Resurrection*. Opening:

> Hail, festal day, venerable throughout all ages,  
> On which God conquered hell and holds the stars, etc.

Already in 1570 Thomasius had warned, in his edition of Lactantius, that these verses were by Venantius Fortunatus. See what we note on p. 270, vol. II of the present edition. Fol. 23: a poem by the same author, *On the Birth and Death of the Phoenix*:

> There is a blessed place, remote in the farthest East,  
> Where the greatest gate of the eternal sky lies open.

**3. VATICAN CODEX**, no. 3381, on parchment, folio, from the books of Fulvio Orsini: Firmianus Lactantius’ exposition of Papinius Statius’ *Thebaid*.—Prologue, or preface: “It is asked in what period this Statius lived; it is certainly established that he lived in the time of Emperor Vespasian,” etc. “Fraternal battle-lines, and kingdoms exchanged by impious brothers”: [Col. 0103C] “because the brothers had agreed that they would reign in alternating years,” etc. It consists of 162 folios.

Learned men know that this exposition of Statius is not by Firmianus Lactantius, but by a certain grammarian—namely Luctatius, or Luctatius Placidus, or even Placidus Lactantius—under whose name certain glosses on Ovid’s *Metamorphoses* also survive.

**4. VATICAN CODEX**, no. 5134, fol. 110. Verses of Lactantius *On the Phoenix*: “There is a blessed place, remote in the farthest East,” etc. Written on paper, like codex 315, fol. 28.

**5. VATICAN CODEX**, no. 5346: Lactantius’ elegy *On the Phoenix*, fol. 21: “There is a blessed place, remote in the farthest East” (as above).

## CODICES NOW IN THE VATICAN, FORMERLY PALATINE

[Col. 0103D] **1. PALATINE CODEX 161**, parchment, twelfth century; it consists of 236 folios: the seven books of Firmianus Lactantius’ *Divine Institutes*—the beginning of the first book is missing; *On the Workmanship of God*, fol. 236—the end is missing.

**2. PALATINE CODEX 162**, parchment, recent, folio; it consists of 213 folios: the seven books of the *Divine Institutes*, fol. 1; *On the Workmanship of the Human Being*, beginning “By no means,” fol. 193; *On the Birth and Death of the Phoenix*, beginning “There is a place in the first …,” etc., fol. 209.

**3. PALATINE CODEX 163**, parchment, recent, 261 folios: *On the Anger of God*, beginning “I have often observed,” fol. 1; the seven books of the *Divine Institutes*, fol. 21; *On the Workmanship of the Human Being*, beginning [Col. 0104A] “By no means,” fol. 233; index of Lactantius’ chapters, fol. 253.

**4. PALATINE CODEX 164**, on paper, folio, 190 folios: the seven books of the *Divine Institutes*, fol. 1; *On the Workmanship of the Human Being*, fol. 157; *On the Anger of God*, fol. 174.

## LACTANTIUS CODICES OF THE URBINO COLLECTION OF THE VATICAN LIBRARY
1. **URBINAS CODEX 58**, an ancient parchment manuscript, folio, 282 leaves: the seven books of the *Divine Institutes*, fol. 1; *On the Workmanship of God*, fol. 234; *On the Wrath of God*, fol. 258; the poem *On the Phoenix*: “There is a place,” etc., fol. 278; the poem *On the Resurrection of Christ*: “Hail, festive day,” etc., fol. 281.

2. **URBINAS CODEX 361**: Lactantius’ commentaries on Papinius Statius’ *Thebaid* and *Achilleid*: “It is asked at what time,” as in Vatican codex 3381. On parchment; it consists of 138 leaves.

## VATICAN CODICES OF THE ALEXANDRINE ROYAL LIBRARY

That is, from the library of Christina Alexandra, Queen of the Swedes.

[Col. 0104B]

1. **ROYAL-ALEXANDRINE CODEX 149**, folio, parchment, written on the sixteenth day of January in the year of the Lord 1434, at Bologna, as is noted on the final leaf. It had belonged to the library of the German cardinal and prince von Dietrichstein, as is noted on fol. 1. It consists of 244 leaves, containing: the seven books of Lactantius’ *Divine Institutes*, fol. 1; *On the Wrath of God*: “I have observed,” fol. 207; *On the Workmanship of God*: “However little,” fol. 226. At the end the following notes were made by the copyist: “1436, February 3: this work was corrected. February 20, 1438: it was corrected a second time. 1439, January 8, at the third hour: I completed my study of it. 1441, February 6: I again completed my study of it, correcting even its orthography.”

2. **ROYAL-ALEXANDRINE CODEX 217**, quarto, parchment. It had belonged to Gerardus Joannes Vossius, as is noted on fol. 1, [Col. 0104C] and afterward to Alexander Petavius, no. 71, in 1656, as is likewise stated there: *On the Wrath of God*: “I have observed,” fol. 1; *On the Workmanship of God*, fol. 25.

3. **ROYAL-ALEXANDRINE CODEX 265**, parchment, consisting of 189 leaves. It contains: the seven books of the *Divine Institutes*, fol. 1; *On the Wrath of God*: “I have observed,” fol. 161; *On the Workmanship of God*, fol. 176.

4. **ROYAL-ALEXANDRINE CODEX 268**, paper. It consists of 155 leaves and was written by Gotardus Stella, as is noted on the final leaf. It belonged to Nicolaus Heinsius, and afterward to Petavius in 1656, as is observed on fol. 1: the seven books of the *Divine Institutes*, fol. 1 (the beginning is missing); *On the Wrath of God*: “I have observed,” fol. 133; *On the Workmanship of God*: “However little leisure I may have,” fol. 145.

5. **ROYAL-ALEXANDRINE CODEX 276**, ancient parchment manuscript, consisting of 241 leaves: the seven books of the *Divine Institutes*: “To one of great and excellent,” fol. 1 through fol. 219.

6. **ROYAL-ALEXANDRINE CODEX 1151**, paper, written by Philip Scholarius of Paris on October 6 in the year [Col. 0104D] of the Lord 1506, as is noted on fol. 108: the seven books of the *Divine Institutes*: “To one of great and excellent,” fol. 58 (incomplete); *On the Wrath of God*: “I have observed,” fols. 77–98.

7. **ROYAL-ALEXANDRINE CODEX 1939**, parchment, written under Pope Nicholas V, as is evident from his coat of arms on the verso of fol. 2. It had belonged to the Theatine Fathers of St. Sylvester, as the inscription placed on fol. 1 shows; it was brought into the Vatican Library by Clement XI. It consists of 289 leaves: the seven books of the *Divine Institutes*: “To one of great and excellent,” fol. 2; *On the Wrath of God*: “I have often observed,” fol. 244; *On the Workmanship of Man*: “However little leisure I may have,” fol. 268.

[Col. 0103]

## VARIOUS EDITIONS OF LACTANTIUS

[Col. 0103D] *The Seven Books of Lactantius Firmianus’ Divine Institutes against the Gentiles, together with His Single Book to Donatus on* [Col. 0104D] *the Wrath of God, along with the Book on the Workmanship of Man, to Demetrianus*, folio, at the venerable monastery [Col. 0105A] of Subiaco, in the year of the Lord 1465, the second year of the pontificate of Pope Paul II, the thirteenth indiction, on the third-to-last day of October. This edition is sometimes called the Roman edition; Dom Bernard de Montfaucon erroneously assigned it to the year 1461 in his *Italian Diary*. It is, moreover, extremely rare. At Rome it is found in the Barberini Library; at Mainz, in the literary collection of the most noble chapter of Mainz; at Paris, in the collection of the most distinguished Claude de Boze, member of the French Academy and the Academy of Inscriptions. Greek is sometimes, though not always, printed in this edition, and it appears to have been taken from only a single manuscript copy. The title of Book I was written by hand. Because this edition was, in the judgment of some, rather inelegant, the Cambridge editor thought it to be a manuscript codex; but the **CAMBRIDGE MANUSCRIPT CODEX** mentioned in the preceding catalogue is different from the printed edition.

—Folio, Rome, in the house of Pietro de’ Massimi, by Conrad Sweynheym, 1468. It survives both in the Royal Library at Paris and in M. de Boze’s collection. It also survives at Rome in the library of His Eminence Cardinal Passionei.

[Col. 0105B]

—Folio, Rome, with a preface by Andrea, bishop of Aleria, by the same Conrad Sweynheym, 1470. It survives in the Royal Library at Paris. It differs from the earlier edition of 1468.

—Folio, Rome, 1471. Johann Ludolph Bünemann saw and collated this edition.

—Folio, Venice, 1472, which Gallaeus wrongly thought to be the first of all. Isaeus, Heumann, and Bünemann saw it.

—Folio, without place or year, but printed in Germany in a crude typeface, dating from the very infancy of the typographical art. His Eminence Cardinal Passionei possesses it at Rome. I found it nowhere else, either in German libraries or in those of our fellow Frenchmen.

—Folio, Rome, 1474. It survives in the Royal Library at Paris; it also survived in the Carpzov Library, from which Christoph Cellarius had obtained it. It also survived in the Hulsius Library.

—Folio, Rome, 1475. Johann Albert Fabricius commends this edition, although Bünemann thinks that it does not exist. [Col. 0105C]

—Folio, Rostock, 1476. Heumann and Bünemann diligently collated it. Blank spaces were left for the Greek passages.

—Folio, Venice, by Joseph of Cologne and Johann Menthen of Gerretzem, 1478. This edition is fairly accurate, and the Greek is printed in it. It survives in the library of the royal Abbey of St. Geneviève, and Heumann used it. Because of the name Joseph of Cologne, the Hulsius catalogue erroneously cites this edition under the year 1478 as though it had been printed at Cologne.

—Folio, Venice, by Andrea de Paltasichis of Cattaro and Bonino de Boninis, 1478. It presents the cited Greek, though in a crude typeface; the *Epitome* was printed in it. It is at Rome in the excellent library of the same His Eminence Cardinal Passionei; Bünemann also possesses it.

—Folio, Venice, by Bernardino de Benali, 1483. Fabricius, Maittaire, and others commend it; Bünemann, however, doubts that it ever existed.

—Folio, Venice, by Theodorus de Ragazonibus of Asola, 1390 (an error for 1490). Isaeus, Gallaeus, Carpzovius, and Cellarius possessed it; [Col. 0105D] the distinguished Claude de Boze possesses it.

—Folio, Venice, by Vincenzo Benali, 1493. It survives in the library of the royal Abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.

—Folio, Venice, 1494, possessed by Carpzovius.

—Folio, Venice, by Simon Bevilacqua, under the supervision of Andrea, bishop of Aleria, 1497. Bünemann thinks it was copied from the edition of 1470.

—Small quarto, Paris, 1500, with annotations by Gilles de Delft.

—Folio, Venice, under the supervision of Giovanni da Tridino, 1502. I myself possessed this edition and sent it to Jean Le Brun in 1709.

—Folio, Venice, under the supervision of the same Giovanni da Tridino, 1509. Carpzovius possessed it.

—Small quarto, Paris, corrected by Gilles of Maizières, 1509. He is the same man who had corrected the edition of 1500.

—Folio, Venice, corrected by Janus Parrhasius, 1510.

—Octavo, Antwerp, 1510.

—Quarto, Paris, 1511.

—Folio, Venice, 1511, by Giovanni da Tridino: it is the same as the Parrhasian edition of 1510; Isaeus and [Col. 0106A] Gallaeus used it.

—Quarto, Paris, by Jean Petit and Nicolas des Prés, 1513, based upon the correction of Gilles of Maizières of Delft. The following title is prefixed to it: *The Delightful Works of Lactantius*, etc.

—Octavo, Florence, the Giunti press, based upon the correction of Mariano Tucci, 1513. The Royal Library possesses it, and Isaeus, Gallaeus, and Heumann used it.

—Octavo, Venice, Aldus, based upon the correction of Giovanni Battista Egnazio of Venice, 1515.

—Folio, Paris, 1521.

—Folio, Venice, reviewed by Janus Parrhasius, 1521. We have seen this edition in the Royal Library; the Greek in it is printed with reasonable accuracy. It is the same as the Parrhasian edition of 1510.

—Quarto, Basel, Cratander, 1521. It was taken chiefly from the Aldine edition, but is nevertheless fairly well corrected.

—Folio or quarto, Basel, Cratander, 1523. Gallaeus said that he used it; Bünemann, however, contends that it is identical with the edition of 1521.

—Quarto, Basel, Cratander, 1524. Bünemann used it in correcting Lactantius.

—Folio, Paris, 1525.

—Folio, Basel, Cratander, 1532. The Cambridge editor used it. Nicolas Lenglet supplied Jean Le Brun with a copy of this edition. [Col. 0106B]

—Octavo, Lyon, 1532.

—Octavo, Antwerp, Jan Grapheus, 1532, with Erasmus’ notes on the book *On the Workmanship of God*. This is the edition which we formerly sent to Jean Le Brun. Heumann possessed it.

—Quarto, Basel, 1534.

—Octavo, Venice, Aldus, based upon the correction made by Onorato Fascitelli of Venice from the Monte Cassino codices, 1535. Thomasius, Isaeus, and Gallaeus used it; in its own day it was the leading edition.

—Octavo, Venice, Paolo Manuzio, 1538.

—Octavo, Cologne, 1539.

—Octavo, Antwerp, Gymnicus, 1539. Erasmus of Rotterdam corrected it in part; his annotations on the book *On the Workmanship of God* appear in it.

—Octavo, Lyon, Gryphius, based upon Fascitelli’s correction, 1541: quite elegant.

—Octavo, Lyon, Gryphius, based upon the same correction, 1543. This edition is less accurate.

—Folio, Cologne, 1544, with notes by Desiderius Erasmus on the treatise *On the Workmanship of God*. This is an excellent and very accurately corrected edition.

—Quarto, Basel, 1545; according to others, 1546.

—Sextodecimo, Lyon, de Tournes, based upon Fascitelli’s correction, [Col. 0106C] 1548. An elegant and handsome edition.

—Sextodecimo, Lyon, de Tournes, 1553, based upon the same correction by Fascitelli.

—Octavo, Antwerp, 1553. This edition is commended by Élie Dupin in his *Ecclesiastical Library*.

—Octavo, Antwerp, Gymnicus, 1555, with Erasmus’ annotations on the book *On the Workmanship of God*.

—Sextodecimo, Lyon, de Tournes, 1556, based upon Fascitelli’s correction: quite handsome.

—Octavo, Antwerp, 1556.

—Folio, Basel, from the press of Heinrich Petri, 1556, where, according to Élie Dupin and Dom Rémy Ceillier, it was published twice. It was indeed published in Johann Herold’s heresiology. Claude Ceillier, however, thinks it was also published separately in that same year, 1556.

—Folio, Basel, Heinrich Petri, 1559.

—Sextodecimo, Paris, Jérôme de Marnef, 1561, based upon Fascitelli’s recension; not very handsome.

—Folio, Basel, with commentaries by Sixtus Betuleius, 1563. It does not entirely meet with the approval of scholars, although Betuleius accumulated in it much material—perhaps more than was proper.

—Octavo, Paris, 1563.

—Sextodecimo, Paris, 1565.

—Sextodecimo, Lyon, de Tournes, [Col. 0106D] 1567: quite elegant, and corrected according to a manuscript codex which de Tournes had acquired for himself.

—Octavo, Antwerp, 1568.

—Octavo, Antwerp, Steelsius, 1570, with Erasmus’ notes on the treatise *On the Workmanship of God*.

—Octavo, Antwerp, from the Plantin press, 1570. Quite elegant, based upon the correction made by Michael Thomasius from two Bolognese and seven Vatican codices. Gronovius was less pleased with it, nor did it entirely please Isaeus, who observes that Thomasius applied a healing hand to certain passages of Lactantius’ text, but left most—and almost countless—passages completely untouched. He therefore informs us that he corrected more than three hundred errors in Thomasius’ text, so as to render Lactantius purer and more complete.

—Octavo, Antwerp, 1579.

—Sextodecimo, Lyon, de Tournes, 1579, corrected according to two manuscript codices.

—Octavo, Antwerp, 1580.

—Sextodecimo, Lyon, de Tournes, 1586.

—Octavo, Antwerp, Plantin, 1587. This is the second edition of Thomasius’ correction; nothing in it, however, was altered. [Col. 0107A]

—Octavo, Lyon, de Tournes, 1587. This edition was corrected according to many manuscript codices and also according to various notes sent by Jacques Cujas.

—Folio, Paris, 1589, in the *Library of the Fathers*.

—Sextodecimo, Lyon, de Tournes, 1594. It does not differ from the edition of 1587.

—Octavo, Paris, 1589, based upon Thomasius’ recension.

—Sextodecimo, Lyon, Thomas Soubron, 1594; fairly well corrected, though less elegant.

—Colonia Allobrogum (that is, Geneva), de Tournes, 1613; corrected from two manuscripts by Jacques Cujas. Gallaeus values it highly; Isaeus nevertheless asserts that he observed Lactantius’ text to be corrupt everywhere in it.

—Sextodecimo, Cologne, 1613, according to Bünemann. Perhaps the same as the preceding edition.

—Sextodecimo, Lyon, 1615 and 1616.

—Sextodecimo, Geneva, 1630.

—Folio, Lyon, 1642.

—Folio, Cesena, 1646. Prepared and corrected by Giuseppe Isaeus, and emended according to two Bolognese and twelve Vatican manuscript codices.

—Folio, Rome, Mascardi, 1650, based upon Isaeus’ correction. It is not, [Col. 0107B] however, a new edition, but precisely the same as the Cesena edition, only the title page having been altered.

—Octavo, Leiden, based upon the correction of Antonius Thysius, 1652; quite handsome, but of little weight among scholars. This edition is corrupt in chapter 15 of Book I, where Plato is discussed.

—Octavo, with selected notes by various scholars, edited by Servatius Gallaeus, Leiden, 1660. It is quite elegant. Gallaeus appropriated almost all the notes from Betuleius’ edition and from Salmasius’ papers; he had, however, collated certain manuscript codices, whose variant readings were added at the end of the book. Since it is not accurately corrected throughout, Jean Le Brun possessed annotations upon it by Pierre Francius, professor of history and eloquence at the Amsterdam Athenaeum. We have likewise used these in our present edition.

—Octavo, Oxford, based upon the recension of Thomas Spark and with certain brief notes by him, 1684. It is elegant and was corrected according to five manuscript codices. The book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* was published in it. We, like Jean Le Brun, have used this edition.

—Octavo, [Col. 0107C] Cambridge, 1685. Quite elegant, but copied from the Thomasian edition. The editor nevertheless used two manuscript codices, whose variant readings he placed before Lactantius’ books. The book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* is likewise found in it. Albert Fabricius, however, wrongly thinks that this editor mistook the Subiaco copy for a manuscript codex.

—Octavo, based upon the recension of Christoph Cellarius, Leipzig, 1698. Although corrected, it is not wholly beyond reproach; nevertheless, it contains certain notes of no slight importance.

—Octavo, based upon the recension of Johann Georg Walch, Leipzig, 1715. He was the first to publish the complete *Epitome* with Lactantius’ other works. A learned inquiry into Lactantius’ life and style is prefixed. Scholars find something wanting in that edition. What wonder? Could the distinguished Walch, who had scarcely reached his twentieth year, display in editing Lactantius the same critical skill and learning that he now possesses at the age of fifty? At the same age, would Walch’s critics have produced—I do not say a more learned—but an equally learned work?

—Octavo, based upon the correction of [Col. 0107D] Christoph August Heumann, Göttingen, 1736. This edition is far more perfect than its predecessors. Cellarius’ text was retained in it, though with certain alterations; and new and learned notes were everywhere added to those of Cellarius. We have read this edition very attentively and have used it.

—Octavo, based upon the correction of Johann Ludolph Bünemann, Leipzig, 1739. Our edition of Lactantius was already hastening toward completion when I received this excellent work from the very learned Johann Daniel Schoepflin, professor of history and eloquence at the Academy of Strasbourg. It is astonishing how much labor and study the distinguished Bünemann devoted to editing Lactantius. We have gathered notes from him, including even those opposed to our own opinions, so that this new edition might, as it were at a single glance, encompass all the others.

**Note.** In the catalogue of the various editions of Lactantius I omitted those included in the *Libraries* [Col. 0108A] *of the Holy Fathers*, among whom Lactantius’ works occupy no insignificant place. Those collections of the Fathers, moreover, were published at least six times, whether at Cologne, Paris, or Lyon. These editions were not corrected according to manuscript codices, but copied from some previously printed exemplar.

Lucius Caecilius Lactantius Firmianus, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, edited with annotations by the distinguished Étienne Baluze, octavo, Paris, 1679, in volume II of the *Miscellanies*.
