# [THE FIRST BOOK OF LACTANTIUS]

[Col. 0109]

## ANALYSIS OF LACTANTIUS’ FIRST BOOK

### SUBJECT

[Col. 0109B]

The general proposition of the first and second books is that the religions of the gods are false. The particular divisions of the first book are four: the preface, chapter 1; the assertion of providence, chapter 2; the assertion of the one true God, chapters 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7; and the refutation of the gods of the Gentiles, from that point to the end.

The preface contains three things:

The reasons for this work.

The address (*προσφώνησις*) to Constantine the Great.

A restatement of the principal reason for this work, where the reason why so few assent to religion is explained.

Five reasons are enumerated by which Lactantius the orator was moved to undertake this discussion of religion.

First: He wishes to aid those to whom the true religion is wholly unknown. Many of them have sought the truth, but in vain, because the mystery of the supreme God cannot be comprehended by intellect and one’s own senses.

[Col. 0109C]

Second: He wishes to aid those to whom the true religion has become known in some measure, but who either despise it, as the learned do, because it lacks capable defenders; or hate it, as the unlearned do, because of the austerity inherent in it.

Third: Because one who imparts the knowledge of speaking well renders less service to human affairs than one who teaches people to live piously and innocently.

Fourth: Because the greatest orators devoted the final stage of life to philosophy; therefore I may more justly devote it to theology.

Fifth: Prudent men have published *Institutes of Civil Law*; it is therefore better that I should pursue *Divine Institutes*.

An address (*προσφώνησις*) to Emperor Constantine, in which he congratulates him upon his recognition of the truth.

He repeats the principal reason for undertaking the discussion—to call people away from their errors—and adds the reason why so few assent to the true religion: [Col. 0109D] because many harden themselves against manifest truth and do not consider why they were born; for this, ignorance of oneself, is the cause of depravity.

The second part of the first book treats the question of providence: Does providence exist? Lactantius writes that this thesis does not require an extensive demonstration, both because the Stoics and Cicero sufficiently and acutely refuted the negative position, and because all peoples agree on this one matter: that providence exists. Chapter 2.

[Col. 0110B] In the third part he asserts that there is one God, the creator and ruler of this world, and confirms this by arguments and authorities.

### BY ARGUMENTS

Because God is perfect. Therefore there can be only one.

Because God admits of no destruction. Therefore neither does he admit of division.

Because one God was able to make the world. Therefore he is also able to govern it.

Because, just as military affairs cannot stand except under a single commander, so too this highest order of things cannot stand unless the power of its individual parts is referred to a single providence.

Because to say that everything is ruled by the decision of many is the same as if someone asserted that many minds exist within a single body, on the ground that the ministries of its members are many and various, although one mind alone governs them all.

[Col. 0110C]

**Objection:** There are indeed many gods, but there is one supreme Ruler.

**Reply:** If they are not all equal, then they are not all gods.

### BY AUTHORITIES

**Of the prophets.** The prophets, who were very numerous, proclaim one God and speak of one God.

**Objection:** We do not admit their testimony; these are human voices.

**Reply:** Their prophecies have been fulfilled; therefore they were neither madmen nor liars, because they restrained others from every kind of fraud. The desire to fabricate and lie belongs to those who seek wealth and desire gains, something far removed from those holy men. Some of them were princes or even kings, against whom no suspicion of fraud can arise.

**Of the poets:** for Orpheus calls the true God *πρωτόγονον* (“first-born”). Virgil and Ovid likewise acknowledge God as the maker of the world.

[Col. 0110D]

**Of the philosophers:** Thales, Pythagoras, Anaxagoras, Antisthenes, Cleanthes and Anaximenes, Chrysippus, Zeno, Aristotle, Plato, Cicero, and Seneca.

**Of Hermes Trismegistus:** *Ὁ δὲ Θεὸς εἷς· ὁ δὲ εἷς ὀνόματος οὐ προσδέεται· ἔστι γὰρ ὁ ὢν ἀνώνυμος*—“God is one; and the One has no need of a name, for He Who Is is nameless.”

**Of the Sibyls,** all of whom proclaim one God.

**Of Apollo,** who, when asked what God was, replied: *αὐτοφυής* (“self-generated” or “self-existent”).

[Col. 0111] In the fourth part of the book he first refutes the common religions of the Gentiles, from chapter 8 through chapter 20, and then the religions peculiar to the Romans, from chapter 20 to the end. He proves that the religions [Col. 0112] of the gods are false because those whom the Gentiles worshipped as gods were born at definite times, lived most wickedly, and finally underwent the law common to all mortals.

[Col. 0111]

# BOOK ONE OF THE DIVINE INSTITUTES OF LUCIUS CAECILIUS FIRMIANUS LACTANTIUS

## ON THE FALSE RELIGION OF THE GODS (C)

### Preface: HOW GREAT THE KNOWLEDGE OF TRUTH IS AND ALWAYS HAS BEEN

[Col. 0111A] Men of great and excellent intellect, when they had devoted themselves wholly to learning, [Col. 0111A]

> **Note: [Col. 0111A] Notes of Various Scholars on columns 111–112**
>
> **Had devoted themselves (*dedissent*).** From the Leipzig and Gotha manuscripts; this is more correct and harmonious than *dedidissent*, as many others have it. The elegant manuscript of His Eminence Cardinal de Rohan has *dedissent*.
>
> **Had devoted themselves (*dedidissent*).**—Cellarius reads *dedissent*, which Reimann’s manuscript also has, since it seemed more rounded. But the reading of most other codices and editions—the first Subiaco edition, the Roman editions, the Venetian editions of 1471 and 1472, both editions of 1478, the Rostock edition of 1476, and very many more—*dedidissent*, comes closer to Cicero, [Col. 0111B] whom Lactantius generally reproduces. *On Duties* I.21: “Those who, being of excellent intellect, devoted themselves to learning.” *On the Orator* III.15: “Men of the most excellent intellect devoted themselves to that pursuit.” *On the Orator* I.3: “To devote themselves wholly to literary study.” Nor does *penitus dedidissent* (“had devoted themselves wholly”) seem less rounded than Lactantius, Book IV, chapter 13, *penitus nescientem* (“wholly ignorant”), and Book VII, chapter 5, *se voluptatibus dediderunt* (“they devoted themselves to pleasures”). De Tournes, 158 [probably 1558; text uncertain], and 1613 read *penitius dedidissent* (“had devoted themselves more deeply”). **BÜNEMANN.**
>
> **To amassing riches.** The manuscripts and fifteenth-century editions read *quam struendis*; but Parrhasius, Cratander, the Giunti, Aldine, Gymnicus, Gryphius, Paris 1513, and Isaeus read *quam aut struendis* (“than either to amassing”); Reimann, Venice 1472, and the de Tournes editions read *quam in struendis* (“than in amassing”). The former was adopted by Heumann; the latter is contrary to Lactantius’ usage, since he always constructs *inhaerere* with the dative. **BÜNEMANN.**
>
> **Because.** The Rohan manuscript reads “since.”
>
> **Can be made more just.** We have thus restored the text from the Rohan manuscript, all the manuscript codices, the old Roman editions, [Col. 0112A] and two Leipzig manuscripts. The other printed editions read “can become.”
>
> **Can be made more just.** Thus the Gotha, Wolfenbüttel, Leipzig, Utrecht, Giunti, Caucchius, Cambridge, Gronovius, and Reimann manuscripts and editions, and the first Subiaco, Roman, Venice 1471 and 1472, Rostock, Paris 1513, and de Tournes editions. It is also preferable in light of Book III, chapter 12: “that anyone can be made happy”; Book IV, chapter 3: “and makes them better”; and Cicero, *On Ends* III.3: “a happy life is produced by virtue.” **BÜNEMANN.**
>
> [Col. 0112B]
>
> **Desired (*cupiverunt*).** Thus most books, more fully; but Parrhasius, the Giunti, Aldus, Cratander, Gymnicus, and Isaeus read *cupierunt*, which in this and similar cases is smoother and closer to Cicero and Lactantius. **BÜNEMANN.**
>
> **And to such a degree.** This is absent from the Rohan manuscript, and rightly so.
>
> **That some cast aside.** Namely Bias, Democritus, etc. See Valerius Maximus, Book VII, chapter 2, and Book VIII, chapter 7. He will speak more fully of each of these in Book III, which is *On False Wisdom*.
>
> **Naked and unencumbered, they might follow naked truth.** Thus Jerome, Letter 13, to Paulinus: “Following the naked cross naked, you ascend Jacob’s ladder more unencumbered and lighter.” In many printed editions and in several manuscripts, “virtue” and “of virtue” are read, rather than “truth” and “of truth.” But in the Oxford manuscripts cited by Spark, “truth” and “of truth” are written, as they also are in the manuscripts used by the editor of the Cologne edition of 1544. Moreover, this chapter does not concern virtue but truth, as may be seen a few lines below; because truth, Lactantius says, cannot be comprehended by intellect and one’s own senses.

they directed whatever labor could be expended—disregarding all private and public occupations—to the pursuit of investigating truth. They considered it far nobler to investigate and know the rational account of human and divine things than to cling either to amassing riches or to accumulating honors. Since these things are frail and earthly [Col. 0112A] and pertain solely to the adornment of the body, no one can thereby be made better or more just. Those men were indeed most worthy of knowing the truth, which they so greatly desired to know; and desired it to such a degree that they placed it before all other things. For it is well established both that some cast aside their family property and that they renounced every pleasure, so that, themselves naked and unencumbered, they might follow truth alone and naked. So great among them was the power of the name and authority of truth [Col. 0113A] that they proclaimed that the reward of the highest good lay in truth itself.

> **[Col. 0113B] Notes of Various Scholars on columns 113–114**
>
> **They proclaimed.** I restored this reading from the manuscript codices and the old printed editions—Roman, Aldine, and Paris 1525—because, according to Cellarius, it more forcefully marks the philosophers’ boastfulness than “they judged,” which appears in the most recent Emmanuel and Cambridge manuscripts and in recent printed editions. Certain printed editions read: “that in it they proclaimed every reward of the highest good” [Col. 0113C] [an evidently corrupt reading].
>
> **Truth, that is, the mystery.** This will be the subject of inquiry in Book IV, which is *On True Wisdom*.
>
> **Of the supreme God.** You will find this expression a hundred times in Lactantius.
>
> **Truth … comprehended.** Book III, chapter 1, and Book VII, chapter 2. **BÜNEMANN.**
>
> **Arrangements (*dispositiones*).** In place of “decrees”; Lactantius is therefore criticized in Erasmus’ *Ciceronianus* for not using the word “decrees” here.
>
> **Arrangements.** Our author is criticized by Erasmus in the *Ciceronianus* for having said “arrangements” instead of “decrees.” We vindicate the usage from Tertullian; compare Lactantius, Book II, chapter 16, and Book VII, chapter 5. **BÜNEMANN.**
>
> **Might become known (*innotesceret*).** Thus the English manuscripts and the Aldine edition; certain others have *notesceret*, but less correctly.
>
> **Might become known.** Thus the de Tournes, Gymnicus, Parrhasius, and Cratander editions, a reading altogether more sonorous here. But the Gotha and Reimann manuscripts, the Leipzig marginal reading, Thomasius, and almost all the early editions—Subiaco, Venice 1472 and 1497, and Paris 1513—have *notesceret*; Heumann also prefers it. It occurs several times in Book IV, chapter 26, and in the *Epitome* from the Turin manuscript. **BÜNEMANN.**
>
> [Col. 0113D]
>
> **To err.** Thus, with the Roman edition, all the manuscripts except Royal 1, and the recent editions, which read “to wander.”
>
> **To wander** prevails in all the editions; but because in Lactantius and other writers this means to stray about something, as I note on Book II, chapter 2, I prefer “to err”; “one who errs” follows. Reimann likewise reads “to err.” **BÜNEMANN.**
>
> **The result of the labor.** Certainly one should not depart from the agreement of the codices, including Reimann. Lactantius again says in Book III, chapter 1: “the result did not follow the intention.” Seneca, *On Tranquillity of Mind*, chapter 11, at the end: “Lest either the labor be fruitless and without result, or the result unworthy of the labor.” **BÜNEMANN.**
>
> **He made the knowledge of truth his own function.** That is, God himself wished to perform the office of teacher by making truth known. For truth is known to him alone, Book III, chapter 1; and “this function belongs to God … and the knowledge of truth belongs to the divine condition.” **BÜNEMANN.**
>
> **None.** That is, of no value, of no advantage. **WALCH.**
>
> In this way authors of purer eloquence interpret the word *nullus* (“none”).
>
> [Col. 0114B]
>
> **Truth in obscurity.** How this is so he teaches in Book III, chapter 28.
>
> **Defenders.** Thus the three old Roman editions of 1468, 1470, and 1474; the Bologna manuscripts of Betuleius and Cellarius; seven Royal, six Colbert, two Sorbonne, Navarre, Victorine, Gatianus, Caucchius, Utrecht, three Leipzig, Cambridge, Emmanuel, Giunti, Gronovius, two Clermont, and two Le Brun manuscripts. This is better and more harmonious [Col. 0114C] than “defenses,” found in two recent Royal manuscripts, the Marmoutier manuscript, and more recent printed editions. On the defenders of the Christian religion, see Book V, chapter 2.
>
> **Mistaken.** That is, deceived.
>
> **That oratorical profession.** Namely, the profane and sophistical one, which he calls “deceptive and captious eloquence” in *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 21. **BÜNEMANN.**
>
> **In which we were long engaged.** He did not, however, enter the forum.
>
> **To instruct.** We have restored this reading from the very ancient and excellent Royal-Puteanus manuscript, three Colbert manuscripts, two Clermont manuscripts, and others, as well as from the old printed Roman editions, the Egnatian or Aldine edition of 1515, Paris 1525, and Cratander 1532. Certain manuscripts and more recent printed editions read “to establish.”
>
> **In greater glory, etc.** On the comparison between the philosopher and the orator, see Plutarch, *On Stoic Self-Contradictions*, near the beginning.

Much, however, did that exercise in fictitious lawsuits, etc. He says “fictitious lawsuits,” for he was never an advocate in real ones, since he did not even enter the forum, as he himself testifies concerning himself in Book III, chapter 13. In former times, when the study of eloquence flourished in Greece and Rome, [Col. 0114D] young men, after learning grammar, were taken to rhetoricians, who proposed to them themes either invented or drawn from history, such as those of which many are still found in the declamations of Seneca the Elder and Quintilian, and among the Greek writers. On these themes boys practiced speaking and writing in the schools, as did Libanius, Carneades, and Dio Chrysostom. They trained these young men so that they might afterwards speak in earnest before the people or the senate; and they were accustomed to treat scandalous subjects. These, then, were the exercises in which Lactantius says a little above that he had long been engaged in that profession of rhetoric, and by which they formerly educated young men, not for virtue, but plainly for clever malice; and he says that his extensive use of them will now benefit him in pleading the cause of truth against the nations. ISAEUS.

**Must be expounded.** *Disserere* means to wish to indicate or explain. Tacitus, *Histories* II: “It will not take long to expound briefly the beginnings of the cult, the site of the temple, and the form of the goddess.” [Col. 0115B] BARTHIUS.—“Perhaps one should read, ‘must be asserted’ (*asserenda est*),” says Petrus Francius in the margin of his copy of Lactantius.]

But they did not attain what they desired either, and they lost both their effort and their diligence, because the truth—that is, the mystery of the supreme God who made all things—cannot be comprehended by ingenuity and one’s own senses. Otherwise there would be no distinction between God and man, if human thought could grasp the counsels and arrangements of that eternal majesty. Because it was impossible for divine reason to become known to man through himself, God did not permit man, while seeking the light of wisdom, to wander any longer and roam without any result from his labor through inextricable darkness. At last he opened his eyes and made knowledge of the truth his own gift, so that he might both show that human wisdom is nothing and reveal to the erring wanderer the way of attaining [Col. 0113B] immortality.

But because few make use of this heavenly benefit and gift, since truth lies hidden, veiled in darkness, and is either despised by the learned because it lacks suitable defenders, or hated by the unlearned because of its inherent austerity, which human nature, prone to vice, cannot endure—for since bitterness is mingled with the virtues, while vices are seasoned with pleasure, people, offended by the former [Col. 0114A] and enticed by the latter, are carried headlong; and, deceived by the appearance of good things, they embrace evils as goods—I believed that these errors must be remedied, so that the learned might be directed toward true wisdom and the unlearned toward true religion. This profession must be considered much better, more useful, and more glorious than that profession of rhetoric in which, after long employment, we used to educate young men, not for virtue, but plainly for clever malice. For now we shall speak much more properly about heavenly precepts, by which we may train human minds in the worship of the true Majesty. Nor does one who imparts the knowledge of speaking well deserve so much from human affairs as one who teaches people to live piously and innocently. For this reason philosophers enjoyed greater glory among the Greeks than orators. The former were regarded as teachers of right living, which [Col. 0114B] is far more excellent, since speaking well concerns only a few, but living well concerns everyone. Yet that exercise in fictitious lawsuits contributed much to us, enabling us now to plead the cause of truth with greater abundance and facility of speech. Although truth can be defended without eloquence, as it has often been defended by many, it must nevertheless be illuminated with clarity and splendor of language and, in a certain manner, expounded, so that it may flow more powerfully into people’s minds, equipped with [Col. 0115A] its own force, [Col. 115A]

[Note: [Col. 115B] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 115–116]]

**Equipped with its own force.** Thus emended from the oldest and best Regius-Puteanus manuscript, as well as seven other Royal manuscripts, six Colbert manuscripts, two Leipzig manuscripts, the Christianus, Emmeranus, Cambridge, two Clermont, and two Bruni manuscripts, and three old Roman editions, the Egnatian or Aldine edition, Paris 1525, the editions of de Tournes, Cratander, Grapheus, Gymnich, and two Leipzig editions. Previously, in the six more recent printed editions, it read: “both by its own force and equipped with religion.” Indeed, the very learned Petrus Francius, professor of history and eloquence at Amsterdam, thought these last two words should be deleted, writing in manuscript notes in the margin of his Lactantius that he suspected *religione* had arisen from what follows.

**The greatest orators.** Cicero especially, who, when more than sixty years old, wrote almost all his philosophical works. Compare the beginning of his *Tusculan Disputations*. BUNEMAN.

[Col. 0115C]

**Veterans.** The comparison is drawn from military service, for some soldiers are veterans and others recruits. Veterans are soldiers who have served for many years and are trained in military affairs through long experience; nevertheless, they remained under the standard, as is clear from Caesar, Book I of *The Gallic War*. See Lipsius on Book I of Tacitus; Budé, in his book *On the As*. Hence orators are called veterans when they have trained themselves through many years of declamation and acquired the faculty and ease of speaking through long practice. GALLAEUS.

**Experts.** That is, jurists; thus in law one speaks of “the opinions of the experts” (*responsa prudentum*). So below, Book V, chapter 12, *prudentes* again means those who are also called jurists; and *prudentia* means jurisprudence in Cicero, *On Old Age*, chapter 9, and *On Friendship*, chapter 1.

**Institutes.** He alludes to the title of the work, after the model of Gaius’s *Institutes of Civil Law*, fragments of which survive today. *Institutes* are books in which the first elements of some art or science to be taught are so summarized that an untrained person may advance by degrees to [Col. 0115D] knowledge of it. Thus among the jurists we read brief writings entitled *Institutes*. BARTHIUS.—By the *Divine Institutes*, Lactantius means discussions concerning the principles and precepts of the Christian religion and the refutation of the impious cults of the pagans.

**Institutes.** Works which, according to Lactantius, Book V, chapter 4, contain the substance of some body of teaching. BUNEMAN.

**Not about dripping water or waters, etc.** In the jurists’ *Pandects*, Book XXX, the third title concerns water and the warding off of rainwater. See Cicero, Book I of *On the Orator*, §38.

**Concerning the laying-on of hands.** According to Gellius, Book XX, chapter 9, “to lay hands” means, when the matter in dispute—whether land or anything else—was physically present, to grasp one’s opponent simultaneously by the hand and claim the thing in question with all the prescribed words. A. GELLIUS.

**This work we now begin under the auspices of your name, etc.** Everything from here to “Therefore, leaving aside” is absent from four Royal, two Bologna, seven Vatican, four Colbert, the Navarre, Victorinus, Christianus, Emmeranus, one Leipzig, [Col. 0116B] Gatianus, de Tournes, Clermont, and Bruni manuscripts, and from the Florentine edition. It is also absent from the Rohannus and Saint-Germain manuscripts. It is present, however, in the oldest Royal manuscript, a codex nine hundred years old, and in four other Royal, five Vatican, two Colbert, the Sorbonne, two Leipzig, one Clermont, the Gothanus, Balliol, and Marmoutier manuscripts, and in the old printed editions: three Roman editions, Aldus 1515, Paris 1525, Grapheus, Cratander, Gymnich, Betuleius, Fasitel, Thomasius, Soubron, two Paris editions, Sparke, and two Leipzig editions. Isaeus rejects these words; but the most distinguished and learned men Stephanus Baluzius, Sebastianus Tillemontius, and Johann Georg Walchius defend them with us on the basis of the consistency of the style and the fact that Lactantius published the work twice. They think that the books of the *Institutes* were first written in troubled times, namely shortly after the year 302, but were revised, enlarged, and issued in a second edition during happier times, and inscribed and dedicated to Constantine around [Col. 0116C] the year 321 or 323. See our preface, no. 10, and Tillemont’s *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. VI, p. 208. “It is unquestionably a genuine offspring of Lactantius,” says Walchius in his Leipzig edition of 1715, p. 13, “as can clearly be inferred from the character of the writing.” On this question see Isaeus in the notes to Book I, appended at the end of this volume.

**Most Mighty Emperor.** Constantine was distinguished by this title when, after defeating his enemies, he alone held the reins of the Roman Empire. Constantine acquired several honorific surnames by degrees. Because, as victor over Maxentius, he had freed the Roman Empire from tyranny, he was called “Liberator of the City” and “Founder of Peace”; when he ruled alone, he was hailed as “Restorer of the Human Race,” “Extender of the Empire,” and “Founder of Eternal Security.”

**Who was the first of the Roman emperors.** He was not so much the first, after rejecting errors, to recognize and honor the majesty of the one true God as the first emperor to grant peace to Christians. Before him, Philip, who reigned from 244 to 249, appears to have been a Christian, as may be gathered from Eusebius’s *Chronicle* and *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VI, chapter 39, p. 234 B, and chapter 34, p. 232 B; Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, or *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 54, p. 285; Vincent of Lérins, Book I, chapter 23; Orosius, Book VII, chapters 20 and 28; and others. Thus the profession of the Christian religion was much less evident in Philip than in Constantine. See Tillemont, *History of the Emperors*, vol. III, p. 300 and p. 643 ff. The cause of Constantine’s conversion was his victory over Maxentius and “the sign of the cross” (*καὶ τὸ τοῦ σταυροῦ σημεῖον*), to which was attached the inscription, “By this, conquer” (*ἐν τούτῳ νίκα*). This happened in the year of Christ 311. He died in 337, on Pentecost, May 22, during the consulship of Felicianus and Titianus. See Philostorgius, Book I of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 6. Others report that he was already a Christian before the victory. Concerning that cross which appeared to Constantine in the year 311, see Jacques Godefroy on Philostorgius; Eusebius, Book I of the *Life of Constantine*, chapter 22; Sebastian Tillemont, *History of the Emperors*, [Col. 0117C] vol. IV, chapter 23, p. 126; and the dissertation of Nicolas de Lestocq appended to this edition.]

and adorned with the light of eloquence.

# CHAPTER I  
## On Religion and Wisdom

Our discussion, then, is instituted concerning religion and divine matters. For if certain of the greatest orators, veterans, as it were, of their profession, after completing the course of their forensic works, finally devoted themselves to philosophy and considered it the most just repose from their labors—even though, by tormenting their minds in the investigation of matters that could not be discovered, they seem to have sought not leisure for themselves but business, and indeed business much more troublesome than that in which they had [Col. 0115B] previously been engaged—how much more justly may I betake myself [Col. 0116A] to that pious, true, and divine wisdom as to some utterly safe harbor, where everything is easy to state, pleasant to hear, readily understood, and honorable to undertake? And if certain legal experts and arbiters of equity published composed *Institutes of Civil Law*, by which they might settle the lawsuits and disputes of citizens at variance, how much better and more properly shall we treat in writing the *Divine Institutes*, in which we shall speak not about dripping water, the warding off of waters, or the laying-on of hands, but about hope, life, salvation, immortality, and God, so that we may put an end to deadly superstitions and most shameful errors?

This work we now begin under the auspices of your name, Constantine, Most Mighty Emperor, who was the first of the Roman [Col. 0116B] emperors, after rejecting errors, both to recognize and to honor the majesty [Col. 0117A] of the one true God. For when that most fortunate day dawned upon the world on which the supreme God raised you to the blessed summit of imperial power, you inaugurated with a glorious beginning a reign salutary and desirable for all, when, by restoring justice after it had been overthrown and removed, you expiated the most loathsome crime of others [Col. 0117A]

[Note: [Col. 0117C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 117–118]]

**The crime of others.** Lactantius here censures the cruelty of Maxentius and Licinius toward Christians, as well as the other persecutors of Christians.

**God will give you happiness.** Thus Saint Augustine says: “God filled the emperor Constantine, who did not supplicate demons but worshiped the true God himself, with earthly gifts so great that no one would have dared wish for as much,” etc., *The City of God*, Book V, chapter 25.

**Even in old age may you hold.** These words are absent from the Subiaco edition.

**The just.** That is, Christians.

**The later, the more severely.** Valerius Maximus, Book I, chapter 1, external example 3: “Divine wrath proceeds with slow step to avenge itself and compensates for the delay of punishment by its severity.” [Col. 0117D] BUNEMAN.

**Bringing forward.** As a little later, “the things we are going to bring forward”; but nine more recent manuscripts, together with several editions, read “asserting.” Here he understands not only the Academics, but all philosophers, who tore the study of wisdom apart through their various opinions.—**Bringing forward nothing certain.** Book III, chapter 7, at the end: “Yet he himself does not bring forward anything for us to follow.” Cicero, chapter 16: “They brought nothing beneficial to life.” *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 1: “They argue in such a way that they wish the things they bring forward to appear proven and known.” In each of these passages also the subject is philosophers.

**Investigating.** Thus the Saint-Germain manuscript and two Leipzig manuscripts; others, however, read “seeking.”

**Seeking out the truth.** Cellarius rightly preferred this from the Leipzig manuscript. Lactantius favors this word. Below, Book VII, chapter 7: “They sought out the truth without a guide.” *On the Wrath of God*, chapter 3: “Let us seek out the truth elsewhere.” BUNEMAN.

**Mystery.** Here *sacramentum* signifies a hidden matter naturally unknown to human reason but divinely revealed, in which sense the true interpreter rendered the word *μυστήριον* (“mystery”). [Col. 0118C] This word sometimes signifies the oath which soldiers formerly gave to the emperor, promising thereby that they would fight faithfully and obey promptly. This meaning can also be applied to the present passage, and Dr. Thysius so understood it. For when Christians were incorporated into the Church through baptism, they bound themselves to Christ by an oath. Hence Saint Jerome to Heliodorus: “Remember the day of your recruitment, when, buried together with Christ, you swore the words of the sacrament.” GALLAEUS.

**To whose assertion.** Thus twenty-two manuscripts, including the older Royal, Bologna, Rohannus, and Saint-Germain manuscripts; this should be preferred to the other, more recent manuscripts and printed editions, which have “of which.”

**A task almost infinite and immense.** There is elegance in these words. Cicero, *On the Orator* I.6: “Nor do I doubt that this will appear immense and infinite to most people.” BUNEMAN.

[Col. 0118D]

**An abundance of material should overflow.** Venice 1471, both editions of 1478, Rostock, Venice 1497, Pierius, Parrhasius, and certain others read *exuperet*. I change nothing: Book IV, chapter 17, “they overflow with an abundance of milk”; chapter 29, “an overflowing spring”; Book VII, chapter 15, “the field overflows”; *On the Wrath of God*, chapter 13, “so that the orchards overflow with fruit”; *Epitome*, chapter 72: “Springs of milk and wine will overflow.” BUNEMAN.

**So that the discourse would find neither the measure nor the end of a book.** Heumann wonders that this passage lay so long in corruption and rewrites *libri* as *liber*. There is no need if, with “neither the measure of a book,” you understand “they would find.” Certainly all manuscripts and editions have *libri*, so that here, in the former position, the verb is *reperiant*.

**Empty.** The Subiaco edition reads “various.”

**Harden themselves against.** The Gothanus manuscript reads, “are hardened against manifest truth.” Cicero uses the verb without the reflexive in *On Ends* III.11: “Who has hardened himself so violently against the natural inclinations?” BUNEMAN.

**Wrongly assert.** Thus the best manuscripts, together with the printed editions. Three recent manuscripts have “bring forward”; ten of the most recent, “prefer.” See below, “those who think wrongly.”]

for which deed God will give you happiness, courage, and length of days, so that even in old age you may hold the helm of the commonwealth with the same justice with which you began as a young man, and may hand over to your children the guardianship of the Roman name, just as you yourself received it from your father. For upon the wicked who still rage against the just in other regions of the earth, the later the same Almighty pays the wages of their crime, the more severely he will pay them, because, just as he is a most indulgent father toward the pious, so toward the impious he is a most just [Col. 0117B] judge. Desiring to defend his religion and divine worship, whom should I invoke, whom should I address, rather than the one through whom justice and wisdom have been restored to human affairs?

Therefore, leaving aside the authors of this earthly philosophy, who bring forward nothing certain, let us enter upon the straight path. Indeed, if I thought them sufficiently suitable guides for living well, I myself would follow them and would exhort others to follow them. But since they differ among themselves with great contention and very often disagree even with themselves, it is apparent that their course is by no means direct. For each has stamped out paths of his own as he pleased, and they have left great confusion to those investigating [Col. 0117C] the truth. But as for us, who have received the mystery [Col. 0118A] of true religion, since the truth has been divinely revealed and since we follow God as teacher of wisdom and guide of truth, we summon everyone, without any distinction of sex or age, to heavenly nourishment. For there is no food sweeter to the soul than knowledge of the truth, to whose assertion and elucidation we have devoted seven volumes, although the subject is a task almost infinite and immense. If anyone wished to expand and treat these matters with complete fullness, so great an abundance of material would overflow for him that his discourse would find neither the measure nor the end of a book. But we shall therefore gather everything together briefly, because the things we are going to bring forward are so clear and luminous that it seems more astonishing that the truth should appear so obscure to human beings, especially to those who are commonly considered wise; or because our sole task will be [Col. 0118B] to instruct people—that is, to recall them from the error in which they are entangled to a straighter path.

If we attain this, as I hope, we shall send them to the doctrine’s own richest and fullest spring, from whose draught they may quench the thirst conceived in their innermost parts and extinguish its burning. Everything will then be easy, accessible, and manifest to them, provided that, in order to receive the discipline of wisdom, they do not begrudge the patience required for reading or listening. For many, clinging stubbornly to empty superstitions, harden themselves against manifest truth, doing a good service not so much to their religions, which they wrongly assert, as a bad service to themselves. Although they have a straight road, they follow winding detours; they abandon level ground to plunge down a precipice; [Col. 0118C] [Col. 0119A]

[Note: [Col. 0119B] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 118–120]]

**To plunge down a precipice.** So too, “plunge,” Book VI, chapter 57; *Epitome*, chapter 69. But two recent Colbert manuscripts and the Rohannus manuscript read “into a precipice”; one Royal manuscript, “headlong.”

**Abandon.** Reimmann, Leipzig 2 and 3 read “utterly abandon” (*derelinquunt*). Lactantius certainly favors this compound: Book I, chapter 18; Book V, chapters 8 and 18; and some manuscripts in Book III, chapter 13. BUNEMAN.

**Be freed.** Francius suggests, “perhaps, to free.” But the Cologne edition of 1544 reads better: “and may at last be willing to be freed from inveterate errors.”

**Why they were born.** From the manuscripts and editions I have added *sint* (“were”), which was missing from the editions of Thysius and also of Servatius Gallaeus.—**Why they were born.** This *sint* is found in Reimmann and in more than thirty editions: the Subiaco edition, two Roman, ten Venetian editions from 1471–1510, three Antwerp, three Basel, five de Tournes, the Junta, Parrhasius, Berutius, Gryphius, and two editions of Isaeus. Thysius, Gallaeus, Sparke, and Cambridge neglected it.

**So that neither … wisdom should be approved.** This is the thesis of the entire Christian profession; Lactantius treats this matter in [Col. 0119C] *On the Wrath of God*, chapter 12.

**I did not consider it so necessary.** Lactantius treats this argument more fully in *On the Wrath of God*, chapters 9, 10, and 11, and in the little work *On the Workmanship of God*, where he refutes the Epicureans.

**By nature; whether there is providence.** Hence Lactantius, *Epitome*, chapter 2, at the beginning: “The first question arises: whether there is providence.” BUNEMAN.

**Are governed.** Thus the best editions and older manuscripts, a reading confirmed by chapter 1 of the *Epitome*, where one reads: “Whether there is some providence which either made or governs the world.” In some manuscripts, however, including the Rohannus and Saint-Germain manuscripts, one reads “are conducted”; in still others also, but wrongly, “are conducted.”

**Democritus.** He attempts to assert that everything was made fortuitously from atoms. See Laertius. Plutarch excellently says: “Nothing beautiful comes into being rashly and by chance, but is produced by some art.” VOSSIUS.—Democritus himself is treated extensively below in Book III, chapter 17. He joins Epicurus to Democritus because the former drew most of his ideas from the latter, according to Cicero, Book V of *On Ends* and Book II of *On the Nature of the Gods*.

[Col. 0119D]

**Protagoras.** A pupil of Democritus. Lactantius speaks of him as follows in *On the Wrath of God*, chapter 9: “Protagoras was the first of all, in the time of Socrates, to declare that it was not clear to him whether there was any divinity or not,” etc. Suidas, under *Protagoras* (*Πρωταγόρας*); Theophilus, *To Autolycus*, Book III; Cicero, Book I of *On the Nature of the Gods*; Epiphanius, Book III *Against Heresies*; Theodoret, Oration II *Against the Greeks*. ELMENHORST.—Protagoras was expelled from Athens because of his impious doctrine. His life is in Laertius, Book IX. Among Plato’s dialogues is a dialogue entitled *Protagoras*.

**Diagoras.** Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I.23 and II.37; Josephus, Book II *Against Apion*; Tatian; Athenagoras, *To the Greeks* (*Πρὸς Ἕλληνας*); Clement in the *Exhortation*, “For the sake of these things” (*Ὧν δὴ χάριν*), etc. “Diagoras of Melos, upon whom antiquity imposed the surname ‘Atheist,’” said Minucius Felix. Theodoret wrote his book *On Providence* against him. The Athenians offered a talent as a reward to anyone who brought them Diagoras’s head (Suidas, under *Diagoras* [*Διαγόρας*]). According to Eusebius, Diagoras lived from the 74th Olympiad onward and was a man [Col. 0120B] of exceptionally acute intellect. The illustrious Vossius thinks he was the same as Diagoras of Athens, who left *Phrygian Discourses*. Tatian, *Against the Greeks*: “Diagoras the Athenian” (*Διογόρας Ἀθηναῖος*), etc. These *Phrygian Discourses* appear to have been a history of matters relating to Cybele, or the Phrygian Mother, and her rites. He himself wrote them for the purpose of turning people away from those rites. From Vossius.—This Diagoras is discussed again by Lactantius in *On the Wrath of God*, chapter 9, and by Theodoret in the sixth book of his *Therapeutic for Greek Diseases*.

**And afterwards Diagoras.** After Protagoras, before Epicurus, and himself a disciple of Democritus. Suidas, ed. Kuster, vol. I, fol. 550. If one understands him correctly, Lactantius believed that he lived after Epicurus, *On Wrath*, chapter 9. This is wrong. Diagoras flourished in the 74th Olympiad; Epicurus was not born until the third year of the 109th Olympiad: Laertius, Book X, §§14–15, and Ménage, p. 453. Vossius therefore followed a corrupt edition of Laertius when, in *On the Greek Historians* I.21, he stated that Epicurus died in the 107th Olympiad; for he concedes that Epicurus was born in the 109th Olympiad, IV.10, Leiden edition, quarto. [Col. 0120C] On the matter compare Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I.1 and 23; III.37; Valerius Maximus I.1, external example 7; Aelian, *Various History* II.31. BUNEMAN.—**Earlier Protagoras … afterwards Diagoras.** Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I.1: “Protagoras thought it doubtful whether gods existed; Diagoras of Melos and Theodorus of Cyrene thought there were none at all.” The same author in the same book, chapter 23: “What of Diagoras, who was called ‘the Atheist’ (*Ἄθεος*), and later Theodorus? Did they not openly abolish the nature of the gods? For Protagoras of Abdera, perhaps the greatest sophist of those times, after placing at the beginning of his book the statement, ‘Concerning the gods I cannot say either that they exist or that they do not exist,’ was, by order of the Athenians, banished from the city and its territory, and his books were burned in the assembly.” CELLARIUS.

**And certain others.** For example, Theodorus. *Epitome*, chapter 68; *On Wrath*, chapter 9. Elmenhorst indicated the passages of the writers in his notes on Minucius, chapter 8; Planner, *System of Pagan Theology*, chapter 2, §2. BUNEMAN.—Bion also excluded the gods; the verses concerning him which survive may be found in Meursius, whom one should not begrudge consulting, in the minor works of Hesychius, p. 12. GALLAEUS.

[Col. 0120D]

**And especially the Stoics.** He commends the Stoics above all, but Plato deserved no less praise, for throughout his writings he calls God “the maker of all things” (*δημιουργὸν ἁπάντων*). VOSSIUS.—Distinguished pronouncements of the Stoics concerning divine providence are found. Lactantius praises the Stoics and the other philosophers. Epictetus in Arrian: “Before all else one must learn that there is one God, that he governs all things and provides for all; and that nothing we do, say, or think can escape his notice.” See Seneca in the *Questions*, *On Benefits*, and *On Providence*. “The Etruscans understand as the same being whom we call Jupiter the guardian and ruler of the universe, the mind and spirit, the lord and craftsman of this cosmic work, to whom every divine title belongs. Do you wish to call him Fate? You will not be mistaken. He is the one upon whom all things depend, from whom all causes of causes proceed. Do you wish to call him Providence? You speak correctly. For it is by his counsel that provision is made for this world, so that it may complete its course unshaken and unfold its operations.” So too [Col. 0121B] Cleanthes in Simplicius: “O God,” he says, “guide me through that cause by which you govern and regulate all things.”]

they leave the light so as to lie blind and feeble in darkness. They must be assisted, lest they fight against themselves, and they must at last be willing to be freed from inveterate errors. They will certainly do this if at some point they discern why they were born. For the cause of this depravity is ignorance of oneself. If anyone, having learned the truth, dispels that ignorance, he will know to what end his life should be directed and how it should be lived. I define the sum of this knowledge briefly: no religion should be adopted without wisdom, and no wisdom should be approved without religion.
