# CHAPTER II  
## That Providence Exists in Human Affairs

Having therefore undertaken the duty of illuminating the truth, I did not consider it so necessary to begin from that question which appears by nature to be the first: whether there is a providence which cares for all things, or whether all things have either come into being or are governed by chance. Democritus is the author of the latter opinion, and Epicurus its confirmer. But Protagoras before him, who called the gods into doubt, and Diagoras afterwards, who excluded them, together with certain others who did not think the gods existed—what else did they accomplish except that providence should be regarded as nonexistent? Yet the other philosophers, and especially the Stoics, refuted them most vigorously, [Col. 0121A]

[Note: [Col. 0121B] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 121–122]]

**Refuted most vigorously.** Book III, chapter 28: “When he had forcefully beaten back the attacks of his enemies”; Book IV, chapter 27: “he beats back the force.”

**Teaching.** Thus the oldest and best manuscripts read. The Rohannus and Saint-Germain manuscripts, however, have “saying,” which amounts to almost the same thing.

**Marcus Tullius.** Cicero followed sometimes the Platonists, sometimes the Stoics, [Col. 0121C] and sometimes Aristotle.

**For no one is so uncultivated, etc.** The very learned Wowerius rightly observes that these are common arguments which almost all who wrote against the nations employed in establishing the existence of divinity. Minucius has the same argument, which he borrows from Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II: “What can be so plain and evident, when we have looked up at heaven, as that there is some divine power of surpassing intelligence by which these things are governed?” The same author, *On the Response of the Haruspices*: “For who is so senseless that, when he has looked up at heaven, he does not perceive that the gods exist, and thinks that things accomplished with such great intelligence that scarcely anyone could, by any art, trace the order and succession of events, have happened by chance? Or, once he has understood that the gods exist, does he not understand that by their divine power this great empire was born, enlarged, and preserved?” etc. ELMENHORST.—Prudentius likewise, in the *Apotheosis*:

> Yet whenever he looked up to heaven, he vested  
> All power in the one God, whom the mighty order  
> Of powers serves, arrayed with manifold ministers.

[Col. 0121D] See Isidore of Pelusium, Book IV. This argument drawn from created things convinces everyone and is known to everyone, so that it is exceedingly powerful for asserting the existence of divinity. The blessed Paul uses this argument in Romans 1:20 to render the nations without excuse: “For his invisible attributes are perceived and understood through the things that have been made since the creation of the world; likewise his eternal power and divinity, so that they are without excuse.” GALLAEUS.—The argument is treated again by Cicero in Book I of the *Tusculan Disputations*.

**Who his eyes.** Thus the manuscripts and old editions. Plutarch teaches where human beings obtained their knowledge of the gods in *Opinions of the Philosophers* I.6. See also Cicero in *On the Universe*.

**Beauty.** Certainly nothing apprehended by the senses is more adorned, beautiful, and complete than the world, as Philo observes in his book *On the Indestructibility of the World* (*περὶ Ἀφθαρσίας κόσμου*); Cicero, Book II of *On the Nature of the Gods*. ELMENHORST.—Cicero affirms the same thing that Lactantius does here, in Book II of *On Divination*. Because of this beauty the world is called *κόσμος* (“orderly world” or “adornment”) by the Greeks. See also Aristotle, *On the World*, and Pliny, Book II, chapter 4. For the word “harmonious balance” which follows, the Subiaco edition wrongly reads “comparison.”

**Because it is constituted by a wondrous order.** Francius reads, “because it is constituted by so wondrous an order.”

[Col. 0122C]

**Certainly.** Thus we have restored the word from the manuscripts and almost all editions. Four recent editions read “therefore.”

**It is necessary.** The Subiaco edition adds “not,” excellently.

**No one who is truly wise.** With the very learned Gronovius I have excellently restored this reading from the Rohannus manuscript, two other Royal manuscripts of good quality, and the Gronovian, one Colbert, two Bruni manuscripts, and Cellarius’s edition. The others have: “There is indeed no one who is wise … who does not understand that there is one.” Five editions insert “God” in the middle, but wrongly, since “one God” has just preceded. Furthermore, on the same matter see Lactantius, Book II, chapter 2: “When they swear and when they make wishes,” etc. Tertullian says in the *Apology* concerning the pagans of his time: “The soul, although enslaved to false gods, nevertheless, when it comes to its senses as though after drunkenness or sleep, names God; and ‘God grant it’ is on everyone’s lips. It also calls upon him as judge: ‘God sees,’ ‘I entrust it to God,’ and ‘God will repay me.’ O testimony of a soul Christian by nature! Finally, when it utters these words, it looks not toward the Capitol but toward heaven, for it knows the seat of the living God.” [Col. 0122D] The poets Aeschylus, Sophocles, Philemon, and Orpheus, as well as Pythagoras, acknowledged one God. See Saint Justin, *On Monarchy*.

**Who both founded all things, etc.** Hierocles writes that God is called *Zēna* and *Dia* (*Ζῆνα* and *Δία*) because through him all things exist and live. Hence Apuleius calls God the “producer of all things.” Proclus calls God “the source of all life” (*πηγὴν πάσης ζωῆς*). Thus Cato in Lucan:

> We all depend upon the gods above, and though the temple is silent,  
> We do nothing except by the will of God.

Sacred Scripture also, in order to assert providence, draws from experience an argument which convinces everyone (Psalm 103:28–29).

**Sinews and strength.** The latter word explains the former. See Davies on Caesar, *Gallic War* I.20: “resources and sinews.” Here I see Cicero, *Fifth Philippic*, chapter 12, reproduced: “He will experience the sinews and strength of a senate acting in agreement.” Compare Lactantius IV.18, “with sinews and strength.” BUNEMAN.

[Col. 0123C]

**Eternal mind.** Seneca, *Natural Questions* I: “What is God? The mind of the universe.” Anaxagoras called God “Mind” (*νοῦν*). Cicero, at the beginning of the *Tusculan Disputations*: “God is a mind unfettered and free, separated from every mortal admixture.” VOSSIUS.—The Platonists speak in this manner. Augustine, however, writes in *On the Trinity* XV that God is something greater than mind by as much as a human being endowed with mind surpasses irrational animals that lack it. On the nature of God see Plutarch, *Opinions of the Philosophers* I.7.]

[Col. 0121A] teaching that the world could neither have been made without divine reason nor continue to exist unless it were governed by supreme reason. Marcus Tullius also, although he was a defender of the Academic school, discussed providence as the governor of things both frequently and at length, confirming the arguments of the Stoics and bringing forward many new arguments of his own. He does this both in all his philosophical books and especially in those entitled *On the Nature of the Gods*.

It was surely not difficult to refute the falsehoods of a few people who think wrongly by the testimony of peoples and nations that do not disagree on this one matter. For no one is so uncultivated, or of such savage character, that when he raises his eyes to heaven, even though he does not know by whose divine providence all that is seen is governed, he does not nevertheless understand from the very magnitude, [Col. 0121B] motion, arrangement, constancy, usefulness, beauty, and harmonious balance of things that some providence exists, and that what is constituted by a wondrous order cannot possibly have been equipped without some higher design. It would certainly be very easy for us to treat this subject as copiously as we pleased. But because the matter has been much debated among philosophers, because those who deny providence appear to have received a sufficient answer from acute [Col. 0122A] and eloquent men, and because throughout this entire work which we have undertaken it will be necessary to speak here and there about the skill of divine providence, let us omit for the present this question, which is so closely connected with the others that it seems nothing can be discussed by us without providence being discussed at the same time.

# CHAPTER III  
## Whether the World Is Governed by the Power of One God or of Many

Let the beginning of our work, then, be the next and second question: whether the world is governed by the power of one God or of many. No one who is truly wise and considers the matter rationally within himself fails to understand that there is one who both founded all things and governs them by the same power with which he founded them. For what need is there of many [Col. 0122B] to sustain the government of the world, unless perhaps we suppose that, if there are several, each possesses less sinew and strength? This is indeed what those who maintain that there are many gods do, because those gods must necessarily be weak, since none of them individually, without the aid of the others, could sustain the helm of so great a mass. But God, who is eternal mind, is certainly in every respect [Col. 0123A] possessed of perfect and consummate power. If this is true, it is necessary that he be one. For absolute power or might retains its own proper firmness. That, moreover, must be considered solid from which nothing can be diminished; [Col. 0123A]

[Note: [Col. 0123C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 123–124]]

**Nothing can be diminished.** Saint Augustine likewise teaches in Book V of *On the Trinity* that no accidents can belong to God, and that whatever is said of God is said essentially, not accidentally.

[Col. 0123D]

**Resources.** That is, abundance, goods, wealth. Below, Book V, ch. 12: “Let all honors, all dominions, all wealth—in short, all resources—be conferred upon him.” Book VII, ch. 23: “Enjoying the delight afforded by innumerable resources.” *On Anger*, ch. 13: “An abundance of possessions and resources . . . to furnish”; and ch. 23: “God nourishes us with innumerable resources.” Hence in Book VI, ch. 11, *wealthy* means “abounding in riches.” Freinsheim on Tacitus, *Annals* III, ch. 54. **Bünemann.**

**But the more perfect nature of virtue, etc.** Thus the Rohan and Saint-Germain manuscripts, and elegantly so. Previously, however, the passage was read with a triple negation: “But the perfect nature of virtue cannot exist except in that in which the whole resides, not in that in which there is a part,” etc. Heumann’s edition, however, reads: “But the perfect nature of virtue resides rather in that in which the whole exists than in that in which there is a part,” etc.

**A nature can exist in that in which the whole exists, than the perfect nature of virtue can exist in that in which the whole exists, than in that.** This reading is entirely correct and should not have been emended by Cellarius; nor is it, as Heumann wrote, an [Col. 0124C] obvious scribal error. “Rather” must be understood. **Bünemann.**

**Because he is perfect.** These words are omitted by the Leipzig and Gotha manuscripts, as well as by Betuleius’s edition. From manuscripts of the first rank and nearly all the others, and from the old Roman editions and Cellarius, *because* has been restored in place of *for*, which appears in the other printed editions.

**Incorruptible.** I find this word frequently in ecclesiastical writers even before our author, in Tertullian, Cyprian, and Arnobius.

**Divine.** The Subiaco edition has “eternal.” **Bünemann.**

**The matter comes back to the same point.** This reproduces Cicero, *Academics* IV, 6: “Unwittingly he comes back to the very point to which he least wishes to return”; *On Divination* II, ch. 5: “You will come back to the same point.” Add *Tusculan Disputations* I, ch. 6. **Bünemann.**

**Fashioned out of nothing.** Paraeus, in his work on *Genesis*, proves [Col. 0124D] that the world was fashioned out of nothing. Theophrastus said the same. The ancient philosophers—the Pythagoreans, Zeno with his Stoics, and Plato himself—asserted that the world was made from some matter coeternal with God. They were followed by the heretics whom Tertullian calls “Materialists” in his book *Against Hermogenes*, ch. 25. See Augustine, *Heresies* 59.

**It is easier . . . to be governed.** Rostock, Subiaco, Venice 1471, both editions of 1478, the editions of 1497, Paris, Pierius, Cratander, the Paris edition, Junta, Aldus, Gymnich, Gryphius, Isaeus, Betuleius, and Heumann order the less necessary word “to be” to be removed. Thomasius inserted it and was followed by Gallaeus, the Cambridge edition, Sparke, Walch, and Cellarius. **Bünemann.**

**We fail.** Heumann thinks that “we are failed” should be read. This accords with Latin usage: “If anyone is failed by money,” says Seneca, *Epistle* 76; “He was failed by his strength,” says Julius Caesar, *Civil War* III, ch. 64, and others similarly.

**So great.** Thus the manuscripts, especially the Rohans manuscript; but seven recent manuscripts, together with the Saint-Germain manuscript, read “so great” in the accusative.

That is perfect to which nothing can be added.

Who could doubt that the most powerful king is the one who holds dominion over the whole world? And rightly so, since everything that exists everywhere belongs to him and all resources from every quarter are gathered to him alone. But if several divide the world among themselves, each will certainly possess less wealth and less strength, since each keeps within his allotted portion. In the same way, if there are several gods, they will possess less power, since the others possess an equal amount in themselves. The more perfect nature of virtue can exist in that in which the whole resides rather than in that in which [Col. 0123B] there is a small part of the whole. But God, if he is perfect—and because he is perfect—as he ought to be, cannot be more than one, so that all things may reside in him. The virtues and powers of the gods must therefore be weaker, because each will lack as much as resides in the others; thus, the more numerous they are, the smaller they will be.

Moreover, can that supreme power over all things, that divine force, be divided even once? Whatever admits division must also admit destruction. But if destruction is far removed from God, because he is incorruptible and eternal, it follows that divine power cannot be divided. God, therefore, is one, since there can be nothing else capable of possessing equal power. Yet those who suppose that there are many gods say that they have divided their duties among themselves; all of these we shall discuss in the proper place. Meanwhile, I maintain the point relevant to the present passage. [Col. 0123C] If they have divided their duties among themselves, the matter comes back to the same point: no one among them can be sufficient for everything. [Col. 0124A] Accordingly, one who could not govern everything if the others ceased their work would no longer be perfect. Thus, for governing the world, there is greater need of the perfect virtue of one than of the weakness of many.

Anyone who thinks that this vast creation cannot be governed by one is mistaken. For he does not understand how great the force and power of the divine majesty are if he supposes that the one God who was able to make the world cannot govern the world he made. But if he conceives in his mind how this immeasurable divine work—although previously there was nothing—was nevertheless fashioned out of nothing by God’s power and design, a work that could not have been begun and completed except by one, he will then understand that what was established by one can much more easily be governed by one.

Someone might perhaps say that even so [Col. 0124B] immense a work as the world could not have been constructed except by several. Let him make them as numerous and as great as he pleases: whatever greatness, power, strength, and majesty he assigns to the many, I gather all of it into one and declare it to exist in one, so that within him there may be as much of these qualities as can neither be conceived nor expressed. Since in this matter we fail both in perception and in words—because neither can the human breast contain the light of so great an understanding, nor can a mortal tongue contain the explanation of such great realities—we must understand and say precisely this.

Again, I see what may be said on the opposite side: that those many gods are each such as we wish the one God to be. But this is in no way possible, because the power of each could not extend any farther when confronted by the powers of the others. Each must either be unable to cross his own boundaries or, if he crosses them, drive another from [Col. 0124C] that other’s territory. Those who believe there are many gods do not see that some of them might desire different things, [Col. 0125A] from which disagreement and conflict would arise among them, just as Homer imagined the gods fighting one another.

[Col. 0125D]  
**Variant Notes on Columns 125–126**

**Just as Homer imagined the gods fighting one another.** Virgil, Ovid, Silius, Lucan, and others follow him. Thus Arnobius, *Against the Nations* IV: “They are said to be wounded, harassed, and to wage wars among themselves in the fury of frenzied conflicts.” Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II; Plato, *Republic* II—from whose accusation Proclus, if it please the gods, absolves Homer by referring the matter to some obscure divisions of emanations and distinctions among substances. Read Augustine, *City of God* IV, ch. 30. Thus Ovid, *Tristia* II:

> Mulciber stood against Troy; Apollo stood for Troy;  
> [Col. 0125C] Venus favored the Trojans, while Pallas opposed them.

See Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II, ch. 28; Tertullian, *Apology* 14: “The gods fought one another over the Trojans and Achaeans, engaging like matched pairs of gladiators.” **Bünemann.**

**The whole.** Turnèbe and others add “power.” See below, *Epitome*, ch. 2: “Nor can the whole order of things stand otherwise.” Reimmann and the old editions read: “the whole itself stand.” **Bünemann.**

**Stand.** Add “power,” as it is read in the excellent Cologne edition of 1544.

**Pertains.** Thus the Rohans and Saint-Germain codices; more recent manuscripts and the printed editions read “may pertain.”

**Wedges.** A wedge (*cuneus*) was a body of soldiers arranged so that it was narrow at the front and gradually broadened. See Turnèbe on Quintilian, *Institutes* I, 13. Pitiscus cites authors abundantly in his *Treasury of Roman Antiquities*, vol. I, fol. 607. **Bünemann.**

**Difference.** Ten recent manuscripts, including the Rohans manuscript, read “differences.” The Subiaco edition also has “differences.”

**The care of the whole entirety.** Thus the manuscripts and the Subiaco, Venice 1471, and 1497 editions. See below, Book I, ch. 5, where God is called “the craftsman of the entire whole”; *Epitome*, ch. 4, “the governor of the whole entirety.” **Bünemann.**

**It is just as if.** Writers on particles have overlooked this elegant use of the words. Book III, ch. 3: “It is, assuredly, just as if we wished to argue.” Book VI, ch. 15: “Which is just as if they wished”; ch. 16: “This is just as if they said.” **Bünemann.**

**By which.** Gronovius’s reading “since indeed” is elegant, although all manuscripts and editions have “by which.” There appears to be a tautology: “by which”—that is, by emotions—“to be moved toward emotions.” **Bünemann.**

**Likewise many emotions by which we are moved, etc.** Lactantius does not deny with the Stoics that there are many emotions in a human being by which we are moved. He denies, rather, that it is properly inferred that there are many minds in a human being simply because, just as there are various services of the limbs, so too there are many emotions, all of which must be traced back to one and the same origin. Gronovius’s manuscript reads: “Likewise many emotions, since indeed we are accustomed to be moved [Col. 0126B] either to anger,” etc. But this is against the evidence of the other manuscripts. One Leipzig manuscript has “many effects,” etc.

**So many.** As though one were to say “many.” Here this expression signifies not magnitude but multitude, so as to form an antithesis with “one.” Similarly, the Greek *τοιοῦτος* (“such”) may mean indifferently either “so many” or “so great.” From **Isaeus**.—**So many things.** That is, “so numerous,” “so many,” in opposition to “one mind.” Lactantius often writes thus: Book V, ch. 13, “so many thousands of people.” Likewise Book III, ch. 19, “how many thousands of people,” that is, “how numerous.” Tertullian, *Apology* 50: “Many among you exhort people to endure pain and death . . . yet their words do not find as many disciples as Christians do by teaching through deeds.” **Bünemann.**

**One mind.** This is the reading, and rightly so, of the old Roman editions, Isaeus, Sparke, both Leipzig codices, and all the manuscripts except one recent Royal manuscript, which has “the human mind,” as do six printed editions. But Lactantius’s argument requires the reading of the manuscripts and old editions. To prove that so many things can adequately be governed by one God, he adduces, among other analogies, the fact that one mind governs all the body’s many and varied actions.

**At the same time.** Eighteen manuscripts incorrectly read “once.”

**Over individual things and parts.** Thus read all the manuscripts and printed editions that I have been able to examine. Gronovius’s manuscript had “over individual things and of the parts,” with a letter written above the line, suggesting that the scribe had intended to write *partitim*, “part by part.” I suspect the reading was: “that they preside over individual things, part by part,” that is, with the parts distributed among them. **Gronovius.**

**Yet so that.** Thus emended from all the manuscripts and old printed editions except Junius’s manuscript and several editions, which read “only so that,” incorrectly.

**Powerful over all.** In Appendix II to the *Symposium*, and here as well, Heumann rewrites this as “parent of all.” God is indeed called “parent of all” by Lactantius in ch. 5; Book II, ch. 16; and Book V, ch. 3. But because all the books consistently read “powerful over all,” and especially because this passage concerns God’s power, nothing should be changed. This is clear from the *Epitome* of this book, ch. 2: “None of them, therefore, could be called omnipotent, which is the true title of God”; and *Divine Institutes* V, ch. 21: “God . . . whom you acknowledge as powerful over all things.” **Bünemann.**

**Appointed.** Thus we have restored the text from nearly all the manuscripts and the old printed editions, and rightly so. Two recent Royal manuscripts and the recent printed editions read “appoints.”

**And they themselves.** Thus we have restored the text from the best manuscripts—two Royal, two Bologna, the Taxaquet manuscript, six Colbert, two Clermont, two manuscripts designated Brun.—and the oldest editions. Four recent Royal manuscripts and nine printed editions have “so that they themselves.”

For some wished Troy to be captured, while others resisted. The world must therefore be governed by the judgment of one. For unless the power over each individual part is referred to a single providence, the whole itself will be unable to stand, because each one cares for nothing beyond what pertains specifically to himself. So too even military affairs cannot function unless they have one commander and ruler. If in a single army there were as many commanders as there are legions, cohorts, wedges, and cavalry wings, the battle line could not even be drawn up in the first place, since each would refuse the danger; nor could it easily be governed or controlled, because all would follow their own plans, whose diversity would do more harm than good. So too in this dominion of the natural world, unless [Col. 0125B] there is one to whom the care of the whole entirety is referred, all things will be dissolved and collapse.

To say that the world is governed by the judgment of many [Col. 0126A] is just as if someone were to assert that there are many minds in one body, because the services performed by the limbs are many and varied: as though each bodily sense were believed to be governed by an individual mind, and likewise the many emotions by which we are accustomed to be moved—to anger, desire, joy, fear, or compassion—so that in all these activities just as many minds were thought to be at work. If anyone actually said this, he would appear not to possess even the one mind that he has.

But if, in a single body, one mind possesses the governance of so many things and attends to them all simultaneously, why should anyone suppose that the world cannot be governed by one but can be governed by many? Because these defenders of the gods understand this, they say that the gods preside over individual things and parts, yet in such a way that there is one supreme ruler. The others, therefore, will no longer [Col. 0126B] be gods, but attendants and ministers whom that one supreme being, powerful over all, has appointed to these duties; and they themselves [Col. 0127A] will serve his authority and his nods.

[Col. 0127B]  
**Variant Notes on Columns 127–128**

**Will serve.** Thus we have restored the text from manuscripts of the highest rank—two Royal, two Bologna, the Taxaquet manuscript, one Colbert, two Brussels—and the older printed editions. Four recent manuscripts and ten printed editions have “may serve.”

**If they are not all equal.** The Subiaco edition reads: “If all the parts are not equal.”

**Impassible.** For a writer earlier than our author, see Tertullian, [Col. 0127C] *On the Resurrection of the Flesh* 57: “impassible flesh”; *Against the Valentinians* 27: “impassible in Christ”; and frequently elsewhere. **Bünemann.**

**Those who think this to be so.** Venice 1493, 1497, and the Paris edition read: “those who think this”—certainly better than the reading of many witnesses, “those who think this thus,” found also in the Gotha manuscript and Reimmann. **Bünemann.**

**A little later.** That is, below, ch. 8.

**Were.** Thus emended from all the manuscripts and printed editions except three—the editions of Thysius, Gallaeus, and Sparke—which have “had been.”

**Speak of one.** Deuteronomy VI and XXVII; Psalms XVII and LXXXV; Wisdom XII; Isaiah LV. Lactantius does not adduce individual testimonies because the writings of the prophets proclaim this one truth throughout.

**Deceitful.** With Cellarius, we have restored “deceitful” from the best manuscripts—two Bologna, six Royal, five Colbert, the Taxaquet, Palatine, Leipzig, Junius, Em., two Clermont, and two manuscripts designated Brun. Three recent manuscripts and the printed editions read “lying.”

**Indeed, however, etc.** Thus Isaeus reads, and rightly; see his annotation on this passage. Others read “and yet,” but less well; the Saint-Germain manuscript reads “and.”

[Col. 0127D]

**Are being fulfilled.** This is the proper reading, according to two Royal manuscripts nine hundred years old, another Royal manuscript of good quality, Gronovius’s manuscript, and one Clermont manuscript in the first hand. Jerome speaks of the prophets in Preface 6 to *Jeremiah*: “We, however, following the authority of the apostles and evangelists, and especially of the apostle Paul, show that whatever was promised literally to the people of Israel has been spiritually fulfilled in us and continues to be fulfilled even today.” **Gronovius.**—Thus also the Cauchy and Utrecht editions read.

**Foretell the future.** Valla reports that his codex read “predict the future.” Seers are elegantly said to “sing” and “sing beforehand.” Lactantius, Book V, ch. 5: “It is established that Zechariah . . . sang.” Book IV, ch. 11: “The prophets had sung long before.” **Bünemann.**

**Driven from his mind.** In place of simply “deranged,” compare Seneca, *Consolation to Polybius* 18. So too Lactantius, Book IV, ch. 27. Two Royal manuscripts, two Colbert manuscripts, the Gotha, Junius, and Brun. manuscripts read “whose mind has been removed,” which also expresses correctly—indeed, more forcefully—what Lactantius intends. For in wishing to prove that the prophets were not insane, he says that madmen, whose minds have been removed, cannot speak both of the future and in a coherent manner. **Gallaeus.**—See also Lactantius on “the minds of men driven away,” *Divine Institutes* IV, ch. 27.

**But also coherently.** Thus all manuscripts and printed editions transmit the text. Valla observes, *Elegances* III, ch. 27, that Lactantius ought to have written “but at least coherently,” “but certainly coherently,” or “but even coherently,” and suspects a scribal error. **Isaeus.**

**Were they, then?** Eight recent manuscripts read “They were not, then.” Both readings are good.—**Were they, then?** Thus read nearly all manuscripts and the Subiaco, Rostock, Venice 1471 and 1472, both editions of 1478, the editions of 1493 and 1497, Junta, Aldus, Paris, Pierius, Cratander, Gymnich, Gryphius, Thomasius, Turnèbe, Isaeus, Gallaeus, Cambridge, and Sparke editions. **Bünemann.**

**Foreign.** Heumann thinks “was” must be added, but we follow the manuscripts.

**Correctors of wickedness.** The Cambridge manuscript and the first Subiaco edition of 1465 read “rebukers.” But the former word is fuller and better suited to the following word, “wickedness.” Note Lactantius, *On Anger* 15, and ch. 17: “for the correction of wickedness.” **Bünemann.**

**Far removed from.** This reading, supported by the manuscripts, is more correct than “without doubt,” found in the Subiaco, Rostock, Venice 1471, 1472, and 1497, Pierius, Paris, Cratander, Gymnich, Gryphius, and Aldus editions. Reimmann reads: “was far removed from them.” **Bünemann.**

**For the preservation of life.** See *Divine Institutes* VII, ch. 4: “Given for its protection”—compare above—“and uses.” Seneca, *To Helvia* 9: “The land is scarcely fertile enough for the preservation of its inhabitants . . . how little is necessary for a person’s preservation.” **Bünemann.**

**For the day.** Book III, ch. 25: “Those who must seek their daily sustenance through labor.” **Bünemann.**

**Food obtained on the spur of the moment.** The Subiaco, Venice 1471 and 1472, both editions of 1478, Rostock, and Paris editions read “temporary food.” Yet even the most sumptuous food is temporary. Venice 1493 and 1479 and the Paris edition read *ex temporali* as two words. Finally, Aldus, Gymnich, Gryphius, and Thomasius print *extemporali* as one word, as do the Gotha and other manuscripts. This is excellent. “Food obtained on the spur of the moment” means food that is easily, quickly, and cheaply procured. **Bünemann.**

**Torture and death.** These are discussed below, Book IV, ch. 11. Epiphanius and Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus, wrote lives of the prophets.

If they are not all equal, then they are not all gods. For that which serves cannot be identical with that which rules. If “God” is the name of supreme power, God must be incorruptible, perfect, impassible, and subject to nothing. Those whom necessity compels to obey one supreme God are therefore not gods. But since those who think this are not deceived without cause, we shall disclose the cause of this error a little later. For now, let us confirm the unity of divine power by testimonies.

## CHAPTER IV. That the Prophets Also Foretold That There Is Truly One God

The prophets, who were very numerous, proclaim one God and speak of one, since, filled with the spirit of the one God, [Col. 0127B] they foretold what was to come with a uniform and harmonious voice. Yet those who are devoid of truth do not think that they should be believed. They say that these voices were not divine but human. Clearly, because the prophets proclaim one God, they must have been either insane or deceitful. Indeed, however, we see that their prophecies have been fulfilled and are being fulfilled every day; and their harmonious divination, agreeing in one judgment, [Col. 0128A] teaches that they were not mad. For what man driven from his mind could not only foretell the future but also speak coherently?

Were they, then, deceitful when they spoke such things? What could be so foreign to them as a motive for deception, when they restrained others from every kind of fraud? They were sent by God precisely so that they might be both heralds of his majesty and correctors of human wickedness.

Moreover, the desire to fabricate and lie belongs to those who seek wealth and desire profit; such motives were far removed from those holy men. They discharged the office entrusted to them in such a way that, abandoning everything necessary for the preservation of life, they labored neither for the future nor even for the day, content with whatever food obtainable on the spur of the moment God supplied. And they not only [Col. 0128B] gained no profit but also suffered torture and death. For the commands of justice are bitter to the vicious and those who live wickedly. Accordingly, the people whose sins the prophets both reproved and prohibited killed them after subjecting them to the most cruel torments. Therefore, since the pursuit of profit was absent from them, the will and motive to deceive were also absent. Moreover, some of them were rulers or even kings, [Col. 0129A] against whom no suspicion of greed or fraud could arise; and yet did they not proclaim the one God with the same prophetic power as the others?

[Col. 0129B]  
**Variant Notes on Columns 129–130**

**Could arise.** Thirteen manuscripts read “can arise.”

**Greed.** Here “greed” means the same as “pursuit of profit” below. Compare below, “without avarice.” **Bünemann.**

**The one God.** That is, the sole and unique God. Nothing is more frequent in Lactantius than *singularis* in the sense of “one” or “unique,” following Cicero’s usage: Book I, chs. 3 and 6; Book II, ch. 16; Book V, chs. 1 and 21; Book VI, ch. 9; Book IV, chs. 12, 26, and 29; Turin *Epitome*, chs. 3 and 4. **Bünemann.**

**From these.** From nearly all the manuscripts and the older editions—the Roman editions, Venice 1490, Erasmus 1539, Betuleius, and Isaeus—we have restored Lactantius’s characteristic expression. So too below, Book V, ch. 15: “Let us teach from their own authorities.” Cicero likewise writes to Lentulus, “that I had bought a house from Crassus”; and in *On the Orator*, “I heard this from my father.” Partly from **Isaeus**. Recent editions read “by these,” a reading that would be more pleasing if it had manuscript support.

**I mean poets and philosophers.** Augustine, *Against Faustus* XIII, ch. 15, shows that the testimony of poets and philosophers is valid for refuting pagan vanity, though not for embracing their authority.

**We must prove one God from these.** Lactantius demonstrates that the ancient pagan sages believed in one God. Saint Justin does the same in his book *On Monarchy*, and Clement of Alexandria in his *Address to the Nations*. See Agostino Steuco, *On the Perennial Philosophy*. From **Isaeus**.

**Forcing . . . brightness upon us.** Compare Minucius 17.3: “It is neither right nor permissible to remain ignorant of the heavenly brightness forcing itself upon our eyes and senses.” On the subject compare Book II, ch. 1, and Book III, ch. 1.—In place of “brightness,” the Subiaco edition has “will.” **Bünemann.**

**The poets, therefore.** Minucius Felix likewise says in ch. 19: “I hear the poets too proclaiming one father of gods and men.” One may see this everywhere among both Greek and Latin poets, who acknowledge no God besides the one. See Orpheus, Phocylides, Xenophanes of Colophon, Hermesianax, Parmenides, and Philemon. And what could be more divine than those verses of Sophocles preserved in Clement of Alexandria’s *Exhortation to the Greeks* and in Cyril’s *Against Julian*? Among the Latin poets, consult Valerius Soranus; Plautus in the *Captives*:

> There surely is a God who both hears and sees what we do;

Manilius, *Astronomica* I:

> God is he who remains unchanged throughout eternity.

Horace, *Odes* I.12:

> He who governs the affairs of men and gods,  
> Who rules the sea and lands and the world  
> Through the changing seasons—  
> Nothing greater than he is brought forth,  
> Nor does anything equal or second to him flourish.

Also Horace, *Odes* III.4; Ovid, *Metamorphoses*:

> Thus the care of God distinguished the enclosed mass  
> By the same numerical order.

[Col. 0130B] Seneca, *Thyestes*:

> God drives our affairs in a swiftly whirling vortex.

Lucan, *Pharsalia* IX, speaking of Jupiter:

> God’s dwelling is wherever there are earth, sea, air,  
> Heaven, and virtue. Why seek the gods any farther?  
> Jupiter is whatever you see, whatever is moved.

**Orpheus, who is the most ancient.** Thus the best and oldest manuscripts—two Bologna, seven Royal, Taxaquet, Leipzig, four Colbert, Junius, two Clermont, Utrecht—and the old Roman edition and Isaeus. Four recent manuscripts and many printed editions read “who,” etc. Tatian says, *Ὀρφεὺς δὲ* etc., that is: “Orpheus lived at the same time as Hercules.” Others, however, say that even the verses attributed to him were composed by Onomacritus, who lived in the time of the sons of Pisistratus, around the fiftieth Olympiad. Tzetzes too, History 399, *Chiliades* 12, makes him a contemporary of Hercules and says that he flourished one hundred years before the Trojan War. This I have transcribed from a distinguished scholar. **Vossius.**—Cyril, *Against Julian* I, asserts that Orpheus, son of Oeagrus, first composed odes and hymns to idols, but later changed his mind and sang a recantation. Among other verses of Orpheus, these occur especially often:

> One is self-generated; from the one all things have been brought forth.  
> Among them he himself moves about, yet no one  
> Beholds him, etc.

Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I, reports that Aristotle stated that this Orpheus never existed; and that the poems circulated under his name were attributed by the Pythagoreans to a certain Cecrops—or, as the text should read, Cercops. From **Vossius**.—Note also that Origen, *Against Celsus* I, denied that any writings of Orpheus still existed in his own time. On Orpheus see below, ch. 22.

**Among the Argonauts.** The Argonauts were the heroes, more than fifty in number, who went with Jason to Colchis. The chief among them were Castor and Pollux, Telamon, Orpheus, Hercules, and the boy Hylas. They received this name from the ship in which they sailed, for that ship was called *Argo* because of its length.

**With the sons of Tyndareus.** Castor and Pollux, who are called “sons of Tyndareus” (*Τυνδαρίδαι*) by an extended use of the term; for they were not both fathered by Tyndareus, but only Castor, while Pollux was fathered by Jupiter. They are nevertheless called sons of Tyndareus because both were born from Leda, Tyndareus’s wife.

**That is, First-Born.** These words should be deleted and are not found in the Rohans and Saint-Germain manuscripts. They are nothing but a gloss, or a copyist’s interpretation.

**All things generated.** On this doctrine of Orpheus, see Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* III.

***Phanes* (Φάνης).** Macrobius, who refers the divine powers of all the gods to Apollo, assigns this epithet to him, although he gives a different explanation of the name. “They also call him Phanes,” he says, “from *to shine* (*ἀπὸ τοῦ φαίνειν*), and Phanaeus, ‘because he appears young’ (*ἐπειδὴ φαίνεται νέος*), since the sun renews itself every day”; Book I, ch. 17. In the following chapter he cites these verses of Orpheus in approximately the same sense. Macrobius’s words are: “Orpheus too, wishing the sun to be understood, says among other things”:

> Melting the divine ether, which previously had been motionless,  
> He revealed to the gods a season most beautiful to behold,  
> Whom indeed they call Earth, Phanes, and Dionysus, etc.

Macrobius, ch. 18.

***First-born*, etc.** That is:

> First-born Phaethon, son of the far-extending air.

## CHAPTER V. On the Testimonies of Poets and Philosophers

But let us indeed set aside the testimonies of the prophets, lest proof derived from those who are not believed at all should seem insufficiently suitable. Let us turn to recognized authorities and summon as witnesses for the proof of truth those very writers whom our opponents customarily employ against us—I mean poets and philosophers. From these we must prove that there is one God, not because they possessed a knowledge of the truth, but because the power [Col. 0130A] of truth itself is so great that no one can be so blind as not to see the divine brightness forcing itself upon his eyes.

The poets, therefore, although they adorned the gods in their songs and magnified their deeds with the highest praises, nevertheless very frequently acknowledge that all things are contained and governed by one spirit or mind. Orpheus, who is the most ancient of the poets and a contemporary of the gods themselves—for tradition says that he sailed among the Argonauts with the sons of Tyndareus and Hercules—calls the true and great God *prōtogonos* (πρωτόγονος), that is, “first-born,” because nothing was generated before him, while all things were generated by him. He also names him *Phanes* (φάνης), because, when nothing yet existed, he was the first to appear and come forth from infinity. [Col. 0131A] Because Orpheus could not comprehend his origin and nature in his mind, he said that he was born from the immeasurable air:

> First-born Phaethon, son of the far-extending air  
> (*Πρωτόγονος φαέθων περὶ μήκεος ἠέρος υἱός*).

For he had nothing further that he could say. He says that this being is the parent of all the gods, for whose sake he created heaven and provided for his children, so that they might have a dwelling and a common abode:

> He built an imperishable home for the immortals  
> (*ἔκτισεν ἀθανάτοις δόμον ἄφθιτον*).

[Col. 0131C]  
**Variant Notes on Columns 131–132**

***He built*, etc.** That is: “He founded an incorruptible home for the immortals.”

**Guided.** Thus nearly all manuscripts and the older and better editions, as well as Lactantius himself below: “likewise guided by nature.” The old Bologna manuscript has “led down”; four recent manuscripts have “taught”; three other recent manuscripts, “speaking.”

**Power of heaven.** Three recent manuscripts and nearly all printed editions read “might.”

**He could not . . . was said.** More on Jupiter and Saturn below, chs. 11 and 12.

**To be an element.** Aristotle, however, would not have admitted this, since in his book *On the World* he held that the ether was “an element distinct from the four, unmixed and divine” (*στοιχεῖον ἕτερον τῶν τεσσάρων, ἀκήρατον καὶ θεῖον*).

**Relevant to truth.** Cyril nevertheless shows in *Against Julian* that Homer knew the one God. See Lactantius [Col. 0131D] below, ch. 19.

**From chaos.** He refutes this in Book II, ch. 8. Compare Grotius, *On the Truth of the Christian Religion* I, §16, where he gives a learned exposition of these matters. **Bünemann.**—**But from chaos, which is a crude, etc.** See Hesiod’s *Theogony*. In Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I: “A crude and undigested mass.” Linus too learned and taught that things had been confused:

> In the primeval age all things were mingled together.

Anaxagoras likewise said: “All things were together; but Mind separated and arranged them, and set in order the things that had been confused.” The Egyptians too understood that the world emerged from chaos, a confused mass. Diogenes Laertius says of them in his preface: *Ἀρχὴν εἶναι τὴν ὕλην*, etc.: “The first principle is a confused mass; from this the four elements were separated, and perfect living beings arose.” The heresiarch Valentinus followed Hesiod: “For he too wishes to introduce thirty gods and heavens; the first is the Depth” (*Τριάκοντα γὰρ καὶ οὗτος θεοὺς καὶ οὐρανοὺς βούλεται προσάγειν· ὁ μὲν πρῶτός ἐστι βύθος*). See Epiphanius, *Heresy* 31. Anaxagoras likewise made undigested chaos the seedbed of all things and added an efficient principle, Mind or God.

[Col. 0132B]

**Produced.** One old Bologna manuscript and one recent Colbert manuscript read “made.” A learned man would prefer “fashioned,” because of what follows, namely “matter formed.”

**Matter formed.** Correctly, for formation pertains to matter and material things. One old Bologna manuscript, one Colbert manuscript, and the Gotha and Saint-Germain manuscripts read “matter made.”

**Made.** Thus restored from nearly all manuscripts. The Bologna and Taxaquet manuscripts, together with the printed editions, read “may have made.”

**On Helicon.** The mountain sacred to the Muses. Poets everywhere proclaim Helicon’s loftiness. Thus Aratus, *Phaenomena* 216, and Strabo IX, chs. 8, 9, and 10. Hesiod had already said at the beginning of the *Theogony*, *Αἵ τ᾽ Ἑλικῶνος*, etc., that is:

> Who dwell upon Helicon, the great and sacred mountain.

**He had come after premeditation and preparation.** Cicero, *Against Verres* II, ch. 40; *Against Verres* II, ch. 6; and *For Publius Quinctius* 11: “When you had come prepared and after due premeditation.” **Bünemann.**

**Was not far from the truth.** Book III, ch. 8: “was not far from this vanity.” **Bünemann.**

**Whom he called mind and spirit.** This is the order in all the manuscripts except two Colbert manuscripts, which, like the printed editions, have “whom he called spirit and mind.”

**May be ignorant.** Thus the excellent Royal-Puteanus codex, the Leipzig manuscripts, three Colbert manuscripts, one Clermont manuscript, and others, together with all the printed editions except Cellarius; twelve manuscripts read “might be ignorant.” Both readings are good. The former seems to me to be Lactantius’s. For if he had written “might be ignorant,” what scribe would have substituted “may be ignorant”?

**That spirit.** Thus we have emended the text from all the manuscripts and the Roman editions of 1468 and 1470, Gymnich, Cratander, Turnèbe, and the two Leipzig editions. Four printed editions incorrectly have “those spirits.”

**For God passes through all things.** Virgil, *Georgics* IV, verse 221. Juvencus, *Gospel History* I:

> We speak nothing while God is absent; no hidden recess  
> Of the breast conceals what lies enclosed: God is present and sees all things.

See Epictetus in Arrian I, ch. 14; Apuleius, *On the World*; Jerome on Paul’s *Epistle to the Ephesians* IV; Augustine, *City of God* IV, ch. 2; Salvian, *On the Governance of God* I; and likewise Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I. **Elmenhorst.**

**Work.** Namely, the *Metamorphoses*, in which pagan theology is expounded.

Guided, therefore, by nature and reason, Orpheus understood that there existed a preeminent power, the creator of heaven and earth. For he could not say that Jupiter was the ruler of all things, since Jupiter was born from Saturn; nor could he say Saturn himself, who was said to have been born from Heaven. Yet he did not dare establish Heaven as the first God, because he saw that it was an element of the world and itself required a creator. This reasoning led him to [Col. 0131B] that first-born God, to whom he assigns and attributes sovereignty.

Homer could give us nothing relevant to truth, since he wrote of human rather than divine affairs. Hesiod could have done so, since in the compass of a single book he included the generation of the gods. Yet he gave us nothing, because he began not with God the Creator but with chaos, which is a confused accumulation of crude and unordered matter. [Col. 0132A] He should first have explained whence, when, and how chaos itself began to exist or acquire consistency. Just as all things were arranged, ordered, and produced by some craftsman, so matter itself must necessarily have been formed by someone. Who, then, made it except God, to whose power all things are subject? But Hesiod avoided this while shrinking in horror from the unknown truth. For he did not pour forth that poem on Helicon under the inspiration of the Muses, as he wished it to appear; he had come after premeditation and preparation.

The first of our own poets, Virgil, was not far from the truth. These are his words concerning the supreme God, whom he called mind and spirit:

> In the beginning, the heavens and the earth,  
> The watery plains, the shining globe of the moon,  
> And the Titanian stars—a spirit sustains them from within;  
> Mind, infused throughout the limbs, sets the whole mass in motion  
> And mingles with the mighty body.

[Col. 0132B] And lest anyone perhaps be ignorant of who that spirit possessing so great a power was, he made it clear elsewhere, saying:

> For God passes through all the lands,  
> The tracts of sea, and the depths of heaven.  
> From him the flocks, the herds, mankind, and every kind  
> Of beast at birth draw their slender lives.

Ovid too, at the beginning of his celebrated work, without any concealment of the name, acknowledges that the world was ordered by God, whom he calls the fashioner of the world and the craftsman of all things. [Col. 0133A] But if either Orpheus or these poets of ours, who—[the supplied source breaks off here]

[Col. 0133B]

**Who.** The Subiaco edition reads “which.”

Thales of Miletus, etc. He said that water was that from which all things were born. “And from which” (*Et qua*) is the reading of twenty-three manuscripts, among them the very ancient Bologna and Royal manuscripts; “were born” (*Nata sunt*) occurs in sixteen. Augustine, *City of God*, book VIII, chapter 2: “The founder of the Ionian school was Thales of Miletus (who died in the first year of the fifty-eighth Olympiad), one of those seven who were called sages. But the other six were distinguished by their manner of life and by certain precepts suited to living well. Thales, however, became eminent by investigating the nature of things and committing his discussions to writing, so that he might also establish a succession of followers; and he was especially remarkable because, having mastered the numerical calculations of astronomy, he was able even to predict eclipses of the sun and moon. Minucius Felix likewise, following Cicero and Laertius, said: “Thales of Miletus said that water was the beginning of things, but that God was the mind which formed all things from water.”

**Of things.** The printed editions read “of all things”; but we have followed the manuscripts, especially the Rohan and Saint-Germain manuscripts. Certainly these two words are unnecessary, since “formed all things” immediately precedes. I suspected that they were not Lactantius’ words but had been inserted by copyists, especially since the codices vary greatly here. For both words are absent from six Royal manuscripts; “all” is absent from the Utrecht, Junius, one Clermont, and the Bruni manuscript, [Col. 0134B] and from Cellarius’ edition; “things” is absent from the editions of Betuleius, Thomasius, Isaeus, and Sparke. **Antisthenes, many, etc.** Below, *On the Anger of God*, chapter 11; Cicero, *The Nature of the Gods*.
