**Mingled.** The common text of Virgil has “commingled.”

**Chrysippus.** “Chrysippus says that divine power resides in reason and in the soul and mind of universal nature; and that the world itself is God, together with the universal diffusion of its soul; and also the shadow of fate and the necessity of future events.” [Col. 0135B] Thus Cicero, *The Nature of the Gods* I. See Aristotle, volume II; Stobaeus, *Physical Extracts*, chapter 2; Diogenes Laertius, book VII. ELMENHORST.]

…they perceived under nature’s guidance; had they defended it forever, they would have held, having grasped the truth, the same doctrine that we follow.

But enough thus far about the poets. Let us come to the philosophers, whose authority is weightier and judgment more certain, because they are believed to have devoted themselves not to fictitious subjects but to the investigation of truth. Thales of Miletus, who was one of the seven sages and is said to have been the first of all to inquire into natural causes, said that water was that from which all things were born, but that God was the mind which formed all things from water. Thus he placed the matter [Col. 0133B] of things in moisture, but established their originating principle and cause [Col. 0134A] in God. Pythagoras defined what God was as follows: “A mind passing through and diffused throughout every part of the world and the whole of nature, from which all living creatures that are born receive life.” Anaxagoras said that God was an infinite mind which moves by itself. Antisthenes said that there were indeed many gods belonging to particular peoples, but only one God by nature, the craftsman of the whole universe. Cleanthes and Anaximenes say that ether is the supreme God. Our poet agreed with this opinion:

> Then the almighty father, Ether, in fertile showers  
> Descends into the bosom of his joyful consort,  
> And, great himself, mingled with her great body, nourishes every offspring.  
> [Col. 0134B]

Chrysippus sometimes calls a natural force endowed with divine reason, [Col. 0135A] and sometimes divine necessity, God. Likewise Zeno [Col. 0135A]

[Note: [Col. 0135B] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 135–136]

**Zeno.** Cicero, *The Nature of the Gods* I, chapter 14: “Zeno holds that the natural law is divine, and that it possesses the power to command what is right and forbid its opposite”; and elsewhere he says that ether is God, as Laertius and Plutarch attest. Cleanthes, his pupil, subsequently followed him. This Zeno of Citium was the founder of the Stoic school.

**Nor is it an objection, etc.** The words of St. Cyprian, *On the Worship of Idols*, are especially pertinent here. “Do not,” he says, “ask God’s name; ‘God’ is his name. Terms are needed where a multitude must be distinguished by individual marks of designation. For God, who alone exists, the term ‘God’ is the whole of his name.” [Col. 0135C]

**Aristotle.** See Aristotle, *Metaphysics* I, chapters 3 and 4; Cicero, *The Nature of the Gods* I; Minucius Felix, *Octavius*, where you will see how greatly that philosopher disagrees with himself.

**Nevertheless, he attests that one supreme mind presides over the world.** He is speaking of Aristotle, who plainly held that there is one God, as is evident from book II *On Generation*, book XII of the *Divine Matters*, and chapter 7 of the treatise *On the World*. See Scaliger, *On Subtlety*, against Cardano, Exercise 365. ISAEUS.

**Plato.** Minucius Felix: “For Plato, in the *Timaeus*, God is, by that very title, the parent of the world.” Plato, *Laws* IV: “God indeed, all things …” (ὁ θεὸς μὲν πάντα etc.); and in the *Sophist* he calls him “the craftsman of all things” (πάντων δημιουργόν). St. Augustine examines Plato’s theology in book VIII of the *City of God*.

**Calls him supreme.** Plato, *Laws* I and II.

**On the Laws.** Cicero wrote these books shortly before his death.

[Col. 0135D]

**Nothing is more excellent . . . nature.** Each of these is Cicero’s own words from *The Nature of the Gods* II, chapter 30. BUNEMANN.

**In the Consolation.** The work is lost; but see Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I, drawing on Plato.

**When he was discussing untimely death.** No book written by Seneca under this title survives. BUNEMANN.

**The authority and majesty.** Thus we have emended the text from nearly all the manuscripts and from the older and better editions. “The author and majesty” crept into the later editions; one recent Royal manuscript, one Colbert manuscript, and one Bruni manuscript have “the truth and majesty.” Shortly afterward, the Subiaco edition reads “of the ruler” instead of “the ruler.”

**The God of all the gods.** Correctly so; thus eighteen manuscripts. Previously the text was: “of the ruler of the earth and heaven, and of the God of all the gods”; but this is less satisfactory.

**Which we worship individually.** Because our author often mentions adoration, it is appropriate at present to note the matters pertaining to the ritual of adoration, [Col. 0136B] lest later, when the same subject recurs, we be forced to scrape the same string. It is now well known to everyone that in the ritual of adoration the hand was customarily brought to the mouth. Brissonius, *On Formulas*, notes an exceedingly clear passage explaining this practice, namely one from Lucian; Dempster too noted it on Rosinus from Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* IV: “And bringing their right hands to their mouths, with the forefinger resting upon the upright thumb, they venerated her in devout adoration as though she were the goddess Venus herself.” The same author, in the *Apology*: “To bring the hand to the lips for the purpose of adoration.” Salmasius correctly observed in his *Plinian Exercises*, p. 936, that worshippers customarily turned their bodies toward the right. Pliny says: [Col. 0136C] “In adoration we bring the right hand to the lips and turn the whole body around.” Plautus and Propertius should also be consulted. Salmasius, in his notes on Flavius Vopiscus, explains this ritual of adoration and teaches that worshippers customarily not only turned the entire body toward the right but also, more specifically, brought the hand to the lips and planted kisses upon it; hence the expression “a lipped kiss” for that of a person who, in adoration, brought his hand to his lips and kissed it. Thus people once adored their divinities, their emperors, and the images of emperors no less than statues of the gods. Jerome, *Against Rufinus*: “Those who adore are accustomed to kiss the hand and bow their heads.” Lipsius has more about this custom in *Select Passages*, book II, p. 20; but there he is wrong to write that worshippers customarily first stretched out the hand and then immediately brought it to the mouth. They did the opposite: they were accustomed to kiss the hand and then extend it toward the person whom they were adoring. This is what they called “throwing kisses” or “tossing kisses” (Tacitus, *Histories* I). “Tossing kisses” occurs in Juvenal, *Satire* 4, and in Phaedrus, book V, poem 87:

> [Col. 0136D] The flute-player  
> Tosses kisses,

that is, he adores the people. Properly speaking, someone is said to “throw a kiss” when he kisses his hand and then extends it toward those to whose honor and veneration he offers that kiss; for by extending the hand they had first kissed, they seemed in a certain sense to extend and throw the kiss itself toward those to whom they paid that honor. Tacitus, speaking of Nero as a singer: “Finally, bending his knee, he venerated that assembly with his hand.” He was playing the part of a true stage performer; for it was the custom of actors, pantomimes, and singers to adore the people upon entering the stage. An old epigram published by Pithoeus, as may be seen in book IV of his *Epigrams*, says:

> On entering the stage, the dancer adores the people.

Charioteers likewise venerated the people with their whips. [Col. 0137B] For since they brought the right hand to the mouth in adoration, charioteers, who held the whip in their right hand, kissed the whip itself and thus performed adoration (Cassius Dio, in *Caracalla*, concerning his chariot-driving). This ritual was customary not only among the Romans but also in the East, as the very learned Drusius correctly noted in *Fragments of the Ancient Interpreters*, p. 834. He proved it from Job 31:26–28: “If I saw the sun when it shone, or the moon proceeding in splendor, and my heart was secretly seduced, and my hand was brought to my mouth, this too would be an iniquity to be punished by the judge, because I would thereby have denied the supreme God.” There the Septuagint renders it: “If I kissed my hand after bringing it to my mouth.” According to Symmachus: “And my hand performed adoration around my mouth.” Jerome: “And I kissed my hand with my mouth.” In Hebrew idiom, kissing signifies adoration, as is evident from the final verse of Psalm 2 and also 1 Kings 19:18: “Every knee which has not bowed itself to Baal, and every mouth which has not kissed him.” In Hosea 13:11, “Let them kiss.” Symmachus and Theodotion rendered it [Col. 0137C] “adoring”; Aquila, καταφιλοῦντες, “kissing.” Jerome says: “For what we translated, following Symmachus and Theodotion, as **adoring**, Aquila interpreted as καταφιλοῦντες, that is, ‘kissing’; for those who adore are accustomed to kiss their own hand, which Job denies having done when he says: ‘If I kissed my hand, bringing it to my mouth’” (from Salmasius). See Martin Kempius, *Dissertation on Kisses* 4, “On the Kiss of Adoration.”

]

calls the divine and natural law God.

Although the opinion of all these men is uncertain, it nevertheless tends toward the same conclusion: their agreement that there is one providence. For whether you call it nature, ether, reason, mind, fated necessity, divine law, or anything else, it is the same thing that we call God. Nor is the diversity of designations an objection, since by their very meaning they all resolve into one. Aristotle, although he disagrees with himself and both says and thinks contradictory things, nevertheless attests that one supreme mind presides over the world. Plato, who is judged the wisest of all, plainly and openly defends monarchy; he does not call it ether, reason, or nature, but God, just as it is, and says that this perfect and wonderful world [Col. 0135B] was fashioned by him. Cicero, who followed and imitated Plato in many respects, frequently acknowledges God and calls him supreme in [Col. 0136A] the books he wrote *On the Laws*. When discussing *The Nature of the Gods*, he argues as follows that the world is governed by him: “Nothing is more excellent than God; therefore the world must be governed by him. God is therefore obedient or subject to no nature; consequently, he himself governs all nature.” In the *Consolation*, moreover, he defines what God is: “Indeed, God himself, as we understand him, can be understood in no other way than as a certain unfettered and free mind, separated from every mortal concretion, perceiving and moving all things.”

Annaeus Seneca too, perhaps the keenest Stoic among the Romans, how often does he celebrate the supreme God with deserved praise! For when he was discussing untimely death, he said: “Do you not understand the authority and majesty of your judge—the ruler of the earth and heaven [Col. 0136B] and God of all the gods, upon whom depend those divinities which we worship and revere individually?” Likewise, in the *Exhortations*: “When he was laying the first foundations [Col. 0137A] of this most beautiful structure and beginning that work than which nature knows nothing greater or better, he begot gods as ministers of his kingdom, so that all things might proceed under their own leaders, although he himself had stretched himself throughout the whole body.” [Col. 0137A]

[Note: [Col. 0137C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 137–138]

**God begot.** Crenius illustrates this in part IX of his *Observations*, p. 30 ff. I have become entirely convinced that the text of Lactantius should here be corrected to “God begot” (*Deus genuit*). The words of book I, chapter 7, where he refers back to this passage, support it: “That God begot the ministers of his kingdom.” The printed editions had “he begot gods” (*deos genuit*). BUNEMANN.

**And almost grasped it.** Thus we have restored the text from four old Royal manuscripts, one Bologna, six Colbert, and the Gronovius, Leipzig, two Clermont, and two Bruni manuscripts, as well as five old editions. Six recent commonly used editions have “nearly” (*prope*).

**Rendered foolish by corrupt opinions.** Thus two manuscript codices belonging to the very learned Gronovius and Clermont—one at first hand—[Col. 0137D] together with four more recent editions. But five Royal manuscripts, one Bologna, three Colbert, one Sorbonne, and the Cauchy, Junius, one Clermont, Leipzig, Pen, Taxius, Utrecht, Erfurt, Cambridge, Christ Church, and Balliol manuscripts, together with the Roman edition of 1468 and the editions of Betuleius and Isaeus, have “tinged” (*infucata*). Three Royal manuscripts, one Colbert, and the Bruni manuscript, with several printed editions, read *fucata*, “colored.” One recent Colbert manuscript has *fuscata*, “darkened”; another Colbert manuscript has the corrupt retrograde reading *infricata*; fourteen manuscripts have “backward.” The reading of the Gronovius and Clermont manuscripts, *infatuata*, “rendered foolish,” seemed truer to us, for through opinions we fall into folly. Lactantius, book IV, chapter 1: “Through the folly of a single age, which adopted various religions and believed that there were many gods, so great an ignorance of oneself was suddenly reached.” The verb, though effective in expressing the matter, is not very common. Cicero, *Philippic* III: “These things explain why his teacher was transformed from an orator into a plowman—to make a foolish man even more foolish at public expense.” *For Flaccus*: “Surely he could not make anyone so foolish as to entrust him with a single coin?” [Col. 0138B] In the aforesaid twenty-three manuscripts and in some editions, the careless mistake of copyists gives *infucata* instead of *infatuata*; some have *fucata*. Yet what can this “custom colored by corrupt opinions” mean? What is it to “color,” unless to alter artificially the definite appearance of a thing? Nevertheless, we do not altogether reject the manuscripts and editions that read “custom colored” or “tinged by corrupt opinions,” since elsewhere one reads of “truth colored by falsehood.” These expressions correspond very closely to one another.

**Divine testimonies.** That is, testimonies regarded by the pagans as divine and possessing divine authority, such as the verses of the Sibyls, the Milesian Apollo, and Hermes Trismegistus, who proclaim only one God.

**Was translated from among men into the gods.** Thus the better manuscripts: the Bologna, two Royal manuscripts nine hundred years old, three other Royal, four Colbert, two Sorbonne, two Clermont, three Leipzig, the Gatianus, and the Marmoutier manuscript. The last, like the oldest Royal manuscript, corruptly reads “was released” instead of “was translated.” Eleven other, more recent manuscripts and most printed editions have “among the gods.”

**Into the gods.** Thus Reimmann, Gotha, Leipzig, three Utrecht manuscripts, Taxius, the Junta and Bologna editions—more elegantly than the Subiaco, Venice 1471 and 1497, [Col. 0138C] and Rostock 1476 editions. Concerning the same Mercury, Lactantius again says, with the constant reading of the codices, in book VII, chapter 13: “Although translated into the gods, he is honored by the Egyptians under the name Mercury.” Cicero himself, *The Nature of the Gods* III, chapter 20: “to translate into the gods”; and already in book I, chapter 13.

**In Cicero.** Namely in book III of *The Nature of the Gods*, which should be consulted.

**Five Mercuries.** The same number is counted by Arnobius; see book III *Against the Nations*: the first was born of Father Heaven and Mother Day; the second was the son of Pharonis and Valens and was also called Trophonius; the third was born of the third Jupiter and Maia; the fourth had the Nile as his father, whose name the Egyptians consider it impious to pronounce; the fifth is he whom the people of Pheneus worship, who is also said to have killed Argus. The Egyptians, they say, call this one Thoyth; yet the chronology does not agree. See Cicero, *The Nature of the Gods* III, and the note placed below.

**For that reason.** Whatever the case, it is certain that Thoyth, or the Mercury of the Egyptians, was much older [Col. 0138D] than the Mercury who killed Argus. This latter Mercury was the son of Jupiter; but Jupiter lived in the nineteenth century before the common era, whereas Thoyth, or the Egyptian Mercury, was ten centuries older than Jupiter, whether he is Thoyth I or his son Thoyth II. On the books published by Thoyth, or the Egyptian Mercury, see Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* VI, where he enumerates them. It is, however, certain that the books we now possess under the name of Mercury Trismegistus are spurious.

**Fled into Egypt.** Thus the manuscripts and printed codices of Lactantius read. Cicero, however, in *The Nature of the Gods* III, from which our author transcribed this passage, has: “and for that reason ruled over Egypt.” Nothing, however, prevents Thoyth from having fled into Egypt and afterward ruled over it.

**Handed down laws and letters to the Egyptians.** Sanchuniathon says that Mercury invented “the writing of the first elements” (τὴν τῶν πρώτων στοιχείων γραφήν) and established the characters of letters.]

And how many other things did Seneca say about God resembling our own teachings! I postpone them now because they are more appropriate elsewhere. For the present it is enough to demonstrate that men of supreme intelligence touched upon the truth and almost grasped it, had not custom, rendered foolish by corrupt opinions, dragged them backward. Under its influence they believed both that other gods existed and that those things which God made for human use were to be regarded and worshipped as gods, as though they were endowed with sensation.

[Col. 0138A]

## CHAPTER VI  
### On Divine Testimonies, the Sibyls, and Their Poems

Let us now pass to the divine testimonies. But first I shall present one which resembles a divine testimony, both because of its extreme antiquity and because the person I shall name was translated from among men into the gods. In Cicero, Gaius Cotta the pontiff, arguing against the Stoics about religions and the variety of opinions customarily held concerning the gods, so that in the manner of the Academics he might make everything uncertain, says that there were five Mercuries. After enumerating four of them in order, he says that the fifth was the one who killed Argus and for that reason fled into Egypt, where he handed down laws and letters to the Egyptians. [Col. 0139A] The Egyptians call him Thoyth. [Col. 0139A]

[Note: [Col. 0139B] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 139–140] [Col. 0139B]

**The Egyptians call him Thoyth.** Nowhere in all the works of Lactantius is there greater variation among the manuscripts and editions than here. Many printed editions give *Thoth*. But the oldest and best of all the manuscripts—the Bologna, one Royal manuscript nine hundred years old, the Marmoutier, Gatianus, and one Sorbonne—have *Thoyth*. Supporting these are one Royal manuscript, which has *Thout*; another Royal, which has Θεουσεν; one Colbert, which has ΝΗΟΥΤΗ; and another Colbert, which has Θεουμ. Five more recent manuscripts—one Royal at first hand, one Colbert, the Navarre, Victorinus, and Bruni manuscripts—seem to have read Θωυθ or Θευθ, as do the editions of Betuleius, Fasitel, and Heinrich Petri of 1556. The remaining manuscripts are greatly corrupted: two recent Royal, one Colbert, one Sorbonne, and one Clermont have Ημουθ or Ηνουθ; two Royal manuscripts, together with the Roman editions of 1468 and 1470, have πνουγνα, πνουγν, etc.; the other Clermont manuscript has πνουσία; and one Colbert has *Hermin*. But I am especially inclined to agree with Johann Gerhard Vossius that the reading should be *Thoyth*. For this is the reading of the best manuscripts and printed codices, and Eusebius, *Preparation of the Gospel* I, chapter 9, likewise shows that it should be read so: [Col. 0139C] “The Egyptians called him Thoyth, the Alexandrians Thoth, and the Greeks translated his name as Hermes” (Αἰγύπτιοι μὲν ἐκάλεσαν Θωὺθ, Ἀλεξανδρεῖς δὲ Θὼθ, Ἑρμῆν δὲ Ἕλληνες μετέφρασαν), that is, Mercury. Similarly, in Cicero, *The Nature of the Gods* III, from which our Lactantius took this passage, the text reads: “The Egyptians call him Thoyth, and among them the first month of the year is called by the same name.” It should further be noted that one Leipzig manuscript has “Moses” instead of “Thoyth.” On the various Mercuries see Isaeus in his notes. On Mercury see also the very learned D. Fourmont’s *Observations on Sanchuniathon*, whose new edition has just appeared in 1747 at Paris from Jean de Bure, volume I.

**Ἑρμόπολις, Hermopolis.** A great city from which the Hermopolitan region, “the Hermopolitan nome” (Ἑρμοπολίτης νόμος), in the inland parts of Egypt west of the Nile, received its name.

**And the Pheneatae worship him religiously.** The same Cicero, *The Nature of the Gods* III, no. 56, speaking of Mercury, says: “The fifth is the one whom the Pheneatae worship and who is said to have slain Argus; for that reason he ruled over Egypt [Col. 0139D] and handed down laws and letters to the Egyptians. The Egyptians call him Thoyth, and among them the first month of the year is called by the same name.” Pausanias likewise, *Arcadia*, book VIII, p. 301: “Of all the gods,” he says, “the Pheneatae venerate Mercury most highly.” The reading should therefore be restored from the Cauchy, one Leipzig, Utrecht, and Christ Church manuscripts and Cellarius’ edition: “and the Pheneatae worship him religiously.” With these agree one Bologna, eight Royal, five Colbert, two Sorbonne, the Gatianus, Marmoutier, one Leipzig, Gotha, Erfurt, Cambridge, and two Clermont manuscripts, in which *Feniatae* is read instead of *Pheneatae*. These are also supported by the Victorinus manuscript, which has *Fenitae*; the Navarre, one Colbert, and the Bruni manuscript, which have *Fenicae*; and another Leipzig manuscript, which has *Fenices*. The Cauchy, Junius, and Cambridge manuscripts, and the Roman edition of 1468, have: “and the Pheneatae preserve and worship him religiously.” The editions of Betuleius, Thysius, Gallus, Sparke, and Walch have: “and the Saitae worship him religiously”; the Paris 1525, Aldine, Fasitel, Cratander, Grapheus, Gymnich, and de Tournes editions have: “and the Saitae preserve and worship him religiously,” [Col. 0140B] which I have found in none of the manuscripts I have seen. Petrus Ciaconius suspects that the text should read: “and both the Saitae and the Pheneatae worship him religiously.” I would prefer: “and the Saitae preserve him, and the Pheneatae worship him religiously,” if I had any manuscript authority for it, so that the meaning would be that he was preserved in Egypt by the Saitae and worshipped in Arcadia by the Pheneatae. It therefore appears that the reading must be *Pheneatae*, because above he had spoken of the Egyptians, from whom he passes to the Arcadian Pheneatae.—**Worship.** Reimmann has “both preserve and worship.” Cambridge, the Junta edition, Cauchy: “preserve and worship.”

**So that his knowledge of many things and arts conferred upon him the surname Trismegistus.** Thus the older and better manuscripts—the Bologna, six Royal, Leipzig, Palatine, and Gronovius manuscripts—and nearly all the printed editions; Cratander and de Tournes have the plural “conferred.” The Cauchy, Junius, and one Colbert manuscripts and the Paris 1525 edition have: “so that because of his knowledge of many things they conferred upon him the surname Trismegistus”; and two recent Royal manuscripts, one Colbert, and the Bruni manuscript have “the name.”

**The surname Trismegistus.** [Col. 0140C] He is also called *Termagnus*, because he founded excellent laws; because, distinguished by the highest priesthood, he established religious ceremonies and sacred rites; and, finally, because he was especially versed in philosophy and taught geometry, which was exceedingly necessary in Egypt, together with other natural sciences. Lactantius will discuss Trismegistus again in *On the Anger of God*, chapter 10.

**By the same names.** See Trismegistus, *Poimandres*, chapter 11; *Asclepius* I. But it is certain that these books of *Poimandres* and *Asclepius* are fictitious.

**Ἀνώνυμον.** In Latin, “without a name.”

**Ὁ δὲ Θεὸς.** In Latin: “But God is one; and the one has no need of a name, for he who is is nameless.”

**God, therefore, has no name.** Minucius Felix, in the *Octavius*: “Do not ask God’s name; ‘God’ is his name.” Likewise, in the *Sentences* of Xystus, and in the Egyptian Hermes, he is called ineffable, not to be named, and to be proclaimed in silence; in Plato too, unuttered and unnameable; in Apuleius, *On the Natural Philosophy of Plato*; Alcinous, *Introduction*, chapter 9; and Porphyry, *History of Philosophy* IV, as quoted by Cyril. [Col. 0140D] See above the testimony of St. Cyprian in the note on the beginning of chapter 5.

**He is one.** Thus St. Cyprian, *Against the Worship of Idols*: “Hermes Trismegistus speaks of one God and calls him incomprehensible and beyond estimation.”

**May think.** Thus restored from nearly all the manuscripts and from the editions of Betuleius and Cellarius. Two Colbert manuscripts, one Clermont, and nearly all the printed editions have the indicative “think.”

**Because they could have erred.** Thus we have restored the text from nearly all the manuscripts. One Clermont manuscript at first hand and many printed editions have “because they erred.”

**Because they themselves were human beings.** Thus we have restored the text from nearly all the manuscripts. The editions and three recent manuscripts have “were”; the printed editions, except Cellarius’, have “these” instead of “themselves.”

**Marcus Varro.** He was born in the 638th year of the City and died, at nearly ninety years of age, in the 727th year of the City. He was a friend of Cicero, who calls him “a writer on every subject” (*universalem polygraphum*) in *Letters to Atticus* V, letter 10. Quintilian likewise, in book XII, attests that Varro transmitted knowledge of nearly everything; [Col. 0141B] see him also in book X, as well as Cicero in the *Academics* I, where he praises Varro exceptionally highly.]

From him the first month of their year, that is, September, received its name among them. He also founded a city which even now is called in Greek Hermopolis (Ἑρμόπολις), and the Pheneatae worship him religiously. Although he was a human being, he was nevertheless of the greatest antiquity and thoroughly instructed in every kind of learning, so much so that his knowledge of many subjects and arts conferred upon him the surname Trismegistus, “Thrice-Greatest.” He wrote books—indeed, many books—pertaining to knowledge of divine matters. In them he asserts the majesty of the supreme and singular God, and calls him by the same names that we do: God and Father. And lest anyone should seek his name, he said that God was “nameless” (ἀνώνυμον), because, precisely on account of his unity, he has no need of the distinguishing property of a name. [Col. 0140A] These are his own words:

> “But God is one, and the one has no need of a name; for he who is is nameless”  
> (Ὁ δὲ Θεὸς εἷς, ὁ δὲ εἷς ὀνόματος οὐ προσδέεται· ἔστι γὰρ ὁ ὢν ἀνώνυμος).

God, therefore, has no name, because he is the only one. Nor is there need of a proper designation except where a multitude requires distinction, so that you may identify each person by an individual mark and appellation. But because God is always one, his proper name is “God.”

It remains to present testimonies from sacred responses and poems, which are much more certain. For perhaps those against whom we are arguing may think that neither poets should be believed, since they invent vain things, nor philosophers, because they could have erred, since they themselves were human beings. Marcus Varro, than whom no one more learned ever lived—not even among [Col. 0141A] the Greeks, much less among the Latins—[Col. 0141A]

[Note: [Col. 0141B] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 141–142]

**Not even among the Greeks . . . lived.** Thus also the Taxius, Cauchy, Junius, Utrecht, and Reimmann manuscripts; the Rostock, Venice 1471, both Venice 1478, and other editions wrongly stuff in “nor among the Latins” or “much less among the Latins.” BUNEMANN.

**Much less among the Latins.** These words are absent from thirty-five manuscripts, as well as from the Rohan and Saint-Germain manuscripts and from the editions of Cellarius and Subiaco. Instead of “much less,” the Roman 1468, Paris 1525, Aldine, Gratianus, Grapheus, and Gymnich editions read “nor.”

**In the books, etc.** On Varro’s books see St. Augustine, *City of God* VI, chapter 3.

**On the Fifteen Men.** On them see Alexander ab Alexandro, *Genial Days* III, chapter 16, and another note below. The following, however, is from Pomponius Laetus: “The Two Men,” he says, “were instituted by Tarquin the Proud, and they alone were to inspect the Sibylline books. Later, when the plebs insisted that members be appointed from its own ranks, ten were appointed from both plebeians and patricians, and afterward fifteen, who were to inspect the Sibylline books.”

[Col. 0141C]

**Sibyl.** On the etymology of the name “Sibyl,” see Servius on *Aeneid* VI.

**Or from the name of a single Delphian woman.** See Antimachus, *On Sibylline Oracles*.

**Or from the counsels of the gods, etc.** This is absurd in many ways and also false. Σίβυλλα, “Sibyl,” is a simple name, not a compound. SALMASIUS.

**Declaring.** Thus we have restored the reading from almost all the manuscripts and from the Roman 1470, Paris 1525, Betuleius, and Cellarius editions. Eight printed editions have “announcing”; one Colbert manuscript has “reporting.”

**Σιοβυλὴν.** Thus we have emended the text from one excellent Royal manuscript, one Sorbonne, one Colbert, and two Bruni manuscripts, which read *Siobulen*. That this must certainly be the reading is evident from the preceding words σιους (“gods”) and βυλὴν (“counsel”). Previously the reading was θεοβούλην.—The words “And so Sibyl . . . Σιοβυλὴν” are absent from the Subiaco edition. As for the Sibyls, both pagans and Christians once transmitted much concerning them and their writings. [Col. 0141D] What judgment they formed concerning these matters does not belong here, nor is there now time to report it. If desired, see St. Augustine, *City of God* XVIII, chapter 23; Vossius; and Blondel, who discussed these matters very well in his book *On the Sibyls*. See also Servatius Gallaeus in his quarto edition of the *Sibylline Poems*, Amsterdam, 1688 and 1689.

**That they were ten in number.** See Antimachus, *On Sibylline Oracles*. Others, among them Suidas, maintain that there were only nine; others, such as Pausanias, four; some, such as Solinus and Ausonius, three. Others, such as Martianus Capella, posit two; finally, some only one. Gaius Pliny, book II, chapter 33, with the support of Aulus Gellius, book I, chapter 19. DEMPSTER. But Giraldi counts more than ten.

**Were accustomed to write repeatedly.** Thus I have restored the text from most of the best manuscripts and from Betuleius’ edition. The Taxius, two Colbert, and one Clermont manuscripts have the indicative “wrote repeatedly.” One Colbert manuscript at second hand and one Clermont at first hand, together with the printed editions, have another indicative form; one Clermont at second hand has a variant subjunctive form. The subjunctive mood is very familiar to Lactantius, as will be evident from what follows.

[Col. 0142B]

**That the first was from Persia.** According to others, she was Chaldaean; according to others, Hebrew, with the personal name Sambethe. BETULEIUS.

**Nicanor.** Perhaps this was Leander Nicanor, the Alexandrian grammarian, who wrote a commentary on Alexander. THYSIUS.

**The second, the Libyssa.** With the Greek termination. Thus seven Royal manuscripts, two of which are nine hundred years old; three Colbert, the Navarre, Utrecht, one Sorbonne, Victorinus, Marmoutier, one Clermont, and another Clermont at second hand; together with the editions of Fasitel, de Tournes, and Sparke. Three Royal manuscripts, the Bologna, Leipzig, Erfurt, Cambridge, Utrecht, Christ Church, three Colbert, one Sorbonne, Gatianus, and one Clermont at first hand, together with most printed editions, have “the Libyan.”

**In the prologue to the *Lamia*, etc.** No *Lamia* survives among the tragedies of Euripides.]

The third, the Delphian. So the Gronovian manuscripts and Cellarius’s edition, as also Lactantius in the *Epitome*, ch. 5, in agreement with Varro, and entirely correctly. For Lactantius said shortly before that some thought the name of the Sibyls was derived from the name of a single Delphian Sibyl. And indeed [Col. 0142C] our reading is supported by four Royal manuscripts—two nine hundred years old, and two others more recent but of good quality—two Colbertine manuscripts, the Navarre, Victorine, and two Brun manuscripts, in which *Delphidam* is read. Who, moreover, does not see from what has been said above that *Delphida* must be read, according to the Greek termination? For our Firmianus sometimes employs Hellenisms. Eleven recent manuscripts and almost all editions have “Delphic.”

*In that book*, etc. This book is not included by Laertius in his list of Chrysippus’s works.

*The fourth, the Cimmerian.* We have thus emended the text from the very ancient manuscripts: two Royal, the Navarre, one Sorbonne, the Victorine, the Utrecht, two Brun, and the Christ Church, as well as Cellarius’s edition. In three other Royal manuscripts, two Colbertine, the Emmanuel, and the Gataker, there is *Cimmeriam*; Lilius Gyraldus also wishes *Cymeriam* to be restored. The Gotha manuscript has *Cymeream*; the Gronovian, *Cimenam* for *Cimeriam*; one Colbertine and the Marmoutier, *Cimoeam*; two recent Colbertine manuscripts, *Cuneam*; five Royal, twelve Vatican, one Sorbonne, two Clermont manuscripts, and many editions, “the Cumaean”—altogether incorrectly, since [Col. 0142D] our author explicitly distinguishes the fourth, the Cimmerian, from the seventh, the Cuman or Cumaean, placed a little below. Isidore likewise does so in *Origins* VIII.8, and the Suda under Σίβυλλα, “Sibyl.” According to Gyraldus, however, she was called the Cimmerian because she once lived at the Italian town of Cimmerium, near Lake Avernus in Campania, according to Pliny III.5.

*Naevius … of the Punic War.* That is, the First Punic War, in which he served. See Vossius, *History of Latin Literature* I.2. BUNEMANN.

*The fifth, the Erythraean.* Salmasius, *Plinian Exercises*, p. 37, maintains that this Erythraean, Cumaean, and Cuman Sibyl was one and the same person.

*To the Greeks.* Four recent manuscripts have “to the Greeks.” But the meaning is the same.

*To the Greeks seeking Ilium … that Homer would write falsehoods.* This occurs in Book 3 of the *Sibylline Oracles* in these words: “Ilium, I pity you; for because of Sparta an Erinys …” (Ἴλιον, οἰκτείρω σε, κατὰ Σπαρτὴν γὰρ Ἐριννύς), etc.

*The sixth, the Samian.* Named Phyto (Φυτώ), whom Valerius Maximus mentions in Book I, *On Omens*, where he discusses the people of Priene. BETULEIUS.

*Writes.* Thus restored from the manuscript codices and the editions of de Tournes [Col. 0143B] and Walch. Many printed editions have “wrote.”]

In the books on divine matters which he wrote to Gaius Caesar, chief pontiff, when speaking of the Fifteen Men, he says that the Sibylline books were not the work of a single Sibyl, but that they were called by the single name “Sibylline” because all female seers were called Sibyls by the ancients—either from the name of one Delphian Sibyl, or from their announcing the counsels of the gods. For in the Aeolian form of speech they called the gods *sious* (σιοὺς), not *theous* (θεοὺς), and counsel *bylē* (βυλὴν), not *boulē* (βουλὴν); hence “Sibyl” was said to derive, as it were, from *siobolē* (σιοβολή). Moreover, there were ten Sibyls in number; and he enumerated them all, citing the authors who had written about each one: the first [Col. 0142A] was from Persia, and was mentioned by Nicanor, who wrote the history of Alexander of Macedon; the second was the Libyan, whom Euripides mentions in the prologue to the *Lamia*; the third, the Delphian, of whom Chrysippus speaks in the book he composed on divination; the fourth, the Cimmerian in Italy, whom Naevius names in his books on the Punic War and Piso in his *Annals*; the fifth, the Erythraean, whom Apollodorus of Erythrae declares to have been his fellow citizen, and who prophesied to the Greeks as they were setting out for Ilium both that Troy would perish and that Homer would write falsehoods; the sixth, the Samian, concerning whom Eratosthenes writes that he found a written record in the ancient annals of the Samians; [Col. 0143A] the seventh, the Cuman [Col. 0143A].

[Note: [Col. 0143B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 143–144]

*The seventh, the Cuman.* See Salmasius, *Plinian Exercises*, p. 73, and you will find that she was the same as the Italian Cumaean; I too agree with this. It should also be noted that the Utrecht manuscript has: “the seventh, the Cuman or Cumaean.” GALLAEUS.—And the excellent Cologne folio edition of 1544 calls her Cumaean. The passage of Justin Martyr refers to her.

*Who is called Demophile or Herophile by others.* Solinus and the Suda call not the Cuman but the Erythraean Sibyl Hierophile, although Solinus and Tibullus, *Elegies* II.5, read *Heriphile*. Eusebius, however, writes that neither the Erythraean nor the Cuman, but the Samian, was called Herophile, and reports that she flourished while Numa was king of the Romans. ISAEUS.

*And that she brought nine books*, etc. Salmasius, in his *Plinian Exercises*, flatly denies that the Sibylline books were offered to Tarquin by the Cuman Sibyl; indeed, he asserts that she was not even a Sibyl. [Col. 0143C] Dionysius of Halicarnassus calls her only “a woman not native to the country” (γυναῖκα οὐκ ἐπιχωρίαν), in Book IV. Gellius I.19: “In the ancient annals the following account of the Sibylline books has been handed down: An old woman, a foreigner and unknown, came to King Tarquin the Proud, carrying nine books which, she said, contained divine oracles, and she wished to sell them,” etc. Anyone desiring more may consult the passage. GALLAEUS.

*Tarquin the Elder.* Varro, Isidore VIII.8, and the Suda name him thus together with Lactantius; but Dionysius of Halicarnassus IV, Pliny XIII.13, and Gellius I.19 name Tarquin the Proud. Yet, says the learned Cellarius, it is more correctly attributed to the Elder, because Solinus, ch. 2, although he calls him the Proud with Pliny, reports that it happened during the fiftieth Olympiad.

*She demanded three hundred philippei.* Servius, on Virgil, adds that these *philippei* were gold coins, which were valuable at that time; yet this was not because those coins had been struck in the name of Philip, namely the father of Alexander the Great, since Philip of Macedon did not yet exist at the time when those books are said to have been purchased. But ancient authors, as the most learned Walch says, write about coinage according to its appearance in their own time; this could be illustrated by many examples. A gold philippeus, moreover, was worth approximately two French gold coins, as Lambinus notes on Plautus. See Budé, *On the As*, Book IV, and Gronovius, Book III, *On Ancient and Modern Money*. Many nevertheless think that all these details savor of fable.

*For three hundred.* See Gellius cited above, and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book IV. *When the Capitol had been rebuilt.* So too Tacitus, *Annals* VI.12: “After the Capitol had been burned in the Social War, Sibylline verses were sought at Samos, Ilium, and Erythrae, and also throughout Africa, Sicily, and the Italian colonies,” etc.

*May have been.* Seventeen manuscripts and fifteen editions have “were.”

*The Hellespontine.* Thus, in agreement with *Epitome* ch. 5, almost all the manuscripts. Two more recent manuscripts have “the Hellespontiac.” The editions have “the Hellespontic.”

[Col. 0144B]

*In the village of Marpessus.* Pausanias likewise reads this in Book X, according to three Greek Royal manuscripts collated by me, where he speaks of Herophile the prophetess. I did not wish to alter the reading received in almost all editions, since Isaeus and Gallaeus assert that *Marpesso* is read in most Lactantian manuscripts. Yet all those I have seen—namely, ten Royal, six Colbertine, the Navarre, two Sorbonne, the Victorine, Gataker, Marmoutier, two Clermont, two Brun, as well as one Bologna, Taxius, Penius, Christ Church, Gotha, Leipzig, Caucchius, Utrecht, Palatine, Rostock, Cambridge, and the three oldest Roman editions—have *Marmesso*; the Suda, at the cited passage, has *Marmisso*. *Gergithium.* On this see Stephanus of Byzantium under Γέργις, “Gergis”; he says that she was buried in the temple of Apollo Gergithius. Gergis is a place in the Troad.—“In the village of Marmessus near the town of Gergithium.” Others have *Marpessus*, whom Tibullus seems to support, II.5.67:

> Whatever Amalthea, whatever the Marpessian Sibyl declared—

[Col. 0144C]

unless even there *Marmessian* should be read with Salmasius on Solinus, p. 55. BUNEMANN.

*Heraclides Ponticus.* A pupil of Plato and afterwards of Aristotle. Vossius, *History of Greek Literature* I.8–9; Diogenes Laertius V.86 ff. BUNEMANN.

*The ninth, the Phrygian.* Capella makes her the same as the Erythraean and Cuman Sibyl. BETULEIUS.

*The tenth, the Tiburtine.* That Albunea was devoutly worshiped at Tibur is indicated by the mountain and spring bearing her name in the territory of Tibur, concerning which see Virgil, *Aeneid* VII.

*Whose oracles the Senate transferred to the Capitol.* Thus we have restored the text from the manuscripts of Junius, Marmoutier, Janus Gulielmus, and four Royal manuscripts, two of them excellent, except that the most ancient manuscripts have “in the Capitol.” The Gataker manuscript has: “whose oracles the Senate brought to the Capitol.” These words are absent from six Royal, six Colbertine, two Sorbonne, the Navarre, Victorine, two Clermont, Taxius, Penius, Emmanuel, Cambridge, two Brun manuscripts, the Roman edition of 1470, and the editions of Betuleius, Walch, and Subiaco. Instead of “oracles,” twelve recent editions read “sacred objects.” That “oracles” must be read is confirmed [Col. 0144D] by the passage of Virgil where Aeneas says to Demophile, the Cuman Sibyl, *Aeneid* VI.72:

> For here I shall place your oracles and the mystic destinies  
> Declared to my people.

For “oracles,” says Servius on this passage, means Sibylline responses.—*Whose oracles … transferred.* Tibullus expressed the same thing with the same word, II.5.67 ff. (in other editions, elegy 6):

> Whatever Amalthea, whatever the Marpessian Sibyl declared,  
> Whatever Herophile, dear to Phoebus, advised,  
> And whatever sacred oracles Albunea carried  
> Along the streams of the Tiber.

Lactantius himself, I.14: “an oracle given to Saturn … the fulfillment of the oracle.” In *Epitome* ch. 28, he joined “oracles and prophecies.”

*Nor is it permitted for anyone except the Fifteen Men to inspect them.* Thus we have restored the text from four Royal, five Colbertine, two Sorbonne, two Clermont, Leipzig, Gotha, Utrecht, Caucchius, Junius, and other manuscripts. The Gronovian manuscripts have “they hold them inspected,” not badly. One Colbertine manuscript and the [Col. 0145A] printed editions have “it is permitted to inspect them.” Concerning this college of Fifteen Men, moreover, it should be noted that at first Tarquin appointed only two; after two hundred and thirteen years, in 388 from the founding of the City, their number was increased, and from their number, ten, they were called the Ten Men. See Livy’s fourth Decade. Afterwards the number rose to fifteen; this occurred between 671 from the founding of the City, when the Capitol burned, and 675, when Sulla resigned the dictatorship, as David Blondel carefully noted in his work on the Sibyls, written in French. The name “Fifteen Men” always remained unchanged, even though they later numbered forty, as Servius notes. This was so even in Christian times, as may be seen in the cited passage. The duty of these Fifteen Men was to preserve the Sibylline oracles carefully and, when necessity required, to consult them at the Senate’s command. GALLAEUS.

Under penalty of death, according to St. Justin, *Second Apology for the Christians*, pagans were forbidden to read the books of the prophets and Sibyls; for it was feared that by reading those writings they would acquire knowledge of the true faith and of good things, and would pass over to the Christian religion. The Sibyls were women whom the ancients regarded as prophetesses. Eight books still survive under their name today, in which many things consonant with the Christian religion are found and were adduced by the ancient [Col. 0145C] Fathers of the Church from the time of St. Justin onward. Scholars now agree that these eight books are either wholly or partly spurious, or at least corrupted; they do not likewise agree about the number of Sibyls. On these matters see Blondel’s excellent discussion. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, however, says the following in Book IV: “The Romans,” he says, “guard nothing, whether holy or sacred, so carefully as the divinely sent Sibylline oracles.”—*They hold them inspected.* Lactantius III.20: “which it is considered unlawful to behold.” The Subiaco edition, Venice 1471 and 1497, Rostock, Junta, Aldine, and others have “it is permitted to inspect them,” which pleases Heumann. So Cicero, *Against Verres* II.V.72: “It was not permitted even to behold the image of Ceres.” BUNEMANN.

] named Amalthea, who by others is called Demophile or Herophile; and that she brought nine books to King Tarquin the Elder and demanded three hundred philippei for them. The king, scorning the enormity of the price, mocked the woman’s madness. She burned three in the king’s sight and demanded the same price for the remainder; Tarquin thought the woman madder still. When she had again burned three others and persisted in the same price, the king was moved and bought those remaining for three hundred gold pieces. Their number was later increased when the Capitol had been rebuilt, because books were gathered from all cities, both Italian and Greek, and especially from Erythrae, and brought to Rome under the name of whatever [Col. 0144A] Sibyl they may have been. The eighth was the Hellespontine, born in the territory of Troy, in the village of Marpessus near the town of Gergithium; Heraclides Ponticus writes that she lived in the times of Solon and Cyrus. The ninth was the Phrygian, who prophesied at Ancyra. The tenth was the Tiburtine, named Albunea, who is worshiped at Tibur as a goddess beside the banks of the river Anio. Her image is said to have been found in its pool, holding a book in her hand; the Senate transferred her oracles to the Capitol.

The poems of all these Sibyls both circulate and are preserved, except those of the Cumaean, whose books the Romans conceal, and no one except the Fifteen Men is permitted to inspect them. There is one individual [Col. 0145A] book belonging to each. [Col. 0145A]

[Note: [Col. 0145C] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 145–146]

*Individual books.* Those books were written not on papyrus rolls but on linen. Symmachus IV, epistle 34: “The divination of the Marcian prophets was indeed inscribed upon perishable bark; the Cuman admonitions took the form of woven linen; you even command my words to be poured into silken rolls, in the Achaemenid manner.” Flavius Vopiscus, *Aurelian*: “I recently found in the Ulpian Library, among the linen books, a letter of the deified Valerian.” Ausonius, epistle 23:

> Through woven threads he uttered his complaints  
> And entrusted the charges to silent fabrics.

It is therefore clear from this that not only the Sibylline books but also others were written upon linen sheets. Pliny disposes of the whole matter in XIII.11: “At first writing was done on leaves of palm trees”—read “mallows,” following Dalechamps’s correction—“then on the inner bark of certain trees. Afterwards public records began to be made in leaden rolls, and presently private documents on linen or wax tablets.”

I saw a man writing excellently upon linen in prison, when his guard refused him papyrus or paper. Those pieces of linen had been lightly pasted together with first-quality bread diluted in water, because flour was lacking. Thus says Jean-Baptiste Le Brun.

*And foretold that she would be called Erythraean.* This has seemed to us the true and genuine reading of the editions of Grapheus, Gymnicus, and Betuleius; of four Royal manuscripts, two of which are very ancient and the other two more recent but of good quality; and also of the old Aldine edition of 1515, Paris 1525, Cratander, and Fasitel, though in four of these “Babylonia” stands for “Babylon.” For what could be more correct than that this Erythraean Sibyl inserted her true and proper name—another name than “Erythraean”—into her poem, and nevertheless foretold that she would someday be called Erythraean, although [Col. 0146B] she had been born at Babylon? There is a strange and inept variation in thirteen other recent manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470, which have: “she calls herself Erythraean, where she foretold it, since she had been born at Babylon”; six other recent manuscripts have “of Babylonia”; one recent Bologna manuscript has “where she spoke at length.” To what, then, will “where” refer? To “Erythraean”? But what a disorderly expression!—*She calls herself where she foretold.* The codex of Janus Gulielmus and the Emmanuel, Taxius, and Penius manuscripts have “she prophesied.” Gulielmus adds that *proloqui* means to prophesy and sing of future things, whence prophets receive their name, because they spoke beforehand. BUNEMANN.

*Foretold.* Or rather, “prophesied,” as found in the margin of the excellent Cologne folio edition of 1544.

*To use.* That is, “to employ.” Thus Terence in the prologue to the *Andria*: “he uses up his labor,” in the sense “he employs it.” Apuleius likewise uses this verb in the same sense, Book IV: “When evening was already advanced, making use of the benefit of darkness, we presented Thrasyleon’s cage to Demochares together with those forged letters.” Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II: “We make use for our benefit of the extraordinarily keen senses of elephants and the sagacity of dogs.” Nazarius, *Panegyric Addressed to Constantine*, no. 30: [Col. 0146C] “Oh, if I were now granted the ability to shape my speech in accordance with the dignity of the subject, I would employ every flower of eloquence and make use of a certain exquisite charm and grace of expression.” Baldric of Noyon III.69: “Perceiving that he could not obtain by blandishments what he sought, the emperor began to employ violence.”

*Curio.* He was consul in the Varronian year 678 of the City, with Gnaeus Octavius. On these matters see below, *On the Wrath of God*, chs. 22 and 23.

*Sibyl.* The ancient Christians once valued the poems of the Sibyls so highly that I thought it pertinent to say something about them. Yet I have decided not to touch upon their number, because it is uncertain and variously reported. It will therefore be sufficient here briefly to submit their authority to examination. It is agreed that certain prophetic women once existed, and were very ancient, whom the ancients called Sibyls. But what they foretold was always obscure, since it was sacrilege to reveal their secret mysteries. Among the Romans only the Two Men—who afterwards increased to fifteen—were permitted to examine their books; but under penalty of death they were forbidden to disclose what they had read. Hence it follows that their poems were always entirely unknown to Christian writers, and that they dealt with nothing except pagan superstitions, as historians note; they were also very obscure, indeed ambiguous and written in a kind of poetic frenzy. But in those poems which certain ancient persons had deceitfully scraped together from all over Greece, and which we now possess, neither the inspired frenzy of poets nor any obscurity is recognizable. Everything recounts the secret mysteries of the Christian religion so clearly and manifestly that it is evident that they were taken both from the Jewish prophets and from the evangelical writers—whether the books were fabricated by the Jews themselves, as Isaac Vossius thought, or by certain early Christians, or were at least interpolated by them, which comes closer to the truth. Some of the ancient Fathers, however, placed little confidence in them. St. Augustine bears witness concerning himself [Col. 0147B] in *The City of God* XVIII.45 and 47. Moreover, these poems seem to have been published after the year 140 of the common era—that is, after the time of Papias of Hierapolis—whose erroneous opinion concerning a thousand-year kingdom of Christians upon earth is found in those books. Yet although Celsus, the Christians’ most hostile adversary, reproaches some of them, according to Origen, *Against Celsus* V, because they adduce the Sibyls’ poems in their defense, the earlier champions of religion are nevertheless not to be blamed for employing arguments so uncertain and fragile in their zeal to vindicate the truth. At that time it was enough, in order to refute the errors of the pagans, that the pagans trusted these poems; hence the ancient Christians rightly argued against them from those texts. The entire question of the Sibyls had already become controversial before the middle of the preceding century; it was debated with the highest critical judgment and much varied learning—not, indeed, by the excessively credulous Crasset, a pupil of the Society of Jesus, but by Louis Ellies Dupin, doctor of Paris; Nicolas Le Nourry; and Father Le Cellier, both of the Order of St. Benedict, the latter from the Congregation of St. Vanne and the former from that of St. Maur. Some very learned outsiders also contributed useful work to the examination of this controversy. They are Jean Daillé, Isaac Vossius, and Servatius Gallaeus, all of whom may be consulted.]

Because these books are inscribed with the name of the Sibyl, they are believed to be the work of one woman; but they are confused and cannot be distinguished and assigned individually to their respective authors—with the exception of the Erythraean, who both inserted her true name into her poem and foretold that she would be called Erythraean, although she had been born at Babylon. We too, however, shall speak indiscriminately of “the Sibyl” wherever it becomes necessary to employ their testimonies. [Col. 0146A] All these Sibyls, therefore, proclaim one God; above all the Erythraean, who is considered more celebrated and distinguished than the rest. For Fenestella, a most diligent writer, when speaking of the Fifteen Men, says that after the restoration of the Capitol the consul Gaius Curio proposed to the Senate that envoys should be sent to Erythrae to seek out the Sibyl’s poems and carry them back to Rome. Accordingly, [Col. 0147A] Publius Gabinius, Marcus Otacilius, [Col. 0147A]

[Note: [Col. 0147C] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 147–148]

*Otacilius.* Thus I read with the excellent Royal manuscript of Puteanus. Martial, *Epigrams* X.78. Many have *Octacilius*.

“One God, who alone exists” (Εἷς θεὸς ὃς μόνος ἐστὶν). Latin translation: “One God who alone exists, surpassing every magnitude, uncreated.” Instead of ἐστὶν, “exists,” an ancient Royal manuscript has ἄρχη; another has ἄρχει, “reigns.”

[Col. 0147D]

“But God” (Ἀλλὰ θεὸς). For the Latin translation see Theophilus, *To Autolycus* II: “But God alone is one, most exalted, who made heaven, the sun, the stars, the moon, the fruit-bearing earth, and the billows of the sea’s water.”

*Most exalted* (Πανυπέρτατος). He appropriately translates it “most surpassingly exalted,” and Spanheim learnedly illustrates it on Callimachus, *Hymn to Zeus* 91, p. 42. BUNEMANN.

“Him alone” (Αὐτὸν τὸν μόνον). Latin:

> Worship him who alone exists, the ruler of the world,  
> Who alone exists forever, and has existed from eternity.

*Has existed* (Ἐτύχθη). Thus it must be read according to the emendation of the distinguished Turnebus and the authority of the best manuscript codices—the Caucchius, one Clermont, and three ancient Royal manuscripts—in one of which it is rendered in Latin “remains.” Some manuscripts have ἐτέχθη, which comes very close to ἐτύχθη, although almost all the remaining manuscripts oppose this and have ἔτυχεν or ἔτυχε, which the metrical scheme cannot bear.

[Col. 0148B]

“I alone am God” (Εἷς μόνος εἰμὶ θεός). This is in Book 3. One Royal manuscript has μόνος γὰρ θεός εἰμι, in Latin, “For I am the one God.” Ranconet thought it should read ὃς μόνος ἐστὶ θεός, in Latin, “Who alone is God.” The Latin translation is: “I alone am God, and there is no other God.”

*Above the rest.* That is, “more than the rest.” I.17: “lest she alone should appear shameless above other women.” In the same place: “above the other living creatures.” Cicero, *On Duties* II.7: “Phalaris is witness, whose cruelty is notorious above that of all others.” More examples are given at *On Wrath* ch. 14.

*At Colophon.* A city of Ionia on the river Halesus, at approximately the [Col. 0148C] thirty-eighth degree of latitude. See Strabo XIV and Solinus ch. 53: “Not far from Ephesus,” he says, “is the city of Colophon, famous for the oracle of Clarian Apollo.” See also Pliny II.103.

*Because he had migrated from Delphi—as I believe.* Thus three Royal, three Colbertine, one Sorbonne, one Leipzig, the Caucchius, Junius, and two Clermont manuscripts, and the Roman editions of 1468 and 1470, the Aldine of 1515, Paris 1525, Cratander, and de Tournes. Seven manuscripts and editions, however, have “had emigrated.” Nor is there any need for the alteration desired by Thomasius, who reads “to which place from Delphi,” as in twelve manuscripts; twelve recent manuscripts have “to which place from Delphi,” with the preposition. He contends that *quod* can in no way be read; indeed, that it must be so read is evident from Lactantius’s purpose and intention. For in order to explain why Apollo gave his response at Colophon, although he ordinarily delivered his oracles in his temple at Delphi, he assigns as the reason that Apollo had migrated from Delphi, drawn by the pleasantness of Asia. The excellent earlier codices named above likewise read thus; and the word “I believe,” which is omitted in some printed editions, is found in those same codices. Who does not see, as Thomasius and Isaeus rightly note, that this little word must certainly be retained because of its elegant irony? Lactantius thus silently undermines the pagan gods, since they are supposedly beings who find recreation in pleasant places. GALLAEUS.—On the Delphic oracle and other oracles see Theodoret, *Cure of the Greek Maladies*, Book X, *On Oracles*; Oenomaus the Cynic; Porphyry, *On the Philosophy of Oracles*; Plutarch, *On the Oracles Which Have Ceased*; and Diogenianus.—*To which place from Delphi.* Gallaeus contradicts himself. In his *Various Readings* he said that B, T, P, and G have *quo*; but in his notes he maintains and defends against Thomasius that the best codices—Bologna, Taxius, Penius, Leipzig, Junius, Caucchius, and others—have *quod*. *Quo* occurs in the Gotha and third Leipzig manuscripts; in the second Leipzig manuscript the stroke is less clear: *quo*, with *quod* written beneath it.

*Pleasantness.* Namely, of the place; for according to Justin’s *History* XXIV, the Delphic shrine was grim with the crags of Parnassus, whereas Colophon, situated on a promontory of Asia Minor, afforded more delight, according to Mela.]

and Lucius Valerius were sent; they carried back to Rome approximately one thousand verses copied from private collections. We have shown above that Varro said the same. In those verses, therefore, which the envoys brought to Rome, there are the following testimonies concerning one God:

> One God, who alone exists, surpassing every magnitude, uncreated.  
> (Εἷς θεὸς ὃς μόνος ἐστὶν ὑπερμεγεθής, ἀγένητος.)

That he alone is the supreme God, who made heaven and distinguished it with lights:

> But God alone is one, most exalted, who made  
> Heaven, the sun, the stars, and the moon,  
> The fruit-bearing earth, and the billows of the sea’s water.  
> (Ἀλλὰ θεὸς μόνος εἷς, πανυπέρτατος, ὃς πεποίηκεν
