> Καρποφόρον γαῖάν τε, καὶ ὕδατος οἴδματα πόντου.)

Since he alone is the builder of the world and the craftsman both of the things from which it is constituted and of the things contained within it, she testifies that he alone ought to be worshiped:

> Worship him who alone exists, the ruler of the world,  
> Who alone exists forever, and has existed from eternity.  
> (Αὐτὸν τὸν μόνον ὄντα σέβεσθ’ ἡγήτορα κόσμου,  
> Ὃς μόνος εἰς αἰῶνα καὶ ἐξ αἰῶνος ἐτύχθη.)

[Col. 0147B] Likewise another Sibyl, whoever she may be, when she declared that she was bearing God’s voice to humankind, spoke as follows:

[Col. 0148A]

> I alone am God, and there is no other God.  
> (Εἷς μόνος εἰμὶ θεός· καὶ οὐκ ἔστι θεὸς ἄλλος.)

I would now pursue the testimonies of the others, if these were not sufficient and if I were not reserving the others for more suitable places. But since we defend the cause of truth before those who, wandering from the truth, serve false religions, what kind of proof should we employ against them more readily than to refute them by the testimonies of their own gods?

## CHAPTER VII  
### On the Testimonies of Apollo and the Gods

Apollo, whom they consider more divine than all the others and preeminently prophetic, when giving a response at Colophon—because he had migrated from Delphi, as I believe, drawn by the pleasantness of Asia—was asked by someone who, or indeed what, God was. He replied in twenty-one verses, of which this is the beginning:

[Col. 0149A]

[Note: [Col. 0149B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 149–150]

*Self-originated* (Αὐτοφυής). Thus Nonnus: “self-grown, and the Word of the self-grown God” (αὐτόφυτος, καὶ λόγος αὐτοφύτοιο Θεοῦ). And the Erythraean Sibyl, Book 3:

> Self-originated, invisible, himself alone seeing all things.  
> (Αὐτοφυής, ἀόρατος, ὁρῶν μόνος αὐτὸς ἅπαντα.)

Plutarch, in *Opinions of the Philosophers*, appends Plato’s and Socrates’ opinion to the opinions of others who say that God is “the One, the uniquely originated and self-originated, the uniquely just, the truly good” (τὸ ἓν, τὸ μονοφυὲς καὶ τὸ αὐτοφυές, τὸ μονόδικον, τὸ ὄντως ἀγαθόν). An ancient Royal manuscript of Puteanus has αὐτοφυής. The Latin translation is:

> Originated from himself, untaught, motherless, unshaken,  
> Whose name cannot be comprehended even in speech, dwelling in fire:  
> This is God; but we angels are a small portion of God.

*Motherless* (Ἀμήτωρ). On this see below, IV.7. *Unshaken* (Ἀστυφέλικτος). Thus Callimachus, *Hymn to Delos* 2, 6: “but a god is always unshaken” (Θεὸς δ’ ἀεὶ ἀστυφέλικτος), a word which Spanheim admirably illustrates, p. 345. Lactantius himself, VI.25: “So that he—the same God—may be always steadfast, immutable, and UNSHAKEN.” BUNEMANN.

*We* (Ἡμεῖς). On these oracles of Apollo see Agostino Steuco of Gubbio, *On the Perennial Philosophy* III.16, where he reports these responses.

*Can anyone.* Thus we emended the text from four Royal manuscripts, two of them very ancient, and from the Emmanuel and Balliol manuscripts. The most learned men agree with us that it should be so read. Others read *Numquid* (“Can it be suspected?”).

*Mercury.* This is Trismegistus, concerning whom see ch. 6, note 5.

*Motherless … fatherless* (ἀμήτορα … ἀπάτορα). Latin: “without mother … without father.”

*From elsewhere.* That is, from another.

*Generated.* Thus we restored the text from almost all manuscripts and six of the older editions. Seven more recent editions and three recent manuscripts—one Royal, one Colbertine, and the Brun—have “may have generated.”

*Who say that there is one.* Thus also the Gotha manuscript, where Subiaco, Venice 1471 and 1497, Rostock, and the others have “who,” which Heumann, following Thomasius, prefers. The words “because we say that there is one” are entirely absent from the Bologna, Taxius, and Penius manuscripts. BUNEMANN.

*To be solitary*, etc. This proposition is false; for the plurality of divine Persons excludes solitude from God, not the company of angels, which are of a different nature. A person is said to be alone in a garden although many plants and animals are there. See St. Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, First Part, question 31, article 3. From ISAEUS. But here Lactantius accommodates himself to the pagans’ understanding somewhat more than is proper; and, in order to put forward something that would appeal to uncultivated minds, he says that the fellowship of angels ensured that God would not be solitary. Yet solitude is not removed through association with something of a different nature.—*Solitary.* Thus they contemptuously called God singular; for example, Caecilius in Minucius, ch. 10: “Whence, or who, or where is that single, solitary, abandoned God?” Hilary has other material on this word “solitary” against the heretics in *On the Trinity* IV, fol. 86 ff., latest Verona edition. BUNEMANN.

*Ministers.* We call these angels, a name of office, not dignity. On them see Philo Judaeus [Col. 0150B] … where you will read much about angels and their ministry and duties.

*To have begotten.* It means “to have created.” See the examples at III.14. Pertinent here is VII.5. BUNEMANN.

*To have begotten the ministers of his kingdom.* Thus the Apostle speaks of the angels in Hebrews 1:14: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent to serve for the sake of those who will inherit salvation?” Hence also blessed John, Revelation 5:11, saw them in a vision “around the throne” (κύκλοθεν τοῦ θρόνου), so that they might execute commands. Moreover, the word “begotten” is used improperly by Lactantius and other ecclesiastical writers for “created.”

*Nor do they wish to be called or worshiped as gods.* “Worshiped,” that is, adored. That the word is to be understood in this sense when God or fictitious gods are discussed is familiar to anyone from many passages of Holy Scripture. Both angels and saints have always forbidden others to adore them (Rev. 19:10 and ch. 22; Acts 10:26 and 14:14, 17). For adoration is due to God alone.

*But if.* Five recent manuscripts have “in that”; the Emmanuel, “in which.”

*Odium.* Two Colbertine manuscripts, by a second hand, have “wrong.”

*That we say there is one God and deny many.* Thus the oldest manuscripts and other excellent ones. Four early editions omit “God.” Two recent Royal manuscripts, one Colbertine, the Victorine, and the Brun have: “That we say there is one God, if we deny many.”

*We demonstrate that there are.* I inserted a full stop: “there are. We demonstrate.” BUNEMANN.

*In the opposite direction.* The manuscripts, including Reimmann’s, both Venice editions of 1478, and most others have this; I interpret it as “to the contrary,” just as Cicero somewhere combined “contrary” and “different.” The words are absent from Venice 1471 and Rostock 1476. The year is incorrect in Heumann: 1479. He himself writes: “there are, and we demonstrate the error of those who think them few.” BUNEMANN.

[Col. 0150D]

*Whose name they cast out.* Thus read nine Vatican, nine Royal, six Colbertine, one ancient Bologna, one Sorbonne, two Clermont, Junius, two Brun, and other manuscripts, together with the editions, except the edition of Betuleius and the Caucchius manuscript, which have *exponunt*; one recent Bologna, Taxius, and Leipzig have *explodunt*. All these readings are good. *Exponunt* means that those who attribute God’s name to many thrust that name out. For God’s name is thrust out and cast away when it is attributed to others. Thomasius, however, believes that “whose name they cast out” (*explodunt*) must be read from ancient codices, because those who attribute God’s name to many are said to cast out and expel it.—*They expose his name.* Caucchius has “erase.” I retain *exponunt*: that is, “they expose it to contempt and mockery.” Sacred writers use the word thus. Ambrose, *On Abraham* I.6, end: “Scripture surely did not expose the faults of the Patriarchs, whom we read were overcome by wine, except that you might learn what to avoid.” Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogue* I, *On the Virtues of the Monks* 8.6: “He omitted nothing that he did not seize upon, tear apart, and expose; he especially assailed vanity.” BUNEMANN.]

> Self-originated, untaught, motherless, unshaken,  
> Whose name cannot be comprehended even in speech, dwelling in fire:  
> This is God; but we angels are a small portion of God.  
> (Αὐτοφυής, ἀδίδακτος, ἀμήτωρ, ἀστυφέλικτος,  
> Οὔνομα μηδὲ λόγῳ χωρούμενον, ἐν πυρὶ ναίων·  
> Τουτὶ θεός, μικρὰ δὲ θεοῦ μερὶς ἄγγελοι ἡμεῖς.)

Can anyone suspect that this was said of Jupiter, who had both a mother and a name? Moreover, what of that thrice-great Mercury, whom I mentioned above? He calls God not only “motherless” (ἀμήτωρα), as Apollo does, but also “fatherless” (ἀπάτορα), because his origin is not from elsewhere. For he who himself generated all things cannot have been generated by anyone. I have sufficiently—as I think—both taught by arguments and confirmed by witnesses what is sufficiently clear in itself: there is one king of the world, one father, one God.

But perhaps someone may ask us the very question that Hortensius asks in Cicero: “If God is one, what blessedness can there be in solitude?” As though we who say that there is one also said that he was abandoned and solitary. [Col. 0149B] For he has ministers whom we call [Col. 0150A] messengers. And what I reported above that Seneca said in his *Exhortations* is true: God begot the ministers of his kingdom. But these are neither gods, nor do they wish to be called or worshiped as gods, since they do nothing apart from God’s command and will. Yet these are not those beings commonly worshiped, whose number is both small and determinate. But if the worshipers of the gods suppose that they worship the very beings whom we call ministers of the supreme God, there is no reason for them to subject us to odium because we say that there is one God and deny that there are many. If multitude delights them, we say that they are not twelve, or three hundred and sixty-five, as Orpheus says, but innumerable; and we demonstrate, to the contrary, the error of those who think there are so few. They should nevertheless know by what name these beings ought to be called, lest they violate the true God, whose [Col. 0150B] name they expose by attributing it to many. Let them believe their own Apollo, who in that same response, just as he took supremacy from Jupiter, likewise took the name of gods away from the others. For the third verse shows that God’s ministers ought to be called not gods but angels. Apollo indeed lied about himself, since he belongs to the number of demons. [Col. 0151A]

[Note: [Col. 0151B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 151–152]

*Demons.* Among the ancients a demon is the same as an angel; but Lactantius, in accordance with the sense of Holy Scripture, understands by the name “demon” the gods of the pagans, according to the verse of the Psalm: “All the gods of the pagans are demons.”

*All-wise* (Πάνσοφε). Latin translation: “All-wise, all-learned, you who move among various things, hear me, demon.”

*Αἰολόστροφε.* Thus MSS. 1 Reg. and that of Guilielmus Canter. Regii 4 reads *πάνστροφε*, and Goth., Clar., and Brun. appear from the Latin translation to have read it thus: “you who move through many things.” Another Clarom., 1 Reg., and 1 Colb. read *ὁλοίστροφε*; 2 Colb. and certain editions, *ἐνολοίστροφε*. “Prayer.” We have thus restored the reading from the MSS.; the word also occurs in Plautus. [Col. 0151C] The printed editions have the plural “prayers.” — “Prayers.” That is, curses and imprecations. See Davies on Caesar, *Gallic War* VI.31.5: “After cursing Ambiorix with every imprecation.” Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XV.505:

> And with a hostile prayer he cursed the head of the departing man [the supplied *euntes* is uncertain; context suggests *euntis*].

Thus the MSS. Bon., Tax., Ultr., and Gron. have the singular, together with Reimm., which reads “with a prayer.” BUNEMANN.

“Smynthian Apollo.” Thus nearly all the best MSS., supported by the Roman edition of 1470, which has *Samnitium*; the printed editions have *Smyntheum*. This epithet is derived from mice, which are called *σμίνθοι*, according to Pausanias, Strabo, and Homer, *Iliad* I:

> Τενέδοιό τε ἶφι ἀνάσσεις, Σμινθεῦ.  
> And over Tenedos you rule in might, O Smintheus.

For when a certain priest of Apollo named Crinis neglected the god’s rites, and consequently gathered no produce at all that year, since everything had been gnawed away by mice, the priest, moved by so great a loss, performed the customary rites for the god. The god immediately destroyed all the mice with his arrows, and from this event [Col. 0151D] was called Smintheus. For the Cretans called mice *Smyntae*. BETULEIUS.

*Ἁρμονίη.* Latin translation:

> Harmony of the world, light-bringer and wise daemon.

> The daemons who range about the earth and about the sea,  
> Tireless, are subdued beneath the scourge of God.

“He wishes to honor himself and place himself in heaven.” Thus the MSS. together with all the editions except Cellarius and seven recent MSS., in which the reading is “to be honored and to be placed”; I would wish that reading to be confirmed by older and better MSS.

“They always attend upon God.” We have added “always” from MSS. 2 Bonon., 4 Reg.—two of which are among the oldest—6 Colb., Pen., 2 Clarom., Em., Cantab., Cauc., Jun., Brun., and the Leipzig MSS., as well as the Roman editions of 1468 and 1470 and Betuleius. “Always” is absent from the recent editions. — “Attend upon.” As God’s attendants; Book II, chapter 16. Bon., Pen., Cauc., Jun., Goth., Lips. 1, 3 Emm., Reimm., Sublac., and the Venice editions of 1471 and 1497 read: “who always attend upon God.” BUNEMANN.

“Their parent and Lord.” He often presses this point; I indicate the passages at Book IV, chapter 3. BUNEMANN.

[Col. 0152B]

“When all paths have been completed.” We emended the text thus from the excellent Royal MS. of Puteanus and four others, from 5 Colb., 1 Clarom., Em., Cantab., and the Leipzig MSS., as well as from the three old Roman editions, Paris 1525, Aldus, Cratander, and Grapheus 1532. Three Reg., 1 Colb., 1 Clarom., and 2 Brun. read “when they have been exhausted”; in the latter of the two, “its own” appears in place of “paths.”

“Anything further.” The older MS. 1 Bonon. and Pen. read “something else further.”

“But because it is impossible that anything which exists did not at some time begin to exist.” An observation of the Reverend Father Giovanni Maria Brasichelli, Master of the Apostolic Sacred Palace, excerpted from the margin of Royal MS. no. 3739: Read all these words cautiously, down to the end [Col. 0152C] of the chapter, for they are strongly at variance with theologians’ customary manner of speaking. God was neither begotten nor brought forth by himself, since nothing is more impossible than for something to beget or produce itself. Nor do Lactantius’ words appear capable of being reduced to any sound meaning unless “begotten from himself” is understood negatively, that is, “not begotten by another.” Finally, in this matter, what could be more absurd than: “It is impossible that anything which exists did not at some time begin to exist”? See Possevino’s *Sacred Apparatus* on Gilbert Génébrard. — “Because it is impossible that anything which exists did not at some time begin to exist.” This passage is free from error, for it must be understood of things that come into existence, as in Book II, chapter 10: “Since it exists, it is apparent that it began at some time. For nothing can exist without a beginning.” Compare below, Book VII, chapter 1. He held a correct view concerning God in Book IV, chapters 12 and 13. Compare Hocker’s *Bibliotheca Heilsbronnensis*, fol. 48 (30). BUNEMANN.

“Since.” Thus the best MSS. and nearly all the printed editions. This is a Ciceronian use of *quando* in the sense of “seeing that” or “because.” MSS. 1 Bonon., 6 Colb., Ultr., [Col. 0152D] 1 Clarom., and Brun. read *quoniam*, “because.”

“Was brought forth from himself.” It must be noted that Lactantius errs when he says that God brought himself forth; Lactantius repeats this error in Book II, chapter 9. GALLAEUS. — “Was brought forth from himself.” This is not stated precisely; similarly in Book II, chapter 8: “He exists from himself.” Gallaeus and Sparke noted Lactantius’ error. BUNEMANN.

*Αὐτοφυής*: Latin, “sprung from himself.”

“By the Sibyl, *αὐτογενής*, etc.” Latin: “self-begotten, unbegotten, and unmade.” Lactantius explains the Christians’ meaning less correctly by the words *αὐτοφυής* and *αὐτογενής*, which exclude creation and generation. They would be explained better by the expression “that he exists from himself,” that is, “self-existent,” as Pearson demonstrates from St. Athanasius.

*Ἀγέννητος* and *ἀποίητος*: that is, “neither begotten nor made.” The words of the Athanasian Creed come to the same thing: “not made, nor created, nor begotten.” On this, see Theophilus of Antioch, *To Autolycus*, Book II.

“A perceptive man.” I restored this from all the MSS. and the old [Col. 0153B] Roman editions; it also occurs in Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* III.83. Nearly all the printed editions read “a perceptive person.” — “A perceptive man.” I prefer the reading of Bon., Tax., Pen., Ultr., Pal., Juntar., Goth., the three Lips., Reim., Sublac., Rost., and the Venice editions of 1471–97, “a perceptive man”; compare *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 1, “a most eloquent man.” BUNEMANN.]

He enrolled himself among God’s angels; finally, in other responses he confessed that he was a daemon. For when he was asked how he wished supplication to be made to him, he replied:

> Πάνσοφε, παντοδίδακτ’, αἰολόστροφε, κέκλυθι, δαῖμον.  
> All-wise, all-knowing, ever-turning, hear us, daemon.

Again, when he was asked to utter a prayer to Apollo Smintheus, he began with this verse:

> Ἁρμονίη κόσμοιο, φαεσφόρε καὶ σοφὲ δαῖμον.  
> Harmony of the world, light-bringing and wise daemon.

What therefore remains except that, by his own confession, he should be subjected to the scourges of the true God and to everlasting punishment? For in another response he also spoke as follows: [Col. 0151B]

> Δαίμονες οἳ φοιτῶσι περὶ χθόνα καὶ περὶ πόντον  
> Ἀκάματοι δάμανται ὑπαὶ μάστιγι θεοῖο.  
> The tireless daemons who range over the earth and the sea  
> Are subdued beneath the scourge of God.

We discuss both classes in the second book [Col. 0152A] (namely, chapter 15). For the present, it is enough for us that, while wishing to honor himself and place himself in heaven, he confessed the reality of the matter: what those who always attend upon God ought to be called.

Let human beings therefore withdraw from their errors, cast aside their corrupt religions, and acknowledge their parent and Lord, whose power cannot be estimated, whose greatness cannot be discerned, and whose beginning cannot be comprehended. When the human mind’s attention, acuteness, and memory have reached him, they halt, cling fast, and fail, as though all paths had been withdrawn and exhausted; nor is there anything further toward which they can advance. But because it is impossible that anything which exists did not at some time begin to exist, it follows that, since nothing existed before him, he was himself brought forth from himself before all things. Hence he is called *αὐτοφυής* (“self-sprung”) by Apollo, and *αὐτογενής* (“self-begotten”), [Col. 0152B] *ἀγέννητος* (“unbegotten”), and *ἀποίητος* (“unmade”) by the Sibyl. Seneca, a perceptive man, saw this in his *Exhortations*: “We,” he says, “depend upon another source. Accordingly, we look to someone [Col. 0153A] to whom we owe that which is best in us. [Col. 0153A]

[Note: [Col. 0153B] [Various Scholars’ Notes to columns 145–146]

“To whom we owe that which is best in us.” Thus all printed editions and MSS. except one Bonon. and four recent editions, which add “the soul” after “in us.” We deleted that word as a gloss.

“And Plato says in the *Timaeus* that his majesty is so great.” Hermes states the same in the *Poemander*, and St. Justin in the *Exhortation*. Clement, in the *Protrepticus*, writes that Plato drew those ideas from Moses and Egyptian teaching; among the Hebrews, the name of God is *ἀνεκφώνητον*, “unutterable.” Basil, *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 18. See Wower on Minucius Felix.

“In the *Timaeus*, Plato.” When Celsus cited this passage in Origen, Book VII, p. 360, Origen examined it and explained more fully how Plato confessed one God. Compare Athenagoras, *Plea for the Christians*, pp. 26–27; Justin Martyr, *Second Apology*, section 11, Oxford edition, p. 27; Minucius Felix, chapter 19.

“Because of his excessive.” MSS. Jun. and Cauc., and six printed editions, add “his,” a word absent from the others. It nevertheless fits the passage remarkably well.

“But could anyone doubt?” We correctly changed the common editions’ *ergo* (“therefore”) to *vero* (“but”), following all the MSS. and Cellarius’ edition.

“Inconceivable.” That is, one whose divine nature and infinite perfections the human mind cannot know by thought and contemplation. “Of such great majesty.” MSS. 2 Bonon. and other recent MSS. read “power.”

[Col. 0153D]

“Thoughtless.” That is, unthinking and inconsiderate. Here Lactantius imitated Plautus, who writes in *The Braggart Soldier*, act II, scene 6, verse 63:

> Only now do I know  
> That I was senseless, blind, and thoughtless.

This word is an affected use of a grander-sounding expression, as are all Virgil’s formations of this kind, by which he commonly lends majesty to his poetry: “a tearful war,” “an inescapable fate,” “a joyless murmur.” Otherwise, Marcus Tullius shows that the ancient Latins were more scrupulous in using words of this sort. After translating *καταληπτόν* as *comprehensibile* (“comprehensible”), as though he had ventured something momentous, he says, “Will you tolerate this?” Seneca likewise notes Maecenas’ use of *irremediabile* (“irremediable”) for *ἀνήκετον*, in Epistle 114. A similar form appears in Lucilius, *monstrificabile* (“monstrific”); and in that most eloquent author Lactantius, *insustentabilis dominatio* (“irresistible dominion”), Book VII, chapter 16, for what the Greeks call *ἀνυπόστατος ἀρχή*, [Col. 0154B] and so forth. ISAAC CASAUBON.

“Differing from dumb animals.” Nearly all the editions and MS. Goth. read “from dumb animals,” and Heumannus reads likewise. With Cellarius, Reimm., the Leipzig MSS., and others, I would prefer to follow those who have the dative “dumb animals,” after the usage of Horace and Cicero. See the examples in Vechner, *Hellenolexia*, p. 440, where Heusinger agrees with us. Here Lactantius imitates Cicero, *On Ends* V.15: “In what do we differ from living creatures?” Thus Grat., Gron., and Verburg. Again Lactantius, Book II, chapter 5: “The sun … and moon differ from the lights of the stars.”

*Οὐ δύνατ’.* Latin: “A God cannot have been formed from a man’s thighs and a woman’s womb.” These Greek words are found in Theophilus, *To Autolycus*, Book II, but in place of *τεταπωμένος* it appears that *τετυπωμένος* should be read.

“As indeed it is.” This expression possesses remarkable elegance. Cicero, *Paradoxes* V.1: “If slavery, as indeed it is, is obedience from a broken spirit.” And *For Sextus Roscius*, chapter 8: “Although he is fortunate, as indeed he is.” Livy VII.35: “If the night is favorable for a sortie, as indeed it is.” — “As indeed it is.” The truth of the matter is thus elegantly confirmed. Nepos, *Eumenes* 1: “Among us, scribes are in fact regarded, as indeed they are, as hired servants.” BUNEMANN.

“Since they are.” Thus the stronger MSS. and the older printed editions—Rom., Ald., Crat., Graph., Fasitel., Gymnic.—as well as our Lactantius in various passages, use *quando* in the sense of “seeing that.” Four Colb., 2 Clarom., and eight recent editions substituted *quandoquidem*; 5 Reg. reads *quoniam*.

“If, therefore, the gods are immortal and eternal.” I read this without punctuation, following MSS. 2 Bonon., the very old 1 Reg. and two others, Tax., Pen., 3 Lips., 6 Colb., 2 Clarom., 2 Brun., and nearly all the editions. MSS. 3 Reg., Goth., and Betul., as well as two recent editions, read “For the gods, if [Col. 0154D] they exist.” The discourse would nevertheless seem more coherent if it read: “For the gods, if they are immortal and eternal, what need is there of the other sex?”

“What need is there of the other sex, since they do not require succession?” Thus MSS. 1 Bonon. ant., Navarr., 2 Brunn., and the editions of Isaeus, Thysius, Gallaeus, Sparke, and 2 Lips. After “the other sex,” MSS. 4 Reg. Vatic., 4 Colb., Gat., Marm., Em., Christ., Pal., Lips., Cauc., and the editions of Fasitel., Betul., and Tornes. add, “namely, so that they may beget.” Four other Reg., 2 Colb., 1 Sorb., 1 Clarom., and the old editions 2 Rom., Paris 1525, Ald., Crat., Graph., and Gymnic. read, “namely, so that they may be begotten,” which we rejected as a gloss, just as we also rejected the following words, “What need is there of offspring itself?”, which are absent from the older Bonon., from Nav., and from many editions. The sense is indeed excellent, and the argument is more forceful when concluded by this brief enthymeme: the gods have no need of both sexes because they have no need of succession, since they will always exist. — “Sex.” After these words the Sublacensian edition reads, [Col. 0155B] “namely, so that they may beget? What need is there of offspring itself?” These words are absent from Gallaeus’ edition; they are nevertheless found in the excellent Cologne edition of 1544, in Betuleius, and in many others, but they are absent from the MSS. cited in the latter part of the preceding note. The following words from the *Orphic Poems* may be referred to this passage:

> Ζεὺς ἀρσὴν γένετο, Ζεὺς ἄμβροτος ἔπλετο νύμφη·  
> Zeus became male; immortal Zeus became a bride.

Soraïcus translated it thus:

> The one and universal God, progenitor and mother of the gods.

Thomasius nevertheless thinks that these words should be deleted as a gloss that crept into the text from the margin. Without them the sense is excellent and the discourse more forceful; therefore delete them if you wish.]

Another brought us forth; another equipped us: God made himself.”

## CHAPTER VIII  
### That God Is Without a Body and Has No Need of Sex for Procreation

It is therefore established by so many and such great witnesses that the world is governed by the power and providence of one God. Plato says in the *Timaeus* that his force and majesty are so great that no one can conceive of them in the mind or express them in words, because of his excessive and inestimable power. But could anyone doubt whether anything is difficult or impossible for God, who devised such great and marvelous works by providence, established them by power, and perfected them by reason; and who now sustains them by his spirit and governs them by his power—himself inconceivable, ineffable, [Col. 0153B] and sufficiently known to no other than himself?

Consequently, when I reflect repeatedly upon such great majesty, those who worship gods sometimes seem to me so blind, so thoughtless, so senseless, and so little different from dumb animals, since they believe that beings born from the intercourse of male and female could have possessed any majesty or divine power, although the Erythraean Sibyl says:

> … Οὐ δύνατ’ ἀνδρὸς  
> Ἐκ μηρῶν μήτρας τε θεὸς τετυπωμένος εἶναι.  
> … A god cannot have been formed  
> From a man’s thighs and a womb.

If this is true, as indeed it is, then it is apparent that Hercules, Apollo, Liber, Mercury, Jupiter himself, and all the others were human beings, since they were born from two sexes. But what is so remote from God as that activity which he himself assigned to mortals for propagating offspring, and which cannot exist without bodily substance?

If, therefore, the gods are immortal and eternal, what need [Col. 0154B] is there of the other sex, since they do not require succession, as they will always exist? For certainly among human beings [Col. 0155A] and other living creatures, diversity of sex, intercourse, [Col. 0155A]

[Note: [Col. 0155C] [Various Scholars’ Notes to columns 145–146]

“Intercourse.” Used for sexual union or coupling; thus Solinus, “the desire for intercourse.” BUNEMANN.

“Since.” Lactantius commonly uses *quando* in the sense of *quandoquidem*, “seeing that.” Several MSS. read *quoniam*, “because.”

“Since God, who is omnipotent, without the use,” etc. In some witnesses “as he is called” follows “omnipotent.” Thomasius, relying upon the authority of the old Bonon. codex and other MSS., judges that phrase to have been ineptly added. God is certainly not merely called omnipotent but truly is so, as even the pagans themselves acknowledge that divine attribute. GALLAEUS.

“Small creatures.” Bees, namely. See Virgil, *Georgics* IV, and Pliny; among more recent authors, Clusius, commonly called de l’Écluse, *On the Generation of Bees*. Quintilian has this statement about the generation of bees in *Declamation* 13: “Pleasure, the enemy of virtues, is absent from their chaste bodies, which are without defilement. Alone of all creatures, they do not bring forth young but make them; and, as befits a laborious animal, they are born from work.”

[Col. 0155D]

“Born from leaves.” These are Virgil’s words about bees, *Georgics* IV.200.

“Because they had been the greatest and most powerful kings.” MSS. Colb. and Brun. read “were.” Maximus of Tyre, *Dissertation* 38: *Καὶ Ἕλληνες*, etc.: “And indeed the Greeks perform sacred rites even for good men, whose virtues they commemorate while omitting their misfortunes.” Much earlier, Persaeus of Citium—the man whom Aratus of Sicyon expelled from Acrocorinth—spoke similarly. Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I: “Persaeus”—write *Persaeus*, as in Greek, *Περσαῖος*—“the pupil of Zeno, says that those persons were regarded as gods by whom some great benefit for the cultivation of life had been discovered, and that useful things themselves were designated by the names of gods,” etc. See the very learned Vossius, *On Idolatry*. Elmenhorst says that Suidas under *Σερούχ* and John of Damascus in his book *On Heresies* attest that Seruch commanded eminent men who had died to be worshiped, their memory to be celebrated annually, their names to be entered in sacred records, and themselves to be judged gods as benefactors; and that from this first arose idolatry and the plurality of gods. See also Wisdom 14:15; Athanasius, *Against the Nations*; Eusebius I.6; Theodoret, Sermon III; and Nazianzen, Oration I against Julian. Because that passage is rather long, I shall not transcribe it here.

Cyprian similarly writes in the treatise *That Idols Are Not Gods*: “That those whom the populace worships are not gods is evident from this: they were once kings, who, because of their royal memory, subsequently began to be worshiped among their own people even after death. Temples were therefore established for them; images were therefore fashioned to preserve the dead men’s faces in representation; for they also sacrificed victims and celebrated feast days by rendering them honor. Hence, for posterity, those observances became sacred rites which had originally been adopted as consolations.” See more on these matters at chapter 15 of this book. Hence Tzetzes, writing about Hercules in his *Various History*, [Col. 0156C] cites Ptolemy as an authority for the custom of calling all kings *θεούς* (“gods”) and queens *θεάς* (“goddesses”).

“Hercules.” Müncker abundantly illustrates the entire chapter in his notes on Hyginus, chapters 29–30; it is not my purpose to copy him out so often.

“Like Africanus.” That is, Scipio Africanus, celebrated for so many virtues. “Like” is absent from MS. 1 Claromont. Recent MSS. 1 Reg., 1 Colb., and Brun. read “nations among the Africans.” The sense is: just as no other Roman is celebrated as surpassing Scipio in virtue, so among the heroes none was more celebrated than Hercules.

“And cleansed it.” Thus many MSS. and editions, with support from MSS. 2 Bonon., the old 1 Reg., Tax., 1 Lips., 3 Colb., 1 Clarom., Brum., and the Roman edition of 1470, which read “and purified it.” In 1 Reg., 3 Colb., Jun., Ultr., Christ., and Em. the reading is “and conquered it,” which pleases some more than the others. Walch considers these two words superfluous and suggestive of a gloss. But *purgare*, Cellarius says, means “to free from monsters and tyrants.” On Hercules, see St. Basil the Great, Sermon 21, and St. Asterius, bishop of Amasea, Sermon 10.

“Acts of debauchery.” Arnobius also attacks Hercules’ divinity with this argument in Book IV: “Thus,” he says, “the holy god Hercules taught the fifty daughters of Thestius—or rather Thespius—in a single night both to surrender the name of virginity and to bear the burdens of motherhood.” Pausanias, *Boeotia*: *Ἡρακλέα ταῖς θυγατράσι*, etc. Romulus Amasaeus translates this into Latin as follows: “They relate that Hercules violated the fifty daughters of Thestius—for that was their number—in the same night, with one exception. When she alone refused to comply, he appointed her his priestess under a law of perpetual virginity. I have nevertheless heard others relate that all fifty daughters of Thestius were violated by Hercules in that same single night and that each bore him male children; indeed, the eldest and youngest bore twins.” Tatian, *Against the Greeks*; Theodoret, *On the Martyrs against the Greeks*, Sermon 8; Clement of Alexandria likewise reproaches Hercules with this in the *Protrepticus*; Suidas under *Θεσπιάδες*; Epiphanius, *Ancoratus*; Nazianzen, Oration I against Julian. ELMENHORST. — Nor did he lie only with these fifty; he also permitted his army to have intercourse with the women of Elis. See Diodorus Siculus, Book IV. He violated Chalciope, daughter of Eurypylus; he carried off Iole, daughter of Eurytus, by force; and Pausanias relates in various passages his intercourse with the daughter of Alcimedon, and so forth. See Betuleius.]

and generation have no other purpose than that all kinds of living things, since they are destined to die under the condition of mortality, may be preserved through mutual succession. But for God, who is everlasting, neither the other sex nor succession is necessary.

Someone will say: so that he may have either servants or subjects over whom he can rule. What need, then, is there of the female sex, since God, who is omnipotent, can beget sons without the use and agency of a female? For if he granted certain small creatures the capacity

> To gather with their mouths their young, born from leaves and fragrant herbs,

why should anyone suppose that God himself cannot beget except through union with the other sex? Accordingly, no one is so inconsiderate that he cannot understand that those whom the ignorant and foolish both call and worship as gods [Col. 0155B] [Col. 0156A] were mortal.

“How, then,” someone will say, “did they come to be believed gods?” Clearly because they had been the greatest and most powerful kings. On account of the merits of their virtues, or their gifts, or the arts they discovered, since they had been dear to those over whom they had ruled, they were consecrated to memory. If anyone doubts this, let him consider their deeds and actions, all of which both poets and ancient historians have transmitted.

## CHAPTER IX  
### On Hercules and His Life and Death

Hercules, who is regarded as the most illustrious because of his valor, and as it were the Africanus among the gods, is said to have traveled through and cleansed the world; yet did he not defile it [Col. 0156B] with debaucheries, lusts, [Col. 0157A] and adulteries? Nor is that surprising, since he himself was begotten through the adultery of Alcmene. [Col. 0157A]

[Note: [Col. 0157B] [Various Scholars’ Notes to columns 157–158]

“Alcmene.” The wife of Amphitryon. Arnobius writes in Book IV that Jupiter kept vigil with Alcmene for nine continuous nights, and that from that union was born Hercules, who in affairs of this sort both inherited and surpassed his father’s prowess. Clement testifies to this in the *Protrepticus*. Servius on *Aeneid* VIII and Lucian in the *Dialogues of the Gods* write that Jupiter made the encounter last three nights; Plautus, in the prologue to the *Amphitryon*, says at least one night, but a longer one; Jerome, volume II, *Against Vigilantius*, chapter 4, Ovid, *Amores* I, Elegy 13, and Hyginus, [Col. 0157C] Fable 39, say that he doubled two nights while he lay with Alcmene. ELMENHORST.

“Performed.” MSS. 1 Colb. and Brun. add “as you maintain.”

“The lion.” He tore apart and mangled the Nemean lion. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IX, Fable 3.

“And the boar.” The Maenalian, or Erymanthian, ravager of Arcadia, whom he captured alive. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IX, Fable 3. — “If he defeated the lion and the boar.” These labors of Hercules are well known; read Hyginus, Fable 30, and Diodorus Siculus IV.9 following.

“If he brought down birds with arrows?” The Stymphalian birds, named after Stymphalus, a town of Arcadia, and Lake Stymphalis. — “If he brought down birds.” Below: “he brings down birds.” *Dejicere*, “bring down,” is a hunter’s term. See Virgil, *Aeneid* V.542 and II.580. BUNEMANN.

“The stable.” That of Augeas, king of Elis, which he cleaned by diverting the river Alpheus through it. Pausanias, *Elis* I.1; Diodorus Siculus IV.13. [Col. 0157D]

“If he defeated the warrior-woman.” Most MSS. and some editions corruptly read “maiden.” With 3 Reg., 1 Colb., Brun., and several printed editions, I prefer to read “warrior-woman,” namely Hippolyta, queen of the Amazons. Justin, who describes Hercules’ war against the Amazons in Book II, speaks not of a belt or girdle (*ζωστήρ*) but of armor. Isaac Tzetzes reports various opinions on this matter in his commentary on Lycophron. BETULEIUS. — “Defeated the warrior-woman.” Some hold that *virago* means a valiant maiden; hence below he calls her a “warlike Amazon.”

“Their master.” Namely Diomedes, king of Thrace, concerning whom see Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IX, Fable 3.

“As the Orator says.” We restored this from all the MSS. except 1 Claromont., which, like most editions, reads “as the Orator states,” that is, Cicero in his speech *For Marcellus*. — “As he says.” Book III, chapter 19. Similar is the expression “what Plato used to say.” Book VI, chapter 11: “And that statement of Cicero is true, when he says,” etc. BUNEMANN.

“Which cannot be weakened or broken by iron.” Thus read all the MSS. and editions I have so far been able to see, and Cicero himself, to whom this maxim belongs. The older Bonon., however, reads: “which cannot be weakened and broken by iron and force.”

“To restrain.” On this victory, see Ambrose, *On Duties*, and Prudentius, where the single combat of the virtues against the vices is described.

“Whoever does these things.” Goth. reads “whoever does this,” just as Graevius restored the text from the Erfurt codex of Cicero. BUNEMANN.

“I do not compare him with the greatest men.” I caused the text to be printed as it stands in the three best MSS.—Reg., the older Bonon., 1 Colb., and 2 Brun.—and in Tullius himself. For the phrase “not only” is very often elegantly left implicit in a negation, in imitation of Greek, although Latins prefer it to be expressed when followed by the adversative “but” or “but even.” ISAAC [CASAUBON], who adduces several examples of this. — Other witnesses read: “I do not merely compare him,” etc.

“I judge him most like God.” Apuleius, in his book *On the God of Socrates*: “Nothing is more like or more pleasing to God than a man whose character is perfectly good.” Pliny, at the beginning of the *Panegyric*: “For what gift of the gods is more excellent [Col. 0158C] or more beautiful than a chaste and holy ruler who is most like the gods?” Musonius says the same on this matter in Stobaeus, Sermon 46. Aristotle likewise, *Politics* III.9, considers a man eminent in virtue *θεὸν ἐν ἀνθρώποις εἶναι*, “to be like a god among human beings.” See more on this in *On the Anger of God*, chapter 19. VALLINUS.

“Like God.” Julius Caesar, namely, because of his clemency.

“Must be considered.” I prefer this reading, supported by nearly all the MSS., including the best and oldest—2 Reg., nine hundred years old, and 2 Bonon.—to “must be judged,” the reading of Cauc., Jun., and the printed editions. See more in Lactantius, *On the Anger of God*, chapter 19.

“Than one who overcomes the violent beast enclosed within himself,” etc. Most printed editions and MSS. read “violence,” but Isaeus, following Thomasius, corrected the text and reads: “one who overcomes a lion, than one who overcomes the violent beast enclosed within himself—anger.” So too 1 Bon. ant., 2 Reg., 1 Clarom., and 2 Colb.; I greatly approve this reading, for the discourse itself is more elegant and weighty. If we read “violence,” I do not see what reason could be given for calling anger a beast enclosed within oneself, since violence is a particularly bitter form of anger. Thus, since he undertakes to compare only one thing with one thing and uses the lion as his example, he undoubtedly compares that lion with the violent beast of anger.

“He brings down the most rapacious birds.” He killed them with arrows; Hyginus, Fable 30. Apollonius denies this in Book II, verse 1055, contending that he drove them away with a bronze rattle and its ringing rather than with a bow. BUNEMANN.

“The warlike Amazon.” The name of the Amazons is derived from the loss of one breast: they burned away the right breast from infancy so that it would not impede the discharge of arrows. That this is not altogether fabulous may be gathered from Plato, *Laws* VII. Hippocrates has something similar in a serious account of the Scythians of his own time. BOCHART.

“Than one who … defeats the destroyer of reputation.” These words are absent from the Sublacensian edition.]

What, then, could have been divine in a man who was himself enslaved to his vices and who, contrary to every law, afflicted both males and females with infamy, disgrace, and shameful abuse? Yet not even the great and marvelous deeds that he performed should be judged such that they might appear attributable to divine powers. For what is so magnificent if he defeated a lion and a boar, brought down birds with arrows, cleared out a royal stable, defeated a warrior-woman and stripped away her girdle, or killed savage horses together with their master? These are the works of a strong man, but still of a human being. For the things he defeated were frail [Col. 0157B] and mortal. As the Orator says, [Col. 0158A] there is no force so great that it cannot be weakened and broken by iron and physical strength.

But to conquer one’s own spirit and restrain one’s anger belong to the strongest of men; Hercules neither ever did nor could do these things. Whoever does them, I do not compare with the greatest men; I judge him most like God.

I wish Cicero had added lust, luxury, greed, and arrogance, so that he might have completed the virtue of the man whom he judged like God. For one who defeats a lion must not be considered stronger than one who overcomes the violent beast enclosed within himself—anger; nor one who brings down the most rapacious birds stronger than one who restrains the most ravenous desires; nor one who defeats a warlike Amazon stronger than one who defeats lust, [Col. 0158B] the destroyer of modesty and reputation; nor one who clears dung [Col. 0159A] from a stable stronger than one who drives vices from his own heart. These are more destructive because they are evils within and belonging to oneself, whereas the former could be both avoided and guarded against. It follows from this that only the man who is self-controlled, moderate, [Col. 0159A]

“Eurystheus.” King of Mycenae. See Diodorus IV.9, [Col. 0159C] and Betuleius.

“Omphale.” Queen of Lydia. See Fulgentius, *Mythologies* II.5; Diodorus Siculus IV.31; Hyginus, Fable 32; Elmenhorst on Arnobius IV; Lucian, *Asclepius*; and Statius.

“Disgrace.” MS. Jun. reads “courage,” but wrongly. See Ovid in the *Heroides*.

“For it is not Lucilius who tells these stories.” Lucilius was a most incisive censor of vices. See Juvenal, Satire 1, concerning this poet Lucilius, and Persius, Satire 1.

“What, finally, is the more certain and truthful mystery?” Thus Reimm. with the remaining witnesses. Heumannus does not believe these to be Lactantius’ words, but they seem to me particularly necessary because the poets who had revealed those mysteries were suspected of falsehood. Hence in chapter 12: “We have revealed the poets’ mystery.” Once they had been rejected, a more certain and truthful mystery had to be sought. Compare chapters 15 and 21.

“He will produce none.” Recent MSS., 3 Colb., and 1 Bonon., together with the Roman edition of 1470, Paris 1525, Graph., Gymnic., and Is., read “no one will produce.”

[Col. 0159D]

“The Argonauts.” The voyage of the Argonauts took place eighty-three years before the destruction of Troy, or thirty-two years before Theseus began to reign. See Apollonius and Valerius Flaccus in their *Argonautica*.

“Troy.” This siege occurred forty years before Troy was plundered by the Greeks; in it Hercules deprived Laomedon of his kingdom.

“His daughter.” Hesione, whom Hercules rescued when she was about to be devoured by a monster.

“Struck by madness.” By Juno, who was hostile to him. See Euripides’ *Heracles Mad* and Seneca’s play as well.

“His wife.” Her name was Megara, daughter of Creon son of Menoeceus. See the *Epitome of Lactantius*, chapter 7, and Apollodorus II.

“Philoctetes.” We restored this form from the MSS., for they all agree upon it. The printed editions have a different form of *Philoctetes*. On him, read Servius on *Aeneid* III. Moreover, concerning the death and *ἀποθέωσις* (“deification”) of Philoctetes, read Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IX, [Col. 0160B] Fable 4. His story is found in Philostratus, *Heroicus*, chapter 6. BETULEIUS.

“Who buried his bones and ashes on Mount Oeta.” Vibius Sequester, *On Mountains*: “Oeta is a mountain of Thrace where Hercules was burned.” Cyprian, *On Idols*: “Hercules is burned in the fires of Oeta so that he may put off the human being.” See the mythographers, Hyginus, Fable 36; Servius on *Eclogue* 8 and *Aeneid* VIII; Augustine, *City of God* XVIII.4. From ELMENHORST. — Arnobius, Book IV, says on the authority of Plutarch that this occurred after the ravages of the epileptic disease; hence Aristotle in the *Problems* calls that disease “Herculean.”

“Oetaean.” It is better to follow nearly all the MSS. than the common editions and certain Vatican MSS., which read “Oeta.” 1 Lips. has “on Mount Oeta in Thessaly.” So too Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* III.40, “on Mount Oeta.”

“Disgrace.” That is, Apollo’s adultery with Arsinoe or Coronis, as Pindar says, and Arnobius in Books I and VII.

“Hippolytus.” Son of Theseus.

“Because he deserved to be struck by lightning by God.” Arnobius, Book IV, testifies that he was pierced by the weapon of the thunderbolt; Tertullian explains why he deserved to be struck by lightning, *Apology* 14: “There is one of the lyric poets—I mean Pindar—who sings that Asclepius was punished by a thunderbolt for his deserved greed, because he practiced medicine harmfully.” The passage to which Tertullian referred is *Pythian Ode* 3. On Asclepius, see Pausanias in the *Corinthiaca*, Diodorus Siculus IV, and Virgil, *Aeneid* VII.

“This man Tarquitius.” Ammianus Marcellinus XXV.6 says concerning this author that the report was drawn “from the books of Tarquitius, under the title *On Divine Matters*.” Macrobius also mentions him, *Saturnalia* III.7. BUNEMANN.

“Chiron.” *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 33. See Apollodorus I, p. 5, and III.3, p. 198. BUNEMANN.

“Stayed at Epidaurus.” Thus nearly all the editions and MSS.; 1 Clarom. reads “dwelt”; MSS. 1 Reg., 1 Colb., and 1 Brun. read “died.” Epidaurus is a city in Achaea, adorned as though with Noric marble and highly celebrated for its temple of Asclepius; hence Asclepius is called “Epidaurian.”

“At Cynosura.” Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* III.22. Cynosura [Col. 0161B] is a city in Arcadia, where there is also a promontory of the same name.]

and just ought to be judged courageous. If anyone reflects on what God’s works are, he will at once judge ridiculous all those things which the most foolish human beings admire. For they measure those deeds not by divine powers, of which they are ignorant, but by the weakness of their own strength.

No one will deny that Hercules served not only King Eurystheus—which might to some extent appear honorable—but also the shameless woman Omphale, who ordered him, dressed in her clothes, to sit at her feet spinning wool: detestable disgrace! But pleasure was worth so high a price.

“What,” someone will say, “do you think the poets are to be believed?” Why should I not think so? For it is not Lucilius who tells these stories, nor Lucian, who spared neither gods nor human beings, but especially those poets who sang the praises of the gods.

Whom, then, shall we believe, if we place no trust in those who praise them? Whoever thinks that these men are lying should produce other authorities whom we may believe, who can teach us who these gods are, how and whence they arose; what their force is, their number, their power; what in them is admirable, what worthy of worship, and, finally, what mystery is more certain and true: [Col. 0160A] he will produce none. Let us therefore believe those who spoke not to censure them, but to proclaim their praises.

He then sailed with the Argonauts and stormed Troy, being angry with Laomedon because the reward promised him for saving his daughter had been withheld; from this it is apparent at what period he lived. The same man, driven by fury and madness, killed his wife together with his children. Do men regard this man as a god? But Philoctetes, his heir, did not: he applied the torch when Hercules was about to be burned; he saw his limbs and sinews consumed and dissolved by the fire; he buried his bones and ashes on Mount Oeta; and in return for this service received his arrows.

## CHAPTER X. On the Life and Deeds of Aesculapius, Apollo, Neptune, Mars, Castor and Pollux, Mercury, and Liber

[Col. 0160B] Aesculapius himself, likewise born from an illicit act of Apollo, did what else that was worthy of divine honors, apart from healing Hippolytus? He certainly had a more illustrious death, because he merited being struck by God’s thunderbolt. Tarquitius, in his discussion *On Illustrious Men*, says that he was born of uncertain parents, exposed, found by hunters, nourished on a bitch’s milk, entrusted to Chiron, and taught medicine; that he was a Messenian, but stayed at Epidaurus. Tullius also says that he was buried at Cynosura. [Col. 0161A]

Mars was a murderer and was acquitted by the Athenians of the charge of murder through favor; then, lest he appear excessively savage and brutal, he committed adultery with Venus. Castor and Pollux, while abducting other men’s brides, ceased to be twins. For Idas, roused by resentment at the injury, ran one of them through [Col. 0162A] with his sword; and the poets relate that they live and die on alternate days, so that they are now the most wretched not only of gods, but of all mortals, since they are not permitted to die once and for all. Yet Homer attests, without qualification—and not in the manner customary among poets—that both of them were dead. For when he represented Helen sitting with Priam upon the walls, recognizing all the leaders of Greece but looking only for her own brothers, he appended to her speech this verse:

> Ὡς φάτο, τοὺς δ᾽ ἤδη κάτεχεν φυσίζοος αἶα.

What did Mercury, thief and scoundrel, leave to his reputation except the memory of his frauds? He was evidently [Col. 0163A] worthy of heaven because he taught wrestling and [Col. 0163A]

> > Eloquent Mercury, grandson of Atlas, [Col. 0163B]

> **And to hold the first place in giving his opinion.** Properly speaking, senators, not consuls, were said to hold the first or second place in giving an opinion. It belonged to the consuls to refer a matter to the senate, and to the senators to state their opinions. The first to be asked their opinions were the consuls designate, or, if there were none, the chief of the senate; hence “senator of the first opinion” and “chief of the senate” mean the same thing. Trebellius Pollio, in *The Usurper Piso*: “Aurelius Fuscus, a consular of the first opinion, who had succeeded Valerian.” Capitolinus, however, in *The Gordians*, calls Valerian “chief of the senate”; Trebellius calls him “the most illustrious chief of the citizen body.” Vopiscus, in *Aurelian*: “Then Ulpius Syllanus, of the first opinion, arose.” Thus one often reads “senator of the first opinion,” even on the stone dedicated [Col. 0163C] in honor of Symmachus: “WHO WAS ACCUSTOMED TO BE ASKED HIS OPINION FIRST IN THE SENATE.” Lactantius alluded to this here. ISAAC CASAUBON.
>

>

He was, however, defeated by the lust with which he burned for Ariadne.
>

Yet with Cellarius I have no doubt that Lactantius wrote *Crete*, because it is more famous than little Dia, which is seventy stadia from the Cretan shore, as Strabo reports near the end of Book X. I trust him more than Diodorus, who says that it was later called Naxos.
>
> **With his half-male retinue.** This consisted of men and women, because Bacchus had not only men but also women in his army. For it was customary among the Persians and Assyrians—in the words of Bochart in his book [Col. 0164A] *On the Colonies of the Phoenicians*—for wives to accompany their husbands on military expeditions. Thus Darius, when preparing to fight Alexander, brought with him his wife and mother and a crowd of other women. [Col. 0164B] Indeed, Indian women συστρατεύουσι (*systrateuousi*), “serve in the army alongside the men,” equipped with every kind of weapon; so Megasthenes reports in Strabo, Book XV. The women who accompanied Liber on his Indian expedition were called Bacchae or Bacchantes, a name derived from mourning (Ezekiel VIII), because the rites of Bacchus were celebrated with much weeping and wailing. See Bochart at the passage cited. The words “with his half-male retinue” are taken from Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.215. On this retinue of Liber, see St. Augustine, *City of God* XVIII.13.
>

> **And made her Libera.** This is a joke. “Since,” he says, “he was Liber, by joining her to himself he made her Libera, and ascended into heaven together with her.” For τὸ *Liberam*, “the word *Libera*,” cannot here be understood as distinguished from a female slave, since it is nowhere related that Ariadne was freed from any servitude through the aid of Father Liber. We have therefore, contrary to the other editions, written this name with a capital letter. Among the nations there was in fact also a goddess called Libera, concerning whom see Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II and *Against Verres*, Actio VI; Tacitus, Book II; Livy, first decad, Book V; Arnobius, Book V; and Augustine, *City of God* VI.19. Some say that she was Ceres, others Venus, and some Proserpina. But Ovid speaks of Ariadne in *Fasti* III.512, verses Lactantius undoubtedly had in mind when he wrote this:
>

Father Liber must possess the highest authority in the senate of the gods and hold the first place in giving his opinion, because, apart from Jupiter, he alone of them all celebrated a triumph, led an army, and conquered the Indians. But that unconquered Indian commander, that greatest of men, was most shamefully conquered by love and lust. For, having been carried to Crete with his half-male retinue, he found a shameless woman on the shore and, trusting in his Indian victory, wished to prove himself a man, lest he appear excessively effeminate. He claimed in marriage this woman who had betrayed her father, murdered her brother, and been abandoned and repudiated by another man; he made her Libera, and together with her ascended into heaven.

What of the father of all these, Jupiter, who in solemn prayer is called Best and Greatest? Is he not discovered to have been impious and almost a parricide from his earliest childhood? For he drove his father from his kingdom and put him to flight, without waiting for the decrepit old man’s death, because of his lust for kingship. After he had seized his father’s throne by violence and armed force, he was assailed in war by the Titans. This [Col. 0165A] was the beginning of evils for the human race. After they had been defeated and peace secured forever, he consumed the remainder of his life in sexual outrages and adulteries. [Col. 0165A]

> [Note: [Col. 0165C] [Various Editors’ Notes on columns 165–166]
>
> **In sexual outrages and adulteries.** Read of Jupiter’s adulteries and sexual outrages in Arnobius, Books IV and V, and Epiphanius, *Ancoratus*.
>
> **I omit, etc.** This manner of speaking is employed repeatedly throughout all the books of Lactantius.
>
> **The maidens whose virginity he impaired.** See a similar expression in *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, ch. 38.
>
> **For that is commonly judged tolerable.** The Subiaco edition has “intolerable,” less correctly.
>
> **Amphitryon and Tyndareus.** Amphitryon was a Theban prince, from whose wife Alcmena Jupiter fathered Hercules. Tyndareus was king of Oebalia in the Peloponnese and had Leda as his wife. Pollux and Helen were born from her and Jupiter.
>
> **Abducted a royal boy for sexual violation.** Namely Ganymede, the son of Tros, king of the Trojans. On him see Homer, *Iliad*; Virgil, *Aeneid* V; Ovid, *Metamorphoses*; Lucian, in several dialogues; Germanicus Caesar, under Aquarius; [Col. 0165D] Herodian, Book I; Orosius I.12.
>
> **Stained.** Polluted, contaminated. Tacitus, *Histories* III.38: “stained by every disgrace.” BUNEMAN.
>
> **Adultery committed contrary to nature.** The most shameful, detestable, and utterly abominable crime of pederasty, which Plato in Book I of the *Laws* execrates as criminal and utterly impure, calling it, as Lactantius does here, τὸ παρὰ φύσιν τόλμημα (*to para physin tolmēma*), “the act of audacity contrary to nature.” The most Christian emperors Constantine and Constantius were the first to confront this criminal audacity, and by passing a laudable law imposing infamy and capital punishment upon these infamous pederasts, they removed this evil from the earth. See Book III of the Theodosian Code, under the Julian Law on Adultery; Book III of the Justinian Code, under the Julian Law on Adultery; Novels LXXI and CXLI. From ELMENHORST.
>
> **The adulteries of Verres … Clodius’s incest.** See Cicero, *Against Verres*, Actio II, and the speech *For Marcus Caelius*.
>
> **Both sister and wife.** See Virgil, *Aeneid* I; Ovid, *Metamorphoses* III; and also Horace, *Odes* III.5; Macrobius; and Plutarch. This was customary among Eastern peoples.
>
> **Mindless.** Without a heart, or without understanding.
>
> **A certain poet wrote a Triumph of Cupid.** The poet’s identity is unknown, and his book has not survived to our time. The author of the book *On Chastity* among the works of Cyprian had this in view when he wrote: “Unchastity subjects a man to the triumph of lust.” Nicolaus Abram likewise admits that the poet’s name is unknown, in his note on Cicero, *Against Piso*, ch. 25. BUNEMAN.
>
> **Power.** Thus in Lucian Jupiter reproaches Cupid for having turned him into a satyr, a bull, gold, and other things that brought disgrace upon Jupiter himself.
>
> **Desire.** Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have the plural, *desires*.
>
> **That Jupiter reigns in heaven.** “We believed Jupiter to reign because he thundered in heaven,” says Horace, *Odes* III.5. Jupiter is imagined to be lord of heaven because the elevated regions fell to his share, and especially Africa, a large part of which lies between the tropics and therefore has the sun and the other planets directly overhead; hence it is thought to be nearest to heaven. [Col. 0166D] See Lucan, Book IX.
>
> **Hymns.** See hymns to Jupiter in Callimachus.
>
> **Temples.** A *delubrum* is a place in which an image of a god has been dedicated. See Festus, Servius, and Macrobius in the *Saturnalia*.
>
> **By Saturn and Rhea.** Thus numerous manuscripts and almost all the printed editions. Ten recent manuscripts, except one, have “by Saturn and Ops.” The meaning is the same, for Rhea is also called Ops, as everyone knows.
>
> **Believed.** This word, which occurs in the ancient Bologna codex, the editions of Thomasius, Thysius, and Gallaeus, and two Leipzig manuscripts, is absent from the others.
>
> **The poet.** Virgil, *Aeneid* XII.820.
>
> **Many thousands existed.** Tertullian refutes Saturn’s divinity with almost the same arguments in *Apology*, ch. 10.
>
> **That another may be.** Perhaps one should read, “that there may also be another.” The text has been altered. Thus Aristotle, in the little work *On the Cosmos*, explains this fiction concerning Jupiter.]

I omit the maidens whose virginity he impaired, for that is commonly judged tolerable. I cannot pass over Amphitryon and Tyndareus, whose households he filled completely with dishonor and infamy. But it was the height of impiety and wickedness that he abducted a royal boy for sexual violation. For it seemed too little that he should be stained and disgraceful in overcoming the chastity of women, unless he also inflicted injury upon his own sex. This is true adultery, committed contrary to nature.

As for the one who did these things, we shall consider whether he is the Greatest; certainly he is not the Best. That title has no place among seducers, adulterers, and the incestuous—unless perhaps we human beings are mistaken when we call those who do such things criminals and degenerates and judge them most deserving of every punishment. Marcus Tullius, then, was a fool to accuse Gaius Verres of adulteries, for Jupiter, whom he worshiped, committed the same acts; and a fool to accuse Publius Clodius of incest with his sister, since for that Best and Greatest god the same woman was both sister and wife. [Col. 0165B]

## CHAPTER XI. On Jupiter’s Origin, Life, Kingdom, Name, and Death, and on Saturn and Uranus

Who, then, is so mindless as to think that Jupiter reigns in heaven, when he should not even have reigned on earth? A certain poet wrote, not without wit, a *Triumph of Cupid*. In that book he represents Cupid not only as the most powerful of the gods, but also as their conqueror. After enumerating the loves of each of them, through which they had come under Cupid’s power and dominion, he arranges a triumphal procession in which Jupiter, together with the other gods, is led in chains before the victor’s chariot. This was indeed elegantly fashioned by the poet, yet it is not far removed from the truth. For whoever is devoid of virtue and is conquered by desire and evil lusts is subject not to Cupid, as the poet imagined, but to everlasting death.

But let us refrain from speaking about his morals; let us consider the matter itself, so that people may understand the wretched errors in which they are entangled. The common people believe that Jupiter reigns in heaven; learned and unlearned alike have been persuaded of this. Religion [Col. 0166B] itself, prayers, hymns, temples, and statues demonstrate it. Yet they admit that this same Jupiter was born of Saturn and Rhea. How can he be regarded or believed to be God—or, as the poet says,

> … the creator of men and things,

when countless thousands of human beings existed before his birth? These, of course, were the people who lived during Saturn’s reign and enjoyed the light before Jupiter did.

I see that one god was king in the earliest times and another in those that followed. It is therefore possible that another may be king hereafter. For if the earlier kingdom was changed, why should we despair [Col. 0167A] of the later kingdom also being capable of change? Unless, perhaps, Saturn was able to beget someone stronger than himself, while Jupiter cannot. Yet divine rule is either always immutable or, if it is mutable—which [Col. 0167A]

> [Note: [Col. 0167B] [Various Editors’ Notes on columns 167–168]
>
> **Which.** One Colbertine and one Brun manuscript read “concerning which.” See Lucian, *Dialogues of the Gods* I.
>
> **Cannot.** An early hand in the Reimmann manuscript wrote “could not” above these words; not badly. BUNEMAN.
>
> **Precisely so.** An elegant formula, as in Book II, ch. 2, and *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, ch. 18. It comes from Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I.7. BUNEMAN.
>
> **Thetis.** See Apollodorus III, p. 218; Hyginus, Fable 54; Crenius, *Observations*, Part IX, p. 48. BUNEMAN.
>
> **Because the oracle declared: greater than his father.** Pindar has the same oracle in the final *Isthmian Ode*, section 4. BUNEMAN.
>
> **And first, there was in him the ignorance of one who was not God.** With Isaeus and Gallaeus we read this from the Royal and Vatican manuscripts, three Colbertine, [Col. 0167C] two Brun manuscripts, and numerous printed editions. But two Bologna manuscripts, the Taxian, Penwortham, Junius, and one Leipzig manuscript, as well as Aldus, have, “prudence in God, not God’s”; three Colbertine manuscripts, one Clermont, and the early Roman editions of 1468 and 1470 and Paris 1525 have, “prudence in God, not God’s,” so that, as Walch says, prudence existed in Jupiter, but it was not divine, because he would not have known unless Themis had foretold it. The genuine reading of Lactantius, however, which stands in the text, is evident from the fact that both here and below in ch. 13 our author charges Jupiter with *imprudentia*, that is, lack of knowledge and ignorance, which is as far removed from God as possible. For *imprudentia* is, as Cicero says, “when the person who is accused is denied to have known something.” It is also clear from Heraldus’s citation of this passage in his note on Arnobius III that he read it as we do. Walch reads and places in the Lactantian text, “First, there was in him ignorance, not the providence of God.” Let the learned judge this reading.—The Subiaco edition reads “prudence” for “ignorance.”
>
> **Consciousness of weakness.** That is, knowledge, the judgment of the mind that convicts people. Thus Pliny has “consciousness of letters,” [Col. 0167D] Book VII, ch. 30, meaning “knowledge.” SALMASIUS.
>
> **Feared.** Therefore he was not God. See ch. 13 and *On Anger*, ch. 15. BUNEMAN.
>
> **He certainly knows.** Thus the Bologna, Taxian, and Penwortham manuscripts; the Utrecht manuscript has “he surely knows”; the very early Caucian manuscript, Rostock editions of 1478, Paris 1513, Parrhasius, Aldus, Cratander 1521–24, and Gymnich have “he surely certainly knows.” I did not wish to omit this combination of particles, which I had not previously observed. BUNEMAN.
>
> **Something greater.** Perhaps read, “someone greater.” At the same place three recent manuscripts have “likewise” for “the same.” One early Bologna manuscript adds after “exist”: “therefore he is neither Best nor Greatest.”
>
> **The same, etc.** Thus the best codices and the better editions read, with a full stop before the word “The same.”
>
> **Swears most solemnly by the Stygian marsh, etc.** The Styx was held in such reverence that the gods were believed to swear by it alone. This is well known from Homer, *Iliad* ο; Hesiod, *Theogony*; Apollonius, *Argonautica* II; likewise Virgil, *Aeneid* IX and XII; [Col. 0168B] Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I; Seneca, *Hercules Furens*; Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* VI; and Virgil, *Aeneid* VI:
>
> > … and the Stygian marsh,  
> > By whose divinity the gods fear to swear falsely.
>
> Whenever any of them committed perjury, according to Hesiod they lay for an entire year devoid of spirit and life. Orpheus, however, gives a somewhat different account, as Servius indicates in his note on *Aeneid* VI: “For Orpheus reports that the gods who swear falsely by the Stygian marsh are punished in Tartarus for nine thousand years.” From Vossius, *On Idolatry* V, and Bochart, *Sacred Geography*, p. 165, who identifies the location [Col. 0168C] of the Stygian marsh from Ptolemy.—
>
> **The same swears by the Stygian marsh.** Here and in ch. 17 Cellarius thought that Lactantius had taken this verse as referring to Jupiter’s oath, although it concerns Juno. But Lactantius added Virgil’s words as a description of the Stygian marsh consecrated by the sacred obligation of oaths. Compare Apollodorus I.2.4 and Vossius, *Gentile Theology* II.81. BUNEMAN.
>
> **Empty superstition.** The passage is from Virgil, *Aeneid* XII.817. We have restored this reading from the codex used by the editor of the folio edition of Lactantius published at Cologne in 1544, p. 15. Nevertheless, the common editions read “One superstition,” in accordance with almost all the manuscripts of Lactantius and the common texts of Virgil. One could also read “Empty superstition” with the French edition of 1563 and the English Christ Church and Balliol manuscripts, since Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII.187, cited by Lactantius in Book IV, ch. 28, reads:
>
> > Empty superstition, ignorant of the ancient gods.
>
> [Col. 0168D]
>
> **Return.** Thus the oldest and best Royal manuscripts, two Bologna, five Colbertine, the Taxian, Junius, Utrecht, and two Clermont manuscripts. That verb is characteristic of Virgil. Three recent manuscripts, one Royal, one Colbertine, and a Brun manuscript, as well as the printed editions, have “descend.”
>
> **The Fates.** The same as the Parcae. Hence the proverb that even the gods do not resist necessity—that is, fate. As for what ἀνάγκη (*anankē*, “necessity”) and εἱμαρμένη (*heimarmenē*, “fate”) mean according to the philosophers, see Plutarch, *Opinions of the Philosophers* I.25, etc.; likewise Aristotle, *On the Cosmos*.
>
> **If the power of the Parcae is so great, etc.** Recent manuscripts, one Royal, one Colbertine, and one Brun manuscript have “of the Fates.” The Parcae are the same as Fate, as you see in this passage and as is perfectly clear in other authors; we shall sample only a few. Fulgentius Planciades, *Mythologies* I: “They assign three Fates to this Pluto, of whom the first is Clotho, the second Lachesis, and the third Atropos.” Procopius: Ἔχει δὲ τὸν ναὸν, etc.—“It has, moreover, in the forum near the senate house, if one passes a little beyond it, a temple of the three Fates. This is what the Romans customarily call the Parcae.” From VOSSIUS.—See in Lucian the dialogue entitled Ζεὺς ἐλεγχόμενος (*Zeus Cross-Examined*), [Col. 0169B] in which the Cynic indicates that, because of this inescapable necessity, the condition of Jupiter and the other gods is no better than the human condition.]

is impossible—it is surely always mutable.

Can Jupiter, then, lose his kingdom just as his father lost his? Precisely so. For although he never spared either virgins or married women, he nevertheless abstained from Thetis alone, because the oracle declared that whoever was born from her would be greater than his father. First, there was in him the ignorance of one who was not God, for unless Themis had told him the future, he himself would not have known it. But if he is not divine, neither can he be God, since “divinity” is named from “God” just as “humanity” is named from “human being.”

Second, there was consciousness of weakness in the one who plainly feared someone greater. Whoever does this certainly knows that he is not the greatest, since [Col. 0167B] something greater is capable of existing. The same god swears most solemnly by the Stygian marsh:

> [Col. 0168A] Empty superstition, rendered to the gods above.

What is this superstition? Or by whom was it rendered? Is there, then, some supreme power that punishes gods who commit perjury? Why is their dread of the infernal marsh so great if they are immortal? Why do they fear what they will never see, unless they are among those who must die? Why, then, do human beings raise their eyes toward heaven? Why do they swear by the gods above, when the gods above themselves return to the underworld and there have something that they revere and adore?

And what are we to make of the assertion that there are Fates which all the gods, even Jupiter himself, obey? If the power of the Parcae is so great that they are stronger than all the heavenly gods and even than their ruler and lord himself, why are the Parcae not rather said to reign, since necessity compels all the gods to obey their laws and decrees? Who can now doubt that one who submits to some authority [Col. 0168B] is not the greatest? For if he were, he would not receive the decrees of fate, but make them.

I now return to another matter that I had omitted. In one [Col. 0169A] therefore— [Col. 0169A]

>
> **Therefore.** Thus emended from the early Roman edition and all the manuscripts except one Brun manuscript, in which, as in the printed editions, the reading is “surely”; less appropriately, since “surely” follows immediately afterward.
>
> **Weak.** Thus we have restored the reading from the oldest and best manuscripts. Ten recent manuscripts and the printed editions have the alternative form *imbecillis*.
>
> **Saved by stealth.** Rhea, therefore, after giving birth to Jupiter, concealed the infant in Crete out of fear of his father, to be nursed by two nymphs, Adrastea and Ida, daughters of Melisseus. See Ovid, *Fasti* V.
>

>

On the story of Jupiter descending in a golden shower, see Terence, *The Eunuch*; Ovid, *Tristia* VI; Horace, *Odes* III; [Col. 0169D] Germanicus Caesar’s translation of Aratus where he discusses Perseus; Hyginus, Fable 63; and also Epiphanius, *Ancoratus*.
