>
> **Catamitus.** *Catamiti* are boys used for prostitution, says Betuleius. The glosses read: “Catamitus: Γανυμήδης (*Ganymēdēs*, ‘Ganymede’).” Festus says: “They used *Catamitus* for Ganymede, who was Jupiter’s male concubine.” Arnobius does likewise.
>
> **Eagle.** Fulgentius likewise says this concerning Jupiter’s deed. See Plato, *Laws* I.
>
> **Had its tutelary deity depicted in the form of an eagle.** I would delete *in aquilam*, “into an eagle,” found in one early Bologna, five Vatican, and two Colbertine manuscripts. The tutelary deity was a god or goddess whose image was depicted on the stern. For the ancients customarily consecrated their ships to particular gods and entrusted them [Col. 0170B] to those gods’ protection. Thus Paris speaks in Ovid’s epistle to Helen:
>
> > We add yards and sails that follow the masts;  
> > The curved stern also receives the painted gods.
>
> Virgil, *Aeneid* X:
>
> > The stern gleamed with a gilded Apollo.
>
> Ships were entrusted not only to the protection of gods but also to that of goddesses. Hence the ship that carried Ovid to Pontus had the goddess Minerva as its protectress. *Tristia* I, Elegy 9:
>
> > My ship has—and, I pray, may it retain—the protection  
> > Of fair-haired Minerva, and takes its name from her painted helmet.
>
> [Col. 0170C]]

Isaeus maintains that not only gods and goddesses were regarded as guardian deities (*tutelae*), but also other things—for example, an eagle and other animals. In my judgment, however, he is mistaken: for what aid or protection could sailors have hoped for from a brute animal? Certainly the very name *tutela* seems to indicate quite plainly that the ancients expected the preservation of a ship from no one other than the god or goddess to whose protection they had entrusted it, or to whom they had consecrated it, and whose image, as a mark of honor, the ship bore depicted on its stern.

The same Isaeus is also mistaken, together with certain other learned men, in thinking that the *tutela* was the ship’s emblem placed upon the prow, that the ship took its name from the *tutela*, and that in Greek the *tutela* was called the παράσημον (*parásēmon*, distinguishing emblem). The occasion of this error was supplied to him and the others by the fact that the Glosses say: “*tutela*, παράσημον τοῦ πλοίου”—“the ship’s distinguishing emblem.” This is not always true; for I affirm with Salmasius that sometimes the *tutela* had nothing in common with the *parasemon*. This is evident in the ship by which Europa was carried: Jupiter was the *tutela*, while the bull was the [Col. 0170D] παράσημον.

Understand the matter, therefore, as follows: one and the same thing was sometimes both the *tutela* and the παράσημον—namely, when the image of the god or goddess under whose protection the ship stood was placed upon the prow. This was done frequently, but not ordinarily. Thus the ship in which Paul was carried, Acts of the Apostles, chapter XXVIII, had the Τῶν Διοσκούρων παράσημον, “the emblem of the Dioscuri,” and at the same time had the Dioscuri as its *tutela*; hence ships of this kind were also called Διόσκουροι, “Dioscuri.” In that case the ship took its name from its *tutela*; otherwise it took its name from the *parasemon*, which represented some animal. A careful distinction must therefore be made between the *tutela*, which was depicted on the stern, and the παράσημον, which was represented on the prow. **GALLAEUS.**

**Like a bull.** The Subiaco edition adds *depicted*. I would not have you understand that the bull was the *tutela* of the ship that carried Europa; rather, it was the παράσημον, while Jupiter was the *tutela*. See Festus under the word *Europa*; Eusebius in the *Chronicle*; Selden, *On the Syrian Gods*, Syntagma II, chapter 16. MSS. 1 Reg., 1 Colb., and Brun. read: *A bull*. See below, *Epitome*, chapter 11, where these things are stated somewhat differently. Eusebius nevertheless [Col. 0171B] says in the *Chronicle*: “Europa was abducted by the Cretans in a ship whose emblem was a bull. For ships had borne emblems from ancient times, and were named after them.”

…alone did he show greater restraint, although he was desperately in love with her—not from any virtue, but from fear of a successor. Such fear surely belongs to one who is mortal, weak, and worthless, since he could have been destroyed at the very moment of his birth, just as his elder brother was destroyed; and if that brother had been able to live, he would never have yielded the sovereignty to the younger. But Jupiter himself, saved by stealth and reared in secrecy, was called Ζεύς or ζῆν, “Zeus” or “to live”—not, as they suppose, from the heat of the celestial fire, or because he is the giver of life, or because he breathes souls into living creatures, a power belonging to God alone (for how could one breathe a soul into another when he himself received his own from elsewhere?), but because he was the first of Saturn’s male children to live.

Men could therefore have had another god as ruler if Saturn had not been deceived by his wife. But, they say, [Col. 0169B] the poets invented these things. Whoever thinks this is mistaken. [Col. 0170A] For the poets were speaking about human beings; but in order to adorn those whose memory they celebrated with praises, they declared them to be gods. Consequently, those things were inventions rather which they said about them as gods, not those which they said about them as human beings. This will become clear from an example which we shall introduce.

When he was about to violate Danaë, he poured gold coins lavishly into her lap. This was the price of the sexual outrage. But the poets, who spoke as though they were speaking about a god, invented the story that he descended in a shower of gold, lest they diminish the authority of his reputed majesty. They used the same figure by which they speak of “iron showers” when describing a multitude of missiles and arrows.

He is said to have carried off Catamitus in an eagle: that is poetic coloring. But either he carried him off by means of a legion whose standard was an eagle, or the ship aboard which he was placed had as its *tutela* an eagle depicted upon it, just as [Col. 0170B] it had a bull when he abducted Europa and carried her across the sea.

In the same way, he is said to have transformed Io, daughter of Inachus, into a cow. In order to escape Juno’s anger, she—already covered with bristles, as the story has it, and already a cow—is said to have swum across the sea, reached Egypt, recovered her original form there, and become the goddess now called Isis. By what argument, then, can it be proved that neither Europa [Col. 0171A]

>
> **Since it is the poet’s function, etc.** Vossius teaches nearly the same thing in *On the Nature and Institution of Poetry*, book III: “Epic poets follow a middle path. For although they invent many things, the principal action is drawn from history and is usually commonly known, because the deeds of kings and commanders cannot remain hidden.” [Col. 0172B]
>
> **Into other forms.** We have corrected the text thus from five Reg. MSS., two of them extremely ancient; five Colb.; one Clarom.; and the editions of Betuleius, Tornes, Soubron, and the French edition of 1563. Other MSS. support this reading: 1 Reg., 1 Colb., and 2 Brun. read *in another form*; Ëm. reads *in other forms*. Two Reg. MSS., one Clarom., and many editions have *into certain forms*.  
> **May have invented.** We have emended the text thus from both ancient and excellent MSS.—2 Bonon., 4 Reg., 1 Colb., Tax., 2 Brun., and 1 Clarom. corrected by a second hand—and from the editions of Isaeus and Cellarius. And rightly so. Twelve recent MSS., together with almost all the editions, read *invented*.
>
> **But also painters and makers of images.** While Bon., Tax., and Pen. read, with Cellarius, “but painters of images also,” Ultr., Pal., Goth., Lips. 1 and 2, Jun., Cauc., and Torn. read more fully: “but also painters and makers of images.” Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I.29, evidently writes: “Jupiter … and the other gods are known to us with the appearance that painters and sculptors have chosen to give them.” **BUN.**
>
> **If this is Jupiter, whom you call God, if he is not the one.** We have restored this reading from almost all the MSS. and the edition of Cellarius; it is more explicit than what is found [Col. 0172D] in the two recent Reg., one Colb., two Clarom. MSS., and many editions: “If this Jupiter, whom you call God, is not the one.”
>
> **If this Jupiter has fallen upon it.** The principal MSS. and the Roman edition of 1470 and the Isaeus edition read thus. *This* is absent from four Colb. MSS. and the most recent editions. The Jun. MS. has “that Jupiter”; Cauc. and the editions of Fasitel, Betuleius, and Tornes have “that Jupiter there”; the Pen. MS. and the Paris 1525, Aldine, Crat., Graph., and Gymnic. editions have “Jupiter himself”; two recent Reg. and three Colb. and two Brun. MSS. have *shall have fallen*.
>
> **Him indeed.** Thus restored from the Isaeus edition and almost all MSS., among them the oldest and best, the Bonon. and Reg. manuscripts. The very learned Francius thought that one should read *indeed*. Inferior editions together with the Cauc. MS. have *then indeed*. The Pen. and Lips. MSS., four Colb. MSS., and many editions have *him truly*.
>
> **For what other argument.** We have added *what* from all the MSS. and editions except Thys., Gall., Spark., and Walch.
>
> **Nothing, therefore, was wholly invented by the poets.** We have restored this from the best and oldest codices: 2 Bon., Cauc., 5 Reg., 3 Colb., and 2 Brun.; *wholly* is absent from some. *In totum* means “altogether.” See book II, chapter 11, and Cicero. In French we say *en tout*. Thirteen recent MSS. and the editions read: “Not everything, therefore, was invented by the poets.”

rode upon a bull, nor Io was changed into a cow? A fixed day is recorded in the Calendar on which the voyage of Isis is celebrated; this fact shows that she did not swim across the sea, but sailed.

Those, therefore, who regard themselves as wise, because they understand that a living earthly body cannot be in heaven, reject the whole Ganymede story as false; and they perceive that the deed was done on earth, because the act itself and the lust involved are earthly. The poets, therefore, did not invent the events themselves; for if they had done so, they would have been utterly frivolous. Rather, they added a certain coloring to actual events. They did not say these things to disparage their subjects, but because they wished to adorn them. [Col. 0171B]

From this men are deceived, especially because, while supposing that all these things were invented by the poets, they worship what they do not understand. For they do not know the limits of poetic license, nor how far one may proceed in invention. The poet’s function is to take things that truly happened and, with a certain elegance, translate them into other forms by indirect figurative representations. But to invent the whole of what one relates [Col. 0172A] is to be an absurd person and a liar rather than a poet.

But suppose they invented those things that are regarded as fabulous: did they also invent what has been said about female gods and the marriages of the gods? Why, then, are they represented in this way and worshiped in this way—unless perhaps not only poets, but painters and makers of images also lie?

If this is Jupiter, whom you call a god—if he is not the one born from Saturn and Ops—then no image except his alone ought to have been placed in all the temples. What is the meaning of the images of women? What is the meaning of the weaker sex? If this Jupiter has fallen under its power, then the very stones will indeed confess that he was a man.

They say that the poets lied, and yet they believe them. Indeed, by the reality of the thing itself they prove that the poets did not lie; for they fashion the images of the gods in such a way that from the very difference of sex it is apparent that the things said by the poets are true. [Col. 0172B] For what other argument is conveyed by the image of Catamitus and the likeness of the eagle when they are placed before the feet of Jupiter in the temples and worshiped together with him, except that the memory of an unspeakable crime and sexual outrage should remain forever?

Nothing, therefore, was wholly invented by the poets. Something may perhaps have been transferred and obscured by indirect figurative representation, so that the truth might be concealed beneath a covering, [Col. 0173A] as in the story about the allotment of the kingdoms.

> [Col. 0173B]  
> **[Variorum Notes to columns 173–174]**
>
> **Of the kingdoms.** This allotment is found in Homer, *Iliad*, book III, in the speech of Neptune addressing Iris; the allotment is explained physically in the *Life of Homer*. See also the mythological explanations of Fulgentius.
>
> **Heaven fell to Jupiter.** See how this occurred at the beginning of this chapter.
>
> **The sea to Neptune.** Neptune was not so named from swimming (*nando*), as Cicero maintained in *On the Nature of the Gods* II, but from covering (*nubendo*) or from *nuptus*, as Lipsius and Varro maintain. Varro says in book IV of *On the Latin Language*: “Neptune is so called because the sea covers the lands, as a cloud covers the sky—from *nuptus*, that is, covering.” Arnobius, book III, also noted this from that passage, as did Vossius in his book *On Idolatry*. [Col. 0173C]
>
> Some maintain that this Neptune is the same as Japheth (Genesis IX.27), since the Latin name *Neptune* is synonymous with the Hebrew name *Japheth*. They placed him over the sea because northern and eastern Asia fell to the line of Shem; the descendants of Ham obtained southern Asia together with Africa; and the continent of Europe, together with the islands of the Mediterranean, fell to Japheth, as Lactantius testifies here.
>
> Some formerly interpreted the allotment among the three brothers in this way. For a long time now, however, learned men have inclined toward interpretations more closely approaching secular history. Yet the very learned Bochart and the celebrated Huet, in his *Evangelical Demonstration*, referred all the stories of mythology to the family and descendants of Noah. But, after more attentive consideration of the matter, Pezron, Banier, and others derived the entire truth, as far as possible, from the source of secular history. Much light is thereby cast upon these stories without circumlocution or metaphor.
>
> **Agesilaus.** Others read *Agelastus*, a name also given to Pluto.
>
> [Col. 0173D]
>
> **Of Marcus Antonius.** All the manuscript codices read thus, with the exception of one Vatican, the older Bologna MS., and the more recent 1 Reg., 1 Colbert., and 1 Sorbon., which read *of Pompey*, as do the Tornes edition of 1579, Soubron, and the Geneva edition of 1613. Pompey, to be sure, was given command of the fleet by the Gabinian law in order to free the sea from pirates.
>
> The other manuscripts and editions that Isaeus, Gallaeus, Cellarius, and I were able to inspect read *of Marcus Antonius*. Coelius Rhodiginus, book VI, chapter 18; Petrus Ciaconius; Latinus Latinius; and Isaeus approved this reading as Lactantius’ genuine text. Indeed, Cicero supports this reading twice: “After,” he says, “they had experienced that boundless command of Marcus Antonius”; and in the speech *On the Grain Supply*: “Thus did Marcus Antonius conduct himself in that boundless command.” I scarcely doubt that Lactantius had these passages in view.
>
> Nevertheless, from the same Cicero and from Plutarch it is clear that the same authority was assigned and delegated to Pompey. I have therefore been unwilling to depart from the received reading, confirmed by so many manuscripts and editions. The oldest Reg. MS. incorrectly has “such as that of Marcus Antoninus” [Col. 0174B]; the Regio-Puteanus has “such as that of Antonius.”
>
> Thomasius nevertheless prefers the reading *of Pompey*, since Cicero, in the speeches *For the Manilian Law* and *On the Agrarian Law*, teaches that Pompey was called Neptune because of his successful outcome. Moreover, Thomasius says, many ancient images of Pompey are found which attribute Neptune’s insignia to him.
>
> **The Senate had decreed.** Plutarch nevertheless states that Caesar Augustus, Marcus Antonius, and Lepidus divided the Roman Empire among themselves in the year 712 from the founding of the city, without the Senate’s authorization and amid universal disorder. Historians called this threefold government the Triumvirate.
>
> **Fell to them.** Cicero, whom Lactantius imitates here, frequently used this verb in connection with allotment; so too Ambrose, *On Duties* I.13: “The poets say that the world was divided into three, so that by the allotment of sovereignty heaven fell to one, the sea to another, and the underworld to another as realms to be governed.” So too *to fall to*: Livy XXI.17: “When they were ordered to draw lots, Spain fell to Cornelius”; XXXII.8: “When lots were drawn … Macedonia fell to Quintius.” Lactantius above uses *to fall by lot* in the same sense. **BUN.**
>
> **Euhemerus.** Author of the *History of the Gods*. Arnobius calls him an Agrigentine in book IV; Strabo, book I, and Plutarch, in *On Isis and Osiris*, make him a Messenian. He lived in the year 438 after the founding of Rome. The ancients counted him among the atheists.
>
> He is also cited by Cicero in *On the Nature of the Gods* I: “This line of reasoning,” he says, “was developed especially by Euhemerus, whom our Ennius translated and followed above all others.” He is also mentioned by Pliny, book XXXV, chapter 22; Josephus, book I *Against Apion*; Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation*; Minucius Felix in the *Octavius*; Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* II.4; Augustine, *City of God* VI.7 and VII.26; Theodoret, *Cure of the Greek Maladies*, at the end of book II and the beginning of book III; Festus under *Sus Minervam*; and others. Theophilus of Antioch, discourse 3, calls this Euhemerus Ἀθεώτατον, “the most atheistic.”
>
> **Messene.** We have emended the text thus from the Regio-Puteanus MS. [Col. 0174D], two other Reg. MSS., one Colb., Goth., Brun., and *Epitome*, chapter 13. And rightly so, for Plutarch calls him a Messenian. One ancient Reg., two Colb., and one Claromont. have *Messena*. Another Clarom., three Colb., one Sorbon., and the editions have *Messana*.  
> **From the city of Messene.** Isaeus, not without error, discussed passages from authors as though Messene and Messana denoted the same city. Lactantius writes correctly in *Epitome*, chapter 13: “Euhemerus was a Messenian.” Lips. 2 wrongly has *Messana*. All the old editions incorrectly have *Messana*. **BUN.**
>
> **Of Triphylian Jupiter.** He was so called because he was worshiped by the Triphylians, peoples inhabiting the Peloponnese.  
> **In the shrine of Triphylian Jupiter.** Triphylia is the region between Elis and Messenia; Strabo VIII, p. 232; book XXXII.5; Pausanias, *Elis* I, p. 151. Pausanias assigns to it the city of Lepreum. Hence “Triphylian Jupiter.” **CELL.**
>
> **Ennius translated it.** Arnobius, book IV, p. 147: “Ennius translated the books of Euhemerus into the Italian language, so that the matter might become clear to everyone.” **CELL.**

For they say that heaven fell to Jupiter, the sea to Neptune, and the underworld to Pluto. Why did the earth not rather enter into the third allotment? Because the event took place on earth.

The truth in the story, therefore, is that they divided the sovereignty of the world and apportioned it by lot in such a way that dominion over the East fell to Jupiter, while the portion of the West fell to Pluto, whose surname was Agesilaus. This was because the region of the East, from which light is given to mortals, appears to be higher, while that of the West appears lower. In this way they veiled truth with falsehood, so that the truth itself would detract nothing from public belief.

The nature of Neptune’s portion is evident. We say that his kingdom was like that boundless command [Col. 0173B] held by Marcus Antonius, to whom [Col. 0174A] the Senate had decreed authority over the entire seacoast so that he might pursue the pirates and pacify the whole sea. In the same way, all maritime regions together with the islands fell to Neptune.

How can this be proved? Ancient histories, of course, teach it. The ancient author Euhemerus, who came from the city of Messene, collected the deeds of Jupiter and of the others who are regarded as gods. He composed a history from the sacred titles and inscriptions preserved in the most ancient temples, especially in the shrine of Triphylian Jupiter. There an inscription indicated that a golden column had been erected by Jupiter himself; upon this column he had written out his own deeds, so that it might remain to posterity as a monument of his achievements. [Col. 0174B] Ennius both translated [Col. 0175A] and followed this history.

> [Col. 0175B]  
> **[Variorum Notes to columns 175–176]**
>
> **And followed.** The books consistently read thus. The meaning is: he both approved the history and made it his own. **CELL.**  
> **Ennius both translated and followed it.** Here Lactantius reproduces Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I.42: “This line of reasoning was developed especially by Euhemerus, whom our Ennius both translated and followed.” Heumann’s correction, “Ennius translated it, whose…,” therefore collapses. **BUN.**
>
> [Col. 0175C]
>
> **Where Jupiter gives Neptune command of the sea.** Thus read very many MSS., among them the oldest and best. Thirteen manuscripts and the old Roman and Isaeus editions have *There*. It is absent from almost all the printed editions.
>
> **So that he might reign over all the islands … over all the places.** We have added the preposition *in*, absorbed by the following syllable, from four Colb. and two Brun. MSS. All MSS. except one recent Reg. read, with the editions of Betuleius and the two Leipzig editions, “were.” In place of *along*, which is the reading of almost all MSS., both old and excellent, two recent Reg., three Colbert., Cauc., Christ., and Ëm. have *otherwise*; while six recent Reg., one Colbert., Christ., Ëm., and Brun., as well as the editions of Cellarius and Walch, have *places*. Cicero similarly uses “along the sea” in *Letters to Atticus* VIII.19 and XVI.8.
>
> **Mount Olympus.** Olympus and heaven were therefore synonymous because Mount Olympus was extremely high and appeared to reach all the way to heaven. See Apuleius, *On the World*, near the end.
>
> **History.** See Ennius.
>
> [Col. 0175D]
>
> **Jupiter on Mount Olympus.** Many mountains bore this name. Which one is meant here? On Olympus in Arcadia, τραφῆναί φασιν τὸν Δία—“they said that Zeus was reared”; Pausanias, *Arcadia*, p. 268. But Olympus in Thessaly is nearer to the war with the Giants. The mountains in Asia and Cyprus are farther away from it. **BUN.**
>
> **Spent the greater part of his life.** That is, “dwelt.” The ancients used *colere* absolutely in the sense “to inhabit.” Aulus Gellius: “The Sauromatae, who dwell far beyond the river Borysthenes.” Varro: “I possess and inhabit houses.” Hence *coligo* is used for “house” in Arnobius; for so we corrected the text from the MSS. in book II: “In the inner chambers of your dwelling you maintain perpetual fires.” Hence also *colium* means the same as “house.” From this the ancients also said *domicolium* for *domicilium*. **SALMASIUS.**
>
> **With multicolored figures.** From almost all the manuscripts and several editions I have restored *multicolored*, a Ciceronian word. Three Reg., one Colb., Brun., and four recent editions have “with figures and various colors.” The *Epitome*, chapter 11, likewise has *multicolored*.  
> **With multicolored figures.** Heumann prefers “with figures and various colors”; thus Goth. The *Epitome*, chapter 11, confirms it: “so that you may cover it with that figure and, as it were, with a multicolored veil.” **BUN.**
>
> **Is represented figuratively.** We have retained this verb in the text from very many MSS. and all editions, as agreeing better with “multicolored figures” than *is fashioned*, which is found in one ancient Bonon., three Reg., one Colb., Gronovius, [Col. 0176C] Pal., Lips., and Brun.
>
> **Two Jupiters.** Rather three, indeed even more, as Plutarch says in *Opinions of the Philosophers* I.6, and as Epiphanius affirms after him. The same was true of the other gods. See Augustine, *City of God* IV.27 and VI.6. Thus Plutarch, in *Opinions of the Philosophers*, enumerates one first cause as natural, another as fabulous, and a third as civil.
>
> **Empty … they assign the name of Jupiter … to God.** See Minucius Felix, chapter 18, near the end; Arnobius I, p. 19; Origen, *Against Celsus* IV, p. 196; V, pp. 261–262; I, pp. 18, 20. Compare Lactantius IV.9; Augustine, *City of God* XIX.22; Selden, who offers better instruction in *On the Syrian Gods*, Syntagma II.1, p. 201 ff. **BUN.**
>
> **Without the companionship.** See Macrobius III.4.  
> **Without the companionship of his wife and daughter.** See Dionysius of Halicarnassus near the end of book IV. Rycquius excellently illustrates the matter from ancient coins in *On the Roman Capitol*, chapter 13, throughout pp. 126–136. **BUN.**
>
> [Col. 0176D]
>
> **What he is is apparent.** Almost all MSS. and the old Roman edition read thus. One Colbert. and Brun. have “who thus.” Two more recent Reg. MSS. and almost all the printed editions have “what he is.” Four more recent manuscripts have “who he is.” But “who he is” is elegant and an imitation of Cicero.
>
> **Jupiter, as though “helping father.”** Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II.25, says: “But Jupiter himself—that is, the helping father—whom, by altering the cases, we call Jove from helping, is called by the poets the father of gods and men; but by our ancestors he was called Best and Greatest, and indeed Best—that is, most beneficent—before Greatest, because it is certainly a greater and more pleasing thing to benefit everyone than to possess great wealth.”
>
> See also Aulus Gellius V.12, where he writes: “The ancient Latins named Jove from helping, and also called the same being by the compound title Father.” Cicero and Cato in *On Agriculture* also held this view, but they are mistaken: *Jupiter* is nothing other than *Jovis Pater*, “Father Jove,” that is, Ἰαοὺ Πατὴρ or Ἰαὼ Πατὴρ, “Jehovah the Father.” The ancients said *Joupater* for *Jovis Pater*, as *Jouglans* for *Jovis Glans*. **GALLAEUS.**
>
> On Jove, Saturn, Rhea, Juno, Hercules, Aesculapius, Apis, [Col. 0177B] Castor and Pollux, Bacchus, Venus, Ganymede, Helen, Japheth, Neptune, Vulcan, Osiris, Isis, Selene, Mars, Cupid, Minerva, Liber, Latona, Pluto or Sarapis, Priapus, Proserpina, Ceres, Eleusina, Dionysius, and so forth, see St. Cyprian, treatise *On the Vanity of Idols*, near the beginning; St. Augustine, *City of God* IV.6 and 18; St. Asterius, Sermon 10; Theodoret, book VIII *On the Martyrs*, and books III and VIII of the *Cure of the Greek Maladies*; Macrobius, Chartarius, Natalis Comes, Giraldus, and D. Fourmont in *Sanchuniathon Explained*.

Its words are as follows:

> “Where Jupiter gives Neptune command of the sea, so that he might reign over all the islands and over all the places situated along the sea.”

The things the poets say are therefore true, but veiled by a certain covering and appearance. Mount Olympus could also have supplied the poets with the figure by which they said that Jupiter received the kingdom of heaven by lot, since *Olympus* is an ambiguous name, denoting both the mountain and heaven.

That same history teaches that Jupiter lived on Olympus, saying:

> “At that time Jupiter spent the greater part of his life on Mount Olympus. People went there to him for judgment if any matters were in dispute. Likewise, if anyone had discovered something new that was useful for human life, he went there and showed it to Jupiter.”

The poets [Col. 0175B] transfer many things in this way—not in order to tell lies about those whom they worship, but to add beauty and charm to their poems through multicolored figures. Those who do not understand how or why each thing is represented figuratively assail the poets as liars and sacrilegious men.

Deceived by this error, even the philosophers, because the things related about Jupiter appeared by no means compatible with God, constructed two Jupiters, one natural and the other fabulous. They saw in part what was true—namely, that the being about whom the poets speak was a man. But in the case of that natural Jupiter they were misled by the common custom of religion, because they transferred the name of a man to God, who, as we said above, has no need of a name because he is one alone.

It cannot be denied that that Jupiter was the one born from Ops and Saturn. Empty, therefore, is the belief of those who assign the name of Jupiter to the supreme God. Some are accustomed to defend their errors with this excuse: when they have been convinced of the one God and cannot deny it, they affirm that they worship him, but that it pleases them to call him Jupiter. What could be more absurd than this? For Jupiter is not customarily worshiped without the companionship of his wife and daughter. [Col. 0176B] From this it is apparent what he is, and it is unlawful to apply that name where there is neither any Minerva nor any Juno.

Moreover, does not the proper meaning of this name express a human power rather than a divine one? Cicero interprets the names Jupiter and Juno as derived from *juvare*, “to help.” Jupiter is thus called, as it were, *Juvans pater*, “the helping father.” [Col. 0177A] That name is by no means appropriate to God, because helping is the action of a human being who contributes some assistance to another person, and conveys only a limited benefit. No one prays to God merely to help him, but to preserve him and grant him life and salvation—which is far more and far greater than helping.

And since we are speaking about a father, no father is said to help his children [Col. 0177A]

> [Col. 0177B]  
> **[Variorum Notes to columns 177–178]**
>
> **And since we are speaking about a father, no father is said [Col. 0177C] to help.** The Subiaco edition omits these words.
>
> **Through whom we exist.** Arnobius: “Do we not all owe to him the very fact that we exist, that we are called human beings?” Apuleius, in *On the World*: “It is an ancient belief, deeply rooted in the thought of all human beings, that God is regarded as the author of the origin of existence.” Compare Euripides, Manilius, and Juvenal. Manilius:
>
> > Is it right to believe that human beings were born  
> > from anything other than heaven?
>
> Juvenal:
>
> > We have derived understanding sent down from heaven’s citadel.
>
> **PRICAEUS.**
>
> **By whom we are fashioned, etc.** Irenaeus: “By whose command human beings are born.” Arnobius, book I: “Does the fact that we walk and breathe come to us from him?” Seneca, *On Benefits* IV.6; and Acts XVII.25: “since he himself gives life and breath to all.” **PRIC.** Thus the Apostle says: “In him we live and move and have our being.”
>
> [Col. 0177D]
>
> **Both from his deeds.** I have added *both* from almost all the MSS.
>
> **He circled the lands five times.** We have restored this from the old Roman edition of 1470, the Isaeus edition, and all MSS. except one recent Colb. and most editions, which read: “after he had circled the earth five times.” But Lactantius also says below, chapter 22, of Jupiter: “when he was circling the lands.”
>
> **Commands.** Almost all MSS. and the editions of Betuleius, Sparke, and Cellarius read thus. But two recent Reg. MSS. and many editions have the singular *command*; one Reg. reads *gave*; two other Reg. MSS. read, incorrectly, “divides and left.” For each person had his own portion, his own command. Cicero, *Letters to Friends* IV.1: “The world, divided among commands, burns with war.” Justin, book II: “His stepmother’s relatives, whom Philip had placed in command.” **GALLAEUS.**
>
> The *Epitome*, chapter 13, likewise reads: “after he had distributed commands among his relatives.”  
> **He divided the commands.** This is indeed his customary usage: book II, chapter 16: “to assign … commands”; book III, chapter 22: “women … to assume commands”; especially *Epitome*, chapter 13: “when he had distributed commands among his friends and relatives”; chapter 38: “he permitted women to hold commands.” **BUN.**
>
> **His lifetime having sunk away.** Thus read four Reg. MSS., two of them extremely ancient; five Colb.; Lips.; Brun.; and the editions of Fasitel, Betuleius, Tornes, Thomasius, Sparke, Isaeus, Thysius, Soubron, Gall., and the two Leipzig editions. They are supported by the editions of Egnatius, Paris 1525, Graph., Crat., Antwerp 1539, Gymnic., Fasitel, Henr., and Petri, which read *pessumata* (“having been brought to its end”). Four Reg., two Colb., one Clarom., and the Roman edition of 1470 and Azul. 1490 read *persumata*, corruptly; one Colb., corrected by a second hand, reads *perfinita* (“having been completed”); one Clarom. reads *perfuncta* (“having been discharged”); two Bologna MSS., Taxaq., Pen., and Boccaccio VII.1 read *pessume acta* (“having been badly spent”), incorrectly.
>
> For since Lactantius wishes to investigate Jupiter’s death, and since Ennius is wholly engaged there in praising Jupiter, he would have mentioned a badly spent life with little appropriateness. Lactantius therefore says that Jupiter’s lifetime had “sunk away” because it had then come to its end. One Vatican MS. has *having been completed*. The sense, therefore, is: “his lifetime having sunk away,” that is, his age descending downward or inclining toward its last stage and end. Thus in Plautus *to sink away*, and in Columella *to sink*, mean “to go down into the depths.”
>
> **Changed his life.** Two Colb., Cantabrig., and one Clarom. MS., together with the Subiaco edition, read *completed*.  
> **Changed his life.** Although Heumann, following the editions of 1472, 1476, and 1478, writes *completed*, Reimmann and the majority more correctly read *changed*. For in the *Epitome*, chapter 13, Lactantius says in the same words that Jupiter “changed his life in Crete and departed to the gods.” **BUN.**
>
> **Curetes.** There are three groups of Curetes: Aetolian, Phrygian, and Cretan. The Aetolian Curetes inhabited Chalcis. On the Curetes see Strabo, book XVIII, and Hyginus, fable 139. The latter were the Cretans themselves, according to Pliny and Solinus.
>
> [Col. 0178D]
>
> **His tomb is in Crete.** “In Crete” is absent from one Reg. MS., the editions of Thysius, Gall., and Walch, the *Epitome*, chapter 13, and Arnobius, book IV. On Jupiter’s tomb on the island of Crete, see Mela II.7 and Solinus, chapter 17. It was still being shown in the times of Theophilus of Antioch, Arnobius, book IV, and Epiphanius in the *Anchored One*.
>
> **In the town of Cnossus.** I write thus with the superior Regio-Puteanus MS., one other Reg., three Colb., one Clarom., and the Roman edition of 1468. They are supported by the less ancient Bologna MS., which has *Enossus*; the older Bologna MS. has *Cossus*; another Reg., two Colb., and the Walch edition have *Cnossus*; one Reg. has *Nessus*; two Reg., Marm., and the Roman edition of 1470 have *Gnosus*; while *Epitome*, chapter 13, four Reg., Navarr., one Colb., Vict., Gat., Brun., and the Aldine, Paris 1525, Graph., Crat., Gymnic., Fasitel, Cellarius, Thysius, Gall., editions have *Gnosus*. Both readings are accepted. Cnossus is a town of Crete; on it see Strabo, *Geography*, book X.
>
> **ZAN.** We judge that this is the correct reading, on the authority [Col. 0179B] of the ancient and excellent Regio-Puteanus MS., another Reg., Gat., Marm., one Clarom., four recent editions, and *Epitome*, chapter 13. One Reg. and three Colb. MSS. have Ζῆνα; another Colb. and one Clarom. have Ζῆνα; one Sorbon. has Ζῆμα; three Reg. and the Roman editions of 1468 and 1470, together with seven other early editions, have Ζεύς. See Callimachus, *Hymn to Jupiter*.
>
> **Δαίμονας.** In Latin:
>
> > Lifeless demons, images of the corpses of the dead,  
> > Whose miserable tombs Crete possesses as her boast.
>
> *Sibylline Oracles*, discourse 8.

when he begets or raises them. For that is too slight a term to express the magnitude of a father’s beneficence. How much more unsuitable is it for God, who is the true Father, through whom we exist and to whom we wholly belong; by whom we are fashioned, given life, and enlightened; who imparts life to us, grants salvation, and supplies manifold nourishment.

A person who thinks that he is merely helped by God does not understand the divine benefits. Therefore, the person who diminishes the power of supreme majesty by the name Jupiter is not merely ignorant but impious. [Col. 0177B]

Accordingly, if we discover from both Jupiter’s deeds and his character that he was a man and reigned upon earth, [Col. 0178A] it remains for us to investigate his death also. Ennius, in his *Sacred History*, after describing everything Jupiter did during his life, finally says:

> “Then Jupiter, after he had circled the lands five times and distributed realms of authority among all his friends and relatives, left laws to humankind, established customs, provided grain, and did many other good things. Having been honored with immortal glory and remembrance, he left everlasting memorials to his people. When his lifetime had sunk away, he changed his life in Crete and departed to the gods. His sons, the Curetes, attended to him and honored him. His tomb is in Crete, in the town of Cnossus, and Vesta is said to have founded this city. Upon his tomb is inscribed, in ancient Greek letters, ΖΑΝ ΚΡΟΝΟΥ—that is, in Latin, ‘Jupiter, son of Saturn.’”

These things are certainly handed down not by poets, but by writers on antiquity; and they are so true that they are confirmed by Sibylline verses, which are as follows:

[Col. 0178B]

[Col. 0179A]

> Δαίμονας ἀψύχους, νεκύων εἴδωλα καμόντων,  
> Ὧν Κρήτη καύχημα τάφους ἴσχει.
>
> Lifeless demons, images of the corpses of the dead,  
> Whose tombs Crete possesses as her boast.

> [Col. 0179C]  
> **[Variorum Notes to columns 179–180]**
>
> **Καύχημα τάφους—“tombs as her boast.”** The Sibylline codex, which has τάφου καύχημα, “the boast of a tomb,” must be corrected from this passage, for the meter there does not scan. Nor should ἕξει, “will possess,” be read there, but, as in our text, ἴσχει, “possesses.” **ISAEUS.** The Cauc. MS. has ἕξει.
>
> **On the Nature of the Gods.** Namely, book III; and, after Cicero, Arnobius, book III.

To be enumerated. Thus I restored the text from Betuleius’s edition and all the manuscripts except Pen., which has “numbered,” a reading also supported by the standard text of the passage in Cicero itself: “To begin with,” he says, “they number three Jupiters.” The other editions of Lactantius have “named.”

The Capitol. The citadel of Rome, in which a temple had been built for Jupiter, whence “Jupiter Capitolinus.” As to why it was actually called the Capitol, see Arnobius, Book VI.

Of such mighty elements. That is, heaven and earth. For Saturn was the son of ether and earth; Saturn was, indeed, the son of Uranus and Titaea. But Uranus is interpreted as both Heaven and Ether, just as Titaea is identical with Earth.

[Col. 0179D] He is said to have possessed the Golden Age. On Saturn’s Golden Age, see below, Book V, chapters 4 and 5. “King Saturn,” says Trogus in Justin, Book XLIII, “is said to have been so just that no one was a slave under him and no one possessed any private property; instead, everything belonged to everyone in common and without division, as though there were a single inheritance for all.” And Virgil, *Georgics* I:

> It was not even lawful to mark the land  
> Or divide the field by boundary lines.

And Ovid, *Amores* III, elegy 7:

> No boundary line marked the earth the digger worked.

Hesiod has the following concerning the same age:

> While King Saturn held dominion over heaven,  
> Mortals lived like gods in perfect peace,  
> And none among them suffered toil or misery.

Add also Martial on Saturn, Book XII, epigram LXIII. This fable was drawn from Scripture; for by [Col. 0180B] Saturn’s Golden Age one must understand the time when, before the world had yet been divided, Noah exercised a natural authority over the whole human race, as a father over his children. That Golden Age also appears to have been derived from Lamech’s prophecy concerning Noah, Genesis 5:29: “He shall comfort us concerning the works and the toil of our hands, in the earth which the Lord has cursed.” BOCHART.—Since the time of Samuel Bochart, however, these things have more correctly been referred not to sacred history but to secular history. Aurelius Victor, in *The Origin of the Roman People*, speaks thus [Col. 0180C] of Saturn: “He was the first to teach agriculture and brought savage men, accustomed to living by plunder, into an ordered way of life.” See above the passage from Justin.

That justice prevailed on earth under him. This too may conveniently be understood of Noah. For he was not merely righteous, but also a diligent herald of righteousness; and since he lived in an age when human morals were utterly corrupt, he left nothing undone to restore mankind, by word and example, to the standard of true piety. They likewise hold that Saturn was a most just king and that, to the best of his ability, he brought the people of his time from a rustic way of life to a more civilized culture; that he consequently received great honors, traveled through many regions of the world, and led everyone to justice and simplicity of character. These are Diodorus’s words in Book V of the *Library*; Aurelius Victor says the same in his book *The Origin of the Roman People*: “He brought savage men, accustomed to living by plunder, into an ordered way of life.” Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII:

> That untrained race, dispersed among the lofty hills,  
> He brought to order and gave laws.

I find something in this. Thus I restored the text from the old and best manuscripts: one Bologna manuscript, three Royal manuscripts, two Colbert manuscripts, and the Bruni manuscript. The Junius manuscript has “concerning him.” Three recent manuscripts, three Colbert manuscripts, two Clermont manuscripts, and the printed editions have “in him.”

Than which I see that something is older. Seven other manuscripts and the printed editions have “because I see”; the Christ Church and Balliol manuscripts have “since I see.”

Before (*priusquam*). Thus I restored the reading from the manuscripts. The printed editions, however, have “before” (*antequam*).

Minucius Felix. His elegant little book against the Gentiles survives. He lived in the third century.

Into Italy, etc. It is remarkable how widely separated in time Saturn the son of Uranus and the Italian Saturn were. The latter lived in the fourteenth century before the Common Era, whereas Saturn the son of Uranus lived in the twentieth century before our era. On Saturn’s [Col. 0181B] arrival in Italy, however, see Diodorus Siculus, Book IV, and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book I. On Saturn the son of Uranus, see the writers on mythology. What happened, however, was that everything done by different Saturns and different Jupiters was combined into a single account. From this arose a certain confusion that can be explained only by examining the times and places.

Those who arrived unexpectedly were said to have fallen from heaven. Thus Tibullus:

> Then I shall come suddenly, and let no one announce me beforehand,  
> But may I seem to stand before you, sent down from heaven.

] **The ill-fated [woman] holds [it]** [ἡ δύσμορος ἴσχει]. Cicero, in *On the Nature of the Gods*, when he said that theologians enumerated three Jupiters, stated that the third was the Cretan Jupiter, the son of Saturn, whose tomb is shown on that island. How, then, can a god be alive in one place and dead in another, have a temple in one place and a tomb in another? Let the Romans therefore understand that their Capitol—that is, the supreme seat of their public religions—is nothing other than an empty monument.

Let us now come to his father, who reigned before him and who perhaps possessed more of what might be considered divine, since he is said to have been born from the union of such mighty elements. Let us see what there was in him worthy of a god. First, there is the claim that he possessed the Golden Age, and that justice prevailed on earth under him. I find something in this [Col. 0179B] that was absent from his son. For what is so fitting for a god as a just government and a pious age? But when I reflect that he was born in the same manner, I cannot [Col. 0180A] regard as the supreme God one than whom I see that something is older—namely, heaven and earth. But I am seeking a God beyond whom there is absolutely nothing, one who is the source and origin of all things. This must be the one who established heaven itself and founded the earth. But if Saturn was born from these, as is supposed, how can he be the primal God when he owes his origin to others? Or who governed the world before Saturn was begotten?

But this, as I said shortly before, is a poetic fabrication. For it could not happen that insensible elements, separated by so great a distance, should unite and beget a son; nor could one born from them fail above all to resemble his parents, yet bear a form his parents did not possess.

[Col. 0180B] Let us therefore inquire what truth lies concealed beneath this figure. Minucius Felix, in the book entitled *Octavius*, argued as follows:

> “Saturn, after he had been driven out by his son and had come to Italy, was called the son of Heaven because we are accustomed to say that those whose excellence we admire, or who arrive unexpectedly, [Col. 0181A] have fallen from heaven; and to call them sons of earth when, because they were born of unknown parents, we call them earth-born.”

[Col. 0181A] [Note: [Col. 0181C] [Various Editors’ Notes on columns 181–182]

Those who arrived suddenly. More recent editors commonly read *repentino*, “by a sudden event,” as it were. But the Leipzig manuscripts and the Aldine and older Aldine, Roman, and Venetian editions have *repentine*, an adverbial form that has still not received much notice. BUNEMANN.

Suddenly. The English, Leipzig, third Gothic, Utrecht, and Caucasus manuscripts, and the Basel 1556, Tournes, Thomas, and subsequent editions, have *repentino*, with *o* as the fourth vowel. Compare the expression in Plautus, *Pseudolus* I.1: “I arose suddenly; I died suddenly”; and Cicero, *For Quinctius*, chapter 4: “and he dies suddenly.” BUNEMANN.

To have fallen from heaven. These words are amply illustrated by the commentators on Minucius, chapter 22. Savaron on Sidonius VI, Epistle 10, p. 378: “It will be regarded as though it had fallen from the pole of heaven.” BUNEMANN.

Born of unknown parents, we call them sons of earth. Tertullian says the same in the *Apology*, as does the author of *The Origin of the Roman People*: “Saturn is believed to have been the first to come to Italy. Such, however, was the simplicity of ancient people that, because they did not know the origins of strangers, they not only themselves believed them to have been born of heaven and earth but also asserted this to posterity.” Aurelius Victor has the same in *The Origin of the Roman People*. [Col. 0181D] For they believed that everything had arisen from heaven and sea. Thus the origin of unknown persons was referred to heaven or the sea, so that they were believed to be sons of Heaven or Neptune. Servius on Virgil. The scholiast on Apollonius writes that monstrous beings were regarded as sons of Earth, and savage ones as sons of Neptune. Naevius in Priscian: “The Titans, sons of Earth.” And Orpheus in the *Hymns*: “Born of obscure and unknown parents.” The same is found in Rhodiginus, *Ancient Readings* II.28, and Politian, *Miscellanies*, chapter 18. WOUWER.

Gave names to heaven and earth. The confusion among the Latins arose because they translated Οὐρανός (*Ouranos*) and Τιταία (*Titaia*), which were patronymic names, as names of actual things. But shortly afterward, in this very chapter, Lactantius reports something more plausible concerning Uranus.

Atlas. He was king of Mauretania and is said to have been transformed into the mountain bearing his name. For his fable, see Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IV.

Inachus. He was the first king of the Argives and is believed to have lived in the nineteenth century before the Common Era. He belonged to [Col. 0182B] the race of the Titans and was related to Saturn and Jupiter. He is said either to have given his name to a river in the Peloponnese or to have been cast into it by Jupiter’s contrivances.

The Aegean. Named after Aegeus, the father of Theseus, who hurled himself into the sea because his son’s death had falsely been reported to him. This happened in the thirteenth century before the Common Era. See Solinus, chapter 15.

The Icarian. Named after Icarus, son of Daedalus; for his fable, see Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VIII. Solinus, following Varro, reports that Icarus the Cretan perished by shipwreck in this sea, and that the place received its name from the man’s death. Thus history [Col. 0182C] gave rise to the fable; but now we are compelled to derive history from the fable. See Solinus, chapter 21.

The Hellespontine. Eighteen manuscripts, together with the Roman 1470, Soubron, and Tournes editions, have “the Hellespont.” Perhaps one should read “Hellespontian,” as above “Hellespontian” at chapter 6. The Hellespontine Sea, or Hellespont, is a narrow strait between the Aegean Sea and the Propontis, separating Asia from Europe by no more than seven stadia. It takes its name from Helle, daughter of Athamas, or from Ἕλλην (*Hellēn*), whence Ἕλληνες (*Hellēnes*), one of the names for the Greeks.

Aventinus. See Livy, Book I.

Tiberinus. The more widespread account is that Tiberinus, the son of Capetus, the tenth king of Alba and a notorious robber, gave his name to the river formerly called the Albula when he drowned while crossing the Tiber.

Who had begotten the most powerful kings. Reimmann: “had been assigned to those whom we read to have been the most powerful kings”; “who had begotten the most powerful kings.” BUNEMANN.

[Col. 0182D]

Trismegistus. See him in *Poimandres*, chapter 10.

That this was done. Thus we restored the text from the Royal manuscripts, six Colbert manuscripts, the Leipzig, Emmeram, Gothic, two Clermont, and two Bruni manuscripts. Our reading is confirmed by the words immediately following: “For Saturn did not do THIS, but Jupiter DID it.” Most printed editions have “that this was said.”

Ennius. Only fragments of his works survive.

Pan leads him onto the mountain. This passage is extremely obscure, and both the manuscripts and the editors display extraordinary variation. From among them I chose this reading, as it has been approved by the judgment of learned men and by the greater number and authority of the manuscripts and editors: namely, many Vatican manuscripts, two Bologna manuscripts, two Royal manuscripts, one Sorbonne manuscript, and the Leipzig, Taxae, Palatine, Cambridge, and Christ Church manuscripts; the 1490 Venetian, Soubron, Tournes 1579, Geneva 1613, and Isaeus editions; and also seven other Royal manuscripts, including the excellent Puteanus, four Colbert manuscripts, and the Gatianus, Marmoutier, one Clermont, and Bruni manuscripts, as well as the Roman editions of 1468 and 1470 and Cellarius, in which *Paneum* is read. Certain Vatican manuscripts and Pen. [Col. 0183B] have *Panaeum*. The oldest Royal manuscript has *Pavenium*; the Emmeram manuscript, *Paneam*; several Vatican manuscripts and eight editions, *Pantum*; one Colbert manuscript, *Pancum*; another Colbert manuscript and the Navarre and Victor manuscripts, *Paucum*; one Clermont manuscript, *Panen*; and the Cratander and Antwerp 1539 editions and Boccaccio, Book III, *Pangaeum*, which is a lofty mountain of Thrace on the Macedonian frontier, overlooking the city of Philippi.—*Paneum*. Also written as one word in the Reimmann, Venice 1471, both 1478, 1497, and Rostock editions: *Paneum*. The first Leipzig, Palatine, Bologna, Taxae, and many Vatican manuscripts divide the words: *Pan eum*, “Pan him”; some of the same read: “Pan leads him onto the mountain of Crete.” BUNEMANN.]

These words are indeed plausible, but they are nevertheless untrue, because it is established that he was regarded in this way even while he was reigning. Minucius could also have argued thus: that Saturn, since he was a most powerful king, gave the names of his parents to heaven and earth in order to preserve their memory, although these had previously been called by other names. We know that names were imposed upon mountains and rivers in the same way. For when the poets speak of the offspring of Atlas or of the river Inachus, they do not chiefly mean that human beings could be born from insensible things; rather, they plainly signify those who were born from the people who, either while alive or after death, gave their names to mountains or rivers. [Col. 0181B] For this practice was customary among the ancients, especially the Greeks. Thus we have learned that seas took their names [Col. 0182A] from those who fell into them, such as the Aegean, the Icarian, and the Hellespontine; and in Latium, Aventinus gave his name to the mountain in which he was buried, while Tiberinus, or Tiber, gave his to the river in which he drowned.

It should therefore cause no surprise if the names of those who had begotten the most powerful kings were assigned to heaven and earth. It is thus evident that he was not born from heaven—which is impossible—but from a man whose name was Uranus. Trismegistus is authority for the truth of this. For when he said that very few men had existed in whom perfect learning was found, he named among them his relatives Uranus, Saturn, and Mercury. Because Minucius did not know these facts, he diverted the history in another direction. I have shown how he could have argued; now I shall say how, where, and by whom this was done. For Saturn did not do this, [Col. 0182B] but Jupiter did. In the *Sacred History*, Ennius relates the following:

> “Then Pan leads him onto the mountain called [Col. 0183A] the Pillar of Heaven.”

[Col. 0183A] [Note: [Col. 0183B] [Various Editors’ Notes on columns 183–184]

The Pillar of Heaven. The learned men Peter Chacón, Isaeus, Baluze, Francius, Cellarius, and others judge that *coeli stela* must unquestionably be read. The Victor manuscript does not disagree, for its first hand has *stelia*, from στήλη (*stēlē*, “pillar”). A *stela* [Col. 0183C] is a column. Martianus Capella, Book II: “Athanasia, examining the markings of the books, ordered them to be inscribed upon certain projecting rocks and placed within the hidden recesses of a cave in the Egyptian manner; and, calling those rocks *stelae*, she said that they contained the genealogies of the gods.” He therefore means that, because of its height, this mountain was called the Pillar of Heaven—that is, a column—as though it appeared to touch and support the sky. Ten Royal, six Colbert, and the Sorbonne, Navarre, Victor, Gatianus, Marmoutier, two Clermont, and Bruni manuscripts, together with the printed editions, have *stella*, “star.”

Which we now call. Many printed editions have “which is called οὐρανός (*ouranos*, ‘heaven’)”; an older Bologna manuscript has simply “which is called,” without οὐρανός. The scholia have the character of a grammarian; but at that time the foremost Roman nobles also cultivated grammar. BARTHIUS.

An eagle flew to him as an omen, etc. Among the ancients, the eagle was particularly suited to auguries. FESTUS.—On this matter see Suetonius’s *Octavian Augustus*, where the people more than once took an eagle circling around him as a favorable omen.

Under his protection. The meaning of “protection” was explained above.

Because he was. For one cannot say of God that he “was”; he is “He Who Is” (Exodus 3), since he remains constant in himself and is always the same.

Whom he killed. Because he is said to have devoured them, or rather to have thrust them into prison.

Whose genitals he is said to have cut off. Thus we restored the text from all the manuscripts except one Colbert manuscript, which has “from whom,” as do the printed editions. Cut off. Some refer this to Jupiter, others to Saturn. After he ascended it, he gazed widely over the lands, and there upon that mountain he established an altar to Heaven. Jupiter was the first to sacrifice upon that altar. In that place he looked up into what we now call heaven, and gave the name Heaven, after his grandfather, to that which was above the world and was called Ether. Praying to what is called Ether, Jupiter first named it Heaven; and the victim that he consecrated there he burned whole.

Nor is Jupiter found to have sacrificed only there. Caesar also, in his commentary on Aratus, reports that Aglaosthenes says that, when Jupiter was setting out from the island of Naxos against the Titans and was offering sacrifice on the shore, an eagle flew to him as an omen; after his victory, he accepted it as a favorable sign and placed it under his protection. The *Sacred History* [Col. 0183B]—that is, that of Ennius—also testifies that the eagle had previously settled [Col. 0184A] upon his head and foretold his kingship. To whom, then, could Jupiter have sacrificed except to his grandfather Heaven, whom Euhemerus says died in Oceania and was buried in the town of Aulacia?

## CHAPTER XII  
### That the Stoics Transfer the Poets’ Fictions into a Philosophical System

Since we have disclosed the poets’ mysteries and discovered Saturn’s parents, let us return to his virtues and deeds. He was just in his kingship. First, from this very fact he is already not God, because he “was” (and so belongs to the past); second, because he was not even just, but impious—not only toward the sons whom he killed, but also toward his father, whose genitals he is said to have cut off, [Col. 0184B] something that perhaps truly occurred. But [Col. 0185A] with reference to the element called heaven, people reject the entire fable as an utterly absurd invention. The Stoics, however, as is their custom, attempt to [Col. 0185A] [Note: [Col. 0185C] [Various Editors’ Notes on columns 185–186]

A physical explanation. See chapter 11, the note there, and Tertullian, *Against Marcion* I.13. BUNEMANN.

Needed. One Colbert manuscript and the Bruni manuscript have “needs,” not without merit.

They regard Vesta. The ancients had two Vestas. One was Saturn’s mother, who was also understood as the earth and was called the Mother of the Gods and the Great Mother. The other was Saturn’s daughter. When Jupiter had defeated the Titans, he gave this latter Vesta her choice, and she chose virginity. This [Col. 0185D] latter Vesta is the subject of the following verses of Ovid, from *Fasti* VI. The rites of this Vesta were among the most ancient at Rome; from her derives the Vestal Virgins’ guardianship and care of the eternal fire.

Who is indeed regarded as fire. Vulcan is thought to have been the first to reveal the use of fire to mortals. In remembrance of this benefit, on a solemn day which the Athenians called the *Lampadōn*, they lit torches at Vesta’s hearth and ran through the city. BETULEIUS.

The poets did not cut him off. We corrected “him” from the manuscripts and the Roman, Soubron, Gymnicus, Fasitel, Tournes, two recent, and Leipzig editions. The Thysius and French editions incorrectly have “her.”

Without the fiery heat of the Sun, etc. On the necessity of the Sun for the generation of all things, see Plato in Book VI of the *Republic* and others.

The course and revolution, etc. Because Saturn, on account of his antiquity, is a kind of symbol of time, on which see Heraclides of Pontus’s *Allegories*, as well as Fulgentius, Macrobius, and Saint Augustine, *City of God* XVII.19. Κρόνος (*Kronos*). On this see Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.22 and 29.—Hence, according to Accius, Saturn’s rites were called the *Kronia*. Compare Savaron on Sidonius, Poem 15, p. 149; Huet, *Demonstratio Evangelica*, p. 257. BUNEMANN.

Saturn, because he is sated. Huet, in the passage cited, p. 290, together with others, derived the name from *latuit*, “he lay hidden.” A. Acoluthus maintains, with the greatest truth, that it is derived from the Armenian or Egyptian *SATOR*, with an appended *N*, so that *Satorn* means “great cutter.” For he is regarded as the inventor of the reaping sickle, which cut down Heaven’s genitals—that is, the grasses, plants, flowers, and crops produced by Heaven’s favor. See Acoluthus’s letter to B. Abbot Molanus of Lucca in Leibniz’s *Collection of Etymologies*, p. 162. BUNEMANN.

To be born from heaven. The Gothic manuscript, together with the Leipzig and Rostock witnesses and the Venice [Col. 0186D] editions of 1471 and 1472, supports “from heaven.” But Heumann says it is readily apparent that “by heaven” ought to be written instead. transfer it to a physical explanation. Cicero, discussing their opinion in *On the Nature of the Gods* II.24, presented it as follows:

> “They held,” he says, “that the celestial, highest, and ethereal nature—that is, the fiery nature—which generated all things by itself, lacked that part of the body which requires union with another for procreation. The same could also have been ascribed to Vulcan, who is indeed regarded as fire; yet the poets did not castrate him. It could also have been ascribed to the Sun, in whom resides the nature and cause of generation; for without the Sun’s fiery heat nothing can either be born or grow. Thus no other element has a greater need of generative organs than heat, by whose warmth all things are conceived, born, and sustained.

Finally, even if matters are as they maintain, why should we suppose that Heaven’s genitals were cut off, rather than that he was born entirely without them? For if he generates by himself, he certainly had no need of genitals [Col. 0186A] when he begot Saturn himself. But if he possessed them and his son cut them off, the origin of things and all nature would have perished.

Moreover, do they not deprive Saturn himself not only of divine perception but even of human perception when they assert that he is called Saturn because he encompasses the course and revolution of spaces and times, and that in Greek he bears a name signifying this very thing? For he is called Κρόνος (*Kronos*), which is the same as χρόνος (*chronos*), that is, a span of time. But he is called Saturn because he is sated with years.

These are Cicero’s words as he expounds the Stoics’ opinion (*On the Nature of the Gods* II.64):

> “Anyone can very easily understand how empty this opinion is. For if Saturn is the son of Heaven, how could either Time be born from Heaven, or Heaven be castrated by Time, or Time afterward be stripped of his dominion by his son Jupiter? [Col. 0186B] Or how was Jupiter born from Time? Or with what years can eternity, which has no end, be sated?”

Does anyone think that one who was driven out, who fled, who hid, is a god? No one is so foolish. For one who flees or hides must necessarily fear violence and death. Orpheus, who lived later than he did, plainly records that Saturn reigned on earth and among human beings:

> Πρώτιστος μὲν ἄνασσεν ἐπιχθονίων Κρόνος ἀνδρῶν,  
> Ἐκ δὲ Κρόνου γένετ’ αὐτὸς ἄναξ, μέγας, εὐρύοπα Ζεύς.
>
> “First indeed Saturn ruled over earth-dwelling men;  
> And from Saturn was born the king himself, great, far-seeing Zeus.”

Likewise our own Maro:

> Golden Saturn lived this life upon the earth;

and elsewhere:

> And golden—as they relate—were the  
> Ages beneath that king: thus he ruled the peoples in tranquil peace.

[Col. 0189B] Above, the poet did not say that he lived his life in heaven, nor below that he ruled the gods above in peace. From this it is evident that he was an earthly king, as the poet declares still more plainly elsewhere:

> He will establish golden  
> Ages—he who once again in Latium, throughout the fields  
> Formerly ruled by Saturn....

Ennius, indeed, in his *Euhemerus* says that Saturn did not reign first, but his father Uranus. “In the beginning,” he says, “Caelus first held supreme power upon the earth; he established and secured that kingdom together with his brothers.” There is no great disagreement, since even the greatest authorities are uncertain concerning the son and the father. Both, however, may be true: Uranus may first have begun to rise [Col. 0189C] above the others in power and to hold leadership, though not kingship; afterward Saturn may have acquired greater resources for himself and assumed the title of king. [Col. 0190A]

## CHAPTER XIV. What the Sacred History of Euhemerus and Ennius Teaches Concerning the Gods

Now, since the *Sacred History* differs somewhat from the accounts we have related, let us set forth what is contained in truthful records, lest we appear to follow and approve the absurdities of the poets in accusing the religions. These are the words of Ennius:

> “After this Saturn took Ops as his wife. Titan, who was the elder by birth, demanded that he himself should reign. Then Vesta, their mother, and their sisters Ceres and Ops advised Saturn not to yield the kingdom to his brother. Then Titan, who was inferior in appearance to Saturn, both for that reason and because he saw that his mother and his sisters [Col. 0190B] were exerting themselves to have Saturn reign, yielded to him and allowed him to reign. And so he made an agreement with Saturn that, if any male child should be born to him, he was not to rear it. He did this so that the kingdom might return to his own sons. Then, when Saturn’s first son was born, they killed him. Afterward twins were born, Jupiter and Juno. They then presented Juno to Saturn’s sight, but secretly concealed Jupiter and gave him to Vesta to be reared, keeping him hidden from Saturn. Likewise Ops bore Neptune without Saturn’s knowledge and secretly concealed him. In the same manner, at her third delivery Ops bore twins, Pluto and Glauca. Pluto in Latin is Dis Pater; others call him Orcus. Then they showed Saturn his daughter Glauca, but concealed and [Col. 0190C] hid his son Pluto. Afterward the little Glauca died.”

*So that they even called them gods, whether because of*, etc. The origin of consecration is of this kind. In the most ancient times it was customary for the highest honors to be decreed after death to the founders of cities or to others who had deserved well of public affairs and the common life; these were called ἡρωικαὶ τιμαί (*hērōikai timai*, “heroic honors”). Flattery, and afterward superstition, invented θεοποιΐα (*theopoiia*, “deification”), and those to whom only heroic honors had previously been decreed gradually began to be regarded as gods; see Plutarch, *On the Excellent Deeds of Women*. Besides Lactantius in this passage, Athenagoras, Eusebius, Theodoret, Minucius Felix, and others also expressly teach that this was the origin of consecration. Hence the phrases so full of flattery—“to enroll among the gods,” “to refer to the gods,” ἀποθεοῦν (*apotheoun*, “to deify”), or θεὸν ποιεῖν (*theon poiein*, “to make a god”)—in which the writings of the ancients abound. In this flattery the Athenians surpassed all other mortals, as is [Col. 0192D] known to everyone who has tasted even lightly of their history. KIRCHMANN.

*In flattery.* See St. Augustine, *The City of God*, book II, chapter 15.

*So that they might obtain some consolation from contemplating the images.* Cyprian, in the treatise *That Idols Are Not Gods*: “That those whom the populace worships are not gods is known from this fact. They were once kings who, because of the memory of their kingship, began afterward to be worshiped among their own people even in death. Hence temples were established for them; hence images were fashioned to preserve through a likeness the features of the dead. For they also sacrificed victims and celebrated feast days in their honor. Hence those observances became sacred rites for posterity which had originally been adopted as consolations.” So too among pagan authors. Servius on *Georgics* I, concerning Silvanus. Seneca, Letter 40, speaking of images: “They alleviate longing for the absent with a false and empty consolation.” See Tacitus, *Annals* XII, etc. From PRICAEUS.]

The lineage and relationship of Jupiter and his brothers has been transmitted to us in this manner from the sacred record. Likewise, a little later he introduces the following:

> “Then Titan, after he learned that sons had been born to Saturn and secretly reared, brought away with him his own sons, who are called Titans, seized his brother Saturn and Ops, enclosed them with a wall, and set a guard over them.”

How true this history is, the Erythraean Sibyl teaches by saying nearly the same thing, except that she differs in a few matters irrelevant to the issue. Jupiter is therefore absolved of the charge of the supreme crime of which he is said to have been guilty in binding his father in fetters. For it was Titan, his paternal uncle, who did this, because Saturn had reared male children contrary to the agreement and his sworn oath. The remainder of the history is connected as follows: [Col. 0191B] when the adult Jupiter heard that his father and mother had been surrounded by guards and cast into chains, he came with a great multitude of Cretans, defeated Titan and his sons in battle, released his parents from their chains, restored the kingdom to his father, and then returned to Crete. After this, then, Saturn received an oracle warning him to beware lest his son drive him from the kingdom. For the purpose of nullifying the oracle and escaping the danger, Saturn plotted against Jupiter in order to kill him. Jupiter, having discovered [Col. 0192A] the plot, reclaimed the kingdom for himself and put Saturn to flight. Saturn, after being driven about through every land while armed men whom Jupiter had sent to seize or kill him pursued him, barely found in Italy a place where he could hide.

## CHAPTER XV. How They Came to Be Called Gods Although They Were Human Beings

Since it is established from these facts that they were human beings, it is not obscure how they began to be called gods. For if there were no kings before Saturn or Uranus, because human beings were few and lived a rustic life without any ruler, there is no doubt that in those times people began to exalt the king himself and his entire family with the highest praises and unprecedented honors, so that they even called them gods—whether because of wonder at their excellence (those still uncultivated and simple people truly believed this), or, as commonly happens, in flattery of present power, or because of the benefits by which they had been brought to civilized life. Then the kings themselves, because they had been dear to those whose lives they had ordered, left behind after death a great longing for themselves. And so people fashioned images of them, so that they might obtain some consolation from contemplating their likenesses; and, advancing further [Col. 0193A] through love of their benefaction, [Col. 0193A]

[Note: [Col. 0193B] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 193–194]

*Through love of their benefaction.* Thus one ancient Bologna manuscript and ten printed editions. *Benefaction* is absent from twenty-five manuscripts and from the old Roman, Betuleius, de Tournes, and Isaeus editions.

*Raise.* We amend it thus from Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book II, chapter 62, and from all our manuscripts and the de Tournes edition. The printed editions have the singular “might raise.”

*And elsewhere: “And in most states.”* The Isaeus, Gallaeus, and Spark editions had “And indeed,” but the latter word is absent from the Royal manuscripts, one Colbert manuscript, two *Brun.* manuscripts, and from Cicero himself, book III of *On the Nature of the Gods*, chapter 50. Five Colbert manuscripts, two Clermont manuscripts, the Christ. manuscript, and almost all the editions have, still more absurdly, “And elsewhere, and elsewhere in most states,” although all the following words of Cicero were taken only from the one passage we have indicated. “And” seems sufficiently useless, but Lactantius retained it without necessity because it was Cicero’s, just as he retained “Tullian, however” from the preceding passage, from book II, chapter 24. “Elsewhere” was repeated to no purpose from what precedes.

[Col. 0193C]
