*Every best man.* That is, every bravest man, as follows: “of brave men.” Compare the note on book III, chapter 17. BUNEMANN.

*It was clearly in this manner that the Romans consecrated their Caesars*, etc. After Romulus, I find no one upon whom this honor was conferred so long as the republic remained free. But after everything began to be conferred upon the Caesars, there was then a return to that ancient custom, and many emperors were enrolled among the gods. See their catalogue in Onofrio Panvinio, book II of the *Fasti*. Julius Caesar was the first to receive this honor, from Augustus. Manilius:

> Now he himself makes gods, and sends to the stars a divinity  
> Greater still, and heaven grows beneath Augustus’ rule.

Consecration was customarily decreed by the Senate, in whose hands authority over this matter lay, unless the emperors reigned as tyrants. On this subject see St. Athanasius, *Against the Pagans*. Hence Aelius Spartianus in the *Life of Hadrian*: “The Senate wished his acts to be annulled; nor was he called *Divus* unless Antoninus requested it.” Julius Capitolinus mentions this senatorial decree several times, as in the *Life of Antoninus Pius*: “He was with delight called *Divus* by the Senate, everyone eagerly assenting”; and in the *Life of Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher*: “Then, when he thanked the Senate because it had consecrated his brother”; and in the *Life of Pertinax*: “Through the Senate and the people, Pertinax was enrolled among the gods.” Herodian describes the rite of consecration fully in book IV. KIRCHMANN.—On this apotheosis of the Caesars, see Theophilus *To Autolycus*, discourse 1. And the Moors consecrated their kings. Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter XXIV: “Each province and city has its own god: Syria has Astarte, Arabia Dusares, Noricum Belenus, Africa Caelestis, and Mauretania its own petty kings.” Cyprian, *On the Vanity of the Nations*: “The Moors openly worship their kings and cover the practice with no disguise.” VOSSIUS.

*Began.* Thus I have restored it from the manuscripts. The editions, however, have an alternative form of “began.”

[Col. 0194B]

*Individual peoples.* Tertullian says this; see the preceding note. Others are provincial gods, who appear in Alexander of Naples, book VI, chapter 4. On this subject one should also consult authors who wrote about the gods of the nations, such as Lilius Giraldus and Vossius.

*The Egyptians, Isis.* On Isis and her rites, see chapter 21 of this book.

*The Moors, Juba.* Juba seems to have been worshiped by the Moors above others, since his name is found expressly stated by authors; or perhaps “Juba” was a name common to the kings of the Moors, like “Pharaoh” or “Ptolemy” in Egypt. On Juba’s enrollment among the gods, see Tertullian’s *Apology*.—*The Moors, Juba.* Cellarius, on Eutropius 6.18.2 and Minucius, chapter 22, noted that Juba was king of the Numidians, not the Moors, understanding this with reference to Juba’s own time. But Gronovius defends Minucius because in Minucius’s time Numidia was included within Mauretania Caesariensis; on this basis Lactantius here, Eutropius, Sextus Rufus, Isidore, [Col. 0194C] and others can also be defended. Davies, on Minucius, p. 137, thinks that the Moors properly so called had kings bearing the name Juba. Cellarius himself, however, on Eutropius, book V, at the end, showed that Latin writers customarily called Mauretanians Numidians, and that this is established concerning Juba from the second civil war. BUNEMANN.

*Cabirus.* Thus most manuscripts and editions. The Roman edition of 1468 has *Cabirim*; Betuleius and de Tournes 1579, *Cabyrium*; two Royal manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470, *Gabyrum*; one Royal manuscript, *Gabirium*; another Royal manuscript and the Marm. manuscript, *Gabirum*; one Royal manuscript, *Sabrium*; another Royal manuscript, the Victorinus, Nav., one Colbert manuscript, and the *Brun.* manuscript, *Scabrum*. On the Cabiri, see Pausanias. *Uranus.* In the oldest Royal manuscript, as also in another recent Royal manuscript in the first hand, *Uranius*.

*Faunus.* He was the third king of the Latins after Janus. According to Virgil he was the son of Picus and father of the Fauns and Latins. He lived, it is believed, 520 years before the founding of Rome. The Romans worshiped him on the Nones of December; see Horace, book III, Ode 18. He will be discussed again below in chapter 22.

*The Sabines, Sancus.* I find this name written in various ways. Some Vatican manuscripts of Lactantius, one ancient Bologna manuscript, the Victorinus, Nav., Marm., and three Royal manuscripts—one of them the oldest—as well as the Gymnicus, Henricus, Petri, Fasit., Soubr., de Tournes, Thomas., Thysius, Gallaeus, and two Leipzig editions have *Sancum*, very correctly. This reading is approved by Joseph Scaliger in his notes on Varro’s *On the Latin Language*. The *Brun.* manuscript has *Saucum* for *Sancum*, *u* for *n*; one Sorbonne and one Clermont manuscript have *Santum*; the Royal-Puteanus and four other Royal manuscripts, five Colbert manuscripts, the Gat., and Ems manuscripts have *Sanctum*, not badly. For Ovid, *Fasti* VI, calls him *Sanctus*. Augustine, *The City of God* XVIII.19, says: “The Sabines also enrolled their first king Sancus—or, as some call him, Sanctus—among the gods.” The Cambridge manuscript, one Clermont manuscript, and the Roman edition of 1468 have *Xanct.*; one Royal manuscript, one recent Bologna manuscript, and the Roman edition of 1470, *Xantum*; one Royal manuscript and the Venetian edition of 1490, *Sabum*; the Paris edition of 1525, the Aldine, Cratander, Grapheus, and Antwerp 1539 editions, *Sangum*; one Colbert manuscript, *Fautum*; one Leipzig manuscript, *Ratum*; the Ultr. manuscript, *Annaeum*. The deity who is Sancus among the Sabines is Hercules among the Greeks and Deus [Col. 0195B] Fidius among the Latins. See Varro, book IV of *On the Latin Language*, chapter 10. Festus: “A sacrifice is performed before departure to Hercules or Sancus, who is of course the same god.” He was also called Semo, as in Ovid, *Fasti* VI.213. In an ancient inscription in Gruter, p. 96, and in the one given by Fulvius Ursinus on Caesar’s *Gallic War*:

> SACRED TO SANCTUS SANCUS SEMO, THE GOD FIDIUS.

Sancus was one of the gods whom Martianus Capella enumerates in the sixteen orders of the heavens. On Sancus see [Col. 0195C] also Gregorius Giraldus, book I of the *History of the Gods*.]

they began to venerate the memory of the dead, so that they might both appear to repay gratitude to those who had deserved well and entice their successors toward the desire to govern well. Cicero teaches this in *On the Nature of the Gods* (II.14), saying:

> “Human life and common custom adopted the practice of raising men who excelled in benefactions to heaven by fame and willing consent. Hence Hercules, hence Castor, hence Pollux, hence Aesculapius, hence Liber.”

And elsewhere:

> “And in most states it can be understood that, for the purpose of sharpening virtue—or so that every best man among the brave might more willingly undergo danger for the sake of the commonwealth—his memory was consecrated [Col. 0194A] with the honor of the immortal gods.”

It was clearly in this manner that the Romans consecrated their Caesars, and the Moors their kings. Thus religions gradually began to exist, when those first people who had known them imbued their own children and grandchildren, and then all their descendants, with that rite. Yet these supreme kings, because of the renown of their names, were worshiped in every province.

Individually, however, each people worshiped with the highest veneration the founders of its own nation or city—whether men distinguished for courage or women remarkable for chastity—such as the Egyptians Isis, the Moors Juba, the Macedonians Cabirus, the Carthaginians Uranus, the Latins Faunus, the Sabines Sancus, [Col. 0195A] and the Romans Quirinus. [Col. 0195A]

[Note: [Col. 0195C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 195–196]

*Quirinus.* What is said about Quirinus is well known; concerning him, see Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, and Plutarch.

*Athens, Minerva.* The city of Athens received its name from her. Concerning her, therefore, see Pausanias in the *Attica*, Plutarch in the *Themistocles*, Isocrates in the *Panathenaicus*, and St. Augustine, *The City of God* XVIII.9.

*Samos, Juno.* Samos is an island in the Ionian Sea, once sacred to Juno, where she had a temple founded by the Argonauts. Concerning it, Virgil, *Aeneid* I:

> Which alone Juno is said to have cherished  
> More than all lands, even with Samos set second.

She will be discussed again below in chapter 17.

*Paphos, Venus.* Thus Virgil, *Aeneid* I:

> She herself, borne aloft, goes to Paphos and gladly revisits  
> Her own abodes, where she has a temple, and a hundred altars glow  
> With Sabaean incense.

[Col. 0195D]

*Lemnos, Vulcan.* See the story in Homer, *Iliad* I, where it is related that Vulcan was hurled down upon the island of Lemnos.

*Naxos, Liber.* Naxos is one of the Cyclades islands, sacred to Liber or Bacchus, formerly called Dionysia, where the vines are excellent and consequently the wine is noble.

*Delphi, Apollo.* On the evidence of seventeen editions, *Delphi* must be read in the nominative case, as the preceding names of cities require. The Royal-Puteanus and four other Royal manuscripts, five Colbert manuscripts, one Sorbonne manuscript, two Clermont manuscripts, the Gat. and Marm. manuscripts in the second hand, and the old Roman editions of 1468 and 1470 have *Delphos*, an error apparently arising from the preceding nominatives ending in *-os*. The other manuscripts have *Delos*. In Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.12:

> The Delian prophet inspires and discloses the future.

*Thus among peoples*, etc. Lilius Gregorius Giraldus collected these local gods in *Syntagma* I.

*And because they could find no other honors to confer upon those deprived of life.* Thus we have restored the text from almost all the manuscripts and from the Paris edition [Col. 0196B] of 1525, Cratander, Grapheus, and Gymnicus. One Colbert manuscript, the *Brun.* manuscript, and eight editions have: “and whatever other honors they might confer upon those deprived of life.” The word “whatever” is absent from the Leipzig, Palatine, and one Colbert manuscript.

*Now pour libations from the bowls*, etc. Virgil, *Aeneid* VII.133.

*These sacred rites of mine.* Thus I restore the text from almost all the manuscripts. So it is also found in several ancient Virgilian manuscripts and in some commonly received texts. Two Colbert manuscripts, one Clermont manuscript in the first hand, and the editions have “these my sacred rites,” but wrongly.

[Col. 0196C]

*Panegyrics.* For a long time now, laudatory speeches have deserved no trust.

*Fickleness.* Lactantius censures the fickleness of the Greeks several times: book I, chapter 18; book III, chapter 14; and it is a common charge against them. See Ludovicus Vives on Augustine, *The City of God* I.4 and II.14; Abramus on Cicero, *For Ligarius*, chapter 4, whom many copy; and Cortius on Sallust, *Catiline* VIII.2, p. 55. BUNEMANN.

*Ἑλλὰς δὴ*, etc. The *Sibylline Oracles*, discourse 3, read differently. Besides omitting the second verse, which reads:

> Θνητοῖς, οἷς οὐκ ἔστι φυγεῖν θανάτοιο τελευτήν;
>
> “To mortals, for whom there is no escape from death’s end?”

they have πορίζεις (*porizeis*, “provide”) where the third verse here has ἀνατίθης (*anatithēs*, “dedicate”), as does the distinguished manuscript of the celebrated Puteanus in the Royal Library. The printed text there has:

> Τίς τοι πλάνην βάλεν ἐν νῷ,  
> Ὥστε σε τάδε ποιεῖν μεγαλοῖο θεοῖο προσώπου;
>
> “Who cast error into your mind,  
> So that you do these things, turning from the countenance of the great God?”

In the very ancient Cauc. manuscript and three Royal manuscripts it is written:

> Τίς σοι πλάνον ἐν φρεσὶ θῆκε [Col. 0196D]  
> Ταῦτα τελεῖν προλιπόντα θεοῦ μεγάλοιο πρόσωπον.
>
> “Who placed delusion in your mind,  
> That you should perform these things, abandoning the countenance of the great God?”

The very learned Francius advised that this was the correct reading. The Latin translation of these verses is as follows:

> Greece, why do you put your trust in ruling men?  
> Why do you dedicate vain gifts to the dead?  
> You sacrifice to idols: who imposed error upon your mind,  
> Making you do these things while abandoning the countenance of the great God?

*Imitator of Plato.* Thus Quintilian in book X calls Cicero Plato’s rival in philosophy; and he was so devoted to Plato that he preferred to err with him rather than hold a correct opinion with others. See Paterculus I.17, where he has excellent remarks on Cicero’s eloquence.

*In that book in which he consoled himself for his daughter’s death.* This book, together with many others, has perished. CELLARIUS.

*Himself.* Two Colbert manuscripts and many editions have the intensive form *se ipsum*.

*Did not hesitate.* Thus all the manuscripts and almost all the printed editions. Gallaeus’s edition has “will not hesitate.”

*The priesthood of augur.* Concerning this, see Cicero himself, book XII of the *Letters to Atticus* and book IV of the *Letters to Friends*.]

In precisely the same manner, Athens worshiped Minerva, Samos Juno, Paphos Venus, Lemnos Vulcan, Naxos Liber, and Delphi Apollo. Thus various sacred rites were adopted among different peoples and regions, because grateful people wished to show gratitude toward their rulers and because they could find no other honors to confer upon those deprived of life. Furthermore, the dutiful affection of their successors contributed greatly to the error; for, wishing to appear born of divine stock, they conferred divine honors upon their parents and commanded that such honors be conferred. Can anyone doubt how the religions of the gods were instituted, when he reads in Maro the words of Aeneas commanding his companions:

> Now pour libations from the bowls to Jupiter, and with prayers invoke  
> Father Anchises.

[Col. 0195B] To Anchises he attributed not only immortality but even power over the winds:

> Let us ask for winds, and may he be willing that each year,  
> Once my city has been founded, I bring him these sacred rites of mine in temples dedicated to him.

Liber, Pan, Mercury, and Apollo evidently did the same concerning Jupiter, and afterward their successors [Col. 0196A] did the same concerning them. The poets were added as well, and, by composing poems intended to give pleasure, raised them to heaven, just as those who attend upon kings—even wicked kings—flatter them with mendacious panegyrics. This evil originated with the Greeks. It is incredible how great a cloud of falsehoods their fickleness, equipped with fluency and abundance of speech, stirred up. And so, in their admiration for those men, the Greeks were the first both to adopt their sacred rites and to transmit them to all nations. Because of this vanity the Sibyl rebukes them as follows:

> Ἑλλὰς δὴ τί πέποιθας ἐπ’ ἀνδράσιν ἡγεμόνεσσι;  
> Πρὸς τί δὲ δῶρα μάταια καταφθιμένοις ἀνατίθης;  
> Θύεις εἰδώλοις· τίς σοι πλάνον ἐν φρεσὶ θῆκε,  
> Ταῦτα τελεῖν προλιπόντα θεοῦ μεγάλοιο πρόσωπον.
>
> Greece, why have you placed your trust in ruling men?  
> Why do you dedicate vain gifts to the dead?  
> You sacrifice to idols: who placed delusion in your mind,  
> That you should perform these things, abandoning the countenance of the great God?

Marcus Tullius, who was not only a consummate orator but also a philosopher—for he alone emerged as an imitator of Plato—did not hesitate, in the book in which he consoled himself for his daughter’s death, to say that the gods publicly worshiped had been human beings. His testimony should be judged especially weighty because he both held the priesthood of augur and declares that he himself worshiped and venerated those same gods. And so, within a few short lines, [Col. 0197A]

[Note: [Col. 0197B] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 197–198]

*Short lines.* An elegant term in place of the common “lines.” Compare book II, chapter 8: “In these ten verses.” BUNEMANN.

*That he would consecrate his daughter’s image in the same manner.* See this manner above, at the beginning of this chapter.

*Males.* The words of Cicero in the *Consolation*.

*Shrines.* Cicero has “temples.”

*Let us assent.* Subiaco 1465, Rostock, Venice 1471 and 1497, and Parrhasius have the singular “let me assent.” Franciscus Fabricius testifies that a manuscript of Lactantius has the plural “let us assent,” and with others he restores the same word in Cicero, *On Duties* I.6. The Gotha manuscript certainly has clearly “let us assent.” This form is favored by Lactantius: book I, chapter 5, “assented”; chapter 18, “assented”; book III, chapter 29, “Virgil assents”; *Epitome*, chapter 12, “the poets assent.” Indeed, Cicero himself, by agreement of the codices, has in *Letters to Atticus* I.14, “they assented to Curio”; II.1, “the Senate assented”; *For the Manilian Law*, chapter 26, “they may have assented to his wishes.” Others were therefore wrong to doubt Cicero’s support for the reading. Compare Quintilian, *Institutes* I.5. BUNEMANN.

*But if any living creature was ever to be consecrated, that one certainly was.* Thus all the manuscripts and editions; namely, the human being. This passage seems corrupt to some. Lactantius took it from Cicero’s lost book *On Consolation*, of which only fragments survive. It reads thus: “But if any living creature was ever to be consecrated—as the Egyptians have consecrated many, although none of them certainly deserved it—if the offspring of Cadmus,” etc.

*The offspring of Cadmus.* Namely Ino, who was made a sea goddess.

*Of Amphitryon.* Hercules, who was enrolled among the gods. “If the offspring of Cadmus, or of Amphitryon”: we have restored these words in this order from the manuscripts and the old editions—Rome 1474, Venice 1490, Florence, de Tournes 1579, Geneva 1613, and Cellarius—and reason itself shows that the passage must be corrected thus. This reading is supported by the fragments of Cicero’s *Consolation* collected by Sigonius and Patricius, who cite this passage from Lactantius. Five recent manuscripts and as many editions read: “If the offspring of Cadmus or Amphitryon”; eight editions corruptly have *Amphion*. For we know of no offspring of Amphion enrolled among the gods, but we do know of Amphitryon’s, namely Hercules, the son of Amphitryon, as Euripides calls him in the *Madness of Hercules*. Partly from ISAEUS.

*Of Tyndareus.* Castor and Pollux, who were therefore called the Tyndaridae.

*Through excessive grief.* Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* IV.29: “We composed the book of *Consolation* in the midst of grief and sorrow—for we were not wise men.” BUNEMANN.

*On the Republic.* A fragment of it indeed survives in the *Dream of Scipio*.

*On Glory.* That book of Cicero has long since perished.

*Following Plato*, etc. This passage must certainly be read thus, and so all the manuscripts and printed editions have it except Thysius, Gallaeus, Spark, and Walch, in which the word “state” is absent. [Col. 0198B] It is astonishing how badly Gallaeus went astray because the noun “state” had been suppressed in the Thysius edition. He took the word *usuram*, which is the future infinitive of the verb *utor* (“to use”), as the noun *usura* (“interest”); from this he took occasion to refute the charge against interest and, on the basis of this mutilated passage of Lactantius, to prove that interest is lawful. This never entered our author’s mind, since he asserts the contrary below in book VI, chapter 18, and in the *Epitome*, chapter 64. The Fathers of the Church, councils, and ecclesiastical writers, theologians and canonists alike, condemned interest, as Dom Ludovicus Bulteau shows in the book which he deliberately published in French against Gallaeus, in defense of our Lactantius, at Paris in 1691. We refer the reader to that work, especially chapters 2 and [Col. 0198C] 3. Francius, seeing that the reading of Gallaeus’s edition was unsound, judged that one should read: “that the just and wise man would use.” The manuscript codices, however, should rather be followed.

*That a just and wise state would use....* All the manuscripts add “state,” including Reimann, as do the editions of Subiaco, Rome, Rostock, Venice 1471, 1472, both of 1478, 1493, 1497, Pierius, Parrhasius, Cratander, Paris, de Tournes, Gryphius, Junta, Aldus, Gymnicus, Thomas, Isaeus, and Canterbury—quite correctly. Lactantius was referring to Plato’s scheme, in which he wished a state to be composed of wise persons; Lactantius III.23. All that Gallaeus and Walch, who wrongly omit the word “state,” have written here about interest is therefore absurd. Ludovicus Bulteau—for he is the author, according to Pez’s *Bibliotheca Benedictina Mauriana* I, p. 62—systematically refuted Gallaeus’s ridiculous discussion of interest in *Defense of Lactantius’s Opinions on the Subject of Interest*, Paris 1672, a work reviewed in the *Journal des Savants* for 1672, pp. 16–19. I therefore think it unnecessary to repeat what I said in *Miscellanea Lipsiensia* III, p. 140. Whether, however, as Walch replied in the same *Miscellanea*, p. 361, “wise interest” can be spoken of in the same way as a “wise excuse” or “wise moderation,” he himself may judge. The same man—in what is the easiest method of extricating oneself—says that these words are probably a gloss: “in which work, following Plato, he wished to lay down laws by which he thought that a just and wise state would use....” Heumann detected no gloss here. Lactantius added those words so that the laws laid down for a wise and just state might be believed to have been given all the more wisely, and so that greater credence might be given to this most weighty testimony—which he presses here—concerning human beings placed in heaven by human beings. Parallel to these words is Lactantius I.5: “Cicero, following and imitating Plato in many matters ... in those books which he wrote *On the Laws*.” The same point is evident from Cicero himself, *On the Laws* II.6: “As Plato did ... that most authoritative writer ... in his work *On the Laws*, I believe that I must do likewise.” See also II.7, 15, 16, 18, and 27; III.1. BUNEMANN.]
gave us two things. For while he professed that he would consecrate the image of his daughter in the same manner in which those men had been consecrated by the ancients, he both taught that they were dead and disclosed the origin of empty superstition.

“Since, however,” he says, “we see that many men and women from among humankind have been numbered among the gods, and since we venerate their most august shrines in cities and countryside, let us assent to the wisdom of those by whose talents and discoveries we possess the whole of life refined and established by laws and institutions. But if any living being was ever worthy of consecration, surely she was. If the offspring of Cadmus, or of Amphitryon, or of Tyndareus deserved to be raised to heaven by fame, this same honor must certainly be dedicated [Col. 0197B] to her. And this I shall indeed do: with the approval of the immortal gods themselves, I shall consecrate you—best [Col. 0198A] and most learned of all—as one placed in their company, in the estimation of all mortals.”

Perhaps someone may say that Cicero was delirious from excessive grief. Yet that entire discourse, perfect alike in learning, examples, and its very style of expression, was the work not of a sick mind but of a steadfast mind and judgment; and this very proposition displays no indication of grief. For I do not think that he could have written with such variety, abundance, and elegance unless both reason itself, the consolation of friends, and the passage of time had softened his sorrow.

What of the fact that he says the same thing in the books *On the Republic*? The same in *On Glory*? For in *On the Laws*, a work in which, following Plato, he wished to lay down laws that he thought a just and wise state would use, [Col. 0198B] he enacted the following concerning religion:

“Let them worship the deities, both those who have always been regarded as heavenly and those whom their merits have placed in [Col. 0199A] heaven— [Col. 0199A]

> **[Note: [Col. 0199B] Variorum Notes to columns 199–200]**
>
> **Whom their merits have placed in heaven.** Two Colbert manuscripts read *collocaverunt* (“have established”). The Roman edition of 1470 reads, “whom their merits have placed into heaven.” Cicero, whose passage occurs in Book II, chapter 19 of *On the Laws*, has: “and those whom their merits have called to heaven”; or, “and those whom their merits have called into heaven above,” as Muretus testifies that some manuscripts of Cicero read, and as he judges should be read in his note on the line of Catullus: “Flavius, the delights of your Catullus.”
>
> **If, however.** We have emended the text thus from the manuscripts and the editions Rome 1470, de Tournes, and Walch. The other printed editions read, “If I should wish.” The passage occurs in Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, Book I, chapter 29.
>
> **Since you have been initiated.** That is, instructed in pagan rites. On initiations and mysteries, and their use among the pagans, consult Cicero, *On the Laws*, Book II, chapter 14. CELLARIUS.
>
> **The knowledge of Atticus.** Here you have Lactantius as a witness that the person designated by the letter A as interlocutor in the *Tusculan Disputations* was Atticus—a matter that is often disputed, as Turnebus notes in *Adversaria* IX, chapter 18. For others, such as Lambinus in his annotations on that book of the *Disputations*, reject Lactantius’ opinion and contend that the letter designates not Atticus but an unspecified person—for example, a Young Man—or a listener, as Robertellus holds in his *Annotations on Various Authors*. ISAEUS.
>
> **Without hesitation.** He uses this word several times: Book II, chapter 7, “he cut the whetstone without hesitation.” Livy expresses it more elegantly in the same story, Book I, chapter 36: “without delaying.” Compare Lactantius, Book VI, chapter 12. Before our author, Cyprian used it in *On the Lapsed*, Basel edition, fol. 286: “Let the work be performed without hesitation and generously”; and in *On Mortality*, near the end: “without hesitation and willingly.” BUNEMANN.
>
> **The gods of the greater nations, etc.** In imitation of the Roman commonwealth, he calls “gods of the greater nations” those known as the twelve *Consentes*. The Fathers whom Romulus had selected were called those “of the greater nations.” Tarquinius Priscus subsequently enrolled one hundred Fathers in the senate; these were called those “of the lesser nations” and “conscript Fathers.” The *Consentes* gods are enumerated in verses of Ennius:
>
> > Juno, Vesta, Minerva, Ceres, Diana, Venus, Mars,  
> > Mercury, Jupiter, Neptune, Vulcan, Apollo.
>
> To these they subsequently added eight supplementary gods, so that there were twenty in number. These divinities were called “select” because of their more important administrations in the world, as Augustine indicates from Varro. Among the Egyptians there were almost similar orders and ranks of gods, as we read in Herodotus’ *Euterpe*. BETULEIUS.—And afterward innumerable gods streamed forth, so that the Caesars themselves, although the worst of men, were placed among the gods.
>
> **The god Julius, etc.** He was the first of the Caesars to be consecrated, and this was done by Augustus; on this see Suetonius, *Julius*, CLXXXVIII. Hence in Julian’s *Caesars*, Silenus calls Augustus Κοροπλαστὴν (*koroplastēn*), “a maker of dolls”; and when Augustus asks the reason for this ridiculous name, Silenus replies that, just as those little men make dolls, so he had made gods, of whom Julius Caesar was the first. Manilius likewise says of him at the end of Book IV:
>
> > Now he himself makes gods and sends to the stars a divinity  
> > Greater still, and heaven grows beneath Augustus’ rule.
>
> —**The god Julius, because … it pleased Antony.** A worthy passage from Pliny’s *Panegyric*, chapter 11, should be compared with ours. “Tiberius,” he says, “dedicated Augustus to heaven, but in order to introduce the divine power of imperial majesty; Nero dedicated Claudius, but to ridicule him; Titus dedicated Vespasian, and Domitian Titus—but the former so that he might appear the son of a god, the latter the brother of one.” CELLARIUS.
>
> **Antony.** According to Tranquillus, while Antony was consul he caused a senatorial decree to be proclaimed by a herald, by which all honors, divine and human alike, had been decreed to Caesar at once. See Cicero, *Second Philippic*.
>
> **The god Quirinus, etc.** This is Romulus, as may be seen at the end of this chapter, for the names of the dead were changed. If you wish to know why Lactantius reports that the shepherds so decided, consult Livy, Book II, chapter 7. There you will find that the senate was selected by Romulus from among shepherds; and here it is said that the shepherds so decided because the senate—created from shepherds—suborned Proculus to announce to the people that he had seen the king in a form more august than human, and that the king had commanded the people to build him a shrine, saying that he was a god and was called Quirinus. On Quirinus, besides the already cited Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, and Plutarch, read St. Cyprian, *On the Worship of Idols*, and St. Augustine, *City of God*, Book III, chapter 4.—**The god Quirinus.** Tertullian, *To the Nations* II.9: “Romulus became a god after his death.” To be sure, Romulus both killed his brother and deceitfully abducted the daughters of others; he is therefore Quirinus because their parents then cried out in lamentation (*quiritatum est*) on his account.
>

Likewise, in the *Tusculan Disputations*, after saying that almost the whole of heaven had been filled with members of the human race, he says:

“If, however, I should attempt to investigate ancient traditions and to draw out from them the things handed down by the writers of Greece, those very gods who are regarded as belonging to the greater nations will be found to have departed from among us here and gone to heaven. Inquire whose tombs are pointed out in Greece; recall, since you have been initiated, the teachings transmitted in the mysteries; then at last you will understand how widely this extends.”

He clearly appealed to Atticus’ own knowledge as a witness that it could be understood from the mysteries themselves that all those who are worshiped had been human beings. And although he confessed without hesitation that this was true of Hercules, Liber, Aesculapius, Castor, and Pollux, [Col. 0199B] he feared openly to confess the same of Apollo and Jupiter, their fathers, and likewise of Neptune, [Col. 0200A] Vulcan, Mars, and Mercury, whom he called the gods of the greater nations. He therefore says that this extends widely, so that we may understand the same thing of Jupiter and the other more ancient gods. If the ancients consecrated their memory by the same reasoning by which Cicero says that he would consecrate his daughter’s image and name, those who mourn may be forgiven; those who believe may not.

For who is so insane as to suppose that heaven is opened to the dead by the consensus and decree of innumerable fools? Or that anyone can give to another what he himself does not possess? Among the Romans Julius was a god because Antony, a criminal man, so decided; Quirinus was a god because shepherds so decided—although Quirinus proved to be the murderer of his twin brother, and Julius the parricide of his country.

For Ennius declares that Romulus was missed by his people. In his work, the people, grieving for their lost king, say:

Because of this longing, Julius Proculus’ lie was more readily believed. He had been suborned by the Fathers to announce to the people that he had seen the king in a form more august than human, and that the king had commanded the people to build him a shrine, saying that he was a god and was called Quirinus. By this act, [Col. 0201B] Proculus both persuaded the people that Romulus had departed to the gods and freed the senate from suspicion of murdering the king.

## CHAPTER XVI  
### Why those distinguished by a difference of sex cannot be gods; and why the function of procreation is incompatible with the nature of God

I might have been content with what I have related; but many matters necessary to the work I have undertaken still remain. For although, by destroying the very foundation of these religions, I have abolished them all, I nevertheless wish to pursue the remaining matters and more fully refute this inveterate conviction, so that at last people may be ashamed of and repent their errors. This is a great work, and one worthy of a human being.

[Col. 0201C]

> I proceed to release minds from the knots of religions,

[Col. 0202A] as Lucretius says—although he could not accomplish this, because he offered nothing true. This is our task, for we both affirm the true God and refute the false ones.

Those, therefore, who suppose that the poets invented fables about the gods, while nevertheless believing that female goddesses exist and worshiping them, unwittingly return to the very thing they had denied: that the gods have intercourse and give birth. For two sexes cannot have been established except for the purpose of procreation. Yet once the difference of the sexes has been admitted, they do not understand that conception necessarily follows—something that cannot apply to God.

But let it be as they suppose; for they say that Jupiter and the other gods have children. New gods, therefore, are born every day, since they are surely not surpassed by human beings in fertility. Thus everything is full of innumerable gods, none of whom, of course, ever dies. For although the mass of human beings [Col. 0202B] is incredible and their number inestimable, they must nevertheless die just as they are born. How many gods, then, are we to suppose there are, who have been born throughout so many ages and have remained immortal? Why, then, are so few worshiped?

Unless perhaps we imagine that the gods have two sexes, not for the purpose of procreation, but solely for obtaining pleasure, and that they practice things which petty humans are ashamed both to do and to undergo.

Since some are said to have been born from others, it follows that they are always being born, seeing that they were born at some time; or, if at some time they ceased to be born, we ought to know why or when they ceased. Seneca says, not without wit, in his books of moral philosophy:

“Why, then,” he asks, “has Jupiter, the most lustful figure among the poets, ceased to acknowledge children? Has he turned sixty, [Col. 0202C] and has the Papian law placed a clasp upon him? [Col. 0203A]

> **[Note: [Col. 0203C] Variorum Notes to columns 203–204]**
>
> **And has the Papian law placed a clasp upon him?** The Christian orator had in view the following lines of Juvenal, *Satire* 6:
>
> > Yet who can affirm that nothing happened upon the mountains  
> > Or in the caves? Have Jupiter and Mars grown so old?
>
> [Col. 0203D]
>
> “To place a clasp upon” is here metaphorical: to forbid marriage because of advancing age, just as in Tertullian “to place the final clasp upon the flesh” means to restrain lust. JOHANNES RHODIUS.—The Papian-Poppaean law “clasped” men of sixty—that is, forbade them to marry—as though their procreative power were already exhausted.… A bronze ring, called a *fibula* (“clasp”), was added to the foreskin extending over the glans of the penis. Hence Martial’s verbs “to remove the clasp” and “to release the clasp.” ISAEUS.—The Papian law had provided that a woman younger than fifty should not marry a man of sixty, nor a man younger than sixty marry a woman of fifty. Apuleius also mentions it in *Apology*, Book I. The emperor Claudius had formerly abolished this provision (Suetonius XIII; Ulpian, *Fragments*, title VI); after its restoration by other emperors, it was again abolished by either Justin or Justinian. Eustathius expresses the sense of this law as follows: “A woman older than sixty may marry a man younger than fifty.” For the senate rightly believed that women could conceive until the age of fifty, and that men could generally procreate until sixty; it did not wish fertile persons of either sex to be joined to the infertile. GROTIUS.—And yet it is well known that men can procreate beyond sixty. See Pliny, Book VII, chapter 14; Solinus, chapter 4; Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 4.
>
> **Or has he obtained the right of three children?** These were privileges and immunities granted, to favor propagation, to parents who had three children. On them see the first law in the Code, *Who May Claim Exemption by Number of Children*; Law I of the Code, *On the Right of Children*; and the section “But these rights” in the Institutes, *On the Tertullian Decree of the Senate*. Plutarch, prologue to *On Love*. Sometimes, however, through the indulgence of the emperor, these privileges were also granted to persons who had fewer children, or even none. Those who had obtained this right enjoyed, among other advantages, the benefit that whenever something was distributed individually among the people, they received shares for three children. See Duarenus, *Disputations* I, chapter 40; Alexander ab Alexandro, *Days of Feasting*, Book IV, chapter 8; Beroaldus and Sabellicus on Suetonius, *Galba*, chapter 14. ISAEUS.

>

>

>

Book II, chapter 3: “is perceived from deeds and conduct”; Book II, chapter 8: “cannot be perceived”; Book IV, chapter 30: “nor did they thoroughly perceive its force and rationale”; Book V, chapter 8: “God perceives their very thoughts.” BUNEMANN.

Or has he obtained the right of three children? Or has it at last occurred to him:

> Expect from another what you have done to another,

and does he fear that someone may do to him what he himself did to Saturn?”

But let those who assert the existence of the gods consider how they will answer the argument we shall advance. If the gods have two sexes, intercourse follows; and if they have intercourse, they must also have houses. For they are surely not devoid of virtue and modesty, so as to do this indiscriminately or in public, as we see dumb animals do.

If they have houses, it follows that they also have cities—and indeed on the authority of Naso, who says:

> The common crowd dwells apart in different places; along this frontage  
> The powerful and renowned heaven-dwellers have established their household gods.

If they have cities, they will consequently also have fields. Now who [Col. 0203B] does not see what follows? They must plow and cultivate them—which is done for the sake of sustenance. Therefore, they are mortal.

The same argument has equal force when reversed. If they have no fields, neither do they have cities; if they have no cities, neither do they have houses. If they lack houses, then they also lack [Col. 0204A] intercourse. If intercourse is absent from them, so too is the female sex. Yet we see that there are females among the gods; therefore, they are not gods. Let anyone solve this argument if he can. For one proposition follows another in such a way that this final conclusion must necessarily be admitted.

Nor will anyone solve the following argument. Of the two sexes, one is stronger and the other weaker. Males are stronger, while females are more feeble. But weakness is incompatible with a god; therefore, so too is the female sex. To this is added the final conclusion of the preceding argument: they are not gods, since there are females among the gods.

## CHAPTER XVII  
### On the Stoics’ view of the same matter, and on the gods’ afflictions and disgraces

[Col. 0204B] For these reasons the Stoics interpret the gods in another direction; and because they do not perceive what is truly the case, they try to connect them with the rational account of natural phenomena. Cicero followed them and delivered the following judgment concerning the gods and their religions:

“Do you therefore see how, from natural phenomena discovered well and usefully, reason was drawn toward imaginary and fictitious gods? This gave rise to false opinions, turbulent errors, and superstitions that are almost those of old women.” [Col. 0205A]

“For the forms, ages, clothing, and adornment of the gods are known to us; in addition, their lineages, marriages, all their kinships, and everything else has been reduced to the likeness of human weakness.”

What could be said more plainly or more truly? The foremost figure of Roman philosophy, invested with the most distinguished priesthood, convicts the gods of being imaginary and fictitious. He testifies that their worship consists of superstitions almost fit for old women, and complains that human beings are entangled in false opinions and turbulent errors. For the whole third book of *On the Nature of the Gods* utterly overthrows and destroys all religions.

What more, then, is expected from us? Can we surpass [Col. 0205B] Cicero in eloquence? Certainly not. But he, being ignorant of the truth, lacked confidence, as he frankly admits in the same work. For he says that he can more easily state what a thing is not than what it is; that is, he understands falsehoods but does not know the truth.

It is therefore clear that those who are thought to be gods were human beings and that their memory was consecrated after death. This is why they also have different ages and distinct images of each: their statues were fashioned in the dress and at the age [Col. 0206A] in which death overtook each of them.

Let us consider, if you please, the afflictions of these unhappy gods. Isis lost her son; Ceres, her daughter. Latona, expelled and driven about throughout the world, scarcely found a small island—Delos—on which to give birth. The Mother of the Gods both loved a handsome young man and, when she discovered him with a rival, cut off his male organs and made him a half-man; for this reason her rites are now celebrated by the Galli priests. Juno most bitterly persecuted her rivals because she herself could not bear a child by her brother.

Varro writes that the island [Col. 0206B] of Samos was formerly called Parthenia because Juno grew up there and also married Jupiter there. Consequently, her most celebrated and ancient temple is on Samos; her image is fashioned in bridal attire, and her annual rites are celebrated after the manner of a wedding. [Col. 0207A] If, therefore, she grew up, if she was first a virgin and afterward a woman—

>
> **Aeneas by Anchises.** Aeneas himself sets forth his lineage in Homer.
>
> **Eryx.** See Hyginus, *Fables*, chapter 260. See also Servius on *Aeneid* V, though he holds a different opinion.
>
> **By Adonius.** We have restored this reading from five Royal manuscripts, two of which are the oldest and best, two Colbert, two Brun., Nav., Vict., Gat., and Marm. Twelve more recent manuscripts and the printed editions read “by Adonis.” The Thomas and Frankfurt editions read “by Adonides.”—**By Adonis.** Witsius, *Egypt* II, chapter 2, no. 15, p. 66, contends that Adonis, the Phoenician divinity, is the same as Osiris and explains the mystery. Witsius followed Vossius, *On Idolatry* II, chapter 4. BUNEMANN.
>
> [Col. 0208B]
>
> **Was killed after being struck by a boar.** I deleted the conjunction “and,” found in six recent manuscripts and the printed editions, on the authority of the other manuscripts and the editions Rome 1468, 1470, and de Tournes 1579. “By a boar’s blow” is read in the Nav. manuscript, one Colbert, Brun., and the original hand of Vict. The fable of Adonis is recounted by the rhetor Aphthonius. See also Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book X, near the end.—**Struck by a boar.** That is, wounded by a boar; Ovid, *Metamorphoses* III.213. “Blow” is properly used of the bite of boars. See the commentators on Phaedrus I, fable 11.6:
>
> > The boar avenged the old injury with a blow.
>
> **In the *Sacred History*.** Namely, that of Euhemerus.
>
> **Established prostitution.** See Theodoret, *Therapeutics*.
>
> **And the author.** Here the word is of feminine gender, as *auctor optima* is in Ovid and Servius, when it is derived from the noun *auctoritas* (“authority”); *auctrix*, however, is used when it comes from *augeo* (“increase”).
>
> **Was in Cyprus.** Thus eight Royal manuscripts, six Colbert, two Clarom., Lips., two Brun., and the printed editions; this is to be preferred to the Christ., Em., and Cambridge manuscripts, where “was in debauchery” is read.
>
> **They made a profit from exposing their bodies to the public.** We have emended the text thus from two Brun. manuscripts. This reading is Lactantian. See below in the same book, chapter 20, “the cheapness of a body exposed to the public”; and Book VI, chapter 23, “one must abstain from bodies public and exposed to all.” In Plautus, too, “to expose one’s body to the public” means to prostitute it. One recent Royal manuscript reads “among the people”; the others, “publicly.”
>
> **But not even those virgins.** Minerva and Diana. CELLARIUS.
>
> **Erichthonius.** He was the fourth king of Athens. On him see St. Augustine, *City of God*, Book XVIII, chapter 12; Pausanias, *Attica*; Hyginus, chapter 166; Servius on *Georgics* III.
>
> **The poets.** Homer, *Iliad* II; Euripides; Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II.
>
> [Col. 0208D]
>
> **As she was accustomed.** Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.

Semen [Seed]. Thus the manuscripts and printed editions, except Gall., where *semel* [once] appears.

Whence Erichthonius was born. Pausanias, *Attica*: “They say that Erichthonius had no human father, but that Hephaestus and Earth were his parents” (Πατέρα δὲ Ἐριχθονίῳ λέγουσιν ἀνθρώπων μὲν οὐδένα εἶναι, γονέας δὲ Ἥφαιστον καὶ Γῆν). Homer in the *Catalogue*; Apollodorus, book III, *On the Origin of the Gods*; Lucian, *Philopseudes*; Origen, *Against Celsus*, book VIII; but especially Augustine, *The City of God*, book XVIII, chapter 12; Jerome, *Against Jovinian*, chapter 4; Tertullian, *On the Spectacles*, chapter 9. Virgin. Concerning her, see Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II.

To three virgins. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II:

> Pallas had enclosed Erichthonius, offspring created without a mother,  
> In a basket woven from Attic wicker,  
> And had given him to the three virgin daughters  
> Of twin-natured Cecrops to be guarded.

Others say that she entrusted him to only two, namely Aglauros and Pandrosos. Germanicus’ commentator says: “Erichthonius was born; Minerva hid him in a basket and, after placing a dragon there as guardian, entrusted him to the two sisters Aglauros and [Col. 0209B] Pandrosos.” Fulgentius says the same in as many words in *Mythologies*, book II, except that for him she is Pandora, who is called Pandrosos by others, etc. MEURSIUS.]

[…] to have been human; whoever does not understand this confesses himself a beast. Why should I speak of the obscenity of Venus, prostituted to everyone’s lusts—not only those of gods, but also of men? From her notorious adultery with Mars she bore Harmonia; by Mercury, Hermaphroditus, who was born androgynous; by Jupiter, Cupid; by Anchises, Aeneas; and by Butes, Eryx. By Adonis, however, she could bear no child, because, while still a boy, he was struck and killed by a boar. She was the first, as is recorded in the *Sacred History*, to establish the harlot’s trade, and she induced the women of Cyprus to earn money by prostituting their bodies. She commanded this so that she alone, in contrast to other women, might not appear unchaste and eager for men. Does she, then, possess anything divine—she whose adulteries [Col. 0207B] outnumber her offspring? Yet not even those [Col. 0208A] virgins could preserve their chastity inviolate.

For whence are we to suppose that Erichthonius was born? From the earth, as the poets wish it to appear? But the fact itself cries out against this. For when Vulcan had made arms for the gods, Jupiter gave him the choice of whatever reward he wished to request, and swore, as was his custom, by the infernal marsh that he would refuse him nothing. The lame craftsman then requested Minerva in marriage. Jupiter, Best and Greatest, bound by so solemn an oath, could not refuse; nevertheless, he warned Minerva to resist and defend her chastity. They say that in the ensuing struggle Vulcan spilled his seed upon the earth, from which Erichthonius was born; and that this name was given him ἀπὸ τῆς ἔριδος καὶ χθονός, that is, from “strife” (*eris*) and “earth” (*chthōn*). Why, then, did the virgin enclose and seal up that boy together with [Col. 0208B] a dragon, and [Col. 0209A] entrust him to the three virgin daughters of Cecrops?

Entrusted. Elegantly used for “deposited,” or, as Hyginus says, *Fables* 166, “gave him in a little chest to be guarded.” Apuleius, *Apology*, p. 308: “entrusted to another’s guardianship.” Shortly afterward, on p. 309, he explains it as “to deposit”; see also Graevius on Cicero, *For Cluentius*, chapter 12: “She carried in her womb the hope entrusted to it by her husband.” On the distinction between the verbs *commendare* [entrust] and *deponere* [deposit], consult Burmann on Phaedrus I, fable 173, p. 43. Ceres and Liber. Thus Virgil begins the books of the *Georgics*: “Liber and nurturing Ceres.”

Minerva. Horace calls her “industrious,” and Ovid “ingenious.” [Col. 0210B]

Men defile themselves with an inexpiable crime. The result will be the same if you emend it to: “men are defiled by an inexpiable crime,” as in book V, chapter 1: “to be defiled and bound by an inexpiable crime.” BUNEMAN.

Discuss. This reading is found in the very ancient manuscripts 1 Bonon., 3 Reg., 1 Colb., Lips., 2 Clarom., Em., 2 Brun., and others, and in the editions of Is. and Cellarius. Manuscripts 1 Reg., 5 Colb., Cauc., Jun., and the printed editions read “said.”

Or be diminished by old age itself. But in certain manuscripts the reading is: “be diminished by old age itself, and at last be ended and brought down by death.” I see no reason to deny that this belongs to Lactantius, especially since he is censuring the opinion that Hercules earned immortality through bodily strength. The jurisdiction of death itself is therefore appropriately invoked: for how could immortality be acquired through that over which death has such complete jurisdiction—what is wholly ended by death? GRONOVIUS.—Concerning this addition, “at last be ended by death,” Bunemann writes as follows:—“Because these words occur only in Gronovius’ codex, Heumann suspected them, and I took care to print them in a different type. Gronovius nevertheless defends them well enough; see his *Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 17, p. 182. Lactantius certainly favors the verb *terminare* [end]. Book III, chapter 12: ‘Life, which ends [Col. 0210D] with the body.’ Compare book VII, chapter 15.”

Nor did he wish to be healed, etc. The ancient Bon. codex reads: “nor did he wish to become healthy, nor to become old.” I approve of this because the resemblance between the words *sanum* and *senem* gives the phrasing a certain elegance. Another Bon. codex reads: “Nor did he wish to be healed, lest he should appear old or more deformed.” This wording too is neither inept nor inharmonious; but because the customary reading, found in thirty manuscripts and all printed editions, has the best sense, we have retained it. This is from THOMASIUS.

Less than himself. For in old men the bones waste away and the flesh is consumed by the acridity of heat. VANDER LINDEN.

From the pyre. Thus we have restored the reading from the Regio-Puteanus manuscript, 2 Colb., Ultr., and the Paris 1525 edition. Manuscripts Cauc., 3 Reg., 1 Bonon., Pen., 1 Colb., 1 Clarom., and many more recent editions read “from the pyre” with *a rogo*.

He had burned himself. This is the manuscript reading; the more recent editors have “his own self.”]

It was, I think, manifest sexual impurity, which cannot possibly be disguised. The other, when she had nearly lost her lover, who had been

> Torn apart by his terrified horses,

summoned the most excellent physician Asclepius to treat the young man; and after he had been healed:

> The nurturing goddess concealed him in secret  
> Dwellings and banished him to the nymph Egeria and her grove,  
> So that, alone and unknown in the Italian woods,  
> He might pass his life and, with his name changed, become Virbius.

What is the meaning of this exceedingly diligent and anxious treatment? Why the secret dwellings? Why banishment either so far away, or to a woman, or into solitude? Why, furthermore, the change of name? Finally, why her so persistent abhorrence of horses? What do all these things signify except consciousness of illicit intercourse and a love by no means virginal? Plainly, she had reason to undertake so much labor for so [Col. 0209B] faithful a young man, who had utterly refused compliance with his enamored stepmother.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Consecration of the Gods Because of Benefits Conferred upon Mankind

At this point those must also be refuted who not only admit that gods were made from human beings, but even boast of this in order to praise them—whether on account of valor, as Hercules; gifts, as Ceres and Liber; or the discovery of arts, as Aesculapius and Minerva. [Col. 0210A] I shall demonstrate from each case how foolish these things are, and how unworthy to be reasons for which human beings defile themselves with inexpiable crime and become enemies of the true God, whom they despise while adopting the rites of the dead.

They say that valor raises a human being to heaven—not that virtue discussed by the philosophers, which consists in the goods of the mind, but this bodily quality called strength. Because it was preeminent in Hercules, he is believed to have deserved immortality. Who is so foolishly absurd as to judge bodily strength a divine or even a human good, when greater strength has also been allotted to beasts and is often broken by a single illness, diminished by old age itself, and brought down? And so, when that same man saw his muscular limbs being disfigured by ulcers, [Col. 0210B] he did not wish to be healed or to grow old, lest at some time he should appear less than himself or more deformed. They believed that from the pyre on which he had burned himself alive he ascended into heaven. Those very things which they so foolishly admired they reproduced in statues and images and set up as consecrated objects, so that monuments [Col. 0211A] to their vanity might endure forever—the vanity of those who believed that men became gods by killing beasts.

But perhaps this is the fault of the Greeks, who have always regarded the most trivial things as the greatest. What of our own people? Are they any wiser? They do indeed despise athletic valor, because it harms nothing; but they so admire royal valor, because it commonly inflicts harm far and wide, that they think courageous and warlike commanders should be placed in the assembly of the gods. [Col. 0211A]

[Note: [Col. 0211B] [Various Notes on columns 211–212]

In the assembly of the gods. Most printed editions read “into the assembly.”

Destroy towns. Six manuscripts read *excindere*; seven, *exscindere*.

If anyone cuts the throat of one man. Cyprian, book II, epistle 2, fol. 33, Basel edition: “When individuals commit homicide, it is a crime; when it is done publicly, it is called valor.” BUNEMAN.

To this earthly dwelling of the gods. Cellarius’ explanation does not fit here. Lactantius means that murderers are not admitted to a temple but excluded from temples. See book III, chapter 17: “that earthly dwelling of Jupiter.”

Ennius. From an epigram, also cited in Cicero’s *Republic*, according to Seneca, epistle 109.

If it is permitted to ascend into the regions of the celestials. Thus we have corrected the text from Cicero, *Republic* III, and from the Lactantian manuscripts Salmas., 1 Lips., Pal., Ultr., and Regio-Puteanus, in which *coelestium* appears in place of *coelestum*. Three Reg., 3 Colb., Nav., Vict., Gat., 2 Brun., Em., and Balliol. concur with this, reading: “If by entering the regions.” Our correction is supported by the most learned Salmasius, Pithaeus, Isaeus, Gronovius, Baluzius, and Cellarius. Eleven more recent manuscripts and the printed editions read:

> If anyone is permitted by slaughter to climb to the realms of heaven.

[Col. 0211D]

Who does not see that through scribal corruption and ignorance *caedendo* [by slaughter] was produced ἀντὶ τοῦ *endo* [in place of *endo*]? Then there followed the faulty judgment partly of other scribes and partly of editors. As if the words immediately following—“Obviously because he extinguished and destroyed a great part of the human race”—necessarily interpreted something contained in Ennius’ verse, they introduced *caedendo*, deleted *plagas* [regions], and substituted *coelestia* for *coelestium* or *coelestum*; that is, they truly made a complete shambles of it. And because Africanus’ glory from all his military exploits is so well known that the poet wishes heaven to lie open to him alone, Lactantius shows that no other reason is apparent for his wishing this except that he

> Sent many valiant souls forth to Hades,

a verse of Homer at the beginning of the *Iliad*—as though one were to say:

> He sent many illustrious souls ahead to the underworld.

Lactantius himself therefore interprets the slaughter and blood [Col. 0212B] of many human beings as having, in popular belief, placed Africanus among the stars, even though he found no word concerning this in the epitaph; for we know Africanus to have become famous through nothing other than slaughter and blood—that is, through war. But many before Lactantius explain it similarly. Seneca, epistle 95: “Crimes are committed under senatorial decrees and resolutions of the people, and things forbidden in private are publicly commanded. Deeds which, if secretly committed, would be punished by death are praised because men in military cloaks committed them. Human beings, the gentlest race, are not ashamed to delight in one another’s blood, to wage wars, and to hand wars on to their children.” GRONOVIUS.—The ancients used *endo* for *in*, relying, I believe, on the argument that *endo*, derived from the Greek ἔνδον [within], is frequently found in Ennius in the sense of *in*, just as Lucretius has *indogredi* for *ingredi* [enter], and several other expressions of that kind. In confirmation of their opinion they also adduce the fact that, when Lactantius saw no reason expressed by Ennius that would have opened the path to immortality for Africanus, he supplied this reason himself.

Did you dwell in darkness, Africanus? Or rather, O poet. Africanus here is Scipio himself, and the poet is Ennius. BUNEMAN.

It truly is so, he says, Africanus. Thus Cicero, *Republic* III; thus the manuscripts together with the printed editions, except 3 Colb. and 1 Reg., in which the reading is: “And indeed, he says, Africanus.” [Col. 0212D] Andreas Patricius, in his scholia on Cicero’s fragments from *Republic* III, thinks it should read, “It truly is so, Africanus,” or simply, “And indeed, Africanus.” For my part, when I find the codices unanimous, I do not readily change anything.

Those same things. A Lactantian expression occurring frequently. Three recent manuscripts and nine recent editions read “those very things.”

To die indeed. Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions, together with four recent manuscripts, read “For my part, to die.”

Have united in concord. I change nothing. Compare the accepted text of Lactantius, book V, chapter 7, below: “The entire multitude has agreed upon it,” where more is said. BUNEMAN.

Public tranquillity. That is, peace.

They will violate the covenant. Thus all printed editions and manuscripts except 1 Clarom., which has “they will break the covenant.” But I observe that Lactantius more than once uses compound verbs for simple ones, and simple verbs for compounds.

The name of gods to Ceres. The Eleusinians especially worshipped Ceres because, when she came into Attica in search of her daughter, she first taught them the sowing of crops and laws. [Col. 0213B] Yet I do not altogether reject the opinion of those who wish *Ceres* to be derived from the Hebrew *charas*, “to plow,” since, as Ovid says in *Metamorphoses* V:

> Ceres first turned the clod with the curved plow.

From VOSSIUS.]

They think there is no other road to immortality than to lead armies, devastate the property of others, erase cities, destroy towns, and either slaughter free peoples or subject them to slavery. Evidently, the more people they afflict, despoil, and kill, the nobler and more renowned they consider themselves; captivated by the semblance of empty glory, they give their crimes the name of valor. Indeed, I would prefer them to fashion gods for themselves from the slaughter of wild beasts rather than approve [Col. 0211B] an immortality so bloodstained.

If anyone cuts the throat of one man, he is regarded as polluted and impious, and they think it unlawful for him to be admitted to this earthly dwelling of the gods. But the man who has slaughtered countless thousands of human beings, flooded fields with gore, and polluted rivers is admitted not merely into a temple but even into heaven. In Ennius, Africanus speaks thus:

> If anyone is permitted to ascend into the regions of the celestials,  
> For me alone heaven’s greatest gate lies open.

[Col. 0212A] Obviously, this is because he extinguished and destroyed a great part of the human race. O Africanus, in what profound darkness you dwelt! Or rather, O poet, who believed that ascent into heaven was opened to human beings by slaughter and blood! Cicero too assented to this vanity: “It truly is so,” he says, “Africanus; for that same gate also stood open to Hercules”—as though he himself had plainly been the gatekeeper in heaven when this happened.

For my part, I cannot decide whether I should think this more deserving of grief or of laughter, when I see grave, learned men—men wise, as it seems to themselves—being tossed about amid such pitiable waves of error. If this is the valor that makes us immortal, I would indeed prefer to die rather than bring destruction upon as many people as possible. If immortality cannot be obtained otherwise than through blood, what will happen if everyone has united in concord? [Col. 0212B] That could certainly occur if, after casting aside destructive and impious madness, people chose to be innocent and just. Will no one, then, be worthy of heaven? Will valor perish because human beings are not permitted to rage against one another?

But those who reckon the overthrow of cities and peoples the highest glory will not tolerate public tranquillity. They will plunder and rage, and, by insolently inflicting injuries, will violate the covenant of human society so that they may possess an enemy whom they can destroy more criminally than they provoked him. Let us now proceed to the remaining matters.

Tradition [Col. 0213A] conferred the name of gods upon Ceres and Liber because of their gifts. [Col. 0213A]

That all things belong to him, etc. An ancient codex reads: “and those very things that could be discovered; the arts also,” etc., so that the words “first discovered” are deleted—and they certainly ought to be deleted. Why not to them also? I have restored *et* [also] from the manuscripts; the printed editions read *etiam* [also].

Who taught how to begin a web. The Sublac. edition adds “reason.” This is the Saitic Minerva, called Neith by the Egyptians, as Plato says in the *Timaeus*; she is the discoverer of the art of weaving. Diodorus includes among her various inventions “the making of clothing” (τὴν τῆς ἐσθῆτος κατασκευήν). According to some, she is the same as Noema or Naamah, the daughter of Lamech mentioned by Moses at Genesis IV.23, if what one reads in Genebrardus’ *Chronicles* and Lippomano’s *Catena* is true: that she discovered wool-working and weaving, and that on account of this discovery she is mentioned contrary to the custom of Scripture, which does not ordinarily mention women in genealogies except because of outstanding virtue or for the sake of a mystery. This becomes still clearer because she is joined to three discoverers of distinguished things: Jabal, Jubal, and Tubal-cain. VOSSIUS.

What of that man? Aesculapius. BUN.

Who were partly beneficial. Thus several books and Reimm. “I rewrite it,” says Heumann, “*per artem profuerunt* [were beneficial through art], because the editions of 1472, 1476, and 1478”—to which the earlier edition of 1478 should also be added—“present *partem*, as though an abbreviation for *per artem*.” Compare chapter 18. Ingenious, except that “were partly beneficial” is here contrasted with “the supreme God, who made all things.” For they worshipped more persons than merely those who were beneficial through art. See this chapter, sections 1–21, and book V, chapter 14. BUN.]

I can demonstrate from divine writings that wine and grain were in human use before the offspring of Heaven and Saturn existed. But let us indeed suppose that these things were discovered by them. Can it seem a greater or more important thing to have gathered grain, crushed it, and taught people to make bread, or to have gathered grapes from vines, pressed them, and made wine, than to have generated the grain and vines themselves and brought them forth from the earth? Let us grant that God left these things to be extracted by human ingenuity. Nevertheless, all things must belong to him who both gave human beings the wisdom to discover and supplied the very things that could be discovered.

The arts too are said to have procured immortality for their inventors: medicine for Aesculapius, [Col. 0213B] craftsmanship for Vulcan. Let us therefore worship those who taught the fulling and shoemaking trades as well. Why, however, is honor not paid to the inventor of pottery? Is it because these wealthy men despise a Samian vessel? There are also other arts whose inventors have been of the greatest benefit to human life. [Col. 0214A] Why were temples not assigned to them too? But of course it is Minerva who discovered them all; and therefore those craftsmen supplicate her. Minerva, then, ascended to heaven from these sordid crafts.

There is indeed reason for anyone to abandon him who first fashioned the earth with its living creatures and heaven with its stars and lights, in order to venerate the woman who taught people to begin a web! What of the man who taught how to heal wounds in bodies? Can he be more excellent than the one who formed the bodies themselves and gave them the capacity to feel and live, and who, finally, devised and brought forth the very herbs and other things of which the medical art consists?

## CHAPTER XIX. [Col. 0214B] That No One Can Worship the True God Together with False Gods

But someone will say that due veneration should be rendered both to this supreme God who made all things and to those who were partly beneficial. [Col. 0215A] First, it has never occurred that anyone who worshipped these gods [Col. 0215A] also worshipped God; nor can it occur, because if the same honor is rendered to others, he is not worshipped at all, since his religion consists in believing that he is the one and only God. For they feared misfortune. Isocrates, in the *Praise of Busiris*, censures the poets’ impious tales about the gods and says that some of them therefore suffered deserved punishments. The supreme poet loudly declares that all those

> Who cultivated life through the arts they discovered

are in the underworld, and that the very discoverer of such medicine and art was cast down by a thunderbolt to the waters of Styx. Thus we may understand how mighty the omnipotent Father is, who destroys even gods with thunderbolts. But perhaps ingenious people had the following reasoning in mind: because God cannot be struck by lightning, it is apparent that this did not happen. On the contrary: because it happened, it is apparent that he [Col. 0215B] was a human being, not a god. For the poets’ falsehood [Col. 0216A] lies not in the event but in the name.

They feared misfortune if, contrary to public belief, they confessed what was true. But if they agree among themselves that gods were made from human beings, why do they not believe the poets whenever they describe their flights, wounds, deaths, wars, and adulteries? From these matters one is given to understand that they could not possibly have become gods, because they were not even upright human beings and performed in their lives deeds that produce eternal death.

## CHAPTER XX. On the Romans’ Own Gods and Their Rites

I now come to the Romans’ own religions, since I have spoken about those held in common. Romulus’ nurse, the she-wolf, was accorded divine honors. I could tolerate this if she had been the animal [Col. 0216B] itself whose figure she bears. Livy is the authority [Col. 0217A]—

Leaena. In Thucydides VI one reads how Hipparchus, the son of Pisistratus, was killed by Harmodius and Aristogeiton. Pausanias adds that when Hippias wished to avenge the death of his brother Hipparchus, he tortured to death a woman named Leaena, whom he knew to be Aristogeiton’s mistress. As a memorial to this event, after the family of Pisistratus had been overthrown, the Athenians set up a bronze lioness because of the torments she had endured. This Leaena’s endurance [Col. 0217D] is celebrated by Pliny, book VII, chapter 23; Athenaeus, *Deipnosophists* XIII; and Eusebius in the *Chronicle*. Since this occurred in the sixty-seventh Olympiad, during the reign of Tarquin the Proud, the Romans could not have imitated the Athenians’ representation of Leaena when fashioning their She-Wolf. For the She-Wolf was sculpted by Ancus Marcius nearly thirty Olympiads before the Athenians made the image of Leaena. Lactantius has therefore made a historical error. Near the end of his *Apology*, Tertullian marvels at the endurance of Leaena, who, according to Eusebius, bit off her own tongue so that she would not betray the secret of her friends and associates. See what Valerius Maximus, book III, chapter 3, reports about Anaxarchus in a similar circumstance.

**Nor is she the only prostitute whom the Romans worship.** We have restored this reading [Col. 0218A] from the oldest and best manuscripts—7 Royal, 2 Bologna, 4 Colbertine, and eleven others—and from the Roman editions of 1470 and 1474 and Cellarius. One Colbertine manuscript has *nor her alone*; another Colbertine has *nor even her alone*, where *even* is a scribal error for *her*. [Col. 0218B]

**But Faula also, etc.** The very learned Vossius thinks that Lactantius wrote *Flaura* in the archaic fashion, that is, *Flora*. For my part, I agree with Vossius that what our author then adds about that Flora is not very probable. There was no prostitute of that name who bequeathed her property to the people. Had Lactantius identified the authors whom he followed, it would be safer to credit him; but on this point he is utterly silent. To make it still clearer that these things were fabricated, note that Flora is placed by Varro, in book IV of *On the Latin Language*, among the gods and goddesses whom the Romans received from the Sabines in the time of Romulus and who were introduced by Tatius. Varro makes it clear that Flora had long been worshipped before the time mentioned by Lactantius. And so that the antiquity of her worship at Rome may be entirely certain, read Varro, *On the Latin Language*, VI, where he says, on Ennius’ authority, that Numa appointed flamens surnamed “Florales.” His words are:

> Ennius says that the same Numa Pompilius appointed flamens, all of whom were surnamed after individual gods. In some cases the etymologies are evident, as why one is called the Martial flamen and another the Quirinal. There are others in whose titles the origins lie concealed, such as most of those appearing in the verses: the Volturnal, Palatual, Furinal, Floral, Falacer, and Pomonal flamens.

Yet because Flora already had sacred rites and flamens in the days of Romulus and Numa, it does not follow that the Floral Games also existed then. These were first celebrated in the year 513 from the founding of the City, when Gaius Claudius Centho and Marcus Sempronius Tuditanus were consuls. Nor were they financed from an inheritance left by Flora or some prostitute, but from fines imposed upon men convicted of embezzlement because they had occupied public land belonging to the Roman people, as Ovid relates in book V of the *Fasti*; see that passage. Such were the beginnings of the Floralia. Thereafter they were not celebrated unless the circumstances of the year demanded it or the Sibylline Books were said to prescribe it. Their annual celebration was finally decreed in the year of the City 580, when Lucius Postumius Albinus and Marcus Popilius Laenas were consuls. The occasion was as follows. Spring weather had repeatedly been severely unseasonable, producing barrenness over several years. The Senate therefore resolved that annual games should be instituted for Flora, so that through the favor of the goddess, now enhanced by so great an honor, all trees and plants might thereafter bloom more successfully. From **Vossius**.

**Flora.** She is not the same as Faula, discussed above. Flora is universally held to have been notorious as a prostitute. It was an image of Larentina—and indeed an image not of her body but of her disposition and character. For she was the wife of Faustulus and, because of the degraded promiscuity of her body, was called a *she-wolf* (*lupa*) among the shepherds, that is, a prostitute; hence a brothel is also called a *lupanar*. Evidently, in portraying her, the Romans followed the Athenians’ example. Among the Athenians, a certain prostitute named Leaena had killed a tyrant; but because it was sacrilegious to set up the image of a prostitute in a temple, they erected the likeness of the animal whose name she bore. Thus, as the Athenians made the memorial from her name, so the Romans made theirs from her profession. A feast day was also dedicated to her name, and the Larentinalia were instituted. Nor is she the only prostitute whom the Romans worship: they also worship Faula, whom Verrius writes to have been the prostitute of Hercules. How great, then, must this immortality be accounted, which even prostitutes attain?

**Those games are therefore celebrated, etc.** When these games were first celebrated in April, they were later transferred into May, as Ovid testifies:

> I postponed your portion in the preceding month.  
> You begin in April and pass into the season of May;  
> when one month comes, it has you as the other flees.

Alexander ab Alexandro, *Days of Festivity* VI.8, says that at these games it was customary for women who earned money by prostituting their bodies to be stripped naked and, with their shameful and obscene parts uncovered, to run about in sport and wantonness and perform shameless jests. The aediles were also accustomed to scatter chickpeas, beans, and other largesse among the common people, and to admit hares, roe deer, and other tame animals into the games. They celebrated them in the Patrician Street or nearby; at night, with torches lit, they ran through the city amid much obscenity of speech and assembled [Col. 0220B] at the sound of a trumpet. Hence our author says that these games were celebrated in a manner fitting the memory of a prostitute. Tightrope-walkers and elephants were also introduced at these games, as appears from Suetonius’ *Galba* and Flavius Vopiscus’ *Carinus*. Ovid left a full explanation of these games in book V of the *Fasti*; consult him. **Rosinus.**—St. Augustine writes against this obscenity in *The City of God*, book IV, ch. 26.—**Therefore those games, with every kind of wantonness.** On the Floral Games, or Floralia, mentioned above, and their license and obscenity, see Seneca, *Letter* 97; Valerius Maximus II.10.1; Martial, book I, epigram 1. **Cellarius.**

**Fittingly.** We have restored this from seventeen of the oldest and best manuscripts. Eight more recent manuscripts and the common editions read *fitting*. On these matters see Tertullian, pp. 697.3 and 216.6, and John Chrysostom, Homilies 6 and 7 on Matthew.

appointed the people her heir and left a fixed sum of money, from the annual interest on which her birthday was to be celebrated by presenting games called the Floralia.
