And the praetor Atilius vowed a temple to Mind in the year 537, the same year in which Quintus Fabius Maximus vowed one to Venus Erycina. Livy, book II of the third decade, and Gruter, p. 99, no. 7.

**The great Cicero.** Cellarius says that this passage of Cicero is lost. If you join section 17 of the present chapter to these words, there can scarcely be doubt that Lactantius had Cicero, *On the Laws* II.11, in view; Turnebus on the Ciceronian passage, fol. 147, thought so as well. **Bünemann.**

**That images of Cupids and Loves.** Thus Cicero among the fragments of book II of *On the Laws*, and our manuscripts and printed editions. Four more recent manuscripts have *of Cupid and Love*. Since this passage is not read in the books of *On the Laws* that we possess, but among their fragments, scholars believe Cicero’s books *On the Laws* to be incomplete.

**Ought to train toward honorable things.** Eleven manuscripts and some printed editions have *toward honorableness*. The Penwortham manuscript, two Colbertine manuscripts, and the Isaeus edition have *should have trained*.

[Col. 0222C]

**Corrupted men.** In book I, ch. 10, Lactantius joined *corrupters* and *adulterers*, following Cicero, *Against Verres* III.2. **Bünemann.**

**And at that age.** The preposition *at* was added from numerous manuscripts and editions.

**For virtues ought.** These are Cicero’s words in *On the Laws*, book II. They should therefore be expressed in the infinitive construction, in agreement with all the manuscripts, four early Roman editions, the Venetian edition of 1490, and Cellarius. The other printed editions have *ought* in the indicative construction.

**Do you not see that the vices will break in?** Thus nearly all manuscript and printed copies. Four recent manuscripts and six printed editions have *perhaps so that*.

**The Romans, Mildew.** He is called Rubigus in book I, in the account of Numa’s reign. Servius on *Georgics* I:

> Mildew is a kind of blight by which stalks perish, called a calamity by country people. This kind of blight commonly arises from mist, when crops blacken and are consumed. Hence also the god Rubigus; his rites on the tenth day before the Kalends of May are called the Rubigalia.

Pompeius Festus, book XVI:

> The Robigalia is a feast on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, on which they sacrificed to the god Robigus, who they thought could avert mildew.

Pliny XVIII.29 agrees, saying that the Robigalia were instituted by Numa in the eleventh year of his reign. See Columella, *On Agriculture* X, and Ovid, *Fasti* IV. From **Dempster.**—Varro, *On Agriculture* I, makes Robigus a god and couples him with Flora.

**Fever.** See Prudentius, *Hamartigenia*:

> Equal is the madness of those whom report says  
> consecrated Fever and Itch as goddesses in dedicated shrines.

Fever was worshipped by the Romans as a sort of goddess; she had a sanctuary on the Capitoline and an altar constructed on the Esquiline. Clement of Alexandria, *Protrepticus*; Pliny II.7; Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* III; Seneca, *The Death of Claudius*; Epictetus I.19; Augustine, *The City of God* III.12; Minucius Felix; Arnobius IV. **Johann Weitz.**—There also survives this inscription to Fever as a goddess:

> TO THE GODDESS FEVER. TO HOLY FEVER. TO GREAT FEVER. CAMILLA AMATA, FOR HER GRAVELY ILL SON.

See Ouzel’s *Inscriptions*, fol. 97, on Minucius Felix.—Valerius Maximus II.5.6: “They worshipped Fever in temples so that she might do less harm; one of these still stands on the Palatine.” Add Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* III.23. **Cellarius.**]

That act of Marcus Marcellus concerning the consecration of Honor and Virtue differs from this in the respectability of the names but agrees with it in substance. With the same vanity, the Senate also placed Mind among the gods; had it actually possessed a mind, it certainly would never have undertaken rites of this sort.

Cicero says that Greece adopted a great and bold policy when it consecrated images of Cupids and Loves in gymnasia. He was, of course, flattering Atticus and mocking his intimate friend. For it should not have been called a great policy—or a policy at all—but the ruined and deplorable wickedness of shameless men. They prostituted to the lust of young men the children whom they ought to have trained toward honorable things. They wished the gods of their crimes to be worshipped by those children, [Col. 0221B] especially in places where naked bodies lie exposed to the eyes of corrupted men, and at that age [Col. 0222A] which, being simple and improvident, can be ensnared and fall into traps before it can guard against them.

What wonder is it if every crime flowed from this people, among whom the very vices are objects of religion, and are not merely not avoided but even worshipped? Therefore, as though Greece were his superior in wisdom, Cicero added to this judgment: “For virtues, not vices, ought to be consecrated.” But if you accept this, Marcus Tullius, do you not see that the vices will break in along with the virtues, since evil clings to good and is more powerful in human minds? If you forbid the vices to be consecrated, that same Greece will answer you that it worships some gods so that they may help and others so that they may not harm.

For this is always the excuse of those who regard their evils as gods, as the Romans do Mildew and Fever. [Col. 0222B] If, then, vices are not to be consecrated—and on this point I agree with you—neither are virtues. For they do not themselves [Col. 0223A] possess wisdom or perception, and they should not be placed within walls or little shrines made of mud, but within the breast and embraced inwardly, lest they be false [Col. 0223A] [Note: [Col. 0223B] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 223–224]

**Lest they be false.** The Emmeram, Venetian 1471, 1493, and 1497, and Rostock editions have *lest they be fables*. **Bünemann.**

**Those.** Bünemann has *olla*, on which word he supplied the following note.—**Olla.** Thus most manuscripts and early editions. But two Leipzig manuscripts, Reimann, de Tournes, Sparke, and Walch have *illa*. Yet *olla* is the true reading. In legal formulas the ancients favored archaic words. This archaic word is repeatedly used in Cicero, *On the Laws* II.8.

**Praiseworthy things.** That is, things worthy of praise and virtues, according to Turnebus on Cicero, ch. 1, fol. 139. **Bünemann.**

**Let there be.** See Cicero, *On the Laws* II.8.

**Which you lack? For virtue must be cultivated.** We have restored this from almost all the manuscripts. Three more recent manuscripts and the printed editions, except Cellarius, have: “which we lack? Virtue must be cultivated.” Augustine says that virtue is not a god but a gift of God.

**And must be cultivated.** In two Bologna manuscripts, the Taxquet manuscript, and some editions, *must be* is absent; it is found in the others.

**As soon as he begins to will.** We have restored this from two Clermont manuscripts, a Colbertine manuscript, and the Roman 1470, Fasitel, Isaeus, and Cellarius editions, with the support of twelve manuscripts and several editions that read *as soon as he has begun to will*. The old Bologna manuscript has *as soon as he commenced*; Junius, one Colbertine manuscript, and five editions have *as soon as he commenced* instead of *as soon as he began*.

**The breast is a temple.** The Apostle has the same statement in 1 Corinthians 6:19.

**Let this be filled with those true names.** The true and excellent reading, found in the Royal manuscripts, three Colbertine manuscripts, and one Clermont manuscript. All the others are plainly wrong in reading “with those true names—indeed, false ones.” Another Clermont manuscript has “this more truly with those names.” By *names*, he means the virtues named above.

**Rushing to poison and the sword.** Thus all the manuscripts. The common editions have *to poison and sword*.

**Privately.** This reading, from the manuscripts and several editions, corresponds very well to the preceding adverb *publicly*. Junius, three Colbertine manuscripts, one Clermont manuscript in the first hand, and some editions read *among private persons*.

[Col. 0224B]

**With the tips of their fingers.** He is mocking the custom of the pagans, who ordinarily took objects prepared for sacrifice with two or three fingers. They cast incense into the flame of the altar in this manner. Jerome, Letter 1: “Service to an idol does not consist only in taking incense with two little fingers and casting it upon the altar’s pyre.” Porphyry, *On Abstinence from Animate Beings* (περὶ ἀποχῆς ἐμψύχων), says—at a materially uncertain passage transmitted as *Pythia Ermionea laetatum*—that, while sacrificing, [someone] took pieces of cake from a pouch with three fingers. Ovid, *Fasti* II:

> And with three fingers he places three grains of incense beneath the light.

See also Lactantius IV.3 and V.19–20. From **Isaeus.**—**With incense and with the tips of their fingers.** That is, with the extremities. He often writes in this way, in agreement with all the best authors, as we note on book V, ch. 10: “of which they bear the outermost shape.” **Bünemann.**

**To shudder at.** I judge, with Thomasius and the manuscripts he cites, that the text must be corrected thus. Add to these the Caucian, three Colbertine, Cambridge, Gotha, and Utrecht manuscripts, the Geneva editions of 1579 and 1613; Betuleius and Isaeus likewise read so. The text itself shows that this must be the reading, for Lactantius rebukes them because they worship vices which they ought instead to avoid and shudder at. The Emmeram manuscript has *to begin shuddering*. Others wrongly read *to worship*.

**The primary error.** This will be treated more fully in book II, which concerns the origin of error.

**When they had made artillery cords from women’s hair, etc.** Sehedius maintains that this happened when Rome was burned by the Senonian Suebi, or Gauls, and the Capitol was hemmed in by a difficult siege. When bowstrings failed, the surviving matrons cut off their hair; strings were made from it and fitted to the bows, and the enemy was finally driven off. Having thus regained their liberty, the Romans, in grateful remembrance of the event, erected a statue to Venus and gave her the epithet “Bald” because the matrons’ hair had been cut off. Vegetius relates this story in *On Military Affairs* IV.9, as does Servius on *Aeneid* I. “This often occurred in ancient wars,” says Isaac Casaubon in his *Notes on Capitolinus*, p. 188. Caesar, *Civil War* III, says of those besieged at Salona that “they cut off all the women’s hair and made artillery cords from it.” Dio also relates, in his account of Severus, that ropes were made from women’s hair in the besieged city of Byzantium. See Aristides’ *Rhodian Oration*. Nothing about this is found in Livy or Plutarch. Nevertheless, the temple of Venus the Bald is mocked by St. Cyprian in these words: “There is also Venus the Bald. She is far more disgraceful here as Bald than she was in Homer as wounded.” Augustine and Vegetius, book IV, also speak of her.]

if they are situated outside the human being. And so I ridicule that celebrated law of yours, which you frame in these words:

> But as for those things through which ascent into heaven is granted to a human being—Mind, Virtue, Piety, Faith—let there be shrines to them and to the praiseworthy things they represent.

Yet these cannot be separated from the human being. For if they are to be cultivated, they must necessarily exist within the human being himself. But if they are outside the human being, what need is there to cultivate things which you lack? For virtue itself must be cultivated, not an image of virtue; and it must be cultivated not by some sacrifice, incense, or solemn prayer, but by the will and purpose alone. For what else is it to cultivate virtue except to embrace and retain it in the mind? [Col. 0223B] Everyone attains it as soon as he begins to will it.

This alone is the worship of virtue; for no religion and reverence is to be maintained except that of the one God. What need is there, then, wisest of men, to occupy with superfluous structures sites that could be turned to human uses? Why appoint priests to worship vain and insensible things? Why slaughter victims? Why expend such great sums either in fashioning or in worshipping images? The human breast is a stronger and more incorruptible temple. Let it be adorned instead; let it be filled with those true names.

The inevitable consequence follows upon these false consecrations. For those who worship the virtues in this way—that is, those who pursue the shadows and images of virtues—cannot possess the things that are real. Thus there is no virtue in anyone, since vices rule everywhere; no good faith, since everyone seizes everything for himself; no dutiful affection, since greed spares neither blood relations nor parents, and desire rushes to poison and the sword; no peace, no concord, since wars rage publicly and private hostilities rage even to bloodshed; no chastity, since unbridled lusts defile every sex and every part of the body. [Col. 0224B] Yet they do not cease to worship the things they flee and hate. For with incense and the tips of their fingers they worship things at which they ought to shudder in their innermost feelings. This entire error descends from ignorance of that primary and supreme good.

When the Gauls occupied the City, the Romans were besieged on the Capitol. After making artillery cords from women’s hair, [Col. 0225A] they consecrated a temple to Venus the Bald. They therefore fail to understand how vain their religions are, even from the very fact that they mock them with such absurdities.

Perhaps they had learned from the Lacedaemonians to fabricate gods for themselves out of events. When the Lacedaemonians were besieging the Messenians, the latter secretly slipped out after deceiving the besiegers and hastened to plunder Lacedaemon; but they were routed and driven into flight by the Spartan women. When the Lacedaemonians learned of their enemies’ tricks, [Col. 0225A] [Note: [Col. 0225B] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 225–226]

**Their enemies’ tricks.** We have restored this from all the manuscripts and several editions. The other common editions have *their enemies’ ambushes*.

**Just as they were.** See above, book I, ch. 8. Here these words indicate the actual circumstances, not an unchanged condition of affairs. Cicero, *Brutus* 14: “Just as he was, wrapped in wool, so he came to the assembly.” Ovid, *Metamorphoses* V, story 10: “Just as I was, I fled without clothes.” Valerius Maximus IV.6: “His friends joined Plautius, just as he was, dressed in his toga and shoes, to his wife’s body”; and V.6, foreign example 4: “Girt with his sword, just as he was, he advanced.” **Bünemann.**

[Col. 0225C]

**The young men previously sent by them, mingled with the maidens.** After comparing the various readings of both manuscripts and printed copies, I judge that the text should be read thus. Three Royal manuscripts, one Colbertine, the Cambridge manuscript, and two Brunswick manuscripts have *previously sent, intermixed with the maidens*. Six Royal, two Bologna, five Colbertine, one Sorbonne, and two Clermont manuscripts, together with three old Roman editions, the Venetian edition of 1490, Egnatius or Aldus, Paris 1525, Florence, Cratander, and Grapheus, have *previously sent with the maidens*. Evidently the word *mingled*, badly copied by scribes, was changed into *sent* and afterward omitted by others as though duplicated. The Gymnich, Fasitel, and Thysius editions have *previously admitted with the maidens*. The Emmeram manuscript and the French and Sparke editions have *previously sent with the maidens*, which gives an entirely incomplete sense.

The history of this matter is related by Strabo. The Lacedaemonians made war upon the Messenians because the latter had killed King Teleclus when he went to perform a sacrifice, in the year 813 before the common era—because maidens had been raped, according to Justin. They swore that they would not return before they had captured Messene. But when their wives bore such a long delay with difficulty, the Lacedaemonians, remembering their oath and taking account of their wives, sent from the camp to Lacedaemon the strongest and youngest men, whom they knew not to be bound by the religious obligation of the oath. They ordered these men to have intercourse with all the maidens, judging that in this way their offspring would be more numerous. Those born in this manner were therefore called *Partheniae*, or “sons of maidens.” See Justin III.4.

**Partheniae.** I read thus with the oldest manuscripts: one Royal, one Bologna, two other Royal, one Colbertine, two Brunswick, and two other Colbertine manuscripts in the first hand. Aristotle, *Politics* V.7; and Justin, *Histories* III.4, read no differently. Nine recent manuscripts, however, together with the printed editions, have *Parthenii*; the Royal-Puteanus manuscript has *Partheni* in the first hand. See Pollux and Strabo, book VI.

**To Venus Armed.** See Pausanias III, in the account of Laconia, and Nonnus, *Dionysiaca* XXXV. At Rome, however, she was called Cluacina, that is, “armed,” from the verb *cluere*, which among the ancients meant “to fight.” From **Schedius.**

**To the Baker.** See Ovid, *Fasti* VI.

**Had warned them in sleep.** The histories say nothing of this dream; on the throwing of the loaves, consult Livy V.48 and Florus I.13. **Cellarius.**

**In sleep.** An elegant expression for “in a dream,” as often in Cicero, *On Divination* I.24; Valerius Maximus I.7, foreign examples 1, 6, and 10; and Lactantius II.7, note. **Bünemann.**

**Had warned.** The customary verb for dreams of this sort; *Epitome*, ch. 20. See Broukhusius on Tibullus 3.4.11, p. 314. **Bünemann.**

**Which they had.** Thus I have restored from the manuscripts. The printed editions have *which they might have*.

**The siege had been lifted.** Thus I have restored from the manuscripts. The printed editions have *the siege was lifted*.

[Col. 0226C]

**Mockery of religions.** Thus all correctly, except the Gotha manuscript, which has *diversity of religions*—wrongly. **Bünemann.**

**Name.** This is the reading of the manuscripts and five early editions. Two more recent Royal manuscripts and eight editions read *divine power*.

**The goddess Furnace.** The Fornacalia and their rites are explained by Plutarch, *Roman Questions*, ch. 89. Ovid, *Fasti* II and VI:

> The Oven (*Fornax*) was made a goddess; at the oven the joyful farmers  
> pray that she may duly regulate their crops.

In ancient times the Romans lived only on porridge, since the use of bread was unknown. Afterward, when they had learned the art of grinding and baking bread, they placed a goddess over their ovens. **Dempster.**

**At the Fornacalia.** Two Colbertine manuscripts and one Brunswick have *Furnacalia*; another Brunswick and three Colbertine manuscripts, together with the Roman edition of 1470, have *at the ovens*. See Ovid, *Fasti* II.—**In celebrating the Fornacalia.** In the month of February; Ovid, *Fasti* II.527:

> The chief Curio now proclaims the Fornacalia with the prescribed words,  
> but does not hold the rites on a fixed day.

**Cellarius.**

[Col. 0226D]

**Perform religious service.** In a sacred sense, as Livy I.31: “He joined them in performing these rites.” **Bünemann.**

**When he hears of the goddess Muta.** Called Tacita by Ovid, *Fasti* II.572. **Bünemann.**

**Lara.** See her story in Ovid, *Fasti* II.

**Caca.** Thus two very old Royal manuscripts and others, together with nearly all the printed editions. Most manuscripts and two editions have *Caeca* or *Ceca*; two Colbertine manuscripts have *Ceta*. Virgil, *Aeneid*, and Ovid, *Fasti* I.—**Caca, who gave Hercules information.** Virgil, book VIII, relates that Hercules found reliable evidence from the reversed tracks; but the betrayal by Cacus’ sister Caca was also added to the story. Servius mentions it on *Aeneid* VIII.190. **Bünemann.**

**Cunina.** Thus the editions and almost all manuscripts. Varro and St. Augustine, *The City of God* IV.8 and 11. But two Bologna manuscripts have *Cunia*; three Colbertine and the Penwortham manuscript, *Cuna*; one Colbertine, *Cuna*; another Colbertine, *Cunena*. On Juno Cunina see Pliny VII.2 and Gruter, *Inscriptions*, p. 96.

**And Stercutus.** Tertullian, *Apology* 25, has the three-syllable form *Sterculus*, as do the manuscripts: one old Royal-Puteanus in the first hand, two other Royal, the Vatican, two Colbertine, Navarre, Gotha, Caucian, Palatine, Victorine, and two Brunswick manuscripts, and the Cellarius edition. One old Bologna and one Colbertine manuscript have *Stercus*; one Royal, one Colbertine, Gataker, and many editions have *Sterculius*; one recent Bologna manuscript and Taxquet have *Sterculinus*. Eight manuscripts, two old Roman editions, and the Turin manuscript of the *Epitome*, ch. 21, have *Stercutus*. Three Royal manuscripts and the Marmoutier manuscript, as well as Augustine, *The City of God* XVIII.15, have *Stercutius*; one Royal has *Stercuatus*; another Royal, one Sorbonne in the first hand, and one Clermont in the second have *Stercatus*; one Colbertine has *Stercautus*; another Colbertine and Junius have *Stercurius*. Sterculus, the son of Faunus, attained immortality for discovering the use of manure on fields. See Tertullian, *Apology* 22, and Pliny XVII.9.—**And Sterculus.** The common text has the four-syllable *Sterculius*, but the Gotha manuscript and Tertullian, *Apology* 25, have the three-syllable form. Thus Prudentius, *Passion of St. Lawrence*, verse 450:

> The Senate worships two-faced Janus  
> and Sterculus.

**Bünemann.**]

the Lacedaemonians went in pursuit. Their armed women came out some distance to meet them. When the women saw their husbands preparing for battle because they thought them to be Messenians, they uncovered their bodies. Recognizing their wives and being aroused to lust by the sight, the men had intercourse with them, indiscriminately, just as they stood under arms; there was naturally no time to distinguish one from another. In the same manner, the young men previously sent by them mingled with the maidens, [Col. 0225B] from whom the Partheniae were born. To commemorate this deed, they erected a temple and image to Venus Armed. Although this originated from a disgraceful cause, it nevertheless seems more honorable to have consecrated an armed Venus [Col. 0226A] than a bald one.

At the same time an altar was also erected to Jupiter the Baker, because he had warned them in sleep to make bread from all the grain they had and throw it into the enemy camp. When this was done, the siege was lifted, because the Gauls despaired of being able to subdue the Romans by famine.

What mockery of religions is this? If I were their defender, what complaint could I make more gravely than that the name of the gods has fallen into such contempt that it is held up to ridicule under the most disgraceful names? Who would not laugh at the goddess Furnace, or rather at learned men performing rites in celebration of the Fornacalia? Who, on hearing of the Mute Goddess, could restrain his laughter? They say that the Lares were born from her, and they call her Lara, or Larunda. What can she provide for her worshipper when she cannot [Col. 0226B] speak? Caca too is worshipped: because she informed Hercules about the theft of the cattle, she attained divinity for betraying her brother. So too Cunina, who guards infants in their cradles and wards off bewitchment; Stercutus, who first introduced the method of manuring [Col. 0227A] a field; and Tutinus, [Col. 0227A]

> **[Note: [Col. 0227B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 227–228]]**
>
> **Tutinus.** It is remarkable how greatly the manuscript codices vary here, as they do in the preceding passage. I have restored *Tutinus* from nine Royal manuscripts, among which are two of the greatest antiquity; one old Bologna manuscript; six Colbert manuscripts; one Sorbonne manuscript; the Navarre, Victorine, Marmi, and Cambridge manuscripts; three Leipzig manuscripts; the manuscripts of Em., two Clermont, Pen., Tornes., and two Brun.; and the Roman edition of 1470 and Cratander’s marginal reading. In one Royal manuscript and the Gat. manuscript the reading is *Futinus*; in the more recent Bologna manuscript, erroneously, *Cutinus* for *Tutinus*, since C and F are easily changed into T. The Roman edition of 1468 has *Titinus*. In Arnobius, Lactantius’ teacher, *Against the Nations*, book IV, it is *Tutunus*, according to the very ancient Royal manuscript. In Augustine it is *Muttunus* and *Tutunus*, who is the same as Priapus. Hence Arnobius, book IV: “You regard it as both auspicious and desirable that your matrons should ride upon his enormous genitals and bristling phallus.” See *The City of God*, book VI, chapter 11. In the Cauc. manuscript, the editions of Tornes., Spark, and Walch, Tertullian’s *Apology*, chapter 25, and ten common editions, it is *Mutinus*. But however one reads it—*Tutinus*, *Tutunus*, or *Mutunus*—it matters little; for this god had both names from the obscene organ of each sex. He possessed the shameful part of both: μυττός (*myttos*), a Sicilian or Aeolic form for μυστός (*mystos*), means the female genital organ; from this came μυττών, μυττῶνος (*myttōn, myttōnos*) and the Roman *Muttonus*. Πόσθη (*posthē*) and ποσθών (*posthōn*) means one who has an enormous male organ, Aeolic ποθθών, ποθθῶνος (*poththōn, poththōnos*); from this came the Latin *Puttunus* and *Tuttunus*, for the Aeolians and the ancient Latins alike interchanged T and P. From Salmasius.—“He himself,” says Augustine in the passage cited above, “is Priapus among the Greeks, if one is not ashamed to say so.” He was also called *Tetinus*.
>
> **In whose shameful lap, etc.** A new bride sat in the lap of this god so that her marriage would not be barren. Augustine, *The City of God*, book VI, chapter 9: “But why should I mention this, when Priapus too, excessively male, is present there, and the new bride was commanded to sit upon his most enormous and disgraceful phallus, in accordance with the most honourable and religious custom of matrons?” Meursius.
>
> **Sit presiding.** *Praesident* is correct in Lactantius; for *praesidere* is the verb properly used of those officiating in a sacred rite. Janus Gulielmus.—**Sit presiding.** Heumann reads *resident* (“sit”) or, preferably, *sedent* (“are seated”). But all the books have *praesident*, which Gulielmus, chapter 1, defends as correct and as the verb properly used of those officiating in a sacred rite. On the matter itself, Arnobius, chapter 1: “Is there also Mutunus, upon whose enormous genitals and bristling phallus you regard it as both auspicious and desirable that your matrons should ride?” St Augustine, *The City of God*, book VI, chapter 9: “Since Priapus too, excessively male, is present there, and the new bride is commanded to sit upon his most enormous and disgraceful phallus.” Book VII, chapter 24: “In the celebration of marriages, the new bride was commanded to sit upon the shaft of Priapus.” Bunemann.
>
> [Col. 0228B]
>
> **Monstrosities.** On these monstrosities see Minucius Felix, chapter 25.
>
> **They venerate.** The Junian manuscript and several editions add “and worship.”—**They venerate.** Thus Bon., Tax., Pen., Cauc., Ult. Pal., Lips., and Goth.; whereas the Venetian editions of 1471 and 1497, Rost., Paris., Parrhas., Crat., Ald., Gymn., Gryph., and Tornes. have “they venerate and worship.” Nor is this a bad reading. Seneca, *On Clemency* I, chapter 19: “Let us behold the gods, venerating and worshipping them.” Lactantius himself couples “venerate and worship” in book II, chapter 5, and book III, chapter 9; and in the *Epitome*, chapter 25: “to be worshipped and venerated.” Compare book I, chapter 15, and book II, chapter 5. Cicero himself, *On the Nature of the Gods* I, chapter 42: “to worship, pray to, and venerate the gods”; and book II, chapter 28: “both to venerate and to worship the gods.” Bunemann.
>
> **What? Those who worship a stone.** Nearly all the manuscripts, as well as the older and better editions, have this reading. The Christ. manuscript, two Colbert manuscripts, and five editions have: “What of the fact that they worship a stone?”
>
> **Terminus.** In ancient times a stone was placed when fields were being bounded. Virgil, *Aeneid* XII:
>
> [Col. 0228C]  
> An ancient, enormous stone that happened to lie upon the plain,  
> Set as the boundary of a field, to distinguish disputed farmland.
>
> Papinius, *Thebaid* V:
>
> With an enormous effort he seizes the stone  
> By which the field was marked off.
>
> It was not only a stone, however, but sometimes also a post, as Lactantius adds later and as the poet relates in book II of the *Fasti*:
>
> Terminus, whether you are a stone or a post abandoned in a field,  
> You too possess a name derived from the ancients.
>
> A statue was erected to this god in the form of a square stone or hewn post, anointed and crowned. See L. Seneca, *Hippolytus*, act II, scene 1. The Terminalia, sacred to this god, are celebrated in February with great rustic solemnity, but their form of worship differed according to the age. Numa would permit no living creature to be sacrificed to this god, as Plutarch reports in his *Life* and in chapter 14 of the *Roman Questions*. Later, however, this method of sacrifice was changed, and a living victim was slaughtered for Terminus, as for the other gods. See M. Cicero, *Philippic* XII, and others. The victim could be a sow, according to Ovid, *Fasti* II. Dempster.—See Florus, book I, chapter 7, and Ovid, *Fasti* II, 690.—**Terminus alone.** On the contrary, the goddess Juventas also proved obstinate together with Terminus, as is attested by other authors whom Rycquius cites in *On the Roman Capitol*, chapter 9, page 81, and chapter 14, at the beginning, concerning Terminus. Compare Livy, book I, chapter 55. Bunemann.
>
> **The Capitol.** The story is found in Livy, book I and near the end of book V; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book II; and Plutarch, *Numa*.
>
> **And in that place.** The manuscripts have *eoque in loco* (“and in that place”); the editions, *atque eo in loco*.
>
> **Would yield.** Thus the manuscripts except three recent ones, which have “were willing to yield.” Several recent editions have, erroneously, “believe” and “to those believing.”
>
> **The poet.** *Aeneid* IX, verse 448:
>
> The Capitol’s immovable rock.
>
> **Now … how great.** Similar irony occurs in book I, chapter 20: “Now how great must that immortality be thought,” etc. Bunemann.

in whose shameful lap brides sit presiding, so that the god may appear to have been the first to violate their chastity; and a thousand other monstrosities, so that we must now say that those who have undertaken to worship these things are even more foolish than the Egyptians, who venerate certain monstrous and ridiculous images. And yet these at least have some form. What of those who worship a shapeless, unworked stone whose name is Terminus? [Col. 0228A] This is the one whom Saturn is said to have swallowed instead of Jupiter; and honour is not undeservedly paid to him. For when Tarquin wished to build the Capitol, and the shrines of many gods stood in that place, he consulted them by augury as to whether they would yield to Jupiter. All the others yielded, but Terminus alone remained. Hence the poet calls him

> The Capitol’s immovable rock.

Now from this very incident we discover how great Jupiter is, [Col. 0229A] since a stone did not yield to him—perhaps confident because it had delivered him from his father’s throat. Accordingly, when the Capitol had been built, an opening was left in the roof directly above Terminus, so that, because he had not yielded, he might enjoy the open sky; [Col. 0229A]

> **[Note: [Col. 0229B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 229–230]]**
>
> **Might enjoy the open sky.** Thus Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* V, 13: “Birds enjoy the open sky.” Seneca, *To Polybius*, chapter 28, at the end: “He now enjoys the unobstructed and open sky.” Bunemann.
>
> **Concerning sacred rites.** Read Alexander ab Alexandro, book VI, final chapter; Tiraquellus; Vossius, *Idolatry* I, chapter 35, and book II; and Crenius, *Annotations*, part IX, pages 77 following. Bunemann.
>
> **Among the Cypriots, a human victim.** We have restored this from all the manuscripts: the two oldest, namely one Bologna and one Royal manuscript; six other Royal manuscripts; two Brun. manuscripts; Cauc.; one Colbert manuscript; Nav.; Pal.; Lips.; Jun.; Vict.; Pen.; Ultr.; one Clermont manuscript; Marm.; as well as the Roman edition of 1470 and Cellarius. The Regio-Puteanus manuscript, four Colbert manuscripts, two Leipzig manuscripts, one Clermont manuscript, one Sorbonne manuscript, Gat., and the Roman edition of 1468 add *autem* (“however”). Many editions have “At Salamis in Cyprus.”—**Among the Cypriots, a human victim.** *Epitome*, chapter 23: “A human victim was customarily sacrificed to Cyprian Jupiter, as Teucer had instituted.” Betuleius elucidates the matter. Bunemann.
>
> [Col. 0229C]
>
> **Teucer.** Strabo, book XIV, attests that Salamis in Cyprus was founded by Teucer in exile. Teucer, the son of Telamon, was exiled because he had not avenged the death of his brother Ajax, who had perished through the intrigues of Ulysses, and because he had returned without him. Moreover, these human sacrifices of the Salaminians were abolished under Hadrian, according to Marcellinus, book XIV.
>
> **During Hadrian’s reign.** Four recent manuscripts have “by the emperor Hadrian.”—**Abolished under Hadrian.** That Hadrian abolished these rites is found neither in Dio, Spartianus, nor Eutropius. Eusebius writes that in Hadrian’s time these mists of impious error were dispersed by the radiance of the Gospel sun. Eutropius, however, says that in Trajan’s time Salaminia—as he, with Pliny, calls it—was destroyed by the Jews. Spartianus does indeed state that Hadrian carefully maintained the Roman sacrifices, but neglected foreign ones. From Acts of the Apostles, chapter 13, it is certain that Paul and Barnabas proclaimed the word of God in the Jewish synagogues at Salamis in Cyprus. [Col. 0229D] It was later called Constantia after Constantius. Betuleius.
>
> **There was a law among the Taurians.** Prudentius recounts this people’s rites in his book *Against Symmachus*, as does Juvenal, satire 15:
>
> In vain do we now habitually arraign the Taurian rites:  
> Human blood is poured out in the Latian ceremony.
>
> Thus Prudentius. King Thoas was the originator of this sacrifice, whence Diana is called *Thoantea* by Silius Italicus. See also Pomponius Mela, book II, in the chapter on European Scythia.—**There was a law among the Taurians.** A people beyond the Euxine Sea. Ovid in exile, *Tristia* IV, elegy 4, verse 63:
>
> Nor far from us is the place where the dreadful Taurian altar  
> Of the quiver-bearing goddess is fed with slaughter. Cellarius.
>
> **The Gauls appeased Hesus.** Lucan, *Pharsalia* I. This Hesus is Mars. In the Hebrew idiom the name means “strong”; for *Hesus* means strength. Mars, moreover, according to the pagans, presides over war; it therefore follows that he is strong. At Edessa in Mesopotamia, Belus, or the Sun, was worshipped in the temple of the Sun from the most ancient times. Alongside him they also worshipped Mercury, whom they called Monimus, and Mars, whom they called Aezizus. Schedius.
>
> [Col. 0230B]
>
> **They appeased Teutates with human blood.** This Teutates is Mercury. Livy, book XXVI: “Scipio turned toward the mound that they call Mercury Teutates.” Teutates, therefore, is to the Gauls the same as Τάαυτος (*Taautos*) to the Phoenicians and Thouth, Theuth, or Thoth to the Egyptians, about whom more was said above. Minucius Felix reports that the Gauls slaughtered human victims for Mercury. Tertullian: “A person of greater age is cut down as a sacrifice to Mercury among the Gauls.” Caesar, *The Gallic War* VI, on the Gauls: “They worship Mercury above all as a god … they sacrifice human beings as victims.” These rites were performed through the Druids; the same author says in the same place: “They—the Druids—take part in divine affairs, conduct public and private sacrifices, and interpret religious observances.” Suetonius writes that this dreadful savagery was completely abolished by Claudius. It was not under Tiberius, but under Augustus, that citizens were forbidden to sacrifice a human being. Pliny relates that in the 657th year from the founding of Rome, when Cornelius Lentulus and Publius Licinius Crassus were consuls, a decree of the Senate was passed [Col. 0230C] forbidding the sacrifice of a human being. See Betuleius, Tertullian’s *Apology*, chapter 8, and Mela, book III. Lucan speaks of these gods in book I in these words:
>
> And those by whom pitiless Teutates is appeased with slaughtered blood,  
> And Hesus, dreadful at his savage altars. Betuleius.
>
> **Latian Jupiter.** Seven manuscripts have *Latiaris*. Both readings are sound. For it is well known that in Latin books Jupiter’s epithet is written both *Latialis* and *Latiaris*. Consequently, some Greeks too retained the *r* in this word, as Porphyry does in *On Abstinence*. Isaac Casaubon. Clement of Alexandria also attacks this abominable ἀνθρωποκτονία (*anthrōpoktonia*, “slaughter of human beings”) in the *Protrepticus*. That inhuman sacrifice had been instituted by Tarquin the Proud on the Alban Mount; see Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book I. The altar of Taurian Diana was notorious for this form of superstition. At Pella, too, a human being was sacrificed to Achilles and Chiron; the Lesbians sacrificed to Bacchus with the same kind of victims. Indeed, the Athenian Erechtheus and the Roman Marius slaughtered their own daughters: the former to Proserpina, the latter to the averting gods. Arnobius, *Against the Nations* II: “Before Hercules’ arrival in Italy, when, at Apollo’s direction, supplication was made to Father Dis and Saturn with human heads.” On this same savagery, see also Athenagoras, justly complaining in his *Plea for the Christians*. Eusebius too has much on these matters in *Preparation for the Gospel* IV, chapter 17. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities* I, relates from Porphyry that Hercules abolished this more-than-bestial savagery in Italy and elsewhere. Petrus Pantinus.—Bunemann reads *Latiaris* and annotates the passage as follows: “I have corrected it,” he says, “from the Goth. and Cauc. manuscripts to *Latiaris*. The manuscript of the distinguished Puteanus also has the same reading in Lactantius here, according to Lambinus on Cicero’s *For Milo*, chapter 31, where this word is defended from a manuscript by Gruter and Graevius. It also appears in the Turin *Epitome*, chapter 23.”—**Latian Jupiter is even now worshipped with blood.** Tertullian raises the same objection in the *Apology*, chapter 9, and the *Scorpiace*, chapter 7; Minucius Felix, page 297—where see Elmenhorst—and Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* I, verse 396. The rite is not sufficiently known. It appears that, at an amphitheatrical spectacle, a criminal or condemned person was customarily slaughtered as a victim for the purpose of taking the auspices. Bunemann.

a sky that even those who thought the stone enjoyed it did not themselves enjoy. Public supplication is therefore made to this god as the guardian of boundaries, although he is not only a stone but sometimes even a wooden post. What am I to say about those who worship such things, except that they themselves are above all stones and wooden posts?
