## CHAPTER XXI  
### Concerning Certain Gods Peculiar to the Barbarians, Their Sacred Rites, and Likewise Those of the Romans

We have spoken about the gods themselves who are worshipped; now a few things must be said about their sacred rites and mysteries. Among the Cypriots, Teucer sacrificed a human victim to Jupiter, and he handed down that sacrifice to posterity; it was only recently abolished during Hadrian’s reign. There was a law among the Taurians, an inhuman and savage people, that foreign guests should be sacrificed to Diana; and that sacrifice was celebrated for many ages. The Gauls appeased Hesus and Teutates with human blood. Nor indeed were the Latins free of this savagery, since Latian Jupiter [Col. 0231A] is even now worshipped with human blood. What good do those who sacrifice in this way pray for from the gods? [Col. 0231A]

> **[Note: [Col. 0231B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 231–232]]**
>
> **What good do those who sacrifice in this way pray for from the gods?** Eleven manuscripts, together with many editions, have “What good do they pray for from these?” One Royal manuscript, one Colbert manuscript, Nav., Vict., and Brun. have “What good do they pray for from such gods?” One Royal manuscript, one Colbert manuscript, and four editions have, erroneously, “What good does he who sacrifices in this way pray for from these?” The Junian manuscript and the French edition of 1563 have “to whom they sacrifice in this way.”—**What good do they pray for from these?** Thus all the manuscripts and editions, which it is fairer to follow than one Gotha manuscript that is not wholly sound; for the latter has: “What good things from the gods?” The sense is straightforward: “What good do they pray for from these,” namely, gods? Bunemann.
>
> **Do they pray for.** Thus, correctly, Goth., three Leipzig manuscripts, Reimm., Rost., the Venetian edition of 1471, the second edition of 1478, the Paris edition of 1513, Tornes., Betul., and Cell., whereas the first editions of 1478, 1493, and 1497, Parrh., [Col. 0231C] Ald., Gymn., Gryph., Crat., Thomas., Isaeus, Gall., and the Cambridge edition erroneously have the singular “does he pray for,” although “they sacrifice” follows in all the witnesses. From this one may recognize the editors’ carelessness. Bunemann.
>
> **Depart from.** Justin, on the Scythians, book II, chapter 2.—**Depart from humanity.** Two Leipzig manuscripts and Reimm. erroneously have “cease from humanity.” In book IV, chapter 11, “depart from the law”; and in *On Anger*, chapter 23, we have restored “depart from piety.” Bunemann.
>
> **Slip into evil deeds.** “I suspect,” says Heumann, “that Lactantius wrote *delabuntur* (‘slide down into’).” But the simple verb is correct. Lactantius, book IV, chapter 1: “having lapsed into these … fragile gods”; book VI, chapter 13: “who slip into sin”; in the same book, chapter 24: “he has slipped onto the path of injustice.” Cicero himself, *For Sestius*, chapter 55: “to slip into an unfamiliar kind of speaking.” Bunemann.
>
> **In Latium.** On this, St Augustine and St Athanasius.
>
> **Milvian.** The Brun. manuscripts have *Molbian*. Today it is called Ponte Molle.
>
> **Oracle.** This oracle is found in Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I, chapter 7.
>
> [Col. 0231D]
>
> **Καὶ κεφαλὰς Ἀΐδῃ** (“And heads to Hades”). We have restored this from the two oldest Royal manuscripts, as well as another, more recent Royal manuscript; one Colbert manuscript; Cauc.; Nav.; Vict.; Marm.; and two Brun. manuscripts. To these may be added one Sorbonne manuscript, which has καὶ κεφαλὰς Αι καὶ instead of Ἀΐδῃ, and one Clermont manuscript, which has Καὶ κεφαλὰς Διί (“And heads to Zeus”). Nine more recent manuscripts and the editions have καὶ κεφαλὰς Κρονίδῃ (“and heads to the son of Cronus”). The Greek is absent from several witnesses. But Ἀΐδῃ is also found in Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I, chapter 7; Pontanus contends in his notes on Macrobius that this is the correct reading, and the very learned Baluzius and Francius agree. In Latin: “Send both heads to Saturn and lights—or a human being—to the father.”
>
> **ΦΩΤΑ.** We have removed every accent so that the ambiguity of the oracle may be preserved, since the line deliberately contains it. This word must always be written without an accent when it is ambiguous, so that it may signify both “a human being” and “light”: with a grave accent it denotes a human being; with a circumflex, light. Isaeus.—Indeed, the circumflex can be restored without destroying the ambiguity, since Φῶτα may be referred either to φώς, φωτός, “human being,” in the accusative singular, or to φῶς, φωτός, “light,” in the accusative plural. The very learned Isaeus does not assert in accordance with grammar that the word ΦΩΤΑ, stripped of every accent, can signify a human being as well as light: for φῶς, understood as “light,” is neuter, but masculine if understood as “human being”; and since every neuter noun has the same form in the accusative as in the nominative in both numbers, it follows that ΦΩΤΑ signifies either “a human being” or “lights.” After Φῶτα, two Bologna manuscripts add *hominem* (“a human being”); two Brun. manuscripts interpret it as *lumina* (“lights”). Because of this ambiguity in the noun, both a torch, says Lactantius, and a human being were customarily thrown in.
>
> **To have thrown into the water.** The Gotha manuscript uses the ablative case, “in the water”; compare *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 21, at the end: “they were thrown in the river.” But Ovid and Lactantius himself below have “was thrown into the Tiber.” Bunemann.
>
> **Throw the counterfeit bodies.** Ovid has *jaci* (“to be thrown”), as does the Lactantian edition. Isaeus.—**To be thrown.** All the manuscripts and editions have *jace* (“throw”), except Isaeus, who here printed Ovid’s *jaci* (“to be thrown”), which I have accepted as more correct; “to have thrown” preceded it. Bunemann.
>
> **For as to the infants who were sacrificed to the same Saturn, etc.** The author again mentions this savage sacrifice a little later in this same chapter; we shall therefore explain the two passages together. Saturn, whom the Greeks call Κρόνος (*Cronos*), is generally thought to be Moloch: infants or children were common victims for both. Those abominable rites appear to have migrated from Syria into Europe and Africa. Anyone investigating the human victims offered to the European Saturn should be referred to Ovid’s *Fasti*, Macrobius, and other readily accessible authors. Of the Carthaginians, who were a colony of the Syrians, Ennius writes:
>
> It was their custom to sacrifice their own children to the gods.
>
> The line is found in Nonius Marcellus under the word *puellis*. Those who lacked children bought them from the poor in order to slaughter them; this we learn from Plutarch. St Athanasius, *Oration Against the Greeks*: Φοίνικες καὶ Κρῆτες τὸν Κρόνον ἐν ταῖς τεκνοθυσίαις ἐθρήσκευον (“The Phoenicians and Cretans worshipped Cronos with sacrifices of children”). Tertullian writes in the *Apology*, chapter 9, that this impious custom endured in Africa until the time of Tiberius: “In Africa,” he says, “infants were sacrificed publicly to Saturn down to the proconsulate of Tiberius.” Similar statements are found in Minucius Felix. Selden.
>
> **What am I to say? I cannot find words; that people were so barbarous.** Thus the oldest Bologna and Royal manuscripts, one Clermont manuscript, and others divide and read the passage, together with nearly all the editions. Eight recent manuscripts and the Roman and Venetian editions have this punctuation: “What am I to say? I cannot discover people so barbarous,” etc. It is an expression of astonishment: “I marvel” or “I am stupefied that people were so barbarous,” etc. The French translation of 1563 followed this reading.
>
> **Should call it a sacrifice … should destroy.** “What victim provokes mercy?” asked Justin, XVIII, 6; see also Curtius, book IV, chapters 3 and 23.
>
> **Innocent.** Gronovius excellently illustrates the force of this word in his note on Minucius, section 2, pages 9–10, on the words “while their years were still innocent.” Bunemann.

Or what can such gods provide for human beings, when it is by their torments that they are propitiated? But there is not so much cause for wonder in the case of barbarians, whose religion accords with their character. Yet are not our own people—who have always claimed for themselves the glory of gentleness and humanity—found to be more savage because of these sacrilegious rites? For those who, although refined by the study of the liberal disciplines, depart from humanity are to be regarded as more wicked than those who, crude and uneducated, slip into evil deeds through ignorance of what is good.

It is nevertheless apparent that this rite of sacrificing human beings is ancient, since Saturn was worshipped in Latium with the same kind of sacrifice—not, indeed, by slaughtering a human being at an altar, but by throwing one from the Milvian Bridge into the Tiber. Varro attests that this practice arose from a certain oracle, whose final line is as follows:

[Col. 0231B]

> Καὶ κεφαλὰς Ἀΐδῃ καὶ τῷ πατρὶ πέμπετε φωτα.  
> And send heads to Hades, and *phōta*—lights/a man—to the father.

[Col. 0232A] Because this appears ambiguous, both a torch and a human being were customarily thrown in for him. But this kind of sacrifice is said to have been abolished by Hercules when he was returning from Spain, though the ritual remained, so that images made of rushes were thrown in place of actual human beings, as Ovid teaches in the *Fasti*:

> Until the Tirynthian came into these fields, each year  
> The grim rites were performed in the Leucadian manner.  
> He threw straw Romans into the water:  
> Let counterfeit bodies be thrown, after Hercules’ example.

The Vestal Virgins perform these rites, as the same author says:

> Then too the virgin is accustomed to throw the rush-woven images  
> Of men of old from the oaken bridge.

For as to the infants who were sacrificed to the same Saturn because of his hatred for Jupiter, I cannot find words; that people were so barbarous and so savage that they called their own murder of their children—that is, an act loathsome and execrable to the human race—a sacrifice; that they should destroy tender and innocent [Col. 0233A] lives, the very age that is especially dear to parents, [Col. 0233A]

> **[Note: [Col. 0233B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 233–234]]**
>
> **Especially … dearer.** A singular construction, in place of “especially dear” or “dearest.” See Heusinger on Vechner’s *Hellenolexia*, page 171. Bunemann.
>
> **Parental affection.** The love of parents toward their children; see book IV, chapter 17, and *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 32. Bunemann.
>
> **Among the altars … crimes.** Cyprian, Oxford edition, folio 17, *To Donatus*; book II, epistle 2, Basel edition: “Transgression is committed amid the very laws; sin amid legal rights.” Bunemann.
>
> **Festus.** Nothing about this is found in the authors, not even in Gregorius Gyraldus. Hence many regard this reading as suspect.
>
> **Relates in the Books of Miscellaneous History.** *Satyra*, or *satura*, in this passage means, according to Vossius’ interpretation, “in a mixed and varied fashion,” without distinction of nation or chronological order; or, according to others, “indiscriminately,” or “in books filled with great variety and abundance”—what we would call a miscellaneous history.
>
> **The Carthaginians to Saturn.** This sacrifice is mentioned by Tertullian, Eusebius, and St Augustine, in addition to Justin and Curtius, already cited; nor was Plato unaware of it in the dialogue entitled *Minos*.
>
> **By Agathocles.** On the deeds of Agathocles in Africa see Justin, book XXI; Diodorus Siculus, books XI and XVII; and Plutarch, *Pyrrhus*.
>
> **So great, etc.** These two verses were written by Lucretius in different places: namely, *On the Nature of Things* I, verse 102, and V, verse 84. The latter, however, is slightly altered here.
>
> **Had killed.** Three thousand Carthaginians are said to have fallen on that occasion. Alexander ab Alexandro collected examples of this sacrilegious sacrifice in his *Genial Days*.
>
> **The Mother of the Gods, etc.** She also had other names; properly she was called Rhea or Cybele. Tatian the Assyrian, *Oration Against the Nations*: “Rhea, whom they call Cybele in the Phrygian mountains, established by law the cutting away of male genitalia because of Attis, whom she loved.” See Prudentius, *Hymn on Romanus*:
>
> But this man dedicates genitals that must be reaped,  
> Appeasing the deity with flesh cut from his groin.  
> Half a man, he offers his shameful organ as a gift to the goddess;  
> By tearing away the channel of his masculine seed,  
> He feeds her and increases her with his flowing blood.
>
> See also Augustine, *The City of God* VII, chapter 6. That emasculation was performed to the sound of a pipe. The music both incited men to mutilation with frenzied madness and immediately afterwards lessened the pain of those who had been castrated. Elias of Crete gives these reasons in his commentary on Nazianzen’s *Oration Against Julian*. For the Phrygian mode has the power to inflame people and inspire them with a kind of frenzy. Hence Lucretius, book II:
>
> And the hollow pipe, with Phrygian rhythm, goads their minds.
>
> Likewise Ovid in *Fasti* IV and in the *Ibis*. It is established that men emasculated in this way were called *Galli*. In the note on chapter 7 of this book, we observed from Betuleius that they were so called after the river Gallus. Vossius also supports this and thinks that they were likewise named after a man named Gallus, who was perhaps Cybele’s first priest. Indeed, one reads in Stephanus: “Both Gallus and Attis cut off their genitals. Gallus came to the river Tyrias, lived there, and named it Gallus; for from him they call those whose genital organ has been cut off *Galli*.” In the rites of Cybele and Attis these Galli imitated Cybele mourning for Attis; accordingly, they both wailed and beat their breasts with their palms. A pine tree was also set up in remembrance of the pine beneath which Attis had castrated himself. Its branches were adorned with garlands because Cybele had honoured the pine in that way. Its trunk was wrapped in wool because Cybele had covered the breast of the lifeless Attis with wool to give it warmth. They abstained from bread because Cybele had abstained from it in her grief. See Arnobius, book V. Vossius.
>
> **Bellona.** See book V, chapter 10, and the commentators on Minucius, chapter 30. Seneca, as quoted by Augustine, *The City of God* VI, chapter 10, splendidly illustrates this reading. It is explained by Lipsius, *Selections* II, chapter 18; Nicolaus Abram on Cicero’s *Against Piso*, chapter 20; and Broekhusius on Tibullus I, chapter 7, page 132. Compare Pitiscus, *Lexicon of Roman Antiquities*, volume I, folio 270. Bunemann.
>
> **In which the priests themselves, etc.** Tertullian, *Apology*, chapters 9 and 24: “Even today, in that place, blood consecrated to Bellona, caught from a slashed thigh in a small shield”—I think *parmulam* must be read—“is given to those initiated with her mark.” Minucius Felix: “Bellona imbues her servant by making him drink human blood.” Lucan, book I:
>
> … whom savage Bellona, when their arms are slashed,  
> Inspires.
>
> [Col. 0234D]
>
> St Augustine, *The City of God* VII, chapter 25, also censures the Galli emasculated in this way. This custom was later changed: only a simulated cutting or severing of limbs was retained, while the real act was abolished. I infer this from Aelius Lampridius in his *Commodus*: “In his zeal for cruelty, he commanded the servants of Bellona actually to cut their arms.” Dempster.—It is probable that they received this custom from the Baalites, for in the worship of their god Baal the priests cut themselves with knives, as may be seen in 1 Kings 18:28. Gallaeus.
>
> **They are carried away; they rave.** Whatever Dempster and Gallaeus may say, we have refused to change anything against the evidence of all the manuscript and printed codices. Indeed, Lactantius himself has “he is carried away; he raves” in book IV, chapter 27, around the middle. He appears to have imitated Cicero, *For Caelius*, chapter 9: “Those who are injured grieve; the angry are carried away; those provoked fight.”
>
> **Quintilian in *The Fanatic*.** The work is not extant. Cellarius.

without any regard for parental affection, and surpass the savagery of all beasts in cruelty, although beasts still love their offspring! O incurable madness! What more could those gods do to them if they were utterly enraged than they do when propitious, since they defile their worshippers with the murder of their children, punish them with bereavement, and strip them of human feeling? What can be sacred to such people? Or what will they do in profane places, when they commit the greatest crimes among the altars of the gods?

Pescennius Festus, in his *Books of Miscellaneous History*, relates that the Carthaginians customarily sacrificed human victims to Saturn; and that, when they had been defeated by Agathocles, king of the Sicilians, they believed that the god was angry with them. Accordingly, to discharge the expiation more scrupulously, they sacrificed two hundred sons of the nobility.

> So potent was religion in persuading men to evil,

[Col. 0233B]

> which has often produced criminal and impious deeds.

Whose interests, then, did those utterly mad people serve by that sacrifice, [Col. 0234A] when they killed as great a part of the citizenry as perhaps even the victorious Agathocles had not killed?

No less insane than this class of rites must those public rites be judged. Some are the rites of the Mother of the Gods, in which men make an offering with their own male organs: for by amputating their sex they make themselves neither men nor women. Others are the rites of Virtus, whom they also call Bellona, in which the priests themselves sacrifice not another’s blood, but their own. For after cutting their shoulders, they run about wielding drawn swords in each hand; they are carried away, they rave, they go mad. Quintilian therefore speaks excellently in *The Fanatic*: “If a god compels this,” he says, “he is angry.”

Are these things too sacred rites? Is it not better to live like cattle than to worship gods so impious, so profane, so bloodthirsty? But where those errors and such great crimes originated we shall discuss in the appropriate place. Meanwhile, let us also examine the other rites that are free of crime, lest [Col. 0235A] we appear, from eagerness to attack them, to be selecting the worse examples. [Col. 0235A]

> **[Note: [Col. 0235B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 235–236]]**
>
> **To be selecting the worse examples.** The manuscripts and both the 1478 editions, as well as those of 1493 and 1497 and others, more correctly have this reading than the Sublac., Venetian 1471, and Rost. editions, which read “to be selecting the better examples.” Cyprian expresses the same idea in book II, epistle 2, folio 34: “Lest we perhaps appear to be selecting the worse examples and, from eagerness to destroy, to be directing your eyes through them.” Bunemann.
>
> **Of Isis.** Diodorus Siculus, in book I of the *Library*, says that *Isis* in the Egyptian language means “ancient.” Under the name of Isis the Egyptians worshipped the moon; hence horns were attributed to her, because the moon presents such an appearance when waxing and waning. They say that she was the first of all to discover wheat and barley in Egypt. Hence the Egyptians had a custom by which reapers plucked ripe ears for a sheaf and, invoking Isis, offered them to the gods. From this it is clear that Isis was the same as the Greeks’ Ceres. From Vossius and Schedius.—**Of Isis.** See Plutarch, *On Isis*; Witsius, *Egyptiaca* II, chapter 3, and III, chapter 4; Tertullian, *Against Marcion* I, 13. Bunemann.
>
> **The Egyptian rites of Isis.** Likewise in Minucius Felix, *Octavius*, page 6. Five Royal manuscripts, four Colbert manuscripts, and Brun. have “of the Egyptian Isis.” Both readings are sound. Augustine, *The City of God* VI, chapter 10, reads: “In the Egyptian rites, the loss of Osiris is mourned”; and before St Augustine, Theophilus, in his first discourse *To Autolycus*, ridicules this vanity. See also Diodorus Siculus, book IV, and Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* II, chapter 1, concerning Osiris and Isis.
>
> **Her priests, their bodies shaved, etc.** Herodotus testifies in *Euterpe* that the Egyptian priests customarily shaved their entire bodies and clipped themselves every third day, lest they incur ritual pollution from the filth of hair while sacrificing, or lest anything in the way of lice or other excremental filth pollute them during the worship of the gods. In the same sense Martial, book X, calls that crowd of petty priests a “depilated cohort”—that is, bald or hairless, with every hair plucked from every part of the body. Henricus Salmuth.—If anyone desires more, let him consult Heraldus on Martial, book XII, epigram 29.
>
> **Their breasts.** One Colbert manuscript and two Brun. manuscripts add “bare.”
>
> **Lucan.** Lactantius is mistaken: the passage is found not in Lucan but in Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IX, verse 793.
>
> **Really happened.** We have restored this from nearly all the manuscripts and editions. Four Royal manuscripts, two Colbert manuscripts, and four editions have “was true.”
>
> **Covered with wood.** Three Royal Lactantian manuscripts, the Balliol manuscript, and Lucan have “covered with linen”; the other manuscripts of Lactantius and all the editions have “with wood.”
>
> **Whom they call Serapis.** Thus nine manuscripts, together with the editions of Tornes., Isaeus, and Cellarius. The other editions, together with four manuscripts, have *Serapin*. Fifteen manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1468 have *Serapem*. Serapis, or Sarapis as the Greeks call him, is the same as Apis, the god of the Egyptians, according to Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* I, and Augustine, *The City of God* XVIII, chapter 5. Most authorities maintain that under the name of Serapis the Egyptians worshipped Joseph, Jacob’s son, because he provided grain for the Egyptians in a time of the greatest scarcity. Firmicus expressly says that Apis was a symbol of Joseph. See Rufinus, book II, chapter 23. Plutarch has a book concerning Isis and Serapis.
>
> **Or Serapides.** Thus all the manuscripts. Several editions have “and Serapides.”
>
> **Was made Quirinus.** We have restored this from the editions of Tornes. and two Leipzig editions, as well as from all the manuscripts except two recent Royal ones. The other editions have “was called.” On the change of his name, see Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Livy, and Plutarch.
>
> **And Leda, Nemesis.** Probus the grammarian likewise observes that Ariadne, after being granted immortality, was called Libera; and Nicanor of Cyrene writes that Melicertes was renamed Glaucus after his death. We read that this privilege was not granted only to the dead, but that the names of the living too were changed and obscured by surnames. For it is established that Polyxena, the mother of Alexander of Macedon, was afterwards called Myrtale, Olympias, and also Stratonice. Hadrianus Junius.—On Leda and Nemesis, see Germanicus Caesar’s *Aratus* on the Swan, and Pausanias in the *Attica*.
>
> **Circe, Marica.** See Hesiod’s *Theogony* and Virgil, *Aeneid* VII:
>
> We understand that he—namely Latinus—was born to Faunus  
> And the Laurentian nymph Marica.
>
> Horace, *Odes* III, 17: “the shores of Marica.”
>
> **Ino.** She was the daughter of Cadmus. Her story is found in Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IV; Hyginus, chapter 20; Pausanias in the *Attica*; and, especially concerning this change of names, Ovid writes in the *Fasti*:
>
> You will be called Leucothea by the Greeks, Matuta by our people.
>
> See also Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I, and *On the Nature of the Gods* II.
>
> **Threw herself down.** Twelve manuscripts and three editions add “into the sea,” which is a gloss.

Leucothea. We have thus restored the reading from all the manuscripts except one Colbertine, and from the printed editions except those of Thysius, Gallus, and Cellarius, in which the form is *Leucothoa*. But Munkerus, in his notes on Hyginus’ *Fables*, p. 15, demonstrates on several grounds that *Leucothea* should be written.

Melicertes. He, also called Palaemon and Portumnus, was himself a sea-god, as was his mother. Thus Plautus in the *Rudens*:

[Col. 0236D] But, O Palaemon, holy companion of Neptune.

Portumnus. He was named from harbors (*portus*), over which he was believed to preside. Among the Romans he had a temple at the Tiber harbor. Varro, book III, *On the Latin Language*: “The Portumnalia are named after Portumnus, for whom on that day a temple was built at the Tiber harbor and a festival instituted.” This was evidently because Portumnus was commonly believed to preside over harbors and to ensure the safety of voyagers. Arnobius, book III: “Portumnus grants the safest voyages to those traveling over the seas.” The Greeks called him Palaemon and instituted the Isthmian Games in his honor. Priapus also says that he presides over harbors, in an ancient epigram:

> Ταῦθ’ ὁ Πρίηπος ἐγὼν ἐπιτέλλομαι ὁ λιμενίτης.
>
> “I, Priapus, guardian of the harbor, give these commands.”

There was also a Venus surnamed Limnesia, who was believed to preside over harbors. Caesar was the first to dedicate a temple to her, after being warned in a dream—if what we read in Servius, book I on the *Aeneid*, is true: “There is also,” he says, “a Limnesian Venus, [Col. 0237B] who presides over harbors; both she herself and the victim and the spinner were consecrated as a result of Caesar’s dream.” Pausanias also mentions her in his *Corinthiaca*, but there she is called not Limnesia but Limenia, which I consider more correct; and I plainly think that *Limnesia* should be written in Servius. Likewise, among Diana’s surnames is Λιμνᾶτις (*Limnatis*) in Artemidorus, book II, chapter 42, for which Cornarius has Λιμνῆτις (*Limnetis*). From this [Col. 0237C] *Limnesia* could easily have arisen, since otherwise the interpretation of the dream does not fit: what was hidden seems to have been found not in a marsh but in a harbor. That Diana, moreover, was among the divinities of sailors is clear from the ancient inscription in Gruterus, p. 37, where she is called:

> QUEEN OF THE WAVES.

SCHEFFERUS.]

The Egyptian rites of Isis concern the loss or recovery of her little son. For at first her priests, with their bodies shaved, beat their breasts and lament, just as she herself did when she lost him. Then the boy is brought forth as though found, and that mourning is turned into joy. Hence Lucan:

> . . . Osiris, never sufficiently sought.

For they are always losing him and always finding him. Thus the rites reproduce the likeness of an event that actually took place—an event which, if we have any understanding at all, certainly shows that she was a mortal woman and nearly childless, had she not recovered her only child. This [Col. 0236A] did not escape that same poet, in whose work the young Pompey, upon hearing of his father’s death, says:

> I shall now cast Isis, a divinity to nations, out of her tomb,
>
> And scatter among the crowd Osiris enclosed in wood.

This is Osiris, whom the common people call Serapis (Latin *Serapim* or *Serapidem*). For the names of the dead are customarily changed when they are consecrated, so that, I suppose, no one may think they were human beings. Thus Romulus after his death became Quirinus; Leda became Nemesis; Circe, Marica; and Ino, after she cast herself down, became Leucothea and Mother Matuta; while her son Melicertes became Palaemon and Portumnus. [Col. 0237A] The rites of Eleusinian Ceres [Col. 0237A]

[Note: [Col. 0237C] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 237–238]

The rites of Eleusinian Ceres. See what we said above concerning Ceres in the notes on chapter 18. These rites were called the Eleusinia, being named after Eleusis, a town of Attica where, according to Strabo, the temple of Eleusinian Ceres stood. See Arnobius, book V, and Augustine, *The City of God*, book VII, chapter 20. Meursius thinks that her rites lasted nine days. They were performed in secret, and it was unlawful to disclose anything about them. If anyone did otherwise, the law required that he be punished with death. From MEURSIUS’ *ELEUSINIA*.

For this reason her rites, etc. Seneca in *Hercules Furens*:

> At silent Eleusis I shall brandish the long torches.

See also *Hippolytus*, act I, scene 2, and Statius, book IV, *Silvae* 8. [Col. 0237D] Smeared with mud and bran, they ran with these torches and, while running, passed them to one another, as the ancient scholiast on Juvenal, Satire 15, verse 141, notes. From DEMPSTER.—Phurnutus too draws a parallel between the two searches: Ceres’ search for her daughter, and Isis’ search for Osiris and eventual discovery of him. See Diodorus Siculus, book IV; Ovid, book V of the *Metamorphoses* and book IV of the *Fasti*; and Claudian, *The Rape of Proserpina*.

Lampsacus. According to Strabo, this is a distinguished city on the Hellespont, in which there is a temple of the Mother of the Gods. From this city Priapus acquired the name “Lampsacene.” See Ovid, book VI of the *Fasti*.

An acceptable sacrificial victim to Priapus. This is the correct reading from the two oldest Royal manuscripts, three other more recent Royal manuscripts, three Colbertine manuscripts, one Sorbonne manuscript, one Clermont manuscript, the Brun manuscript, and eight printed editions. So too Lactantius, *Epitome*, chapter 65, near the end: “This is a more acceptable sacrificial victim before God.” Three Royal manuscripts, one Colbertine, one Sorbonne, and five printed editions have *letabilis*; one Royal has *lectabilis*; two Bolognese manuscripts, *litalis*; one Clermont manuscript, *letalis*; and the Gronovius manuscript, *habilis victima*, “a suitable victim.” [Col. 0238B] This Priapus was the patron of obscenity. A *litabilis victima* is a victim that is pleasing and proper, by which a favorable omen is obtained and a deity appeased. You will read *litabilem hostiam* in the same sense in Minucius Felix, chapter 32.

Silenus used to ride. He was a nursling of Bacchus and one of the petty kings of Caria, who ruled at Nysa. They say that Silenus generally rode on an ass and remained inseparably attached to Bacchus, the god of vineyards, [Col. 0238C] as his companion. Hence Silenus is assigned to the treading of grapes. But nothing is so impious as the fiction that Silenus was always drunk. See Pausanias in his *Eliaca*.

Thwarted. The reading we have restored here is that of nearly all the manuscripts and the earliest editions. The other printed editions and the recent manuscripts—two Royal, one Colbertine, and one Sorbonne—read “exposed.”

Crowned with loaves. Loaves were fashioned in various shapes; these loaves represented the form of a crown. ISAAC CASAUBON.

Have written. Here it is not Aratus himself, but Theon of Alexandria in his commentary on Aratus. See also Hyginus, book II, *On the Celestial Constellations*, in the chapter on Cancer, where he agrees with Lactantius. Φαινόμενα (*Phaenomena*, “appearances”) are those things visible in the heavens which concern astronomers.

Concerning the two stars of Cancer . . . which they call ὄνους. Read Hyginus, *Poetic Astronomy*, book II, chapter 23. CELLARIUS.

Concerning the size of the obscene part. The recent manuscripts, three Royal, three Vatican, one Clermont, and most printed editions add “member.” But it is more correct to delete this word, because that is more modest, especially [Col. 0238D] since Lactantius says below: “I shall not probe so shameful a mystery, nor strip Priapus bare.” One Royal and one Colbertine manuscript read “concerning the size of obscene things”; the Junius manuscript, “concerning the image of obscene things”; and one Colbertine manuscript, “because of the size of obscene things.”

Worthy of laughter. Francius conjectured that the reading should be “unworthy of sight.”

What, then, it is. I have thus restored the reading from the manuscripts and from the editions of Turnèbe, Isaeus, and Cellarius. The other printed editions have “What, then, they are”; incorrectly. See the preceding and following passages.—What it is. Thus the Bolognese, Taxianus, Penius, and Caucianus manuscripts, excellently. Supply: “the shamefulness.” BUNEMANN.

Has horns. See Claudian, book I, *The Rape of Proserpina*.

Appeases. From Ovid, *Fasti* I.385; Justin, book X.

Persia. *Persis* is the region put for its inhabitants; in Greek Περσίς, -ίδος. Lindus. See Philostratus, *Imagines*, book II.

Εὐφημίᾳ. From Lactantius himself it is apparent that this is a word belonging to sacred rites, for it does not simply mean praise, [Col. 0239C] but contains within itself a kind of religious enthusiasm. Thus we read that Ammon, in an oracle, preferred the prayers of the Spartans to the sacrifices of the Greeks. BETULEIUS. Or it means the auspicious words that had to be spoken during sacred rites, in accordance with Ovid, *Fasti* I.72:

> Now on this auspicious day auspicious words must be spoken.

Εὐφημία. The Greek εὐφημεῖν is, in Latin, *linguis favere*, “to keep reverent silence” or “speak words of good omen.” Spanheim learnedly illustrates these expressions in his notes on Callimachus, *Apollo*, verse 17, p. 58 ff., and *Ceres*, verse 18, p. 676. BUNEMANN.

Should inadvertently . . . escape someone’s lips. The Venice 1471 edition and both 1478 editions, as well as the Rostock edition, have “shamelessly”; incorrectly. Things uttered thoughtlessly are elegantly said to “escape”:

> And so great a crime escaped his father’s lips.

Virgil, *Aeneid* II.658.

On this passage Emmenessius cites Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VII.171: “What crime,” he says, “escaped your lips?” BUNEMANN.]

are not unlike these. For just as there Osiris, the boy, is sought amid his mother’s lamentation, so here Proserpina, carried off into an incestuous marriage with her uncle, is sought. And because Ceres is said to have searched for her in Sicily with torches kindled at the summit of Etna, her rites are therefore celebrated by brandishing blazing torches.

At Lampsacus the ass is an acceptable sacrificial victim to Priapus. The reason for this sacrifice is given in the *Fasti* as follows. When all the gods had assembled for the festival of the Great Mother and, sated with feasting, were spending the night in amusements, Vesta lay down upon the ground and fell asleep. There Priapus plotted against her sleep and chastity; but she was awakened by the untimely braying of the ass on which Silenus rode, while the lust of the would-be violator was thwarted. For this reason the people of Lampsacus became accustomed to slaughter an ass to Priapus, as though in vengeance; among the Romans, however, [Col. 0237B] that same animal is crowned with loaves during the rites of Vesta, in honor of chastity preserved. What could be more shameful? What more disgraceful than that Vesta should owe her virginity to an ass? But the poet invented the fable. Is that account, then, any truer which is related by those who have written the Φαινόμενα (*Phaenomena*), when they speak of the two stars in Cancer which the Greeks call ὄνους (*onoi*, “asses”)? [Col. 0238A] They say that these were asses which carried Father Liber across when he was unable to cross a river; that he gave one of them, as a reward, the power to speak with a human voice; that a contest consequently arose between that ass and Priapus over the size of their obscene parts; and that Priapus, defeated and enraged, killed the victor. This is indeed far more foolish; but poets are permitted to say whatever they please. I shall not probe so shameful a mystery, nor strip Priapus bare, lest anything appear that is worthy of laughter. The poets certainly invented these stories, but they must have been invented to conceal some still greater shamefulness. Let us therefore inquire what it is. It is, in fact, obvious. For just as a bull is slaughtered to the Moon because it similarly has horns, and:

> Persia appeases with a horse Hyperion, girdled with rays,
>
> Lest a sluggish victim be offered to the swift god,

[Col. 0238B] so in this case, because the size of the male member is enormous, no victim more suited to that monster could have been found than one capable of imitating the very being to whom it is sacrificed.

At Lindus, a town of Rhodes, there are rites of Hercules whose ritual differs greatly from all others. For they are celebrated not with εὐφημία (*euphēmia*, auspicious or reverent speech), as the Greeks call it, but with curses and execration; and they regard the rites as profaned if, during the solemn ritual, a good word should ever inadvertently escape someone’s lips. [Col. 0239A] The following explanation is given for this custom, if indeed any explanation can [Col. 0239A]

[Note: [Col. 0239C] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 239–240]

If indeed any can exist. One old Bolognese manuscript, one Colbertine, and the editions of Thysius and Gallus incorrectly add “explanation,” a word that immediately precedes. The Royal-Puteanus, Caucianus, Junius, Lipsius, Utrecht, and Brun manuscripts have “unless.”

[Col. 0239D]

Indeed, he refused. This is the reading of the manuscripts and printed editions. “Indeed” is absent from one old Bolognese manuscript and the editions of Thomas, Isaeus, Sparke, and Gallus. The more recent manuscripts—one Royal and the Cambridge manuscript—have “But to whom.”

Young bullocks. I have thus restored the reading from the old printed editions and nearly all the manuscripts, among them the oldest and best. But six manuscripts and sixteen commonly used editions have “draught animals.” See above and below.—Young bullocks. Martial IV, Epigram 55: “He tills his fields with strong young bullocks.” BUNEMANN.

Hercules. See Apollodorus, book II, p. 218, and Gale’s note, p. 50; Origen, *Against Celsus*, book VII, p. 368; Erasmus, *Adages*, chiliad 2, century 5, no. 19; Hadrianus Junius, *Observations*, book IV, chapter 2. BUNEMANN.

βοὺζυγον. One Royal manuscript has βούζουγον; another Royal manuscript, βούζηγον; the Aldine edition, Paris 1525, and Fasitellus have βουζιγον. Three Royal manuscripts, one Colbertine, and many printed editions add “that is, a yoke of oxen,” which is a Latin translation of the Greek word that crept from the margin into the text.

A pair of yoked oxen. This is the more correct reading, with the manuscripts and the Venice 1493 and 1497, Parisian, Cratander, Paris, and Aldine editions, rather than “defeated,” as in the Subiaco, Venice [Col. 0240C] 1471, and Rostock editions, or “bound,” as in both 1478 editions. BUNEMANN.

Because he declared that he had never feasted . . . more pleasantly. He elegantly imitates Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* V.34: “He declared that he had never drunk more pleasantly . . . nothing was more pleasant to him than bread”; and chapter 35: “a pleasant dinner.”

Is said. Thus six old editions, together with all the manuscripts except three, which have “is led,” as do fourteen editions. BUNEMANN.

Amalthea. Some make Amalthea herself the goat; others make her one of the daughters of Melissus, who nourished Jupiter with the milk of a certain goat whose name was Amalthea. See Ovid, book V of the *Fasti*.

Musaeus is the authority. The celebrated Vossius, in his book *On the Nature and Constitution of the Poetic Art*, thinks that no Musaeus ever existed, but that it is a name from the ancient Phoenician language used by Cadmus and, for some time afterward, his descendants. He derives the name Musaeus from *Musa*, or Μῶσα. Borrichius, however, in *On the Poets*, p. 8, thinks that there were three men named Musaeus, according to the *Suda*. But the Musaeus whose poem we possess on the love of Hero and Leander was a grammarian who lived after the fifth Christian century, and his diction does not savor of antiquity. [Col. 0240D] Αἰγίοχος. In Latin, “bearing the shield.” See Pindar in the *Nemeans*, Nicander in the *Theriaca*, and Homer, *Iliad* I.—Αἰγίοχος. Spanheim, in his notes on Callimachus, *Jupiter*, verse 49, p. 19, reproduces a coin on which the infant Jupiter rides upon a goat. Add Montfaucon, volume I of *Antiquity Explained*, where there is more. BUNEMANN.

Sallust. This passage is not found in Sallust today. “The first originators of understanding the divine.” With the very learned Cellarius I read the passage thus in both occurrences, on the authority of all the manuscripts and the Rome 1470 edition. The other printed editions have “divine things.”—The first originators of understanding the divine. Thus the Bolognese, Taxianus, Penius, Caucianus, Palatine, Lipsius, Emmanuel, Cambridge, Subiaco, Venice 1471 and 1472, both 1478 and the 1497, Rostock, Paris, and Parisian editions. The Gotha manuscript errs in number: “was the first originator of understanding.” “The first originators of understanding the divine” means, from chapter 22, the first authors of the worship of the gods. BUNEMANN.

Magnifying it. Thus the printed editions and manuscripts, except one Colbertine manuscript and six printed editions, which have “magnifying them.”

Fosterers of Jupiter. The editions of Thomas and Cellarius have “for Jupiter.” [Col. 0241B] The matter itself cries out that one must write “magnifying,” not “magnifying them,” and “of Jupiter,” not “for Jupiter.” For Sallust did not mean that antiquity was magnified by the Curetes, but rather that this deed of the Curetes—this invention and conceptual formulation of religion—was magnified by antiquity itself. Sallust elsewhere used almost the same expression, “to celebrate on a larger scale,” as did, unless I am mistaken, the learned poet Claudian in imitation of him: Sallust, *Jugurtha*; Claudian, *Panegyric*. From ISAEUS.]

exist in matters of utter vanity. When Hercules had come to that place and was suffering from hunger, he saw a certain plowman at work and began asking him to sell him one ox. The man, however, refused, because his entire hope of cultivating the land depended upon those two young bullocks. Hercules, employing his customary violence, took both because he could not obtain one. But when the unhappy man saw his oxen being slaughtered, he avenged his wrong with curses. This greatly delighted that refined and urbane man. For while he prepared a feast for his companions and devoured another man’s oxen, he listened with laughter and loud guffaws [Col. 0239B] as the man assailed him with the bitterest abuse.

But after it was decided, out of admiration for his valor, to confer divine honors upon Hercules, the citizens set up an altar to him, which, after the event, he named βούζυγον (*bouzygon*, “ox-yoking”), and at which two yoked oxen were to be sacrificed, like those he had taken from the plowman. He appointed that same man as his priest and commanded him always to use the same curses in celebrating the sacrifices, because Hercules declared that he had never feasted more pleasantly. These are no longer sacred rites but sacrileges, in which something is called sacred that, if done elsewhere, is punished with the greatest severity.

What else do the rites of Cretan Jupiter show [Col. 0240A] than how he was either stolen away from his father or nourished? There is the she-goat belonging to the nymph Amalthea, which fed the infant from its udders. Concerning her Germanicus Caesar says in his poem on Aratus:

> . . . She is believed
>
> To have been Jupiter’s nurse—if Jupiter truly, as an infant,
>
> Drew milk from the most faithful udders of the Cretan goat,
>
> Who by her bright constellation attests her grateful foster-child.

Musaeus is the authority for the claim that Jupiter used this goat’s hide as a shield when fighting against the Titans; hence he is called by the poets αἰγίοχος (*aigiochos*, “aegis-bearing”). Thus whatever was done in concealing the child is itself enacted symbolically in the sacred rites. His mother’s mystery also contains the same thing, as Ovid explains in the *Fasti*, book IV, verse 207:

> Long now has lofty Ida resounded with ringing,
>
> [Col. 0240B] So that the boy may safely wail with an infant’s mouth.
>
> Some strike shields with staffs, others empty helmets:
>
> The Curetes have this task, and so do the Corybantes.
>
> The matter remained hidden, and imitations of the ancient deed endure;
>
> The goddess’s companions beat bronze and rumbling hides;
>
> Cymbals are struck in place of helmets, drums in place of shields;
>
> The pipe gives forth Phrygian measures, as it did before.

Sallust rejected this entire account as though invented by the poets, and attempted ingeniously to explain why the Curetes were said to have been the fosterers of Jupiter. He writes as follows: “Because they were the first originators of understanding the divine, antiquity, which magnifies other things as well, celebrated them as the fosterers of Jupiter.” How greatly that learned man erred is now [Col. 0241A] revealed by the matter itself. For if Jupiter is the chief both of the gods and of religions; if before him no gods were commonly worshiped because those who are worshiped had not yet been born, it is apparent that the Curetes [Col. 0241A]

[Note: [Col. 0241C] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 241–242]

The Curetes. Two Royal manuscripts, one Colbertine, and the Brun manuscript have “the Curetes” in the accusative.

That they were the first originators not of understanding the divine. The manuscripts just cited again have “divine” in this passage—that is, they did not impart understanding and knowledge of God and divine worship but introduced error. BUNEMANN.

Those, I mean. One Colbertine manuscript, the Brun manuscript, and the editions of Turnèbe, Cellarius, Soubronius, and Walchius have “of those, I mean.”

Dance in leaping steps. He alludes to the Salii, the priests of Mars. Isaeus reads *saltu*, “in leaping,” in the Gotha manuscript. BUNEMANN.

Naked, etc. These are the Luperci, in accordance with Virgil, book VIII:

> Hence the exulting Salii and the naked Luperci,
>
> Their wool-bearing caps and shields that fell from heaven.

Or smeared with mud. Four recent manuscripts have *obliniti*. He indicates the Salii and the Luperci. BUNEMANN.

What shall I say of the shields, etc.? These were the *Ancilia*. Virgil at the end of *Aeneid* VIII. Those shields were fashioned after the shape of the small shield, or *ancile*, which, as the story goes, fell from heaven in Numa’s time and was consecrated by him. See Festus and Plutarch’s *Numa*.

They think that they are carrying the gods themselves upon their shoulders. Just as the Jews were accustomed to carry the Ark of the Covenant, so the Gentiles imitated the sacred practices of the Jews of which they knew. In processions and supplications they once carried the emblems, weapons, or principal implements of their own gods, and bore their images upon their shoulders during a purification ceremony, sometimes with litanies, fasting, or abstinence, sometimes with the washing of the images in a lake, while all wore crowns and carried laurel branches in their hands. Besides Lactantius, the witnesses to these pagan rites are Ovid, *Fasti*, book IV, verses 292–335; Titus Livy, Decade I, book X, year 458; Decade III, book II, year 537; Decade IV, book X, p. 339; Lucian, p. 1074; Trebellius Pollio, p. 178; and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book II, p. 91; book VIII, p. 510; book IX, pp. 597 and 599; and book VII, p. 475, where he says: “The men in whose hands lay the supreme power led a procession for the gods from the Capitol through the Forum to the Circus Maximus, [Col. 0242B] in which their sons who were approaching puberty went before them.” And below, p. 478: “The images of the gods closed the last rank of the procession, borne upon men’s shoulders; they displayed the same form in which they are represented among the Greeks, the same dress and emblems, and likewise the gifts that each is said to have discovered and bestowed upon humankind. . . . When the procession had been completed, the consuls and priests sacrificed immediately.” See Eustathius on Homer’s *Iliad* I.422. Christians likewise, following the example of the Hebrews, instituted [Col. 0242C] both supplications and other sacred rites. Read much of this kind in letter 5 of Vigilius, bishop of Trent, to St. John Chrysostom, *On the Martyrdom of Saints Sisinnius, Martyrius, and Alexander, the Martyrs of Anagnia*.

Is numbered. One Colbertine manuscript and the Brun manuscript have “is commemorated.”

were, on the contrary, the first originators not of understanding the divine, but of the entire error that was introduced and by which the memory of the true God was destroyed. From the mysteries and ceremonies themselves, therefore, they ought to have understood that they were making supplication to dead human beings.

Accordingly, I do not demand that anyone believe the poets’ fictions. Let the person who thinks they lie consider the writings of the pontiffs themselves and examine all the literature pertaining to sacred rites. He will perhaps find more than we have presented, from which he may understand that everything regarded as sacred is empty, foolish, and fabricated. But if anyone, upon attaining wisdom, lays error aside, he will certainly laugh at the absurdities of people who are almost insane—I mean those who dance in disgraceful, leaping steps, [Col. 0241B] or run about naked, anointed, crowned, masked, or smeared with mud.

What shall I now say of shields rotted with age? When they carry them, they think that they are carrying the gods themselves upon their shoulders. For Furius Bibaculus is numbered among the foremost examples of piety because, although he was praetor, he nevertheless carried an *ancile*, preceded by his lictors, even though, by privilege of his magistracy, he was exempt from that duty. [Col. 0242A] He therefore was not Furius, but plainly *furiosus*—mad—because he thought that he adorned his praetorship by this service.

Rightly, then, since these things are done by men who are neither uneducated nor ignorant, Lucretius exclaims:

> O foolish minds of men, O blinded hearts!
>
> In what darkness of life, and amid what great dangers,
>
> Is this span of existence, whatever it may be, passed!

Who that possesses any sanity would not laugh at these mockeries, when he sees people, as though bereft of reason, seriously doing things which, if anyone did them in play, would make him appear excessively wanton and foolish?

## CHAPTER XXII [Col. 0242B]

### Who was the author of the aforesaid vanities in Italy among the Romans, and who among other nations

The author and founder of these vanities among the Romans was that Sabine king who above all entangled the rude and ignorant minds of men [Col. 0243A] in new superstitions. To do this with some show of authority, he pretended that he held nocturnal meetings with the goddess Egeria [Col. 0243A]

[Note: [Col. 0243B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 243–244]

With the goddess Egeria, etc. This story is related by Livy, book I; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities*, book II; Valerius Maximus, book I, in the chapter *On Feigned Religion*; Cicero, book II, *On the Laws*; Ovid, book III of the *Fasti*; and Plutarch, *Numa*. Egeria was named from *egerere*, “to bring forth,” and pregnant women sacrificed to her so that they might more easily bring forth the contents of the womb, according to Festus. Concerning her, see Arnobius, at the beginning of book V; Tertullian, *On the Prescription of Heretics*, and *Apology*, chapter 25; Augustine, *The City of God*, book VII, chapter 35, etc. BETULEIUS. See also Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book IX. BETULEIUS.

[Col. 0243C]

Arician. Three recent Royal manuscripts and the editions of Thomas, Thysius, and Gallus have “Arian.” We have emended it to “Arician” from two Royal and two Bolognese manuscripts, two of which are the oldest of all, from one Colbertine manuscript, the first hand of the Marble manuscript, and all the printed editions. This is supported by one Colbertine manuscript and the Navarre, Victorinus, and Brun manuscripts, which have “Arocian”; also by four Royal manuscripts, among them the Royal-Puteanus, four Colbertine, three Lipsius, the Gotha, Emmanuel, Cambridge, one Clermont, Gataker, and the second hand of the Marble manuscript, which have “Erycinian.” One Royal manuscript has “neighboring,” incorrectly. But Aricia and the Arician grove are well known.

Hence the belief that Minos was Jupiter’s son. Concerning him, see Homer, *Odyssey* λ; Horace, “Minos admitted to Jupiter’s counsels”; Hesiod, βασιλεύτατον, “most kingly”; Lucian, “most just”; but Cyril calls him τυραννικώτατον, “most tyrannical.” BETULEIUS.

Having remained there a long time. That is, for nine years, as many have related. Davisius, however, teaches that “every ninth year” is the more correct view, agreeing with Valerius, in his note on Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* II.13, p. 127. BUNEMANN.

Salii. That is, “dancers,” because during the festival of the *Ancilia* they performed dances to the measures of pipes. See Livy, book I; Florus, book I, chapter 2; and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities*, book III, p. 45. WALCHIUS.

Urban praetor. Perhaps Petilius had both praenomina.

Burned them in an assembly of the people. In well-ordered commonwealths it is customary to burn books that derogate from religions. Arnobius, book IV: “But if you possessed any indignation on behalf of your religions, it is rather these writings, these books, that you ought long ago to have burned; these theaters rather that you ought to have demolished and destroyed, in which the disgraces of the divinities are daily published in shameful fables. For why did our writings deserve to be given to the flames?” See Valerius Maximus, book I, chapter 1: “Because the Greek books were thought to tend in some measure toward the dissolution of religion, Lucius Petilius, the urban praetor, on the senate’s authority, had a fire lit by the sacrificial attendants and burned them in the sight of the people.” ELMENHORST.

Because they are. Thus the manuscripts and printed editions. With Heumann, I would prefer “because they were.” BUNEMANN.

Yet not have the matter pass into memory. Thus all the manuscripts and printed editions, though the expression is somewhat obscure. In that way the matter would not have passed into memory, or been handed down to remembrance. Augustine, *The City of God*, book VII, chapter 35, illustrates this. Reimmann neglected the word “matter.” BUNEMANN.

To demonstrate. In French, *faire entendre*, “to make understood.”

Faunus. Faunus is called the cultivator of Latium because he was the first, or among the first, to institute the cultivation of Latium, as Aurelius Victor relates in *The Origin of the Roman People*. The same author says that he filled Italy with various superstitions. In Calpurnius he calls himself the guardian of forests and fields:

> I, Faunus, born of the upper air, who guard the ridges and the forests.

Propertius also placed fowling under his charge, as Turnebus notes in *Adversaria*, book XXVI, chapter 19. BARTHIUS.

Impious rites. Because infants were sacrificed to Saturn. [Col. 0245A] Tertullian reproaches the Gentiles with this crime in the *Apology*, chapter 9.]

at night. There was a very dark cave in the Arician grove, from which a stream flowed from a perennial spring. He was accustomed to withdraw there, after removing all witnesses, so that he could falsely claim that, at the prompting of the goddess who was his wife, he was handing down to the people those rites that were most acceptable to the gods. He plainly wished to imitate the cunning of Minos, who secluded himself in the cave of Jupiter and, after remaining there a long time, brought forth laws as though they had been delivered to him by Jupiter, so that he might bind men to obedience not only through sovereign authority but also through religion.

It was certainly not difficult to persuade shepherds. Accordingly, he created pontiffs, flamens, Salii, and augurs, and distributed the gods among families. Thus he softened the fierce dispositions [Col. 0243B] of the new people and drew them away from warfare toward the pursuits of peace. But although he deceived others, he did not deceive himself. For many years later, in the consulship of Cornelius and Baebius, two stone chests were found by laborers in the field of the scribe Petilius beneath the Janiculum. In one [Col. 0244A] was Numa’s body; in the other were seven Latin books written on pontifical law, and likewise the same number of Greek books on the discipline of wisdom. By these he dissolved not only the religions that he himself had instituted, but all the rest as well.

When the matter was reported to the senate, it was decreed that these books should be destroyed. Thus Quintus Petilius, the urban praetor, burned them in an assembly of the people—foolishly, indeed. For what good did it do that the books were burned, when the very fact that they were burned because they derogated from religions has been handed down to memory? There was therefore no one in the senate at that time who was not utterly foolish. They could have destroyed the books without allowing the matter itself to pass into memory. Thus, while wishing to demonstrate even to posterity how piously they had defended their religions, they diminished the authority of those very religions by their own testimony.

[Col. 0244B] But just as Pompilius was the founder of foolish religions among the Romans, so before Pompilius was Faunus in Latium. Indeed, he instituted impious rites for his grandfather Saturn, honored his father Picus among the gods, and likewise his sister [Col. 0245A] Fatua Fauna, [Col. 0245A]

Fatua Fauna. That this is the correct reading is clear from what follows, and the most learned men agree with us; yet most manuscripts read it otherwise and in many different ways. Two Royal manuscripts, two Colbertine, and one Sorbonne have *Fauta Fauna*; one Clermont, *Fauta Fanna*; another Clermont, *Feuteia Fauna*; one old Bolognese, *Fenteia Fauna*; two Royal and the Marble manuscript, *Fena Fauna*; two Royal manuscripts nine hundred years old, the Caucianus, three Colbertine, and the Gataker manuscript, *Senta Fauna*; another Royal adds *Sentum* above *Faunam*. *Fautam* is absent from two Royal manuscripts, the Penius and Brun manuscripts, and the Rome 1468 and 1470 editions; it is also absent from one Colbertine and the Navarre and Victorinus manuscripts, in which the reading is *Fannam*. Arnobius, like Lactantius, calls her Fatua Fauna in books I and V.
