**They sacrifice in a covered place.** So Bon., the two oldest Reg. manuscripts, two Brun. manuscripts, and the other best manuscripts; not, as it is corruptly printed in some editions, *in apertos* (“into the open”), which conflicts with Lactantius’ meaning and also with the historical account. ISAeus.—**In a covered place.** Cicero correctly calls the place of the rites *the covered place of the Good Goddess*, *Paradoxa*, ch. 4; and Pliny calls them *covered rites*, book X, sect. 77, *On the Good Goddess*; Lactantius, book III, [Col. 0246A] ch. 20. BUN.—**They sacrifice in a covered place.** In a place removed from all men, for whom it was sacrilege to take part in these rites, [Col. 0246B] which were celebrated by women of the highest rank in the house of a consul or praetor (Plutarch, *Caesar*, p. 711), or of the chief pontiff (Livy, *Epitome*, 103). CELL.

**Sextus Clodius.** From Arnobius, book V, p. 168. See Vossius, *Hist. Gr.*, book IV, part III, p. 511; Onuphrius Panvinius, *Civit. Rom.*, ch. 37; Bosius and Graevius on Cicero, *Ad Atticum*, book IV, ep. 15. BUN.

**Faunus’ . . . wife.** Plutarch says that she was the wife of Flavius the diviner. Macrobius tells the story very differently.

**She had drunk a jar dry.** Meursius thinks that *Obbam* should be read; an *obba* was a kind of drinking vessel. But I did not wish to alter anything, for all the manuscript codices consistently read *Ollam* (“a jar”), except one Clarom. manuscript, which has *Olam*. Arnobius, in recounting this story in book V, has *seriam* in place of *Olla*; a *seria* was an elongated earthenware wine vessel. ISAEUS.—Romulus enacted a law that no woman should drink wine, and that if one [Col. 0246C] had drunk it, her husband was permitted to punish her as an adulteress. See Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book II; Pliny, book XIV; Plutarch, *Problems*; Athenaeus, book X; Gellius, book X, ch. 13.

**With myrtle rods.** See Plutarch’s *Problems*, where he recounts this story as follows: she was the wife of Flavius the diviner; after she had secretly drunk wine rather freely, she was caught by her husband and beaten with scourges. From this arose the custom that myrtle was not brought into her temple, and that the wine which the women drank in the temple was called not wine but milk. BETULEIUS.

**Every prudent person.** Our author generally, and more elegantly, joins *quisque* (“each”) with the superlative. Yet again in book VI, ch. 12: “all good judges.” Bangius collected similar examples from Justin, Suetonius, and Tacitus, *Observ. Philol.*, book II, p. 831. BUN.

**In these verses.** So I restored the text from the three old Roman editions, Isaeus and Cellarius, and all the manuscripts, except Cauc. and the more recent printed editions, which have “in these words.”

[Col. 0246D]

**Earth-dwellers.** Bunemann reads *Terriculas* (“bogeys”); on this word he supplied the following note.—**Bogeys.** Since *terricolas* (“earth-dwellers”), which stood in almost all copies, does not fit, on the authority of the Reimm. manuscript and the very old Turin codex, and with the agreement of Davis from the *Epitome*, ch. 22, I have written *terriculas*, as Fruterius long ago proposed by conjecture. Ezechiel Spanheim likewise reads *Terriculas Lamias*, “Lamia-bogeys,” in his *Observations on Callimachus’ Diana*, v. 67, pp. 174–175. BUN.

**Thus those men regard all fictions.** This is after the Greek manner; otherwise something is lacking from the meter. Lucretius sometimes does not elide.

**They believe that a heart is present in bronze statues.** Thus we emended the text from two Royal manuscripts nine hundred years old, one other Royal manuscript, two Colbert manuscripts, and two Brun. manuscripts; and it is read no differently in the *Epitome*, ch. 22. Another Royal manuscript has, corruptly, “is present in them”; one Clarom. manuscript has, badly, *inesse anis*; the other Clarom. manuscript, “is present in stone statues.” In the margin of the old Bologna manuscript stands *inanis* (“empty”).

**Studio.** It is a part of a house projecting outward and overhanging, of the kind that our craftsmen call “jutting.”

He also consecrated that same wife; Gabius Bassus relates that she was called Fatua because she was accustomed to sing prophecies (*fata*) to women, just as Faunus did to men. Varro writes that she was of such great chastity that, for as long as she lived, no male except her own husband ever saw her or heard her name. For that reason women sacrifice to her in a covered place and call her the Good Goddess. Sextus Clodius, in the book he wrote in Greek, reports that she was the wife of Faunus and that, because contrary to custom and royal decorum she had secretly drunk a jar of wine dry and become intoxicated, she was beaten to death by her husband with myrtle rods. But afterward, [Col. 0246A] when he regretted his deed and could not endure his longing for her, he bestowed divine honor upon her. For this reason, at her rites an amphora of wine is placed under a covering.

Faunus, therefore, also left no small measure of error to posterity, though all prudent persons perceive it. For Lucilius mocks the stupidity of those who think images are gods in these verses:

> He trembles at the earth-dwelling Lamiae of Faunus,  
> Which the Pompilii and the Numae established; he trembles at these; this man places everything [in them].  
> As infant children believe that every bronze statue  
> Lives and is human, so those men regard all fictions  
> As true; they believe that a heart is present in bronze statues.  
> A painter’s booth—nothing true; everything is fictitious.

[The precise reading and syntax of the opening lines are materially uncertain; see the apparatus above.]

[Col. 0247A] The poet indeed compared foolish men to infants. But I say that they are far more senseless. Infants think images are human beings; these men think them gods. Age causes the former to think that something exists when it does not; stupidity causes the latter. The former certainly cease to be deceived in a short time; the vanity of the latter both endures and continually increases.

**The rites of Father Liber** [Col. 0247A]

[Note: [Col. 0247B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 247–248]]

**The rites of Father Liber.** Valerius Flaccus, book II of the *Argonautica*, describes these rites most elegantly. On them see also Livy, book XCIV; Arnobius, book V; St. Augustine, *City of God*, book VI, ch. 9, and book XVIII, ch. 13.

**On the mountain of Boeotia nearest Thebes.** As Strabo describes it, book IX, p. 279, Mount Cithaeron is in the western part of Boeotia, above the Crisaean Gulf. BUN.

**It was called Cithaeron.** See *Aeneid* IV, 303.

**Orphic.** Those mysteries are called *orgia*, “orgies,” **from anger** (*ἀπὸ τῆς ὀργῆς*), concerning which Clement of Alexandria writes. The emblem of the Bacchic orgies is the serpent initiated into the mysteries. [Col. 0247C] Nazianzen, in the oration *On the Lights*; Epiphanius; Theodoret, book I, *Therapeutic*; Macrobius, book I, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*. BETUL.

**Was torn apart.** So all manuscripts and printed editions. The simple verb is used for the compound *discerptus est* (“was rent apart”), a usage common in Lactantius.

**Faunus and Laomedon.** So read two Bologna manuscripts, four Royal manuscripts, two of which are nine hundred years old, Tax., Ultr., Gronov., Em., three Colbert manuscripts, Gat., and the editions of Isaeus, Sparke, Cellarius, and Walch. In the remaining printed editions, especially the Subiaco edition, and in sixteen recent manuscripts, *Picus* wrongly stands in place of *Faunus*. For Faunus was the father of Latinus, just as Laomedon was the father of Priam. See Virgil, *Aeneid* VII, v. 45 ff. Accordingly, it is uncertain which was earlier, Orpheus or Faunus. For if Orpheus came with the Argonauts to the Trojan coast during Picus’ reign, then it is beyond doubt that Orpheus was older than Faunus.

**Who first originated the worship of the gods.** The beginning of the worship of the gods must be traced not merely to the period after the Flood, but even to a time long before it, roughly one or two ages after the beginning of things. For this is how the passage Genesis 4, last verse, must be understood: “Then profanation began in invoking the name of Jehovah.” For *chalal*—whence the Hophal form—is very often rendered “to profane,” as in Leviticus 19:12. The Chaldean Paraphrase also understands this passage in this way. Rabbi Solomon Jarchi has the following: “Then profanation began in invoking—that is, the names of men and the names of images—together with the name of that Holy One, blessed be God, so that they made idols and made them gods.” The Erpenian Arabic likewise says: “Then men began to fall away from the worship of God.” It is therefore as though Moses had said that that most sacred name, which designates the Creator and Lord of the entire universe, was impiously bestowed upon created things.

Josephus, book I, ch. 4, testifies that the worship of idols was in use long before Noah’s time, down to the seventh generation; and almost immediately after the Flood had withdrawn from the lands, abominable idolatry began anew. “And they sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons. God sent a storm-wind against them; and the wind was Typhon. [Col. 0248B] And the wind shattered all the idols and demolished the temples of the idols, until they had been reduced to heaps of dust; and those heaps remain even now.” From Selden and Schedius. *Extiterit* is the manuscript reading; the printed editions have *extitit*. On the origin of idolatry, however, see the Book of Wisdom, ch. XIII, etc.

**Didymus in his books.** There were several men named Didymus. According to Vossius, this one bore the surname Chalcenterus, as in Ammianus XXII, ch. 42, as though “strong for studies and labors with intestines of bronze.” He is said to have flourished under Caesar the dictator and the triumvirs. CELL.

**King of the Cretans.** Hence Servius says that the Cretans were the inventors of religious rites. [Col. 0248C]

**Amalthea and Melissa.** Book I, ch. 21. Bochart, *Hierozoicon*, p. 11, ch. 51, fol. 630, teaches from Galen, Callimachus, and others that these two nurses were assigned to Jupiter because goats’ milk cannot safely be drunk without honey, and that this practice was very common among the ancients. BUN.

**As soon as he had come into any region.** Ten manuscripts and almost all printed editions have “as soon as he came into each”; one Clarom. manuscript and four common editions have *veniret*, wrongly. *Ut* means “as soon as,” “immediately when.” Terence, *Hecyra*:

> As each man arrived, I approached him.

**Or leading men.** So the oldest and best manuscripts, together with many printed editions. Five recent manuscripts have “and leading men.”

**To Jupiter Atabyrius.** In six Royal manuscripts, one old Bologna manuscript, and two Colbert manuscripts, *Ataburio* is written, evidently with the pronunciation by which the early Latins represented the Greek Υ with *u*; one Royal, one Colbert, and the Brun. manuscript have *Atavirio*, with *u* in place of *b*. He had a temple on Mount Atabyrium, from which Jupiter was called Atabyrius. Diodorus, book V: “upon Mount Atabyrus” (*ἐπὶ δ’ ὄρους Ἀταβύρου*; so it should be read, not as corruptly printed in the editions). Partly from BOCHART.—**Atabyrius.** On him Bochart has much learned material in *Geogr. S.*, book I, ch. 7, fol. m. 369; Meursius, *Rhodes*, book I, ch. 8, p. 23; Gyraldus, *History of the Gods*, Syntagma II, Leiden ed., fol. 98. BUN.

**To Jupiter Labrandius.** It is remarkable how great a variety of readings the manuscripts have here; from them I conjecture that the true reading is *Labrandio*. One Royal manuscript reads *Labradio*; in three Royal manuscripts, one of which is nine hundred years old, three Colbert manuscripts, one Sorbonne manuscript, and one Clarom. manuscript, I read “to Jupiter Labrandius”; in the Regius-Puteanus and three other Royal manuscripts, two Colbert manuscripts, Gat., Em., the Cambridge manuscript, and the Roman editions of 1468 and 1470, *Labriando*; in two Bologna manuscripts and one Clarom., *Labiandro*; in one Royal, one Colbert, Vict., and Brun., *Labrianderio*; in Marm., *Labriandrio*; in Cellarius’ edition, *Labrandreo*; and in nearly all printed editions, *Labradeo*. He is called Lavrandenus by Strabo XIV, pp. 450, 453. Labranda was a village of the Mylasians in Caria, famous for the temple of Jupiter Labrandeus. The image of this Jupiter carried an axe in its hand; after Gyges killed Candaules, he carried that axe [Col. 0249B] into Caria and placed it in the god’s hand. Hence Plutarch, *Greek Questions* 45, held that Jupiter was called Labrandenus because the Lydians call an axe *labrys* (*λάβρυς*). From CELLARIUS and THYSIUS.—Yet Lactantius maintains that he was so called after his guest. Aelian, however, writes that Jupiter was given this name for another reason: “Jupiter,” he says, “was named Labradeus because it had rained very heavily.” ISAEUS.

The rites of Father Liber were first introduced into Greece by Orpheus, who first celebrated them on the mountain of Boeotia nearest Thebes, where Liber was born. Because it frequently resounded with the music of his lyre, it was called Cithaeron. Those rites are still called Orphic, and in them Orpheus himself was afterward torn limb from limb and rent apart. He lived at approximately the same time as Faunus. But it may be doubted which of them was earlier in age, since Latinus and Priam reigned in the same years, as did their fathers Faunus and Laomedon; and during Laomedon’s reign Orpheus [Col. 0247B] came with the Argonauts to the Trojan coast.

Let us therefore proceed further and inquire who first originated the worship of the gods altogether. Didymus, [Col. 0248A] in his books *Exposition of Pindar* (*ἐξηγήσεως Πινδαρικῆς*), says that Melisseus, king of the Cretans, was the first to sacrifice to the gods and to introduce new rites and ceremonial processions. He had two daughters, Amalthea and Melissa, who nourished the infant Jupiter with goats’ milk and honey. From this arose the poetic fable that bees flew to him and filled the child’s mouth with honey. Melissa, moreover, was appointed by her father as the first priestess of the Great Mother, whence the ministers of that same Mother are still called *Melissae*.

Sacred History, however, testifies that Jupiter himself, after he had gained mastery of affairs, reached such a pitch of arrogance that he established temples to himself in many places. For when he traveled through the lands, as soon as he had come into any region he bound its kings or leading men to himself by hospitality and friendship; and when he departed from each one, he ordered [Col. 0248B] a temple to himself to be created in the name of his host, as though the memory of their friendship and treaty could thereby be preserved. Thus temples were established to Jupiter Atabyrius and Jupiter Labrandius. [Col. 0249A] For Atabyrius and Labrandius were his hosts and assistants in war. Likewise, to Jupiter Laprius—

[Col. 0249A]

[Note: [Col. 0249B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 249–250]]

**To Jupiter Laprius.** One old Bologna manuscript and the more recent manuscripts—one Royal, one Colbert, Nav., Lips., and Brun.—have *Labrio*. That *b* was often written by scribes in place of *p*, and conversely, is universally known. No author other than Lactantius mentions this name of Jupiter.

**To Jupiter Casius.** So I read with two very old Royal manuscripts, two other Royal manuscripts, one Colbert, Nav., Vict., Gat., Marm., Em., Christ., and Brun., as well as the editions of Betuleius and Cellarius. And correctly so. He is likewise *Cassius* in Suidas and Stephanus. In Lucan, book VIII:

> And to prefer him to Casian Jupiter.

Likewise in Pliny, book V, ch. 12: “From Pelusium is Mount Casius and the shrine of Jupiter Casius.” Thirteen more recent manuscripts of Lactantius and the same number of printed editions have *Cassio*.

**In the same fashion.** It is remarkable how greatly the various names of Jupiter have increased in number. Varro relates that there were three hundred Jupiters, with various epithets and surnames; but the deeds belonging to the several individuals were attributed to one. Hence arose the error of the ancients in recounting the history of Jupiter. After Lilius Gyraldus, Xystus Betuleius collected two hundred Greek names given to him in his notes on chapter 22 of this book of Lactantius, and one hundred and sixty Latin names. The same happened with Hercules [Col. 0249D] and Mercury, and also with Belus in ancient Assyrian and Babylonian history.

**And hence they willingly submitted to his rule.** On the advice of learned men I restored *hinc* (“hence”) from two Colbert and two Brun. manuscripts in place of *huic imperio ejus* (“to this rule of his”), which stands in the others.

**Related.** Here we restored *tradidit* (“related”) from almost all the manuscripts and the editions of Tornesius and Walch. Three Royal manuscripts, one Colbert, Gat., Brun., and the Roman edition of 1470 have *tradit* (“relates”). Yet nearly all printed editions read, “or from Jupiter himself as well, as Euhemerus related”; but less correctly, because this is contrary to the testimony of the manuscripts.

**Euhemerus.** The Subiaco edition adds “relates.”

**Jupiter, the grandson.** That is, the grandson of Uranus, who was the first to rule the whole world. For by his wife Tellus he fathered Saturn; Saturn by Rhea fathered Jupiter. So Apollodorus. Lactantius also immediately adds here his grandmother Tellus, who was the wife of Uranus. Uranus, therefore, was Jupiter’s grandfather, and Jupiter his grandson, as he also says above, ch. 5, and at the end of ch. 2. This, then, is the correct reading acknowledged by almost [Col. 0250B] all printed books, not “great-grandson,” which appears in the manuscripts and the Roman, Tornesius, Soubron, Isaeus, and Plantin marginal editions. That reading is contrary to Lactantius, who makes Saturn Jupiter’s father and Saturn the son of Uranus, or Heaven.

**Tellus.** On her temple in the city of Rome, read Pliny XXXIV, 9; Valerius Maximus VI, 3; Augustine, *City of God* IV. Macrobius has more in *Saturnalia* I. The Persians also worshiped Mother Earth (Herodotus, *Clio*), as did the Scythians (the same author, *Melpomene*); and the Germans too, under the name Hertha, according to Tacitus XL, 3. So Freinshemius on Tacitus.

**Theophilus.** This was the sixth bishop of the church of Antioch, according to Jerome, and he flourished under the emperor Antoninus Verus, that is, soon after the age of the apostles. Eusebius likewise testifies concerning him in book IV of his *Ecclesiastical History*. BETULEIUS.—He lived approximately around the year 160 of the common era.

**On Times.** Among the other surviving works of Theophilus there is not a book *On Times*, but a work against the pagans addressed to Autolycus in three books. In the first book Theophilus teaches what God is; in the second he refutes the idolatry and superstition of the pagans; in the third he treats the chronology of the pagan gods. Today, however, the chronology of ancient history has been clarified to some extent from ancient records.

**Thallus.** So it is read in almost all the manuscripts. In two recent Royal manuscripts, Vict., Nav., and Brun., it is *Thallium*; in four Colbert manuscripts, *Thallion*; in one Clarom., *Thalion*; in most printed copies, *Thalum*. But *Thallum* should be written, on the evidence of Tertullian, *Apology* II, Minucius, and Lactantius himself above, ch. 13, as Meursius observes.

[Col. 0250D]

**That Belus, etc.** I consider this Belus to have been Nimrod, because the beginning of his kingdom in the land of Shinar was Babylon (Gen. 10:10); but the pagans call Belus the founder of Babylon. Among them is the ancient poet Dorotheus of Sidon:

> Ancient Babylon, the city founded by Tyrian Belus.

Artabanus, in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book IX, ch. 41, after relating how all things were initially submerged in water, adds that Belus dried the places and enclosed Babylon with walls. For this reason Servius calls Belus the first king of the Assyrians. His tomb was at Babylon, but Xerxes destroyed it, as Strabo reports at the beginning of book XVI. There is a notable passage on the worship of this Belus in the first book of Claudian’s *Praises of Stilicho*; but it is corrupt, since according to Scaliger’s most certain emendation in book VI of *On the Correction of Chronology*, *Beli* must be read in place of *Belli*. Belus was worshiped together with the Sun. VOSSIUS.

[Col. 0251B]

**By three hundred and twenty-two years.** Pererius clearly demonstrates the error of Thallus, whom Theophilus and then Lactantius followed, in his commentary on Daniel, book XVI, ch. 14, and book II of the *Disputation on the Seventy Weeks*, part I, question 2. Although chronologists vary remarkably in this calculation, nevertheless, after weighing all their opinions, it is established that Belus was older than the fall of Troy by no less than approximately eight or nine hundred years. ISAEUS.—Yet nothing certain can be determined on this matter because of the various Babylonian and Assyrian kings named Belus, who ruled those nations at different times.

—to Jupiter Molion, to Jupiter Casius, and others named in the same fashion. He devised this most cunningly, so that he might obtain both divine honor for himself and, for his hosts, a perpetual name joined with religion. They therefore rejoiced and hence willingly submitted to his rule, and for the sake of their own name celebrated annual rites and festivals.

Aeneas did something similar in Sicily (see *Aeneid* V), when he gave the city he had founded the name Acesta, after his host, so that Acestes might thereafter gladly and willingly cherish, enlarge, and adorn it. In this way Jupiter spread the religion of his own worship throughout the world and gave the others an example to imitate.

Whether, therefore, the rites of worshiping the gods flowed from Melisseus, as Didymus related, [Col. 0249B] or from Jupiter himself as well, according to Euhemerus, the period when the gods began to be worshiped is nevertheless established. Melisseus was indeed far earlier in age, since he [Col. 0250A] had raised Jupiter, the grandson [of Uranus]. It is therefore possible that he instituted the worship of the gods either earlier or while Jupiter was still a child—that is, the worship of his foster-child’s mother, of the foster-child’s grandmother Tellus, who was the wife of Uranus, and of the foster-child’s father Saturn—and that by this example and institution he advanced Jupiter himself to such pride that he afterward dared to assume divine honors for himself.

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### On the Ages of Vain Superstitions and the Periods in Which They Began

Now that we have discovered the origin of vain superstitions, it remains for us also to calculate the periods during which those persons whose memory is worshiped lived. Theophilus, in the book *On Times* written to Autolycus, [Col. 0250B] says that Thallus, in his history, states that Belus, whom the Babylonians and Assyrians worship, is found to have been older than the Trojan War by three hundred and twenty-two [Col. 0251A] years; and that Belus was contemporary with Saturn, and both reached maturity at the same time. This is so true that it can be inferred by reason itself. For Agamemnon, who conducted the Trojan War, was Jupiter’s great-great-grandson; Achilles and Ajax were his great-grandsons, and Ulysses was related to him in the same degree; Priam, however, through a long line.

But certain authorities relate that Dardanus and Jasius were the sons of Coritus, not of Jupiter. For if that had been so, Jupiter could not have taken his own great-grandson Ganymede for immoral purposes. Therefore—

[Col. 0251A]

[Note: [Col. 0251B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 251–252]]

**Therefore.** This word is found in the manuscript codices and in nine old printed editions. Recent editions have “thus.”

**If you divide the corresponding years.** Ten more recent manuscripts together with the printed editions have “in agreement.” Chronologists vary greatly, and Lactantius did not take meticulous care over chronological calculations. ISAEUS.

**No more than . . . years ago.** The calculation appears false. Arnobius adopted another method of calculation and writes, near the end of book II, that almost two thousand years elapsed from Jupiter down to his own time. ISAEUS.

**Lest it exceed due measure.** Two recent Royal manuscripts, Vict., Nav., one Colbert, Gat., and Brun. add “the discourse,” but incorrectly.

—if you divide the corresponding years among the parents of those whom I named above, the number will agree. From the destruction of the city of Troy, moreover, 1,470 years are reckoned. From this chronological calculation it is evident that Saturn, who was also the progenitor of all [Col. 0252A] the gods, was born no more than 1,800 years ago.

Let them not, therefore, boast of the antiquity of their rites, since their origin, rationale, and chronology have been discovered. Some matters still remain that have very great force for disproving false religions. But I have now resolved to bring the book to an end, lest it exceed due measure. For those matters must be treated more fully, so that, after everything which appears to oppose the truth has been refuted, we may be able to instruct in true religion those who, through ignorance of the good, wander in uncertainty.

The first step of wisdom is therefore to understand what is false; the second, to know what is true. Accordingly, anyone whom this first course of instruction of ours—in which we have exposed falsehood—has benefited will be aroused to knowledge of the truth, than which no pleasure is more delightful to a human being; and he will then be worthy of the wisdom of heavenly teaching, if he approaches the knowledge of the remaining matters willingly and prepared.

[LACTANTIUS, BOOK TWO]

[Col. 0251]

## ANALYSIS OF BOOK TWO, ENTITLED *ON THE ORIGIN OF ERROR*

[Col. 0251C] The book has two parts: the first concerns the Vanity of the religion of the gods; the second, the Origin of error.

He proves that the religions of the gods are vain:

1. Because they are adopted against conscience, since even those who, when affairs proceed according to their wishes, run eagerly to the temples of the gods, flee to the one God amid calamities.

2. Because they do not accord with human reason, for they bend a heavenly creature down to worship earthly things. An upright posture and upturned countenance were given to humanity so that one might look upward, not downward (ch. 1).

3. Because they worship images, which are representations either of dead gods, absent gods, or present gods. If of the dead, they worship foolishly; if of the absent, the gods should not be worshiped if they neither see what we do nor hear what we pray. If of the present, then, because gods cannot be absent, images are superfluous. Furthermore, the image of an eternally living God ought to be living and capable of sensation. But their images lack every sense. The human being is, as it were, the parent of images. Therefore, the one who makes them is better than the things that are made. In an image there is [Col. 0251D] nothing of a human being except a shadow; therefore, much less is there anything of God (ch. 2). To these points is appended a forceful exhortation against the worship of images, extending to the end of ch. 2, and a rebuke of Cicero, who, although he understood the vanity of religions, nevertheless wished neither to lead others away from it nor to abandon it himself (ch. 3).

Again, he asserts that images possess no majesty: because they were under the power of a mere man; because they can be broken, burned, and destroyed; because they cannot protect themselves; because, when violated, they remain unavenged unless their worshipers avenge them; because they are subject to the eyes and consequently are not immortal; and because gifts are therefore offered to them in vain. Hence Dionysius, tyrant of Sicily, rightly despised, despoiled, and mocked [Col. 0252C] such gods, and did so with impunity. Gaius Verres likewise committed so many acts of sacrilege with impunity (ch. 4).

4. Because they prefer the works of God to God, their parent—not only barbarians but also the Stoic philosophers, who number among the gods all the heavenly bodies that move. He refutes them not only by the truth but also by their own words (chs. 5 and 6).

5. Because they form images of the sun, moon, fire, water, etc., in human shape and consecrate to them their spoils and plunder, thinking that God loves whatever they themselves covet (ch. 7).

**OBJECTION:** But these very gods often display their majesty through prodigies, dreams, auguries, and oracles. (Here many miracles of the gods are enumerated.)—To explain the cause of these miracles, Lactantius begins his narrative at a deeper level, namely with the creation of things itself. He begins to discuss it in ch. 9, in which he refutes the philosophers’ errors concerning the world and God its maker. He then continues the history of creation in chs. 10, 11, 12, and 13, repeatedly interspersing short disputes with [Col. 0252D] philosophers concerning creation. Third, he touches upon the history of the Flood and derives the origin of errors from the apostasy of Ham and the Hebrews, ch. 14. Fourth, as human wickedness increased, he writes that God sent angels to earth to protect the human race. When the devil had enticed them into vice and defiled them through intercourse with women, he made those angels his attendants; those conceived from them were neither angels nor human beings. Thus two classes of demons came into existence, one heavenly and the other earthly. These are the unclean spirits and the authors of the evils that are committed; they fill everything with snares, deceits, and errors, and insinuate themselves into human [Col. 0253A] bodies (ch. 15), although they can harm no one except a person whom they hold under their power (ch. 16).

Their inventions are astrology, haruspicy, augury, oracles, necromancy, and the magical art. They attempt to turn human beings away from the worship and knowledge of true majesty. From them come the miracles mentioned in ch. 7. For since they foresee God’s arrangements, Lactantius continues, because they were once his ministers, they interpose themselves in these matters so that whatever either has been done or is being done by God may appear to have been done principally by them. Whenever some good, according to God’s ordinance, is about to befall a people or the world, they promise through prodigies, dreams, or oracles that they will bring it about, if temples, honors, and sacrifices are granted to them.

**OBJECTION:** Why, then, does God allow this to happen?—**Response:** So that evil things may contend with good things; so that vices may stand opposed to virtues; and so that he may have some whom he punishes and others whom he honors.

[Col. 0253B] Thus far this discussion, which Lactantius takes up again in the latter part, ch. 18, but in general terms. He appends to it a forceful exhortation against the religions of the gods and against images, ch. 19; and in the final ch. 20 he explains both what he has treated thus far—namely, that he has driven out inveterate errors—and what he intends to treat next. [Col. 0254A]

The second part of this book concerns the Origin of error, which is presented in this book not continuously but at scattered points. He discusses the origin of errors first specifically, then generally.

Specifically, he discusses the origin of errors in Roman religion: when Romulus founded the city and admitted all the worst men into it, he selected for the senate those among them who surpassed the others in age and called them “fathers”; and these fathers and hide-clad old men issued decrees concerning religion which the Romans now obey. He therefore urges them to change their mind, because while those shepherds lived, no one would have judged them worthy of kinship by marriage (ch. 6). He next argues that especially in that matter on which the conduct of life depends, each person ought to trust himself and rely on his own judgment and his own senses in investigating and weighing the truth (ch. 7).

Generally, he says that there are two causes of all errors: [Col. 0254B] the apostasy from God of Ham and the posterity of the pious Noah (ch. 14), and the snares of the devil (ch. 16). SCULTETUS.

[Col. 0253]

# BOOK TWO  
## ON THE ORIGIN OF ERROR

## CHAPTER ONE  
### That Forgetfulness of Reason Makes Human Beings Ignorant of the True God, Who Is Worshiped in Adversity and Despised in Prosperity

Although in the first book I demonstrated that the religions of the gods are false, because those whose varied and dissimilar cults the consensus of humanity has adopted throughout the whole earth under a foolish persuasion were mortal, and, when they had completed their lives, yielded through death to the divine necessity, nevertheless, lest any doubt remain, this second book will disclose the very source of errors and explain all the causes by which human beings were deceived, so that at first [Col. 0254B] they believed that there were gods and afterward, through an inveterate persuasion, persevered in the religions they had most perversely adopted.

For I am eager, Emperor Constantine—

[Col. 0254A]

[Note: [Col. 0253] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 253–254]]

**For I am eager, Emperor Constantine.** These final two words appear in the very old Royal codex of nine hundred years, in another Royal manuscript, seven Vatican manuscripts, two Leipzig manuscripts, the Balliol and Marm. manuscripts, and the editions of Soubron, Fasitel 1543, Gymnicus 1555, Betuleius, Tornesius, two Paris editions, Thomas, Thysius, Gall., Sparke, Cellarius, and Walch. But they are absent from the Rohan and Saint-Germain manuscripts, Soubron, and many copies of the two Paris editions. The Regius-Puteanus has in the title, “To the Emperor Constantine.”

**Now that the empty gods have been refuted.** So I restored the text from six Royal manuscripts, two of which are very old, one Leipzig manuscript, Em., Gat., Marm., and the marginal reading of Vict.; the Roman edition of 1470; Gymnicus, Fasitel, Tornesius, Thomas, Isaeus, Thysius, Cellarius, and Walch. I prefer this reading together with the learned men Jean Le Clerc, *Ars Critica*, part III, section I, ch. 4, p. 44, Cellarius, and Walch. For I am entirely persuaded that *m* was written in place of *in*, something well known to have happened often among copyists. The reading must certainly be *inanibus*, namely “empty gods,” which are more correctly contrasted with the one God than are the *manes*. One Clarom. manuscript has “now that the empty gods have been refuted”; one Colbert manuscript wrongly has “now that the empty things have been joined”; sixteen other recent manuscripts and five editions have “now that the shades have been refuted.” See below, book III, ch. 30: “now that the philosophical schools have been refuted,” etc.

[Col. 0254C]

**Vanity exposed.** The Goth. manuscript has, not badly, “vanity cast down.” BUN.

**Undertaking.** Some editions have “suspecting,” which amounts to the same thing.

**Certain philosophers.** Lactantius glances here at the Epicureans.

**Both nothing and born wholly in vain.** So we restored the text from seven Royal manuscripts, two of which are very old, four Colbert manuscripts, Goth., Ult., the less old Bologna manuscript, Em., Cambridge, Brun., and the editions of Egnatius, Paris 1525, Fasitel, and Graph. In two more recent Royal manuscripts, three Leipzig manuscripts, Cauc., Pen., Rostoch., Pal., two Clarom. manuscripts, Christ., one Colbert manuscript, and the Roman 1470, Gymnicus, Betuleius, Tornesius, and Cellarius editions, the text is “and nothing,” which is absent from one old Bologna manuscript and five recent editions. One Colbert manuscript has “and toward nothing and in vain.” In some places *nihili* (“worthless”) is read in place of *nihil* (“nothing”); Bunemann has the following note on this passage.—**And worthless.** Cellarius rightly adopted this from three Leipzig manuscripts and Betuleius; it is also found in the C.C.C., Reimm., Ultr., Cauc., and Pal. manuscripts and Tornesius. I confirm the earlier reading from Lactantius, book I, ch. 11: “who is both mortal and weak and worthless”; and book VI, ch. 22: “He is foolish, inept, and worthless.” BUN.

**Of concern to no God.** This matter was also discussed in the earlier chapters of book I and will be discussed again in the work *On the Anger of God*. “No” is construed with “concern.”

[Col. 0254C]—now that the empty gods have been refuted and the impious vanity of human beings exposed, to vindicate the majesty of the one God, undertaking the more useful and greater duty of recalling human beings from perverse paths and restoring them to reconciliation with their own selves, lest they despise themselves so greatly, as certain philosophers do, or think themselves weak, superfluous, nothing, and born wholly in vain.

This opinion drives very many people into vice. For when they think that we are of concern to no God, or that after death we shall be nothing, they abandon themselves entirely to their lusts; and because they think everything permitted to them, [Col. 0255A] they thirstily devote themselves to draining pleasures—

[Col. 0255A]

[Note: [Col. 0255B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 255–256]]

**They thirstily devote themselves to draining pleasures.** One Brun. manuscript and the Paris edition of 1525 have “thirsting.” Two Colbert manuscripts and one Clarom. have, wrongly, “knowingly.” The genuine reading is *sitienter*, “thirstily,” that is, greedily. Cicero, *Tusculans* 2.17a: “Nor thirstily seeking anything.” Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* IV, v. 88: “To drink thirstily.” WALCH.

**Their Lord.** So the Rohan and Saint-Germain manuscripts, which is more correct than “their God,” as the common editions have.

**Delights.** Thus we restored the reading from two Bologna manuscripts and five Royal manuscripts, two of which are very old, Tax., two Leipzig manuscripts, Goth., one Colbert, and two Clarom. manuscripts. The recent manuscripts and printed editions have “pleasures.”
