**Might retain.** So we restored the reading from the older Bologna manuscript and one Clarom. manuscript. The others have “could be retained”; one Royal manuscript has “might retain” in the singular. [Col. 0255D]

**They have adopted.** Perhaps “they might adopt.”

**They prefer.** Rostoch. and Ultr. have “set before.”

**And those buried in the earth to him.** One Clarom. manuscript and seven recent editions add “place before”; incorrectly, since the verb “prefer” immediately preceded.

**Of the name.** Heumann believes that *numinis* (“of the divinity”) should be read. But we do not alter the reading of the manuscripts and editions.

**Whom it is wholly impossible for a human being not to know.** That is, whom it cannot happen that a human being should fail to know altogether. For he has affirmed that error did not arise from ignorance of the divine name. Relevant is Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 17: “This is the supreme fault of those who refuse to acknowledge one whom they cannot fail to know.” BUN.

**But name God.** Cyprian, *The Vanity of Idols*, ch. 5: “We frequently hear it said: ‘O God’; ‘God sees’; ‘I entrust it to God’; ‘God will repay me’; ‘What God wills’; and ‘If God grants it.’ And this is the supreme fault: to refuse to acknowledge one whom you cannot fail to know.” BUN.

**Ought.** So I restored the reading from all the manuscripts and four editions. [Col. 0256B] Fourteen printed editions have “should,” but wrongly.

**If some necessity.** So Lucretius, book III:

> . . . In straitened circumstances—
They turn their minds more keenly to religion. Rivetus remarks very well in his manuscript notes on this author: “It is established that we are at our best while we are ill”; hence Pliny rightly wishes that, when healthy, we might continue to be such as we profess that we shall be when ill.

**Refuge is sought.** This reading, found in almost all the manuscripts, connects better with what follows than *they seek refuge*, which is the reading of two recent Royal manuscripts and of the editors.

**Rather.** Thus I restore the text from all the manuscripts and from the old Roman editions. Fourteen more recent editions have *immediately*. See the preceding passage.

**Name.** Thus I have restored the text from all the manuscripts, from the old Roman and Cratander editions, and from the marginal reading in Grapheus; and this indeed suits the words used by those begging alms, “in the name of the Lord.” In [Col. 0256D] almost all editions the reading is *divinity*.

**They are in adversity.** That is, in adverse circumstances. Book VI, ch. 25: “Let him give thanks even in adversity.” Cicero, *For Cluentius*, ch. 61: “The one refuge amid adversity from calamity.” BUN.

**They crown these.** It was customary among the Gentiles to crown the images of the gods. Arnobius, book VII: “Are even the gods presented with garlands, crowns, and flowers?” See also Clement of Alexandria, *The Instructor* [παιδαγωγός], book II, ch. 8. Tertullian, *On the Soldier’s Crown*, ch. 7: “Pherecydes reports that Saturn was crowned before all others; Diodorus says that Jupiter was crowned after the Titans had been defeated. The same author also gives ribbons to Priapus and a garland to Ariadne.” Pliny, book XVI, ch. 4, says that in ancient times no one except the gods was customarily adorned with crowns; and book XXI, ch. 24: “Crowns were an honor paid to the gods and to the public and private Lares.” Artemidorus, *Interpretation of Dreams*, book II, ch. 34. But not only were the gods crowned; so also were those who performed the rites, and indeed even the vessels and the victims, whose horns were gilded, etc. From HERALDUS and ELMENHORST.

**To pour darkness over them.** Again, book II, ch. 16: “They pour darkness over them; they veil the truth in gloom.” In the same place: “Errors . . . [Col. 0257C] pour darkness over them”; book VII: “The darkness with which the sky will be overspread.” *On the Anger of God*, ch. 1: “By which darkness human thought has been overshadowed.” BUN.]

through which the unwary run into the snares of death; for they do not know what the nature of the human being is. If they were willing to preserve it, they would first acknowledge their Lord, follow virtue and justice, not prostrate their souls before earthly fabrications, and not seek the deadly pleasures of lusts. In short, they would value themselves highly and understand that there is more in a human being than appears—whose power and condition they could preserve in no other way than by laying aside depravity and embracing the worship of their true parent.

For my part, as is proper, when I often reflect upon the totality of things, I am accustomed to marvel that the majesty of the one God, which contains and governs all things, has fallen into such oblivion that, although it alone ought to be worshiped, it alone above all is neglected; and that human beings [Col. 0255B] themselves have been brought to such blindness that they prefer the dead to the true and living God, and prefer earthly beings, buried in the earth, to him who was the founder of the earth itself.

And yet pardon could be granted for this human impiety if this error arose entirely from ignorance of the divine name. But since we often see the worshipers of the gods themselves both acknowledge and proclaim the supreme God, what pardon can they hope for their impiety, when they do not acknowledge the worship due to him whom it is not possible for a human being wholly to ignore? For when they swear, when they make wishes, and when they give thanks, they name not Jupiter or many gods, but God. To such an extent does truth itself, under the compulsion of nature, burst forth even from unwilling hearts. Yet they do not do this in prosperous circumstances. For God slips most completely from human memory precisely when, enjoying his benefits, they ought to render honor for divine generosity.

But if some grave necessity presses upon them, then they remember God. If the terror of war has roared, if the deadly force of disease has settled upon them, if a long drought has denied nourishment to the crops, if a savage storm or hail has swept down, refuge is sought in God, help is requested from God, and God is entreated to come to their aid. If someone is tossed upon the sea while the wind rages, he calls upon God. If someone is afflicted by some violence, he implores God rather than any other. If someone, reduced to the last necessity of begging, requests sustenance with entreaties, he appeals to God alone, and through God’s divine and unique name [Col. 0256B] seeks human mercy for himself.

Thus they never remember God except while they are in adversity. After fear has departed and dangers have receded, then indeed they hurry cheerfully to the temples of the gods; to these they pour libations, to these they sacrifice, and these they crown. But to God, whom they had called upon in their very hour of necessity, they do not give thanks even in a word. Thus luxury is born from prosperity, and from luxury, just as all other vices are born, so too is impiety toward God.

What cause should we suppose produces this, unless there is some perverse power that is always hostile to truth, that delights in human errors, and whose sole and perpetual work is to pour darkness over them [Col. 0257A] and blind human minds, so that they may not see the light, may not, in short, look up to heaven, and may not preserve the natural posture of their own body [Col. 0257A]?

[Note: [Col. 0257C] [Various Notes on columns 257–260]

**The natural posture of their own body.** He means the upright condition of the human body. He presses this argument often, both here and elsewhere. In some respects he followed Cicero, *On the Laws*, book I, ch. 9: “Whereas he had cast down the other living creatures toward their food, he raised the human being alone upright and roused him to behold heaven, as though it were the home of his kinship and his former dwelling.” Book II, *On the Nature of the Gods*, ch. 56: “God raised human beings from the ground and established them tall and upright, so that by contemplating heaven they might acquire knowledge of the gods.” BUN.

**Whose origin, etc.** These words appear in the very ancient Bologna manuscript and in the first Clermont manuscript, and in the editions of Thomasius, Isaeus, Thysius, Gallaeus, Sparke, and Walch; they are absent from the others. They must nevertheless be retained, both because of their elegance and because they fit aptly with the subject under discussion here.

**Toward the ground.** Heumann rightly judges that *toward* should be deleted, since the expression would be more elegant in accordance with Lactantius’ phrasing.

[Col. 0257D]

**But raised him from the ground, etc.** With Thomasius, and on the authority of nine Royal manuscripts, the first and older Bologna manuscript, five Colbert manuscripts, the Rostock, Palatine, Cambridge, Caucian, Junius, and Utrecht manuscripts, three Vatican manuscripts, and the Roman edition of 1470 and the Geneva, Tornesius, Soubiron, and Isaeus editions, I maintain that this passage should be read in this way, not, as most editions corruptly read, *for indeed he raised him from the ground*. There will be no sense if that reading is retained; for one would have to say that the human being is an animal capable of reason because God raised him from the ground, which is clearly absurd in the case of the other animals: although they too are composed from the ground, they nevertheless are not capable of reason. From GALLAEUS.

**The Greeks.** See Plato in the *Cratylus* and the *Timaeus*, and also Philo the Jew.

**It has been granted to us . . . to look upon it while upright and standing.** The expression is like that of Claudian, *Against Rufinus*, book I: “Nature granted all to be blessed”; that is, nature permitted all to be blessed. Horace, *Satires*, I.4.36: “Those to whom I would grant that they are poets”; *Art of Poetry*, 372:

[Col. 0258C] Neither human beings, nor gods, nor booksellers’ pillars  
Have permitted poets to be mediocre.

**Upright.** That is, erect. Book II, ch. 17: “He fashioned the human being upright.” *On the Workmanship of God*, ch. 8: “He raised him upright for the contemplation of heaven.” BUN.

**Since.** Thus we restore the text from almost all the manuscripts. Four more recent manuscripts and the common editions have *which*. That reading is nevertheless not inelegant. The first Clermont manuscript has *because*. But we prefer to adopt the reading of the manuscripts.

**Should be.** Thus all the manuscripts and old editions. Twelve printed editions read *is*.

**So that it may imitate that which it ought to govern.** Thus we have emended the text from the Royal manuscripts, the older Bologna manuscript, six Colbert manuscripts, and the Caucian, Junius, Utrecht, Leipzig, Palatine, Peniarth, Rostock, Tornesius, Betuleius, Clermont, Cambridge, Emmanuel, and Brussels manuscripts, and from the three old Roman editions, Venice 1490, Paris 1525, and the editions of Grapheus, Betuleius, Antwerp 1539, Isaeus, and Cellarius, and the marginal reading of the Geneva edition. Eight recent editions corruptly have *lest it imitate*. Isaeus asserts that the reading must be *so that*, and the text itself proves it: namely, so that by raising itself toward heaven the mind may imitate the posture of the body, which is upright.

**As though, indeed.** We have added *indeed* from the manuscripts and the editions of Soubiron and Tornesius. It is, however, absent from the common editions.

**Therefore.** The Rohannus manuscript reads *accordingly*, which means the same thing.

**It is not the images themselves, they say, that we fear, etc.** Eusebius likewise, in the preface to book IV, reports that this was evident even to the Gentiles: that images are not gods. His words are: “That lifeless carved images are not gods is indeed evident even to them” [Ὅτι μὲν οὖν οὐ θεοὶ ἄψυχα ξόανα, προφανὲς καὶ αὐτοῖς]. The same qualification may be seen in Arnobius, book VI; Origen, *Against Celsus*, book VII; and Augustine on Psalm 113. From GALLAEUS.

**By their names.** Thus we have restored the text from the manuscripts and the editions of Tornesius and Soubiron; this is more elegant than *of the gods*, as in the common editions, since the word *gods* has just preceded.—**Calling upon . . . their names.** Thus all the books; that is, *invoking*. Again below: “to call upon names in prayers.” Book II, ch. 5: “By what names and with what prayers we should call upon each star.” The lexicons have not noticed this meaning. BUN.]

We shall relate the origin of this body in its proper place; for now let us expose these deceptions. For since the other living creatures look toward the ground with bodies bent downward, because they have not received reason and wisdom, while an upright posture and a face raised high have been given to us by God the craftsman, it is clear that those religions of the gods do not belong to human reason, because they bend a heavenly animal down to the veneration of earthly things.

For that one and only being is our parent; and when he fashioned the human being—that is, an intelligent animal capable of reason—he raised him from the ground and set him upright for the contemplation of his craftsman. The gifted poet expressed this excellently (*Metamorphoses* I):

> And while the other animals gaze downward at the earth,  
> He gave the human being a face held high and commanded him to look  
> [Col. 0257B] Upon heaven and raise his upright countenance toward the stars.

It was surely for this reason that the Greeks called him *anthrōpos* [ἄνθρωπος], because he looks upward. Those, therefore, who do not look upward but downward renounce themselves and surrender their claim to the name of human beings—unless perhaps they think that the very fact that we are upright was attributed to humanity without a cause.

God willed us to look upon heaven, surely not without purpose. For birds and almost all the dumb animals see heaven too; but it has been specially granted to us to look upon heaven while upright and standing, so that we may seek religion there, and so that we may contemplate in our mind the God whose dwelling it is, since we cannot do so with our eyes. [Col. 0258A] The person who venerates bronze or stone, which are earthly things, certainly does not do this.

Yet it is utterly perverse that, although the posture of the body—which is temporal—is upright, the mind itself—which is eternal—should be made lowly, since bodily shape and posture signify nothing other than that the human mind ought to look in the same direction as the face, and that the mind ought to be as upright as the body, so that the mind may imitate the body, which it ought to govern. But human beings, forgetful both of their own name and of reason, cast their eyes down from on high and fix them upon the ground, and they fear the works of their own fingers, as though anything could be greater than its craftsman.

## CHAPTER II  
### What the first cause of making images was; concerning the true [Col. 0258B] image of God and his true worship

What madness, therefore, is it either to fashion things that they themselves will afterwards fear, or to fear things that they have fashioned? “It is not the images themselves,” they say, “that we fear, but those in whose likeness they were fashioned and in whose names they were consecrated.” Of course you fear them because you suppose that they are in heaven; for if they are gods, it cannot be otherwise. Why, then, do you not raise your eyes to heaven and, calling upon their names, celebrate your sacrifices in the open air? Why do you look toward walls, wood, and stones, rather than toward that place where you believe them to be? What purpose do temples serve? [Col. 0259A]

[Note: [Col. 0259C] [Various Notes on columns 259–261]

**What purpose do temples serve?** It must not be supposed that Lactantius here forbade all the faithful to consecrate any place to divine worship, since by the term *temples* he means only buildings sacred to the gods of the Gentiles. Christians so abhorred that word that they designated the place in which they assembled to perform sacred rites only by the name *church* or *meeting-house*. SPARKE.—That churches were built for Christians from the earliest centuries is established from Lampridius, Flavius Vopiscus, Tertullian’s *On Idolatry*, and likewise *To His Wife*, book II, ch. 9; *On the Veiling of Virgins*, ch. 13; and frequently elsewhere. Cyprian too, who flourished in the year 250, mentioned the church under the name *the Lord’s house* in his book *On Works and Almsgiving*; and finally this is established from Diocletian’s edict ordering the destruction of churches and the burning of Christian books, cited by Eusebius, *History*, book VIII, chs. 2 and 3, who laments that disaster, as does Arnobius at the end of book IV and Lactantius himself below in book V. See him in book V at the end, and in *On the Anger of God*, ch. 8. FROM ISAEUS.

[Col. 0259D]

**What do altars signify?** Namely, the altars on which the Gentiles were accustomed to make sacrifices to the gods. For it is otherwise sufficiently established from Holy Scripture that Christians had altars of their own. SPARKE.

**Of making.** On this see St. Justin in the *Exhortation*. See also *Wisdom*, chs. 13 and 14.

**In whose category shall we place them?** With the sixth case, that is, the ablative. Lactantius, book II, ch. 5; book III, ch. 4; *On Anger*, ch. 22. Cicero likewise, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book III, ch. 9 and chs. 19–20; *On the Orator*, book I, ch. 13. BUN.

**Names.** Heumann thinks that *divinities* should be read, but this is contrary to the testimony of the manuscripts and editors.

**The souls of the dead, etc.** We read something similar in Gregory of Nyssa’s treatise *On the Soul and the Resurrection*, around the middle.

**Wander.** The Gentiles believed that the souls of those whose bodies had not yet been buried wandered upon the earth until the remains of the dead were committed to the tomb.—**That souls wander around tombs . . .** Ammianus Marcellinus, book XIX, [Col. 0260C] ch. 12: “If anyone was accused, on the evidence of malicious persons, of having passed by a tomb in the evening, he was condemned to death as a sorcerer collecting the honors of tombs and the vain phantoms of souls wandering there.” They derive this from Plato, to whom Origen appeals in *Against Celsus*, book II, p. 97, where see Spencer; and book VII, p. 334. BUN.

**If anyone should contemplate an image.** Seneca, Epistle 40, at the beginning: “If images of absent friends are pleasant to us, because they renew our memory and relieve our longing for the absent by a false and empty consolation, how much more pleasant are letters, which convey the true traces and true marks of an absent friend?” BUN.

**So that from it.** Twenty manuscripts read *and from it*.

**And yet the image of a human being.** The English and Leipzig manuscripts, together with the Roman edition, have *and yet*, not *for indeed*, as the others read. CELL.

**Diffused.** Thus Virgil also: “All things are full of Jupiter.”

**Empty and vain.** The C.C.C., Emmanuel, Cambridge, Caucian, and Junius manuscripts, and the Subiaco and Rostock manuscripts, Venice 1471, 1472, both editions of 1478, those of 1493 and 1497, and the editions of Pierius, Parrhasius, Paris, and Cratander read *empty and void*. They vary similarly in book VII, ch. 6. Nevertheless, I change nothing. See book II, chs. 1, 3, and 17; and book III, ch. 4, where *empty* and *vain* are likewise joined. BUN.

**Capable of sensation.** That is, not devoid of sensation. FRANCIUS.

**Which neither perceive.** Thus we have restored the text from the editions of Soubiron, Tornesius, and Thysius and from all the manuscripts except the Christianus manuscript and the Aldine edition, which have *which perceive nothing*.

**The human being.** That is, the human being who was created in the image of God, Genesis 1:26. “But the greater a person is,” says Cicero in *On Duties*, book I, “the more humbly he should conduct himself.” See also St. Augustine, *City of God*, book XII, ch. 23.

**Would of their own accord have worshiped the human being by whom.** Thus we have restored the text from almost all the manuscripts, as it corresponds better to what follows than the reading of two recent Royal manuscripts and the editions, which have, *would have worshiped the human beings by whom*. The second Bologna manuscript has *would have worshiped the human being, by whom*; one Colbert manuscript has *from whom*.

**Looks up to.** Thus we have emended the text from the oldest and best manuscripts—two Royal, two Bologna, three Colbert, Tornesius, Gothic, the first Clermont—and from several editions. The others have *receives*.

[Col. 0261B]

**They throw coins to them.** According to Festus, a *stips* is a stamped coin. This is also indicated by the fact that money given to soldiers is called *stipendium*, and the pledging of money *stipulatio*. HOSPINIANUS.]

[Col. 0259A] What do altars signify? What, finally, do the images themselves signify, when they are memorials either of the dead or of the absent? For the entire rationale for making likenesses was invented by human beings so that the memory of those who had either been taken away by death or separated by absence could be preserved.

In which category, then, shall we place the gods? If among the dead, who is so foolish as to worship them? If among the absent, then they ought not to be worshiped, if they neither see what we do nor hear what we pray. But if gods cannot be absent, since, being divine, they see and hear everything from whatever part of the world they may occupy, then images are superfluous when the gods themselves are present everywhere, since it is sufficient to call upon the names of those who hear us in our prayers.

“But they are present only at their own images.” Exactly so—[Col. 0259B] in the way that the common people suppose the souls of the dead to wander around tombs and the remains of their own bodies. Yet once that god has begun to be present, there is no longer any need for his image.

For I ask: if someone frequently contemplates an image of a person who is far away, so that from it he may receive the consolation of the absent person, would he appear to be sane if, once that person had returned and was present, he persisted in contemplating the image and preferred to enjoy it rather than the sight of the person himself? Certainly not. For the image of a human being seems necessary when that person is far away, but will be superfluous when he is present. God, however, whose spirit and divine power are diffused everywhere, can never be absent; [Col. 0260A] his image, therefore, is always superfluous.

But they fear that their entire religion would be empty and vain if they saw nothing present to worship. They therefore set up images which, because they are images of the dead, resemble the dead, for they are devoid of every sense. But the image of the eternally living God ought to be living and capable of sensation. If an image takes its name from likeness, how can these images be judged similar to God when they neither perceive nor move?

Therefore the image of God is not that which is fashioned by human fingers from stone, bronze, or some other material, but the human being himself, since he both perceives and moves and performs many great actions. Nor do these utterly foolish people understand that, if the images could perceive and move, they would of their own accord have worshiped the human being by whom they were polished, since they would have been either an unworked and rough stone or shapeless and crude material had they not been formed by a human being.

The human being, therefore, must be regarded as a kind of parent of those images: through his hands they were born, and through him they began to possess appearance, shape, and beauty. The maker is consequently better than the things that were made. Yet no one looks up to or reveres the maker himself; people fear the things he made, as though there could be more power in a work than in its craftsman.

Seneca therefore rightly says in his moral writings:

> They venerate the images of the gods, supplicate them on bended knee, adore them, sit or stand beside them throughout the entire day, throw coins to them, and slaughter victims for them; [Col. 0261A] and although they hold these in such high esteem, they despise the craftsmen who made them. What could be more self-contradictory than to despise the sculptor, yet worship the statue, and not even admit into your company the man who makes gods for you?

What force or power, then, can they possess, when the very person who made them possesses none? But he could not even give them the faculties that he possessed: seeing, hearing, speaking, and moving. Is anyone, then, so foolish as to think that there is anything of a god in an image in which there is not even anything of a human being except the shadow? But no one considers these things, for they have been steeped in persuasion, and their minds have thoroughly drunk in the dye of folly.

[Col. 0261A] [Note: [Col. 0261C] [Various Notes on columns 261–262]

**They have thoroughly drunk in the dye of folly.** Thus read three very old and excellent Royal manuscripts, the Caucian and Oxford manuscripts, together with one Colbert, one Sorbonne, one Clermont, and the Gattian manuscript, and the Aldine, Fasitelian, Thomasius, Isaeus, Sparke, and Walch editions, as well as the old Bologna manuscript, in which the reading is *they saw through it*; the Marmoutier manuscript has *they asserted it*, corruptly writing *h* for *b*. Eighteen more recent manuscripts have *the juice*, although eight have *they asserted*. “The first reading can be retained,” says Gallaeus, “if the metaphor is taken from colors; for cloths are rightly said to be dyed with color, as is evident from those verses in Gellius, book XX, ch. 8:

> Carpets now senseless, drunken with dye,  
> Which the purple shell has imbued with its poison;

this was the reading preferred by Antonio Agustín, bishop of Lérida. Yet I would prefer the alternative reading, *the juice of folly*, which agrees better with the verb *have drunk in*. This latter reading, however, is approved by Michael Thomasius in his notes on this passage.”

—**They have thoroughly drunk in the juice of folly.** The second Bologna manuscript, some Vatican manuscripts, and the Taxian, Peniarth, Junius, and Emmanuel manuscripts, together with Venice 1493 and 1497 and the Paris, Gymnich, Parrhasius, Cratander, Betuleius, and Tornesius editions, have *juice*; and Thomasius, Gallaeus, Cellarius, and Walch prefer it because it agrees with the verb “to drink in.” Ovid certainly uses the expression often. *Metamorphoses* XIII.944: “Scarcely had his throat fully drunk in the unknown juices.” *Letters from Pontus* IV.4.1: “Drink the juices.” *Art of Love* III.187: “Wool drinks in so many juices, or still more.” *Remedies for Love* 237: “I have often drunk juices”; verse 308: “You should drink juices.” The very old Bologna, Reimmann, Leipzig, Gothic, Caucian, and Cambridge manuscripts and the Aldine and Gryphius editions present *dye*, a word favored by Antonio Agustín, bishop of Lérida, Isaeus, and Heumann, so that the metaphor is from the colors with which cloth is dyed. Heinsius noted at various passages in Ovid that *succus* (“juice”) and *fucus* (“dye”) are frequently confused in manuscripts. BUN.

**Stationed upon some lofty watchtower.** Cyprian echoed this in *To Donatus*, Oxford edition, fol. 6: “Oh, if only you could, stationed upon that lofty watchtower—incorrectly *mirror* in the Basel edition—direct your eyes into hidden places.” BUN.

**That saying of Persius.** Namely, Satire II. Lactantius employs the testimony of Gentile writers against the Gentiles. St. Augustine likewise, *City of God*, book IV, ch. 30, uses the authority of Varro. See Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 11, and Arnobius, book VI. But in place of the verse “O souls bent down,” etc., certain manuscripts and editions read:

> O cares of human beings! O how much emptiness there is in things!

This, however, is found nowhere in Persius.

**God, your craftsman.** Thus read the very old Bologna, Leipzig, Palatine, Utrecht, Junius, and two Brussels manuscripts, and three Vatican manuscripts. I approve Thomasius’ reasoning in asserting that this is the proper reading, because he had first spoken of images, whose craftsman is a human being; now, in speaking to human beings about God, he rightly calls God *your craftsman*.

**Toward their own parent.** Thus I have restored the text from the old Roman editions and almost all the manuscripts. Four recent manuscripts and the common editions have *toward their own father*.—**Toward their own parent.** Thus the Bologna, Taxian, Peniarth, English, and Rostock manuscripts, Venice 1471 and 1472, both editions of 1478, and the marginal reading in Tornesius 1587 and 1613—correctly. Book II, ch. 17: “Let us worship . . . the unique divinity of our sole craftsman and parent”; book II, ch. 18: “Whom his own parent recognizes as not bent low . . . but . . . upright.” BUNEMAN.

[Col. 0262D]

**Be placed on the same level as earthly creatures that bend toward the ground.** Thus I read with the oldest manuscripts—the first Bologna, four Royal, the Caucian, five Vatican, and eleven others—and with five editions. But two Royal, one Colbert, and one Clermont manuscript have *be made equal*; the remaining common editions, together with eight recent manuscripts, have *associate*. I do not approve this latter reading, since there is no one who does not associate with earthly things. Thomasius rightly says that those who do not know God and seek only earthly things are said to be placed on the same level as beasts.—**Be placed on the same level as earthly creatures.** I confirm this from *On the Anger of God*, ch. 7: “Nor did he place the rational animal on the same level as dumb and irrational creatures.” Compare book V, ch. 14. BUNEMAN.

**Deprive.** Thus I have restored the reading from the very old first Bologna and two Royal manuscripts, as well as from fifteen others and the edition of Isaeus. Twelve recent manuscripts and the common editions have *deprived*.

**May be able.** Thus I have restored the text from the older and better manuscripts—the Royal-Puteanus, both Bologna, the Taxian, and others. Twelve recent manuscripts and the common editions have *might be able*.

**Dead things.** That is, images.]

Thus those who possess sensation adore insensible things; those who possess wisdom, irrational things; those who live, lifeless things; and those who have their origin from heaven, earthly things. It is pleasing, therefore, as though stationed upon some lofty [Col. 0261B] watchtower from which everyone can hear, to proclaim that saying of Persius:

> O souls bent down toward the earth and empty of heavenly things!

Look instead upon heaven, to whose contemplation God, your craftsman, raised you. He gave you a face held high; you bend yourselves toward the earth. You depress toward lower things your lofty minds, raised together with your bodies toward their own parent, as though you regretted not having been born quadrupeds.

It is not right for a heavenly [Col. 0262A] animal to be placed on the same level as earthly creatures that bend toward the ground. Why do you deprive yourselves of heavenly benefits and, bent forward, prostrate yourselves on the ground of your own accord? For you wretchedly roll in the soil when you seek below what you ought to have sought on high.

What else are those playthings of mortal fingers and fragile fabrications, formed from any kind of material whatever, but earth, from which they were born? Why, then, do you subject yourselves to inferior things? Why do you place earth above your own heads? For when you submit yourselves to the earth and make yourselves lower, you voluntarily plunge yourselves into the underworld and condemn yourselves to death, because nothing is lower or more abject than the earth except death and the underworld.

If you wished to escape these, you would despise the earth subjected beneath your feet while preserving the posture of your body—a posture you received upright for this reason, [Col. 0262B] so that you might direct your eyes and mind toward him who made you. To despise and tread upon the earth means nothing other than not worshiping images, because they were fashioned from earth; likewise, not coveting riches and scorning bodily pleasures, because wealth and the body itself, whose lodging we use, are earth. Worship the living one, that you may live; for the person who has assigned himself and his soul to dead things must necessarily die.

[Col. 0263A]

## CHAPTER III  
### That Cicero [Col. 0263A]

[Note: [Col. 0263C] [Various Notes on columns 263–264]

**Cicero.** Namely, in his excellent books *On the Nature of the Gods*.

**Yet he says that those matters should not.** He says this in a certain lost book, for it is not found today among Cicero’s surviving works. CELL.

**What are you to do with him?** Thus I read with the better and older manuscripts—six Royal, four Colbert, the Leipzig, Gothic, Emmanuel, and Brussels manuscripts. Eight recent manuscripts and the common editions have *What will you do to him?*—**What will you do with him?** Cellarius says this is preferable to the common reading, *to him*. The Leipzig, Bologna, Reimmann, and Subiaco manuscripts, Venice 1471 and 1497, the Rostock and Paris editions, and the rest have *to him*, which is not contrary to the idiom of Cicero and Lactantius. Here, book III, ch. 18: “What shall we do with Cicero?” Chapter 20: “What are you to do with those who wish to investigate what is not permitted?” Book V, ch. 12: “What are you to do with those who call slaughterhouses justice?” Cicero, *For Caecina*, ch. 11, at the beginning: “What are you to do to this man?” BUNEMAN.

**He deliberately dashes himself against stones.** The two Leipzig manuscripts rightly insert *himself*, which is omitted in the common text, since the character of the verb “dash against” requires it. BUNEMAN.

**He tears out his own eyes.** *On the Workmanship of God*, ch. 8: “His eyes having been torn out and gouged out.” It is an established expression. Seneca, *Suasoriae* 7: “Your own eyes will be torn out.” Seneca the Younger, *On Providence*, ch. 5. Justin, book V, ch. 8. BUNEMAN.

**Knowingly and consciously places his foot in the snare.** Venice 1497 corruptly reads only *knowingly and consciously*. With similar elegance, book VI, ch. 12: “Knowingly and consciously he brings himself into these snares.” Cicero, *For Marcellus* 5: “So that knowingly and consciously, as though toward voluntary destruction.” See Abramus there for more. BUNEMAN.

**Exercise your powers.** The Gothic and Reimmann manuscripts, with the Subiaco and Rostock manuscripts, Venice 1471 and 1472, both editions of 1478, and the rest, read *bring forth*, that is, *display*, as Arnobius, book I, p. 11: “Let them display and test their inward powers.” But *exercise* is preferable, the reading also presented by the Paris edition of 1513. Our author regularly uses it thus: book III, ch. 16: “Wisdom, in order to exercise its power”; book VII, ch. 4: “Let it exercise the power of its reason.” BUNEMAN.

**Lest eloquence fail you in so good a cause.** A Ciceronian expression, found in the best manuscripts and in many editions. Eight recent manuscripts and five printed editions have *fail for you*.

[Col. 0264C]

**But of course you fear Socrates’ prison.** Lactantius attacks Cicero here because Cicero was unwilling to reveal the truth to the Romans and thereby face the danger of death. Valerius Maximus, Xenophon, and Diogenes Laertius relate with what courage Socrates, condemned by the Athenians, received the draught of poison from the executioner’s hand. Plato relates this history in the *Phaedo*.

**And it would indeed have been much nobler.** This must be read on the authority of the old Bologna manuscript, with which six Royal, six Colbert, five Vatican, two Clermont, and the Brussels manuscripts agree. Indeed, unless the conjunction *and* is added, the sentence cannot stand. THOMASIUS.—The Caucian, Leipzig, Palatine, and Junius manuscripts likewise have it. Isaeus and the Thysius edition read thus, as do the very old edition of 1490 and the Betuleius edition. Twelve manuscripts omit *indeed*.

**Philippics.** Cicero had written nine invectives against Marcus Antonius, to which, in imitation of Demosthenes, he gave the title *Philippics*. These speeches were the reason Antonius obtained Cicero’s death from Augustus.

[Col. 0264D]

**Recalled.** This is certainly the correct reading in the manuscripts and in the editions of Parrhasius, Aldus, Cratander, Gymnich, Gryphius, Betuleius, the first Tornesius editions, Thomasius, and those that followed, so that the terms correspond: “dispelled . . . and . . . recalled.” Moreover, the expression “minds recalled to sanity”—that is, to sounder and more correct counsels—is elegant. Thus Hirtius, *Alexandrian War*, ch. 24: “To recall the citizens to sanity.” BUNEMAN.

**For that which is exposed to the eyes, etc.** Here Lactantius follows Plato, for Plato in the *Alcibiades* located the essence of the human being in the intellectual soul. Nevertheless, the body is not merely an instrument; it truly belongs to the essence of the human being, who consists of two parts, namely the body and the intellectual soul. But Lactantius names the whole from the better and more worthy part, for the soul is the principal part of the human being, and from it the principal dignities of humanity shine forth. Anyone who desires further discussion should consult Isaeus’ notes on Lactantius. We have added these at the end of this volume.]

and other more learned men sinned by not turning the peoples away from error

But what benefit is there in addressing the common people and the uneducated in this way, when we see even learned and prudent men, although they understand the vanity of the religions, nevertheless persist through some inexplicable depravity in worshiping the very things they condemn?

Cicero understood that the things human beings worshiped were false. For after saying many things capable of overthrowing the religions, he nevertheless says that those matters should not be discussed before the common people, lest such a discussion extinguish the religions publicly adopted.

What are you to do with a man who, although he realizes that he is in error, deliberately dashes himself against stones so that the entire populace may stumble? Who tears out his own eyes so that everyone may be blind? Who does no good either to others, whom he permits to remain in error, or to himself, since he joins in the errors of others and does not at last employ the benefit of his wisdom by fulfilling in deeds what he has perceived in his mind, but knowingly and consciously places his foot in the snare, so that he himself may be caught together with the others whom, as the more prudent man, he ought to have liberated?

Rather, Cicero, if there is any virtue in you, make trial of rendering the people wise. This is a worthy cause in which to exercise all the powers of your eloquence. There is no need to fear that eloquence will fail you in so good a cause, [Col. 0264A] since you often defended even bad causes copiously and forcefully. But of course you fear Socrates’ prison, and therefore do not dare undertake the defense of truth. Yet as a wise man you ought to have despised death. And it would indeed have been much nobler for you to die because of things well said than because of invectives. Nor could the *Philippics* have brought you greater praise than the dispelling of the error of the human race and the recall of human minds to sanity through your disputation.

But let us make allowance for timidity, which ought not to exist in a wise man. Why, then, do you yourself remain involved in the same error? I see you venerating earthly and handmade things. You understand that they are vain, and nevertheless you do the very same things as those whom you yourself acknowledge to be utterly foolish. What benefit was it to you, then, to have seen the truth when you were neither going to defend nor follow it?

If even those who realize that they are in error willingly persist in error, how much more will the uneducated common people do so, when they delight in empty processions and look upon everything with childish minds? They are amused by trifles and captivated by the appearance of images, and cannot weigh each matter within themselves so as to understand that nothing perceived by mortal eyes ought to be worshiped, because it must necessarily be mortal.

Nor is it surprising that they do not see God, since they do not even see the human being whom they believe they see. For that which is exposed to the eyes is not [Col. 0265A] the human being.

[Col. 0265A] [Note: [Col. 0265B] [Various Notes on columns 265–266]

**Not the human being.** On this see above, ch. 1, col. 255, note . . .

**They are bodies devoid of human beings.** The word *human beings* must be read here on the authority of two Bologna, nine Royal, three Vatican, five Colbert, and the Caucian, Taxian, Palatine, Peniarth, first Sorbonne, Leipzig, Utrecht, [Col. 0265C] first Clermont, Emmanuel, Cambridge, and Brussels manuscripts, and of several editions. In this Platonic doctrine the word means the same as *souls*. Four recent manuscripts and some editions have *souls*; but, according to Thomasius, *human beings* should be read, since it is far more elegant. For Plato locates the essence and nature of the human being in the soul.—**Bodies devoid of human beings.** Hear Lactantius in *On the Workmanship of God*, ch. 1: “The body is a vessel . . . in which the soul—that is, the true human being himself—is contained.” In the same work, ch. 19: “The little body . . . is the receptacle of the human being”; book V, ch. 21: “The soul, in which alone the human being resides,” etc. BUNEMAN.

**Have surrendered.** Thus I have restored the text from the edition of Isaeus and almost all the manuscripts. Two Colbert manuscripts, the Caucian and Cambridge manuscripts, and the common editions have *have given*.

**The bodily faculty of sight.** Book VII, ch. 13: “Since the mind’s faculty of sight is much clearer . . . than that of the body.” Some deny without cause that *acies* can be used of the eyes. Cicero himself, *On Ends*, book V, ch. 28: “Unimpaired sight is good; blindness is wretched.” BUNEMAN.

[Col. 0265D]

**Veiled.** The first and older Bologna manuscript has *made common*. But the former reading is correct, for those who worshiped the gods had their heads veiled. See Plutarch, *Roman Questions* [ἐν Ῥωμαϊκοῖς]; Plautus, *Amphitryon*; Virgil, *Aeneid*, book III, verse 545.

**To turn oneself toward a stone.** Thus I read with the old Roman and Tornesian editions, Soubron, and all the manuscripts except the recent Emmeranus and Cambridge manuscripts and the edition of 1514, in which the reading is *vertier ad lapidem* (“to be turned toward a stone”), as it is read in Lucretius.—**To be turned toward a stone.** Thus the Lucretian manuscripts; moreover, Lucretius also commonly uses that form *vertier* in Book I, p. and line 2,926. Therefore this reading, *vertier ad lapidem*, is to be preferred to the *vertere se* of Aldus, Cratander, Gymnich, Gryphius, Betuleius, the Rostock, Paris, Parrhasius, and Tornesian editions. BUNEMANN.

**And to fall prostrate.** Thus the manuscripts and the Roman, Cratander, and Tornesian editions. In the commonly printed editions: *nor to fall prostrate*.

**To be called away.** Thus I corrected the text from almost all the manuscripts and the old editions. In two recent manuscripts and the printed editions: *advocari*; in the Brunsvigian manuscript: *evocari*.—**To be called away.** We confirm this from Lactantius himself, Book VI, ch. 6: “So that, called away from heavenly things and plunged into earthly things … they may destroy him”; and below: “Nor is it right that a soul [Col. 0266B] intent upon heavenly goods … should be called away from its own immortal goods.” BUNEMANN.

**And in this way.** With Thomasius, I judge that this must be read on the authority of the Bologna, Utrecht, two Brunsvigian, and other manuscripts. The sense is that, after false religions had been refuted and no certain religion established, the critics of religions were led by this, as though by a certain method and path, to say that no religion existed at all—an error more serious than that of those who followed a false religion. *In the same way*, however, as it stands in eight editions and impressions, cannot possibly be read, because no one becomes a despiser of religions or a follower of false religion in the same way or for the same reasons, but in opposite ways and for plainly contradictory reasons. GALLAEUS.

**Since the distinction between human beings and dumb animals is …** See below in this same book, ch. 9; Book III, ch. 10; and *On the Anger of God*, ch. 7. This opinion is believed to have flowed from Pythagoras’s doctrine of metempsychosis; Plato also held it, and Plutarch writes about it in *Opinions*, V, ch. 20. One is suddenly astonished at Basil, who says in his *Homily on Paradise* that before Adam’s fall all brute animals lived harmoniously with one another, heard one another, and spoke sensibly with one another. But St. Augustine argues against this in Book II of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, ch. 29. Finally, the Holy Spirit teaches that reason was granted to humanity alone [Col. 0266D], Psalm 31: “Like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding”; and Psalm 44: “He has been compared to senseless beasts.” Lactantius himself likewise asserted this in *On the Anger of God*, chs. 7 and 13, and in *On the Workmanship of God*, chs. 2 and 3. Philastrius attributes this heresy concerning brute animals’ participation in reason to the Gnostics and Manichaeans. ISAEUS.

**It is easier to judge the affairs of others.** He had in mind the passage of Terence cited by Lactantius, Book III, ch. 4; Seneca, Letter 109: “People see more in another’s business than in their own”; Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, Book III, ch. 30: “It is characteristic of folly to perceive the faults of others and forget one’s own.” BUNEMANN.

**A certain scent of wisdom.** That is, a certain trace of wisdom.—**A certain scent of wisdom.** He is very fond of this elegant expression. Book VI, ch. 12: “As though detained by a certain scent of truth.” Ibid., ch. 22: “Whom not even the scent of virtue has reached.” Book VII, ch. 1: “The philosophers scented truth so faintly that they nevertheless had no perception at all of the source from which [Col. 0267C] that scent of wisdom, so sweet and delightful, breathed upon them.” BUNEMANN.]

but the receptacle of the human being; and his quality and form are perceived not from the outlines of the little vessel in which he is contained, but from his deeds and character. Those, therefore, who worship images are bodies devoid of human beings, because they have surrendered themselves to bodily things and see no more with the mind than with the body, although it is the soul’s function to discern more subtly those things which bodily sight cannot behold. That same philosopher and poet sternly accuses such people as low and abject because, contrary to the rational principle of their own nature, they cast themselves down to worship earthly things. For he says (*On the Nature of Things*, Book VI, v. 51):

> And they make men’s minds abject through fear of the gods,  
> And crush them down, bowed to the earth.

He did, indeed, have something else in mind when he said this: namely, that nothing [Col. 0265B] at all ought to be worshipped, because the gods do not concern themselves with human affairs.

Finally, in another passage he admits that the religions and worship of the gods are an empty duty (ibid., Book V, near the end):

> Nor is there any piety in often being seen, with veiled head,  
> To turn oneself toward a stone, and to approach every altar,  
> And to fall prostrate upon the ground, and spread one’s palms  
> Before the shrines of the gods, nor to sprinkle the altars  
> With the abundant blood of four-footed beasts, nor to bind vow upon vow.

Surely, if these things are futile, lofty and [Col. 0266A] exalted minds ought not to be called away and pressed down to the earth, but should think of nothing except heavenly things.

False religions, therefore, were attacked by the more discerning because they perceived that they were false; but the true religion was not introduced, because they did not know what kind it was or where it was. And so they regarded matters as though there were no religion at all, because they could not discover the true one. In this way they fell into an error much greater than that of those who held to a false religion. For although these worshippers of fragile things are foolish, because they locate heavenly things in corruptible and earthly objects, they nevertheless retain something of wisdom and can receive pardon, because they maintain the highest duty of humanity—if not in actual fact, at least in intention—since the sole, or certainly the greatest, distinction between human beings and dumb animals lies in religion. But [Col. 0266B] the more wisely the others recognized the error of false religion, the more foolish they became in supposing that no true religion existed. And because it is easier to judge the affairs of others than one’s own, while they saw the downfall of others, they failed to look ahead at what lay before their own feet. On both sides, therefore, one finds both the height of folly and a certain scent of wisdom, so that you may doubt which group should especially be called the more foolish: those who adopt a false religion [Col. 0267A], or those who adopt none. But, as I have said, pardon may be granted [Col. 0267A]—

[Note: [Col. 0267C] [Notes of the Various Editors on columns 267–268]

**May be granted.** Thus we have restored the text from nearly all the manuscripts and several editions. The other commonly printed editions and two recent manuscripts have *might be granted*.

**And who admit that they are not wise.** Thus the text must be read on the authority of both Bologna manuscripts, the Royal manuscripts, and the Caucian, Taxian, Leipzig, and Palatine manuscripts, together with the editions of Isaeus, Thysius, Gallaeus, Sparke, and Cellarius. The negative must be placed before *to be*, not immediately before *admit*, as it is in several manuscripts and editions.

**Could have.** Thus I restored the text from almost all the manuscripts and a great many old editions. Seven manuscripts and the same number of recent editions have *ought to have*.

[Col. 0267D]

**By reason.** The Apostle likewise teaches this in the *Epistle to the Romans*, ch. 1, vv. 19, 20, 21, etc.

**That some true religion exists.** I restored *true* from twenty-seven manuscripts and the old editions, including the three Roman editions, Venice 1490, Betuleius, Tornesius, and Soubron; these lack the word *religion*. The latter word, without *true*, is found in the two Bologna manuscripts, the Caucian and Rostock manuscripts, Junius, and the editions of Thomasius, Isaeus, Thysius, Gallaeus, and Sparke. Both words are found in the Vatican and Utrecht manuscripts, together with the editions of Aldus, Fasitelus, Grapheus, Cratander, Gymnich, Cellarius, and Walch. Thomasius contends that the word *true* must be inserted, because, although they did not know the true religion, they could nevertheless understand that some religion existed; for Lactantius employs the long discourse that follows to demonstrate this point.

**Mystery** (*sacramenti*). That is, a mystery. Either he means the sacred rites of the Christian religion or the mystery of eternal wisdom, of which Paul speaks in 1 Corinthians, ch. 2, v. 7.

**This, however, unless it is taught, etc.** This statement argues against the Socinians and accords with the Apostle in 1 [Col. 0268C] Corinthians 2:14.

**Beyond this level.** Because neither flesh nor blood can reveal Christ, but the Father who is in heaven.

**What it is not … rather than what it is.** From Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, ch. 21, at the end: “I could say more quickly what it is not than what it is.” BUNEMANN.

**What majesty, therefore, can they possess, etc.?** See Isaeus’s discussion of these matters in his notes, and Lactantius himself in *On the Anger of God*, ch. 16, where he says that those who are persuaded that justice is pleasing to God worship him with constant prayers and frequent vows, offer him gifts and sacrifices, and, finally, earn his favor through righteous works.

[Col. 0268D]

**Fig-wood.** In proverbial usage, *fig-wood* signifies something useless and fragile. Fig-wood is altogether contemptible and fragile timber. Moreover, learned men have reproduced such representations of Priapi in their collections, and the ancient poets also mocked them, as may be seen in the ancient little book entitled *The Priapeia, or the Diversions of Various Poets on Priapus*.

**Who would not be, etc.?** This is not a Horatian half-line, as seems to have been supposed in some printed editions, but prose composed by Lactantius himself in an ironic vein. ISAEUS.

**Erection** (*tentiginem*). It means sexual arousal, a word also used by Virgil and Horace.

**Perch upon.** Thus I read with the older and better Royal, Bologna, four Colbertine, and other manuscripts. Four Royal, one Colbertine, one Clermont, and almost all the printed editions have *sit upon*; three other Royal manuscripts, one Colbertine, and one Clermont have *lie in wait for*, incorrectly.

**In this alone.** Thus I restored the text from all the manuscripts and the old Roman editions. The commonly printed editions have *alone*; one Clermont manuscript, *only*.]

to the ignorant and to those who admit that they are not wise; but it cannot be granted to those who, professing wisdom, display folly instead. I am not, to be sure, so unfair as to suppose that they could have divined the truth and discovered it by themselves; I admit that this cannot be done. But I require from them what they could have achieved by reason itself. For they would have acted more prudently if they had both understood that some true religion exists and, after attacking the false religions, openly declared that the true religion was not possessed by human beings.

But perhaps they were troubled by the consideration that, if any true religion existed, it would reveal and vindicate itself and would not permit anything else to exist. For they could in no way perceive why, or by whom, or how the true Religion [Col. 0267B] was being suppressed; this belongs to the divine mystery and the heavenly secret. No one can possibly know it unless instructed. The essence of the matter is this: the ignorant and foolish regard false religions as true because they neither know the true one nor understand the false ones. The more discerning, however, because they do not know the true religion, either persist in those which they understand to be false, so that they may appear to hold to something, or worship nothing at all, lest they fall into error—although the greatest error of all is precisely to imitate the life of cattle under human form. To understand what is false does indeed belong to wisdom, but to human wisdom. A human being cannot advance beyond this level; and so many philosophers, as I have shown, abolished religions. But knowledge of the truth belongs to divine wisdom. A human being cannot by himself attain this knowledge [Col. 0267C] unless instructed by God. Thus the philosophers attained the summit [Col. 0268A] of human wisdom: they understood what the truth is not; but they were unable to attain the point of saying what it is. Cicero’s remark is well known (*On the Nature of the Gods*, Book I): “Would that I could discover the truth as easily as I can refute falsehood.” Because this exceeds the powers of the human condition, the capacity for that task has been assigned to us, to whom God has transmitted knowledge of the truth; the final four books will be devoted to explaining it. For the present, let us continue, as we began, to expose falsehood.

## CHAPTER IV. Images, the Ornaments of Temples, and Their Contempt Even by the Gentiles Themselves

What majesty, therefore, can images possess when it lay within the power of some insignificant man either to make them into something else [Col. 0268B] or not to make them at all? For this reason Priapus speaks as follows in Horace:

> Once I was a fig-wood trunk, a useless piece of timber;  
> When the craftsman, uncertain whether to make a bench or Priapus,  
> Preferred that I should be a god. And so I became a god,  
> The greatest terror of thieves and birds.

Who would not be safe with so mighty a guardian? Thieves, evidently, are so foolish that they fear Priapus’s erection; while the very birds which people imagine are driven away by the terror of his sickle or his groin perch upon the skillfully fashioned images—that is, images made entirely in the likeness of human beings—build nests upon them, and foul them. Flaccus, however, as a writer of satirical verse, mocked human vanity. But those who make these images believe that they are doing something serious. Finally, the greatest of poets, a man discerning in other matters, in this alone showed himself foolishly senile rather than poetic when, in those most highly polished books, he actually ordered this to be done:

[Col. 0269A]

> And let the guardian—

[Note: [Col. 0269B] [Notes of the Various Editors on columns 269–270]

**And let the guardian.** These are Virgil’s verses in the fourth book of the *Georgics*. **Of the Hellespont.** Priapus was worshipped at Lampsacus, which Strabo describes as a renowned city of the Hellespont; hence Priapus was called both Lampsacene and Hellespontine. On him, see Ovid, Book VI of the *Fasti*, and Lactantius, Book I, ch. 21.

**Protection.** Emmenessius, on this passage of Virgil, says that *protection* means an image. But I doubt that the word has that meaning apart from a ship’s figurehead, as stated by Lactantius, Book I, ch. 11. Here, therefore, it properly means defense, as is apparent from the passage below: “What vanity it is to hope for protection from things that cannot protect themselves!” Arnobius, Book II, p. 89: “Among you, particular gods possess particular protections, permissions, powers,” etc. BUNEMANN.

**Can be burned and destroyed.** Thus all the manuscripts read, together with the editions of Gymnich, Tornesius, Soubron, and Cellarius—a smoother wording than that of two recent Royal manuscripts and the other printed editions: “can be burned [Col. 0269C] and destroyed.” The edition of Betuleius has “could be burned and destroyed.”

**To fear those things on whose behalf, etc.** Gallaeus, following Gronovius, not inelegantly observes that it would be better to delete the word *on behalf of* and read: “to fear things for which collapse, fire, or theft is feared.” Thus in Silius Italicus:

> At once they feared the worst for both nation and city.

**For which … is feared.** The other manuscripts and editions read *on behalf of which*, as Celsus, Book III, ch. 11, has “those on whose behalf we fear.” BUNEMANN.

**To hope for.** Thus, with Cellarius and Walch, I read on the authority of all the manuscripts and the Paris 1525, Cratander, Gymnich, Tornesian, Soubron, Cellarius, and Walch editions. The Roman 1470, Fasitelus, Egnatius, Thomasius, Isaeus, Thysius, and Sparke editions have *to look for*, which is not bad. *To look for*, in the sense of *to expect*, is perhaps Lactantius’s genuine reading, since he frequently uses simple verbs for compounds, as I have observed elsewhere.—**To hope for protection.** He imitates Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*, fol. 328: “Be ashamed to worship those whom you yourself defend; be ashamed to hope for protection from those whom you yourself protect.” I have shown in the note on the *Epitome*, ch. 64, that *to hope*, *to look for*, and *to expect* are frequently confused in manuscripts: “To hope for some protection from them.” On the subject, compare Lactantius, Book V, ch. 20, and Justin Martyr, *Apology* I, sect. 9, at the end, with Grabe’s note. BUNEMANN.

**Which cannot protect themselves.** Thus the older and better manuscripts, together with all the printed editions. The more recent manuscripts—two Royal, four Colbertine, the Emmeranus, and the Brunsvigian—have: “which can in no way protect themselves.”

**To resort to … protection.** Just as *to succor* means to bring aid, so *to resort to protection* means to implore assistance and help. In Book II, ch. 14, and Book VI, ch. 10, he combines the expressions: “to have resorted to others, to have implored protection.” BUNEMANN.

**Embellish and adorn.** The one word explains the other. See note 6 on ch. 13, where the phrase *to embellish images* occurs twice. Thus Cyprian, Book II, Letter 2, *To Donatus*: “When you know that you yourself should rather be embellished, that you yourself should instead be adorned.” BUNEMANN.

**For by the same reasoning they smear the bodies of the dead with perfumes, etc.** That the anointing of the dead was customary even among [Col. 0270B] pagans is evident from Pliny the Younger, Book V, Letter 16: “I cannot express in words how deeply my spirit was wounded when I heard Fundanus himself directing that what he had intended to spend on clothing, pearls, and gems should instead be spent on incense, ointments, and perfumes.” From Ovid, *Fasti* IV:

> She pressed final kisses to the body laid upon the bier,  
> And said: “Brother taken from me against my will, farewell.”  
> And she anointed the limbs soon to be burned.

And from Apuleius, *Apology*: “Even if you suppose that incense, cassia, myrrh, and other perfumes of that kind are purchased only for funerals, although they are also prepared for medicine and sacrifice.” This custom is extremely ancient and seems to have originated among the Egyptians. Thus in the final chapter of Genesis: “He, Joseph, commanded his servants, the physicians, to embalm his father with aromatic substances.” See also the final verse of that chapter. Herodotus, Book II, and [Col. 0270C] Diodorus Siculus, *Historical Library*, Book II, ch. 5, relate how this was done. That this custom also prevailed among the Jews is established from Matthew 26:10 and following; it then passed to the Christians. Tertullian, *On Idolatry*: “They are useful even to human beings as medicinal spices, and to us in addition as consolations in burial”; likewise *Apology*, ch. 42. The bodies of the dead were customarily not only anointed but also washed; hence Virgil, *Aeneid* VI:

> And they wash and anoint the body of the cold dead man.

This rite of washing also prevailed in the primitive Church, as is established from Acts 9:37, where we read that Tabitha was washed immediately after her death. From KIRCHMANN.—And this custom persists even now, not only in almost all monasteries and convents, but also commonly in certain provinces and dioceses, such as Avranches, Gascony, and Béarn, in the case of deceased laypersons. We have discussed these matters more fully in our *Liturgical Itinerary*, published in French at Paris in 1718. Thus JEAN LE BRUN.

[Col. 0270D]

**And with costly garments.** Pagans also clothed the bodies of the dead. Lucian wittily mocks this custom in *On Mourning*, alluding to the superstition of the ancients, who believed that the dead shivered in the underworld without clothing and were consumed by cold; see also Herodotus, Muse V. Such were the ravings of the petty Greeks. The Romans, however, as will be evident from what follows, had a different purpose when they wrapped the dead in garments. Juvenal, Satire 3, teaches us that the toga was the customary covering throughout virtually all Italy:

> There is a large part of Italy, if we admit the truth, in which  
> No one assumes the toga except when dead.

And Martial, Book IX, Epigram 58:

> And the pallid toga of the dead member of his tribe.

Apuleius, *Florida*, Book I: “For there too he had seen a man preside, a man fight, and a toga prepared alike for a vow and for a funeral”; likewise corpses and [Col. 0271B] philosophers were covered with the cloak. That toga, however, varied according to the condition of those whose funeral was being held. In the case of ordinary citizens and a quiet funeral, I believe the ordinary toga, which was white, was used. In this sense Plutarch is to be understood in the *Problems*, where, among other reasons why women wear white garments in mourning, he offers this one: that the dead person himself is clothed in a garment of this kind. Homer also mentions this rite, which even today remains current among Greek Christians, in the *Iliad*, in connection with the funeral of Patroclus. The poor and people of slender means, however, do not appear to have been borne forth in white, as Artemidorus, Book II, ch. 3, indicates. I believe instead that they were wrapped in cheap rags, being guided by Eusebius in the *Chronicle*: “Cassius Severus, a distinguished orator, died in extreme poverty in the twenty-fifth year of his exile, with scarcely a rag covering his private parts.” For otherwise it was customary for corpses to be carried out in their most honorable clothing [Col. 0271C]. Valerius Maximus, Book IV, ch. 5: “When he recognized that the man was his own brother, he vehemently and at length assailed the gods with reproaches for the gift of an impious victory, carried him near the camp, and placed him upon the pyre covered in costly clothing.” Jerome, *Life of Paula*: “Why do you wrap your dead in garments embroidered with gold?” Suetonius, *Nero*, ch. 50: “He was buried at a cost of two hundred thousand sesterces, in white coverlets interwoven with gold which he had used on the Kalends of January.” Hence those who had held public office or had won honor in war were clothed in garments that indicated these achievements (Polybius, Book VI), etc. Livy, Book XXXIV, and Valerius Maximus, Book V, ch. 1, testify to the same thing. This distinction in clothing was observed at Rome not only for men but also for matrons. That women whose sons had held curule magistracies were borne forth in more honorable clothing is evident from Propertius, Book IV, final elegy:

> And yet I earned the noble honors of the garment.

[Col. 0271D]

In the East the custom still persists of carrying Christian bodies to the tomb and burying them clothed in their more costly garments; in the West, only priests and monks are buried in their everyday garments.]

> —against thieves and birds, with his willow sickle,  
> The protecting presence of Hellespontine Priapus keep guard.

They therefore worship mortal things, since they were made by mortals. For they can be broken, burned, and destroyed. Indeed, they are often shattered when roofs collapse from age; consumed in a fire, they dissolve into ashes; and very frequently—unless their own size gives them assistance or diligent custody encloses them—they fall as plunder to thieves. What madness, then, is it to fear things on whose behalf collapse, fire, or theft must be feared? What vanity it is to hope for any protection from things that cannot protect themselves! What perversity, to resort for protection to beings which, when they themselves are violated, remain unavenged unless their worshippers [Col. 0270A] avenge them! Where, then, is truth? It is where no force can be applied to Religion, where nothing appears that can be violated, and where sacrilege cannot be committed.

But whatever is exposed to eyes and hands is, because it is fragile, entirely foreign to every rational conception of immortality. In vain, therefore, do people embellish and adorn their gods with gold, ivory, and gems, as though the gods could derive any pleasure from those things. What use are costly gifts to beings that feel nothing? Is it the same use they have for the dead? For by the same reasoning, people smear the bodies of the dead with perfumes, wrap them in costly garments, and bury them in the ground, just as they honor the gods, who neither perceived anything when they were being made nor know anything when they are worshipped; for they did not acquire sensation through consecration. Persius disapproved of golden vessels being brought into temples [Col. 0271A]—

[Note: [Col. 0271D] [Notes of the Various Editors on columns 271–272]

**Being brought in.** The Brunsvigian manuscript and Latinus have *were brought in*, not badly.

**Established.** See Persius, Satire 2, near the end. *Established law* means human law that has been written down and ratified, just as *divine right* (*fas*) is sacred and religious law.

**Steeped.** One ancient Bologna manuscript has *in an assembly*.—**Steeped.** I note more on this at *On the Anger of God*, ch. 13: “Steeped in moist things.” Gothofredus incorrectly reads *untouched*. BUNEMANN.

**Ridiculously.** Thus I restored the text from the oldest and best manuscripts: Bologna, Royal, five Colbertine, one Clermont, and the Brunsvigian. One recent Colbertine manuscript and the printed editions have *ridiculous*. Both readings are good. One other Clermont manuscript has *in a ridiculous manner*.

**Gold in temples.** I judge that this must be read on the authority of the Rostock, Palatine, two Brunsvigian, Caucian, Junius, Vetus, and many other manuscripts [Col. 0272B], and most printed editions. The editions of Thomasius and Thysius incorrectly read *golden*. GALLAEUS.

**Dolls given by a maiden.** This too is taken from Persius, Satire 2, whose complete verses are:

> But you,  
> Pontiffs, tell me: what is gold doing in a sacred place?  
> Exactly what the dolls given to Venus by a maiden are doing.

Dolls, therefore, were customarily dedicated to Venus by maidens who had reached puberty or were about to marry, just as boys dedicated their *bullae*, because at every transition it was customary to dedicate to the gods the emblems or instruments of one’s former life. Horace:

> Vetanius, his weapons  
> Fastened to Hercules’ doorpost, lies hidden away in the countryside.

[Col. 0272C]

The same poet elsewhere:

> He asked whether he had yet given to the Lares,  
> In fulfillment of his vow, the chain …

Thus women about to marry suspended their maidenly girdle; and there are many testimonies to the practice. *Doll* is Greek *plangōn* (πλαγγών), whence Cicero’s *planguncula* in a letter to Atticus.

**Polyclitus, etc.** These were outstanding sculptors. Polyclitus is mentioned by Pliny in Book XXXIV, Quintilian, and Aelian in *Various History*. Polyclitus lived around the eighty-seventh Olympiad. Euphranor, a contemporary of Praxiteles, was a distinguished painter and sculptor and lived around the 104th Olympiad; he is mentioned in the same book of Pliny. Phidias, no less outstanding, was an Athenian and lived around the eighty-second Olympiad. He is mentioned by Pliny in Book XXXV. On this subject, see also Tatian’s *Oration Against the Greeks*.

**Not twice children.** This is an old proverb; see Erasmus on it.

[Col. 0272D]

**They do indeed have mouths.** He alludes to the saying of David: “They have mouths and will not speak.”

**To these they give robes and costly clothing.** The gods had their own coverings and mantles, with which they were clothed and adorned. Suetonius, *Caligula*: “In the temple stood a golden portrait-statue, and it was dressed each day in clothing of the kind he himself wore.” Philo, in his *Explanation of the Decalogue*, elegantly observes that the craftsmen who make images very often struggle against every sort of misery, while the images fashioned and formed by them are adorned with purple, gold, and other costly ornaments. HERALDUS.—**To these … costly clothing … to these … they consecrate silver.** I am close to accepting the reading of the Bologna manuscript: “to these … they consecrate costly clothing; to these … they bring silver,” for he has attached a separate verb to each preceding object. Compare the *Epitome*, ch. 25. BUNEMANN.

**Which they no more possess.** The Bologna manuscript again has a more elegantly complete reading: “which they have no more use for.” BUNEMANN.

**After gaining possession of Greece by victory.** Justin, drawing from Trogus, Book XX, chs. 1 and 5, relates that Magna Graecia, [Col. 0273B] the part of Italy, was subdued by Dionysius; Diodorus Siculus, Book XIV, says no more. But Cicero, when about to describe his sacrilege in Book III of *On the Nature of the Gods*, ch. 34, says: “When he had brought his fleet to the Peloponnese and had entered the sanctuary of Olympian Jupiter.” The uncertainty is not removed, because there was also at Syracuse, in the Acradina district, a temple of Olympian Jupiter [Col. 0273C]; Cicero, *Against Verres*, Book VI, ch. 53. It is more probable that the golden mantle in question had been presented either by the Sicilian Gelon, as Cicero has it in the passage cited, or by Hiero, as Valerius Maximus states in Book I, ch. 1; both agree that it had been made from spoils taken from the Carthaginians. CELLARIUS.

**Dionysius … with jokes.** Arnobius treats all these matters more fully in Book VI, p. 205. Add Perizonius on Aelian, *Various History*, I, ch. 20. Thus Justin says of a certain Alexander in Book XXXIX, ch. 2: “He orders that the solid-gold image of Victory be removed from Jupiter’s temple, disguising his sacrilege with witty jokes; for he said that Jupiter had lent Victory to him.” Thus Brennus, too (Justin, Book XXIV, ch. 6), jested like a buffoon that wealthy gods ought to make gifts to human beings, etc. BUNEMANN.]

because he considered it superfluous in religious rites, since it was an instrument not of sanctity but of greed. For it is better to bring to the God whom you rightly worship these things as a gift:

> Established justice and divine right within the soul, its holy inner recesses,  
> And a heart steeped in noble honor.

His thought was excellent and wise. But he ridiculously added that this is what gold in temples amounts to:

> Dolls given to Venus by a maiden,

which he perhaps despised because of their smallness. For he did not perceive that the images and likenesses of the gods, fashioned from gold and ivory by the hands of Polyclitus, Euphranor, and Phidias, were nothing other than large dolls [Col. 0272A], consecrated not by maidens, whose play can be pardoned, but by bearded men. Seneca therefore rightly mocks even the folly of old men. “We are not,” he says, “children twice over, as the common saying goes, but always children. The difference is that our toys are larger.” Thus to these playthings—these adorned and enormous dolls—they bring ointments, incense, and perfumes; to them they sacrifice rich and fat victims, though they do indeed have mouths, but mouths devoid of the function of teeth; to them they give robes and costly clothing, although they have no use for covering; to them they consecrate gold and silver, which those who receive them no more possess than those who gave them away.

Not without reason, therefore, did Dionysius, the tyrant of Sicily, after gaining possession of Greece by victory, despise, plunder, [Col. 0273A] and mock gods of this kind; for he even accompanied his acts of sacrilege with jocular remarks. When he had stripped the golden mantle from Olympian Jupiter [Col. 0273A]—

**When he had stripped the golden mantle from Olympian Jupiter.** The tyrant Gelon had adorned it with this from the spoils of the Carthaginians, as Cicero says. On this jocular deed and the witty remarks, see Valerius Maximus, Book I [Col. 0273D], in the chapter *On Neglected Religion*. On this and other similar acts, see Epiphanius in the *Ancoratus*, Clement of Alexandria in the *Protrepticus*, Arnobius, Book VI, and Cicero, Book III of *On the Nature of the Gods*.—**They have a mantle.** Two Royal manuscripts, the Brunsvigian manuscript, and the Roman 1470, Paris, Aldine, Cratander, Grapheus, Isaeus, and Walch editions have *covering*; one Clermont manuscript, *little mantle*.

**Stripping Aesculapius of his golden beard.** See Cicero and Valerius in the passages cited. Aesculapius, moreover, was represented with a beard to signify the wisdom of old age required by a physician. The phallic poet, Poem 36:

> Aesculapius’s beard is always unshorn.

CELLARIUS.

**Still beardless.** Thus the same Apollo is called *smooth-faced* by Horace, *Odes* IV, 6. Our author follows Minucius Felix, ch. 21: “Apollo smooth-faced throughout so many ages, Aesculapius well bearded,” etc. BUNEMANN.

**Smooth-faced.** We have correctly restored this from one Clermont manuscript and the editions of Fasitelus, Tornesius, Soubron, Thomasius, Cellarius, and Walch. Six other manuscripts together with four editions have *light*; five Royal manuscripts, four [Col. 0274B] Colbertine manuscripts, one Clermont, the Brunsvigian manuscript, and the Roman 1470 edition have *gentle*.

**Bowls, ornaments, and certain small statuettes.** Cicero reports the same things in Book III of *On the Nature of the Gods*, ch. 34; consult him. He himself calls them “little Victories, bowls, and crowns,” which were held in the images’ outstretched hands. CELLARIUS.—**Small … statuettes.** Compare the note on Book VII, ch. 3: “As though little statuettes,” etc.

[Col. 0274C]

**Outstretched hands.** Thus correctly the second edition of 1478. The first edition of 1478 incorrectly has *powerful*. The Subiaco, Rostock, Venice 1493, and Venice 1497 editions have *portentous*. Cicero, Book III of *On the Nature of the Gods*, ch. 34, and Valerius Maximus, Book I, external example 3, have *with hands extended*, which is the same as *outstretched*, from *to stretch forth*. BUNEMANN.

**And handed the kingdom over … into his hands.** See *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, ch. 24. Thus Livy, Book I, ch. 3: “He handed the kingdom over into Aventinus’s hands.” BUNEMANN.

**Could not.** Four Colbertine manuscripts and the Brunsvigian have *were unable*.

**It would have been proper.** *It was proper* is used for *it would have been proper*, as in Book VI, ch. 24: “He could have been a true worshipper of God if someone … had shown him”; and *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, ch. 27: “He could easily have been captured in flight if anyone had pursued him.” BUNEMANN.

**Racks.** Pitiscus provides an illustration and description of the rack in his note 19 on Curtius, Book VI, ch. 10. Compare Cuper on *The Deaths of the Persecutors*, ch. 23. BUNEMANN.

**When they punish.** The same point occurs in Book V, ch. 20. Although the Fathers press this argument rather frequently—for example, Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*, ch. 12, fol. 328, and Arnobius, Book I, p. 11—Heraldus nevertheless rightly warns, on Arnobius, Book I, pp. 18–19, that these statements are not true *without qualification* (ἁπλῶς), because God wills impiety to be punished even by human beings. BUNEMANN.

**Especially to them—why not?** The reading of Gothofredus, Reimann, and the third Leipzig edition is almost better: “For why do they not especially leave it to the gods themselves?” BUNEMANN.
