**Punishments should fall upon themselves.** Five Colbertine manuscripts, Junius, the Rostock manuscript, one Clermont manuscript, and the Roman 1470 edition have “punishments should fall upon themselves”; one Colbertine and one Clermont manuscript, by a second hand, have *should expose*. One ancient Bologna manuscript and the Caucian manuscript have “punishments should seek them out.” Isaeus would prefer this reading if *punishments* had been written in the accusative.

**They suppose, because of the crimes of others.** Four Colbertine manuscripts and the Roman 1470 edition have *they suppose* in the indicative.

**To his companions.** See Cicero at the end of Book III of *On the Nature of the Gods*.

**From Plato.** Dionysius kept him with himself for a long time, as is evident both from Diogenes Laertius and from the Platonic letters.]

he ordered a woolen one to be put upon the statue, saying that gold was heavy in summer and cold in winter, whereas wool was suitable for both seasons. Likewise, when he stripped Aesculapius of his golden beard, he said that it was incongruous and unjust for the son to appear bearded before his father, when his father Apollo was still beardless and smooth-faced. He also removed bowls, ornaments, and certain small statuettes held in the images’ outstretched hands; and he said that he was accepting them, not taking them away, since it was exceedingly foolish and ungrateful to refuse to accept things freely offered by those from whom people prayed that good things might come to them. He did these things with impunity because he was king and victor. Indeed, his customary good fortune continued to accompany him [Col. 0273B]: he lived to old age and handed the kingdom over into his son’s hands. Since human beings could not avenge these acts of sacrilege upon him, it would therefore have been proper for the gods themselves to be their own avengers. But if some lowly person commits such an act, whips, fires, racks, crosses, and whatever else angry and frenzied people can devise are ready at hand for him. Yet when they punish those caught in sacrilege, they themselves show distrust in the power of their gods. For why do they not especially leave to the gods the opportunity to avenge themselves, if they believe that the gods can do anything? Indeed, they even suppose that it occurred through the gods’ divine power that robbers of sacred objects were caught and detained; and they rage not so much from anger as from fear that, if they fail to avenge the injury done to the gods, punishments will fall upon themselves. Their vanity is, of course, incredible: they suppose that the gods will harm them because of other people’s crimes, although those gods could by themselves do no harm to the very people by whom they were violated and plundered. “But,” they say, “the gods themselves have also often taken vengeance upon sacrilegious persons.” That may have happened by chance, since it occurred sometimes, not always. Yet I shall show a little later how it happened. For the present, I ask why they did not avenge so many and such great acts of sacrilege upon Dionysius, who mocked the gods not secretly but openly. Why did they not keep this powerful sacrilegious man away from their temples [Col. 0274B], rites, and images? Why, even after the sacred objects had been carried away, did he enjoy a prosperous voyage? He himself attested to this in a joke, as was his custom. “Do you see,” he said to his companions when they feared shipwreck, “what a prosperous voyage the immortal gods themselves grant to sacrilegious men?” But perhaps he had learned from Plato that there are no gods.

[Col. 0275A] What of Gaius Verres, whom Tullius, his prosecutor—

[Note: [Col. 0265C] [Notes of the Various Editors on column 275]

**Prosecutor.** Cicero, *Against Verres*, Action VI, at the end.

**Of Catina.** Thus I restored the text from the manuscript codices and the old Roman editions of 1468 and 1470. Pomponius Mela likewise calls it *Catina*; Cicero calls it *Catina* or *Catine* in Action VI *Against Verres*, at the end; and so does Silius in Book XIII. Many printed editions have *of Catana*. Catina is now Catana, at the foot of Mount Etna, and has suffered greatly from its eruptions in recent times.]

Ennensian. Ἔννη (*Ennē*), Enna, a city in the very center of Sicily, famous for the worship of Ceres, as is also attested by Strabo and Mela. Thus Ceres is also called “Ennaean” in Claudian and Silius Italicus.

**So great was the religious sanctity of the other.** “Of the other,” namely, the Catanian. On its religious sanctity, see Cicero at the place cited, chapter 45. CELL.

**In the time of the Gracchi.** When, after the killing of Tiberius Gracchus, portents foretold the fear of great dangers. From Cicero, *On Famous Orators*, chapter 45. CELLAR.—On these disturbances at Enna, see Livy, Decade IV.

**Ceres.** On the worship of Ceres, see above, Book I, chapter 21.

**By Gaius Verres.** In the first consulship of Gnaeus Pompey and Marcus Crassus, Gaius Verres, after completing his quaestorship, legateship, and urban praetorship, and after holding the government of Sicily for three years and conducting himself there licentiously, greedily, and cruelly, was prosecuted by the Sicilians on a charge of extortion. Seven speeches by Cicero against Verres survive. For the present subject, however, the sixth should be read above all the others. The story is also related by Valerius, Book I, chapter 1.

**He had also removed them from heaven.** I have restored this reading from the early printed editions and all the manuscripts except one Colbert manuscript, which has *sustulerit* (“has removed”). Twelve printed editions read *sustulisset* (“had removed”).

**To you, Marcus Tullius—that is, to a human being.** So the early Bologna manuscripts read. Some printed editions read: “To you, Marcus Tullius—that is, to you yourself, a human being,” which is less correct because of the pointless repetition, as Thomasius observes.

**Could.** I have restored this from all the manuscripts and from the editions of Rome 1470, Paris, Cratander, Tornesius, Soubron, and Cellarius. Aldus 1515 has “will be able”; the other common editions have “were able.”

**Was condemned.** For he had carried off forty million sesterces, according to Cicero; according to Plutarch, as interpreted by Budaeus, three million sesterces—that is, seventy thousand gold crowns, by the computation of the same Budaeus.

**By which he either crushed his defenders.** The first early Bologna manuscript and Walch’s edition have “which”; Junius and the Aldine, Paris, and Grapheus editions have “because”; the Rome 1468 edition has “by which either [he crushed] those who exposed him.”

**Who seemed to have fallen.** On the proscription of the triumvirs, read Eutropius, Book VII; Appian, Book IV; Plutarch’s *Antony*; Florus, Book IV, chapter 5; Orosius, Book VI, chapter 18; Velleius Paterculus, Book II; and others. Yet nowhere, so far as I know, is Verres mentioned. Lactantius may perhaps have read this in certain lost writings.

**Standing.** That is, safe and unharmed. He echoes Cicero, *Letters to Friends*, Book VI, letter 6. BUNEMANN.—**While all stood.** I read this with the editions of Tornesius, Soubron, and Walch, and with all the manuscripts except two recent Royal manuscripts and fourteen editions, which have “while everyone stood.”

**How much more right, therefore, it is.** The first early Bologna manuscript, one Clermont manuscript, and the Cotton manuscript have: “How much more honorable and right, therefore, it is.”

[Inherited source gap: the subject and antecedent are missing] …of him, compares [him] with that same Dionysius, with Phalaris, and with all tyrants. Did he not plunder the whole of Sicily, carrying away the statues of the gods and the ornaments of their shrines? It would be tedious to pursue every individual case. I wish to recall one instance (see *Against Verres* IV), over which the accuser lamented with every power of eloquence and, indeed, with every exertion of voice and body: the case of Ceres of Catana or of Enna. So great was the religious sanctity of the former that it was forbidden for men to approach the secret inner chambers of her temple; so great was the antiquity of the latter that all histories relate that the goddess herself first discovered grain in the soil of Enna and that her virgin daughter was abducted from that same place. Finally, in the time of the Gracchi, when the commonwealth had been thrown into disorder by seditions and portents, and it was discovered in the Sibylline verses that the most ancient Ceres had to be propitiated, envoys were sent to Enna. [Col. 0275B]

This Ceres, then—either the most sacred, whom males were not permitted to see even for the sake of worship, or the most ancient, whom the Senate and People of Rome had propitiated with sacrifices and gifts—was carried away with impunity from her secret and ancient inner sanctuary by Gaius Verres, who sent in his robber-slaves. When Cicero himself affirmed that he had been asked by the Sicilians to undertake the province’s case, he used these words: “They said that they no longer had even gods in their cities to whom they might flee for refuge, because Gaius Verres had removed their most sacred images from their most holy shrines”—as though, if Verres had removed them from the cities and shrines, he had also removed them from heaven. From this it is evident that those gods possess nothing beyond [Col. 0275C] the material from which they were fashioned.

And not without reason, Marcus Tullius, did the Sicilians flee to you—that is, to a human being—for in the course of three years they had learned by experience that those gods had no power. They would have been exceedingly foolish if, in order to defend themselves against injuries inflicted by human beings, they had fled to gods who could not even become angry with Gaius Verres on their own behalf. But, it will be said, Verres was condemned for these crimes. It was therefore not the gods who exacted vengeance, but Cicero’s diligence, by which he either crushed Verres’ defenders or withstood their influence.

What of the fact that, for Verres himself, that condemnation was not a punishment but a holiday? Just as the immortal gods had granted Dionysius a favorable voyage while he carried away the gods’ spoils, so they also seem to have granted Verres a pleasant repose in which he could enjoy his acts of sacrilege undisturbed. For when civil wars subsequently began to rage, under cover of his condemnation he remained removed from every danger and fear, hearing of the grievous misfortunes [Col. 0276B] and pitiable deaths of others. He who alone had seemed to have fallen while all others stood was in truth the only one who stood when all others fell, until the triumviral proscription carried him off, after he had been sated both with the wealth acquired by sacrilege and with life, and worn out by old age—the very same proscription, of course, that carried off Tullius, the avenger of the violated majesty of the gods. Indeed, Verres was fortunate even in this: before his own death, he heard of the exceedingly cruel death of his accuser. The gods evidently took care that this sacrilegious plunderer of their religious rites should not die before deriving consolation from the vengeance.

## CHAPTER V  
### That the one Creator, God, alone is to be worshiped, and not the elements or the heavenly bodies; and a refutation of the Stoic opinion that the stars and constellations are gods

[Col. 0276C] How much more right, therefore, it is to abandon insensible and [Col. 0277A] empty things and direct our eyes toward the place where the dwelling of the true God is—

**Where the dwelling is.** On this opinion of Lactantius, see Plutarch, *Opinions of the Philosophers*, Book I, chapter 6.

**Who [suspended] the earth with stable [firmness].** In his book *On the World*, Philo Judaeus asks what the foundation of the universe is; he finally concludes that it is the law and decree of the eternal God. Compare Psalm 148:6.

**Suspended the earth.** Book III, chapter 3: “On what foundations the earth is balanced or suspended.” BUN.

**As an indication, etc.** Similar words are found in St. Augustine, *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*.

**Surrounded the lands with seas.** So read all the manuscripts and common editions except four recent editions, which have “surrounds.” **Commanded.** This is from the beginning of Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*, Book I.

**Who was born seventeen hundred years ago.** The Christ Church manuscript has: “Who was born after a thousand years,” etc. Either reading is sound and signifies the same thing. For when speaking of time, Lactantius commonly uses “before” in the sense of “after,” as in Book IV [Col. 0277D] of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 10: “Before the tenth day of the Kalends of April, the Jews fastened Christ to the cross”; but in *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 2, at the beginning: “After the tenth day of the Kalends of April,” etc., as we shall demonstrate more fully there and in the Dissertation on that book itself.

**That maker.** Ovid, at the passage cited above, shortly afterward.

**For the uses of man.** Three recent Royal manuscripts and the printed editions have “for the uses of men”; but six Royal manuscripts, two of which are extremely ancient, two Colbert manuscripts, and two Clermont manuscripts have “of man,” from which “for human uses” arose in two recent Royal manuscripts, four Colbert manuscripts, and the Emmeram and Christ Church manuscripts.

**To serve.** The Subiaco edition and the first Venice edition of 1478 incorrectly have “to be familiar”; the manuscripts and the Rostock, Venice 1471, and the second editions of 1478, 1493, 1497, and others correctly have “to serve.” In *On the Anger of God*, Book XXIII [sic], chapter 21: “to serve earthly things.” BUN.

**Who preferred his works to God himself, their most indulgent Father.** So read the older and better manuscripts—two Bologna, the Royal, Taxius, Junius, Penworth, six Colbert, Leipzig, Palatine, Brunswick, and two Clermont manuscripts—together with the editions of Rome 1468 and 1470, Isaeus, and six more recent printed editions, except that one Clermont and one recent Royal manuscript omit “and,” as do six printed editions. The Caucasus manuscript has: “who [preferred] his own works to God, his most indulgent Father.” Early editions used *suus* and *ille* indiscriminately.

**Lucilius.** This is taken from Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book II, section 54, where those who attribute divinity to the heavenly bodies are censured. Clinias also, in Plato’s *Laws*, Book X, attributes a soul to the sun, moon, and stars. I find “Lucilius” written thus in nine Royal manuscripts, two Bologna manuscripts, Taxius, Penworth, six Colbert manuscripts, two Clermont manuscripts, and the Emmeram, Cambridge, and Brunswick manuscripts; in the editions of Gymnicus, Betuleius, Tornesius, Soubron, Isaeus, Cellarius, and Walch; and in Cicero himself. The Leipzig, Junius, Bodleian, and Cotton manuscripts and the editions of Rome 1470 and Cratander have *Lucillius*; seven editions have *Lucillus*.—**Lucilius the Stoic.** Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book I, chapter 6: “Quintus Lucilius Balbus, who had made such progress among the Stoics that he was compared with the most eminent Greeks in that school.” CELL.

**In such varied [courses].** The preposition “in” has been added from all the manuscripts and almost all the editions; it is absent from five recent common editions.

**It remains.** This is from Cicero, at the same place, section 44.

**But also acts impiously if he denies that they are gods.** Plato in the *Cratylus*. The Stoics speak similarly, as does Posidonius in Stobaeus. St. Augustine, *City of God*, Book IV, chapter 11: “They—the Stoics—say that all the stars are parts of Jupiter, that they are all alive and possess rational souls, and that they are therefore gods beyond dispute.” VOSSIUS.

**For they regard the sun and moon.** Various nations had the custom of worshiping the Sun and Moon. Herodotus says of the Persians in *Clio*: “They also sacrifice to the Sun, Moon, Earth, Fire, Water, and Winds; for an ancient custom has prevailed that they sacrifice to these alone.” He likewise says of the peoples of Libya in *Melpomene*: “They sacrifice to the Sun and Moon alone, to whom all the peoples of Libya customarily offer victims.” SCHEDIUS.

—who suspended the earth with stable firmness; who adorned heaven with gleaming stars; who kindled the sun, the brightest and unique light for human affairs, as an indication of his unique majesty; who surrounded the lands with seas and commanded the rivers to flow in an everlasting course:

> He commanded the plains to spread, the valleys to sink,  
> The woods to be clothed with foliage, and stony mountains to rise.

Certainly Jupiter did not make all these things, for he was born seventeen hundred years ago, but rather:

> That maker of things, the source of a better world,

who is called God. Since his beginning cannot be comprehended, it ought not even to be sought. For full and perfect wisdom, it is sufficient for a human being [Col. 0277B] to understand that God exists. The force and essence of this understanding is that one should look up to and honor the common Parent of the human race and the maker of these marvelous things.

Hence certain people of dull and obtuse mind worship as gods the elements, which were themselves made and lack sensation. Although they marveled at the works of God—that is, heaven with its varied lights, earth with its plains and mountains, and the seas with their rivers, pools, and springs—they were stupefied by admiration for these things and, forgetting the craftsman himself, whom they could not see, began to venerate and worship his works. They were never able to understand how much greater and more marvelous is he who made those things out of nothing. Although they see these things obedient to divine laws, serving the benefits and uses [Col. 0278A] of man by perpetual necessity, they nevertheless suppose them to be gods. They are ungrateful for divine benefactions, for they have preferred his works to God himself, their most indulgent Father.

But what wonder is it if barbarians or uneducated people go astray, when even philosophers of the Stoic school hold the same opinion, judging that all the heavenly bodies that move ought to be counted among the gods? Thus Lucilius the Stoic speaks in Cicero:

> This constancy in the stars, this great agreement of times throughout all eternity amid such varied courses, I cannot understand without mind, reason, and design. Since we see these present in the heavenly bodies, we cannot fail to place those very bodies among the number of the gods.

Likewise, a little earlier:

> It remains, he says, that the motion of the stars is voluntary. Whoever sees these things acts not only ignorantly but also [Col. 0278B] impiously if he denies that they are gods.

We, however, firmly deny it; and we prove that you philosophers are not merely ignorant and impious, but blind, foolish, and deranged, for you have surpassed the ignorance of the uneducated in your delusion. They regard the sun and moon as gods; you regard even the stars as gods.

Teach us, then, the mysteries of the stars, so that we may erect altars and temples to each of them; so that we may know by what rite and on what day we should worship each one, and by what names and prayers we should invoke them—unless perhaps we ought to worship such innumerable and tiny gods indiscriminately, all in a heap. What of the fact that the argument by which they infer that all the heavenly bodies are gods actually supports the opposite conclusion? For if they suppose them to be gods because they follow fixed and rational [Col. 0279A] courses, they are mistaken.

**Rational.** The Brunswick manuscript has “reasoning”; Francius also preferred that reading.

**To depart from their orbit.** Cyprian, Book I, letter 12: “Departing from its orbit and straying from the way of truth.” BUN.

**At random.** That is, without order, without fixed laws, as they pleased, as the context of all the words reveals. I note this at Book II, chapter 6, and Book III, chapter 9. BUN.

**As it pleased.** So all editions and manuscripts except six recent ones, which have “as it pleases.”

**It is borne wherever [the mind leads it].** Two recent manuscripts have “they are borne.”

[Col. 0279D]

**The motion of the stars is therefore not voluntary.** The ancients said that the heavenly bodies “moved” when they rose or set.

**Conscious of its duty.** Compare Book II, chapter 14, “knowing things”; and the *Epitome*, chapter 5, “those who know things.” BUN.

**Or did Archimedes, etc.?** Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I: “For when Archimedes bound the motions of the moon, the sun, and the five wandering planets into a sphere, he accomplished the same thing as Plato’s God, who built the world in the *Timaeus*: a single revolution governed motions highly dissimilar in slowness and speed. If this cannot happen in our world without God, Archimedes could not have imitated those same motions in his sphere without divine genius.” Julius Firmicus, Book VI, chapter 3: “This is that man of ours by whose genius a sphere was fashioned which displays the revolution of heaven and the courses of all the stars as an image of divine imitation.” Solinus, chapter 21: “Here was the home of Archimedes, who was a mechanical interpreter according to the science of the stars.” Yet he was celebrated not only for this machine but also for others, acclaimed by everyone, during the siege of Syracuse. There was also a certain hydraulic machine praised by Tertullian [Col. 0280C] in *On the Soul*, chapter 14: “Consider,” he says, “the most prodigious generosity of Archimedes—I mean the hydraulic organ: so many members, so many parts, so many joints, so many pathways of voices, so many concentrations of sounds, so many exchanges of modes, so many ranks,” etc. BARTHIUS. Cicero also mentions this sphere in *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book II, and *Tusculan Disputations*, Book V. See also Claudian’s epigram on Archimedes.—**Archimedes.** Lactantius evidently had in view Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book II, chapter 36: “They suppose that Archimedes achieved more in imitating the revolutions of the sphere than nature did in producing them.” Add chapter 34. BUNEMANN.

**Unequal motions.** On these, see Pliny, Book II.

**Revolutions.** That is, the returns of the sun from one tropic to the other. See Pliny, Book XVIII.

**Or fixed stars.** This is the reading of all the manuscripts except one Oxford manuscript, and of the two early Roman editions, Venice 1490, Betuleius, Isaeus, Sparke, Cellarius, and Walch; that is, the fixed stars. Several editions incorrectly have “wandering”; for that is the same as τὸ *vagarum* (“the wandering stars”), which follows. One Clermont manuscript and the Cotton manuscript have *vagantium*.

**The sun to stand still.** See Pliny, Book II, chapter 19. **That the heavenly bodies are animals.** Origen also fell into this error in his book *On First Principles*.

**And tiny lights.** Tiny, that is, to the eye.

**Φαινόμενα.** This book by Ovid, or translation from Aratus’ *Phaenomena*, was derived from that work. Plutarch quotes these verses from Aratus in Greek in *Opinions of the Philosophers*, Book II, chapter 19.

Indeed, from this very fact it is evident that they are not gods: they are not permitted to depart from the paths prescribed for them. But if they were gods, they would be carried here and there at random, without any necessity, just as living creatures on earth wander this way and that because they possess free wills, as it pleases them; each is borne wherever its mind leads it. The motion of the stars is therefore not voluntary but necessary, because they are subservient to prescribed laws and duties.

Yet when the Stoic discussed the courses of the stars, which from the very harmony of events and times he understood not to be accidental, he supposed them to be voluntary, as though they could not move in such a well-arranged and orderly manner unless there were in them a faculty of sensation conscious of its duty. O how difficult truth is for those who do not know it, and how easy for those who do! [Col. 0279B] “If the motions of the stars,” he says, “are not accidental, nothing remains except that they be voluntary.” On the contrary: just as it is evident that they are not accidental, so too they are not voluntary.

How, then, do they preserve their constancy in completing their courses? God, the maker of the universe, plainly arranged them and contrived them in such a way that they would run through the expanses of heaven according to a divine and marvelous plan, producing the variety of seasons that succeed one another. Or did Archimedes the Sicilian have the power to construct in hollow bronze a likeness and representation of the universe, arranging the sun and moon within it so that they produced unequal motions and revolutions resembling the heavenly revolutions, as though day by day, and so that, as it turned, that sphere displayed not only the approaches and withdrawals of the sun and the waxing and waning of the moon, but [Col. 0279C] also the differing courses of the stars, both fixed and wandering? Could God, then, not contrive and produce in reality what human skill was able to represent by imitation?

If a Stoic had seen the shapes of the stars painted and modeled on that [Col. 0280A] bronze, would he say that they moved by their own design, rather than by the ingenuity of the craftsman? There is, then, a rational plan adapted to the stars’ completion of their courses; but that plan belongs to God, who both made and governs all things, not to the stars themselves, which are moved. For if he had wished the sun to stand still, there would certainly be perpetual day. Likewise, if the stars had no motion, who could doubt that night would have been everlasting? But so that there might be alternations of day and night, he willed them to move—and to move with such variety that there would be not only mutual successions of light and darkness, establishing alternate intervals of labor and rest, but also of cold and heat, so that the force and influence of the different seasons might be suited either to producing or to ripening crops.

Because the philosophers did not perceive this skill of divine power in contriving the paths of the stars, [Col. 0280B] they supposed that the heavenly bodies were animals, as though they proceeded on feet and of their own accord, rather than according to the divine plan. Why God devised them, however, who does not understand? Obviously, it was so that, when the sunlight withdrew, an excessively blind night would not become oppressive with grim and dreadful darkness and harm living creatures. Thus at one and the same time he adorned heaven with marvelous variety and softened the darkness itself with many tiny lights.

How much wiser, then, was Naso than those who suppose themselves devoted to wisdom, since he understood that God established those lights to drive away the horror of darkness! He concluded the book in which he briefly treated the Φαινόμενα (*Phaenomena*, “Appearances”) with these three verses:

> So many images in number and of such form did God  
> Set in heaven and scatter through the black darkness,  
> Commanding them to give bright light to the frosty night. [Col. 0280C]

But if it is impossible for the stars to be gods, neither the sun nor the moon can be gods, since they differ from the lights of the stars not in kind but only in magnitude. And if these are not gods, neither can heaven itself, in which all these things are contained, be a god.

[Col. 0281A]

## CHAPTER VI  
### That neither the whole universe nor the elements are God or living beings

Similarly, if the earth upon which we tread [Col. 0281A]—

**If the earth upon which we tread, etc.** Many nations worshiped the earth as a goddess. The Phrygians worshiped her under the names Rhea, Cybele, and so forth. The Assyrians likewise regarded her as a goddess, according to Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book I, chapter 23: “The Assyrians gave the name Adad to the god whom they worship as highest and greatest. They join to him a goddess named Adargatis and attribute to these two all power over every thing, understanding them as the sun and earth.” The Egyptians also rendered divine honors to her under the name Isis, according to Servius on *Aeneid* VIII: “In the language of the Egyptians,” he says, “Isis is the earth, which they understand Isis to be.” Likewise Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book I, chapter 20: “Isis is celebrated in a conjoined religious observance; she is either the earth or the nature of things lying beneath the sun.” The Germans also worshiped this goddess, as Tacitus attests, saying that she was called Hertha. See Vossius, *On Idolatry*, chapter 55.

**Which we subdue and cultivate for sustenance.** We have restored this from the early editions and all the manuscripts except the first early Bologna manuscript, in which “and cultivate” is absent. Cato speaks of this in Cicero’s *On Old Age*.

[Col. 0281D]

**Not even the fields.** I read “not even the fields,” as in Venice 1493 and 1497. BUN.

**Likewise, if water.** Of all nations, the Egyptians and Persians appear especially to have venerated water. Plutarch says of the former in *On Isis and Osiris*: “Nothing is held in greater honor among the Egyptians than the Nile.” Among our writers, Athanasius, himself an Egyptian, says in his *Oration Against the Nations*: “Others worship rivers and springs; the Egyptians above all especially venerate water and call it a god.” Julius Firmicus speaks similarly in *On the Error of Profane Religions*. VOSSIUS.

**Not even the springs.** On the basis of the Gotha manuscript, the third Leipzig manuscript, Venice 1471, and Rostock, I read “not even the springs,” as many books have “not even the earth,” “not even the rivers,” and “not even the universe.” Hence I thought “not even heaven” should be corrected in the same way. Compare Graevius and others on *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 4, note 8, and my note on Lactantius, Book VI, chapter 15. BUN.

**Not even the rivers.** I have substituted “nor” for “not” from two Royal manuscripts, three Colbert manuscripts, the Brunswick manuscript, and many editions, as the preceding words require.

**Which are parts of the universe.** Cicero expresses the same opinion in *On the Nature of the Gods*: namely, that the parts of the universe are not parts of God.

**Therefore not even the whole universe is God.** On this Stoic doctrine, see Cicero in Book IV of the *Academic Questions*. For the Stoics, the universe itself was God. See Plutarch, *Opinions of the Philosophers*, Book I, chapters 3 and 7; Epiphanius, preface to the *Heresies*; Seneca, *Natural Questions*, Book II, chapter 45: “Do you wish to call the universe God? You will not be mistaken. For he himself is the whole that you see, wholly inserted into his works and sustaining himself by his own power.” Manilius, *Astronomica*, Book I:

> How it may be revealed that the universe turns by divine power,  
> And is itself God.

So too Cato in Lucan, Book IX:

> Jupiter is whatever you see, whatever is moved.

**The propositions are indeed true … but the assumptions false.** Lactantius speaks in Ciceronian fashion. He calls that part of a syllogism which the Schoolmen name the “major” the “proposition,” and what the Schoolmen call the “minor” he calls the “assumption.” From ISAEUS.

**The universe [is] a dwelling.** Thus Cicero says in *On Ends*, Book III: “They hold that the universe is governed by the divine power of the gods, that it is, as it were, the common city and state of human beings and gods, and that each one of us is a part of that universe.”

**What inhabits it is one thing.** I have restored this reading from all the manuscripts and early editions. Many printed editions have “worships.” See the preceding words.

**The consequence.** Reimmann and Tornesius have “the consequent.” Reimmann likewise reads “therefore even beasts of burden”; correctly. BUN.

**But also.** This is the reading of all the manuscripts; the printed editions have “but even,” except Tornesius and Soubron.

**Beasts of burden and cattle.** This is confirmed by Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, chapter 1, verse 23.

**For the Egyptians worship even these.** They were especially devoted to the more absurd superstitions. On the religious superstitions of the Egyptians, see Herodotus, Book II; Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, Book V; Philostratus, *Life of Apollonius*, Book VI; Lucian, *On Sacrifices*; Solinus, chapter 45; and Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book II, chapter 1.

—and which we subdue and cultivate for sustenance, is not a god, neither will the fields and mountains be gods. But if these are not gods, the whole earth cannot be regarded as God. Likewise, if water, which serves living creatures for drinking or washing, is not a god, neither are the springs from which water flows. If the springs are not gods, neither are the rivers that gather from the springs. If the rivers too are not gods, then the sea, which consists of rivers, cannot be regarded as God. And if neither heaven, earth, nor sea, which are parts [Col. 0281B] of the universe, can be gods, then not even the whole universe is God—although these same Stoics contend that it is both living and wise, and for that reason God. In this they were so inconsistent that they said nothing which they themselves did not overthrow.

For they argue as follows: “It is impossible for that which generates sentient beings from itself to lack sensation. But the universe generates the human being, who is endowed with sensation; therefore, the universe itself is sentient.” Likewise: “That of which a part possesses sensation cannot be without sensation. Therefore, because a human being is sentient, sensation also inheres in the universe, of which the human being is a part.” [Col. 0282A]

The propositions are indeed true: that what begets something endowed with sensation is itself sentient, and that a thing whose part is furnished with sensation itself possesses sensation. But the assumptions by which they complete their arguments are false, because the universe does not generate the human being, nor is the human being a part of the universe. For at the beginning the same God made both the human being and the universe. A human being is not a part of the universe as a limb is a part of the body; for the universe can exist without the human being, just as a city or a house can. Rather, just as a house is the habitation of one person and a city of one people, so the universe is the dwelling of the entire human race. What is inhabited is one thing; what inhabits it is another.

But while they strive to confirm what they have falsely assumed—that the universe is both sentient and God—they fail to perceive the consequence of their own arguments. [Col. 0282B] For if a human being is a part of the universe, and the universe is sentient because the human being senses, then because the human being is mortal, the universe too must necessarily be mortal—and not merely mortal, but subject to every disease and passion.

Conversely, if the universe is God, its parts are certainly immortal. Therefore, a human being too is God, because, as you say, the human being is a part of the universe. If a human being is God, then so too are beasts of burden, cattle, and the other kinds of wild animals, birds, and fish, since they too sense in the same manner and are parts of the universe. Yet this is tolerable, for the Egyptians worship even these. But the matter goes so far that [Col. 0283A] even frogs—

**So that even frogs.** I have restored “even” from the manuscripts and early Roman editions. One Clermont manuscript has “so that even spiders,” perhaps the genuine reading, which agrees better with gnats and ants than “frogs” does.

**These same men.** Namely, the Stoics. Compare Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book II, chapters 53 and 62; and Lactantius, *On Anger*, chapter 13 and following. BUNEMANN.

**That the universe was constructed.** Plato also uses both forms of expression in the *Timaeus*. If the universe was made by God out of nothing, as the Christian confession believes, it was not generated. For γένεσις (*genesis*, generation) occurs when matter assumes another substantial form. [Col. 0283D] BETULEIUS.

**A ship. There is, therefore.** I have punctuated it thus, as all editions do, whereas Cellarius has “a ship is. Therefore.” After “ship,” understand “was built.” BUN.

**Now how contradictory and absurd is this.** One Royal manuscript has “For.” The Penworth manuscript and the editions of Isaeus and Sparke have “how absurd.”

**They affirm.** This is the reading of nearly all the manuscripts and of the Rome 1468 edition. One Colbert manuscript, one Clermont manuscript, and almost all common editions have “they assert.”

**But if the universe is God.** Reimmann gives a better order: “But if the universe is God.” BUN.

**Which certainly cannot by themselves receive the name of God.** We have restored this from a great many manuscripts. Two Royal manuscripts and the printed editions have “of God alone”; two Royal, two Colbert, and two Clermont manuscripts have “of the solid [God].”

**Become insensible.** So read the editions of Sparke, Cellarius, and Walch, and all the manuscripts except three Colbert manuscripts and many printed editions, which have “decay,” an entirely corrupt reading. “Become insensible” means, in Lactantius, “lose sensation.”—**Become insensible.** Book VII, chapter 12: “It is not the soul that becomes insensible when the body fails, but the body when the soul departs, because the soul draws all sensation away with it.” In both passages Lactantius is speaking of sensation, not decay. BUN.

**Nor can the house exercise ownership over itself.** This must be read on the authority of both Bologna manuscripts and five Vatican manuscripts. Thomasius rightly judges that the copyists negligently omitted an *i*, and the text itself proves that this is the proper reading; for because a house does not possess ownership of itself, the universe likewise does not enjoy that right. In addition to the manuscripts praised by Thomasius, I find this reading in the Royal manuscripts, three Colbert manuscripts, and the Caucasus, Junius, Utrecht, Emmeram, Cambridge, one Leipzig, one Clermont, and Brunswick manuscripts, and in the editions of Rome 1470 and 1474, Aldus, Cratander, Gymnicus, Grapheus, Soubron, Isaeus, Gallasius, Sparke, Cellarius, and Walch.

**Of the sun and moon.** Eusebius argues against this Greek superstition in *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book III, chapter 2.

**They offer sacrifice in the open.** So read all the printed editions and almost all the manuscripts. Junius has “they sacrifice.” One Royal and one Colbert manuscript have “they offer sacrifice under cover,” incorrectly. The first early Bologna manuscript has “they offer sacrifice at the crossroads”; the other, more recent Bologna manuscript and Taxius have “they offer sacrifice in an openly occurring event.”

**The sheen dazzles their eyes.** Instead of the received text, the *Epitome*, chapter 25, has “the brilliance would dazzle their eyes.” Cicero, *On Ends*, Book IV, chapter 14: “You dazzle the keenness of our minds with the splendor of virtue.” BUNEMANN.

**They therefore consecrate the spoils of war to the gods.** Florus, Book I, chapter 7, on Tarquinius Superbus: “From the proceeds of captured cities he erected a temple.” Nonius Marcellus teaches what *manubiae* properly are and how they differ from booty or spoils, saying: “The ancients held that *manubiae* differ from booty in this respect: booty consists of the actual objects that are captured, whereas *manubiae* are the money obtained from selling the booty.”

**Weak.** The Gotha manuscript and Reimmann have the masculine accusative *imbecillos*. Very well, to prevent so many instances of the second vowel (*e*) from clustering together. I have therefore rejected *imbecilles*.

—and gnats and ants seem to be gods, because sensation is present in them too and they are parts of the universe. Thus arguments derived from falsehood always produce foolish and absurd conclusions.

What of the fact that these same men say that the universe was constructed for the sake of gods and human beings, like a common house? Therefore, if it was constructed, the universe is neither God nor a living creature, for a living creature is not constructed but born. And if it was built, certainly like a house or a ship, then there is some craftsman who is the God of the universe. The universe that was made will be one thing, and he who made it another.

Now how contradictory and absurd is this: although they affirm that the heavenly fires and the other elements of the universe are gods, they likewise call the universe itself God. How can one God be composed from a heap of many gods? If the stars are gods, then the universe is not God but the dwelling [Col. 0283B] of gods. But if the universe is God, all the things within it are not gods but members of God, and these certainly cannot by themselves receive the name of God. No one would rightly say that the members of one human being are many human beings.

Yet the comparison between a living creature and the universe is not analogous. Since a living creature is endowed with sensation, its members also possess sensation and do not become insensible unless severed from the body. What sort of thing, then, does the universe resemble? They themselves plainly teach us when they do not deny that it was made to be, as it were, a common house for gods and human beings. If, therefore, it was constructed like a house, neither is it God nor are the elements that form its parts gods, because neither can a house exercise ownership over itself, nor can the materials [Col. 0283C] of which a house consists. They are therefore refuted not only by the truth but [Col. 0284A] also by their own words. For just as a house, made for the purpose of habitation, has no sensation in itself and is subject to the master who made or inhabits it, so the universe, having no sensation in itself, is subject to God its maker, who made it for his own use.

## CHAPTER VII  
### On God and the religions of the foolish; on greed and the authority of the ancestors

The foolish therefore err in two ways: first, because they prefer the elements—that is, the works of God—to God; and second, because they worship representations of those very elements embodied in human form. For they fashion images of the sun and moon in human form; likewise of fire, earth, and sea, which they call Vulcan, Vesta, [Col. 0284B] and Neptune. Nor do they offer sacrifice to the elements themselves in the open.

So great is the hold that desire for images has upon human beings that the real things are now considered of less value: they delight, of course, in gold, gems, and ivory. The beauty and sheen of these things dazzle their eyes, and they suppose there is no religion wherever such objects do not glitter. Thus, under the pretext of gods, greed and desire are worshiped. For they believe the gods love whatever they themselves covet—whatever it is on account of which thefts, robberies, and murders rage every day, and on account of which wars overthrow peoples and cities throughout the world.

They therefore consecrate to the gods their spoils of war and their plunder. Those gods must surely be weak and devoid of supreme power if they are subject to desires. For why should we suppose them heavenly if they desire something from the earth; or blessed [Col. 0285A] if they lack anything; or incorruptible if they take pleasure in things whose pursuit makes human desire deservedly subject to condemnation? They therefore come to the gods not so much for the sake of religion—which can have no existence among things wickedly acquired and corruptible—as in order to drink in gold with their eyes and the sheen of polished marble—

**The sheen of polished marble, etc.** See Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 12; Justin Martyr, *Second Apology for the Christians*.

**So completely [does] their religion.** We have restored this from nine Royal manuscripts, two Bologna manuscripts, several Vatican manuscripts, six Colbert manuscripts, two Clermont manuscripts, and the Emmeram, Cambridge, Christ Church, Cotton, and Balliol manuscripts, as well as the Rome 1470 edition. Eight printed editions have “so completely does the religion of the gods”; Egnatius, or Aldus 1515, Paris 1525, and Grapheus have “is the religion of the gods for that reason?”

“It is said to be a crime.” This is the reading to be adopted from both Bologna codices and three Vatican manuscripts; because, Thomas says, although learned and wise men pretended to esteem highly the authority of the ancients, they did indeed say that it was a crime to investigate it, yet did not regard that act as a crime, since they themselves often ridiculed many things belonging to their ancestors. Not only is *dicatur* (“it is said”) found in 2 Bologna codices and 3 Vatican manuscripts, but also in 5 Colbertine manuscripts, Jun., Lips., Tax., Ultr., Em., Cambridge, Rostock, Pen., 2 Clermont manuscripts, and the two old Roman editions, as well as Is., Gall., Spark., Cellar., and Walch.; as though the learned pagans speak thus even though they think otherwise. In 4 Royal manuscripts, 1 Colbertine, Brun., and 8 printed editions, [Col. 0285D] the reading is *ducatur* (“it is regarded”).

“Indiscriminately.” That is, rashly, without any reason. See the note above and Book III, ch. 9. BUN.

“Lucilius.” Thus restored from almost all the manuscripts and printed editions. In 1 recent Royal manuscript and 4 editions, *Lucillus*; in the Graph. edition, *Lucillius*. These words of Cicero are from Book III of *On the Nature of the Gods*, not far from the beginning.

“Balbus.” Balbus is Lucilius himself (see ch. 5), and Cotta is also the pontiff. Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book I, ch. 22.

“It is reasonable to believe.” The words *rationis est* (“it is reasonable”) are absent from Cicero’s books; Gruter, however, does not object to them. CELL.

“Which certainly was not suggested to you by another.” So read 2 Bologna manuscripts, Tax., Pen., 5 Vatican, 5 Colbertine, Em., Cant., Cauc., Pal., Lips., Rostock, Ult., 2 Clermont manuscripts, Brun., and the old Roman, Paris, and Is. editions; four other Royal manuscripts and some editions lack the negative, which must necessarily be added for the sense to stand.

“Chosen.” Fourteen manuscripts read *elata est* (“was elevated”). Thomas, indeed, thinks that the reading should be *Elata est*.

[Col. 0286C]

“But if piety urges us to follow our ancestors.” Thomas notes that in the Bologna codex the following words had been written above this sentence in smaller letters: “But if truth is greater, which urges us.” Yet this is not found thus in any other codex that we have seen; therefore we have judged that nothing should be changed. GALL.—Thomas does not wish this reading to be altered because of the antiquity of the codex. Nevertheless, in smaller letters in the same codex one reads: “But if truth is greater, which urges you, then admit.”

“Admit.” Thus I have restored it from the manuscripts and the old Roman editions. The other commonly used editions have *fateris* (“you admit”).

“Served.” This is the reading of almost all the manuscripts. The Jun. manuscript and six old editions have *serviunt* (“serve”); six other printed editions have *servierint* (“have served”).—“Have served.” This is more correct than *servierunt* in the single Bologna manuscript and in Reim. and Goth., or *serviunt* in the Sublac., Rost., Venice 1471–97, Paris, Junt., Crat., Ald., Parrh., and Gymn. editions. BUN.

“Of whose falsity you are convicted.” Thus I read with 5 Royal manuscripts, two of which are very ancient, 7 Vatican manuscripts, 4 Colbertine manuscripts, and many others, as well as 10 old editions. In 19 manuscripts, [Col. 0286D] among them 1 ancient Bologna manuscript, and in 6 more recent printed editions, the reading is *conviceris* (“you may convict”). Thomas nevertheless thinks that on the authority of 1 Bologna and 5 Vatican manuscripts the reading should be “of whose falsity you may convict.” This, he says, refers to Cicero, who was saying: “He who, out of piety, followed things which he might convict of being false.”

“Let us at last see.” Eleven manuscripts and 6 old editions, in place of *tandem* (“at last”), repeat *tamen* (“nevertheless”), which immediately preceded.

“Asylum.” On this see Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Livy, Plutarch, and Strabo.

“Indiscriminately.” Perottus, in *Cornu copiae*, Aldine ed., fol. 844, explains *passim* here as “from every direction.” Rather, here it means “without distinction, without order,” as the words “without any discrimination” suggest. BUN.

“Propertius.” Book IV, Elegy 1, in which he compares the frugality of the ancient Romans with the luxury of his own time.

“The trumpet summoned,” etc. This is the order in the manuscripts and old editions; many commonly used editions place the earlier couplet after the latter. By these verses Propertius means that the earliest senators did not wear purple-bordered togas, [Col. 0287C] but skins, after the fashion of countrymen, whose garments were hides. WALCH. Nevertheless, in all the editions of Propertius that I have seen, the couplet “The senate-house, which now,” etc., is placed before “The trumpet summoned,” etc.; but these differences do not alter the meaning. See, therefore, Propertius, Book IV, Elegy 1.

—or gaze upon ivory; so that with insatiable contemplation they may handle garments distinguished by precious stones and colors, or cups set off with glittering gems. And the more richly adorned the temples and the more beautiful the images have been, the greater the majesty they are believed to possess: to such a degree their religion is nothing other than that which human desire admires.

These are the religions which they persist most stubbornly in protecting and defending as handed down to them by their ancestors. They do not consider what sort of religions they are, but trust that they are approved and [Col. 0285B] true because the ancients handed them down; and so great is the authority of antiquity that it is said to be a crime to investigate it. Consequently, belief is given to it indiscriminately, as though to an acknowledged truth. Finally, in Cicero, Cotta speaks thus to Lucilius:

> “You have heard, Balbus, what Cotta thinks and what the pontiff thinks. Now let me understand what you think; for from you as a philosopher I ought to receive a rational account of religion, but as for our ancestors, even when no reason has been given, it is reasonable to believe them.”

If you believe, why then do you ask for a reason, which may cause you not to believe? But if you ask for a reason, and [Col. 0286A] think that it must be sought, then you do not believe. For that is precisely why you seek it: so that, when you have found it, you may follow it. See now—reason teaches you that the religions of the gods are not true. What will you do? Will you follow your ancestors instead, or reason? Reason, indeed, was not suggested to you by another, but was discovered and chosen by yourself when you uprooted all religions entirely. If you prefer reason, you must depart from the institutions and authority of your ancestors, since that alone is right which reason prescribes. But if piety urges you to follow your ancestors, then admit both that those men were foolish who served religions devised contrary to reason, and that you are senseless for worshiping that of whose falsity you are convicted. Yet because the name of our ancestors is so insistently set against us, let us at last see who those ancestors were, from whose authority it is regarded as sacrilege to depart.

[Col. 0286B] When Romulus was about to found the city, he summoned the shepherds among whom he had grown up; and when that number seemed insufficient for founding a city, he established an asylum. To it the very worst people fled indiscriminately from neighboring places, without any discrimination of status. Thus he fashioned a people from all of them; and he chose for the senate those who were advanced in age and called them “Fathers,” conducting everything by their counsel. Of this senate Propertius, the writer of elegies, speaks as follows:

> The trumpet summoned the ancient Quirites to hear the words:
>
> Those hundred in the meadow were often his Senate.
>
> [Col. 0287A] The lofty senate-house, which now gleams with its purple-bordered Senate,
>
> Once held skin-clad Fathers with rustic hearts.

These are the Fathers whose decrees learned and prudent men obey with utter devotion, so that all posterity should judge as true and immutable whatever a hundred skin-clad old men wished to establish—men whom, nevertheless, as was said in Book I, ch. 22, Pompilius enticed into believing that the rites he himself handed down were genuine. Is there truly any reason why their authority should be so highly valued by their descendants, when no one, whether highest or lowest, judged them worthy of marriage ties while they were alive?

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Use of Reason in Religion; and on Dreams, Auguries, Oracles, and Portents of That Kind

[Col. 0287B] Therefore, especially in the matter with which the ordering of life is concerned, each person ought to trust himself and rely more upon his own judgment and perceptions in investigating and weighing the truth than, by believing the errors of others, to be deceived as though he himself were devoid of reason. God has given wisdom to everyone in an equal share, [Col. 0287B]

[Note: [Col. 0287C] [Variorum Notes on columns 287–288]

“In an equal share.” That is, equally; for jurists generally interpret *portiones viriles* as equal shares—namely, those established according to the number of persons and per capita, so that there are as many shares as there are persons. BETULEIUS.—“In an equal share.” Hence Lactantius says, “Wisdom is given equally to all”; and Book III, ch. 35: “Wisdom has been given to all without any discrimination,” etc. Add the remainder. BUN.

“Cannot be preempted.” Seneca puts it elegantly at the end of Epistle 33: “Truth lies open to all; it has not yet been occupied; much of it has been left even for those to come.” CELL.

“Undiminishable.” An exceedingly rare word. One Colbertine manuscript, Em., and the Cambridge manuscript read *illabilis*; 1 Leipzig manuscript, *illibalis*; Gronovius, *habilis*.—“Undiminishable.” That is, nothing can be taken or plucked away from it. Gronovius writes learnedly on Seneca, Epistle 83, p. 347: “DELIBATUM: that which is taken from another and propagated without injury to it; one light is kindled from another.” There is more there. BUN.

“Of the human heart.” That is, of our soul, of our understanding: Lactantius speaks in the Hebrew manner. WALCH.

“After the manner of cattle.” Seneca, *On the Happy Life*, ch. 1: “Let us not follow the flock of those ahead after the fashion of cattle, proceeding not where one ought to go, but where people go … judging those things best which have been received with great assent and of which many examples lie before us, and living not by reason but by imitation.” Compare Book II, ch. 3.

“Descendants.” That is, posterity; ch. 13. Virgil often uses the word thus; on him consult Servius, Erythraeus, Taubman, and Cerda at greater length; and on Juvenal, Satire 1, line 148. RIGALT.

“The false things which they had devised.” The reading *quae* (“which things”) is skillfully preserved in the Royal manuscripts, 3 Colbertine manuscripts, Goth., 1 Clermont manuscript, and the old editions. Three Colbertine manuscripts, 1 Clermont manuscript, Brun., and the recent commonly used editions have *qui* (“who”).

“And auguries.” Auguries were highly valued not only among the Greeks but [Col. 0288C] among every barbarian nation; Aelian, *Various History*, Book II, ch. 31. Suidas, under the entry Τηλέγ[ονος] (*Telegonus*), states that this art passed to the Greeks through Telegonus, its first inventor. But the Etruscans claimed themselves as its originators and said that a certain Tages had been its discoverer. Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book XV:

> The natives called him Tages, who first taught
>
> The Etruscan nation to disclose events to come.

Anyone who wants more concerning auguries should consult Dempster, from whom we have drawn this material. The examples that follow are taken chiefly from Cicero’s books *On the Nature of the Gods* and *On Divination*. See also Valerius Maximus, Book I, ch. 4 and following.

“Accius Navius.” Thus almost all manuscripts and editions; 1 ancient Bologna manuscript and 1 Colbertine manuscript, by a second hand, have *Naevius*. Some call him Actius Navius. Two Royal manuscripts have *Attus*; the commonly printed text of Cicero has *Attius Navius*. On this story see Cicero, Book II of *On the Nature of the Gods* and Book I of *On Divination*. It occurs in Livy, Book I; Florus, Book I, ch. 5; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, [Col. 0288D] Book III; and Valerius Maximus, Book I, in the chapter on Auspices.

“To undertake.” This word is absent from the Cambridge manuscript, without loss of meaning. Nevertheless, the codices I have been permitted to see have “began to undertake,” as is read in this edition of ours.

“Unless it had first been inaugurated.” *Inaugurare* here means “to consult the auguries.” Places were also inaugurated when they were consecrated. And because newly appointed magistrates did not enter upon the offices assigned to them without auguries, they were “inaugurated”—that is, as people today barbarously say, “invested.” On this see Francis Petrarch, *Memorable Matters*, Book IV, treatise 5, ch. 3. BET.

“And cut it apart with a razor.” All the manuscripts have this; and I judge with the distinguished Puteanus that it should be so read. He learnedly explains the verb *dissicio* as though it meant *disseco*, “I cut apart.” This word should likewise be read in our author Lactantius, Book III, ch. 17, rather than *disjice*, as nearly all the printers incorrectly have it—except, however, the Rostock edition of 1476, which has *dissice*. On this matter see Pareus in his *Critical Lexicon*, where he explains the verb from ancient authors. The Rohan manuscript reads *deffice*, but wrongly; the Saint-Germain manuscript has *dissice*, as do the other codices.]

so that they may both investigate things they have not heard and weigh things they have heard. Nor, because those men preceded us in time, did they also precede us in wisdom; for if wisdom is given equally to all, it cannot be preempted by those who came before. It is undiminishable, like the light and brightness of the sun, because, just as the sun is the light of the eyes, so wisdom is the light of the human [Col. 0288A] heart. Therefore, since wisdom—that is, the search for truth—is innate in all, those who approve the discoveries of their ancestors without any judgment and are led by others after the manner of cattle deprive themselves of wisdom. But what deceives them is this: once the name “ancestors” has been introduced, they do not think it possible either that they themselves might be wiser because they are called “descendants,” or that the former might have been foolish because they are called “ancestors.” What, then, prevents us from taking an example from them, so that just as they handed down false things of their own devising to posterity, we, who have found the truth, may hand down better things to posterity?

An immense question remains, the discussion of which proceeds not from natural ability but from knowledge, and which will have to be explained at greater length so that nothing at all may remain doubtful. For perhaps someone will take refuge in those things handed down by many authorities who are not open to doubt: [Col. 0288B] that those very beings whom we have shown not to be gods very often displayed their majesty through portents, dreams, auguries, and oracles. And certainly many things worthy of wonder can be enumerated.

First among them is the event involving Accius Navius, the chief augur. When he warned Tarquinius Priscus not to begin any new undertaking unless the auguries had first been consulted, the king, making light of the credibility of his art, told him to consult the birds and report whether something the king had conceived in his mind could be done. When Navius affirmed that it could, the king said: “Then take this whetstone and cut it apart with a razor.” But Navius accepted it without hesitation and cut it.

[Col. 0289A] Next is the event in which Castor and Pollux—

[Col. 0289A] [Note: [Col. 0289B] [Variorum Notes on columns 289–290]

“And Pollux.” This story is found in Plutarch’s *Paulus Aemilius*; it is also mentioned by Valerius Maximus, Book I, in the chapter on Miracles; Ovid, *Fasti*, Book I; and Cicero, Books II and III of *On the Nature of the Gods*.

“Of Juturna.” One recent Royal manuscript, 1 Colbertine, and Brun. read *Diuturnae*; another Royal manuscript, Tornes., and 1 Colbertine, *Miturnae*; 1 Clermont manuscript, *Uniturnae*; 1 ancient Bologna manuscript, *Saturni*. Juturna was the daughter of Daunus and sister of Turnus, king of the Rutulians; a spring and lake flowing into the river Numicius in Latium, not far from Lavinium, bore her name. She is mentioned by Ovid in Book II [Col. 0289C] of the *Fasti*.—“At the lake of Juturna.” See Gronovius on Minucius Felix, ch. 7, p. 62. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities*, Book VI, fol. 351, is indeed an authority for a similar event’s having occurred in the Latin War; but at the cited passage he more correctly assigns this story to another time, namely the Macedonian War, as does Florus, Book II, ch. 12. Lactantius has therefore erred: for how could the temple of the Castors have stood open during the Latin War, when it was dedicated by Postumius only after that war, according to Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book III, ch. 5; Livy, Book II, ch. 42; and Dionysius, at the cited passage? BUN.

“The temple … was … had opened.” Goth. reads in the plural: “the temples which adjoined the spring had opened,” referring to the sanctuary. This is not a bad reading, as Alexander ab Alexandro teaches against Valla in *Genial Days*, Book VI, ch. 9, concerning two temples. Livy, Book XL, ch. 34: “Two temples were dedicated … these temples were dedicated”; and Book XLV, ch. 2. See Vossius, *On Analogy*, Book I, ch. 43. BUN.

“Publius Vatienus.” Thus we have restored the name from 10 Royal manuscripts, 5 Colbertine, 2 Clermont, and the Roman edition of 1470 and Betul., [Col. 0289D] supported by 1 Colbertine manuscript and Brun., which have *Vatrenus* for *Vatienus*; many editions have *Vatinius*. In Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book III, no. 11, read *Vacienus*, with *Vatienus* in the margin; *c* and *t* are often confused in manuscripts.

“King Perses had been defeated and captured that day.” From the end of Livy, Book XLIV, the beginning of Book XLV, and likewise Plutarch’s *Aemilius*, fols. 266–269, it is clear that four or more days elapsed between the defeat and the capture; Lactantius, however, follows Cicero. Florus, Book II, ch. 12: “On the same day on which Perses was defeated in Macedonia, it became known at Rome.” Pliny, Book VII, ch. 23: “The Roman Castors announced the victory over Perses on the very day it occurred”;  and Minucius, ch. 7: “They announced the victory on the same day on which they had won it.” These authors spoke only of his defeat; Cicero expressly adds his capture as well in *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book II, ch. 2: “The Tyndarids announced that Perses had been defeated. For when P. Vatienus … was traveling by night, two young men with white horses told him that King Perses had been captured that day, and he announced it to the senate.” It appears that Vatinius added on his own that Perses had been captured that day after hearing that he had been defeated, [Col. 0290B] or that Cicero led Valerius Maximus and Lactantius into error. Compare Freinshemius and Duker on Florus at the cited passage, p. 405. BUNEMAN.

“A female image of Fortune.” Thus I have restored the reading from the older and better manuscripts. The more recent manuscripts and commonly used editions have *muliebris* (“feminine”). On this read Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book VIII; Plutarch’s *Coriolanus*; Livy, Book II; Valerius Maximus, Book I, in the chapter on Miracles; and St. Augustine, *City of God*, Book IV, ch. 19.

“Of Juno Moneta.” One ancient Bologna manuscript reads *Monita*. Juno was surnamed Moneta from *monendo*, “warning”: Cicero, *On Divination*, Book I, ch. 45, and Book II, ch. 32. The story of Juno Moneta is in Livy, Book V, and Valerius Maximus, Book I, in the chapter on Miracles. Plutarch writes in his *Camillus* that the temple of Moneta [Col. 0290C] stood in the place where the house of Manlius Capitolinus had been.

“Asked.” Thus the older and better manuscripts. The more recent manuscripts and printed editions read *interrogaret* (“were to ask”).

“Claudia also.” This story occurs in Livy, Book IX of the Third Decade; Herodian, Book I; and Ovid, *Fasti*, Book IV.—“Claudia.” Savaro has cited several authorities concerning her in his notes on Sidonius Apollinaris, Poem 24, p. 207. BUNEMAN.

“Is presented as an example.” Thus I print from Reimm., Goth., and Lip. III. The Old Latin translation of Nahum 3:6 has: “I shall present you as an example.” Minucius Felix, ch. 36, aptly says “to proclaim someone as an example.” Indeed Lactantius himself does so again in Book III, ch. 6: “That which is usually presented as … an example.” BUNEMAN.

“Aesculapius from Epidaurus.” Livy, Book X, and Plutarch, in the *Questions*, mention this story.

“Appius Claudius the Censor.” See Valerius Maximus, Book I, ch. 1, and Livy, Book IX, ch. 29. CELL.

[Col. 0290D]

“Contrary to the response.” These two words are absent from 1 ancient Bologna manuscript and 3 Royal manuscripts.

“Was deprived.” On the blindness of Appius Claudius, read Cicero’s *Cato the Elder*.

“And the family of the Potitii.” Livy at the cited place: “The Potitian family, which had possessed the hereditary priesthood at the Great Altar of Hercules,” etc. At that time it was divided into twelve families, making it all the more remarkable that they all became extinct, root and branch, within a year. Livy, in the same place. CELL.

“Fulvius the Censor.” On him read Livy, Fifth Decade, Book II, and Valerius Maximus, on Neglected Religion.

“Of Juno Lacinia.” This reading is supported by the better Royal manuscripts, 5 Colbertine manuscripts, Tornes., 1 Clermont manuscript, Brun., and almost all editions, as well as Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book III, line 552; Pliny, Book II, ch. 7; and Arnobius, Book VI. One Clermont manuscript has the corrupt *Lasciniae*; 1 ancient Bologna manuscript, 1 Royal manuscript, and the Jun. edition have *Lucinae*; 1 Colbertine manuscript, *Liciniae*. See Valerius Maximus, Book I, ch. 1, no. 20. Juno was surnamed Lacinia from the promontory of the [Col. 0291B] same name near Croton; thus Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book III:

> Dread Lacinia rises opposite.

]

—were seen during the Latin War at the lake of Juturna, washing the sweat from their horses, while their temple, which adjoined the spring, had opened of its own accord. The same gods, during the Macedonian War, are said to have appeared on white horses to Publius Vatienus as he was coming to Rome by night, announcing that King Perses had been defeated and captured that day—an event which letters from Paulus showed a few days later to have been true.

Also wonderful is the tradition that a female image of Fortune spoke more than once; likewise the image of Juno Moneta, when, after the capture of Veii, one of the soldiers sent to move it jokingly and playfully asked whether it wished to migrate to Rome, and it answered that it did.

Claudia also is presented as an example of a miracle. For when the Idaean Mother had been summoned in accordance with the Sibylline books, and the ship in which she was being carried had become stuck in a shallow of the river Tiber [Col. 0289B] and could not be moved by any force, Claudia—who had always been regarded as unchaste because of her excessive attention to bodily adornment—is said to have knelt and prayed to the goddess that, if she judged her chaste, she should follow her girdle. Thus the ship, which could not be moved by the entire body of young men, was moved by one woman. Equally wonderful is the report that, when a plague was raging, Aesculapius, summoned from Epidaurus, freed the city of Rome from a long-lasting pestilence.

Sacrilegious men may also be enumerated whose immediate punishments are believed to show that the gods avenged the injuries done to them. When Appius Claudius the Censor, contrary to the response, transferred the rites of Hercules to public slaves, he was deprived of his sight, and the family of the Potitii, which betrayed those rites, became extinct within the space of one year. Likewise Fulvius the Censor, after removing marble [Col. 0290B] tiles from the temple of Juno Lacinia with which to roof the temple of Equestrian [Col. 0291A] Fortune—

[Col. 0291A] [Note: [Col. 0291B] [Variorum Notes on columns 291–292]

“The temple of Equestrian Fortune.” He had vowed it as proconsul during the Celtiberian War, Livy, Book XL, ch. 40, and six years later dedicated it as censor, or out of the funds of his censorship, in the same author, Book XLII, ch. 18. An ancient inscription in Gruter, p. 75, no. 4:

> SACRED TO EQUESTRIAN FORTUNE.

CELLARIUS.

[Col. 0291C]

“Turullius.” Thus most manuscripts and printed editions. But 1 recent Royal manuscript has *Curullius*; 1 Clermont, *Turallius*; 1 Colbertine, *Turtullius*; another Colbertine, *Turculius*; 3 Colbertine manuscripts and Brun., *Thurillius*; Torn., *Turillus*; another Clermont and Em., *Tertullius*. On him see also Valerius Maximus in the chapter already cited.—“Turullius, a prefect of Marcus Antonius.” He was one of Caesar’s assassins and afterward a friend of Antony the triumvir, as Dio, Book LI, p. 448, relates. CELL.

“Place.” One Clermont manuscript and the Ald., Paris 1525, Graph., and Is. editions read *grove*; but wrongly, since after the grove had been destroyed only the place remained.

“Caesar.” Augustus, that is.—“By Caesar’s soldiers.” By the soldiers of Caesar Octavianus the triumvir, to whom Turullius was handed over by Antony [the source’s “44” here is uncertain, apparently a stray reference marker]; Dio, in the same place. CELL.

“Pyrrhus.” On him see Valerius in the same place.

“From the treasury of Proserpina at Locri.” Concerning this plundering, see Valerius Maximus, Book I, ch. 1, external example 1, and Livy, Book XXIX, ch. 8. Both also mention another plundering of the same sanctuary by Pleminius, Scipio’s legate, which likewise did not go unpunished. CELL.

[Col. 0291D]

“Of Miletus.” On her see Valerius.

“The city was captured.” In Faber’s *Thesaurus* we read: “In Lactantius the word *civitas* is used for *urbs*”; Walch also noted this in his *Diatribe*, p. 60, from Lactantius, Book III, ch. 21. Add Book IV, ch. 13; Book VI, ch. 6; Book VII, chs. 26 and 24—not to mention Vossius’s assertion that Caesar, *Civil War*, Book I, ch. 1, used *civitas* for the city of Rome. BUN.

“A blaze of fire cast before them.” The very learned Francius suspected that the reading should be *objecti fulgor ignis*, “the blaze of a fire set before them.”

“Dreams.” The whole of Valerius Maximus, Book I, ch. 7, pertains to this. BUN.

“During sleep.” The Latin writers neatly use the term *quiet* to signify dreams. CELLAR.—On this see Valerius in the chapter on Dreams; Cicero, *On Divination*, Book I; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book VII; Plutarch’s *Coriolanus*; and St. Augustine, *City of God*, Book IV, ch. 26.

“Lead dancer.” Almost all the manuscripts and editions have *praesultorem*, as does Valerius Maximus at the cited place. Cicero and Arnobius, Book IV, however, have *praesulem*; Livy has *praesultatorem*, one who by dancing begins [Col. 0292B] the games.

“Antonius.” Bunemann’s edition reads *Antronius* and gives the following note on this name.—“Antronius.” Thus the Leipzig and Goth. manuscripts, and the Rostock, Venice 1471, and both Gryph. editions. Gronovius’s 1670 edition of Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book I, ch. 21, reads *AUTRONIUS*. In my rarer Brescia edition of 1485 and another Venice edition of 1500, Macrobius has *ATRONIUS*. Many Lactantius editions—Venice 1493 and 1497, Parrh., Paris, and several others—have *Antonius*. From the word “a certain” he might seem to have been an obscure man. [Col. 0292C] But Dionysius, *Antiquities*, fol. 473, calls him ἀνὴρ οὐκ ἀφανής, “a man not without distinction.” Lipsius, *On the Cross*, Book III, ch. 3, regards *Autronius* as the more correct name. Cicero mentions P. Antronius in *Brutus*, ch. 68. BUN.

“A slave under the fork.” It was customary to beat untrustworthy slaves with rods beneath a fork-shaped yoke; one subjected to this kind of punishment was called a *furcifer*, “fork-bearer,” as Plutarch reports in the *Life of Coriolanus*. GALLAEUS.

“But he himself was stricken by a serious illness … carried on a litter,” etc. Thus I have restored the text from the better manuscripts: 2 Royal, 2 Colbertine, and 2 Clermont. In both clauses supply the verb “is said,” which preceded; otherwise the syntax will not stand. Nor does it stand in the reading “he was stricken,” found in 1 Colbertine manuscript, Brun., and the Roman editions of 1468 and 1470 and Paris 1525; or in “but that he himself was stricken by a serious illness … carried on a litter,” which is found in 2 Royal and 2 Colbertine manuscripts and most printed editions.

“That dream also,” etc. The authors vary somewhat; for some report that Augustus went down into the battle line because of that dream, while others say that because of the same dream he was not present at the battle. Lactantius used Valerius, Book I, in the chapter on Dreams, [Col. 0292D] as his authority. See also Plutarch, *Brutus*, near the end; Suetonius, *Augustus*, chs. 13 and 9; Appian, near the end of Book IV of the *Civil Wars*; Paterculus, at the same place; Florus, Book IV, ch. 6; and Tertullian, *On the Soul*. ISAEUS.

“Augustus.” Since the authors disagree concerning this, see Suetonius, Plutarch, Paterculus, and Florus.

“Appeared before.” Rostock, Venice 1471, both editions of 1478, 1493, and 1497, and Paris have *observata* (“observed”); but the manuscripts and the Parrh., Ald., Gymn., Gryph., Tornaes., Thomas, and the editions following him more correctly and elegantly read *obversata* (“appeared before”). So above: “Jupiter appeared before him during sleep.” These words are also confused in the codices of Valerius Maximus, Book I, ch. 7: “And the same form appeared before his mind.” BUNEMAN.

“ incur the charge.” Thus the books, without the preposition *in*. Again in Book VI, ch. 25: “Lest anyone incur the charge of pride and arrogance.” This usage is customary among ecclesiastical writers. Arnobius, Book IV, p. 138: “incur the charge of folly.” Cyprian, *Exhortation to Martyrdom*, fol. 385: “incur eternal punishments.” Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogues*, Book II, ch. 9: “we encounter a band of hunters.” [Col. 0293B] BUNEMAN.]

—was driven out of his mind and, after losing his two sons while they were serving in Illyricum, was consumed by the deepest grief. Turullius, a prefect of Marcus Antonius, after destroying the grove of Aesculapius at Cos to build a fleet, was later killed in that same place by Caesar’s soldiers.

To these examples is added Pyrrhus, who, after taking money from the treasury of Proserpina at Locri, suffered shipwreck and was dashed upon the shores near the goddess’s sanctuary, so that nothing except that money was found undamaged. Ceres of Miletus also added greatly to the reverence people felt for her. For when the city had been captured by Alexander and the soldiers had burst in to plunder her, a blaze of fire suddenly cast before them blinded them all.

Dreams are also found which seem to demonstrate the power of the gods. [Col. 0291B] For Jupiter is said to have appeared during sleep to Tiberius Attinius, a commoner, and to have instructed him to tell the consuls and senate that at the most recent Circus games their lead dancer had displeased him. The reason was that a certain Antonius Maximus had led a slave, beaten with rods under the fork, through the middle of the circus to punishment; the games therefore had to be celebrated anew. When Attinius neglected this, he is said to have lost his son that same day and himself to have been stricken by a serious illness. When he again saw the same figure asking whether he had paid sufficient penalties for neglecting the command, he was carried on a litter to the consuls; after explaining the whole matter in the senate, he recovered bodily strength and returned home on his own feet.

That dream also occasioned no less wonder by which Caesar Augustus is said to have been saved. During the civil war against Brutus, when Augustus was afflicted by a serious illness and had determined to abstain from battle, an apparition of Minerva appeared to his physician Artorius, warning that Caesar should not keep himself within the camp because of his physical weakness. He was therefore carried on a litter into the battle line, and on that same day the camp [Col. 0292B] was captured by Brutus.

Many similar examples can be brought forward besides these; but I fear that, if I linger too long in presenting matters contrary to my position, I may appear either to have forgotten my purpose or to incur the charge of loquacity.

[Col. 0293A]

## CHAPTER IX. On the Devil, the World, God, Providence, Man, and His Wisdom

I shall therefore explain the rationale of all these things, so that difficult and obscure matters may be understood more easily, and I shall expose all these deceptions of pretended divinity—

[Col. 0293A] [Note: [Col. 0293B] [Variorum Notes on columns 293–294]

“And I shall expose all these deceptions of pretended divinity.” Thus most of the Royal and Vatican manuscripts, 6 Colbertine manuscripts, Pen., 1 Clermont manuscript, Brun., and all printed editions except the Roman editions of 1468 and 1470, which have *simulatas* (“pretended deceptions”). The Royal-Puteanus manuscript has: “and I shall expose all these deceptions of simulations in these”; the ancient Bologna manuscript: “and I shall expose all these causes of simulations in these deceptions”; 1 Clermont manuscript: “and I shall expose all these causes of simulations in these deceptions, the deceptions of pretended divinity.”

“Misled.” One ancient Bologna manuscript and 1 Clermont manuscript read *indocti* (“unlearned”).

“May be equipped.” Thus very many manuscripts and Cellarius’s edition. Eight recent manuscripts and almost all printed editions have *instituatur* (“may be instructed”).

“Beginning.” From Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book II.

“May perceive the errors.” After these words the following passage is found in ten recent manuscripts and most printed editions:
