> Just as the mother gave birth without precedent to her own Creator, so the Father must be believed ineffably to have begotten one coeternal with himself. From the mother was born one who already existed before; from the Father, one who at some time did not exist. Let faith believe this; let understanding not inquire, [Col. 0293C] lest it either think what has not been discovered incredible or refuse to believe what has been discovered because it is unique.

But those words are not found in the most ancient manuscripts—1 Bologna, 2 Royal, Cauc., 3 other Royal manuscripts, 8 Vatican, 1 Sorbonne, 4 Oxford, Tornes., Betul., Gat., 2 Colbertine, 1 Clermont—nor in the Is., Spark., and other editions. In the margin of 1 Clermont codex it is written: “I do not believe these to be Lactantius’s words.” In the very old editions of 1475 and 1490, a little after the middle, one reads “did not fail,” as also in the Rohan and Saint-Germain manuscripts. It is better simply to remove those words than to waste effort emending them, as others do. For they were added by Arians and savor of the Arian heresy, which so often declared concerning Christ: Ἦν ὅταν οὐκ ἦν, “There was a time when he did not exist.” Because of the manuscripts, which are exceedingly numerous, I agree with Gallaeus that these words should not be admitted into the text. Betuleius, who admits them into the text of Lactantius, nevertheless notes that they are absent from the old codex; he leaves no stone unturned to assign them a Catholic meaning, though he admits that they savor of the Arian heresy. The excellent Cologne [Col. 0293D] edition of 1544 does not admit them except in smaller type and notes that they are not found in the manuscripts used by its editor.

“God, most provident in devising.” Many of the most ancient and best manuscripts have this reading, which is confirmed by what follows below: “And he placed his greatest Son over the whole work, and used him at once as counselor and craftsman in devising, adorning, and perfecting things, since he is perfect in providence, reason, and power.” And below: “Providence for devising, and skill and power for making.” Eight recent manuscripts and the printed editions have *prudentissimus*, “most prudent.”

“Should undertake this work of the world.” After these words, in the Marm. and Goth. manuscripts and many printed editions, the following appears:

> In the beginning he made good and evil. I shall explain more openly what this means, lest anyone think that I speak as poets are accustomed to speak, who embrace incorporeal things in certain figures as though they were visible, especially since it itself did not yet exist—or, with the variant *praeter*, since nothing yet existed besides him.

But because these words assert the Manichaean heresy, from which Lactantius was plainly alien, [Col. 0294B] as is evident from what follows, we have removed them from the text as additions made by an interpolating hand. For they are not found in the most ancient Bologna manuscript, Tax., 8 Royal manuscripts, 6 Colbertine, 2 Clermont, 11 Vatican, 2 Br., nor in the Oxford, Jun., Rohan, or Saint-Germain manuscripts. They are likewise absent from the best editions: Rome 1468 and 1470, Venice 1490, Florence, Plantin, Cratander 1524, Aldus 1515, Gymnicus’s Antwerp edition of 1539, and Grach. GALLAEUS.

“Good.” Thus we have restored the reading from the most ancient and best manuscripts: 2 Bologna, 12 Vatican, 6 Royal—one of which is nine hundred years old—6 Colbertine, Tax., Pen., 1 Clermont; and from the Tornes., Is., and Cellar. editions. The Cauc. manuscript, 2 recent Royal manuscripts, and 12 editions have *bono* (“for the good”). The Royal-Puteanus, Ultr., Clermont, and Brun. manuscripts have *bonus* (“good,” masculine). All three readings are acceptable and supported by manuscript authority.

“A spirit like himself.” St. Jerome, in his *Letter to Pammachius*, reproves Lactantius for error because he called the Son of God “the spirit of God,” although this expression was used by other Fathers: Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 21; *On Prayer*, ch. 1; *Against Marcion*, Book I, ch. 19, Book III, [Col. 0294C] chs. 6 and 16, Book IV, ch. 21; *Against Praxeas*, ch. 26; Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, no. 71 according to Pamelius, etc. See St. Thomas, Part I, question 36, article 1. From ISAEUS. The Brun. and Colbertine manuscripts read “like himself.” Lactantius, however, spoke wrongly in saying that the Father “produced” the Son; for the Son was not produced, but begotten.

How he willed this, however, we shall attempt to explain in the fourth book, etc. This is how the text should be read, with 7 Royal manuscripts, 12 Vatican, 2 Bologna, the Cauc., Tax., Pen., 6 Colbertine, 3 Oxford, Ultr., 2 Clermont, Em., Cambridge, Brun., Jun., Sic.; likewise the old Roman edition of 1468, the Venetian of 1490, the Aldine of 1515, and seven other editions. Some, together with 3 Royal manuscripts and the Balliol manuscript, have *fecerit* (“did”) in place of *voluerit* (“willed”), and add “when he was alone”; but wrongly, because Christ can never be said to have been alone, as was stated in the notes on Book I, chapter 7. ISAeus.—“How he willed this, however”: Heumann thinks these words are an interpolation.—Bunemann has: “How he did this, when he was alone, we shall attempt to explain in the fourth book,” etc.; and he supplies the following two notes on this passage.—“How, however,” etc.: [Col. 0294D] Book IV, chapter 6 and following: “God, therefore, the designer . . . of things, as we said in the second book, before he undertook . . . the work of the world, begot a holy . . . spirit.” In the same place he expresses this from Hermes as ἐπεὶ τὸν δεύτερον ἐποίησε θεόν, “since he made the second god”; likewise from the Sibyl, ἐποίησε, “he made.” In Lactantius, however, *made*, *begot*, *produced*, and *procreated* are synonyms. Hence, further on in Book IV, chapter 8, he asks, as he does in our passage: “How, then, did he procreate him?” The *Epitome*, chapter 42, suggests the same: “he begot a son for himself”; then, “he made a second, visible god . . . When, therefore, he had first made him.” Pfaffius conveniently explains these passages in the Preliminary Dissertation to the *Epitome*, §28, p. 35, from Acts 2:36 and Hebrews 2:2.—“Did this, when he was alone.” I thought these words should be inserted into the text from the Gryphius edition; the Gotha manuscript, however, reads, “did this, when he is alone.” For in Book IV, chapter 8: “God . . . while he was still alone . . . did not need the association of another for creating” (that is, begetting or engendering). BUN.

“He was infected by envy as though by poison.” This is confirmed by Wisdom 2:24: “Through the envy of the devil death entered into the world.” Irenaeus also, Book IV *Against Heresies*, chapter 78, and Book V, chapter 24; and Cyprian, in the book *On Jealousy and Envy*, shortly after the beginning, asserted that the devil sinned through pride, with envy joined to it by an indissoluble bond—according to Augustine, Book I *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 14—directed both against the Son of God and against humankind, according to Lactantius, Book II, chapters 8 and 12. See Estius on Book II of the *Sentences*, distinction 6, §§2–3.—“And so through his own envy.” Not as his first sin; for the holy Fathers Basil, Chrysostom, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Gregory the Great, and St. Thomas hold that the devil first sinned with the sin of pride. He is then said to have sinned with the sin of envy as a consequence, by aspiring to a certain singular excellence. In the sacred text he is said “not to have stood in the truth” (John 8:44).]

by which human beings, once led astray, withdrew still farther from the path of truth. But I shall begin again from a much earlier point, so that if anyone devoid and ignorant of the truth approaches this work to read it, he may be instructed and may understand what, ultimately, is

the head and cause of these evils; [Col. 0294A] and, once he has received the light, may discern his own errors and those of the entire human race.

Since God was supremely provident in devising and supremely skillful in executing, before he began this work of the world—because the source of full and consummate goodness was within him, as it always is—he produced a spirit like himself, so that goodness might arise from him like a stream and flow far abroad; this spirit was endowed with the virtues of God the Father. How he willed this, however, we shall attempt to explain in the fourth book (namely, chapter 6). He then made another, in whom the character of the divine stock did not remain. And so he was infected by his own envy as though by poison and [Col. 0295A] passed from good to evil; and by his own free choice, which God had given him, [Col. 0295A]

[Note: [Col. 0295B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 295–296]]

“Which God had given him as free.” These words could be absent, and they are almost as suspect to me as the same words in Book II, chapter 14, where they are absent from the best manuscripts. BUN.

“Envy.” See Wisdom 2:24.

“Once approved, he is also beloved.” I restored this from the most ancient manuscripts—1 Bologna, 1 Royal-Puteanus, 1 other Royal, 1 Colbertine, and others—with the support of 1 Royal, 1 Colbertine, the Palatine, Leipzig, and Brun. manuscripts and the Gymnich edition, in which the reading is “having been approved”; in 1 Clermont manuscript and the Aldine, Paris, Cratander, and Grapheus editions, “then having been approved”; in 4 Colbertine manuscripts, 1 Clermont manuscript, and six printed editions, “then approved.”

“Made evil by himself.” These words conflict with the doctrine [Col. 0295C] of the Manichaeans, who believe God to have been the author of evil. Here, on the contrary, an angel who had been good was made evil by himself.

“Reports them to God.” After these words, in one 900-year-old Royal manuscript, another recent Royal manuscript, the Marm., Balliol manuscript, and some printed editions, the following appears:

> Why a just God willed him to be such, however, I shall attempt to explain as far as the limited capacity of our understanding permits. When God was about to fashion this world, which was to consist of things mutually opposed and discordant, he first established diverse elements and before all else made two sources of mutually opposed and conflicting things: namely, those two spirits, the upright and the depraved, one of whom is, as it were, God’s right hand, the other his left, so that those opposing things might lie within their power, and that the world and everything within it might consist of their mixture and tempering. Likewise, when he was about to make the human being, to whom he would set virtue before him as the rule for living through which he might attain immortality, he made good and evil so that virtue could exist; unless virtue is assailed by evils, it will either lose its force or not exist at all. For just as the bitterness of poverty makes wealth appear good, [Col. 0295D] and the darkness of shadows commends the attractiveness of light, and the pleasure of well-being and health is recognized through sickness and pain, so in this life good cannot exist without evil. And although the two are contrary, they nevertheless cohere in such a way that, if you remove one, you remove both; for good can neither be comprehended and perceived without the rejection and avoidance of evil, nor can evil be guarded against and overcome without the aid of good that has been comprehended and perceived. It was therefore necessary for evil also to be made, so that good might come into being. And because it was not right that evil should proceed from God—for he will not act against himself—he appointed that spirit the inventor of evils. When he made him, he gave him ingenuity and cunning for devising evils, so that both a depraved will and consummate wickedness might reside in him; and God willed those things contrary to his own virtues to arise from him, and willed him to contend with himself as to whether God would grant more good things or he more evil ones. But again, because resistance to the supreme God is impossible, God assigned to that avenger (*ultori*; perhaps read *alteri*, “other”) authority over his good things—the one whom we said above was good and perfect. [Col. 0296A] Thus he matched and equipped two contestants; but he loved one of them as a good son and disowned the other as a bad son. Afterward, however, he begot many others as ministers of his works, whom the Greeks call ἀγγέλους (*angelous*, “angels”); and these were of one nature, though a nature containing the same opposition as that of the two. Yet that corruptible part was assuredly not corrupted immediately at the beginning of its origin; rather, after the world had been composed and ordered, as we shall soon explain, it defected from the [Col. 0296B] vigor of the heavenly substance through its perverted will. At the beginning, however, all were equal before God and of equal condition, and for that reason all were angels, while those two were their leaders. When God had appointed one of these two over good and the other over evil, he began the construction of the world, with all those whom he had created serving him and assigned to definite offices.

But we were unwilling to admit this passage into the text, as though it were spurious; for it is absent from 12 Vatican manuscripts, 8 Royal, 1 Bologna, the very ancient Tax., Pen., Leipzig, Nav., Palatine, 2 Brun., 4 Oxford, Tornes., Rostock, 6 Colbertine, Gat., Vict., 1 Sorbonne, and 2 Clermont manuscripts. It is also absent from the Rohan and Saint-Germain manuscripts and is not found in the oldest Roman edition, the Venetian edition of 1490, the Aldine of 1515, the Paris edition of 1525, Grapheus, the Antwerp edition of 1539, Cratander’s of 1524, Isaeus, etc. Nor should it be admitted in any way, although it savors of Lactantius’ style, since it contains many errors. First, it teaches the Manichaean error, namely, that God created two principles, one of good and the other of evil. It is also false that good and evil cohere in such a way that, if you remove one, you also remove the other; [Col. 0296C] for this does not hold true in heaven. It next compares the devil with the Son of God, which is plainly impious and was devised by some Arian. This ἀντίγραφον (*antigraphon*, “text”) also says that God had the angels as ministers of his work in creation; indeed, it even contradicts Lactantius, who says in this same chapter: “How, then, would that divine power differ from a human being, if God, like a human being, required the aid of another?” GALLAEUS.

“That first and greatest Son.” Take care not to suppose that Lactantius believes the angels to be sons of God by nature, and thus either raises them to the nature of God or lowers the Son of God to the nature of angels. Lactantius both knew and taught that Jesus is the one Son of God, as below in this book, chapter 17, and in Book IV, chapter 8; and in the same chapter 8 and chapter 18 of that fourth book he confesses him to be God from God: “What,” he says, “shall we say of the indignity of this cross, on which God was suspended and fastened by the worshipers of God?” He has the same teaching in Book IV, chapters 10, 13, 14, and 29; likewise “light from light” in chapter 29, and in the same chapter one in substance with the Father: “Both,” he says, “have one substance”; of the same power with him, in chapter 17 of this same book: “He alone,” he says, “possesses power over all things together with the Son”; and one with the Father throughout that same chapter. In chapter 8 of Book IV he also quotes and confesses that saying of John: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,” in which the Son’s divinity and coeternity are clearly asserted. Finally, he confirms that all things were made through him in this passage and in Book IV, chapters 6 and 8, at the end. Arius is therefore refuted by Lactantius rather than receiving even the least support from him. Accordingly, when Lactantius here and in Book IV, chapter 6, appears to designate angels by the name “sons of God,” he must be understood to use that name not univocally but equivocally in relation to the Word, that is, the only-begotten Son of God.

“Craftsman.” This accords with Paul’s words to the Colossians, 1:16–17, where the creation of the world is attributed to the Word.

“Adorning.” One ancient Bologna manuscript reads “ordering.” But below also: “to have both arranged and adorned the world.”]

he took for himself a name contrary to himself. From this it is apparent that envy is the source of all evils. For he envied his predecessor, who, by remaining faithful to God the Father, is both approved and beloved. [Col. 0296A] The Greeks therefore call this being, who made himself evil from good, διάβολον (*diabolon*, “devil”); we call him “the accuser,” because he reports to God the crimes into which he himself entices people.

God, therefore, when he began the construction of the world, placed that first and greatest Son over the whole work and employed him both as counselor and as craftsman in devising, adorning, and perfecting things, because [Col. 0297A] he is perfect in providence, [Col. 0297A]

[Note: [Col. 0297C] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 297–298]]

“Because he is also perfect in providence.” One Royal manuscript, the Rostock manuscript, and the Roman editions of 1468 and 1470 read “prudence,” which is not very appropriately said of God. Prudence is a virtue proper to human beings, but providence to God, as Thomasius rightly observes.

“The poets.” Namely Hesiod and Ovid, at the beginning of Book I of the *Metamorphoses* and Book I of the *Fasti*. See above, Book I, chapter 5. Lactantius does not rebuke the poets because they posited a kind of chaos from which the beauty of the universe later emerged, but because they made it coeternal with God. For it is known from the sacred Scriptures that God created from nothing a confused and unformed mass, that is, chaos.

“Arranged.” So almost all manuscripts and printed editions. But one ancient Bologna and one Clermont manuscript, together with Isaeus’ edition, have “ordered.”

[Col. 0297D]

“They believe” (*credant*). This is the reading of the manuscripts; the printed editions have *credunt* (“they believe”).

“On the Nature of the Gods.” Namely, in fragments of Book I *On the Nature of the Gods*.—“For Cicero, when discussing the nature of the gods.” This indicates the subject of the discussion, not the title assigned to the book, because these words are not found in the three books *On the Nature of the Gods* that we possess. They therefore either come from a lost book or the extant books on the nature of the gods were once more extensive.

“Divine providence.” On this, see Lactantius’ book *On the Anger of God*.

“Not what he himself would make.” Perhaps read, “what he himself had made.”

“In these ten verses.” Among Latin writers *versus* means not only metrical verses but any lines of writing. Cicero: “I shall count not merely the pages of the letter, but even its lines and syllables.”

“Let us grant this to the custom.” This is the reading to be adopted from all the manuscripts and editions except Tornes., Soubron, Thomasius, and Walch, which have “to this custom,” and the Roman edition of 1470, 2 Paris editions, the Aldine, Fasitel., and Betuleius, which have “in this manner”; wrongly. Cicero argued according to the custom of the Academics, and Lactantius was saying that this custom must be granted to him. From ISAEUS.

“Let us consider the propositions themselves.” From 4 old Royal manuscripts, the Gotha manuscript, 1 Clermont manuscript, and Cellarius’ edition, with Francius’ approval, I restored “themselves,” which is more forceful than others’ “his.”

“Do you establish?” This is the reading of all the manuscripts and of the Roman editions of 1468 and 1470, Tornes., and Soubron. Fourteen printed editions read, “do you prove?”

“For you have said nothing.” So most Royal manuscripts, 6 Colbertine, 2 Clermont, Em., Cambridge, Brun., and the printed editions cited above. Two Bologna manuscripts, six others, and some printed editions have “For it is not.”

[Col. 0298D]

“How, then, will it differ from a human being?” Thus with the Roman edition of 1470, Thysius, Gallaeus, Cellarius, and all manuscripts except the recent manuscript, 2 Colbertine, Jun., and twelve printed editions, which have “In what way?”

“That divine power will differ.” I restored this from the oldest manuscripts—1 Royal-Puteanus, 1 Bologna, 4 Colbertine, 1 Clermont, and Brun.—and the edition of Gallaeus of 1563, with support from 1 very ancient Royal manuscript, Jun., Leipzig, Palatine, Pen., Ultr., 1 Colbertine, 1 Clermont, and printed editions which have the future “will differ,” except the Roman edition of 1470, in which, as also in 1 Bologna, 1 Royal, and 1 Colbertine manuscript, the reading is the present “differs.”

“Requires the aid of another . . . requires.” The indicative is the reading of almost all manuscripts and old editors; the other printed editions, 1 Royal, 1 Colbertine, and Brun. have the subjunctive, “would require.”

“Creator.” The reading varies: elsewhere “fashioner,” elsewhere “maker.” This term has not yet been noted in my Faber. Thus Tertullian, Book V *Against Marcion*, chapter 5: “He calls the Father Lord and creator and founder both of humankind and of the universe.”

“Received.” This is the reading of the manuscripts, the old editors, and Cellarius. The recent common editions have “assumed.”]

reason, and power. I shall now say less about him, because elsewhere (namely, Book IV, chapter 6 and following) I shall have to explain his virtue, his name, and his nature. Let no one ask from what materials God made works so great and so marvelous; for he made all things from nothing.

Nor should we listen to the poets, who say that chaos existed in the beginning, that is, a confusion of things and elements, but that afterward God divided that entire mass and, separating individual things from the confused heap and arranging them in order, both structured and adorned the world. It is easy to answer those who fail to understand God’s power and believe that he can accomplish nothing except from material already lying ready at hand—an error into which the philosophers also fell. For [Col. 0297B] Cicero, when discussing the nature of the gods, speaks as follows:

> First, therefore, it is not probable that the material of things from which all things arose was produced by divine providence; rather, it possesses and has possessed its own force and nature. Accordingly, just as a builder, when he is about to construct something, does not himself make the material but uses what lies ready at hand, and similarly a sculptor uses wax, so material must have been available to that divine providence—not material that he himself would make, but material that he would have ready at hand. But if matter was not made by God, then neither earth, water, air, nor fire was made by God.

Oh, how many faults there are in these ten lines! First, a man who in other discussions and in almost all his books was a defender of providence, and who attacked with the sharpest arguments those who said that providence does not exist, [Col. 0297C] now, like some traitor or deserter, attempted [Col. 0298A] to abolish providence. If you wished to contradict him on this point, neither thought nor labor would be required; his own words need only be recited to him. For Cicero can be refuted more forcefully by no one than by Cicero himself. But let us grant this to the custom and practice of the Academics, so that exceedingly free human beings may be permitted to say and think whatever they please. Let us consider the propositions themselves.

“It is not probable,” he says, “that the material of things was made by God.” By what arguments do you establish this? For you have said nothing to explain why it is not probable. To me, on the contrary, it appears probable in the highest degree; nor does it appear so rashly, when I consider that there must be something greater in God, whom you plainly reduce to human weakness by granting him nothing but craftsmanship. How, then, will that divine power differ from a human being if God, just like a human being, requires [Col. 0298B] the aid of another? Yet he does require it if he can attempt nothing unless material is supplied to him by someone else. If that is so, his power is necessarily imperfect, and the creator of matter must now be judged more powerful. By what name, then, will the one who surpasses God in power be called? For it is a greater thing to make one’s own materials than to arrange another’s. But if it is impossible for anything to be more powerful than God, who must necessarily be perfect in virtue, power, and reason, then the fashioner of matter is the same being who fashioned the things composed from matter. For nothing either could or ought to exist if God had not made it and had been unwilling that it exist.

“But it is probable,” he says, “that the material of things possesses and has always possessed its own force and nature.” What force could it possess when no one had given it? What nature, when no one had generated it? If it possessed force, it received that force from someone. From [Col. 0298C] whom, however, could it have received it except God? Further, if it possessed [Col. 0299A] a nature—which is assuredly so called from being born—it was born. By whom, however, could it have been brought forth except by God?

For if nature, from which you say [Col. 0299A]

[Note: [Col. 0299C] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 299–300]]

“From which you say.” I restored this from the Roman editions of 1468 and 1470, Betuleius, Tornes., and Soubron, and from all manuscripts except 1 Clermont manuscript, which has the singular, “from which you say”; the other Clermont manuscript and many printed editions have “which is said.”

“And of making.” Thus several printed editions and all manuscripts except the Cotton manuscript, which has “and also of making”; many printed editions have “or of making.”

“Seneca.” See Seneca, Book IV *On Benefits*, chapter 7. Add Pliny, Book II, chapter 7, and Book XXVII, chapter 3. On this, see below, Book III, chapter 18.

“For indeed.” *Enim* (“indeed”) was added from the Royal manuscripts, 3 Colbertine, 2 Brun., and the older and better editions; it is absent from 9 manuscripts.

“Although it is natural to him, he gave it to himself.” Thus 2 Bologna, 9 Royal, 4 Colbertine, and 2 Clermont manuscripts. In the Tax., Pen., Cambridge, and Brun. manuscripts and several printed editions, “it is natural.” In 1 recent Royal manuscript and the Roman edition of 1470, Aldine of 1515, Paris of 1525, Cratander, Grapheus, Gymnich, Fasitel., and Cologne edition of 1544: “Although it is natural to him, he gave it to himself,” with a slightly different Latin construction, which I would consider more suitable. In Em.: “Although it is natural to him, he gave it to himself,” with *eam* in place of *illam*. [Col. 0299D] These last two readings do not displease me.

“God himself is nature.” Thus I read with 2 Bologna, 8 Royal—two of which are very old—3 Colbertine, 2 Clermont, Tax., Brun., and other manuscripts. Lactantius has the same below, Book III, chapter 26. In 1 Royal, 3 Colbertine, Jun., and many printed editions: “God is nature itself.”

“You are stuck in the same mud,” etc. These two expressions are from Terence’s *Phormio*, Act V, scene 2, verse 15. It is a proverb signifying that some people become entangled in an affair from which they cannot extricate themselves. See, if you wish, Erasmus’ *Adages*, Century I, Section IV, Adage 99. Lactantius himself recalls the former expression in Book VII, chapter 2.—“You are stuck in the same mud.” Again in Book VII, chapter 2: “They became stuck in the same mud, as the comic poet says.” BUN.

“You pay off one loan by contracting another, Geta.” One ancient Bologna manuscript, 3 Royal, Ultr., Brun., and others add “Geta.” Muretus reads *vorsuram*; others maintain that Terence wrote *vorsura*. According to Budaeus, those are said “to pay off one loan by contracting another” who, in order to discharge one written obligation and free themselves from one bond, again borrow money at greater interest, etc. [Col. 0300C] The expression applies to those who become so entangled in a difficult affair that they cannot extricate themselves without great loss. ERASMUS.—The metaphor is taken from travelers who, as soon as they fall into mud, attempt to pull out one foot and sink the other more deeply.

“You deny to be made.” Thus the oldest and best manuscripts—1 Bologna and 2 Royal, 6 Colbertine, Cambridge, Em., 2 Clermont, and Brun.—and 2 old Roman editions, the Aldine, Paris, Grapheus, Cratander, and the French translation. But the recent manuscripts, 2 Royal and 7 printed editions, wrongly add “the world” after “to be made.” See the preceding words.

“Which he himself would make.” Perhaps read, “which it itself had made.”

“Will build.” I restored this from the manuscripts except 1 Royal, in which “built” is read, *v* in place of *b*. The printed editions have “builds.”

“He makes from it.” Thus the manuscripts and old printed editions. Eight recent printed editions have “he made.”

“Prepared, and prepared from it.” Thus the Bologna codices and one Vatican manuscript, according to Thomasius, who [Col. 0300D] finds this repetition elegant; previously the printed editions had only one occurrence: “prepared from it.”

“It is impious.” Thus I restored the text from the manuscripts. Two recent Royal manuscripts and the printed editions have “it would be impious.”

“For if anything exists before him, he will lose the power and name of God.” Thus we emended the text from the most ancient manuscripts—1 Bologna, 5 Royal, 4 Colbertine, 1 Clermont, Em., Balliol, and 2 Brun. The remaining manuscripts and printed editions vary remarkably, and their readings seem incongruous to us. The reading we admit, however, produces excellent sense, which was previously absent from texts reading: “For if anything made exists before him.”

“They will not be able.” Thus I read with nearly all the manuscripts and old printed editions. The remaining common editions, together with 2 Colbertine manuscripts, have “they were able.”

“And so either God.” “Either” was added from all the manuscripts and a very large number of printed editions.

“Except in that which perceives, which understands.” We added “which perceives” [Col. 0301C] from all the manuscripts and old printed editions. See the preceding discussion.]

all things to have arisen, possesses no rational purpose, it can accomplish nothing. But if it has the power of generating and making, then it possesses rational purpose and must therefore be God. No other name can be given to that power in which there reside both the providence to devise and the skill and power to execute.

Seneca, therefore, the most acute of all the Stoics, spoke better when he perceived that “nature is nothing other than God. Shall we therefore,” he says, “not praise God, whose virtue is natural to him?” For he did not learn it from anyone. Indeed, we shall praise him; for although it is natural to him, he gave it to himself, since God himself is nature.

When, therefore, you attribute the origin of things to nature and take it away from God, you are stuck in the same mud; [Col. 0299B] you pay off one loan by contracting another, Geta. For what you deny is made by one, you plainly confess is made by that same one after changing the name.

There follows a most inept comparison:

> Just as a builder, he says, when he is about to construct something, does not himself make the material but uses what lies ready at hand, and similarly a sculptor uses wax, so material must have been available to that divine providence—not material that he himself would make, but material that he would have ready at hand.

Quite the contrary: it need not have been so. For God will possess lesser power if he makes something from material already prepared, which is what a human being does. A builder will construct nothing without wood because he cannot make the wood itself; inability, however, belongs to human weakness. But God makes [Col. 0300A] his own material for himself because he has the power to do so. For ability belongs to God; if he lacks the power, he is not God.

A human being makes from what exists because through mortality he is weak and, through weakness, possesses limited and moderate power. God, however, makes from what does not exist because through eternity he is strong and, through strength, possesses immeasurable power, which is without boundary or limit, just like the life of its maker. What wonder is it, then, if God, when about to make the world, first prepared the material from which he would make it, and prepared it from what did not exist? For it is impious that God should borrow anything from elsewhere, since all things are in him or from him. For if anything exists before him, and if anything was made that was not made by him, he will thereby lose both the power and the name of God.

“But matter was never made, just like God, who made this world from matter.” Two eternal things are therefore posited, and indeed things [Col. 0300B] mutually opposed—something that cannot occur without discord and destruction. For things whose force and nature are different must necessarily collide. Thus both will not be able to be eternal if they oppose one another, because one must necessarily overcome the other. It is therefore impossible that the nature of the eternal should not be simple, so that all things have flowed down from it as from a spring.

And so either God arose from matter or matter from God. Which of these is truer can easily be understood. Of these two, one is capable of perception, while the other lacks perception. The power to make anything can exist only in that which perceives, understands, thinks, and moves. Nor can anything be begun, made, or completed [Col. 0301A] unless it has first been rationally planned; [Col. 0301A]

[Note: [Col. 0301C] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 301–302]]

“Planned.” Thus we restored the text from the Vatican manuscripts, 2 Bologna, 8 Royal, Tax., Pen., Leipzig, Palatine, Brun., the Roman editions of 1468 and 1470, and Isaeus’ edition. Two Colbertine, 1 Clermont, and almost all printed editions have “foreseen.” See below: “by reason and providence.”

“And how.” Twice in the aforementioned 29 manuscripts. “Or” is read twice in 2 Royal, 1 recent Bologna, 1 Colbertine, the Clermont manuscript, and almost all printed editions. In Em. and Christ.: “how it may come to be before it has been made.”

[Col. 0301D]

“A living creature through reason.” Lactantius appears here to suggest that animals are endowed with reason.

“With a tangible body.” Thus we emended the text from 7 Royal, 6 Colbertine, 2 Clermont, Brun., and other manuscripts, and the editions of Tornes. and Thomasius. In the remaining common editions and three recent Royal manuscripts it is “contractible.”

“And inanimate things.” Thus 2 Bologna and 2 very ancient Royal manuscripts and numerous printed editions. In 1 Clermont manuscript, “inanimate beings”; in 4 Royal, 3 Colbertine, and 1 Clermont, “inanimate things,” with a different Latin form; in 3 other Royal, 3 Colbertine, and Brun., “things lacking life.”

“Matter.” See Plutarch, *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*, Book I, chapter 9.

“For what has always existed never ceases always to exist.” From all the older and better printed codices and all manuscripts, we added “always to exist,” which is absent from many common editions and 3 Oxford manuscripts.

“Which, by changing, might dissolve him.” One ancient Bologna manuscript reads: “Which might change and dissolve him.”

“Impassible.” See the annotations on the book *On the Anger of God*.

[Col. 0302C]

“Of the Sibyls.” Namely, at the beginning of the first discourse.

“Of the prophets.” I understand this not of the true prophets but of foreign ones, such as Orpheus and Zoroaster, or the Persian Magi, the Indian Gymnosophists, or the Gallic Druids or Semnothei. Augustine, too, sometimes mentions seers of this kind. Lactantius’ purpose is to convict the nations by the testimonies of their own people. For what point would there have been in counting Moses and the others, who expressly assign the making of the world to the true God, among the pagans? BETULEIUS.—Yet this also seems to me capable of being understood [Col. 0302D] of the true prophets. Compare Huet, *Evangelical Demonstration*, p. 497.

“For this.” Thus I emended the text from the oldest manuscripts—2 Bologna, 2 Royal, another 4 Royal, 4 Colbertine, Gotha, 1 Leipzig, 2 Clermont, and Brun.—and the editions of Tornes., Cellarius, and Walch; this is more suitable than the “the same also” of most common editions, or “for the same” in 2 Colbertine manuscripts and Isaeus’ edition.

“Pythagoreans.” Thus I restored the text from almost all manuscripts. Three Colbertine, Brun., and the common editions have “Pythagorics.” Plutarch, in *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*, says that Pythagoras established God as the principle of all things.

“Stoics.” They taught that we possess knowledge of God from the beauty and magnitude together of the things made by him, as Galen reported in the *History of Philosophy*, chapter 27. In Laertius’ *Life of Zeno*, they define God as Θεὸν εἶναι ζῶον ἀθάνατον, “God is an immortal living being.” I wonder what came into Jerome’s mind when, in chapter 9 of his commentary on Ezekiel, he denied that the Stoics affirm the providence of God, especially since the Stoic Seneca’s excellent book *On Providence* survives. Moreover, Salvian, near the beginning of his work, where he presents almost the same testimonies, by no means passes over the Stoics in silence. [Col. 0303B–C] BETULEIUS.]

and how it is to come into being before it exists, and how it is to be constituted after it has been brought into being. In short, something is made by one who possesses both the will to make it and hands for carrying out what he has willed. But that which lacks perception always lies inactive and sluggish, and nothing can arise from a place where there is no voluntary motion.

For if every living creature is constituted through reason, it certainly cannot be born from something that is not endowed with reason; nor can that which is not present in the source from which it is sought be received from elsewhere. Yet no one should be disturbed because certain animals seem to be born from the earth. For the earth does not produce these by itself; rather, the spirit of God does so, without which nothing is generated.

God, therefore, does not arise from matter, because that which possesses perception can never arise from that which lacks it; the wise from the brutish; the impassible from the passible; [Col. 0301B] or that which is free of body from the corporeal. Matter, rather, comes from God. For whatever exists in a solid and tangible body is subject to external force. Whatever is subject to force is dissoluble. What is dissolved perishes. What perishes must necessarily have arisen. What has arisen had a source from which it arose, that is, some maker who perceives, exercises providence, and possesses skill in making. This maker is assuredly God and no other.

Because he is endowed with perception, reason, providence, power, and virtue, he can create and produce both animate and inanimate things, since he understands how each thing is to be made. Matter, however, cannot always have existed, because it would not be capable of change if it had. For what has always existed never ceases always to exist; and where a beginning was absent, an end must likewise be absent. Indeed, it is easier for that which had a beginning [Col. 0301C] to lack an end than for that which lacked a beginning to have an end.

If, therefore, matter was not made, nothing can be made from it either. If nothing can be made from it, [Col. 0302A] it will not even be matter. For matter is that from which something is made. Everything from which something is made, however, is destroyed because it has received the craftsman’s hand and begins to be something else. Therefore, since matter reached an end when the world was made from it, it also had a beginning. For what is destroyed was built; what is loosened was bound; what is ended was begun. If, therefore, from matter’s transformation and end it is inferred that it had a beginning, by whom other than God could it have been made?

God alone, therefore, who was not made and for that reason can destroy other things, cannot himself be destroyed. He will always remain what he was, because he was not generated or born from elsewhere, nor does his birth depend upon some other thing which, by changing, might dissolve him. He exists from himself, as we said in the first book (namely, chapters 3 and 7); and he is therefore such as he willed himself to be: impassible, [Col. 0302B] immutable, incorrupt, blessed, and eternal.

The conclusion with which Tullius ended his proposition is still more absurd:

> But if matter was not made by God, then neither earth, water, air, nor fire was made by God.

How cleverly he flew past the danger! For he assumed the preceding claim as though it required no proof, although it was far more uncertain than the proposition for whose sake it was assumed. “If,” he says, “matter was not made by God, neither was the world made by God.” He preferred to infer what is false from a falsehood rather than what is true from the truth. And although uncertain propositions ought to be proved from certainties, here he drew his proof from an uncertainty in order to overthrow what was certain.

For it is agreed among almost all philosophers that the world was produced by divine providence—to say nothing of Trismegistus, who proclaims this; nothing of the poems of the Sibyls, which announce the same; nothing of the prophets, [Col. 0302C] who with one spirit and a concordant voice testify that the world is God’s work and craftsmanship. For this is the teaching of the Pythagoreans, Stoics, and Peripatetics, [Col. 0303A] who are the leaders of every school. [Col. 0301A]

[Note: [Col. 0303C] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 303–304]]

“School,” that is, sect. Our author frequently uses the word in this way, together with Cicero, Macrobius, and others. Terence, *Eunuch*, Act II, scene 2: “The schools of philosophers derive their names from the philosophers themselves.” Cicero, Book I *On the Nature of the Gods*, chapter 7: “You have assembled as three leaders of three schools”; Book V *Tusculan Disputations*, chapter 32: “Almost all the philosophers of every school.” Compare Lactantius, Book II, chapter 5; Book III, chapters 12, 14, 15, 17, 28, and 30. BUN.

“Who are the leaders of every school.” I restored this reading, which seemed better than the following readings of more recent witnesses. Four manuscripts have “which are the leaders of the school of all”; 2 Bologna, 8 Royal—two of which are ancient—3 Colbertine, Palatine, Leipzig, Ultr., 1 Clermont, Brun., and the Roman editions of 1468 and 1470 have “which are the principal representatives of every school”; 2 Royal and 3 Colbertine manuscripts have “who.”

“As far as Socrates, as far as Plato.” I thus emended the text from two 900-year-old Royal codices and another, more recent Royal manuscript of good quality. This is the true reading. Many other manuscripts and printed editions have “from Socrates down to Plato.” Thus [Col. 0303D] Thales, according to Laertius, says that the world is the work of God.

“Many centuries.” Lactantius errs here; Epicurus lived not many centuries after Plato but only a few years after him. Epicurus was born in the second year of the 109th Olympiad, whereas Plato died in the first year of the 108th Olympiad.

“Barking all around.” He appears here to allude to the Cynics.—“Barking all around.” This is better evidence than the examples in the lexicons from Avienus and Nolanus. I also find in Seneca, *To Marcia*, chapter 22, “to bark all around a man,” and in Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XVI: “Envy barked all around Arbetio.” Add Falster’s *Supplement*, Book I, p. 54. BUN.

“Structured by providence.” Thus all witnesses. Heumann reads: “the world structured by providence,” adding “by.” The preposition can be absent, as in Book I, chapter 2: “structured by design”; *On Anger*, chapter 9: “the world itself structured by no reason, art, or craftsmanship”; and *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 2: “that the world is structured and governed by no providence.” BUN.

“Than providence conglobated with matter.” Thus reads the older first Bologna manuscript, supported by three Vatican manuscripts, one Leipzig manuscript [Col. 0304B], and the Gotha manuscript, in which the reading is “providence of matter conglobated” [Col. 0304C]. But the man who says that providence was conglobated together with matter believes that providence existed at the same time as matter, and supposes that providence could have effected nothing unless it had possessed matter beforehand or simultaneously. By this, indeed, much is detracted from providence. THOMASIUS.—Twenty-eight manuscripts and the old Roman edition read “matter conglobated by providence”; twelve printed editions, “of matter conglobated by providence.”—“Than matter conglobated by providence.” In *On Anger*, ch. 9: “the nature of things conglobated from certain minute and indivisible seeds”; and ch. 10: “this conjunction and conglobation of atoms produces all things.” BUN.

“Whereupon Lucilius.” Most manuscripts and printed editions transmit it thus. Nine manuscripts and two printed editions read “since Lucilius”; the first old Bologna manuscript and the Roman edition of 1470, “because Lucilius”; some common editions, “Lucillius.” See this in Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book I. In Cicero, Lucilius defends the Stoics’ position.

“Let Cotta extricate himself.” I read thus with all the manuscripts and almost all the printed editions. Some common editions wrongly have “Let C. Cotta explain” [Col. 0304D]. Cotta, of course, was an Academic in Cicero.—“I have him . . . I have him . . . let him extricate himself.” An elegant formula used when one disputant has confined himself in a difficulty and the other rejoices in victory. Cicero, *Academics* IV.48: “I have you, I said,” etc.; *For Quinctius*, ch. 20: “Here I have you”; and *Against Verres*, Book III, ch. 60. BUN.

“He will not wish.” Two recent Royal manuscripts read “he may not wish”; five recent manuscripts, “he would not wish”; the Royal Putéanus manuscript, “he does not wish.”

“With what hands.” See Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book I.

“With what machines . . . levers . . . contrivance.” Add below, “tools.” He had in view Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I.8: “What contrivance? What tools? What levers? What machines?” BUN.

“Perhaps he would have seen,” etc. Nine manuscripts read: “You might have seen . . . you might have been able.” The first old Bologna manuscript and the Palatine manuscript: “Perhaps you might have been able to see . . . you might have been able.”

“When he made it.” The first Colbert manuscript reads “he may have made”; several read “when God made it,” among them Bunemann, who annotates this passage as follows:—“When God made it.” “God” is added by the Leipzig, Gotha, Emmanuel, Bodleian, Cottonian, Subiaco, Venice 1471, 1472, and 1497 [Col. 0305C], Rostock, Pierius, Parisian Cratander, Aldine, Gymnicus, and Tournes editions. But Thomasius and subsequent editors wrongly omitted it.]

Finally, from those first Seven Sages down to Socrates and Plato, it was regarded as confessed and indubitable, until many centuries afterward there arose a single madman, Epicurus, who dared to deny what is most evident—evidently from an eagerness to discover something new, so that he might establish a school under his own name. And because he could discover nothing new, he nevertheless wished to overthrow the old doctrines so that he might seem to disagree with everyone else. In this, all the philosophers barking around him convicted him of error. It is therefore more certain that the world was furnished by providence than that providence was conglobated with matter. Accordingly, one ought not to have supposed that the world was not made by divine providence merely because its matter had not been made by divine providence; rather, because the world was produced by divine providence, [Col. 0303B] its matter too was divinely made. For it is more credible that matter was made by God, since God can do all things, than that the world was not made by God, since nothing can be made without mind, reason, and design.

But this is not Cicero’s fault; it is the fault of his school. For when he had undertaken a disputation intended to abolish the nature of the gods, about which the philosophers babbled, through ignorance of the truth he supposed that all divinity had to be abolished. Thus he could abolish the gods, because they did not exist. But when he attempted to overthrow divine providence, which exists in the one God, because he had begun to strive against the truth, his arguments failed him [Col. 0304A], and he necessarily fell into this pit, from which he could not extricate himself. Here, therefore, I have him caught; I have him pinned fast at the point where Lucilius, who argued against him, fell silent. Here, then, is the pivot of the whole matter; everything turns upon this. Let Cotta extricate himself from this abyss, if he can; let him produce arguments by which he may prove that matter has always existed and was produced by no providence. Let him show how anything ponderous and heavy could either have existed without an author or have been capable of undergoing change, and how that which had always existed ceased to be, so that something which had never existed might begin to be.

If he proves these things, then at last I shall assent that not even the world was established by divine providence; and yet I shall assent in such a way that I may catch him in other snares. For he will be driven back to the very point to which he does not wish to return: he must say that both the matter from which the world exists and the world [Col. 0304B] which exists from matter arose by nature, while I contend that nature itself is God. For no one can perform marvelous works—that is, works constituted by the highest rationality—unless he possesses mind, providence, and power. Thus it follows that God made all things, and that absolutely nothing can exist which did not derive its origin from God.

Yet whenever this same man becomes an Epicurean and refuses to admit that the world was made by God, he is accustomed to ask with what hands, with what machines, with what levers, and by what contrivance God made so great a work. Perhaps he would have seen, had he been able to exist at the time when God made it. But lest man should perceive [Col. 0305A] the works of God—

[Col. 0305A]

[Note: [Col. 0305C] [Notes of the Various Commentators on columns 305–306]

“But lest man should perceive the works of God,” etc. This opinion of Lactantius is false.

“Benumbed by excessive rigors.” Thus all printed editions except the old Roman edition. Almost all manuscripts read “embodied,” which agrees less well with “rigors.” But near the beginning of the next chapter Lactantius also writes, “is numb with cold and frost”; and Turpilius too used *torporavit* (“benumbed”), according to Nonius.

“The sun not yet established.” Thomasius reads, as in the Bologna and first Clermont manuscripts, “the soil not yet established,” which seems to accord better with what follows concerning crops and animals [Col. 0305D], which live upon the soil. I have presented the reading accepted by all the other manuscripts and printed editions. Besides, Lactantius had already spoken of the soil or earth, and anyone who examines the text will understand that Thomasius’s reasoning has no weight. ISAEUS.

“That man was God’s final work.” Genesis, ch. 2. If anyone wonders why God assigned the last place to his most excellent work, let the Creator’s supremely wise will suffice for him. Yet if anyone wishes to know some reasons, let him have these. Man needed a dwelling, and one that was neither empty nor unsightly, since he was God’s noblest creature and, as it were, a kind of demigod. Therefore God first constructed the most beautiful and perfect theater of the universe—that is, one adorned with things and filled to overflowing with everything conducive to use and every kind of delight. Afterward he introduced man into this most august palace, thus prepared, and set him as ruler over all creatures. For if man had found the world empty and bereft of the sun [Col. 0306C], heavenly lights, plants, fruits, and, finally, living creatures moving through air, water, and earth, solitude would certainly have been extremely burdensome to him, and the lack of necessary things would have disturbed his happiness in various ways. Whoever desires more should read Philo’s *Cosmopoeia*, Gregory of Nyssa’s *On the Making of Man*, ch. 2, and Ambrose’s letter to Herontianus, which is no. 38. PARAEUS.

“How it is built.” Thus the manuscripts, including two of the oldest of all—the first Bologna and first Royal manuscripts—the four Colbert manuscripts, Junius, Brunus, and very many printed editions. Four manuscripts and two common editions read “how it is being built”; two Royal manuscripts and one Leipzig manuscript, “how it might be built”; the first Clermont manuscript and the Tournes and Soubron editions [Col. 0306D], “how it is constructed.”

“Hermes.” Trismegistus in Stobaeus, *Collections*, discourse 80, *On the Gods*.

“Perception.” This is what the whole section above requires. Borrichius too recognized it in his *Deficiency of the Lexicons*. Again Lactantius, *On Anger*, ch. 1: “from perception of the truth.” I have also found this rather rare word, hitherto unknown from earlier authors, in Augustine, *The City of God* VIII.4: “Contemplation claims for itself the perception of truth.” BUN.

“Enclosed in the custody.” Plato speaks thus of body and soul in the *Phaedo*. So too Lactantius himself, in *On the Workmanship of God*, ch. 20, says of man in accordance with the Platonists: “For this little body in which we are clothed is the receptacle of man.”

“Only those things to know . . . inquisitive.” Compare below, Book II, ch. 11; Book III, ch. 20; *On the Workmanship of God*, ch. 15. Tertullian, *On the Soul*, ch. 1, end: “It is better not to know through God, because he has not revealed it, than to know through man, because he himself has presumed it.” BUN.]

—he did not wish to bring him into this world until everything had been completed. Indeed, man could not even have been brought into it: for how could he have subsisted while heaven was being constructed above and the earth was being founded below; while moist substances perhaps either congealed, benumbed by excessive rigors, or, baked and solidified by fiery heats, hardened? Or how could he have lived when the sun had not yet been established and neither crops nor animals had been born? Therefore man necessarily had to be made last, when the finishing hand had already been placed upon the world and all other things.

Finally, the sacred writings teach that man was God’s final work and was thus brought into this world as though into a house already prepared and furnished, for all things were made on his account. The poets too acknowledge this. Ovid, at the beginning of the *Metamorphoses*, after the world had already been completed and every kind of animal fashioned, added this [Col. 0305B]:

> A creature holier than these and more capable of lofty thought  
> Was still lacking, one that could rule the rest:  
> Man was born.

So great an impiety must it be deemed to scrutinize those things which God wished to remain concealed! But Cicero inquired not from a desire to hear or learn, but to refute, because he trusted that no one could explain it. As though one should therefore suppose these things not to have been made divinely because it cannot be perceived how they were made.

If you had been raised in a crafted and ornamented house but had never seen any construction, would you have supposed that house not to have been built by a human being because you did not know how it was built? You would surely ask about the house the very same questions that you now ask about the world: with what hands and with what tools [Col. 0305C] a human being had contrived such great works—especially if you saw enormous stones, immense masses of masonry, vast columns [Col. 0306A], and the whole structure towering aloft. Would these things not seem to you to exceed the measure of human strength, because you did not know that they had been made not so much by physical strength as by reason and craftsmanship?

But if man, in whom nothing is perfect, nevertheless accomplishes through reason more than his slight strength would allow, why should it seem incredible to you when the world is said to have been made by God, in whom, because he is perfect, neither wisdom can have a limit nor strength a measure? His works are visible to the eyes. Yet how he made them is not visible even to the mind, because, as Hermes says, the mortal cannot approach the immortal, the temporal the perpetual, or the corruptible the incorruptible—that is, it cannot draw nearer and follow with understanding.

And therefore an animal still earthly does not grasp the perception of heavenly things [Col. 0306B], because it is held enclosed by the body as though in custody, which prevents it from beholding all things with an unfettered and free faculty of perception. Let the person who investigates ineffable matters therefore know how foolishly he acts. For this is to transgress the limit of his created condition and not to understand how far it is permissible for a human being to approach. Finally, when God disclosed the truth to humanity, he wished us to know only those things which it was important for a human being to know in order to attain life. But matters belonging to an inquisitive and profane desire he left unspoken, so that they might remain secret. Why, then, do you seek things which you can neither know nor become happier by knowing? Wisdom is perfect in a human being if he knows both that there is one God and that all things were made by him.

## CHAPTER X [Col. 0306C]

### On the World and Its Parts, the Elements, and the Seasons

Now, since we have refuted those who think wrongly about the world and [Col. 0307A] about its maker—

[Col. 0307A]

[Note: [Col. 0307C] [Notes of the Various Commentators on columns 307–308]

“And about its maker.” The preposition “about” has been restored from almost all the manuscripts. It is absent from four recent manuscripts and many printed editions. On the work of the six days, see St. Ambrose, St. Basil, St. Augustine, *Confessions*, Book XII, and Theodoret, *On Providence*, Books I and II.

“Be surrounded by flowing water.” Passive, as in Macrobius, *Dream of Scipio* II.9: “the whole body of the earth is surrounded by the twin circuit of Ocean.” BUN.

“His own dwelling.” Here and in Book VII, ch. 5, our author understands “heaven” as the whole mass of the heavens, insofar as it also includes the empyrean heaven. ISAEUS.

[Col. 0307D]

“But darkness, which is contrary to these.” Nothing should be changed: “which is” signifies “that is,” in the customary usage of other authors and of Lactantius, Book VI, ch. 23: “The divine law joins two in marriage, which is, into one body. . . .” *Turin Epitome*, ch. 13, end: ΖΑΝ ΚΡΟΝΟΥ, “which is, Jupiter, son of Saturn.” BUN.

“The east is assigned to God.” Thus thirty-six manuscripts and several printed editions. That is, “is attributed.” Two recent Royal manuscripts and some printed editions read “is judged similar to God,” which is a gloss. Lactantius appears here to indulge too much in allegories.

“To the corrupt mind.” Here and below Lactantius speaks with insufficient orthodoxy, as though an evil mind exercised supreme dominion over the West.

“The northern region.” Thus I have restored the text from the older and better manuscripts: the first Bologna manuscript, the Royal Putéanus, two other Royal manuscripts of good authority, the Palatine, and the Leipzig. The common editions and several manuscripts read “of the north.”

“Spring to the east.” On these allegories, see also St. Ambrose, *Hexaemeron*, Book IV.

“Autumn belongs to the west, winter to the north.” Thus the manuscripts and the old Roman edition, using the genitive case. The other common editions [Col. 0308C] use the dative case: “to the west . . . to the north.” Most manuscripts have “wintry weather” instead of “winter.” Our reading comes closer to the normal order of the Latin language.

“Which intervals.” Thus six Royal manuscripts, three Colbert manuscripts, two Brunus manuscripts, and a great many of the older and better printed editions. Some manuscripts and seven editions read “which.”

“Complete.” The Gotha manuscript reads “finish”; I prefer the former. Book VII, ch. 14: “As the days revolve in succession, the cycles of years are completed”; and the *Epitome*, ch. 25: “so that . . . they might complete their courses and fixed intervals.” BUN.

[Col. 0308D]

“Brings on.” Thus almost all manuscripts and printed editions, and rightly so, since it corresponds to the preceding “supplies.” The first Royal manuscript and the Thysius and Gallæus editions read “brought on.”

“Even in this.” I restored these words from all the manuscripts and printed editions except five more recent editions, in which they are absent.

“Which rises to form the day.” Thus I emended the text from all the manuscripts except one recent Royal manuscript and the editions, which read “in the day.”

“The light of perfect fullness.” Heraclitus calls the sun the source of heavenly light, according to Macrobius—whether it lends its own light to the other stars, according to Pliny, or whether, as Cicero maintained, the other stars except the moon possess their own light, while the sun itself is the leader, prince, and governor of the lights. See Plato’s *Timaeus*, Cicero’s *On the Universe*, and Macrobius, *Dream of Scipio*, Book I, above, ch. 20. BETULEIUS.

“With most powerful heat.” Thus all printed editions and many of the better manuscripts. The first old Bologna manuscript, three Royal manuscripts, the Leipzig, and the Palatine read “with most potent heat.”

“Antigod.” That is, the devil. *Antitheus*, a Greek word, signifies one who is opposed to God, or God’s adversary.

“Display.” Thus very many printed editions and almost all the manuscripts. One recent Royal and one Colbert manuscript read “may display”; one Leipzig manuscript and three printed editions, “bring forth”; three recent Royal manuscripts and six editions [Col. 0309C], “convey.” Bunemann also reads “convey” and presents the following note.—“Convey.” *On the Workmanship of God*, ch. 7: “It is marvelous that a single arrangement . . . displays innumerable varieties of living beings.” There many editions had surreptitiously introduced “conveys.” *On the Workmanship of God*, ch. 8: “It is incredible how much beauty it displays.” BUNEMANN.]

—let us return to the divine construction of the world, concerning which an account is handed down in the secret writings of the holy religion.

First of all, therefore, God made heaven and suspended it aloft, so that it might be the abode of God himself, the Creator. Then he founded the earth and placed it beneath heaven, so that humanity might inhabit it together with the other kinds of animals. He willed it to be surrounded and bounded by flowing water. But he distinguished and filled his own dwelling with brilliant lights: namely, he adorned it with the sun, the shining orb of the moon, and the radiant constellations of twinkling stars. Darkness, however, which is contrary to these, he established upon the earth; for the earth contains no light in itself unless it receives it from heaven, in which he placed perpetual light, the beings above, and everlasting life, while, conversely, upon the earth he placed darkness, the beings below [Col. 0307B], and death. For these earthly things differ from those higher things as much as evils differ from goods and vices from virtues.

He also established two parts of the earth as contrary and diverse to one another, namely east and west. Of these, the east is assigned to God, because he is himself the source of light and the illuminator of things, and because he causes us to arise to everlasting life. The west, however, is attributed to that disordered and corrupt mind, because it hides the light, continually brings on darkness, and causes people to fall and perish through sins. For just as light belongs to the east, and the principle of life is found in light, so darkness belongs to the west, and death and destruction are contained in darkness.

Then, by the same principle, he measured out two other regions, the south and the north, which are joined by association [Col. 0307C] to the former two. For the region which burns more intensely with the heat of the sun is nearest to and contiguous with the east. But the region which is numb with cold and perpetual frost belongs to the same order as the farthest west. For just as darkness is contrary to light [Col. 0308A], so cold is contrary to heat. Therefore, as heat is nearest to light, so the south is nearest to the east; and as cold is nearest to darkness, so the northern region is nearest to the west.

To each of these regions he assigned its own season: namely, spring to the east and summer to the southern region; autumn belongs to the west, and winter to the north. In these latter two regions too—the southern and northern—the figure of life and death is contained, because life is in heat and death in cold. And just as heat derives from fire, so cold derives from water.

In accordance with the measurement of these regions he also made day and night, so that in alternating succession they might complete intervals and the perpetual, revolving cycles of time which we call years. The day, which the east first supplies, necessarily belongs to God, as do all things whatsoever that are better. But the night, which the farthest west brings on [Col. 0308B], belongs, of course, to the one whom we have called God’s rival.

God, foreknowing the future, made these two things even in this respect, so that through them a kind of image might be displayed both of true religion and of false superstitions. For just as the sun, which rises to form the day, though one, is apparently called *sol* for that reason—as Cicero maintains in *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book II—because, when the stars are darkened, it alone (*solus*) appears, yet because it is the true light of perfect fullness, it illuminates all things with most powerful heat and most brilliant radiance; so in God, although he is one, majesty, power, and splendor are perfect.

But the night, which we say is assigned to that corrupt antigod (*antitheus*), represents by analogy his many and various religions. For although innumerable stars appear to twinkle and radiate [Col. 0308C], nevertheless, because they are not full and solid lights, they display no heat at all and do not overcome the darkness by their multitude.

Accordingly, two primary things are found which possess powers diverse and contrary to one another: heat and moisture. God devised these in a marvelous manner [Col. 0309A] for sustaining and generating all things—

[Col. 0309A]

[Note: [Col. 0309C] [Notes of the Various Commentators on columns 309–310]

“In a marvelous manner.” The first Colbert manuscript and the first Brunus manuscript read “in a very useful manner.”

“Philosophers.” Empedocles, namely, concerning whom see Diogenes Laertius and Plutarch, *Opinions of the Philosophers* I.3.

“And poets.” Such as Ovid, in the verses to be presented shortly, and Horace, *Epistles* I.12.19, concerning the struggle of the elements:

> What discordant concord wills and can accomplish.

“They did not see.” Thus we have restored the text from all the manuscripts and the Tournes, Betuleius, and Soubron editions. The other printed editions read “they have not seen.”

“Heraclitus, from fire.” This is reported among his doctrines by Diogenes Laertius. Cicero mentions it in *Academic Questions*, Book IV. It is also refuted by Lucretius in Book I. BETULEIUS.

“Thales.” Concerning whom something was said in Book I, ch. 8; see also Diogenes Laertius [Col. 0309D].

“The substance of fire is heat; of water, moisture.” Because they subsist and are preserved by these. See below and ch. 12.

“Ovid.” *Metamorphoses*, Book I, in the same passage where he writes about the fertility of the Nile.

“So that the marriage compact might be solemnized by the sacrament of fire and water.” Pompeius Festus, Book I: “Water is so called because people are aided by it; one is customarily forbidden water and fire, which brides receive, evidently because these two things sustain human life above all.” The same appears in Plutarch, *Roman Questions*, ch. 1. Festus again, Book VI: “At weddings they carried a torch before the bride in honor of Ceres, and the new bride was sprinkled with water, either so that she might come to her husband chaste and pure, or so that she might share fire and water with her husband.” Valerius Flaccus, *Argonautica*, Book VIII:

> Pollux carried before them the fire and nuptial water,  
> So that together they might turn into a favorable course.

Ovid, *The Art of Love*, Book II:

> Let those men pursue such things, if they have already approved pursuing them,  
> Whom fire and water make lawful husbands.

At the threshold they presented water, into which they dipped a firebrand. Marcus Varro, quoted by Turnebus, Book XXIX, ch. 27: “From the new husband in turn, when a firebrand from the hearth, taken from a fruitful tree, and water in a basin had been brought” [Col. 0310B]. Dempster. See Brissonius, *On the Rite of Marriage*.

[Col. 0310C]

“Be embodied and animated.” Pliny similarly joined the two terms in *Natural History* VII, section 13, at the end, on the generation of humanity. Jerome, *To Pammachius*, fol. m. 170: “Once warmed, he gives it body; once embodied, he distinguishes it into limbs.” Compare Lactantius, *Institutes* II.8, and Barthius, *Adversaria* VII.2, fol. 313. BUN.

“Neither can the moisture be embodied nor the body animated.” This must be read from the Soubron and Tournes editions and the manuscripts, not, as is wrongly printed in some editions, “embody, nor animate the body.” That this is the necessary reading will be evident to anyone who considers Lactantius’s purpose, for the body does not animate but is animated. From ISAEUS.—*Corporari*, “to be clothed with a body,” and *animari*, “to receive a soul,” are rare words. They occur additionally in *Institutes* IV.26.

“Exiles too.” That prohibition, without any change of territory, consisted in forbidding anyone to share water, fire, or shelter with the person thus interdicted, as Appian says concerning Metellus when thus interdicted. A person who received, concealed, or harbored someone forbidden fire and water was also liable under the Julian Law on private violence, as Paulus says in *Sentences* V.26. A similar punishment was also in use among the Greeks. Electra, speaking in Euripides’ *Orestes* about herself, Pylades, and Orestes, says: “It has been decreed at Argos that no one may receive us matricides with shelter, fire, or speech.” SELDEN.—We read in Usuard’s *Martyrology*, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January, that St. Valerian, a bishop in Africa, was afflicted with the same punishment. When he was more than eighty years old, during the Vandal persecution under the Arian king Genseric, he was ordered to be expelled alone from the city; and orders were given that no one should allow him to dwell either in a house or on an estate. Instead, he lay naked beneath the open sky on a public road for a long time and completed the course of his blessed life in the confession of Catholic truth and the defense of holiness. From Victor of Vita, *History of the Vandal Persecution* I.12.

“One of these is common to us,” etc. Lactantius does not make this argument in order to teach that the human being consists only of fire and water. For the human body, like those of all other animals, consists of the four elements, as Aristotle and Hippocrates testify. Rather, by analogy he teaches that the soul’s origin is heavenly, while that of the body is from the same elements of which all things consist, but chiefly from moisture—perhaps because both semen and blood are fluids; for Thales’s opinion was rejected by Lactantius himself a little above. But in attributing a fiery nature to the soul, he contradicts his own arguments by which he had not long before refuted Heraclitus’s doctrine. BETULEIUS.]

For since God’s power resides in heat and fire, if a material consisting of moisture and cold had not been mixed in to temper its heat and force, nothing could have been born or held together; rather, whatever had begun to exist would immediately have perished in a conflagration. Hence some philosophers and poets said that the world consists through discordant concord, but they did not perceive the underlying reason at all. Heraclitus said that all things were born from fire; Thales of Miletus, from water. Each saw something, but each nevertheless erred, because if either element had existed alone, neither could water have arisen from fire nor, conversely, fire from water. The truer account is that all things are generated from both together, commingled.

Fire itself cannot be mixed with water, because the two are mutually hostile [Col. 0309B]; and if they come into close contact, whichever overcomes must destroy the other. But their substances can be mixed. The substance of fire is heat; that of water, moisture. Ovid therefore rightly says:

> Indeed, when moisture and heat have attained a temperate mixture,  
> They conceive, and from these two all things arise;  
> And although fire is hostile to water, moist vapor creates  
> All things, and discordant concord is suited to offspring.

[Col. 0310A] For one is, as it were, the masculine element, the other the feminine; one is active, the other receptive. And therefore it was instituted by the ancients that the marriage compact should be solemnized by the sacrament of fire and water, because the offspring of living creatures are embodied through heat and moisture and animated into life.

For since every animal consists of soul and body, the material of the body resides in moisture, and that of the soul in heat. This may be learned from the embryos of birds: unless productive heat warms them when they are full of thick moisture, neither can the moisture be embodied nor the body animated. Exiles too were customarily forbidden fire and water; for it still appeared impious to inflict capital punishment upon human beings, even if they were evil. Thus, by forbidding the use of those things upon which human life depends, the person who had received that sentence [Col. 0310B] was regarded just as though he had been punished with death. So fully were these two elements regarded as primary that people believed neither human birth nor life could subsist without them.

One of these is common to us and the other animals; the other was given to humanity alone. For because we are heavenly and immortal animals, we use fire, which has been given to us [Col. 0311A] as evidence of immortality, since fire comes from heaven. Because its nature is mobile and strives upward, it contains the principle of life. But the other animals, because they are entirely—

[Col. 0311A]

[Note: [Col. 0311C] [Notes of the Various Commentators on columns 311–312]

“Entirely.” Note the use of the word “entirely” in the plural nominative.

“Because it is mobile and inclines downward.” Except for the first Bologna manuscript, which reads “immobile”—written by a second hand—all the manuscripts and printed editions read “mobile.” This reading, although Isaeus opposes it, appears preferable. For since Lactantius appeals to experience and says that water is immobile and nevertheless inclines downward, how, I ask, can water move downward—as he admits—while itself remaining immobile? We shall certainly grasp Lactantius’s thought more successfully if we look back to the preceding words. There he says that we use fire, all of whose motion is upward, whereas the other animals share their condition with water, which, devoid of fiery vigor, is borne along by a very different motion and inclines downward with whatever force it possesses. SPARK.

“In pairs.” See Genesis 1 and compare ch. 6, verse 20.

[Col. 0311D]

“For clothing.” Thus I restored the text from most manuscripts, including the oldest and best—the Royal, Bologna, and others. Eight recent manuscripts and the printed editions read “for a garment.”—“For clothing.” Thus I print from the Bologna, Palatine, Utrecht, and first Leipzig manuscripts, and from a parallel passage in *On Anger*, ch. 13, according to the better copies: “partly for food, partly for clothing.” BUN.

“To procreate innumerable souls.” From this passage some argue that Lactantius believed all souls to have been created in the beginning. But in Book III, ch. 18, he ridicules and refutes that Platonic fiction concerning souls created before bodies. Indeed, Lactantius is speaking here not of the actual creation of souls, but of the divine decree to create them, which he denotes by the words “he resolved and devised.”

“Form.” For the image or divine character implanted in humanity by the Creator, see not Plato but Paul: 2 Corinthians, ch. 3; Colossians, ch. 3; and Ephesians, ch. 4.

“Godlike” (*θεοειδὴν*). Rather *θεοειδῆ* or *θεοειδές*, as it stands in Plato himself, *Republic*, Book VI. Thus Philo Judaeus calls the soul an *ἀπόσπασμα θεοῦ*, “a fragment of God,” attributing to it what Paul, in Hebrews 1, attributes to Christ, the only-begotten Son of God. In *On the World*, he calls the soul *τύποθεν σφραγῖδα θεοῦ*, “a seal impressed by God,” whose character, he says, is eternal reason. Pythagoras says that mortals are a *θεῖον γένος*, “divine race”; so too Aratus: *τοῦ γὰρ καὶ γένος ἐσμέν*, “for we are also his offspring.” Paul himself did not reject this at Athens, Acts 17. From these passages, I say, we can readily gather how close studious antiquity came to the truth through the midst of darkness. For truly, as Lactantius says, it was not the reality but the artisan’s name that deceived them: they attributed to the best and greatest God the name of Jupiter, which Scripture does not recognize. BETULEIUS.

“An image,” etc. *Sibylline Oracles*, discourse 8. Latin translation:

> Man is my image, possessing right reason.

See also the first discourse of the *Sibylline Oracles*, where it treats of the creation of humanity.

[Col. 0312D]

“Prometheus.” Different authors relate this myth differently. Concerning it, see Hesiod’s *Works*, Plato’s *Protagoras*, Ovid at the beginning of the *Metamorphoses*, Horace, *Odes* I.16, Propertius III.3, Fulgentius’s *Mythologies*, and Servius.

“With everyone adding something to what he had heard.” I restored the text thus from the manuscripts and the old Roman edition.
