The printed editions had: “with everyone adding something to what they had heard.” You might perhaps suppose the reading in the text to be a scribal error; but I judge it to be a deliberate Hellenism of Lactantius himself. Thus Terence in the *Andria*: “Restore me to the position in which you received me.” Thus Livy, Book I: “And the place in which they first disembarked is called Troy.” Gronovius. This reading is also confirmed by the Leipzig, Utrecht, and two Brunus manuscripts. Three recent Royal manuscripts read “to that which.”

“Prometheus.” One of the Titans. For Iapetus was the son of Uranus and Titaea. These events took place around the time of Saturn, namely more than nineteen centuries before the Common Era.]

—mortal, use only water, which is a corporeal and earthly element. Because its nature is mobile and inclines downward, it displays the figure of death. Therefore cattle neither look up toward heaven nor possess a sense of religion, because the use of fire is foreign to them. But from what source, or in what manner, God either kindled or distilled these two primary elements, fire and water, only he who made them can know.

## CHAPTER XI

### On Living Creatures, Humanity, Prometheus, Deucalion, and the Fates

[Col. 0311B] When the world had therefore been completed, God commanded that animals of various kinds and dissimilar forms, both great and small, should come into being. And they were made in pairs—that is, each kind was made of differing sex; from their offspring the air, the earth, and the seas were filled.

God gave all these creatures, kind by kind, nourishment from the earth, so that they might be of use to humanity: some, of course, for food, and others for clothing; but those possessing great strength were given to assist in cultivating the earth, whence they were called beasts of burden (*jumenta*).

When all things had thus been arranged according to a marvelous design, God resolved to prepare an eternal kingdom for himself [Col. 0312A] and to procreate innumerable souls to which he would grant immortality. Then he made for himself a sensible and intelligent representation—that is, one formed according to his own image, than which nothing can be more perfect. He fashioned man from the clay of the earth; hence man was named *homo*, because he was made from the soil, *humus*. Finally, Plato says that the human form is godlike; and the Sibyl says:

> *Εἰκών ἐστ᾽ ἄνθρωπος ἐμή, λόγον ὀρθὸν ἔχουσα.*  
> Man is my image, possessing right reason.

Although corruptly, the poets too handed down no different account of this fashioning of humanity: for they said that man was made from clay by Prometheus. It was not the reality that deceived them, but the artisan’s name. For they had encountered no writings of truth. Instead, what had been handed down by prophetic utterance and was contained in God’s sanctuary, they gathered from myths and obscure report, distorted it, and incorporated it into their poems—as truth, when dispersed among the populace through various accounts, is customarily corrupted—with everyone adding something to what he had heard [Col. 0312B]. In this they were indeed foolish, because they assigned so marvelous and divine a work to a human being.

For what need was there to fashion man from clay when he could have been generated in the same manner in which Prometheus himself was born from Iapetus? If Prometheus was a man, he could beget a man; he could not make one. That he was not one of the gods, moreover, is demonstrated by his punishment on Mount Caucasus [Col. 0313A].

[Col. 0313A]

[Note: [Col. 0313B] [Notes of the Various Commentators on columns 313–314]

“His punishment on Mount Caucasus.” Tzetzes interprets him as having been bound upon the Caucasus [Col. 0313C].—“His punishment on Mount Caucasus.” Books are full of the myth of Prometheus. Concerning his punishment, Propertius II.1.71:

> The same man will free Prometheus’ arms  
> From the Caucasian rock and drive the bird from the center of his breast.

And Martial, *Spectacles*, poem 7:

> Just as Prometheus, bound upon a Scythian rock,  
> Fed the ceaseless bird from his immense breast.

CELLARIUS.

“His uncle Titan.” He was his paternal grandfather. THYSIUS.

“It was in Saturn’s power alone.” “Was” appears in all the manuscripts and the old printed editions; “may have been,” in the more recent printed editions. Saturn too was a son of Uranus and Titaea, and accordingly the brother of Iapetus.

“That a flood occurred,” etc. Nonnus, *Dionysiaca*, Book III, enumerates three *κατακλυσμούς* (“cataclysms” or “floods”). Isidore, *Origins* XIII.22, lists three floods. MEURSIUS.—That the flood occurred because of sin is described most elegantly by Ovid in *Metamorphoses*, Book I. Anyone who desires more testimony on this subject should consult Grotius’s notes on his book *On the Truth of the Christian Religion*.

[Col. 0313D]]

If, therefore, the cataclysm occurred for this reason. Thus nearly all the manuscripts and the editions of Tornesius and Soubron. But two old editions and two recent manuscripts have *a Deo* (“by God”) instead of *ideo* (“for this reason”); many printed editions have both: *a Deo ideo* (“by God for this reason”). The universal Flood is acknowledged by all who do not call Holy Scripture into doubt. The other floods, however, of which some record has been handed down, rest upon exceedingly uncertain evidence. Nevertheless, some scholars, Grotius among them in his annotations on chapter 16 of Book I *On the True Religion*, mingle later events with earlier ones and suppose the floods of Noah, Ogyges, and Deucalion to have been the same, although long intervals of time separate these very floods.

Deucalion. On the story of Deucalion, see Justin, Book II, and Lucian in the dialogue *On the Syrian Goddess*. Cyril relates that Prometheus, Deucalion’s father, was born in the seventh year of Moses.

What they relate concerning Prometheus’s craftsmanship. Thus all the manuscripts and most of the older printed editions. The editions of Betuleius and Gymnicus add *iidem* (“the same men”) after *opificio* (“craftsmanship”); six others have *itidem* (“likewise”); one Clermont manuscript has *idem* (“the same”).

Prometheus fashioned an image of a man, etc. We have restored this reading from the oldest and best manuscripts: two Bolognese, four Royal, [Col. 0314B] two Colbertine, the Sorbonne, Pen., Tax., and two Clermont manuscripts. Ten recent manuscripts [Col. 0314C] and ten editions have *Prometheum*; one Royal and one Leipzig manuscript have *Prometheo*.

And that from him the art first arose. Thus nearly all the manuscripts and the old Roman edition. *Esse* (“to have”) is absent from two recent manuscripts and from many editions.

Temples to be established. Many editions and all the manuscripts use the infinitive, so that it may be referred to *coeperunt* (“began”), which follows. One recent Colbertine manuscript and six recent commonly used editions have *constituit* (“he established”).

The fashioning . . . from clay belongs to God. Understand these words thus: “The fashioning . . . of man from clay belongs to God,” or: “God is the fashioner of man from clay.” I have therefore, with Walch, placed a comma after *limo* (“from clay”). BUNEMANN.

Which Hermes also handed down. *Tradidit* (“handed down”), which occurs in six Royal manuscripts, four Colbertine manuscripts, the Brun manuscript, and others, is required by the following verbs, “said . . . attempted”; six recent manuscripts, together with the editions, have *tradit* (“hands down”). Hermes testifies that man was created in the image of God—namely, in chapter 1 of the *Poimandres*. And lest anyone suppose that the name τοῦ δημιουργοῦ (*tou dēmiourgou*, “of the Creator”) was attributed to God, the supreme architect, only by Plato and Hermes, as we have already seen rather frequently, let him know that it is also found in the apostolic writings. Paul, *To the Hebrews*, chapter 11: δημιουργὸς ὁ [Col. 0314D] Θεός (*dēmiourgos ho Theos*, “God is the Creator”), etc. But our Lactantius treated this workmanship in a separate work, which he himself now testifies that he had written for his pupil Demetrianus. Hermes, however, followed Pythagoras, the Pythagorean Iamblichus, and others. BETULEIUS.

Made. Nine manuscripts have “fashioned.”

And Cicero followed them. I have thus restored the reading from nearly all the manuscripts. Instead of *Tullius*, three recent Royal manuscripts and the editions have *Cicero*; five Colbertine manuscripts and the Brun manuscript have “and Cicero followed them.” — See Cicero, Book II of *On the Nature of the Gods*, and Book I of *On the Laws*.

Touches upon. I read thus with six Royal, four Colbertine, two Clermont, the Brun, and other manuscripts, as well as the Roman editions of 1468 and 1470, Soubron, Tornesius, and Cellarius. Three recent Royal and two Colbertine manuscripts, together with several editions, have “touched upon.” The book: that is, *On the Workmanship of God*, addressed to Demetrianus. You will find it below in volume II of our edition.

Men and the other animals. See Orpheus, Pacuvius, and Diodorus Siculus, Book I, where he treats of myths.

It is Virgilian: “And the earth-born race of men,” etc. In Virgil, *Georgics* II.341. Some editions read *Ferrea* (“iron”), especially Heinsius’s; but wrongly: that verse should be corrected from this passage. If *Ferrea* had been read in Virgil in Lactantius’s time, the verse here would in no way have suited his purpose. To prove the assertion of the philosophers who supposed that men had arisen from the earth without any craftsman, he adds, “whence that Virgilian line.” Three Royal manuscripts have *Ferrea*. — “And the man.” I have added this word, which supports Lactantius’s argument, from the Bolognese manuscript, two Royal manuscripts nine hundred years old, and two other recent but reliable Royal manuscripts.]

But no one called either his father Iapetus or his uncle Titan gods, because the exalted rank of kingship belonged to Saturn alone, through which he, together with all his descendants, obtained divine honors. This fiction of the poets can be refuted by many arguments. It is agreed among all that the Flood occurred to destroy and remove wickedness from the face of the earth. Philosophers, poets—namely Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I—and writers of ancient history all say the same; and on this matter especially they agree with the language of the prophets. If, therefore, the cataclysm occurred in order that the wickedness which had increased through the excessive multitude might be destroyed, how was Prometheus the fashioner of man, when those same authors say that his son Deucalion alone was preserved because of his righteousness? How could a single [Col. 0313B] generation and a single line of descent have filled the world with human beings so quickly? But plainly they corrupted this story too, just as they did the earlier one, since they did not know at what time the cataclysm occurred upon the earth, who through righteousness merited preservation when the human race perished, how he was preserved, or with whom—all matters taught by the prophetic writings. It is therefore evident that what they relate concerning Prometheus’s craftsmanship is false.

Yet because I had said that poets (namely, Book I, chapter 11) are not accustomed to lie altogether, but envelop and obscure what they say in figures, I do not say that they lied, but that [Col. 0314A] Prometheus was the first of all to fashion an image of a man from rich and pliant clay, and that from him first arose the art of fashioning statues and images; for he lived in the time of Jupiter, when temples first began to be established and new forms of worship of the gods began. Thus the truth was disguised with falsehood; and the deed said to have been done by God began also to be ascribed to a man who imitated the divine work. The fashioning of a real, living man from clay, however, belongs to God. This Hermes also handed down: he not only said that man was made by God in the image of God, but also attempted to explain by what subtle design God fashioned every individual member of the human body, since there is none that contributes no less to beauty than to necessary use. The Stoics likewise [Col. 0314B] attempt to do this when they discuss providence; and Cicero, who followed them, does so in several passages. Yet he touches only briefly upon so abundant and fertile a subject. I pass it over now because I recently wrote a separate book on the matter for my pupil Demetrianus. But at this point I cannot pass over the assertion of certain erring philosophers that men and the other animals arose from the earth without any craftsman; whence that Virgilian passage:

> And the earth-born race of men raised its head from the hard fields. [Col. 0315A]

Those who deny that providence exists were especially committed to this opinion. The Stoics, by contrast, attribute the structure of living creatures to divine skill. Aristotle, however, freed himself [Col. 0315A] [Note: [Col. 0315C] [Notes of Various Commentators on columns 315–316]

Aristotle, however, freed himself from the trouble, etc. Book I of *On the Heavens*, chapter 10, and Book II, chapter 1. This opinion does not have Aristotle alone as its author; others also followed it. Thus Heraclitus of Ephesus, in Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* VI; and Pliny, Book I, chapter 1. Lucretius refutes this opinion in Book V, verse 325 and following. GALLAEUS.

Three times. This is the Stoic division of time: they make the past and future infinite, but the present finite. Some deny that the present time exists; on this dispute, however, read Aristotle, Book IV of *Lectures on Nature*, [Col. 0315D] chapter 10 and following; or, if you prefer, Augustine, *Confessions* XI, chapters 17 and 18. This entire argument, however, is employed to establish the providence of God. BETULEIUS.

The subsistence of the present. That is, the present time, which now exists, stands in being. So too below: “the subsistence of the present time.”

Three Fates. This myth concerning the three Fates took its origin from Hesiod’s *Theogony*. See also Plato, Book X of *The Republic*, near the end, and especially Aristotle’s book *On the Cosmos*, where, enumerating very many names of the one God, he attributes to that same one God the rationale and functions of the Fates. — Fates. Compare Vossius, *Idolatry* II, chapter 44 throughout. Leipzig manuscript 3 wrongly has “three parts.” BUNEMANN.

Begins the thread of life for human beings. I read thus with the oldest manuscripts: the Bolognese, Royal-Putean, three Colbertine, and two Clermont manuscripts, and with nearly all the editions. One Royal manuscript nine hundred years old, fifteen recent manuscripts, and two Roman editions have “for a human being.”

Will come to an end. I have thus corrected the text from the Royal-Putean, one Colbertine, the Gotha, Leipzig, one Clermont, and several other manuscripts. “Will come to an end” refers, understand, either to time or to the whole species mentioned above. One Brun manuscript and one Colbertine have “will fail”; another Brun manuscript has the feminine form “will fail”; one Colbertine and two editions have the feminine “will come to an end”; one Royal manuscript nine hundred years old has another feminine form of the same.

Phaethon. His story may be read in Ovid near the end of Book I of the *Metamorphoses* and at the beginning of Book II. Lucian, however, in *Astrology*, believes that Phaethon observed the course of the sun and discovered it, just as Endymion did that of the moon.

At the direction of divine providence. Thus all printed editions and manuscripts except one old Bolognese and one Clermont manuscript, which have “is granted by divine providence.”

As a whole. That is, altogether: Book IV, chapter 1; Book VII, chapter 20; *Epitome*, chapter 61; *On the Anger of God*, chapter 21; *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 8.

Aristotle will not be able to maintain. This is the reading of nearly all the manuscripts and five editions, and is required by what precedes and follows; the Junius manuscript, moreover, has “was able.” One Royal manuscript has “is able”; five recent manuscripts and ten printed editions have “was able.”

[Col. 0316D]

Unwillingly. Here *ingratis* is an adverb. So too in Plautus, *Amphitryon*, act I, scene 1, verse 10. That is, “against their will”; or, according to Sparkius, “whether they will or not.” One Clermont manuscript and four editions have the adjective “ungrateful.”

Epicurus will wrest it away. Read Plutarch, *On the Opinions of the Philosophers* II.4, and Galen, *Philosophical History*, chapter 42.

At greater length. One Clermont manuscript and seven recent editions wrongly add “we shall pursue,” which is absent from all the other manuscripts and printed editions. Instead of “at greater length,” one recent Royal and two Colbertine manuscripts have “more fully”; one Colbertine and the Brun manuscript have “more extensively.”

They say, etc. Namely, the Epicureans. For Censorinus, in *On the Birthday*, writes as follows about this opinion of Epicurus: “Democritus of Abdera thought that human beings were first generated from water and mud. Epicurus’s view was not very different: he believed that, when the mud had grown warm, certain womb-like structures—I know not what—grew from the roots of the earth; and that, after they had brought forth infants from themselves, nature supplied them with nourishment, the moisture of milk; and that, having been thus reared and grown to maturity, they propagated the human race.” On this matter see Lucretius, Book V, verse 806. BETULEIUS. — See Cicero, *On the Laws* I.]

from labor and difficulty by saying that the world had always existed, and consequently that the human race and the other things within it had no beginning, but had always existed and would always exist. Yet since we see each individual animal, which previously did not exist, begin to exist and cease to exist, it follows necessarily that the entire species began to exist at some time and will come to an end at some time, because it had a beginning.

For all things must necessarily be contained within three times: past, present, and future. Origin belongs to the past, subsistence to the present, dissolution to the future. All these are evident in individual human beings: we begin when we are born, we exist while we live, and we cease when we perish. Hence they also conceived of three Fates: [Col. 0315B] one who begins the thread of life for human beings, another who weaves it together, and a third who breaks and ends it. In the human race as a whole, however, because only the present time is evident, the past—that is, its origin—is nevertheless inferred from it, as is the future—that is, its dissolution. For since it exists, it is evident that it began at some time, since nothing can exist without a beginning; and because it began, it is evident that it will at some time come to an end. For a whole composed of mortal beings cannot itself be immortal. Just as all of us perish one by one, so it can happen through some circumstance that all perish at once: either through barrenness [Col. 0316A] of the lands, which commonly occurs piecemeal; through a plague spread everywhere, which very often ravages individual cities and regions; through a conflagration sent throughout the world, such as is said already to have occurred under Phaethon; or through a flood of waters, such as is handed down concerning the time of Deucalion, when the entire race except for one man was destroyed. If that flood occurred by chance, then it could certainly also have happened that the single survivor perished. But if he was preserved, at the direction of divine providence—which cannot be denied—in order to restore humankind, it is evident that either the life or the destruction of the human race lies within God’s power. But if he can destroy it as a whole because he destroys it in parts, it is evident that it arose at some time; and just as its frailty reveals a beginning, so too it reveals an end. If these things are true, Aristotle will not be able to maintain that the world itself did not also have a beginning. But if Plato and Epicurus wrest this concession from Aristotle, the same Epicurus will in turn wrest from Plato and Aristotle, though eloquent men who supposed that the world would exist forever, the unwilling concession that it follows that the world must also have an end. But we shall discuss these matters at greater length in the final book. Let us now return to the origin of man.

## CHAPTER XII

### That animals did not arise spontaneously but by divine ordering, of which God would have made us aware if it were expedient for us to know

They say that, through certain revolutions of the heavens and movements of the stars, a certain maturity for sowing animal life came into existence; and consequently that the new earth, retaining generative seed, brought forth from itself certain sacs resembling wombs, concerning which Lucretius says:

> Wombs grew, attached to the roots of the earth; [Col. 0317A]

[Col. 0317A] [Note: [Col. 0317C] [Notes of Various Commentators on columns 317–318]

Attached to the roots of the earth. The Lucretian manuscript codices have precisely this reading, as do six Royal and one Clermont manuscript of Lactantius and eight printed editions. But the Royal-Putean, one other Royal, four Colbertine and the Brun manuscripts, and the Roman edition of 1470 have “earth” in the ablative; two other Royal, two Colbertine, one [Col. 0317D] Clermont manuscript, and the Roman edition of 1468 and Paris edition of 1525 have “earth” in the accusative.

Had matured. Bunemann reads “had ripened,” and writes as follows concerning this reading: “Thus I have printed it from the Utrecht manuscript; Munckerus also preferred to read it thus here and thus corrected Hyginus, *Fables* 136, p. 203.” BUNEMANN.

Living creatures were nourished. I have restored this from the manuscripts. The printed editions read *nutritos* (the masculine form, “were nourished”).

How, then. I have thus restored the reading from all the manuscripts, supported by five more recent manuscripts and the edition of Betuleius, in which “therefore” occurs; the editions have “but how.” Lucretius in the same Book V.

Nor. I have restored this from two Royal manuscripts nine hundred years old and eight others. Two others have “or”; the rest, “and.”

Living. I have thus restored the reading from four old editions and all the manuscripts except one belonging to Tornesius, in which, as in ten printed editions, the word is “seeing.”

Were poured forth from their mothers’ wombs. Arnobius, Book II: “We are born and poured forth from our mothers’ wombs.” Augustine, volume X, *Sermon 2 on St. John*: “He was poured forth from the confines of a corruptible womb.” Quintilian, *Declamation* VI; Cicero, *Against Piso*.

[Col. 0318C]

Inextricable. This alteration was made from two Bolognese manuscripts, one old Colbertine, the Junius, Utrecht, and two Brun manuscripts, and the editions of Tornesius and Soubron. Walch’s edition has *inexpricabilis*, a typographical error; the rest have “inexplicable.” — “A wondrous and inextricable provision.” The Bolognese, Utrecht, Junius, and Gotha manuscripts have “wondrous and inextricable.” But he again combined the words in *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 8: “The subtlety is inexplicable and wondrous.” BUNEMANN.

And would not also be overwhelmed by the moisture. Thus restored from the editions of Tornesius and Cellarius and all manuscripts except the Em. manuscript, in which “also” is absent, and one Leipzig and one Colbertine manuscript, which have “and not from the moisture.”

And would not be overwhelmed by that moisture of the earth. The Emman. and Leipzig manuscripts have *ac non* (“and not”); others, *annon* (“whether not”). *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 16: “Can anyone comprehend . . . and not understand from that very fact?” BUNEMANN.

Which. Three excellent Royal manuscripts, one Colbertine, two Brun manuscripts, and most of the printed editions and manuscripts have “that which.”

Brought forth fully grown. Since all manuscripts and editions of Lactantius have *excreta*, I retain it; so Virgil, *Georgics* III.397:

> Many already keep the fully grown kids from their mothers.

BUNEMANN.

By the supreme God. Thus nearly all manuscripts, the editions of Tornesius, Soubron, and Walch, and all the Ciceronian codices. Two recent Royal manuscripts have “by the God above”; three Colbertine and two Royal manuscripts, together with many editions, have “by the highest God.”]

and that, when they had matured, they were broken open under the compulsion of nature and poured forth tender animals. They say, furthermore, that the earth itself overflowed with a certain moisture resembling milk and that the living creatures were nourished by this food. How, then, could they endure or avoid the force of cold or heat, or indeed be born at all, when the sun scorched and the cold constricted them? “At the beginning of the world,” they reply, “there was neither winter nor summer, but a perpetual mildness and an equable spring.” Why, then, do we see none of these things occurring even now? “Because,” they say, “it was necessary for them to happen once, so that [Col. 0317B] animals might be born; but after animals began to exist and were granted the faculty of reproduction, the earth ceased to give birth and the condition of the seasons changed.” O how easy it is to refute falsehoods! First, nothing can exist in this world without continuing in the manner in which it began. For surely the sun, moon, and stars were not then nonexistent; nor, when they existed, were they without their courses; nor did the divine governance that regulates and directs their courses fail to begin simultaneously with them. Next, if matters are as they say, providence must necessarily exist, and they fall into the very position they especially seek to avoid. For before animals had yet been born, someone surely provided that they should be born, lest the world be desolate, uncultivated, and dreadful. Moreover, for them to be capable of being born from the earth without the service of parents, provision must necessarily have been made with profound design: first, that [Col. 0317C] the moisture congealed from the earth should be fashioned into the various forms of bodies; and then that, from the sacs in which they were covered, they should receive the capacity for living and sensing and be poured forth as if from their mothers’ wombs. This is a wondrous and inextricable provision. But let us suppose that this too occurred by chance: the things that follow certainly cannot be accidental—that the earth should continually flow with milk and that the temperature of the air should be equable. If it is agreed that these things [Col. 0318A] occurred so that the newly born animals might either have nourishment or be free from danger, it necessarily follows that someone provided for them by some kind of divine design.

But who can provide unless it is God? Let us nevertheless see whether the very thing they repeatedly assert could have happened—namely, that human beings were born from the earth. If anyone considers how long and by what means an infant is reared, he will certainly understand that those earth-born children could not have been nourished without any caregiver. For they would necessarily have lain abandoned for a great many months, until, their sinews having grown firm, they could move themselves and change position—a capacity that can scarcely be attained within the span of a year. Now consider whether an infant could have lain for many months in the same manner and the same place in which it was poured forth, and would not have been overwhelmed and corrupted, and so died, by that moisture of the earth which the earth supplied for nourishment, [Col. 0318B] mixed together with the excretions of the infant’s own body. Thus it is in no way possible that it was not reared by someone—unless, perhaps, all animals were born not tender but fully grown, something it never occurred to them to assert. Their entire account, therefore, is impossible and empty—if indeed an account can be so called whose purpose is to abolish all rational account. For one who says that all things arose spontaneously and attributes nothing to divine providence certainly does not uphold reason but overthrows it. But if nothing can either be made or born without reason, it is evident that providence is divine, since what is called reason belongs peculiarly to it. God, therefore, the contriver of all things, made man.

Cicero, although without knowledge of the heavenly writings, nevertheless perceived this. In Book I of *On the Laws* he handed down the very same teaching as the prophets. I append his words:

> This provident, sagacious, versatile, acute, mindful creature, full of reason and counsel, whom we call man, was generated in an especially glorious condition by the supreme God; for among all the kinds and natures of living creatures, he alone participates in reason and thought, while all the others are devoid of them. [Col. 0318C]

Do you see how this man, although far removed from knowledge [Col. 0319A] of the truth, nevertheless understood—because he preserved an image of wisdom—that man could be generated only by God? Yet divine [Col. 0319A] [Note: [Col. 0319C] [Notes of Various Commentators on columns 319–320]

Divine. But only according to the pagans. Ὃς μόνος, etc. Latin translation:

> He who alone is God, existing as the unconquerable Creator,
>
> Himself established the figure of the form of human beings,
>
> Himself mingled the nature of the generation of every living thing.

These verses come from the *Sibylline Oracles*, discourse 1.

Αὐτὸς ἔμιξε (*Autos emixe*, “Himself mingled”). Thus the editions and manuscripts except one Clermont manuscript and the Roman edition, which have Αὐτὸς ἔλιξε (*Autos elixe*, “Himself wound”). Betuleius wishes to restore αὐγὰς μίξε (*augas mixe*, “mingled rays”). Isaeus notes that this is the reading in the Sibylline codex.

The sacred writings. Namely Genesis I, and David in the Psalms.

Man. That is, the male, the man. Below, once again, “man” κατ’ ἐξοχήν (*kat’ exochēn*, “preeminently”) stands for the male. BUNEMANN.

He breathed into him a soul from the vital source, etc. “Breathed” stands for “breathed into,” which occurs in one Clermont manuscript. Lactantius commonly uses the simple verb for the compound. Above, [Col. 0319D] our author said that the soul is something fiery and a kind of heat, and in this chapter, “But if the soul is fire, as we have shown.” Here he writes that it is from God, as though souls were particles of the divine essence; for besides saying here that God breathed the soul from the vital source, he says below, when explaining this, that the soul arises from God—indeed, that it consists of God. “It is from heaven and God,” he adds shortly afterward; these words sufficiently disclose his meaning. Augustine refutes this opinion in Letter 28 to Jerome, as does Thomas Aquinas in *Against the Gentiles* II.85. Thus Leo I says concerning this opinion: “Excessively proud, therefore, and excessively blind are those who, when they say that the human soul is of the divine substance, do not understand that they are saying nothing other than that God is mutable and that he himself undergoes whatever can be inflicted upon his nature.” They took the occasion for this error from a misunderstanding of Genesis 2:7, where these words are read: “And he breathed into his face the breath of life.” These words in no way say that God breathed the breath of life from his own substance; [Col. 0320C] they merely signify that God infused a soul by which the body made from earth might live, not that it was breathed from the very essence of God. This is peculiar only to the Holy Spirit, who is the essential breath of the Father and the Son; and if the passage concerning man had to be understood in this way, man would have been made God. GALLAEUS.

Empedocles. His *Life* is indeed found in Laertius among the *Lives* of the other philosophers; Cicero, however, more frequently numbers him among the poets. Yet in Book I of *On the Orator*, Cicero denies that natural philosophers and poets are called the same thing on the ground that Empedocles, a natural philosopher, composed an excellent poem. Many of his verses are found in the collection of Henri Estienne entitled *Philosophical Poetry*, published in octavo format.

Four elements. On these, see St. Epiphanius, Book III, *Against Heresies*, and Plutarch, *On the Opinions of the Philosophers* I.3. See also Laertius in the *Lives of the Philosophers*. — Empedocles . . . Varro. He follows [Col. 0320D] Quintilian, *Institutes* I.4. Empedocles among the Greeks, and Varro and Lucretius among the Latins, handed down precepts of wisdom in verse. Aristotle, *Poetics* 1, calls Empedocles φυσιολόγον μᾶλλον ἢ ποιητήν (*physiologon mallon ē poiētēn*, “a natural philosopher rather than a poet”). BUNEMANN.

Following Trismegistus. Something of this kind occurs in the third dialogue of the *Poimandres*.

Said to have been made by God. See the same Trismegistus in Stobaeus, *Collection*, Discourse 11, *On Truth*.

May be immortal. That is, perpetually blessed. He himself explains it: “may abide in perpetual light.” This should be noted against Dodwell, concerning whom more is said at Book VII, chapter 5, under “Immortal” and “Immortality.” BUNEMANN.

And in death. Because the word “death” is ambiguous in sacred inquiry, that ambiguity had to be removed for pagans, for whom the word “death” signifies nothing of this kind. In the sacred pages, however, the departure of the soul from the body is more rarely denoted by the word “death,” and more frequently by “rest” or “sleep.” Thus Lazarus is said to sleep; and [Col. 0321B] 1 Thessalonians 4:13 says: “God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus.” It was a Hebrew manner of speaking to say that the deceased had fallen asleep with their fathers. It is a thoroughly devout and hopeful phrase, by which they signified that the resurrection of the dead is as certain as awakening from sleep. Platonic philosophy, however, also uses the same word. As for Lactantius’s calling darkness death, the prophetic writings commonly speak of “the shadow of death.” “Death,” says Paul, [Col. 0321C] “entered through sin.” BETULEIUS.]

testimonies are needed, lest merely human ones prove insufficient. The Sibyl testifies that man is the work of God:

> Ὃς μόνος ἐστὶ Θεὸς κτίστης ἀκράτητος ὑπάρχων,
>
> Αὐτὸς δὲ ἐστήριξε τύπον μορφῆς μερόπωντε,
>
> Αὐτὸς ἔμιξε φύσιν πάντων γενεῆς βιότοιο.
>
> He who alone is God, existing as the unconquerable Creator,
>
> He himself established the pattern of the form of mortals,
>
> He himself mingled the nature of the generation of all life.

The sacred writings contain the same teaching. God, therefore, performed the office of a true father. He himself fashioned the body; he himself infused the soul by which we breathe. Whatever we are belongs wholly to him. If it were necessary for us to know how he did this, he would have taught us, just as he taught the other things that brought us knowledge both of our former error and of the true light.

## CHAPTER XIII [Col. 0319B]

### Why there are two sexes in humanity; what man’s first and second death are; and concerning the fault and punishment of the first parents

When, therefore, God had first fashioned the male in his own likeness, he then also formed the female according to the likeness of the man himself, so that the two sexes, mingled with one another, might propagate offspring and fill the whole earth with their multitude. In fashioning man himself, moreover, he brought to completion the design of those two substances which we have said are contrary to one another—fire and water. For when the body had been fashioned, he breathed into it a soul from the living source of his own spirit, which is everlasting, so that man might bear the likeness [Col. 0320A] of the world itself, which consists of contrary elements. For man consists of soul and body—that is, as it were, of heaven and earth—since the soul by which we live arises, as it were, from heaven, from God, while the body comes from the earth, from whose clay we have said it was formed.

Empedocles—whom one would not know whether to number among the poets or among the philosophers, because he wrote in verse about the nature of things, as Lucretius and Varro did among the Romans—established four elements: fire, air, water, and earth. Perhaps he followed Trismegistus, who said that our bodies were constituted by God from these four elements, since they contain something of fire, something of air, something of water, and something of earth, and yet are neither fire, nor air, nor water, nor earth. These assertions are indeed not false. For the principle [Col. 0320B] of earth is present in the flesh; that of moisture, in the blood; that of air, in the breath; and that of fire, in vital heat. But blood can no more be separated from the body than moisture from earth; nor can vital heat be separated from breath any more than fire from air. Thus only two elements of all things are found, whose entire principle is comprehended in the fashioning of our body.

Man, therefore, was made from diverse and mutually opposed things, just as the world itself was made from light and darkness, from life and death. God ordained that these two should contend with one another in man, so that if the soul, which arises from God, should prevail, it may be immortal and abide in perpetual light; but if the body should conquer the soul and subject it to its dominion, it may be in everlasting darkness and in death. The power of this death is not [Col. 0321A] such that it utterly extinguishes unrighteous souls, [Col. 0321A] [Note: [Col. 0321C] [Notes of Various Commentators on columns 321–322]

The power of this death is not such that it utterly extinguishes unrighteous souls, etc. These words must be carefully observed against the Socinians, since they teach what the opinion of the Fathers at that time was concerning the state of the impious after death. For the impious are not annihilated, as those heretics assert, but, as Christ says in John 5:29: “Those who have done evil will proceed to the resurrection of judgment.” Read Matthew XXV and Acts 24:15, where Paul expressly mentions δικαίων τε καὶ ἀδίκων (*dikaiōn te kai adikōn*), “both the righteous and the unrighteous.” GALLAEUS.

The dissolution of living nature. The same is read in Plato’s *Phaedo* and Cicero’s *Tusculan Disputations* I: “Death is the departure of the soul from the body.”

And the separation of the soul. Four Colbertine manuscripts and the Brun manuscript have “and the dissolution of the soul.” — Separation. That is, division or severance, as in Book VII, chapter 12. From this I confirm the reading of Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.385:

> And when cold death has severed the limbs from the soul.

BUNEMANN.

The second. We have thus emended the text from the manuscripts and several [Col. 0321D] editions. Six commonly used editions wrongly have “second” in the nominative, for we read “the first” a little above.

The lower part, however, etc. Do not suppose that Lactantius followed Marcion’s error in this, as though he believed that the human body had been fashioned by the devil; for above, in chapters 12 and 13, he said it was formed by God. Rather, his meaning is that, according to John and Paul in 2 Corinthians 4:4, power over the earth was permitted to the devil, and that our body belongs to the devil because God left him the capacity to entice and impel human beings to sin and to harm them. This is therefore not to be understood physically but morally: namely, the “body of sin,” as Paul calls it, is from the devil, not from God. GALLAEUS.

For it is like a little vessel. I judge that this is the correct reading, and not the erroneous reading of most manuscripts and editions: “For the earth is like a little vessel,” etc. The author is not discussing the earth here, but the body made from earth; nor is the earth properly called the little vessel of our spirit. The words must instead be referred to the body, which is like a little vessel or a temporary dwelling used by the spirit, as he immediately adds. In view of Lactantius’s purpose, therefore, I read as the oldest and better manuscripts present the text—namely, one Bolognese, four Royal, the Cauc., Utrecht, one Colbertine, and the Brun manuscripts, and six printed editions.

This heavenly spirit. From all the manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470 and the editions of Tornesius and Soubron, we have added the pronoun, which is absent from the other printed editions.

[Col. 0322C]

And the devil. From the manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470 and the editions of Gymnicus and Cellarius, it was necessary to add the particle “and,” which similarly appears in the first clause, “from heaven and God.” Here, however, it is absent from many editions.

Sallust. See the preface to his history *The Conspiracy of Catiline*.

Service. Used instead of “servitude.” The same occurs in Book IV, chapter 10, “grievous service,” and Book VII, chapter 15, “not to have endured service.”

For he served the foulest pleasures, etc. Suetonius, in his book *On Illustrious Grammarians*, says that he was savaged in a satire by Lenaeus and called a glutton, a scoundrel, and a tippler, monstrous both in life and writings. Aulus Gellius, Book XVII, chapter 18, relates from Varro that he was caught in adultery by Milo and soundly beaten with straps; after paying money, he was released. JURETUS.

And just as fire can burn. Thus all the manuscripts together with the editions, except one old Bolognese manuscript, which reads “For just as,” and one Clermont manuscript, “For also just as.”

Is sustained. That is, is nourished. Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II.54: “The life of living creatures is sustained by three things: food, drink, and breath.” Compare chapter 55, at the beginning, and chapter 11: “Human beings and beasts [Col. 0322D] are sustained by heat.” A little earlier: “are preserved and flourish.” BUNEMANN.

In the regions of the East. It was an eastern location in relation to Judaea, Egypt, or Arabia, where Moses wrote; and indeed it was part of the region called Eden, from “delight,” because it was the most beautiful and fertile part of the entire world. PARAEUS.

Planted. I read thus, as this passage is cited by everyone and as it appears in the Bolognese, Tax., and Pen. manuscripts. So below, chapter 14: “He planted a vineyard with his own hand”; and plantings of trees are called *consitiones*. ISAEUS. — One Colbertine manuscript and seven editions have “sowed together”; one recent Royal manuscript corruptly has “constructed.” But the oldest Royal manuscripts, two Bolognese, the Cauc., and thirteen others, as well as the Roman edition of 1470, the Venetian edition of 1490, and eleven other editions, read “planted”; nor does Lactantius read otherwise in the *Epitome*, chapter 27.

Free from labors. These words must not be understood as though man lived idly in Paradise without any work. If Lactantius understands “free from labors” in this way, he contradicts Holy Scripture, which says that Adam was placed by God in Paradise so that he might cultivate it. I therefore understand the phrase as referring to burdensome and painful labor, which alone is the punishment of sin. Thus GALLAEUS.]

but rather such that it punishes them eternally.

We call that punishment the second death, which is itself perpetual, just as immortality is. We define the first as follows: death is the dissolution of the nature of living creatures; or thus: death is the separation of body and soul. The second we define as follows: death is the endurance of eternal pain; or thus: death is the condemnation of souls, according to their deserts, to eternal punishments. This does not touch dumb beasts, whose souls, being composed not of God but of the common air, are dissolved by death.

In this association of heaven and earth, therefore, whose likeness is expressed in man, the things belonging to God occupy the higher part—namely, the soul, which has dominion over the body; while those belonging to the devil occupy the lower part—namely, the body. [Col. 0321B] Because it is earthly, it ought to be subject to the soul, just as the earth is subject to heaven. For it is like a little vessel, which this heavenly spirit may use as a temporary dwelling. The functions of each are these: that which is from heaven and God should command, while that which is from the earth [Col. 0322A] and the devil should serve. This indeed did not escape the wicked man Sallust, who says:

> But all our power is situated in mind and body; we employ the mind for command and the body rather for service.

He spoke rightly—if only he had lived as he spoke. For he served the foulest pleasures and himself overthrew his own maxim by the depravity of his life.

But if the soul is fire, as we have shown above (chapter 10), it ought to strive toward heaven, as fire does, lest it be extinguished—that is, toward the immortality which is in heaven. And just as fire cannot burn and live unless it is sustained by some rich material in which it may find nourishment, so the soul’s material and food is righteousness alone, by which it is sustained for life.

After this God placed man, generated in the manner we are about to explain, in Paradise (see Genesis II)—that is, in a most fertile and delightful garden—which he planted [Col. 0322B] in the regions of the East with every kind of wood and tree, so that man might be nourished by their various fruits and, free from every labor, might serve God his Father with the highest devotion.

Then he gave him definite commandments. If he had observed them, [Col. 0323A] he would have remained immortal. [Col. 0323A] [Note: [Col. 0323B] [Notes of Various Commentators on columns 323–324]

He would remain immortal. These words militate against Pelagius and his followers, the Socinians, who contend that Adam was created mortal by nature. That this is false is demonstrated by Romans 6:23 and 1 Corinthians 15:53–54; and, as Isaeus notes, it was condemned at the Council of Milevis.

From the tree, etc. That is, from the fruit of the tree. The common people suppose that this tree was an apple tree (*malum*), misled by the ambiguity of the word *pomum* (“fruit”), which has a broader meaning and includes the fig as well. The ancients do not agree: most maintain that it was a fig tree, while others hold that it was a citron tree; Drusius cites their passages. But the matter is extremely uncertain. GROTIUS.

Which was. Thus the Royal-Puteanus manuscript and one other Royal manuscript of excellent authority. [Col. 0323C]

In which he had placed, etc. This statement must not be understood as though the tree were rational and knew good and evil; nor is it called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil because it possessed the power to impart an understanding of good and evil. Rather, it was so named from the outcome, because this would happen to the man: he would know what good he had lost and what evil he had acquired, and what difference there was between the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience. Adam acquired this understanding after eating the forbidden fruit, for he immediately began to be ashamed of himself and saw that he was naked. From ISAEUS. The accuser mentioned here is none other than the devil.

To deceive the man. Thus, with Bon., Witeb., Lips., Reimm., and other manuscripts, almost all editions read. Emman., Goth., and the editions of Tornes. 1587 and 1613 read: “to cast down the man”—a reading surely beyond the invention of copyists and in keeping with Lactantius’ characteristic usage, book III, chapter 29: “If he accomplishes nothing by deceit, he tries to cast him down by violence”; book IV, chapter 27: “The demons established various forms of worship for the purpose of casting man down.” Cyprian, *On the Unity of the Church*, at the beginning: “The persecution which rages for the overthrow and [Col. 0323D] downfall of God’s servants.” BUN.

That he might overstep God’s law. Correctly. See above: “He gave him definite commands, which … if he overstepped, he would be punished with death.” Only one ancient Bononian manuscript reads: “that he might transgress.”

God expelled the man from paradise. Some have supposed paradise to have been a certain pleasant place outside this habitable world; and since Holy Scripture relates that our first parents were expelled from paradise, they maintain that this should be understood to mean that they were banished from that place into this world. This is supported by no foundation whatever, and the contrary will be evident to anyone who examines the text more attentively; for it mentions rivers watering the garden, rivers that still exist in the natural world even now. It must therefore be said that, while dwelling in paradise, they also inhabited this earth of ours, and that when they were expelled from paradise they merely changed their location within this world. GALLAEUS.

Sentence having been passed upon the sinner. I restored this reading from the very ancient manuscripts Cauc., two Bononian, and Pal., and from the edition of Is. and the *Epitome*, chapter 27; it is also supported by two Royal manuscripts and twelve printed editions, in which the reading is “passed upon the sinners.” But seven Royal manuscripts, two of them of the greatest antiquity, six Colbertine manuscripts, Jun., Ultr., two Claromontane, and Brun., together with the editions of Tornes. and Walch., have: “sentence having been given against the sinners.” [Col. 0324B]

Procure. I thus emend on the authority of all the manuscripts and of the Roman editions of 1468 and 1470 and the edition of Walch., except that three Colbertine manuscripts read “complain,” another Colbertine manuscript “acquire,” and ten printed editions “they might procure,” less correctly. For God condemned only the man to labor, but the woman to the pain of childbirth (Genesis 3:16–17, 19).

He surrounded it with fire. The opinions of learned men vary on this matter. Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chapter 46, St. Thomas, and certain others said that Moses intended to signify in figurative language that paradise was situated beneath the torrid zone and was therefore inaccessible to human beings; for, according to the accepted opinion, the torrid zone was formerly thought uninhabitable because of its excessive heat. The experience of our age sufficiently refutes that opinion. Ambrose interprets it differently; Lyranus, as Lactantius does. By the “flame of the sword” we apparently ought to understand the weapons with which the Cherubim angels guarded the garden: with fiery sword-points, which they brandished in a terrifying fashion, they rendered paradise inaccessible. Partly from PARAEUS. [Col. 0324C]

Until he holds the final judgment. Lactantius, together with Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chapter 46, errs in saying that after the Last Judgment the righteous will be brought into the earthly Paradise. Certain ancients had derived this opinion from Papias of Hierapolis, who, through a misunderstanding of chapter 20 of the Apocalypse, imagined a thousand-year kingdom before the blessed were brought into their heavenly fatherland. On this matter see Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, chapter 39. Had Lactantius meant the heavenly kingdom, he would have spoken truly; for Christ expressly testifies that they will enter the kingdom of heaven, Matthew 25:34; and blessed Paul says in 2 Corinthians 5:1: “We know that if our earthly house of this habitation is dissolved, [Col. 0324D] we have a building from God, a house not made by hands, eternal in the heavens.”

The sacred utterances teach. I restored this reading from the editions of Soubr., Bet., Tornes., and Walch., and from nearly all the manuscripts. Two recent Royal manuscripts and twelve printed editions read “the sacred writings.” But the manuscript reading is to be preferred; Lactantius also used it in book IV, chapter 26, as did Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History*, book II, shortly after the middle, in his account extending to the age of Constantine the Great.

Οἳ δὲ Θεὸν. Latin translation:

> But those who honor the true God assuredly possess  
> Everlasting life by hereditary right, themselves  
> Dwelling for all time in paradise, in a luxuriant garden.

These are final matters, in the final part. The recent manuscripts and several printed editions read: “These are final matters, all in the final part.”

The Sibyl. On her, see Discourse I, near the beginning, and Discourse 8, around the middle.]

—if he overstepped them, he would be punished with death. The command was that he should not taste from one tree which stood in the middle of paradise, in which God had placed the understanding of good and evil. Then that accuser, envying the works of God, directed all his deceits and cunning toward beguiling the man, so that he might deprive him of immortality. First he enticed the woman by deceit to take the forbidden food; and through her he persuaded the man himself also to overstep God’s law. Having therefore acquired the knowledge of good and evil, the man began to be ashamed of his nakedness and hid himself from the face of God, something he had not previously been accustomed to do. Then God expelled the man from paradise, sentence having been passed upon the sinner, so that [Col. 0323B] he would procure his sustenance for himself through labor; and God surrounded paradise itself [Col. 0324A] with fire, lest the man be able to approach it until God holds the final judgment upon the earth and, death having been abolished, recalls to that same place the righteous men who worship him. So the sacred utterances teach, as does the Erythraean Sibyl (see Theophilus, *To Amphilochius*, book II), when she says:

> Οἵ δὲ Θεὸν τιμῶντες ἀληθινὸν, ἄεναὸν γε  
> Ζωὴν κληρονομοῦσι, τὴν αἰῶνος χρόνον αὐτοὶ  
> Οἰκοῦντες παράδεισον ὁμῶς ἐριθηλέα κῆπον.
>
> But those who honor the true God inherit  
> Everlasting life, themselves dwelling for all eternity  
> In paradise, alike a luxuriant garden.

But since these are final matters, we shall treat them in the final part of this work. Let us now explain the things that came first. Death, therefore, followed mankind in accordance with God’s sentence; this the Sibyl also teaches in her [Col. 0324B] poem, saying:

[Col. 0325A] Ἄνθρωπον πλασθέντα [Col. 0325A]

[Note: [Col. 0325B] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 325–326]

Ἄνθρωπον πλασθέντα. I restored this reading from the three oldest Royal manuscripts, the Cauc. manuscript, and the Sibylline manuscript used by Isaeus; two Brun. manuscripts agree with them. Printed editions have πεπλάσται. Latin translation:

> Man fashioned by the hands of God.

Ὅν κε. I restored this from the old Royal manuscripts, supported by three Colbertine manuscripts, one Claromontane, one Brun. manuscript—the one possessed by Masurus—and the Roman edition of 1468, which read Ὃν καί. Some [Col. 0325C] manuscripts and several printed editions have ὅν τε, “whom indeed the serpent deceitfully led astray.”

Ὅν γε would not be a bad reading. In Latin:

> So that he might come to the allotted fate of death and receive knowledge of good and evil.

Ἐπὶ μοῖραν. Opsopoeus, in his Sibylline manuscript, reads μ᾽ ἐπὶ, with the negative added, and ἐπελθεῖν in place of ἀνελθεῖν.

Which was extended to a thousand years, etc. No one lived for a thousand years on earth. It must therefore be said that life was prolonged toward a thousand years—that is, that it approached as nearly as possible to that number—as in the cases of Methuselah, Jared, and Noah. From ISAEUS.

He endeavored. Thus most of the best manuscripts and the editions of Rome and Gymnic.; from this seven more recent manuscripts produced “he seemed.”

That months were counted as years. This was not a permanent practice among the Egyptians, although Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I, chapter 12, asserts that among the Egyptians alone the year always had a fixed measure. It is more accurate to say that the Egyptians varied the year and sometimes made it consist of three months, more often four, as the spurious Xenophon has it in his book *On Equivocal Terms*: “The year varies; for the Egyptians sometimes use a one-month year, often a two-month year, not rarely a three-month year, often a four-month year, and sometimes a solar year.” Solinus, chapter 3, writes that the Egyptian year consisted of four months; and St. Augustine, *City of God* XV, chapter 12, says that it sometimes consisted of four months and sometimes of one month. Plutarch, in his *Numa*, relates that the Egyptians first had a one-month year and then a four-month year. Pliny, book VII, chapter 48, and Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, nevertheless write that they generally measured it by the span of a month, according to the course of the moon. On the different forms of the year among various nations, see Alexander ab Alexandro, *Genial Days* III, chapter 24, and Gyraldus, *On Days, Years, and Months*. ISAEUS.—And Fabricius’ *Menologium*, quarto edition, Hamburg, 1712. [Col. 0325D]

The moon, which traverses that circle of the zodiac in the space of thirty days. Thus all the manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470. I restored *lustrat*, “traverses,” in place of *illustrat*, “illuminates,” which appears in the printed editions. Ambrosius Calepinus also cites this passage under *Lustro*. The word is used in the same sense by Cicero [Col. 0326B] and by Virgil:

> The sun traversed the lands with his lamp.

They relate. Philo, *On the Giants*; Josephus, *Antiquities* I, chapter 5.

Fourteen hundred months, etc. Thus nearly all manuscripts and printed editions. One recent Royal manuscript has “three hundred”; one ancient Bononian manuscript, “one thousand four hundred and forty months”; the edition of Spark omits “four hundred”; Walch.’s edition has, incorrectly, “one thousand and four hundred months.” [Col. 0326C]

One, which. Thus all the witnesses. Heumann says: “I am strongly inclined to rewrite it as ‘one, who.’” I think the neuter *quod* refers to “example.” Note examples in which this pronoun refers not to a preceding but to a following noun: for example, Lactantius II, chapter 11, “the living creature whom we call man”; VII, chapter 9, “fire, which is an element”; and II, chapter 9, “they use water, which is an earthly element.” Livy XXX, chapter 7: “The Suffetes—an office that was among them like consular authority—summoned the senate.” Cicero, *On Divination* I, chapter 23: “The Magi said—this class was regarded among the Persians as one of wise and learned men....” BUNEMANN.

He constructed an ark. The Septuagint calls κιβωτός a kind of vessel constructed and roofed over in the manner of a chest, without sails or oars; Josephus calls it λάρναξ, whence θήβατα in Clement, *Stromata* V. Vessels of this kind were made either of wood, as Noah’s ark was, or of papyrus, as was that rush-woven craft which carried the infant Moses. The Septuagint calls the latter θίβη, preserving a fairly clear trace of the Hebrew word. DRUSIUS. [Col. 0326D]

He fixed the limit at one hundred and twenty years. According to Brasichellus’ observation, St. Jerome in his *Hebrew Traditions* on Genesis 6, St. John Chrysostom in Homily 20 on Genesis, and nearly all the others disagree with this opinion of Lactantius, which was also Josephus’ opinion. See Sixtus, *Bibliotheca* V, Annotation 75, and the more recent interpreters of Genesis 6.

Yet we know that very many people exceeded one hundred and twenty years, not only from the sacred writings but also from secular authors. Consequently, according to Isaeus, what Lactantius here reports from Moses in Genesis 6 appears to refer not to the time allowed for living but to that allowed for repentance. It is as though God said: “I shall punish him here and overwhelm him with waters; indeed, before I punish him, I shall give him time for repentance, and his days for repentance shall be one hundred and twenty years.” The Lord’s words, therefore, express not severity but clemency and compassion. They are so interpreted by Chrysostom, Homily 22 [Col. 0327B] on Genesis; St. Jerome in his *Hebrew Questions*; St. Augustine, *City of God* XV, chapter 24; Hugh of St. Victor on Genesis; and others. From ISAEUS.—“At one hundred and twenty years he fixed the limit.” Our author repeated this from others. Hence in chapter 12 he says: “Trustworthy authorities relate that people are accustomed to reach one hundred and twenty years.” Thus Arnobius, book II, page 94: “They may have lived for twenty years and a hundred; for it is denied that human life can be prolonged beyond that.” Again, Lactantius, *Turin Epitome*, chapter 27: “Life … was reduced to one hundred and twenty years.” There is a remarkable passage in Trebellius Pollio, *The Deified Claudius*, chapter 2: “The most learned mathematicians judge that one hundred and twenty years have been allotted to man for living, and proclaim that no more has been granted to anyone. They add that Moses alone—the intimate of God, as the books of the Jews call him—lived for 127 years; and when he complained that he was dying young, they report that an unknown divine power answered him that no one would live longer.” BUNEMANN. [Col. 0327C]]

> Θεοῦ παλάμαις ἐνὶ αὐταῖς  
> Ὅν κε πλάνησεν ὄφις δολίως, ἐπὶ μοῖραν ἀνελθεῖν  
> Τοῦ θανάτου, γνῶσίν τε λαβεῖν ἀγαθοῦ τε κακοῦ τε.
>
> Man, fashioned by the very hands of God,  
> Whom the serpent deceitfully led astray, so that he came  
> To the allotted fate of death and received knowledge of good and evil.

Thus human life was made temporary, though nevertheless long, being extended toward a thousand years. This had been handed down in the divine writings and made common knowledge among all; and since Varro was not unaware of it, he endeavored to argue why the ancients were thought to have lived for a thousand years. He says that among the Egyptians months were counted as years, so that a year was constituted not by the sun’s circuit through the twelve signs, but by the moon, which traverses that circle of the zodiac in the space of thirty days. This argument is manifestly false. For no one then exceeded his thousandth year. But now those who reach their hundredth year—as very frequently happens—certainly live for twelve hundred months. And trustworthy authorities relate that people are accustomed to reach one hundred and twenty years. [Col. 0325B] But because Varro did not know why or when human life had been shortened, he himself shortened it, although he knew that a human being could live for fourteen hundred months.

[Col. 0326A]

## CHAPTER XIV. On Noah, the Inventor of Wine; on Those Who First Possessed Knowledge of the Stars; and on the Origin of False Religions

Afterward, when God saw that the world was filled with wickedness and crimes, he resolved to destroy the human race by a flood. Nevertheless, to restore the population he chose one man who, when all others had been corrupted, remained as the unique example of righteousness. When this man was six hundred years old, he constructed an ark as God had commanded him. In it he himself was saved, together with his wife, his three sons, and the same number of daughters-in-law, when the water had covered all the highest mountains. Then, when the world had dried, God, execrating the unrighteousness of the preceding age, gradually diminished the length of human life through each successive generation, lest longevity should once again become the cause of devising evils; and he fixed the limit at one hundred and twenty years, which it was not permitted to exceed. But when Noah [Col. 0327A] had gone out of the ark, [Col. 0327A]

[Note: [Col. 0327C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 327–328]

When he had gone out of the ark. Genesis 9. “In Armenia.” The place is called ἀποβατήριον, “the place of disembarkation.” Epiphanius locates these mountains midway between Armenia and the Cardyaeans. He calls the mountain itself upon which the ark came to rest Lubar. These details are derived from an ancient tradition which Josephus incorporated into his *Antiquities*. He says: “It is reported that a certain part of this vessel still survives in Armenia, near the mountain of the Gordyaeans, and that some people have carried away bitumen scraped from it.”

He planted a vineyard with his own hand. Thus nearly all manuscripts and printed editions. The Royal-Puteanus manuscript, Jun., Ultr., one Claromontane manuscript, and the Paris edition of 1525 read “his own vineyard”; the ancient Bononian manuscript and one Claromontane manuscript read “he planted a vineyard”; one recent Royal manuscript reads “he uprooted vineyards with his own hand.”

By many ages. That Liber who is under discussion here was the son of Jupiter and Semele; but Jupiter, who was worshiped in Greece, lived in the nineteenth century before the common era, whereas Noah died more than twenty—or even twenty-six—centuries before our era. Hence Tertullian says that Liber did not so much invent wine as make it known. [Col. 0327D]

He disowned and expelled his son. There is nothing about this in Genesis, but it appears clearly in Berossus, book III; the works that survive today, however, are not Berossus’. The term “disowning” is one used by the jurists, signifying a disgraceful emancipation. On these matters see Valla V, chapter 102. BETULEIUS.

From his name. Thus, together with Cellarius’ edition, all the manuscripts except one recent Royal manuscript, in which, as in the common editions, the reading is “from his own name.” It was named not from the name of Ham, but from that of his youngest son, who was called Canaan. After Canaan’s descendants had been driven out, the people of Israel received that land upon its surrender. Hence Judaea also retained the name Canaan, as Josephus attests, book I, chapters 12 and 15. BETULEIUS.—But Ham also penetrated into Egypt, which according to Plutarch was formerly called Chemia, and which is called “the land of Ham” in the Prophets; hence also Jupiter Ammon among the Egyptians.

[Col. 0328B]

The first nation. One ancient Bononian manuscript alone reads “the first progeny.”

Cursed by him. This word must be understood as a prophetic declaration of divine judgment against the impiety of Ham, which the Holy Spirit placed in the mouth of Noah, so that, as God’s minister, he might pronounce sentence against the descendants of the profane man. Since this sentence was ratified before God, it had its effect in part at the very time when it was pronounced; yet its greater part, by divine dispensation, was deferred until that time when the descendants of Canaan had either to be utterly destroyed or, in their surviving remnant, reduced to servitude. The holy man, therefore, must not be accused as though he had uttered these words in the heat of vengeance [Col. 0328C] or through impatience at the injury he had received. Rather, one must recognize in him a zeal for justice and an extraordinary impulse of the Holy Spirit. Otherwise it could scarcely have happened that a man so kindly and not devoid of natural affection (*στοργή*) would have thundered such harsh words against his grandson, unless, moved by the will of God and assuming the character of a judge, he had for a time put off the character of a father and grandfather. RIVETUS.

Hebrews. There are some who think that the Hebrews were so called from the particle *eber*, “across” or “beyond,” Greek πέρα, as though they were περώται, “those from beyond,” because their patriarch Abraham came from beyond the Euphrates. Among the ancients, Africanus, Origen, Diodorus of Tarsus, Chrysostom, and Theodoret held this view; among more recent scholars, Scaliger and others did so. But then the name “Hebrew” would have been peculiar to Abraham, not shared with his descendants, since he alone came from beyond the Euphrates. Moreover, the Hebrew nation is also called Eber in Numbers 24:24, and “the sons of Eber” in Genesis 10:21; from this you may know that the name of the Hebrews is derived from Eber just as surely as that of the Jews is derived from Judah. [Col. 0328D] Theodoret objects in vain that in Scripture only the Jews are called Hebrews, not all the sons of Eber—namely, the Joktanites, Ishmaelites, Idumaeans, Amalekites, Moabites, Ammonites, Midianites, and so forth—who are nowhere called Hebrews although they acknowledge Eber as their father. The reason is readily apparent: they are not called Hebrews because, having neglected the Hebrew language, they adopted the speech of the peoples among whom they lived. Thus Laban in Mesopotamia became accustomed to the Syrian language, and the Ishmaelites in Arabia to Arabic. BOCHART.

Nor in that region is the sky overlaid with any clouds. Four Vatican manuscripts and eleven printed editions read: “for it is not overlaid with any clouds,” etc. But the particle “for” is absent from the other manuscripts and from the two old Roman editions and the editions of Betuleius and Cellarius; I have therefore deleted it as superfluous. Thomas says that there is no rain in those regions because God provided for them through the inundation of the Nile. In place of “is overlaid,” one Leipzig manuscript has “is withdrawn”; some others have “is covered.” See Tibullus I, Elegy 7, and Lucan VIII, verse 846. Moreover, Mela, book I, also testifies that in that region the sky [Col. 0329B] is not covered by clouds: “Egypt,” he says, “is without rain, yet wonderfully fertile,” etc. Pliny, book II, chapter 1, writes that clouds do form there, although they are rare and thin. Democritus, as reported by Plutarch, *Opinions* IV, chapter 1, maintained that the Nile’s rise occurs because snow situated in the northern regions melts and disperses around the summer solstice; clouds are then condensed from the vapors, driven southward and toward Egypt by the Etesian winds, and dissolved into great and violent rainstorms, by which both the marshes and the Nile are filled. Diodorus also, book I, chapter 2, testifies that rain does occur there, though rarely. But we can reconcile these writers from Philo, who writes in book I of his *Life of Moses* that slight and infrequent rains occur there in the coastal regions, but above Memphis there is none at all. There he also explains admirably why winter is superfluous to Egypt. ISAEUS.—“The sky is overlaid with clouds.” Thus the witnesses read, not “is covered.” The ancient poets use the same expression. Lucretius V, verse 467:

> With a compact body the clouds overlay the sky.

And Virgil, *Aeneid* III, verse 582:

> …to overlay the sky with smoke.

]

—as the sacred writings teach, he diligently cultivated the earth and planted a vineyard with his own hand. This refutes those who suppose Liber to have been the inventor of wine. For Noah preceded not only Liber but also Saturn and Uranus by many ages. When he had taken the first fruit from this vineyard, he became joyful and drank to the point of intoxication, and lay naked. When one of his sons, whose name was Ham, saw this, he did not cover his father’s nakedness but went outside and told his brothers as well. They, however, took a cloak, entered with their faces turned away, and covered their father. When the father learned what had happened, he disowned and expelled his son. The latter, now an exile, settled in that part of the earth which is now called Arabia; and that land was named Canaan from his name, and his descendants were called Canaanites. [Col. 0327B] This was the first nation that did not know God, because its chief and founder, having been cursed by his father, [Col. 0328A] did not receive from him the worship of God. He therefore left ignorance of the divine nature to his descendants.

From this nation all the neighboring peoples successively arose as the population increased. The descendants of the father himself, however, were called Hebrews, and among them the religion of God remained. But afterward, when their number had multiplied immeasurably and the narrow limits of their territories could no longer contain them, young men—either sent away by their parents or voluntarily becoming exiles when scarcity compelled them—were dispersed here and there in search of new homes for themselves. They filled all the islands and the whole world; and, torn away from the stock of the holy root, they established new customs and institutions for themselves according to their own judgment. But the first of all were those who occupied Egypt: they began to gaze up at and worship the heavenly bodies. Because they were neither sheltered by houses [Col. 0328B] on account of the quality of the climate, nor was the sky in that region overlaid with any clouds, they observed the courses and [Col. 0329A] eclipses [Col. 0329A]

[Note: [Col. 0329C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 329–330]

Eclipses. Six recent manuscripts read “effects.”

Worshiping them. Betuleius’ edition reads “tracking them,” and Joannes Caucchius likewise thinks that this is how the passage should be read. The conjecture does not seem inappropriate, for everyone knows that “to track” can mean “to investigate with the greatest diligence.” If this reading were retained, that would be the meaning of the word in this passage. The Bononian manuscript reads: “While frequently worshiping them, observing them with greater curiosity and freedom.” GALLAEUS.

Portent-producing. This is a very rare word, also found in *Divine Institutes* IV, chapter 15, and one which perhaps you will find nowhere else except in Ovid. [Col. 0329D]

In the course of time. On the expression, see book III, chapter 6; *On the Anger of God*, chapter 13. Arnobius II, page 55: “Arts gradually formed by practice in the course of time.” BUN.

When, therefore, the number of human beings began to increase, etc. This chapter 15 must be read circumspectly, for Lactantius introduces several errors. The first is that God granted the devil power over the earth from the beginning. The second is that the angels were not sent to protect human beings until after the human race had begun to increase. The third is that God commanded the good angels not to be stained by contact with the earth, lest they lose the dignity of their heavenly substance. The fourth is that the devil gradually enticed the good angels into vices and defiled them through intercourse with women. The fifth is that this was the sin on account of which the angels fell from heaven. The sixth is that from that intercourse of angels with women there was born a third kind of beings, who were neither heavenly angels, nor human beings, nor infernal demons, but a certain race [Col. 0330B] of earthly demons who are the tempters and deceivers of human beings and the authors of magical arts, human calamities, and evils. All these teachings are absurd, erroneous, and wholly alien to the sound doctrine of theologians. Consult Sixtus, *Bibliotheca* V, Annotation 77, and other interpreters of Genesis 6. BRASICHELLUS.—Lactantius is mistaken in saying that angels were not assigned as guardians until the number of human beings began to increase; for from the first parents onward, every soul, from the beginning of its creation, has had an angel appointed to guard it. Neither those first parents nor any human beings whatever have lacked one. Origen on the book of Numbers; Jerome [Col. 0330C] on Matthew 18, “Of their angels,” etc.; St. Bernard, *Sermon on the Angels*, and on Psalm 8, “What is man, that thou art mindful of him?” etc.; the Master and all the theologians on the Second Book, distinction 11; St. Thomas, part I, question 113, article 4. ISAEUS.

The devil. The Bononian manuscript has *Zabulus*, as in *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 16: “You defeated Zabulus”; and below, “Zabulus was defeated.” BUN.

Destroy. I thus emend from the old Royal manuscripts, two Bononian manuscripts, Cauc., five Vatican, six Colbertine, and fifteen others, as well as the Roman edition of 1470 and the editions of Betuleius, Isaeus, Spark, and Cellarius. Here we follow the Rohan manuscript. One recent Royal manuscript, two Vatican manuscripts, Jun., and ten editions have “scatter.”

Which. Restored from ten Royal manuscripts, two Bononian, five Vatican, six Colbertine, and ten others, and from the Roman editions of 1468 and 1470 and the edition of Isaeus. Two Vatican manuscripts, Cauc., Jun., and eleven printed editions read “whom.”

In the beginning. Two Bononian manuscripts, five Vatican, Tax., Pen., one Claromontane, and five recent printed editions add “of things”; these words are absent from thirty other manuscripts and ten older printed editions.

The cultivation of the human race. That is, the nurture or care of the human race.—“For the protection and cultivation.” Lactantius himself explains this in the *Epitome*, chapter 27: “He sent angels to cultivate the life of human beings and protect them from every evil.” BUN. [Col. 0330D]

Because free choice had been given to them. These words are absent from ten Royal manuscripts, six Colbertine, Cauc., Tornes., Lips., Goth., Jun., Ultr., Em., Cant., one Sorbonne, Nav., Vict., Gat., Marm., one Claromontane, two Brun., and Rohan, and from the two old Roman editions and the editions of Aldus, Paris 1525, Graph., Crat., and Betuleius. Are they a gloss? They appear in some other witnesses and must at least be understood. For Lactantius wrote similarly in book II, chapter 8, concerning the creation of the angel: “By his own choice, which had been given to him freely by God, he assumed a name contrary to himself.”

He enticed them into vices and defiled them through intercourse with women. Genesis 6:11, misunderstood by Lactantius, Sulpicius Severus in *Sacred History* I, and certain others, gave occasion to the fables that follow, in which angels are said to have coupled with women. Several of the ancients followed this error. Nothing else appears to be meant here than that the progeny of Seth, like that of Cain, degenerated into the utmost impiety, or at least that they mingled with Cain’s descendants in foul intercourse. For, as Aben Ezra reports, some understand the “sons of God” to mean the sons of Seth, and the “sons of men” to mean the descendants of Cain. SPARK.—This certainly appears to be the genuine interpretation. See Augustine, *City of God* XV, chapter 23, and Estius on Book II of the *Sentences*, distinction 6, §12.—“Through intercourse with women.” Tertullian likewise teaches this in *On Idolatry*, chapter 9; *On the Dress of Women* I, chapter 2; *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 7; Cyprian, *On the Dress of Virgins*, folio m. 109; Commodian, *Instructions*, page 4; and several others. See Kortholt on Justin Martyr, folio 19, and Suicer, *Thesaurus Ecclesiasticus*, vol. I, fols. 37–40. BUN. [Col. 0331C]]

—of the stars, while frequently worshiping them and observing them with greater curiosity and freedom. Later they devised portent-producing animal forms for themselves to worship, having been prompted by certain prodigies; we shall shortly disclose the originators of these forms. The others, however, who had been dispersed throughout the earth, admired the elements of the world—the sky, the sun, and the earth—and wrongly worshiped them without any images or temples, celebrating sacrifices to them in the open air.
