In the course of time, however, they made temples and images for their most powerful kings and established the practice of worshiping them with sacrificial victims and incense. Thus, by straying from the knowledge of God, they began to be Gentiles. Those therefore err who contend that the worship of the gods existed from the beginning of things and that paganism is earlier than the religion of God, which they suppose to have been invented later because they are ignorant of the source and origin [Col. 0329B] of truth. Let us now return to the beginning of the world.

[Col. 0330A]

## CHAPTER XV. On the Defilement of the Angels and the Two Kinds of Demons

When, therefore, the number of human beings began to increase, God, foreseeing that the devil—to whom he had granted power over the earth from the beginning—might either corrupt human beings by his deceits or destroy them, as he had done in the beginning, sent angels for the protection and cultivation of the human race. Because free choice had been given to them, he commanded them above all not to lose the dignity of their heavenly substance by being stained through contact with the earth. Plainly, he forbade them to do what he knew they were going to do, so that they could have no hope of pardon. Accordingly, while they were dwelling among human beings, that most deceitful ruler of the earth gradually enticed them into vices through their very association [Col. 0330B] and defiled them through intercourse with women. Then, not being received back into heaven because of the sins in which [Col. 0331A] they had immersed themselves, they fell to the earth. Thus the devil made them, from angels of God, into his own attendants and ministers. Those who were procreated from them, because they were neither angels nor human beings, [Col. 0331A]

[Note: [Col. 0331C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 331–332]

They were neither angels nor human beings. In several printed editions the first two words were missing; I restored them from all the manuscripts and twelve old printed editions. The following words also require them: “possessing a certain intermediate nature,” namely, between angels and human beings.

Thus there are two kinds of demons, etc. These are fables arising from the passage that we explained above, which was misunderstood.

The grammarians, however, call them demons, etc. Plato approves this etymology in the *Cratylus*, following Hesiod’s opinion. He also says that good men, after being honored with great honors, become *daimones* after death, the term being derived from prudence and wisdom. He readily assents to the view that every excellent person, whether alive or dead, is rightly called a *daimōn*. Posidonius, according to Macrobius, *Saturnalia* II, derived the word from ἀπὸ τοῦ δαίειν, that is, “from burning,” because they consist of an ethereal substance. Eusebius rejects both etymologies and holds that they are named ἀπὸ τοῦ δειμαίνω, “from terrifying” or “causing fear,” as demons are accustomed to do.

[Col. 0331D]

“All” is the reading of the manuscripts; the printed editions have “these.”

It is not permitted to know. I restored this from all the manuscripts and from the Roman edition of 1470 and the edition of Gymnicus.

Responses in ambiguous terms. On these, read Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* V, chapter 10.

Οἱ μὲν δαίμονες…. In Latin:

> These, then, are, by the will of great Zeus, good terrestrial  
> Demons, guardians of mortal human beings.

Hesiod, *Works and Days*, where he discusses the Golden Age. On this passage see Plato, *Republic* V and the *Cratylus*; and Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* V, chapter 4.

And that God may not be worshiped. These words are absent from one ancient Bononian manuscript, Tax., and Lips. They appear in the other manuscripts and in the common editions.

They discuss these beings. Thus read six Royal manuscripts, including the two oldest, one Colbertine, two Claromontane, two Brun., and the editions of Gymnicus and Spark. The others read “they spoke.” Either reading is sound.

[Col. 0332B]

And that Socrates had a demon constantly attending him, etc. This demon of Socrates is frequently mentioned by Plato, as in the *Euthyphro*, *Apology*, *Theaetetus*, *Phaedrus*, *Theages*, and *Euthydemus*; by Xenophon in *Memorabilia of Socrates*; by Cicero in *On the Nature of the Gods* I; by Maximus of Tyre; and by Plutarch in the *Table Talk* IX, in almost the final chapter. Apuleius likewise wrote a short work on this subject, *On the God of Socrates*, in which he explains the kind of divinity Socrates had attached to himself and bound to him in friendship. Socrates is said to have been accustomed to receive warnings from it to refrain [Col. 0332C] from acting whenever what he wished to do would not turn out successfully. See also St. Augustine, *City of God* VIII, chapter 14, and Diogenes Laertius. Some have said that this genius of Socrates was a sneeze, whether his own or another person’s. If Socrates was beginning to do something and heard someone sneeze on his right, he allegedly regarded it as a sign that he should proceed with the action; but if the sneeze came from his left, he should abandon his purpose entirely. Plutarch testifies to this in his book *On the Genius of Socrates*, though he subsequently refutes it himself. Sneezing was formerly regarded as an omen. Aristotle, *Problems*, section 33, §11, teaches that a morning sneeze was unlucky but a midday sneeze auspicious, especially if it occurred on the right, according to Plutarch in his *Themistocles*. Hence people offered good wishes to those who sneezed. Apuleius, book IX: “She caused him to sneeze repeatedly; and because he thought that the sneeze had come from her, he had wished her health in the customary phrase.” This custom also existed among the Hebrews. The rabbis maintain that many people died while sneezing and that from this arose the custom of bidding a sneezer to preserve his life. For the rest, I consider this Socratic demon entirely fabulous—either invented by Socrates himself or falsely publicized by his friends for the purpose of gaining authority for him among the ignorant common people. GALLAEUS. [Col. 0332D]

As a boy. Bunemann reads “from boyhood” and supplies the following note.—“With him from boyhood.” I have printed the reading found in Betuleius, on the recommendation of the *Epitome*, chapter 28: “From earliest boyhood.” Lactantius appears to have followed Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapter 1: “They say that a *daemonion* had attached itself to Socrates from boyhood.” BUNEMANN.]

The magi’s . . . through their breathings. See Tertullian, *Apology*, chapters 22 and 23, and especially Minucius, chapter 26: “Whatever wonders the magi perform, they perform through demons; when these breathe upon them and inspire them, they produce illusions, making things that do not exist appear, or things that do exist disappear.” BUNEMANN.

**Suppose.** The preceding words support this correction, which is found in almost all the manuscripts and editions. Three recent manuscripts and the same number of editions read *they suppose*.

**For they attach themselves to individual human beings, etc.** Empedocles expressed the same opinion in Plutarch, *On Tranquillity* (*περὶ εὐθυμίας*). So too Menander, whose verses survive in Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* V; Stobaeus, *Physical Extracts*, book I, chapter 9; the scholiast on Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXI; and Theocritus, *Idyll* 1. On this subject see Acts 12:15; Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapter 37, and Pamelius there, chapter 39; Justin Martyr, *Responses to the Orthodox* (*Ἀπόκρισις πρὸς ὀρθοδόξους*), question 30; Origen, *Homilies on Numbers* 20, and *On First Principles* (*περὶ Ἀρχῶν*) III.2; Jerome, on Matthew 18 and Isaiah 66; Augustine, *Soliloquies*, chapter 27; John Cassian, *Conferences* XIII.12; Burchard, bishop of Worms, *Decrees* XX.46–47; and Servius on Virgil’s words, “Each of us suffers his own spirits of the dead.” The being whom Menander calls a *mystagogue* (*μυσταγωγός*), Plato—according to Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* V—calls a *guardian* (*φύλαξ*), as do Hesiod in *Works and Days* and Apuleius in *On the God of Socrates*; Arrian, *Discourses* I.25, calls him a *trustee* (*ἐπίτροπος*); Seneca, Epistle 110, a tutor; Censorinus, a constant observer; and Martianus Capella, *Philology* II, a protector, guardian, and most faithful brother. LINDENBROGIUS.—Symmachus says that, just as souls are assigned by fate to those who are born, so fateful guardian spirits are allotted to peoples. Prudentius recounts his opinion in these verses:

[Col. 0333C] “Just as,” he says, “different souls fall by lot  
To children at their birth, so too the hour and day  
Bestow upon cities, when their walls first rise,  
Either a fate or a guardian spirit, under whose governance they are to rule.”

Claudian also spoke of the guardian spirit of a kingdom:

“What could accomplish our purpose through the voice of the serene writer:  
The kingdom’s guardian spirit, or the love of dutiful affection?”

Dio, *History* L, where he speaks of the monkey, teaches that at Rome a particular temple had been dedicated to the guardian spirit of the people. From Ammianus Marcellinus, *History* XXII, we also gather that Alexandria had a temple of the guardian spirit; in books XX and XXV he likewise mentions the public guardian spirit. PETRUS FABER.]

But because they possess a certain intermediate nature (see St. Augustine, *City of God* VIII.14), they were not received into the lower regions, as their parents were into heaven. Thus two classes of demons arose, one heavenly and the other earthly. These are the unclean spirits, the authors of the evils that are committed, and the same devil is their prince. Hence Trismegistus calls him the *ruler of demons* (*δαιμονιάρχης*). Grammarians say that demons (*δαίμονες*) are so called as though they were *δαήμονες*, that is, expert and knowledgeable about affairs; for people suppose these beings to be gods. They do indeed know many future events (see St. Augustine, *City of God* IX.20), but not all, since they are by no means permitted to know God’s counsel fully. Therefore [Col. 0331B] they are accustomed to frame their answers so that they admit of ambiguous outcomes. The poets both know that these beings are demons and speak of them as such. Hesiod relates:

[Col. 0332A] “Through the counsels of great Zeus, they are spirits divine,  
Noble, dwelling upon the earth, guardians of mortal human beings.”

This was said because God had sent them as guardians of the human race; but although they are themselves destroyers of human beings, they nevertheless wish to appear to be their guardians, so that they themselves may be worshipped and God may not be worshipped. Philosophers also discuss them. Plato even attempted to describe their natures in the *Symposium*. Socrates, too, used to say that a demon was constantly about him, which had attached itself to him from boyhood and by whose judgment and nod his life was directed. The entire art and power of the magi likewise depends upon the breathings of these beings. When invoked, they deceive human sight by blinding it with illusions, so that people do not see what exists and suppose themselves to see what does not exist. These contaminated [Col. 0332B] and ruined spirits, as I say, wander throughout the whole earth and seek consolation for their own ruin by ruining human beings. Accordingly, they fill everything with snares, frauds, tricks, and errors. For they attach themselves to individual human beings and occupy every house from door to door, so as to assume for themselves the name of guardian spirits [Col. 0333A]; [Col. 0333A]

[Note: [Col. 0333C] [Notes of Various Commentators on columns 333–334]

**The name of guardian spirits.** See Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, chapter 2: “The guardian spirit,” he says, “is the god under whose protection each person, from the moment he is born, lives. . . . It is certainly called *genius* from *gignere*, ‘to beget.’”

[Col. 0333D]

**They pour out undiluted wine to them every day.** So almost all the early editions. This reading has support from Pliny XIV.19, where he says that the ancients were accustomed to pour out undiluted wine to the guardian spirits and household gods. Almost all the manuscripts, however, omit the word *wine*. But this sentence—as anyone can see—must be completed by some word. Thus whether one reads with Betuleius, “they pour out blood,” or with many editions, “they pour out undiluted wine,” the sense is the same; for it is well established that the pagans poured out blood as well as wine to their idols. As to blood, our author testifies to this above, book I, chapter 21, where the notes should be consulted. But if conjecture has any place, I would venture to affirm that the reading should be “they pour out undiluted wine,” as I have just shown. My reason is that Lactantius is expressly speaking about guardian spirits, and it is known from Horace, *Odes* III.17, that undiluted wine was customarily poured out to them:

[Col. 0334A] “Tomorrow you will appease your Guardian Spirit  
With undiluted wine and a two-month-old pig.”

[Col. 0334B]

Persius, *Satires* 6:

“Pour out undiluted wine to your Guardian Spirit.” GALLAEUS.

Furthermore, *profundere* means to exhibit lavish and excessive generosity, as in Terence, *The Brothers*, act I, scene 2, verse 54:

“Let him squander it, ruin himself, and waste it.”

**As though they were warders-off of the evils . . . they themselves cause.** Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 22: “First they inflict harm; next they prescribe remedies, marvellously novel or contrary. After that they cease to harm, and are believed to have effected a cure.” Minucius, chapter 27; Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, chapter 4. Shortly afterward, all correctly read *they inflict* (*irrogant*). Venice 1471 wrongly reads *they irrigate* (*irrigant*). BUNEMANN.

**Because they are subtle spirits.** The ancients tended toward calling God alone *incorporeal* (*ἀσώματος*), while holding that angels possess some kind of body—not one like human bodies, but something fine and subtle. Hence Lactantius calls them “subtle spirits.” Tertullian, *On the Flesh of Christ*, chapter 6: “It is agreed that angels did not bear flesh of their own, inasmuch as they possess a spiritual nature and, if they have any body, one of their own kind; yet they can be transformed temporarily into human flesh, so that they may be seen and associate with human beings.” Cassian, *Conferences* VII.13, says that angels have a body, though a subtler one than ours; so too Macarius, *Homily* 4. VOSSIUS.—But anyone who reads Holy Scripture can see that this opinion is erroneous.

**Working.** Almost all the manuscripts and some editions prefer this reading. One early Bologna manuscript reads *they work*; two recent Royal manuscripts and several printed editions wrongly read *covered*, for the word *secretly* would then be superfluous.

**They stir up diseases.** That is, they arouse or excite them: the simple verb is used for the compound, as *breathed* for *inspired* in *Divine Institutes* II.12, and *lay blows* for *direct blows* in the same book, II.17, and so forth.

**Deceptions.** On these deceptions of the demons, see St. Augustine, *City of God* IX.18.

**When they cease to harm.** Hence the ancient Romans worshipped Fever, Dread, and Pallor, and the Babylonians worshipped the dragon, so that they would not harm them.

**They fear the righteous.** See Acts 16 and 19, and the well-known passage of the Gospel where the demons say to Christ Jesus: “Why have you come to torment us before the appointed time?”

**When adjured in his name, they depart from bodies.** Observe the extremely ancient use of exorcisms in the Church and the believers’ power over demons. So too book IV, chapter 27. Add Justin, *Dialogue with Trypho*, on the truth of the Christian religion, and his *Address to the Greeks*; Tertullian, *The Soldier’s Crown*, chapter 11; *On Idolatry*, chapter 11, at the end; *To Scapula*, chapter 2; and *Apology*, chapter 23; Cyprian, *To Demetrianus* and *To Donatus*, Epistle II, and *On the Vanity of Idols*; Minucius, *Octavius*; Epiphanius, *Heresies* 30; and Prudentius, *Apotheosis against the Jews*. That there were also exorcists in the synagogue may be gathered from Acts 19; Josephus likewise testifies to it, relating certain remarkable things in *Jewish Antiquities* VIII.2, as does Epiphanius, *Heresies* 30. ISAEUS.—Justin, *Dialogue with Trypho*: “The demons tremble at and dread the power of Christ’s name, and even today, when adjured by the name of Jesus Christ who was crucified, they submit.” (*Τὴν τοῦ ὀνόματος Χριστοῦ ἰσχὺν καὶ τὰ δαιμόνια τρέμει, καὶ σήμερον ἐξορκιζόμενα κατὰ τὸ ὄνομα Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τοῦ σταυρωθέντος ὑποτάσσεται.*) Likewise: “We who believe in Jesus our crucified Lord expel all demons and evil spirits by adjuring them.” (*Ἡμεῖς οἱ πιστεύοντες ἐπὶ τὸν σταυρωθέντα Ἰησοῦν Κύριον ἡμῶν, τὰ δαιμόνια πάντα καὶ πνεύματα πονηρὰ ἐξορκίζοντες.*) God had granted apostolic men this gift of casting out demons and performing other miracles, so that they might confirm the truth of the Gospel all the more powerfully. Pagans and Jews also had their own exorcists. Justin, in the passage cited: “The Jewish exorcists, or your adjurers, employ in their adjurations a certain art like that of the Gentiles and make use of incense and binding spells.” (*Οἱ ἐκ Ἰουδαίων ἐξορκισταὶ τῇ τέχνῃ ἧπερ καὶ τὰ ἔθνη χρώμενοι ἐξορκίζουσι, καὶ θυμιάμασι, καὶ καταδεσμοῖς χρῶνται.*) That the pagans had their own exorcists is clear from Lucian’s *Lover of Lies*, which you should consult; you will find much there concerning this matter. Plutarch, *Table Talk* VII, question 5, testifies that those possessed by demons had to recite the Ephesian letters at the magi’s command.]

For this is how *demons* are translated into Latin. People consecrate these beings in their innermost chambers; they pour out undiluted wine to them every day; and although they know them to be demons, they venerate them as earthly gods and as though they warded off the evils that they themselves cause and inflict. Because these are subtle and imperceptible spirits, they insinuate themselves into human bodies; working secretly within the entrails, they impair health, stir up diseases, terrify minds with dreams, and buffet them with fits of madness, so that by these evils they may compel human beings to resort to their aid.

[Col. 0344A]

## CHAPTER XVI  
### Demons can do nothing against those who are firmly established in faith

The nature of all these deceptions is obscure to those who have no experience of the truth. For they suppose that the demons help them when they cease to do harm, although they can do nothing except harm. Someone might perhaps say: “Then they should be worshipped so that they do not harm us, since they have the power to harm.” They do indeed harm, but only those by whom they are feared, whom God’s mighty and exalted hand does not protect, and who are excluded from the mystery of truth. They fear the righteous, however—that is, the worshippers of God. When adjured in his name, they depart from bodies; scourged by their words as though by whips, they not only confess that they are demons but also disclose their names, namely, those worshipped in the temples, [Col. 0335A] and they very often do this in the presence of their own worshippers; [Col. 0335A]

[Note: [Col. 0335C] [Notes of Various Commentators on columns 335–336]

**They very often do this in the presence of their own worshippers.** I consider this passage, which seems to me very corrupt, should be restored as follows from Cyprian and Minucius, from whom Firmianus derived nearly all this material: “And they very often do this in the presence of their own worshippers; certainly not to bring reproach upon their religion and honor, because they can lie neither to God, by whom they are adjured, nor to the righteous, by whose voice they are tormented.” Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*: “They confess where they come from and when they depart, even while those who worship them are listening.” Minucius: “They declare what they are, and certainly do not lie to their own shame, especially when some of your own people are present.” ISAEUS.—**Very often.** Recent editors had printed *and very often*. [Col. 0335D] I removed the conjunction on the authority of the third Leipzig edition, Reimmann, Venice 1471 and 1472, both editions of 1478, and those of 1493 and 1497, as well as Rostock, Paris, Tornes, so that the discourse might flow better. Heumann agrees. BUNEMANN.

**Certainly not to bring reproach upon their religion and honor, because neither to God, etc.** This passage, which comes from Cyprian’s *On the Vanity of Idols*, should certainly be restored thus from the oldest manuscripts—one Bologna and two Royal—as well as two other Royal manuscripts of good quality and Isaeus: in these *but* is absent, as it is also in some printed editions. In many manuscripts and editions, however, the text reads: “Certainly not to bring reproach upon their religion, but upon their honor, because neither to God”; wrongly. See below: “not because they desire any honor.” For what honor belongs to the ruined? Chapter 17, near the middle. In place of *because*, one early Bologna manuscript has *who*.—**Certainly not to bring reproach upon their religion, but upon their honor.** [Col. 0336B] All the books consistently and correctly read thus. Isaeus and Sparke are therefore wrong when, without manuscript support, they emend it in their notes to “Certainly not to bring reproach upon their religion and honor.” Lactantius therefore means that when the demons are adjured, they confess that they are demons, not gods, and disclose their names, not in reproach of the Christian religion, but in reproach of their own demonic honor—that is, to their own disgrace and shame. Heumann conjecturally reads: “Not reproach upon religion, but honor.” BUNEMANN.

**Attacks.** I restored this reading from the Roman edition of 1470, Cellarius, and all the manuscripts except one Colbert manuscript, which, like many common editions, reads *incursions*.

**Μία, etc.** In Latin: “There is one safeguard,” he says, “piety; for neither an evil demon nor fate has power over a pious person. For God rescues the pious person from every evil; for the one and only good among human beings is piety.”

**Εἱμαρμένη.** In the *Asclepius*, Hermes teaches that Fate (*εἱμαρμένη*), Necessity, and Order were made at God’s command, who governs the world by his law and divine reason. [Col. 0336C] Augustine uses the word *Fate* in different senses in various passages, sometimes even for the decree of the stars, which theologians wholly reject. In his third discourse *On Fate and Providence*, Chrysostom says that observing such decrees is as manifestly contrary to God’s law as neglect of the Sabbath, murder, or adultery. That faith—for I say that faith is true piety (*εὐσέβεια*)—breaks the laws of Fate is shown by Hezekiah’s example, whose span of life was extended by fifteen years; by Lazarus restored to life; and by many other cases enumerated by Paul in Hebrews 11. Epiphanius, where he discusses the errors of the Pharisees, abolishes fate by setting judgment in opposition to it, for he says that the two cannot coexist. BETULEIUS.

**Ἡ γὰρ εὐσέβεια.** In Latin: “For piety is knowledge of God”; so too Trismegistus in *Poimandres*, chapter 9. This agrees with what Christ said in John 17:3 and 3:15. Augustine teaches in the *Enchiridion* that wisdom and piety are the same.

[Col. 0336D]

**Explained.** Nine recent manuscripts read *expounded*, not inappropriately.

**Ἀγγέλους πονηρούς.** In Latin, “evil angels.” Demons are often so called in Holy Scripture: either “the devil’s angels,” as in Matthew 25, or “angels of Satan,” as in 2 Corinthians 12.

**Astrology.** Judicial astrology, namely, which claims to predict the future from the aspects of the stars. Tertullian treats it in *Apology*, chapter 35, and in *On Idolatry* condemns all the arts under discussion here. Cicero also discusses them in *On the Nature of the Gods* I, and Giovanni Francesco Pico demolishes them in an excellent volume entitled *On the Foreknowledge of Events*. ISAEUS.

**The magic art.** See St. Augustine, *City of God* VII, final chapter, where he testifies that these arts had been prohibited by nine laws of the Gentiles even before Christ’s birth. See also Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I.]

Certainly not to bring reproach upon their religion and honor, because they can lie neither to God, by whom they are adjured, nor to the righteous, by whose voice they are tormented. Accordingly, after often uttering the loudest howls, they cry out that they are being beaten and burned and are now, this very moment, about to depart. Such is the power possessed by the knowledge and righteousness of God! Whom, then, can they harm except those whom they hold in their power? Finally, Hermes affirms that those who have come to know God are not merely safe from the demons’ attacks, but are not even subject to fate:

“There is one safeguard,” he says, “piety; for neither an evil demon nor fate has power over a pious person. For God rescues the pious person from every evil; for the one and only good among human beings is piety.” (*Μία φυλακὴ εὐσέβεια· εὐσεβοῦς γὰρ ἀνθρώπου οὐ δαίμων κακός, οὔτε εἱμαρμένη κρατεῖ. Θεὸς γὰρ ῥύεται τὸν εὐσεβῆ ἐκ παντὸς κακοῦ· τὸ γὰρ ἓν καὶ μόνον ἐν ἀνθρώποις ἐστὶν ἀγαθὸν εὐσέβεια.*)

What *piety* (*εὐσέβεια*) is, he testifies elsewhere in these words: [Col. 0336A] “For piety is knowledge of God” (*ἡ γὰρ εὐσέβεια γνῶσίς ἐστι τοῦ Θεοῦ*). Asclepius, his pupil, also explained the same view at greater length in the *Perfect Discourse* that he wrote to the king. Both affirm that demons exist and are the enemies and tormentors of human beings. Trismegistus therefore calls them “evil angels” (*ἀγγέλους πονηρούς*): so far was he from being unaware that, having been corrupted from their heavenly state, they began to be earthly beings.

## CHAPTER XVII  
### Astrology, haruspicy, and similar arts are inventions of demons

Their inventions are astrology, haruspicy, augury, the things called oracles, necromancy, the magic art, and whatever other evils human beings practice, either openly or secretly. All these things [Col. 0337A] are false in themselves, as the Erythraean Sibyl testifies:

“. . . . . . Since all these things are delusions,  
Which foolish men investigate day after day.”

[Col. 0337A]

[Note: [Col. 0337C] [Notes of Various Commentators on columns 337–338]

**Ἐπεὶ πλάνα.** I restored this from the extremely ancient Royal manuscript, nine hundred years old; the oldest Royal-Puteanus and Cancellarius manuscripts do not differ greatly, reading *ἐπίπλανα*. The learned Francius likewise judged that *πλάνα* should be read. In many manuscripts the Greek is absent; four Royal manuscripts and the common editions read *πλαγή*. The Latin translation is:

“Since all these things are erroneous,  
Which foolish human beings investigate every day.”

These lines were taken from the *Sibylline Oracles*, discourse 3, verse 166.

**And fashioned.** Bunemann reads *fashioned*, and presents the following note on this passage.—**Fashioned likenesses of dead kings.** The Emman., Gotha, and Leipzig manuscripts read *fashioned*; the common reading *and fashioned* is wrong. CELLARIUS.

**They assumed certain characters.** The manuscripts agree with the editions except for one early Bologna manuscript and the Cotton manuscript, which read *they introduced*. The common reading nevertheless appears to deserve retention, since it is the usage of Cicero and Titus Livy. See Isaeus in the notes. Characters are properly said to be “assumed.”

**Whom . . . sorcerers, etc.** In the *Code*, book IX, title 18, there is a constitution of Caesar Constantine—or rather Constantius—issued in 357: “Let no one,” he says, “consult a haruspex or astrologer; let no one consult a soothsayer. Let the depraved avowal of augurs and seers fall silent. Let the Chaldaeans, magi, and all others whom the common people call sorcerers because of the magnitude of their crimes make no attempt in this direction. Let curiosity about divination be perpetually silent among all; for whoever refuses obedience to our commands will suffer capital punishment, struck down by the avenging sword.” BETULEIUS.

**They summon them by their true names.** At the beginning of book V, Arnobius relates how Numa was taught the method of drawing Jupiter forth. Livy, book I, treats the same Numa. The method of summoning the tutelary gods out of cities that the Romans were going to capture may be found in Macrobius, *Saturnalia* III.9.

**Impure.** Here these are evil spirits that incline human beings toward filth; thus Cicero speaks of an “impure mouth.”

**Wandering.** Because they inhabit the air, as St. Augustine says from Apuleius, and Apuleius from Plato.

[Col. 0338C]

**Pour errors upon human hearts.** I restore this from the oldest and best manuscripts—one Bologna, two Royal, and six others—as well as the Roman edition of 1470 and Betuleius. Lactantius similarly says below, “they pour darkness upon them,” and above in the same book, II.1, near the middle, “to pour darkness upon.” Two Royal manuscripts, one Leipzig manuscript, three Colbert manuscripts, and Cellarius’s edition read *pour upon hearts*; three other Royal, three Colbert, two Clermont manuscripts, and the Brunswick manuscript read *pour forth*; eleven common editions read *infuse*.

**Do nothing except at his command.** So most manuscripts—the Royal-Puteanus, twelve others, and six printed editions. One early Bologna manuscript, one Royal, two Colbert manuscripts, and Tornes read *command*; five other manuscripts read *commands*, for which one Royal manuscript and the Roman editions of 1468 and 1470 have *just things*; the Palatine has *commanded*; one Royal manuscript, the Marmoutier manuscript, and seven printed editions read *at his command*.

**The business is conducted.** Eight manuscripts and Cellarius’s edition read *the affairs are conducted*. The others agree with the text.

**With the Son.** So all the printed editions and thirty manuscripts, including the Royal-Puteanus. These two words are absent from thirteen manuscripts.

**Nor is there in the angels.** I restored *is* from the manuscripts and early editions; it was absent from several recent printed editions.

[Col. 0338D]

**Not because.** I restored this from all the manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1468. The other common editions read *because*. But *quo* in place of *quod* occurs in Cicero: “Not because you heard it from somewhere,” *Letters to Atticus* X.1, and elsewhere.

**Not because they desire any honor, etc.** St. Augustine holds a different view in *City of God* IX.20. “In the demons,” he says, “there is knowledge without love; and therefore they are so puffed up—that is, so proud—that they have contrived to have divine honors and the service of religion, which they know is owed to the true God, rendered to themselves, and still strive to achieve this as far as they can.” Moreover, St. Thomas asserts that evil spirits persist in the same sin by which they first sinned as regards their appetite, though not as regards their belief that they can attain their object. SPARKE. **To turn them away from the worship and knowledge of the true Majesty.** I restored this from eight Royal manuscripts, including the two oldest, six Colbert, two Oxford, and eight other manuscripts, as well as six common editions. Two recent Royal and three Oxford manuscripts, together with nine printed editions, read *from the cultivation*.]

Yet these same authors make these things appear true by their presence. Thus, by falsely assuming divinity, they mock human credulity, because it is not in their interest to disclose the truth to human beings. They are the beings who taught people to fashion images and statues. In order to turn human minds away from the worship of the true God, they caused fashioned likenesses of dead kings, adorned with exquisite beauty, to be erected and consecrated, and assumed their names as though they were certain characters. But the magi—and those whom the common people rightly call sorcerers—when practicing their accursed arts, summon these beings by their true names, those heavenly names that are read in Holy Scripture. Moreover, these impure [Col. 0337B] and wandering spirits, in order to throw everything into confusion and pour errors upon human hearts, sow and mingle falsehoods with truths. For they fabricated the claim that there are many heavenly gods and that Jupiter is the one king of them all, because there are many angelic spirits in heaven and one God, the Father and Lord of all. But by wrapping the truth in fictitious names, they removed it from sight.

For God, as I taught at the beginning (namely, book I, chapter 6), has no need of a name, since he is alone. Nor do the angels, since they are immortal, either permit or wish themselves to be called gods. Their one and only duty is to serve God’s commands and to do absolutely nothing except at his command. For we say that the world is governed by God in the same way that a province is governed by its governor. No one would call the governor’s attendants his partners in governing the province, although its business is conducted through their service. Yet they can do something beyond the governor’s commands because of his ignorance, which belongs to the human condition. But that ruler of the world and governor of the universe, who knows all things and from whose divine eyes nothing is hidden, alone possesses power over all things together with the Son; nor is there anything in the angels except the necessity of obedience. Accordingly, they wish no honor to be paid to themselves, since all their honor is in God. But those who have deserted God’s service, because they are enemies of truth and violators of their duty to God, strive to claim for themselves the name and worship of gods—not because they desire any [Col. 0338B] honor, for what honor belongs to the ruined? Nor because they wish to harm God, who cannot be harmed, but because they wish to harm human beings, whom they strive to turn away from the worship and knowledge of the true Majesty, so that they cannot attain the immortality that the demons themselves lost through their wickedness. They therefore pour darkness upon them and envelop the truth in gloom, so that they may know neither their Lord nor their Father. To entice them easily, they hide themselves in temples, are present at every sacrifice, and often produce wonders by which human beings, dumbfounded, place their trust in images as possessing divinity and [Col. 0339A] divine power. Hence it is that a stone was cut by an augur’s razor; [Col. 0339A]

[Note: [Col. 0339B] [Notes of Various Commentators on columns 339–340]

**An augur.** See above, chapter 8 of this book, shortly after the beginning.

**Juno of Veii.** He called her Moneta in chapter 8 of this book.

**Fortune.** See St. Augustine, *City of God* IV.19.

**Claudia.** See above, chapter 8.

**Juno despoiled, etc.** This is Juno Lacinia, whose temple the censor Fulvius stripped of its marble tiles; Proserpina of Locri, whom Pyrrhus despoiled; Ceres of Miletus, who punished Alexander’s sacrilegious soldiers with blindness; Hercules in the case of Appius, whom the god deprived of sight after he transferred Hercules’ rites to slaves; Jupiter in the case of Atinius, who had reported Jupiter’s commands to the senate; Minerva, whose form had appeared to Artorius, Augustus’s physician; and the serpent, Aesculapius. On these see above, chapter 8.

**Δαιμονιάρχης.** This word is absent from the two oldest Royal manuscripts.

**In his own form.** Namely, in the form of a serpent.

**Was conveyed.** I restored this from a great many of the earlier manuscripts. Three manuscripts and all printed editions read *was conducted*.

**They conveyed.** The Emman. and Gotha manuscripts elegantly read *they conveyed*. Torrenius correctly perceived, in Valerius Maximus I.8.2, that the text should be read as one expression, “caused himself to be conveyed to our city.” There this story is related more fully. BUNEMANN.

**Profane.** That is, strangers to the faith.

**Were.** Six recent manuscripts read *may have been*.

**God’s decree.** I emended this from the manuscripts and early printed editions. Two recent manuscripts and seven editions read *condition*.

**Because he had placed a handsome boy on Jupiter’s sacred carriage to hold the divine trappings.** The Subiaco edition has *in the temple* in place of *on the sacred carriage*. In all the printed editions and many manuscripts this passage is extremely corrupt. Some have “in Jupiter’s temple to keep watch”; others, “in Jupiter’s temple to hold the trappings.” So the Bologna, Junius, Taxius, Penius, three Royal, one Sorbonne, and twelve Vatican manuscripts, and the two Bologna, Venetian, Florentine, Junta, Gymnich, Cratander, Aldine, Grapheus, Tornes, and thirty-eight early editions, among others. Six recent manuscripts read *exceptional things*; six editions, *watches*. I emend the text in accordance with the better codices, reading *sacred carriage* for *temple*, and *trappings* for *watches*. So read the Palatine and five early Royal manuscripts. The Isaeus manuscript has *itemtesa*; the Caucian manuscript reads *in tentaesa*; and the Emman. manuscript *tentesea*. Joannes Caucus believes that the scribe wrote this incorrectly for *in tensa*, “on the sacred carriage,” and I subscribe to his conjecture. Two manuscripts and the Utrecht manuscript read *in centesa*, but this too is a corrupt form written through a copyist’s carelessness. [Col. 0340B] I believe the error entered the text in the following manner: scribes who did not know what *tensa* meant—for the word is obsolete—thought that *templo*, “in the temple,” should be read, especially since *Jupiter’s* immediately follows and the beginning of *tensa* is not very unlike *templo*. They consequently thought that Jupiter’s temple was being mentioned. I conjecture that *excubias*, “watches,” entered in place of *exuvias*, “trappings,” in the manner Isaeus suggests: old manuscripts had *exubias* or *exsubias* in place of *exuvias*. The ancients commonly wrote *b* for *v* and vice versa, as we showed in the notes on the *Epitome*; they also added *s* after *x*, as is clear in *exsequor*, *exsul*, and so forth. Consequently, in place of what we now call *exuvias*, they wrote *exsubias*. Scribes who did not understand the meaning of that word wrongly substituted *excubias*. What a *tensa* is, moreover, is known from Sisinnius Capito in Festus: namely, a vehicle on which the gods’ trappings were carried into the circus and to the sacred couch during the Circus games. This vehicle was drawn not by beasts of burden but by human beings. Hence Suetonius, *Augustus* 43: “During votive Circus games it happened that, when seized by illness, he led out the sacred carriages while reclining in a litter.” Those who led out the *tensae* were called *adtensatores*. They were generally pairs of men who undertook the burden of transporting them. From ISAEUS.—Tertullian, *On the Spectacles*, chapter 7, mentions chariots, sacred carriages, seats, crowns, and divine trappings in the Circus games. From this it is clear that the reading must be “on Jupiter’s sacred carriage to hold the divine trappings.” Gallaeus would prefer to read *renowned* for *handsome*. But the reading must be *handsome*, as is established both by all the manuscripts and editions of Lactantius and by Valerius Maximus, from whom Lactantius took these details, *History* I.2, where the text reads “a boy of exceptional beauty,” and so forth. Arnobius also relates these matters at the end of book IV.—**On Jupiter’s sacred carriage.** Tertullian, *On the Spectacles*, chapter 7, at the end: “If it carries even a single sacred carriage of Jupiter . . . it is a wagon.” Cuperus illustrates this passage of our Lactantius admirably in his quarto edition of *Harpocrates*, page 134 and following.—**On Jupiter’s sacred carriage to hold the divine trappings.** *Tensae*, or *thensae*, are vehicles of the gods in which their objects were led into the Circus. Suetonius, *Augustus* 43: “During votive Circus games it happened that, when seized by illness, he led out the sacred carriages while reclining in a litter.” BUNEMANN.

**Why did Varro?** The story is in Livy, book II of the Second Punic War. See Valerius Maximus, book I, chapter “On Neglected Religion.”—**Why did Varro alone escape?** The consul Terentius Varro escaped from the battle of Cannae. BUNEMANN.]

that Juno of Veii replied that she wished to migrate to Rome; that Fortuna Muliebris announced danger; that a ship followed Claudia’s hand; that Juno, when despoiled, took vengeance upon the sacrilegious, as did Proserpina of Locri and Ceres of Miletus; as did Hercules in the case of Appius, Jupiter in the case of Atinius, and Minerva in the case of Caesar. Hence also the story that a serpent, summoned from Epidaurus, freed the city of Rome from pestilence. For the ruler of demons (*δαιμονιάρχης*) himself was conveyed there in his own form, without any disguise, since the envoys sent for this purpose brought back with them a dragon of extraordinary size.

They deceive most of all through oracles, whose illusions those profane from the truth cannot understand. Therefore they suppose that empires, victories, wealth, and prosperous outcomes of affairs are bestowed by these beings, and finally that the republic has often been freed by their command from imminent dangers—dangers that they both announced in their responses and, after being appeased with sacrifices, averted. But all these things are deceptions. For since they foresee God’s dispositions, because they were once his ministers, they interpose themselves in such affairs so that whatever has been done or is being done by God may appear above all to be done, or to have been done, by them. Whenever some good is impending for a people or city in accordance with God’s decree, they promise through prodigies, dreams, or oracles that they will bring it about, provided that temples, honors, and sacrifices are granted to them. Once these have been given and the event that must occur has occurred, they procure the highest veneration for themselves. Hence temples are vowed, new images are consecrated, and herds of sacrificial victims are slaughtered. But even after these things have been done, the life and safety of those who performed them are nevertheless sacrificed as well.

Whenever dangers threaten, they declare themselves angry over some foolish and trivial cause—as Juno did with Varro because he had placed a handsome boy on Jupiter’s sacred carriage to hold the divine trappings; and for this reason the Roman name was almost annihilated at Cannae. But if Juno feared a second Ganymede, why did the youth of Rome pay the penalty? Or if the gods care only for commanders and neglect the rest of the multitude, why did Varro alone escape, although it was he who [Col. 0341A] did this, while Paulus, [Col. 0341A]

[Note: [Col. 0341C] [Notes of Various Commentators on columns 341–342]

**Paulus.** He had chickens that ate eagerly and nevertheless fell at Cannae, as Cyprian taunts him.

**Who had deserved nothing.** That is, who had done nothing worthy of punishment. Lactantius again, VII.10: “Good people are thought to deserve nothing like what they often suffer.” BUNEMANN.

**Hostile.** Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII.667. See Silius Italicus, book X.

**By cunning.** Lactantius, *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 2: “They protect themselves by cunning.”

**She could not dare.** Heumann correctly explains this as “she did not dare.” The expression is nevertheless unusual, although the ancients sometimes use *to dare* for *to be able*, and *to be able* for *to dare*. See Broukhusius on Propertius I.15.37, page 64 and following. BUNEMANN.

**The offspring.** Virgil, at the beginning of *Aeneid* I. See also Valerius at the passage cited.

[Col. 0341D]

**Hiding beneath the names of the dead.** He follows Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 21: “A contrary divinity, hiding beneath the names and images of the dead, establishes belief in its divinity by means of certain signs, miracles, and oracles.” See also *On the Spectacles*, chapter 10. BUNEMANN.

**For the living.** Four Colbert manuscripts, one Clermont manuscript, and the Brunswick manuscript add *human beings*. In the same passage Lactantius uses *lay blows* for *direct blows*, the simple verb for the compound, meaning, as it seems to me, “lay snares.”

**Among all nations.** The final word, *nations*, was added from all the manuscripts and editions except Thysius, Gallaeus, and Sparke.

**They have become deeply rooted.** Compare II.1, “through a deeply rooted persuasion,” and II.19, where he speaks of “deeply rooted errors.” BUNEMANN.

**God therefore postpones.** For no more grievous wrath of God and no greater punishment can threaten us than when God punishes sins with sins. God is indeed *long-suffering* (*μακρόθυμος*) and does not desire the sinner’s death, but that he should turn and live, Ezekiel 3. “It is great wrath on God’s part,” as Jerome writes to Castrutius on the authority of Ezekiel, “when he does not correct sins but punishes blindness with blindness. [Col. 0342C] For this very reason God sends the effective power of delusion, as Paul writes to the Thessalonians, so that they may believe a lie and all who have not believed the truth may be judged. Those, I say, who dig cisterns for themselves are unworthy of the living fountain.” Jerome 2. BETULEIUS.

**In power.** That is, *by means of power*. A Scriptural mode of expression.

**The predictions of pious seers.** I restored this from the two oldest Royal manuscripts, two other Royal manuscripts, the Caucian, four Colbert, and the Emman. manuscripts, and from manuscripts of Virgil. Six recent manuscripts and the common editions read *earlier seers*. Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.—**The predictions of pious seers.** I print this from the Caucian and Emman. manuscripts, which are in different hands. This is a received epithet. Thus Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.662: “And the pious seers”; Silius Italicus VI.288: [Col. 0342D] “Nor were the pious seers silent.” BUNEMANN.

**Some.** The Epicureans. See *On the Wrath of God*, chapter 4.

**That God is not even angry at all, because by passions, etc.** This, like the other passions, belongs to God not affectively but effectively, as the rule has it. That is, anger does not disturb or affect God with pain as it does human beings; rather, when God is said to be angry, he does what angry people customarily do—namely, punishes and afflicts. Thus anger in God is not a passion, but the will to punish. GALLAEUS.—See St. Thomas, part I, question 21, article 3.]

Why was one who had deserved nothing killed? Evidently nothing then befell the Romans

> . . . . . through the fates imposed by hostile Juno,

when Hannibal destroyed two armies of the Roman people by both cunning and valor. For Juno could not venture either to defend Carthage, where her arms and chariot were, or to harm the Romans, because

> . . . . . she had heard that a race descended from Trojan blood  
> Would one day overthrow the Tyrian citadels.

But these are the tricks of those who, hiding beneath the names of the dead, lay snares for the living. Accordingly, if an impending danger can be avoided, they wish it to appear that they, once appeased, averted it; but if it cannot, they contrive matters so that it may seem to have occurred because they were treated with contempt. Thus they engender authority and fear for themselves among people who [Col. 0341B] do not know them. By this cunning and these arts they have caused knowledge of the true and only God to grow obsolete among all nations. For, ruined by their own vices, they rage and ravage in order to destroy. Therefore these enemies of the human race themselves also devised human sacrifices, so that they might devour as many souls as possible.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On God’s patience and vengeance, the worship of demons, and false religions

Someone will say: Why, then, does God permit these things to happen, and why does he not bring aid amid such grievous errors? So that evils may contend with goods; so that vices may stand opposed to virtues; so that he may have some whom he punishes and others whom he honors. For he has appointed the final times for judging the living and the dead [Col. 0341C]; concerning that judgment there will be a discussion in my final book. [Col. 0342A] He therefore postpones it until the end of the ages comes, when he will pour out his wrath in heavenly power and might, just as

> . . . . . the predictions of pious prophets  
> Fill men with dread through their terrible warning.

For the present, however, he permits human beings to err and even to behave impiously toward himself, while he himself remains just, gentle, and patient. For it cannot be that one in whom virtue is perfect should not also possess perfect patience. Hence some suppose that God does not become angry at all, because he is not subject to passions, which are disturbances of the mind; for every creature that is affected and agitated is frail. This conviction utterly abolishes truth and religion. But let us set aside for the present this occasion for discussing the wrath of God, both because the subject is more extensive and because it must be treated at greater length in a work of its own (namely, the book *On the Wrath of God*). [Col. 0342B] Whoever, therefore, has worshiped and followed those most wicked spirits will obtain neither heaven nor light, which belong to God, but will fall into that which, in our discussion of the distribution of things, we showed to have been assigned to the principle of evil itself: namely, darkness, the underworld, and everlasting punishment.

I have demonstrated that the religions of the gods are vain in three ways. First, because those images that are worshiped are likenesses of dead human beings; but that it is perverse and incongruous for the image of a human being to be worshiped by the image of God—for the image of God then worships what is inferior and weaker; further, that it is an inexpiable crime to abandon the living God in order to serve the memorials of the dead, who can give neither life nor light to anyone, since they themselves lack them; and that [Col. 0342C] there is no other God whatsoever besides the one God, to whose judgment [Col. 0343A] and power every soul is subject. Secondly, [Col. 0343A]

because the sacred images themselves, which the most empty-headed people serve, are devoid of every sense, since they are earth. Who does not understand that it is sacrilege for an upright creature to bend down in order to worship the earth? The earth was placed beneath our feet for this very reason: that it should be trodden upon by us, not worshiped. For this reason we were raised from it and received an elevated posture beyond that of the other living creatures, so that we should not roll back downward or cast this heavenly countenance toward the earth, but should direct our eyes to the place to which the constitution of their nature has pointed them, and should adore nothing else, worship nothing else, except the unique divinity of our sole maker and father. He fashioned the human being upright for this reason: that we might know that we are summoned to the things above and in heaven. Thirdly, because the spirits who preside over those [Col. 0343B] religions, condemned and cast off by God, wallow over the earth. Not only are they unable to confer anything upon their worshipers, since power over all things resides with the one God, but they also destroy them through deadly enticements and errors, since this is their daily work: to draw darkness over human beings so that the true God may not be sought by them. They must not therefore be worshiped, because they are subject to God’s sentence. For it is the greatest sacrilege to bind oneself over to the power of beings over whom, if you follow righteousness, you could be more powerful, and whom you could drive out and put to flight by adjuration in the divine name. But if it is evident that these religions are vain in all the ways I have demonstrated, it is manifest [Col. 0344A] that those who either make supplication to the dead, venerate the earth, or make over their souls as property to unclean spirits do not retain the rational character of human beings; and that those who, rebelling against God, the father of the human race, have violated every sacred obligation by undertaking inexpiable rites will pay the penalties of their impiety and crime.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the worship of images and earthly things

Whoever, therefore, strives to preserve the mystery of humanity and to retain the rational character of his own nature should raise himself from the ground and, with his mind erect, stretch his eyes toward heaven. He should not seek God beneath his feet, nor dig out from under his footsteps something to worship, because whatever lies beneath a human being must necessarily be lower than a human being. [Col. 0344B] Rather, let him seek on high; let him seek at the summit, because nothing can be greater than a human being unless it is above a human being. But God is greater than a human being; therefore he is above, not below, nor should he be sought in the lowest region rather, but in the highest.

Consequently, there is no doubt that there is no religion wherever there is an image. For if religion derives from divine things, and there is nothing divine except among heavenly things, images therefore lack religion, because nothing heavenly can exist in something made from earth. This indeed can become apparent to a wise person from the name itself. For whatever is *simulatur* (“represented” or “imitated”) must necessarily be false; nor can that which counterfeits truth by embellishment and imitation ever receive the name of truth. [Col. 0345A] But if every imitation is not so much a serious reality as a kind of play and jest, [Col. 0345A]

then there is not religion in images, but a mime of religion. The true must therefore be preferred to all false things; earthly things must be trampled underfoot so that we may attain heavenly things. For the matter stands thus: whoever has prostrated his soul, whose origin is from heaven, toward the infernal and lowest things falls to the place to which he himself has cast it down. Therefore, mindful of his reason and his posture, he must always strive and reach only toward the things above. Whoever does this will be judged truly wise, truly righteous, truly human, and finally worthy of heaven, when his father recognizes him not as lowly and cast down toward the earth in the manner of quadrupeds, but rather as standing and upright, just as he made him.

## CHAPTER XX. [Col. 0345B] On the philosophers and on truth

A great and difficult portion of the work undertaken has therefore, unless I am mistaken, been completed; and with heavenly majesty supplying us with the ability to speak, [Col. 0346A] we have driven away errors grown inveterate. But now a greater and more difficult contest with the philosophers lies before us. Their supreme learning and eloquence are set against me like some massive obstacle. For just as there—that is, in the second book—we were oppressed by the multitude and nearly unanimous agreement of all nations, so here we are oppressed by the authority of men preeminent in every kind of distinction. Who does not know that greater weight resides in a smaller number of learned people than in a larger number of the uneducated?

Yet we must not despair that, with God and truth as our leaders, these men too can be dislodged from their position. Nor do I think they will be so obstinate as to deny that they see the brightest sun with sound and open eyes. Provided that what they themselves are accustomed to profess is true—that they are held by zeal for investigating truth—I shall certainly bring it about [Col. 0346B] that they believe the truth they had long sought has at last been found, and confess that it could not have been discovered by human intellects.

# [LACTANTIUS, BOOK THREE]

[Col. 0345]

# ANALYSIS OF LACTANTIUS’ THIRD BOOK: THE VANITY OF PHILOSOPHY AND OF THE PHILOSOPHERS

[Col. 0345C] There are three parts to this book. The first concerns philosophy; the second, the vanity of the philosophers; the third again demonstrates that philosophy is not wisdom.

In the opening he wishes for himself the eloquence of Tullius to demonstrate the vanity of philosophy; he shows by the following arguments that philosophy is empty and false.—I. Philosophy is the pursuit of wisdom; therefore it is not wisdom.—II. Wisdom is not reached through that pursuit; therefore philosophers are not even pursuers of wisdom (Chapter 2).—III. In philosophy there is neither knowledge nor opinion; therefore it is not wisdom: not knowledge, because Socrates and the Academics abolished it; not opinion, because Zeno and the Stoics rejected it (Chapter 4).—IV. Philosophy destroys itself. For each individual school is convicted of folly by the judgment of the many other schools; all of them, therefore, are vain and empty (Chapter 4).—V. Either there is knowledge of nature, or there is not, as Arcesilaus maintains. Not the former, because no inward and proper knowledge can exist in a human being, on account of the frailty of the human condition; not the latter, because there are many things that nature itself, frequent experience, and the necessities of life compel us to know. Both kinds of philosophy therefore collapse: the old, which claims knowledge for itself, and the new, which disposes of it (Chapter 5).—At this point he corrects the philosophers in matters of physics. “The Academics,” he says, “argued from a few obscure matters that there is no knowledge; the natural philosophers, from certain evident and clear matters, argued that everything can be known. Arcesilaus indeed rightly reproved the arrogance of the philosophers, but he should have added an exception and said that only the causes and rational principles of natural things cannot be known, because they are hidden and no one teaches them; nor ought they to be sought, because they cannot be found” (Chapter 6).—VI. In ethics the philosophers disagree concerning the highest good. Here he recounts the philosophers’ various opinions concerning the highest good (Chapter 7), which he refutes (Chapters 8 and 9). He himself locates the highest good solely in religion (Chapter 10), showing that the philosophers could have discovered the highest good by deduction: that it is not pleasure, riches, [Col. 0347B] kingship, or virtue, but immortality. From this he concludes that ethical philosophy is vain (Chapters 11 and 12).—VII. Logic and physics do not pertain to living rightly; therefore the whole of philosophy is thus empty. On this occasion he refutes Cicero’s commendation of philosophy (Chapters 13 and 14), and Seneca’s definition of philosophy, who said that philosophy is the rational method of living rightly (Chapter 15).—VIII. From philosophy one seeks not usefulness but amusement; therefore it must be rejected.—IX. The beginning and origin of philosophy are evident; therefore it is not wisdom (Chapter 16).

In the second part, he says that the philosophers themselves are occupied with great vanity, and proves this:—from the tenets of Epicurus, namely that there is no providence, that souls are mortal, and so forth (Chapter 17);—from the tenets of the Stoics and of Pythagoras [Col. 0347C] concerning the migration of souls from one body into other [Col. 0348A] bodies, concerning the goodness of death, and concerning the evil of life; and above all from Plato’s thanksgiving, in which he said that he gave thanks to nature both because he had been born a human being rather than a dumb animal, because he was male rather than female, because he was Greek rather than barbarian, because he was Athenian, and because he lived in the time of Socrates (Chapter 18). Lactantius assails this thanksgiving with remarkable force (Chapters 19, 20, and 21);—from various deeds and sayings of lesser philosophers: because Democritus allowed his fields to become public pastureland; because Zeno makes all sins equal and places compassion among the vices; because Xenophanes believed those who said that the globe of the moon was twenty-two times larger than the earth (Chapter 22);—from those who introduce the antipodes, that is, human beings whose feet are higher than their heads (Chapter 23).

In the third part he again proves that philosophy is not wisdom, because:—it is restricted by some to philosophers alone;—the Stoics and Epicureans admitted everyone, yet they could not accomplish what they wished (Chapter 24);—it cannot accomplish what true religion accomplishes: making the irascible person calm, the greedy person generous, and the cruel person merciful;—the wisdom of the philosophers, at most, does not root out vices but conceals them. Yet God’s few precepts so transform the whole person, and after casting out the old make him new, that you would not recognize him as the same person (Chapters 25 and 26);—the philosophers themselves confess that they are unwise: Empedocles, Anaxagoras, Democritus, and Socrates (Chapter 27);—out of sheer unwisdom and ignorance of the true God they invented the names Nature and Fortune (Chapter 27), although fortune is nothing in itself, but merely the sudden and unexpected outcome of accidental events (Chapter 28).

The conclusion of the book follows. There is therefore one hope for humanity, one salvation, placed in this teaching that we defend. The whole wisdom of humanity consists in this one thing: knowing and worshiping God.

[Col. 0347C]

# BOOK THREE: ON THE FALSE WISDOM OF THE PHILOSOPHERS

## CHAPTER ONE. A comparison of truth with eloquence; why the philosophers did not attain truth; on the simple style of the Scriptures

I wish that, since truth is still believed to lie hidden in obscurity—whether through the error and ignorance of the common people, who serve various foolish superstitions, or through philosophers who, by the depravity of their intellects, confuse rather than illuminate it—I might possess some capacity for eloquence, even if not of the quality found in Marcus Tullius, since his was preeminent and admirable, yet at least one approaching it. [Col. 0347D] Thus, to the degree that truth prevails by its own inherent power, it might likewise, supported by intellectual powers, at last display itself and, after dispersing and refuting both public errors and those of the persons regarded as wise, bring the clearest light to the human race. [Col. 0348C]

I would wish this to happen for two reasons: either because people who believe even a lie, captivated by ornate speech and the allure of words, might more readily believe truth when adorned; or certainly so that the philosophers themselves might above all be crushed by us with their own weapons, in which [Col. 0348D] they are accustomed to take pleasure and place confidence.

and naked truth should be more luminous, because it is sufficiently adorned in itself and is therefore corrupted when painted over with ornaments added from without, whereas falsehood should give pleasure through an appearance alien to itself, because, being corrupt in itself, it vanishes and dissolves unless it has been coated and polished with ornament sought from elsewhere, I calmly accept that only moderate intellectual ability was granted to me.

Yet I have undertaken this work in confidence not in eloquence but in truth—a work perhaps greater than can be sustained by my powers. Nevertheless, even if I fail, truth itself will complete it with the aid of God, whose office this is. For since I know that even the greatest orators have often been defeated by advocates of middling ability, because the power of truth is so great that, even in insignificant matters, it defends itself by its own brightness, [Col. 0349B] why should I think that, in the greatest case of all, it will be crushed by those admittedly ingenious and eloquent men who nevertheless speak falsely? Why should I not think that truth, even if it is less supported by our discourse, which flows very thinly from a meager spring, will nevertheless appear bright and illustrious by its own light?

Nor, even if the philosophers proved remarkable in literary learning, would I therefore grant them knowledge and cognition of the truth, which no one can attain by reflection or disputation. Nor do I now condemn [Col. 0350A] the pursuit of those who wished to know the truth, because God made human nature exceedingly eager to attain truth. What I charge and refute is this: that their honorable and excellent intention was not followed by achievement, because they knew neither what truth itself was nor how, where, or with what disposition it should be sought. Thus, while desiring to remedy human errors, they led themselves into snares and the greatest errors. The very sequence of the subject I have undertaken has therefore brought me to this task of reproving philosophy.

For since every error arises either from false religion or from false wisdom, it is necessary, in refuting error, to overthrow both. Since it has been handed down to us in the divine writings that the thoughts of philosophers are foolish, that very point must be demonstrated by facts and arguments, lest [Col. 0350B] anyone, enticed by the honorable name of wisdom or deceived by the splendor of empty eloquence, prefer to believe human teachings rather than divine ones, which have indeed been delivered briefly and plainly. For it was not fitting otherwise that, when God spoke to a human being, he should vindicate his words with arguments, as though he would not be believed; rather, as was proper, he spoke like the supreme judge of all things, whose role is not to argue but to pronounce judgment. But he himself spoke as God. We, however, since we possess testimonies of the divine voice concerning each individual matter, will certainly demonstrate [Col. 0351A]
