Indeed, Pythagoras. See Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book XIV, chapter 1, and *The City of God*, book VIII, chapter 2; and Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, book V. God himself, therefore, is supreme wisdom; but the worship of God is human wisdom, of which we are now speaking. For the wisdom of this [Col. 0352D] world is foolishness with God. Accordingly, with reference to this wisdom, which is the worship of God, Holy Scripture says (Wisdom 6:26): “A multitude of wise men is the health of the world.” But if one is to discuss the wisdom of the wise, the example of Pythagoras should be imitated: since he had not dared to profess himself a wise man, did he not answer instead that he was a philosopher, that is, a lover of wisdom? This name, originating with him, thereafter so pleased posterity that, however much anyone seemed to excel, either in his own judgment or that of others, in learning concerning matters pertaining to wisdom, he was called nothing more than a philosopher. Besides St. Augustine at the passage cited above, see Cicero, preface to book I of the *Tusculan Disputations*, and Laertius at the beginning.

**The perfect name of an imperfect thing.** Laertius, at the passage cited, reports from Heraclides Ponticus these words of Pythagoras: μηδένα εἶναι σοφὸν ἄνθρωπον, ἀλλ’ ἢ Θεόν, “No human being is wise, but only God.” Seneca, Letter 89: “I shall state the difference between wisdom and philosophy: wisdom is the perfected good of the human mind; philosophy is the love and pursuit of wisdom.” BUN.]

how much more surely truths could be defended by arguments, when even falsehoods are so defended that they commonly appear true. Therefore there is no reason for us to pay philosophers such great honor or to fear their eloquence. For they could speak well, as educated men, but they could by no means speak truly, because they had not learned the truth from one who had mastery of it. Nor indeed shall we accomplish anything very great by convicting them of the ignorance which they themselves very frequently confess; for they are not believed in the one matter in which alone they ought to have been believed. I shall attempt to show that they were never so truthful as when they pronounced judgment concerning their own ignorance.

[Col. 0351B] CHAPTER II. On philosophy, and how empty its occupation was in expounding the truth.

Now, since in the two preceding books the falsity of religions has been demonstrated, and the very origin of the whole error has also been explained, the task of this book is to show how empty and false philosophy likewise is, so that, when every error has been removed, the truth may stand forth revealed in its brightness. Let us therefore begin with the common name of philosophy, so that, once the head itself has been [Col. 0352A] destroyed, an easier approach may lie open to us for cutting down the whole body—if indeed that can be called a body whose parts and members are at variance, are joined together by no connecting structure, but, as though scattered and dispersed, seem rather to twitch than to live. Philosophy is—as its name indicates and philosophers themselves define it—the study of wisdom. From what, then, may I prove more conclusively that philosophy is not wisdom than from the meaning of its own name? For one who studies wisdom is assuredly not yet wise, but studies in order that he may be able to become wise. In the other arts, it is evident what study accomplishes and toward what it tends. When anyone has mastered them by learning, he is no longer called a student of the craft, but a craftsman. But, it will be said, out of modesty they called themselves students of wisdom, not wise men. Indeed, Pythagoras, who first [Col. 0352B] devised this name, because he was a little wiser than those earlier men who thought themselves wise, understood that no human study could attain to wisdom, and that one therefore ought not to impose a perfect name upon something unattained and imperfect. Accordingly, when he was asked what he professed himself to be, he answered: a philosopher, that is, a seeker after wisdom. If, therefore, philosophy seeks wisdom, it is not itself wisdom, because that which seeks must necessarily be one thing, and [Col. 0353A] that which is sought another; nor is the search itself sound, [Col. 0353A]

[Note: [Col. 0353B] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 353–354]

**Nor is the search itself sound.** I read thus with four printed editions and sixteen manuscripts, two of which are very ancient. Six others read “question”; the Pen. manuscript, several Vatican manuscripts, and seven printed editions read, “nor is the search for wisdom sound.” I have nevertheless deleted “for wisdom,” which is absent from the manuscripts.

**Opinion.** *Opinatio* is opinion as opposed to knowledge, and is called probability by the more recent philosophers. From Walch.

**Knowledge from the mind.** That is, from the soul. For below, in chapter 6, he says that knowledge comes from the soul, ignorance from the body. See chapter 1 of *On the Wrath of God*. Some call that metaphysical light divinely kindled in our minds wisdom, others knowledge—as does our author here—although knowledge properly concerns things perpetual and constant within mutable nature. That light is implanted in mortal minds by nature itself; and although it is obscured by bodily darkness, there is nevertheless more light in some and less in others, and for that reason more knowledge in some and less in others. This is indeed not surprising, since Augustine, teacher of divine wisdom, denies that any of the saints has received the whole of heavenly wisdom. For this assertion he has Paul himself as his most authoritative (*authentikōtaton*, αὐθεντικώτατον) witness. BETULEIUS.

**For this reason he opened the eyes and ears, etc.** Socrates, in the *Theaetetus*, in the second definition, defines knowledge (*epistēmē*, ἐπιστήμη) as perception (*aisthēsis*, αἴσθησις). Aristotle teaches how they differ from one another in *On the Soul*, book III, chapter 8. BETULEIUS.

**Might flow through.** I have restored this from the two Bonon. manuscripts and the Lips., Pal., and Tax.; for the older and better manuscripts concur in this reading. The Regio-Put. has “might remain”; the Cauc., three Reg., Ultr., and one Brun. have “remains” for “might flow through”; one Colb. has “might pass through.” Five other recent Reg., five Colb., two Clarom., and the printed editions have “might arrive”; one Reg. and one Brun. have “may arrive.” — **Might flow through.** Aptly expressed, as in Cicero: “to flow through to the mind, to the senses, to the ears.” All editions have “might arrive,” which is itself elegant. BUN.

**Whether the sun, etc.** Lucretius, on the heavenly bodies generally, book V:

> Whatever it is, it is borne along in no larger shape  
> Than it appears to be when we behold it with our eyes.

This is a doctrine of Epicurus. On this subject see Plutarch’s words from *The Opinions of the Philosophers*, book II, chapter 11, where he said that the sun is twenty-seven times larger than the earth. Galen agrees, *On the History of Philosophy* (*peri philosophias historias*, περὶ φιλοσοφίας ἱστορίας), chapter 58. But in Cicero’s *Academic Questions* it is believed, according to mathematical calculation, to be more than eighteen times larger than the earth; in the preceding chapter of Plutarch this same claim is attributed to Anaximander. Yet in his *Life* in Laertius he is said to have asserted, τὸν ἥλιον οὐκ ἐλάττονα τῆς γῆς, καὶ καθαρότατον πῦρ, “that the sun is no smaller than the earth and is the purest fire.” Plato held nearly the same opinion in the *Epinomis*. Macrobius, *On the Dream of Scipio*, book I, chapter 20, attributes to Eratosthenes what [Col. 0354B] Plutarch and others ascribed to Anaximander, reporting it thus: “Eratosthenes says as follows in his books on measurements: ‘The measure of the earth, multiplied twenty-seven times, will produce the measure of the sun.’” Macrobius himself, however, concludes that the sun is eight times larger than the earth. But Franciscus Philelphus, in book I of the *Convivialia*, concludes from Ptolemy that the sun is one hundred sixty-six and three-eighths times larger than the earth. Read further concerning the size of the sun Cleomedes, book II, and Pliny, book II, chapter 11. BETULEIUS. — See Descartes, if you wish.

**Whether the moon is spherical.** See Plutarch, *Opinions*, book II, chapter 27. Cleomedes reports that the ancients set forth only three shapes of the moon: crescent-shaped, halved, [Col. 0354C] and full; and that Diana was consequently called Trivia. He nevertheless testifies that a fourth, bulging on both sides, was added by later writers; for Valla seems to have rendered ἀμφίκυρτον (*amphikyrton*) in this way, whereas Budaeus rendered it “convex on both sides.” Pliny, book II, chapter 9, and Theon on Aratus mention the former shapes but make no mention of this one. Martianus, however, mentions it in book VIII, Macrobius in *On the Dream of Scipio*, book I, chapter 6, and the Moon herself in Lucian’s *Icaromenippus*. To these we shall add what Cicero reports in *Academic Questions*, book IV, concerning Xenophanes, who said that the moon was habitable and was an earth containing many cities. Natural philosophers certainly called the moon an ethereal earth, as Macrobius attests. On all these matters see Philelphus’s *Convivial Discourses*. Aristotle, *On the Heavens*, book II, chapter 11, makes all the stars σφαιροειδῆ (*sphairoeidē*), “spherical”; so too does Cicero in the *Dream of Scipio*, where Macrobius calls the bodies of the stars spheres. But some were found who thought otherwise: Cleanthes, Anaximenes, and others. BETULEIUS.

**And whether the stars adhere to the heavens, etc.** I have restored this from the editions of Tornesius and Soubron and from all the manuscripts, [Col. 0354D] except two recent Reg. and the printed editions, in which it reads, “and whether the stars cohere with the heavens.” It records a doctrine of Xenocrates—or, as Galen has it, Xenophanes; on these matters see Plutarch. Today, certainly, neither is that arrangement of the stars accepted, nor is it doubted that the fixed stars revolve with the whole universe. Why Lactantius repeatedly says that the heavenly bodies are borne through the air is without rationale, unless he used “air” for “aether.” The expression is altogether improper (*akyron*, ἄκυρον), or was taken from the popular belief, which, as Plato teaches in the *Phaedo*, arises from the weakness and slowness of our vision; or else from the fact that what is aether to those above is air to us, as Plato likewise reports there. BETULEIUS.

**Whether it is at rest and immovable.** Thus read the Jun., Cantabrig., two Reg., and other manuscripts, together with several printed editions; three other Reg. have “or movable”; the Cauc. manuscript, “immortal.” I emend the text from the four best and most ancient Reg., one Bon., the antiq., Ultr., Goth., Em., four Colb., two Brun., and the editions Graph., Gymnic., Tornes., Soubron., Paris., Cellar., and Walch., to read “and immovable.” Isidore, *Origins*, book II, chapter 24, quotes this passage word for word in precisely this form; and there follows in addition, “or whether it revolves at incredible speed.” See Copernicus, Cardinal Nicholas of Cusa, Descartes, and the other authors cited below—namely Macrobius, *On the Dream of Scipio*, book I, chapter 17; Pliny, book II, chapter 3; Aristotle, in book II of *On the Heavens*, *On the Cosmos*, and elsewhere. Cicero, *On the Universe*, §17, writes: “Accordingly, in one vast revolution, which is always the same, it twists and turns about itself.” See col. 355, line 2.]

because it can discover nothing.

Indeed, I would not concede that philosophers are even students of wisdom, because that study does not attain wisdom. For if the capacity to discover truth were subject to this study, and if that study were, as it were, a road to wisdom, wisdom would at some point have been discovered. But since, after so many ages and so many intellects have been worn out in seeking it, it has not been grasped, it is apparent that no wisdom is present there. Those who philosophize, therefore, do not study wisdom; they merely think that they study it, because they do not know where or of what kind the thing they seek is. Whether, then, they study wisdom or do not study it, they are not wise, because what is either sought wrongly or not sought at all can never be found. Let us nevertheless consider [Col. 0353B] this very point: whether anything can be found by this study, or nothing.

[Col. 0354A] CHAPTER III. Of what philosophy consists, and who was the first principal founder of the Academic school.

Philosophy appears to consist of two things, knowledge and opinion, and of nothing else. Knowledge cannot come from the mind or be grasped by thought, because to possess proper knowledge within oneself belongs not to man but to God. Mortal nature, however, does not receive knowledge unless it comes from without. For this reason divine craftsmanship opened the eyes, ears, and other senses in the body, so that through them knowledge might flow into the mind. For to investigate the causes of natural things, or to wish to know whether the sun is merely as large as it appears, or is many times larger than this whole [Col. 0354B] earth; likewise, whether the moon is spherical or concave; whether the stars adhere to the heavens or are borne through the air in a free [Col. 0355A] course; of what size and material the heavens themselves consist; whether they are at rest and immovable or revolve at incredible speed; how thick the earth is, [Col. 0355A]

[Note: [Col. 0355C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 355–356]

**How thick the earth is.** Macrobius, *On the Dream of Scipio*, book I, chapter 20, concludes—as he himself declares, by the most evident and indisputable measurements—that the circumference of the entire earth, wherever it is either inhabited or lies uninhabitable, is 252,000 stadia, while its diameter is 80,000 stadia, [Col. 0355D] or not much more. He derives this from the calculation of Eratosthenes, which Cleomedes also follows in book I. Read in addition Ptolemy’s *Great Construction*, book V, chapter 16, Theon’s *Commentaries* there, and Martianus in his *Geometry*. Plato, however, discusses the size of the earth without determining it in the *Phaedo*. BET.

**Upon what foundations it is balanced, etc.** See Simmias in Plato’s *Phaedo* near the end; Cicero in the *Academics*; Ptolemy, *Almagest*, book III, chapter 7.

**By debating.** One ancient Bon. manuscript reads “to debate.”

**We suppose.** I have restored this from thirteen of the best and most ancient manuscripts and from the four editions Torn., Soubr., Cellar., and Walch. Seven recent manuscripts and sixteen printed editions have “we do suppose.”

**Those who investigate nature.** He is not disparaging that natural science which is the foundation of medicine, as will become clear below in chapters 5 and 6, but that whose proper task, as Laertius says, is to debate the cosmos and the things existing within it.

**Socrates, therefore, was right, etc.** Even Laertius himself makes it clear that the Academy flowed from the teaching of Socrates. Plato, of course, a pupil of Socrates, founded the Academy. Although the Academics seem to some to have followed the best mode of teaching, nevertheless, because their profession is founded solely upon opinions, Carneades the Stoic’s judgment concerning them appears true to us: he said that the wise man who holds opinions will err; for he who holds an opinion knows nothing. Knowledge is therefore removed from their midst. Augustine argues against the Academic heresy in three books whose title is taken from the subject itself; Epiphanius in book I. BETUL.

**He holds an opinion . . . about what he does not know.** Book III, chapter 4. Here Lactantius reproduces Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, book IV, chapter 11: “Opinion is judging that one knows what one does not know.” BUN.

**Truer.** I have restored this from nearly all the manuscripts. Two very recent manuscripts together with the printed editions have “more certain”; three have “truly more certain.” [Col. 0356D] The subject here is truth. See what follows.

**Fall within the nature of things.** I have restored the accusative form from nearly all the manuscripts and from the old printed editions—the two Roman editions, Tornesius, and Soubron. Very many common editions, together with four manuscripts, have the nominative “nature.”

**No one, therefore.** I have accepted this reading from all the manuscripts and the editions of Cellarius and Walch. Fourteen printed editions have “for no one.”

**Will descend.** Namely, from heaven. Reimm. has “will disagree,” not badly. For the received reading compare Livy, book VI, chapter 18: “They will never descend from heaven on my account.” Compare Lactantius, book III, chapter 20. BUN.

**Although he seems to shut his eyes.** Yet, according to Thomasius, one Vatican manuscript reads “although he seems to remain silent,” which he strongly prefers; and he says that “shut his eyes” conveys nothing pertinent to the matter.

**Supreme foolishness.** On this see Paul, 1 Corinthians 3:19.]

and upon what foundations it is balanced and suspended—all this, I say, to wish to comprehend by debate and conjecture is surely like wishing to discuss what we suppose a city of some extremely distant nation to be like, when we have never seen it and have heard nothing of it except its name. If we claim knowledge for ourselves in a matter that cannot be known, do we not seem insane, daring to affirm something in which we can be refuted? How much more must those who think they know natural things, which cannot be known by man, be judged mad and demented. Socrates, therefore, and the Academics who followed him rightly abolished knowledge, which belongs not to one who reasons but to one who divines. It remains that opinion alone exists in philosophy. For wherever knowledge is absent, opinion possesses the whole field. Each person holds an opinion about what he does not know. Those who debate natural things hold the opinion that matters are as they argue. They therefore do not know the truth, since knowledge concerns what is certain, opinion what is uncertain.

Let us return to the preceding example. Come, let us form an opinion about the condition and character of that city which is entirely unknown to us except for its name. It is plausible that it is situated on a plain, with stone walls, lofty buildings, many streets, and magnificent, richly adorned temples. Let us describe, if you please, the customs and dress of its citizens. [Col. 0355C] But when we have said these things, another person will argue the opposite; [Col. 0356A] and when he too has finished speaking, a third will rise, then others in succession, and they will form opinions very different from those we have formed. What, then, among all these will be truer? Perhaps nothing. Yet everything has been said that falls within the nature of things, so that something among them must necessarily be true. But it will not be known who spoke the truth. It may happen that all have erred in some respect and touched the truth in another. We are therefore fools if we seek this by disputation, for someone may come along who laughs at our opinions and regards us as insane for wishing to form an opinion about what we do not know the character of. But there is no need to seek distant places from which perhaps no one will come to refute us. Come, let us form an opinion about what is now being done in the forum or in the senate-house. Even that is too far away: let us say [Col. 0356B] what is happening on the other side of a single intervening wall. No one can know it unless he has heard or seen it. No one, therefore, dares to state it, because he will immediately be refuted, not by words but by the present fact itself. Yet philosophers do precisely this when they debate what is happening in heaven; but they suppose that they can do so with impunity because no one appears to expose their errors. If they thought that someone would descend to prove that they were raving and lying, they would never debate matters that they cannot know. Yet their shamelessness and audacity should not be thought more fortunate merely because they are not refuted: for God, to whom alone the truth is known, refutes them, although he seems to shut his eyes, and counts this wisdom of men as supreme foolishness.

[Col. 0357A] CHAPTER IV. That knowledge was abolished by Socrates, and opinion by Zeno.

Zeno and the Stoics, therefore, rightly repudiated opinion. For to suppose that you know [Col. 0357A]

[Note: [Col. 0357C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 357–358]

**To suppose . . . that you know.** The word “know” must not be absent: it is necessary here, and all editions correctly contain it. The passage of Cicero cited by me at chapter 3 requires it, as does the *Epitome*, chapter 31: “To suppose, however, that you know what you do not know is rashness and foolishness.” BUN.

**Know.** “Know” is absent from the Emmanuel. and Gothan. manuscripts.

**Who were the leading figures in philosophy.** The Academics and Stoics were the leading philosophers. Socrates laid, as it were, the foundation of the Academic school; Zeno was the founder of the Stoic.

**Constituted.** On this see Terence, *The Self-Tormentor*, act III, scene 1, verse 97. From this arose the saying that no one is a competent judge in his own case.

**Those Sown Men of the poets.** I think the text should be read thus, with Johannes Caucus and Isaeus; it is printed so in the Florentine, Juntine, Aldine editions of 1515 and 1535, the Venetian editions of 1509 and 1521, and the editions of Parrhasius, Paris 1525, Antwerp, Grapheus 1532, Cratander, and Gymnicus. Those “Sown Men” of the poets are the men who sprang from the serpent’s teeth sown by Cadmus; the story is too familiar to require retelling. I shall add only that those men are called *Sparti* from the Greek verb σπείρω (*speirō*), “I sow”; hence σπάρτοι (*spartoi*), “sown, seeded.” Lactantius wrote this word in the Latin manner. Similarly, the Vulgate translator at John 5:2 and Pliny wrote a Greek name as though it were Latin by saying *probata* for “sheep.” In book VII, chapter 2, Virgil somewhere similarly used *acta*, which is Greek ἀκτή (*aktē*), “shore.” Here too I agree with Isaeus that an error crept in because scribes, failing to understand the meaning of this word and suspecting corruption, substituted *Spartiatae* for *Sparti*. GALLAEUS. — I suspect this word arose from *Sparti, sati*—“the Sown Men, the sown”—the latter term having been added as an interpretation in some old manuscripts, intruded into the text, and finally corrupted into [Col. 0358C] *spartiati* or *Spartiatae*, which appears in twenty-eight manuscripts and nine printed editions. See also Euripides’ *Phoenician Women* and Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book III.

**Arcesilaus.** The founder of the New, or Middle, Academy. In the *Academic Questions*, Cicero calls Plato’s Academy the Old Academy, and the New that which continued down to Carneades, who was fourth from Arcesilaus and persisted in Arcesilaus’s method. Cicero, *On the Orator*, book III: “Arcesilaus, who had studied under Polemo, was the first to seize chiefly upon this doctrine from Plato’s various books and the Socratic dialogues: that there is nothing certain which can be perceived either by the senses or by the mind.” BETULEIUS.

**A new philosophy of not philosophizing.** Just as Fabius Maximus devised a new kind of fighting: not to fight. Florus II.6. FRANCIUS.

**Takes it away.** This is the reading of all the manuscripts and the old Roman edition; the recent printed editions have “tears it apart.”

[Col. 0358D]

**As though a civil war, etc.** Cicero, in the book entitled *Lucullus*, declares that Arcesilaus overthrew a well-established philosophy in the same way as Tiberius Gracchus overthrew the commonwealth, and that he sheltered behind the authority of those who denied that anything could be known or perceived. From their number Cicero excludes both Socrates and Plato. BET.

**A band of recruits.** He means the followers of Arcesilaus and the New Academics.

**The veterans.** That is, the Platonists.

**Without destroying itself.** I have added “itself” from the Bon., Tax., Pen., Cauc., Junt., Cant., Sublac., Rost., Ven. 1471, both editions of 1478, the 1493 and 1497 editions, Pier., Junt., Ald., Parrh., Crat., Gymn., Gryph., and Tornes. I do not see why Thomas. and his followers expelled the word “itself.” BUN.

**Prevails.** I have restored this from the manuscripts. The printed editions and one recent Reg. have “prevailed.” Either, however, can be said.]

what you do not know belongs not to a wise man, but rather to a rash man and a fool. Therefore, if nothing can be known, as Socrates taught, and one ought not to hold opinions, as Zeno taught, all philosophy has been abolished. What of the fact that it is overthrown not only by these two, who were the leading figures in philosophy, but by all philosophers, so that it now appears to have long since been destroyed by its own weapons? Philosophy is divided into many schools, and all hold different views. In which of them do we locate truth? Certainly it cannot be in them all. Let us designate any one we please: then, plainly, [Col. 0357B] there will be no wisdom in all the rest. Let us pass through them one by one: in the same way, whatever we grant to one we shall take away from the rest. For every school overthrows all the others in order to confirm itself and its own doctrines; nor does it allow any other to be wise, lest it confess itself foolish. But just as it abolishes the others, so it too is abolished by all the others. For those who accuse it of foolishness are philosophers nonetheless. Whichever school you praise and call true is censured by philosophers as false. Shall we therefore believe one school praising itself and its own teaching, or the many that condemn the ignorance of that one? What the majority thinks must necessarily be more correct than what one person thinks. For no one can judge himself correctly, as the renowned poet testifies. For the nature [Col. 0357C] of all human beings has been so constituted that they see and judge the affairs of others better than their own. Since, therefore, all things [Col. 0358A] are uncertain, either everyone must be believed or no one. If no one, then they are not wise, because each one, affirming something different, thinks himself wise. If everyone, they are equally not wise, because each one is denied by everyone to be wise. Thus they all perish, and, like those Sown Men of the poets, they slaughter one another so that no one of them remains. This occurs because they have a sword but no shield.

If, therefore, each individual school is convicted of foolishness by the judgment of many schools, all are found to be empty and vain. Thus philosophy consumes and destroys itself. When Arcesilaus, founder of the Academy, understood this, he gathered together the criticisms made by all the philosophers against one another and the confession of ignorance by renowned philosophers, [Col. 0358B] and armed himself against them all. He thus established a new philosophy of not philosophizing. With him as its founder, therefore, there began to be two kinds of philosophy: one, the old kind, which claims knowledge for itself; the other, a new and opposing kind, which takes knowledge away. In these two kinds I see dissension and something like a civil war. On which side shall we place wisdom, which cannot be taken away? If the nature of things can be known, this band of recruits will perish; if it cannot, the veterans will be destroyed. If they are evenly matched, philosophy, the leader of them all, will nonetheless perish, because it has been taken away; for nothing can be contrary to itself without destroying itself. But if, as I have taught, there can be no inward and native knowledge in man because of the frailty of the human condition, [Col. 0358C] Arcesilaus’s troop prevails. Yet not even it will stand, because it cannot be the case that absolutely nothing is known.

[Col. 0359A] CHAPTER V. That knowledge of many things is necessary.

There are many things which nature itself, frequent practice, and the necessity of life compel us to know. Thus one must perish unless one knows which things are useful for life, so as to pursue them, and which are dangerous, so as to flee and avoid them. Moreover, there are many things which practice has discovered. For the various courses of the sun and moon, the paths of the stars, and the reckoning of times have been ascertained; physicians have discovered the nature of bodies and the powers of herbs, [Col. 0359A]

[Note: [Col. 0359C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 359–360]

**The powers of herbs.** Galen assigns the invention of herbal medicine to Chiron the Centaur; Macer assigns it to Artemisia. BETULEIUS.

**And also of rains.** Christ himself concedes this in Matthew 16 and Luke 11. Aratus above all treats these matters, and Virgil in the *Georgics*. BETUL.

**Arcesilaus, therefore, ought.** According to Mela, Arcesilaus, leader of the Academy that affirmed nothing, so removed all knowledge of things from human beings that he left it to God alone, as Epiphanius writes of him in volume II, book III, *On Heresies*. BETULEIUS.

**Had reduced himself to the crowd.** He said “reduce to the crowd” in the sense of “reduce to the ranks.” On this manner of speaking, see Budaeus on the Law *Divus Marcus*, *Digest*, *On the Office of a Provincial Governor*. — **Had reduced himself to the crowd.** That is, had counted himself among the common run of philosophers. According to Priscian and Raphael Regius, Quintilian, *Institutes*, book I, chapter 4, used “reduce to the ranks” to mean “reckon among the base and contemptible.” BUN.

**You prove.** This is the reading of the manuscripts and the three old Roman editions, Tornesius, and Soubron; the other printed editions have “you will have proved.”

**Arcesilaus.** Nearly all manuscripts and the old Roman editions have *Archesilaus*. But one very ancient Reg. and the common editions have *Arcesilaus*, as does Diogenes Laertius in *Lives of the Philosophers*.

**Finished off.** A term from gladiatorial combat, used of a gladiator pierced by many wounds. Cicero, [Col. 0360C] *Against Catiline* II, chapter 11: “that finished and wounded gladiator.” CELLAR.

**Among themselves.** I have restored this from twenty-nine of the better and older manuscripts. In place of “themselves,” the printed editions and six recent manuscripts substituted “philosophers” because of the beginning of a new chapter. Four others and the edition of Isaeus added “philosophers” after “themselves”—evidently a gloss from the book’s margin admitted into the text.

**From the mind, which.** Nearly all manuscripts and five printed editions use the masculine gender. Fourteen printed editions have “from the soul, which.” Above, in chapter 3, he said that knowledge comes from the mind.

**Toward the left.** *Sinistrorsus* occurs in Caesar, *Gallic War* VI; I miss it in my lexicons. BUN.

**Of a few things.** Thysius and Gallaeus, with one Bonon. manuscript, add “and.”

**Because.** Francius thought that “than” should be read here and below.

**With hands joined in combat.** A proverb meaning “with the utmost contention,” a metaphor taken from wrestlers. Or it is an allusion to that ancient forensic custom which they called *manum conserere* in legal proceedings. Besides Budaeus and Erasmus, see Gellius, book XX, chapter 9. BETUL. — **With hands joined in combat.** Sparkius interprets this “with the utmost effort.” It means “fighting,” as in book V, chapter 6: “Then they began to join battle with one another.” BUN.

**Situated in the middle, which.** Nearly all witnesses read thus. I understand “knowledge, which.” BUN.]

and farmers have gathered knowledge of the nature of soils, as well as signs of coming rains and storms. In short, there is no art that does not consist of knowledge. Arcesilaus, therefore, if he had possessed any wisdom, ought [Col. 0359B] to have distinguished what could be known from what could not. But if he had done this, he would have reduced himself to the crowd. For common people are sometimes wiser, because they are wise only so far as necessary. If you ask a common person whether he knows anything or nothing, he will say that he knows what he knows and confess that he does not know what he does not know. Arcesilaus was therefore right to abolish the teachings of others, but wrong to establish his own. For ignorance of all things cannot be wisdom, whose distinctive property is knowledge. Thus, when he had defeated the philosophers and taught that they knew nothing, he himself also lost the name of philosopher, because his doctrine is to know nothing. For one who censures others for their ignorance ought himself to possess knowledge. But when he knows nothing, what perversity and arrogance it is to set himself up as a philosopher for precisely the reason for which he abolishes the others! For they can answer him thus: “If [Col. 0359C] you prove that we know nothing, and therefore are not wise because we know nothing, are you, then, wise because you too confess that you know nothing?” What, therefore, did Arcesilaus accomplish, except that, after finishing off all the philosophers, he pierced himself also with the same sword-point?

[Col. 0360A] CHAPTER VI. On wisdom, and on the Academics and natural philosophers.

Is wisdom, then, nowhere to be found? Indeed, it was among the philosophers themselves, but no one saw it. Some thought that all things could be known; these were certainly not wise. Others thought that nothing could be known; neither were these wise—the former because they granted too much to man, the latter because they granted too little. Both lacked moderation in opposite directions. Where, then, is wisdom? It lies in neither thinking that you know everything, which belongs to God, nor that you know nothing, which belongs to a beast. For there is a certain middle condition proper to man: namely, knowledge joined and tempered with ignorance. Knowledge in us comes from the mind, which arises from heaven; ignorance comes from the body, which comes from earth. Hence we share something both [Col. 0360B] with God and with animals. Thus, since we are composed of these two elements, one endowed with light and the other with darkness, a portion of knowledge and a portion of ignorance have been given to us. It is possible to cross by this bridge, so to speak, without danger of falling; for all those who inclined themselves toward either side fell either to the right or toward the left. I shall explain how each side erred. The Academics argued against the natural philosophers from obscure matters that there was no knowledge; satisfied with examples of a few incomprehensible things, they embraced ignorance, as though they had abolished knowledge altogether because they had abolished it in part. Conversely, the natural philosophers drew from evident things the argument that everything could be known; satisfied with what was manifest, they retained knowledge, [Col. 0360C] as though they had defended it altogether because they had defended it in part. Thus neither did the natural philosophers see what was obscure, nor the Academics what was clear; but both, while with hands joined in combat they either retained knowledge alone or snatched it away, failed to see that knowledge, situated in the middle, would convey them to wisdom.

[Col. 0361A] But Arcesilaus, teacher of ignorance, in attacking Zeno, the leader of the Stoics, so as to overthrow all philosophy, adopted from Socrates [Col. 0361A]

[Note: [Col. 0361C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 361–362]

**Socrates.** Xenophon discusses this teaching of Socrates fully and elegantly in *Sayings and Deeds of Socrates*, not far from the beginning.

**Adopted this proposition, etc.** On this Cicero, *On the Orator*, book III: “Arcesilaus, who had studied under Polemo, was the first to seize chiefly upon this doctrine from Plato’s various books and the Socratic dialogues: that there is nothing certain which can be perceived either by the senses or by the mind.” Arnobius, book II: “Who does not believe Arcesilaus and Carneades, who held that nothing can be comprehended by man and that all things are enveloped in blind obscurity?” Lucretius refutes this proposition in book IV:

> Finally, if anyone thinks that nothing can be known,  
> He does not know whether even this can be known, since he confesses that he knows nothing, etc.

**Estimate.** I have restored this from the manuscripts. The printed editions have “valuation.”

**Mortal.** The Sublac. edition has “immortal.”

**Suddenly the Academy arose.** Understand: the New Academy. On the threefold Academy—Old, Middle, and New—read the highly learned discussion of Georg Horn, *History of Philosophy*, book III, chapter 20.

**Incoherent (ἀσύστατον).** For among dialecticians the Greeks call a kind of fallacy ἀσύστατον (*asystaton*), and the Latins “insoluble,” as in: “I know nothing.” “Therefore, you know this: that you know nothing.”

**For in order that nothing is to be known.** Thus all the manuscripts except one very recent Reg. and one Clarom., which insert “can be known” after “nothing,” as do four printed editions. **An exception having been made.** Among jurists an exception is the exclusion of an action.

**Nor can it be known.** The reading found in three old Reg. manuscripts and one Clarom. seemed to us truer and better than the reading of the others, “cannot be unknown.” See what follows.

**They cannot.** Bunemann reads “they may not be able,” and gives the following account of this word: — I print the subjunctive “they may not be able” from the Goth. and second Lips., for “because he teaches” has preceded it. Heumann saw the same point. BUN.]

From others. Thus I read with almost all the manuscripts and the editions of de Tournes and Soubron. Five recent manuscripts and the printed editions have “from these.”

As we can. Thus almost all the manuscripts and the Paris edition of 1525. The other editions, together with six recent manuscripts, have “as we may be able.”

He adopted this position, affirming that nothing can be known. He thus exposed the conceit of the philosophers who had supposed that truth had been unearthed and discovered by their own intellectual powers. Indeed, because that wisdom was mortal and had been established only a short time before, it had now reached its greatest development; and, so that it should now necessarily grow old and perish, the Academy suddenly arose, like the old age of philosophy, to finish it off when it was already past its bloom. Arcesilaus rightly saw that those who think that knowledge of the truth can be grasped through conjecture are arrogant—or rather, foolish. Yet no one can refute one who speaks falsely unless he already knows what is true. Arcesilaus, attempting to do this [Col. 0361B] without having learned the truth, introduced an *asystaton* (ἀσύστατον) kind of philosophy, which in Latin we may call unstable or inconsistent.

For there to be no knowledge, something must necessarily be known. For if you know absolutely nothing, that very claim—that nothing can be known—will be eliminated. Accordingly, one who pronounces, as though stating a settled opinion, that nothing can be known is presenting it as an acknowledged and established doctrine. Therefore, something can be known.

Similar to this is the example customarily proposed in the schools as an instance of the inconsistent kind: someone dreamed that he should not believe dreams. For if he believes the dream, it follows that it should not be believed; but if he does not believe it, then it follows that it should be believed. So too, if nothing can be known, it is necessary that this very fact be known: that nothing is known. But if it is known that nothing can be known, then the claim [Col. 0361C] that nothing can be known is false. Thus a doctrine is introduced which contradicts itself and dissolves itself.

But the cunning man [Col. 0362A] wished to deprive the other philosophers of knowledge so that he might conceal it in his own house. For one who makes an assertion in order to deprive others of knowledge certainly does not deprive himself of it. Yet he accomplishes nothing; for knowledge becomes visible and betrays the man who stole it. How much more wisely and truthfully he would act if, after making an exception, he were to say that only the causes and principles of celestial or natural things, because they are hidden, cannot be known, since no one teaches them, and ought not to be investigated, since they cannot be discovered through investigation. By introducing this exception, he would both have warned the natural philosophers not to investigate matters exceeding the limits of human thought, and have freed himself from the odium of malicious criticism; and he would certainly have given us something to follow.

But now, since he has drawn us away from following them, lest we wish to know more than we can, he has no less drawn us away from following himself. For who would wish to labor so that he may know nothing? [Col. 0362B] Or to undertake a doctrine of such a kind that he even loses ordinary knowledge? If it is a doctrine, it must necessarily consist in knowledge; if it is not, who is so foolish as to think that he should learn something in which either nothing is learned or even what one knows is unlearned? Therefore, if neither can everything be known, as the natural philosophers thought, nor nothing, as the Academics thought, all philosophy has been extinguished.

## CHAPTER VII. On Ethical Philosophy and the Highest Good

Let us now pass to the other part of philosophy, which they themselves call moral philosophy, in which the rationale of philosophy as a whole is contained; for while in natural philosophy there is only pleasure, in this there is also usefulness. And since a graver error is committed, with greater danger, in ordering one’s condition of life and shaping one’s character, greater diligence must necessarily [Col. 0362C] be applied so that we may know how we ought to live. For in the former pardon may be granted, because whether they say something, they do no good, or whether they rave, they do no harm. [Col. 0363A] Here, however, there is no room for disagreement and no room for error. All must hold one opinion, and philosophy itself must give instruction as though with a single voice, because if any error is made, the whole of life is overturned.

In that former part, just as there is less danger, so there is greater difficulty, because the obscurity of the subject’s rationale compels people to adopt diverse and varying opinions. Here, just as there is greater danger, so there is less difficulty, because practical experience itself and daily trials can teach what is truer and better. Let us therefore see whether they agree, or what they offer us by which life may be conducted more rightly.

It is not necessary to make the entire circuit. Let us choose one subject, and indeed the most important: that which is the highest [Col. 0363A]

[Note: [Col. 0363B] [Notes of Various Commentators on columns 363–364]

That which is the highest. For the philosophers’ doctrines concerning ends, or the highest good, see Cicero in Book II of the *Academic Questions*. See also Book II of *On Ends*. Consult also St. Augustine, Book XVIII of *The City of God*.

The pivotal point turns. Thus Reimmann and all the witnesses. Heumann says, “I think *vertitur* (‘turns’) ought to be written.” But Lactantius himself confirms the received *versatur* in *On the Anger of God*, chapter 6: “Upon this the whole sum and pivotal point of religion and piety turns.” BUNEMANN.

Epicurus judges the highest good to consist in pleasure of the mind. This is an excellent opinion, which those who later followed him foolishly interpreted perversely. In addition to Gassendi, Stanley’s *History of Philosophy*, p. 1052, should be consulted here. WALCHIUS.—Lactantius, being somewhat inconsistent with himself, below in chapter 17 calls him an advocate of bodily pleasure, and in chapter 27 a pleasure-loving man, following Cicero’s second *Tusculan Disputation*. Yet it is evident from Seneca’s letters that Seneca, the greatest of the Stoics, whose doctrines strongly recoil from bodily pleasures, was a most devoted admirer of Epicurus; for he wished to conclude almost all his letters with some precept of Epicurus. You have Seneca’s judgment about him in chapters 12 and 13 of *On the Happy Life*. What Epicurus himself declares to be the highest good, however, and what pleasure he calls the end, he states in clear and explicit words in his letter to Menoeceus, preserved by Laertius in his life of Epicurus. Cicero also mentions this opinion in Book I of *On Ends*. Petrus Victorius, *Various Readings*, Book XXVII, chapter 14, contends that Epicurus was very similar to Socrates; and Laertius testifies that most people maintained that he was exceptionally temperate, to such an extent that he was content with water and ordinary bread alone. ISAEUS.—In the following chapter we shall see to what extent pleasure of the mind is, for Epicurus, the end of goods.

Aristippus. Below, Lactantius portrays him as a man fit for every stage-play, whose sole aim was to accommodate his mind and [Col. 0363D] character to any person’s disposition. His *Life* survives in Laertius, Book II. Read many accounts of his debauchery in Athenaeus, Book XII of the *Deipnosophists* (δειπνοσοφιστικῶν, “Banquet-Sophists”). Among ecclesiastical writers, moreover, Epiphanius notes his doctrine in vol. II, Book III, *Against Heresies*. Aristotle also argues against those who make pleasure the end of goods in Book X of the *Ethics*. BETULEIUS.

Callipho. Cicero, *On Ends*, Book II, chapter 6: “Callipho joined pleasure to moral worth”; and Book IV of the *Academics*, chapter 45, at the end. BUN.

Callipho and Dinomachus. Many manuscripts and printed editions add “the Cyrenaics,” but wrongly; three Royal manuscripts reject this word, two of which are the oldest of all. Cicero distinguishes them from the Cyrenaics in Book III of *On Duties*, near the end, as do Lactantius here and below in chapter 8, and also in Book VII, chapter 7. Rightly so: for both these philosophers, who in defining the highest good joined moral worth with pleasure, were certainly alien to the opinion of Aristippus, who located the highest good in bodily pleasures alone. The difference between them is enormous. Certainly, that Aristippus was the founder of the Cyrenaics and that this philosophical school derived from him is attested by Cicero at the end of the *Lucullus* and in Book III of *On Duties*; by Strabo at the end of Book XVII; by Laertius in his life of Aristippus; by the Suda under the letter K; and indeed by Lactantius himself in chapter 15 of this same book. Partly from ISAEUS.—Hence Cicero, speaking of Aristippus, says “from whom the Cyrenaics derive,” and distinguishes Callipho from the Cyrenaics. On Callipho and Dinomachus, see Cicero, Book V of *On Ends*, from which Lactantius drew these statements.—Callipho and Dinomachus: moral worth. In the *Epitome*, chapter 33: “Dinomachus and Callipho approved morally worthy pleasure.” BUNEMANN.

Diodorus, together with freedom from pain. Hieronymus placed the highest good in not suffering pain. Thus several manuscripts, among them two Royal manuscripts, one Colbertine manuscript, three old editions, and the *Epitome*, chapter 56. This passage must certainly be read and punctuated in this way, as Ciacconius long ago observed; both the rationale itself and Cicero—from whom Lactantius borrowed almost all this material—conclusively prove it. For if you read: “Diodorus placed the highest good in freedom from pain; Hieronymus in not suffering pain,” as the passage is commonly read, what difference will there be between the opinions of Diodorus and Hieronymus? Yet it is evident from Cicero that the difference was this: Diodorus did not simply place the highest good in not suffering pain, but joined moral worth to freedom from pain. Hieronymus, however, located it simply in not suffering pain, without adding anything. See Cicero, Book II of *On Ends*, shortly after the beginning. ISAEUS.—There were many men named Diodorus devoted to philosophy; but the one discussed here was a disciple of Socrates. That Hieronymus was a philosopher from Rhodes. He is certainly distinct from St. Jerome.

The Peripatetics. On how the Stoics differ from the Peripatetics, and what the three kinds of Peripatetics are, read Cicero in Book IV of *On Ends* and the founder of the Peripatetics himself in Book I of the *Ethics*, chapter 8. BETULEIUS.

Herillus. He was a Chalcedonian—or rather, a Carthaginian: “the Carthaginian” (ὁ Καρχηδόνιος), says Laertius. He was a disciple of Zeno; concerning him, see Cicero in Book IV of the *Academic Questions* and Book II of *On Ends*. Herillus, moreover, referring everything to knowledge, perceived a certain single good, but neither the best good nor one by which life could be governed. Accordingly, he himself was rejected long ago.

Of Zeno. Cicero attributes these ideas to the ancient Peripatetics. But the same Cicero reports that, for Zeno, the highest good is that which is derived from affinity with nature. Meanwhile, remember that Zeno calls those things which others call goods *proēgmena* (προηγμένα, “preferred things”): some Latin writers translate them as “things placed before,” others as “things advanced.” Perhaps more will be said about these elsewhere. Of the Stoics. A book entitled *On the Stoics and Epicureans* survives under the name of St. Augustine, in which he says: “For Epicurus, the end of goods is the pleasure of the body; for the Stoic, virtue of the mind; for the Christian, the gift of God.”

In all. Heumann deletes “in,” following six old editions.]

and principal good, upon which the pivotal point of all wisdom turns. [Col. 0364A] Epicurus judges the highest good to consist in pleasure of the mind; Aristippus, in pleasure of the body; Callipho and Dinomachus joined moral worth with pleasure; Diodorus joined it with freedom from pain. Hieronymus placed the highest good in not suffering pain; the Peripatetics, however, placed it in goods of mind, body, and fortune. The highest good of Herillus is knowledge; that of Zeno, to live in harmony with nature; that of certain Stoics, to follow virtue. Aristotle located the highest good in moral worth and virtue.

These are the opinions of almost all of them. Amid such great diversity, whom shall we follow? Whom shall we believe? Authority is equal in them all. If we can choose [Col. 0365A] what is better, we no longer need philosophy, because we are already wise, since we can judge among the opinions of the wise. We come. I have restored this from the manuscripts and many printed editions; some have “we have come.”

Who. I have added this from the better and older Royal manuscripts and others, and from ten printed editions. It is omitted in some; most have “what.”

Draw us back by his cloak. Isidore thinks that *pallium* (“cloak”) derives from *pelles* (“skins”), because the ancients first wore pelts over their clothing—as though the word were *pellea*—or that it derives from *palla*. This was the distinctive garment of philosophers, as appears from the saying of Herodes Atticus in Gellius, Book IX: “I see,” he says, “a beard and a cloak; I do not see a philosopher.” It was particularly common among the Greeks as well. Hence “cloak-wearers” (*palliati*) means Greeks, just as “toga-wearers” (*togati*) means Romans. Plays in which Greeks were introduced were therefore called “cloak-plays” (*fabulae palliatae*), just as those in which Romans appeared were called “toga-plays” (*togatae*). That the garment was common to both sexes may be gathered from Ulpian and Tacitus, who calls cloaks “common to both.” Martial:

> I veil her who wanders freely, clad in a little cloak.

Lampridius also wrote that royal matrons ought to be content with a single cloak sprinkled with gold. Ovid, *Amores*, Book I, elegy 2, seems to indicate that the ancients used them in bed as well:

> Nor do our cloaks remain upon the bed.

Leaving aside the frenzied litigants. how can we judge, when we have not yet begun to be wise? Especially since the Academic is standing nearby, ready to draw us back by his cloak and forbid us to believe anyone, while nevertheless offering nothing himself for us to follow.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Highest Good, the Pleasures of Mind and Body, and Virtue

What therefore remains, except that, leaving aside the frenzied and obstinate litigants, we should come to that judge, [Col. 0365B] namely the giver of simple and tranquil wisdom? This wisdom can not only shape us and lead us onto the path, but can also pronounce judgment upon their controversies. It teaches us what the true and highest good of the human being is. Before I begin to speak about this, however, all those opinions must be refuted, so that it may become apparent that none of those men was wise.

Since the question concerns the duty of the human being, the highest good of the highest animal must be established in something that cannot be shared with the other animals. Just as teeth are proper to wild beasts, horns to herds, and wings to birds, so something of his own must be assigned to the human being, without which he would lose the defining principle of his condition. For whatever has been given to all beings for the sake of living or procreating is indeed a natural good; yet the highest good is only that which [Col. 0365C] is proper to each individual kind.

Therefore, the man who believed that the highest good was pleasure of the mind [Col. 0366A] was not wise, because that pleasure—whether it is security or joy—is common to all. I do not even think Aristippus deserves a reply. No one doubts that he, always rushing headlong into bodily pleasures and serving nothing but his belly and Venus, was not a human being. For he lived in such a way that there was no difference between him and a beast except this one thing: he could speak.

But suppose the power of speech were given to a donkey, a dog, or a pig, and you asked them what they wanted when they pursued females so rabidly that they could scarcely be torn away, neglecting even food and drink; why they either drove other males violently away or, even when defeated, did not withdraw but, though often battered by stronger animals, pursued them all the more; why they feared neither rain nor cold, undertook labor, [Col. 0366B] and did not refuse danger. What else would they answer but that bodily pleasure is the highest good; that they seek it so that they may be affected by the most delightful sensations; and that these sensations are worth so much that, for the sake of attaining them, they think they should refuse neither any labor, nor wounds, nor death itself? Shall we therefore seek precepts for living from those who hold the very same opinion as souls devoid of reason?

The Cyrenaics say that virtue itself should be praised because it produces pleasure. “True,” says the obscene dog, or that mud-soiled pig. “For that is why I fight my rival with the utmost exertion of my strength: so that my valor may produce for me the pleasure of which I must necessarily be deprived if I depart defeated.” Shall we therefore learn wisdom from those who are distinguished from cattle and beasts not by their opinion [Col. 0366C] but by their tongue?

To regard freedom from pain [Col. 0367A] as the highest good is an opinion not, certainly, of Peripatetic [Col. 0367A]

[Note: [Col. 0367C] [Notes of Various Commentators on columns 367–368]

Not, certainly, of the Peripatetics. Janus Guilielmus, in *Questions on Plautus’ Menaechmi*, chapter 4, thinks that the reading should be “of wandering Peripatetics” (*plano peripateticorum*), so that, through a novel verbal compound, Lactantius might ridicule both the inconsistency of the Aristotelians’ discourse and their wandering about; for it is well known that vagabonds are called *planes*. ISAEUS.

But of bedridden philosophers. The manuscript has *Clynicorum*. Nothing is more certain than that Lactantius wrote “bedridden philosophers” (*clinicorum philosophorum*). He mockingly calls them “bedridden philosophers”: sick men confined to their beds and discoursing on the happy life of the healthy according to what their present illness dictates. He alludes to clinical physicians, who, belonging to the school of Hippocrates, go around the beds of the sick and prescribe treatments. JANUS GUILIELMUS.—We too approve this emendation. Besides the manuscript cited above, it should be known that this reading is found in three Royal manuscripts, two of which are the oldest; in two Colbertine manuscripts; the Cauc., Vict., Lips., Pal., Em., Ultr., and Brun. manuscripts; and also in one other Royal, one other Colbertine, and one Clermont manuscript. In these last three, “bedridden” appears to have been written by the first hand. The Navarre manuscript and one Clermont manuscript have “pagans,” written by a second hand; the Marmoutier manuscript has the erroneous *Chinicorum* for the genuine *Clinicorum*. For Lactantius adds: “Who does not understand that this was argued by men who were ill and suffering some pain?” Likewise Cyprian, Letter 69, to Magnus: “Let them not be asked whether they are bedridden or Peripatetics”—that is, whether they walk while debating, like the Peripatetics or the Stoics, who customarily discoursed in the portico, or lie in bed suffering from a most serious illness, like the bedridden. For *clinicus* was the name [Col. 0368C] for a person who, without any hope of recovery, could not rise from bed. Certain editions, however, among them Cologne 1544, Betuleius 1563, and de Tournes 1567, read “Cynics” in place of this word “bedridden.”

and Stoic philosophers, but of bedridden philosophers. For who does not understand that this was argued by men who were ill and suffering some pain? What could be more ridiculous than to regard as the highest good something a physician can give? We must therefore suffer pain in order to enjoy the good—and indeed suffer severely and often, so that afterward not suffering may be more pleasant. The most wretched person, therefore, is one who has never suffered pain, because he lacks the good—although we regarded him as most fortunate because he lacked the evil.

Not far removed from this folly was the man who said that suffering no pain whatsoever was the highest good. For, in addition to the fact that every animal flees pain, who can secure for himself this good, whose occurrence we can do nothing but wish for? The highest good, however, cannot make anyone happy [Col. 0367B] unless it is always within his own power. Yet this is provided to all living creatures not by virtue, instruction, or labor, but by nature itself.

Those who joined pleasure to moral worth wished to escape this commonality, but they produced a self-contradictory good, because one who is devoted to pleasure must necessarily lack moral worth, while one who pursues moral worth must lack pleasure.

The Peripatetics’ good is excessively complex and—excepting the goods of the mind, whose identity is itself a matter of great dispute—it may be seen to be shared with beasts. For bodily goods—that is, soundness, painlessness, and health—are no less necessary to dumb animals than to human beings; perhaps they are even more necessary, because a human being can be assisted by medicines and attendants, whereas dumb animals [Col. 0367C] cannot. The same applies to what they call the goods of fortune. For just as a human being needs wealth to sustain his life, so animals [Col. 0368A] need prey and food. Thus, by introducing a good not within the human being’s power, they subjected the whole human being to another’s dominion.

Let us hear Zeno as well, for he sometimes dreams of virtue. “The highest good,” he says, “is to live in agreement with nature.” We must therefore live in the manner of beasts. For all the things that ought to be absent from a human being are found in them: they seek pleasures, fear, deceive, lie in wait, and kill; and, what is most pertinent, they do not know God. What, then, does he teach me when he tells me to live according to nature, which is itself inclined toward what is worse and, by certain gentler enticements, hurls us into vice? Or if he says that dumb animals have one nature and human beings another, because the human being was born for virtue, then he says something of value. Nevertheless, this will not be a definition of the highest good, [Col. 0368B] because there is no animal that does not live according to its own nature.

The man who made knowledge the highest good assigned something proper to the human being. But people seek knowledge for the sake of something else, not for its own sake. For who is content merely to know, without desiring some fruit from his knowledge? Skills are learned so that they may be practiced; they are practiced either to provide the necessities of life, or for pleasure, or for glory. Therefore, something not sought for its own sake is not the highest good.

What difference does it make, then, whether we regard knowledge as the highest good or those very things that knowledge produces from itself—namely livelihood, glory, and pleasure? These are not proper to the human being and therefore are not even the highest goods. For the desire for pleasure and sustenance is present not only in human beings but also in dumb animals. What of the desire [Col. 0368C] for glory? Is it not found in horses, when the victors exult and the defeated grieve?

But if the things produced by knowledge are shared with other animals, knowledge is therefore not the highest good.

Moreover, it is no slight defect in this definition that bare knowledge is posited. For all who know some skill will begin to appear happy—even those who know evil things—so that one who has learned to compound poisons will be as happy as one who has learned to heal. I therefore ask: to what end is knowledge to be referred? If to the causes of natural things, what happiness will be set before me if I know where the Nile originates, or whatever the natural philosophers rave about concerning heaven? What of the fact that there is no knowledge [Col. 0369B] of such matters, but only conjectural opinion, which varies according to people’s intellectual abilities?

It remains that knowledge of good and evil should be the highest good. Why, then, did he prefer to call knowledge, rather than wisdom itself, the highest good, when the meaning and force of the two are the same? Yet no one until now has said that wisdom is the highest good, though that could have been said more fittingly. For knowledge is insufficient for undertaking good and fleeing evil unless virtue is also added. Many philosophers, although they discoursed about good and evil, nevertheless lived otherwise than they spoke, under the compulsion of nature, because they lacked virtue. Virtue joined with knowledge, however, is wisdom.

It remains for us also to refute those who regarded virtue itself as the highest good, an opinion held even by Marcus Tullius. In this they were exceedingly thoughtless. [Col. 0369C] For virtue is not itself the highest good, but is the producer and mother of the highest good, because that good cannot be reached without virtue. Both points are easy to understand.

For I ask whether they think that illustrious [Col. 0370A] good can be reached easily or only with difficulty and labor. Let them sharpen their wits and defend their error. If it can be reached easily and without labor, it is not the highest good. For why should we torment and exhaust ourselves by striving day and night, when what we seek lies so ready to hand that anyone can grasp it without any exertion of mind? But if even any ordinary and moderate good is attained only through labor—because the nature of goods is situated on a steep ascent, while that of evils lies on a downward slope—then the highest good must necessarily be attained through the highest labor.

If this is entirely true, then another virtue is needed so that we may attain the virtue that is called the highest good. This is incongruous and absurd: that virtue should arrive [Col. 0370B] at itself through itself. If no good can be reached except through labor, it is apparent that virtue is that through which it is reached, because the force and function of virtue consist in undertaking and enduring labors.

Therefore, that through which one must necessarily arrive at something else cannot be the highest good. But those men, since they did not know what virtue produced or toward what it tended, and could find nothing more honorable, halted at the mere name of virtue. They said that it should be sought without any advantage set before it and established for themselves as a good something that required another good.

Aristotle did not depart far from them when he regarded virtue together with honorability (*honestas*) as the highest good—as though any virtue could exist without being honorable, or as though, if it possessed anything shameful, it would not cease to be virtue. But he saw that it could happen that virtue might be judged wrongly through perverse judgment; he therefore thought [Col. 0370C] that one must submit to human estimation. Yet whoever does so departs from what is right and good, because it is not within our power to ensure that virtue is honored according to its merits.

For what is honorability (*honestas*) except enduring honor bestowed upon someone by the people’s favorable report? [Col. 0371A] What, then, will happen if, through human error and depravity, an evil reputation follows? Shall we cast virtue aside because the unwise judge it scandalous and shameful? Since virtue can be oppressed and harassed by envy, so that it may itself [Col. 0371A]

A good that is proper and perpetual ought to need no external assistance, but to rely upon and stand firm through its own powers. Accordingly, it must neither hope for any good from man nor shrink from any evil.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Highest Good and the Worship of the True God; and a Refutation of Anaxagoras

I now come to the highest good of true wisdom, whose nature must be defined in this way: first, it must belong to man alone and not fall to any other animal; [Col. 0371B] second, it must belong to the mind alone and be incapable of being shared with the body; finally, it must be incapable of coming to anyone without knowledge and virtue. This delimitation excludes and disposes of all those opinions, for none of the things they have proposed is of this kind.

I shall now state what it is, so that I may demonstrate—as I undertook to do—that all the philosophers were blind and foolish, since they could never see, understand, or even surmise what had been established as man’s highest good. When Anaxagoras was asked for what purpose he had been born, he answered, “To see the heavens and the sun.” Everyone admires this saying and judges it worthy of a philosopher. But I think that, because he could not discover what answer to give, he blurted this out at random rather than remain silent. Yet if he had been wise, [Col. 0371C] he ought to have had the matter considered and pondered within himself; [Col. 0372A] for if anyone does not know the reason for his own existence, he is not even truly a man.

But let us suppose that this statement was not blurted out on the spur of the moment. Let us see how many and how great were the errors he committed in three words. First, he placed the whole function of man in the eyes alone, referring nothing to the mind but everything to the body. What if a man were blind? Would he lose the function of a human being—something that cannot happen without the destruction of the soul? What of the other parts of the body? Will they each be deprived of their respective functions? What of the fact that more depends upon the ears than upon the eyes, since both learning and wisdom can be apprehended through the ears alone, but cannot be apprehended through the eyes alone?

Were you born for the purpose of seeing the heavens and the sun? Who brought you into this place of observation? Or what does your seeing contribute to the heavens and to the nature of things? Presumably it is so that you may praise this immense and wondrous work. Acknowledge, therefore, [Col. 0372B] that God is the founder of all things, who brought you into this world as a witness and eulogist, so to speak, of so great a work of his. You believe it a great thing to see the heavens and the sun; why, then, do you not give thanks to him who is the author of this benefit? Why do you not measure in your mind the excellence, providence, and power of the one whose works you admire? For the one who accomplished wondrous things must necessarily be far more wondrous.

If someone invited you to dinner and you were treated splendidly there, would you seem sane if you valued the pleasure itself more highly than the author of the pleasure? To such an extent do the philosophers refer everything to the body and absolutely nothing to the mind; nor do they see beyond what comes before their eyes. Yet, when all the functions of the body have been set aside, the defining principle of man must be placed in the mind alone. We are therefore not born so that we may see the things that [Col. 0372C] have been made, but so that we may contemplate the maker himself of all [Col. 0373A] things—that is, perceive him with the mind.

Accordingly, if anyone were to ask a man who is truly wise [Col. 0373A]—

—for what purpose he was born, he will answer fearlessly and readily that he was born for the purpose of worshiping God, who brought us into being precisely so that we might serve him. To serve God, moreover, is nothing other than to uphold and preserve justice through good works.

But Anaxagoras, as a man unskilled in divine matters, reduced the greatest subject to the smallest by selecting only two things that he might say were to be observed. Even if he had said that he was born to contemplate the world, although he would thereby have embraced everything and employed a grander expression, he still would not have fulfilled the function of man; for by as much as the soul is of greater value than the body, by so much is God of greater value than the world, because God made and governs the world. It is therefore not the world that must be contemplated by the eyes, since both the world and the eye are bodies, but God [Col. 0373B] must be contemplated by the mind; for just as God himself is immortal, so he willed the mind to be everlasting.

The contemplation of God, moreover, consists in reverencing and worshiping the common father of the human race. But if this was absent from the philosophers, and if they were cast down upon the earth through ignorance of divine things, then Anaxagoras, who said that he had been born to see those things, must be judged to have seen neither heaven nor the sun.

The defining principle of man, therefore, is evident, provided that he is wise: its distinctive quality is humanity. For what is humanity itself but justice? What is justice but piety? And what is piety but acknowledgment of God as father?

[Col. 0374A]

## CHAPTER X. It Is Distinctive of Man to Know and Worship God

The highest good of man, therefore, consists in religion alone; for the other things, even those thought to be distinctive of man, are also found in other animals. Since they distinguish and recognize their respective voices by signs peculiar to themselves, they appear to converse with one another. Some capacity for laughter also appears in them when, with ears caressed, mouth contracted, and eyes relaxed in playfulness, they either play up to a human being or each to their own mates and offspring. Do they not impart something resembling mutual affection and tenderness?

Again, because they make provision for themselves against the future and store away food, they certainly possess foresight. Signs of reason, too, are detected in many of them. For when they seek things useful to themselves, guard against evils, avoid dangers, and prepare hiding places opening apart into several exits, [Col. 0374B] they clearly understand something. Can anyone deny that reason is present in them, when they often outwit man himself? For when those whose task is producing honey occupy the dwellings assigned to them, fortify their camp, construct their homes with indescribable skill, and serve their king, I do not know whether perfect prudence is not found in them.

It is therefore uncertain whether the qualities attributed to man are shared with other living creatures; they are certainly devoid of religion. For my part, I judge that reason has been given to all animals, but to mute animals only for the preservation of life, whereas to man [Col. 0375A] it has also been given for its perpetuation.

And because reason itself is perfect in man, it is called wisdom; and this makes man exceptional, because to him alone it has been given to understand divine things. On this subject Cicero’s statement is true:

> “Among so many kinds of creatures,” he says, “there is no animal except man that possesses any knowledge of God; and among human beings themselves there is no nation either so uncivilized or so savage that, even if it does not know what sort of God it ought to acknowledge, it nevertheless knows that a God ought to be acknowledged.”

From this it follows that the person who recognizes God is, as it were, remembering the source from which he arose. Therefore, those philosophers who wish to free minds from every fear also abolish religion and deprive man of his proper and unique good, which means being cut off from right living and from all humanity; for just as God subjected all [Col. 0375B] living creatures to man, so he subjected man himself to himself—that is, to God.

For why do those very same men argue that the mind must be directed to the place toward which the face is raised? If we must look toward heaven, it is surely for no other purpose than religion. If religion is abolished, we have no relationship with heaven. Accordingly, we must either look there or sink down upon the earth. Even if we wished, we whose posture is upright could not sink down upon the earth. We must therefore look toward heaven, to which the nature of the body summons us.

But if it is agreed that this must be done, it must be done either so that we may serve religion or so that we may understand the rational order of heavenly things. Yet we can in no way understand [Col. 0376A] the rational order of heavenly things, because nothing of that kind can be discovered by thought, as I demonstrated above. Religion, therefore, must be served. Whoever does not embrace it casts himself down upon the earth and, by adopting the life of cattle, renounces his humanity. The untaught, therefore, are wiser: even if they err in choosing a religion, they have nevertheless remembered their own nature and condition.

## CHAPTER XI. On Religion, Wisdom, and the Highest Good

It is therefore established by the consensus of the whole human race that religion ought to be embraced; but the manner in which error occurs within it must be explained. God willed the nature of man to be such that he would desire and seek two things: religion and wisdom. But men are deceived [Col. 0376B] because they either embrace religion while neglecting wisdom, or devote themselves to wisdom alone while neglecting religion, although neither can be true without the other.

They therefore fall into manifold religions, which are false precisely because they have abandoned wisdom, which could have taught them that there cannot be many gods. Or else they devote themselves to wisdom, but to a wisdom that is false precisely because they have neglected the religion of the Most High God, who could have instructed them in knowledge of the truth. Thus people who embrace either one without the other follow a path leading astray and filled with the greatest errors, because in these two things, inseparably joined, are contained both the function of man and the whole truth.

I therefore marvel that not one of all the philosophers ever discovered the seat [Col. 0377A] and dwelling place of the highest good. For they could have investigated it in this way: whatever the highest good is, it must necessarily be set before everyone. Pleasure is sought by all; but it is also shared with beasts, [Col. 0377A]—
