—and it does not possess the quality of moral goodness, brings satiety, is harmful when excessive, diminishes with the advance of age, and does not fall to many people; for those who lack resources—and they are the greater number—must also lack pleasure. Pleasure, therefore, is not the highest good, nor indeed a good at all.

What of riches? Much more so. For they fall to fewer people, generally by chance, often to the indolent, and sometimes through crime; and they are desired by those who already possess them. What of kingship itself? Not even that. For not all people can reign, whereas everyone must necessarily be capable of the highest good.

[Col. 0377B] Let us therefore seek something that is set before everyone. Is it virtue? It cannot be denied that virtue is both a good and certainly a good available to everyone. But if it cannot be blessed, because its power and nature lie in the endurance of evils, it is assuredly not the highest good.

Let us seek something else. Yet nothing more beautiful than virtue and nothing worthier of a wise man can be found. For if vices must be avoided because of their disgracefulness, virtue must therefore be sought because of its beauty. What then? Can something acknowledged to be good and honorable lack recompense and reward, and be so barren that it produces no benefit from itself? That great labor, difficulty, and struggle to overcome the evils with which this life is filled must necessarily produce some great good. What shall we say that good is? [Col. 0378A]

Pleasure? But nothing disgraceful can arise from what is honorable. Riches? Political powers? But those are fragile and fleeting. Glory? Honor? The remembrance of one’s name? But all these do not reside in virtue itself; they depend upon the estimation and judgment of others. For virtue is often hated and afflicted with evil.

The good arising from virtue, however, ought to adhere to it so closely that it cannot be severed or torn away; nor can it otherwise be regarded as the highest good unless it is both proper to virtue and of such a nature that nothing can be added to or taken from it. What of the fact that the functions of virtue consist in despising all these things? For not to covet, seek, or love pleasures, riches, powers, honors, and all those things regarded as goods, as others do when conquered by desire, [Col. 0378B] is assuredly the work of virtue.

Virtue therefore brings about something else, something higher and more glorious; nor does it resist these present goods in vain, except because it desires greater and truer goods. Let us not despair of being able to discover it, provided only that thought examines everything. For the rewards being sought are neither trivial nor frivolous.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Twofold Struggle of Body and Soul, and on Seeking Virtue for the Sake of Eternal Life

But since the question is why we are born, we may investigate what virtue brings about in the following way. There are two things of which man consists: mind and body. [Col. 0379A] Many things are proper to the mind, many to the body, and many are common to both, as virtue itself is. [Col. 0379A]—

> **Founder of the Megarian school.** He now begins a new argument against those who dimly and, as it were, through a mist perceived the highest good. The argument resembles Paul’s argument against the Athenians concerning the altar of the unknown God. These observations appear to have been taken from Cicero’s fourth book of the *Academic Questions*. I shall quote the whole passage: “Nor did the Megarians depart far from Plato. Their school was renowned, as I find it written, and its founder was Xenophanes, followed by Parmenides and Zeno. Accordingly, these philosophers were called Eretrians. Later came Euclides, a disciple of Socrates, a Megarian, from whom those same men are called Megarians, [Col. 0380C] who said that the sole good was that which was one, similar, and always the same. They too derived much from Plato. But from Menedemus, because he was an Eretrian, they were called Eretrians. Their entire good was placed in the mind and in the mind’s keenness, by which the truth was discerned.” From these words it is evident that Lactantius’s text is incomplete, for it was also relevant to the description of the highest good that it should be one. In his *Philosophical History*, [Col. 0380D] Galen traces the origin of this school to Stilpo the Megarian, a pupil of Euclides. But both reason itself and the authority of Laertius make Cicero’s account more probable. BETULEIUS.

>
> **They deny, etc.** On this, see Cicero, Book V of the *Tusculan Disputations*.

Whenever virtue is referred to the body, it is called strength, for the sake of distinction. Since strength is therefore applicable to each, a struggle is set before each and, from the struggle, victory for each. Because the body is solid and tangible, it must necessarily fight with solid and tangible things. But because the mind is subtle and invisible, it engages enemies that cannot be seen or touched.

What are the mind’s enemies but desires, vices, and sins? If virtue conquers and drives these away, the mind will be spotless and pure. From what, then, can it be gathered what the strength of the mind brings about? Clearly from its conjoined and corresponding counterpart—that is, from bodily strength. When bodily strength enters into an encounter [Col. 0379B] and contest, what does it seek from victory other than life? For whether you fight with a man or with a beast, the struggle is for preservation.

Therefore, just as the body attains by victory the result that it does not perish, so too does the mind attain the result that it endures. And just as the body, when conquered by its enemies, is punished with death, so the mind, when overcome by vices, must necessarily die. What difference, then, will there be between the struggle of the mind and that of the body, except that the body seeks temporal life, whereas the mind seeks everlasting life?

If, therefore, virtue is not blessed through itself, since its entire power lies, as I have said, in enduring evils; if it neglects everything coveted as good; if its highest degree lies open to death, since it often rejects the life sought by others and courageously accepts the death that others fear; [Col. 0379C] if it must necessarily produce some great good from itself, because labors endured and overcome even to the point of death cannot be without reward; if no reward worthy of it is found on earth, since it despises everything fragile and [Col. 0380A] fleeting—what remains except that it must produce something heavenly, since it disdains all earthly things, and must strive toward higher things, since it looks down upon the lowly? This can be nothing other than immortality.

Euclides, therefore, a philosopher deservedly not without distinction and the founder of the Megarian school, dissented from the others and said that the highest good is that which is similar and always the same. He certainly understood the nature of the highest good, although he did not explain what it was. It is immortality, and absolutely nothing else, because it alone can neither be diminished, increased, nor changed.

Seneca too, unwittingly, happened to acknowledge that there is no reward of virtue other than immortality. For in praising virtue in the book he wrote *On Untimely Death*, he says:

> “Virtue is the one thing [Col. 0380B] that can bestow immortality upon us and make us equal to the gods.”

The Stoics also, whom he followed, deny that anyone can be made blessed without virtue. The reward of virtue, therefore, is the blessed life, if virtue—as has rightly been said—produces the blessed life. Virtue must therefore not, as they say, be sought for its own sake, but for the sake of the blessed life that necessarily follows virtue. This argument could have taught them what the highest good was.

This present bodily life, however, cannot be blessed, because through the body it is subject to evils. Epicurus calls God blessed and incorruptible because he is everlasting. Blessedness must be perfect, so that there is nothing capable of troubling, diminishing, or changing it. Nor can anything be considered blessed unless it is incorruptible. [Col. 0380C] But nothing is incorruptible except that which is immortal. Immortality alone, therefore, is blessed, because it cannot be corrupted or dissolved.

But if virtue can belong to man—and no one can deny that it can—blessedness can belong to him as well. For it cannot happen that one endowed with virtue should be [Col. 0381A] miserable. If blessedness can belong to man, then immortality can belong to man as well, which—

Moreover, that many in antiquity were involved in the same error can be gathered from Alfonso de Castro’s *On Heresies*, in the chapter on the Resurrection. Rejecting the advice of his father, who urged exile instead, the son killed himself for the preservation of his country. This tragic story is found in Euripides’ *Phoenician Women*, in Book X of Statius’s *Thebaid*, and in Philostratus, no. 4. Plutarch mentions it in *Pelopidas*, and Juvenal in Satire 14:

The highest good, therefore, is found to be immortality alone. No other animal and no body attains it, nor can it come to anyone without the virtue of knowledge—that is, without knowledge of God and justice. How true and upright the desire for it is is shown by the longing for this present life: although it is temporary and utterly full of toil, it is nevertheless sought and desired by everyone. Old people and children alike, kings and the lowest alike, and, finally, the wise and the foolish alike desire it. So great is the value—as Anaxagoras thought—of contemplating heaven and the light itself that one may willingly endure every kind of misery. Since, therefore, this laborious and brief life is regarded as a great good by the common agreement not only of human beings but also of all other living creatures, [Col. 0381B] it is evident that this same life becomes the highest and perfect good if it is both without end and free from every evil. Finally, no one would ever have existed who despised even this brief life or submitted to death except in the hope of a longer life. For those who voluntarily offered themselves to death for the safety of their fellow citizens—Menoeceus at Thebes, Codrus at Athens, Curtius at Rome, and the two Mures—would never have preferred death to the advantages of life unless they had believed that they would attain immortality in the estimation of their fellow citizens. Although they did not know the immortal life, nevertheless the reality did not deceive them. For if virtue despises riches and wealth because they are fragile, and pleasures because they are brief, then it also despises [Col. 0381C] a fragile and brief life in order to attain one that is substantial and [Col. 0382A] everlasting. Thus thought itself, proceeding in orderly fashion and considering the whole, leads us to that excellent and singular good for whose sake we are born. If the philosophers had done this—if they had not preferred stubbornly to defend whatever they had once taken hold of—they would certainly have arrived at this truth, as I have just shown. Even if this insight did not belong to those who extinguish heavenly souls together with their bodies, nevertheless those who discuss the immortality of the soul ought to have understood that virtue was set before us so that, once our passions had been subdued and our desire for earthly things overcome, our souls, pure and victorious, might return to God—that is, to their origin. For this reason alone among living creatures we stand erect to look upon heaven, so that we may believe that our highest good is in the highest place. For this reason we alone [Col. 0382B] apprehend religion, so that from this we may know that the human spirit is not mortal, because it both desires and recognizes God, who is immortal.

Accordingly, of all the philosophers who embraced either knowledge or virtue as the highest good, they did indeed hold to the path of truth, but they did not arrive at its summit. For these are the two things that together produce what is sought. Knowledge enables us to know how and where we must go; virtue enables us to arrive. One is worthless without the other, for virtue arises from knowledge, and the highest good from virtue. The blessed life, therefore, which philosophers have always sought and still seek, is found neither in the worship of the gods nor in [Col. 0382C] philosophy; and for this reason it could not be discovered by them, [Col. 0383A] because they did not seek the highest good in the highest place but in the lowest. What, then, is the highest, if not heaven and God, from whom the soul originates? What is the lowest, if not the earth, from which the body comes? And so, although some philosophers assigned the highest good not to the body but to the soul, nevertheless, because they referred it to this present life, [Col. 0383A]

By his simplicity he so stopped the mouth of the man who was arguing arrogantly that the latter fell silent, to the astonishment of everyone. they turned back toward the body, to which belongs all this time that is spent on earth. It is therefore no wonder that they did not comprehend the highest good, because whatever pertains to the body and is devoid of immortality must necessarily be the lowest. Blessedness, then, does not befall a human being in the manner in which the philosophers supposed. Rather, it befalls him not so that he is blessed while he lives in the body—which, of course, must decay in order to be dissolved—but when the soul, [Col. 0383B] released from association with the body, lives in spirit alone. In this one way we can be blessed in this life: if we appear to be anything but blessed; if, fleeing the enticements of pleasures and serving virtue alone, we live amid every toil and misery, which are the exercises and supports of virtue; and if, finally, we keep to that rough and difficult road that has been opened for us toward blessedness. The highest good, therefore, which makes people blessed, can exist only in that religion and doctrine to which the hope of immortality is joined.

## CHAPTER XIII  
### On the Immortality of the Soul, and on Wisdom, Philosophy, and Eloquence

[Col. 0383C] The subject appears to require at this point that, since we have shown [Col. 0384A] immortality to be the highest good, we should also establish that the soul itself is immortal. On this matter there is immense disagreement among the philosophers; yet those who held a true view of the soul were unable to explain or prove anything. For, being without this divine instruction, they brought forward neither true arguments by which they might prevail nor testimonies by which they might prove their position. But we shall treat this question more suitably in the final book, when we shall have to discuss the blessed life.

There remains that third part of philosophy which they call *logikēn* (λογικὴν, “logic”), in which the whole of dialectic and every method of speaking are contained. Divine instruction has no need of this, because wisdom is not in the tongue but in the heart; nor does it matter what kind of language you employ, for realities, not words, are sought. We are not discussing the grammarian or orator, [Col. 0384B] whose knowledge concerns how one ought to speak, but the wise person, whose doctrine concerns how one ought to live. But if neither that physical system nor this logical one is necessary, because they cannot make anyone blessed, it follows that the entire power of philosophy is contained in ethics alone, to which Socrates is said to have devoted himself after casting all else aside. Since I have also shown that the philosophers erred in this part, because they did not comprehend the highest good for the sake of attaining which we were born, it is evident that all philosophy is false and empty, because it neither trains us for the duties of justice nor confirms the function and rational purpose of the human being. Let those, therefore, who suppose philosophy to be wisdom know that they are mistaken. Let them not be drawn by anyone’s authority, but rather favor [Col. 0384C] and approach the truth. There is no room here [Col. 0385A] for rashness: the eternal penalty of folly must be endured if either an empty personage or a false opinion has deceived us.

GALLAEUS.—Like pipes. A proverb concerning a chance occurrence, derived from the story of Marsyas the Phrygian. But I think the story should be related from Hyginus as follows. Minerva is said to have been the first to make pipes from a stag’s bone and to have come to play them at a banquet of the gods. When Juno and Venus mocked her because she was gray-eyed and puffed out her cheeks, she appeared ugly and was ridiculed for her playing. She went into the forest of Ida, to a spring, and, playing there, looked at herself in the water and saw that she had deserved the ridicule. She therefore cast away the pipes there and pronounced a curse that whoever picked them up should suffer severe punishment. Marsyas, the son of Oeagrus, a shepherd and one of the Satyrs, found them. By practicing on them continually, he made their sound sweeter day by day, to such a degree that he challenged Apollo to a contest between the pipes and the lyre. When Apollo arrived, they appointed the Muses as judges. Just as Marsyas was about to depart victorious, Apollo turned his lyre over and produced the same sound; Marsyas could not do this with the pipes. Apollo therefore handed the defeated Marsyas, bound to a tree, over to a Scythian; from Marsyas’ blood the river was named Marsyas. See the mythology in [Col. 0387B] Fulgentius, Book III. Plato and Ovid write that he was a satyr. Whoever wishes to know more should see Plutarch’s *On Music* and Apuleius, Book I of the *Florida*. Moreover, concerning his contest with Apollo and the flaying of Marsyas, read Ovid, Book VI of the *Metamorphoses*, and Diodorus Siculus, Book IV of the *Antiquities*. BETULEIUS.]

whatever sort of creature he may be, if he trusts himself—that is, if he trusts a human being—even if I do not call him a fool for failing to see his own error, he is certainly arrogant, because he dares claim for himself something that the human condition does not admit.

How greatly that very man, the highest authority on the Roman language, is mistaken may be clearly seen from the following statement. After saying in his books *On Duties* that philosophy was nothing other than the pursuit of wisdom, and that wisdom itself was knowledge of divine and human things, he then added:

> “As for the man who censures its pursuit, I cannot at all understand what he thinks worthy of praise. For if delight of mind and relief from cares are sought, what can be compared with the studies of those who [Col. 0385B] are always investigating something that pertains and contributes to living well and blessedly? Or if account is taken of constancy and virtue, either this is the art through which we attain them, or there is no art at all. To say that there is no art of the greatest matters, when there is no artless treatment of the smallest, is characteristic of people who speak without sufficient consideration and who err in the greatest matters. But if there is some discipline of virtue, where will it be sought once you have departed from this kind of learning?”

For my part, although I have taken pains to acquire such slight ability in learning as I could for the sake of my pursuit of teaching, nevertheless I have never been eloquent, since I have not even set foot in the forum. Yet the very excellence of my case must necessarily make me eloquent; for eloquently and copiously defending it, knowledge of divinity and truth itself are sufficient. I would therefore wish Cicero to rise from the dead for a little while, so that the most eloquent of men might be instructed by an insignificant, unpolished man: first, what the person who censures the pursuit called philosophy considers worthy of praise; then, that philosophy is neither an art through which virtue and justice are learned, nor is there any other such art, as he supposed; and finally, since there is a discipline of virtue, where it should be sought after one has departed from that kind of learning. This was something he did not ask in order to hear and learn. From whom could he have heard it, when no one knew it? But, as he was accustomed to do in legal cases, he wished to press the matter by a question and lead his opponent to an admission, as though confident that absolutely no answer could be given that would prevent philosophy from being the teacher of virtue.

Indeed, in the *Tusculan Disputations* he openly professed this, turning his speech toward philosophy itself, as though displaying himself in a declamatory style of speaking:

> “O philosophy, guide of life,” he says, “O discoverer of virtue and expeller of vices, what could not only we, but human life altogether, have been [Col. 0386B] without you? You were the inventor of laws; you were the teacher of morals and discipline.”

As though philosophy itself possessed any perception, and the one who bestowed it ought not rather to be praised! He might in the same way have given thanks to food and drink because life cannot continue without them, although in those things there is no consciousness and therefore no awareness of conferring a benefit. Yet just as those things are nourishment for the body, so wisdom is nourishment for the soul.

But if one reads with the commonly used editions, “lest I censure the Greeks,” it is not apparent to what this could refer. Nevertheless, this latter reading is found in all the printed editions and almost all the manuscripts. So says Thomasius.

Fickleness. Cicero speaks of this especially in his speech *For Lucius Flaccus*.

Calls it an invention of the gods, and praises it personified in poetic fashion. I have restored this from all the manuscripts and most printed editions. See Cicero in Book I of the *Tusculan Disputations*, where his words are: “Philosophy, indeed, the mother of all the arts—what else is it but, as Plato says, a gift, or, as I say, an invention of the gods?” See the passage in Plato’s *Timaeus*.

Praises it to its face. Elegantly, as Horace, *Satires* I.5: “Having made very many jokes to his face.” The same expression occurs in Terence’s *Brothers* II.4: “To praise someone openly to his face.” BUN.

Would anyone? I read thus with the manuscripts and almost all the editions. The Graphius, Thysius, and Gallaeus editions have, “Who, then, would?”—I print it thus on the authority of the Emmanuel, Cambridge, and Reimmann manuscripts and all the early editions from 1465 to 1513. Lactantius, Book V, chapter 10: “Would anyone think?” Cicero, *Second Philippic* 32: “Can anyone divine?” *Tusculan Disputations* V.2: “Does anyone dare censure it?” BUN.

To be sewn, in your judgment, into a sack. This was once the punishment of parricides who had killed their father or mother. Isidore of Seville, in his glosses: “A sack is a garment made from esparto grass in the manner of a purse, coated at public expense with pitch and bitumen. Parricides were enclosed in it with an ape, a snake, and a cock; once sewn shut, it was cast into the sea, and as the animals struggled with one another, the human being was afflicted with still greater punishment.” This statement must certainly be understood with qualification, for at first nothing was sewn into the sack with the parricide. See Valerius Maximus, Book I, chapter 1; and Plautus, concerning the sea, in the lost *Vidularia*, as quoted by Priscian:

> Order this man to be sewn into a sack  
> And carried out to sea, if you desire a good  
> Grain supply.

As the number of parricides increased day by day, the severity of the punishment was augmented. Previously, therefore, they were beaten with blood-colored rods, as Modestinus reports in Book IX of the *Digest*, on the *Lex Pompeia concerning Parricides*. Their heads were also wrapped, according to Festus under the word *obvolvere*. But when they began to sew parricides into sacks, they also began to enclose snakes with the guilty person, as Plutarch records concerning Gaius Villius; see Lucius Seneca, *Controversies* V.4; Livy, Fifth Decade, Book VIII; and Valerius Maximus, Book I, chapter 1. Later they added an ape (Juvenal, Satire 13). Finally, they also sewed a dog and cock into the sack, according to Isidore in the passage cited above. This seems first to have been added by Constantine, in the sole law of the Code, “Concerning Those Who Have Killed Parents or Children.” Dempster.—Eight Royal manuscripts, including two of the oldest, three Colbert, two Brussels, and the Utrecht, Leipzig, and one Clermont manuscript, as well as the Roman editions of 1468 and 1470, have *culleum*; the ancients pronounced the word in this way. Parricides sewn into this sack were cast into rivers or the sea under Roman law. See Cicero, *For Sextus Roscius*, chapter 11; Seneca, *On Clemency*, Book I, chapter 23; and Suetonius, *Augustus* 33. This applied if the sea was near; otherwise, according to an enactment of the deified Hadrian, they were to be exposed to wild beasts.

And created the human being. Thus read one ancient Bologna manuscript; seven Royal manuscripts, two of which are among the oldest; and the Caucasus, Penitentiary, Palatine, Junius, Utrecht, Gotha, five Oxford, six Colbert, Sorbonne, three Leipzig, Turnèbe, two Clermont, and Brussels manuscripts, together with five printed editions. Lactantius commonly uses “beget” in the sense of “create,” here and elsewhere. Two recent Royal manuscripts, the Cambridge manuscript, and twelve commonly used editions have “fashioned,” a word likewise familiar to Lactantius: *Divine Institutes* IV.4 and VII.14; *Epitome* 65, etc. [Col. 0389C] It is also a frequent expression in Cicero for God to be said to “beget” the human being—that is, to create him. Certain editors, not understanding that force of the word, substituted “fashioned.”]

of wisdom was praised as a god—for this is what he says:

> No one, I think, will ever be born in a mortal body.
>
> For if, as the very majesty of things, once known, demands,
>
> We must speak, he was a god, a god, illustrious Memmius—

nevertheless, God ought not to have been praised on the ground that he discovered wisdom, but because he made the human being capable of receiving wisdom. For one diminishes praise when one praises a part instead of the whole. But Lucretius praised him as a human being, though for that very reason he ought to have regarded him as a god, because he discovered wisdom. For he says:

> Surely it will be fitting  
> To deem this man worthy of a place among the gods?

From this it is apparent that he wished to praise either Pythagoras, who, as I said above (chapter 2), was the first to call himself a philosopher, [Col. 0387B] or Thales of Miletus, who is reported to have been the first to discuss the nature of things. Thus, while he seeks to [Col. 0388A] exalt a human being, he debases the subject itself. For it is not something great if it could be discovered by a human being. Yet he may be granted indulgence as a poet.

But that same man who was the perfect orator and the greatest philosopher both censures the Greeks, whose fickleness he always condemns, and nevertheless follows them. He personifies wisdom itself in poetic fashion—which elsewhere he calls sometimes a gift and sometimes an invention of the gods—and praises it to its face. He also complains bitterly that some people have arisen who censure it:

> “Would anyone,” he says, “dare to censure the parent of life, stain himself with this act of parricide, and be so impiously ungrateful?”

We, then, Marcus Tullius, are parricides and, in your judgment, must be sewn into a sack because we deny that philosophy is the parent of life? Or are you the parricide, because you are so impiously ungrateful toward God—not this god whose image you venerate [Col. 0388B] seated on the Capitol, but him who made the world and created the human being, and who also [Col. 0389A] bestowed wisdom itself among his heavenly benefits? [Col. 0389A]

[Note: [Col. 0389C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 389–390]

Among his heavenly benefits. Thus all the manuscripts, together with the old Roman and Paris editions. The other editions have “among his other heavenly benefits.”

Can you profess? I have emended this from nine editions and nineteen handwritten copies. See what follows. Two other Royal manuscripts and four printed editions read “can he profess?”

As yet. That is, “until now.”

The most powerful consul. Marcus Antonius, who held the consulship with Gaius Caesar in the year in which Caesar was killed, 710 from the founding of the City. Cicero wrote nine invective speeches against him, which, according to Fabius, he called *Philippics* in imitation of Demosthenes. BETULEIUS.

Rendered illustrious. See Cicero in the preface to Book I of the *Tusculan Disputations*.

Tell me. *Cedo* is an old imperative verb and means “say”; it occurs very frequently in this sense in Terence. It is also used in the sense of “give” or “hand over.” Phaedrus, Fable V.2: “Give me that man,” he says. See Paraeus’ *Critical Lexicon*, p. 185.

That you know nothing. On this saying, see Cicero, Book I of the *Academic Questions*, concerning Socrates.

But to me. This passage of Cicero is missing in its entirety; it is found only among the fragments of the *Academic Questions*. With her teaching. This is the reading of the manuscripts and of the editions of Isaeus in the margin, Cellarius, and Walch; the other editions have “teaching her.”

But how you admitted the truth of philosophy. Thus read nineteen manuscripts and all the printed editions. Thomasius prefers “but how, trusting in philosophical truth,” as found in one ancient Bologna and three Royal manuscripts, or “trusting to philosophical truth,” as in another recent Bologna manuscript and the Balliol, Caucasus, Palatine, and Leipzig manuscripts. I have judged that nothing should be changed and have retained the reading of the other manuscripts, because the word “admitted” is entirely suitable and appears in every printed edition.

To his son, etc. In *On Duties*, indeed, he denies that the duties of justice can be preserved apart from social association, and for that reason condemns the idle and inactive life of philosophers, as Lactantius himself will indicate below, chapter 16. But I find these words nowhere in Cicero. BETULEIUS.—They occur only among the fragments.

Of folly and emptiness. The Emmanuel and Leipzig manuscripts have “of folly and vanity,” which is more suitable to the subject and matter, though not to the rhythm of the orator. BUN.

Of folly and emptiness. Thus the majority of Sparke’s manuscripts, and the Gotha, Reimmann, Bologna, Roman, Subiaco, Rostock, and Venice editions of 1471 and 1497—indeed, all the printed editions—read; compare Book III, chapter 13: “It is apparent that all philosophy is empty”; and Book VII, chapter 26: “Those who defend empty philosophy.” BUN.

You admit the truth. I have restored this from the oldest manuscripts—two Bologna, the Caucasus, three Royal, Taxius, and Penitentiary manuscripts. Thirteen recent manuscripts, two old Roman editions, and thirteen printed editions have “you used to admit.”

Seneca. We do indeed find this thought scattered throughout his books, but not these exact words in their entirety; perhaps they were taken from a lost book. CELL.

Philosophy is nothing other than. Seneca’s teaching is everywhere interspersed with ideas of this kind. The words quoted here, however, have perished with most of his other writings. In Letters 90 and 95 he argues that philosophy is the law of life. BETUL.

The right method of living. Thus the editions of Cellarius and Walch, together with all the manuscripts except two recent Royal manuscripts and the Junius manuscript, which have “living rightly,” as do the printed editions.]

Do you call her the teacher of virtue or the parent of life, when anyone who approaches her must necessarily become far more uncertain than he was before? Of what virtue is she the teacher, when the philosophers themselves still cannot explain where virtue is situated? Of what life is she the parent, when the teachers themselves have been worn out by old age and death before they determined how one ought to live? Of what truth can you profess her to be the discoverer, when you often testify that, although there has been so great a multitude of philosophers, nevertheless no wise person has yet existed? What, then, has that teacher of life taught you? Was it to assail the most powerful consul with abuse and, through venomous speeches, make him an enemy of his country? But let us pass over those things, which can be excused under the name of fortune.

You certainly studied philosophy, and did so [Col. 0389B] more diligently than anyone ever did, since you became acquainted with every branch of learning, as you yourself are accustomed to boast, rendered philosophy itself illustrious in Latin literature, and showed yourself an imitator of Plato. Tell me, then, what you learned, or in what school you discovered the truth. In the Academy, of course, which you followed and approved. But it teaches nothing except that you should know that you know nothing. Your own books therefore convict you of how nothing useful for life can be learned from philosophy. These are your words:

> “But to me we seem not merely blind to wisdom, but dull and obtuse even toward those very things that appear in some measure capable of being discerned.”

If, therefore, philosophy is the teacher of life, why did you regard yourself as blind, dull, and obtuse, when, with her teaching, you ought both to have perceived and understood and to have walked in the clearest [Col. 0389C] light? But how you admitted the truth of philosophy [Col. 0390A] is shown by the precepts you composed for your son, in which you advise that the precepts of philosophy should indeed be learned, but that one must live in a civic manner.

What more contradictory statement could be made? If the precepts of philosophy must be learned, they must surely be learned so that we may live rightly and wisely. Or, if one must live in a civic manner, philosophy is therefore not wisdom, since it is better to live in a civic manner than philosophically. For if that which is called philosophy is wisdom, the person who does not live according to philosophy certainly lives foolishly. But if the person who lives in a civic manner does not live foolishly, it follows that the person who lives philosophically does live foolishly. By your own judgment, therefore, philosophy has been condemned as folly and emptiness.

In the *Consolation* also—that is, in a work that was not written in jest—you delivered this judgment concerning philosophy:

> “But I do not know what error, or what pitiable ignorance of the truth, holds us.”

Where, then, is philosophy’s authority as teacher? Or what did that parent of life teach you, if you pitiably remain ignorant of the truth? But if this confession of error and ignorance was forced almost against your will from the depths of your heart, why do you not at last admit the truth to yourself: that philosophy, which you exalted to heaven with praises even though it teaches nothing, cannot be the teacher of virtue?

## CHAPTER XV  
### Seneca’s Error in Philosophy, and How the Philosophers’ Teaching Conflicts with Their Life

Seneca, led by the same error—for who could keep to the true path when Cicero was going astray?—says: “Philosophy [Col. 0390C] is nothing other than the right method of living, or [Col. 0391A] the knowledge of living honorably, or the art of conducting life rightly.” [Col. 0391A]

[Note: [Col. 0391C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 391–392]

*Ars rectae vitae agendae* (“the art of conducting a right life”). Francius preferred to read *recte* (“the art of conducting life rightly”), with four Royal, two Clermont, and the *Brun.* manuscript.

And whoever has said. I have restored this from five commonly used editions and all the manuscripts except the Caucasus and Emmanuel manuscripts and seven editions, which have “said.”

Because he called it the rule of life, he restored its own name to it. I wished the word “name” to be enclosed in brackets, because it is absent from the English and Leipzig manuscripts, and when it is removed the sentence is sufficiently polished and ornate. CELL.

To the common name of philosophy. Thus each of the philosophers looked not to other schools but especially to his own. Yet I wonder why Lactantius here makes Seneca an Academic when he was professedly a Stoic; that Lactantius was not ignorant of this is evident from other passages. From BETULEIUS.

To be named. I have restored this from the editions of Turnèbe, Cellarius, and Walch and from all the manuscripts except two recent Royal manuscripts and thirteen commonly used editions, which have “to be called”; the Florence edition has “to call.”

Which renders everything uncertain. Thus the Royal-Puteanus and many other manuscripts. Others, together with the printed editions, have “in order that it may render everything uncertain.”

To train life. The second Leipzig manuscript and the Rostock edition have “to establish life.” The accepted reading is correct. Book III, chapter 30: “They do not train life but disturb it.” Hence Book III, chapter 13: “Nor does philosophy train us for the duties of justice.” BUN.]

Good without learning. Cicero, *For Archias*, ch. 7: “I acknowledge that many men have possessed an excellent character and virtue, and that without learning . . . they have proved self-controlled and serious,” etc. BUN.

Although countless persons exist . . . worthy of praise, who, then, is there? Nearly all the manuscripts have this punctuation. But Cauc., Jun., and eight printed editions read: “although countless persons exist . . . worthy of praise. Who, then, is there?”

If anyone carefully investigates their conduct. Better in the Regio-Puteanus manuscript, two other Royal manuscripts, two Colbertine, two Clermont, the Cottonian, and the Merton manuscript than in the others, which lack the preposition.

Doing at home those things. Nine manuscripts place *then* before this. Four others read: “when they do those things at home.”

Acknowledges. The passage occurs near the beginning of Cicero’s second book of the *Tusculan Disputations*.

Who regards true discipline, not a display of his knowledge. Thus the ancient codices, according to Thomasius. Others omit [Col. 0392D] *true* and write “of his own knowledge”; but the Thomasian reading seems more convenient and appropriate.

One may see. Thus nearly all the manuscripts and printed editions. Three manuscripts and the same number of printed editions have “one might see”; the Caucasian manuscript and four editions have “but one might see.”

So that their life. Thus the manuscripts and nearly all printed editions. Cornelius Nepos also. The manuscripts and four printed editions give this more fully than two recent Royal manuscripts and eleven commonly received editions, which read: “and Cornelius Nepos.” It is found among the fragments of Cornelius Nepos, not in the surviving work of Cornelius itself.]

“We shall not go wrong if we say that philosophy is the law of living well and honorably. And whoever calls it the rule of life has given it its due.” Here he plainly did not have regard to the common name of philosophy. For since philosophy is divided among several sects and schools, and possesses nothing certain—indeed, nothing upon which all agree with one mind and one voice—what could be more false than to call philosophy the rule of life, when the diversity of its precepts obstructs and confuses the straight path? Or to call it the law of living well, when its principal provisions are widely discordant? Or the science of conducting life, when, by frequently asserting contradictory things, it accomplishes nothing except that no one knows anything?

For I ask whether he thinks the Academy is philosophy or not. I do not suppose he will deny it. [Col. 0391B] But if it is, then none of those descriptions applies to philosophy, which renders everything uncertain, repeals law, recognizes no art, overthrows reason, corrupts the rule, and utterly abolishes knowledge. All those descriptions are therefore false, because they cannot apply to something always uncertain and still explaining nothing. Accordingly, no rational system, science, or law of living well has been established except in this one, true, and heavenly wisdom, which was unknown to the philosophers. For earthly wisdom, because it is false, becomes various and manifold and is wholly at variance with itself. And just as there is one God, the creator and ruler of this world, and one truth, so wisdom [Col. 0391C] must be one and simple, because whatever is true and [Col. 0392A] good cannot be perfect unless it is unique.

But if philosophy were able to shape one’s life, none except philosophers would be good, and all who had not learned it would always be evil. Yet countless people exist, and have always existed, who are or were good without any learning, whereas among philosophers it has very rarely happened that anyone did something in life worthy of praise. Who, then, does not see that those men are not teachers of the virtue which they themselves lack? For if anyone carefully investigates their conduct, he will find them irascible, greedy, lustful, arrogant, insolent, and concealing their vices beneath the pretense of wisdom—doing at home the very things they would have denounced in the schools.

Perhaps I am lying for the sake of making an accusation. Does not Tullius himself both acknowledge and lament this very thing? “How rare is it,” he says, [Col. 0392B] “to find a philosopher whose character, disposition, and manner of life are such as reason demands? Who regards true discipline not as a display of knowledge but as the law of life? Who obeys himself and complies with his own decrees? One may see some possessed by such frivolity and boastfulness that it would have been better for them never to have studied; others greedy for money, others for glory; and many enslaved to lusts, so that their speech is astonishingly at war with their life.”

Cornelius Nepos also writes thus to the same Cicero: “So far am I from thinking philosophy the mistress of life and the perfecter of a happy life that I believe no one has greater need of teachers in living [Col. 0392C] than most of those who occupy themselves in discussing it. [Col. 0393A] For I see that a great proportion of those who most acutely teach modesty and self-restraint in the school themselves live amid desires for every kind of lust.”

Likewise Seneca in his *Exhortations*: [Col. 0393A]

*Exhortations.* This book will be cited below, in Book VI, the final chapter; it has long since perished, as have other works of the same philosopher.

Eloquent in denouncing themselves. Minucius, ch. 38, calls philosophers “eloquent against their own vices.” Jerome, to the monk Rusticus, folio mark 47: “We often accuse what we ourselves do, and, eloquent against ourselves, inveigh against our own vices.” BUN.

You would think they had publicly declared evidence against themselves. Thus I emended the text from the oldest and best manuscripts—three Royal, one Bologna, Cauc., Jun., and one Colbertine—and the commonly received editions Aldus, Paris 1525, Gymnicus, Junta, Craphius, Tornesius 1553. With Lais. Lais, the most famous courtesan, is called the Corinthian because, when she was carried away as a little girl from Sicily to the Peloponnese among other captives, she lived at Corinth. Ovid, *Amores*, Book I, elegy 5, v. 13:

> And Lais, loved by many men.

The courtesan was plainly wiser. To a most notorious courtesan. Arguing that pleasure, etc. For that reason Xenophon, hostile toward him, composed a book against pleasure, as Laertius reports in his life of Aristippus. ISAEUS.

Why should I speak of the Cynics? Thus Augustine also thinks in many passages that the Cynics were named from their doglike shamelessness; for this reason Cicero too, in *On Duties*, seems to exclude them from the discussion of propriety. Others, however, think they were so named from barking and doglike biting. Laertius indeed testifies that the name arose ἀπὸ τῶν σκωμμάτων, “from their taunts”; Galen says δι’ ἔνστασιν, “because of their contentious opposition.” In Lucian’s *Auction of Lives*, however, they are characterized as ὑλακτοῦντες καὶ δάκνοντες, “barking and biting.” BETUL.—The founder of the Cynics was Antisthenes, a pupil of Socrates and teacher of Diogenes, a man more acute than learned.]

“Most philosophers,” he says, “are of such a kind: eloquent in denouncing themselves. If you heard them declaiming against greed, lust, and ambition, you would think they had publicly declared evidence against themselves, so thoroughly do the reproaches they utter in public rebound upon themselves. They should be regarded no differently from physicians whose signboards promise remedies while their boxes contain poisons. Some, moreover, are not even restrained by shame over their vices, but devise defenses for their depravity, so that they may appear to sin honorably.

“‘The wise man,’ says the same Seneca, ‘will even do things he will not approve, in order to find a passage to greater things. He will not abandon good morals, but will [Col. 0393B] adapt them to the occasion; and the things which others use for glory or pleasure, he will use for the sake of accomplishing his business.’”

Then, shortly afterward:

> “The wise man will do everything that the profligate and the ignorant do, but not in the same manner or with the same purpose.” Yet it makes no difference with what intention you do what it is vicious to have done, because deeds are seen, but intention is not.

Aristippus, master of the Cyrenaics, had relations with Lais, a celebrated prostitute. That serious teacher of philosophy defended this disgrace by saying that there was a great difference between himself and the other lovers of Lais: [Col. 0394A] he possessed Lais, whereas the others were possessed by Lais. O splendid wisdom, worthy of imitation by the good! Would you entrust your children to this man’s instruction, so that they might learn to possess a courtesan? He said that there was some difference between himself and ruined men: namely, that they squandered their property, while he indulged in luxury for nothing.

In this the courtesan was plainly wiser, for she used the philosopher as a pimp, so that all the young men, corrupted by their teacher’s example and authority, might flock to her without any shame. What difference, then, did the intention with which the philosopher resorted to the most notorious courtesan make, when the people and his own rivals saw him as more depraved than all other ruined men? Nor was it enough for him to live in this fashion: he also began to teach lusts, and transferred his conduct from the brothel to the school, arguing that bodily pleasure is the highest good. [Col. 0394B] That execrable and shameful doctrine was born not in the philosopher’s heart but in the courtesan’s bosom.

For why should I speak of the Cynics, whose custom it was to have intercourse with their wives in public? What wonder is it if they also derived their title and name from dogs, whose way of life they imitate? There is therefore no instruction in virtue in this discipline, since even those who prescribe more honorable conduct either do not themselves do what they recommend or, if they do it—which rarely happens—it is not their discipline but nature that leads them to what is right; and nature even more frequently drives the unlearned toward praiseworthy conduct.

[Col. 0395A] CHAPTER XVI. That philosophers who teach rightly live badly, as Cicero testifies; hence one must devote oneself not so much to philosophy as to wisdom.

They spend their life in nothing but speaking. Heumann says this expression is characteristic of Lactantius. I go further and declare—with due modesty—that it is an expression used by all the best writers, as shown by examples cited by Gronovius from Livy and by Burmann from Cicero and others. BUN.

[Col. 0395D]

For wisdom. From the manuscripts I restored *for*, which is more correct than the editors’ *but*. Wisdom: for if the praise of virtue consists in action, the same is certainly true of wisdom. Cicero teaches this in Book I of *On Duties*, in the chapter on Prudence. Hence Aristotle also says in the *Magna Moralia* that wisdom which issues in action deserves the name of virtue, but other wisdom does not.

And Tullius rightly. This passage is missing from Cicero. Nevertheless, in Book I of *On Duties*, in the chapter on Prudence, he condemns philosophy that lacks practical knowledge.

Or for the sake of pleading. Here Lactantius uses the word *advocandi* in the sense of pleading a case. Three manuscripts have *avocandi*; eight recent manuscripts have *vacandi*.—Or for the sake of summoning. I thought that one must supply an object: “or for the sake of summoning hearers, an assembly, or the people.” For he is discussing philosophers here and below; and of Epicurus he says in ch. 17: “that he may draw the multitude to himself.” Below in the same place: “he gathers a circle”; and the complete phrase occurs in *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, ch. 28: “He summoned the people.” BUN.

To have goodness on their lips. Thus I restored the reading from the editions of Cellarius and Walch and from all manuscripts except two recent ones and the other commonly received editions, which have *labiis* instead of *labris* for “lips.” One recent Colbertine manuscript and Brun. have “goodwill” instead of “goodness”; Tornesius and the Cottonian have “truth.”

Assuredly, he says, the whole discourse of those men, etc. This passage is believed to have dropped out of Cicero’s *Hortensius*, or *On Philosophy*. In it one must read “those men,” as found in eight older editions and in all manuscripts except two recent Royal manuscripts, which have “of those same men”; five printed editions absurdly have “just men”; and one Colbertine manuscript has “philosophers.”

[Col. 0396D]

I fear that . . . leisure. Thus I emended the text from the oldest and best manuscripts: one Bologna, two Royal, four other Royal, and one Colbertine. The word “business” also seems to require “leisure.” Perhaps this passage of Cicero should be restored from these excellent manuscripts. Twenty-two recent manuscripts and old editions have “lest it has brought . . . a certain pleasure of leisure.” Most other editions, including Gothofredus’ edition of Cicero, lack *not*.

All philosophy must therefore be cast aside. Lactantius is mistaken if he means true and genuine philosophy. But if by the name philosophy he designates the trifles and errors of those who philosophize, it is true that all such philosophy must be abolished. The Apostle Paul does not wish all philosophy to be exterminated, but only philosophy that is empty and deceitful, as may be seen in Colossians 2:8. This statement must therefore be taken with a grain of salt. From DAVENANTIUS.

Lacks. The manuscripts, two old Roman editions, Tornesius, Soubron, and Walch have “may lack”; the other commonly received editions have “lacks.”]

they surrender themselves to perpetual idleness, pursue no virtue, and spend their whole life in nothing but speaking, what else should they be considered but idle? For wisdom, unless it is embodied in some action through which it exercises its power, is empty and false. Tullius therefore rightly prefers to teachers of philosophy public men who govern the state, who either establish new cities or protect established ones through justice, and who preserve the safety and liberty of citizens by good laws, wholesome counsels, or weighty judgments.

For one ought rather to make people good [Col. 0395B] than, shut away in corners, to prescribe what ought to be done—things which not even those who speak about them do themselves. And because they have withdrawn from real activity, it is apparent that they invented the very art of philosophy for the sake of exercising their tongues or summoning an audience. But those who merely teach and do not act themselves diminish the weight of their own precepts. For who would obey when the teachers themselves teach people not to obey? It is good to prescribe what is right and honorable; but unless you also do it, it is a lie. It is incongruous and absurd to have goodness not in the heart but on the lips.

They therefore seek from philosophy not usefulness but pleasure. Cicero himself testified to this:

> “Assuredly,” he says, “although the whole discourse of those men contains the richest sources of virtue and knowledge, nevertheless, when compared with their actions and accomplished deeds, I fear that it may appear to have brought not so much usefulness to human affairs as pleasure to leisure.” [Col. 0395C]

He should not, indeed, have been afraid when he was speaking the truth. But [Col. 0396A] as though he feared being summoned by the philosophers on a charge of betraying their mystery, he did not dare confidently to declare what was true: that they engage in debate not in order to teach but to amuse themselves in their leisure. Because they are advisers about things that ought to be done while doing nothing themselves, they must be regarded as mere talkers.

But assuredly, because they brought nothing good to life, they did not themselves obey their own decrees; nor through all those centuries has anyone been found who lived according to their laws. All philosophy must therefore be cast aside, because one must not study wisdom—a pursuit which has neither end nor measure—but must be wise, and indeed without delay. For we are not granted a second path, such that in this life we may seek wisdom and in another be wise: both must necessarily be accomplished in this one. Wisdom must be found quickly, so that it may quickly be embraced, lest any portion be lost from a life whose end is uncertain. [Col. 0396B]

Cicero’s Hortensius, while arguing against philosophy, is ensnared by a subtle conclusion: although he said that one ought not to philosophize, he nevertheless appeared to philosophize, since it is the philosopher’s function to discuss what should or should not be done in life. We are immune and free from this captious objection, because we abolish philosophy on the ground that it is an invention of human thought; but we defend wisdom (*sophia*), because it is a divine tradition, and testify that it ought to be embraced by everyone. When Hortensius abolished philosophy without presenting anything better, he was thought to be abolishing wisdom, and was therefore more easily driven from his position, because it is agreed that the human being is born not for folly but for wisdom.

Moreover, another argument against philosophy [Col. 0396C] is especially powerful, an argument which the same Hortensius employed: that one can understand that philosophy is not wisdom from the fact that its beginning and origin are apparent. “When,” he asks, “did philosophers begin to exist? Thales [Col. 0397A] was the first, as I suppose; this age, then, is recent.”

[Col. 0397A] [Note: [Col. 0397B] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 397–398]

A recent . . . age. Thales was born in the second year of the thirty-fifth Olympiad and died in the first year of the fifty-eighth Olympiad.

Likewise Lucretius says. Thus I restored the text by emendation from the old Regio-Puteanus manuscript, one other Royal manuscript, four Colbertine manuscripts, two Brun., and the edition of Betuleius. And rightly so. Thirteen manuscripts and the same number of printed editions incorrectly have “The same Lucretius says,” for nothing from Lucretius appears in this chapter or the preceding one. The passage from Lucretius is at the beginning of Book V.

First among the first. Thus I restored the text from the manuscripts Jun., Lips., Pal., twelve editions, and Lucretius himself as emended by Lambinus on the basis of five manuscript codices. Others have “first with the first” or “first with the first man.”

A thousand years. This cannot refer to Thales, who lived not even seven hundred years before Seneca. It must refer either to Homer or to what is called barbarian philosophy.

Were set in motion. Thus I corrected the text from nearly all manuscripts and from the old editions Rome 1468, Rome 1470, Venice 1490, and Cellarius. The other printed editions and one recent Colbertine manuscript read “were known”; two Royal manuscripts have “were born”; one Colbertine has “arose.” With Cellarius and Walch, I think that “the beginnings were set in motion” means “the foundation was laid,” or “discussion of the matter was first begun.” This passage does not [Col. 0397D] survive today among Seneca’s works.—The beginnings . . . were set in motion. I retain “were set in motion,” because *movere* can mean “to begin.” Virgil, *Aeneid* VII.45: “I set in motion a greater work.” Compare v. 40, “beginnings,” and v. 44, “is born.” Hence Ciofanus, on Ovid, *Fasti* III.6,

> The work which I sought for my Muse to begin,

rightly explains the verb *movere* as “to make a beginning.” BUN.

Persius, ridiculing this, etc. Lactantius takes this passage of Persius perversely, as though the hateful declamation against philosophers belonged to Persius, when it belongs to Bestius. Yet neither Bestius nor, after him, Lactantius wished to condemn all philosophers under the same charge, but only the empty and deceitful philosophizers mentioned shortly above. Partly from Theodorus Marcilius on Persius, Satire 6, v. 38.

With flavorful wares, etc. Robertus Titius, *Controversial Passages*, Book IX, ch. 3, has offered what I consider the true and uncorrupted interpretation: namely, that Lactantius thought Persius meant in this passage that philosophy [Col. 0398B] had been brought into the City together with *saporis mercibus*, that is, flavorful and savory wares, such as pepper and [Col. 0398C] other spices of that kind, which had begun to be imported from Asia not long before. At the same time, he thought Persius was alluding to the name of wisdom, *sapientia*, which, as though contemptuously, he wished to derive from flavor, *sapor*—the flavor it acquired from the wares together with which it was conveyed to us. Accordingly Titius judges that *saporis* is the plural ablative of the adjective *saporus, -a, -um*, newly coined by Lactantius, indeed, but in imitation and on the model of similar formations: from *odor*, *odorus*; from *vapor*, *vaporus*; from *canor*, *canorus*; and from *honor*, *honorus*. ISAEUS.

Because. Thus I restored the text from all the manuscripts except one recent Royal manuscript, one Colbertine, and the printed editions, which have “who.”

Did not know. Others have an alternative Latin form with the same meaning.

Through ignorance of the truth. The manuscript used by the Cologne editor of 1544 has “because of ignorance of the truth,” which is not displeasing.

Contend with them. Thus I read with many manuscripts and eight printed editions. Sixteen manuscripts and three printed editions have “contend with those same men”; four printed editions and one Clermont manuscript have “with the same men.” The Regio-Puteanus has “I may obtain leave . . . to contend”; three other manuscripts have “I may obtain leave . . . to contend” with a variant verb form.

[Col. 0398D]

The popular name of pleasure attracts many. Thus nearly all the manuscripts and seven printed editions. One recent Royal manuscript and seven printed editions have “toward the popular name”; the old French translation reads: “because it invites and summons many to that name of pleasure, so greatly loved and desired by the people.” The Subiaco edition reads “many toward the popular.”

Moreover. Thus nearly all manuscripts and printed editions. Cauc., one recent Royal manuscript, and six recent printed editions have “For that reason.”

Forbids him to study literature. Epicurus himself is censured for not having learned the subjects that make a person truly educated. Writing to Philocles, this philosopher says that all learning must be avoided.

The sluggish man to be exercised. Thus I restored the text from the manuscripts and the editions Rome 1470, Tornesius, Soubron, and Walch. The other commonly received editions incorrectly have the active infinitive, “to exercise.”

That they care about nothing. On this see *On the Anger of God*, ch. 27.

Life can be sustained. Thus I restored the text from the most ancient Royal manuscript, four other Royal manuscripts, five Colbertine, two Clermont manuscripts, and others, as well as from the editions of Rome 1468, Rome 1470, Tornesius, Soubron, and Walch. [Col. 0399B] Six recent manuscripts, one Colbertine, and twelve printed editions have the active infinitive, “to sustain.” Yet Epicurus practiced such frugality that he lived on bread and water alone and was devoted to no pleasure, as St. Jerome says in Book II *Against Jovinian*. It is added, however, that he rejected pleasure only because of the inconveniences that followed from it. On this matter see Stobaeus.—Life . . . can be sustained. Taubmann, on Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII.409, affirms that the verb *tolerare*, “to sustain,” signifies scantiness and frugality. BUN.]

Where, then, among earlier people was this love of investigating the truth concealed? Likewise Lucretius says:

> In short, this nature and rational account of things  
> Has only recently been discovered; and I myself am now found  
> First among the first able to render it in my native tongue.

And Seneca:

> “It is not yet a thousand years,” he says, “since the beginnings of wisdom were set in motion.”

For many centuries, then, the human race lived without reason. Persius, ridiculing this, says:

> After wisdom came to the City  
> With pepper and dates—

as though wisdom had been imported together with flavorful wares. But if wisdom accords with human nature, it must necessarily have begun with humanity itself; if it does not, human nature could not even receive it. But because human nature has received it, wisdom must necessarily have existed [Col. 0397B] from the beginning. Therefore philosophy, because it did not exist from the beginning, is not identical with true wisdom.

But clearly the Greeks, because they had not encountered the sacred writings of truth, did not know how wisdom had been corrupted. And therefore, because they thought human life was devoid of wisdom, they invented philosophy: that is, they wished through discussion to unearth the truth that was hidden and unknown to them, and through ignorance of the truth they regarded this pursuit as wisdom.

[Col. 0398A] CHAPTER XVII. He passes from philosophy to the philosophers, beginning with Epicurus; and explains how Epicurus had Leucippus and Democritus as the authors of his error.

I have spoken about philosophy itself as briefly as I could. Now let us come to the philosophers—not to contend with men who cannot stand, but to pursue them as they flee and lie overthrown upon our field.

The school of Epicurus was always much more celebrated than the others, not because it offers anything true, but because the popular name of pleasure attracts many. For everyone is prone to vice. Moreover, so that he may draw the multitude to himself, [Col. 0398B] Epicurus speaks in a manner adapted to each individual disposition. He forbids the idle man to study literature; frees the miser from public generosity; prohibits the cowardly man from entering public life, the sluggish man from being exercised, and the timid man from serving in war.

The irreligious man hears that the gods care about nothing. The inhuman man who serves his own interests is commanded to give nothing to anyone, for the wise man does everything for his own sake. Solitude is praised to one who flees the crowd. One who is excessively frugal learns that life can be sustained on water and porridge. One who [Col. 0399A] hates his wife—

[Col. 0399A] [Note: [Col. 0399C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 399–400]

One who hates his wife. On this see St. Jerome near the end of Book I *Against Jovinian*.

Against impious parents. This is Gothofredus’ word order. Hence, by removing one letter, I conjecture: “to the impious man, against his parents,” that is, “it is said,” as immediately follows and as appears shortly before: “to one who has bad children.” Now Epicurus flatters an impious son against his parents. BUNEMANN.

To court kings. On this see Plutarch, *On Tranquillity of Mind*, and Stobaeus, Discourse 27.

Dispositions. Thus I restored the text from thirty-one manuscripts and seven editions. One recent Royal manuscript corruptly has “motions”; two recent Royal manuscripts, Tornesius, one Colbertine manuscript, and ten editions have “manners.”

Gathers. This is the reading of the oldest and best codices: two Bologna, nine Royal, four Colbertine, Tornesius, two Clermont, and the Cambridge manuscript, as well as the old Roman editions and eight others. One recent Royal manuscript, two Colbertine, Goth., Em., Brun., and five printed editions have “collects.”—Gathers a circle. I have recalled the precise verb *cogit*, “gathers,” which was rejected by Cellarius and Walch, and earlier by Tornesius in 1587. For the oldest and most numerous manuscript and printed books have the elegant expression “to gather a circle”; it means the same as to collect or assemble a company—or, as above in this chapter, “to draw the multitude to himself.” For *circulus* in the sense of a company or surrounding ring, see Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, Book II, p. 120: “When, enclosed by a circle of a large crowd, he unraveled the destinies before a ring of bystanders.” BU.

Epicurus saw that adversities always befell the good, etc. From this he concluded that there was no providence and that God exercised no care for human beings, but that everything happened by chance. Hence not only Epicurus but others as well—Seneca in *Hippolytus*, act III, and Lucan, Book VII:

> Assuredly, there are no divine powers for us:  
> Since all things are swept along by blind chance,  
> We falsely claim that Jupiter reigns.

Ovid, *Amores*, Book III, elegy 8:

> Since evil fates sweep good men away, forgive my confession:  
> I am troubled into thinking that there are no gods.

[Col. 0400B]

GALLAEUS.—Thus falsely thought those who possessed no certainty concerning what would happen after death.

Infants are carried off. In the manner of the ancients. Suetonius, *Caligula*, ch. 7: “carried off while still infants.” Pliny, *Letters* VI.6: “I grieve that he was most undeservedly carried off by an untimely death.” Justin, Book VII, ch. 2: “carried off by an untimely death.” BUN.

[Col. 0400C]

His own. Printed editions of Lucretius have “often his own.”

The Capitol. Among ancient authors, no one treats the fires of the Capitol more fully than Plutarch in the *Life of Publicola* and Cornelius Tacitus in Book XIX of the *Annals*. Tarquinius Priscus, son of Demaratus, began to build a temple to Jupiter during the Sabine War on the Tarpeian Hill, which had previously been called Saturnian. While the workmen were opening the foundations, a human head was discovered. The augurs said that this omen signified that this citadel would become the head of the world, and for that reason the name Capitoline was given to the hill.

But Priscus, overtaken by death, left the structure unfinished. Tarquinius Superbus, his grandson, afterward completed it from the spoils of captured Pometia; but before he could conduct its dedication, he was expelled because of his tyranny. The dedication was therefore performed after Tarquin’s expulsion, in the 247th year from the foundation of the City.

The Capitol, founded upon squared stone—a work worthy of admiration even amid later magnificence—was consumed by fire during the Marian wars, when L. Scipio Asiaticus and C. Norbanus Balbus were consuls, that is, in the 671st year from the foundation of the City, 424 years after its dedication, not [Col. 0400D] 415, as Tacitus asserts—an error later followed by Alexander of Naples. Sulla restored it. Quintus Catulus consecrated the restored building; Pliny also mentions him in Book XIX, ch. 1.

It endured until the Vitellian war, when it was burned a second time by the soldiers. Vespasian restored it; but while he was still living it was consumed by fire a third time, and Vespasian himself died along with the Capitol. Domitian then made it more magnificent than it had ever been before. The words of Lucretius, however, must refer to the Marian fire. But I do not see when it was burned by Jupiter’s lightning. BETUL.—The Capitol . . . struck by lightning. See Arnobius, Book VI, p. 245, octavo edition of Elmenhorst: “When devouring fire so often consumed the Capitol and seized Capitoline Jupiter himself together with his wife and daughter, where was the wielder of the thunderbolt at that time . . . that he might avenge it?” BUNEMANN.

Of his consulship. We do not possess this book, but see Book II of *On Divination*, ch. 20, where the same verses are read.]

—the advantages of celibacy are listed for him. To one who has bad children, childlessness is praised; against impious parents, he is told that there is no bond of nature. To one who is impatient and delicate, pain is said to be the greatest of all evils; to the courageous man, that the wise man is happy even under torture. One who strives for distinction and power is instructed to court kings; one who cannot endure vexation is instructed to flee the royal court.

Thus this cunning man gathers a circle from various and diverse dispositions; and while striving to please everyone, he came into greater conflict with himself than all the philosophers did with one another. We must now explain where his whole doctrine came from and what origin it had.

Epicurus saw that adversities always befell the good—poverty, labors, exile, and the loss of loved ones—[Col. 0399B] while the wicked, by contrast, were prosperous, increased in power, and honored. He saw that innocence enjoyed less protection and that crimes were committed with impunity. He saw death rage without selection according to character and without order or distinction of age: some reached old age; others were carried off as infants; others died when already mature; others were extinguished by untimely funerals in the first flower of youth; and in wars it was especially the better men who were both defeated [Col. 0400A] and killed.

What disturbed him most of all, however, was that especially religious people were afflicted by more grievous evils, while those who either wholly neglected the gods or worshiped them irreverently suffered either lesser misfortunes or none at all. Even temples themselves were often burned by lightning. Lucretius complains of this in Book II of *On the Nature of Things* when he says of God:

> Then let him hurl his thunderbolts and shatter  
> His own temples; and, withdrawing to deserted places,  
> Let him rage there, practicing with a weapon that often  
> Passes by the guilty and strikes the innocent and undeserving dead.

If Lucretius had been able to catch even the faintest breath of truth, he would never have said that God shattered his own temples, since he shatters them precisely because they are not his. The Capitol, which is the supreme head of the city and religion of Rome, [Col. 0400B] was not once but repeatedly struck by lightning and burned.

What ingenious men thought about this is apparent from a statement of Cicero’s. He said that the fire had arisen by divine agency, not to destroy that earthly dwelling of Jupiter, but to demand a loftier and more magnificent one. On this matter, in the books concerning his consulship, he also said the same thing as Lucretius:

[Col. 0401A]

> For the high-thundering Father, resting upon starry Olympus,  
> Himself—

[Col. 0401A] [Note: [Col. 0401C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 401–402]

Himself, etc. This second verse is read as follows in Cicero, Book II of *On Divination*:

> He himself once struck his own hills and temples.

Ensnared himself. Thus I restored the text from the best and oldest Regio-Puteanus manuscript, one other more recent Royal manuscript, three Colbertine, one Leipzig manuscript, Em., and Brun., with the support of sixteen others, which have “enclosed,” as do ten old printed editions. *Concludere* in this sense is Terentian: to thrust or entangle oneself, in French *s’engager, s’embarrasser*. Three Royal manuscripts [Col. 0401D] and six printed editions have “cast himself.”

There is no arrangement. See Lucretius, Books II and V, near the beginning. See also Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book I.

And the divine man discovered things to criticize. These words are incorrectly printed in many editions as if they were the words of Epicurus, although they are Lactantius’ ironic words. I have therefore had them printed in ordinary type. BUNEMANN.

Providentially. Goth. has “prudently.” Compare Book VI, ch. 15; *On Anger*, ch. 10. It is also found in Pliny’s *Panegyric*, ch. 1: “Because human beings rightly and providentially undertook nothing without the counsel and honor of the immortal gods.” BUNEMANN.

For there are seeds. We shall reserve this discussion of atoms for chapter 10 of *On the Anger of God*. Meanwhile, see St. Basil’s first homily εἰς τὸ ἑξαήμερον, “On the Six Days of Creation,” on this subject, and the third chapter of the first book of the *Placita* in Plutarch. BETULEIUS.

Except Leucippus alone. On him, see Galen’s *Philosophical History*. But we shall discuss these matters in *On the Anger of God*.

[Col. 0402C]]

If They Are. This is the manuscript reading; the printed editions have “if they be.”

In Various Order. On this see Lucretius, book II.

But If They Are Smooth and Lack Hooks. Thus the Bologna manuscript reads, on the basis of which this passage must be corrected. For although the other manuscripts and all the printed editions read “and lack moisture,” that reading is nevertheless corrupt. This is clear from the argument soundly advanced by Thomasius: namely, moisture added to smoothness would produce not merely no cohesion but rather slipping. GALLAEUS.

So That They Can Be Cut Apart. Here again you have the archaic verb *dissicio* [Col. 0402D], whose explanation may be seen above, book II, chapter 8. Note that two recent Royal manuscripts, one Colbert manuscript, and the printed editions wrongly have *disjici*. GALL.

May Be Constructed. One old Bologna manuscript has “may be joined together”; twelve recent manuscripts and ten printed editions have “may be constituted.”

This Is He. Namely Epicurus, to whom these verses taken from the end of Lucretius, book III, refer.

He Dimmed the Stars. Four Royal manuscripts, the Cauc., Lips., Pal., Jun., and Cant. manuscripts, and four printed editions have *restinxit*; six printed editions, *restrinxit*; six Royal manuscripts, six Colbert manuscripts, one Sorbonne and one Clermont manuscript, Brun., and two old editions, including the Roman, have “extinguished.” But Lucretius, as emended by Lambinus, reads “dimmed” (*praestinxit*), and he uses the same verb in books II and IV. *Praestinguere*, moreover—as Nonius teaches—means to darken or obscure, as the rising sun obscures the brilliance of the stars. There can be no doubt that “dimmed,” rather than “quenched” or “extinguished,” must be read; for the rising sun does not extinguish the stars’ splendor but merely dims it. “Quenches” is much less suitable still, since *restinguere* [Col. 0403C] is said of heat or burning, not of light or brilliance. From LAMBINUS.]

> He sought his citadels and renowned temples,
>
> And cast fire upon the Capitoline seats.

Thus, in their obstinate folly, they not only failed to understand the power and majesty of the true God, but even aggravated the impiety of their error by striving, against every divine law, to restore a temple repeatedly condemned by heavenly judgment.

When Epicurus, therefore, considered these things, he was led on by what seemed to be their unfairness—for so it appeared to one ignorant of their cause and rationale—and concluded that there was no providence. Once he had persuaded himself of this, he also undertook to defend it; and so he enclosed himself within inextricable errors. For if there is no providence, how was the world produced with such order and arrangement? “There is no arrangement,” he says, “for many things were made [Col. 0401B] otherwise than they ought to have been.” And the godlike man found things to criticize! If there were time to refute every one of them, I could easily show that this man was neither wise nor sane.

Again, if there is no providence, how have the bodies of living creatures been ordered with such foresight that each and every member, arranged according to a marvelous design, performs its own function? “No providential design,” he says, “was at work in producing living creatures. Eyes were not made for seeing, ears for hearing, the tongue for speaking, or feet for walking, since these things came into being before speaking, hearing, seeing, and walking existed. Thus they were not born for use; rather, use arose from them.”

If there is no providence, why do rains fall, crops spring up, and trees put forth leaves? “These things,” [Col. 0401C] he says, “do not always occur for the sake of living creatures, since they contribute nothing to providence; everything necessarily comes about of its own accord.” From what, then, do all the things that happen arise—or how do they come about? (See Lucretius, book II.) “No work of providence is involved,” [Col. 0402A] he says. “There are seeds flying through the void; when these randomly cluster together, all things are generated and grow.”

Why, then, do we not perceive or see them? “Because,” he says, “they have neither color nor any heat nor odor; they are also devoid of taste and moisture, and are so minute that they cannot be cut or divided.”

Thus, because he had adopted a falsehood at the outset, the necessary consequences led him into ravings. Where are these little bodies, or where do they come from? Why did no one dream of them apart from Leucippus alone? Instructed by him, Democritus left Epicurus an inheritance of folly. If these little bodies exist, and are indeed solid, as they say, surely they can come within the range of sight. If all of them have the same nature, how do they produce different things? [Col. 0402B] “They come together,” he says, “in different orders and positions, just as letters, though few in number, nevertheless produce innumerable words when arranged in different ways.”

But letters have different shapes. “So too,” he says, “do these first principles themselves: some are rough, some hooked, and some smooth.” They can therefore be cut and divided, if there is something projecting from them. But if they are smooth and lack hooks, they cannot cohere. They must therefore be hooked, so that they can be linked to one another. Yet since they are said to be so minute that they cannot be cut apart by any iron blade, how can they have hooks or angles? Because these project, they must necessarily be capable of being torn away.

Then by what compact do they meet, or under the direction of what intelligence, so that something may be constructed from them?
