If they lack sensation, they cannot come together in such an orderly fashion, since nothing rational can be accomplished except by reason. [Col. 0402C] In how many ways could this vanity be refuted! But my discourse hastens onward. This is he

> Who surpassed the human race in intellect, and dimmed  
> All the stars, rising like the ethereal sun.

[Col. 0403A] I can never read these verses without laughing. For he was not saying this even of Socrates or Plato, who are regarded as the kings of the philosophers, but of a man more foolishly deranged than any sick person ever was while this man remained sane and vigorous. Thus the utterly empty-headed poet did not adorn a mouse with a lion’s praises; he overwhelmed and crushed it beneath them.

Yet this same man frees us from the fear of death, concerning which these are his exact words:

> “When we exist, death does not; when death exists, we do not; [Col. 0403A]

[Note: [Col. 0403C] [Various Notes on columns 403–404]

When Death Exists, We Do Not. That this is the genuine reading is established from the Bologna, Tax., Pen., two Brun., six Colbert, two Clermont, and all the Vatican manuscripts, and from Epicurus himself in his letter to Menoeceus in Laertius—not the common reading, “When we do not exist, death does.” ISAEUS. This correction by Isaeus is confirmed by the Lips., Pal., Ult., and Jun. manuscripts and the Plantin, Gymn., Geneva, Aldine, Cratander, Is., and Thysius editions. The passage of Epicurus addressed to Menoeceus reads: Ὅταν δὲ ὁ θάνατος παρῇ, τόθ’ ἡμεῖς οὐκ ἐσμέν, “But when death is present, then we do not exist.” GALLAEUS. On this reasoning see Lucretius, book III; Laërtius, in his *Epicurus*; Aulus Gellius, book II, chapter 8; Plutarch, *On Tranquillity of Life*; and Stobaeus, Discourse 15.

By Which Sensation Has Now Been Taken Away. I have restored this from the old Roman and Venetian editions, as well as the editions of de Tournes and Cellarius and all the manuscripts except one Royal manuscript and seventeen editions, which have “because.” See below: “by which sensation is taken away.”

During Which We Still Exist. I approve Isaeus’s observation on this passage. In place of the reading in the printed editions, “during which we too now no longer exist,” he thinks it should be read in the form in which we have had it printed. His reasoning is very sound: for if there is some time during which we no longer exist and death does not yet exist, Epicurus was right to say that during that time death is nothing to us. Lactantius, however, intends the contrary, as is evident from his purpose if the text is carefully weighed. And certainly it was easy for *non* to be substituted for *num*. The editions of Grapheus and Gymnicus and the Jun. manuscript confirm our emendation, for they lack the negation found in the remaining manuscripts and printed editions. GALLAEUS.

When Death Also Begins to Exist. Seventeen manuscripts and five editions have “because death also”; one old Bologna manuscript and Brun. have “during which death also.”

Bring. This reading comes from the manuscripts and nine old editions; the more recent printed editions have “may bring.”

Rather, Bring It About That Pain Is Not an Evil. I have thus restored the text from ten editions and the very ancient manuscripts—two Royal and twenty-one others—except that two have “bring about,” six “brings about,” and one other Royal manuscript has “that pain may not be an evil.” The French translator also followed our reading: *O Epicure, fais plutôt que douleur ne soit point mal*—“O Epicurus, bring it about instead that pain should not be an evil.” Six editions read, “This circumstance rather brings it about that pain is an evil.”

Because Souls Do Not Perish. “But souls perish.” I have thus emended the text from a Royal manuscript four hundred years old and of the finest quality, with support from two very ancient Royal manuscripts, another recent Royal manuscript, and the Betuleius edition, in which “souls” occurs only once; fifteen manuscripts and eleven common editions have “truly, he says”; three have “but.”

It Is Necessary. After Epicurus, Lucretius dreams this in book III.

For My Final Work. Lactantius carries this out in book VII, chapters 7, 8, and following, and in the *Epitome*, chapter 10.

Democritus, Etc. He was the Abderite who devised atoms. He lived in the fifth century before the Common Era and died at the age of 109, in the sixty-fourth Olympiad. Dicaearchus, however, was a Messenian philosopher who held that the human race had always existed and that everything in a human being perishes simultaneously.

Of the Most Shameful Pleasure. Here our author forgot himself, for above he had said that Epicurus placed the highest good in pleasure of the mind.

Impunity. Thus Cicero says in the *Pro Milone*: “The hope of impunity is the greatest inducement to wrongdoing.”

To Do Evil. Cicero, by contrast, teaches in *On Duties* that a good man will never sin even if impunity is offered him. For nothing is advantageous unless it is honorable.

Thus the Person Who Hears These Crimes. I have thus restored the text from the manuscripts. The common editions have, “And so the person who hears,” etc.]

> death, therefore, is nothing to us.”

How cleverly he has deceived us! As though what is feared were death already completed, by which sensation has now been taken away, and not the very act of dying, by which sensation is taken away. For there is some time during which we still exist, while death does not yet exist; and this very condition seems wretched, when death begins to exist and we cease to exist.

[Col. 0403B] It was therefore not said without reason:

> Death is not wretched;  
> The approach to death is wretched.

That is: wasting away from disease, suffering a blow, receiving a sword into one’s body, burning in fire, and being torn apart by beasts’ teeth. These are the things that are feared, not because they bring death, but because they bring great pain. Rather, bring it about that pain is not an evil. “It is the greatest of all evils,” he says. How, then, can I avoid fearing it, if that which precedes or causes death is an evil?

Moreover, what of the fact that this entire argument is false, because souls do not perish? “But souls perish,” he says. “For what is born together with the body must necessarily perish together with the body.” I have already said above that I defer this subject for a more appropriate place and reserve it for my final work, so that I may refute this conviction of Epicurus—whether it belonged [Col. 0403C] to Democritus or Dicaearchus—both by arguments and by divine testimonies.

But perhaps he promised impunity [Col. 0404A] to his own vices, for he was an advocate of the most shameful pleasure, for the sake of obtaining which he thought that the human being was born. Who, on hearing this affirmed, would abstain from vices and crimes? For if souls are destined to perish, let us seek riches so that we may enjoy every delight; and if we lack them, let us take them from those who possess them—secretly, by deception, or by force. All the more, if no God concerns himself with human affairs, whenever the hope of impunity smiles upon us, let us rob and kill. For it is the part of a wise man to do evil if doing so is both advantageous and safe, since, if there is any God in heaven, he is angry with no one. It is equally foolish to do good, since just as he is not stirred by anger, neither is he affected by favor.

Let us therefore serve pleasures in whatever way we can, for in a short time we shall be utterly nothing. Therefore let us allow no day, and indeed no single point [Col. 0404B] of time, to pass for us without pleasure, lest, because we ourselves are destined one day to perish, the very life we have lived should perish as well.

Although he does not say this in words, he teaches it by the substance of his doctrine. For when he argues that the wise man does everything for his own sake, he relates everything he does to his own advantage. Thus the person who hears these crimes will think that no good deed should be done, since doing good concerns another’s advantage, and that one need not abstain from crime, because plunder is joined to wrongdoing.

If some arch-pirate or leader of brigands were exhorting his men to pillage, what other language could he use than to say the same things that Epicurus says? That the gods care for nothing; that they are affected neither by anger nor by favor; that punishments in the underworld need not be feared, [Col. 0404C] because souls perish after death and no underworld exists at all; that pleasure is the highest good; that there is no human fellowship; that each person should look after himself; that no one loves another except for his own sake; [Col. 0405A]

[Note: [Col. 0405B] [Various Notes on columns 405–406]

Except for His Own Sake. Yet Cicero, in the *Laelius*, condemns profit-seeking friendship and admits no end of friendship other than moral worth; and Plato himself teaches that a human being is born not so much for himself as for each of his neighbors.

Even If He Is Tortured. I have restored “who” from numerous manuscripts, since it agrees with the context better than the reading “indeed not” found in others.

That Souls Are Not Born. Antoninus, book IV, §21, maintains that souls are dissolved, transformed, poured back, and rekindled, so that, as others succeed and replace them, they may make room each day, just as he had said of bodies dissolved into earth. And perhaps this is what Epiphanius meant when he said of the Stoics, II, *Heresy* 5: Μεταγγισμούς τε ψυχῶν καὶ μετενσωματώσεις, “transfusions of souls and reincarnations”; and, following Epiphanius, John of Damascus in his book *On Heresies*: “The Stoics maintain that the soul migrates from body to body.” On this account Lactantius in this passage joins the Stoics to the Pythagoreans. Servius says on *Aeneid* III [Col. 0405C] that the Stoics followed a middle way: Plato said that the soul is everlasting and passes immediately into different bodies according to the merits of the preceding life; Pythagoras, however, says that there is not *metempsychōsis* (μετεμψύχωσις), transmigration of souls, but *palingenesia* (παλιγγενεσία), rebirth—that is, that it returns, but only after an interval. GATAKER. See Augustine, *City of God*, book X, chapter 30.

And Migrate from Some Bodies into Others. The Egyptians were the first to hand down this opinion concerning the *metempsychōsis* (μετεμψύχωσις), or transmigration, of souls. Pythagoras derived it from them, according to Herodotus in *Euterpe*. The Gauls held the same belief. *Gallic War* VI: “Above all, they wish to persuade people of this: that souls do not perish, but after death pass from some persons to others.” There is, however, this difference between the opinion of the Gauls and that of Pythagoras: the Gauls thought that souls passed only into other human beings, whereas Pythagoras thought they also passed into other living creatures. The Pharisees likewise believed this opinion, according to Josephus, *Antiquities* XVIII, chapter 2. Modern Jews too find these ideas pleasing. GALLAEUS.

And That Souls Are Born. Lactantius seems here to contradict himself. For above, in book II, chapter 12, near the end, he states that God infuses into the body the soul by which we breathe; but here he teaches that souls are born. On this matter, however, one should consult St. Jerome’s *Apology Against Rufinus*, book II, whose words are as follows:

> “I have read,” says Jerome, “certain persons who say that, together with the body, souls too are propagated through the transmission of the human body; and they confirmed this by such arguments as they could. Among the Latins I think that Tertullian held this opinion, and perhaps Lactantius and certain others. Others assert that, once bodies have been formed in the womb, God daily creates souls and infuses them. Others maintain that souls were made long ago—that is, when God created all things from nothing—and that now, by his judgment, he disposes them to be born in bodies. . . . But although I have read each of these views, I say before God that down to the present I hold nothing certain and settled concerning this question; rather, I leave it to God to know what occurs in the womb, and to reveal it to anyone to whom he himself deigns to do so.”

On this matter see also Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book XIII, chapter 10, and Cassiodorus, *On the Soul*, chapter 9.

They Did Not Know What the Rationale of the Human Being Was. This must be read from the old manuscripts—one Bologna and two Royal—as Thomasius judges, and not “human beings,” as is commonly found in the printed editions and other manuscripts. For the question is not what they knew about human beings in general, but what the Pythagoreans and Stoics knew, whom he says to have been ignorant of the rationale of the human being. GALLAEUS.—Much the same appears in *Divine Institutes* VII, chapters 3 and 5.

Such as Cleanthes. The Stoic philosopher who was called φρεάντλης, “well-drawer,” because at night he drew water in gardens to earn his livelihood, so that he might be free to philosophize by day. He voluntarily ended his life by starvation, as Laertius reports in book VII, in his *Life* of Cleanthes. Lucian mentions him in *The Long-Lived*. BETULEIUS.

[Col. 0406C]

Such as Chrysippus. He was a disciple of Zeno and, after Cleanthes, the head of the Stoic school. Laertius reports two accounts of his death: one that he died after too copious a draught of sweet wine, the other that he died from excessive laughter. Seneca, Epistle 57, relates that incessant greeting brought him to his death. BETUL.

Such as Zeno. Zeno of Citium, founder of the Stoic school. Laertius writes thus of his death: as he was leaving his school, he stumbled and broke his toe. Striking the ground with his hand, he uttered the line from *Niobe*: Ἔρχομαι, τί μ’ ἀΰεις; “I am coming; why do you summon me?” In the Paris edition of Laertius of 1585 it reads: Ἔρχομαι, τί με καλεῖς; “I am coming; why do you call me?” Immediately afterward he strangled himself and died. BETULEIUS.

Such as Empedocles. A philosopher and poet. Laertius reports various opinions about his death, but the more consistent tradition, also reported by Strabo in book VI, prevailed. In Lucian’s dialogue between Menippus and Aeacus, Menippus asks Empedocles himself why he leapt down; Empedocles replies: Μελαγχολία τις, ὦ Μένιππε, “A certain melancholy, Menippus.” Menippus instead attributes the deed to arrogance and the pursuit of empty glory. He is also censured in the *Icaromenippus*. Tertullian, in his book *To the Martyrs*, adduces him as an example of contempt for death. Tatian also mentions him in *Against the Greeks*, as does Gregory of Nazianzus in his excellent poem addressed to Nemessus.

Ἐμπεδόκλεις, etc., which may be rendered in Latin as follows:

> Empedocles, Aetna’s craters show that you fell in death,  
> Greatly swollen with arrogant pride.  
> Behold, their surges cast forth the bronze sandals  
> Of the mad divinity, giving mortals cause for laughter.  
> How grievously empty Glory drives you to destruction!

An Imitator of Socratic Vanity. I thus restore the reading from all manuscripts and printed editions except Betul., Spark., and Gall., who, contrary to the authority of all the manuscripts, substituted “Stoic,” because Cato really was a Stoic. Yet nothing prevents Cato, though a Stoic, from being called by Lactantius an imitator of Socratic vanity, since he imitated Socrates and spurned death with no little ostentation. When he killed himself, he had read Plato’s book *On the Eternity of Souls*, in which, of course, Socrates’ death is described. Is this not enough for him to be called an imitator of Socratic vanity? NOURRY. On Cato’s death see Plutarch, volume II, and Augustine, *City of God*, book I, chapter 23.—An Imitator of Stoic Vanity. Although the manuscripts and the editions printed from 1465 to 1650 protest against it, I have adopted “Stoic” in place of “Socratic,” chiefly for these reasons: Cato acted “to obey the decrees of the Stoics, whom he followed.” Compare Plutarch, *Cato the Younger*, fol. 792 ff.: “Cato came to the paradoxes of the Stoics.” BUN.]

that death is not to be feared by a brave man, nor any pain, and that even if he is tortured or burned, he should say that he cares nothing for it. Is there any reason at all for anyone to think that this utterance belongs to a wise man, when it could most suitably be applied to brigands?

## CHAPTER XVIII  
### The Pythagoreans and Stoics, in affirming the immortality of souls, vainly recommend voluntary death

Others, however, argue the contrary: that souls survive after death. These are chiefly the Pythagoreans and Stoics. Although they should be pardoned because their opinion is true, [Col. 0405B] I nevertheless cannot refrain from censuring them, because they fell upon the truth not through judgment but by chance. Thus, even in the very matter in which their opinion was correct, they went wrong in some respect. [Col. 0406A]

For because they feared the argument by which it is inferred that souls must perish together with bodies, since they are born together with bodies, they said that souls are not born but are instead introduced into bodies and migrate from some bodies into others. They did not think it otherwise possible for souls to survive bodies unless they appeared to have existed before bodies. The errors of the two parties are therefore equal and almost identical. But the one view is false concerning the past, the other concerning the future. For no one perceived what is most true: both that souls are born and that they do not perish, because they did not know why this occurred or what the rationale of the human being was.

Many of them, therefore, because they supposed souls to be eternal, laid hands upon themselves as though they were about to migrate to heaven: Cleanthes, Chrysippus, Zeno, and Empedocles, who cast himself into the fiery crater of Aetna in the dead of [Col. 0406B] night so that, when he suddenly disappeared, people would believe he had departed to the gods; and, among the Romans, Cato, who throughout his entire life was an imitator of Socratic vanity. [Col. 0407A]

[Note: [Col. 0407C] [Various Notes on columns 407–408]

For Democritus. He called cheerfulness the greatest good and sadness the greatest evil, being utterly remote from Stoic severity. We shall quote in full the passage of Lucretius from which this verse is taken:

> Finally, when ripe old age warned Democritus  
> That the memory-bearing motions of his mind were growing weak,  
> Of his own accord he went to meet death and offered up his head.

But Laertius gives a different account: namely, that by holding warm loaves of bread to his nostrils he fulfilled his destiny over three days. It must, however, be understood that he had previously resolved to die by starvation. Thus authors differ concerning the manner of his death: Lucian affirms that he died τῆς τροφῆς ἀποσχόμενον, “abstaining from food,” which Laertius also reports; Athenaeus says that he sustained his life for a time with honey, until the festival of the *Thesmophoria* had passed, so that public rejoicing would not be interrupted by private mourning. Antoninus, differing from all of them, reports that he was consumed by lice. [Col. 0407D] From BETULEIUS (book III, §3).

Of His Own Accord. In Lucretius, *On the Nature of Things*, book III, near the end. Authors nevertheless differ concerning the manner of his death, as I have said: ancient writers report either that he died through abstinence from food or that he was consumed by worms or lice.

Just as into This Life, Etc. He follows Cicero in *Cato the Elder*, chapter 20, and in the *Dream of Scipio* as cited by Macrobius, book I, chapter 23. BUN.

So Again from This Dwelling of the Body. Cicero in *Cato the Elder* attributes these words to Pythagoras: “Pythagoras forbids us to depart from the guard-post and station of life without the commander’s order—that is, God’s.” And in the fragment of the *Republic*, Scipio says to his grandson: “Therefore, Publius, you too, and all righteous men, must keep the soul in the custody of the body; nor should you depart from human life without the command of him by whom the soul was given to us, lest you appear to have deserted the human duty assigned by God.” These words evidently derive from Plato. BETULEIUS.—On this matter see Plato’s *Phaedo*.

Must Be Endured. I have thus restored the reading from six old editions and all the manuscripts [Col. 0408B] except the Marm. manuscript, in which the reading found in most common editions was written by the first hand.

When an Innocent Person’s Soul Has Been Extinguished. That is, “life”; perhaps, “when an innocent person has been killed without vengeance.” I note similar passages at book VI, chapters 11 and 20, and book VII, chapter 11. Terence, *The Brothers* III.2: “I would extinguish the old man’s life.”

The Great Judge. I have thus restored the reading from all the manuscripts and the old Roman edition and Cellarius, whatever Walchius may say—as though vengeance did not belong to the great Judge. Thirteen printed editions read “the great avenger.”

Vengeance Always Remains Entire. Almost all the manuscripts agree with three printed editions in this reading. Lactantius likewise uses *in totum* and *in integro*; and we French also say *en tout, en son entier*, “as a whole, in its entirety.” Six recent manuscripts and ten printed editions have “vengeance remains intact.”—Remains Entire. This is our author’s customary usage, as in book I, chapter 11: “That rests upon the truth”; in the same book, chapter 17: “What rests upon the truth”; and book V, chapter 1: “The cause of this matter lies open.” Likewise in Cicero, *On the Orator* III, chapter 4: “But since these things can no longer remain untouched for us,” certain persons had substituted “intact.” BUN.

And Cato Himself, the Foremost Figure of Roman Wisdom, Etc. Plutarch testifies that Cato’s counsel was regarded as an oracle, and in his *Life* assigns the same reasons for his voluntary death. Cicero, in *On Duties* I, when speaking of the propriety suitable to different persons, says that this deed was especially fitting for Cato’s dignity, but by no means for the others who had belonged to the same cause. We shall more properly listen to Augustine, who denies human beings every right to voluntary death. In *City of God* I, chapter 23, when examining this example, he thinks that the cause was not Cato’s reading of Plato but his belief that it would be disgraceful to fall into the hands of the victorious Caesar; he also judges the deed to have proceeded from a weaker rather than a stronger spirit. Josephus likewise inveighs against it [Col. 0408D] in *The Destruction of Jerusalem* III, chapter 21. Under civil law, those who laid hands upon themselves because of a guilty conscience were not mourned, nor did their relatives name them during preparation for burial: law *Liberorum*, § *Non solent*, Digest, *On Those Branded with Infamy*. But it was foolish not to include those who killed themselves from weariness of life as well. BETUL.

Plato’s. This book is the *Phaedo*.

Driven by the Philosopher’s Authority. Plato did not teach this; the contrary is evident from the beginning of the *Phaedo*. Thus he was driven to that crime not by the philosopher’s authority but by his own madness, since he did not understand the philosopher’s meaning. ISAEUS.

The Ambraciot. This is Cleombrotus, a young man born in the Greek city of Ambracia in Epirus, who threw himself headlong into the sea.—What of That Ambraciot? This is Cleombrotus, whom he named above. Cicero says of him in *Tusculan Disputations* I, chapter 34: “There is Callimachus’s epigram on Cleombrotus of Ambracia, who, he says, though nothing adverse had befallen him, threw himself from a wall into the sea after reading Plato’s book.” It is epigram 24 in Th. Graevius’s edition and 28 in that of Anna Tanaquil. CELL.]

Democritus [Col. 0407A] held a different conviction. Nevertheless,

> Of his own accord he went to meet death and offered up his own head,

than which nothing more criminal can be done. For if a murderer is wicked because he destroys a human being, a person who kills himself is bound by the same crime, because he kills a human being. Indeed, this deed must be judged all the greater because its punishment lies with God alone.

For just as we did not enter this life of our own accord, so we must depart again from this dwelling of the body—which was assigned to us to guard—at the command of the same being who introduced us into this body, to possess it until he orders us to be released. If some violence is inflicted upon us, it must be endured with equanimity, since, when an innocent person’s soul has been extinguished, it cannot remain unavenged, and since we have a great Judge with whom alone vengeance always remains entire.

[Col. 0407B] All those philosophers were therefore murderers, including Cato himself, the foremost figure of Roman [Col. 0408A] wisdom. Before killing himself, he is said to have read Plato’s book concerning the eternity of souls, and he was driven to the highest crime by the philosopher’s authority. Yet he at least appears to have had some reason for dying: his hatred of servitude.

But what of that Ambraciot, who, after reading the same book, threw himself headlong for no other reason than that he believed Plato? A doctrine is utterly accursed and must be shunned if it drives human beings from life. But if Plato had known and taught by whom, how, upon whom, for what deeds, and at what time immortality is bestowed, he would not have driven Cleombrotus to voluntary death, nor Cato either, but would instead have instructed them toward life and justice.

For Cato seems to me to have sought a reason for dying not so much to escape Caesar as to obey the decrees of the Stoics, whom he followed, and to make his name illustrious through some great deed [Col. 0409A];

[Note: [Col. 0409C] [Various Notes on columns 409–410]

Make Illustrious. An ecclesiastical term used frequently in the New Testament by the author of the Vulgate Version, as well as by Sedulius and others.

He Was Merciful. On Caesar’s clemency read Plutarch, Suetonius, Paterculus, and other historians, but especially Cicero’s speeches *For Marcellus* and *For Ligarius*.

I See. I thus restore the reading from the editions of de Tournes, Soubron, and Walchius and all the manuscripts except two recent Royal manuscripts, which, like the printed editions, have “I find.”

That Foolish Old Man. Namely Pythagoras, on whom see Laertius, Philostratus, *Life of Apollonius* VIII, and Gellius IV, chapter 11. Observe here how Lactantius ridicules the doctrine that souls were created before bodies—a doctrine some have ascribed to Lactantius himself. ISAEUS.—That Euphorbus whom Pythagoras falsely claimed formerly to have been was a noble Trojan killed by Menelaus in the Trojan War.

Who Claimed That in a Previous Life, Etc. The second part of this refutation concerns the Pythagorean *palingenesia* (παλιγγενεσία), or *metempsychōsis* (μετεμψύχωσις), concerning which no pagan writer treats more fully than Ovid in *Metamorphoses* XV. After Laertius, read Gellius IV, chapter 11, and Philostratus, *Life of Apollonius* VIII. It is mocked as it deserves by Lucian both elsewhere and in *The Cock*. Among ecclesiastical writers it is noted by Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 46; Tatian, *Against the Greeks*; Origen, *Against Celsus* I; and again by our Lactantius, book VII, chapter 23; Jerome, *Against Jovinian* II and *Apology Against Rufinus*; Augustine, *On the Trinity* XII; Chrysostom, in a homily on John XII; and Cyril, *Against Julian* VII. BETULEIUS.

That He Had Been Euphorbus. Euphorbus was a Trojan killed by Menelaus. CELL.

Pythagoras’s Unique Memory. He says of himself in Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XV, verse 160:

> Was I that man?—for I remember—in the time of the Trojan War  
> I was Euphorbus, son of Panthous, in whose breast there once lodged  
> The heavy spear of the younger son of Atreus.

CELL.

Who Thinks That Life Is Not a Punishment. This is the reading of very many manuscripts and four editions. Seven manuscripts add *malis* (“with evils”); five, like six common editions, give *malis plenam* (“full of evils”).

He Said by Way of Preface. Thus the oldest manuscripts read: one Bologna, three Royal, the Lips., Pal., and one Colbert corrected by a second hand. Fifteen recent manuscripts and the printed editions read “declared”; four recent manuscripts, “professed.” “He said by way of preface” means “he said above.”

Let Us Congratulate Ourselves, Etc. These words are not found in Cicero’s books *On the Laws*. The thought is indeed found, though not in the same words, near the beginning of *Tusculan Disputations* I.

When Devoid of Sensation. One old Bologna manuscript and the Cotton manuscript have “when sensation has perished.” Cicero, five printed editions, and one recent Royal manuscript have “when devoid of sensation.”

As It Seemed to Him. This refers to Cicero, who preceded and immediately follows. Three manuscripts add “he spoke.” Seven manuscripts and the same number of editions have “it seems”; eight manuscripts, “they seem.”

The Scriptures. Namely Daniel XII; Matthew III, XIII, and XXV; John XII and L [probably an uncertain or corrupt citation].

As the Same Tullius. I have added the final word from thirteen printed editions and all the manuscripts except one recent Royal manuscript, which has “Cicero”; it is absent from three recent manuscripts. (See below.)]

yet I see nothing bad that could have happened to him if he had lived. For Gaius Caesar, merciful as he was, even amid the very heat of civil war wished to accomplish nothing other than to appear to have deserved well of the Republic by preserving its two best citizens, Cicero and Cato.

But let us return to those who praise death as a good. You complain of life as though you had lived, or as though you had ever formed any rational understanding of why you were born at all. Would not that true and common Father of all therefore justly rebuke you with Terence’s words? (See Terence, *The Self-Tormentor*, act V, scene 2.)

> First learn what it is to live;  
> If life displeases you, then make use of that course.

You are indignant that you are subject to evils—as though you deserved anything good, when you do not know your Father, your Lord, and your King; when, although you gaze with your eyes upon the most brilliant light, you are nevertheless blind in mind and lie in the profound darkness of ignorance. [Col. 0409B]

This ignorance has caused some people to feel no shame in saying that we were born for the purpose of paying penalties for crimes; and I do not see what more deranged statement could be made. For where, or what, crimes could we have committed when we did not exist at all? Unless perhaps we are to believe that foolish old man who falsely claimed that in a previous life he had been Euphorbus. Since, I suppose, he was born of an obscure family, he adopted a lineage for himself from Homer’s poems.

O marvelous and unique memory of Pythagoras! O wretched forgetfulness of all the rest of us, who do not know who we were before! But perhaps it came about through some error or special favor that he alone did not reach the stream of Lethe or taste the water of oblivion. Clearly, the vain old man [Col. 0409C], as idle old women are accustomed to do, invented tales for credulous [Col. 0410A] children. Had he thought properly of those to whom he spoke these things—had he regarded them as human beings—he would never have claimed for himself so wanton a license to lie. But the vanity of this utterly frivolous man deserves ridicule.

What, then, shall we do with Cicero? At the beginning of his *Consolation* he said that human beings are born for the purpose of paying penalties for crimes, and later repeated the same thing as though rebuking one who thinks that life is not a punishment. He was therefore right when he said by way of preface that he was held fast by error and by a pitiable ignorance of the truth.

## CHAPTER XIX  
### Cicero and other very wise men teach the immortality of souls, but without faith; and death must be judged good or evil from the life previously lived

Those who argue that death is a good, because they know nothing [Col. 0410B] of the truth, reason as follows: “If there is nothing after death, death is not an evil, for it removes the sensation of evil. But if souls survive, death is also a good, because immortality follows.”

Cicero explained this opinion in *On the Laws* as follows:

> “And let us congratulate ourselves, since death will bring either a better condition than that which exists in life, or certainly one no worse. For when the mind flourishes without the body, life is divine; when it is devoid of sensation, there is assuredly no evil.”

Cleverly argued, as it seemed to him—as though nothing else were possible. Yet both alternatives are false. For the divine Scriptures teach that souls are not extinguished, but are either rewarded for justice or punished eternally for crimes. Nor is it right that the person who was wicked but prosperous in life should escape what he deserves, or that the person who was most wretched [Col. 0410C] because of justice should be defrauded of his reward.

This is so true [Col. 0411A] that the same Tullius, in his *Consolation*, assigns them different dwelling places—

[Col. 0411A] [Note: [Col. 0411C] [Various Notes on columns 411–412]

**The same abodes.** The poems of Homer and Virgil teach this same doctrine.—**Not the same abodes.** This passage of Cicero has indeed been lost; but a passage entirely parallel to it survives in *Tusculan Disputations* I.30, and is most worthy of reading. Compare Lactantius VII.7 and Pfanner, *Theologia Gentilis*, ch. 21. **BUNEMANN.**

**But chaste souls, etc.** Euripides says in the *Suppliants* that the soul, upon departing from the body, flies up to heaven, from which it had fallen, while the body is returned to the earth from which it arose. **HERALDUS.**

**To fly to the gods by a light and easy course.** Cicero, in the passage cited: “For these men an easy return lay open to those gods from whom they had proceeded.” **BUNEMANN.**

**A human being born.** There is elegance underlying the combination of these words. Book VI, ch. 3: “He denies immortality to no human being born.” Book VII, ch. 5: “If indeed every human being born were to become immortal.” Seneca, *On the Constancy of the Wise Man*, ch. 6: “There is no reason for you to doubt whether a human being born can raise himself above human things.” **BUNEMANN.**

[Col. 0411D]

**Aristides.** Here the name is used for any just man, just as Phalaris stands for a tyrant, Cato for a good citizen, and Catiline for a wicked man; their histories are very well known.

**Or Phalaris.** He is the notorious tyrant of Acragas in Sicily, famous for his bronze bull. On him see Cicero, *Against Verres* VI.33.

**Does not perceive.** This is the reading of the older and better manuscripts and of thirteen printed editions. But fifteen recent manuscripts, together with two old Roman editions, read “does not feel.”

**Depends upon the character of one’s life.** In accordance with the maxim that one must await the end of life. Hence Pliny, book VII, ch. 40, says: “So indeed it is: one day judges one person and another day another, and yet the final day judges them all.”

**But if, on the other hand.** I have restored this reading from the two best and oldest manuscripts, the first Bologna manuscript and the Regius-Puteanus. The others read “but if otherwise” or “if otherwise.”

**Do not weigh.** The Subiaco edition reads “do not counterbalance.”

**That foolish saying.** See Euripides in Plato’s *Gorgias* and in Stobaeus, *Sermon* 121; Aristophanes, *Frogs*; [Col. 0412C] Cicero, *Dream of Scipio* and *Tusculan Disputations* I. Cicero nevertheless does not shrink from endorsing this saying, which Lactantius calls foolish, in *Letters* XVI.8.—**That foolish saying, etc.** He is referring to Euripides, whose lines were preserved by Origen, *Against Celsus* VII, p. 366:

> Τίς οἶδεν, εἰ τὸ ζῆν μέν ἐστι κατθανεῖν,  
> Τὸ κατθανεῖν δὲ ζῆν;
>
> Who knows whether living is dying,  
> and dying living?

Add Spencer on this passage, p. 89. Closely parallel to these are Euripides, *Trojan Women* 631–632, and *Uncertain Tragedies*, fr. 331. **BUNEMANN.**

**It is attributed to Silenus.** Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I.48: “A certain tale is told about Silenus. When he had been captured by Midas, it is related that, as the price of his release, he bestowed this gift upon him: he taught the king that by far the best thing for a human being was not to be born, and the next best to die as soon as possible.” On Silenus compare Perizonius on Aelian, *Varia Historia* III.18. **BUNEMANN.**

**Not to be born.** This passage also occurs in *Tusculan Disputations* I, not far from the end. Pliny likewise says in the preface to book VII: “And so there have been many who judged it best not to be born, [Col. 0412D] or else to be extinguished as quickly as possible.”

**To die as soon as possible, as though escaping from a fire the violence of fortune.** The word “to die,” which is absent from twenty-six recent manuscripts and six editions, I have restored from three Royal manuscripts, six Vatican manuscripts, the manuscripts of Caucius and Junius, the first old Clermont manuscript, the Roman edition, and nine others, as well as from Cicero himself, from whom this passage was taken. But in Cicero the word “violence” is lacking, although it is supplied by thirty-seven manuscripts and fourteen printed editions and is also required by the sense.—**To die as soon as possible, and as though.** I added “to die” and “and” from six Vatican manuscripts, the editions from 1465 to 1539, and all the editions of de Tournes from 1548 and 1614. **BUNEMANN.**

**To escape the violence of fortune.** The words “the violence of fortune” occur in ten Vatican manuscripts, five of Sparke’s manuscripts, the Emmanuel and Cambridge manuscripts, and three Leipzig manuscripts—except that the third reads “and the violence of fortune.” Heumann nevertheless goes further and declares that the words “the violence of fortune” should be expunged. In my judgment they should be retained, because in the refutation below Lactantius makes mention of fortune. **BUNEMANN.**

**Plato’s saying is not dissimilar.** On this saying of Plato see Plutarch at the end of his *Marius*.

He declared that the just and the impious inhabit the same abodes. For, he says, those same wise men did not think that the same path into heaven lay open to everyone: they taught that those contaminated by vices and crimes are thrust down into darkness and lie in mire, but that chaste souls—pure, whole, uncorrupted, and refined by good studies and disciplines—fly to the gods by a light and easy course, that is, to a nature resembling their own. This opinion contradicts the earlier argument. For that argument was framed as though every human being born must necessarily be endowed with immortality. What distinction, then, will there be between virtue and crime if it makes no difference whether someone is Aristides or Phalaris, Cato or Catiline? But no one perceives this contradiction between facts [Col. 0411B] and opinions unless he possesses the truth.

If, therefore, someone asks us whether death is good or evil, we shall reply that its character depends upon the character of one’s life. For just as life itself is good if it is lived with virtue, but evil if it is lived with crime, so death too must be weighed according to the deeds of the preceding life. It therefore follows that, if life has been spent in the worship of God, death is not an evil, because it is a passage to immortality. But if the contrary is true, death must necessarily be an evil, since it transfers a person to eternal punishments, as I have said.

What, then, shall we say except that those people are mistaken who either desire death as a good or flee from life [Col. 0411C] as an evil? The truth is that they are utterly unfair, because [Col. 0412A] they do not weigh fewer evils against more numerous goods. For although they spend their entire lives amid elaborate and varied pleasures, they wish to die if some trace of bitterness happens to befall them; and they act as though they had never fared well merely because they had fared badly at some time. They therefore condemn life in its entirety and suppose it to be filled with nothing but evils.

From this arose that foolish saying that what we regard as life is death, while what we fear as death is life; and thus that the first good is not to be born, and the second to die sooner. To give the saying greater authority, it is attributed to Silenus. Cicero, in his *Consolation*, says:

> By far the best thing is not to be born and not to fall upon these rocks of life; but the next best, if you have been born, is to die as soon as possible, as though escaping from a fire the violence of fortune.

[Col. 0412B] That Cicero believed this utterly frivolous saying is apparent from the fact that he added something of his own to embellish it. I therefore ask: for whom does he suppose it best not to be born, when there is no one at all there to perceive it? For perception is what makes anything good or evil. Next, why did he suppose that all of life is nothing but rocks and fire—as though it had been within our power not to be born, or as though fortune, rather than God, bestowed life upon us, or as though the manner of living bore any resemblance to a fire?

Plato’s saying is not dissimilar. He said that he gave thanks to nature: first, because he had been born [Col. 0412C] a human being rather than a speechless animal; next, because [Col. 0413A] he had been born male rather [Col. 0413A] than female; because he was a Greek rather than a barbarian; and finally, because he was an Athenian and had been born in the time of Socrates.

[Col. 0413B]

**Variorum Notes to Columns 413–414**

**Because he was male.** I have restored this reading from three old Roman editions, the Venice edition of 1490, and eight other editions, as well as from all the manuscripts [Col. 0413C] except five, which, together with seven common editions, read “because he was masculine.” **Rather than female.** The Jewish teachers likewise say in *Pesachim*, fol. 65, and elsewhere: “Happy is he whose children are males; woe to him whose children are females.” **BUNEMANN.**

**Because he was an Athenian.** The Cambridge manuscript and seven printed editions add “not a Theban,” which appears to be a gloss. Diogenes Laertius, book I, attributes the same saying to Socrates. The Subiaco edition adds “not a Theban.”

**Nothing more insane was ever said.** One must not pass over in silence what the Jews have in the prayers specifically prescribed for their men: “Blessed are you, O Lord God, because you created me a man, not a woman; an Israelite, not a foreigner.” **GATAKER.**

**That it had been born.** Bunemann reads “that he had been born,” with the masculine participle, and gives the following account of this alteration.—I restore the masculine form from the third Leipzig manuscript, the manuscripts of Reimann and Rost, the Venice editions of 1471, 1472, both editions of 1478, the 1493 edition, and the Paris, Juntine, Gymnich, Aldine, Isaeus, and Gruter editions. **BUNEMANN.**

**But plainly he believed Pythagoras, etc.** Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, also testifies that Plato followed the teaching of Pythagoras. And the same Augustine, *Against Julian* II, quotes the following words from Ambrose’s book against Plato:

> I marvel how so great a philosopher could enclose the soul—which he credits with the power to confer mortality—in owls and twigs, and even clothe it in the savagery of beasts, when in the *Timaeus* he had stated that it was the work of God and belonged among the immortal things made by God. Yet he asserted that the body did not appear to be the work of the supreme God, because the nature of human flesh differs in no respect from the nature of an animal’s body.

Plato bought the books of Philolaus the Pythagorean from some poor women; hence he stole from them everything he wrote about the immortality of the soul. Tzetzes, *Chiliades* II, *Various Histories*. **BETULEIUS.**

**Pass.** Minucius Felix expresses this at ch. 37: “Souls repeatedly pass into other, new bodies.” **BUNEMANN.**

**Which is both futile and impossible.** Lactantius appears to have held a different view about the souls of the impious: namely, that an evil spirit has power over them, so that through magical art they may be changed into wolves. Such a transformation is acknowledged not only by Virgil, *Eclogue* IX, and other poets, but also by Pliny, book VIII, ch. 22. But whether the souls that pass into beasts belong to the pious or the impious has little bearing on the matter. For one complete animal to be made from another complete animal altogether far surpasses created power; and what God has denied to all creatures cannot be attributed to them without impiety, etc. **VOSSIUS.**

**Like a river.** Eight recent manuscripts read “like lightning.”

**Be enclosed.** Six recent manuscripts read “be introduced.”

**Give thanks.** I have restored this reading from all the manuscripts except two recent Royal manuscripts, which, like the printed editions, read “boast.” Similarly below: “whose times the wise man congratulates himself on having been born in”; and earlier, “give thanks to nature.” Nowhere, however, does the text read “boast.”

**Provide.** Eleven manuscripts read “give.”

**Alcibiades also and Critias.** In the *Busiris*, Isocrates denies that Alcibiades was a pupil of Socrates, refuting Polycrates, who had asserted it. And in Plato’s *Gorgias*, Socrates himself calls Alcibiades his companion, ἑταῖρος (*hetairos*). For the rest, concerning the career of Alcibiades read Justin, book V; Thucydides, book VI; and Plutarch’s *Nicias* and elsewhere. Concerning the Thirty Tyrants, [Col. 0414D] read Xenophon, *Hellenica* II, and Justin, book V. **BETULEIUS.**—**Alcibiades … hearers of Socrates.** Nepos, *Alcibiades* 2: “He was educated by Socrates.” Xenophon says the same in *Memorabilia* I, fol. 713 ff.; Lactantius follows him here above the others and calls Alcibiades an enemy of his country. Nepos, to be sure, asserts the contrary; but Cicero, *On the Orator* I.34, says: “What of Critias? What of Alcibiades? Though certainly not good citizens of their own states, they were nevertheless learned and eloquent. Were they not educated through Socratic discussions?” Compare Maximus of Tyre, *Dissertation* VIII, p. 90. **BUNEMANN.**

**That he had been born in his times.** Reimann reads: “that he had been born in those times.” But the pronouns “his” and “himself” are combined no less elegantly.

**Inquisitive eyes.** If you read at the same time what appears below, you will understand that our author is here imitating Cicero, *On the Responses of the Soothsayers* 17, where he says of the rites of the Good Goddess: “That sacrifice excludes not only inquisitive eyes,” etc. **BUNEMANN.**

**Intrude.** On these matters see St. Augustine, *City of God* VIII.3.

It is impossible to say how great a blindness and how many errors ignorance of the truth produces in human minds. For my part, I would maintain that nothing more insane has ever been said concerning human affairs. As though, if he had been born a barbarian, a woman, or even an ass, he would still have been that same Plato, rather than the very thing he had been born as!

But plainly he believed Pythagoras, who, in order to forbid people to eat animals, said that souls pass from bodies into the bodies of other animals. This is both futile and impossible. It is futile because there was no need to introduce old souls into new bodies, since the same Craftsman who had once made the first souls could always have made new ones. It is impossible because [Col. 0413B] a soul endowed with right reason can no more alter the nature of its own condition than fire can strive downward or pour out its flame sideways like a river.

Thus this wise man believed that it could have happened that the soul then present in Plato might be enclosed in some speechless animal while remaining endowed with human perception, so that it could understand and grieve that it had been burdened with an unsuitable body. How much more sensibly he would have acted if he had said that he gave thanks because he had been born intelligent and teachable, and amid such wealth that he could receive a liberal education.

For what benefit was there in the fact that he was born at Athens? Did there not arise in other cities very many men of outstanding ability and learning, each of whom was better than all the Athenians? How many thousands of people should we suppose were born both at Athens and in the time of Socrates, yet remained uneducated and foolish? For neither walls nor the place where someone is poured forth from the womb gives a person wisdom.

And what purpose was served by his congratulating himself on having been born in the time of Socrates? Could Socrates provide ability to those who studied under him? It did not occur to Plato that Alcibiades and Critias had also been constant hearers of the same Socrates. One of them was his country’s most bitter enemy, and the other the cruelest of all tyrants.

## CHAPTER XX  
### Socrates Was More Prudent Than Others in Philosophy, Although He Was Foolish in Many Matters

Let us now see what was so great in Socrates himself that the wise man was justified in giving thanks for having been born in his time. I do not deny that he was somewhat more sensible than the others who thought that the nature of things could be comprehended by human ingenuity. In this I judge that they were not merely senseless but even impious, because they wished to intrude inquisitive eyes into the secrets of that heavenly providence.

We know that at Rome and in very many cities there are certain sacred rites [Col. 0415A] which it is held unlawful for men to witness.

[Col. 0415C]

**Variorum Notes to Columns 415–416**

**It is held unlawful.** The comparison proceeds from the lesser to the greater, though only according to the pagans’ opinion.

**Or by some accident.** I have restored this reading from eight old editions and all the manuscripts except three Royal and two Leipzig manuscripts, which, like seven printed editions, read “someone”; one Colbert manuscript reads “by anyone.” Note in passing the use of *quopiam* in the ablative, as in Arnobius, book VI near the end and book VII near the beginning.

**This heavenly temple, etc.** Scipio similarly called the universe a temple in Cicero’s *Dream of Scipio*. On that passage Macrobius says:

> The whole universe is rightly called the temple of God, because of those who suppose that God is nothing other than heaven itself and the heavenly things we see. Accordingly, to show that the power of the supreme God can scarcely be understood and can never be seen, he called everything subjected to human sight the temple of him who is apprehended by the mind alone. Thus one who venerates these things as temples must nevertheless know that the highest worship is owed to their Creator; and whoever is admitted to the use of this temple must know that he should live according to the discipline of a priest, etc.

**BETULEIUS.**

**Of the Good Goddess, etc.** Lactantius discusses her shortly below and above at I.22; Propertius, IV, Elegy 9, says concerning the rites of the Good Goddess:

> [Col. 0415D] Places closed to men for the female goddess, and springs requiring purification,  
> sacred mysteries exposed with impunity to no man.

Not only was it unlawful for men to enter the temple of the Good Goddess, but even paintings of male figures in the temple were veiled, as Juvenal, *Satire* 6, and Seneca, *Letter* 97, attest. On these mysteries of the Good Goddess or of Vesta see Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book II; Cicero’s speech *On His House*; Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.11–12; and Servius on *Aeneid* IV.

**Sense.** Here “heart” is used for mind, prudence, or wisdom.—**He possessed some human sense.** That is, as above, “he was somewhat more sensible.” Lactantius, together with others, located wisdom in the heart. Hence III.13: “Wisdom is in the heart”; *On the Workmanship of God* 10: “The heart is the dwelling place of wisdom”; ch. 12: “The human heart is formed first, because all life and wisdom are in it.” **BUNEMANN.**

**What is above us has no concern for us.** Jerome also mentions this in his *Apology Against Rufinus*. Yet Lactantius appears somewhat unfair to Socrates and contradicts himself, since elsewhere he praises Socrates highly. Nevertheless, we must not go so far as to speak like Erasmus of Rotterdam, who often said that he could scarcely refrain from saying: “Saint Socrates, pray for us.”

**Let us cast ourselves down … upon the earth.** Minucius Felix, ch. 8, interprets the saying more fairly. Tertullian, *To the Nations* II.4, attributes it to Epicurus. Those who have written about Socrates have rightly reproved Lactantius for this adverse interpretation. **BUNEMANN.**

**Falls apart.** This is the reading of eleven older and better manuscripts and several printed editions; the others read “flows down,” less appropriately.

**But the same man swore by the dog, etc.** Athenaeus, *Deipnosophistae* IX, mentions this oath. Apollonius, in Philostratus VI, excuses Socrates on the ground that he swore by these things not as gods but in order to avoid swearing by the gods. What shall I say of the theologians? Tertullian, *Apology* 14, says: “I say nothing of the philosophers, contenting myself with Socrates, who, in contempt of the gods, swore by the oak, the goat, and the dog.” But Socrates was condemned precisely because he destroyed the gods. Augustine, *On True Religion* 2, interprets this more leniently. Meanwhile, we shall not deny that the dog was a god among the Egyptians, as is attested not only by Eusebius in the *Preparation for the Gospel* but also by Plato himself in the *Gorgias*. **BETULEIUS.**—Socrates was called the Attic buffoon because he delivered many of his teachings jokingly. Besides Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I.34 and *On Ends* V, see Minucius Felix in the *Octavius*, shortly before the end.

**O buffoon of a man … Zeno the Epicurean.** Lactantius follows Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I.34: “Zeno attacked with abuse not only his contemporaries—Apollodorus, Syllus, and the others—but even Socrates himself, the father of philosophy, saying in Latin that he had been an Attic buffoon.” **BUNEMANN.**

**As Zeno the Epicurean says.** He must be distinguished from Zeno of Citium, the Stoic, and also from Zeno of Elea. Among eight men named Zeno, Diogenes Laertius places this Epicurean eighth and identifies him as a native of Sidon. **BUNEMANN.**

Those, therefore, who are not permitted to contaminate those rites abstain from looking at them; and if by chance, error, or some accident a man witnesses them, the transgression is expiated first by his punishment and then by a repetition of the sacrifice. What are you to do with people who wish to investigate what has not been granted to them? Surely those who seek to profane the mysteries of the universe and this heavenly temple with impious disputations are far more criminal than those who enter the sanctuary of Vesta, the Good Goddess, or Ceres. For although men are not permitted to approach those inner shrines, they were nevertheless constructed by men.

Yet these men not only escape the charge of impiety but—what is far more shameful—acquire a reputation for eloquence and the glory of genius. What if they were actually able to discover something? For they are as foolish in making assertions as they are unscrupulous in conducting inquiries, since they can neither discover anything nor defend it even if [Col. 0415B] they have discovered it. For if by chance they glimpse the truth, as very often happens, their conduct causes others to refute it as false. No one comes down from heaven to render judgment on the opinions of each individual. Consequently, no one should doubt that those who investigate such matters are foolish, absurd, and insane.

Socrates, then, possessed some human sense because, understanding that these matters could not be discovered, he withdrew from questions of this sort; yet I fear that this was the only matter in which he did so. For many of his teachings are not merely unworthy of praise but most worthy of censure, and in these he closely resembled his own fellows. From among them I shall select one that has won everyone’s approval.

Socrates had this celebrated maxim: “What is above us has no concern for us.” Let us therefore cast ourselves down upon the earth and turn into feet the hands that were given to us for noble works. Let heaven, for the contemplation of which we have been raised upright, have no concern for us; indeed, let light itself have no concern for us—even though the cause of our nourishment certainly comes from heaven.

But if what he meant was that heavenly matters ought not to be debated, neither could he comprehend the nature of those things that lay beneath his feet. What, then? Did he perhaps misspeak? That is unlikely. Rather, what he meant by his words was plainly that religion should not be practiced at all; for if he had said this openly, no one would have tolerated it.

Who does not perceive that this universe, fashioned according to so marvelous an order, is governed by some providence, [Col. 0416B] since nothing can remain in existence without any ruler? Thus a house abandoned by its inhabitant collapses; a ship without a pilot goes to destruction; and a body deserted by its soul falls apart. Much less, then, should we suppose that so immense a mass could either have been constructed without a craftsman or have remained standing for so long without a ruler.

If Socrates wished to overthrow those public religions, I do not condemn him; indeed, I shall praise him—provided that he himself discovered something better. But this same man swore by the dog and the goose. O buffoon of a man—as Zeno the Epicurean calls him—absurd, ruined, and beyond hope, if he wished to ridicule religion; mad, [Col. 0417A] if he acted seriously and regarded the most disgraceful of animals as God! Who would now dare to condemn the superstitions of the Egyptians, when Socrates confirmed them at Athens by his own authority?

And was it not the height of folly that, before his death, he asked his friends to sacrifice on his behalf the cock [Col. 0417A] that he had vowed to Asclepius?

[Col. 0417B]

**Variorum Notes to Columns 417–418**

**A cock to Asclepius.** On this matter see Tertullian, *On the Soldier’s Crown*.

**Sacrifice on his behalf.** This is the reading transmitted by all printed editions and almost all manuscripts, including four of the oldest. Two old Royal manuscripts, as also the *Epitome*, ch. 37, have *prosecrarent*, a word that the Latin language does not admit. Two more recent manuscripts read *prosecant*; others, *procurarent*; and three, *consecrarent*.—Bunemann, however, reads *prosecrarent* and gives the following explanation of the word: “Amid so great a variation among the books, I thought it safer to present the reading of the oldest codices.” Étienne Baluze, on *The Deaths of the Persecutors* 33, says: “The Royal manuscript 3735, which reads *prosecrarent*, is better, in my judgment.” **BUNEMANN.**

**Rhadamanthus.** A judge of the underworld. Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.566.

**Reciperator.** I have restored *reciperatorem* from a very old Royal manuscript nine hundred years old; and the learned men Theodore Canter, Johannes Caucius, and Gallaeus judged that it should be so read. For *recuperator* and *recupero* derive from the ancient verb *reciperare*, as Paulus Francius of Besançon rightly observed in his *Treasury of Scholastic Learning*, folio, Frankfurt, 1622. Our reading is supported by the Marmoutier manuscript, which has *receperatorem*; manuscript 29 and nine editions abbreviate it as *receptorem*; one recent Royal manuscript and nine recent editions read *recuperatorem*; the Utrecht manuscript corruptly reads *imperatorem*. *Reciperatores*, or *recuperatores* if one prefers, were those who adjudicated the recovery and restoration to its owner of private property removed by deceit and fraud. Gellius XX.1; Livy XXVI.48.

**Thinks.** This reading comes from eighteen manuscripts, including the oldest Royal manuscripts. The rest, together with the printed editions, read “would think.”

**To have been.** This likewise ought to be read on the authority of the oldest manuscripts—the first Bologna manuscript, two Royal manuscripts, and three others—rather than “to be” in the remaining witnesses.

**Of justice, etc.** I would prefer to read “in equality” with Thysius, because of what follows: “on an equal footing … so that they may be equal.” But *aequitas* too is used by Seneca in the sense of equality. **The force of justice in equity.** I would prefer “equality,” not because *aequitas*, called ἐπιεικές (*epieikes*) by the Greeks, is not the foundation of justice, as Plato and Aristotle and, after them, Cicero abundantly teach; rather, the community under discussion proves that Lactantius means τὸ ἴσον (*to ison*), or τὴν ἰσότητα (*tēn isotēta*), which Cicero usually translates as *aequalitas*, “equality.” Yet there are some who also translate ἰσότης (*isotēs*) as *aequitas*, understanding by it what Varro calls *parilitas*, “parity.” See Plato, *Laws* V and VI, and Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics* V. **BETULEIUS.**

**In equality.** Bunemann does in fact read “in equality” and supplies the following note.—**In equality.** So too in V.14 and the following chapter: “By equality I mean … making oneself equal with others, which Cicero calls evenness … all are equal, that is, peers … he bestows equality upon all … with equal right.”

**Possess.** The first old Bologna manuscript reads “will possess.”

**This may be tolerated.** Two recent manuscripts, together with five editions, read “may be done”; one recent Royal manuscript reads “This cannot be done.”—**This may be tolerated so long as.** In place of the received reading, the *Epitome*, ch. 38, has: “With regard to property, it is tolerable … it can in some way be tolerated.” **BUNEMANN.**

**Marriages also, etc.** Plato discusses this elsewhere and especially in *Republic* V. Aristotle argues against it in *Politics* II. Among ecclesiastical writers, Eusebius does so in *Preparation for the Gospel* XIII.12. Plato is censured by Epiphanius II.III, by Chrysostom in his first homily on Matthew and on Acts II, and likewise by Epiphanius II.I. **BETULEIUS.**

**If they are patient.** Ten manuscripts and four common editions read “patient”; the Aldine edition reads “wise.”

**In their turns.** I have restored this reading from nearly all the better manuscripts and nine older editions. Seven manuscripts and eight recent common editions read “and in their turns.”

[Col. 0418D]

**States would be happy.** This opinion belongs to Socrates in *Republic* V. See Cicero, *To Quintus His Brother* I.1, whose words are:

> Plato, that foremost man in genius and learning, believed that commonwealths would finally be happy if either learned and wise men began to govern them or those who governed devoted all their effort to learning and wisdom.

A treatise by Plutarch survives on the same subject. Lactantius’ purpose is not to condemn this saying, but to show from the outcome that neither Socrates nor Plato should be numbered among the wise and, as St. Ambrose says, that they described not a true commonwealth but merely a fictitious and shadowy one. **BETULEIUS.**

**Who.** I have restored this word from six Royal manuscripts, six Colbert manuscripts, and seven others, together with eight old and three recent editions. It is absent from three Royal manuscripts and an equal number of printed editions.

**But what reason did he offer for this most disgraceful proposal?** Eight recent editions read “But when.” I have restored “what” with interrogative force from the old printed editions and all the manuscripts, except that fifteen read “nevertheless” instead of “indeed.”

Socrates was evidently afraid that, before Rhadamanthus as *reciperator* (recovery judge), Asclepius might hold him liable for his vow. I would think him utterly mad if he had died while afflicted by disease. But since he did this while of sound mind, the person who thinks that Socrates was wise is himself insane. Behold the man in whose time the wise Plato congratulated himself on having been born.

## CHAPTER XXI  
### On Plato’s Teaching, Which Would Destroy Commonwealths

Let us nevertheless see what Socrates taught Plato, [Col. 0417B] since, after rejecting the whole of natural philosophy, he turned to an inquiry into virtue and duty. I therefore do not doubt that he instructed his hearers in the precepts of justice.

Thus, under Socrates’ instruction, it did not escape Plato that the force of justice consists in equity, since all are born on an equal footing. “Therefore,” he says, “let them possess nothing private or belonging to themselves; instead, so that they may be equal, as the principle of justice requires, let them possess everything in common.” [Col. 0418A] This may be tolerated so long as it appears to be said about money. I could show by many arguments how impossible and unjust this very arrangement is. Let us nevertheless grant that it can be done. For everyone will be wise and will despise money.

Where, then, did this community lead him? “Marriages also,” he says, “will have to be held in common”: evidently so that many men may rush upon the same woman like dogs, and so that the one who prevails in strength may take possession of her; or, if they are patient, as philosophers are, they may wait and visit her in their turns as though visiting a brothel.

O marvelous equality of Plato! Where, then, is the virtue of chastity? Where is marital fidelity? If you abolish these, all justice is abolished. Yet the same man said that states would be happy if either [Col. 0418B] philosophers ruled or kings became philosophers. Would you give royal power to so just and equitable a man, who would take their own possessions from some, grant the property of others to others, and prostitute the chastity of women—something no king, or even tyrant, has ever done?

But what reason did he offer for this most disgraceful proposal? He says: “The state will be harmonious and bound together by ties of mutual love if everyone is everyone’s husband and father, wife and child.” [Col. 0419A] What a confusion of the human race this is! How can affection be preserved where there is nothing certain to be loved? How will a man love a woman, or a woman a man, unless they have always lived together, unless a devoted mind [Col. 0419A] and fidelity maintained toward one another have made their love indivisible?

[Col. 0419C]

**Variorum Notes to Columns 419–420**

**A devoted mind.** Thysius explains “a devoted mind” as “bound by vows”; but *devotus* has a stronger force, as does the noun *devotio*. Consider V.7: “faith devoted to its God”; II.12: “to serve with the utmost devotion”; *On the Workmanship of God* XIX: “not to betray faith and devotion.” **BUNEMANN.**

**Indivisible love.** This follows Cyprian’s style, II.4 in Erasmus’s edition: “Indivisible love unites us to your honor.” **BUNEMANN.**

**The community therefore perishes for that one person.** I have restored “for that one person,” namely, the son. This reading is supported above all others [Col. 0419D] by nineteen manuscripts and the old Roman, Egnatius, Fasius, and Betuleius editions. Three Royal manuscripts and five more recent common editions read “that one”; the Gothic manuscript reads “that single one”; in place of these, five printed editions read “of marriage.”

**He intends.** I have restored this reading from the oldest Royal manuscript and six others, taking the reference to be to Plato. Both what precedes and what follows require the singular. Seven manuscripts, together with the editions, read “they intend.”

**Who always.** Seven recent manuscripts read “who often.”

**In external things.** The Stoics believed not only that things subject to fortune but even bodies themselves lie outside us, as is clear from Epictetus’ *Enchiridion*. This agrees quite well with Christ’s own teaching, when he affirmed that acts of robbery and adultery—that is, ὀρέξεις (*orexeis*, “desires”) proceeding from us—alone defile a person. **BETULEIUS.**

**When their minds have become equal.** Lactantius uses “equal in mind” by a Greek idiom. I have restored “have become” from the manuscripts and the editions of Betuleius, de Tournes, Walch, and Soubron. “Are” is the reading of the other common editions.

[Col. 0420B]

**For if justice, etc.** Justice embraces all the virtues within itself, as Aristotle says in *Nicomachean Ethics* V. Lactantius calls it the mother of the other virtues because it cherishes the others like daughters within its own bosom and embrace. On this see also Johannes Stobaeus.

**Removed.** *Tulit* is often used in the sense of “took away” or “abolished.” Lactantius himself uses it again in the *Epitome*, ch. 29, quoting Gellius: “If you remove the one, you take away both.” Ambrose, *On Duties* I.32: “Take benevolence out of human practice, and it will be as though you had removed the sun from the world.” *On Duties* III.5: “He merely took the spear … and the little jar of water.” **BUNEMANN.**

[Col. 0420D]

**Since there would be nothing belonging to another from which one might abstain.** This reading is retained by a great many manuscripts and printed editions, and it is excellent, whatever Thomasius may say. For we quite correctly say that a thing is “abstained from,” as though it were held at a distance and prohibited. Lactantius, VII.17: “It withheld the rains,” etc. Livy: “Fortune kept Alexander the Great away from war with Rome.” Sixteen recent manuscripts and eight editions read: “since there would be nothing from which one might abstain.” The Bologna manuscript reads: “since there would be no one who abstained from another’s property.” From Isaeus.

**And spendthrifts.** That is, consumers and dissipators. Horace, *Epodes* I: ἄσωτοι (*asōtoi*), “profligates,” the intemperate and squanderers of patrimony. One Royal, one Colbert, the Palatine, and the Brun manuscript read “and ruined men,” which is an interpretation of the word *nepotes*, “spendthrifts.”—**Luxurious men and spendthrifts.** Cicero, *For Quinctius* 12: “What spendthrift so ruined and extravagant, even when his money had not yet been eaten away but was still abundant, would have been as dissolute as Sextus Naevius was?” **BUNEMANN.**

**I shall say.** So the manuscripts. The printed editions read “I say.”

Likewise, if all children belong to everyone, who will be able to love children as his own when he either does not know or doubts that they are his? Who will render honor to someone as his father when he does not know from whom he was born? The result is that he will not only regard another man as his father but also his own father as a stranger.

Moreover, a wife can be common, but a son cannot, since he must necessarily be conceived from one man alone. The community therefore perishes for that one person, with nature herself crying out against it. [Col. 0419B] It remains, then, that Plato intends wives alone to be held in common for the sake of harmony. Yet there is no more powerful cause of discord than many males’ desire for a single woman. If reason could not warn Plato of this, examples certainly could: both those of speechless animals, which fight with the utmost ferocity for this very reason, and those of human beings, who have always waged the gravest wars among themselves over the same matter.

## CHAPTER XXII  
### On Plato’s Precepts and Their Refutation
It remains, then, that this community possesses nothing other than adultery and lusts—precisely those things for whose utter eradication virtue is most necessary. Accordingly, he did not [Col. 0419C] find the concord he sought, because he did not see whence it arises. For justice has no force in external arrangements, [Col. 0420A] not even in the body; rather, it is wholly concerned with the human mind. Whoever wishes, therefore, to make human beings equal ought not to take away marriages or possessions, but arrogance, pride, and conceit, so that the powerful and exalted may know themselves to be the equals even of the most destitute. For once insolence and injustice have been removed from the rich, it will make no difference whether some are rich and others poor, provided their minds are equal; and nothing except religion toward God can bring this about.

He therefore thought that he had discovered justice when he had completely overthrown it, because community ought to be a community of minds, not of perishable things. For if justice is the mother of all the virtues, justice itself is subverted when those virtues are individually removed. Yet Plato removed frugality before all else; for frugality plainly does not exist where nothing [Col. 0420B] is privately owned. He removed abstinence, since there would be nothing belonging to another from which one might abstain. He removed self-control; he removed chastity—virtues of the highest importance in both sexes. He removed reserve, modesty, and propriety, if things customarily judged shameful and disgraceful begin to be regarded as honorable and lawful. Thus, while wishing to give virtue to everyone, he takes it away from everyone. Private ownership supplies the material both for vices and for virtues, whereas community of property supplies nothing but license for vice. Men who have many women can be called nothing other than dissolute spendthrifts. Likewise, women who are possessed by many must be, not adulteresses—since there is no definite marriage—but prostitutes and harlots.

He therefore reduced human life to the likeness [Col. 0420C]—I will not say of dumb animals, but of cattle and wild beasts. For nearly all birds contract marriages, pair off, [Col. 0421A] and defend their nests as though they were marriage beds, with harmonious devotion; and because they are certain of their offspring, they love them, while if you place another’s offspring among them, they drive it away.

[Col. 0421A]

> [Note: [Col. 0421B] Variorum Notes on columns 421–422]
>
> **Pair off.** So MSS. 3 Royal, 2 Bologna, Cauc., Jun., Cambridge, Cotton, 1 Colbert, etc., and the old Roman, Aldine, Paris, and Florence editions, together with seven others. One Royal MS. and two Leipzig MSS. have “are joined”; very many MSS. have “pair”; three recent MSS. and several editions have “join together.” The race of doves is especially celebrated for this by Aristotle, *History of Animals*, Book IX, chapter 7, and by Pliny, Book X, chapter 34.
>
> [Col. 0421C]
>
> **Marriage beds.** The best reading, found in very many MSS. and in the editions of Isaeus, Sparke, and Walch. The other commonly printed editions and ten MSS. have “generative beds.” But *lectus genialis*, “marriage bed,” occurs in Horace, *Epistles* I.1, and Persius, *Satires* 2.3.
>
> **And since he saw.** In Book VII of the *Laws*, Plato confounds all the duties of males and females and adduces as examples the Amazons, Spartan maidens, and the women of the Sarmatians and Pontus. Indeed, in Book V of the *Republic*, does he not teach that women are as fit as men to undertake public duties, except that they are somewhat weaker? Aristotle, however, criticizes this arrangement in Book II, chapter 4, of the *Politics*. These same views are censured by Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book III, chapter 12. In the Christian commonwealth, women are barred from ecclesiastical offices. **BETULEIUS.**
>
> **That wool and the loom should be assigned to men, etc.** St. Epiphanius, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, writing against various heresies, reviews in his third book the customs of various nations, [Col. 0421D] and reports something of this kind concerning the Seres.
>
> **Nor so vain.** I restored this from nearly all the MSS. and ten old printed editions. One Colbert MS. and the Aldine edition read “so varied” in place of “so foolish”; MSS. 3 Royal and Marmoutier, together with seven recent printed editions, read “nor so wise.”
>
> **Amid such folly.** Five printed editions together with one Royal MS. read “amid such variety.”
>
> **Lesser men.** That is, philosophers of lesser reputation, who will be discussed presently.
>
> **In calm water.** The Gotha MS., the third Leipzig edition, and Reimann have “into calm water,” that is, the sea. I prefer the received reading from the other MSS. and all the old editions. Calm is opposed to tempest: “in calm water” means “when it is calm.” Seneca, *Agamemnon* III.682: “Trusting too little in calm weather, they boldly entrust themselves once more to the sea.” Livy, Book XXVI: “We are not sailing in calm weather, but have already been almost sunk by several storms.” Again in Book XXVI: “The soldiers advanced into deep water while it was calm.” **BUN.**
>
> **From which they could.** I restored this from all MSS. and editions except two recent Royal MSS. and five editions, which read, [Col. 0422B] “from which they think.”
>
> **Democritus.** Valerius Maximus, Book VIII, chapter 7, gives a different account: “But Democritus,” he says, “although he might have been counted among the wealthy—for his riches were so great that his father could easily have provided a banquet for Xerxes’ army—in order that he might apply himself to literary studies with a mind all the freer, retained only a very small sum and gave his patrimony to his country.” Laertius writes that he divided his share among his brothers and reserved for himself some money as traveling expenses. Seneca, in his book *On Providence*, says: “Democritus cast away riches, considering them a burden upon a good mind.” Cicero, *On Ends* V, comes closer to Lactantius: “Why did Democritus do these same things, who—whether the report be true or false is a question—was said to have deprived himself of sight? Certainly, so that his mind might be distracted as little as possible from its reflections, he neglected his patrimony and left his fields uncultivated. What else was he seeking but the happy life?” Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 46, gives a different interpretation of his voluntary blinding. **BETULEIUS.**—Democritus is praised. On this matter it is worth reading Philo, *On the Contemplative Life*, fol. 891, Leipzig edition; Jerome, *To Pammachius*, fol. 164 ff.; *To Lucinius*, fol. 193; letter *To Julianus*, fol. 207; and *Against Jovinian*, Book II, fol. 76; Clement of Alexandria, *On the Salvation of the Rich*, Ilt. edition, chapter 11, p. 24. **BUN.**
>
> **What of the man?** Namely Crates of Thebes, the Cynic philosopher and disciple of Diogenes. Jerome mentions him [Col. 0422D] in his letter to Paulinus, *On the Training of a Monk*, and in Book II *Against Jovinian*, reporting his apophthegm: “Begone and perish, evil desires; I shall drown you, lest I myself be drowned by you.” That theologian indeed counts this to his credit, considering nothing other than his contempt for money.
