But Apollonius, as Philostratus reports, criticized him with the same argument as Lactantius, since he had been useful neither to beasts nor to human beings. Neither Laertius nor Plutarch, however, mentions this drowning. **BETUL.**
>
> **What of the man who converted his patrimony into coin?** This is Crates of Thebes. Jerome, Letter 13 to Paulinus, *On the Training of a Monk*: “That Crates of Thebes, once a man of immense wealth, when he was setting out for Athens to study philosophy, cast away a great weight of gold and did not think that he could possess both virtues and riches at the same time.” **BUNEMAN.**
>
> **Poured away.** Our author uses the word literally here. Cicero uses it figuratively in *On Duties* II.15: “Many have poured away their patrimonies through thoughtless largesse.” Several authorities report that Crates distributed his property to the Theban people. See Ménage on Laertius, Book VI, fol. 87, and Perizonius on Aelian, *Various History* III.6. **BUN.**

Yet the wise man, contrary to human custom and contrary to nature, chose for himself still more foolish things to imitate. And since he saw that among the other animals the duties of males and females were not divided, he thought that women too ought to serve as soldiers, participate in public deliberations, hold magistracies, and assume commands. Accordingly, he assigned them arms and horses. The logical consequence is that wool and the loom, and the carrying of infants, should be assigned to men. Nor did he see that the things he said were impossible, from the fact that nowhere in the world has any nation yet arisen so foolish or so vain as to live in this way.

## [Col. 0421B] CHAPTER XXIII. On the Errors of Certain Philosophers, and on the Sun and Moon

Since, therefore, even the leading philosophers are caught amid such folly, what are we to think of those lesser men, who never seem to themselves [Col. 0422A] so wise as when they boast of their contempt for money? A courageous spirit. But I am waiting to see what they do and what result that contempt produces. They flee from and abandon the patrimonies handed down to them by their parents as though these were evil. And so that they may not suffer shipwreck in a tempest, they deliberately cast themselves overboard in calm water, courageous not through virtue but through perverse fear—like those who, fearing that they may be slaughtered by an enemy, slaughter themselves in order to escape death by means of death. In the same manner these men squander without honor and without gratitude the property from which they could have acquired the glory of generosity.

Democritus is praised because he abandoned his lands and allowed them to become public pastures. I would approve if he had given them away. Nothing, however, is done wisely if, were everyone to do it, the result would be useless and harmful. Yet this negligence is tolerable. What of the man who converted his patrimony into coin and poured it into the sea? I am uncertain [Col. 0422B] whether he was sane or mad. “Begone into the deep,” he said, “evil desires; I shall drown you, lest I myself be drowned by you.” If your contempt for money is so great, turn it into a benefaction, turn it into an act of humanity, and distribute it to the poor. What you intend to destroy could aid many people and prevent their dying of hunger, thirst, or nakedness. Imitate at least the madness and frenzy [Col. 0423A] of Tuditanus: scatter it among the people for them to seize. You can both escape money and yet place it to good use, because whatever has benefited many remains secure.

[Col. 0423A]

> [Note: [Col. 0423B] Variorum Notes on columns 423–424]
>
> **Tuditanus.** Concerning him, see Valerius Maximus, Book VII, chapter 8. Cicero also, *Philippic* III.6: “Tuditanus, of course—that man who used to scatter coins among the people from the Rostra while wearing a woman’s robe and tragic buskins.”
>
> **Zeno’s assertion, however, that offenses are equal, etc.** Jerome notes that Jovinian was tainted by this error. For theologians rightly maintain distinctions among sins. See Cicero’s *Paradoxes*. Among the Stoics, however, it is a paradox that **ὅτι ἴσα τὰ ἁμαρτήματα**—“offenses are equal.” Cicero summarizes the Stoic doctrines in a concise bundle in his speech *For Murena*: “There was,” he says, “a man of the highest genius named Zeno, whose imitators are called Stoics. Among his doctrines are precepts of this sort: that the wise man is never moved by favor and never forgives anyone’s offense; that no one is compassionate unless he is foolish and frivolous; that it is not characteristic of a man either to be prevailed upon by entreaty or to be appeased; that only the wise are—if utterly misshapen—beautiful; if utterly destitute, rich; if they live in slavery, kings.” **BETUL.**
>
> **To refute the error of a madman.** The Emmanuel and Cambridge MSS. and Reimann, together with the Subiaco, Rostock, Venice 1471 and 1497 editions, down to the Gymnich edition, read “to restrain.” The word seemed appropriate because “madman” follows, and madmen are more properly restrained than refuted. **BUN.**
>
> **Because he places compassion among the vices and diseases.** Stoic doctrine held that compassion is distress, or a disturbance and contraction of the mind alien to reason; consequently, the wise are not compassionate. See Laertius, Book VII, on Zeno; Cicero, *For Murena* and *Tusculan Disputations* IV.18. Plato and Aristotle, by contrast, taught that it belongs to a good man to feel compassion. Indeed Euripides, in direct opposition to the Stoics, says in the *Antiope*, as quoted by Stobaeus, vol. II, title 3:
>
> > It is not an ignorant impulse to feel compassion,  
> > But that of a wise man; and ruin threatens  
> > When those who think themselves wise are wise beyond measure.
>
> Seneca explains this Stoic doctrine with the utmost clarity in *On Clemency* II.4–5: “Most people praise compassion as a virtue and call a good man compassionate; but it is a vice of the mind. For it is the vice of a petty mind that collapses at the sight of another’s misfortunes.” And shortly afterward: “Compassion is distress caused by the sight of another’s miseries; but distress does not befall the wise man.” Finally, chapter 6: “Compassion is the vice of minds excessively indulgent toward misery; if anyone demands it from a wise man, he comes close to demanding lamentation and proud groaning over the misfortunes of others.”
>
> Because these statements might appear rather harsh and severe, Seneca attempts to soften them in the same work, where he adds in chapters 5 and 6: “The wise man, therefore, does not feel compassion, because compassion cannot exist without misery of mind. Nevertheless, all the things that compassionate people would do in sorrow, he will do willingly and with a cheerful countenance. He will bring aid to another’s tears but will not join them; he will extend a hand to the shipwrecked, hospitality to the exile, and alms to the needy; he will restore her son to a mother’s tears, order chains to be removed, rescue a man from the arena, and even bury the corpse of a criminal. And he will do these things with a tranquil mind and his natural countenance. The wise man, therefore, will not feel compassion, but he will give aid, he will benefit others, being born for the common assistance and public good,” etc.
>
> Indeed Augustine himself, *On the Morals of the Catholic Church* I.27, says: “Therefore those who dutifully and humanely furnish all the things by which evils and hardships of this kind are resisted are called compassionate, even if they are so wise that they are no longer disturbed by any sorrow of mind. For who does not know that the word *misericordia*—‘compassion’—was so named because it makes the heart (*cor*) miserable through sharing grief at another’s evil?” Although in truth *misericordia* was named rather because another’s misery is a concern of the heart. Augustine continues: “And who would not concede that a wise man ought to be free from every misery when he aids the needy, frees the oppressed, and finally extends his humanity even to the burial of the dead? Even if he does this with a tranquil mind, impelled by no stings of grief but moved by the duty of goodness, he must nevertheless be called compassionate; for the name does him no harm when misery itself is absent.” Cicero says (*Academics*, Book IV) that the Stoics themselves are not accustomed to say who is or ever has been wise; and in portraying the wise man—or rather the ideal of the wise man—they depict someone whom no mortal has ever attained.
>
> **Would become savage at the sight of another human being.** Isaeus judged correctly that in place of the reading *auferretur*, “would be carried away,” found in one recent Royal MS., the Bologna MS., Tax., the reading should be *efferaretur*, “would become savage.” For human minds become savage when compassion is taken away. Thus read thirty MSS. and most printed editions. From **GALLAEUS.**—**Would become savage at the sight …** Hence *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 4: “If the human being … possessed sufficient strength to repel dangers and needed no other person’s assistance, what society would there be? … Or what would be more repulsive than man? What more savage? What more inhuman?” **BUN.**
>
> **Solitary.** That is, creatures that naturally love to live alone, as opposed to those that live in groups, such as bees, ants, and many others.—**Whose nature is solitary.** *Tusculan Disputations* V.13 contrasts solitary beasts with gregarious ones. And *On Duties* I, penultimate chapter: “A solitary condition is opposed to community.” **BUN.**
>
> **Who said that snow is black.** Anaxagoras, as Galen reports in his book *On Simple Medicines*. The man about whom Galen writes in Book IX, chapter 1 of the same work struggled no less against common sense when he said that nothing prevented one from asserting that snow possessed both the same quality and the same power as fire. **BETULEIUS.**
>
> **That he might see heaven.** See above, chapter 9, and below, Book XI, chapter 1.
>
> **Xenophanes.** Cicero in the *Academics*: “Xenophanes says that the moon is inhabited and is an earth upon which strange forms of many cities and mountains are seen.” On this matter read Lucian’s *Icaromenippus*. **BETULEIUS.**

Who approves, however, Zeno’s assertion that offenses are equal? But let us pass over a doctrine that has always been mocked by everyone. To refute the error of this madman it is enough that he places compassion among the vices and diseases. He deprives us of the affection upon which nearly the whole ordering of human life depends. For human nature is weaker than that of the other animals, which heavenly providence has armed with natural defenses, either for enduring the violence of the weather or for warding attacks away from their bodies. But because none [Col. 0423B] of these defenses has been given to man, he received in place of them all the affection of pity, [Col. 0424A] which is properly called humanity, by which we protect one another.

For if a human being were to become savage at the sight of another human being—as we see happen among living creatures whose nature is solitary—there would be no human society and no concern or rational basis for founding cities. Nor would life itself be sufficiently safe, since human weakness would be exposed to the other animals, and human beings themselves would rage against one another after the manner of wild beasts. There is no less madness in the others.

For what can be said of the man who declared snow to be black? The logical consequence was that he should also call pitch white. This is the man who said that he had been born for the purpose of seeing heaven and the sun, though he saw nothing [Col. 0424B] on earth while the sun was shining.

[Col. 0425A] Xenophanes most foolishly believed the mathematicians when they said that the moon’s sphere was eighteen times larger than the earth; and, consistently with this frivolity, he said that within the moon’s concave hollow there was another earth, and that another race of human beings lived there in the same way that we live upon this earth. Those lunatic human beings, therefore, have another moon to give them light by night, just as this moon gives light to us. And perhaps this world of ours is the moon of some other, lower earth.

Seneca says that there was a man among the Stoics who deliberated whether he should assign populations to the Sun as well. Foolishly, of course, since he hesitated. For what would he have lost if he had assigned them? But I suppose the heat deterred him from committing so great a multitude to danger, lest, if they perished from excessive heat, so great a calamity should be said to have occurred through his fault.

> [Note: [Col. 0425B] Variorum Notes on columns 425–426]
>
> **When the mathematicians said, etc.** I do not know whether he means Anaximander, whose pupil Xenophanes is believed to have been. [Col. 0425C] Anaximander said that the circle of the moon was nineteen times greater than the earth, as Plutarch reports in *Opinions*; or, according to Galen, that the moon’s circle was sixty times greater than the earth. But in Plutarch the opinion of Xenophanes is **σελήνην εἶναι νέφος πεπιλημένον**, that is, “the moon is a compacted or conglomerated cloud”; in Galen, however, it is **νέφος πεπυρωμένον**, that is, “an inflamed cloud.” But these are nothing other than dreams.
>
> **Eighteen.** He is a scrupulous observer of elegance: with a few changes, he follows Cicero, *Academics* IV.26 and 41.
>
> **Within the moon’s concave hollow.** Cicero, *Academic Questions* IV.39: “Xenophanes says that the moon is inhabited and is an earth of many cities and mountains.” **CELL.**
>
> **Seneca says.** Nothing on this subject survives today in Seneca.
>
> **What of those who suppose that there are Antipodes with their feet opposite ours?** Concerning them, see Cicero in the *Lucullus*. Lactantius certainly asserts many paradoxes in this chapter, on account of which some writers hiss him off the stage. Although I admit that he departed from the truth, nevertheless, since—as I shall now show—he had men of the greatest authority and wisdom either as the sources or the followers of his opinions, I should certainly think that those men are more deserving of being hissed off who thought that so distinguished a man ought to be hissed off so rashly.
>
> In the first place, he judges that there are no Antipodes, a view also maintained by Eratosthenes, Polybius, Strabo, Tzetzes in the *Chiliads*, and Lucretius near the end of Book I. This position is also asserted in Plutarch’s dialogue *On the Face in the Orb of the Moon*. Among our own writers, St. Augustine thought the same in *City of God* XVI.9, though led by different reasons: for he feared that if he conceded the existence of Antipodes, the human race would have another progenitor besides Adam. Nicholas of Lyra likewise denies the Antipodes at the beginning of his commentary on Genesis, as afterward did all who denied that the earth is spherical.
>
> The true opinion concerning the Antipodes, contrary to Lactantius, is nevertheless established by Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio* I.5, where he overturns Lactantius’ arguments; Pliny, *Natural History* II.65; Cleomedes, *Meteorology* I.2; and St. Augustine—contradicting himself—in *The Literal Meaning of Genesis* II.9, etc. Nor in these times, certainly, can any further doubt about the matter be entertained, since through the genius and courage of that illustrious Ligurian hero Christopher Columbus, the formerly unknown peoples of the other hemisphere have now been discovered and thoroughly explored. **ISAEUS.**
>
> **Hanging gardens.** He means the hanging gardens of Semiramis, concerning which see Diodorus, Book II, chapter 10; Strabo 16, p. 508; and Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapter 14.
>
> **What reasoning, therefore, led them to the Antipodes?** I added the preposition *ad*, “to,” from twenty MSS. and ten printed editions, as being necessary. Two Colbert MSS. have “Antipedes.”
>
> **That the world was round.** The reasoning is derived from its daily motion; for that motion reveals that the world, and especially the heaven, moves spherically, or in the manner of a sphere, around its own axis and poles. For all the planets and stars—indeed even the elements themselves—revolve in a circle from east to west, just as occurs in a sphere. All these things are evidence that the highest part of heaven is spherical or globular, and consequently that the world is endowed with a spherical form.
>
> **And from the motion of the stars they supposed that heaven revolved.** Not only Lactantius denied that heaven revolved, but also several philosophers and a great many of the holy Fathers and doctors: Justin Martyr, in his response to Question 93 to the Orthodox; John Chrysostom, Homilies 6 and 13 on Genesis and Homily 12 to the People of Antioch; Caesarius, at the end of Dialogue I; Elias of Crete, on Gregory Nazianzen’s Oration VII; Isidore, *Etymologies* III.49; likewise Severianus and Acacius, who thought the world hemispherical, heaven motionless and stretched out like a tent, vault, or chamber; Junilius in the *Hexaemeron*; Richard in the second book of *Selections*; and Diodorus and Procopius in their commentaries on Genesis. In his book *On Heresies*, Philastrius writes that this opinion is consonant with Holy Scripture, whereas the contrary opinion is absurd and agrees more with pagan folly than with Christian truth. St. Augustine, in *The Literal Meaning of Genesis* II.10, thinks that it can be defended. It has nevertheless been rejected by most philosophers and mathematicians, especially in Aristotle, *On the Heavens* II, text 43 ff. **ISAEUS.**

## [Col. 0425B] CHAPTER XXIV. On the Antipodes, Heaven, and the Stars

What of those who suppose that there are Antipodes with their feet opposite ours? Do they say anything rational? Is anyone so foolish as to believe that there are human beings whose feet are higher than their heads? Or that things which lie flat among us hang upside down there? That crops and trees grow downward? That rains, snows, and hail fall upward to the earth? And does [Col. 0426A] anyone marvel that the hanging gardens are numbered among the seven wonders, when philosophers make fields, seas, cities, and mountains hang suspended?

The origin of this error too must be disclosed by us. For they are always deceived in the same manner. Once they have adopted something false at the beginning, led astray by its resemblance to truth, they necessarily fall into the consequences that follow from it. Thus they fall into many absurdities, since things consistent with false premises must themselves be false. Yet once they have put their faith in those first premises, they do not look around to see what kind of things follow from them, but defend them in every possible way, although they ought to judge from the consequences whether those first premises are true or false.

What reasoning, therefore, led them to the Antipodes? They observed the courses of the stars proceeding toward the west, and that the sun [Col. 0426B] and moon always set in the same direction and always rise from the same direction. But since they did not perceive what mechanism regulated their courses or how they returned from west to east, and since they thought that heaven itself sloped downward in every direction—as, because of its immense breadth, it necessarily appears to do—they concluded that the world was round like a ball. From the motion of the stars they supposed that heaven revolved, so that the stars and sun, after setting, were carried back to the east by the revolution of the world itself.

Accordingly, they fabricated bronze spheres [Col. 0427A] in imitation, as it were, of the shape of the world, and engraved them with certain monstrous figures that they said were stars. From this supposed roundness of heaven it followed that the earth should be enclosed within its central hollow. But if that were so, the earth itself would likewise resemble a globe, since it could not be that something held enclosed by a round body would not itself be round.

[Col. 0427A]

> [Note: [Col. 0427B] Variorum Notes on columns 427–428]
>
> **This roundness of heaven, therefore.** The roundness of heaven was denied not only by Lactantius, but also by Justin Martyr in his responses to Questions 59 and 130 to the Orthodox; Basil, Homily 1 on Genesis; Chrysostom, Homilies 14 and 27 on Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews and Homily 2 *On the Incomprehensible Nature of God*; Ambrose, Book I of the *Hexaemeron*; Theophylact and Theodoret on chapter 8 of the Epistle to the Hebrews; Caesarius and Procopius in the places cited above; Haimo, Severianus, and Acacius; likewise Primasius on the Epistle to the Hebrews; Euthymius on Psalm 103; and Elias of Crete in the place cited above.
>
> The contrary opinion, however, is true and has been established by all philosophers and astronomers—namely, that heaven is round. Ptolemy demonstrates this with nine arguments in Book I, chapter 3, of the *Great Composition*; Aristotle, *On the Heavens* II, text 22 ff. The holy Fathers have asserted the same: Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 4 against Julian, Oration 2 on Theology, and his oration on Holy Baptism; Chrysostom, Homily on Psalm 103; Ambrose, Sermon 12 on Psalm 118; St. Augustine, *The Literal Meaning of Genesis* I.10 and II.9; Bede, *On the Six Days*, the oration and questions on Genesis. It also seems more consonant with Holy Scripture. At the beginning of Ecclesiastes: “The sun rises,” etc.; on that passage St. Jerome should be consulted. Likewise Ecclesiasticus 24: “The circuit of heaven,” etc.; Job 9: “Beneath him those who bear the world are bent”; Proverbs 8. To Psalm 103 and Isaiah 40, where heaven is said to have been stretched out by God like a tent, chamber, or skin, St. Augustine responds in *The Literal Meaning of Genesis* II.9. **ISAEUS.**
>
> **Enclosed.** Two Royal MSS. and seven printed editions read “confined.”
>
> **The earth itself would likewise resemble a globe.** The earth is round and spherical—not geometrically so, indeed, but in a rough fashion, since valleys and mountains make its surface uneven. The first argument for this is that the sun, stars, and eclipses appear successively around the earth to all its inhabitants just as if they were moving around a perfectly round sphere—that is, regularly and uniformly—so that they appear one hour earlier in places, for example, fifteen degrees farther east. This occurs everywhere on earth in proportion to the earth’s circuit extending from east to west, as is evident from the infallible prediction of eclipses, according to which they are foretold to appear, not to everyone at the same hour, but at different hours. Such reliable prediction presupposes that the earth is round.
>
> There is also the experience of sailors, who, [Col. 0428B] while circumnavigating the whole circuit of the earth, everywhere observe the same uniform and regular appearance of the stars. **Jos. BLANCANUS.**
>
> **How do all things not fall?** One Royal-Puteanus MS. reads “how would they not fall?” Ten MSS. and two old printed editions read “How, then?” One Colbert MS. has [Col. 0428C] “therefore.”
>
> **Are carried away from the center.** I restored this from ten printed editions and all MSS. except three Royal MSS., which have “are separated,” as do three recent commonly printed editions.
>
> **Display.** I restored this from the MSS. and two old Roman editions. The other commonly printed editions read “make a display of.”
>
> **By many arguments.** Rather, by none.
>
> **Might be understood.** Seven MSS. and the same number of printed editions read “might be understood” in the plural.
>
> **Now a few things must be said by us about philosophy.** Read this chapter cautiously. For if Lactantius censures all the philosophy of the ancient pagans, he acts without sufficient judgment, since that philosophy contained many things both true and right which were of use and benefit to human life. But if he condemns philosophy universally, he is on no account to be tolerated and contradicts the common judgment of the Fathers and the Church. See Alfonso de Castro, *Against Heresies*, Book XIII, under the word “Knowledge.” **BRASICHELLI.**
>
> **In general.** This is the reading of all MSS. except four more recent ones, which read, as do the printed editions, “in common.”—**In general.** I restore this from the Bologna, Tax., Cauc., Utrecht, and Gotha MSS. I have illustrated the expression more fully at Book III, chapter 21. Here I add from Tertullian, *On Patience*: “Mindful of patience in general.” **BUNEMAN.**
>
> **That supreme man of ours.** **Διαβολή**, “disparagement,” by irony. The passage is in the preface to the second book of the *Tusculan Disputations*. One old Bologna MS. reads, “Cicero, that supreme man of ours.” For the passage runs as follows: “Plato indeed makes a selection in political matters, excluding the **νόθους**—that is, ‘illegitimate’—from the study of wisdom and admitting the **γνησίους**—that is, ‘legitimate.’” But Plato says in the *Euthydemus* that since happiness is the goal set before all human beings universally, and happiness consists in wisdom, it follows that everyone must devote himself to the study of wisdom.
>
> **May be able.** So many of the best and oldest MSS. Two recent MSS. read “are able”; three recent MSS. and the printed editions, “would be able.”
>
> **Since if wisdom.** The third Leipzig edition and Reimann give this order: “since wisdom, if.” That is satisfactory; so too the Subiaco, Rostock, Venice 1471, and both 1478 editions: “since wisdom, if.”

If the earth too were round, it would necessarily present the same face toward every part of heaven—that is, raise mountains, spread out plains, and cover itself with seas. If this were so, the final consequence would follow: that there is no part of the earth not inhabited by human beings and the other animals. Thus the roundness of heaven invented those hanging Antipodes.

If you ask those who defend these monstrosities [Col. 0427B] how everything does not fall into that lower region of heaven, they answer that this is the nature of things: heavy bodies are borne toward the center, and all things are fastened to the center as we see spokes fastened in a wheel; while things that are light, such as mist, smoke, and fire, are carried away from the center and seek heaven.

I do not know what to say about men who, once they have gone astray, steadfastly persist in folly and defend one absurdity with another—except that I sometimes think that they either philosophize for amusement [Col. 0428A] or knowingly and deliberately undertake to defend falsehoods, as though to exercise or display their talents upon bad subjects. I could prove by many arguments that heaven can in no way be lower than the earth, were it not that this book must now be concluded and that some matters remain which are more necessary to the present work. And since surveying the errors of every individual is not the task of a single book, let it suffice to have enumerated a few, from which the character of the rest may be understood.

## CHAPTER XXV. On Learning Philosophy and How Much Is Necessary for Its Study

[Col. 0428B] Now a few things must be said by us about philosophy in general, so that, having established our case, we may bring the argument to its conclusion. That supreme man of ours, an imitator of Plato, thought that philosophy was not for the common people, because only learned men could attain it. “Philosophy,” Cicero says (*Tusculan Disputations* II.1), “is content with a few judges and deliberately shuns the multitude.”

It is not wisdom, therefore, if it recoils from the society of human beings; for if wisdom was given to humanity, it was given indiscriminately to everyone, so that there should be absolutely no one [Col. 0429A] incapable of receiving it. Yet they embrace virtue, which was given to the human race, in such a way that they alone of all people seem to wish to enjoy the public good; they are as grudging as if they wished to bind up people’s eyes—

> [Note: [Col. 0429C] Variorum Notes on columns 429–430]
>
> **As grudging as if they wished to bind up people’s eyes.** Quintilian, *Institutes* II.17, has “to bind a wound,” in place of others’ “to bind” or “to fasten”; thus “to bind the eyes” is also correct. Compare the note on Lactantius, Book V, chapter 1. **BUN.**
>
> **The light.** “That enlightens every human being coming into this world.”
>
> **It would also have been necessary for craftsmen.** From the MSS. I added the word “also,” which the following passage appears to require.
>
> **The people … to be formed.** Cicero’s elegant expression, which Lactantius has already used in Book II, chapter 6.
>
> **Its mystery is proclaimed by the beard alone, etc.** Philosophers wore long beards and were wrapped in the philosopher’s cloak, concerning which see above. See also below, Book V, chapter 2. Herodes Atticus therefore rightly answered a beggar who professed philosophy by his clothing, as reported by Gellius, Book IX, chapter 2: “I see a beard and a cloak; I do not see a philosopher.” See the proverb “A Tragic Monkey,” and likewise the other, “Wise Only as Far as the Beard.”—**It is proclaimed only by beard and cloak.** By the dress of philosophers, especially Greek philosophers. Below, Book V, chapter 2, concerning a false philosopher: “He concealed his vices beneath his hair and cloak.” And Gellius, Book XIII, chapter 8, concerning men of the same kind: “Covered by beard and cloak, they turn the morals and benefits of philosophy into matters of the tongue and verbal arts.” **CELL.**
>
> **The Stoics.** On this matter see Seneca’s letter to Marcia.
>
> **Likewise Plato.** One very old Royal MS. reads “the same”; the Cotton MS., “Thus Plato did not.”
>
> **These common branches of learning must be studied.** The Clermont and Brun. MSS. read, “The common branches of learning must be studied.”—**Common branches of learning.** Cicero, *On the Orator* II.17: “Common literature and the more refined humanities.” Lactantius similarly said “common knowledge” in Book III, chapter 6. **BUN.**
>
> **Tullius.** See Cicero in the passage cited in the note above, at line 2.
>
> **Themista.** He perhaps means the wife of Leontius, to whom Epicurus is known to have written. What are we to say of Themistoclea, the sister of Pythagoras? What of many others, a very long catalogue of whom Textor provides? **BETULEIUS.**—See Gilles Ménage’s *History of Women Philosophers*, Lyon, 1682, duodecimo. Yet these authors do not enumerate them all.—**A single Themista in all recorded history.** Perhaps no age, not even antiquity, was without learned women. Themistoclea, the sister of Pythagoras, is praised; other women are praised as well. **BUN.**
Phaedo. Twenty-eight manuscripts corruptly read *Pythagoras*. In Laertius it is uncertain whether Crito or Alcibiades redeemed him at Socrates’ urging. Gellius, however, agrees with Lactantius; in Book II, chapter 18, he writes as follows concerning Phaedo:

> Phaedo of Elis belonged to that Socratic circle and was exceedingly intimate with Socrates and Plato. Plato gave his divine book on the immortality of the soul Phaedo’s name. This Phaedo was a slave, of handsome appearance and a freeborn disposition, and, as some have written, while still a boy was forced by his master, a pimp, to earn money through prostitution. Cebes the Socratic is said, at Socrates’ urging, to have purchased him and instructed him in the disciplines of philosophy; and afterward he became a distinguished philosopher, and his discourses concerning Socrates are read as works of [Col. 0430D] considerable elegance.

After this, read Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.2. BETULEIUS.—For *Phaedonem*, in twenty-eight manuscripts and two old Roman editions, the name *Pythagorae* seems to have been intruded; but wrongly, for nowhere do we read that Pythagoras was a slave, purchased by Cebes, and imbued with philosophy.

Cebes, they report. *Cebetem* is absent from the manuscripts and two old Roman editions. Fourteen manuscripts have *traduntur* (“they are reported”).

Plato. On Plato’s enslavement by Dionysius the Younger, the tyrant, see Laertius.

And Diogenes. Gellius and Macrobius, in the same passages:

> Diogenes the Cynic also underwent slavery; but he had passed from freedom into slavery by being sold. When Xeniades of Corinth wished to buy him and asked what craft he knew, Diogenes said, “I know how to command free men.” Then Xeniades, astonished by his answer, bought and manumitted him; and, entrusting his sons to him, said, “Take my children, whom you may command.”

Compare Laertius as well. BETULEIUS.]

or to gouge out the eyes of the rest, lest they see the sun. For what else is it to deny wisdom to human beings than to take away from their minds the true and divine light? But if human nature is capable of wisdom, craftsmen, countrymen, women, and, in short, all who bear the human form ought to have been taught, so that they might become wise; and a people ought to have been assembled from every language, condition, sex, and age. It is therefore the strongest possible argument that philosophy neither tends toward wisdom nor is itself wisdom, that its mystery is celebrated only by the beard and cloak. The Stoics indeed perceived this, for they said that both slaves and women should philosophize; [Col. 0429B] so too Epicurus, who invites those untrained in all literature to philosophy; likewise Plato, who wished to compose his state of wise persons.

They did indeed attempt to do what truth demanded, but they could not proceed beyond words. First, because many arts are needed before philosophy can be approached. Those common branches of learning must be mastered for the practical purpose of reading, because amid so great a variety of subjects not everything can be learned by listening, nor retained [Col. 0429C] in the memory. No small amount of labor must also be given [Col. 0430A] to grammar, so that one may know the proper method of speaking. This must necessarily consume many years. Nor, indeed, may rhetoric be left unknown, so that one may be able to set forth and express what one has learned. Geometry, music, and astronomy are also necessary, because these arts have some association with philosophy. Yet women cannot thoroughly learn all these things, since before the end of their marriageable years they must learn duties that will shortly prove useful in household affairs; nor can slaves, who must above all serve during those very years in which they could learn; nor the poor, craftsmen, or countrymen, who must seek each day’s sustenance through labor. For this reason Tullius says that philosophy shrinks away from the multitude. “But Epicurus will receive the uneducated.” How, then, will they understand the things said about the first principles of reality, things so intricate and involved that even cultivated persons [Col. 0430B] scarcely grasp them?

In matters, therefore, entangled in obscurity, confused by the diversity of intellects, and embellished with the elaborate discourse of eloquent men, what place is there for an untrained and uncultivated person? Finally, they never taught any women to philosophize except one, Themista, in all recorded history; nor any slaves except one, Phaedo, whom, they report, Cebes redeemed from wretched servitude and instructed. They also enumerate Plato and Diogenes, [Col. 0430C] who, however, were not slaves, but happened to undergo slavery, [Col. 0431A] for they had been captured. A certain Anniceris is indeed said to have redeemed Plato [Col. 0431A].

[Note: [Col. 0431B] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 431–432]

Plato . . . a certain Anniceris is said to have redeemed. When Plato had answered Dionysius, tyrant of Sicily, rather sharply concerning tyranny, Dionysius handed him over to Pollis, the Spartan envoy, to be carried away and sold; Pollis offered him for sale at Aegina. He was then redeemed for twenty minas by Anniceris of Cyrene and sent back to his friends at Athens. CELLARIUS.

[Col. 0431C]

For eight sesterces. This amounts to a sum of two hundred gold crowns.

Mad. Heumann believes that Lactantius wrote *furiosius* (“rather madly”). I can scarcely believe it. All the books, including Reimmann’s, have *Furiosus* (“Mad”), and rightly so; this accords with Lactantius’ manner in Book VI, chapter 15: “The Stoics, therefore, are mad, who . . .” BUNEMANN.

As it seems to me. I have deleted *quidem* (“indeed”), which is absent from all the manuscripts and several editions.

A great sum of money. I restored this from all the manuscripts and from the old editions—the two Roman editions, Turnèbe’s, and Soubron’s. Twelve common editions have *multum pecuniae* (“much money”).

When Hector was dead. The story is found in Homer’s *Iliad*, Dictys of Crete, Book III, and Virgil’s *Aeneid*, Book I. In the seventh speech against Verres, Cicero charges Verres with this crime: although he had killed many people in Sicily, he returned their corpses to their fathers and relatives for burial only after receiving payment.

Anacharsis the Scythian. He was the brother of the king of the Scythians, born of a Greek mother, and traveled from his homeland to Athens. His life is in the first book of Laertius. A notable dialogue of Lucian is inscribed with his name; in it he debates with Solon concerning the exercises of youth. On Anacharsis, see Plutarch’s *Life of Solon*. BETULEIUS.

And literature. I deleted *Graecas* (“Greek”), because it is absent from all the manuscripts and the old editions—the two Roman editions and Betuleius’. Bunemann has: “And (Greek) literature.”—And (Greek) literature. I enclosed *Graecas* in parentheses; the word is absent from Bon., Tax., Pen., Cauc., Pal., Ultr., Jun., Goth., Lips. 1 and 3, Reimm., Emman., and Cant., as well as from all the old editions: Sublac., Rost., Ven. 1471–97, and Paris 1513. But Aldus and the subsequent editors admitted it. BUNEMANN.

At nature’s demand. That is, at the dictate of natural law—not that corrupted law, but the original one. For near the end of this chapter he uses the word “nature” for that corrupted nature, and thus for disposition or, to speak with the Apostle, the law of the flesh. BETULEIUS.

But the commandments of God, etc. Not by themselves, but through the accompanying efficacy of the Holy Spirit.

So gentle. This comes from Terence’s *The Brothers*, act IV, scene 1; and Lactantius teaches that nothing becomes a Christian more than simplicity.

Distributing with full hands. The best reading of the older manuscripts and of several editions. Thirteen manuscripts and six common editions have *propriis* (“his own”).

[Col. 0432C]

With full hands. That is, abundantly, copiously, lavishly, and by no means grudgingly. Thus Erasmus in the *Chiliades*. In his Epistle, chapter III, verses 13 and following, James compares worldly wisdom with heavenly wisdom.—With full hands. Cicero, *Letters to Atticus* II.25: “He urged him with how full a hand,” etc. There Corradus notes that “with a full hand” is proverbial, like “with a full measure.” Seneca uses it frequently: *To Polybius*, chapter 28, “He left him heaping up gifts with a full hand”; Epistle XXXIII, “Yet if you demand it, I shall not deal with you like a pauper, but it shall be done with a full hand”; and Epistle CXX, “We saw him, when there was occasion to bestow something, giving with a full hand.” BUNEMANN.

Crosses. The French version wrongly translates this here as *afflictions*; in this passage it means instruments of execution. BUNEMANN.

He will despise crosses, fires, and the bull. Learned men and we ourselves judged this reading more correct than the intrusive *et pericula* (“and dangers”) of twenty-three manuscripts and seven editions. In place of it one Cauc. manuscript has *et Perilli* (“and Perillus’”), and three manuscripts and four printed editions have *et Phalaridis* (“and Phalaris’”); all of these seem to us glosses.—He will despise crosses, fires, and the bull of Phalaris. Bon. has “crosses and fires, every danger, and the bull.” The unique Cauc. manuscript has: “he will despise crosses and fires and the bull of Perillus.” For Perillus invented that bronze bull, about which Salvagninus writes learnedly and at length in his note on Ovid, *Ibis* 439:

> In Perillean bronze imitate real bullocks;

and *Tristia* V.1:

> Phalaris himself allowed him, in Perillean bronze,  
> To utter bellows and complain through a bull’s mouth.

BUNEMANN.

A debauchee. One who devotes himself to taverns and more shameful banquets. See Cortius on Sallust, *Catiline* 13, p. 90, and 14, p. 94. BUNEMANN.

For by one washing, etc. That is, by the sacred font of baptism.

Drives out folly in one single onslaught. That is, baptism drives away human wickedness and all sins.]

for eight sesterces. And so Seneca assailed this very redeemer with reproaches because he had valued Plato so cheaply. Mad, as it seems to me, was the man who grew angry with someone because he had not lost a great sum of money! Apparently he ought to have weighed out gold, as though for the dead Hector, or heaped up as much coin as the seller had not demanded. Of the barbarians, however, they name none except Anacharsis the Scythian, who would never even have dreamed of philosophy unless he had first learned both the language and literature.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Wisdom Is Bestowed by Heavenly Teaching Alone; and How Powerful the Law of God Is

[Col. 0431B] What, therefore, they perceived must be done at nature’s demand, but nevertheless could neither do themselves nor saw could be done by philosophers, this heavenly teaching alone accomplishes, because it alone is wisdom. Will they, forsooth, be able to persuade anyone, when they persuade not even themselves? Or will they suppress anyone’s desires, [Col. 0432A] moderate anger, and restrain lust, when they themselves both yield to vices and confess that nature is more powerful? But daily experience shows how powerful the commandments of God are in human souls, because they are both simple and true. Give me a man who is irascible, abusive, and unbridled: with a very few words of God,

> I shall render him as gentle as a sheep.

Give me one who is covetous, avaricious, and tightfisted: presently I shall give him back to you generous and distributing his own money with full hands. Give me one afraid of pain and death: presently he will despise crosses, fires, and the bull. Give me a lustful man, an adulterer, a debauchee: presently you will see him sober, chaste, and continent. Give me one cruel and thirsting for blood: presently that frenzy will be changed into true clemency. Give me one unjust, foolish, and sinful: immediately [Col. 0432B] he will be just, prudent, and innocent. For by one washing all wickedness will be abolished. So great is the power of divine wisdom that, once poured into the human breast, it drives out folly, the mother of transgressions, in one single onslaught. To accomplish this there is no need of payment, books, or nocturnal studies. These things are done freely, easily, and quickly, [Col. 0433A] provided that the ears are open and the breast thirsts for wisdom.

[Note: [Col. 0433B] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 433–434]

The breast . . . thirsts. Rost. wrongly has “the breast . . . knows.” He imitates Cyprian, Book II, Epistle 2, Erasmus’ edition: “Only let our breast thirst and lie open.” BUNEMANN.

Let no one be afraid: we do not sell water. Nine Reg. manuscripts, three Colbert manuscripts, six others, and the Roman edition of 1470 punctuate the sentence in this way. In three Colbert manuscripts there is no punctuation. In two recent manuscripts and seventeen printed editions it reads: “Let no one fear us; we do not sell water.”—We do not sell water. As you see, he means the matter used in Baptism; that is, we confer that sacrament freely upon everyone. In later times councils in various kingdoms forbade the demanding of anything for the conferral of baptism. Among these are the Councils of Elvira, canon 48; Braga, canon 7; Mérida in 666; Tribur in 895; Limoges in 1034; Bourges in 1438; the Council of Milan under St. Charles Borromeo; Pope Gelasius’ epistle to all the bishops of Lucania, chapter 7; the Constitutions of Gallo, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, around the year 1208, chapter 2; and all the Rituals.—Let no one be afraid: we [do not sell] water. This entire passage is excellently illuminated from Cyprian, Book II, Epistle 2, in the Basel and Gryphius editions, in the epistle *To Donatus*:

> Nor for this is there need of payments, influence, or labor . . . but the freely given gift from God is received by a devout mind, and it is easy; and just as the sun shines spontaneously, daylight illuminates, a spring waters, and rain bedews, so the heavenly Spirit pours himself in.

Lactantius himself, Book VII, chapter 27: “And who is there who would wish to procure and acquire these goods? . . . Let those who thirst come, that they may draw saving water in the fullest draughts from the perennial and heavenly spring”; and Book I, chapter 1. BUNEMANN.

Cuts out the vices. So read nearly all manuscripts. Three Reg. manuscripts from Marmoutier and six editions have *exscindit*; ten printed editions have *excindit*.

Having put off the old. See Paul to the Ephesians IV and Colossians III. “Having put off the old,” namely the old man—that is, having cast him out. Canterus and others think that *expuncto* (“having erased”) should be read in place of *exposito* (“having put off”); this conjecture is not to be despised—if only it were supported by manuscripts!—Having put off the old. This is the style of Lactantius and of the ancient sacred and ecclesiastical writers. Again Lactantius, Book VII, chapter 5: “A man purified by the heavenly washing has put off infancy together with every stain of his former life”; here Heumann vainly attempts to substitute *deponit* (“lays aside”). Cyprian often writes in this way; for example, *Against Demetrianus*, Basel edition, fol. 103; Oxford edition, fol. 193: “Having put off earthly birth, we have been recreated and reborn by the Spirit.” The same author, Epistle XI, Oxford edition, fol. 26: “They put off the conduct of the old man.” Book II, Epistle III—in the Oxford edition, Epistle LXIII, fol. 153: “All sorrow is put off . . . let the memory of the old man be put off.” The same author, *On the Dress of Virgins*, near the end: “There they put off the old man through the grace of the spiritual washing.” The matter is established still more securely by verses 609–610 of Paulinus of Nola, Poem XXIII:

> Lest I remain the earthly Adam, let me be born from virgin earth,  
> And, when the old has been put off, be fashioned as a new image.

BUNEMANN.

Which comes from knowledge. Thus read the two oldest Reg. manuscripts and several others, together with nearly all the editions. One Bonon. manuscript and ten recent manuscripts have “which comes to knowledge.”

The Stoics say that virtue is. Laertius cites Zeno and Chrysippus as authors of this assertion. Cicero, in the fifth book of the *Tusculan Disputations*, and Seneca, Epistle 92, discuss this question. Lactantius approves the pagans’ opinion, though he understands it differently from them: namely, that the virtue born from Christian faith is sufficient for attaining eternal happiness. The pagans’ meaning, however, is that virtue is sufficient in itself, needs neither anyone’s praise or glory nor the aid of fortune, and produces and perfects happiness. Hence Cicero too, in Book I of *On the Laws*, defined virtue as “nature perfected in itself and brought to its highest point.” BETULEIUS.

The wise man, he says, is always happy. In Cicero, near the beginning of Book II of the *Tusculan Disputations*, we read the following concerning Epicurus’ constancy:

> Epicurus affirms that if the wise man is burned, if he is tortured—you perhaps expect him to say, “He will endure it, bear it, and not succumb.” A mighty praise, by Hercules, and worthy of Hercules himself, by whom I have sworn. But this is not enough for Epicurus, a harsh and unyielding man. If he is in Phalaris’ bull, he will say, “How pleasant this is! How little I care for it!” Pleasant, even? Is it not enough if it is not bitter? etc.

The story of Perillus is too well known to require recounting. See, if you wish, Pliny, Book XXXIV, chapter 8, and the proverb “The rule of Phalaris” in Erasmus. BETULEIUS.

If it is for the glory of endurance, he will not enjoy it. So read six Reg. manuscripts, one Colbert manuscript, Bon., two Brun., Em., Cauc., and Ultr.; and I contend that this is the proper reading. For, as Thomasius rightly affirms, if we read *patientia fruetur* (“he will enjoy endurance”), as in four other manuscripts and the editions, we shall have no sense. Lactantius’ point is that human beings will not be as happy amid calamities as Epicurus proclaims. For if a man suffers for the glory of endurance, he will not be able to enjoy that glory, since he is about to die under torture. One Reg. manuscript, Pal., and the Roman edition of 1468 have *fruatur* in place of *fruetur*.]

Let no one be afraid: we do not sell water, nor do we supply sunlight for payment. God’s most abundant and overflowing spring lies open to all, and this heavenly light rises for everyone who has eyes (see John, chapters I and VI). Did any philosopher ever provide these things, or could he provide them if he wished? Although they consume their lifetimes in the study of philosophy, they can make neither anyone else nor themselves better, if nature offers even a little resistance. And so their wisdom, even when it achieves as much as possible, does not cut out the vices but conceals them. A few commandments of God, however, so transform the whole person and, having put off the old, render him new, that you would not recognize him as the same man.

## CHAPTER XXVII. How Little the Philosophers’ Precepts Contribute to True Wisdom, Which You Will Find in Religion Alone

[Col. 0433B] What then? Do they prescribe nothing similar? On the contrary, very many things; and they frequently approach the truth. But those precepts have no weight, because they are human and lack a greater authority, namely the divine. No one, therefore, believes them, because the hearer considers himself just as human as the one who gives the instruction. Furthermore, [Col. 0434A] among them nothing is certain, nothing that comes from knowledge. But since everything is conducted by conjecture, and many divergent and varied claims are advanced, it is the mark of an utterly foolish person to wish to obey precepts whose truth or falsity is in doubt; and therefore no one obeys, because no one wishes to labor toward an uncertainty.

The Stoics say that virtue is what alone makes life happy. Nothing truer can be said. But what if a man is tortured or afflicted by pain? Can anyone be happy among torturers? “Indeed, pain inflicted upon the body is material for virtue; and so he is not wretched even under torture.” Epicurus speaks much more boldly: “The wise man,” he says, “is always happy; and even if enclosed in Phalaris’ bull, he will utter this cry: ‘It is pleasant, and I care nothing for it.’” Who would not laugh at him? Especially because this devotee of pleasure has assumed the role [Col. 0434B] of a courageous man—and beyond all measure. For it cannot happen that anyone regards bodily torments as pleasures, when it is enough, for fulfilling the duty of virtue, to bear and endure them.

What are you saying, Stoics? What are you saying, Epicurus? “The wise man is happy even while being tortured.” If this is because of the glory of his endurance, he will not enjoy it, for perhaps he will die under torture. If because of its remembrance, then either he will not be conscious of it, if souls perish, or, if he is conscious, he will gain nothing from it.

[Col. 0435A] What other fruit, then, is there in virtue? What happiness of life? That he may die with an untroubled mind? You bring me the good of a single hour—or perhaps a single moment—for the sake of which it is not expedient to be worn away by miseries and labors throughout one’s entire life. How much time, however, does death occupy? When it comes—

[Note: [Col. 0435C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 435–436]

Comes. Correctly. Others have “has come.”

Whether you undergo it with an untroubled or a troubled mind. I restored the two words *an iniquo* (“or a troubled”), omitted in the old Bologna manuscript and five printed editions, from the other editions and twenty-seven manuscripts, except that two Colb. manuscripts and one Clarom. have *aut iniquo*.

Will not follow. That is, glory will not follow. One recent Bon. manuscript and Is.’s edition have *non sequitur* (“does not follow”). The Jun. manuscript and nine editions have *non sequenda* (“not to be followed”), which does not cohere. Thomasius interprets our reading as saying that, according to Lactantius, corrupt human judgments will cause no glory to arise from virtue where there has been true and substantial glory, or a life worthy of that glory.

Thus those who said these things. So read the oldest and best manuscripts—Bonon., Reg., and others—together with five editions. Fifteen recent manuscripts and eleven printed editions have “And so those who said these things”; one corrected Reg. manuscript and one Colb. have “And so those who said this.”

They saw. Restored in both places from the manuscripts. The editions have “they have seen” twice.

Fixed. Eight recent manuscripts and five editions have “turned aside.” The others read as in the text.

Displayed herself. This is the reading of the manuscripts; the editions have “showed herself,” as do the common texts of Lucretius. That verse is from the beginning of Book I of Lucretius.

For virtue. I emended this from the manuscripts and better editions. Six printed editions have “by virtue.”

When they seek things that cannot be tracked down. Thus the old manuscript codices. More recent manuscripts and printed editions wrongly have “when they seek things that cannot be investigated.” Lactantius’ meaning is that those who have no religion and consider the soul mortal have no reason to look toward heaven, because if they seek there the mortality of souls and impiety, they seek things that cannot be tracked down—that is, things that cannot be found. But if you read “cannot be investigated,” the sense will be contrary and wholly nonexistent. This is from Thomasius. Nevertheless Cellarius and Heumann, relying on the authority of the old editions, think that “cannot be investigated” should be read. Let learned readers therefore consider which reading they think ought to be embraced.

Or embrace religion. The most learned Rivetus, in his manuscript Notes, reads *suspicere* (“look up to”); but, so far as I know, no manuscript reads thus. GALLAEUS.—Below: “do not embrace religion.”

Is in heaven. For our thought ought to be in the heavens, says Paul.

By the appearance of false virtue. One Colbert manuscript and Brun. have “by false appearance.”

Invented the name of nature. According to Galen, Plato, Hippocrates, Empedocles, Parmenides, Melissus, Alcmaeon, Heraclitus, and Epicurus wrote on nature. The word “nature” is used in various senses by Latin authors. Sometimes it is taken for character, disposition, or habit; sometimes for mind; more often for substance, especially in Cicero. Its more common use, however, is to denote the condition and principle of coming into existence. Lactantius, meanwhile, by confusing these meanings, entangles himself rather than explaining himself. Otherwise, he rightly condemns those who, defrauding God the creator of things of his glory, establish a certain Nature as the creator and administrator of things, although Nature (*physis*, φύσις) is nothing other than the law and eternal will of God, who through it creates and administers all things. For Greek verbal nouns in *-sis* (-σις) very often signify action and the capacity for acting.

One might wonder why he endeavors to make the word “Nature” suspect, since readers encounter it frequently not only in the books of both Testaments but also among the most ancient ecclesiastical writers. For it neither exists nor moves of itself, being nothing other than God’s command and, as I have said, his eternal will. God, however, can indeed be called Nature, if by this you understand not *physis* (φύσις, “nature”) but *ousia* (οὐσία, “being” or “substance”). For not only Cicero but Augustine himself translated *ousia* as *creatura* (“creature”), not only concerning God but concerning other substances as well. In Book II of *On the Morals of the Manichaeans*, chapter 1, Augustine says that the substantive verb—whether you understand *eimi* (εἰμί, “I am”), from which *ousia* is derived, or *sum* (“I am”), from which *essentia* (“essence”) is derived—implies the meaning of a nature that abides in itself and remains unchangeably constituted. We can call this nothing other than God. The same Augustine says so in Book II of *On the Soul*. Thus Lactantius appears to censure more harshly than it deserves something that could be read and understood in a sound sense. He raises this same question again in chapter 10 of *On the Anger of God*. BETULEIUS.]

whether you undergo it with an untroubled or a troubled mind no longer matters. It therefore follows that nothing is sought from virtue except glory. But this is either superfluous and brief, or else will not follow because of corrupt human judgments. There is therefore no fruit from virtue where virtue is mortal and perishable. Thus those who said these things saw a sort of shadow of virtue; they did not see virtue itself. For they were fixed upon the earth and did not raise their faces on high, so that they might behold her,

> Who displayed herself from the regions of heaven.

[Col. 0435B] This is why no one obeys their precepts: either they train people for vice, if they defend pleasure, or, if they uphold virtue, they threaten no punishment for sin except its shamefulness alone, and promise no reward for virtue except honor and praise alone, although they say that virtue is not to be sought for its own sake.

The wise man, therefore, is happy under torture; but when he is tortured for faith, for justice, and for God, that endurance of pain will make him most blessed. For there is a God who alone can honor virtue; and its sole reward is immortality. Those who do not seek immortality, and do not hold to the religion beneath which eternal life lies, assuredly know neither the power of virtue, whose reward they do not know, [Col. 0435C] nor do they look toward heaven, though they themselves think they do, [Col. 0436A] when they seek things that cannot be tracked down. For there is no other reason for looking toward heaven except either to embrace religion or to believe that one’s soul is immortal. Whoever understands either that God must be worshiped or that the hope of immortality has been set before him has his mind in heaven; and although he does not behold it with his eyes, he nevertheless beholds it with the light of the soul.

Those who do not embrace religion are earthly, because religion comes from heaven; and those who think that the soul perishes with the body likewise look toward the earth, because beyond the body, which is earth, they see nothing further that is immortal. It is therefore of no benefit that the human being was fashioned so that with an upright body he might look toward heaven, unless with an uplifted mind he discerns God and his thought is wholly occupied with the hope of everlasting life.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On True Religion and Nature; Whether Fortune Is a Goddess; and on Philosophy

[Col. 0436B] Therefore there is nothing else in life upon which our reason and condition may rest except the acknowledgment and reverent and devout worship of God, who begot us. Since the philosophers strayed from this, they certainly were not wise. They did indeed seek wisdom; but because they did not seek it rightly, they slipped still farther away and fell into such great errors that they did not retain even common wisdom. For they not only refused to uphold religion but actually abolished it when, led on by the appearance of false virtue, they attempted to free souls from every fear. [Col. 0436C] This overthrow of religion invented the name of nature. [Col. 0437A] For since they either did not know by whom the world was made or wished to persuade others that nothing had been perfected by a divine mind, they said that nature was the mother of all things, as though they were saying that all things had been born of their own accord. By this word they plainly confess their lack of understanding. For nature, once divine providence and power are removed, is absolutely nothing. But if they call God “nature,” [Col. 0437A]

[Note: [Col. 0437C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 437–438]

If they call God “nature.” This was Seneca’s opinion. See above, Book I, chapter 9.

But. I restored this from the manuscripts; the editions have “because.”

By a not dissimilar error. St. Augustine attacks this error of the pagans in *The City of God* IV.18–19.

Matched themselves against her. A gladiatorial expression, used when pairs were matched; this was also called “joining” or “pairing.” Here Firmianus had in mind Seneca, *On Providence*, chapter 2: “Behold a pair worthy of God: a courageous man matched against adverse Fortune.” BUNEMANN.

And the loss of loved ones. Compare below, “he had lost his dearest daughter.” *Interitus* (“death”) and *amissio* (“loss”) are not infrequently used for decease. So sacred and profane authors alike. Tertullian, *On Patience*, chapter 14: “the loss of those dearest to us.” Compare chapter 9, beginning. Cyprian, *On the Good of Patience*, no. 9: “A manifold variety of trials is inflicted: from losses of property . . . from the torments of wounds, from the loss of loved ones.” Arnobius, Book II, no. 98: “the loss of children.” Seneca, *To Marcia*, chapter 7: “Departure, not merely the loss of those dearest to us, necessarily causes anguish.” Cicero himself, *On Duties* III.5: “the loss of children, relatives, and friends”; and *Tusculan Disputations* III.30, beginning. The second Lips. manuscript reads “because of the death and loss of loved ones.” BUNEMANN.

Is assailed. This is the reading of nearly all the manuscripts and editions. One old Bon. manuscript, one Colb., and three editions read “is occupied”; one recent Reg. has “fears.”

And had been overcome by him. Three Reg. manuscripts, Lips., Goth., and Cellarius’ edition add *semper* (“always”) after *a se* (“by him”); the other manuscripts and editions reject it, and it seems unnecessary, since the same thought has just preceded. See also Cicero’s *Tusculan Disputations*, Book V: “I have forestalled you, Fortune,” he says, “and captured you, and blocked all your approaches, so that you could not breathe upon me.”—And had always been overcome by him. Lips. and Goth. insert *semper*, which others omit, perhaps because they believed it repeated from what precedes. Yet the repetition is neither displeasing nor alien to the author’s character. BUNEMANN.

He says. The same Cicero in the fragments of the *Consolation*.

And I raise my hand. This is how the text must be read according to the manuscripts and Cicero himself. Theodorus Canterus corrected it thus. So read the very old Roman edition of 1470 and the Venetian edition of 1490; the other editions read, “Look, I raise my hand.” Those who were overcome and acknowledged themselves defeated would offer their hand; hence Virgil in *Aeneid* XII says “to stretch forth the palms.” Cicero in *Laelius*: “At last let him give his hands and allow himself to be conquered.” Likewise Theocritus, Idyll 23.

Who should lie so low? That is, who should be so cast down, afflicted, and broken. Hence Cicero frequently joins “afflicted and prostrate,” and “cast down and prostrate.” Compare Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 1. BUNEMANN.

He says. Thus all the manuscripts and the old Roman and Paris editions. Twelve common editions have “you say.”

You give. I have followed the authority of nearly all the best manuscripts. Five very recent manuscripts have “he gives”; one Lips. has “have been given”; two recent Reg. manuscripts and one Colb., together with the editions, have “are given”—not badly.

Who is wise. I restored this from all the manuscripts and most editions. The other common editions have “is wise.”

They do. Some editions have “they may do.”

Invent. This is the reading of nearly all the manuscripts and the common editions. Three Colb. manuscripts have *affigere* (“attach”); the Turnèbe manuscript has *attingere* (“touch”). The common editions read *effingere* (“fashion”).

Anaxagoras, etc. These remarks appear to have been taken from Cicero’s first book of the *Academics*, where he writes concerning the Academics’ *akatalepsia* (ἀκαταληψία, “inapprehensibility”). Cicero’s words are:

> Then I said: Arcesilaus, as we have learned, directed his whole contest against Zeno, not from obstinacy or a zeal for victory—as it seems to me—but because of the obscurity of those matters which led Socrates to confess his ignorance, and similarly Democritus, Anaxagoras, Empedocles, and nearly all the ancients, who said that nothing can be known, apprehended, or understood; that the senses are narrow, minds feeble, the circuits of life brief, and—as Democritus said—that truth is sunk in the depths.

This final statement is also read in the other surviving fragment of the *Academic Questions*: “Blame nature, which, as Democritus says, has hidden truth utterly in the depths.” BETULEIUS.]

what perversity it is to name nature rather than God! But if nature is the principle, necessity, or condition of coming into existence, it is not perceptible in itself; rather, there must necessarily be a divine mind which by its providence supplies the first principle of birth to all things. Or if nature is heaven and earth and everything that has come into being, then nature is not God but God’s work.

By a not dissimilar error they believe that Fortune exists as a kind of goddess who mocks human affairs through various accidents, because they do not know whence good and evil befall them. They believe themselves matched against her in combat, yet give no account at all of by whom or for what reason; they merely boast that at every moment they are locked in combat with Fortune. Moreover, all who have consoled others because of the death and loss of loved ones have torn the name of Fortune to pieces with the fiercest accusations; [Col. 0438A] and there is no discussion of theirs concerning virtue in which Fortune is not assailed.

Marcus Tullius, in his *Consolation*, says that he had always fought against Fortune and that she had been overcome by him when he courageously repelled the attacks of his enemies; that he had not been broken by her even when he was driven from his home and deprived of his homeland; but that, when he had lost his dearest daughter, he shamefully confessed himself conquered by Fortune. “I yield,” he says, “and raise my hand.” What could be more wretched than a man who should lie so low? “It was foolishly done,” he says—but he professes himself a wise man. What, then, is the point of assuming that name? What of that contempt for worldly things that is paraded in magnificent words? What of his dress, unlike everyone else’s? Or why do you give precepts of wisdom at all, if no one who is wise has yet been found?

And does anyone make us odious because [Col. 0438B] we deny that philosophers are wise, when they themselves confess both that they know nothing and that they possess no wisdom? For whenever they have become so exhausted that they cannot even invent something—as they do in other matters—then at last they are reminded of their ignorance and, as though raving, leap up and cry out that they are blind and witless. Anaxagoras declares that all things are surrounded by darkness. Empedocles complains that the pathways of the senses are narrow, [Col. 0439A] as though he required a carriage and four horses for thinking. Democritus says that truth lies sunk as though in a well (see Cicero, *Academics*, chapter 12) so deep that it has no bottom—foolishly, of course, like everything else. For truth is not sunk as though in a well, [Col. 0439A]

[Note: [Col. 0439C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 439–440]

Truth sunk in a well. Thus, together with eight old printed editions, read all the manuscripts except two recent Reg. manuscripts, which have “into a well.” But Cicero too, in *Academic Questions* I.12, expresses it in the ablative: “Democritus said that truth was sunk in the depths.”

At the top for them. The old editions read “for them at the top.”

Except this one thing. See this in Plato’s *Apology*, *Phaedo*, and *Crito*, and in Cicero, near the beginning of *Academic Questions* I.

Often. Six recent manuscripts have “always.”

What they thought, what they wanted. Ten recent manuscripts, together with Betuleius’ edition, have “what they think, what they want.” The Cotton manuscript has “what they wished to think.”

To determine. Thus the oldest codices—Bonon., three Reg., Cauc., and three Oxon.—together with eight editions. Twenty-three more recent manuscripts, together with eight old printed editions, have “adequately to determine.”

They perish by their own sword. One Clarom. manuscript, corrected by a second hand, has “they killed themselves by their own sword.” This is a proverb; see Terence, *The Brothers*.]

Whom their own [discourse] itself destroys. Thus nearly all the manuscripts, together with almost all the editions. Three editions have “itself [destroys] its own”; the recent manuscripts 1 Colb. and Brun. have “itself its own”; 1 recent Reg. has “their own themselves.”

Afflicts. Thus I have restored the reading from the best and oldest Regio-Puteanus manuscript, five other Reg. manuscripts, six Colb. manuscripts, and seven others, as well as from the old Roman edition of 1470. Three manuscripts and fourteen editions read “harasses”; 1 recent Reg. reads “inflicts.” But in Cicero and Columella, the simple verb “to affect” likewise means “to harass, afflict”; ignorant copyists substituted the latter word.

Either the greatest fools or the greatest boasters. This reading [Col. 0440C] is found in nearly all the best manuscript codices; seven recent manuscripts and five printed editions read “or boastful.”

At what time? In what manner? When is it? This rarer usage may be supported from Cicero, *On Invention* I.25, beginning: “In his manner of life one ought to consider among whom, in what fashion, and at whose discretion he was brought up.”

As though it possessed some sensation. Read: “as though they possessed some sensation.” HEUMANN.—As though it possessed some sensation. Cicero omits the preposition in *On the Nature of the Gods* II.15: “that the creature possesses both the keenest sensation and the swiftest mobility.” But it is well known that the ancients often added *in*. BUNEMANN.

But they say that it is a god. I have not yet read that the philosophers did this—unless perhaps one understands Plutus, who in Aristophanes is likewise represented as blind. The Romans, however, worshiped both Fortune as male and Fortune as female, as Plutarch writes in his book *On the Fortune of the Romans*. Augustine mentions both in the passage cited above. A temple of Male Fortune was erected by Ancus Marcius, the fourth king of the Romans, because he believed that fortune had aided him somewhat more than courage in attaining victory. There was also another shrine [Col. 0440D] of Male Fortune beside the temple of Venus, according to the same Plutarch, who lists both the names and the sanctuaries of various Fortunes. But this passage will acquire greater clarity if I transcribe in full the words of Cicero cited here, from the first book of the *Academic Questions*; for there that perfection of things is called by many different names. Cicero’s words, where he speaks about natural philosophy, run as follows:

> “They hold, moreover, that all things contained within the world are parts of the world, and that they are maintained by a sentient Nature in which perfect reason resides, a Nature likewise everlasting—for there is nothing more powerful by which it might perish. This force they call the Soul of the world, and likewise a perfect mind and wisdom, which they call God: a kind of providence governing all things subject to it, especially the heavenly things, and then, upon the earth, those that concern human beings. Sometimes they call this same force Necessity, because nothing can happen otherwise than has been established by it, through an order that is, as it were, a fated and immutable succession from eternity. Sometimes, indeed, they call it Fortune, because it brings about many things unforeseen and unexpected by us, owing to the obscurity of causes and our ignorance of them.”

But in Cicero’s second book *On Divination*, the question is debated whether there can be divination concerning fortuitous events. The counterargument is this: if Fortune exists, fate is abolished; but if all things occur from eternity and by fate, Fortune is abolished. Lactantius added that this same God is sometimes called Nature and sometimes Fortune. Plutarch, however, in his *Problems*, proposes this distinction: Fortune is the principle of all things, whereas Nature consists by chance. But on these matters read John of Damascus, *On the Orthodox Faith* II.15.]

into which it might descend or even fall, but as though it stood upon the very summit of a lofty mountain—or rather in heaven, which is most true. For what reason had he to say that it was cast down to the lowest depth rather than raised to the highest point? Unless perhaps he also preferred to locate the mind in the feet, or in the lowest heels, rather than in the breast or the head.

So exceedingly remote were they from truth itself that not even the posture of their own bodies reminded them that truth was to be sought above them. From this despair [Col. 0439B] arose that confession of Socrates by which he said that he knew nothing except this one thing: that he knew nothing. From this flowed the doctrine of the Academy—if indeed that can be called a doctrine in which ignorance is both learned and taught. Yet not even those who laid claim to knowledge were able consistently to defend the very things that they supposed themselves to know. Because their reasoning did not cohere, through ignorance of divine things they were so various and uncertain, and so often advanced arguments contrary to themselves, that one cannot determine and judge what they thought or what they wanted. Why, then, should you fight against [Col. 0440A] men who perish by their own sword? Why labor to destroy those whom their own discourse destroys and afflicts?

Aristotle, says Cicero (*Tusculan Disputations* III), accusing the ancient philosophers, said that they had been either the greatest fools or the greatest boasters for supposing that philosophy had been perfected by their own abilities; but that he saw that, since a great advance had been made in a few years, philosophy would shortly be brought to complete perfection. What, then, was that time? In what manner? When is it, or by whom was it perfected? For what he says—that those who supposed wisdom to have been perfected by their own abilities were the greatest fools—is true. Yet he himself was not sufficiently prudent either, since he thought that it had been begun by the ancients, increased by the more recent thinkers, or would soon be perfected by their successors. For that which is not sought along its proper path can never be discovered. [Col. 0440B]

## CHAPTER XXIX. Again on Fortune and Virtue

But let us return to what we omitted. Fortune, therefore, is nothing in itself; nor should it be regarded as though it possessed some sensation. For Fortune is the sudden and unexpected outcome of accidental events. But the philosophers, lest they should ever fail to err, wish to be wise in a foolish matter: they change Fortune’s sex and say that it is not a goddess, as the common people believe, but a god. [Col. 0441A] Yet they sometimes call the same being Nature, [Col. 0441A]

[Note: [Col. 0441C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 441–442]

Sometimes Nature. These two words are absent from twelve manuscripts and from Thomas’s edition.

Brings about things unexpected by us. Thus all the editions and manuscripts except the two most recent, Em. and Cant., which read: “brings about things unforeseen and unexpected by us.” See Cicero near the end of the first book of the *Academic Questions*.

In a very serious work. This phrase indicates *On Duties* II.2, near the end, though with certain alterations. “We arrive”: Bunemann reads “we are carried,” and explains the reason for this change as follows.—I have adopted this reading, which agrees with Cicero, from Reimm., the manuscripts, and Tornes. 1587, where previously “we arrive” was printed. BUNEMANN.

[Col. 0441D] When it blows adversely. Thus the printed and manuscript codices read, except for eight that have “when it gives us breathing-space,” and 1 Reg., “when it gave breathing-space.” But “blows adversely,” which comes from Cicero’s passage, corresponds excellently to “a favorable wind” (*prospero flatu*), which appeared shortly before. So too below: “what this wind is,” and “what this adverse wind is.”—When it blows adversely. Emman. and Goth. read “when it gives breathing-space.” Cicero’s codices have the received reading, as does Lactantius himself below: “what wind … and what adverse wind.” BUNEMANN.

Assent must be withheld. But see rather Cicero himself in the preface to *On Duties*, where he meets this objection: “We are, however, confronted,” etc. You may consult that answer.

For they fashion its image, etc. Bupalus made for the people of Smyrna—as Volaterranus cites from Pausanias—a statue of Fortune with a cornucopia, a celestial sphere above her head, and the horn of plenty in her other hand. In Galen also Fortune holds a rudder in her hands. As for her depiction as blind and standing upon a rolling globe, see, besides Galen, the *Tablet of Cebes* and the verses of Pacuvius in the *Rhetoric to Herennius* II, in the chapter on Faulty Argumentation. HEUMANN.

[Col. 0442B] And of human affairs, etc. Pliny, book II: “Throughout the whole world, in every place and at every hour, Fortune alone is praised by every voice, Fortune alone is accused and worshiped with abuse; fickle, and indeed regarded by most as blind, she alone turns both pages in the whole account of mortals.” So too Minucius Felix: “Fortune, released from laws, holds dominion.”

Virgil. These are his words in *Aeneid* VIII.334. Aeneas speaks:

> Driven from my homeland, pursuing the farthest reaches of the sea,  
> Almighty Fortune and ineluctable fate  
> Have placed me in these lands, etc.

There Servius says that the poet spoke according to the Stoics, who assign birth and death to the fates, but all that lies between them to Fortune, because everything in human life is uncertain.
