And the historian, etc. Sallust spoke thus in the prologue to his history of Catiline. Very many testimonies to this effect could be collected from Greek and Latin authors. But that is not part of our undertaking. Plato likewise speaks thus in book IV of *The Laws*.

Or, if it only. Others posit two Fortunes, one good and one evil. But Augustine refutes with powerful arguments the possibility that there are different Fortunes, *City of God* IV.18.

Who established her as the tormentor of the human race. Thus I have restored the text from the best and almost all the manuscripts. The manuscripts Em. and 1 Clarom. have “of humankind”; 1 recent Reg. and all the editions have “of the race of men.” Yet below, in chapter 30, Lactantius uses a similar construction: “One hope has been established for man”; and shortly afterward, “so hostile to human beings.”—The tormentor of the human race. They rend the injustice of Fortune. Cicero, *Philippic* XI.2: “After he had rent that excellent man with verbal abuse.” Valerius Maximus IV.4, at the end: “Why do we … rend Fortune with prolonged abuse, as though it were the principal evil of the human race?” BUNEMANN.]

and sometimes Fortune, “because,” says the same Cicero, “it brings about many things unexpected by us, owing to the obscurity of causes and our ignorance of them.” Since, therefore, they do not know the causes on account of which something happens, and do not know the very agent who brings it about, this consequence is inevitable.

The same man, in a very serious work in which he presented to his son precepts for life drawn from philosophy, says: “Who does not know that Fortune has great power in either direction? For when we enjoy her favorable wind, we arrive at the outcomes we desire; and when she blows adversely, we are afflicted.”

First, the man who denies that anything can be known said this as though both he himself and everyone else knew it. Next, the man who attempts to render doubtful even what is clear supposed this to be clear, though it ought above all to have been doubtful to him; for to a wise man it is altogether [Col. 0441B] false. “Who,” he says, “does not know?” I, for my part, do not know. Let him teach me, if he can, what that power is, what this wind is, and what this adverse wind is.

It is therefore shameful for an intelligent man to say something that, if you deny it, he cannot prove. Finally, the very man who says that assent must be withheld, because it is characteristic of a foolish person to assent rashly to unknown matters, plainly [Col. 0442A] believed the opinions of the common people and the uneducated, who suppose that Fortune exists and bestows good and evil upon human beings. For they fashion its image with a cornucopia and a rudder, as though it both bestowed riches and held the governance of human affairs. Virgil assents to this opinion, calling Fortune omnipotent; so does the historian who says: “But assuredly Fortune rules in every matter.” What place, then, remains for the other gods? Why is Fortune not either said to reign, if she is more powerful, or worshiped alone, if she governs everything?

Or, if she only sends evils, let them offer some reason why, if she is a goddess, she envies human beings and desires their destruction, although she is devoutly worshiped by them; why she is fairer to the evil but less fair to the good; why she plots against, afflicts, deceives, and destroys them; who established her as the perpetual tormentor of the human race; [Col. 0442B] and finally, why she obtained such evil power that she celebrates or obscures all things according to caprice rather than truth. These, I say, are the questions that the philosophers ought to have investigated, instead of rashly accusing innocent Fortune. Even if Fortune were something real, they could offer no reason why she should be as hostile to human beings as she is supposed to be. Accordingly, all those discourses in which they rend the injustice [Col. 0443A] of Fortune and boast most arrogantly of themselves and their own virtues [Col. 0443A]

Therefore let them not envy us, to whom God has disclosed the truth. Just as we know that Fortune is nothing, so we know that there exists a corrupt and treacherous spirit who is hostile to the good and an enemy of justice, who does things contrary to God; the cause of his envy we explained in the second book (ch. 13). He, therefore, plots against all. Those who do not know God he obstructs with error, overwhelms with folly, and surrounds with darkness, so that no one may be able to attain knowledge of the divine name, in which alone are contained both wisdom and eternal life. Those who know God he attacks by deceits and cunning, so that he may entangle them in greed and lust and, having corrupted them [Col. 0443B] by alluring sins, drive them to death; or, if deceit has accomplished nothing, he attempts to cast them down by force and violence.

For this reason, at the beginning of his transgression, he was not immediately thrust down by God to punishment: so that through his malice he might train man in virtue. Unless virtue is tested, unless it is strengthened by continual harassment, it cannot be perfect; for virtue is the courageous and unconquered endurance of evils that must be borne. From this it follows that there is no virtue if there is no adversary. Perceiving, therefore, the force of this corrupt power opposing virtue, but not knowing its name, they invented for themselves the empty term “Fortune.” How far removed this is from wisdom Juvenal declares in these verses:

> No divine power is absent, if prudence is present; but we  
> Make you, Fortune, a goddess and place you in heaven.

Folly, therefore, and error and blindness—and, as Cicero says, [Col. 0444A] ignorance of things and their causes—introduced the names Nature and Fortune. But just as they do not know their adversary, so they do not even know virtue, knowledge of which derives from knowledge of the adversary. If virtue is joined with wisdom—or, as they themselves say, is itself identical with wisdom—they must necessarily be ignorant of the things in which it consists. For no one can be equipped with true arms if he does not know the enemy against whom he must be armed; nor can one conquer an adversary if, in combat, he strikes not at the true enemy but at a shadow. He will be laid low, because, intent upon something else, he neither foresaw nor guarded against the blow coming upon his vital parts.

## CHAPTER XXX. Epilogue to What Has Been Said Above, and the Manner in Which One Must Pass from the Vanity of the Philosophers to True Wisdom [Col. 0444B] and Knowledge of the True God, in Whom Alone Are Virtue and Happiness

I have shown, insofar as my modest ability permitted, that the philosophers followed a path far astray from the truth. I perceive, however, how many things I have passed over, because a disputation against the philosophers was not my particular subject. But it was necessary to make this digression in order to show that so many and such great intellects were expended upon false things, lest anyone, perhaps, after being shut out from corrupt religions, should wish to turn to the philosophers as though he would find something certain.

One hope, therefore, one salvation, has been established for man in this doctrine that we defend. All human wisdom consists in this one thing: knowing and worshiping God. This is our doctrine; this is our conviction. With as powerful a voice as I can command, therefore, I testify, proclaim, and announce it. Here, here is that [Col. 0445A] which all the philosophers sought throughout their entire lives but were never able to discover, comprehend, or retain, because they either retained a corrupt religion [Col. 0445A]

[Note: [Col. 0445B] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 445–446]

Retained. Thus I have restored the reading from the editions Tornes., Soubron., and Walch., and from all the manuscripts except 2 recent Reg. and fourteen printed editions, which read “held.”

Thus [Col. 0446B] Lactantius in II.18 speaks of “the mystery of man.”—Know the mystery of his birth. Very close to our passage is this from VII.5: “Why he made man”; above: “if they had known the mystery of man”; and above again: “because he alone was formed in such a way that his eyes were directed toward heaven … raised up.” BUNEMANN.

The same author says at the end of IV.2: “Wisdom is so closely connected with religion that the two cannot be torn apart”; IV.3: “Wisdom is bound to religion by an inseparable bond”; IV.4: “It is evident how closely wisdom and religion are joined to one another”; IV.5: “Wisdom and religion cannot be separated.” BUNEMANN.

And this. Namely, in the third book; this coheres well with the preceding books. I have therefore restored “this,” with Cellarius, from the manuscripts except six Reg. manuscripts, which read “and here,” as do nearly all the printed editions.]

or abolished religion altogether. Let all those depart, therefore, who do not guide human life but throw it into confusion. What do they teach? Or whom do they instruct, when they have not yet instructed themselves? Whom can the sick heal, or the blind guide? Let all of us, therefore, who care for wisdom, gather here. Shall we wait until Socrates knows something? Or until Anaxagoras finds light in the darkness? Or until Democritus draws truth out of the well? Or until Empedocles broadens the pathways of his mind? Or until Arcesilaus and Carneades see, feel, and perceive?

Behold, a voice from heaven teaching the truth and showing us a light clearer than the sun itself. Why are we unjust to ourselves? [Col. 0445B] Why do we hesitate to receive the wisdom that learned men, after wearing away their lifetimes in seeking it, were never [Col. 0446A] able to find? Whoever wishes to be wise and happy should hear the voice of God, learn justice, and know the mystery of his birth. Let him despise human things and receive divine things, so that he may attain that highest good for which he was born.

Now that all religions have been dissolved, and all the arguments that either customarily were or could be advanced in their defense have been refuted, and then the systems of philosophy have been convicted, we must come to true religion and wisdom, since the two, as I shall show, are joined together. We must vindicate it by arguments, examples, and competent witnesses; and we must show that the folly which those worshipers of the gods never cease to charge against us is not at all on our side, but lies wholly with them. Although in the preceding books, when I denounced false religions, and in this book, when I demolished false wisdom, I have shown where the truth lies, the next [Col. 0446B] book will nevertheless indicate more plainly what true religion and true wisdom are.

## [LACTANTIUS, BOOK FOUR]

[Col. 0445]

## ANALYSIS OF THE FOURTH BOOK, ENTITLED *ON TRUE WISDOM AND RELIGION*

[Col. 0445C] This book has four parts: the Preface, chs. 1, 2, 3, and 4; the Instruction concerning Christ, from ch. 5 through ch. 29; the resolution of the question how two persons, the Father and the Son, are one God, ch. 29; and an admonition concerning the causes of heresies, ch. 30.

The Preface contains three things: a complaint concerning the introduction of the worship of the gods, which was followed by every kind of injustice and impiety; the reasons why wisdom was not discovered by the philosophers—namely, because they sought it beyond their own boundaries and did not approach the Jews, having undoubtedly been abandoned by divine providence, and therefore could not learn the truth from them; and finally, a discussion of the bond between wisdom and religion. There it is taught that wisdom is joined with religion only among Christians, by whom one God is worshiped, and not among the pagans, whose religion is vain and separate from philosophy, and whose divine worship is likewise contrary to all reason.

The Instruction concerning Christ comprises doctrine concerning the knowledge, person, name, birth, two natures, miracles, passion, and cross of Christ.

He admonishes that knowledge of Christ must be drawn from the prophets, who are older than all pagan writers (ch. 5).

He demonstrates from the testimony [Col. 0446C] of Trismegistus, the Sibyls, and Solomon’s Proverbs that Christ existed as a subsistent person before the creation of the world and was begotten by God (ch. 6).

He writes that Christ’s proper name is known to God the Father alone and was not to be made public before God’s dispensation had been fulfilled. Yet among human beings he is called Jesus; “Christ,” however, is not his proper name but a designation of power and kingship (ch. 7).

A twofold birth of Christ is asserted, one in spirit and the other in flesh. The former is said to have proceeded incomprehensibly, with voice and sound, from the mouth of God like a word—not from marriage and union with some woman, nor from a God who is both male and female, as Orpheus and Hermes supposed. Hence he is deservedly called God’s speech and word, though more correctly *logos* (λόγος) among the Greeks (chs. 8 and 9).

By the latter birth he is shown to have been born of a virgin; Lactantius explains the necessity, manner, place, and purpose of this birth. Its necessity was this: because the Jews, though endowed by God with great benefits, had departed from the divine law, God commanded his firstborn Son to descend from heaven in order to transfer the holy religion to the nations (chs. 10 and 11). Its external manner was despised and humble, so that the people ungrateful to God might be led into the greatest error (ch. 11). Its internal manner consists in his choosing a virgin and entering her womb. This ought by no means to appear incredible, since [Col. 0447A] certain animals are accustomed to conceive from wind and air, and since this kind of birth of Christ had been foretold by the prophets.

The place of his birth is identified as Judaea. He wished to be born there, and indeed from the seed of the Jews, lest, if he had been a foreigner, they might offer as a just excuse under the law that they had not received him. Lactantius lists various purposes of the birth, including the revelation to every nation under heaven of the sacred mystery of the one true God (ch. 12). Another purpose was that he should be like the supreme Father in all respects, and should himself, like the Father, be *apatōr* (ἀπάτωρ), “without a father,” and *amētōr* (ἀμήτωρ), “without a mother” (ch. 13).

The author also affirms two natures in Christ, divine and human. The divine nature, because it was manifested by the works he performed, and because Isaiah, Jeremiah, and David proclaimed Christ to be God. The human nature, because it was manifested by the suffering that he endured; and likewise because Jeremiah, Isaiah, Moses, and Nathan foretold that Christ would be the Son of Man (ch. 14). The prophet Zechariah also determined his priesthood and his very priestly person. [Col. 0447B]

Various miracles of Christ are enumerated; in chapter 15 it is shown that they were foretold both by the prophets and by the Sibyls, and therefore were by no means magical.

Concerning Christ’s passion, its efficient and impelling causes, form, consequences, and accompanying circumstances are taught. Its efficient causes were the Pharisees and priests. The impelling causes were Christ’s teaching and the offense taken at his humility, as well as his abrogation of the law of Moses by not resting on the Sabbaths, rendering circumcision ineffectual, and removing abstinence from pork. Yet Lactantius teaches that all these things had previously been foretold by the prophets (chs. 16 and 17).

The form of the passion is set forth through a historical account of Christ’s arrest and crucifixion. To this are added a denunciation of the deed and an exposition of the testimonies by which that passion was foretold (ch. 18).

Six consequences of the passion are enumerated: miracles, the guarding of the tomb, the resurrection, Christ’s own explanation to his disciples of Scripture concerning the dispensation of Christ, the ascension into heaven, and the full revelation [Col. 0447C] of the Gospel through the apostles (chs. 19, 20, and 21). The accompanying dignity of the passion is defended against the pagans, who took offense at Christ’s humility and suffering (ch. 22).

Lactantius affirms that Christ had to be not only God but also man, and had to suffer, by the following argument:

> “Whoever gives precepts to human beings and shapes the life and conduct of others must himself carry out those precepts, so that others may see that the things he commands are possible and may not despise their teacher. He must likewise come from heaven, since an inward and distinctive doctrine can in no way reside in a human being, and since a heavenly teacher must be perfect [Col. 0448A] and complete in his teaching. Finally, he must assume a human body, because mortal eyes cannot behold the brightness of God, nor can God, without a body, teach human beings. Likewise, he cannot refute those who use the flesh as an excuse for their sins unless he himself has been clothed in flesh, so as to show that even flesh is capable of virtue” (chs. 23 and 24).

But Christ was given to us by God the Father as just such a teacher, one who was to instruct human beings through his precepts of justice. Therefore, he had to be God so that he might present perfect doctrine and, by heavenly authority, impose upon human beings the necessity of obedience; and he had to be man so that he might provide humanity with examples of virtue and, by subduing the desires of the flesh, teach that sinning is not a matter of necessity but of purpose and will (ch. 25).

The author then continues: Christ was embodied so that he might offer humanity both examples of virtue and incentives toward it. He suffered so that, just as he foreshadowed certain mysteries by other miracles, so through the things he suffered he might signify [Col. 0448B] that wisdom would be hated and that the good would experience afflictions and various hardships. He also suffered in order to teach humanity patience and contempt for death.

Finally, in treating the cross, he first gives the reasons why Christ wished to undergo this infamous form of punishment: namely, so that there might be absolutely no one unable to imitate him; secondly, so that his body might be preserved intact, since it had to rise from the dead on the third day; and furthermore, because he had to be raised up upon the cross so that the passion of God might become known to every nation. In the same way, by the extension of his hands upon the cross, he prefigured the gathering of the nations from every place into the Church (ch. 26).

From this he discusses the power of the sign of the cross, which puts demons to flight and confounds soothsayers; from these effects he demonstrates the truth of the Christian religion (ch. 27). He consequently infers that vanities must be cast away and that the true God must be known and worshiped (ch. 29).

In the third part of the book, the question is resolved how, although we say that we worship one God, we nevertheless assert [Col. 0448C] that there are two, God the Father and God the Son. Lactantius answers that both have one mind, one spirit, and one substance, just as a spring and its stream, the sun and its ray, and a hand and its body are one; and just as, in civil law, a household is called one and its master one when the Father grants the Son the title and authority of Master. Finally, he shows from the prophets Isaiah and Hosea that both the Father and the Son are one God (ch. 29).

In the final part he discusses the causes of heresies, which he says are greed and pride, ignorance of Scripture, and admiration for false prophets (ch. 30).
