…that former condition of the human race, and it likewise commonly seems both astonishing and shameful that, through the folly of a single age which embraced various religions and believed that there were many gods, humanity suddenly fell into such profound ignorance of itself that, once the truth had been taken from its sight, neither the religion of the true God nor the principle of humanity was maintained, since human beings sought the highest good not in heaven but on earth. For this reason, certainly, the happiness of former ages was transformed. For, abandoning God, the parent and founder of all things, they began to venerate the insensible artifacts of their own fingers. What this depravity accomplished, and what evils it brought, the facts themselves disclose. For, turning away from the highest good—which is blessed and everlasting precisely because it cannot be seen, touched, or comprehended—and from the virtues consonant with that good, which are equally immortal, they fell away to [Col. 0449B] these corruptible and frail gods. By devoting themselves to things by which the body alone is adorned, nourished, and delighted, they sought perpetual death for themselves together with their gods and bodily goods, because every body is subject to death.

Injustice and impiety therefore followed religions of this kind, as was inevitable. For people ceased to raise their faces toward heaven; instead, human minds, cast downward, clung to earthly goods just as they did to earthly religions. Dissension within the human race followed, together with fraud and every wickedness, because, after despising the eternal and incorruptible goods which alone ought to be desired by a human being, they preferred temporal and short-lived goods. Human beings placed greater confidence in evil, preferring what was depraved to what was right because it was [Col. 0449C] more immediately present.

Thus gloom and darkness overtook human life, which in former ages had dwelt in the brightest [Col. 0450A] light; and, as was consistent with this depravity, only after wisdom had been removed did people finally begin to claim the name of sages for themselves. Yet no one was called wise when everyone was wise. Would that this name, once common to all, had retained its force even when it had been reduced to a few! For perhaps those few might, by their talent, authority, or constant exhortations, have freed the people from vices and errors. But wisdom had so completely perished that, from the very arrogance of the title, it appears that none of those who were so called was wise. And yet, before this thing which is called philosophy was found to exist, seven are said to have existed who, because they were the first of all to dare to inquire and dispute about natural phenomena, deserved to be regarded and called [Col. 0450B] wise.

O wretched and calamitous age, in which throughout the whole world only seven existed who could be designated by the name “human”! For no one can rightly be called human unless he is wise. But if all the others apart from those seven were foolish, not even they were wise, because no one can truly be judged wise by the judgment of fools. Wisdom was so far removed from them that not even afterward, as learning increased and many great intellects continually directed themselves toward this very end, could the truth be perceived and comprehended. For after the renown of those seven sages, it is incredible with what zeal all Greece caught fire for the investigation of truth. At first they considered the very name of wisdom presumptuous, and called themselves not sages but students of wisdom. By [Col. 0450C] doing this, they both condemned as erroneous and foolish those who had rashly appropriated the name of sages for themselves, and [Col. 0451A] also acknowledged their own ignorance, which indeed they did not deny. For whenever the nature of things had, as it were, set its hand against their intellects—

[Col. 0451A] [Note: [Col. 0451B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 451–452]

*Had set its hand against.* The Gotha manuscript has “had placed against.” Lipsius, worse, has “they had placed against.” Seneca, Book II of *On Anger*, chap. 4: “Then above all must a hand be set against it.” Seneca, *Hercules on Oeta*, line 1243: “These hands I set against it.” The books likewise varied at Ovid, Book IV of the *Fasti*, line 178: “and he set his hand against it.”

*Perceived.* Some read “to perceive.”

*Had believed.* This reading comes from very many of the oldest [Col. 0451C] manuscripts and five old printed editions; the others have “believed.”

*No wisdom anywhere.* This is how I write with nearly all the manuscripts and common editions. The Aldine, Thomasius, Thysius, and Gallaeus editions have “none,” erroneously; one recent Royal manuscript has “that wisdom.”

*There.* Ten recent manuscripts have “in that place.”

*The designation of folly.* See Paul in First Corinthians, chap. 1, verses 20, 22, 24, etc. See also St Hilary, Book IV of *On the Trinity*, near the end.

*The mystery of his divine work.* After “mystery,” one old Bologna manuscript and four recent editions add “highest,” which is absent from the others and which I deleted as a gloss.

*Although Pythagoras,* etc. Hermippus the Pythagorean says the contrary; Aristobulus too does not deny that Pythagoras learned many things from the law of Moses. Clement, Book I of the *Stromata*; Eusebius, Book IX of the *Preparation*, chap. 3; and Josephus, Book I *Against Apion*. Among more recent writers, Selden plausibly [Col. 0451D] asserts that Pythagoras knew not only other things but also the tetragrammaton Jehovah as the name of the Trinity, and called it the *tetraktys* (τετρακτήν); *Syntagma* II, *On the Syrian Gods*, chap. 1. He certainly gave one of his daughters a Jewish name. He had two, Sara and Myia, as stated in Photius, codex 259. HORN. — *Although Pythagoras.* On these matters, see Valerius, Book VIII, *On Study and Industry*. We shall collect the judgments of ecclesiastical writers concerning them. Read the first of Jerome’s letters in volume IV, written to Paulinus, which agrees wonderfully with this chapter. Augustine, Book VIII of *The City of God*, chap. 4: “Plato,” he says, “although an Athenian, born among his own people to an honorable station, and although by his marvelous talent he far surpassed his fellow students, nevertheless thought that neither he himself nor the Socratic discipline was sufficient for the perfection of philosophy. He therefore traveled as far and wide as he could, wherever the fame of some distinguished body of knowledge to be acquired drew him. Thus in Egypt too he learned whatever great things were held and taught there,” etc. He recalls the same matter in Book III of *Against the Academics*, chap. 23. Ambrose too, sermon 18 on Psalm 118, testifies that Plato went to Egypt for the sake of learning, so that he might become acquainted with the oracles of the Mosaic law and the sayings [Col. 0452B] of the prophets. Know that the Platonic and Pythagorean disciplines flowed in large part from the teaching of Moses. Eusebius demonstrates this concerning Plato throughout the whole eleventh book of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, with many evident examples. Cyril says the same thing with clear testimonies in *Against Julian*. Origen, *Against Celsus*, Book VI, testifies that Plato copied from the Hebrews what he wrote in the *Phaedrus*. Ambrose, writing to a certain Irenaeus in Letter VI, Book I, testifies that Pythagoras derived his lineage from the Jewish people, read Moses, and took his symbols from that source. It is therefore astonishing why Lactantius says that they did not reach the Jews. BETUL.

*Did not approach the Jews.* But other Fathers relate that they not only associated with Jews but also went to Egypt precisely in order to learn the teaching of Moses. Malchus, in the *Life of Pythagoras*, confirms that Pythagoras visited not only the Arabs and Egyptians but also the Hebrews and Chaldaeans. BUN.

*Were turned away … so that they could not know.* Vockerodt observed that this explanation is baseless, indeed false, in his dissertation *On the Knowledge of the Divine Writings among the Nations*, p. 276. BUN.

*To become known.* I restored this from the oldest manuscripts—five Royal, two Bologna, the Caucian manuscript—and from five other more recent manuscripts. Three recent manuscripts have “to know”; ten recent manuscripts and the common editions have “to become acquainted with.”

*The last age.* By “the last age,” Lactantius means the age of the new covenant. Kimchi has not inappropriately observed, with many examples, that this expression is used in the sacred text for the age of the New Testament. WALCH.

*A great leader,* etc. He calls Jesus Christ “Great” by comparison with Moses or Joshua. The prophets sometimes called Christ a prince, as in Isaiah, chap. 55, to which passage he appears to have referred here. “Behold,” the Father says, “I have given him as a witness to the peoples, a leader and teacher to the nations. Behold, you shall call a nation that you did not know,” etc.

*To foreign peoples.* Correctly—that is, to the pagans, whom our author contrasts with the Jews. Below as well, chap. 11, he says, “that he might turn to foreign nations.” Betuleius’s edition has “to the other peoples,” but less suitably; other editions read “to the other nations.” Heumannus correctly reads “to foreign peoples” from the old printed editions. — *To foreign peoples.* This reading, which Cellarius rejected, is found in the Subiaco, Rostock, Roman, and other editions. Compare chap. 43: “that he might gather for himself another, more faithful people from foreign nations.” BUN.]

—they used to testify that they knew nothing and perceived nothing, since they could give no account of the matter. Hence those who perceived themselves, at least to some degree, are found to be far wiser than those who had believed themselves wise.

## CHAPTER II  
### Where wisdom is to be sought; why Pythagoras and Plato did not approach the Jews

Therefore, if neither those who were called wise were wise, nor those who came later, who did not hesitate to confess their ignorance, what remains except that wisdom must be sought elsewhere, since it was not found where it was being sought? [Col. 0451B] What, moreover, should we suppose was the reason why, though sought by so many intellects, over so many ages, with the greatest zeal and labor, it was not discovered, unless because the philosophers sought it beyond their own boundaries? Since, after traversing and investigating everything, they comprehended no wisdom anywhere, and since that wisdom must necessarily exist somewhere, [Col. 0452A] it is evident that it must especially be sought where the designation of folly appears. Beneath the covering of that folly, God concealed the treasure of wisdom and truth, so that the mystery of his divine work would not lie exposed in public.

Hence I am indeed accustomed to wonder that, although Pythagoras and afterward Plato, inflamed by love for investigating the truth, penetrated as far as the Egyptians, the Magi, and the Persians in order to learn the rites and sacred institutions of those peoples—for they suspected that wisdom was situated in religion—they nevertheless did not approach the Jews, who alone then possessed it and whom they could have reached more easily. But I believe that they were turned away by divine providence so that they could not know the truth, because it was not yet lawful for people of foreign birth to become acquainted with the religion of the true God and with righteousness. For God had determined, as the last age approached, to send from heaven a great leader [Col. 0452B] who would take it away from an unfaithful (see Matthew 21) and ungrateful people and reveal it to foreign peoples. I shall undertake to discuss this matter in this book, if I first demonstrate that wisdom and religion are so closely connected that the two cannot be torn apart.

[Col. 0453A] ## CHAPTER III  
### Wisdom and religion cannot be separated; it is necessary that the Lord of nature be the father of every person

The worship of the gods, as I taught in the preceding book, possesses no wisdom: not only because it casts the human being, a divine creature, beneath earthly and frail things, but also because nothing is discussed there that contributes to the cultivation of morals and the shaping of life. Nor does it contain any investigation of truth, but only a ritual of worship, which consists not in an activity of the mind—

[Col. 0453A] [Note: [Col. 0453C] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 453–454]

*Activity of the mind.* For this reason the law commands us to love the Lord with our whole heart.

*Thus.* This is the reading of the old Roman edition and all the manuscripts except the most recent—one Royal and two Colbert manuscripts—which, like the printed editions, have “Therefore.”

*This religion.* I have understood “true” as implicit.

[Col. 0453D] *Which it lacks.* I restored this from the manuscript and twelve old editions. The more recent printed editions have “because it lacks.”

*Both must be true.* Francius conjectured that one should read “both must be true” with the feminine forms.

*But where wisdom coheres with religion by an inseparable … fulfill.* This entire section was omitted from the earliest editions—the Subiaco, Rostock, and Venetian of 1471, especially the Subiaco edition. BUN.

*Is joined? There, namely.* From the manuscript and most printed editions I added “There,” which is absent from four manuscripts and two recent editions.

*Life and action.* In our author, as in Minucius and others, *actus* often means “action.” See Book III, chap. 19; Book IV, chap. 3; Book V, chap. 9; *On the Anger of God*, chaps. 12 and 17. BUN. *Teachers of wisdom.* This occurred in the Christian religion, because the apostles are teachers and priests: they preach the doctrine of the Gospel and preside over the sacred mysteries.

*As Father.* The author strips the gods of the nations of the epithet “father” by the authority of both natural and civil law, for it certainly does not apply to them. The name “father” belongs not only to God alone but also belongs to him eternally. They, however, because they began at a certain time both to be fathers and to be called fathers, cannot be gods. For God is the timeless (*achronos*, ἄχρονος) Father, who also begot a timeless (*achronon*, ἄχρονον) Son. He is, indeed, a “begetter of equal age” (*homēlikos genetēr*, ὁμήλικος γενετήρ), as Nonnus addresses him. The gods themselves, however, were born in time, if we are willing to trust Hesiod. There is no need here to cite the authority of Christ, who in Matthew, chap. 23, says that there is one Father—namely, he who is in heaven. BETULEIUS.

*Father, let the name be applied to one.* F. Douza and Selden read, “Let us all speak of one.” See Selden, *On the Syrian Gods*, Syntagma II; the distinguished Vossius likewise printed it thus in *On Idolatry*, Book II, chap. 16. GALLAEUS. — These three verses were taken from Lucilius’s *Satires*.

*Many fathers.* I read “many” with the manuscripts and Cellarius. The common editions have “more fathers.”

*The principle of civil law demonstrates.* Fathers once possessed supreme power over their children, to such an extent that they had the right of life and death, just as masters had over slaves (*Digest*, law 11, *On Direct and Statutory Heirs*; final law of the *Code*, *On Paternal Power*; Book I of the *Theodosian Code*, *On Cases concerning Free Status*). Sopater on Hermogenes and Simplicius on Epictetus. This paternal sovereignty over children migrated from Attic law to Rome under the consuls; [Col. 0455B] for at Athens Solon enacted the law *concerning persons not yet judged* (περὶ τῶν ἀκρίτων), by which a parent was permitted to kill his son, as Sextus Empiricus states in Book III of the *Outlines of Pyrrhonism*.]

—but in the service of the body. And therefore that religion must not be judged true, because it educates no one through precepts of justice and virtue and makes no one better. Thus philosophy, because it does not possess true religion—that is, the highest piety—is not true wisdom. For if the divinity that governs this world sustains [Col. 0453B] the human race with incredible beneficence and cherishes it with, as it were, fatherly indulgence, it surely desires that gratitude be returned to it and honor given to it. Nor can the principle of piety remain sound in a person if he proves ungrateful for heavenly benefits—which is certainly not characteristic of the wise.

Since, therefore, as I have said, philosophy and the religion of the gods are separated and far removed from one another—since some are teachers of wisdom, through whom one certainly does not approach the gods, while others are ministers of religion, through whom one is not taught to be wise—it is evident that the former is not true wisdom, nor the latter true religion. Consequently, philosophy could not comprehend the truth, nor could the religion of the gods give an account of itself, which it lacks. But where wisdom coheres with religion in an inseparable [Col. 0453C] bond, both must be true, because in worshiping we must also be wise—that is, know what we ought to worship and how—and in being wise we must also worship—that is, fulfill in fact and action what we have come to know.

Where, then, is wisdom joined with religion? There, namely, where one God is worshiped; where all life and action are referred to one head and one supreme end; [Col. 0454A] finally, where the same persons are both teachers of wisdom and priests of God. Nor should anyone be troubled because it has often happened, and can happen, that some philosopher undertakes a priesthood of the gods. For when this occurs, philosophy is nevertheless not joined with religion; philosophy will cease during the sacred rites, and religion when philosophy is being treated. For that religion is mute, not only because it belongs to mute beings, but because its rite lies in the hands and fingers, not in the heart or tongue, as does ours, which is true. Therefore religion is present in wisdom and wisdom in religion. Hence it cannot be separated, because to be wise is nothing other than to honor the true God with just and pious forms of worship.

That the worship of many gods is not in accordance with nature can also be gathered and comprehended from this argument: every god worshiped by a human being must, amid [Col. 0454B] solemn rites and prayers, be called “father,” not only for the sake of honor but also by reason, because he is older than the human being and supplies life, health, and sustenance, as a father does. Thus Jupiter is called father by those who pray, as are Saturn, Janus, Liber, and all the others in succession. Lucilius mocks this in his council of the gods:

> So that no one among us fails to be “Father, best of the gods”:  
> Father Neptune, Liber, Father Saturn, Mars,  
> Father Janus, Father Quirinus—the name is applied to each and every one.

But if nature does not permit one person to have many fathers—for he is generated from one—then to worship many gods is also contrary to nature and contrary to piety.

[Col. 0454C] One, therefore, must be worshiped who can truly be called Father. He must also be Lord, because just as he can show indulgence, so too can he restrain. He must be called Father because he bestows many great things upon us; Lord because he possesses the supreme power of chastising and punishing. The principle of civil law also demonstrates that the same person who is Father is Lord. [Col. 0455A] For who could raise children unless he possessed a master’s authority over them?

[Col. 0455A] [Note: [Col. 0455B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 455–456]

*Unless he possessed a master’s authority over them.* This reading is found in many manuscripts, among them the two oldest [Col. 0455C] Royal manuscripts, and in five editions. Thus Lactantius too writes “by the right of masters” in Book V, chap. 6. Six manuscripts and ten printed editions read “authority of ownership,” a word absent from two recent Royal manuscripts and two old Roman editions.

*Head of a household,* etc. A person is called the *paterfamilias*, or head of a household, when he possesses dominion in the house, even if he has no son. Thus we are also accustomed to call a body of slaves a *familia*, on the authority of Ulpian, law *Pronuntiatio*, § *Familiae appellatio*, in the *Digest*, *On the Signification of Words*. For this reason, as Macrobius testifies, the ancestors, removing all ill-will toward masters and all degradation from slaves, called the master “father of the household” and the slaves “members of the household.” BETULEIUS.

*And a son is manumitted.* This is by catachresis (καταχρηστικῶς), to be sure. Properly speaking, children are emancipated and slaves manumitted. The latter is clear from title 5 of the *Institutes*, *On Freedmen*; the former from title 12, which teaches by what means the right of paternal power is dissolved. Both terms are derived from *manus*, “hand”—that is, authority. Moreover, the verb “to emancipate” also pertains to other things; on this point Budé should be consulted in his earlier *Annotations*. BETUL.

*Receives the name of patron.* Masters, when paying their slaves the supreme price of freedom, gave them from their own names either a second or even a third name. Persius’s Dama received the praenomen Marcus from his patron. Juvenal also mentions the third:

> As though you had three names.

That is: as though through manumission you had acquired, in addition to your servile name, a praenomen and nomen from your patron. This was done in the same manner by which heirs under a will were adopted into a name and family. Of those manumitted by their masters, some became Roman citizens, others *dediticii*, and others Latins. On this subject, after Theophilus the paraphrast of the *Institutes*, see Poliziano, *Miscellanies*, chap. 34; Alciatus, *Parerga*, Book I, chap. 14; and Alexander ab Alexandro, Book IV, chap. 10 of *Genial Days*. BETUL.

*Because both to show indulgence.* This is the reading of all the manuscripts together with all printed editions, except one Royal manuscript, in which the first hand had “who”; I would prefer to read it thus. See what follows.

[Col. 0456B] *Because he is Father.* Added from nearly all the manuscripts and most printed editions.

*If there are many.* Hence that slave in Terence wished to know how many masters he had. Thus Philo Judaeus, following Homer, *Iliad* VI, says that the rule of many is not good; therefore let there be one lord, one king.

*And incestuous.* Four recent manuscripts and eight printed editions have “uncertain,” but less suitably.

*Uncertain.* Thus all manuscripts except one more recent Royal manuscript, and all editions except four, which have “incestuous.” Thomasius rightly defends the reading “uncertain.”

*God.* The construction of the phrase is faulty; he should have said: “We ought both … to love God.”

*Sustains both roles.* Thus *On the Anger of God*, chap. 23: “Both roles are venerable in him.” *Persona* means office or condition. Cicero often uses “to hold” or “sustain a role”; for example, Book II of *On the Orator*, chap. 24: “I alone sustain three roles—my own, that of my opponent, and that of the judge.” BUN.

*And fear him because we are slaves.* Among the Prophets, fear generally signifies reverence for the divine majesty, and thus religion, whereas the Apostle, together with the philosophers, calls fear an expectation of evil accompanied by hatred, in accordance with that tragic and tyrannical saying: “Let them hate, provided they fear.” In this manner they fear the Lord who consider not his inestimable goodness but his inescapable justice: they do not love him as Savior but dread him as Judge and as a kind of Vejovis. The Greek translation testifies that fear is the same as religion in the Prophet and the Sage: it calls *eusebeia* (εὐσέβειαν), that is, religion—for so Tertullian interprets it—the same thing as wisdom. In the same way they also render the prophetic oracle: “the spirit of knowledge and piety shall fill him” (πνεῦμα γνώσεως καὶ εὐσεβείας ἐμπλήσει αὐτόν). From these examples it is easy to gather the sense in which the word “fear” must be understood in each passage. Nor was Lactantius without a scriptural precedent when he bound fear—that is, religion—to wisdom by so close a bond. Lactantius appears to allude to Malachi 1: “A son honors his father and a slave his lord. If, therefore, I am Father, where is my honor? And if I am Lord, where is my fear?” In this passage the word “fear” must undoubtedly be understood as veneration and as solicitude lest the one whom we worship and love with the highest devotion be offended through us—and that for his sake, not our own. BETULEIUS.]

Nor is he undeservedly called the *paterfamilias*, even if he has only sons: for the name “father” plainly includes slaves as well, because “household” follows it, and the name “household” also includes sons, because “father” precedes it. Hence it appears that the very same person is both the father of slaves and the lord of sons. Finally, a son is manumitted as though he were a slave, and a liberated slave receives the name of patron as though he were a son. But if he is called *paterfamilias* so that it may be evident that he is endowed with a twofold authority—because he must both show indulgence, because he is Father, and restrain, because he is Lord—then the same person is slave and son, and the same person is Lord and Father. Therefore, just as by the necessity of nature there can be only one Father, so too there can be only one Lord. For what [Col. 0455B] is a slave to do if many masters give different commands? Religions of many gods are therefore contrary to reason and nature, since there can be neither many fathers nor many lords, yet gods must necessarily be called both fathers and lords.

Truth, therefore, cannot be maintained where the same person is subject to many fathers and lords, where the mind, dispersed among many objects, wanders here and there. Nor [Col. 0456A] can religion possess any stability when it lacks a definite and settled dwelling place. The forms of worship offered to the gods therefore cannot be true, just as it cannot be called marriage when one woman has many husbands; rather, she will be called either a prostitute or an adulteress. For since modesty, chastity, and fidelity are absent from her, she must necessarily lack virtue. So too the religion of the gods is immodest and incestuous, because it lacks fidelity, because that unstable and uncertain honor has no head or origin.

## CHAPTER IV  
### Again concerning wisdom and religion, and concerning the rights of a father and lord

From these matters it is evident how closely wisdom and religion are joined to one another: wisdom relates to sons and demands love; religion relates to slaves and [Col. 0456B] demands fear. For just as the former must love and honor their father, so the latter must worship and revere their lord. But because God, who is one, sustains both roles, that of Father and that of Lord, we ought both to love him because we are sons and to fear him because we are slaves. Therefore neither can religion be separated from wisdom nor wisdom severed from religion, because the same God must both be understood, which belongs to wisdom, and honored, which [Col. 0457A] belongs to religion. But wisdom precedes and religion follows, because knowing God comes first and worshiping him follows from it. Thus there is one force in the two names, although it appears to be different.

[Col. 0457A] [Note: [Col. 0457C] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 457–458]

*Although it appears to be different.* This is the reading of the better manuscripts and very many printed editions. The more recent manuscripts, together with five common editions, have “although they appear to be different.”

*Disowned sons or fugitive slaves.* It was a custom among the Greeks that children who persistently resisted their father’s will and honorable conduct should be disowned by their parents once the grounds for disowning them had been proved before a judge. [Col. 0457D] Cases concerning disowning are found in Lucian and in Quintilian’s *Declamations*. A disowned son was deprived of support and all assistance from his father during the latter’s life, and after his death of succession to his property. Disowning is mentioned by Aristotle at the end of Book VIII of the *Ethics* and by Seneca in Book III of the *Controversies*. This custom was not permitted to pass to the Romans, as appears from the law *Abdicatio* in the *Code*, *On Paternal Power*, which Alciatus explains and restores in the second book of his *Dispunctiones*, chap. 28. ISAEUS. — The punishment of fugitive slaves was combat with wild beasts. An example is the slave Androclus in Gellius, Book V, chap. 14. We nevertheless read that masters marked them with brands when imposing a more merciful punishment. BETULEIUS.

*Will receive.* I restored this from nearly all the manuscripts and Cellarius’s edition; in the other clause “will escape” follows. Four Royal manuscripts and Junius have “receive.”

*Plato … and Marcus Tullius.* The former chiefly in the *Timaeus*, the latter in Book I of *On the Laws*. See also Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book II, chap. 15. — *Marcus Tullius, who acknowledges that the human being was generated in a distinguished.* Cicero, *On the Laws*, Book I, chap. 7: “This provident, sagacious, complex, acute, mindful creature, full of reason and judgment, whom we call the human being, was generated by the supreme God in a certain distinguished condition.” CELL.

*Who created.* That is, begot or generated, as below in chap. 8. Thus Phaedrus, Book I, fable 6, at the end: “if he should beget children.” [Col. 0458D] BUN.

*That the human being was fashioned by the gods.* Seven recent manuscripts have “by them”; the Royal-Putean manuscript and eight printed editions have “by these.”

*Who possesses the power of life and death,* etc. He alludes to the ancient power of masters over slaves, over whom they possessed the power of life and death. This was later prohibited by a constitution of Emperor Antoninus, lest they rage beyond measure against their slaves without a cause recognized by law, as stated in Book I of the *Institutes*, *On Those Who Are under Their Own or Another’s Jurisdiction*, and in the *Code*, *On the Correction of Slaves*. But God possesses not only the power of death but also, after death, that of casting into Gehenna, as stated in Luke, chap. 12. BETULEIUS.

*To be pulled apart.* Thus our author, *On the Workmanship of God*, chap. 9: “When the line of sight of each eye is pulled apart.” Seneca, Letter 113: “They must be separate. Thus the one must be pulled apart from the other so that they are two.” The same author, *On the Happy Life*, chap. 6: “They deny that pleasure can be pulled apart from virtue.” BUN.

*Beneath the covering of folly.* Isaeus has “beneath the covering of justice,” incorrectly. See the note on chap. 2: “Beneath the covering of which”—that is, of folly. Several old editions also have “beneath the covering” here.]

For one is situated in perception, the other in action. Yet they are like two streams flowing from one spring. The spring of wisdom and religion is God; if those two streams stray from him, they must dry up. Those who do not know him can be neither wise nor religious.

Thus philosophers and worshipers of the gods are like either disowned sons or fugitive slaves, because the former do not seek their Father and the latter do not seek their Lord. And just as disowned sons do not obtain their father’s inheritance, nor fugitives impunity, so philosophers will not receive immortality, which is the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom [Col. 0457B]—that is, the highest good which they especially seek—nor will worshipers of the gods escape the punishment of everlasting death, which is the true Lord’s sentence against fugitives from his majesty and name.

Both groups were ignorant that God is Father and likewise Lord: the worshipers of the gods no less than the teachers of wisdom themselves. For they either thought that absolutely nothing should be worshiped, or approved false religions, or—even if they understood the force and power of the supreme God, as did Plato, who says that the one God is the maker of the world, and Marcus Tullius, who acknowledges that the human being was generated in a certain distinguished condition by the supreme God—they nevertheless did not render him the worship owed to him as supreme Father, although this was the consequent and necessary course.

Not only their multitude, as I demonstrated above—that is, in the preceding chapter—but also reason declares that the gods cannot be either fathers or lords. For tradition neither says that the human being was fashioned by the gods, [Col. 0457C] nor shows that the gods themselves preceded the origin of humanity, since it is evident that human beings existed on earth before Vulcan, Liber, Apollo, and Jupiter himself were born. But neither is the fashioning of the human being customarily ascribed to Saturn, nor to his father, Heaven.

[Col. 0458A] But if none of those who are worshiped is said to have formed and established the human being at the beginning, then none of them can be called the human being’s father—or even God. Therefore it is not right to venerate those by whom the human being was not generated, because neither can he be generated by many. One and one alone, therefore, must be worshiped: he who preceded Jupiter, Saturn, Heaven itself, and earth. For he who completed heaven and earth before the human being must necessarily have fashioned the human being. He alone who created must be called Father; he alone who rules must be called Lord—he who possesses the true and everlasting power of life and death. Whoever does not adore him is both a foolish slave, who either flees or does not know his Lord, and an impious son, who either hates or is ignorant of his true Father.

[Col. 0458B] ## CHAPTER V  
### The oracles of the prophets must be examined; and concerning their times and those of the judges and kings

Now, since I have taught that wisdom and religion cannot be pulled apart, it remains for us to discuss religion and wisdom themselves. I realize, indeed, how difficult a discussion of heavenly matters is; nevertheless, it must be attempted, so that the truth, once illuminated, may become manifest and many may be delivered from error and destruction—people who disdain and reject it while it lies hidden beneath the covering of folly.

But before I begin to speak about God and his works, I must first say a few things about the prophets, whose testimonies it is now necessary to employ; in the preceding books I refrained from doing so. Above all, anyone who seeks to comprehend the truth must not only direct his mind toward understanding the utterances of the prophets, but must also investigate most diligently the periods in which each of them lived, so that he may know both what future events they predicted and how many years afterward those predictions were fulfilled. Nor is there any difficulty in collecting this information, for they testified under which king each experienced [Col. 0458C] the inspiration of the divine Spirit. And many written books—

[Col. 0459A] [Note: [Col. 0459B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 459–460]

*And many written books,* etc. This is how I write it with eight old printed editions and all the manuscripts except one recent Royal manuscript and five editions, which give “writers.” Of those who before Lactantius’s time wrote on Jewish affairs, nothing, so far as I know, survives apart from the writings of Josephus, the works circulated under the name of Philo, and the five books of Hegesippus together with an *anakephalaiōsis* (ἀνακεφαλαίωσις, “recapitulation”). A certain Justus of Tiberias in Galilee wrote in imitation of Josephus; he was nevertheless accused of falsehood by Josephus himself, as Jerome relates in the *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*. Aristobulus, Demetrius, and Eupolemus wrote *On the Primeval Origin* (Περὶ τῆς ἀρχαιγονίας) of Moses and the Jewish people, but these works too had perished by Jerome’s time. Melito of Asia’s book *On the Lives of the Prophets* has perished. A book *On the Lives of the Prophets* by Epiphanius, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, survives. [Col. 0459C] We possess the *Synopsis* of Theodore and Dorotheus; and the third discourse of Theophilus is likewise a chronicle. BETULEIUS.]

About seven hundred years. I have thus restored the text from two old Roman editions, the edition of Isaeus, and the marginal readings of many others, as well as from more than thirty manuscripts, two of which are of the greatest antiquity. This comes closer to the chronology generally considered more accurate than *nine hundred years*, or *nine hundred*, found in four recent Royal manuscripts, five Vatican manuscripts, one Sorbonne manuscript, one Clermont manuscript, the first hand of the *Marm.* manuscript, and eleven printed editions. Yet I think both these computations erroneous. I consider Bucholcer’s more probable: he thinks that Moses preceded the Trojan War by approximately 415 years. Eutropius believes that 410 years intervened. GALLAEUS.—About nine hundred years. The impious Porphyry’s calculation of the years was nearly the same: according to Eusebius, he made Moses almost 850 years older than the Trojan War. Eusebius himself, however, correcting Porphyry’s error in the *Chronicle*, places 328 years between Moses’ leadership and the destruction of Troy; but in Eusebius’ actual chronology I find [Col. 0459D] 347 years. The same Eusebius, in *Preparation for the Gospel*, book X, chapter 3, says: “From the capture of Troy, if you go back four hundred years, you will arrive at Moses and earth-born Cecrops.” Cyril, book I *Against Julian*, reports that Troy was conquered 410 years after Moses, Esebon—or Abesam—then being judge among the Hebrews. But from the *Chronicle* of Phrygio I find that no more than 322 years intervened between Moses’ leadership and the destruction of Troy. For he places Moses in the year 2454 from the creation of the world, but Troy’s destruction in 2775. From the Anglo-Saxon Bede I calculate 308 years. He places Labdon, judge of the Hebrews, in the year 2708, and writes that Troy was captured in his third year. Augustine also writes something about the age of Moses in book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 8. BETULEIUS.—But this entire method of calculating the periods is not so easy, because of disagreements in determining the periods of the judges. These matters, however, concern students of chronology, not theologians. Whatever one says, Moses is at least three hundred years and more [Col. 0460B] earlier than the Trojan War. Yet some, such as Pezron and Vossius in recent centuries, following the Seventy Translators, hold that Moses was approximately seven hundred years older than the destruction of Troy. But we leave these matters to others.

*Jesus.* I read thus with the two old Roman editions and all the manuscripts except two recent ones, which have *Josue*; one other, *Josua*; another, *Josuam*; and nine editions, *Josuem*.

*Twenty-seven.* In this computation the chronologists do not agree among themselves about the duration of Joshua’s leadership. But these matters belong to others.

*They were under judges for three hundred and seventy years.* The Palatine manuscript has 380. But Scripture, Acts 13:20, says four hundred and fifty years.

*For four hundred and fifty years.* I have restored this reading to Lactantius from seven Vatican manuscripts, six Royal manuscripts—two of which are [Col. 0460C] of the greatest antiquity—the Caucasus, Junius, four Colbert, Navarre, Victorinus, Gattius, Tornesius, Utrecht, Emenius, one Clermont, and the Bruni manuscript. The manuscripts vary greatly here. Two Bologna manuscripts have *four hundred and forty*; five Vatican manuscripts, four Royal manuscripts, the Penna manuscript, and fifteen printed editions have *four hundred and sixty*; one Colbert manuscript and Sparks’s edition have, erroneously, *four hundred and seventy*; one Royal, one Clermont, and one Sorbonne manuscript have only *for four hundred years*. But whichever reading you follow, these calculations do not agree with the chronologists. See, if you wish, Jean-Baptiste Le Brun’s *Harmony of Kings and Chronicles*, published at Paris in 1691, or at least the Chronological Table prefixed to it.

*The Jews were captured.* On this see 4 Kings 25; Jeremiah 39 and 52.

*In the seventieth year thereafter he restored them*, etc. This had been foretold by Jeremiah: *After the year, Cyrus the Great [restored] them to their lands and dwellings.* The Subiaco edition has: *After the years, Cyrus the Great [restored] the captive Jews to their lands and dwellings.* Indeed, in place of *them*, thirty-one manuscripts and six editions have *the captive Jews*, which I could never persuade myself Lactantius wrote, since [Col. 0460D] *and the Jews were captured* has just preceded.—Cyrus began his rule over the Persians in the sixty-first Olympiad, in 536 before the common era.

*At Rome, Tarquin the Proud.* See Orosius, book II, chapter 6. Eusebius and Bede agree. But it is established that Zerubbabel was leader of the Jews, with Jehoshua as high priest, in the thirty-second year of Servius Tullius, which was the year 207 from the founding of the City, 3417 from the creation of the world, and the fifty-eighth Olympiad. Moreover, in Tarquin’s time Cambyses prohibited the construction of the Temple, and Darius subsequently permitted it again. BETULEIUS.

*Prophesied.* That is, foretold.

*So much more ancient*, etc. That the prophets are older than the Greek writers is taught by Theophilus, *To Autolycus*, discourse 3; Justin Martyr, *To the Gentiles*; Josephus, *Against Apion*; Eusebius, book X of *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 3; and Augustine, book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 37. Pythagoras, who flourished at the same time as the last of the prophets, was among the earliest and most ancient of the Greeks.]

[They] published works concerning chronology, beginning with the prophet Moses, who preceded the Trojan War by approximately seven hundred years. After governing the people for forty years, he had Jesus as his successor, who held the leadership for twenty-seven years.

Thereafter they were under judges for three hundred and seventy years. Then, when their form of government was changed, they began to have kings. While these held power for four hundred and fifty years, down to the reign of Zedekiah, the Jews were attacked by the king of Babylon and captured, and endured a long servitude, until, in the seventieth year thereafter, Cyrus the Great restored them to their own lands and dwellings. [Col. 0459B] At the same time Cyrus assumed rule over the Persians [Col. 0460A] as Tarquin the Proud did at Rome. Therefore, since the whole chronological sequence may be assembled from Jewish, Greek, and Roman histories, the periods of the individual prophets can also be determined. The last of them was certainly Zechariah, who is known to have prophesied under King Darius, in the second year of his reign, in the eighth month. Thus the prophets are found to be older even than the Greek writers. I present all this so that those who attempt to condemn Sacred Scripture as something new and recently fabricated may recognize their error, since they do not know the source from which the origin of the holy religion flowed. But if anyone, after collecting and examining the chronological periods, lays a sound foundation for this teaching, he will both comprehend the truth thoroughly [Col. 0460B] and, once the truth is known, put aside error.

[Col. 0461A] CHAPTER VI. God begot an omnipotent Son; and the testimonies concerning him from the Sibyls and Trismegistus.

God, therefore, the designer and founder of all things, as we said in the second book—namely, chapter 9—before undertaking this splendid work of the world, [Col. 0461A]

[Note: [Col. 0461B] [Various Notes on columns 461–462]

*Undertaking.* I would prefer to read *adordiretur* with the Junius manuscript and one Clermont manuscript. GALLAEUS.

*Holy and incorruptible.* The Junius and Penna manuscripts, the marginal reading of one Colbert manuscript, and the Paris 1525, Aldine, Grapheus, and Isaeus editions add *and incomprehensible*; hence the Roman edition [Col. 0461C] of 1470 has *irreprehensible*, as do four recent Royal manuscripts, four Colbert manuscripts, the Caucasus manuscript, eight others, and eight printed editions. This expression, however, is absent from the older and better manuscripts: two Bologna manuscripts, two Royal manuscripts, three other recent Royal manuscripts, the Taxius manuscript, one Sorbonne manuscript, one Clermont manuscript, and the editions of Thysius and Gallaeus. As for what Lactantius says here—“He begot a holy and incorruptible spirit, whom he called his Son”—take care not to understand him to mean that the Holy Spirit is the Son, but that, as it is said, God is spirit.

*Had created through him.* I think those two words, *through him*, should be added, so that the text says that God made the world through his Son, as the sacred writers John and Paul also teach. These two words, *through him*, are found in two Bologna manuscripts, the Caucasus manuscript, seven Royal manuscripts, twenty others, the two old Roman editions, and six other editions. Some manuscripts and printed editions have *through himself*; the words are absent from three Royal manuscripts, one Clermont manuscript, and the editions of Gymnicus and Fasitel.

*With the designation of the divine name*, etc. Rather, he possesses this by nature, not because God deigned to honor him with the designation of the divine name. GALLAEUS.

[Col. 0461D] *Trismegistus.* Τρισμέγιστος means “thrice greatest.” This occurs in the *Asclepius*, chapter 4. Augustine Steuchus writes extensively about the authority of Hermes Trismegistus in book VII of *Perennial Philosophy*. BETULEIUS.

Ὁ λόγος τέλειος. In Latin, “The Perfect Word.”

Ὁ Κύριος, etc. In Latin: “The Lord and Maker of all things, whom we have considered it proper to call God, made a second god, visible and perceptible. I call him perceptible not because he himself perceives—for the question here is not whether he himself perceives—but because he directs things toward sense-perception and understanding. Therefore, since he made him first, alone, and one, and he appeared beautiful to him and most fully endowed with every good thing, he sanctified him and loved him greatly as his own son.”

*At the beginning.* See this passage in Theophilus, book II, *To Autolycus*.

Παντοτρόφον. On the Sibylline poems see above, book I, chapter 6, page 28, where one may read what judgment should be formed of them. In Latin:

[Col. 0462B] “The nourisher and creator of all things, who placed a sweet spirit in all and made God ruler of all.”

Θεόν. I have restored this reading from the two most ancient Royal manuscripts, one Sorbonne manuscript, three Colbert manuscripts, the Bruni manuscript, the Roman edition of 1468, and [Col. 0462C] the edition of Gymnicus. With Opsopoeus, I prefer to read Θεόν, “God,” because Lactantius calls the Son of God the Leader and Commander of all things, rather than Θεῶν, “of gods,” from the more recent manuscripts and printed editions. *Sibylline Oracles*, discourse 3.

Ἄλλ᾽ ὃν. I have restored this from four Royal manuscripts, two of which are of the greatest antiquity, two Colbert manuscripts, one Clermont manuscript, one Bruni manuscript, and others. Opsopoeus also read it thus. This verse is incomplete in the Sibylline codex.

“But him whom God gave faithful men to honor.”

*Sibylline Oracles*, discourse 8.

Αὐτὸν σόν. Thus the same manuscripts and printed editions. One Clermont manuscript and the Roman edition of 1468 have σου. In Latin:

“Know him as your own God, who is the Son of God.”

*Namely, he himself is the Son of God.* Thus the two most ancient Bologna manuscripts, two Royal manuscripts, two other Royal manuscripts, the Taxius and Penna manuscripts, and five printed editions. In the Caucasus and Junius manuscripts, eighteen recent manuscripts, and eight printed editions, *also* is added.

[Col. 0462D] *God created me*, etc. The passage is from Proverbs 8:22–31. Let it suffice to warn the reader once that the passages of Sacred Scripture quoted by Lactantius are quoted almost always, like those of the other ancient Fathers, from the translation of the Seventy Translators. ISAEUS.—*Created*: according to the Hebrew text, read: “possessed me from the beginning,” etc., which confirms the catholic doctrine concerning the eternity of the Word. But all these matters must be referred back to the original text.

*And uninhabitable regions.* I have restored this from all the manuscript codices, whereas the printed editions have *and uninhabitable lands*.

*When he set the mountains firmly in place.* This is the reading of all the printed books, and the preceding words require it. *He was setting* is the reading of the manuscripts. In the Septuagint, Tertullian, and Cyprian one reads *he was setting the springs*; one recent Colbert manuscript has *he was setting the winds*.

*At his side, arranging.* The Bruni manuscript has: “At his side, arranging all things”; one Colbert manuscript, by contrast, has *for* in place of *all things*.]

begot a holy and incorruptible spirit, whom he called his Son. And although he later created innumerable others through him, whom we call angels, he nevertheless deemed this one alone, the firstborn, worthy of the designation of the divine name, since he was endowed with his Father’s power and majesty. That he is the Son of the Most High God, endowed with supreme power, is demonstrated not only by the harmonious testimony of the prophets but also by the proclamation of Trismegistus and the prophecies of the Sibyls. [Col. 0461B] In the book entitled Ὁ λόγος τέλειος (*The Perfect Word*), Hermes used these words:

> Ὁ Κύριος καὶ τῶν πάντων ποιητὴς, ὃν Θεὸν καλεῖν νενομίκαμεν, ἐπεὶ τὸν δεύτερον ἐποίησε θεὸν ὁρατὸν καὶ αἰσθητόν· αἰσθητὸν δέ φημι οὐ διὰ τὸ αἰσθέσθαι αὐτόν, περὶ γὰρ τούτου οὐκ ἔστι πότερον αὐτὸς αἴσθοιτο, ἀλλ᾽ ὅτι εἰς αἴσθησιν ὑποπέμπει καὶ εἰς νοῦν. Ἐπεὶ τοῦτον ἐποίησε πρῶτον, καὶ μόνον, καὶ ἕνα, καλὸς δὲ αὐτῷ ἐφάνη, καὶ πληρέστατος πάντων τῶν ἀγαθῶν, [Col. 0462A] ἡγίασέ τε καὶ πάνυ ἐφίλησεν ὡς ἴδιον τόκον.

> The Lord and Maker of all things, whom we have considered it proper to call God, made a second god, visible and perceptible. I call him perceptible not because he himself perceives—for the question here is not whether he himself perceives—but because he directs things toward sense-perception and understanding. Since, therefore, he made him first, alone, and one, and he appeared beautiful to him and most fully endowed with every good thing, he sanctified him and loved him greatly as his own offspring.

At the beginning of her poem, which she commenced with the Most High God, the Erythraean Sibyl proclaims the Son of God as Leader and Commander of all in these verses:

> Παντοτρόφον κτίστην, ὅστις γλυκὺ πνεῦμ᾽ ἐν ἅπασι  
> Κάττετο, χ᾽ ἡγητῆρα Θεὸν πάντων ἐποίησε.

> The all-nourishing Creator, who placed a sweet spirit in all things  
> and made God the leader of all.

And again, at the end of the same poem:

> Ἄλλ᾽ ὃν ἔδωκε Θεὸς πιστοῖς ἀνδράσσι γεραίρειν.

> But him whom God gave faithful men to honor.

And another Sibyl commands that he must be known:

> Αὐτὸν σὸν γίνωσκε Θεὸν Θεοῦ υἱὸν ἐόντα.

> Know him as your own God, who is the Son of God.

Namely, he himself is the Son of God, who through Solomon, the most wise king, filled with the divine Spirit, spoke the words we append:

> “God created me at the beginning of his ways, for his works before the ages. He established me in the beginning, before he made the earth and before [Col. 0462B] he established the abysses; before the springs of waters came forth. Before all the hills the Lord begot me; he made the regions and the uninhabitable bounds beneath heaven. When he prepared heaven, I was present with him; and when he marked off his own seat, when he made the clouds strong above the winds, and when he set the mountains firmly in place beneath heaven; when he made the strong foundations of the earth, I was at his side, arranging. I was the one in whom he rejoiced; daily [Col. 0463A] I delighted before his face, as he rejoiced in the completed world.”

For this reason Trismegistus called him δημιουργὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ, “the craftsman of God,” [Col. 0463A]

[Note: [Col. 0463B] [Various Notes on columns 463–464]

Δημιουργὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ. In Latin, “the craftsman of God.” Trismegistus in the *Poimandres*, chapter 1. Irenaeus also calls him *Demiurge* in the passage already cited, and frequently elsewhere when refuting the Valentinian “psychic Demiurge”; so too does the Apostle in Hebrews 2. BETULEIUS.

Σύμβουλον. In Latin, “counselor,” from one Colbert manuscript, one Leipzig manuscript, and the Bruni manuscript. Lactantius used this word below, book IV, chapter 11.

*Because he was endowed with such wisdom and power.* I have restored this from all the manuscripts except one Colbert manuscript, which has the corrupt reading *quot* in place of *quod*.

*Perhaps someone may ask.* The Paris, Juntine, Aldine, Cratander, and Gymnicus editions have the future, “Perhaps someone will ask,” and Heumann approves it because Lactantius speaks thus elsewhere as well. Quite rightly; but the other reading, “Perhaps someone may ask,” is equally correct and is supported here by the Leipzig, Gotha, Gryphius, Tornesius, Betuleius, Thomasius, and remaining manuscripts. Lactantius, book I, chapter 3, and book IV, chapter 26: “Perhaps someone may say.” In chapter 29: “Perhaps someone may ask.” *On the Anger of God*, chapter 15: “Here perhaps someone may ask.” I note more examples on the *Epitome*, chapter 29. BUNEMANN.

*Constructed by his power.* Thus the manuscripts and editions. Francius conjectures *virtus* (“power”) instead. *It is proper for us to know that his name is not known even to the angels.* This reading has the greater authority, being found in ten Royal manuscripts, two of which are of the greatest antiquity, six Colbert manuscripts, six others, the two old Roman editions, and Betuleius’s edition. Two Royal manuscripts have *nor* in place of *not even*. The Caucasus, Junius, Leipzig, and Palatine manuscripts and four editions have *nor yet*; four printed editions—the Aldine, Paris 1525, Cratander, and Grapheus—have: “It is not proper for men to know his name, nor is it known even to the angels.”

[Col. 0463D] *Not even to the angels.* Because, as Paul says in Philippians 2, he gave him the name that is above every name.

Αἰτία. In Latin: “The cause of this cause, however, is the will of the divine Good, which brought forth God, whose name cannot be spoken by a human mouth.”

Θείου ἀγαθοῦ. A very few manuscripts have Θεοῦ, “of God.” The marginal reading in the Tornesius edition is *of God*, from a manuscript.

Ἔστι, etc. In Latin: “There is, O son, a certain secret discourse of wisdom, holy concerning the sole Lord of all and the Lord apprehended beforehand by the mind; to speak it is beyond man.”

Ὅσιος περὶ τοῦ μόνου κυρίου πάντων. These words, which are absent from some manuscripts, have been restored to Lactantius—or rather to Hermes—from the Bologna, Caucasus, Royal, Taxius, Emenius, Canterbury, Bruni, and two Colbert manuscripts. One Royal manuscript, one Sorbonne manuscript, and some printed editions omit καὶ προεννοουμένου Θεοῦ, “and of God conceived beforehand.”

Θεοῦ. I have restored this from the two most ancient Bologna manuscripts, the Caucasus manuscript, one Royal manuscript nine hundred years old, two other Royal manuscripts, two Colbert manuscripts, [Col. 0464B] two Bruni manuscripts, the Roman edition of 1470, the edition of 1497, and Isaeus’s Roman edition of 1650. But two manuscripts and seven printed editions have κυρίου, “of the Lord.” Most manuscripts omit both words.

*Jesus.* In Latin, “savior.”

*Chrestus.* Suetonius reports that the Jews were continually causing disturbances “at the instigation of Chrestus.” He meant Christ himself, though falsely and impiously; for the ancient pagans, through ignorance of the correct name, said *Chrestus* and *Chrestians*, not *Christus* and *Christians*. This passage of Tertullian’s *Apology* taught me the same thing here: “If,” he says, “the hatred is directed against the name, what guilt attaches to a name? What accusation can be made against words, unless perhaps some name sounds barbarous, ill-omened, abusive, or indecent? Yet even when ‘Chrestians’ is incorrectly pronounced by you—for you do not even possess certain knowledge of the name—it is formed from ‘sweetness’ or ‘kindness.’ Thus even an innocent name is hated in innocent men.” Thus far Tertullian; from his words I believe that what I proposed has certainly been established. Χρηστός means “pleasant, gentle, and kind.” See Suetonius, *Claudius*, chapter 25, and Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 3.

*To the priesthood or the kingship*, etc. Both have their place in Christ, who is both a king, whose kingdom will have no end, as the angel promised the Most Blessed Virgin, and a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek. Hence Peter rightly called the Church—that is, the kingdom of Christ—a royal priesthood. On the anointing of a king, read the First Book of Samuel; on the priestly chrism, Leviticus 8. No one treats the priesthood of Christ, and therefore his anointing, more learnedly or fully than Paul in the Epistle to the Hebrews. BETULEIUS. *Or the kingship.* This custom nevertheless later spread to other nations as well.

*The purple garment is the insignia of royal dignity.* It is a royal ornament, signifying by this reddish color the dominion of blood and the power to inflict death. Perhaps it is in this sense that Horace calls tyrants “purple-clad,” *Odes* 1.35:

> The purple-clad tyrants fear  
> lest with destructive foot you overturn  
> the standing column.

And undoubtedly because of this majesty God commanded the priest’s garment to be made purple (Exodus 39); and when Christ, the sole restorer of our salvation, was hailed as king by the dissolute soldiers, we read that he was clothed in purple. SALMUTH.

Αὐτούς. See below. In Latin:

“The maidservants washed them and anointed them with oil.”

]

and the Sibyl calls him σύμβουλον, “counselor,” because he was endowed by God the Father with such wisdom and power that the Father employed both his counsel and his hands in the construction of the world.

CHAPTER VII. On the name of the Son, and why he is called Jesus and Christ.

Perhaps someone may ask at this point who this being is who is so powerful and so dear to God, and what name he bears, whose first birth not only preceded the world but also arranged it by his wisdom and constructed it by his power. First, it is proper for us to know that his name is not known even to the angels who dwell in heaven, but only to himself and to God the Father; nor, as has been handed down in the sacred writings, will it be made public before God’s dispensation has been fulfilled. [Col. 0463B] Secondly, it cannot be uttered by a human mouth, as Hermes teaches when he says:

[Col. 0464A]

> Αἰτία δὲ τούτου τοῦ αἰτίου ἡ τοῦ θείου ἀγαθοῦ βούλησις, ἣ θεὸν προήνεγκεν, οὗ τὸ ὄνομα οὐ δύναται ἀνθρωπίνῳ στόματι λαληθῆναι.

> The cause of this cause, however, is the will of the divine Good, which brought forth God, whose name cannot be spoken by a human mouth.

And a little later, to his son:

> Ἔστι τις, ὦ τέκνον, ἀπόρρητος λόγος σοφίας, ὅσιος περὶ τοῦ μόνου κυρίου πάντων, καὶ προεννοουμένου Θεοῦ, ὃν εἰπεῖν ὑπὲρ ἄνθρωπόν ἐστι.

> There is, O son, a certain ineffable discourse of wisdom, holy concerning the sole Lord of all and God conceived beforehand; to speak it is beyond man.

But although no one other than himself knows the name that the Most High Father imposed upon him from the beginning, he nevertheless has one designation among the angels and another among human beings. Among human beings he is called Jesus; for *Christ* is not a proper name but a designation of power and kingship, since this is what the Jews called their kings. But the meaning of this name must be explained because of the error of the ignorant, who commonly change one letter and call him *Chrestus*. [Col. 0464B] The Jews had previously been commanded to prepare a sacred ointment with which those called to the priesthood or the kingship might be anointed. And just as among the Romans today the purple garment is the insignia of assumed royal [Col. 0465A] dignity, so among them anointing with the sacred ointment conferred the name and power of kingship. Now, because the ancient Greeks used χρίεσθαι to mean “to be anointed,” for which they now use ἀλείφεσθαι, as that Homeric verse indicates—

> Αὐτοὺς δὲ δμωαὶ λοῦσαν, καὶ χρῖσαν ἐλαίῳ·  
> The maidservants washed them and anointed them with oil—

for this reason we call him *Christ*, that is, “the Anointed,” who in Hebrew is called *Messiah*. Hence in certain Greek writings that were badly translated from Hebrew, [Col. 0465A]

[Note: [Col. 0465B] [Various Notes on columns 465–466]

*Were translated.* I have corrected the text thus from the manuscripts and several printed editions. Others have, erroneously, *was translated*. Francius thought the reading should be *translated*. Yet *were translated* is Lactantius’s genuine reading; he uses this verb here passively, as does Cicero in *On Divination* I.53, as do Jerome and Augustine frequently, and also the jurist Paul: “In wills,” he says, “the intentions of testators are interpreted,” etc. Indeed, Gellius, book XV, chapter 13, says that this verb is common—that is, it possesses both an active and a passive voice.—*Were translated.* In a passive sense, as in Tertullian, *Against Hermogenes*, chapter 19: “That which can be interpreted as matter”; *On the Flesh of Christ*, chapter 8: “the headings having been interpreted”; book V *Against Marcion*: “we find it interpreted.” Indeed, Cicero himself, *On the Laws* II.12: “We retain almost the same Greek name translated.” *On Divination* I.52: “Badly conjectured and badly interpreted things are false.” Compare Vossius, book III, *Analogy*, chapter 6; Gronovius on Gellius XV.14, page 683; Duker, *On the Latin of the Ancient Jurists*, page 334 following. BUNEMANN.

Ἠλειμμένος. In Latin, “treated by anointing.” I have removed from the text these four Latin words, which interpret the Greek expression, since they were intruded into the text from the margin of a book and are found only in four very recent manuscripts and several printed editions.

[Col. 0465D] Ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀλείφεσθαι. In Latin, “from being anointed.”

*A king is signified.* Thus almost all manuscripts and editions. Some have *a thing*.

*The time for taking which*, etc. Lactantius is mistaken, for a time will never come when Christ is to receive an earthly kingdom, since his kingdom is not earthly but entirely spiritual. Lactantius speaks thus because he thinks that Christ will reign in this world for a thousand years before leading us into heaven; we shall refute this opinion in its proper place. GALLAEUS.

*Jeremiah.* But this earlier prophecy is to be understood of Jesus Christ only in a secondary and more elevated sense; for the context sufficiently indicates that in its primary sense it concerns Jeremiah himself. See Jeremiah 1.

*And again in the same prophet.* The most ancient Royal manuscript has: “And again in the same man.” These words are absent from five recent manuscripts.

*Blessed is he who existed.* This passage is not found in Jeremiah—indeed, not even in the whole Bible. I therefore do not know [Col. 0466B] from what source the author drew it. Perhaps it came from somewhere in the Septuagint version or in some other version. The holy Fathers sometimes cite passages as drawn from Scripture which one nevertheless seeks there in vain. [Col. 0466C] GALLAEUS.—Perhaps they have been lost. Because it was considered insufficiently consistent with divine majesty, this was rejected at the Council of Nicaea and prohibited by anathema. On this matter see the words of Eusebius preserved in Theodoret, book I of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 12: Καὶ τὸν ἀναθηματισμὸν δὲ τὸν μετὰ τὴν πίστιν πρὸς αὐτὸν τεθέντα, δεκτὸν εἶναι ἡγησάμεθα, etc.: “We also judged that the anathema placed after the creed and directed against him should be accepted,” etc. We repeat this passage from a little farther back because above, in book II, chapter 9, the two preceding statements—namely, “from nothing,” and also, “There was a time when he did not exist”—were cited by Lactantius. BETULEIUS.

*Was born again.* That is, was born a second time. FRANCIUS.

Αὐτοπάτορα καὶ αὐτομήτορα. In Latin, “himself his own father and himself his own mother.” After these words, the recent Royal, Gattius, Navarre, Victorinus, and Bruni manuscripts insert the following: “And eternal is what God said, ‘Let there be light,’ because the Word of God, God with God, the only-begotten Son, is coeternal with God the Father. For although words such as *when* and *at some time* belong to time, nevertheless in the Word of God it is eternally determined when something ought to be made, and it is made when it ought to have been made; this exists in that Word in whom there is no *when* or *at some time*, because that entire Word is eternal. But how the words ‘Let there be light’ could have been spoken temporally through the creature whom he made before time is difficult to discover. For we do not”—or, in another reading, “we”—“understand that it was spoken by the sound of a voice.” But these words are foreign to Lactantius’s style.]

the word ἠλειμμένος, “anointed,” is found written, from ἀλείφεσθαι, “to anoint.” Nevertheless, by either name a king is signified—not because he obtained this earthly kingdom, for the time for taking it has not yet come, but because he obtained the heavenly and everlasting kingdom, which we shall discuss [Col. 0465B] in the final book. For now, however, let us speak of his first birth.

CHAPTER VIII. On the birth of Jesus in spirit and in flesh; on spirits and the testimonies of the prophets.

First of all, we testify that he was born twice: first in spirit and afterward in flesh. Hence it is said in Jeremiah: “Before I formed you in the womb, [Col. 0466A] I knew you.” And again in the same prophet: “Blessed is he who existed before he was born”; this happened to no one other than Christ. Although he was the Son of God from the beginning, he was born again a second time according to the flesh. This twofold birth of his introduced a great error into human hearts and spread darkness even around those who retained the mysteries of the true Religion. But we shall demonstrate the matter plainly and clearly, so that lovers of wisdom may be instructed more readily and carefully. Whoever hears someone called the Son of God ought not to conceive such great impiety in his mind as to imagine that God procreated him by union and intercourse with some woman. Only a corporeal animal subject to death acts in that way. But since God is alone, with whom could he have intercourse? Or, since his power was so great that he could accomplish whatever he wished, [Col. 0466B] he certainly did not require another’s partnership in order to create—unless perhaps we suppose, as Orpheus thought, that God is both male and female because he could not otherwise beget unless he possessed the power of both sexes, as though he either coupled with himself or could not procreate without intercourse.

But Hermes also held the same opinion when he called God αὐτοπάτορα καὶ αὐτομήτορα, “himself his own father and himself his own mother.” If this were so, then just as the prophets call him Father, they would also call him Mother. [Col. 0467A] How, then, did he procreate? First, divine works can neither be known by anyone nor described, [Col. 0467A]

[Note: [Col. 0467C] [Various Notes on columns 467–468]

*Described.* Thus in three Royal manuscripts, four Colbert manuscripts, the Gotha and Bruni manuscripts, and only Cellarius’s edition, in accordance with the prophet’s saying: “Who shall describe his generation?” The others have *narrated*.

*Speech, or also reason.* These last three words, which are present in the fourth ancient Bologna manuscript, Isaeus’s edition, and some others, are absent from ten Royal manuscripts, six Colbert manuscripts, and almost all the manuscript and printed copies.

*For speech is spirit*, etc. This definition is by no means sufficient to establish the divinity of the Word. Human speech does not contain within itself the substance of the one who utters it. But both the catholic faith and Tertullian, in *Against Praxeas* and elsewhere, affirm that the Word who is the Son of God and who became flesh is of the same essence as the Father. BETULEIUS.

*For conveying to man.* I have restored this from two Bologna manuscripts, two Royal manuscripts, the Junius, Gotha, and Leipzig manuscripts, and five editions. Many read *for carrying through*; one Clermont manuscript, *for setting before*.

*Which he himself.* Supply “word,” so that the sense is: “which very Word God first spoke in this manner.”

[Col. 0467D] *So that through him he might speak to us.* This is the reading of nearly all the manuscripts and editors, with *he himself*, which the printed editions, one recent Royal manuscript, and the Emenius and Leipzig manuscripts insert, deleted. The last three have “to us” in a different construction.

*The Word of God.* This will be discussed in the following chapter.

*Vocal.* It is absent from one Colbert manuscript. The Emenius manuscript has *living*.

*Other spirits of his likewise into angels.* I have added the pronoun *of his* from nearly all the manuscripts and the editions of Betuleius, Cellarius, and Walch. It is absent from the other printed editions, four recent Royal manuscripts, and the Colbert manuscript.

*Our spirits are dissoluble.* Here I would understand *spirit* to mean breath; for Lactantius continues to speak about speech and utterance. He should not be thought to assert this of our souls, since he teaches everywhere that they are immortal. ISAEUS.

*Accompanied by perception and power.* *Accompanied* is used here passively, as in Virgil, “accompanied by Achates alone”; in Justin XXX.2, “now they are greeted, now accompanied”; [Col. 0468B] and in Cicero, *Letters to Atticus* IX.2.

[Col. 0468C] *The latter of whom … preceded the destruction of the city of Troy by 140 years.* Thus one Vatican and three Colbert manuscripts, and this appears to be the certain reading. The commonly printed texts, however, have *the other*, incorrectly; for Solomon began his reign in 1019 before the common era, whereas Troy was captured either in 1209 or 1184 before the same era. The interval is therefore at least 165 years; but in chronological matters so remote an error of a few years is scarcely regarded. Chronologists do not agree in this computation of the periods: Eusebius gives 170 years; Glareanus, 147, which comes closest to Lactantius’s calculation. If the common reading were accepted, Lactantius would be mistaken. The destruction of Troy preceded the common era by twelve centuries, whereas Solomon lived only in the tenth century before the common era. Solomon therefore did not precede Troy’s destruction; rather, this king of Israel lived in the second century after Troy’s devastation. According to the Oxford Marbles, Troy was destroyed in 1209 before the common era. Solomon began building the Temple in 1015 before [Col. 0468D] our era. The destruction of Troy is therefore much older than Solomon; Solomon is not older than Troy’s destruction.

*By the Word of God the heavens were established.* In Cyprian, *Testimonies Against the Jews*, book II, chapter 3, the reading is “were made firm.” Both readings, however, occur in Augustine, *Exposition 3 of Psalm 32*. In Hebrew, Psalm 33:5 reads thus: “By the word of Yahweh the heavens were made, and by the spirit of his mouth all their host.”

*And by the spirit of his mouth.* Thus all the manuscripts, together with nine old editions and two recent ones, the Septuagint, the Vulgate, and Cyprian and Augustine cited above. Seven printed editions read “in the spirit.”

*Likewise Solomon.* Rather, the son of Sirach, Ecclesiasticus 24:3 and following. These words were hitherto attributed to Solomon because it was believed that Jesus, whose surname was Sirach, drew his sayings from Solomon’s abundance. CELLARIUS.—*Likewise Solomon.* Many Fathers attribute the book of Sirach to Solomon. Pamelius laboriously collected their passages in his notes at the beginning of Cyprian’s *To Quirinus*, book II, in order to prove that it belonged among the canonical books, for which he was criticized by Goulart. Serarius likewise collects passages from the ancients who attribute Ecclesiasticus to Solomon, in his notes on St. Boniface’s first Epistle. BUNEMANN.]

yet the sacred writings teach—Wisdom 18—that the Son of God is God’s speech, or reason, and likewise that the other angels are spirits of God. For speech is spirit uttered together with a voice signifying something. Nevertheless, because spirit and speech are emitted through different parts—spirit proceeding through the nostrils, speech through the mouth—there is a great difference between this Son of God and the other angels. For they went forth from God as silent spirits because they were created not to transmit God’s teaching but for ministry. He, however, though himself also spirit, proceeded from God’s mouth with voice and sound, like a word, precisely because he was to employ God’s voice in addressing the people; [Col. 0467B] that is, because he was to become the teacher of God’s doctrine and was to convey the heavenly mystery to humanity. He was the very Word whom God first spoke, so that through him he might speak to us and so that he might reveal to us God’s voice and will.

He is therefore rightly called God’s speech and Word, because by an inconceivable power and potency of his majesty God enclosed the vocal spirit proceeding from his mouth—whom he had conceived not in a womb but in his mind—within a form endowed with its own perception and wisdom; and he likewise fashioned other spirits of his into angels. [Col. 0468A] Our spirits are dissoluble because we are mortal. God’s spirits, however, live, remain, and perceive, because he himself is immortal and the giver of perception and life. Our voices, although they mingle with the air and vanish, nevertheless often remain when embodied in letters. How much more must it be believed that God’s voice both remains eternally and is accompanied by perception and power, which it derived from God the Father like a stream from its spring? If anyone marvels that God could be begotten from God by the utterance of voice and spirit, once he has learned the sacred sayings of the prophets, he will surely cease to marvel.

Perhaps even those who have never touched the divine writings know that Solomon and his father David were exceedingly powerful kings and were also prophets. The latter of these, who reigned later, preceded the destruction of the city of Troy by one hundred and forty years. The father of this man, the author of divinely inspired hymns, says thus in Psalm 32: “By the Word of God the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their host.” Again, in Psalm 44: “My heart has uttered a good word; I declare my works to the king.” He thereby testifies that God’s works are known to no one other than the Son alone, who is the Word of God and who must reign forever.

Likewise Solomon shows that he is the very Word of God by whose hands these works of the world were constructed. “I,” he says, “came forth from the mouth of the Most High before [Col. 0469A] every creature. I caused an unfailing light to arise in the heavens, and I covered the whole earth like a cloud. I dwelt in the heights, and my throne was in a pillar of cloud.” John too handed it down thus: [Col. 0469A]

*Handed down.* Eight manuscripts and four editions have the present tense, “hands down.”]

**Zeno.** Substantially the same things are reported in Laertius and in Cicero’s Book I *On the Nature of the Gods*. [Col. 0469D]

**Whom he also calls Fate.** Laertius likewise says: “There is one and the same being—God, Mind, Fate, and Zeus” (Ἕν τε εἶναι θεὸν, καὶ νοῦν, καὶ εἱμαρμένην, καὶ Δία); and that he is designated by many other names: Zeus (Ζῆνα), namely, Athena (Ἀθηνᾶν), Hera (Ἥραν), Hephaestus (Ἥφαιστον), Poseidon (Ποσειδῶνα), and Demeter (Δήμητραν). But Aristotle, near the end of the book *On the World*, lists several names of this same God from the Orphic writings. BETULEIUS.

**By which he acknowledges.** Seven printed editions have *in quo* (“in which”). I deleted the preposition, which is absent from all the other printed editions and all the manuscripts.

**To have proceeded from the beginning.** Six recent manuscripts and seven printed editions have *praecessisse* (“to have preceded”).

**So that, when he had discharged his teaching office.** The author uses the same expression below, chapter 16: “when he had discharged that teaching office and embassy of God.”

**And to the man whom he had put on.** This is a customary manner of speaking among the Fathers, who say that the divine Word assumed, or put on, a man. Thus Cyprian at the end of the book *On the Vanity of Idols*; Augustine, at the beginning of chapter 26 of the book *On Faith against the Manichaeans*; and Hilary, Book X *On the Trinity*, near the middle. This must be understood as meaning that we say a man was assumed because his nature was assumed, and because the assumption culminated in this: that the Son [Col. 0470C] of God should be man. See St. Thomas, Part III, question IV, article 3. ISAEUS.—**To the man whom he had put on.** “To the man,” that is, to the human nature which he had put on—the concrete term in place of the abstract. Cyprian often speaks this way, for example at the end of *On the Vanity of Idols*: “He who, as mediator of the two, put on man . . . so that the man whom he loved, whom he put on . . . he might carry victorious to the Father.” Arnobius, Book I, p. 38: “The man whom he had put on and himself carried with him.” So too among the Greeks Irenaeus, Origen, and Athanasius; among the Latins Hilary, Ambrose, and Augustine.
