## CHAPTER IX. On the Word of God

But the Greeks speak more aptly of the *Logos* (λόγος) than we do of the “word” or “speech”; for λόγος signifies both speech and reason, because he is both the voice and the wisdom of God. Not even the philosophers were ignorant of this divine Speech. For Zeno proclaims the λόγος to be the arranger of nature and the craftsman of the universe, whom [Col. 0469B] he also calls Fate, the necessity governing things, God, and the mind of Jupiter—following, of course, the convention by which they commonly take Jupiter to stand for God. But the words present no obstacle when the thought accords with the truth. For he is the Spirit of God, whom Zeno called the mind of Jupiter.

For Trismegistus (*Pimander*, chapter 4 of the *Asclepius*), who somehow investigated almost the whole of the truth, often described the power and majesty of the Word, as is shown by the example cited above, in which he acknowledges that there is a certain ineffable and holy Speech, the exposition of which surpasses the capacity of man.

I have spoken briefly, as well as I could, concerning the first birth. Now the second birth must be discussed at greater length, since the controversy concerning it is very great, so that we may hold forth the light of understanding to those who desire to know the truth.

[Col. 0469C]

## CHAPTER X. On the Coming of Jesus; on the Misfortunes of the Jews and Their Government Down to the Passion of the Lord

First of all, therefore, people must know that the arrangement of the supreme God proceeded from the beginning [Col. 0470A] in such a way that, as the end of the age drew near, it became necessary for the Son of God to descend to earth, so that he might establish a temple for God and teach righteousness. Yet he was to come not in the might of an angel or in heavenly power, but in the form of a man and in a mortal condition, so that, when he had discharged his teaching office, he might be delivered into the hands of the impious and undergo death; and so that, after overcoming death also through his power, he might rise again and bring to the man whom he had put on and whom he bore both the hope of conquering death and admission to the rewards of immortality.

Therefore, lest anyone remain ignorant of this arrangement, we shall teach that everything which we see fulfilled in Christ was foretold. Let no one give credence to our assertion unless I demonstrate that, long ages beforehand, the prophets proclaimed that the Son of God would one day be born [Col. 0470B] as a man, perform marvelous works, sow the worship of God throughout the whole earth, and finally be fastened to a gibbet and rise again on the third day. When I have proved all these things from the writings of those very people who maltreated their God while he was using a mortal body, what further obstacle will there be to making it clear that true wisdom is found in this religion alone? The origin of the entire mystery must now be recounted from the beginning.

Our ancestors, who were the leaders of the Hebrews, when afflicted by barrenness and want, went into Egypt to obtain grain. After remaining there for a considerable time, they were oppressed beneath an intolerable yoke of slavery. Then God took pity on them, led them out, and freed them from the hand of the king of the Egyptians after four hundred [Col. 0470C] and thirty years, under the leadership of Moses, through whom the law was afterward given to them by God. In this departure God displayed the power of his majesty. For he conducted the people through the middle of the Red Sea, while the angel went before them and divided the water, [Col. 0471A]

[Col. 0471A]  
[Note: [Col. 0471B] Variorum Notes on columns 471–472]

**While the angel went before them and divided the water.** Gallaeus, in his Notes, draws the contrary conclusion from Moses, because Exodus 14:18 says: “And the angel of God, who went before the camp of Israel, moved and went behind them, and together with him the pillar of cloud.” [Col. 0471C] But these words do nothing against Lactantius. For although the angel was behind them, the light had nevertheless continued to go before them; thus what Holy Scripture affirms of the light which the angel carried before them may not improperly also be said of the angel who carried that light. Nor perhaps is Gallaeus’s charge that Lactantius incorrectly wrote that the water was divided by the angel of any greater weight. The text which Gallaeus cites from verse 21 of the same chapter reads: “And when Moses had stretched out his hand over the sea, the Lord drove it—the sea—away by a strong wind,” and so forth. This was indeed done by God; but I would not therefore think that the ministry of the angel is excluded—the angel, I mean, of the covenant, who so often manifested himself to the Hebrew people and whose guidance the Israelites were already following at that time. SPARK.

**Curved.** Virgil, *Georgics* IV, 361, where he tells the story of the shepherd Aristaeus.

**Pursuing with a great body of his men.** See Josephus II, 6; but no infantry took part, as is evident from Moses. For he mentions only cavalry, chariots, and those who fought from them. The Septuagint calls their officers τριστάται, “third men,” as though one might call them *triarii*; because, according to Cajetan, there were nine on each chariot, three on each of its three sides. According to others, there were three on each chariot: the driver and two defenders.

**Was destroyed together with his whole army.** Justin XXVI: “The Egyptians were forced by storms to return home.” Orosius, Book I, chapter 12: “Even now the surest monuments of these events remain. For the tracks of the chariots and the impressions of the wheels can be clearly seen, not only on the shore but even in the depths, as far as sight can reach.” DRUSIUS.—But this observation by Orosius appears insufficiently certain. See Josephus. Pharaoh himself perished, but last of all, so that he might be more grievously tormented by first witnessing the destruction of his men. So the Rabbis and Alphonsus Tostatus report.

**Having entered the wilderness, they saw many marvelous things.** I emended the text in this way from a very ancient and excellent Royal-Puteanus manuscript, supported by one Clermont manuscript, which has “having entered in the wilderness,” etc.; another Clermont manuscript, “having entered in the wilderness, many,” etc., the letter *m* having been absorbed because of the following *m* in *multa*; and by one very old Royal manuscript, another Royal manuscript, seven recent manuscripts of good quality, four Colbert manuscripts, one Sorbonne manuscript, Em., and Brun., which have: “Having gone out into the wilderness, they saw many marvelous things.” “Into the wilderness,” that is, into the desert. The other manuscripts, together with the printed editions, have: “Having gone out, in the wilderness they saw many marvelous things.”

**By a stroke of the rod, when the rock was struck, etc.** Exodus 15. The gentiles fabricated the story that water was discovered under the guidance of an ass. From this arose the tale that the Jews worshiped an ass. Tacitus, *Histories* V; Plutarch, *Table Talk* IV. This springing forth of water was not a benefit lasting only one day; they continued to use it afterward in those deserts, and it endures to this day. So the cosmographers and Tostatus of Ávila.

**Of heavenly food.** That is, manna. Exodus 15.

**Quails into their camp, etc.** Josephus says πλῆθος ὀρτύγων, that is, a great mass or multitude of quails. The passage is in Book III, chapter 1: “Not long afterward, a great mass of quails—a species which the Arabian Gulf produces more abundantly than other regions—after crossing the intervening sea and becoming exhausted by their long flight, which in any case is not high, was carried down among the Hebrews.” See Diodorus, Book I, on the inhabitants of Rhinocolura; Pliny, Book X, chapter 23: “They wish to be carried by the breeze”—that is, migrating quails—“because of the weight of their bodies and the weakness of their strength; therefore they fly especially with a north wind, under the leadership of the quail-king.” See Aristotle, *History of Animals*, Book VIII, chapter 12. DRUSIUS.

**The wind carried in.** I restored this reading from three very ancient manuscripts—one Bologna and two Royal—likewise from two more recent Royal manuscripts of excellent quality, one Colbert manuscript, Goth., the Leipzig manuscripts, and Brun. Twelve recent manuscripts and the printed editions have “brought in”; one Clermont manuscript has “carried through.”

**Yet for these divine benefits.** The Royal-Puteanus manuscript, two other recent Royal manuscripts, Jun., and six printed editions have “for such divine benefits.”

**A golden head of an ox.** Some Fathers agree with our Lactantius that only the head of the calf was fashioned, rather than the entire calf: Tertullian, *Against the Jews* I, XX, 3; Clement, *Recognitions* I, 13; Cyprian, *On the Benefit of Patience*, near the end; St. Ambrose, Epistle 62; Jerome, on Jeremiah 7, Amos 5, and Hosea 4; and St. Augustine on Psalm 73.

**Apis.** Apis was a calf, an Egyptian ox also called Serapis: the chosen calf mentioned in Jeremiah 46. It was an ox maintained and worshiped by the Egyptians, according to Theodoret’s commentary on this passage of Jeremiah.

**To go before them as a standard.** I emended the text in this way from the Gymnicus edition, the two oldest Royal manuscripts, and fifteen other manuscripts. But ten manuscripts and nine printed editions lack the preposition *in*. One Royal manuscript, the Cambridge manuscript, and two old Roman editions lack the words “as a standard.” Eleven manuscripts and three common editions have “into a standard”; one Clermont manuscript reads “a standard going before them”; the manuscript seen by Barthius reads “that God might go before them by a sign.” But I find the word *God* inserted nowhere else.

**To the law.** The commentators rightly observe that Moses ascended the mountain to receive the law before the Jews fashioned the image of the calf. The law in question here is therefore not the Decalogue, but the ceremonial precepts, and so forth.

**They lost their ancient name, etc.** They were called Hebrews after Eber, who was a great-grandson of Noah through Shem. Eber was the son of Shelah and the grandson of Arphaxad. On him see Genesis 10; Josephus, *Antiquities* I, chapter 14; Jerome, *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*; Augustine XVI, chapter 11. I do not see, however, what Judas Lactantius imagines here as a leader after the time of Moses, unless it is the man who, as stated in the first chapter of Judges, was declared leader of the people against the Canaanites at the Lord’s command and, after defeating them, burned Jerusalem. This Judas, I say, was regarded by some as a kind of interrex between the leaders and the judges. Yet the common agreement not only of the Bible but also of ecclesiastical writers holds that Judaea and the tribe of Judah were named after Judah, the son of Israel and the patriarch and progenitor of the Judaean family. He was born to his father Jacob by the handmaid Leah in Mesopotamia and was Joseph’s more steadfast defender against the injustice of his brothers. From his line and succession of descendants the kingdom of the Israelites flourished for a considerable time, and the true king of the Jews—namely Christ—was born. The Hebrews, however, did not bear the name Jews until after Solomon; before him they were called Israelites, or the sons of Israel.—**Hebrews.** This name is derived either from Eber, the great-grandson [Col. 0473C] of Noah, or rather from Abraham, whom they called a Hebrew, that is, “one dwelling beyond the river,” because Abraham, at the command of the supreme Deity, moved from the eastern bank of the Euphrates to the western. From his former dwelling the holy patriarch bore the name “Hebrew.”

so that the people could proceed on dry ground. As the poet more truly says:

> The wave, curved into the shape of a mountain, stood all around.

When the Egyptian tyrant heard of this, he pursued them with a great body of his men and rashly entered the sea while it was still open. When the waters came together, he was destroyed along with his entire army. The Hebrews, however, entered the wilderness and saw many marvelous things. For when they were suffering from thirst, a spring of water burst forth when the rock was struck by a blow of the rod, and it revived the people. When they were again hungry, a rain of heavenly food descended. Indeed, the wind also carried quails into their camp, so that they were filled not only with heavenly bread [Col. 0471B] but also with a richer banquet. [Col. 0472A]

Yet they did not render honor to God for these divine benefits. Once they had been freed from slavery and relieved of thirst and hunger, they lapsed into self-indulgence and turned their minds toward the profane rites of the Egyptians. For when Moses, their leader, had ascended the mountain (Exodus 32) and remained there for forty days, they fashioned a golden head of an ox, whom they call Apis, to go before them as a standard. Offended by this sin and crime, God afflicted the impious and ungrateful people with severe punishments, as they deserved, and subjected them to the law which he had given through Moses.

Afterward, when they had settled in a certain desert region of Syria, [Col. 0472B] they lost their ancient name of Hebrews. [Col. 0473A] And because the leader of their host [Col. 0473A]

[Note: [Col. 0473C] Variorum Notes on columns 473–474]

**Host.** I change nothing. *Examen* is here used for an army or flock. Horace, *Epistles* I.19: “The leader governs the host.” Lactantius is clearly imitating Tertullian, *Apology* 39: “Palestine had not yet received the Jewish host out of Egypt.”

**They were called Jews.** Josephus testifies in Book XI, chapter 5, that they were called Jews from the time of their return from the Babylonian captivity. BETULEIUS.—In the earliest times they were called either Hebrews, Israelites, or the people of Israel, as we have already said.

**For a year.** So all the manuscripts and nearly all the printed editions. Some printed editions have “annually.”

[Col. 0473D]

**Royal power.** Not immediately, for a hierarchy intervened for eighty years. Eli the priest and Samuel his successor each held sovereignty over the Israelite nation for forty years. The First Book of Samuel teaches us their history. Writers, however, disagree with one another concerning these years.

**Had adopted.** The older Bologna manuscript has “adopted.”

**Subjected.** Through periods of servitude. Judges 3, 4, 6, 10, and 13.

**From that time they had tetrarchs, etc.** After the return—indeed, during the return itself—the affairs of the Jews were brought under a hierarchy, beginning with Zerubbabel and then continuing under others, concerning whom see Eusebius and Bede. The tetrarchies began after Jewish affairs came under Roman power, though not immediately at the outset; for the hierarchy of Hyrcanus degenerated into some sort of kingdom under Herod. To reduce Herod’s power, four sons of Herod were appointed tetrarchs: namely Herod, Antipater, Lysanias, and Philip. This occurred by the favor of Caesar Augustus. BETULEIUS.

[Col. 0474A]

**In his fifteenth year, etc.** Two new questions arise here: in what year Christ suffered, and on what day. On both points the authority of Lactantius is cited. [Col. 0474B] Paulus of Middelburg, in the second part of his *Paulina*, which concerns the Lord’s Passion, chapter 10—for his *Paulina*, published in 1513, may have relied on a somewhat corrupt edition of Lactantius—teaches there that Lactantius followed the authority of Tertullian and of Julius Africanus, the most celebrated doctor of the Church, and that the historian Orosius agrees with them. Eusebius, Bede, and certain others assign the Lord’s Passion to the eighteenth year of Tiberius; but, relying upon Luke’s authority, they appear to present the truer account. For in Luke, chapter 3, we read a most careful reckoning of the times: “In the fifteenth year,” he writes, “of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governor of Judaea, Herod tetrarch of Galilee, his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, under the high priests Annas and Caiaphas, the word of the Lord came to John the son of Zechariah,” and so forth. It is established, however, that Christ suffered more than three years and several months after his baptism. [Col. 0474C] Tertullian, Chrysostom, Jerome, Cyril, Augustine, and Bede assigned the day of the Passion to the eighth day before the Kalends of April.

**In the consulship of the two Gemini.** Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, chapter 8: “The Passion belonging to this destruction was completed within the period of seventy weeks, under Tiberius Caesar, when Rubellius Geminus and Fufius Geminus were consuls, in the month of March, at Passover time, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April.”

**On the day before . . . they fastened him to the cross.** This is indeed the reading of the best and older manuscripts: nine Royal, eight Vatican, Bologna, Gat., Marm., Tax., Pen., Cauc., Navarre, Victorinus, Jun., Ultr., Tornes., two Brun., Cambridge, Em. corrected by the same second hand, six Colbert, one Sorbonne, two Clermont; and of the Roman editions of 1468 and 1470, Cratander in the margin, Betuleius, and Isaeus. Some manuscripts and printed editions read: “On the seventh day before the Kalends of April.” Marcellus Francolinus explained this passage of Lactantius in a long and most excellent discussion in his *Treatise on the Times of the Canonical Hours*, chapters 73 and 74, which we shall summarize. [Col. 0474D] By the words “on the tenth day before the Kalends,” Lactantius means not the eleventh day before the Kalends, as Paulus of Middelburg thought in the *Paulina* (“quinto Paulin.”), p. 2, chapter 4, and Thomasius in his Notes on this author, but the actual tenth day before the Kalends of April. In this manner of speaking both terminal days are understood to be counted—that is, the day being specified and the day of the Kalends itself—as Marcellus, following Alciatus, rightly observes in the cited chapter 73, number 18, after refuting the objection drawn from the section *Ante diem* in the law *Anniculus amittitur*, Digest, *On the Meaning of Words*, and admirably explaining the same section. By these words, therefore, Lactantius held that Christ the Lord suffered on the twenty-third day of March. Theophilus of Caesarea, who lived close to apostolic times, held the same position in his synodical Epistle *On Easter*, printed among the works of Bede, volume II, at the end. Eusebius of Caesarea held the same in his comprehensive *Canonical History of the Chronicles*, a fragment of which survives in Anastasius of Antioch, [Col. 0475C] *Various Questions*. So too St. Augustine, Sermon 22 *On Time*, which is Sermon 18 *On the Nativity of the Lord*; Bede, *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 65, in the *Chronicle*; Ado of Vienne, *Short Chronicle*, at the beginning of the first age; Anselm, Book II *On the Image of the World*, chapter 17; Nicetas and almost all the Greeks; and others. From FRANCOLINUS and ISAEUS.—See our Dissertation on the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, and the letter of that most learned and illustrious man Étienne Baluze to Henry de Noris concerning the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, printed below in volume II of this edition of Lactantius.

was Judas, they were called Jews, and the land which they inhabited, Judaea. At first, indeed, they were not subject to the rule of kings. Instead, civil judges presided over the people and the law. They were not appointed for a single year, like the Roman consuls, but were supported by permanent jurisdiction.

Then the title of judge was abolished and royal power was introduced. Yet while the judges held their government, the people had often adopted corrupt religions; and God, offended by them, repeatedly subjected them to foreigners, [Col. 0474A] until, appeased once more by the people’s repentance, he freed them from servitude. Likewise, under the kings they were harassed by the wars of neighboring peoples because of their offenses. Finally, they were captured and carried away to Babylon, where they paid the penalty for their impiety through harsh servitude, until Cyrus came to the throne and immediately restored the Jews by an edict.

From that time they had tetrarchs down to Herod, who lived under the rule of Tiberius Caesar. In the fifteenth year of Tiberius—that is, when the two Gemini were consuls—on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, the Jews fastened Christ to the cross. [Col. 0475A] This sequence of events, [Col. 0475A]

[Note: [Col. 0475C] Variorum Notes on columns 475–476]

**Sequence of events.** Just as *textus* here means “sequence and order,” so *textus* and *series* are joined by Arnobius, Book V. Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XX, chapter 8: “This is the sequence of events.” On the word, compare Borrichius, *Vindiciae Latinae*, p. 229 ff. The Subiaco edition has “outcome.” BUNEMANN.

**Those very men.** I added “very” from the manuscripts and almost all the printed editions.

**The prophet Jeremiah.** This testimony is for the most part from Jeremiah 44. Certain things are added from chapters 7, 13, 16, and perhaps others, without preserving the change of persons that is very frequent among the Greeks and Hebrews. BETULEIUS.

**From your most wicked inclinations.** I restored this reading from almost all the manuscripts and most of the printed editions. Four recent Royal manuscripts, one Colbert manuscript, one Sorbonne manuscript, and thirteen printed editions—including those of Gallaeus and Cellarius—read “affectations.”

**The prophet Ezra also.** This passage is found in Nehemiah 9, a book which among the Greeks is incorporated into Second Ezra; and this speech is attributed to Ezra, not Nehemiah. The passage is, as I have said, Nehemiah 9. Augustine discusses whether Ezra was a prophet in Book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 36. **Behind their body.** I restored this reading from the editions of Isaeus, Cellarius, and Walch, and from all manuscripts except two recent Royal manuscripts, which, like twelve printed editions, have “behind their heart”; the old Bologna manuscript has “behind their back.” The Greek book of Nehemiah, which Lactantius reproduced—or a translation of it—agrees with the reading of our text: ὀπίσω σώματος αὐτῶν, “behind their body.” From CELLARIUS.

[Col. 0476C]

**With zeal I have been zealous.** So the old Roman edition reads, together with all manuscripts except one very recent Royal manuscript and almost all the printed editions, which read: “Being zealous, I have been zealous.”

**Disowned.** Fathers disown degenerate children—that is, exclude and alienate them: ἀποκηρύττουσι. For ἀποκήρυξις means “disowning,” as in Justinian’s Code, *On Paternal Authority*; Alciatus, Book II, chapter 28. BETULEIUS.

**Counselor.** The Subiaco edition has “comforter.”

**Ordered to descend from heaven.** So the better and older manuscripts and very many printed editions. Recent manuscripts and some printed editions have simply “to come down.”—**To descend . . . from heaven.** Lactantius elegantly varies *labi* and *delabi* in the sense “to descend,” as in the *Epitome*, chapter 43. Tertullian, *Apology* 21, says of Christ: “having descended into the virgin.” BUNEMANN.

**Had declared that he would do.** I read this with the older and better manuscripts and six printed editions. One old Bologna manuscript and the Leipzig manuscript have “had declared himself about to do”; six manuscripts and four printed editions have “had announced”; Pen. has “they announced.”

**The prophet Malachi indicates.** Two very old Royal manuscripts and two other Royal manuscripts read “Malachiel.” “Prophet” is absent from seven early printed editions. For “indicates,” one Royal manuscript has “announces”; the Leipzig manuscript has “announced.” The Gotha manuscript simply has “the prophet Malachi says,” namely in chapter 1.

**I will not regard the sacrifice as acceptable.** I restored this reading from the two oldest Royal manuscripts and four Colbert manuscripts, correctly. It is read no differently in Cyprian, Book I of the *Testimonies against the Jews*, chapter 16. The Septuagint and the Vulgate have “I will not receive”; two other Colbert manuscripts and two Clermont manuscripts have “I will not accept sacrifices,” which comes to the same thing. Two more recent Royal manuscripts, Brun., and the printed editions have “I do not regard it as acceptable.” Bunemann reads “I will not regard it as acceptable” and presents the following note on this variant.—Betuleius, alone, gave by far the best reading: “I do not regard it as acceptable”; for this is plainly supported by the Turin codex, the *Epitome*, chapter 48, and Cyprian, chapter 16, whom Lactantius follows especially closely. Yet the Hebrew and Greek have the future tense. Isaeus also saw this. BUNEMANN.

this order, is contained in the mysteries of Holy Scripture. But first I shall show why Christ came to earth, so that the foundation and rationale of the divine religion may become clear.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Cause of Christ’s Incarnation

Since the Jews repeatedly resisted saving precepts and departed from the divine law, straying into the impious worship of gods, God would fill just and chosen men with the Holy Spirit and establish them as prophets in the midst of the people. Through them he rebuked the sins of the ungrateful people with threatening words, while nevertheless exhorting them to repent of their wickedness. If they did not repent and, after casting aside their vanities, return to their God, he declared that he would change his covenant—that is, [Col. 0475B] transfer the inheritance of immortal life to foreign nations—and gather for himself from among foreigners another and more faithful people.

But when they were rebuked by the prophets, they not only rejected their words but, offended because their sins were being held against them, killed those very men with elaborately contrived tortures. Holy Scripture preserves all these things in writing.

For the prophet Jeremiah says:

> I sent to you my servants the prophets; I sent them before dawn, but you did not listen to me or incline your ears when I said to you: “Let each one turn [Col. 0476A] from his evil way and from your most wicked inclinations, and you shall dwell in this land which I gave to you and to your fathers, from age to age. Do not walk after foreign gods to serve them, and do not provoke me by the works of your hands, causing me to destroy you.”

The prophet Ezra also, who lived in the time of the same Cyrus by whom the Jews were restored, speaks as follows:

> They departed from you, cast your law behind their body, and killed your prophets, who solemnly entreated them to return to you.

Likewise Elijah, in the Third Book of Kingdoms (chapter 19):

> With zeal I have been zealous for the Lord God Almighty, because the children of Israel have abandoned you, demolished your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword; and I alone am left, and they seek my life, to take it from me.

Because of these acts of impiety, God disowned them forever, [Col. 0476B] and so ceased sending prophets to them. But he ordered that firstborn Son of his, that craftsman of all things and his counselor, to descend from heaven, so that he might transfer God’s holy religion to the gentiles—that is, to those who did not know God—and teach the righteousness which the faithless people had cast aside.

He had long before declared that he would do this, as the prophet Malachi indicates, saying:

> I take no pleasure in you, says the Lord, and I will not regard sacrifice from your hands as acceptable; for from the rising of the sun to its setting [Col. 0477A] my name shall be glorified [Col. 0477A]

[Note: [Col. 0477C] Variorum Notes on columns 477–478]

**Shall be glorified.** In Greek, “has been glorified”; and so it is read in Tertullian and in Cyprian, *Against the Jews*.

**Which are far away.** Tertullian, Book V *Against Marcion*: “You who were far away have been brought near.” Cyprian, Book I *To Quirinus*, chapter 21: “He will raise a standard among the nations which are far away”; and a little earlier in this very passage, “which are far away”; likewise chapter 22. BUNEMANN.

**That he would do this.** Nine recent manuscripts have “that this would happen.”

**Cut apart with a saw, etc.** This is one of the elaborately contrived punishments mentioned above by Lactantius, by which the prophets were tortured to death. Thus Jehu was killed by Elah (3 Kingdoms 16); Isaiah was cut into two parts with a wooden saw under Manasseh, who killed very many prophets; Jeremiah died in Egypt, overwhelmed with stones by the people, or—as most maintain—was drowned in a lake; Ezekiel was killed by a leader of the people in Babylon; Naboth died overwhelmed with stones (3 Kingdoms 21); Amos was killed with a nail by the son of the priest Amaziah; Micah was thrown down by Joram, son of King Ahab; Zechariah was killed between the altar and the temple by King Joash [Col. 0477D] (Luke 11:2; 2 Chronicles 24). Nothing concerning Isaiah’s punishment is found either in the sacred monuments of the Bible or in Josephus, who wrote of Manasseh’s tyranny in Book IV, chapter 10; in the Bible, however, we read of the latter—Manasseh’s tyranny—in 4 Kingdoms 21 and 2 Chronicles 33. Although these accounts belong among the apocryphal writings concerning Isaiah, Origen nevertheless considers that faith should be placed in Paul, who says in Hebrews 11: “They were stoned, they were cut apart”; the latter statement is to be understood of Isaiah. Both Talmuds mention this cutting apart, as do, among ecclesiastical writers, Justin Martyr in the *Dialogue with Trypho*; Origen, Homily I on Psalm 37 and Homily I on Isaiah; Tertullian, in the book *On Patience*; Chrysostom, Homily 33 on Matthew 19. Jerome likewise mentions it in his commentary on Isaiah 57; Ambrose in *On Jacob and the Blessed Life*, Book II, in Sermon 3 on Psalm 118, and in his commentary on Luke 20; and Hilary likewise in *Against the Emperor Constantius*. Epiphanius does not omit it in his *Life of Isaiah*. If Eusebius is to be believed, Isaiah was killed in the seventeenth Olympiad, when Numa Pompilius reigned among the Romans. BETULEIUS.

[Col. 0478C]

**The measuring has been made in vain; the scribes are false, and they have been confounded.** So read all the oldest and best manuscripts—six Royal, two Bologna, two Clermont, and others—together with all printed editions except the Roman edition of 1470 and twelve recent manuscripts, which have: “The measuring is false; the scribes have been confounded.” One Colbert manuscript has: “The measuring is false, the scribes also have been confounded”; similarly the edition of Cellarius, but with “also” deleted. The Royal-Puteanus manuscript agrees with the text, with the conjunction “and” struck out. The Septuagint and Cyprian have: “The false measuring belongs to the scribes, and they have been confounded.” Jerome has: “The lying pen of the scribes has produced falsehood. The wise have been confounded, terrified, and captured.”

**God is merciful and gracious toward his own.** Here *pietas* signifies God’s mercy. Antoninus was called Pius because he was most merciful. Augustine, *The City of God*, Book X, chapter 1: “In common usage, however, this word”—*pietas*—“is also frequently used of works of mercy. From this customary manner of speaking it has come about that God himself is also called *pius*,” and so forth. HERALDUS.

**Whom he hated.** See Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, chapter 5.

[Col. 0478D]

**Had rejected.** One old Bologna manuscript, four recent printed editions, and the edition of Thomasius add: “which he knew that they would do.” These words, as a gloss, are absent from the others.

**Descending.** That is, when the fullness of time came. Galatians 4.

**But if certain animals are accustomed to conceive from wind and air, etc.** Two Royal manuscripts and six recent printed editions read only “air”; the others have “and air.” The conjunction “and” is also found in Virgil. Virgil writes that mares conceive from the west wind in *Georgics* III, verse 272:

> And often, without any unions,  
> Pregnant by the wind—marvelous to tell.

Varro, *On Agriculture* II, chapter 1: “Concerning reproduction,” he says, “there is something incredible in Spain, but it is true: in Lusitania, by the Ocean, in the region where the town of Olisipo stands, on Mount Tagrus, certain mares conceive from the wind at a particular time; just as hens here also commonly do, whose eggs they call *hippenemia* (‘wind-eggs’),” and so forth. Pliny mentions this in Book IV, [Col. 0479B] chapter 22; Book VIII, chapter 42; and Book XVI, chapter 24. This comparison argues from the lesser to the greater, but I fear that in those days it did not possess much authority. [Col. 0479C]

among the gentiles.

Likewise David says in Psalm 17:

> You will appoint me as head of the gentiles; a people whom I did not know will serve me.

Isaiah too speaks as follows, namely in his final chapter:

> I come to gather all nations and languages; and they shall come and see my glory. I shall set a sign upon them and send those of them who have been preserved to nations which are far away, which have not heard of my glory; and they shall proclaim my glory among the gentiles.

Therefore, when God wished to send the measurer of his temple to earth (Ezekiel 41; Revelation 11), he did not wish to send him in heavenly power and glory. His purpose was that the people ungrateful toward God should be led into the greatest error and pay the penalty for their crimes, since they would not receive their Lord and God. The prophets had long ago sung that he would do this.

For Isaiah, whom the Jews themselves most cruelly killed by cutting him apart with a saw, speaks as follows (chapter 1):

> Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken: I begot sons and raised them up, but they despised me. The ox recognized its owner, and the ass its master’s manger; but Israel did not know me, and my people did not understand me.

Jeremiah likewise says (chap. 8): “The turtledove and the swallow have known their appointed time, and the sparrows of the countryside have observed the seasons of their return; but my people have not known the judgment of the Lord. How do you say, ‘We are wise, and the law of the Lord is with us’? The measuring-rod has been made in vain; the scribes are false and have been confounded; the wise have trembled [Col. 0478A] and been taken captive, because they rejected the word of the Lord.”

Therefore—as I had begun to say—when God had determined to send a teacher of virtue to humankind, he commanded him to be born again in the flesh and to become like the human being whose leader, companion, and teacher he was to be. Yet because God is merciful and gracious toward his own, he sent him to those very people whom he hated, lest he close to them forever the way of salvation, but might give them the free opportunity to follow God, so that they might both obtain the reward of life if they followed—as very many of them do and have done—and, through their own fault, incur the penalty of death if they rejected their king. He therefore commanded him to be born again among them and from their stock, lest, if he had been a foreigner, they could plead as a legitimate excuse under the law that they had not received him; and at the same time so that there might be no nation at all on earth to which the hope of immortality was denied.

## CHAPTER XII. On Jesus’ Birth from a Virgin, His Life, Death, and Resurrection; and the Testimonies of the Prophets Concerning These Matters

Accordingly, that holy Spirit of God, descending from heaven, chose a holy Virgin into whose womb he might enter. But she, filled by receiving the divine Spirit, conceived; and without any contact with a man, her virginal womb suddenly swelled. Now if it is known to everyone that certain animals are accustomed to conceive from the wind and the breeze, why should anyone think it remarkable [Col. 0479A] when we say that the Virgin was made pregnant by the Spirit of God, for whom whatever he wills is easy? [Col. 0479A]

> **Note: [Col. 0479C] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 479–480]**
>
> **The Virgin was made pregnant.** Thus all printed editions and manuscripts except four recent ones, in which the reading is *gravidatam* (“made pregnant”). The first Colbert manuscript, by a second hand, reads *gravidam* (“pregnant”). And below, *gravata est* (“she was made pregnant”) also occurs in the manuscript codices.
>
> **Solomon speaks as follows.** So many manuscripts report. Among the others, some add, “in the nineteenth Ode”; others, “in the nineteenth Psalm”; two, “in the twentieth Psalm.” All these appear to me to be glosses. Two other recent Royal manuscripts and eight printed editions read, “Solomon says as follows.” These words of Solomon are not found in his books.
>
> **Behold, a Virgin shall receive in her womb.** Thus the very ancient Royal-Puteanus manuscript, the first Colbert, the Emanensis, and the first Clermont; nor does St. Cyprian read otherwise in Book II of the *Testimonies against the Jews*, chap. 8. Two Royal manuscripts and twelve printed editions read *into the womb*; nineteen more recent manuscripts and eight printed editions read, “shall conceive in the womb.” The Subiaco edition has “shall conceive.”
>
> **You shall call.** Thus nine Royal manuscripts, including two of the most ancient, and others together with nine printed editions. Six recent manuscripts, together with the same number of printed editions, have “he shall be called”; another recent manuscript has “you shall call.” This occurs in Isaiah, chap. VII. See Irenaeus, Book III, chaps. 24 and 16.
>
> **Who denied him.** Thus all printed editions together with the manuscripts, except two Royal, the de Tournes edition, two Colbert, and one Clermont, in which the reading is “who killed him.” See the same expression below, chap. 18.
>
> **But he was never called Hemanuel, etc.** It is true that he was never so called as a proper name; yet it is certain that he was our true Emmanuel, not with respect to the outward designation of the name, but either with respect to its effect or to the application of the reality signified by that name.
>
> **Who raised up.** The first ancient Bologna manuscript reads “because.”
>
> **Raised up from the earth the shepherd of the sheep.** In place of “from the earth,” the Septuagint reads, “brought up from the sea”—*ἐκ τῆς θαλάσσης* (“from the sea”)—“the shepherd of the sheep.” Thus also the Hebrew and St. Jerome in his own version. In the other witnesses, *ἐκ τῆς γῆς* (“from the earth”), and in Jerome, “from the earth.” Paul, who appears to have had this passage in mind at the end of the Epistle to the Hebrews, rendered it somewhat differently: “God … who brought up from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep”—*ὁ ἀναγάγων ἐκ νεκρῶν* (“who brought up from the dead”). See Isaiah, chapters [Col. 0480B] LXIII and XLV. [Col. 0480C]
>
> **For I, the Lord God, created him, etc.** You must not imagine for yourself some created Son of God. To ward off this error, the Council of Nicaea took care that the creed should thereafter say, *Γεννηθέντα, οὐ ποιηθέντα* (“begotten, not made”). On this, read Basil’s letter written to the Antiochenes and another by Eusebius, which Theodoret inserted into Book I, chap. 12 of his *Ecclesiastical History*. See in Epiphanius—that most rigorous investigator of heretical perversity and most diligent reconciler of prophetic utterances—Book III, what difference there is between being created and being begotten. —BETULEIUS.
>
> **Behold, etc.** Isaiah IX. But these words do not occur verbatim in Scripture; hence one may infer that Lactantius quoted the Holy Scriptures from memory.
>
> **Sole.** A theological term, says Betuleius; but no more so than “one” or “only,” in place of which he often elegantly uses “sole.” I noted this at the end of Book I, chap. 4. Likewise here, as in Book I, chap. 13, he said, “the sole and true God.” —BUNEMANN.
>
> [Col. 0480D] **Taken away from the faithless people.** The Gotha manuscript wrongly reads, “the faithless people having been taken away.” Book IV, chap. 2: “God had determined … to send a leader who would reveal to the other nations that righteousness”—here, “the holy mystery”—“which had been taken away from the faithless and ungrateful people.” —BUNEMANN.
>
> **Daniel likewise foretold similar things.** Chap. VII. The Hebrews do not number him among the prophets. The reason is that he led not a prophetic but a satrap’s life, just as David led a kingly one. Accordingly, they say that these men did indeed write through the Holy Spirit, but were not prophets. Nevertheless, Christ, Josephus, and the catholic Church call Daniel a prophet. From PERERIUS.
>
> **Which shall not be corrupted.** Bunemann omits “which”: “Previously,” he says, “all editions had printed, ‘and his kingdom, which shall not be corrupted.’ The Hebrew text has ‘which,’ as does Tertullian in Book III *Against Marcion*: ‘And his kingdom, which shall not be impaired.’ Nevertheless, I omitted it on the authority of the Gotha codex, which, like the very ancient Turin manuscript in the *Epitome*, chap. 47, clearly reads: ‘and his kingdom shall not be corrupted.’” —BUNEMANN.

This could certainly seem incredible, had the Prophets not foretold many centuries before that it would occur. Solomon speaks as follows: “The womb of a virgin became weak, and received a fetus, and she became pregnant, and in abundant compassion she became a virgin mother.” Likewise the prophet Isaiah, whose words are these: “For this reason God himself will give you a sign: Behold, a Virgin shall receive in her womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Hemanuel.” What could be said more plainly than this? The Jews who denied him read these words. If anyone thinks that we have fabricated them, let him inquire of the Jews and take them especially from the Jews. That testimony which is supplied by one’s enemies themselves is sufficiently strong to prove the truth.

But he was never called Hemanuel, but Jesus, which in Latin [Col. 0479B] means “salvation-bringer” or “savior,” because he came bringing salvation to all nations. Yet through this name the prophet declared that God was to come to humankind in the flesh. For Hemanuel means “God with us”: namely, because after his birth through a virgin, people had to confess that God was with them—that is, upon earth and in mortal flesh. Hence David says in Psalm LXXXIV: “Truth has sprung from the earth,” because God, in whom truth resides, assumed an earthly body in order to open the way of salvation to those who are earthly.

Likewise Isaiah himself says: “But they did not believe, [Col. 0480A] and they provoked the holy Spirit, and he was turned to enmity against them. And he himself fought against them, and he remembered the days of old, who raised up from the earth the shepherd of the sheep.”

Who that shepherd would be he declared in another place, saying: “Let the heavens above rejoice, and let the clouds put on righteousness; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Savior. For I, the Lord God, created him.” Now the Savior is Jesus, as we said above. But in another place the same prophet also proclaimed as follows: “Behold, a child has been born to us, and a son has been given to us; his government is upon his shoulders, and his name has been called ‘Messenger of the Great Counsel.’” For he was sent by God the Father for this reason: to reveal to all nations under heaven the holy mystery of the sole and true God, which had been taken away from the faithless people who often sinned against God.

Daniel likewise [Col. 0480B] foretold similar things: “I saw,” he says, “in a vision of the night; and behold, one coming upon the clouds of heaven like a son of man, and he came as far as the Ancient of Days. And those who stood by presented him, and a kingdom and honor and dominion were given to him; and all peoples, tribes, and languages shall serve him. His power is eternal and shall never pass away, and his kingdom shall not be corrupted.”

How, then, do the Jews both confess and hope for the Christ of God, when they rejected this man precisely because he was born from a human being? For since it was so ordained by God that the same [Col. 0481A] Christ should come to earth twice— [Col. 0481A]

> **Note: [Col. 0481C] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 481–482]**
>
> **That Christ should come to earth twice, etc.** This is false. Such was the opinion of those who are called Millenarians, whose error we shall later refute when Lactantius treats that question expressly. —GALLAEUS.
>
> **Was to be clothed in flesh upon earth.** The Junius manuscripts, the first Colbert, the first Clermont, and the Aldine, Grapheus, and Cratander editions read, “ought to be clothed in flesh upon earth.” But *was to* is the true reading, confirmed by the authority of all the other codices and by Lactantius below, chap. 30, shortly after its beginning, and Book VII, chap. 6, near the end.—“Was to be clothed.” Heumann says, “I read *ought to*, as in the editions of 1513 and 1515. This is the style of Lactantius and the sacred writers.” Lactantius, Book IV, chap. 20: “Which was to be given through Christ.” In the same book, chap. 30: “That … heresies were to arise.” Tertullian, *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chap. 5: “From whom Christ was to be born”; chap. 11: “It had to be answered on the opposing side.” *Against the Jews*: “Circumcision was to be given”; chap. 8: “Was to be destroyed”; chap. 11: “Had to be erased”; chap. 14: “Has to be acknowledged”; *On Baptism*, chap. 16: “Has to be baptized.” *On the Flesh of Christ*, chap. 7: “Was to be born”; *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chap. 14: “Have to be judged.” —BUNEMANN.
>
> [Col. 0481D] **As far as the Ancient.** The Subiaco and Venice 1471 editions read “as far as Ancient.” As I noted at Book I, chap. 22, I do not approve this here, for all the others have “as far as the Ancient”; the wording, however, varies here. See above, “as far as the Ancient of Days.” Cyprian, Book II of the *Testimonies*, chap. 26, has “as far as the Elder of Days.” —BUNEMANN.
>
> **Isaiah.** Namely, chap. XLV. Although this prophecy applies by name to Cyrus, theologians nevertheless assign it in some measure to Christ.
>
> **I shall go before you.** Thus I have restored the text from nearly all the manuscripts and from the old Roman, Cellarius, and Walch editions. “You” is absent from three [Col. 0482C] Royal manuscripts, two recent Colbert manuscripts, and twelve commonly used editions. It is present in the Hebrew text and in the Septuagint; the Leipzig manuscripts read, “I shall go before him.” And immediately after “invisible,” the Septuagint adds, “I shall open for you.”
>
> **He possesses dominion and honor.** Thus the most ancient manuscripts and seven printed editions. But seventeen recent manuscripts and seven commonly used editions read, “he possesses dominion, he possesses honor.” This latter reading is not without elegance, and is Lactantian.
>
> **When he shall come again.** Lactantius returns again to his natural bent and once more dreams of a thousand-year kingdom, which he had in mind.
>
> **Like the supreme Father.** The Leipzig manuscripts, the first Colbert, Emanensis, and Brunner manuscripts read, “the supreme God and Father.” Here, however, the likeness must be understood as consisting not in accidents—which have no place in God—but in essence. For he appears plainly to wish to establish the *τὸ ὁμοούσιον* (“consubstantiality”), which was afterwards established at the Council of Nicaea: namely, that against the Arians and other heresies they should confess *Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν υἱὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ, γεννηθέντα ἐκ τοῦ Πατρὸς μονογενῆ, τουτέστιν ἐκ τῆς οὐσίας τοῦ Πατρὸς, Θεὸν ἐκ Θεοῦ, καὶ φῶς ἐκ φωτὸς, θεὸν ἀληθινὸν ἐκ θεοῦ ἀληθινοῦ*, etc.—“Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the only-begotten born of the Father, that is, from the essence of the Father, God from God, and light from light, true God from true God,” etc. Christ was also like a human being in such a way that he appeared to be a sinner. Romans VIII: “God sent the Son in the likeness of sinful flesh.” Hence in the next chapter he also appears in Zechariah’s vision clothed in filthy garments. —BETULEIUS.
>
> **Ἀπάτωρ and ἀμήτωρ** (“fatherless” and “motherless”). Cyril makes this same observation against Julian. Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews, chap. VII, receives much light from this passage, nor will this passage be correctly understood without that one. For there the Apostle teaches that Melchizedek, king of Salem, who was also high priest of the Most High God, prefigured Christ in that Genesis XIV says that his father and mother were unknown. —BETULEIUS.—See also Cunaeus, *On the Commonwealth of the Hebrews*, Book III, chap. 4.

—once, to proclaim the one God to the nations, and then again, to reign—how do they believe in his second coming when they did not believe in the first?

And yet the prophet encompassed both his comings in a few words. “Behold,” he says, “one coming upon the clouds of heaven like a son of man.” He did not say, “like a son of God,” but “a son of man,” to show that he was to be clothed in flesh upon earth, so that, after assuming a human form and mortal condition, he might teach righteousness to humankind; and, after fulfilling God’s commands and revealing the truth to the nations, he might also be punished with death, so that he might conquer and unseal the lower regions as well, and only then, rising again, depart to the Father, borne aloft in a cloud.

For the prophet added: “And he came as far as the Ancient of Days, and was presented [Col. 0481B] to him.” He called the supreme God “the Ancient of Days,” because his age and origin cannot be comprehended, since he alone existed from eternity and will always exist throughout eternity.

David testified in Psalm CIX, in these words, that after his passion and resurrection Christ would ascend to God the Father: “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.’” Since that prophet was a king, whom could he call his lord, who would sit at God’s right hand, except Christ the Son of God, who is King of kings and Lord of lords?

Isaiah shows this more openly, saying: “Thus says the Lord God to Christ my lord, whose right hand I have held: I shall make the nations obey before him, and I shall shatter the strength of kings. I shall open gates before him, [Col. 0481C] and cities shall not be closed. I shall go before you and level the mountains; I shall break bronze doors and shatter iron bars; and I shall give you hidden and invisible treasures, [Col. 0482A] so that you may know that I am the Lord God, who call you by your name, the God of Israel.””

Finally, because of the virtue and faith that he displayed toward God upon earth, a kingdom and honor and dominion were given to him; and all peoples, tribes, and languages shall serve him; and his power is eternal and shall never pass away, and his kingdom shall not be corrupted. This is indeed understood in two ways. Even now he possesses perpetual power, since all nations and all languages venerate his name, confess his majesty, follow his teaching, and imitate his virtue; he possesses dominion and honor, since all the tribes of the earth obey his precepts. And later, when he shall come again in power and glory to judge every soul and restore the righteous to life, then he will truly obtain sovereignty over the whole earth. [Col. 0482B] Then, when every evil has been removed from human affairs, a golden age—as the poets call it—that is, a just and peaceful time, will arise.

But we shall discuss these matters more fully in the final book, when we speak about the second coming. For now, let us explain the first, as we began to do.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Jesus as God and Man; and the Testimonies of the Prophets Concerning Him

Therefore, when the supreme God and parent of all wished to transfer his religion, he sent from heaven a teacher of righteousness, so that in him or through him he might give a new law to new worshipers—not as he had done before through a human being. Nevertheless, he wished him to be born as a human being, so that in every respect he might come to be like the supreme Father. [Col. 0482C] For God the Father himself, the source and beginning of all things, because he has no parents, is most truly called by Trismegistus *ἀπάτωρ* and *ἀμήτωρ*—“fatherless” and “motherless”—because he was begotten from no one. [Col. 0483A] For this reason the Son also had to be born twice, so that he too might become [Col. 0483A]

> **Note: [Col. 0483C] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 483–484]**
>
> **So that he too.** I added “too” from nearly all the manuscripts.
>
> **Was begotten.** The Caucian and Junius manuscripts, two Royal manuscripts, and eleven commonly used editions read “was brought forth.”
>
> **Virginal.** Heumann reads “from a virginal womb.”
>
> **Meanwhile.** Reimann and others read “again,” by which the variant reading “again” is indicated. In the Subiaco, Rostock, Venice 1471 and 1472, and both 1478 editions, the text reads: “Whole and to have been God, he testifies. That he was a human being mingled from both kinds we learn from the prophecies of the prophets. Isaiah testifies that he was God.” It is evident that the typesetters omitted the words “that he was God,” because the words “that he was God” followed twice. The Paris 1513 edition reads, “Whole and to have been God, etc.,” and contains everything. The Subiaco edition has, “Whole and to have been God, he testifies with these words: ‘Egypt has labored,’ etc.” —BUNEMANN.
>
> **Mingled from both kinds.** Not by a confusion of natures, [Col. 0483D] but in such a way that a single *ὑφιστάμενον* (“subsisting entity”), or one person, was constituted, while the properties of each nature were preserved. RIVET, in his manuscript notes.—That is, so that there might be one suppositum. Otherwise, it is well known that there were the heresies of Arius, Apollinaris, Nestorius, and Eutyches, which assailed the person and nature of Christ and were condemned by the first four ecumenical councils.
>
> **Isaiah.** Chap. XLV; this too is understood first of Cyrus and subsequently of Christ.
>
> **And the commerce of the Ethiopians.** Thus I have restored the text from all the manuscripts and the old Roman, Egnatius, Paris 1525, Cratander, Grapheus, Isaeus, and Cellarius editions. The true reading, according to the Hebrew, the Septuagint, and the Vulgate itself, also occurs in Jerome. Eight printed editions wrongly read “nation.”
>
> **And the Sabaeans.** I have restored *Sabaim* from all the manuscripts except two recent ones, and from the editions, which read “and Saba.”
>
> **And they shall pray to you.** Thus I have restored the text from the very ancient Royal-Puteanus manuscript, two other Royal manuscripts of excellent quality, and the Leipzig manuscript, as it also stands in the Greek.
>
> [Col. 0484C] **Jeremiah speaks as follows.** This passage is not read today in Jeremiah, but in Baruch, chap. III, which nevertheless is itself entitled *Ἰερεμίας Βαρούχ* (“Jeremiah–Baruch”) in the Greek Bibles and is included among Jeremiah’s writings before Lamentations. Read Augustine, Book XVIII of *The City of God*, chap. 33. —BETULEIUS.
>

>

In the Vulgate: “a rod from Israel.” Likewise in Justin, *ἡγούμενος* (“a leader”) from Israel, as also in Cyprian, Book I *Against the Jews*, §10. In Symmachus: “a scepter.”—**From Israel.** The third Leipzig manuscript and Reimann add: “And he shall rule the nations.” In *On the Anger of God*, chap. 14: “That he might rule over all things.” Add Cyprian, Book II *Against the Jews*, chap. 10.
>
> **The Milesian Apollo.** He was so called from the city of Miletus, which once, as Mela says, was the foremost city of all Ionia in the arts of war and peace. According to the same Mela, this oracle was formerly delivered at Branchidae and afterward at Didyma; on this see also Strabo and Herodotus. —BETULEIUS.
>

>

>
> **Wonder-working.** [Col. 0484D] Thus the de Tournes, Soubron, and Thomasius editions. Lactantius himself likewise reads this below, around the middle of this chapter and chap. 15, as well as above, Book II, chap. 13. In place of “by nails and a cross,” four Colbert manuscripts have “pierced through.”
>
> **Ἀλλ᾽ ὑπὸ Χαλδαίων, etc.** In the Caucian manuscripts it reads: *Ἀλλ᾽ ὑπὸ Χαλδαίοισι δίκας πολιέτιν ἄλωσας*—“But under the Chaldaeans … judgments … you were captured” [the intervening Greek is corrupt and materially uncertain].

*ἀπάτωρ* and *ἀμήτωρ*, “fatherless” and “motherless.” For in his first, spiritual birth he was *ἀμήτωρ*, “motherless,” because he was begotten by God the Father alone, without a mother’s agency. But in his second, carnal birth he was *ἀπάτωρ*, “fatherless,” because he was brought forth from a virginal womb without a father’s agency. Thus, bearing a substance intermediate between God and humanity, he could, as if by the hand, lead this fragile and feeble nature of ours toward immortality.

He was made both the Son of God through the Spirit and the son of man through the flesh; that is, both God and man. The power of God in him was revealed by the works that he performed; human frailty, by the suffering that he endured. Why he underwent it I shall explain a little later.

Meanwhile, from the prophecies of the prophets we learn both that he was God and that he was a human being mingled from both kinds. Isaiah testifies in these words that he was God: “Egypt has labored, and the commerce of the Ethiopians and the Sabaeans; [Col. 0483B] tall men shall come over to you and shall be your servants. They shall walk behind you bound in shackles, and they shall worship you and pray to you, because God is in you and there is no other God besides you. For you are God, and we did not know you—the God of Israel, the Savior. All who oppose you shall be confounded and put to shame, and shall fall into confusion.”

Likewise the prophet Jeremiah speaks as follows: “This is our God, and no other shall be accounted apart from him, who discovered the whole way of wisdom and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. After these things he was seen upon earth and associated with human beings.”

Likewise David says in Psalm XLIV: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the rod of equity is the rod of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated injustice; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness.” By that word he also disclosed the name, since—as I taught above—he was called Christ from the anointing.

Then Jeremiah teaches that the same one was a human being, saying: “He is also a man; and who has known him?” Likewise Isaiah says (chap. 19, in the Septuagint): “And God will send them a man who will save them, and by judging he will heal them.” Moses also speaks as follows in Numbers (chap. XXIV): “A star shall arise from Jacob, and a man shall arise from Israel.”

For this reason, when the Milesian Apollo was consulted as to whether he was a god or a man, he answered in this manner:

> *Θνητὸς ἔην κατὰ σάρκα, σοφὸς, τερατώδεσιν ἔργοις,*  
> *Ἀλλ᾽ ὑπὸ Χαλδαίων κριτῶν ὅπλοις συναλωθείς,*  
> *Γόμφοις καὶ σκολόπεσσι πικρὴν ἀνέτλησε τελευτήν.* [Col. 0484B]
>
> Mortal he was according to the flesh, wise in wonder-working deeds;  
> But, seized by force of arms under Chaldaean judges,  
> By nails and a cross he endured a bitter end.

In the first verse he did indeed speak the truth, but he craftily deceived the questioner, who was wholly ignorant of the mystery of the truth. For he seems to have denied that Christ was God. But when he admits that he was mortal according to the flesh—which we too proclaim—it follows that according to the spirit he was God, which we affirm. For why was it necessary to mention the flesh, when it would have been enough to say that he was mortal? But, constrained by the truth, Apollo could not deny how the matter stood, just as he could not deny what he said about Christ’s being wise.

What do you answer to this, Apollo? If he is wise, then his teaching is wisdom, and no other teaching is; those who follow him are wise, and no others are. Why, then, are we commonly regarded as foolish, empty, and witless because we follow a teacher whom even the gods themselves confess to be wise? For when Apollo says that he performed wonder-working deeds—the very reason he especially earned belief in his divinity—he now appears to agree with us, since he says the same things in which we glory. But he pulls [Col. 0485A] himself together [Col. 0485A]:

> **Note: [Col. 0485C] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 485–486]**
>
> **But he pulls himself together, etc.** Because, bewildered by frenzy, he had uttered contradictory things. Eusebius collects many oracles of this sort in the *Preparation for the Gospel*, as does Augustine in *The City of God*, Book XIX, chap. 23. It is certain that the whole vanity of the oracles collapsed at Christ’s birth. —BETULEIUS.
>
> **The truth had forced from him.** I restored this wording from all the manuscripts and from the three old Roman editions, as well as Betuleius and Cellarius. The other printed editions read “had extorted.”
>
> **The Jews.** For they said that Jesus cast out a demon by the power of a demon; see Matthew, chap. XII, Mark, chap. III, and Luke, chap. XI. The later Jews said the same, as may be seen in the *Life of Jeshua the Nazarene*, published by Huldricus in octavo, Leiden, 1705.
>

>

These words, which are absent from the others, are highly approved by Thomasius and Isaeus, for in this way the Jews’ malice is demonstrated more clearly, and the miracles are explained as having been of such a kind that they ought to have believed them.—**Those miracles which the Prophets had foretold to them would occur.** Since Thomasius added the words “which the Prophets had foretold to them would occur” from the ancient Bologna manuscript, and Isaeus confirmed them from the same, I rightly think that they should be restored. I am especially persuaded by the *Epitome* of our passage, chap. 45, where it clearly says: “When the Jews saw those things, they thought that they were being done by magical power, not knowing that all the things being done by him—the miracles—had been foretold by the prophets.” And again, chap. 46: “The Prophets … had foretold that all these things … would happen.”

>

For “shall come forth” is read above at the beginning of this chapter, as also at the end of Book VII, chap. 16. In the Vulgate at Matthew: “from you shall come forth a leader”; likewise in Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, chap. 13, quoting Micah.
>

>

>
> Sibyl, Discourse 6.
>
> **In the second book.** Namely, chap. 7, where some things refer in their literal sense to Solomon, but secondarily to Christ.
>
> **To construct.** Four recent Royal manuscripts, two Colbert, Betuleius, Bodley, Cotton, and two Clermont manuscripts read “to build.”
>

>

>
> **Built a temple for God and named the city … after himself.** Our author is mistaken, for Solomon neither founded this city nor named it after himself. Its founder was Melchizedek, as is gathered from Psalm LXXVI, 3, and Genesis XIV, 18, where he is called “king of Salem,” that is, “founder of Salem”; for founders of cities were once called kings of cities. Some think that Jerusalem or Hierosolyma is a Greek name, although it is plainly Hebrew. Eusebius thinks that it is a word compounded from the Greek *ἱερόν* (“temple”) and the Hebrew *Σολομών* (“Solomon”). Lactantius also appears inclined toward this view, since, as soon as he spoke [Col. 0487B] about the construction of the temple, he immediately added, “and the city,” etc. Others compound it from Jebus and Salem: since it was first called Salem and then Jebus, the name Jerusalem supposedly arose from this. But Solomon cannot be called its founder and builder, because it had been constructed many centuries before him, as is evident from the books of Joshua and Judges—unless we wish to interpret Lactantius in this manner: that Solomon embellished and greatly enlarged Jerusalem. In that case, this meaning could be tolerated. Secular writers generally used *Jerosolyma* in the plural, although the singular is also found. In part from GALLAEUS.—On the construction of the temple, see III Kings, chapters VI and IX, and II Chronicles, chapters III, VII, and VIII. See also, if you please, Josephus, Book VII of the *Antiquities*, chap. 3; likewise Book VII of *The Jewish War*, chap. 18; and Jerome, *On Hebrew Places*.

—but returns to demonic deceptions. For since he had spoken the truth under compulsion, he now appeared to be a betrayer of the gods and of himself, unless he concealed with a deceptive lie what the truth had forced from him. He therefore says that Christ did indeed perform marvelous works, but not by divine power; rather, by magic.

What wonder is it that Apollo persuaded those who were ignorant of the truth of this, when the Jews also—worshipers, as they seemed, of the supreme God—thought this same thing, although before their eyes every day [Col. 0485B] those miracles were being performed which the Prophets had foretold to them would occur? Yet even the sight of such great powers could not move them to believe that the one whom they saw was God.

For this reason David, whom they read especially beyond the other Prophets, condemns them as follows in Psalm XXVII: “Render to them their recompense, because they did not understand in the works of the Lord.”

Both David himself and the other Prophets announced that Christ would be born according to the flesh from David’s own house. In Isaiah (chap. XI) it is written as follows: “And on that day there shall be the root of Jesse, and one who shall arise to rule the nations; in him the nations shall hope, and his resting place shall be held in honor.” And in another place: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and [Col. 0485C] a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of God shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him.” [Col. 0486A]

Now Jesse was the father of David, from whose root the prophet foretold that a flower would rise—namely, the one of whom the Sibyl says, *ἀνθήσει δ᾽ ἄνθος καθαρόν*: “But a pure flower shall blossom.”

Likewise, in the second book of *Kingdoms* (*βασιλειῶν*), the prophet Nathan was sent to David when he wished to construct a temple for God; and the word of the Lord came to Nathan, saying (see II Kings, chap. 7): “Go and say to my servant David: Thus says the almighty Lord: You shall not build me a house to dwell in. But when your days have been fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I shall raise up your seed after you and establish his kingdom. He shall build me a house in my name; and I shall establish his throne [Col. 0486B] forever. I shall be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me; and his house and his kingdom shall obtain faithfulness forever.”

But the reason the Jews did not understand these things was that Solomon, the son of David, built a temple for God and named the city Hierosolyma after himself. Accordingly, they referred to Solomon what was spoken by the Prophet. Solomon, however, received the government of the kingdom from his own father. But the Prophets were speaking about the one who would be born after David had rested with his fathers.

Moreover, Solomon’s rule was not perpetual, for he reigned for forty years. Furthermore, he was never called the Son of God, but the son of David; and the house that he built did not [Col. 0486C] obtain faithfulness, as did the Church, which is the true [Col. 0487A] temple of God, which is not in walls but in the heart. [Col. 0487A]

In those times, as Eusebius indicates, the kings were expelled from the city of Rome, while Zerubbabel and Jesus, on returning, began to build the temple. This is that Jesus the priest, son of Jozedek. Whatever is shown to the Prophet concerning him in this vision is rightly applicable to Christ, the eternal high priest of Jerusalem. —BETULEIUS.

and by the faith of those who believe in him and are called faithful. But that temple of Solomon, because it was made by hand, fell by hand. Finally, his father prophesied in Psalm 126 concerning the works of his son in this manner: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who built it have labored in vain; unless the Lord guards the city, he who guarded it has watched in vain.”

## CHAPTER XIV. The Priesthood of Jesus as Foretold by the Prophets

From these things it is evident that all the prophets announced concerning Christ that the time would come when, born bodily from the line of David, he would establish for God an eternal temple, which is called the Church, and would summon all nations to [Col. 0487B] the true religion of God. This is the faithful house, this the immortal temple; and anyone who does not offer sacrifice in it will not possess the reward of immortality. Since Christ was the builder of this great and eternal temple, he must also possess an everlasting priesthood within it. Nor can anyone reach either the entrance of the temple or the sight of God except through him who established the temple.

David teaches precisely this in Psalm 109, saying: “Before the morning star I begot you. The Lord has sworn and will not repent: you are a priest forever [Col. 0488A] according to the order of Melchizedek.” Likewise, in the First Book of Kingdoms (chap. 2): “And I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who will do everything that is in my heart; and I will build him a faithful house, and he will pass before me all his days.”

Moreover, Zechariah, even giving the name, taught most explicitly who this future person was to be to whom God promised an eternal priesthood. For he spoke as follows:

> And the Lord God showed me Jesus, the great priest, standing before the face of the angel of the Lord; and the devil stood at his right hand to oppose him. And the Lord said to the devil: “May the Lord, who chose Jerusalem, command you; and behold, a brand cast out of the fire.” And Jesus was clothed in filthy garments and stood before the face of the angel. And he answered and said to those standing before his face: “Take the filthy garments [Col. 0488B] from him, clothe him in a robe reaching to the feet, and place a clean tiara upon his head.” And they covered him with a garment and placed a clean tiara upon his head. And the angel of the Lord stood and bore witness, saying to Jesus: “Thus says the Lord Almighty: If you walk in my ways and keep my commandments, you shall judge my house, and I will give you those who may dwell among these who stand here.” Hear, therefore, O Jesus, great priest.

Who, then, would not suppose that the Jews were at that time mentally captive [Col. 0489A] when, although they read and heard these things, they laid their impious hands [Col. 0489A]—

> **[Note: [Col. 0489C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 489–490]]**
>
> **Their impious hands.** The Caucasian manuscript and eight recent manuscripts, together with the editions of Tornesius and Soubrenius, read *criminal hands*.
>
> **Was crucified.** Francius proposed the correction *was fastened to the cross*. Thus the Latin writers, and Lactantius himself three times below in this same book, chap. 18.
>
> **Nearly five hundred years are counted.** Thus all the manuscripts and six printed editions. In nine common editions *nearly* is absent. This word is highly appropriate and must be retained, since precisely five hundred years are not counted. Eusebius, in his *Chronicle* under Olympiad 202, calculates five hundred and fifty-eight years. See the chronologists.
>
> **Of Darius and Alexander.** Of Darius, the fourth king of the Persians. This Alexander, however, is not the one called “the Great,” son of Philip, the twenty-third king of the Macedonians, whom Eusebius places under Olympiad 114, but Alexander X, king of the Macedonians, whom the same Eusebius dates under Olympiad 69. ISAeus.
>
> **Not long before, etc.** Thus I read from one Colbert and one Cotton manuscript, together with Betuleius and Sparkius. In seventeen others and in the printed editions the reading is *after*. Rather, it was approximately seven years *before* Tarquin the Proud was expelled. They place the overthrow of the kings in the final year of Olympiad 67. The temple, however, while Zechariah was still prophesying, was completed in Olympiad 66, according to Eusebius. BETULEIUS. Unless Lactantius—or a copyist—made a mistake by writing *after* in place of *before*.
>
> **Was scorched.** Thus I restored the text from nine Royal manuscripts, two Colbert manuscripts, the Gothic manuscript, one Sorbonne, one Brun, the Leipzig manuscript, and others, and from three old Roman editions, as well as those of Betuleius, Tornesius, Soubron, and Cellarius. Six recent manuscripts and nine printed editions have *was burned*. The verb *amburo* (“scorch”) is familiar to Lactantius in Book VII, chaps. 17 and 21.
>
> **Torments.** According to Walchius, this word is not particularly common, but it occurs rather frequently in our author, for example Book IV, chap. 30; Book V, chap. 2 and chap. 22; *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chap. 49. Arnobius, Book I, p. 26; indeed, also Cicero, *Philippic* IX, chap. 4. BUN.
>
> **For the common people call a brand, etc.** Apuleius likewise says in *Metamorphoses*, Book VII: “He ran to the hearth carrying a burning brand”; and Quintilian, Book X of the *Declamations*: “As though she were lying and fabricating everything, he killed her with extreme cruelty by thrusting a glowing brand between the middle of her thighs.”
>
> **He sent his Son as an envoy to mankind.** The oldest manuscripts—one Bononian and the Royal-Putean—as well as the editions of Thomasius, Isaeus, Thysius, Gallaeus, and Sparkius, have precisely this reading. Thirty-one manuscripts and ten printed editions, however, add after *his Son* the words *the chief of the angels*. Thomasius thinks these two words were added by some Arian. Unless by this expression Christ is signified as the first of the envoys or messengers, as Lactantius calls him below in chaps. 25 and 29 and in *On the Anger of God*, chap. 2; or as the head of the angels, according to the Apostle’s words in Colossians 2: “Who is the head of every principality and power.”
>
> **Nor did he ever call himself God.** Gallaeus accuses Lactantius of falsehood to no purpose on the ground that John 10 reads: “I and the Father are one.” For Lactantius’ meaning is that Christ nowhere said that he possessed a divinity distinct from the Father’s nature. What follows sufficiently proves this: for that would have been to conduct not the business of the one who sent him, but his own business, and to separate himself from the one whom he had come to reveal. SPARKIUS.
>
> **Whom he had come to reveal.** Thus I restored the text from seven Royal manuscripts, two Bononian, five Oxford, four Colbert, and thirteen others, as well as eight printed editions. Six manuscripts and twelve printed editions have *revealed*; either reading is sound. The Caucasian manuscript, one Royal, one Leipzig, and the Palatine read: *whom he had come to reveal* [literally, “for whose revealing he had come”].
>
> **Because for himself.** Heumann reads: *and because for himself*.

—against their God? Yet from the time of Zechariah to the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when Christ was crucified, nearly five hundred years are counted. For Zechariah flourished in the age of Darius and Alexander, who lived not long before Tarquin the Proud was expelled.

But they were again deceived and mistaken in the same way, thinking that these things were said about Jesus the son of Nun, who succeeded Moses, or about the priest Jesus the son of Josedec. Yet none of the things related by the prophet applies to them. For they were never clothed in filth, since one of them was a most powerful ruler and the other a priest; nor did they suffer any adversity such that they might be regarded as a brand cast out of the fire. Did they ever stand in the sight [Col. 0489B] of God and the angels? Or was the prophet speaking about the past rather than the future?

He was therefore speaking about Jesus, the Son of God, in order to show that he would come first in humility and in the flesh. For this is the filthy garment: that he might prepare a temple for God and be scorched by fire like a brand—that is, endure torments at the hands of men and finally be extinguished. For the common people call a half-burnt, extinguished torch drawn from the hearth a *titio*, or brand.

The Spirit of God also declared through the prophet how and with what commands he would be sent by God to the earth, teaching that, after he had faithfully and steadfastly fulfilled the will of the supreme Father, he would receive judicial authority and everlasting sovereignty. “If you walk in my ways,” he says, “and keep my commandments, you shall judge my house.”

What the ways [Col. 0489C] of God were, and what his commandments were, is neither doubtful nor obscure. [Col. 0490A] For when God saw that wickedness and the worship of false gods had grown so strong throughout the world that his name had now almost been erased from human memory—since even the Jews, to whom alone the mystery of God had been entrusted, had abandoned the living God, become entangled by the deceits of demons, and strayed into the worship of fabrications, and, although rebuked through the prophets, refused to return to God—he sent his Son as an envoy to mankind, so that he might turn them from impious and empty forms of worship to the knowledge and worship of the true God; and likewise that he might lead their minds from folly to wisdom, and from injustice to works of righteousness.

These are the ways of God in which he commanded him to walk. These are the commandments that he ordered him to keep. And he displayed faithfulness toward God. For he taught that there is one God and that he alone ought to be worshipped; nor did he ever [Col. 0490B] call himself God, because he would not have preserved his faithfulness if, having been sent to abolish the gods and assert the one God, he had introduced another besides the one. That would have been, not to make proclamation concerning the one God, nor to conduct the business of the one who sent him, but to conduct his own business and to separate himself from the one whom he had come to reveal.

Therefore, because he proved so faithful, because he assumed absolutely nothing for himself in order that he might fulfill the commands of the one who sent him, he received the dignity of perpetual priest, the honor of supreme king, the power of judge, and the name of God.

## CHAPTER XV. The Life and Miracles of Jesus, and Testimonies Concerning Them
