Since we have spoken about the second birth, by which he showed himself to mankind in the flesh, let us come to those [Col. 0490C] marvelous works which, although they were indications of heavenly power, [Col. 0491A] the Jews believed to be works of magic.

When he first began to approach maturity, [Col. 0491A]—

> **[Note: [Col. 0491C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 491–492]]**
>
> **When he first began to approach maturity.** Lactantius extends the meaning of this word more broadly, for he was “about thirty years old” (*hōsei etōn triakonta*, ὠσεὶ ἐτῶν τριάκοντα; Luke 3:23). Lucretius likewise used it in this sense in Book III, verse 450, and Virgil in *Aeneid* XII, verse 438, with reference to the greater maturity of advancing years.
>
> **Was immersed.** This is the meaning of the word *baptizesthai* (βαπτίζεσθαι); but “to baptize” is now a consecrated word among Christians. On this baptism of Jesus Christ, see Luke 3, Matthew 3, John 1, and Mark 1.
>
> **Might abolish.** The Bodleian manuscript reads *might wash away*. The sins, indeed, of the flesh—not his own, but those belonging to the human condition—“might abolish through washing.” The Merton manuscript reads “might wash away through washing.” Aptly indeed; yet the received reading is supported by Book III, chap. 26: “All wickedness will be abolished by a single washing”; and Book VI, chap. 24: “He abolished the stain of his former life.” BUN.
>
> **By the sprinkling of purifying dew.** Thus all the manuscripts. But the Aldine, Plantin, Fasitel, and Thysius editions read *of the purified*. It may consequently be concluded that in the primitive Church the practice prevailed that those being baptized were not only immersed in water but also sprinkled with water, as is practiced in these regions. GALLAEUS.
>
> **The Spirit of God, formed into the appearance of a white dove.** I do not know where Lactantius obtained the claim that the dove which descended upon Jesus at his baptism was white, unless from some ancient Christian tradition; for nowhere in the Gospel is its color indicated.—**A white dove.** Majus the younger, in his *Sacred Observations* on Luke 3:22, maintains that the Holy Spirit was not formed into an appearance, but descended like a dove in a gentle glide. BUN.
>
> **Not by magical illusions, which display nothing true or substantial.** The Gentiles maliciously alleged that Christ was a magician. Augustine, *Sermon XI on Matthew*: “The pagans say that the Lord Christ performed miracles through magical arts.” Augustine refutes them in *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, and Eusebius in *Demonstration*, Book III, chaps. 3 and 8. Lactantius rightly said that magical illusions display nothing true or substantial. Hence Minucius elegantly writes: “Whatever miracle magicians make sport of, they perform through demons; with the demons inspiring them and pouring their power into them, they produce illusions, either making things that do not exist appear to exist, or things that do exist appear not to exist.” ELMENHORST.
>
> **Which long before, etc.** One Colbert manuscript and the Cratander edition read *which also long before*; three Royal manuscripts, three Colbert, four others, and four printed editions read *which even before that*.
>
> **Prodigious.** On these, see above, chap. 13; Matthew 4, 9, and 14 [correcting an obvious OCR corruption]; Mark 1, 2, and 10; Luke 5, 7, and 11.
>
> **Wherever he made a journey.** The second Leipzig manuscript has *whithersoever*, incorrectly. He imitates Cicero, *Against Verres* I.16: “Wherever he made a journey”; *On the Nature of the Gods* II.33: “Wherever we go, wherever we move.” Add the note on Lactantius, Book VI, chap. 18. Again in Book V, chap. 17: “Wherever he makes a journey.” BUN.
>
> **The sick and disabled.** The sick are those affected by disease; the disabled are those deprived of the use of some part of their limbs. Thus shortly afterward our Lactantius speaks of restoring wholeness to the disabled.
>
> **Disabled in all their limbs.** Arnobius, chap. 1: “They used to report that those disabled in their limbs rose up and even carried their own beds, though shortly before they had been borne upon the shoulders of others.” BUN.
>
> **Sprinkled with spots.** Five recent manuscripts read *rough*; one very ancient Royal manuscript and Junius read *with spots sprinkled upon them*; the Cambridge manuscript and seven recent editions read *and scattered with spots*.
>
> **Or any remedy.** Except for the blind man whom he healed with clay in John 9.
>
> **Πάντα λόγῳ.** In Latin translation:
>
> > Accomplishing all things by a word, and curing every disease.
>
> **And let the feeble knees be strengthened.** Thus I read with one very ancient Royal manuscript, and the sense demands it. One Colbert manuscript has: “and let the feeble knees be fortified.” “Be comforted, you who are….” The Hebrew, Chaldean, and Vulgate have *strengthen*; the Syriac, *be strengthened*; the Septuagint and almost all the manuscripts, *be comforted*, so that it is connected, less appropriately, with what follows. See the preceding and following words.
>
> **Νεκρῶν δὲ.** The Sibylline poems, Discourse 8, in Latin:
>
> > But there will be a resurrection of the dead,  
> > And the lame will run swiftly, and the deaf will hear;  
> > [Col. 0493C] The blind will see, and the mute will speak.

—he was immersed by John the prophet in the river Jordan, so that through a spiritual washing he might abolish, not his own sins—which of course he did not have—but those of the flesh which he bore; so that, just as he saved the Jews by undertaking circumcision, he might likewise save the nations by baptism, that is, by the sprinkling of purifying dew. Then a voice was heard from heaven: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2). This voice is found foretold in David. And the Spirit of God descended upon him, formed into the appearance of a white dove.

From that time he began to perform the greatest mighty works, not by magical illusions, which display nothing true or substantial, but by heavenly force and power, which had long before been proclaimed by the prophets. These works are so numerous that one book would not be enough to include them all. I shall therefore enumerate [Col. 0491B] them briefly and by general categories, without specifying persons or places, so that I may reach the explanation of his passion and cross, toward which my discourse has long been hastening.

His mighty works were those which Apollo called prodigious: wherever he made a journey, by a single word and in a single instant he restored to health the sick, the disabled, and those suffering from every kind of disease. Those who were disabled in all their limbs were suddenly strengthened when their powers were restored, and themselves carried back the little beds on which they had shortly before been carried. To the lame and those afflicted by defects of the feet he granted the ability not only to walk but even to run. Then he restored the eyes [Col. 0492A] of those whose blind vision had been buried in the deepest darkness to their former sight. He also loosened the tongues of the mute for speech and discourse. Likewise, by opening the ears of the deaf, he introduced hearing into them. He cleansed those who were polluted and sprinkled with spots. And he did all these things not with his hands or with any remedy, but by his word and command, just as the Sibyl also foretold (Discourse 8, after the middle):

> Accomplishing all things by a word, and curing every disease  
> (*Panta logō prattōn, pasan te noson therapeuōn*; Πάντα λόγῳ πράττων, πᾶσάν τε νόσον θεραπεύων).

And it is certainly no wonder that he performed wonders by his word, since he himself was the Word of God, sustained by heavenly force and power. . . . Nor was it enough that he restored strength to the weak, wholeness to the disabled, and health to the sick and languishing, unless he also raised the dead (Matt. 12; Mark 3; Luke 7 and 11; John 2), released as though from sleep and recalled to life.

[Col. 0492B] When the Jews of that time saw these things, they charged that they were being performed by demonic power, although their secret writings contained everything that was to happen just as it did happen. For they read, among the words of the other prophets, those of Isaiah, who said (chap. 25):

> Be strengthened, you loosened hands, and let the feeble knees be strengthened. You who are fainthearted, do not fear; do not be afraid. Our Lord will render judgment; he himself will come and save us. Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will hear. Then the lame man will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute will become fluent, because water has broken forth in the desert, and a stream in a thirsty land.

But the same Sibyl also sang in these verses:

> . . . There will be a resurrection of the dead, [Col. 0493A]  
> And the lame will run swiftly, [Col. 0493A]—

> **[Note: [Col. 0493C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 493–494]]**
>
> **Καὶ χωλῶν δρόμος ἔστ’ ὠκύς** (“And the lame will run swiftly”). An old parchment reads: **καὶ χωλῶν δρόμος ὠκύτατος** (“and the course of the lame will be swiftest”). OPSOPOEUS.
>
> **Had remained.** Thus I restored the text from very many manuscripts, more appropriately than *was remaining*, which occurs in eight manuscripts and the common editions. See Matthew 15 and Mark 8.
>
> **How much food they were carrying with them.** Francius thought the text should read *how much food they had with them*. See Matthew 14; Mark 6; Luke 9; and John 6.
>
> **Divided into groups of fifty.** In the older Bononian manuscript, two Colbert manuscripts, and certain editions, *divided* is absent.
>
> **And when he had ordered the disciples to set it before the people.** Thus I restored the text from two very ancient Royal manuscripts, five other Royal manuscripts, four Colbert, the Emmeram, one Clermont, the Brun manuscript, and two old Roman editions. Many others have *to be set before them*.
>
> **Twelve baskets.** The *cophinus* was a kind of measure for measuring dry and liquid substances, for which reason the Jews were especially well known for it. Hence Juvenal says:
>
> > The sanctuaries are let  
> > To Jews, whose furnishings are a basket and hay.
>
> **Εἰν ἄρτοις, etc.** The Sibylline codex reads: **ἐκ δ’ ἄρτων ἅμα πέντε, καὶ ἰχθύος εἰναλίοιο** (“and from five loaves together and a fish of the sea”). OPSOPOEUS. The Sibyl’s former verse should be corrected from Lactantius, four Royal manuscripts, and one Colbert manuscript. **Ἐξ ἄρτων** is erroneous because of the following **ἰχθύεσσι**. One Clermont manuscript and two old Roman editions have **Ἐν ἄρτοις**. In Latin:
>
> > With five loaves together and two fishes,  
> > He will satisfy five thousand men in the desert;  
> > And, taking all the remnants after the fragments,  
> > He will fill twelve baskets for the hope of many.
>
> **For nothing else.** From very many manuscripts and printed editions I have added the preposition *for*, which is missing in nine manuscripts and seven editions.
>
> **To delude.** That is, to deceive, to mislead. Thus *circumscriptio* also means fraud and deception in Cicero, *For Cluentius* 46 and *On Duties* III.61.
>
> **At evening.** Thus I restored the text from the very ancient Royal-Putean manuscript, two Bononian, two Colbert, two Clermont, and twelve printed editions. *In the evening* occurs in seven other manuscripts and in the editions of Gallaeus and Sparkius. One Colbert manuscript has *breeze*.
>
> [Col. 0494C] **On solid ground.** That is, on solid earth. Virgil, *Georgics* II.231:
>
> > And you will order a well to be sunk deep  
> > In solid ground. BUN.
>
> **Orion.** Theon of Alexandria tells the story in his work on Aratus’ *Phenomena*.
>
> **Awakened from sleep.** We added the preposition from the manuscripts and from three old Roman editions, as well as those of Cratander, Cellarius, and Walchius. Two Colbert and Clermont manuscripts have the redundant *from from sleep*. The preposition is absent in nine printed editions.
>
> **At his word.** Lactantius himself again says in Book VII, chap. 17: “These things will happen at his word.” Lucretius likewise says in Book IV, verse 786:
>
> > Nature creates and prepares all things at the word.
>
> Creechius interprets this as “at his command.” I interpret Lactantius’ *at his word* as “while he was still speaking and commanding.” BUNEMANN.
>
> **Τοὺς ἀνέμους.** In Latin:
>
> > He will restrain the winds by a word and lay the sea flat,  
> > Treading the raging sea with the feet of peace and faith.
>
> **Κύματα.** Sibylline Book VI, Discourse 6. In Latin:
>
> > He will walk upon the waves and release mankind from infirmity;  
> > He will raise [Col. 0494D] the dead and drive away many pains,  
> > And from the bread of a single pouch there will be a filling of men.
>
> [Col. 0494D] **He will raise the dead.** One very ancient Royal manuscript and the Brun manuscript have *he will cause the dead to rise*.
>
> **Στήσει.** Thus I corrected the text from the oldest Royal manuscripts, the Putean, the Caucasian, one Colbert, one Brun, and the Basel edition of 1569. Four recent Royal manuscripts, one Sorbonne, one Clermont, and eight printed editions have **Ζήσει**; two other Royal manuscripts and one Colbert have **Ζεύσει**. I would prefer **Ζώσει**. The Greek is absent from most manuscripts.
>
> **Ἄλγεα πολλά.** Thus I restored the text from one very ancient Royal manuscript, another Royal, one Colbert, and the Brun manuscript, with the support also of the very ancient Royal-Putean manuscript, which corruptly has **τολλα** for **πολλά**. Six manuscripts have **πολλοῖς**.
>
> **Πήρης.** Thus I restored the text from the two oldest Royal manuscripts, with the support of the Latin translation *perionis*, found in four Colbert manuscripts and the Brun manuscript; in its place perhaps *peridionis* should be read, a Greek word meaning a sack, concerning which it was stated above that they said they had five loaves and two fish in a pouch. Therefore I think the Greek text should read **πήρης**, not **πηγῆς**, as in eight recent manuscripts. The alteration from **πήρης** to **πηγῆς** would have been easy.

> —and the deaf will hear;  
> The blind will see, and those who did not speak will speak.

Because of these mighty works and divine deeds, a great multitude followed him, consisting either of disabled or sick persons or of those who wished to present their relatives to be healed. He ascended a certain deserted mountain to worship there. When he had remained there for three days and the people were suffering from hunger, he called his disciples and asked how much food they were carrying with them. They replied that they had five loaves and two fish in a pouch.

He ordered these to be brought and the multitude to recline after being divided into groups of fifty. When the disciples had done this, he himself broke the bread into small pieces and divided the flesh of the fish, and both increased in his hands. When he had ordered the disciples to set it before the people, five thousand people were satisfied, and in addition twelve baskets were filled [Col. 0493B] from the remaining fragments.

What more marvelous thing can either be said or done? Yet the Sibyl had long ago sung that this would happen, and her verses are transmitted as follows:

> With five loaves together and two fishes,  
> He will satisfy five thousand men in the desert;  
> And, taking all the remnants after the fragments,  
> He will fill twelve baskets for the hope of many.  
> (*Ein artois hama pente, kai ichthyesi doioisin,  
> Andrōn chiliadas en erēmō pente koresei,  
> Kai ta perisseuonta labōn meta klasmata panta,  
> Dōdeka plērōsei kophinous eis elpida pollōn*;  
> Εἰν ἄρτοις ἅμα πέντε, καὶ ἰχθύεσσι δοιοῖσιν,  
> Ἀνδρῶν χιλιάδας ἐν ἐρήμῳ πέντε κορέσσει,  
> Καὶ τὰ περισσεύοντα λαβὼν μετὰ κλάσματα πάντα,  
> Δώδεκα πληρώσει κοφίνους εἰς ἐλπίδα πολλῶν.)

I therefore ask what magical art could have contrived here, when its skill avails for nothing except deluding the eyes.

Likewise, when he was about to withdraw to a mountain to pray, as was his custom, he commanded his disciples to take a little boat [Col. 0494A] and go ahead of him. But when they had departed, with evening already pressing on, they began to struggle against a contrary wind. When they were already in the middle of the sea, he entered the sea on foot and caught up with them, walking as though on solid ground. This was not like the poets’ false tale about Orion walking in the sea, who, with part of his body submerged,

> Towers with his shoulder above the waves.

And again, when he had fallen asleep in the boat and the wind had begun to rage to the point of extreme danger, he was awakened from sleep and immediately ordered the wind to be silent. The waves, which had been surging with enormous force, grew calm, and immediately, at his word, tranquility followed.

Perhaps the sacred Scriptures are lying (Luke 8; Mark 4; Matt. 8) when they teach that he possessed such power that by his command he compelled the winds to obey, the seas [Col. 0494B] to serve, diseases to retreat, and the lower regions to submit. But what of the fact that the Sibyls taught these same things beforehand in their poems? One of them, whom we mentioned above, says:

> He will restrain the winds by a word and lay the sea flat,  
> Treading the raging sea with the feet of peace and faith.  
> (*Tous anemous pausei te logō, strōsei de thalassan  
> Mainomenēn, posin eirēnēs pistei te patēsas*;  
> Τοὺς ἀνέμους παύσει τε λόγῳ, στρώσει δὲ θάλασσαν  
> Μαινομένην, ποσὶν εἰρήνης πίστει τε πατήσας.)

And again another, who says:

> He will walk upon the waves and release mankind from disease;  
> He will raise the dead and drive away many pains,  
> And from the bread of a single pouch there will be a filling of men.  
> (*Kymata pezeusei, noson anthrōpōn apolysei,  
> Stēsei tethneōtas, apōsetai algea polla,  
> Ek de mias pērēs artou koros essetai andrōn*;  
> Κύματα πεζεύσει, νόσον ἀνθρώπων ἀπολύσει,  
> Στήσει τεθνηῶτας, ἀπώσεται ἄλγεα πολλά,  
> Ἐκ δὲ μιᾶς πήρης ἄρτου κόρος ἔσσεται ἀνδρῶν.)

[Col. 0495A] Refuted by these testimonies, some are accustomed to take refuge in the claim that these are not Sibylline poems but fabrications [Col. 0495A]—

> **[Note: [Col. 0495C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 495–496]]**
>
> **Fabrications.** Thus the text was restored from seven old editions and all the manuscripts except one recent Royal manuscript, which has *fabricated*. In one recent Royal manuscript and the Brun manuscript the words *and composed* are absent. On how much trust should be placed in the Sibyls, see above, col. 000.
>
> **Cicero.** Book II of *On the Nature of the Gods*. And Varro, concerning whom see chap. 6 of the First Book above and chap. 22 of *On the Anger of God*.
>
> **Φήσουσι.** This occurs in Discourse 3 and is thus translated into Latin: [Col. 0495D]
>
> > They will call the Sibyl  
> > Insane and deceitful. But when all these things have happened,  
> > Then you will remember me, and no one will any longer  
> > Call me insane, but a prophetess of the great God.
>
> **Ψευστείραν.** Thus I corrected the text from two very ancient Royal manuscript codices, with support from another Royal manuscript, which has **Ψεστείραν**. Six recent manuscripts and nine editions have **Ψεύστριαν**, incorrectly and contrary to the requirements of meter; likewise one Royal manuscript and the Roman edition of 1470, which have **Ψειύστριαν**.
>
> **Προφῆτιν.** Five very old Royal manuscripts have **προφῆτιν**; three others, like the editions, have the masculine **προφήτην**, incorrectly.
>
> **Lay hidden.** Thus I restored the text from two very ancient Royal manuscripts, two other good Royal manuscripts, four Colbert, one Leipzig, the Emmeram, Cambridge, and Brun manuscripts, and the Roman edition of 1468. *Jacuerunt* means “they lay hidden.” The verb is used in this sense by Cicero and Plautus. More recent copyists incorrectly substituted *latuerunt* (“were concealed”).
>
> **But they were recognized afterward, when.** That is: they were recognized when Christ’s birth and passion afterward disclosed the mysteries. Thus *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chap. 5: “But afterward when . . . he ended.” See the note above. BUNEMANN.
>
> **Or more.** This is the reading of the Royal-Putean manuscript, two Bononian, four Colbert, the Emmeram, Cambridge, and other manuscripts, three old Roman editions, and three others. Seven recent manuscripts and as many printed editions have *and more*.
>
> **Which is cast at us as though a reproach, etc.** The pagans cast it at Christians as a reproach that they worshipped a man who had been crucified and had died a slave’s death. Augustine, *Sermon 1 on the Conversion of St. Paul*: “Let us not be ashamed of the name of Christ. Let us be insulted because we believe in one crucified and killed.” The same author, *Sermon 8 on the Words of the Apostle*: “The wise of this world insult us on account of Christ’s cross and say: ‘What sort of heart do you have, you who worship a crucified God?’” ELMENHORST.
>
> **Divinity.** Thus I restored the text from the editions of Isaeus and Cellarius and from all the manuscripts except one recent Royal and one Colbert, in which *dignity* is corruptly read in place of *divinity*, as well as two recent Royal manuscripts and thirteen common editions, which have *religion*.—**Devoid of true divinity.** Book V, chap. 10: “The more religiously they serve these earthly images, the more criminal they prove themselves against the name of true divinity.” BUNEMANN.
>
> **Not only look up to.** Thus I corrected the text from a Royal manuscript only four hundred years old but of excellent quality, and from two old Roman editions of 1470 and 1474. Betuleius, Rivetus, Meursius, Gallaeus, Sparkius, and Cellarius likewise prefer this reading to the *take up* found in the others. The same correction occurs above in Book II, chap. 2, near the middle. *Suspiciunt* means “admire.”
>
> **The leaders.** Our author reproduced Cyprian, *The Vanity of Idols*: “Their teachers and leaders . . . handed this man over”; and Cyprian reproduced Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 21: “The leaders of the Jews,” and so forth. BUNEMANN.

—and compositions made by our people. Certainly no one who has read Cicero and Varro, and the other ancient authors who mention the Erythraean Sibyl and the others, will think so. It is from the Sibyls’ books that we produce these examples; and those authors died before Christ was born according to the flesh.

I do not doubt, however, that in earlier times these poems were regarded as ravings, since no one then understood them. For they announced certain monstrous wonders, without indicating their rationale, time, or author. Finally, the Erythraean Sibyl says that she would be called insane and deceitful:

> . . . They will call the Sibyl [Col. 0495B]  
> Insane and deceitful. But when all these things have happened,  
> Then you will remember me, and no one will any longer  
> Call me insane, but a prophetess of the great God.  
> (*Phēsousi Sibyllēn  
> Mainomenēn pseusteiran; epan de genētai hapanta,  
> Tēnika mou mnēmēn poiēsete, k’ ouk eti m’ oudeis  
> Mainomenēn phēsei me theou megaloio prophētin*;  
> Φήσουσι Σίβυλλην  
> Μαινομένην ψευστείραν· ἐπὰν δὲ γένηται ἅπαντα,  
> Τηνίκα μου μνήμην ποιήσετε, κ’ οὐκ ἔτι μ’ οὐδεὶς  
> Μαινομένην φήσει με θεοῦ μεγάλοιο προφῆτιν.)

They therefore lay hidden for many centuries; but they were recognized afterward, when Christ’s birth and passion disclosed the mysteries. The same is true of the words of the prophets: although they had been read by the Jewish people for fifteen hundred years or more, they were nevertheless not understood until Christ interpreted them both by his word and by his works. For the prophets announced him, and the things of which they spoke could in no way be understood unless they had all been fulfilled.

## CHAPTER XVI. The Passion of Jesus Christ, and That It Was Foretold

I now come to the passion itself, which is commonly cast [Col. 0495C] at us as though a reproach: that we worship both a man and one who was subjected by men to an extraordinary punishment and tortured [Col. 0496A]. I shall show that this very passion was undertaken by him according to a great and divine rationale, and that in it alone are contained virtue, truth, and wisdom.

For if he had been most blessed upon earth and had reigned throughout his entire life in the greatest prosperity, no wise person would have believed him to be God or judged him worthy of divine honor. This is what those devoid of true divinity do: they not only look up to perishable riches, fragile power, and benefits bestowed by another, but even consecrate them; and knowingly enslave themselves to the memory of the dead, worshipping a fortune already extinguished—although the wise have never thought that even a living and present fortune ought to be worshipped by them.

Nothing among earthly things can be venerable or worthy of heaven. Virtue alone, justice alone, [Col. 0496B] can be judged a true, heavenly, and everlasting good, because it is neither given to anyone nor taken away. Since Christ came to earth furnished with this virtue and justice—indeed, since he himself is virtue and he himself is justice—he descended to teach it and to form the human being. Having discharged this office of teacher and embassy from God, he both deserved and was able to be believed God by all nations, on account of that very virtue which he both taught and practiced.

Therefore, when a great multitude repeatedly gathered around him, either because of the justice that he taught or because of the miracles that he performed, heard his commandments, and believed that he had been sent by God and was the Son of God, then the leaders and priests of the Jews were goaded by anger because he rebuked them as sinners, corrupted by envy because they saw themselves being despised and abandoned as the multitude gathered around him, and—what was the crown of their crimes—blinded by folly and error, and forgetful [Col. 0496C] of the heavenly commandments and the prophets. They united against him and formed an impious [Col. 0497A] plan to destroy and torture him [Col. 0497A]—

> **[Note: [Col. 0497C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 497–498]]**
>
> **To torture.** Compare chap. 18; chap. 22; *Epitome*, chaps. 46 and 48. Lipsius illustrates the term in *On the Cross*, Book I, chap. 3, and Columbus in his note on *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chap. 2. BUNEMANN.
>
> **And Solomon in the Book of Wisdom.** Jerome is more sensible in his preface to the Proverbs of Solomon—which is Epistle 115. He says: “The pseudepigraphal book entitled *The Wisdom of Solomon* is nowhere found among the Hebrews; its very style has the flavor of Greek eloquence, and some ancient writers affirm that it is the work of Philo the Jew.” BUN.
>
> [Col. 0497D] **Unpleasant.** Lactantius frequently uses this word: Book V, chap. 1; *Epitome*, chaps. 45 and 64; *On the Anger of God*, chap. 20.
>
> **As though from impurities.** Lactantius does not avoid this word. Book IV, chap. 17: “from impurities.” Lipsius, in his note on Seneca, *On Anger* III.34, preferred *impurities* on the authority of an ancient book. BUN.
>
> **And boasts that God is his Father.** Earlier editors had printed: “and boasts that he has God as his Father.” But the very ancient Turin codex, chap. 45, reads: “And boasts that the Lord is his Father” (read *God*). Accordingly, I print it as I do. BUN.
>
> **One thousand and ten years.** This agrees sufficiently well with the chronology of sacred history. For Solomon died in the year 980 before the common era. Christ, according to the ancient teachers of the Church, was fastened to the cross during the consulship of the two Gemini, that is, in the year 29 of the Christian era. If you add this number to 980, you obtain 1,009 years.
>
> **We add nothing.** The Emmeram and Brun manuscripts read: *We ourselves add nothing*.
>
> **Jesus.** Thus very many of the most ancient manuscripts and all printed editions. Seven recent manuscripts have *him*.
>
> **Peaceful.** Absent from seven recent manuscripts.
>
> **Unremarkable.** Here the word does not mean unclean, nor miserly as opposed to frugal, as in chap. 1 and Book VI, chap. 14, but obscure, despised, and undistinguished. This is clear from the cited saying of Isaiah, no. 15, and Lactantius, Book VI, chap. 14. BUN.
>
> **In the humility of the flesh.** Compare Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 21: “In the humility of the human condition”; Lactantius, Book IV, chap. 14; compare chap. 22: “Why did he make himself so humble and weak?”; chap. 26: “He had come in humility to bring aid to the humble and lowly,” etc. Compare Book II, chaps. 1–4; Book V, chap. 14: “From the humble to the powerful.” BUN.
>
> [Col. 0498D] **We proclaimed, etc.** The Hebrew reads: “and he came up like a shoot before him.” The Septuagint and Augustine read: “We shall proclaim before him, like an infant.” Why say more? In human judgment it is *paradoxon* (παράδοξον), paradoxical, to seek supreme power in humility. The carnal wisdom of the Jews was not discerning enough to understand what Zechariah had foretold: “Your king comes to you in meekness.” BETULEIUS.
>
> **He suffers for us.** I restore the true reading from the third Leipzig, Gothic, Reimmann, Rostock, and Venice 1471 manuscripts, and both the 1478, 1493, and 1497 editions, as well as the Paris editions of Tornesius of 1587 and 1613. It agrees with the Hebrew and the Septuagint, and also with Cyprian, Book II *Against the Jews*, chap. 13. The more recent Paris, Aldine, Gryphius, Thomasius, and subsequent editions had unnecessarily printed *he suffers here for us*. BUN.
>
> **Οἰκτρὸς, etc.** Sibylline Discourse 8. In Latin:
>
> > Pitiable, dishonored, without beauty, he will offer hope to the pitiable.
>
> **Ἐλπίδα δώσει.** Thus the Royal-Putean manuscript, five other Royal manuscripts, one Clermont, and two Colbert manuscripts. The Greek is absent from the others. The distinguished Puteanus’ parchment is incorrectly cited as reading **δώσῃ**, not **δώσει**; nevertheless, some manuscript must have contained that wording, since one Brun manuscript translates it: “so that he may offer hope to the pitiable.”

—a plan which the prophets had described long before.

For David too, at the beginning of his Psalms (Ps. 1), foreseeing in the spirit how great a crime they were going to commit, declares blessed the man who has not gone away into the counsel of the ungodly. And Solomon, in the Book of Wisdom (chap. 2), used these words:

> Let us lie in wait for the righteous man, because he is displeasing to us and reproaches us with sins against the law. He professes to have knowledge of God and calls himself the Son of God. He has become a reproof of our thoughts. He is grievous to us even to behold, because his life is unlike that of others, and his ways have been changed. We are regarded by him as triflers. He keeps himself from our ways as from impurities, prefers the final lot of the righteous, and boasts that he has God as his Father. Let us see, [Col. 0497B] therefore, whether his words are true, and let us test what will happen to him. Let us examine him with insults and torments, so that we may know his reverence and test his patience. Let us condemn him to the most shameful death. These things they devised, and they went astray. For their own folly blinded them, and they did not know the mysteries of God.

Did he not describe that impious conspiracy undertaken by the ungodly against God so precisely that he seems plainly to have been present? Yet from Solomon, who uttered these words, to the time when the event took place there were one thousand and ten years. We fabricate nothing; we add nothing. Those who committed these deeds possessed these words; those against whom these things were spoken read them. Even now, moreover, the heirs of their name and crime possess them and, in their daily readings, proclaim in the words of the prophets the condemnation foretold against themselves; yet they never admit them into [Col. 0497C] their hearts—which itself is part of their condemnation. The Jews, therefore, having often been rebuked by Christ, who reproached [Col. 0498A] them for their sins and injustices, and having been almost deserted by the people, were incited to kill him.

His humility gave them the boldness to do this. For although they read with how great power and glory the Son of God was to come from heaven, they saw Jesus as humble, quiet, mean in appearance, and without beauty, and therefore did not believe that he was the Son of God. They did not understand that two advents of his had been foretold by the prophets: the first obscure, in the humility of the flesh; the second manifest, in the might of majesty. Of the first, David says in Psalm 71:

> He will descend like rain upon a fleece, and in his days righteousness will arise, and an abundance of peace, until the moon is exalted.

For just as rain, if it descends upon a fleece, cannot be perceived because it makes no sound, so he said that Christ would come to earth without anyone’s suspicion [Col. 0498B], to teach righteousness and peace. Isaiah likewise handed down the following (chap. 53):

> Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? We proclaimed before him like children, and like a root in thirsty ground. He has neither form nor splendor; and we saw him, and he had neither form nor beauty. But his appearance was without honor, and deficient beyond the rest of mankind. He is a man placed under affliction, knowing how to bear weakness, because he was turned away from and was not esteemed. He bears our sins and suffers for us; and we thought him to be in pain, under affliction, and in distress. But he was wounded because of our crimes and weakened because of our sins. The discipline of our peace was upon him; by his bruising we have been healed. We have all gone astray like sheep, and God delivered him [Col. 0498C] up for our sins.

And the Sibyl spoke in the same manner:

> Οἰκτρὸς, ἄτιμος, ἄμορφος, ἐν οἰκτροῖς ἐλπίδα δώσει.
>
> Pitiful, dishonored, without beauty, he will give hope among the pitiable.

[Col. 0499A] Because of this humility, they did not recognize their God and entered into a detestable conspiracy to deprive of life him who had come to give them life.

## CHAPTER XVII  
### On the religious observances of the Jews and their hatred of Jesus

But for their anger and envy, which they kept shut up within their hearts, they put forward other reasons: [Col. 0499A]

> **[Col. 0499C] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 499–500]**
>
> **For their envy … they put forward.** Manuscripts 1 Royal and Cauc. and three recent editions read: “their malice being shut up within, they put forward reasons.”
>
> **Annulled.** See Matt., chap. 12; Mark, chap. 3; Luke, chap. 6; and John, chap. 9.
>
> **Working for salvation.** Thus the Turin manuscript, *Epitome* 47: “That they might … work for the salvation of mankind.” And Cyprian, *On Almsgiving*, at the beginning: “Many and great are the divine … benefits by which, for our salvation, the … mercy of God has both worked and continues always to work.” Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 33: “I work more effectively for his salvation.” BUN.
>
> **Of swine’s flesh.** This is not found in the Gospel history.
>
> **Had withdrawn to Christ.** Ancient Bologna manuscript 1 reads “had approached.” [Col. 0499D] Eight manuscripts and four editions read “had withdrawn from Christ.” But “had withdrawn to Christ” is here a “pregnant” verb, as they call it, which also includes another action: in the sense that the portion had not yet withdrawn and betaken itself to Christ. For example, Velleius Paterculus, book I, 18.1: “So completely were the bodies of that people separated into other states”; that is, they were separated and distributed among other states. This mode of expression is especially frequent in the sacred Hebrew text.
>
> **And will choose powerful nations.** The verb “will choose” is missing from the Royal-Puteanus manuscript. Other manuscripts have “will love,” “will bind,” “will reduce,” or “will direct.” Almost all editions, together with several manuscripts, have “will choose,” which Lactantius appears to have read in a corrupt Greek biblical manuscript in which ἐκλέξει, “will choose,” had been written instead of ἐξελέγξει, “will convict” or “will rebuke.” Perhaps “will refute and reduce powerful nations” is not a bad reading, as found in recent Royal manuscript 1, the editions of de Tournes, and Claromontanus manuscript 1. Much is missing here from the oldest Royal manuscript, and the Greek is absent from many manuscripts.
>
> [Col. 0500C] **Will choose.** The Vulgate has “will rebuke.”
>
> **On Mount Horeb.** “In the desert of Arabia.” Thus, following the Greek text, I have restored the passage from the Royal-Puteanus manuscript, six other Royal manuscripts, five Colbert manuscripts, the Cauc. manuscript, and very many others. Recent Royal manuscript 2, Colbert manuscript 1, and eleven editions read “Oreb.” Horeb, however, is Sinai. The rock was therefore in the wilderness of Sinai, though nearer to Rephidim than to Mount Sinai. MENOCHIUS.—That entire mountainous region, in which Sinai also stood, was called Horeb. JUNIUS.—The western part was Horeb, the eastern Sinai.
>
> **Ἀλλ᾽ ὅτε, etc.** In Latin:
>
> > But when all the things I have spoken of have been fulfilled,  
> > Then the whole law will be annulled in him.
>
> *Sibylline Oracles*, book 8.
>
> **Εἰς αὐτὸν, etc.** I have thus emended the text from the Royal-Puteanus manuscript, one other Royal manuscript of the highest quality, and Betuleius:
>
> > Εἰς αὐτὸν τότε πᾶς λύεται νόμος.
> >
> > Then the whole law is annulled in him.
>
> [Col. 0500D] And rightly so, because of the metrical rule. The other texts read λύσεται, “will be annulled,” and omit τότε, “then.”
>
> **A greatest prophet would be sent by God.** I have restored this from the two old Roman editions and five others, as well as from all the manuscripts except two Royal manuscripts, which, together with eight editions, read “may be sent by God.”
>
> **In Deuteronomy.** This is cited by St. Stephen in Acts of the Apostles, chap. 7.
>
> **Given through a mortal.** This reading, found in the oldest Royal manuscript, many others, and twelve editions, is the best and genuine reading; for, by the relation between cognate terms, it corresponds to “eternal,” which follows. Thirteen manuscripts and three printed editions read “through Moses.” Who would have changed the very familiar name “Moses” into “a mortal”?
>
> **Isaiah prophesied thus.** Lactantius is mistaken, for the words are Jeremiah’s, chap. 4, verses 3–4.
>
> **Circumcise a second time.** That is: renew the circumcision long omitted in the wilderness, which God commanded to be restored after its interruption.

They alleged that he annulled the law of God given through Moses—that is, that he did not refrain from activity on the Sabbaths, but worked for the salvation of mankind; that he rendered circumcision void; and that he abolished abstinence from swine’s flesh. The rites of the Jewish religion consist in these things. For these reasons, therefore, the remainder of the people, which had not yet withdrawn to Christ, was incited by the priests to judge [Col. 0499B] him impious because he annulled the law of God, although he did this not by his own judgment but according to God’s will and the prophets’ predictions.

For Micah (chap. 4, v. 2) announced that he would give a new law, in this manner:

> The law will go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem; and he will judge among many peoples, and will refute and choose powerful nations.

For that earlier law, which was given through Moses, was given not on Mount Zion but on Mount Horeb. The Sibyl showed that it would be annulled by the Son of God:

> Ἀλλ᾽ ὅτε ταῦτ᾽ ἂν ἅπαντα τελειωθῇ ἅπερ εἶπον,  
> Εἰς αὐτὸν τότε πᾶς λύεται νόμος.
>
> But when all the things I have spoken of have been fulfilled,  
> Then the whole law is annulled in him.

Moses himself also—through whom they had received the law, yet while they stubbornly defend it they have [Col. 0500A] fallen away from God and failed to recognize God—had foretold that a greatest prophet would be sent by God, one who would be above the law and would convey the will of God to mankind. In Deuteronomy he left it written as follows:

> And the Lord said to me: “I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brothers, like you, and I will put my word into his mouth; and he will speak to them whatever I command him. And whoever does not hear the things which that prophet speaks in my name, I will exact vengeance upon him.”

Through the lawgiver himself, therefore, the Lord announced that he would send his Son—that is, the living and present law—and would annul that old law given through a mortal, so that through him who was eternal he might establish anew an eternal law.

Likewise, concerning the annulment of circumcision, Isaiah prophesied as follows: [Col. 0500B]

> Thus says the Lord to the men of Judah who dwell in Jerusalem: Renew a newness among yourselves, and do not sow among thorns. Circumcise yourselves for the Lord your God, and circumcise the foreskin of your heart, lest my wrath go forth like fire and burn, with no one to extinguish it.

Likewise Moses himself (Deut. 30):

> In the last days the Lord will circumcise your heart, so that you may love the Lord your God.

Likewise Jesus, the son of Nave and his successor:

> And the Lord said to Jesus (Josh. 5:1): “Make for yourself exceedingly sharp knives of stone, and sit down, and circumcise the children of Israel a second time.”

He said that there would be a second circumcision—not of the flesh, as the first was, which the Jews still practice even now, but of the heart and spirit, which [Col. 0501A] Christ, who was the true Jesus, handed down. For the prophet does not say, “And the Lord said to me,” [Col. 0501A]

> **[Col. 0501C] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 501–502]**
>
> **And the Lord said to me.** Thus emended by me from the seven older Royal manuscripts, and from de Tournes, Betuleius, Gothofredus, Emen., six Colbert manuscripts, one Sorbonne manuscript, two Claromontanus manuscripts, Brun., and Lactantius himself a little above. Many manuscripts and editions incorrectly read “Jesus.”
>
> **That he was not speaking about himself.** The reading has been restored from the manuscripts and ten editions; eight printed editions have “about him.”
>
> **Who was at first called Auses.** Numbers 13. He was previously named Hosea; he is also called Hose, whence the Greek edition has Ause, which should be aspirated to give Hause. His father was Nun, corruptly called Nave. DRUSIUS.—See St. Augustine, *City of God*, book XVI, chap. 43. See also Tertullian, *Against the Jews*.
>
> **A new law.** Christ did not bring a new law but fulfilled the old.
>
> **A concealed breast.** Compare Seneca, *Natural Questions*, book I, preface: “You do not have a counterfeit expression, nor speech composed to please another, nor a concealed heart.” BUN.
>
> **We should conceal.** The author ought to have said *velaremus*, “we should conceal.” There is more than one faulty change of tense from here to the end of the chapter.
>
> **The prohibition of swine’s flesh also has the same purpose, etc.** This was imposed in Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14. I indicated above that the prohibition of pork is nowhere expressly criticized in the Gospel history. In general, certainly, Christ condemns all superstition, signifying that what comes out of a person defiles him, not what enters him. It was certainly believed [Col. 0502C] and observed that human beings assume the habits of the animals whose flesh they eat. Peter best indicates the nature of swine in his second canonical epistle, chap. 2:22, where he censures in these words those who, after knowing the way of truth, return again to their former impurity: “The whole sow is in the wallowing-place of mud.” BETUL.
>
> **Cast down upon the ground.** Suspecting that the text should read “upon the ground,” [Col. 0502D] I found precisely that reading in the editions of de Tournes, 1587 and 1613, and Walch. *On the Workmanship of God*, chap. 8: “So that … cast down upon the ground with their whole body, they might serve their belly and their food.” BUN.
>
> **Always its belly.** The de Tournes manuscript reads “lust.”
>
> **That they should not use pork.** The Palatine and Leipzig manuscripts and four editions read “eat it.” On swine’s flesh see Varro, *On Agriculture*, book II, chap. 4; Cicero, *On Ends*, book V; and Pliny, book VIII, chap. 51.
>
> **They smear themselves.** Compare my notes on book V, chap. 1. Again Lactantius, VI, chap. 23: “Whoever has immersed himself in mire must necessarily be smeared with mire.” BUN.
>
> **It was necessary.** See Matt. 20; Mark 10; Luke 18; John 7, 8, and 11.
>
> **That it was necessary for it to happen in this manner.** I have restored this reading from almost all the manuscripts and seven old editions. Two Royal manuscripts, Emen., Cambridge, Brun., and nine printed editions have “that it is necessary.”
>
> **Would be betrayed.** Matt. 27; Mark 14; Luke 22; John 18.
>
> **Delivered the Son of God to the Jews.** I have restored this from the two oldest Bologna manuscripts, the Royal-Puteanus manuscript, and eight others, as well as from three old Roman editions and eight others. Recent manuscripts read “delivered him to the Jews.”

but “to Jesus,” in order to show that he was not speaking about himself but about Christ, to whom God was then speaking. For that Jesus bore the figure of Christ. When he was at first called Auses, Moses, foreseeing the future, commanded him to be called Jesus, so that, since he had been chosen as commander of the army against Amalek, who was attacking the children of Israel, he might both defeat the adversary through the figure of the name and lead the people into the land of promise. For this reason he also succeeded Moses, to show that the new law given through Christ Jesus would succeed the old law, which had been given through Moses.

For that circumcision of the flesh is certainly without rational basis, because if God had desired it, he would have fashioned man from the beginning so that he had no foreskin. But [Col. 0501B] it was a figure of this second circumcision, signifying that the breast must be laid bare—that is, that we ought to live with an open and sincere heart—because that part of the body which is circumcised has a certain resemblance to the heart and is a shameful part. For this reason God commanded it to be laid bare, so that by this representation he might admonish us not to have a concealed breast—that is, not to conceal within the hidden places of conscience any deed of which we should be ashamed.

This is the circumcision of the heart of which the prophets speak, which God transferred from mortal flesh to the soul, which alone will endure. For, wishing in his eternal loving-kindness to provide for our life and salvation, he set repentance before us in that circumcision, so that if we lay bare our heart—that is, if, after confessing our sins, we make satisfaction to God—we may obtain pardon. This pardon is denied to the obstinate and to those who conceal what they have committed by [Col. 0501C] him who looks not upon the face, as a human being does, but upon the innermost and hidden things of the breast.

The prohibition of swine’s flesh also has the same purpose. When God commanded them to abstain from it, he chiefly intended it to be understood that they should abstain from sins and impurities. [Col. 0502A] For this animal is muddy and unclean and never looks up to heaven, but, cast down upon the ground with its whole body and mouth, always serves its belly and its food. Nor, while it lives, can it provide any other service, as other animals do: they either furnish a vehicle for riding, assist in the cultivation of fields, draw wagons with their necks, carry burdens on their backs, provide clothing from their hides, abound in a plentiful supply of milk, or keep watch in guarding houses.

He therefore forbade them to use pork—that is, to imitate the life of swine, which are fattened solely for death—lest, by serving the belly and pleasures, they should be useless for the practice of righteousness and be put to death. Likewise, they were not to plunge themselves into foul lusts, like the sow which gorges itself with mud; or [Col. 0502B] to serve earthly images and defile themselves with clay. For those who worship gods—that is, who worship clay and earth—smear themselves with clay. Thus all the precepts of the Jewish law aim at the practice of righteousness, because they were given indirectly, so that spiritual realities might be understood through the figure of carnal things.

## CHAPTER XVIII  
### On the Lord’s Passion and the fact that it had been foretold

Since, therefore, Christ was fulfilling the things which God willed to be done and which he had foretold through his prophets many centuries before, they were incited by those very deeds and, not understanding the divine writings, conspired to condemn their own God. Although he knew that this would happen and repeatedly said that it was necessary for him to suffer and be killed for the salvation of many, he nevertheless withdrew with [Col. 0502C] his disciples (Mark 3), not in order to avoid what he necessarily had to undergo and endure, but to show that in every persecution it was necessary to act in this way, lest anyone appear to have fallen into it through his own fault. He also announced that he would be betrayed by one of them. And so Judas, enticed by a reward, delivered the Son of God to the Jews.

They arrested him and brought him before [Col. 0503A] Pontius Pilate, who was then governing Syria as legate. [Col. 0503A]

> **[Col. 0503B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 503–504]**
>
> **Was governing Syria as legate.** Thus read Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 21, and Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, near the end. Lactantius here uses the title “legate” generally for one who has been sent to perform some office, just as Varro too explains this word in book V of *On the Latin Language*. ISAEUS.—Lactantius’ statement that Pontius Pilate was legate of Syria is by no means free of suspicion or placed beyond all risk of controversy; for Pilate was only procurator of Judaea. Tacitus: “Christ, the founder of that name, had been subjected to punishment under the emperor Tiberius by the procurator Pontius Pilate.” Although Christian chronologists, with a certain carelessness, call him governor, after considering the matter I would judge Lactantius’ manuscripts to be corrupt and that the text should read “who governed Judaea under Silanus.” For Silanus was then governor of Syria, and Judaea was governed by Pilate under him. Judaea was not then a separate province but belonged to Syria. [Col. 0503C] They were, however, divided in time of war, just as Judaea obeyed Vespasian and Syria Mucianus during the Vitellian disturbances. The statement about Silanus is so true that the Jews at one time even accused Pilate before him. BARTHIUS.—There were two kinds of these procurators. Some were called *rationales* and attended solely to the collection of revenues. Others, in addition, governed smaller provinces in the governor’s stead, with a degree of power, and exercised a measure of jurisdiction among the provincials when no governor was present, although otherwise legal action was permitted only before magistrates who were provincial governors, such as proconsuls and propraetors. SCULTETUS.—Nevertheless, it is certain that most historians, though less precisely, call Pilate a governor.
>
> **If you destroy.** See John 2; Matt. 26 and 27; Mark 14.
>
> **Which was built in forty-six years.** I have retained this number, which is confirmed by John the Evangelist, chap. 2, verse 20; by twelve Vatican, eight Royal, six Colbert, one Sorbonne, two Claromontanus, and Brun. manuscripts; and by all editions. But the oldest Royal manuscript 1, two Bologna manuscripts, Tax., and the Cambridge manuscript wrongly have “forty years.”—“Which was built in forty-six years.” From John 2:20, the number of years must be understood not of Zerubbabel’s work, which was completed in four years, Ezra 6:15, but of the restoration under Herod and his successors, to whom the Romans had granted responsibility for the temple. See Josephus, book XV, chap. 14, and book XX, chaps. 3 and 8. CELL.
>
> **I will raise it up again.** Restored from very many of the best manuscripts and twelve printed editions. Two ancient Bologna manuscripts, Cauc., six others, and five editions read “I will raise it up.”
>
> **To appear.** A word from the ancient judicial formula.
>
> **Most unjust accusers.** The Royal-Puteanus manuscript, another very ancient Royal manuscript in its first hand, one other recent Royal manuscript, and Brun. read “most just,” but ironically.
>
> **To demand with violent cries.** Thus the manuscripts and editions, whereas the Cellarius edition incorrectly has “of one willing.” Thus Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, chap. 7: “Demanding his cross and death with violent and obstinate votes.” And our *Epitome*, chap. 45: “And they demanded his death with impious cries.” Among Latin writers, the verb *flagitare* itself indicates vehement persistence in making a demand. Compare Lactantius, VI, chap. 20. BUN.
>
> **Yet he did not himself pronounce sentence.** Luke says: “He delivered him to their will”—that is, to the will of the Jews—that he might be crucified, indeed by his authority, but not by a sentence declaring him worthy of the cross. For it cannot be proved that Pilate pronounced a sentence against him as one guilty of death. Thus the sentence which is read in Adrichomius appears to be fictitious. He did indeed sit on the tribunal, but merely adjudged that their petition should be granted, as Luke says: namely, that he who had been condemned by them should be delivered to them to be crucified, as they demanded. JANSENIUS.—Nevertheless, see Luke 23:24 and John 19:16.
>
> **They led him away.** That is, they dragged him to death, for the verb *ducere*, “to lead,” also has this meaning.
>
> **Crowned with thorns.** The ancients thought these were white thorns, which are consequently called health-giving and are useful in medicines. Marcellus Empiricus, chap. 23: “The health-giving herb—that is, the white thorn with which Christ was crowned—which bears something like a cluster of grapes, will heal the spleen when rubbed gently upon the same place.” BARTHIUS.
>
> **And they gave him gall for food and mixed for him a drink of vinegar.** Matt. 27:48. The Syriac and Arabic also read ὄξος, “vinegar,” but the common text has οἶνον, “wine,” which Beza testifies he read in his own very ancient copy. So too the Hebrew Gospel: “And they gave him wine mixed with gall to drink.” Mercerus’ copy omits “to drink.” Beza regards this reading as the truest, so much so that even ὄξος would not mean what we call vinegar but seasoned wine, because Mark 15:23 mentions οἶνος ἐσμυρνισμένος, “wine mixed with myrrh.” I would prefer, however, to take ὄξος as vinegar in the proper sense, and also to understand Mark’s οἶνος, “wine,” as vinegar, which is nothing other than sour wine. For I think that taking ὄξος to mean seasoned wine lacks both example and authority. As for the most learned man’s interpretation of χολή, “gall,” not as gall but as bitterness in general, such as that of genuine myrrh, I readily agree with him: both because Mark has σμύρνα, “myrrh,” in place of χολή, and because the Septuagint also translated “wormwood” by χολή in Prov. 5:4 and Lam. 3:15. Accordingly, the Arabic translator, who here has “myrrh” for μετὰ χολῆς, “with gall,” is not greatly to be blamed. For χολή can signify any bitterness, whether of gall, wormwood, or myrrh. This passage is taken from Ps. 68:22. The Septuagint has καὶ ἔδωκαν εἰς τὸ βρῶμά μου χολήν, “and they gave gall for my food.” There it may simply mean “bitterness,” as may be gathered from Deut. 29:18, Heb. 12:15, and Jer. 23:15, where the Septuagint translated it as ὕδωρ πικρόν, “bitter water.” Matthew and Mark therefore explain one another. Matthew explains Mark’s οἶνος, “wine,” by ὄξος, “vinegar,” and Mark in turn explains Matthew’s χολή, “gall,” by σμύρνα, “myrrh.” Hence it is clear, contrary to what very learned men have supposed, that nothing here was done in accordance with the accepted Jewish custom by which they ordinarily performed this service for those about to die: giving them wine with a grain of incense so that their minds might be carried away. Here, on the contrary, they offered vinegar in place of wine and the bitterness of myrrh in place of pleasantly flavored incense, so that nothing might be lacking by which they could reveal their venomous disposition toward the Savior. LUDOVICUS DE DIEU.

They demanded that he be nailed to the cross, charging him with nothing other than saying that he was the Son of God and king of the Jews, and also that he had said:

> If you destroy this temple, which was built in forty-six years, I will raise it up again without hands in three days,

signifying that his Passion would shortly occur and that, after being killed by the Jews, he would rise again on the third day. For he himself was the true temple of God. They denounced these words of his as ominous and impious.

When Pilate heard them, and when Jesus said nothing in his own defense, Pilate declared that nothing worthy of condemnation appeared in him. But those most unjust accusers, [Col. 0504A] together with the people whom they had incited, began to shout and to demand his crucifixion with violent cries.

Then Pontius was overcome both by their clamor and by the instigation of Herod the tetrarch, who feared that he might be driven from his kingdom. Yet he did not himself pronounce sentence, but delivered him to the Jews so that they themselves might judge him according to their law. They therefore led him away after he had been scourged, and before nailing him to the cross they mocked him. For they clothed him in a scarlet-colored garment, crowned him with thorns, and saluted him as a king; and they gave him gall for food and mixed for him a drink of vinegar. After [Col. 0505A] this, they spat upon his face, [Col. 0505A]

> **[Col. 0505B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 505–506]**
>
> **They spat upon his face.** I have retained this reading, which is found in the three oldest Royal manuscripts and ten editions. The preposition in the phrase “upon the face” may be omitted, though it is found in more recent manuscripts and seven printed editions. Thus in Seneca, chap. 13, *To Helvia*: “Aristides was being led to punishment at Athens, and everyone who met him cast down his eyes … yet one man was found who spat upon his face.”
>
> **For we are not describing the cross of Gavius.** This is the best reading, found in three Royal manuscripts, one Sorbonne manuscript, and nineteen editions, and supported by Cicero’s *Against Verres*, Oration 10. The Royal-Puteanus manuscript, three other Royal manuscripts, four Colbert manuscripts, and Brun. have the erroneous *Gabianam*, with *b* in place of *v*. One Colbert manuscript and the Roman edition of 1468 have *Gabiniam*; one Royal manuscript, the Roman edition of 1470, and the Florentine edition have *Gabinianam*; the oldest Royal manuscript has *Gavinianam*; one Claromontanus manuscript has *Ganianam*, erroneously for *Gavianam*; one Royal and two Colbert manuscripts have *Gravianam*; the de Tournes manuscript has *Gravinianam*; Junius has *Grabianam*; and three editions have the corrupt *Cannianam*. See Cicero, *Against Verres*, second action, books V, VI, and VII. He alludes to Publius Gavius of Consa, a Roman citizen whom Verres, contrary to law and legal right, had scourged and nailed to a cross—that is, subjected to the punishment of slaves.
>
> **All.** Thus I have restored the text from eight Royal manuscripts, two of which are very ancient, six Colbert manuscripts, two Claromontanus manuscripts, and others. But two recent manuscripts and eleven editions read “all of.”
>
> [Col. 0505D] **Sinews.** Ten manuscripts and five editions read “words,” but less satisfactorily.
>
> **With such abundant richness.** Ten very recent manuscripts read “so great.”
>
> **And all the elements of the world mourned.** The word “world” is missing from one Colbert manuscript and seven editions. Students of grammar should note our author’s use of *toti* in the plural in book I of the *Divine Institutes*, chap. 11, and Augustine’s use of it in Psalm 148; Plautus’ use of *totae*, as well as its occurrence in the creed *Quicumque* attributed to Athanasius; and Lactantius’ use of *tota* in the nominative plural in book II, chap. 9, at the end, and book IV, chap. 18. See the following chapter.
>
> **And they did not understand.** I read this with the older and better manuscripts—seven Royal, four Colbert, and one Claromontanus—and with almost all printed editions. Augustine reads it in the same way in his second exposition of Psalm 34. Nine recent manuscripts and two old editions read “and he did not understand.”
>
> **They tested.** Restored from the manuscripts; printed editions have the contracted form *tentarunt*.
>
> [Col. 0506B] **And they mocked me with mockery.** The third Leipzig edition and Reimmann read: “They mocked me and gnashed their teeth.” Augustine and Jerome: “They derided me with derision.” Augustine very effectively applies the earlier wording to Christians. The words “and they mocked me with mockery” are missing from the *Epitome*, chap. 46, but are present in the Hebrew and the Septuagint. BUN.
>
> **Εἰς ἀνόμων χεῖρας.** *Sibylline Oracles*, book 8. In Latin:
>
> > Afterward he will come into the hands of lawless and unbelieving men;  
> > With unholy hands they will give blows to God,  
> > And from unclean throats, venomous spittle;  
> > Then he will simply surrender his pure back to the scourge.
>
> These and the following lines are read in the same form in Royal-Puteanus manuscript no. 3736 and in Augustine, *City of God*, book XVIII, chap. 23, no. 2, who excerpted them from our author, except that he has “lawless hands … venomous spits … holy back.” In Brun. and other manuscripts and printed copies of the Latin translation, the text reads “then his innocent back”; in some, “then his pure back.”
>
> **Ἀνόμων.** I have restored this from the excellent Royal-Puteanus manuscript, Betuleius, the Paris editions of 1525, 1561, and 1565, Cratander, Gymnicus, Graphius, de Tournes, Soubron, and the French translation. Musurus, Betuleius, and Sparke also judged that it should be read thus, and the syntax is consequently better established. The distinguished Heumann likewise emended it in this way. But eleven manuscripts, others, and seven editions have ἀνόμους.
>
> **Τὰ πτύσματα.** This reading is found in the Royal-Puteanus manuscript, three other Royal manuscripts, three Colbert manuscripts, one Sorbonne manuscript, and all editions. The Cauc. and two Royal manuscripts have ἐμπτύσματα, “spittings”; Betuleius’ manuscript has ἐκπτύσματα, “things spat out,” on page 261 of his commentary.
>
> **Καὶ κολαφιζόμενος.** *Sibylline Oracles*, book 8. In Latin:
>
> > And while receiving blows he will remain silent, lest anyone recognize  
> > What Word he is, or whence he came to speak to mortals;  
> > And he will wear a crown of thorns.
>
> Augustine, in the passage cited above, reads “to speak to those below.” Musurus and Thomasius, with two Colbert manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470, de Tournes, two Paris editions, and Soubron, read “to speak to the dead.”
>
> **Τίς λόγος ἢ πόθεν ἦλθεν.** Thus three Royal manuscripts, two of which are very ancient, three Colbert manuscripts, and all editions. But the Sibylline manuscript has Τίς πνος ὢν πόθεν ἦλθεν [an uncertain and apparently corrupt reading]; Betuleius’ manuscript has Τίς πνος ὤ [likewise corrupt]. Augustine, however, follows Lactantius’ reading, which Betuleius also considers more satisfactory.

and struck him with their palms. When the executioners themselves contended over his garments, they cast lots among themselves for his tunic and cloak. And while all these things were being done, he uttered no sound from his mouth, as though he were mute. Then they suspended him between two criminals who had been condemned for robbery and nailed him to the cross.

What am I to lament here, amid so great a crime? Or with what words am I to bewail so great an impiety? For we are not describing the cross of Gavius, which Marcus Tullius treated with all the sinews and powers of his eloquence, as though pouring forth all the fountains of his genius, proclaiming it an unworthy crime that a Roman citizen had been raised upon a cross contrary to every law. Although that man was innocent and undeserving of that punishment, he was nevertheless mortal, and was subjected to it by a wicked man who [Col. 0505B] knew nothing of justice.

What shall we say of the indignity of this cross, upon which God was suspended and transfixed by the worshipers of God? Who will arise so eloquent and equipped with so great an abundance of matter and words? What discourse could flow with such abundant richness as fittingly to lament that cross, which the world itself and all the elements of the world mourned?

That these things would happen in this manner was announced both by the voices of the prophets and by the Sibylline verses. In [Col. 0506A] Isaiah (chap. 50) it is found written as follows:

> I am not disobedient, nor do I contradict. I offered my back to the scourges and my cheeks to blows; but I did not turn my face away from the foulness of spittle.

Similarly, David in Psalm 34:

> Scourges gathered against me, and they did not understand. They were dissolved and felt no remorse. They tested me and mocked me with mockery, and gnashed their teeth against me.

The Sibyl likewise revealed that these same things would occur:

> Εἰς ἀνόμων χεῖρας καὶ ἀπίστων ὕστερον ἥξει·  
> Δώσουσι δὲ θεῷ ῥαπίσματα χερσὶν ἀνάγνοις,  
> Καὶ στόμασιν μαροῖσι τὰ πτύσματα φαρμακόεντα·  
> Δώσει δ᾽ εἰς μάστιγας ἁπλῶς ἁγνὸν τότε νῶτον.
>
> Afterward he will come into the hands of lawless and unbelieving men;  
> With unholy hands they will give blows to God,  
> And with defiled mouths venomous spittle;  
> Then he will simply surrender his pure back to the scourge.

Likewise, concerning his silence, which he resolutely maintained even to death, Isaiah spoke again as follows (chap. 53):

> He was led like a sheep to slaughter, and like a lamb [Col. 0506B] voiceless before its shearers, so he did not open his mouth.

And the Sibyl mentioned above:

> Καὶ κολαφιζόμενος σιγήσει, μή τις ἐπιγνῷ  
> Τίς λόγος, ἢ πόθεν ἦλθεν ἵνα φθιμένοισι λαλήσῃ·  
> Καὶ στέφανον φορέσει τὴν ἀκάνθινον.
>
> And while receiving blows he will remain silent, lest anyone recognize  
> What Word he is, or whence he came to speak to the dead;  
> And he will wear the crown of thorns.

Concerning the food and drink which they offered him before nailing him to the cross, David says in Psalm 68:

> And they gave me gall for food; and in my thirst they [Col. 0507A] gave me vinegar to drink.

[Col. 0507A]

> **[Col. 0507B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 507–508]**
>
> **They gave me vinegar to drink.** This reading is found in six Royal manuscripts, two of which are the oldest, one Sorbonne manuscript, two Colbert manuscripts, two Claromontanus manuscripts, and six editions. Thirteen very recent manuscripts and seven printed editions read: “They made me drink vinegar.”
>
> **That this same thing would happen.** One recent Royal manuscript, one Claromontanus manuscript, and the French edition and Sparke read “Likewise.”
>
> [Col. 0507C] **Εἰς δὲ τὸ βρῶμα.** *Sibylline Oracles*, book 8. In Latin:
>
> > For food they gave gall, and for thirst vinegar;  
> > This table of inhospitality they will display.
>
> **Αὐτὴ γὰρ δύσφρων.** I have restored this from the two oldest Royal manuscripts. But one recent Royal manuscript, three Colbert manuscripts, one Claromontanus manuscript, and eleven editions have ἄφρων, “foolish.” The Greek is absent from the other manuscripts I have seen. The Latin translation is:
>
> > For you yourself, devising harm, did not recognize your God  
> > Playing with mortal thoughts; but with thorns  
> > You crowned him with a crown, and mixed dreadful gall.
>
> Augustine has “foolish” in place of “devising harm”; and in the following verse both Augustine and one Brun. manuscript have “Playing with the minds of mortals”; the other Brun. manuscript has “Mocking human minds.” These lines are from the *Sibylline Oracles*, book 6.
>
> **Παίζοντα θνητοῖσι.** I have restored this from three Royal manuscripts, two of which are the oldest, one Claromontanus manuscript, and three Colbert manuscripts—except that one has θνητισι—and from the Roman edition of 1468. The manuscript seen by Betuleius has πταίοντα, “offending,” which appears to him more appropriate, since Christ had offended in the judgment of mortals. Seven printed editions have παίζοντ᾽ ἐν θνητοῖσι, “playing among mortals.”
>
> **Ἔστεψας.** I have thus emended the text from seven Royal manuscripts, among which two are the oldest, three Colbert manuscripts, one Sorbonne manuscript, one Claromontanus manuscript, the two old Roman editions, and eight others. Six printed editions have ἔστρεψας, “you twisted.”

In Esdras it is written thus, etc. Justin Martyr, in his *Dialogue with Trypho the Jew*, 83, transcribes certain passages from Scripture which he maintains were deleted by the Jews out of hatred for Christ. *Τοῦτο τὸ πάσχα ὁ σωτὴρ ἡμῶν*, etc. (“This Passover is our Savior,” etc.), which Lactantius reports and translates as follows. These words, however, occur neither in the Hebrew text nor in the Greek or Latin manuscripts. Justin indeed complains that they were deleted and erased by the Jews: “From the words,” he says, “in which Esdras recalled the law and ordinance of the Passover, they removed this passage: ‘And Esdras said [Col. 0508B] to the people: This Passover is our Savior,’” etc. They must, however, have been in those books which the Jews received into the canon.

**Humble him on the sign.** Thus nine printed editions agree with the manuscripts; and St. Justin Martyr has *ἐν σημείῳ*, “on the sign.” In the manuscripts [Col. 0508C] 1 recent Royal, 1 Colbertine, the Brunswick manuscript, and seven printed editions, it reads “on the wood.”

**Whom they denied.** Thus the two most ancient Royal manuscripts, many others, and all the printed editions. He used the same expression above, chapter 12. In the very ancient Bologna manuscript and fifteen other recent manuscripts, it reads “whom they killed.”

**In his humiliation, etc.** Lactantius followed the Greek translation of the Septuagint almost everywhere; to it is due the phrase “his generation,” that is, *γενεάν*, which the Latin Vulgate also adopted. CELLARIUS.

**I am a lamb without malice.** I restored this from the two most ancient Royal manuscripts, another Royal manuscript, and two Brunswick manuscripts. It is no different in Cyprian’s *Testimonies against the Jews*, book II, chapter 15, and in the Septuagint at Jeremiah XI: *Ἐγὼ δὲ ὡς ἀρνίον ἄκακον*, “But I was like an innocent lamb.” The recent manuscripts and printed editions have “without blemish”; the Vulgate has “gentle.”

**The wood, however, signifies the cross, and the bread his body.** I corrected the text thus from one Royal manuscript of the highest quality, one Colbertine, and two Brunswick manuscripts, as well as from the old French translation of 1563, which reads: *Or le bois signifie la croix, et le pain son corps*—“Now the wood signifies the cross, and the [Col. 0508D] bread his body.” Seventeen manuscripts and eighteen printed editions incorrectly have: “and the bread [signifies] his body.” — **The wood, however, etc.** Origen, Tertullian, and Jerome explain it in the same way, understanding the body by the bread and the cross by the wood, and referring it to the sacrament of Christ’s body. BETULEIUS.

**Because he himself is food.** That is, because he himself is that bread which came down from heaven (John VI).

**The life of all.** I restored “of all” from three old Roman editions, the Venice 1490 edition, Cellarius, and Walch, and from all the manuscripts except two recent Royal, one Sorbonne, and one Colbertine manuscript, which have “the life of men.”

**On which he hung.** Thus the most ancient manuscripts: one Bologna, the Royal-Puteanus, six Colbertine, the Brunswick, and two Clermont manuscripts, together with two old Roman editions. One Royal manuscript, one Colbertine at first hand, and seventeen printed editions have “upon which he hung.”

**And your life shall hang.** Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, chapter 11; Cyprian, *Against the Jews*, book II, chapter 20; and Augustine, book XVI *Against Faustus*, [Col. 0509B] chapter 21, also interpret this of the cross of Christ. From CELLARIUS. — This occurs in Deuteronomy, chapter XXVIII, but Lactantius’ interpretation seems excessively allegorical.]

The Sibyl also proclaimed that this would happen:

> For food they gave him gall, and for thirst vinegar;  
> They will display this table of inhospitality.

And another Sibyl rebukes the land of Judaea in these verses:

> For you yourself, malevolent, did not recognize your God,  
> Who played with mortal thoughts; but with thorns  
> You crowned him as with a crown, and mixed dreadful gall.

That the Jews would lay hands upon their God and kill him had been foretold by these testimonies of the prophets.

In Esdras it is written thus: “And Esdras said to the people: This Passover is our Savior and our refuge. Consider, and let it rise into your heart, that we must humble him on the sign; and after these things we shall hope in him, lest this place be forsaken for all eternity, [Col. 0507B] says the Lord God of hosts. If you do not believe him or heed his proclamation, you will become a laughingstock among the nations.” From this it is evident that the Jews have no other hope unless they cleanse themselves of blood and place their hope in the very one whom they denied.

Isaiah also (chapter LV) marks out their crime and says:

> In his humiliation his judgment was taken away. Who shall recount [Col. 0508A] his generation? For his life shall be taken from the earth; because of the crimes of my people he was led to death. And I shall give the wicked for his burial, and the rich for his death, because he committed no crime and spoke no deceit with his mouth. Therefore he shall obtain many, and shall divide the spoils of the mighty, because he was delivered to death and numbered among criminals; and he himself bore the sin of many and was delivered up because of their crimes.

David likewise says in Psalm XCIII:

> They will lie in wait for the life of the righteous man, and will condemn innocent blood; and the Lord became my refuge.

Jeremiah says (chapter XI):

> Lord, reveal it to me, and I shall know; then I saw their designs. I, like a lamb without malice, was led to the sacrifice. They devised a scheme against me, saying: “Come, let us put wood into his bread, and root out his life from the earth, and his name shall no longer be remembered.” [Col. 0508B]

The wood, however, signifies the cross, and the bread his body, because he himself is the food and the life of all who believe in the flesh which he bore and in the cross on which he hung.

Moses himself, however, foretold this more openly in Deuteronomy:

> And your life shall hang before your [Col. 0509A] eyes, and you shall fear by day and by night, and shall not trust your life.

The same man again in Numbers [Col. 0509A]

[Note: [Col. 0509B] [Various Notes on columns 509–510]

**Numbers.** This interpretation is no less metaphorical.

**The Lord is suspended.** Bunemann reads “God . . .,” and gives the following reason for this wording. — **God is suspended.** I restore “God” from Leipzig II, 3, Reimmann . . . the Subiaco and Rostock manuscripts, and both Venetian editions of 1478. The contrast with “man” requires it; so too the Septuagint, *ὁ θεός*, “God,” and Cyprian, book II *Against the Jews*, chapter 20. BUNEMANN.

**Zechariah.** This prophecy is interpreted of Christ by the evangelist John, chapter XIX.

**So many years are reckoned.** Quite rightly: from the death of David to the Common Era there are 1,019 years, but to the Passion there are 1,052 years. Yet if, according to the ancients, Christ died when the two Gemini were consuls—that is, in the year 29 of the Common Era—the total will be 1,048 years, which amounts to the same thing.

**Solomon.** These words are found in III Kings, chapter IX, and II Chronicles, chapter VII; but it is not true that Jerusalem was founded by Solomon.

**Turn away from me.** III Kings, chapter IX. But some things have been added by Lactantius and others omitted, as will be evident to anyone who consults the passage.

**A reproach.** I restored this from the two most ancient and best Royal manuscripts, one 900 years old and another Royal manuscript 400 years old but of the highest quality. Many more recent [Col. 0509D] manuscripts and printed editions read “a disgrace.”

**Because they forsook.** Thus the second Leipzig manuscript; Reimmann has, with a closely similar reading, “For this reason they left.” But the Turin manuscript and the *Epitome*, chapter 46, read as I have printed it. BUNEMANN.

**And persecuted the king.** I do not know from what tradition he added these words, of which no trace appears in III Kings 9 or II Chronicles 7. CELLARIUS.

**Concerning the crime of the Jews.** I restored this from the two oldest Royal manuscripts, four other Royal manuscripts of good quality, and others. The printed editions and many more recent manuscripts wrongly read “concerning the crimes,” since only one crime is under discussion here, namely that committed in the death of Christ.

**An earthquake occurred, etc.** Matthew XXVII, Mark XV, Luke XXIII, John XIX. It occurred in several places, not only in Judaea. For God wished the memory of this portent to survive. See what is written in Phlegon and Thallus. It is entirely true that among the prophets an earthquake signifies in some places a change in affairs, and elsewhere the majesty of God; but here the meaning is more evident and could be understood equally by the Jews and other nations—namely, divine anger at human crimes (Psalm XVIII, 8; Joel XVI). [Col. 0510B] Thus Virgil joined an earthquake to the sun’s darkness; Lucan and Seneca did likewise. Certainly the centurion and those who were with him interpreted the prodigy in this way, for from it they concluded that Jesus had been unjustly condemned (Luke XXIII, 45). GROTIUS.

**And from the sixth hour, etc.** Among the Romans judicial proceedings began at the third hour of the day:

> The third hour puts the hoarse advocates to work. [Col. 0510C]

Pilate’s inquiry also fell within that period.
