Ignatius aptly says in his letter to the Smyrnaeans: *Τῇ οὖν παρασκευῇ τρίτῃ ὥρᾳ ἀπόφασιν παρεδέξατο τοῦ Πιλάτου*—“On the day of Preparation, therefore, at the third hour, he received Pilate’s sentence.” Thus Christ was crucified before the sixth hour; after the sixth the darkness began; and Christ died shortly after the ninth. The same Ignatius says: *ἕκτῃ ὥρᾳ ἐσταυρώθη, ἐννάτῃ ἀνέπνευσε*—“At the sixth hour he was crucified; at the ninth he expired.” This understanding is also found in the fairly ancient work entitled the *Constitutions of Clement*, book V, chapter XIV, and book VIII, chapter XXXIV. These authorities should restrain us from altering anything in the text of Mark or John contrary to the authority of the most ancient manuscripts and translators (*μεταφρασταί*).

Nor do those evangelists contradict one another. The manner of speaking arose from the practice of the Temple, where sacrifices and prayers were customarily performed at the third, sixth, and ninth hours. Jerome, besides the Hebrews, notes this on Daniel VII. Especially on feast days, those very times were announced by the sound of a trumpet, as Numbers X, 10 teaches us. Consequently, these hours were commonly spoken of as the best known; and wherever fixed prayers are mentioned, you will find no other names [Col. 0510D] for the hours. See Acts III, 1; X, 3 and 9; and Tertullian, *On Fasting*, where he calls these hours particularly distinguished in human affairs: they divide the day, distinguish its business, and are publicly sounded. With this agree the statements of Cyprian in *On the Lord’s Prayer* and Jerome both to Laeta and to Demetrias. The same point is relevant above at XX, 3 and 5, where no hour between the third, sixth, and ninth is named, although after the ninth the eleventh is mentioned. Whatever happened between those fixed times of prayer is said to have occurred at the third or sixth hour, just as intervening events are customarily referred now to one boundary and now to the other. GROTIUS.

**There was darkness.** The sun, of course, was darkened, as Luke teaches us—not because the moon intervened, since it was then full, nor because a cloud covered it, but by some means unknown to humankind. The phrase here, *ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν*, “over all the land,” which Mark expressed as *ἐφ’ ὅλην τὴν γῆν*, cannot be understood of the entire globe, since in many regions it was not daytime. Yet I would not restrict it to [Col. 0511B] Judaea alone, since ancient astrologers and chronographers recorded this darkness without adding any place-name, from which it may be inferred that it extended widely.

Phlegon, in book XIII of his *Olympiads*, writes:

> In the fourth year of the 202nd Olympiad there occurred the greatest eclipse of the sun known in earlier times; at the sixth hour of the day it became night, so that even the stars appeared in the sky. A great earthquake also occurred throughout Bithynia and destroyed most of Nicaea.

He names the location of the earthquake but not of the darkness; and when he records a darkness greater than those seen before, such that at the very height of noon it was like night, he sufficiently demonstrates that this spectacle was not peculiar to Judaea. Eusebius cites another Greek author, whom he does not name, writing thus on the event:

> The sun failed. Bithynia was shaken. Most of Nicaea fell.

Tertullian says in the *Apologeticum*:

> Yet, when fastened to the cross, he displayed many signs peculiar to his death. For with a word he voluntarily dismissed his spirit, forestalling the executioner’s task. At that same moment the day was withdrawn, although the sun marked the middle of its circuit. Those who did not know that this too had been foretold concerning Christ naturally thought it an eclipse. And yet you have that catastrophe of the world recorded in your archives. [Col. 0511C]

Here I see no reason to understand by “archives” anything other than the Roman public records, to which, unless I am mistaken, the martyr Lucian also appeals in Eusebius. And by calling it “a catastrophe of the world,” Tertullian sufficiently guarded against its being thought peculiar to Judaea. GROTIUS.]

**Shall be darkened.** I restored this reading from the ancient Royal-Puteanus manuscript, four other Royal manuscripts, the Junius manuscript, six Colbertine, two Sorbonne, two Leipzig, the Emmeram, Canterbury, two Clermont manuscripts, and the editions: three old Roman editions, Venice 1490, Aldus, Paris 1525, Cellarius, and Walch. In three more recent Royal manuscripts, one Leipzig, the Brunswick manuscript, and eleven printed editions, it reads “shall be made dark”; in one very ancient Royal manuscript, “shall grow dark.” The verb *tenebrare*, that is, “to bring on darkness,” is also used by Apuleius in book VIII, Chrysologus, and Ammianus. — **Shall be darkened.** Bunemann, however, reads “shall be made dark” and gives the following explanation of this variant. — **Shall be made dark.** Greater authority ought to be assigned to the very ancient [Col. 0511D] Turin manuscript, in which the *Epitome*, chapter 46, has this reading, as does Cyprian, whom Lactantius follows here even in the order of the sayings, in book II *Against the Jews*, chapter 23; so too the first Leipzig manuscript and the editions of Fasitelus, Gryphius, de Tournes, Betuleius, Thomasius, Isaeus, Thysius, Gallæus, and Sparke. It is likely to be Lactantius’ reading, since it is found in the Septuagint and in St. Cyprian, book II of the *Testimonies*, chapter 23.

> There shall be vast, dark night for three hours.

Instead of “vast,” three Colbertine manuscripts, one Brunswick manuscript, and Augustine, *The City of God*, book XVIII, chapter 23, read “exceedingly dark.”

[Col. 0512B] ***Σχισθῇ τὸ πέτασμα*.** I corrected the text thus from the two most ancient and best Royal manuscripts, the Sibylline manuscript seen by Betuleius, and the one seen by Isaeus. Nor can it be read otherwise if the metrical scheme is to stand, for the meter has a redundant syllable in four other recent Royal manuscripts, three Colbertine, one Sorbonne, one Clermont manuscript, and nine printed editions, which read *σχισθήσεται*; one Royal manuscript has *σχισθητοίσατα*; three common editions, *σχισθῆται*; Isaeus’ edition, *σχίσθητε*; and the Caucian manuscript, *ἐσχίσθη*.

**They took him down from the cross.** Thus the manuscripts and printed editions except the Emmeram manuscript, which has “they took him down from the cross” with a different case construction, while the de Tournes edition reads “from the cross.” Below, chapter 26, past the middle, it says: “The body was taken down from the gibbet.” See Acts XIII.

**Intact from the tomb.** I restored this from the manuscripts and very many printed editions. One Clermont manuscript has “from the tomb”; one recent Colbertine and the edition of Fasitelus, “away from the tomb”; four common editions, “entirely from the tomb.” See Matthew XVI and XXVIII, Mark XVI, and John XX.

**In the tomb, however, etc.** It is certain that our Lord’s tomb, like Lazarus’ tomb, was sunk within a vault or cave. Sidonius calls it a crypt: “On the left side is the little hill of Golgotha, where the Lord was crucified. From there, about a stone’s throw away, is the crypt where his body was laid and from which he rose on the third day.”

This crypt seems to have been constructed in no other manner or form than Lazarus’ tomb: it was underground, built of stone, covered by a vault, and opened by an aperture closed with a stone, as all crypts intended to conceal the dead were built. Some nevertheless maintain that the Lord’s crypt was cut from living rock, being led to this view by Mark’s words, *ἦν λελατομημένον ἐκ πέτρας*, “which had been hewn from rock.” Others translate *πέτρα* as “cliff,” as though there had also been a cliff in the garden where the monument in which the Lord’s body was placed stood.

But their reasoning deceives them. In ancient Greek, *πέτρα* certainly signifies the same as “rock”; here, however, it means a monument built from cut and polished stone. The common people and the poorest class, who because of their means could not build tombs for themselves, placed their dead in sunken graves and covered them with earth. [Col. 0512D] This custom prevailed not only in Judaea but equally among the Greeks and Romans. Those who possessed adequate resources had monuments built for themselves and their families.

That monument of Joseph, therefore, in which Christ’s body lay, was indeed a cave or crypt, hollowed out of the earth but built of stone and vaulted, just as all wine cellars, which we call *cavae*, are constructed today. It stood in a garden. The ground in which that monument was built underground was not rocky or craggy but was, as was fitting, garden soil, containing neither cliffs nor rocky ledges. Nor is it credible that the garden soil itself was *ὑπόπετρον*, “rocky underneath.”

That cave or crypt, made by human hands and serving as a tomb, consisted of masonry and a vault and lay beneath the garden soil. In the surface itself was an opening upon which a stone was laid to serve as a lid. The monument stood within the garden plot, enclosed underground by dressed stone and covered with a vault, with an opening above which was closed by rolling a stone over it.

It is moreover certain that the Jews did not place the bodies of the dead in chests, couches, or sarcophagi, but carried them into the monument covered and wrapped only in strips of linen. Niches suitable for receiving individual bodies were carved in the sides of the monument, and the bodies, veiled in strips [Col. 0513C] or bands, were inserted into them. These cavities, hollowed into the monument’s wall and receiving the corpse, served in place of the couches or little chests in which the bodies of the dead were customarily deposited in Greece.]

**They call it a testament.** *Διαθήκην*, a word which among the Septuagint signifies a testament, pact, and covenant. Let Moses provide evidence, Deuteronomy XXIX: *Καὶ φυλάξεσθε ποιεῖν πάντας τοὺς λόγους τῆς διαθήκης ταύτης*—“And you shall take care to perform all the words of this covenant.” Here it signifies “covenant,” and is translated so because the sense plainly requires it. For the living enter into a covenant with the living, while a dead person makes a testament with the living. The former belongs to the law of nations, the latter to civil law.

If you desire prophetic testimony, take this from Malachi, chapter II:

[Col. 0514A] ## CHAPTER XX. On Jesus’ departure for Galilee after the resurrection, and on both Testaments, the Old and the New

Having therefore departed for Galilee—for he did not wish to show himself to the Jews, lest he bring them to repentance and restore the impious to health—he gathered the disciples together again and disclosed the meaning of the sacred writings, that is, the mysteries of the prophets. Before he suffered, these could in no way be perceived, because they announced him and his Passion.

For this reason Moses and those same prophets call the law given to the Jews a “Testament,” because unless the testator has died, a testament can neither be confirmed nor its contents known, since it is closed and sealed. Thus, unless Christ had undergone death, the testament could not have been opened—that is, the mystery of God could not have been revealed [Col. 0514B] and understood.

All Scripture, however, is divided into two Testaments. That which preceded Christ’s advent and Passion—that is, the Law and the Prophets—is called the Old; but those writings composed after his resurrection are called the New Testament. The Jews use the Old, and we [Col. 0515A] the New; yet they are not different, [Col. 0515A]

because the New is the fulfillment of the Old, and in both Christ is the same testator. By undergoing death for us, he made us heirs of the eternal kingdom, while disowning and disinheriting the Jewish people, as the prophet Jeremiah bears witness (chapter XXXI) when he speaks thus:

> Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I shall consummate a new testament for the house of Israel and the house of Judah—not according to the testament which I established for their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; because they did not persevere in my testament, and I disregarded them, says the Lord.

Since his inheritance is the heavenly kingdom, he certainly does not say that he hates the inheritance itself, but rather the heirs, who proved ungrateful and impious toward him. “My inheritance,” he says, “became to me like a lion”; that is, I became prey and something to be devoured by my heirs, who sacrificed me like an animal. “It raised its voice against me”; that is, they pronounced against me a sentence of death and crucifixion.

For when he said above that he would consummate a new testament for the house of Judah, he showed that the old testament given through Moses was not perfect, but that the one which was to be given through Christ would be consummated. Isaiah teaches who that race would be (chapter XLII), where the supreme Father speaks to the Son, saying:

Since we formerly sat in darkness as though blind and shut within the prison of folly, ignorant of God and the truth, we have been illuminated by him who adopted us through his testament, freed us from evil chains, led us forth into the light of wisdom, and admitted us to the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom.

[Col. 0516B] ## CHAPTER XXI. On Jesus’ ascension, its prediction, and the preaching and deeds of the disciples

Having arranged for his disciples the proclamation of the Gospel and of his name, a cloud suddenly enveloped him and raised him into heaven on the fortieth day after the Passion, just as Daniel had shown would happen (chapter VII), saying:

The disciples, meanwhile, dispersed throughout the provinces and everywhere laid the foundations of the Church. They themselves also performed, in the name of the Teacher who is God, great and almost incredible miracles, because, when departing, he had equipped them with the strength and power by which the doctrine of the new proclamation could be founded and confirmed. [Col. 0516C] He also disclosed to them all future events, which Peter [Col. 0517A] and Paul [Col. 0517A]

[Note: [Col. 0517C] [Various Notes on columns 517–518]

Peter and Paul, etc. Certain Protestants dispute the question whether Peter was ever at Rome; and, if he was there, it may be learned from St. Jerome and the ancient writers that he presided over the Church there as its pastor. The most learned Protestants have, moreover, long inclined toward the sounder opinion. For if we wish to proceed by the testimony of the Fathers, we shall find that Peter preached at Rome, suffered there, and was buried there. Jerome thus committed it to record in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*. Likewise Theodoret, in his commentary on Romans 1; Irenaeus, the most ancient and very close to the times of the Apostles, in book III, chapter 3, testifies that the Roman Church was founded by Paul and Peter. Epiphanius followed him in the second tome of his first book, when recounting the catalogue of the bishops of Rome. Tertullian likewise mentions this in *The Prescription Against Heretics*. Eusebius, in his *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 25, adduces the testimony both of a certain Gaius, an ancient writer, and of Peter’s tomb—as Jerome also does against Vigilantius. [Col. 0517D] He likewise mentions it in book III, chapter 2. And the same Eusebius again, in his *Chronicle*, testifies that Peter exercised the pontificate at Rome from the beginning of Claudius’s reign, and that in Nero’s fourteenth year he died gloriously for the name of Christ. Hegesippus, a very ancient historian who composed an ecclesiastical history extending from the Lord’s Passion down to his own times, writes much about Peter’s deeds at Rome and his suffering under Nero, in the first three chapters of book III. Nor is Clement silent. Augustine and Chrysostom also mention this matter, upon which writers of the highest authority are in substantial agreement. **BETULEIUS.**—See the very learned *Historico-Critical Exercises* of Samuel Basnage of Flottemanville, on the year 44, no. 25, pp. 547–564. Indeed, all critics now acknowledge as beyond dispute Peter’s preaching and suffering at Rome. Consult David Blondel in his *Dissertation*, and Pearson in his *Posthumous Works*. See also *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter II, around the middle.

[Col. 0518C] **Written as a memorial.** This was the title of a certain spurious book, now lost; concerning it, see Fabricius in the *Codex Apocryphus Novi Testamenti*, p. 800.

**Cities.** Several manuscripts and printed editions have the plural; but Subl., Rost., and Ven. 1471 have the singular, *the city*, namely Jerusalem, to which these statements especially apply; Luke 19:43.

**When Nero had put them to death.** It is certain that Paul suffered martyrdom at Rome. The ancients generally agree that his punishment was by the sword; thus Eutychius, in *The Origins of Alexandria*: “He slew Paul with the sword.” See Samuel Basnage at the place cited above. Peter and Paul, moreover, were crowned with martyrdom on June 29 in the year 66 of the Christian era, when Suetonius Paulinus and L. Pontius Felesinus were consuls—not under Bassus and Tuscus, who were consuls in the year 258, the year in which the translation of the Holy Apostles took place, on the very day when their feast was celebrated.

**May perceive clearly.** Thus very many manuscripts and printed editions, as also Lactantius below at the end of this chapter, “he will easily perceive clearly”; and chapter 30, around the middle, “he perceived thoroughly its force and rationale.” 2 Reg. and 1 Clarom. have “may foresee”; 1 Colb., Tornes., and 1 Clarom., “may believe”; the Aldine edition, Paris 1525, Crat., and Graph., “may see.”

**He wished.** The Tornes. manuscript, 3 Colb., and five printed editions have “was able”; Em. has “will be able”; Reg. rec. has “they wished.”

**Openly professing God.** This is the reading of the Vatican manuscripts, 9 Reg., Cauc., 6 Colb., 1 Sorbon., 5 Oxon., Ultr., Em., Cant., Tax., Pen., 2 Clarom., 1 Bonon. rec., Brun., and fourteen old editions. In 1 Reg. it is “professing God”; in 1 Lips. and Goth., “a profession of God”; in 1 Bonon. antiq., “by God’s precepts.” Manuscripts 2 Reg. rec. and Cantabrig., 1 Colb. in the margin, and three old Roman editions, the Aldine, and nine others prefix “they say.” “Openly professing God” means one who declared himself to be God and did not conceal it. Thus Mars is called “openly professed”—not secret or hidden beneath the veil of peace, but openly displaying and avowing war. The greater part of the manuscripts reads thus. 1 Bonon. reads “as by God’s precepts,” and Thomas follows that reading; but whatever he may say, we have judged that nothing should be changed. **GALLAEUS.**

They preached at Rome, and that preaching remained written as a memorial. In it, among many other marvelous things, they also said that this would come to pass: after a short time God would send a king who would subdue the Jews, level their cities to the ground, and besiege them until they were exhausted by hunger and thirst. Then they would feed upon the bodies of their own people and consume one another; finally, they would be captured and fall into the hands of their enemies, and before their own eyes would see their wives subjected to the bitterest abuse, virgins violated and prostituted, children carried off, infants dashed to pieces, and, in short, everything devastated by fire and sword, while the captives were banished forever from their own lands—all because they had exulted over the most loving and most approved Son of God. Accordingly, after their death, when Nero had put them to death, [Col. 0517B] Vespasian extinguished the name and nation of the Jews and did everything that they had predicted would occur.

## CHAPTER XXII. The Arguments of Unbelievers Against Jesus’ Incarnation

The things regarded as false and incredible by those who have not been imbued with the true teaching of the heavenly writings have, I think, been confirmed. Yet, so that we may also refute those who are excessively wise—not without harm to themselves—and who detract from belief in divine things, let us also expose their error by means of their own arguments, so that at long last [Col. 0518A] they may perceive clearly that it had to happen in the manner in which we have shown that it did happen. And although, before fair judges, either testimonies without arguments or arguments without testimonies would possess sufficient force, we are nevertheless not content with either one alone, since both are available to us; thus we leave no perversely ingenious person any opportunity either not to understand or to argue against us.

They deny that it could have happened that an immortal nature suffered any loss. Finally, they deny that it was worthy of God that he should wish to become a human being and burden himself with the weakness of the flesh, subjecting himself to passions, pain, and death—as though it were not easy for him to reveal himself to human beings without the frailty of a body and to teach them justice, if indeed that was what he wished, with greater authority, as one openly professing himself God. For then, they say, everyone would have obeyed the heavenly precepts [Col. 0518B] if the might and power of God, who issued them, had accompanied them. Why, then, they ask, did he not come as God to teach human beings? Why did he make himself so lowly and weak that he could be both despised and punished by human beings? Why did he suffer violence at the hands of weak mortals? Why did he not either repel human hands by his power or elude them through his divinity? Why did he not reveal his majesty at least in the very moment of death? Instead, he was led to judgment as one powerless, condemned as one guilty, and killed as one mortal.

I shall refute these claims carefully and shall permit no one to remain in error. For those events were accomplished according to a great and marvelous rationale; [Col. 0519A] whoever [Col. 0519A]

[Note: [Col. 0519C] [Various Editors’ Notes on columns 519–520]

**Whoever.** I have restored this from manuscripts 2 Bon., Regio-Put., 6 other Reg., 6 Colb., the Leipzig manuscripts, and ten other recent manuscripts, as well as the old Roman edition, Cellar., and Walch., referring it, of course, to the “marvelous rationale.” 2 Reg., Cauc., Jun., and fifteen printed editions have “which things,” referring it to the events.

**Gives human beings precepts for life.** Thus restored by me from the old Roman editions, Paris 1525, Crat., the old French translation, and all the manuscripts except 2 Reg. rec.; in these, as also in fifteen commonly received editions, the reading is “and life.”

**Among whom he lives.** It is preferable to confirm this from Lactantius himself rather than from others: book IV, chapter 27, “When he lived among human beings”; *On the Anger of God*, chapter 1, “Living in mortal flesh”; *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 10, beginning, “When he lived in the regions of the East.” **BUN.**

**Among whom he lives; he himself must live in the same way.** [Col. 0519D] Eleven recent manuscripts have “he himself dwells”; six recent manuscripts, “let him dwell.” “Dwells” or “let him dwell” appears to be a gloss on *agit* (“lives”), which is the reading of the oldest manuscripts. Thus the same author says below, at the beginning of chapter 27: “When he lived among human beings.” For St. John Chrysostom says: “He who speaks differently from the way he has lived teaches how God ought to punish him.” And in these latter centuries the Count of Mirandola says that each person knows only as much as he puts into practice.

**Bind.** I have thus restored the text from all the manuscripts and from three old Roman editions, as well as Cellar. and Walch.; the term is appropriate because it is opposed to “undoes.” “To bind” and “to undo” are indeed more properly opposed than “to establish” and “to undo,” which occur in thirteen printed editions.—Compare Cicero, *For Cluentius*, chapter 57: “Lest under that law, from whose judicial investigation he thinks himself released and free, he should be bound by a small number of judges.” Lactantius himself, book IV, chapter 24: “So that by fulfilling his own precepts in deeds, he may constrain others by the necessity of obedience.” **BUN.**

**Will reply.** Restored by me from the two old Bonon. manuscripts, 7 Reg., 5 Vatican, Colb., 3 Lips., and six others. Cauc. and the Betul. edition have “may reply”; three recent manuscripts have “replied”; three other recent manuscripts and the printed editions, “will reply.” [Col. 0520C]

**You forbid pain; you forbid the fear of death.** Eleven recent manuscripts have “pain or death”; six old editions and 2 Reg., “he says, death”; 1 Reg. rec., “you forbid grieving; you forbid the fear of death.”

**Will do.** Thus the Sangerm. manuscript and the editions of Cellarius and others; many have “may do.”

**Hence.** Restored from eight old editions and all the manuscripts, except 4 Reg., 1 Colb., and ten commonly received editions, which have “thence.”

**They prefer examples to words.** “Deeds” (*τὰ ἔργα*) have greater power for the conversion of others than “mere words” (*ψιλοὶ λόγοι*), says Chrysostom, Homily 19 on the Epistle to the Hebrews. “The voice of deeds is more effective than that of speech,” says Bernard. “The manner of living has more force than the manner of speaking,” Augustine, Epistle 112. “It is best to teach by example rather than by sayings,” Hilary, chapter 5 on Matthew. **JOHANN GERHARD.**—I shall add our own Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, book III, [Col. 0520D] chapter 16: “Those who merely teach and do not act themselves deprive their own precepts of weight. . . . It is good to prescribe what is right and honorable; but unless you also do it, this is falsehood, and it is inconsistent and absurd to possess goodness not in the heart but only upon the lips.” And St. Leo, pope, says in his sermon on fasting: “Examples are more powerful than words, and teaching is conveyed more fully by deed than by voice.”

**Would that, indeed.** I have thus correctly restored the text from very many manuscripts and printed editions, because of the “but” that follows. Three Reg. and seven commonly received editions have “and would that.” In 1 Lips., “indeed” is omitted.

**Had existed.** Restored from the two oldest Bonon. manuscripts, Cauc., 8 Reg., Jun., 4 Colb., eleven others, and three printed editions; 2 Reg., 2 Colb., and eight commonly received editions read “exists.”

**The highest virtue and perfect justice agreed with the highest learning and knowledge.** I am extraordinarily pleased by Betuleius’s reading: “the highest learning and knowledge, the highest virtue and perfect justice,” which Sparkius deservedly reproduced. The alternative is found in all the manuscripts and the remaining editions. Traces of the true reading occur in Emman.: “In whom the highest degree of learning and knowledge.” **BUN.**

**Agreed.** Lactantius likes to speak thus throughout. Two recent manuscripts and recent editions have the plural, “agreed.”]

perceives it will not only cease to be amazed that God was tormented by human beings, but will also easily perceive that he could not even have been believed to be God if the very things criticized by these people had not occurred.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On Teaching and Acting

Whoever gives human beings precepts for life and shapes the character of others—should he himself, I ask, do what he prescribes, or should he not? If he does not do it, his precepts are nullified. For if the things prescribed are good, if they establish human life in its best condition, the teacher himself ought not to separate himself from the number and fellowship of the human beings among whom he lives; he himself must live in the same way in which he teaches that one ought to live, lest, if he lives otherwise, he himself detract from the credibility of his precepts [Col. 0519B] and weaken his teaching by undoing in practice what he strives to bind by words.

For whenever anyone hears a person issuing precepts, he is unwilling to have the necessity of obedience imposed upon him, as though his right to liberty were being taken away. He therefore replies to the teacher in this manner: “I cannot do what you command because it is impossible. You forbid me to become angry, you forbid me to desire, you forbid me to be stirred by lust, you forbid pain, you forbid the fear of death. But this is so contrary to nature that every living creature is subject to these passions. Or, if you think that nature can indeed be resisted, then do yourself what you prescribe, so that I may know that it can be done. But when you yourself do not do it, what arrogance is this, that you wish to impose upon a free human being laws which you yourself do not obey? [Col. 0519C] Learn first, you who teach, and correct your own character before you correct that of others. [Col. 0520A]”

Who would deny that this reply is just? Indeed, such a teacher will even fall into contempt and will in turn be mocked, because he will seem to be mocking others himself.

What, then, will that instructor do if these objections are raised against him? How will he deprive the recalcitrant of their excuse unless he teaches them by present deeds that what he teaches is possible? Hence it happens that no one obeys the precepts of the philosophers. For human beings prefer examples to words, because speaking is easy, while performance is difficult. Would that as many people acted well as speak well. But those who prescribe without acting possess no credibility. If they are human beings, they will be despised as frivolous; if the teacher is God, the excuse of human frailty will be raised against him. It remains, therefore, that words should be confirmed by deeds, [Col. 0520B] something the philosophers are unable to do. Accordingly, since those instructors are themselves overcome by the passions which they proclaim ought to be overcome, they can train no one in the virtue that they falsely proclaim. For this reason, they think that no perfect wise person has yet existed—that is, one in whom the highest virtue and perfect justice agreed with the highest learning and knowledge. This was indeed true. For since the foundation of the world no such person has existed except Christ, who both delivered wisdom by his word and confirmed his teaching by his actual virtue.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Refutation of the Arguments Raised Above

Come, then; let us now consider whether a teacher sent from heaven can fail to be perfect. [Col. 0520C] I am not yet speaking of this one whom they deny to have come from God. [Col. 0521A] Let us suppose that someone is to be sent from heaven to instruct human life in the rudiments of virtue and form it toward justice. No one can doubt that this teacher, who is sent from heaven, must be perfect both in knowledge of all things and in virtue, lest there be no difference between a heavenly teacher and an earthly one. For teaching that is innate and proper to a human being can in no way exist. The mind, enclosed in earthly organs and obstructed by the body’s corruption, can neither comprehend by itself nor grasp the truth unless it is taught from elsewhere. [Col. 0521A]

[Note: [Col. 0521C] [Various Editors’ Notes on columns 521–522]

**Unless it is taught from elsewhere.** Because flesh and blood, according to Christ himself, do not reveal mysteries to us.

[Col. 0521D] **For himself.** This word is absent from the editions of 1476, 1497, 1513, and 1515.

**And yet leaves liberty, etc.** He attributes to free will what belongs to it; but without divine assistance human beings cannot merit eternal life. For we do not conquer sins because Christ is an example, but because he supplies strength—unless, perhaps, by the “extension of the hand” one wishes to understand the power of Christ’s Spirit.

**And punishment for those who do not obey, because they could have obeyed if they had wished.** These words are absent from twelve manuscripts and three printed editions, but they appear necessary.

**Which becomes angry, which grieves, which fears to die.** This is the reading of the Bonon. manuscripts, Regio-Put., 6 Colb., very many others, and fourteen commonly received editions. In 1 Reg., which is very ancient, and in another Reg. manuscript, the reading is, “which becomes angry, which to grieve, which fears to die.” In the editions of Thom., Thys., and Gall., “which to become angry, which grieves,” incorrectly and contrary to the connection of the words.

**And so I am carried along against my will, etc.** Yet Paul too complains of this. For in Romans 7:15 [Col. 0522C] he writes: “For the good that I will, I do not do; but the evil that I hate, that I do.” The will to do good was indeed present within him [Col. 0522D], but he did not find in his own powers the capacity to perform it. But in the following chapter, verse 3: “What was impossible for the law, in that it was weakened through the flesh, God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and concerning sin, condemned sin in the flesh,” etc.

**Will confute.** This is the reading of the manuscripts and the Tornes. edition. “Will refute” is the reading of one Colb. manuscript and the printed editions.

**Become as like a human being as possible.** Nine manuscripts and the printed editions have “entirely like human beings.” 1 Bonon. antiq. and Ultr. have “entirely like a human being.” Jun. has “like a human being.”

**Persistent.** That is, obstinate and persevering in the opinion he had advanced.

**Because one cannot live otherwise in this body.** The word “live,” which was absent from several editions, has been added. The Em. manuscript has, “because I cannot live otherwise.”

**Nor can a human being possess perfect teaching.** Manuscripts 2 Colb., 2 Lips., 2 Clarom., and the Tornes. edition have “of perfect teaching”; 1 Reg. antiq. and Em., “perfect in teaching”; 1 Colbert., “perfect teaching for a human being.”

(See below, col. 523, line 12.)]

And even if it could do so fully, the mind nevertheless cannot attain the highest virtue and resist all the vices whose material is contained within the bodily organs. It follows that an earthly teacher cannot be perfect. But a heavenly teacher—to whom divinity imparts knowledge and immortality imparts virtue [Col. 0521B]—must necessarily be perfect and consummate in teaching as in all other things. Yet that cannot happen at all unless he assumes a mortal body for himself.

The reason why it cannot happen is clear. For if he comes to human beings as God—to omit the fact that mortal eyes cannot behold and endure the radiance of his majesty—God himself certainly will not be able to teach virtue, because, being without a body, he will not do the things he teaches, and through this his teaching will not be perfect. Otherwise, if the highest virtue consists in patiently enduring pain for justice and duty; if it is virtue not to fear death itself when threatened, and to bear it courageously when inflicted—then that perfect teacher must both teach these things by prescribing them and confirm them by doing them. For whoever gives precepts for living ought to cut off every avenue of excuse [Col. 0521C], so that he may impose upon human beings the necessity of obedience—not by any force, but by shame—and yet leave them liberty, so that both a reward may be appointed for those who obey, because they could have refused to obey if they had wished, and punishment for those who do not obey, because they could have obeyed if they had wished.

How, then, can an excuse be cut off unless the one who teaches does what he teaches, goes ahead like a guide, and extends his hand to the one who will follow? But how can he do what he teaches if he is not like the person whom he teaches? For if he is subject to no passion, [Col. 0522A] a human being can reply to him as teacher in this way:

“I certainly wish not to sin, but I am overcome; for I am clothed in frail and weak flesh. It is this which desires, which becomes angry, which grieves, which fears to die. And so I am carried along against my will and sin, not because I wish to, but because I am compelled. I myself perceive that I am sinning, but the necessity of frailty drives me on, and I cannot resist it.”

What will that instructor in justice reply to these things? How will he confute and convict a person who uses the flesh as an excuse for his offenses, unless the teacher himself has been clothed in flesh, so that he may show that even flesh can attain virtue? For obstinacy cannot be convicted except by example. The things you teach cannot possess firmness unless you have first done them yourself, because human nature, being prone to vice, wishes to appear to sin not merely with pardon but even with reason. [Col. 0522B]

It is necessary for the master and teacher of virtue to become as like a human being as possible, so that by conquering sin he may teach a human being that sin can be conquered by him. But if he is immortal, he can in no way provide an example for a human being. For some persistent person will arise and say:

“You do not sin because you are free from this body; you do not desire because nothing is necessary for one who is immortal. But I need many things to preserve this life. You do not fear death because it has no power over you. You despise pain because you cannot be affected by any force. But I, being mortal, fear both because they inflict upon me the most grievous torments, which the weakness of the flesh cannot endure.”

Therefore, the teacher of virtue also had to remove this excuse from human beings, lest anyone attribute his sin to necessity rather than to his own fault [Col. 0522C]. Accordingly, for him to be perfect, nothing should be capable of being raised against him by the person who is to be taught. Thus, if the latter should happen to say, “You prescribe impossible things,” he may reply, “See, I myself do them.”

“But I am clothed in flesh, whose peculiar property is to sin.”

“And I bear the same flesh, and yet sin does not rule in me.”

“It is difficult for me to despise wealth, because one cannot live otherwise in this body.”

“See, I too have a body, and yet I fight against every desire.”

“I cannot endure either pain or death for justice because I am frail.”

“See, [Col. 0523A] pain and death have power over me too, and I conquer the very things you fear, so that I may make you a conqueror of pain and death. I go first through the things you claim cannot be endured. If you cannot follow one who commands, follow one who goes before you.”

In this manner every excuse is removed, and a human being must confess that it is through his own fault that he is unjust if he does not follow the teacher of virtue, who is also his guide.

You see, then, how much more perfect a mortal teacher is than an immortal one: a mortal can be a guide to one who is mortal, whereas one who is not subject to passions cannot teach endurance. Yet the point of this is not that I should prefer a human being to God, but that I may show that neither can a human being possess perfect teaching unless he is also God, so that by heavenly authority he may impose upon human beings the necessity of obedience; nor can God possess it unless he is clothed in a mortal body, so that by fulfilling his own precepts in deeds he may constrain others by the necessity of obedience. It is therefore plainly apparent that the one who is the guide of life [Col. 0523B]

[Note: [Col. 0523C] [Various Editors’ Notes on columns 523–524]

**Who is the guide of life.** He is not merely the guide of life and the teacher of justice, but also its giver; indeed, he is life and justice itself.

**Unless it has a root, etc.** I follow 6 Reg., 6 Colb., nine other manuscripts, and eleven old editions. Three Reg. manuscripts and six commonly received editions have “and has,” with “unless it has” deleted. But Heumann reads “which has.”

**And stable.** Manuscripts 2 Lips. and Goth., and the Roman edition of 1474 and Venice 1490, have “which, stable.”

**And receive into himself the virtue of which he is the teacher.** Thus very many manuscripts, including the oldest, together with nine printed editions. Eight recent manuscripts and five printed editions have, “receive the teacher’s virtue, so that he may.”

**Let them learn.** Some printed editions have “let them say.”

**Mortality.** That is, mortals, or human beings. Curtius also uses the word in this sense, book VIII.

**Be subjected to torment.** Thus all the manuscripts together with six printed editions, except one Colb., which has in the first hand “be fastened by torment” [Col. 0523D], and in the second “be afflicted”; five old printed editions have “be fastened to the cross”; Crat., “be fastened upon a cross.”

**A living law.** Not in the sense in which Cicero said in book III of *On the Laws* that a law is a mute magistrate, while a magistrate is a living law, but as Paul speaks in Romans of “the law of the Spirit of life,” which—as had been foretold through the prophet—is written in the human heart and makes a person eager. Concerning this life-giving law it is thus written in Romans 8. **BETUL.**

**A new temple.** For, as Paul says in Hebrews 8:2, Jesus is the minister of the sanctuary and of the true tabernacle.

**That even in a human being he was heavenly, etc.** Thomasius nevertheless notes that the ancient Bologna codex reads, “that even that human being was heavenly,” etc. The sense of those words is clear and manifest, and fits this passage especially well.

**Without the agency of a begetter.** Two Lips. manuscripts have “without the agency of a begetter,” incorrectly. Book I, chapter 7: “Since God . . . can beget sons without the use and agency [Col. 0524C] of a woman.” Book IV, chapter 13: “He was begotten in a virgin’s womb without a father’s function.” **BUN.**

**Spiritual.** The Aldine, Fasit., and Thys. editions have “special,” corruptly; Thomas has “heavenly.” Betuleius correctly observes that “spiritual” should be read in place of “special.” The error arose from manuscript abbreviations.

**The mother of his body was a virgin.** Against Valentinus, Apollinaris, Eutyches, and others who denied that Christ received anything from the Virgin Mary. See Irenaeus, book III, *Against Heresies*; St. Augustine, *On Heresies*; Theodoret, *Heretical Fables*, book IV, at the end.

**Intermediate.** Again in the *Epitome*, chapter 44: “Made intermediate between God and a human being.” This is more elegantly expressed than “mediator.” A more refined age—though not the most ancient—also called *τὸν μεσίτην* (“the mediator”) “the one intermediate,” according to Salmasius in his *Plinian Exercises*, fol. 462. **BUN.**

[Col. 0524D] **Μεσίτην.** Others translate it “mediator,” a word employed in sacred matters and much better than Erasmus’s translation “reconciler.” 1 Timothy 2: “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus” (*Εἷς γὰρ Θεός, εἷς καὶ μεσίτης Θεοῦ καὶ ἀνθρώπων, ἄνθρωπος Χριστὸς Ἰησοῦς*), etc. And in the Epistle to the Hebrews he is called, in more than one place, “mediator of the new covenant” (*μεσίτης διαθήκης τῆς καινῆς*). And in Galatians 3 it says that a “mediator” (*μεσίτην*) is not of one. Augustine teaches what the office of a mediator is in *The City of God*, book IX, chapter 15, as does Epiphanius in the *Ancoratus*. **BETUL.**—See Suicerus in the *Thesaurus*, under the word *μεσίτην*.

**To immortality.** That is, to blessedness and immortal glory.

**To earn by works of justice.** Correctly, “to earn”—that is, to acquire or obtain—by works of justice, so that the spirit may become eternal, that is, be endowed with blessed immortality; book III, chapter 19. For a more exact understanding of these things, the following words from book VII, chapter 5 should be read carefully: “So that we may either lose that true and perpetual life through vice or earn it through virtue.” **BUN.**]

and teacher of justice ought to be corporeal; nor can his teaching be full and perfect in any other way, unless it has a root and foundation and remains stable and fixed among human beings. He himself must undergo the weakness of flesh and body and receive into himself the virtue of which he is the teacher, so that he may teach it both by words and by deeds. Likewise, he must be subject to death and every passion, since the duties of virtue are exercised both in enduring suffering and in undergoing death. As I have said, the consummate teacher must endure all these things so that he may teach that they can be endured.
