## CHAPTER XXV. On Jesus’ Advent in Flesh and Spirit, So That He Might Be the Mediator Between God and Humanity

Let human beings therefore learn and understand why the supreme God, when sending his delegate and messenger to train mortals in the precepts of his justice, wished him to be clothed in mortal flesh, subjected to torment, and punished with death. For since there was no justice on earth, he sent a teacher as a kind of living law, so that he might establish a new name and temple and sow true and devout worship throughout the whole earth by word and example.

Yet, so that it would be certain that he had been sent by God, he ought not to have been born as a human being is born, formed from two mortal parents; [Col. 0524B] rather, so that it might be apparent that even in a human being he was heavenly, he was created without the agency of a begetter. For he had God as his spiritual father; and just as the father of his spirit was God without a mother, so the mother of his body was a virgin without a father.

He was therefore both God and a human being, established as one intermediate between God and humanity. Hence the Greeks call him *μεσίτης* (“mediator”), so that he might be able to lead humanity to God—that is, to immortality. For if he had been God alone, as was said above, he could not have provided a human being with examples of virtue; if he had been a human being alone, he could not have compelled human beings toward justice unless authority and a power greater than the human were added.

For since a human being consists of flesh and spirit, and the spirit ought to earn through works of justice that it may become [Col. 0525A] eternal, the flesh—because it is earthly and therefore mortal—drags the spirit joined to it along with itself and leads it away from immortality toward death. Therefore, a spirit devoid of flesh could in no way serve as a guide for a human being toward immortality, because the flesh hinders the spirit from following God. For it is frail and subject to sin, while sin is the food of death. [Col. 0525A]

[Note: [Col. 0525C] [Various Editors’ Notes on columns 525–526]

**Sin is the food of death.** That is, the nourishment of evils that engender the death of the soul.

**And might snatch away.** I have deleted “so that,” which is inserted by manuscripts 1 Bonon., Lips., Pal., and Cant., and by an equal number of printed editions, but is absent from all the other manuscripts and printed editions.

**Dominion over the flesh.** I follow nearly all the manuscripts and printed editions. [Col. 0525D] Three Reg. and five printed editions read “in the flesh”; Jun. and two old Roman editions, Paris, Crat., and Graph., “condemnation against the flesh.”

**Nor dominion.** Entirely correct; Betuleius formerly and Heumann more recently judged that it should be read thus. It has accordingly been restored, book II, chapter 5: “Nor can a house possess dominion over itself.” Likewise book II, chapter 12: “The soul commands . . . by the rule of the mind”; and especially, “The soul, which possesses dominion over the body.” **BUN.**

**Imparts the reward of immortality.** Two Bonon. manuscripts and four recent editions insert “to us.” Three recent manuscripts and seven printed editions have, “imparts the reward of immortality that we must seek.” Three recent manuscripts and six commonly received editions have the variant verb “shares.” Thomasius correctly observes that the word “to be sought” should be deleted, because if he imparts immortality as a reward, it is then not to be sought, since no one seeks what he possesses. Heumann wishes “to us” to be added after “reward.”

**Preferred.** Heumann reads “wished,” with the Em. manuscript, because there is no comparison here.—“Preferred to undergo.” The verb “prefer” is often used without being followed by the comparative particle “than.” Heumann himself certainly recognized this [Col. 0526C] below: “Why God preferred the cross.” Thus book VI, chapter 17: “When compelled . . . to betray the faith, let us prefer to undergo death.” Ibid., chapter 21: “Whoever prefers temporal things will be deprived of eternal things.” Book VII, chapter 1: “Without doubt they prefer that it be fictitious.” **BUNEMANN.**

**Which preceded as true concerning Christ.** The reading of absolutely all the books appears sound to me in this sense: the prophetic divination concerning [Col. 0526D] Christ that preceded the event was true—that is, certain and confirmed by the outcome, not doubtful, deceptive, or false. **BUN.**

**Significance.** The word is African. See Faber in the *Lexicon*. The same occurs immediately below and in chapter 28: “Glosses.” “Significance,” *Σημασία*. Fabius Victorinus, preface to book I of Cicero’s *On Invention*: “An art is that which does not possess significance of itself”; “this word has a threefold generic significance.” The Jun. and Lips. manuscripts and the editions have “signification.”

**Signified.** See Mark 8 and 10; Luke 4, 7, and 14.

**Opened.** See Matthew 11, Mark 7, Luke 7.

**Only this far.** That is, “only this much.” See the note on the *Epitome*, chapter 68, and *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 10. The margin of Paris 1513 interprets “only this far” as “only for the present time.” **BUN.**

**Marvelous.** Matthew 9 and 15; Mark 7.

**Feet.** See Matthew 11, 15, and 21; Luke 7.

**Affliction.** See Matthew 8 and 11; Mark 1; Luke 7.

**Sufferers from elephantiasis.** I have restored this reading on the authority of the oldest and best manuscript codices: 2 Bonon., 6 Reg., Cauc., Jun., 2 Colbert., 2 Lips., 1 Sorbon., Ultr., Pal., 1 Clarom., Brun. In 2 Reg., 1 Colbert., and 1 Clarom. the reading is “those afflicted with elephantiasis”; in two other Reg., [Col. 0527C] 1 Lips., 3 Colb., three old Roman editions, and thirteen other printed editions, “elephantiacs.” “Sufferers from elephantiasis,” or “elephantiacs,” are those commonly called lepers, who are often mentioned in the Gospel. See Pliny, book XXVI, chapter 1; Celsus, book III, chapter 25.]

For this reason the mediator came—that is, God in the flesh—so that the flesh might be able to follow him and he might snatch the human being, over whose flesh death possesses dominion, away from death. He therefore clothed himself in flesh so that, by subduing the desires of the flesh, he might teach that sinning is not a matter of necessity but of purpose and will.

For our one great and principal struggle is with the flesh. Its boundless desires oppress the soul and do not permit it to retain dominion; instead, they enslave it to pleasures [Col. 0525B] and seductive delights and subject it to eternal death. So that we might be able to resist these things, God both opened and showed us the way to overcome the flesh. This virtue, perfect and complete in every respect, imparts to the victors the crown and reward of immortality.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On Jesus’ Cross and His Other Torments, and on the Figure of the Lamb Prescribed by the Law
I have spoken of humility, frailty, and suffering, and why God preferred to undergo these things; now an account must be given of the cross itself, and its power explained. What the supreme Father ordained from the beginning, and how he ordered everything that was done, is taught not only by the prophetic foretelling [Col. 0525C] that came beforehand and proved true concerning Christ, but also by the very rationale of his Passion. For none of the things that he suffered was without purpose; rather, they possessed a figurative character and profound significance, just as did those divine works that he performed. Their force and power were effective in the present, but they also disclosed something that was to come.

The heavenly power opened the eyes of the blind and [Col. 0526A] restored light to those who could not see. By this deed it signified that, when he turned to the nations that did not know God, he would illuminate the hearts of the foolish with the light of wisdom and open the eyes of their hearts to contemplate the truth. For those who do not see heavenly things, but are surrounded by the darkness of ignorance and worship earthly and perishable things, are truly blind.

He opened the ears of the deaf. That heavenly power was certainly not operative only to that extent; rather, it disclosed that before long those who were without the truth would both hear and understand the divine words of God. For those who do not hear heavenly and true things, and the things that must be done, may truly be called deaf.

His wondrous power loosened the tongues of the mute for speech, even while the deed was being performed; but this power contained another significance, indicating that those who had until recently been ignorant of heavenly things would soon, after receiving the discipline of wisdom, discourse [Col. 0526B] about God and the truth. For one who does not know the rational account of divinity is truly speechless and mute, even if he is the most eloquent of all. Only when the tongue begins to speak the truth—that is, to interpret the power and majesty of the one God—does it at last perform its natural function. But so long as it speaks falsehood, it is not fulfilling its proper use; and therefore one who cannot utter divine things must necessarily be an infant.

The praiseworthy might of the divine work also restored the feet of the lame to the function of walking; but the figure contained this meaning: that once the errors of worldly and wayward life had been restrained, the path of truth would be opened, along which human beings might walk to obtain the grace of God. For the person who, entangled in the gloom and darkness of foolishness and ignorant of where he is going, proceeds with stumbling and [Col. 0526C] falling steps along the road of death must truly be regarded as lame.

Likewise, no insignificant works of immortal power cleansed away the sores and stains of defiled bodies; but this power portended that his teaching would purify, by instruction in righteousness, those defiled by the sores of sins and the stains of vices. For those whom either endless [Col. 0527A] desires drive to crimes or insatiable pleasures drive to outrages, branding them with stains of disgrace and afflicting them with an everlasting corruption, must truly be regarded as leprous and elephantiasic.

He raised the prostrate bodies of the dead and, calling them by their names, summoned them back from death. [Col. 0527A]

> **Note: [Col. 0527C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 527–528]**
>
> **Summoned them back from death.** See Matthew 9; Mark 5; Luke 7; John 11.
>
> **Added everlasting times.** Thus nearly all the manuscripts and printed editions. *Everlasting* is absent from four Regius manuscripts and eleven common editions. The Emmanuel manuscript has *of everlasting*.—**Added times.** Heumann, adding *and*, reads as the Emmanuel manuscript does: “Added, and revealed the mysteries of everlasting death.” **Bunemann.**
>
> **In damaged bodies.** The editors could have learned the force of the word from later in this [Col. 0527D] chapter, where an intact body is contrasted with a damaged and diminished body. **Bunemann.**
>
> **In damaged and afflicted bodies.** Correctly; that is, in mutilated, enfeebled, and diseased bodies. Two recent Regius manuscripts and nine printed editions have *undamaged*, corruptly; Betuleius’ edition has *and distressed*.—**And afflicted.** *Afflicted bodies* are diseased bodies. Thus Seneca often writes; for example, *To Polybius*, ch. 32: “To heal one who is ill and afflicted”; *On Benefits* IV.11: “So afflicted that he has no hope of recovery.” **Bunemann.**
>
> **Displayed.** I restored this from thirty-five manuscripts. The Caucasus manuscript, two recent Regius manuscripts, and nineteen editions have *applied*. **Works of a power not earthly.** This “power not earthly” is described in other words earlier in this chapter: “heavenly power”; likewise, “heavenly force”; likewise, “wondrous power”; likewise, “the praiseworthy might of the divine work”; likewise, “no insignificant works of immortal power”; likewise, “inexpressible power.” **Bunemann.**
>
> **Might display works of a power not earthly.** Thus the three very ancient Regius manuscripts. Nine manuscripts and five common editions [Col. 0528C] place *to us* before the negation. In seven manuscripts and fourteen printed editions, *not* is absent and the reading is *earthly*.
>
> **Therefore.** He will now explain the figures of the Passion of Jesus Christ.
>
> **Promised.** Thus the manuscripts and printed editions; Lactantius uses the same manner of expression throughout. Francius thought that *they promised* should be read, as in three recent Regius manuscripts.
>
> **Token.** Two Regius manuscripts have *appearance*.
>
> **For “crown” is used, etc.** Festus Pompeius thinks the word derives from *chorus*, with the aspirate removed, of course. Cicero uses the word *corona* in this sense in the opening itself of *For Milo*; Livy uses it of an armed gathering. **Betuleius.**
>
> **Chosen, therefore, from thorn bushes.** The Regius-Puteanus manuscript reads: “For those chosen [Col. 0528D] from thorn bushes”; eleven recent manuscripts and four common editions, *struck*—in what sense? Betuleius’ edition has *interwoven*.—**From thorn bushes and brambles.** He has correctly joined the terms, as Virgil does in *Aeneid* IX.380–81, whom he imitates:
>
> “And they ring every approach with a guard.
>
> There was a wood, widely bristling, black with thorn bushes and holm oak,
>
> which dense brambles had filled on every side.”
>
> **Bunemann.**
>
> **And by deeds performed in the present.** I added *and* from almost all the manuscripts and printed editions. These words are absent from the Regius-Puteanus manuscript.
>
> **Might attain.** Some printed editions have *attains*.
>
> **Was embodied.** That is, he assumed a body. He uses the same verb twice in Book II, ch. 10, as does Tertullian in *On the Flesh of Christ*, chs. 3 and 6. Hence, in the same author’s Book IV, *embodiment* means the assumption of humanity. **Barthius.**
>
> **Pattern.** That is, an example. Cicero, *Laws* III.3: “Let that order be free from fault; let it be a pattern for the rest.” Quintilian, *Institutes* III.1: “Marcus Tullius … provided among us the sole pattern of oratory.” **Bunemann.**
>
> **He endured, etc.** He omits what was most important: namely, [Col. 0529C] that the cross has God’s curse attached to it. But Christ had to be accursed so that we might be justified. **Rivet.**

What could be more fitting for God? What could be more worthy of the wonder of all ages than to restore a life that had run its course, and, when human spans had been completed, to add everlasting ages and reveal the mysteries of death? But this inexpressible power was an image of a greater power, showing that his teaching would possess such force that the nations throughout the whole world—which, estranged from God, had been subject to death—would be given life through the knowledge of the true light and attain the rewards of immortality. For those who, not knowing God the giver of life and dragging their souls down from heaven to earth, fall into the snares of eternal death may rightly be regarded as dead. [Col. 0527B]

The things, therefore, that he was then doing in the present were images of things to come. What he displayed in damaged and afflicted bodies bore a figure of spiritual things, so that he might both display in the present works of a power not earthly and demonstrate for the future the power of his heavenly majesty.

Therefore, just as his works also possessed the significance of a greater power, so too his Passion did not occur as something simple, superfluous, or accidental. Rather, just as the things he did signified the great power and efficacy of his teaching, so the things he suffered announced that wisdom would be hated. For the drink of vinegar and the food of gall promised bitterness and harshness in this life to the followers of truth. And although the Passion itself, bitter and harsh in its own right, gave us a token of the future [Col. 0527C] torments that virtue itself sets before those who remain in this world, nevertheless that kind of drink and food entering the mouth of our teacher furnished us with an example of afflictions, [Col. 0528A] hardships, and miseries. All these things must necessarily be borne and endured by those who follow the truth, since truth is bitter and hated by all who, devoid of virtue, devote their lives to deadly pleasures.

The crown of thorns placed upon his head declared that he would gather for himself a divine people from among harmful persons. For *corona* (“crown”) is also the name for a people standing in a circle. But before the knowledge of God, we were unrighteous: we were thorns—that is, evil and harmful—ignorant of what was good, estranged from the knowledge and works of righteousness, and defiling everything with crime and lust. Chosen, therefore, from thorn bushes and brambles, we encircle the holy head of God; for, summoned by him and gathered around him on every side, we stand beside God as our master and teacher, and we crown him as the king [Col. 0528B] of the world and the Lord of all living things.

As for the cross, it possesses great power and meaning, which I shall now attempt to demonstrate. For when God—as I explained above—had determined to liberate humankind, he sent a teacher of virtue to the earth, who would both shape human beings for innocence by saving precepts and, by works and deeds performed in the present, open the path of righteousness along which a person, walking and following his teacher, might attain eternal life.

He, therefore, was embodied and clothed in the garment of flesh so that he might furnish the human being whom he had come to teach with both examples of virtue and incentives toward it. But when he had provided a pattern of righteousness in all the duties of life, then, in order that he might also transmit to humanity the endurance of pain and contempt for death, by which virtue is made perfect and complete, he came into [Col. 0528C] the hands of an impious nation, although he could both have avoided them by the knowledge of the future that he possessed and repelled them by the same power with which he performed wonders. He therefore endured torments, lashes, and thorns. Finally, he did not refuse even to undergo [Col. 0529A] death, so that humanity, under his leadership, might triumph over death, subdued and chained together with its terrors. [Col. 0529A]

> **Note: [Col. 0529C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 529–530]**
>
> **Might triumph over death together with its terrors.** Similarly, at the end of Book VI, ch. 23, Lactantius says, “He will triumph over the earth”; elsewhere too he commonly says “to live life.”—**Might triumph over death together with its terrors.** With the accusative, as in VI.23: “He will triumph over the earth”; *Epitome*, ch. 46: “He triumphed over the captives”; and see my notes on *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, ch. 16: “You have triumphed over the age together with its terrors.” **Bunemann.**
>
> **Why by an infamous kind of punishment.** I restored these words from all the manuscripts and very many printed editions; they were absent from five common editions.—**Why by an infamous kind of punishment.** They appear to have fallen out of Gallaeus’ edition, for all my manuscripts and printed editions contain them. In the same sense in which he says *infamous* here, he says in IV.16, “a conspicuous punishment,” and in IV.30, “an execrable gibbet.” Arnobius, Book I, p. 20 at the beginning: “The gods are hostile to you for this reason … because you maintain that a man who was born, and who was put to death by the punishment of the cross—which is infamous for persons [Col. 0529D] of humble rank—was God.” **Bunemann.**
>
> **Unworthy of a free person.** For the cross was a punishment for slaves. Horace, *Satires* I.3; Juvenal, *Satire* 2: “Set up the cross for the slave”; Seneca, *On Clemency* I.26; Cicero, *Against Verres* V, where the Roman orator says: “Would you reserve for Roman citizens who had not been condemned the cross that you had set up for condemned slaves?” See also Julius Capitolinus in his *Opilius Macrinus*. **Faber.**
>
> **So that he might bring aid to the humble and lowest.** I restored this from the most ancient manuscripts—one Bononiensis, one Regius, two other Regius manuscripts of good quality—and four editions, as the following words also require. The same reading occurs below in those manuscripts and seven others. Twenty-two have *the weak*.
>
> **Whom on the third day.** Thus the printed editions together with almost all the manuscripts. Two Claromontanus manuscripts have “on the third day”;  one Regius manuscript of the highest quality and one Brunensis have “because on the third day.” But at John 19:36 a better reason is given: namely, that what was said in Exodus 12 and Numbers 9 might be fulfilled: “You shall not break a bone of it,” where the words concern the Passover lamb, which was a figure of Jesus dying. [Col. 0530C]
>
> **From the lower world.** One Claromontanus manuscript and the Brunensis have “from the dead,” which amounts to the same thing.
>
> **Foretelling his Passion beforehand.** This is the reading of the older and better manuscripts—two Bononiensis, the Regius-Puteanus, eleven others—and of nine editions. Eighteen recent manuscripts have “predicting beforehand,” since the prefix *prae-* means the same as “before.”
>
> **When, therefore, he had been fastened up, because he had relinquished his spirit.** I restored this from the most ancient manuscripts: one Regius, one Bononiensis, and two other Regius manuscripts. Sixteen recent manuscripts and two old editions have, “when he had voluntarily relinquished his spirit.” Two Regius manuscripts and the de Tournes edition, together with eight other editions, have, “when he had voluntarily relinquished his spirit”; the Canterbury manuscript has, “was relinquishing.”
>
> **Might be rendered incapable.** This is not a valid reason, for God, who created the body, was able to restore what was mutilated. This will also occur in the resurrection, when mutilated bodies will rise sound and whole.
>
> **Be raised up.** He appears here to allude to Christ’s own saying in John 12: “And I, if I am raised up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.”
>
> [Col. 0530D] **When they mark their doorposts with the blood of a lamb.** Cyprian understood it in this way too, in *Against the Jews* II §22, and Jerome on Isaiah 66, as did Lactantius.
>
> **A white lamb.** Exodus 12 says “without blemish,” referring not to color but to deformity, such as being lame, scabby, or afflicted by some other defect or disease. This is said of every victim in Leviticus 22. **Menochius.**
>
> **The firstborn.** I corrected this from all the manuscripts and printed editions except the Emmanuel and Canterbury manuscripts and five recent editions, in which the reading is “of the firstborn.” But *the firstborn* is also the correct reading, since the term embraces both human beings and livestock, according to Exodus 12:29.
>
> **Had been an image.** Although there were more than enough arguments by which the truth of the Christian religion could be confirmed, it must nevertheless be admitted that it was once customary among certain ecclesiastical writers to appropriate to their own cause everything that bore some appearance of truth—whether signs or prophecies, even when interpreted allegorically and mystically—as we see Lactantius doing here. Yet no one denies that the Passover lamb was a figure of the true Lamb, that is, of our Savior.
>
> **For the lamb.** This is the reading of all the manuscripts; the printed editions have, “for a lamb.”

Why, however, did the supreme Father choose precisely that kind of death and allow him to be subjected to it? The reason is this. Someone might perhaps say: “If he was God and wished to die, why was he not at least subjected to some honorable kind of death? Why specifically the cross? Why an infamous kind of punishment, one that seems unworthy even of a free person, though guilty?”

First, because he who had come in humility, in order to bring aid to the humble and lowest and to show everyone the hope of salvation, had to be subjected to the kind of punishment that the humble and lowest commonly suffer, so that there might be absolutely no one unable to imitate him. Second, so that the body of him who had to rise from the lower world on the third day might be preserved intact.

[Col. 0529B] No one should be ignorant of the fact that, in foretelling his Passion beforehand, he himself also made it known that he possessed the power to relinquish his spirit whenever he wished and to take it up again. Therefore, because he had relinquished his spirit while fastened to the cross, the executioners did not think it necessary to break his bones—as their custom required—but merely pierced his side. Thus his intact body was taken down from the gibbet and carefully enclosed in a tomb. All these things were done so that a damaged and diminished body might not be rendered incapable of rising again.

There was also another principal reason why God preferred [Col. 0530A] the cross: he had to be raised up upon it and the Passion of God had to become known to all nations. For since one who is suspended from a gibbet is both visible to everyone and elevated above the rest, the cross was chosen in preference to other punishments to signify that he would become so conspicuous and so exalted that all nations from the entire world would come together alike to know and worship him. In short, there is no nation so inhuman and no region so remote that either his Passion or the sublimity of his majesty is unknown to it.

During his Passion, therefore, he extended his hands and measured out the world, so as to show even then that a great people, gathered from all languages and tribes, would come under his wings from the rising of the sun to its setting, and would receive upon their foreheads that greatest and exalted sign.

[Col. 0530B] The Jews display a figure of this even now, when they mark their doorposts with the blood of a lamb. For when God was about to strike the Egyptians, in order to keep the Hebrews unharmed by that plague, he commanded them to sacrifice a white lamb without blemish and place a sign from its blood upon their doorposts. Accordingly, when the firstborn of the Egyptians perished in a single night, the Hebrews alone were protected by the sign of blood—not because the blood of an animal possessed such power in itself that it could bring salvation to human beings, but because it had been an image of things to come.

For the white lamb without blemish was Christ—that is, innocent, righteous, and [Col. 0531A] holy—who, sacrificed by those same Jews, is salvation for all who inscribe upon their own forehead the sign of his blood, that is, of the cross on which he shed his blood. [Col. 0531A]

> **Note: [Col. 0531B] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 531–532]**
>
> **On which he shed his blood.** Some printed editions have *which*, incorrectly.
>
> **Inscribe upon …** Elsewhere our author varies the expression in this way below: “to mark the sign … of blood upon the highest part of one’s body”; ch. 27: “to sign the forehead”; *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, ch. 10: “to place the immortal sign upon the forehead.” **Bunemann.**
>
> **It is called Passover, ἀπὸ τοῦ πάσχειν.** These Greek words are absent from the Bononiensis manuscript, one Colbertinus, the Junius manuscript, and the editions of Thomasius and Thysius. But because they are [Col. 0531C] found in the other manuscripts and printed editions, it seemed best not to omit them. Lactantius is mistaken, however, in thinking that *Pascha* is a Greek word, for it is Hebrew and derives from the verb *pāsaḥ*. That feast is celebrated in memory of the angel’s passing, when he passed through the land of the Egyptians, killing their firstborn but sparing the Israelites. **Gallaeus.**
>
> **So that it might be apparent.** I restored this from most of the better manuscripts and the early printed editions. Three Regius manuscripts, the Brunensis, and six editions have “so that it would have been apparent.”
>
> **All will be protected.** Seven manuscripts and six printed editions have “all people.”
>
> **Will have marked.** Nine manuscripts and six common editions have “have marked.”
>
> **How great the power of this sign is.** Thus the Regius-Puteanus manuscript and six others, with support from three other manuscripts and five editions, in which the reading is “concerning the power of this sign.” The celebrated Heumann likewise adopts this reading, because Cicero says “to explain concerning a certain matter.” Ten manuscripts and nine printed editions have simply “the power.”
>
> **How terrifying this sign is to demons.** See what follows [Col. 0531D] and below, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chs. 10 and 12.
>
> **And restored deranged human minds.** Thus the manuscripts and printed editions. Lactantius likewise writes in I.4, “Who, being of a deranged mind”; and in *On the Workmanship of God*. See Matthew 4; Mark 1; Luke 4.
>
> **The rites in no way produce favorable omens.** *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, ch. 10: “When they sacrifice animals and seek in their livers the things that are to come”—that is, future things—“they do not see the customary marks in the entrails.” Below: “The slaughtered victims reveal nothing.… The rites give no response.” **Bunemann.**
>
> **Nor can responses.** Virgil, *Georgics* III.491.
>
> **Certain attendants of ours, etc.** I restored *ours* from the Regius-Puteanus manuscript and seven other Regius manuscripts, the Bononiensis, two Claromontanus manuscripts, and the Brunensis, as well as the Fasitel edition. *Ours* means “from among us,” namely, from among the Christians; some printed editions incorrectly read “of our people.” One very ancient Regius manuscript has, “Certain attendants from among the worshipers of God”; the Aldine, Cratander, and Grapheus editions simply have, “Certain of our people, when attending those who were sacrificing.” “Certain attendants from among the worshipers of God” is the reading in Bunemann, who supplies the following note.—**Certain attendants from among the worshipers of God.** Thus it is written in two older Paris Regius manuscripts, [Col. 0532B] according to Nurrius in his dissertation on *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, p. 181. We have therefore preferred it to the other, more obscure readings, for it comes very close to the words at the beginning of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, ch. 10: “Certain attendants who knew the Lord”; and II.15: “They fear the righteous,” he says, “that is, the worshipers of God.” **Bunemann.**
>
> **Were attending their masters while they sacrificed.** The Gothanus manuscript alone has, “were attending the demons as they sacrificed.” I change nothing. It is the role of attendants to attend their masters. **Bunemann.**
>
> [Col. 0532C] **To portray future events in the entrails of the victims.** The Canterbury manuscript has “beasts.” *To portray* is used metaphorically for “to observe.”—**In the entrails of the victims.** Thus most manuscripts and printed editions; but the Canterbury manuscript and the Sublacensis, Rostock, Venice 1493 and 1497, and Paris editions have “in the entrails of beasts.” This too is correct, as in *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, ch. 10: “The emperor … an investigator of future events, sacrificed livestock and sought in their livers”—the livers of the livestock, that is, “in the entrails of beasts” in the present passage—“the things that were to come.” The matter comes to the same thing. **Bunemann.**
>
> **Sacrifice to them.** I read this from two Regius manuscripts, with the support of the Palatinus and four Oxford manuscripts, in which the reading is “were sacrificing.” Indeed, the ancients used this verb when sacrifices were under discussion. We read in Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 46: “Yet, at the very end, he ordered a cock to be sacrificed to Aesculapius.” Six Regius manuscripts, five Colbertinus manuscripts, four others, and four printed editions have “consecrate”; eleven manuscripts and the same number of printed editions have “had consecrated”; Junius and the Ultrajensis have “had consecrated.” In the *Epitome*, chs. 23 and 37, we read the verb *to dedicate* from the Turin manuscript.—[Col. 0532D] **To whom they sacrifice.** This is the genuine reading, because *prosecare* is a technical verb of sacrifice. Suetonius, *Augustus*, ch. 1: “When he was performing a sacred rite to Mars, he cut up the half-raw entrails after they had been snatched from the fire.” **Bunemann.**
>
> **Profane persons.** The haruspices here call Christians “profane persons,” just as in *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, ch. 10: “Because profane persons were present at the divine rites”—that is, Christians who were alien to the rites of the Gentiles. **Bunemann.**
>
> **Drove their rulers into a fury.** I read this with the two most ancient Regius manuscripts, another recent manuscript likewise Regius, and the editions of Fasitel, Thomasius, Isaeus, Thysius, Gallaeus, and Sparke. *Drove* stands for “impelled” or “forced,” a simple verb for a compound, as is customary in Lactantius. Twenty-one recent manuscripts and thirteen printed editions have “forced”; one recent Regius manuscript has “compelled”; one Sorbonicus, two Claromontanus manuscripts, and the Soubron edition have “forced the rulers themselves into a fury.”—**Forced their rulers into a fury.** Terence, *The Brothers* I.2: “You will drive me to madness.” I still lack examples from ancient writers in which they say “to drive into something,” for they generally repeat the same preposition *ad*. Lactantius expresses it differently in V [Col. 0533C].21: “They incite the ignorant to fury”; and VII.20: “To rouse their minds to fury.” **Bunemann.**

For the forehead is the highest doorpost of the human being, and wood smeared with blood signifies the cross. In short, the sacrifice of the animal is called by those very people who perform it *Pascha* (“Passover”), ἀπὸ τοῦ πάσχειν, “from suffering,” because it is a figure of the Passion that God, with foreknowledge of the future, delivered through Moses for his people to celebrate. But at that time the figure was effective in the present to ward off danger, so that it might be apparent how greatly the truth itself will prevail in protecting the people of God amid the final crisis of the whole world. How, or amid what plague, all who have marked the sign of this true and divine blood upon the highest part of their body will be protected, I shall explain in the final book.

[Col. 0531B]

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the Wondrous Effects Produced by the Power of the Cross, and on Demons

For now it is enough to explain how great the power of this sign is. Anyone who has seen how far demons, when adjured through Christ, flee from the bodies they have possessed will know how terrifying this [Col. 0532A] sign is to them. For just as he himself, when he lived among human beings, drove away all demons by a word and restored human minds that had been deranged and driven into frenzy by evil assaults to their former senses, so now his followers drive those same unclean spirits out of human beings both by the name of their teacher and by the sign of his Passion.

Proof of this matter is not difficult. For when they sacrifice to their gods, if someone bearing a signed forehead is present, the rites in no way produce favorable omens.

Nor can the seer, when consulted, give responses.

And this was often the chief reason why evil kings persecuted righteousness. For when certain attendants of ours were attending their masters while they sacrificed, by placing the sign [Col. 0532B] upon their foreheads they put those masters’ gods to flight, so that they could not portray future events in the entrails of the victims. When the haruspices understood this, under the instigation of those same demons to whom they sacrifice, they complained that profane persons were present at the sacred rites and drove their rulers into a fury, [Col. 0533A] so that they might overthrow God’s temple [Col. 0533A] and contaminate themselves with true sacrilege, which was to be expiated by the most grievous punishments inflicted upon the persecutors.

> **Note: [Col. 0533C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 533–534]**
>
> **So that they might overthrow God’s temple.** I corrected this from almost all the manuscripts and printed editions, correctly, as I think. “Overthrow God’s temple” means, namely, the temple at Nicomedia, which was destroyed by Diocletian and Maximian and is discussed in ch. 1 of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*. This chapter thus provides further confirmation that our Lactantius was the author of that work. One recent Regius manuscript and six editions read “cleanse”; one Vatican manuscript, “expiate.”
>
> **Which was to be expiated by the most grievous punishments of the persecutors.** On these, read our Lactantius’ *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*.

> [Col. 0533D] **Not out of fear.** I corrected this from all the manuscripts and several printed editions. Most common editions have “at a nod.”
>

> **Whom the immortal sign has fortified.** That is, the sign of the cross. The early Christians very frequently signed themselves with it, as Tertullian attests in *On the Crown*, §4: “At every advance and movement; at every entrance and departure; when dressing, putting on shoes, bathing, approaching tables, lighting lamps, going to beds, sitting down—whatever activity occupies us—we wear away our forehead with the seal of the cross.” See also his *Against Marcion* III.18; Augustine, *Confessions* I.11.17; *Tractates on John* III.2, on John 1; and frequently elsewhere. He likewise explains in *Exposition IV of Psalm 30*, §7, and on Psalm 50, §1: “But if Christians in the circus happen for some reason to become afraid, they immediately sign themselves and stand there bearing upon their forehead what they would leave that place if they bore it in their heart.” See below, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, ch. 10.

>

>
> **With the demons.** That is, with the *genii*.

The Ultrajensis manuscript has “throughout a different region”; one Regius, one Lipsiensis, and the Brunensis have “throughout different regions”; one ancient Bononiensis, “throughout the various religions”; the Palatinus and one Lipsiensis, “throughout a different religion”; four recent Regius manuscripts, four Colbertinus manuscripts, and five others, together with seven common editions, have “by perverse religion.”

Yet blind human beings cannot understand from this very fact either that this is the true religion, since it possesses such great power to conquer, or that the other is false, since it cannot stand firm or enter into conflict.

But they say that the gods do this not out of fear, but out of hatred—as though anyone could hate someone unless that person either harmed him or was capable of harming him. Indeed, it would have been more consistent with their majesty to punish those whom they hated with immediate penalties rather than flee from them. But because they can neither approach those in whom they see the heavenly mark nor harm those whom the immortal sign has fortified like an impregnable wall, they assail them through human agents and persecute them with the hands of others. If they indeed admit that these beings exist, we have conquered. For this religion must necessarily be true, since it knows the nature of demons, understands their cunning, breaks their power, and forces them, tamed and subdued by spiritual weapons, to yield to it.

If they deny them, they will be refuted by the testimony of poets and philosophers. But if they do not deny either that demons exist or that they are evil, what remains except for them to say that gods are one thing and demons another? Let them therefore explain to us the difference between the two kinds, so that we may know what is to be worshiped and what execrated, and whether they have some association with one another or are instead enemies.

If they are joined by some bond, how shall we distinguish them? Or how shall we combine the honor and worship of both kinds? But if they are enemies, why do the [Col. 0533C] demons either not fear the gods, or why are the gods unable to put the demons to flight?

Here, for example, is someone struck by the impulse of a demon: [Col. 0534A] he is demented, carried away, insane. Let us take him into the temple of Jupiter Best and Greatest; or, since Jupiter does not know how to heal human beings, into the shrine of Aesculapius or Apollo. Let the priest of either god command in the name of his god that the harmful spirit depart from the person: this cannot be accomplished by any means. What, then, is the power of the gods, if they do not keep the demons subject to themselves?

Yet these same demons, when adjured by the name of the true God, flee at once. What reason is there for them to fear Christ but not Jupiter, unless they are the very demons whom the multitude supposes to be gods? Finally, if both a person known to be suffering a demonic assault and a seer of Delphic Apollo are placed together in the midst, they will shudder alike at the name of God; and Apollo will depart from his seer as swiftly as that demonic spirit departs from the person, [Col. 0534B] and, when his god has been adjured and driven away, the seer will fall silent forever. Therefore, those whom they admit must be execrated as demons are the same beings as the gods to whom they offer supplication.

If they do not think that we should be believed, let them believe Homer, who placed that supreme Jupiter among the demons, and also the other poets and philosophers who call the same beings now demons and now gods. One of these designations is true, the other false. For wherever those utterly wicked spirits are adjured, they confess that they are demons; wherever they are worshiped, they falsely claim to be gods, so that they may introduce errors among human beings and divert them from knowledge of the true God, through which alone eternal death can be avoided.

They are the same beings who, for the purpose of casting humanity down, established various forms of worship for themselves throughout the various regions, though under fabricated and adopted names, so that they might deceive. For because [Col. 0534C] they could not claim divinity in their own persons, they appropriated the names of powerful kings so that, under those kings’ [Col. 0535A] titles, they might claim for themselves the honors of gods. This error can be dispelled and brought forth into the light of truth. [Col. 0535A]

So too the *Epitome*, at the end of the preface: “Truth must be brought forth into the light.” Many earlier printed editions have: “And it can be brought forth into the light of truth.” Compare, however, III.1: “When the errors have been dispelled and refuted, truth … sheds the brightest light.” **Bunemann.**
>

That word certainly cannot be retained. See, therefore, Trismegistus in the *Poimandres*, ch. 1. The Sublacensis edition has: “Who said everything about God the Father, and many things about the Son.”

Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book II, chapter 28. Lactantius rejects Cicero’s derivation from *relegere* (“to go over again”) [Col. 0536C] and derives the etymology of *religio* (“religion”) from *religare* (“to bind”). St. Ambrose agrees with Lactantius in his book *On Virgins*, where he presents virgins espoused to God as being, so to speak, bound (*religatas*) to him. He says that “religion” is so called for this reason—an etymology truer in substance than in word. Jerome supports Lactantius still more explicitly in his commentary on Amos, chapter IX: religion is so called because we are, as it were, tied together in the Lord’s bundle and bound to him. Augustine, however, varies somewhat, approaching more nearly to Cicero’s explanation. For in *The City of God*, Book X, chapter 4, he indeed thinks that the word is derived from *religere* (“to choose again”), through a play upon the name improvised for the occasion—as Vives thinks. His own words are: “For he himself is the source of our blessedness; he himself is the end of every desire. In choosing him—or rather, choosing him again (*religentes*), for we had lost him through neglect (*negligentes*)—in choosing him again, therefore, from which religion (*religio*) is said to derive its name, we tend toward him in love, so that by attaining him we may rest: blessed for this reason, because we are perfected by that end.” BETULEIUS.

**He spoke as follows.** The manuscripts have *he spoke as follows*; the printed editions, *he speaks as follows*.

But Goth., Lips., Fasit., Gryph., Torn. 1548, Thomas. and the following editions have *elegant*, a reading which, because it is preferred in many manuscripts of Cicero, I do not condemn here either. **Words.** I added this word from all the manuscripts and printed editions; it is also found in Cicero. It is absent, however, from the other printed texts.

**There is no difference.** The difference between religion and superstition lies not so much in form as in matter. Religion consists in the true and prudent worship of the true divinity; superstition is a spurious form of that same worship. Religion embraces the true piety, faith, life, laws, rites, and sacraments of Christian teaching. Superstition belongs to a feeble and senile mind, which either adheres to falsehood or worships the truth, but not as it ought.

**If . . . to do it once.** Thus Jerome, *Against Vigilantius*, vol. II of the *Works*, fol. m. 124: “For what it is good to have done once [Col. 0537C] cannot be evil if it is done frequently.” You know the rest. BUN.]

For if anyone desires to inquire more deeply, let him gather those skilled in summoning souls from the underworld. Let them call forth Jupiter, Neptune, Vulcan, Mercury, Apollo, and Saturn, the father of them all. They will all answer from the underworld; when questioned, they will speak and will confess the truth about themselves and about God. After this, let them call forth Christ: he will not be present; he will not appear, because he was in the underworld for no more than two days. What more certain proof than this can be produced? For my part, I do not doubt that Trismegistus arrived at the truth by some such means, since he spoke at length about God the Son concerning matters contained among the divine mysteries.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On Hope and True Religion, and on Superstition

Since these things are as we have shown them to be, it is evident [Col. 0535B] that no other hope of life has been set before humankind except that, after casting aside vanities and wretched error, one should know God and serve God, renounce this temporal life, and train oneself through the rudiments of justice for the worship of true Religion. For we are born under this condition: that we render just and due service to God who begot us; [Col. 0536A] that we know him alone and follow him. By this bond of piety we are obligated and bound to God; from this Religion itself received its name—not, as Cicero interpreted it, from *relegere* (“to go over again”). In the second book of *On the Nature of the Gods*, he spoke as follows:

> “For not only philosophers, but also our ancestors, distinguished superstition from religion. Those who spent entire days praying and offering sacrifice so that their children might survive them were called ‘superstitious.’ Those, however, who carefully reconsidered and, as it were, went over again everything pertaining to the worship of the gods were called ‘religious,’ from *relegere* (‘to go over again’), just as *elegantes* (‘discerning’) comes from *eligere* (‘to choose’), *diligentes* (‘diligent’) from *deligere* (‘to esteem’), and *intelligentes* (‘intelligent’) from *intelligere* (‘to understand’). For all these words contain the same force of *legere* that is present in ‘religious.’ Thus, of ‘superstitious’ and ‘religious,’ the former became the name of a fault and the latter of something praiseworthy.”

How inept this interpretation is [Col. 0536B] may be understood from the matter itself. For if superstition and religion alike are occupied with the worship of the same gods, there is little—or rather, no—difference between them. For what reason could he give me for thinking that to pray once for the safety of one’s children is the act of a religious man, while to do the same thing ten times is the act of a superstitious man? For if to do it once [Col. 0537A] is excellent, how much more excellent is it to do so more often? If it is excellent during the first hour, then it is so throughout the entire day. If one sacrificial victim is propitiatory, then surely numerous victims are still more propitiatory, [Col. 0537A]

[Note: [Col. 0537C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 537–538]

**Numerous victims.** I restored this reading from many manuscripts and printed editions. Four Reg. manuscripts, Brun., and seven printed editions read *more victims*.

**Win favor.** This is the excellent reading of a great many manuscripts and nine printed editions. Ignorant copyists corrupted it in two Colbert manuscripts, the Tornesian edition, and two Clarom. manuscripts, substituting *earn God*; in one Colbert manuscript and four printed editions, *earn acts of service*.—“Win favor rather than give offense.” Lips. 2 and 3, Reimm., Torn., and a marginal reading in the manuscript of 1587 have: “They earn God rather than give offense.” I cannot rashly reject this, remembering Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 21: “by which they were instructed concerning meriting God’s favor and not [Col. 0537D] offending him.” BUN.

**Acquire a blameworthy name.** Eleven recent manuscripts and sixteen printed editions have *receive*.

**Honors the gods more.** From the oldest manuscripts—one Bonon., one Reg., and six others—and from four printed editions, I restored *more*, which certainly fits better than *enough*, the reading in the rest.

**Not how you worship.** This was expressed rather poorly by Lactantius. On the matter, see St. Augustine, *The City of God*, Book IV, chapter 30. The religious person is best distinguished from the superstitious person in this way: the superstitious person fears God as an enemy, whereas the religious person reveres God as a parent.

**What you pray for.** Six recent manuscripts and the same number of printed editions have *what you may pray for*.

**Therefore, better.** Nine recent manuscripts and seven printed editions have *Therefore, so much the better*.

**Lucretius.** These words of Lucretius from Book I of *On the Nature of Things* were already quoted above, in Book I, chapter 16.

**Who says.** This is the reading of the manuscripts and four printed editions. Eleven commonly used editions have *because he says*; wrongly.

**Worshiped their images.** Some manuscripts and editions have *celebrate*, which can mean nothing in this passage.

[Col. 0538C] **In place of gods.** Thus a great many of the oldest manuscripts and eight printed editions. Nine manuscripts and eleven printed editions have *into the place of gods*; three recent manuscripts, *the places*.

**Empty superstition, etc.** These are Evander’s words to Aeneas in Book VIII of the *Aeneid*. On that passage Servius gives an account of this word different from that of Lactantius—or Cicero: “Superstition,” he says, “is an excessive and deranged fear; or the term derives from old women, who, because they survive (*superstites*) to a great age, become deranged and foolish; or, according to Lucretius, superstition is an empty and excessive fear of things standing above us—that is, heavenly and divine things that stand over us.” So much for Servius. The law was: “No one shall possess gods separately, nor privately worship new or foreign gods unless they have been publicly adopted.” [Col. 0538D]

**Perhaps.** This chapter appears to have been written either against Paul of Samosata or against the Arian heresy.

**May ask.** Heumann reads *will ask*.

**Has driven.** Thus the manuscripts and printed editions. The Cauc. and three Reg. manuscripts and eight printed editions have *drives*.

**We are wavering.** Thus a great many manuscripts and sixteen printed editions. That is, “vacillating,” or rather, “erring.” Six recent manuscripts and two old Roman editions have *we are laboring*; seven recent manuscripts, *labor*; the first hand of Regio-Put., two Bonon. manuscripts, and Tax. have *we are slipping*.

**Neither can the Father exist without the Son, nor can the Son be separated from the Father.** Thus the Regio-Put., Cauc., Jun., five Colb., Pal., one Lips., Em., Cant., one Sorbon., two Clarom., Brun. manuscripts, and fourteen old editions. Some printed editions omit *exist*. But one ancient Bon., three Reg., one Lips., one Colb. manuscript, and the Is. edition read: “Neither can the Father be separated from the Son, nor the Son from the Father.” I think this was said against the Arians.—This reading is confirmed by the end of *Epitome*, chapter 49: “One retains neither of them who separates either the Father from the Son or the Son from the Father.” BUN.]

because multiplied acts of service win favor rather than give offense. For we do not regard as hateful those servants who are constantly and frequently in attendance upon us, but rather as more dear. Why, then, should one who either loves his children more or honors the gods more be at fault and acquire a blameworthy name, while one who does less is praised? This argument is also valid in reverse. For if it is a crime to pray and offer sacrifice throughout entire days, then it is also a crime to do so once. If it is wrong repeatedly to wish that one’s children may outlive one, then even the person who wishes this only rarely is superstitious. Or why should it be the name of a fault, if it is derived from something than which nothing more honorable or more just can be desired? For as to his statement that religious persons were named from *relegere* [Col. 0537B] because they carefully reconsider what pertains to the worship of the gods, why, then, do those who do this frequently during the day lose the name of religious persons, although through that very constancy they surely go over the rites by which the gods are worshiped much more carefully?

What, then, is the truth? Clearly, religion is the worship of what is true, and superstition the worship of what is false. What matters altogether is what you worship, not how you worship or what you pray for. But because worshipers of the gods consider themselves religious when they are superstitious, and can neither distinguish religion from superstition nor express the significance of the names, we have said that the name Religion is derived from the bond of piety, because God has bound humankind to himself and constrained it by piety; for we must serve him as Lord and obey him as Father. Lucretius, therefore, interpreted this name better [Col. 0537C] when he said that he was untying the knots of religions. People are called superstitious not [Col. 0538A] because they wish their children to survive them—for we all wish this—but either because they honor the surviving memory of the dead, or because, after surviving their parents, they used to worship their images at home as household gods. For those who adopted new rites for themselves, so that they might honor the dead in place of gods—persons whom they believed to have been received from among human beings into heaven—were called superstitious. Those, however, who worshiped the public and ancient gods were called religious. Hence Virgil:

> Empty superstition, ignorant of the ancient gods.

But since we find that the ancient gods too were consecrated in the same manner after death, those, therefore, who worship many false gods are superstitious. We, however, are religious, because we supplicate the one true God.

[Col. 0538B]

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the Christian Religion and the Union of Jesus with the Father

Perhaps someone may ask how, although we say that we worship one God, we nevertheless assert that there are two, God the Father and God the Son. This assertion has driven very many into the gravest error. Although what we say appears credible to them, they think that on this one point we are wavering, because we confess both a second God and a mortal God. We have already spoken about mortality; let us now teach concerning unity. When we say God the Father and God the Son, we do not say that they are different, nor do we separate the two; because neither can the Father exist without the Son, nor [Col. 0538C] can the Son be separated from the Father, since the Father cannot be named without the Son, nor can the Son be begotten without the Father. Since [Col. 0539A] the Father, therefore, makes the Son, and the Son makes the Father, [Col. 0539A]

[Note: [Col. 0539C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 539–540]

**The Father makes the Son, and the Son the Father.** Relatively speaking, of course. Thus ten Reg., two Bon., six Colb., one Sorbon., Em., Cant., two Clarom., two Brun. manuscripts, and others, together with thirteen old printed editions. The Cauc. manuscript and some recent commonly used editions have *and the Son comes to be*.—“Both the Father makes the Son and the Son the Father.” Indeed, Tertullian answers in *Against Praxeas*, chapter 10: “The Father makes the Son, and the Son makes the Father.” BUN.

[Col. 0539D] **There is one substance.** The Son is of one substance with the Father; this is directed against Arius. Although Lactantius seems catholic concerning the divinity of the Word, he nevertheless stammers excessively, because he attempts to explain that supreme mystery by natural comparisons.

**Likewise neither.** This is the reading of all the manuscripts; printed editions have *likewise nor*, which sounds awkward.

**Minister.** Six recent manuscripts and twelve more recent printed editions wrongly added *is*. Three old Roman editions and a great many manuscripts reject it; and shortly afterward *are* follows.

**Above.** Namely, in Book IV, chapter 13 of this work, from chapters XLIV and XLV of Isaiah.

**Besides me there is no God.** Thus the manuscripts and a great many printed editions. This is certainly correct, and Lactantius reads no differently below. Six printed editions have *besides me no one is God*.

**Because whatever is in the Father, etc.** Thus also Christ our Savior, John 10:30: “I and the Father are one.” Hence too he says elsewhere, namely in the same John, chapter 3, verse 35: “The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand.” [Col. 0540C]

**Not even the Father.** The verb *worships*, which immediately precedes, is understood. One recent Reg. manuscript and six printed editions have *nor*. Seven recent manuscripts and four commonly used editions have *nor does he even worship the Father*. Eight manuscripts and three old Roman editions have *does not even worship the Father*.

[Col. 0540D] **He, however, together with the Son.** Seven recent manuscripts and the same number of printed editions have *he truly*. But the remaining manuscripts and three commonly used editions have *he, however*.

**Light.** Thus all manuscripts and printed editions. Isaeus thought that *liquid* should be read.

**And heresies would have to arise.** Thus the manuscripts and printed editions, except Goth., which lacks *and heresies*; Cauc. has *that very many sects would arise*. The Aldine edition has *ought to* in place of *would have to*, and Gallaeus thought that this should be the reading. But indeed *heresies would have to arise* is the true reading. For Lactantius likes to speak in this way: Book IV, chapter 12, around the middle, “would have to be clothed in flesh on earth”; Book VII, chapter 6, before the end, “have to say.” Cicero likewise has “I have to promise,” Book I, letter 5, to Lentulus, and “I have to write,” Book II, letter 22, to Atticus. Paul says that heresies must exist in 1 Corinthians 11:19: “There must be heresies among you, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you.” See also 2 Peter 2:1.]

there is one mind, one spirit, one substance in both. But the former is like an overflowing fountain, the latter like a stream flowing down from it; the former is like the sun, the latter like a ray extended from the sun. Because the Son is both faithful and dear to the supreme Father, he is not separated from him, just as neither the stream from the fountain nor the ray from the sun is separated; for the water of the fountain is in the stream, and the light of the sun is in the ray. Likewise, neither can the voice be separated from the mouth, nor power or the hand be torn from the body. Since, therefore, the prophets call the same one the hand, power, and Word of God, there is surely no distinction; for the tongue, the minister of speech, and the hand, in which power resides, are inseparable portions of the body.

I wish to use a closer example. When someone has a son whom he loves above all others, but who nevertheless remains in his household and under his authority, even if he grants him the name and power of lord, [Col. 0539B] nevertheless, by civil law, both the household is called one and its lord one. So this world is the one household of God; and the Son and Father, who dwell in the world with one mind, are one God, because the one is as though two, and the two as though one. Nor is this surprising, since the Son is in the Father because the Father loves the Son, and the Father is in the Son because the Son faithfully obeys the Father’s will and never does or has done anything except what the Father either willed or commanded. Finally, Isaiah shows that both the Father and the Son are one God in the passage we cited above, when he said: “They will worship you and pray to you, because God is in you; and there is no other God besides you.” In another place he likewise says: “Thus says God, the king of Israel, and God eternal, who rescued him: I am the first, [Col. 0539C] and I am the last; and besides me there is no God.” Although he had introduced two Persons—God the King, that is, Christ, and God the Father, who raised him from the underworld after his Passion, just as we said the prophet Hosea had shown when he said, “And I will rescue him from the hand of the underworld”—he nevertheless referred the conclusion to both Persons: “And [Col. 0540A] besides me there is no God,” although he could have said “besides us.” But it was not lawful to create, by a plural number, a separation within so close a union.

For there is one sole, free, supreme God, lacking an origin, because he himself is the origin of all things; and in him the Son and all things are contained together. Therefore, since the mind and will of the one is in the other—or rather, since there is one mind and will in both—both are rightly called one God, because whatever is in the Father flows into the Son, and whatever is in the Son descends from the Father. The supreme and singular God, therefore, cannot be worshiped except through the Son. Whoever thinks that he worships the Father alone does not worship the Son, and likewise does not even worship the Father. Whoever, however, receives the Son and bears his name worships the Father together with the Son, because the Son is the representative, messenger, and priest of the supreme Father. He is the gate of the greatest temple, the way of light, the guide of salvation, the doorway [Col. 0540B] of life.

## CHAPTER XXX. On Avoiding Heresies and Superstitions, and on Which Is the One True Catholic Church

But since many heresies have arisen and the people of God have been divided by the promptings of demons, we must briefly define the truth and establish it in its own proper dwelling, so that, if anyone desires to draw the water of life, he may not be led to worn-out pools that possess no spring, but may know the most abundant fountain of God, by which, once watered, he may obtain everlasting light. Above all, we ought to know that both he himself and his messengers foretold that very many sects and heresies would have to arise, which would rupture the harmony of the holy body; and that they warned us to exercise the greatest [Col. 0540C] prudence, lest we should ever fall into the snares and deceptions of that adversary of ours with whom God has willed us to struggle. Then they gave definite commandments which we were to observe forever. Forgetful of these, very many deserted the heavenly road and constructed for themselves divergent paths through winding passages and precipices, by which they might lead a portion of the unwary and simple people into darkness and death. How this came about, I shall explain. There were certain persons among us either less firmly established in faith, [Col. 0541A]

[Note: [Col. 0541B] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 541–542]

**Established in faith.** One Lips. manuscript and Goth. have *firmly established in faith*; Brun., *firm in faith*.

**Rending.** Thus the old editions.—“Create a rending of unity.” I print *rending* (*discidium*, from *discindere*, “to tear apart”) from Lips. 3 and Reimm.; Venice 1471 and both editions of 1478 come very close with *descidium*. This reading is certainly demanded by the phrases “rupture the harmony” and “dissipate . . . unity,” as well as by the frequent imitation in this chapter of Cyprian, *On the Unity of the Church*, Oxford edition, fol. 105: “He invented heresies and schisms by which . . . he might rend unity”; and fol. 119: “Unity cannot be torn apart, nor can the one body be separated by a rupture in its joining” (Gryph. wrongly has *dissension*). Likewise, Letter 59, [Col. 0541C] Oxford edition, fol. 129; Erasmus edition, Book I, letter 3: “No one should rend the Church by a rupture of unity.” BUN.

**Rather than endure them as superiors.** The extremely ancient Bonon. manuscript has *nor* in place of *rather than*; five old printed editions have *make* in place of *endure*. These words appear to refer to Novatian.—“Rather than endure them as superiors.” Bon. has: “nor endure them as superiors.” Superiors of the Church are often mentioned in Cyprian—for example, Book I, letters 3, 4, 5, and 11, and elsewhere in Erasmus’s edition; likewise Letter 59, Oxford edition, fol. 130: “to persecute the superior of the Church.” BUN.

**That God should be enclosed in a woman’s womb.** Thus Regio-Put., three Colbert, Em., Cant., one Lips. manuscript, three old Roman editions, and Cellar. and Walch.; more correctly and appropriately than “that God should enclose himself in a woman’s womb,” which is the reading of seven manuscripts and thirteen printed editions. The oldest Reg. manuscript has *had enclosed himself*, not badly, because of the following phrase “could have been brought down.”

**The prophets and he himself had foretold.** Five recent manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470 have the plural, *had foretold*. But Lactantius frequently employs throughout his writings this form of expression, with the verb [Col. 0541D] stated in the singular.

**Phrygians.** These are the Cataphrygians, concerning whom see Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book V, chapters 3, 14, and following. They received their name from the province of Phrygia because they arose and lived there. Their founders were Montanus, who presented himself as the Paraclete, and his two insane prophetesses, Priscilla and Maximilla. According to Epiphanius, they accepted both Testaments and believed that we ought to receive χαρίσματα (*charismata*), that is, gifts of prophecy. According to Epiphanius they arose in the ninth year of Antoninus Pius, that is, in the Christian era 148; according to Eusebius, however, in the eleventh year of Antoninus Verus, that is, in the year of Christ 174. See also Nicephorus, Book IV, chapter 23, and Augustine, *On Heresies*, no. 26.

**Novatians.** They most arrogantly and offensively called themselves Cathars, as though pure and free from sins, although, according to Jerome, they were the most polluted of all. They did not admit second marriages; they denied repentance to those who sinned after baptism; they rebaptized those who came to them from the Catholic Church; and they followed the heretic Novatus—or else Novatian, the schismatic presbyter of the Roman Church and rival of Pope Cornelius. St. Cyprian, Letter 8, Book II; Epiphanius, *Heresies* 50; Augustine, *Heresies* 38; Rabanus, *Instruction of Clerics*, Book II, chapter 58. [Col. 0542B]

**Valentinians.** They were named from Valentinus, who lived under Antoninus Pius, in the year 146. They asserted that there had existed thirty aeons, or ages, whose first principle was the Deep. From that Deep—that is, from the Father—they said that Christ was sent, bringing a spiritual or heavenly body and assuming nothing from the Virgin Mary, but passing through her, as through a crack or tube, without taking any flesh from her. They also denied the resurrection of the flesh. They called themselves Gnostics, as though endowed with supreme knowledge or enlightened; Augustine, *Heresies* 11. Irenaeus and Tertullian wrote chiefly against them. [Col. 0542C]

**Marcionites.** Marcion of Pontus followed Cerdo’s doctrine concerning two first principles. See Irenaeus, Book I, chapter 26, Tertullian, and Epiphanius. Marcion lived in the time of Antoninus Pius.

**Anthropians.** Isaeus understands by these those who declared Jesus Christ to have been merely a ψιλός (*psilos*, “mere” or “bare”) man, such as Ebion and Cerinthus. Yet those who imagined God as corporeal may also be reckoned under this name, such as the Audians and Anthropomorphites, who in their thought fashioned God as fleshly, in the likeness of the image of corruptible man. On these, see Alfonso de Castro, fol. 145, Antwerp edition. SPARK.—**Anthropians.** They are mentioned in Cyprian, Letter 73, Oxford edition, fol. 200. They were distinct from the Anthropomorphites: denying that Christ was God, they asserted that he was a mere man, as Isaeus taught more precisely than Spark and Cellarius. Ittigius supports him in his dissertation *On the Heresiarchs of the First and Second Centuries*, section I, chapter 6, pages 62–63, believing that others called the same people “Homuncionites.” BUN. [Col. 0542D]

**Or Arians.** Isaeus rejects these words as an addition made by some later person, because, he says, when Lactantius wrote, the name of the Arians was not yet known. But although they are absent from the oldest manuscripts—one Bonon., two Reg., and Cauc.—as well as from another recent Reg., Marm., one Clarom., and three printed editions, they are found in more than forty manuscripts and fourteen commonly used editions; therefore we have left them in the text. Isaeus says that the Arian heresy became known around the year 315 and that Lactantius was moved to write in the year 302. But Cardinal Baronius, Betuleius, Baluzius, and others think otherwise and approve and defend our reading, confirmed by so many manuscripts and old editions. Isaeus’s assertion rests upon the premise that Lactantius wrote [Col. 0543A] his books of the *Divine Institutes* in the year 302. Betuleius and others, however, contend that Lactantius wrote or dedicated them in or around the year 316; Tillemont, on the other hand, argues that it was not before the year 321, for reasons he gives in his *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. VI, page 208, which the reader should not begrudge consulting. Some maintain that the seven books of the *Divine Institutes* were first [Col. 0543B] published in the East, and then a second time around the year 321, or later, in the West; and that, having been written earlier, they were revised and expanded by Lactantius and dedicated to Constantine the Great after the time when hateful cruelty was raging. See Book V, chapter 2. I write *Ariani* with a single *r*, as the Greeks customarily do, since Arius was Greek and the Greeks knew better than the Latins how his name was written. I find it written in this way in four Reg., one Sorbon., one Colb., Gat., one Clar., Em., and Cant. manuscripts, and in the Cellar. edition.—**Or Arians.** According to Isaeus, these words are read in the Vatican and other manuscripts, including the second Bonon. and Taxaq.; according to Baronius, in nine Vatican manuscripts and two manuscripts of the Vallicellian Library; according to Baluzius, in Ultr., Jun., Palat., four manuscripts of the Royal Library at Paris, and six Colbert manuscripts; also in seven English manuscripts, three Lips., Goth., Reimm., and the Wolfenbüttel manuscripts, which I have seen, and in absolutely all editions before Thomasius. After weighing the arguments on both sides, Baluzius, at the beginning of his expanded notes on *The Deaths of the Persecutors*, regards them as genuine; I willingly agree with him and other very distinguished men. BUN.] [Col. 0543C]

or less learned, or less cautious, who created a rending of unity and dissipated the Church. But those whose faith was unstable, while pretending to know and worship God, pursued an increase in wealth and honor, aspired to the highest priesthood, and, when defeated by worthier men, preferred to withdraw with their supporters rather than endure as superiors those over whom they had themselves desired to be appointed.

Others, however, who were not sufficiently instructed in the heavenly writings, could not answer the accusers of the truth when they objected that it was either impossible or unfitting for God to be enclosed in a woman’s womb, and that the heavenly majesty could not have been brought down to such weakness [Col. 0541B] that he became an object of contempt, mockery, insult, and ridicule to human beings, and finally even endured torments [Col. 0542A] and was fastened to an accursed cross. Since they could neither defend nor refute any of these things by intelligence or learning—for they did not thoroughly perceive their force and rationale—they were corrupted away from the straight path and corrupted the heavenly writings, so that they might devise for themselves a new doctrine without any root or stability.

Still others, enticed by the prophecy of false prophets—concerning whom both the true prophets and he himself had foretold—fell away from the doctrine of God and abandoned the true tradition. But all these, entangled in demonic deceptions that they ought to have foreseen and guarded against, through imprudence lost the divine name and worship. For when they are called Phrygians, Novatians, Valentinians, Marcionites, Anthropians, Arians, or by any other name, they have ceased to be Christians, since, having lost the name of Christ, they have put on human and foreign designations. [Col. 0542B] The Catholic Church alone, therefore, retains the true worship.

[Col. 0543A] This is the fountain of truth, this the dwelling of faith, [Col. 0543A]

[Note: [Col. 0543C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 543–544]

**This the dwelling of faith.** The printed editions have “This is,” etc. But I deleted the verb *is*, which is elegantly absent from the manuscripts [Col. 0544A] and is not found in the following clause.

**If anyone has not entered it.** Thus all the manuscripts and printed editions except one ancient Bonon. manuscript and the Gymnic., Soubron., two Paris, and Torn. editions, which have *because*.

**In which there is confession and repentance, which wholesomely treats the sins . . .** These shafts are directed against Novatian [Col. 0544B] and his followers, who did not admit to repentance those who had fallen into sin. They denied that remission of sins was found in the Church and that Christ had given it the keys of opening and releasing. On this matter see Pacianus, Letter I to Sympronianus, and St. Augustine, *On the Christian Struggle*, chapter 31. ISAEUS.

**And more abundantly.** We have emended the text thus from two Reg. manuscripts nine hundred years old; from another Reg. manuscript four hundred years old and of the best quality; from two Brun., one Lips., and Ultr. In the other manuscripts and printed editions, except the Leipzig edition, the corrupt reading *more truly* is found. For who would think Lactantius so absurd as to affirm that he had not written with sufficient truth in what he had set forth before, and that in another work he would deal with the matter “more truly”? Moreover, if that separate and independent work against heresies—or, as Lactantius says, against all sects of falsehood—ever existed, it has not survived to our time.—**More fully and more abundantly.** The ancients frequently join these words, as Cicero, *On the Distinguished Orators*, chapter 33: “No one was fuller and more abundant in speaking”; *Second Oration*, *Philippic* I: “What could be fuller, what more abundant?” Caesar, *Civil War* I, chapter 53: “They wrote these things still more fully and more abundantly.” BUN.] [Col. 0544C]

this the temple of God. If anyone has not entered it, or if anyone has departed from it, he is estranged from the hope of life and eternal salvation. No one ought to flatter himself through obstinate disputation. For life and salvation are at stake; unless they are provided for cautiously and diligently, they will be lost and extinguished.

Nevertheless, because every individual assembly of heretics regards itself above all others as Christian and believes that its own is the Catholic Church, it must be known that the true Church is the one [Col. 0544A] in which there is confession and repentance, which wholesomely treats the sins and wounds to which the weakness of the flesh is subject. For the present I have related these few things by way of admonition, lest anyone who desires to flee error become entangled in a greater error through ignorance of the innermost sanctuary of truth. Later, in a distinct and separate work, we shall contend more fully and abundantly against all sects of falsehood. It follows that, since we have spoken sufficiently concerning true religion and wisdom, we should discuss justice in the next book.

# [LACTANTIUS, BOOK FIVE]

[Col. 0543]

# ANALYSIS OF BOOK FIVE: ON JUSTICE

This book has two parts. The first gives the reasons why he undertook this labor of writing (chapters 1, 2, 3, and 4); the second pursues the teaching concerning legal justice from that point [Col. 0543D] to the end.

After first requesting that the Gentiles read his works before judging them, he recounts both the final and the motivating causes of the present composition. He gives these final causes: to recall those who wander from the wrong path; to strengthen those who waver in the faith; and to delight the conscience through profession of the truth (chapter 1).

He mentions two motivating causes. One is that, until now, no one has written elegantly about the Christian religion: neither Minucius Felix nor Tertullian, who was rather unpolished and very obscure in expression; Cyprian, however, did indeed speak elegantly, but mystically. The other is that this very scarcity of learned writers provoked certain persons to dare to write against a truth unknown to them. For, among others, a certain philosopher sharpened his pen against the Christians. Likewise, one of the judges composed two little books in which he attempted to accuse Scripture of falsehood, on the ground that it was wholly self-contradictory; he also said that Christ was a magician and inferior to Apollonius. The author refutes all these charges in chapter 3.
