In the second part he treats the following matters in order:

That the age under Saturn was golden because mortals then worshiped one God (chapter 5).

[Col. 0544D] That under Jupiter the golden age was changed because people abandoned true religion (chapter 9).

But that now, through the messenger of God—Christ—the semblance of that golden era has returned, and justice—that is, the pious and religious worship of the one God—has been restored (chapter 7).

That this justice was not given to all, because virtue cannot be discerned unless it has contrary vices, nor can it be perfect unless it is exercised amid adversities; and further, because piety would have been nothing if nature had given equal affections to everyone. And because God did not remove evil, the present age is therefore not called golden, although justice has been sent to humankind (chapter 7).

That people are evil and unjust because gods are worshiped; and that all evils therefore daily grow more oppressive in human affairs, because God, the maker of this world, has been abandoned. If he were worshiped by all, then there would truly be a golden age (chapter 8).

That justice—even the justice they consider true—would, were it to come, have no place among the pagans, since they kill the followers of justice, either from hatred of truth or because they are ashamed to be wicked [Col. 0545A] in the presence of the just; that they mock the bodies of those cruelly slain and turn against just people the reproaches that properly apply to themselves. Since none of these reproaches can be made against the Christian people, the pagans can understand even from this that they themselves are impious and the Christians pious (chapter 9).

That impiety itself appears to the Gentiles as piety, just as Virgil called Aeneas pious although he killed not only those who did not resist, but even those who begged for mercy; and that, in accordance with the desert of their impiety, they are therefore often afflicted by more grievous evils, whose cause they ascribe to fortune (chapter 10).

Furthermore, that the worshipers of the gods cannot be good and just, since they worship bloodthirsty Mars, Jupiter who expelled his father, Saturn the ἄστοργος (*astorgos*, “devoid of natural affection”), an adulterous goddess, and Mercury the thief (chapter 10).

That from this comes their great rage and monstrous cruelty: they are headlong in killing, devise severe forms of torture, and finally enact impious laws against the pious (chapter 11).

Moreover, that the Gentiles are unjust and utterly blinded by malice and madness is evident even from the fact that, although they must judge Christians to be either wise or foolish, they nevertheless neither imitate them if wise nor spare them if foolish (chapter 12). Further, they do not see that wisdom stands on the side of the Christians, whose worship of God is the same throughout the whole world, whose patience is everywhere the same, and whose contempt for death is the same; whose number increases during persecution itself; and who possess the constancy praised by philosophers. Finally, they think that they have utterly destroyed religion if they have defiled people, as though access to God were barred to those who have fallen if they come to their senses (chapters 13 and 14).

That the philosophers themselves could neither discover nor defend Justice, because they were ignorant of the chief parts of justice, piety and equity (chapter 15). That true equality and fraternity are seen among Christians alone (chapter 16).

Yet the error of those who think Christian sages foolish is not without grounds. For justice by its very nature presents a certain appearance of folly. Carneades teaches this in Cicero [Col. 0545C]: having divided justice into two parts, the one civil and the other natural, he taught that civil justice was indeed wisdom but not justice, while natural justice was indeed justice but not wisdom. Thus the just man is a fool if he does not take a plank from a shipwrecked man, or a horse from a wounded man, in order to save his own life (Chap. 17).

In truth, however, justice has no alliance with folly. The situation proposed by Carneades can never befall a just man. For a just man, to whom his own possessions suffice, does not sail or seek anything from a foreign land; nor does a peaceable man wage war. And even if such a situation should befall him, so great is the power of justice that, when he raises his eyes to heaven, he merits all things from God, by whom he is delivered amid the very dangers of wars and storms. And even if he is not delivered, he will himself die rather than kill. Reason likewise cannot teach that the same man is both just and foolish, or both wise and unjust, since the fool does not know what is good [Col. 0545D] and just, whereas the just man [Col. 0546A] abstains from every sin. The same point is clear from the definition of folly. For since folly is error in deeds and words through ignorance of what is right and good, the man who does not spare even himself, provided that he does no harm to another, is not a fool (Chap. 18).

The reason why the just appear foolish is that the pagans do not know of the soul’s immortality, nor how great an impiety it is to worship anything other than the true God. The reason why God wishes justice to be concealed beneath the guise of folly is that the mystery of truth and of his religion may remain secret; that he may condemn the world’s wisdom as vanity; and finally that, by setting difficulty before us, the exceedingly narrow path may lead to the sublime reward of immortality (Chap. 19).

The persecutors of the Church therefore commit an inexpiable crime: both because they slaughter themselves by serving the most ruinous demons, and because they do not permit God to be worshipped by others.

The killers of souls also falsely claim that they are acting for the Christians’ benefit and wish to recall them to a sound mind. For they ought to proceed not by force and torture, but by reason [Col. 0546B] and exhortation. Religion cannot be compelled; Christians are prepared to listen; they themselves teach, prove, and demonstrate their doctrines. Religion must be defended not by killing, but by dying; not by cruelty, but by patience; not by crime, but by faith. Religion must indeed be defended—but the true religion, not one in which nothing is seen but a ritual pertaining only to the fingers, such as that of the pagans; in which a foolish libation is required in place of a pure heart; to which all the most criminal men come without discrimination; and in which each person thinks that he has sacrificed piously if he has washed his skin (Chap. 20).

The pagans themselves destroy their own gods by compelling the unwilling to sacrifice, for they thereby show distrust in their gods’ power. Finally, they confer no benefit either upon the gods to whom Christians sacrifice under compulsion or upon those whom they compel: not upon those whom they compel, because what is forced upon one who refuses it is no benefit; and not upon the gods, because what is extorted from an unwilling person is no sacrifice.

Their objection that those who destroy religions ought to be punished is of no weight [Col. 0546C], since the Egyptians, who worship the most shameful forms of beasts; certain philosophers, who say that there are no gods at all; and the Epicureans, who abolish providence, truly abolish religion, and yet are tolerated—indeed, are even honored (Chap. 21).

From this it is evident that the pagans rage against the Christians not because the latter do not worship the gods, but because the truth is in their possession. Thus the pagans do not know what they are undergoing and, driven by polluted spirits, are carried away by blind and irrational fury (Chap. 22).

God indeed permits these things: that he may test the patience of his own people; that he may not allow them to be corrupted by perishable and mortal goods; that he may correct offenders with blows and scourges; and that God’s people may be increased, as the cruelty of the impious and the constancy of the faithful are set before human eyes. Yet the persecutors will not go unpunished, but will pay God severe penalties because they served as agents of indignation against the Christians (Chaps. 23 [Col. 0546D] and 24). **SCULTETUS.**

[Col. 0545]

# BOOK FIVE. ON JUSTICE

## CHAPTER I. That defendants must not be condemned before their case has been heard; why philosophers have despised the Sacred Writings; concerning the first defenders of the Christian religion

I have no doubt, most mighty Emperor Constantine, [Col. 0546D]

> **Note: [Col. 0545D] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 545–546]**
>
> **Most mighty Emperor Constantine.** These three words are absent from manuscripts 1 old Bologna, 1 Royal, Palatine, and 1 Leipzig [Col. 0546D], and from Isaeus’ edition; they are, however, present in all the other manuscripts and printed editions. This first chapter is, as it were, a preface to the whole [Col. 0547B] book. In it he complains about the persecutors of the Christian name because they persist in inflicting punishment upon innocent Christians without first hearing their case. Its argument is precisely the same as that of Tertullian’s *Apologeticum*.

that this work of ours, in which that unique [Col. 0547A] creator of all things and ruler of this immensity [Col. 0547A]

> **Note: [Col. 0547B] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 547–548]**
>
> **Ruler of this immensity.** Colbert manuscript 1, by a second hand, and six editions read “ruler of this immense work”; recent Colbert manuscript 1 and Brunswick manuscript 1 read “ruler of the universe.” Lactantius, Book II, chap. 5, has “craftsman of the universe,” and chap. 17, “ruler of the universe.”
>
> **Impatient.** The Rostock edition, Venice 1471 and 1472, and both editions of 1478 incorrectly read “imparting”; Heumann therefore conjectures “powerless.” But the Wolfenbüttel, Leipzig, Gotha, Reimmann, Venice [Col. 0547C] 1493 and 1497, Parisian, and Paris manuscripts and editions—and the rest—read “impatient,” which I retain because of what follows: “let him read patiently or listen.” **BUNEMANN.**
>
> **By the right of humanity.** That is, by the law of nations, or even by natural law.
>
> **That he should not condemn before.** In what follows he plainly follows Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 1: “Truth desires only one thing in the meantime: that it not be condemned without being known.” Likewise Minucius Felix, chap. 27, at the end: “So that men begin to hate us before knowing us, lest, once they have come to know us, they should either be able to imitate us or be unable to condemn us.” Lindenbrog supplies parallels in his note on Ammianus, Book XV, chap. 7, p. 99: “To condemn a man neither seen nor heard is the ultimate impiety,” etc. **BUNEMANN.**
>
> **Has learned the whole matter.** For if being a Christian was then a capital charge, the law of nations required a fully comprehensive examination of the case, as the jurists teach.
>
> **For if sacrilegious men, etc.** Aristides, in his second oration against Plato, praises the saying, *Πάταξον μὲν, ἄκουσον δὲ*—“Strike me, but hear me.” There was a law of Lycurgus *περὶ ἀκρίτων*—“concerning those not yet judged,” as Sextus Empiricus III calls it—which forbade the punishment of persons who had not been condemned, according to Valerius [Col. 0547D] Maximus VII, chap. 3, §12. See also Ambrose, Letter 28; Salvian, Book VIII; Augustine, Letters 50 and 372. **GROTIUS.**—Tacitus, *Annals* II: “For the defendant must not be prevented from presenting everything by which his innocence might be supported.” In Seneca’s *Apology*: “Tell me,” etc., “why did you condemn anyone among those men and women whom you killed before investigating the case, before hearing them?”
>
> **If there should be anyone who.** In what follows there is an evident imitation of Cicero, *First Action against Verres*, chap. 18: “If there should be anyone who … desires it, he will hear.” The Paris edition of 1513 does well to enclose the words “if there should be anyone” in parentheses in Lactantius; the remainder then flows properly. **BUNEMANN.**
>
> **At some point surrender.** That is, acknowledge themselves defeated. For some, “to give one’s hands” means the same as to assent; thus Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid* XI: “had given his hands”—“had assented.” Likewise in Clement’s *Recognitions*, Book II, in Rufinus’ translation. Seneca, *Natural Questions* II, chap. 38: “Suppose that I surrender to you and admit that this too is embraced by fate”; and Lucretius, Book II:
>
> > If these things seem true to you,  
> > Surrender.
>
> **ELMENHORST.**
>
> **They shout him down.** Chap. 4: *Obstrepere* properly means to disturb and impede by making a noise. See Duker on Florus, Book II, chap. 19, p. 469. Aptly Curtius, Book VI, chap. 9: “The clamor of men expressing indignation on every side … shouted him down.” Add Pitiscus on Curtius, Book VII, chap. 7.
>
> **They intervene.** Manuscripts 3, the recent Royal manuscript, four Colbert manuscripts, the Brunswick manuscript, and the Paris 1525 and Grapheus editions read “they interrupt.”
>
> **And they press their own eyes shut.** Minucius calls this “refusing to recognize the heavenly brightness that thrusts itself before one’s eyes.” See Paul, 2 Corinthians 4:4.—**They press their own eyes shut.** Heumann writes “they close their own eyes.” There is no need to depart from the consensus of all the books and exchange an elegant expression [Col. 0548C] for a more familiar one. Others supplied precedents for it: Valerius Maximus II, chap. 6: “He summoned his daughters’ hands for the final duty of closing his eyes”; on which consult Vorstius. In the same manner the Latins say “to press shut the mouth, face, or throat.” The familiar line of Terence is “Shut your mouth.” Ovid, *Metamorphoses* III.5 ff.:
>
> > … A god wished to close  
> > The speaker’s mouth …
>
> **BUNEMANN.**
>
> **By this they plainly display their distrust, etc.** Two recent Royal manuscripts and one Leipzig manuscript read “which.” Royal manuscript 1 and three Leipzig manuscripts have “distrust” in the nominative.—**By this they plainly display their distrust …** From the Gotha and Reimmann manuscripts I have restored the reading of all editions before Cellarius, which accords with our author’s style in Book VI, chap. 19: “By this they plainly display.” Cellarius’ reading, “which they display through distrust,” has a less plain and suitable sense. **BUNEMANN.**
>
> **They dare.** Heumann reads “they should dare.”
>
> **From our midst.** This verse is from Ennius, *Annals* VIII. On it see Aulus Gellius, Book XX, chap. 9. See also Cicero, *For Murena*, §30.
>
> [Col. 0548D] **That the innocence itself be established.** Heumann reads “that their innocence be established.” Nothing should be changed. Again, *Epitome*, chap. 52: “They condemn them as the most guilty without investigating the case, because they have refused to establish their very innocence.” It is a phrase of Quintilian, *Institutes* VII.2, Burmann edition, p. 601: “If our innocence has first been established.” **BUNEMANN.**
>
> **Although they could correct themselves.** The Gotha manuscript alone reads “although they could not correct themselves”; all other manuscripts and printed editions omit the negative particle. Below he says: “Because they resist their own salvation.” **BUNEMANN.**
>
> **They heap up.** Thus the manuscripts and printed editions read. The Bologna manuscript has *coacerbant* instead of *coacervant*, with *b* substituted for *v*. Relying on this ancient codex, Thomasius thinks that *coacerbant* should be read, as though it meant “they aggravate”; he regards this mode of expression as thoroughly Latin and its sense as excellent.—**They heap up.** Thomasius says that *coacerbant* must be read on the authority of an ancient manuscript, since the verbs *acerbare* and *exacerbare* are thoroughly Latin; and the sense itself is excellent, namely, that they are not content merely to follow their errors unless they make them still more bitter by their cruelty. But if one reads “they heap up errors,” there is no suitable meaning, and it is manifest [Col. 0549B] that this form arose from the other by changing *b* to *v*. In numerous examples in my note on the *Epitome*, chap. 2, from the Turin manuscript [Col. 0549C], I show that the oldest codices often put *b* for *v*. Thomasius’ case therefore collapses here, and *coacervant*, that is, “they accumulate,” must be read. And who among the ancients said *coacerbare*? It is just as legitimate to say “they heap up errors with cruel deeds” as Cicero says in *For Roscius of Ameria*, chap. 11: “They heap these misdeeds upon other abominations and increase them.” **BUNEMANN.**

is vindicated, will be attacked even with curses if any of those foolishly religious men should touch it—for they are impatient through excessive superstition—and, after perhaps scarcely reading its opening, he will cast it down, throw it away, and curse it. He will think himself polluted and bound by an inexpiable crime if he either reads these things patiently or listens to them. Yet, if possible, we request of such a man, by the right of humanity, that he not condemn before learning the whole matter. For if sacrilegious men, traitors, and poisoners are given the opportunity to defend themselves, and no one may be condemned in advance before his case is known, we do not seem to make an unjust request: if there should be anyone who happens upon these writings, let him, if he reads them, read them through; if he listens, let him defer judgment until the end.

But I know the obstinacy of men: we shall never obtain this. For they fear that, if refuted by us, they may at some point be compelled to surrender when truth itself cries aloud. They therefore shout us down and intervene so that they may not hear; they press their own eyes shut so that they may not see the light we offer. [Col. 0548A] By this they plainly display their distrust in their own ruined system, since they dare neither examine nor engage with us, because they know that they can easily be defeated. And therefore, once debate has been removed,

> Wisdom is driven from our midst; the matter is conducted by force,

as Ennius says. And because they are eager to condemn as guilty those whom they assuredly know to be innocent, they refuse to allow their very innocence to be established. As though it were a greater injustice to condemn innocence once it had been proved than to condemn it unheard! But, as I have said, they fear that, if they hear, they will be unable to condemn.

And therefore they torture, kill, and exterminate the worshippers of the supreme God—that is, just men. Those who hate so vehemently cannot themselves give reasons for their hatred: because they themselves are in error, they are angry with those who follow the true [Col. 0548B] way; and although they could correct themselves, they instead heap additional errors upon their own by cruel deeds, are stained with the blood of the innocent, and tear out minds dedicated to God from disemboweled [Col. 0549A] bodies.

> **Note: [Col. 0549C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 549–550]**
>
> **From disemboweled bodies.** Quintilian, *Declamation* 12, at the end: “The sun shone upon the disemboweled bodies.” Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* II, chap. 9: “Behold with pity the disemboweled body of your mangled father.” **BUNEMANN.**
>
> **From that wandering path.** The Subiaco edition has “from death.”
>
> **Have had some contact with literature.** I read *attigerunt* with the printed editions and manuscripts except for three recent manuscripts and five printed editions, which have *attigerint*.
>
> **Poets are harmful.** How harmful they were to religion through their fictions! This was why Plato expelled them from his republic, in *Republic* I and in the *Laws*. Indeed, Pythagoras said that Homer was being tortured in the underworld because he had invented those tales about the gods [Col. 0549D] and woven them into his poem. Aristotle likewise warns in *Politics* VIII that great care must be exercised in children’s education with regard to the narration of myths. **RITTERSHUSIUS.**
>
> **These are honey concealing poison.** These words occur in ten printed editions and in the oldest Royal manuscript, nine hundred years old; likewise in one other Royal manuscript, the Gotha and the Marmoutier manuscripts, except that the first old Royal manuscript has “poisons,” and three others have “producing [poison].” They are absent, however, from one old Bologna manuscript, the Cauchy manuscript, eight Royal, six Colbert, two Sorbonne, and sixteen other manuscripts, and from nine printed editions. “They are honey”: that is, poems flowing with honeyed sweetness, an expression taken from Horace. Thus “a honeyed sword” and “a deadly honeyed drink” are proverbial.
>
> **May not only do no harm … but … may benefit.** The third Leipzig manuscript reads, “may not only harm religion and justice, but also”; thus “not only” is used for “not only not,” as I have occasionally observed, including in my note on *The Workmanship of God*, chap. 19. But here I prefer the reading of the others, “not only no harm,” which is itself elegant, as in Book VI, chap. 20: “Because not only do they contribute nothing … but they also do the greatest harm.” In these words he reproduced Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II, chap. 36: “Not only do they do no harm [Col. 0550B] to the earth, but they benefit it.” **BUNEMANN.**
>
> **Should be better instructed in the virtues.** I added the preposition “in” [Col. 0550C] from two Bologna and five Royal manuscripts, two of the latter being very old, as well as six Colbert, the Taxius, two Clermont manuscripts, and three editions.
>
> **Food of the soul.** Book I, chap. 1: “No food is sweeter to the soul than knowledge of the truth.” Book III, chap. 3: “Thus wisdom is the soul’s nourishment.” Cicero, *On Ends* V, chap. 19: “That cultivation of the mind was for him a kind of nourishment of humanity.” **BUNEMANN.**
>
> **We do not sing, etc.** A proverb from Virgil, *Eclogue* X.
>
> **For affairs are not in so evil a condition.** Two Bologna manuscripts instead read *Non enim* (“For … not”). Some printed editions, together with the two oldest Royal manuscripts and the Marmoutier and Gotha manuscripts, have: “For impure spirits are not permitted more than the holy.” This is a useless addition. Some have “unjust” instead of “impure.” So Thomasius judges.
>
> **Human affairs.** This word is absent from several manuscripts.
>
> **It is smeared around.** He alludes to the thought of Lucretius I.936 ff., who says of nurses that they smear the rims of cups with the sweet, golden liquid of honey, so that the unsuspecting age of children may be deceived and, once beguiled, may not realize it has been caught. **RIVETUS.**
>
> [Col. 0550D] **With the heavenly honey of wisdom.** Twelve recent manuscripts and nine printed editions read “of heavenly wisdom.”
>
> **Adhere to their minds.** Six manuscripts and eight printed editions read “inhere.”—**Adhere to their minds.** The English, Leipzig, Gotha, Reimmann, Venice 1472, both 1478 editions, the Parisian, Paris, Giunta, Aldine, Cratander, and Gymnicus editions, and the rest read “inhere in their minds,” as in Book VI, chap. 20. But the Rostock and Venice 1493 and 1497 editions read “adhere.” **BUNEMANN.**
>
> **Soothes with a sound.** This is the manuscript reading; the printed editions have “thoroughly soothes.” The Royal and Puteanus manuscripts and Rome 1474 read, incorrectly, “they soothe.”
>
> **To such an extent.** The Turnèbe and Emmenius manuscripts and four printed editions read “For this reason.”
>
> **Can inspire pleasure.** The first Venice edition of 1478 stands alone here in reading “can induce pleasure.” All my other witnesses have “inspire.” The verb is used even of something flattering and pleasant, as in Lucretius I.20:
>
> > Inspiring soothing love through every breast.
>
> Thus also Tertullian, *Against Marcion* III, chap. 20: “You will make me laugh.” **BUNEMANN.**
>
> **Should happen to be thoroughly eloquent.** Fourteen recent manuscripts and six printed editions read “fully.”

We now endeavor to encounter and dispute with such men, and to draw away from their foolish conviction to the truth those who would more readily drink blood than the words of the just. What, then? Shall we waste our labor? By no means. For even if we are unable to win back from death those who rush toward it with the greatest violence; even if we cannot recall them from that wandering path to life and light, because they resist their own salvation, we shall nevertheless strengthen our own people, whose conviction is not stable or founded and fixed upon solid roots.

For very many waver, especially those who have had some contact with literature. Philosophers, orators, and poets are harmful in this respect, because they can easily ensnare unwary minds by the charm of their language and by the sweet modulation of flowing verse. These are honey concealing poison. For that reason I wished to unite wisdom with Religion [Col. 0549B], so that that empty learning could do no harm to students; so that knowledge of literature might now not only do no harm to Religion and justice, but even benefit them as greatly as possible, provided that the person who has learned literature is better instructed in the virtues and wiser in the truth.

Moreover, even if it benefits no others, it will certainly benefit us: the conscience will delight in itself, and the mind will rejoice that it dwells in the light of truth. This is food for the soul, steeped in an extraordinary delight. Yet we must not despair. Perhaps

[Col. 0550A]

> We do not sing to the deaf.

For affairs are not in so evil a condition that sound minds should be lacking—minds to which the truth is pleasing, and which both see and follow the right path when it has been shown to them. Only let the cup be smeared around with the heavenly honey of wisdom, so that bitter medicines may be drunk by the unwise without offense, while the enticing sweetness at the outset conceals the bitterness of the harsh flavor under the guise of pleasantness.

For this above all is why Holy Scripture lacks credibility among the wise, the learned, and the rulers of this age: the Prophets spoke in common and simple language, as if addressing the people. They are therefore despised by those who wish to hear or read nothing unless it is polished and eloquent; nor can anything adhere to their minds unless it soothes their ears with a more pleasing sound. Things that seem unrefined [Col. 0550B] are regarded as old women’s tales, foolish, and commonplace. To such an extent do they think nothing true unless it is pleasant to hear, and nothing credible unless it can inspire pleasure. No one weighs a matter by its truth, but by its ornament.

They therefore do not believe the divine writings because those writings lack artificial coloring; nor do they believe even those who interpret them, because the interpreters themselves are either wholly untrained or at least insufficiently learned. For it very rarely happens that they are thoroughly eloquent, and the reason is evident. Eloquence serves the present age; it longs to parade itself before the people and to win favor in evil causes. Indeed, it very often attempts to conquer truth [Col. 0551A] in order to display its own power; it seeks wealth, covets honors, and finally demands the highest rank of dignity. It therefore despises these matters as though they were lowly, and shuns mysteries as contrary to itself, since it rejoices in publicity and desires crowds and renown. Hence it comes about that wisdom and truth lack suitable heralds.

> **Note: [Col. 0551D] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 551–552]**
>
> **Truth lacks suitable heralds.** The Turnèbe manuscript and one recent Colbert manuscript read “commendations.”
>
> **Minucius Felix.** We possess his elegant defense of the Christian religion under the title *Octavius*. He lived in the year of the Christian era 235, when Tertullian also lived. He has already been mentioned above, Book I, chap. [Col. 0551C] 11, after the midpoint.
>
> **Tertullian.** He is sufficiently well known from his published writings. He was furnished with every kind of learning. Works composed by him in Greek are extant in the Royal Escorial Library of Spain, as the Marquis of Santa Cruz de Marcenado—a man in every respect adorned with integrity and learning—had learned from the Catholic King Philip V. It is remarkable that these works have not yet been published in both languages. St. Cyprian valued Tertullian so highly that he passed no day without reading him; and, according to St. Jerome, the holy bishop was accustomed to say, “Give me the master,” meaning Tertullian. Something further will be said about him below in chapter 4.
>
> **Since he had also gained great.** Royal manuscript 1, recent, and the Brunswick manuscript read “the greatest.” Three recent manuscripts and six printed editions read “who” instead of “since.”
>
> **Had gained.** In place of “had acquired”; Lactantius frequently uses the simple verb for the compound. See *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*.
>
> **Or more felicitous.** Thus read the oldest manuscripts: one Bologna, two Royal [Col. 0551D], another recent but reliable Royal manuscript, one Colbert, the Rohan, Utrecht, and Brunswick manuscripts. More recent manuscripts, including the Saint-Germain manuscript, together with the printed editions, have “more fluent.” Either reading is good, for shortly before he wrote “of fluent genius,” etc.
>
> **Coprianus.** As if one were to say “Dung-man,” or, if you prefer, “Buffoon,” or “one who speaks filthy and worthless things.” The Victorinus and one Colbert manuscript read “Ciprianus,” contrary to Lactantius’ meaning; nor are the readings “Caprianus” in recent Royal manuscript 1, the Turnèbe manuscript, and one Colbert manuscript any better. It is a taunt based on an allusion to *κοπρία*, “dung.” Buffoons were called *copriae*. **GALLAEUS.**—Rhetoricians, sycophants, pettifoggers, buffoons, and the multitude of men of this sort, who promise and threaten great and numerous things and make marvelous claims about themselves, were commonly called *κοπρολόγοι*, “dung-talkers,” and *κοπρίαι*, “dung-men.” The *copriae*, οἱ κοπρίαι, in Suetonius, *Tiberius*, chap. 61, are buffoons who, to provoke laughter, made numerous empty boasts and promises about themselves. Hence also the verb *incopriare*, “to act the mountebank and sell smoke,” an activity they also called “smoking,” as the Greeks called it [Col. 0552B] *καπνίζειν*. Isidore’s glosses state: “A buffoon: one who *incopriat*”; other glosses state: “A buffoon: one who smokes.” Likewise Isidore: “A mountebank: one who smokes.” Thus triflers, liars, and empty talkers were called *copriae*. In this way certain pagans of old called Cyprian *Coprianus*, changing one letter, because he had, as they alleged, inserted old women’s tales and many lies [Col. 0552C] into his writings. **SALMASIUS.**—See also Casaubon on Suetonius’ *Tiberius*, and Lipsius, *Selections* II, chap. 17. Of St. Cyprian, Jerome says that it is unnecessary to compile a catalogue of his books, since his works are brighter than the sun. Not only the Latins but also the Greeks, such as Nazianzen, sang his praises. On Cyprian’s eloquence, read Prudentius, St. Augustine’s *On Christian Doctrine* IV, and Jerome’s letter to Paulinus.
>
> **Who.** Thus the Cambridge manuscript and four printed editions; many others read “because.”
>
> **Had applied.** Isaeus testifies that after this verb he found the following statement in the old Bologna manuscript: “From this it is evident that, so far as refuting the sacrilegious is concerned, this most eloquent and learned man lacked not the ability to speak, but judgment—especially because he constrained Demetrianus, who was devoid of truth, not by the method of worldly prudence, which he ought to have used at the beginning, but by the authority of heavenly precepts, of which Demetrianus confessed himself an enemy.”
>
> [In the manuscript the reading is “of learning.” This statement occurs neither in the Rohan nor Saint-Germain manuscripts, nor in the others.]
>
> [Col. 0552D] **Among us.** I have restored this from the Turnèbe and Soubron editions and all the manuscripts except one recent Royal manuscript, in which, as in the commonly printed editions, the reading is “our men.”
>
> **Attacked.** Two old Roman editions and almost all the manuscripts give us *lacessierunt*, a smoother reading than *lacesserunt*, which is found in the other commonly printed editions and five recent manuscripts. The latter is erroneous according to Latin usage.
>
> **Rhetorical literature, etc.** At Nicomedia, namely. He taught rhetoric there, as Jerome also relates in his biography: Latin rhetoric in Greece, perhaps because the Romans even at that time wished their language to be propagated throughout the Roman world—but perhaps in vain, for he lacked students. Bithynia was a province of Asia Minor, opposite Constantinople, on the Black Sea. King Nicomedes had bequeathed it to the Roman people. Today this province is called Anatolia.

And if any men of letters happened to devote themselves to the truth, they were unequal to its defense.

Among those known to me, Minucius Felix held no obscure place among advocates. His book, entitled *Octavius*, shows what a suitable defender of the truth he could have been if he had devoted himself wholly to that pursuit. Septimius Tertullian too was skilled in every kind of literature, but his expression was not very fluent, still less polished, and was very obscure [Col. 0551B]. Therefore he too attained insufficient renown.

Cyprian alone, then, emerged as outstanding and distinguished, since he had gained great glory for himself from the profession of rhetoric and had written very many works that are remarkable in their kind. For his genius was fluent, abundant, agreeable, and—what is the greatest virtue of discourse—clear, so that you could not determine whether he was more ornate in expression, more felicitous in exposition, or more powerful in persuasion. Yet he cannot please those who are ignorant of the mystery beyond the level of his words [Col. 0552A], because the things of which he spoke are mystical and intended to be heard only by the faithful.

Consequently, he is commonly ridiculed by the learned of this age who happen to become acquainted with his writings. I myself heard a decidedly eloquent man who, changing a single letter, called him *Coprianus*—“Dung-man”—as though he had applied an elegant genius, suited to better subjects, to old women’s tales. If this happens to a man whose eloquence is not disagreeable, what, then, should we suppose happens to those whose language is meager and unpleasing, and who could possess neither power of persuasion, subtlety of argument, nor any sharpness whatever in refutation?

## CHAPTER II. How greatly Christian truth was attacked by reckless men [Col. 0552B]

Therefore, because among us there were lacking suitable and skilled teachers who would refute public errors forcefully and keenly, and defend the whole cause of truth with ornate and abundant speech, this very scarcity provoked certain men to dare to write against a truth unknown to them. I pass over those who attacked it fruitlessly in earlier times.

When I had been summoned to Bithynia to teach rhetoric, it happened [Col. 0553A] at that same time that the temple of God was overthrown.

> **Note: [Col. 0553B] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 553–554]**
>
> **The temple of God.** Lactantius appears here to allude to Diocletian’s persecution in the year 302, approximately the time when Lactantius was summoned to Nicomedia by Diocletian to teach rhetoric, according to Jerome. Lactantius discusses the rebuilding of this temple at the beginning of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* in these words: “The Church, lately laid waste, rises again, and by the Lord’s mercy the temple of God, which had been overthrown by the impious, is built with greater glory.”
>
> **One of whom professed himself a high priest of philosophy, etc.** It is remarkable that he suppressed their names. Consider from this how little malice he bore his enemies, whose names he spared. Nor is there any need for curious investigation into a matter that our author wished to keep concealed. From **BETULEIUS.**—Some nevertheless think that this was the philosopher Maximus whom Julian, called the Apostate, heard at Nicomedia. That philosopher was an Ephesian who was put to death for allegedly practicing magical arts. Others believe that Lactantius indicates not Maximus but Porphyry. According to the *Suda*, Porphyry lived from the time of Aurelian down to Diocletian; yet no one is unaware how fiercely he raged against the Christians. Holstenius, however, proves in chapters 3 and the final chapter of his *Life of Porphyry* that this philosopher was not Porphyry. Bayle holds the same view in his *Historical Dictionary*, under “Hierocles.”
>
> **His vices beneath his hair, etc.** Philosophers customarily grew beards, which a poet therefore called wise. Horace, *Satires* II.3:
>
> > At the time when, to console me,  
> > He ordered me to nourish a wise beard.
>
> Hence philosophers were often called “bearded masters.” Thus Persius, *Satire* IV:
>
> > Believe that it is a bearded master  
> > Who says this—a man whom a dreadful draught of hemlock carries off.
>
> They grew beards because they believed that a beard bestowed a certain majesty upon them. When Diogenes was asked why he grew so large a beard, he replied: “So that, seeing [Col. 0554B] and touching it, I may remember that I am a man.” Hence men also affected [Col. 0554C] holiness through their beards, as did the philosopher whom Lactantius discusses here. See the same Lactantius, *On the Anger of God*, chap. 22.
>
> **Whom he was driving from their homes and lands.** Five recent manuscripts and seven printed editions have “buildings,” with the first letter omitted, perhaps through a copyist’s carelessness, since it is identical with the final letter of the preceding word.
>
> **Might recover their soundness.** Lactantius similarly uses *resanaret* in Book IV, chap. 20, at the beginning, and *resanati* below in Book V, chap. 22, at the end. You will scarcely find these words in any other Latin authors.
>
> **And not cruel.** Nine recent manuscripts and six printed editions read “nor.”
>
> **In other matters.** Eight manuscripts and the printed editions add “human,” which is rejected by many preferable and older manuscripts and by the Rome 1474 edition.
>
> **Human.** This word is absent from several manuscripts.
>
> **And old-womanish superstition.** An appropriate epithet for extreme superstition, because the female sex is supposedly more inclined to superstition; hence Strabo, Book VII, called women *τὰς δεισιδαιμονίας ἀρχηγούς*, “the originators of superstitions.” To the weakness and levity of the sex there is also added the feebleness of age. **HERALDUS.**
>
> **Empty.** Colbert manuscript 1, by its first hand, the Cotton manuscript, and one Clermont manuscript read “inconstant.”
>
> **Kept silent.** Thus the English and eleven other manuscripts, together with the better editions of 1476 and 1497 and the Turnèbe and Soubron editions. Some other witnesses read “closed their eyes”; one recent Royal manuscript has the corrupt *coniberent*; one Leipzig and one Colbert manuscript read “restrained”; the Utrecht and one Brunswick manuscript read “were restrained”; one Colbert manuscript reads “assembled”; four manuscripts and as many printed editions read “became silent”; one recent Bologna manuscript reads “became silent” in the singular; and one old Royal manuscript reads: “For if any of our people had been present … he would have closed his eyes … he would have mocked.”
>
> **That he would instruct others in the truth.** Lactantius uses the same expression in Book III, chaps. 11 and 27; Book V, chaps. 2 and 11; Book VI, chap. 2; Book VII, chap. 14; and *On the Anger of God*, chap. 23.

There arose in that same place two men who assailed truth, as it lay prostrate and cast down, with an insolence that I cannot tell whether to call more arrogant or more importunate. One of them professed himself a high priest of philosophy; yet he was so vicious that, while posing as a master of self-restraint, he burned with avarice no less than with lusts. His manner of life was so extravagant that, while presenting himself in the school as a defender of virtue and a eulogist of frugality and poverty, he dined more disgracefully in the palace than at home.

Nevertheless, he concealed his vices beneath his hair and philosopher’s cloak and—what is the greatest covering of all—his wealth. To increase that wealth, he forced his way into the friendship of judges by extraordinary canvassing and quickly placed them under obligation to himself through the authority of his false title. He did so not merely that he might sell their verdicts, but also that, through this power, he might deter his neighbors—whom he was driving from their homes and lands—from reclaiming their property from him. [Col. 0553B]

This man, who refuted his own arguments by his conduct—or condemned his conduct by his arguments—and who was his own severe censor and most vehement accuser, vomited forth three books against Religion and the Christian name at the very time when the just people were being criminally torn apart. Before all else, he professed that it was the philosopher’s duty to remedy men’s errors and recall them to the true way—that is, to the worship of the gods, by whose divine power and majesty, as he said, the world is governed. He declared that philosophers must not allow ignorant people to be enticed by the deceits [Col. 0554A] of certain persons, lest their simplicity become the prey and food of cunning men.

He therefore claimed that he had undertaken this task, worthy of philosophy, in order to hold out the light of wisdom before those who could not see: not only so that, by taking up the worship of the gods, they might recover their soundness, but also so that, after laying aside their stubborn obstinacy, they might avoid bodily torments and not choose to endure cruel mutilations of their limbs in vain.

To make evident the purpose for which he had elaborated that work, he poured himself out in praises of the rulers. Their piety and providence, as he asserted, had become illustrious both in other matters and especially in defending the religions of the gods. At last, he said, provision had been made for human affairs: impious and old-womanish superstition had been restrained so that all people might devote themselves to lawful rites and experience the gods as propitious toward them. [Col. 0554B]

But when he attempted to undermine the rational basis of the religion against which he was declaiming, he appeared foolish, empty, and ridiculous. For that weighty counselor of another’s welfare knew neither what he was attacking nor even what he was saying. Those of our people who were present, although they kept silent out of regard for the circumstances, nevertheless mocked him inwardly. They saw a man professing that he would illuminate others although he was himself blind; recall others from error although he did not know where to place his own feet; and instruct others in the truth although he had never seen even a single spark of it [Col. 0555A]—since, while professing wisdom, he was striving to destroy wisdom.

Yet everyone condemned the fact that he had undertaken such a work at precisely that time when hateful cruelty was raging. [Col. 0555A]

> **Note: [Col. 0555B] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 555–556]**
When hateful cruelty was raging. He means the time of the persecutions under the emperors. From this it may be inferred that Lactantius wrote after those times. [Col. 0555C]

Because of his vanity. Thus the Gotha manuscript and the editions of 1476 and Gymnich; others read “emptiness.” “Another wrote on the same subject.” In place of *de eadem materia* (“on the same subject”), our Lactantius more than once takes pleasure in using the accusative case instead of the ablative.

More caustically. The Venetian edition of 1471 stands alone here in reading “more moderately.” Compare below: “so that he might be thought to have offered humane and kindly counsel.” BUN.

Another wrote more caustically on the same subject. This was Hierocles, who prefixed to the books he wrote against the Christians the title φιλαληθής (*philalēthēs*), that is, “Lover of Truth,” as Eusebius reports; Eusebius also splendidly refuted them in a treatise. ISAEUS.—Hierocles lived at the same time as Lactantius, namely, at the beginning of the fourth century after Christ’s birth. Hierocles so pleased Diocletian by his eagerness to persecute Christians that some scholars believe he was promoted from judge at Nicomedia to prefect at Alexandria. On this subject see *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, ch. 16. Epiphanius discusses his cruelty in *Heresy* 68, and because of [Col. 0555D] it Hierocles had an evil reputation.

Who was then one of the judges. At that time he held the Augustal prefecture of Alexandria, as Epiphanius reports, *Heresies* 68. ISAEUS.

Demosthenes. An antonomasia for “a supreme orator,” just as shortly afterward Aristophanes stands for an empty-headed poet, and Aristarchus for a very learned man who, as a critic of others’ scholarship and an ὀβελίζων (*obelízōn*, “marker with an obelus”), became proverbial. Indeed, “Aristophanes’ lamp” also became proverbial because of his extraordinary diligence. Lactantius therefore means men who were certainly learned, but profane and ill-suited to grasping the mysteries of God. BETULEIUS.

Had assented. This must be emended, in accordance with the Rohans and Saint-Germain manuscripts, to *assensus*, not, as Jean-Baptiste Le Brun had corrected it, *accensus*. Here Lactantius indicates that Hierocles had embraced the faith which he afterward abjured, and this is correctly expressed by the verb *assensus*, that is, “having assented to the religion.” *Accensus fidei*, “enrolled into the faith,” would be less properly said. Moreover, it is perfectly correct to say “to assent to a religion or faith.” Yet here is Jean-Baptiste Le Brun’s note, which we rightly reject:

> “Thus I emended it to *accensus* from a great many manuscripts, among which are two very ancient Royal manuscripts and the Caucianus. Seven recent manuscripts and fifteen printed editions corruptly read *assensus*; recent manuscript 1, the Colbertine, and manuscript 2, the Leipzig, read *ascensus*. But *accensus* is best, meaning ‘enrolled,’ from *accenseo*. This word denotes an attendant of a magistrate, one substituted for a deceased soldier, or one added to a legion already at full strength. See Vegetius, *On Military Affairs*, book II, ch. 19.”

On the same word *accensus*, Bunemann writes as follows:

*Accensus.* All editions from 1465 through 1685, including the Rostock edition—although Heumann writes otherwise—have *assensus*. But Janus Gulielmus, in his *Questions on Plautus’ Menaechmi*, ch. 4, was the first to restore *accensus* from parchment manuscripts; so too the Gotha, Leipzig 1, Emmanuel, Caucianus, and Utrecht manuscripts. Compare Lactantius, book II, ch. 9: “He is enrolled” (*accensetur*); and shortly afterward in the same passage, “He is registered” (*adscribitur*). BUN.

He was far removed from faith and truth. From all the manuscripts and several printed editions I have added “from faith,” which is missing from the rest. Manuscripts 1 and 1 Royal and 1 Colbertine have “charity” instead of “truth.”

Aristophanes … Aristarchus. As Heumann observes, the conjunction makes it probable that Aristophanes of Byzantium, the grammarian and teacher of the grammarian Aristarchus mentioned here, is meant. Fabricius gives more about both in *Bibliotheca Graeca*, vol. VII, pp. 51 and 53. BUN.

From these men. That is, from the apostles, whom he mentions in the preceding chapter.

Or who could. The Junius and Colbertine manuscripts and four printed editions read “could have.” In recent manuscripts 2 Royal, 3 Colbertine, Bodleian, Cottonian, and 1 Clermont, the reading is “as if anyone could.”

Consistent with one another and coherent. See book I, ch. 4. Cicero, *Second Philippic*, ch. 8:

> Were you so senseless that throughout your entire speech you contradicted yourself, so that you uttered not merely things consistent with one another—understand “not merely not”—but things utterly disconnected and contradictory?

BUN.

Agrees. On the disagreements and contradictions among the philosophers, and on the harmony of the sacred Scriptures, read St. Augustine, *The City of God*, book XVIII, ch. 41.

For not for gain. I have restored this reading from four very ancient [Col. 0557B] manuscripts—1 Bologna, Junius, Caucianus, and Regius-Puteanus—and the edition of Isaeus. In the others “therefore” stands in place of “for.”]

O philosopher turned flatterer and servant of the times! But in this case he was despised for his vanity: he both failed to obtain the favor for which he hoped, and the glory he pursued was converted into blame and reproach.

Another wrote more caustically on the same subject. He was then one of the judges and had been among the principal instigators of the persecution. Not content with that crime, he also attacked in writing those whom he had afflicted. For he composed two little books, not *against* the Christians—lest he appear to assail them as an enemy—but *to* the Christians, [Col. 0555B] so that he might be thought to have offered humane and kindly counsel. In them he tried to accuse sacred Scripture of falsehood on the ground that it was wholly self-contradictory. For he set forth certain passages which seemed to conflict with one another, enumerating matters so numerous and so intimate that he appears formerly to have belonged to the same discipline. But if he did, what Demosthenes could defend him against the charge of impiety, when he had become a traitor to the religion to which he had assented, to the faith whose name he had assumed, and to the sacrament he had received? Unless, perhaps, the divine writings happened by chance to fall into his hands. [Col. 0556A] What rashness, then, was it to dare dismantle something that no one had interpreted for him? It is just as well that he either learned nothing or understood nothing. For the divine writings are as far from contradiction as he was far removed from faith and truth. Above all, however, he mangled Paul and Peter and the other disciples as sowers of deceit, although he also testified that these same men were uncultivated and uneducated; for some of them had earned their living by the fisherman’s trade—as if it grieved him that the account had not been contrived by some Aristophanes or Aristarchus.

## CHAPTER III  
### On the truth of Christian teaching, the vanity of its adversaries, and the fact that Christ was not a magician

[Col. 0556B] These men, therefore, lacked both the intention and the cunning to fabricate, since they were uneducated. Or how could an uneducated man fabricate things consistent with one another and coherent, when the most learned of the philosophers—Plato, Aristotle, Epicurus, and Zeno—made statements that were self-contradictory and mutually opposed? For this is the nature of falsehoods: they cannot cohere. But the apostles’ tradition, because it is true, fits together on every side and agrees wholly with itself; and it therefore persuades because it is supported by consistent reasoning. For they did not devise that religion for the sake of gain or [Col. 0557A] advantage, since both in their teachings and in actual practice they pursued a life that is without pleasures and despises everything counted among goods. Not only did they undergo death for the faith, but they also knew and foretold that they would die and that afterward all who followed their discipline would suffer bitter and unspeakable torments.

Apollonius performed equal deeds, etc. It is written of Apollonius of Tyana that, when he stood before Domitian, he suddenly disappeared from the imperial council. So that you may know the story, we shall give a brief summary. Apollonius of Tyana, as Philostratus relates in book IV, was a very great professor of philosophy, a magician—or, as the Pythagoreans prefer, [Col. 0557D] a philosopher. After traveling to the Brahmans, hearing the hierarch seated upon his throne, freeing the Ephesians, and performing many deeds by divine power, he was accused of disloyal sentiments toward Domitian, of practicing magic, and of other ridiculous things of that kind. At Domitian’s command Apollonius hastens to Rome; he presents himself before the judge, is cast into prison, and is kept in fetters for trial. Damis, who alone had followed him, is confined with him. To convince Damis that it was within his power to leave prison whenever he wished, Apollonius showed him the fetters, from which he withdrew his feet and into which he inserted them again at his own pleasure. When Damis saw this, he then plainly believed Apollonius to be a divine man. Apollonius sent him ahead to Puteoli and foretold the hour at which Damis should await him on the shore. Apollonius is brought out of prison and placed before Domitian’s tribunal. The emperor acquits him. But when he was forbidden to depart and Domitian reminded him that there were matters he wished to discuss with him, [Col. 0558B] Apollonius answered him as follows before a very large assembly:

> I would have you know, my lord, that I am subject to you by no decree of fate; and, so that you may know it more fully, no power over my life is granted to you. Farewell.

Having spoken these words, he suddenly vanished, while everyone stood amazed and, because of the novelty and miraculous character of the event, could scarcely believe his own eyes. Apollonius hurried to Damis, whom he found walking anxiously on the shore and troubled about the Tyanean himself. From Jerome. Johannes Baptista Pius.

[Col. 0558C] Eunapius, in his preface, makes him a kind of demigod and says that Philostratus ought to have entitled his work not Ἀπολλωνίου βίον (*Apollōníou bíon*), “The Life of Apollonius,” but θεοῦ εἰς ἀνθρώπους ἐπιδημίαν (*theoû eis anthrṓpous epidēmían*), “A God’s Advent among Human Beings.” The emperor Caracalla esteemed him so highly that he thought he should be honored with a heroic monument. The blasphemous Hierocles dared compare him with Christ, and Eusebius refuted Hierocles in a book devoted to that purpose. MEURSIUS.—All scholars, however, maintain that this story about Apollonius is a fable. Arnobius numbers Apollonius among famous magicians in book I. St. Jerome nevertheless considers that, amid the many plainly fabulous elements in his story, some things are true. *Letter to Paulinus*.

Why do they procure statues, why portraits? Porphyrion, commenting on Horace’s words, “a funeral procession and triumphal portraits,” bears witness that portraits were used at the funerals of nobles. The commentator says:

> At the funeral of every highly distinguished person, portraits of his ancestors were customarily carried before him, a practice we see observed at the funerals of rulers.

Authors frequently mention this rite. Cicero, *Eleventh Oration*:

> Brutus, why are you sitting there? What do you wish that old woman to report to your father? What to all those whose portraits you see being carried? What to your ancestors?

Valerius Maximus, book VIII, ch. 15:

> Africanus has a portrait placed in the shrine of Jupiter Best and Greatest. Whenever a funeral must be celebrated for someone of the Cornelian family, it is fetched from there.

Livy, *Epitome* XLVIII, on Lepidus:

> He instructed his sons to carry him out upon a bier covered neither with linen nor with purple, saying that the funerals of the greatest men were customarily ennobled by the sight of ancestral portraits, not by expenditure.

Tacitus, *Annals*, book III, relates that at Junia’s funeral twenty portraits of the most illustrious families [Col. 0559B] were carried before her. The same author, book IV, concerning Drusus’ funeral:

> The portraits of the Claudii and Livii were grouped around the bier; he was mourned in the Forum and praised before the rostra.

Tacitus, book II, states that they were not carried before Germanicus at his funeral:

> The funeral lacked portraits and procession, but was illustrious through praise and the memory of his virtues.

These portraits were nothing other than wax likenesses of the body down to the shoulders, preserved for consolation. Roman nobles adorned their atria with portraits of this kind, arranging them in order in certain wooden cases or cabinets, from which they were taken at the time of funerals. This may be gathered from Pliny, book XXXV, ch. 2:

> Likenesses of faces modeled in wax were arranged in separate cabinets, so that portraits might be present and accompany the funerals of the clan; and whenever anyone died, the entire people of his family who had ever existed was present.

At the funerals of rulers, however, portraits not only of members of the clan but of every great and outstandingly virtuous man were carried in front, as at the funeral of Augustus in Dio, book LVI. The same was done at other funerals. If anyone had been condemned for a shameful and monstrous crime, his portrait was customarily condemned and broken, and it was not carried in funeral processions. See Juvenal, Satire 8, and Tacitus, *Annals*, book I. Thus Tacitus teaches that the portraits of Brutus and Cassius had been suppressed, at the end of *Annals*, book III, 20. It therefore appears that as many little funeral couches were carried in front as there were ancestral portraits, so that each portrait had its own couch upon which it was borne. Yet one may not unreasonably judge that these portraits were sometimes carried not on couches of this kind but on long poles or spears, as the displays in triumphs customarily were. Silius, book X, on Paulus’ funeral, leads us toward this conjecture:

> Neither wife nor sons were present, nor a throng of men  
> united to him by kindred blood; nor, as customary,  
> did an ancient portrait, borne aloft on a bier,  
> precede and adorn the funeral procession.

Furthermore, not only portraits but also effigies of conquered peoples [Col. 0559D] and cities, the names of defeated enemies written beneath captions, and the very spoils captured from enemies were customarily carried in front and exhibited at emperors’ funerals, as appears in Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book VIII, on Coriolanus’ funeral. Tacitus, on Augustus’ funeral procession:

> Then the honors were considered; among them the most distinguished appeared to be the proposal that the funeral should pass through the triumphal gate. Gallus Asinius proposed that the titles of the laws Augustus had enacted and the names of the peoples he had conquered should be carried before it.

Dio, book LVI, says that this too was done. The same author, book LXXIV, reports the same thing concerning Pertinax’s funeral:

> Then passed all the nations subject to the Roman Empire, represented in bronze statues and adorned according to each nation’s native custom.

Lucan understood this in book VIII, when he says that Pompey does not seek

> that a funeral procession should carry his ancient triumphs before him.

Indeed, Polybius, book VI, relates that lictors with fasces and the other insignia of the magistracies which the deceased had formerly held went before the procession. [Col. 0560B] It should also be noted that these fasces were customarily reversed, as we learn from Tacitus, *Annals*, book III, concerning Germanicus’ funeral:

> The ashes, therefore, were carried upon the shoulders of tribunes and centurions; before them went unadorned standards and reversed fasces.

Virgil appears to have touched upon this custom in the *Aeneid*, book XI. Albinovanus, on Drusus’ funeral:

> The fasces that I first saw, I saw at a funeral;  
> and I saw them reversed, a sign of disaster.

JOHANNES KIRCHMANNUS.—It should further be noted that these wax portraits were once carried with the highest honor even at the funerals of our own kings.]

Alexicacus. That is, “averter of evils.” When Ephesus was suffering from a plague, Apollonius freed it in the following way—if Philostratus is to be believed. After summoning the people to an assembly for the performance of sacred rites, a man in beggar’s garb appeared, who could readily move people to pity, and ordered the Ephesians to overwhelm him with stones. When the people hesitated out of compassion, Apollonius continued to press them until he induced at least some to pick up stones. After the beggar once and again displayed fiery eyes, the entire crowd, believing him to be a demon, overwhelmed him with stones. When the stones were afterward removed, the lifeless corpse of a dog lay in their midst. Thus freed from the plague, the Ephesians erected a statue to Apollonius as to an ἀποτρόπαιος (*apotrópaios*, “averter”) Hercules—for that is the reading in Philostratus, not ἀλεξικάκος (*alexíkakos*, “averter of evils”). The latter is otherwise an epithet of Hercules. BETUL.

O mind blacker than the Cimmerian darkness, as they say! The Cimmerians were a Scythian people from whom the Cimmerian Bosporus took its name. At its mouth stood the town of Cimmerion, which was also called Cerberion, as Pliny states in book V. Strabo, in book VII, thinks that it was called the Cimmerian Bosporus as though “Cimbrian,” from the Cimbri, who wandered without fixed abodes and carried on warfare as far as Lake Maeotis. The ancients believed the climate of the Cimmerians to be obscure and dark, as Strabo also records in book I. Homer too mentions the matter when speaking as follows of the Cimmerians:

> Upon them the sun never sheds Phaethon’s light;  
> destructive night is always stretched above them.

Tibullus too, emulating Homeric song, sang as follows in a heroic poem:

> He also approached the shadowy citadels of the Cimmerians,  
> which day never visited with its gleaming dawn,  
> whether Phoebus ran above the earth or beneath it.

Since, therefore, the region of the Cimmerians was dark and its air gloomy, the proverb “Cimmerian darkness” was derived from it.

him, and as the Jews then thought, if all the prophets had not foretold with one spirit that Christ would do precisely those things. This could not then, nor can it ever, happen to Apollonius, Apuleius, or any magician.

After pouring forth such ravings of ignorance, after striving utterly to extirpate the truth, he dared entitle his impious and God-hating books Φιλαληθεῖς (*Philalētheîs*), “Lovers of Truth.” O blind [Col. 0561B] heart! O mind blacker than the Cimmerian darkness, as they say! Perhaps this man was a disciple of Anaxagoras, for whom snow was ink. Yet it is the same blindness both to apply the name of falsehood to truth and the name of truth to a lie. Obviously, the crafty man wished to conceal the wolf under sheep’s clothing so that he might ensnare the reader with a deceptive title.

But let it be so: suppose you did this through ignorance, not malice. What truth, then, did you bring us, except that, after championing the gods, you finally betrayed those very gods? For after pursuing the praises of the supreme God—whom you confessed to be king, greatest of all, creator of the universe, fountain of good things, parent of all, and maker and sustainer of living beings—you took the kingdom away from your Jupiter, drove him from supreme power, [Col. 0561C] and reduced him to the number of servants. Your [Col. 0562A] epilogue therefore convicts you of folly, vanity, and error. For you affirm that gods exist, yet you subject and enslave them to that God whose religion you are trying to overthrow.

## CHAPTER IV  
### Why this work was published; and again concerning Tertullian and Cyprian

When, therefore, the men of whom I have spoken expounded their sacrilegious writings while I was present and grieving, I was spurred by their arrogant impiety, by my consciousness of the truth itself, and—as I believe—by God, to undertake this duty: to refute the accusers of justice with all the powers of my intellect. I did this not to write against those men, who could have been crushed in a few words, but to rout with one single [Col. 0562B] assault all who everywhere are doing or have done the same kind of work. For I do not doubt that very many others, in many places, have constructed a monument to their injustice not only in Greek but also in Latin writings. Since I could not answer every one of them individually, I thought I should plead this case in such a way as both to overturn the earlier writers together with all their writings and to cut off from future writers every opportunity to write or reply.

Only let them lend me their ears: I shall certainly bring it about that everyone who comes to know these things will either embrace what he formerly condemned or, at the very least, finally cease to ridicule it. Although Tertullian fully pleaded the same case in the book entitled *Apologeticus*, nevertheless it is one thing to answer accusers—which consists solely in defense or denial [Col. 0562C]—and another to give systematic instruction, which is what we are doing [Col. 0563A] and in which the substance of the entire doctrine must be contained. I therefore did not shrink from this labor, so that I might fill out the subject which Cyprian did not fully treat in the discourse in which he attempts to refute Demetrianus, [Col. 0563A]

[Note: [Col. 0563B] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 563–564]

In which he addresses Demetrianus, etc. That Demetrianus was not the proconsul of Africa but a Carthaginian judge of lower rank. He said that all the evils then oppressing the world were to be blamed upon the Christians.

[Col. 0563C] Barking at and clamoring against the truth. These are Cyprian’s own words at the beginning of his book.

For he ought not to have been refuted by testimonies from Scripture … but by arguments and reason. Augustine thinks very differently. Lactantius and Jerome unjustly criticize St. Cyprian here for bringing forward the testimony of sacred Scripture, or of the Hebrew prophets, against the pagan proconsul Demetrianus. For Augustine says in *Against Faustus*, book XIII, ch. 7:

> We demonstrate the reliability of the prophets from the things which they foretold would come and which are now seen to have come.

And in the same book, ch. 10:

> Through their books, indeed, we prove that these things were not written down by us after we had been warned by the event itself, but were foretold and preserved long ago in that kingdom and are now manifested and fulfilled.

And in ch. 2 of the same book:

> To say that Hebrew prophecy is not suited to bringing the Gentiles to belief in Christ, when one sees all nations believing in Christ through Hebrew prophecy, is ridiculous madness.

The ancient author of the *Treatise against Five Heresies*, formerly published under Augustine’s name, thinks no differently. [Col. 0563D] In ch. 7, Appendix, vol. VIII, p. 9, he says:

> Come here, pagan, and hear what the prophet says. I did not write for myself whatever I wished. The book in which these things are found written is kept in a Jew’s cabinet. My enemy is my witness; ask him yourself. Open, read, and believe.

Ignorant of the truth. Walchius correctly saw this, illustrating it from Cicero, *On Duties*, book III, ch. 6:

> This one virtue, justice, is the mistress and queen of all the virtues.

Why multiply examples? Lactantius himself says again in this book, [Col. 0564D] ch. 14:

> Justice is called the supreme virtue because it embraces all the virtues together.

> God himself is the fountain of goodness.

In the same book, ch. 21:

who, as Cyprian himself says, was “barking at and clamoring against the truth.” He did not handle this subject as he should have done; for Demetrianus ought to have been refuted not by testimonies from Scripture—which he naturally regarded as empty, fabricated, and fictitious—but by arguments and reason. For since Cyprian was dealing with a man ignorant of the truth, he should have set aside the divine readings for a little while and formed him from the beginning as one still untrained, gradually showing him the first principles of light, lest he be blinded when the whole light was placed before him.

For just as an infant, because of the tenderness of its stomach, cannot take the strength of solid and substantial food, but is nourished by the fluidity [Col. 0563B] and softness of milk until, its powers having grown firm, it can feed on stronger fare, so too, because this man was not yet able to grasp divine things, human testimonies—that is, those of philosophers and historians—ought first to have been presented to him, so that he might be refuted chiefly by his own authorities. Because he did not do this, carried away by his exceptional learning in the divine writings so as to be content with those alone upon which faith rests, I undertook, by God’s inspiration, to do it myself, and at the same time to prepare a path for others to imitate. [Col. 0564A] And if, at our exhortation, learned and eloquent men begin to direct themselves to this subject and prefer to display their talents and power of speech in this field of truth, no one will doubt that the false religions will shortly vanish and that all philosophy will fall, if everyone is persuaded that this alone is religion and this alone is also true wisdom. But I have wandered farther than I intended.

## CHAPTER V. The True Justice That Existed Under Saturn Was Driven Away by Jupiter

We must now return to the proposed discussion of justice, which is either itself the highest virtue or itself the source of virtue. Not only philosophers sought it, but poets as well, who lived much earlier and, before [Col. 0564B] the name “philosophy” was born, were regarded as wise men. They clearly understood that justice was absent from human affairs, and imagined that, offended by the vices of men, it had withdrawn from the earth and migrated to heaven. And in order to teach what it means to live justly—for they are accustomed to give their precepts through circumlocutions—they draw examples of justice from the age of Saturn, which they call the Golden Age, and relate the condition of human life while justice remained on earth. [Col. 0565A] This, indeed, should be regarded not as a poetic fiction but as truth. For during Saturn’s reign, before the worship of the gods had been instituted and before any nation [Col. 0565A]

had yet been consecrated into belief in its divinity, God was certainly worshipped. And therefore there were neither dissensions, nor enmities, nor wars.

> Not yet had madness drawn the frenzied swords,

as Germanicus Caesar speaks in his poem on Aratus:

> Nor had discord been known among those of common blood.

Indeed, it was unknown even among foreigners; nor were there any swords at all to be drawn. For while justice was present and flourishing, who would think either about defending himself, when no one plotted against him, or about destroying another, when no one coveted anything?

[Col. 0565B]

> They preferred to live content with modest provision,

as Cicero relates in his own work—a quality proper to our religion.

> It was not even lawful to mark or divide the field by a boundary;  
> They sought their provisions for the common stock.

For since God had given the earth to all in common, so that they might live a common life, and not so that ravenous and raging greed might claim everything for itself, no one was deprived of what was produced for everyone. The poet’s statement must be understood, not as meaning that at that time there was no private property whatever, but as a poetic figure: we are to understand that people were so generous that they did not shut away the crops produced for them, nor brood alone over hidden stores, but admitted the poor to a share in the fruits of their own labor. [Col. 0565C]

[Col. 0566A]

> Now rivers of milk, now rivers of nectar flowed.

Nor is this surprising, since the storehouses of the just stood generously open to everyone. Greed did not intercept divine benefits and thus create hunger and thirst among the populace; instead, all enjoyed equal abundance, since those who had gave liberally and plentifully to those who had not. But after Saturn was driven out by his son and conveyed to Latium—

> Fleeing the arms of Jove, an exile from his stolen kingdom—

when the people, corrupted either through fear of the new king or of their own accord, had ceased to worship God and had begun to regard the king as God; and when he himself, almost a parricide, served as an example to others for violating filial piety:

[Col. 0566B]

> The most righteous maiden swiftly abandoned the earth;

but not, as Cicero says:

> And settled in Jove’s kingdom and a region of heaven.

For how could she settle or remain in the kingdom of one who expelled his father from his kingdom, pursued him in war, and drove him as an exile throughout the whole world?

> He added evil venom to the black serpents  
> And ordered the wolves to prey:

that is, he implanted hatred, envy, and deceit in men, so that they might be as venomous as serpents and as rapacious as wolves. This is indeed what those men truly do who persecute the just and those faithful to God, and give judges the power to rage against the innocent. [Col. 0566C] Perhaps Jupiter did something of this kind in order to assault and abolish justice; and for that reason he is said to have made [Col. 0567A] the serpents savage [Col. 0567A]

> [Note: [Col. 0567C] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 567–568]

Latin authors, however, do not say that a covenant or association is “plundered” (*diripere*), but that it is “dissolved” (*dirimere*). Thus our author, from Cicero, book VI, chapter 6: “These men … dissolve society.” BUN.
>

>

The more recent manuscripts and printed editions have *aliis* (“to others”), which does not agree with the verb *participare*. For *participare* is regularly joined with the accusative. Plautus said “to give a slave a share in his plan,” *Cistellaria*, Act I, scene III, verse 17; and Cicero, “to give one person a share with another,” *On the Laws* I, no. 33.—**Those men did not impart to others.** *Participare alicui* (“to impart to someone”) occurs very frequently in the ancient translation of Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, which Grabe and Fabricius thought was produced at the end of the second century: book I, chapter 1, fol. 10, “Nous was devising a way to impart the Father’s greatness to the remaining aeons”; book I, chapter 9, fol. 59, “Who imparted his grace to him”; book II, chapter 61, fol. 191, “The soul imparting life to its own body … imparting life to the body”; book IV, chapter 28, fol. 316, “Wishing to impart his glory to his disciples.” BUN.

The old French translator already recognized this, rendering it “for the use of all men.” BUN.

and sharpened the wolves.

> Then came the madness of war and the love of possessing.

And not without reason. For once religion toward God had been removed, men also lost knowledge of good and evil. Thus the communal life of mankind came to an end, and the covenant of human society was dissolved. Then they began to join hands in combat with one another, to lay ambushes, and to obtain glory for themselves from human blood.

## CHAPTER VI. With Justice Driven Out, Desire, Unjust Laws, Audacity, Greed, Ambition, Pride, Impiety, and Other Vices Reigned

The source of all these evils was desire, which of course erupted from contempt for true majesty. [Col. 0567B] Those to whom anything accrued not only failed to give others a share, but also seized what belonged to others, drawing everything into private profit; and the things for which individuals had previously labored for human uses were amassed in the houses of a few. For in order to subject the rest to servitude, they began first to withdraw and collect the necessities of life and to keep them securely shut away, so that they might make heavenly benefits their own—not from humanity, of which there was none in them, but so that they might scrape together every instrument of desire and greed. They also enacted for themselves, under the name of justice, the most inequitable and unjust laws, [Col. 0567C] by which they might protect their plunder and greed against the power [Col. 0568A] of the multitude. Thus they prevailed as much by authority as by physical force, wealth, or wickedness. And since there was no trace in them of justice, whose duties are humanity, equity, and mercy, they now delighted in proud and swollen inequality; and by a retinue of guards, steel, and distinctive clothing, they made themselves higher than other men. Hence they invented honors, purple robes, and fasces for themselves, so that, supported by the terror of axes and swords, they might command the stricken and fearful as though by the rightful authority of masters. Into this condition that king brought human life who, after defeating and driving away his father, seized not a kingdom but an impious tyranny by force and with armed men. He abolished that golden and just age and compelled men to become wicked and impious, even by this very fact [Col. 0568B]: that he turned them away from God to worship himself—something that the terror of his most insolent power had extorted.

For who would not fear a man surrounded by arms and encircled by the unfamiliar glitter of steel and swords? Or what stranger would he spare, when he had not spared even his own father? Whom, indeed, would he fear, after defeating in war the robust and exceptionally powerful race of the Titans and destroying it utterly? What wonder, then, if the whole multitude, oppressed by an unfamiliar fear, went over to flattering a single man? They feared him and rendered him the greatest honor. And because imitating the character and vices [Col. 0568C] of the king is judged to be a form of obedience, they all cast aside [Col. 0569A] piety, lest by living piously they should appear to reproach the king for his crime. Thus, corrupted by continual imitation, they abandoned divine right, and little by little the habit of living wickedly became custom. [Col. 0569A]

> [Note: [Col. 0569B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 569–570]
>
> **The habit became custom.** Arnobius, II, p. 58, reverses this: “For through custom the habit will become familiar.” Perottus, *Cornu Copiae*, Aldine edition, fol. 653: “Custom is properly defined [Col. 0569C] as a manner of life confirmed by habit.” For Varro, custom is an established disposition of mind which habit ought to follow. BUN.

He calls justice “put to flight.” BUN.
>

Six recent manuscripts and twelve printed editions read: “… sang—that is, to the kingdom of Jove.” The Rohault manuscript and the Subiaco edition read: “Foolish, therefore, are the poets who sang that she had fled for refuge to heaven, to the kingdom of Jove.” The Saint-Germain manuscript, however, reads: “Foolishly, therefore, the poets who sang that she had fled for refuge to the kingdom of Jove.” Choose whichever you please.
>
