But these last three could have learned from Isaeus’s marginal note that the passage is from the speech *For Deiotarus*, chapter 9: “To be called frugal does not carry much praise in a king; brave, just … generous, beneficent, liberal—these are royal virtues.” BUN.

See book IV, chapter 23: “In which … he has agreed”; *On the Anger of God*, chapter 9: “In which all their predecessors had agreed”; ibid., chapter 11: “To such an extent does universal nature agree in unity.” Cicero himself, *For Sestius*, chapter 51: “In which cause all agree.” BUN.

Yet there it is not exercised by adversities. **God therefore.** After these words, one very old Royal manuscript, the Caucus, Gotha, and Marmoutier manuscripts, and five printed editions add “intending to bring justice back.” In place of “evil,” the Penitential manuscript has “wickedness.” As to his statement that God “did not exclude evil,” that is, permitted evil, here are Thomasius’s scholia on this passage. These are his words:
>
> “The words ‘intending to bring justice back’ must also be struck out, for they certainly appear to have been transferred from the margin into the text. In this chapter Lactantius indeed seems to say many things by which he would in some fashion make God the author of evil. Yet if each statement is properly considered, he does not assert this. For he either says that God does not exclude evil, or that he permits it so that virtue may have something against which to struggle. Here, [Col. 0571B] and elsewhere when he discusses evils, by the term ‘evils’ he often understands not so much morally base things themselves, or their baseness, as adversities and things contrary to nature, such as [Col. 0571C] unhappy events, poisons, and the like. These are not evils properly and in themselves, but because they are harmful to us they are commonly called evils. Ambrose, in his *Exposition of Psalm 128*, Sermon 16, said the same thing that Lactantius says here, except that what Lactantius, following common usage, called ‘evils,’ Ambrose called ‘harsh things.’ ‘God,’ says Ambrose, ‘did not create evils, but those things which seem harsh to us—lashes, death, and other things of this kind—which have been ordained for the correction of the guilty.’ In evil and in every sin, as theologians hold—and Augustine in particular argues at length in *Against Julian*, book V, chapter 3—two things can be considered: the baseness itself and the punishment. The baseness has no relation to God; yet God can rightly be called the author of punishment. Lactantius may indeed be defended in this passage by this distinction, although what we said earlier seems capable of being fitted more suitably to Lactantius’s words. If anyone nevertheless thinks that Lactantius here says that God is simply the author of evil, let him know that we utterly abominate that opinion and have therefore undertaken this labor, so that it may become clear that this opinion [Col. 0571D] had no authors except the Manichaeans.”
>
> Thus Thomasius in his notes on Lactantius.]

Nothing now remained of the pious and excellent condition of the preceding age. Instead, justice, driven out and drawing truth away with herself, left mankind error, ignorance, and blindness. Foolish, therefore, are the poets who sang that she had fled for refuge to the kingdom of Jove. For if justice was on earth in the age they call golden, she was certainly driven away by Jove, who changed the Golden Age. But the transformation of the age and the expulsion of justice must be understood, as I have said, as nothing other than the abandonment of divine religion. This alone causes one man to hold another dear and to know that he is bound to him by the bond of brotherhood, [Col. 0569B] since the same God is Father to all; it causes him to share the benefits of God, their common Father, with those who have none; to injure no one, oppress no one, close his doors to no guest and his ear to no petitioner; but to be generous, beneficent, and liberal—qualities Tullius regarded as royal praises. This assuredly is justice, and this is the Golden Age. Corrupted first under Jove’s reign and then, when both he and all his offspring had been consecrated and the worship of many gods adopted, it was entirely abolished.

[Col. 0570A]

## CHAPTER VII. On the Coming and Fruit of Jesus, and on the Virtues and Vices of His Age

But God, like a most indulgent father, as the final age drew near, sent a messenger to bring back that ancient age and justice which had been put to flight, lest the human race be tossed about by the gravest and perpetual errors. The likeness of that Golden Age therefore returned, and justice was indeed restored to the earth, but assigned to a few. Justice is nothing other than the pious and reverent worship of the one God. But someone may perhaps be troubled as to why, if this is justice, it has not been given to the whole human race, and why the entire multitude has not agreed upon it. It requires a substantial discussion to explain why God, when He gave justice to the earth, [Col. 0570B] retained diversity. I have explained this elsewhere, and it will be discussed whenever the subject fittingly arises. For now it is sufficient to indicate it very briefly: either virtue cannot be discerned unless it has contrary vices, or it is not perfect unless exercised by adversities. For God willed this distinction between good and evil so that we might know the character of good from evil, and likewise that of evil from good; nor can the nature of either be understood if the other is removed. God therefore did not exclude evil, so that the nature of virtue might remain established. For how would patience retain its power and its name if there were nothing that we were compelled to endure? How would faith devoted to its God merit praise unless there were someone who wished to turn it away from God? For it was also for this reason [Col. 0571A]

> [Note: [Col. 0571D] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 571–572]
>
> **For it was also for this reason.** The conjunction “also” is missing from one Bologna-Royal-Puteanus manuscript and three printed editions.
>
> **The unjust to be more powerful.** Twelve recent manuscripts and the old Roman and Aldine editions read “superior.”
>
> **Which is rare.** I restored this from one old Bologna manuscript, five Royal manuscripts, one Clermont manuscript corrected by a second hand, and the Gymnicus edition. Many have “which”; the Royal-Puteanus has “whereby”; recent witnesses, “which is rarely found.”
>
> **In the work entitled *With His Head Covered*.** This was the title of a declamation, now lost.—**In *With His Head Covered*.** This work has perished. *Obvolutum* means “covered,” as in book I, chapter 22: “that an amphora covered with wine be placed.” Plautus, *Mostellaria* II, 1: “Let him flee with his head covered … flee and cover your head.” The phrase also occurs in book I, chapter 22: “that a covered amphora of wine be placed.” BUN.
>
> **Would innocence be a virtue.** Two Bologna manuscripts, one recent Royal manuscript, and the Taxius edition read “of innocence.”
>
> **Toward that upon which they have fastened.** This is the reading of two old Bologna, six Royal, three Colbertine, one Clermont, the Brunswick, and the Cambridge manuscripts. Four recent Royal and twenty-three Colbertine manuscripts have “may have fastened,” which Bunemann also prints.—**Toward that upon which they may have fastened.** The Bologna, Reimmann, and Leipzig 2 witnesses have “toward that upon which they have fastened.” All, however, have *in id quod* for *in id in quod*: by ellipsis the preceding preposition is not repeated. Thus *Epitome* 27: “Lest anyone fall into the same snares into which those ancients fell.” BUN.
>
> **To be free from fault.** For, according to Jerome, to live in the flesh apart from the flesh is an angelic life rather than a human one. To Cicero, indeed, as he writes to Marius in the seventh book of his *Letters*, “To be free from fault is a great consolation.” And conscience is certainly a thousand witnesses; but Paul subjects the whole mortal race to guilt. BETULEIUS.—“And if we say that we have no sin, the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).
>
> **If nature had given equal passions to all.** I emended this from the Royal-Puteanus, five other Royal, six Colbertine, two Clermont, the Emmanuel, Cambridge, and Brunswick manuscripts, and eleven printed editions. Three manuscripts and the same number of common editions read “to the passions”; some read “effects,” wrongly.
>
> **There would be no virtue.** One old Bologna manuscript reads “virtue would be nothing.”
>
> **And the more frequently it is assailed, the more firmly it is strengthened.** I restored this from all the manuscripts. Lactantius wrote thus, in an idiom peculiar to some ecclesiastical writers; the more customary wording, “the more frequently … the more firmly,” occurs in the printed editions. But the manuscripts have the positive adverbs, “frequently” and “firmly.” St. Augustine likewise, omitting the comparative, which he likes to leave understood, says in *Retractations* II, chapter 15, no. 6: “Which seems to me a light declamation”—that is, a lighter declamation—“rather than a grave confession.”—**The more frequently … the more firmly.** Sparke, Cellarius, Walchius, and Heumann maintain complete silence about this reading; yet it is presented by the Bologna, Taxius, and Penitential witnesses and almost all Isaeus’s manuscripts. The wording is perfectly good Latin, provided that “more” is understood. See Gronovius on Livy I, chapter 25, and Livy XXXIV, chapter 4; Tacitus, *Annals* III, chapter 46: “The richer in money and more opulent in pleasures the Aedui are, the more unwarlike you will prove them”; *Annals* XII, chapter 11: “He should embrace clemency and justice, the more unknown they were to barbarians, the more tolerable they were.” What Tacitus and others do in only one member of the comparison, Tertullian often does in both; for example, *To the Nations* I, 7: “The more inclined you are to wickedness, the more receptive you are to belief in evil.” BUN.
>
> **Place.** Twelve recent manuscripts and six printed editions read “Establish.”]

that He permitted the unjust to be more powerful, so that they might compel others to evil; and for this reason He permitted them to be more numerous, so that virtue, which is rare, might be precious. Quintilian excellently and briefly demonstrates this very point in *With His Head Covered*:

> “For,” he says, “what virtue would innocence be unless rarity had given it praise? But because nature has so arranged matters that hatred, desire, and anger drive blind men toward whatever they have fastened upon, it seems superhuman to be free from fault. Otherwise, if nature had given equal passions to all, piety would be nothing.”

How true this is, the very necessity of reason teaches. For if virtue consists in bravely resisting evils and vices, [Col. 0571B] it is apparent that there can be no virtue without evil and vice. In order to render virtue absolute and perfect, God retained what was contrary to it, so that it might have something against which to struggle. For when it is agitated by battering evils, it acquires stability; and the more frequently it is assailed, the more firmly it is strengthened. This, assuredly, is the reason why, although justice has been sent to mankind, it is nevertheless said that there is no Golden Age: because God did not remove evil, so that He might retain the diversity which alone contains the mystery of divine religion.

[Col. 0572A]

## CHAPTER VIII. On Justice, Which Is Known to All but Not Embraced; on the True Temple of God and His Worship, That All Vices May Be Crushed

Those, therefore, who think that no one is just have justice before their eyes, but are unwilling to see it. For why do they describe her either in poems or in every kind of discourse, complaining of her absence, when it is very easy to be good if they wish? Why do you depict an empty justice for yourselves and wish for her to fall from heaven, as though represented in some image? Look: she is before your eyes. Embrace her, if you can, and place her in the dwelling of your heart; do not consider her difficult to attain or alien to the times. Be equitable [Col. 0572B] and good, and the justice you seek will follow you of her own accord. Lay aside every wicked thought from your hearts, and immediately that Golden Age will return to you—something you cannot attain in any other way than by beginning to worship the true God. You, however, desire justice on earth while the worship of the gods remains, which can happen by no means whatever. Nor, indeed, could it have happened even at the time when you suppose it did; for since those gods whom you impiously worship had not yet been born, the worship of the one God must necessarily have prevailed throughout the earth: namely, of Him who abominates wickedness [Col. 0573A] and requires goodness, whose temple is not stones or clay [Col. 0573A]

> [Note: [Col. 0573B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 573–574]
>
> **Not stones or clay.** The Brunswick manuscript reads “not stone or clay.”
>
> **Not with gifts of gold and jewels.** I follow the six older Royal and four Colbertine manuscripts. Eight recent manuscripts and the printed editions have “with gold.”
>
> **Is adorned.** Some printed editions read “may be adorned.”
>
> **Learn.** I restored this from very many printed editions and from all the manuscripts except one recent Royal manuscript, which in its first hand has the singular “Learn,” as do some printed editions.
>
> [Col. 0573C] **If you have any mind remaining.** Walchius says that the “remaining mind” is that which remained to men after the Fall. To me the words mean the same as in book I, chapter 21, “If you possess any sanity”; book V, chapter 3, “If you have any heart”; ibid., chapter 9, “If you have any wisdom.” Heumann writes *reliquum* instead of *reliquae*, but there is no need to depart from the reading of all the books. Thus Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* XI, 94–95: “If any sound mind remains within you.” Burmann cites Suetonius, *Tiberius*, chapter 62: “The corpses being cast out by a band of marines, without any remnant of breath remaining in any of them.” BUN.
>
> **And unjust because the gods are worshipped.** He effectively turns the charge of the alleged evils and impiety back upon the nations. Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chapter 41: “It is therefore you who are troublesome to human affairs, you who are guilty of public calamities, you who are always the enticers of evils, among whom God is despised and statues worshipped.” Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*: “When those things occur which reveal the wrath of an indignant God, they do not occur because of us, by whom God is worshipped, but are inflicted because of your sins and deserts, by whom God is neither sought at all nor feared.” ELMENHORST. **Therefore evils … grow heavier.** The passage bears traces of Cyprian’s *Against Demetrianus*. The Gentiles alleged that Christians were the causes of every evil. To refute such claims, Arnobius wrote his books *Against the Gentiles*, Augustine his work *The City of God*, and Orosius his *History*. BUN.
>
> **United.** Without any punctuation before it. I restored this from seven Royal manuscripts, among which two are very old, four Colbertine manuscripts, many others, and the old Roman edition. Seven recent manuscripts and most printed editions read the nominative “united.”
>
> **Would prepare.** I restored this from the Royal-Puteanus and very many other manuscripts and the old Roman editions, supported by another very old Royal manuscript in which “will have prepared” is read. Four recent Royal manuscripts, two Colbertine manuscripts, and nine printed editions read “prepares.”
>
> **Sees through.** I restored this from the great majority of manuscripts and two old Roman editions. Lactantius uses this verb throughout his works, and it is more appropriate than “sees,” the reading of six manuscripts [Col. 0574B] and eight printed editions. The words “secret” and likewise “thoughts” support it.
>
> **So that to frail beings.** I added “so that” from six printed editions and all the manuscripts except one Colbertine and one Clermont manuscript; it is also missing from nine common editions. At the same place, for “might prefer,” Francius wrote “to prefer” in the margin of his copy of Lactantius.
>
> **A woman … should seek.** The Brunswick manuscript and Betuleius’s edition read “women … should seek.”
>
> **Men restrained their lust.** The genuine reading, restored by me from the Betuleius and Cellarius editions and all the manuscripts except two recent Royal manuscripts, which, together with the other printed editions, read “despised their lust.”
>
> **A religious contribution.** That is, alms collected together.
>
> **There would therefore not be, as I have said.** One old Bologna manuscript and five recent editions read, absurdly, “Nor would there be mutual things, as I have said.”
>
> **If by all.** Restored from almost all the manuscripts. Two recent Royal manuscripts, three Colbertine manuscripts, and sixteen printed editions have “if by men.”
>
> **All conspired to uphold the law of God.** That is, combined together, or, as Gallus and Francius maintain, “swore together.” For the word *conjurare* is generally taken in a bad sense by writers. Lactantius therefore intended it in its proper sense of “swearing together,” and alludes to the ancient custom by which holy men bound the Jews by oath to observe the law of God and not deviate from it in any way. Such a *conjuratio* is good and praiseworthy. GALLUS.—Nevertheless, we must not depart from the consensus of all the manuscripts and editors. For although the word is generally taken in a bad sense, Servius nevertheless says on Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII, 5: “It must be noted that a *conjuratio* can be spoken of in connection with a good cause.” There are the well-known lines of Claudian, *On the Third Consulship of Honorius*, pp. 96, 98:
>
> > O you too greatly beloved by God, for whom the air does battle,  
> > And winds, joined in alliance, come at the trumpet’s call.
>
> **Remained.** Were Lactantius not fond of speaking in this way, as I have already noted, I would gladly write the plural “remained” with Francius; but I do not dare to do so against the authority of the manuscripts and editors.
>
> **So many.** Sensible and wise men long ago said that many laws are evidence of corrupt morals in a commonwealth. Hence Cicero in *On Duties* II and Sallust said that good laws arise from bad morals.
>
> **Governors.** Those who presided over the provinces.
>
> **Would voluntarily train men for works of justice.** I added the preposition “for” from the manuscripts and printed editions; it is absent from one old Bologna manuscript and five editions. See below, chapter 10, “they are trained for injustice”; and at the end of chapter 11, “They train their worshippers for these works.”]
but the human being himself, who bears the image of God. This temple is adorned, not with corruptible gifts of gold and jewels, but with the eternal offerings of virtues. Learn, therefore—if any sound mind remains to you—that human beings are evil and unjust because the gods are worshipped, and that all evils daily weigh more heavily upon human affairs because God, the maker and governor of this world, has been forsaken; because impious religions have been adopted, contrary to what is right; and, finally, because you do not permit God to be worshipped even by a few.

But if God alone were worshipped, there would be no dissensions or wars, since human beings would know that they were children of one God; and therefore, since they would be joined by the sacred and inviolable bond of divine kinship, there would be no treacherous attacks, because they would know what punishments God prepares for murderers of souls [Col. 0573B]—God who sees through secret crimes and even thoughts themselves. There would be neither fraud nor robbery if, at God’s command, they had learned to be content with what was their own and with little, preferring things substantial [Col. 0574A] and eternal to things frail and transient. There would be no adulteries, sexual violations, or prostitution of women if it were known to everyone that God condemns whatever is sought beyond the desire for procreation. Nor would necessity compel a woman to profane her modesty in order to obtain a most shameful livelihood for herself, since men would restrain their lust, and the pious and religious contributions of those who possessed means would relieve those who had none.

Therefore, as I have said, none of these evils would exist upon earth if everyone were united under oath to the law of God; if all did what our one people practices. How blessed, how golden, would be the condition of human affairs if gentleness, dutiful devotion, peace, innocence, equity, temperance, and good faith remained throughout the whole world! Finally, there would be no need for so many and such varied laws to govern human beings, since the one law of God would suffice for perfect innocence; nor would there be need of prisons, swords for protection, or the terror of punishments, since the saving power of the heavenly commandments, infused into human hearts, would of itself instruct human beings in the works of justice. [Col. 0574B]

But now [Col. 0575A] they are evil—

> **Note: [Col. 0575C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 575–576]**
>
> **They are evil.** The Cambridge manuscript and six old editions wrongly add *human beings*.
>
> **For, when discussing.** The Gothic manuscript, one Leipzig manuscript, and the Bruni edition read *arguing forcefully*, omitting *for*.
>
> **Just as one, etc.** This passage is found neither in the books *On the Laws* nor in Cicero’s other works. From this and other evidence it may be inferred that Cicero’s books have been mutilated and greatly corrupted.
>
> [Col. 0575D] **Under one and the same protection.** Six more recent manuscripts read *under one and the same protection* with the ablative construction.
>
> **Human beings would assuredly live the life of gods.** Sixteen more recent manuscripts and five editions have, “human beings would assuredly live by the life of gods.” But the actual phrase occurs among the fragments of Book I of Cicero’s *On the Laws*: “all would assuredly live the life of gods.” And Cicero, Fourth Verrine Oration, no. 118: “They think that they will live a safer life under my protection.” I was nevertheless unwilling to change *human beings* to *all*, contrary to the authority of all the Lactantian codices. Our Lactantius also said elsewhere, Book I, chapter 14: “They lived a rustic life”; Book VII, chapter 24: “Human beings will live a most tranquil and abundant life”; and *On the Anger of God*, chapter 7: “He will live the life of cattle beneath a human appearance.”
>
> **Meanwhile.** Five more recent manuscripts and the old Roman edition read *again*.
>
> **Because they perform good deeds.** Thus I read with the five older Royal manuscripts, several others, and nine old editions. Three more recent manuscripts have “who perform good deeds”; five more recent manuscripts and seven commonly received editions, “because they perform good deeds” with a different verbal form; two printed editions have “who.”
>
> **Yet the conquered are spared, etc.** Augustine, in Book I, chapter 1 of *The City of God*, complains that the city of Christ, which is the Church, lives in exile in this world and is afflicted by those very people whose art, according to the poet, and peculiar glory is:
>
> > To spare the subjected and subdue the proud.  
> > (Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.853)
>
> And in the next chapter he teaches by several examples that no wars were ever waged in which the victors spared the conquered. [Col. 0576C–D]
>
> **Amid arms.** See Cicero, *Oration for Marcellus*.
>
> **Wolves.** See Virgil, *Aeneid* II.356.
>
> **Shall we say?** Thus all manuscripts and editions except one Colbert manuscript and three editions, which have “shall we say?” with the future form.
>
> **Truth.** Terence, *The Woman of Andros*, Act I, scene 1. These words are spoken by the freedman Sosia.
>
> **Inspired by a divine spirit.** Eight more recent manuscripts and four editions read “instructed”; the rest, “inspired.”
>
> **They regard them as burdensome.** This passage is plainly a twin of Book V, chapter 21: “They persecute holy and just men, whom they feel to be burdensome to themselves … so that … they may remove them altogether from the earth, lest there be any who can restrain their wickedness.”
>
> **As though their life were thereby convicted.** Compare chapter 6 on the matter. Sulpicius Severus, Book II, chapter 28: “Vices are always hostile to virtue, and all the best people are regarded by the wicked as though they reproached them.” Seneca, *On the Happy Life*, chapter 19: “It is advantageous to you that no one should appear good, as though another’s virtue were a reproach for your offenses.” **BUN.**
>
> **Before whom they are ashamed to live wickedly.** Thus almost all manuscripts and most editions. And correctly, by anastrophe; that is, the pagans are ashamed to live wickedly before those Christians. But the Oxford manuscripts and eleven commonly received editions printed “whom they are ashamed to live wickedly before,” as though the pronoun *whom* had to be construed with *are ashamed*.—Anastrophe is not infrequent in our author. Book VI, chapter 5: “Among whom we dwell.” Ibid., chapter 17: “Against whom they argue.” The sense is that the pagans are ashamed to live wickedly before Christians. He expressed the same sense above: “They are ashamed to be wicked in the presence of the just and good.” **BUN.**

through ignorance of what is right and good. Cicero indeed saw this, for in discussing the laws he says:

> Just as the world, being one and governed by one and the same nature, coheres and is sustained through the mutual concord of all its parts, so all human beings, though mingled together by nature, are divided by depravity. They do not understand that they are kindred and that all are subject to one and the same protection. If this truth were maintained, human beings would assuredly live the life of gods.

Therefore, the unjust and impious worship of the gods has introduced all the evils by which the human race destroys itself in mutual conflict. For those who, like prodigal and rebellious children, had disowned God, the common Father of all, could not retain dutiful devotion.

## CHAPTER IX [Col. 0575B]  
### On the Crimes of the Impious and the Tortures of Christians

Sometimes, nevertheless, they perceive that they are evil; they praise the condition of former ages and infer from their own conduct and deserts that justice is absent. Yet when justice stands before their very eyes, they not only fail to receive or recognize it but even hate it violently, persecute it, and strive to exterminate it.

Let us suppose for the moment that this which we follow is not justice. How, when that justice which they consider true arrives, will it be received by people who tear apart and kill those whom they themselves acknowledge to be imitators of the just because they perform good and just deeds? Even if they killed only the evil, they would be unworthy of a visit from justice, whose sole reason for leaving the earth was the shedding of human blood. How much more is this so when they kill the pious [Col. 0575C] and regard the very followers of justice as enemies—indeed, as worse than enemies? For although the lives, property, and children of enemies are attacked by sword and fire, the conquered are nevertheless spared, and amid arms there remains room for clemency; or, if men have chosen to rage with utter savagery, nothing further is done to them than that they are killed or led away into slavery. But what is done against those who do not know how to do wrong is beyond description. No one is considered more harmful than those who are the most innocent of all. [Col. 0576A]

Thus the vilest of men dare to mention justice—men who surpass wild beasts in savagery and ravage God’s most gentle flock:

> Like ravening wolves  
> In black mist, driven blindly forth  
> By the wicked frenzy of their bellies.

Yet these men have been made savage not by frenzy of the belly but by frenzy of the heart. They do not range about in black mist but engage in open plunder; nor does consciousness of their crimes ever call them back, to prevent them from violating with that mouth the holy and pious name of justice—a mouth which, like the jaws of beasts, drips with the blood of the innocent. [Col. 0576B]

What shall we say is the chief cause of such great and persistent hatred? Is it that

> Truth breeds hatred,

as the poet says, seemingly inspired by a divine spirit? Or are they ashamed to be wicked in the presence of the just and good? Or rather, is it both? For truth is always hated because the person who sins wants an unrestricted opportunity to sin, and thinks that he cannot enjoy the pleasure of wrongdoing more securely unless there is no one to whom his crimes are displeasing. They therefore strive to uproot and remove them completely, as witnesses of their crimes and wickedness, and regard them as burdensome, as though their own life were thereby convicted.

For why should there be some who are inconveniently good, who, when public morals have been corrupted, cast reproach upon others by living well? Why should not all be equally evil, rapacious, unchaste, adulterous, [Col. 0576C] perjured, greedy, and fraudulent? Better still, why not remove those before whom they are ashamed to live wickedly—those who strike and scourge the shamelessness of sinners, if not by words, since they remain silent, nevertheless by the very example of their different manner of life? For whoever dissents appears to administer correction.

[Col. 0577A] Nor is it greatly surprising that such things are done against human beings, since even against God himself—

[Col. 0577A]

> **Note: [Col. 0577B] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 577–578]**
>
> **God himself.** That is, Christ.
>
> [Col. 0577C] **A people established in hope.** That is, the Jewish people, concerning whom Acts 26:6 says: “In the hope of the promise made by God to our fathers.”
>
> **The just.** That is, Christians.
>
> **By their own faithlessness.** One Royal-Puteanus manuscript and eight more recent manuscripts, together with the editions, read *of their own accord*; Bruni reads *by persuasion*. The other manuscripts, including one very old Bologna manuscript and one very old Royal manuscript, read as in the text, “have deserted the heavenly mystery”; that is, the religion of Christ.
>
> **And enrich them with honors.** That is, they increase and heap honors upon them, as in Plautus and Cicero. One Colbert manuscript and Bruni read *magnify them*. Francius might perhaps prefer *entice them*. But *enrich* is Lactantius’ genuine reading. Thus below, chapter 10, “enriches them with misfortune.”
>
> **They call them desperate, etc.** *Desperate* is παράβολος (*parabolos*). Those otherwise called *finishers* were so named: they fought wild beasts and devoted their labor to killing them, and were consequently called παράβολοι, “desperate men.” Christians were also designated in this way in antiquity because they did not spare themselves and willingly laid down their lives for their God. **SALMASIUS.**—And they preferred to be torn apart rather than violate the faith pledged to Christ.
>
> [Col. 0577D] **For they call them impious.** Christians were commonly assailed by pagans as impious, ill-omened, atheistic, irreligious, profane, and sacrilegious, because they rendered absolutely nothing to the gods and did not sacrifice for the emperors. Tertullian: “You say: ‘You do not worship the gods, and you do not offer sacrifices for the emperors,’ etc.; and so we are prosecuted as guilty of sacrilege and treason.” Arnobius, Book IV: “Because you call us impious and irreligious.”
>
> **So completely has all shame vanished.** Three more recent manuscripts and six old editions read: “Indeed, so completely has all shame vanished.”
>
> **They turn back.** The Junius manuscript and five printed editions read *turn aside*; two Colbert manuscripts and one Clermont manuscript, *turn*.
>
> **Being themselves, of course, pious and averse to human blood.** This is said ironically. Fourteen manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470 wrongly read “being themselves, of course, impious,” for that does not cohere with “and averse to human blood.”
>
> **Not from our number, but from theirs.** Thus most manuscripts, including the old ones. Twelve more recent manuscripts read *from* twice; Bruni reads *out of* twice.
>
> [Col. 0578B] **If they are exceedingly pious.** The Gothic manuscript reads: “If they are less pious.” But those who exposed their children wished to appear more pious than those who strangled them. Otherwise it would be easy to emend the text to: “if, to be sure, they are pious.” I have shown at Book I, chapter 10 that these expressions vary in the manuscripts. **BUN.**
>
> **Expose them.** Thus Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 9: “First of all, you expose your children, to be taken up by some unrelated mother.” Aristotle, *Politics* VII.17. Under Athenian law people were permitted to kill or expose any newborn child they did not want—such cruelty even among the people considered wisest! The Thebans provided the contrary by law: if anyone exposed an infant, he was to be punished with death. Aelian, *Various History* II.7. Infants were often exposed with tokens, which were called by the general name γνωρίσματα (*gnōrismata*, “means of recognition”) in Greek and *crepundia* (“recognition trinkets”) in Latin. Terence, *The Eunuch*, Act IV, scene 6:
>
> > Where is the little chest? Bring it with the tokens.
>
> These *crepundia* were added as provisions supplied by fortune, so that whoever found the infants would have something with which to support them. Various kinds of such tokens are enumerated in Longus, Book I of the *Pastorals* (*ποιμενία*); there he speaks of swaddling bands, a little sword, a headband, sandals, and other things of this kind. **BETUL.**
>
> **Priestess.** That is, a Vestal virgin; thus *Aeneid* I.277, “the royal priestess,” for “the royal Vestal.”
>
> **Nor the sack.** I write this with the old editions and with one Royal-Puteanus manuscript, four other Royal manuscripts, two Colbert manuscripts, one Sorbonne manuscript, the Navarre, Victorinus, Gattius, and Marmoutier manuscripts, one Clermont manuscript, two old Roman editions, and the edition of Fasius of 1543. But one Colbert manuscript and Bruni read “nor any”; one more recent Royal manuscript, four Colbert manuscripts, one Clermont manuscript, and six printed editions, “nor the sack” with a variant spelling; one old Royal manuscript, two Colbert manuscripts corrected by a second hand, and Junius, “nor the little horse.” I discussed this kind of punishment at Book III, chapter 14.
>
> **And customary among them.** Thus very many manuscripts transmit the text, among them two very old Royal manuscripts and one Bologna manuscript, which also adds “among them.” But the Caucianus, Leipzig, Palatine, and Utrecht manuscripts read “and not customary”; other more recent manuscripts and the same number of editions, “and unusual.” We have followed the reading reported by Thomasius from an old Bologna codex, which that most learned editor confirms by this example: “The fraudulent substitution of wills in order to seize inheritances was very customary among the pagans; Marcus Crassus, one of the leading men of the Roman Republic, acquired a bad reputation on this account. Since this occurred in the case of a leading man, what are we to believe concerning others?”

—for the same reason there rose up even a people established in hope and not ignorant of God; and the just are subject to the same necessity that assailed the very author of justice. They therefore harass them and torture them with ingenious forms of punishment; nor do they consider it enough to kill those whom they hate unless cruelty also makes sport of their bodies.

If any, from fear of pain or death, or through their own faithlessness, have deserted the heavenly mystery and consented to death-dealing sacrifices, they praise them and enrich them with honors, so that by their example they may entice the others. But those who have highly valued their faith and have not denied that they are worshippers of God they assail with all the strength of their torture chambers, as though thirsting for blood. They call them desperate because they by no means spare their own bodies—as though [Col. 0577B] anything could be more desperate than torturing and tearing apart someone whom you know to be innocent. So completely has all shame vanished among those from whom all humanity is absent! [Col. 0578A] And they turn back upon just men insults that properly belong to themselves.

For they call them impious—being themselves, of course, pious and averse to human blood! Yet if they considered both their own actions and those of the people whom they condemn as impious, they would at once understand how mendacious they are and how much more deserving they themselves are of everything they say or do against the good.

For it is always not from our number but from theirs that there arise men who lie armed in ambush along roads and plunder the seas; or, if open brigandage is not permitted, secretly compound poisons; who murder their wives to profit from their dowries, or their husbands in order to marry their lovers; who strangle the children born to them or, if they are exceedingly pious, expose them; who do not restrain incestuous lust even from a daughter, sister, mother, or priestess; who conspire against their own fellow citizens and country; who do not [Col. 0578B] fear even the sack; who, finally, commit sacrilege and despoil the temples of the gods they worship. And, to mention things that are slight and customary among them, they court legacies, forge wills, remove or exclude rightful heirs; they prostitute their bodies to lusts; and finally, forgetful of the sex in which they were born, they vie with women in passive submission. [Col. 0579A]

>
> **They vie with women in passive submission.** Against those who burn with lust for men.

> [Col. 0579C] **Who pollute even the most sacred part of their body in defiance of every divine law.** That is, when they admit into themselves an accursed frenzy “which does not spare even the head,” as he says in Book VI, chapter 33; thus **ISAEUS**. Is this to be understood of the offense committed when a man violates continence upon himself?—**The most sacred part of the body.** Namely, the head. See the authors cited by me at Book VI, chapter 23. Here he has reproduced Cicero, *After His Return*, chapter 5: “Who could not repel the impure intemperance of men even from the most sacred part of his body.” See Graevius on this passage, p. 367. **BUN.**
>
> **Who reap their male organs with the sword.** Arnobius, Book V: “And do we not daily see those who have reaped away these parts from themselves?”
>
> **Seneca’s books.** Among his surviving works, read the second letter of Book XVI, where he inveighs against various crimes, but especially against corrupt judges. The same things may be seen in Tertullian’s *Apology*, chapter 12.
>
> **Take in hand.** Cicero, *On the Orator* III.4: “Those who take these works in hand.” *Tusculan Disputations* II.3: “He takes Epicurus in hand.” Pliny, *Letters* I.16: “When you take his speeches in hand.” Quintilian, *Institutes* X.1, p. 882: “Whose speeches we have taken in hand.” **BUN.**
>
> **And equally throughout the day.** Thus the Royal-Puteanus manuscript and others. Seventeen more recent manuscripts and five editions read “days.” One old Royal manuscript reads “and equally indeed.”
>
> **In the forum (*induforo*).** It is remarkable how greatly the manuscripts vary here. I read *induforo* from one very old Royal manuscript, the Palatine and Penwortham manuscripts, and Lucilius himself as edited by Franciscus Dousa. Supporting these are the Caucianus, four Royal, five Oxford, three Colbert, Junius, Utrecht, Navarre, Gattius, Marmoutier, Emmanuel, two Clermont manuscripts, Bruni, and six editions, which have *indeforo* for *induforo*, by archaism, just as in Lucretius IV.318, Lambinus’ edition reads *indugredi* or *endogredi* for *ingredi*, “to enter.” For the ancients used *indu* and *endo* for *in*, as Lambinus observes there, pp. 456 and 277. In the same Lucretius, *indu manu* and *indu statu* stand for “in the hand” and “in a condition”; in Book V, *indu manus* for “into the hands”; and in Book VI, *indu mari* for “in the sea.” One old Bologna manuscript and four other more recent manuscripts have *induforum*; two Royal manuscripts, *induforus*; one Royal and five commonly received editions, *indufori*; one Colbert manuscript and the Victorinus manuscript, “to see in the forum,” corruptly. *Induforo* is also found in Ennius, Book VII. [Col. 0580B–C] Betuleius thinks the *indufori* are those who spend their leisure in the forum, just as *inforare* in Plautus means to make something public in the forum. Roughly similar forms are Virgil’s *induperator* for *imperator*, and Lucretius’ *indugredi* and *indupeditus* for *ingredi* and *impeditus*. Thomas Spark nevertheless thinks that *endo forum* should be read, because Lucretius similarly has, in Book II:
>
> > If anyone may lawfully climb into the regions of heaven;
>
> and *endogredi* in the same Lucretius for *ingredi*.
>
> **Vie in flattery.** Thus nearly all the manuscripts and editions, nor is it read otherwise in Lucilius. One more recent Royal manuscript, the Balliol manuscript, and six commonly received editions read “to flatter, to vie.”
>
> **Our.** Thus Tertullian also.
>
> **Would follow throughout all the rest.** Thus almost all manuscripts and printed editions. The Royal-Puteanus manuscript and printed editions have “follows”; one old Bologna manuscript, “would be sought”; two more recent Royal manuscripts, one Colbert manuscript, the Canterbury manuscript, and three old editions, “is prevalent.” Our reading greatly pleased Antonio Agustín, a man of the keenest literary judgment.
>
> [Col. 0580D] **And therefore it cannot happen.** I restored this from many editions and all manuscripts except two Royal manuscripts and seven editions, which have “equally”; Thomasius’ edition has “And”; one old Bologna manuscript, “And indeed.” This emendation belongs to the Antonio Agustín just praised, who read: “what is supreme, would follow throughout all the rest, and therefore it cannot happen, etc.” Thomasius found this reading very attractive. But Bunemann has: “Equally, it cannot happen,” and supplies the following note on this word.—Lactantius frequently uses *equally* in this way, though manuscripts have here and there corrupted it by substituting “and therefore.” Thus Book III, chapter 17: “It is characteristic of the wise man to do evil.… Equally, it is characteristic of the fool to do good.” Ibid., chapter 27: “Those who do not embrace religion are earthly, because …; and those who think that the soul … perishes equally look toward the earth, because,” etc. **BUN.**
>
> **That they are not also deceived in religion.** From all the manuscripts and very many editions I have restored the negative particle, which is absent from some editions. Six printed editions have “not also.”
>
> **Would preserve its tenor in all other matters.** This is the reading of very many manuscripts and seven editions. The Royal-Puteanus manuscript, seven other more recent manuscripts, and five editions read “preserves and”; the Junius manuscript, “they preserve.”

They pollute and profane even the most sacred part of their body in defiance of every divine law; they reap their male organs with the sword and, what is more criminal, do so in order to become ministers of religion; they do not spare even their own lives but sell their lives to be publicly extinguished. If they sit as judges, they either destroy the undeserving after being corrupted by a bribe or allow the guilty to go unpunished. They even assault heaven itself with sorcery, as though the earth could not contain their wickedness. These crimes, I say, and more than these, are assuredly committed by those who worship the gods.

Amid so many and such great crimes, what place is there for justice? I have collected examples from many sources, not in order to prosecute them but to demonstrate the fact. Those who wish to know everything should take Seneca’s books in hand, for he was both the most truthful describer and the sharpest accuser of public morals and vices. Lucilius too concisely and precisely depicted that dark life in these verses:

> But now, from morning until night, on holidays and working days,  
> Throughout the whole day alike, both people and senators,  
> All parade themselves in the forum and never withdraw;  
> All have devoted themselves to one and the same pursuit and art:  
> To deceive with words cautiously, to contend deceitfully,  
> To vie in flattery, to feign oneself a good man,  
> And to devise snares, as though everyone were everyone’s enemy. [Col. 0580A]

But which of these things can be charged against our people, whose entire religion consists in living without crime and without stain? Since, therefore, they see both themselves and their own people doing the things we have described, while our people do nothing except what is equitable and good, they could, if they possessed any wisdom, understand from this that those who do good are pious and that they themselves, who commit abominations, are impious. For it cannot happen that those who do not err in any of the actions of their lives should err in the supreme matter itself—that is, in religion, which is the head of all things. Impiety adopted in that which is supreme would follow throughout all the rest. And therefore it cannot happen that those who err throughout their whole lives are not also deceived in religion, since piety, holding the rule in the highest matter, would preserve its tenor in all other matters. Thus, on either side, the nature of the supreme principle itself may be known from the condition of the actions performed.

[Col. 0580B]

## CHAPTER X  
### On False Piety, and on False and True Religion

It is worthwhile to examine their piety, so that from the things they do with clemency and piety it may be understood what sort of deeds they perform contrary to the laws of dutiful devotion. And lest I appear to assail anyone without mercy, I shall assume a poetic character who is, perhaps, the greatest possible example of piety. In Maro, that famous king—

[Col. 0581A]

> **Note: [Col. 0581C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 581–582]**
>
> **That famous king.** Namely, Aeneas; Virgil, *Aeneid* I.544.
>
> **He had bound.** Virgil, *Aeneid* XI.81.
>
> **To the shades.** The shades are the souls of the dead.
>
> **Funeral offerings.** These are rites for the dead performed on the thirtieth, fortieth, and anniversary days, with sprinkling over the tomb. See Virgil, Book V.
>
> **With slain blood.** For “with the blood of the slain”; as likewise *Aeneid* X.520 has “with captive blood” for “with the blood of captives.”
>
> **Intending to sprinkle.** From almost all the manuscripts and fifteen printed editions; better than “those intending to sprinkle,” as found in one more recent Royal manuscript, Junius, one Colbert manuscript, and six old editions. Three more recent manuscripts wrongly read “things intending to sprinkle.”
>
> **More merciful.** Ironically. Thus one very old Royal manuscript, two Bologna, four other Royal, four Colbert, three Leipzig, the Bodleian, Cotton, Marmoutier, one Clermont manuscript, the old Roman edition of 1474, and seven others. And correctly. See above, “with clemency” and “without mercy,” and what follows below. The Junius manuscript, with Francius, reads “more unmerciful”; the Royal-Puteanus manuscript, thirteen more recent manuscripts, and ten editions, “more insane.” Gallaeus defended this last reading rather inappropriately, for he failed to observe that Lactantius is here being ironic against the pagans. See the note on chapter 36 of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*: “What can be more merciful than this piety?”—The Junius manuscript reads “more unmerciful,” from which Columbus, on chapter 31 of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, concludes that the true reading is: “What can be more unmerciful than this piety? What more insane than to feed the dead …?” His intended meaning would then be: nothing is more unmerciful, and therefore nothing more unworthy of Aeneas, who boasted that he was pious—for clemency too was called *pietas*, as was shown above—than cruelly slaughtering and burning innocent human beings; nothing is more unsuitable for an experienced and prudent commander than believing that the dead feed upon human blood. Heumann, in his addenda, believes that Columbus emended the passage ingeniously and successfully. **BUN.**
>
> [Col. 0582C] **Who defiled a man renowned for piety with a notorious crime.** Virgil, *Aeneid* I. This reading is derived from the Royal-Puteanus, five other Royal, six Colbert, Canterbury, and two Clermont manuscripts, and six editions, except that four manuscripts and the same number of printed editions read “defiled”; the rest, “may have defiled.” Two Royal manuscripts and seven commonly received editions read “who defiled that renowned man.”
>
> **Behold pious Aeneas.** Thus I restored the text from the manuscripts and printed editions, except one old Bologna manuscript and three editions, which have “Then pious Aeneas,” less suitably for Lactantius’ purpose.
>
> **Sulmo.** This comes from *Aeneid* X.517. Pliny says that Sulmo was a town in ancient Latium.
>
> **Here four young men … whom he might sacrifice to the shades.** Tertullian: “In former times, because it was believed that the souls of the dead were propitiated with human blood, captives or slaves were sacrificed at funerals.”
>
> **At that very same time.** Lactantius uses “that very same” frequently.
>
> [Col. 0582D] **Indeed.** Virgil, *Aeneid* XI.111.
>
> **Good.** Ironically, from Virgil, Book II.
>
> **For he was adjured by that same father.** *Aeneid* X.524:
>
> > By your father’s spirit and the hopes of rising Iulus,  
> > I beg you, preserve this life.
>
> **CELL.**
>
> **And by the hopes of rising Iulus.** From Virgil, *Aeneid* X.524. I have restored the word “by” from three Royal manuscripts, two of them very old. Ten more recent manuscripts and six printed editions have “and the hope.”
>
> **By the Furies.** Virgil, *Aeneid* XII.946.
>
> **And of his father’s spirit.** Three Colbert manuscripts and one Clermont manuscript read “hand”; the Emmanuel manuscript, “lifeless.”
>
> **Those who were not resisting.** One old Bologna manuscript reads “those who were fighting”; Junius, “those who were pleading.”
>
> **Someone will say, etc.** An excellent description, teaching what Christians are, or ought to be.
>
> **They become.** Heumann reads “they are”; correctly.
>
> **Nothing pertains to the gods.** On this subject see *On the Anger of God*, chapter 4, and above, Book III, chapter 17.
>
> **Who judges.** One old Bologna manuscript reads “who protests.”

—than whom

> None was more just, none greater  
> In piety, war, and arms—

what lessons in justice has he offered us?

> He had bound their hands behind their backs, intending to send them  
> As funeral offerings to the shades and sprinkle the flames  
> With the blood of the slain.

What can be more merciful than this piety: to sacrifice human victims to the dead and feed fire with human blood as though with oil? But perhaps this was not the fault of Aeneas himself, but of the poet,

> Who defiled a man renowned for piety with a notorious crime.

Where then, O poet, is that piety which you so frequently praise? Behold pious Aeneas:

> Here he seizes four young men born to Sulmo,  
> And as many whom Ufens rears, while they are still alive,  
> To sacrifice them as funeral offerings to the shades  
> And drench the pyre’s flames with captive blood. [Col. 0581B]

Why, then, did he say, at the very same time when he was sending bound men to be sacrificed,

> Indeed, I would have wished to spare the living,

when he ordered those whom he held alive in his power to be killed like cattle? But this, as I have said, was not the fault of Aeneas, who perhaps had received no literary education, but yours: although you were learned, you nevertheless did not know what piety was, and you believed that the very act which he performed impiously and abominably was a duty of piety. Evidently he is called pious for this one reason alone: that he loved his father. What of the fact that

[Col. 0582A]

> Good Aeneas slaughtered those who pleaded and were not to be despised?

For he was adjured by that same father and by

> The hopes of rising Iulus,

yet he showed no mercy,

> Inflamed by the Furies and by anger.

Could anyone, then, think that this man possessed any virtue within himself, when he blazed up with fury like stubble and, forgetting his father’s spirit by which he was entreated, could not bridle his anger? He was therefore in no way pious, since he killed not only those who were not resisting but even those who pleaded with him.

Someone will say here: “What, then, is piety? Where is it, and what is its nature?” Assuredly it is found among those who know nothing of wars, who preserve concord with everyone, who are friends even to their enemies, who love all human beings as brothers, [Col. 0582B] who know how to restrain anger and to soothe every frenzy of the mind through tranquil moderation.

How great, then, is the darkness, how great the cloud of gloom and error that has covered human hearts! For just when they think themselves most pious, they become most impious. The more religiously they serve these earthly images, the more criminal they prove themselves against the name of the true divinity. Consequently, in accordance with the deserts of their impiety, they are often afflicted by more grievous evils. Since they do not know the cause of these evils, all blame is assigned to fortune; and Epicurus’ philosophy finds an opening, judging that nothing pertains to the gods and that they are neither touched by favor nor moved by anger, because people often see those who despise the gods prospering and their worshippers suffering misery.

This [Col. 0582C] happens because, although they appear religious and are good by nature, [Col. 0583A] they are thought to deserve nothing like what they often suffer. Nevertheless, they console themselves by accusing fortune, without perceiving that, if any such power existed, it would never harm its own worshippers. Such piety is therefore deservedly followed by punishment; and the offended divinity, because of the crime of perversely religious human beings, overwhelms them with grievous misfortune.

[Col. 0583A]

> **Note: [Col. 0583C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 583–584]**
>
> **Overwhelms them with misfortune.** So too in Plautus, *Amphitryon*, Act IV, scene 2, and *Curculio*, Act IV, scene 3; Terence, *Phormio* V.8.39. Thus above, “to enrich with honor,” meaning “to heap honor upon.”
>
> **With the greatest good faith.** Here only civic good faith is at issue, which in Cicero’s *On Duties* is the foundation of justice.
>
> **Mars, etc.** Enough has been said against these vanities in Books I and II.
>
> **Saturn.** The Subiaco edition has “who worship Saturn.”
>
> **Prostituted.** Leipzig manuscripts 2 and 3 and Reimmann read “abandoned.” But more manuscripts, and indeed all the editions, read “prostituted.” Lactantius himself says of this same Venus in Book I, chapter 17: “Why should I speak of the obscenity of Venus, prostituted to the lusts of all?” Compare Book III, chapter 22: “Not an adulteress … but a prostitute.” **BUN.**
>
> [Col. 0583D] **Are represented.** The Emmanuel manuscript reads “are displayed.”—**Are represented.** Thus all manuscripts and editions except the Emmanuel manuscript, and correctly. It is the proper term in this context. *Epitome*, chapter 63: “The shameless gestures of actors … teach the lusts which they represent in dancing.” He clearly reproduces Cyprian, Book II, Letter 2, Erasmus’ edition, fol. 33: “They represent the unchaste Venus, adulterous Mars,” etc.
>
> **Are instructed in injustice.** The subject requires this reading, as do almost all manuscripts and editions. Some manuscripts and commonly received editions wrongly read “in justice.”
>
> **The most religious act of worship is imitation.** Augustine: “The highest form of religion is to imitate the one whom you worship.” Seneca, Letter 95: “Whoever has imitated him has worshipped the gods sufficiently.”
>
> **To those men, therefore, etc.** Three Royal, two Colbert, the Bodleian, Cotton, and one Clermont manuscript read: “Those men, therefore … because they regard justice as burdensome and bitter.”
>
> **They are called beasts.** See Ezekiel 34:5, 8, 25, and 28; Zephaniah 2:14–15; Exodus 26:6 and 22. Likewise, in Daniel 7, four tyrannical kingdoms are described by four animals.
>
> [Col. 0584C] **Marcus Tullius therefore excellently said.** Betuleius says that this passage is not extant, but a similar one occurs in *On Duties* III.3.
>
> **To die.** Cicero has “to die,” with a different Latin verb.
>
> **The form of a beast.** On the similar but fabulous transformation of human beings into beasts, see Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 22.
>
> **To be savage in mind.** The Merton manuscript reads “to have a savage mind.”
>
> **More savage.** The edition of 1476 reads “more brutish.”
>
> **What Caucasus, etc.** This refers to Dido’s words in *Aeneid* IV.365:
>
> > Faithless man, but bristling Caucasus begot you  
> > From its hard rocks, and Hyrcanian tigresses gave you suck.
>
> They attribute savagery to Caucasus because of the story of Prometheus; I prefer to think it is because of the multitude of panthers with which Philostratus, in his *Life of Apollonius*, writes that it is filled. India and Hyrcania are formidable for their tigers. Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 18. On the elephant, tiger, and ant of India, read Arrian, Book VIII, which concerns Indian affairs. I pass over Heliodorus in his tale of Theagenes and Chariclea. **BETUL.**
>
> **That is the true beast.** Insofar as conjecture is permissible, he means Diocletian, whose edicts and persecution are described by Eusebius in *Ecclesiastical History* VIII, especially the cruelty at Nicomedia in chapters 5 and 6 of that book, and in *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*.
>
> **Command.** Thus also below, “agents of the impious command.” This word is not very Latin.
>
> **Is poured out, etc.** Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.646 and II.368.
>
> **Rages against the ashes.** This passage elucidates the end of chapter 21 of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, causing me to explain it of Galerius no less than of Diocletian, to whom Betuleius had referred it. Compare Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VIII.5–6. A similar event under Julian is narrated in Ammianus Marcellinus XXII.11: “After setting fire beneath them and burning them, the crowd cast the ashes into the sea, fearing, as it cried out, that if their remains were collected, temples would be built for them, as for the others who, after being compelled to depart from religion, endured agonizing punishments, advanced with undefiled faith even to a glorious death, and are now called martyrs.” **BUN.**

Although they live with holy conduct, in the highest good faith and innocence, nevertheless, because they worship gods whose impious and profane rites the true God hates, they are estranged from justice and from the name of true piety.

Nor is it difficult to show why worshippers of the gods cannot be good and just. For how will those who worship bloodthirsty gods—Mars and Bellona—abstain from bloodshed? How will they spare either their parents, when they worship Jupiter, who drove out his own father, or the infants born to them, when they worship Saturn? [Col. 0583B] How will they safeguard chastity, when they worship a goddess who is naked and adulterous and, as it were, prostituted among the gods? How will they refrain from robbery and fraud, when they know of Mercury’s thefts, which teach that deceiving is not fraud but cleverness? How will they restrain their lusts, when they venerate Jupiter, Hercules, Liber, Apollo, and the rest, whose adulteries and violations of males and females are not only known to the educated but are also represented in the theaters and sung in songs, so that they become even more widely known to everyone? Can people be just amid such things when, even if they are good by nature, they are nevertheless instructed in injustice by the gods themselves? For in order to appease the God whom you worship, you must employ those things in which you know that he rejoices and takes delight. [Col. 0583C] Thus it comes about that a god forms the lives of his worshippers in accordance with the character [Col. 0584A] of his own name, since the most religious form of worship is imitation.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Cruelty of the Gentiles toward Christians

Because justice is burdensome and bitter to those whose conduct accords with the character of their gods, they violently exercise against the just the same impiety that they employ in all other matters. Nor is it without reason that the prophets call them beasts. Marcus Tullius therefore spoke admirably:

> “For if there is no one,” he says, “who would not rather die than be transformed into the shape of some beast, even though he would retain a human mind, how much more wretched is it to possess the mind of a wild beast in human form? To me, at least, it seems as much more wretched as the mind is more excellent than the body.”

They therefore disdain the bodies of wild animals, [Col. 0584B] although they themselves are more savage than beasts; and they are so pleased with themselves for having been born human beings, though they bear nothing human except the outlines and general shape. For what Caucasus, what India, what Hyrcania has ever reared beasts so monstrous and bloodthirsty? The rage of every wild animal runs only until its belly is satisfied and, once its hunger has been appeased, it immediately becomes quiet. But that is the true beast at whose single command:

> Everywhere dark blood is poured forth . . .  
> Everywhere there is cruel  
> Mourning, everywhere terror, and death in countless forms.

No one can adequately describe the monstrous savagery of this enormous beast, which, although reclining in a single place, nevertheless rages throughout the whole world with iron teeth; it not only tears apart the limbs of human beings but even crushes their very bones [Col. 0584C] and rages against their ashes, lest any place remain for burial.

[Col. 0584C]

> **Note: [Col. 0585C] Variorum Notes on columns 585–586**
>
> **A place for burial.** He undoubtedly means Dorotheus, Peter, and Gorgonius. Although they were courtiers, their bodies, after being miserably stripped of their flesh, were committed to the earth, but were soon afterward dug up by order of the tyrant and cast into the sea. Eusebius writes about them.
>
> **The earth to the dead.** See St. Augustine, *The City of God*, book I, chapter 12.
>
> **Advancement (*provectio*).** I am still seeking stronger authority for the use of this word among ancient authors. It is not noted by Kresbius in *On the Style of Lactantius* or by Walch in his *Diatribe*. Pliny uses *provehere ad dignitatem*, “to advance to a dignity,” in his *Letters*. BUN.
>
> **Kinds of cruelty.** See these in the *Acts of the Martyrs* collected by that equally learned and devout man, Theodoric Ruinart, a Benedictine of the Congregation of St. Maur.
>
> [Col. 0585D] **Each raged (*quisque saeviit*).** Thus the oldest manuscripts, one Bologna, Cauc., Betul., two Colbertine manuscripts, and Cellarius’s edition. It flows more agreeably than *saevivit*, the reading of three Royal manuscripts, Marm., and as many editions. Twelve recent manuscripts have *saevit*; five recent manuscripts, *quique saeviunt*.
>
> **Through excessive timidity.** Thus eight Royal manuscripts, including two of the oldest, Cauc., five Colbertine manuscripts, and others, together with thirteen printed editions. This is more appropriate to attendants and servants, who wished not to appear to have done less than they had been commanded. Five manuscripts read “arrogance” (*tumiditate*). For no one is more cruel than a timid man when he believes himself superior in strength. Almost the same statement occurs in *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 11: “Some, from their personal hatred of Christians, judged that they ought to be destroyed; and those who thought otherwise, once they understood the emperor’s will, either through fear or through a desire to please him, concurred in the same opinion.”
>
> **Than he was commanded.** Two recent handwritten codices read *jubeatur*; seven recent manuscripts and as many printed editions, *jubebantur*; three recent manuscripts, erroneously, *videbantur*.
>
> [Col. 0586B] **Some (*aliqui*).** Heumann deletes this word.
>
> **In Phrygia.** See the account in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, chapter 11.
>
> **Together with its very meeting-house.** The account is found in Eusebius. The early Christians, moreover, did not have temples but meeting-houses, buildings, and so forth, for they recoiled from the word “temple,” which the Gentiles used.
>
> **The more merciful.** Eleven recent manuscripts, together with the Roman edition of 1468, wrongly read “the more insane” (*dementior*). The others, including the oldest, have “the more merciful” (*clementior*). He calls the brevity of the punishment—namely, burning—mercy in comparison with a lingering and more protracted death.
>
> **In devising kinds of punishments.** Cyprian, *Against Demetrianus*: “You apply prolonged tortures to rend bodies; you multiply numerous punishments to tear apart their entrails; nor can your savagery and monstrous cruelty be content with customary tortures: ingenious cruelty devises new punishments.” Compare Lactantius, book VI, chapter 17; *Epitome*, chapter 54; Seneca, *On Clemency*, book I, chapter 25 (“Cruelty”): “It seeks out new punishments, summons ingenuity, and devises instruments by which pain may be varied and prolonged,” etc. BUN.
>
> [Col. 0586D] **They think only of victory.** Thus, together with the old Roman edition, all the manuscripts except one recent Royal manuscript, which, like the other printed editions, has *excogitant*, “devise.”
>
> **He seemed.** Five recent handwritten codices and nine printed editions read “he seemed” (*visus est*).
>
> **They avoid nothing else.** Thus two very old manuscripts, one Royal manuscript and Cauc., two other Royal manuscripts, many others, and eight printed editions. Fourteen recent manuscripts and five printed editions read *aliud evitant*; one old Bologna manuscript and one very old Royal manuscript, *aliud vitant*.
>
> **Those being tortured should die.** That is, during the actual punishment.
>
> **The more severe the tortures have been.** I restore this reading from Lips. 2, Reimm., Rost., Venice 1471 and 1472, both editions of 1478, those of 1493 and 1497, Parrh., Paris, Junt., Ald., Crat., Gymn., Tornes., Betul., Fasit., and Gryph., in place of the reading of the more recent editions of Thomasius, Isaeus, Thys., Gall., Spark., Cell., and Walch: “the tortures which, the more . . . may produce.” If they wished “make them blessed” to be understood after “tortures,” they should have printed *pariunt*, not *pariant*. BUN.
>
> **Constitutions.** Namely, those quoted by Eusebius.

[Col. 0585A] As though those who confess God desired people to come to their tombs, rather than desiring themselves to come to God.

What savagery, what frenzy, what madness it is to have denied light to the living and earth to the dead! I therefore say that nothing is more wretched than those people whom necessity either found or made the agents of another’s fury and the attendants of an impious command. For that was not an honor or an advancement in rank, but the condemnation of a human being to the work of a butcher, and by God to everlasting punishment. It is impossible to recount what individuals did throughout the whole world. For what number of volumes could contain such countless and varied kinds of cruelty? Once power had been granted, each person raged according to his own character. Some, through excessive timidity, ventured to do more than [Col. 0585B] they were commanded; others acted from their personal hatred of the just; some from the natural savagery of their minds; and others so that they might please their superiors and, by this service, pave for themselves a road to higher office. Some showed themselves eager to kill, as did one man in Phrygia, who burned an entire community together with its very meeting-house. Yet the more savage this man was, the more merciful he is found to have been. The worst kind, however, is the one flattered by a false appearance of mercy: the executioner who determines to kill no one is more grievous and more savage. It is therefore impossible to say how many and how terrible the kinds of torture were that judges of this sort devised [Col. 0586A] in order to attain their intended result.

They do these things not only so that they may boast of having killed none of the innocent—for I myself have heard some boasting that their administration had been bloodless in this respect—but also from envy, lest either they themselves be defeated or their victims attain the glory of their courage. Thus, in devising kinds of punishments, they think of nothing but victory. For they know that this is a contest and a battle. In Bithynia I myself saw a governor wonderfully elated with joy, as though he had subdued some barbarian nation, because one man who had resisted with great courage for two years seemed at last to have yielded. They therefore struggle to win and inflict exquisitely contrived pains upon bodies; and they avoid nothing except allowing those under torture to die. As though death alone made people blessed, and not also tortures, [Col. 0586B] which produce a greater glory of courage in proportion to their severity. In their obstinate folly, moreover, they order diligent care to be given to the tortured, so that their limbs may be restored for further torments and fresh blood renewed for punishment. What could be more dutiful, beneficent, or humane? They would not have cared so solicitously for people whom they loved. This is the discipline of the gods. For these works they train their worshippers; these are the rites they desire. Indeed, those most criminal murderers even enacted impious laws against the devout. For sacrilegious imperial constitutions and unjust discussions by jurists are read. Domitius, [Col. 0587A]

[Col. 0587A]
