in the seventh book of *The Office of the Proconsul*, collected the wicked rescripts of the emperors in order to explain with what punishments those who confessed themselves worshippers of God ought to be afflicted.

## CHAPTER XII. On True Virtue, and on Being Regarded as a Good or Evil Citizen

What are you to do with people who call the butcheries perpetrated by ancient tyrants raging furiously against the innocent “law”? Although they are teachers of injustice and cruelty, they nevertheless wish to appear just and legally expert—blind, dull, and ignorant both of reality and of truth. Is justice so hateful to you, O ruined minds, that you equate it with the greatest crimes? Has innocence so utterly perished among you [Col. 0587B] that you judge it unworthy even of a simple death? Is it to be accounted worse than every crime to commit no crime and to keep one’s heart pure from all contamination of wrongdoing? Since we are speaking generally with worshippers of the gods, permit us, so far as you are concerned, to do good together with you. For this is our law, this our work, this our religion. If we seem wise to you, imitate us; if foolish, despise us, or even laugh at us if you please, for our folly benefits us. Why do you tear us apart? Why do you afflict us? We do not envy your wisdom. We prefer this folly; this we embrace. We believe it advantageous to us that we should love you and bestow every benefit upon you yourselves, who hate us.

There is in Cicero a passage not far removed from the truth, in the argument that Furius delivers against justice:

> “I ask,” he says, “suppose there were two men, one of whom was an excellent man, most equitable, possessed of the highest justice and exceptional fidelity, [Col. 0587C] while the other was notorious for crime and audacity; [Col. 0588A] and suppose that the state were under such a misconception that it regarded the good man as criminal, wicked, and impious, while on the contrary it supposed the thoroughly wicked man to possess the highest integrity and fidelity. Suppose that, in accordance with this opinion of all the citizens, the good man were harassed and dragged away, his hands finally cut off and his eyes gouged out, that he were condemned, bound, burned, exiled, and reduced to destitution, and at last, with the fullest right, seemed utterly wretched to everyone; while on the contrary the wicked man were praised, honored, and loved by all, and every honor, every command, all wealth, and finally all resources were conferred upon him; and he were judged, in the estimation of all, the best of men and most deserving of every kind of fortune: who, then, would be so insane as to hesitate which of the two he would prefer to be?”

Surely, as though divining what evils [Col. 0588B] were going to happen to us because of justice, and in what manner, he proposed this example. For our people suffer all these things through the perversity of those in error. Behold, the state—or rather the entire world itself—is under such a misconception that it persecutes, tortures, condemns, and kills good and just men as though they were wicked and impious. For when he says that no one is so insane as to hesitate which of the two he would prefer to be, he himself—speaking as one arguing against justice—meant that a wise person would prefer to be wicked while enjoying a good reputation rather than good while suffering a bad one.

But far be this madness from us, that we should prefer falsehood to truth. Will the character of our goodness depend upon the errors of the populace rather than upon our own conscience and the judgment of God? Or will any happiness ever entice us into preferring anything other than true goodness accompanied by every evil to false goodness accompanied by every prosperity? Let [Col. 0588C] kings keep their kingdoms for themselves, the rich their riches—as Plautus says [Col. 0589A]—and the wise their own wisdom. Let them leave us our folly, which is shown to be wisdom by this very fact: that they envy us for it. For who would envy a fool unless he himself were the greatest fool? Yet they are not so foolish as to envy fools; rather, by the very fact that they persecute them carefully and anxiously, [Col. 0589A]

> **Note: [Col. 0589B] Variorum Notes on columns 589–590**
>
> **They persecute.** Thus ten Royal manuscripts, four Colbertine manuscripts, and very many others. But the Bologna, Tax., one Colbertine, two Clermont manuscripts, and Fasit. read *prosequuntur*, “pursue.”
>
> **With their worm-eaten gods.** That is, gods that fall apart through decay and rottenness. Thus Arnobius, book VI, says that images of the gods are loosened by decay. I have chosen this as the better reading. It is found, together with the Aldine edition of 1535, in one nine-hundred-year-old Royal manuscript and another more recent manuscript. In two other manuscripts, one of each period, the word is absent. Isaeus and Francius approve our reading; it is also supported by Gymn., Tornes., Soubron., Betul., Fasit., and two Paris editions, which read *curiosis*; two Colbertine manuscripts, Marm., and Cant. read *variosis*. In addition, two recent Royal manuscripts, one Colbertine, Em., and one Clermont read *nariosis*; two Bologna, two Royal, two Colbertine manuscripts, and four printed editions have *narinosis*; Jun. has *narosis*; one Sorbonne manuscript, *narinosos*. They are supposedly so called because they imbibe incense through their nostrils. Two Royal manuscripts, Tornes., five Oxford manuscripts, and the Roman edition of 1470 read *varicosis*; Ultr., *nanosis*; one Colbertine and one Brun., *vanosis*; one Royal, Vict., Gatian., Nav., and the other Brun., *ventosis*; one Colbertine, *viciosis*. The Cologne edition of 1544 reads from manuscripts: “Let them be left with their own *narinosi* gods—whom they call *narinosi* because they are worshipped with the odors of incense.” This interpretation intruded into the text. In the margin one reads *varicosis* and *curiosis*. More correctly, read *diis cariosis*, “decayed gods,” that is, gods that either are being consumed or have been consumed by worms and moths. Thus in Columella soil is called *cariosa*. For decay (*caries*) is an infestation by worms.—This passage varies astonishingly among the books. Cellarius had adopted Joannes Clericus’s conjecture *araneosis*, “cobwebbed,” from *Ars Critica*, part III, section I, chapter 8, section 9. Tertullian certainly says in the *Apologeticus*, chapter 12, that Christians deserve praise if they do not worship statues and cold images resembling their dead, which kites, mice, and spiders understand. Arnobius, book VI, p. 202: “Do you not see webs and treacherous snares being begun by spiders upon the face of an image?” etc. Minucius, chapter 24: “Spiders weave over the face of the idol and suspend their threads from its very head.” Nevertheless, with Isaeus, Gall., Spark., and Heumann, I have preferred *cariosis*; for decay is attributed not only to wood, as Cellarius thought here, but also to other things. Hence Phaedrus, book V, fable X, verse 5, wrote of a dog “with decayed teeth.” Indeed, Arnobius, book VI, p. 202, says that “the images of the gods . . . are loosened after the manner of rottenness by DECAY”; and, still more explicitly, Prudentius, *Against Symmachus*, book I, verses 433–434: “I shall not suffer you to venerate the monstrous forms [Col. 0590B] of decayed gods.” But, as Plautus says, anyone who wishes to scent out the true reading here must necessarily have a keen nose. BUN.
>
> **What do they fear?** Ten recent manuscripts and nine printed editions read “what are they afraid of?”
>
> **Should increase from the worshippers of the gods.** The preposition “from” is absent from nine editions. This chapter should be compared with the end of Tertullian’s *Apologeticus*. The preposition is present in six old editions of the fifteenth century.
>
> **Yet it is never, etc.** The Christian faith is not only not extinguished by persecution but is propagated more and more. For it has been divinely ordained that the evangelical field should grow richer from the blood of the devout and innocent in proportion as that blood is poured out more abundantly. For “the just man will flourish like the palm tree.” See Tertullian at the end of the *Apologeticus*.
>
> **Who, then, is so senseless?** Thus I read with the two oldest Royal manuscripts and seven others. In five recent manuscripts *tamen*, “nevertheless,” is read in place of *tandem*, “then”; in one old Bologna manuscript, two Leipzig manuscripts, the Roman edition of 1474, and other commonly printed texts, “so insane,” which anyone can see arose from *tandem*. Both words are absent from four recent Royal manuscripts, four Colbertine manuscripts, and eight old printed editions. One Colbertine manuscript has “deranged.”—“Who, then, is senseless and so blind?” Perhaps the fuller reading should be: “Who, then, is so insane, so senseless, and so blind?” Below, chapter 12: “Who, then, will be so insane?” BUNEMAN.
>

Chapter 10: “Whom he had alive in his power”; chapter 18: “He does not have it in his power to.” Compare *On the Anger of God*, chapter 21. Minucius, however, chapter 37, writes “although they had it in their own power to be released,” adding the pronoun; and Seneca, letter 9: “He has it in his own power how quickly he may recover it.” Thus both forms are correct. BUNEMAN.
>
> **Is senseless.** I have restored this from nearly all the manuscripts and seven old editions, as is required by the verb “lacks” below. Five manuscripts and as many printed editions have “has become senseless.”
>
> **Surely the countless others.** Regio-Put. reads “the others also”; Francius conjectures *ut quae*.
>
> **Lacks discernment.** Thus very many manuscripts, including the three oldest: one Royal, one Bologna, and Cauc. Regio-Put., seven others, and the printed editions read “foresight.”
>

they concede that we are not fools. For why do they rage so cruelly unless they fear that, as justice grows stronger from day to day, they will be left alone with their worm-eaten gods? If, therefore, the worshippers of the gods are wise and we are fools, why do they fear that the wise will be enticed by fools?

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Growth and Punishments of the Christians

Since our number always increases from among the worshippers of the gods [Col. 0589B] and yet is never diminished, not even during persecution—for people can sin and be defiled by sacrifice, but they cannot be turned away from God, since truth prevails by its own power—who, then, [Col. 0590A] is so senseless and so blind that he cannot see on which side wisdom stands? But they are blinded by malice and frenzy so that they cannot see; and they suppose those people to be fools who, although they have it in their own power to avoid punishments, nevertheless prefer to be tortured and to die. Yet from this very fact they could perceive that it cannot be folly upon which so many thousands of people throughout the whole world agree with one and equal mind. If women fail through the weakness of their sex—for those people sometimes call it a womanish or old-woman’s superstition—men, surely, possess discernment. If children and adolescents lack foresight because of their age, mature people and the elderly surely possess settled judgment. If one city is senseless, the countless others surely cannot all be foolish. If one province or one nation lacks discernment, all the others must necessarily possess an understanding of what is right. But since [Col. 0590B] the divine law has been received from the rising of the sun to its setting, and every sex, every age, nation, and region serves God with one and equal mind, with the same endurance everywhere and the same contempt for death, they ought to have understood [Col. 0591A] that there is some rational basis in a cause that is defended to the point of death not without reason; that there is some foundation and solidity which not only keeps that religion from being dissolved by injuries and persecution, but continually increases it and makes it stronger. For their malice is also refuted in this respect: they believe that they have utterly overthrown the religion of God if they have defiled its adherents, although it is possible to make satisfaction to God, and no worshipper of God is so wicked that, once the opportunity is given, he does not return to appease God;

[Col. 0591A]

> **Note: [Col. 0591B] Variorum Notes on columns 591–592**
>

One recent Royal manuscript and nine recent editions read “who . . . does not.” Cauc. and one Leipzig manuscript read “to the placid God.”
>
> **With greater devotion.** It sometimes happens that the fallen who return to a sounder life love God with greater devotion than before, but not always with greater devotion than those who have never fallen. The faith of penitents is therefore not firmer than the faith of those who have preserved it religiously. Every Catholic theologian will accordingly take proper exception to this opinion of Lactantius.
>

Three Colbertine manuscripts, one Clermont, and fourteen printed editions read “what reason, then, is there that?”—Book I, chapter 17: “There plainly was reason why.” Ibid., chapter 18: “There is indeed reason why.” Compare book II, chapter 6; book III, chapter 17; Heinsius on Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II.518: “There is indeed reason why.” Closer still to our passage, book II, chapter 8: “What reason is there why?”; book VI, chapter 11: “What cause is there why?”; ibid., chapter 9: “What reason, then, does he have why?” Finally, exactly as here, *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 1: “What reason, then, is there why he should regard us as hateful?” BUNEMAN.

Cicero, *Letters to Friends*, book III, letter 13, at the end: “I shall withdraw myself from my anxieties and transfer my mind to those matters.” BUNEMAN.

>

BUNEMAN.

> **Let the Romans go, etc.** Lactantius nevertheless misinterprets here two examples of Roman endurance and courage. Regulus returned to the Carthaginians even at the risk of torture and death in order to keep his pledged word, and preferred to overcome his tortures through endurance rather than take his own life. Mucius, for his part, displayed no less endurance and courage by willingly submitting to punishment because he had failed through error to kill Porsenna. On these men see St. Augustine, *The City of God*, book I, chapters 15 and 24, and book IV, chapter 20.—**Let the Romans go . . . and boast.** He imitates Cyprian, book II, letter 4 in Erasmus’s edition; Oxford edition, letter 37, p. 73: “Let the magistrates now go, and let consuls or proconsuls boast of the insignia of their annual dignity and their twelve fasces: behold.” BUNEMAN.

and indeed with greater devotion. For consciousness of sin and fear of punishment make a person more religious, and the faith restored by repentance is always much firmer.

If, therefore, when they suppose that their gods are angry with them, they nevertheless believe that those gods can be appeased by gifts, sacrifices, and incense, [Col. 0591B] what reason is there for them to suppose our God so unyielding and implacable that a person who, under compulsion and against his will, has poured a libation to their gods seems incapable of ever again being a Christian? Unless perhaps they suppose that those once defiled will transfer their allegiance and begin of their own accord [Col. 0592A] to do what they did under torture. Who willingly undertakes a duty that began with injury? Who, when he sees the scars upon his sides, will not hate all the more the gods on whose account he bears permanent marks of punishment and brands impressed upon his flesh? Thus it comes about that, when peace is granted by God, those who had been turned away return, and another, new people joins because of the miraculous display of courage. For when the common people see human beings torn apart by various kinds of torture and maintaining unconquered endurance even when their executioners are exhausted, they conclude—correctly—that neither the agreement of so many nor the perseverance of the dying is meaningless, and that endurance itself could not overcome such terrible tortures without God. Robbers and physically powerful men are unable to endure lacerations of this kind: they cry out and utter groans, [Col. 0592B] for they are conquered by pain because they lack divinely inspired endurance. Our people, however—to say nothing of the men—even boys and mere women silently defeat their torturers, and not even fire can force a groan from them. Let the Romans go and boast of Mucius or Regulus: the one delivered himself to the enemy to be killed because he was ashamed to live as a captive; the other, after being captured by the enemy, when he saw that he could not escape death, thrust his hand into the fire so that he might make satisfaction to the enemy whom he had wished to kill for his criminal act, and through that punishment received the pardon that he had not deserved. [Col. 0593A]

Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 23, follows: “Take care lest this too contribute to the charge of irreligion: to take away freedom of religion and forbid the choice of divinity, so that I may not be permitted to worship whom I wish, but am compelled to worship whom I do not wish.” Compare Lactantius, *Epitome*, chs. 53 and 54: “Nor can necessity be imposed upon anyone to worship what he does not wish.” BUN.

**Will be left.** The Regio-Puteanus MS., 1 Colbertinus, and the Brun.: *relinquatur* (“may be left”); 1 recent Regius: *relinquitur* (“is left”).

**Extorts.** The oldest Regius MS. 1 and the Aldine edition of 1515, Graph., Crat.: *extorqueat* (“should extort”).

**Seneca.** This passage is among the fragments found [Col. 0594D] at the beginning of Seneca’s works—namely, in *On Accidents*. Thus it is read in Tertullian at the conclusion of the *Apology*: “Many among you exhort people to endure pain and death, as Cicero does in the *Tusculans*, Seneca in *On Accidents*, Diogenes, Pyrrho, and Callinicus.”

**Virtue.** Brun. 1: “justice.”

**The height of perversity.** Regius 1: “the supreme degree of perversity”; 1 old Bononiensis: “the height of depravity.”

**Sibyl.** See *Discourse* 8, and Theophilus, *To Autolycus*, Book II.

**Earth fashioned by their fingers.** That is, shaped into an image and formed by their fingers. Thus St. Remigius in his testament, in Brisson, *Formularies*, Book VII: “I order a censer and a figured chalice to be made for you, heir of my aforementioned church.” ISAEUS.—Lactantius used the verb *imaginor* passively, although it is always active.—He expressed it more elegantly in *On the Anger of God*, ch. 20: “They adore works wrought by human fingers . . . they venerate things fashioned and formed from earth.” BUN.]

Behold: the weaker sex and fragile age permit themselves to be torn throughout the whole body and burned—not from necessity, since they could avoid it if they wished, but voluntarily, because they trust in God.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Fortitude of Christians

But this is true virtue, which even boastful philosophers vaunt, not in deed but in empty words, when they argue that nothing is so consonant with the dignity and constancy of a wise man as his being incapable of being driven by any tortures from his conviction and purpose; but that it is worth being [Col. 0593B] tortured and dying rather than betraying one’s faith, abandoning one’s duty, or, overcome by fear of death or bitter pain, doing anything unjust. Unless, perhaps, they think Flaccus is raving in his *Lyrics* when he says:

> The just man, steadfast in his purpose,  
> Is shaken in his settled mind neither  
> By the fury of citizens commanding evil,  
> Nor by the threatening tyrant’s countenance.

Nothing truer than this can be said, provided that it is applied [Col. 0594A] to those who refuse no tortures and no death rather than depart from faith and justice; who do not tremble before tyrannical commands or the swords of governors, so as to be prevented from defending true and solid liberty with an unwavering mind—for in this alone must wisdom be maintained. For who is so insolent, so arrogant, as to forbid me to raise my eyes to heaven? Who could impose upon me the necessity either of worshipping what I do not wish, or of not worshipping what I do wish? What more will be left to us if another’s caprice extorts even this, which ought to be done voluntarily? No one will accomplish that, if we possess any virtue with which to despise death and pain. If we maintain this constancy, why are we judged fools for doing what the philosophers praise?

Seneca, therefore, rightly reproached human beings for their inconsistency when he said: “To them, greatness of spirit seems the highest virtue.” Yet the same people regard one who despises [Col. 0594B] death as a madman—which is certainly the height of perversity. But those worshippers of vain religions level that same reproach from the same folly by which they fail to understand the true God. The Erythraean Sibyl calls them κωφοὺς καὶ ἀνοήτους, “deaf and senseless”—that is, deaf and mindless people who neither hear divine things nor perceive them, but fear and worship earth fashioned by their fingers.

## [Col. 0595A] CHAPTER XV. On Folly, Wisdom, Piety, Equity, and Justice

But as to the reason [Col. 0595A]—

**He, when serving as ambassador, etc.** Concerning this embassy, the following is written in Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book I, ch. 5: “I mean those whom the Athenians once sent as ambassadors to the Senate to obtain the remission of the fine which it had imposed upon their city because of the devastation of Oropus; that fine had been almost five hundred talents. It is said that, for the sake of displaying their abilities, each of them separately delivered discourses in the busiest places of the city before a great gathering of people. He stated these things concerning the occasion of the embassy, which Gellius mentions near the end of Book XVII.

**Galba and Cato the Censor.** Nineteen later manuscripts and six editions have “the censors.” But “Cato the Censor” is very rightly preferred by six Regius MSS., two of them among the oldest, 1 Sorbonicus, 2 Colbertini, Marm., 1 Lipsiensis, 1 Claromontanus, and thirteen printed editions. For it was not Galba but L. Valerius Flaccus who held the censorship with Cato, as everyone familiar with the historical monuments knows from Livy and Plutarch. Nor does this have anything to do with the censors. Rather, these two, as the most celebrated orators of that age—as is evident from Cicero’s *Brutus*—are represented as having heard the eloquence of those most eloquent men. [Col. 0596B] BETULEIUS.—**Cato the Censor.** The following relevant passage from Quintilian, *Institutes*, Book XII, ch. 1, p. 1053, settles the matter: “Nor was that Carneades—who at Rome, with Cato the Censor listening, is said to have argued against justice with no less force than he had spoken in favor of justice the day before—himself an unjust man.” BUN.

**But the same man, etc.** Quintilian, Book V, ch. 1: “For neither do the Academics, when they argue both sides of a question, fail to live in accordance with one of them; nor was that Carneades—who at Rome, with Cato the Censor listening, is said to have argued against justice with no less force than he had spoken in favor of justice the day before—himself an unjust man,” etc. Plutarch writes at length about how reluctantly Cato endured these orators declaiming in the city. Pliny, Book VII, ch. 30, touches upon the same matter in very few words: “Cato the Censor,” he says, “during that famous embassy from Athens of three eminent sages, after hearing Carneades, recommended that the ambassadors be dismissed as soon as possible, because, when that man argued, it was far from easy to discern what was true,” etc.

**Whose judgment ought to be firm and stable.** Eleven recent manuscripts and two editions have “whose prudence ought to be firm,” etc. Ten recent manuscripts have “of prudence.” The older manuscripts and fifteen printed editions reject this word.

In the Regio-Puteanus: “bringing forward whatever one pleases.” The Cauc., twelve other recent manuscripts, and two editions have “asserting anything whatever.” Four recent manuscripts and two others have “asserting whatever proposition.” Regius 1 and Colbertinus 1 have “discussing anything whatever.”

**Justice is overthrown.** Eleven later manuscripts and five editions: “is subverted.”

**To undermine.** Three Regius MSS., 1 Sorbonicus, 1 Colbertinus, and 2 Claromontani: “to be undermined.” Eleven recent manuscripts add, “so that he might say that one laboring breathlessly was toiling”; two have “with labor”; nine editions, “so that he might say that one was laboring fruitlessly.”

**Was perceived.** The Tornesianus MS. and Colbertinus 1, by a second hand, the Roman edition of 1470, and Crat. in the margin: “was said.”

**Not even the second.** Twelve recent manuscripts: “nor the second.”

**Justice, although, etc.** This is a proverb which Aristotle often cites, especially in Book V of the *Ethics*, ch. 1. He understands by it general justice, which embraces particular justice, together with the other parts of moral goodness, within the scope of its generality.]

—why they regard those who are wise as fools, there is an important rationale, for they are not deceived without cause. It must be carefully explained by us, so that they may at last, if possible, recognize their errors. Justice by its very nature has a certain appearance of folly, which I can confirm by both divine and human testimonies. But perhaps we shall accomplish nothing among these people unless we teach them from their own authorities that no one can be just—which is inseparably joined to true wisdom—without also appearing to be a fool.

Carneades, a philosopher of the Academic school: anyone who does not know what force he possessed in argument, what eloquence, and what acuteness, may learn it [Col. 0595B] from Cicero’s praise of him, or from Lucilius, in whose work Neptune, discussing a matter of extreme difficulty, shows that it could not be explained even if the underworld sent Carneades himself back. When Carneades had been sent to Rome as an ambassador by the Athenians, he argued at length about justice, while Galba and Cato the Censor, the greatest orators of the time, listened. But on the following day this same man subverted his argument with a contrary argument and abolished the justice he had praised the day before. He did so not with the seriousness of a philosopher, whose judgment ought to be firm and stable, but as a kind of oratorical exercise in arguing both sides of a question. This he was accustomed to do so that he could refute others when they brought forward any proposition whatever.

In Cicero, L. Furius recalls that argument by which justice is overthrown. I believe Cicero introduced it because he was discussing the republic and wished to introduce a defense and praise of justice, without which he thought a republic could not be governed. Carneades, however, in order to refute Aristotle and Plato, the champions of justice, gathered together in that first argument everything that was said in favor of justice so that he might thereafter overthrow it, as he did. For it was extremely easy to undermine a justice that had no roots, because at that time no justice existed on earth by which philosophers might perceive what justice was or what its character was.

And would that men so numerous and so distinguished had possessed as much knowledge for completing the defense of the highest virtue as they possessed eloquence [Col. 0596B] and spirit! Its origin lies in religion and its rationale in equity. But those who did not know that first component were unable even to grasp the second. I wish first, however, to show concisely and briefly what justice is, so that it may be understood that the philosophers were ignorant of it and could not defend what they scarcely knew. Although justice embraces all the virtues together, there are nevertheless two [Col. 0597A] chief virtues which cannot be torn away or separated from it: piety and equity. For faithfulness, self-restraint, uprightness, innocence, integrity, and the other virtues of this kind can exist either by nature—

[Col. 0597A] [Note: [Col. 0597C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 597–598]

**Either by nature.** In Plutarch there is a discussion of whether virtue can be taught.

**Can exist in those people.** Four very recent Regius MSS., four Colbertini, and 1 Claromontanus: “can exist in the same people”; six old editions and 1 recent Regius: “can be present in the same people.”

**But piety, etc.** See above, Book II, ch. 16. Philosophers and orators, however, define piety differently. Cicero says in his *Rhetoric*: “Piety is that by which dutiful and diligent respect is accorded to those joined to us by blood, to our country, and to our benefactors.” He therefore confuses one species with another, for he calls the worship of the gods “religion.” That division of Cicero must therefore be entirely disregarded, since it not only contributes nothing to this discussion but even greatly impedes it. Cicero likewise defines piety, in *On the Nature of the Gods*, as justice toward the gods, and sanctity as knowledge of the worship due to the gods.

**Trismegistus.** In the *Poimandres*, ch. 9.

**Elsewhere.** See Book II, ch. 16, and Book III, ch. 9.

**Can know justice itself.** The word “itself” is absent from two Regius MSS. and seven printed editions. Claromontanus 1 has “to know.”

[Col. 0597D] **Who.** I emend thus from the MSS.: 1 old Bononiensis, 6 Colbertini, 1 Claromontanus, the Roman edition of 1470, the Paris edition of 1525, and eleven others. The rest wrongly have “which.”

**Plato.** Near the beginning of the *Timaeus*.

**Socrates.** Note that Socrates denied that there were many gods.

**What would happen to those people.** Thus I have restored the reading from almost all the manuscripts and fifteen editions. Two Colbertini have “to all these”; some printed editions read “among people.”

**To defend.** Colbertinus 1 and Brun.: “would defend.” Either reading is sound.

**Single.** That is, “sole” or “unique,” a word characteristic of Lactantius.

**The other part of justice is equity.** Thus read the two oldest Regius MSS., three other Regius MSS., 1 Colbertinus, Marm., and the manuscripts. Sixteen recent manuscripts and printed editions add “therefore.”

**Which Cicero calls impartiality.** Thus the older and better manuscripts and twelve editions. Sixteen recent manuscripts and five printed editions read “equality.” Either reading is sound and occurs in Cicero. See Cicero, *On the Orator*, Book II, and *On Duties*, Book I, ch. 32. So too Cicero, *On Duties*, Book II, [Col. 0598C] ch. 25: “Flexibility must also be exercised in maintaining the impartiality of the law.”

**All equal, etc.** Politianus did not hesitate to assert from Plato: “There is no king who is not descended from slaves, nor any slave who does not have a king as his ancestor; for time has intermingled all these things.” Let the ancient sage Boethius be heard, in Meter VI:

> The whole race of human beings on earth  
> Arises from a similar origin,  
> For there is one Father of all things,  
> One who provides for all, etc.

Euripides in the *Alexander* concurs. JOH. WEITSIUS.

**No one is excluded from his benefits.** Book I, ch. 5; Book IV, ch. 23; Book VII, ch. 18. Here and in what follows, with alterations in wording, Lactantius follows Cyprian, *On Almsgiving*, Oxford edition, fol. 208: “Nor is anyone barred from his benefits and gifts so as to prevent the entire human race from enjoying divine goodness and generosity equally. Thus the day gives light equally, the sun shines, rain waters, the wind breathes; sleepers have one common sleep, and the radiance of the stars and moon is shared by all. By this example of equality”—I read “equity” from the Bodleian MS., Book I, ch. 2—“one is an imitator of God the Father.” BUN.

**Is a slave.** A certain equitable civil law has been established for the Christian commonwealth, which all who have given their allegiance to God may enjoy. This sharing of legal status is mentioned in many places by the blessed Paul: in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, ch. XII, and the Epistle to the Ephesians, ch. IV.

**Most illustrious . . . most perfect.** With these epithets Lactantius likes to allude to the titles by which many persons were honored according to their rank. Thus the prefect of the city was called “most glorious man”; the praetorian prefects for Illyricum, “most eminent men”; the prefect of Egypt, “admirable man”; governors of provinces, “most illustrious men”; and the governor of Gaul, “most perfect man.” On this matter see Du Cange’s glossary under the words *Perfectissimus*, *Clarissimus*, and *Egregiatus*. See the note on ch. 21 of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, and Panciroli, *Notes on the Notitia Dignitatum*, ch. 2 and following.]

—or through parental instruction, among people who do not know justice, as they always have. For the ancient Romans, who used to glory in their justice, were assuredly glorying in those virtues which, as I have said, can proceed from justice and yet be separated from the source itself.

Piety and equity, however, are like channels issuing from justice, for the whole of justice consists of these two sources. But its head and origin lie in the first, while its entire force and rationale lie in the second. Piety is nothing other than knowledge of God, as Trismegistus most truly defined it, as we have said elsewhere. If, therefore, piety consists in knowing God, and the sum of that knowledge is to worship him, [Col. 0597B] then whoever does not hold to the religion of God is certainly ignorant of justice. For how can one know justice itself when one does not know its origin?

Plato indeed said much about the one God, by whom, he says, the world was constituted; but he said nothing about religion, for he had dreamed of God, not known him. If he himself, or anyone else, had wished to complete the defense of justice, he ought first of all to have overthrown the religions of the gods, because they are contrary to piety. Because Socrates attempted to do this, he was cast into prison, so that it might already then become apparent what would happen to those who began to defend true justice and to serve the one God.

[Col. 0598A] The other part of justice is equity. By equity I do not, in this instance, mean judging rightly, although that too is praiseworthy in a just person, but placing oneself on an equal footing with others, which Cicero calls evenness (*aequabilitas*). For God, who brings human beings into existence and breathes life into them, wished them all to be equal—that is, peers. He established the same condition of life for everyone, brought everyone into being for wisdom, and promised immortality to everyone: no one is excluded from his heavenly benefits. For just as he distributes his one light equally to all, sends forth springs for all, supplies food, and grants the sweetest repose of sleep, so he bestows equity and virtue upon all.

In his sight no one is a slave and no one a master. For if the same Father belongs to all, we are all free by equal right. No one is poor before God except one who lacks justice; no one is rich except [Col. 0598B] one who is full of virtues; finally, no one is distinguished unless he is good and innocent; no one “most illustrious” unless he has performed works of mercy generously; no one “most perfect” unless he has completed every degree of virtue.

Therefore, neither Romans nor Greeks could possess justice, because they kept human beings unequal through many grades: from poor to rich, from lowly to powerful, and finally from private citizens all the way to the loftiest powers of kings. For where all are not equal, equity does not exist; and inequality itself excludes justice, whose entire force consists in making equal those who have entered this condition of life by an equal lot.

## [Col. 0599A] CHAPTER XVI. On the Duties of a Just Man and the Equity of Christians

When those two sources of justice have thus been altered, every virtue and every truth is removed, and justice itself returns to heaven. Accordingly, the true good was not discovered by the philosophers, because they did not know either whence it arose or what it accomplished. It has been revealed to no people except ours.

Someone will say: “Are there not among you some who are poor and others rich—”

[Col. 0599A] [Note: [Col. 0599A] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 599–600]

**Are there not among you some who are poor and others rich, etc.?** Below, following Salmasius, we observe from the mutual designation “brother” among the earliest Christians that they also lived as brothers, contributing what they possessed to the common stock, except their wives, as Tertullian notes. Yet this should not be understood as though all the possessions of all were held in common among them, as certainly happened in the time of the apostles in the Jerusalem church. That this was not so is clear from this passage of Lactantius and from the very passage of Tertullian just cited, *Apology*, on the same page: “Even if there is a kind of common chest,” he says, “its fund is not assembled from an admission fee, as though religion had been purchased. Each person, on the monthly day, or whenever he wishes—and only if he wishes and is able—contributes a modest offering. For no one is compelled; each contributes voluntarily. These are, as it were, deposits of piety.” If each person contributed as much as he wished, and did so monthly, this was not a contribution of all possessions, but only of a modest offering. This was plainly a form of ἔρανος (*eranos*, voluntary contribution), customarily collected each month in the individual Christian churches. Tertullian immediately adds the purpose for which it was expended: namely, supporting [Col. 0599C] and burying the needy. “For it is not spent on banquets or drinking parties or thankless gluttony, but on supporting and burying the poor, and on boys and girls deprived of property and parents, as well as elderly persons confined to the household.” Justin Martyr, in his Second *Apology*, mentions the same contributory offering, or ἔρανος, which Christians customarily made, except that he says nothing about a monthly day.

How, therefore, if they employed only this kind of contribution, could Tertullian himself say that everything among them was held without distinction? Do these statements not conflict? For a general contribution of all possessions makes poor people equal to the rich and ensures that, in a community where every person contributes everything he possesses, no one is rich or poor, but all are mutually equal. Yet it is evident from Tertullian that there were then some poor and some rich within the Church, for the rich contributed toward the support of the poor. I do not know whether such equality ever obtained in the Christian Church, not even in the age of the apostles. Indeed, it is evident from Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians, ch. XVI, that collections of this kind were frequently made under the apostles and at their direction. One may read there how he prescribed that they should be made. From that time onward, the custom of collections described by St. Justin and Tertullian was preserved in the churches.

But what need would there have been for collections of this kind if every individual had contributed all his possessions to a common fund? That communal arrangement appears to have existed only in the Jerusalem church, as Luke relates in Acts, ch. IV. Even there, however, each person was free either to do this or not to do it, as Peter said in the following chapter to Ananias, who had withheld part of the price from the property he sold and laid the remainder at the apostles’ feet.

But how can what the authors write about the customary sharing of personal property among Christians be reconciled with the absence of the community of possessions which most people imagine existed? Justin, at any rate, who mentions that collection in which each person contributed to the common chest at his own discretion, also relates in the same *Apology* that it was characteristic of Christian discipline to contribute what they possessed to the common stock. He shows the difference in this respect between a Gentile and a Christian: “Formerly,” he says, “when we were Gentiles, we were accustomed to pursue income and profit above all things; now we contribute what we possess to the common stock and share it with everyone in need.” [Col. 0600B] Those who persuaded themselves on the basis of these testimonies that the ancient Christians actually held all their possessions in common, contributing them jointly as an undivided fund for each person to enjoy, have certainly strayed very far from the truth. Just as equality of rank among them existed not in their actual social positions but in the disposition by which a superior treated an inferior as his equal, and a master treated his slave no differently than if he were a brother, so too it is evident that their community of possessions existed not in the possessions themselves, but solely in the willingness to share them—a willingness followed by action whenever the need arose. SALMASIUS.

**We bestow upon one another the name of brothers.** Clement, *Stromata* II: “We are therefore brothers because we have been regenerated by the same Word.” Eusebius of Emesa, Homily IV: “Brothers and sisters—not by nature but by duty and affection; for we customarily call those whom we love by these names.” WOUWER.—As we noted previously, God did not wish any needy person to be found among his people, but intended all to live together as brothers, since all sprang from one parent. This designation “brother” [Col. 0600C] also remained in use among Christians for some time, and not only while the Church of Christ stood within the city of Jerusalem under the apostles, but also in other places into which it was propagated, especially as long as it was afflicted by persecutions.

They called one another brothers not merely because human beings have one God as Father, because they share the same faith, and because they are coheirs of the same hope, as Minucius says, but also because they lived together in a brotherly manner, as brothers customarily do when they jointly enjoy their paternal possessions without division. They contributed whatever each possessed to the common stock, held common banquets called by the name “love-feasts,” and finally held nothing without distinction except their wives, as Tertullian says in the *Apology*, ch. 39. He also gives this reason for the shared designation “brother” among Christians:

“How much more worthily are those called and regarded as brothers who have acknowledged one God as Father, who have drunk one Spirit of holiness, and who have awakened from the one womb of the same ignorance into the one light of truth! But perhaps we are considered less legitimate because no tragedy cries out concerning our brotherhood, or because we are brothers by virtue of our family property, which among you generally sunders brotherhood. And so, because we are united in mind and soul, we have no hesitation about sharing possessions. Among us everything is held without distinction except our wives.”

**Bodies.** Heumann thinks that “slaves” should be read.

**Except in what they can, etc.** The Cauc., Jun., three recent Regius MSS., and fourteen printed editions have “except those whom.” Either reading is sound. But the reading in the text seemed genuine to us, being taken from the MSS. 2 Bononienses, 5 old Regii, 6 Colbertini, and many others, together with the edition of Is., and confirmed by what precedes and follows. See above, “except because we believe ourselves equal,” and below, “because they also lack nothing.”

**Not because they possess riches, but because they use them.** Thus eight Regius MSS., five Colbertini, Brun., and others, together with several printed editions. Correctly. See below, “because they also lack nothing.” The Cauc., Jun., 2 recent Regius MSS., 1 Colbertinus, and eight printed editions have: “not those who possess riches, but those who”—a reading that is nevertheless not inappropriate.]

“—some [Col. 0600A] slaves and others masters? Is there not some difference between individuals?” None. There is no other reason why we bestow upon one another the name of brothers except that we believe ourselves equal. For since we measure all human things not by the body but by the spirit, although bodily conditions may differ, they are nevertheless not slaves to us; rather, we both regard and call them brothers in spirit and fellow servants in religion.

Nor do riches make people distinguished, except insofar as they can render them more illustrious through good works. For people are rich not because they possess riches, but because they use them [Col. 0601A] for works of justice. And those who appear poor—

[Col. 0601A] [Note: [Col. 0601C] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 601–602]

**And those who appear poor.** Thus I restored the reading from the Regio-Puteanus MS., five other Regius MSS., 1 Colbertinus, 2 Claromontani, and others, as well as fifteen printed editions. Nine manuscripts and several printed editions have “and because.”

**Because they also lack nothing.** Thus four old Regius MSS. and many others, together with several printed editions. Eleven recent manuscripts and three printed editions omit the word “not.”

**Is more exalted.** He appears to allude to the saying of Cicero in *On Duties*, that each person is the more exalted the more humbly he conducts himself.

**In this temporal life.** That is, this life within time, as below in ch. 18 and in Book VII, chs. 4 and 11. Something appears to be missing here, for the sentence is incomplete.

**From the reasoning of a wise man.** Six manuscripts have “from wisdom.” From the oldest manuscripts and several others I have deleted “and,” which occurred in some editions.

[Col. 0601D] **More remote.** Five manuscripts: *submotius*; six: *summotius*; two: *remotius*. The rest and all printed editions have *semotius*. Compare Lucretius, Book I, verse 46: “removed from cares.”

**Before God.** 1 Corinthians I. **Firm.** Brun. MS.: “highest.”

**Exalts himself.** Luke XIV and XVIII; Matthew XXVIII.

**I have explained, etc.** Up to this point we lacked the complete *Epitome* of Lactantius. The fragment of it began at this place. Now, through Pfaff’s care, we possess it almost complete. I therefore mention this so that the student may diligently compare it with the work itself. He will thereby understand that the same subject can often be expressed well in different ways; he will moreover enlarge his command of expression by this means and will experience the truth that it belongs to the same craftsman to speak both briefly and copiously. Furthermore, once the ornament of fuller eloquence has been removed, he will perceive the subject itself more directly. BETULEIUS.

**Which were brought forward by the philosophers.** Thus the older and better manuscripts and ten printed editions. Ten recent manuscripts and four editions have “were asserted”; three recent manuscripts and three old Roman editions [Col. 0602C] have “were discussed.”

**Of refuting.** In the Junianus MS. the following words, which do not appear in the printed editions, occur: “Wishing civil law to be one thing and natural law another; civil law to be called civil wisdom, and natural law to arise without wisdom, as though both were nothing.” I decided not to admit this sentence into the text, for it is not found expressly in any other manuscript. GALLAEUS. See Cicero, *On Duties*, Book III.

**Who held possession of the whole world.** Thus almost all the manuscripts and printed editions. And rightly so, for this verb also readily takes the genitive in Cicero, *Academics* IV, 126, and *On Ends* I, 7; in Velleius Paterculus, “to gain possession of the kingdom”; in Caesar, “they hope that they can gain possession of the whole of Gaul”; and in Plautus, “to gain possession of the enemy.” Some, not understanding this, added “dominion,” as in the Junianus MS., two recent Regius MSS., and two old Roman editions; but entirely without reason, since “rule” has just preceded. St. Augustine, in the books of *The City of God*, and Tertullian, in ch. 25 of the *Apology*, reproach the Romans themselves for their injustices.

**And in poverty.** Thus I restored the reading from the oldest MSS., 1 Bononiensis and 1 Regius, three other Regius MSS., 1 Colbertinus, 1 Lipsiensis, Goth., Brun., the edition of Is., and Lactantius himself in the *Epitome*, ch. 56: “But if all the peoples in whose hands rule resides, and the Romans themselves, who have possessed the whole world, should wish to follow justice and restore to each what they occupied by force and arms, they will return to huts and poverty.” The Cauc. and fifteen recent manuscripts have “in necessity.” Those four words are absent from the Regio-Puteanus.

**If he discloses it, he will indeed be good because.** Five recent Colbertini MSS., two Claromontani, and ten editions read: “If he discloses that the slave is a fugitive, he will indeed be good.” But these three interpolated words are absent from the others. Thomasius rightly teaches that they must be deleted, because the statement refers not only to a fugitive slave but also to an infected house and similar things.]

—are nevertheless rich, because they lack nothing and desire nothing.

Since, therefore, we who are free are equal to slaves, and we who are rich equal to the poor, through humility of mind, we are nevertheless distinguished before God by virtue. Each person is the more exalted, the more just he is. For if justice consists in making oneself equal even to one’s inferiors, although one excels by the very fact that one has placed oneself on an equal footing with those beneath oneself, yet if one has conducted oneself not merely as their equal but even as their inferior, one will certainly, in God’s judgment, attain a far higher degree of dignity.

For assuredly, in this temporal life, because all things are brief and perishable, people both prefer themselves to others and contend over rank—nothing is more shameful, more arrogant, or more remote from a wise man’s reasoning. [Col. 0601B] For all these earthly things are contrary to heavenly things. Just as the highest wisdom of human beings is folly before God, whereas folly, as I have shown, is the highest wisdom, so before God a person is lowly and abject if he has been conspicuous and exalted on earth.

For, to say nothing of the fact that these present earthly goods to which great honor is accorded are contrary to virtue and enervate the mind’s vigor, what nobility, what wealth, what power can ultimately be secure, when God can make even kings themselves lower than the very lowest? Therefore, in providing for us, God placed this teaching foremost among his divine commandments: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” The salutary character of this commandment teaches that whoever makes himself level with others and presents himself as humble among human beings [Col. 0601C] is regarded as preeminent and distinguished before God. [Col. 0602A] Nor indeed is that saying false which is found in Euripides and runs as follows: “The things regarded as evil here are good in heaven.”

## CHAPTER XVII. On the Equity, Wisdom, and Folly of Christians

I have explained the reason why the philosophers could neither discover justice nor defend it. I now return to what I had set out to discuss. Because the arguments brought forward by the philosophers were weak, Carneades ventured to refute them, since he understood that they could be refuted.

The substance of his argument was this:

> Human beings have established laws for themselves according to utility; these laws naturally vary according to customs and are often changed among the same people as times change. But there is no natural law. All human beings and other living creatures are carried toward their own advantages under nature’s guidance. Consequently, either justice does not exist at all or, if it does exist, it is the height of folly, since in consulting the interests of others it would harm itself.

And he advanced the following arguments:

> If all peoples flourishing in power, and the Romans themselves, who held possession of the whole world, should wish to be just—that is, if they restored what belongs to others—they would have to return to huts and lie in poverty and misery.

Then, leaving general examples aside, he proceeded to particular cases:

> If a good man possesses a fugitive slave or an unhealthy and infected house, whose defects he alone knows, and therefore advertises it for sale, will he disclose that he is selling a fugitive slave or an infected house, or will he conceal the matter from the buyer? If he discloses it, he will indeed be good [Col. 0603A] because he will not deceive—

[Col. 0603A] [Note: [Col. 0603A] [Various Scholars’ Notes on columns 603–604]

**He will not deceive.** Eleven manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1468 have “he does not deceive.” But the following verbs, “he will consult” and “he will deceive,” require the future “he will not deceive.”

**He will consult his material interest.** The old Bononiensis MS. 1 and the edition of Is. have “he will consult his own interest.”

**Because he will deceive.** Five recent manuscripts have “because he deceives.”

**Or will he disclose it?** The Cauc., Jun., and nine editions have “or will he disclose that?”

**He proceeded beyond.** Thus the older and better manuscripts in very great number, together with many printed editions. Ten manuscripts and five printed editions have “he passed on.”

**Could.** Bononiensis MS. 1, four recent manuscripts, and the same number of printed editions have “can”; Claromontanus 1 has “may be able.”

Now that man is just. I have retained this reading, found in one Royal manuscript and in the Aldine, Florentine, Junta, Paris 1525, Cratander, Gymnich, Grapheus, Fasius, Betuleius, Gallaeus, Sparke, and Walch editions, despite the opposition and protest of both manuscript and printed codices, which read *now that man is not just*, except for one recent Royal manuscript, one Colbert manuscript, and the Brünn edition, which report *now that man is not wise*. Our reading agrees best with Carneades’ position, whereas the adversative reading is altogether incompatible with it; for in this debate it was not injustice but justice that was joined with folly, while injustice was joined with wisdom itself. Thus it was said that the man would indeed be just but foolish; if, however, he acted contrariwise, the same man would be considered wise but would be unjust. This is clear from the next example as well. ISAEUS.—Heumann, however, thinks that one should read *but now that man is just*, as in the early printed editions.—*But now that man is just, he is nevertheless foolish.* I preferred this reading because the other, *now that man is not just*, conflicts with Carneades’ position, with the whole of Lactantius’s chapter 17—especially the passage below—and with the words of the *Epitome*, chapter 56: [Col. 0604C] “Will he . . . knock him from the plank . . . from the horse, so that he himself may escape? If he wishes to be just, he will not do so; but that same man will be judged foolish, because, while sparing another’s life, he betrays his own. If he does it, he will indeed be wise . . . but . . . wicked.” BUN.

While sparing another’s. The accepted reading is confirmed by chapter 17: “It is folly to spare another’s life at the cost of one’s own destruction,” and by the words quoted shortly before from the *Epitome*, chapter 56. BUN.

Poisonous. Heumann suspects that Lactantius wrote *almost invincible*. I alter nothing against the manuscripts, because these arguments were pointed, pernicious, and weighty, and he therefore calls them “poisonous.” Thus, in Book III, chapter 14, he called Cicero’s speeches against Antony [Col. 0604D] “poisonous.” BUN.

Could not refute. Thus all manuscripts and printed editions, apart from four recent manuscripts and three editions, which have *was able*.

Makes . . . reply. An elegant construction, as in Book I, chapter 10: “He makes him sit beside him.” Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book I, chapter 12: “He makes Socrates dispute.” Compare Book I of *On the Nature of the Gods*, chapter 8. BUN.

And on behalf of justice. Lactantius writes thus elsewhere; and I so read with three editions and all manuscripts, except for two recent Royal manuscripts and almost all editions, which have *and on behalf of justice* with the conjunction in a different position.

Unrefuted. A new word, meaning “not refuted.”

Who, to be sure, though he was wise. His wisdom is celebrated by Cicero in Book II of *On Ends*, Book II of *On Duties*, and especially in *On Friendship*, which bears Laelius’s name. BETULEIUS.

Who. Heumann reads *because*, from the printed editions.

Plato. His ten books *On the Republic* are entitled *On Justice*.

Aristotle. In Book V of the *Ethics*.

Yet he will nevertheless be judged foolish, because he will either sell it cheaply or not sell it at all. If he conceals the fault, he will indeed be wise, because he will attend to his own interest; but that same man will be wicked, because he will deceive. Again, if he finds someone who thinks he is selling orichalcum when it is actually gold, or lead when it is silver, will he remain silent so as to buy it cheaply, or disclose the truth and thus buy it dearly? It plainly seems foolish to prefer to buy it dearly.”

From this he wished it to be understood both that one who is just and good is foolish, and that one who is wise is wicked. And yet it is possible, without mortal danger, for people to remain content with poverty. He therefore passed on to more serious cases, in which no one could be just without endangering his life. For he said:

“Justice, surely, means not killing a human being and not touching anything belonging to another. What, then, will a just man do if by chance he has been shipwrecked [Col. 0603B] and someone weaker than he has taken hold of a plank? Will he not knock the man from the plank, climb upon it himself, and escape by relying upon it—especially since there is no witness in the middle of the sea? If he is wise, he will do so; for he himself must perish unless he does. But if he prefers to die rather than lay hands upon another, then that man is just, but foolish, because he does not spare his own life while sparing another’s.

“Likewise, if his own battle line has been routed, the enemy has begun to pursue, and that just man comes upon a wounded person sitting on a horse, will he spare him and so be killed himself, or throw him from the horse so that he himself may escape the enemy? If he does so, he is wise, but also wicked; if he does not, he must be just, but also foolish.”

Thus, after dividing justice into two parts, saying that one was civil and the other natural, he overthrew both: civil justice, he argued, is indeed wisdom, but is not justice; natural justice, on the other hand, is indeed justice, but is not wisdom. These arguments are certainly ingenious and poisonous, and Marcus Tullius [Col. 0604A] could not refute them. For although he makes Laelius reply to Furius and speak on behalf of justice, he passed these arguments by unrefuted, as though skirting a pit. Consequently, that same Laelius appears to have defended not natural justice, which had been charged with folly, but civil justice—the kind that Furius had conceded to be wisdom, though unjust.

## CHAPTER XVIII  
### On Justice, Wisdom, and Folly

As far as the present discussion required, I have shown how justice bears the appearance of folly, so that it may be evident that those who think the adherents of our religion foolish are deceived not without cause, since they appear to do the sort of things that he proposed. [Col. 0604B] I now perceive that something greater is required of me: I must show why God wished justice, wrapped in the guise of folly, to be removed from human sight—after I have first answered Furius, because Laelius answered him insufficiently. For although Laelius was undoubtedly wise, as he was called, he could in no way defend true justice, since he did not grasp the very head and fountain of justice.

For us, however, this defense is easier, because through a heavenly benefaction justice is familiar and thoroughly known to us, and because we know it not merely by name but in reality. Plato and Aristotle, indeed, wished with honorable intent to defend justice and would have accomplished something if knowledge of divine things had supported their good efforts, their eloquence, and their intellectual power. Accordingly, their work lay empty and [Col. 0604C] useless; nor could they persuade any human being to live according to their prescription, because that teaching had no foundation from heaven. Our [Col. 0605A] work must necessarily be more certain, for it is God who has taught us.

[Col. 0605A] [Note: [Col. 0605C] [Various Notes on columns 605–606]

For us. Thus very many of the oldest manuscripts and four printed editions. The others, together with nine recent manuscripts, read *because*.

Presented. I have restored this from the five oldest manuscripts, one Bologna manuscript, two Royal manuscripts, three other Royal manuscripts, two Colbert manuscripts, and two Clermont manuscripts. Ten manuscripts and ten editions read *asserted*; others, *discussed*.

Perceived. I have corrected the text thus from the five older Royal manuscripts, four Colbert manuscripts, two Clermont manuscripts, the Brünn manuscript, and the Betuleius edition; the Caucian manuscript, one recent Bologna manuscript, and the Tax edition support it with the reading *may have perceived*. One old Bologna manuscript, five recent Royal manuscripts, two Colbert manuscripts, and eleven common editions have *foresaw*.

And nevertheless the reason. I added *nevertheless* from ten editions and all the manuscripts except one old Bologna manuscript, the Pen manuscript, and four recent editions, in which it is absent.

The dogma of his school. Seneca says much about such dogmas in Letter 95. Arnobius, Book II, page 48: “While the philosophers undermine, destroy, and tear down one another’s dogmas, they have rendered everything uncertain.” BUN.

To defend the dogma of his school. That is, the dogma of the Academic school that nothing can be known with certainty—or, as follows, that nothing can be apprehended as certain. He used *decretum* for an established dogma, Greek ἀρεστόν (*arestón*, “an accepted tenet”). Partly from BETULEIUS.

For why should he sail, etc.? Other Fathers likewise condemned commerce as an illicit activity. See Tertullian, *On Idolatry*, Book XI. Their reasoning was that it can scarcely be practiced without greed and falsehood. GALLAEUS.

Dwells. Francius reads *dwells* in another tense. See what precedes. One recent Royal manuscript has that reading from a second hand. Heumann likewise reads it so.

Who does not know how to seek profit, etc. Above, he said that a just man seeks absolutely nothing belonging to another, and here, that he does not seek profit, etc. I do not wish these words to be understood as though anyone who seeks profit must be accused of injustice. What our author here asserts generally he plainly means of immoderate desire, in which sense his assertion is true.

Watch. This refers to Christian laws, under which it was unlawful to attend gladiatorial spectacles.

Or may even be compelled against his will to undergo these things. That is, to perform killing when compelled to serve as a soldier. For in that age, not only under pagan emperors but also under Christian ones, when recruits were levied, those who were of military age and stature, and whose status did not grant exemption from military service, were driven to take the military oath and could not evade it. Once they had taken that oath, it was unlawful for them to leave the standards before completing their service, unless they had obtained discharge for a just and meritorious reason; anyone who otherwise deserted military service was punished with death. These, therefore, are the people whom Lactantius said were compelled by the necessity of the laws, against their will, to enter military service—that is, the lawful art of slaughtering human beings—and whom both he and the Fathers of the Council of Nicaea, canon 12, consequently imply should be excused. SALMASIUS.

O Carneades. Thus several manuscripts and printed editions. Two recent Royal manuscripts and two Colbert manuscripts have *O Carneades*; the Brünn manuscript, *you, Carneades*; one Colbert manuscript, *you, O Carneades*.—*O Carneades.* Thus the manuscripts and editions. Heumann rightly defends this form and illustrates it from Vossius, *Analogy*, Book II, chapters 3 and 10. Gronovius likewise defends *O Socrates* as a vocative form in the fragments of Cicero, Verburg edition, page 3936. BUN.

Who do not understand the mystery of man. That is, the true principle and condition of man. Above, Book II, chapter 18: “Whoever, therefore, strives to understand the mystery of man and the principle of his own nature.” WALCH.

Upright. Horace, *Odes* I.22.

The Hydaspes washes. Thus the older and better manuscripts, twelve editions, and the Horatian manuscripts. Sixteen recent Lactantian manuscripts and three early editions from Rome have *encircles*, not inappropriately.

For they depicted and imagined in words a justice that was not present to view, and they could not confirm what they presented by examples before their eyes. Their listeners could answer that it was impossible to live as they prescribed in their discussion, since no one had yet appeared who followed that manner of life. We, however, show that what we say is true not only by words but also by examples drawn from reality.

Carneades, therefore, perceived the nature of justice, except that his perception did not reach deeply enough to see that it is not folly—although I think I understand the intention with which he acted. For he did not truly believe that the just man was foolish; rather, although he knew that he was not, he did not comprehend the reason why he appeared so, and therefore wished [Col. 0605B] to show that truth lay concealed in a hidden place, so as to defend the dogma of his school, whose chief tenet is that nothing can be apprehended.

Let us therefore see whether justice can have any alliance with folly. “A just man,” he says, “if he does not take a horse from a wounded man or a plank from a shipwrecked man in order to save his own life, is foolish.”

First of all, I deny that such an accident can possibly befall a man who is truly just, because the just man is neither an enemy to any living person nor does he covet anything whatever that belongs to another. For why should he sail, or what should he seek from a foreign land, when his own possessions suffice him? Why, moreover, should he wage war and involve himself in the frenzies of others, when perpetual peace with humanity dwells in his mind? Surely a man who does not know how to seek profit, being satisfied with his sustenance, [Col. 0605C] will delight in foreign merchandise or human blood; and he will regard as unlawful not only to perform killing himself but also to be present among those who do it and to watch. [Col. 0606A]

But I pass over these points, since it is possible that he may be compelled against his will to undergo such things. Do you therefore suppose, O Furius—or rather, O Carneades, to whom that whole speech belongs—that justice is so powerless, so superfluous, and so despised by God that it can do nothing and possesses nothing within itself capable of preserving it?

Plainly, those who do not understand the mystery of man, and therefore refer everything to this temporal life, cannot know how great the power of justice is. For even when they discuss virtue, although they understand that it is utterly full of hardships and miseries, they nevertheless say that it must be sought for its own sake; for they have no perception whatever of its rewards, which are eternal and immortal. Thus, by referring everything to this present life, [Col. 0606B] they plainly reduce virtue to folly, since it assumes such great labors in this life fruitlessly and vainly. But these matters will be treated more fully elsewhere.

Meanwhile, let us continue, as we began, with justice, whose power is so great that, when it raises its eyes to heaven, it merits all things from God. Flaccus therefore rightly said that the power of innocence is so great that it needs neither weapons nor physical strength for its protection, wherever it may journey:

> The man upright in life and pure of crime,  
> Has no need, Fuscus, of Moorish spears,  
> Nor bow, nor quiver laden  
> With poisoned arrows:
>
> Whether he means to journey through the burning Syrtes,  
> Or through the inhospitable  
> Caucasus, or those regions that the fabled  
> Hydaspes washes.

It cannot therefore happen that heavenly protection should fail to preserve the just man amid the dangers [Col. 0606C] of storms and wars. Even if he sails with murderers and criminals, either the wicked too will be spared so that the one just and innocent soul may be delivered, or, at any rate, while all the others perish, he alone will be preserved. [Col. 0607A]

But let us grant that what the philosopher proposes can happen. What, then, will the just man do if he encounters either a wounded man on a horse or a shipwrecked man on a plank?

[Col. 0607A] [Note: [Col. 0607C] [Various Notes on columns 607–608]

A shipwrecked man on a plank, etc. Ambrose, *On Duties*, Book III, chapter 4, says and thinks the same as Lactantius.

What dearer. Twelve recent manuscripts and three editions read *clearer*.

You have carried. Six recent manuscripts read *he has carried*, not inappropriately.

[Col. 0607D] Will you judge. Ten recent manuscripts and thirteen editions have *will be judged*; two Colbert manuscripts and the Pen manuscript, *he will judge*. But I write *will you judge*, with one very old Bologna manuscript, one very old Royal manuscript, one other Royal manuscript of good quality, five other manuscripts, and the Betuleius edition. See the preceding words.

Pythagoreans. Two recent Royal manuscripts, one Clermont manuscript corrected by a second hand, the Rome 1470 edition, and the Florentine edition read *Pythagorics*: namely Damon and Pythias, concerning whom see Valerius, Book IV, chapter 7, and Cicero, *On Duties*, Book III, chapter 10.

The tyrant. Namely Dionysius of Syracuse.

Was being led away. That is, to execution. The verb is used absolutely, in the manner of the ancients. Seneca uses it three times of Piso, who had ordered a soldier to be led away, in *On Anger*, Book I, chapter 16. BUN.

Because one. This is the reading of the older and better manuscripts. Four recent manuscripts and four editions have *of whom one*; thirteen recent manuscripts and five common editions have *when one*.

To them. I have restored this from the manuscripts and many editions. Some have *here*.

Is said to have entreated. That is, “to have asked.” Book VI, chapter 20: “Entreating mercy.” Compare *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapters 41, 46, and 52, and Valerius Maximus, Book IV, chapter 7. The ancients often use the word in this sense. BUN.

Is resolved. One Colbert manuscript has *will be resolved*; one Colbert manuscript, one Leipzig manuscript, and the Em edition, *is solved*.

Provided that he does not. Thus the old and better manuscripts and editions. It is a Ciceronian expression, *dum ne*, rather than the more recent *dummodo non*: Cicero, *To Atticus*, Book VI, letter 1, “provided that it is not to the businessman”; and Book VIII, letter 13, “provided that it is not to you, I am not concerned.”

Conciliator. See Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book I, §104.

Because it is evil. That is, insofar as it is evil.

For they do not know that it is evil to harm. Lactantius and other sacred writers—Tertullian, Augustine, and especially Cyprian hundreds of times, to say nothing of the Vulgate translation—after *I know* and other verbs of perception use *because* with the indicative, with the same force as the accusative and infinitive or *that* with the subjunctive. Lactantius, Book VI, chapter 22: “For he knows that pleasure is the maker of death.” We note several further examples there and at Book IV, chapter 12: “That you may know that I am the Lord.” BUN.

But the human being who. Thus the oldest manuscripts—one Bologna, three Royal, one of which is of the highest quality, and six others—as well as six printed editions and six early editions of the fifteenth century. Twelve manuscripts and eight printed editions have *because*.

By which he is distinguished from dumb animals. Three recent manuscripts and two editions read *from many*.

But cunning and craftiness exist among dumb animals. I added *but* from twenty-one manuscripts. After *dumb animals*, eight recent manuscripts and fourteen printed editions add *also*.

Not unwillingly do I acknowledge it: he will die rather than kill. Yet justice, which is the distinctive good of the human being, will not on that account receive the name of folly. For what should be better or dearer to a human being than innocence? It must surely be the more perfect, the further you carry it to its utmost limit and prefer to die rather than allow anything to be subtracted from the principle of innocence.

“It is folly,” he says, “to spare another’s life at the cost of one’s own destruction.” Will you also judge it [Col. 0607B] foolish to perish for friendship?

Why, then, are those Pythagorean friends praised by you, one of whom gave himself to the tyrant as a pledge that he would die in place of the other, while the other appeared at the appointed time when his guarantor was already being led away, and by his arrival freed him? Their virtue would not be held in such great glory—because one was willing to die for his friend and the other even for his pledged word—if they were regarded as fools.

Indeed, precisely because of this virtue, the tyrant granted them favor by preserving them both, and the nature of that most cruel man was transformed. He is even said to have entreated them to receive him as the third member of their friendship—not, surely, as fools, but as good and wise men. I therefore do not see why, when dying for friendship and good faith is reckoned the highest glory, [Col. 0607C] it should not likewise be glorious for a human being to perish for innocence.

Those, therefore, are the greatest fools who charge us as a crime with being willing to die for God, while they themselves exalt to heaven with the highest praises a man who was willing to die for another human being.

Finally, to conclude the argument, reason itself teaches that the same man cannot be both just and foolish, or both wise and unjust. For one who is foolish does not know what is just [Col. 0608A] and good, and therefore always sins. He is led along as though captive by vices and cannot resist them in any way, because he lacks the virtue that he does not know. The just man, however, abstains from every sin, which he cannot do unless he possesses knowledge of right and wrong.

But who can distinguish right from wrong unless he is wise? It follows that no one who is foolish can ever be just, nor anyone who has been unjust be wise. If this is most true, it is evident that the man who does not take either the plank from the shipwrecked man or the horse from the wounded man is not foolish, because to do these things is a sin, from which the wise man abstains.

I nevertheless acknowledge that he appears foolish through the error of people who do not understand the proper nature of each thing. Thus this whole question is resolved not so much by arguments [Col. 0608B] as by definition. Folly, then, is error in deeds and words through ignorance of what is right and good. Therefore, the man who does not spare even himself, provided that he does not harm another—which is evil—is not foolish. Both reason and truth itself prescribe this for us.

For in all animals we see that, because they lack wisdom, nature acts as a conciliator on their own behalf. They therefore harm others in order to benefit themselves, for they do not know that it is evil to harm. But the human being, who possesses knowledge of good and evil, abstains from causing harm even at a cost to himself—something that an irrational animal cannot do. For this reason, innocence is numbered among the highest human virtues. From these facts it is evident that the wisest man is the one who prefers to perish rather than cause harm, so that he may preserve the function by which he is distinguished from dumb animals.

For the man who does not correct a seller’s error so that he may buy gold cheaply, or who does not disclose that the slave he is selling is a runaway or that the house he is selling is pestilential, attending to his own profit and advantage, is not wise, as Carneades wished him to appear, but cunning and crafty. Cunning and craftiness exist even among dumb animals, whether they lie in wait for others and capture them by guile in order to devour them, or evade the snares of others [Col. 0609A] in various ways.

Wisdom, however, belongs to the human being alone. For wisdom is understanding directed either toward doing what is good and right or toward abstaining [Col. 0609A] from wicked words and deeds.

[Col. 0609A] [Note: [Col. 0609C] [Various Notes on columns 609–610]

Or toward abstaining. I have restored this from the oldest manuscripts—one Bologna and two Royal—and the editions of de Tournes, Soubron, and Isaeus. See the preceding phrase, *toward doing good*. A great many manuscripts and printed editions have *or abstinence*.

Of words and deeds. This is the reading of a great many manuscripts, among them the oldest Royal and Bologna manuscripts, and of eleven editions. Correctly; see what follows. Ten manuscripts and three early editions read *of offenses and deeds*.

By which alone. Four recent manuscripts and seven early editions have *by which alone* in the feminine; another has *which alone*; a Colbert manuscript, *which alone* with a different gender.—*By which alone*: that is, by which thing alone, namely wisdom. Since the word *wisdom* occurred somewhat further back, he used the neuter, as elsewhere, to refer to everything said about wisdom.

But surely this cause brings it about, etc. Up to this point he has refuted Furius, the advocate of injustice. He will now indicate why Laelius, who was considered supremely wise, did not defend the cause of justice as its dignity required—namely, because his wisdom did not come from heaven. He also shows that Laelius asserts mutually contradictory things. At the beginning of the chapter, moreover, he investigates the source of the errors of philosophers and of the common people: namely, that the doctrine concerning the hope of resurrection is believed not to have been sufficiently established. From these foundations he concludes that:

> Virtue lives among the gods above and has its own rewards.

[Col. 0610C] By “virtue” he means justice itself, which is the subject matter of this entire fifth book.
