Who should be in want. One old Bologna manuscript and one Clermont manuscript in the first hand read *because*.

From which persuasion. The Canterbury manuscript and five editions read *And from that persuasion*.

This present. Supply “life,” which the Gotha manuscript has added, I think received from a gloss. CELLARIUS.

Never. One recent Royal manuscript and fifteen editions have *by no means*; in one recent Royal manuscript, *you will never be able*.

Uncertain and wavering judgment. Seven manuscripts and two editions have *slipping*; one recent Royal manuscript, *struggling and*.

His eyes be gouged out. Three recent manuscripts and twelve printed editions insert *his*, although it occurred just before.

A very narrow path. The Brünn manuscript has *by a very narrow path*; four Colbert manuscripts, corruptly, *very narrow paths*. Six recent manuscripts and five common editions have *through very narrow paths*. Read concerning this below, Book VI, chapter 3.—*A very narrow path . . . might lead.* For everywhere he establishes only one way, one path, to immortality; hence Book VII, chapter 20: “Very narrow is the path by which justice leads a human being into heaven.” The whole of Book VI, chapters 3 and 4, teaches the same, especially chapter 7: “The false way . . . has many paths . . . the way of truth . . . is both simple . . . and narrow . . . and steep,” etc. BUN.

The wise man, moreover, never strives after profit, because he despises these earthly goods; nor does he permit anyone to be deceived, because it is the duty of a good man to correct human errors and lead people back onto the way. For human nature is social and beneficent; through wisdom alone the human being has kinship with God.

## CHAPTER XIX  
### On Virtue, the Tortures of Christians, and the Rights of Father and Master

[Col. 0609B] But surely this is the reason why a man who prefers to be in want or to die rather than harm or take anything from another appears foolish: people believe that the human being is annihilated by death. From this conviction arise all the errors both of the common people and of the philosophers.

For if we are nothing after death, it is certainly the mark of the most foolish person not to provide for this life, so that it may be as long as possible and filled with every advantage. Whoever does this must necessarily depart from the rule of justice.

But if a better and longer life remains for the human being—a truth that we learn both from the arguments of great philosophers, from the responses of seers, and from the divine utterances of prophets—then it is the part of a wise person to despise this present life with all its goods, since every loss he suffers is compensated by immortality.

In Cicero, that same Laelius, the defender of justice, says: “Virtue plainly desires honor, and virtue has no other reward.” It certainly has another, and one most worthy of virtue, which you, Laelius, could never have suspected, because you knew nothing of the divine writings.

“Yet,” he says, “virtue receives honor readily but does not demand it harshly.” You are gravely mistaken if you think that a human being can pay virtue its reward, when you yourself said with perfect truth elsewhere: “What riches will you offer to this man? What commands? What kingdoms? He regards these things as human, but judges his own goods divine.” [Col. 0610A]

Who, then, would think you wise, Laelius, when you contradict yourself and, a little later, take away from virtue what you had given it? Plainly, ignorance of the truth makes judgment uncertain and wavering.

What do you then add? “But if all are ungrateful, or many are envious, or powerful enemies despoil virtue of its rewards—” O how frail and empty a virtue you have introduced, if it can be despoiled of its reward! If it judges its goods divine, as you said, how can there arise people so ungrateful, so envious, or so powerful that they are able to despoil virtue of goods bestowed upon it by God?

“Indeed,” he says, “virtue delights itself with many consolations and above all sustains itself by its own beauty.” With what consolations? With what beauty, when it is often brought under accusation and that beauty is turned into punishment? [Col. 0610B]

For what if, as Furius said, it “is seized, tormented, banished; reduced to want; has its hands cut off and its eyes gouged out; is condemned, bound, burned, and killed by wretched forms of death”? Will virtue lose its reward? Or rather, will virtue itself perish?

By no means. It will both receive its reward from God as judge and live and flourish forever. If you take these things away, nothing in human life can appear so useless or so foolish as virtue. Its natural goodness and honorableness can teach us that the soul is not mortal and that a divine reward has been established for it by God.

But God wished virtue itself to be concealed beneath the guise of folly so that the mystery of truth and of his religion might remain secret; so that he might condemn for vanity and error these religions and earthly wisdom, which exalts itself too highly and takes great satisfaction in itself; and finally so that, by setting difficulty before us, a very narrow path might lead to the sublime reward of immortality. [Col. 0610C]

I have explained, I think, why our people are regarded as foolish among fools. For preferring to be tortured and killed rather than take incense in three fingers and cast it upon a hearth [Col. 0611A] appears just as senseless as caring more for another’s life than one’s own when one’s life is in danger.

[Col. 0611A] [Note: [Col. 0611C] [Various Notes on columns 611–612]

Cast it upon a hearth. Ten manuscripts read *lie upon a hearth*; the de Tournes manuscript, *lie upon hearths*.

Anything other than God. One Colbert manuscript, one Clermont manuscript, and Francius read *apart from God*. The same variation appears below: *apart from food* and *anything other than food*.

His own master. I have restored this from all the manuscripts and several editions; correctly. See what follows. Some printed editions have, incorrectly, *the supreme master*.

Disinherited. A title concerning the disinheritance of children occurs in the Imperial *Institutes*, Book II, chapter 13. Fourteen causes for disinheritance are enumerated in the constitutions of the law. BETULEIUS.

Of master and father. See Book IV, chapter 3: “One is your Father, who is in heaven.” Matthew 23.

Apart from food. Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have *anything other than food*.

Does not have it in his power. I have restored this from the Rome 1470 edition and all manuscripts except one recent Royal manuscript and twelve editions, which read *does not have the power*.

Except those that God himself has established? All books contain the words “except that God himself established,” and everything is correct provided one supplies, “except those that . . . he established?” This refers back to the penalty established above. Thus Book VI, chapter 25: “What is worthy of God, except what he himself . . . demanded?” BUN.

For the impious. Isaiah, final chapter; Ecclesiasticus 7; Judith 16; Psalm 10.—*The fire, which he himself . . . threatens.* The books consistently have the neuter *which*, which is often used for the matter under discussion, as I said at chapter 17: namely, that he has prepared eternal fire for the unjust. Thus earlier in this chapter: “There remains . . . a longer life, which . . . we learn.” BUN.

[Col. 0612C] Their own robbers. Walch says that by “robbers” he means the pontiffs and priests; rather, he means the demons, for there immediately follows: “whom they believe to be gods.” Again, chapter 20: “They worship their enemies and appease their robbers and murderers with victims,” etc. Compare Book II, chapter 16, and Book V, chapter 21. BUN.

Instigations. Book IV, chapter 27: “At the instigation . . . of demons”; chapter 30, “by the promptings of demons.” Book V, chapter 21: “Lost spirits . . . drive the ignorant into madness.” BUNEMANN.

Clinging to the common persuasion. One old Bologna manuscript has *cling*; the other, more recent Bologna manuscript, *they cling*. Eighteen manuscripts have *while the common persuasion clings*.—*While the common persuasion clings.* The Rostock, Venice 1471, 1472, and both 1478 editions, the Paris, Junta, Aldine, and the remaining editions read *clinging to the common persuasion*. The participle better expresses their will, for he immediately says that they willingly err; similarly, Book I, chapter 1: “For many, clinging stubbornly to empty superstitions, harden themselves against manifest truth.” BUN.

Ignorance. Thus the older and better manuscripts and eight printed editions. This word is characteristic of Lactantius. Eighteen recent manuscripts and seven printed editions read *lack of knowledge*.

Do those things to bodies. An elegant expression. Cicero, *Against Verres*, Action I, chapter 5: “Nor did he do this only to statues and ornaments.” Compare Cortius on Sallust, *Catiline* 11, note 4, page 47: “To perpetrate foul and cruel deeds against citizens.” BUNEMANN.

Darkness. These words allude to Isaiah 5:20: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil; who put darkness for light and light for darkness; who put bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter.”

For they do not understand how great a sacrilege it is to worship anything other than God, who founded heaven and earth, fashioned the human race, breathed life into it, and endowed it with light.

If a slave who deserts his master by fleeing is considered utterly wicked, and is judged most deserving of scourging, fetters, the workhouse, the cross, and every evil; and if, in the same way, a son who abandons his father so as not to obey him is regarded as depraved and impious, and is therefore thought worthy of disinheritance and of having his name erased from the family forever—how much more is this true of one who abandons God, in whom the two equally venerable titles of master and father converge? [Col. 0611B]

For what benefit does the man who purchases a slave confer upon him apart from food, which he supplies for the sake of his own advantage? And the man who begets a son does not have it in his power that the child should be conceived, born, and live. From this it is apparent that he is not the father, but only the agent of generation.

Of what punishments, then, is the deserter of him who is both true Master and Father worthy, except those that God himself has established? He has prepared eternal fire for unjust spirits, which he himself threatens against the impious and rebellious through his prophets.

## CHAPTER XX  
### On the Vanity and Crimes of Impious Religions, and the Tortures of Christians

[Col. 0611C] Let those who murder both their own souls and the souls of others therefore learn what an inexpiable crime they commit: first, because they slaughter themselves by serving the most depraved demons, whom God has condemned to eternal punishments; [Col. 0612A] and second, because they do not permit God to be worshiped by others but strive to divert human beings toward death-dealing rites. With the utmost diligence they endeavor to ensure that no soul remains unharmed on earth and looks up to heaven with its condition intact.

What else should I call them but wretches, since they obey the instigations of their own robbers, whom they believe to be gods? They know neither their condition, origin, names, nor nature; but, clinging to the common persuasion, they willingly err and indulge their own folly.

If you ask them for the rationale of that persuasion, they can give none. Instead, they take refuge in the judgments of their ancestors: those men were wise, those men approved it, those men knew what was best. Thus they deprive themselves of perception and renounce reason while placing faith in the errors of others. Entangled in such ignorance of all things, they know neither [Col. 0612B] themselves nor their gods.

And would that they wished to err alone and be foolish alone! They also drag others into fellowship with their evil, as though they would derive consolation from the destruction of many. This very ignorance causes them to be so wicked in persecuting the wise, while pretending to be acting for their benefit and wishing to recall them to a sound mind.

Do they therefore attempt to do this through discourse or by presenting some rational argument? By no means, but through violence and torture. O astonishing and blind madness! An evil mind is thought to exist in those who try to preserve their faith, but a good mind in their torturers.

Is the evil mind found in those who, contrary to the law of humanity and every divine ordinance, are mangled? Or rather in those who do to the bodies of the innocent what neither the cruelest robbers, the most enraged enemies, nor [Col. 0612C] the most savage barbarians have ever done?

Do they deceive even themselves to such a degree that they interchange and transpose the names of good and evil? Why, then, do they not call day night and the sun darkness? Otherwise, it is the same [Col. 0613A] shamelessness.

[Col. 0613A] [Note: [Col. 0613D] [Various Notes on columns 613–614]

It is shamelessness. Eight recent manuscripts read *imprudence*; Junius, *prudence*.

Lest, if our. One Colbert manuscript and certain printed editions read *nor*, [Col. 0613C] but incorrectly.

The religion of God increases . . . is oppressed. See the note on chapter 13 and chapters 22 following. Tertullian, at the end of the *Apology*: “Yet no refinement of cruelty profits you at all. It is rather an enticement to the sect. We become more numerous whenever we are mown down by you.” BUNEMANN.

Pontiffs. It is apparent that those ancient Roman priesthoods still flourished in Lactantius’s time. BETULEIUS. Whether lesser or chief pontiffs. Numa instituted the pontiffs and set over them his son-in-law Marcius as *Pontifex Maximus*, in whose hands rested supreme authority over ceremonies. BETULEIUS.—There were lesser pontiffs, scribes of the pontiffs who maintained the calendars and commentaries and preserved a faithful record of events, which were called the *Annales Maximi*. Those attendants who committed the deeds of every age to writing were called “lesser pontiffs.” Alexander ab Alexandro, Book II, chapter 8.

Flamens. Whether the *Diales* or *Martiales*, instituted by Romulus, or the *Quirinales*, instituted by Numa. BETULEIUS.

[Col. 0613D] Augurs. They are believed to have derived their origin from the Chaldaeans, from whom they passed to the Greeks, from the Greeks to the Etruscans, and from the Etruscans to the Latins.

Sacrificial kings. They were instituted after the expulsion of the kings, to preside over the royal rites. On them, read Pomponius Laetus, Lucius Fenestella, Alexander ab Alexandro, Blondus, etc., who, drawing on Livy, Dionysius, Varro, and others, have handed down much concerning the Roman priesthoods. BETULEIUS.—Seven Royal MSS., two Colbert MSS., Tornesius, two Clermont MSS.: *sacricolae* (“sacrificers”).

Let them exhort us to. The word *nos* (“us”), added by me, is repeated by the English edition, Lipsius’ third edition, Reimmann, and the editions of 1465 and 1524, as well as Gymnicus and Isaeus; it is omitted by Fasius, Gryphius, and the rest, and is understood with sufficient elegance. BUNEMANN.

What reward awaits in worship, what punishment in contempt. Heumann, here assailing all the editors, finally says: “Write: ‘what reward awaits worship, what punishment contempt.’” The common reading of all the books seems sufficiently elegant to me, with the accusative *mortales* (“mortals”) or *homines* (“human beings”) understood. BUNEMANN.

Let them draw the edge of their intellects. Previously all editions printed *distringant*, as does the Gotha manuscript. That verb is less suitable here, for it means “to pull in different directions”—unless one understands it in the rarer sense, where it means “to bind” or “constrain.” Just as among Latin authors *destringere aciem, gladium* means “to draw the edge, the sword,” so Lactantius, Book III, chapter 8, says: “Let them bring forth their keenness.” BUNEMANN.

Let it be brought forward. I have thus restored the text from nearly all the manuscripts—nine Royal, six Colbert, and many others—and from the Roman edition of 1470. Junius’ manuscript and two Leipzig manuscripts have *asserant* (“let them assert”), not badly; one Clermont manuscript has *asserantur* (“let them be asserted”). Three Oxford manuscripts and fourteen commonly printed editions have *afferatur*.

And the rationale. This is how it should be read with one Colbert manuscript, unless one prefers *ut rationem* (“that they explain the rationale”), which occurs in the old manuscripts—one Bologna, one Royal, Caucianus, and fifteen others—and in two old Roman editions, Isaeus, and Cellarius. Six other recent handwritten copies and seventeen printed ones have *aut* (“or”).

Who lacks devotion and faith. Emman.: “who lacks faith and reason.” The former reading should not be altered. Below: “The worship of God demands the greatest devotion and faith”; chapter 22: “That it may strengthen devotion and faith”; *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 19: “If anyone has not manifested his faith and devotion”;  *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 18: “No force could deprive you of faith and devotion.” Compare Book V, chapter VII. BUNEMANN.

[Col. 0614D] Let them open their mouths. I read thus with one Royal manuscript and fourteen printed editions. Because they did not understand this, the copyists of eight Royal manuscripts, six Colbert manuscripts, Junius, Penius, Lipsius, Palatinus, the second Utrecht manuscript, two Clermont manuscripts, Brun’s manuscript, and five old editions wrote *discant* (“let them learn”) instead of *hiscant* (“let them open their mouths”); two Bologna manuscripts and Taxius have *dicant* (“let them speak”). Titus Livy, Book VI, 16: “They will not dare either to raise their eyes or to open their mouths.” Arnobius, Book IV: “whether to mutter, whether to open the mouth.”

It will be laughed at. This is the reading of all the manuscripts and of the old Roman edition. The other printed editions have “it will be mocked”; in the oldest Royal manuscript, “justice will be laughed at.”

From deaths. Thus the older and better manuscripts and eight printed editions. Sixteen recent manuscripts and six commonly printed editions have “from conduct.” This is also the reading in Bunemann, who presents the following note on this variant.—From conduct. This reading is confirmed by Book I, chapter 11: “From Jupiter’s deeds and conduct we discover that he was a human being,” etc. Compare *On the Wrath of God*, chapter 11; St. Augustine, *The City of God*, Book VII, chapter 18: “For each of the gods, rites were established according to his disposition, conduct, deeds, and fortunes.” BUNEMANN.]

—to impose upon the good the name of the wicked; upon the wise, that of fools; upon the just, that of the impious. Indeed, if they have any confidence either in philosophy or in eloquence, let them arm themselves and refute these arguments of ours, if they can. Let them engage us at close quarters and examine each individual point. It is fitting that they undertake the defense of their gods, lest, if our cause should grow strong—as it grows stronger every day—the gods be abandoned together with their shrines and their objects of ridicule. And since they can accomplish nothing by force—for the religion of God increases the more it is oppressed—let them act instead through reason and exhortation.

Let the pontiffs, whether lesser or chief, come forward into public; the flamens, augurs, likewise the sacrificial kings, and all who are priests and prelates of their religions. Let them summon us to an assembly; let them exhort us to undertake [Col. 0613B] the worship of the gods. Let them persuade us that there are many gods by whose divine power and providence all things are governed. Let them reveal the origins and beginnings of the rites and of the gods, and how they were handed down to mortals. Let them explain what their source is and what their rationale is. Let them set forth what reward awaits in worship and what punishment in contempt; why the gods wish to be worshiped by human beings; and what human piety contributes to them if they are blessed. Let them confirm all these things, not by their own assertion—for the authority of a mortal human being has no force—but by some [Col. 0614A] divine testimonies, as we do.

There is no need for violence and injury, because religion cannot be compelled. The matter must be conducted with words rather than blows, so that there may be willing assent. Let them draw the edge of their intellects. If their reasoning is true, let it be brought forward. We are ready to listen if they teach; but we certainly believe nothing when they are silent, just as we do not yield even when they rage. Let them imitate us and explain the rationale of the whole matter. For we do not entice people, as they charge; rather, we teach, prove, and demonstrate. Accordingly, no one is detained by us against his will, for one who lacks devotion and faith is useless to God. And yet no one departs, because truth itself holds him fast.

Let those men teach in this manner, if they have any confidence in the truth. Let them speak; let them open their mouths; let them dare, I say, to debate some such matter with us. Then assuredly [Col. 0614B] their error and folly will be laughed at by the old women whom they despise and by our children. For although they are thoroughly learned and know from books the genealogy, deeds, dominions, deaths, and tombs of the gods, and although they know that the very rites into which they have been initiated arose either from human deeds, from human fortunes, or even from human deaths, it is incredible madness to regard as gods those whom they do not dare deny were mortals. Or, if they are so shameless as to deny it, their own writings and [Col. 0615A] those of their people will expose them, [Col. 0615A] [Note: [Col. 0615B] [Various Notes on columns 615–616]

Will expose. Twelve recent MSS. and eight printed editions: “will expose” in the future indicative. See the preceding “let them dare” and the following “let them convict.” Junius: “let them be exposed.”

[Col. 0615C] Let them convict. Ten recent MSS. and six editions: “they will convict.”

Although they are. In place of *quum*, which occurs in the better manuscripts and printed editions, many printed copies had *quam*. Three recent Royal manuscripts, Brun’s manuscript, and the Aldine, Cratander, and Grapheus editions read “who are.”

Lest they be mocked by our people as well. I restored the conjunction from six Royal manuscripts, five Colbert manuscripts, five others, and seven editions. The oldest Royal manuscript has *aut* (“or”) instead of *et* (“and”). Five recent manuscripts and twelve commonly printed editions omit *et*.

For the common people generally. Thus twelve manuscripts. The Caucianus manuscript, sixteen recent manuscripts, and the printed editions have: “For perhaps the common people.”

Uncorrupted judgment. Here *incorruptum* means “pure, unimpaired,” as in Cicero: “an uncorrupted and upright witness,” “uncorrupted testimony.” *For Marcellus*, chapter 9: “Those who will judge . . . perhaps more incorruptly than we do.” BUNEMANN.

Faithful silence. Virgil, *Aeneid* III, verse 112. When these rites were commanded, the formula was: “Favor us with your tongues”—that is, “Keep reverent silence.” Hence the proverb, “Bar the door, profane ones.” The canon in the Decretals, *On Consecration*, distinction 2, which bars the laity from the presbyterium, agrees with this proverb. BETULEIUS.

[Col. 0615D] Why do they either not believe us? One recent manuscript has “why should they believe?”; two recent Royal manuscripts, Junius, the Cambridge manuscript, and many printed editions have: “Why do they not believe either us or our people?”

They say. See above, at the beginning of Book III of the *Institutions*, chapter 3.

Oh, with what honorable intention. Ironical. So read three manuscripts, one of them the oldest and another of good quality. The Caucianus manuscript, nineteen other recent manuscripts, and six editions have “dishonorable.”

Not by killing, but by dying. This is the reading of nearly all the manuscripts and of eight editors, and rightly so. For “to kill” and “to die” are correlatives. See below: “that you defend religion by endurance or death.” Two recent Royal manuscripts and six commonly printed editions have “by admonishing.” St. Bernard, Sermon 61 on the *Song of Songs*: “Faith must be persuaded, not commanded”; and Sermon 64: “Let heretics be captured rather than allowed to escape; captured, I say, not by arms, but by arguments by which their errors may be refuted.” Athanasius, *Apology* II: “Slaughter and chains are foreign to our Church.” In place of “by dying,” Cellarius and Heumann have “by admonishing,” which, they say, refers to the persecutors, who defended their superstitions with sword and flame.—Not by killing, but by dying. Augustine aptly writes in *The City of God*, Book II, chapter 29, that Roman Christians “struggled against the most hostile powers and conquered them by dying bravely.” BUNEMANN.

If by evil. Here the reading of nearly all the others, *malo*, is correct. *Malo* means “by wickedness,” which is evil and belongs to evil persons. See above and chapter 20: “People should be brought to good by good . . . not by evil.” BUNEMANN.

It is already abolished; it is already nothing. One old Bologna manuscript: “now no supplication exists.”

Faith preserved. Junius’ manuscript and five old editions have “consecrated,” less well. See shortly below: “preserves faith . . . and faith must be preserved.”

Obtains. One recent Royal manuscript and Brun’s manuscript have the future “will obtain.” See the preceding clause.

Has met death. Thus very many manuscripts and nearly all printed editions, just as Lactantius uses the cognate expression “to live life” in *Divine Institutes*, Book I, chapter 14; Book V, chapter 8; Book VII, chapter 24; and, in *On the Workmanship of God*, “let us serve an indefatigable military service for God.” But “to live life” is also Cicero’s expression, *Against Verres* IV, no. 118. The scribes therefore wrongly wrote “has died by death” in five Royal manuscripts, one Colbert manuscript, Brun’s manuscript, and the Roman editions of 1470 and Isaeus.—Has met death. *Occumbere mortem* is correct Latin and frequently used. See Pitiscus on Curtius, Book IV, chapter 15: “Each regarded it as glorious to meet death before the eyes of his king”; and Gebhard, Gruter, and Davies on Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I, 42, end: “who would not hesitate to meet death for his country.” BUNEMANN.

Can pay to the dead the reward of virtue. One old Bologna manuscript: “will pay the reward of death.”

Since it is a heavenly military service, it demands the greatest devotion, etc. This is taken from bodily military service, for soldiers devoted themselves wholly to the commonwealth or consecrated themselves to Caesar. Vegetius: “They swear by God, by Christ, by the Holy Spirit, and by the majesty of the emperor, which, after God, is to be loved and revered by the human race. For when the emperor has received the name Augustus, faithful devotion must be rendered to him as to a present and embodied god, and sleepless service must be expended upon him.”

Or grant the petitioner. Two recent Royal manuscripts read “the one asking” in place of “the one praying.”]

Finally, the very origins of their rites will convict them. Let them understand from this fact alone how great the difference is between truth and falsehood: although they themselves are eloquent, they cannot persuade, while the unlearned and uncultivated can, because the subject itself and truth itself speak.

Why, then, do they rage? In attempting to diminish their folly, they increase it. Torture and piety are utterly different things; neither truth with violence nor justice with cruelty can be joined. But with good reason they do not dare to teach anything about divine matters, lest they be mocked by our people and abandoned by their own. For if the common people generally, whose judgment is simple and uncorrupted, were to learn that those mysteries had been established in memory of the dead, they would condemn them and seek something else, something truer, to worship.

Hence faithful silence was established for the rites [Col. 0615B] by cunning men, so that the people would not know what they worshiped. But since we are thoroughly acquainted with their teachings, why do they either not believe us, who know both systems, or envy us because we have preferred truth to falsehood?

“But,” they say, “the rites publicly adopted must be defended.” Oh, with what honorable intention those wretched people go astray! For they perceive that nothing in human affairs is more excellent than religion and that it ought to be defended with the utmost force; but just as they err in religion itself, so too they err in the manner of its defense. [Col. 0616A] Religion must be defended not by killing, but by dying; not by savagery, but by endurance; not by wickedness, but by faith. The former belong to the evil, the latter to the good. Good, not evil, must necessarily be practiced in religion. For if you wish to defend religion with blood, torture, or evil, it will no longer be defended but polluted and violated.

Nothing is so dependent upon the will as religion; if the mind of the person sacrificing is averse to it, religion is already abolished—it is already nothing. The correct principle, therefore, is that you defend religion by endurance or death. In such defense, faith preserved is both pleasing to God himself and adds authority to religion. For if a man who, in this earthly military service, preserves faith with his king in some outstanding exploit lives afterward, he becomes more acceptable and dearer; if he perishes, he obtains the highest glory because he has [Col. 0616B] met death for his commander. How much more must faith be preserved with God, the emperor of all, who can pay the reward of virtue not only to the living but also to the dead?

Therefore, since the worship of God is a heavenly military service, it demands the greatest devotion and faith. For how will God love his worshiper if he himself is not loved by that person? Or how will he grant the petitioner whatever he has prayed for, when the petitioner approaches prayer neither sincerely nor reverently?

But when these people come to sacrifice, [Col. 0617A] they offer their gods nothing inward, nothing of their own: no integrity of mind, no reverence, no fear. And so, when their empty sacrifices have been performed, they leave their entire religion in the temple and together with the temple, [Col. 0617A] [Note: [Col. 0617C] [Various Notes on columns 617–618]

In the temple and together with the temple. The words “and together with the temple” are absent from three recent manuscripts.

And from it they neither bring nor carry anything away with them. In one old Bologna manuscript, “from it” is absent; in one Royal manuscript, “nor” is absent.

Nor firm and unchangeable. Thus one Bologna manuscript, six Colbert manuscripts, five others, and nine old editions. Others have “nor firm and unchangeable” in the masculine plural. But our reading is better, for he contrasts false religions with the true religion, which is firm and unchangeable.

Forward procuresses. He learnedly calls the procuresses who, as stated below, “strip many people of their property,” *procaces*. Festus: “*Procari* means to demand; hence both suitors (*proci*) and importunate prostitutes (*procaces meretrices*) derive their names from continual demanding.” BUNEMANN.

That they may kill. Nine Royal manuscripts, one Clermont manuscript, and eight editions have the singular, “that he may kill.” Either reading is good.

What does the poisoner ask? Two recent Royal manuscripts, one Colbert manuscript corrected by a second hand, Tornesius, Emman., the Cambridge manuscript, and three old Roman editions have: “What does the moneylender ask, except to deceive”—that is, to act covertly and conceal his schemes?—What does the poisoner ask? *Venenarius* is used above for *veneficus* (“poisoner”); and who deceives more than a poisoner or dealer in poison? Hence the parallel passage in Book V, chapter 9: “If they are not permitted to assault openly, let them mix poisons secretly—those who kill their wives to obtain their dowries, or their husbands so that they may marry their adulterous lovers . . . those who assail heaven itself with sorceries.” BUNEMANN.

Except that she should wish for her husband’s death or that her unchastity should be concealed. Thus the editions of Betuleius, Cellarius, Walch, and Heumann, and a few manuscripts, namely the Cambridge and Leipzig manuscripts. Other manuscripts and editions read “except either her husband’s death, or that her unchastity should be concealed,” which produces a defective sentence.

What does the procuress ask? Ten manuscripts have the masculine *leno* (“pimp”). All the rest read as in the text.

To sacrifice. Thus six old editions together with all the manuscripts except two Royal manuscripts and eleven editions, which have “to have sacrificed”; one recent Royal manuscript has “to make satisfaction.”

If they have washed their skin. They expiated all kinds of crimes with water. Cato, *Origins* 3; Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapter 5; Seneca, *Hercules Furens*; Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, Book XI; Dio, Book XLVIII; Euripides, *Iphigenia in Tauris*; Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* VII. They washed either the entire body or only their hands, according to the commentator on Sophocles and Athenaeus, Book IX: “It was customary among the ancients, whenever they had committed either the killing of a human being or other acts of slaughter, to wash their hands in expiation of the offense. Among the ancients, indeed, washing the hands was regarded as an excellent and solemn act.” Justin Martyr, *Apology* II: “And the demons, learning of this bath proclaimed by the prophet, brought it about that those approaching their rites should sprinkle themselves, and ordained that they should offer libations and fragrant fumes when performing such ceremonies; indeed, they arranged that those approaching should wash themselves before ascending to the rites, and thereafter, purified, perform the sacred ceremonies.” They also believed that bloodshed could be removed by sprinkling, a practice to which Virgil alludes in *Aeneid* II. Hence Pilate washes his hands to declare himself harmless or innocent of Christ’s death. See Matthew 27:24.

Wash away. Ovid says almost the same in the *Fasti*:

> O far too credulous are you, who think  
> The grim guilt of murder can be washed away  
> With river water!

Is defiled. An ecclesiastical term that you will not find among authors of sound Latinity; but the adjective *sordidatus* (“soiled”) occurs frequently in Cicero.—That any rivers should wash away. As is clear from chapter 20 below, here too he had in view Cicero, *On the Laws* II.10: “The law commands that one approach the gods chastely—that is, in one’s mind, in which all things reside; nor does it abolish bodily purity . . . for bodily impurity may be removed by a sprinkling of water . . . but the stains of the mind cannot vanish through length of time or be washed away by any rivers.” BUNEMANN.

But these people. Four manuscripts and eight editions have “They themselves.” All the other manuscripts and printed editions have “But these people.”]

just as they found it. From religion they neither bring nor carry anything away with them. Hence religions of this kind can neither make people good nor be firm and unchangeable.

People are therefore easily led away from them, because nothing concerning life, wisdom, or faith is learned there. For what is the character of their superstition concerning those gods? What is its force, its discipline, its origin, its rationale, its foundation, its substance? Toward what does it aim? Or what does it promise, so that it could be faithfully preserved and bravely defended by a human being? In it I see nothing but a ritual [Col. 0617B] pertaining solely to the fingers.

Our religion, however, is firm, substantial, and unchangeable precisely because it teaches justice, because it is always with us, because it resides entirely in the worshiper’s mind, and because it regards the mind itself as a sacrifice. There nothing is required except the blood of animals, smoke, and a senseless libation; here, a good mind, a pure heart, and an innocent life.

To their rites come, indiscriminately, unchaste adulteresses, forward procuresses, and obscene prostitutes; gladiators, brigands, thieves, and poisoners come, and they pray for nothing except that they may commit crimes with impunity. For what does a brigand who sacrifices, or a gladiator, ask except that they may kill? What does a poisoner ask except that he may deceive? What does a prostitute ask except that she may sin as much as possible? [Col. 0618A] What does an adulteress ask except that she should wish for her husband’s death or that her unchastity should be concealed? What does a procuress ask except that she may strip many people of their property? What does a thief ask except that he may steal more?

Here, however, there is no room even for a slight and commonplace sin. If anyone comes to sacrifice without an unblemished conscience, he hears what God threatens against him—God who sees the hiding places of the heart, who is always hostile to sins, who demands justice, who requires faith. What room is there here for an evil intention or an evil prayer?

But those unhappy people do not understand even from their crimes how evil the object of their worship is. Although stained by every shameful deed, they come to pray and think that they sacrifice piously if they have washed their skin—as though any rivers could wash away the lusts enclosed within the breast, or any seas purify them. How much better it is instead to wash the mind, [Col. 0618B] which is defiled by evil desires, and to drive away every vice with the single cleansing of virtue and faith! Whoever has done this is sufficiently pure, however polluted and filthy the body he bears.

## CHAPTER XXI  
### On the Worship of the Gods and of the True God, and on the Beasts Worshiped by the Egyptians

But these people, because they do not know either what is to be worshiped or how it is to be worshiped, blindly and foolishly fall into the opposite error. And so they adore their enemies; they appease their robbers and murderers with victims; and they place upon detestable altars their own souls, to be burned together with the incense itself. In their incredible mental blindness, the wretched people are even angry [Col. 0619A] that others like them do not perish, [Col. 0619A] [Note: [Col. 0619B] [Various Notes on columns 619–620]

Alike. Heumann reads *simul et* (“at the same time also”).

They are angry with us. One old Bologna manuscript: “with the good.”

In whose power they have no confidence. “In” is absent from two Royal manuscripts; in the other recent manuscript the reading is “in whose power.”

When chastely. Slaying his opponents with their own sword, [Col. 0619C] he cites a law of the Twelve Tables from the second book of Cicero’s *On the Laws*, whose first provision is: “Approach the gods chastely.” He spoils a splendidly expressed matter by his prolix inflection.

Piety, etc. The second provision is: “Employ piety.” Piety is a disposition of the mind by which God is worshiped, in accordance with the saying: “God is spirit; therefore he must be worshiped in spirit and in truth.” BETULEIUS. See Cicero near the beginning of Book II of *On the Laws*.

Remove riches. This is the law’s third provision: “Remove riches.” It is taken, I think, from Plato’s *Second Alcibiades*, whose title is *Περὶ προσευχῆς* (*Peri proseuchēs*, “On Prayer”). Betuleius, however, thinks that in place of *facit* (“does”), the reading should be *faxit* (“shall do”), to preserve the majesty and style of the ancient laws.

God himself will be the avenger. Francius: perhaps “for that person himself.” One Clermont manuscript: “God will be his judge.”

If he cannot avenge his own. Thirteen MSS. and five editions: “who cannot avenge his own.”

Those whom they compel, etc. *Epitome*, chapter 53. Tertullian, *To Scapula*, chapter 2: “It is no part of religion to compel religion, which ought to be adopted voluntarily, not by force, since even sacrificial victims are required to be offered from a willing mind. Thus, even if you compel us to sacrifice, you will render no service to your gods, for they will not desire sacrifices from the unwilling unless they are contentious; but God is not contentious.” BUNEMANN.

It is not a benefit. Hence, conversely, the jurists say: “No injury is done to one who consents.”

Either destroy them in wretched ways. “Either” was added from the manuscripts and very many editions; it is absent from some.

Render them useless. Lactantius alludes to this in Book VI, chapter 11: “Give . . . to the disabled, the lame . . . they are useless to human beings but useful to God”; and below: “to feed the needy and useless.” BUNEMANN.

They perform. That is, they sacrifice. The verb occurs in this sense in Varro, *On the Latin Language*, Book V, chapter 4, and Virgil, *Eclogue* 3, verse 77.

To whom with tears. This should be read from the manuscripts and very many editions; *cum* (“with”) is absent from some printed editions.

Who is the God of all. That is, God, for “God” has just preceded. The word *creator* is therefore wrongly added in the Caucianus manuscript, two recent Royal manuscripts, the Cambridge manuscript, and eleven editions; it is absent from the rest.

Whether he wishes or not. Thus very many manuscripts, including the oldest and best—one Bologna, three Royal, five Oxford, three Leipzig, two Colbert, and others. Thirteen manuscripts and five editions have the plural, “whether they wish or not.” Bunemann also admits this latter reading and presents the following note.—I have adopted the plural from Caucianus, two Leipzig manuscripts, the third Gotha manuscript, Emman., Reimmann, the Venice edition of 1472, and both editions of 1478. On the subject, Tertullian, *Apologeticum* 23: “It is well that he is the God of all, to whom, whether we wish it or not, we all belong.” BUNEMANN.

As also. I added “also” from three commonly printed editions and all the manuscripts except two recent Royal manuscripts, in which it is absent, as it is in most editions.—As also of his servants. I add that “as also” is found in the Gotha manuscript, Reimmann, and Emman., and I confirm it as conforming to Lactantius’ style, so that Heumann can raise no objection. It occurs in *On the Wrath of God*, chapter 13: “All things set before the human being, both good things and also evil”; and *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 48: “Both I, Constantine Augustus, and also I, Licinius Augustus.” BUNEMANN.

Afflictions. That is, calamities.

We do not resist even with a word. *Epitome*, chapter 53. These words counter the slanders alleging that Christians conspired against the emperors. BUNEMANN.

But we leave it to God. *Remittimus* means “we reserve.” Book VI, chapter 8: “Let him not assume his own vengeance, but reserve it for God’s judgment.” BUNEMANN.

Who wish to appear defenders of their gods. Ten recent MSS. and the same number of editions add “that they are.”

Savage ferociously. All witnesses read thus. Nothing concerning this little word, not previously observed in older authors, appears in the dictionaries, Krebs’s dissertation, or Walch’s treatise. BUNEMANN.

Any worse. Correctly. See what follows. One Bologna manuscript has: “Rather more.”

Of the Egyptians. The superstition of the Egyptians is condemned not only by writers of Christian philosophy but also by the prophets. No one has written more fully about the animals worshiped as gods by the Egyptians than Herodotus in *Euterpe*. See also Philostratus, *Life of Apollonius*, Book VI, and Athenaeus, Book VII. Cicero also mentions it in the fifth book of the *Tusculan Disputations* and in Book I of *On the Nature of the Gods*, as does Lucian in the dialogue [Col. 0621A] *On Sacrifices*. See also Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book II, chapter 1.]

since what can those see who do not see the sun? As though, if those beings were gods, they would require human assistance against those who despise them.

Why, then, are these people angry with us if their gods can do nothing? It can only be because they themselves destroy their gods, in whose power they have no confidence, and are more irreligious than those who do not worship at all. Cicero, in his *Laws*, when prescribing that people approach sacrifices chastely, says: “Employ piety; remove riches. Whoever acts otherwise, God himself will be the avenger.” This is indeed correctly said. For it is wrong to despair of a God whom you worship precisely because you regard him as powerful. How can he avenge an injury done to his worshiper if he cannot avenge his own?

I should therefore like to ask these people whom they think they chiefly benefit by compelling the unwilling [Col. 0619B] to sacrifice. Do they benefit those whom they compel? But what is forced upon someone who refuses it is no benefit. “Yet one must provide even for those who are unwilling, since they do not know what is good.” Why, then, do they harass, torture, and maim them so cruelly if they wish them to be safe? Or whence comes a piety so impious that they either destroy in wretched ways or render useless the very people whose welfare they claim to desire?

Do they, then, benefit the gods? But what is extorted [Col. 0620A] from an unwilling person is no sacrifice. Unless it is performed voluntarily and sincerely, it is a curse, as when people driven by proscription, injuries, imprisonment, and torture perform sacrifices. If those who are worshiped in this manner are gods, they ought not to be worshiped for this reason alone: that they wish to be worshiped in such a manner. They are plainly deserving of human detestation, since libations are offered to them with tears, groaning, and blood flowing from every limb.

We, by contrast, do not demand that anyone unwillingly worship our God, who is the God of all, whether one wishes it or not; nor are we angry if someone does not worship him. For we trust in his majesty, which is able to avenge both contempt for himself and also the afflictions and injuries of his servants. And therefore, although we suffer such unspeakable things, we do not resist even with a word, but leave vengeance to God. We do not act as those who wish [Col. 0620B] to appear defenders of their gods and who rage with savage ferocity against those who do not worship them.

From this one may understand how far the worship of the gods is from being good. For people ought to have been brought to good by good, not by evil. But because the object itself is evil, its service also lacks good. “Yet those who destroy religions must be punished.” Do we destroy them any worse than the Egyptian nation, who worship the most shameful forms of wild and domestic animals, [Col. 0620D] [Note: [Col. 0621A] [Various Notes on columns 621–622]

Who worship the most shameful forms of wild and domestic animals. There were two corresponding cults among the Egyptians: one called Mnevis and practiced by the Heliopolitans; the other regarded Apis as divine and was practiced by the Memphites. So Plutarch in his book *On Isis and Osiris*. Tibullus means Apis when he says in Book I, Elegy 7:

> The barbarian race sings of you and marvels at its Osiris,  
> Trained to mourn the bull of Memphis.

For he calls him “the bull of Memphis” *διακριτικῶς* (*diakritikōs*, “by way of distinction”), differentiating him from the bull worshiped at Heliopolis under the name Mnevis. Cicero also writes of Apis in Book I of *On the Nature of the Gods*: “What, then, do you think? Does not that Apis, the sacred bull of the Egyptians, appear to the Egyptians to be a god?” Likewise Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 46: “In Egypt a bull is worshiped even in place of a divinity; they call him Apis.” And shortly afterward: “There are twin shrines for him, which they call chambers and which serve as omens for the peoples. His entering one is a joyful sign; in the other he portends calamity.”

Pseudo-Clement of Rome, *Recognitions* V: “Some Egyptians taught that the bull called Apis was to be worshiped.” Apis is also mentioned by Clement of Alexandria in the *Exhortation to the Nations*; Mela, *Description of the World*, Book I, [Col. 0621C] chapter 19; Solinus, chapter 35; Lucian in *The Council of the Gods* and *On Sacrifices*; Spartianus in his *Hadrian*; Diodorus Siculus, Book I; and Aelian, *On Animals*, Book XI, chapter 10, and elsewhere.

Under the form of the bull, however, the Egyptians worshiped the sun. Macrobius, Book I, chapter 21: “That the bull is associated with the sun is shown in many ways by Egyptian worship: either because at Heliopolis they especially worship the bull consecrated to the Sun, whom they surname Neton, or because in the city of Memphis the bull Apis is received as an image of the Sun.” There, in place of *Neton*, I think we should read *Mnevis*, as he is called by other authors; this is undoubtedly the true reading. After writing this, I happened upon a passage in the distinguished Selden’s *Syntagma* I, *On the Syrian Gods*, where I see that he had already noted that *Mnevis* should be restored in Macrobius.

Aelian, however, says in *History of Animals* XI.11 that Apis was not a symbol of the sun but of the moon, and that, just as the Heliopolitans consecrated their bull to the sun, so the Memphites consecrated theirs to the moon. Some of the ancients hold that the golden calf which the Israelites erected and worshiped in the wilderness derived its origin from this Egyptian Apis. Thus [Col. 0621D] Lactantius, Book IV, chapter 10: “Having fallen into luxury, they turned their minds toward the profane rites of the Egyptians. For when Moses, their leader, had ascended the mountain and remained there for forty days, they fashioned a golden head of the Bull whom they call Apis, to go before them as a standard.”

The same tradition is also given concerning Jeroboam’s calves, discussed in I—or III—Kings 12:28, by St. Ambrose, or some other author, in the commentary on Romans 1. St. Jerome likewise takes the same view of both in his commentary on Hosea 4: “It therefore seems to me,” he says, “that the people of Israel made for themselves in the wilderness the head of a calf to worship, and that Jeroboam son of Nebat fashioned golden calves, so that what they had learned in Egypt—namely, that *Ἄπιν καὶ Μνεῦιν* (*Apin kai Mneuin*, ‘Apis and Mnevis’), worshiped under the form of bulls, were gods—they might preserve in their own superstition.”

We know, however, that the worship of certain animals was common to all Egyptians, while that of others was observed only in particular cities. We shall add some remarks on each.

After the bull, whose worship we have already discussed, Strabo adds the dog. Cicero also speaks of its veneration in Book V of the *Tusculan Disputations*: “Who does not know the custom of the Egyptians? Their minds are steeped in pernicious errors, and they would undergo any torture rather than harm an ibis, an asp, a cat, a dog, or a crocodile.” He also mentions the veneration of the dog [Col. 0622B] in Book I of *On the Laws*, as do Plutarch in *On Isis and Osiris* and Juvenal, Satire 15:

> There whole cities worship the dog, but no one Diana.

Clement of Alexandria also mentions it in his *Protrepticus* (“Exhortation”), indicating that the dog was worshiped especially by the Cynopolitans: *Κυνοπολῖται δὲ (σέβουσι) κύνα* (*Kynopolitai de [sebousi] kyna*), “The people of Cynopolis [worship] the dog.”

Herodotus in *Euterpe* and Diodorus Siculus, Book II, also discuss the worship of the dog. They add that Egyptians in whose homes a dog died customarily shaved the entire body as a sign of mourning.

They also venerated the cat with the highest worship. On this subject, besides Herodotus and Plutarch, see Cicero, *On the Laws* I; *Tusculan Disputations* V.78; and *On the Nature of the Gods* I: “It has never even been reported that a crocodile, ibis, or cat was harmed by an Egyptian.” Juvenal likewise says in Satire 15:

> There they worship cats; here, a river fish . . .  
> . . . they worship.

[Col. 0622C] For *aeluros* (“cats”) should be read there, not *coeruleos* (“blue ones”), as in the commonly printed editions, a point excellently noted by Brodaeus, *Miscellanies* VII.2.

Diodorus Siculus, *Historical Library* I, also gives the reason for this worship: the cat is useful against the bites of asps and other serpents. Plutarch also mentions the worship of the cat in *Table Talk* IV, question 5. So does Pseudo-Clement of Rome in *Recognitions* V, in a passage already cited in part above: “Some Egyptians taught that the bull called Apis was to be worshiped, others the goat, and others cats.”

By *gattas* he plainly means cats, or *aeluri*. For that was how people spoke at the time: they called cats *gattae* or *cattae*. Hence the gloss: “*Catta*: *αἴλουρος* (*ailouros*, ‘cat’).” And other glosses: “*Κάττα, Catta*.” The scholiast on Callimachus likewise says that *αἴλουροι* (*ailouroi*), or cats, were popularly called *κάτται* (*kattai*). Evagrius, Book VI, chapter 24, similarly uses the word *catii*. The author of the *History of Barlaam* also uses it when treating Egyptian superstitions: “Some of them,” he says, “worshiped a sheep; some a goat; others a calf and a pig; some a raven, [Col. 0622D] a hawk, a vulture, and an eagle. Others worshiped a crocodile; some a cat, a dog, a wolf, an ape, a dragon, and an asp; others onions, garlic, and thorns.”

Moreover, in the cited book of Herodotus we read that, upon the death of a cat, the Egyptians did not shave their entire bodies, as at the death of a dog, but only their eyebrows. He then adds that dead cats were customarily salted and carried in that state to Bubastis, where they were buried.

About whom mimes are even performed. Thus nearly all the manuscripts, together with four editions. Two recent Royal manuscripts, one Colbert manuscript corrected by a second hand, the Cambridge manuscript, and eleven commonly printed editions have: “to be performed through mimes.”—Mimes to be performed. Here *mimi* are not the actors themselves but the plays; and “to perform mimes” is a familiar expression, restored by me also in the *Epitome*, chapter 55. On the matter itself, Augustine, *The City of God* IV.26: “In theatrical games . . . the crimes of the divinities are repeatedly displayed.” BUNEMANN.

To have arisen spontaneously. Thus the old editions of the fifteenth century; many others omit “to have.”

By chance. Thus the better and far more numerous manuscripts, including six Royal and four Colbert manuscripts, and the printed editions. Nine manuscripts, eight of them very recent, have *fortuito*. But *fortuitu* occurs in Lactantius himself, Book I, chapter 2, and Book VII, chapter 9; in Cicero, *Philippic* X.2; *Letters to Atticus* X.6; *On Duties* I.103; and *Rhetoric to Herennius* II.16.]
[Col. 0621A] even worship as gods certain things shameful to mention? Is this any worse than what those very same people do? For although they say that they worship the gods, they nevertheless publicly and disgracefully ridicule them, and permit even mimes about them to be performed amid laughter and pleasure. What sort of religion, or how great a majesty, must that be thought to possess, which is adored in temples and mocked in theaters? And those who have done these things do not pay the penalty for violating the divine power, but depart honored and even praised. Do we [Col. 0622A] destroy religion any worse than certain philosophers who say that there are no gods at all, but that everything arose of its own accord and that everything which happens occurs by chance? Any worse than the Epicureans, who indeed say that gods exist, but deny that they care about anything, that they become angry, or that they are moved by favor? By these assertions they assuredly persuade men that the gods are not to be worshiped at all, since they neither regard those who worship them nor become angry with those who do not. Moreover, [Col. 0623A] when they argue against fear [Col. 0633A]

MSS. and Jun., *expelluntur* (“are expelled”); one Reg., *exultantur*; one Reg. and Marm., *exultant* (“exult”); what worse reading could be proposed? For I remember reading this word in the ancient Fathers when they discuss the power of exorcisms; among them Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*: “Yet demons, when adjured by us through the true God, immediately yield, confess, and are compelled to depart from the bodies they possess. they attempt to accomplish nothing other than that no one should fear the gods. And yet such things are both gladly heard and discussed by men without punishment.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Fury of the Demons against Christians, and the Error of Unbelievers

They do not therefore rage against us because the gods are not worshiped by us, but because the truth is in our possession, and truth—as has been most truly said—produces hatred. What, then, are we to suppose, except that those men do not know what they are suffering? For they proceed in blind and irrational fury; we see that fury, but they do not recognize it. It is not the men themselves who persecute us, for they have no reason to be angry with innocent people; [Col. 0623B] rather, those polluted and ruined spirits, to whom the truth is both known and hateful, insinuate themselves into their minds and incite the ignorant to fury. For as long as there is peace among God’s people, these spirits flee from the righteous and are afraid; and when they take possession of human bodies and torment their souls, they are adjured by the righteous and put to flight by the name of the true God. On hearing it, they tremble and cry out, and testify that they are being burned and beaten; and when questioned as to who they are, when they came, and how they crept into the person, they confess. Thus, wrenched out and racked by the power of the divine name, they are released. Because of these blows and threats, they have always hated holy and righteous men. And because they can do them no harm by themselves, they persecute through public hatred those whom they perceive to be burdensome to them; and they exercise their savagery as violently as they can, either to diminish their [Col. 0623C] faith through pain or, if they cannot accomplish that, to remove them altogether from the earth, so that there may be no one capable of restraining their wickedness. [Col. 0624A]

I am not unaware of what may be answered on the other side: Why, then, does that one and supreme God, that great God whom you acknowledge as sovereign over the universe and Lord of all, permit these things to happen, and neither avenge nor protect his worshipers? Why, finally, are those who do not worship him wealthy, powerful, and prosperous, and why do they possess offices and kingdoms, and hold those very worshipers subject to their own dominion and power?

An explanation of this matter too must be given, lest any error remain. For the principal reason why the religion of God is thought to possess no power is that men are beguiled by the appearance of earthly and present goods, which in no way pertain to the welfare of the mind. Because they see the righteous lacking these goods and the unrighteous abounding in them, they suppose the worship of God to be empty, since they do not perceive those goods to be contained in it; and they regard the rites of the gods as true because their worshipers enjoy riches, honors, and kingdoms. [Col. 0624B]

But those who hold this opinion do not look more deeply into the power and nature of man, which lies wholly not in the body but in the mind. For they see nothing beyond what is visible, namely the body; because it can be handled by the eyes and the hand, it is feeble, fragile, and mortal. To it belong all those goods that are objects of desire and wonder—wealth, honors, and dominions—because they bring pleasures to the body; and therefore they are as perishable as the body itself. But the mind, in which alone the human being consists, is not subject to the eyes, nor can its goods be inspected; these are situated in virtue alone. Therefore the mind must necessarily be as stable, constant, and everlasting [Col. 0624C] as virtue itself, in which the good of the mind resides.

[Col. 0625A]

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the Righteousness and Patience of Christians

It would take too long to set forth all the forms of virtue, [Col. 0625A]

> **Is subject.** Some place within brackets the addition: “Desire to dominate free men, because he has no self-restraint,” a fragment. But those words are rejected by the Bon., Tax., Pen., Pal., Jun., Angl., Lips., and Reimm. manuscripts, and by the editions of 1645, 1524, and those of Gymn., Thomas., Isaeus, Gall., Spark., and the rest. BUN.
>
> **Because all those things are human.** In a great many MSS. and seven common editions, “are” is added; it is absent from three very old MSS. and eight editions.
>

What kingdoms? He regards those things as human, but judges his own goods to be divine”; and below: “What virtue, if it judges its own goods to be divine?” BUN.

Eleven recent MSS. read, “And from this is added the fact that”; two recent Reg. MSS. and six printed editions likewise read, “And from this is added the fact that”; one Bon. MS. and three common editions read, “There is added the fact that”; one recent Reg. MS., “Let there be added the fact that.”
>

MSS. read: “That is, no arrogance”; one Reg., Jun., and four old editions read: “and no arrogance”; six MSS. and four common editions read “fear” (*timoris*), wrongly. For there is an antithesis with the preceding passage, where he had said that the impatient man “swells insolently with an exalted spirit.”

He does not even desire it. Hence he said of the same man above: “Nor does he covet anything belonging to another”; and Book VI, chapter 24: “Let him seek absolutely nothing, covet nothing belonging to another.” BUN.

See above: “the righteous man must be subject to the unrighteous”; and below: “For this reason he wished them to live under another’s dominion and rule... he wished them to be oppressed by those into whose hands he had placed them.” But Bunemann accepts the second reading and defends it as follows:
>
> [Col. 0627B] “**And the latter has virtue within himself.** He has just said, ‘The righteous man must be subject to the unrighteous’; to what purpose would he say again that the righteous man goes into servitude because he is righteous? By contrast, if you read, ‘has virtue within himself,’ there is a proper opposition between sin and virtue. Thus the righteous and wise man, because he acquires virtue, ‘has patience within himself.’ The phrase occurs in Book V, chapter 10: ‘Can anyone suppose that this man possessed any virtue within himself?’” [Col. 0627C]

so as to teach concerning each one how necessary it is for a wise and righteous man to shrink far from those goods which, because the unrighteous enjoy them, cause the worship of the gods to be believed true and efficacious. For the present question, it is enough if we prove from one virtue what we intend.

Patience, certainly, is a great and preeminent virtue, which alike the public declarations of the common people, philosophers, and orators celebrate with the highest praises. But if it cannot be denied that patience is the highest virtue, the righteous and wise man must necessarily be in the power [Col. 0625B] of an unrighteous man, so that he may acquire patience. For patience is the endurance with equanimity of evils either inflicted upon us or befalling us. Therefore the righteous and wise man, because he acquires virtue, has patience within himself; but he will lack it altogether if he suffers nothing adverse. By contrast, one who lives amid prosperity is impatient and lacks the greatest virtue. I call him “impatient” because he suffers nothing.

Nor can he preserve innocence, which is itself a virtue proper to the righteous and wise man. Rather, he often does harm, covets what belongs to others, and seizes by injury what he has desired; because, being devoid of virtue, he is subject to vice and sin, and, forgetful of his frailty, swells insolently with an exalted spirit.

Hence the unrighteous and those ignorant of God flourish in riches, [Col. 0625C] power, and honors. For all these things are the rewards of unrighteousness, [Col. 0626A] because they cannot be everlasting and are sought through greed and violence. But the righteous and wise man, because all those things are human, as Laelius said, judges his own goods to be divine. He does not covet anything belonging to another, lest he violate anyone contrary to the law of humanity; nor does he desire any power or honor, lest he injure anyone. For he knows that all, begotten by the same God and under the same condition, are united by the law of brotherhood.

He is also content with what is his own, and with little, because, mindful of his frailty, he seeks no more than that by which he may sustain life; and even from what he possesses he shares with one who has nothing, because he is dutiful—and dutifulness is the highest virtue. To this is added the fact that he despises perishable and vicious pleasures, for whose sake wealth [Col. 0626B] is sought, because he is self-controlled and a conqueror of passions. Likewise, bearing no arrogance or insolence, he does not raise himself too high or lift a proud head, but is gentle, harmonious, gracious, and unassuming, because he knows his condition.

Since, therefore, he injures no one, does not desire what belongs to another, and does not even defend his own possessions if they are taken from him by force; since he knows how to bear with moderation even an injury inflicted upon him, because he is endowed with virtue—it is necessary that the righteous man be subject to the unrighteous, and the wise man be treated with contempt by the foolish, so that the former may sin because he is unrighteous, and the latter go into servitude because he is righteous.

But if anyone wishes to know more fully why God permits the wicked and unrighteous to become powerful, prosperous, and rich, [Col. 0626C] while permitting the dutiful, by contrast, to be humble, wretched, and poor, [Col. 0627A] let him take up that book of Seneca entitled *Why Many Evils Befall Good Men, Although Providence Exists*, [Col. 0627A]

in which he expressed many things, not with the ignorance of a merely secular writer, but wisely and almost divinely:

> “God,” he says, “regards human beings as his children; but he permits the corrupt and vicious to live luxuriously and delicately, because he does not consider them worthy of his correction. The good, however, whom he loves, he corrects more frequently and trains for the exercise of virtue by continual hardships; nor does he allow them to be corrupted and depraved by perishable and mortal goods.”

Hence it ought to seem surprising to no one if we are often corrected by God for our offenses. Indeed, when we are harassed and oppressed, then especially do we give thanks to our most indulgent Father, because he does not permit our corruption to proceed farther, but corrects us with wounds and blows. From this we understand [Col. 0627B] that God cares for us, because when we sin, he becomes angry.

For although he could have bestowed both riches and kingdoms upon his people, as he had formerly given them to the Jews, whose successors and descendants we are, for this very reason he wished his people to live under another’s dominion and rule: lest, corrupted by the prosperity of favorable circumstances, they should fall into luxury and despise God’s commandments, as did those ancestors of ours, who, often enervated by these earthly and fragile goods, strayed from discipline and broke the bonds [Col. 0628A] of the law.

God therefore made provision to grant peace to his worshipers so long as they kept his commands, and yet to correct them if they did not obey his precepts. And so, lest they be as corrupted by ease as their fathers had been by license, he wished them to be oppressed by those into whose hands he had placed them, so that he might strengthen those who were wavering, restore the corrupted to fortitude, and test and try the faithful. For how can a commander prove the courage of his soldiers unless he has an enemy? Yet an adversary rises against a human commander contrary to his will, both because he is mortal and because he can be defeated. But because God cannot be resisted, he himself raises up adversaries against his own name—not to fight against God himself, but against his soldiers—so that he may either test or strengthen the devotion and faith of his own people, until by the blows of affliction [Col. 0628B] he binds together their lax discipline.

There is also another reason why he permits persecutions against us: so that the people of God may increase. Nor is it difficult to show why or how this occurs. First, very many are driven away from the worship of the gods by hatred of its cruelty. For who would not shudder at such sacrifices? Next, some are pleased by virtue and faith themselves. Some suspect that the worship of the gods is not without reason regarded as evil by so many people that they would rather die than do what others do in order to live.
