what that good is which is defended even unto death; which is preferred to everything pleasant and dear in this life; from which neither the loss of possessions, nor the loss of light, nor bodily pain, nor the torments of the entrails can deter them. These things possess very great force. But the following causes have especially always increased our number.

The surrounding populace hears them saying amid the very tortures that they do not sacrifice to stones made by human hands, but to the living God who is in heaven. Many understand this to be true and admit it into their hearts. Then, as usually happens in uncertain matters, while they ask one another what the cause of such perseverance may be, many things pertaining to religion are circulated and learned through reports gathered in turn; and because these things are good, [Col. 0629B] they must necessarily be pleasing.

Moreover, the vengeance that followed, as always happens, powerfully impels them to believe. Nor is this a trivial cause: the unclean spirits of demons, once permission has been received, plunge themselves into the bodies of many; and after they have subsequently been cast out, all who have been healed adhere to the religion whose power they have experienced. All these causes, brought together, wonderfully acquire a great multitude for God.

[Col. 0630A]

## CHAPTER XXIV. On Divine Vengeance against the Torturers of Christians

Whatever evil rulers devise against us, God himself permits to happen. Yet the most unrighteous persecutors, to whom the name of God has been an object of contempt and mockery, must not suppose that they will escape punishment because they served, as it were, as ministers of his indignation against us. For they will be punished by God’s judgment: having received power, they abused it beyond the measure proper to humanity, insolently insulted even God, and impiously and wickedly cast down his eternal name beneath their feet to be trampled.

For this reason he promises that he will swiftly avenge himself upon them and exterminate the evil beasts from the earth. Yet the same God, although he is accustomed to avenge the harassments of his people even here in the present, nevertheless commands us to await patiently that day of heavenly judgment, [Col. 0630B] when he himself will either honor or punish each person according to his deserts.

Therefore sacrilegious souls must not hope that those whom they thus crush will remain despised and unavenged. There will come—there will come—to the rabid and ravenous wolves their due reward, because they tortured righteous and innocent souls who had committed no crimes. Let us labor only so that nothing else in us may be punished by men except righteousness alone. Let us strive with all our strength to deserve from God both vengeance for our suffering and its reward.

# [THE SIXTH BOOK OF LACTANTIUS]

[Col. 0629]

## ANALYSIS OF THE SIXTH BOOK, ON TRUE WORSHIP

Thus far we have spoken about the knowledge of God. I shall now teach by what rite or by what sacrifice God ought to be worshiped.

The worship of God is either false or true. The false worship is that of the pagans, who judge that whatever is rare in appearance, whatever is costly in workmanship [Col. 0631A] or fragrance, is pleasing to their gods (Chapter 1).

Accordingly, they slaughter fat victims for them as though they were hungry; pour out wines as though they were thirsty; and kindle lights as though they lived in darkness.

True worship is that in which the worshiper’s mind presents itself to God as an undefiled victim. This subject must now be treated in such a way that, while the philosophers’ precepts concerning uprightness remain in place, we build upon them the precepts of dutifulness and righteousness (Chapter 2).

Just as worship is twofold, so too is the road along which human life must proceed: one road that carries upward into heaven, and another that presses downward to the lower regions.

The philosophers wished the one to be the road of the virtues and the other of the vices; the former, indeed, to be arduous at its first approach but pleasant at the summit; the latter, by contrast, to be pleasant at its first entrance but rugged over the remaining distance. This, indeed, they taught wisely—if only they had known the forms of the virtues, if only they had known the limits of the virtues.

The poets wished this fork in the road to be in the lower regions; [Col. 0631B] in this they are mistaken, because they set those roads before the dead.

We therefore say more correctly that those two roads lead respectively to heaven and the lower regions, because immortality has been set before the righteous and eternal punishment before the unrighteous. This is also the reason why we explain these roads in a far different manner from the philosophers (Chapter 3).

There is, therefore, one road of virtue, which leads to heaven and is difficult and steep. Upon this road God placed righteousness, self-restraint, patience, faith, and the other virtues; but together with them poverty, disgrace, hardship, and so forth.

There is also one road on the left, which sends a person to Orcus. Its appearance seems level, open, and delightful with every kind of flower. On it have been placed wealth, honor, rest, pleasure, and every enticement; but together with these, unrighteousness, cruelty, pride, faithlessness, lust, and the other vices.

If anyone patiently treads the former road, he is rewarded with the crown of virtue—that is, immortality. If anyone travels the latter, he is cast down to the lower regions. On the former, temporal evils are presented first, together with eternal goods; on the latter, temporal goods are presented first, together with eternal evils.

It is therefore better to balance brief evils against everlasting goods [Col. 0631C] than to endure everlasting evils for the sake of brief and perishable goods. We labor in this world and contend with our enemies so that afterward we may be at rest. With great labor we obtain for ourselves things which can once again perish. Therefore we must contend against our spiritual enemy, and no labor by which we may obtain what can in no way be lost must be refused—especially since God wishes us always to stand ready for battle, while our enemy ensnares us by various arts, raging against each person according to his nature and character.

The philosophers did indeed seek the road of virtue, but they did not find it, since they could neither define virtue nor understand what good and evil are.

Lucilius defined virtue as knowledge of good and evil. This was false, for knowledge cannot be virtue, because it is not within us but comes to us from outside, and can exist without virtue, as it did in a great many philosophers.

Horace described virtue as flight from the vices. This was foolish, because he defined it by its contrary (Chapter 5).

[Col. 0631D] They did not know what good and evil are because they knew neither God, the author of good things, nor the adversary of the human race, the author of evils. Consequently, they referred the end of good things to this brief life. This is evident from Lucilius, who located virtue in seeking those things in the contempt of which the power of virtue is revealed, and who thinks it a virtue to extend the borders of one’s native land, although such extension is joined with the greatest unrighteousness. Cicero himself admits that the Romans possess no firm and express image of true law and genuine righteousness (Chapter 6).

There were indeed some who were regarded and called wise; [Col. 0632A] but even these bore only the likeness and appearance of wise men. For just as the road of wisdom has something resembling foolishness, so the road of the vices, although it is wholly foolishness, has something resembling wisdom; and this is what those who perceive the foolishness of the public seize upon. These are the arts of the devil: after displaying to human beings an appearance of truth and goodness, he leads them by various paths to the same death (Chapter 7).

The reason why the philosophers did not find the road of truth and virtue is that they sought it on earth, where it cannot appear. But the law of God has been revealed to us, and, just as the stars shine by night for sailors, it shines before us upon the road of wisdom.

That law is right reason, consonant with nature, diffused among all, constant and everlasting; it summons to duty by commanding, and, by forbidding, deters from fraud—as Cicero portrayed it splendidly in Book III of *On the Republic*.

Some principles of this law are primary and others secondary. The primary principles are two: one concerning dutifulness toward God, the other concerning humanity (Chapter 8).

[Col. 0632B] Dutifulness toward God consists in knowing and worshiping God. Ignorance of this God causes a human being to serve foreign gods; to embrace the laws of his own nation as though they were true law, although expediency rather than righteousness devised them; and consequently causes all the virtues of the pagans to resemble a body without a head.

Whoever, therefore, has not acknowledged God is impious; and all his virtues are found upon that death-bearing road which consists wholly of darkness. Likewise, the person who, once the hope of immortality—which God promises to those engaged in his religion—has been taken away, seeks virtue for its own sake and undergoes dangers of every kind is insane.

By contrast, the wise man is one who knows God and attends upon him with the dutifulness that is his due (Chapter 9).

Humanity is the virtue that unites us with another human being; it is also called mercy. This virtue is most worthy of a human being: because we all arise from one human being and therefore are blood relatives; because God likewise commands that hostilities must never be initiated by us and must always be ended; and, finally, because we have all been inspired and given life by one God.

The opposite of humanity is savagery, or bestial inhumanity, which, contrary to the law of humanity, [Col. 0632C] despoils, tortures, kills, and exterminates human beings.

Therefore the philosophers who removed compassion from humanity are mistaken. First, they contradict themselves, for they teach that the fellowship of human society must be maintained, and yet exclude humanity itself from the human being. Next, human beings were brought together either so that they might protect their weakness through mutual assistance, or for the sake of humanity itself. If the former is true, then aid must be given to a person who needs help. But if the latter is true, one human being certainly ought to acknowledge another as such. And if those primitive and savage human beings did this, then surely people who have been civilized and accustomed to human society ought much more to do so (Chapter 10). Whoever does not do this strips himself of the designation “human.” Moreover, if they concede that it belongs to humanity to give aid in those circumstances that bring danger to a person’s life, there is no reason why they should not think aid must also be given when a person is hungry, thirsty, or cold.

Cicero too is mistaken when, in his books *On Duties*, he advises that one should not be generous without qualification; restraining [Col. 0632D] people from humanity, he admonishes them to guard their household property carefully and to prefer preserving their strongbox rather than justice.

He is likewise mistaken in writing that one’s household resources should be shared with **suitable** persons, because he measures the duties of humanity by utility; whereas generosity should be shown not to suitable persons—that is, those capable of returning a favor—but to those who are not suitable. He also contradicts himself, for in many passages he proclaims that virtue is not mercenary. From this it is easy to conclude that, if virtue is to be sought for its own sake, justice must be valued not according to our advantage but according to its own worth. I pass over the fact that these men, because they neither preserve the natural order nor understand the reward [Col. 0633A] inherent in what is done, lose while they fear to lose: whether they squander their patrimonies, spend their wealth on presenting public entertainments, seek remembrance for their name by erecting public works, or, finally, distribute gifts to members of their tribe or to their clients (Chapter 11).

The branches of humanity are hospitality, the redemption of captives, the protection of widows, the care of the sick, and the burial of strangers and the poor.

Hospitality is a pre-eminent virtue commanded by God. Yet Cicero again erred concerning it, for he wished our houses to stand open to distinguished guests. Our houses, however, ought to stand open to the humble and the outcast.

The redemption of captives is likewise a work proper to the just and is to be preferred by far to the lavish distribution of gifts.

The protection of orphans and widows has been entrusted to everyone by divine law.

He who cares for and comforts the sick acquires a living sacrifice for God; and what he gives to another for a time, he himself will receive from God for eternity.

[Col. 0633B] The burial of strangers and the poor is also a very great duty of piety. The philosophers did not address it at all.

The question is asked here whether everything ought to be bestowed upon the needy.

**Answer.** It is good not to fear poverty; and one who is rich before God can never be poor. Next, each person ought to practice justice according to his ability, so that, to the same degree that he surpasses others in wealth, he may also surpass them in deeds (Chapter 12).

Generosity, therefore, must be practiced, because sins are removed through giving, and no one can be without fault so long as he is burdened with the garment of flesh (Chapter 13).

From this it is clear how far the Stoic philosophers were removed from human goodness, since they always regarded this virtue—I mean compassion—as a vice. By removing the vices, they removed the virtues themselves, and through imprudence eventually fell back into the very position at which the Peripatetics arrive by reasoning: because vices cannot be removed, they must be moderated (Chapters 14 and 15).

[Col. 0633C] Yet the Peripatetics themselves also erred when they conceded that these were vices but tempered them to a moderate degree; for even moderate vices must be avoided, and it must be shown that it is not the emotions themselves but their causes that must be moderated (Chapter 16).

[Col. 0634A] If fear and desire are cast down toward earthly things, they become vices; but if they are directed toward divine things, they become virtues. These emotions, therefore, must neither be uprooted, as the Stoics maintain, nor moderated, as the Peripatetics wish, but directed onto the true path (Chapter 17).

The secondary precepts of the law are these: that a worshiper of God should never lie; that, if he has lent any money, he should not take interest; that he should not accept a gift from a poor person; that he should answer one who speaks ill of him with a good word; that he should not make an enemy through his own fault; and that he should not avenge an injury inflicted upon him.

Cicero therefore gives a poor definition of the good man as one who benefits everyone and harms no one unless provoked by an injury. For if he harms another when provoked, by that very fact he loses the name of a good man, since harming another is not in accordance with human nature. If he harms another, he is not innocent and not patient. And Cicero himself, contrary to his own precept, placed the forgetting of injuries among the highest objects of praise (Chapter 18).

The Peripatetics also err when they say that anger is the companion [Col. 0634B] of virtue. So too do the poets, who said that there were three Furies: Anger, Desire, and Lust. For God has set definite limits upon these emotions; only when they transgress those limits are they transformed into diseases and vices (Chapter 19).

Finally, the worshiper of God must overcome and suppress by virtue the pleasures of the five senses: namely, the pleasure of the eyes, by not attending public spectacles or stage performances (Chapter 20); the pleasure of the ears, by not delighting himself in the sweetness of songs (Chapter 21); the pleasure of taste and smell, by not serving the belly and gluttony (Chapter 22); and the pleasure of touch, by curbing lust or restraining it through marriage, not through fornication or adultery, whether in deed or in thought (Chapter 23).

But if anyone has slipped onto the path of injustice, let him not despair of himself; rather, having turned toward better things, let him make satisfaction to God, to whom even our innermost thoughts [Col. 0634C] lie open (Chapter 24).

If, moreover, the worshiper of God wishes to sacrifice, he will offer God two incorporeal things: integrity of mind and praise of the divine name. For God created us to receive these things; Hermes Trismegistus taught that these gifts should be offered to God (Chapter 25). **SCULTETUS.**

[Col. 0633]

# BOOK SIX: ON TRUE WORSHIP

[Col. 0633D] ## CHAPTER ONE  
### On the worship of the true God and innocence, and on the worship of false gods

With the divine Spirit instructing me and truth itself supporting me, I have completed the duty involved in the undertaking I assumed. The responsibility for defending and illuminating that truth [Col. 0634D] was imposed upon me by my conscience, my faith, and our Lord himself.

[Col. 0634D] **[Note: [Col. 0633D] Variorum Notes on Columns 633–634]**

**“The responsibility for defending and illuminating that truth was imposed upon me by my conscience, my faith, and our Lord himself.”** I have restored the text in this form from one very ancient Royal manuscript, one other Royal manuscript of excellent quality, and two Brun. manuscripts, with the support of the first Lips. manuscript, which has *conscientiam*; likewise the manuscripts two Reg., two Claromont., Bodl., Cotton., one Sorbon., one Colbert., and Walch’s edition, except that they have *scientia*. Two Reg., three Oxon., one Colb., and eight printed editions read: “the responsibility upon me, and knowledge and faith,” etc. Four Colb., Em., Cant., Got., Marm., and the editions Rome 1474, Parr., and Cellar. read: “the responsibility upon me, and knowledge, and faith the Lord himself,” [Col. 0634D] etc. In Jun. and the first Clarom., *God* stands for *Lord*, with the earlier occurrence of *himself* deleted. “To illuminate the truth” is a familiar expression in Lactantius: *Divine Institutes*, Book I, chapter 1, twice, and chapter 2; Book IV, chapter 5; Book VI, chapter 1; Book VII, chapter 7; and *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 20. In Bunemann the text reads: “And knowledge and faith the Lord himself.” — **WALCH.**

“The responsibility upon me both knowledge and faith and the Lord himself.” Book III, chapter 13: “For defending which—the goodness of the cause—knowledge of divinity and truth itself suffice.” **BUN.**

**[End of note]**

Without him nothing can be known or explained. I now come to what is the highest and greatest part of this work: to teach by what rite and by what sacrifice God ought to be worshiped. For this is the duty of the human being, and in this alone consist the supreme principle of all things and the whole rationale of a blessed life; since for this purpose [Col. 0635A] we were fashioned—

[Col. 0635A] **[Note: [Col. 0635B] Variorum Notes on Columns 635–636]**

**Fashioned.** The manuscripts two Reg. rec., Jun., Tornes., Pal., and five early editions read *made*.

**Anaxagoras.** He was discussed above, Book III, chapters 9 and 23.

**And the God of heaven.** One ancient Bonon. manuscript reads: “and the Lord of heaven.”

**I defended.** Nine manuscripts read: “we defended”; the Paris and Graph. editions read: “I would defend.”

**“For that holy and unique majesty desires nothing else from a human being but innocence alone.”** This is not because an outward sacrifice also is not highly acceptable to God; rather, the ancient Fathers repeatedly impressed these things upon the ears of the pagans, who, though covered with every crime, considered themselves religious if they stained temples and altars with the blood of victims, as though God needed sacrificial animals. But concerning the most holy sacrifice of the Eucharist instituted by Christ the Lord—which we call the Mass, and which heretics quite rashly defame on the basis of this and other passages of the same kind—see the testimonies of the most ancient Fathers: Ignatius, a contemporary of Christ and disciple of the Apostles, Epistle 10; Epistle 9 to the Philadelphians; Epistle 14 to the Ephesians; Epistle 15 to the Romans. Irenaeus, the disciple of Polycarp, who was a hearer of John the Apostle, Book IV, chapter 32, where he says: “He took bread from creation, gave thanks, and said, ‘This is my body’; and similarly the cup, which comes from that creation to which we belong, he acknowledged as his blood, and taught the new offering of the New Testament, which the Church, receiving it from the Apostles, offers to God throughout the whole world.” And chapter 34: “Therefore the Church’s offering, which the Lord taught to be offered throughout the whole world, has been reckoned a pure sacrifice before God and is acceptable to him.” Likewise Tertullian, Book II *To His Wife*, *On Monogamy*, *On the Soldier’s Crown*, *On Prayer*, *On Chastity*, *On the Dress of Women*, Book I *Against Marcion*, and often elsewhere; Cyprian, Epistle 63 to Caecilius and Epistle 66; Nazianzen in his poem to the bishops; Chrysostom in his homily *On the Betrayal of Judas* and upon the *Epistle to the Hebrews*; Jerome to Damasus, *On the Prodigal Son*; Augustine, *City of God*, Book XVII, chapter 20; Cyril, *Mystagogical Catecheses*; Gregory the Great, *Dialogues* IV, chapter 58; Leo I to Dioscorus, Epistle 9; Fulgentius to Monimus, Book II, etc.

**“If they moistened the hearths with an outpouring of fragrant and aged wine,” etc.** This is the reading of seven Reg. manuscripts, among which are two very ancient ones, eleven Colb., four Oxon., Marm., Brun., and others, as well as nine printed editions and the first ancient Lips. manuscript, and also Cellar.’s edition, in which *or* occurs instead of *and*. One Reg. and one Colb. have the corrupt reading *worshiped*; one Clarom. has *they may have smelled*; the other Clarom. has the erroneous *they may have given off a smell*; Cauc., Jun., one Colb., and six printed editions read *they may have burned*. “If they have made the hearths fragrant.” SA. and Jun. read *they may have burned* instead of the printed *fragrant*. The editions of Gymnicus 1539, Cratander 1524, and Aldus 1515 have the same. Isaeus attests that he found this reading in other very ancient manuscripts. The Venetian edition of 1490 reads: “if they have worshiped at the hearth”; L. C.: “if they have worshiped the hearths.” I was unwilling to alter the received [Col. 0636B] reading, since it is relevant to the subject and carries no absurdity with it. **GALLAEUS.**

**Outpouring.** Six recent manuscripts and seven editions read *pouring over*. Arnobius, Book VII: “Undiluted wine is the companion of incense; we similarly request an explanation of why it is poured over the burning incense.”

**“They offer it as if to those about to taste something from it.”** *About to taste* is entirely correct—that is, to gods about to taste it. Hence chapter 2: “They slaughter sacrificial animals … for God, as though he were hungry; they pour out wines, as though he were thirsty.” *Epitome*, chapter 28: “A libation is poured out to these every day, as to household gods”; as though the gods were about to drink or taste it, as Bel does in the story of Daniel. **BUN.** — **“They offer it as if to those about to taste something from it. Whatever,”** etc. Eleven recent manuscripts and five editions read *about to pour a libation*; one Colb. manuscript reads *let them offer*. In my judgment, however, *libaturis* is used here for *delibaturis*, “about to taste,” a simple verb in place of a compound, which is characteristic of Lactantius; or else *de-* dropped out because of the similarity of the preceding syllable. See Arnobius, Book VII, around the middle.

**“That this is pleasing to their gods.”** Sixteen recent manuscripts and five editions read: “and that these things are pleasing.”

**Earthly riches.** Two recent Reg. manuscripts, Jun., one Clarom., and five early editions read *works*.

**Enslaved.** For according to Sallust, we ought to be so constituted that we employ the soul for command and the body for service.

**“They give the reins to their lusts.”** He appears to allude to Socrates’ story in Plato’s *Phaedrus*, where he divides the soul into three parts.

**“They exercise no moderation or reflection.”** Lips. 2 and 3 and Reimm. read: “nothing with moderation and reflection.” He imitates Sallust, *Catiline* XII.2, and compare *Catiline* 5.6; consult Cortius, who at the former passage explains “to have nothing measured or considered” as “not to reflect upon anything or handle it temperately.” **BUN.**

**“Surrounded by crowds of household slaves.”** I corrected the text in this way from seven Reg. manuscripts, among which are two of the greatest antiquity, three Colb., Goth., two Lips., one Clarom., Brun., three early editions, the Roman edition, and the recent editions of Cellar. and Walch—that is, “by a gathering of slaves” or “with a large household staff.” For *familia* means “slaves” in Phaedrus, Book II, Fable 8, on the stag and the ox; Book III, Fable 7, on the wolf and the dog; Fable 10 of the same book; and also Fable 19, on Aesop and the chatterer; and, as it appears, in the *Institutes*, *On the Lex Fufia Caninia*. Three recent Reg. manuscripts, two Colb., one Clarom., and nine common editions read *familiarium*, “attendants,” which means the same thing but was perhaps less customary at that time. For Seneca places it among obsolete expressions in Epistle 47: “They called the master ‘father of the household,’” he says, “and the slaves ‘members of the household,’ a term that survives even in mimes.” Partly from **CELLARIUS.**

**“They continually walk through a crowd made to move aside.”** Thus nine Reg. manuscripts, of which two are extremely old, four Colb., three Lips., two Clarom., Brun., and six editions. That is, the crowd was moved aside from the road by slaves, or, if the person were a magistrate, by a lictor. One Reg., Tornes., one Colb., and several others, as well as eight old printed editions, have the corrupt *subdued*. — **“Through a crowd made to move aside.”** Gronovius illustrates this more fully in his note on Livy, Book XXVIII, chapter 2. The verb *submovere*, “to clear away,” is more frequent in this connection; hence Livy, Book III, chapter 48: “Lictor, clear the city; make way for the master.” **BUN.**

**[End of note]**

—and inspired by him, not so that we might look upon the sky and the sun, as Anaxagoras thought, but so that we might worship with a pure and uncorrupted mind the God who fashioned the sun and the sky. Although in the preceding books I defended the truth according to the modest measure of my ability, it can nevertheless shine forth most clearly from the very rite of worship itself. For that holy and unique majesty desires nothing else from a human being but innocence alone. If anyone offers this to God, he has sacrificed with sufficient piety and religious devotion.

Human beings, however, neglect justice and, although polluted by every disgraceful act and crime, consider themselves religious if they stain temples and altars with the blood of sacrificial animals, or moisten the hearths with an outpouring of fragrant and aged wine. Indeed, they even prepare sacred banquets and elaborate feasts, offering them as though the gods were about to taste something from them. Whatever is rare in appearance, whatever is precious [Col. 0635B] in workmanship or fragrance, they judge to be pleasing to their gods—not on the basis of any understanding of divinity, which they do not possess, but on the basis of their own desires; [Col. 0636A] nor do they understand that God has no need of earthly riches.

For they comprehend nothing but the earth and assess good and evil solely by bodily sensation and pleasure. Just as they weigh religion according to the body’s judgment, so they arrange all the actions of their life. And because they have once turned themselves away from contemplation of heaven and enslaved that heavenly faculty to the body, they give the reins to their lusts, as though they were going to carry pleasure away with them. They hurry to seize it at every moment, although the mind ought to employ the body in its service, not the body the mind. These same people judge riches to be the greatest good. If they cannot acquire them by honorable means, they acquire them by evil ones: they defraud, seize, plunder, lay snares, perjure themselves. In short, they exercise no moderation or reflection, provided only that they glitter with gold and shine with silver, jewels, and garments, heap riches into their insatiable [Col. 0636B] bellies, and, surrounded by crowds of household slaves, continually walk through a crowd made to move aside. Thus [Col. 0637A] bound over and enslaved—

[Col. 0637A] **[Note: [Col. 0637B] Variorum Notes on Columns 637–638]**

**“Thus bound over and enslaved.”** The metaphor comes from civil law. Among jurists, *addicti* are debtors—also called *nexi*—who under the Law of the Twelve Tables were assigned to their creditors in temporary servitude because of debt. And rightly so. For slavery to sin is more truly an assignment for a fixed term than any other servitude: from it, through repentance and by Christ’s beneficence, the door to freedom lies open to those who return to their senses. **BETULEIUS.**

[Col. 0637C] **“Which belong to the earth.”** Thus the manuscripts and very many editions. Some printed texts have the erroneous *who*.

**From heaven.** Thirteen recent manuscripts and seven editions read *from the sky*.

**“The same blindness everywhere oppresses these wretched people.”** All the books agree upon the printed reading. These words correspond to Book III, chapter 24: “For they are always deceived in the same way.” **BUN.**

**“As though he were hungry.”** Thus Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* VIII, p. 215: “They demand from a certain man … an exceedingly fat ram, which might satisfy the hungry Syrian goddess with its sacrifice.” Observe Lactantius’ abundance of expressions such as “as though,” “just as,” and “as if.” **BUN.**

**“They light lamps.”** It was a custom common to almost all peoples to light fires as an expression of joy; nothing occurs more frequently among ancient authors than mention of *λυχνοκαΐαι* (*lamp-lightings*) and of kindled torches on occasions of public or private rejoicing. They lit lamps not only in temples, but also in their individual homes, and hung them at doors and windows. Juvenal, in Satire 12, describes the preparations for a festival day—not according to Jewish observance, but according to Roman custom:

[Col. 0637D]  
> All things shine; the doorway has raised its long branches  
> And, festive, is covered with lamps from early morning.

**“As though he dwelt in darkness.”** Lactantius could reproach the pagans for lighting lamps by day in the temples of their gods, as though those gods dwelt in darkness, without any necessity, since they sacrificed in the open air, as he himself says in *Divine Institutes*, Book II, chapter 2. Gallaeus ought not to have concluded from the words of our author quoted above that in Lactantius’ time the custom of lighting candles did not exist in Christian meeting places. The early Christians necessarily had to use lamps and lanterns, since for fear of persecution they held their gatherings before dawn and celebrated the sacrifice in crypts. Lamps were therefore absolutely necessary there. While once visiting the most celebrated cities of Gaul, I saw in the Church of Saint Peter in the city of the Andecavi, or Andegavi—Angers in French—two very ancient crypts. In one of them, namely beneath the choir, many hooks still fixed into the vault can be seen, as well as [Col. 0638B] several pulleys from which lamps or candles were suspended.

The Church, accustomed to this practice, retained it all the more willingly because light was necessary in sacred buildings constructed after the persecutions had subsided, which were very dark. Several such buildings still exist, including those at Bourges, Chartres, and the Sainte-Chapelle in Paris. In them I have seen lighted candles required for singing solemn Mass and Sext from the books in winter at ten o’clock in the morning. The same is true of churches of the Cistercian Order, in which, according to its manuscript ordinal or ceremonial preserved at the Abbey of Vaux-de-Cernay in the diocese of Paris, a light was placed and lit in a concealed position, necessary for reading by the priest who celebrated Mass after Terce. [Col. 0638C] What was formerly an absolute necessity—and still is so in some churches—is done in others for the sake of majesty, as an expression of joy and a testimony of gladness, as Jerome demonstrates against Vigilantius. See Athanasius in his epistle to the Orthodox; Eusebius, *History*, Book VI, chapter 33; Saint Epiphanius to John, bishop of Jerusalem; Saint Paulinus, poems 3 and 6 on the birthday of Saint Felix; Saint Augustine, *Sermons on the Liturgical Year*, 215; Theodoret, *History of the Holy Fathers*, chapter 21, on James; Bellarmine, Book II *On the Relics of the Saints*, chapters 3 and 4; and Baronius, *Annals*, vol. I, at the year of the Lord 58. From Saint Justin’s *Dialogue with Trypho the Jew*, it appears that lamps were lit in the liturgy among Christians. These observations are by **J.-B. LE BRUN.**

**“They would recognize.”** Heumann reads: “they would have recognized.”

**“They will perceive.”** Three Reg. manuscripts, two Colb., and eleven editions read: “let them perceive.”

**“How little need he has.”** Thus nearly all the manuscripts, among them Bonon. and Reg., and the early Roman, Is., and Cellar. editions. One recent Reg. manuscript reads *because*; Cauc., Jun., one recent Reg. manuscript, and thirteen editions read *that*.

[Col. 0638D] **“So brilliant, so radiant a light.”** In the passage cited from the *Epitome*, he called it simply “the sun.” Here, however, he learnedly calls the light *candida*, “radiant,” following the example of Ennius, Cicero, and others. Ennius in Cicero, *On Divination*, Book I, chapter 48:

> Then radiant light, struck by the rays, poured itself forth.

Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book II, chapter 15: “the radiance of the sun illuminates.” **BUN.**

**“Than a human head.”** Heraclitus said that the sun was a foot in breadth; Epicurus, that it was only as large as it appears, as Plutarch reports in *Opinions of the Philosophers*. Laertius also ascribes the latter view to Heraclitus. Cleomedes argues against Epicurus in Book II. For the size of the sun, moreover, read Pliny, Book II, chapter 11; Macrobius, *On the Dream of Scipio*, Book I, chapter 20; Ptolemy himself, *Almagest*, Book V, chapter 16; Theon at the same passage, and the same author again in his work on Aratus.

**“Cannot gaze upon it.”** The Torn. manuscript reads: “is unable to gaze upon it”; two Clarom. manuscripts read: “cannot look upon it.”

**“So great a measure of these things.”** That is, so great a measure of radiance [Col. 0639C] and heat. Lactantius and Cicero often use the expression in this way. Our author, *Institutes*, Book I, chapter 3: “So that there may be in him—God—so great a measure of these things,” that is, magnitude, power, virtue, and majesty, “as,” etc. **BUN.**

**[End of note]**

—to pleasures, they extinguish the force and vigor of the mind; and while they suppose that they are living most fully, they hasten with the greatest speed toward death. For, as we taught in the second book, the principle of heaven is in the mind, while that of the earth is in the body. Those who neglect the goods of the mind and seek those of the body dwell in darkness and death, which belong to the earth and the body, because life and light come from heaven. Since they are without these things through serving the body, they are far removed from an understanding of divine realities. The same blindness everywhere oppresses these wretched people: just as they do not know who the true God is, so they do not know what true worship is.

## CHAPTER II  
### On the worship of false gods and of the true God

They therefore slaughter choice and fat sacrificial animals for God, [Col. 0637B] as though he were hungry; pour out wines, as though he were thirsty; and light lamps, as though he dwelt in darkness. But if they could conjecture or comprehend in their minds what those [Col. 0638A] heavenly goods are—whose greatness we cannot grasp by our senses while still enveloped in an earthly body—they would then recognize themselves as utterly foolish in performing these empty duties. Or if they were willing to contemplate the heavenly light that we call the sun, they would then perceive how little need God has of their lamps, since he himself gave so brilliant and radiant a light for human use. And yet, although it appears within so small a circle that, because of its distance, it seems no larger than a human head, its radiance is so great that the sight of mortal eyes cannot gaze upon it; and if you fix your gaze upon it even briefly, dimness and darkness follow in your dazzled eyes. What light and what brilliance, then, are we to suppose exist in the presence of God himself, with whom there is no night? [Col. 0638B] He so regulated this very light that it would harm living creatures neither through excessive radiance nor through violent heat; and he gave it so great a measure of these things [Col. 0639A] as mortal bodies could endure—

[Col. 0639A] **[Note: [Col. 0639C] Variorum Notes on Columns 639–640]**

**“Could endure.”** I corrected the text in this way from three editions and all the manuscripts, as is required by the preceding “would harm” and the following “required.”

**Required.** Heumann reads: “requires.”

**Wax candles.** One old Reg. manuscript reads *cerorum*; one recent Reg. manuscript and Is.’s edition read *cereorum*; one other recent Reg. manuscript reads *cerearum*. The others have the reading printed in the text.

**Poet.** Lucretius, Book V, *On the Nature of Things*.

**“But clear.”** That is, bright or pure, the metaphor being drawn from wine strained free of its dregs. Thus Virgil, *Eclogue* 6:

> And at the same time of clear fire;

and Lucretius:

> May that renowned golden heat  
> Of clear fire fly down to earth,

[Col. 0639D] they said. These terms appear altogether contrary to fire, for *liquidus* derives from liquid; but here *liquidus* means pure, unpolluted by smoke. **TURNEBUS.**

**“We are called φῶτες.”** I restored this reading from two very ancient Reg. manuscripts, with the support of the very old Cauc., one Bonon., and the recent two Reg., Marm., one Clarom., and Brun., which have “it is called *φῶτες*”; Ultr. has *fortes*; two recent Reg. manuscripts, *φωτος*; one Reg. and the Roman edition of 1474, *phantes*; one Reg., one Bonon., Pen., and the Florentine and Aldine 1515 editions, *Phanetes*; one Clarom., *focus*; one Reg. and two Colb., *focos*; one other Colb., *fodes*; another Colb. has the erroneous *fontes* in place of *φῶτες*, which means “we are called men.” One Reg., two Colb., and printed editions have “it is called *φῶς*,” that is, “it is called light.” Grammarians say that *φὼς*, when it means “man,” is written with a grave accent, but *φῶς*, when it means “light,” with a circumflex.

**“Feed upon it.”** That is, upon the blood. The use of *vesci*, “feed,” for drinks is rather rare. Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book II, chapter 23: “The gods feed neither upon food nor upon drink.” **BUN.**

[Col. 0640C] **“Of this kind.”** Thus restored from almost all the manuscripts and the Paris edition of 1525. Two recent Reg. manuscripts and almost all editions have *hujuscemodi*. Persius, Satire 2, verse 30.

**“Purchase the ears.”** That is, purchase a favorable hearing.

**“With greasy entrails.”** That is, with fat intestines.

**“Not with flesh … to appease.”** Cicero expresses this excellently in *For Cluentius*, chapter 68: “Nor does he understand that the minds of the gods can be appeased by piety, religion, and just prayers, not by superstition or by slaughtered victims offered for the accomplishment of a crime.” **BUN.**

**“Noble through natural integrity.”** He added the word *natural* to the words of Persius, a point some have misunderstood. That word was inserted because natural qualities adhere most firmly, as in the case of native colors and similar things—unless, however, Lactantius called integrity “natural” with the Stoic doctrine in mind. He said “noble” because true piety is noble and full of good hope; superstition, by contrast, is fearful and cast down to the ground. Accordingly, Plato argues that superstition is not *θεραπείαν* (*service*) of the divine but *κολακείαν* (*flattery*), a vice characterized by *τὸ ταπεινόν* (*abasement*), which is incompatible with a noble mind. **ISAAC CASAUBON.**

> A heart steeped in noble integrity.

**PERSIUS.**

**“On Duty.”** The little books *On Duties* were therefore written before the *Hortensius*, which has been lost.

**“For the seditious man Cornelius.”** Not Balbus, whose trial concerned citizenship. Cicero himself mentions the speeches *For Cornelius* in *On the Orator* and *On Canvassing for the Consulship*. I think, however, that these words of Cicero were taken from the *Hortensius*. **BETULEIUS.**

**“I believe, in order to recommend the books.”** I restored this reading from Cellar.’s edition and all the manuscripts except two recent Reg. manuscripts, in which, as in the common editions, the text reads “little books.”

**Attests.** Cicero, at the beginning of *On Duties*.

**Endless.** One Colb., Brun., the Roman edition of 1470, and Is. read *lowest*.

**Perfect.** Among the philosophers, some were making progress and others were perfect.

**[End of note]**

—or as the ripening of crops required. Should we therefore regard as being in possession of his reason a man who offers to the author and giver of light the light of lamps and wax candles as a gift? God requires from us another kind of light—one that is not smoky but, as the poet says, clear and bright: namely, the light of the mind, on account of which the poets call us *φῶτες* (“men,” with a play on *φῶς*, “light”). No one can present this light unless he has acknowledged God.

Their gods, however, because they are earthly, need lamps so that they may not be in darkness. And since their worshipers understand nothing heavenly, they bring even the religions they serve back down to earth. For on earth there is need of light, because its principle and nature are dark. Accordingly, they attribute to the gods not a heavenly but rather a human mode of sensation. They therefore believe that those things necessary and pleasing to us are also necessary and pleasing to the gods: food when they are hungry, [Col. 0639B] drink when they are thirsty, clothing when they are cold, or light when the sun has set, so that they may be able to see.

From no circumstance, therefore, can it be proved and understood so clearly that those gods once lived and are now dead as from the very rite of worship, which is wholly derived from the earth. For what heavenly good can there be in the shed blood of cattle with which they defile their altars—unless perhaps they believe that the gods feed upon something that human beings disdain even to touch? And whoever has supplied them with this fattening fare, even if he is a brigand, adulterer, poisoner, or parricide, will be blessed and fortunate. Him they love, him they protect, and upon him they bestow everything he has wished for. Persius therefore deservedly [Col. 0639C] ridicules superstitions of this kind in his customary manner:

[Col. 0640A]

> At what price, he says, do you purchase  
> The ears of the gods—with lung and greasy entrails?

He evidently understood that flesh was not needed to appease the heavenly majesty, but a holy mind, a just disposition, and a heart—as he himself says—noble through its natural integrity. This is heavenly religion: not one composed of corruptible things, but one composed of the virtues of the mind, which has its origin in heaven. This is true worship, in which the worshiper’s mind presents itself to God as an undefiled victim. The discussion of this book will teach how this very thing is to be attained and accomplished. For nothing can be so excellent or so fitting for humanity as to instruct human beings in justice.

In Cicero’s *Hortensius*, Catulus, preferring philosophy to all other things, says that he would rather have even one [Col. 0640B] small book *On Duty* than a long speech on behalf of the seditious man Cornelius. This opinion should certainly be regarded not as Catulus’—who perhaps did not say it—but as Cicero’s, who wrote the work. I believe he did so in order to recommend the books he was going to write *On Duties*. In those very books he attests that nothing in all philosophy is better and more fruitful than giving precepts for life.

But if those who have no knowledge of the truth do this, how much more ought we to do so, who, having been instructed and enlightened by God, can give true precepts? We shall not, however, teach as though we were transmitting the first elements of virtue, for that would be an endless task; instead, we shall proceed as though we had undertaken to teach someone who already appears [Col. 0640C] perfect among them. While retaining their precepts which [Col. 0641A] they customarily and correctly give for moral uprightness—

[Col. 0641A] **[Note: [Col. 0641C] Variorum Notes on Columns 641–642]**

**“Correctly give.”** I corrected the text in this way from all the manuscripts and from the early Roman and Betul. editions. And it must be read thus: “which they—that is, those authors—customarily and correctly give for moral uprightness.” Thirteen editions read: “to be given.”

**“There are two paths.”** Gallaeus states that after these words many manuscripts add “Emperor Constantine”; I also found the addition in one very old Reg. manuscript, another Royal manuscript, Marm., and six editions. It is absent from two Bon., seven Reg., six Colb., five Oxon., and eighteen other recent manuscripts, as well as three early Roman editions and nine other editions.

**“Which the poets also.”** Hesiod, in the *Works*.

**“And the philosophers.”** Xenophon—or, in Xenophon’s *Memorabilia*, Book II—has Socrates recount, from Prodicus, Hercules’ dream, in which Virtue and Pleasure appeared to him, each striving to entice the young man to devote himself to her. The verses of Hesiod cited by us are quoted in that passage. On the subject, see also Philostratus on Prodicus and Cicero, *On Duties*, Book I. In Plato’s *Protagoras*, Prodicus himself is introduced speaking about this hill of virtue. Plato again mentions it in Book IV of *The Laws*. Nor are the things Cebes depicted for us in his *Tablet* dissimilar.

[Col. 0641D] **“To be, and the virtues.”** The *and* is absent from one ancient Bonon. manuscript and five editions.

**“The course of human life resembles the letter Y.”** Among ecclesiastical writers, Jerome mentions the Pythagorean letter in an epistle to Laeta and again to Pammachius on the death of Paulina; and in his commentary on Ecclesiastes 10 he clearly cites this passage with praise. Ausonius describes it in these little verses:

> The letter of Pythagoras, divided by its two-branched fork,  
> Appears to display the image of human life.  
> For virtue’s path seeks the steep hill to the right  
> And at first offers a difficult approach to those who behold it,  
> But at the highest summit it gives rest to the weary.  
> The broad path displays an easy road, but at its final bound  
> Hurls down those it has ensnared and rolls them over jagged rocks.  
> For whoever through love of virtue has overcome  
> Hard trials will win praise and honor for himself;  
> But he who pursues sloth and idle luxury,  
> While heedlessly fleeing the hardships set before him,  
> Will pass his life in shame, poverty, and misery alike.

Palingenius also touches upon the subject in *Sagittarius*. It is perhaps called the Pythagorean letter because Y and Z are believed to have been invented by Pythagoras. From **BETULEIUS**, who incorrectly cited these verses under Virgil’s name, although they are by Ausonius, as Francius observed. See Servius on Book VI of Virgil’s *Aeneid*.

**“When he has reached the threshold of early adolescence.”** Thus all the manuscripts except two recent Reg. manuscripts, in which, as in the common editions, the text reads “the first.”

**“Directions.”** This is drawn from Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.540.

**“Divides.”** One Reg., one Brun., and the Thomas. edition read *splits*.

**“Onto the left-hand path, which falsely assumes the appearance of the better.”** Five editions read “toward the left.” The manuscripts Cauc. and Jun. and the Gymnic. and Betul. editions read: “which falsely assumes the appearance of virtue and of the better.”

**“To fall.”** I corrected the text in this way from the older and better manuscripts—one Bonon. and two Reg.—as well as Is.’s edition. Isaeus and Francius also judged that this was the proper reading. Other codices read “to walk.”

**“They appear.”** Heumann reads: “they may appear.”

**“In the underworld.”** This will be discussed in the following chapter.

**[End of note]**

—we shall build upon them what is unknown to those philosophers, in order to perfect and bring to completion the justice they do not possess. But I shall pass over those matters that can be common to us and them, lest I appear to borrow anything from those whose errors I have resolved to refute and expose.

## CHAPTER III  
### On the paths, the vices and virtues, the rewards of heaven, and the punishments of the underworld
There are two paths, Emperor Constantine, along which human life must proceed: one that leads to heaven, the other that plunges down to the underworld. Poets have introduced them in their poems, and philosophers in their discussions. The philosophers, indeed, held that one [Col. 0641B] belonged to the virtues and the other to the vices. They maintained that the path assigned to the virtues is steep and rugged at its first approach; but that if anyone overcomes the difficulty and reaches its summit, thereafter he has a level road, a bright and pleasant plain, and reaps all the rich and delightful fruits of his labors. Those, however, whom the difficulty of the first approach frightens away slip and turn aside into the path of the vices. At its entrance this path seems pleasant and is far more well-trodden; but when they have advanced a little farther along it, its appearance of pleasantness is suddenly withdrawn, and a precipitous road arises—now rough with rocks, now overgrown with thorns, now broken by chasms, or made violent by torrents—so that they must struggle, become stuck, slip, and fall. All these things are put forward [Col. 0641C] to show that the greatest labors attend the acquisition of the virtues, but the greatest fruits and solid, incorruptible pleasures attend their possession; whereas the vices [Col. 0642A] entice human minds with certain natural allurements and, having captivated them with the appearance of empty delights, lead them to bitter anguish and misery. This would be an altogether wise argument, if they knew the forms and boundaries of the virtues themselves. For they had learned neither what the virtues are nor what reward from God awaits them; this we shall teach in these two books.

Because, however, they did not know—or doubted—that human souls are immortal, they assessed both virtues and vices in terms of earthly honors or punishments. This entire discussion of the two paths therefore concerns sobriety and luxury. For they say that the course of human life resembles the letter Y, because every person, upon reaching the threshold of early adolescence and coming to the point

> [Col. 0642B] Where the road divides into its two branches,

stands there wavering and does not know toward which side he should preferably incline. If he finds a guide to direct him, while hesitating, toward better things—that is, if he learns philosophy, or eloquence, or some honorable art by which he may come to good character, something that cannot be achieved without the greatest labor—they argue that he will complete an honorable and prosperous life. But if he finds no teacher of sobriety, he falls into the path on the left, which falsely assumes the appearance of the better path; that is, he surrenders himself to idleness, sloth, and luxury. These do indeed seem pleasant for a time to one ignorant of true goods, but afterward, when all dignity and property have been lost, he will live amid every misery and disgrace. They therefore referred the ends of those paths [Col. 0642C] to the body and to this life that we lead on earth. The poets perhaps did better when they held that this fork in the road lies in the underworld. But they err in that they set those paths before the dead. Both groups, therefore, spoke truly [Col. 0643A], but neither spoke correctly; for the paths themselves ought to have been referred to life, and their ends to death. We, then, speak better and more truly when we say that these two paths are the paths of heaven and the underworld, because immortality has been set before the just, and eternal punishment before the unjust.

How these paths [Col. 0643A]—

> **Note: [Col. 0643C] Variorum Notes on columns 643–644**
>
> **How these paths.** Thus the editions of Betuleius and Isaeus, and all the manuscripts except two recent Royal manuscripts and the Canterbury manuscript, in which, as in fourteen printed editions, the reading is “these paths”; four printed editions wrongly have “these lives.” Lactantius is not speaking about lives, but continues in the allegory of the two paths, one of which leads to heaven and the other to the underworld.
>
> **I shall disclose.** Most printed editions wrongly add *-que* here: “and I shall disclose what.” Such expressions have often been corrupted in books by those who thought the sequence *que quae* sounded wrong. Yet above we likewise find “and the one (*eamque*) that is assigned”; Book VI, ch. 18: “and patience (*Patientiaeque*), which is the greatest of all the virtues”; Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I.2: “and many things (*Multaque*) that will be said”; ibid., ch. 42: [Col. 0643D] “and those things (*Eaque*) which”; and *On the Nature of the Gods* III.7: “and all things (*Omniaque*) which.” Cortius defended this usage in Sallust and illustrated it at *Catiline* III.5, p. 25. —Bünemann.
>
> **For whether you implant the virtues, the vices will depart of their own accord; or remove the vices.** Six recent Royal manuscripts and three editions read “For if”; thirteen recent manuscripts and eight printed codices wrongly read “introduce.” See below, “the virtues to be implanted.” After “or,” seven manuscripts add “also,” which is rejected by the older and better manuscripts and printed editions.
>
> **The vices to be removed.** Sixteen recent manuscripts and two editions read “drawn back.” Shortly afterward follows “without the removal of the vices.”
>
> **Nor the virtues be implanted.** Thus all the manuscripts and many printed editions. The Paris edition of 1525, Cratander, and Isaeus read “introduced.” See above, “you implant the virtues.” —**The virtues be implanted.** Correctly. *Epitome*, ch. 60: “The vices must first be removed from our minds, and only then must the virtues be implanted”; ch. 61: “These roots of the vices must be torn out, so that the virtues can be implanted … nor can they be removed … implanted by nature.” Below: “Neither are they to be removed … God implanted.” —Bünemann.
>
> [Col. 0644C] **And presides over the good.** The Subiaco edition has “is endowed with good qualities.”
>
> **Will possess perpetual light.** The word “perpetual” is missing from the Venetian editions of 1493 and 1497, perhaps because it dropped out owing to the similar word “reward.” I defended it at Book IV, ch. 30: “may possess perpetual light.”
>
> **Accordingly.** The Junius and Utrecht manuscripts and five old editions read “therefore.”
>
> **But the left-hand path exacts the punishments of the wicked.** Virgil’s words from *Aeneid* VI are cited by Jerome also in his commentary on Ecclesiastes, chapter 10. A similar argument from the same subject occurs in Chrysostom, *Against the Detractors of the Monastic Life*, Book II.
>
> **With every kind of flower.** I deleted the superfluous conjunction “and,” which eight manuscripts and the same number of common editions place before it, but which is absent from many manuscripts of good quality and five old editions.
>
> **To be.** This verb is missing from the Bologna, Taxius, and Penius manuscripts.
>
> **All things have been placed.** I restored this from the two Bologna manuscripts, the Regius-Puteanus manuscript, two other Royal manuscripts, three Leipzig manuscripts, two Colbert manuscripts, and the Junius, Tours, Bodleian, Christ Church, two Clermont, and other excellent and very ancient manuscripts, as Michael Thomasius observed. Isaeus also prefers this reading to “God placed all things,” found in one ancient Royal manuscript and thirteen very recent manuscripts, nine editions, as well as three Oxford manuscripts; four common editions omit the name “God.” For God placed no vices there. As Thomasius very rightly observes, those things that are evil, or have a certain appearance of evil, must not be referred to God, but to us, who create evils for ourselves by our sins and use good things to our own destruction.
>
> **Of this path.** Five recent manuscripts and four editions have this reading. Certain witnesses read “of this life,” but wrongly.
>
> **When the end has been reached.** Seneca, *On the Shortness of Life*, ch. 3: “As soon as the matter comes to the wasting of time.” Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.45: “They had come to the threshold.” Silius Italicus XV.510: “When the summit was reached.” —Bünemann.

—either raise people to heaven or cast them down to the underworld, I shall explain. I shall disclose what the virtues unknown to the philosophers are; then I shall show what their rewards are, and at the same time what the vices are and what punishments belong to them. For perhaps someone expects me to discuss vices and virtues separately, although, when we discuss good or evil, its contrary can also be understood. For whether you implant the virtues, the vices will depart of their own accord; or remove the vices, the virtues will enter of themselves. The nature of good and evil is so constituted that they always [Col. 0643B] fight and expel one another. It thus follows that the vices cannot be removed without the virtues, nor can the virtues be implanted without the removal of the vices.

We therefore present these paths very differently from the way philosophers usually present them. First, we say that over each of them has been placed a guide, both guides being immortal: one honored, who presides over the virtues and good things; the other condemned, who presides over the vices and evil things. The philosophers, however, place a guide only on the path to the right, and not one single and perpetual guide. For they introduce any teacher of a respectable art, who recalls people from idleness and teaches them to be sober. Nor do they cause anyone to enter that path except boys and adolescents, evidently because the arts are learned at those ages. We, however, [Col. 0643C] bring every sex, race, and age onto this heavenly journey, because God, who is the guide of that path, denies immortality to no human being who has been born.

The shape [Col. 0644A] of the paths themselves is likewise not as they supposed. What need is there of the letter Y in the case of contrary and divergent things? Rather, the better path is turned toward sunrise, and the worse toward sunset; for whoever follows truth and justice will, after receiving the reward of immortality, possess perpetual light. But whoever, enticed by that evil guide, prefers vices to virtues and falsehood to truth must be carried toward sunset and darkness. I shall therefore describe each path and show their distinctive qualities and character.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Paths of Life, on Pleasures, and also on the Hardships of Christians

There is accordingly one path of virtue and good things, which leads [Col. 0644B], not to the Elysian Fields, as the poets say, but to the very summit of the universe:

> But the left-hand path exacts the punishments of the wicked  
> And sends them down to impious Tartarus.

For this is the path of that accuser who, after establishing corrupt religions, turns people away from the heavenly journey and leads them onto the path of destruction. The appearance and form of this path have been fashioned to the eye in such a way that it seems level and open, delightful with every kind of flower and fruit. For on it have been placed all the things that are regarded as goods on earth: I mean wealth, honor, leisure, pleasure, and every enticement; but together with these are injustice, cruelty, pride, treachery, lust, greed, discord, ignorance, falsehood, folly, and the other [Col. 0644C] vices.

The end of this path, however, is as follows. When the end has been reached, from which it is no longer [Col. 0645A] possible to turn back, the path is cut off so suddenly, together with all its beauty, that no one can perceive the deception before being hurled headlong and falling into a profound depth.

> **Note: [Col. 0645C] Variorum Notes on columns 645–646**
>
> **Fall into a profound depth.** I corrected the text thus from almost all the manuscripts and editions. I do not think this reading should be rejected, as Thomasius rejected it; for since “height” differs from “depth,” so to speak, only conceptually, *altitudo* is often used for depth or the deep. Thus: “the depth of the sea,” Psalm 68:2; “He brought them out of the depth of the underworld,” Wisdom 10:19; “from the depth of the belly of the underworld,” Ecclesiasticus 51:7; “Put out into the deep,” Luke 5:4; and “the well is deep,” John 4:11, that is, the water there is deep. Caesar, *Gallic War* IV, and Cicero, *To Atticus* IX, also used this word in the same sense: “The earth descends to an infinite depth”; likewise *On Divination* I, and “the shrine has been sunk to an astonishing depth,” *Against Verres* VII; Celsus VII.7. Lactantius himself, *Divine Institutes* III.28: “In a well so deep that it has no bottom.” In the *Epitome*, ch. 72: “The valleys will sink into a profound depth,” according to the Turin manuscript—and correctly. See the following note. Moreover, although “height” and “depth” appear to be opposites, nevertheless, according to Augustine, “*Altitudo* in the Latin language signifies both: that which extends upward bears the name of *altitudo*, and that which extends far downward bears the name of *altitudo*.” St. Augustine, Sermon 165, *On the Words of the Apostle*, Ephesians III. Thus there is no need for the emendation of the ancient Bologna manuscript adopted by Thomasius, Isaeus, Thysius, Gallaeus, Sparkius, and Walchius, namely, “falls from a height into the depths.” —**Fall into a profound depth.** Seneca, Letter 70: “What a brave man! … with what courage he had cast himself into the profound depth of the sea!” Arnobius [Col. 0646C], Book V, p. 173, speaks of “a cavern of profound depth.”
>
> **Placed.** Supply “God” as the understood subject.
>
> **Bitternesses.** The Christ Church, Merton, and Emmanuel manuscripts read “illnesses.”
>
> **Enter those narrow places.** Paulinus of Nola, Letter 29, ch. 2: “The Pharisee … could not enter, because narrow places do not admit those burdened with baggage. Nor could broad ostentation be received where narrow humility gathered itself together and, narrower than narrowness itself, penetrated through the meagerness of a contrite heart.”
>
> **Come about.** Elegantly expressed. Shortly afterward the same author uses “advance.” Justin VII.6: “When affairs were turning out successfully.” Cicero, *On Ends* I.14: “Nor does he foresee what will come about.”
>
> **With difficulty.** Adverbially. Pliny II.18: “extricating themselves with difficulty”; XVII.23, near the end: “they recover with difficulty”; and often elsewhere. The word is now almost neglected; Faber cites only two passages for it, from Cicero and Velleius.
>
> **Greed or pleasure.** The first ancient Bologna manuscript, the Caucian and Junius manuscripts, and the Leipzig manuscripts read “greed and pleasure.”
>
> **For on the one path.** The ancient Bologna manuscript reads “For on its own path.”
>
> **Fall into evils.** Correctly, in contrast with the preceding “attain goods.” Fourteen recent manuscripts and eight editions read “will fall.”
>
> **Bodily life.** Thus very many ancient and excellent manuscripts. The Caucian manuscript and nine recent manuscripts, together with the editions, have “temporal.” But the antithesis there is between bodily and spiritual. —Isaeus, and before him Thomasius.
>
> **When at the same time.** Twelve manuscripts read “once.” One may often observe “once” and “at the same time” being confused in manuscripts.
>
> **Pledges.** That is, children. —**With his pledges safe.** That is, his children. Compare Book VI, ch. 12, note. Cyprian frequently uses the term, for example *On Almsgiving*, Gryphius edition, p. 334: “to provide for dear pledges … Give useful and saving precepts to your pledges.”

For whoever is captivated by the appearance of present goods and occupied in acquiring and enjoying them, and does not foresee what will follow after death, but turns himself away from God, will be cast down to the underworld and condemned to eternal punishment.

The heavenly path, however, has been set before us as difficult and steep, either rough with bristling thorns or obstructed by projecting rocks, so that everyone must advance with the greatest exertion and wearing of the feet, and with great anxiety about falling. On this path God has placed justice, temperance, patience, faith, chastity, abstinence, concord, knowledge, truth, wisdom, and the other [Col. 0645B] virtues; but together with them poverty, disgrace, toil, pain, and every bitterness. For whoever extends his hope farther and prefers better things will lack these earthly goods, so that, unencumbered and light, he may overcome the path’s difficulty. One who surrounds himself with royal equipage or burdens himself with wealth cannot even enter, much less remain within, those narrow places.

From this it is understood why the things the wicked and unjust desire come about more easily for them: their path slopes downward and is steeply descending. But the things the good desire come about with difficulty, because they walk along a difficult and arduous road. Therefore the just person, because he has entered a hard and rough journey, must necessarily be an object of contempt, ridicule, and hatred. For all whom greed or pleasure drags headlong envy the person who has been able to grasp virtue [Col. 0645C], and they resent another’s possessing what they themselves do not possess. He will accordingly be poor, humble, obscure, and [Col. 0646A] exposed to injury, yet will endure everything bitter. And if he carries his unbroken patience to that highest stage and final destination, the crown of virtue will be given to him; and in return for the labors that he endured in life for the sake of justice, God will bestow immortality upon him.

These are the paths that God assigned to human life. On each he displayed both goods and evils, but in a reversed and inverted order. On the one path he displayed temporary evils first, together with eternal goods; this is the better order. On the other he displayed temporary goods first, together with eternal evils; this is the worse order. Thus whoever chooses present evils together with justice may attain goods greater and more certain than those he despised; but whoever prefers present goods to justice may fall into evils greater and more lasting [Col. 0646B] than those he fled. Because this bodily life is brief, its goods and evils must therefore also be brief. But because that spiritual life, which is the opposite of this earthly life, is everlasting, its goods and evils are therefore also everlasting. Thus eternal evils follow brief goods, and eternal goods follow brief evils.

Accordingly, since goods and evils have been set before a person at the same time, everyone ought to consider within himself how much better it is to compensate brief evils with everlasting goods than to endure everlasting evils in exchange for brief and transitory goods. For in this world, when a contest with an enemy lies before us, one must labor first so that afterward one may be at leisure. One must hunger, thirst, endure heat and cold, rest on the ground, keep watch, [Col. 0646C] and undergo danger, so that, with one’s children, house, and property safe, one may enjoy all the goods of peace and victory [Col. 0647A]. But if you prefer present leisure to labor, you necessarily bring the greatest evil upon yourself; for the adversary will forestall you when you offer no resistance, the fields will be laid waste, the house plundered, wife and children carried off as spoil, and you yourself killed or captured. To prevent all these things from happening, present advantage must be postponed so that a greater and more lasting advantage may be obtained.

So throughout this entire life, because God has left us an adversary so that we may acquire virtue, present pleasure must be relinquished lest the enemy overwhelm us. We must keep watch, stand guard—

> **Note: [Col. 0647B] Variorum Notes on columns 647–648**
>
> **Stand guard.** An imitation from the fragment *On the Republic*. Hence also his designation of God as commander (*αὐτοκράτορα*, “supreme commander”). On this, see above, Book III, ch. 18. —Betuleius.
>
> **All the more readily because.** Many manuscripts, including the Witt, Leipzig, and Reimm manuscripts, together with all the editions, read “all the more readily, the more”; but I printed from the Wolfenbüttel and Gotha parchment manuscripts, “all the more readily because.” Thus our author in ch. 6: “They do … many things that the good do, all the more readily because they do them for the sake of deceiving.” —Bünemann.
>
> **By which this is acquired.** Three recent manuscripts read “whereby this is acquired.” Eight editions read “whereby this may be acquired.”
>
> **Against the snares of a single enemy.** One Royal manuscript and the Bruni manuscript read “against the snares of this enemy”; the Caucian manuscript, one Royal and one Colbert manuscript, and seven editions, “against the snares of the invisible enemy”; three Royal, four Colbert, two Clermont, and the Canterbury manuscripts, and the Roman edition of 1470, “against the snares of a single or invisible enemy.” **To serve pleasure and the body.** One recent Royal manuscript and the Bruni manuscript read “serving the pleasure of the body.”
>
> **Puffs others up with ambitions.** I corrected the text thus from the oldest and best manuscripts: the first ancient Bologna manuscript, three Royal manuscripts, the Caucian, one Leipzig, the Palatine, and Bruni manuscripts, and Isaeus’s edition. But seven recent Royal, six Colbert, one Clermont manuscript, and fourteen printed editions read “inflames,” which is unsuitable, especially since “inflames with the goads of anger” immediately preceded. One Clermont manuscript reads “inflames and puffs up with ambitions.” —**Puffs others up with ambitions.** Thus Book VI, ch. 24: “he is puffed up, swollen with pride”; Book VII, ch. 1: “puffed up with ambition.” Compare the note on Book V, ch. 22. Cyprian, Book II, Letter 2: “Let pride puff up, let irascibility inflame.” Cicero used “ambitions” in the plural in the *Verrines*. Compare Lactantius, Book IV, ch. 16, “injustices.” —Bünemann.
>
> **And upon the years.** Perhaps “upon the year” should be read: “and bestow their name upon the year.” It would take too long to relate here how varied and manifold antiquity was in reckoning its years. Consult Augustine, *City of God* XII.10 and XV.14; Pliny VII.48; Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights* III.48; Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, ch. 15, at greater length; Janus Parrhasius, Letter 63; Petrus Nannius, *Miscellanies* V.7; Carolus Sigonius, *Emendations* II.16; and Servius Honoratus on *Aeneid* I:
>
> > Thirty great months completing their cycles.
>
> Before writing was invented, the Egyptians, the earliest of mortals, fashioned a serpent holding its tail in its mouth as a symbol of the reciprocal movements and revolutions of the stars [Col. 0648B], and as a representation of the year. Isidore of Seville, *Etymologies* V.36, and others. The same Servius, on *Aeneid* V:
>
> > When a gliding serpent from deep within the shrine …
>
> They dedicated the year to Jupiter, but the months to Juno. Plutarch, *Roman Questions* 77. It is also established that originally the year comprised the span of only one month; because they measured it by the moon’s course, they called it lunar. Joannes Jovianus Pontanus, *Urania* II, *On the Moon*:
>
> > Cycle upon cycle  
> > She changes as she circles round, completing her little year.
>
> Others limited the year to a span of two months, among them the Egyptians. The same Pontanus, in the same place:
>
> > The ancient Egyptians first made it two months long.
>
> Those same Egyptians sometimes divided their year into three months and sometimes into four. Plutarch, *Numa*. The Carians and Acarnanians enclosed the year within a span of six months. Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, ch. 19. The Hebrews likewise made the year six months long according to the moon’s motion: Suidas, under the word ἐνιαυτός, “year.” These peoples revered the moon as the supreme deity and therefore bounded their years according to its course. Others took a different view: they recognized the sun as the leader of the heavenly bodies and, measuring its courses, conformed their years to its motion. Servius on *Aeneid* III:
>
> > Meanwhile the sun completes the great year.
>
> —**So that they may mark the fasti and bestow their name upon the years.** Lactantius is speaking of those whom ambition has so puffed up that they think of nothing except holding public office, especially offices associated with marking the *fasti* and bestowing a name upon the years; that is, he is speaking of the consuls, from whom the consular *Fasti* were named, and those same consuls bestowed their names upon the years. Aptly Seneca, near the end of Book I of *On Anger*: “Ambition is not content with annual honors; if possible, it wishes to occupy the *fasti* with a single name and to display its titles throughout the whole world.” Salvian, Book VI, Bremen edition, p. 106: “Since all these things are done by the very men—the consuls—who confer their names upon the years, and from whom the years themselves take their beginning.”
>
> **Entangles in various religions.** I read thus with the most ancient manuscripts: the two Bologna manuscripts, the Regius-Puteanus, Junius, three other Royal, and two Colbert manuscripts. Four Royal manuscripts, the Caucian, three Colbert, the Emmanuel, two Clermont manuscripts, and thirteen editions read “entangles in vain religions”; one Colbert manuscript, “may fill with vain religions”; one recent Royal, the Penius and Canterbury manuscripts, and six common editions, “entangles in empty religions”; one recent Royal manuscript reads “may fill with empty religions.” —**In vain … religions.** The Bologna, Junius, and Gotha manuscripts read “various”; the Penius manuscript and the Subiaco, Rostock, Venice 1471 and 1515, Paris, Cratander, Gymnich, and Isaeus editions read “empty”; the Caucian, Leipzig, and Reimm manuscripts and the Fasius, Gryphius, Tours, Thomasius, and subsequent editions read “vain.” —Bünemann.

—undertake military expeditions, finally shed our blood, and patiently endure everything bitter and burdensome; all the more readily because our commander, God, has established eternal rewards for our labors. And since in this earthly military service people exhaust so much labor to procure things that can perish in the same manner in which they were obtained [Col. 0647B], surely no labor must be refused by us, for whom that is acquired which can in no way be lost.

For God, who brought human beings into existence for this military service, willed them to stand unencumbered in the battle line and, with minds keenly intent [Col. 0648A], to keep watch against the snares or open assaults of a single enemy. Like skilled and experienced commanders, he seeks to capture us by various arts, raging against each person according to his nature and character. Into some he sends insatiable greed, so that, bound to their riches as though by fetters, they may be driven from the path of truth. Others he inflames with the goads of anger, so that, intent on doing harm instead, they may be turned away from the contemplation of God. Others he plunges into immoderate lusts, so that, serving pleasure and the body, they cannot look toward virtue. Into others he breathes envy, so that, occupied with torments of their own making, they think of nothing except the happiness of those whom they hate. Others he puffs up with ambitions. These are the people who direct all the labor and concern of their lives toward holding public offices, so that they may mark the *fasti* and bestow their names upon the years.

The greed of some aims higher—not merely to govern provinces [Col. 0648B] with a temporal sword, but to wish themselves called lords of the entire human race with unlimited and perpetual power. Those whom he sees to be devout he entangles in various religions, so as to make them impious. Before the eyes of those who seek wisdom, however, he thrusts philosophy [Col. 0649A], so that he may blind them with the appearance of light—

Thirteen recent manuscripts and seventeen printed editions have “I shall begin.” But likewise in Book III, ch. 8: “before I begin to speak.”

>

Yet although no one can teach the root of virtue, which lies either in a naturally benign disposition itself or in the operation of divine grace, we can nevertheless learn its boundaries, attributes, and circumstances only from prudent teachers.
>
