> **But knowledge, etc.** This argument is not so much true as plausible. For faith, which in Plato’s *Theaetetus* is true knowledge of God, is a virtue; yet faith, as Paul wrote to the Romans, comes from hearing. Therefore it must be considered more carefully to what extent it is, or is not, within us. If we believe those philosophers that our learning is nothing other than recollection, we shall readily understand that there is something within us that is awakened by teaching, which the dialecticians call φυσικὴ δύναμις (*physikē dynamis*, “natural capacity”) and the moral philosophers φυσικὴ ἀρετή (*physikē aretē*, “natural virtue”). I pass over the fact that heavenly teaching does not enter us merely because a teacher instructs us from without and kindles the mind’s light through his teaching, unless the heavenly teacher at the same time penetrates our hearts by a certain hidden power—any more than true virtue itself can enter them, which no one but the sanctifier can form in human hearts. So far is that virtue from being within our own power that whatever is in us from ourselves has no efficacy for salvation unless it has been corrected and reformed by the divine power through regeneration.

—lest anyone comprehend and retain the truth. Thus he has blocked every approach for human beings and obstructed the paths, rejoicing in widespread errors. So that we might dispel these errors and conquer the very author of evils, God has enlightened us and armed us with true and heavenly virtue, which I must now discuss.

## CHAPTER V. On False Virtue and True Virtue, and on Knowledge

But before I begin to explain the individual virtues, virtue itself must be defined, since the philosophers did not correctly define what it was, in what matters it consisted, what work it performed, or what duty it possessed. They therefore retained only the name, but lost its power, principle, and effect. Whatever they are accustomed to say in defining virtue is collected and set forth by Lucilius in a few verses, [Col. 0649B] which I prefer to quote, so that I may not become longer than necessary by refuting the opinions of many:

> Virtue, Albinus, is to pay the true price;  
> To attend to the affairs among which we act and live.  
> Virtue for a human being is to know what each thing contains.  
> Virtue for a human being is to know what is right, useful, and honorable;  
> What is good, and likewise what is evil; what is useless, base, and dishonorable.  
> Virtue is to know the end and limit of what is to be sought.  
> [Col. 0650A] Virtue is to be able to assign wealth its proper value.  
> Virtue is to give to honor what is truly owed to it;  
> To be the foe and enemy of people and practices that are evil;  
> And, conversely, the defender of people and practices that are good;  
> To hold these in high regard, wish them well, and live as their friend;  
> Furthermore, to regard the advantages of one’s country as coming first,  
> Then those of one’s parents, and our own as third and last.

From these definitions, which the poet briefly comprised, Marcus Tullius derived the duties of life, following Panaetius the Stoic, and enclosed them within three volumes.

We shall soon see how false these statements are, so that it may become evident how much divine favor has bestowed upon us by revealing the truth to us. He said that virtue is to know what is good and evil, what is base and honorable, what is useful and what is not. He could have expressed it more briefly if he had mentioned only good and evil, because nothing can be useful or honorable without also being good, and nothing useless or base without also being evil [Col. 0650B]. This also seems true to the philosophers, and Cicero himself demonstrates it in the third book of the work mentioned above.

But knowledge cannot be virtue, because it is not within us but comes to us from outside. What can pass from one person to another is not virtue, because each person’s virtue is his own. Knowledge, therefore, is the benefit of another [Col. 0651A], because it is founded upon hearing. Virtue is wholly our own—

> **Note: [Col. 0651C] Variorum Notes on columns 651–652**
>
> **Virtue is wholly our own.** He teaches something otherwise true from insufficiently solid foundations. For Paul indeed wished to do right, as the spirit directed him, but did not find within himself the power to accomplish it; likewise, flesh and blood had not revealed true wisdom to Peter. We should therefore establish that virtue and knowledge either alike exist in a person or alike do not. The light of knowledge exists in a person if it has been kindled from heaven; likewise, true virtue is not within us unless it has been awakened in us by divine power. Yet while we live in this flesh it is so weak that it often succumbs in conflict and possesses no strength unless that strength is divinely supplied.
>
> [Col. 0651D] **Of doing good.** I restored this from four very ancient and excellent manuscripts: one Bologna, two Royal, and the Caucian. Fifteen other recent manuscripts have “doing good things”; one Royal and the Canterbury manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1468 read “doing a good thing”; the Tours manuscript, one Royal manuscript, and another Royal manuscript in a second hand read “doing well.”
>
> **In traveling along a road.** Twenty-eight older and better manuscripts, together with the Roman edition of 1470, read *celebrando*; eighteen editions read *celerando*, “hastening.” Cicero uses *celebrare viam* in *For Caelius* 4, and both “the crowdedness of the road” and “a much-traveled road” occur in the same Cicero. Lactantius uses “a frequented field” in *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*. —**In traveling along a road.** *Celebrare* sometimes means to frequent and to travel swiftly; hence Cicero several times says *celebrare viam*. Jerome follows Cicero in Letter 14 to Celantia, f. m. 109: “That road is frequented and trodden by many; this one is scarcely found by a few.” —Bünemann.
>
> **Strength is available.** I restored this from five editions and all the manuscripts except two recent Royal manuscripts, in which, as in eleven printed editions, it reads “they supply.”
>

>

>

>
> **Purity.** That is, chastity. Tacitus, *Annals* XIV.60: “Most persisted in defending their mistress Octavia’s purity … more chaste,” etc. Lactantius VI.24: “Let him look chastely upon another man’s wife.” —Bünemann.
>
> **Let us do right things.** The Tours manuscript and one Colbert manuscript read “let us act rightly.”
>

“Let me define.” I have restored this reading from the old Roman edition and all the manuscripts except one Clermont manuscript, which has “let them be defined”; thirteen printed editions have “let us define.”

“Because almost.” I have restored this from almost all the manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470. Six recent manuscripts and thirteen editions have “because”; the Paris edition, “fully”; one recent Royal manuscript, “plainly”; Junius, “well.”]

because it is situated in the will to do good. Therefore, just as in making a journey it is no advantage to know the road unless the effort and strength needed for walking are available, so knowledge is of no advantage if one’s own virtue is lacking. For even those who sin generally perceive, though not perfectly, what is good and what is evil; and whenever they do anything wickedly, they know that they are sinning and therefore try to conceal it. But although they are not deceived about the nature of good and evil, they are overcome by evil desire and so commit sin, because virtue—that is, an upright and honorable desire to act—is lacking in them.

From this, therefore, it is apparent that knowledge of good and evil is one thing and virtue another, since knowledge can exist without virtue, as it did in very many philosophers. In this matter, since failure to do what you know you should do is rightly counted as guilt, [Col. 0651B] a corrupt will and a vicious disposition, which ignorance cannot excuse, will rightly be punished. Therefore, just as virtue is not knowing good and evil, so virtue is doing good and not doing evil. Yet knowledge is joined to virtue in such a way that knowledge precedes virtue and virtue follows knowledge, because cognition is of no advantage unless action follows it.

Horace, therefore, puts it somewhat better:

> Virtue is to flee vice; and the beginning of wisdom  
> Is to have escaped folly.

But he speaks ineptly in defining virtue by its contrary, as if he were to say: “Good is that which is not evil.” For when I do not know what virtue is, neither do I know what vice is. Both, therefore, require definition, because the nature of the matter is such that both must either be understood or not understood. [Col. 0651C]

But let us do what he ought to have done. Virtue is [Col. 0652A] to restrain anger, curb desire, and check lust; for this is to flee vice. Almost everything done unjustly and wickedly arises from these passions. For if the impulse of that agitation called anger is blunted, all evil conflicts among human beings will be quieted: no one will plot against another, and no one will leap forward to do harm. Likewise, if desire is moderated, no one will range violently over land and sea, and no one will lead an army in order to seize and devastate the property of others. Likewise, if the heat of lusts is suppressed, every age and sex will preserve its chastity (*sanctitas*); no one will either suffer or commit anything shameful.

Thus, when these agitations have been calmed by virtue, every crime and disgraceful deed will be removed from human life and conduct. This calming of agitations and passions has as its purpose that we should do everything rightly. The whole [Col. 0652B] duty of virtue, therefore, is not to sin. Certainly no one who does not know God can fulfill this duty, since ignorance of him from whom good things arise must necessarily drive an imprudent person into vices. And so, to define more briefly and significantly the chief duties of both things: knowledge is to know God; virtue is to worship him. Wisdom is contained in the former, justice in the latter.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Highest Good and Virtue, and on Knowledge and Justice

I have stated first that knowledge of the good is not virtue, and then what virtue is and wherein it consists. It follows that I should also show briefly that the philosophers did not know what good and evil are, [Col. 0652C] because this was almost fully demonstrated in the third book, when I discussed the Highest Good. [Col. 0653A]

[Col. 0653A] [Note: [Col. 0653C] [Various Editors’ Notes on columns 653–654]

Moreover, because they did not know what the highest was, they must necessarily have erred concerning the other good and evil things that are not highest; for no one who does not grasp the fountain from which they descend can examine them with true judgment. Now the fountain of good things is God, while the fountain of evil things is that other being, namely the perpetual enemy of the divine name, of whom we have often spoken. Good and evil arise from these two principles. Those things which come from God have the purpose of procuring immortality, which is the Highest Good; but those which come from that other being have the function of turning a person away from heavenly things, plunging him into earthly things, and consigning him to eternal punishment, which is the highest evil.

Is there therefore any doubt that all those men were ignorant of what good and evil were, since they knew neither God nor God’s adversary? And so they referred the end [Col. 0653B] of good things to the body and to this brief life, which must of course be dissolved and perish; they advanced no farther. But all their precepts and all the things they present as goods cling to the earth and lie upon the ground, since they die together with the body, which is earth. For they relate not to procuring life for a human being, but to seeking or increasing wealth, honors, glory, and power—all of which are mortal, just as mortal as the person who labored to obtain them for himself. Hence the saying:

> Virtue is to know the limit and measure of acquiring property.

For they prescribe by what methods and arts a private fortune is to be acquired, because they see that it is commonly acquired by evil means. But virtue of this kind is not the objective set before the wise person. For acquiring wealth is not virtue, since neither its [Col. 0653C] discovery nor its possession lies within our power. Consequently, both its acquisition and its attainment come more easily to the evil than to the good. Virtue, therefore, cannot consist in seeking those things in contempt of which the force and principle of virtue become apparent; nor will virtue take refuge in those very things which it longs to tread underfoot and crush with a great and lofty spirit. Nor is it right for a soul intent upon heavenly goods to be turned away from its immortal works [Col. 0654A] in order to acquire these fragile things for itself. Rather, the principle of virtue consists especially in acquiring those things which neither any human being nor death itself can take away from us.

Since this is so, the next statement is true:

> Virtue is to be able to pay wealth its proper price.

This verse signifies almost the same thing as the first two. But neither the poet himself nor any of the philosophers could know the price itself—either its nature or what it was. For by this the poet, and all those whom he followed, understood using wealth rightly, that is, being thrifty: not furnishing banquets extravagantly, not giving recklessly, and not squandering one’s private fortune on superfluous or shameful things.

[Col. 0654B] Someone may perhaps say: “What about you? Do you deny that this is virtue?” I certainly do not deny it, for if I did I might appear to approve its contrary. But I deny that it is true virtue, because it is not heavenly but wholly earthly, seeing that it accomplishes nothing except what remains on earth. What it means to use wealth rightly, and what fruit should be sought from riches, I shall explain more openly when I begin to speak about the duty of piety.

The remaining statements that follow, however, are in no way true. For declaring hostility against the wicked or undertaking the defense of the good can be common even to evil men. Some, by feigned integrity, pave a path to power for themselves and perform many things that good men commonly perform—all the more readily because they do them for the sake of deception. Would that it were as easy to exhibit goodness as it is to simulate it! But when such men have begun [Col. 0654C] to possess the object of their design and desire and have attained the highest degree of power, then, casting off their disguise, they reveal their true character. They seize, violate, and harass everything; they persecute those very good people whose cause they had undertaken, and cut away the steps by which they themselves ascended, [Col. 0655A] lest anyone be able to imitate them against themselves.

Nevertheless, let us suppose that this duty—to defend the good—belongs only to the good. Undertaking it is easy; fulfilling it is difficult, because once you have committed yourself to contest and conflict, victory lies in God’s power, not your own. And wicked men are generally stronger than the good both in numbers and in conspiracy, so that overcoming them requires not so much virtue as good fortune. Does anyone not know how often the better [Col. 0655A] [Note: [Col. 0655C] [Various Editors’ Notes on columns 655–656]

“Does anyone not know how often the better,” etc. I have restored this from five old editions and twenty manuscripts, among which are the very old first Bologna and two Royal manuscripts.

“Gnaeus Pompey.” Four Royal, three Colbert, and two Clermont manuscripts have *Gneius*; Junius, one Colbert manuscript, and the Aldine, Paris, Junt., Crat., and Graph. editions have “For Gnaeus Pompey”; Ultr. and Brun. have “For when Pompey.” On Gnaeus Pompey’s love for the republic, see Plutarch, Appian of Alexandria, and especially Cicero’s letters throughout.

“The same man.” I have restored this from all the manuscripts and the old Roman and Betuleius editions. The others read, “He nevertheless, when defeated.”

“Perished.” Thus almost all manuscripts and printed editions. Three Royal manuscripts, Junius, and five old editions have “is killed”; one Colbert manuscript has “fell.”

“By Egyptian eunuchs.” He means the royal eunuch Pothinus, who administered the kingdom in place of the youthful Ptolemy. BETULEIUS.

“If concord among human beings is abolished, there is no virtue whatsoever.” The word “virtue” is absent from eight Royal, six Colbert, Cauc., Junius, and ten other witnesses. Fourteen manuscripts read “nothing” instead of “no.”

“The advantages of the fatherland.” The law of nature or humanity binds and unites the entire human race; whoever violates it overthrows nature itself. Those who, for the sake of their own advantage, take away what properly belongs to others sin against this law. According to Cicero, this is more contrary to nature itself than death, pain, or any other evils. From this it may be inferred that this human law is absolutely nothing other than the law of nations; whoever destroys it must also be thought to destroy every association of the human race. For no law is to be regarded as just if it is either established in fraud of nature or does not flow from the eternal law. Hence all privileges introduced contrary to the equality of human association are also incompatible with equity. By means of this note the whole of this passage in Lactantius, which confuses just defense with unjust aggression, should be corrected.

and more just side has been defeated? Hence cruel dominations over citizens have always arisen. All history is full of examples, but we shall be content with one. Gnaeus Pompey wished to be a defender of good men, since he took up arms for the republic, the Senate, and liberty. Yet the same man, when defeated, perished together with liberty itself; beheaded [Col. 0655B] by Egyptian eunuchs, he was cast away unburied.

It is therefore not virtue either to be an enemy of the wicked or to be a defender of the good, because virtue cannot be subjected to uncertain contingencies.

> Moreover, to regard the advantages of one’s fatherland as foremost for oneself.

If concord among human beings is abolished, there is no virtue whatsoever. For what are the advantages of one’s fatherland except the disadvantages of another state or nation? They consist in extending borders violently taken from others, enlarging dominion, and making taxes greater. All these are certainly not virtues, but the overthrow of virtues. For above all, the bond of human society is abolished; innocence is abolished; [Col. 0655C] abstention from the property of others is abolished; and finally justice itself is abolished—[Col. 0656A] justice, which cannot endure the division of the human race and which, wherever weapons flash, must necessarily be driven away and banished.

For Cicero’s statement is true:

> Those who say that account must be taken of citizens but deny that it must be taken of foreigners destroy the common society of the human race; and when that has been abolished, beneficence, generosity, goodness, and justice are utterly abolished.

For how can one be just who harms, who hates, who plunders, who kills? Yet all these things are done by those who strive to benefit their fatherland. For those who consider nothing useful and nothing advantageous except what can be grasped by the hand do not understand what this very “benefiting” means; yet that alone cannot truly be grasped, because it can be taken away.

Therefore, whoever acquires these so-called goods for his fatherland—that is, whoever has destroyed cities, annihilated nations, filled the treasury with money, seized lands, and made his fellow citizens wealthier [Col. 0656B]—is extolled to heaven with praises; in him the highest and perfect virtue is thought to reside. This error belongs not only to the people and the uneducated, but also to the philosophers, who even provide precepts for injustice, lest folly and wickedness be deprived of the authority of doctrine. And so, when they discuss duties pertaining to military affairs, their whole discourse is adapted neither to justice nor to true virtue, but to this life and to civil custom. Both the facts themselves and Cicero’s own testimony show that this is not justice:

> “But,” he says, “we possess no solid and clearly expressed likeness of true law and genuine justice. We employ a shadow and images; and would that we followed even those! For they are derived from the best examples of nature and truth.” [Col. 0656C–0657A]

[Col. 0657A] [Note: [Col. 0657B] [Various Editors’ Notes on columns 657–658]

“From the best examples of nature and truth.” Thus all Lactantius’s manuscripts and editions, so far as I know. Some editions of Cicero have “from the best principles of nature and examples of truth,” which is more correct. Some editions, however, do not contain the word *principiis*, “principles.”

[Col. 0657C] “Or when Fabricius or Aristides is called just, an example of courage is sought from those men, or of justice from these men, as though from a wise man.” I have emended and restored this passage not only from eight Royal, four Colbert, and other manuscripts, but also from Cicero, deleting the word “brave” after “Fabricius,” so that “the former” refers to the two Decii and the two Scipios, whom Cicero had just mentioned as brave men. The passage occurs thus in Cicero, *On Duties*, Book III, chapter 4: “Nor indeed, when the two Decii or the two Scipios are commemorated as brave men, or when Fabricius or Aristides is called just, is an example of courage sought from the former or of justice from the latter as though from a wise man,” etc. From this you see that Cicero introduces Fabricius not as an example of Courage, but of Justice. Hence the word “brave” appears superfluous here, and the passage should be restored from Cicero. From ISAEUS. — “Or when Fabricius.” Heumann wishes to read “nor when Fabricius.”

“Cato and Laelius.” On the latter, see Cicero himself in *Laelius, or On Friendship*, and on the former in *Cato, or On Old Age*. See above, Book V, chapter 18.

“Of the wise.” Thus the manuscripts, except two Brun. manuscripts and four editions, which have “of wisdom.” One recent Royal manuscript and the Roman edition of 1470 have the erroneous “wisdom”; three editions have “of wise men.”

“If therefore even the philosophers.” I added “therefore” from all the manuscripts and twelve common editions.

“Unless he is just and wise.” After these words I added, from twelve editions and all the manuscripts except three, “But no one is just and wise,” which is absent from one Royal, one old Bologna, and one Sorbonne manuscript. The last two of these and four editions have “because no one is”; one Royal manuscript has “no one is.”

“For all those men.” I restored “For” from the two old Roman editions, Isaeus, and Cellarius, as well as from all manuscripts except one recent Royal manuscript, which has “Now,” as do fifteen printed editions.

“Schools of learning.” This must be read on the authority of all the manuscripts and twelve editions. Several common editions corruptly read “pupils,” evidently through the fault of printers or copyists, as is clear from the following feminine forms, “unlike and diverse.” [Col. 0658B] If Lactantius had written “pupils,” the following words could not have been expressed in the feminine gender. Moreover, the author’s purpose also makes the proper reading clear: the pupils are carried toward destruction not because of the variety of the pupils themselves, but because of the variety of the schools of learning. GALLAEUS.

“Unlike in human life.” One Colbert manuscript and seven editions have “in a human being’s life.”

“Which they may seize upon.” I have restored this from the very old Bologna manuscript, two Royal manuscripts, Cauc., four recent Royal manuscripts, four Colbert manuscripts, others, and three old editions. Seven manuscripts and fourteen common editions have “which they seize upon.”

“The forerunner of that road.” Thus almost all editions and manuscripts, among which are the oldest and best. This is the correct reading because Lactantius is speaking of being led into deception, something that can be said more appropriately of a “forerunner” than of a “traverser,” the reading of some manuscripts and editions.

“Displayed.” The first old Bologna manuscript alone has “showed.”

“That immortal mystery of his.” The first old Bologna manuscript has “immortality, thus the mystery.” “For God, in order that that immortal mystery of his,” etc. The passage is very obscure, says Thomasius, and at first sight Lactantius seems to make God the author of shameful and evil things. But the passage must be understood from what he said earlier in the same chapter, and especially from the final chapter of the preceding book.

He therefore says that God placed in his road those things commonly regarded as shameful or evil, such as crosses, reproaches, scourging, and death. Why? First, so that the elect might be tested; then, so that many who were seeking wisdom, upon seeing Christians steadfastly endure every torment and death itself for the religion and discipline they had embraced, might inquire what that discipline was to which they professed themselves devoted. Thus those who had turned away from wisdom and truth—that is, from the true doctrine of the Christians—yet were seeking wisdom without any guide and did not know how to seek it, fell into the very thing they wished to avoid and flee: namely, the Christian religion and wisdom itself, or those same torments and crosses which they had previously resolved to avoid.

Justin, philosopher and martyr, indeed taught this by his own example. He says of himself that, while he delighted in Plato’s philosophy, [Col. 0659C] he heard that many of our martyrs were meeting death with the greatest steadfastness for the Christian religion, and therefore wished to learn about the religion for which they were dying so willingly. When he had understood it most perfectly, he afterward did not hesitate to pour out his own life most willingly for the same cause, experiencing in himself what he had previously admired in others. We write these things in order to clear Lactantius of every error, lest it be said that this most weighty author made God the author of evil—an error from which, on the evidence of other passages in this writer, he appears to us to be free.

— “His mystery might be concealed.” Lactantius refers us to the preceding book, namely the fifth, where chapter 18 says: “For this reason God willed virtue itself to be concealed beneath the guise of folly, so that the mystery of his truth and religion might remain secret.” What is said in our passage, “his mystery might be concealed,” is expressed in the fifth book as “so that the mystery … might remain secret.” He says the same in Book IV, chapter 2: [Col. 0659D] “Under the veil of folly, lest the mystery of his divine work lie exposed, God concealed the treasure of wisdom and truth.” Likewise, chapter 5: “Many disdain and reject the truth hidden beneath the veil of folly.” BUN.]

Therefore, what they regarded as justice is a shadow and image of justice. What of wisdom? Does Cicero not likewise confess that none exists among the philosophers?

> “Or,” he says, “when Fabricius or Aristides is called just, an example of courage is sought from those men, or of justice from these men, as though from a wise man. For none of these men was wise in the sense in which we wish a wise man to be understood. Nor were those who were regarded and called wise—Marcus Cato and Gaius Laelius—truly wise; nor indeed were the Seven. But through their frequent fulfillment of intermediate duties, they bore a certain likeness and appearance of wise men.”

If, therefore, by their own confession wisdom has been taken away even from the philosophers, and justice has been taken away from those who were regarded as just, then all those descriptions of virtue [Col. 0657B] must necessarily be false; for no one can know what true virtue is unless he is just and wise. But no one is just and wise unless God has instructed him through heavenly precepts.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Road of Error and Truth: That the Latter Is Simple, Narrow, and Steep, and Has God as Its Guide

For all those men who are considered wise because of the acknowledged folly of others [Col. 0658A] are led on by the appearance of virtue and grasp shadows and images, but nothing true. This happens because that deceptive road which leads to destruction has many tracks, owing to the variety of pursuits and schools of learning, which are unlike and diverse in human life. For just as that road of wisdom possesses something resembling folly, as we demonstrated in the preceding book, so this road, although it belongs wholly to folly, possesses something resembling wisdom which those who recognize the common folly may seize upon. Just as it has manifest vices, so it has something that appears similar to virtue; just as it has open crime, so it has a certain image and appearance of justice.

For how could the forerunner of that road, whose entire force and power consists in deceiving, lead everyone into deception [Col. 0658B] unless he displayed plausible things to human beings? For God, in order that that immortal mystery of his might remain concealed, placed in his own road things which human beings would disdain as evil and shameful, so that, having turned away from wisdom and truth—which they were seeking without any guide—they might fall into the very thing they wished to avoid and flee. Accordingly, he made that road of destruction and death manifold, either because there are many kinds of life or because there are many gods who are worshiped.

The guide of this road is a transgressor and deceiver. In order to make it appear that there is some distinction between false and true, evil and good, he leads the luxurious by one way and those called thrifty by another; the uneducated by one and the learned by another; the sluggish by one and the energetic by another; [Col. 0659A] [Note: [Col. 0659D] [Various Editors’ Notes on columns 659–660]

“The sluggish by one and the energetic by another.” Goth. has “the inept by one and the energetic by another”—ineptly. The remaining witnesses rightly have “the sluggish,” for the strong are distinguished from the sluggish. The sluggish are opposed to the brave and energetic. Compare the note on Book VI, chapter 14: “the peaceful from the sluggish”; and chapter 18: “He will be regarded as idle and sluggish,” where “brave and energetic” is likewise opposed to it. Thus in Valerius Maximus, Book VIII, chapter 8, the sluggish and the energetic are opposed to one another. Boethius, Book IV, Meter 7: “Go now, brave men … Why, you sluggish men, do you not turn your backs?” BUN.

“Over rugged places.” Thus I write on the authority of the two very old Bologna manuscripts, Betuleius, and the first hand of one Royal-Puteanus manuscript. The word occurs in Virgil and Quintilian. Our reading is supported by the old Roman edition of 1468, which corruptly has *fragrosa*. Many other recent manuscripts and editions have *confragrosa*.

[Col. 0660C] “Are not other roads.” The old Bologna manuscript alone has “are not steep.”

“Are carried back.” That is, “are carried back again.” Francius.

“One seat.” The first old Bologna manuscript alone, together with four recent editions, adds “pleasant,” a word which appears deserving of rejection. — “It has one seat and is simple.” “Simple” is used here in opposition to the deceptive road, which was said above to have many tracks; hence Lactantius calls that road manifold. BUN.

“Because.” Heumann reads “whereby.”

“Nor do they follow any guide.” I restored the final word “any,” neglected by five recent editions, from the other editions and all the manuscripts except the first old Bologna manuscript, which reads: “Nor do they follow a guide. This principle.” One recent Royal, one Colbert, and one Brun. manuscript have “that” instead of “any.”

“Must not follow a human being.” “Must” is absent from the first old Bologna manuscript.

“The sun is much brighter than this,” etc. I have restored this from three Royal manuscripts, two of which are among the oldest, two Colbert manuscripts, Goth., Marm., one Clermont manuscript, and with the support of two Royal and two Colbert manuscripts which read “is much brighter than the sun”; Brun. reads “much brighter than the sun is.” Four recent Royal, two Colbert, two Leipzig, one Clermont manuscript, and the editions have “is much more brightly than the sun.”

“Which we see with mortal flesh.” Thus the manuscripts and editions, except Pal. and six editions, which have “which we see in mortal flesh.”

“Thus he will direct.” I added these words from the manuscripts and most editions; they are absent from some printed editions.

“To the highest harbor of wisdom.” Thus I restored the text from the manuscripts and very many old editions. Six common editions have “to the highest point.”

“May direct.” David had already said: “Your word is a lamp to my feet.”

“Law.” Cicero similarly says in Book I of *On the Laws*: “Law is the highest reason, implanted in nature, which commands the things that must be done.”

“It is unlawful to supersede this law.” Thus read the very old first Royal manuscript, Ultr., Pal., Leipzig, Brun., and six editions. Latinius, Joan., Caucius, Betuleius, and Francius judge that the text should be emended accordingly. Others corruptly read “repeal,” “promulgate,” “propagate,” or “prolong.”

“To supersede.” According to Ulpian, a law is superseded (*obrogatur*) when an earlier law is abolished; it is partially repealed (*derogatur*) when part of the first law is abolished; it is supplemented (*subrogatur*) when something is added; it is repealed (*abrogatur*) when something is changed. SPARK. — This interpretation is Ulpian’s own.]

fools by one way and philosophers by another—and even the latter not by a single track. For those who do not reject pleasures or riches he separates only slightly from this public and crowded road; but those who wish either to follow virtue or to profess contempt for material things he drags over certain rugged precipices. Nevertheless, all those routes that display the appearance of good works are not other roads, but byways and paths. They indeed appear to branch off to the right from that common road, but at the very end they are all carried back to the same road and the same single outcome.

For there that guide unites everyone at the point where the good ought to have been separated from the evil, the brave [Col. 0659B] from the sluggish, and the wise from fools: namely, in the worship of the gods. There, because they have all been foolish without distinction, he slaughters them with a single blade and casts them headlong into death.

But this road—the road of truth, wisdom, virtue, and justice, all of which have one fountain, one power, and one seat—is simple, because with like-mindedness and the greatest concord we follow and worship one God. It is narrow, because virtue has been granted to fewer people; and it is steep, because the good, which is highest and most exalted, cannot be reached except with the greatest difficulty and labor.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Errors of the Philosophers and the Variety of Laws

[Col. 0659C] This is the road the philosophers seek; but they therefore [Col. 0660A] fail to find it because they seek it upon the earth, where it cannot appear. Thus they wander as though upon a vast sea and do not understand where they are being carried, because they neither discern the road nor follow any guide. For this road of life must be sought in the same manner in which ships seek their course on the open sea: unless they observe some heavenly light, they wander along uncertain courses.

But whoever strives to keep to the road’s straight course must look not toward the earth but toward heaven; and, to speak more plainly, he must follow not a human being but God; serve not these earthly images but the heavenly God; refer all things not to the body but to the mind; and devote his labor not to this life but to eternal life. Therefore, if you always direct your eyes toward heaven, observe where the sun rises, and take it as the guide of your life just as of a ship, your feet will of their own accord [Col. 0660B] be directed onto the road. And that heavenly light, which to sound minds is much brighter than this sun which we see with mortal flesh, will so direct and govern you that it will bring you without any error to the highest harbor of wisdom and virtue.

The law of God, therefore, which directs us onto this journey, must be accepted: that holy and heavenly law which Marcus Tullius, in the third book of *On the Republic*, depicted in language almost divine. To avoid speaking at greater length, I have appended his own words:

> “There is indeed a true law: right reason, consonant with nature, diffused among all, constant and everlasting. By commanding, it calls us to duty; by forbidding, it deters us from wrongdoing. Yet it neither commands nor forbids the upright in vain, nor moves the wicked by commanding or forbidding. [Col. 0660C] It is unlawful to supersede this law, nor is it permissible to detract anything from it, nor can it be repealed in its entirety. Neither the Senate nor the people can release us from this law. Nor need any other expounder or interpreter of it be sought. There will not be one law at Rome and another at Athens,” [Col. 0661A]

[Col. 0661A] [Note: [Col. 0661C] [Various Editors’ Notes on columns 661–662]

“There will not be one law at Rome and another at Athens.” This is evidently a characterization of civil law—not merely that of one commonwealth but also that of another. On this see § *Sed jus*, *Institutes*, *On Natural, Gentile, and Civil Law*, and the Pontifical *Decretals*, chapter 2, distinction 1.

“But both all nations.” The first old Bologna manuscript has “for every nation.” “Will embrace; and there will be one.” The same Bologna manuscript has “and if each person embraces it, there will be one.” Cicero therefore says in Book II of *On the Laws*, concerning natural law: “I see that this, then, was the opinion of the wisest men: that law was neither contrived by human intelligence nor constituted by any decree of peoples, but was something eternal that governed the whole world through the wisdom of commanding and forbidding.”

Nevertheless, in accordance with Thomasius’s view, we do not wish to deprive the reader of the old reading of the Bologna codex, which runs as follows: “but for every nation and at every time there is one everlasting and immutable law; and if each person embraces it, there will be one common teacher, as it were.” These words also present an excellent sense. [Col. 0661D]

“Author.” Thus Demosthenes, speaking of civil law, when he says, **πάντα τὸν νόμον εὕρημα καὶ δῶρον θεῶν εἶναι**, “that every law is an invention and gift of the gods,” signifies that such laws flow from natural law and are therefore true and must be abolished at no time. Other laws, which do not take their origin from natural law, may be either disregarded or repealed without offense. From this book it will readily be understood which laws do not emanate from this eternal law: namely, those which conflict with true religion and love of one’s neighbor. Because these laws rest principally upon force, they do not deserve the name “law,” either among the Greeks or among the Latins. For among the latter *lex* signifies a selection, the word evidently deriving from *legere*, “to choose”; among the former, *νόμος* derives **ἀπὸ τοῦ νέμειν**, “from distributing,” because it renders to each person what is his own. “We owe nothing to anyone,” says the Apostle, “except love.” For “the end of the commandment is love,” 1 Timothy, chapter 1. **Having despised.** Thus I have emended from the very oldest Bononian and Royal manuscripts and very many others, as well as three old editions. But two recent Royal manuscripts, two Colbert manuscripts, and two Clairvaux manuscripts have *aspernatur* [“he despises”]; ten printed editions, *aspernabitur* [“he will despise”].

**Could.** So very many manuscripts, among them the oldest Bononian, eight Royal, Junius, four Colbert, Brunck, and five old editions. Six recent manuscripts and twelve common editions: *may be able*.

**Unwitting.** Thus I have restored it from almost all manuscripts and two old editions. In one recent Royal manuscript, one Colbert manuscript, and fourteen printed editions it is *unwittingly*. Old French translation: “Those who, without knowing it, speak true things.”

**As though divining, inspired by some spirit.** For *divining*, one Leipzig manuscript has *mad*. One Colbert manuscript, one Clairvaux manuscript, and Brunck: “as though divining, instructed by some spirit.” Junius and five printed editions: “as though instructed by a divine spirit.” See above, in the same book, at the beginning of chapter 1: “with a divine spirit instructing.” Of the eternal law, St Augustine spoke more excellently than other ecclesiastical writers in Book I of *On Free Choice of the Will*.

**Would have been.** One Colbert manuscript: *was*; three Royal manuscripts and thirteen editions: *would be*.

**Of this law.** One old Bononian manuscript and one recent Royal manuscript: *of which*.

**To worship him alone.** Exodus 20; Deuteronomy 5; Psalm 80.

**That he may serve foreign gods.** Brunck: *others*. One old Bononian manuscript: “causes him to serve foreign gods.”

**Of goodness. Or if.** Brunck manuscript and Betuleius edition: “of goodness and truth. Or if”; one old Bononian manuscript: “of goodness. Lest if.”

**He will wish to pursue the justice of God.** Heumann wishes the word *God* deleted; and it could be absent, since Lactantius often says simply “to pursue justice” [*iustitiam sequi*], even when speaking of the divine, as in Book II, ch. 17, and Book VII, ch. 11. But all copies have it here. Compare below. BUNEMAN.

**Who, through the Fetiales, declared wars.** In two recent Royal manuscripts, Leipzig, Utrecht, Brunck: “who frequently, through the Fetiales, etc.” One old Bononian manuscript: “who, by declaring treacherous wars.” The Fetiales’ office was to ensure that no unjust war was inflicted upon anyone; if the Romans had been injured, they sent envoys to demand restitution of their right; and if the allied party despised the envoys or their words, then they made demands and declared war. They likewise concluded peace, or rendered an unlawful peace void; they also judged injuries done to envoys, etc. On them see Dionysius and Pliny. GALLAEUS.

**And committing injuries lawfully.** This is the reading of almost all manuscripts, two old Roman editions, Isaeus, Cellarius, and Walch. In Caucasianus, Emendatus, Cantabrigianus, and eleven printed editions one reads *inflicting*. *Lawfully* means according to Roman laws.

**By coveting what belongs to others.** Leipzig manuscripts 2 and 3, Reimmann, Tornæsius 1587, [Col. 0663B] 1613, Geneva 1630: “by taking what belongs to others.” I prefer the former. Book V, ch. 22: “He covets what belongs to others and seizes, through injustice, the things he has coveted.” Compare the note to Book V, ch. 22. BUNEMAN.]

“...now one thing, hereafter another; but one law, eternal and immutable, shall bind all nations and at every time; and there shall be, as it were, one common master and ruler of all, God—the inventor, judge, and giver of this law. Whoever does not obey him will flee from himself; and, having despised human nature, will for that very reason pay the greatest penalties, even if he has escaped the other punishments which are thought to exist.”

Who, knowing the mystery of God, could set forth God’s law so expressively as this man, far removed from knowledge of the truth, expressed it? [Col. 0661B] For my part, I think that those who unwittingly speak truths ought to be regarded as though they were divining, inspired by some spirit. And if, just as he perceived the force and rationale of the holy law, he had also known or explained in what precepts the law itself consists, he would not have discharged the office of a philosopher, but of a prophet. Since he could not do this, it must be done by us, to whom the law itself has been delivered by that one master and ruler of all, God.

[Col. 0662A] ## Chapter IX. On the Law and Commandment of God; on Mercy; and on the Error of Philosophers

The first head of this law is to know God himself, to obey him alone, and to worship him alone. For one who does not know God, the parent of his own soul, cannot possess human reason; and that is the greatest impiety. This ignorance causes him to serve foreign gods, than which nothing more criminal can be committed. From this point the descent to wickedness is already easy, through ignorance of the true and unique good; for God, whom he refuses to know, is himself the fountain of goodness. Or if he wishes to pursue the justice of God, yet being ignorant of divine right, [Col. 0662B] he embraces the laws of his own nation as true law; laws which justice certainly did not discover, but expediency did. For why have diverse and varying laws been established among all peoples, except because each nation enacted for itself what it judged useful to its own affairs? But how far expediency departs from justice is taught by the Roman people itself, which, by declaring wars through the Fetiales, by committing injuries lawfully, always coveting and seizing what belonged to others, acquired possession for itself of the whole [Col. 0663A] world. Yet these men think themselves just [Col. 0663A]

> **These men think themselves just, if.** I added *if* from almost all manuscripts and printed editions. It is absent in the Cambridge manuscript and five editions. “Not therefore . . . .” One old Bononian manuscript: “Not on that account.”

> **The framers of the Twelve Tables.** The Decemvirs. Indeed, they were unjust, because, though appointed for one year for the purpose of framing laws, they seized the commonwealth by a kind of oligarchic force and refused to lay down either their magistracy or their army—especially Appius Claudius, who, with a tyranny worse than Sicilian tyranny, strove contrary to law and right to claim Verginia as a slave. On him see Pomponius, Book II of the *Digest*, “On the Origin of Law.” Read among historians Livy, Book V of *From the Founding of the City*; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Books X and XI; Valerius Maximus, Book VI, ch. 1; Florus, Book I, ch. 24; Eutropius, Book I, ch. 12; Orosius, Book II, ch. 13; Pliny, *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 21. In the work entitled *On the Delayed Vengeance of the Deity*, Plutarch recounts several trivial [Col. 0663D] and useless laws of the Athenians, Spartans, and Romans; Favorinus too, in Gellius, censured the Decemviral laws under the same designation. In his paraphrase Theophilus mentions certain laws which, though certainly very useful in one commonwealth, would be of no importance in another. BETULEIUS.
>
> **And he must necessarily be ignorant of justice itself.** That this is the proper reading is clear from the author’s aim and from all manuscripts except one Cambridge manuscript, in which, as also in seven editions, one reads: “and he must necessarily be ignorant of God himself.” The meaning of the reading which we follow in the text is clear and easy: he wishes to prove that the Romans, because they were ignorant of God, were likewise ignorant of justice itself. But the contrary would follow if one read, as in certain common editions, “whom whoever does not know must necessarily be ignorant of God himself”; this would by no means fit the foregoing argument.—“Whom whoever does not know, and justice itself.” Aldus, Fasiolus, Gryphius; Tornæsius, Betuleius, Thomasius, Thysius, and the Cambridge edition: “which justice whoever does not know must be ignorant of God himself.” But both Bononian manuscripts, Taxander, Penz, Junius, Leipzig, Gothanus, Reimmann, English, Roman, Rostock, Venice [Col. 0664C] 1471, 1472, both 1478 editions, 1490, 1493, 1497, Pierius, Parrhasius, Paris, Juntine, Cratander, Gymnasium, Isaeus, Gallæus, Spark, Walch, Heumann: “Whom whoever does not know, and justice itself.” BUNEMAN.

if they do nothing contrary to their own laws; though this also may be attributed to fear, if they refrain from crimes out of dread of present penalties. But let us grant, certainly, that they do by nature, or—as the philosopher says—of their own accord, what they are compelled to do by laws. Will they therefore be just because they obey the institutions of men, who themselves could either be mistaken or unjust? Such were those framers of the Twelve Tables, who certainly served public utility according to the conditions of their times. Civil law, therefore, which varies everywhere according to customs, is one thing; true justice, which God has set forth as uniform and simple for all, is another. Whoever does not know him must necessarily be ignorant of justice itself as well.

But let us suppose it possible that someone, by a natural and inborn goodness, might attain true virtues—such as Cimon is said to have been at Athens: he gave aid to the needy, invited the poor, and clothed the naked. Yet, since that one thing which is greatest—the recognition of God—is lacking, all those good things are already superfluous and empty, so that he has laboured in vain to attain them. For all his justice will be like a human body without a head: although all its limbs remain both in their proper places, and in form and arrangement, still, because that which is chief of all is absent, it is without both life and [Col. 0664A] every sensation. Thus those limbs have only the appearance of limbs, not their use—just as a head without a body has. Like it is the person who, though he is not ignorant of God, lives unjustly. For he has that alone which is supreme, but in vain, since he lacks virtues as though they were limbs.

Therefore, for a body to be living and sentient, both the recognition of God is necessary, as though it were the head, and all the virtues, as though they were the body. Thus a human being will become complete and alive; but the whole sum is nevertheless in the head. Although it cannot exist without all the limbs, it can exist without certain ones. It will indeed be a defective and weak living creature, yet it will live—like one who both knows God and sins in some respect. For God grants pardon for sins. Thus one may live without certain limbs, but in no way without a head. [Col. 0664B] This explains why philosophers, even if they are naturally good, nevertheless know nothing and understand nothing. All their learning and virtue are without a head, because they do not know God, who is the head of virtue and learning. Whoever does not acknowledge him, though he sees, is blind; though he hears, is deaf; though he speaks, is tongue-tied. But when he has known the creator and parent of things, then he will see, hear, and speak. For he has begun to have a head, in which all the senses are situated—namely, the eyes, ears, and tongue. For assuredly that person sees who has beheld with the eyes of the heart either the truth in which God is, or [Col. 0665A] God in whom truth is; that person hears who fastens divine utterances and life-giving precepts [Col. 0665A]

upon his breast; that person speaks who, discoursing of heavenly things, sets forth the virtue and majesty of the one God. Therefore, there is no doubt that whoever has not acknowledged God is impious; and all the virtues which he thinks that he possesses or maintains are found on that death-bearing path which is wholly one of darkness. Accordingly, no one has reason to congratulate himself if he has acquired these empty virtues; for not only must the person who lacks present goods be miserable, but the person who undertakes the greatest labours in his life in vain must also be foolish. For if hope of immortality is removed—the hope which God promises to those engaged in his Religion, and for the attainment of which virtue must be sought and whatever evils may happen must be endured—[Col. 0665B] it will surely be the greatest folly to wish to submit to virtues which vainly bring calamities and labours upon a human being. For if virtue is courageously to endure and undergo poverty, exile, pain, and death—things feared by others—what good, after all, does it possess in itself, that philosophers should say it is to be sought for its own sake? Clearly they delight in superfluous and empty punishments, though they are able to live peacefully.

For if souls are mortal, if virtue will come to nothing when the body is dissolved, why do we flee the goods bestowed upon us, as though ungrateful or unworthy to enjoy divine gifts? To possess these goods, one must live wickedly and impiously, because poverty follows virtue—that is, justice. Therefore, a person is not sane if, with no greater hope set before him, he prefers labours, tortures, and miseries to the goods which others [Col. 0665C] enjoy in life. But if virtue, as these men most rightly say, must be embraced because it is established that a human being is born for it, some greater hope must underlie it, bringing great and splendid consolation for the evils and labours which it belongs to virtue to bear. Nor can virtue, harsh as it is in itself, be considered a good in any other way than by compensating for its bitterness with a supreme good. [Col. 0666A] Likewise, one must abstain from these present goods only if there are other, greater goods for the sake of which it is worth both foregoing pleasures and enduring every evil. But there are no other such things, as I taught in the third book, except everlasting life. And who can bestow this except God, who himself set virtue before us? Therefore, the whole sum of things rests in the acknowledgment and worship of God. In this is all human hope and salvation; this is the first step of wisdom: that we know who is our true Father, pursue him alone with due filial devotion, obey him, serve him with the utmost devotion, and place every act, concern, and work in winning his favour.

## Chapter X. On Religion toward God and Mercy toward Human Beings; and on the Origin of the World

[Col. 0666B] I have said what is owed to God; I shall now say what must be given to a human being, although that very thing which you give to a human being is given to God, because a human being is God’s image. Yet the first duty of justice is union with God; the second, union with a human being. The former is called Religion; the latter is called mercy or humanity. This virtue belongs especially to the just and to worshippers of God, because it alone preserves the principle of common life. For God, who did not give wisdom to the other animals, generated them safer from attack and danger by their natural defenses. But because he formed the human being naked and frail, in order that he might rather equip him with wisdom, he gave him, besides other things, this feeling of affection: that one human being might protect, love, and cherish another, and both receive [Col. 0666C] and render aid against every danger. Humanity, therefore, is the highest bond among human beings. Whoever has broken it must be judged wicked and a parricide. For if we all spring from one human being whom God fashioned, we are certainly blood-relations; and therefore it must be considered the greatest crime to hate a human being, even a guilty one. For this reason God commanded that enmities should never be created by us and should always be removed: namely, so that we may soften those who are [Col. 0667A] our enemies by reminding them of their kinship. Likewise, if we have all been inspired and given life by one God, what else are we but brothers? Indeed, we are more closely joined by our souls than by our bodies. [Col. 0667A]

Therefore those who harm human beings, who despoil, torture, kill, and exterminate them contrary to the law of humanity and every sacred right, must be regarded as savage beasts.

Because of this bond of brotherhood, God teaches us never to do evil and always to do good. What this doing good is, he himself prescribes: to render aid to those brought low and in distress; [Col. 0667B] to share food with those who have none. For because God [Col. 0668A] is compassionate, he wished us to be a social creature. Therefore, in other human beings we ought to think of ourselves. We do not deserve to be delivered in danger if we do not come to others’ aid; we do not deserve help if we refuse it. Philosophers have no precepts for this part, since, captivated by the appearance of false virtue, they removed mercy from human life and, while wishing to heal, corrupted it. And although they themselves commonly admit that fellowship in human society must be maintained, they utterly separate themselves from it by the severity of their inhuman virtue. This error of those who think that nothing ought to be shared with anyone must therefore also be refuted here. They have advanced more than one origin and cause for the founding of cities. Some recount that human beings, born originally from the earth, while they led a wandering life through forests and fields, [Col. 0668B] were prey to beasts and stronger animals because they had no bond among themselves either of speech or of law, [Col. 0669A] but had leaves and grass for beds, caves and caverns for homes. they gradually perfected the practice of speaking. But since they did not see even the multitude itself safe against beasts, they also began to fortify towns, either to make their night’s rest safe, or to repel the raids and assaults of beasts not by fighting but by interposing embankments.

O intellects unworthy of human beings, which produced these absurdities! [Col. 0669B] O wretched and pitiable men, who committed their own folly to writings and memory! Although they saw that even dumb animals have an inborn capacity both to gather together, to seek one another, flee danger, avoid harm, and prepare beds and hiding places for themselves, they nevertheless supposed that human beings themselves could only have been instructed and learned by examples what they ought to fear, avoid, and do; or that they would never have come together or discovered speech unless beasts had eaten them. These things seemed mad to others, as they were, and they said that mauling by wild beasts was not the cause of coming together, but rather humanity itself: thus human beings had gathered among themselves because human nature shunned solitude and sought fellowship and society. [Col. 0669C] There is no great dispute between them. For the causes differ, but the matter is the same.

Both things, therefore, might have happened, since they are not incompatible; yet neither is in any way true. For human beings were not born from the earth across the whole earth, scattered abroad like seed from the teeth of some dragon, as poets tell; rather, one human being was fashioned by God, and from that one the whole earth was filled with the human race, by the same principle, of course, as again after the flood. This they certainly cannot deny. Therefore, no such gathering occurred in the beginning; nor has there ever been a human being on earth who did not speak beyond infancy, as anyone not lacking reason will understand. Yet let us suppose true the things which idle and foolish old men invent, so that we may refute them especially by their own judgments and arguments.

If human beings gathered together for this reason—namely, to protect their weakness by mutual [Col. 0670B] assistance—then help must be given to a human being who needs assistance. For since human beings entered into and sanctioned society with human beings for the sake of protection, to violate or fail to preserve that treaty struck among human beings from the beginning of their origin must be considered the greatest impiety. For one who withdraws from rendering assistance must necessarily withdraw himself also from receiving it, because the person who denies his own service to another thinks that he needs no one’s service. But one who separates and severs himself from the body must live not in a human manner, but after the fashion of beasts. And since this is impossible, the bond of human society must therefore be preserved by every means, because a human being cannot in any way live without another human being. The preservation of society is community: that is, rendering assistance so that we may be able to receive it.

But if, as those others argue, the gathering of human beings took place for the sake of humanity itself, then one human being certainly ought to acknowledge another. If those crude and still savage people did this, and did it before any system of speaking had been established, what should we think of civilized human beings, and of speech [Col. 0671A]

Misled by the ambiguity of this word, Lactantius unjustly attacks Cicero’s words in *On Duties* II.15: “Often one must share one’s property with suitable needy persons” [Col. 0673B]. In Lactantius’s age, *idonei homines* almost invariably meant no others than worthy and wealthy persons; hence he reproves this precept as crafty and Epicurean, as though one should share only with those able to repay, VI.11. ## CHAPTER XI. On the persons upon whom a benefit should be conferred

Humanity, then, must be preserved if we are to wish to be called human beings in the proper sense. And what else is it to preserve humanity itself but to love a human being because he is human and is the same as we are? Therefore discord and dissension are not in accordance with human nature. And Cicero’s statement is true, when he says that a person obedient to nature cannot harm another person. [Col. 0671B] Therefore, if harming a human being is contrary to nature, helping one must necessarily be in accordance with nature. Whoever does not do this strips himself of the name of man, because it is the duty of humanity to come to the aid of a person’s need and danger.

I ask, therefore, those who do not think that it belongs to a wise person to be moved or to pity: if a man were seized by some beast and begged for help from an armed man, would they think that he ought to be rescued, or not at all? They are not so shameless as to deny that what he asks and what humanity demands ought to be done. Likewise, if someone is surrounded by fire, crushed by a collapse, submerged in the sea, or swept away by a river, do they think it humane not to help? They are not themselves human if they think so. For no one can be free from exposure to dangers of this kind. [Col. 0671C] Indeed, they will say that it belongs both to a human being and to a brave man [Col. 0672A] to save one who is perishing.

If, therefore, in such cases as bring danger of death to a human being, they grant that it is humane to provide aid, what reason is there why, if a person is hungry, thirsty, or cold, they should not think that aid ought to be given? Although these conditions are by nature equivalent to those accidental emergencies and demand one and the same humanity, they nevertheless distinguish them, because they measure everything not by its true reality but by immediate advantage. For they hope that those whom they snatch from danger will return their favor. But, since they have no such hope concerning the needy, they think that whatever they bestow upon persons of that sort is lost.

From this comes that detestable saying of Plautus:

> He does ill who gives a beggar something to eat.  
> For what he gives is lost,  
> And he prolongs that man’s life for misery. [Col. 0672B]

But perhaps the poet spoke in character.

What does Marcus Tullius say in his books *On Duties*? Does he not advise the same thing: that one should not give liberally without qualification? For he says:

> “Liberality which is exercised from one’s estate exhausts the very fountain of kindness; thus kindness is destroyed by kindness: the more uses to which you have applied it, the less able you are to apply it to many persons.”

And shortly afterward he says:

> “What is more foolish than, when you gladly do something, to take care that you may be unable to do it longer?”

The professed teacher of wisdom, plainly, restrains people from humanity and advises them carefully to preserve their estate; he would have them prefer preserving their money-chest to preserving justice. Yet, recognizing this to be inhuman and impious, immediately in another chapter, as though seized by repentance, he says:

> “Yet sometimes one should give liberally; nor should this kind of kindness be wholly [Col. 0672C] rejected; and often one should share one’s estate with suitable needy persons.” [Col. 0673A]

Who are “suitable”? Obviously, those who can make restitution and return the favor. If Cicero were alive now, I should certainly cry out: “Here, Marcus Tullius, here you have departed from true justice; with a single word you have destroyed it, when you measured the duties of piety and humanity by advantage.”

[Col. 0673A] [Note: [Col. 0673C] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 673–674]

“You measured.” Lactantius used an archaism, *metitus es*, for *mensus es* (“you have measured”).—“You measured duties by advantage.” Reimmann and all editions also preserve this archaism, discussed by Vossius, *On the Life of the Latin Language* I.24 and *On Analogy* III.33. BUN. “As much as he can.” One Clarom., 2 recent Reg., and 2 Colb. manuscripts have *potes* (“you can”).

“You say that you possess.” I restored this from the two most ancient Reg. manuscripts. Seven recent manuscripts and 14 editions have *dicitis* (“you say,” plural). See below; Cicero, *On Duties* III.17.

Mercenary. Cicero, *On Laws* I.1 and *On Duties* III.1.—“In many places you proclaim that virtue is not mercenary.” Among these is the passage to which he shortly appeals, *On Laws* I.18: “Is liberality gratuitous or mercenary? If it is kindly without payment, it is gratuitous; if for remuneration, it is hired.” CELL.

“And kindly.” In Cicero, *benignusve* (“or kindly”) is better. [Col. 0673D] Cicero, *On Laws* I, near the end.

Persons of ample means. That is, moneyed and wealthy persons: *copia* by itself signifies riches. Cyprian, *Sermon on Mortality*: “Faith is firm and the soul devout when it is not moved by the abundance of the present life.” BARTHIUS.—“Ample.” The following passages explain it: VII.27, “He shall come to God rich; he shall come wealthy”; VI.3, “to lead an abundant life.” BUN.

Utmost necessity. That is, extreme need. *Epitome* 34: “Utmost hunger.” Elsewhere, namely VII.27, “utmost necessity” signifies death. BUN.

Reward. I restored this from all manuscripts and 14 editions. Others have “justice.” I recall having read somewhere: “Virtue is sufficiently its own reward.” Here read *dicis* (“you say”), as above, not *dicitis*; for he addresses Cicero.

“As you say.” Cicero, *On Duties* III.3 and *On Laws* I.

Justice. I write this with the manuscripts and most editions; other printed editions have *justitia* [in a different construction].—“Justice, the mother.” One of the latter forms is required by the sense and is the genuine reading. III.22: “Justice is the mother of all virtues.” BUNEMAN.

Esteem. Attribute it especially to her. I follow the most ancient codices—2 Reg., 6 other Reg., 4 Colbert., and others—as well as the Roman edition of 1470, which reject the conjunction *-que* or *et*, found in 4 recent manuscripts and many editions.

[Col. 0674C] “They must die.” One old Bonon. manuscript has “they must live less.”

“Who keeps them in life, who grants breath.” Thus I read with all manuscripts except 5 recent ones, which have *spiritum*, and 1 old Bonon. and 2 recent Reg. manuscripts, which read: “who gives them life, who grants breath.” The Thysius and Gallius editions approach our reading: “who grants them life, who grants breath.” The others read as in our text. “Who grants breath,” etc. Here Lactantius alludes to the Gospel saying: “who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust,” Matthew V.44. Yet whatever Monsieur le Brun may say, we should prefer the reading of the ancient Bologna manuscript, “who gives them life, who grants breath”; for in Latin one does not say *retinere in vita* (“keep in life”).

“He who can come to the aid of one perishing,” etc. Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* VII: “Do you not know that even those who denied life-saving help to persons dying are customarily punished, because they did what is contrary to good morals?” PRICAEUS. Ambrose, on Psalm CXVIII: “This is to kill a human being: to deny the aids of life.” And elsewhere: “Feed one dying from hunger. Whoever could save a person by feeding him, but did not feed him, has killed him.” This passage is cited by Gratian, *Decretum*, Distinction 86, chapter 20, under the name of St. Ambrose’s *On Duties*, where it is not found, but it occurs in Anselm. It is also found in St. Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* II–II, question 32, article 5, in the body of the article. Gregory the Great, too, *Pastoral Rule* III, admonition 22: “Therefore those vainly consider themselves innocent who privately claim for themselves God’s common gift; when they fail to give what they have received, they are active in the slaughter of their neighbors.”

Populist frivolity. That is, prompted by slight or paltry reasoning—namely, the pursuit of popular applause. “The ancients,” says Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights* XVI.11, “called those *leves* [light] whom we now commonly call cheap and worthy of no honor.” A *popularis* person is one who strives to win the people’s favor; *populare* means what pleases the people. Lactantius thus used “populist frivolity” through hypallage. WALCHIUS.]

One ought not, then, to give liberally to suitable persons, but, so far as possible, to unsuitable persons. For what one does without hope of repayment is just, pious, and humane.

This is that true and genuine justice, whose solid and exact form you say that no one possesses. You yourself proclaim in many places that virtue is not mercenary; and in your books *On Laws* you acknowledge that liberality is gratuitous, in these words:

> “There is no doubt that the person called liberal and kindly pursues duty, not profit.”

Why, then, do you give more readily to suitable persons, unless in order to receive a reward afterward? Thus, with you as author and teacher of justice, whoever is not suitable will perish through nakedness, thirst, and hunger; and persons of abundant means, overflowing even to luxury, will not come to the aid of utmost need. If virtue does not demand a reward, if, as you say, it is to be sought for its own sake, then esteem justice, the mother and chief [Col. 0674A] of virtues, by her own worth, not by your advantage. Give especially to one from whom you hope for nothing.

Why do you choose persons? Why do you inspect limbs? Whoever entreats you because he considers you human ought to be regarded by you as a human being. Cast away those shadows and images of justice, and hold fast to justice itself, true and exact. Give liberally to the blind, the disabled, the lame, and the destitute; unless you give to them, they must die. They are useless to human beings, but useful to God, who keeps them in life, who grants breath, who deems them worthy of light. So far as lies in you, sustain human souls by humanity lest they be extinguished. Whoever can aid one perishing and does not aid him, kills him.

But these people, because they retain neither nature nor know what the reward in this matter is, lose while fearing loss; and they fall into what they most avoid: whatever they give either wholly perishes or helps only for the briefest time. For those who deny a small alms to the wretched, who wish to preserve humanity without loss to themselves, pour out their estates in order either to acquire for themselves things that will perish and are fragile, or certainly to gain nothing at the cost of their greatest losses.

What, indeed, is to be said of those who, led by populist frivolity, [Col. 0675A] spend resources sufficient for great cities [Col. 0675A] [Note: [Col. 0675B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 675–676]

“Resources sufficient for great cities,” etc. It is astonishing how much the ancients spent upon theatrical and scenic games; this is still evident today from the various theatres built at great expense which remain in different parts of the world—at Rome, Padua, Nîmes, Avignon, and other cities. On these scenic expenses see Budé, *On the As* II.—“Resources sufficient for great cities … upon public entertainments.” Lipsius illustrates this, *On the Greatness of Rome* II.11. On Cyprian, *On Works and Almsgiving*, Oxford edition, fol. 206: “How great, how precious, and how laboriously acquired are the gifts which they procure with lavish displays, their property being either mortgaged for obtaining the gift or sold,” etc. BUN.

On presenting public entertainments. Namely, gladiatorial games and other spectacles. See Tertullian, *On Spectacles*; our Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* VI.20; *Epitome* 63, otherwise 6; and Lipsius, *Saturnalia* I.7. The person who staged such games was called *munerarius* or *munerator*, sometimes *editor*. WALCH.

“Which both they themselves lose and no one … receives.” He imitates Cyprian, *To Donatus*, Oxford edition, fol. 8: “By these losses the favor of the crowd was purchased and … popular applause sought. It was utterly foolish and empty waste to wish, by the pleasure of a disappointing spectacle, to procure something which neither the people received nor the magistrate retained.” BUN.

“Or if they have pleased so greatly.” Thus I read with the two most ancient Reg. manuscripts, 3 Colbert., 2 Brun., the Paris edition of 1525, and Betuleius. Twelve recent manuscripts and 3 printed editions have *placuerint*; 1 Lips. has *placaverint*; 1 Reg., 1 Colb., 1 Clar., and 5 editions have *placuerint*; 1 Reg. and 1 Colb. have “and if they have pleased so greatly.”

“Estates … are squandered.” Venice 1493 and 1497 have *patrocinia* (“patronages”), incorrectly. I recall Tertullian, *On Modesty* 8: “God’s substance having been squandered”; chapter 9: “all substance having been squandered.” Jerome, letter to Sabinianus, fol. 228: “his father’s substance having been squandered.” BUN.

“Those who, after erecting public works,” etc. See Gruter’s *Inscriptions*, which extensively demonstrates this vanity from p. 158 through p. 225 with many examples and inscriptions. GALLAEUS.

“Nor do these men act rightly: [they] bury.” This passage has hitherto been wrongly punctuated, for everyone read continuously: “Nor do these men rightly bury their goods in the earth.” But what does it mean “rightly to bury their goods in the earth”? I therefore punctuate it thus: “Nor do these men act rightly” (that is, they do not act rightly). For there preceded: “Do those men therefore act more wisely who … seek?” The answer is: “Nor do these men act rightly.” Hence follows below: “Those, therefore, act better.” Chapter 15: “The Peripatetics, therefore, act more correctly.” BUN.

“In the earth.” Thus I restored it from 3 printed editions and all manuscripts except 2 recent Reg. manuscripts, which, like many editions, have “into the earth.”

“Nothing is made by labor and hand that age does not wear out and consume.” Thus all manuscripts and editions. In Cicero one reads: “For there is nothing made by labor or hand which age does not at some time wear out and consume.” And immediately: “But this justice and gentleness of spirit flourishes.” Cicero, *For Marcellus* 10, where he teaches that Caesar’s clemency will be immortal if compared with other things that are fleeting and perishable.

“But this justice and gentleness flourishes.” Most manuscripts and editions. “And these,” incorrectly. The rest read as in the text, except Brun. and 1 Clarom., which have “will flourish more each day,” as in Cicero, *For Marcellus* 11.

“To their fellow-tribesmen.” Thus most manuscripts with the editions. [Col. 0676D] One recent Reg., 1 Colb., Ultr., and Brun. read “to their fellow-tribesmen,” that is, partners in the same tribe. One older Bonon. manuscript has “to their needy friends.”

“There is none.” On beneficence read Seneca’s books *On Benefits*, in which he discusses it as well and splendidly as a pagan and person alien from Christ can.

“It must therefore be held.” One old Bonon. manuscript: “It must be held [feminine].”—“It must be held.” That is, it must be known and regarded as certain; not, as Bonon. has it, “It must be held [feminine].” BUN.

“In every way.” Six recent manuscripts and 5 old editions have “entirely,” which occurs at the end of this period.

“Must be expected.” Thus I emended from all manuscripts except 3 Colb., 1 Clarom., and the Fasitel edition, which have *expectenda*, incorrectly; and 2 recent Reg. and 1 Colb., which have “must be sought,” as in the printed editions.

“Usury upon a benefit.” Two Goth., 2 Colb. manuscripts, and 2 old Roman editions have “repayment.”

“He who does what he does.” Thus I restored from the most ancient manuscripts—1 [Col. 0677C] Bonon., 2 Reg., 17 others—and 5 printed editions. The Cauc. manuscript and 5 others, along with 15 common editions, have “did.”]

on presenting public entertainments? Unless they are madmen and lunatics, who provide for the people something which they themselves lose and none of those for whom it is provided receives. Accordingly, since every pleasure is fleeting and brief, especially that of the eyes and ears, people either forget and regard another person’s losses as nothing owed in return, or are even offended if the craving of the crowd is not satisfied; so that these utterly foolish persons have acquired one evil for themselves by another evil. Or, if they have indeed pleased greatly, they gain nothing more than empty favor and gossip lasting a few days.

Thus the estates of the most frivolous persons are daily squandered on superfluities. Do those, then, act more wisely who offer more useful and lasting gifts to their fellow citizens? Namely, those who, after erecting public works, seek remembrance for their name? Nor do these men act rightly. [They] bury their goods [Col. 0675B] in the earth, because remembrance contributes nothing to the dead, nor are their works everlasting. For they are either shattered and collapse in one earthquake, or are consumed in some accidental fire, or are destroyed by hostile assault, or finally, dissolved by age itself, fall into ruin.

> “For, as the orator says, nothing is made by labor and by hand which age does not wear out and consume. But this justice and gentleness flourish more every day.”

Those, therefore, act better who give liberally to their fellow-tribesmen or clients. [Col. 0676A] For they provide something for human beings and are useful to them. Yet that is not true and just liberality. For there is no beneficence wherever there is no necessity. Thus whatever is bestowed upon the non-needy for the sake of favor perishes, or returns with interest, and there will be no beneficence. Even if it is pleasing to those who receive it, it is nevertheless not just, because no harm follows if it is not done. The one certain and true duty of liberality, then, is to support the needy and the helpless.
