## CHAPTER XII. On the kinds of beneficence and the works of mercy

This is that perfect justice which preserves the human fellowship of which philosophers speak. This is the greatest and truest fruit of riches: not to use [Col. 0676B] wealth for the private pleasure of one person, but for the welfare of many; not for one’s present gain, but for justice, which alone does not perish.

It must therefore be held in every way that all hope of repayment should be wholly absent from the duty of mercy. For the reward of this work and duty must be expected from God alone. If you expect it from a human being, it will no longer be humanity, but usury upon a benefit. Nor can one seem to have deserved well who, in what he does, serves not another but himself. Yet the matter [Col. 0677A] comes to the same thing: [Col. 0677A] [Note: [Col. 0677C] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 677–678]

“It comes to the same thing.” *Eodem* was restored from the most ancient manuscripts, 2 Bonon., 2 Reg., and 5 others. The rest, with the editions, have *eo*.

“The same God.” Fourteen recent manuscripts and 5 editions have “Likewise.”

“Who cannot invite [them] back.” That is, back to a meal. *Revocare* is a word of invitation and absolutely means to invite in return a person who previously received us at a banquet. WALCHIUS.

“Let him not think that fellowship with friends or affection for relatives has been forbidden him.” This is the reading of the older and better manuscripts—1 Bonon., Regio-Put., 3 other Reg., Tax., 1 Colb., 1 Clarom.—with 4 editions, and rightly so. For *interdicere* is more frequently construed with the dative and ablative. In vain do Cauc., 1 recent Reg., Jun., 2 Lips. manuscripts and 12 editions read “that fellowship … or affection has been forbidden”; 1 ancient Reg., 15 other recent manuscripts, and the Sublac. edition read “that fellowship … or affection,” etc. Buneman also has “affection.”—“Forbidden … fellowship … affection.” Just as futures in *-rum* were often indeclinable among the ancients—for example Cicero, *Against Verres* V.65: “that this thing would be a protection for him”—so the same sometimes happens with passive perfect participles. BUN.

“True and just.” Heumann writes “truly just.” But all books have the received reading; and in chapter 11: “But that is not true and just liberality.” BUN.

“Ought.” Thus I restored from all manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470 and Betuleius. Nearly all editions have “ought [infinitive].”—“Thus we ought.” I understand it thus: to do good to friends and relatives—that is, kinsmen—belongs to a human being; it is a merely human work. But to do good to those who cannot return the favor is a divine work, and the reward of that beneficence must be expected from God. See above and chapter 10. BUN.

Hospitality. Romans XII; Hebrews XIII; 1 Peter IV; Matthew XXV.

Cicero. *On Duties* II, from Theophrastus’s chapter on wealth in his book *On Character*.

[Col. 0678C] Suitable persons. On suitable persons, see above, note on chapter 11.

“What advantage it brings.” The Paris editions of 1513 and 1525 have this reading, and Betuleius and Isaeus advise that it should be read so. Common editions have “what he does,” etc.; 1 recent Reg. has “does”; 2 Reg. in a second hand and Brun. have “what a powerful person does”; Jun. has “who does.” This is from Cicero, *On Duties*, near the end.—“What advantage it brings.” Here he expresses Cicero’s thought rather than his words, which are, *On Duties* III.18: “It is … highly advantageous for those who honestly wish to have great influence to be powerful among foreign peoples through guests, by means of resources and influence.” BUN.

“Might be convicted.” Thus I restored from all manuscripts except 2 recent Reg. manuscripts, which, like the editions, have “might be refuted.”

“The same man also denies that it belongs to a straightforward and open man.” He argues in much this way concerning the straightforward and open person in *On Duties* I.30. CELL.

“For me.” *Mihi* is elegantly superfluous, in the same way as *tibi* is in III.14: “Why do you not confess the truth to yourself?” Cicero, *Letters to Friends* VII.1, suitably: “Support for me this weakness of your health.”

[Col. 0678D] “You run about through every gate … for your own advantage.” Heumann in his edition had six lines printed in a different typeface, saying that these are Cicero’s words, or rather words falsely attributed to him by Lactantius. On the contrary, Lactantius, with these words, as it were mockingly taunts Cicero. Compare above. Thus no difference in type should be made here. BUN.

“You [wish to appear] just.” In certain printed editions *humanum* (“humane”) is absent.

“Knowingly and deliberately.” Cicero, *For Marcellus* 5 also shows this: “that knowingly and deliberately I might rush, as it were, toward voluntary destruction.” *Letters to Friends* VI.6: “Thus knowingly and deliberately I set out toward ruin placed before my eyes.” BUN.

“He brought himself into these snares.” Thus the ancient manuscripts—1 Bonon., 2 Reg., 3 other Reg., Cauc., and 9 others—and the Roman edition of 1470, Isaeus, and Cellarius. Three recent manuscripts have “cast”; 9 recent manuscripts and 14 printed editions have “led.” See below, chapter 24, “may be led into snares.” Cicero, *Against Verres* IV.24: “into how many snares he brought himself.” Thus Thomas’s claim that no one said “to bring oneself into snares” is false.]

whatever each person has done for another, expecting no advantage from him, he truly does for himself, because he will receive his reward from God.

The same God commanded that, whenever we have prepared a dinner, we should invite to the meal those who cannot invite us back or return the favor, so that no action of our life may lack the gift of mercy. Yet let no one think that fellowship with friends or affection for relatives has been forbidden him. But God has made known to us what is the true and just work. Thus we ought to live with our relatives, provided that we know that the one pertains to humanity, the other to God.

Hospitality, then, is the chief virtue, as philosophers too say; but they twist it away from true justice and drag it toward advantage.

> “Hospitality,” Cicero says, “has rightly been praised by Theophrastus. For it is, in my opinion, highly becoming for the houses of distinguished persons to be open to distinguished guests.” [Col. 0677B]

He erred again in the same way as when he said that one should give to suitable persons. For the house of a just and wise man ought not to be open to the distinguished, but to the humble and lowly. Those distinguished and powerful people can lack nothing, since their wealth both protects and honors them. But a just man ought to do nothing except what is a benefit. A benefit, however, when it is returned, perishes and comes to an end; for we cannot retain intact something for which its price has been paid to us.

Therefore the principle of justice is concerned with benefits [Col. 0677C] which remain safe and uncorrupted. They remain [Col. 0678A] only if they are bestowed upon persons who can in no way be useful in return. But in receiving distinguished guests Cicero considered nothing other than advantage, and the ingenious man did not conceal what benefit he hoped to obtain from it. For he says that the person who does this will become influential among foreigners through the favor of rulers, whom he will have bound to himself by the bond of hospitality and friendship.

With how many arguments could Cicero’s inconsistency, if I undertook it, be convicted! He would be refuted not so much by our words as by his own. For he himself says that, insofar as anyone refers whatever he does chiefly to his own advantage, he is least of all a good man. He also denies that it belongs to a straightforward and open person to canvass for favor, to pretend and make a show of something, to appear to do one thing while doing another, and to feign that he performs a service for another when he serves himself; these belong rather to the malicious, crafty, deceitful, and treacherous person.

How, then, could he defend that ambitious hospitality from being malice?

> “You run about through every gate, so that you may invite into your house the rulers of peoples and cities when they arrive, in order to gain influence among their citizens through them; and you wish to appear just, humane, and hospitable, when you are pursuing your own advantage.”

But did he not do this rather incautiously? What, indeed, is less fitting for Cicero? Yet through ignorance of true law, knowingly and deliberately he brought himself into these snares. That he may be forgiven for this, he testified that he gives precepts not for true justice, which he does not possess, [Col. 0678C] but for a shadow and image of justice. Therefore this shadowy and imaginary teacher [Col. 0679A] must be forgiven; [Col. 0679A] [Note: [Col. 0679B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 679–680]

“Shadowy teacher.” He calls him *umbraticus* playfully, because he had said that Cicero gave precepts for a “shadow and image of justice.” [Col. 0679C] BUN.

“And this beneficence.” *Atque* (“and”) was restored from all manuscripts and 7 old editions; the others have *itaque* (“therefore”).

The poor. Tobit IV; Ecclesiasticus IV; Matthew XXV.

“For them it is a matter of the highest praise.” One ancient Reg. manuscript has “of the highest praise,” and not badly. BUN.

“Whom no one expected would do such things.” Davisius proposes, “whom no one expected to do such things.” It is not displeasing, but we did not adopt it without manuscript support. BUN.

“No great praise.” Here Lactantius seems to allude to the Lord’s saying, Matthew V.46: “If you love those who love you, what reward will you have?”

“Their estates.” Here Crates is noted; see above, book III, chapter 23.

“Of those who cast away.” For variety he here says “cast away.” Chapter 11: “pour out their estates”; below, “squander upon superfluities”; likewise, “bury in the earth.” Chapter 12: “spend upon superfluities.” Cicero uses a related term, *On Duties* I–II.17: he criticizes Pericles “for having thrown so much money into … the Propylaea.”

Divine law. Exodus XXII; Job XXIX and XXXI; Psalm LXVII; Ecclesiasticus IV; James I. Orphans and widows are commended in many Davidic psalms. Isaiah, chapter X, inspired by divine power, attacks legislators, or *nomophylakes* (“guardians of the laws”), through whose negligence, injustice, or avarice orphans and widows were exposed to them as prey. Cicero distinguishes two kinds of injustice: that of those who inflict injury and that of those who, when able, do not repel injury from those upon whom it is inflicted. Unjust judges not only fail to repel injury from orphans and widows; they even greedily pursue as prey those whom they ought to defend. BETULEIUS.

“That they should cherish them out of natural humanity.” This is the reading of very many manuscripts and nearly all printed editions. Two Bonon., 5 Reg., Cauc., and 11 others have “that they should favor them.” But below *foveri* is used in the same sense.

“Are properly ours.” Goth. and Rom. have “proper.” But the received reading too is good and praiseworthy. Cicero, *Letters* IX.15 to Paetus: “That you yourself are so lovable, so sweet, and so pleasant in every respect—that is properly your own.” CELL.

“Ours, who have received the law.” I added these final two words, absent in some editions, from all manuscripts and most printed editions. On these works see Deuteronomy XXVII and Isaiah I.

“Commands [them] to be defended and cherished.” Twelve recent manuscripts and 6 old editions have “protected” instead of “cherished,” repeating the word that occurred shortly before; but, in my judgment, the active or deponent verb is incorrectly joined with a passive. Six older Reg. manuscripts and others, as well as 10 printed editions, have “cherished.”

“Of their pledges.” *Pignora* is used for children.—“Their pledges.” Cyprian repeatedly, *On Works and Almsgiving*, Oxford edition, fol. 205: “father of many pledges … pledges to be fed and supported … the greater abundance of pledges … the number of pledges.” BUN.

“Who lack someone to attend them.” Jun., 3 Colbert. manuscripts, and 5 editions have “who lack persons to attend them.”

“It is a work of great service.” In the *Psychomachia*, verse 575, Service is opposed to Avarice; there Aldus, Antonius, Nebrissensis, and Georgius Fabricius had introduced the similar gloss “compassion,” contrary to the manuscript authority reported by Rosweyde and Nicolaus Heinsius. Prudentius writes excellently in that passage.]

nor should truth be demanded from one who confesses that he does not know it.

The redemption of captives is a great and splendid duty of justice, and Tullius himself approved it:

> “And this beneficence,” he says, “is also useful to the commonwealth: the redemption from slavery of prisoners, and the enrichment of the poorer. I far prefer this practice of kindness to the lavish distribution of public gifts. It belongs to serious and great men.”

It is, then, the particular work of the just to feed the poor and redeem captives, when among the unjust, if any perform these acts, they are called serious and great. For it is a matter of the highest praise for them to do good to those whom no one expected would do such things. For one who does good to a kinsman, a relative, or a friend [Col. 0679B] either deserves no praise or certainly no great praise, because he ought to do it; and he is impious and detestable if he does not do what both nature itself and the bond of relationship demand of him. If he does it, he acts not so much to gain glory as to avoid blame.

But one who does good to a stranger and an unknown person is truly worthy of praise, because humanity alone prompted him to act. Therefore justice is present where there is no bond of necessity to doing good. Thus Cicero should not even have preferred this duty of kindness to the lavish distribution of public gifts, [Col. 0680A] as though comparing two goods and choosing the better. For that distribution—the empty and frivolous largesse of people casting their estates into the sea—is far removed from every kind of justice. Therefore such things ought not even to be called gifts, in which no one receives except one who does not deserve to receive.

No less great a work of justice is it to protect and defend orphaned and widowed persons who are destitute and in need of assistance. Indeed, that divine law prescribes this to all; since all good judges consider it part of their duty to cherish such persons with natural humanity and to strive to help them. Yet these works belong properly to us, who have received the law and the words of God himself commanding them. For those others indeed perceive that it is naturally just to protect persons who lack protection; [Col. 0680B] but they do not discern why this is so. For God, whose mercy is perpetual, commands that widows and orphans be defended and cherished, lest anyone, through concern and pity for his own dependants, be held back from undergoing death for justice and faith; rather, he should undertake it unhesitatingly and bravely, knowing that he leaves those dear to him in God’s care and that they will never lack protection.

To undertake the care and support of the sick also, when they lack anyone to attend them, is an act of the highest humanity and of great service. Whoever does this will obtain for God a living sacrifice; [Col. 0681A] and what he gives another for a time, he himself will receive from God for eternity. That final and greatest duty of piety is the burial of strangers and the poor. [Col. 0681A]

[Note: [Col. 0681C] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 681–682]

**The burial of strangers and the poor.** That greatest duty of piety—as Lactantius calls it—consists in the burial of strangers and the poor. Burial has always been a sacred matter. Ahab was deemed so much more unfortunate because he lacked burial; and Jehoiakim because he received an ass’s burial. Isaiah, chapter IV, foretells to the king of Babylon that he himself will be cast out from his tomb. Whether it harms Christians’ bodies if they are cast away unburied is discussed by St Augustine, *City of God*, book I, chapters 12 and 13. Even now it is customary that persons guilty of great crimes be deprived of burial. Servius says concerning piety in burial, in his commentary on *Aeneid* VI: “Those who have written on the kinds of piety wished burial to hold first place. Hence, although it was unlawful for pontiffs to look upon a corpse, it was nevertheless more unlawful if, having seen it, they left it unburied.”

Moreover, the cathedral church of Vienne in Dauphiné provides burial with the greatest generosity. For if any stranger and poor person, falling ill at Vienne and fortified with the divine sacraments, should at the point of death request burial in the cemetery of the cathedral [Col. 0681D] church, situated in the middle of the cloister, once dead he is there committed to the earth, with bells ringing, just as at the funeral rites of a canon. Not only the canons and clergy of that church attend the funeral rites of that person, but the archbishop himself as well, if he happens then to be in the city; the cross and silver candlesticks go before, and they make the funeral splendid.

**All duties.** Twelve recent manuscripts and seven editions add *sua*, “their own.” But Cellarius and Heumann rightly judge that *sua* should not be added.

**They wandered less far.** Thus five Royal manuscripts read, two of which are very ancient; likewise one Colbert manuscript, two Clermont manuscripts, and two Bern manuscripts: “so that they had not wandered so far from the right way.” This, says Walchius, is what the particle *propius* (“more nearly,” “less far”) means. Three recent Royal manuscripts, three Colbert manuscripts, the Emendated text, and eight editions read *oberraverunt*; one Royal, the Juntine, Palatine, and two Leipzig manuscripts read *aberraverunt*; three Royal, two Colbert, one Leipzig, the Canterbury manuscript, and two old Roman editions read *aberrarunt*. Heumann considers this verb more correct than the others’ *oberraverunt*.

**They made burial superfluous.** One Royal manuscript, one Colbert manuscript [Col. 0682B], and the Bern manuscript read *supervacuam*, “superfluous.” The Emendated text reads: “they said that burial was superfluous.” Diogenes the Cynic, Menippus, and Theodorus of Cyrene considered burial useless; see Ludovicus Vives’s commentary on St Augustine’s *City of God*. [Col. 0682C]

**Unburied.** That is, without burial.

**Divine utterances.** Likewise in book IV, chapter 26: “Holy Scripture.”

**Therefore we shall not permit.** Thus I restored the text from the most ancient manuscripts—two Bologna, eight Royal, five Colbert, and others—and from the Tornesian edition. Two recent Royal manuscripts, one Colbert manuscript, and the printed editions have *enim* (“for”), which occurred immediately before. But Heumann wishes *enim* also to be deleted and *ergo* (“therefore”) to be read, as we read it.

**But we shall return it to the earth.** Thus restored from four Royal manuscripts, four Colbert manuscripts, the Emendated text, the Canterbury and Pen. manuscripts, and ten printed editions; the following words require it: “we shall perform the duty owed to those nearest.” Eleven manuscripts and six printed editions read: “but let us return.”

**Even in the case of an unknown person, etc.** These words give an entirely complete sense; and thus read two Bologna manuscripts, the Caucasian manuscript, and the two most ancient Royal manuscripts, the Tax. manuscript, and the Marm. manuscript in its first hand. Other manuscripts and editions variously insert words which appear to have crept into the text as glosses from the margin of the book; I therefore rejected them. After *necessariorum* (“those nearest”), nineteen recent manuscripts, two old Roman editions, the Juntine, Parrhasian, Gymnasium, [Col. 0682D] and Is. editions add: “burial must be denied to no one.” Following the manuscripts, Heumann, like ourselves and the most learned Cellarius, judges these three words should be erased; yet, he says, Thomasius rightly omitted them in his edition. Five Oxford editions and seven printed editions read: “a service must be denied to no one.” Four handwritten manuscripts and the Betuleian edition read: “we shall provide burial, to be denied to no one”; one recent Royal manuscript and the Gat. edition read: “by providing the burial of those nearest and friends, to be denied to no one, we shall fulfil a service and duty.”

**Will be lacking.** One Colbert manuscript, the Emendated and Canterbury texts, and the Roman edition of 1470 read *desiderabit*, “will be lacking.”

**When this is done.** The words *quae fit* (“which is done”) occur in the two Bologna manuscripts and some editions, and are absent in others. That is: when that is done which pertains to humanity. But the relative word *quae* was omitted in many copies because of the conjunction *-que* attached to the word *justior*. From THOMAS.

**Sacrifice.** For God requires mercy from us rather than sacrifice.

**Which even your philosophers praise.** See Seneca, *Letters* 17, 20, and elsewhere.]

This is something which those teachers of virtue and justice did not touch at all. Nor could they perceive it, since they measured all duties by utility. For in the other matters mentioned above, although they did not maintain the true limit, yet because they detected some advantage in them, as though held by a certain scent of truth, they wandered less far from the right path. But this they abandoned because they could perceive in it no advantage.

Indeed, there were even some who made burial superfluous and said that there was no evil in lying unburied and cast aside. All humankind rejects their impious wisdom, as do [Col. 0681B] the divine utterances that command this to be done. Yet they do not dare say that it ought not to be done; rather, they say that, should it perhaps not be done, there is no harm. Thus in this matter they perform the role not so much of those commanding as of those consoling: so that, if this should happen to a wise man, he may not think himself miserable on that account. But we do not say what a wise man must endure; we say what he himself ought to do. Therefore, we are not now asking whether the whole practice of burial is useful or not; rather, even if it is futile, as they suppose, it must nevertheless be done, if only because [Col. 0682A] it appears to be done well and humanely among human beings. For it is the intention that is sought, and the purpose that is weighed.

Therefore we shall not allow the form and workmanship of God to lie as prey for wild beasts and birds; but we shall return it to the earth from which it arose. And even in the case of an unknown person, we shall perform the duty owed to those nearest; in their place, because they are absent, humanity shall succeed, and wherever a human being is lacking, there we shall consider our duty to be demanded. In what, moreover, does the principle of justice consist more than in this: that what we provide for our own through affection, we provide for strangers through humanity—which is much more certain and more just? When this is done, the service is no longer rendered to a human being, who feels nothing, but to God alone, to whom a just work is a most dear sacrifice.

Perhaps someone will say: “If I do all these things, I shall have nothing. For what if a great number of persons should be needy, cold, taken captive, or dying, [Col. 0682B] so that one who does these things must necessarily be stripped of his estate in a single day? Shall I lose the family property acquired by my own labour or that of my ancestors, so that I myself must then live by another’s mercy?”

Why do you fear poverty with such faintness of heart? Even your philosophers praise it, declaring that nothing is safer or more tranquil. What you fear is a harbour from anxieties. Do you not know to how many dangers and misfortunes you are exposed along with those evil riches? They will have dealt kindly with you if they pass away without your bloodshed. But you go about burdened with plunder and carry spoils that provoke even the minds of your own people. Why then do you hesitate to place well what perhaps [Col. 0683A]

[Note: [Col. 0683B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 683–684]

**Perhaps.** Three recent Royal manuscripts and sixteen editions read *forsitan*.

[Col. 0683C] **To entrust your treasures to God as guardian.** That is, to deposit them with God. For Tertullian, in *Apology*, chapter 39, where he speaks of Christian discipline, writes as follows: “On a monthly day, or whenever he wishes, each person contributes a modest offering, provided only that he is able. For no one is compelled; rather, each gives voluntarily. These are, as it were, deposits of piety. For they are not spent on banquets, drinking, or ungrateful gluttonous feasts, but on feeding and burying the needy; on boys and orphans deprived of resources and parents; on elderly persons worn down by age; likewise on shipwrecked persons; and on any who are in mines, islands, or prisons merely because, as adherents of God’s sect, they make confession of their faith,” etc. BETUL.—The Venice editions of 1493 and 1497 read *tradere* (“to hand over”) for “to entrust to God as guardian.” I change nothing. He imitates Cyprian, *On Works and Alms*, Oxford edition, folio 205: “An inheritance entrusted to God is neither snatched away by the state, nor invaded by the treasury, nor overturned by any legal accusation. The inheritance is placed in safety when it is preserved with God as guardian.” Compare Lactantius, *Epitome*, chapter 65. BUN.

[Col. 0683D] **Rust.** Matthew VI; Luke XII.

**Can.** The Caucasian and Juntine manuscripts and five editions read *poterit*, “will be able.”

**That you bring your riches to God’s altar.** Thus I read from the most ancient manuscript codices: two Bologna, six Royal, and the Tax. manuscript. One Colbert manuscript has *iram* (“anger”) for *aram* (“altar”). Thomasius says that a person brings riches to the altar when, by giving them to the poor, he gives and offers them to God. But *arcam* (“chest”), read in twelve recent editions and printed texts, cannot be read, because God does not receive riches in order to store them away.

**More secure.** The Sublacensian text: “better.”

**Redeem the captives.** Seven recent manuscripts: “captives.”

**From the source from which you procure men for the sword.** You buy gladiators from a trainer (*lanista*) in order to set them before the people’s pleasure. CELLAR.—A *lanista* was one who trained gladiators in the gladiatorial art.

**Beast-fighters.** *Bestiarii* were persons who fought beasts in public shows in the amphitheatre, either hired for payment or condemned to this as punishment. WALCHIUS.

**For these true gifts.** In one recent Royal manuscript, *his* (“these”) is absent. I would prefer to read “for these vain gifts,” or “for these gifts to the earth,” [Col. 0684B] as in one Clermont manuscript.

[Col. 0684C] **If you hear.** Matthew V; Luke VI, where these words occur not verbatim but in sense.

**And I will turn your own disposition against you.** I shall be merciless toward you, just as you have been toward others. Seven manuscripts and an equal number of printed editions omit *tuum* (“your”), which is read in the rest and is certainly necessary. From THOMASIUS and CELLARIUS.

**Worthy to be heard.** Thus nearly all manuscripts read, more elegantly than the printed editions’ *exaudiri* (“to be granted a hearing”), and three recent manuscripts. *Dignus* with an infinitive is used in the manner of poets.—“Worthy to be heard.” *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapters 1 and 52: “You who deserve to be heard by God”; as Cyprian often writes in *On the Lord’s Prayer*, Oxford edition, p. 427: “Cornelius the centurion, when he prayed, deserved to be heard”; and p. 428: “They themselves too deserve to be heard by God.” BUN.

**Because you have sinned.** Thus three very old manuscripts and nine others, with three editions, read. The more recent texts read: “because you had sinned.”

**He commands repentance to be performed.** Thus I write with the most ancient Bologna manuscripts, two Royal manuscripts, and twelve others, and seven editions. Six recent manuscripts and eight common editions read *agere*, “to perform.” Jeremiah XVIII; Ezekiel [Col. 0684D] XVIII; Luke V.

**To perform repentance … is to profess and affirm that one will sin no more.** Lactantius explains this at length in chapter 24: “For one who repents of his deed understands his former error … one whom his fault pains, and who rebukes himself for folly, confirms his mind to live more rightly; then he especially takes care not to be led again into the same snares.” And elsewhere, book IV, chapter 17: “If we uncover our heart—that is, if we confess our sins and make satisfaction to God—we shall obtain pardon.” No one, he says, who has slipped into the path of injustice because overcome by greed, driven by lust, or compelled by force, ought to despair of salvation, if he repents of what he has done and, converted to better things, makes satisfaction to God. Here you see repentance openly distinguished from satisfaction.

Before Lactantius, Tertullian had said: “Where there is no amendment, repentance is necessarily vain.” For, as Gregory the Great says, *Pastoral Rule*, book III, Admonition 31: “Those who abandon their committed sins but do not lament them should not suppose their faults already forgiven; although they do not multiply them by action, they cleanse them with no tears. For a writer, if he ceases writing, has not thereby erased what he had written merely because he adds no more; nor has one who inflicts insults made satisfaction merely because he has kept silent, since it is certainly necessary that he combat the words of previous pride with words of subsequent humility; nor is a debtor released because he adds no further debts, unless he also pays those by which he was bound.” Nor, as St John Chrysostom says, is it enough for the recovery of a wounded person merely to draw the weapons from the body; remedies must also be applied to the wounds.]

will be taken from you either by a single act of brigandage, or by a sudden proscription, or by some hostile plundering? Why are you afraid to make a fleeting and fragile good everlasting, or to entrust your treasures to God as guardian, where you need fear neither thief nor robber, neither rust nor tyrant? Whoever is rich with God can never be poor. If you value justice so highly, pursue it after casting off the burdens that weigh you down. Free yourself from shackles and chains, so that unencumbered you may run to God. It belongs to a great and exalted mind to despise and trample mortal things.

But if you do not attain this virtue, so as to bring your riches to God’s altar and obtain more secure things in exchange for frail ones, [Col. 0683B] I shall free you from fear. All these precepts are not given to you alone, but to the whole people joined in mind and adhering together as one human being. If alone you are unequal to great works, perform justice according to your capacity, yet in such a way that, as much as you surpass others in riches, so much you surpass them in service. Nor should you suppose that you are now being advised to diminish or exhaust your family estate; rather, redirect to better purposes what you would have spent on superfluities. From the source from which you buy beasts, redeem captives; from the source from which you feed wild animals, feed the poor; from the source from which you procure men for the sword, bury innocent [Col. 0684A] dead persons. What good is it to enrich beast-fighters for ruinous wickedness and equip them for crimes? Transfer to a great sacrifice what would otherwise perish badly, so that in exchange for these true gifts you may receive from God an eternal gift.

Great is the reward of mercy, to which God promises that he will forgive all sins. “If,” he says, “you hear the prayers of your suppliant, I too shall hear yours. If you have pity on those who labour, I shall have pity in your labour. But if you do not look upon them or help them, I too shall turn your own disposition against you, and I shall judge you by your own laws.”

## CHAPTER XIII. On repentance, mercy, and the forgiveness of sins

[Col. 0684B] Therefore, whenever you are asked, believe that you are being tested by God as to whether you are worthy to be heard. Examine your conscience and, insofar as you can, heal its wounds. Yet do not suppose that, because sins are removed by generosity, you are given permission to sin. For they are removed if you give generously to God because you have sinned; but if you sin in reliance upon your future generosity, they are not removed. For God especially desires human beings to be cleansed from sins, and therefore commands repentance to be performed. But to perform repentance is nothing other than to profess and affirm that one will sin no more.

Accordingly, pardon is granted [Col. 0685A] to those who fall into sin [Col. 0685A]

[Note: [Col. 0685C] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 685–686]

**Sin.** The Sublacensian text adds “unknowingly.”

**The person who sins knowingly has no pardon.** That is, one who, after receiving baptism, commits sins from malicious and harmful wickedness, or evil intention—for example, slander or premeditated murder—obtains pardon from God only with the greatest difficulty. For, as Basil the Great says in his discourse *To Young Men, on How Benefit May Be Derived from Greek Authors*: “To one who fails involuntarily in the fitting duty, some pardon from God may perhaps be granted; but to one who deliberately chooses worse things no excuse can be granted, such that he should not undergo a multiple punishment.”

For it is exceedingly difficult that those who commit such crimes after baptism—crimes due neither to ignorance [Col. 0685D] nor to human weakness—be restored through repentance: first, because it is difficult for them to perform true and sincere repentance and bring forth fruits of repentance and satisfaction worthy, as the Gospel requires; and secondly, because the severity of Christian discipline demands from such people a hard and difficult exercise of repentance. Ambrose, indeed, *On Repentance*, book II, chapter 10, no. 96, says that he found more readily people who had preserved innocence than people who had performed repentance fittingly. Yet in two books he exhorts sinners to it, especially in book I, chapter 16, no. 90: “If anyone, having secret crimes, nevertheless diligently performs repentance for Christ’s sake … I wish that the guilty person should hope for pardon; let him seek it with tears, seek it with groanings, seek it with the weeping of the whole people; let him entreat that he may be forgiven,” etc.

**Which may remove them.** That is, which ought to redeem them.

**For the healing of wounds.** That is, of sins. Cyprian, *On the Lapsed*, chapter 13: “Let one’s entire estate be expended for the healing of the wound.” The same writer, at the end of *On Works and Alms*, Oxford edition, folio 209: *operatio*—that is, almsgiving—is called the remedy for sin. BUN.

[Col. 0686B] **No one can be.** III Kings, chapter VI, 2 Chronicles, chapter VI; Ecclesiastes VII; Proverbs XX and XXIV, 1 John, chapter I.

[Col. 0686C] **To abstain.** III John, verse 10; Psalm XXXIII, 1 Peter III, verse 11. **In thought.** Isaiah I; Jeremiah IV, 1 Corinthians XIII.

**He who has ascended the first step is sufficiently just.** He is not sufficiently just if, while abstaining from evil works, he nevertheless either speaks or thinks evil; Lactantius himself both acknowledges and teaches this below, chapter 23, and book VII, chapter 27, where he says that God will judge even perverse thoughts. ISAEUS.

**Not even to admit into thought, etc.** Thirteen recent manuscripts and two editions read “not even in thought”; four editions read “nor in thought.”

**A life-sustaining man.** That is, a man worthy of life, upright, and attentive to business; thus Horace, book II, *Satires* 7:

> A slave to his master, yet upright; and this is enough:
>  
> That you consider him fit for life.

And Seneca, book V, Letter 39: “It belongs to a great mind to despise great things and to prefer moderate things to excessive ones. For those things are useful and life-sustaining.” See Turnebus, *Adversaria*, [Col. 0686D] book XXVIII, chapter 27.

**Insensible.** Lacking sensation. FRANCIUS.

**And cannot give thanks for what they have received.** I restored *quod* (“for what”) from the old Roman edition and all manuscripts except one recent Royal manuscript and sixteen editions, which read *qui acceperint* (“who have received”); another Royal manuscript reads *qui acceperunt*.

**Living images of God.** That is, human beings.

**That you may win the favour of the living one.** Thus the most ancient Bologna manuscripts, four Royal manuscripts, the Caucasian and Juntine manuscripts, and three printed editions read. But more recent manuscripts and almost all editions read: “that you may deserve to find the living one.” Two Royal, two Colbert, two Tornesian, and two Clermont manuscripts read: “that you may deserve to see the living one.”—“That you may win the favour of the living one.” Relevant to this are the words of Cyprian, *On Works and Alms*, Oxford edition, folio 203: “That we may understand that these works are given to God, and that whoever does these things wins the Lord’s favour.” There, folio 209: “He wins Christ the judge.” BUN.

**And he will approve.** The word *et* (“and”) is added from all manuscripts and most printed editions.]

unwisely and incautiously; the person who sins knowingly has no pardon. Yet, if anyone has been purified from every stain of sin, he should not think that he must refrain from works of generosity because he has no sins to remove. Rather, then all the more ought he to practise justice, once he has become just, so that what he had previously done to heal wounds, he may afterwards do for the praise and glory of virtue. Moreover, no one can be without fault as long as he is burdened with the garment of flesh. Its weakness is subject to the dominion of sin in three ways: in deeds, words, and thoughts.

By these steps justice advances to its highest summit. The first step of virtue is to abstain from evil actions; the second, also from evil words; the third, also [Col. 0685B] from thoughts of evil things. Whoever has ascended the first step is sufficiently just; whoever has ascended the second already possesses perfect virtue, since he sins neither in deeds nor in speech; but whoever has ascended the third seems truly to have attained the likeness of God. For it is almost beyond human capacity not even to admit into thought what is either evil to do or shameful to say.

Therefore even just persons, who can restrain themselves from every unjust act, are nevertheless sometimes overcome by their very frailty, so that in anger they may say something evil, or, at the sight of delightful [Col. 0686A] things, may silently desire them in thought. But if the mortal condition does not allow any human being to be wholly pure from every stain, the sins of the flesh must therefore be removed by continual generosity. For the one work of a wise, just, and life-sustaining man is to invest his riches in justice alone. Whoever lacks this, though he surpass Croesus or Crassus in riches, must be considered poor, naked, and a beggar.

Accordingly, effort must be made that we may be clothed in the garment of justice and piety, which no one may strip from us and which may provide us with everlasting adornment. For if worshippers of the gods cultivate insensible images and devote to them whatever precious things they possess—though these images can neither use them nor give thanks for what they have received—how much more just and true is it to care for the living images of God, that you may win the favour of [Col. 0686B] the living one? As these make use of whatever they receive and give thanks, so God, in whose sight you have done good, will both approve and repay the reward of piety.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the passions, the Stoics’ view of them, and virtue, vices, and mercy

If, therefore, mercy is a splendid and outstanding good in a human being, and is judged best by divine testimonies and by the agreement of good and bad alike, [Col. 0687A] it is apparent that philosophers have been far removed from the human good—[Col. 0687A]

[Note: [Col. 0687C] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 687–688]

**From the human good.** Nothing should be altered against the manuscripts: *ab humano bono* means “from the good proper to human beings,” from humanity, from mercy. BUN.

**But virtue.** Almost all printed editions insert the article *hanc* (“this”), which, since the manuscripts reject it, the Roman edition of 1470 and Cellarius also reject; I have deleted it as unnecessary. St Augustine disputed against the Stoics’ opinion concerning the passions in *City of God*, book XIV, chapters 8 and 9.

**The liberal person from the prodigal.** The philosopher, in book IV of the *Ethics*, thus defines the scheme of liberality and its extremes: prodigality, liberality, meanness, avarice. Therefore thrift, which Cicero, where he maintains the Stoic position, calls a great source of revenue, considers sparing, grasping, [Col. 0687D] and dry persons vicious, because they are deficient in giving. But Lactantius seems to understand by *parcus* a frugal person. BETULEIUS.

**Sparing.** Three recent manuscripts read *purum*, “pure”; one Colbert manuscript, “from the splendid person.”

**The calm person from the sluggish.** “Calm” is deficient, sluggish, excessive, irascible. For I think this is altogether what Aristotle taught in *Nicomachean Ethics* I and V, chapter 4. Lactantius seems, I say, to have called the gentle person “calm” and the foolish person “sluggish.” BETULEIUS.

**Or the cautious from the timid.** Aristotle makes timidity a deficiency of courage, just as rashness is an excess. In *Tusculan Disputations* IV, Cicero translates the Stoics’ *εὐλάβεια* (*eulabeia*, “caution”), distinguishing it from fear on the ground that fear avoids dangers contrary to reason, while caution avoids them in accordance with reason. BETULEIUS.

**Becomes impudence.** Thus the older manuscripts and many printed editions read. Thus *ut*, which occurred immediately before, is used in the sense “just as,” as in Cicero; Cellarius did not observe this, nor Francius, who wished to read *sit impudentia*, “is impudence,” as in one Royal manuscript, the Bern manuscript, and the Marm. manuscript in its first hand.

**Is changed.** Thus I restored the text from many printed editions and all manuscripts except one Colbert manuscript, which reads *convertatur*; four editions read *convertetur*. See the following: “is obstinacy”; “becomes savage cruelty.”

**Liberty likewise, etc.** *Παῤῥησία* (*parrēsia*, frankness), which Erasmus frequently renders in the New Testament as *fiducia* (“confidence”), has very clear examples in the Lord Christ himself, in Peter, and in Paul, who bravely resisted Pharisees and priests hostile to them. It is therefore a kind of courage, perhaps the same thing which Cicero calls *fidentia* (“confidence”) and the Greeks *καρτερία* (*karteria*, steadfastness). Plutarch, in the work entitled *On the Distinction Between a Flatterer and a Friend*, teaches that *παῤῥησία* is proper to a friend and how it should be tempered lest its harshness give offence. BETULEIUS.

**Liberty.** Relevant here is the excellent passage in Valerius Maximus, book VI, chapter 2: “Liberty, placed between virtue and vice, deserves praise if it moderates itself in a wholesome manner; if it pours itself out where it ought not, it deserves blame.” BUN.

**Obstinacy.** It is opposed to liberty. This is illustrated by a passage in Macrobius, *Saturnalia* II, chapter 5: “Who did not marvel that a soldier, not merely exhibiting liberty but even rashness … departed without having offended Caesar, though obstinate?” In Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 52: “Neither liberty nor obstinacy was thereby harmful to anyone.” Graevius there defines *contumacia* as a disposition to contradict and an appetite for passing judgment. BUN.

**Savage cruelty.** According to the saying: “The strictest law is the greatest injustice.”

**Which … are shaken.** Namely, the condition of all living things. Augustine too uses the phrase “to be shaken by passions,” *City of God* XIV, near the end of chapter 9; both following Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* III, chapter 6: “to be shaken by grief as by a storm.”

**Become.** Thus I restored the reading from all manuscripts and many editions. Eight common editions read “are.”]

from the good proper to humanity—since they neither taught anything of this kind nor practised it. Instead, they have always regarded as a vice a virtue that is almost singularly distinctive of humanity.

Here I should like to insert one discussion concerning philosophy, in order to refute more fully the errors of those who call mercy, desire, fear, and mental disorders. They do indeed try to distinguish virtues from vices, which is certainly very easy. For who could not distinguish a liberal person from a prodigal one, as they do; or a sparing person from a miser; or a calm person from a sluggish one; or a cautious person from a timid one? The reason is that these things which are good have their limits, and if they exceed them, they fall into vices. Thus constancy, unless undertaken for truth, becomes impudence; likewise courage, if it undergoes a certain danger without necessity compelling it or not for an honourable cause, [Col. 0687B] is changed into rashness. Liberty likewise, if it attacks others rather than resists those attacking it, is obstinacy. Severity too, unless it confines itself within penalties appropriate to the guilty, becomes savage cruelty.

Accordingly, they say that those who seem wicked do not sin voluntarily or choose evils in preference; rather, deceived by the appearance of good things, they fall into evils while ignorant of the distinction between goods and evils. These statements are not false; but they all refer to the body. For to be sparing, constant, cautious, calm, courageous, or severe are indeed virtues, but virtues of this temporary life. We, however, who despise this life, have other virtues set before us—virtues of which philosophers could not by any means [Col. 0687C] even have formed a suspicion. Accordingly, they regarded certain virtues [Col. 0688A] as vices and certain vices as virtues.

For the Stoics remove from the human being every passion by whose impulse the mind is moved: desire, joy, fear, and grief. The first two arise from goods, future or present; the latter two from evils. In the same way they call these four “disorders,” as I have said, not so much implanted by nature as adopted through false opinion. They therefore judge that these can be uprooted entirely if the false opinion of goods and evils is removed. For if the wise person judges nothing to be good and nothing to be evil, he will neither burn with desire, exult in joy, be terrified by fear, nor be contracted by grief.

We shall shortly see whether they accomplish what they wish, or what they do accomplish. Meanwhile, their project is arrogant and almost mad: they believe themselves able to cure and strive against the force [Col. 0688B] and order of nature.

## CHAPTER XV. On the passions and the Peripatetics’ view of them

For the condition of all living things demonstrates that these are natural, not voluntary, since all are shaken by the same passions. The Peripatetics are therefore more correct in denying that all these things can be removed, because they were born together with us. They attempt to show how providently and necessarily God—or nature, as they say—has armed us with these passions. Yet, because they usually become vicious if excessive, they hold that a human being can beneficially moderate them by applying measure, so that only as much may remain in a person as is sufficient for nature. This is not an unintelligent argument, if, as I said, everything were not referred to this life. [Col. 0688C]

The Stoics, therefore, are mad, since they do not moderate these things but cut them off, and—[the supplied text breaks off with *rebusque a natura insitis*, “and things implanted by nature”]. [Col. 0689A]

[Note: [Col. 0689C] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 689–690]

**And things implanted by nature.** Eleven recent manuscripts lack the preposition.—“Implanted by nature.” Reimmann, with the editions, reads “implanted by nature.” But Lactantius is accustomed to use this expression without a preposition, as below, “implanted by nature”; and in chapter 14, “they call disorders not so much implanted by nature.” *Epitome*, chapter 61: “indeed, implanted by nature.” Cicero, *For Sulla*, chapter 30: “This is implanted by nature.” BUN.

**Fear from deer.** Poets portray deer as timid. Thus Ovid, *Tristia* V:

> Yet the tracks of the timid hind, once found …

**Gentleness from cattle.** He said in book III, chapter 26: “Give me an irascible man … and I shall make him as gentle as a sheep,” where I noted that Terence was expressed. Likewise, *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 14: “the gentler animals.” Seneca, *On Anger* II, chapter 8: “This is an assembly of wild beasts, except that they are gentle among themselves.” Indeed, the very word *placiditas* belongs to the golden age; Varro uses it in *On Agriculture* II, chapter 1, no. 4: “They think sheep were adopted both for usefulness and for gentleness. For they are especially … quiet,” etc. BUN.

**Physicians affirm.** Thus I restored the text from the manuscripts. Three recent manuscripts and the editions read “say”; one Royal manuscript reads “report.”

**In the spleen.** Some think that laughter is removed from a human being along with the spleen and that immoderate jesting is determined by the spleen’s size. Pliny, book II, chapter 37: “The reason is that it draws to itself the melancholic humour, so that pure blood may pass through to the brain and other parts.” BETULEIUS.

[Col. 0689D] **Anger in the gall.** Pliny, in the same passage: “But in the gall,” he says, “when it is black, lies the cause of madness and, when it is wholly discharged, of death for a human being.” Hence *bilis*, “gall,” is also used as an accusation concerning character. Such great poison resides in this part when it flows into the mind. Hence gall is the symbol of anger. BETULEIUS.

**Lust in the liver.** Tityus is said by poets to pay his penalty in his liver because, inflamed by lust there, he dared to solicit Latona for sexual violation, according to Heraclides Ponticus. Alexander of Aphrodisias says in the *Problems* that pigs are so given to pleasure because they have a larger liver. Ovid sums up the seats of the passions in a couplet in the *Tristia*:

> The heart is wise, the lung speaks, gall stirs angers;
>  
> The spleen causes laughter; the liver compels love.

BETULEIUS. See Lactantius’s *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 14.

**Fear in the heart.** Pliny, in the passage already cited so often, says: “Animals are thought dull whose heart is stiff and hard; bold if it is small; timid if it is very large.” Hence, according to the same Heraclides, in the *Odyssey* Ulysses, angry with the suitors, strikes his heart, as though it were a certain dwelling-place of *τῆς μισοπονηρίας* (*tēs misoponērias*, “hatred of wickedness”). But, if we consider the matter more correctly, the heart is the principal organ of all passions. [Col. 0690B] Read concerning these chapter 14 of *On the Workmanship of God*. BETUL.

[Col. 0690C] **For if virtue is, etc.** What follows must be understood cautiously; for it is clear that these statements are not absolutely true of glorified saints, but concern this life.

**As the vices give way.** The Canterbury manuscript and Roman edition of 1470 read “as the vices fall”; one Colbert manuscript, “as the thorns fall.”

**He placed … the material of vices … in vices.** These words, somewhat awkwardly expressed, may indeed be softened from *Epitome*, chapter 61, where he treats of the passions: “For those things which God rationally implanted in human beings are not evil in themselves … they become evil by being used badly.” Yet our author does not appear to have been wholly sound in his teaching concerning the origin of evil, as will be noted on *Epitome*, chapter 29. BUN.

**Either appears or is established.** The Juntine manuscript and five editions read “either may appear or may be established”; one Colbert and one Clermont manuscript read “either may appear or is established,” incorrectly.

**From an opinion of goods.** The Greeks call this *δοκοῦντα* (*dokounta*, “things that seem good”); Cicero calls them *opinata*, “matters of opinion.” But the wise person is not led by opinions. He therefore desires what he ought, rejoices in honourable things, fears true evils, and grieves and bears with distress whatever painful event occurs. Thus Ludovicus Vives is much more correct, as he discusses these matters excellently in book III of *On Philosophy*. BETULEIUS.

[Col. 0690D] **So that in place of desire.** Thus one ancient Bologna manuscript and several editions read.

**Than to will.** I have deleted *malum* (“evil”), a word absent from the Betuleian manuscript and incapable of being retained in a sound sense. For Lactantius is dealing with the Stoics, whose customary practice was wordplay; he therefore asserts that the word “to desire” contains so little vice in itself that, provided this passion concerns a good thing, it is much better to desire than to will. SPARK.—“To desire a good rather than to will it.” There is greater force in the word *cupere* (“to desire”) and *cupiditas* (“desire”) than in *velle* (“to will”) and *voluntas* (“will”). This is clear from book VI, chapter 17: “The Stoic will say that will, not desire, is needed to attain these things. On the contrary, it is too little to will. Many persons will; but when pain reaches the inward parts, the will yields, while desire persists.” BUN.]

…their rationale failed them in changing the name. Thus I have corrected it from the very oldest manuscripts: 2 Bonon., Regio-Put., Cauc., Tax., [Col. 0691C] Pen., and the editions of Betuleius. In six others it is *deficit* (“fails”). In nine others one reads, “their rationale fails them in the name”; in five recent manuscripts and in the printed editions, “the rationale of its name fails.” But below, too, the perfect tense occurs: not that the thing was lacking to them, but the word.]

They in some sense wish to castrate the human being. This is as though they wished to remove fear from deer, venom from snakes, anger from wild beasts, or gentleness from domesticated animals. For the qualities assigned severally to dumb animals have all been assigned together to human beings. And if, as physicians maintain, the affection of joy resides in the spleen, anger in the gall, desire in the liver, and fear in the heart, it is easier to kill the living creature itself than to tear something out of its body—which is to wish to alter the nature of a living being. Yet these prudent men do not understand that, when they remove vices from a human being, they also remove virtue, for which alone they make room. For if virtue consists in holding oneself in check and restraining oneself amid the onset of anger—as they cannot deny—then whoever lacks anger lacks virtue. If it is virtue to restrain bodily desire, then one who has no desire to restrain must necessarily lack virtue. If it is virtue to curb desire from craving what belongs to another, then surely one can possess no virtue who lacks that upon which the use of virtue is brought to bear for restraint. Therefore, where there are no vices, there is no place even for virtue—just as there is no place for victory where there is no adversary. Thus it comes about that in this life good cannot exist without evil.

The affections, therefore, are as it were the natural fertility [Col. 0690A] of souls. For just as a field that is naturally fertile runs wild in brambles, so an uncultivated mind, as vices spontaneously grow strong, is overgrown as with thorns. But when the true cultivator approaches, the vices at once give way and the fruits of virtue spring up.

Accordingly, when God first fashioned the human being, by wonderful providence He first implanted in him these stirrings of the mind, so that he might receive virtue as the earth receives cultivation; and He placed the material of vices in the affections, and that of virtue in the vices. Virtue indeed either will not exist at all, or will be unable to be put into practice, if the things through which its power either appears or is established are absent. Let us now see what those same men, who eradicate vices utterly, have accomplished. The four affections which they think arise from judgments about goods and evils, and which, once uprooted, they believe the mind of the wise person to be healed [Col. 0690B]—since they understand both that these are implanted by nature and that without them nothing can be moved or done—they replace with certain others in their place and stead: in place of desire they substitute will, as though it were not far preferable to desire the good than merely to will it; likewise, in place of joy, gladness; and in place of fear, caution. But in the fourth case their rationale failed them in changing the name. Thus they utterly removed distress—that is, sadness and pain of mind—which absolutely [Col. 0691A] cannot be done. For who could fail to grieve if pestilence had exhausted his country, or an enemy had destroyed it,

[Col. 0691C] **Variant Notes on Columns 691–692**

**“An enemy had destroyed it.”** Four manuscripts and five editions read “had invaded it.”

**“Good men.”** One old Bononian manuscript reads “neighbours.”

**“Imposed, or at any rate not greatly.”** Cauc., Jun., and eight editions insert “or not at all,” wrongly, since, as Thomasius says, it disturbs the whole argument.

**“Manifest gladness.”** Three recent manuscripts and the printed editions read “profuse gladness.” But nearly all the manuscripts more correctly have *professum*, that is, open gladness shown by outward signs. The edition of Isaeus has “suffused.”

[Col. 0691D] **“Should be moderated moderately.”** Thus I restored the text from all manuscripts except seven, and from the Roman edition of 1470 and the Gymnic edition. The reading is also confirmed by what follows below: “they moderate moderately.” *Medie* means “moderately,” “in a moderate manner,” as one recent Regius manuscript has it. In seven recent manuscripts and the printed editions one reads *medio temperanda sint*: because the word *medie* seemed uncommon, they made it *medio*. Yet *medie* occurs in Apuleius, *On the Doctrine of Plato*, II, p. 22, *medie morati* (“moderately disposed”); and in Eutropius VII.8, concerning Claudius, *medie imperavit* (“he ruled moderately”). The Gryphian and Betuleian editions read merely *temperanda*, as does the Tornesian; but this last notes that its manuscript has *medie temperanda*. Yet if you suppress *medie*, the sentence will be equally correct and elegant.

**“For nothing defective can be born.”** These words should be read cautiously. David confesses that he was conceived in iniquities. Nevertheless, it is true that the affections are not sins by their own nature, unless consent is given to evil affections. Consult Saint Augustine. BETULEIUS.

**“One should walk quietly.”** Correctly so. One recent manuscript and seven editions read “moderately.” [Col. 0692C]

**“What if I show?”** I write this in the present tense, with the three old editions, the Roman and Betuleian editions, the Gymnic edition, and all manuscripts except two recent Regius manuscripts and one Claromontanus, in which one reads *ostendero* (“I shall show”), as in fifteen editions.

**“To rejoice for a moment.”** That is, for an instant or moment of time. Thus above, VIII.17, he said: “Let us not allow a single day, indeed not a single instant of time, to pass without pleasure.” Likewise VII.12.

**“Should curb.”** Thus I corrected from five Regius manuscripts, including the two oldest, and many others; nine other recent manuscripts support this, reading “should restrain.” Two recent Regius manuscripts and editions read “should restrain [plural],” and seven common editions “should curb [plural]”; incorrectly. See above: “the wise person … should see.”

[Col. 0692D] **“Indeed, even in the former case, to rejoice a little,” etc.** He speaks according to the opinion of Gentile philosophers, against whom the argument was directed, in order to refute them from their own premises; for he had professed that he would do this in these books, V.4. He does not speak according to the doctrines of Christian wisdom, by which we are taught to wish every good even for enemies; on this he himself argues admirably below, chapter 18. ISAEUS.—**“Indeed, even in the former case, to rejoice a little.”** This is Lactantius’ meaning: no one doubts that, if some evil befalls one’s enemy, even to rejoice a little—that is, in the slightest degree—is a most serious sin, because the truly wise person wishes well to his enemy and is not *εὐχαιρέκακος* (“one who rejoices in another’s misfortune”). Conversely, if liberty and safety have been won for one’s fellow citizens, to rejoice only slightly—that is, inadequately and coldly—is an equally great fault; for such a person would show that he preferred unjust servitude and the city’s ruin. This is clearer than the sun from what precedes: “What if I show a case in which it is wrong not merely to rejoice moderately, but even for an instant,” etc. BUN.

or if a tyrant had oppressed it? Can anyone fail to grieve if he sees liberty taken away; if he sees relatives, friends, or good people either banished or most cruelly slaughtered—unless his mind has become so stupefied that every sense has been taken from him? They therefore ought either to have removed everything, or this curtailed and feeble argument ought to have been completed; that is, something should also have been substituted for distress, since, once the foregoing points had been arranged as they were, this followed necessarily.

For just as we rejoice in present goods, so we are troubled and grieve at evils. Therefore, if they gave joy another name because they considered it defective, then they should consistently have assigned another term to distress also, because they considered it defective as well. From this it is apparent that [Col. 0691B] it was not the thing that was lacking to them, but the word; through lack of which they wished, contrary to what nature permitted, to remove the entire affection, which is perhaps the greatest of all. I could refute those changes of names more extensively and show either that many names have been applied to the same things for the sake of adorning speech and increasing its richness, or at least that those terms do not differ much from one another. For desire begins from will; caution arises from fear; and joy is nothing other than manifest gladness. But let us suppose, as they themselves wish, that they are different. They will then say, of course, that desire is a persistent and enduring will; joy, an exultant gladness carried beyond bounds; and fear, a caution excessive and exceeding measure. Thus it turns out that the things they think should be removed are not removed, but moderated; since they change merely the names, while the things themselves remain. Therefore these unwise men [Col. 0691C] are brought back to the same conclusion that the Peripatetics reach by reasoning: namely, that vices, because they cannot be removed, [Col. 0692A] should be moderated moderately. They therefore err, because they do not accomplish what they wish and, by a long and rough detour, return to the same road.

## Chapter XVI. On the affections, and the refutation of the Peripatetic view concerning them: what is the true use of the affections, and what is their bad use

But I do not think that even the Peripatetics have approached the truth, although they concede that there are vices and moderate them in measure. Vices, even moderate ones, must be avoided; indeed, the first task ought to have been to ensure that there were no vices. For nothing defective can be born; rather, vices arise if we use the affections badly, while virtues arise if we use them well. Next, it must be shown that not the affections themselves but their causes ought to be moderated. “One must not,” they say, [Col. 0692B] “be excessively elated with joy, but moderately and in due measure.” This is like saying that one should not run at speed but should walk quietly. Yet a person who walks can go wrong, while a person who runs can keep the straight road. What if I show that there is something in which to rejoice not merely moderately but even for a moment is wrong, and, conversely, something in which even to exult with joy is by no means blameworthy? What benefit, after all, will this moderation bring us? I ask whether they think the wise person should rejoice if he sees some evil happen to his enemy; or whether he should curb his joy if, after enemies have been defeated or a tyrant overthrown, liberty and safety have been secured for the citizens.

No one doubts that both to rejoice even slightly in the former case and to rejoice too little in the latter is a very great wrong. The same may be said concerning the other affections. But, as I have said, the principle of wisdom does not concern itself with moderating [Col. 0692C] them, but with their causes, because they are stirred from without; nor ought [Col. 0693A] restraints to be imposed chiefly upon the affections themselves,

[Col. 0693C] **Variant Notes on Columns 693–694**

**“To impose restraints.”** Most editions, with all manuscripts except Jun., read *fraenos imponi* (“restraints to be imposed”); Jun., like four common editions, has *fraena imponi*. Both readings are accepted; see below, chapter 23, shortly before the end, “to impose restraints,” and chapter 18, after the middle, “to loosen the reins.” I follow the manuscripts.

**“Can.”** Thus I corrected from all manuscripts and many editions; some have “may.” But “can” is correct. See what follows: “and can be greatest.”

**“But if it desires what belongs to another.”** Namely, the marriage-bed mentioned above. One Regius, one Colbertinus, one Lipsiensis manuscript, and the Tornesian and Soubron editions read “what belongs to another [feminine].”—**“It desires what belongs to another.”** Take *alienum* here as neuter; it should not be referred to the marriage-bed, because he condemns every desire forbidden by laws, not adultery alone. BUN.

[Col. 0693D] **“But to be prone to anger.”** This disposition, then, is defective; a sudden movement of mind, especially from a just cause, is free from fault, in accordance with “Be angry, and do not sin,” etc. You see, therefore, that circumstances matter greatly in defending the cause. To say *Racha* against one’s brother is a sin; but we see that the Apostles, following their teacher’s example, more than once flared into anger against vices without fault. BETUL.

**“Or when one ought not.”** Seven manuscripts and twelve common editions read “or at a person whom one ought not.”

**“The impulse toward those things.”** I added *rerum* (“things”) from the manuscripts; it is absent in Thys. and Gall.

**“Lacks.”** Three recent manuscripts and five editions read “lacks [present indicative].”

**“The highest fear.”** This fear is not supreme in itself, for it is joined with love and joy; rather, it is supreme in relation to Him who is feared, who is certainly supreme. For he means fear of God, which one might more truly call reverence. CELL.

**“But whoever fears God,” etc.** Not as a stern judge—this is what theologians call servile fear. Rather, the fear of which Lactantius speaks here is nothing other than the love with which good children are accustomed to regard their parents; because this love is mingled with a measure of fear, it is then called *reverentia* (“reverence”) or *veneratio* (“veneration”) in Latin.

**“For they have always been witnessed, and are still witnessed.”** Thus nearly all manuscripts. Two Bononian manuscripts and Tax. read “and are always witnessed”; Cauc., one Colbertinus, and nine editions omit “always.”

**“The mind shudders to recall.”** An ancient elegance, customary among the finest writers. Livy, II.37: “The mind shudders lest anything be done rashly and heedlessly.” Pliny, VI.20: “The mind shudders to remember.” Lactantius, VII.15: “The mind shudders to say.” BUNEMAN.

[Col. 0694D] **“Of savage beasts.”** He means the most cruel human beings—tyrants and others whose service emperors used in persecuting Christians. The ashes of martyrs were often attacked, so that by this novel contrivance of cruelty they might cut off every hope of resurrection for Christians. See chapter 2 of the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, where one may read that the bones of martyrs were crushed into powder and thrown into a river or the sea.

**“Fear of God.”** That is, reverence, or a person’s fear of displeasing God.

**“Fears must be removed.”** The plural is frequent in our author. V.20; VII.16; Seneca, *Epistle* 13: “No fears are so pernicious, so irrevocable, as frenzied fears.” *Epistle* 24: “The fears of the underworld are vain.” BUN.

**“So that this one alone may remain.”** Thus I restored the text from two old Bononian manuscripts, seven Regius, four Colbertinus, others, and three printed editions. Seven recent manuscripts and twelve common editions have “so that he”; the Roman edition of 1470, “so that these.”

**“Desire.”** It is longing; thus in Celsus, “the desire for food returns,” and in Quintilian, “the desire for light.” Desire is not a vice unless it adheres to evil.]

because they can be small in a very great crime, and can be greatest without fault. Rather, they ought to have been assigned to definite times, circumstances, and places, so that things which may rightly be used should not be vices. For just as it is good to walk rightly but evil to go astray, so it is good to be moved by the affections in the right direction and evil to be moved by them in the wrong direction. For if sexual desire does not wander outside the lawful marriage-bed, it is free from fault, even if intense. But if it desires what belongs to another, it is nevertheless a very great vice, even if moderate. Therefore it is not a disease to be angry, to desire, or to be stirred by sexual desire; but it is a disease to be irascible, greedy, and lustful. For one who is irascible grows angry even with someone with whom he should not be angry, or when he should not; one who is greedy desires even what he does not need; and one who is lustful seeks even what the laws forbid. Therefore the whole principle [Col. 0693B] ought to have concerned this: since the impulse toward such things can neither be restrained nor ought to be restrained, because it is necessarily implanted for maintaining the duties of life, it should instead be directed onto the straight road, where its very course is free from obstruction and danger.

## Chapter XVII. On the affections and their use; on patience and the highest good of Christians

But my zeal for refutation has carried me too far, although my purpose is to show that the things philosophers considered vices are not merely not vices, but are in fact great virtues. For the sake of instruction I shall select from the rest those things which I think most relevant to the matter. They place fear, [Col. 0693C] or dread, among the greatest vices, and think it the utmost [Col. 0694A] weakness of mind; courage, they think, is its opposite, and if it is present in a human being, there is no place for fear. Does anyone, then, believe that the same fear can be the highest courage? By no means. For nature does not seem capable of allowing something to turn into its opposite. Yet I shall show, not by some subtle inference such as Socrates uses in Plato, forcing those against whom he argues to acknowledge the things they had denied, but plainly, that the highest fear is the highest virtue.

No one doubts that it belongs to a timid and weak mind to fear pain, poverty, exile, prison, or death; whoever does not shrink from all these is judged most courageous. But whoever fears God does not fear all those things. No arguments are needed to prove this: the punishments inflicted on worshippers of God have always been witnessed, and are still witnessed throughout the world. In torturing them, new and unheard-of torments have been devised. The mind shudders to recall the kinds of death, when the butchery of savage beasts has raged beyond death itself. Yet happy and unconquered patience endured these execrable mutilations of bodies without a single groan. This virtue presented the greatest miracle to all peoples, provinces, and even to the torturers themselves, when cruelty was conquered by patience. Yet nothing but fear of God produced this virtue. Therefore, as I was saying, fear must not be uprooted, as the Stoics wish, nor moderated, as the Peripatetics wish; rather, it must be directed into the true way, and fears must be removed—but so that this one alone remains. Since it is lawful and true, it alone brings it about that all other things can be without fear. [Col. 0694C]

Desire also is reckoned among vices; but if it desires earthly things, it is a vice, whereas it is virtue if it desires heavenly things. For whoever desires to attain justice, God, everlasting life, eternal light, and all the things God promises to humanity will despise riches, honours, powers, [Col. 0695A] and kingdoms themselves.

Perhaps a Stoic will say that will, not desire, is necessary for attaining these things. Indeed, it is not enough to will. Many will; but when pain has reached their inward parts, will yields while desire perseveres. And if desire causes all things sought by others to be held in contempt, it is the highest virtue, since it is the mother of self-restraint. Therefore we should rather bring about this: that the affections, the wrong use of which is a vice, should be directed aright. For these stirrings of the mind are like a chariot yoked together, [Col. 0695B] in the proper control of which the chief duty of the driver is to know the road. If he keeps it, he will not collide, however swiftly he goes. But if he strays, even though he travels gently and slowly, he will either be jolted over rough ground, plunge over precipices, or at least be carried where there is no need to go. Thus that chariot of life, drawn by the affections as by swift horses, will perform its duty if it keeps the straight road. Fear and desire, therefore, become vices if they are cast down to earthly things, but virtues if they are directed toward divine things.

They count frugality also in the place of a virtue. But if it is eagerness to possess, it cannot be a virtue, because it is wholly occupied with increasing or preserving earthly goods. We, however, do not refer the highest good to the body; rather, we measure every duty by the preservation of the soul alone. And if, as I taught above, one must by no means spare one’s estate in order to preserve humanity and justice, then being frugal is not a virtue; the term deceives and misleads under the appearance of virtue. For frugality is indeed abstinence from pleasures; but it is a vice for this reason: it comes down from love of possession, [Col. 0696A] although one ought both to abstain from pleasures and not to be sparing of money. For to use money sparingly—that is, moderately—is a kind of smallness of mind: either of one who is over-fearful that it may fail him, or of one who despairs of being able to restore it, or of one who cannot grasp contempt for earthly things. But they, conversely, call prodigal the person who does not spare his own property. For they distinguish the liberal person from the prodigal in this way: the liberal person gives generously to those who deserve it, when it is fitting, and as much as is enough; but the prodigal pours things out both upon those who do not deserve them, when there is no need, and without regard for his estate.

What then? Shall we call prodigal one who, for mercy’s sake, gives food to the needy? Yet it makes a great difference whether you give lavishly to prostitutes because of lust, [Col. 0696B] or to the miserable because of humanity; whether seducers, gamblers, and pimps plunder your money, or you devote it to piety and to God; whether you put it into your belly and throat, or lay it up in the treasury of justice. Therefore, just as it is a vice to pour it out for an evil purpose, so it is a virtue to pour it out for a good one. If it is a virtue not to spare wealth that can be restored in order to sustain a human life that cannot be restored, then frugality is a vice. I would therefore call nothing other than mad those who deprive the human being, a gentle and social animal, of its own designation; who, after uprooting the affections in which all humanity consists, wish to lead it to an immovable stupor of mind while they endeavour to free the mind from disturbances and, as they themselves say, render it calm and tranquil. This is not only impossible, because its power [Col. 0696C] and principle lie in motion; it ought not even to be attempted. For just as water always lying still and quiet is unhealthy and more turbid, so a motionless and torpid mind is useless even to itself. Nor can it preserve life itself, because it will neither do anything nor think; since thought [Col. 0697A] itself is nothing other than the movement of the mind.

[Col. 0697C] **Variant Notes on Columns 697–698**

**“Movement of the mind.”** As Thales says, the mind is a substance which is always moved, and moved from itself; that is, with God supplying the principle of motion.

**“Immobility of mind.”** The Cantabrigian manuscript and five old editions read “immutability.”

**“And all.”** The Cantabrigian manuscript and nine editions read “as,” a particle which occurred shortly before.

**“This is true constancy.”** Two recent Regius manuscripts, Jun., two Colbertinus manuscripts, and Brun. read “This is the true constancy.”

**“Cicero’s,” etc.** An argument from authority. In the same way Cicero himself, *On Duties* III.8, says that to take something from another for one’s own advantage is more contrary to nature than death, pain, and the rest. No work of Seneca survives under this title; doubtless it has perished.

**“Flame must be seized with the mouth.”** The Roman edition of 1470, Cellarius, and all manuscripts except one Regius read this; in that manuscript, as in many editions, one finds “must be received.”

**“He endures these things.”** Pierr., Parrh., Ald., Crat., and Gymn. read “Nor does he endure,” incorrectly. More correctly the manuscripts and Rost., Venice 1471 and 1497, Paris., Fasit., Gryph., and the rest read: “He endures these things.” Reimm. has “This endures.” BUN.

**“Therefore he is just.”** From the very old Regio-Put. manuscript, five other Regius, four Colbertinus, five others, and three editions I added *est* (“is”), which seems necessary.
