**“They know nothing.”** He means the Academics.

**“As the highest knowledge.”** These words breathe Lactantius’ style; thus in *On Anger*, chapter 1: “So that he might profess as the highest learning precisely that he had learned to know nothing.” *Pro summa scientia* means “as though it were the highest knowledge,” a usage customary with our author; for example, III.3: “He regards wisdom as the greatest folly.” BUN.

**“Put forward.”** Thus I restored the text from the very oldest manuscripts: two Bononian, Cauc., eight Regius, five Colbertinus, three Lipsiensis, eight others, and eight editions. Two recent Regius manuscripts and twelve editions read “display publicly,” which means the same.

**“Perceive.”** Two recent Regius manuscripts read “foresee.” Two Bononian, three Regius, Jun., Tax., one Colbertinus, two Claromontanus, and four editions read “apprehend.”

[Col. 0698D] **“Having comprehended these virtues; for example, ‘Let him not lie.’”** Thus I punctuated it. For here *ut* means “for example,” if the reading is genuine. BUN.

**“There is no place for falsehood.”** Away, then, with the “officious lie,” unworthy of a Christian. See Augustine, *On Lying* and *Against Lying*, and Jonas, bishop of Orléans, *On the Instruction of Laypeople* II.27.

**“He will receive.”** Buneman reads “Let him receive,” and confirms his reading thus: “Heumann says that one should read ‘he will receive,’ because ‘he will say,’ ‘he will think,’ and ‘he will commit’ have preceded. But nothing should be changed: the things which he says a worshipper of God must observe he expresses in the present subjunctive; when illustrating them, he varies the tenses. Such precepts are: ‘Let him not lie,’ above; ‘Let him not take interest,’ below; ‘Let him not accept a gift from a poor person,’ below; ‘Let him answer one who curses with a blessing,’ below; ‘Let him take care not to make … an enemy,’ below; ‘Let him preserve innocence,’ etc.” BUN.—**“If he has lent any money, he will not take interest.”** Thus I read with nine Regius manuscripts, two of them very old, two Bononian, five Colbertinus, Jun., and many others. I think that Lactantius and other authors used this idiom; at least the Vulgate has Psalm 117:22: “The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the head of the corner”; and John 14:24: “The word which you have heard is not mine, but the Father’s who sent me.” One recent Regius manuscript and three others read “of money”; Ultr. and Brun. have “and money.” Goth. and Lips. have “if anyone has lent money”; *si qui* stands for *si quis*, as is often found in manuscripts of Cicero. Eleven manuscripts have “let him take.” But “he will say,” “he will think,” and “he will commit” occurred shortly before, and “he will not omit,” “he will not defile,” and “he will bring about” follow. As to usury understood by Gallaeus from this passage and I.15, consult, if you wish, the French book published in Paris in 1677, entitled *Défense des sentiments de Lactance sur le sujet de l’Usure* (“Defence of Lactantius’ Views on the Subject of Usury”). See also Leviticus 25, Deuteronomy 23, Psalm 4, and Ezekiel 18.]

Finally, those who uphold this immobility of mind wish to deprive the mind of life, because life is active and death is still. They also rightly count certain things as virtues, but they do not preserve their proper measure.

Constancy is a virtue: not so that we may resist those who inflict injury, for we must yield to them—I shall shortly explain why this ought to be done—but so that, when people command us to do something contrary to God’s law and to justice, no threats or punishments may terrify us into preferring a human command to God’s command. Likewise, it is a virtue to despise death: not so that we seek it and voluntarily inflict it upon ourselves, as many, even very great, philosophers often did—which is wicked and impious—but so that, when compelled to abandon God and betray [Col. 0697B] the faith, we may prefer to undergo death; that we may defend liberty against the foolish and mad violence of the powerful; and that we may challenge every threat and terror of the world by courage of mind. Thus, with a lofty and unconquerable mind, we trample pain and death, which others fear. This is virtue; this is true constancy: it must be guarded and preserved for this one purpose, that no terror and no force may be able to turn us away from God.

That saying of Cicero, therefore, is true: “No one,” he says, “can be just who fears death, pain, exile, or poverty.” Likewise Seneca, in his books of moral philosophy, says: “This is the honourable man—not distinguished by a pointed cap or purple robe, nor by the attendant service of lictors, but diminished by nothing—who, when he sees death nearby, is not disturbed as though he had seen something new; who, whether torments must be endured throughout the whole body, or flame must be seized with the mouth, or his hands must be stretched out upon a crossbeam, asks not what he suffers, but how well.” But whoever worships God endures these things and does not fear. Therefore he is just. From these considerations [Col. 0698A] it follows that no one wholly alien from the religion of the one God can either know or preserve virtues, or their most exact boundaries.

## Chapter XVIII. On certain commands of God and on patience

But let us leave philosophers aside: those who either know absolutely nothing and put forward this very fact as the highest knowledge; or who do not perceive even what they know; or who, because they think they know what they do not know, foolishly and arrogantly act without wisdom. Let us, therefore—to return to our purpose—we alone to whom truth has been revealed by God and wisdom sent from heaven, do what God our illuminator commands. Let us bear with one another and endure the burdens of this life by mutual assistance. Yet if we do some good work, [Col. 0698B] let us not seek glory from it. For God warns that a worker of justice ought not to boast, lest he appear to have performed the duty of humanity not so much in obedience to heavenly commands as from a desire to please, and so receive already the reward of glory which he sought and fail to receive the recompense of that heavenly and divine reward.

The other things a worshipper of God must observe are easy, once those virtues have been comprehended: for example, let him never lie for the purpose of deceiving or harming. It is impious for one devoted to truth to be deceitful in any matter and to depart from the truth itself which he follows. On this path of justice and every virtue there is no place for falsehood. Therefore that true and just traveller will not utter the Lucilian verse:

> It is not my way to lie to a friend or intimate,

but will consider that it is not his way to lie even to an enemy or stranger; nor will he ever allow his tongue, the interpreter of the mind, to disagree with his feeling and thought. If he has lent any money, he will not take interest, [Col. 0699A] so that the kindness by which he assists someone in need may remain unimpaired,

[Col. 0699C] **Variant Notes on Columns 699–700**

**“By which he assists.”** Thus I restored the text from all manuscripts and very many editions. Five common editions have “may assist.”

[Col. 0699D] **“Let him accept.”** Thus several manuscripts and nine editions read, and the following words require it. Cauc., Jun., one Colbertinus, and six printed editions have “he will accept.” On gifts not to be received, read Exodus 23, Proverbs 15, Deuteronomy 16, Luke 6, and Romans 15.

**“Let him answer.”** See Matthew 5, Luke 6, and Romans 12. **“That no evil word.”** Thus with all manuscripts, the old Roman edition, and Cellarius. The other common editions have “nor.”

**“Who worships the good Word.”** That is, Jesus, the Son of God, who is the Word of the Father.

**“And let him not take vengeance upon himself.”** I added *suam* (“his own”), absent from one old Bononian manuscript and four editions, from the remaining witnesses.

**“Let him reserve it for God the judge.”** Thus I read with the two oldest Regius manuscripts, which is preferable to “reserve it for God’s judgment,” in the other manuscripts and editions, except one old Bononian manuscript and five editions, which have “let him preserve.” On not taking revenge, see Deuteronomy 32, Hebrews 10, and Romans 12.

[Col. 0700C] **“The observer and witness of all.”** He follows Minucius, chapter 32: “How much more is God the author of all and observer of all, from whom no secret can be hidden,” etc. Many similar passages occur in Lactantius II.16; VI.24: “He knows all things … let us suppose … that we are looked upon from above by Him who will himself be both judge and witness,” etc.; and *On Anger* 8. BUN.

**“For sluggish and inert.”** Thus the Regio-Put. manuscript, four other Regius, five Colbertinus, three Lipsiensis, others, and the passage below read; in three Regius, one Colbertinus, and sixteen printed editions, “inert.”

**“Although he can benefit more people.”** Thus I restored the reading from nearly all manuscripts and from the editions of Cellarius and Walch, deleting all instances of *vel* (“or”), which exist only in the margin of one Colbertinus manuscript and in ten editions. *Pluribus* (“more people”) is also absent in four Regius manuscripts, one of them very old, one Colbertinus, and Brun.

**“In ethical works.”** Two recent manuscripts and fifteen printed editions add “books,” a word absent from the others and unnecessary, since shortly before the end of chapter 17 the saying of Cicero, taken from the second book of *On Duties*, had already occurred.

[Col. 0700D] **“Unless provoked by injury.”** After these words the following sentence occurs in the Latin manuscripts: “Here Cicero wrongly added ‘unless provoked by injury.’”

**“A most shameful tail.”** Perhaps some, out of a concern for chastity, did not wish to name a tail, as in Lactantius I.17 and *Epitome* 9 they omitted “semen” from manuscripts. The rest and Fasit. and Gryph. rightly read “tail.” BUN.

**“But if patience.”** Thus I corrected from all manuscripts and many editions; some have “wisdom.” The correction is certain. See what precedes and follows.

**“As though.”** One recent Regius manuscript, one Colbertinus, and nine editions wrongly add “if,” absent from the others, and rightly so. Below, at the beginning of chapter 19: “as though no one could fight bravely against enemies.” Likewise, “as though fire.” Cicero too compares wickedness to a conflagration, *Against Verres* I.58: “Such wickedness must be extinguished by the common defence as though it were some conflagration.” BUNEMAN.]
to necessity, and should entirely refrain from what belongs to another. For in this kind of duty a man ought to be content with his own, though at other times he must not spare even his own property in doing good; but to receive more than he has given is unjust. Whoever does this lies in wait, as it were, in order to prey upon another’s need.

But the just man will never fail to do something merciful; nor will he defile himself by gain of this sort. Rather, he will ensure that, without any loss to himself, the very thing which he lends is reckoned among good works. Let him accept no gift from a poor man, so that, if he has himself bestowed anything, it may be good precisely because it was gratuitous. Let him answer one who curses with a blessing; let him never curse himself, lest an evil word proceed from the mouth of a man [Col. 0699B] who worships the good Word. Indeed, let him carefully beware lest at any time he make an enemy through his own fault; and if anyone should prove so insolent as to injure a good and just man, let him bear it mildly and moderately, and not take vengeance upon himself, but reserve it for God the judge. Let him preserve innocence always and everywhere. This precept has force not merely to prevent him from inflicting injury himself, but also to prevent him from avenging an injury inflicted upon him. For there sits the greatest and most equitable judge, the observer and witness of all things. Let him prefer this judge to man; let him choose that this judge pronounce upon his case, since no one can escape His judgment, either by anyone’s defence or by favour.

Thus it comes about that a just man is held in contempt by all; and [Col. 0700A] because he is thought unable to defend himself, he is considered sluggish and feeble. But he who has avenged himself upon an enemy is judged strong and vigorous: men honour him, and all fear him. Yet though the good man may be able to benefit more people, they nevertheless admire the man who can harm rather than the man who can benefit. But the perversity of men will not be able to pervert the just man from striving to obey God; and he will prefer to be despised, provided that he always performs the duty of the good man and never that of the bad. Cicero, in the same *On Duties*: “But if anyone,” he says, “wishes to unfold the closely wrapped conception of his own mind, let him now teach himself that that man is good who benefits those whom he can, and harms no one, unless provoked by injury.”

O how he corrupted a simple and true sentence by adding two words! For what need was there [Col. 0700B] to add “unless provoked by injury”? It was as though he attached vice, like a most shameful tail, to a good man, and deprived him of patience, which is the greatest of all virtues. He said that a good man will harm someone if he has been provoked; but by that very fact he must lose the name of a good man if he does harm. For it is no less evil to return an injury than to inflict one. For whence do conflicts among men arise, whence battles and strifes, except because impatience, set against wickedness, often stirs up great storms? But if you set patience—than which no virtue truer, none more worthy of man, can be found—against wickedness, it will immediately be extinguished, as if you had poured water upon fire.

[Col. 0701A] But if that provocative wickedness finds impatience as its equal, then, as though doused with oil, it will kindle so great a conflagration that no river, but an outpouring of blood, will extinguish it. Great, therefore, is the principle of patience, which the wise man has taken away from the good man. For this alone ensures that no evil is done; if it were granted to all, there would be no crime and no fraud in human affairs. What, then, can be so disastrous and so contrary to a good man as to give the reins to anger, which will strip him not only of the title of good, but even of that of human? For, as he himself most truly says, to harm another is not in accordance with human nature. Even cattle, if provoked, resist either with a kick or with a horn; and serpents and wild beasts cause no trouble unless you pursue them in order to kill them. And, to return to examples among men [Col. 0701B], even the unskilled and foolish, when they receive an injury, are led by blind and irrational rage and endeavour to repay in kind those who harm them.

In what, therefore, does the wise and good man differ from the bad and foolish, except that he possesses invincible patience, which fools lack? Except that he knows how to govern himself and moderate his anger, whereas they, because they lack virtue, cannot restrain it? But evidently this consideration deceived him: when he was speaking of virtue, he thought that victory in any contest was a matter of virtue; nor could he see at all that a man who yields to grief and anger, indulges the passions which he ought rather to resist, and rushes wherever wickedness has provoked him, does not maintain the office of virtue. For he who strives to return an injury longs to imitate the very man [Col. 0701C] by whom he has been injured. Thus he who imitates evil can in no way be good.

**Notes on columns 701–702**

**“Its equal” (*comparem*).** Here wickedness and impatience are matched like a pair of gladiators. See Book VI, ch. 20 and *On the Workmanship* ch. 19, in the notes: “Unless there is some equal opponent.” BUNEMAN.

**“What then” (*quid igitur*).** Five recent manuscripts and twenty printed editions read *quid ergo*, “what therefore.” One ancient Bologna manuscript, Cauc., and one Colbert manuscript have *enim*, “for,” instead of *igitur*, because it immediately preceded. The great majority agree with the text.

**“When he was speaking of virtue” (*quod cum de virtute*).** I have restored *quod* from almost all manuscripts [Col. 0701D]. Three recent manuscripts and the printed editions read *quia*, “because.”

**“Was speaking” (*loqueretur*).** Thus restored from the very ancient manuscripts: one Bologna and one Regius; two other recent Regius manuscripts, one of them of excellent quality; Lips., Pal., one Colbert, and Marm. in the first hand. Eight manuscripts and ten printed editions have *quaereretur*, “was being sought”; eleven recent manuscripts and seven common editions, *quaeritur*, “is sought.”

**“And rushing wherever wickedness has provoked him.”** Thus almost all manuscripts. Brun. has *provocaverit*, “has provoked.” “In part” is to be understood, perhaps from a gloss: two recent Regius manuscripts, Cantabrig., and the third old Roman edition adopted *in quacumque parte*, “in whatever part,” as do the notes and one Colbert manuscript in the margin. Eight common editions read *in quamcumque partem*, “in whatever direction.” Explain *et* as “also,” says Walch; the sense will lack obscurity.

**“Dog-like eloquence.”** Many refer this to a saying of Appius, on which Wasse is fuller in his notes on Sallust, *Fragments*, Book VI, ch. 11, p. 88. All have overlooked the passage in Jerome very close to Lactantius, *Letter to the monk Rusticus*, fol. 47: “They go out in public in order to exercise dog-like eloquence.” Isidore, *On the Highest Good*, Book III, ch. 60: “The ancients called forensic eloquence ‘dog-like eloquence,’ because advocates, in contests of cases, abandoning the matters at issue, bark at one another like dogs and turn the disputes of their cases into personal insults.” BUN.

**“Reports” (*refert*).** In Nonius, under *Rabula*; Quintilian, Book XII, ch. 9.

**“In a dog-like fashion” (*canino modo*).** Three recent manuscripts read *canino more*, “in a dog-like manner.”

**“Whence will an example be sought?”** Three recent manuscripts and three editions have *peteretur*, “would be sought.”

**“Of his teacher.”** One Regius manuscript and the printed editions read *doctoris*, that is, of Cicero himself, by his death [Col. 0702D].

**“But if provoked” (*quod si lacessitus*).** Jun. and five editions read *qui*, “who.”

**“Orations inscribed under another’s title.”** The *Philippics*, which he so entitled in imitation of Demosthenes. Read the account in Plutarch, *Life of Cicero* and *Life of Antony*; and in Appian, Book IV of the *Civil Wars*. Cicero can scarcely be excused for having avenged so vehemently an injury done to himself by Antony rather than a public injury.

**“So that a just man might acquire it” (*quam ut caperet homo justus*).** Thus I have restored the passage from the very ancient manuscripts—one Bologna, two Regius, and eighteen others—and from seven old editions: that is, “so that a just man might be able to possess it.” Ten manuscripts and an equal number of common editions read: “so that a just man might not lack it.”

**“He is conquered.”** One Clairmont manuscript: “he will be conquered”; Jun.: “there is no virtue”; one older Bologna manuscript: “there is no virtue at all.” The rest agree with the text.

**“He rules himself.”** One recent Regius manuscript and twelve printed editions add the conjunction *and*, which the others rightly reject as superfluous. Likewise at the end of ch. 19: “this man is patient, this man strong, this man just.”

By two words, therefore, he took away from the good and wise man the two greatest virtues, innocence and patience. But because he himself practised that dog-like eloquence which Sallust [Col. 0702A] reports to have been so called by Appius, he wished man also to live in a dog-like fashion, biting back when provoked. From what source might a more fitting example be sought of how destructive such retaliation for insult is, and of what devastations it commonly produces, than from the most lamentable fate of his own teacher, who, while striving to obey these precepts of the philosophers, destroyed himself? If, when provoked by injury, he had maintained patience; if he had learned that it belongs to a good man to overlook and bear an insult; then impatience, fickleness, and madness would not have poured forth those famous speeches inscribed under another’s title. He would never have bloodied with his own head the rostra from which he had formerly flourished; nor would that proscription have utterly destroyed the commonwealth.

It is not, therefore, the part of a wise and good man to wish to contend and expose himself to danger: for victory is not in [Col. 0702B] our power, and every contest is uncertain. Rather, it is the part of a wise and excellent man not to wish to remove his adversary, which cannot be done without crime and danger, but to remove the contest itself, which can be done both advantageously and justly. Patience, therefore, must be regarded as the highest virtue. In order that a just man might acquire it, God wished him, as was said above, to be despised as feeble. For unless he is subjected to insults, it will remain unknown how much strength he possesses in restraining himself. But if, when provoked by injury, he begins to pursue the person who has harmed him, he is conquered. If, however, he suppresses that impulse by reason, he plainly rules himself; he can govern himself. This support of oneself is rightly named patience: the one virtue opposed to all vices and passions. It restores the disturbed and wavering mind to its own tranquillity [Col. 0702C]; it softens; it restores a man to himself.

Therefore, since it is impossible and useless to resist nature so as never to be moved at all, yet before that agitation bursts forth into harm, it should, so far as possible, be lulled to rest promptly. God commanded [Col. 0703A] that we should not let the sun go down upon our anger, lest it depart as a witness to our rage. Finally, Marcus Tullius, contrary to the precept of which I spoke a little before, placed forgetfulness of injuries among great praises: “I hope, Caesar,” he says, “that you, who are accustomed to forget nothing except injuries.” If he did this, though he was a man far removed not only from heavenly justice but also from public and civic justice, how much more ought we to do so, who are, as it were, candidates for immortality?

**Notes on columns 703–704**

**“We are, as it were, candidates for immortality” (*immortalitatis velut candidati sumus*).** Thus I emended the text from twelve manuscripts and four editions. The fifteenth-century editions read likewise, a reading also approved by Thomasius from old manuscripts. In his edition Gallaeus rewrote it as *immortalitatis velamine candidati*, “clothed in the veil of immortality”; this is also found in two recent Regius manuscripts, one Colbert manuscript in a second hand, Jun., Cantabrig., and some more recent editions. In one Colbert, Nav., Marm., and Victor. manuscript: *immortalitatis velo candidati*, “candidates under the veil of immortality.” But the best and ancient codices—four Regius, one Bologna, Tax., Cauc., Pal., Brun., Emmanuel, one Colbert in the first hand, and the editions Betul., Is., Spark., Walch.—read: “we are, as it were, candidates for immortality.” Correctly so, supported by five Regius, Gat., Tornes., one Sorbonne, two Clairmont, Cott., and Bodl. manuscripts, which read *immortalitate velut candidati sumus*, “we are, as it were, candidates by immortality.” One ancient Bologna manuscript has *immortalitate candidati sumus*, “we are candidates by immortality.” Lactantius indeed calls Christians “candidates for immortality” in the same sense in which Cyprian calls virgins candidates for integrity and modesty, and Tertullian calls men of ruined conscience candidates of the devil. The analogy is drawn from Roman custom: those seeking a magistracy came forward clothed in a white toga [Col. 0703D], came thus dressed to the elections, and sat upon the hill so that all might see them. Lactantius therefore calls Christians candidates for immortality, just as candidates for the consulship or praetorship were those seeking the consulship or praetorship. Since certain copyists did not understand the little word *velut*, “as it were,” they made it *velamine*, “with a veil,” which is plainly absurd, according to Thomasius.

**“The Stoics.”** Fifteenth-century editions read “Stoics.”

**“Correct indeed.”** Thus the manuscripts and editions. Francius would prefer “They indeed [are correct].” But in this chapter Lactantius disapproves the doctrine of the Peripatetics, who maintain that the passions in man are necessary. Lactantius’s doctrine throughout this chapter accords especially well with Catholic truth.

**“They say that it is the whetstone of virtue.”** This is the reading of the manuscripts: one Regio-Putianus, four Colbert, Jun., Ultr., Nav., Vict., Marm., two Lips., Em., Brun., the codex used by Janus Guilielmi, and four editions [Col. 0704C]. And correctly. Undoubtedly our author reproduced Cicero, *Academic Questions*, Book IV, ch. 44: “They used to say that anger was, as it were, the whetstone of courage”—namely, the adherents of the Old Academy. One ancient Regius, two Colbert, one Sorbonne, Gat., Cant., the second old edition, Roman, Venetian 1490, Fasit., and Thys. read *comitem*, “companion.” Ald., Parrhas., and nine other editions go farther astray, preferring *fomitem*, “fuel.”

**“If it has been given to us for this purpose.”** He criticizes the final cause, which raises a further question: whether it is permissible for a Christian to wage war. For brevity’s sake we leave this unresolved; man is an animal born for peace. Lactantius seems here to criticize matters found in Aristotle, *Ethics*, Book III, ch. 7. BETULEIUS.

**“Drive” (*agant*).** Thus I restored it from the ancient manuscripts Regio-Putianus, Cauc., Jun., and seven others, and from five old editions. Twelve manuscripts and fourteen common editions read *agunt*, “drive”; one Brun. manuscript has *faciunt*, “make.”

**“They said.”** Orpheus, in the hymn to the Eumenides; Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book XII [Col. 0704D].

**“Agitate” (*exagitent*).** Thus restored from almost all manuscripts and editions, as above with *agant*. So too the fifteenth-century editions. Two recent Regius manuscripts, two Colbert, and one Clairmont manuscript, with five printed editions, have *exagitant*, “agitate”; the other Clairmont has *agitant*, “stir.”

**“Lust, for the propagation of offspring.”** *On Anger*, ch. 18: “He gave lust for the sake of producing offspring.” *Epitome*, ch. 61: “The passion of lust is implanted and inborn for begetting children.” Hence recognize an abundant occurrence. Isaeus reads: “lust, for begetting offspring.” This is not bad, since in Book VII, ch. 5 he says “to beget offspring”; but all manuscripts read “for the propagation of offspring,” as our author says in Book I, ch. 8. BUN.

**“That is.”** Restored from all manuscripts and eight editions.

**“Those who curse.”** Matthew IX. Thus I emended the text from the very ancient Regio-Putianus and Cauc. manuscripts, sixteen others, and nine editions, whereas previously it read *maledictis*, “accursed,” erroneously, in eight recent manuscripts and fifteen printed editions. One Bologna and three Regius manuscripts have *inimicis*, “enemies,” in place of *maledicis*; this is said in accordance with the command of Christ the Lord concerning the love of enemies.

## Chapter XIX. On the passions and their use, and on the three Furies

When the Stoics endeavour to uproot the passions from man as diseases, the Peripatetics oppose them. They not only retain the passions but even defend them, and say that there is nothing in man which has not been implanted by great reason [Col. 0703B] and providence. This is correct indeed, if they knew the true limits of particular things. Thus they say that anger itself is the whetstone of virtue, as though no one could fight bravely against enemies unless stirred by anger. By this they clearly show both that they do not know what virtue is and why God gave anger to man. If it has been given to us in order that we may use it to kill men, what is more savage than man? What should be judged more like wild beasts than the animal which God made for fellowship and innocence?

There are, therefore, three passions that drive men headlong into every crime [Col. 0704A]: anger, desire, and lust. For this reason the poets said that there are three Furies which agitate the minds of men: anger desires vengeance, desire wealth, lust pleasures. But God established fixed limits for all these; if they cross them and begin to grow greater, they must corrupt their own nature and turn into diseases and vices. What these limits are, however, is not difficult to show.

Desire was given to us for acquiring the things necessary to life; lust, for propagating offspring; the passion of anger, for restraining the faults of those who are in our power—that is, so that younger age may be formed toward uprightness and justice by stricter discipline. Unless it is restrained by fear, licence will produce audacity, which will issue in every disgraceful deed and crime. Therefore, as it is both just and [Col. 0704B] necessary to use anger against inferiors, so it is both destructive and impious to use it against equals. It is impious because humanity is violated; destructive because, when they resist, one must either destroy or be destroyed. That this is the reason why the passion of anger has been given to man can be understood from God’s own commands: He orders that we not be angry with those who curse and injure us; but that we always keep our hands over inferiors—that is, that we correct those who sin by continual beatings—lest, through useless affection and excessive indulgence, they be brought up toward evil and nurtured in vices.

But men ignorant of things and unacquainted with reason have banished beyond their proper limits the passions given to man for good uses [Col. 0705A], and they wander more widely than reason requires. Hence life is conducted unjustly and impiously. They use anger against equals: hence dissensions, hence banishments, hence wars contrary to justice have arisen. They use desire for amassing wealth: hence frauds, hence robberies, hence every kind of crime has arisen. They use lust merely for obtaining pleasures: hence fornications, hence adulteries, hence all corruptions have arisen. Whoever, therefore, has brought those passions back within their own limits—which those ignorant of God cannot do—this man is patient, this man strong, this man just.

**Notes on columns 705–706**

**“They have banished” (*exterminaverunt*).** That is, they have sent them beyond their boundaries. *Exterminare* is used in the novel sense “to send beyond one’s boundaries.” Hence Nonius says: “*Exterminatus* means sent outside the boundaries.”

**“They use anger.”** One ancient Bologna manuscript inserts *impie*, “impiously,” which occurred immediately before; it is absent from the following clauses.

**“For amassing” (*congerendas*).** Thus the fifteenth-century editions. Common editions read *congregandas*, “for gathering”; others, *cogendas*, “for collecting.”

**“Have arisen.”** With the editions Torn., Sonbron., and Cellar., all manuscripts so read except one recent Regius, which, like the printed editions, reads “arose.”

**“Corruptions.”** That is, corruptions of maidens; the word is used in this sense by Cicero, *On Divination*, Book I, ch. 53, and Suetonius, *Claudius*, ch. 16 [Col. 0705D].

**“Against the pleasures of the five senses.”** Two Vatican manuscripts read: “against the pleasures of the five bodily senses”; one ancient Bologna manuscript: “against the unjust senses of pleasure.” Yet Thomasius prefers “against the unjust senses of pleasure” or “of pleasures”: “It is said too scholastically and childishly,” he says, “to speak of ‘the pleasures of the five senses.’”

**“Other living creatures, etc.”** Lactantius errs somewhat in his knowledge of natural things. For Aristotle and Gellius demonstrate clearly that sight, hearing, and smell are distinctive to man, while touch and taste are shared with beasts; although, in the meantime, I could show by very obvious examples that some dumb animals derive pleasure even from smell, and indeed, if necessary, from hearing and sight as well. BETUL.

**“Reject.”** “Eating.” Between these words Lips. 2 and Reimm. elegantly and barbarously insert: “They reject. And many men whom I myself have known measure the function of eating and drinking by the fullness of the belly.” BUN.

**“Because He set before him.”** Thus all manuscripts and almost all editions; some have “who.”

**“A domestic enemy.”** The law of the flesh, also called the law of death and of sin, is a domestic and internal enemy.

**“Fornications, etc.”** Heumann considers these words added and introduced from the margin into Lactantius’s text.

**“Every disgraceful deed.”** One ancient Bologna manuscript: “all disgraceful deeds.”

**“In the kingdom of pleasure.”** These words are not found in Cicero [Col. 0706D].

**“Cicero … stand.”** Thus all books. Heumann thinks that all these words were formerly inscribed in the margin and are not Lactantius’s; that the argument hangs together better if they are omitted and is more impeded if they are retained. Nor does he think Lactantius would have written: “Cicero says that fornications are excited,” but rather: “Cicero: ‘Fornications are excited.’” Indeed, he thinks the words would not have been attributed to Cicero, but to their author, Archytas of Tarentum. BUN.

**“But on the contrary.”** Up to this point, Cicero.

**“Pleasures.”** Pleasure is the food of evils, according to Plato.

**“Subject him to its dominion.”** Pleasure is not God. For those subjected to the dominion of pleasure and serving it alone are condemned to everlasting death. CELL.

**“The philosophers.”** Archytas, Cato, Cicero. *Caelum*, “heaven,” rather than *caelata*, “engraved works”: a paronomasia. Without doubt he alludes to the etymology of *caelum* given by Varro and Pliny, namely that it is so named from *caelare*, “to engrave.” BETULEIUS.

## Chapter XX. On the senses and their pleasures in beasts and man; and on the pleasure of the eyes and spectacles

[Col. 0705B] It remains for me to speak briefly against the pleasures of the five senses; for the extent of the book itself now demands an end. Since all these pleasures are corrupt and deadly, they must be conquered and subdued by virtue, or, as I said a little earlier concerning the passions, brought back to their proper measure. Other living creatures feel no pleasure besides the one concerned with generation. They therefore use the senses for the necessity of their nature: they see in order to seek the things needed to preserve life; they hear one another and recognize each other, so that they may gather together. Things useful for food they discover by smell or perceive by taste; useless things they reject or refuse. They measure the function of eating and drinking by the fullness of the stomach.

But providence, that of the most skilful artificer, gave man infinite pleasure, tending toward vice, because He set before him virtue, which was always to fight against pleasure [Col. 0706A] as against a domestic enemy. Cicero, in *Cato the Elder*: “But fornications,” he says, “and adulteries, and every disgraceful deed, are aroused by no other allurements than pleasure. And since either nature or some god has given man nothing more excellent than the mind, nothing is so hostile to this divine endowment and gift as pleasure. For when lust rules, there is no place for temperance; nor can virtue stand in the kingdom of pleasure.” But on the contrary, God gave virtue for this purpose: that it might assault and conquer pleasure, restraining it, when it goes beyond the limits assigned to it, within the prescribed boundary, lest it make man—softened and captured by delights—subject to its dominion and punish him with everlasting death.

The pleasure of the eyes is various and manifold; it is [Col. 0706B] derived from the sight of things pleasing to men either by nature or by workmanship. The philosophers have most rightly abolished this. For they say that it is far more splendid and more worthy of man to gaze upon heaven rather than engraved works (*caelata*), and to admire this most beautiful work, adorned as though with flowers by the gleaming lights of the stars, rather than painted and fabricated objects distinguished with gems. Yet though they have expressly exhorted us to despise earthly things and summoned us to the spectacle of heaven, they do not despise these public spectacles. Thus they delight in them and willingly attend them. Since these are the greatest incitements to vice and have the strongest power to corrupt minds, they must be removed from us, because they contribute nothing to the blessed life and indeed are exceedingly harmful.

For the person who counts it as pleasure to see before his eyes a man, even one condemned on account of his crimes, slaughtered, defiles his conscience, just as much as if [Col. 0707A] he were spectator and participant in a murder committed secretly. Yet they call these games in which human blood is shed. So far has humanity departed from men that, when they destroy human lives, they think they are amusing themselves—more guilty than all those whose blood they hold to be a pleasure.

**Notes on columns 707–708**

**“So far has humanity departed from men.”** I write *recessit*, “has departed,” after Lips. 2, 3, Reimm., Torn., 1587, 1613, Gen. 1630, and Walch, whereas many editions have *secessit*, “has withdrawn.” BUN.

**“They hold blood to be a pleasure.”** Cyprian, Book II, Letter 2: “A gladiatorial show is prepared so that blood may delight the lust of cruel eyes … a man is killed for another man’s pleasure.” BUN.

**“I ask now.”** Ten manuscripts: “Ask.”

**“But they even demand.”** *Et* has been restored from the manuscripts and two editions, since “not only” demands it. *Et* means “also.” Two Regius manuscripts and sixteen editions have *sed efflagitant*, “but they vehemently demand.”

**“Nor satisfied with blood.”** Add what Pliny writes, Book XXVIII, ch. 1: that spectators were accustomed to drink the blood of gladiators.

**“They order those struck down and lying on the ground to be struck again.”** Gladiators sometimes repeated their blows and put their hands into the wound, lest anyone deceive spectators by feigning death.

**“It is not fitting that they be associates and participants.”** Salvian, *On Providence*, VI, laments that in ancient spectacles the bellies of beasts were filled with human flesh amid the joy of the onlookers; and he says that this is almost no less to be devoured by the eyes of men than by the teeth of beasts. Jerome, *Against Rufinus*: “Far be it from Christian morals that men should be murderers in will, though without a sword.” Writing to St Augustine, he says: “Heretics whom they cannot kill with the sword, they kill by their desire.” Minucius in the *Octavius* expressly declares that Christians may neither see nor hear homicide, and that in former times they so avoided human blood that they did not know even the blood of cattle as food. JURETUS. See also Tertullian, *On Spectacles*; Cyprian, Letter 1 to the people; Augustine, *City of God*, Book III, ch. 8 ff.

**“Thus it will not be permissible for a just man to serve as a soldier.”** Lactantius follows an Anabaptist doctrine only for that period of the primitive and still young Church, which neither possessed the sword nor was suited to employ arms, but was to grow only through sufferings and miracles. Yet that a just man may serve as a soldier, and that military service is sometimes just, Gratian demonstrates from Saints Ambrose, Augustine, Gregory, and the other Fathers in the *Decretum*, the whole of Cause 23, Questions 1, 2, and 3; and Sixtus of Siena, *Bibliotheca*, Book VI, note 156. ISAEUS. These remarks must be understood only of unjust wars and killings, which Lactantius also calls, in ch. 19, “wars contrary to justice.” See St Thomas, *Summa theologiae*, II–II, question 40, Book I, and Bellarmine, *On the Laity*, Book III, ch. 14 [Col. 0708B].

**“Nor indeed to accuse anyone of a capital crime.”** This is not simply true. Just grounds of accusation may exist, either when the accuser is summoned to court, or when he understands that a crime will result in the ruin of the commonwealth. St Gregory in Gratian, canon *Si quis super his*; canon *Metropolitanum*; and Gelasius, canon *Qua propter*, Second Question 7; St Thomas, *Summa theologiae*, II–II, question 68, article 1. ISAEUS. It is not permissible for a Christian wholly to give himself over to private vengeance. See Bellarmine, *On the Laity*, Book III, chs. 12–13.

**“He wished man to be a sacred creature.”** Lactantius here takes *sanctum*, “sacred,” in its proper sense: protected and defended from human injury. Donatus: “That is called sacred which is inviolable under every protection; thus laws are called sacred,” etc. ISAEUS.

**“Newly born.”** From the very ancient manuscripts—two Regius, one Bologna, and eight others—and from the old Roman, Betul., and Is. editions, I restored *recens*, used adverbially. Ten recent manuscripts and fifteen editions read *recentes*, “newborn”; seven manuscripts, *recenter*, “recently.” See Tertullian, *Apology*, chs. 2 and 9.

**“Crush to death” (*oblidere*).** It means to suffocate by crushing or pressing. *Oblidere* occurs in Arnobius and in almost all Lactantian manuscripts and printed codices; Merton, Christ., and Em. have *elidere*, “dash to death,” and one ancient Bologna manuscript, *allidere*, “crush against.” The old fifteenth-century editions agree with the text.

**“Lives” (*animis*).** Used for *animas*, “souls/lives”; so Cicero, *Letters*, Book XIV, Letter 14 [Col. 0708D].

**“They deny them light,” etc.** He speaks of that barbarity by which women drink potions to procure abortion. Paul the jurist, *Sentences*, Book V, ch. 23: “Those who administer an abortifacient or love-potion, even if they do not do so maliciously, nevertheless, because it is an evil example, are punished—persons of lower rank by condemnation to the mines, persons of higher rank by relegation to an island with loss of part of their property. But if a man or woman dies from this, they are subjected to the highest penalty.” ELMENHORST.

**“False affection.”** Unless I am wholly mistaken, this false affection was the belief that it was more dutiful and innocent to expose an infant than to strangle it. This is evident from Book V, ch. 9: “Those who either strangle the children born to them or, if they are too affectionate, expose them.” BUN.

**“Their own entrails.”** That is, their own children. So Statius, *Thebaid*, VII.751; see Barthius on this passage, p. 730. “Their own entrails”: here, infants and children only. Elsewhere parents and friends also are thus called—those dear to us, “our entrails”—as Pitiscus shows on Curtius, Book IV, ch. 14. BUN.

I ask now whether those can be pious and just men who permit persons placed under the stroke of death and begging for mercy not merely to be killed, but even demand it and cast cruel and inhuman votes for death; who are neither sated with wounds nor satisfied with blood; who even order those struck down and lying on the ground to be struck again, and corpses to be mangled by blows, lest anyone deceive them by feigning death. They are angry even with combatants unless one of the two is quickly killed; and as though [Col. 0707B] they thirsted for human blood, they hate delays. They demand that fresher opponents be matched against them, so that they may satiate their eyes as quickly as possible. Steeped in this habit, they have lost humanity. Accordingly, they do not spare even the innocent, but practise upon all what they have learned in the slaughter of criminals.

Therefore, those who strive to keep the way of justice ought not to be associates and participants in this public homicide. For when God forbids killing, He does not merely forbid us to commit robbery—which is not permitted even by public laws—but commands that those things also not be done which are considered lawful among men. Thus it will not be permissible for a just man to serve as a soldier, whose military service is justice itself; nor indeed to accuse anyone of a capital crime, because it makes no difference whether you kill with a sword or rather with a word, since killing itself is forbidden. Therefore, in this command of God no exception whatsoever ought to be made: it is always unlawful to kill a human being, whom God wished to be a sacred creature.

Therefore let no one suppose that even this may be permitted: to crush to death newborn children, which is the greatest impiety. For God breathes souls into life, not into death. But men, lest there be any crime [Col. 0708B] by which they do not defile their hands, deny light—not given by themselves—to souls still unformed and simple. Should anyone expect them to spare another’s blood when they do not spare their own? These men are unquestionably wicked and unjust. What of those whom false affection compels to expose their children? Can they be considered innocent when they set their own entrails as prey before dogs, and, so far as lies in them, kill them more cruelly than if they had strangled them?

**Notes on columns 709–710**

**“Can they … than if they had strangled them?”** I have restored *num*, “can they?” with an interrogative force, as more pointed and vigorous, from the very ancient manuscripts—two Regius, one Bologna, and twelve others—except that four Regius manuscripts and two others have *num possint*, “can they be able?” One Colbert manuscript has *extrangulassent*, “had strangled completely.”

**“To another’s mercy.”** Rost. reads “to the mercy of another.” But this is the conventional expression in this matter. Tertullian, *To the Nations*, I.16: “You expose infants to another’s mercy.” Minucius Felix, ch. 30: “Children born at home you frequently expose to another’s mercy.” BUN.

**“Who gives place to another’s mercy.”** I have deleted *non*, “not,” from the two very ancient Regius manuscripts and nine others, which reject the negation; nor should it be admitted, otherwise our author’s meaning would be reversed. For what follows is: “If what he wished happens to him, that the child is reared.” This is indeed another’s mercy. “Gives place.” Lips. 2, 3, Reimm., and all editions before Cellarius incorrectly read “does not give place.” But exposing a child was, in a certain respect, to give place to another’s mercy. Hence Paul, Book IV of the Digest, *On Acknowledging and Supporting Children*, aptly says: “He seems to kill not only the man who suffocates his offspring—Lactantius says *elidit*, *oblidit*—but also the man who exposes it in public places out of a mercy which he himself does not possess.” BUN.

**“To slavery.”** If it is a male.

**“To a brothel.”** If it is a female.

**“Of Oedipus.”** He who, having been exposed as an infant by his father Laius, unknowingly killed him when grown up and married his mother Jocasta. The tragic story was celebrated by Sophocles himself in the play entitled *Oedipus*, or *Oedipus Tyrannus*; by Seneca in the *Thebaid* and *Oedipus*; and by Statius in Books II and XII of the *Thebaid*. It is also written by Hyginus, *Fables* 67. BETUL.

**“Confounded by a double crime.”** Rather, by a fourfold one: he was his father’s killer, his mother’s husband, thus his own stepfather, and his children’s brother. Orosius, Book I, ch. 12. See Plato, *Laws*, Book VIII, and Plutarch, *On Curiosity*.

**“In his power.”** Added from all manuscripts and almost all editions.

**“Poverty.”** Fifteenth-century editions: “indigence.”

**“Nor is it at all permitted to be present, lest any blood stain the conscience.”** It is not lawful for a just man to be present at the killing of a man; so greatly does the Church abhor bloodshed. On this matter see Minucius Felix in the *Octavius*, already cited above at col. 707, note “and participants.”

**“Blood … is provided.”** That is, slaughter is performed for the people in order to delight them. Lactantius, Book V, ch. 5, end: “to acquire glory from blood.” BUN.

**“I do not know whether it is.”** *Nescio an*, *haud scio an*, and *dubito an* have the appearance of doubt but most often an affirmative sense … Yet sometimes they are used simply in a doubtful sense. I believe the former applies here. Thus *Epitome*, ch. 63: “What of the stage? Is it any holier?” Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book II, ch. 4: “A very wise man, and I do not know whether the most excellent of all, preferred to confess his fault, though it could have been concealed,” etc. Valerius Maximus, Book II, ch. 9: “This crime is perhaps greater than the preceding one”; Book IV, ch. 6: “But perhaps this was braver.” BUN.

In theatrical performances, I do not know whether there is any corruption more vicious. Lactantius himself says below: “What shall I say of mimes, who offer instruction in corruptions, who teach adultery while they feign it?” That scenic and shameful games, and every kind of spectacle, have always been forbidden to ecclesiastics and to all Christians is attested by the Fathers and Councils. Council of Laodicea, canon 54: “Priests or clerics ought not to attend any spectacles in theatres.” Likewise the Third Council of Tours, canon 7; and the Third Council of Carthage, canon 11 adds that, since all laypeople too are prohibited from spectacles. For this has always been forbidden to all Christians: that they should not go where there are blasphemers. See Tertullian, *On the Spectacles*, where he prohibits them to all Christians; Cyprian, Epistle 1, calls them “the Devil’s business”; Minucius in the *Octavius*: “in scenic performances there is no less frenzy and more prolonged obscenity: now the mime either displays adulteries or represents them”; Arnobius, p. 172; Augustine, *On Instructing Beginners*, ch. 16; Homily 21, Book L of Homilies; and *City of God*, II.8–9; and Ludovicus Vives on this passage of Augustine.

Comic plays speak of the violations of maidens; Tertullian, [Col. 0710D] *On the Spectacles*, calls comedies and tragedies the bloody, lascivious, impious, and extravagant authors of lusts and crimes.

“Or the loves of prostitutes.” 2 Reg. and Brun.: “lovers” (*amatoribus*).

“Crimes in the buskin.” That is, crimes of mimes, whose shoes, raised by cork soles, made them taller, so that, when playing the parts of kings and princes, they might appear of greater stature. Lactantius therefore calls the great and lofty crimes presented by tragedians “buskined crimes.” NOURRY.

“And teach.” Thus I write with all manuscripts except 3 Reg. rec., in which the conjunction *et* is absent, as in the printed editions.

“Women . . . counterfeit by their gestures.” Columella, Preface to Book I: “Astonished, we admire the gestures of effeminate men, because by womanly movement they counterfeit a sex which nature denied to men, and deceive the eyes of the spectators.”

“What shall I say of mimes?” On these see Book I, chapter 20, and Epitome, chapter 6; also Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 15.

[Col. 0709A] Who can doubt that he is impious who assigns his child to another’s mercy? Even if it happens to him as he wished—that the child is reared—he has nevertheless consigned his own blood either to slavery or to a brothel. And who does not understand, who is ignorant, what may or commonly does happen through mistake in either sex? The example of Oedipus alone, entangled in a double crime, makes this plain. Therefore it is as wicked to expose a child as to kill one. But parricides complain of narrow means, and allege that they cannot support the upbringing of several children—as though possessions were in their owners’ control, or as though God did not daily make poor persons from the rich and rich persons from the poor. Therefore, if anyone cannot rear children because of poverty, it is better that he refrain from intercourse with his wife [Col. 0709B] than that he corrupt the works of God with criminal hands.

[Col. 0710A] Therefore, if it is by no means lawful to commit homicide, neither is it permitted at all to be present at it, lest any blood stain the conscience; for that blood is supplied for the people. In theatrical performances too, I do not know whether there is any corruption more vicious. For comic plays speak of the violations of maidens and of the loves of prostitutes; and the more eloquent those who invented these enormities are, the more their elegance of expression persuades, and their rhythmic and ornate verses adhere more easily to the memory of their hearers. Likewise tragic histories place before the eyes parricides, the incestuous acts of wicked kings, and exhibit buskined crimes. What else do the utterly shameless movements of actors do but both teach and incite lusts? Their enervated bodies, softened into a womanly gait and dress, counterfeit immodest women in disgraceful [Col. 0710B] gestures. What shall I say of mimes, who offer instruction in corruptions? Who teach [Col. 0711A] adultery—

[Col. 0711A] [Note: [Col. 0711B] Variorum Notes to columns 711–712]

“They [the mimes] teach adultery,” etc. Valerius Maximus, II.6.7, at the end, excellently says: “Massilia is a most vigilant guardian of severity, granting mimes no entry to its stages, since their plots for the most part contain enactments of sexual violations, lest the habit of viewing such things take up also the license of imitating them.” Compare Tertullian, *On the Spectacles*, ch. 17, and Salvian, *On the Governance of God*, VI, p. 108. BUN.—“They teach adultery while they feign it.” Cyprian, *On Grace, to Donatus*, p. 6: “Adultery is learned while it is seen; and, through the evil enticement to vices of public authority, the matron who perhaps went out modestly to the spectacle returns from the spectacle immodest.” And Minucius Felix, p. 345: “While the actor feigns love, he inflicts it.”

“Things [learned] by sight,” etc. And I do not know how it happens that even in our dramas scarcely anything is sufficiently inviolate and sacred. For it is received with far greater applause when old men watch Susanna about to bathe and already putting sandals on her legs, than [Col. 0711C] when, about to go to punishment, she bids farewell to her pledges; when Judith flatters Holofernes with wanton gestures, than when, clothed in sackcloth, she pours forth prayers to the Lord; when Sarah permits her female servant to her husband, than when the father, anxious over his son’s sacrifice, prays to God; when Potiphar’s wife solicits Joseph to adultery, than when Jacob is pressed by shortage of grain. To such an extent are eyes readier to look upon vain matters than serious ones. BETUL.

“Prefigures” (*praefigurat*). Compare the Epitome, ch. 12, beginning. Lexicographers pause at Lactantius’s authority. Before him Tertullian used this word, *Prescription against Heretics*, ch. 26: *praefiguraverat*. Cyprian, II.3: “a prefigured sacrament . . . the truth of the prefigured image.” BUN.

“With premature vices.” Thus the manuscripts and printed editions. Francius preferred to read “premature in vices” (*praematuros vitiis*), not badly. Yet immediately before occurs “with vices adhering.”

“Whom it is no longer fitting to sin.” After these words, manuscripts 2 Reg. rec., Jun., Cant., and 1 Colb. in the margin, as well as nine printed editions, add: “they slip down into such a path of vices”; the others reject this. “No longer to sin,” that is, any longer. See Passeratius on Cicero, *For Quinctius*, ch. 1: “To me it is now sacred and inviolate in the state.” Compare Vorstius, *Latina Neglecta*, p. 230. Lactantius often uses it so; e.g. III.17: “There is a time . . . when we too no longer exist”; V.13: “so that he may appear no longer to be a Christian.” BUN.

“Circus games.” Tarquinius Priscus first established at Rome the Circus called Maximus, in which he gave games more richly and splendidly equipped than the other kings; Livy, Book I, is the authority. The Circus—Plutarch calls it ἱππικὰ θέατρα, “equestrian theatres”—was between the Palatine and Aventine hills; see Pomponius Laetus, *Roman Antiquities*. Varro, *On the Latin Language*, IV: “The Armilustrum,” he says, “is named from the circuit of the purification; the same place is called the Circus Maximus because it was built around with viewing-places. Games are held there; and because the procession is borne around the turning-posts there, and horses run.” There were seven turning-posts. Propertius:

> Or before, with the race unfinished, he demands the prize,  
> Before the seventh wheel has worn away the turning-post.

[Col. 0712B] In circus games, as is clear from Suetonius, very noble young men drove four-horse chariots, two-horse chariots, and trick-riding horses. Yet it appears even from Livy that this custom was not very ancient. For in the fourth place of Book V of the *Decades*, writing of the events of the year 583 [A.U.C.], he says: “The custom then was—not yet having introduced this extravagance—to fill the circus with beasts of every nation and seek out varied kinds of spectacles; and, after a four-horse chariot had been sent once and a trick-rider once, scarcely an hour’s time completed both races.” Circus games are sometimes called Great, and sometimes Roman, by writers; they are called circus games, if we believe Servius, either from their circuit or from the swords (*enses*) around which they went. BETUL.

“May lie in wait” (*insidat*). Thus nearly all manuscripts and four editions. In 2 Reg. is *insidiat*; in 5 Reg., 1 Colbert., and fourteen printed editions, *insideat*.

Likewise below, after the beginning of the following chapter, from very many manuscripts.

[Col. 0712C] “And at first indeed the hunts.” I do not recall reading this elsewhere than in Alexander, who undoubtedly copied it from Lactantius; except that Donatus, in the prolegomena to Terence, also testifies that comedies and tragedies were sacred to Father Liber. But in his commentary on the *Andria* he testifies that comedy was customarily established for Apollo and tragedy for Bacchus. Servius, on *Aeneid* VIII, says that circus games were sacred to Consus, that is, equestrian Neptune. Consus was so called because he is the god of counsels. Tertullian too, near the end of his book *On Women’s Dress*, testifies that he published a volume on secular spectacles. BETUL.

“Shows” (*munera*). The designation *munera* pertains not only to gladiators but also, beyond doubt, to those who dispatch beasts, in Pliny, Book LXXXIV [probably OCR corruption; perhaps Book VIII], ch. 3, indeed also in most other authors. Suetonius, *Julius*, ch. 75, and *Caligula*, ch. 27, somewhere mentions beasts procured for a public show. See Seneca, *On Benefits*, ch. 12.

[Col. 0712D] “But circus games to Neptune. Yet gradually.” Thus I emended from the six Reg. manuscripts, two of which are very ancient; five Colb.; three Lips. Em.; Brun.; and the editions of Cellarius and Walch. In the Roman edition of 1470, *vero* appears twice; in 1 Colb.: “circus vows to Neptune. Yet gradually,” where *vota* is corrupt for *vero*. In 4 Reg. rec. and twelve common editions: “circus games to Neptune.”

“Each individual game,” etc. Arnobius, *Against the Nations*, VII: “You are persuaded that the gods delight in and are affected by the ringing of bronze and the sound of pipes, by horse-races and theatrical games, and that their anger, sometimes conceived, is softened by such appeasement.”

“Names” (*nominibus*). Thus I restored it from all manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470. Nearly all printed editions have “divinities” (*numinibus*). But what sense would there be in: “to bestow honour upon the other gods and to consecrate games to their divinities”? From the manuscripts, “names” is much better: namely, games whose designation derives from the names of fictitious gods, such as the Saturnalia from Saturn, the Martial games from Mars, the Apollinarian from Apollo, the Cerealian from Ceres, the Floralia from Flora, etc.

—while they feign it, and by simulated acts instruct people in real adultery? What are young men or maidens to do when they see that these things are both done without shame and gladly watched by everyone? They are certainly instructed in what they can do, and are inflamed by lust, which is especially aroused by sight; each person imagines himself in those scenes according to his sex, approves them while laughing, and returns to the bedroom more corrupt, with vices adhering—not merely boys, whom it is not fitting to imbue with premature vices, but also old men, whom it is no longer fitting to sin.

What does the character of circus games contain except frivolity, emptiness, and madness? For minds are driven into frenzy with as much force as [Col. 0712A] the racing there is driven; so that those who come to watch now provide more spectacle when they begin to shout, be carried away, and leap up. Therefore all spectacles must be avoided, not merely lest some vice lie in wait in hearts which ought to be calm and peaceful, but lest the habit of any pleasure seduce us and turn us away from God and good works. For the celebrations of games are festivals of gods, since they were instituted for their birthdays or for the dedications of new temples. At first, indeed, hunts, called *munera*, were assigned to Saturn; theatrical games to Liber; circus games to Neptune. Yet gradually the same honour began to be bestowed on the other gods as well, and individual games were consecrated under their [Col. 0713A] names, as Sisinius Capito [Col. 0713A] teaches in his books *On Spectacles*. Therefore, whoever attends spectacles to which people gather for the sake of religion has departed from the worship of God and transferred himself to the gods whose birthdays and festivals he has celebrated.

[Col. 0713A] [Note: [Col. 0713C] Variorum Notes to columns 713–714]

“Sisinius Capito.” Heumann thinks that Asinius Capito should be read, the very learned man whom Aulus Gellius mentions, V.20, and likewise Festus. Yet St Jerome calls him Sisinnius Capito, *Questions on Genesis*, on chapter X.

“People gather” (*convenitur*). Only the ancient manuscripts 1 Bon. and 1 Reg. have *convenit*.

“Deepest” (*intimum*). Eight recent manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470 have *integrum*, “whole.” “The deepest sense.” Goth., Venice 1471, Rost.: “the whole sense.” The former is more suitable; Gronovius, on Minucius Felix, ch. 1, p. 4, illustrates its elegance and force from Cicero’s “deepest feelings” (*intimis sensibus*). So Lactantius, I.20: “which ought to have caused horror in the deepest senses.” BUN.

“From this, educated persons.” Therefore, in the preface to Book III, he wished for himself Ciceronian eloquence: not because truth, whose speech is simple, needs verbal ornament, but on account of those who disdain every discourse unless it tinkles with some sweet sound. But enough has been said there on this subject. BETULEIUS.

“When they come to God’s religion.” From the end of the preceding chapter 20, “to come to God’s religion” means to depart from the worship of gods and to betake oneself to God, or to God’s religion; or, with reversed terms, in the Epitome, ch. 63, beginning: “having abandoned profane rites, to pass to the worship of God”; or from VII.22: “to leave the gods and turn oneself to the worship and religion of the one God”; or finally the same as VII.11: “to follow the heavenly religion of God, namely justice.” BUNEMAN.

“If they have not been grounded by some expert teacher.” Of those who laid less solid foundations he spoke more elegantly, V.1: “Their judgment is not established and fixed with stable and solid roots.” For very many waver, especially those who have attained something of letters. BUNEMAN.

“When they have come, if they have not been grounded by some expert teacher, they believe less.” “If they have not,” etc. Heumann deletes these words. But I restored this passage from the most ancient manuscripts, 1 Bonon. and 1 Reg., supported by 1 Regio-Put., 1 other Reg., 2 Colb., 1 Clarom., 2 Lips., and the Roman edition of 1468, in which it reads: “they have come, grounded by some expert teacher”; “if they have not been” is absent. The Cauc., Jun., sixteen other manuscripts and fourteen printed editions have: “they have come, grounded by some unskilled teacher”; 2 Reg.: “in some unskilled [teacher]”; the Cant. manuscript and the editions of Thom., Thys., and Gall.: “they have come, if they have not been [grounded] by some unskilled [teacher],” altogether wrongly. Since all this is not sufficiently disentangled in this note of Dom Jean-Baptiste Le Brun, we have thought it should be explained rather more fully, so that the reading represented by our text may be confirmed better and more clearly. The sense is that Lactantius says that educated persons, trained in polished literature, when they come to religion, are accustomed to believe less because they disdain the simplicity of the speech of the sacred Scriptures. This, however, will not happen if those coming to true religion have a teacher of religion trained in sacred matters, skilled and learned. The common reading formerly had: “From this, educated persons, when they have come to God’s religion, grounded by some unskilled teacher, believe less.” This presents almost the same sense as the reading in our text, but its expression is less elegant and more obscure. Those words, “grounded by a teacher,” which are often not read in authors of older Latin eloquence, nevertheless occur among jurists, who call persons “grounded in law.” Thus *fundo* means the same as “I teach.” So Livy has “lightly grounded belief.”

“Lies in wait” (*insidit*). Thus nearly all manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470. Two recent manuscripts have *insistit*; 1 Colb. has *et sedit*; four recent manuscripts and eleven common editions have *insidet*.

“Both of mind and voice.” Nor is voice without mind. In Latin, *vox* is used improperly also of inanimate and mute things—for noise and sound—although Aristotle attributes voice even to mute beings. BETULEIUS.

“To be without cosmetic.” On the simplicity of Holy Scripture see Isidore of Pelusium, XI.5.

“Which bind the soul to themselves.” Manuscripts 1 Bon. ancient, 1 Lips., and Brun. have *subjiciunt*: “subject the soul to themselves.” Thus Buneman reads.—“They subject the soul to themselves.” I conjectured that *viciant*, that is, *vitiant* (“corrupt”), should be read; for Rost. almost always writes *viciant* for *vitiant*, e.g. II.2. Thus the passage above, “vicious pleasure,” would be relevant. The verb *vitiant* is therefore appropriate to the complete text, since it is said of both soul and body. BUN.

CHAPTER XXI. On the pleasures of hearing and the sacred Scriptures.

The pleasure of hearing is received from the sweetness of voices and songs; and it is as vicious as that pleasure of the eyes of which we have spoken. For who would not judge luxurious and worthless a man who keeps theatrical arts at home? Yet it makes no difference whether one practices luxury alone at home or with the people in a theatre. But enough has now been said about spectacles. One thing remains for us to overcome: lest we be captured by things that penetrate the deepest sense. For all those things which lack words—that is, the sweet sounds of wind and string instruments—can easily be despised, because they do not cling to the mind and cannot be written down. But a poem composed with sweetness, and eloquence that deceives through sweetness, captures minds and drives them wherever it wishes. Hence, when educated persons come to God’s religion, if they have not been grounded by some expert teacher, they believe less. For, accustomed to sweet and polished prose or poetry, they disdain the simple and common speech of the divine Scriptures as vulgar. For they seek what caresses the sense [Col. 0714A] But whatever is sweet persuades and, while delighting, settles deep within the mind. Can God then—the maker of mind, voice, and tongue—not speak eloquently? On the contrary, in his supreme providence he wished divine things to be without cosmetic, so that all might understand what he himself spoke to all.

Therefore, whoever devotes himself to truth and does not wish to deceive himself must cast away hostile and harmful pleasures, which bind the soul to themselves as sweet foods bind the body. Let true things be preferred to false, eternal things to brief, useful things to pleasant. Let nothing be pleasing to sight except what you see done piously and justly; let nothing be sweet to hearing except what nourishes the soul and makes you better. Above all, this sense must not be perverted to vice, since it was given to us so that we might receive the teaching of God. Thus, if it is pleasurable to hear songs and poems, let it be pleasant to sing and hear God’s praises. This is true pleasure, [Col. 0714B] the companion and associate of virtue. It is not fleeting and brief like those pleasures sought by people who, like cattle, are slaves to the body; it is perpetual and delights without any interruption. Whoever exceeds its limits and seeks from pleasure nothing except pleasure itself meditates upon death; for as perpetual life lies in virtue, so death lies in pleasure. Whoever prefers temporal things will lack eternal things; whoever prefers earthly things will not possess heavenly things.

[Col. 0715A] CHAPTER XXII. On the pleasures of taste and smell.

[Col. 0715A] [Note: [Col. 0715C] Variorum Notes to columns 715–716]

“Concerning pleasures.” *Ad* is used in the sense “with regard to.” Nothing needs to be supplied here. The ancients elegantly, though more rarely, used “to discuss with regard to something” and “to discourse with regard to something.” Lactantius again, from Gellius, in Epitome, ch. 29: “When Chrysippus discoursed concerning these matters.” BUN.

“There is nothing for us to discuss.” Cauc. and Jun. manuscripts and edition 7: “There is nothing else for us to discuss,” etc.

“Belly and throat.” Paul teaches that these must be avoided, Philippians 3:19: “whose god is their belly.”

“If anointed with perfumes,” etc. Arnobius, V: “Why adorned with violet crowns?” To smell of perfume was rejected by satyrs [satyr plays?] and stages as soft and contrary to manly dignity. Aristotle, *Ethics*, III.10, places among the ἀκόλαστοι (“intemperate”) those who delight excessively in scents and in sweet musical harmony; yet he maintains that the more intemperate are those “who delight in the smells of perfumes” (*τοὺς τῶν μύρων ὀσμαῖς χαίροντας*). Aristotle, however, is most deserving of censure because he assigns temperance to the body and not likewise to the soul. Moreover, ecclesiastical writers condemn the smell of flowers and the use of garlands. Tertullian, in the book entitled *On the Soldier’s Crown*, denounces the use of flowers in crowns. In *Apology*, ch. 46, he approves the fact that Christians nevertheless contribute their portion to the fellowship of life, even though they do not bring flowers to their nostrils and watch no spectacles. Minucius: “Forgive us for not crowning our heads; nor do we crown the dead, since the blessed person does not need, and the miserable person does not rejoice in, flowers.”

“Thus he made everything.” 1 Bonon. ancient: “And he made all this.”

[Col. 0716C] “By human beings.” Thus I restored it from the editions Torn. and Soubron., and all manuscripts except 2 Reg. rec. and 1 Colb., in which, as in the printed editions, it reads “by human beings, or from all”; 1 Brun. and the Betul. edition: “by others.”

“Because.” It stands for “that.” Lactantius and other authors use it so everywhere.

“Pleasure from touch.” Touch (ἁφή) employs the organ of the entire body, while each of the other senses has its own separate instrument. Thus, proportionately, lust and the sweetness received from intercourse are greatest—for in all the rest of this sense there is no vice; the whole body opens itself. See Aristotle, *On the Generation of Animals*, I.18. BETUL.

“Desire.” On this see Pliny, X.63.

“That there might be praise.” 1 Colb. in the first hand, and the Is. edition in the margin: perhaps, “that there might be praise for him.”

“Which some preferred to call necessity.” He seems to me to have meant Hermes Trismegistus and Apuleius, whom he had read. Apuleius, *Apology*, p. 327: “He ascribes to fate . . . either the rationale or the necessity of marrying.” BUN.

“He places before,” etc. Thus I emended from nearly all manuscripts and twelve printed editions. Reg. 1 rec. and Goth.: “He therefore places before the eyes”; 1 Bonon. ancient: “And he places before the eyes”; some printed editions: “And he places before the eyes,” wrongly, for “and suggests” follows immediately.

“Then in the inmost entrails.” I added the preposition, which the following syllable absorbed in most books, from Reimm., Torn. 1587 and 1613.

“He also established brothels.” Namely through his agents. For in accounts of Caligula and Heliogabalus we read that they established brothels. On brothels, moreover, Book I, ch. 20 has spoken. Tertullian, *On the Pallium*: “Look upon the she-wolves [prostitutes], the marketplaces of popular lusts.”

Concerning the pleasures of taste and smell, which two senses pertain only to the body, there is nothing for us to discuss—unless perhaps someone demands that we say it is shameful for a wise and good person to be enslaved to belly and throat, to walk about anointed with perfumes and crowned with flowers. Whoever does this is surely foolish, unsuitable, and worthless, a person whom not even the scent of virtue has touched. Perhaps someone will say: “Why, then, were these things made, unless for us to enjoy them?” But it has already often been said that virtue would not exist unless it had things to overcome. Therefore God made all things to equip the contest between the two things. These enticements of pleasures, then, [Col. 0715B] are the weapons of him whose sole work is to overcome virtue and exclude justice from humankind. By these blandishments and sweetnesses he titillates souls. For he knows that pleasure is the maker of death. As God calls a human being to life only through virtue and labour, so that one calls him to death through luxuries and pleasures; and as one comes to true good through deceptive evils, so one comes to true evil through deceptive goods. These pleasures must therefore be avoided as snares and traps, lest, captured by the softness of their sweetnesses, we be reduced, together with the body itself to which we have enslaved ourselves, under the dominion of death.

[Col. 0716A] CHAPTER XXIII. On the pleasure of touch and lust, and on marriage and continence.

I come now to the pleasure perceived through touch, a sense that belongs indeed to the whole body. But I think I must speak not of adornments or clothing, but of lust alone, which must especially be restrained because it especially harms. When God devised the arrangement of two sexes, he granted them the desire for one another and delight in union. Accordingly, he mingled into the bodies of all living creatures a most ardent desire, so that they might rush most eagerly into these affections and, by this means, species might be propagated and multiplied. [Col. 0716B] This desire and appetite is found more vehement and acute in a human being, either because he wished the number of human beings to be greater, or because he gave virtue to the human being alone, so that there might be praise and glory in restraining pleasures and in self-restraint. Therefore that adversary of ours knows how great the force of this desire is—which some preferred to call necessity—and transfers it from what is right and good to what is evil and depraved. For he introduces unlawful desires, so that people may defile what belongs to others, though they are permitted to possess their own without fault. He sets provocative forms before the eyes, suggests incentives, and supplies nourishment to vices; then, in the inmost entrails, he disturbs and stirs every spur, and excites and inflames that natural ardour until he deceives the entangled and ensnared human being. And lest there should be anyone who, through fear of punishments, refrained from what belongs to another, he also established brothels [Col. 0717A] and made public the shame of unfortunate women, so that he might make a mockery both of those who act and of those who must suffer it.

He plunged souls born for holiness into these obscenities as into a whirlpool of filth; he extinguished shame and destroyed chastity.

[Col. 0717A] [Note: [Col. 0717C] Variorum Notes to columns 717–718]

“He destroyed chastity.” Thus the editions of Cellarius and Heumann, and rightly, so that there is a climax: “he plunged,” “he extinguished,” “he destroyed.” Others have *flagitavit*, as though one were to say “to solicit earnestly toward sexual violations and disgraces,” or “to address a virgin more insistently for sexual violation.” Six Vatican manuscripts, 1 Reg. rec., 1 Lips., 1 Clarom., and Aldus among the corrections to the errors of his edition have *flagitiavit*, an unusual word. Marm. and 1 Reg. in the second hand have *profugavit*; 2 Reg. rec., *fugavit*. But these variant readings, and neither Betuleius’s nor Isaeus’s corrections, please me. “He solicited chastity” (*pudicitiam flagitavit*) appears in many manuscripts. Thus Ulpian, *On Private Offences*, ch. 2, and Digest, *On Private Offences*, law 2, §5: “to solicit another’s maidservant.” But these do not seem sufficiently pertinent to the matter.—“Chastity.” Here weigh what was said in Book I, ch. 20: “There is no chastity, when unbridled lusts defile every sex and every part of the body.” BUN.

“He joined males to males.” 1 Bon. ancient: *applicuit*, “he applied.”

“The institution of God.” Thus I restored it from fourteen old editions and all manuscripts, except Em. and 1 Clarom., which have “the justice of God,” as in five common editions.

“Unless they also impiously,” etc. Thus manuscripts 2 Bonon., Tax., Pen. In Cauc., Jun., and eight editions, *et* stands for *etiam*. Seven Reg. manuscripts, including two very ancient ones, and eleven other recent manuscripts have: “unless they also impiously [make sport of] their own sex”; five recent manuscripts and the same number of printed editions have: “unless they impiously [make sport of] their own sex,” wrongly repeating the word “sex,” which occurred immediately after.

“He does not even spare the head.” We say nothing of this sin because of its obscenity. If you can do so without loss of modesty, see what Suetonius relates about the monster of a human being, Tiberius; for in this matter it would be a crime to have learned it. Hieronymus Magius treats this sin fully; see *Gruter’s Critical Treasury*, II, p. 1353. From GALLAEUS.

“May obtain.” I restored this from the editions Torn. and Soubron. and all manuscripts except 1 Reg., which has *exequatur*. 2 Reg. rec., 3 Colb., and sixteen printed editions have *assequatur*.
