“Will forbid.” Manuscript 1 Reg.: *cohibebit*, “will restrain”; eight other recent manuscripts and six editions: *prohibet*, “forbids”; 1 Colb.: *prohiberet*, “would forbid.” The rest, as in the text.

“From others’, which.” After *alienis*, many manuscripts and nearly all printed editions add *toris*, “beds,” which cannot stand with the relative *quae*. 1 Reg. rec. has *quos*.—Yet Buneman has *alienis toris* and supplies the following note on this word:—“From others’ beds, which.” The books consistently read thus, so that *torus* may be said in both genders: *torum, tori, tora*, like *forus, forum; lectus, lectum*. BUN.

“To set before oneself.” Thus I emended from Cellarius’s edition and all manuscripts except 2 Reg. rec. and 1 Clarom., which have *praeponere*, as do eighteen printed editions.

“To this.” Manuscript 1 Bon. ancient: “to which.”

“And condemn [it] to death.” Thus I restored from manuscripts and nearly all printed editions. 1 Bon. ancient alone, and some printed editions, have: “and condemn [it] by death.”

“Over which death has power.” I restored *quod* from the two most ancient Reg. manuscripts, one other excellent Reg. manuscript, and two Brun. In seven Reg., six Colb., two Clarom., and seventeen editions, one reads *quo*.

“Shame.” Sixteen manuscripts and twelve editions add *-que*, but in vain, for it is absent from the following member.

“To revolt to worse things.” Thus I restored it from manuscripts 1 Bon. ancient, Pal., and 2 Reg., supported by the most ancient Regius manuscript, where *desuescere* (“to become unaccustomed”) is read, corruptly for *desciscere*. Sixteen manuscripts and nineteen editions have *descendere* (“to descend”).

He also joined males to males and contrived unspeakable intercourse contrary to nature and contrary to God’s institution; thus he trained and armed human beings for every wickedness. For what can be holy for those who have subjected immature age, weak and in need of protection, to be ravaged and defiled by their lust? This deed cannot be described in proportion to the greatness of its crime. I can call these people nothing more than impious persons and parricides: the sex given by God does not suffice for them unless they also impiously and wantonly [Col. 0717B] make sport of their own. Yet among them these things are trivial and, as it were, honourable. What shall I say of those who practise not an abominable lust but rather a madness? I am ashamed to speak; but what are we to think will happen to those who are not ashamed to do it? And yet it must be spoken of, because it happens. I speak of those whose utterly foul lust and execrable frenzy do not even spare the head. With what words, or with what indignation, should I pursue so great a crime? The magnitude of the wickedness surpasses the office of speech. Since, therefore, this lust produces such works and devises such deeds, we must arm ourselves against it with the greatest virtue. Whoever cannot bridle those impulses should restrain them within the prescribed limits of lawful marriage, so that he may obtain what he eagerly seeks and yet not fall into sin. For what do ruined human beings want? Surely pleasure follows honourable acts; if they seek it in itself, they may enjoy it justly and lawfully.

But if some necessity prevents this, then [Col. 0718A] the greatest virtue must be applied, so that continence may resist desire. God commanded abstinence not only from others’ bodies, which it is not permitted to touch, but also from public and common bodies; and he teaches us that when two bodies have been joined to each other, they become one body. Thus whoever immerses himself in filth must necessarily be smeared with filth. The body can indeed quickly be washed; but a mind polluted by the contagion of an immodest body cannot be cleansed of the filth that has adhered to it except by long time and many good works. Therefore each person must set before himself that the union of two sexes was given to living beings for the sake of procreation, and that this law was laid down for these impulses: that they may produce offspring. Just as God gave us eyes not that we might look and take pleasure, but that we might see for those actions which concern [Col. 0718B] the necessities of life, so we received the generative part of the body—as the very name teaches—for no other purpose than producing offspring. This divine law must be obeyed with the utmost devotion. Let all who profess themselves disciples of God be so disposed and trained that they can govern themselves. For those who indulge pleasures and comply with lust enslave their soul to the body and condemn it to death, because they have consigned themselves to the body, over which death has power. Therefore, as far as possible, let each person form himself for modesty, cultivate shame, and defend chastity in conscience and mind; and let him not merely obey public laws, but stand above all laws, since he follows God’s law. If he accustoms himself to these goods, he will then be ashamed to revolt to worse things—provided only that upright and honourable things please him, [Col. 0718C] things more pleasant to the better than depraved and dishonourable things are to the worse.

[Col. 0719A] I have not yet set forth all the duties of chastity, which God confines not only within private walls but also within the prescribed bounds of the marriage-bed, so that, when a man has a wife, he should have neither a slave woman nor a free woman—

[Col. 0719A] [Note: [Col. 0719C] Variorum Notes to columns 719–720]

“Neither a slave woman nor a free woman,” etc. For this reason the Julian law in the civil law of the Romans is to be criticized: it recognizes adultery or *stuprum* only among free persons; otherwise it leaves to the plaintiff an action for injuries or for corrupting a slave against one who has intercourse with a slave woman. Digest, *Inter liberas*, and *Julian Law on Adultery*. No less an error belongs to the same jurists, who say that a person has committed adultery or *stuprum* if he has had intercourse either with your spouse or has violated your daughter, while you, even if you have broken faith with your wife, will not be an adulterer unless the other party brings an accusation against you. Thus they measure adultery from those who suffer it, not those who commit it. To them, an adulterer is someone who has intercourse with another’s wife, even if he is not a husband. He is said to have committed *stuprum*, even if he is a husband, if he has relations with a virgin or widow. But the sacred Scriptures say that the person who has broken marital faith is guilty of adultery. BETULEIUS.

[Col. 0719D] “Only the woman is an adulteress,” etc. This should not be understood as though an action were not granted either against the adulterer of your wife or against the violator of your daughter—provided that Modestinus’s distinction is admitted, which Ulpian confesses is rather improperly confused (*καταχρηστικώτερον*)—but because the Julian law does not permit a woman to bring a public accusation of adultery, as the emperors Severus and Antoninus rescripted to Cassia, law 1, Code, *On the Julian Law on Adultery*. BETULEIUS.

A husband, however, etc. From Petitus, the law of Solon—partly preserved in Lysias, partly in Plutarch—runs as follows: “Let no one be seized as an adulterer in the case of a woman who prostitutes herself either in a brothel or publicly.” Women who prostitute themselves publicly are also subject to the wrongs committed by slaves; for through brothels and maidservants lust is permitted. Jerome, *Life of Fabiola*; see also Augustine, *City of God*, XIV.17. Hence Quintilian, VII.4, asks whether one caught with another man’s wife is an adulterer, because the uncertainty concerns not the designation but the force of the act—[Col. 0720C] whether he has sinned at all.

Divine law. Matthew XIX; Mark X; I Corinthians VII; Ephesians V.

Woman alone of all creatures, etc. Pliny says, VII.11: “Apart from woman, few animals know sexual intercourse while pregnant.” Among those few are the mare and the sow, as Pliny himself says at the end of X.63; but Aristotle mentions only the mare, *Generation of Animals*, IV.5.

Lust would compel men to seek another thing. The Brunensis manuscript reads *another*; Francius, *another woman*.

For it is unfair, etc. Ulpian, in the book *If a Wife*, § “The Judge,” Digest, *On the Julian Law concerning Adultery*: “The judge,” he says, “must keep before his eyes and inquire whether the husband, living chastely himself, has also encouraged his wife to cultivate good morals. For it seems most unfair that a husband should demand chastity from his wife which he does not himself exhibit. This circumstance can also condemn the husband, though it does not, by compensation of a reciprocal offense, make the matter common between the two.” BETULEIUS.

Has brought about. Ten recent manuscripts and four old editions read “has brought this about”; five others, [Col. 0720D] “brings this about.”

Stirred by the example itself. Thus I restore it from ten Royal manuscripts, five Colbert manuscripts, and eight others. One Colbert and one Claramontanus have “stirred by her own example”; twelve editions, “incited by the example itself”; in four other printed copies *itself* is absent.—“Stirred … by example”: Cicero, *On Ends*, II.19, “stirred by ardor of mind”; Lactantius, I.10, “stirred by the pain of injury”; and plainly, as here, he has said in *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, 9, “stirred by domestic examples.”

To avenge herself. The Roman edition of 1470 and all manuscripts read this, except one Colbert manuscript, which, like seventeen common editions, reads “to avenge.”

Those provisions are added. Thus I corrected it from two very ancient Royal manuscripts and six others. Thirteen manuscripts and the same number of editions read “let those provisions be added”; one ancient Bologna manuscript and four others, “are brought in.”

Has taken a divorced woman. One Colbert manuscript: “a separated woman”; one ancient Bologna manuscript: “has taken one cast out.” Luke VI.

The mind becomes adulterous. Ovid: “The mind is adulterous.” FRANCIUS.]

…may furthermore wish to possess, but let him keep faith in marriage. For it is not so, as the principle of public law has it, that the woman alone is an adulteress when she has another man, while the husband, even if he has several women, is free from the charge of adultery. Rather, divine law joins two persons in marriage—into one body—on equal terms, so that whoever has torn apart the union of the body in different directions is held an adulterer.

Nor for any other reason, when God wished the other animals to resist males after conceiving offspring, did he make woman alone among them all receptive to the male: namely, lest, if women resisted, lust should compel men to seek another object [Col. 0719B] and thereby fail to retain the glory of chastity. Yet neither could a woman attain the virtue of modesty if she were unable to sin. For who would call a dumb animal chaste because, after conceiving, it resists the male? It does this because it must suffer pain and danger if it admits him. There is therefore no praise in not doing what one cannot do.

Chastity is praised in a human being because it is not natural but voluntary. Faith must therefore be kept by each toward the other; indeed, the wife must be taught by an example of continence to conduct herself chastely. For it is unfair to demand what you yourself cannot provide. This unfairness has certainly brought it about that adulteries exist: women, resenting that those who do not themselves keep faith do not show reciprocal affection. In short, there is no adulteress of such ruined modesty that she does not allege this as an excuse for her vices: she says that in sinning she is not committing an injury but returning one.

Quintilian expressed this very well: “A man who neither abstains from another’s marriage nor guards his own—things naturally connected with one another.” For a husband occupied in corrupting the wives of others cannot attend to the sanctity of his own household; and when a wife falls into such a marriage, stirred by the very example, she thinks either that she is imitating or that she is avenging herself.

We must therefore take care not to provide occasions for vice by our own lack of self-control. Rather, let the habits of the two become accustomed to one another, and let them bear the yoke with equal minds. Let us think of ourselves in the other person. For almost the whole of justice [Col. 0720B] consists in this: do not do to another whatever you would not wish to suffer from another. These are the things God commands concerning continence.

Yet, lest anyone think that he can evade the divine commands, those provisions are added, in order that every pretext and opportunity for fraud may be removed: that he is an adulterer who takes a woman dismissed by her husband; and likewise he who dismisses his wife, except for the crime of adultery, in order to take another. For God did not wish the body to be dissolved and torn apart. Moreover, not only adultery but even the thought must be avoided: let no one look upon another’s wife and desire her in his heart. For the mind becomes adulterous if it has even painted for itself an image of pleasure. It is indeed the mind that sins, which embraces in thought the fruit of unrestrained lust: [Col. 0721A]

[Note: [Col. 0721C] Various Notes on Columns 721–722]

**Embraces the fruit of lust in thought.** Augustine, *Against the Manichaeans*: “Justice holds a person guilty by evil will alone, even though he may have been unable to accomplish what he wished.” Salvian, VI: “The very desire for a shameful deed is condemned as an act.” Ambrose, *On Duties*, I: “Adultery is committed not only by the pollution of the deed, but also by the intentness of the gaze.” PRICAEUS.

**Since it is proposed to human beings.** Nine recent manuscripts and ten old editions: “to all human beings.”

**Even to conquer.** Thus restored from five old printed editions and almost all manuscripts, except one Leipzig manuscript, which has “and to conquer it”; one Colbert manuscript and eight editions: “to conquer it.”

**By this heavenly manner of life.** That is, celibacy. FRANCIUS, in the margin of his copy.

**But as though he permits.** In the older Royal manuscript alone: “but as one who grants freedom to choice”; this is a gloss.

**He shall triumph over the earth.** In the accusative, as elsewhere he said “to live life,” “to meet death,” “to wage warfare.” By “triumphing over the earth,” Lactantius means triumphing over earthly goods and pleasures. See the *Epitome*, chapters 51 and 66.

**Has taken.** Junius, one Colbert manuscript, and five editions: “will have taken.”

**For because virtue.** One ancient Royal manuscript: “for if”; Bologna, eight Royal, Taxensis, Penuensis, two Colbert, and two Claramontanus manuscripts: “for virtue indeed”; Brunensis: “for since virtue.” The rest, with all editions, as in the text; this seems more suitable.

**We must make our way out.** *Exire* is said of a work brought to its end by application and labor. CASAUBON.

**Or despair of himself.** One ancient Royal manuscript: “and”; Brunensis: “of himself.” In eight recent manuscripts and six editions, *himself* is absent.

**Has slipped into the path of injustice.** Two Colbert manuscripts: “of justice,” corruptly; six recent manuscripts and the Betuleius edition: “has slipped from the path of justice.”

**In the third Academic.** Cicero informs Atticus that he condensed four books of the *Academic Questions* into two. Yet a fourth book is cited by Nonius Marcellus; it is the second of the two that survive, just as the third is cited by Lactantius. This third, however, has perished with most of the others.

[Col. 0722C] **But if it were permitted to those, etc.** This passage of Cicero does not survive today. ISAEUS.

**A devious path.** Thus I emended it from several manuscripts and editions. In French, *la mauvaise voie*, “the bad road”: a more suitable reading than “the devious life” of ten others. For our reading is confirmed by other passages in Lactantius: *Divine Institutes*, IV.30, “they made for themselves devious paths,” and V.1, “from that devious road.” In these, of course, he imitated Cicero.—Bunemann reads: “A devious life.” Gotha, Rostock, Venice 1471 and 1515, Paris, Cratander, Gymnasium, and Tornesius: “thus, a devious path.” Here *path* has no place, and hence Leipzig, Reimmann, Fasius, Gryphius, Betuleius, Thomas, and the rest read “a devious life.” Thus “a devious life” is a life turned away from the true path of virtue, according to Graevius on Cicero, *On Friendship*, 25. More on Lactantius, III.11.

**Easier.** Thus restored from all manuscripts and several editions; “happier” appears in nine printed copies.

**Our children.** This point is elegantly set forth in the prodigal son, Luke XV.

**We receive, cherish, embrace.** Twelve recent manuscripts and the Gymnasium edition prefix “support”; two Royal manuscripts, one of them very ancient, reject “cherish”; two other Royal manuscripts and the Brunensis read “let us receive, cherish, embrace.”

**Can be appeased by repentance.** One ancient Bologna manuscript: “cannot.”

**Will blot out.** This reading belongs to the most ancient manuscript codices: two Bologna, seven Royal, three Caucasian, Colbert, one Claramontanus, Ultramontanus, two Leipzig, two Brunensis manuscripts, and sixteen editions. Eleven recent manuscripts and four common editions have “will forget.” Does he refer to Isaiah XLIII.25: “I who blot out your iniquities for my own sake, and will not remember your sins”?

**Old sins [do not harm] the corrected person.** One recent Royal manuscript: “the corrected woman,” wrongly; another Royal: “the rebuked person,” worse; one Royal, Tornesius, and one Claramontanus manuscript have “old [sins] [do not harm] one corrected”; one very ancient Royal manuscript: “and vices [do not harm] one corrected.”

**For he whose deed repents him.** Thus the very ancient Royal-Puteanus, Caucasian, Junius, and seven other manuscripts, together with thirteen common editions. In one very ancient Royal, one Bologna, twelve other recent manuscripts, and seven editions: “for he whose sin repents him,” etc. In one Colbert manuscript: “for he whose sin repents him.”]

…which we may call in Latin *resipiscentia*, “coming to one’s senses.” For one comes to one’s senses and, as it were, recovers one’s mind from madness when one is sorry for one’s error; one chastises oneself for folly and strengthens one’s mind to live more rightly. Then one takes especial care not to be led again into the same snares.

Even dumb animals, when they are caught by a trick, if somehow they have extricated themselves in flight, become afterward more cautious and always avoid everything in which they have perceived fraud and ambushes. Thus repentance makes a person cautious and diligent in avoiding sins into which he has once fallen through deception.

No one can be so prudent, so watchful, as never to stumble. And therefore God, knowing our weakness, in his mercy opened [Col. 0723B] for humankind a harbor of salvation, so that the remedy of repentance might assist this necessity to which our frailty is subject. Whoever, therefore, has gone astray should turn back, and as quickly as possible recover and reform himself:

> But to recall one’s step and escape to the upper air—  
> This is the task, this is the toil.

For once they have tasted pleasures that are sweet to their harm, they can scarcely be torn away from them. They would follow the right path more easily if they had not experienced their sweetness. But if they free themselves from this evil slavery, every error will be forgiven them, if they correct their error by a better life.

Let no one think he gains anything by having no accomplice aware of his offense. For he knows all things, in whose sight we live; and even if we can conceal ourselves from all human beings, we cannot conceal ourselves from God, to whom nothing can be hidden or secret. Seneca ended his exhortations with an admirable statement: “There is,” he says, “some great divinity, greater than can be conceived, to whom we devote our efforts by living. Let us commend ourselves to him. For it is of no use for conscience to be shut up within: we lie open to God.”

What truer thing could be said by one who knew God than was said by a man ignorant of true religion? For he expressed God’s majesty by saying that it is greater than human thought can comprehend; and he touched the very fountain of truth in judging that human life is not superfluous, as the Epicureans maintain, but that people render God service by living, provided [Col. 0725A] they live justly and devoutly.

[Note: [Col. 0725C] Various Notes on Columns 725–726]

**A true worshipper of God.** Thus the manuscripts and editions. Francius preferred “of the true [God].”

**If someone had shown him.** The true God.

**Zeno.** He was leader of the Stoic school.

**And his teacher Sotion.** Jerome, at the end of Augustus’s reign in the Eusebian Chronicle: “Sotion, an Alexandrian philosopher and teacher of Seneca, is reckoned famous.” Seneca himself, *Letters*, XLIX: “Recently I sat as a boy with the philosopher Sotion; recently I began to plead cases.” BUNEMANN.—**Sotion.** A Spanish philosopher who was Seneca’s teacher.

**A confession of ignorance.** Emendation: “a confession of one ignorant.”

**It is of no use for conscience to be shut up within.** Thus restored from almost all manuscripts and the Isaeus edition. In the Caucasian, two recent Royal, Emendatus, Cantabrigiensis manuscripts, and thirteen printed editions: “to keep conscience shut up within.”

**But the divinity of God cannot be excluded even by inner chambers.** For God searches hearts and reins, Psalm VII.10. Minucius, in the *Octavius*: “He is present in darkness; he is present in our thoughts.”

[Col. 0725D] **You can never.** Ten Royal manuscripts, two Colbert manuscripts, and the Betuleius edition: “can,” wrongly.

**Suppose, madman, it has happened to you that you escape the eyes of all human beings.** Seneca, *On Clemency*, I.26: “But suppose cruelty to be safe.” *On Benefits*, III.30: “Suppose I have returned life for life.” Letter LXIV: “Suppose remedies have been left to us.” BUNEMANN.

**Not to have an accomplice while possessing conscience.** “To have an accomplice” is absent from certain editions, which read “while possessing awareness.” This emendation is Nicolas Le Nourry’s, in his *Apparatus to the Library of the Fathers*, II.

**Tully.** Cicero, *On Duties*, III.3.

**His own mind, etc.** Marcus Aurelius, XII.26: “Each person’s mind is a god.” Hermes, *Poimandres*, 12: “Mind in human beings is god.” Hence Synesius, *Encomium on Baldness*, on the head as God’s temple because it is the seat of the mind. Cicero, *On Duties*, III.44, cited by Lactantius, *Institutes*, VII; and Euripides in Theon the Sophist, *Progymnasmata*. GATAKER.

**As though we must render an account.** Seneca, Letter XII: “Death ought to be before the eyes of the young no less than of the old.” Epictetus, *Enchiridion*, 28; see the whole passage there. Augustine, Homily 13: “He wished the last day to be unknown, so that everyone might be watchful.” Gregory of Rome, *On Job*, XXII: “The last day is beneficially unknown, so that it may always be believed near.” For how can you sin by putting matters off from day to day, when you do not know whether this is your last day? Horace, *Epistles*, I.4:

> Believe that every day which has dawned for you is your last.

And Jerome on Matthew XXIV: “Let us so live every day as though we were to be judged on that day.” GATAKER.

**Said.** In the last action against Verres.

**The same witness.** Sixteen recent manuscripts and six editions read “the witness himself.”

[Col. 0726D] **Will remove envy.** Thus the most ancient manuscripts—two Royal, one Bologna, Junius, Emendatus, Cantabrigiensis—and the Betuleius edition. Eighteen Royal manuscripts and seventeen common editions read “will scatter.”

**Swollen, he is inflated by pride.** One ancient Bologna manuscript, Emendatus, Cantabrigiensis: “inflated by the swelling of pride.”

**Let him look chastely upon another’s wife.** Horace: “with an unturned eye.” FRANCIUS.—Curtius, III.12, on Alexander: “He regarded virgins of outstanding beauty as chastely as if they had been born of the same parent as himself.”

**Let him not covet what belongs to another.** Thus I read with the Royal-Puteanus, three other Royal, three Colbert, one Claramontanus, Emendatus, Cantabrigiensis manuscripts, and four old editions. In eleven manuscripts and thirteen printed copies, *nothing* stands in place of *not*.

**This man is a worshipper of the true God.** Thus the most ancient manuscripts—one Bologna, one Royal, three others—and the Isaeus edition transmit it. See above, “He could have been a true worshipper of God.” Twenty-one manuscripts and eighteen common editions read: “This man is a worshipper of God.”]

He could have been a true worshipper of God, if someone had shown him [God]; and he would certainly have despised Zeno and his teacher Sotion if he had found the guide of true wisdom. “Let us commend ourselves to him,” he says. It is an altogether heavenly utterance, were it not preceded by a confession of ignorance: “It is of no use for conscience to be shut up within; we lie open to God.”

There is, therefore, no place for falsehood or pretense. For walls exclude human eyes; but the divinity of God cannot be excluded even by inner chambers from seeing and knowing the whole person. In the first book of the same work Seneca says: “What are you doing? What are you contriving? What are you concealing? Your guardian follows you. Travel has removed one companion from you, death another, illness another; this one clings to you, and you can never be without him. Why do you choose a hidden place and remove witnesses? [Col. 0725B] Do you think it has happened to you that you escape the eyes of all human beings? Madman! What good is it to you not to have an accomplice, when you have conscience?”

Tully speaks no less admirably concerning conscience and God: “Let him remember,” he says, “that he has God as witness; that is, as I judge it, his own mind, than which God himself has given nothing more divine to man.” Again, when speaking of the just and good man: “Therefore such a man,” he says, “would not dare not only to do but even to think anything which he would not dare to proclaim publicly.”

Let us therefore cleanse conscience, which lies open to God’s eyes; and, as the same author says, “let us always live as though we believed that we must render an account.” Let us suppose that at every moment [Col. 0726A] we are watched, not in some theater of the world, as he said, by human beings, but from above by him who will be both judge and witness; and when he demands an account of life, it will not be permitted to deny our deeds.

It is therefore better either to escape conscience, or of our own accord to lay our mind open and, by reopening the wounds, pour out their ruin: wounds which no one can heal except him alone who restored the power of walking to the lame, sight to the blind, cleansed defiled limbs, and raised the dead. He will extinguish the burning of desire, root out lusts, remove envy, moderate anger. He will restore true and everlasting health.

All should seek this remedy, because the soul is troubled by a greater danger than the body; treatment must be applied as quickly as possible to hidden diseases. For even if someone enjoys sharp sight, sound limbs [Col. 0726B] throughout, and the strongest health of the whole body, I should nevertheless not call him healthy if he is carried away by anger, puffed up and swollen with pride, enslaved to lust, burning with desires. Rather, I would call healthy the person who does not raise his eyes toward another’s prosperity, does not admire riches, looks chastely upon another’s wife, desires absolutely nothing, does not covet another’s possessions, envies no one, despises no one, is humble, merciful, beneficent, gentle, and humane, and has enduring peace dwelling in his soul.

That person is healthy, just, and perfect. Whoever therefore obeys all these heavenly commands is a true worshipper of God, whose sacrifices [Col. 0727A] are gentleness of mind, an innocent life, and good deeds. Whoever renders these things sacrifices as often as he does something good and devout.

[Note: [Col. 0727B] Various Notes on Columns 727–728]

**For God does not desire a victim.** In several editions *not* is absent; I restore it from all manuscripts and many editions.

**Nor are vervain, purificatory offerings, or turf-altars needed, etc.** By *februa* he means entrails, the part for the whole. Those preparing to perform rites placed upon altars a turf of grass or sacred herbs (*verbenae*). Vervain and laurel were likewise frequent in fumigations. Virgil, *Eclogues*, VIII:

> Bind these altars with a soft fillet;  
> And burn rich vervains, etc.

ISAEUS.

[Col. 0727C] Donatus, on *Andria*, says that *verbena* is so called as though *herbena*, and that verbenas are all grasses and festive branches used to crown altars. No plant had greater distinction at Rome, according to Pliny, XXV.9. “With it,” he says, “Jupiter’s table is swept; the house is purified and cleansed.” Hence Dioscorides, IV, says it was called *hierobotanē* (ἱεροβοτάνη), “sacred plant.” BETULEIUS.—**Purificatory offerings (*februis*).** Thus I read from the most ancient Royal manuscript, supported by another Royal-Puteanus manuscript, a very ancient and excellent codex, which has *febris* for *februis*. Others transmit *fibris*. But that *februis* must be read is shown by Varro’s words: “The Sabines call purification *februum*, and it is a word used in our rites.” Festus is no less explicit: “Whatever is used for the sake of purification in any sacrifices is called *februa*; and that which is purified is said to be *februatus*,” as also Augustine, *City of God*, VII.7, and Ovid.

**From the innermost breast.** Thus restored from all manuscripts except four recent ones and their edition, which have “heart”; but the latter word follows shortly.

[Col. 0727D] **Upon the altar of God, which is truly greatest.** He alludes to the *Ara Maxima* of Hercules. Virgil, *Aeneid*, VIII.271–272.—**Which is truly greatest.** Heumann rightly observed that our author has reference to the *Ara Maxima* mentioned by Livy, I.7, and Virgil, *Aeneid*, VIII.271; compare Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, III.12. He sets this altar, truly greatest, as it were against Rome’s *Ara Maxima*.

**As Cicero has said.** I add *has*, from all manuscripts and many editions. This is Cicero’s, in the first book *On Laws*.

**Now we shall say a few things about sacrifice itself.** Lactantius does not argue very judiciously in this chapter concerning the external worship of God, temples and their ornamentation, votive gifts, and sacrifice. For he seems to disapprove all external worship of God. Indeed, the Church’s chief sacrifice, the Eucharist, is also external in large part and is offered in an external rite. Moreover, although inward worship of mind and spirit is primary, and what God chiefly requires from each of us—for external worship without inward worship brings no salvation to a Christian—yet our external worship of God is in itself devout, holy, good, and pleasing to God. The external adornments of churches, consisting partly in buildings, partly in golden vessels, silken vestments, and so forth, by their very nature contribute to the devout and holy worship of God. To think otherwise is the heresy of the Petrobrusians, Wycliffites, and the Innovators of our age. See Bellarmine, *On the Cult of the Saints*, III.6, and Baronius, *Annals*, I, year 57. As for Lactantius’s meaning in this chapter, Thomasius rightly brings it to a sound sense: he speaks against those who thought religion consisted in external worship alone. Nevertheless, Lactantius speaks with insufficient caution.

**“Ivory,” Plato says, “is not a pure gift for God.”** Plato, *Laws*, XII, about the middle. Pliny, VIII.10, indicates that ivory had been used very extensively in religious rites: “Tusks,” he says, “are of immense value, and furnish the most highly praised material for images of gods. Luxury has discovered another recommendation: it seeks in the hand worn at the neck a force of flavor; I think for no other reason than that ivory itself seems to eat.” “The size of the tusks seems especially important in temples,” etc. Pliny also, XII.1: “With wood we plough the seas and bring lands near; with wood we build roofs. Images of divinities too were made from wood, before value had been devised for the corpse of a beast; before, by a right of luxury as though born from the gods, the same ivory was seen both in the faces of gods and the legs of tables.” BETULEIUS.

**Incorporeal.** Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, I.

[Col. 0728D] **Seneca.** In the book *On Superstition*, which is also cited by Tertullian and St Augustine.

**Close at hand.** That is, nearest. Cyprian, *Testimonies to Quirinus*, III.23: “The time is now close at hand”; or, as Elmenhorst in his index to Apuleius, *in proximo*: in the vicinity.

**But with a pure mind, etc.** Paulinus, Letter XXXII:

> Most chaste in body, mind, and faith, Severus joyfully built  
> These dwelling places for God.  
> Since he himself flourishes wholly as God’s temple, with Christ as guest,  
> And bears in his humble heart the Lord who rejoices.

But Christ had already begun his temple in his mother’s breast, and the beginning of his holy dwelling. Augustine, *Confessions*, II.3.—**With a pure mind.** Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, II: “The worship of the gods is best, and at once most pure, most holy, and most full of piety, when we always venerate them with mind and voice pure, whole, and uncorrupted.”

**What God is.** The Bologna manuscript, one recent Royal manuscript, and the Taxensis have *quis* (“who”); one Royal manuscript has *qui* (“who”).

**Which things, if a human being should also despise them.** All editions except the old Roman edition add *quis* after *si*; I have deleted it, and the handwritten manuscripts reject it.

**By divine law.** Sacrifices are treated in Leviticus, and votive offerings in Exodus, chapter XXV and following.

**But among them … it is a gift, etc.** Lactantius is mistaken: for the distinction he refutes is itself the true and proper distinction between a gift and a sacrifice, as Chrysostom teaches in Homily 18 on the Epistle to the Hebrews, Theophylact on chapter VIII of the same epistle, and St Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, II–II, question 85, article 3. ISAEUS.

**Trismegistus.** Trismegistus, *Poimandres*, chapter 12.

**The worship of God consists solely in not being evil.** Christians ought not merely to abstain from evil, but to do good, as Christ, the Prophets, the Apostles, and the holy Fathers of the Church attest and require.]

God does not desire a victim: neither that of a dumb animal nor one of death and blood, but that of a human being and life. For this sacrifice there is no need of vervain, purificatory offerings, or turf-altars—things certainly most vain—but of those things brought forth from the innermost breast. Thus justice, patience, faith, innocence, chastity, and abstinence are laid upon God’s altar, which is truly greatest, established in the human heart and incapable of being defiled by blood.

This is the truest rite; this is that splendid and divine law of God, as Cicero has said, which always commands what is right and honorable and forbids what is wicked and shameful. One who obeys this most holy and most certain law must necessarily live justly and lawfully. I have set forth only a few heads of this law, because I promised to speak only of those matters which place the highest crown upon virtue and justice. Whoever wishes to comprehend all the rest should seek it from the fountainhead itself, from which this stream has flowed down to us.

## CHAPTER XXV. On sacrifice, on a gift worthy of God, and on the manner of praising God

Now we shall say a few things about sacrifice itself. “Ivory,” Plato says, “is not a pure gift for God.” What then? Surely painted and precious woven cloth? On the contrary: nothing that can be stolen, nothing that can be corrupted, is a pure gift for God. But although Plato saw that one ought not offer to a living being anything derived from a dead body, why did he not see that a bodily gift ought not be offered to an incorporeal being?

How much better and truer is Seneca: “Do you wish,” he says, “to conceive of God as great and gentle, a friend to be revered with mild majesty and always close at hand? He is not to be worshipped with sacrifices and much blood—for what pleasure is there in the slaughter of innocent beings?—but with a pure mind and a good and honorable purpose. Temples are not to be built for him out of stones piled to a height: he must be consecrated in the breast of each person.”

In that perfect discourse, etc. Ἐν λόγῳ τελείῳ (“in the perfect discourse”), likewise cited above, Book IV, ch. 6. This testimony occurs at the end of the *Asclepius*. Since the Greek is unavailable to us, I shall set down Apuleius’ translation, beginning a little earlier:

> But when they had come forth from the sanctuary and begun to pray to God, they faced south. For at sunset, whoever wishes to pray to God ought to face in that direction, just as at sunrise he ought to face that quarter called east. Then, as they were speaking the prayer, Asclepius said: “In a low voice, let us suggest to the Father as he prays what he has commanded: that, with incense and spices added, we offer prayer to God.” Trismegistus, hearing this and disturbed, said: “Speak better omens, better omens, O Asclepius. For it is like sacrilege, when you pray to God, to burn incense and the rest; for nothing is lacking to him who himself is all things. But let us worship while giving thanks. For these are God’s highest offerings of incense: thanks rendered by mortals.”

Then follows the thanksgiving. BETUL.

Asclepius asking his son. From the manuscripts and almost all editions I have restored *quaerentem*, “asking.” In the editions of Thysius and Gallæus, *quae*, wrongly.

“Speak good omens, good omens, O Asclepius.” This is certainly the reading required by the manuscripts—the Regio-Palatine, the old Bologna manuscript—and by Hermes Trismegistus’ *Asclepius* itself, cited in the preceding observation, as well as by Apuleius’ version. The Regio and Bologna manuscripts agree with Lipsius, Palatine, and the editions of Spark and Walch in reading *o mi nate* (“O my son”), in twenty-five manuscripts and eighteen printed editions. The letters *r* and *t* have almost the same shape in manuscripts. The old Bologna manuscript corruptly reads *o Asclepiades*. In the final chapter of the *Asclepius*.

Impiety. This is true if we suppose that he is to be worshipped by incense alone and by odours alone; this seems indicated by the following words [Col. 0730D].

Needing. Old Bologna manuscript 1: *indiget*, “needs.”

“For his sacrifice is blessing alone.” And rightly. For one must sacrifice by means of the Word. The Brunswick manuscripts add *est* after *benedictio*; the Oxford manuscripts place it after “And rightly.” In five editions: “His sacrifice is blessing alone; rightly so. Therefore one must sacrifice by means of the Word.” Old Bologna manuscript 1: “Whose sacrifice is blessing alone. Rightly, therefore.” At this point Lactantius’ teaching is true, because he is disputing against the Gentiles, whose whole sacrifice consisted in costly offerings, with no regard for the inward sacrifice—namely, innocence, an upright and pious life, humility, fear, and integrity. This too is Trismegistus’ purpose, whose words Lactantius reports. So also St Paulinus, Epistle XII. Thomasius held the same view.—“Blessing.” And rightly, *Epitome*, ch. 68: “The Stoics say that [the world] was made for human beings.” And rightly. Cicero himself, in the *Brutus*, ch. 51: “Plato,” says Antimachus, “alone is worth all the thousands to me.” And rightly. BUN.

“And with humility.” I have prefixed *et* (“and”) from nine old editions and all the manuscripts except two Bologna and two recent Royal manuscripts.

Therefore, if anyone thinks that garments, jewels, and the other things held in esteem are dear to God, he plainly does not know what God is: he supposes that God takes pleasure in things which, if a human being despised them, he would deservedly be praised. What, then, is chaste, what is worthy of God, except what he himself required in that divine law of his?

There are two things which ought to be offered: a gift and a sacrifice—a gift permanently, a sacrifice for a time. But among those who in no way understand the nature of divinity, a gift is whatever is fashioned from gold and silver; likewise, whatever is woven from purple and silk. A sacrifice is a victim and whatever is burned upon the altar [Col. 0729B]. Yet God makes use of neither, because he himself is incorruptible, while that whole is corruptible. Therefore both must be offered to God in incorporeal form, which he does use. The gift is integrity of mind; the sacrifice, praise and hymn. For if God is not seen, then he must be worshipped by things not seen. Therefore no other religion is true except that which consists in virtue and justice.

How God makes use of human justice is easy to understand. For if a human being is just, having received immortality he will serve God forever. Both the ancient philosophers and Cicero too suppose that human beings are born for justice alone. For, discussing laws, he says:

> “But of all the matters treated in the discussions of learned men, surely nothing is more excellent than to understand clearly that we are born for justice.” [Col. 0730A]

Therefore we ought to present and offer to God only that for receiving which he himself created us. Hermes Trismegistus is a competent witness to the supreme truth of this twofold kind of sacrifice. He agrees with us—that is, with the prophets whom we follow—both in words and in substance; and he spoke thus concerning justice:

> “This word, O son, worship and cultivate. But the worship of God is one thing: not to be evil.”

Likewise, in that perfect discourse, when he had heard Asclepius asking his son whether it pleased his father that incense and other odours should be offered for the sacrifice of God, he cried out:

> “Speak good omens, good omens, O Asclepius. For it is the greatest impiety to admit into one’s mind any such thought concerning that one and unique Good [Col. 0730B]. These things, and things like them, do not suit him. For he is full of all things whatsoever exist and is least of all in need of anything. But let us worship while giving thanks. For his sacrifice is blessing alone.”

And rightly.

For one must sacrifice to God by means of the Word, since God is Word, as he himself confessed. Therefore the highest rite of worshipping God is praise directed from the mouth of a just person to God. Yet for that praise itself to be acceptable to God, great humility, fear, and devotion are necessary, lest anyone, trusting in his integrity and innocence, incur the fault of pride and arrogance and thereby lose the grace of virtue. But in order to be dear to God [Col. 0731A] and free from every stain, he should always implore God’s mercy and pray for nothing else except forgiveness for his sins, even if there are none.

[Col. 0731A] [Note: [Col. 0731A] [Various Notes on columns 731–732]

“Even if there are none.” That is, none known to himself. And how many are hidden from us! Hence the Psalmist says: “Cleanse me, O Lord, from my hidden faults.” Psalm XVIII [19]:13. For who can be clean from every sin? See Lactantius above, ch. 13. And: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” First Epistle of John 1:8.

Make satisfaction. By producing fruits worthy of repentance, Luke III. For, according to Augustine, *On Repentance*, repentance does not consist merely in changing one’s conduct for the better and turning away from evil deeds; unless one also makes satisfaction to God for what has been done, through the sorrow of repentance [Col. 0732A], through the groaning of humility, through the sacrifice of a contrite heart, with almsgiving cooperating.

“Let him acknowledge that this happened to him because of his sins.” Two recent manuscripts and editions read *illud*, “that”; Bologna manuscript 1 and recent Royal manuscript 1, *venisse*, “has happened.” The others as in the text.

“Let him give thanks even in evils.” Old Bologna manuscript 1 adds *suis*, “his own.” *Etiam* (“even”) is absent in two recent Royal manuscripts and five editions, for which the Brunswick manuscript has *et* (“and”).—“Let him give thanks even in evils”: that is, in adversities and calamities; Book II, ch. 11: “They never remember God except when they are in evils.” BUN.

“If he has served God, Father and Lord.” Who is the Father and Lord of all. FRANCIUS.]

If he desires anything else, there is no need to tell one who knows what we want. If any good happens to him, let him give thanks; if any evil, let him make satisfaction and acknowledge that it happened to him because of his sins. Nevertheless, even amid evils let him give thanks, and amid good things let him make satisfaction, so that he may always be the same—steadfast, unchanging, and unshaken. Nor should he suppose that this is to be done only in a temple [Col. 0732A], but also at home and even in his own bedchamber. Finally, let him always keep God consecrated with him in his heart, because he himself is God’s temple. And if he serves God, Father and Lord, with this constancy, this obedience, and this devotion, justice is complete and perfect; whoever has maintained it has obeyed God, and has fulfilled both religion and his own duty, as we have previously attested.

[THE SEVENTH BOOK OF LACTANTIUS.]

[Col. 0731]

ANALYSIS OF THE SEVENTH BOOK, ON THE BLESSED LIFE.

[Col. 0731C] The Seventh Book has nine parts:

The first investigates the highest good, or reward of virtue, from chapter 1 to 7, and determines that it is immortality.

The second discusses the immortality of the soul, from chapter 7 to 14.

The third teaches to what extent blessedness is granted to human beings, chapter 14.

The fourth teaches when it is granted, discussing the end of the world and the preceding signs, both more remote and nearer ones (chapters 15, 16, 17, 18, 19).

The fifth treats of the last judgment (chapters 20, 21, 22, 23).

The sixth treats of the rule of Christians on earth for a thousand years (chapter 24).

The seventh again discusses the time of the end of the world, and more specifically (chapter 25).

The eighth teaches what will happen when the thousand years have elapsed (chapter 26).

[Col. 0731D] To all these is appended the general conclusion of the entire work, which is the ninth part of this book.

Lactantius himself gathers up the sum of the FIRST PART at the beginning of chapter 6. “For this reason,” he says, “the world was made: that we may be born; for this reason we are born: that we may know God, the maker of the world and of ourselves; for this reason we know him: that we may worship him; for this reason we worship him: that we may receive immortality as the reward of our labours; for this reason we are endowed with the reward of immortality: that, made like angels, we may serve the supreme Father forever.” He says that this is the sum of theology, which the philosophers did not grasp, although every school perceived something of it. Therefore immortality is established as the highest good.

In the SECOND PART the immortality of the soul, which some philosophers denied and others affirmed, is defended (ch. 8). The following arguments are used.

I. If the gods are without bodies, human souls must likewise subsist by the same reasoning.

II. The soul’s eternity is discerned from the fact that no other animal has knowledge of God [Col. 0732C].

III. Humanity alone uses the heavenly element, namely fire, the element of light and life. Therefore humanity has received an immortal condition.

IV. Virtue, given to humanity alone, harms the present life; therefore it will benefit the future life (ch. 9).

V. The very perpetuity of virtue indicates that the human mind, if it has attained virtue, endures.

VI. Cicero himself thought in the *Tusculan Disputations* that the highest good comes to humanity only after death (ch. 10).

VII. As God is everlasting, so are the goods which he grants to the pious.

VIII. Just as bodily works are mortal because the body itself is mortal, so the soul appears immortal because we see that its works are not mortal.

IX. The mind desires not fragile things but eternal ones; it is therefore credible that it too is eternal.

X. If the body is mortal because it is subject alike to sight and touch, then the soul is immortal for that reason, because it can neither be touched nor seen [Col. 0732D] (ch. 11).

Lucretius, Book III, objects: the soul is born with the body; therefore it also perishes.

Reply.—The two cases are not alike, because the body consists of earth, the soul of heavenly spirit. Indeed, even the body does not immediately dissolve after the soul’s departure; much more, then, does the soul remain.

The same writer objects: perception is vigorous in children and young people and diminishes in old people; therefore the soul is mortal.

Reply.—Mind and soul differ. The former increases or diminishes with age; the latter always remains in its own condition.

He objects: the soul is liable to pain and grief; therefore it is also liable to mortality.

Reply.—This is why virtue is necessary: that grief may be repelled and pleasure overcome through abstinence.

He objects: an eye torn out of the body sees nothing; therefore the separated soul too perceives nothing.

Reply.—The comparison is dissimilar. The soul is not a part of the body [Col. 0733A], but is in the body (ch. 12).

The remaining objections are not of great importance and are therefore omitted here.

XI. Hermes also, and the Sibylline verses, taught the soul’s immortality (ch. 13).

In the THIRD PART of the book he teaches to what extent immortality is granted to humanity. He says that justice alone brings eternal life to humanity, and God alone bestows the reward of eternal life. Those said to have become immortal by their own merits, since they lacked true justice, acquired for themselves not immortality but death through sins.

In the FOURTH PART he discusses the end of the world and its signs.

Concerning the end he boldly declares that consummation will come when six thousand years have been completed, because God created and completed all things within the span of six days (ch. 14).

He enumerates the preceding signs, both more remote and immediate.

The more remote are: the extreme impiety of human beings and the destruction of the Roman Empire [Col. 0733B] (ch. 15). Here one may read Lactantius’ remarkable conjectures about the time and manner of the Roman Empire’s destruction throughout chapters 16, 17, and 18.

He lists these nearer signs: he says that a sword will fall from heaven, that Christ will descend with angels accompanying him into the middle of the earth, and that the power of the angels will hand over the reprobate into the hands of the just (ch. 19).

In the FIFTH PART he treats of the last judgment. Briefly describing its form, he says that those who knew God will be judged, and their deeds—that is, evil works weighed against good ones—will be weighed: if the good are more numerous and weightier, they will be justified unto a blessed life; but if the evils prevail, they will be condemned to punishment. Here he examines this question: how can an immortal soul be afflicted? He writes that the Stoics maintain that the souls of the impious have a certain intermediate nature, between immortal and mortal [Col. 0734A] (ch. 20). He himself invokes God’s power, which grasps even incorporeal things and affects them as it wills. He then explains the manner of the affliction:

> Divine fire, by one and the same power, will burn and restore the impious; and whatever it consumes from their bodies it will replace, itself supplying its own everlasting fuel.

But when he has judged the just, he will also test them by fire. Then those whose sins prevail in weight or number will be scorched and burned by fire. But those whom full justice has ripened will not feel that fire (ch. 21). Lactantius adds what the poets wrote concerning the last judgment and what philosophers wrote concerning resurrection (chapters 22, 23).

In the SIXTH PART, following the dream of the Chiliasts, he teaches that Christ will dwell among human beings for a thousand years and govern them by a most just rule (ch. 24).

In the SEVENTH PART he defines the time of the world’s end more specifically. “The whole expectation,” he says, “seems to be no more than two hundred years” [Col. 0734B] (ch. 25).

The EIGHTH recounts what will happen once the thousand years are completed. “The world,” he says, “will be renewed by God; heaven will be folded up; earth will be changed; and God will transform human beings into the likeness of angels. They will be white as snow, will always remain in the sight of the Almighty, and will sacrifice and serve their Lord forever.” At the same time will take place that second, public resurrection of all, in which the unjust will be raised for everlasting torments (ch. 26).

The CONCLUSION of the whole work follows, in which he congratulates the Church on the peace established through Constantine, and exhorts all, individually and collectively, to cast aside the worship of gods, devote themselves to the true God, and thus escape the punishments to come. SCULTETUS.

[Col. 0733]

BOOK SEVEN. ON THE BLESSED LIFE.

[Note: [Col. 0733C] [Various Notes on columns 733–734]

“On the Blessed Life.” In chapter 5, in the old Roman edition and in the manuscripts, the title of this seventh book is *On the Blessed Life*, except in Colbert manuscript 1 and two Royal manuscripts, where it is *On the Reward of Virtue*. In most printed editions it is *On the Divine Reward and the Last Judgment to Come*. The former reading is supported by chapter 1, where one reads “the divine reward of perpetual blessedness”; the latter by chapter 2: “It remains for us to discuss God’s judgment,” etc., and chapter 15. Thomasius wisely observes that in this seventh book of Lactantius there are many errors, taken partly from philosophers, especially Platonists, and partly from Origen; for the same errors are found in the earlier books. It is sufficient to give this warning at the beginning of the book.

“Good: the foundations have been laid.” Lipsius manuscripts 2 and 3, Reims: *Bene hactenus*, “Good thus far.” Venice 1493, 1477: *Bene habeat*, “May it be well.” Camerarius, on Cicero at this place, supplies “the matter fares well.” But Cicero and other ancient writers do not add the words “the matter.” Seneca, *Hercules Furens* IV.10.35: “Good: the house of the shameful king has been destroyed.” *Oedipus* V.998: “Good: it has been accomplished.” BUNEMAN.

“Bearing the work forward.” Excellent; for foundations bear a work or building, rather than complete it. The copyists in five recent manuscripts and the Roman editions of 1468 and 1470 therefore altered it wrongly to “completing the work.”

“False religions.” False religions were discussed in Books I and II.

“The true [religion].” Lactantius treats this in Book VI.

“False wisdom.” This is treated in Book III.

“What the true [wisdom] is.” The author teaches this in Book IV.

“Heavenly justice.” See Book V.

“Unless it.” I have restored this from the older and better manuscripts: two Bologna, Regio-Palatine, Taxius, two Clairvaux [Col. 0735B], and others. Three Royal manuscripts have *eamdem* (“the same”); two recent Royal manuscripts and the editions have *eum* (“him”); three Colbert manuscripts, Brunswick, and the Cratander edition, *cum* (“with”), *nisi eam* being understood as “justice.” If one reads *nisi eum*, supply “worship.” — “Unless it.” Thus I print, from Bologna, Taxius, Lipsius 2 and 3, Reims, *eam*, namely virtue. Observe that Lactantius, by a remarkable artifice, embraces in this third section the titles of the seven books of the *Divine Institutes*. BUNEMAN.]

[Col. 0733C] CHAPTER ONE. On the world; on those who will believe and those who will not; and a rebuke of the faithless.

Good: the foundations have been laid, as the eminent Orator says. Yet we have not merely laid foundations, firm and suitable for bearing the work forward; we have carried the entire building, with great and strong masses, almost to its summit. What remains is much easier: either to roof it or adorn it. Yet without this, the previous labours are both useless and ungrateful. For what advantage is there in being freed from false religions, or in understanding the true one? What advantage is there in discerning the vanity of false wisdom, or in recognizing what true wisdom is? What advantage, I say, is there in defending that heavenly justice? What advantage is there in maintaining, amid great difficulties, the worship of God, which is the highest virtue, unless the divine reward [Col. 0735A] of perpetual blessedness follows it?

This is what we must discuss in this book, lest all that has preceded appear futile and fruitless if we leave uncertain that for the sake of which those things were undertaken. Otherwise someone might suppose that such great labours are undertaken in vain, since he distrusts their heavenly reward, which God has appointed for one who has despised these pleasant earthly goods for the sake of virtue alone, bare and unadorned. Let us do enough for this part as well, both by testimonies from the divine Scriptures and by probable arguments, so that it may be equally clear that future things are to be preferred to present, divine things to earthly, and perpetual things to brief; because the rewards of vices are temporal, but those of virtues everlasting.

I shall therefore explain the rationale of the world, so that it may readily be understood [Col. 0735B] both when and why it was made by God. Plato, who discussed the world’s formation, could neither know nor explain this, since he was ignorant of the heavenly mystery, which is learned only by prophets and through God’s teaching. Therefore he said that the world was made for eternity. But the truth is very different: for whatever possesses a solid and heavy body, just as it once had a beginning, must also have an end.

For Aristotle, not seeing how so vast a mass of things could perish and wishing to escape this limitation [Col. 0736A], said that the world had always existed and would always exist. He saw absolutely nothing; for whatever exists must at some time have had a beginning, and nothing at all can exist unless it began. For since we see earth, water, and fire—the parts of the world—perishing, being consumed, and extinguished, it follows that the whole whose members are mortal is mortal. Thus whatever can perish has been born. Moreover, everything that comes under the eyes’ sight must, as Plato says, be both bodily and dissoluble.

Epicurus alone, following Democritus’ authority, spoke truthfully in this matter. He said that the world had at some time arisen and would at some time perish. Yet he could give no account of it: neither the causes for which so great a work should be dissolved nor the time at which it would be dissolved [Col. 0736B]. But because God has revealed this to us, and we do not attain it by conjectures but by heavenly tradition, we shall teach it diligently, so that students of truth may at last see that the philosophers neither saw nor understood truth, but merely caught so faint a scent of it that they in no way perceived whence that scent of wisdom—so sweet and pleasant—had breathed upon them.

Meanwhile, I think it necessary to warn readers that corrupt and vicious minds will either not understand at all what we set forth—for their perception is blunted [Col. 0737A] by earthly desires, which weigh down and weaken all their senses—or, even if they understand it, will nevertheless dissemble and refuse to acknowledge it as true. For they are drawn by vices and knowingly favour their own evils, whose sweetness captivates them; and they abandon the way of virtue, offended by its harshness.

For those who burn with avarice and with a certain insatiable thirst for wealth, because they cannot live modestly after selling or generously giving away what they love, undoubtedly prefer that to be false which compels them to renounce their desires. Likewise, those stirred by the goads of lust, who, as the poet says,

> Rush into madness and fire,

certainly say that we bring forward incredible things, because the precepts of self-restraint wound their ears. Those precepts prohibit their pleasures, to which they have adjudged their souls together with their bodies [Col. 0737B]. Those, moreover, who are swollen with ambition or inflamed by love of power, and have devoted all their effort to acquiring honours, would not credit that teaching even if we held the sun itself in our hands. It commands them, having despised every power and honour, to live humbly—and so humbly that they can receive an injury and refuse to return it when received.

Such are the people who, with eyes closed, bark against truth in every fashion. But those who are sound, or will become so—that is, not so immersed in vices as to be incurable—will both believe these things and gladly approach them. Everything we say will seem to them clear, plain, simple, and, what matters most, true and unassailable.

[Col. 0737C] No one favours virtue except one who can follow it; but not everyone can easily follow it. Those can do so whom poverty and lack of resources have trained and made capable of virtue [Col. 0738A]. For if virtue is endurance of evils, those who have always enjoyed good things do not embrace virtue, because they have neither experienced evils nor can bear them, owing to their habituation to and desire for the good things which alone they have known. Consequently, poor and humble people, who are unencumbered, believe God more readily than the rich, who are entangled in many hindrances. Indeed, they are chained and fettered, serving at the beck of their mistress, desire, who has ensnared them in inextricable bonds. They cannot look toward heaven, because their mind bends down toward earth and is fixed in the ground.

But the path of virtue does not admit those carrying heavy burdens. The track by which justice leads a human being to heaven is exceedingly narrow. No one can keep to it unless unencumbered and naked. But these wealthy people, laden with many vast loads, walk along the way of death [Col. 0738B], which is extremely broad, because destruction rules widely. Bitter things and poisons to them are what God commands for justice and what we set forth concerning virtue and truth under God’s instruction. If they dare oppose these, they must confess themselves enemies of virtue and justice.

I shall now undertake what remains, so that the work may be brought to its conclusion. What remains is to discuss God’s judgment. It will be established when our Lord has returned to earth, in order to pay each person either reward or punishment according to merit. Therefore, just as in the fourth book we spoke of his first coming, so in this book let us relate his second coming, which the Jews also acknowledge and await, but in vain. For he must return to confound those to whom he had first come to summon. For those who impiously violated him in humility will experience him as victor in power; and all that they read without understanding, they will suffer when God repays [Col. 0739A], since, polluted by every sin and moreover stained with the holy blood, they are destined for eternal punishments by that very one against whom they laid their impious hands. But we shall have a separate subject against the Jews, in which we shall refute them concerning their error and wickedness.

CHAPTER II. On the error of the philosophers and divine wisdom; and on the golden age.

Let us now instruct those ignorant of the truth. By the ordering of the most high God it has been so arranged that this unjust age, when the course of time has run out, shall reach its end; and that, once all wickedness has forthwith been extinguished and the souls of the pious restored to the blessed life, a quiet, tranquil, peaceful—in short, golden, as the poets call it—age shall flourish, with God himself reigning. [Col. 0739B]

The primary cause of all these errors among the philosophers was that they did not grasp the rational order of the world, which contains the whole of wisdom. That order cannot be grasped by one’s own perception and inward understanding—yet this is what they wished to accomplish for themselves, without a teacher. Thus they fell into various opinions, often contrary to one another, from which they had no way out; and they hesitated in the same mire, as the comic poet says. For their reasoning did not correspond to their assumptions: they had indeed assumed truths, but truths which could neither be asserted nor proved without knowledge of truth and of heavenly realities. Such knowledge, as I have often already said, cannot exist in a human being unless it is received through God’s teaching.

For if a human being can understand divine things, he will also be able to do them; for to understand is, as it were, to follow immediately in the tracks. [Col. 0739C] But he cannot do what God does, because he is clothed in a mortal body; therefore he cannot even understand what God does. That this cannot be done may readily be measured by anyone from the immensity of divine things and works. For if you wish to contemplate the world with all that is in it, [Col. 0740A] you will surely understand how greatly God’s work surpasses human works. Accordingly, as great as the difference between divine and human works, so great must be the distance between the wisdom of God and that of humankind. For because God is incorruptible and immortal, and therefore perfect because eternal, his wisdom likewise, just as he himself is, is perfect; nor can anything obstruct it, because God himself is subject to no thing.

But since a human being is subject to passion, his wisdom too is subject to error; and just as many things impede human life from being perpetual, so too human wisdom must necessarily be impeded by many things from being perfect in thoroughly discerning truth. Therefore there is no human wisdom if it strives by itself toward acquaintance with truth and knowledge; [Col. 0740B] for the human mind, bound to a frail body and enclosed in a dark dwelling, can neither range about more freely nor perceive truth more clearly. Knowledge of it belongs to the divine condition. For God alone knows his own works. A human being cannot attain it by thinking or disputing, but by learning and hearing from him who alone can know and teach.

Therefore Marcus Tullius, rendering Plato’s account of Socrates, who said that the time had come for him to depart from life and for those before whom he was pleading his case to continue living, says: “Whether it is better, the immortal gods know; I think that no human being knows.” Hence all philosophical schools must necessarily be alien to truth, because they were established by human beings; and those which are supported by no oracles of divine utterance [Col. 0740C] can possess no foundation or firmness.

## CHAPTER III. On Nature and the World; and a Refutation of the Stoics and Epicureans

And since we are speaking of the errors of the philosophers, [Col. 0741A] the Stoics divide nature [Col. 0741A]

> **[Note: [Col. 0741B] Notes of Various Scholars on columns 741–742]**
>
> **The Stoics divide nature.** In Cicero, in the first book of the *Academica*, this division of Nature is assigned not to the Stoics but to the Old Academy, etc. Add to this that Aristotle, *Physics*, book II, makes nature twofold: namely, matter and form; and he makes form the final cause. Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, book I, chapter 2: “Others,” he says, “divided the world into two things: one of which acts, the other suffers,” etc. What is more, Augustine too, in *On the Soul and Its Origin*, to the presbyter Peter, book II, chapter 3, recognizes two natures: one, the Creator—namely God; the other, the creature from God. BETUL.
>
> **One which acts, etc.** Seneca, *Letters* 64: “Our Stoics say that there are two things in the nature of things from which all things are made: cause and matter. Matter lies inert, ready for anything, and would remain inactive if no one moved it. Cause, however—that is, reason—forms matter, turns it wherever it wishes, and produces various works from it.” And shortly afterward, in different words: “Plainly, the universe consists of matter and God. God regulates these things which, encompassing him, follow their ruler and leader. Yet that which acts, namely God, is more powerful than the matter which suffers God’s action.” GATAKERUS.
>
> **Nor can either exist without the other.** Thus, with the old Roman edition, all manuscripts except two recent Royal manuscripts. In two other recent Royal manuscripts: “nor can one exist without the other.” And Lactantius a little below: “and they say that neither can do anything without the other.”
>
> **Intermingled with the world.** Twelve manuscripts, including the ancient first Bolognese manuscript and the Caucasian manuscript, read “bounded by the world,” but, Betuleius says, without authority. “Intermingled” is the true reading. [Col. 0741D] See below: “they mingled him with the world.”
>
> **So that God himself is the mind of the world.** This has been discussed in book I, chapter 5. Epiphanius lists this doctrine among Zeno’s errors in book III, tome II. I recall having reported elsewhere from Hermes that God is neither mind, nor spirit, nor light, but the cause that these things are. BETUL.
>
> **And the world is God’s body.** In the *Timaeus*, Plato calls the world “a living creature endowed with soul and intellect” (*τὸν κόσμον ζῶον ἔμψυχον καὶ ἔννουν*). Plato, however, makes the world the body of a god—not of that first Creator, but of some god who is to come. Perhaps from this Pliny too judged that the world ought to be believed divine. BETUL.
>
> **And that he himself did not make the world.** *Himself*, which I have added from all manuscripts and very many editions, is absent in some recent editions.
>
> **For the sake of human beings.** This is true even among the Gentiles. Pliny, in the preface to book XXXVI, says that all things were created for the sake of humankind.
>
> **Since God is a divine and eternal mind, free and released from body.** *Is* is lacking in the ancient first Bolognese manuscript and in four [Col. 0742B] recent editions, but they read: “let a mind be called free from body.” A similar definition of God from the teaching of Socrates and Plato occurs in Plutarch, *Opinions*, book I, chapter 1. Moreover, Diogenes Laertius reports this doctrine of the Stoics on the authority of Chrysippus and Posidonius. BETUL.—See also Cicero in the fragments of the *Consolation* and in book I of the *Tusculan Disputations*, chapter 5; and this from Plato.
>
> **Virgilian.** From Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, verse 726; above, chapter 5, and *On the Anger of God*, chapter 11.
>
> **As mind governs body.** Macrobius, book II, chapter 12, of the *Dream of Scipio*: “The soul,” he says, “which is the true human being, is alien to every condition of mortality, so much so that, in imitation of God governing the world, it too governs the body while the body is animated by it. Therefore the natural philosophers said that the world is a great human being, and a human being a little world,” etc. BETUL.
>
> **And mortal.** Correctly. See above: eleven manuscripts and nine editions add *is*.
>
> **That the members are mortal.** Macrobius in the same place, from the doctrine both of ancient philosophers and of Cicero, notes that the world appears mortal in a certain respect, like an animal deprived of life, a fire extinguished, or moisture dried up. BETUL.
>
> **The earths have gaped.** See Pliny, book II, chapters 80, 92, 106.
>
> **Have sunk down.** Three recent manuscripts and fifteen printed editions read “have descended”; seven Royal manuscripts, the Junius manuscript, and two Colbert manuscripts have “have fallen down”; one Royal manuscript, “have fallen.” But “have sunk down” is the reading of very many manuscripts, including the very ancient two Bolognese and Caucasian manuscripts, and the second old Roman edition. This reading is genuine and Ciceronian: *desidere* means “to sink down.” Cicero, *On Divination* I.97: “The collapse of the Privernian field, when the earth had sunk down to immeasurable depth.” Ibid. 78: “Many towns had collapsed, landslides had occurred in many places, and the earths had sunk down.” See Pliny, book II, chapter 91.
>
> **Fruit-bearing fields.** An example is the Dead Sea. Ovid, book XV:
>
> > I myself have seen what once was most solid earth  
> > Become a strait; I have seen lands made from the sea,  
> > And marine shells lying far from the shore,  
> > And an ancient anchor found on the highest mountains, etc.
>
> See more in Philo, *On the World*, and in Vadianus on Mela, book I, in the chapter on Numidia. BETUL.
>
> **Have dried up lakes.** Thus the manuscripts and editions. That *siccare* should be taken in an intransitive sense is unheard of.—**Have dried up lakes.** Sparkius says: “Since the manuscripts are silent, I shall use my conjecture until a better presents itself, and write: ‘dry places have become parched’ (*sicca aruerint*). For to take it in an intransitive sense is unheard of.” But [Col. 0743C] who does not know that active verbs are often used passively? Apicius, *On Cookery*, book IV, chapter 2, uses this very word: “When they have dried, sprinkle ground pepper over them.” Book IX, chapter 1: “Locusts are roasted on a grill; when they have dried, add to them on the grill whenever they have dried.” BUN.

into two parts: one which acts, the other which offers itself as pliable for being acted upon. In the first, they place the power of perception; in the second, matter; and they hold that neither can exist without the other. How can that which handles and that which is handled be the same? If someone should say that the potter is the same as the clay, or that the clay is the same as the potter, would he not plainly seem mad? Yet these men comprehend under the single name of nature two utterly different things: God and the world, maker and work. And they say that neither can do anything without the other, as though nature were God intermingled with the world.

For at times they so confuse matters that God himself is the mind of the world, and the world is God’s body. As if the world and God had begun to exist at the same time, and he himself had not made the world. Yet they themselves admit this on other occasions, when they declare that it was fashioned for the sake of human beings and that God can, if he wishes, exist without the world; since God is a divine and eternal mind, free and released from body. Because they could not understand his power and majesty, they mingled [Col. 0742A] him with the world—that is, with his own work. Hence that Virgilian passage:

> Mind, poured through all its limbs,  
> Sets the whole mass in motion and mingles with the mighty body.

Where, then, is what these same men say: that it was made by divine providence and is governed by it? For if he made the world, he existed without the world. If he governs it, he does so not as mind governs body, but as a master governs a house, a helmsman a ship, a charioteer a chariot. Yet they are not mingled with the things which they govern. For if all these things which we see are God’s members, God is thereby made insensible, since members lack sensation; and mortal, since we see that the members are mortal.

I can enumerate how often the earths, shaken by sudden [Col. 0742B] movements, have either gaped or sunk down into an abyss; how often cities and islands, overwhelmed by waves, have gone down into the deep; how marshes have flooded fruitful fields; how rivers and lakes have dried up; how mountains [Col. 0743A]

> **[Note: [Col. 0743C] Notes of Various Scholars on columns 743–744]**
>
> **Mountains also.** Pliny counts among marvels that mountains too have rushed together; see him, book II, chapter 83.
>
> **Consumes.** Nearly all manuscripts have the present tense, and rightly so. For several internal fires still remain in the mountains of Italy—Etna and Vesuvius—and on the island of Lipara, etc. The ancient first Bolognese manuscript, the Tax manuscript, and one Colbert manuscript read “consumed,” though Heumann approves this.
>
> **Seas are built up.** An example is Tyre. Pliny, book V, chapter 19: “Tyre,” he says, “once an island, separated by seven hundred paces of very deep sea, is now mainland through the works of Alexander as he besieged it.” Curtius treats this fully in book IV. BETUL.
>
> **Mountains are cut away.** He seems to allude to the Isthmus, which some tried to cut through in vain, as the proverb has it; or to Mount Athos, from whose breadth Xerxes is said to have cut away fifteen hundred paces, according to Pliny, book IV, chapter 10. The account is in Herodotus, book VII. BETUL.
>
> **Riches to be dug out.** Thus Ovid on the Iron Age:
>
> > Riches are dug out, incitements to evils.
>
> So Pliny, in the preface to book XXXIII: “We go down into its entrails, and in the abode of the dead seek riches, as though the earth were not sufficiently kind and fertile wherever it is trodden.”
>
> **Yet not in such a way that God himself.** The Junius manuscripts read *nor* for *not*. *In such a way* is absent from one ancient Bolognese manuscript, four Colbert manuscripts, and one Claromontane manuscript; *so that* from the Pen manuscript.
>
> **Established.** The ancient editions have “instituted,” which Heumann approves.
>
> **The mystery of the world and of humankind.** Thus below, chapter 5, at the beginning: “if they had known the whole mystery of humankind.”
>
> **That the world was made by God and made for the sake of human beings.** *And* is absent in one ancient Bolognese manuscript; nine recent manuscripts and nine editions have: “that the world was made by God, and was for the sake of human beings.”
>
> **If they are mortal.** In place of “if those for whose sake it was made are mortal.” Thus Heumann.
>
> **Itself mortal.** Minucius Felix, chapter 34: “Although Plato said that the world itself was made perpetual and indissoluble, he nevertheless adds that it too is both dissoluble and mortal to its maker, God alone.” BUN.
>
> **The reasoning would fit.** Thus at the beginning of chapter 5: “their reasoning does not fit”; and at the end of chapter 7: “their reasoning would not fit.”
>
> **For its own sake.** Book III, chapter 17: “the wise person does everything for his own sake.” Book V, chapter 17: “they say that virtue must be sought for its own sake.” BUN.
>
