> **These so great works.** The Bolognese manuscript, Isaeus, and Lactantius himself, book II, chapter 8, confirm this elegant reading: “By what contrivance he made this so great work.” BUN.—**To have undertaken these so great works.** Twenty-four manuscripts and three editions read “so great” in some copies, but wrongly.
>
> **And of the other living creatures.** Thus Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II, chapter 53: “For whose sake, then, will anyone say that the world was made? Surely for those living creatures that use reason. These are gods and human beings.” BUN.
>
> **God wished us to be seen.** Thus the old editions. The ancient first Bolognese manuscript and five editions have “to see.” In the rest, *us* is absent.
>
> **Little seals.** That is, small images. For the human being was created in God’s image, with proportion preserved.

also have either fallen down in collapse or been levelled to plains. A hidden and inward fire consumes very many regions and the foundations of many mountains. And is this too little—that God does not spare his own members—unless it is also permitted to humankind to do something to God’s body? Seas are built up; mountains are cut away; and, in order to dig out riches, the inner entrails of the earth are excavated. Moreover, not even ploughing can occur without the tearing of the divine body. Thus we are already wicked and impious because we violate God’s members. Does God, then, suffer his body to be harassed and allow himself to be made weak either by himself or by human beings? Unless perhaps that divine sense which is intermingled with the world and all parts of the world has abandoned the earth’s surface and plunged itself into the depths, so that it might feel no pain from the continual tearing.

But if this is empty and absurd, then they themselves were as much in need of sense as these things are, since they did not perceive that the divine spirit is indeed diffused everywhere and that all things are thereby held together, yet not in such a way that God himself, who is incorruptible, is mingled with heavy and corruptible elements. More correct, then, is what they took from Plato in the *Timaeus*: that the world was made by God and governed by his providence. Plato, therefore, and those who thought the same ought to have taught and explained what cause and rationale there was for constructing so great a work; why he made it, or for whose sake.

But the same Stoics say: “The world was made for the sake of human beings.” I hear them. But Epicurus does not know why human beings themselves were made, or who made them. For Lucretius, when he said that the world was not established by the gods, thus says [Col. 0743C] in book V of *On the Nature of Things*:

> Further, to say that they wished to prepare  
> The splendid nature of the world for the sake of human beings—

[Col. 0744A] Then he adds:

> Is madness. For what advantage could our gratitude  
> Confer upon the immortal and blessed,  
> That they should undertake to do anything for our sake?

And rightly so. For they offered no reason why the human race had been either created or established by God. It is our task to expound the mystery of the world and of humankind. Being strangers to it, they could neither attain nor see the sanctuary of truth. Therefore, as I said a little earlier, although they assumed what was true—namely, that the world was made by God and made for the sake of human beings—nevertheless, because reasoning failed them in what followed, they could not defend what they had assumed.

Finally, lest he make God’s work weak and ruinous, Plato said that it would endure forever. If it was made for the sake of human beings, and made so as to be eternal, why then are those for whose sake it was made not everlasting? If those for whose sake it was made are mortal, then it too is mortal and dissoluble. For it is not more valuable than those for whose benefit it was made. But if his reasoning had fitted, he would have understood that it would perish because it was made, and that nothing can remain forever except what cannot be touched.

But whoever denies that it was made for the sake of human beings maintains no rational account. For if he says that the Maker himself undertook these so great works for his own sake, why then were we born? Why do we enjoy the world itself? What is the purpose of the creation of the human race and of the other living creatures? Why do we appropriate benefits belonging to another? Why, finally, do we grow, diminish, and perish? What rational basis does generation itself possess? What does perpetual succession mean? Surely God wished us to be seen, and to fashion us as little seals by his various images, so as to delight himself; and [Col. 0745A] nevertheless, if this were so, he would care for living creatures, and especially for the human being, to whose command he subjected all things.

But as for those who say that the world has always existed, I pass over the fact that its very existence [Col. 0745A]

cannot be without some beginning, from which they cannot extricate themselves. But I say this: if the world has always existed, it can possess no rational order. For what could rational order have devised in something which never took a beginning? Before something is made or constructed, counsel is needed, so that it may be arranged how it is to be made; and nothing can begin without the foresight of reason. Thus rational order precedes every work. Therefore that which was not made has no rational order. But the world has a rational order by which it both consists and is governed; therefore it too was made. If it was made, it will also be dissolved. Let these men, then, give an account, if they can, of why it was either made in the beginning or dissolved afterward. [Col. 0745B]

Because Epicurus or Democritus could not teach this, he said that it arose of its own accord, when seeds combined randomly with one another, and that, when these were again dissolved, separation and destruction would follow. Thus he corrupted what he had correctly perceived; and, through ignorance of rational order, utterly overturned all rational account. He reduced the world and all that happens in it to the likeness of some utterly empty dream, since no rational order can subsist in human affairs.

Yet since a wonderful rational order governs the world and all its parts, as we see; since the tempering of heaven, the course—equal amid its very variety—of the stars and heavenly lights, the constant and wonderful ordering of the seasons, the varied fruitfulness of lands, the level defences of plains and ramparts of mountains, the greenness and abundance [Col. 0745C] of forests, the most wholesome emergence of springs, the fitting overflow of rivers, the rich and abundant spread of the sea, the varied and useful blowing of winds, and all else consist in supreme rational order—who is so blind as to suppose that those things were made without a cause, in which shines forth a wonderful arrangement of most provident rational order? [Col. 0746A] Therefore, if nothing either exists or comes to be at all without a cause; if the providence of the most high God is manifest from the arrangement of things, his power from their greatness, and his authority from their governance: then those who have said that providence does not exist are dull and mad. I would not disapprove if they said that gods do not exist in order to say that one God exists; but when they say it in order that no god may exist, who does not think them mad is himself mad.

## CHAPTER IV. That All Things Were Created for Some Use, Even Those Which Seem Evil; Why a Human Being, in So Frail a Body, Possesses Reason

But we have said enough about providence in the first book. Since it exists—as is apparent from the wonder of its works—it is necessary that it also created human beings and the other [Col. 0746B] living creatures. Let us therefore see what rationale there was for the formation of the human race; for it is established that what the Stoics say is true: the world was fashioned for the sake of human beings. Yet even in this they err not slightly, in saying not “for the sake of the human being,” but “for the sake of human beings.” For the singular designation of one human being encompasses the entire human race. They say this because, ignorant that one human being was formed by God, they think that people have been generated in every land and field like mushrooms.

But Hermes did not fail to know that the human being was fashioned both by God and in God’s likeness. But I return to the subject. There is nothing, I think, made for its own sake; rather, whatever is made at all must necessarily be made for some use. For who is either so foolish or so idle as to undertake making something to no purpose, from which he expects no usefulness and no benefit? A person who builds a house does not build it merely so that there may be a house; rather, he does so in order that it may be inhabited. A person who makes a ship does not expend effort merely so that a ship may appear; [Col. 0747A] rather, he does so in order that one may sail in it. Likewise, one who makes and shapes some vessel [Col. 0747A]

does not do so merely in order to seem to have made it, but so that the finished vessel may hold something necessary. Similarly, all other things whatever that are made are produced not certainly in vain, but for some useful purposes.

Therefore the world was made by God not, certainly, for the sake of the world itself; for, being without sensation, it has no need of the sun’s heat, light, the blowing of winds, the moisture of rains, or the nourishment of crops. But neither can it be said that God made the world for his own sake, since he can exist without the world, as he existed before; and God himself does not use all the things which are in it and which come to be in it. It is evident, therefore, that the world was constructed for the sake of living creatures, [Col. 0747B] since living creatures enjoy those things of which it consists; and, so that they may be able to live and endure, all necessities are supplied to them at fixed times.

Again, that the other living creatures were fashioned for the sake of the human being is clear from the fact that they serve humankind and were given for human protection and uses. For whether they are land animals or water animals, they do not perceive the rational order of the world as the human being does. At this point the philosophers, and especially Cicero, must be answered. He says: “Why, when God made all things for our sake, did he make so great a multitude of water-snakes and vipers? Why did he scatter so many harmful things over land and sea?” This is a vast subject for discussion, but it must be touched upon briefly in passing.

Since the human being is composed of diverse and opposing things—[Col. 0747C] soul and body, that is, heaven and [Col. 0748A] earth; the subtle and the comprehensible, the eternal and the temporal, the sentient and the brute, that which is endowed with light and that which is dark—the rational order and necessity of the matter itself required that both good things and evil things be set before humankind: good things to use, evil things to avoid and beware of.

For this reason wisdom was given to the human being: so that, once the nature of good and evil had been known, he might exercise the power of his reason both in seeking good things and in avoiding evil ones. For because wisdom was not given to the other animals, they were both protected by natural coverings and armed. But instead of all these things, God gave to the human being that which was chief: reason alone. Therefore he formed him naked and unarmed, so that wisdom might both arm and clothe him. He established his protections and adornment not outside but within, not in the body but in the heart.

Unless, then, there were evils for him to avoid and distinguish from good and useful things, wisdom would not be necessary to him. Let Marcus Tullius therefore understand either that reason was given to the human being so that he might catch fish for his own use and avoid water-snakes and vipers for the sake of his safety, or that good and evil were set before him because he had received wisdom, whose whole power lies in distinguishing good things from evil.

Great, therefore, right, and admirable is the power, rational order, and authority of the human being, for whose sake God made the world itself and all things whatever exist. And he bestowed so much honor upon him that he set him over all things, because he alone could admire God’s works. Therefore our Asclepiades, discoursing excellently on the providence of the most high God in the book which he wrote to [Col. 0748C] me, says: “And therefore,” he says, “one may rightly judge [Col. 0749A] that divine providence gave the place nearest to itself to the one who could understand [Col. 0749A]

This is fire: who uses it?” Therefore the supreme God established these things not for Himself, since He needs nothing, but for humankind, who would use them fittingly.

## CHAPTER V. On the creation of humankind, the ordering of the world, and the highest good

Let us now give the reason why God made humankind itself [Col. 0749B]. If philosophers had known this, they would either have defended those things which they had discovered to be true, or would not have fallen into the greatest errors. For this is the sum and hinge of all things. Whoever has not grasped it, all truth escapes him. This, finally, is what makes their reasoning fail to cohere. Had it shone upon them, had they known the whole mystery of humankind, the Academy would never have cut down their disputations and their entire philosophy across the grain.

Therefore, just as God did not make the world for Himself, because He has no need of its advantages, but for humankind, which uses it, so He made humankind itself for His own sake. “What benefit,” says Epicurus, “does God derive from humankind, that He should make it for His own sake?” Surely, that there might be one who could understand His works, admire in thought and proclaim in speech His providence in ordering, His reason in making, and His power [Col. 0749C] in bringing things to completion. The sum of all this is that one should worship God. For the person who understands these things worships Him; the person who, with due reverence, follows the Maker of all things and his true Father [Col. 0750A], measuring the power of His majesty from the discovery, undertaking, and perfection of His works.

What clearer proof can be offered that God made the world for humankind and humankind for His own sake, than that, of all living creatures, humankind alone was so formed that its eyes are directed toward heaven, its face looks toward God, and its countenance is shared with its parent? Thus God seems, as though extending His hand, to have raised humankind from the ground and stirred it up to contemplate Himself.

“But,” he says, “what does human worship contribute to God, who is blessed and in need of nothing? Or, if He held humankind in such great honour as to construct the world for its sake, to furnish it with wisdom, make it lord of living creatures, and love it as a son, why did He make it mortal and frail? Why did He expose to every evil [Col. 0750B] the one whom He loved, when humankind ought both to be blessed, as joined and nearest to God, and everlasting like God Himself, for whose worship and contemplation it was fashioned?”

Although we have taught these matters here and there in the earlier books, nevertheless, since the subject now especially requires it, because our purpose is to discuss the blessed life, they must be unfolded more carefully and fully, so that God’s ordering, work, and will may be known. Though He could continually produce innumerable souls from His immortal spirits, as He generated angels, whose immortality is secure without any danger or fear of evils, He nevertheless devised an inexpressible work: how to create an infinite multitude of souls, which He would first establish, bound to frail and weak bodies [Col. 0750C], midway between good and evil, so that He might set virtue before beings constituted from both natures; lest they attain immortality delicately and easily, but instead reach that ineffable reward of eternal life [Col. 0751A] with the greatest difficulty and through great labours.

[Note: Variorum Notes to columns 751–752]

**“And vexing limbs” (*vexabilibus membris*).** I have restored this from all manuscripts and from the second old Roman edition, the Florentine, Cratander, Isaeus, and Cellarius. Twelve printed editions read *nexibilibus*, a word which I judge not to be Latin; the Gymnic edition has *nexilibus*; the Paris edition of 1525 and Grapheus have *exibilibus*, wrongly. “Vexing limbs” are laborious limbs, as physicians say, or limbs suited to cause weariness, such as legs, arms, feet, and hands.

**“They could not subsist in the empty middle.”** Leucippus and Democritus believed that primary bodies move in a void, as Aristotle reports in *On the Heavens* II, although there is no empty space or void beneath the aether. The question of the void is treated in Aristotle, *Physics* IV.6 ff. Read the opinions of the philosophers in Plutarch, I.18. BETULEIUS.—See also Descartes.

**“He devised the splendid works of the world.”** Thus nearly all manuscripts agree with all printed editions. Lactantius likewise says above, chapter 3, that He “devised these works,” and below, chapter 9, “when we see His works splendid and wonderful.” Yet two recent Royal manuscripts, of good quality, one Colbert manuscript, and the Brun manuscript have “the splendid work of the world”; and I remember having read the same expression somewhere, unless I am mistaken, in Cicero.

**“Suspended on high.”** For according to the laws of nature everything light rises and everything heavy descends. Ovid elegantly described this arrangement in these words:

> He bound together things separated in place by a harmonious peace;  
> The fiery force of the joined and weightless heaven  
> Flashed forth and chose its place in the highest citadel;  
> Next to it came the air in lightness and position;  
> The denser earth drew down the great elements  
> And was pressed by its own weight. The encircling moisture  
> Occupied the outermost place and enclosed the solid globe.

**“Whose regulation, brightness, and motion … is suitably ordered.”** Five manuscripts and eight recent editions read “whose regulations, brightnesses, and motions … He ordered”; but three have “is ordered.”

**“Fertility for producing diverse things.”** Fourteen recent manuscripts and five editions have “varied”; one Colbert manuscript, “fruitful abundance for producing diverse things.”

**“That by the abundance of crops.”** Junius and five editions: “that abundance.”

**“And green herbs.”** Thus five printed editions and all manuscripts except five and the fourth edition, which read “living.”

**“Of each kind.”** I have restored this from ten editions and all manuscripts except the Caucasian manuscript, which has “for each kind,” as do nine printed editions.

**“Should supply nourishment.”** Fasitellus, Gryphius, Betuleius, Tournès, Thysius, Gallaeus, Sparke, and Cellarius read “administer.” In *On the Workmanship*, chapter 6: “that nourishment of milk may be supplied to the young.” In the *Epitome*, chapter 72: “God will supply sustenance.” Our author does not use *administrare* in this sense. Elsewhere Lucretius, II.1149: “Nature supplies what is enough.” BUN.

**“And compounded.”** Heumann thinks that *and* should be deleted.

**“Could not remain for ever,” etc.** Nor is this true. For if Adam had remained innocent, he would certainly have been immortal; “the wages of sin is death.” Therefore the Council of Carthage, held in A.D. 418, canon 1, anathematizes those who affirm that Adam, even if he had not sinned, would nevertheless have died, “not through the desert of sin but through necessity of nature” (*mē tē axia tēs hamartias, alla tē physeōs anankē*).

**“Why did He make him mortal?”** Gallaeus and Sparke charge Lactantius with a very grave error because he said that man could not remain forever and was made mortal (see above, and *On the Anger of God*, chapter 15). But the statement must be explained from Book II, chapter 12, “he would have remained immortal”; and *On the Workmanship*, chapter 4, where he admits that the creature God made passed voluntarily into death; and *Epitome*, chapter 27. BUN.

**“Endurance of evils and labours.”** What he discusses in this chapter concerning the bearing of hardships and labours, and in Book VI, chapter 11, concerning works of mercy, should be noted against Luther and his followers, who deny that good works are necessary for salvation. ISAEUS.—One Royal manuscript and one Brun manuscript have “and pains”; four recent manuscripts and six editions, “and goods.”

**“Two lives.”** In Aldus, Cratander, and Gymnicus, “two ways,” corruptly. Book VII, chapter 10: “Two lives are set before humankind, one of the soul, the other of the body.” BUN.

**“We receive it by being born.”** Thus Tertullian says against Marcion: “God had granted a human being life, having made him a living soul; but had enjoined right living, having admonished him to obey the law.” Six recent manuscripts and twelve editions have “we have received.”

**“Lest immortality [be] for humankind.”** From all manuscripts and many editions I have added “for humankind.”

Therefore, in order to clothe them with burdensome and vexing limbs—since they could not subsist in the empty middle, pressed downward by the weight and heaviness of the body—He decided first that a seat and dwelling must be created for them. Accordingly, by ineffable strength and power He devised the splendid works of the world: suspending the light elements on high and pressing the heavy ones down into the depths; He established the heavenly things and set the earthly things in place. It is unnecessary now to recount each item, since we have set them all forth in the second book.

He therefore placed lights in heaven, whose regulation, brightness, and movement are most fittingly ordered for the benefit of living creatures. To the earth, which He willed to be their dwelling-place, He gave fertility for producing and bringing forth diverse things, [Col. 0751B] so that through the abundance of crops and green herbs it might supply nourishment according to the nature and use of every kind.

Then, once He had completed everything belonging to the constitution of the world, He fashioned humankind from the earth itself, which He had prepared from the beginning as its habitation. That is, He clothed and enclosed His own spirit in an earthly body, so that, being compounded of diverse and opposing things, [Col. 0752A] it might receive good and evil; and, just as the earth itself is fruitful for producing crops, so the human body, taken from the earth, received the capacity for generation and the ability to produce offspring, so that, since it was formed from frail matter and could not remain forever, it might yield when the span of temporal life had ended and renew through perpetual succession that frail and weak thing which it bore.

Why, then, did He make humankind mortal and frail, when He had built the world for its sake? First, that an infinite multitude of souls might be generated and fill the whole earth with a population; next, that He might set virtue before humankind—that is, endurance of evils and labours—through which it could attain the reward of immortality. For because a human being consists of two things, body and soul, one of which is earthly [Col. 0752B] and the other heavenly, two lives have been assigned to humankind: one temporal, allotted to the body; the other everlasting, belonging to the soul. We receive the former by being born; we attain the latter by labouring, lest immortality for humankind, as we said before, be secured without any difficulty. The former is earthly, like the body, and therefore comes to an end; the latter is heavenly, like the soul, and therefore has no limit.

We receive the first unknowingly; [Col. 0753A] the second knowingly. For it is given to virtue, not nature, because God willed that we should acquire life for ourselves in life.

[Note: Variorum Notes to columns 753–754]

**“We receive unknowingly.”** Four recent manuscripts and fourteen editions: “we have received.”

**“To acquire in life.”** One Colbert manuscript: “unto life”; one Leiden manuscript and the Brun manuscript: “in this life.”

**“Or earn it by virtue.”** Although God has set fire and water before us, and it is within us to stretch out the hand to either, nevertheless the second death is set before us only so that we may avoid it; but God gives aid so that we may earn the second life.

**“By divine necessity.”** I interpret “by divine necessity” as “by divine law.” Likewise, Book II, chapter 2: “having discharged … they yielded to the divine necessity by death.” *On the Anger of God*, chapter 15: “Let us consider divine necessity; for I do not wish to call it nature.” Chrysippus called God “divine necessity.” BUN.

**“Will be dissolved.”** Thus I have restored it from seven old editions and all manuscripts except one recent Royal manuscript, which has “is dissolved,” like the other printed editions.

**“For which fact.”** Thus almost all manuscripts. The Caucasian manuscript and eight other recent ones have “of which fact,” as do almost all printed editions.

**“The nature and constitution of the body furnish [an argument].”** One ancient Bologna manuscript and four recent editions have “the constitution of nature and the nature of the body furnish.” I think the reading of the text should be understood thus: the nature and constitution of the body furnish an argument for the point that the highest good belongs to the spiritual life, because the body is too unstable for the highest good to be located in it.

**“Immortality is not a consequence of nature.”** Understand: blessed immortality is not a consequence of nature. BUN.

**“Although.”** Rather *cum* or *quum*.

**“Not immediately when he is born.”** Eight recent manuscripts and as many printed editions: “not immediately when”; three other recent manuscripts: “when.”

**“It is common to us with dumb animals.”** As if infants were not capable of baptism immediately from birth, when the primitive Church, long before Lactantius, thought quite differently. For Cyprian, in his letter to Fidus, p. 159 of the Oxford edition, when Fidus had raised with him the question whether infants should be admitted to the washing within three days, concludes the letter thus: “And therefore, dearest brother, this was our judgment in council: that no one should be prevented by us from baptism and the grace of God, who is merciful, kind, and gracious to all. Since this ought to be observed and maintained with regard to all, we think it should especially be observed with regard to infants themselves and the newly born,” etc. Read Irenaeus, Book II, chapter 10, on this.

**“That is.”** Added from all manuscripts except one Royal manuscript, where it is absent, as also in some printed editions.

**“Pleasures.”** Thus also below, in the plural, in the following chapter. Two recent manuscripts and four editions have the singular, “pleasure.”

**“Because.”** Two recent Royal manuscripts: “who himself.”

**“Strive toward the highest.”** Thus almost all manuscripts; fifteenth-century editions, one Colbert manuscript, and two Clermont manuscripts have “to strive”; one Brun manuscript, “to be raised”; the other as in the text. I have deleted “good,” which followed in three recent manuscripts and seven editions but is absent from the rest. “He will live badly for a time” means inconveniently, subject to evils; and below “to live well” means conveniently, luxuriously.

**“With what reward He will recompense the person who has honoured God.”** Thus one Bologna manuscript, the Regio-Put manuscript, two other Royal manuscripts, and the edition of Isaeus. Twelve recent manuscripts have: “He who has honoured God, He rewards with this reward.” Cellarius and Walchius agree with our edition.

For this reason He has given us this present life: that we may either lose that true and everlasting life through vices or earn it by virtue. In this bodily life there is no highest good; for, just as it has been given to us by divine necessity, so it will again be dissolved by divine necessity. Thus what has an end does not possess the highest good. But in that spiritual life, which we ourselves acquire through our own efforts, the highest good is contained, because it can have neither evil nor end. The nature and constitution of the body furnish an argument for this.

For all other animals bend toward the ground, because they are earthly; nor do they receive immortality, which is from heaven. But humankind looks upright toward heaven because immortality is set before it; yet it does not come unless it is bestowed upon humankind by God. For there would be no difference between the just and the unjust if every human being were born immortal. Therefore immortality is not a consequence of nature, but the reward and prize of virtue.

Finally, a human being does not walk upright immediately upon being born, but is at first four-footed, because the constitution of the body and of this present life is common to us with dumb animals. Then, when its strength has been established, it rises upright, its tongue is released into speech, and it ceases to be a dumb animal. This reasoning teaches that a human being is born mortal, but afterward becomes immortal when it begins to live from God—that is, to follow justice, which consists in the worship of God—when God has raised the human being to behold heaven and Himself. This happens when the human being, purified by the heavenly washing, [Col. 0753C] lays aside infancy together with every stain of its former life and, having received an increase of divine strength, becomes a complete and perfect human being.

[Col. 0754A] Therefore, because God has set virtue before humankind, although soul and body are united, they are nevertheless opposed and attack each other. The goods of the soul are evils to the body: namely, the avoidance of wealth, the prohibition of pleasures, and contempt for pain and death. Likewise, the goods of the body are evils to the soul: namely, desire and lust, by which both riches and the enjoyments of various pleasures are sought, and by which the enervated soul is extinguished.

For this reason the just and wise person must be amid every evil, because courage is the conqueror of evils; but the unjust are amid riches, honour, and power. For these are bodily and earthly goods. Such persons live an earthly life and cannot attain immortality because they have surrendered themselves to pleasures, which are enemies of virtue. Thus this temporal life must be [Col. 0754B] subject to the eternal one, as the body is subject to the soul.

Therefore whoever has preferred the life of the soul must necessarily despise the life of the body; nor can one otherwise strive toward the highest unless one has despised what is lowest. But whoever has embraced bodily life and cast his desires upon the earth cannot obtain that higher life. Yet whoever prefers to live well forever will live badly for a time and be afflicted with every discomfort and labour while on earth, so that he may have divine and heavenly consolation. And whoever prefers to live well for a time will live badly forever; for by God’s judgment he will be condemned to eternal punishment because he placed earthly goods before heavenly ones.

Therefore God seeks to be worshipped and honoured by humankind as a father, so that humankind may hold fast to virtue and wisdom, which alone produce immortality. [Col. 0754C] Since no one besides God Himself can bestow it, because He alone possesses it, He will recompense the human being’s devotion, by which it has honoured God, with this reward: that it may be blessed forever, be with God, and always be with God.

[Note: Variorum Notes to columns 755–756]

**“And always with God.”** The Marmoutier manuscript, about 500 years old, and one Royal manuscript of about 400 years, no. 3976; Gryphius, Tournès, Betuleius, the Antwerp edition of 1570, and Soubron of 1594 append after these words a long discourse which I find neither in the better manuscripts nor in the remaining editions; therefore I have not wished to admit it as genuine. This discourse also contains many statements that are ill-suited, indeed false, and savour of the heresy of Mani; yet neither Jerome nor St Augustine accuses Lactantius of it.

**“Nor,” etc.** Thomasius observes that this long discourse, extending to the end of this fifth chapter, is absent from two Bologna manuscripts; after Thomasius, Isaeus teaches that it is also absent from twelve Vatican codices. Indeed it is not read in almost all French manuscripts, except two. It must therefore be admitted that this entire passage was interpolated by someone—a very subtle and skilled Manichaean—in order to support his error by Lactantius’s authority. All editors agree, therefore, that it should be removed. But lest anything be lacking in our edition, we append it here, marked in the margin so as to distinguish it from Lactantius’s text.

The following material is found in certain manuscripts and ancient editions. More recent interpreters deny that it belongs to Lactantius; but lest anything be omitted, it has seemed proper to place it here, while warning that it is not thoroughly Catholic. It reads as follows:

> “Nor should anyone now take refuge in saying that the blame belongs to Him who established both good and evil. For why did He will evil to exist if He hates it? Why did He not make only good, so that no one might sin and no one do evil? Although I have taught this in nearly all the earlier books and have already touched upon it above, though lightly, it must nevertheless be repeatedly recalled, because the whole argument rests upon it. For no virtue [Col. 0755B] could exist unless He had made opposites; nor can the power of good appear at all except by comparison with evil. Indeed evil is nothing other than an interpretation of good. Therefore, if evil is removed, good also must necessarily be removed.
>
> “If you amputate the left hand or foot, neither will the body be whole nor life itself remain sound. So fittingly are left things joined with right things to preserve the structure of the body. Likewise, if you make the gaming counters equal, no one will play. If you assign one colour to the Circus, no one will think it worth seeing, when all the pleasure of the Circus games has been removed. Certainly the person who first established those games was a lover of one colour; but he set another beside it as a rival, so that there might be a contest and some charm in the spectacle. Thus, when God established good and gave virtue, He also established opposite things with which it might contend. [Col. 0755C] If an enemy is lacking, there is no battle and no victory. Remove competition, and virtue itself is nothing. How many contests among human beings are there, established by how many different arts? Yet no one would be thought stronger, swifter, or more excellent if he did not have an adversary with whom to compete. Where victory is absent, glory and reward must necessarily be absent as well. Therefore, in order that He might strengthen virtue itself by continual exercise and make it perfect through conflict with evils, He gave both together, because neither can retain its force without the other. Therefore diversity is that on which the whole rationale of truth rests.
>
> “I am not unaware what may be objected here by the more learned. If good cannot exist without evil, how do you say that the first human being was in good alone before offending God, or will afterward be in good alone? We must examine this question, which I omitted in the earlier books in order to complete it here. We said above that human nature consists of opposing elements. For the body, because it is earth, is tangible, temporal, brutish, and dark. But the soul, because it is from heaven, is subtle, eternal, sentient, and bright. Since these are opposed to one another, humankind must be subject to good and evil. Good is assigned to the soul because it is indissoluble; evil to the body because it is frail. Therefore, because body and soul are joined and united, good and evil must likewise adhere together; nor can either be separated from the other except when those two are separated.
>
> “Accordingly, knowledge of good and evil was given to the first human being at the same time. Once it had been received, he was immediately driven from the holy place in which evil does not exist. While he was in good alone, he did not know that that very thing was good. But after he received understanding of good and evil, it was already unlawful for him to remain in the place of blessedness; and he was banished into this common world, so that he might experience together both things whose nature he had equally come to know. It is clear, therefore, that wisdom was given to humankind so that it might distinguish good from evil, distinguish advantageous things from disadvantageous, useful things from useless, and have judgment and reflection concerning what it ought to avoid, seek, flee, and follow. Therefore wisdom cannot exist without evil; and that first founder of the human race lived, as long as he was in good alone, like an infant ignorant of good and evil. Yet afterward humankind must necessarily be both wise and blessed without any evil. But this cannot happen as long as the soul is clothed in the dwelling of the body.
>
> [Col. 0756C] “But when the separation of body and soul has occurred, then evil will be separated from good. And just as the body perishes while the soul remains, so evil will perish and good endure. Then, having received the garment of immortality, humankind will be wise and free from evil, like God. Therefore whoever wishes us to be in good alone chiefly desires that we live without a body, in which evil resides. If it [i.e. evil] is removed, either wisdom, as I said, or the body will be taken away from humankind: wisdom, so that it does not know evil; the body, so that it does not feel it. But now, because humankind is furnished both with wisdom, so that it may know, and with a body, so that it may feel, God willed both to exist together in this life, so that the rationale of virtue and wisdom might stand.
>
> “He therefore placed humankind midway between the two, so that it might have freedom to follow either evil or good. But with evil He mixed certain apparent goods—various pleasant delights—so that by their allurements He might lead humankind to the hidden evil. With good He mixed certain apparent evils—hardships, miseries, and labours—so that the soul, offended by their harshness and difficulty, might recoil from the hidden good. Here, therefore, the office of wisdom is required: that we should see more with the mind than with the body. Very few can do this, because virtue is difficult and rare, while pleasure is common and public. Thus the wise person must be thought foolish: while seeking goods that are not seen, he lets go of those that are visible and within his hands; and while avoiding evils not seen, he falls into evils that are before his eyes.
>
> “This happens to us when we do not refuse either torture or death for the faith, when we are compelled to the utmost crime: to betray the faith, deny the true God, and pour libations to dead and death-dealing gods. This is the reason why God made humankind mortal and subjected it to evils, although He had built the world for its sake: namely, that it might receive virtue, and that virtue might grant it immortality. And virtue, as we have shown, is the worship of the true God.”

## CHAPTER VI. Why the world and humankind were created; how empty the worship of gods is

Let us now mark out the whole argument in a brief outline. The world was made so that we might be born; we are born so that we may acknowledge God, the maker of the world and of ourselves; we acknowledge Him so that we may worship Him; we worship Him so that we may receive immortality as the reward for our labours, because the worship of God consists in the greatest labours; we are rewarded with immortality so that, having become like angels, [Col. 0757C] we may serve the supreme Father and Lord forever, and may be God’s everlasting kingdom.

[Note: Variorum Notes to columns 757–758]

**“God’s kingdom.”** Revelation 1 and 5.

**“If they are many, if for this reason only … and whatever other things,” etc.** Thus seven older Royal manuscripts and others, as well as six editions. Nine recent manuscripts have “who are feigned … and whatever other things”; six recent manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1468, “if many were born … we are fashioned”; two recent manuscripts and five printed editions, “if they are many,” etc., as in the text.

**“So vain.”** For according to the Apostle’s meaning, if there is no resurrection, the entire Christian religion is superfluous and empty.

**“How human a thing, and how the world itself.”** Thus I read with two editions and very many manuscripts, including the very ancient Bologna manuscript and six Royal manuscripts. Eight editions and one Colbert manuscript have “how”; eight recent manuscripts and five printed editions have “and how this world.”

**“So wonderful.”** One ancient Bologna manuscript and one Leiden manuscript: “then wonderful”; one recent Royal manuscript: “and wonderful”; one Royal manuscript and the Gotha manuscript: “and admirable.”

**“Constructed.”** One Colbert manuscript and five editions: “constituted.”

**“You see.”** Fourteen recent manuscripts and five editions: “we see”; one Royal manuscript: “we see.”

**“Have to say.”** *Habeo dicere*, “I have to say,” means “I can” or “I ought to say.” It is a Greek idiom, which Lactantius also uses elsewhere, namely Book IV, chapter 12, near the middle, and in the last chapter; see the notes there.

**“That we may give them grain.”** *Far* is a general word denoting every kind of grain: wheat-grain, barley-grain, and so forth. GALLAEUS.

**“Was established.”** Eleven recent manuscripts and seven editions: “was made.”

**“Begotten? Why are they born?”** From manuscripts and editions I have added “why,” absent from one Colbert manuscript and some editions.

**“Who after death.”** One Leiden manuscript and the Roman edition of 1474: “who after decease.”

**“Souls after decease.”** This is the reading of five old printed editions and all manuscripts except two Royal manuscripts and nine editions, in which the reading is “after death”; but that word occurred just above.

**“Are reduced.”** Four recent manuscripts: “are dissolved.”

This is the sum of things, this is God’s hidden secret, this is the mystery of the world. Those are strangers to it who, following present pleasure, have devoted themselves to earthly and frail goods and sunk souls born for heavenly things into death-dealing pleasures as into mud and filth.

Let us now ask in turn whether any rationale can stand in the worship of the gods. If they are many; if human beings worship them only so that they may grant them wealth, victories, honours, and all other things of merely present value; if we are born for no purpose; if no providence is at work in the generation of human beings; if we are born by chance for our own sake [Col. 0758A] and that of our pleasure; if after death we are nothing—what can be so superfluous, so empty, so vain as the human race and the world itself? Though it is of incredible magnitude and constructed with such wonderful reason, it would nevertheless be occupied with useless matters.

For why should gusts of wind drive clouds? Why should lightning flash, thunder roar, and rain fall, so that the earth may produce crops and nourish various offspring? Why, finally, should the whole nature of things labour so that nothing may be lacking of those things by which human life is sustained, if life is empty, if we perish into nothing, if there is nothing in us of greater benefit to God? But if it is impious even to say this, then neither should it be thought possible that what we see to possess the greatest rational order has been established without some very great reason. What rationale, then, can there be in these errors of perverse religions and in this philosophers’ persuasion that souls perish? Surely none.

For what can they say as to why the gods so diligently provide human beings with everything at its proper time? Is it so that we may give them grain and wine, the fragrance of incense, and the blood of cattle? Such things can please neither immortals, because they are perishable, nor beings without bodies, because these things were given for bodily use. And yet, if they desired them, they could supply them to themselves whenever they wished.

Therefore, whether souls perish or remain forever, what rationale does the worship of the gods contain, or from whom was the world established? Why, when, how long, and to what extent are human beings begotten? Why are they born, perish, succeed one another, [Col. 0758C] and are renewed? What do the gods gain from the worship of those who will be nothing after death? What do they provide? What do they promise? What do they threaten that is worthy either of human beings or of gods?

Or, if souls remain after death, what do the gods do with them, or what will they do? What need do they have for a treasury of souls? From what source do those gods themselves arise? How, why, or whence are there many of them? Thus it comes about that, if you depart from that sum of things which we have set forth above, every rationale perishes and everything is reduced to nothing.

## CHAPTER VII. On the diversity of philosophers and their truth

Because philosophers did not grasp this sum, [Col. 0759A] they could not grasp truth, although they both perceived and explained almost all the matters of which that sum itself consists. But they presented them separately and in different ways, without joining together either the causes of things or their consequences, [Col. 0759A] [Note: Variorum Notes to columns 759–760]

Dicaearchus. “Dicaearchus,” says Suidas, “son of Phidias, a Sicilian from the city of Messene (others say he was a Mamertine), a pupil of Aristotle, philosopher, rhetorician, and geometer,” etc. He, as Cicero recalls in *Tusculan Disputations* I [Col. 0761B] and the *Academic Questions*, argued against the immortality of the soul. “He,” Cicero says, “wrote three books called *Lesbiaca*, because the dialogue takes place at Mytilene, in which he seeks to establish that souls are mortal.” But the same Dicaearchus wrote, as we read in the same book of Cicero, a dialogue set at Corinth, which he expounds in three books, in which he argues that there is absolutely no such thing as soul, and that the whole thing is empty sound in name; that animals and living beings are called such in vain; and that neither a mind (*animus*) nor a soul (*anima*) exists in a human being or in a beast. Cicero likewise mentions him in the *Academic Questions*. Yet, as Plutarch reports in the *Opinions of the Philosophers*, Dicaearchus held the soul to consist of the four elements. BETULEIUS.]

nor reasons, whereby they might both join together and fill out that supreme whole which contains the universe. It is easy, moreover, to show that almost the whole truth has been divided among the philosophical schools. For we do not overthrow philosophy as the Academics customarily do, whose purpose is to answer everything—a practice that is rather to cavil and to mock. Rather, we show that no school was so misguided, nor any philosopher so empty, that he did not perceive something of the truth. But while they rage with zeal for contradiction, while they defend even their own falsehoods, they overthrow the truths of others as well [Col. 0759B]. Thus truth has not merely escaped them, though they pretended to seek it; through their own fault they have especially lost it.

If, therefore, someone had arisen who gathered into one the truth scattered among individual thinkers and diffused among the schools, and reduced it into a coherent body, he surely would not disagree with us. Yet no one can do this except one who is acquainted with and knows the truth. And to know truth belongs only to one taught by God. For no one can otherwise reject what is false and choose and approve what is true. But even if he achieved this by chance, he would be philosophizing most truly; and although he could not defend those truths by divine testimonies, truth itself would nevertheless shine forth by its own light.

Therefore incredible is the error of those who, once they have approved some school and committed themselves to it, condemn all the rest [Col. 0759C] [Col. 0760A] as false and empty. They arm themselves for battle, knowing neither what they ought to defend nor what to refute; and indiscriminately assail everything advanced by anyone who disagrees.

Because of these exceedingly obstinate controversies among them, no philosophy arose that came nearer to truth; for truth in its entirety was grasped by them piecemeal. Plato said, in the *Timaeus*, that the world was made by God. The prophets say the same; and the same is apparent from the verses of the Sibyl (Discourse 1). Therefore those are mistaken who have said either that all things were born spontaneously or that they arose from minute seeds gathered into a mass. For so great, so ordered, so vast a work could neither be made nor arranged and ordered without some most wise author; and the very rational order by which all things are perceived to subsist and be governed acknowledges an artificer of most skillful mind [Col. 0760B].

The Stoics say that the world, and all things in it, were made for the sake of human beings; our sacred writings teach the same. Democritus, therefore, was mistaken in supposing that human beings poured forth from the earth like little worms, without an author and without rational design. Why the human being was formed belongs to the divine mystery; and because he could not know this, Democritus reduced human life to nothingness. Ariston maintained that human beings are born for the attainment of virtue; the prophets likewise admonish and teach us so. Aristippus, therefore, was wrong: he subjected humanity to pleasure—that is, to evil—as a beast of burden. Pherecydes and Plato argued that souls are immortal; and this [Col. 0760C] is a doctrine proper to our religion. Therefore Dicaearchus [Col. 0761A], together with Democritus [Col. 0761A]

Together with Democritus. Democritus and Epicurus say that the soul dies along with the body. Plutarch; Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I.

Arguments. Two recent manuscripts and ten printed editions read “proofs” (*documenta*); the rest, as in the text. See what follows and the beginning of chapter 9.

Yet they possess little firmness. As all philosophical propositions are merely opinions (*δοκοῦντα*), and are not held with certainty even by their authors, so in theological disputes they possess no authority merely because someone has pronounced them. For that reason one must not believe Plato or Pythagoras merely because he said something—even if he said the truth—but because it is true and accords with heavenly authority. Such is the power of divine oracles that their very utterance confers being (*τὸ εἶναι*) upon the matter; and for this very reason it is true that life is everlasting, because the sacred Scriptures have transmitted it—not less truly than if you say, “The flesh shall rise again; therefore sacred doctrine is true.” For the heavenly voice supplies the cause whereby the thing is. BETULEIUS.

We can draw out the truth. So I read with the Bologna manuscripts, the two good Regius manuscripts, the Brunensis, and Betuleius’s edition—and rightly. Thus Plautus and Cicero, *Academic Questions* IV, use “draw out the truth” (*verum elicere*). Seven others read “choose” (*eligere*). [Col. 0762C] Plato, however, argued thus: in the *Phaedo*, *Meno*, *Republic* I, and *Laws* XII. In Lactantius the word “perceiving” (*sentiendi*) has intruded, I know not whence; it is not even in Cicero, who translated these same words in *Tusculan Disputations* I as follows: “That which is always moved is eternal; but that which imparts motion to something else, and is itself moved from elsewhere, when its motion comes to an end must necessarily also have an end of life. Therefore that alone which moves itself, because it is never abandoned by itself, never even ceases to move.” BETULEIUS.—For Plato’s argument, see Macrobius, *Dream of Scipio* II.13 ff.; St Athanasius, *Oration against the Idols*; St Thomas, *Against the Gentiles* II.82.

And perceives. It is absent from the *Phaedo* and from Cicero’s *Tusculan Disputations*.

Abandoned by itself. Bologna manuscript I, ancient: “cannot be lacking to itself” (*desiderari a seipso non potest*); but, as Thomasius rightly observes, the sense of each reading is excellent.—“It cannot be abandoned by itself.” He has expressed Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I.23: “That which moves itself, because it is never abandoned by itself, never even ceases to move . . . the mind perceives itself to be moved . . . to be moved by its own force, not another’s, and that it cannot happen . . . that it should ever be abandoned by itself.” BUNEMAN.

This argument, etc. For its universal proposition is: “Every soul is immortal” (*πᾶσα ψυχὴ ἀθάνατος*). Yet perhaps *the Beautiful* (*τὸ καλόν*)—for this is the title of the discourse—will defend Plato from Lactantius’s criticism, since it has a place not in beasts but in human beings, and thus in the rational soul.

He added. See Plato in Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I; and toward the end of *Cato the Elder, or On Old Age*, and *Consolation* I; as below, *On the Anger of God*, chapter 10, near the end.

Whose wonderful ingenuity. These words were added not by Plato but by Cicero himself.

Learning. Six manuscripts and four editions read “distinguishing” (*discernendi*). See below, chapter 22, at the end: “In children there are capacities easy to receive, because they seize so quickly what they learn that they seem not then to learn it for the first time, but to recognize and remember it.”]

was mistaken in arguing that it perishes and is dissolved with the body. Zeno the Stoic taught that there is an underworld, and that the abodes of the pious are distinct from those of the impious: the former inhabit peaceful and delightful regions, while the latter pay penalties in dark places and in horrible gulfs of mire. The prophets plainly make the same known to us. Epicurus, therefore, was mistaken in thinking this a poetic fiction, and in interpreting the punishments of the underworld that are related as belonging to this life. Thus philosophers touched upon the whole truth and every mystery of divine religion. But, when others refuted them, they could not defend what they had discovered, because the reasoning of each did not cohere and they could not reduce into a whole what they had truly perceived, as we have done above.

[Col. 0761B] CHAPTER VIII. On the immortality of the soul.

There is, therefore, one supreme good: immortality. We were formed from the beginning and born in order to attain it. Toward it we tend; human nature looks to it [Col. 0762A]; virtue advances us toward it. Since we have discovered this good, it remains to speak also of immortality itself.

Although Plato’s arguments contribute much to the matter, they nevertheless possess little firmness for proving and establishing the truth, because he had neither brought the rationale of the whole great mystery to completion and gathered it into one, nor comprehended the supreme good. For though his view concerning the immortality of the soul was true, he did not discuss it as the supreme good. We, therefore, who have learned truth not by uncertain conjecture but through divine transmission, can draw it out by surer signs.

Plato, however, argued thus: whatever both perceives through itself and is always in motion is immortal; for that which has no beginning of motion will have no end either [Col. 0762B], since it cannot be abandoned by itself. This argument would grant eternity even to dumb animals, had he not distinguished the matter by adding wisdom. Therefore, to escape this common consequence, he added that the human mind must necessarily be immortal, since its marvelous ingenuity in discovery, speed in thought, ease in comprehension and learning, memory of the past [Col. 0763A], foresight of the future, and knowledge of arts almost beyond number—of which other living creatures are devoid—appear divine and heavenly. For no origin of a mind able to grasp and contain such things is found on earth, since it has nothing mingled in it from earthly concretion. Rather, whatever in a human being is weighty and dissoluble must necessarily be resolved into earth; but what is light and subtle is indivisible, and, liberated from the dwelling of the body as though from a prison, flies away to heaven and to its own nature. Such, briefly assembled, are Plato’s arguments, which he himself expounds at length and abundantly.

As though freed from prison. From Plato: Cicero calls the body a vessel, receptacle, dwelling, and custody; Seneca further calls it a workhouse and chains. Methodius, in Epiphanius against the Origenists, teaches that the body is neither the soul’s bond nor prison. Peter meanwhile calls it a tent (*σκήνωμα*), and in Job the human body is called a house of clay. The words by which Lactantius here exalted Platonic doctrine are Cicero’s, from *Laelius*, on Scipio’s death, spoken by Laelius: “If this is so—that the soul of every best man most easily takes flight in death, as though from the custody and chains of the body—for whom should we think the journey to the gods was easier than for Scipio?” BETULEIUS.

Pherecydes, etc. This whole doctrine of Plato, Pythagoras, and Pherecydes concerning the soul’s immortality was not pure, but infected by transmigration of souls (*metempsychosis*) as by a kind of hereditary disease. Concerning this, Cicero says in *Tusculan Disputations* I: “Pherecydes of Syros was the first to say that human souls are everlasting—an ancient writer indeed, for he lived during my countryman Servius Tullius’s reign. His pupil Pythagoras especially confirmed this opinion. When Tarquinius Superbus reigned, Pythagoras came into Italy and gained mastery over that Great Greece by reputation, learning, and authority; and for many ages afterward the name of the Pythagoreans flourished so greatly that no others seemed learned.” Thus far Cicero. Their lives are found in Laertius. On Pherecydes, see Augustine, *Against the Academics* III.17 and Letter 3 to Volusianus. BETULEIUS.

Pythagoras had held the same opinion before him, as had Pherecydes, Pythagoras’s teacher, whom Cicero reports to have been the first to dispute concerning the eternity of souls. Although all these excelled in eloquence, those who argued against this opinion had no less authority in this particular controversy: first Dicaearchus, then Democritus, and finally Epicurus. Thus the matter itself over which they fought with one another was brought into doubt.

Finally Tully himself, after setting forth all their opinions concerning immortality and death, declared that he did not know what was true. “Which of these opinions is true,” he says, “some god will see.” And again elsewhere: “Since each of the two opinions,” he says, “had most learned authors, nor can one divine what is certain.” But we have no need of divination, since divinity itself has disclosed truth to us.

[Col. 0764A] CHAPTER IX. On the eternity of the soul, and on virtue.

Accordingly, the eternity of souls can be proved and understood by these arguments, which neither Plato nor anyone else discovered, and which we have briefly assembled, because our discourse hastens to set forth the great judgment of God, which will be held on earth as the end of the ages draws near.

First of all, because God cannot be seen by human beings, lest anyone should therefore think that God does not exist because he could not be seen by mortal eyes, among the other miracles of his institutions God also made many things whose force is manifest but whose substance cannot be seen—such as voice, scent, and wind. Thus, by the argument and example of these things, although God did not come before our eyes, we might nevertheless perceive him through his power, effect, and works [Col. 0764B]. What is clearer than a voice? What stronger than wind? What more forceful than scent? Yet, when these are borne through the air and come to our senses and strike them by their power, they are not seen by the sight of the eyes, but are perceived by other parts of the body.

Likewise, God is not to be grasped by sight or by any other fragile sense, but to be contemplated with the eyes of the mind, when we see his splendid and wonderful works. For those who have said that there is absolutely no God I would call not merely non-philosophers, but not even human beings. Like dumb animals, consisting of body alone, they perceived absolutely nothing with the mind [Col. 0765A], but referred everything to bodily sensation, thinking that nothing existed except what they beheld with their eyes. And because they saw adversity happen to the good and prosperity to the wicked, they believed that all things happen by chance and that the world was established by nature, not providence.

From this point they slipped into absurdities that necessarily followed such an opinion. For if God exists and is incorporeal, invisible, and eternal, then it is not credible that the soul perishes because, after departing from the body, it is not seen—since it is established that something perceptive and active exists which does not come under sight. But it is difficult for the mind to comprehend how the soul can retain perception without those bodily parts in which the function of perceiving resides. What of God? Is it easy to comprehend how he [Col. 0765B] is active without a body? If they believe that gods exist—and if they exist, they are certainly without bodies—then human souls must subsist by the same reasoning, since reason and intelligence itself show that there is some likeness between the human being and God.

Finally, the argument also perceived by Marcus Tullius is sufficiently strong: the soul’s eternity can be recognized from the fact that no other animal has any awareness of God, and religion is almost the only thing that distinguishes the human being from dumb creatures. Since religion belongs to the human being alone, it surely testifies that we seek, desire, and worship that which is akin and will be near to us.

Can anyone, after considering the nature of other living creatures, which the providence of the supreme God made with bodies bent downward, lowered and cast upon the earth—so that one may understand from this that they share no rational affinity with heaven—fail to understand that of all creatures the human being alone is heavenly and divine? His body has been raised from the ground; his face is lifted up; his erect posture seeks its origin; and, as though despising the lowliness of earth, he strives upward because he perceives that the supreme good must be sought for him on high. Mindful of his condition, in which God made him outstanding, he looks to his Maker [Col. 0765C]. This looking Trismegistus most aptly called *theōpida* (*θεώπιδα*, “contemplation of God”); among dumb animals it does not exist.

Since wisdom, given to human beings alone, is nothing other than knowledge of God, it is evident that the soul neither perishes nor is dissolved, but remains forever, because it both seeks and loves God, who is eternal, compelled by nature itself and perceiving both whence it arose and whither it is to return.

Moreover, there is no small argument for immortality in the fact that the human being alone employs the heavenly element. For since the nature of things consists of these two elements, fire and water, which are opposed and hostile to one another—one assigned to heaven, the other to earth—other living creatures, being earthly and mortal, employ the earthly and heavy element; the human being alone uses fire, an element light, lofty, and heavenly [Col. 0766B]. Things that are heavy press downward toward death; things that are light raise upward toward life, because life is on high and death below. And just as light cannot exist without fire, so life cannot exist without light. Fire, therefore, is the element of light and life. Hence it is evident that the human being who uses it has received an immortal condition, because that which produces life is native to him.

The sun is the source of all lights. Besides, who does not know that our smoky and vaporous lights consist of fire? BETULEIUS.

Virtue belongs to the human being alone. Cicero, *On the Laws* I, makes virtue common to God and human beings.

Which would not be. Understand: “virtue.” Some editions have “which would not even be”; seven recent manuscripts and the Cratander edition have “which would not be.”

Which would not be according to nature. This reading is much more fitting than “which would not even be according to nature.” Therefore our reading is more probable; for, speaking of virtue, he says that if regard were to be had only for the body, virtue ought not be called according to nature. For if the soul perished, virtue would rather be called contrary than according to nature, since it weakens the body and subjects it to various hardships. [Col. 0767C]]

Virtue likewise, given to the human being alone, is a strong argument that souls are immortal. It would not accord with nature if the soul is extinguished, for virtue harms this present life. For this earthly life, which we share with dumb animals [Col. 0767A], seeks pleasure and delights in its various and pleasant fruits; it flees pain, whose harshness wounds the nature of living beings with bitter sensations and strives to bring them to death, which dissolves the living creature.

If, therefore, virtue both forbids the human being those goods naturally desired and impels him to endure evils naturally avoided, virtue is evil and hostile to nature; and one who follows it must be judged foolish, since he harms himself both by fleeing present goods and by pursuing evils likewise, without hope of a greater reward. For since we are permitted to enjoy the most pleasant pleasures, do we not seem devoid of sense if we prefer to live in lowliness, poverty, contempt, and dishonor—or even not to live, but to be tortured by pain [Col. 0767B] and to die—if from these evils we obtain nothing further by which the abandoned pleasure can be compensated?

But if virtue is not evil, and acts honorably in despising vicious and shameful pleasures, and courageously in fearing neither pain nor death in order to preserve duty, it must necessarily attain some greater good than the things it despises. Yet, once death has been undergone, what further good can be hoped for except eternity?

CHAPTER X. On vices and virtues, and on life and death.

Let us now turn in turn to those things opposed to virtue, so that the soul’s immortality may also be inferred from them. All vices are temporal, for they are stirred up for the present. The onset of anger is appeased when vengeance has been taken [Col. 0767C]. The pleasure of lust ends with the body. Desire is destroyed either by satiety in the things it seeks or by the stirrings of other affections. Ambition grows old after it has gained the honors it desired. Likewise, the other vices cannot stand or remain; they are ended by the very reward they seek. Therefore they withdraw and return.

But virtue is perpetual without any interruption, and one who has once embraced it cannot depart from it. For if it has an interval, if we can ever be without it, the vices that always attack virtue will immediately return. It has not therefore been comprehended if it abandons us, if it ever withdraws. But once it has established for itself a fixed dwelling, it must be active in every deed; and it cannot faithfully drive out and banish vices unless it fortifies with perpetual guard the breast in which it has taken its seat [Col. 0768A].

Thus the perpetuity of virtue itself indicates that, if the human mind has embraced virtue, it endures, because virtue too is perpetual and the human mind alone receives virtue. Since vices are contrary to virtue, their entire principle must be different and contrary. Since vices are motions and disturbances of the mind, virtue, by contrast, is gentleness and tranquillity of mind [Col. 0768B]. Since vices are temporal and brief, virtue is perpetual, constant, and always equal to itself. Since the fruits of vices—that is, pleasures—are, like the vices themselves, brief and temporal, the fruit and reward of virtue is everlasting. Since the benefit of vices belongs to the present, that of virtue belongs to the future.

Thus it comes about that virtue has no reward in this life, because virtue itself is still ongoing. For just as, when vices are ended in their operation, their pleasure and rewards follow, so virtue’s recompense follows when virtue has ended. But virtue is never ended except by death, since its highest duty consists even in undergoing death. Therefore the reward of virtue is after death.

Finally, Cicero in the *Tusculan Disputations*, though doubtfully, nevertheless held that the supreme good comes to the human being only after death: “With confident mind,” he says, “if circumstances so require, he will advance to death, in which we have learned that there is either the supreme good or no evil.” Death, therefore, does not extinguish the human being, but admits him to the reward of virtue. But one who, as the same author says, has defiled himself with vices and crimes and has been enslaved to pleasure is condemned and will pay an eternal punishment, which the divine writings call the second death, and which is both perpetual and full of the most grievous torments [Col. 0769A].
