For just as two lives are set before the human being—one of the soul and the other of the body—so two deaths are set before him: one belonging to the body, which everyone must undergo according to nature; the other belonging to the soul, acquired by crime and avoided by virtue. And as this life is temporal and has fixed limits because it belongs to the body, so death also is temporal and has a fixed end because it affects the body.

CHAPTER XI. On the final times, and on the soul and body.

When, therefore, the times which God has appointed for death have been fulfilled, death itself will come to an end. And because temporal death follows temporal life, it follows that souls will rise again to everlasting life, because temporal death has received its end. Again, just as the life of the soul is everlasting, in which it receives the divine and ineffable fruits of its immortality, so its death must necessarily be perpetual, in which it pays enduring penalties and infinite torments for its sins. Thus the matter stands such that those who are blessed in this bodily and earthly life will hereafter always be miserable, because they have already obtained the goods they preferred. This happens to those who worship gods and neglect God. Then those who, pursuing righteousness, have in this life been miserable, despised, poor, and often harassed with insults and injuries for righteousness itself—since virtue cannot otherwise be maintained—will hereafter always be blessed; so that, having already endured evils, they may also enjoy goods. This assuredly befalls those who, despising earthly gods and fragile goods, follow the heavenly religion of God, whose goods, like him who bestows them, are everlasting.

What of the works of body and soul? Do they not show that the soul is exempt from death? For the body, since it is itself fragile and mortal, produces only works equally perishable. For Cicero says that there is nothing wrought by human hands which is not at some time reduced to destruction, whether by human violence or by age itself, the destroyer of all things.

But we see that the works of the mind are eternal. For all those who, despising present things, have left memorials of great talents and deeds for remembrance, plainly sought an indelible name for their mind and virtue. Therefore, if the works of the body are mortal because the body itself is mortal, it follows that the soul appears immortal because we see that its works are not mortal. In the same way, the desires of body and soul declare that the one is mortal and the other everlasting. For the body desires nothing but temporal things: food, drink, clothing, rest, pleasure; and yet it can neither desire nor attain even these without the prompting and assistance of the soul. But the soul of itself desires many things which do not redound to the service or benefit of the body; and these are not fragile but eternal—for example, the renown of virtue and the memory of one’s name. For the soul desires even against the body the worship of God, which consists in abstinence from desires and lusts, endurance of pain, and contempt for death. Hence it is credible that the soul does not perish but is separated from the body; for the body can do nothing without the soul, whereas the mind can do many great things without the body.

Moreover, the things visible to the eyes and tangible to the hand cannot be eternal, because they can suffer external force. But those things which come neither under touch nor under sight, and whose power, principle, and effect alone appear, are eternal, because they suffer no force from without. Therefore, if the body is mortal because it is subject alike to sight and touch, the soul is consequently immortal because it can neither be touched nor seen.

[Note: Variant readings to cols. 771–772]

“**But those things which**”: Francius reads, “but indeed those things which.”

“**Because no**”: some printed editions read, “who no.”

“**Body**”: Lactantius, Book VII, chapter 21, concerning the impious: “They will again be clothed with flesh, so that they may pay the penalty in their bodies.” —Buneman.

“**But if the body is mortal for this reason**, etc.” If this argument held, it would follow that after the resurrection the body would be neither visible nor tangible. —Rivet.

“**They argue against**”: so very many manuscripts, including the most ancient and the excellent Bononiensis and Regio-Putianus. Seven recent manuscripts and twelve printed editions have *contra dixerunt*, “they spoke against”; three other manuscripts and five editions, *contradixerunt*, “they contradicted,” as one word.

“**Lucretius**”: in Book III of *On the Nature of Things*, among other things he writes:

> Must it not be confessed  
> That mind and soul consist of bodily nature?  
> Moreover, you see that the mind acts together with the body  
> And agrees with it as one within our body.

And in the same book he says:

> Moreover, we perceive that the mind is produced together with the body,  
> Grows with it as one, and likewise grows old with it.

“**With eyes and hand**”: eight recent printed editions add, “it is seen and touched.” These words are absent from the other printed editions and from all manuscripts, and are wholly superfluous. See the note on *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 1.

“**Thin, and eluding touch and sight**”: yet Lucretius says that the soul is also subject to touch. Claudianus Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, who flourished in the middle of the fourth century, left posterity three eloquent books *On the State of the Soul*, addressed to the patrician Sollius Sidonius, against a certain man who had asserted that the mind was corporeal because it could be limited by quantity and enclosed in a place. —Betuleius.

“**Made solid**”: four recent manuscripts and as many printed editions read *consolidatum*, “made firm.”

“**Plato**”: in Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I, and at the end of *Cato*, as above, chapter 8.

“**Unless it derived its origin from heaven**”: Lactantius commonly speaks in this manner, which has the flavor of the error of those who believed that the soul was cast down into bodies from the third heaven, where they place Paradise. But, lest we rashly accuse our author of error, we should suppose that he himself was not ignorant of this; and a little below he will confess that the soul was breathed into man from the mouth—that is, from the power—of the Creator. For, as Scripture says, “He breathed into him the breath of life.” Yet I do not deny that some understand this only of the vital soul. —Idem.

“**Because it comes under sight and touch**”: I read thus with the better twenty-four manuscripts. Six manuscripts and four printed editions read, “it comes under sight and under a blow”; three recent manuscripts read, “under sight and under touch.”

“**Like a little vessel**”: seven recent manuscripts read *vehiculum*, “vehicle.” “Little vessel”: Book II, chapter 12: “The body is like a little vessel.” *On the Workmanship*, chapter 1: “The body is, in a manner, an earthen vessel.” —Buneman.

“**Is called**”: some printed editions read, “may be called.”

“**Returns**”: nine common editions and all manuscripts, except two recent manuscripts and seven printed editions, read *recedit*, “returns” or “withdraws”; these have *redit*, “returns.”

“**What was from earth is resolved into earth**”: thus ten printed editions with all manuscripts, except two recent manuscripts, which omit *id* (“that”), and two Bononienses, the Taxianus, and three editions, which read *solvitur*, “is dissolved”; one Colbertinus has *revolvitur*, “is rolled back.”

“**The same Lucretius**”: the passage is Book II, line 998, written somewhat differently today in printed books and in the Aldine, Cratander, and Gryphian editions of Lactantius:

> Likewise, what was formerly from earth withdraws back  
> Into the earth; and what was sent from the regions of ether,  
> The shining temples of heaven in turn receive again.

“**Which he concludes**”: two recent Regii, one Colbertinus, the Brunensis, and six editions read *quo*, “whereby.”

“**And often, when embalmed, it lasts for a very long time**”: Tacitus thought that the Jews had learned from the Egyptians to preserve corpses rather than burn them in the Roman fashion. In this he erred, as those know who have read in the Scriptures of the burials of Sarah, Abraham, and others. If, however, Tacitus intended both *condere* (“to lay away”) and *condire* (“to preserve, embalm”) when he wrote this, his judgment would have been true in part, though not wholly. For the Hebrews do seem to have received from the Egyptians the custom of applying spices to corpses, as Genesis 50:2 sufficiently indicates. But the actual manner of preserving corpses practiced by the Egyptians was neither learned nor, I think, ever practiced by the Hebrews: their embalming was performed internally, after the body had been disembowelled and the brain drawn out through the nostrils; this the Greeks called *taricheuein* (ταριχεύειν). The Hebrews, by applying ointments and spices externally to the body and then wrapping it in bandages—a practice which Herodotus also attributes to the Egyptians—prepared their dead, as the examples of the Lord and Lazarus show. —Isaac Casaubon.

## CHAPTER XII. On the soul and body, their union, departure, and return

Let us now refute the arguments of those who argue against this view, which Lucretius set forth in his third book. “Since,” he says, “the soul is born with the body, it must necessarily perish with the body.” But the condition of the two is not alike. The body is solid and apprehensible, both by eyes and hand; the soul, however, is thin and eludes both touch and sight. The body is formed and made solid from earth; the soul has in itself nothing compacted, nothing of earthly weight, as Plato argued. For it could not possess such ingenuity, such power, such swiftness, unless it derived its origin from heaven. Therefore the body, since it is formed from a weighty and corruptible element and is tangible and visible, decays and dies; nor can it repel force, because it comes under sight and touch. But the soul, because by its subtlety it eludes every touch, cannot be dissolved by any blow.

Therefore, although they are born joined and associated with one another, and the one which is formed from earthly substance is like a little vessel for the other, which is derived from heavenly subtlety, when some force has separated them both—that separation being called death—then each returns to its own nature: what was from earth is resolved into earth; what was from heavenly spirit remains and is always strong, since the divine spirit is everlasting. Finally, the same Lucretius, forgetting what he asserted and what doctrine he defended, set down these verses:

> What formerly was from earth withdraws back  
> Into the earth; but what was sent from the regions of ether,  
> The shining temples of heaven receive again.

This was not for one to say who argued that souls perish with bodies. But he was overcome by truth, and the true reasoning slipped in unawares.

Moreover, the very inference which he draws—that the soul is dissolved, that is, perishes together with the body, because they are born together—is both false and capable of being turned to the contrary conclusion. For it does not perish together with the body. Rather, when the soul has departed, the body remains intact for many days and often, when embalmed, lasts for a very long time. For if, as they are born together, they also perished together, the soul would not suddenly depart and abandon the body; but both would simultaneously be scattered in a single instant of time, and the body itself, while breath still remained in it, would dissolve and perish as quickly as the soul withdraws. Indeed, when the body had been dissolved, the soul would vanish, like liquid poured out from a broken vessel.

[Note: Variant readings to cols. 773–774]

“**Like liquid from a broken vessel**”: Lucretius also said this in the following lines:

> Now therefore, since you see liquid flow out  
> When vessels are shattered on every side, and moisture disperse;  
> And since mist and smoke depart into the air,  
> Believe that the soul too is diffused and perishes  
> Much more swiftly, and that its first bodily particles dissolve more quickly,  
> Once it has withdrawn and departed from all the limbs.  
> For indeed the body, which stood as its vessel,  
> Cannot contain it when shattered by some cause  
> And made porous as blood is withdrawn from the veins—  
> How then can you believe that any air can contain it,  
> When it is more rarefied than our body, which cannot contain it?  
> —Betuleius.

“**Because it grows**, etc.” Lucretius, *On the Nature of Things* III, continues:

> Moreover, we perceive that the mind is produced together with the body,  
> Grows with it as one, and likewise grows old with it.  
> For just as children move about with weak and tender  
> Bodies, so a weak judgment of mind attends them.  
> Then, when age has grown strong in robust powers,  
> Counsel too becomes greater and the mind’s force increased.  
> Afterwards, when the body has been shaken by the mighty powers of age  
> And the limbs have fallen with blunted strength,  
> Talent falters, the tongue raves, and the mind;  
> All things fail and vanish at one time.  
> Therefore it is fitting that the whole nature of the soul too be dissolved,  
> Like smoke into the high airs of the sky.  
> —Betuleius.

“**Mind is not the same thing**”: *analysis* (ἀνάλυσις), by which a part is separated from the whole. For mind is a part of the soul, or a *power* (*dynamis*, δύναμις), which the Greeks call *nous* (νοῦς), from *noein* (νοεῖν, “to think”); others translate it “understanding.” He uses this same distinction below in *On the Workmanship of Man*, chapter 18. Moreover, what follows shows that he is not speaking merely of the vital soul. —Betuleius.

“**That by which we live; that by which we think**”: fourteen recent manuscripts and one old Roman edition read, “that by which we live, and that by which we think.”

“**The mind of sleepers**, etc.” That is, the exercise of reason rests.

“**And in the mad the mind is extinguished**”: it is false that the mind is extinguished, even if the exercise of reason is lost through a defect of the organs. —Rivet.

“**Either increases**, etc.” Hence, I suppose, Augustine was led to derive the name *mens* (“mind”) from *mēnē* (μήνη), “moon,” in *On Spirit and Soul*, chapter 11, because it waxes and wanes like the moon. Yet he was not unaware that some derived it from *memnēmai* (μέμνημαι), or *mnēmē* (μνήμη), while others derived it from *emineo* (“I stand out”). In *On the Trinity* XIV he says that an infant’s mind cannot fail to know itself, but cannot think. —Betuleius.

“**Receives the faculty**”: thus I restore the reading from all manuscripts except four recent ones, which, like the printed editions, have “received.”

“**And old age**”: see Cicero’s *Cato* on this subject.

“**Memory fails**”: two Regii manuscripts and thirteen editions read “failed”; one Colbertinus, “was lacking.”

“**He says**”: Lucretius, Book III, thus:

> To this is added that we see the body itself  
> Receive terrible diseases and harsh suffering;  
> So too the mind receives sharp cares, etc.

“**Maker**”: Lactantius here mocks this verse of Lucretius:

> For pain and disease are each the maker of death.

“**And forgetfulness**, etc.” He explains lethargy. For Lucretius has:

> And sometimes one is borne by heavy lethargy into a deep  
> And eternal sleep, with eyes and nodding head drooping.

*Lethargy* (λήθαργος), as Celsus teaches in Book III, chapter 20, is the opposite disorder to frenzy: namely, melancholy and an almost unconquerable necessity of sleeping. For it derives its name from *lēthē* (λήθη), “forgetfulness,” and, in my judgment, from *argos* (ἀργός), “inactive.” Some Latins call it *veternus*, on which Caelius Rhodiginus writes in his *Ancient Readings*.

For if the earthly and fragile body does not immediately dissolve and waste away into the earth from which it originated after the soul has departed, then the soul, which is not fragile, remains forever, because its origin is eternal. “Because,” he says, “sensation grows in children, is vigorous in youths, and diminishes in old men, it is evidently mortal.” First, mind and soul are not the same thing: one thing is that by which we live, another that by which we think. For the mind of sleepers, not the soul, is put to rest; and in the mad the mind is extinguished, while the soul remains. Thus they are called not lifeless but demented. Mind, therefore—that is, intelligence—either increases or diminishes according to age. The soul is always in its own state; and from the time when it receives the faculty of breathing, it remains the same to the end, until, released from the prison of the body, it flies back to its own dwelling.

Further, although the soul has been breathed in by God, because it is enclosed in the dark dwelling of earthly flesh, it does not possess the knowledge that belongs to divinity. It therefore hears and learns all things, and acquires wisdom by learning and hearing. Old age does not diminish wisdom but increases it, provided that youth has been passed in virtue. But if extreme old age has broken the limbs, it is not the fault of the soul if sight has failed, the tongue has become sluggish, or hearing has grown deaf; it is the body’s fault. “But memory fails.” What wonder, if the mind is oppressed by the collapse of its decaying dwelling and forgets things past, no otherwise than it will know things divine to come once it has escaped the prison in which it is confined?

“But,” he says, “it is subject to pain and grief, and is made mad by drunkenness; hence it appears fragile and mortal.” Virtue and wisdom are necessary for this very reason: that grief, contracted by suffering and seeing what is unworthy, may be repelled by courage; and that pleasure, not only in drinking but in all other matters, may be overcome by abstinence. For if it lacks virtue and is softened by devotion to pleasures, it will become subject to death, because virtue, as we have taught, is the maker of immortality, and pleasure the maker of death. Death, however, as I have shown, does not utterly destroy and annihilate, but subjects persons to everlasting torments. For the soul cannot perish altogether, since it took its origin from God’s spirit, which is eternal.

“The soul,” he says, “also feels bodily illness, suffers forgetfulness of itself, and, just as it becomes ill, is also often healed.” This, therefore, is why virtue must especially be employed: lest it be broken by any bodily pain, and lest not the soul but the mind suffer forgetfulness of itself. Because the mind is situated in a definite region of the body, when some force of disease injures that part, it is displaced and, as though shaken, leaves its seat, destined of course to return when treatment and health have restored its dwelling.

[Note: Variant readings to cols. 776–777]

“**Leaves its seat**”: the preposition is absent from ten manuscripts and six editions. In the Bononiensis, Junianus, and five common editions one reads, “migrates from its seat.”

“**Torn away and separated from the body**”: thus almost all manuscripts. But the printed editions, with six recent manuscripts, read, “torn away from the body and separated.” Lucretius has *avulsus*. “Just as,” he says, “the eye, torn away … from the body.” This is the poet’s sense, not his actual words. For he had written in Book III, line 562:

> Clearly, torn away from its roots, the eye itself cannot  
> See any object separately from the whole body.  
> —Buneman.

“**It is not a part of the vessel**”: this comparison is framed less correctly, although it accords with the doctrines of the Platonists, who imagined two bodies: one subtler, serving as the vehicle of the soul; the other bearing the senses and being tangible and visible.

“**As though it were eternal**”: one Claromontanus manuscript, in a second hand, and four editions read, “if it were,” with Betuleius’s approval.

“**So that, as the limbs gradually grow cold, the soul is breathed out**”: thus all manuscripts except one Claromontanus, which has “as the limbs grow cold again”; one recent Regius manuscript and five editions read, “and as the limbs gradually grow cold.” Here *ut* means “so that.” The old French translation has *tellement que*.

“**Like light in oil**”: he will establish nothing by this comparison, though we use it commonly even today. For when the oily liquid or material of flame fails, the light vanishes into the air. If, therefore, mind or soul is extinguished in the same way, it will follow that it likewise vanishes while it exhales. The refutation drawn from contrary causes and effects is therefore stronger. —Betuleius.

“**Consumed by the heat of fevers**”: fever is, according to Galen’s definition, a conversion of innate heat into a more violent heat.

“**Becomes brutish**”: three recent Regii manuscripts, three Colbertini, two Claromontani, and almost all printed editions read *putrescit*, “rots,” wrongly. The rest have the text’s reading. Above he called the body *brutum* in the same sense, that is, without sensation; thus here *brutescit* means “becomes devoid of sensation.” So also Book II, chapter 6.

“**Its sensation**”: *suum* (“its”) is absent from thirteen recent manuscripts and sixteen editions.

“**Like a serpent**”: for how serpents cast off old age, see Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 17; Aristotle, *History of Animals* VIII.17 and V.17. These verses are from Lucretius, Book III, line 611.

“**Would rejoice**”: Nicander also describes the joy of this renewal.

“**Indeed**”: the Caucian manuscript and seven editions read, “But indeed”; the Regio-Putianus, “And indeed.”

“**Of his dissolution**”: one recent Regius manuscript and twelve recent editions read “of his own dissolution.”

“**How can it be known**, etc.” He kills them with their own sword. For Epicurus says in Laertius: “Death is nothing to us. For what has been dissolved is deprived of sensation; and what lacks sensation is nothing to us.” They are therefore caught by their own dilemma. —Betuleius.

“**When he has been dissolved**”: these words are absent in seven manuscripts.

“**But before**”: thus seven old editions and all manuscripts except one recent manuscript, which, with twelve recent printed editions, adds *non* (“not”) after *enim* (“but”).

For, since the soul is joined with the body, if it lacks virtue, it becomes sick through the body’s contagion, and weakness is communicated from its association with fragility to the mind. But when it has been separated from the body, it will flourish by itself and will no longer be assailed by any condition of fragility, because it has cast off its fragile garment.

“Just as,” he says, “the eye, torn away and separated from the body, can see nothing, so too the separated soul can feel nothing, because it too is a part of the body.” This is false and dissimilar. For the soul is not a part of the body, but is in the body. Just as what is contained in a vessel is not part of the vessel, nor are things in a house said to be parts of the house, so the soul is not a part of the body, because the body is either the vessel of the soul or its receptacle.

That argument is still more empty by which he says that the soul seems mortal because it is not emitted from the body more swiftly, but gradually unfolds itself from all the limbs, beginning at the feet; as though, if it were eternal, it would burst forth in a single instant of time. This happens to those who die by the sword. But those whom disease kills exhale their breath more slowly, so that, as the limbs gradually grow cold, the soul is breathed out. Since it is contained in the material of the blood, like light in oil, when that material is consumed by the heat of fevers, the outermost parts of the limbs must grow cold, because the narrower veins extend to the extremities of the body, and the farthest and finest streams dry up when the spring-vein fails.

Yet because bodily sensation fails, we must not suppose that the soul’s sensation is extinguished and dies. For it is not the soul that becomes brutish when the body fails; rather, the body becomes brutish when the soul departs, because the soul carries all sensation away with it. But since the soul, when present, imparts its own sensation to the body and makes it live, it cannot be otherwise than that it itself both lives and feels by itself, because it is itself both sensation and life. For he says:

> If our mind were immortal,  
> It would not, when dying, complain so much that it was dissolved;  
> Rather, it would rejoice to go forth and leave its garment behind, like a serpent.

I have certainly never seen anyone complain, at death, of being dissolved. But perhaps he had seen some Epicurean still philosophizing while dying and discoursing upon his dissolution in his last breath.

How can it be known whether he feels himself being dissolved or set free from the body, when at the end the tongue becomes mute? For while he feels and can speak, he is not yet dissolved; when he has been dissolved, he can no longer either feel or speak. Thus he either cannot yet complain of dissolution, or can no longer complain. “But before he is dissolved, he understands that he will be dissolved.” What then? We see that most dying persons do not complain that they are being dissolved, as he says, but testify that they are going out, departing, and journeying; and they signify this either by gesture or, if they are still able, pronounce it with their voice. Hence it appears that dissolution does not occur, but separation; and this shows that the soul remains.

The remaining arguments of Epicurean doctrine are opposed to Pythagoras, who argues that souls migrate from bodies worn out by age and death and insinuate themselves into new and newly born bodies, and that the same souls are always reborn—now in a human being, now in cattle, now in a beast, now in a bird—and are immortal on this account, because they repeatedly exchange the dwellings of various and dissimilar bodies. Since this opinion is that of a madman, ridiculous and more fit for a mime than a school, it ought not even to have been seriously refuted; for whoever does so seems to fear that someone may believe it. We must therefore pass over those arguments advanced, falsely, against a falsehood. It is enough to have refuted those which were argued against truth.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the soul, and testimonies to its eternity

I have shown, I think, that the soul is not dissoluble. It remains to cite witnesses by whose authority the arguments may be strengthened. I shall not now call the Prophets as witnesses, whose teaching and prophecy rest wholly upon this: that they teach that human beings were created for the worship of God and for receiving immortality from him. Rather, let us call those whom these men who reject truth must necessarily believe.

Hermes, describing human nature in order to teach how it was made by God, said this:

> “And from both natures, the immortal and the mortal, he made one nature of man, making the same man in one respect immortal and in another mortal; and placing him midway between the divine and immortal nature and the mortal and changeable nature, so that, seeing all things, he might also marvel at all things.”

But perhaps someone will count him among the philosophers, although the Egyptians honor him as a god under the name Mercury, and will grant him no greater authority than Plato or Pythagoras. Let us therefore seek a greater testimony. A certain Polites consulted the Milesian Apollo whether the soul remains after death or is dissolved; Apollo answered in these verses:

> So long as the soul is held in bonds to the body,  
> Perceiving perishable affections, it yields to mortal pains.  
> But when, after the body has wasted away, it has found  
> The swiftest human release, it is wholly borne into the ether,  
> Ever ageless, and remains altogether without suffering for eternity.  
> For the first-begotten providence of God ordained this.

What of the Sibylline verses? Do they not declare this to be so when they announce that at some time God will judge the living and the dead? We shall give examples of them a little later. False, then, is the opinion of Democritus, Epicurus, and Dicaearchus concerning the dissolution of the soul. Certainly they would not have dared to argue, in the presence of some magician who knew how by fixed spells to summon souls from the underworld, make them present, present them to human eyes to be seen, make them speak and foretell the future, that souls perish. Or if they had dared, they would have been overcome by the thing itself and by the evidence before them. But because they did not discern the nature of the soul, which is so subtle that it escapes the eyes of the human mind, they said that it perishes.

[Note: Variant readings to cols. 779–780]

“**Aristoxenus**”: Cicero says that, because Aristoxenus was skilled in music, he did not depart in this opinion of the soul from his own art. See *Tusculan Disputations* I. Aristoxenus was a Tarentine, though he lived at Mantinea. He was an eminent philosopher and musician. He heard Lamprus, the philosopher of Erythrae; then Xenophilus the Pythagorean; and finally Aristotle. When Aristotle was dying, Aristoxenus reproached him for preferring Theophrastus to him as successor in the school of the Peripatetics. He wrote in every field of learning, but especially on music, and held that the soul was nothing other than harmony. Aristoxenus was both contemporary and fellow pupil of Dicaearchus, mentioned above. Cicero in the place cited.

“**From the tension of the strings in a lyre**”: one Regius manuscript, one Colbertinus, and the Brunensis read *extensione*, “from extension.”

“**By what he ought to live**”: thus emended from all manuscript codices except two recent Regii, which have, as do twelve printed editions, “who”; the Junianus and four editions read “because.”

“**Ought**”: from all manuscripts except five recent ones and three editions, which read “must.”

“**Decrees**”: there was a law in the Twelve Tables specifying which gods were to be worshipped among the Romans; and Romulus had forbidden the worship of any foreign gods except Faunus.

“**That gods had been made … either because they had discovered arts, or**, etc.” Apollo, Pallas, Ceres, Bacchus, Minerva, Vulcan, Hercules. —Francius. Apotheosis was discussed above, Book I.

“**They had handed down**”: the Cantabrigian manuscript and four old editions read *providerant*, “had foreseen,” wrongly. For Cicero, *On Old Age*, chapter 7, says: “We ought to hand down to posterity those things which we have received from our ancestors.”

“**They deserved**”: our author often uses *merere* in the sense “to receive” or “to obtain,” as observed at Book V, chapter 23 and elsewhere. Here the ordinary meritorious sense may have a place. —Buneman.

“**Which they pay**”: Heumann says that Latin speakers say *poenas pendere*, “to pay penalties”; our author has also dared to say *pendere supplicia*, “to pay punishments,” following the lead of the poet, *Aeneid* VI.740. I add that Lactantius cited this very passage of Virgil in Book VII, chapter 20, and again said in Book II, chapter 17: *supplicia pensuros*, “they will pay punishments.” Lactantius could all the more easily venture upon this because many others did the same—for example Pliny, whose words illustrate both *merere* and *supplicia pendere*. Book XXIX, chapter 4, section 14: “We have spoken of the honor which geese deserved … For the same reason dogs pay annual penalties … alive … fixed [to crosses].” —Buneman.

“**Plato**”: at the beginning of the *Timaeus*, he introduces an Egyptian priest conversing with Solon. Among other things, the priest says that Athens among the Greeks and Sais among the Egyptians were founded by the same Pallas—the former nine thousand years and the latter eight thousand years before his own time. But Egyptian measures of years are so uncertain that nothing definite can be determined from this calculation. On these myriads of years among the ancients, see Augustine, *City of God* XII.10.

“**Many thousands of ages … since**”: an ancient elegance: *ex quo*, elliptically, means “since the time when.” In the *Epitome*, chapter 24: “It is not more than 1,800 years since … the human race fell into error.” So Book III, chapter 16, where Seneca is quoted: “It is not yet a thousand years since the beginnings of Wisdom were set in motion.” Cyprian, *Exhortation to Martyrdom*, preface: “Six thousand years are fully completed since the devil attacks man.” —Buneman.

**Textual variant: “since this most beautiful adornment of the world came into being.”** I added this from all the manuscripts and a very large number of printed editions; it is absent from some printed copies. Three recent Royal manuscripts, three Colbert manuscripts, Tornesius, and one Clermont manuscript read: “since this most beautiful world came into being in ordered form.”

**Textual variant: “perhaps following the Chaldeans.”** Almost all the manuscripts read thus. [Col. 0781B] Thomasius, Johannes Caucius, and Isaeus rightly judge this to be the genuine reading. One Clermont manuscript and five old editions read, “just as perhaps the Chaldeans”; two recent manuscripts and thirteen common editions, “just as perhaps the Chaldeans did.” The latter reading is corrupt, since in affirming the proposition he would not have introduced persons about whose assertion he was uncertain. For he did not doubt that the Chaldeans held the same opinion as Plato; he doubted only whether those philosophers had followed the Chaldeans or some others. —GALLAEUS

who denied outright that there is any soul, even while it lives in the body? Rather, just as in lyres a harmonious sound and melody—what musicians call harmony—is produced by the tension of the strings, so in bodies the capacity for sensation arises from the joining of the internal organs and the vigor of the limbs. Nothing more insane could be said. Yet he had sound eyes, but a blind heart: he did not perceive that he himself lived and possessed the mind by which he had thought that very thing. But this happens to many philosophers: they suppose that nothing at all exists which does not appear to the eyes, although the vision of the mind ought [Col. 0779B] to be far clearer than that of the body for discerning those things whose force and rationale are sensed rather than seen.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Earlier and Later Times of the World

Since we have spoken of the immortality of the soul, it follows that we should explain to what extent, and when, it is granted to humanity, [Col. 0780A] so that in this matter too those who suppose that certain mortals were made gods by the decrees and judgments of mortals may perceive the errors of their perversity and folly—whether because they had discovered arts, taught the use of certain crops, disclosed things useful to human life, or killed savage beasts. How far such merits are removed from immortality we have shown in the earlier books and shall now show again, so that it may appear that justice alone begets eternal life for humanity, and God alone grants the reward of eternal life. For those who are said to have become immortal through their merits, since they possessed neither justice nor any true virtue, gained for themselves not immortality but death through sins and lusts; and they earned not a heavenly reward but infernal punishments, [Col. 0780B] which they suffer together with all who worshipped them. I shall show that the time of this judgment is approaching, so that a fitting recompense may be paid to the righteous and deserved punishment imposed upon the impious.

Plato and many other philosophers, since they did not know the origin of things or that earliest point in time at which the world was made, declared that many thousands of ages had passed since this most beautiful adornment of the world came into being, perhaps following the Chaldeans. For they, as Cicero [Col. 0781A] related

Let us condemn, I say, these men for folly, vanity, or impudence: they claim that their records embrace 470,000 years; let us judge that they lie and that they do not fear the judgment which all subsequent ages will pass upon them.” In the second book he explains what those records were in these words: “For when they say that the Babylonians spent 470,000 years testing and observing every child who was born, they deceive us.” You will find the tracks of Plato and Cicero in Macrobius, *On the Dream of Scipio*, book II, chapter 10. —BETULEIUS

> This opinion that the world would endure for six thousand years arose from an ancient tradition of the Hebrews, discussed in the volume of the Talmud entitled *Sanhedrin*. Moreover, these are St. Augustine’s words: “They supposed that the first resurrection would be bodily, being moved, among other things, especially by the number of a thousand years, as though it were fitting that a Sabbath rest of so long a duration should thus be granted to the saints—a holy repose after the labors of the six thousand years [Col. 0782B] since the creation of humanity and its banishment, because of the guilt of that great sin, from the happiness of Paradise into the miseries of this mortality. in the first book *On Divination*, deliriously claim that they possess records embracing 470,000 years. Since they did not think themselves liable to refutation on this point, they believed themselves free to lie. But we, whom the divine writings instruct in the knowledge of truth, have learned the beginning and the end of the world. We shall now discuss the latter at the end of this work, since we explained the former in the second book.

Let philosophers, then, who count thousands of ages from the beginning of the world, know that the six-thousandth year has not yet been completed. When that number has been fulfilled, a consummation must take place, and the condition of human affairs must be reformed for the better. The proof of this must first be set out, so that the reasoning may become clear. God completed the world and this admirable work of the nature of things, as is contained in the hidden mysteries [Col. 0781B] of sacred Scripture, within the space of six days; and he sanctified the seventh day, on which he rested from his works. This is the Sabbath day, [Col. 0782A] which in the Hebrew language took its name from the number; hence the number seven is lawful and complete. For there are seven days, by whose recurring revolution the cycles of years are completed; seven stars that do not set; and seven heavenly bodies called “wandering,” whose unequal courses and irregular movements are believed to produce variations in things and times.

Therefore, since all God’s works were perfected in six days, the world must remain in this condition through six ages—that is, six thousand years. For the great day of God is bounded by a cycle of a thousand years, as the prophet indicates when he says: “Before your eyes, Lord, a thousand years are as one day.” And just as God labored during those six days in constructing such great things, [Col. 0782B] so religion and truth must labor during these six thousand years, while wickedness prevails and rules. And again, since, once his works had been completed, he rested on the seventh day and blessed it, [Col. 0783A]

> **“And blessed it.”** The nature of Latin requires the verbs *benedicere* and *maledicere* (“to bless” and “to curse”) to govern the dative; nevertheless, they are joined with the accusative by some authors, including Apuleius in the *Asclepius*, Petronius in the *Satyricon*, and frequently in our Vulgate translation.
>

>
> **“Thus this day of ours.”** So the older printed editions read, with almost all the manuscripts. Here *ut* means “just as.” Three manuscripts and twelve recent printed editions read “and.”
>
> **“For a thousand years,” etc.** Up to this point he has taught, against those among the Gentiles who denied the immortality of the soul, that there will be another life and that it will be eternal. He will next teach where that reward is to be expected. In this matter, however, he becomes insufficiently cautious—as we have already often noted—and entangles himself in the errors of the Chiliasts, though not in a stubborn or partisan spirit. Rather, because, through the circumstances of his times, he had absorbed this disease almost as an inheritance and lacked the sound judgment of heavenly wisdom, he wandered somewhat from the truth, deceived, as some maintain, by Sibylline and other oracles. He will more readily deserve pardon for his error than our own Chiliasts, who, driven by a lust for domination and imagining that they had hastened the millennium through certain conjectures, dared to seize a sufficiently tyrannical millennial sovereignty. Such among the Dutch were Augustine Weher in 1530, Thomas Müntzer in Westphalia in 1525, and John of Leiden in 1534. They drew this doctrine from a misunderstanding of Revelation, chapter 20. Concerning it Justin Martyr writes as follows against Trypho the Jew:

> *Ἔστι καὶ παρ’ ἡμῖν ἀνήρ τις, ᾧ ὄνομα Ἰωάννης, εἷς τῶν Ἀποστόλων τοῦ Χριστοῦ, ὃς ἐν ἀποκαλύψει γενομένῃ αὐτῷ χίλια ἔτη ποιήσειν ἐν Ἱερουσαλὴμ τοὺς τῷ ἡμετέρῳ Χριστῷ πιστεύσαντας προεφήτευσε· καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα τὴν καθολικὴν, καὶ συνελόντι φάναι αἰωνίαν, ὁμοθυμαδὸν ἅμα πάντων ἀνάστασιν γενήσεσθαι, καὶ κρίσιν.*
>
> “There is also among us a certain man named John, one of Christ’s apostles, who, in a revelation made to him, prophesied that those who believed in our Christ would spend a thousand years in Jerusalem; and that afterward the universal—and, to speak briefly, eternal—resurrection of all together would take place, followed by judgment.”
>
> John was the teacher of Papias, bishop of Hierapolis, concerning whom Jerome writes as follows in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*: “He is said to have published a Jewish *δευτέρωσις* (*deuterōsis*, ‘repetition’ or ‘secondary teaching’) concerning a thousand years. He was followed by Irenaeus and Apollinaris, St. Martin, bishop of Tours, according to the testimony of Sulpicius Severus, and others who say that after the resurrection the Lord will reign in the flesh with the saints. [Col. 0784B] Some make Cerinthus the author of this doctrine, a man who would stop at nothing for his belly and was wholly devoted to lusts and pleasure. Tertullian too, in his book *On the Hope of the Faithful*, Victorinus of Poetovio, and Lactantius are led by this opinion. Nor are there lacking those who accuse Jerome himself of this error.”
>
> Eusebius also mentions a certain Chiliast named Nepos, book VII, chapter 23. Theodoret, in book III of his *Heretical Fables*, writes that Nepos agreed with the doctrines of the Church in all other respects, but erred concerning the divine promises because he believed that they would be fulfilled on earth and would involve food, drink, Jewish festivals, and a cycle of a thousand years to be spent in these things; and that Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, wrote against him. [Col. 0784C]

Epiphanius, book III, tome II, writes against the Chiliasts, though he does not attack them very bitterly, lest he appear to turn his pen against the apostles themselves, who likewise seem to have conceived a vain hope for the restoration of the kingdom of Israel: the sons of Zebedee, for example, and Cleopas in Luke XXIV, who says that he had hoped the Lord was the one who would redeem Israel. it is necessary that at the end of the six-thousandth year all wickedness be abolished from the earth, that justice reign for a thousand years, and that there be tranquillity and rest from the labors which the world has long endured. But I shall explain in due order how this will occur.

We have often said that lesser and small things are figures and foretokens of greater things: thus this day of ours, bounded by sunrise and sunset, bears the likeness of the great day which a cycle of a thousand years determines.

In the same way, the formation of the earthly human being foreshadowed the future formation of the heavenly people. For just as, after perfecting all things which God had fashioned for human use, he made the human being himself last, on the sixth day, and introduced him into this world as into a house already carefully furnished, [Col. 0783B] so now on the sixth great day the true human being is formed by the word of God: that is, the holy people are shaped unto justice by God’s teaching and commandments. And just as then a mortal and imperfect human being was formed from the earth to live in this world for a thousand years, so now a perfect [Col. 0784A] human being is formed out of this earthly age, so that, made alive by God, he may rule in this same world for a thousand years.

Anyone who has searched the divine writings will discover how the consummation is to come and what kind of end threatens human affairs. But the voices of secular prophets also accord with those of heaven: they announce the end and setting of all things after a short time, depicting the final old age of a world exhausted and falling into ruin. What the prophets and seers say will come to pass before that final conclusion arrives, I shall now append, gathered from all sources and brought together.

## CHAPTER XV. On the Devastation of the World and the Change of Empires

[Col. 0784B] It is contained in the hidden mysteries of the sacred writings that, compelled by a scarcity of grain, the leader of the Hebrews went down into Egypt with his entire household and family. When his descendants, having remained in Egypt for a long time, had increased into a great nation and were oppressed under the heavy and unbearable yoke of slavery, God struck Egypt

> **“Egypt … for foolish superstitions,” etc.** The superstition of the Egyptians has already been discussed above; we shall now pursue the remaining matters. The cat has been treated thus far; next come the *ἱέρακες* (*hierakes*, “hawks”). On them see also Plutarch in his book *On Isis and Osiris* and Diodorus Siculus, book I. The latter afterward adds the reason for their worship: the hawk purges Egypt of horned snakes, scorpions, and other harmful animals. Eusebius also adduces this explanation from Diodorus in book XI of the *Preparation for the Gospel*. Diodorus supplies another explanation as well, which he immediately appends. [Col. 0786C]
>
> Aelian does not agree with Strabo’s statement that the hawk was worshipped throughout Egypt. In the *History of Animals*, book X, chapter 24, he expressly says that it was worshipped by the people of Tentyra. He then adds that crocodiles, by contrast, were honored by the people of Coptos, and that hawks, as enemies of crocodiles, were often crucified by them. This is certainly exceedingly far removed from venerating them. Strabo too, in book XVII, relates that the people of Philae—inhabitants of the island of Philae, which borders Egypt and Ethiopia—worshipped in a temple a bird which they called a hawk. Cicero, in book III of *On the Nature of the Gods*, places the hawk among the animals that were accorded divine honors by barbarians.
>
> Concerning the worship of the ibis, besides Herodotus in *Euterpe* and Diodorus Siculus, book II, see also Juvenal, Satire 15:
>
> > That land reveres the ibis, glutted with serpents.
>
> Pliny, book X, chapter 28: “The Egyptians also invoke their ibises against the coming of serpents.” Before Pliny, Cicero wrote in *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I: “The Egyptians consecrated no animal except on account of some benefit which they received from it. Thus ibises destroy a very great number of serpents. Being tall birds, with stiff legs and a long, horny beak, they ward off disaster from Egypt by killing and consuming the winged snakes carried out of the Libyan desert by the south wind; as a result, the snakes harm no one by their bite while living or by their stench when dead.” [Col. 0786D]
>
> See Diodorus Siculus, book XI. Cicero also mentions the worship of the ibis in *Tusculan Disputations*, book V; so too Plutarch, *Table Talk*, book IV, question 5, and *On Isis and Osiris*; and Lucian in *The Council of the Gods*. Ammianus Marcellinus likewise writes in book XXII: “Among the birds of Egypt, whose variety cannot be comprehended by any number, the ibis is sacred, beloved, and harmless, because by bringing serpents’ eggs to its nests as food, it causes those deadly pests to become rare through their destruction.” Herodotus, however, says in *Euterpe* that among the Egyptians it is a capital offense for anyone, knowingly or unknowingly, to kill either an ibis or a hawk.
>
> Concerning the *oxyrhynchus*, which Strabo here says was worshipped by all Egyptians, he had earlier said that it was worshipped by the people of Oxyrhynchus. Clement of Alexandria reports the same in his *Exhortation to the Greeks*, as does Plutarch in *On Isis and Osiris*. For Hadrianus Junius, in the chapter on fish in his *Nomenclator*, the oxyrhynchus is a kind of ray called *βάτος ὀξύρυγχος* (*batos oxyrhynchos*, “sharp-snouted ray”). Others, such as Petrus Bellonius, *Observations*, book II, chapter 32, maintain that it is the pike, inferring this from the abundance of pike in the Nile. [Col. 0787B]
>
> Strabo says that the sheep was worshipped by the people of Sais and Thebes. Clement of Alexandria likewise attests this in the *Protrepticus*: *Σαΐται δὲ καὶ Θηβαῖοι πρόβατον*—“The people of Sais and Thebes [worship] a sheep.” Strabo next adds the wolf, which was venerated by the inhabitants of Lycopolis, as is also attested by Plutarch in *On Isis and Osiris* and Clement of Alexandria in the passage cited repeatedly above. Diodorus Siculus, book I, says that the reason for its worship, by which the Egyptians were moved to hold the wolf in honor, was its very close affinity with dogs.
>
> The worship of the cynocephalus is also mentioned by Tertullian in the *Apology*, chapter 6, and Augustine in *The City of God*, book XI, chapter 13. The cynocephalus is a member of the tailed species of apes; but, as Aristotle says, it is larger, stronger, and fiercer than the *cebus*, or long-tailed monkey, and its face more closely resembles that of a dog. In book II of the *History of Animals*, chapter 8, he says of the *cebi* that they are apes bearing tails. Hence Martial, book XIV, epigram 202:
>
> > A clever ape, skilled at eluding the spears cast at me—  
> > If I had a tail, I should be a long-tailed monkey.
>
> Juvenal discusses the worship of the long-tailed monkey in Satire 15. Prudentius alludes to it in book II *Against Symmachus*, when he says:
>
> > For Isis, Serapis, the Ape with its great tail,  
> > And the Crocodile are what Juno, Laverna, and Priapus are.
>
> [Col. 0787C] The worship of the ape is also mentioned by Lucian in *The Council of the Gods*. What Strabo says about the worship of the eagle can likewise be read in Diodorus Siculus, book I.
>
> Strabo afterward adds the lion, worshipped by the people of Leontopolis. Its worship is also mentioned by Plutarch, *Table Talk*, book IV, question 5. He says that the lion was consecrated to the Sun because, among quadrupeds with curved claws, the lioness alone gives birth to offspring that can see; because the lion sleeps only for a very brief period and its eyes shine while it sleeps; and because the springs and channels of Leontini are found newly filled with water when the Sun passes through Leo. [Col. 0787D]
>
> Strabo attributes the veneration of the she-goat and he-goat to the people of Mendes; Herodotus agrees in *Euterpe*. Clement of Alexandria also writes of the he-goat in the *Exhortation to the Greeks*: *Μενδήσιοι (σέβουσι) τὸν τράγον*—“The people of Mendes [worship] the he-goat.” Other Egyptians too seem to have regarded the he-goat as a divinity. See Diodorus, book II. Lucian also mentions the worship of the he-goat in *The Council of the Gods*. —From VOSSIUS

[Col. 0785A] with an incurable plague and freed his own people. He led them through the midst of the sea, with the waves divided and moved apart on either side, so that the people might walk on dry ground. When the king of Egypt attempted to pursue the fugitives, the sea returned to its former state, and he was overwhelmed with all his forces.

Although this deed, so famous and wonderful, displayed God’s power to people at the time, it was nevertheless a foreshadowing and figure of a greater event which the same God will accomplish at the final consummation of time. For he delivered his people from the grievous slavery of the world. But because at that time there was only one people of God, dwelling among one nation, Egypt alone was struck. Now, however, because God’s people, gathered from every language, dwell among all nations and are oppressed by those who rule them, all nations—that is, the whole world—must [Col. 0785B] be scourged with heavenly plagues, so that the righteous people who worship God may be delivered. And just as signs were then given to show the Egyptians their impending destruction, so at the end astonishing prodigies will occur throughout all the elements of the world, so that the approaching end may be understood by all nations.

[Col. 0786A] Therefore, as the end of this age draws near, the condition of human affairs must change and decline for the worse as wickedness gains strength. Thus even these present times of ours, in which injustice and malice have grown to the highest degree, may nevertheless be judged happy and almost golden by comparison with that incurable evil. Justice will become so rare, and impiety, avarice, greed, and lust will so abound, that any good persons who may then happen to exist will become prey to criminals and be harassed from every side by the unjust. The wicked alone will be wealthy; the good will be tossed about amid every insult and in destitution.

All law will be confounded, and laws will perish. No one will then possess anything unless it has either been wickedly acquired or defended by force. Audacity and violence will possess everything. There will be no faithfulness among human beings, no peace, no humanity, no modesty, no truth; [Col. 0786B] and thus no security, no government, and no rest whatever from evils. For the whole earth will be in turmoil; wars will rage everywhere; all nations will be under arms and attack one another. Neighboring cities will fight among themselves. Egypt, first of all, will pay the penalty for foolish superstitions and be covered with blood [Col. 0787A] as though by a river.

Then the sword will range over the world,

> **“The sword will range over the world.”** I restored this from seven old printed editions and all the manuscripts except the Caucianus, one Royal manuscript, two recent manuscripts, and the editions of Gymnicus and Fasius, which read “destruction will range over the world.”
>
> **“Laying all low like a harvest.”** Precisely as Catullus writes concerning the wedding of Peleus, poem 65:
>
> > [Col. 0788B] For just as a reaper, laying low the thick-set ears,  
> > Reaps the yellowing fields beneath the burning sun,  
> > So with hostile steel they lay low the bodies of the sons of Troy.
>
> —BUNNEMANN
>
> **“The Roman name,” etc.** This is Sibylline: *ἔσται Ῥώμη ῥύμη*—“Rome will become a mere street” [a Greek wordplay on *Rhōmē* and *rhymē*]. Lactantius writes below, chapter 25: “But when that head of the world has fallen,” etc. There was an old tradition of those times that, as soon as the Roman Empire had collapsed, Antichrist would come and the world would perish shortly afterward. Tertullian writes thus in his book *To Scapula* and in the *Apology*, chapter 32, as does Optatus of Milevis in *Against the Donatists*, book II. A tradition of this kind seems to have arisen from the prophecy of Daniel, chapter II, and the Apostle’s words in 2 Thessalonians, chapter II, according to Augustine, *The City of God*, book XX, chapter 19. St. Thomas, however, commenting on the said chapter II of Paul’s epistle, lecture I, understands it as a departure from the Roman Empire not only temporally but also spiritually—that is, from the Catholic faith of the Roman Church. [Col. 0788C] —From ISAEUS
>
> **“And imperial power will return to Asia.”** Betuleius understands the Muhammadan empire, so that from past events you may readily infer that Lactantius will prove a truthful prophet concerning the future as well. —THE SAME
>
> **“On so great a scale.”** Lactantius seems to have had in mind Virgil’s line:
>
> > So great was the toil of founding the Roman nation!
>
> **“Nothing wrought by human powers,” etc.** Twelve recent manuscripts and five editions read “nothing wrought *by* human powers,” etc. But the preposition “by” has been wrongly added, for it is absent from the corresponding clause as well.
>
> **“For the Egyptians,” etc.** His purpose is not to enumerate the monarchies signified either in Daniel or in Revelation, among which there is no Egyptian monarchy and no Greek monarchy other than the Macedonian. Moreover, although the people of God served the Egyptian and the Assyrian, they were protected by the Persian and the Macedonian. Otherwise Antiochus too would have had to be numbered here. The author is therefore doing only this: showing by example that Roman power can perish, because the most flourishing empires of the world have fallen. [Col. 0788D] —BETULEIUS
>
> **“The greater will be their fall … things higher than others have more weight for their ruin.”** Claudian:
>
> > They are raised on high  
> > That they may fall with a heavier crash.
>
> —FRANCIUS
>
> **“Seneca aptly,” etc.** What he cites here as Seneca’s is by Florus. Lactantius was misled by the praenomen *Annaeus*, which some codices attribute to Florus; some even acknowledge that name while omitting the name Florus, for *Annaeus* is the distinctive praenomen of the Senecas. Those who suppose that Seneca the philosopher was the author of this division into ages are also mistaken. From Johannes Isaacus Pontanus and Salmasius. Anyone who desires more on this matter should consult the most distinguished Vossius, *On the Latin Historians*.
>
> **“Divided … into ages.”** Eight recent manuscripts and the same number of editions read “according to ages.”

mowing down everything and laying all low like a harvest. The cause of this devastation and confusion will be that the Roman name, by which the world is now ruled—my mind shudders to say it, but I shall say it because it will happen—will be removed from the earth, and imperial power will return to Asia; the East will again rule, and the West will serve.

Nor should anyone find it surprising that a kingdom founded on so great a scale, enlarged for so long by so many and such great men, and finally strengthened by such vast resources, should nevertheless at some time collapse. For there is nothing wrought by human powers that cannot equally [Col. 0788A] be destroyed by human powers, because the works of mortals are mortal. So too other kingdoms before it, although they had flourished for a long time, nonetheless fell. For the Egyptians, Persians, Greeks, and Assyrians are recorded to have held dominion over the earth; after all these had been destroyed, the supreme power in affairs also came to the Romans. And the more they surpass all other kingdoms in magnitude, the greater will be their fall, because things higher than others have more weight for their ruin.

Seneca aptly divided the periods of the city of Rome into ages. He says that its first stage was infancy under King [Col. 0789A] Romulus, by whom Rome was both begotten and, as it were, reared; then came childhood under the remaining kings, by whom it was enlarged and formed through many disciplines and institutions. But under Tarquin’s reign, when it had already begun, as it were, to become adult, Rome did not endure slavery; throwing off the yoke of arrogant domination, it preferred obedience to laws over obedience to kings. When its adolescence had been terminated by the end of the Punic War, then at last, its strength having been established, it began to enter its youth. For, with Carthage destroyed,

But thirteen recent manuscripts and seventeen common editions read “Hydaspes.”
>
> He is cited under the name Hystaspes by St. Justin Martyr, *Apology* 2, in Greek *Ὑστάσπις*, Paris edition, 1636, page 66, letter c, and in the genitive *Ὑστάσπου*, page 82, c; and by St. Clement of Alexandria in book VI of the *Stromata*, Paris edition, 1641, page 636, in Greek *Ὑστάσπην*, when he says: “Take up the Greek books as well; recognize how the Sibyl signifies one God and the things that are to come. Take up Hystaspes also and read him, and you will find it written far more clearly and openly concerning the Son of God, and how many kings who hate him will draw up a battle line against Christ, and against those who bear his name, his faithful people, his endurance, and his advent.” [Col. 0789D]
>

> **“Who is now called Hydaspes.”** There are two rivers named Hydaspes: one in Media, concerning which Virgil writes in *Georgics* IV, verse 211, “Median Hydaspes.” Whether it is the same as the Choaspes, or as the river called the Median—since both arise in Media—is uncertain. The other is in India and is amply known from the historians of Alexander’s campaigns. —CELLARIUS
A wondrous dream. So MS 1, the ancient Bologna manuscript, and five recent editions, supported by 1 recent Regius manuscript and Marm., in which the reading is “wondrous of all things”; Goth. has “wondrous of all.” Moreover, Isaeus maintains that *a wondrous dream* is the true reading, as is evident, he says, from what follows: “of the prophesying boy.” Unless one prefers “wondrous of all things” from 1 Colb. and 2 Lips. Yet in almost all manuscripts and old printed codices one reads “most wondrous of all things.”

“Under interpretation.” Heuman thinks these words ought to be deleted.

“Wars.” See Matthew 24:6–7; Mark 13:12; Luke 21:9–11.

“Ten kings,” etc. They are figuratively represented by ten horns, by which some understand governors (*eparchs*, ἐπάρχας); Irenaeus and Jerome, together with Lactantius, understand ten kings. Others take a definite number as standing for an indefinite fullness; nevertheless, these concede that an enumeration of the greatest provinces fits tolerably well. They count Italy, Spain, Gaul, Germany, Illyricum, Greece, Africa, Egypt, Asia, and Syria, adding that neighboring regions should be included with each: Macedonia with Greece, Pannonia with Illyricum, etc. —Betuleius.

“They shall divide [the world] for its consumption.” This is the true reading, found in five editions and almost all manuscripts, among them 2 Bologna, 6 Regius, 3 Colbert, 3 Lipsius, and Junius. In Regio-Put. *for its consumption* is absent; in 3 Colbert and some printed editions one corruptly reads, “they shall suffer [it] to be brought to consummation”; in 3 recent Regius manuscripts, 1 Claromontanus in a second hand, and nine common editions, “they shall divide [it] for consummation.”

“These, having increased their armies beyond measure.” Thus restored from nine editions and all manuscripts except 1 recent Regius, which has “having assembled [their armies],” as do several common editions.

“Then suddenly,” etc. Most of what is said here can be applied to the dominion of the Turks. —Rivet, in manuscript notes.

“A most powerful enemy,” etc. Some understood Antiochus; others Nero; some understand Muhammad, others Antichrist. See the interpreters on Daniel chapter 12 and Revelation chapter 12; Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book 5, chapters 25–26; Theodoret, *On Daniel*, Oration 7. Lactantius interprets all these things, somewhat too confidently, in accordance with his own view.]

…which for so long had rivalled the empire, stretched out its hands over the whole world by land and sea; until, having subdued all kings and nations beneath its dominion, when the material of wars had already failed, it made evil use of its own strength, by which it exhausted itself. This was its first old age: torn by civil wars and oppressed by its internal disease, it again fell back into the rule of a single empire, as though it had returned to a second infancy. For, having lost the liberty which it had defended under Brutus as leader and founder, it so grew old as though it could not support itself unless it leaned upon the assistance of rulers. But if these things are so, what remains except that destruction should follow old age? And the prophets’ utterances announce that this will happen shortly, under the disguise of other names, lest anyone easily understand.

Yet the Sibyls [Col. 0790A] speak openly of Rome’s destruction, indeed by God’s judgment, because its name has been hateful and, as an enemy of justice, it slaughtered a people nurtured in truth. Hystaspes also, who was the most ancient king of the Medes, from whom likewise the river now called Hydaspes received its name, handed down for posterity the memory of a wondrous dream, interpreted by a prophesying boy; and he foretold long beforehand that the Roman empire and name would be removed from the world, before that Trojan people had been founded.

## Chapter XVI. On the devastation of the world and its portents

But lest anyone think this incredible, I shall show how it will happen. First, the empire will be multiplied, [Col. 0790B] and the supreme power in affairs, dispersed and divided among many, will be diminished. Then civil dissensions will be sown forever; there will be no respite from destructive wars, until ten kings arise together and divide the world, not in order to govern it but to consume it. These, having increased their armies beyond measure and abandoned cultivation of the fields—which is the beginning of overthrow and ruin—will destroy, crush, and devour everything.

Then suddenly a most powerful enemy [Col. 0791A] will arise against them from the furthest borders of the northern region. Having destroyed three from that number,

[Col. 0791A] [Notes of Various Writers on columns 791–792]

“Having destroyed three from that number.” I have added *from that number* (*eo*) from almost all manuscripts and fourteen common editions; it is absent in some printed editions. In 2 Colbert it reads “from them.”

“He will change the laws and establish his own.” By substituting, as Betuleius understands it, the Qur’an for the Gospel. With respect to the reading of the text, I follow the older and better manuscripts: 1 Bologna, Regio-Put., and 2 other Regius manuscripts of good quality. But eight recent manuscripts and twelve editions have “he will change … he will establish.”

“He will defile.” Perhaps he had in view the crimes and lust of soldiers, concerning which this word *contaminare*, “to defile,” is used. He employs it in book 1, chapter 20: “with unrestrained lusts defiling every sex …” —Buneman.

“With the name changed and the seat of empire transferred.” Supply from the preceding phrase: “with the name of the empire changed”; unless one prefers transposition, as in the *Epitome*, chapter 71: “he will change the name and seat of the empire.” —Buneman.

“Then indeed.” 1 Clarom.: “then”; Junius, 3 Colbert, Brun., and five editions: “so.”

“They will be overthrown.” Seven recent manuscripts and five old editions have “they will be dug up” in others. The same variation of readings occurs below, at the beginning of chapter 17.

“Frequent famine.” 1 Brun.: “frequent death.”

“For the air will be corrupted.” Lactantius does not say whence he obtained these particulars, although some have been drawn from the Scriptures concerning the signs of the coming judgment. Thomasius rightly observes that many things in this book were taken from Plato and Origen and are to be avoided by all. —Rivet, manuscript notes.

“Now by untimely.” In six manuscripts and eight editions the conjunction *and* precedes; it is absent from the others.

“No crop.” Four recent manuscripts and almost all printed copies have “nor”; 1 Colbert: “no crops.”

“Bitterness.” Lipsius 2: “bitternesses”; *Epitome*, chapter 71: “all water will partly be changed into blood, partly spoiled by bitterness.” —Buneman.

“And the hair of comets,” etc. A pleonasm. “For comets,” Pliny says, “the Greeks call them, our people call *crinitas* [hairy stars], bristling with bloody hair and shaggy on their crowns in the manner of locks.” —Betuleius.

“And darkness of the sun.” Revelation 6; Acts 2; Joel 2; Matthew 24.

“Unseen by the eyes.” That is, “not seen.” Today it belongs almost to neglected Latin. The ancients often used *invisus* in this sense. Cicero, *On the Response of the Haruspices*, chapter 27: “Rites hidden and not only unseen but even unheard of by men.” —Buneman.

“Stars.” Matthew 24; Mark 13.

“Sibyl.” In the Acrostic Poem, Book 8.

“Trumpet.” Latin translation from the ancient Bologna manuscript:

> A trumpet from heaven will give forth a voice with many wailings.

“Against men.” Three recent manuscripts and seven editions: “against.”

“Who did not acknowledge justice.” I have struck out “of God,” following the Isaean edition and nearly all manuscripts. It is found, however, in nine very recent manuscripts and in the common editions.

“Imminent.” Thus restored from all manuscripts and six editions. Ten common editions read “impend”; the Gymnich and Betuleius editions, “will be imminent.”

“Not even night.” Six recent manuscripts and sixteen editions: “nor.”

“They gnash their teeth.” Three recent manuscripts and twelve editions: “will gnash.” Both readings are good, for both *strideo* and *strido* are used.

“The world will be without adornment,” etc. Latin translation:

> The world will be without adornment, as human beings perish.

“There will be a world without adornment,” etc. This alludes to the meaning of *world* (*κόσμος*); for just as among the Greeks, so among the Latins, *mundus* derives its name from adornment. On this subject see Hermes, Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, and Pliny. This Sibylline verse occurs in Book 7.]

…he will be accepted into partnership by the rest and established as ruler over all. By unbearable domination he will afflict the world; he will mingle divine and human things; he will devise deeds unspeakable and abominable. He will turn new schemes over in his heart, so that he may establish an empire of his own, change the laws, and enact his own; he will defile, plunder, despoil, and kill. Finally, with the name changed and the seat of empire transferred, confusion and disturbance of the human race will follow. Then indeed there will be an accursed and abominable time, in which life will be pleasant to no one.

Cities will be utterly overthrown and perish, not only by sword and fire, but also by continual earthquakes, [Col. 0791B] floods of waters, frequent diseases, and recurrent famine. For the air will be corrupted, becoming foul and pestilential, now by untimely rains, now by useless drought; at one time by cold, at another by excessive heat. Nor will the earth yield fruit to humanity: no crop, no tree, no vine will bear anything. But when they have given the greatest hope in blossom, they will disappoint in fruit. Springs also, together with rivers, will dry up, so that not even drink will be available; and the waters will be changed into blood or bitterness. Because of these things, quadrupeds on earth, birds in the air, and fish in the sea will perish.

Marvelous portents in heaven will also overwhelm human minds with the greatest terror: the hair of comets, darkness of the sun, the moon’s color, and the fall of falling stars. Yet these will not occur in the customary way; rather, stars unknown and unseen by the eyes will suddenly [Col. 0791C] appear. The sun will be darkened continually [Col. 0792A], so that day can scarcely be distinguished from night. The moon will no longer be eclipsed for three hours, but, continually drenched in blood, will travel extraordinary courses, so that it will not be easy for humanity to recognize either the courses of the stars or the reckoning of times. For summer will come in winter, or winter in summer. Then the year will be shortened, the month diminished, and the day compressed into narrow limits. Very many stars will fall, so that the entire heaven will appear blind, without any lights. The highest mountains also will collapse and be levelled with the plains; the sea will become unnavigable.

And lest anything be lacking to the evils of humankind and earth, a trumpet will be heard from heaven. The Sibyl announces this in the following manner:

> A trumpet from heaven will send forth a voice of much lamentation.

[Col. 0792B] Therefore all will tremble and quake at that mournful sound. Then, by the wrath of God against people who did not acknowledge justice, sword, fire, famine, disease, and, above all, ever-imminent fear will rage. Then they will pray to God, and he will not hear them; death will be desired, and it will not come. Not even night will grant rest from fear, nor will sleep come upon their eyes; anxiety and wakefulness will wear down human souls. They will weep and groan and gnash their teeth; they will congratulate the dead and mourn the living. By these and many other evils, the earth will become a wilderness, and the world will be disfigured and deserted, as is said thus in the Sibylline poems:

> The world will be without adornment, as human beings perish.

[Col. 0792C] For the human race will thus be destroyed, so that scarcely a tenth [Col. 0793A] of humankind will remain; and where a thousand had gone forth, scarcely will there come forth

“They will come forth.” So the manuscripts and editions read. I discussed this form at book 4, chapter 13, before the end.

“Which shall have been.” Correctly, from manuscripts and editions. In some printed copies: “had been.”

“A great prophet.” He means Elijah the Tishbite, as is clear from the fragment on the Last Judgment placed below under Lactantius’ name, which you will read after the book. “Will proceed … from [his] mouth.” Lipsius 2 and 3: “out of [his] mouth,” as in book 6, chapter 18: “let no evil word proceed out of [your] mouth,” etc. But the author of the elegant letter to Celantia in the Appendix to Paulinus of Nola, p. 15 (which is Jerome, Letter 14), says: “Let no evil word ever proceed from your mouth.” Lactantius himself uses *proceed from the mouth*, *out of the mouth*, and *from [the] mouth*. —Buneman.

“It will burn him.” This verb is familiar to Lactantius. Caucasian and Junius manuscripts, nine recent manuscripts, and six editions have “will burn.” See below, chapter 21: “they will be scorched by fire and burned.”

“This man will fight against God’s prophet.” There is nothing certain in these and the following statements, which depend upon fabulous traditions. —Cellarius. “That king.” See Matthew 24:2; 2 Thessalonians.

“Image.” Heumann wishes to read “images,” that is, idols.

“At his word.” That is, while he is still speaking. I defended this expression at length at book 4, chapter 15: “And immediately at his word.” —Buneman.

“By which miracles.” Revelation 13:2; 2 Thessalonians 2.

“He will attempt to destroy God’s temple.” 1 Regius, 1 Colbert, and Brun.: “overthrow.”

“To lay waste the world.” Daniel 7; Revelation 2.

“Forty-two.” Tornes. manuscript: sixty; 1 Colbert: forty-three.

“They will prey upon [the good].” Three recent manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470: “they will fight.”

“Military discipline.” Reimm.: “discipline of wickedness,” as also, wrongly, Cellarius’ edition of the *Epitome*, chapter 71; there Taur. and others read: “Neither the dignity of empire nor military discipline will be preserved.” —Buneman.

“By one common banditry.” Junius, 1 Colbert, and ten editions: “by common and grievous banditry.”

“When these things shall be so.” Thus I read with Regio-Put. and many others, and five editions; three recent manuscripts: “When these things have thus been done.” Ten recent manuscripts and seven common editions: “When these things have been done.”

“Then the righteous.” Four manuscripts and an equal number of editions: “then.”

…a hundred. Of God’s worshippers also, two parts will perish, and the third which has been tested will remain.

## Chapter XVII. On the false prophet, the afflictions of the pious, and his destruction

But I shall explain more plainly how this will occur. When the end of times is already imminent, a great prophet will be sent by God, to turn people to the acknowledgment of God and receive power to perform miracles. Wherever people do not listen to him, he will shut heaven, withhold the rains, change water into blood, and torment them with thirst and famine. And whoever [Col. 0793B] attempts to injure him, fire will proceed from his mouth and burn that person. By these signs and powers he will convert many to the worship of God.

When his works have been completed, another king will arise from Syria, born of an evil spirit, an overthrower and destroyer of the human race, who will destroy the remnants of that earlier evil together with him. He will fight against God’s prophet; he will conquer and kill him and allow him to lie unburied. But after the third day he will come to life again; and, as all look on and marvel, he will be snatched up into heaven.

That king, moreover, will indeed be most foul, but a prophet of lies. He will establish and call himself God, and [Col. 0793C] command himself to be worshipped as the Son of God. Power will be given him [Col. 0794A] to perform signs and wonders; when these are seen, he will ensnare people so that they worship him. He will command fire to descend from heaven, the sun to stand still in its courses, and an image to speak; and these things will occur at his word. By these miracles even very many of the wise will be enticed by him. Then he will attempt to destroy God’s temple and persecute the righteous people; and there will be distress and crushing such as has never been from the beginning of the world.

Whoever believes and joins him will be marked by him like cattle; but those who refuse his mark will either flee to the mountains or, if seized, be killed by exquisite tortures. He will wrap righteous people in the books of the prophets and burn them thus. And he will be given forty-two months to lay waste the world. This will be the time in which justice [Col. 0794B] is cast down and innocence is hated; in which the wicked will prey upon the good as enemies. No law, order, or military discipline will be maintained; no one will reverence grey hair or acknowledge the duty of filial affection; none will spare sex or childhood. Everything will be thrown into confusion and mixed together contrary to what is right, contrary to the laws of nature. Thus the whole earth will be ravaged as though by one common act of banditry.

When these things are so, then the righteous and followers of truth will separate themselves from the wicked and flee into wildernesses. On hearing this, the impious king, inflamed with anger, will come with a great army and, bringing up all his forces, encircle the mountain on which the righteous dwell, so that he may seize them. [Col. 0794C] But when they see themselves shut in and besieged on every side, [Col. 0795A] they will cry out to God with a loud voice and implore heavenly aid; and God will hear them and send a king
