“And send a king.” Thus I restored it from all manuscripts and the old Roman edition; the other printed editions read “and will send forth a king.” The older fifteenth-century editions read “will send.”

“Hystaspes.” See above, the note at the end of chapter 15 of this book 7 of the *Divine Institutes*. On Hystaspes the philosopher see Stanley, *History of Chaldaean Philosophy*, book 2, chapter 2.

“They will stretch out.” MS 1 Claromontanus and seven editions: “they will stretch out.”

“That the Son of God will then be sent by the Father.” Thus I corrected from manuscripts and most editions.

“Hermes.” In the *Asclepius* translated by Apuleius, we read this:

> Then the earth will not stand firm, the sea will not be navigated, the heaven will not maintain the courses of the stars, nor will the course of the stars remain fixed in heaven. Every divine voice will fall silent in necessary silence; the fruits of the earth will decay, the soil will not be fruitful, and the very air will languish in a gloomy season. This and such an old age of the world will come: irreligion, disorder, and the irrationality of good human beings.

“Perfect discourse” (*logos teleios*, λόγος τέλειος). “Perfect discourse,” mentioned above in book 4, chapter 6.

“When these things have happened thus, O Asclepius,” etc. Latin translation:

> When these things have thus happened, O Asclepius, then the Lord and Father and God, the creator of the first and only God, looking upon what has happened and opposing his own will—that is, the good—to such disorder, recalling error and cleansing away wickedness, partly washing it away with much water, partly burning it with swift fire, and sometimes wiping it out by wars and plagues, brought and restored his world to its former state.

Apuleius translates the *Asclepius* somewhat differently. For “and God, creator of the first and only God,” he gives “God the first and greatest, governor of the one world.” Comparison shows that neither the Greek nor Apuleius’ reading is sound or complete. Trismegistus, *Asclepius*, chapter 9.

“Having washed [it] away” (*καταλύσας*). Davisius, chapter 1, corrects it to “having inundated [it]” (*κατακλύσας*). Very well; for Apuleius, chapter 1, has “washing it away by a flood”; hence *cataclysm* (*κατακλυσμός*), and in our Lactantius, book 2, chapter 10, *cataclysmus*. —Buneman.

“And restored” (*καὶ ἀποκατέστησεν*). Thus Regio-Put. and two other good Regius manuscripts, supported by the old Colbert manuscript, which has “he will restore” (*ἀποκαταστήσει*). In most manuscripts the Greek is absent. In the Paris edition of 1525 and Walch it is “he restored” (*ἀποκατέστησε*); in the other printed copies, *ἀπεκατήστησε*; in Latin, “he restored.”

“One [Sibyl] has thus handed it down.” These verses occur in Book 5, though there the reading varies remarkably.

“To his own people” (*ἐπ’ ἰδίων*). In the Regio-Put. manuscript it is “against him” (*ἐπὶ τοῦτον*).

“There will be judgment” (*κρίσις ἔσται*). Thus restored from the best manuscripts, Regio-Put. and another Regius manuscript of four hundred years, 2 Colbert, and 1 Brun.: “there will be judgment.” In four recent Regius manuscripts, 2 Colbert, and the editions it is “he will be judged” (*κρινεῖται*).

“From the immortal [one]” (*ἀφθίτου*). Thus I read with M. Masur, for metrical reasons, as in 6 Regius, the ancient Bologna manuscript, 2 Colbert, 1 Claromontanus, the old first Roman edition, and the Isaean and Florentine editions—not *ἀφθίτοις*, “by immortal men,” as in other editions, wrongly. Sibyl, Book 5: “thus will it be imperishable” (*οὕτως ἔσται ἄφθιτον*).

“And then.” In Book 3, Latin translation:

> And then God will send a king from the sun,
>
> Who will bring the whole earth to rest from evil war.

“From the sun” (*ἠελίου*). The Sibylline verses read *ἠελίοιο*; 2 Regius has *ἠλισί*; 1 Colbert, *ἤελοιο*.

“Our servitude.” Three recent Regius manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470 read “the yoke of our servitude.” Latin:

> He will remove from the neck  
> The unbearable yoke of our servitude,  
> And will dissolve godless ordinances and violent bonds.

“Therefore, when the world is oppressed,” etc. Observation: Lactantius, not sufficiently knowledgeable in the sacred Scriptures, as St. Jerome says, and not fully grasping the words of Revelation 16, sets forth in this chapter several things concerning Antichrist that are not sufficiently consistent. They are carefully examined by Thomas Malvenda, *On Antichrist*, book 10, chapters 11 and 13.]

…great from heaven, who will rescue and liberate them and destroy all the impious by sword and fire.

## Chapter XVIII. On the calamities at the end of the world, and their prediction by seers

That these things will happen has been sung both by all the prophets through God’s Spirit and by seers through the prompting of demons. For Hystaspes, whom I mentioned above, after describing the wickedness of this final age, says that the pious and faithful, separated from their persecutors, will stretch out their hands to heaven with weeping and groaning and implore the protection of Jupiter; that Jupiter will look upon the earth, hear human voices, and destroy the impious. [Col. 0795B] All these things are true except one: he said that Jupiter would do what God will do. But through the fraud of demons, this too has not been entirely suppressed: that the Son of God will then be sent by the Father, so that, after all evils have been destroyed, he may deliver the pious. Hermes, however, did not conceal this.

For in the book entitled *The Perfect Discourse* (*λόγος τέλειος*), after enumerating the evils of which we have spoken, he added the following:

> When these things have thus happened, O Asclepius, then the Lord and Father and God, the creator of the first and only God, looking upon what has happened, and by his own will opposing the good to such disorder, recalling error and [Col. 0795C] cleansing away wickedness, partly washing it away with much water, partly [Col. 0796A] consuming it with very swift fire, and sometimes suppressing it by wars and plagues, brought his world back to its ancient state and restored it.

The Sibyls likewise show that it will be no otherwise than that the Son of God will be sent by the highest Father, to deliver the righteous from the hands of the impious and destroy the unjust together with raging tyrants. One of them has thus handed it down:

> He will come, wishing to destroy the city of the blessed;
>
> And a king sent by God to his own people
>
> Will destroy all great kings and most excellent men;
>
> And thus there will be judgment upon mortals from the immortal [one].

Likewise another Sibyl:

> And then God will send a king from the sun,
>
> Who will bring the whole earth to rest from evil war.

And again another:

> …He will remove from the neck  
> [Col. 0796B] the unbearable yoke of our servitude,  
> And will dissolve godless ordinances and violent bonds.

## Chapter XIX. On Christ’s coming for judgment and the defeat of the false prophet

Therefore, when the world has been oppressed, and human resources have failed to destroy a tyranny of immense strength—for, having captured the world, it will press upon it with great armies of brigands—that vast calamity will require divine aid. God, therefore, moved by the double danger and the pitiable lamentation of the righteous, will immediately send a deliverer. Then, in the middle of a seasonless and dark night, the heaven will be opened [Col. 0796C] so that throughout the whole world [Col. 0797A] the light of the descending God may appear like lightning.

[Col. 0797A] [Notes of Various Writers on columns 797–798]

“Like lightning.” These words are from Matthew 24:27, where it is written: “As lightning comes out of the east and appears even to the west, so also will be the coming of the Son of Man.” The Sibyl speaks in these verses, which I have not yet found. But scarcely anything is said in these chapters which is not found in the Sibylline poems—not once only, but repeatedly—as anyone will observe who carefully compares the Sibyls with Lactantius.

“When he comes,” Latin translation:

> When he comes,  
> There will be fire and darkness in the middle of the black night.

“This is the night.” The conjunction *and* precedes in the Caucasian manuscripts and five editions.

“Which is celebrated by us.” I have added the preposition from fifteen editions and all manuscripts except 1 Colbert, in which it is absent, as also in four common editions.

“Is celebrated with a vigil.” Fifteen recent manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470: “with a vigil.” How celebrated the Paschal Vigil was among the ancients is attested by ecclesiastical writers who dealt with liturgical matters; if you wish, you may consult them.

“A sword will suddenly fall from heaven.” These things are plainly apocryphal.

“He will falsely claim to be Christ.” Thus I read with the older and better manuscripts. Eight recent manuscripts and the editions have “he himself”; Brun.: “that he is.” 2 Thessalonians 2.

“The true [one].” Supply: Christ.

“They will be brought bound.” Tornes. manuscripts: “all will be brought”; 1 Colbert: “all will be led.”

“And couches,” etc. *Pulvinaria* were properly couches spread in temples of the gods, upon an altar or in a higher place in the temple. Images of gods were placed on them; hence the name *lectisternia*. Livy: “A lectisternium was arranged and held for three days, while the decemvirs oversaw the sacred rites; couches stood in view for Jupiter and Juno.” They then used to feast. Flaccus, Ode 37, book 1.

“They will crush” (*τρίψουσιν*). The very ancient Colbert manuscript has this. Three recent Regius manuscripts, Bodleian, 1 Colbert, 1 Claromontanus, and seventeen printed editions have *τρίψουσι*. Regio-Put. and two other recent Regius manuscripts read *τρίψωσιν*, wrongly in the subjunctive; yet Regio-Put. has the Latin “they will crush” in the indicative, as do 5 Colbert, 1 Claromontanus, and Brun. Opsopoeus and Isaeus would prefer *πίψουσι* [uncertain reading]. Latin translation:

> Human beings will crush the idols and all wealth.

In the Sibylline poems, Book 8.

“The works,” etc. Book 3. Latin translation:

> The handmade works of the gods will be burned up.

“They will be utterly burned” (*κατακαυθήσονται*). Thus I corrected from Regio-Put. and two other good Regius manuscripts. Very well, also for metrical reasons. Four recent Regius manuscripts, 2 Colbert, 1 Claromontanus, and fifteen editions have *συνεκκαύσονται*.

“The dead will rise.” From Ezekiel 37:5 and following, and Revelation 20.

“When,” Book 3 of the Sibylline poems. Latin translation:

> But when that day has received its destined end, and to mortals  
> The judgment of the immortal God has come,  
> Great judgment and rule will come upon human beings.

But these words have been slightly altered in the text.

“Tartarean.” Latin:

> Then the earth, gaping open, will display Tartarean chaos;  
> And all will come before the tribunal of God the King.

“Heaven.” (See below, column 799, line 2.) Book 8. Latin:

> I shall roll up heaven and open the hidden places of the earth;  
> And then I shall raise the dead, undoing fate  
> And the sting of death; afterward I shall lead them to judgment,  
> Judging the lives of pious and impious human beings.]

The Sibyl spoke thus in the following verses:

> …When he comes,  
> There will be fire and darkness in the middle of the black night.

This is the night which we celebrate with a vigil because of the coming of our King and God. There is a twofold reason for this night: on it he received life again after he had suffered, and afterward he will receive the kingdom of the world. For he is the deliverer, judge, avenger, king, and God whom we call Christ. Before he descends, he will give this sign: a sword will suddenly fall from heaven, so that the righteous may know that the commander of the holy host is about to descend. He will descend with angels accompanying him into the middle of the earth; an unquenchable flame will go before him; and the power of the angels will deliver into the hands of the righteous [Col. 0797B] that multitude which has surrounded the mountain. It will be cut down from the third hour until evening, and blood will flow like a torrent. When all its forces have been destroyed, the impious one alone will escape, and his power will perish from him.

This is the one called Antichrist. But he will falsely claim to be Christ, fight against the true Christ, and, defeated, flee. He will repeatedly renew the war and repeatedly be defeated, until in a fourth battle, after all the impious have been vanquished, he himself is subdued and captured, and at last pays the penalty for his crimes. The other rulers and tyrants also, who crushed the world, will be brought bound [Col. 0798A] with him before the king. He will rebuke and convict them; he will reproach them with their deeds, condemn them, and hand them over to deserved torments.

Thus, when wickedness has been destroyed and impiety suppressed, the world will rest, having endured through so many ages a foul slavery, subject to error and crime. Gods made by human hands will no longer be worshipped. Rather, images cast down from their temples and sacred couches will be given to fire; together with their marvelous gifts, they will burn. The Sibyl, agreeing with the prophets, likewise foretold that this would happen:

> Human beings will crush the idols and all wealth.

The Erythraean Sibyl likewise promised the same:

> The handmade works of the gods will be utterly burned.

## Chapter XX. On Christ’s judgment, Christians, and the soul

After these things the underworld will be opened and the dead will rise. The same king and God will hold the great judgment concerning them; the highest Father will give him the greatest authority both to judge and to reign. Of this judgment and reign the Erythraean Sibyl speaks thus:

> But when that day has received its destined end, and to mortals  
> The judgment of the immortal God has come,  
> Great judgment and rule will come upon human beings.

Then another [Sibyl]:

> Then the earth, gaping open, will display Tartarean chaos;  
> And all will come before the tribunal of God the King.

[Col. 0799A] And elsewhere in the same [Sibyl]:

> Rolling up heaven…

“...I shall open the hidden places of the earth;

And then I shall raise the dead, having loosed the portion

And the sting of death; and afterward I shall lead them to judgment,

Judging the lives of godly and ungodly men.”

Yet not all will then be judged by God, but only those who have been occupied with God’s religion. For those who have not acknowledged God, since no sentence of acquittal can be pronounced concerning them, have already been judged and condemned, the sacred writings testifying that the ungodly will not rise for judgment. Therefore those who have known God will be judged, and their deeds—that is, their evil works weighed against their good ones—will be assessed; so that, if their good and righteous works are more numerous and weightier, they may be granted a blessed life; but if evils prevail, they may be condemned to punishment.

Here perhaps someone will say: If the soul is immortal [Col. 0799B], how is it represented as capable of suffering and feeling punishment? For if it is punished according to its merits, it will certainly feel pain, and thus also death. If it is not liable to death, neither is it liable to pain; therefore it is not capable of suffering.

The Stoics meet this question, or argument, as follows: human souls indeed endure and are not dissolved into nothing through the intervention of death; but the souls of those who have been righteous return, pure, incapable of suffering, and blessed, to their heavenly abode, whence they derive their origin; or are borne away to certain fortunate fields, where they enjoy wonderful pleasures. But the souls of the ungodly, because they have defiled themselves with evil desires, possess a kind of nature intermediate [Col. 0800A] between immortality and mortality, and retain some weakness from the contagion of the flesh. Addicted to its desires and lusts, they carry with them a certain indelible stain and earthly blemish; and when this has thoroughly adhered through long duration of time, souls are reduced to such a condition that, if not wholly extinguishable, since they are from God, they nevertheless become capable of torment through the stain of the body, which, branded by sins, imparts the sensation of pain. The poet expressed this view thus:

> For even when, with life’s last light, they have departed,  
> Still every evil does not leave the wretched, nor do all  
> Bodily plagues wholly quit them; and it must needs be  
> That many things, long congealed, grow deep by wondrous means.  
> Therefore they are exercised by punishments and pay  
> The penalties of their former evils.

These things are very nearly true. For the soul, when it has parted from the body, is—as the same poet says—

[Col. 0800B]

> Equal to the light winds, and very like a flying dream,

because it is a spirit, incomprehensible by reason of its very subtlety to us, who are bodily beings, yet comprehensible to God, to whom the power to do all things is subject.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the torments and punishments of souls

First, then, we say that God’s power is so great that it embraces even incorporeal things and affects them in whatever manner he wills. For angels too fear God, because they can be chastised by him in some ineffable way; and demons dread him, because they are tortured [Col. 0801A] and punished by him. What wonder, then, if souls, though immortal, are nevertheless capable of suffering at God’s hands?

[Col. 0801A] [Note: [Col. 0801B] Various Notes on columns 801–802]

**“Capable of suffering at God’s hands.”** This word is used both actively and passively. See above three times.

[Col. 0801C] **“To whom belongs power.”** Three recent manuscripts read “whose power.” Both readings are good.

**“Sacred writings.”** See John 5; 1 Corinthians 15.

**“They shall render.”** In two recent Royal manuscripts and fifteen printed editions, *laturi* (“shall bear”) stands in place of *daturi* (“shall render”). Both readings are good.

**“For because they contracted sins in their bodies, they will again be clothed with flesh.”** Lactantius thought, mistakenly, along with Justin, Irenaeus, and a few of the ancient Fathers, that every judgment of souls is deferred until after the resurrection of bodies. Therefore, he says, although God by his power can act with fire upon souls even stripped of bodies, he nevertheless more fittingly wills them to suffer with the body, because they sinned in the body, and therefore they will again be clothed with flesh, etc. From Isaeus.

**“With everlasting fire.”** The ancients gave various names to this fire. Arnobius, book II: “fierce fire”; the same author, book IV: “the inextinguishable flames of Gehenna”; Cyprian, *To Demetrian*: “living flames”; Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 48: “unending fire”; Augustine, Sermon 17 on Paul’s conversion: “eternal flames.” Others spoke differently. Elmenhorst.

[Col. 0801D] **“Divine.”** That is, fire.

**“And clear.”** *Liquidus* fire, from *liquet*, is bright fire, not clouded by any smoke. See Turnebus.

**“Will restore.”** Francius says “will create anew”; “with fibres reborn,” says Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.

**“What the poets transferred to Tityus’s vulture,” etc.** Homer, *Odyssey* II, and Virgil after him, *Aeneid* VI:

> And Tityus, offspring of almighty Earth, was there to see, etc.

Tibullus, I, Elegy 3; Ovid, *Letters from Pontus* I, Elegy 2. Other writers also remembered this who described punishments in the underworld: Lucretius, Silius, Lucian, Claudian, and Boccaccio. Betuleius.

**“Of bodies growing vigorous again.”** Thus restored from the editions of Betuleius and Cellarius and nearly all manuscripts. In two recent Royal manuscripts, Junius, Penance, and six common editions stands *reviviscentium* (“reviving”); in one Royal manuscript and ten printed copies, *virescentium* (“growing vigorous”).

**“But when he has judged even the righteous, he will also test them in fire.”** In three Royal manuscripts, *et* stands in place of *etiam* (“also”). Ten recent manuscripts and thirteen editions lack the preposition *in*. By “the righteous” Lactantius means Christians.

[Col. 0802B] **“Then those whose sins...”** This error of Lactantius, concerning the cleansing by fire of the bodies of the righteous after the universal judgment, has been rejected by the schools of theologians. See Sixtus, book V of the *Bibliotheca*, annotations 170–171. On this fire see St Thomas, *Sentences*, IV, distinction 47, article 4, reply to 3; and there St Bonaventure, question 4, at the end; and part 7 of the *Breviloquium*, chapter 4.

**“Either by weight or by number.”** See above, col. 799, the note “Good and righteous,” etc., toward the end of the verse.

**“The maturity of virtue has steeped them.”** Reimmann reads *intoxerit* (“has poisoned”), wrongly; *incoxerit* is correct: “has thoroughly imbued.” He alludes to the passage from Persius cited by Lactantius, book II, chapter 4:

> ...a breast steeped in noble honour. Bunemann.

**“They will not feel that fire.”** That fire is called “wise” by St Paulinus of Nola; of it he says in Letter 28, formerly 9, to Severus: “If we should deserve by such works to become fellow citizens of the saints, our work will not burn; and that wise fire, when we pass through its testing, will not surround us to punish us with a severe burning, but, receiving us as approved, will touch us with a gentle lick, so that we may say: ‘We passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment.’”

**“They have something of God in themselves, which has power...”** Thus restored from eleven editions and all manuscripts except the Ultramontane manuscript and the Gymnic edition, which have “they have something in themselves which”; four common editions wrongly read “they have in themselves something from that which has power.” The fifteenth-century editions agree with our reading.

[Col. 0802D] **“And repels.”** Five recent manuscripts and as many editions read “rejects.”

**“Power.”** Recent manuscripts read “authority,” as do printed editions.

**“Yet let no one suppose that souls are judged immediately after death.”** Lactantius held that the punishments and rewards of souls are postponed to the day of universal judgment after the resurrection of bodies, and that meanwhile they are kept in one common confinement, as we said above in this same chapter. Certain ancient Fathers held the same opinion: the spurious Clement of Rome, *Recognitions* I, at the end; Justin Martyr, *Dialogue with Trypho* and question 76; Irenaeus, book V *Against Heresies*; Tertullian, IV *Against Marcion* and *On the Soul*, penultimate chapter; Origen, Homily 7 on Leviticus and books II and IV of *First Principles*; Victorinus, on Revelation, at “I saw beneath the altar.” The Church, however, thinks otherwise and holds with certainty that souls, immediately upon departing their bodies, undergo a private judgment, either for punishment or for blessed life in heaven. This is confirmed by the example of the beggar Lazarus in Abraham’s bosom and of the rich man in hell, etc., Luke 16. Partly from Isaeus.—See Sixtus, book VI of the *Bibliotheca*, [Col. 0803B] annotation 345; Bellarmine, book I *On the Blessedness of the Saints*, chapters 1–6; Coccius, [Col. 0803C] volume I of the *Catholic Treasury*, book V, article 2.]

For since souls have in themselves nothing solid or tangible, they can suffer no force from solid and bodily things; but because they live among spirits alone, they can be handled by God alone, whose power and substance are spiritual. Yet the sacred Scriptures teach us how the ungodly are to render punishment. For because they contracted sins in their bodies, they will again be clothed with flesh, in order that they may pay the expiation in their bodies. Yet that flesh will not be like this earthly flesh which God put upon humanity, but indissoluble and enduring forever, so that it may suffice for torments and everlasting fire. The nature of that fire differs from that of ours, which we use for the necessities of life and which is extinguished unless nourished by the fuel of some material.

[Col. 0801B] But that divine fire always lives and flourishes through itself, without any fuel, and has no smoke mingled with it; rather, it is pure and clear, fluid in the manner of water. For it is not driven upward by any force, as ours is, which the burden of the earthly body by which it is held, together with its mingled smoke, compels to leap upward and to fly with restless movement toward the heavenly nature.

Therefore this same divine fire, by one and the same force and power, will both burn the ungodly and restore them; and whatever it consumes from their bodies, it will restore in equal measure, supplying itself with everlasting nourishment. This the poets transferred to Tityus’s vulture: thus, without any loss to bodies growing vigorous again, it will burn only so much as to inflict the sensation of pain. But when he has judged even the righteous, he will also test them in fire. Then those whose sins prevail either by weight or by number will be touched and burned by the fire; but those whom full righteousness and mature virtue have steeped will not feel that fire. For they have something of God in themselves which [Col. 0802B] repels and rejects the force of the flame. So great is the power of innocence that that harmless fire recoils from it: a fire which has received from God this power, to burn the ungodly and obey the righteous.

Yet let no one suppose that souls are judged immediately after death. For all are held in one common [Col. 0803A] confinement,

[Col. 0803A] [Note: [Col. 0803C] Various Notes on columns 803–804]

**“For all are held in one common confinement.”** This is plainly *agraphon* and *antigraphon* [an unwritten and contrary tradition].

**“Into the same darkness.”** See above, cols. 799, 801.

**“Although they are much older than historians and orators.”** This controversy cannot easily be decided, since among secular poets one cannot go earlier than Homer. For Vossius, *On Poetry*, teaches that all those said to have existed before the Trojan War were invented by the poets themselves. Eusebius in his *Chronicle* reports, according to some, that Homer flourished around the time of Samuel. The origin of history is referred to Cadmus, about the period of the Hebrew Judges; if there is any truth in this reckoning, the crown of antiquity must be awarded to history. But since nearly all these ancient matters not contained in sacred writings are uncertain, let it suffice that Moses long before excelled in both, whether one considers history or poetry. From Sparke.—Yet according to the Arundelian Marbles, Epoch XXVIII, Homer lived at the end of the tenth century before the common era, three hundred years after the destruction of Troy; Samuel died before the middle of the eleventh century before the common era, namely about 1061 before Christ’s birth.

**“Had reached them through an obscure report.”** Thus restored from the ancient and best Regius-Puteanus manuscript and the editions of Betuleius, Sparke, and Walch. The most learned Francius also thought it should be read thus. Similarly, I read in Cicero, book III, letter 4 to Curio, “through an obscure report.” Most manuscripts and printed copies have *obscurorum ore* (“from the mouth of obscure persons”), where one sees that the same letters appear as in *obscuro rumore*. One Royal and one Colbert manuscript have *obscuro more* (“in an obscure manner”); the Isaeus edition, *obscuro ore* (“from an obscure mouth”); one Royal manuscript, *oraculorum more* (“in the manner of oracles”); the Tornesian manuscript and four editions, *obscurior pervenerat* (“had reached [them] more obscurely”).

**“As Maro.”** Virgil, namely *Aeneid* VI, verse 266.

**“That [they agree] in part with the prophets.”** Five recent manuscripts read “wherein.”

**“For when the prophets...”** In John 5, Christ himself says [Col. 0804B] that he received from the Father the office of judging. Psalm [Col. 0804C] 71: “O God, give your judgment to the king.” There are many passages throughout the prophets, both on the judgment of the great day and on the universal judgment by which sinners are perpetually condemned through the divine word. Betuleius.

**“Ruler of heaven.”** One ancient Bolognese manuscript and eleven other Royal manuscripts add “Lord”; the Caucasian manuscript and four common editions add “God.”

**“But him.”** Thus restored from one Royal manuscript, one ancient Bolognese manuscript, one Leipzig manuscript, and one Palatine manuscript, supported by another Royal manuscript reading “but also him.” “Him” is absent from nine recent manuscripts. Eight others and thirteen editions have “God.”

**“Minos.”** On the judges of the underworld see Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I, from Plato’s *Apology*. He, like Aeacus and Rhadamanthus, was a son of Jupiter, and so righteous and upright that he was judged worthy to preside over the underworld. “Minos sits as judge of Orcus,” says Propertius, book III, Elegy 19. Horace says of Aeacus, book II, Ode 13:

> How nearly we saw the realms of dark Proserpina,  
> And Aeacus sitting in judgment.

[Col. 0804D] On Rhadamanthus, see Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, verse 566.

**“Scattered.”** Heumann and Bunemann read *dissipatam*, and the latter presents the following note on this variant.—Thus not only in book VII, chapter 7, he said “truth divided ... scattered,” but also “dispersed.” Book II, chapter 10: “Truth, dispersed among the people through various reports, is usually corrupted.” Bunemann.

**“By Maro.”** Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, verse 768.

**“Restored to life.”** One Leipzig, one Colbert, and one Claromontane manuscript read “divine,” but wrongly.

**“Except for the water of forgetfulness,” etc.** Hence Maro’s words:

> They drink the carefree waters and long forgetfulness.

This is a circumlocution for the river Lethe. *Lēthē* means “forgetfulness”; hence the river Lethe. On this river read Macrobius, book I, *Dream of Scipio*, chapter 22.]

until the time comes when the supreme judge shall examine their merits. Then those whose righteousness has been approved will receive the reward of immortality; but those whose sins and crimes have been discovered will not rise again, but will be shut away with the ungodly in the same darkness, assigned to fixed punishments.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the error of the poets and the soul’s return from the underworld

Some think these are fictions of the poets, not knowing whence the poets received them; and they deny that these things can occur. It is no wonder that they seem so to them. For the poets relate matters otherwise than they are. Though they are much older than historians, orators, and the other [Col. 0803B] kinds of writers, nevertheless, because they did not know the mystery of the divine sacrament, and because a report of the future resurrection had reached them obscurely, they handed down what they had heard rashly and superficially in the form of an invented tale. Yet these same poets testified that they were following not a certain author but an opinion; as Maro says:

> May it be permitted me to speak what I have heard.

Although, therefore, they corrupted the mysteries of truth in part, the matter itself is found all the truer because they agree in part [Col. 0804A] with the prophets; and this is sufficient for us as proof of the matter. Yet some rationale underlies their error.

For when the prophets proclaimed in continual sermons that the Son of God would judge the dead, and this proclamation was not concealed, because they thought that the ruler of heaven was none other than Jupiter, they handed down that Jupiter’s son would judge in the underworld. Yet they named not Apollo, Liber, or Mercury, who are thought heavenly, but one who had been both mortal and just: Minos, Aeacus, or Rhadamanthus.

Thus the poets corrupted by poetic license what they had received; or else opinion, dispersed through diverse mouths and varied reports, altered the truth. For their song that, after a thousand years spent in the underworld, souls are restored again to life—as Maro says:

[Col. 0804B]

> All these, when they have rolled the wheel for a thousand years,  
> God calls in a great throng to the river Lethe,  
> So that, forgetful, they may revisit the vault above  
> And again begin to desire return into bodies—

was mistaken in this respect: the dead will rise, not a thousand years after their own deaths, but so that, restored again to life, they may reign with God for a thousand years. For God will come in order, after purging this world of every stain, to receive the souls of the righteous restored to life, in renewed bodies, unto eternal blessedness. Therefore all the rest is true except the water of forgetfulness, which they invented [Col. 0805A] lest someone should object:

[Col. 0805A] [Note: [Col. 0805C] Various Notes on columns 805–806]

**“Lest someone should object.”** Twenty-two manuscripts and nine editions read “to them.”

**“So many ages have already passed: who ever, even one person, [returned] from the underworld?”** As Rigaltius long ago observed, this derives from Minucius, chapter 11: “So great an age has passed; innumerable centuries have flowed by. What single person, anyone at all, has returned from the underworld, even by the lot of Protesilaus, with leave to travel only for a few hours, so that we might believe by an example?” Rigaltius also says that he read the word *ullus* (“anyone”) omitted in a copy of Lactantius, I think the Paris Royal manuscript. Bunemann.

**“Furthermore.”** Thus the Bolognese manuscript and early editions. But twenty-seven manuscripts and seven editions read “to the same [point].”

**“Man-made.”** Thus restored from seven old printed editions and all manuscripts except the Marmoutier manuscript, which has *manufabricatorum*; the Caucasian manuscript, one recent Royal manuscript, and eight editions read *fabricatorum*.—“Gods made by hand.” Paris, Juntine, Cratander, Gymnic, Isaeus: “gods made by hand.” The other editors ought not to have altered this. Book VII, chapter 19: “The gods made by hand will no longer be worshipped.” Bunemann.

**“Are held so cheaply, are so easily...”** Three Royal manuscripts read “and so easily”; one ancient Bolognese manuscript, “and so easily”; five editions, “by such ease.”

**“Whose death has been unsealed.”** Book IV, chapter 26: “What is more worthy of wonder than to have unsealed a life that had run its course, added ages after completing the human span, and disclosed the secrets of death?” Bunemann.

**“Virgil.”** *Aeneid* VI, verse 719. He gives Aeneas’s words to his father.

**“To return to sluggish bodies.”** The Tornesian manuscript reads “to be sent back.”

**“Therefore.”** Thus restored from twelve old editions and all manuscripts except one Colbert manuscript, which reads “likewise.” Six common editions read “thus.”

**“Whence Plato also.”** Plato, *Meno* and *Apology of Socrates*; Cicero cites this passage in *Tusculan Disputations* I.

**“They grasp so quickly.”** Four manuscripts and eight editions read “take.” — Thus Cicero, *Cato Major*, chapter 8, on this argument of Plato: “And it is a great proof that men know many things before they are born, because even when boys learn difficult arts, they seize innumerable things so swiftly that they appear not to receive them for the first time then, but to recollect and remember them.” Bunemann.

[Col. 0806C] **“So that they do not.”** Heumann reads “that they do not.”

**“And recollect.”** These are Plato’s words in the *Phaedo*; hence Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I, chapter 24: “Plato wishes memory to be a recollection of a former life.” — “But to recognize again and recollect.” Arnobius refutes this at length, book II, pp. 58–64. Compare Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I.24: “First, they possess memory, and this is of infinitely many innumerable things; Plato indeed wishes it to be recollection of a former life ... from which Socrates wishes to infer that learning is nothing other than recollecting ... that they do not then learn these things but recognize them through recollection.” Bunemann.

[Col. 0806D] **“But they will rise.”** Perhaps Lactantius could have said this in a sound and proper sense, I think: that God will again raise them up as fit to animate bodies, just as above he said *recreabit*, “he will make alive anew.” This is spoken metaphorically. They will “rise,” namely when, after their bodies have long been dead, they are again clothed with them by God. For Lactantius did not believe the soul mortal; he strove with all the powers of his intellect to prove its immortality.

**“Placed and enjoying.”** Thus the older and better manuscripts and the older Roman and Gymnic editions. Seven manuscripts and fourteen printed editions have the feminine *collocatae*.

**“Anastasis.”** Here and below, at the end of this chapter, he uses the Greek word with a Latin ending for “resurrection,” as he does *asystati* for “unstable,” above in book III of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 6, after the middle; *Sophia*, book III, chapter 16; and *cataclysmus* for “flood,” book VI, chapter 11.

**“Pythagoras.”** He has been discussed above, book III, chapter 18.]

Why, then, do they not remember that they once lived, or who they were, or what they did? Nevertheless, it is not thought plausible, and the whole matter is rejected as if it were freely and fabulously invented.

But when we affirm and teach the resurrection, and say that souls will return to another life not forgetful of themselves but in the same consciousness and form, this objection is raised: So many ages have now passed—who has ever risen from the underworld, even a single person, so that we may believe from his example that this can happen? But resurrection cannot occur while injustice still rules. For in this age people are killed by violence, the sword, plots, and poison; they are afflicted by wrongs, poverty, prisons, tortures, and proscriptions. Furthermore, righteousness is hated; all who wish to follow God are not merely [Col. 0805B] objects of hatred, but are harassed by every insult, tortured by many kinds of punishments, and compelled to the impious worship of gods made by hand, not by reason or truth but by the wicked mutilation of their bodies.

Must people then rise again to these same conditions and return to a life in which they cannot be safe? Since the righteous are held so cheap and removed so easily, what should we suppose would have happened if anyone returning from the underworld had received life again? He would certainly have been taken from human sight, lest, when he was seen or heard, all should abandon the gods and turn to the worship and religion of the one God. Therefore resurrection must occur once, when evil has been removed, [Col. 0805C] because those who have risen may neither die again [Col. 0806A] nor be harmed in any way, so that they may live a blessed life, whose death has been unsealed.

But because the poets knew that this age abounds in every evil, they introduced a river of forgetfulness, lest souls mindful of their toils and evils should refuse to return to the world above. Hence Virgil:

> O father, must we think that any souls go hence  
> Sublime to heaven, and return again to sluggish  
> Bodies? What so dread a longing for light possesses the wretched?

For they did not know how or when this ought to happen. Thus they thought that souls were reborn, rolled back again into the womb, and returned to infancy. Whence Plato too, in discussing the soul, says that souls can be known to be immortal and divine from this: that children’s minds are quick-moving and ready to receive, and that they grasp what they learn so swiftly that they appear not [Col. 0806B] to learn it for the first time then, but to recognize and recollect it. In this the wise man believed the poets most foolishly.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the resurrection of the soul and the testimonies to it

Therefore souls will not be reborn, since that is impossible; but they will rise and be clothed by God with bodies. They will remember their former life and all their deeds; and, placed amid heavenly goods and enjoying the delight of innumerable blessings, they will give thanks to God present with them because he has destroyed every evil and raised them to everlasting kingdom and life.

The philosophers too have tried to say something about this *anastasis* [resurrection], as corruptly [Col. 0806C] as the poets. For Pythagoras argued that souls pass [Col. 0807A] into new bodies; but foolishly, since he held that they pass from human beings into beasts, from beasts into human beings, and that he himself had been restored from Euphorbus. Chrysippus did better, whom Cicero

[Col. 0807A] [Note: [Col. 0807B] Various Notes on columns 807–808]

**“Cicero.”** In *Academica* IV, section 75.

**“Of the Stoics.”** They were named from the *Stoa*, that is, the Portico, where they customarily met at Athens and discussed philosophical matters.

**“Which he wrote on Providence.”** *On Providence* (*Peri tēs pronoias*). Plutarch also cites this book, but Laertius does not.

[Col. 0807C] **“τούτου δὲ...”** In Latin: “Since this is so, it is evident that nothing is impossible, and that when we have ended life, after certain revolutions of time have elapsed, we shall again be restored to the state in which we now are.”

**“The Sibyl says this.”** One Leipzig manuscript reads “the Sibyl says.” Five recent manuscripts and seven editions read “the Sibyl says again,” deleting *haec* (“this”). Sibylline Books, Book 4, near the beginning.

**“Δύσπιστον.”** Latin translation:

> For the whole race of mortals is difficult to persuade; but when  
> The judgment of the world and of mortals comes, which God himself  
> Will conduct, judging the ungodly and the godly together,  
> Then indeed he will send the ungodly into darkness, into fire.  
> But those who practise piety will live again upon the earth,  
> The Spirit of God giving them honour and life together.

**“Καὶ τότε...”** These verses occur somewhat differently in the Sibylline codex.

**“τιμὴν ἅμα καὶ βίον αὐτοῖς.”** Thus five Royal manuscripts, two Colbert manuscripts, one Claromontane manuscript, the Roman editions of 1470 and 1474, and other editions. In place of *timēn*, “honour,” stands *psychēn*, “spirit,” in the manuscript seen by Colomesius and in the Sibylline text:

> ...and life and favour together to them.

**“And the poets.”** Absent from the Tornesian manuscript.

**“Anastasim.”** Seven recent manuscripts read *anastasin*.

**“Who made [him] new.”** Thus Prudentius: “I who was able to form [him] anew shall restore [him] when slain.” — “Let us believe that he who made [him] new can restore [him] old.” Thus Minucius Felix, chapter 34: “Besides, who is so foolish or brutish as to dare deny that humanity, having been able to be fashioned by God at first, can be refashioned by him again ... just as it was possible to be born from nothing, so it is possible to be refashioned from nothing?” Compare Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 48. Bunemann.

**“That he may judge the living and the dead,” etc.** This is said with scriptural warrant and without prejudice to Catholic faith; would that the rest were said with equal soundness. By “the living” we understand those whom the Lord’s advent will find remaining and surviving. The clearest testimonies to this are in Paul’s epistles. For in 2 Timothy 4:1 he says: “Before God and Jesus Christ, who will judge the living and the dead.” And in 1 Thessalonians 4: “For this we say to you in the word of the Lord: that we who are living and remain until the Lord’s coming shall not precede those [Col. 0808B] who have fallen asleep. For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel and the trumpet of God; and the dead in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive, who remain, shall together with them be caught up in clouds to meet the Lord in the air; and so we shall always be with the Lord.” No earthly kingdom is mentioned in these words. By “the dead,” moreover, we understand those who will have died before the day of the great judgment.

**“Πάσης γὰρ...”** Sibyl, Book 8. Latin:

> For then there shall be confusion of the mortals of the whole earth,  
> When the Almighty himself comes upon the judgment-seat to judge  
> The souls of the living and the dead, and the whole world.

**“Will have restored.”** Thus manuscripts and editions. Betuleius and Francius consider that *instauraverit* should be read, denying that *restaurare* is Latin. Yet it is found in Tacitus.

**“He will dwell among people for a thousand years,” etc.** These are fables and the error of the Millenarians; see Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VII.22, and Jerome on Papias.

[Col. 0808D] **“Κλύετε δέ...”** In Latin:

> Hear me, mortals: the eternal king rules.

These words are not found in the codex of Sibylline poems.

**“Then those who are...”** This is an error, as above.

**“But during the same thousand years they will produce an infinite multitude.”** Observe this: the things Lactantius discusses at length in the last three chapters of this book, namely chapters 24, 25, and 26—concerning the first resurrection of humanity; Christ’s golden kingdom on earth for a thousand years after that first resurrection; the binding of the devil for a thousand years; his release; and the battle of Gog and Magog—drawn from prophecies of Revelation 20 wrongly understood, are nearly all wholly alien to the sense of sacred Scripture and to the teaching of the Church and holy Fathers, and plainly erroneous, as Father Thomas Malvenda, Dominican theologian, shows at length in book I, “On Antichrist,” chapters 3–11.]

says supports the Porch of the Stoics. In the books which he wrote *On Providence*, when he was speaking of the renewal of the world, he inserted these words:

> τούτου δὲ οὕτως ἔχοντος, δῆλον ὡς οὐδὲν ἀδύνατον, καὶ ἡμᾶς μετὰ τὸ τελευτῆσαι, πάλιν περιόδων τινῶν εἰλημμένων χρόνου, εἰς ὃν ἐσμεν καταστήσεσθαι σχῆμα.

> Since this is so, it is evident that nothing is impossible, and that when we have ended life, after certain revolutions of time have elapsed, we shall again be restored to the state in which we now are.

But let us return from human things to divine. The Sibyl says this:

> For the whole race of mortals is hard to persuade; but when at last  
> The judgment of the world and of mortals comes, which God himself  
> Will conduct, judging the ungodly and the godly together,  
> Then he will send the ungodly into darkness, into fire.  
> But all who practise piety will live again upon the earth,  
> The Spirit of God granting them honour and life together.

If not only prophets, therefore, but also seers, poets, [Col. 0807B] and philosophers agree that the resurrection (*anastasis*) of the dead will occur, let no one ask us how it can occur. For no account can be rendered of divine works. But if in the beginning God formed humanity in some ineffable manner unknown to me, let us believe that he who made humanity new can restore it when old.

[Col. 0808A]

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the renewed world

I shall now append what remains. Therefore the Son of the supreme and greatest God will come to judge the living and the dead, as the Sibyl testifies and says:

> For then there shall be confusion of the mortals of the whole earth,  
> When the Almighty himself comes upon the judgment-seat to judge  
> The souls of the living and the dead, and the whole world.

But when he has destroyed injustice, conducted the greatest judgment, and restored the righteous who have existed from the beginning to life, he will dwell among people for a thousand years and rule them by a most just government. Elsewhere the Sibyl, prophesying and crying out in frenzy, declares:

> Hear me, mortals: the eternal king rules.

[Col. 0808B] Then those who are alive in bodies will not die; but during the same thousand years they will produce an infinite multitude. Their offspring will be holy and dear to God. But those who are raised from the underworld will preside over the living as judges. The nations, however, will not be wholly destroyed; some will be left for the victory [Col. 0809A] of God, that they may be triumphed over by the righteous and subjugated.

See there John’s words, whose meaning St Augustine first set out and explained before the rest in *City of God* XX.7 and several following chapters; after him Eugippius recounted it, volume I, chapter 134 and following. Betuleius. **“He will be in confinement.”** See Revelation 20.

**“After his coming.”** That is, the coming of the Son of God. He returns to what was said below: “The Son of the supreme and greatest God will come.” Bunemann.

**“The Sibyl,” etc.** In Book 5, where the verses differ slightly. Yet Lactantius’s reading is more pleasing.

**“Καὶ πόλιν...”** In Latin:

Nine manuscripts and six printed editions read “heaven will be overspread and darkened”; the manuscripts of Betuleius and nine editions read “heaven was overspread and darkened.”

**“Brightness.”** Nine recent manuscripts read “clarity.”

**“But the sun,” etc.** This is Isaiah 30. But Isaiah himself teaches how this should be understood, chapter 60: “You shall no longer have the sun as light by day, nor shall the brightness of the moon shine for you; but the Lord shall be for you an everlasting light, and your God your glory. Your sun shall no longer set, nor shall your moon diminish, because the Lord shall be your everlasting light,” etc. The prophet said “everlasting,” not “of a thousand years.” And John, after describing the city, says: “The city has no need of sun or moon to shine upon it, for the glory of God illuminates it and its lamp is the Lamb,” etc. These words utterly remove *chiliasmos* [millenarianism]. But concerning the seventh and eighth age of the future world, as concerning the day of the Lord and the time of Antichrist, read Bede, *On the Nature of Things*, chapter 76 and several following chapters. [Col. 0810B] [Col. 0810C] Betuleius.

St Augustine, *City of God* XX.7.—“They will sweat honey.” In the *Epitome*, chapter 72, this and the following words vary thus: “Honey will drip from the rocks; springs of milk and wine will overflow.” Bunemann. **“Of evil, impiety, crime, and error.”** I have added “and crime” from seventeen editions and all manuscripts, except that the Regius-Puteanus manuscript has “terror.”

] to perpetual bondage. At the same time the prince of demons, who is the contriver of all evils, will also be bound in chains; and he will be kept in custody for the thousand years of the heavenly kingdom, during which righteousness will reign in the world, so that he may devise no evil against the people of God. After his coming, the righteous will be gathered from the whole earth; and, when judgment has been completed, the holy city will be established in the midst of the earth, in which God the Creator himself will dwell together with the righteous who reign. The Sibyl describes this city when she says:

> And the city which God made—he made it  
> > Brighter than the stars, and the sun, and the moon.

Then those darknesses by which heaven is veiled and obscured will be removed from the world; and the moon will receive the brightness of the sun and will no longer wane. The sun, moreover, will become seven times brighter than it is now. The earth will open its fertility and, of its own accord, will produce most abundant crops; the rocks of the mountains will sweat honey, wines will run through the streams, and rivers will overflow with milk. Finally, the world itself will rejoice, and the whole order of nature will exult, having been rescued and liberated from the dominion of evil, impiety, wickedness, and error. During this time beasts will not feed upon blood, nor birds upon prey; rather, all things will be calm and peaceful. Lions and calves will stand together at the manger; the wolf will not seize the sheep; the dog will not hunt; hawks and eagles will do no harm; an infant will play with serpents. In short, then those things will come to pass which poets said had occurred in the golden age, when Saturn was already reigning. Their error arose from this: prophets commonly utter and proclaim many future things as though they had already been accomplished. For visions were presented to their eyes by the divine spirit, and they saw them before themselves as though they were happening and being brought to completion. When report had gradually spread these prophecies abroad, because those outside the sacrament did not know in what sense they were spoken, they supposed that all those things had already been fulfilled in the ages of old—things which certainly could not happen or be fulfilled while a human being reigned.

But when impious religions have been destroyed, wickedness suppressed, and the earth subjected to God,

> > Then the field will yellow with soft ears of grain;  
> > And the red grape will hang from uncultivated brambles;  
> > And hard oaks will sweat dewy honey,  
> > Nor will wool learn to counterfeit varied colours.  
> > But the ram himself, in the meadows, will now change his fleece—  
> > Now with the pleasant purple of blushing murex, now with saffron dye.  
> > Of its own accord sandyx [scarlet] will clothe the grazing lambs.  
> > The she-goats themselves will bring home their udders swollen with milk,  
> > And herds will not fear great lions.

These are the words which the poet uttered in accordance with the verses of the Cumaean Sibyl. The Erythraean Sibyl, however, says:

The kings of the nations will come from the ends of the earth with gifts and offerings, to worship and honour the great King, whose name will be illustrious and venerable among all nations beneath heaven and among the kings who rule on earth.

## Chapter XXV. On the last times and the city of Rome

These are the things which the prophets declare will happen. I have not thought it necessary to set forth their testimonies and words, since this would be endless, and the compass of a book could not contain so great a multitude of matters, when so many speak similar things under one Spirit. At the same time, I wished to avoid wearying readers by heaping together translated passages collected from them all; and besides, I wished to confirm what I was saying chiefly by writings not our own, rather than ours, and to show that the truth which they refuse to acknowledge is preserved under seal not only among us, but even among those who persecute us. But if anyone wishes to know these matters more diligently, let him draw from the fountainhead itself, and he will find more marvels than we have embraced in these books.

Perhaps someone may now ask when those things which we have described will occur. I have already shown above that this change must occur when six thousand years have been completed, and that the supreme day of the final consummation is now drawing near. It is possible to know from the signs foretold by the prophets; for they foretold signs by which the consummation of the times is to be expected and feared by us day by day. Yet when this total will be completed is taught by those who have written about times, calculating from sacred writings and from various histories the number of years from the beginning of the world. Although they differ, and the total of their reckoning diverges somewhat, the entire expectation appears to be no more than two hundred years.

The condition of affairs itself also declares that the collapse and ruin of things will occur soon—except that, while the city of Rome remains unharmed, nothing of this kind seems to be feared. But when that head of the world has fallen and has begun to be a *rhymē* [“street”; reading uncertain in context], which the Sibyls say will happen,

**[Col. 0813A–0814D] [Variorum Notes to columns 813–814]**

**Sibyllae** (“the Sibyls”). Sibylline Oracles, Books 3 and 8.

**Illa, illa est civitas** (“That, that is the city”). Thus I read with the most ancient Regius-Puteanus manuscript, two other good Regius manuscripts, one Colbert manuscript, Pen., Ultr., one Claromontanus manuscript, and two Brunensis manuscripts. The editions read *Illa est enim*; in most manuscripts and two old editions *illa* is not repeated, and *enim* is absent.

**Precandusque nobis** (“must be entreated by us”). Lactantius uses this verb both actively and passively. Ausonius likewise used it passively: *Deus precandus est mihi*, “God must be entreated by me.”

**Abominabilis** (“abominable”). Lactantius likes to speak thus, as I have already noted above; copyists altered it by emendation in four manuscripts and fifteen editions to *abominandus* (“to be abominated”).

**Diximus, etc.** Our author links many fables in this chapter; readers are therefore warned not to give them credence too readily.

**Tunc veniet** (“Then will come”). These things resemble those prophesied by Ezekiel, chapter 38; indeed, I do not know whether they are not altogether the same. Similar, indeed much more dreadful, things occur in the Sibyls, Book 3; because they are rather numerous, I refrain from noting them. BETULEIUS.

**Et debellabit eas** (“and he will defeat them”). One Regius and one Brunensis manuscript read *et delebit eas* (“and he will destroy them”). An excellent reading, too, in seven recent manuscripts and twelve printed editions is *et debellabit eos* (“and he will defeat them”). See Revelation 16.

**Usque ad unum** (“to the last one”). Two recent manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470 read *usque ad imum* (“down to the bottom”). But Heumann rightly reads *usque ad unam*.—*Usque ad unum*: as Caesar, *Civil War* II.14: “He inflicted punishment upon every slave and free person down to those under age, and killed them to the last one.” BUN.

**Concident** (“will fall”). Thus four old editions and all manuscripts except one recent Regius manuscript, which has *corruent*, as do eleven printed editions.

**Occultabitur** (“will be hidden”). Sublacensis: *occultatus erit* (“will have been hidden”).

**Et extremum judicium terminetur** (“and the final judgment be completed”). Thus corrected from five old editions and all manuscripts except one recent Regius manuscript, which has *terminet*, as in nine printed editions, without the preceding conjunction.

**Perpetes** (“continual”). As in *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 33, *per annum perpetem* (“for a continual year”); and *Epitome*, chapter 71, *gemitus perpetes* (“continual groans”). BUN.

**Renovabitur, etc.** See Isaiah 65 and 66, and Revelation 21: “There will be a new heaven and a new earth.” The Chiliasts seize on these words as an occasion for error. Catholics interpret them in a good sense. In Revelation mention is made of the first and second death, but absolutely no mention of a second resurrection. Yet the Chiliasts infer that if there is a first, why should there not also be a second? By the same reasoning they might infer that there are more. For among writers who speak accurately, “first” is said either of several things or of two. Moreover John himself says that over the holy person who has a part in the first resurrection the second death has no power; from this it follows that there can be no resurrection from the second death. BETULEIUS.

**Secunda illa et publica omnium resurrectio, in qua excitabuntur injusti ad cruciatus sempiternos** (“that second and public resurrection of all, in which the unjust will be raised for everlasting torments”). Above, in chapter 21, Lactantius said that the impious, when the holy rise to reign with God on earth for a thousand years, are shut up in darkness, destined for fixed punishments. Accordingly he now devises a second resurrection, in which they must be raised from the common prison for everlasting torments. For he seems to have seized his occasion for error from the fact that Revelation mentions a first resurrection, in which the righteous are said to have their part; he infers a second, fitted for punishing the wicked, although St John does not mention it at all. SPARK.

**Excitabuntur** (“will be raised”). Nine recent manuscripts and nine editions read *excitabuntur impii* (“the impious will be raised”); Florentinus has *exterminabuntur impii* (“the impious will be exterminated”). But God will raise them also when the second resurrection has taken place, etc. This is read at the end of chapter 2 of the *Epitome*.

**Injusti** (“the unjust”). Nine recent manuscripts and as many editions have *impii* (“the impious”).

who can doubt that the end has now come for human affairs and the whole world? That, that is the city which still upholds all things. Therefore God of heaven must be entreated and worshipped by us—if indeed his decrees and purposes can be deferred—that the abominable tyrant may not come sooner than we think, to undertake so great a crime and dig out that light, at whose extinction the world itself will fall. Let us now return to the remaining matters that are to follow.

## Chapter XXVI. On the release of the demon and the second great judgment

A little earlier we said that, at the beginning of the holy kingdom, the prince of demons would be bound by God. But when the thousand years of the kingdom—that is, when the seven thousand years—begin to come to an end, he will be released again and, having been sent forth from custody, will go out. He will stir up all the nations then under the rule of the righteous to wage war upon the holy city. An innumerable people of nations will be gathered from the whole earth; they will besiege and surround the city. Then the final wrath of God will come upon the nations and will destroy them to the last one. First he will shake the earth with the greatest violence; from its motion the mountains of Syria will split, hills will sink into chasms, and the walls of all cities will fall. God will cause the sun not to set for three days; he will set it ablaze; and excessive heat and a great burning will descend upon hostile and impious peoples, together with showers of sulphur, hailstorms of stones, and drops of fire. Their spirits will melt in the heat, their bodies will be crushed in the hail, and they themselves will strike one another with the sword. The mountains will be filled with corpses and the plains covered with bones. But for those three days the people of God will be hidden in cavities of the earth, until God’s wrath against the nations and the final judgment are completed.

Then the righteous will come out from their hiding places and find everything covered with corpses and bones. The entire race of the impious will perish utterly; and no nation whatever will remain in this world except the nation of God alone. Then for seven continual years the forests will remain untouched; no timber will be cut from the mountains. But the weapons of the nations will be burned, and there will no longer be war, but peace and everlasting rest. When the thousand years have been completed, the world will be renewed by God, heaven will be rolled up, and earth will be changed. God will transform human beings into the likeness of angels; they will be white as snow, will always move in the sight of the Almighty, and will sacrifice to and serve their Lord forever. At the same time there will occur that second and public resurrection of all, in which the unjust will be raised for everlasting torments. These are those who worshipped things made by hand, who either did not know or denied the Lord and Father of the world. Their lord also, together with his attendants, will be seized and condemned to punishment; along with him the entire multitude of the impious will be burned forever in everlasting fire, before the angels and the righteous, for their deeds.

**[Col. 0815A] [Variorum Notes to columns 815–816]**

**In abdito** (“in secret”). Sublacensis: *in abscondito* (“in concealment”).

**Istos veri profanos** (“these truly profane persons”). Thus the Roman edition of 1470 and all manuscripts except one Colbert manuscript, which, like nineteen editions, has *vere* (“truly”).

**Qui nomen fidei gerimus** (“who bear the name of faith”). From this Christians were called *fideles* (“the faithful”). *Epitome*, chapter 66, beginning: “Faith … must especially be preserved by us who bear the name …” BUN.

**Opiniones** (“allegations”). See Tertullian, *Apology*.

**Quae finxerint, credunt** (“they believe the things they have invented”). The older and better manuscripts and old editions have *finxerint*; the more recent ones, *finxerunt*; one Colbert manuscript, *finxerant*.

**Imperator** (“Emperor”). We give this epilogue to Emperor Constantine from Regius manuscript no. 3976, an excellent manuscript about four hundred years old, and from the Antwerp editions of 1570 and 1587, Gymnicus, Fasitellus, Gryphius, Paris 1561 and 1565, Betuleius, Tornesius 1579, Lyons, and Soubron 1594; we gladly admit it into the text, since it is wholly Lactantian, as it seems to learned men and to us. Betuleius, Walchius, and Francius thought thus; the latter wrote in the margin of his Lactantius: “An elegant and vigorous speech; nor do I doubt that it is genuine.” Indeed, it has Lactantius’s character, style, and idiom, as is evident in various places, and fits and coheres excellently with what precedes. Lactantius used an epilogue in his writings, after Cicero’s manner: see *Divine Institutions* I.1, II.1, the beginnings of books IV and V, VI.26; *On the Workmanship of God* 20; and *On the Wrath of God* 22, where Lactantius himself says: “This is what I had to say about the wrath of God, dearest Donatus … It remains that, after Cicero’s manner, we use an epilogue for the peroration,” etc. Sparke nevertheless removes this speech from the text and relegates it to the notes; yet we have not wished, with the other editions, to remove it from its place. We do, however, state in which editions it is absent; for we cannot deny that this speech, although elegant and worthy of Lactantius, is absent from the Cambrai, Rohan, and Saint-Germain manuscripts. The reason for this is given in the preliminary dissertation.—**Sanctissime Imperator** (“most holy Emperor”): Lactantius calls the same young Constantine *Constantinus sanctissimus adolescens* (“Constantine, most holy young man”) in *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 18.

**Figmenta** (“fictions”). *Figmentum*, that is, an invention. Thus Lactantius, *Divine Institutions* VII.22, beginning: “These fictions of the poets … in the manner of a fabricated tale,” etc.; VII.7, “that this is a fiction of the poets”; and II.11, “this fiction of the poets can be refuted by many arguments.”

**Sopita sunt** (“have been laid to rest”). Lactantius, *Divine Institutions* I.1, about the middle: “might lay controversies to rest”; and there: “We shall speak of hope, life, salvation, immortality, and God, that we may lay to rest deadly superstitions and most disgraceful errors.” Here likewise: “But now, most holy Emperor, all fictions have been laid to rest, since,” etc.

**Deus summus** (“the supreme God”). Lactantius uses this expression throughout: *Divine Institutions* I.1; IV.12, 13, 29; VII.2, 3, 4; *On the Wrath of God* 11, 23; *On the Workmanship of God* 1; *Epitome* 3, 4, etc. You will encounter it a hundred times in Lactantius’s works.

**Ad restituendum justitiae domicilium** (“to restore the dwelling-place of justice”). Lactantius similarly uses *domicilium* elsewhere: *Divine Institutions* III.18 and VII.2, 8, “from this dwelling-place of the body”; *On the Wrath of God* 1; IV, final chapter, “the dwelling-place of faith”; *Epitome* 52, “the dwelling-place of piety”; chapter 54, “the dwelling-place of liberty”; and *On the Workmanship of God* 10. In the epilogue to the same Emperor, *Divine Institutions* I.1, he says: “By restoring justice, overthrown and taken away, you expiated the most shameful crime of others”; shortly thereafter: “Since you wish to defend divine worship, whom should I rather call upon, whom address, than him through whom justice and wisdom have been restored to human affairs?” VII.5: “Has justice been assigned to few persons?”

**Ad tutelam generis humani excitavit** (“raised you up to protect humankind”). In the aforesaid epilogue, *Divine Institutions* I.1: “The supreme God raised you to the blessed height of empire … that even as an old man you may hold the helm of the commonwealth, and hand down to your children, as you yourself received from your father, the protection of the Roman name.” Also II.15: “for the protection and cultivation of humankind”; V.18: “may heavenly protection guard the righteous man amid the dangers of storms and wars”; *On the Workmanship of God* 2: “no one lacks a defence for his own protection”; V.5, “protection of himself.”

**Cultores Dei** (“worshippers of God”). Lactantius, *Divine Institutions* VI.24: “a worshipper of God,” and shortly afterwards, “this is the worshipper of the true God”; II.16: “the righteous, that is, worshippers of God”; V.1 and 2, and frequently elsewhere.

**Illustrata veritate** (“truth brought to light”). Lactantius, *Divine Institutions* I.1 and 2, beginning: “Having therefore undertaken the office of bringing truth to light”; and at the end of *On the Workmanship of God*, “to bring truth itself to light among others,” etc.; IV.5; VI.1; VII.7.

**Dei nomen exprobrat** (“reproaches [us with] the name of God”). Lactantius, I.20: “the name of the gods … may be made a mockery by the most shameful names”; V, final chapter: “the name of God was an object of insult and mockery”; and frequently elsewhere, especially in *On the Wrath of God*.

**Irreligiosus** (“irreligious”). Lactantius, V.21: “more irreligious.”

**Religiosi sumus** (“we are religious”). Lactantius, III.28: “religious and pious worship”; IV.28: “worshippers of the gods were called religious”; VI.1: “they think themselves religious.”

**Contemptis imaginibus mortuorum, vivum colimus et verum Deum** (“despising images of the dead, we worship the living and true God”). Lactantius uses the same expression in the contrary sense in II.1: “I am accustomed to wonder … that human beings themselves have been led to such blindness as to prefer the dead to the true and living God,” etc. II.2: “they worship images, which are likenesses of the dead”; and below, chapter 18, he says that it is an inexpiable crime to desert the living God in order to serve monuments of the dead.

This is the teaching of the holy prophets which we Christians follow; this is our wisdom. Those who worship either fragile things or uphold empty philosophy mock it as folly and vanity, because we are not accustomed publicly to defend and assert it, God commanding us to keep his mystery quietly and silently hidden and within our own conscience, and not to contend in obstinate dispute against these truly profane persons. For they assail God and his religion cruelly, not for the sake of learning but for the sake of accusation and mockery. The mystery must indeed be concealed and guarded with the utmost fidelity, especially by us who bear the name of faith. But they accuse our silence as though it were a bad conscience; hence they invent certain execrable allegations about chaste and innocent people, and readily believe the things they have invented.

> “But now, most holy Emperor, all fictions have been laid to rest, since the supreme God raised you up to restore the dwelling-place of justice and to protect humankind. Under your governance of the Roman commonwealth, worshippers of God are no longer regarded as criminal and wicked. Now that truth is emerging and has been brought to light, we are no longer accused as unjust because we endeavour to perform works of justice. No one now reproaches us with the name of God. No one is any longer called irreligious who alone among all people are religious, because, despising images of the dead, we worship the living and true God.
>
> “The providence of the highest divinity has advanced you to the imperial summit,

**[Col. 0817A–0818D] [Variorum Notes to columns 817–818]**

**Te providentia summae Divinitatis ad fastigium principale provexit** (“the providence of the highest divinity has advanced you to the imperial summit”). Lactantius, VII.4: “the providence of the supreme God”; *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* 48: “so that the highest divinity may be able for us,” etc.

**Ad fastigium principale provexit** (“advanced [you] to the imperial summit”). Lactantius says something similar of Decius in *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* 4: “as though he had been advanced to that imperial summit for this very purpose”; that is, to imperial rank.

**Male consulta rescindere** (“to annul ill-conceived measures”). *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* 3: “the acts of the tyrant having been annulled”; ibid. 1: “who annulled the impious and bloody reigns of tyrants.” BUN.

**Quae sit vera majestas** (“what true majesty is”). Lactantius, I.1: “to the worship of true majesty”; II.17: “human beings whom they strive to turn away from the worship and knowledge of true majesty,” etc.; V.6: “the source of all these evils was desire, which, that is, burst forth from contempt of true majesty.”

**Qui ut impias religiones defenderent** (“those who, in order to defend impious religions”). Lactantius, V.8: “impious religions have been undertaken contrary to what is right.”

**Coelestis ac singularis Dei cultum tollere voluerunt** (“wished to abolish the worship of the heavenly and unique God”). Lactantius, V.5: “those who persecute persons righteous and faithful to God … to attack and abolish justice, that is, the worship of God.” See above the note on the word *justitia*, and “unique God,” the note on chapter 1 of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*.

**Profligati jacent** (“lie defeated”). Lactantius, VI.20: “they order those struck down and lying [there] to be attacked again”; and *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* 1: “the Church recently defeated”; shortly thereafter: “those who had struggled against God lie [fallen].”

**Illi poenas sceleris sui et pendunt et perpenderunt** (“They both pay and have paid the penalties of their wickedness”). *Epitome* 53: “Of all those who dared this crime, we have learned of the wretched ends of some and see those of others.” Compare IV.27. Lactantius’s *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* pertains to this passage and is strikingly illuminated here and there by this speech, long suspected. BUN.

**Te dextera Dei potens ab omnibus periculis protegit** (“God’s mighty right hand protects you from every danger”). Lactantius also, II.15: “whom the mighty and exalted hand of God protects.”

**Rerum Dominus ac rector** (“Lord and ruler of all things”). Lactantius, *On the Workmanship of God* 16: “that which governs the universe by reason, just as the Lord and ruler of the world himself is above.”

**Te potissimum delegit, per quem sanctam religionem suam instauraret** (“chose you above all others, through whom he might restore his holy religion”). Of the same man Lactantius says, I.1: “For when that most blessed day dawned upon the world, on which the supreme God raised you to the blessed height of empire, you inaugurated a saving and desirable rule for all with a distinguished beginning, when by restoring justice, overthrown and taken away, you expiated the most shameful crime of others,” etc.

**Antiquorum principum gloriam, quos tamen fama inter bonos numerat** (“the glory of ancient rulers, whom reputation nevertheless counts among the good”). Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* 3: “Many Roman rulers were good, though pagan: Nerva, Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus Pius, and that pair of brothers, Verus and Lucius.” On the good rulers who permitted liberty of belief to our people, used their service in palace and provinces, and advanced them to the highest dignities, see Eusebius at the beginning of book VIII of the *Ecclesiastical History*. In part from BALUZIUS.

**Qui enim moderatorem universitatis Deum ignorat** (“For one who does not know God, the governor of the universe”). Lactantius, *On the Workmanship of God* 16: “Nor is anything more exalted than that which governs the universe by reason, just as the Lord and ruler of the world himself is above”; II.16, “ruler of the universe.”

**Similitudinem justitiae assequi potest: ipsam non potest** (“can attain a likeness of justice, but not justice itself”). Lactantius, III.27: “They saw a certain shadow of virtue; they did not see virtue itself.”

**Provecti sumus** (“we have advanced”). Thus the better and older manuscripts and the great majority of editions. Seventeen manuscripts have *pervecti sumus* (“we have arrived”); Gat. has *praevecti*.

**Illicibiles** (“alluring”). Lactantius is remarkably fond of such formations. Eight recent manuscripts: *allicibiles*; Betuleius’s edition: *illices*.—**Illices voluptates** (“alluring pleasures”). More in Elmenhorst on chapter 1. Tertullian, *Apology* 41: “You are allurers of evils”; *On Repentance* 9: “enjoining a conduct alluring to mercy,” where Cyprian, *On Jealousy and Envy*, beginning: “It sets alluring forms before the eyes.” BUN.

**Perniciosa** (“ruinous”). This is the reading of all manuscripts except two recent Regius manuscripts, which have *perniciosissima* (“most ruinous”), as do the editions.

so that in true devotion you might annul others’ ill-conceived measures, correct their sins, provide with paternal clemency for the welfare of human beings, and finally remove from the commonwealth those very wicked persons whom God, in his supreme mercy, delivered into your hands after their overthrow, so that it might be clear to all what true majesty is.
>
> “For those who, in order to defend impious religions, wished to abolish the worship of the heavenly and unique God, lie defeated. But you, who defend and love his name, pre-eminent in courage and good fortune, enjoy most happily your immortal glories. They both pay and have paid the penalties of their wickedness. God’s mighty right hand protects you from every danger and grants you a peaceful and tranquil government, amid the supreme rejoicing of all. Nor without reason did the Lord and ruler of all things choose you above all others, through whom he might restore his holy religion. For among all men you alone have arisen to furnish outstanding examples of courage and holiness, by which you not only equal the glory of ancient rulers—whom reputation nevertheless counts among the good—but even, what is greatest, surpass it.
>
> “They, perhaps, were only naturally similar to the righteous. For one who does not know God, the governor of the universe, can attain a likeness of justice, but not justice itself. You, however, by an inborn holiness of character and by knowledge of truth and of God, bring works of justice to completion in every action. It was therefore fitting that, in shaping the condition of humankind, divinity should employ you as its author and minister. To it we offer daily prayers: first, that it may preserve you, whom it wished to be the guardian of affairs; then, that it may inspire in you the will always to persevere in love of the divine name. This is salutary for all: for you, unto happiness; for others, unto peace.”

## Chapter XXVII. Exhortation and confirmation of the pious
