Since, having traversed the seven divisions of the work proposed, we have advanced to the goal, it remains to exhort all people to embrace wisdom together with true religion. Its power and function consist in this: that, despising earthly things and casting away the errors by which we were formerly held—serving frail things and desiring what is frail—we may direct ourselves toward the eternal rewards of the heavenly treasure. In order that we may grasp these rewards, the alluring pleasures of this present life, which soothe human souls with ruinous sweetness, must be abandoned as soon as possible.

**[Col. 0819A–0820D] [Variorum Notes to columns 819–820]**

**Aestimanda est** (“should be judged”). Thus almost all manuscripts. Five recent manuscripts and the printed editions read *existimanda est* (“should be considered”).

**Terentiana** (“Terentian”). Terence, *Phormio*, act II, scene 1.

**Usque in pistrino** (“at the mill”). Thus I have restored it from Terence himself and the manuscripts. Three recent Regius manuscripts, one Colbert manuscript, and ten printed editions have *usque in pistrinum*; many editions of Terence read likewise.

**Sine divino praemio** (“without divine reward”). *Divino* is absent from recent manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470.

**Ut susceptis operatisque virtutibus** (“when virtues have been undertaken and practised”). Junius manuscript: *vel ut susceptis*; twenty-two other manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470 have *vel susceptis*. I have deleted *vel* as useless, since there is no antithesis. Observe in passing that Lactantius uses *operari* passively.

**Qui solem cum caeteris sideribus induxit** (“who introduced the sun with the other stars”). Eight recent manuscripts: *illuxit* (“shone upon”).

**Terram vallavit montibus, mari circumdedit, amnibusque distinxit** (“He enclosed the earth with mountains, surrounded it with sea, and marked it off with rivers”). Thus Betuleius reads; nor is it read otherwise in the manuscripts, except that five recent manuscripts and eight editions have *mare*. Disregard what Pricaeus says concerning a transposition of the words.

**Lucretius.** Book VI of *On the Nature of Things*, at the beginning.

**Veridicis hominum.** Lucretius has *Veridicis igitur*.

**Et finem statuit cuppedinis** (“and set a limit to desire”). Thus the editions of Gymnicus and Paris 1561 and 1565, and Betuleius, with double *pp*, so that the first syllable, naturally short, becomes long by the addition of one letter *p*. Lucretius has the same. Lambinus noted that it was no different in his manuscripts, which he used to revise, correct, and annotate Lucretius’s works. One good Regius manuscript, the editions of Tornesius and Soubron 1594, read *cupidinis*; eight editions, *cupedinis*; one Regius-Puteanus manuscript, *turpidinis*; the manuscripts and six printed editions, *torpedinis*.

**Limite parvo** (“by a narrow path”). Old French translation: *par un chemin étroit*. Lactantius seems to have read *limite* in his copy; all printed editions and manuscripts have it, except one Junius manuscript, which reads *tramite*, as the Lucretian manuscripts seen by Lambinus do; these read *prono*, with Victorius, Navagerius, and three old Roman editions. In the Regius-Puteanus manuscript and two other Regius manuscripts, Marm., Balliol., and three editions, the reading is *limite puro* (“by a pure path”).

**Quam innocens ad judicem veniat** (“how innocently he may come to the judge”). Sixteen recent manuscripts and seven editions: *ad judicium veniat* (“may come to judgment”).

**Non ut faciunt, quorum caecis mentibus lux negatur, qui** (“Not as those do whose blinded minds are denied light, who”). Thus I read with the ancient Caucasian manuscript, one excellent Regius manuscript, and the editions of Gymnicus, Fasitellus, two Paris editions, Betuleius, Tornesius, Soubron, and Walchius. Some editions have *quorum caecis mentibus, qui*. In thirty-two manuscripts and ten printed editions it reads: *Non ut faciunt quidam caecis mentibus nixi, qui* (“Not as certain persons do, relying on blinded minds, who”).

**Lux negatur** (“light is denied”). Because they voluntarily close their eyes.

**Ut cupidius, ut ardentius** (“the more eagerly, the more ardently”). Many manuscripts and editions have *et ardentius* (“and more ardently”).

**Et acquirere** (“and acquire”). The manuscripts have *et*; the editions, *ac*.

**De perenni fonte** (“from the perennial fountain”). Thus I read, as in the text, with all editions except the old Roman one and all manuscripts except two Regius manuscripts, which insert *coelestique* (“and heavenly”), an interpolation in my judgment, since “heavenly food” has already preceded.

How great a happiness should it be judged to depart from these earthly miseries to that most equitable judge and most indulgent father, who grants rest for labours, life for death, light for darkness, and eternal, heavenly goods for earthly and brief goods. The hardships and miseries that we endure in this world while performing works of justice cannot in any way be compared or made equal with such a reward. Therefore, if we wish to be wise and blessed, we must reflect upon and set before ourselves not only those Terentian words, “One must grind at the mill, be beaten, and wear fetters,” but things far harsher still: prison, chains, and tortures must be endured; pains must be borne; finally, death itself must both be undertaken and endured, since our conscience makes clear that neither this fragile pleasure will be without punishment nor virtue without divine reward.

All, therefore, must strive to set themselves as soon as possible upon the right path; so that, having embraced and practised the virtues, and patiently undergone the labours of this life, they may deserve to have God as their comforter. For our Father and Lord, who created and established heaven, who brought forth the sun with the other stars, who surrounded the earth, poised by his greatness, with mountains, encompassed it with sea, and marked it out with rivers, and who fashioned and perfected from nothing whatever exists in this work of the world—having observed human errors—sent a Guide to disclose to us the path of righteousness. Let us all follow him; let us hear him; let us obey him with the utmost devotion; since he alone, as Lucretius says,

> Cleansed men’s breasts by his truth-speaking words,  
> And set a limit to desire and fear;  
> [Col. 0819C] He showed what that highest good was, toward which we all tend,  
> And pointed out, along a narrow track, the way  
> By which we might hasten straight toward it.

Nor did he merely point it out, but also went before us, lest anyone should shrink from the path of virtue because of its difficulty. Let the way of destruction and deceit be abandoned [Col. 0820A], if that be possible, the way in which death lies concealed beneath the alluring enticements of pleasure.

And insofar as each person sees himself, as the years decline into old age, drawing near to that day on which he must depart from this life, let him consider how pure he departs, how innocent he comes before the Judge. Let him not act as those do whose blinded minds are denied the light, and who, when their bodily strength is already failing, are warned by this of the impending final necessity only to apply themselves more greedily, more ardently, to draining pleasures. Let each free himself from this abyss while he may, while opportunity remains, and turn himself to God with his whole mind, so that he may await without anxiety that day on which God, the governor and lord of the world, will judge the deeds and thoughts of every individual. Whatever is sought here, let him not merely disregard [Col. 0820B], but flee from it; and let him judge his own soul more precious than those deceptive goods, whose possession is uncertain and fleeting. For they pass away daily; they depart far more swiftly than they came; and yet, even if we were permitted to enjoy them to the very end, they must certainly be left to others. We can carry nothing with us except a life lived well and innocently. He will arrive rich before God, he will arrive wealthy, at whose side stand self-control, mercy, patience, charity, and faith. This is our inheritance: it can neither be taken from anyone nor transferred to another. And who is there who would wish to procure and acquire these goods for himself?

Let those who hunger come, that, filled with heavenly food, they may lay aside everlasting hunger; let those who thirst come, that they may draw the saving water from the perennial fountain with throats filled to overflowing [Col. 0820C]. By this food and drink of God, the blind shall see, the deaf hear, the mute speak, the lame walk, the foolish become wise, the sick recover health, and the dead rise again. For whoever has trampled underfoot, through virtue, the corruptions of earth, him that highest and true Judge [Col. 0821A] will raise to everlasting light and life. Let no one trust in riches, in offices of state, or even in royal power: these do not make one immortal. For whoever has cast away human reason and, following present things, has thrown himself down upon the ground, shall be punished as a deserter of his lord, commander, and father. Let us therefore devote ourselves to righteousness, which alone, as an inseparable companion, will lead us to God; and, [Col. 0822A] while the spirit governs these limbs, let us serve God in an unwearied campaign.

[Col. 0822A] [Note: Variorum Notes on columns 821–822]

“Let us serve God in an unwearied campaign” (*Infatigabilem militiam Deo militemus*). A manner of expression familiar to Lactantius, concerning which I spoke above in the note at the end of chapter 24 of this book. This reading is found in ten editions and very many manuscripts, among them the most ancient: the two Bolognese manuscripts, Regio-Put., Cauc., Jun., three other Royal manuscripts, three Colbert manuscripts, and others. In fifteen recent manuscripts and four printed editions [Col. 0822A] there is: “with an unwearied campaign” (*infatigabili militia*).

“That we may obtain from the Lord” (*A Domino consequamur*). The Cantabrigian and Junian manuscripts, and the Aldine, Parisian, Cratander, and Grapheus editions, read “from God” (*a Deo*); two recent Royal manuscripts and three old ones add, “Amen.” The Junian manuscript adds: “Who lives and reigns, God, through the immortal ages of ages. Amen.”]

Let us keep our stations and watches; let us engage bravely with the enemy whom we know, so that, victorious and triumphing over the vanquished adversary, we may obtain from the Lord the reward of virtue which he himself promised.

[FRAGMENT CONCERNING THE LAST JUDGMENT.]

[Col. 0821]

NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING FRAGMENT.

[Col. 0821B] In 1679 Stephen Baluze was the first to publish the following fragment under the name of Lactantius, relying upon this single argument: that he had read it at the end of certain manuscripts of the *Divine Institutions*. [Note: [Col. 0821B]

It occurs in certain later manuscripts: first, in three Royal manuscripts; secondly, in one Victorine manuscript; thirdly, in one Sorbonne manuscript; fourthly, in three English manuscripts—but without Lactantius’s name.

] But, with all respect to so learned a man, I would say that this is insufficient. For nowhere in these manuscripts is it attributed to Lactantius [Col. 0822B]; indeed, in Royal manuscript 3977 it is copied under the name of St Augustine, with these words: “Augustine, in Book XX of *The City of God*.” The copyist appended this fragment to Lactantius in order to dispel his errors and those of the millenarians, errors which our author spreads everywhere, and especially in Book VII of the *Divine Institutions*. (We have extracted this annotation from the *Examination of the Doctrine of the Holy Fathers* by the most learned des Essarts.)

[Col. 0821]

FRAGMENT OF SAINT AUGUSTINE CONCERNING THE LAST JUDGMENT.

[Col. 0821C] No one either denies or doubts that through Jesus Christ there will be such a judgment as is foretold in the Sacred Scriptures—unless he does not believe those same Scriptures through some inexplicable hostility or blindness, though they have already demonstrated their truth to the whole world. In that judgment, or around that judgment, we have learned that these things will occur: Elijah the Tishbite; the faith of the Jews; Antichrist’s persecution; Christ’s judging; the resurrection of the dead; [Col. 0822C] the separation of the good and the evil; the conflagration of the world; and its renewal. All these things, indeed, must be believed to be future. But by what means and in what order they will come, experience of events will then teach more fully than human understanding can now perfectly grasp. Yet I think that they will occur in the order in which I have mentioned them.

[Col. 0821C] [Note: Variorum Notes on columns 821–822]

“Is foretold” (*praenuntiatur*). Thus I have restored the reading from the new edition of St Augustine and the manuscripts, except one Colbert manuscript, in which there is *pronuntiatur* (“is declared”), as in Baluze’s edition.

“Will be” (*esse*). Added from Royal manuscript 1, Colbert manuscript 1, Em., and St Augustine.

“Through some inexplicable” (*qua incredibili*). See the *Epitome*, ch. 67, near the middle; elsewhere ch. 8, near the end.

“That” (*illud*). Thus I read with Royal manuscript 1, Colbert manuscript 1, the Sorbonne and Victorine manuscripts, Em., and the new edition of St Augustine. The other Colbert manuscript and Baluze’s edition [source text breaks off].

“Tishbite” (*Thesbiten*). This is the reading of St Augustine and the Lactantian manuscripts, except one Colbert manuscript, which, with Baluze’s edition, has *Thesbitem*.

[Col. 0822C]

“Separation” (*diremptionem*), that is, *separationem*. The Victorine manuscript has in the margin *discussionem* (“distinction” or “examination”); five manuscripts and Baluze’s edition read *direptionem* (“plundering”), incorrectly. With St Augustine I read *diremptionem*, a word though unusual and scarcely Latin, having the same sense as Cicero’s *diremptus*, who says: “Death is, as it were, a departure, a separation, and a sundering of those parts which before death were held together by some union,” *Tusculan Disputations* I.71.

“And its renewal” (*ejusdemque*). Thus I restore the text from Royal manuscript 1, the Sorbonne and Victorine manuscripts, Colbert manuscript 1, Em., and St Augustine. The other Colbert manuscript and Baluze’s edition read: “and finally its” (*ejus denique*).]

[Col. 0823]

DISSERTATION ON THE SEVEN BOOKS OF THE *DIVINE INSTITUTIONS*, BY DOM NICOLAS LE NOURRY, O.S.B.

[Col. 0823A] CHAPTER ONE. Analysis of the seven books.

ARTICLE I. Analysis of the first book.

Lactantius began this book with a fairly lengthy preface, in which he sets forth before the eyes and view of all the reasons for the work he has undertaken. He relates (ch. 1) that many men of great and distinguished ability, having abandoned all private resources and public occupations, devoted themselves wholly to the pursuit of truth, but utterly wasted both oil and labour. For truth, he says, being the secret of the supreme God, cannot be comprehended by any powers of human intellect alone. [Col. 0823B] Yet God, taking pity on man as he sought it with such zeal, did not permit him to wander long; rather, he showed him the light of wisdom and the way to attain immortality. But because that way is still obstructed by the greatest difficulties, few avail themselves of this heavenly gift. Lactantius therefore judged that these persons ought to be aided, so that he might direct the learned to true wisdom and the unlearned to true religion. By the example of Greek orators and philosophers, he shows this to be far more useful and glorious than the art of rhetoric, in which he himself had long been engaged, instructing young men not in virtue but in a thoroughly subtle malice. Yet he does not deny that by this exercise he acquired the capacity to defend and plead the cause of truth with greater abundance and power of speech—though it can be defended even without these [Col. 0823C].

He accordingly declares that he has all the more right to undertake a discussion of religion and divine matters because the greatest orators, at the very end of their lives, vainly and uselessly consumed laborious effort in the study of philosophy. Moreover, if certain men issued *Institutions of Civil Law* in order to settle the disputes of quarrelling citizens, how much more should Divine Institutions be committed to writing, by which deadly superstitions and most shameful errors may be lulled to sleep and uprooted.

If the various manuscript and printed copies are to be trusted, our author there addresses Constantine the Great, praises him for restoring the worship of the true God, and unhesitatingly promises him and his sons happiness to be given by God. He hopes that in seven volumes he will establish and illuminate the truth of our religion briefly, indeed, in proportion to the abundance of material [Col. 0824A], but so clearly and perspicuously that it is remarkable that it should seem obscure to men, especially to the wise or philosophers. Once they have recognized it, he will send them to the most abundant fountain of doctrine; by drinking from it, provided that they do not cling too stubbornly to their superstitions, everything will become easy and clear to them. Then all will readily recognize this as the sum of true religion: that no religion is to be embraced without wisdom, nor any wisdom approved without religion.

After this preface, he openly declares that he did not think it proper to begin this work from the question which appears first: whether providence governs all things, or whether all things have been made and are conducted by chance, as the Epicureans dreamed [Col. 0824B] (ch. 2). This error of theirs belongs either to atheists or to fools; it has been sufficiently refuted by other pagan philosophers, especially the Stoics and Cicero himself, though an Academic, and will be refuted throughout these books. He therefore begins from another question, though one close to the former: whether the world is ruled by the power of one God or many. First, then, Lactantius demonstrates by various arguments drawn from natural reason that this world was created by one God and is governed by his providence, and overturns the opposing sophisms of his adversaries (ch. 3). He next proves the same conclusion by the authority of the prophets, which, although the pagans cannot reject it, he treats more briefly because of their blindness and obstinacy [Col. 0824C] (ch. 4). He presses them more vigorously (ch. 5) with the testimonies of their own pagan authors whom they praised: especially the poets Orpheus, Homer, and Hesiod; then the philosophers Thales, Pythagoras, Anaxagoras, Antisthenes, Cleanthes, Anaximenes, Chrysippus, Aristotle, Cicero, and Seneca; and finally seers inspired, as those pagans themselves believed, by a divine spirit—Mercury surnamed Trismegistus, whom the Egyptians called Thoyth (ch. 6) and whom others worshipped as a god; and the Sibyls. Concerning the Sibyls’ name, authority, number, and preserved verses, he offers much preliminary discussion, and then presents many of their poems, omitting others. To these he appends a celebrated oracle of Delphic Apollo, confirmed by Trismegistus (ch. 7).

Then he replies to those who, following Cicero, might perhaps ask him what the blessed solitude of one God could be [Col. 0825A]. God, he says, as Seneca writes, begot ministers of his kingdom—namely angels—who are not gods and neither wish to be worshipped nor called gods. The pagans, however, bestowed the venerable name of divinity upon their fictitious deities, deceived by Apollo’s false testimony, for Apollo once enrolled himself among the angels, although elsewhere he admitted that he was a demon. Accordingly, he exhorts the pagans to cast off their errors and acknowledge the true God, whose power cannot be measured, whose greatness cannot be discerned, and whose beginning cannot be comprehended (ch. 8). He confirms this by the testimony of Apollo, the Sibyl, and Plato. Therefore God is sufficiently known to no one but himself, he who created all things by infinite power.

[Col. 0825B] Turning then to the gods of the pagans, he rejects their false and invented divinity because they were said to have been born of a male and female, and therefore were neither incorporeal nor immortal—the qualities which, as the Sibyl says, the true God must possess. Nor does he allow the objection that God needs sex in order to have ministers. For if he gave certain living creatures, that is, bees, the power to gather for themselves offspring born from flowers with their mouths, how much more can he himself, being omnipotent, create ministers and others at will without sexual union.

Furthermore, in a longer exposition our author makes it clear to all that the ridiculous troop of gods consists of human kings who had been beloved by their subjects because of outstanding deeds or benefits conferred (ch. 9). He places Hercules at the head of their company [Col. 0825C]: born from Alcmena’s adultery, he polluted the world with his debaucheries and adulteries. Nothing divine, therefore, could be in him—unless perhaps his various labours and contests, which are here recounted one by one. Yet these, as Cicero also testifies, show that he was a very brave man, but by no means a god. What, moreover, of the fact that his weakness and depravity were most clearly apparent when he served, shamefully, King Erythraeus, and, more shamefully still, the wanton woman Omphale? Nor should anyone say that no faith should be given to the poets who invented these things. For no other writers could be produced who either denied them or related what was admirable and divine in their gods.

What deed of Aesculapius, born from Apollo’s crime, was worthy of divine honours? Was it because he healed Hippolytus? But precisely for this he was struck by a thunderbolt [Col. 0825D] (ch. 10). Tarquitius recounts his origin from uncertain parents and his other human deeds, just as Cicero identifies his tomb. Nor was his father Apollo any better: he tended another man’s flock, built walls for Laomedon, and violated a boy. Mars, a murderer and Venus’s adulterer, and Castor and Pollux, abductors of brides, are sung of by the poets as living alternately, and are said by Homer to have been buried. Although Mercury was a thief and rascal, he was nevertheless enrolled among the gods because he was said to have invented the lyre and taught wrestling. Liber received the same honour because of his expedition into India, but burned with mad love for a woman.

[Col. 0826A] Even Jupiter, whom they call best, greatest, and father of all, was impious from childhood: he drove his father from his kingdom and, after conquering the Titans, lived a life infamous for so many and such horrible crimes that he ought never to have reigned on earth, much less in heaven (ch. 11). Thus a certain poet did not absurdly sing that he was led in chains before the chariot of triumphant Cupid. Lactantius presses the point that he is invoked by all pagans as God, though he was, as they said, born of Saturn and Rhea; that he alone abstained from Thetis lest he have anyone greater than his father; that he swore by the Stygian marsh; that he obeyed fate and the power of the Fates; and that he is called Ζεύς (*Zeus*) because he was the first of Saturn’s children to be saved alive.

There Lactantius again refutes those who objected [Col. 0826B] that these were poets’ inventions and lies. For the poets did not invent the deeds themselves, as he proves through various examples; rather, by poetic license they added many things to them, in order to persuade people that they were recounting them not of men but of gods. And if the poets lied, why do the pagans worship and represent their gods as the poets had depicted them? Moreover, the pagans could not deny that Euhemerus had written a true history of the gods, which Ennius later translated. But because poets had transferred additional features from it to the gods for the charm of their poems, certain people accused them of lying. He proves this by various examples, from which he concludes that what the poets say is true, but related under some covering and appearance. Yet when philosophers recognized these things as false, they imagined two Jupiters, though in no lesser error: one natural, the other wholly fabulous. Nor indeed could anyone answer that by the name Jupiter he understands and worships the true God. For Jupiter, Lactantius says, is not customarily worshipped apart from the society of his wife and daughter; and his name signifies only a human, not a divine, power. Finally, by the already cited testimonies of Ennius, the Sibyl, and Cicero, he conclusively proves that this Jupiter died and was buried in Crete, and that the Capitol is his empty memorial. The pagans could never prove these claims to be poets’ inventions.

Lactantius continues that there was likewise nothing in Saturn worthy of divine majesty. Although they vaunted that he had introduced the Golden Age [Col. 0826D], it was nevertheless more certain that he had been born from Heaven and Earth, just as other gods were said either to have been born from mountains and rivers or to have given their names to seas. For from Trismegistus and Ennius we learn that his father was Uranus, to whom Jupiter first sacrificed, having set up an altar on a mountain, and whose name he gave to Heaven. Nor did he perform only this sacrifice, but another also on the shore, when he set out from the island of Naxos against the Titans, as Aglaosthenes says. But this same Heaven, or Uranus, died in Ocean, as Euhemerus reports, and was buried in the town of Aulatia.

[Col. 0827A] Lactantius rightly concludes from this account that Saturn was not a god, since he was an impious man who cut off his father’s genitals and devoured his sons, born from Rhea or Ops—except Jupiter, who was removed by the stratagem of his mother and the Corybantes (chs. 12 and 13). There he again rejects the Stoics’ reply, by which they attempted to convert this fable into a physical explanation (ch. 13). Saturn proved himself to be a man not only by the crimes mentioned, but also because, stripped of his sovereignty and a fugitive, he came by ship to Italy. There, after lying hidden, he was received by Janus and reigned first—or, at least, second after Uranus. Our author makes clear that these matters were transmitted by various historical writers and poets, whom he names. But [Col. 0827B] because Ennius differed somewhat from them, he briefly describes what Ennius and the Sibyl recount in nearly the same manner concerning Saturn’s deeds (ch. 14).

Taking the opportunity, he recounts what he considers to have been the origin of idolatry (ch. 15). In the time of this Saturn, he says, men still uncultivated called their king and all his descendants gods, whether through wonder at their power, flattery of present authority, or gratitude for benefits received. Later others made images of their dead kings, either to console their grief or to stimulate virtue. Hence came the fabricated divinity of Hercules, Castor, Pollux, Aesculapius, and Liber. Hence the Egyptians’ Isis, the Moors’ Juba, the Macedonians’ Cabirus, the Carthaginians’ Uranus, and the Romans’ Quirinus [Col. 0827C] and their Caesars. Hence others worshipped others as true gods.

Furthermore, certain persons, led by false piety—such as Aeneas, Liber, Pan, Mercury, and Apollo—paid divine honour to their parents and by their example led others into the same error. But this crime was later enlarged by those who, deceived by poets’ inventions and lying panegyrics, handed on to other peoples the utterly impious rites they themselves had adopted; yet they are severely rebuked by the Sibyl. Cicero was one of them. Although, following Plato, he declared that the gods of his pagans had been men, he nevertheless professed that he would consecrate an image of his dead daughter as though she were a goddess. Certainly, if something must be allowed to those grieving so bitterly, no pardon can be granted to those who seriously believe such things. For what could be madder than to declare and worship Julius Caesar as a god because it pleased the criminal Antony, and Quirinus or Romulus because Proculus committed perjury [Col. 0827D] (ch. 16)? He further exposes the madness of these and other pagans who worship such gods by noting that they asserted them to be male and female. For if difference of sex exists among them, then they have intercourse and bear children; therefore they inhabit houses and cities; therefore they cultivate fields for sustenance; and accordingly they are not gods, but mortal and weak creatures. Moreover, the female sex is weaker than the male. But no such weakness, nor any other, belongs to the true God.

[Col. 0828A] After our Lactantius had established this by Cicero’s testimony (ch. 17), he utterly overturns their fabricated divinity—joined by the Stoics to an account of natural things—by pointing out the age and death represented in the image of each, their celebrated sufferings, for example those of Isis, Ceres, Latona, and Juno, and the publicized crimes, debaucheries, and adulteries of Venus, who instituted the art of prostitution; likewise those of Vulcan, Minerva, Aesculapius, and many others whom he names individually (ch. 18). No less plainly does he show the folly of those who thought that men had become gods through bodily strength, or through discovering grain, wine, or particular arts (ch. 19). Nor should it be said that they are owed even some veneration and worship. For it cannot happen that one who worships these should worship the true God. Then Virgil sang that they are all among the dead below. Yet he and other poets, although they are mistaken in calling them gods, do not err in recounting their various deeds, wars, adulteries, wounds, and death.

Lactantius then turns to the Romans’ particular religions and clearly shows that they placed prostitutes and courtesans among the number of gods, especially the she-wolf who nursed Romulus, just as the Athenians had previously placed a lioness there [Col. 0828B] (ch. 20). But undoubtedly the Romans’ impiety was greater when, in honour of the she-wolf, they established both a festival day and the Larentalia. They also worshipped Faula, Hercules’ prostitute, and Flora, a courtesan, in whose memory they celebrated the most obscene Floralia. What, too, of the fact that Tatius consecrated Cloacina; Tullus Hostilius, Terror and Pallor; Marcellus, Honour and Virtue; and the Senate, Mind; while—worse still—others consecrated and worshipped Rust and Fever as true gods? Why say more? As the Lacedaemonians made an image of armed Venus, so the Romans made a temple to Bald Venus and, at the same time, an altar to Jupiter the Baker. Finally, their divine powers included Fornax, Muta or Lara, Caca, and Cunina; the god Sterculius and Termin​us; and a thousand other monstrosities of the blind and wandering human mind.

If, therefore, the pagans displayed such madness in creating their gods, their madness was surely greater in instituting and celebrating their solemn rites (ch. 21). For what is madder and more cruel than the human sacrifices offered [Col. 0828D] to Jupiter, Diana, Hesus, Teutates, and Saturn? The rites of the Mother of the Gods, of Virtue or Bellona, and of Egyptian Isis were customarily performed either by castration, by the shedding of human blood, or by shaving the body and beating the breast. And because in these rites the name of the sought-for Osiris had been changed, Lactantius proves there by various examples that the names of gods were altered after their deaths. But let us proceed, if you please. The mysteries of Eleusinian Ceres, he says, were performed with the greatest obscenity; he censures this as it deserves and shows in the same place that the rites of Hercules and Jupiter are sheer sacrilege. He refutes Sallust and others who wished to interpret such things ingeniously. By the writings of the pontiffs and by the example of Furius Bibuculus [Col. 0829A], he demonstrates with what credulity, shamefulness, and impiety the pagans celebrated all these things.

The author of these vanities among the Romans was the Sabine king, that is, Numa Pompilius. In order more safely to deceive the people, he pretended to converse with Egeria, just as Minos had once pretended to converse with Jupiter (ch. 22). But books on pontifical law, discovered long after his death, exposed the wickedness of this deceitful king; in them the impious king dissolved all religion. Although these books were burned by decree of the senate, the memory of this deed was not thereby abolished but rather commended to posterity. Earlier, Faunus in Latium prescribed wicked rites to Saturn, his grandfather, and numbered among the gods his father Picus and his sister Fatua Fauna, whose ridiculous mysteries Lactantius there recounts. He adds the rites of Father Liber introduced into Greece by Orpheus, and inquires whether Orpheus was older than Faunus. He then makes plain to us what were the opinions of Didymus and Euhemerus concerning the origin of idolatry, and how temples were built to Jupiter Atabyrius, Labradeus, Laprius, Molion, and Cassius. Finally, from the writings of Theophilus of Antioch, he concludes that the pagans boast vainly of the antiquity of their gods and rites, since Saturn, progenitor of all the gods, had been born no more than 1,800 years before these books of law were made public [Col. 0829B] (ch. 23).

ARTICLE II. Analysis of the second book.

In this book Lactantius undertakes to disclose the foul and utterly corrupt source of the error by which men fell into idolatry, and to establish the supreme majesty of the one God [Col. 0829C] (ch. 1). First, he marvels that men had come into such forgetfulness both of God and of themselves that, denying God’s providence, they preferred the dead to him and believed their own soul to be mortal. For, he says, knowledge and awareness of the true God are so deeply implanted in their minds that, when swearing, making wishes, giving thanks, and especially in adversity, they name him alone and not other gods. But blind men, once danger had passed or in prosperity, eagerly rushed, at the devil’s instigation, to temples of the gods; they sacrificed to these false gods and crowned them. Yet these impious men had forgotten that their upright stature, raised toward heaven, and the name ἄνθρωπος (*anthrōpos*, “human being”) admonished them to acknowledge God, and not, turning toward images, fear or venerate the works of their own fingers [Col. 0829D].

Our author clearly demonstrates how absurd this superstition is from the fact that these images represent men who were absent and dead long ago and are wholly without sensation (ch. 2). Being fashioned by human hands, they ought rather to worship men than to be worshipped by them. For they receive no power from the artisan, who cannot give them the capacity which he possesses for seeing, hearing, speaking, or moving himself. Lactantius shows that this opinion concerning image-worship was held not merely by unlearned men but by learned men as well, and especially by Cicero [Col. 0830A]. Although Cicero accumulated many arguments throughout his books for overthrowing the religions of those pagans, he nevertheless, fearing Socrates’ prison, denied that these matters should be publicly discussed (ch. 3). Our author rightly rebukes this foolish fear in so great an orator, acting against his own conscience. He consequently declares Cicero and others like him less worthy of pardon than the ignorant multitude, who are deceived by the appearance of images. Yet if these people had sound minds, they certainly ought to have understood that whatever we see with our eyes is truly mortal and therefore neither divine nor to be worshipped. Still less was it lawful for them to turn to a stone and worship it with covered head and prostrate body, to slaughter victims for it, and to make utterly useless vows.

Then, after our author had most plainly established that false religions were rightly assailed by the more prudent, but that the true religion—which God alone can teach—had not been discovered by them, he again attacks the images of gods (ch. 4). It lay in the power of a mere man to make them, or to make something else, or to make nothing. Once made, birds perch and nest upon them and defile them with their droppings. Moreover, these images can perish and be burned. Very often they have been reduced to ashes or become plunder for thieves. The pagans therefore adorned them in vain with gold, ivory, gems, and precious clothing. They were nothing else than larger dolls, like those which girls dedicated to Venus. In addition, Dionysius, tyrant of Sicily, and the impious Verres mocked, stripped, and carried them off with impunity. Lactantius particularly presses the case of the image of Ceres of Catana or Enna, taken away by Verres [Col. 0830C].

He therefore concludes that those impious cults must be abandoned and that our eyes must be raised to heaven, in order that we may acknowledge and honour him who created it and all things [Col. 0830C] (ch. 5). By various arguments he proves false the opinion of philosophers who attributed soul and divinity to the elements, and especially of the Stoics, who attributed them to the stars or the world. He further reproves those who not only worshipped figures of the elements represented in human form and adorned with gold, ivory, and gems, but also consecrated to them their spoils and plunder [Col. 0830D] (ch. 6). Yet they defended those absurd superstitions with such obstinacy that they cried out that it was a crime to investigate them. But by the example of Romulus and Numa, our author proves that truth must be sought not through unjust tradition or the errors of others, but through intelligence and wisdom (ch. 7).

The pagans, however, thought that the strongest argument for retaining their religions was derived from prodigies, dreams, auguries, and oracles, by which they asserted that the gods had made their majesty manifest to all. For, they said, Accius Navius could not have cut a whetstone with a razor without a great miracle; Castor and Pollux were seen fighting and announcing victory over King Perseus. The images of Fortuna Muliebris and Juno Moneta also spoke. Claudia Quintia drew by her girdle the ship that carried the image of the Idaean Mother [Col. 0831A]. Aesculapius stopped a plague at Rome. The censor Claudius was blinded because of his sacrileges against the gods; Fulvius died mad; Turullius was killed; Pyrrhus suffered shipwreck; and Alexander’s soldiers were deprived of the light of their eyes. Indeed, Attinius, who had not obeyed Jupiter’s command given in a dream, was struck down and finally recovered his former health through obedience. Finally, Caesar Augustus escaped danger through Artorius’s dream. From all these prodigies and miracles, which they thought could not occur without the assistance of their gods, the pagans concluded that those gods truly existed and were omnipotent.

But Lactantius replies that none of these things was done by the power of those gods, but by the deceits of demons [Col. 0831B] (ch. 8). To make this manifest to all, he begins again from the very origin of the matter. God, he says, at the beginning of the world brought forth a spirit like himself and made another who, through envy, became evil from being good and received the name devil. By various arguments and ancient testimonies, our author proves against Epicurus that neither the world nor matter existed from eternity, but were made from nothing by God, who placed his Son over their creation. The last of all creatures to be created was man, whose role is not to search out secrets which God willed to remain hidden; rather, man’s highest wisdom is to acknowledge this true God, by whom all those things were made [Col. 0831C] (ch. 9). He began so great a work with heaven, distinguished by the lights of the stars, and established the opposed regions of the earth: east set against west, and north against south. From the east our day rises, and night from the west; and the latter belongs to the devil, as the former belongs to God. To those four regions of the earth belong heat and cold and the various changes of seasons; while to fire and water belongs the generation of all things. From this, undoubtedly, certain philosophers taught that all things are formed from a discordant harmony, or from fire, as Heraclitus held, or from water, as Thales of Miletus taught. Yet the material of living bodies is in moisture, whereas that of the soul is in fire. But living creatures use water, and man alone uses fire.

God created living creatures of various kinds; and when He had resolved to create innumerable souls, He made man like Himself from the earth, whence man derived his name [Col. 0831D] (ch. 10). Mere fables, therefore, are those of the poets in which man is said to have been fashioned by Prometheus, father of Deucalion, whom they invent to have been the sole survivor of the flood. But it is true, Lactantius says, that from this same Prometheus came the art of fashioning statues and images, and that in his time temples were first built and the worship of false gods introduced. He further confirms, on the authority of Hermes, that man was produced by God; and he rejects the foolish errors of philosophers who babbled that living creatures had sprung from the earth without any maker, or that the world had always existed, or would always exist. There he attacks Lucretius at greater length. Lucretius, in his usual manner, peddles nonsense when he sings that animals and men derived not only their food but also their origin [Col. 0832A] from the earth’s little sacs, as though from their wombs (ch. 11). Since these things could not have happened by chance, divine providence—by which man was truly created, as Cicero and the Sibyl attest—had to be acknowledged even by that poet against his will.

After God had formed the body of man and infused a soul into it, He then fashioned woman, that offspring might be propagated from the two (ch. 12). Although the opinion of Trismegistus and Empedocles that man is composed of four elements is not wholly false, Lactantius nevertheless maintains that these are reducible to two, fire and water: the latter enclosed in the body, the former in the soul. Thus man consists of body and soul, images respectively of heaven and earth, so that the soul, which is from God, holds dominion and the higher place over the body; whereas the body, [Col. 0832B] which belongs to the devil, occupies the lower. Since man is composed of these two opposing things, there is within him a mutual conflict between them, as between light and darkness, life and death. If the soul conquers, it will become immortal, or enjoy blessed immortality; but if it is conquered, it will be afflicted with the second death—that is, eternal punishments.

Thus created, man was placed in paradise to serve God free from every labor. But because the first woman, at the devil’s instigation, and then man, broke the law given by God, their expulsion from paradise was followed by death. Human life was extended to a thousand years; and, after all those persons had subsequently perished in the flood because of their crimes, to one hundred and twenty years (ch. 13). After that flood Noah—and by no means Bacchus—planted a vineyard with his own hand. Intoxicated by its fruit, he lay naked; and he disowned his son Ham, who had not covered his nakedness. Ham, a fugitive, at last established his dwelling in that part of the earth which was called Canaan. His descendants, the Canaanites, were the first of all to abandon the worship of the true God, which remained among the Hebrews. Afterwards the Egyptians began to worship the stars, and then monstrous figures of animals. The others, scattered over the earth, honored the elements without images or temples and offered sacrifices to them in the open air, until, in the course of time, they built temples for the most powerful kings.

Moreover, since God had from the beginning given the devil power over the earth, He sent angels to guard men, lest the devil corrupt those who had begun to multiply [Col. 0832D] (ch. 14). But these angels, at the devil’s persuasion, had intercourse with women; for so great a crime they fell to earth and became attendants of that same devil. From them were begotten very many unclean spirits, having a nature intermediate between angels and men. Under their prince, the devil, they are authors of every evil and are recognized by poets and philosophers. They know many things, though not all, and therefore give ambiguous answers to those who consult them. Moreover, they wish to appear as guardians of men so that they may be worshiped by them, but they deceive them through magical arts. To lead men more easily into error, they roam throughout the earth under the name of genii, and, by the subtlety of their spirit, insinuate themselves into [Col. 0833A] human bodies, afflicting them with diseases and terrifying them with dreams.

It must not be said that they ought to be worshiped so that they may do no harm. For they harm none except worshipers of idols and those who fear them (ch. 15). On the contrary, they fear worshipers of the true God: adjured by His name, they are put to flight and, even against their will, proclaim who they themselves are. Indeed, Hermes and Asclepius once testified that worshipers of the true God are safe from their assaults. From these spirits, Lactantius says, astrology, divination from entrails, augury, necromancy, and other evil arts were invented; through all these deceptions they falsely claim to be gods and, once idolatry has been introduced, mock mankind (ch. 16). Magicians, however, by their accursed art summon them by their true names. Yet these wandering and incestuous spirits so disturb everything and mingle falsehood with truth that, although other holy and immortal angels neither wish nor permit themselves to be called gods, these most wicked spirits have very often claimed for themselves the name and worship of gods.

Having thus explained these matters, our author resolves the argument proposed above, by which pagans wrongly endeavored to infer from the aforementioned prodigies, dreams, auguries, and oracles that their gods exist and ought to be worshiped. For he maintains that these things have been done by the evil arts, illusions, deceits, and frauds of the demons we have described—demons who hide themselves in temples and attend the sacrifices of the impious. Having reconsidered and examined one by one all the alleged prodigies and miracles, as they called them, he makes this altogether plain and evident to anyone.

[Col. 0833C] “Why then,” the pagans asked, “does God permit these things to occur?” “So that evils may contend with goods,” Lactantius replies, “and that God, whose patience and wrath are perfect, may render to pious and impious men, after the end of the world, eternal rewards or punishments” (ch. 17). Finally, by a brief recapitulation of what he had written in this book, he concludes that God is to be sought neither on earth nor in images, which present nothing but what is feigned and false, but in heaven, whence our souls originate. Then, having set forth the subject of the following book, he brings this one to an end.

## ARTICLE III. Analysis of the Third Book

[Col. 0833D] Lactantius, intending in this book to dispute against pagan philosophers, wishes for an ability approaching Cicero’s eloquence, by which he might more easily demonstrate the vanity of philosophy and philosophers (ch. 1). Yet, relying upon the power of truth, which reveals itself by its own brightness, he hopes to prove by the most certain arguments that the opinions of those philosophers are as false as their own confession of ignorance is true.

His first argument is drawn from the name philosophy, or “love of wisdom.” By it Pythagoras, its author, although somewhat wiser than others, indicated that no human effort can attain true wisdom (ch. 2). For philosophers cannot truly be called lovers of wisdom, since, after the longest study through so many ages, they have not obtained it.

There are three branches of philosophy: physics, logic, and ethics; these must rest either upon knowledge or opinion (ch. 3). But what knowledge can there be in physics, when we cannot discern the causes of natural things? Who has ever clearly ascertained the size of the sun’s body, the nature of the moon’s, the arrangement of the stars, or the thickness of the earth? Socrates and the Academics therefore rightly took knowledge away from all philosophers. Thus opinion alone is found in this first part of philosophy (chs. 4–5). Yet opinion provides nothing certain and leaves us so doubtful that we may affirm nothing on either side [Col. 0834B]. Hence Zeno and the Stoics rightly rejected opinion itself. Those who boast that physics contains some pursuit of wisdom are therefore mistaken.

Furthermore, philosophers are divided into so many schools, so widely at variance with one another, and the defenders of those schools fight among themselves so fiercely that, by mutual wounds, they kill and destroy both themselves and philosophy with them. From these disputes emerged Arcesilaus, who asserted that nothing whatever can be known. But by overthrowing the opinions of others, he established his own no more firmly than they had established theirs. For, just as we are ignorant of many things, so we have clear knowledge of many others (ch. 6). We should not suppose that we know everything—that belongs to God—nor that we know nothing—that belongs to a beast. Man therefore possesses knowledge joined with ignorance [Col. 0834C]: the former arises from the body, the latter from the mind. Thus the physicists who babbled that they could know everything are wholly astray; and Arcesilaus is deceived, together with the Academics, in judging that nothing can be known.

Lactantius then turns to the other branch of philosophy, called ethics, in which error is attended by far greater danger (ch. 7). How far philosophers departed from the truth in it, he clearly demonstrates from their various opinions concerning the highest good, upon which the whole hinge of wisdom turns. How numerous those opinions were may be inferred from the fact that he enumerates and refutes, one by one, not all of them but ten principal ones (ch. 8). He next rebukes Anaxagoras, who dreamed that the highest good lay in believing himself born for the purpose of beholding heaven and the sun [Col. 0834D] (ch. 9). Man is born, indeed, to contemplate, honor, and serve alone the Creator of heaven and all things. From this our author concludes that the highest good is recognized only by those who profess the worship of the true God and true religion (ch. 10). Moreover, by several arguments—not insignificant ones—he proves that this highest good cannot be attained by any but worshipers of true religion, which ought therefore to be embraced by all. Nor did philosophers deny that true religion should be embraced; but because they did not know that it could not be separated from wisdom, they failed to perceive what that religion is from which the highest good must be sought—a good which cannot be placed in pleasure, riches, kingship, or glory [Col. 0835A] (ch. 11). For virtue, than which nothing is more beautiful and honorable, despises all such fleeting and fragile goods and fights against unlawful desires and vices, so that, once these have been overcome, man may become unstained and attain blessed immortality (ch. 12).

Lactantius proves, by the authority of Euclid, Seneca, the Stoics, and Anaxagoras, and maintains by various arguments, that this good lies precisely in immortality. Indeed, as he adds, Menoeceus, Codrus, Curtius, and Mures met death steadfastly in hope of immortality. Certainly, philosophers who judged the soul immortal ought plainly to have approved this, had they not clung to their errors with excessive obstinacy. Others, however, who placed the highest good in knowledge or virtue, held the path of truth but did not arrive at the true highest good. For it lies in that happy immortality to which virtue leads, and which is granted only to worshipers of true religion.

Then, postponing the question of the soul’s immortality, Lactantius teaches that the other part of philosophy, called logic, is not needed for acquiring divine instruction, because wisdom lies not in words but in things and in the heart (ch. 13). But if this branch of philosophy, and likewise physics, cannot make one blessed and are therefore unnecessary; if in physics and in ethics, to which Socrates devoted himself, errors are so great as has been said—what remains except to conclude that pagan philosophy is false and empty?

[Col. 0835C] Those therefore err who think philosophy to be wisdom, and above all Cicero, who had said that it could not be criticized and was the teacher of virtue and justice. In this very matter he is convicted of greater inconsistency than Lucretius. For that poet extols Epicurus, the founder of his school, with extravagant and foolish, but always identical, praises. Cicero, however, never ceases to accuse of intolerable fickleness the Greeks whom he praises and follows (ch. 14). He also calls philosophy the parent of life, yet denies that anyone has ever been wise. He often boasts that he studied philosophy diligently; but, following the position of the Academics, he could surely attain nothing certain through so great a study.

If Cicero erred, who will ever assert with certainty that he has attained truth [Col. 0835D]? Certainly not Seneca, who wrongly defined philosophy as the method, art, or science of living rightly and honorably (ch. 15). For it is false, diverse, manifold, and contrary to itself. Moreover, there are good people without philosophy. Philosophers, on the other hand, are angry, greedy, lustful, and arrogant. Lactantius demonstrates this from examples drawn from Cicero, Cornelius Nepos, Aristippus, the Cynics, and Seneca himself.

Why say more? Philosophers spent their lives not in works of virtue but in the study of eloquence (ch. 16). From philosophy itself they sought not usefulness but pleasure [Col. 0836A]. Finally, Cicero, Lucretius, and Seneca acknowledge that philosophy has a recent origin. Persius, moreover, sang that it was brought to Rome in a later age along with pepper and dates. But wisdom began with man and preceded pagan philosophy by many ages.

Lactantius then advances to the philosophers themselves and utterly overthrows their chief doctrines. Beginning with Epicurus, whose school was more celebrated than the rest, he shows that Epicurus indulged everyone in what suited his disposition best and foolishly contradicted himself in maintaining that pleasure was the highest good. Next our author explains why Epicurus denied providence and attacks this error with several arguments. By similar arguments he uproots another opinion, no less absurd, which Epicurus had received from Leucippus and Democritus: namely, that all things happen by the chance collision of atoms. He continues his attack upon Lucretius, who flattered that view. Finally, he declares still more false the claim proclaimed by that impious man that our souls are mortal.

He judges the Pythagoreans and Stoics no more tolerable, since they taught that souls enter bodies but migrate from one body to another (ch. 18). Those who supposed them immortal, he says, laid violent hands upon themselves, as though about to migrate to heaven: Cleanthes, Chrysippus, Zeno, Empedocles, and Cato. Democritus, though guided by another opinion, and Ambraciotes, after reading Plato’s book on the immortality of the soul, imitated them. But what madness, insanity, and frenzy, pray, could be greater than that of these murderers?

[Col. 0836C] Lactantius also inveighs against those—and especially against Cicero—who taught that life is evil and death good, or that man’s first good is not to be born and his second to die quickly (ch. 19). With no feeble arm he shakes this error and rightly concludes that death is good or evil according to the deeds of one’s former life. Nor was Plato wiser. Embracing Pythagoras’s error of the transmigration of souls—and the error of Pythagoras foolishly proclaiming himself to have been Euphorbus—he gave thanks to nature that he was a man, a male, an Athenian, and had lived in Socrates’ time. Did not Alcibiades and Critias constantly hear Plato [Col. 0836D]? Yet the one became an enemy of his country, the other a tyrant.

Lactantius nevertheless admits that Socrates was somewhat more sensible than the other philosophers who asserted that the nature of things could be comprehended by human intelligence (ch. 20). For these were doubtless more criminal than those excessively inquisitive persons who entered, contrary to prohibition, the shrine of Vesta, the Good Goddess, or Ceres. Yet he maintains that many of Socrates’ doctrines deserve the strongest censure, especially the saying: “What is above us is nothing to us.” He is to be praised, indeed, if by this pronouncement he intended to overthrow the public religions of the pagans; but in this he was superstitious, like the Egyptians, that he swore by a dog and a goose, and before death ordered that a cock which he had vowed be sacrificed to Aesculapius on his behalf [Col. 0837A].

As regards Plato, what, I ask, is more contrary to modesty, marital fidelity, human society, and justice than his doctrine that marriages ought to be held in common? In this way he reduced human life to the likeness of beasts (chs. 21–22). Was he also of sound mind when, seeing that the functions of the same beasts, male and female alike, were common, he inferred that our women also should bear arms and undertake magistracies and rule? Why, by the same reasoning, did he not assign to men spinning wool and carrying infants?

Did Democritus not also talk nonsense among the lesser philosophers when he made his fields public pastureland (ch. [Col. 0837B] 23)? Was not he more mad who converted his estate into money and threw it into the sea? Certainly, like Tuditanus, each should have distributed it among the people—or rather bestowed it upon the needy. Is not Zeno likewise ridiculous, when he taught that sins are equal and classed mercy among vices and diseases? What should one make of another philosopher who declared snow to be black? What of Xenophanes, who thought that the globe of the moon was eighteen times larger than the earth, and inhabited by people other than those of this earth? Finally, what should one make of Seneca, who doubted whether some peoples might inhabit the globe of the sun?

Lactantius also judges those to stray from truth who confidently affirm the existence of antipodes and, as he calls them, “men hanging downward” (ch. 24). For these, he says, ought to have excited greater wonder in us than the hanging gardens so much celebrated of old in everyone’s discourse.

He then returns to philosophy, which Cicero declares to flee the multitude and to be acquired only by the learned (ch. 25). “That,” Lactantius says, “is not wisdom, which, bestowed upon men without any distinction, can be apprehended by all.” Contrary to Cicero’s opinion, the Stoics held that slaves and women should philosophize; Epicurus, that the uneducated should do so; and Plato, that a state should be composed of wise men. But none of them brought this to completion. For grammar, rhetoric, geometry, music, and astronomy must first be learned. Yet women and the uneducated are not allowed to learn these sciences and arts. Therefore no woman besides Themistoclea, no slave besides Phaedo, and no barbarian besides Anacharsis cultivated philosophy [Col. 0837D]. Plato and Diogenes, who devoted themselves to it, were not slaves, as some suppose; slavery merely befell them.

On the contrary, all easily acquire the heavenly teaching handed down in the Christian religion; and, by observing its decrees—the only wisdom—they become, from wicked and unjust persons, righteous and good (ch. 26). For by a single washing, given freely, all wickedness is wiped away; when the old man has been laid aside, a new one is restored.

Lactantius admits that philosophers have many precepts; but they are, he says, of such little force that no one obeys them on their account [Col. 0838A] (ch. 27). There he thoroughly refutes the Stoics, who claimed that virtue alone produces the blessed life, and Epicurus, who declared the wise man blessed even amid tortures: first, because not every kind of torture, but only those endured for faith, justice, and God, makes a person blessed; and second, because God alone can give virtue its due reward, namely immortality and eternal blessedness. Philosophers, therefore, who seek this reward but do not hold true religion are wholly ignorant of the power and recompense of virtue.

Through ignorance of true religion, of the one supreme God, and of the worship due to Him, the same philosophers fell into the greatest errors (ch. 28). Hence they imagined Nature to be the mother of all things, or Fortune to be a goddess. Hence Empedocles complains that the paths of our senses are narrow [Col. 0838B]. Hence Anaxagoras dreamed that all things were surrounded by darkness; Democritus, that truth was submerged in a well; and the Academics, that nothing could be known. Lactantius overturns all these false opinions, especially the assertion that Fortune, a goddess, rules all things; and he completely refutes Cicero, its defender (ch. 29). Christians, he says, know well that no such Fortune exists, but rather an evil spirit, the enemy of justice and the ambusher of all good things, who has not immediately been thrust by God into punishment, in order that he may exercise man in virtue. Finally, having recapitulated what he had said in this book and set forth the subject of the preceding and following books, he brings it to an end.

## ARTICLE IV. Analysis of the Fourth Book

[Col. 0838C]

Lactantius marvels at and laments the blindness of men, who, abandoning the worship of the true God, began to venerate many invented gods and their images (ch. 1). From this, indeed, proceeded injustice, impiety, dissensions, frauds, crimes, gloom, and darkness. Yet seven men, after wisdom had been taken away, discussed natural matters and were called, by antonomasia, “the Wise.” But the small number of these men, themselves condemned by others for arrogance and ignorance, exposed the folly of all the rest. Philosophers after them, moreover, sought wisdom in vain where it was not to be found (ch. 2). For Pythagoras and Plato approached Egyptians, Magi, and Persians in order to investigate it and the truth, but by no means the Jews, among whom alone it remained. Lactantius judges that they were turned away from them by divine providence, lest they should know the truth which God had determined, as the last age approached, to disclose through the great Leader. He undertakes to demonstrate this in the present book, after showing that wisdom cannot be separated from religion.

He first makes clear what he had already demonstrated in the first book: wisdom is not found in the worship of many gods, but in true religion, in which one God only is worshiped, and it therefore cannot be separated from wisdom (ch. 3). For the worship of many gods is contrary both to reason and nature: as one man has one father and one master, so there is but one God [Col. 0839A]. Indeed, just as a marriage cannot be true where one woman has many husbands, so no religion is true which venerates many gods. Wisdom therefore commands us to love one God alone as Father, and religion commands us to fear Him as God (ch. 4). Neither, then, can be separated from the other. Accordingly, philosophers, like disowned sons or runaway slaves, will not receive the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, because they ignored God, the fountain of wisdom and of religion, wisdom’s inseparable companion. Do not reply that Plato and Cicero recognized Him. They did not render to the one true God the worship due to the sole Father, Lord, Governor, and holder of the power of life and death over all things.

The true God revealed this wisdom and religion to us. Before our author discusses Him and His works, he judged that the age of our sacred prophets, who foretold many things concerning Him, should briefly be explained (ch. 5). From this account all will readily understand, first, that they were earlier than Greek writers; and second, that what they prophesied concerning Christ is true, since we have seen fulfilled what they foretold.

Having prefaced these matters, he relates that, before undertaking the work of the world, God begot a spirit endowed with the Father’s power, whom He called His Son and God (ch. 6). He proves that this generation was announced by all prophets, both profane and sacred, specifically by the testimony of Trismegistus, the Sibyl, and Solomon. Although the name of the Son of God—who created the world by His own power and wisdom—is known only to Him and His Father, He is nevertheless called Jesus by men (ch. 7). Lactantius gives various reasons why He is called Christ by an appellation of power and kingship rather than by a proper name, and why He is Christ (*Christus*), not Chrestus (*Chrestus*), as some ignorant persons said.

Moreover, he clearly shows that not only Christ’s first and eternal generation, but also His second generation, by which He became man, was announced repeatedly by Jeremiah (ch. 8). But because this double generation had cast no small darkness over the minds of most men, including certain Christians, he explains the former as follows: the Son of God was begotten by His Father alone, without union with a woman. Although no human being can know or narrate how He was begotten, we learn from sacred writings that He is God’s speech and reason. He is the spirit whom God the Father conceived and begot from God as God: not silently, like angels, but vocal from His own mouth; not from a womb, but from His mind. Therefore He is rightly called the speech and word of God and remains forever. Our author endeavors to explain this more clearly by comparing it with the creation of angels and with human speech; and he establishes and confirms it by the words of the prophets David and Solomon and of John the Evangelist. Since He is the voice and wisdom of God, the Greeks have therefore called Him more aptly *logos* (λόγος) than the Latins have called Him *verbum* or *sermo*, “word” or “speech.” Lactantius adds that this *logos* was not wholly unknown to Zeno and Trismegistus (ch. 9).

[Col. 0840A] By the supreme ordinance of God, as the end of the age approached, He had to descend to earth—not “in the power of an angel,” nor in heavenly authority (these are our author’s own words), but in the form of a man and in a mortal condition—in order to teach men righteousness and establish for God a temple, that is, the Church (ch. 10). So that all might more readily recognize that wisdom is found in this Church or religion alone, he promises to demonstrate that the oracles fulfilled their purpose: the sacred prophets foretold that the Son of God would be born as a man, perform wonders, spread God’s worship throughout the earth, be fastened to a cross, and rise on the third day.

He thus begins the matter from its first origin. Our ancestors, the rulers of the Hebrews, left their native homes because of famine and migrated into Egypt. But because they were oppressed by an intolerable yoke of slavery, they were led out from there under Moses, after 430 years, and passed with him through the miraculously divided waves of the Red Sea [Col. 0840B]. When they had afterwards traversed vast wildernesses, they were not moved by the miracles performed by Moses and adopted the profane rites of the Egyptians. For this reason they paid the most grievous penalties for such ingratitude and so many crimes, and were sent under the yoke of the Mosaic law. Later, when they had settled in a part of Syria, that land was called Judaea and they themselves Jews. There, established first under judges and then under kings, they were afflicted, because of their sins and the adoption of corrupt religions, by wars and various forms of servitude; the last of these occurred at Babylon. Thereafter they had tetrarchs down to Herod and the fifteenth year of the emperor Tiberius, in which they put Christ to death by crucifixion.

Accordingly, after the Jews had thus defected to impious worships of gods, and had despised and killed the sacred prophets sent to them by God to exhort them to better conduct, God sent His Son—the maker of things and His counselor—to transfer holy religion to the nations, as Jeremiah, Ezra, Elijah, Malachi, David, and Isaiah had foretold [Col. 0840C] (ch. 11). Yet the Son of God, in order to leave those Jews free to follow God, chose a virgin from their nation and entered her womb, as Solomon, Isaiah, David, and Daniel had foretold long before (ch. 12). Our author therefore rightly rebukes them because they expect another Messiah. He plainly proves, from further words of Daniel, David, and Isaiah, that Christ is the true Messiah, born of this virgin and made truly human. Moreover, that by His first generation He came from the eternal Father without a mother’s office, just as by His second He came from His mother without a father’s office, and is true God and true man, was established not only by His deeds but also by the words of Isaiah, Jeremiah, David, and Moses cited by Lactantius, and even by Apollo of Miletus—although the latter speaks more obscurely of His divinity (ch. 13).

He then makes clear that the same prophets foretold in their oracles that Christ would be born of David’s family [Col. 0841A]. This is signified by the words of Isaiah and Nathan, which the Jews mistakenly tried to twist toward Solomon. With no less evidence he teaches that the priesthood of this same Christ in the Church founded by Him was predicted by the divine oracles of David, of the author of the First Book of Kings, and of Zechariah. The Jews vainly attempted to interpret these of Joshua, or of the priest Jesus son of Jozadak (ch. 14).

He proceeds from there to Christ’s miracles sung beforehand by those same sacred prophets, after demonstrating that they likewise foretold the voice heard at His baptism (ch. 15). Washed in that baptism, He healed by innumerable miracles—“wonder-working powers,” as Apollo calls them—paralytics, the lame, the blind, the mute, the deaf, lepers, and persons afflicted by any kind of disease, not by hand or medicines but by His word alone; and He restored many dead persons to life [Col. 0841B]. Moreover, in the wilderness He satisfied five thousand people with five loaves and two fish, calmed storms, and walked with dry feet upon the sea. Lactantius shows that these things had been announced beforehand either by the prophecies of our prophets or by the songs of the Sibyls, whose authority pagans then wrongly attempted to undermine.

Many, however, far more unjustly objected that a man executed by the shameful punishment of death could not be worshiped by other human beings without madness (ch. 16). Yet, besides the fact that no one would have believed Christ to be God or worthy of divine honor had He lived a most prosperous life in this world, the manner of His death, undertaken with great and divine power, had been prophesied many centuries earlier by David and Solomon. Blinded by anger and envy, the Jews crucified Him because they did not know that He would have two comings into this world, the first of which, as David, Isaiah, and the Sibyl foretold, had to be attended with dishonor and humiliation [Col. 0841C].

The Jews nevertheless pressed the allegation that Christ had been an impious man, since He abolished Moses’ law, the prohibition of swine’s flesh, and circumcision (ch. 17). But in vain, Lactantius says. For just as Micah, the Sibyl, and Moses himself, so Isaiah—likewise Moses and Joshua son of Nun, a type of Christ—had foretold that a new law would be brought, by which the old law and circumcision would be abolished [Col. 0841D]. Moreover, Jewish circumcision prefigured the holy circumcision of heart and spirit announced by the prophets, just as the prohibition of swine’s flesh showed that one must abstain from sins and foul deeds.

Furthermore, Christ had foretold Judas’s betrayal and His own death, and Pilate, without acting prematurely, handed Him over to the Jews though falsely accused (ch. 18). By them He was scourged, disfigured with spittle, given gall and vinegar to drink, was silent like a lamb, led to sacrifice, and suspended upon the wood of the cross—as Isaiah, the Sibyls, and David had foretold. Of His own accord He underwent a death more cruel than that of Gavius, and one which no power of eloquence can adequately lament. Moreover, we read that Christ’s death and the events that afterward occurred had previously been recorded in writing by Ezra, Isaiah, David, Jeremiah, Moses, Amos, and the Sibyl [Col. 0842A] (ch. 19).

No less clearly had our sacred prophets long before announced that Christ would be restored to life on the third day after His death. Our author cites David, Hosea, and the Sibyl (ch. 20). He then relates how Christ, returned to life, went into Galilee, where He showed Himself not to the Jews—lest He should bring them to repentance—but to His disciples. To them He disclosed the mysteries of sacred Scripture, which until then no one had been able to understand. This sacred Scripture is called the Old Testament, not as something distinct from the New. For the latter is its fulfillment, and in both Christ is the same testator; by His death He made Christians, after rejecting the Jews, heirs of the eternal kingdom, as Jeremiah testifies [Col. 0842B].

Finally, on the fortieth day after His death, He ascended into heaven, as Daniel had earlier written (ch. 21). His disciples afterwards dispersed throughout the whole world, performed great and almost countless miracles, and laid the foundations of the Church. Of these, Peter and Paul, preaching at Rome, were killed by Nero. There survives, Lactantius says, that preaching of Peter which foretold the ruin of the Jewish nation during Vespasian’s reign.

Yet the enemies of the Christian religion insisted that it was impossible for anything ever to depart from an immortal nature, and unworthy of God that one who was to teach men should become a man, subject to the weaknesses of our flesh and to death (ch. 22). Would Christ not have taught men with greater and more effective authority if He had come as God?

No, says Lactantius. For a teacher and instructor ought to teach the precepts of conduct and life handed down by him not by word alone, but also to fulfil them by example (ch. 23). And this, indeed, after the creation of the world, Christ alone, as both God and man, accomplished. For an earthly teacher cannot attain the highest doctrine and virtue unless he is taught by others (ch. 24). But a heavenly master, unless he is a man, cannot go before men by his example and show beforehand what ought to be done. Therefore Christ had to be born of a virgin, and to be at once man and God, so that, appointed mediator between God and men—or, as the Greeks say, *mesitēs* (μεσίτης)—he might found the Church [Col. 0842D], teach humankind, and lead them to immortality (ch. 25).

Lactantius gives two reasons why he chose to die fixed to a cross (ch. 26). First, because this manner of his death had been foretold by the prophets. Second, just as the miracles performed by Christ, which our author recounts one by one, so also the draught of vinegar, the crown of thorns, and the other torments that he endured, signified something great. Finally, by such numerous and severe sufferings, and by so cruel a death, he taught humankind both endurance and contempt for death.

“But,” they said, “why did he prefer to end his life by the punishment of the cross rather than by some other, more honourable death?” Lactantius replies: in order to bring aid to the weak and humble; to furnish an example to all; to preserve his body whole [Col. 0843A] and fit for resurrection; to make his death known to all; and to show that a people from every region of the earth was to be gathered beneath his wings—a people destined to receive the sign of the cross. He added that the lamb sacrificed by the Jews when they departed from Egypt was a figure of Christ’s death.

He next shows the wondrous power of the sign of the cross, by which demons are expelled together with Christ’s name, and, when consulted, cannot give responses (ch. 27). Nor should it be said that they do this from hatred rather than fear. For they ought rather to punish than flee Christians protected by this sign of the cross. Moreover, if demons—who in truth were the gods of the Gentiles—cannot harm Christians who bear the sign of the cross, and are conquered by them, then the Christian religion is certainly true and victorious [Col. 0843B]. Lactantius proves by various arguments that these demons are identical with the gods of the pagans, especially because, when summoned by the arts of necromancy, they did indeed answer concerning themselves and concerning God, but from no place other than the underworld, where Christ remained only for two days.

Trismegistus, moreover, spoke much concerning him and God his Father, whom we are altogether bound to acknowledge and serve (ch. 28). And from this comes the name *religio*: that is, from the bond of piety by which we are bound fast (*religati*), not from “reading again” (*relegendo*), as Cicero supposed. And just as religion is the worship of the true God, so superstition—whose name derives from the word *superstes*—is the impious worship of false gods.

After this Lactantius teaches that Christ, the Son of God [Col. 0843C], is one God, of the same substance as his supreme Father (ch. 29). For he proceeds from him as a stream from a fountain and a ray from the sun, and cannot be separated from him. Having explained this by certain examples, he confirms it by a double testimony from Isaiah. From this he concludes that the supreme Father is to be worshipped together with the Son.

Yet not only the most hostile Gentile and Jewish enemies of the Christian religion attacked this true doctrine; heretics also, as had been foretold, endeavoured to undermine it (ch. 30). For some of those who, through a wavering faith and their errors, brought about a rupture in ecclesiastical unity, were intent on increasing their wealth and attaining honour, and aspired to the highest priesthood; or they believed it either unfitting [Col. 0843D] or altogether impossible that God should be clothed in human flesh; or finally they were deceived by the prophecies of false prophets. Lactantius names individually the authors of the heresies, so that we may guard against them more carefully, and makes plain which is the true Catholic Church. Finally, he promises to dispute against all heretics in a separate work, and sets before us the subject of this and the following book.

## ARTICLE V. Analysis of the Fifth Book
