In the prologue of this book Lactantius declares that he has no doubt that people foolishly devoted to religion, perhaps scarcely having read [Col. 0844A] the beginning of his work and of others, will immediately cast them aside and curse them (ch. 1). Yet he asks of them, by the law of humanity, that they read them before condemning them. But he admits that he will not obtain this from those who tortured and slaughtered Christians by every kind of punishment without a hearing. Nevertheless, he hopes that he will not lose all his labour entirely. For he will strengthen wavering Christians, or at least rejoice that he himself lives in the light of truth. Nor does he predict that one should altogether despair that the sweetness and charm of his discourse may draw sound minds to hear him. For the pagans did not believe our sacred writers because of their rough and unpolished manner of speaking. Therefore, since the wisdom and truth of the Christian religion needs suitable heralds, and those who had hitherto [Col. 0844B] undertaken its defence—such as Minucius Felix, Tertullian, and Cyprian—had not sufficed for its defence, many men ventured to write against a truth unknown to them.

He mentions two such men, very well known to him and his contemporaries. One, professing the office of philosopher, destroyed his own disputations by his utterly corrupt morals (ch. 2). In three books which he vomited forth against the Christian religion, he showed himself vain, inept, and ridiculous both in defending the worship of the gods and in attacking our religion. The other, one of the judges and a leading instigator of the persecution, composed two pamphlets entitled in Greek *Philalētheis* (φιλαληθεῖς, “Lovers of Truth”). In these he sought to demonstrate that sacred Scripture contradicted itself; that Paul [Col. 0844C] and Peter and Christ’s other disciples were fishermen, unlearned and ignorant, and disseminators of deceits; that Christ, driven out by the Jews, gathered a band of nine hundred men and committed thefts and robberies; that Apollonius had performed miracles equal or greater than his; and finally that this Apollonius, who did not claim divinity for himself, was more modest than Christ (ch. 3). Having refuted and utterly overthrown all these points as briefly as decisively, our author reminds us that he was moved to undertake the writing of these books by the published treatises of these impious and sacrilegious writers. In them he will defend and demonstrate the truth of the Christian religion more fully and abundantly than Tertullian in the *Apologeticus* and Cyprian in his discourse *To Demetrianus* (ch. 4) [Col. 0844D]. If learned men follow, at his urging and example, the path thus marked out, he does not doubt that within a short time false religions will disappear and the Christian religion alone remain.

Having concluded this preface, he comes to his intended discussion of justice (ch. 5). Justice, he says, is the highest virtue, or the source of virtue; poets and philosophers vainly imagined that it had departed from earth to heaven. For while Saturn reigned, the worship of the true God, supreme peace, and temperance reigned everywhere. But after Jupiter took the kingdom from Saturn, his own father, he drew men away from God by the terror of an utterly insolent power, so that they might worship himself (ch. 6). Then the worship of the true God was removed, and ignorance [Col. 0845A], blindness, error, vice, greed, idolatry, and every evil afterwards flooded in so greatly that no trace of justice remained. But God, most merciful, as the final time approached, sent his messenger, who at last brought back to us this justice, which is itself the pious and religious worshipper of the one God (ch. 7).

“Why then,” you ask, “did he not give it equally to all?” Although Lactantius had already answered this question sufficiently, he nevertheless replies again that God did not wholly exclude evils, but permitted them in order that virtue might have its adversary, without which it cannot exist, and that the faith and constancy of Christians might be exercised. Therefore those who thought justice absent from the world are mistaken. It stood before their eyes and can readily be embraced by all [Col. 0845B], if they are willing to worship the true God and fulfil his commands. For if these were duly observed, there would be no wars at all, no dissensions, plots, frauds, robberies, fornications, adulteries, or other crimes; no sexual intercourse outside the desire for procreation; and throughout the whole world gentleness, piety, peace, innocence, equity, temperance, and faith would flourish. For impious worship of the gods introduced all evils with it (ch. 8).

Therefore no justice could exist among worshippers of false gods, since, by afflicting and killing innocent Christians—who, as they themselves admitted, were imitators of the just—with every kind of horrible punishment, they surpassed wild beasts in ferocity (ch. 9). Such cruelty and hatred had been produced by the truth [Col. 0845C] and the piety and holiness of Christians, by which the crimes of evil people are usually exposed and condemned. Christians were indeed as pious as the Gentiles were impious, as our author proves through a lengthy enumeration of crimes and wicked deeds in which the latter wallowed daily, and by the testimony of Seneca and Lucilius. And what of the fact that, by the example of Aeneas, he shows that they were then especially impious when they wished to appear pious to everyone (ch. 10)?

Accordingly, in proportion to their impiety they were often afflicted with more grievous evils, which they wrongly attributed to fortune. For, having offended the true God, they and others who seemed among them religious and good by nature paid most deserved penalties. They worshipped Jupiter, Venus, and other gods infamous for detestable crimes [Col. 0845D]. And, so that their worshippers might imitate all these deeds with impunity, they were not ashamed to represent them in theatres.

Their impiety and cruelty were therefore such that they stirred up against Christians a persecution of the utmost savagery and, indeed, horrible even to describe, which Lactantius vividly portrays (ch. 11). Indeed, most criminal men enacted sacrilegious laws collected by Domitius, so that everyone might know by what punishments Christians ought to be penalized. But pagans, if they were wise, should imitate these men; if truly foolish, they should despise and ridicule them, or leave them their own folly (ch. 12). For who but the most foolish person [Col. 0846A] envies a fool? Yet these same pagans, when they rage so cruelly against Christians, admittedly do not consider them fools; rather, they fear that, as the Christians’ justice gains strength daily, they themselves will be abandoned together with their snub-nosed gods. And certainly the number of Christians, diminished neither by tortures nor by death, always increased (ch. 13). Who, on considering the unconquered endurance—not only of men but also of women and children—among all peoples in the most savage and terrible punishments, and their ever-increasing number, would not immediately understand both that they were by no means foolish and that their religion was true?

Lactantius does not permit the objection that some yielded under torture. For when an opportunity was granted them and peace given to the Churches, they immediately returned to the Christian profession; and, after repentance for their sin, their faith became stronger [Col. 0846B]. Moreover, though our martyrs could very easily have avoided the death inflicted on them through most savage torments, they voluntarily encountered it far more gloriously than Mucius and Regulus. Thus in these martyrs were true virtue and wisdom—the virtues praised by Horace and Seneca—whereas among the Gentiles, worshippers of fictitious gods, there was sheer impiety and folly, as the Sibyls proclaim.

Lactantius explains why Christians, though wise, were called foolish by pagans: justice bears a certain appearance of folly (ch. 14). But before showing this by the two speeches, for and against justice, of the Academic Carneades—greatly praised by Cicero and Lucilius—he makes it [Col. 0846C] clear to us that justice has two parts: piety and equity. Piety is the knowledge and worship of God. Equity, or equality, makes all people equal and alike. Yet pagans neither know nor venerate the true God. Among them too were poor and rich, and wholly differing conditions of persons, as well as different ranks of honours and dignities. Therefore among them there was neither piety nor equity, and consequently no justice. But all Christians worship the true God; and although differing in bodily condition, they were nevertheless equal and alike in spirit, in sincere lowliness or humility of mind, in contempt for human affairs, and in sharing possessions and resources (ch. 15). He then offers the following summary of Carneades’ speech against that justice which the philosophers could neither discover nor defend [Col. 0846D] (ch. 16). In it Carneades divided justice into civil and natural. He attempted to overthrow both on the ground that civil justice is indeed wisdom but is not justice, whereas natural justice is justice but not wisdom. For, he said, many things which appeared to be done wisely were plainly unjust; as is clear from the example of a man who conceals the defects either of a house offered for sale, or who, to preserve his own life, snatches from another man suffering shipwreck with him a plank, or takes a horse from another man wounded by enemies in a shared battle. But this whole speech of Carneades, which the more learned pagans could not answer, is refuted by our author with firm reasons and by a true definition of wisdom and folly, and is utterly demolished (ch. 17) [Col. 0847A].

In his other speech, in favour of justice, Carneades seeks to prove that it is honoured and acquired by men because honour is the reward due to virtue (ch. 18). But Lactantius refutes this speech as well, because that Academic absurdly contradicted himself and did not ascertain what the reward of virtue is. For it can be given only by the true God, who willed that virtue should lie hidden under the appearance of folly. No less clearly, our author shows that Christians are counted among fools by mad pagans because they preferred to be tortured and killed rather than burn incense to false gods with three fingers.

He proves that those are guilty of an inexpiable crime who impiously serve such gods—or rather demons—whose origin and name they did not even know, and do not permit the true God to be worshipped by others (ch. 19) [Col. 0847B]. Before using force against Christians, they certainly ought to have proved who and what sort their gods were, by what worship they were to be honoured, and whether the world is governed by their providence. For, he says, religion cannot be compelled: it ought to be defended and commended not by force and arms, not by crime and cruelty, not by tortures and slaughter, but by the invincible force of reasons, by endurance, and by voluntary death. It is voluntary for this reason: God loves only one who loves him and hears only one who prays from the heart. Now the religion of the pagans consists wholly in external rites, by which they worship false gods; that of Christians wholly in the mind, by which they adore and pray to the true God.

Therefore one who does not worship the gods commits no injury against them; or, if he does commit one, it ought to have been repelled by the gods themselves, not by others (ch. 20) [Col. 0847C]. Nor was anyone permitted to compel Christians to sacrifice to them. What is extorted from an unwilling person is an execration, not a sacrifice; nor could it benefit either gods who were willing or Christians who were unwilling.

But the pagans objected that those who overthrow religion ought to be punished. Yet Christians, Lactantius replies, destroyed it less than Egyptians, who worshipped beasts and things shameful even to mention; less than other pagans, who worshipped their gods in temples and mocked them in theatres; less than philosophers, who taught either that there were no gods or that everything happened by itself or by chance; and less, finally, than those who declared that the gods had no concern for earthly things, were never moved by anger or favour, and were to be feared by no human being. But the Gentiles, truly mad and blinded by a frenzy inspired by demons, killed Christians who refused to sacrifice to fictitious gods by every kind of most atrocious punishment (ch. 21) [Col. 0847D].

But these same people asked Christians why their God allowed his worshippers not only to be tortured but also to be poor, miserable, and dishonoured (ch. 22). Lactantius easily answers this question. Having set forth a definition of endurance, which no one can deny to be the greatest virtue, he shows most clearly that God permits these things because one must look not to the frail goods of the body but to the everlasting goods of the soul [Col. 0848A]. God further allows Christians to be tested by such adversities lest prosperity corrupt them; in order to prove their faith and devotion; in order that their number may increase; and so that very many, finally abandoning the worship of the gods, may follow their example. Yet tyrants who rage against them with such inhumanity will not bear this with impunity, but will be punished at the final judgement. He rightly concludes from this that all persons ought to devote themselves to justice, endurance, and the other virtues, so that, when the course of this life is finished, they may receive an eternal reward.

## ARTICLE VI. Analysis of the Sixth Book

In this book Lactantius teaches by what rite and sacrifice God ought to be worshipped, and what is the true worship of God in which the supreme good consists (ch. 1) [Col. 0848B]. “There is no other,” he says, “than innocence, which alone God requires from human beings.” Accordingly, he demonstrates that pagans have erred throughout, in believing that their gods ought to be worshipped with victims, sacrifices, libations, and other external rites, as though they needed these things (ch. 2). For the true worship of God is that by which the worshipper’s mind presents itself to him as an unstained offering. How this is to be done, our author says he will next explain, so that people may be instructed in justice, than which, Cicero testifies, nothing is better.

First, he teaches that there are two paths of human life: one is that of virtue and leads to heaven; the other is that of vices and presses down to the underworld (ch. 3). He explains to us in detail how unknown the ends of each path were to philosophers and poets, and how greatly they differ from Christians in expounding each. He then shows that the path of vice is as smooth, easy, and pleasant as the way of virtue is difficult, thorny, and harsh; but the former ends in everlasting punishment and the latter in blessed immortality (ch. 4) [Col. 0848C]. For this eternal happiness is granted only after the greatest labours have been endured steadfastly in this life. Therefore God willed that human beings should have a common adversary, who might lie in wait for them by every deceit and artifice, and strive to entice them into sin and divert them from the straight path of virtues.

Before coming to expound the individual virtues, he rejects and refutes the descriptions of virtue given by the poet Lucilius, from which Cicero had drawn the duties of life expounded in his books (chs. 5–6) [Col. 0848D]. He then makes it clear that virtue does not consist precisely, as they thought, in knowledge of good and evil, or in increasing one’s household estate, seeking wealth, paying a price for riches, defending goods or evils, or procuring advantages for one’s country. He concludes that Lucilius and the others were deceived in laying down definitions of virtue because, since no one can know what true virtue is unless instructed by God, they pursued only its shadow and images (ch. 7). Added to this is the fact that, deceived by a false appearance of virtue and wisdom, they did not perceive the various paths of vice and the underworld, by which the devil, according to the inclination of each person’s mind [Col. 0849A], leads and drags people to destruction. Nor did they understand any better that there is a single path of virtue and truth: namely, the worship of the true God, by which alone we can enter the harbour of salvation.

Lactantius then teaches that God’s law must be embraced. Cicero praised it in a wonderful manner but never recognized its precepts (ch. 8). The first and chief of these is to know God, worship him, and obey him alone. Therefore ignorance of him is the greatest evil. Civil law and the particular laws of nations were invented for utility (ch. 9). Whoever follows them while ignorant of the divine law cannot become just. Whatever virtues such persons possess—such as those of Cimon—which seem acquired through natural ability and without knowledge of the true God, their good works are superfluous and empty, like a human body lacking a head [Col. 0849B]. Whoever has not known God lacks true piety, and all actions that appear good are found on the deadly path of darkness. But one who knows God and lives unjustly is like a diseased and feeble animal, though he can be healed. For a person to be perfectly healthy and live justly, knowledge of God is wholly necessary to him as the head is necessary to the body, and virtues as the limbs are necessary to that same body. Therefore the first duty of justice, in which human salvation and the supreme concern of all things consist, is to know the true God, pursue him with the worship due to him, always obey him, serve him with the utmost devotion, and devote all one’s effort to winning his favour.

Just as the first duty of justice is union with God, and this is called religion, so the second is association with humankind, and this is called mercy or humanity (ch. 10; the supplied text reads “ch. 20”) [Col. 0849C]. This distinctive virtue of the righteous includes fellowship in common life. For God created people unarmed and endowed them with wisdom so that they might love one another and protect one another by reciprocal services. Accordingly, enmities must be removed, as God commands, and good must always be done to others. Lactantius therefore rightly rebukes Plautus and Cicero, who denied that aid should be given to the needy, and refutes others who hated mercy and would not help one person even when he was about to perish (ch. 11). Cicero, however, later, as though moved by repentance, admitted that something from one’s estate should be shared with worthy needy persons [Col. 0849D]. But Lactantius refutes him because by “worthy persons” he understands persons able to return the favour. He does admit that it is better to give generously to one’s own fellow citizens; but he insists that the true duty of mercy and generosity is to sustain the needy and useless and help others in necessity, without any expectation either of pursuing human glory or of receiving any return at interest. For in doing good to another, one ought to expect one’s reward from God alone.

The author then argues against the same Cicero concerning hospitality, the redemption of captives, the protection of orphans, widows, and others deprived of assistance, care for the sick, and the burial of strangers and the poor [Col. 0850A]. This last duty of mercy had been neglected by the pagans (ch. 12).

He then rebukes the pagans by various arguments, because they objected that the estate of one person would be exhausted in a single day by these duties of piety and mercy. By various arguments he demonstrates that such poverty need not be feared, and that at least what is superfluous should be distributed.

He teaches that the reward of mercy is great: God promises a person that, provided there is henceforth a resolve not to sin, he will forgive all sins (ch. 13). Nor may anyone put forward the pretext that he is conscious of no sin. For, apart from the fact that such a person should on that account devote greater effort to justice [Col. 0850B], surely no one is wholly free and pure from every stain of any sin whatever. Riches must be placed in justice alone; whoever lacks it is poor. And indeed, if pagans spend their wealth in making and adorning images of gods, how much more fitting it is to bestow it generously upon needy people, who are living and breathing images of God.

After this Lactantius attacks and opposes the Stoics, who held that mercy and every other affection of the soul ought to be removed from human beings (chs. 13–14). He clearly shows that individual affections are implanted by nature in individual mute animals, and all of them in human beings; and that this Stoic opinion falls back into the error of the Peripatetics, who dreamed that vices, since—as they said—they cannot be removed, must be moderated by a mean (chs. 15–16) [Col. 0850C]. For he insists, not without reason, that even moderate vices must be avoided. Moreover, virtue and vice can exist in the greatest as in the smallest affections. Anger, sexual desire, and appetite are neither disease nor vice; rather, it is a vice to be irascible, lustful, and covetous (ch. 17). Indeed fear is sometimes the highest courage. Does not the fear of God make people unconquered amid horrible and most cruel tortures and death itself? Fear, therefore, must not be uprooted, as the Stoics thought, nor moderated, as the Peripatetics believed, but directed into the true path. Likewise, desire is not a vice if we desire not earthly but heavenly things. He therefore again refutes the Stoics, who babbled that these things are done not by desire but by will, and that humans can be led to an immovable stupor of mind, or *apatheia* (ἀπάθεια) [Col. 0850D]. For the force and reason of the mind lie in motion; and, as thought is the mind’s activity and life active, so death is still. Their error, however, arose because they did not know the prescribed limits of virtue. For it is not virtue to despise death in the manner of certain philosophers, but to endure it steadfastly when people seek to compel us to abandon God or betray the true faith. Lactantius affirms and confirms this by the testimony of Cicero and Seneca.

He returns from this to explain other commands of God, which prohibit anyone from seeking the fragile glory of good works, lying, taking interest on money entrusted to him, accepting any gift from a poor person, responding to one who curses otherwise than with blessing [Col. 0851A], making another person an enemy through his own fault, injuring anyone, or bearing an injury inflicted upon him impatiently (ch. 18). Here Cicero is rightly reproved for deciding that penalties may deservedly and lawfully be exacted from one who has provoked us. Whoever exacts punishment from one who injures him has already been conquered. Moreover, God forbids the sun to set upon our anger. Nor without reason did Cicero praise Caesar especially for being accustomed to forget nothing except injuries.

Here our author again turns against the Peripatetics and condemns them for ignorance because they taught that anger is the fuel of virtue, by which one fights more bravely against enemies (ch. 19). For anger, desire, and lust—from which poets invented the three Furies—hurl a person headlong into every sin, unless the limits established for them by God are rightly observed [Col. 0851B]. And just as the pagans overstepped those limits, so one who remains within them is enduring, courageous, and just.

He proceeds to the pleasures of the five bodily senses, which must be restrained or, like the affections of the soul, recalled to right reason (ch. 20). In beasts he thinks there is only one, that relating to procreation; but in human beings they are countless and must be repressed by virtue. One of them is the pleasure of the eyes, which some philosophers rightly condemn—unless they approve public spectacles and take delight in them. He teaches that circus games, and especially gladiatorial shows, are forbidden by the general law of God, which utterly prohibits everyone from committing or seeing any homicide, or exposing newly born children [Col. 0851C]. With no less severity he condemns comedies, tragedies, hunts dedicated to Saturn, scenic games to Liber, the aforementioned circus games consecrated to Neptune, and all other celebrations of such games.

“No less vicious,” he says, “is the pleasure of the ears,” which is chiefly received from the sweetness of voice, speech, and song, especially on the stage and in the theatre (ch. 21). For this reason God willed that the divine Scriptures should be written in simple language. But if songs and poems give any person pleasure, Lactantius says, it ought to be pleasant for that person to sing and hear praises of God.

The pleasures of taste and smell must likewise be avoided (ch. 22). For it is shameful for a good and wise man to serve his belly and throat, or to walk crowned with flowers [Col. 0851D]. Moreover, the enticements of pleasures furnish the devil with weapons by which he tickles souls and attempts to conquer their virtue.

Lactantius admits that the pleasure of touch is a sensation of the whole body, but discusses only lust (ch. 23). Although this is far greater and more ardent in humans than in other living creatures, the devil sharpens and inflames it in various ways, especially by openly and with impunity establishing brothels. We must therefore arm ourselves with the greatest strength against its assaults. But if anyone cannot restrain this affection, let him confine it within the prescribed bounds of a lawful marriage-bed. No man may in any way have several women at once, nor any woman several men [Col. 0852A]. Both spouses must preserve marital fidelity; and it is forbidden to all to use its lawful pleasure except for the purpose of begetting offspring. Therefore not only every adultery but also a corrupt thought must be avoided, so that no one, on seeing another’s wife, may desire her in his mind. Nor should it be objected that it is difficult to put restraints upon pleasure. For very many, our author says, have retained the blessed and uncorrupted integrity of their bodies. Yet this kind of continence, which God does not command but only advises, is, as it were, the completion of virtue, by which a human being becomes like God himself.

But if anyone sins through lust, desire, or in any other way, forgiveness of the sin must not be despaired of; God grants it to one who repents sincerely and truly. Nor should anyone flatter himself concerning a hidden sin [Col. 0852B]. For nothing, as Lactantius there confirms by various words of Seneca and Cicero, is concealed from God. Therefore the conscience must be cleansed of every stain of sin and opened to him alone who can heal it (chs. 24–25).

Whoever is endowed with every virtue and obeys God’s commands is his true worshipper and truly sacrifices to him. For God does not demand vervain, entrails, turf, ivory, or any woven or painted work; nor sacrifices and the blood of cattle; nor magnificent temples. Rather, he demands a pure mind, a chaste and innocent life, praises, hymns, and thanksgivings. These, as Trismegistus says, are the true gifts and sacrifices which God requires from a human being born for justice, as Tully says. This justice and virtue constitute true worship of God and true religion [Col. 0852C]. Besides this, all must implore God’s mercy, seek forgiveness of sins, and consecrate God himself within their hearts.

## ARTICLE VII. Analysis of the Seventh Book

At the beginning of this book Lactantius openly declares that he will undertake a discussion concerning the divine reward of perpetual happiness, which he confidently expects to demonstrate by various testimonies of the sacred Scriptures and probable arguments (ch. 1). But first he thought it necessary to prove why the world was made, and to refute Plato’s opinion that it will always remain, and Aristotle’s assertion that it always existed and always will exist [Col. 0852D]. He considers truer the opinion of Epicurus who, following Democritus, maintained that the world both arose and will perish. But neither he nor the other philosophers, he says, who faintly scented the truth, could give a reason why the world will dissolve. Indeed, entangled in vices and desires, they never understood that what Christians teach is true.

The principal origin and source of so many and such great errors was undoubtedly that they wished to comprehend by their own powers of intellect things which cannot be understood by a human being unless instructed by God (ch. 2). He particularly reproves the Stoics, who at one time divided nature into two parts, the active and the passive, neither of which can exist without the other; at another maintained that God is the mind of the world and the world the body of God (ch. 3) [Col. 0853A]. Plato had indeed gone before them in teaching that the world was made by God and governed by his providence, but he did not explain why or for whose sake it was made. The Stoics proclaimed that it had been created for the sake of human beings. But Epicurus rejected this view, maintaining that it arose spontaneously from the chance collision of atoms; yet he admitted that he did not know for what reason it was made. Our author therefore attacks and destroys all these errors (ch. 4). By various arguments he demonstrates that the world was created by God, not indeed for its own sake, nor for the sake of him who created it and can exist without it [Col. 0853B], but for the sake of living creatures, and living creatures for the sake of humankind.

“Why then,” philosophers asked, and Cicero with them, “was so great a multitude of destructive beasts and serpents created?” Lactantius replies that good and evil were set before humankind, endowed with wisdom, so that they might avoid the latter and use the former. Having confirmed this answer by the testimony of Asclepiades, he teaches that humankind was created precisely for God’s own sake: that it might understand his works, marvel at them, proclaim them, and worship and venerate him as its true Father (ch. 5). From this he readily answers Epicurus, who wrongly asked what advantage God derived from the creation of humankind.

Yet that impious philosopher pressed the point that, if these things are true, man ought not to have been created mortal and subject to so many diseases. But before Lactantius replies to this frivolous argument, already overthrown in the preceding books, he again briefly sets forth the creation of the world. He says that man was created mortal after all the other creatures, so that an infinite force, or multitude, of souls might be generated, and so that man himself, through endurance of labours and evils, might attain the supreme good of immortality, which is to be attributed not to nature but to virtue. Man is therefore first born mortal and afterwards becomes immortal; and he will be endowed with immortal happiness, provided that, despising earthly goods, he preserves sound, whole, and undefiled justice—content with the worship of the true God and received through the heavenly washing—by holy works.

Therefore those err who worship many gods and prate that the world was made without reason, merely for our pleasure [Col. 0853D], that it is governed by no providence of God, and that the human soul will perish with the body (ch. 6).

Although the pagan philosophers did not understand the substance of this heavenly teaching, nevertheless there was no school among them that did not perceive something true; but its adherents are shown to have corrupted it through their own fault and their eagerness to contradict (ch. 7). Plato, indeed, rightly said that the world was made by God; others most wrongly said that it came into being of itself or from atoms. The Stoics rightly proclaimed that it was created for man's sake; Democritus most wrongly thought that men had sprung from the earth, like little worms, without reason and without any author. Aristotle rightly maintained that man was born for virtue; Aristarchus most wrongly, for the pursuit of pleasure. Zeno rightly taught that there are infernal regions [Col. 0854A]; Epicurus most wrongly rejected this as a fiction of poets.

Lactantius then proceeds to prove the immortality of the human soul. Plato demonstrates it from the fact that it perceives by itself and is always in motion (ch. 8). But lest he should grant the same immortality to dumb animals, he very properly added wisdom to this perpetual motion which man possesses of himself. Pythagoras and Pherecydes held the same view, though Dicaearchus, Democritus, Epicurus, and even Cicero vainly attempted to make it doubtful and uncertain.

Nor should it be objected that the soul is no longer seen after the death of the body. For voice, wind, scent, and God Himself, though they do not fall beneath our eyes, are nevertheless perceived by the penetration of our mind and from their effects [Col. 0854B]. Therefore no one ought to insist that it is difficult to understand how the soul can retain sensation without bodily organs. For it is no easier to understand how God is active without a body. Besides, pagans were in any case compelled to believe that their gods existed, although they declared them to be devoid of bodies (ch. 9).

Lactantius demonstrates the soul’s immortality by further arguments. First, because there is no living creature other than man that possesses knowledge, worship, and religion of God. Secondly, because man alone among animals uses fire, the heavenly element of light and life. Thirdly, because virtue, he says, having been given to man alone, is a great argument that souls are immortal [Col. 0854C]. By this virtue man despises the sweet and pleasant pleasures of this life—indeed, he fights against them even unto death. But some reward is due, and will be given by God, for this struggle and victory; and it can be nothing other than blessed immortality after this life.

Fourthly, vices and the pleasure derived from them come to an end, but virtue must be perpetual (ch. 10). Therefore its reward, and the human mind which alone among living beings desires it, must, as Cicero says, be immortal. Fifthly, those who follow virtue and justice, since in this bodily life they are for the most part unhappy, must in another life be eternally blessed, like God Himself, who bestows eternal goods. Sixthly, just as the works of the body are perishable and mortal, so those of the mind must be eternal [Col. 0854D], as no one fails to see that memorials of intellects and illustrious deeds are everlasting (ch. 11). Seventhly, the body desires absolutely nothing except something temporal, whereas the soul desires many things neither bodily nor frail, but eternal. Yet this desire has not been implanted in it in vain. Therefore it must be eternal. Finally, the body is subject to sight and touch, but the soul can neither be touched nor seen. Therefore, as the former is mortal, so the latter is immortal.

After this Lactantius weakens and entirely refutes Lucretius’ contrary arguments (ch. 12). For Lucretius objected: “The soul is born with the body; therefore it must perish with it.” Lactantius admits that the body is born, since it is solid and formed by an earthly concretion [Col. 0855A]; but he maintains that the soul, being exceedingly subtle and not falling under any bodily sense, is drawn down from heavenly subtlety—or created by God—as Lucretius himself elsewhere sang. It is false, however, that the body perishes as soon as the soul departs. For it remains whole for many days afterwards, and, preserved with certain aromatics, lasts a very long time.

Lucretius pressed further: sensation grows in children, flourishes in youths, and diminishes in old men. Therefore sensation, or the soul, is mortal. Lactantius replies that the mind by which we live is one thing, and the soul by which we think another. The mind, he says—that is, intelligence—increases and diminishes in man according to age; but the soul remains always in the same condition. Moreover, if memory and knowledge undergo any increase or decrease [Col. 0855B], or even wholly fail, this is a defect of the body, not of the soul.

The same Epicurean urged that the soul is liable to pain and sorrow, and therefore to frailty and death. On the contrary, says our author, the soul repels grief by wisdom and virtue, which is the maker of immortality.

With the same ease he refutes Lucretius’ further assertion that the soul is affected, along with its body, by disease and forgetfulness. For virtue, he says, must therefore be employed, so that the mind, not the soul, may not be broken by any pain of the body or suffer forgetfulness of itself.

Lucretius made no progress at all by again objecting that the soul is a part of the body and, once separated from it, no more feels than an eye torn from the body [Col. 0855C]. Lactantius denies—and emphatically denies—that the soul is a part of the body, just as all rightly deny that what is contained in a vessel or a house is a part of that vessel or house.

He considers still weaker and more futile than all the rest the Epicurean poet’s renewed objection that the soul gradually departs from the dying parts of the body. For in those killed in a single instant, the soul immediately bursts forth from the body. If it seems gradually to disengage itself from the cooling limbs of others suffering a prolonged illness, that occurs from the failure of the body, not of the soul.

Moreover, Lactantius laughs at Lucretius, who finally presses the ridiculous fiction of a soul complaining that it is being dissolved. For who has ever heard such a complaint from the soul of any dying person, even an Epicurean [Col. 0855D]? What complaint can there be, moreover, from a dead man? Finally, very many dying persons indicate by word or gesture that they are rather going out and departing than dying.

Our author could indeed have opposed to the Epicureans the Pythagorean opinion concerning the transmigration of souls. But he passes it over, as absurd and unworthy of mention or refutation. He establishes and confirms the true doctrine of the soul’s immortality not only by the testimonies of Trismegistus, Apollo of Miletus, and the Sibyls, but also because no one would dare deny it in the presence of a certain magician, who knows how to summon souls by his spells. He thinks no one more foolish and stupid than Aristoxenus [Col. 0856A], who, while saying that there was no soul, failed to understand that he himself lived and possessed the mind by which he had thought this (ch. 13).

In explaining when and how, after the body’s death, impious men are to be punished by eternal penalty and the righteous rewarded with blessed and immortal recompense, Lactantius confidently asserts that the time of judgment is approaching and that the world—which certain philosophers had dreamed had existed for many thousands of ages—will be consumed when six thousand years from its beginning have elapsed. Yet he attempts to establish this opinion only by arguments drawn from a certain correspondence or congruity (ch. 14).

Many signs, however, he says, will precede this final ruin of the world (ch. 15). Everywhere, all manner of calamities, miseries, impiety, and a flood of every vice will overwhelm the earth. Egypt will be covered with blood as with a river. The Roman Empire, whose various ages Seneca described, will be overthrown, as the Prophets, the Sibyl, and Hystaspes foretold (ch. 16). After civil wars, ten kings will divide it among themselves, until there arises from the furthest northern regions a most powerful king, who will destroy three of these ten kings and be established as ruler over all. Our author sets forth in detail what and how great evils and portents will occur under his reign [Col. 0856B].

He adds that God will send a great prophet who, having performed many miracles, will convert many to the worship of God (ch. 17). But this prophet will be killed by another king, sprung from Syria; left without burial, he will revive on the third day and be caught up into heaven. That impious king and prophet of lies will establish and call himself god, and will perform signs and wonders in order to be worshipped. He will attempt to destroy the temple of God, command his followers to be marked like cattle, lay waste the world by most savage cruelty, and besiege the mountain to which worshippers of the true God will flee. But God, moved by their prayers, will send from heaven a great king, who will deliver them and destroy all the impious. He judges that all these things were foretold by the testimony of Hystaspes and by the words he has produced from both Hermes and the Sibyls (ch. 18) [Col. 0856C].

Further, that great king, after the sword has fallen, will descend from heaven at night, on the very vigil of Passover, attended by angels, who will hand over to the righteous the impious men besieging the mountain (ch. 19). When these have been destroyed and the mountain cut away, the impious Antichrist alone will flee; afterwards defeated in a fourth battle, he will pay the penalty for his crimes together with their leaders and tyrants. At last, evil having been extinguished, the world will rest, and images of gods and every form of idolatry will be utterly destroyed.

Afterwards the dead will rise, and worshippers of the true God will be judged by the great king, the Son of God; each will receive either reward or punishment according to his deserts (ch. 20). There Lactantius explains how and by what fire the souls of wicked men, although immortal and spiritual, will truly be tormented. He even adds that the righteous too are to be tested by fire (ch. 21) [Col. 0857A].

These things, he says, are not mere fictions of poets, as some suppose—poets more ancient than other writers. For these men, not sufficiently understanding the true doctrine of the resurrection of human beings, preached in the constant proclamations of our prophets, either altered or corrupted it. He confirms this by the testimony of Maro [Vergil], and further shows that this most certain proof cannot be shaken or weakened on the ground that, after so many ages, no living person has returned from the underworld (ch. 22).

He therefore declares false those who taught that souls are reborn or migrate from bodies into other bodies. For the dead will truly rise, when their souls, as Chrysippus and the Sibyl handed down, are again clothed by God with their own bodies [Col. 0857B]. Nor does he think that one should inquire too curiously how this can occur. Even though no account can be given of God’s works, we must nevertheless believe that He will restore the old man in an indescribable manner—He who created the new (ch. 23).

But after the great judgment, he says, and after the righteous have been recalled to life, Christ will reign among men for a thousand years and dwell with them (ch. 24). He warns us that he will briefly recount what he believed would occur during that time and what manner of life human beings would lead. Yet, because of differing opinions concerning the number of years elapsed since the world’s origin, he admits that it is difficult to say when those six thousand years will be completed; at their end, as he had said above, the world will fall and perish. He nevertheless thinks that, from the time when he was writing [Col. 0857C], no more than two hundred years remained (ch. 25).

He then places before our eyes the great evils which, when Christ’s thousand-year reign ends, the prince of demons with his followers will commit; how he will utterly perish with them; and how the people of God alone will remain for seven years (ch. 26). When these are at last completed, he says, the world will be renewed, human beings will be transformed into the likeness of angels, and the unjust will rise in order to be tormented with the devil and his ministers by fire and everlasting punishment. He further declares this to be the teaching of the holy prophets; because Christians concealed it, pagans falsely attributed execrable opinions to them [Col. 0857D]. There is appended thereafter, but only in certain editions, an epilogue in which Lactantius praises the piety of Constantine the Great and rejoices in the restoration of the Christian religion. But because these matters are omitted in the better manuscripts, they seem as spurious and interpolated as it is certain that our author exhorts all to embrace true religion, despise frail and passing goods, and devote themselves always to justice and the other virtues, so that they may attain the reward of everlasting happiness promised by God (ch. 27).

[Col. 0858A]

## CHAPTER II. On the author, title, subjects, number, division into chapters, and reasons for publication of these books

### ARTICLE I. On the author and title of these books; what is meant by the name *Divine Institutions*; and on the titles, subjects, number, and division into chapters of the entire work and its individual books

Such great and unanimous agreement has always existed among all men that Lactantius is the true author of these seven books on the Divine Institutions that no controversy, not even the slightest, can seem possible on this matter. There is therefore no need for us to assemble the almost infinite testimonies—especially of recent writers—by which this might be proved [Col. 0858B]. Yet we shall invoke as one witness standing in place of all, and beyond every exception, Jerome, who most explicitly affirms that our Lactantius composed the seven books of the *Divine Institutions against the Gentiles* (Jerome, *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, §80, p. 121). Likewise, in his letter to the orator Magnus: “Arnobius,” he says, “published seven books against the Gentiles, and his disciple Lactantius the same number; he also composed two volumes *On Wrath* and *On the Workmanship of God*. If you wish to read them, you will find in them an epitome [ἐπιτομή] of Cicero’s *Dialogues*” (*Epistle* 83, to Magnus, p. 656). And again, in another letter, to Pammachius and Oceanus, he writes: “Who can forbid me to read his—Lactantius’—books of the *Institutions*, in which he wrote most forcefully against the Gentiles?” (*Epistle* 41, to Pammachius and Oceanus, p. 345) [Col. 0858C].

Would you have yet surer testimony given you? Behold the testimony of Lactantius himself, who in another work, where he attacks the impious worshippers of false gods, wrote these very words: “But we have already refuted the ignorance of these persons in the second book of the *Divine Institutions*” (Lactantius, *On the Wrath of God*, ch. 2). Later he rebukes others who held mistaken views concerning Christ the Lord: “These,” he says, “we have already refuted in part in the fourth book of the aforesaid work.” There too he notes the Peripatetics’ opinion about moderating anger: “To these,” he says, “we responded in the sixth book of the *Institutions*” (ibid., ch. 17). What more need be said? Again, in the same treatise: “We have sufficiently shown, I think, in our *Institutions*, that there cannot be many gods” (ibid., ch. 11). Finally, we have made clear that, in these books of the *Divine Institutions*, his book *On the Workmanship of God* is cited by him. Thus he himself indicates that he composed both this book and the others. It is therefore wholly settled and certain that our Lactantius is the author and parent of these books [Col. 0858D].

No less must it be constant and fixed from the words of Lactantius and Jerome already cited that the title placed by Lactantius upon the books under discussion was none other than *Divine Institutions*. Why, however, did he entitle them thus? We may gather this from his own words: “If certain prudent men and arbiters of equity published written institutions of civil law, by which they might settle the lawsuits and disputes of disagreeing citizens, how much better and more rightly shall we set forth in writing divine institutions, in which we shall speak not about dripping eaves, diverting waters, or laying hands in litigation, but about hope, life, salvation, immortality, and God, so that we may put to rest deadly superstitions and most shameful errors” (*Institutions*, I.1). Therefore, just as very many men, as is clear from their works, and others of the highest rank, as Cicero says (*On the Laws*, I), published books on civil law and laws—on, to use Cicero’s own words, the law of dripping eaves and walls, or the drafting of formulas for stipulations and lawsuits—and called them *institutions of civil law*, so Lactantius thought it far better and more appropriate that his books, which concern the overthrow of the worship of false gods and the establishment of the worship of the true God [Col. 0859A], should be inscribed with the name and title *Divine Institutions*.

If you ask what is signified by the name “institutions,” we shall answer that some have thought it denotes books in which the first elements of some art or science to be taught are so explained that persons still untrained and unlearned may attain it gradually. But Lactantius employed the name in a broader sense. For he openly declares that in this work he discussed all the doctrines of the Christian religion and the false superstitions of the pagans much more fully and copiously than the defenders of Christianity down to his own time had debated them. Accordingly, by the name *Divine Institutions* he denotes a full and complete discussion for the exposition and vindication of the precepts and institutions of the Christian religion [Col. 0859B], and for the refutation of the impious cults of the pagans. Therefore, when he or others cite these books merely by the name *Institutions*, no one, I think, will deny that this is done for the sake of brevity.

Although this is the general title of the whole work, he nevertheless seems to have prefixed to each book its own particular inscription, as is read in the most ancient editions. We are indeed aware that these inscriptions were sometimes altered in certain more recent editions. Yet we shall easily be persuaded that they proceeded from Lactantius himself without these corrections. For they are presented in the same manner not only in those ancient editions but also in manuscript codices, both recent and ancient, at the end of each book and the beginning of the next [Col. 0859C]. Further, may not this also be gathered from Lactantius himself? At the end of the third book he explains the title and subject of the fourth book thus: “The next book will show what true religion and wisdom are” (*Institutions*, III.30). In like manner he concludes the fourth book thus: “It follows that, since we have spoken sufficiently about true religion and wisdom, we should discuss justice in the next book” (IV.30). If, however, anyone maintains that from this an official charged with copying the most ancient codices took occasion to inscribe titles upon the individual books, he may retain his opinion; and if he proves it properly, we shall yield at once.

What we have said about the differing inscriptions of the whole work and of each book must likewise be said of their subjects. For one general subject is treated throughout the work, and a particular subject in each individual book. Lactantius states the subject common to all the books in these words: “We undertake a discussion concerning religion and divine matters” (*Institutions*, I.1) [Col. 0860A]. This discussion has two parts: in the first, he utterly overthrows the false religions of the pagans in the first three books; in the second, he asserts, establishes, and demonstrates the truth and holiness of the Christian religion in the other following books (IV.30).

He also supplies us with the particular subject of each book. In the first, which he calls the first institution, he uncovers, in his own words, the false religions of the gods. In the second, he reveals the source and causes by which men first believed that there were many gods and later persisted in their corrupt worship (*Institutions*, I.23; II.1) [Col. 0860B]. Then, in the third (chs. 1, 2, 25, 30), he rejects the vain philosophy of the pagans. In the fourth book (chs. 3, 30), he shows what true wisdom and religion are; there he argues especially against the Jews concerning Christ the Lord. In the fifth book (ch. 1), confronting the pagans specifically, he discusses justice. In the sixth book (chs. 1–3), he teaches what true worship is—or, as he says, “by what rite or sacrifice God ought to be worshipped”—and what the virtues are, with their forms and limits. Finally, the subject of the seventh book (ch. 1) is “the divine reward of perpetual blessedness,” as Lactantius himself says; or, elsewhere, “what reward virtue deserves from God”; and, more briefly in another passage, “the blessed life.” How he treats this subject may be learned from these words of his: “We shall satisfy this part sufficiently, both by testimonies of the divine writings and by probable arguments.” After the last word, the oldest Bolognese codex is noted as adding *vatum*, “of prophets.” But if this reading is true and genuine, the name “prophets” must undoubtedly mean Hystaspes, Hermes, and above all the much-celebrated oracles of the Sibyls, which are cited more frequently in this book (*Institutions*, VI.3; III.13; I.1) [Col. 0860C].

The Jerome cited by us a little earlier most explicitly testifies that the whole work of the *Divine Institutions* was divided by Lactantius himself into these seven books, and no more. Even if Jerome had been entirely silent on this point, what, pray, could be clearer than Lactantius’ own words: “No food is sweeter to the mind than the knowledge of truth, for the assertion and illumination of which we have allotted seven volumes” (*Institutions*, I.1). Furthermore, in the first book (ch. 23), he indicates that he has brought it to an end in these words: “But I have now resolved to make an end of the book, lest it exceed its proper measure.” Likewise in the third book (ch. 30): “The next book will show more clearly what religion … is”; and in the fourth (ch. 30): “In the next book we shall discuss justice.” At the very beginning of the second book (ch. 1): “Although,” he says, “I have shown in the first [Col. 0861A] book that the religions of the gods are false.” In the same book (ch. 3), he indicates the four later books thus: “The four later books will serve the exposition of the knowledge of truth”; and in the seventh he recalls the earlier books. Added to this is the fact that he sends us from one book to another. For besides the matters noted a little earlier, in these books he refers us from the third and fourth books to the second; from the sixth to the third; and from the seventh to the second. Finally, after having often said in various places that the seventh book of the *Institutions* would be the last, we read these very words in its epilogue: “Having traversed the seven courses of the proposed work, we have reached the goal” [Col. 0860D].

Therefore, as true and manifest as it is that this work was divided by Lactantius himself into seven books, so certain must it be for everyone that the divisions of these books into chapters, together with the subjects of those chapters, were not composed by Lactantius but by another and much more recent writer, who lived not long after the age of the first edition. For these are not found in the old manuscript codices that it has been possible to examine, but only in more recent ones [Col. 0861B].

### ARTICLE II. The reasons that led Lactantius to compose these books; and whether Minucius Felix, Tertullian, and Cyprian failed to satisfy fully the undertaking of defending the Christian religion

Lactantius gives various reasons that led him to publish these books. First, he testifies that he applied himself to their composition in order to labour for the illumination of truth; to show true wisdom to learned men and true religion to the unlearned; and to direct minds, individually imbued with heavenly precepts, to the true worship of the divine majesty (*Institutions*, I.2) [Col. 0861C].

Moreover, since eminent orators at the end of their lives devoted themselves to the vain philosophy of the pagans, and jurists composed certain institutions of civil law, he judged it far more equitable, prudent, and useful to commit these divine institutions to writing and to betake himself to true, pious, and divine wisdom as though to a most safe harbour—“in which,” he says, “all things are easy to speak, pleasant to hear, easy to understand, and honourable to undertake.” Yet he did not undertake the work merely for his own special benefit and personal use, but in order, after deadly superstitions and most shameful errors had been quieted and wholly extinguished, to demonstrate the truth of the Christian religion. He therefore allotted seven volumes to asserting and illuminating it, so that pagans might be instructed and might no longer, hardened or made more obstinate, fight against themselves and against the lights of right reason clearer than the light of the sun itself, but might at last be freed from inveterate errors. If some especially stubborn persons should still close their ears, he hopes that there will not be lacking men of sound mind to whom truth, delivered in a style not wholly disagreeable or unpolished, will be pleasing [Col. 0861D]. But if no one of them should yet wish—which is difficult to suppose—to return to a sound mind and the way of salvation, his writings will at least strengthen wavering Christians. Finally, if they should benefit no one—which is not credible—they will surely benefit himself, and he will rejoice to dwell in the light of truth (*Institutions*, IV.5; V.1) [Col. 0862A].

One principal reason and occasion for composing these books was that our author was convinced that, down to his own age, capable and expert teachers had been lacking who had vigorously and keenly rebuked the public errors of the pagans and defended the entire cause of the Christian religion with elegance and completeness (*Institutions*, V.2). Two pagan writers, to be discussed shortly, emboldened by this lack of valiant champions, had dared, while Lactantius himself was present and grieved, to assail and attack the Christian religion in sacrilegious writings [Col. 0862B]. Provoked and compelled by such proud impiety and by consciousness of the truth, he composed these books in order to break their vain assaults and present a defence of the Christian religion complete and perfected in every respect. But these matters need to be explained by us somewhat more fully.

It may indeed seem remarkable to many how Lactantius can assert with such confidence that capable defenders of the Christian religion had been lacking down to his own time, unless he spoke expressly only of those known to him. More remarkable still may appear to some the fact that he included among them Minucius Felix, Septimius Tertullian, and Cyprian, while passing over his teacher Arnobius in profound silence [Col. 0862C]. For Arnobius treated the cause of the Christian religion no more perfectly than they did. Yet the dignity of his teacher may perhaps have been the cause of so great a silence. Perhaps too the writings which Arnobius had recently published in Africa were unknown to him. For Lactantius had left that region while still young and had gone so far away that he could have been ignorant of what his teacher had written there. But whatever may be the case concerning Arnobius, someone may ask what these three other celebrated writers, mentioned by Lactantius, lacked that prevented them from discharging so illustrious an office as defenders of the Christian religion. Lactantius answers freely that Minucius Felix did not devote himself wholly to that study; that is, he did not, as he could readily have done, set forth a full and complete discussion in defence of the truth of the Christian religion [Col. 0862D]. But we have already treated this matter in our dissertation on his book (*Dissertation on Minucius Felix’s Octavius*, ch. 2, art. 1).

Lactantius finds two deficiencies in Tertullian’s *Apology* for the Christian faith: an exposition of Christian doctrine and elegance and clarity of language. “In speaking,” these are Lactantius’ words, “he was not very fluent, was insufficiently polished, and was very obscure” (*Institutions*, V.1). Nor did Jerome differ greatly from this judgment; he wrote to Paulinus in these words: “Tertullian is rich in thoughts, but difficult in expression” (Jerome, *Epistle* 49, to Paulinus, p. 567). But others will say: however great the barbarism and obscurity of his style may be, both are rightly compensated by the very great force, strength, and weight of his arguments [Col. 0863A].

Nevertheless, as regards establishing our doctrine, Lactantius admits that Tertullian in that book properly answered the absurd accusations of the pagans, but denies that the doctrines of our religion were sufficiently explained or proved by him. “It is one thing,” he says, “to answer accusers, which rests solely in defence or denial; it is another to instruct, which is what we do, and in which the entire sum of doctrine must be contained” (Lactantius, V.4).

But Tertullian had no other purpose in his *Apology* than to show plainly to all that Christians, accused by pagans of even the gravest crimes, were condemned entirely without merit, though never heard and still less convicted. Accordingly, in his *Apology* he undertook to prove nothing else than to make manifest to all the true teaching of Christians, their innocence, the highest integrity of their lives and morals, and that pagans were in truth guilty of the same crimes of which they most falsely accused Christians. And he accomplished all this most brilliantly in his book, although he set forth, with as much integrity as brevity, not all but only the principal doctrines of the Christian religion, and demonstrated them briefly but very clearly. Since he therefore fully satisfied his purpose, neither he nor any author whatever ought to be blamed for not saying more than he judged relevant to the argument he had undertaken [Col. 0863B]. But Lactantius undoubtedly wished that the defence of Christians undertaken by Tertullian should not be confined within such narrow bounds (*Dissertation on Tertullian*, ch. 4, art. 4) [Col. 0863C].

His complaint concerning Cyprian is greater. For the more highly he praises Cyprian’s talent and eloquence, the more sharply he rebukes him because, in his disputation against Demetrianus, who barked against the Christian religion, he was unable to make “the mystery pleasing beyond words to those ignorant of it,” that is, to pagans (Lactantius, IV.2 and IV.4). If you ask him the reason, he answers: “Because what he said was mystical, and prepared to be heard only by faithful Christians.” Later he explains what these mystical matters were: “For he, Demetrianus, had to be refuted not by testimonies of Scripture, which he certainly considered empty and fabricated, but by arguments and reason.” Indeed, he openly recounts, with scarcely any excuse, that Cyprian was not only ridiculed for this by learned men of that age, but that he himself heard a very eloquent man call Cyprian “Coprianus,” changing one letter, “as though a refined talent, fitted for better things, had been applied to old women’s tales” (ibid., ch. 1) [Col. 0863D]. Certainly the name *Coprianus*, or *Copreus*, and *Coprea*—or, as others read in Suetonius, *Coprias*—is derived from the Greek κοπρία and κοπρίον, “dung” or “filth”; it signifies a buffoon, pettifogger, sycophant, or worthless person, accustomed indeed to proclaim great things about himself but to peddle old women’s and foolish tales (Suetonius, *Life of Nero*, §6; *Life of Claudius*, §8) [Col. 0864A].

No one should be surprised that the pagans attempted to harass Cyprian, their religion’s most implacable enemy, with taunts, mockery, and insults. But Lactantius will cause many readers astonishment, since he dismissed these only with the words: “Carried away by his outstanding learning in the divine writings, he was content with those alone by which faith is established” (Institutions, book V, ch. 4). Lactantius therefore judged that, in his disputation against Demetrian, Cyprian ought first to have adduced human testimonies from philosophers and historians rather than divine testimonies from Holy Scripture. For, since Demetrian “was not yet,” as Lactantius says, “able to grasp these things, he ought especially to have been refuted by his own authorities.” [Col. 0864B] Perhaps this would not have been badly said had this been Cyprian’s first debate with Demetrian concerning the truth of the Christian religion. But Cyprian indicates from the very beginning of his address that he had had several such encounters with him before, where he addresses Demetrian thus: “Since you often came to me more from a desire to contradict than from a wish to learn, and, resounding with clamorous voices, preferred shamelessly to thrust forward your own opinions rather than patiently to hear ours.”

Some therefore reply that the passages of Holy Scripture cited by Cyprian are testimonies drawn from the prophets, which, as we shall see, furnish a most powerful argument against the heathen for the establishment of the Christian religion. But Cyprian’s defence is better served by the fact that in this treatise he undertook to refute the slander of Demetrian [Col. 0864C] and other pagans, who loudly alleged that Christians were the cause of all the evils by which the world was shaken. He overthrows this charge by those testimonies of Holy Scripture in which such evils were foretold as impending in punishment for crimes committed by the heathen. But since these events occurred as they had long beforehand been predicted, the same pagans could not deny the divine authority of these oracles and of our entire Holy Scripture. Moreover, he refutes Demetrian’s foolish accusation by certain arguments which are by no means weak.

Finally, concerning that judgment of Lactantius, Jerome wrote these words to the orator Magnus: “Cyprian, a man powerful in eloquence and in martyrdom, is criticized, as Firmian relates, because, writing against Demetrian, [Col. 0864D] he employed testimonies of prophets and apostles, which the latter said were fictitious and fabricated, rather than those of philosophers and poets, whose authority, as a pagan, he could not oppose” (Jerome, Epistle 93, to Magnus, p. 655). But what, I ask you, did he intend to signify by the word *mordetur*, “is bitten” or “criticized”? Surely some disparagement and a reproach not wholly fair? For we read Terence using it in this sense: “All envy me, secretly bite at me” (Terence, *Eunuch*, act 3, scene 1, v. 20). One may perhaps not improperly infer that Jerome himself uses it in the same sense from his following words: “With what brevity, with what knowledge of all histories, with what brilliance of words [Col. 0865A] and thought Cyprian showed that idols are not gods” [the transmitted text has *perstrinxit perstrixit*] (Jerome, cited passage, p. 657). Do not these words signify that Cyprian properly fulfilled his office as a defender of Christianity, if not in the one address against Demetrian alone—as Lactantius thought—then at least in his other discourses against the heathen?

## ARTICLE III. On the two pagan philosophers whose impious writings moved Lactantius to publish these books; and whether he defended the cause of the Christian religion more completely than others, and by what method.

Lactantius portrayed in their natural [Col. 0865B] colours, though without naming them, both philosophers who, as we said a little earlier, compelled him to write these books of the *Divine Institutions*. He further assures us that they existed at the time when he was teaching rhetoric in Bithynia and the temple of God was being overthrown (Institutions, book V, ch. 2).

The first professed philosophy, but was notorious for every vice, which he sought to conceal under long hair and the cloak—that is, under the profession of philosophy—and under wealth. A most severe accuser of others, he destroyed by his corrupt conduct his own disputations about virtue. He vomited forth three books against the Christian religion when tyrants were raging with the utmost cruelty against it. Yet this imprudent man, wholly ignorant both of what he was attacking and of what he was saying, appeared in these books so foolish, empty, and ridiculous that he was as universally despised as he was mocked.

[Col. 0865C] The other, one of the judges and an instigator of the persecution against Christians—whose faith he had at one time seemed to embrace—attempted in two books, which he had entitled with the deceptive title *Philalēthēs* (“Lover of Truth”), to prove the falsity of Holy Scripture on the ground that it was wholly self-contradictory. He then endeavoured to show that Apollonius had performed miracles equal to, or even greater than, those performed by Christ (Lactantius, ibid.; Caecilius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, ch. 16).

This second philosopher seems to be none other than Hierocles, whom Eusebius refuted in a work published after his *Demonstration of the Gospel*, and elsewhere. For Eusebius gives the same title of the work: “These are the words of Hierocles himself, in the discourse entitled *Philalēthēs*, written against us” (Greek: Ταῦτα ῥήμασι αὐτοῖς Ἱεροκλεῖ τῷ τὸν καθ’ ἡμῶν ἐπιγεγραφότι φιλαλήθῃ λόγον εἴρηται). [Col. 0865D] “These are the words of Hierocles himself in the discourse written against us, entitled *Philalēthēs*” (Eusebius, *Against Hierocles*, p. 513). At the very beginning of the book Eusebius also mentions this same title, and adds that Hierocles had reached such a pitch of shamelessness that he did not hesitate, as Lactantius had said, to compare Apollonius of Tyana with our Saviour Christ. Moreover, Eusebius transcribed Hierocles’ words by which he denounced Peter, Paul, and Christ’s other disciples as liars, unlearned men, and impostors, because they had exaggerated the deeds performed by their divine teacher. Likewise our Lactantius says: “Above all, he tore to pieces Paul and Peter and the other disciples, as sowers of falsehood; yet he himself testified that these same men were uneducated and unlearned” [Col. 0866A] (Lactantius, *Institutions*, book IV, ch. 2).

We are indeed not unaware that some hold Eusebius of Caesarea not to be the author of this book, but another Eusebius of the same name who, according to Photius, refuted books published by Hierocles concerning fate and providence around the time of Theodosius the Younger. Yet these persons do not seem to have paid sufficient attention to what the same Photius had earlier committed to writing: “A short refutatory book of Eusebius Pamphili against Hierocles’ discourses on behalf of Apollonius of Tyana was read” (Greek: Ἀνεγνώσθη Εὐσεβίου τοῦ Παμφίλου ἀνασκευαστικὸν βιβλιάριον πρὸς τοὺς ὑπὲρ Ἀπολλωνίου τοῦ Τυανέως Ἱεροκλέως λόγους). Nor should anyone object that Lactantius mentions only two little books, whereas Eusebius refuted seven. For Eusebius attacks not only the books of Hierocles, [Col. 0866B] but also those of Philostratus. But another occasion will be given for discussing this Hierocles.

It is, however, far more difficult to say who the first writer and philosopher addressed by Lactantius was. Baronius held that he was Porphyry, the most hostile enemy of the Christian religion, who in A.D. 302, the nineteenth year of the Emperor Diocletian, was in the sixty-ninth year of his life and lived on to extreme old age (Baronius, under the year 302, §51). For this Porphyry, like the writer cited by Lactantius, while performing above all the office of philosopher, professed himself to be a chief representative of philosophy (Institutions, book V, ch. 2). Augustine likewise calls Porphyry most learned and most renowned among philosophers, [Col. 0866C] a most bitter enemy of Christians, who boasted that he was a lover of virtue and wisdom (Augustine, *City of God*, book XIX, ch. 22; book XXII, ch. 3; book X, ch. 28). Nor is Baronius troubled by the fact that Lactantius says that the person he cites wrote only three books, while Suidas says that Porphyry composed fifteen. For the most learned author of the *Annals* considers that Porphyry first published three separately and subsequently added twelve more.

But several considerations seem to oppose this view. There is no way to prove that these books were published separately. Who could readily persuade himself that Porphyry, at seventy years of age, was tainted by those vices of lust and gluttony which Lactantius plainly and openly reproached in his philosopher? If someone replies [Col. 0866D] that he could, like many lustful old men, have been stained by these vices, we shall say that this still needs to be proved.

Moreover, Eusebius and Jerome state without hesitation that Porphyry published his books against the Christian religion while he was living in Sicily (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, ch. 19; Jerome, *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, §81). Yet Lactantius affirms that, in his own presence, while he was teaching rhetoric in Bithynia, this philosopher and the other one of whom we have spoken “set forth their sacrilegious writings” (Institutions, book V, chs. 2 and 4).

Baronius replies that Jerome believed Porphyry had completed them in Sicily because [Col. 0867A] he had migrated there from Rome. Yet it is not Jerome alone, but also Eusebius, whom we have cited, who expressly asserts that they were composed by him in Sicily. Furthermore, Baronius ought to have told us when Porphyry withdrew to Sicily and how long he remained there (Baronius, under the year 302, §57).

Finally, from Lactantius’ words already cited it may not unreasonably be inferred that both those philosophers were refuted by him before all others. But if this is so, it may be concluded that he indicates someone other than Porphyry. For we learn from Jerome that other works against this Porphyry were composed by Methodius, who, according to him, “at the end of the last persecution,” or, as others affirm, “under Decius and Valerian, was crowned with martyrdom at Chalcis in Greece” (Jerome, *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, §83; *Apology against Jovinian*; *Against Rufinus*, book II; Epistle 83, to Magnus). [Col. 0867B] He reports there two opinions about the time at which that most holy martyr died for the faith of Christ. The first is that he died under Decius and Valerian, that is, between A.D. 250 and 260. The second is that he departed this life at the end of the final persecution raised by Diocletian, that is, around A.D. 311. The first opinion cannot stand together with the books published by Methodius against Porphyry, who in A.D. 263 was in his thirtieth year. For Porphyry does not appear yet to have issued to the public the books which Methodius refuted. If the second opinion is truer, then Lactantius, who composed the *Divine Institutions* a little [Col. 0867C] after A.D. 311, must be said not to have read Methodius’ books against Porphyry at that time. For in these *Institutions* he indicates that he himself was the first of all to refute him. But since it is scarcely at all credible that Methodius’ *Apology* was unknown to him, does it not follow that Lactantius denotes someone other than Porphyry?

These, then, are the arguments of both parties, which in accordance with our practice and duty we set before the eyes of all after examination, so that each may form his own judgment concerning them and embrace whichever he considers truer. But if anyone should certainly prove to us that the philosopher of whom Lactantius speaks was not Porphyry, he will draw us all the more readily to his opinion because we are firmly persuaded that there is no reason why Lactantius, [Col. 0867D] while refuting Porphyry’s books, should have spared his name.

Whatever may be determined concerning this philosopher—whose writings and perhaps even name have not come down to us—it must be certain that Lactantius composed these books of the *Divine Institutions* in order to refute the published treatises against the Christian religion of that man and of the other impious writer, and to demonstrate its truth more fully and completely than the defenders of the Christian religion had hitherto done. But whether he himself completely satisfied this purpose may be a question—and not a small one. For Jerome wrote to Paulinus concerning him in these words: “Lactantius is like a certain river of Ciceronian eloquence; would that he had been able to establish our doctrines as forcefully as he easily overthrew those of others” (Jerome, Epistle 49, to Paulinus). [Col. 0868A] What else do these words mean than that Lactantius fell into the very fault which he reproached in others and promised to correct? “Those of others,” says Jerome—that is, the errors of the heathen—he easily overthrew; but “our doctrines,” surely, he could not establish, prove, and confirm with equal facility. Yet it is certain that in these books of the *Divine Institutions* the doctrines and ordinances of our religion are defended and confirmed much more fully than in the treatises of Minucius Felix, Tertullian, and Cyprian cited by him, not only against the heathen but also against the Jews. Whether he defended them well or badly, clearly and completely or meagrely and thinly, [Col. 0868B] we shall consider later. But Jerome seems to have delivered the judgment mentioned above concerning these books for no other reason than that he thought he had observed in them errors opposed to the doctrines of our sincere faith. Yet whatever those errors may have been—of which we shall speak later—he nevertheless openly affirms that they were never any obstacle to his reading these books of the *Divine Institutions*, in which, he says, Lactantius wrote most vigorously against the heathen (Jerome, Epistle 41, to Pammachius and Oceanus; Jerome, *Commentary on Ecclesiastes*). In another book he calls the *Divine Institutions* a distinguished work, in which Lactantius discussed vices and virtues most fully.

Moreover, what Jerome added—that Lactantius was [Col. 0868C] like a river of Ciceronian eloquence—is certainly true, as everyone readily grants and willingly agrees with Jerome. But we have already discussed Lactantius’ eloquence.

Finally, Jerome writes in his letter to Magnus that in the books of the *Divine Institutions* and *On the Workmanship of God* there is an *epitomē* (ἀπιτομή, “epitome” or “abridgment”) of Cicero’s dialogues (Jerome, Epistle 83 to Magnus). But in what sense he said this has been observed by us above. We shall therefore add only that Cicero is very often refuted by Lactantius, especially where the sacred doctrines of the Christian religion and of moral discipline are treated.

# CHAPTER III. On the date of these books, the various fragments which seem ineptly inserted into them, and the errors attributed to Lactantius.

[Col. 0868D]

## ARTICLE I. At what time Lactantius wrote these books, and whether he published two editions of them.

When Lactantius published his books of the *Divine Institutions*, some conjecture is indicated by his own words: “From the destruction of the city of Troy 1,470 years are reckoned.
