From this chronological calculation it is evident that Saturn, who was also the begetter of all the gods, was born not more than about 1,800 years ago” (Lactantius, *Institutions*, book I, ch. 23). Isaeus therefore thinks [Col. 0869A] that it may be inferred from this that Lactantius published these books in A.D. 302. For, he says, according to Glareanus’ precise chronology of Livy, 432 years elapsed from Troy’s destruction to the founding of Rome; 751 years from Rome’s founding to Christ’s birth; and, if 302 years are added, the total comes to 1,485 years. But if this method of reckoning years is true, it follows from it that Baronius’ opinion—rejected by Isaeus—that Lactantius composed these books in A.D. 316 is the more probable. For 317 years must be counted from the total. Isaeus is therefore compelled to admit that chronologists’ opinions on this matter are so varied that nothing certain can be determined. He then adds, quite truly, that Lactantius takes little care to supply a precise method for calculating dates. Indeed, [Col. 0869B] he undertakes there to prove nothing but that Saturn, the father of the gods, according to the pagans’ own chronology, was born not more than about 1,800 years earlier, and that they therefore boast vainly of the antiquity of their impious rites. Accordingly, in the following book he speaks thus about Jupiter’s age: “who was born 1,700 years ago” (same author, book II, ch. 5). Was Jupiter, then, Saturn’s son, a hundred years younger than his father? It is therefore clear that nothing can be drawn from all this by which the date of these books may be certainly defined.

Although Isaeus admits this, he nevertheless believes that they were in fact composed in the very year A.D. 302. For Lactantius testifies that, while he was teaching rhetoric in Bithynia and the temple of God was being overthrown, he was stirred by the impious writings of the two pagans of whom [Col. 0869C] we spoke a little earlier to publish his *Divine Institutions* (Institutions, book V, ch. 2). But that temple was destroyed in A.D. 302, when Diocletian, by issuing an edict, ordered all Christian churches to be destroyed. No one, says Isaeus, will find it probable that Lactantius, provoked no less by the immense impiety and audacity of these pagans than inflamed by the highest zeal to defend true religion, delayed devoting his labour to composing these books against them for as much as fourteen years. Nor is he troubled by Lactantius’ address to Constantine, included in certain copies of the books. For he wholly rejects and repudiates this address, of which we shall speak below, as spurious and interpolated.

Others reply that it is not at all astonishing [Col. 0869D] if Lactantius did not immediately refute the impious inventions of pagan writers, although they had been spread and disseminated abroad in public writings—as often happens with authors. For who would dare to assert whether it was in his power to publish books against pagans during the period when Christians were shaken by various and most violent storms of persecution? Other reasons unknown to anyone may also have arisen, for which he judged that a more opportune occasion for writing should be awaited. Whatever the case, they are persuaded that quite strong arguments can prove that these books appeared publicly long after A.D. 302.

[Col. 0870A] But these writers are still divided into two parties. Baronius thinks that Lactantius published them in A.D. 316 itself (Baronius, under the years 315, §§20–21, and 316, §55). Others, on the contrary, have maintained that he wrote them no earlier than A.D. 321. That most eminent Cardinal sought to establish his opinion chiefly by two arguments. The first he draws from the fact that Lactantius devoted himself to composing these books while Licinius was harassing the Church and Constantine was preparing an expedition against him. For our author in the preface to this work foretells the victory which Constantine would win over Licinius. The second he derives from the fact that the same author [Col. 0870B] mentions the Arian heresy as something known and already everywhere widespread, although it had raised its head in A.D. 315 (Institutions, book I, ch. 1; book IV, ch. 30, p. 449).

Others answer that it may be doubted whether that preface and the term “Arian” were not inserted into Lactantius’ text by some idle writer. Furthermore, even if it were wholly certain that these came from Lactantius, Baronius could derive nothing from them except something against his own opinion. For, they say, it can be demonstrated by certain and invincible arguments that Licinius’ persecution did not arise before A.D. 319. If Lactantius therefore mentions this persecution, he must be said to have composed these books not in A.D. 316 but after A.D. 319.

The entire question, then, rests upon whether Lactantius [Col. 0870C] speaks of Licinius’ persecution and when it was raised. As to the first point, supporters of both views admit that he did indeed mention that persecution. “He was writing,” says Baronius, “in the year in which Licinius’ persecution harassed the Church” (Baronius, under the year 316, §55). Lactantius thus declares in words far from obscure not that it was about to arise, as some think, but that it had already arisen.

Certainly, Lactantius described Diocletian’s monstrous cruelty in raging against Christians, and the horrible and until then unheard-of punishments inflicted on Christians during his reign, as events already past, some of which he himself had seen (Institutions, book V, ch. 11). But elsewhere he recalls that other sufferings wholly similar or exactly the same were still being inflicted while he wrote these books: [Col. 0870D] “They torture, kill, and exterminate the worshippers of the most high God—that is, righteous persons, namely Christians—and they themselves cannot give reasons for the hatred they so violently feel, because they themselves are in error. They are angry with those who follow the true way, and, though they might correct themselves, they heap up their errors further by cruel deeds; they stain themselves with the blood of innocents and wrench from bodies, after their entrails have been torn out, minds consecrated to God. With such persons we now strive to engage and dispute.” Later: “Behold, the city—or rather the whole world—is in such error that it persecutes, tortures, condemns, and kills good and righteous men as though they were wicked and impious. … For why do they rage so cruelly, unless because they fear that, as righteousness grows stronger day by day, [Col. 0871A] they will be left behind with their wide-nostriled gods?” (Institutions, book V, ch. 12). Again, in another book: “The punishments of the worshippers of God have been seen and are still being seen throughout the world; in torturing them, new and unprecedented torments have been devised. For the mind shudders to recall the modes of death, since the slaughter inflicted by savage beasts has raged beyond death itself” (book VI, ch. 17). Finally, we shall not now heap up further proofs of an admitted matter, to be treated later, by which he openly makes clear that the number of Christians was not diminished but always increased by so many and such cruel torments and killings. From the passages of Lactantius quoted, it is understood sufficiently clearly that he mentions two persecutions: one begun by Diocletian, the other by Licinius (book V, ch. 12).

[Col. 0871B] It remains, therefore, to determine when this second persecution began. Baronius dates it to A.D. 314, when, after hostilities had arisen between Constantine and Licinius, the latter was routed and defeated in the battle of Cibalae; Eusebius’ *Chronicle* and other writers assign this battle to that same year, 314. Others, however, thought that Licinius’ persecution began in the nineteenth year after 300, that is, in A.D. 319. For the author of the same Eusebian *Chronicle*, as also Theophanes and Cedrenus, says that Licinius expelled Christians from his palace in 319 or 320. Yet he undoubtedly expelled them from there when he first began openly to rage against the Christian religion. Moreover, the same chronicle states that in 321 Basil, [Col. 0871C] bishop of Amasea in Pontus, gained the crown of martyrdom under Licinius. Theodore also, according to Nicephorus, gained the same crown on Saturday, the seventh day of February, as we read in the Acts of his martyrdom published by Bollandus. But 7 February fell on a Saturday in A.D. 319, marked by the dominical letter D, not in 316. Lactantius therefore did not publish the books of the *Divine Institutions* before A.D. 319.

Does not some further strength and support accrue to this later opinion from the fact that Lactantius seems to indicate that he had left Bithynia—whence, as we have said, he had been summoned by Diocletian—before he published his books of the *Divine Institutions*? (Institutions, book V, ch. 2). [Col. 0871D] For it may not wholly improperly be inferred that he composed them after he had gone to Gaul and Crispus had been entrusted to his instruction there. This happened in A.D. 318 or a little later.

Some more recent critics, however, seem to themselves to have removed the difficulties of both Baronius’ opinion and that of the others by saying that Lactantius issued two editions of these books. They suppose that he first set hand to their composition while he was living in Bithynia during the raging persecution of Christians; then, after peace had been granted to the Church, revised and enlarged them and brought them out publicly in a second recension. They consider that this later edition was published long after the battle of Cibalae, [Col. 0872A] while Lactantius was living in Gaul with Caesar Crispus, where he dedicated it to Constantine the Great. This opinion may perhaps seem to receive no small support from the large number of manuscripts and especially from their variation in presenting certain fragments.

But what, pray, prevents us from ascribing this discrepancy to some idle and dishonest corrupter of ancient books? Moreover, as we noted a little earlier, Lactantius indicates quite plainly that he did not compose these books as long as he remained in Bithynia.

Perhaps someone will press the point that, after the *Divine Institutions* had been published, Lactantius issued an epitome of them. But why did he prepare it except because [Col. 0872B] very many derived the greatest benefit from these books? Could he not therefore, for the same reason, publish a second edition of the same books, more carefully prepared than the first, as generally happens, and consequently more useful than the other? We shall not deny that this could have happened; but no sufficiently certain and firm argument establishes whether it actually did. Jerome is our witness that the first and larger part of this epitome had already been lost in his time, although it was found and published a few years ago, as we shall say. But why, pray, in the entire epitome—at whose beginning he excuses himself from the labour of composing it—did Lactantius make no mention of a twofold edition of the *Divine Institutions*? Nor is there found in the epitome we possess any trace whatsoever [Col. 0872C] of a second edition of these books, except one wholly uncertain and deceptive. Therefore either he never made this second edition, or we have lost it.

Let an impartial assessor of matters judge which of these different opinions concerning the date of the books is truer, and embrace it. But whatever judgment is made, it must be admitted that these books were published between A.D. 316 and 322. Yet this interval of only six years will not appear so important to many that the thread of discussion should for that reason be drawn out further. Meanwhile, let us consider whether these books were really dedicated to Constantine the Great, a point which may assist in establishing their date.

## ARTICLE II. Whether Lactantius dedicated these books to Constantine the Great and addressed him in one or two speeches.

[Col. 0872D]

Two passages occur especially in these books of the *Divine Institutions* in which Lactantius addresses Constantine the Great and testifies that this work was begun under the auspicious omen of his name. In the first, the author expressly asserts that Constantine was the first of Roman emperors to reject pagan errors, worship the true God, and embrace the true religion—that is, Christ’s religion—restored by himself (Lactantius, book I, ch. 1). He therefore promises him that God will grant him prosperity as long as he holds the helm of empire, and that as an old man [Col. 0873A] he will hand over to his sons the empire which he himself received as a young man from his father. He promises no less confidently that, for so excellent and pious a deed, Constantine will receive from God a worthy reward, and that others in other regions of the earth, who were still then raging against Christians, will pay the penalties for so great a crime.

In the second, longer than the first, he again congratulates the Emperor Constantine because, raised up by God for the protection of humankind and the restoration of the Christian religion, no one would any longer dare to cast even the name Christian as a reproach upon anyone; because, all tyrants having been destroyed, Constantine had escaped very many dangers and alone held the empire of the whole world. He further adds that all pray to God that, protected and guarded by Him, Constantine may persevere in His love (Lactantius, book VII, ch. 26).

[Col. 0873B] But Isaeus, and afterward Thomasius, consider the first address wholly spurious and interpolated for various reasons. First, it is absent from seven Vatican manuscripts and very many other manuscripts written in different hands, as well as from certain printed copies; especially, it is absent from the very ancient manuscript exemplar of St Saviour at Bologna. Next, he says, this address conflicts with Lactantius’ genuine books, in which he indicates that Christians were then still most cruelly harassed by pagans and tyrants throughout the entire world. You have already heard us quote above his words; nor do the following appear less clear: [Col. 0873C] “No one can describe as it deserves the monstrous savagery of this immense beast, which, though lying in one place, nevertheless rages with iron teeth throughout the whole world and not only tears apart human limbs, but crushes the very bones and rages even against ashes, lest any place remain for burial” (book V, ch. 11). Yet in the address to Constantine the Great tyrants are said to rage against Christians not everywhere but only in certain regions of the world.

But this apparent and merely verbal contradiction does not greatly trouble others. For we have already observed that Lactantius denotes two most bitter persecutions of Christians: one raised by Diocletian, the other by Licinius; the former indeed past, the latter present. If, therefore, he sometimes speaks—as in the passage just cited—of the former also as though it were still present, he follows there not the manner of a historian but of an orator, by whom past events are not infrequently presented as present. [Col. 0873D] It is enough correctly to distinguish the two that the time of the one’s passing and the other’s present duration be indicated. Nor is anything to prevent Licinius’ persecution, which did not rage everywhere, from being meant.

That objection pressed by Isaeus is undoubtedly of lesser weight: that Lactantius, when recalling the most celebrated defenders of the Christian religion, said nothing of Arnobius, his teacher, who was defending the Christian cause at the same time as he. For we have given reasons why Lactantius passed Arnobius over—or, if you prefer, spared his name and the ever-venerable dignity of his teacher (above, ch. 3, art. 2).

Nor does another argument of the same Isaeus seem more compelling, drawn from the fact that various writers, [Col. 0874A] and above all Jerome, who carefully catalogued Lactantius’ works, nowhere said that these books of the *Divine Institutions* were inscribed to the name of Constantine the Great or that he was addressed in them. For Jerome himself similarly passed over in silence to whom Lactantius’ most beautiful book, as Jerome calls it, *On the Anger of God*, and another, *On Persecution*, were inscribed and dedicated.

Nor indeed should Isaeus have insisted that Lactantius was compelled to publish these books when he saw the Christian church, as we have said, utterly destroyed in A.D. 302; and that he therefore delayed their publication until the time when Constantine the Great restored peace to the churches. For what is remarkable if Lactantius awaited a more opportune time: namely, when that most pious emperor, after defeating Licinius, favoured Christians as greatly as Licinius was raging and fuming against them in certain provinces?

[Col. 0874B] The chief, indeed almost the entire, difficulty seems to rest in the authority of manuscript copies. For Constantine’s name and the words in which Lactantius addresses him are wholly omitted in the very ancient Bolognese manuscript and in manuscripts of various dates, and also in many printed editions; but they are found in others no fewer in number. For, to pass over five Vatican copies and others copied either earlier or later, all these things appear in the manuscript of the former monastery of Fleury, now the Royal Library, numbered 3735 there, which seems to have been written about A.D. 900. In another manuscript, formerly belonging to Claude Puteanus and now likewise in the Royal Library, number 3736, copied about A.D. 800, Lactantius’ address to Constantine does not occur; nevertheless, the title of the second book is found there: “Here begins the second book of Lactantius Caecilius Firmianus, *On the Origin of Error*, to Constantine.” Nor should you think that this was written casually by a copyist. For in the same manuscript Constantine’s name is likewise prefixed at the beginning of the third book: “I would wish, Emperor Constantine, since truth, etc.” Similarly at the beginning of the fourth: “While I reflect, Emperor Constantine, and in my mind, etc.” Again, at the opening of the fifth: “There is no doubt with me, Emperor Constantine, that this work, etc.” It would be a long, and perhaps not very useful, task [Col. 0874D] to enumerate all the other manuscripts in which all these things are read. For their number is greater, although not many were written long before the editions published in print.

[Col. 0874C] Among the editions in which Constantine’s name and Lactantius’ speech to him are found, the first to be mentioned is that published at Rome from the press of Peter de Maximo in 1468. It is also read in Betuleius’ edition of 1563 and in most other editions. Thomasius, however, observes in his notes to the edition which he published in 1570 that this address of Lactantius to Constantine is absent from two Bolognese and five Vatican manuscripts; [Col. 0875A] for this reason Isaeus afterward removed it, as he did Constantine’s name, from Lactantius’ text.

It is therefore beyond doubt that so great a divergence among manuscript codices keeps the minds of many in suspense, lest they incline too hastily to one side rather than the other. And certainly, if the greater antiquity of the Bologna codex seems to outweigh the others, nevertheless the age of those copied in Gaul—being only one or two centuries later—has its own weight and authority. To this is added that no reason appears why Lactantius’s address and Constantine’s name should either have been added to or removed from these books. For they contribute nothing to Lactantius’s purpose; and whether they are added or deleted, his books are neither less complete nor better or worse. Finally, [Col. 0875B] critics of no small distinction recognize Lactantius’s style in that address, which could more easily have been removed than added.

Yet these arguments might perhaps carry greater weight, if there were not several other fragments which seem to have been fraudulently inserted into these same books of the *Divine Institutions*. Besides several others which must shortly be discussed, another address of Lactantius to Constantine—longer than the former, as we have observed—is read near the end of the entire work as genuine in some editions, while in certain others it has been relegated to the margin (*Institutions*, VII.26). But Isaeus declares that he found it neither in the two Bologna manuscripts, nor in twelve Vatican manuscripts, nor in the other manuscripts which he was able to examine. Nor did others [Col. 0875C] who supervised the later English editions at Cambridge and Oxford find it in the English manuscripts which they used. It is also absent from the Roman edition published in 1468, and from the manuscript codex of the Royal Library, no. 3736, which we carefully collated, copied, as we have said, about eight hundred years ago. Nothing, however, can be determined concerning another and older exemplar from the same library, since its final leaves were torn away or lost after the middle of chapter 9 of Book VII.

Since, then, this address or allocution lacks the authority of so many older codices, can it not be concluded with considerable certainty that it is altogether spurious and adulterated? But if this is counterfeit and fabricated [Col. 0875D] by some trifler, why not the other, earlier address as well? The case, however, does not seem at all parallel. For this second address bears far greater marks of a forged interpolation than the first. The first indeed occurs, as we have already observed, in many manuscripts both older and more recent; the latter in very few, and those of the latest date. Moreover, the later address contradicts not only the earlier one, but Lactantius’s genuine text itself. In the former, as has been observed, the writer says that Christians were being tortured, struck down, and killed with horrible punishments in at least a great part of the world; in the latter, on the contrary, he says that there was no one who held the name of God against Christians. In the first address tyrants and most bitter enemies of the Christian religion are said then to have been ruling; [Col. 0876A] in the second it is asserted that, having paid the penalty for their crimes, they lay overthrown, and that Constantine alone possessed supreme power. Can it not therefore be concluded without absurdity that this second address is supposititious and stitched into Lactantius’s genuine text as inappropriately as the other appears to be genuine and truly issued by him? If this is so, it must be said that these books of the *Divine Institutions* were published by Lactantius, as we have stated, in the year 320 or 321, when hostility and rivalry had already arisen between Licinius and Constantine, and Licinius was raging against the Christians. Nevertheless, since forgers and corruptors even of the most ancient codices dared with such audacity to lay their impious hands upon Lactantius’s books, consider, I pray you, what judgment should be made about these addresses, [Col. 0876B] and pronounce upon it. Meanwhile, other passages in these books must be examined which are likewise said to have been spurious, or even corrupted and adulterated.

## ARTICLE III. On several fragments which appear spurious and to have been inappropriately inserted into Lactantius’s text

All who read Lactantius’s writings encounter many things which very many persons, not wholly without reason, consider to have been wrongly introduced into his text. First is this:

> “As the mother without precedent gave birth to her own author, so the Father must be believed, in an ineffable manner, to have begotten one coeternal with himself. He was born from the mother who already existed before; from the Father, who at some time did not exist. Let faith [Col. 0876C] believe this; let understanding not inquire into it—lest it judge incredible what has not been discovered, or fail to believe what has been found to be unique.”  
> (*Lactantius*, II.8–9)

Many, however, think that these words were altogether inappropriately added by some utterly foolish writer. For Isaeus has informed us that they are absent from the most ancient Bologna manuscript, eight Vatican manuscripts, and other excellent codices. Others have observed that they are likewise absent from the copies which they had before them for correcting the edition of these books of Lactantius. They are also missing from the two older exemplars of the Royal Library, copied nine hundred and eight hundred years ago.

Moreover, whoever reads even cursorily what precedes and follows this fragment will immediately discover that Lactantius’s discourse is completely disturbed by it. We further notice an open contradiction in this very short addition. For there the Son of God is asserted to be coeternal with his Father and yet at some time not to have existed—that is, not to be coeternal. We know that Betuleius observed that the second Roman edition reads: “Who was not at some time absent.” But who does not see that this correction was made by a more clear-sighted writer, in order to remove so obvious a contradiction? Rightly, therefore, these words are enclosed in asterisks in some editions; more properly, in others they are transferred from the text to the margin; and the notes identify them as spurious. There are nevertheless certain learned men who consider them genuine and spoken in a catholic sense. But we shall examine their reasons below, when we deal with the divinity of the Son of God.

[Col. 0877A] Not long afterward, where Lactantius begins to discuss the creation of all things, this sentence likewise seems to have been added:

> “In the beginning he made good and evil. What this precisely means I shall explain more clearly, lest anyone suppose that I speak as poets customarily do, who comprehend incorporeal things by certain figures as though visible, especially since he himself was still nothing.”

This entire sentence is plainly incoherent and wholly unworthy of Lactantius; it has been rejected by nearly all editions, both because it is not found in the Bologna manuscripts, eleven Vatican manuscripts, and very many others, and because it seemed to many to smell of Manichaean errors. Yet we read it in the older manuscript codex of the Royal Library, no. 3735, though not in the other, marked by the succeeding number. Yet this nonetheless shows that it was ineptly added to our Lactantius’s text long ago. Nor without reason. For these words disrupt and confuse Lactantius’s discourse there. Some further maintain that these words signify that God made good and evil not only before the creation of the world, but even before the generation of his Son. If this is so, nothing could surely be imagined more contrary to Lactantius’s teaching, as we shall later show.

A little later, in the older royal codex, between the words “He is also so beloved” and “Therefore, this one, made evil out of good by himself, the Greeks call *diabolos* [διάβολον],” the following words were inserted:

> “He too is beloved. Of him I shall speak more sparingly now, because elsewhere we must set forth for ourselves both his power, his name, and the explanation of it. Meanwhile, I shall speak more fully about him here, in order that the divine arrangement may be known; because neither can good be understood without evil, nor evil likewise without good, and wisdom is the knowledge of good and evil. Therefore this evil spirit, whom the Greeks call *diabolos* [διάβολον], etc.”

But these words occur neither in other handwritten codices nor in many printed editions; nor has any writer noted anywhere that he read them. If, therefore, this fragment is genuine, those by whom it was torn out or omitted undoubtedly erred. If it is spurious and counterfeit, far more wicked are those who deliberately dared to insert it into Lactantius’s text.

A very few words later, and before “God, therefore, having begun, etc.,” another addition is inserted, much larger than the rest, whose length does not allow us to transcribe it in full. There we read that the world was created by God in order that it might consist of contrary and mutually opposing things; that two spirits also were made, one good and the other evil, so that the things in the world which oppose each other might be in their power. Likewise, as is there asserted, God, when about to create humanity, made good and evil in order that virtue might exist. Yet because evil may not proceed from God, he established the evil spirit as the inventor of evils and gave him intelligence and cunning for devising evils, so that he might possess both a wicked will and perfect malice. He arranged those two spirits for conflict in such a way that he placed one over good and the other over evil. Afterwards he created many angels of an opposing nature, such as that of the gods, a part of whom, after the world had been established, apostatized from the power of the heavenly substance. [Col. 0878A] All the angels, moreover, whose leaders were those two spirits, were in the beginning equal and of the same condition before God.

Such, indeed, are the matters narrated in this very lengthy interpolation. But Isaeus maintains that it is not found in the most ancient Bologna codex, nor in twelve Vatican manuscripts, nor in many others. Spark notes that it is likewise absent from the English manuscripts accessible to him, except the Bullion manuscript. It is also lacking in the Roman edition published in 1568 and in other more corrected editions, as likewise in the extremely ancient royal exemplar no. 3736. We admit that we found it in the other older manuscript, no. 3735; but beside it was added this verse:

> Reader who reads these things, beware of pits and snares.

The copyist, therefore, or the person charged with correcting the codex, thought that this fragment administered the poison of the Manichaeans, who foolishly proclaimed two principles, one good and the other evil. This was also Isaeus’s opinion; in his notes he observes that this impious doctrine is nowhere else asserted more clearly. Spark, however, criticizes Betuleius because he wrote in his commentary on this passage that Lactantius was there combating the error of the Origenists and Manichaeans, who wished God to be the author of evil. Yet Betuleius wanted this interpolation enclosed in asterisks, because he considered it either adulterated or at least wholly doubtful. That some deadly Manichaean poison is subtly and artfully insinuated in it may be inferred from the fact that its author openly declares that God [Col. 0878C] made good and evil. But since these words could appear too harsh, he added shortly afterward, in order to correct or soften them:

> “And because it was not lawful for evil to proceed from God—for he would not act against himself—he established that one as the inventor of evils; and when he made him, he gave him intelligence and cunning for devising evils, so that there might be in him both a wicked will and perfect malice. He wished things contrary to his virtues to arise from him, and for him to contend with God, whether God himself would bestow more goods or he more evils.”

But what, someone may ask, did that shifty writer intend by this deceitful correction? Had he not read what our Lactantius himself had truly written just before: that God made the other spirit, in whom the disposition of the divine stock did not remain?

> “Therefore,” he says, “he was infected by his own envy as by poison, passed from good to evil, and by his own choice—which God had granted him freely—assumed for himself a name contrary to his nature. Hence it is evident that envy is the fountain of all evils.”

Were not these words orthodox, as well as sufficiently clear and plain? What need was there for some obscure and malicious interpretation to be added in the same place a few lines later? However much it may be explained in some good sense, who, I ask you, will find it credible that Lactantius added all this entirely without purpose?

Moreover, in this interpolation the two spirits whom Lactantius states were first created by God are called leaders of the angels. Yet in Book IV, to which the author of that interpolation refers us, the first spirit is called by Lactantius [Col. 0879A] the true Son of God (IV.6–7). Furthermore, angels in the same fragment are imagined to be not of one nature, but of a contrary nature, such as that of the gods. But where, I ask, did Lactantius ever speak in this way? And what of the fact that that writer so departed from imitation of Lactantius’s style that within two lines the words “he began the construction of the world” are repeated? Finally, as much as Lactantius’s discourse is badly interrupted by this addition, so completely, when it is removed, does it cohere with itself and join together most aptly.

Another fragment, longer than the preceding one, is presented in Book VII (VII.5). Its author declares that in the other books, and a little before, he had answered those who objected that the blame of humanity must be laid upon God, who made evil as well as good. Further, he says, there could be no virtue unless God had made opposites; for if evil were removed, good too would be removed. God therefore made good and evil, so that by exercise and conflict with evils he might make virtue perfect. For there is no victory without an enemy and a contest. He then introduces someone arguing against him in this manner: “If good cannot exist without evil, how do you say that the first human being was in good alone before offending God, or that he will later be in good alone?” He immediately answers that he had omitted this question in the earlier books so that it might be discussed there in a more appropriate place. Accordingly, in order now to resolve it, he first teaches that a human being consists of an earthly body and a subtle yet eternal soul; and because these are opposed to one another, humanity must necessarily be subject to good and evil. [Col. 0879C] “Good,” he says, “is attributed to the soul because it is indissoluble; evil to the body because it is fragile.” Therefore good and evil cannot be separated unless the soul is separated from the body. Moreover, knowledge of good and evil was simultaneously given to the first human being; but while he existed in good alone, he did not know that good itself was good. But once he first attained an understanding of good and evil, he was banished from the place of blessedness into the common world, so that he might experience the good and evil whose nature he had recognized. Hence it is clear that wisdom was given to human beings to distinguish good from evil, and wisdom cannot stand without evil.

The first human being, he continues, so long as he existed in good alone, lived like an infant ignorant of good and evil. But one cannot be wise and, before the separation of soul and body, blessed without any evil. For then, just as the body, so evil too will perish, and good alone will remain forever with the blessed soul. Thus God placed humanity in this life between the two, so that it might have freedom to follow either good or evil. But because evils are mingled with goods, and apparent goods with evils, the office of wisdom is needed, by which we see more with the mind than with the body. Since this is difficult and rare, the wise person who despises fragile goods, and the Christian who for faith refuses neither tortures nor death, is considered foolish. Therefore humanity was made mortal and subject to evils by God in order that it might acquire virtue, and virtue might confer immortality upon it.

Thus argues the author of this fragment. But that it is spurious and attributed to Lactantius is inferred from the fact that Isaeus affirms that it is absent from the Bologna manuscripts, twelve Vatican manuscripts, and others; while Spark states that it is absent from all the English manuscripts. Nor did we find it in the ancient royal codex no. 3736. Nothing can be determined about the other, older codex, because it was there truncated and mutilated. It is likewise omitted in the ancient Roman, Florentine, Antwerp, and other better editions. Betuleius suspected that Gryphius was the first of all to publish it in print.

For this reason most reject it as adulterated. Some suspect it was manufactured by a certain trickster, as ingenious as he was cunning, who correctly imitated Lactantius’s style. Yet that was undoubtedly not difficult for one who had gathered his statements from Lactantius’s own various books. For our part, however, we shall not readily be persuaded that Lactantius employed in one place as many comparisons as this writer has crammed into the first part of this fragment. Still less do we think Lactantius used the comparison drawn from the Circus, against which he declaims so vehemently and so deservedly. Moreover, he clearly indicates that the matters disputed in the first part of that fragment had already been sufficiently treated by him: “But,” he says, “it has already often been said that no virtue could have come to exist unless it had something to overcome” (*Lactantius*, ch. 22). But the author of this addition openly declares—or rather pretends—that he had touched upon these matters only lightly, although what he wrote there was taken from Book V and especially Book VI of the *Divine Institutions* (V.7, 21; VI.15; II.12; VII.4–5; *On the Anger of God*, 15). Nor could he with greater reason say that the question of the human being, who cannot exist without evil, had been omitted in the preceding books. For anyone may easily recognize that nearly everything he set forth there was excerpted from Books II and VII of the *Institutions* and from *On the Anger of God*. We know indeed that Lactantius published *On the Anger of God*, as we shall show more fully below, after the seven books of the *Divine Institutions*, where we read this addition. Yet surely, if he had written it there and resolved this question with such care, then in *On the Anger of God*, where he reconsidered it, he would not have omitted, as was his usual custom, to refer us to this passage or make some mention of it.

[Col. 0880D] Moreover, although Isaeus rejected this passage like the preceding fragments and did not permit them to be printed in Lactantius’s text, nevertheless relying solely upon the authority of the Bologna codex, he inserted into its text the following words, where Lactantius discusses Cyprian:

> “Hence it is evident that to this most eloquent and learned man, so far as refuting sacrilegious persons was concerned, there was lacking not ability in speaking but judgment—especially in that he extinguished Demetrianus, who was devoid of truth, not by the reasoning of human prudence, which he ought to have employed at the outset, but by the authority of the heavenly precepts, of which the latter confessed himself an enemy.”  
> (V.1)

But Isaeus’s customary diligence is lacking here, since he did not expressly explain to us in which Bologna manuscript—whether the very ancient one or the other, more recent one—these words were written. Yet even if they appeared in the former, must the authority of that one alone prevail over all the rest? Are there not in it, as in others, some copyists’ errors? But that this is an addition by some writer is clear from the fact that the same things concerning Cyprian are later said more elegantly. Nor is it probable that Lactantius judged these insulting words worthy of repetition—words which, as we have seen, were by no means deservedly spoken of so eminent a writer. Is it not therefore much more probable, not to say more certain, that this repetition is attributable to a negligent copyist? (*Lactantius*, ch. 4.)

Finally, the distinguished Stephen Baluzius (Balus., *Miscellanies*, II, p. 46) published another short fragment concerning the final judgment, which he had found copied in codex 1095 of the Colbert Library after the seven books of the *Divine Institutions* [Col. 0881B] and before *On the Anger of God*. Supported by the authority of this codex, he thought that it had truly come from Lactantius. Thomas Spark followed Baluzius and afterwards had it printed from two English manuscripts in the Oxford edition. We, however, saw two other manuscripts in the Colbert Library, to be discussed shortly, in which the same fragment is found in the same manner. But how could it happen that it occurs only in these exemplars, which are certainly very recent, and not in many others which are far more numerous and older? Why also was it not copied in its proper place in these books written in so recent a hand? Can it not be concluded from this that there is no reason why it should be said to have been transcribed from the books of our Lactantius rather than those of another author? Be that as it may, this short fragment is not of sufficient importance for us to linger longer in investigating its parentage. For it supplies nothing new except the name of Elijah the Tishbite, who, as is there related, pursued the Antichrist of the Jews by faith—or, in two English manuscripts, “faith.” But I fear that these words too may not agree with what Lactantius has set forth in Book VII of the *Institutions* and in the epitome on the final judgment.

Yet it is astonishing with what confidence a certain recent critic (Simon, *Selected Letters*, XXV, Rotterdam, 1704) asserted in one of his selected letters that all the fragments hitherto discussed are genuine and sound, and that they had been cut from Lactantius’s text by those who in former times supervised the correction of ancient codices in monasteries. He wished us to be informed there that, lest that letter become too long, he would examine these same fragments only in another letter. Whether he fulfilled his promise is unknown to us. In the cited letter, however, he admits that those additions in which Manichaean errors are detected are not found in the greater part of the better manuscript codices. Yet he boldly affirms that for many centuries correctors of these codices removed from authors’ texts these and many other things which did not seem orthodox to them. Finally, he unhesitatingly declares that Lactantius, who was not perfectly instructed in our theological doctrines, might have been infected by the false opinions of the Manichaeans, derived from the Gnostics.

[Col. 0882A] But observe, I pray, the altogether unusual acuteness of a man to whom the name of critic is so dear and delightful, and indeed a new kind of argumentation. “Lactantius,” says that critic, “could have been contaminated by Manichaean errors; therefore he actually was contaminated by them; therefore he wrote the fragments in question; therefore the monastic correctors cut them out.” An argument indeed worthy of so great a critic! But in order to accuse monks of so great a crime, he first had to prove that Lactantius had actually been contaminated by these Manichaean errors; then that Lactantius wrote those additions; and when they were cut out by monks or not copied into later codices. But he will certainly never prove these things, nor will anyone else be able to prove them. Furthermore, we have demonstrated by many arguments that all these additions are counterfeit and spurious, especially those which seem to smell of the poison and venom of the Manichaeans. Nor less clearly and plainly have we shown that Lactantius’s discourse is inappropriately disrupted by most of these same fragments and errors contrary to his teaching are defended. But it is shameful to waste further effort in refuting the calumnies by which that modern writer vainly attempted throughout his writings to disparage not only the faithfulness of monks but also the teaching of the most ancient writers. Yet the man should be spared, since before he gave up his spirit in 1712 he publicly sought pardon from those whom he had offended as grievously as undeservedly, and died in the bosom of the Catholic Church. One may only wish that he had turned his mind and learning toward better things.

## ARTICLE IV. On various errors ascribed to Lactantius

If any errors of Lactantius occur in the additions thus far enumerated, most people rightly judge, as we have seen, that they must be attributed not to our Lactantius but to others abusing their leisure. Yet many false opinions and errors of every kind are attributed to Lactantius himself, which many have believed they found scattered through his writings. Their number is indeed so great that scarcely any other writer seems ever to have erred so often in so few books. Some formerly counted one hundred and seventy of his errors; others later reduced them to somewhat more than ninety-four; still others to a smaller number. The greater part of them concerns orthodox faith, the lesser part moral teaching, and the least part physical matters. But the larger the number imagined for them, the more readily everyone understands that many of the passages marked are sound and altogether unworthy of being branded with the mark of censorious severity. Therefore, in the Roman edition of Lactantius’s works published in 1468, Brother Antonius Raudensis, theologian, is rebuked by Brother Adam of Genoa, as we read there, in these verses:

> Anthony, in foolish daring, wrongly rebuked  
> The author in many places, where he ought to be excused.  
>
> One ought not say that the star of a wandering image is in darkness,  
> Or that a bright radiance lacks light.  
>
> Finally, since it is known that the devout lights of the holy Church  
> Have fallen silent in obedience to so great a man,  
>
> You, whose tongue is forbidden Latin speech, go to bed;  
> For hellebore is prescribed for you.

[Col. 0883A] Nevertheless, among more recent heterodox writers there were afterwards not a few who either accused Lactantius of still further errors or made him conscious supporter and advocate of false doctrines which they vainly attempt to defend. But we have judged that such audacity should be corrected later in a more appropriate place, lest the same matters be repeated.

The testimony of Pope Damasus ought beyond doubt to have more serious weight. In his letter to Jerome he gives this judgment concerning the letters of our Lactantius:

> “I confess to you that I do not gladly read the books of Lactantius which you gave me long ago, because both his very many letters extend to thousands of lines, and they rarely discuss our doctrine. Thus their length produces weariness in the reader; and if any are short, they are better suited to schoolmen than to us, discussing metres, the position of regions, and philosophers.”  
> (Several manuscripts and editions read “discussed”; others, “discussing.”)

But by Damasus’s words, “rarely discuss our doctrine,” he seems to mean nothing else than the questions concerning certain passages of Holy Scripture which Jerome had proposed. Furthermore, this judgment of Damasus seems to concern only Lactantius’s letters, if his name is written there, and not the books of the *Divine Institutions*, in which—as in his other writings—he discusses many matters concerning our doctrines and tenets neither sparsely nor unlearnedly, as may readily be discerned from their analysis and from other things to be said more fully below. And what of the fact that Jerome, to whom Damasus wrote, speaks thus of the same books of Lactantius: “Our Firmianus too, in the distinguished work of his *Institutions*, mentions the letter Y and has discussed most fully right and left—that is, vices and virtues” (Jerome, *Commentary on Ecclesiastes*, p. 770). Of his letters themselves we can determine nothing certain, since none has reached us.

“But at least Gelasius I,” someone may say, “in the Roman council rejected Lactantius’s works among others which the Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church does not receive, in these words: ‘The works of Lactantius: apocryphal.’” Yet many formerly doubted whether those words were genuine and authentic. We, however, know with the greatest certainty that they are found in all the older and better-regarded manuscript codices. But it is no less established [Col. 0884A] that in this decree of Pope Gelasius several writings of ancient Fathers of the Church, such as Tertullian, Eusebius Pamphilus, and others, are dismissed as apocryphal, though everyone readily admits that they are nonetheless sound and orthodox. They were marked by this designation either because of other writings by the same authors infected with errors or because of certain mistakes with which they are here and there stained. No one can deny that our Lactantius, in composing these books of the *Divine Institutions*, struck upon several reefs of error, especially the one invented by the Chiliasts concerning Christ’s thousand-year reign on earth after the final judgment. Could not that error alone have given occasion for Damasus’s judgment mentioned above? We have dealt with it and shall say something more about it below.

[Col. 0884B] We shall, moreover, expound in their proper place with our customary candor his other errors, whether genuine or attributed to him, so that, after explaining them without any concealment, we may make plain to all what in them is worthy of reproach. But with the same frankness we shall clear him of others which are ascribed to him by some through thoughtlessness or ill will. For nothing is dearer to some modern writers than to magnify and multiply the slips and errors of the ancient Fathers of the Church. Sometimes, however, these crafty persons pretend to excuse them somewhat, because to err is human, or because ancient writers who came to Christ’s religion from paganism had not yet sufficiently investigated our sacred teachings. But by this subtle and fraudulent excuse they do nothing other than weaken and diminish the authority of those Fathers and of ancient, ever-venerable tradition.

Whatever Lactantius’s blemishes or errors may be, we shall soon show that he demonstrates the truth of the Christian religion by the strongest weight of arguments. Nor can it be denied that in his books he correctly explains, asserts, and confirms many teachings of Christian faith concerning Holy Scripture, God, Christ the Lord, the old and new law, and the precepts and ordinances of the latter. These matters, however, are more clearly and fully presented in the books of the *Divine Institutions*. Hence they are rightly considered his principal work, composed with great care and strenuous application. Yet it is filled not only with sacred learning, but also with profane learning, varied and abundant in many kinds.

[Col. 0883]

## [NOTES OF JOSEPH ISAEUS OF CESENA ON THE SEVEN BOOKS OF THE *DIVINE INSTITUTIONS*]

## NOTES ON THE FIRST BOOK OF THE *DIVINE INSTITUTIONS* OF LACTANTIUS FIRMIANUS

### CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0883D] “For some have cast away their possessions, etc.” [Col. 0884D] These were Socrates, Democritus of Abdera—concerning whom Lactantius himself also speaks in Book III, chapter 23—Anaxagoras of Clazomenae, and others.

[Col. 0885A] “For because bitterness is mixed with virtues, while vices are seasoned with pleasure, offended by the former and enticed by the latter, they rush headlong, etc.” He says the same in *On the Anger of God*, ch. 19. This reason is advanced, among others, why, although virtue is in accordance with human nature and vice contrary to it—as is found in Seneca, *On Anger* II.13 and Letter 123; in Quintilian, Book XII, final chapter; and as St Thomas demonstrates excellently in Part II, question 71, article 2—so few embrace the former and so many the latter. The reason is that, although the good of virtue accords with human nature according to its rational part, the sensible good by which we are lured into vice also suits it according to the sensitive part, which opposes reason. Although the rational portion is the more important in a human being, nevertheless a person follows the good of sense rather than the good of reason, because he begins from sensible good to know and love the good of reason. But those beginning are far more numerous than those who reach completion. Therefore, there are more who remain and abide among the goods of sensitive nature than those who attain to embrace the goods of [Col. 0885B] reason—especially because the inducement to remain and rest in those goods is powerful: they have been in use from earliest age; they are more familiar, being known by the evident experience of the senses; and finally they move us more strongly, both because pleasure is immediate and because the opposing sorrow is imminent. The good of reason, however, which is virtue, is perceived at a more advanced age; it is little known and moves little. For it has sadness and bitterness mingled with it, at least in the beginning, as Lactantius says; but it promises reward and pleasure for the future, as Aristotle says, *On the Soul* III, text 53. Cajetan, on question 71.

Yet that exercise in fictitious lawsuits benefited us greatly, etc. He says “fictitious lawsuits”; for he was never an advocate in real ones, since he never even set foot in the forum, as he himself testifies in Book III, chapter 13. In former times, when the study of eloquence flourished in Greece and at Rome, young men, after mastering grammar, were brought to rhetoricians, who set before them themes either composed for the purpose or drawn from histories [Col. 0885C], such as those still found in abundance in the declamations of the elder Seneca and Quintilian and among Greek writers. In these schoolboys practised speaking and writing, so that later they might speak seriously before the people or the senate. They were also accustomed to argue both sides, and to handle *adoxous theses* (θέσεις ἀδόξους), that is, unexpected propositions, and disreputable subjects, concerning which see Gellius, Book XVII, chapter 12. Thus they became ready and equipped to speak upon any matter whatsoever. Those trained in this method of speaking at school were said to declaim, and speeches of this kind, composed in imitation of forensic proceedings, were called declamations. Hence St Jerome, in the Questions to Damasus: “Nor are the ears to be soothed with Quintilian’s little flowers and schoolroom declamation.” On these matters see at considerable length Quintilian, Book II, chapter 10, and Book IV, chapter 2; Seneca, in the Prologue to his *Declamations*. Libanius the sophist flourished in this genre of speaking, and was therefore especially pleasing to the Emperor Julian [Col. 0885D], concerning whom Eunapius wrote. Carneades also flourished in it, of whom Lactantius himself makes mention in Book V, chapter 15. Likewise Paulus of Tyre was so beloved under this name by the Emperor Hadrian that he obtained from that emperor for Tyre, his native city, the status of metropolis, as Suidas writes. These, therefore, were the exercises by which Lactantius, a little above, says that he had long been occupied in that rhetorical profession; exercises which formerly trained young men not in virtue, but plainly in subtle wickedness, and whose practice, he says, would now greatly assist him in pleading the cause of truth against the Gentiles.

“But if certain very great orators,” etc. He perhaps means Marcus Tullius himself, whom we know from the opening of the *Tusculan Disputations* and the first book of the *Academic Questions* to have rested, as in a harbour, from forensic business and the administration of the republic in the study of philosophy.

“And if certain prudent men and arbiters of equity published compiled Institutes of civil law,” etc. These were Gaius, Ulpian, Paulus, Florentinus, Callistratus, and Martianus.

“And let us put to sleep the most shameful errors.” In some printed books the following speech is appended after these words:

> “This work we now begin under the auspices of your name, Constantine, greatest Emperor. You, the first of Roman rulers, having rejected errors, both acknowledged and honoured the majesty of the one and true God. For when that most fortunate day dawned upon the world, on which the supreme God raised you to the blessed summit of empire, you inaugurated, by a splendid beginning, a rule salutary and desirable for all. By restoring justice, which had been overthrown and removed, you expiated the most foul crime of others. For this deed God will grant you prosperity, strength, and long duration, so that with the same justice with which you began as a young man, you may hold the helm of the state even in old age; and that you may hand down to your children, as you yourself received it from your father, the guardianship of the Roman name. For upon the wicked, who still rage against the just in other parts of the earth, that same Almighty One will pay the recompense of crime with the greater severity the later he does so; because, as he is a most indulgent father toward the pious, so he is a most righteous judge against the impious. Desiring to defend his religion and divine worship, whom should I rather invoke, whom address, than him through whom justice and wisdom have been restored to human affairs?”

This speech addresses Constantine when he was already openly embracing the Christian religion and turning away from impiety. At that time Licinius, Constantine’s colleague in the Empire, was disregarding the agreement made with Constantine for the protection of the Christian religion and was harassing the Church of God throughout the eastern region; whereas the West, having fallen to Constantine’s rule, enjoyed the utmost peace and tranquillity. For this reason certain men of the greatest weight and renown have thought that from this passage they had discovered the time when Lactantius elaborated these books of his *Institutions*. They think that this occurred in the year of our Lord 316, when Licinius’s persecution harassed the Church and Constantine was preparing an expedition against him; and that Firmianus, in this preface supposedly addressed to Constantine [Col. 0886C], prophesied the disaster and destruction of Licinius and Constantine’s victory.

For my part, I cannot but agree with Thomasius that passages of this kind, in which Constantine is either named or addressed, are spurious and interpolated. For I have observed that they are absent from the most ancient manuscript of San Salvatore at Bologna, from most Vatican manuscripts, and from other more reliable witnesses. Indeed, this entire speech is absent not only from that most ancient manuscript and another manuscript of the same monastery, but also from seven Vatican manuscripts, from the Florentine printed editions, and from many other manuscripts and printed books. After the words “and let us put to sleep the most shameful errors,” the text immediately reads, “Therefore, omitting the authors of this earthly philosophy,” etc. We also have other passages of Lactantius, supported by the authority of absolutely all manuscripts and admitting no controversy or ambiguity, which do not agree sufficiently with what is read in this speech.

In Book V, chapters 2 and 4, when he states the reason why he undertook to write, he says that when he was teaching rhetoric in Bithynia and the temples of God were being destroyed, and when he learned that two men—he means Porphyry and Hierocles—were there insulting truth more arrogantly and importunately and vomiting forth their impieties and blasphemies against the Christian religion, he was stirred by their proud impiety to undertake the task of writing, in order with all the powers of his intellect to refute the accusers of justice. The destruction of the temples by Diocletian’s decree, however, and the publication of Porphyry’s three books against Christ, fall in the year of our Lord 302. But in this passage he is said to begin this work only when evils had already ceased in the West, though in other parts of the earth men were still raging against the just: namely, when Constantine was preparing an expedition against Licinius, which occurred in the year of Christ 316. How, then, can it appear at all likely that Lactantius, provoked—as he himself says—by the impious disputations of Porphyry and [Col. 0887A] Hierocles, and inflamed with righteous anger on behalf of God’s religion, delayed for fourteen years, held back his pen, and did not immediately undertake writing and devote himself at the earliest opportunity to refuting their impieties?

It is also of no small importance that, at the time Lactantius was writing the *Institutions*, the cruelty of tyrants against Christians was being exercised throughout the whole world. He expressly testifies to this in Book V, chapter 11: “That beast, lying in one place, nevertheless rages throughout the whole world with iron teeth,” etc.; and in chapter 12 of the same book: “Behold, the whole world itself is in such error that it persecutes, tortures, condemns, and kills good and just men as though they were evil and impious.” And in Book VI, chapter 17: “For throughout the world the punishments of worshippers of God have been seen and are still continually seen; in torturing them new and unheard-of torments have been devised,” etc.

But at the time of Licinius’s persecution, when this speech is pretended to have been addressed to Constantine [Col. 0887B], the Christian religion was almost everywhere at peace; it suffered some harassment only in the East. This is also shown by the speech itself, where it says: “For upon the wicked, who still rage against the just in other parts of the earth, that same Almighty One will pay the recompense of crime with the greater severity the later he does so.” Since this harassment did not touch the West, Severus did not regard it as such as should be counted among the other persecutions of the Church. Thus he writes in Book II of his *History*: “Certainly at that time Licinius, because he contended with Constantine for the Empire, ordered his soldiers to sacrifice and dismissed from military service those who refused; but this is not counted among the persecutions, so slight a matter was it, not such as to pertain to the wounds of the churches.” Eusebius also, in Book I of the *Life of Constantine*: “Thus,” he says, “the Roman Empire, divided into two parts, seemed in all respects like the darkness of night and the brightness of day. For those who possessed the East were overspread as it were by the gloom of night; but upon the inhabitants of the other part shone the splendour of the brightest day.” Finally Sozomen, Book I, chapter 2: “At the same time Christians who lived eastward as far as the Libyans, who border upon Egypt, did not dare to hold assemblies openly, because Licinius had changed his benevolent disposition toward them; but the Greeks, Macedonians, and Illyrians, whose homes lay westward, worshipped God with free and secure minds through the agency of Constantine, who presided over that part of the Roman Empire.”

Perhaps someone may also be moved by the fact that, if Arnobius wrote in the year of our Lord 302 and swiftly and hastily published his work as a pledge of his faith, so that he might be admitted among the faithful as soon as possible, it would certainly seem very likely that Lactantius saw that work fourteen years later, if we wish to maintain that he wrote in 316. Yet no reason is apparent why, although he mentions Theophilus once, Tertullian twice, Cyprian twice, and Minucius twice—all of whom had long before pleaded the Christians’ cause against the Gentiles (for he mentions Theophilus at the end of this Book I, Tertullian in Book V, chapters 1 and 4, Cyprian in the same chapters, and Minucius in Book I, chapter 11, and Book V, chapter 1)—he should have suppressed in such profound silence Arnobius, his own teacher, who had conducted the same cause no less keenly and lucidly than any of them, but much more recently and at closer hand. Unless it was because both were writing at the same time, and Lactantius had perhaps not yet been able to see Arnobius’s books.

But St Jerome also, who could have seen the first edition of Lactantius’s books—for he was almost Lactantius’s contemporary, the infancy of Jerome, as may be believed, nearly touching Lactantius’s final days—and who reviewed his works so diligently that he did not omit to say to whom each had been dedicated, simply passes over the books of the *Institutions* without mentioning any dedication to anyone, and nowhere mentions the Emperor Constantine [Col. 0888A], although he surely understood that the dignity and esteem of these books could be greatly increased among all persons by Constantine’s name. Nor does Honorius of Autun mention him, though in the same manner he compiled a catalogue of the same works of Lactantius nearly five hundred years ago. We think for no other reason than that these books were not at all dedicated by their author to Constantine: since, as we have proved, they began to be elaborated in the year 302 and therefore, as it is reasonable to believe, had already been completed, finished, and published before Constantine openly rejected impiety and embraced the Christian faith.

Thus I hold that not only Methodius and Arnobius, at the same time when Porphyry’s blasphemous commentaries against Christ were published—that is, in 302—but also our Lactantius, undertook to refute by opposing writings the sacrilegious impieties of the heathen; and that this speech, rejected for so many reasons, is spurious and interpolated. Nor can the view of Thomasius be maintained, that Lactantius may have written these books before Constantine’s time but published them in Constantine’s time. For here he is not said to have published them then, but to have begun them at that time under the auspices of Constantine’s name.

## CHAPTER III

**“So many.”** This word here signifies not magnitude but multitude, so as to form an antithesis with “one.” Thus the Greek τοσοῦτος may indiscriminately mean both “so many” and “so great.” Antonius Augustinus noted that jurists use the word in this same sense, *Emendations*, Book II, chapter [uncertain OCR], from Law *Si ita legatum*, Digest, *On Legacies*, where one reads: “But not among more than ten who are legatees; if there are fewer, among as many as are found.” Likewise *quantus* means “how many,” as in that law and in Law 2, § *Si vero*, Code *On the Prefect of the Praetorium of Africa*: “And how many frontier-soldiers are stationed in those places or on those frontiers.” I add Vegetius, Book III, chapter 5, from the best manuscripts: “How many kinds of military standards are there?” And in the same book, chapter 9: “That they may kill as many men as they can while their own forces remain intact.” So too the interpreter of Luke 15, whom Valla rashly condemns: “How many hired servants in my father’s house abound in bread!”

## CHAPTER IV

**“But indeed they have been fulfilled,” etc.** Thus I read, not *atqui*, following B. and T. Arnobius, Book VI, at the beginning: “But indeed we think that every god,” etc. Book III: “But indeed I had thought a little before that the kindnesses of the gods were spontaneous.” Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 2: “But indeed we find that even investigation against us has been forbidden.” Papinian, in the law *Debitor*, § 1, Digest *On the Trebellian Decree of the Senate*: “But indeed, whether the creditor-plaintiff and at the same time heir possesses the thing, or does not possess it.” Paulus, in Law *At quin natura*, Digest *On the Conduct of Affairs*: “But indeed by nature he was a debtor.” And Barnabas Brissonius, in his *Parerga*, testifies that it is written thus in the Florentine Pandects, where he also points out other passages.

**“But also their coherence.”** Valla observes, *Elegances*, Book III, chapter 27, that Lactantius ought to have said “but at least their coherence,” or “but certainly their coherence,” or “or even their coherence,” and suspects a scribal error.

## CHAPTER V

**“Concerning those whom wholly,” etc.** Thus it is read in B. and T. So below, Book V, chapter 15: “Let us instruct from their own authors.” Cicero, *To Lentulus*: “I bought a house from Crassus.” *On the Orator*: “I heard this from my father.” More recent editions read, “from those by whom,” etc.; but the older ones, “concerning those whom wholly,” etc.

**“From these we must necessarily prove one God.”** Lactantius demonstrates that the ancient pagan sages believed in one God. Clement of Alexandria does the same in the *Exhortation to the Gentiles*. See Augustine of Eugubium, *On Perennial Philosophy*.

**“Homer could give us nothing,” etc.** On the contrary, he could and did provide it; for Cyril, *Against Julian*, demonstrates that Homer asserted one God.

[Col. 0889A] **“He said that water was that from which all things were born,” etc.** Besides those noted in the margin of the text, see Plutarch, *Opinions*; Laertius; Eusebius, *Preparation*, Book I, chapter 5, and Book VII, chapter 5; Ambrose, *Hexaemeron*, Book I, chapter 2; Augustine, *City of God*, Book VIII, chapter 2; Cyril, *Against Julian*.

**“And Anaximenes,” etc.** Cicero, where he is speaking of Anaximenes, and Laertius in his account of Anaximenes, read not “ether” (*aethera*) but “air” (*aera*).

**“Intermingled.”** The received reading of Maro has *commistus*, “mingled together.”

**“Yet he testifies that one supreme Mind presides over the world.”** He speaks of Aristotle, who is known from *On Generation*, Book II; Book XII of the *Metaphysics*; and chapter 7 of the little work *On the World* to have believed in one God. The most learned modern men have demonstrated this: Trapezuntius, *Comparison of Aristotle and Plato*, Book II; Scaliger, *On Subtlety against Cardano*, Exercise 365; and several others.

**Plato.** In the *Parmenides*, *Timaeus*, *Phaedo*, *Laws*, and *Republic*. Cardinal Bessarion, Book II *Against the Calumniator of Plato*, should be consulted.

**“Perceiving and moving all things.”** I have followed the reading of Tax. and P., and of Cicero himself in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*: “perceiving all things and moving all things.”

**“On Untimely Death.”** The book has perished.

**“Likewise in the Exhortations.”** Here too a book of Seneca has perished.

## CHAPTER VI

**“And for this reason he fled into Egypt.”** Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book III—from which Lactantius took this passage almost word for word—reads: “and for this reason he presided over Egypt.”

**Thoyth.** From the same passage of Cicero I corrected Lactantius’s text, which in some copies has *Thoth*. Eusebius also writes in Book I of the *Preparation* that Mercury is called *Thoth* by the Alexandrians and *Thoyth* by the Egyptians. We may further confirm this reading from a most beautiful passage of Martianus Capella. In Book II he says:

> “And so he first investigates by number whether the marriage is advantageous and whether the winged swiftness of the ethereal summit may be united to him by a fitting bond; then he distributes upon his fingers and counting-board his own name and the appellation of Cyllenius—not that which the discordant difference of nations or the diverse rites of peoples, according to their locations and cults, invented for him, but that which deceptive human curiosity asserts to have been joined, at his birth, with the star from Jupiter himself by an act of naming, and made widely known solely through Egyptian fables. From this he takes the final letter on each side, which closes the first and perfect limit of number; next he takes that which holds sway in all shrines by cubic solidity; and he also takes, in the next place, the letter which the wise Samian held to signify the twofold way of mortality; and thus there shone forth the number one thousand two hundred and eighteen.”

For the Greeks express numbers by letters.

**Pheneatae.** Thus Cicero in the passage cited above. Pausanias too, in his *Arcadia*: “Of all the gods,” he says, “the Pheneatae most revere Mercury,” etc. And indeed Hermopolis (ἑρμούπολις), of which Lactantius speaks here, may be thought, on the evidence of Stephanus, to have been in Arcadia. But because most books here read, instead of “the Pheneatae,” “the Saitae”—these are peoples in Egypt, named after the city called Sais—and because Lactantius, *On the Anger of God*, chapter 11, testifies that Cicero wrote that among the Egyptians Hermes was counted among the gods, namely he who was called Trismegistus because of his excellence and knowledge of many arts, and of whom the present discussion concerns the same person, the most distinguished Petrus Ciacconius suspected that the reading here should be: “both the Saitae and the Pheneatae reverently worship him”; and in Cicero, “whom the Saitae and the Pheneatae worship,” so that he may be said to be worshipped in Egypt by the Saitae and in Arcadia by the Pheneatae. In some manuscripts of Lactantius, *Femete* is corruptly read for *Pheneatae*.

**“But God is one,” etc.** I do not find these words verbatim in Hermes, but similar ones at the end of chapter 5 of the *Pimander*.

**“Therefore God has no name, because he alone is,” etc.** Minucius Felix says likewise in the *Octavius*. Dionysius, Book I, chapter *On the Divine Names*, says that God has neither name nor conception. St Thomas, *Prima Pars*, question 13, article 1, says that God cannot be named by us with a name signifying his essence as it is, because we name as we conceive, and names are signs of concepts; but in this life we cannot know God’s essence. Whether the blessed can impose such a name upon God is disputed by theologians in the first book of the *Sentences*, distinction 22, and in the *Prima Pars*, question 13, article [uncertain OCR]. For how ancient philosophers named God, see Augustine of Eugubium, *On Perennial Philosophy*, Book III.

**“God is a proper name.”** For θεός (*theos*, “God”) is said to derive from θεᾶσθαι (*theasthai*, “to see”), as though he foresees all things and provides for all, as Damascene writes, *Orthodox Faith*, Book [uncertain OCR], chapter 12. Thus the name *Deus*, “God,” has been derived from the universal providence of things to signify the divine nature.

**“That there were ten Sibyls,” etc.** On the Sibyls in general, see Solinus, chapter 8; Aelian, *Various History*, Book XII; Martianus Capella, Book II; St Jerome, *Against Jovinian*, Book [uncertain OCR]; Suidas under *Herophila* and σιβυλλει; Francesco Petrarch, *Memorabilia*, Book IV, chapter 3; Ficino, *On Christian Doctrine*; Juan Luis Vives on Book XVIII, chapter 23 [of Augustine’s *City of God*]; St Augustine, *City of God*; Gyraldus, Dialogue 2, *On the History of Poets*; Onofrio Panvinio, *On the Sibyls and Sibylline Poems*. Most, following Lactantius—or rather Varro—maintain that there were ten. Some think there were more. Others, on the contrary, contend that there was only one Sibyl and that the Sibylline poems read under the names of several Sibyls belong to one woman; still others maintain that there were only two. It should also be observed that what one writer ascribes to one Sibyl is often likewise assigned by another to a different Sibyl. From this the good reader will understand that reports concerning the Sibyls are very perplexed and tangled.

**“The fourth, the Cumaean, in Italy.”** Cumae is a city of Campania, where this Sibyl is said to have uttered oracles, and of which Servius speaks on the following passage in the third book of the *Aeneid* [Col. 0890C]:

> “When you have been brought hither and have reached the city of Cumae,” etc.

There is another city in the Locrian territory of Ionia in Asia Minor, called in Latin *Cuma*, -ae, or *Cume*, whose genitive is *Cumes*, near Erythrae; and there too another Sibyl is reported to have prophesied. From the names of both cities—or rather from this one name shared by both—are derived the adjectives *Cumaeus* and *Cumanus*. These have often afforded our Lactantius, as well as other writers, an occasion for ambiguity, since they often attribute to one Sibyl what belongs to another, and confuse the Cumaean with the Cuman, and the Erythraean—because Erythrae is near Cumae in Ionia—with both. Here, when Lactantius calls her the Cumaean in Italy, he sufficiently distinguishes her from the other, who may be called the Ionian Cumaean or Cuman and whom he later, following Varro, lists as seventh. Aristotle mentions this Italian Cumaean in *On Marvellous Things Heard*, chapter 91; Justin Martyr, at the end of the *Exhortation to the Gentiles*; and Silius, Book XII.

I do not know how Servius can write, on the passage from the third *Aeneid*:

> “Whatever verses the maiden has written upon leaves,” etc.,

that she was called Phemonoe by her proper name, when Virgil in Book VI calls her Deiphobe, and Servius himself confirms there that this was her proper name. Because Gregory Gyraldus, Dialogue 2, *History of Poets*, and Petrus Ciacconius saw that Lactantius below speaks of the Cuman Sibyl, they thought this passage corrupt and proposed reading “Cimmerian” for “Cumaean,” following Suidas under Σίβυλλαι, who enumerates these Sibyls in the same order as Lactantius: “the fourth, the Italian, from Cimmeria of Italy” (τετάρτη ἡ ἰταλικὴ ἡ ἐκ Κιμμερία τῆς Ἰταλίας), and Isidore, *Origins*, Book VIII, chapter 8, who seems to have taken everything from this passage, so that one might not unreasonably suspect that Lactantius perhaps once read thus. Yet, although she could also have been called Cimmerian because, as some think, she was born at the Campanian town of Cimmerium near Cumae [Col. 0891A], she is nevertheless rightly called Cumaean by most writers because she gave responses at Cumae. We learn this from others and from Justin, who testifies in the passage cited above that he visited her cave there. Moreover, this is how it is read in twelve Vatican manuscripts and in all the other manuscripts and printed editions, from which I have not dared to differ; and Suidas’s translator reads not Κιμμερία (*Kimmeria*) but Κύμη (*Kyme*). As we have said, Lactantius sufficiently distinguishes one from the other when he calls this one the Cumaean of Italy; therefore the other Cuman must be understood as deriving her name from Cumae in Ionia.

**“The fifth, the Erythraean.”** Some say that she is the same as the Ionian Cumaean; nor is it surprising that this error entered on account of the proximity of the places—namely, Erythrae in Ionia, where some say she prophesied, and Cumae in Ionia, as we said above. But why Aristotle, chapter 91 of *On Marvellous Things Heard*, should have identified the Italian Cumaean and the Erythraean, I do not see, unless we say that the Erythraean too was called Cumaean, as Martianus Capella asserts in Book II, perhaps because she also prophesied at Cumae on occasion. For some write that several women prophesied at Cumae, all of whom were called by the name Sibyl. They went there either to become more skilled in divination through Apollo’s oracles—who had there a very great shrine with a cave—or to preside over his rites, which were customarily performed only by women. Afterwards they were all called Cumaeans or Cumans from that city. Clement, the first Pope, mentions this Sibyl in his Epistle to the Corinthians; Lactantius himself again, *On the Anger of God*, chapter 22; the Emperor Constantine the Great, in the Address to the Assembly of Saints, in Eusebius’s *Life of Constantine*; and St Augustine, *City of God*, Book XVIII, chapter 23.
