**“The seventh, the Cuman.”** We can now understand this as none other than the one who prophesied at Cumae in Ionia. Servius, on the verse of Maro [Virgil],

> “Phoebus, ever grievous to Troy,” etc.,

notes that Varro attributed the whole story of the Sibylline books offered to Tarquin not to the Cuman Sibyl, of whom Lactantius here speaks from Varro, but to the Erythraean, as Suidas also attributes it under *Herophila*. Virgil, however, and Solinus, chapter 8, refer the same story not to her but to the Italian Cumaean, whom Solinus calls Cuman. Indeed, Virgil quite clearly suggests that the prophecies of the Cumaean Sibyl were kept at Rome, in those verses of Book VI in which Aeneas addresses her:

> “Great sanctuaries in our realms also await you;  
> For here I shall set up your lots and secret destinies,  
> Utterances for my people,” etc.

Others call her Demophile or Herophile. Solinus and Suidas in the passage cited above call not the Cuman but the Erythraean Herophile; although in Solinus and Tibullus, Elegy 5, Book II, one reads *Heriphile*. Eusebius, however, writes that it was neither the Erythraean nor the Cuman but the Samian who was called Herophile, and reports that she flourished while Numa, king of the Romans, was alive.

**“And that she brought nine books.”** Dionysius of Halicarnassus says the same at the end of Book IV, *Roman Antiquities*; so do Gellius, Book I, chapter 19; Suidas under Σίβυλλαι; Servius in the passage cited; Pliny, Book XIII, chapter 13; and Solinus, chapter 8. Suidas under *Herophile* writes that the Sibyl offered Tarquin three books, not nine, full of oracles, and that after two had been burned only the third remained.

**“To King Tarquinius Priscus.”** Pliny, in the chapter cited, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Solinus, and Gellius in the passage cited write that the books were offered not to Tarquinius Priscus but to Tarquinius Superbus. Suidas under Σίβυλλαι and Isidore, *Origins*, Book VIII, chapter 8, follow Lactantius—or rather Varro as reported by Lactantius. The latter view seems closer to the truth and more congruent with the chronology, if the event is referred to the Italian Cumaean Sibyl, as Virgil and Solinus do. For she, according to Solinus, took part in Roman affairs in the fiftieth Olympiad; and Tarquinius Priscus, according to Glareanus’s chronology on Livy and the common view of other writers, took up kingship in the second year of the forty-first Olympiad [Col. 0892A] and reigned thirty-eight years. But the reign of Tarquinius Superbus begins in the fourth year of the sixty-first Olympiad, so that from the Sibyl’s time to the reign of Tarquinius Superbus eleven Olympiads elapsed, that is, forty-four years and more. This nevertheless does not prove Pliny’s, Dionysius’s, and the others’ view false, for the Sibyl could have lived to her eightieth, ninetieth, or even later years; but, as we said, the other view seems more likely.

Those who refer the story to the Erythraean are utterly mistaken, if we maintain either that the Erythraean prophesied even during the Trojan War, as Solinus thinks and as St Augustine reports at the end of the same chapter 23 that certain others also held; for that war preceded the reign of Tarquinius Priscus by 570 years, and that of Superbus by 650; or that she flourished in Romulus’s time, as Augustine reports there that others held, among whom he numbers Eusebius in the *Chronicle*. That time certainly preceded the reign of Priscus by about 160 years and that of Superbus by 244.

**“She demanded three hundred Philippics.”** Servius, on the verse “For here I shall set up your lots,” etc., supports Lactantius—or Varro. For my part, I have nowhere found in authors that Macedonian coinage was ever struck or used at Rome.

**Marpessus.** Hermolaus Barbarus, *Emendations* on Pliny, Book V, chapter 30, thinks that *Mermissus* should be read, on the authority of Stephanus of Byzantium under Μερμήσσος. Pausanias, however, Book X, where he speaks of the prophetic Herophile, has *Marpessus*, as does the greater part of Lactantius’s manuscripts here. Others read *Marmissus*, after Suidas under Σίβυλλαι. The T. and P. manuscripts here have *Marmessus*; Achilles Statius, in his notes on Tibullus, judged that *Marinessus*—as some printed editions also read—or *Marmessus* ought to be read.

**“The tenth, the Tiburtine, named Albunea.”** Tibullus, Elegy 5, Book II, seems to have called her Alban.

**“Whose sacred rites the Senate transferred to the Capitol.”** T., P., and some old printed editions do not acknowledge these words. But if they are retained, as most retain them, I would prefer, with Janus Gulielmius, to read *sortes*, “lots/oracles,” rather than *sacra*, “sacred rites.” Those prophecies were plainly called *sortes*, as is evident from Virgil and Tibullus; and Janus himself testifies, in his Questions on Plautus’s *Menaechmi*, chapter 4, that this is how it is written here in some manuscripts.

**“Besides that of the Cumaean, whose books,” etc.** Here is the ambiguity (ἀμφίβολον) mentioned above. Lactantius himself calls Cumaean here the one whom above, from Varro, he had called Cuman. For the books that were carefully concealed and to which only the fifteen men could have access were those sold by the Sibyl to Tarquin, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus testifies in Book IV and Gellius in the cited chapter 19; yet Lactantius himself called that Sibyl Cuman a little above. He reports the same thing in *On the Anger of God*, Book [chapter] 23.

**“And she foretold that she would be called Erythraean.”** T., P., and the older printed editions have: “And she calls herself Erythraean, when she prophesied.” Janus Gulielmius, in the work cited above, reads: “when she prophesied,” since *proloqui* properly means to prophesy and chant future things; whence prophets are so called because they foretell the future.

**“On the Fifteen Men,” etc.** See Onuphrius at length.

**“They should be sent to Erythrae.”** He writes the same in *On the Anger of God*, chapter 22. Yet Sibylline poems were sought not only from Erythrae but also, as he said a little above, from all cities, both Italian and Greek. Tacitus, *Annals*, Book V, and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book IV, also note this. For in the burning of the Capitol, which occurred in the year before Sulla’s dictatorship, they had been consumed, whether through treachery or by chance.

**“One God, who alone is” (Εἷς θεός, ὃς μόνος ἐστίν).** Thus it is read in the Sibylline poems: “One God alone, who is ruler” (εἷς θεὸς μόνος, ὃς ἄρχει).

**“Most high” (Πανυπέρτατος).** In the Sibylline poems it is corruptly written πάντων ὑπέρτατος, “highest of all,” which metre rejects; although the annotator in the margin of the Sibylline book observes that manuscripts have the reading found in our text.

[Col. 0893A] **Ἔτυχεν.** Metre rejects this, since the second syllable is short. The correct reading in Theophilus is ἐτέχθη, “was born.” Yet all manuscripts of Lactantius agree, and therefore I would not dare alter it.

**“I alone am God” (Εἷς μόνος εἰμὶ θεός).** This verse frequently occurs among the Sibylline poems, but in these words:

> “For he alone is God, and there is no other”  
> (Αὐτὸς γὰρ μόνος ἐστὶ θεός, καὶ οὐκ ἔστιν ἔτ᾽ ἄλλος).

## CHAPTER VII

**“Because he had emigrated from Delphi, I suppose.”** Thus B., T., P., and the oldest printed editions correctly read, though *I suppose* (*credo*) is absent from some other manuscripts. The phrase is clearly ironic, as in Cicero, first *Philippic*: “Hannibal, I suppose, was at the gates”; Tertullian, chapter 46: “I suppose, for the honour of his father”; and Lactantius below, Book III, chapter 18: “This man, I suppose, because he was born of obscure rank,” etc., and chapter 23: “But, I suppose, the heat deterred him,” etc.

**“If God is one, what blessed solitude can there be?”** A fragment from Cicero’s *Hortensius*, or *On Philosophy*, which we have lost.

**“For he has ministers, whom we call messengers.”** Lactantius seems, in order to remove solitude from God, to summon angels and associate them with that deity. This was by no means appropriate. For it does not follow from the nearly infinite number of holy souls and angels with God that he is not called solitary; nor would their absence make him solitary. The theologians expressly teach this in the first book, distinction 21, where Richard [of St Victor], question one, and St Thomas, *Prima Pars*, question 31, article 3. For solitude is not removed by the companionship of something of an extraneous nature: a man is said to be alone in a garden, although many plants and animals are there. Thus God, even with angels and all beings existing with him, would truly be called alone or solitary if there were not several persons in the Godhead. But since from eternity there was indeed no essence other than the divine essence, yet in that essence there is and has been from eternity a plurality of persons [Col. 0893C], which excludes solitude from God, this proposition is false and inadmissible: “God was alone from eternity”; for its meaning is that he was solitary from eternity. We note this for Catholics.

Nevertheless, Lactantius is not without excuse, since he had to descend to the understanding of the Gentiles and put forward something that could please untutored and dull minds. For, as Archelaus the bishop truly said while disputing against the impious Manes, in Cyril, *Catechesis* VI: “We do not disclose the mysteries concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to Gentiles; indeed, we do not state the mysteries so openly even to catechumens. Rather, we often speak more obscurely, so that believing persons who know may understand, and those who do not know may not be corrupted.”

God begot the ministers of his kingdom. The word “begetting” (*gignendi*) is sometimes used improperly not only by Lactantius and other ecclesiastical writers, but also in the sacred Scriptures. For the books of Moses concerning the creation of the world bear the title *Genesis*; and in Paul, Acts chapter XVII, we are God’s offspring; and James I says, “God voluntarily begot us.” But the account of generation set forth by Aristotle, *Ethics* VIII, chapter 12, and *Metaphysics* VII, text 28 and following, and treated by St Thomas, *Prima Pars*, question 27, article 2, properly applies to God only in the procession of the uncreated Word, of which we shall speak below at book IV, chapter 8.

“They explain his name,” etc. T. has *explodunt* (“they cast out”). The sense is the same in either reading; for something is said to be *exponi*, as though placed outside, just as it is *explodi* when it is sent out and expelled. Thus at the end of book III, chapter 26: “having put away the old, they render the new.”

Ἐνολόισροφε [unintelligible as transmitted]. William Canter, *New Readings*, book III, chapter 30, prefers ἀιολόσροφε, that is, “turning swiftly.” Yet in my copy of the Antwerp edition of 1571, through a printer’s error, ἀιολόσροφε is printed—a form which means nothing.

“He himself, before all things, was begotten out of himself.” He says the same at the end of book II, chapter 9. Yet the proposition “whatever existed began at some time to exist” is truly asserted of all creatures; but when we speak of God, it is altogether falsely maintained. For if God is eternal, as the truth requires and Lactantius himself everywhere affirms, and if beginning is incompatible with eternity, there was no reason why he should be called begotten, generated, or made from himself—as St Bernard shows at the beginning of book VI of *On Consideration*, addressed to Eugenius, and St Thomas in book I, chapter 15, *Against the Gentiles*. Moreover, all theologians following the Master condemn in the first book, distinction 4, the proposition: “God begot himself as God.”

## CHAPTER VIII

“What, moreover, is so far removed from God as that work which he himself assigned to mortals for propagating offspring?” Much to this effect may be found among our writers in Arnobius, book III, at the beginning; and among the pagans in Pliny, book II, chapter 7.

## CHAPTER IX

“Which cannot be weakened and broken by iron and force,” etc. Thus indeed most editions, and Cicero himself, whose saying it is. Bononiensis, however, has: “which cannot be weakened and broken by iron and force.”

“But to conquer the mind,” etc. St Ambrose discusses this victory admirably in *On Duties*, where he treats courage.

“I do not compare him with the greatest men,” etc. Some editions have: “I not only compare him with the greatest men,” etc. I caused the text to be printed as it stands in B. and in Tully himself; for *tantum*, *solum*, and *modo*, in elegant imitation of the Greeks, often have an understood negation, which Latin writers prefer to express after an adversative follows, although *quamvis*, *et*, *aut*, *etiam*, or *non* is not added. Ulpian, in Law *Invitum*, Digest, *On Urban Praedial Servitudes*: “By unwilling, however, we must understand not one who objects, but one who does not consent.” Likewise, in the opening law, at the beginning, Digest, *On Daily and Summer Water*: “Daily water is not that which is conducted daily, but that which one may use daily if he wishes.” Celsus, in Law *Littus est quousque*, Digest, *On the Meaning of Words*: “We say estates belong to certain persons, not necessarily to persons holding them in common, but where one holds one thing and another another.” Other passages are collected by Antonio Agustín, *Emendations*, book II, chapter 1.

“But Philoctetes did not think himself his heir, though he placed the torch beneath him as he was about to burn.” Writers generally hold that Philoctetes set fire to Hercules’ pyre and became heir to his arrows, as Lactantius writes here: Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IX; Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* II; Diodorus Siculus, book V; Justin, *History*, at the beginning of book 20; Calaber, book X; the scholiast on Homer, *Iliad* III; Seneca, *Hercules on Oeta*; Philostratus, *Heroicus*, chapter 6; Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid* III, “The small [arrows] of Philoctetes.” Peter Victorius, therefore, wrongly rejected this view in *Various Readings* II, chapter 15—a view supported by so many writers—moved by the authority of Apollodorus alone, who assigns this act in *Library* II to Poeas, Philoctetes’ own father. For although, as Victorius says, Philoctetes served under Agamemnon with Neoptolemus, Hercules’ son, in the Trojan War, which occurred much later than Hercules’ death, this happened when Philoctetes was already very old. Thus it could have happened that he, when young, lived with Hercules already worn out by age and was present at his death, as Brodaeus notes against Victorius in *Miscellanies* I, chapter 5.

## CHAPTER X

Tarquitius, in discussing illustrious men, says that he was born of uncertain parents and exposed. Theodoret, recounting this same story of Asclepius near the beginning of book VIII of *Cure of Greek Affections*, writes:

“And, to pass also to others, Apollodorus is witness that Asclepius was thought by some to be the son of Arsinoë, but by others of Coronis, who, made pregnant by Apollo in a secret and violent intercourse, is said afterwards to have exposed the child when born. This child, Apollodorus says, was found by chance by hunters, taken from the teats of a nursing bitch, brought to the centaur Chiron, and there reared; he then applied himself to the medical art, in which he first displayed his powers in the cities of Tricca and Epidaurus.”

I think Theodoret took from Apollodorus only this: “Asclepius was thought by some to be the son of Arsinoë, but by others of Coronis.” But I judge that the words concerning the secret intercourse, and everything following, were taken from no one other than Tarquitius—plainly, either from Tarquitius’ own book or from this passage in Lactantius. For although various writers have written differently concerning Asclepius’ birth, upbringing, and education—Homer in the *Hymns*, Pindar in *Pythian Ode* 3, Pausanias in books II, IV, and VIII, Diodorus Siculus in book IV, chapter 9, and book V, chapter 15, Ovid in *Metamorphoses* II, Cicero in *On the Nature of the Gods* III, Tarquitius, Apollodorus, and very many others—you will find no one at all, apart from Tarquitius alone, who recounts the story as Theodoret does.

Moreover, Theodoret could not have copied it from Apollodorus, who says neither that Asclepius was exposed by his mother, nor that he was found by hunters, nor that he was suckled at a bitch’s teats. Rather, he writes that when Apollo had killed the mother and she, already dead, was burning on the pyre, the child was immediately snatched from the pyre and brought to Chiron to be reared. I append Apollodorus’ words from book III:

“She [Arsinoë], impregnated by Apollo, bore Asclepius. But some say that Asclepius was born not of Arsinoë, daughter of Leucippus, but of Coronis, daughter of Phlegyas in Thessaly. Apollo, as soon as he had fallen in love with her, is said immediately to have lain with her; but they say that, because he had possessed her against her father’s will, she was joined to Ischys, son of Elatus. Apollo, however, cursed the informing raven with excessive imprecations, and changed it, though it had been white until that day, into black. He struck and killed pregnant Coronis; and when she was burning, he snatched the child from the pyre and brought him to Chiron the Centaur to be reared,” etc.

Therefore, where Theodoret’s text reads, “this child, Apollodorus says,” I suspect a scribal error, and that one should read, “this child, Tarquitius says.” Indeed, if Theodoret were recounting the entire story from Apollodorus, whom he had cited at the beginning, it would serve no purpose immediately to name him again. But he named Tarquitius. Thus, together with Lactantius, we have Theodoret as a witness to this fragment which has disappeared from Tarquitius’ book. Theodore Canter, failing to notice this, thought in *Various Readings* II, chapter 19, that the material here cited by Firmianus from Tarquitius had been drawn from Tarquitius himself, and then again by Theodoret from Apollodorus.

“He most disgracefully tended another’s flock.” That is, he tended Admetus’ cattle, as Ovid has it in *Metamorphoses* II; Tertullian also mocks this in *Apology*, chapter 14, as does Cyprian in *On the Vanity of Idols*.

“And he built the walls for Laomedon.” The story is indeed told by Neptune himself near the end of Homer’s *Iliad* XXI. Herodotus, however, denies that Apollo or Neptune served Laomedon. Tertullian and Cyprian touch upon the same story in the passages cited above, as do Minucius and Clement of Alexandria in *Exhortation to the Greeks*, and Tatian in *Against the Greeks*. See Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II, and Apollodorus, *Library* II. They say that Laomedon did not go unpunished for that fraud, as Lactantius relates here, but that Apollo sent a plague upon the city and Neptune a flood. When he sought an oracle concerning the means of averting these evils, he was commanded to expose his daughter Hesione to be devoured by the sea-monster; Hercules afterwards rescued her, as the author says above toward the end of chapter 9. But here Lactantius seems to have followed Homer, from whom we understand that the gods departed unavenged, *Iliad*, in the passage cited.

“Greatest Indian.” He plays on the title customarily used by emperors after conquering nations: they were called “greatest Parthian conqueror,” “greatest German conqueror,” and so forth.

“He was most shamefully conquered by love and desire.” With Michael Thomas, I restored this passage from B. and T. in place of the printed reading, “on account of love and desire.” For Liber was not conquered by someone because of love or desire in that Indian expedition; he was nevertheless conquered by love itself, with which he burned for Ariadne. Diodorus also writes that he burned with love for other women in India, in book V, where he gives the story; Orosius gives it as well, book I, chapter 9.

“For he was carried to Dia.” Dia is an island adjoining Crete, according to Strabo, book X. This, I think, is the genuine reading, found in all printed books of Lactantius and in Diodorus Siculus, book V; also in Ovid, *Metamorphoses* V, and Catullus, *Marriage of Peleus and Thetis*, though B., T., and P. have “Crete.” Plutarch should also be consulted, for he reports different opinions concerning Ariadne in his *Theseus*.

“With his half-manly retinue.” He alludes to *Aeneid* IV:

> “And now that Paris with his half-manly retinue,” etc.

He calls Bacchus’ troop “half-manly,” because it contained not only men but also women, who were called Bacchae, as St Augustine writes, *City of God* XVIII, chapter 13.

“And he made her free (*liberam*),” etc. This is a jest. Since he was Liber, Lactantius says, by joining her to himself he made her free, and ascended to heaven with her. For *Libera* cannot here be understood as the opposite of “a female slave,” since nowhere is it recorded that Ariadne was made free from any slavery through Father Liber’s help. Therefore, contrary to the other editions, we printed this name with an initial capital. Among the pagans there was also a goddess called Libera, of whom Cicero speaks in *On the Nature of the Gods* II and in the sixth action *Against Verres*; likewise Tacitus, book II; Livy, decade I, book 5; Arnobius, book V; and St Augustine, *City of God* VI, chapter 13. Some say she was Venus, others Ceres, and some Proserpina. But Ovid certainly speaks of Ariadne in *Fasti* III, in verses to which Lactantius undoubtedly alluded when he wrote this:

> “Liber had already heard the words of her complaint,  
> as by chance he followed behind.  
> He forestalls her with an embrace and dries her tears with kisses;  
> ‘Let us seek together heaven’s highest places,’ he says.  
> Joined to my bed, you shall take a name joined to mine;  
> changed, your name shall be Libera.’”

“In solemn prayer he is called Optimus Maximus.” You have an example of such a prayer from Marcus Tullius at the end of his speech *For His House*, and in his speech *For Gaius Rabirius on a Charge of Treason*.

“He carried off the royal boy.” He speaks of Ganymede, who was the son of Tros, king of the Trojans. Plato indeed condemns the authors of this story in book I of *Laws*. On it see Homer, *Iliad* XX; Virgil, *Aeneid* V; Ovid, *Metamorphoses* X; Lucian; Herodian, book I; and Orosius, book I, chapter 12. Xenophon, however, in the *Symposium*, reports that he was carried off not because of bodily beauty but because of beauty of soul.

“For Jupiter himself, whom he worshipped, committed the same act.” Thus the young Terentian Chaerea relates in the *Eunuch* that, moved by Jupiter’s example—having looked at a painting depicting Jupiter’s rape—he violated a virgin. Clement of Alexandria says more on this in his *Exhortation to the Greeks*, as does St Augustine, *Confessions* I, chapter 10. Read about Jupiter’s adulteries and rapes in Arnobius, books IV and V, and Epiphanius, *Ancoratus*.

## CHAPTER XI

“A certain poet wrote the triumph of Cupid,” etc. I have not discovered who this poet was, nor has this poem come down to us. We bear its loss with less regret because we possess Francesco Petrarch’s splendid poem of the same title, written in his native tongue.

“Lack of prudence” (*imprudentia*). Thus I read it, however much B., T., P., and most printed editions object, having *prudentia* (“prudence”). The Aldine edition and some others nevertheless support it, as does Lactantius himself, who shows from the very context that it must be read thus. For not being able to know future things by oneself, but needing to be warned by another, is lack of prudence, or a deficiency of prudence. Lactantius therefore removes prudence from Jupiter in order also to remove his divinity, which was the purpose of the entire argument. Something similar occurs below, chapter 13, where, speaking of Saturn, he says: “Again, I must criticize his lack of prudence; for why did he receive an answer from another?” There he both alludes to this passage and shows that he here marked Jupiter’s lack of prudence.

“Unless Themis had told him the future.” Lactantius followed Apollonius, who writes that Jupiter was warned by Themis; Lucian prefers Prometheus, who for that reason also was released from Caucasus. Apollodorus, *Library* III, where he speaks of Peleus, reports both accounts.

“If the Fates,” etc. See Lucian, who makes almost the same jest against the gods.

“Zeus was named from ζῆν (‘to live’),” etc. In his book *On the Instruction of Literary Studies*, Budé criticizes Lactantius at this point as one who considered these things too little accurately and failed to see that all of them were said symbolically. Yet Budé himself considered Lactantius’ whole purpose too little accurately. Lactantius strives to eliminate all such symbolic interpretations, invented by Stoics and others as pagan trifles—not merely as ridiculous and foolish, but as impious and criminal, since they generated, as Lactantius himself notes below in chapter 17 from Cicero, false opinions, turbulent errors, and almost senile superstitions. Arnobius at the end of book V, Lactantius himself admirably below in chapters 12 and 17 and often elsewhere, St Augustine in books VII and XVIII of *City of God*, Tatian likewise—who hisses down the allegories of Metrodorus of Lampsacus—and certain other holy Fathers did the same.

“They call them iron rains.” He alludes to Virgil’s verses, *Aeneid* XII:

> “A storm of weapons, darkening, goes over the whole sky,  
> and an iron rain rushes down.”

“Or the ship in which he was placed bore the figure of an eagle as its *tutela*.” Read: “Or the ship in which he was placed had an eagle represented on its *tutela*,” with *navis* as a genitive: “of the ship.” The following phrase, “just as [he carried off Europa] in a bull,” proves that this is how the passage must be written. Yet I do not condemn the expression “a *tutela* represented in an eagle,” which Lactantius himself uses below, book V, chapter 8, where he says that justice is represented, as it were, in some image. But I maintain that he did not write it thus here because he adds, “just as [in] a bull,” etc. Otherwise, if we read, as is commonly printed and as six Vatican manuscripts have it, “he had a tutela represented in an eagle,” or “represented as an eagle,” as B. and five Vatican manuscripts read, then, to make the latter agree with the former, one would have to say, “just as in a bull,” or “just as into a bull.”

To clarify this passage of Lactantius, which is not so readily understood: a *tutela* was an emblem mounted upon a ship’s prow, called in Greek παράσημον (*parasēmon*). It was an image of some god or animal after which the ship itself was named, as in Virgil’s *Pistris* and *Centaur*:

> “He sails on the great Centaur.”

Hence certain ships were called κριοί (*krioi*, “Rams”) and by other such names, as Strabo, Plutarch in the *Banquet of the Seven Sages*, and Lucian in the dialogue *The Ship or the Wishes* attest. Seneca mentions *tutela* in this sense in book X, letter 77:

> “A ship is called good not because it is painted in costly colours, nor because it has a silver or golden beak, nor because its tutela is carved in ivory,” etc.

Ovid likewise means a ship’s *tutela* in *Tristia*, book I, elegy 3:

> “And the wave lashes the painted gods.”

Silius Italicus says:

> “And the gods who serve as tutelae float.”

Thus Lactantius again says at the end of this chapter: “An eagle flew to him as an omen, and after his victory he accepted it as a favourable omen and made it subject to his tutela.”

“Just as when he carried off Europa in a bull and transported her.” Baptista Pius, in chapter 98 of his *Annotations*, seems to have read “just as in a represented bull,” and some printed editions have this. Although I do not approve adding that word to the text, especially since far more and better manuscripts oppose it, I do not deny that it may be understood as a gloss. Lactantius’ meaning is this: just as Ganymede is said to have been carried off by Jupiter in an eagle because perhaps he was carried off in a ship whose *tutela* bore an eagle figure, so Jupiter is said to have carried off Europa in a bull because he took her away in a ship on which a bull was represented. Eusebius asserts this in the *Chronicle*: “Europa was carried off by Cretans in a ship whose emblem was a bull.” Palephatus, however, says that there was a man of Cnossus named Taurus, who, waging war upon the Tyrian territory, carried off other maidens as well as Europa, daughter of Phoenix, from Tyre; hence the fable arose.

“A voyage is celebrated.” *Navigium* (“voyage”) here means “navigation,” as in Ulpian, first law, § *Ait Praetor*, Digest, *On Rivers*, and Scaevola, Law *Qui Romae*, § *Callimachus*, Digest, *On Verbal Obligations*.

“Whose surname was Agesilaus.” He was called Agesilaus, παρὰ τὸ ἄγειν τοὺς λαούς, “from leading peoples,” because he leads peoples; for he is god of the dead and of the underworld. Callimachus also calls him this, saying: φοιτῶσι μεγάλῳ Ἀγεσιλάῳ, that is, “they go to great Agesilaus.” Therefore I do not approve the contention of some that *Agelastus* or *Agathalius* should be read here, though I know that Pluto was called both Agelastus and Agathalius and by other surnames. Gyraldus supports our reading in *On the Gods of the Gentiles*, Syntagma 8; so does Coelius Rhodiginus, *Ancient Readings* VI, chapter 18.

“Marcus Antonius possessed that unlimited command.” Thus read eleven Vatican manuscripts and all others I have seen, manuscript or printed, except one Vatican manuscript and B., which has “Pompey’s,” etc. This Marcus Antonius, as Asconius relates in his commentaries on Cicero’s first, third, and fourth speeches against Verres, obtained, through the favour of the consul Cotta and the faction of Cethegus, unlimited charge of the entire seacoast within Roman dominion. He was not only thoroughly dissolute and worthless himself, but, through utterly wretched companions, ravaged Sicily and all the provinces. Finally, having declared war on the Cretans and conducted it unsuccessfully, he perished there, before Pompey was sent against the pirates. Cicero says: “After they had experienced that unlimited command of Marcus Antonius.” And in *On the Grain Supply*: “Thus Marcus Antonius conducted himself in that unlimited command.” You may see that Lactantius perhaps had these passages in view.

Yet I would not dare reject the reading of the Bologna manuscript, since Cicero in many places, Plutarch, Asconius in the cited passages, and others make clear that at another time the Senate also assigned Pompey the province of clearing the sea and freeing it from pirates; and that he thereby received not merely command of the fleet but virtually unlimited power. Plutarch, in his *Pompey*, writes:

> “It was chiefly the pressure of scarcity in the grain supply, and fear of a great famine, that induced the Romans to send Pompey to recover the sea from the pirates. Gabinius, a friend of Pompey, proposed a law granting not command of a fleet, but plainly free dominion and authority over all mortals. That law gave him command of the whole inland sea within the Pillars of Hercules, for fifty miles from the sea. This space excluded very few regions of the Roman world, but included the greatest nations and most powerful kings.”

Velleius, speaking of the pirate war entrusted to Pompey by the Gabinian law, says: “By this senatorial decree, almost the sovereignty of the whole world was conferred upon one man.” Thus it is now also clear why Lactantius called it “that unlimited command,” even if you prefer to think he was speaking of Pompey. I, however, would not readily depart from the more generally received readings. Coelius Rhodiginus, book VI, chapter 18, Peter Ciacconius, and Latinius Latinus approved our reading; Thomasius approved the other in his notes.

“From the city of Messana.” Strabo also calls him a Messenian in book I; so do Plutarch in *On Isis and Osiris*, Aelian in *Various History* II, and Athenaeus, who cites book III of his *Sacred Description*. Athenaeus, however, calls him a Coan; others call him a Tegean, as Theodoret does at the beginning of book III of *Cure of Greek Affections* and often elsewhere. Cicero mentions him at the end of book I of *On the Nature of the Gods*, as do Sextus Empiricus at the beginning of book VIII *Against the Mathematicians* and Theophilus, bishop of Antioch, in his third discourse.

“Ennius translated this history.” See Arnobius, book IV; Minucius in the *Octavius*; St Augustine, *City of God* VI, chapter 7; Crinitus, *On Poets*, under Ennius; and Politian, *Miscellanies*, chapter 35.

“For Jupiter is not customarily worshipped without the shared dwelling of his wife and daughter.” In the temple dedicated to Jupiter on the Capitol there were three shrines: Jupiter’s in the middle; on either side, one of Juno and one of Minerva, under the same roof and pediment. See Dionysius of Halicarnassus, on the Capitoline temple of Jupiter at the end of book IV of *Roman Antiquities*, and Macrobius, *Saturnalia* III, chapter 4.

“Brought to ruin” (*pessum acta*). I prefer this reading to the others; others before me preferred it as well. It is read in the Aldine and Plantin editions; and although one Vatican manuscript has *persumata* in the text, the margin has *pessum acta*. Among Latin writers *pessum ire* means to fall to the bottom or lowest part of something. Why, then, should Lactantius not say metaphorically that Jupiter’s age was “brought to ruin,” since it had reached its lowest or final stage and its end? Most Vatican manuscripts and P. corruptly have *persumata*; B. and T. have *pessume omnium*, “most badly,” or *pessume acta*. For how could Ennius say there that Jupiter spent his life most badly, when he is entirely engaged in Jupiter’s praises? Another Vatican manuscript has *consummata* (“completed”), and Politian cites the passage thus in *Miscellanies*, chapter 35.

“And his tomb is in Crete.” Arnobius, book IV at the end; Minucius; Theophilus, *To Autolycus*; Epiphanius, *Ancoratus*; Mela, book II, chapter 7; Solinus, chapter 16.

“In the town of Cnossus.” Others prefer Mount Jasius; Marcus Varro, in Solinus, cited chapter 16, prefers Ida. Besides the authors already noted, see Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* III; Diodorus Siculus, book IV; Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*; Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* III, chapter 3; and Politian, cited above.

Καύχημα τάφους (“boast of tombs”; the transmitted Greek is grammatically uncertain). From this the Sibylline manuscript, which has τάφου καύχημα, must be corrected; for the metre does not work there. Nor should ἕξει be read as there, but, as in our text, ἴσχει.

“That is, the chief seat of the public religions.” Arnobius, therefore, was not the only one, as Theodore Canter thought in *Various Readings* I, chapter 11, to provide us with the source of the name *Capitolium*. Canter supposed that Livy, Plutarch, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, and other historians of Roman affairs had not known it. But Lactantius himself supplies the origin of the word here and in book III, chapter 17, though differently from Arnobius himself at the beginning of book VI, Dionysius at the end of *Roman Antiquities* IV, and Suidas.

“That we call those born of unknown parents sons of Earth.” Tertullian says the same in *Apology*, chapter 11. Hence arose the proverbial expression, discussed at length by the author of the *Adages* under “Son of Earth,” by Rhodiginus, *Ancient Readings* XI, chapter 28, and by Politian, *Miscellanies*, chapter 18.

“Pan [gave] him.” Thus B., T., and many Vatican manuscripts, though some of these have *Pantum*; some other manuscripts write it as one word, *Panaeum*, while P. and others have *Panem*. Boccaccio, book III, chapter 1, reports this passage of Ennius somewhat differently and reads *Pangaeum*: “On Mount Pangaeum,” he says, “he established an altar,” etc. Since I can produce nothing further, it is enough to indicate the variant readings; for I think everyone will recognize that the passage is corrupted. If Ennius’ *Sacred History*, from which it is taken, survived, the whole matter would be clear; but that is only to wish for something.

“The stela of heaven.” We owe this passage’s most ingenious restoration to Peter Ciacconius, who first advised that it should be read *stela*, with one *l*, not *stella*, “star,” with two, as it is corruptly read in all books. *Stela*, Greek στήλη (*stēlē*), means “column.” Pliny, book VI, chapter 28: “On it are written stone stelae in unknown letters.” Thus it is printed in my copy of the Aldine Venetian edition, corrected by Paulus Manutius and Gelenius; Barbarus corrects that passage in his emendations of Pliny, Budé cites it in his annotations on Law *Sicuti*, § *Competit*, Digest, *If a Servitude Be Claimed*, as do the compilers of the Greek-Latin lexicon printed at Basel in 1568 under Στήλη, and the author of the *Treasury of the Latin Language* under *stela*. Martianus Capella, book II:

> “When Athanasia had examined the signs of the books, she ordered them to be inscribed on certain projecting rocks and placed within a cave in the hidden places of Egypt, calling those same rocks stelae, and [saying that they] contained the genealogies of the gods.”

For there too *stelas* must be read, as Pliny and the word’s derivation establish. Thus the mountain, on account of its height, was called the column of heaven, as though it touched and even supported heaven.

“And there, on that mountain, he creates an altar to heaven.” Ciacconius thought certain words had been added here, and that Lactantius wrote thus: “After he ascended there, he contemplated the lands far and wide. On that mountain he creates an altar; and Jupiter was the first to sacrifice on that altar. In the place where he looked upward, he called that which was above the world, and which was called aether, the first heaven.” He understood “that which was above the world” to mean “that which had previously been called the world.”

“He made it subject to his tutela.” See Diodorus Siculus, book VI; and we have explained above what *tutela* means here.

## CHAPTER XIII

[Col. 0900B] “Ancient coins.” On the first coinage, see Strabo, book VIII; Pliny, book XXXIII, chapter 3; Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I, chapter 7; Eutropius; Tertullian, *Apology*; Minucius, *Octavius*; Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*; and the fragment of Athenaeus in Theodore Canter, *Various Readings* II, chapter 23.

“Safe he would have remained upon the shores.” Virgil: “he would have remained safe upon the shores.”

“Who returned to Latium.” Thus I read, as in Maro, instead of the reading in other editions, “which returned,” etc. For there he speaks of Augustus.

## CHAPTER XIV

“Sacred History.” That is, Euhemerus’.

“These are the words of Ennius.” Namely, as translator of Euhemerus’ *Sacred History*.

“Son.” In place of “son [accusative].” An antiptosis, as: “The speech which you heard is not mine”; “The city which I establish is yours.”

“Pluto in Latin is Diespiter; others call him Orcus.” Everyone knows that Jupiter was called Diespiter, that is, “father of day,” as Varro explains in *On the Latin Language* IV, chapter 10, and Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I, chapter 15. But I do not know that this surname was assigned to Pluto, unless perhaps in Varro himself in the cited passage, in these words: “This same Diespiter is called the lower air, which is joined to the earth, where all things arise and perish; because that is their end, he is called Orcus,” etc. I would certainly have called this one father of night and darkness, rather than father of day, as the Fate addresses him in Claudian:

> “O greatest ruler of night  
> and powerful lord of shades!”

Fulgentius the Mythographer says: “They also said that he was devoted to darkness, because earth’s material alone is darker than all the elements.” Perhaps our author and Varro wrote *Dis pater* (“Father Dis”); for Pluto’s being so called is very well known. And *Dis*, or Latin *Dives*, is certainly what Greek Πλοῦτων (*Ploutōn*) means, as Lactantius says. Diespiter is not the same. Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II: “But all earthly force and nature is dedicated to Father Dis, who is Dis, as among the Greeks Πλοῦτων, because all things return to earth and arise from earth.” Arnobius, near the end of book II: “When, at Apollo’s command, sacrifice was offered to Father Dis and Saturn with human heads.” Isidore, *Etymologies* VIII, chapter 11, almost suggests this emendation.

“And he surrounded them with a wall.” I find no Latin author speaking so. I think Lactantius wrote, “and he led a wall around them,” for *circumagere* means nothing other than “to lead around,” as in Virgil, *Aeneid* IX:

> “He whirled the whistling sling around his head.”

Or: “he surrounded them with a wall.”

## CHAPTER XV

“Through affection, the remembrance of the dead,” etc. Others read: “through affection for merit, the remembrance of the dead,” etc. But *meriti* is not found in T. and P. manuscripts and was absent from Francesco Petrarch’s manuscript, who cites this passage in book II of *On Religious Leisure* and does not acknowledge that word.

“Would exalt.” Cicero has “would exalt [plural],” and hence Castor and Pollux.

“And indeed in most [cities],” etc. All books have an error where they read “and another in most [cities],” etc. Lactantius cites the other passage of Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, chapter 3, where the reading varies slightly: “and in most states it may be understood that [this was done] for the sake of increasing virtue, so that more willingly,” etc.

“Sancus.” There is a remarkable variety of readings concerning this name, as is clear to anyone inspecting the Vatican manuscripts; see Gregory Gyraldus, *On the Gods of the Gentiles*, Syntagma I. See also Varro, *On the Latin Language* IV, chapter 10; Propertius, book IV, elegy at the end; Silius, *Punica* VIII; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities* II; likewise the book circulating under the name of Gaius Sempronius, *On the Division of Italy*, with Annius’ commentaries; and St Augustine, *City of God* XVIII, chapter 19. Our reading is given by manuscript B., some Vatican manuscripts, and the Aldine and Plantin editions; Joseph Scaliger approves it in his conjectures on Varro in the cited passage, both from Propertius there and from the etymology of the name supplied there by Propertius himself.

“My sacred rites.” Thus Maro reads in some editions. In others it is “me sacred,” and this too is reported in certain old Virgilian manuscripts in Velutello’s edition and in Pierio Valeriano’s *Corrections on Virgil*, though Lactantius’ reading does not please him.

Ἑλλὰς εἰὴ τί πέποιθας (“Hellas, what have you put your trust in?”; the transmitted εἰὴ is uncertain). These verses are read somewhat differently in the Sibylline Oracles.

“An imitator of Plato.” Indeed a rival, as Quintilian thinks, book X, chapter 1, near the end.

“That certainly was the case.” As Andreas Patricius notes in his scholia on Cicero’s fragments, and Sigonius in the dialogue entitled *The Accuser, or On Cicero’s Consolation*, this passage, which Lactantius took from Cicero’s own little book *Consolation*—mentioned by Cicero himself in the *Tusculans* and elsewhere, and often by Lactantius in the *Institutions*—is plainly corrupted. While all learned men lamented that this work was lost, seventeen years ago a book appeared bearing the same title and name of Cicero. There was much controversy among learned men of that time over whether it was Cicero’s genuine and authentic work. In that little book, therefore—whether Cicero or another is its author—the following is read most plainly and correctly: “But if any animal whatsoever was ever to be consecrated, such as the Egyptians consecrated many—for certainly none was—if of Cadmus …,” etc.

“Of Amphitryon.” The Aldine, Plantin, and some other editions contain an error in reading “of Amphion.” Our reading is supported by that little *Consolation*, and by Sigonius and Patricius when citing this passage from Lactantius among Cicero’s fragments; likewise by the best manuscripts T. and P., the Florentine edition, and others; indeed by the argument itself. For we know of no offspring of Amphion admitted among the gods, whereas everyone knows Amphitryon’s offspring, namely Hercules. Although he was born of Jupiter as father and Alcmene as mother, as Apollodorus relates in *Library* II and Homer in the *Hymn to Hercules*, he was nevertheless called the son of Amphitryon by Euripides in *Heracles Mad* and by others.

“And those whom their merits placed in heaven.” Cicero, whose passage occurs in *On the Laws* II, has: “and those whom their merits have called into heaven”; or, as some manuscripts of Cicero are reported to read and Muretus judges should be read in commenting on Catullus’ “Flaccus’ darling to his Catullus”: “and those whom their merits have called in heaven.”

“Atticus’ knowledge.” You have here Lactantius as a witness that Atticus was the man designated by the letter A as interlocutor in the books of the *Tusculan Disputations*, a matter usually disputed. Turnebus notes this in *Adversaria* IX, chapter 18. Others, however—for example Lambinus in his annotations on the first book of those *Questions*—refute Lactantius’ opinion and contend that the letter denotes not Atticus but an unspecified person, perhaps a young man, or an auditor, as Robertellus holds in his annotations on various authors.

“Because it pleased that wicked man Antony.” See Cicero, *Philippics* II, near the end.

“Twin brother.” Janus Gulielmius reports in his notes on Plautus’ *Menaechmi*, chapter 3, that some manuscripts have the better and more pointed reading, “twin brother,” rather than “full brother.” A twin brother is one born in the same birth and on the same day. Plautus, at the end of the *Menaechmi*:

> “I hope that you will find two full brothers,  
> twins born of one mother and one father, on one day.”

Virgil says of Romulus and Remus in book VIII:

> “Around her udders two twin boys  
> played, hanging,” etc.

“Parricide of his country.” So Cicero, *On Duties* III, chapter 3, near the end: “Behold for you the man who [is] king of the Roman people,” etc.

## CHAPTER XVI

[Col. 0902B] “The minds [bound] by the knots of religions,” etc. Lucretius: “the mind [bound] by the knots of religion,” etc.

And did the *lex Papia* put a clasp upon him? Seneca jokes about Jupiter; for the *lex Papia Poppaea* “clasped” sexagenarians—that is, forbade them to marry, as though their generative capacity were already exhausted. Claudius Caesar later repealed this law, as Suetonius writes in his *Claudius*, where *Pompeia* is corruptly read for *Poppaea*; likewise in Isidore, *Origins* IV.15, as reported in the Decretals, chap. *Quaedam*, distinction 2. Beroaldus followed this error in his commentary on Suetonius, cited above, chapters 19 and 23; likewise Rivallius in *History of Civil Law* II—though in book IV, on Claudius, he used the correct name. But Alciatus refuted the same error, *Dispunctions* III.3; Tiraquellus, *On Marriage Laws*, law VI, no. 20; Prateius, *On the Laws of the Roman People*, under *Papia Poppaea*, from Dio book LVI, Tacitus book III, and Ulpian, *Epitome*, title 29. Finally, Emperor Justinian too repealed that law, in the final law of the Code, *On Marriages*.

Seneca said “put a clasp upon him” (*fibulam imposuit*) by a metaphor taken from persons who were infibulated—[Col. 0902C] either to preserve the voice, which sexual intercourse alters, or for health. In such persons the skin extending over the glans of the penis was pierced through on both sides, and a bronze ring, called a *fibula* (“clasp”), was added. Hence in Martial, book IX, epigram 28, *refibulare*, “to unclasp,” means to undo the clasp. For more on the infibulation of young men, see Celsus. In certain printed copies *tabulam* (“tablet”) or *fabulam* (“story”) is corruptly read here for *fibulam*; Beroaldus notes this too on Claudius, cited chapter 19.

“The right of three children” (*ius trium liberorum*)? These were privileges and immunities granted, in the interest of increasing the population, to parents with three children. See the first law of the Code, *Those Excused by Number of Children*; the first law of the Code, *On the Rights of Children*; and § *Sed hae* of the Institutes, *On the Senatus Consultum Tertullianum*. Plutarch, *On Love*, prologue. Yet by the emperor’s favour these privileges were sometimes also granted to those with fewer children, or even none. Those who had obtained this right enjoyed, besides other advantages, this benefit as well: when something was distributed individually to the people, [Col. 0902D] they received the share allotted to three children. See Duarenus, *Disputations* I.40; Alexander of Naples, *Days of Genius* IV.8; Beroaldus and Sabellicus on Suetonius, *Galba* 14.

## CHAPTER XVII

“Do you see then,” etc. In a few particulars the reading differs in Cicero.

That is: they understand falsehoods and do not know truths. “Would that,” Cicero says, “I could discover truths as easily as I can expose falsehoods!”

“As is contained in the sacred history.” That is, in Euhemerus’s history concerning the gods, discussed above in chapter 11.

“He summoned Aesculapius to treat the young man.” Ovid recounts the story in *Metamorphoses* XV.

## CHAPTER XVIII

“If it is right to climb to the heavenly realms by slaughter,” etc. Seneca reports these two [Col. 0903A] little verses from Ennius’s *Epigrams*, cited by Cicero in his books *On the Republic*, in book XIX of the *Letters*, letter 109: “The matter about which you ask,” etc. Crinitus, however, writes in *On the Honourable Disciplines* XIX.3 that the first verse is corrupt in Seneca. Yet he does not give the verse as it stood in Seneca; editions of Seneca vary in their reading. I think Crinitus read in Seneca: “If by inflicting wounds one may ascend to the heavenly realms,” etc. This reading did not please Erasmus, in his annotations on that letter, any more than it pleased me, though Pincianus in his *Emendations* on the same Seneca considers it superior to the reading offered by Erasmus, namely: “If it is lawful for anyone to ascend to the regions of the heavenly beings,” etc. Crinitus therefore thought Seneca should be read as Lactantius has it; Erasmus too considered Lactantius’s reading not unreasonable.

Pithoeus, however, *Adversaria* I.11, condemns Lactantius’s reading and maintains that Ennius wrote: “If it is lawful for anyone to ascend into the regions of the heavenly beings,” etc. The ancients, he says, [Col. 0903B] commonly used *endo* for *in*. Africanus would not have been wrongly criticized if the passage in Ennius had stood as it does in Firmianus’s reading, for he added the condition “if it is right by slaughter,” etc., which might not be true. But he was rightly and deservedly criticized for boasting that heaven lay open to him, defiled by so many and such great slaughters, provided only that it was lawful for any mortal to enter into the regions of the heavenly beings. Pithoeus’s reading, which greatly pleases me, is also approved by Scipio Gentilis in the *Origins* and by Lambinus in his annotations on the fragments of Cicero’s *Republic* III. It is nearly identical with the reading Erasmus says he restored by divination and conjecture; but Pithoeus’s seems more Ennian. See Gruter’s observations on Seneca.

“It is indeed so, Africanus,” he says. Andreas Patricius, in his scholia on the fragments of Cicero’s *Republic* III, thinks that one should read: “It is indeed so, Africanus,” or simply, “Indeed, Africanus.” Where I find all manuscripts unanimous, I do not readily alter anything; nevertheless, I do not suppress the opinions of learned men.

[Col. 0903C] “To teach through divine writings.” Genesis IV, where the discovery and cultivation of crops and vines are attributed to Adam and Noah; Lactantius himself discusses this again below, book II, chapter 14, as does St Augustine, *On Genesis according to the Letter* VIII. Pliny, therefore, at the end of book VII, and the other pagans talk nonsense when they attribute these things to Ceres and the Athenian Eumolpus, or to Dionysus—that is, Osiris—as Diodorus writes, book I, chapter 2.

“As medicine to Aesculapius, craftsmanship to Vulcan.” Pliny VII.56; Polydore Vergil, *On the Inventors of Things*.

“To the inventor of pottery.” Namely Rhoecus and Theodorus, according to some, as Pliny reports in book XXXV, chapter 12.

“Samian vessels.” Pliny, same book, chapter 16.

“There is indeed reason why anyone,” etc. I have restored this as it stands in B., T., P., and the Plantin edition, rather than as in certain other editions, “There is indeed a cause why anyone,” etc. For they preferred simply “there is reason” or “there is cause.” Plautus [Col. 0903D] *Aulularia*: “There is reason why I should inspect the house”; Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II:

> There is indeed reason why anyone would not wish to offend Juno.

Lactantius above, at the end of chapter 17: “There plainly was reason for so great a labour,” etc.; and below, book II, chapter 7, at the end: “There is indeed reason why their authority,” etc.

## CHAPTER XIX

“For they feared harm if they confessed contrary to public belief.” He gives an example concerning Cicero below, book II, chapter 3, at the beginning. St Augustine said the same of Varro in *City of God* VI, and of Scaevola in book IV, chapter 27.

## CHAPTER XX

“If it had been the very animal whose form it bears.” Yet [Col. 0904A] writers were not lacking who reported that it was indeed the animal itself: namely, a real she-wolf that offered her teats to Romulus and Remus. Virgil, book VIII:

> And in Mars’s green cave, newly delivered, etc.

Ovid, *Fasti* II: “She came to the exposed infants,” etc.; and III: “With what milk did she nourish the infants,” etc. Propertius II, elegy VI: “Romulus, nurtured by the hard,” etc. Nor did poets alone say this, but historians too, and distinguished ones, cited by Dionysius of Halicarnassus at the end of the first book of his *Roman Antiquities*: Pliny VIII.17; Strabo under the relevant entry; Justin the historian, books XXXVIII and XLIII and at the end of XLIV; Plutarch, *Parallel Lives* XXXVI and *Roman Questions* XXI; Hyginus, chapter 252.

The more generally accepted view, however, is that this “she-wolf” was a woman named Acca Larentia, surnamed Lupa because she was a prostitute. For women who made their bodies public were called *lupae* (“she-wolves”), just as Cicero often calls Antony’s harlots *lupae* in the *Philippics*. Most of the above-mentioned authors report this, besides others: Ovid, *Fasti* III; Pliny XVIII.2; [Col. 0904B] Plutarch, *Romulus*; Festus; Livy, book I of the first Decade; Massurius, quoted by Gellius VI.7; and Macer the historian, book I, quoted by Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.10. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, cited above, writes that this opinion accords better with history.

“Larentia.” I have followed this reading both because of the authority of the better manuscripts B., T., and P., and because a little below her festival is called *Larentinalia* in all Lactantian manuscripts without dissent. There is, however, much variation among writers concerning the woman’s name and her festival. Cicero in the letters to Brutus, Varro, Festus, Livy, Ovid at the beginning of *Fasti* III, and Pliny cited above call her Laurentia. But Gellius VI.7, Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.10, Tertullian, *Apology* 13 and 24, Minucius in the *Octavius*, and Plutarch in *Romulus* call her Larentia.

“The Romans, of course, followed the Athenian example in fashioning her likeness.” How the Athenian citizens Harmodius and Aristogiton killed Hipparchus the tyrant is related at length in Thucydides, in the preface and book VI. Plato mentions them in the *Symposium*; Aristotle, *Rhetoric* II.25; Cicero at the end of the first *Tusculan Disputation*; and Aelian, *Various History* II. [Col. 0904C] After the tyrant’s murder, a prostitute—Harmodius’s mistress, according to Athenaeus XIII.24, and familiar with both conspirators through lyre-song, according to Pliny XXXIV.8—was captured and cruelly tortured by the tyrants Pisistratus and Hippias, so that she might reveal the entire plan for killing him and betray the accomplices in the crime. Nothing could be extorted from her. Indeed, as Tertullian writes at the end of the *Apology*, when the executioner was already exhausted, she finally spat out her own bitten-off tongue into the face of the raging tyrant, so that she might spit out her voice as well, lest she should be able to confess the conspirators even if, overcome, she had wished to do so. Pliny VII.23, however, when speaking of Leaena, assigns this deed not to her but to Anaxarchus when he was tortured for a similar reason; Valerius III.3 does likewise.

The Athenians therefore erected in her honour the image of the animal whose name she bore, [Col. 0904D] but forbade the artist to add a tongue. Pausanias, in his *Attica*, mentions the bronze lioness set up by the Athenians for her. Athenaeus and Pliny, cited above, recall the story; so do Tertullian, cited above and *To the Martyrs* 6, and Eusebius of Caesarea in the *Chronicle*, who records Hipparchus’s murder under Olympiad 65.

Hence I do not sufficiently understand how Lactantius can write that the Romans took their example from the Athenians in making the image of the she-wolf. For since the deed of Lupa—Acca Larentia, that is—preceded the deed of Leaena by about two hundred and fifty years, it seems highly probable that the Romans portrayed Lupa long before the Athenians portrayed Leaena. The Athenians, therefore, could rather have taken such an example from the Romans than the Romans from the Athenians. Moreover, because the prostitute was privy to the conspiracy and did not prevent the murder—which she surely could have prevented by denouncing the conspirators—Lactantius rightly writes that she too killed the tyrant, although she did not herself perpetrate the killing.

[Col. 0905A] “Larentinalia.” Those who call the woman Laurentia call her festival *Laurentialia* or *Laurentalia*, as Ovid does near the beginning of *Fasti* III. Those who call her Larentia call it *Larentialia* or *Larentiala*; those who call her Laurenta call it *Laurentinalia*; and thus those who call her Larentina call it *Larentinalia*.

“But Faula also,” etc. Plutarch discusses her in *Roman Questions* 35, where he calls her Larentia Fabola.

“Floralia.” On these, see Varro, at the beginning of *On Agriculture*; Pliny XVIII.29; Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.4.

“Those games, therefore, are celebrated with every sort of licentiousness,” etc. Every kind of depravity and obscenity was performed in these games by naked women acting as mimes. When Cato once attended them, the people, out of respect for his dignity and severity, did not dare demand that the women strip naked. Valerius Maximus recounts this more fully in book II, chapter *On Dignity*; Seneca, letter 98: “You are mistaken, my Lucilius.” [Col. 0905B] These games fell on the fourth day before the Kalends of May and on the Kalends of May themselves, as Pliny writes in cited chapter 29, and Ovid at the end of *Fasti* IV and beginning of V.

I think Gyraldus mistaken when, in his *On the Gods of the Gentiles*, first Syntagma, where he treats Flora, he left it written that the Floralia were the same as the festival of Maiuma, concerning which see the sole law in Code XI, *On Maiuma*, and law XV, title 6, of the Theodosian Code. The Floralia were held at Rome; but the spectacle of Maiuma was presented not on western shores but eastern ones, as the most learned Cardinal Baronius demonstrates in his notes on the martyrology under 26 December, refuting Suidas’s opinion that Maiuma was a Roman festival customarily held in May at the mouths of the Tiber—though almost everyone follows Suidas. See Alciatus’s annotations on the cited sole law of the Code, *On Maiuma*, and *Parerga* V.5; Cujacius on the same law; Girardus; Prateius; Brissonius in their lexicons under *Mauma*; Stewechius on Vegetius III.39; and others.

Yet their opinion in no way supports Gyraldus, since they write that Maiuma’s festivals were customarily held at [Col. 0905C] the mouths of the Tiber but do not maintain that they were identical with the Floralian games, which were celebrated in the city itself, as Alexander of Naples notes, *Days of Genius* VI.8.

“Fear and Pallor.” Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* III; Pliny II.7.

“He might have them present.” This is the accepted reading of manuscripts and printed editions and should not rashly be rejected, as Thomasius idly does. Everyone knows that *praesentem habere* or *praesentem esse*, “to have present” or “to be present,” means “to be at hand,” an extremely frequent expression among all Latin writers, especially Lactantius himself: *Divine Institutes* II.2 at the end; *On the Anger of God*; and elsewhere. B., however, reads *secum haberet*, “might have them with him.”

“Mind.” Cicero and Pliny, cited above.

“Cicero said that Greece had undertaken a great and bold design,” etc. Sigonius and Patricius think that a passage has dropped out of Cicero’s *Laws* II, in their scholia on Cicero’s fragments.

“For virtues, not vices, ought to be consecrated.” [Col. 0905D] Cicero: “It is fitting to consecrate virtues, not vices.”

“Fever.” Cicero and Pliny, cited above.

“But that.” In Cicero: “But that one” (*ast olla*).

“By superfluous constructions.” Namely temples consecrated to gods, or rather to demons.

“Images.” Idols of demons.

“With the tips of their fingers.” He mocks the pagan custom of taking things prepared for sacrifice with two or three fingers. Thus they threw incense into the flame of the altar. St Jerome, letter 1: “It is not only service to an idol if someone casts into the altar’s burning ash incense held between two little fingers.” Lactantius V.19: “For they preferred to be tortured and killed rather than cast incense, grasped with three fingers, upon the hearth,” etc. Porphyry, *On Abstinence from Animate Beings*, says: “The Pythia at Hermione rejoiced while sacrificing, taking pieces of cake from a bag with three fingers.” Ovid, *Fasti* II:

> And beneath the threshold she places three grains of incense with three fingers. [Col. 0906A]

This also explains other passages of Lactantius: IV.3, “For that religion is mute, not only because it belongs to mute things, but because its rite lies in hand and fingers”; V.20, “In it I see nothing but a rite pertaining only to fingers.”

“To shudder.” This is from manuscripts cited by Thomasius; for *colere*, “to worship,” found in printed editions, contradicts Lactantius himself.

“When they had made instruments of torture from women’s hair,” etc. Vegetius, *On Military Matters* IV.9; Capitolinus, *Maximinus*.

“Just as young men previously sent by those same persons together with virgins, from whom the Partheniae were born,” etc. This reading occurs in many Vatican manuscripts, in the very ancient B. and another manuscript likewise of the library of San Salvatore at Bologna, in Florentine and Venetian Tridentine editions. For the whole history of the Partheniae, see Strabo VI; Justin the historian at the end of book III; and Isidore, *Origins* IX.2, though he made the error of writing Spartans for Partheniae.

The very learned Latinus Latinius thought that the reading of the Aldine edition, *ante admissi* (“previously admitted”), [Col. 0906B] was not merely neither absurd nor senseless, as Thomasius judged, but very apt and precisely consistent with the story. It appears from this story that before the war was ended, those young men were sent back to Lacedaemon by command, to have intercourse indiscriminately with all the virgins for the procreation of offspring. Now *admittere*, besides its other meanings, is to bring male to female or female to male for intercourse; whence *admissio*, *admissura*, and *admissarius*. Petrus Ciacconius suspected that one should read *antea dimissi*, “previously dismissed.”

“Partheniae.” Others read *Partheniae*, as does manuscript B. here. Aristotle, *Politics* V.7; Pollux, under Παρθενίας; Strabo, cited above.

“To armed Venus.” See Pausanias, *Laconica*; Quintilian, *Institutes* II.4.

“To Jupiter the Baker also,” etc. The story is in Livy, book V of the first Decade; Frontinus, *Stratagems* III.15; Ovid, *Fasti* VI; Suidas.

[Col. 0906C] “Mute.” A nymph of the Tiber first called Lara, according to Varro, *On the Latin Language* IV; afterwards Muta, according to Ovid, *Fasti* II, who recounts the story; called Larunda by Ausonius; and finally elsewhere Mania by the same Varro, Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.7, and Arnobius at the end of book III.

“Cunina.” Thus it is read in Varro and St Augustine, *City of God* IV.8 and 11. B. has *Cunia*; P., *Cuna*.

“Sterculius.” Thus Tertullian, *Apology* 24; Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.7: *Stercutius*; Pliny XVII.9; Servius on the first *Georgic*; Isidore, *Etymologies* XVII.1; others, however, have *Stercutus*. Varro, *On the Life of the Roman People* II: *Sterquilius*. Manuscript B. here has *Stercus*; T., *Sterculinus*; P., *Stercutus*.

“Mutinus.” Thus Tertullian, cited *Apology* 24; this reading is approved by Vives on *City of God* IV.11 and by Gulielmus, *Verisimilia* I.23. Festus Pompeius: “Musinus Tusinus; the shrine of Musinus Tisinu,” he says, “was on the Veliae,” etc. Arnobius IV: *Mutunus*. But St Augustine, cited chapter 11, has *Musunus* and *Tutunus*. Manuscripts B. and P. here have *Tutinus*.

[Col. 0906D] “Terminus.” See Apollodorus at the beginning of the *Library*; Pausanias, at the end of the *Boeotica*.

“For when Tarquinius wished to build the Capitol,” etc. Livy, at the end of book I of the first Decade and at the end of book V; Ovid, *Fasti* II; St Augustine, *City of God* IV.23 and 29; Servius on *Aeneid* IX.

## CHAPTER XXI

“A human victim.” He notes the cruelty of pagans who sacrificed human victims. On this subject see Plutarch, *Pelopidas*; Tertullian, *Apology* 9; Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Greeks*; Minucius, *Octavius*; Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* IV.7; Nazianzen, *Oration on the Epiphany*; St Augustine, *City of God* VII.19; Theodoret, *Therapeutics* VII.

“Esus and Teutates.” Lucan speaks of them in book I. [Col. 0907A] Some interpret Esus as Mars. Teutates, however, is Mercury; see Livy, book VI of the third Decade; Caesar, *Gallic War* VI, where he discusses human victims; Arnobius II.

“Jupiter Latiaris.” He is also called Latiaris. Franciscus Juretus testifies in his notes on Symmachus’s letters, book I, letter 9, that this was written in certain Lactantian manuscripts.

“From the Milvian Bridge.” Varro has “from the Sublician Bridge.” “Argei,” he says, “are images of men made from rushes, and every year they are customarily thrown from the Sublician Bridge by priests.” Thus Epicadus, quoted by Macrobius, *Saturnalia* II.11; but Dionysius of Halicarnassus, at the beginning of the *Roman Antiquities*: “They cast thirty images of men into the river Tiber from the Sacred Bridge; these are called Argei.”

> Καὶ κεφαλὰς ᾅδῃ  
> “And heads to Hades.”

Perhaps Varro took this little verse from Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.7, where ᾅδῃ occurs—that is, “to Dis”—rather than Κρονίδῃ, “to Saturn,” as in every Lactantian book, through an obvious scribal error. For here τὸ πατρὶ (“to the Father”) can designate no one but Saturn, to whom whole human bodies were sacrificed, as is clear from Ovid, Macrobius cited above, and *Saturnalia* II.11; Lactantius confirms the rest in this very passage. Therefore τὸ ἅδῃ [sic] ought to have been restored in Firmianus, so that we understand Dis, as Pontanus also advises in his notes on Macrobius cited above.

“Φῶτα.” We have removed not merely the Latin interpretation of this word—which is absent from most editions, though present in many manuscripts in forms such as *φῶτα, id est hominem* (“φῶτα, that is, a man”) or *id est lumina* (“that is, lights”)—but every accent as well, so that the ambiguity of the oracle may be preserved, an ambiguity deliberately contained in the verse. It is removed whether one place a grave or circumflex accent on the word, as is incorrectly found in every printed edition, both in Macrobius, cited chapter 7 and 11, and in Plutarch. With a grave accent it is restricted to the meaning “a human being”; with a circumflex, to “light,” as Suidas and others teach under φώς. It is likewise removed whether one prefix the article, [Col. 0907C] or even more so if, by adding an interpretation, one determines it in one sense or the other. Why φῶς can mean both “man” and “light,” Plutarch explains in the cited passage. I would ask you, reader, to recall the arguments by which we have refuted this reasoning concerning the different accents and meanings of ΦΩΤΑ, as wholly contrary to the rules of modern grammar (see the note at col. 241 of this volume).

“To be thrown.” *Jace* is incorrectly read in all Lactantian books; we therefore corrected it as in the poet:

> Such evils could Religion persuade,

> which often produced, etc.

Lactantius joined, arranged, and elevated for his own purpose two verses of Lucretius, separated from each other at the beginning of *On the Nature of Things* I. For there the following comes first:

> Because formerly, more often,  
> Religion was able to prompt wicked and impious deeds.

Then, after a few intervening lines, [Col. 0907D] comes the verse:

> Such evils could Religion persuade.

“The Egyptian rites of Isis.” On these see above, chapter 17; Arnobius I; Minucius; St Augustine, *City of God* VI.10.

“Lucan.” A mnemonic error: he put Lucan for Ovid.

“And covered with wood.” Namely, enclosed in a wooden chest—thus the Lactantian books read; or, as all manuscripts of Lucan have it, “and covered with linen,” that is, wrapped in linen cloths, etc.

“Osiris.” Gyraldus wonders in Syntagma 8 that Lactantius here makes Osiris the son of Isis, since Plutarch, with whom Diodorus agrees in book I, chapter 2, calls him not Isis’s son but her brother and husband in *On Isis and Osiris*. But Gyraldus should have remembered what he himself had assembled in Syntagma 6, where he discusses Serapis; in 8, where he discusses Osiris; and in 12, where he discusses Isis: namely, that the history is entangled and very obscure. He could have understood that Lactantius, though departing from Plutarch’s opinion, [Col. 0908A] may nonetheless have followed the account of other writers scarcely less weighty than Plutarch.

First, Firmianus himself asserts above, chapter 11, that the woman whom Jupiter violated was the same as the goddess Isis worshipped in Egypt. Ovid, at the end of *Metamorphoses* I; Apollodorus, at the beginning of *Library* II; Lucian, *Dialogues of the Gods*; and others say this. Hence Propertius, speaking of her rites performed at Rome in his own time, calls her Inachian, II, penultimate elegy:

> Would that she might perish by the Nile, etc.

Likewise in the elegy of book II beginning “Jupiter, having conceived desire,” etc.:

> Io had once lowed, her head transformed, in her first years;  
> now she is the goddess-cow who drinks the streams of Nile.

Aelian too writes that the Greeks affirm this. She bore Epaphus by Jupiter; in Egypt he was worshipped and had a temple joined to that of his mother, as Ovid and Aelian report. [Col. 0908B] Now Epaphus among the Greeks is the same as Apis among the Egyptians, as Herodotus writes. We know from Aridaeus of Argos and Nymphodorus of Amphipolis, quoted by Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* X, and from Varro, quoted by Augustine, *City of God* XVIII.5, that Apis is the same as Serapis. Rufinus, Suidas, and others write that this was commonly believed.

Tacitus, at the end of book XX, writes that Serapis was believed to be the same as Osiris. Diodorus Siculus, book I, chapter 2, asserts that Serapis is called both Osiris and Dionysus. Lactantius himself says the same here. Indeed Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*, says: “It is preferable to make Osiris the same as Bacchus, and Serapis the same as Osiris.” And again, in the same work, Plutarch reports that Apis was held by Egyptian priests to be the same as Osiris; Strabo likewise, speaking of Memphis, book XVII. Lactantius could therefore, following these authors, call Osiris the one who was continually sought and found in the rites of Isis, and say that he was Isis’s son, as the story relates.

[Col. 0908C] “The steep height has long resounded.” The reading of these verses differs somewhat in Ovid. There it is “some with their hands [raise] shields,” and:

> The deed escaped the father’s notice, and imitations of the ancient act.

“Because they are to be understood as chief authorities.” The passage is not now found among Sallust’s works.

“Antiquity embellishing it into something greater.” I followed the reading of the Florentine edition, approved by Carrio, *Ancient Readings* II.7, rather than the other reading, “those embellishing antiquity into something greater.” Sallust did not mean that the Curetes had embellished antiquity; rather, that the Curetes’ deed—both the discovery and understanding of religion, since they were first in understanding divine matters—had been magnified by antiquity itself. For this reason they were called the foster-fathers of Jupiter and celebrated under that name.

“I mean those who stamp in an unseemly dance.” He means the Salii, priests of Mars.

“Or those naked and anointed.” He means the Luperci, priests of Pan, [Col. 0908D] god of shepherds.

“What of shields already rotten with age,” etc. These were the *ancilia*. Virgil speaks of all these at the end of book VIII:

> Hence he had displayed the leaping Salii and naked Luperci,  
> wool-bearing priests with pointed caps, and the *ancilia* fallen from heaven.

“O foolish minds of men, O blind hearts! However much in darkness,” etc. In these verses Lucretius has “wretched” for “foolish,” and “of what kind” for “however much.”

“Less sane and foolish.” With Thomasius I followed the reading of manuscript B., instead of “too wanton and foolish,” etc., found in certain printed editions. Yet I also greatly like the conjectural reading proposed by Ludovicus Carrio, *Ancient Readings* II.7: “less wanton and foolish,” etc. [Col. 0909A] Here *lascivia* is not lust but cheerfulness and rather forward jesting. Ulpian, in the Cornelian law, Digest, *On the Cornelian Law concerning Assassins*: “When someone through playful conduct had given occasion for death,” etc. So Cicero at the beginning of *On Ends* and *On Divination* I; Varro at the beginning of *On Agriculture*. See Budé’s annotations on the law *Ex conducto*, § *Si vis tempestatis*, Digest, *On Letting and Hiring*.

## CHAPTER XXII

“That Sabine was a king.” Numa Pompilius, concerning whom here you have much drawn from Livy, book X of the fourth Decade, and Plutarch’s *Numa*.

“Impious rites.” Because infants were sacrificed to Saturn; Tertullian reproaches the pagans with this crime too, *Apology* 9.

“Fatua, Fauna.” Some call her Fatua, others Fauna, others jointly Fatua Fauna, as Lactantius does here and Arnobius in books I and V. Why she was called by both names is explained by Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.12.

“They sacrifice indoors.” Thus B. and all other manuscripts and the best editions read, not the erroneous “outdoors” in inferior printed editions, which contradicts Lactantius’s meaning and the history of this goddess’s rites. See Cicero, [Col. 0909B] speech *On the Response of the Soothsayers*; Macrobius cited above; Plutarch, *Caesar* and *Cicero*; Seneca, *Letters* XVI, letter 98, “You are mistaken, my Lucilius,” where even corrected editions read “indoors.” This error has nevertheless been corrected here in the Aldine, Florentine, and Plantin editions.

“And Sextus Clodius.” See Suetonius, *On Famous Rhetoricians*.

“He drank a potful.” Whatever I find anywhere devised by learned men concerning our Lactantius, I gladly share with the reader, so that nothing may be wanting to him for either usefulness or pleasure. Yet I would urge every reader, again and again, never to think that ancient and received readings should be abandoned if they can be defended and sustained in any way. Otherwise, if ancient words and meanings are altered and overturned in accordance with each person’s own fancy, and removed whenever one wishes by continually introducing new ones, we shall assuredly possess no longer the memorials of ancient writers but our own inventions.

[Col. 0909C] Johannes Meursius, *Arnobian Criticism* V.6, thinks that *obba* should be read here. An *obba*, according to Nonius, was a kind of drinking-cup. Arnobius, recounting this history in book V, calls it a *seria*; this too was an elongated earthenware vessel for wine. Arnobius agrees with Lactantius—or rather with Sextus Clodius—that Fatua Fauna was beaten to death by her husband after drinking wine too freely, as Plutarch also relates in the *Problems*. But Macrobius recounts the matter quite differently in the cited chapter 12.

“Earth-born Lamiae of Faunus,” etc. These verses are thought to have fallen out of Lucilius’s *Satires*: “to proceed, and to be human beings,” etc. This little verse should be read as in Lucilius himself in the collections of fragments of ancient pagan poets, in B., T., and P.; nor should the conjunction be omitted, as it is in certain printed editions.

“Bronze.” In the margin of one manuscript, *inanis* (“empty”) was written for *ahenis* (“bronze”), and I suspect this is the true reading. A stop should be placed after *inesse*, and then one should read continuously: “the empty workshop of painters,” to which the following words most aptly apply: “nothing true, everything fabricated.”

[Col. 0909D] “Likewise, their fathers Faunus and Laomedon.” “Their,” that is, Latinus’s and Priam’s: Laomedon was Priam’s father, Faunus Latinus’s father, and Picus his grandfather. I therefore read here with B. and T. not *Picus*, as in many editions, but *Faunus*. Virgil, speaking of Latinus in book VII:

> Him we receive as born of Faunus and the Laurentian nymph Marica;  
> Picus was Faunus’s father, and he traces you, Saturn, as his ancestor.

But Arnobius II also says: “Who [made] Picus the father of Faunus and grandfather of Latinus,” etc.

“Sacred history testifies,” etc. Namely Euhemerus’s history concerning the gods, discussed so often above.

“Whenever he came into a region.” Thus I read it, as in B.: *ut*, in the sense “as soon as,” “from the moment when,” has a remarkable charm. Plautus, *Poenulus*:

> As each of them encountered the birdlime,  
> so thickly they fell to the ground like pears.

[Col. 0910A] Terence, *Hecyra*:

> As each person arrived,  
> I went up to him.

Others read: “into whatever region he came”; others: “into whatever region he might come.”

“Atabyrius.” In B. it is written *Ataburius*, following the pronunciation by which the Latins of old represented Greek upsilon with *u*: thus *Musia* for Mysia, *Tumpanum*, *Assurius*, *Sulla*, *Purrhus*, *Poluposus*, and similar forms are found in the Florentine Pandects, as Brissonius testifies in the *Parerga*. Appian is corrected, who in his Mithridatic History calls Jupiter Tabyrius rather than Atabyrius.
