For it is clear from this passage, Stephanus, Strabo, Apollodorus, *Library* III, and Pindar’s Olympian ode celebrating Diagoras and its scholiast, that the former form is both to be spoken and written. Stephanus and Strabo, however, hold that Jupiter was called thus not from a host, as Lactantius says, but from Mount Atabyrius.

“Labradeus.” Thus Plutarch, *Greek Questions* 45, and Aelian. Strabo and Stephanus, however, have *Labradeus* [Col. 0910B] or *Labrandenus*. Aelian writes that Jupiter was named not from a host, as Lactantius relates here, but for another reason: “Jupiter was called Labradeus because it had rained very heavily.”

“Cassius.” I have written it as I find it in every manuscript and in Theophilus, with double *s*: for he writes Κάσσιος Ζεύς, “Cassian Zeus.” Stephanus, however, says that this name was bestowed on Jupiter not from a host but from Mount Casius and the Egyptian city: “Casion,” he says, “is a mountain and city of Egypt, from which comes also Zeus Casios,” etc. Pliny too mentions Mount Casius and the sanctuary there of Jupiter Casius, book IV and V, both chapter 12; as do Strabo XVI, Solinus chapters 46, 47, and 49, and Suidas. If we prefer to think Jupiter named from this, it should be written not *Cassio* with double *s*, but *Casio* with one *s*, as in Lucan, [Col. 0910C] book VIII, speaking of Pompey’s tomb:

> And to prefer it to Casius’s Jupiter, etc.

“Nephew.” Namely, of Uranus or Heaven, who first ruled the whole universe. By his wife Earth he begot Saturn; Saturn begot Jupiter by Rhea, as Apollodorus writes at the beginning of the *Library*. Lactantius himself adds here that Earth was Jupiter’s grandmother, being Uranus’s wife. Uranus therefore was Jupiter’s grandfather and Jupiter his grandson, as Lactantius says above, chapter 5 and at the end of chapter 11. This, then, is the correct reading, acknowledged by all printed books, not “great-grandson,” as B. reads in the margin of the books of the Plantin edition, as also T. and P.

## CHAPTER XXIII

“Theophilus in the book *On Times*,” etc. This is the third of the books that Theophilus himself wrote against the pagans, addressed to Autolycus. See St Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.

“Thallus.” We have written this, following Meursius in the *Hypocritica*, from Tertullian, *Apology* 11, Minucius, and Lactantius himself above, chapter 13 of this book, rather than *Thalus*, found in all printed editions.

Benedictus Pererius clearly demonstrates, in his commentary on Daniel XVI.14 and book XI of his *Disputation on the Seventy Weeks*, part I, question 2, Thallus’s error of 322 years, which Theophilus followed, [Col. 0910D] and then Lactantius. Although chronologists differ astonishingly in this calculation, once all views have been weighed, it is nevertheless certain that Belus was older than the fall of Troy by no fewer than about eight or nine hundred years. See Hermannus Contractus in the *Chronicle* and others.

“One thousand four hundred and seventy.” If it is true that Lactantius wrote this in A.D. 302, as I have maintained above in the notes on chapter 1, then according to Glareanus’s chronology of Livy, compiled from the most approved authors, the total would be 1,485 years. For he writes that 432 years elapsed from the fall of Troy to the founding of the City; from the City’s founding to Christ’s birth, 751; adding 302 years produces a total of 1,485 years. Those, however, who maintain that Lactantius wrote this in 316 must concede that he diverged even further from the [Col. 0911A] true total. But, as I have said, chronologists differ greatly, and Lactantius is not careful in chronological calculations.

Before no more than eighteen hundred years ago, etc. [Col. 0912A] It is already clear from what precedes that the calculation is false. Arnobius adopted another method of reckoning and writes, near the end of Book II, that almost two thousand years had elapsed from Jupiter to those times.

[Col. 0911A]

## BOOK II

## CHAPTER I

“For I rejoice, when vain things have been convicted,” etc. Another reading: “For I rejoice, Emperor Constantine, when vain things have been convicted,” etc. But the words “Emperor Constantine” are absent from most Vatican manuscripts, two manuscripts of San Salvatore at Bologna, T. P., the Florentine edition, and certain others.

That there is some perverse power, namely the Devil.

“We shall recount his origin in its place; for the present let us expose his deceits.” We wished to restore this passage in our edition from manuscript B, as also Thomasius did in the Plantin edition: it is lacking from the others. [Col. 0911B]

“God willed that we should look upon heaven,” etc. “Man,” he says, “was made upright so that he might gaze upon heaven.” Thus Plato in the *Timaeus*, where he treats of the use of the eyes; Seneca, *Epistle* 95, “That part,” etc., at the end; Philo the Jew, in *On the Planting of Noah*; Basil, *Homily* 9 on the *Hexaemeron*. Galen nevertheless contests this assertion in Book III of *On the Use of the Parts*, chapter 3.

“That he may imitate that over which he ought to rule.” This is how it should be read, as in B. and P.; the text itself proves it—not, as in most printed editions, “lest he imitate that,” etc.

## CHAPTER II

“What is the point of temples?” Thus concerning temples made by human hands: Book I, chapter 20; Book VI, chapter 25; and at the end of the final chapter of *On the Wrath of God*. Arnobius likewise, at the beginning of Book VI: “For neither,” he says, “do we construct sacred buildings for the offices of veneration,” etc.; and a little below: “But we build no temples for them,” etc. And Minucius, near the end of the *Octavius*: “What temple should I build for him?”

We, however, have learned, affirm, and teach that the human soul is the worthier and more principal temple of God, and that it especially ought to be adorned, dedicated, and consecrated to Him. Yet we do not maintain that these temples made by human hands ought therefore to be abandoned, in which the external worship also due to Him is rendered. For by God’s own command we know that temple at Jerusalem was built by Solomon with a magnificence, solidity, richness, and beauty surpassing belief, as Sacred History in II Kings, Josephus the Jew in *Antiquities* and *The Jewish War*, and Eupolemus in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book IX, testify. We know also that the very Son of God, our Lord, often rendered it illustrious by the glory of his own presence and dwelling; that he expelled those conducting profane business there; and that he called it his Father’s house, a house of prayer: John II; Mark XI.

Accordingly, from the very earliest times after the creation of the world, some place dedicated to divine worship has always existed among the faithful, though called by different names, as every page of the Old Testament testifies: Genesis XXVIII and XXXV; Daniel VII; Amos IV; Isaiah LVI; Exodus XXV; Deuteronomy XII; everywhere in the Prophets and Psalms. After the departure of the Lord and Saviour, moreover, the Apostle Paul mentions the Church at Corinth in this sense in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter XI.

It is useful also to call upon outside witnesses from those times. Philo the Jew, a contemporary of the Apostle Peter—for he is said also to have met with him at Rome while acting there as ambassador to Gaius on behalf of the Jews—in *On the Contemplative Life*, where he describes the habits of the faithful dwelling at Alexandria under Mark the Evangelist, testifies that they had sacred little buildings, which they called *Semnea*, or monasteries, where solitary persons devoted themselves to the mysteries of holy life. Eusebius also cites him, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, chapter 17.

There is also a passage in the *Philopatris* of that impious Lucian, the most bitter enemy of Christians, who lived in the times of the Apostles and even of Trajan. From it one may understand with what expenditure, ornament, and cost churches were then raised among Christians. There he introduces a certain Critias, who, when persuaded by one of the faithful to become a Christian, was led by him to the place where the Christian assembly was held. He describes the place thus: “We passed through iron gates and brazen thresholds, and, having now surmounted many stairs, ascended into a house distinguished by a gilded roof, such as Homer imagines Menelaus to have had. I indeed contemplated all the things that young islander had seen; but I saw not Helen, by Hercules, but men with bowed and pale faces,” etc. [Col. 0912A]

Lampridius, a contemporary of Lactantius—for he wrote in the early years of Constantine—testifies in his *Alexander* that Alexander himself, who assumed imperial power in A.D. 224, assigned a place to the Christians for erecting a church. “When,” he says, “the Christians had occupied a certain place that had been public property, and the tavern-keepers claimed that it ought to belong to them, he replied that it was better for God to be worshipped there in whatever manner than for it to be given over to tavern-keepers.” [Col. 0912B]

Flavius Vopiscus offers this testimony concerning the church of Christians in a rescript of the Emperor Valerian, who held imperial power after about A.D. 257, addressed to the senate: “I am surprised, holy fathers, that you have so long hesitated about opening the Sibylline books, as though you were deliberating in a Christian church and not in the temple of all the gods.”

Evaristus, moreover—to return to our own writers—who occupied the see in A.D. 112, divided the *tituli*, that is, the churches, in the city of Rome among the presbyters, as is clear from the *Book of the Roman Pontiffs*. Tertullian, who flourished about A.D. 200, mentions the church in this sense in *On Idolatry*, likewise in *To His Wife*, Book II, chapter 9; *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 13; and frequently elsewhere.

Cyprian also, who flourished shortly before Lactantius, after A.D. 250, referred to a church under the name *Dominicum* in his *On Works and Almsgiving*, as did the Council of Laodicea, canon 28, reported in the chapter *Non Oportet*, Distinction 42. Eusebius gives the reason for this name in his *Oration in Praise of Constantine*; so too Walafrid and Strabo, *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 7.

The same *Book of the Roman Pontiffs* records that Pope Fabian, in A.D. 245, when Christians enjoyed tranquillity, built churches, by means of which the tombs of the martyrs, hidden beneath the earth in crypts of sand-pits, were made clear and conspicuous by buildings raised above them and suitable for Christian use.

St Gregory of Nyssa, in the *Life of St Gregory Thaumaturgus*, has left in writing that St Gregory himself, in the same period of Fabian, at Neocaesarea in Pontus—of which city he was bishop—erected a distinguished church through the contributions of money and labour from the whole body of the faithful. Because it was most acceptable to God, it was never shaken by earthquakes. Although that city was nearly destroyed by earthquakes, that temple is said always to have remained whole and unharmed; nor was it even attacked by force at the time when, by Diocletian’s decree, all Christian churches were ordered to be destroyed. It still stood intact in the age of Nyssen himself, who likewise testifies elsewhere that Christians erected temples and altars while Fabian occupied the see. [Col. 0912D]

Finally, shortly before Arnobius, Minucius, and Lactantius wrote, Diocletian’s edict ordering churches to be demolished and Christian books to be burned was issued, as is clear from Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VIII, chapters 2 and 3. He laments that disaster, as Arnobius himself does at the end of Book IV in these words: “Why have our writings deserved to be consigned to flames? Why are the meeting-houses, in which the supreme God is prayed to and peace and forgiveness are sought for all—magistrates, armies, and kings—cruelly demolished?” [Col. 0913A]

At the same time, under the same edict, Lactantius testifies below, Book V, chapter 2, that in his presence a building in Bithynia dedicated to divine worship—rightly called by him a temple of God—was destroyed. He also explains his opinion concerning Christian temples at the end of Book VI, where he teaches that thanks should indeed be given to God in temples, yet not in temples alone, but also at home and even in one’s bedroom. In chapter 8 of *On the Wrath of God*, he admits that to build temples, offer sacrifices, and bestow gifts is an act of obedience rendered to God by one who worships him.

A certain heretic, Eustathius, directed a venomous tongue against churches, just as Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon—a type of the devil, of whom II Kings XXV speaks—once directed his engines against them, and as that wicked Diocletian did. Against Eustathius the Council of Gangra had to be summoned around the time of the First Council of Nicaea. It decreed in chapter 5 of its canons: “If anyone teaches that the house of God ought to be despised, and likewise the assemblies held in it, let him be anathema.”

Later the Patarene heretics, as Hugh of Ferrara writes, raised this heresy again from hell in A.D. 1200. They were followed by the Waldensians, Wycliffites, Hussites, and Taborites. [Col. 0913B]

“What is the purpose of altars?” Thus concerning sacrifices: Book I, chapter 20; Book VI, chapters 1, 20, and 25; Book VII, chapter 6; and *On the Wrath of God*, chapter 21; Philo the Jew, *On the Worse Attacking the Better*; Arnobius, at the end of Book IV. The ancient Fathers, that is, cried out against those who sacrificed to God as though he needed victims and sacrificial offerings. Lactantius himself shows this, Book VI, chapter 2: “They slaughter rich and fat victims for God as though he were hungry; they pour out wine as though he were thirsty; they light lamps as though he were in darkness.” Or they spoke against those who performed outward rites in such a way as utterly to omit the inward sacrifice—namely, of a contrite, humbled heart devoted to God.

We, however, maintain that both the inward sacrifice, by which the mind is offered to God, and also the outward sacrifice are owed by us to Him. We know that Holy Scripture so often mentions holy altars and sacrifices: Genesis IV, VIII, XII; Leviticus II and VI; Numbers V; II Chronicles, chapter 28; and countless other places. St Thomas writes, *Second Part of the Second Part*, question 85, article 1, that outward sacrifice has always been due to God, even by natural reason. For natural reason dictates to man that he should submit himself to some superior because of the deficiencies which he perceives in himself, in respect of which he needs to be helped and directed by some superior; and whatever that may be, it is what all call God.

But as lower things in nature are naturally subject to higher, so natural reason dictates to man, according to his natural inclination, that he should offer submission and honour, in his own manner, to that which is above man. The manner fitting to man is to use sensible signs to express certain things, since he receives knowledge from sensible things. Therefore it follows from natural reason that man should use certain sensible objects, offering them to God as a sign of the submission and honour due to Him, just as persons offer certain things to their masters in acknowledgment of lordship. This belongs to the notion of sacrifice, which was formerly offered to God even at his own command in victims. Now we offer, in the most holy Eucharist, the unbloody and ineffable sacrifice instituted by Christ the Lord; more on this at the first chapter of Book VI.

Hence Lactantius himself says in *On the Wrath of God*, chapter 19: “Those who are persuaded that justice is pleasing to God, and who venerate him because he is Lord and Father of all, offer him gifts and sacrifices with constant prayers and frequent vows,” etc.; and in the same work, chapter 8: “To build temples, to offer sacrifices, to bestow gifts,” etc. [Col. 0913D]

“And finally, what of the images themselves?” Lactantius often treats of images or representations below, chapters 3, 7, 18, and 19. With the holy Seventh Synod, one may well marvel at the madness—worthy of mourning with every fountain of tears—of the unhappy “chapters” that impiously twist passages of the holy Fathers directed against idolaters into arguments against images of the saints, which the Church reverently venerates. For the Fathers rightly reproached the nations because they worshipped statues and other images that were nothing but likenesses of dead people, and believed the divinities to be confined within those very representations. This is clear from Arnobius, Book VI: “But you are mistaken,” they say, “and go astray; for neither do we [worship] the bronzes,” etc. [Col. 0914A]

But all who embrace the Catholic faith do not worship images of the dead, but images of the living—for the saints live unto God. They do not worship them with the adoration of *latria*, which is due to God alone, but honour them with the veneration fitting to them. Nor do they halt their minds at the images themselves, as though the divinities were bounded within them; rather, they are directed toward the heavenly persons whose images they venerate, because through them they are powerfully stirred to remembrance, love, and imitation of those persons, as St Gregory the Great says in his letter to Secundinus.

Moreover, no one even slightly acquainted with sacred histories can doubt that from the times of Christ and the Apostles images of Christ himself, of his most holy cross, of his virgin Mother, and of the Apostles themselves were held in veneration among the faithful. Very weighty authorities relate that the image of Christ—not made by any mortal hand, but impressed by Christ the Lord himself and sent by him to Abgar, ruler of Edessa—existed: Evagrius, *History*, Book IV, chapter 26, where he also treats of the miracles of that image, verified and proved at the Second Council of Nicaea; John Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, Book IV, chapter 17; Nicephorus, *History*, Book II, chapter 7; Constantine Porphyrogenitus in Metaphrastes, under 10 August; and, under 15 November, in the Acts of Saints Samonas and Gurias.

Indeed, the Greeks celebrate an annual feast of the same image on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September, as appears in their *Menologion*. Pope Adrian I, writing to Charlemagne in an epistle extant in volume III of the new edition of the Councils, testifies that the same account of Christ’s image sent by him to Abgar was known and received by Pope Stephen in a Roman council; and its miracles are also recorded by Theophanes, *Miscellaneous History*, Book XVII, and Metaphrastes, in the place cited above. What other testimony on behalf of holy images could be adduced stronger or more illustrious than this testimony of Christ himself? [Col. 0914B]

Eusebius, *History*, Book VII, chapter 14, and Damascene, *Orations on Images*, third oration, report the statue of Christ erected by the Syrophoenician woman who had been healed by the Lord himself when she suffered from an issue of blood, as the Evangelists write.

There is a canon of a synod held by the Apostles themselves at Antioch concerning the image of the Saviour customarily painted in churches, in these words: “Lest those who are saved be deceived through idols, let them instead paint, over against idols and Jews, the hand-made, unmixed image of the true God and our Saviour Jesus Christ, both divine and human, and of his servants; and let them not err in idols nor be like the Jews.”

Tertullian, in *On Modesty*, mentions paintings on chalices in which Christ the shepherd was depicted with the sheep he had found. From the final law of the Code *On Pagans* in the Theodosian Code, and from the law *Decernimus* in the Code *On Bishops and Clergy*, we learn that churches were anciently marked with the banner of the cross, as though with an affixed title, and hence were also called by the name *tituli*.

St Irenaeus, who was close to the times of the Apostles—for he had as his teacher Polycarp, a disciple of the Apostle John—condemns the Encratites for misusing images of Christ the Lord and of the Apostle Paul, Book I *Against Heresies*, chapter 24. [Col. 0914D]

Theodor… writes at the beginning of his commentary on Luke of images of the Virgin Mother of God painted by St Luke the Evangelist; so too Nicephorus Callistus, *History*, Book II, chapter 43; Book VI, chapter 15; Book XIV, chapter 2; Book XV, chapter 14. The same Nicephorus, *History*, Book I, chapter 43, and the cited chapter 15 of Book VI, writes of images of the Apostles Peter and Paul also painted by St Luke. Dionysius the Areopagite, a disciple of the Apostle Paul, mentions images of angels that were painted at that time, *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, chapters 1 and 2; Pope Adrian I cites him in his book against Pseudo-Charlemagne addressed to Charlemagne.

Finally, St Paulinus, bishop of Nola and a contemporary of Lactantius, writing to Severus in Epistle 12, bears witness that sacred and venerable crosses and other images of saints were customarily painted in the apses of churches, in these verses:

> The Trinity shines forth in the full mystery, etc.

Thus far concerning holy images held in use and veneration before the time of Lactantius and in Lactantius’ own time. After the time of Constantine the Great, and from Constantine himself onward, it is so manifest that sculpted and painted images were everywhere present and thereafter continually in the Church of God that the matter needs no proof.

They say that Bishop Epiphanius once held this error concerning the prohibition of images; this is clear from his own statements in *Against Heresies*, heresy 79, and in a letter written by him to John, bishop of Jerusalem. In the time of St Gregory the Great, likewise, there was a certain Serenus, bishop of Marseilles, whom St Gregory sharply rebuked in a letter because, from an inconsiderate zeal, he had broken certain images of saints out of fear that the people might worship them. [Col. 0915B]

Neither of these two bishops, however, was branded a heretic, since the Church had not yet decreed anything on the subject, and since they did not hold this opinion with such obstinacy as to be unwilling to assent if the Church taught the contrary.

Many Greek emperors were supporters of the same error: Leo III, who on that account was deprived by Gregory III of communion with the faithful and of the empire; Constantine V, who died after being struck by God with the disease of elephantiasis; and Leo IV. After Leo’s death, his wife Irene, governing the empire in the name of her son Constantine VI, arranged for the Second Council at the city of Nicaea to be assembled. There the opinion against holy images was condemned as heresy under a perpetual anathema by 350 bishops. The Greeks call this council the Seventh General Synod. It met in A.D. 781, when Constantine and his mother Irene ruled and Pope Adrian I occupied the see.

This heresy was held by Samaritans, Saracens, Arians, Theopaschites, and, in a more recent time, Waldensians, Wycliffites, and other sons of wickedness and darkness called Iconoclasts or Iconomachs. It was condemned not only in the said Seventh General Synod, but also in the Eighth Ecumenical Council gathered at Constantinople under Adrian II; in three Lateran councils; at Frankfurt; and finally at Trent, Session 25. Its adherents were refuted by the distinguished disputations of John Damascene, Jonas of Orléans, John Molanus in their books on images and paintings; of all the doctors in the chapter *Venerabiles*, *On Consecration*, Distinction 3; and of St Thomas, Third Part, question 25, article 3. [Col. 0915C]

“In his moral writings.” These have perished, to great loss.

“They have imbibed the dye of folly.” Manuscript B of San Salvatore, the older one, agrees with this reading; but another manuscript of the same monastery, several Vatican manuscripts, T. and P., and the Florentine edition have “the juice of folly,” etc. I have followed the former reading, presented by the Aldine and Plantin editions and approved by Antonio Agustín, as Thomasius testifies in his notes. The metaphor is thus taken from the dyes with which cloths are coloured, since Lactantius says in the same passage that the pagans were “dyed” with persuasion, etc. Thus Pliny, Book XXII, chapter 2: “We know that garments are dyed with marvellous *fucus*.” And Gnaeus Matius in Gellius, Book XX, chapter 8:

> Now soft-coverings, drunk with dye,  
> Which the purple-bearing shellfish, steeping them, has stained with poison.

## CHAPTER III

“He nevertheless says that these matters ought not to be publicly discussed,” etc. This passage is placed among the fragments of Cicero’s Book III, *On the Nature of the Gods*.

“For that which is subject to the eyes is not the man, but the receptacle of the man,” etc. He calls the human body the receptacle of the human being; above, at the end of chapter 2, a lodging; below, chapter 13, a little vessel and dwelling; Book IV, chapter 26, clothing; and perhaps elsewhere by other such names. In Book V, chapter 22, he says that the human being exists in the mind alone.

What he states here he also wrote in Book VII, chapter 12, and in *On the Workmanship of God*, chapters 1 and 20, where he has almost copied word for word a passage of Cicero at the end of the *Dream of Scipio*: “But strive thou,” etc. Pythagoras was the originator of this opinion, and Plato its advocate. In the first *Alcibiades*, or *On the Nature of Man*, Plato tries to prove that the human being is the intellectual soul alone, not the body, which the soul uses as an instrument for carrying out actions.

For, seeing the soul to be of a simple and incorporeal nature, he thought it could not be united with the body, since incorporeal things do not coalesce with bodies. He also believed that the contrary position led to the absurdity that the soul would perish with the body and would be contaminated by its contagion. Since, if we consider the purity of its nature, it is free from such contamination, he judged that it was not combined with the body but set over it like a governor. He therefore does not call the human being a composite of body and soul, frightened by the difficulty of their union; rather, he says that the soul is placed in the body and rules it. [Col. 0916B]

Ammonius, Plotinus’ teacher, investigated the matter more carefully and said that intelligible things have such a nature that they can penetrate bodies and, retaining their purity, attach themselves to them. We see this in the illumination of air: light, though incorporeal, suffuses and illuminates the corporeal air, yet is not in the least defiled. Thus he thinks that an incorporeal soul is attached to a body without being mingled with it, but, remaining incorrupt, brings it life, movement, and every sense.

Gregory of Nyssa teaches the same in *On the Soul and Resurrection* and *On the Making of Man*, where he also endeavours to show the nature of this union of body and soul. St Thomas most excellently treats the matter, as is his custom, in *Against the Gentiles*, Book II, chapter 56 and following. Lactantius was unable to do so when he attempted it in chapter 16 of *On the Workmanship of God*.

Yet Plato’s position appears especially suited to commending virtue and shaping morals. Therefore Aristotle himself, though the opposite is asserted from his metaphysical teachings, when speaking of morals is almost indistinguishable from Plato’s mode of expression: *Nicomachean Ethics*, Book IX, chapters 4 and 8. The holy Fathers also sometimes seem to speak in this manner. Arnobius, Book II: “For what are we human beings except souls shut up in bodies?” Thus he often says that souls are bound to bodies. Sacred Scripture likewise uses this same manner of speech: Genesis I, “Let us make man,” etc.; Job X, “You clothed me with skin and flesh.” Thus the body is called a tent by the Apostle Paul, II Corinthians V; elsewhere a house of clay, Job IV; a prison and confinement, Psalm CXLI.

Plotinus wrote an entire book on this question, the first of the First Ennead. Whatever the Platonists may think, true philosophy and divine theology require us to affirm that the human soul is the informing and substantial form of the body itself, not merely an attendant upon it like a sailor upon a ship. Lactantius himself appears at times to have held this, from Book VII, chapter 3: “If it rules,” he says, “not indeed as the mind rules the body,” etc. Aristotle teaches this in many places: *On the Soul*, Book II, text 24; *Metaphysics*, Book XII, text 16. So too St Thomas: First Part, question 76, articles 1, 6, and 7; *Against the Gentiles*, Book II, chapters 56, 57, 68 and following; *Quodlibet* XII, article 12. The same holy doctor argues that Aristotle held this view of the intellectual soul against Averroes, *Against the Gentiles*, Book II, chapter 59; so too Gregory of Rimini, *Commentary on the Sentences*, Book II, distinctions 16 and 17, question 1. This is a conclusion of faith, as appears in the Clementine constitution *Fidei*, *On the Supreme Trinity*. [Col. 0916D]

Therefore, since in composite substances the “this particular thing” is neither form alone nor matter alone, but both together, as Aristotle and the Commentator teach in *Metaphysics*, Book VII, commentary text 27, and as St Thomas discusses at length in *On Being and Essence*, chapter 2, with Cajetan there, and in the First Part, question 75, article 4, and *Quodlibet* 76, article 1, one must not say that the human being is soul alone or body alone, but soul and body together—that is, the whole composite.

Since this position contributes greatly both to establishing the resurrection of bodies, as in Athenagoras’ *On the Resurrection*, St Thomas’s *Commentary on the Sentences*, Book IV, distinction 43, sole question, article 1, and other disputations concerning the resurrection of the dead, and to confirming other positions of faith, concerning which John Andrew speaks in the said Clementine constitution *Fidei*, under the word *Intellectivae*, *On the Supreme Trinity*, I wished to warn that one ought not depart from it. One should beware of such expressions as calling the body the vessel, instrument, receptacle, clothing, or lodging of the soul. For they seem partly to allude to Plato’s doctrine that the soul is not the form of the body, and partly to his other teaching in the *Phaedrus* and *Phaedo* that souls were created before bodies. This was adopted by Origen in *On First Principles*, Book I, chapters 7 and 8, and refuted by Lactantius himself in Book III of this work, chapter 18.

It is also refuted by St Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, Book II, heresy 64; the Master of the Sentences, Book II, distinction 18; Alexander of Hales, Second Part, question 62, member 3; St Thomas, *Against the Gentiles*, Book II, chapters 83 and 84; First Part, question 47, article 2; question 90, article 4; question 118, article 3; and St Bonaventure, *Commentary on the Sentences*, Book II, distinction 18, article 2, question 2. Finally, the Council of Vienne and Pope Clement V condemn it as heresy, as we read in the cited Clementine constitution *Fidei*. [Col. 0917B]

The passages of Sacred Scripture and the holy Fathers cited on the other side are to be explained by saying with St Thomas, cited question 75, article 4, reply to the first objection, that because what is principal in a thing seems especially to be that thing, what is considered principal in the human being comes to be called “man.” Thus sometimes, in truth, the intellectual part is called the inner man; and sometimes, in the estimation of those occupied solely with sensible things, the sensitive part together with the body. Still less should the body be called the snare, bond, or prison of the soul, as I shall say below, Book VII, chapter 5.

“Bodies are things lacking human beings.” Thus I read, as in B., T., P., and certain Vatican manuscripts, rather than “things lacking souls,” as is commonly read. For Lactantius plainly held the opinion that the mind and soul of each individual are themselves the human being. [Col. 0917C]

“And they produce minds.” Lucretius: “they bring about minds.”

“To turn into stone, and all to approach the altars, nor to fall prostrate upon the ground,” etc. I have followed the reading of the Aldine, Plantin, and several other editions, which seemed more genuinely Lucretian, since it is given by all manuscripts of Lucretius, although B., T., and P. disagree, having “to turn themselves,” etc., and “and to fall prostrate,” etc.

“For indeed the sole, or at least the greatest, distinction in religion between human beings and dumb animals is.” Elsewhere he states his opinion more clearly: namely, that brute animals possess reason and differ from human beings only by religion, not by reason or speech—below in this same Book, chapter 9; Book III, chapter 10; and *On the Wrath of God*, chapter 7. This opinion is thought to derive from Pythagoras, who, raving in his doctrine of metempsychosis, believed that the souls of human beings and brute animals are the same—he himself surely more irrational than all brute animals.

Virgil mentions this opinion in the *Georgics*:

> Following these signs and examples, some have said  
> That bees possess a share of the divine mind  
> And heavenly draughts, etc.

Plato also held it, as Plutarch writes, *Opinions of the Philosophers*, Book V, chapter 20; and Porphyry followed him in Book III *On Sacrifices*. Plutarch discusses it extensively in *Whether Brute Animals Possess Reason* and *On the Intelligence of Animals*. Galen says at the beginning of his exhortation to the liberal arts: “Whether no reason at all has been given to the class of animals called irrational is certainly doubtful. For though it lacks the reason that operates in speech, which they call discourse, it may perhaps share in that which is conceived in the mind, which they call reasoning, although it has been allotted more sparingly to some and more generously to others,” etc. [Col. 0917D]

Arnobius speaks in the person of a brute animal at the beginning of Book VII: “But they are rational, and utter articulated sounds. And how do they know whether I too do what I do by my own reasoning, and whether this voice which I bring forth is speech of my kind and understood only by us?” etc.

Plato says in the *Statesman* that in the Golden Age not only human beings conversed with human beings, but also with beasts, questioning them and in turn receiving answers from them. Eusebius also records Plato’s opinion, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book XII, chapter 9. What of the fact that Pythagoras and Melampus, Tiresias, Thales, and Apollonius devoted themselves to interpreting the languages of birds? Democritus, indeed, says Pliny, Book XXIX, chapter 4, composes certain compounds from these things so that the speech of birds may be understood.

But such ravings have been ridiculed by wiser pagans, not to speak of our theologians. For what could be more absurd than to suppose that brute animals possess either reason or speech because by natural instinct they perform certain actions in which some appearance of prudence, as Aristotle says, may seem to be present, and because by the same instinct they utter among themselves certain sounds known to one another? What was the point, moreover, of asserting that human beings differ from brute animals only in religion? Just as they were deceived concerning reason, they could be deceived concerning religion. Pliny, Book X, chapter 41, attributes religion even to domestic hens; and the same author has left for posterity in Book VIII, chapter 1, remarkable accounts of the deeds of elephants that appear to manifest religion and piety.

Yet all such things are performed by them:

> Not, surely, because a divinely given intelligence  
> Or greater knowledge of things by fate belongs to them,

as Virgil says; but because, just as art, prudence, and wisdom belong to human beings, so brute animals possess a certain natural power of this sort. Under its guidance bees, spiders, dogs, foxes, elephants, and other animals of that kind which seem more clever perform certain remarkable actions. In them reason indeed shines forth, but not their own reason: it is that of a higher power directing them. [Col. 0918C]

Thus an arrow flies directly toward its mark by motion impressed upon it by one taking aim, as if it itself possessed directing reason. The same is evident in the movements of clocks and other things made by human skill. As artificial things stand in relation to human art, so all natural things stand in relation to divine art. Hence order appears in things moved according to nature, as in things moved according to art, as is said in *Physics*, Book II.

Accordingly, certain forms of cleverness appear in the works of brute animals insofar as they have an inclination toward certain most orderly processes—ordered, that is, by supreme art. Some animals are therefore called prudent or clever, not because they possess reason or choice. This is clear from the fact that all things of one nature act alike, as St Thomas teaches in the First Part of the Second Part, question 13, article 2, reply to the third objection. Lactantius himself says nearly the same below, chapter 5, when disputing against Cicero, who attributes reason to the stars.

See also what the holy doctor discusses in the First Part, question 78, article 4, and in the First Part of the Second Part, question 11, article 2. Aristotle therefore rightly says, at the beginning of the *Metaphysics*, in Books VIII and IX of *History of Animals*, chapter 1 in each case, at the end of Book I *On the Generation of Animals*, and in *Nicomachean Ethics*, Book VI, chapter 7, not that prudence belongs to animals, but that they possess an image of prudence.

Since they lack reason, it was fitting that they should lack speech also, as Aristotle shows, *Politics*, Book I, chapter 2. If some animals trained by art appear to utter certain words, this is not speech properly so called, because they do not understand what they pronounce, but do it from a kind of habituation.

Once these points are known, one is moved to wonder here that Josephus the Jew, *Antiquities*, Book I, chapter 3, thought—as Tostatus asserts, question 429 on Genesis XIII—that the serpent which deceived the first woman was a real and natural serpent, naturally endowed at that time with the capacity of understanding and speaking; and that Basil, in his *Homily on Paradise*, says that all brute animals lived harmoniously together before Adam’s fall, heard one another, and spoke much with understanding. But St Augustine argues to the contrary, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Book XI, chapter 29. [Col. 0919A]

Finally, the Holy Spirit teaches that reason was bestowed on human beings alone: Psalm XXXI, “Like horse and mule,” etc.; Psalm XLIV, “He is compared to the beasts,” etc. Lactantius himself also affirms this in *On the Wrath of God*, chapters 7 and 13, and *On the Workmanship of God*, chapters 2 and 3. Philastrius attributes this heresy—that brute animals share in reason—to the Gnostics and Manichaeans.

## CHAPTER IV

“Who would not be secure under so great a guardian?” This is not a Horatian half-line, as appears to have been thought in the other printed editions, but prose by Lactantius himself, speaking ironically.

That golden vessels should be brought into temples, etc. The heretics draw other such statements from Lactantius concerning gifts and precious offerings made to God, especially for the adornment of churches: below, chap. 7; book V, chap. 8; [Col. 0919B] book VI, chap. 25; and *On the Anger of God*, chap. 21. Yet these things were rightly and repeatedly urged upon pagan ears. For they approved external offerings and gifts in such a way as to foster avarice under the pretext of holiness—as Lactantius here affirms on Persius’s authority; or they offered them to God as though he were needy, as Lactantius himself says in book VI, chap. 2; or, finally, these charges are rightly made against those who give lavishly to God in such a manner that they place their entire hope in external worship and ornament, wholly neglecting inward worship and the offering of the spirit, by which we especially please God. The inward worship of the mind, therefore, must above all be rendered to him; yet outward worship also must not be omitted. For external gifts and offerings are most acceptable to him insofar as—as St Thomas says in the *Second Part of the Second Part*, question 85, article 2—they are signs of an inward offering; for the external acts of religion are ordered toward inward acts.

That the adornment of temples pleases God, everyone may readily understand from Exodus, chap. XXV and following, and from book II of Kings, chap. VI and following, where they will learn how immense a quantity of gold and silver Solomon expended upon the furnishings of that admirable temple, which the Lord adorned with innumerable privileges as most acceptable to himself, as is read in book II of Chronicles, chap. VII. The most ancient Christian custom of adorning churches is also evident from the acts of Constantine the Great in the Ecclesiastical Histories. Thus sacred matters are indeed conducted more fittingly and magnificently, and minds are stirred to an extraordinary degree to glorify God. For we offer nothing to God as though he were needy, since he is Lord of all; rather, as Irenaeus says, book IV, chap. 34, we do so in thanksgiving. “For,” says Justin Martyr in the *Second Apology for the Christians*, “just as we understand that God does not need our offerings, so we know that we need to offer something to him.” Hence Lactantius himself, in *On the Anger of God*, chap. 16, acknowledges that those persuaded that righteousness pleases God worship him with constant prayers, offer him gifts and sacrifices through frequent vows, and finally win his favor by righteous works.

[Col. 0919D] “No,” he says, “twice boys.” You have a similar passage in the same Seneca, *Letters*, book XXI, letter 116, “too anxious”; and on the saying “Old men twice boys,” see the author of the *Adages*.

Dionysius, tyrant of Sicily, etc. Cicero has this at the end of book III of *On the Nature of the Gods*; Valerius Maximus, book I, chapter “On Neglect of Religion”; Aelian, *Various History*, book I; Arnobius, at the end of book VI.

“Let punishments seek them out themselves.” All the printed editions and the Vatican manuscripts read thus. Since this is not at all a customary phrase, I should think it can be sustained only if we understand *Poenae* (“Punishments”) here as certain divine beings—namely Furies and avenging goddesses—as in Plutarch: “. . . as though not a man, but some punishment and abominable daemon had invaded the city.” Manuscript B reads: “Let punishments seek them out.” This would be the genuine reading, in my judgment, if *poenas* had been written there instead of *poenae*. But that was the copyist’s error. Certainly it is probable that Lactantius wrote: “Let them seek punishments upon them,” just as Livy, in the prefatory book, says that “the divine power of the gods, beginning from its very head, would exact punishment upon all the Alban name”; and a little above: “so that all might exact upon him the disasters of this war.”

“Why this so powerful sacrilegious man,” etc. Janus Gulielmus, in his *Questions on Plautus’s Menaechmi*, chap. 4, testifies that certain manuscripts read: “Why this nevertheless powerful man,” etc. Therefore he thinks, by conjecture, that it should be read: “Why this so powerless man,” etc.

“Do you see,” he says, etc. The reading varies in Cicero.

“Of Catania.” It is a city of Sicily, called *Catina* or *Catine*, with the penultimate syllable shortened by Cicero, in the conclusion of the sixth action against Verres, and by Silius in book XIII. Strabo, however, Diodorus, Ptolemy, and Lactantius here write not *Catinum* but *Catanam*, and hence *Catanians*.

## CHAPTER V

“By hollow bronze.” Namely, the sphere of which Cicero writes in the *Tusculan Disputations* and in the second book of *On the Nature of the Gods*, where he writes that a similar sphere was also made by Posidonius. Sextus Empiricus, at the beginning of the eighth book *Against the Mathematicians*, under the heading “Whether There Are Gods”; Claudian, in that celebrated epigram:

> Jupiter in a small [sphere], etc.

“Either of the non-wandering [stars], or of the wandering.” Thus in the best manuscripts B, T, P, in place of what the printed editions corruptly read, “either of the erring, or of the wandering.” For the erring are the same as the wandering; but we call the fixed stars *inerrant*.

## CHAPTER VI

“The propositions are indeed true.” Here *propositio* is taken not for θέσις (*thesis*), but for πρότασις (*protasis*), that is, for the proposition of a syllogism which the Schoolmen call the major premise. Cicero, in the first book of *On Invention*, simply calls it a proposition. Lactantius speaks in his own manner—that is, in Cicero’s manner.

“The assumptions are false.” Cicero and Quintilian call *assumptio* that which the Schoolmen call the minor premise.

## CHAPTER VII

[Col. 0920C] “You have it, Balbus,” etc. This passage varies somewhat in Cicero.

## CHAPTER VIII

“God gave wisdom to all in equal shares.” Jurists generally interpret *virile portions* as equal shares: namely, shares established according to the number of persons and distributed per head, so that there are as many shares as persons. Ulpian, law 1, § *Si pupillis*, Digest, *On Guardianship and the Accounting of Property to Be Sold*; Papinian, law *Pupillus*, Digest, *On Sureties*; Paul, law XLIII, Digest, *On Res Judicata*. Thus, a little below: “if [wisdom] is given equally to all, it cannot be seized first by those who arrive earlier.” Lactantius appears to call wisdom, causally rather than identically, that faculty and light divinely implanted in all people for seeking and attaining heavenly doctrine and true religion. See also book III, chap. 25, 26, and following.

Accius Navius. Authors vary greatly in the name of this augur, as Glareanus notes on the first book of Livy’s first Decade [Col. 0920D]. For Valerius Maximus, book I, chap. 4, calls him Decius Accius Naevius; Pliny, book XXXIV, chap. 5, Accius Navius, as do Lactantius and Livy; Dionysius, however, book III, writes that his personal name was Nevius and his surname Accius. Some write *Naevius* with a diphthong, others *Actius*. But the matter is of no great importance. See all these authors; Pliny the Second in the book *On Illustrious Men*, under Tarquinius, who writes “Accius Navius”; Cicero, book I of *On Divination*, where “Actius Navius” is written; and Festus under *Navia*.

Castor and Pollux in the Latin War, etc. Cicero, book II of *On the Nature of the Gods*; Ovid, at the end of the first book of the *Fasti*; Valerius, book I, chap. 8; Plutarch, *Aemilius*.

The same in the Macedonian War. Valerius, in the same place; likewise Plutarch, who relates the matter somewhat differently, in the same place.

“That the female statue of Fortune spoke more than once,” etc. Valerius, in the same place; Plutarch, *Coriolanus*; Halicarnassus [Dionysius], book VIII; St Augustine, book IV of *The City of God*, chap. 19.

[Col. 0921A] Likewise, that of Juno Moneta, etc. Valerius, in the same place; Livy, the fifth book of the first Decade.

Claudia also, etc. Minucius ridicules the story; Ovid relates it in the fourth book of the *Fasti*; Livy, book IX of the third Decade; Fenestella, chap. 12, *On Roman Priests*; Pliny the Second, *On Illustrious Men*, chap. 46; Herodian, book I.

Aesculapius summoned from Epidaurus, etc. Valerius, in the same place; Plutarch, *Roman Questions*, question 94; Arnobius, book VII, who ridicules the matter.

Appius Claudius the Censor, etc. Valerius, book I, chapter “On Neglect of Religion”; Livy, at the end of book IX of the first Decade.

Of Juno Lacinia, etc. This should be read here from Valerius, in the same place; Livy, book II of the fifth Decade and book IV of the second Decade; Arnobius, book VI, who recount the story. Virgil, at the end of the third *Aeneid*:

> The goddess Lacinia rises up in opposition.

B. Junius wrongly reads *Lucinae*, “of Lucina.”

Turullius, etc. Valerius, in the same place.

Ceres of Miletus also, etc. Valerius, in the same place.

[Col. 0921B] “For Tiberius Attinius,” etc. Livy, book II of the first Decade, calls him Titus Latinius; Valerius simply Latinius, book I, chapter “On Dreams.” But Dionysius, book VII; Plutarch, *Coriolanus*; St Augustine, book IV of *The City of God*, chap. 26, call him Titus Latinius; Macrobius calls him Annius, *Saturnalia*, book I, chap. 11. On the story, besides the authors noted, see Cicero, book I of *On Divination*; Arnobius, book VII; Minucius, in *Octavius*.

“That dream also,” etc. The writers differ somewhat. Some report that Augustus entered battle because of that dream; others that for the same reason he was absent from the battle. Lactantius had Valerius as his source, book I, chapter “On Dreams.” See also Plutarch, at the end of *Brutus*; Suetonius, *Augustus*, chaps. 13 and 91; Appian, at the end of book IV of *The Civil Wars*; likewise Paterculus, Florus, book IV, chap. 6; and Tertullian, *On the Soul*.

## CHAPTER IX

“Let him discern the errors.” After these words, certain printed books contain the following:

> “As a mother without precedent gave birth to her own author, so he must be believed to have begotten, ineffably, one coeternal with himself. He was born of the mother who already existed before; from the father, he who at one time did not exist. Let faith believe this; let understanding not investigate it, lest it deem what is not discovered incredible, or fail to believe what is discovered unique.”

But that Lactantius’s argument begins from the words, “Since God was most provident in devising,” etc., and that the whole passage which I rejected contains nothing whatever of Lactantius’s style, all will immediately and readily understand—unless they are utterly senseless. For even those numerous ὁμοιοτέλευτα (*homoioteleuta*, like-ending phrases), which Lactantius does not employ, betray the forgery and imposture itself. It is clearly an inept addition by some Arian who maintained that the Son of God was a creature and that there had been some time when he did not exist. Yet this most foolish man asserts the same thing, while nevertheless truly declaring him coeternal with the Father. In what follows I shall show not only that Lactantius does not favor the Arians, but that he held so correct a view concerning the Son of God as almost to have expressed for us the confession of the great Council of Nicaea.

Moreover, this entire passage is absent from the most ancient manuscript B, from eight Vatican manuscripts, and from other excellent manuscripts which I carefully examined. After the words, “let him discern the errors,” it immediately reads, “since God was most provident in devising,” etc. Since pious men who detected Arianism in that passage failed to observe this, they considered correcting the passage, I think, rather than utterly deleting it—as ought to have been done—and expelling it from Lactantius’s writings. Consequently, in some copies the passage is amended to read: “From the father, who at no time was absent.” I have removed the whole spurious and interpolated passage.

“Most provident in devising.” The holy Fathers and Holy Scripture itself sometimes speak improperly and μεταφορικῶς (*metaphorically*) in this way, although in God there is no thought, and therefore no prudence; for he does not deliberate or reason after the manner of human beings. Rather, in one single and simple act he understands, knows, and does all things, as St Thomas teaches, *Against the Gentiles*, book I, chap. 57 and following, and *First Part*, question 14, article 7.

“Before he began this work of the world.” After these words, certain printed editions continued as follows:

> “In the beginning he made good and evil. I shall explain more plainly what this means, lest anyone suppose that I speak in the way poets do, who comprehend incorporeal things by certain figures as though they were visible. When besides himself nothing yet existed, since *pleni* . . .”

This entire passage is absent from B and T; from eleven Vatican manuscripts and many other manuscripts; likewise from the Florentine and Plantin editions and the other better editions. Therefore someone maintained that it had been inserted by the Manichaeans. I confidently rejected it as contradicting both the claim that the devil was created by God evil by nature and from the beginning, and Lactantius himself, as we shall shortly see.

“That he might arise as a stream,” etc. The Fathers often use the comparison of a spring and a stream in order somehow to signify the Son’s emanation from the Father, which no tongue can utter and no understanding comprehend—as Lactantius does here. They also use that of the sun and its ray, as Tertullian does in the same chapter, chap. 29 *Against Praxeas* and chap. 21 of the *Apology*; and Cyprian, or Rufinus, in the exposition of the Apostles’ Creed. Thus Paul, Hebrews 1, calls him ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ, “the radiance of his glory.” This does not diminish in any respect the Son’s equality with the Father; but because, as theologians teach, God the Father is the source and principle of divinity, and is said to possess the fullness of Deity in the first sign of origin, since he has it of himself; whereas the Son possesses it in the second sign, because by generation he receives from the Father the same numerically identical essence communicated to him. Hence nothing is diminished from their equality.

“Like himself.” In likeness of nature. For the procession of the Word in the Godhead has the character of generation because it proceeds by way of an intelligible action, which is an operation of life, from a conjoined principle, and according to a likeness—not merely any likeness, but likeness in nature. For the conception of the intellect is a likeness of the thing understood, existing in the same nature, since in God understanding and being are one. Therefore the procession of the Word in the Godhead is most truly and properly called generation, and the Word himself most truly and properly Son, as St Thomas teaches, *First Part*, question 27, article 2. I have said more on this subject in my notes on book IV, chap. 8.

“Spirit.” Because Lactantius perhaps calls the Son of God “the Spirit of God” here and in book IV, chaps. 6, 8, 9, 18, and elsewhere, St Jerome charges him with error in the letter to Pammachius and Oceanus, *On the Errors of Origen*, as though he had not held a correct view of the person of the Holy Spirit. Yet—with due respect to so great a Father—this expression is not absurd, nor was it used by Lactantius alone; Tertullian, Cyprian, and others also used it, calling the Son of God the Spirit of God, in the sense in which God is called Spirit in John III and 1 John, chap. IV, as St Thomas notes, *First Part*, question 36, article 1. Thus Tertullian must be understood in *Apology*, chap. 21; *On Prayer*, chap. 1; *Against Marcion*, book I, chap. 19, book III, chaps. 6 and 16, book IV, chap. 21; *Against Praxeas*, chap. 26. So too Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, section 71, according to one reading there noted by Pamelius; and the author of *On Mounts Sinai and Zion*, among Cyprian’s works.

[Col. 0922D] “But how he intended this, we shall endeavor to teach in the fourth book.” Thus read twelve Vatican manuscripts and two codices of San Salvatore at Bologna, T, P, the Plantin and Florentine editions, and other better manuscripts and printed editions, instead of the faulty Aldine reading: “But how he made this, when he was alone, we shall teach in the fourth [book],” etc. For the Son of God was not made but eternally begotten of the Father, who therefore never existed alone, as I said in book I, chap. 7.

“Then he made another,” etc. He speaks of the highest angel, whom he says was created before this world; for a little above he had said, “before he began this work of the world.” Lactantius, however, says nothing here concerning the creation of the other angels. Three opinions are found regarding the time of their creation. Gennadius and Acacius thought that angels were created after the corporeal world; this opinion indeed has no weight. Others think that angels were created many ages before this world: Origen, at the beginning of book I of *On First Principles* and in the fourth homily on Isaiah; Gregory Nazianzen, homily on the Nativity of the Lord, cited by St Thomas, *First Part*, question 61, article 3; Basil, Homily I on the *Hexaemeron*; John Damascene, book II of *On the Orthodox Faith*, chap. 3; and many other Greeks. Among Latin writers also, Hilary, book XII of *On the Trinity* and *Against Auxentius*; Ambrose, book I of the *Hexaemeron*, chap. 5, and preface to Psalm I; Isidore, book I, *On the Highest Good*; Jerome, on chap. I of the Epistle to Titus; Cassian, who in *Conferences*, book 8, chap. 7, writes that no believer can doubt this matter; and Bede, *Book of Separate Questions*, question 9.

Certain learned men of the school of St Thomas have asserted that this opinion today entails error in faith: namely, Ferrariensis in his commentary on the *Summa Against the Gentiles*, book II, chap. 83; Master Cano; and Soto Major. Others, however—such as Cajetan, *First Part*, question 61, article 3; Sixtus of Siena, book V of the *Bibliotheca*, annotation 5; and St Thomas himself in the same article—deny that it is an error in faith, since it has been approved by so many and such great Fathers, especially Gregory Nazianzen, against whose writings, as St Thomas says there, no one has ever dared bring a charge. St Augustine also, book II of *The City of God*, chap. 32, says that one who says angels were created before this visible world asserts nothing contrary to faith, provided that he does not say they were created from eternity; and Theodoret says nearly the same in question 3 on Genesis.

We, following what we judge the truer opinion, hold that not only the highest angel—which Lactantius here denies—but also all the other angels, who were all created together with the highest angel—which Lactantius omits, and Bede denies in *Separate Questions*, question 9—were created together with this world. This is taught by Bonaventure, book II, distinction 2, article 2, question 3, and distinction 2, article 4, question 1, and by others: Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, book II, heresy 65; Theodoret, the said question 3; St Augustine, book II of *The City of God*, book XII of the *Confessions*, book IV *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*; Gregory the Great, book XXXII of the *Morals*, chaps. 20, 24, and 25; Bede, Rupert, Hugh, the Master of the Sentences, and all theologians on book II, distinction 2; St Thomas, *First Part*, question 61, article 3. We judge the contrary opinion, if it does not contain an error in faith, nevertheless certainly to be rash in the present age, insufficiently consonant with the Church’s teaching and the testimonies of Holy Scripture; and the Lateran Council, reported in the chapter *Firmiter*, “On the Supreme Trinity and the Catholic Faith,” appears to oppose it.

“Offspring of the divine stock,” etc. This is not because the first angel of whom he speaks was Son of God by nature; rather, these words must be understood improperly and abusively, just as when we call God the Father of angels or human beings, and angels or human beings sons of God, as I said above, book I, chap. 7, note.

“By his own envy.” Lactantius says that the sin of the highest angel was the sin of envy, which must be understood not as the first sin, but as consequential; for his first sin was the sin of pride. Basil, homily *That God Is Not the Author of Evil*; Chrysostom, homily on Adam; Ambrose on Psalm XXXVI, “I saw the wicked,” and Psalm CXVIII, “You rebuked the proud”; St Augustine, book XII of *The City of God*, chap. 16, and book XIV, chap. 13; Jerome on Isaiah, chap. 14; Gregory, book XXXIV of the *Morals*, chap. 14; Anselm, *On the Fall of the Devil*, chap. 4; all the Doctors on book II of the *Sentences*, distinctions 5 and 6; Alexander of Hales, part II, question 109, member 2; St Thomas, *First Part*, question 63, articles 2 and 3. This assertion is so supported by the testimonies of all the other saints and theologians that some have called the contrary view not merely very rash but erroneous.

He is said to have sinned consequentially by envy, since, having coveted a certain singular excellence, and since that singularity ceases through another’s excellence, the sin of envy immediately followed the sin of pride. St Thomas, book II, distinction 5, article 2, and *First Part*, question 63, article 2.

“And he passed from good to evil.” Thus a little below: “Therefore this one, made evil in himself out of good,” etc. This is directed against the Manichaeans and Priscillianists, who maintain that the devil was created evil by nature from the beginning.

[Col. 0924A] “For he envied that predecessor of his,” etc. I said that the devil’s sin was not first, but consequentially, envy. Theologians therefore ask in relation to whom he was moved by that envy. Lactantius appears to have thought that the devil’s envy rose up against one of the divine persons, namely against the Son of God. St Thomas, *First Part*, question 63, article 2, says that after the sin of pride the sin of envy followed in the sinning angel, insofar as he grieved at the good of humankind, and also at divine excellence, insofar as God, against the devil’s own will, would make use of this for divine glory. For the angel knew by faith the mystery of the Incarnation from the beginning of his creation as to the substance of the mystery itself, though not as to its particular rationales and certain circumstances, as St Thomas teaches in book II, distinction 11, article 3. On this question see the Doctors in their commentaries, and the Master, book II, distinction 5; St Thomas, question 63, article 2; Alexander of Hales, part II, question 109, member 9; William of Paris, book II *On the Universe*; Cassian, *Conference* 8, chap. 8 and following.

[Col. 0924B] “By persevering with God the Father, he is both approved and beloved.” “By persevering, he is approved”: I would by no means approve this. For the word *persevering*, in its formal meaning, appears to imply a continuation of action together with a certain possibility of failing. Thus Lactantius has used words that cannot be fittingly applied to God’s only-begotten Son; for since he is God, one with the Father, and in every respect coequal and consubstantial with him according to divinity—as Lactantius himself everywhere acknowledges—he is certainly good by nature and cannot fail from goodness.

“The Greeks call [him] διάβολος (*diabolos*), we [call him] accuser,” etc. On the meaning of this name, and why the enemy of humankind is so called, see Tertullian, *Against Marcion*; Basil, letter to the Neocaesareans; Suidas under Σατάν (*Satan*) and under Συκοφαντεῖν (*to slander*); and Isidore, book VIII of the *Origins*, chap. 11.

“Let him carry [the accusation] to God.” After these words, the Aldine editions immediately append the following speech, though marked and enclosed with asterisks, so that its suspect character is readily apparent:

> “But why the just God wished him to be such, I shall endeavor to explain as far as the limited measure of our understanding permits. God, about to fashion this world, which would consist of things mutually contrary and discordant, first established diversity and before all things made two sources of mutually opposing and contending things: namely, those two spirits, the upright and the perverse, one of whom stands to God as his right hand, the other as his left; so that those contrary things might be in their power, by whose mixture and tempering the world and all things within it would subsist.
>
> “Likewise, when he was about to make man, to whom he would set before him virtue for living, through which he might attain immortality, he made good and evil, so that virtue might exist; for unless it is stirred by evils, it either loses its force or does not exist at all. For poverty’s bitter hardship makes wealth seem good, and the darkness of shadows commends the pleasantness of light; the pleasure of health and soundness is known through sickness and pain. Thus good cannot exist in this life without evil. Although both are contrary, they are so joined that if you remove one, you remove both; for neither can good be understood and perceived without turning away from and fleeing evil, nor can evil be avoided and conquered without the aid of good understood and perceived. Evil therefore had necessarily to be made in order that good might be made.
>
> “And since it was not lawful for evil to proceed from God—for he will not act against himself—he established that inventor of evils. When he made him, he gave him ingenuity and cunning for devising evils, so that in him there might be a perverse will and perfect wickedness; and he willed that things contrary to his virtues should arise from him and contend with him, whether God himself would bestow more goods or that other more evils. But again, since the supreme God cannot be resisted, he assigned authority over his goods to that victor whom we said above was good and perfect. Thus he matched and equipped two for the contest; but he loved one as a good son and repudiated the other as evil.
>
> “Afterward he begot many others, ministers of his works, whom the Greeks call ἄγγελοι (*angeloi*, ‘angels’); and they were of the one, but opposing, nature possessed by the two. Yet that corruptible part was certainly not corrupted immediately at the beginning of its origin; rather, after the world had been put together and ordered—as we shall soon teach—it defected from the vigor of heavenly substance through a perverse will. But in the beginning all were equal before God in equal condition, and therefore all were angels, whose leaders were those two. When, however, God had set one of these two over good and the other over evil, he began the construction of the world, all those whom he had created ministering, each assigned to definite duties.”

This discourse contains many errors. First, the doctrine of two principles, of which I speak below in chap. 10, is asserted here more clearly and explicitly than anywhere else in Lactantius. Next, it speaks insufficiently exaltedly and fittingly of the Son of God, making Lucifer almost his equal; hence it plainly appears that the whole was fabricated by some Arian. It says that the other angels were created not with Lucifer but after him, whereas above I noted that St Bonaventure and other Doctors teach the contrary in book II, distinction 2. It also says that all angels were begotten before this world, not together with it; I have said that the Lateran Council and all Doctors today teach the contrary. It further says that the evil angels sinned not immediately at the beginning of their origin but much later, namely after the world had already been put together and ordered; concerning this error, see below, chap. 15. Finally, it says that angels cooperated with God instrumentally or ministerially in the construction of the world, a proposition rejected by all Doctors on the first chapter of Genesis. Most people strongly suspect that this is not Lactantius’s discourse; and I certainly do not recognize Lactantius’s manner of expression here. The Aldine edition does contain it, but, as I have said, marks it with asterisks. It was not received in the Florentine, Plantin, and other better corrected editions; Michael Thomasius gives his reasons in his notes. Finally, it is absent from twelve Vatican manuscripts, the most ancient Bologna manuscript, T, P, and many other manuscripts. Therefore I too judged that it should by no means be admitted into our text.

[Col. 0925C] “That first and greatest Son.” Take care not to think that Lactantius considers angels to be sons of God by nature, thus either raising them to God’s nature or bringing down the Son of God to angelic nature. Lactantius both knew and taught that Jesus alone is Son of God, as below in this book, chap. 17, and in book IV, chap. 8. In that same book IV, chaps. 8 and 18, he confesses him to be God from God. “What,” he says, “shall we say of the indignity of this cross, upon which God was suspended and fastened by worshippers of God?” He says the same in book IV, chaps. 10, 13, 14, and 29. Likewise, concerning light from light, in the same chap. 29: “He,” he says, “is as the sun, this one as a ray stretched forth from the sun.” In the same chapter he calls him consubstantial with the Father: “Both,” he says, “have one substance and the same power.” In book IV, chap. 17: “He alone,” he says, “has with the Son power over all things”; and he calls him one with the Father throughout that chapter. In chap. 8 of the same book IV, he cites and confesses John’s statement: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” In this the Son’s divinity and coeternity are explicitly asserted. Finally, he affirms both here and in book IV, chap. 6, at the beginning and end, and chap. 8 at the end, that all things were made through him.

Do you not therefore recognize here the confession of the most sacred Council of Nicaea convened against Arius? Arius is thus pierced by Lactantius rather than receiving from him even the slightest support, as some rashly suspect because Lactantius occasionally uses certain expressions that Catholics would not today be permitted to use, which I have carefully noted in their appropriate places above and shall note below. It should indeed have been remembered that in that age of the nascent or growing Church it had not yet been determined which expressions writers ought to use and which to avoid. Later, when heresies became frequent, it became necessary to establish and decree this, lest we agree in any way, even in expressions, with heretics who had abused them to insinuate their impious doctrines.

[Col. 0926A] Since, therefore, we hold Lactantius’s wholly correct judgment concerning the Son of God, no sound person can suspect that he considers angels gods, he who throughout this whole work has overthrown the plurality of gods with such great weight of arguments. In chap. 17 of this book he says that there are many spirits of angels in heaven, but that there is one parent of them and Lord of all, God; and a little below in the same chapter: “Nor do angels permit or wish themselves to be called gods; their sole and only office is to serve the commands of God and do absolutely nothing except at his command.” Further below in the same chapter: “There is nothing in angels but the necessity of obedience.” He further affirms, book VII, chap. 21, that angels fear God, since they can in some ineffable manner be punished by him. Thus it is clear from Lactantius himself that angelic nature differs infinitely from the nature of the Son of God.

Accordingly, if he ever calls angels “sons of God,” he uses the term *sonship* equivocally and μεταφορικῶς (*metaphorically*). For Scripture itself sometimes does not refrain from such language, as at the beginning of Job: “When on a certain day the sons of God came”; and chap. XXXVIII: “And all the gods rejoiced.” Thus each passage is read in Jerome’s version according to the Hebrew truth. Hence Chrysostom is shown to have erred: following the edition of the Seventy in both places, which translates “angels of God” for “sons of God,” he asserted in Homily 22 on Genesis that angels are never called sons of God in Holy Scripture, indeed not even sons. Nor is this opposed by Paul’s writing at the beginning of Hebrews: “To which of the angels did he ever say, ‘You are my Son’?” For there the Apostle does not deny that angels are sometimes called sons of God by grace, but only by nature, in which sense Christ alone is truly called and is the Son of God. Thus we noted above, on chap. 7 at the beginning of the book, that the term *generation* too is sometimes improperly used by the Fathers and Holy Scripture. Therefore, when Lactantius here and in book IV, chap. 6, appears to regard angels as sons of God, he must be understood to use that name not univocally but equivocally in relation to the Word, that is, the only-begotten Son of God.

[Col. 0926C] “And he used him at once as counsellor and craftsman.” From Proverbs VIII, which passage he cites in book IV, chap. 6, and Ecclesiasticus XXIV, which passage he mentions in book IV, chap. 8, at the end, where Scripture speaks of Wisdom and the Word of God cooperating with God the Father in the creation of the world.

“Poets are not to be heard,” etc. A lengthy argument is undertaken here against those who asserted that God did nothing in creating the world except separate, arrange, and order the things themselves from eternal, uncreated matter which was nevertheless rough, unformed, and confused. Among heretics, a certain Hermogenes held and spread this error; Tertullian wrote against him. Lactantius maintains that even prime matter was created by God from nothing, and that afterward God himself arranged and ordered the world from it. At the end of this chapter he also says that humankind was made last, when the final hand had already been laid upon the world and the other things; he teaches the same in book VII, chap. 14.

From these passages it appears that Lactantius held, as the greater part of the holy Fathers and theologians held, that prime matter was created before every day, both in the order of nature and in the order of time or duration: not altogether formless—that is, lacking every form whatsoever—but lacking that completing and distinguishing form which the Lord afterward gave it through intervals of six natural, proper, successive days, precisely in the manner transmitted by Moses in the book of Genesis. Thus Dionysius wrote, book IV of *The Divine Names*; St Basil, Ambrose, and Bede, in their *Hexaemerons*; Chrysostom on John; Gregory the Great, book XXXIII of the *Morals*, chap. 10; Rupert, book I *On the Works of the Trinity*, chap. 37, and book II, chap. 18; Hugh of St Victor, first book *On the Sacraments*; the Master [of the Sentences], book II, distinction 12; Alexander of Hales, part II, question 47; St Bonaventure, book II, distinction 12, article 1, question 2; Scotus, book II, distinction 14, question 1; St Thomas, *First Part*, question 66, articles 1 and 4, and *Questions on Power*, article 2.

Although very weighty and holy men also held the contrary: namely, that matter was created in perfect actuality, and that its formlessness preceded its formation not in time but in nature; and consequently that the world was created in one instant of time, not through intervals of six days; and that the days enumerated by Moses were not real days but were to be understood metaphorically and referred to the knowledge of created things instilled by God in angelic minds: Philo the Jew in the book of *Allegories*; Origen, book IV of the *Periarchon*, chap. 2; St Augustine, book IV of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chap. 21 and following; Procopius of Gaza; and Cajetan on Genesis.

As for this argument undertaken by Lactantius against those who posit the eternity of matter and assert that it is coeval with God, see Tertullian, *Against Hermogenes*; John the Grammarian, in the book against Proclus *On the Eternity of the World*; Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book X, chap. 8; Gregory of Nyssa, *On the Making of Man*, chap. 25, and the book *History of the Six Days*.

“The first, therefore, is not probable,” etc. This passage is thought to have fallen out of book III of *On the Nature of the Gods*.

[Col. 0927B] “To die.” Thus read from B, T, P, the Florentine edition, and others, not “custom,” as in the Aldine edition. For it was Cicero who argued in the manner of the Academics, and Lactantius said that “to die” must be conceded to him; Sigonius also reports the passage thus in his fragments.

“Always.” I added this word, which is absent from some copies, from B, because the argument here concerned the eternity of matter.

Seneca, the most acute of all the Stoics. Lactantius is lavish in his praise of Seneca in many places—and rightly and most deservedly so; for, with a few things in his doctrine either removed or added, you have an excellent Christian. And, as Lactantius says in Book VI, chapter 24, he might have been a true worshipper of God if he had found a guide to true wisdom. Francesco Petrarch, in his letter addressed to Seneca himself, among the letters to distinguished men of antiquity, and at the end of the *Apology against the Gauls*, reports that Plutarch wrote that, although he had compared the Romans with Greek men in every other virtue and discipline, he had no Greek whom he could set against Seneca as an equal in moral precepts. [Col. 0927C]

“Therefore,” he says, “shall we not praise God,” etc. You have similar passages in Seneca himself, Book IV of *On Benefits*, chapter 7, and in Pliny, Book II, chapter 7, and Book XXVII, at the beginning of chapter 3.

“You stick fast in the same mud; you pay off one loan by another.” In Terence: “You stick fast; you pay off one loan by another.” Those are said to stick fast in the same mud, as the author of the *Adages* explains, who become so entangled in some business that they cannot extricate themselves: the expression is transferred from travellers who, as soon as they have fallen into mud, when they try to pull out one foot, sink the other more deeply. Then, in order to draw this one out, the other, which they had withdrawn, must again be planted in the mud. “To pay off one loan by another,” moreover, is said, as Budé explains on law *vit.* D. *On the Action concerning Pledged Property*, of those who, to discharge one written obligation and free themselves from one security, borrow money at higher interest. Thus Lactantius says that this happens to those who attribute the origin of things to nature and take it away from God; for they deny that the world was made by Him by whom, under a changed name only, they plainly acknowledge it to have been made—since in reality nature is nothing other than God. So too below, Book III, chapter 28.

“Before the sun had been established.” Thomasius reads, as in B., “before the soil had been established,” which seems to fit better with what follows concerning crops and animals, which dwell upon the soil. I have retained the reading received in all the other manuscripts and printed editions. Besides, Lactantius had already spoken of the soil, or earth; and anyone who examines the text will see that Thomasius’s reason carries no weight.

“Thus it was necessary for man to be made last.” See other most beautiful reasons in Gregory, *On the Making of Man*, chapter 2.

## CHAPTER X

“He distinguished his own dwelling with bright lights,” etc. In this passage Firmianus is charged with error, as though he had established God’s seat and the dwelling-place of the blessed in the starry heaven, and had placed the sun and moon in it.
