Here, however, I think that by “heaven” he understands the whole mass of the heavens, insofar as it embraces all that is above fire, upward as far as, and including, the empyrean heaven itself. He says that this mass of heavens was adorned with sun, moon, and glittering stars—namely, with lights assigned to each heaven; and I believe this may be clearly gathered from his own words, where he says: “God therefore first of all made heaven, and suspended it on high, that it might be the seat of the Creator himself,” etc. Yet he placed on high not only the starry heaven, but the whole mass of the heavens. He adds: “Then he founded the earth and placed it beneath heaven,” etc. And in Book VII, chapter 5, as though explaining this passage, he says: “He therefore placed the lights in heaven, but the earth,” etc. Is the earth, then, placed beneath one starry heaven alone? Thus “heaven” is taken by him in both places and distinguished from the elements which he mentions; and it means, as I said, the whole mass of the heavens, insofar as it includes even the outermost empyrean.

[Col. 0928B] “From these, the east is assigned to God,” etc. Thus B., T., P., and the other better manuscripts read, not, as in the printed editions, “from these, the east is judged similar to God.” *Accenseri* means the same as “to be attributed”; hence soldiers were called *accensi*, as though *accensiti*, because they were assigned to decurions and centurions—that is, attributed to them—as Varro wrote in Book XX of his *Rhetoric* and Book III *On the Life of the Roman People*, and Nonius Marcellus, chapter 12. Lactantius affirms that the east, light, life, and day are attributed to God; but the west, darkness, death, and night to the devil. Below, chapter 13, he says that the soul belongs to God and the body to the devil; and in chapter 18, that heaven and light belong to God, while darkness, the underworld, and punishments were assigned, in the ordering of things, to the prince of evils. In Book VI, chapter 3, he establishes two leaders: one presiding over virtues and goods, the other over vices and evils; and in chapter 6 of the same book he says that God is the fountain of goods, while the enemy of the divine name is the fountain of evils: from these two principles goods and evils arise. From all these passages we must beware, because the author seems in some measure to have favoured the condemned doctrine of Cerdon and Marcion in those times, concerning two principles, one of good things and the other of evil things—a doctrine later embraced by Mani. Yet Lactantius seems to differ from them in this: he asserts that the devil is not without a principle and is not evil by nature; rather, he says that the devil was created good by God, but passed into evil by his own choice, since free will had been given him; and thus, as stated above near the beginning of chapter 9, he became the prince of all evils. But those men posited two principles without principle: one good by nature, the other evil by nature, as St Augustine writes in *On Heresies*, heresies 21 and 22; Philostratus on Cerdon and Apelles; and Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, heresy 66. St Thomas refutes this heresy in Book II *Against the Gentiles*, chapter 41.

“Cicero thinks that the sun appears to have been so called.” So too Varro, Book IV *On the Latin Language*, chapter 10; Isidore, *Origins*, Book III, chapter 70.

“Because they are not full and solid lights.” As though they were in some manner lights by their own nature, and Lactantius therefore thought that the stars shine by their own proper light. All those philosophers, and those Fathers, must be thought to have held this opinion who taught that the luminaries and stars were made as vehicles of the primordial light: Basil, Ambrose, and Nazianzen; much more those who say that the primordial light was distributed by God into the luminaries—that is, into the sun, moon, and stars—as Apollinarius and Didymus in Lipomano’s *Catena*, Athanasius, Questions 83 and 85, Theodoret, Questions 14 and 16 on Genesis, Procopius in the first chapter on Genesis, and Damascene, Book II of *The Orthodox Faith*, chapter 7. Avicenna and Macrobius are said to have held the same view, the latter excepting the moon alone in chapters 19 and 20 of the *Dream of Scipio*. But Plato in the *Timaeus*, Pliny, Book II, chapter 6, and most astronomers assert the contrary. Hugh of St Victor, in his annotations on Genesis, chapter 6, says that the sun alone has its own light and is made from fire, while all the other stars, made of aerial matter, reflect light rather than shine. St Augustine, *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Book II, chapter 16, says that Holy Scripture makes it plainly known that the brightness of the stars is unequal, since the Apostle says in chapter V of the First Epistle to the Corinthians that there is one brightness of the sun, another of the moon, and another of the stars, and that star differs from star in brightness; but whether the stars receive their light from the sun or not cannot be gathered or determined from Sacred Scripture. [Col. 0929A]

“That the world consists by discordant harmony,” etc. He indicates the opinion of Empedocles, who said that all things consist of strife and friendship—namely, of the elements; Aristotle discusses this in Book I of the *Physics*, Book I *On the Soul*, and Book I *On Divination*.

“That the bonds of marriage may be ratified by the sacrament of fire and water.” As is clear from the law *Seia Sempronio*, D. *On Gifts between Husband and Wife*, explained from Festus under *Aqua*; Budé on the said law; and Cyriacus, *Observations*, Book II, chapter 2.

“The material of the body is in moisture.” Especially so, perhaps, because both semen and blood are fluids; otherwise the body of an animal, like all other things, consists of the four elements, as Lactantius himself explains, following Empedocles, below in chapter 13.

“The material of the soul is in heat.” This was Democritus’s opinion, which Aristotle refutes at the beginning of *On the Soul*. Nor indeed do I see how Lactantius can here assert that the soul’s material is fiery or heat, when he certainly knows that the human soul is immortal, as he himself shows in Book III, chapters 12, 13, and 17, of *On the Workmanship of God*. Below, in chapter 13, he expressly writes that the soul is fire—contradicting himself, since he denied this in the said chapter 17 of *On the Workmanship*, and elsewhere writes that the soul is from God’s substance, as below in chapter 13, where we shall discuss it.

“Neither can moisture be embodied, nor body enlivened.” The printed editions read: “Neither can moisture embody, nor body enliven.” Our reading is exhibited by the Vatican manuscripts, two codices of San Salvatore at Bologna, T., and P. “Neither can moisture,” he says, “be embodied,” that is, be condensed into that body; “nor can the body itself be enlivened,” not “enliven,” because body does not enliven but is enlivened. Thus Budé too correctly cites this passage in his annotations on Book II, D. *On Penalties*. [Col. 0929C]

“Fire and water also used to be forbidden to exiles.” On interdiction from fire and water: Ulpian, Book II, D. *On Penalties*, and Budé there in the annotations on the *Pandects*; Festus under *aqua*; Isidore, *Origins*, Book V, chapter 27, at the end.

“It is motionless and tends downward,” etc. Thomasius rightly corrected from the B. manuscript the reading of the printed editions, which has “it is mobile,” etc. For an antithesis is manifestly required here; and indeed he had spoken of fire, whose nature, because it is mobile and strives upward, contains the principle of life. He therefore rightly added concerning water: its nature, because it is motionless and tends downward, displays the image of death. It could not display the image of death if it were mobile, because, as Lactantius himself says in Book VI, chapter 17, and Book *On the Wrath of God*, chapter 17, life is active and death is still. Its nature, therefore, is motionless and quiet; for it approaches the heaviness of earth. It moves with difficulty, and only downward, unless it is stirred by blasts of wind or motion is imparted to it externally in some other way.

“Therefore cattle do not look up to heaven.” Galen, Book III *On the Usefulness of the Parts*, chapter 3, says that this was said by men who had never seen the fish called *ouranoskopos* (οὐρανοσκόπος), that is, “heaven-observer”; for this fish, even against its will, always looks at heaven. Yet it truly contemplates nothing whatever there, as man does.

## CHAPTER XI

“That they might assist in cultivating the earth, whence they are called *iumenta* [beasts of burden].” So too Columella, Book V, and Isidore, *Origins*, Book XII, chapter 1, and Book XV, chapter 17. But Nonius, chapter 1, the jurist Pomponius in the law *Boves*, D. *On the Meaning of Words*, and other ancients, as Gellius testifies, Book XX, chapter 1, prefer to derive the word not from *iuvare*, “to help,” but from *iungere*, “to yoke.”

“And to bring forth innumerable souls,” etc. So below, chapter 14: “He resolved to destroy the human race by a flood, yet did not immediately send the flood.” The sense is that God decreed and determined in his eternal predestination that, as time proceeded and while the world endured, innumerable souls should be brought forth for human bodies when formed, and infused into those bodies in their creation. This is the Catholic opinion and consonant with Lactantius, who says in chapter 19 of *On the Workmanship of God*: “All the rest belongs to God: namely, conception itself, the formation of the body, the breathing-in of the soul, and safe delivery,” etc. From this you may readily understand that, after the body’s formation, the infusion of the soul is performed by God. Lactantius mocks and refutes, in Book III, chapter 18, the fiction of souls created before bodies, which some rashly attribute to him from this passage. [Col. 0930A]

“Whence man is called *homo*, because he was made from *humus* [earth].” So too at the end of chapter 10 of *On the Wrath of God*. Here “man” means the human body. Quintilian, Book I, chapter 6, does not approve this etymology; Isidore, *Origins*, Book II, chapter 1, does. See Rhodiginus, *Ancient Readings*, Book I, chapter 41.

[Col. 0930B] *Theoeidē* (Θεοειδῆ), “godlike.” I have corrected the corrupt reading found in all copies, *theoeidēn* (θεοειδὴν). Plato, *Republic*, Book VI: “Inferring from that which Homer also called among men godlike and God-resembling” (*ap’ ekeinou tekmairomenoi, ho dē kai Homēros ekalesen en tois anthrōpois theoeides te kai theoeikelon*; ἀπ’ ἐκείνου τεκμαιρόμενοι, ὃ δὴ καὶ Ὅμηρος ἐκάλεσεν ἐν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις θεοειδές τε, καὶ θεοείκελον).

“Earth-born offspring,” etc. Editions which read “iron-born” in Virgil ought, Turnebus warned, to be corrected on this basis: *Adversaria*, Book XXI, chapter 22; Rhodiginus, *Ancient Readings*, Book IV, chapter 19; Pierio Valeriano, *Hieroglyphics*, Book LVII, chapter on papyrus. Yet those who think Lactantius’s text corrupt, as Pierius himself reports in his Virgilian corrections on that passage of Virgil, are not seriously mistaken either, since Lactantius here says that animals arose from the earth without any craftsman; hence he cites “earth-born offspring.” The word “iron-born” has no bearing whatsoever upon his argument.

“The substance of the present.” Yet there have been those who doubted whether present time exists; Aristotle discusses this in Book IV of the *Physics*, text 87 and following; St Augustine, *Confessions*, Book II, chapter 14 and following. See also Censorinus, *On the Birthday*.

“Without favour.” Thus B., T. of Florence, and also the Plantin edition in the margin. It is an adverb, meaning “apart from favour and merit.” “Not willingly,” Donatus says, “but under compulsion”; another reading: “ungratefully.”

## CHAPTER XII

“They say that through certain revolutions,” etc. He explains and refutes the account of the first origin of living creatures advanced by Anaximander and Democritus, as Lactantius himself relates below, Book VII, chapter 7, and by several other ancient philosophers. Lucretius discusses it in Book V, Cicero in Book I *On the Laws*, and Diodorus, Book I, chapter 1, at the beginning; there Diodorus also adds something from Euripides’ *Menalippe*—Euripides being a pupil of Anaxagoras—by which he judges that Euripides held the same view. Lactantius likewise ridicules this opinion—which asserts that men first sprang from the earth like mushrooms, and then poured forth like certain little worms—in Book VII, chapters 4 and 7. Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, chapter 3, reports various opinions on the primeval generation of animals.

[Col. 0930D] “They say.” Namely, some men, among them Lucretius in Book V, in these verses:

> But the newness of the world produced neither harsh cold  
> Nor excessive heats, etc.

“From the highest God.” The manuscripts of Cicero read, “from the supreme God.”

“He himself mingled” (*autos emixe*, Αὐτὸς ἔμιξε). The Sibylline manuscript has “he mingled rays” (*augas mixe*, αὐγὰς μῖξε).

## CHAPTER XIII

“He breathed into him a soul from the life-giving fountain of his own spirit,” etc. Below in this chapter: “whose souls do not consist of God, but of the common air,” etc. Again: “that which is from heaven and rules over God,” etc. And Book VII, chapter 12: “That which consists of heavenly spirit,” etc.; and a little later in the same place: “Since it is from God’s spirit, which is eternal,” etc. From these passages Lactantius seems to think that the human soul is from God’s substance. Yet why say “seems to think”? What precisely he thinks on this matter, I certainly cannot grasp. Above, at the end of chapter 10, he said that the soul is something fiery, namely heat; and below in this same chapter he says it is fire. Aristotle ridicules this position in Book II *On the Parts of Animals*, chapter 7: “For if,” Lactantius says, “the soul is fire, as we have shown, it must strive upward into heaven, like fire,” etc. But whatever he may have thought elsewhere, in the passages noted above he does seem to judge the soul to be from God’s substance. This opinion flowed from the school of the Platonists; following it, Marcus Tullius often says that human minds are portions, draughts, or fragments drawn from the divine nature. Philo too seems ensnared by this error in the book *That the Worse is Accustomed to Attack the Better*, as does Tertullian, concerning whom Gennadius says in *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*: “Let us believe that nothing from the essence of the Trinity has been transferred into created nature, as Plato and Tertullian [held],” etc. Likewise, according to Theodoret, the heretics Cerdon, Marcion, the Gnostics, and the Manichaeans were misled by their erroneous understanding of Genesis 2: “He breathed into his face the breath of life.” Because breath appears to be drawn forth from the body of one breathing, they believed that the soul had been breathed into man from God’s substance. [Col. 0931B]

But that passage in Genesis gives no support to the error. For a human being, from whom they claim the analogy is taken, does not emit breath from his own substance but from inhaled air, which is not from the substance of the body, much less of the soul. Further, the soul cannot produce breath except from the body, since it is not creative. But God, being of infinite power, can create the soul from nothing; and he is thus said to have breathed insofar as he created human breath. So the Master and all doctors teach, especially St Thomas in Book II, distinction 17. That divine breathing was not bodily, just as his speech was not bodily when he said, “Let there be light; let there be a firmament,” etc. Theodoret says: “By the name of breath we do not understand some part of the divine essence, according to the madness of Cerdon and Marcion; rather, by it is denoted the nature of the soul, because the soul is a rational and intellectual spirit.” This heresy was condemned in the First Council of Toledo, in its profession of faith; by Leo I, Epistle 91; and in the First Council of Braga, chapter 5. Against it argue Irenaeus, Book I *Against Heresies*, chapter 24; the whole school of theologians in the said distinction 17; and St Thomas, Book II *Against the Gentiles*, chapter 85, and *Prima Pars*, question 90, article 1.

“Empedocles, whom you would not know whether to count among poets,” etc. Aristotle indeed writes in the *Poetics* that he should be considered among philosophers rather than poets; and Plutarch, *On Listening to Poets*, says that his poems should be called discourses rather than poetry.

“Second.” The printers’ error has been corrected; in other editions they had printed “second” (feminine).

“For it is, as it were, a little vessel,” etc. Another reading: “for earth is, as it were, a little vessel,” etc. But *terra* [earth] is rightly absent in B.; for he continues to speak of the body, which he says is like a vessel and dwelling of the soul. I noted above, on chapter 3, that we ought to beware of and abstain from such expressions.

“For he served the foulest pleasures,” etc. Add Suetonius, *On Illustrious Grammarians*, chapter 6; Gellius, Book XVII, chapter 18.

“He planted.” Thus I read, as this passage is cited by everyone and as it stands in B., T., and P. So below, chapter 14: “And he planted a vineyard with his own hand”; and the planting of trees is called *consitiones*. Nevertheless, most printed editions read *conseruit*, a reading defended by Cyriacus, *Observations*, Book II, chapter 39, from the Florentine *Pandects*, in the law *in fundo alieno*, D. *On Vindication of Property*, Aurelius Victor, and Livy. [Col. 0931D]

“If he had observed these, he would have remained immortal.” Against Pelagius, who asserted that Adam died not because of sin but by a natural condition, according to which he would have perished even if he had not departed from God’s command. This heresy was condemned in the Council of Milevis, chapter 1.

“In which he had placed the knowledge of good and evil.” Below in this same chapter: “Having therefore received the knowledge of good and evil,” etc. What species of tree this tree was is variously discussed by commentators on Genesis, but nothing is determined with certainty. The question is asked why it was called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. The Hebrews have thought that the first parents were created utterly simple, like infants without the use of reason; and that because this tree had the power to accelerate the use of reason and free choice, it was called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. For according to the idiom of Scripture, to know good and evil means to possess the use of reason. Lactantius followed this opinion, supported also by the Sibyls, as is read below in note 97; but it is commonly rejected by all. For it is a grave error, not to say heresy, to assert that Adam at the beginning was ignorant of good and evil, but acquired knowledge of good and evil by eating the fruit of that tree. For how could he who gave names to all animals—which surely must correspond to their natures—and who possessed the admirable faculty of prophecy which he displayed in speaking of the woman, “This now is bone,” etc., not know what was good and what evil? It was also fitting that, just as he was established in a perfect state with respect to his body, so that he could immediately beget offspring, he should likewise be established in a perfect state with respect to his soul, so that he could immediately instruct and govern others. Such arguments are drawn from St Augustine in several passages on Genesis and Book XIV of *The City of God*, chapter 17, and from St Thomas in the *Prima Pars*, question 94, article 3. Chrysostom likewise disputes against that opinion in Homily 16 on Genesis; and see Philo’s excellent discussion of the perfection of the first man at the end of *On the Creation of the World*. [Col. 0932B]

Moreover, almost all agree that this name, “knowledge of good and evil,” did not belong to that tree by a nature implanted in it by God: Eucherius, Book I on Genesis; Cyril, Book III *Against Julian*; St Augustine on Genesis and the said chapter 17; Theodoret, Question 26 on Genesis; likewise Bede and Strabo, whom the Master follows in Book II of the *Sentences*, distinction 17. A second opinion is that of Josephus the Jew, Book I of the *Antiquities*, chapter 3: that it was so called because its fruit, if eaten by man, would have power to sharpen intelligence, ingenuity, and thoughtful prudence, and would contribute greatly to the acquisition of knowledge. Lyra refutes this opinion. A third is that of Rupert, Book II *On the Trinity*, chapter 27; Tostatus on Genesis chapter XIII, questions 154 and 155; and Pererius, Book III on Genesis: that it was so called ironically because of the serpent’s lie and deceptive promise, by which he promised that if they ate they would become like gods, knowing good and evil, so that even the tree’s name might preserve for posterity a memorial of that notable diabolical lie. They therefore think that the name was given either by Adam after the sin or by Moses. Although in the history of Genesis, before the serpent’s encounter with Eve, the tree is twice called by that name, they say this is by anticipation; in fact, it had not previously borne the name. When God commanded Adam not to eat from it, they say, he either called it by another name or pointed it out, as it were with his finger, or designated it in some other way.

The more common opinion is that held by Chrysostom on Genesis, Augustine, Book VIII *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapters 6 and 15, Cyril, Bede, Strabo, and the others cited in the first place: namely, that the name was not implanted in it by God as its nature, as though it gave or contained knowledge of good and evil, as Lactantius writes, but was assigned from the event which later followed. For as soon as man ate the fruit of that tree, he began to know in practice and by experience the distinction of good and evil, which previously he knew only speculatively, and how great was the difference between the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience. St Augustine, in the said chapter 15, further writes that God had imposed this name on the tree even before the serpent’s conversation with Eve. [Col. 0932D]

“A sentence was pronounced upon the sinner, that he should procure his sustenance by labour.” Thus it is read in B. and other excellent manuscripts, and in the Genesis narrative itself, from which these words are taken. For there it is written: “And the Lord God sent him forth from the Paradise of delight, to work the earth,” etc. Other copies read: “A sentence was pronounced upon sinners, that they should procure their sustenance by labour.”

“And he surrounded Paradise itself with fire.” The history at the end of Genesis chapter III reads thus: “And he placed before the Paradise of delight Cherubim and a flaming and turning sword, to guard the way of the tree of life.” Various opinions have existed about what is meant there by the flaming sword. Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 46, seems to have understood by the flaming sword the torrid zone and its most burning heat, which, in the manner of a sword, strikes those approaching it; Paradise is surrounded by this zone. St Thomas follows Tertullian in II–II, question 165, final article. But this exposition does not accord with the letter. St Basil cries out in Homily 3 and at the beginning of Homily 9 on Genesis, St Augustine at the beginning of Book VIII of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Bede on the words “In the beginning God created,” and other very weighty and holy men, that Moses’s teaching in the work of the six days of creation is wholly historical; therefore it must be understood historically, properly, and literally, not figuratively, mystically, or anagogically. The torrid zone was there even before humanity’s fall; but Scripture says that God placed the flaming sword there after Adam had been driven out. [Col. 0933B]

Lactantius judges that the flaming sword was nothing other than some immense force and quantity of fire, placed before Paradise’s entrance like a wall, fortification, or rampart, as he says here. Peter Comestor, Nicholas of Lyra, and Tostatus seem to have followed Lactantius on that Genesis passage. This opinion is rejected by some as incomplete because it makes no mention of the Cherubim, and as improper and not at all literal. Some understand obstacles to be indicated by which man, after sin, is prevented from entering the heavenly Paradise. But this interpretation too is far from the literal sense. St Ambrose, on that verse of Psalm CXVIII, “Reward thy servant,” etc., interprets the flaming sword as purgatorial fire. So too Rupert, Book III on Genesis, chapters 32 and 33; but they are refuted on the same grounds. The flaming sword was placed before the earthly Paradise, whereas theologians locate purgatorial fire beneath the earth. Finally, another opinion, approved by Benedict Pererius, Book VI on Genesis, is that these words of Genesis are to be understood wholly historically as they sound: namely, that Cherubim—that is, angels—were stationed to guard Paradise in the appearance and form of men, holding sharp swords in their hands, which flashed with sparks and flames, as it were, when brandished.

“Until he shall make the supreme judgment upon the earth and restore the righteous men, his worshippers, to that same place,” etc. Here we note an error of Lactantius and Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 46: they think that after the universal judgment the souls of the righteous will be brought into the earthly Paradise. Yet neither do the Holy Scriptures teach this anywhere, as Lactantius says, nor does the Sibyl say it, who, in naming Paradise, perhaps meant the heavenly one. Christ the Lord announces that after the universal judgment he will call the righteous into the kingdom of heaven: Matthew XXV, “Come, ye blessed,” etc., as all the saints and doctors interpret there.

“And those who honour God,” etc. (*Hoi de Theon timōntes*, Οἱ δὲ Θεόν τιμῶντες, etc.). These verses are read in Theophilus, *To Autolycus*, Book II; but in the Sibylline manuscript there are not precisely these verses but similar ones, Discourse 1, near the beginning, namely:

> … whom he commanded, dwelling in ambrosial Paradise,  
> Man, etc.  
> (*Ton dē keleth’ en paradeisō / Ambrosiō naiōn / Anthrōpon*,  
> Τὸν δὴ κέλετ’ ἐν παραδείσῳ / Ἀμβροσίῳ ναίων / Ἄνθρωπον, etc.)

These verses occur in the Sibylline poems, Discourse 1 near the beginning, and Discourse 8 about the middle, but there they vary somewhat. In Discourse 1:

> … but the serpent deceitfully greatly deceived [them].  
> (*Tous de mal’ ainos / Exapatēsen ophis dolios*,  
> Τοὺς δὲ μάλ’ αἶνος / Ἐξαπάτησεν ὄφις δολίως.)

In Discourse 8:

> And man, having been formed,  
> Whom the deceitful serpent deceived, etc.  
> (*Kai anthrōpon plasthenta, / Ont’ eplatēsen ophis dolios*,  
> Καὶ ἄνθρωπον πλασθέντα, / Ὄντ’ ἐπλάτησεν ὅφις δολίος, etc.)

In these poems it is false that Adam was deceived in order to gain, from eating the fruit, a knowledge of good and evil—if “knowledge” is understood as speculative knowledge, as was said above in this same chapter. [Col. 0934A]

“Both of good and of evil” (*agathou te, kakou te*, Ἀγαθοῦ τε, κακοῦ τε). Thus I read it, as in the Aldine and Plantin printed editions and in the Sibylline manuscript, Discourse 1; not as in the Florence edition and the Sibylline manuscript, Discourse 8, “both of good and of evil” (*agathou te, kai kakou*, ἀγαθοῦ τε, καὶ κακοῦ), for the metre does not scan.

“Which should be extended to a thousand years,” etc. Certainly, you will find in Scripture no one who lived for a thousand years, whatever he himself says below, at the end of Book VII, chapter 14, concerning the duration of Adam’s life, where we refuted him. Yet we do not speak absurdly in saying that the life of those who came very near that number was extended to a thousand years, such as Jared, Methuselah, and Noah, of whom Genesis chapters V and IX speak.

“For he says that among the Egyptians months were counted as years,” etc. This was not perpetual among the Egyptians, although Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book I, chapter 12, affirms that the year always had a fixed measure among the Egyptians alone. For it is truer that the Egyptians varied the year, sometimes making it a year of three months, more often of four months. Xenophon is reported to have written in his book *On Equivocal Terms*: “The year varies; for the Egyptians themselves use a year sometimes of one month, often of two, not infrequently of three, frequently of four, and sometimes a solar year.” Solinus, chapter 3, writes that the Egyptian year had four months; and St Augustine, *The City of God*, Book XV, chapter 12, says that it was sometimes of four months, sometimes of one month. Plutarch also, in his *Numa*, relates that the Egyptians’ year was monthly, then of four months. Yet Pliny, Book VII, chapter 48, and Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, write that they generally measured it by the period of a month according to the moon’s course. On the variety of years among different peoples, see Alexander of Naples, *Genial Days*, Book III, chapter 24; Camers on Solinus, chapter 3; and Giraldi, *On Days, Years, and Months*. [Col. 0934B]

“But that argument is plainly false,” etc. He nevertheless appears to agree with Varro and Pliny in the said chapter 48, whom St Augustine cites in the passage mentioned above. Yet Lactantius rightly refutes Varro and asserts what the fact requires: namely, that the years which Scripture says men lived before the Flood were not lunar months, as Varro said, but equal to our years, as St Augustine also demonstrates, *The City of God*, Book XV, chapter 14. For in Genesis chapter VII, in the one year during which the Flood lasted, Scripture mentions the first, second, and tenth months. And lest anyone might quibble that those months consisted of fewer days than ours, it also mentions the seventeenth day of the second month, the twenty-seventh day of the seventh month, and the twenty-seventh day of the second month. Indeed, if anyone computes all the days Moses mentions in his description of the Flood within that one year, he will find them to amount to three hundred and sixty. Josephus the Jew writes that it should neither be surprising nor seem false that such long lives are reported for the ancients, because the Lord granted them longer spans of life on account of their invention of sciences and arts, especially astronomy. Anyone may readily find many other reasons in commentators on Genesis.

## CHAPTER XIV

“He set the limit at one hundred and twenty years.” The Lord’s words which Moses reports at the beginning of Genesis VI—“And his days shall be one hundred and twenty years”—provided the cause for an erroneous understanding in Philo, *On Giants*; Josephus the Jew, *Antiquities*, Book I, chapter 5; Arnobius, Book II *Against the Gentiles*; Lactantius; Diodorus, bishop of Tarsus; Rupert, Book IV on Genesis, chapter 13; and Tostatus on Genesis VI, chapter 11. They thought that God had set the limit of human life after the Flood at one hundred and twenty years. But the words should be explained thus: “His days,” that is, man’s days, “shall be one hundred and twenty years,” not for living but for repenting. The Lord said this twenty years before the ark began to be built, as St Jerome writes; the ark is recorded as having been made over one hundred years. Or, according to Strabo, he spoke from the year in which the ark began to be made. But because men remained in wickedness, they were destroyed before the appointed time, namely in the hundredth year. “It repents me,” says the Lord, “that I made man”—that is, I shall do what a man commonly does when angry and regretting his work: he demolishes what he has made. Thus I shall destroy the man whom I made. Yet “my spirit shall not remain in man for ever”—that is, my anger shall not remain against man eternally as it does against the devil—“because he is flesh,” that is, frail. Rather, I shall punish him here and overwhelm him with waters; indeed, before I punish him, I shall give him time for repentance: his days for repentance shall be one hundred and twenty years. Thus the Lord’s words are not words of severity but of clemency and compassion. Chrysostom, Homily 22 on Genesis; St Jerome, *Hebrew Questions*; St Augustine, *The City of God*, Book XV, chapter 24; Strabo; Hugh of St Victor in the annotations on Genesis; and finally the Master of the *Scholastic History*, Book of Genesis, chapter 31, interpret them thus. [Col. 0935A]

This explanation also agrees with the Hebrew text, which reads: “My spirit shall not judge these men for ever, because they are flesh”; that is, as Rabbi Solomon interprets it, “My spirit shall not contend or dispute with them in judgment,” etc. Certainly we know that very many persons exceeded one hundred and twenty years, not only from Sacred Scripture—Genesis chapters XI, XXIII, XXV, XLVII, and elsewhere often—but also from secular authors: Pliny, Book VII, chapters 48 and 49, and Athenaeus, Book X, chapter 11.

“And that land was called Canaan after his name.” It ought therefore rather to have been called after Canaan himself, the son of Ham, rather than after Ham, as Lactantius says; likewise the Canaanites themselves were named after Canaan, Genesis chapter X.

“Nor is the sky woven over with any clouds in that region.” In both Bolognese codices, P., and some Vatican manuscripts, the particle *enim* [for] is absent and the clause is not enclosed in parentheses, as though it did not give the reason for the preceding assertion—why that people lived in the open air—but presented another reason why they could continually contemplate the stars. I have written it as it stands in all printed editions. What Lactantius says here, that clouds do not form in Egypt, is doubtful. For Pliny, Book II, chapter 50, writes that clouds form there, although they are rare and thin. Democritus, according to Plutarch, *Opinions*, Book IV, chapter 1, taught that the Nile rises because snow, melted and spread abroad at the summer solstice in northern regions, thickens clouds from vapours; driven southward toward Egypt by the Etesian winds, these dissolve into great and violent rains, filling both the marshes and the Nile. Diodorus too, Book I, chapter 2, testifies that rains occur there, though rarely. Mela agrees with Lactantius: “Egypt,” he says, “is without rains, yet wonderfully fertile,” etc. But the writers can be reconciled from Philo, who in Book I of *The Life of Moses* writes that rains there are slight and rare, occurring in maritime places, while above Memphis there are none at all; there he also discusses most elegantly why winter is superfluous in Egypt.

“Prodigious forms of animals.” On these, Cicero, Books I and III *On the Nature of the Gods*, and Philo, *On the Decalogue*.

## CHAPTER XV

[Col. 0935D]

When, therefore, the number of human beings had begun to increase, etc., he sent angels for the protection and cultivation of the human race. He is mistaken in saying that angels were not given for guardianship before the number of human beings had begun to increase. For from the first parents onward, every soul, from the beginning of its creation, has an angel assigned for its protection; neither the first parents themselves nor any human beings whatever lacked such an angel. Origen, on Numbers; Jerome, on Matthew XVIII, “Their angels,” etc.; St Bernard, Sermon on the Angels and on Psalm VIII, “What is man, that thou art mindful of him,” etc.; the Master and all theologians on II, distinction 11; St Thomas, Part I, question 113, article 4.

Because free will had been granted to them. He writes that the sin of the remaining evil angels occurred when the multitude of human beings had already begun to increase—that is, a long interval after Lucifer’s sin [Col. 0936A]—and that this sin was one of luxury and lust, because they mingled with women. We say, rather, that only a very brief delay intervened between the creation of Lucifer, the highest angel, and his fall. St Augustine, On Genesis, book XII, chapter 23: “Having been made, he immediately turned himself away from the light of truth, swollen with pride,” etc. Isidore, On the Highest Good, book I, chapter 10: “As soon as he was made, he burst forth into pride and was cast down from heaven.” It is altogether certain that he had already become guilty of sin and condemnation when he approached to tempt the first woman, as Serenus the abbot expressly argued against the opinion of Germanus in Cassian, Conference VIII, chapter 10.

Secondly, we say that the evil angels sinned either simultaneously and in one instant of time with Lucifer, as Alexander of Hales writes, Part II, question 110, member 5; St Thomas, First Part, question 63, article 8; or perhaps after some delay had intervened, as St Bonaventure, on II, distinction 5, article 2, question 2, and Scotus, on the same distinction, question 2, hold—but a delay imperceptible and almost nonexistent, as may be gathered from those same writers. It is likewise clear from the same holy Fathers and doctors, in the places cited, that the sin of the evil angels [Col. 0936B] was the same as Lucifer’s: namely, the sin of pride, of which I spoke on chapter 9, and which Lucifer persuaded them to commit. As soon as they sinned, moreover, they were condemned and cast down from heaven along with Lucifer: Revelation XII; St Isidore, cited above; John Damascene, On the Orthodox Faith, book II, chapter 4.

Some doctors indeed judge that the devil, that is Lucifer, was immediately thrust into hell; others, into this darksome air. But they hold that, after he had been defeated by Christ in the temptation, he was cast into hell. So the Master in II, distinction 6—though he doubts whether Lucifer is now in hell. Lactantius below, book III, chapter 29, considers him to have been permitted to remain in this world, so that by his malice he may exercise men unto virtue. Concerning the other demons, St Thomas writes, on the said distinction 6, article 4, and First Part, question 64, article 4, that some were cast into this darksome air, while others, who sinned more gravely, were thrust into hell. But St Bonaventure, on the said distinction, article 2, question 1, affirms that until the Day of Judgment the place of the other demons [Col. 0936C] is not hell but the darksome air. Whether any have been thrust into hell, he confesses himself not to know; yet he says that some descend thither in order to torment souls. But wherever they are, they always carry with them the torments of flames, as the ordinary Gloss says on James III, “set on fire by hell,” etc.; this is also cited and approved by St Thomas, on the said distinction 6, article 4.

It is also clear from Holy Scripture that evil angels, immediately after their sin and the sentence of condemnation, remained obstinate in evil, and will remain forever in their condemnation, obstinacy, and punishment: Alexander of Hales, Part II, question 118, member 1, articles 1 and 4; St Thomas, First Part, question 64, article 2; the Doctors with the Master in II Sentences, distinction 7, especially St Bonaventure, article 1; Scotus, sole question; Durandus, question 2; Gabriel, question 1. This is indeed a matter of faith and is defined in the chapter *Firmiter*, On the Supreme Trinity and the Catholic Faith. From these points many errors of Lactantius may be noted and avoided. The first [Col. 0936D] is that he writes here that God then commanded the angels not to be stained by the contagion of earth and so lose the dignity of their heavenly substance; for they had long before been defiled and stained by sin, and indeed confirmed in that stain and obstinacy, as we have said.

He enticed them to vices. Fables. It has already been said that they were seduced into sin by Lucifer much earlier, namely before the fall of the first parents, and were immediately condemned for it.

And defiled them by intercourse with women. What the sin of the evil angels was, and when it was committed, has been set out above. Yet Lactantius was not alone in thinking that angels had sexual relations with women in Noah’s time; very many other Fathers thought so too, on the basis of the wrongly understood passage in Genesis chapter VI: “The sons of God went in unto the daughters of men, and they bore,” etc. Josephus the Jew, *Jewish Antiquities*, book I, chapter 5; Tertullian, On the Veiling of Virgins; Justin Martyr, both Apologies; Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, books III and V; Cyprian, On the Discipline and Dress of Virgins; Methodius, Sermon on the Resurrection; Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book V.

The occasion for this opinion was supplied by the ancient Greek version of the Seventy Interpreters, which those writers followed after Philo. It offered the reading οἱ ἄγγελοι τοῦ Θεοῦ, “the angels of God,” and the Old Latin or Italic version—so Ambrose, Augustine, and Procopius report—likewise read *angeli Dei*, “angels of God.” Later, according to the Hebrew text, the Greek read οἱ υἱοὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ, “the sons of God,” and the Latin edition *filii Dei*, “sons of God”; Augustine and Procopius knew both readings in their time. Therefore by the angels, or sons of God, the sons of Seth must be understood, since they were religious and worshippers of God; and by the daughters of men, daughters of the line of Cain must be understood. This is how the passage is explained by the interlinear Gloss; Theodoret, Question 47 on Genesis; Cyril, Against Julian, book IX, and Allegories on the Pentateuch, book II, sermon 1; Augustine, *City of God*, book XV, chapter 23; Jerome, Hebrew Traditions on Genesis, book IV, chapter 12; Suidas under μιαιγαμίαι and under “Seth”; Bede, Aimo, [Col. 0937B] and Rabanus on Genesis; Rupert likewise on Genesis, book IV, chapter 12; the Master, *Scholastic History*, Genesis, chapter 31; St Thomas, First Part, question 51, article 3, reply to 6.

Indeed Philastrius, On Heresies, chapter 108, lists among heresies the proposition that angels mingled with women before the Flood. It is also rejected by St John Chrysostom, Homily 22 on Genesis, and by his disciple Cassian, *Conferences*, book XII, chapter 8. Finally, St Ambrose, Letter 84 to Demetrias, says that the cause of Lucifer’s and the other evil angels’ condemnation was not lust but pride, and that he, together with his followers, fell from heaven through pride before the fall of man.

Then, not received into heaven because of the sins in which they had immersed themselves, they fell to earth. These fables follow from those above. As to the place of the evil angels after their fall, I set out the opinions a little earlier.

But those who are begotten from them, etc. Fables.

Thus two kinds of demons were made: one heavenly, the other earthly, etc. If these words are separated from what precedes, [Col. 0937C] they can acquire a true sense. We may say that the heavenly kind of demons is that which moves about in the darksome air—for “heaven” is frequently used for air, not only in profane but also in sacred writings—whereas the earthly kind is that which, as we said according to St Thomas’s opinion, has been cast into the lowest depths of the earth and into hell.

But that aerial kind wanders through all the elements, so that with violent winds and foul storms it agitates the air; and thence it not only hurls hail and thunderbolts, but also, as is related among prodigies, sometimes rains down wool, stones, wax, iron, and flesh. It stirs up the sea’s waves, intent upon drowning sailors, and haunts wells, lakes, springs, and rivers for the destruction of human beings, as Tertullian writes in On Baptism. It either shakes the earth with unusual tremors or otherwise harms and disturbs it. Hence Orpheus in the poem addressed to Musaeus, Marcus in Psellus’s book On Demons, [Col. 0937D] and Porphyry in his book Responses from the Oracles of Apollo held that there are six kinds of demons in all. Whoever wishes may consult those writers.

Δαιμονιάρχην. Just as the Pharisees call him δαιμονίων ἄρχοντα, “ruler of demons,” in Matthew XII.

Δαήμονας. Thus I have restored this word, which is corruptly read in all copies as δαίμονας. For the derivative must differ in some respect from its etymon. They maintain that δαίμων, written with αι, is so called as though δαήμων, from δαῆναι, “to understand” or “to know”: Plato, *Cratylus*; Martianus Capella, book II; Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book I, chapter 23.

They certainly know many future things, but not all. What future things? Origen answers, On First Principles, book IV, chapter 2; St Augustine, On the Divination of Demons, and On Genesis, book II, chapter 17, and *City of God*, book IX, chapter 22; Gregory the Great, *Morals*, book XXVIII, chapter 6; Isidore, On the Highest Good; Damascene, On the Orthodox Faith, book II; the Master, II Sentences, distinction 7; and there St Bonaventure, article 3, question 3; Durandus, question 3; likewise St Thomas, First Part [Col. 0938A] question 57, article 3; II–II, questions 95 and 192; and Against the Gentiles, book III, chapter 154.

To frame responses with ambiguous outcomes. See Cicero, On Divination, book II; Tertullian, Apology, chapter 22; Lactantius again below, book IV, chapter 13; Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book IV, chapter 1, and book V, chapter 10, where he treats at length the falsity of oracles; St Augustine, *City of God*, book III, chapter 17, and book XIX, chapter 23.

And they seek the consolation of their own ruin by ruining human beings. The theologians aptly inquire whether demons derive any consolation and joy from human sins and condemnation. Minucius says this too in the *Octavius*, and St Leo in Sermon 2 on the Nativity of the Lord, near the beginning. Alexander of Hales answers, Part II, question 100, member 5, article 1, that this is a kind of consolation for them, not real but apparent, and mingled with every bitterness, because that joy arises not from the apprehension of what is simply fitting, but of what seems fitting to them. St Augustine also writes, On Genesis against the Manichaeans, chapter 17, that demons have power over [Col. 0938B] those who despise God’s commandments and rejoice in that most unhappy power.

Yet that joy becomes punishment for them. Therefore St Thomas, in the books of the Sentences, as cited and explained by Dominicus Bannes on First Part, question 64, article 3, doubt 2, calls that joy deceptive and, as it were, fantastic, because it is immediately followed by new torment and pain. Other theologians simply and absolutely deny that any joy or consolation can be found in demons, since the greatest pain admits no joy alongside itself, even concerning a distinct object, as Aristotle teaches in the seventh book of the *Ethics* and experience demonstrates. They support this by arguing that, if demons could have any consolation and joy, they would not be in a state of the greatest and most extreme misery—which must not be asserted.

They reply to St Augustine and Thomas that joy or consolation is not there taken formally but causally: demons are said to rejoice in the victory they gain over human beings because that victory fulfills their desire, by which, through envious zeal, they strive to cast human beings down [Col. 0938C] from attaining the heavenly kingdom. The fulfillment of that desire is called joy and gladness, not formally and in reality, but only causally, because by its nature it would be capable of producing pleasure and joy, and would actually produce it in demons if their will were not forestalled by the greatest and most extreme pain that consumes them.

They derive this explanation from the same St Thomas, in his commentary on the Master, where he says that demons are said to rejoice in our evils in the same sense in which blessed angels are customarily said to grieve over our evils. Yet it is certain that blessed angels do not grieve formally, because their state does not allow it; therefore neither do demons rejoice or acquire any consolation formally, but only causally, as has been said.

They pour out unmixed wine for them every day. Τὸ *merum*, “unmixed wine,” is absent from B. T. P. I have retained the reading of all printed editions; for *profundunt*, “they pour out,” used absolutely, is unusual, and we know that pagans customarily poured unmixed wine for the genii; Horace, Odes, book III, ode 17, said, “to tend one’s genius with unmixed wine.” In the margin of the Plantin editions stands: *his quotidie procumbunt*, “they daily prostrate themselves before them.”

They are subtle spirits, etc. If you wish to take the author as speaking properly, it is scarcely doubtful that he means us to understand that he attributes to demons a substance of some subtle aura, and so agrees with those who assign an exceedingly subtle body to angels. This opinion, flowing from the springs of Plato, who taught that God alone and the Mind produced by him are wholly without body, was adopted by Philo in On the Creation of the World; Tertullian, On the Flesh of Christ; Origen, On First Principles, book II, chapters 2 and 8; Methodius, Athanasius, Basil, and John, bishop of Thessalonica, cited at the Second Council of Nicaea, session 4; St Augustine, *City of God*, book VIII, chapter 9, and book II, chapter 23; *Enchiridion*, chapters 45 and 59; On the Nature of Demons; and it is reported in chapter *Sciendum*, question 26, question 3; in On Genesis Literally, book VII, chapter 17; and often elsewhere; Cassian, *Conferences*, book VII, conference 7, [Col. 0939A] chapter 13; Damascene, Theology, book II, chapter 3, and book III Against the Iconoclasts; and perhaps Lactantius too in this passage, as I have said.

For *tenue*, “subtle,” means in Latin the same as Greek λεπτόν: that is, nothing other than thin, extended, yet solid, and bounded within limits; and this can properly be said only of bodies. Its opposite is *spissum*, “dense”; for they are relatives. But nothing lacking quantity is either subtle or dense, since these are affections peculiar to the arrangement of parts. Nevertheless, this opinion about angelic bodies has now been rejected by the unanimous judgment of all doctors, who teach that all angels are wholly without bodies. So teach Dionysius the Areopagite, On the Divine Names, chapter 21; Nazianzen, at the end of On Theology and in the Oration on the Nativity of the Saviour; Chrysostom, Homily 22 on Genesis; Gregory the Great, *Morals*, book IV, chapter 9; Hugh of St Victor, On the Sacraments, book I, part 5, questions 7 and 8; Alexander of Hales, Part II, question 20, member 3, reply to 3; Albert the Great, St Thomas, Bonaventure, and Major on II Sentences, distinction 8; again St Thomas, First Part, question 51, articles 1 and 2, Against the Gentiles, chapter 88 and following; [Col. 0939B] John Duns Scotus, II, distinction 2, question 6, and distinction 8, question 1; Thomas of Strasbourg, II, distinction 3, question 1; Marsilius, question 2.

Finally, the Lateran Council under Innocent III, reported in the chapter *Firmiter*, On the Supreme Trinity and the Catholic Faith, expressly calls the angelic creature spiritual and the worldly creature corporeal. For this reason all doctors at the present time affirm that this is more probable even on natural grounds, while the contrary position contains, if not a manifest error in faith, at least rashness.

They work. If you read *operti*, “covered,” as many editions have it, then *occulte*, “secretly,” appears superfluous. I have followed the reading of B. and T., placed in the margin of Plantin.

They impair health. Yet one must beware the heresy of the Gnostics, who affirmed that diseases are demons and must be cured not by natural remedies but by incantations. Plotinus wrote against this, *Enneads*, book IX, Ennead 2, chapter 14. One must again beware the error of the physicians Peter of Abano and Pomponazzi, who attribute every condition of those possessed by demons [Col. 0939C] to melancholic humour and contend that they should be treated not by adjurations but by natural remedies. See Tertullian, Apology, chapter 22; Minucius, *Octavius*; Psellus, On Demons; Fernel, On the Hidden Causes of Things, book II; Levinus Lemnius, On the Occult Things of Nature, book II, chapter 1.

## CHAPTER XVI

Adjured by his name, they depart from bodies. Observe the most ancient use of exorcisms in God’s Church and the authority of believers over demons. So too book IV, chapter 27. Add Ignatius, To the Antiochenes, letter 12; Justin, On the Truth of the Christian Religion and in the Oration to the Gentiles; Tertullian, On the Soldier’s Crown, chapter 11; On Idolatry, chapter 11, at the end; To Scapula, chapter 1; and Apology, chapter 23; Cyprian, To Demetrian and To Donatus, letter 2, and On the Vanity of Idols; Minucius, *Octavius*; Epiphanius, Heresy 30; Prudentius, *Apotheosis* against the Jews. That exorcists also existed in the synagogue may be inferred from Acts of the Apostles, chapter XIX; Josephus testifies to this and recounts certain marvels, *Jewish Antiquities*, book VIII, chapter 2; as does Epiphanius, Heresy 30.

And what they for the most part do in the presence of their worshippers. I judge that this passage, which seems very corrupt to me, should be restored from Cyprian and Minucius, from whom Firmianus drew nearly all these things, as follows: “And this too they for the most part do in the presence of their worshippers—not surely to the disgrace of their religion and honour, but because they cannot lie either to God by whom they are adjured or to the righteous by whose voice they are tortured.” Cyprian, On the Vanity of Idols: “You may see them confess, in the hearing even of those who worship them, whence they come and when they depart.” Minucius: “They declare what they are; and certainly they do not lie to their own disgrace, especially while some of you are standing by.”

Μία (he says) φυλακὴ εὐσέβεια, etc. I do not find these words verbatim, but similar ones occur in chapter 10 of *Asclepius*: “For a just man, religion toward God and the highest piety are a safeguard; for God protects such persons from every evil,” etc.

## CHAPTER XVII

Astrology. That is, judicial astrology, which claims by the configurations of the stars to foretell future events. See Tertullian, Apology, chapter 35, and On Idolatry. Cicero too condemns all these arts of which he speaks here, in On the Nature of the Gods, book I; and Giovanni Francesco Pico demolishes them in an excellent volume entitled *On the Foreknowledge of Things*.

Ἐπεὶ πλάνα πάντα, etc. These verses are not found among the Sibylline poems.

They put on. I have retained the reading of the Vatican manuscripts and all printed editions; B.’s reading, *induxerunt*, “they introduced,” did not please me. Lactantius followed the best authors in this expression. Cicero, On Ends, book II: “From his spoils he put on both a torque and a surname.” Livy: “My care and fidelity put on for me the name of patron of the plebs.” Persons too are properly said to be “put on.”

For we say that the world is ruled by God as a province by its governor. A most beautiful comparison. Aristotle, in the little work On the World, says that God stands in relation to the world as an emperor to an army.

Not because they desire any honour, etc. On the contrary, they seek honour, as above, book I, chapter 7, and in this book, chapter 15. St Augustine, *City of God*, book IX, chapter 20, and all theologians affirm this. For, as St Thomas says, First Part, question 64, article 2, reply to 3, evil spirits remain in the same sin in which they first sinned in respect of their desire, though not in respect of believing themselves able to obtain what they desire. But that sin was the sin of pride. Hence the devil, tempting Christ the Lord, dared to say: “All these things I will give thee, if thou wilt fall down and worship me.” Matthew IV.

Hence it is that a stone was cut by a razor at an augur’s command, etc. Here ends the discussion which he began in chapter 9 concerning the devil and his companion angels: namely, their creation, sin, condemnation, expulsion, deception of the first parents, and finally their nature and hostility toward human beings. His purpose was to explain certain marvellous works and deceptions sometimes brought about by them and enumerated in chapter 8 of this book; here he provides their epitome.

And victories. An example may be drawn from the voice of Silvanus sent out from the Arician wood, as in Livy at the beginning of the second book of the first Decade; Valerius, book I, chapter 8; Plutarch, *Publicola*.

Because he had placed a handsome boy in the temple of Jupiter to hold the *exuviae*. In Valerius Maximus, from whom Lactantius took it, this story is written as follows, book I, chapter 2: “It was believed that the consul Varro fought so unsuccessfully against the Carthaginians at Cannae because of Juno’s anger, since, when as aedile he was holding the Circensian games, he had placed in the temple of Jupiter Best and Greatest a strikingly handsome boy, an actor, to keep watch.” This passage is read in remarkably corrupt form in both Valerian and Lactantian manuscripts, and has been noticed neither by Pighius, who published an emended Valerius, nor by anyone else.

It is known from Sisinnius Capito, cited by Festus under *Tensa*, that in the procession of the Circensian Games the *exuviae* of the gods were also brought from the temples to the Circus in *tensae*: “Sisinnius Capito”—for that is the reading required there, not “Sinnius,” from Lactantius below, book VI, chapter 20—“says that *tensa* is the name of the vehicle in which the *exuviae* of the gods are carried to the Circus and its couch in the Circensian games; it was made of ivory, as in Titinius’s *Barbatus*, and also of silver.” Tertullian, On Spectacles, chapter 27: “But the display of the Circensian games is somewhat more splendid, and this alone properly bears the name *pompa*, ‘procession’; it proves its own character from the succession of images, the procession of statues, the chariots, the *tensae*, the armamaxes, the seats, the crowns, the *exuviae*,” etc.

Asconius Paedianus: “The *tensae* are sacred vehicles, part of the procession of ranks, victims, and functions; so called because straps—or, according to another reading, cloths—are stretched in front of them, which those leading them delight to hold and touch. Others prefer to derive the word from θεῖον, ‘divine thing’; then it is written *thensa*, with *th*.” By the boys assigned as guardians while these *tensae* and the gods’ *exuviae* were being carried in the procession, I understand those mentioned by Cicero in the speech On the Response of the Haruspices: “If an actor stopped, or a flute-player suddenly fell silent, or if that boy whose parents were both living did not touch the ground, or let go of the *tensa* or the strap, or if the aedile made an error in word or gesture, were the games not duly performed?” Arnobius repeats this passage almost word for word at the end of book IV.

Therefore in Valerius the passage must first be punctuated and written thus, with a comma after *faceret*, “was holding”; then what follows must be read continuously and entirely without punctuation: “Because, when as aedile he was holding the Circensian games, in the temple of Jupiter Best and Greatest, a boy of striking appearance, an actor,” etc. Thus “in the temple of Jupiter Best and Greatest” belongs to the latter phrase, so that it is understood that the aedile placed the handsome boy in Jupiter’s temple, as Lactantius has it. A comma or semicolon must not be placed after *templo*, as erroneously in all Valerius manuscripts, because then “in the temple of Jupiter Best and Greatest” is joined to the earlier phrase, signifying that the aedile held the Circensian games in Jupiter’s temple [Col. 0941B]—which is plainly false.

For those games were not held in temples, but either in the Circus, as their very name and the testimony of Sisinnius Capito cited above show, together with Dionysius at the end of *Roman Antiquities*, book VII; Cassiodorus, letter to Faustus; and Volaterranus, Commentaries, book XXIX, chapter “On the Celebration of Games”; or in the forum, as Volaterranus states there. Nor was this Valerius’s meaning, as Lactantius shows. Secondly, in both authors *exuvias*, “the sacred ornaments,” must be read in place of *excubias*, “watches,” on the basis of the passages cited above. Thus all the best manuscripts of Lactantius—B., T., P., the twelve Vatican manuscripts—and many editions, Venetian, Tridentine, and the Florentine Juntas, read here, although eight Vatican codices of Valerius, every printed copy we have seen, and likewise the Aldine edition of Lactantius have *excubias*. Without doubt, therefore, Valerius must be corrected from Lactantius. For what Latin writer ever said *tenere excubias*, “to hold watches,” for *agere* or *habere excubias*, “to keep” or “maintain watches”?

I conjecture that the error entered because ancient codices had *exubias* or *exsubias* for *exuvias*. In antiquity they often substituted *b* for *v*: thus they pronounced *connibere* and *coacerbare*, and similar words, for *connivere* and *coacervare*, as I noted in book III, chapter 4, and book V, chapter 1. They also added *s* after *x*, pronouncing *exspecto*, *exsul*, and *exsequor*. It therefore seems most likely that scribes or printers, not having understood the meaning of the word as written in the manner I have described, either added or substituted the letter *c*, and so wrote or printed it in the corrupt form that is now read.

By the fates of hostile Juno. He refers to these lines of Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII:

> That he, beneath king Eurystheus,  
> endured a thousand harsh labours  
> by the fates of hostile Juno, etc.

When Hannibal destroyed two armies of the Roman people by both strategy and valour. The history is in Livy, third book of the second Decade; Plutarch, *Hannibal*.

## CHAPTER XVIII

That evils may contend with goods, etc. He says the same in book V, chapter 7; book VI, chapters 15 and 22; and book VII, chapter 4, at the end; also St Thomas, Against the Gentiles, book III, chapter 71, in the fifth argument, where throughout that excellent chapter he explains why God permits evils to occur and why divine providence does not entirely remove evil from things. Seneca also composed an outstanding book on this subject, entitled *On Divine Providence*. See further Dionysius the Areopagite, On the Divine Names, chapter 3; Basil, Homily “That God Is Not the Author of Evil”; Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapters 11 and 96.

This persuasion utterly destroys truth and religion. Lactantius thought that certain affections, and especially anger, truly and properly exist in God; and he tried to persuade others of the same, not only here but in an entire book entitled On the Anger of God, where he expressly asserts it, especially in chapters 16 and 17. He could at least have learned the falsity of this position and opinion from his own teacher Arnobius, who often reproaches the Gentiles with it, at the beginning of book I and in many places in book VII. We also know that Tertullian was entangled in the same error, from On the Testimony of the Soul, chapter 2; On the Soul, chapter 26; and elsewhere.

Against this, Catholic truth is established by St Thomas, Against the Gentiles, book I, chapter 89: anger belongs to God neither in respect of its genus, insofar as it is a passion, [Col. 0942B] nor in respect of its proper species. Whenever anger is ascribed to God in Holy Scripture, it is understood metaphorically. Since God exercises punishment and vengeance upon the wicked—an effect which in human beings commonly belongs to anger—we therefore say that God is angry. But because he is altogether simple and immutable, anger, mercy, repentance, and other things of this kind cannot be said of him properly and according to a passionate affection, but only according to a likeness of effect, as St Thomas teaches in the First Part, question 21, article 3.

## CHAPTER XIX

Which counterfeits truth by colouring and imitation. Yet the Bolognese reading, “which counterfeits truth by appearance,” is not displeasing; for *facies*, “appearance,” is frequently used for likeness. Virgil, *Georgics* IV:

> The curving wave stood round in the appearance of a mountain.

Sallust, *Histories* II: “Sardinia, in the African sea, has the appearance of a human footprint.”

But less of religion, etc. I read thus with Petrus Faber, *Semestria*, book II, chapter 16, as I found it in a copy of the Florentine edition and several others. For, because he had said that the religion of the pagans is a simulation and therefore falsehood, he consequently says that it contains not truth but mime—that is, a mere imitation of religion and truth. For the business of a mime is precisely to imitate and simulate. Seneca, Letters, book V, letter 26: “Just now I was saying: Thus I am preparing myself for that day on which, the artifices and cosmetics removed, I shall pronounce judgment upon myself—whether I speak brave words or feel them; whether there has been any simulation and mime in whatever defiant words I have hurled against fortune.” Another reading: “But less of religion.”

Whose origin is from heaven. Thus above, chapter 2, at the end: “Earthly things, which arise from heaven.” Since human souls are produced by God, who is said in a particular manner to be in heaven, he says that they derive their origin from heaven. In this sense it is rightly said that human souls derive their origin from heaven, or are heavenly or divine—not because they were produced in heaven before their bodies. For, as was said above on chapter 11 of this book, Lactantius himself does not accept this.

## CHAPTER III
