For to investigate the causes of natural things, etc. So Socrates in Xenophon, *Memorabilia of Socrates*, book I, at the beginning; Cicero treats the same subject in *Academic Questions*, book IV.

Whether the sun is as large as it appears, etc. Aristotle, *Meteorology*, book I, summary I, chapter 3, at the end, says that it is very childish to think each of the things carried in heaven small because it appears so to those looking from here; and in On Dreams, chapter 2, he writes that the sense is deceived in this, that the sun appears a foot in breadth. Read Plato, *Epinomis*; Lucretius V; Cicero, *Academics* II; Cleomedes, book II; Pliny II, chapter 11; Plutarch, *Opinions of the Philosophers*, book II, chapter 21 and following; Laertius on Anaximander; and Epicurus’s letter to Pythocles in Laertius’s *Epicurus*; Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, book I, chapter 20; Basil, Homily 6 on the Hexaemeron. In general, on all these questions mentioned here by Lactantius, see Giovanni Francesco Pico, On the Vanity of the Learning of the Gentiles, book I, chapter 12.

[Col. 0943A] The moon is spherical, etc. Plutarch, *Opinions of the Philosophers*, book II, chapter 27.

And whether the stars adhere to heaven. This was Anaximander’s opinion, according to Plutarch, *Opinions of the Philosophers*, book II, chapter 16, and Aristotle, On the Heavens, book II; today it is accepted by all philosophers and mathematicians.

Or whether they are carried through the air in a free course. This question was debated not only by the Stoics, as in Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods, book II, and by other philosophers, but also by the Fathers: whether the stars are so fixed to their spheres that they are turned only by the revolution of those spheres, or whether, while heaven remains unmoved—or, as Chrysostom put it, through a spread-out air, permeable and yielding—they are borne and wheeled around by divine decree or under the guidance of a soul.

Procopius, Commentary on Genesis, chapter I: “Some declare that the luminaries wander in the air, at a great distance from heaven, far removed from heaven,” etc. Elias of Crete, on Nazianzen’s Oration 7: “And therefore, they say, not even all the stars are fixed in heaven, but rest upon the air, which supports them just as it does birds,” etc. Junilius shows what is here meant by “air” in the *Hexaemeron*: “It must be understood that birds are said to fly according to the firmament of heaven because this name also denotes the ether, that is, that upper region of air extending from this turbulent and dark place in which birds fly up to the stars, and which is rightly believed to be entirely tranquil and full of light. For the seven wandering stars, said to move about in this region of ether, Scripture says were placed in the firmament of heaven,” etc.

Anselm of Canterbury, On the Image of the World, book I, chapter 3: “Fire is called ether, as though pure air, and rejoices in perpetual brightness. From this angels take bodies when they are sent to human beings. In it the seven stars are carried in their several circles contrary to the world, and because of their wandering course are called planets, that is, wanderers,” etc. Philo the Jew too, in On Giants, thought that the stars are moved by their own motions rather than fixed to heaven; likewise Justin Martyr, Against Aristotle and Orthodox Questions 59 and 93; Origen, Against Celsus, book V, and On First Principles, book I, chapter 7; Lactantius below, chapter 24; Eusebius of Emesa [Col. 0943C] on Genesis I, cited in Lipomani’s *Catena*; Diodorus of Tarsus, as in the same *Catena*; and Chrysostom, Homily 6 on Genesis.

Whether it is at rest or in motion, etc. This is the more commonly received reading. But manuscript B reads: “whether it is at rest and immovable,” with which Isidore agrees, reproducing this entire passage word for word in *Origins*, book II, chapter 24. Seneca, *Natural Questions*, book VII, chapter 2: “This too will belong to that examination, so that we may know whether, while earth stands still, the world moves around it, or whether, while the world stands still, earth turns,” etc. Nicetas of Syracuse believed that heaven is at rest and earth alone moves, according to Theophrastus as cited by Cicero, *Academic Questions*, book IV; so too Cleanthes of Samos, according to Plutarch, On the Face in the Orb of the Moon. Plato too, according to some, although he expressed it somewhat obscurely. The same most paradoxical opinion, παραδοξότατον, I see approved by certain more recent writers: Cardinal Nicholas of Cusa, On Learned Ignorance, book II, chapter 12; Coelius Calcagninus; and Copernicus. See the notes on chapter 24 of this same book.

How great is the thickness of the earth. Plato, at the end of the *Phaedo*; Cleomedes, book I; Macrobius, Commentary on the Dream of Scipio, book I, chapter 20.

By what foundations it is balanced. Plato, cited above; Ptolemy, *Almagest*, book III, chapter 7; Cicero, *Academics*.

Although it seems to wink. This reading is found in most copies; some manuscripts have *conticere*, “to fall silent”; B has *connibere*, a spelling reflecting the old pronunciation in which *b* was used for *v* in certain words. Thus *connibentia* for *conniventia* is frequently found in the Theodosian Code and in Vatican manuscripts of John Cassian, *Conferences*, book VI, chapter 9, and book VIII, chapter 8. The Glossary too has *connibentia*, ῥᾳθυμία, “slackness.” Petrus Ciacconius noted this in his annotations on the same Cassian.

## CHAPTER IV
Sparti, those men of the poets. I cannot believe, with Janus Guilielmius in his *Questions on Plautus’ Menaechmi*, ch. 4, that Lactantius wrote *Spartiatae*, as it appears in nearly all printed editions [Col. 0944A]; that would plainly have been the act of an ignorant man. Rather, he wrote the Greek Σπάρτοι, that is, “sown” or “seeded men,” as Pliny too translates this Greek name at the end of Book XIX, ch. 1; or, more probably, Lactantius wrote *Spartae* in Latin letters, with οι rendered by the diphthong *oe*, treating it as one of those names which Latin speakers customarily pronounced in Latin form, though with Greek inflection. Thus *acta*, ἡ ἀκτή, “shore.” Virgil, Book V:

> But far away upon the solitary shore the Trojan women  
> Wept for the lost Anchises, etc.

Cicero, *Against Verres*, Book VII: “His wife could scarcely keep him with her, in a spirit untroubled and free, for so many days on the shore.” Likewise *probata*, πρόβατα, “sheep”: Pliny, Book VII, ch. 2: “At their praise let the sheep perish, let the trees wither,” etc. Not understanding the meaning of this word, scribes immediately suspected an error, seized upon another similar word at hand, and substituted *Spartiatae* for *Spartae*. They thereby introduced into this passage a conspicuous corruption, which crept into almost all manuscripts [Col. 0944B] as well as printed copies. For the edition corrected by Janus Parrhasius and the Florentine Juntine edition preserve the true reading.

The story of Euripides, Ovid, and others is well known; the author himself mentions it again in Book VI, ch. 16. Cadmus sowed the dragon’s teeth, from which armed men sprang up; in Greek they were called Σπάρτοι, that is, “the Sown Men.” Censorinus, *On the Natal Day*, ch. 3: “But now,” he says, “the licence of poetic invention has advanced to such a point that it invents things scarcely tolerable to hear. After human memory, when nations had already been propagated and cities founded, it represents men as brought forth from the earth in various ways: thus, in the Attic region, Erichthonius is said to have arisen as a man from Vulcan’s seed; and in Colchis or Boeotia, after the teeth of a serpent had been sown, armed *Spartae*”—for so, or Σπάρτοι, must also be read there, not, as corruptly in printed editions, *armati partus*, “armed births,” as the same Guilielmius most rightly observed in Book III of his *Verisimilia*, ch. 5—“are said to have sprung forth; after mutually killing one another, a few are said to have survived, who assisted Cadmus in founding Thebes,” etc.

Apollodorus, near the beginning of Book III of the *Library*, where he treats of Cadmus [Col. 0944C]: “Therefore Cadmus, angered, killed the dragon; and, at Minerva’s advice, sowed its teeth. When these had been sown, armed men sprang from the earth, to whom the name *Sparti* was given. Later they killed one another with mutual wounds: some indeed engaged in combat even unwillingly, while others did so because none recognized another,” etc. On them see Gellius, Book XVII, ch. 3. He reports that Marcus Varro mentions the Homeric line occurring near the beginning of Iliad II:

> And now the timbers have decayed, etc.

Euripides also mentions them both elsewhere and in the *Phoenician Women*; so does Eustathius on the phrase in Iliad II, φάριντε, Σπάρτηντε; and Stephanus of Byzantium, under “Sparta.”

Arcesilaus, founder of the Academy. That is, of the New Academy; for the Old Academy was Platonic: Diogenes Laertius, in *Arcesilaus*; Cicero, *On Ends*, Book I; *Academic Questions*; and *On the Orator*, Book III.

## CHAPTER VI

“For, in order to know that nothing can be known, it is necessary that something be known,” etc. Ancient and modern writers have asked whether those who denied all apprehension of truth could nevertheless reserve and retain for themselves the truth of this one proposition as the conclusion of their philosophy: namely, that no truth can be given, upon which the denial of every other truth depended. That is: this truth is granted—that no truth can be granted. Lactantius affirmed this here, and long before him Socrates, Antipater, Antiochus the pupil of Philo—of whom Cicero speaks in the *Academics*—then Clement of Alexandria at the end of the *Stromata*, Averroes, *Metaphysics*, Book IV, text 28, St Thomas, *Prima Pars*, question 2, article 1, reply to objection 3, and his interpreter Cajetan there. Arcesilaus and Carneades denied it in Cicero, as cited above; likewise Metrodorus of Chios, Lucretius, Book IV, John Duns Scotus, *Sentences*, Book I, distinction 2, question 2, reply to objection 3, and Gregory of Rimini, same distinction, question 1, reply to objection 2. On this matter see Mazzoni, my fellow citizen, who discusses it subtly and sheds light upon this passage of Lactantius: Book I, *On the Comparison of Plato and Aristotle*, section 3, ch. 2.

## CHAPTER VII

[Col. 0945A]

Epicurus holds that the highest good consists in pleasure of the mind. What is stated here concerning philosophers’ opinions about the highest good is almost entirely drawn from the end of Cicero’s *Lucullus* and from Book II of *On Ends*. Some indeed believed this concerning Epicurus, although most writers affirm that he placed the human good in bodily pleasures. Moreover, Lactantius himself is not wholly consistent: below, in ch. 17, he calls Epicurus an advocate of bodily pleasure, and in ch. 27 a man devoted to pleasure. From Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, Book II, it is clear that Seneca—though the greatest of the Stoics, whose doctrines strongly reject bodily pleasures—was an especially zealous admirer of Epicurus; for he wished almost all his letters to conclude with some precept of Epicurus. His judgment of Epicurus appears in chs. 12 and 13 [Col. 0945B] of *On the Happy Life*.

But Epicurus himself states clearly and expressly what highest good, and what pleasure, he declares to be the end, in his Letter to Menoeceus, preserved by Laertius in his *Epicurus*; Cicero also mentions this doctrine in Book I of *On Ends*. Pietro Vettori, *Various Readings*, Book XXVII, ch. 14, contends that Epicurus was very similar to Socrates. Laertius testifies that most people said he was extremely self-controlled, so that he was content merely with water and coarse bread.

Callipho and Dinomachus, Cyrenaics. I do not fully understand how Lactantius calls these philosophers Cyrenaics, since they combined moral excellence with pleasure in establishing the highest good, whereas this position differs enormously from the doctrine of Aristippus, who placed the highest good in bodily pleasures alone. Certainly Cicero, at the end of the *Lucullus* and in Book III of *On Duties*, Strabo at the end of Book XVII, Laertius in *Aristippus*, Suidas under eta, and Lactantius himself in this same book, ch. 15, testify that Aristippus was the head of the Cyrenaics and that this philosophical school derived from him.

Diodorus, with freedom from pain. Hieronymus placed the highest good in not suffering pain. This passage must unquestionably be read and punctuated thus, as Ciacconius long ago observed; both reason itself and Cicero, from whom Lactantius borrowed almost all this material, prove it. For if one reads: “Diodorus placed the highest good in freedom from pain; Hieronymus in not suffering pain,” as is commonly printed, what difference will remain between Diodorus’ opinion and Hieronymus’ opinion? But Cicero makes clear that the difference is this: Diodorus did not place the highest good simply in not suffering pain, but joined moral excellence to freedom from pain; Hieronymus, however, placed it simply in not suffering pain, with no addition. Cicero, *On Ends*, Book II, shortly after the beginning: “Callipho added pleasure to moral excellence; Diodorus added freedom from pain to the same moral excellence.” And a little below: “Callipho added nothing to virtue but pleasure, Diodorus nothing but freedom from pain”; and later: “Thus there are three ends devoid of moral excellence: one of Aristippus or Epicurus, another of Hieronymus, and the third of Carneades; and three in which moral excellence is joined with some addition: those of Polemo, Callipho, and Diodorus,” etc. He repeats the same point at the end of the *Lucullus* and in Book III of *On Duties*.

## CHAPTER VIII

“The Cyrenaics say that virtue itself is to be praised because it produces pleasure,” etc. Thus Cicero at the end of *On Duties*: “Those called Cyrenaic and Annicerean philosophers, following Aristippus, placed every good in pleasure; and they held that virtue was to be praised because it produced pleasure.” These positions therefore do not conflict: they both placed the highest good in pleasure and nevertheless regarded virtue as praiseworthy. For they embraced pleasure simply and for its own sake, whereas they embraced virtue not for its own sake but for pleasure itself—that is, only insofar as it was, as it were, a cause or occasion of pleasure for them.

Not exactly of the Peripatetics. Janus Guilielmius, in his *Questions on Plautus’ Menaechmi*, ch. 4, thinks one should read *plano Peripateticorum*, so that, by a novel compound formation, Lactantius mocked both the inconsistency of Aristotelian argument and the wandering walk of the Aristotelians; for wandering rogues are known as *plani*.

But of the Cynics. Here too Janus thinks, in the same place, that *Clinicorum*, “of the Clinicians,” should be read; he testifies that it is so read in some manuscripts. Lactantius would then be making the ridiculous assertion that the “Clinicians” were sick men fixed to beds and discussing the happy life of healthy persons—what their present illness dictated—and would be alluding to clinical physicians, who attend the beds of the sick.

That no philosopher whatever has arisen who discovered the seat and dwelling-place of the highest good. He refutes the ancient opinions concerning the highest good: Aristotle, *Ethics*, Book I, ch. 6; Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy*, Book II; St Thomas, *Against the Gentiles*, Book III, ch. 27 ff.; and *Summa Theologiae*, I–II, entire question 2.

“And they are desired,” etc. The negation must not be added, as in B., which reads “and they are not desired,” etc. For he denies that riches are the highest good, and proves it by the argument that they do not fill the mind; indeed, they are desired ever more and more even by those who possess them. Seneca, Letter 120, “Whenever something”: “Money,” he says, “has made no one rich; indeed, on the contrary, it has instilled in everyone a greater desire for itself. Do you ask the cause? I think that because *Mures* was not a sufficiently familiar name, it was rejected as if an error; hence “and the two Decii never,” etc., was written, as in Vatican manuscript 1 and Pen. Or perhaps τὸ Decii, placed in the margin as a gloss upon the words “and the two Mures,” at length crept into the text, producing: “and the two Mures Decii never,” etc., as many printed editions have it. “In this one respect we can be happy in this life: if we appear least happy.” These words accord wonderfully with those of our Saviour in John 12: “He who hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life.”

“To which, casting aside all else, Socrates is said to have devoted himself.” Namely, by Xenophon, *Memorabilia of Socrates*, Book I; Aristotle, *Metaphysics*, Book I, ch. 5 and Book XIII, *Summary*, Book II, ch. 1, and *Parts of Animals*, Book I, ch. 1; and Laertius, in *Socrates*.

## CHAPTER XIV

“For you, a vessel at the fountain.” All printed editions and many manuscripts read *tibias ad fontem*, “pipes at the fountain.” When, in order to discover the explanation of this saying, I had gone through all Greek and Latin authors and made no progress, I at last suspected an error and thought of consulting the Vatican manuscripts [Col. 0947B]. In ten of them I found it written as I have had it printed: certainly aptly and most suitably to Firmianus’ meaning. I think the error entered because perhaps the exemplar from which copyists transcribed had these two words joined as *tibivas*; since that had no sense, they immediately wrote *tibias*. “For you, a vessel at the fountain” is, I think, a proverb borrowed from some comic poet. It can apply to one for whom something falls out according to wish and advantage without effort, by analogy with someone who comes to a fountain without a jar but nevertheless, by good fortune, finds there a vessel ready at hand with which to draw and carry away water. Yet I have nowhere else thus far discovered the proverb.

Accordingly, Lactantius jokes in his usual way and attacks Lucretius, who said that wisdom was discovered by some man, as though that man whom he praised—whether Pythagoras, Thales, or whoever else he was—had encountered wisdom lying somewhere ready-made, so that the proverb [Col. 0947C] “For you, a vessel at the fountain” could apply to him.

“And fashioned man.” All printed editions so read; but B. and P. have “and begot man.” Both expressions are familiar to Lactantius: Book IV, ch. 4: “For it is necessary that he fashioned man,” etc.; Book VII, ch. 14: “The fashioning of the earthly man prefigured the future formation of the heavenly people”; Epitome, ch. 7: “For since human nature is weaker than that of the other living creatures, which God fashioned both equipped for inflicting force and fortified for repelling force.”

“But for me, not merely toward wisdom,” etc. Sigonius thinks this passage has fallen out from some book of the *Academic Questions*.

“The precepts of philosophy must indeed be known,” etc. These are thought to have fallen out from the letters to his son Marcus.

## CHAPTER XV

[Col. 0947D]

Philosophy, etc. You have similar passages in Letter 90, “A useful thing”; 91, “Who doubts”; and 95, “That part of philosophy.”

“How few philosophers,” he says, etc. This passage is read somewhat differently in the *Tusculan Disputations*.

“You would think they had volunteered evidence.” I have followed the reading of manuscript B. and the Juntine edition, together with Thomas: namely, *indicium professos putes*. The alternatives found in some manuscripts and printed editions—*in judicium suum*, *in judicium sui*, or *judicium suum professos putes*—seem insufficiently Latin, as Budé also observes, and insufficiently suited to express Lactantius’ meaning. To “volunteer evidence” (*indicium profiteri*) means voluntarily to report and denounce oneself and one’s accomplices as parties to a crime. Martianus, Law I, Digest, under the Cornelian Law on Assassins: “Or whoever, being a magistrate or presiding over a public court, has exerted himself so that someone might volunteer false evidence.” This is how Budé reads the passage in his *Annotations on the Pandects*. Prateius, *Treasury of Civil Law*, under “to volunteer evidence,” and Brisson, Books IX and XIV, *On the Meaning of Words*. Scaevola, in the law *Athales*, Digest, under the Cornelian Law on Forgery: “He volunteered evidence”—thus the Florentine Pandects read—“against Maximilla,” [Col. 0948A] etc. Sallust, *Jugurthine War*: “But when he himself was apprehended, at the encouragement of many, and especially of the consul Albinus, he volunteered evidence.” Asconius: “Nor can a person of senatorial rank volunteer evidence while the laws remain intact.” Suetonius, *Domitian*: “Having volunteered evidence concerning the conspiracy and for this reason been admitted, he read aloud a written statement handed over by himself and, while [the emperor] was astonished, stabbed him in the groin.” Pliny, *Letters*, Book III, Letter 16: “When she volunteered evidence before Claudius against Scribonianus’ wife, he said: ‘Am I to hear you, in whose lap Scribonianus was killed, and you still live?’”

Thus, while philosophers fiercely declaimed against the lustful, the greedy, and seekers after honour, they themselves were overwhelmed by the same crimes. Everyone understood that the abuse which they launched publicly overflowed back upon themselves, so that by their arguments they seemed to achieve nothing except to confess voluntarily that they were guilty of the same vices, and deserving of the same censure and punishment. They accused and denounced before the people not others alone, but themselves along with them. This, as we said, is “to volunteer evidence.”

[Col. 0948B]

“Aristippus, master of the Cyrenaics, had an affair with the famous courtesan Lais,” etc. Cicero, *Letters to Friends*, Book IX, final letter, to Papirius Paetus; Athenaeus, Book XII, ch. 20; Laertius, in *Aristippus*.

“Maintaining that bodily pleasure is the highest good.” Therefore Xenophon, hostile toward him, composed a book against pleasure, as Laertius reports in *Aristippus*.

## CHAPTER XVI

“Civic men, who govern the republic.” This passage of Cicero has been lost.

“Certainly,” he says, “the whole discussion of those men,” etc. This passage is thought to have fallen out from Cicero’s *Hortensius*, or *On Philosophy*. There one should read *istorum*, “of those men,” as Andreas Patricius also observed in his *Annotations on Cicero’s Fragments*, and as is found in all Vatican manuscripts and B., T., P., and the other best manuscripts; not *justorum*, “of the just,” as corruptly in printed editions. Then, in the clause, “I fear that it seems to have brought to human affairs not so much an enjoyment of leisure,” I have followed the more accepted reading [Col. 0948C]. For this is the reading of nine Vatican manuscripts, P., the Aldine edition, and Lambinus’ corrected edition of Cicero’s works; Patricius approves it in the cited *Annotations*. The printed editions read “not so much”; the manuscripts read “lest not so much”; B. reads: “lest it seem to have brought to human affairs as much benefit as enjoyment to leisure.” Patricius also offers other readings; but, to confess the truth, none pleases me, nor do I wish to guess.

“Not yet a thousand years ago,” he says, etc. See also Seneca’s Letter 91, “Who doubts.”

“With wares of flavour,” etc. Gulielmus Canter, *New Readings*, Book III, ch. 30, reads *Saporis* with a capital S, thinking Lactantius speaks of the wares of Sapor, king of the Persians. But this explanation cannot be accepted in any way, since it cannot be fitted to the verse of Persius cited here, who lived many years before King Sapor. It was therefore rightly refuted by Robert Titius, *Controversial Passages*, Book IX, ch. 3. He provided, as I think, the true and sound interpretation: namely, Lactantius thought that Persius in this place meant that philosophy had been brought into the city with wares of flavour—that is, flavoured or savoury goods—which had begun not long before to be imported from Asia, such as pepper and other spices of that sort. Meanwhile Lactantius alluded to the name *sapientia*, “wisdom,” which he wishes, almost contemptuously, to derive from *sapor*, “flavour,” as though wisdom acquired its name from those wares with which it was itself brought to us. Titius accordingly holds that *sapōris* is the plural ablative of the adjective *saporus, sapora, saporum*, newly formed indeed by Lactantius, but by imitation and analogy of similar words: from *odor*, *odorus, odora, odorum*; from *vapor*, *vaporus*; from *canor*, *canorus*; from *honor*, *honorus*, etc.

## CHAPTER XVII

[Col. 0948D]

“But because the popular name of pleasure attracts many.” Yet Lactantius above, ch. 7, maintained that Epicurus was an advocate not of sensory pleasure [Col. 0949A] but of pleasure of the mind.

“Let him himself disturb his own.” Lucretius: “often let him disturb his own,” etc.

“In the books of his Consulship.” These have been lost; but the verses which he cites occur in *On Divination*, Book II, where the second verse differs slightly. There it reads:

> He himself once sought his own tombs and temples.

“There is no ordering,” he says; “for many things occurred otherwise than they ought to have occurred,” etc. Everything which Lucretius raves is Epicurus’, as Firmianus himself said in *On the Workmanship [of God]*, ch. 6. Here, therefore, he alludes to Lucretius, Book II, near the beginning:

> But some, ignorant of matter, argue against these things, etc.

And Book V, near the beginning:

> If I were now ignorant what the first beginnings of things are, etc.

“Nothing,” he says, “in the procreation of living creatures,” etc. Lucretius, Book IV:

[Col. 0949B]

> There is in these matters one very grave fault, and that error  
> Must be avoided and shunned by forethought:  
> Do not make lights for the eyes, etc.

“But everything must occur spontaneously,” etc. Namely, by the collision of infinitely many atoms. Lucretius, Book II, near the end:

> First, in every direction around us, etc.

“There is no need,” he says, “of providence; for seeds fly through the void,” etc. Lucretius, Book II:

> Now come, by what motion the generative bodies of matter  
> May produce various things, etc.

“Because they have neither colour,” he says, “nor any heat,” etc. Lucretius, Book I:

> Now come: since I have taught that things cannot be created  
> From nothing, etc.

Likewise in Book II:

> Now come, receive what has been sought by my sweet labour and expressed,  
> etc., to the end of the book.

[Col. 0949C]

“These little bodies?” Aristotle, *On the Soul*, Book I, text 20; Lucretius, Books I and II *On the Nature of Things*; Cicero, *On Ends*, Book I, and *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book I; Plutarch, *Opinions*, Book I; Laertius in *Epicurus*; and Lactantius himself again, *On the Anger of God*, ch. 10.

“They meet in varying order and position.” Lucretius, Book II:

> Now come: next, what are the beginnings of all things, etc.

“So he says, and these first elements themselves: for some are rough, some hooked,” etc. Lucretius, Book II:

> It is now very easy for us to unravel the reasoning of the mind.

“He dimmed the stars.” I did not hesitate to restore this verse in Lactantius, as it is read in corrected editions of Lucretius. For *extinxit*, “extinguished,” which is also found here in some editions of Lucretius [Col. 0949D], or *restrinxit*, “checked,” found in others, do not seem to express Lucretius’ meaning as he intended it. See Lambinus, *Corrections on Lucretius*, Book III, verse 1056.

“When death is, we are not.” This is certainly the true reading from B., T., P., all Vatican manuscripts, and Epicurus himself in the Letter to Menoeceus preserved by Laertius; not the commonly printed reading, “when we are not, death is.”

“At which point even we are no longer.” I think this reading cannot possibly be approved, although it is found in every manuscript and printed edition; for it conflicts with Lactantius’ argument against Epicurus. If there is some time when we are no longer and death is not yet present, Epicurus rightly says that at that time death is nothing to us. But Lactantius wishes to show the actual fact: namely, that there is some instant when we still are—when we begin to die—and yet death is not yet [Col. 0950A] present, that is, completed and past, but has merely begun. At that time it inflicts great pains and miseries upon the dying person, and consequently is to be feared. Therefore I believe that I can confidently swear that Lactantius wrote: “at which point we still are,” etc. This reading fits the preceding as well as the following words most aptly. For he says: “as though completed death were feared, because sensation has already been removed, and not dying itself, by which sensation is removed.” You see that Lactantius speaks of death not as completed, but as impending—namely, at the point when it removes sensation. If it removes sensation, then we still are. He also says: “and this very thing seems wretched: that death begins to be, and we begin to cease to be.” How do we begin to cease to be if, according to the earlier reading, we are already no longer? In truth, we begin to cease because we have not yet ceased; we still are, and death is not yet completed and past, because it is only beginning to exist and to inflict pains. Hence it rightly ought to be feared, as Lactantius said and Epicurus denied. The genuine reading, in my judgment, is therefore supplied by a very slight change: merely placing the conjunction after the pronoun and replacing the negative particle in the word *num*.

## CHAPTER XVIII

“Like Cleanthes.” He wasted away by voluntary starvation. Laertius.

“Like Chrysippus.” This is not so certain concerning Chrysippus; some report that, after drinking rather too freely, he was distressed by shortness of breath and finally died; others that he expired from excessive laughter. Laertius.

“Like Zeno.” Laertius likewise asserts that he was killed not by a voluntary death but by death inflicted by others.

“Like Empedocles, who cast himself into burning Etna,” etc. Horace’s well-known lines in the *Art of Poetry*:

[Col. 0950C]

> While he longed to be deemed an immortal god,  
> The ardent Empedocles leapt into burning Etna, etc.

“He leapt,” etc. But Strabo, Book VI, says this is fabulous, and Laertius observes that writers give varying accounts of his death.

Cato. Namely the Younger, as in Seneca, Letter 24, “The anxious man,” and Plutarch’s *Life of Cato*.

Democritus. Besides Lucretius, Athenaeus, Book II, ch. 3, and Laertius.

“For, just as we do not come into this life by our own will,” etc. Lactantius took this from Cicero’s *Dream of Scipio* and *Tusculan Disputations*, Book I; Cicero from Plato, at the beginning of the *Phaedo*.

“And, compelled by philosophy’s authority, he was driven to the greatest crime.” But Plato did not teach that. On the contrary, he maintained that man is under God’s guardianship and may not depart unless God wills it, as is clear from the beginning of the *Phaedo*. He did indeed advise that the soul should be separated from the body: that it should be separated from disturbances through purification by moral discipline, then from the senses and imagination itself through the concentration of contemplation. Therefore Cleombrotus was driven to so great a deed not by philosophy’s authority but by his own madness, since he failed to understand philosophy’s meaning.

[Col. 0950D]

“That Ambraciot,” etc. Namely Cleombrotus, concerning whom Callimachus and Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, Book I.

“That foolish old man,” etc. Namely Pythagoras, concerning whom Laertius, Philostratus, *Life of Apollonius*, Book VIII, and Gellius, Book IV, ch. 11. Observe here how Lactantius mocks the doctrine that souls were created before bodies—a doctrine some have attributed to Lactantius himself.

## CHAPTER XIX

“And let us rejoice.” This passage has fallen out from those books *On the Laws*.

“That foolish opinion.” Of Euripides and others. Stobaeus and Theodorus Canter, *Various Readings*, Book II, ch. 12, produce the verses of Euripides from Greek writers, and likewise those of Aristophanes. Plato’s words occur in the *Gorgias*: “Yet that life which you call grievous is grievous; nor should I be surprised if Euripides spoke truly in this matter: ‘Who knows whether to live is really to die, and to die to live?’” etc. [Col. 0951A] Cicero, *Dream of Scipio*: “Indeed,” he says, “those live who have flown out from the chains of their bodies as from a prison; but your so-called life is death.” And in the first *Tusculan Disputation*, somewhat after the middle: “For this life is indeed death, which I could lament, if I wished.”

“To die as soon as possible, as though escaping a fire, [is to escape] the violence of fortune.” Andreas Patricius approves this reading in his *Annotations on Cicero’s Fragments*. Some old books, and Francesco Petrarch, *Seniles*, Book I, letter to Giovanni Boccaccio, read: “to escape fortune as soon as possible, as though escaping a fire.” Six Vatican manuscripts, whose reading Sigonius follows in his notes on Cicero’s fragments, read: “to die as soon as possible, and as though escaping a fire, to escape the violence of fortune.” Four other Vatican manuscripts: “as soon as possible, as though escaping a fire, to escape the violence of fortune.”

[Col. 0951B]

“It did not occur to Plato that Alcibiades too and Critias,” etc. This appears to have been taken from Xenophon, *Memorabilia of Socrates*, Book I, who testifies that Socrates’ accusers also added to their charges that Critias and Alcibiades, after hearing Socrates, inflicted many evils upon the state. Xenophon refutes that slander at length there. But Isocrates, in the *Busiris*, denies that Alcibiades was ever Socrates’ pupil.

## CHAPTER XX

“Doubtless he meant what he said: that religion is by no means to be observed.” He presses a calumny against Socrates; Xenophon explains in the *Memorabilia* how Socrates’ statement should be understood. Besides, who among pagans ever discoursed more devoutly about the gods above, divine providence, and religion than Socrates himself, disputing with Euthydemus at the beginning of Book IV of Xenophon’s *Memorabilia*, and frequently in Plato?

“The same man swore by a dog and a goose.” As one often reads in Plato, and as Athenaeus mentions, Book IX, ch. 20. Tertullian reproaches Socrates in ch. 14 of the *Apology* because he swore not only by a dog, as an insult to God, [Col. 0951C] but also by a sheep and an oak. But Apollonius, discussing the matter with Thespion in Philostratus, *Life of Apollonius*, Book VI, says that Socrates customarily swore by such things not because he regarded them as gods, but so as not to swear by the gods. St Augustine likewise interprets these oaths of Socrates favourably in *On True Religion*, ch. 20.

“A recuperator.” Thus it should be read, as in the Aldine edition, although B., T., P., and the Florentine edition have *receptorem*. Lactantius says ironically that Socrates feared that, if summoned by Aesculapius before Rhadamanthus the judge in a recuperatory action, he might be condemned by the recuperator for the cock he had vowed. Recuperators were judges, as Theophilus writes in the section *Eadem*, *Institutes*, “By what causes manumission is not permitted,” because through them each person recovered what was owed to him. I would have preferred *recuperabat*, so that it better served the etymology he offered. Recuperators are mentioned by Cicero, *On Invention*, Book II, and at the end of the speech *For the Manilian Law*; Suetonius, *Vespasian*, ch. 3; Pliny, second-last letter of Book III.

## CHAPTER XXI

[Col. 0951D]

“To consist in equality.” Here *aequitas* is not ἐπιείκεια, “equity,” but ἰσότης, “equality.”

“Marriages too,” he says, “must be held in common.” Aristotle also writes against Plato on this in *Politics*, Book II; but Cardinal Bessarion explains him in Book IV, ch. 3, *Against the Calumniator of Plato*.

“The city will be harmonious,” etc. Plato does not state this verbatim, but the doctrine is gathered throughout Book V of the *Republic*.

## CHAPTER XXII

“For there will be nothing withheld as another’s property.” Very many printed editions and manuscripts preserve this reading, and it is excellent, whatever Thomasius may say. For we speak quite correctly of an object being “withheld” (*abstineri*), as though held at a distance and kept back. Lactantius, Book VII, ch. 17: “He will withhold the rains,” etc. [Col. 0952A] Livy: “In the Roman war Fortune kept Alexander the Great away.” The Florentine edition reads: “for there will be nothing by which one is withheld,” etc.; Bon.: “for there will be no one whom he keeps from another’s property.” But the first expression, which we approve, is as much more elegant as it is more recondite and less commonplace.

“Marriage-beds.” I restored *geniales toros*, as I found it in certain Vatican manuscripts, and as Pietro Faber long ago advised in Book II of the *Semestria*, ch. 1, and Johannes Meursius in Book IV, ch. 10, of his *Critical Notes on Arnobius*. Others read *genitales toros*.

“In the circle of the earth.” I do not sufficiently understand on what rhetorical principles the consummate rhetor Lactantius here—and in Book II, ch. 14; Book IV, chs. 1, 14, and 24; and frequently elsewhere—calls it the *orbis terrae*, “circle of the earth,” while below, ch. 24, he denies that the earth has a spherical shape.

## CHAPTER XXIII

“If he had given [it away].” Valerius Maximus, Book VIII, chapter “On Study and Industry,” writes that he did indeed give it to his country. Lactantius followed Cicero, *On Ends*, Book V; Seneca, *On Divine [Col. 0952B] Providence*, near the end; and Philo, *On the Contemplative Life*, near the beginning.

“What of the man who converted his patrimony into money and poured it into the sea?” He means Crates the Theban philosopher, following Philostratus in the *Life of Apollonius*, who writes that he came to poverty in this way; Suidas says the same under Anaxagoras. But Demetrius of Magnesia, cited by Laertius in *Crates*, and Suidas under Crates Asconidae, say that he deposited his whole estate, converted into cash, with a banker on the condition that, if his sons were ordinary men, it should be restored to them, but, if philosophers, it should be distributed to the needy; for he thought that philosophers would lack nothing.

“Who approves Zeno’s equal sins?” Cicero approves them in the *Paradoxes*, and Cato in Cicero’s speech *For Murena* and at the end of Book IV of *On Ends*.

“That has always been ridiculed by everyone.” Plutarch indeed reports that it was ridiculed by the entire Senate, in his comparison of Demosthenes with Cicero, while Cicero himself, pleading Murena’s case against Cato, mocked that doctrine of Zeno.

[Col. 0952C]

“That he might become savage at the sight of another person.” This is the reading of the Aldine and Florentine editions, Pen., and many other manuscripts, from which I did not wish to depart, though Thomas, with B. and T., reads: “that he might be removed from the sight of another person.” Lactantius speaks against Zeno, who removed the emotion of pity from man. But if pity were removed, human feeling would necessarily become savage. “If man,” Lactantius says, “became savage in the manner of solitary-roaming animals, society would be abolished.”

“He who said that snow is black.” He alludes to Anaxagoras, as below in Book V, ch. 3; Galen reports this of him in *On the Powers of Simple Medicines*, Book II. Aristotle, *Topics*, Book I, end of ch. 9, said that he lacked understanding.

“This is that man,” etc. He argued against him above, ch. 9.

“That another earth exists within the hollow bosom of the moon.” Besides Xenophanes, who is said in Cicero’s *Lucullus* to have held this view, Pythagoras too seems to have believed that the moon and other stars contain the four elements, mountains, valleys, plants, and everything found among us. Yet, as Iamblichus warns in *On Pythagorean Symbols*, these things were stated mystically by them; St Thomas reports this at the end of his commentary on Aristotle, *On the Heavens*, Book II, text 49: because the forms of effects are in some manner in their causes, and the heavenly bodies are causes of lower bodies, etc.

[Col. 0952D]

“Seneca says that among the Stoics there was [one] who,” etc. I have read nothing of this in Seneca.

## CHAPTER XXIV
What of those who think that there are Antipodes, opposite to our own footprints? Cicero discusses them in the *Lucullus*. Lactantius indeed asserts many paradoxes in this chapter, for which reason he is hissed at by some. Although I admit that he departed from the truth, yet since, as I shall presently show, he had very weighty and very wise men as either authors or adherents of his opinions, [Col. 0953A] I should certainly think those more deserving of hissing who have thought that so distinguished a man ought so rashly to be hissed at. First, he holds that there are no Antipodes—a view also maintained by Eratosthenes, Polybius, Strabo, Tzetzes in the *Chiliads*, and Lucretius at the end of Book I. This position is likewise asserted by Plutarch in the dialogue *On the Face in the Orb of the Moon*. Among our own writers, St Augustine, *City of God*, XVI.9, Nicholas of Lyra at the beginning of his commentary on Genesis, and afterward all who denied that the earth is spherical, held the same view; concerning these, a little below. Yet the true view concerning the Antipodes, contrary to this, is established by Macrobius, Book I of the *Dream of Scipio*, where in chapter 5 he refutes Lactantius’ arguments; by Pliny, *Natural History* II.65; Martianus Capella at the beginning of Book VI; Cleomedes, *Meteorology* II.2; Manilius, *Astronomy* I; and St Augustine, contradicting himself, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis* II.9. The philosopher Posidonius, disciple of Panaetius, and Avicenna too are reported formerly to have held this opinion; nor can any doubt on the matter remain even in these times, [Col. 0953B] since, through the genius and courage of that most illustrious Ligurian hero, the glory of our Italy, Christopher Columbus—rival of the sun—the peoples of the once unknown other hemisphere have now been discovered and thoroughly explored.

“Hanging gardens,” etc. Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapter 14.

“And from the motion of the stars they supposed that heaven revolves.” Lactantius denies that heaven revolves; and with him also the philosophers whom I listed above, chapter 3, final note, col. 354, and very many Holy Fathers and Doctors: Justin Martyr, answering Question 93 to the Orthodox; Chrysostom, Homilies 6 and 13 on Genesis, and Homily 12 to the people of Antioch; Caesarius at the end of Dialogue I; Elias of Crete on Oration 7 of Nazianzen; Isidore, *Etymologies* III.49; likewise Severianus and Acacius, who believed the world to be a hemisphere and heaven to be motionless, stretched out like a tent and vaulted like an arch or chamber; Junilius, *On the Hexaemeron*; Richard, *Exceptions* II; Diodorus and Procopius in their commentaries on Genesis. Philastrius writes in his book *On Heresies* that this opinion accords with the sacred [Col. 0953C] Scriptures, whereas the contrary opinion is discordant and agrees rather with pagan vanity than Christian truth. St Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis* II.10, thinks it can be defended. It has nevertheless been rejected by most philosophers and mathematicians, as may be seen in the proper places, especially in Aristotle, *On the Heavens* II, text 43 and following.

“This, therefore, roundness of heaven.” Not Lactantius alone denied that heaven is round, but also Justin Martyr, answering Questions 59 and 130 to the Orthodox; Basil, Homily 1 on Genesis; Chrysostom, Homilies 14 and 27 on Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews, and Homily 2, *On the Incomprehensible Nature of God*; Ambrose, *Hexaemeron* I; Theophylact and Theodoret on chapter VIII of the Epistle to the Hebrews; Caesarius and Procopius, cited above; Haimo, Severianus, and Acacius; likewise Primasius on the Epistle to the Hebrews; Euthymius on Psalm CIII. Elias of Crete, cited above, says this:

> Isaiah taught that heaven is not spherical or globular, but has a shape resembling half a globe and is motionless, when he says: “He set heaven like a chamber”; likewise, “he fixed heaven.” Many similar statements are found in the same prophet, both concerning the stretching out of heaven in the form of a tent and concerning its firm establishment. David too mentions the ends of heaven, as does Christ himself in the Gospels. But neither a chamber-like form nor extremities have a place in a sphere or globe, which is carried round in every direction; nor likewise do establishment, solidification, or other motions of this sort. Hence almost all Fathers skilled in divine things, rejecting the spherical or globular figure of heaven and its circular motion as a fabrication of the Greeks and a product of reasoning, followed the words of the prophets as divinely inspired.

The contrary view, namely that heaven is round, is approved by all philosophers and astronomers. Ptolemy demonstrates it by nine arguments, Book III, chapter 1 of the great edition; Aristotle, *On the Heavens* II, text [Col. 0954A] 22 and following. The Holy Fathers also affirmed the same: Nazianzen, Oration 4 against Julian; Oration 2 on Theology; Oration on Holy Baptism; Chrysostom, Homily on Psalm CXVIII; St Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis* I.10 and II.9; Bede, *On the Six Days of Creation* and in the *Questions on Genesis*. It also seems more consonant with Sacred Scripture. At the beginning of Ecclesiastes: “The sun rises and sets and returns to its place; and, rising again there, it turns through the south and bends toward the north. The wind proceeds, surveying all things in its circuit, and returns to its circles.” On this passage see St Jerome. Likewise Ecclesiasticus XXIV: “I alone traversed the circuit of heaven,” etc. The Greek is more expressive and exact: ἐκύκλωσα, “I led around; I made round; I made spherical.” Job IX: “Under him are bent those who bear the world.” Proverbs VIII: “When by a fixed law and circle he enclosed the deeps.” To the passages of David, Psalm CIII, and Isaiah XL, where heaven is said to have been stretched out by God like a tent, chamber, or skin, St Augustine responds in the cited chapter 9 of Book II, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*.

[Col. 0954B] “Even the earth itself, like a globe.” Plato too, in the *Timaeus*, assigns not a spherical shape to the earth but a cube; nevertheless, almost all assign it a spherical shape. See Strabo, Book I; Pliny, Book II, chapter 64; Martianus Capella, Book VI. Ovid’s verses in *Fasti* VI are most beautiful: “The earth is like a ball,” etc. Sacred Scripture likewise shows it to be globe-like, when it so often calls it the *orbis* of the earth; for that word *orbis*, as Lactantius himself explains in chapter 8 of *On the Workmanship of God*, signifies nothing but roundness. Isaiah XL: “He who sits above the circle of the earth”; or, according to the Hebrew reading: “He who sits above the globe of the earth.” Moreover, Lactantius himself very often calls it the *orbis* of the earth, as we noted a little above; and in *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 8, he admits that every roundness belongs to perfect reason and form. Was the world then suited to an imperfect form and figure, or rather to the most perfect of all, from the supreme maker? The opinion, therefore, of all philosophers, astronomers, and cosmographers is that the earth, [Col. 0954C] heaven, and indeed the world are spherical. The theologians agree in *Sentences* II, distinction 14, especially St Bonaventure, article 2, question 1; Durandus, question 4; and St Alexander of Hales, Part II, question 50, member 6, article 3. They clearly show that this shape suits it above all by reason of its simplicity, capacity, perfection, and nobility.

## CHAPTER XXV

“The mystery of his beard alone is celebrated, and of his cloak.” For those who profess philosophy, he says, seem to possess nothing philosophical except a deep beard and a cloak; hence arose the proverb, “wise only as far as the beard.” On this see the author of the *Adages*. Thus below, *On the Anger of God*, chapter 22: “They boast of wisdom in their hair and dress.” For in former times those professing philosophy wore long hair and a beard, and clothed themselves in a cloak. Gellius recounts a witty jest about this, Book IX, chapter 2.

“Phaedo.” Diogenes Laertius notes, in his lives of Socrates and Phaedo, that he was redeemed from captivity. Thus it should be read, not, as it is corruptly given in some copies, “Protagoras” or “Pythagoras.”

“They report Cebes.” So Gellius, Book II, chapter 18, and Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.11. Laertius, however, in his life of Phaedo does not state clearly enough whether Phaedo was redeemed, at Socrates’ urging, by Alcibiades or by Crito. Yet afterward, in his life of Socrates, he writes that it was by Crito.

“Plato and Diogenes.” See Seneca, Letter 47, *Libenter*; Gellius and Macrobius, cited above; Laertius in Plato.

“But slavery had befallen them; for they were captives.” Phaedo too was not a slave, as Lactantius seems to think; rather, slavery had come upon him, if we follow Laertius, who writes that he was born of a noble family and captured with his native city. Yet Gellius and Macrobius, cited above, agree with Lactantius.

“He ought to have weighed out gold.” I think he alludes to the beginning of Iliad XXIV, where Homer represents Priam weighing out gold to ransom Hector’s corpse from Achilles:

> Χρυσὸν δὲ στήσας etc.  
> “Having weighed out gold,” etc.

## CHAPTER XXVII

“Which [rises] from heaven.” Lucretius: “which [rises] from the head of heaven,” etc.

“When things are not traceable.” Thus the old manuscript codices; the printed editions corruptly read: “when things are not investigable.”

## CHAPTER XXVIII

“And I raise my hand.” Thus B., T., and P.; Petrarch recognized this reading in *Seniles* VIII, Letter 1, and Patrizi approved it in his notes on Cicero’s fragments. Others: “from raising my hand.”

“Aristotle, says Cicero, [accused] the ancient philosophers,” etc. Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* III, reads: “Aristotle, accusing the ancient philosophers who had thought philosophy perfected by their own talents, said that they had been either exceedingly foolish or exceedingly boastful; but that he saw,” etc.

## CHAPTER XXIX

“Because, says the same Cicero, it produces many things unforeseen by us,” etc. Cicero: “because it brings about many things unforeseen and not expected by us,” etc.

“Therefore, in the beginnings of transgression, he was not at once cast down by God into punishment,” etc. He does not deny that the devil is now afflicted with essential punishment, as I showed above, Book II, chapter 15; rather, he speaks of the punishment of being cast down, by which he denies that the devil is now afflicted, as is clear from the text. I gave the Doctors’ opinions in the cited chapter 15. See also below, Book VII, chapter 26.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0955]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0955B]

“While I reflected, and often considered with my mind,” etc. Others: “While I reflected, Emperor Constantine, and with my mind,” etc. But in B., T., the Florentine edition, and several others, the words “Emperor Constantine” are not read.

## CHAPTER II

“Yet they did not approach the Jews.” I do not know whether they approached the Jews; but they did go to Egypt, as Lactantius himself admits, and there drew some teaching from Moses, as Justin Martyr says in the *Exhortation to the Greeks*. They also learned certain mysteries of the Jews who had remained in Egypt, so much so that Numenius affirmed of Plato himself that he was “Moses speaking Attic.” On this subject see much material in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* II, and Theodoret at the beginning of *Cure of Greek Affections* I.

“But I think that they were turned away by divine providence, lest they might know the truth.” Not because God turned them away, but because he permitted them to be turned away by their free choice. Since this permission of God is willed by him through a positive act, [Col. 0955C] as theologians teach, God’s permission is therefore often called an action of God, not only by the Fathers but sometimes by Sacred Scripture itself: because he permits a person to be hardened, blinded, or turned away, he is said to harden, blind, or turn that person away. I shall explain this more fully below, chapter 20.

## CHAPTER III

“His hand and fingers are in it,” etc. What is said here, and seems like an enigma, I explained in Book I, chapter 20.

“And the son is manumitted like a slave,” etc. Although *emancipate* properly applies to children and *manumit* to slaves, the latter is nevertheless sometimes said also of children, since to manumit is nothing other than to release from the hand—that is, from authority. See § *Praeterea*, *Institutes*, “By what means the right of paternal power is dissolved.” The jurist uses this word in Law II, *Digest*, “On the Office of a Proconsul”; Law 28, *Digest*, “On Adoption”; Law 107, *Digest*, “On Verbal Obligations”; and the title “If anyone is manumitted by a parent.”

“And a freed slave takes the patron’s name.” Examples are the two freedmen of Marcus Tullius Cicero, one called Marcus Tullius Tiro and the other Marcus Tullius Laurea; and the poet Livius [Col. 0955D] Andronicus, whom Eusebius in the *Chronicle* reports to have been granted freedom by Marcus Livius Salinator, whose sons he had educated. See Politian, *Miscellanies*, chapter 31.

## CHAPTER IV

“Disinherited sons.” It was a Greek custom that children who stubbornly opposed their father’s will and honourable conduct should be disinherited by their parents, once the ground for disinheritance had been approved before a judge. Grounds of disinheritance are read in Lucian and Quintilian’s *Declamations*. A disinherited child lacked maintenance and every form of paternal assistance during the father’s life, and after his death lacked succession to his property. Disinheritance is mentioned by Aristotle at the end of Ethics VIII and by Seneca, *Controversies* III. This custom was not permitted to pass to the Romans, as stated in the law *Abdicatio*, *Code*, “On Paternal Authority,” which Alciato explains and restores, *Dispunctiones* II.28.

## CHAPTER V

“About seven hundred years.” Most printed editions read “about nine hundred years” or “about nine hundred years” [accusative]. Two Vatican manuscripts have “about nine hundred years.” Seven others of the same Vatican manuscripts have “about seven hundred years” or “about seven hundred years” [accusative]. Finally, one of them, while having “nine hundred” in the text, has written in the margin: “elsewhere, seven hundred.” Therefore, this reading of seven hundred years seems more common in the manuscripts; at least it certainly contains less error. For we cannot deny that Lactantius erred, whichever reading one follows. Although chronologists differ remarkably, and although Eusebius himself does so in the *Chronicle* and in *Preparation for the Gospel* X.3, it is nevertheless agreed that Moses lived no more than about four hundred years before the Trojan destruction. If you read “about nine hundred years,” the error is greater, and Lactantius will have followed the calculation of the impious Porphyry, which Eusebius corrects in the preface to the *Chronicle*. The reader should further be warned not to accuse Lactantius or any other writer too severely should he perhaps be found mistaken somewhere in calculating chronology; rather, he should judge him worthy of pardon and excuse. For histories and chronographies concerning matters of so remote a time are surrounded by so many and such great obscurities; opinions vary so widely; scribal errors are so numerous, especially in numerical signs, that nowhere is it easier to err, even for men of the greatest learning, diligence, and memory, than in chronology. Besides Eusebius, one should consult Cyril, who writes in *Against Julian* I that Troy was destroyed 410 years after Moses; Eutropius I; Bede, *On the Reckoning of Time* II; and Vives on chapter 8 of *City of God* XVIII.

“He had Jesus as successor.” As is evident from the end of Deuteronomy. Instead of “Jesus,” which is in B., T., P., and in Lactantius himself below in this book, chapters 14 and 17, “Joshua” is commonly read; and indeed the one whom the Hebrews call both Joshua and Jesus is called by the interpreters both Joshua and Jesus. The Apostles themselves and the Septuagint correctly call him Jesus, because he prefigured our Lord Jesus Christ not only by his deeds but by his very name, [Col. 0956D] as Lactantius himself says below, chapter 17.

“Who held command for twenty-seven years.” So too Eusebius in the *Chronicle*, St Augustine, *City of God* XVIII.10, Sulpicius Severus, Isidore, and Carion. But Josephus, *Antiquities* V.4, writes twenty-five years, followed by Hermann in his *Chronicle* and the author of the *Sacred Chronicle*; Bede, John Lucidus, and some others give seventeen.

“Afterward they were under judges for three hundred and seventy years.” To see that Lactantius’ total may come very near the truth, observe first that from the number of judges whom he thinks governed the people for so many years, he excludes Moses and Joshua, as the expression “afterward” plainly indicates. Second, it must be noted that this total includes only the years during which the people were under the judges themselves, while subtracting and not counting the years of interregna, during which they were under foreign kings, mentioned in Judges III, IV, VI, X, and XIII. Therefore the twelve judges who governed the people after Moses and Joshua, and whose history is set forth in the sacred Book of Judges, governed for 299 years, as Sacred Scripture itself and all chronographers and historians unanimously report. See Hermann in the *Chronicle*, under Samson, and the Master of Scholastic History, Book of Judges, chapter XX, at the end. Now let us add Eli and Samuel to those twelve judges. Let us give forty years to Eli’s government, a number found in Josephus at the end of the final chapter of Book V of the *Antiquities*, and in the old and Vulgate Latin edition at 1 Samuel 4, and likewise in the printed Greek codices of the version of the Septuagint; as Flaminius de Nobilibus observes in his annotations on the Old Testament translated into Latin from that Greek version and recently printed at Rome, as does Melchior Cano, *On Theological Topics* II.5, at the end, and Genebrard in *Chronography* I under Eli. To Samuel, however, let us assign from the same Josephus, *Antiquities* VI.13, twelve years during which he alone governed the people after Eli; for Sacred Scripture does not state how many years Samuel governed separately from Saul, [Col. 0957B] who was the first king. Then let us add eighteen years during which he governed with Saul, as Josephus reports in the same Book VI, chapter 13 and at the end of chapter 14, along with very many chronographers, especially Genebrard in the cited Book I of *Chronography*, under Samuel and Saul. We shall thereby arrive at precisely the total of 370 years, lacking only one year, during which Lactantius says that judges governed the people after Joshua until the kings.

Nothing in the Greek text of Acts of the Apostles, chapter XIII, stands against this sum of 370 years, where the Apostle Paul in his address to the Hebrews says:

> Καὶ καθελῶν ἔθνη ἑπτὰ ἐν γῇ Κανάαν κατεκληροδότησεν αὐτοῖς τὴν γῆν αὐτῶν, καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα ὡς ἔτεσι τετρακοσίοις, καὶ πεντήκοντα ἔδωκε κριτὰς, ἕως Σαμουὴλ τοῦ [Col. 0957D] προφήτου·

That is: “And having destroyed seven nations in the land of Canaan, he distributed their land to them by lot; and after these things, for about four hundred and fifty years, he gave judges, until Samuel the prophet.” For most learned men consider this text to contain an error and believe it should be restored according to the reading of the Vulgate Latin edition, so that it reads:

> Κατεκληροδότησεν αὐτοῖς τὴν γῆν αὐτῶν ὡς μετὰ τετρακόσια καὶ πεντήκοντα ἕτη, καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα ἔδωκε κριτὰς ἕως Σαμουὴλ προφήτου·

That is: “He distributed their land to them by lot, as though after four hundred and fifty years; and after these things he gave judges until Samuel the prophet,” etc. Here the number of approximately 450 years is understood by the Apostle Paul as referring to the time of the children of Israel’s dwelling in Egypt, not to the age of the Judges, as Genebrard shows at length in *Chronography* I, under the age of Jacob and under the age of Samuel; and Bede, the Master of Scholastic History, [Col. 0958A] Lyra, the Carthusian, and the rest likewise understand the same passage of Acts.

“Then, after the order had changed, they began to have kings; and while these held power for four hundred and sixty years, until the reign of Zedekiah,” etc. B. and seven Vatican manuscripts read “for four hundred and fifty years.” I have given the reading found in five Vatican manuscripts, in P., and in the Aldine, Florentine, and other printed editions, because it contains less error. To show this more clearly and remove every ambiguity, I first note that in examining this calculation one must not take account of the reign of the kings of Israel, but of the reign of the kings of Judah. We must recall what is related in 1 Kings XII and 2 Chronicles X: in the first year of the reign of Rehoboam, son of Solomon—Rehoboam being the fourth king of the Hebrews—a rebellion arose among the Hebrews. For the ten tribes, fearing that Rehoboam would be a harsh and cruel king, made Jeroboam their king; while the tribes of Judah and Benjamin followed Rehoboam. Thus the Hebrew monarchy was split into two kingdoms, which never afterward returned to unity. [Col. 0958B] The kingdom of the two tribes was called the kingdom of Judah, or of the Jews, because of the dignity of the royal tribe. The kingdom of the other ten tribes was called the kingdom of Israel, retaining the name of their father Jacob because of their greater number. Nineteen kings are counted in this kingdom of Israel: Jeroboam, who began to reign in the first year of Rehoboam king of Judah, son of Solomon, as stated; Nadab, Baasha, Elah, Zimri, Omri, Ahab, Ahaziah, Joram, Jehu, Jehoahaz, Joash, Jeroboam, Zechariah, Shallum, Menahem, Pekahiah, Pekah, and Hoshea. In the ninth year of the latter’s reign this kingdom came to an end. That ninth year was the sixth of the reign of Hezekiah, sixteenth king of Judah, as stated in 2 Kings XVIII. The whole kingdom of Israel thus comprises 241 years, seven months, and seven days, as is evident from Scripture itself in 2 Kings XIV, XV, XVI, and XXII, and 2 Kings XVIII. I say, therefore, that this kingdom is not counted, because Lactantius plainly indicates that in giving this total of 460 years he looked to the succession of the kings of Judah when he says: “Then, after the name had changed, they began to have kings.” So too below, chapter 10. For immediately after the judges came Saul’s reign, then those of David and Solomon, kings of Judah; and the series of the kingdom of Israel did not begin until the first year of Rehoboam, son of Solomon, as we have said. Lactantius further adds “until the reign of Zedekiah,” who belongs to the kingdom of the Jews, for he was its final king. Thus it is plainly evident that Lactantius, in mentioning both the beginning and end of the kingdom of the Jews here, had regard to the kingdom of Judah.

In this kingdom I find twenty-three kings of the Jews after Samuel, whom we have placed in the position of the last judge, beginning with Saul, but only from the time when he reigned alone after Samuel’s death. That period was two years, as is clear from 1 Samuel XIII and Josephus, *Antiquities* VI, at the end of the final chapter. Counting through Zedekiah, as Lactantius says, inclusively [Col. 0958D]—that is, including Zedekiah’s own eleven years of rule—I find that these twenty-three kings reigned in all for 475 years, six months, and ten days, although Josephus, *Antiquities* X.10, writes 514 years, six months, and ten days. See Eusebius, Hermann, and others. Thus Lactantius’ calculation lacks fifteen years, six months, and ten days.

[Col. 0959B] “Until the reign of Zedekiah: attacked by the king of Babylon and taken captive, the Jews endured a long servitude.” I have written “Zedekiah,” not “Sedechiah,” as in earlier editions; for I think Lactantius pronounced and wrote the name as it appears in the Septuagint and the Vulgate. “Until the reign of Zedekiah,” he says—that is, inclusively, as we have said. For the attack on the Jews by the king of Babylon occurred in the ninth year of Zedekiah’s reign, 2 Kings XXV; Jeremiah XXXIX and LII. It lasted until the eleventh, that is, final, year of his reign; in that year the captivity of the city Jerusalem and its people followed, as is stated in the same passages. From this it is clear that the opinion is correct of those who hold that the seventy years of this captivity must be reckoned and begun from no other point than this eleventh year of Zedekiah’s reign, just as Lactantius begins and reckons them here: Josephus, *Antiquities* X.10; Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* I; Africanus, *Annals* V; Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* III, final chapter, and *Demonstration* in the discussion of the seventy weeks; Jerome on Ezekiel IV; Cyril, *Against Julian*; Isidore, *Origins* V, final chapter; Bede, *On the Six Ages*. Although I know that the same years are begun and reckoned elsewhere by other very eminent writers: some reckon them from the thirteenth year of King Josiah, of whom Eusebius makes mention without naming them in the *Chronicle* under Olympiad 58; others from the captivity of King Jehoiakim, which occurred in the first year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign, such as Sulpicius, *History* II; Theodoret on Daniel 9; Lyra on Ezra I; Vatablus in his annotations on Daniel IX; and still others from the deportation of Jehoiakim or Jeconiah, such as Rabbi Solomon, cited by Lyra and Cajetan on the final chapter of 2 Chronicles, and Scaliger, *On the Correction of Times*.

“Until, in the seventieth year thereafter, Cyrus the Great restored them to their lands and homes.” Here too authors differ concerning the date when the Jewish captivity was ended. Some prefer that the seventy years of the Jewish captivity were not completed before the second year of Darius Hystaspes, by which forty years had elapsed from the first year of Cyrus. On this view, only thirty years elapsed from the desolation of Jerusalem to the first year of Cyrus. Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* I; Eusebius in the *Chronicle* and *Preparation for the Gospel* X, final chapter, and *Demonstration* VIII; Jerome in the prologue to Haggai, on Zechariah I, and Daniel IV; Augustine, *City of God* XVIII.26; and Isidore, *Origins* V, final chapter, held this view. Others distinguish between the years of the Jews’ captivity, which they begin with the deportation of Jeconiah and end in the first year of Cyrus, and the years of the desolation of the city and Temple, which they begin in the eleventh year of Zedekiah’s reign and end in the second year of Darius Hystaspes, as Theodoret on Daniel 9. But Lactantius’ position is truer and more accepted: namely, that Cyrus ended the captivity. This is written not only by Josephus [Col. 0960A] in *Antiquities* II.1, Africanus, *Annals* V; Sulpicius, *History* II; Cyril, *Against Julian* VIII; Bede, *On the Reckoning of Time*; and Pererius on Daniel X.9, but also by many of the writers listed above who hold the other opinion in other places: namely, Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* X, final chapter, and St Jerome on Jeremiah 29.

“Who assumed rule over the Persians at the same time as Tarquinius Superbus at Rome.” This does not altogether accord with the chronology of the others; for about twenty years elapsed between Cyrus’ assumption of power and the reign of Tarquinius Superbus, though writers differ slightly, as happens in nearly all chronologies. See Eusebius in the *Chronicle*.

“That those may recognize their error who strive to accuse Sacred Scripture as new and recently invented,” etc. See Josephus, *Against Apion* I; Justin Martyr, *Against the Gentiles*; Theophilus, *To Autolycus* III; Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* X.3; Theodoret, *Cure of Greek Affections* II. Certainly Pythagoras, considered the most ancient of Greek sages, is placed by Eusebius in the *Chronicle* as contemporary with Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, the last of the prophets.

## CHAPTER VI

“He had created through him.” From B., T., P., the Florentine edition, and Plantin, I have restored to the text the words *through him* (*per ipsum*), omitted by the Aldine and certain other editions; for Lactantius’ statement thus agrees beautifully with John 1: “All things were made through him,” etc.

“He honored him with the appellation of the divine name.” No; rather, he possesses it by his own nature, as Lactantius himself admits below, chapter 29, and frequently elsewhere.

> Παντατρόφον κτίστην  
> “Creator who nourishes all things.”

Eugubinus explains these verses in *On Perennial Philosophy*; they occur in Theophilus, *To Autolycus* II, but not in the Sibylline Oracles.

> Αὐτὸν ἔδωκε etc.  
> “Him he gave,” etc.

This verse is defective in the Sibylline poems; for there it reads:

> Ἀλλ᾽ ὃν ἔδωκε θεὸς πιστὸν ἄνδρα γεραίρειν.  
> “But [he gave] whom God [appointed], to honour a faithful man.”

> Αὐτὸν σὸν etc.  
> “Him, your …,” etc.

In the Sibylline codex, σοῦ (“of you”) is read in place of σόν (“your”).

“God created me,” etc. The passage is from Proverbs VIII. Let it be sufficient to warn the reader once that the Scripture passages quoted by Lactantius are generally quoted, like those of the other ancient Fathers, from the version of the Septuagint interpreters, although he sometimes differs somewhat even from the version which we now possess, as we shall carefully note in the appropriate places. One might therefore reasonably suspect that the Septuagint edition of those times differed in some places from that now extant. Here, certainly, instead of “God,” the Septuagint, Vulgate, Tertullian in *Against Hermogenes* and *Against Praxeas*, and Cyprian in *Against the Jews* II, have “the Lord.”

“In the beginning of his ways.” Thus the Vulgate. But Tertullian, *Against Hermogenes*, and Cyprian, *Against the Jews* II.1, from the Septuagint: “the beginning of his ways.”

“In his works before the ages. He founded me in the beginning,” etc. In the punctuation and division of this passage, Lactantius and Tertullian differ from the Septuagint and Cyprian. For the Septuagint reads: “in his works. Before the age he founded me in the beginning,” etc.; Cyprian: “in his works, before the age he founded me. In the beginning,” etc.

“In the beginning.” Lactantius, Cyprian, and Irenaeus, Book IV, chapter 37, give it better than Tertullian, who omits these two words, which occur in the Hebrew, Chaldean, and Greek text.

“Fountains came forth.” The Septuagint and Cyprian: “fountains proceeded.”

“He begot me.” So too Tertullian and Cyprian, in place of the Septuagint’s γεννᾷ με, “he begets me.”

“He made regions and uninhabitable lands under heaven.” B. and T.: “he made regions and uninhabitable boundaries,” etc. The Septuagint: “The Lord made regions, and uninhabitable places, and their inhabited heights under heaven.” Cyprian: “he made regions and uninhabitable places”; others: “inhabited places and uninhabitable boundaries under heaven.”

“When he prepared heaven,” etc. Others here read “when he brought forth.” I followed the best manuscripts of Lactantius, which have the same reading as the Septuagint, Tertullian, Cyprian, and Hilary.

[Col. 0961A] “When he separated his seat, when he made strong clouds above the winds.” In the Septuagint we read the passage divided so that “above the winds” is joined with “seat,” not with “clouds”: “when he separated his seat above the winds, and when he made the clouds strong from above,” etc. Yet it is rightly noted here that Tertullian, Cyprian, and Hilary have precisely Lactantius’ reading. For Tertullian: “and when he made strong above the winds those clouds which are aloft”; Cyprian: “when he made strong clouds from above, over the winds”; Hilary: “when above the winds he made strong clouds in the height.”

“And when he set the mountains firm under heaven.” Instead of “mountains,” the Septuagint reads “fountains”: “and when he set firm his fountains which are under heaven.” Tertullian likewise: “and when he set firm his fountains which are under heaven”; and Cyprian: “and when he set firm fountains under heaven.”

“I rejoiced before his face, when he rejoiced.” The Septuagint: “I rejoiced in his presence at all times, when he rejoiced,” etc. The phrase “at all times” is also found in the Vulgate and Cyprian, though Tertullian omits it, as Lactantius does.

## CHAPTER VII

“His name is unknown even to the angels.” The theologians dispute whether holy angels and blessed souls, who clearly behold God, can comprehend his true and proper name; see *Sentences* I, distinction 22, and St Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, Part I, question 13, article 1, as I noted above on Book I, chapter 6.

> Ὅσιος περὶ τοῦ μόνου Κυρίου πάντων, καὶ προεννοουμένου Θεοῦ.  
> “Holy [is he] concerning the sole Lord of all, and God conceived beforehand.”

I have restored these words to Lactantius—or rather to Hermes—from codices B. and T.; some lack ὅσιος περὶ τοῦ μόνου Κυρίου (“holy [is he] concerning the sole Lord”), while others lack καὶ προεννοουμένου Θεοῦ (“and God conceived beforehand”).

“Christ is not a proper name,” etc. The author of the *Exposition of the Apostles’ Creed* among the works of Cyprian.

“Those who customarily call him Chrestus, with a letter changed.” Even then the name bears the meaning “good,” for it is derived from ἀπὸ τοῦ χράομαι [“to use; be useful”] and means “good, pleasant, suitable, useful.” Justin Martyr, *Apology for Christians* to Antoninus Pius; Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 3.

> Αὐτοὺς δὲ δμωαὶ etc.  
> “And the handmaidens [them],” etc.

A verse of Homer, slightly altered from the beginning of *Odyssey* IV; there it reads: τοὺς δ᾽ ἐπὶ οὖν δμωαί etc. (“then the handmaidens [attended] them,” etc.).

## CHAPTER VIII

“Blessed was he,” etc. I find nowhere the passage from Jeremiah that Lactantius adduces.

“From the beginning.” That is, from eternity; for this expression is often thus explained even in Scripture: Ecclesiasticus XXIV, “From the beginning, and before the ages, I was created,” etc.

“How, then, did he beget?” Sacred Scripture sometimes also uses the vocabulary of creation when speaking of uncreated Wisdom and the eternal emanation of the Word. Since the procession of the eternal Word is ineffable and is revealed to a rational creature wholly unfit for understanding divine things, the Holy Spirit ordinarily employs many different expressions to explain it. The Holy Fathers afterward sometimes borrowed these expressions; they must be understood not properly but metaphorically (*μεταφορικῶς*) and loosely. Divine Wisdom and the uncreated Word are said to be created, not because they are made from nothing, but so that we may understand that the Word is not produced from pre-existing matter; likewise, that the Father undergoes no change or alteration, as happens in created generations. Such expressions, however, must not be used by us, but must be interpreted according to the sense of the Church whenever they occur in Sacred Scripture or the writings of the Holy Fathers.

“Or even reason.” I understand that these words, absent from the printed editions, have rightly been restored by me from codex B.; for at the beginning of the following chapter Lactantius says that the Greeks call the Son of God more aptly *logos* (λόγος), because, since he is the voice and wisdom of God, *logos* signifies both “word” and “reason.”

There is a great difference between this Son of God and the other angels [Col. 0962A], etc. Above, on the words in Book II, chapter 9, “That first and greatest Son,” etc., we have plainly shown that Lactantius held a true and correct view concerning the only-begotten Son of God: that he believed him to be true God and consequently believed his nature to differ infinitely from the nature of angels. Therefore, as we said there, when he calls angels “sons of God” together with the divine Word, that designation is not to be referred univocally to the Word himself and to the angels, as though it applied to all equally; rather, it is equivocal—that is, proper to the divine Word, but improper and metaphorical in regard to angels. So here we observe that, conversely, where Lactantius calls the Son of God an Angel—as here, above in chapter 10, and below in chapter 14, according to the alternative reading—the name “Angel” is not to be referred univocally to the Son of God himself and to angels. Rather, it applies properly to angels, as signifying their nature and substance; but improperly to God’s only-begotten Son, so that the term denotes not his nature but the ministry and office of an envoy and messenger. [Col. 0962B] For *angelus* in Greek is called *nuntius*, “messenger,” in Latin, because the only-begotten Son of God performed the greatest of all embassies—namely, that of redeeming the human race—an office for which no other was sufficiently fit. In this sense St Augustine, vol. VI, in the tract on “I am who am,” judges that Christ the Lord may safely be called an angel: in office, namely, not in nature. We shall speak again below, in chapter 14.

“For those silent spirits went forth from God.” And below: “But the spirits of God both live and remain,” etc. I fear that he thinks angels proceed from God’s substance! I have shown above, on Book II, chapter 13, that he says something of the kind somewhere concerning human souls. I warn the reader to be on guard.

“But he, although himself also spirit, nevertheless proceeded from the mouth of God with voice and sound, like a word,” etc. He now attempts to explain the Son’s emanation from the Father and why he is called the Word of God. But he merely circles around the matter; he does not reach it. Nor should this surprise anyone, for the mystery of the most holy Trinity remained profoundly hidden and concealed in God’s Church for many [Col. 0962C] centuries. Indeed, he ineptly employs the analogy of a created spoken word in order to lead us toward knowledge of that uncreated divine Word. Yet it is not by an analogy of a spoken word, but of the mental word within us, that, as St Augustine says in *On the Trinity*, XV.11, the Word of God is in some fashion seen “as in a mirror, in an enigma.” Lactantius himself here admits that God the Father conceived it in his mind; and since God is wholly incorporeal, the divine generation can be understood only according to an intellectual emanation. Setting aside, therefore, what Lactantius puts forward, let us instruct the reader thirsting for Catholic truth.
