First, the word of the mind is nothing other than knowledge, or a conception of the mind: St Augustine, *On the Trinity*, IX.7 and 11, and XV.10; St Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, I, question 34, article 1, and on John 1. This inner conception, which St Thomas sometimes calls a “species,” as in *Commentary on the Sentences*, I, distinction 27, question 2, article 2; sometimes “the conception of the thing understood,” as in *Against the Gentiles*, I.11; and “the understood intention” [Col. 0962D], as in *Against the Gentiles*, IV.11; and “the conception of the intellect,” in the same work, IV.12—this is properly, and most properly, called a word, because by means of it the soul speaks: St Augustine, cited chapter 10. For there is in the mind a true and proper utterance and speech, and a proper and true saying and speaking, which is understanding; and consequently there is a true and proper word, namely the very conception of the mind. This is indeed much more true and proper than a spoken word; and the name “word” principally signifies the conception of the mind, as St Augustine teaches in the place cited above. For that reason, the position that the conception of the mind is not properly a Word would not be free from danger. For in the signification in which “Word” signifies knowledge, it also signifies the Son of God. Therefore, if it signified a conception improperly, it would likewise signify the Son of God improperly; and hence the Son of God would improperly be Word, and consequently would not be Word—positions which are heretical and contrary to John 1: “In the beginning was the Word,” etc. St Thomas, in *Commentary on the Sentences*, I, distinction 27, question 2, article 1, teaches that it must be confessed without any doubt that the Son of God is the Word and is properly called Word; and in *Summa Theologiae*, I, question 34, article 1, reply to the first objection, he asserts that it is an error of the Arians to deny that the Son of God is properly Word.

Now the same St Thomas—the summit alike of all divine and human wisdom—teaches in *Against the Gentiles*, IV.11, how the uncreated Word is produced in the divine mind. There are, namely, several modes and degrees of understanding, just as there are several degrees of intellectual life. For although the human intellect can understand itself, it takes the beginning of its knowledge from without, because it does not understand without a phantasm. Therefore, in angels there is a more perfect mode of understanding: their intellect does not proceed from anything external in order to know itself, but knows itself through itself. Yet something is lacking to complete and absolute perfection, because although the understood intention is wholly intrinsic to them, [Col. 0963A] that understood intention is not itself their substance, since in them understanding and being are not identical. The final perfection of life therefore belongs to God, in whom understanding is not one thing and being another. Hence the intention understood by God—that is, his Word—must be the divine essence itself.

Therefore, in God understanding himself, there is the Word of God, as it were God understood, just as the word of a stone in the intellect is the stone understood. But because the divine intellect does not pass from potency into act, but is always actual, it is necessary that God has always understood himself; and because he understands himself, it is necessary that his Word is in him. Thus the Word of God has always existed in God and is therefore coeternal with him. Again, since the divine intellect is not only always actual, but is itself pure act, the substance of the divine intellect must be its own understanding, which is the act of intellect. But the being of the inwardly conceived Word, or understood intention, is its being understood. Therefore the being [Col. 0963B] of the divine Word and of the divine intellect is the same, and consequently the same as that of God himself, who is his own intellect. But God’s being is his essence or nature—which is the same thing as God himself. Therefore the Word of God is divine being itself, his essence, and true God himself.

Finally, the production of the Word in the divine mind is generation in the strictest sense, and the Word produced is, in the strictest sense, the Son of God. This is demonstrated from the definition of generation properly so called, which St Thomas draws in *Summa Theologiae*, I, question 27, article 2, from Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics* VIII and *Metaphysics* VII. For generation is the origin of a living being from a conjoined living principle, in likeness of nature. But in divine things the living divine Word proceeds from the living Father, and there is there a principle conjoined with both generator and generated: for the divine essence, which is most inward to the Father and is the root of generation, is conjoined—or rather, communicated in its very self—to the generated Son. And the proceeding Word proceeds according to the character of likeness, because the conception of intellect is the likeness of the thing understood; and it proceeds in the same nature, for in God understanding and being are identical. Therefore there is there, in the strictest sense, a Son of God, and sonship and generation much more fully than in created things. For, as St Thomas teaches, *Summa Theologiae*, I, question 13, articles 5 and 6, because certain things are found in God and in creatures, they are present in God in a more noble and perfect manner and are first predicated of him. [Col. 0963D]

Accordingly, he is rightly called both the Speech and the Word of God. He is called Speech in Wisdom 18, John 17, and by the Fathers: Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*; Cyprian, *Against the Jews*, II.1 and 5, who, when citing John 1, “In the beginning was the Word,” puts *Sermo*, “Speech,” for “Word”; Augustine, who, expounding John 17, “His speech is truth,” etc., teaches that it makes no difference whether we say *Sermo* or *Verbum*; Hilary, who in his books *On the Trinity* calls him now Word, now Speech; and likewise Jerome, on the Epistle to the Ephesians. Yet he seems more fittingly called Word than Speech, since *verbum* properly signifies one thing and a single utterance, whereas *sermo* signifies either one or many. Therefore, in order to show that the Son of God is one and utterly simple, insofar as he is God, he is more fittingly called Word than Speech. [Col. 0964A]

“Our spirits are dissoluble, because we are mortal.” Here I would suppose that by “spirit” he means breath, for he continues speaking about speech and utterance. He should not be thought to assert this of our souls, since everywhere he teaches that they are immortal.

“How much more the voice of God,” etc. Thus a little below: “If anyone is astonished that God came forth from God by the utterance of a voice,” etc. All expressions of this sort ought to be avoided. The passages of Scripture which he adduces speak of the mouth of the heart and of the mental word.

“Of whom the latter, who reigned later, preceded the destruction of the city of Troy by one hundred and forty years.” This reading, found in one of the Vatican manuscripts, is beyond doubt the true and authentic reading. In saying that the destruction of Troy occurred before Solomon (for I shall speak later of the number of years), it agrees with all chronographers and with Lactantius himself. The alternative reading of nearly all other manuscripts and printed editions, which has “of whom one,” etc., produces the opposite sense and says that Solomon existed before the destruction of Troy. This certainly greatly contradicts the chronology of history and Lactantius’s view explicitly stated elsewhere. At the end of the first of these books he reckoned 1,470 years from the destruction of Troy to the time at which he was writing. He was writing, as we showed above, in the year 302 after Christ’s birth. Therefore, if from that sum of 1,470 years you subtract the 269 years that elapsed from Christ’s death to Lactantius’s writing, surely 1,201 years elapsed, according to Lactantius’s reckoning, from the destruction of Troy to the death of Christ the Lord. [Col. 0964B]

Now if you follow the common reading and add to this total the 140 years which you would suppose elapsed from Solomon to the destruction of Troy, the whole period from Solomon to Christ’s death would be 1,341 years. This plainly conflicts sharply with Lactantius’s statement below, in chapters 16 and 18 of this book, as noted there, that only 1,010 years elapsed from Solomon to Christ’s death. But if, on the contrary, you adopt our reading and subtract from the said total of 1,201 years the 140 years which we maintain elapsed from the destruction of Troy to Solomon, you will see that all Lactantius’s statements agree with one another; and there emerges a total of 1,061 years from Solomon to the death of Christ the Lord, according to Firmianus’s view.

Do not, however, be surprised that more years emerge—namely fifty-one beyond the said total of 1,010 years given in the cited chapter 16. You will understand that approximately the same period is designated in both places if you observe that here the years are reckoned from the destruction of Troy to Solomon’s birth, and from that birth to Christ’s death; whereas there the calculation begins, not with Solomon’s birth, but from the time when he was already reigning and uttering that prophecy about Christ which Firmianus there cites, and continues to the death of Christ the Lord. Solomon reigned for forty years, as is clear from Sacred Scripture, 3 Kings 2 and 2 Paralipomenon 9; from Josephus, *Antiquities* VIII.7; and from Lactantius below, chapter 13. He lived ninety-four years, as Josephus likewise reports in chapter 7. Thus fifty-one years, and indeed three years besides, may well have elapsed from Solomon’s birth to the earliest time at which he prophesied about Christ. From this it is altogether most likely that Lactantius wrote thus, and not otherwise through a lapse of memory, as Vives thought in his note on Augustine, *City of God* XVIII.20, and Thomasius here in his notes. [Col. 0964C]

From the destruction of Troy to Lactantius’s writing: years 1470  
From these, subtract the years from Christ’s death to Lactantius’s writing: 269  
There remain from the destruction to Christ’s death: years 1201  
Add the years from Solomon to the destruction, according to the common reading here: 140  
There result from Solomon to Christ’s death: years 1341  
Contrary to Lactantius, who below, chapter 16, calculates from Solomon’s prophecy to Christ’s death: years 1010  

Again, from the destruction to Christ’s death: years 1201  
From these subtract the years from the destruction to Solomon’s birth, according to the authentic reading of this passage: 140  
There remain from Solomon’s birth to Christ’s death: [Col. 0965A] years 1061  
From these subtract the years from Solomon’s birth to the time when he prophesied: 54  
There remain from the time of Solomon’s prophecy to Christ’s death: years 1007.

“Preceded by one hundred and forty years.” Chronologists do not agree: Eusebius has 170 years; Glareanus, 147.

“By the Word of God.” Tertullian: “by the Speech of God”; Cyprian likewise.

“And by the spirit of his mouth.” Aldus and Plantin have “and in the spirit,” etc. I have retained the reading of the Florentine edition, which is found in the Septuagint, the Vulgate, and Cyprian. But Tertullian, *Against Praxeas* and elsewhere, has “and by his Spirit.”

“A good Word.” Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, II; Cyprian, *Testimonies* II.3: “a good Speech.”

“Likewise Solomon,” etc. This passage is cited from Ecclesiasticus 24. Although this book is not by Solomon but by Jesus son of Sirach, as appears from the prologue of that book in the Bibles, the custom of those times prevailed—as St Augustine notes, *City of God* XVII.20—of calling it Solomon’s, either because of its likeness in style or because it seemed compiled from Solomon’s sayings. Therefore it is cited under Solomon’s name not only by Lactantius, but also by other Fathers: Cyprian, who adduces this same passage in *Against the Jews* II.1; Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* VII; Basil, *Against Eunomius* IV; Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 8; and very many others; likewise the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 43. [Col. 0965B]

“I,” he says, “came forth from the mouth of the Most High before every creature.” Cyprian agrees with Lactantius. But St Ambrose, *On the Faith* IV.4, gives the Septuagint’s reading, which has merely, “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High”; while the Vulgate has: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn before every creature.”

“I caused unfailing light to rise in the heavens.” These words are not found in the Septuagint, but in the Vulgate and in Cyprian.

“And I covered the whole earth with a cloud.” Cyprian has the same. But the Septuagint has, “and like a cloud I covered the earth”; the Vulgate: “And like a cloud I covered the whole earth.”

“I dwelt in the heights.” What is read in the Septuagint as *en hypsēlois* (ἐν ὑψήλοις), Lactantius renders *in altis*, “in the heights.” Cyprian’s manuscripts vary: some have this, others “in the highest places”; and so do the recent Latin translation from the Septuagint and the Vulgate.

“And without him nothing was made.” Here a full stop is placed; then follows, “but the Greeks better [punctuate it],” according to nine Vatican manuscripts and all printed editions. But two of the same Vatican manuscripts read: “And without him nothing was made.” Full stop. Then: “but the Greeks better,” etc. One Vatican manuscript has: “And without him nothing was made”: here a colon is placed, and then follows continuously, “What was made in him was life.” Here again there is a full stop; then follows, “but the Greeks better,” etc. From these readings it seems sufficiently clear that Lactantius punctuated and read the passage of John’s Gospel thus: “And without him nothing was made. What was made in him was life”—taking “what was made” not with the preceding words, “and without him nothing was made,” but with the words of the following clause, “in him was life.” This is contrary to the view of Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Euthymius. [Col. 0965C]

For Chrysostom says in Homily 4 on John: “When we have said, ‘Without him nothing was made,’ we must not mark this with a full stop, as the heretics suppose; for they, wishing the Spirit to be a creature, read: ‘What was made in him was life.’ But this expression can certainly be understood in no way.” Theophylact says in his Commentary: “The Pneumatomachians, who deny that the Holy Spirit is God, read this clause thus: ‘And without him nothing was made.’ Then, placing a full stop here, they read, as though from another beginning, ‘What was made in him,’ etc., and interpret this passage according to their own view, saying that the Evangelist is speaking here of the Holy Spirit: ‘What was made in him,’ that is, the Holy Spirit, ‘was life.’ The Macedonians say this in attempting to show that the Holy Spirit is a creature and to number him among things made. But we do not read it thus; rather, after placing a full stop after ‘what was made,’ we begin anew: ‘In him was life,’ etc.” Euthymius says nearly the same.

But however much one places a full stop after the word “nothing,” the passage in no way supports the error, nor does it do anything for the heretics. Cyril, Augustine, and St Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, I, question 18, article 4, read it in this manner; so too, as some report, does the Complutensian Bible—although all the Bibles in my library, especially those printed at Rome by command of Sixtus V in 1593, have it entirely as Chrysostom does. [Col. 0966A]

## CHAPTER IX

“And the wisdom of God.” That which is wisely devised is called someone’s wisdom. But in God, as St Thomas teaches, *Against the Gentiles* IV.12, wisdom must be called so from the fact that he knows himself. But because he knows himself not through some species but through essence—indeed, because his very act of understanding is his essence—God’s wisdom cannot be a habit, but is God’s essence itself. But the Son of God is the Word and the conception of God understanding himself; therefore the Word of God itself, as wisely conceived in the divine mind, is properly called the wisdom of God.

“Even the philosophers did not fail to know this divine Speech.” Their testimonies are adduced by Augustine of Eugubium, *On the Perennial Philosophy* I.23 ff.

## CHAPTER X

“And the man whom he had put on, whom he bore,” etc. Such expressions are familiar to the Fathers: they say that the divine Word assumed, put on, or bore a man. Thus Cyprian speaks at the end of the book *On the Vanity of Idols*; Augustine, in *On Faith against the Manichaeans*, at the beginning of chapter 26; and Hilary, *On the Trinity* X, about the middle. Yet these expressions are not to be understood properly, so that we say that a man was assumed, because his nature was assumed and because the assumption terminated in this—that the Son of God should be man. Otherwise the proposition, simply and properly taken, “The Son of God put on, assumed, bore a man,” is false and heretical. St Thomas gives the reason in *Summa Theologiae*, III, question 4, article 3. For the term “man” signifies human nature concretely, that is, as existing in some supposit; and therefore, just as we cannot say that a supposit was assumed, so we cannot say that a man was assumed. There St Thomas adds the words of Pope Felix and of Martin at the Council of Ephesus. [Col. 0966B]

“After four hundred and thirty years.” Thus it should be read, not “three hundred and thirty,” as in Aldus and the Florentine edition. For the former number is found in the best manuscripts, B, T, P, nine Vatican manuscripts, and Theophilus in *On Times*; indeed, in Sacred Scripture itself, both in the Septuagint and Vulgate editions, Exodus 12, and in Paul, Galatians 3. But not only the years of servitude in which the Hebrews were oppressed in Egypt are to be counted, but also those of their dwelling in the land of Canaan. The beginning is to be taken from the seventy-fifth year after Abraham’s birth, when he entered Canaan, as Hermannus Conradus notes in his Chronicle on Jacob, and the Master of Scholastic History, Exodus 27. For in the Septuagint, whose edition the Fathers used, Exodus 12 reads: “The dwelling of the children of Israel, which they dwelt in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan, was four hundred and thirty years.” St Augustine cites the passage in this form in *Questions*, question 47, where he also discusses this number of years; likewise Suidas under Μωῦ, and Bede.

“When he was hungry again, a rain of heavenly food descended.” The history is narrated here in a different order from that of Scripture, for they were first afflicted by hunger: Exodus 16.

“The golden head of a bull, whom they call Apis,” etc. This too is reproached to them in Psalm 105: “They made a calf in Horeb,” etc.

“The Hebrews lost their former name.” They had been so called after Heber, Noah’s great-grandson through Shem, according to Josephus, *Antiquities* I.14; Eusebius, *Chronicle*, at the beginning; Augustine, *City of God* XVI.11; Suidas; and Isidore, *Etymologies* IX.2, no. 40. [Col. 0966C]

“And because Judah was the leader of their examination, they were called Jews.” I find no Judah who presided over the Jewish people after Moses. For the Judah of whom it is written in Judges 1, “And the Lord said, Judah shall go up,” etc., is understood by the Hebrews and by Josephus, *Antiquities* V.1, not as the name of an individual but as a patronymic denoting the whole tribe from which Othniel was taken. They therefore say that Judah—that is, the tribe of Judah together with the tribe of Simeon—captured the king of Hebron, Adoni-bezek, etc. Thus they generally prefer that the children of Israel should be called Jews from Judah. See Eusebius, *Chronicle*, and Isidore in the place cited above.

“Under the rule of Tiberius Caesar; in his fifteenth year, that is, when the two Geminus were consuls,” etc. This is the thirty-first year of Christ the Lord, according to Eusebius and chronographers generally. Thus Lactantius says that the Savior suffered after completing the thirtieth year of his life. Tertullian also says so, *Against the Jews*; Clement, *Stromata* I; Africanus, *Annals* V; Jerome, on Daniel 9 and in Epistle 22; Augustine, *City of God* XVIII.54 and XXII.15, and Epistle 80 to Hesychius; Orosius VII; and Cassiodorus, *On the Consuls*. Others prefer the thirty-first year of his life, such as Apollinaris, bishop of Laodicea, in Jerome on Daniel 9; Cyril on Isaiah 29; Philastrius, *On Heresies*; Severus, *History* II; and other later writers reported by John Lucidus, *On the True Day of the Passion*, chapter 9. The thirty-second year, and more than three months in addition, was the opinion of others, vigorously defended by Benedictus Pererius in his commentary on Daniel, II, in the disputation on the seventy weeks, question 7. But Bede, *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 45; Albertus Magnus, on the Epistle of Dionysius the Areopagite; Onuphrius, *Fasti* and *Chronicle*; and Cardinal Baronius, *Annals* I, judged it to be the thirty-third year and three months. Finally, some others asserted that he was about fifty, as St Augustine reports, *On Christian Doctrine* II.28. [Col. 0966D] Some attribute this view, refuted by all, to Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* II.39–40; others say it was foisted upon him and doubt the deception, such as the Cardinal in the place cited above.

“The Jews crucified Christ on the tenth day before the Kalends of April.” This is the reading of B, T, P, and eight Vatican manuscripts, although some printed editions read, “on the seventh day,” etc. I have retained the reading supported by the greater number and better exemplars. Marcellus Francolinus—lest we deprive him of his due praise—expounded this passage of Lactantius in a long and very fine discussion in his *Treatise on the Times of the Canonical Hours*, chapters 73 and 74, which we shall relate briefly. By “the tenth day before the Kalends,” Lactantius means not the eleventh day before the Kalends, as Paul of Middelburg, *Fifth Pauline [work]*, part 2, chapter 4, and Thomasius in his notes on this author thought, but the tenth day itself before the Kalends of April. In this expression both terminal days are included in the reckoning: the day designated and the day of the Kalends itself. Marcellus rightly notes this in the cited chapter 73, no. 18, refuting the objection from the section “Ante diem” in the law *Anniculus amittitur*, *Digest*, “On the Meaning of Words,” and explaining that section well. Thus, by these words Lactantius thought that Christ the Lord suffered on 23 March.

Theophilus of Caesarea, near to the times of the apostles, held the same view in the synodical letter on Easter printed among Bede’s works, volume II, at the end, as Marcellus proves against Middelburg and Thomasius, chapter 73, no. 19, and at the beginning of chapter 74. Eusebius of Caesarea likewise held it throughout his *Chronological Canons*, of which a fragment survives in Anastasius of Antioch, *Various Questions*, as Turrianus reports in his exposition of chapter 6, Book II of Clement of Rome’s *Apostolic Constitutions*, and as Marcellus reports. So also St Augustine, Sermon 22 *On Time*, which is sermon 18 on the Nativity of the Lord; Bede, *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 65; the Chronicle of Ado of Vienne, at the beginning of the first age; Anselm, *On the Image of the World* II.17; Nicetas and all the Greeks; and others cited by Middelburg, *Pauline [work]* II, Book V, chapters 1–2. [Col. 0967A]

Let us now review the other opinions on the day of whatever month on which the Lord suffered. Hugolinus Martellus, *On the Restoration of the Complete Year*, chapter 19, reports from St Augustine that some asserted that the Lord suffered on the Nones of March, that is, 7 March. St Epiphanius, *Heresies* 50, against the Tessarescaedecatites, says that he found the *Acts of Pilate*, in which Pilate indicated that the Lord died not on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, as the Tessarescaedecatites alleged, but on the fifteenth day before those Kalends—that is, 18 March. But Epiphanius himself, in the cited *Heresies* 50 and 51, against those who reject the Gospel of John and the Apocalypse, thinks it was on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April—i.e. the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April itself—namely 20 March. The author of the Exposition on Matthew 27 among Anselm’s works gives the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, that is, 21 March. Lactantius and others, as above, give 23 March. Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, about the middle; Chrysostom, sermon on the Nativity of John the Baptist; Augustine, *City of God* XVIII, last chapter, and *On the Trinity*, chapter 5, and elsewhere; Bede; Usuard; Wandelbert; and others in the martyrologies wrote that it was 25 March, the day on which he also deigned to be incarnate. Again, Bede in *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 28, relates that very many teachers of the Church held the same view: Cyril, in the letter to the Council of Carthage; St Thomas, on John 2, lecture 3; St Antoninus, *Chronicle*, title 5, chapter 7; and countless others. It is thus readily apparent that this opinion was more commonly received.

Victorinus of Limoges, an ancient teacher and excellent calculator, thought it was 26 March, as did others mentioned by Bede, *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 59; Franciscus Maurolicus in his Martyrology; and Onuphrius in his Ecclesiastical Chronicle. Middelburg, *Pauline [work]* II, Book XIV, chapter 2, sought by an extended argument, rejecting the opinions of all others, to prove 30 March. Some also give 2 April, as Martellus reports in *On the Restoration of the Complete Year*, chapter 19. Roger Bacon, John of Murs, Paul of Burgos, Abulensis, Lucidus, Pontacus, Zarlino, and most modern writers give 3 April. John of Königsberg, cited by Middelburg, *Pauline [work]* II, Book V, chapters 1–2, gives 11 April. [Col. 0967B]

So numerous and so diverse are writers’ opinions concerning the day of the Lord’s Passion that one may rightly wonder and regard it as some great secret of God: the day of his Incarnation was then known only to the Virgin Mother, and the day of his Nativity to very few, yet thereafter both became known to the whole Church; but the day of his Passion—endured in a most populous and celebrated city, with leading men and peoples acting together, a Roman governor rendering judgment, natives and foreigners openly witnessing its execution, heaven and all the elements displaying terrifying signs, more marvelous than anything remembered by humankind, and these proclaimed throughout the whole world—has still remained so little established and known.

## CHAPTER XI

[Col. 0969A]

“I sent to you,” etc. Nearly the same also in Cyprian, *Against the Jews* I.2.

“Let each one turn from his evil way.” Manuscript B has “each one of you,” although *vestrum*, “of you,” is absent from the Bibles and from Cyprian.

“Behind his body.” Thus it is read in B, T, P, in the Septuagint here, and in the Vulgate, 3 Kings 14. The passage is taken from Nehemiah 9, which circulates under the title of the second book of Ezra. The Vulgate here has “behind their backs”; Cyprian, who cites the same passage under Ezra’s name, “behind his back”; recent editions of Lactantius, “behind his heart.”

“I have been jealous with jealousy for the Lord.” Cyprian cites it in nearly the same manner in the cited chapter 2.

“And I remained alone.” Cyprian likewise. But the Septuagint, with which the Vulgate agrees, has, “and I was left alone.” The Greek, moreover, is *monōtatos* (μονώτατος), “most solitary.”

“And they seek to take my life from me.” The Septuagint and Vulgate have, “and they seek my life, to take it,” or “that they may take it.” Cyprian, in the place cited above: “and they seek to take my life from me.”

“And I have no acceptable sacrifice.” Cyprian, *Testimonies against the Jews* I.16, more correctly has, “I shall have no acceptable sacrifice,” since both the Septuagint and the Vulgate read, “I shall not regard”; and Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, “I shall not receive,” or “I shall not accept.”

“Will be glorified.” The Greek is *dedoxastai* (δεδόξασται), “has been glorified”; and so in Tertullian and Cyprian, *Against the Jews*.

“Among the nations.” As in Cyprian. The Septuagint has *en tois ethnesin* (ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσι), as does the Vulgate, “among the nations.” Tertullian: “among all nations.”

“Will serve me.” The Septuagint, Vulgate, Tertullian, and Cyprian have, “has served me.”

“I come to gather,” etc. Cyprian cites it word for word.

“My splendour.” The Septuagint and Vulgate: “my glory.” [Col. 0969B]

“And I shall send some of those saved among the nations,” etc. The Fathers often cite passages of Scripture not word for word, but briefly and *paraphrastically* (παραφραστικῶς), extracting only what is sufficient for their purpose. Firmianus is especially accustomed to do this, as I shall note in the relevant places; and here he omits a few things found in the Septuagint and the Vulgate.

“So that a people ungrateful toward God might be led into the greatest error.” Yet the leading itself, or the Jews’ persistence in error, must not be ascribed to God as its cause. See the notes on chapter 20 of this book concerning the subject of reprobation.

“Whom the Jews themselves most cruelly killed by cutting him with a saw.” This is reported by Tertullian, *On Patience*; Origen, Homily 1 on Psalm 37; the author of the book *Against the Jews Who Persecuted Christ*, among Cyprian’s works; Chrysostom, on Matthew 19; and the Master of Scholastic History, in the history of 4 Kings, chapter 32.

“I begot sons.” So Tertullian, *On Prayer*, and many Cyprian manuscripts at the beginning of the book *On the Lord’s Prayer* and of *On Jealousy and Envy*, and the Latin translation from the Septuagint; although elsewhere in Tertullian and Cyprian one finds, “I generated [them].”

“And my people did not understand me.” Thus Tertullian, *Against Marcion* V, and Cyprian, *On the Lord’s Prayer*, although *Testimonies* I.30 has, “and my people did not understand.” In many manuscripts, *mou* (μοῦ, “of me”) is noted in place of *me* (μέ, “me”) in the Latin translation from the Septuagint; these indeed have, “and my people did not understand me.” St Jerome affirms that they wrote thus, not, as Pamelius says in his note on Cyprian, *On the Lord’s Prayer*, “and my people did not understand.” Tertullian, *Against Marcion* III and IV, Basil, and Cyril followed the Septuagint reading.

In vain was the measuring-line made: the scribes are false, and they have been confounded; the wise have trembled. What is here called “measuring-line” (*metatura*), and likewise in Cyprian, *Testimonies* I, ch. 3, is in the Greek Bibles σχοῖνος, a word properly meaning “reed.” Hence the recent Latin translation of the Bible from the Septuagint reads: “In vain has the lying reed been made for the scribes; the wise have been confounded and terrified,” etc. There “reed” is understood for pen and stylus; for the ancients formerly used sea-reeds for writing, and therefore St Jerome translated more clearly in the Vulgate: “Truly the lying stylus of the scribes has wrought falsehood; the wise have been confounded and terrified,” etc. The word also signifies a rope, since ropes, as Pliny relates, were woven from seaweed and reed. Hence, by a certain *metalepsis*, σχοῖνος also signifies a measure by means of a rope; for the ancients measured fields with ropes, as is evident from Isidore, *Origins*, book XV, ch. 14, and this custom came from the Hebrews: Amos VII, “and thy land shall be measured by a cord”; Psalm LXXVII, “and he divided the land among them with the cord of distribution.” This geometrical cord was called an *arvipendium*. Glossary: “*Arvipendium*, σχοῖνος γεωμετρικός.” And the land which they had measured was called σχοίνισμα, as is evident from the author of the *Etymologicum*. Indeed, even in Herodotus σχοῖνος is taken as a Persian measure of land. Those, therefore, who in this passage translated the Greek σχοῖνος into Latin as *metatura* (“measuring-line”), as Lactantius here and Cyprian did, had regard to this final meaning of the word. Cyprian thus cites the passage [Col. 0970B]: “In vain was the false measuring-line made; the scribes have been confounded, the wise have trembled,” etc. From this it appears that Lactantius translated and punctuated it less correctly; for the scribes are not called false in the Bibles or in Cyprian, but rather “a false measuring-line for the scribes,” or “of the scribes.” The Greek indeed reads σχοῖνος ψευδής; and “scribes” in the Bibles is not joined with “have been confounded,” as in Lactantius and Cyprian, but with “false measuring-line.”

## CHAPTER XII

“If it is known to all that certain animals are accustomed to conceive from wind and breeze,” etc. This was, of course, reported concerning mares by Homer, *Iliad* XX; Virgil, *Georgics* III; Silius, books III and XVI; Varro, *On Agriculture* II, ch. 1; Columella, book VII, ch. 25; Pliny, book IV, ch. 22; Solinus, book III, chs. 26 and 47; Justin, *History*, at the beginning of book XLIV, book VIII, ch. 42, book XVI, ch. 45; Martianus Capella, book VI, chapter “On the Division of the Earth.”

“The womb of the Virgin was weakened,” etc. This passage of Solomon [Col. 0970C] may perhaps have fallen out from those books which Scripture reports that he composed, 3 Kings [1 Kings], ch. IV, at the end, but which are now missing. Yet I would say either that this passage did not fall out of any canonical book of Scripture, or that Solomon did not utter it concerning the Virgin Mary; since it is certain that that most blessed and holy woman suffered no injury or pain from the Conception or Nativity of the Saviour, whereas the contrary seems to be inferred from this passage. For Isaiah XXXV says: “It shall bud forth as a lily, and shall rejoice with gladness and praise.” The holy Fathers and all the Doctors likewise maintained this: Cyprian, *On Works*; [uncertain citation:] “Card., on the Nativity of Christ”; St Zeno the bishop, Sermon 6 *On the Nativity*; St Augustine, sermon *On the Assumption*; St Thomas, Part III, question 35, article 6, reply to the first objection.

“She shall conceive in the womb.” Thus Luke I; and from this passage of Isaiah, Tertullian, *Against Marcion* III and *On the Trinity*; Cyprian, Epistle 9, according to Morellius’s edition and other older editions. Yet according to Manutius’s edition, which Pamelius there approved and adopted, and in *Testimonies* II, ch. 9, and Ambrose, *Cain and Abel* I, ch. 3, they have “she shall receive in the womb.” Pamelius thought this came nearer to the reading of the Seventy, who have ἐν γαστρὶ λήψεται; and St Jerome testifies, *On the Best Method of Translating*, that it was formerly read thus among them as well. But if we consider the proper meaning of the verb *concipio*, “in the womb” is not attached to it without reason, nor is there any difference whether we say “she shall conceive in the womb” or “she shall receive in the womb.” For the verb *concipere*, when used absolutely, does not mean “to receive in the womb,” but simply “to take hold of”; and therefore the translators in the recently published Latin version of the Greek Bibles, together with the Seventy themselves, translated λήψεται not “shall receive” but, like Lactantius and the others cited above, “shall conceive.” The Aldine and Plantin editions here read *in uterum*, “into the womb.” I have followed the Florentine Juntine edition, *in utero*, “in the womb,” which agrees with Tertullian, Cyprian, and others. The Vulgate edition in Isaiah simply reads “she shall conceive.”

“And thou shalt call his name Emmanuel.” Thus most manuscripts of Lactantius read, as do Tertullian *Against the Jews*, Cyprian [*Testimonies*], ch. 9, and Jerome, *To Pammachius on the Best Method of Translating*. The Florentine Juntine edition here reads “he shall be called,” together with the Vulgate and the Cambron manuscript of Cyprian’s Epistle 9, as Pamelius testifies there. But the Septuagint, along with Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, according to St Jerome, translated “thou shalt call”; and most of the ancients read it thus, although Chrysostom in his commentaries on Isaiah and on Psalm XLIV, and Cyril, prefer καλέσουσι, “they shall call,” with the Evangelist Matthew.

“But they did not believe,” etc. This passage is read somewhat differently from Lactantius both in the Septuagint and in the Vulgate. In the Septuagint: “But they did not believe and embittered his Holy Spirit, and he was turned to them in hostility; he fought against them, and remembered the ancient days. Where is he who brought up from the sea the shepherd of the sheep?” etc. The Vulgate: “But they provoked to anger and afflicted the Spirit of his Holy One, and he was turned to them as an enemy, and he himself defeated them, and remembered the days of Moses of old and of his people. Where is he who brought them up from the sea with the shepherds of his flock?” etc. We see that in both Bibles it reads not “from the land,” as in Lactantius, but “from the sea,” as in the Hebrew. Yet it is noted on the Latin version from the Septuagint that in the other versions it is written as in Lactantius, ἐκ τῆς γῆς, “from the land.”

“Let the heavens rejoice from above,” etc. Here Lactantius has something in common with the Septuagint and something with the Vulgate. For the former reads: “Let heaven rejoice from above, and let the clouds scatter righteousness; let the earth sprout and bring forth mercy, and let righteousness spring up together. I am the Lord who created thee,” etc. The Vulgate: “Drop down dew, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the Just One; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Saviour, and let righteousness arise together. I, the Lord, have called him.”

“Behold, a child has been born to us,” etc. Cyprian, *Testimonies* II, ch. 21, cites this entire passage exactly thus; but in the Septuagint it is “because a little child has been born to us,” and in the Vulgate “a little child has been born,” etc. Likewise the Septuagint and Vulgate have ἐπὶ τοῦ ὤμου, “upon the shoulder.”

“He was called.” The Septuagint and Aquila have this. Ignatius, Epistle to the [Col. 0971C] Antiochenes, and Eusebius, *Demonstration* VII, have καλεῖται, “he is called,” as also Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* IV, ch. 66. The Vulgate, Symmachus, and Tertullian have κληθήσεται, “he shall be called.” Theodotion has ἐκάλεσε, “he called.”

“Messenger of great counsel.” So the manuscript codices of Cyprian read, as Pamelius attests, not “of great thought,” as some printed copies have. The former reading is supplied by the Septuagint, μεγάλης βουλῆς, and likewise by Tertullian, Ambrose at the beginning of book III on Luke, and Jerome in his Commentary.

“And all the peoples.” P. has “and all the people,” etc., as does the Florentine edition. But I retained the reading of the Aldine, Plantin, and better manuscripts, which the Septuagint and Vulgate have, as do the author of the *Exposition of the Apostles’ Creed* among Cyprian’s works, and Lactantius himself at the end of this chapter, with no manuscript differing.

“And his power is eternal,” etc. B. has “and his powers are eternal, which shall never pass away.” But here too I retain the former reading of the best manuscripts and of all printed editions; it agrees with the Septuagint and Vulgate, with Tertullian, likewise with Cyprian *Against the Jews*, and with Lactantius himself at the end of the chapter.

“Thus says the Lord God to Christ, my Lord.” Tertullian indeed often gives this reading, as does Cyprian, *Against the Jews* I, ch. 21. It is deservedly condemned by St Jerome in his Commentary: “I know,” he says, “that in this chapter very many not only of the Latins but also of the Greeks grievously err, thinking that it is written, ‘Thus says the Lord to Christ, my Lord,’ so that it may be understood in accordance with what we read elsewhere: ‘The Lord rained from the Lord,’ and ‘The Lord said to my Lord.’ For it is not κυρίῳ, which means ‘Lord,’ but Κύρῳ, that is, ‘Cyrus,’” etc. The Septuagint indeed reads: Οὕτω λέγει Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς τῷ Χριστῷ μοι Κύρῳ, “Thus says the Lord God to my anointed one, Cyrus.” And the Vulgate: “Thus says the Lord God to my anointed one, Cyrus.” This Cyrus was the first king of the Persians who afterwards released the captive Jews, as Josephus relates, *Antiquities* XI, ch. 1, and Lactantius above, chs. 5 and 10.

“And the cities shall not be shut.” Thus the Septuagint, Tertullian [Col. 0972A], Cyprian, and Cyril read. Some prefer πύλαι, that is, “gates,” as in the Vulgate.

“I shall open for thee.” I added this from the Bononian manuscript and from the Septuagint, although it is absent from many copies of Lactantius. Tertullian, *Against Marcion* IV and V, has “I shall open for them”; but the Hebrew, Chaldee, Greek, and Latin text reads as in ours.

“Then, when every evil has been removed from human affairs, the golden age,” etc. He falsely believed, of course, that this golden age would be that period of a thousand years which he and certain others devised. We shall discuss it in the notes on book VII, ch. 24.

## CHAPTER XIII

“Without a father’s office he was begotten in the virginal womb.” Observe this passage against the Carpocratians and Cerinthians, who blasphemously asserted that Christ had been conceived from Joseph’s seed. Thus above, ch. 12, “the holy Virgin,” etc.; and below, ch. 5, at the beginning.

“That, bearing a substance intermediate between God and man.” That is, between [Col. 0972B] the divine and human natures. So below, ch. 25: “He was therefore both God and man, established as a middle being between God and man,” etc. In these passages Lactantius calls Christ the Lord *medius*, “middle” or “intermediate.” But in the said ch. 25 he is called *mediator*. To say that Christ is intermediate differs from saying that he is mediator, as St Bonaventure teaches in *Sentences* III, distinction 19, question 2. For *medius* indicates conformity with the extremes; *mediator* indicates not only conformity but also the office of reconciliation: the former is μέσος in Greek, the latter μεσίτης, as Lactantius himself states in the said ch. 25. Therefore, as St Bonaventure writes there, Christ is said to be intermediate between the divine and human natures because those two natures concur in him as in one person, insofar as he is one person in those two natures—not in the divine alone nor in the human alone, but in both. He is said to be intermediate also in another way, because there were in him properties corresponding to the two natures, namely, blessedness and mortality together: in the former he is compared with God, in the latter with man.

[Col. 0972C] “Bearing a substance.” Here *substantia* is not φύσις, that is, “nature,” so that Christ the Lord is understood to bear an intermediate substance—that is, a sort of third nature between the divine and human, forged and constituted from the divine and human natures confused and mixed together—as Eutyches madly dreamed. He was condemned and refuted in disputations at the Councils of Constantinople and Chalcedon under Leo I, at the Second Council of Seville, and by Leo himself in many of his letters, especially Letters 14 to the Synod of Ephesus and 17 to the Empress Pulcheria; and by Pope Gelasius, John Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith* III, Boethius, *On the Two Natures*, and St Thomas, *Against the Gentiles* IV, ch. 35. For we confess that Christ the Lord bore not one but two natures, divine and human, in such a manner that both remained perfect, unmixed, and unconfused, and neither was changed into the other. We therefore profess that Christ consists from both natures and in both natures: in both, because both remain; from both, because from both, through the union of what remains, there comes to be the one person of Christ, as the Council of Chalcedon itself defines and as Boethius teaches at length in the said book *On the Two Natures*. Nor is *substantia* here taken for οὐσία, “essence,” or for οὐσίασις, “substance,” but properly for ὑπόστασις. For the term that is *substantia* among the Latins is ὑπόστασις among the Greeks. Yet because substances properly, principally, and most fully so called are primary substances, that is, the individuals of secondary substances—which in rational and intellectual nature are called supposita and persons—the name ὑπόστασις is taken in this proper sense, signifying an individual, a supposit, or a person, as Boethius teaches in the cited place, ch. 3, and St Thomas in Part III, question 2, article 3, reply to the second objection. Thus also *substantia*. Therefore Lactantius says, “that, bearing an intermediate substance,” that is, existing as a person intermediate between God and man, that is, between the divine and human [Col. 0973A] natures—since it consists from two and in two natures in the manner stated—he might, as it were by the hand, lead our frail and weak nature forth to immortality.

“Mixed from each kind,” etc. There was once a question long debated: whether the terminus of the union of the uncreated Word with humanity was a simple or a composite person. Many ancient theologians did not venture to affirm the latter, as we learn from the Master of the Sentences, book III, distinction 2; St Thomas, question 2, article 3; Bonaventure, article 1, question 2; Scotus, question 3; Durandus, question 3; Richard, article 2, question 2; Gabriel, question 1, article 3; Marsilius, question 6, article 3, doubt 3; Almain, question 1, conclusion 2; Alexander of Hales, Part III, question 6, member 2, article 5; Cajetan on Part III, question 2, article 4, and Part I, question 3, article 8. For they said that composition, taken absolutely, in its formal concept implies imperfection in each component, and therefore is incompatible with the divine Word. But it is easily answered that this is true in other compositions, in which the components are by their nature established and ordered for composing; in those cases the components perfect one another, and the composite is more perfect than the individual components, and therefore such a mode of composition implies imperfection. But in this admirable composition the Word is not by its nature ordered to this or to any other composition, though by grace he accommodates himself to composing this man. In him it is not the Word that is perfected, but the humanity. Nor is anything taken from his perfection, because he is not changed and loses none of his perfection. Therefore this composite is not simply or intensively more perfect than one of its components, namely the Word, because the latter is simply infinite and contains eminently within itself whatever perfection exists in humanity; yet extensively it formally includes some perfection which the Word alone does not include. Finally, although the being of the Word, considered in itself, does not result from the Word and humanity, the being of this man as such results from the union [Col. 0973C] of both. And, formally speaking, nothing else belongs to the nature of composition or of a composite than that it be truly one thing resulting from the real union of several things. This formal account of composition does not imply imperfection in either component, or at most in one; the other features which entail imperfection are accidental to the account of composition as such. Therefore, because, as has been said, Christ is one thing from diverse things—and this is an argument taken from St Basil near the end of *Against Eunomius* II—we are compelled to deny that the terminus of this union is simple and consequently to affirm it composite; for these two are plainly contradictory. This is further confirmed because Christ, as this man, is more composite than humanity alone; for Christ intrinsically includes humanity and something else. Accordingly, all modern theologians teach that it must absolutely and simply be said that the terminus of the uncreated Word’s union with humanity is a composite person, and that this union is a true and proper composition: St Thomas, Part III, question 2, article 4. This is the conclusion defined at the Fifth Synod, Session VIII, Canons 4 and 7; and at the Sixth Synod, Session IV, Epistle 1 of Agatho; Session XI, Epistle of Sophronius; Session XIII, Canon 6; and at the Lateran Council under Martin III, Consultation V, Canon 17, which condemns those who deny that the matters defined concerning Christ in those councils are properly and truly stated [the source text is corrupt at this point]. There too Canon 6 defines that Christ subsists properly and truly in two natures and from two natures; and that particle *from* undoubtedly denotes composition. The holy Fathers also acknowledge this: Dionysius, *Divine Names* ch. 1 and *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* ch. 3, part II; Damascene, book III, ch. 3 and following; Gregory, Homily 38 on the Gospels; Athanasius, at the beginning of the Oration “That Christ Is One”; Peter the Deacon, *On the Incarnation and Grace*: “The Lord Christ,” he says, “is proclaimed by the holy Fathers as [Col. 0974A] composite through the union of divinity and humanity.” He says that this was defined at a certain Council of Antioch against Paul of Samosata. Therefore, in order to explain this composition and the reality of this union, the Fathers also used other names: namely, “mixture” or “commixture,” as Lactantius does in this place, and Eusebius of Emesa in the Homily on John III, “Amen, amen, I say to you, a servant is not greater,” etc. Gregory Nazianzen calls this composition “a new mixture” and “an admirable blending” in Oration 42. Tertullian, *On the Flesh of Christ* and *Apology* ch. 21, says that in Christ there is a man mixed with God; and Hilary says nearly the same in *On the Trinity* II, ch. 13. They likewise used the term “union,” “joining,” or “conjunction from two,” as Chrysostom, Homily 10 on John; Justin, *Exposition of the True Faith*, near the end; Cyril, Epistle to Nestorius. They also used “concretion,” as Cyprian, *Against the Jews* II, ch. 10: “Christ is man and God, concreted from each kind.” Yet expressions which speak of mixture are not to be understood properly; for since each nature remained perfect and unconfused in itself, as was determined against Eutyches, there could not properly be mixture or mingling there. Rather, they were employed by the holy Fathers only to suggest the reality of this composition. But we must wholly refrain from using them; nor should we imitate the Fathers in every expression, as St Augustine says, *On Christian Doctrine* IV, ch. 3, because we have not received equal graces.

“Egypt has been wearied.” Thus Cyprian, *Testimonies* II, ch. 6, following the Septuagint, ἐκοπίασεν Αἴγυπτος, instead of what the Vulgate has according to the Hebrew letter, “the labour of Egypt.”

“And Saba, tall men.” It must be written precisely thus, with *Saba* joined to “tall men,” and without an intervening stop, as it is mistakenly printed in all copies of Lactantius. Thus the sense is that the tall men of Saba shall pass over, etc., according to the reading of all Hebrew, Greek, and Latin Bibles, Tertullian *Against Praxeas*, Cyprian in the place cited, and other Fathers. Where Lactantius [Col. 0974C] has *Saba*, the Septuagint, Vulgate, Tertullian, and Cyprian have *Sabaim*. But it makes no difference, because by either name the Sabaeans are meant—namely, those descended from Saba son of Cush, mentioned in Genesis X, who inhabited that part of Arabia Felix extending toward the Red Sea, also called the Arabian Sea. For this is what the Hebrew has here [the Hebrew is omitted in the supplied text]. Other Sabaeans were descended from Saba son of Raamah, mentioned in the same chapter of Genesis; they inhabited the part of Arabia Felix that extends more toward the Persian Gulf. Hence Pliny, book VI, ch. 28, says that the Sabaeans dwell with peoples extending to both seas. He means the Arabian or Red Sea and the Persian Sea, and both peoples of Sabaeans: both those originating from Saba son of Cush and those deriving their origin from the son of Raamah. Although secular writers did not know this distinction, known to us from the Sacred Writings, but described both as one people, and Greeks and Latins alike called both Saba and their inhabitants Sabaeans without any distinction in the name, as Pererius notes on Genesis in the place cited. The Hebrews, however, distinguish the names of the two in this way: Saba, son of Cush, they write with *samekh* as the first letter, a thin and weak *s*; but the son of Raamah they mark with *shin* as the first letter, a thick *s*. See Isidore, *Origins* IX, ch. 2, no. 30. Thus the former would correctly seem to be called Seba, and his descendants Sebaeans; the latter rather Sceba, and his descendants Scebaeans. Psalm LXXI mentions both peoples, where what is in Hebrew “the kings of Sceba and Seba” is read in the Vulgate and Septuagint: “the kings of the Arabs and Saba shall bring gifts,” etc. That is, St Jerome and the Septuagint, translating “Arabs” for Sceba, intended to designate the offspring descending from Saba son of Raamah and ruling the Arabian land by the Persian Gulf.

“And after thee they shall walk bound in fetters, and they shall worship,” etc. The Septuagint reads: “And after thee they shall follow, bound in manacles, and shall pass over to thee, and shall worship thee.” But while Lactantius omits “and shall pass over to thee,” he agrees with the Vulgate, Cyprian, *Testimonies* II, ch. 6, Cyril, and Eusebius, *Demonstration* V.

“And they shall pray to thee.” Thus the Vulgate; but Cyprian, and Lactantius himself below, ch. 29, read: “And they shall pray in thee,” a reading with which the Septuagint agrees: καὶ ἐν σοὶ προσεύξονται.

“Jeremiah.” This passage is not found in Jeremiah, but in Baruch, ch. III. It is also cited under Jeremiah’s name by St Augustine, *City of God* XVIII, ch. 32; Cyprian, *Testimonies* II, ch. 6; Chrysostom, Homily *On the Trinity*; Cassiodorus on Psalm LXXXI. For because Baruch was Jeremiah’s scribe and disciple, very many ancients customarily cite testimonies from the Book of Baruch under Jeremiah’s name—especially Clement of Alexandria, beginning of the *Pedagogue*, ch. 10; Hilary, *On the Trinity* IV; Basil, *Against Eunomius* IV; Ambrose, beginning of *On Repentance*, ch. 8, and beginning of the *Hexaemeron*, ch. 14; and others.

“And no other shall be reckoned apart from him, who found every way of prudence.” The Septuagint: “And no other shall be esteemed beside him; he discovered every way of knowledge.” The Vulgate [Col. 0975B]: “And no other shall be esteemed against him; he discovered every way of discipline.” But Cyprian cites this whole passage exactly as Lactantius does.

“Thy throne.” Thus it is in Greek in Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews I: ὁ θρόνος σου; and Aquila, Symmachus, Tertullian, and Cyprian read thus. On this matter see Eusebius on this passage, Jerome to Principia, and Chrysostom.

“A rod of equity.” Thus Cyprian too, instead of what is found in the Vulgate and Septuagint, “a rod of rectitude.”

“And thou hast hated injustice.” The Septuagint, Vulgate, Tertullian, and Cyprian have “iniquity”; Aquila, according to Eusebius, has ἀσέβημα, “ungodliness.”

“With the oil of exultation.” Thus the Septuagint, ἐλαίῳ ἀγαλλιάσεως; and Cyprian, St Augustine, and Jerome likewise read so, instead of the Vulgate, Tertullian, and Aquila’s ἐλαίῳ χαρᾶς, “with the oil of joy.” Others have ἐλαίῳ ἀγλαϊσμοῦ, “with the oil of brightness and splendour,” as Symmachus does; this reading is close to the Hebrew *sason*, that is, “beauty, glory, ornament.”

“And he is a man; and who has known him?” Thus the Septuagint gives the entire passage, except that there, as in the Vulgate [Col. 0975C], it reads “shall know” rather than “has known.” Tertullian and Cyprian *Against the Jews*, and Epiphanius, *Against the Ebionites* I, likewise cite the passage. Since it occurs somewhat differently in the Vulgate—namely, “The heart of all is perverse and inscrutable; who shall know it?”—some thought that it is no longer extant in Jeremiah today.

“And God shall send them a man,” etc. The Septuagint: “And he shall send them a man who shall save them; by judging he shall save them.” The Vulgate: “And he shall send them a Saviour and defender, who shall deliver them.”

“And a man shall arise.” Thus also Cyprian according to the Septuagint; but Symmachus preferred, instead of “man,” as does the Vulgate, σκῆπτρον, “sceptre” or “rod.”

“They did not understand the works of the Lord.” Thus codex B, Cyprian *Against the Jews* I, ch. 3, and the Septuagint read: “They did not understand in the works of the Lord.” But the Florentine, Aldine, and Plantin editions read as does the Vulgate: “They did not understand the works of the Lord.”

“And he who shall arise.” Thus Cyprian, *Testimonies* I, ch. 21 [Col. 0975D], and Paul’s interpreter on Hebrews ch. XV; the Septuagint has καὶ ὁ ἀνιστάμενος, “and he who rises.”

“In him the nations shall hope.” Thus Paul’s interpreter in the cited place and Cyprian in the manuscripts, from which Pamelius arranged for “in him” to be printed as *in illum*, against the Vulgate printed copies’ *in illo*. The Septuagint in the recent Roman edition has ἐπ’ αὐτῷ, “in him,” although Pamelius read in Greek ἐπ’ αὐτόν, “upon him.”

“And his rest shall be in honour.” I suspect that Lactantius’s Bible had an error in the word “their”; for that prophecy is spoken of Christ, and the Septuagint and Cyprian have: “And his rest shall be honour.” The Vulgate: “And his sepulchre shall be glorious.”

“The Spirit of knowledge and godliness.” This must be read as in B., T., P., and the Plantin edition, not as in the Florentine and Aldine editions, “the Spirit of godliness”; for the words “of knowledge and” are in the prophet himself and in Cyprian.

“And the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him.” This reading of Lactantius agrees [Col. 0976A] with the Vulgate and Cyprian, *Testimonies* II, ch. 11, although the Septuagint punctuates it so that a comma follows “him”: “The spirit of knowledge and godliness shall fill him, the spirit of the fear of the Lord.”

“And I shall prepare his kingdom.” Thus B., T., P., the Septuagint, Vulgate, Cyprian *Against the Jews* I, ch. 15, and II, ch. 11, read, instead of the printed reading here: “And I shall prepare his seed.”

“And the city which he called Jerusalem from his own name.” Solomon did not found it, as Lactantius falsely states here and below, ch. 13. For how could Sacred Scripture so often mention it when speaking of the times of Joshua, the Judges, and the Kings, which were certainly long before Solomon was born? Joshua chs. X, XII, XV, XVIII; Judges I and XIX; 1 Kings [1 Samuel] ch. XVIII; 2 Kings [2 Samuel] chs. V, VIII, IX, X, and elsewhere. It is believed rather to have been founded by King Melchizedek about the year 2023 from the creation of the world, in Abraham’s time, and to have been called in Hebrew Salem and in Greek Solyma. He seems to have possessed it for fifty years, after which the Jebusites, descended from Jebus the son of Canaan, occupied it. From them it was for a while called Jebus and Jebusite, at which time Joshua slew its king. The Jebusites held it for eight hundred and twenty-four years; and they relied so greatly on the city’s strength that when King David was about to attack it, they contemptuously stationed blind, lame, and mutilated persons upon the walls, boasting that these would suffice to repel the enemy. But when David had driven out the Jebusites and gained possession of the city, he restored it, fortified its citadel, and made it the metropolis of all Judaea. It was then called Jerusalem, as though *Jebus-Salem*, with the letter *b* changed to *r* for euphony; in Greek, with the word inflected, Hierosolyma. Eupolemus, however, in Eusebius, *Preparation* IX, thinks that it was called Hierosolyma from the most magnificent temple Solomon built there, as if ἱερὸν τοῦ Σαλομῶνος, “the sanctuary of Solomon”; for ἱερόν means “temple” in Greek because it is sacred. Lactantius, however, having himself thought that the city was named from Solomon, was deceived by that designation and falsely believed it was founded by Solomon. Strabo writes in book XVI that it was built by Moses. But besides the passages noted, see Josephus, *Antiquities* VII, ch. 3, and *Jewish War* VII, ch. 18; Hegesippus; likewise Jerome, *On Hebrew Places*, to Dardanus and to Damasus; and Suidas under “Melchizedek.”

“Those who built it.” The Vulgate has “those who build it”; the Septuagint, “those building.”

“He watched in vain.” Thus also the Septuagint, εἰς μάτην ἀγρύπνησεν; and St Jerome cites the passage this way several times, as does Cassian, book XII, ch. 9. The Vulgate: “he watches in vain.”

“He guarded.” The Septuagint and Vulgate: “he guards.”

## CHAPTER XIV

“He must necessarily possess in him an everlasting priesthood.” Cyprian discusses the same point in *Against the Jews* I, ch. 16. On Christ’s priesthood, see St Thomas, Part III, question 22.

[Col. 0976D] “Who shall do all things that are in my heart.” The Septuagint: “Who shall do all things that are in my heart and in my soul.” Cyprian agrees with Lactantius, except that for “shall do” he has “will do,” with the Septuagint and Vulgate.

“And he shall pass before me.” The Septuagint: “And he shall pass before my anointed one,” agreeing with the Vulgate and Hebrew. St Augustine cites the passage thus. Other versions have τῶν χριστῶν μου, “my anointed ones”; and Cyprian, *Testimonies* I, ch. 17: “Before my anointed ones.”

“And the Lord God showed me Jesus,” etc. The word *God* does not appear in the Vulgate, the Septuagint, or Cyprian, *Testimonies* II, ch. 13.

“That he might oppose him.” Thus the Septuagint and Vulgate; but codex B has “that he might contradict him.”

“May the Lord rule over thee in thee.” The Septuagint and Vulgate: “May the Lord rebuke thee in thee.”

“And behold, a firebrand cast out of the fire.” The Septuagint: “Behold, is not this one like a tower snatched from the fire?” In the Complutensian Bible, and in Theodoret and St Jerome: “Is not this one a firebrand,” etc., as in the Vulgate.

“Take the filthy garments from him.” After these words, the Septuagint and Cyprian add: “And he said to him: Behold, I have taken away thy iniquities”; and the Vulgate: “Behold, I have taken away thy iniquity.” Lactantius perhaps omitted this, like a few other things, for brevity.

“And clothe him.” Thus the Septuagint, Tertullian, and Cyprian; but the Vulgate continues the speech addressed to Jesus: “and clothe thyself.”

“A robe reaching to the feet.” Lactantius translated τὸ ποδήρη, found in the Septuagint, Tertullian, and Cyprian, as *tunicam talarem*, “a robe reaching to the ankles”; St Jerome supports this rendering.

“And I shall give thee those who may walk among these who stand around.” Thus it is read in the Septuagint; but the Vulgate differs little: “And I shall give thee walkers from among those who now stand by.” The preceding words found before these in both Bibles are omitted: καὶ ἐὰν διαφυλάξῃς τὴν αὐλήν μου, “and if thou shalt keep my court.”

[Col. 0977B] “Nearly five hundred years are counted.” Thus B., T., P., nine Vatican manuscripts, and the Plantin edition read. But the Aldine, Florentine, and several other editions lack *nearly*. Now Zechariah prophesied in the second year of Darius, the fourth king of the Persians, as is found in Zechariah I and Ezra [Esdras] I, ch. V; in Eusebius’s *Chronicle* under Olympiad 64; and in Jerome’s prologue to his Commentary on Zechariah. From that time to the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, Eusebius calculates five hundred and fifty-eight years in the *Chronicle* under Olympiad 202.

“Darius.” The fourth king of the Persians, as stated, whom Eusebius places under Olympiad 64.

“And Alexander.” This Alexander is not the one called the Great, son of Philip and twenty-third king of the Macedonians, whom Eusebius places under Olympiad 111; but Alexander, tenth king of the Macedonians, whom the same Eusebius places under Olympiad 69.

“Who lived not long before Tarquinius Superbus [Col. 0977C] was expelled.” It is certain that Darius was not after, but before Tarquin’s expulsion; for he assumed rule over the Persians in Olympiad 64 according to Eusebius, whereas Tarquin was expelled in Olympiad 67.

“He sent his Son as envoy to men.” Many manuscripts and printed editions have: “He sent his Son, the prince of angels, as envoy to men.” If anyone prefers to follow them and retain “prince of angels,” I shall not greatly object, since I understand the word “angels” here not to indicate some nature but a function and office: it is much the same as if he had said “first of envoys” or “messengers.” For *angel* in Greek is *nuntius*, “messenger,” in Latin; and under this name, in Sacred Scripture as well as in Lactantius, Cyprian, *Testimonies* II, ch. 5, and others, Christ is called an angel: Isaiah IX in the Septuagint, “the angel of great counsel”; Cyprian gives the passage thus in the sermon on Christ’s Nativity; Lactantius above, ch. 12, preferred the Latin expression “messenger of great counsel”; Malachi III, “the Angel of the Covenant”; and John, Revelation XX, “I saw an angel descending from heaven,” etc., a passage which most interpret of Christ the Lord. Christ is rightly called prince of messengers or envoys—for below, chs. 25 and 29, and in *On the Wrath of God*, ch. 2, Lactantius calls him by this name also—because he discharged the greatest embassy of all to humankind, as we said above, ch. 8. Or he called him prince, that is, head of angels, in accordance with the Apostle’s words in Colossians II: “Who is the head of all principality and power,” etc. The same reasoning applies to angels of all the other orders, as St Thomas teaches, Part III, question 8, article 4. I have followed the reading of codex B, to which I assign very great weight because of its remarkable antiquity, and of the Plantin edition.

## CHAPTER XV
When he first began to grow into youth, he was baptized by John the prophet in the Jordan, etc. Jesus was about thirty years old [Col. 0978A] when he was baptized (Luke 3), whether we explain the passage as meaning that he was two months short of thirty, as Epiphanius, *Heresies* 51, and Jansenius in the *Harmony* do; or that he was in the very thirtieth year of his age, as the African Tertullian does in Jerome, *On Daniel*, ch. 9, and the Master of Scholastic History, *History of the Gospels*, ch. 33, who reports that he had begun his thirtieth year in such a way that he had completed only thirteen days of it. This was also the view of many Holy Fathers: Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, II.10; Gregory Nazianzen, Homily on St. Lawrence; Theophylact and Euthymius on Luke 3; and later writers—the Carthusian, Cajetan on the same ch. 3, and others. Or finally, it may mean that he had already completed his thirtieth year and begun his thirty-first, as Ignatius the Martyr, *To the Trallians*; Chrysostom, Homily 10 on Matthew; and Euthymius on Matthew 3 hold. At any of these ages, I think, no one would have begun adolescence.

“By the sprinkling of purifying dew.” This is how it should be read from B, T, P, and the Florentine edition—not “purified,” etc., as [Col. 0978B] in the Aldine and Plantin editions. From this passage one may perhaps infer that in the primitive Church the practice of baptism was not to immerse those to be baptized, nor to pour water over them from above, but merely to sprinkle them. This is to be supposed to have occurred at that time because of the multitude of candidates for baptism, often assembled together. Yet, since in immersion the image of Christ’s burial is represented more expressly, the mode of baptizing by immersion or pouring, which the Church uses today, is more praiseworthy, as St. Thomas maintains, III, q. 66, art. 7.

“You are my Son,” etc. This passage is found somewhat differently in Matthew 3, Mark 1, and Luke 3.

“Strengthen the feeble hands,” etc. The wording and punctuation of this passage vary slightly in the Septuagint, the Vulgate, Tertullian, *Against Marcion* IV, and Cyprian, *Testimonies* II, ch. 7. See the annotations of Franciscus Lucas of Bruges on the Bible.

“Of the mute.” This is how it stands in the Vulgate and in Cyprian, in place of the Septuagint’s μογιλάλων, “those who speak with difficulty,” or stammerers.

“And a stream in thirsty land.” Cyprian too, *Against the Jews*, ch. 7, rendered καὶ φάραγξ ἐν γῇ διψώσῃ in this way. The Septuagint: “and a valley in thirsty land”; the Vulgate: “and torrents in the wilderness.”

Καὶ χωλῶν δρόμος ἐστὶ ὠκύς: “and the course of the lame is swift.” In the Sibylline manuscript: χωλῶν δὲ δρόμος ὠκύτατος, “but the course of the lame is most swift.”

“He went up onto a certain deserted mountain, in order to worship there. When he had remained there for three days, and because of hunger, etc.” Lactantius seems to have confused the narratives of the two miracles in which the Lord satisfied a multitude. The first occurred when, withdrawing from Nazareth, he crossed by boat into a deserted place, and crowds followed him by land; this is narrated in Matthew 14, Luke 9, Mark 6, and John 6. There Jesus had not gone up a mountain before performing the miracle, nor had the crowds remained for three days. Rather, five loaves and two fish were multiplied; the crowd was arranged in groups of fifty; five thousand men were fed; and twelve baskets were filled with the remaining [Col. 0978D] fragments. The other miracle occurred when, withdrawing from Tyre and Sidon, he came beside the Sea of Galilee; going up a mountain, he sat there, and great crowds followed him. Jesus had compassion on them because they had already remained fasting for three days, as Matthew 15 and Mark 8 relate. But there were seven loaves and a few small fish, about four thousand persons, and seven baskets of leftover fragments. Both miracles are mentioned in Matthew 16.

Εἰν ἄρτοις ἅμα πέντε: “[with] five loaves together.” In the Sibylline manuscript these verses vary somewhat.

Πίστει τε: “and by faith.” Thus the error in the Aldine edition, which has πύστειτε, should have been corrected from the Florentine and Plantin editions and from the Sibylline manuscript itself.

Κύματα πεζεῦσι, etc.: “Waves [for] pedestrians,” etc. These too vary slightly there.

## CHAPTER XVI

[Col. 0979A]

“And they do not merely admire the good things of another’s beneficence,” etc. Meursius, *Critics* V, Arnobius, ch. 10, conjectures that it should rather read: “And they do not merely admire the gifts of another’s beneficence,” etc.

“And he reproaches us with the sins of the law.” Here, however, the words which precede these in both Bibles and in Cyprian have been omitted: “and he is contrary to our works.”

“He boasts that God is his father.” This is indeed better, as in the Vulgate and Cyprian according to the corrected editions of *Testimonies* II, ch. 14; Lucifer [of Cagliari], [the work attributed to] St. Athanasius, Augustine, *City of God* XVII.20; than the Septuagint’s “he boasts that God is father.”

“Their folly.” The Septuagint, Vulgate, and Cyprian have “their wickedness.” For the Greek is ἡ κακία, “wickedness.”

“There were one thousand and ten years.” In Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, under Olympiad 202, I find that one thousand and sixty years elapsed from Solomon to the death of Christ the Lord. [Col. 0979B]

“Let the moon be exalted.” In all the Latin manuscripts of the Psalms: “let the moon be taken away.”

“We announced before him as children.” This is exactly how Cyprian has it, *Against the Jews* II, ch. 13. The Septuagint, according to St. Jerome: “we announced [him] as a little child in his sight”; and it is also found in St. Jerome himself, in the Commentary [reference uncertain], in Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, and in *Against Marcion* II: “we announced concerning him as a little child.” The Vulgate is very different.

“A man set in affliction,” etc. In citing this passage of Isaiah, Lactantius changes some things and mutilates others. The Septuagint: “A man set in affliction and knowing how to bear weakness; because his face has been turned away, he was despised and not esteemed,” etc. Cyprian: “A man set in affliction and knowing how to bear infirmity; because his face has been turned away, he was dishonoured and not counted.” Let the reader compare the rest.

## CHAPTER XVII

“That he was abolishing the law; although he did this not by his own judgment,” [Col. 0979C] etc. He used the term *solving* [*solvendi*] in the sense of abolishing or nullifying, terms used by Paul in Hebrews 8 and Ephesians 2, drawn metaphorically from the bonds of ropes, which lose their force as soon as they are untied. Christ the Lord preferred the proper term “fulfilling” in Matthew 5, because when a law is repealed which was not perpetual but established for a fixed time, after that time it is not properly said to be dissolved or removed, but ended and completed. Thus the Saviour there, because the old law was not established forever but until the fullness of time should come, said that he had come not to dissolve it—as if it were perpetual—but to fulfil and complete the realities of which it bore shadows. Lactantius likewise means this when he says that Christ acted according to the predictions of the prophets; and below, ch. 20, he acknowledges that the New Testament was the fulfilment of the Old.

“And he shall choose mighty nations,” etc. Yet in the Septuagint, both in Micah and in Isaiah, one reads ἐξελέγξει, which the Vulgate translator and others rendered “he shall rebuke,” as in Isaiah, or “he shall correct,” as in Micah; for this is what ἐξελέγχω means. Cyprian also, *Against the Jews* II, ch. 18, cites from Isaiah “he shall convict,” and the author of the tract *Against the Jews* among Cyprian’s works has “he shall correct.” But since the Aldine edition of Lactantius, the Plantin edition, and most others read *deliget*, “he shall choose,” I suspect that Lactantius’s Greek biblical manuscript in Micah contained an error and gave ἐκλέξει, “he shall choose,” in place of ἐξελέγξει. Yet why in the same Cyprian, *Against the Jews* I, ch. 10, also citing Micah, one reads *deteget*, “he shall expose,” or here in Lactantius’s Florentine edition *diriget*, “he shall direct,” I can find no explanation; and I think it was a printer’s error. But I think that the genuine text of Cyprian and Lactantius had *deliget*, and that they thus wrote—though wrongly—deceived, as I have said, perhaps by an error in the Greek text of Micah.

“Horeb.” It is also called Choreb, and perhaps more correctly. [Col. 0980A] For among the Hebrews the first letter of this name is represented among the Greeks by χ. It is a ridge of Mount Sinai, and hence the mountain of God is called by a single name; and it is written that the law was given on Sinai, as in Exodus 19 and 34, Leviticus 26, and on Horeb, as in Deuteronomy 9 and Malachi 4. We read that some have written that the eastern part of this mountain is called Sinai and the western Horeb: Jerome, *On Hebrew [Names]* and *On the Forty-Two Stations*; Ortelius and certain other modern writers think that the same mountain is now called Sinai, now Horeb. The more accepted opinion, however, is that these mountains are distinct from one another but joined at their bases, and that Horeb is much lower in height than Sinai.

Εἰς αὐτὸν πᾶς λύσεται, etc.: “Into him everyone shall be released,” etc. The verse is mutilated; it is restored from the Sibylline manuscript, where it reads: Εἰς αὐτὸν τότε πᾶς λύεται, etc., “Then everyone is released into him,” etc.

“Isaiah prophesied thus.” An error of memory: he put Isaiah in place of Jeremiah, who has this in ch. 4.

“Renew.” The Florentine edition has “recall.” But manuscripts, the Aldine and Plantin editions, and the Bible—both Vulgate [Col. 0980B] and Septuagint—together with Tertullian and Cyprian, support our reading.

“Newness.” Thus Cyprian, *Testimonies* I, ch. 8, and Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, though Tertullian in *Against Marcion* I has *novamen novum*, “a new newness,” in place of the Septuagint’s plural νεώματα, “newly cleared fields”; whereas in Hebrew, Chaldaic, and the Vulgate it is singular, *novale*, “newly cleared field.”

“Circumcise the foreskin of your heart.” Thus Cyprian, *Against the Jews* I; but Tertullian has “be circumcised [in] the foreskin,” or “foreskins, of your heart,” as in the Hebrew, Chaldaic, and Latin according to the Vulgate edition, in place of what is now read in the Septuagint, κληροκαρδίαν ὑμῶν, “the hardness of your heart.”

“And let it burn up.” Most copies do not have these words; we added them from B, for Cyprian has precisely this wording, and the prophet in the Septuagint and Vulgate reads “and it shall be kindled,” or “and let it be kindled.”

“In the last days.” The Septuagint and Vulgate do not have these words, but Cyprian does.

“The Lord will circumcise.” It agrees with the Vulgate and Cyprian; Augustine, *Questions* 53, agrees with the Septuagint: “he will cleanse all around.” But here the words “and the heart of his seed,” which appear in both Bibles and in Cyprian, are absent.

“Very sharp stone knives.” It agrees with the Septuagint, Cyprian, and Theodoret. In the manuscripts: “stone knives from a sharp rock.” St. Augustine, *Questions* 6: “Make for yourself knives from a sharp rock”; or, as the Greek has it, “from a sharp rock.”

“For the prophet does not say thus: ‘And the Lord said to me.’” All copies contain an error, reading “Jesus” in place of “Lord.” But the text of Sacred Scripture itself has it as we have caused it to be printed; and Firmianus himself cited it correctly a little earlier, to which passage these remarks refer.

“Auses.” In accordance with the Septuagint of Numbers 13, Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, and St. Augustine, *Against Faustus* XVI.19, render this name: τὸν Αὐσὴν υἱὸν Ναυῆς, “Auses, son of Naue.” The Vulgate, following the Hebrew, has Hosea.

## CHAPTER XVIII

“That this ought to be done in every persecution.” Observe the testimony of a most ancient Father concerning the lawful resort to flight in time of persecution, against the Marcionites and Montanists. Clement of Alexandria refutes them in *Stromata* IV; so do Origen on John, ch. 31; Cyprian in his Letter to the Thibaritans, *On the Exhortation to Martyrdom*, and *On the Lapsed*; Nazianzen in the Oration in Praise of Caesarius and the Oration in Praise of Basil; Athanasius in the *Apology concerning His Flight*; and St. Augustine in his Letter to Honoratus.

“The legate governed Syria.” He uses the title *legate* as common to all who were sent publicly on any official business; Varro likewise interprets the term so in *On the Latin Language* V. But in its strict sense it was the particular title of a magistracy and office. Some call Pilate a procurator, as Luke’s Gospel, ch. 3, and Tacitus, *Annals* XV; others governor of Syria, as Ignatius the Martyr in his Letter to the Trallians.
