“Forty-six years.” I have retained this number, supported by twelve Vatican manuscripts, P, and the Florentine, Aldine, [Col. 0981A] Plantin, and other editions, and given by John’s Gospel itself, ch. 3, although B and T have “forty years.”

“Nothing worthy of condemnation appeared to be in him.” This was an ancient judicial formula. Seneca, *Natural Questions* I.16: “And yet he did not pronounce that he appeared to have been lawfully killed.” Pliny, XIV.13: “The judge pronounced that the woman appeared to have drunk more wine than [was needed] for health’s sake.” They also used the same formula not infrequently in decrees of the senate. Sallust: “When Cicero consulted [the senate], the full senate decreed that the judgment concerning Tarquinius appeared false.” Cornificius, I: “The senate decreed that, if he should bring that law before the people, he appeared to be acting against the republic.” It was used also in laws and plebiscites. Livy, XXV: “The plebs resolved that he should be considered to be in exile.” Cujas, *Observations* III.26, produces other examples from the replies of ancient jurists and other authors.

“Yet he himself did not pronounce the sentence,” etc. On the contrary, it is certain from John and Luke that Pilate pronounced a sentence of condemnation against Christ. John, ch. 19, says that Pilate sat upon the tribunal, which belongs only to one exercising judgment; Luke, ch. 23, says that he judged concerning him, for this is the sense of ἐπέκρινε. The Apostle Peter likewise, speaking of Jesus in 1 Peter 2, says: “He entrusted himself to him who judged unjustly”—namely, Pilate. St. Ignatius expressly relates this in his Letter to the Trallians; likewise St. Augustine on Psalm 63, and Pope Leo, Sermons 1 and 8 on the Lord’s Passion.

“With a garment of crimson colour.” That garment was a *chlamys*, as Matthew 27 has it: χλαμύδα κοκκίνην, “a scarlet cloak”; the Romans called it a *paludamentum*. Kings, emperors, and soldiers wore it over their armour. Its colour was red. Hence Martial, XIV:

> Rome is more clothed in dark colours, Gaul in red;  
> and this colour pleases boys and soldiers.

For soldiers were not deceived or frightened if blood flowed from their wounds. Thus they designated that red colour sometimes as scarlet, as Matthew the Evangelist; sometimes as purple, as Mark 15 and John [Col. 0981C] 19; sometimes as crimson, as Lactantius does here. For all these colours in some way denote red, whether intensifying or softening it, or tempering it with a certain mixed shade. Everyone knows from Pliny, IX.41, that *coccum* is red; and in XXII.2 he writes that it was assigned to imperial military cloaks. Plutarch too, in his *Fabius*, reports that for Roman commanders a scarlet tunic stretched above the praetorium was a sign of an impending battle. Pliny, IX.8, writes that the finest purple is that which displays the colour of congealed blood; hence blood is called purple in Homer.

As for crimson, also called Phoenician—called φοῖνιξ or σπάδιξ by the Greeks, because the end of a palm branch torn from the tree with its fruit is called *spadix*, as Gellius testifies, III.9—I offer the following from Fronto in the same Gellius, II.26, disputing with the philosopher Favorinus concerning colours: “For these are not the only terms indicating red which you have just mentioned, *rufus* and *ruber*. We also have many others, beyond the Greek words named by you. *Fulvus*, *flavus*, *rubidus*, *Phoeniceus*, *rutilus*, *luteus*, and *spadix* are names for red colour: they either sharpen it, as if setting it ablaze; mix it with green; darken it with black; or gradually brighten a greenish shade with white. For *Phoeniceus*, which you called φοῖνιξ in Greek, is ours; and *rutilus* and *spadix* are synonyms (συννώνυμα) of *Phoeniceus*, which, rendered into Greek, denotes an abundance and splendour of redness, like the fruit of a palm tree not very much ripened by the sun; hence the names *Spadix* and *Phoeniceus*. For the Dorians call *spadica* the end torn from a palm tree together with its fruit,” etc.

Accordingly, Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XIII, and Statius, *Achilleid* I, also attribute this colour to blood. Plutarch, *Laconic Institutions*, *Aemilius Paulus*, and *Marcellus* relate that it was likewise a sign of impending battle, and that soldiers preparing for combat customarily put it on. Others maintain that the colour took its name not from the palm, as stated, but rather from the rind of the pomegranate; others derive it from παρὰ τὸν φόνον, “from slaughter,” because that shrub—which, like *androsemon*, yields blood, though in another manner—was called φόνος by Theophrastus. Thus, in reference to one and the same cloak of Christ, these three colours were named—not because they are identical, for in their proper senses they differ, as Brodaeus argues against Parrhasius, Guarinus, and others, *Miscellanies* I.8, and Bayfius, *On Dress* 3—but because, as stated, all in some way display the same colour, namely red. They could therefore be used by the Evangelists and Lactantius for one and the same colour. I wished to discuss these few points in order to show that Lactantius agrees with the Evangelists, and the Evangelists with one another, although passages that seem to conflict caused some difficulty for learned men, especially Lazarus Bayfius in the work cited above.

“The Gavian cross.” The Florentine edition has “Gabian,” an error noted by Andreas Patricius at the beginning of his Scholia on the fragments of Cicero’s Orations. [Col. 0982B] For the passage must refer to the cruel act of Verres, who fastened P. Gavius—not Gabinius—to a cross; Cicero discusses this in the seventh oration *Against Verres*.

“They did not know.” St. Augustine has this as well, in place of the Vulgate and Septuagint’s “I did not know”; Symmachus: “I did not know.”

Εἰς ἀνόμιους, etc.: “Into lawless [hands],” etc. Lactantius joined these verses, which in Sibylline Oracles, Book 8, are separated and scattered from one another. For there one first reads καὶ στόμασιν μιαροῖσι, etc., “and with defiled mouths,” etc.; then, after several intervening verses, δώσει δ᾽ εἰς μάστιγας, “he shall give [him] to scourges”; finally, after other verses intervene, occur those which stand first here: εἰς ἀνόμους χεῖρας, etc., “into lawless hands,” etc.

Τὶς λόγος, ἢ πόθεν ἦλθεν: “What word—or whence did he come?” The Sibylline manuscript has: τίς τινος ὤν, πόθεν ἦλθεν, etc., “who is he, whose [son] is he, whence did he come?” etc.

Αὐτοῦ γὰρ σὺ ἄφρων: “For you are foolish concerning him.” I do not find these verses among the Sibylline poems.

Ἀκάνθαις: “with thorns.” I would prefer ἀκάνθης, “of a thorn.”

“And Esdras said to the people.” A notable passage, which we no longer possess. Justin Martyr, in the *Dialogue against the Jews*, affirms that it was removed by the Jews from the books of Ezra, together with other passages there specified.

“His birth.” Tertullian and Cyprian have this too. But the Septuagint and Vulgate have τὴν γενεὰν, “his generation.”

“He was led to death.” This is how nearly all manuscripts of Lactantius read. The Florentine edition has “he was taken away,” a reading which did not please Pamelius, who reports that it is also read in certain manuscript codices of Cyprian. Tertullian has “he was conducted [to death].”

“Because he committed no crime, nor spoke deceit with his mouth.” The Septuagint: “because he did no injustice, nor [was there] deceit in his mouth”; the Vulgate: “because he did no injustice, nor was deceit in his mouth”; Tertullian, *Against the Jews*: “Nor was deceit found in his mouth,” or, as in the manuscripts, “nor was deceit in his mouth”; Cyprian: “because he committed no crime, nor spoke deceit with his mouth.” The Florentine Juntine edition here has: “because he committed no crime, nor was deceit found in his mouth.” But we followed the manuscripts and the more numerous and better editions.

“He shall obtain many.” This is the reading in the Aldine and Plantin editions [Col. 0982D] and in Cyprian as edited by Pamelius, where, however, John Coster read “he shall possess,” as is now read in the recent Latin translation from the Septuagint, whose Greek has κληρονομήσει. I would translate this “he shall inherit,” as the Florentine edition has here, and Tertullian, *Against the Jews*: “he shall have as an inheritance.”

“Because he was delivered to death.” Cyprian from the Septuagint: “Because his soul was delivered to death.” The Vulgate: “because he delivered his soul unto death.”

“The sins of many,” etc. Thus I read with B, T, and the other better manuscripts and printed editions, along with the Septuagint, Vulgate, Tertullian, and Cyprian, although the Florentine edition has “the sin of many,” etc.

“They will hunt for [his] soul,” etc. B has “they will hunt [his] soul.” I have presented the reading of all the other manuscripts of Lactantius, the Septuagint, and the Vulgate.

“Like a lamb without blemish.” The Septuagint has ὡς ἀρνίον ἄκακον, which later translators of that version rendered “like an innocent lamb.” Cyprian, *Testimonies* II, ch. 15, has “like a lamb without malice”; the Vulgate, “like a gentle lamb.”

“They devised a thought.” As Cyprian, *Testimonies* II, ch. 15: “They devised a devising”; the Vulgate: “they devised plans.” The Septuagint: ἐλογίσαντο λογισμὸν πονηρόν, “they devised an evil thought.”

“Let us root out.” Thus the Vulgate and the printed books of Cyprian, *Testimonies* II, chs. 15 and 20; but the manuscripts, according to Pamelius, have “let us remove” or “let us pluck out.” Tertullian is closer to the Septuagint and Jerome: the former in *Against the Jews*, and the latter in his Commentary, have “let us crush.” The Greek is ἐκτρίψωμεν, “let us wipe out.”

“From the land of his life.” Cyprian likewise has this; but the Septuagint, Vulgate, and Tertullian have “him from the land of the living.”

“He shall not be remembered.” The Septuagint and Vulgate: μὴ μνησθῇ, “let him not be remembered.” Tertullian and Cyprian agree with Lactantius.

“The Lord is not as a man,” etc. Thus the Septuagint, except that for “Lord” it has “God”; Cyprian, *Testimonies* II [Col. 0983B], ch. 20, and Theodoret, *Questions* 43. But the Vulgate: “God is not as a man, that he should lie, nor as a son of man, that he should change.” Origen, Homily 16, and Philo, *On the Life of Moses* I, are nearly the same.

“Whom they pierced.” The Vulgate: “whom they transfixed”; Cyprian, *Testimonies* II, ch. 21: “upon whom they pierced”; Tertullian, *Against the Jews*: “whom they stabbed.” St. Jerome, who discusses the diverse readings of this passage, nevertheless recognizes in the Septuagint ἀνθ᾽ ὧν κατωρχήσαντο, “because they danced in triumph.”

“They dug.” The Greek is ὤρυξαν; Pamelius read this in Cyprian from the manuscripts, not “and they dug,” as in the printed editions, because the conjunction is nowhere present. Tertullian sometimes has “they dug,” like the Septuagint, Vulgate, and Justin, as in *Against Marcion* IV; sometimes “they destroyed,” as in *Against the Jews*.

“My hands and my feet.” Thus the Vulgate, Tertullian, *Against Marcion* IV, Cyprian, St. Augustine, and others. But Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, with the Septuagint, has merely “my hands and feet,” with nothing further; Justin likewise: “my feet and hands,” with nothing further.

“But the Spirit of God was speaking through him, who was to suffer those things.” That is, the Son of God himself, whom Lactantius here, as often elsewhere, calls the Spirit of God—in the sense in which God is called Spirit, as we said in Book II, ch. 9—not so as to confuse the person of the Son with that of the Holy Spirit.

“After one thousand and fifty years.” For that is the total number of years gathered from David’s reign to Christ’s crucifixion. From the beginning of David’s reign, the sum indeed falls somewhat short according to Eusebius’s *Chronicle*. He assigns forty years to David’s reign; after him his son Solomon reigned. From Solomon and the first construction of the Temple—which occurred in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign, as 3 Kings 6 states—to the year of the Lord’s Passion, Eusebius under Olympiad 202 calculates one thousand and sixty years. But this accords exactly with Lactantius’s calculation, who above, ch. 16, counted 1,010 years from the time of Solomon’s prophecy, which we begin from the first year of his reign. Adding the forty years of David’s reign therefore yields precisely the total of one thousand and fifty years. [Col. 0983D]

“But if you turn away,” etc. The wording of this passage varies greatly in the sacred text: here some things have been altered, others omitted or added. Let whoever wishes compare them.

## CHAPTER XIX

“And the day of light shall be darkened.” Thus Cyprian, *Testimonies* II, ch. 23, and nearly Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, where one reads: “and the day of light shall grow dark over the earth.” The Septuagint: “and light shall be darkened over the earth by day”; the Vulgate: “and I shall make the earth grow dark in the day of light.”

“And your songs.” The Septuagint, Vulgate, Tertullian, and Cyprian: “and all your songs.”

“She was terrified.” Cyprian agrees with Lactantius; but the Septuagint and Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* IV.66, read ἐκενώθη, “she was emptied”; the Vulgate, “she was weakened.”

[Col. 0984A] “She who gives birth.” Thus Irenaeus and Cyprian. The Vulgate and Septuagint add ἑπτά, “seven”: Vulgate, “she who bore seven”; Septuagint, “she who bears seven.”

“And the soul was weary.” Cyprian: “and her soul was weary”; Vulgate: “her soul failed.” For the conjunction is absent, as also in the Septuagint, which has ἀπεκαύκησεν ἡ ψυχὴ αὐτῆς, “her soul was afflicted.”

“And the sun went down upon her.” Thus the Florentine edition; but the Plantin and Aldine editions, like the Vulgate, have “and the sun set upon her.” I retained the reading which I judged Lactantius more probably to have expressed, namely that of the Septuagint, ἐπέδυ, and Cyprian.

Ναοῦ δὲ σχίστητε πέτασμα, etc.: “And let the veil of the temple be torn,” etc. I have presented this verse as Marcus Musurus corrected it at the end of the Aldine edition. But here in the text, in nearly all copies, one reads ναοῦ δὲ σχισθήσεται πέτασμα, etc., “and the veil of the temple shall be torn,” etc. In the Sibylline manuscript: ναοῦ σχίσσθε τὸ καταπέτασμα, “let the curtain of the temple be torn.” In both cases the metrical form is unsound.

“In Hades.” Cyprian likewise has this; where the Septuagint and Vulgate have εἰς ᾅδον, “into hell.”

“Destruction.” The Greek is διαφθοράν, “corruption,” as in the Septuagint, Vulgate, and Cyprian.

“And I took sleep.” Thus Cyprian and St. Augustine, in place of the Septuagint’s Greek ὕπνωσα, “I slept”; yet St. Augustine acknowledges that some manuscripts have, as the Vulgate now does, “I fell asleep.”

“He helped me.” Thus Cyprian; but the Septuagint has ἀντιλήψεταί μου, “he will support me,” followed by St. Augustine. The Vulgate has “he supported me,” as does Justin Martyr: ἀντελάβετό μου.

“This is my wise son,” etc. Lactantius cites this passage neither sufficiently faithfully, having omitted, added, and changed certain things, nor interprets it sufficiently correctly concerning the Son of God. The Septuagint: “This is your wise son”; the Vulgate: “he himself is not a wise son.” Scripture speaks there of Ephraim’s iniquity; and by Ephraim different interpreters understand different things: St. Jerome, a tribe prone to idolatry; Lyra, an unwise son who has turned from piety to impiety; others simply a sinful human being. The Septuagint continues: “For [Col. 0984C] he shall not now stand in the breaking of children. From the hand of Hades I shall deliver [them], and from death I shall redeem them. Where is your case against them, O death? Where is your sting, O Hades?” The Vulgate: “For now he shall not stand in the breaking of children. From the hand of death I shall deliver them; from death I shall redeem them. I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your bite, O Hades.”

“He shall not stand.” B lacks the negation, which must certainly be retained, as the prophet has it. For the Septuagint reads “he shall not remain”; the Vulgate, “he shall not stand.”

“I shall deliver him.” Scripture has not “him” but “them,” both in the Septuagint and in the Vulgate.

“He will make us alive after two days; on the third day.” This passage of Hosea is read in Lactantius mutilated and wrongly punctuated, as also in Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, and Cyprian in the old edition of *Testimonies* II, ch. 25. It should have been cited as it stands in the prophet: “He will make us alive after two days; on the third day we shall rise,” as the Septuagint has; or “on the third day he will raise us up,” as the Vulgate has.

Θανάτου: “of death.” This should be read as it stands in the Sibylline manuscript and as Musurus once corrected it here, not θάνατος, “death,” corruptly printed in [Col. 0984D] the Florentine and Aldine editions.

## CHAPTER XX
So that he might not bring them to repentance and heal the ungodly. Lest, pious reader, you take any offence from this, and that we may at the same time defend Lactantius against the calumny by which some charge him here with error, attend again and again to this point: it is most certain and a matter of faith that some human beings are rejected by God; Mal. I, Rom. IX, II Tim.; since it belongs to divine providence to permit some things to fail of their end which by their own nature can fail of it—such as man, who through freedom of choice can fall away from blessedness—in order that the harmonious ordering of the universe may be preserved. Nor does that well-worn saying, I Tim. II, “God wills all human beings to be saved,” etc., stand in the way; for it is understood not of the consequent will, by which God is said simply to will, but of the antecedent will, by which he is not said simply [Col. 0985A] to will, as Damascene says, *On the Orthodox Faith*, ch. 2; Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter*, ch. 33, and *On Rebuke and Grace*, ch. 15. St Thomas gives other explanations of that passage, First Part, question 19, article 6.

The question now is whether, with regard to the reprobate, the divine will has any positive act, so that it positively concurs; or whether it is only purely negative. The answer is that four things befall the reprobate: first, they are permitted to fall into sin; second, the fault itself and sin; third, they are abandoned by God and persevere in fault until the end of life; fourth, punishment itself and eternal penalty.

With regard to the first, God has a positive will to permit sins and to permit some persons, by their own freedom, to sin and fall short of blessedness. This is so, first, because in fact he thus permits it, and therefore wills that permission; for permission and operation are signs of the divine will of good pleasure: St Thomas, First Part, question 19, article 12. Since this is a consequent will, it is a positive act in God. Secondly, since nothing occurs unless God wills it to occur, either by allowing it to occur or by doing it himself (St Augustine, *Enchiridion*, ch. [Col. 0985B] 95), and since sin does indeed occur, though not by his doing it or willing it to occur, it therefore occurs because he wills to permit and allow it to occur. Again, to permit evils is good and is directed to a greater good, and this belongs to divine providence: St Thomas, First Part, question 22. Therefore this permission must be said to be willed by God by a positive act.

Nor should it be objected that, if such permission of sin in the reprobate is willed by God through a positive act, God must at least indirectly be judged the cause of the reprobate’s sin—as though God withdrew the efficacious aid by which, if it remained, the reprobate would not sin. For one who removes an obstacle is, at least indirectly, the cause of the consequent effect, as we say of a stone’s fall after the column by which it was held up has been removed.

The answer is that, although he withdraws efficacious aid, he never withdraws sufficient aid; and sin does not follow immediately from the withdrawal of efficacious aid, but from the free will of the sinner. For reprobation takes away nothing of the power or freedom of the reprobate, as St Thomas teaches [Col. 0985C] in the First Part, question 23, article 2, reply to objection 3. But when an effect does not follow necessarily and immediately after the removal of an obstacle, the remover of the obstacle is not always said to concur in the effect or to be its cause.

And we rightly say “not always”; for sometimes the remover of an obstacle is called the moral cause of an effect where he was obliged to prevent the effect. For then, although the effect does not follow immediately from the removal of the obstacle, it is nevertheless imputed to the remover, because he could have prevented it, was obliged to prevent it, and did not prevent it. Thus thefts which occur are imputed to a magistrate, and he is called their cause, although they do not follow immediately from him, because he is obliged to prevent them. But the sins of a prostitute—an utterly corrupt policy, especially unworthy of a Christian—are not imputed to the person who permits them, nor is she called their cause, because she ought not to prevent them; indeed, it belongs to her good government to permit them.

From this it is especially clear why God is not said to be in any way the cause of the reprobate’s sins, either by nature or morally, although [Col. 0985D] he permits them and removes the obstacle: because he is not obliged to prevent them. Rather, it belongs to his good governance and to the harmonious ordering of the world to permit some persons to sin and to fall short of their end, as St Bonaventure teaches in I *Sentences*, distinction 4, article 2, question 2.

With respect to the fault for which the reprobate is damned, God certainly does not will it: Hos. XIII, “Your destruction,” etc.; Rom. IX, “He endured with much patience,” etc. Otherwise God would be the author of sin and his will would be evil, since its object would be sin and evil—blasphemous assertions. But neither does he have an absolute and efficacious unwillingness toward it; for since nothing can resist the absolute and efficacious divine will, no sins whatsoever would exist if God had such an absolute unwillingness concerning them.

Thirdly, God positively wills to abandon the reprobate, to permit them to persevere in sins, and to be handed over to the desires of their hearts: Rom. I, “God handed them over to their desires,” etc.; Ps. LXXX, “I dismissed [Col. 0986A] them according to their desires,” etc.; Rom. IX, “He has mercy on whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills.” These passages indicate a positive act of the divine will concerning the abandonment of the reprobate.

The same is also supported by reason. Whatever is reasonable and just, God wills by a positive act. But it is of this sort for a human being to be abandoned by God when he has first abandoned God himself by sinning. Yet care must be taken that, where Sacred Scripture says that God abandons, forsakes, hardens, or blinds, the sense is not that God introduces or produces in the souls of the reprobate any hardness or blindness, as though some darkness; nor that God is the cause that the reprobate fall into sins and remain in them. Rather, it means that by his will God does not bestow his grace and warmth, by which the reprobate’s heart is softened, nor infuse the light by which it can be enlightened (St Augustine, *On Predestination and Grace*, ch. 4; Epistle 105; and the Epistle to Simplicianus); or he is said to harden, blind, and so forth because he permits them to be hardened and blinded. For it is a phrase and mode of speech of Scripture to call that which is properly [Col. 0986B] God’s permission God’s action, because God wills that permission by a positive act. Damascene teaches this, *Theology*, IV, ch. 14; Euthymius, on John, ch. 15.

Finally, God positively wills to inflict punishment on the reprobate for fault; for this is especially just and reasonable and pertains to the rectitude of a judge. From this it is clear that reprobation is not the cause of the reprobate’s damnation as predestination is the cause of the predestined person’s salvation. For permission to sin puts nothing into the sinner, as justification puts something into the penitent; nor does God’s reprobation take anything away from the reprobate’s power, nor is the reprobate rendered incapable of obtaining grace by an absolute incapacity, but only by an incapacity under a supposition, which does not diminish freedom, as St Thomas teaches, First Part, question 23, article 3.

Therefore Lactantius did not speak absurdly when he said that Jesus did not wish to show himself to the reprobate Jews, lest he bring them to repentance, etc. For by these words is signified the abandonment by which they were abandoned by God, [Col. 0986C] and the permission that they should remain in the sin of unbelief, together with the withdrawal of the efficacious divine aid by which their hearts would be softened and enlightened. Yet their sin, or their perseverance in it, cannot be referred back to God as its cause.

“I have forsaken my house,” etc. In quoting this passage Lactantius omitted the words, “I have given my beloved soul,” which occur in both Bibles: “I have forsaken my house; I have abandoned my inheritance; I have given my beloved soul into the hands of her enemies.” And indeed the sense varies greatly. On the other hand, he added the word *ipsa* (“herself”), which neither the Bibles nor Cyprian have.

“In righteousness.” Aldine and Plantin have this reading; the Florentine edition has “unto righteousness.” I should prefer “in righteousness,” as in the Vulgate, the Septuagint, and Cyprian.

“And I will hold your hand.” So also the Septuagint; but the Vulgate has, “and I took hold of your hand.” Cyprian: “that I might hold your hand.”

“And I will strengthen you.” The Septuagint and Cyprian have, “and I will make you strong.” [Col. 0986D] The Vulgate has, “and I preserved you.” Therefore that pronoun must be retained in the text of Lactantius, as it appears in the Florentine edition, though it is lacking in the Aldine and Plantin editions.

“Of my race.” So Cyprian and Cyril; but in the Vulgate and Septuagint the word *mei* (“my”) is absent.

“Those sitting in darkness.” The Vulgate agrees with Lactantius, as do Tertullian, III *Against Marcion* and *Against the Jews*, Cyprian, and Cyril. But in recently published editions of the Septuagint the conjunction is added: “and those sitting,” etc.

## CHAPTER XXI

“As the Son of Man.” The Florentine edition lacks the particle *ut* (“as”), which is recognized by the others, by the manuscript books, by Lactantius above in chapter 12, likewise by the Septuagint and Vulgate, and by Tertullian, *On the Flesh of Christ* and III *Against Marcion* and elsewhere: “as the Son of Man.”

“Which Peter and Paul preached at Rome.” This is to be noted as a notable fragment indeed of this prophecy concerning the coming [Col. 0987A] destruction of Jerusalem, and of the preaching of Peter and Paul delivered at Rome, concerning which we have nothing in the sacred writings or elsewhere. The testimony of this most distinguished and ancient Father is also to be noted against heretics who deny that the Apostle Peter was ever at Rome.

## CHAPTER XXIII

“Whoever gives precepts to human beings,” etc. I pass over as empty the entire discussion of this and the following chapter; for no one could rightly deny that God himself, having assumed flesh, was the true and perfect giver of the law of Moses and teacher of virtue. Isa. XXXIII: “The Lord is our judge; the Lord is our lawgiver.” Therefore attention should be given to the truer reasons for the incarnation of Christ the Lord, divinely expounded by St Thomas, Second Part, question I, article 1, and by the other Doctors, especially St Bonaventure in III *Sentences*, distinction I.

## CHAPTER XXV

“His mother in respect of his body, a Virgin.” Against Valentinus, [Col. 0987B] Apollinaris, Eutyches, and others who denied that Christ the Lord received anything from the Virgin Mary. See Irenaeus III, *Against Heresies*; St Augustine, *On Heresies*; Theodoret, *Compendium of Heretical Fables*, book IV, at the end.

## CHAPTER XXVI

“In bodies injured and afflicted.” In the earlier editions *uninjured* is corruptly read.

“Lest there should be anyone at all who could not imitate him.” This same reason is also given by St Thomas in the Third Part, question 46, article 4; for he teaches that it was most fitting for Christ to undergo death on the cross for the example of virtue.

“As their custom required,” etc. He rightly says “their,” namely the Jews’; for they alone used to break the legs of those hanging [on crosses] so that they might bury them dead on the same day, according to the law of Deuteronomy, chapter XXI. Among other nations, however, the breaking of legs had nothing to do with crucifixion, but was an altogether separate kind of punishment, as Caesar Baronius, Cardinal, noted in the *Martyrology* under 23 May, and Lipsius in books II and III of *On the Cross*, chapter 14 in both places.

“Lest his injured and diminished body should be rendered unfit for resurrection.” A worthless reason—as though an injured, cut, or mutilated body could not have been raised to life by God.

“Passover is called ἀπὸ τοῦ πάσχειν,” that is, “from suffering.” These Greek words are absent from B., but retained by all the other manuscripts and printed editions. That he himself thought the name *Passover* derived from that verb is sufficiently indicated also by what follows. Tertullian has the same error at the end of *Against the Jews*, as does the author of the gloss, whom St Jerome rejects in his commentary on Matthew, chapter XXVI; Isidore, *Origins*, book VI, chapter 18. For it is derived not from a Greek verb, but from the Hebrew *Phasach*, which means “passage,” as Josephus teaches, *Antiquities*, book II, chapter 13; Jerome, in the place cited and on Isaiah XXXI and Micah VII; Ambrose, *On Cain and Abel*, chapter 8, and Sermon 53; Augustine, Epistle 119, *On the Trinity*, book II, chapter 17, and *City of God*, book XVI, chapter 43. This festival was celebrated in memory [Col. 0987D] of the angel bearing the plague passing over the thresholds of doorways marked with the blood of the lamb.

## CHAPTER XXVII

“For the present it is enough [to speak] of his power,” etc. This passage should be noted against the heretics of our time, enemies of the cross of the Lord. Tertullian treats the same argument in *Against the Jews* and III *Against Marcion*, and Cyprian in II *Against the Jews*, chapters 21 and 22.

“To depict things to come.” Future things were said metaphorically to be depicted in the entrails of sacrificial victims, insofar as they were in some manner prefigured in them; and perhaps this was a verb peculiar to haruspices, like *litare* (“to offer an acceptable sacrifice”) and *porricere* (“to present an offering”).

“With which they *prosecrant*.” That is, with which they sacrifice for a long time, or otherwise perform sacred rites; for it is a compound verb of the preposition *pro*, which when joined to a verb has temporal force, and the verb *sacro*, “I perform a sacred act.” Thus indeed I find it in the manuscripts and most printed editions. [Col. 0988A] The Florentine edition, however, corruptly reads *prosecarant*. This reading led me strongly to suspect that one should read *prosecuerant*; for that verb too fits beautifully when entrails are being discussed. Livy V: “He who had *prosecuisset* the entrails of that victim,” etc. Tertullian, *Apology* IX: “Among the Gauls, the elder age is *persecratur* to Mercury.” The word *prosecrant* is not easily found in any other author; but perhaps scribes carelessly omitted those two letters.

“The temple of God.” Understand: of Jupiter, Apollo, or any other demon, whom he often calls gods when speaking in the person of pagans, as in book I, chapters 17, 20, 21; book II, chapter 4; and elsewhere.

“Who added that supreme Jupiter to the demons.” I think this passage alludes to the place where Homer speaks of Minerva, *Iliad* I, near the beginning, who is said to have returned to heaven, to the dwellings of aegis-bearing Jupiter among the other gods:

> ἠδ᾽ Ὀλυμπόνδε βεβήκει,  
> Δώματ᾽ ἐν αἰγιόχοιο Διὸς μετὰ δαίμονας ἄλλους.

> “And she had gone up to Olympus,  
> to the halls of aegis-bearing Zeus, among the other demons.”

## CHAPTER XXVIII

[Col. 0988B]

“Whence religion itself received its name.” Lactantius thinks that *religio* is so called from *religare*, “to bind fast.” Ambrose seems to follow Lactantius in *On Virgins*, where he calls virgins consecrated to God *religiosae*, as though bound fast to God. So too Jerome, on Amos, chapter IX; Isidore, *Origins*, VIII, chapter 2; St Augustine, *On True Religion*, where he says, “May religion bind us fast to the one almighty God”; Nigidius Figulus in Gellius, book IV, chapter 9; Servius on Vergil’s line VIII, “Even then religion terrified,” etc.

But Masurius Sabinus in Gellius, in the place cited, and Servius Sulpicius in Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book III, chapter 3, prefer that it be derived from *relinquere*, “to leave behind,” as though that which is religious were understood to be something left by us, removed, and set apart.

“Not, as Cicero interpreted it, from *relegere*.” Yet a certain ancient writer in Gellius, in the passage cited, follows Cicero almost exactly, saying: “One ought to be observant [*relegens*]; to be religious [*religiosus*] is impious.” Arnobius at the end of book IV, St Augustine, *City of God* X, [Col. 0988C] chapter 4, and St Thomas approve all the etymologies of *religion* noted here, *Second of the Second*, question 81, article 1.

“Superstition is false [worship]. And it makes an absolute difference what you worship, not how you worship,” etc. This is false. For superstition is not only worship that is false, but also worship of the true [God] improperly offered, as St Thomas teaches in II–II, question 92. Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II, says that religion consists in devout worship of the gods; superstition, in which there is an empty fear of the gods. Fabius, book VIII, chapter 3, says that superstition differs from religion as the over-curious from the diligent. Varro, in St Augustine, *City of God* VI, distinguishes the religious from the superstitious on this ground: he says that gods are feared by the superstitious as enemies, but revered by the religious as parents. Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*, said that superstition was no less slight a vice than impiety.

“To free themselves from the bonds of religions.” He alludes to Lucretius, book I:

> Then I proceed to free minds from the knots  
> of religions by the art [of poetry].

“Unacquainted with the ancients.” Pierius and Velutello, in their annotations on Vergil, testify that this is found in the Roman Vergilian codex and many other ancient copies; but now all printed editions have “or of the ancients,” etc.

## CHAPTER XXIX

“Yet let us affirm two: God the Father and God the Son.” Since he was here speaking of only two persons, Father and Son, he therefore called them simply “two,” with no noun added. We may safely understand “two beings,” taking *beings* not substantively but adjectivally, and again understanding, namely, two persons. Thus the Master [Peter Lombard] in I *Sentences*, distinction 25, and St Thomas there, single question, article 4, and St Bonaventure in his explanation of the text.

“Since therefore both the father makes the son, and the son the father,” etc. He does not take these names for the divine Persons; for he would not have been so foolish as to say that the Father is made by the Son. Rather, he takes them as relative names, one of which constitutes and presupposes the other, and neither can exist without the other. For before these words he had said: “For neither can the Father be named without the Son, nor can the Son be begotten without the Father.” By this example, evidently, he wished to show that coexistence and coeternity of Father and Son in the Godhead—as does also the author of the *Exposition of the Apostles’ Creed* among the works of Cyprian.

“One substance.” Therefore the Son is consubstantial with the Father, against Arius.

“Since the Son is in the Father because the Father loves the Son, and the Father in the Son because he faithfully obeys the Father’s will.” The Son according to divinity is equal to the Father in all things and one with him, therefore in will, as Lactantius says here and St Thomas in IV *Against the Gentiles*, chapter 36, argument 7; but not in will alone, but also in nature, essence, and substance, as the author himself confessed a little above. For innovators have not been lacking—such as Erasmus, in his annotations on I John, chapter V—who interpreted the Gospel passage John X, “I and the Father are one,” which all the holy Fathers and Catholic doctors have always used against the Arians, as referring only to unity of will, harmony, and agreement, and not to unity of essence. Against them argue Alphonsus de Castro, book V *Against Heresies*, under “God,” Heresy 6; Torres, commentary on question 27, First Part; St Thomas, article I, disputation I, Part II.

“And they shall pray in you.” Others: “and they shall pray to you,” as above in chapter 13, where we spoke of it.

“And he who rescued him.” So the Septuagint: καὶ ῥυσάμενος αὐτόν, “and he who delivered him.” The Vulgate: “and his redeemer.”

“Eternal God.” In both Bibles the reading is “God Sabaoth,” that is, “God of hosts.”

“And I am the last.” So too the Vulgate, in place of what the Septuagint has: καὶ ἐγὼ μετὰ ταῦτα, “and I after these things.”

## CHAPTER XXX

“Or the Anthropians, or any others,” etc. I do not think that anthropomorphites are designated here, to whose error I shall say below, in chapter 18 of the book *On the Anger of God*, that Lactantius at one time assented. Rather, by the name *Anthropians* I think he means heretics who denied that Christ was God and maintained that he was a mere ἄνθρωπος, that is, a human being. Thus they were called Anthropians—as one might say in Latin, “humanists”: Ebion, Carpocrates, Cerinthus, Theodotus or Theodosion, Paul of Samosata, Photinus, and others, whose heresy was condemned by the great Nicene Synod, that of Ephesus, that of Chalcedon, and many others.

In the Vatican and certain other manuscripts and printed editions the reading is: “Or the Anthropians, or the Arians, or any others,” etc. I retained the reading of B., also found in the Plantin edition, both because of the authority of a codex of remarkable antiquity and because of the argument. For the Arian [Col. 0990B] heresy became known about the year of our Lord 315. But these books of Lactantius were begun, completed, and published long before, as was said above on chapter 1 of book I. Yet Catholics lose nothing from this, since so many passages of Lactantius establish that he abhorred Arian impiety and condemned it beforehand, before it had arisen, as we showed above in book II, chapter 9, and in this book, chapters 8, 14, and 29.

“In which are confession and repentance, which beneficially heal the sins and wounds to which the weakness of the flesh is subject.” These darts are directed against Novatian and his followers, who did not admit those fallen into sin to repentance, denying that remission of sins could be found in the Church and that Christ had given her the keys of opening and loosing. On this matter see Pacian, Epistle 1 to Sympronianus; St Augustine, *On Christian Combat*, chapter 31.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0989]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0989C]

“For I have no doubt that this work of ours,” etc. In certain printed editions: “For I have no doubt, Emperor Constantine, that this work,” etc. I followed the reading of B., which seems supported by reason, as I said on chapter 1 of book I.

“They embittered.” Thus it is written in B., perhaps for *coacervant* (“they heap up”), as above in book III, chapter 3, *connibere* for *connivere*. Thus St Cyprian in manuscript Epistle 42 to Cornelius, according to Pamelius’ edition, has *acerbationibus* (“embitterings”) where the printed editions read *acervationibus* (“heapings up”). So too “embittered scourges” in Tertullian at the end of the *Apology*, where see Pamelius and the said Epistle 42. Thomasius, however, here prefers to derive it from *acerbo*, “I make bitter.”

“Sacrilegious.” I prefer this reading, as in B., to “eloquent,” as in the Florentine, Plantin, and Aldine editions; for he did not mean to praise but to condemn that sacrilegious pagan who had given that name to the most holy man Cyprian.

“Coprianus.” It should be read thus, as in Plantin and Aldus, not *Caprianus*, as the Florentine Juntine edition reads. [Col. 0989D] It is a jibe at Cyprian through an allusion of words; for κοπρία means “dung,” whence *Coprianus*, as if “one handling dung” or “a dung-worker.” Or he calls him Coprianus as if he were a ridiculous person and buffoon; for buffoons were anciently called *Copriae*, as Joseph Scaliger notes in his *Castigations* on Festus under *Scurra*, and as the most learned men observe in correcting this passage: Lipsius, book II, chapter 17; Jacobus Durantius, *Variations* I, chapter 13. That is, having abandoned the worship of the gods, his noble talent had devoted itself to the base and foul kind of teaching, and to the old wives’ and ridiculous tales of Christians.

“Whence it appears,” etc. We added this whole period, down to “but if this happens,” etc., from codex B., both because it fits most aptly with the other material here and because it plainly appears to be Lactantian.

## CHAPTER II

“One of whom professed himself the chief priest of philosophy,” [Col. 0990C] etc. He means Porphyry. Consult Cardinal Baronius, *Annals*, vol. II, under the year of our Lord 302.

“He spewed forth three books against religion and the Christian name.” Three at first indeed, but afterward others up to fifteen, as Suidas writes. The calumnies and impieties of Porphyry were sharply refuted in substantial volumes by Methodius, bishop of Tyre, Eusebius, and Apollinaris, as Jerome reports in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and afterward incidentally and as occasion arose by Cyril, Jerome, Augustine, and others.

“Another wrote on the same subject more bitterly,” etc. This was Hierocles. Eusebius writes that he gave the books which he wrote against Christians the title *Lover of Truth*, and Eusebius also refuted them in an excellent treatise.

“Who was then among the number of judges.” At that time he held the Augustal prefecture at Alexandria, as Epiphanius reports, *Heresies* 68.

“Assent.” Janus Gulielmius testifies in his questions on Plautus’ *Menaechmi*, chapter 4, that certain copies read *accensus* (“inflamed”), evidently through a metaphor drawn from military affairs, as above in book II, chapter 10.

## CHAPTER III

“No one [mentions] Apollonius.” Baptista Pius, in his later annotations, chapter 99, thinks that one should read here “no one [mentions] Apuleius,” since he testifies that some corrupt copies have “no one [mentions] Apollo.” I read altogether as I find it in all the books: “no one [mentions] Apollonius.” For the discourse concerned him; and perhaps Pius also wrote thus, for the edition of those annotations in my possession abounds excessively in printers’ errors.

“He suddenly failed to appear at the trial.” Philostratus also relates this, *Life of Apollonius*, book IV.

## CHAPTER IV

“He did not employ this material as he ought,” etc. St Jerome too holds this view in his letter to Magnus.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0991A]

“Not even to signify,” etc. Pierius and Velutello testify that this is the reading in the Roman Vergilian codex, though the printed copies vary: some have this, others “nor even to signify.”

## CHAPTER VI

“For human uses.” I would gladly read “for the use of all,” so that there might be an antithesis to “individual persons” and “a few.”

## CHAPTER VII

“And the more frequently it is assailed, the more firmly it is strengthened.” B., T., P., and nearly all manuscripts: “the more often it is assailed, the more firmly it is strengthened.” I followed the reading of the Florentine, Aldine, and Plantin editions, which seemed more correct; for Valla condemns the other in *Elegances* I, chapter 16. Although indeed, as Franciscus Floridus aptly notes even against him, *Miscellaneous Readings* II, chapter 20, certain words and phrases peculiar to Cyprian, Tertullian, Boethius, and especially other ecclesiastical Latin writers—writers whom even Valla himself judges not altogether bad—are by no means to be adopted for imitation. Yet one should not rightly criticize them in those authors, but rather approve and kiss them as one approves certain moles on a beautiful face, the slight blemishes of great men.

## CHAPTER VIII

“As one and the same nature,” he says. This passage is thought to have fallen out of the first book *On Laws*.

## CHAPTER IX

“They compete in passivity with women.” Namely, when men marry women in order to bear a man, as is said in the law *Cum vir*, Code *On the Julian Law concerning Adultery*. So too Quintilian, *Declamations* 3: “When lust, incurred by males polluted to the point of womanly passivity, now falls upon its own sex.”

“Who pollute even the most sacred part of their own body against every law,” etc. Namely, while they admit into themselves an execrable madness, which spares not even the head, as he says below, book VI, chapter 23.

“All [go] *induforum*,” etc. I read as B. has it, or *induforo*, as P. has it and as Robert Estienne read it in the fragments of Lucilius collected and published by him—not, as Aldus and Plantin corruptly print, *indufori*. It is an epenthesis for *in forum* (“into the forum”) or *in foro* (“in the forum”). But perhaps Lucilius wrote *Endoforum* or *Endoforo*; for all know that the ancients used *endo* for *in*.

“To compete in flattery.” Robert Estienne reads thus in the place cited, following the Florentine edition, which is surely more Lucilian, although Aldus and Plantin have “to flatter, to compete,” etc.

“It follows through all the rest.” B. has: “through all the rest it would be sought.” Although that reading can itself be accepted, the former is more common and more approved by Antonio Agustín and Thomas.

## CHAPTER X

[Col. 0991D]

“About to scatter the flames with blood.” The reading in Vergil varies. Some editions have *sparsuros* (“about to scatter”), which Pierius approves more; others have the reading found in our text. Pierius and Velutello testify that *flamma* (“flame”), rather than *flammas* (“flames”), is also read in the Roman Vergilian codex, but our reading is more widely received.

“Then pious Aeneas.” On the authority of codex B. this corrects the printed editions, which have “Behold pious Aeneas,” a reading contrary both to Vergil and to the sense of the verse.

“Indeed, I should be willing to yield even to the living.” Pierius, Velutello, and Bergizomus on Vergil report that several ancient codices have, “Indeed, I should prefer to yield to the living.”

“They are instructed in injustice.” The word *justice* is an error in the Aldine and Plantin editions, opposed alike by the author’s meaning, B., T., P., the other manuscripts, and the Florentine edition.

## CHAPTER XI

[Col. 0992A]

“For if there is no one,” he says, etc. I do not find the passage among Cicero’s works; but there is a similar one in *On Duties* III, chapter 3: “For what difference is there whether someone changes himself from a human being into a beast, or, in human form, bears the savagery of a beast?”

“Like one in Phrygia,” etc. Eusebius recounts the story, *Ecclesiastical History* VIII, chapter 11.

“Sacrilegious constitutions.” Read them in Eusebius.

“Domitius.” Ulpian.

“In the seventh book.” Others: “in seven books.” But manuscripts B. and P. and the printed Florentine editions support our reading; Cujas approves it, *Observations* X, chapter 34, and Thomasius in his notes.

## CHAPTER XII

“I ask,” he says, “if there are two,” etc. This passage was excerpted from the argument against justice, which Sigonius supposes was in Cicero’s *On the Republic* III, in his scholia on the fragments of Cicero, where he discusses this excellently. See also *Letters to Atticus* IV, Epistle 15.

“And against one who is most wicked, let him think,” etc. Others: “but against one who is most wicked, let it be thought,” etc. But Andreas Patricius seems to me most correctly to have restored this passage, although on conjecture alone. His words in his scholia on the fragments of Cicero’s *On the Republic* III are these:

> Formerly the reading was *existimetur* [“let it be thought”]; but, having myself divined what I think is the true reading, I afterward found that it had been noticed by others. What if, moreover, it read thus: “and against one who is most wicked, let him think,” etc.? For neither here nor shortly afterward does “but against” please me; and a copyist could easily have omitted *in* in “let him think and against,” especially if he had seen it written as many things remain written in the Florentine Pandects: *put Et contra*, which is equivalent to my writing *putet et contra*, etc.

Patricius’ conjecture is aided by the observation that scribes often omitted one of two instances of the same repeated word or clause, as Gulielmus Fornerius notes, *Selections* II, [Col. 0992C] chapter 24. Thus, where Varro, *On the Latin Language*, has “customary around altars,” he advises reading “customary then around [the] altars”; and in law *Poenales*, §1, Digest *On the Lex Falcidia*, where the reading is “the argument of the matter,” he reads “the argument then of the matter”; and in law *Omnes*, Digest *On Restoration in Full*, for “let him examine whether they are true,” he reads “let him examine, and whether they are true,” etc. You may see other examples there. Cujas also notes this, *Observations* II, chapter 11, and X, chapter 30.

“Reputation.” Patricius, in the place cited, approves this reading, which appears in the Plantin and Aldine editions. The Florentine has “valuation.”

“Worm-eaten.” I retained this as the better reading, which Aldus has. By insult he calls the gods worm-eaten—that is, their images, which, being made of wood or some other such material, contracted rot and decay. Others read “nostrilly” or “varicose.”

## CHAPTER XIII

[Col. 0992D] “And let them glory in Mucius.” On him see Cicero, Livy II, first Decade, Valerius III, chapter 3, Seneca, *On Divine Providence* and Epistle 24, Tertullian, *To the Martyrs*, chapter 4, St Augustine, *City of God* IV, chapter 20.

“Or in Regulus.” On him see Cicero, *On Duties* III, at the end; Seneca, *On Divine Providence*; Pliny, *On Illustrious Men*; Gellius, book VI, chapter 4; Tertullian, *To the Martyrs*, in the passage cited, and at the end of the *Apology*; Augustine, *City of God* I, chapters 15 and 24; Suidas under ῥήγουλος.

## CHAPTER XIV

“The earth fashioned by his fingers.” An unusual expression; that is, shaped and formed by his fingers into an image. So St Remigius in his will, in Brisson, *Formulas* VII: “I direct that a censer and an embossed [*imaginatum*] chalice be made for you, my heir, the church above mentioned.”

## CHAPTER XV

“When he was an ambassador,” etc. Macrobius relates the story, *Saturnalia* I, chapter 5; Gellius, book VII, chapter 14, and book XVII, at the end; Quintilian, book XII, chapter 1.

“Which Cicero calls equality.” In *On the Orator* II: “And all the more if they arrogantly vaunt themselves and, by the superiority of their rank or fortune, go beyond the equality of common right,” etc. And at the end of the same book: “In praise of justice, it will need to be explained what the person praised has done in connection with good faith, equality, and such other duties”; and *On Duties* I, chapter 32: “But in free peoples, and in the exercise of equality of rights, affability too [is required],” etc.

## CHAPTER XVI

“Nor is there any other reason why we mutually bestow the name of brothers upon one another,” etc. So also Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 39.

“The things thought evils here,” etc. I do not find this little verse in Euripides.

## CHAPTER XVII

“Either that justice does not exist at all, or, if there is any, that it is the height of folly,” etc. Thrasymachus treats this argument in Plato’s first book *On the Republic*.

“A good man,” he says, “if he has a runaway slave,” etc. Cicero discusses some of these questions, as well as several others of the same kind, *On Duties* III, chapter 3.

“If he declares [it], he will indeed be good,” etc. Others: “If he declares to the buyer that [the slave] is a runaway, he will indeed be good,” etc. But the words “to the buyer that [he is] a runaway” are absent from B. and P., because *profitebitur* (“he will declare”) must refer not only to a runaway slave, but also to an unhealthy house and other like matters of which he had spoken, as Thomasius also notes.

“Now that just man is foolish.” I retained this reading of the Aldine and Florentine Juntine editions, despite the opposition and protest of codices B., T., P., and the Plantin edition, where the reading is “now [he is] not just,” etc. That reading conflicts with Carneades’ own argument; for in this discussion it was not injustice but justice that was joined with folly, while injustice itself was joined with wisdom. Thus it was said that he indeed would be just but foolish; whereas, if he did the contrary, he would be thought wise but would be unjust. This is clear from the other example which follows immediately.

## CHAPTER XVIII

“For why should he sail?” etc. See Seneca, *Natural Questions* V, chapter 18.

“Those Pythagorean friends.” He speaks of Damon and Pythias; their story may be found in Valerius, book IV, chapter 7; Cicero, *On Duties* III, chapter 3, near the beginning.

## CHAPTER XIX

“In Cicero, Laelius himself, that defender of justice, says,” etc. The opinions of this Laelius reported in this chapter have fallen out of the same discussion in Cicero’s third book *On the Republic* mentioned above [Col. 0994B] in chapter 12, where Cicero introduced Laelius arguing for justice against Furius.

## CHAPTER XXIII
God, he says, regards human beings as his children, etc. You will certainly not find these very words in Seneca; but their meaning occurs near the beginning of his little work *On Divine Providence*. Therefore one must either say that the words have dropped out, or that Lactantius expressed Seneca’s own view as though in Seneca’s words—a practice I observe that he often employs elsewhere. Thus above, Book III, chapter 21, he attributes to Plato the words: “The state will be harmonious,” etc.; and in this book, chapter 18, the words of Carneades in Cicero: “The just man, he says, if [he finds] either a horse belonging to a wounded man,” etc.; and below, Book VI, chapter 12: “If you hear the prayers,” he says, etc. These words of the Lord are found nowhere, but their meaning—Matthew V and Luke VI—is expressed in Lactantius’ own words.

## BOOK SIX

[Col. 0993]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0993C]

“For that holy and singular Majesty desires nothing else from man,” etc. Not because outward sacrifice also is not most acceptable to God, as was said above in Book II, chapter 2; but because the ancient Fathers frequently pressed these points upon the ears of pagans, who, though covered with every crime, believed themselves religious if they drenched temples and altars with the blood of victims—as though God had need of sacrifices. But concerning the most holy sacrifice of the Eucharist, instituted by Christ the Lord, which we call the Mass, and which heretics rashly malign on the basis of this or other similar passages, see the testimonies of the most ancient Fathers: Ignatius, a contemporary of Christ and disciple of the apostles, Epistle 10, and *To the Philadelphians*, Epistle 9; *To the Ephesians*, Epistle 14; *To the Romans*, Epistle 15; Irenaeus, a disciple of Polycarp, who was a hearer of the Apostle John, Book IV, chapter 32, where he says:

> He took bread from the created order and gave thanks, saying: “This is my body”; and likewise the cup, which is from that created order which is according to us, he acknowledged as his blood, and taught the new offering of the New Testament, which the Church, receiving from the apostles, offers to God throughout the whole world, etc.

And chapter 34:

> Therefore the Church’s offering, which the Lord taught should be offered throughout the whole world, has been reckoned a pure sacrifice before God and is acceptable to him.

Likewise Tertullian, Book II *To His Wife*, *On Monogamy*, *On the Soldier’s Crown*, *On Prayer*, *On Chastity*, *On Women’s Dress*, Book I *Against Marcion*, and often elsewhere; Cyprian, Epistle 63 to Caecilius and Epistle 66; Gregory Nazianzen, in the poem *To Bishops*; Ambrose, in the preparatory prayer for Mass; Chrysostom, in the Homily *On the Perdition of the Jews* and on the Epistle to the Hebrews; Jerome, to Damasus, *On the Prodigal Son*; Augustine, *City of God*, Book XVII, chapter 20; Cyril, *Mystagogical Catecheses*; Gregory the Great, *Dialogues*, Book IV, chapter 58; Alexander, in the decree found among the general councils concerning priests not to be harassed [Col. 0994C]; Leo, in Epistle 9 to Dioscorus; Fulgentius, to Moncimus, Book II; finally, the councils: the Second Council of Toledo, chapter 5; Ephesus, in its letter to Nestorius; the Lateran Council, cited in chapter *Firmiter*, *On the Supreme Trinity*; and Trent, Session 22.

## CHAPTER II

“They light lamps, as though he acted in darkness.” Likewise, a little below: “Let them now perceive how little God needs their lamps,” etc. Those, therefore, who light lamps for God in the belief that he acts in darkness or needs lights are most deservedly condemned. Yet the holy Church of God lights lamps in churches even during the day, in order to awaken in the souls of believers reverence toward God and his saints, along with a certain religious joy; and so that, under the symbol of bodily light, that Light may be shown of which the Gospel reads: “There was the true Light, which enlightens every person.” This is stated in the *Canon Cleros*, distinction 21, from Isidore, *Origins*, Book VII, chapter 12. Their pious use is approved both by Holy Scripture and by the testimonies of the saints. For Exodus XXV mentions the lampstand in God’s temple having seven lamps. Cyprian, Epistle 55, mentions the candle-bearers or acolytes, whose office it is to carry lighted candles in church for the sacred ceremonial of the mysteries. St Jerome disputes against the heretic Vigilantius, who reproached Catholics for using lights. St Athanasius laments, in his letter *To the Orthodox*, that candles offered by the faithful had been taken away by Arian heretics. See further Eusebius, *History*, Book VI, chapter 23; St Epiphanius, to John, bishop of Jerusalem; St Paulinus, poems for the third and sixth Natals of St Felix; St Augustine, Sermon on the Seasons 215; St Evodius, *On Miracles of St Stephen*, Book I, chapter 3, and Book II, chapter 2. Likewise the councils: Rome under Sylvester, and Carthage IV, chapter 2 and following.

That this sign of piety is most pleasing and acceptable to God is testified by remarkable miracles performed by means of wax taken from candlesticks or oil from lamps: St Augustine, *City of God*, Book XXII, chapter 8; Theodoret, *History of the Holy Fathers*, chapter 21, on James; St Gregory of Tours, *Miracles of St Martin*, chapter 2, near the end; St Gregory the Great, *Dialogues*, Book III, chapter 30; Paul the Deacon, *Deeds of the Lombards*, Book II, chapter 9. [Col. 0995A]

## CHAPTER III

“There are two ways through which human life…” The Aldine edition reads: “There are two ways, Emperor Constantine, through which,” etc. But B. T. P., the Florentine, Juntine, and Plantin editions contain nothing concerning Constantine.

“They wished one to be that of virtues, the other of vices.” Prodicus of Ceos invented the tale that, when Hercules came to this fork in the road, he was uncertain in mind as to which road he should take. Xenophon relates it in a most beautiful narrative at the beginning of Book II of the *Memorabilia of Socrates*; Cicero, *On Duties*, Book I, chapter 43; Suidas under the word *prodicen* (πρόδικεν); the commentator on Aristophanes’ *Clouds*; Philo the Jew, in *On Not Bringing the Earnings of Prostitutes into the Treasury*; and Basil, *On Drawing Benefit from Greek Literature*. There is a most charming epigram of Virgil on the letter Y concerning this matter.

“But how are these ways…?” I have restored this from both Codices of St Saviour, B. T. P., in place of the printed reading, “But how are these lives,” etc.; for the allegory of the two ways continues.

## CHAPTER IV

“As poets speak.” For Virgil, *Aeneid* VI:

> The right-hand way, which leads beneath the walls of mighty Dis,  
> by this road lies our way to Elysium, etc.

“All things have been placed.” I read thus with B., T., and other best manuscripts, not as in some printed copies, “God placed all things”; for God placed no vices.

“Let him fall from height into the depths.” I have followed the reading of the very ancient manuscript B. Yet I do not think the alternative reading, “Let him fall into deep height,” should be rejected, as Thomasius thought when he said: “For one can in no way be said to fall into a height, since that is to be raised, not to fall.” For, since height differs from depth only in relation, *height* is often used for *depth*. Thus Cicero, *Letters to Atticus*, Book IX, and Caesar, *Gallic War*, Book IV, speak of “the height of the sea”; Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book II, of caves “of concave height”; *On Divination*, Book I, “the earth descends to an infinite height”; *Against Verres*, Book VII, “the stone was sunk to a remarkable height”; Celsus, Book VII, chapter 7, says that the depth of a wound should reach the cartilage; and Pliny, Book X, chapter 33, speaks of a cave dug to a depth of six feet. [Col. 0995C]

## CHAPTER V

“But knowledge cannot be virtue.” Plato holds otherwise in the *Laches*, the *Meno*, and elsewhere; Aristotle criticizes him in *Ethics*, Book VI, chapter 13; *Magna Moralia*, Book I, chapter 1; and *Eudemian Ethics*, Book I, chapter 3 and Book VII, chapter 6.

“To have lacked folly.” B. T. P. and the Florentine edition do not contain these words. I followed the Aldine edition and restored them because they belong with the words, “and wisdom first,” rather than with the preceding statement, “virtue is to flee vice.”

## CHAPTER VI

[Col. 0995D]

“Neither God nor his adversary.” This reading is received in all printed editions and in three Vatican manuscripts and P. Nine others of the same Vatican manuscripts read, “neither God nor the adversary of God.” Nor does that reading contain anything absurd, as Thomasius suspects, since not only the devil but also any sinners whatsoever may rightly be called adversaries of God. Moses says in the Song of Exodus XIII: “You have cast down your adversaries”; and in the Song of I Kings, chapter II: “The adversaries of the Lord shall fear him.” Lactantius himself, above, Book II, chapter 10, called the devil *antitheus* (ἀντίθεος), that is, God’s adversary. But B. reads, “the adversary of the human race.”

“These men dissolve the common fellowship of the human race.” Only a few words have been transposed; for Cicero reads: “These men dissolve the common [fellowship] of the human race,” etc.

“From the best examples of nature and truth.” But Cicero, in Lambinus’s corrected text—which I think preserves the genuine reading—has: “from the best principles of nature and examples of truth.” Yet some other editions of Cicero lack the word *principles* (*principiis*).

“Or when Fabricius, he says, is brave,” etc. Cicero’s passage is mutilated and somewhat altered in our author. Cicero reads:

> Nor indeed, when the two Decii or the two Scipios are commemorated as brave men, or when Fabricius or Aristides is called just, is an example of courage sought from the former or of justice from the latter as from a wise man, etc.

Cicero never adduces Fabricius as an example of courage, but of justice; and in the same Book III of *On Duties* he says that Fabricius at Rome was the same as Aristides at Athens. Hence perhaps the word *brave* here seems superfluous, and the entire passage should be restored from Cicero.

## CHAPTER VII

“That his immortal secret might be kept concealed.” Nearly all manuscripts and printed editions read, “might be kept open,” a reading contrary to Lactantius’ meaning. I therefore followed the Juntine reading, which is clear, coherent, and intelligible. For he speaks of that eternal and infallible mystery, unsearchable by any human minds, by which God reprobates some and permits them to err, so that, having turned away from wisdom and truth by their own free choice, they fall into precisely what they seek to avoid—namely, everlasting punishment. We discussed this at chapter 20 of Book IV. B. reads: “He willed immortality, and likewise his secret, to be open.”

## CHAPTER VIII

“It is not lawful for this law to be annulled,” etc. I think it should be read thus with Thomasius in his notes, and with Patrizi and Sigonio in their scholia on this passage among the fragments of Cicero’s Book III *On the Republic*. For three kinds of weakening a law are here stated: *obrogatio*, *derogatio*, and *abrogatio*, concerning which see Festus, Cicero, *On Invention*, Book II, and Ulpian, title 1 of the *Institutes*. “To be extended,” found here in some copies, is irrelevant.

“And having despised human nature, by this very fact he will pay the greatest penalties,” etc. Nearly all manuscripts read, “he will despise”; and because the conjunction seemed to demand the future, Patrizi read: “he will despise, and by this very fact he will pay,” etc. Franciscus Balduinus, in his *Institutes of Justinian*, reads: “he will despise, and by this very fact he will pay.” Manuscript B. removes every difficulty by showing that the text should be read as above. [Col. 0996C]

## CHAPTER IX

“And by inflicting injuries lawfully.” He speaks ironically against the Romans, who customarily declared war through the fetial priests and first solemnly protested in a fixed verbal formula that they were undertaking war justly against the nation which they sought to subdue. Then they thought everything permissible for themselves and believed that they did everything lawfully. See Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *History*, Book II.

“Therefore civil law is one thing, varying everywhere according to customs.” Philosophers discuss this in *Nicomachean Ethics*, Book V, chapter 7, and *Magna Moralia*, Book I, chapter 31; jurists, in the *Institutes* and *Pandects*, under the title *On Justice and Law*.

[Col. 0996D] “And he must necessarily be ignorant of justice itself.” From both Codices of St Saviour, B. T. P., and the Florentine edition, the books are corrected which read, “and he must necessarily be ignorant of God himself,” etc.

## CHAPTER X

“Therefore, gathered together with one another, because human nature…” See Aristotle, *Politics*, Book I, chapters 1 and 2, and Book III, chapter 4.

## CHAPTER XI

“Those who think that to be moved or to pity is not the part of a wise man.” Such are the Stoics, according to Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, Book III, and the speech *For Murena* against Cato; likewise Seneca, *On Clemency*, Book II, chapter 5; and the most courageous commander Agesilaus, whose saying Plutarch reports in the *Laconic Sayings*: that it is difficult to pity and be wise at the same time.

“He deserves ill,” etc. In Plautus this verse is read thus, concerning a beggar:

> He does ill who gives him food to eat or drink to drink.

“What you have done without hope of receiving [anything in return].” Seneca treats this excellently in *On Benefits*, Book IV, chapter 3 and following.

“And generous.” Cicero reads *or generous* (*benignusve*).

“For there is nothing,” etc. Cicero: “For there is nothing made by work or hand which he does not at some time finish,” etc.

## CHAPTER XII

“What those teachers of virtue and justice never addressed at all.” For although one may find something in Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, or perhaps other pagans concerning burying the dead, they regarded this more as the duty of a good man than as something ever commanded by the precept of any lawgiver; and they are understood to speak rather of burying parents and relatives, or those who had served the republic well, than strangers and the poor. See Hieronymus Magius, who expounds this passage in *Miscellanies*, Book II, chapter 19.

“Those who made burial superfluous.” Hence that saying of Virgil, near the end of *Aeneid* II: “The loss of burial is easy.” See Seneca, *On Remedies for Chance Misfortunes*. [Col. 0997B]

“If you hear, he says, the prayers of your suppliant,” etc. These words are not taken from any place in Holy Scripture; rather, Lactantius himself expressed in them the thought of the Lord the Saviour, Luke VI: “Be merciful, as your Father is merciful. Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you. For with the same measure with which you have measured, it will be measured back to you.”

## CHAPTER XIII

“He has no pardon who sins knowingly.” He explains this from the preceding statements: namely, if the sinner does not repent, confess, and resolve not to sin further in this way.

“He who has ascended the first step is sufficiently just.” He is not sufficiently just if, while abstaining from evil deeds, he nevertheless speaks or thinks wickedly; Lactantius himself both acknowledges and teaches this below, chapter 23, and in Book VII, chapter 27, where he says that God will judge even depraved thoughts. [Col. 0997C]

## CHAPTER XIV

“For the Stoics remove from man all the affections by whose impulse the mind is moved,” etc. Seneca argues for these Stoics in many places: Epistle 86, “I had spared”; Epistle 117, “Whether it is better”; Book I *On Anger*, chapters 10, 11, and following; and throughout Book II. The Peripatetics, on the other hand, contend that they should not be removed altogether but moderated. For Aristotle denies in *Ethics*, Book II, chapter 30, that virtues are simply states of freedom from passion and calmness, as Lactantius says in Book VII, chapter 10. See Cicero, Books III and IV *On Ends*, and Book IV of the *Tusculan Disputations*; Plutarch, *On Moral Virtue*; St Augustine, *City of God*, Book IX, chapter 4, and Book XIV, chapters 8 and 9. Our author argues against both.

## CHAPTER XVI

“Indeed, even to rejoice in that small thing,” etc. This is according to the view of the pagan philosophers against whom the argument was directed, so that he might refute them from their own premises—as he declared that he would do in these books, Book V, chapter 4—not according to the doctrines of Christian wisdom, by which we are taught to wish every good thing even for our enemies. Lactantius himself discusses this excellently below, chapter 18. [Col. 0997D]

## CHAPTER XVII

“For these excitements of the mind are like a yoked chariot,” etc. Perhaps he alludes to the chariot of which Plato speaks in the *Phaedrus*.

“This is that honourable man,” etc. A saying of Seneca, excerpted from books of moral philosophy which we have lost; but he expresses similar thoughts everywhere—in Epistle 24, “Anxious”; *Natural Questions*, Book VI, chapter 32; and elsewhere.

## CHAPTER XVIII

“He who worships the good Word.” That is, Jesus, the Son of God, who is called the “good Word” at the beginning of Psalm XXIV, the passage to which he refers. [Col. 0998A]

“By this very fact he must lose the name of good man,” etc. This argument is directed not only against Cicero, but also against Aristotle, who maintains in *Nicomachean Ethics*, Book IV, and *Eudemian Ethics*, Book III—chapter 5 in both—that not avenging an injury is the part of an ignoble and servile man.

“Inscribed with another’s title.” Namely, with the title *Philippics*, in imitation of Demosthenes.

“Caesar, I hope,” he says, “that you forget,” etc. The word *Caesar* (Καῖσαρ) is absent from Cicero’s text; there it reads: “I hope also that you, who forget,” etc.

## CHAPTER XIX

“Accordingly, they call this very anger the whetstone of virtue.” I have followed both the judgment and the testimony of Janus Gulielmius, who testified in his *Questions on Plautus’ Menaechmi*, chapter 4, that this reading occurs in some manuscripts of Lactantius. Indeed Cicero, from whom Lactantius borrows all this, reads near the end of the *Lucullus*: “Anger itself is, as it were, the whetstone of courage,” etc. [Col. 0998B]

## CHAPTER XX

“But fornications and adulteries,” he says, etc. Some things have been transposed, some omitted. Cicero reads:

> But fornications and adulteries, and every shameful act of that kind, are excited by no enticements other than pleasure. And since nature, or some god, had given nothing more excellent to man than the mind, there is nothing so hostile to this divine gift and endowment as pleasure. For when lust rules, there is no place for temperance; nor at all in the kingdom of pleasure, etc.

Yet some manuscripts of Cicero read: “Incited by no other enticements than those of pleasure,” as is noted in the margin of Lambinus’s editions; and: “For when lust rules, there is no place for temperance at all, nor in [the kingdom] of pleasure,” etc.

“Yet they do not despise these public spectacles,” etc. See Tertullian, *On Spectacles*; Cyprian, Epistle I to the people; St Augustine, *City of God*, Book III, chapter 8 and following.

“Nor will it be lawful for a just man to serve as a soldier,” etc. He speaks only of that time of the primitive and youthful Church, which had neither the sword nor, at that point, any fitness to use arms, but was to increase solely through sufferings and miracles, as Hugh of St-Cher writes in his annotations on Mark, explaining Luke 22: “Let him sell his garment and buy a sword.” Yet that a just man can serve as a soldier, and that military service is sometimes just, is shown from Sts Ambrose, Augustine, Gregory, and the other Fathers by Gratian in the *Decree*, throughout Cause 23, Questions 1, 2, and 3; and the contrary assertion of the Manichaean heretics, Oecolampadius, Agrippa, Luther, and Erasmus is refuted by Sixtus of Siena, *Bibliotheca*, Book VI, Annotation 156, and Alphonsus de Castro, *Against Heresies*, Book III, under “War.”

“Nor indeed [will it be lawful] to accuse anyone of a capital crime.” This is not simply true. There may be circumstances in which it is not only permitted to a just man to accuse a criminal but in which he is obliged to bring an accusation: namely, when he understands that the crime tends to the destruction of the commonwealth and can be proved by suitable witnesses. St Gregory in Gratian, canon *If anyone concerning these matters*; in the canon *Of Metropolitans*; Gelasius, canon *Wherefore*, Question 7; Pope Pius, canon *If anyone by a hair*, Cause 22, Question 1; St Thomas, *Summa*, II–II, Question 68, Article 1; Soto, *On Justice and Law*, Book V, Question 5, Article 1. [Col. 0998D]

“Therefore, in this commandment of God no exception at all ought to be made, so that it is always unlawful to kill a human being,” etc. John Duns Scotus, *Sentences*, Book IV, distinction 15, question 3, comes close to Lactantius’ position. But that commandment of God is not so general that it rejects every exception; and that there can be circumstances in which one human being lawfully puts another to death is demonstrated by St Thomas, II–II, Question 64, and Domingo de Soto, *On Justice and Law*, Book V, Question 1.

“Whom God willed to be a sacred living creature,” etc. The word *sacred* (*sanctum*) is here taken in its proper sense and means that which is protected and secured from human injury, as Martianus the jurist writes in the law *Sacred*, *Digest*, *On the Division of Things*. Donatus says: “That is called sacred which is inviolate under every observance.” Cicero, *Philippics*, Book II: “So great is the love of country that I was sacred even to your legions.” Thus sacred laws are those forbidden to be violated under the sanction of penalty, in Ulpian, law *Sacred*, *Digest*, *On the Division of Things*. Likewise the walls of towns are sacred according to Pompeius Festus, *On Ancient Words*; the jurist Gaius in the first law; and Cassius, Sabinus, and Marcianus in the said law *Sacred*, *Digest*, *On the Division of Things*. [Col. 0999A]

## CHAPTER XXIII

“So that they might rush most eagerly into these passions, and by this means kinds might be propagated and multiplied,” etc. Thus also Galen, *On the Usefulness of the Parts*, Book XIV, chapter 2. So also St Basil: “For this appetite,” he says, “was divinely given to mortals for the propagation of offspring,” etc. And Seneca, speaking of man in the *Consolation to His Mother*, chapter 13: “If you consider,” he says, “that lust was given to man not for pleasure but for propagating the race, every other desire will pass by untouched anyone whom this secret and inborn destruction, fixed in the very entrails, has not violated.”

“He urgently demanded chastity.” Thus B., six Vatican manuscripts, and almost all other manuscripts and printed editions. Six other Vatican manuscripts, and Aldus in the errata correction at the end of his edition, read *flagitiavit* (“she disgraced” / “violated shamefully”). I have no sufficient reason to approve either reading, nor can I discover what to conjecture. Since *flagitare* has no meaning other than to demand vehemently and urgently, one may properly say that a girl is solicited by someone, as in Ulpian, law II, *Digest*, *On Private Offences*, a passage adduced by Thomasius; but it gives him no help, because it is one thing to solicit a girl and another to solicit chastity. Guilielmus Fornerius, *Selections*, Book II, chapter 11, says that *flagitare* properly means the same as “to be sexually violated.” He produces authorities which others may examine. I would prefer *flagitiavit*, so that it here means “he afflicted and defiled chastity by shameful conduct,” were I not deterred by the highly unusual word.

[Col. 0999C] “He does not even spare the head.” Beroaldus on Suetonius, *Tiberius*, chapter 45; Brodaeus, *Miscellanies*, Book II, chapter 21; and Magius, *Miscellanies*, Book II, chapter 20, explain this saying of Lactantius, who also inveighed against these impious persons above, Book V, chapter 9.

“But God commanded abstention even from common and public bodies; and he teaches us, when two bodies unite with one another,” etc. From this the heresy of Ebion and the Elkesaites is refuted. They rejected all the Epistles of the Apostle Paul, as Irenaeus writes in Book I *Against Heresies*, and Eusebius in *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, chapter 27, and Book VI, chapter 27. For since these words are drawn from the end of chapter 6 of I Corinthians, it is clear that even in those times Paul’s Epistles were numbered by the faithful among the divine and divinely inspired Scriptures. Elsewhere he also cites other sayings of Paul as divine oracles: above in this book, chapter 18, and in *On the Anger of God*, chapter 21.
