Accordingly, the heresy of Simon Magus, Saturninus, the Nicolaitans, Florinians, Adamites, and Waldensians is also overthrown by this, since they dared to approve the promiscuous use of all women.

[Col. 0999D] “Of all females, he made woman alone receptive of man,” etc. But Aristotle writes that a mare too may be mounted after she has conceived, *History of Animals*, Book VII, chapter 4. And Pliny relates, *Natural History*, Book VII, chapter 11, that other animals besides woman, although few, know intercourse while pregnant.

[Col. 1000A] “For it is unjust that you should demand what you yourself cannot provide.” Ulpian expressed this in nearly the same words in the law *If a wife*, section *Judge*, *Digest*, *On the Julian Law Concerning Adultery*. Seneca, Epistle 95, “That part,” etc.

## CHAPTER XXIV

“But if it were permitted to those who had gone astray on a journey,” etc. This passage no longer exists today.

“Having followed.” Others read “having followed [masculine].” The first reading pleased Patrizi more, and me as well.

“Something great, he says, I know not what,” etc. Seneca has the same golden saying at the beginning of the twelfth book of his *Letters*, Epistle “Each day”: “Certainly,” he says, “we ought to live as though we lived in sight,” etc.

“We need neither vervain, nor entrails, nor turfs,” etc. By *entrails* (*fibrae*) he means intestines—a part for the whole. Those intending to perform rites placed a turf of grass or vervain upon altars. Vervain and laurel were also common in fumigations. Virgil, *Eclogues* VIII:

> Bind these altars with a soft fillet,  
> and burn rich vervain, etc.

For that reason vervain was called ἱεροβοτάνη (*hierobotanē*), that is, “sacred herb,” by Dioscorides, Book IV, and by Pliny, Book XXV, chapter 9. [Col. 1000B]

“As Cicero said,” etc. I find the passage nowhere except among fragments of books of uncertain identification.

## CHAPTER XXV

“Ivory,” Plato says, “is not a pure gift for God.” The passage is in Plato’s *Laws*, Book XII, where he teaches what offerings should be made to the gods. Ivory is mentioned because it was commonly used among the Gentiles in making statues of gods, as Pliny writes, *Natural History*, Book VIII, chapter 10, and Book XII, chapter 1; Virgil, *Georgics*, Book I:

> And the ivory weeps mournfully in the temples, etc.

“But among those who in no way understand the nature of divinity, whatever is made of gold … is a gift.” Lactantius is mistaken; for the distinction he refutes is itself the true and proper distinction between a gift and a sacrifice, as Chrysostom teaches in Homily 18 on the Epistle to the Hebrews; Theophylact on chapter 8 of the same Epistle; and St Thomas, II–II, Question 85, Article 3.

“Therefore both must be offered to God immaterially. . . . The gift is integrity of mind; sacrifice, praise and hymn,” etc. The prophet also often mentions a sacrifice of praise in the Psalms, as does Paul in Hebrews XIII; a contrite spirit is called a sacrifice in Psalm L; and every good work in the Epistle to the Hebrews. All these are called sacrifices improperly and metaphorically. Properly, however, sacrifices are things offered over which something is done: such as formerly animals, which were slain and burned; and now bread, which is blessed, broken, and eaten, as Chrysostom, Theophylact, and St Thomas teach in the passage cited above. Both sacrifices are owed to God. See what we said above, Book II, chapter 2, and in this same book, chapter 1. [Col. 1000C]

“In that perfect discourse.” Thus above, Book IV, chapter 6: ὁ λόγος τέλειος, “the perfect Word”; and below, Book VII, chapter 18. He means the *Asclepius*.

“Speak a good omen.” This should be read from manuscript B. and from Hermes’ *Asclepius* itself, where he says this more than once; for he says it also in the *Pimander*, chapter 9. The Aldine, Juntine, and Plantin editions read: “Good, good, O my son,” etc.

“O Asclepius.” All printed books rightly read this, as does Hermes himself. B. incorrectly reads, “O Asclepiades.”

## BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 0999]

## CHAPTER ONE

“As Plato says.” He refers to that passage in the *Phaedo*: “Do you wish, then,” he says, “that we posit two kinds of things, one of visible things and the other of invisible things,” etc.

“Who says that it both once arose and will at some time perish.” This is clear from Lucretius’ poems, Book II, near the end.

## CHAPTER III

“The Stoics divide nature into two parts.” See Cicero, *Academics*, Book I.

“Or the earth may gape.” Pliny, *Natural History*, Book II, chapter 80.

“How often both cities and islands have been submerged by waves,” etc. Pliny, same book, chapter 92.

[Col. 1001A] “And a hidden, inward fire consumes the foundations of many mountains.” Pliny, same book, chapter 106.

“Seas are built up.” Pliny, Book V, chapter 19.

“Mountains are cut through.” As Athos was once by Xerxes, king of the Persians; Pliny, Book IV, chapter 10.

“And the inner bowels of the earth are dug out to extract riches.” Pliny complains of this in *Natural History*, Book II, chapter 63, and in the preface to Book XXXIII; Seneca, *Natural Questions*, Book V, chapter 15.

“But when, as we see, a marvellous order governs the world and all its parts.” Aristotle speaks divinely in the little work *On the World*, chapter 7.

## CHAPTER IV

“And they think that human beings have sprung up in every land and field like mushrooms.” He discussed this opinion above, Book II, chapter 12.

“And not by the heat of the sun, or light, or the blowing of winds,” etc. I have followed this blameless reading of Taxaq. P., the other and less ancient manuscript of St Saviour B., and the Plantin edition, since the others can in some fashion be challenged. Aldus reads: “either by the heat of the sun or the light of the moon”; the Florentine and Juntine editions: “either by the heat of the sun, or the moon, or the blowing of winds,” etc. That reading may be retained according to the view of those who believe that the moon, like the sun, warms bodies. Suidas, under *moon* (σελήνη). [Col. 1001B]

“Why, when God made all things for our sake, did he create so great a multitude of water-snakes and vipers?” In addition to Cicero’s *Lucullus*, Lucretius, Book V:

> Moreover, why does nature nourish or increase  
> the race of dreadful wild creatures hostile to humankind  
> by land and sea? etc.

Basil answers in Homily 9 on the *Hexaemeron*: “Nor should anyone accuse the Creator because he brought forth animals that emit poison, harmful and hostile to our life; for by the same reasoning one might also accuse a teacher because he restrains the power and inclination of youth within duty and corrects intemperance by blows and lashes,” etc. The same in Homily 5, not far from the beginning; Augustine, *Against the Manichaeans on Genesis*, Book I, chapter 16. But in the manuscript of Cicero, in place of “Why does the earth [produce] so many destructive things,” etc., it reads: “Why does the earth [produce] so many deadly, destructive things,” etc.

“But to man, in return for all these things, he gave reason alone, which was the chief thing. Thus he formed him naked and unarmed,” etc. Lactantius says the same in *On the Workmanship of God*, chapters 2 and 3; likewise Aristotle, *Parts of Animals*, Book IV, chapter 10. Therefore Pliny unjustly complains about Nature in the preface to Book VII, because, although she clothed and protected all other living creatures in some manner, she formed man naked and unarmed.

“Our Asclepiades.” He wrote a book *On God’s Providence* addressed to Lactantius; Lactantius in turn wrote two books to him, of unknown title, as Jerome, Honorius of Autun, and others report.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 1001D] “And bound to weak bodies,” etc. Lactantius often calls the body the soul’s snare, bond, enclosure, prison, custody, etc., imitating Plato in the *Gorgias*, *Phaedo*, and *Cratylus*, and Cicero in the *Dream of Scipio*, the first *Tusculan Disputation*, and elsewhere. We ought to refrain from such ways of speaking. Methodius, Epiphanius in the second *Panarion*, Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, Book I, Jerome in the letter to Pammachius, and Cyril, Book I of the Commentary on John, condemned them in Origen. See above, on chapter 3 of Book II.

“Endurance of evils and labours,” etc. What he discusses in this chapter concerning the bearing of hardships and labours, and in Book VI, chapter 11 concerning the exercise of works of mercy, should be observed against Luther and his followers, who deny that good works are necessary for salvation.

“And always with God.” In both manuscripts B., in twelve Vatican manuscripts, T. P., and all other manuscripts, as well as in the Juntine and Plantin editions, chapter 5 ends here, and chapter 6 begins immediately with the words: “Now let us unfold the whole argument,” etc. Hence no slight suspicion arises that the whole fairly lengthy discourse which I shall now append, and which is joined after these words in the Aldine edition, is spurious and inserted by another. Yet its author must certainly have been an extremely ingenious and remarkably vigorous forger, able to imitate Lactantius’ style so wonderfully. The discourse is as follows:

> Nor should anyone now take refuge in saying that the fault belongs to him who established both good and evil. For why did he will evil to exist if he hates it? Why did he not make only good, so that no one might sin, no one do evil? Although I have taught this in nearly all the preceding books, and have already touched upon it above, though lightly, it must nevertheless be recalled repeatedly, because the whole argument rests upon it. For virtue could not exist unless he had made opposites; nor can the power of good appear at all except by comparison with evil. Evil, indeed, is nothing other than the interpretation of good. Therefore, if evil is removed, good also must necessarily be removed.
>
> If you amputate the left hand or foot, neither will the body be whole nor life itself continue. Thus the left limbs are most suitably joined with the right for the ordering of the body’s structure. Likewise, if you made the contestants equal, no one would play. If you gave the Circus only one colour, no one would think it worth watching, all the pleasure of the races having been removed. The man who first established them was surely a lover of one colour; but he set another against it as a rival, so that there might be a contest and some charm in the spectacle.
>
> Thus, when God established good and bestowed virtue, he also appointed opposites with which they might contend. If there is no enemy and no battle, there is no victory. Remove the contest, and virtue itself is nothing. How many contests among people are there, established by how varied arts? Yet no one would be considered stronger, swifter, or superior if he had no opponent against whom to contend. Where victory is absent, glory and reward must also be absent. Therefore, in order to strengthen virtue itself by continual exercise and make it perfect through struggle with evils, he gave both together, because neither can retain its force without the other. Therefore, diversity is that upon which the entire rationale of truth rests.

I am not unaware what may be objected at this point by those more learned. If good cannot exist without evil, how do you say that the first man, before he offended God, was in good alone, or that afterwards he will be in good alone? We must examine this question, which I omitted in the earlier books in order to complete it here. We said above that human nature consists of conflicting elements. For the body, because it is of earth, is tangible; it is temporal, brutish, and dark. But the soul, because it is from heaven, is subtle, eternal, sentient, and bright. Since these are opposed to one another, man must necessarily be subject to good and evil. Good is ascribed to the soul, because it is indissoluble; evil to the body, because it is fragile. Therefore, since body and soul are associated and joined, good and evil must likewise cling together; nor can they be separated from one another unless those themselves are separated. Finally, knowledge of good and evil was given simultaneously to the first man [Col. 1002D]. Once he had received it, he was immediately driven from the holy place, in which evil does not exist. While he was there in good alone, he did not know that this itself was good. But after he received understanding of good and evil, it was now unlawful for him to remain in the place of blessedness; and he was banished into this common world, so that he might experience both together, whose nature he had come to know alike.

It is therefore apparent that wisdom was given to man in order that he might distinguish good from evil; that he might separate advantages from disadvantages, useful things from useless; that he might have judgment and deliberation as to what he ought to avoid, desire, flee, and pursue. Wisdom, therefore, cannot exist without evil; and that founder of the human race lived, so long as he was in good alone, like an infant, ignorant of good and evil. “But afterwards man must necessarily be both wise and blessed without any evil.” Yet this cannot happen so long as the soul is clothed in the dwelling-place of the body.

But when the separation of body and soul has occurred [Col. 1003A], then evil will be separated from good. And just as the body perishes while the soul remains, so evil will perish and good endure. Then man, having received the garment of immortality, will be wise and free from evil, like God. Therefore, whoever wishes us to be in good alone chiefly desires that we should live without the body, in which evil exists. If this is removed, either wisdom, as I said, or the body will be taken from man: wisdom, so that he may not know evil; the body, so that he may not feel it.

But now, since man is equipped both with wisdom, that he may know, and with a body, that he may feel, God willed both alike to exist in this life, so that the rationale of virtue and wisdom might stand. He therefore placed man midway between the two, so that he might have the freedom to follow either evil or good. But he mixed into evil certain apparent goods, that is, various pleasant and delightful charms, in order by their enticements to lead man toward concealed evil. Into good, however, he mixed certain apparent evils, that is, hardships, miseries, and labors, so that the mind, offended by their harshness and unpleasantness, might recoil from the concealed good. Here, therefore, the task of wisdom is required: that we see more with the mind than with the body [Col. 1003B]. Very few indeed can do this, because virtue is difficult and rare, while pleasure is common and public. Thus the wise man must necessarily be considered foolish: while he seeks goods that are not seen, he lets slip from his hands those that are seen; and while he avoids evils that are not visible, he falls into evils that are before his eyes.

This happens to us when we refuse neither torture nor death for the faith, when we are compelled to the utmost wickedness: to betray the faith, deny the true God, and pour libations to dead and death-dealing gods. This is the reason why God made man mortal and subjected him to evils, although he had built the world for his sake: namely, that he might acquire virtue, and that virtue might give him immortality. Virtue, moreover, as we have shown, is the worship of the true God.

Nothing is asserted in this passage that Lactantius has not also said elsewhere. For he taught that God willed good and evil to exist in the world also in Book II, chapter 18; Book V, chapter 7; Book VI, chapters 15 and 22; and *On the Anger of God*, chapter 15. Likewise, using that manner of speaking which pertains to the subject of reprobation, discussed in Book IV, chapter 20—namely, that God mixed into evil [Col. 1003C] certain apparent goods, that is, various pleasures, in order by their enticements to lead man toward concealed evil, and so forth—he used it above in Book IV, chapters 2 and 11. That Adam, before eating the forbidden fruit, was equally ignorant of good and evil, and so forth, he asserted in Book II, chapter 13.

## CHAPTER VII

The Stoics say that the world, and all things in it, were made for the sake of human beings. Thus testifies the speaker debating with a Stoic in Tertullian’s *Lucullus*, near the end: “Why, when God made all things for our sake—as you maintain—did he make such a great multitude of water-snakes,” etc.

Aristotle maintained that human beings are born to acquire virtue. He alludes to a passage of Aristotle which no longer exists among his works, but which Cicero reports in *On Ends*, Book II, in these words: “These men have not perceived that, just as a horse is for running, an ox for ploughing, a dog for tracking,” etc.

The Stoic Zeno taught that the underworld exists, etc. [Col. 1003D] I find nothing of the kind concerning Zeno in the writers, but concerning Socrates in Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, Book I, about the middle. “For this was his opinion,” he says, “and thus he argued: there are two roads and two courses for souls departing from the body; for those who had defiled themselves with human vices,” etc.

## CHAPTER VIII

“But Plato argued thus: that it is immortal,” etc. On this argument of Plato see Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, Book II, chapter 13 and following; St Athanasius, *Oration against the Idolaters*, who seems largely to have approved it; and St Thomas, *Against the Gentiles*, Book II, chapter 82. From this [argument] he inferred that Plato believed the souls of brute animals to be immortal, because he stated without qualification that soul exists of itself and moves itself. But Lactantius here defends Plato, on the ground that, by adding wisdom, he distinguished the human soul from the souls of speechless animals.

“He added, therefore, in order to escape this commonality, that the mind cannot but be immortal,” etc. [Col. 1004A] He had in view two passages of Cicero in which Cicero gathers Plato’s arguments for the immortality of souls: one in *Tusculan Disputations*, Book I: “No origin of souls can be found on earth,” etc.; the other near the end of *Cato the Elder, or On Old Age*: “Why say much? This is how I have persuaded myself, this is my conviction: when there is such swiftness of minds,” etc.

“Which of these opinions is true,” he says, “some god may know.” These words are found spoken by Cicero while the substance of the soul, not immortality—the subject here in Lactantius—was being discussed.

“Since both of these opinions,” he says, etc. From which book of Cicero these words have fallen is uncertain.

## CHAPTER IX

He most rightly named it *theōrian* (θεωρίαν, “contemplation”). For the word is compound and derived from the noun *tou theou* (τοῦ θεοῦ), “of God,” and the verb *horaō* (ὁράω), “I look upon, behold,” as Plutarch also relates in his little treatise *On the World*. Hence it appears that Codex B incorrectly reads not *theōrian* [Col. 1004B], but *opida* (ὀπίδα). That word, however, is frequent in Trismegistus. Thus, at the end of *Pimander*, chapter 12: “But if you wish to contemplate him” (*ei de boulei auton theōrēsai*, εἰ δὲ βούλει αὐτὸν θεωρῆσαι), etc.; chapter 13, near the beginning: “Am I not contemplated with these eyes?” (*ouk ophthalmois toutois theōroumai?*, οὐκ ὀφθαλμοῖς τούτοις θεωροῦμαι;); at the end of the hymnody in the same chapter: “What I behold, I tell you” (*ha theōrō legō soi*, ἃ θεωρῶ λέγω σοι), etc.; and at the beginning of chapter 14: “Let there be contemplation” (*genētai hē theōria*, γένηται ἡ θεωρία).

“Which will not be according to nature,” etc. Thus B, P, Juntine, and Plantin; that is: virtue will not be according to nature if account is to be taken only of the body and not of the soul’s eternity. For the body is rather broken and wasted away by virtuous actions, as Thomasius correctly explains. Others read: “which indeed will not be according to nature.”

“For since we are permitted to enjoy the most pleasant pleasures,” etc. The apostle Paul employs the same argument in 1 Corinthians, chapter 15: “If in this life only,” etc.

## CHAPTER X

“And tranquility of mind is,” etc. Aristotle does not approve this without qualification in *Ethics*, Book II, chapter 3; on this matter see above at Book VI, chapter 14.

## CHAPTER XII

[Col. 1004C]

“Since the soul is born with the body,” he says, etc. He advances Epicurean arguments against the soul’s immortality from Lucretius, *On the Nature of Things*, Book III; and this is the first argument:

> Moreover, we perceive that it is begotten together with the body,  
> and grows along with it, etc.

“It likewise gives way backward,” etc. These verses are read somewhat differently in Lucretius; there they are:

> What was formerly of earth returns again  
> into the earth; and what was sent from the regions of ether,  
> the temples of heaven receive again, restored.

“Like liquid from a broken vessel,” etc. He alludes to what follows there:

> Now therefore, since the vessels are shattered on every side, etc.

“Since sensation increases in children,” he says, etc. Lucretius:

> For just as children wander about weak and tender, etc.

[Col. 1004D] “First, mind and soul are not the same,” etc. He tries to dissolve that objection concerning sensation, which increases in children and fails in old people. But not very convincingly. Aristotle, *On the Soul*, Book I, text 65: he teaches that, if old people become delirious, it is not a defect of the soul but of the body; and that old age is not in the soul but in its instruments, etc.

“For in sleepers the mind, not the soul, sleeps.” Lactantius, you do not seem to me to have sufficiently understood what soul and mind are. Did it not occur to you from the divine teacher, *On the Soul*, Book I, text 89 and following, and Book II, texts 19 and 31, that the soul is one thing, possessing several powers; that the higher of these is what Aristotle calls *nous* (νοῦς), and we call intellect and mind; and that he teaches in *On the Soul*, Book III, text 6, that it is neither mixed with the body nor attached to a bodily organ? Therefore he wrote, *On Sleep and Waking*, chapter 2, that sleep occurs not in the mind but in the inner sense. For sleep is nothing else [Col. 1005A] than the cooling of the primary sensory faculty, in the same work, chapter 3, and *On the Parts of Animals*, Book II, chapter 7.

“And in madmen the mind is extinguished, while the soul remains.” Nonsense. What does “is extinguished” mean? Is not this part of the soul that divine fire which you yourself mentioned in chapter 8 of *On the Workmanship*? Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, Book I: “Panaetius advances another argument: whatever can feel pain can also be sick; and whatever can fall into disease can also perish. Souls, however, feel pain; therefore they also perish. These arguments can be refuted; for they belong to one ignorant that, when the eternity of souls is discussed, the reference is to the mind, which is always free from every turbulent motion, not to those parts in which ailments, anger, and desires operate—parts which the person against whom these things are said thinks separated and excluded from the mind,” etc.

“They are called demented.” This is an improper usage: not because they are without mind, but because they appear to be so, when they cannot employ reason, owing to injury to the organs of the lower powers, which serve the mind in reasoning.

[Col. 1005B] “It will fly back to its own seat.” As Cicero says in the *Dream of Scipio*: “Having departed from here, they return here”; and at the end of the first *Tusculan Disputation*: “Let us migrate back to our own home”; and often elsewhere. Carried away by imitation of such passages, Firmianus rashly uttered this phrase. But we ought to refrain from expressions of this sort, for they generally favor the doctrine that souls were created before bodies and fell from heaven to earth. Lactantius himself mocks that doctrine above, Book III, chapter 18; and St Augustine, after saying in Book II of the *Academic Books* that the more serious mind would return to heaven, condemns this form of speech in *Retractions*, Book I, chapter 1, and says that he ought to have written not “would return,” but “would go,” for the reason stated above. See the notes on Book II, chapter 3.

“But memory fails.” For, as Seneca the Elder says in the prologue to his *Declamations*, memory is, of all parts of the mind, the most delicate and fragile, and the first upon which old age makes its attack.

“But it is subject to pain and grief,” he says [Col. 1005C], etc. The second argument. Lucretius:

> To this is added that we see the body itself  
> contract terrible diseases, etc.

“The soul,” he says, “also feels bodily illness,” etc. The third argument. Lucretius:

> Indeed, in diseases the mind often wanders from its path  
> in the body, etc.

“Forgetfulness of itself.” Lethargy, concerning which Lucretius says in the same place:

> And sometimes it is borne into deep sleep by heavy lethargy, etc.

“It becomes ill through the contagion of the body.” Not very wisely said. If it becomes ill, it finally also perishes.

“Just as the eye,” he says, “when torn from the body,” etc. The fourth argument. Lucretius:

> Clearly, once torn out by the roots, the eye itself cannot  
> look upon any object, etc.

[Col. 1005D] “Like that which is contained in a vessel,” etc. An absurd comparison. The soul is not contained in the body as something is in a vessel; it is not contained as something is in a place. Rather, the soul contains the body than is contained by it: *On the Soul*, Book I, text 90. It is in the body as form is in matter: *Physics*, Book IV, text 23.

“That the soul seems mortal because it is not emitted from the body more quickly,” etc. The fifth argument. Lucretius:

> Finally, we often see a man gradually pass away, etc.

“But if our mind were immortal, it would not, when dying, so…” The sixth argument; but Lucretius reads:

> It would not, when dying, so…

## CHAPTER XIII

“Whenever [there is] dissolution” (*Hēnika d’ analysin*, ἡνίκα δ᾽ ἀνάλυσιν). Thus we read it with Musurus and the Juntine edition; for in the Aldine and Plantin editions *de* (δέ) is absent.

“But just as in lyres, from the tension of the strings,” etc. On this opinion of Aristoxenus, also mentioned in *On the Workmanship*, chapter 16, see Plato, *Phaedo*; Aristotle, *On the Soul*, Book I, text 54 and following; Lucretius, at the beginning of Book III; and Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, Book I.

## CHAPTER XIV

“Plato.” In his *Timaeus* are found those fictions concerning a certain Egyptian priest recounting to Solon that Athens had been founded nine thousand years before Solon’s time, and that all the notable deeds of that age were preserved, carefully recorded, in the sacred books of the Egyptians.

“Perhaps following the Chaldeans.” With Thomasius I have approved the reading of both codices, S. Salvator B, T, P, in place of that found in others, “just as perhaps the Chaldeans.” They indeed boasted that they possessed countless thousands of years, as Lactantius says here and St Augustine, *City of God*, Book XII [Col. 1006B], chapter 10; Lucretius also refutes them in Book V: “Why, before the Theban war,” etc.; and Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, Book II.

“That the six-thousandth year has not yet been completed,” etc. St Augustine says the same in the chapter just cited.

“When this number has been completed, the consummation must take place.” This error concerning the world’s duration of six thousand years is said to have become widespread from an ancient Hebrew tradition, concerning which there is a discussion in the fourth order of the Talmudic volumes, tractate 4, entitled *Sanhedrin*. They say that it was fostered not only by a certain Rabbi Isaac, on Genesis chapter 1, and several others of his sect, but also by some notable men among our own writers. For, besides Lactantius, Justin Martyr, Question 72; Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, final chapter; Hilary, *On Matthew*, chapter 17; Jerome, in the exemplar exposition of Psalm 89 addressed to Cyprian and in his commentary on Micah, chapter 4; and Augustine, *City of God*, Book XX, chapter 7, held this opinion.

Germanus, bishop of Constantinople, however, in his book *On the Theory of Ecclesiastical Things*, following Hippolytus the Martyr and Cyril in the book *On Antichrist*, affirms that the world will endure for six [Col. 1006C] thousand years and more than five hundred. Against this error stands the authority of other Fathers: Ambrose, *On Luke*, Book VII, expounding Matthew’s words, “After six days he was transfigured,” etc.; Augustine on Psalm 89; Bede in *On the Reckoning of Time*; and finally the Savior himself, testifying in Acts 1 that it is not ours to know the times or seasons which the Father has placed in his own power, and in Matthew 13: “But concerning that day or hour no one knows,” etc.

The fact itself also stands against it. For since it was inferred from that error that a period of about two hundred years remained from that time until the world’s consummation, as below in chapter 25, assuredly not merely two hundred years but nearly thirteen hundred have now passed. St Thomas gives reasons why it is fitting that the great day of the Lord should be unknown.

“This is the day of the Sabbath, which in the Hebrew language received its name from number,” etc. Lactantius thinks that the name *Sabbath* is derived from *Sebang*, which means “seven” [Col. 1006D], because it is the seventh day; Theophilus also says so in *To Autolycus*, Book II. Others prefer *Sciabath*, that is, “Sabbath,” to mean rest, and to be derived from the verb *Sciabath*, “to rest.” Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book I, chapter 1; Philo, at the beginning of *On Abraham*; and *On the Migration of Abraham* support them. Plutarch, however, and certain other pagans very foolishly suppose a different derivation. For Plutarch, in Question 5 of his *Table Talk*, derives it from Bacchus, who is Sabbus, because on that day the Hebrews invite one another to drink. Others derive it from *sabbos*, a kind of Egyptian disease in which the groin is filled with sores; they say that the Hebrews suffered from it while leaving Egypt, rested on the seventh day, and therefore called that day Sabbath.

Certainly Manetho the Egyptian—according to Josephus disputing against him in *Against Apion*, Book I—and Justin the historian, Book XXXVI, slandered Moses as the leader of lepers and persons afflicted with scabies in the departure from Egypt. Justin says that, after recovering Damascus, his ancient homeland, Moses occupied Mount Sinai—elsewhere *Synam* [Col. 1007A]—and that, when he and his people, worn out by seven days’ fasting through the deserts of Arabia, had at last come there, he called the seventh day Sabbath according to the custom of the nation and consecrated it to fasting forever, because that day had ended their hunger and wandering, etc.

“As the Prophet indicates, saying,” etc. But that passage provides no support for the error, since there the number one thousand is used for an indefinite number, as in Psalm 104: “Of the word which he commanded for a thousand generations”; and in Ecclesiasticus: “One who fears God is better than a thousand impious sons,” etc. Many examples of this kind are found among secular writers.

“That he might live a thousand years in this world.” I find in Genesis chapter 5 that Adam’s entire lifetime was nine hundred and thirty years.

## CHAPTER XV

[Col. 1007B] “That the Roman name,” etc. And below, chapter 25: “But when that head of the world has fallen,” etc. There was an ancient tradition of those times that when the Roman Empire first failed, Antichrist would come, and shortly afterward the world would perish. Thus Tertullian writes in his book *To Scapula* and in the *Apology*, chapter 32; and Optatus of Milevis in *Against the Donatists*, Book II. This tradition seems to have arisen from Daniel’s prophecy, chapter 2, where four kingdoms are enumerated and, after them, the coming of Antichrist is announced; and also from the Apostle’s words in 2 Thessalonians, chapter 2, where he says that Antichrist will not come before the apostasy has arrived, namely, the departure of peoples from the Roman Empire, according to Augustine, *City of God*, Book XX, chapter 19.

But how can this be, since the nations long ago departed from the Roman Empire and Antichrist has not yet come? St Thomas answers, in his commentary on the cited chapter 2 of Paul’s epistle, lecture 1, in these words: “It must be said that it has not yet ceased, but has been changed from temporal into spiritual, as Pope Leo says in his sermon on the Apostles. Therefore, departure from the Roman Empire must be understood not only as from the temporal empire but also from the spiritual, namely from the Catholic faith of the Roman Church.” This is a fitting sign: Christ came when the Roman Empire ruled over all; conversely, the sign of Antichrist’s coming is departure from it.

“Seneca distributes the ages of the Roman city into periods,” etc. [Col. 1007C] I do not find this passage in Seneca, but something of the sort in Bede, *On Times*, chapter 66.

“Hystaspes also, who was a most ancient king of the Medes,” etc. Paul the Apostle also mentions prophecies under Hystaspes’ name in Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, Book VI, in these words: “Take up the Greek books also; recognize how the Sibyl signifies one God and the things to come; take up Hystaspes and read,” etc. Since these words are not found in Paul’s letters, it is likely that Clement, a very ancient theologian, recorded them from Paul’s public sermons, committed to memory and then transmitted to posterity by a tradition.

Justin Martyr likewise mentions Hystaspes by name more than once in his *Second Apology for the Christians*. In this place seven Vatican codices read *Hystaspes*, instead of *Hydaspes*, as in other printed books. Therefore we restore to Lactantius the true name of this king, as Theodore Canter also approves in *Various Readings*, Book II, chapter 19. Yet what he brings forward from the historian Agathias, Book II, and Ammianus, Book XXIII, concerning Hystaspes, father of Darius, cannot apply to this Hystaspes of ours. For Darius’s father, who is also called Hydaspes in some places, was not a king, as is clear from Herodotus. And since Rome was founded around the sixth Olympiad, as is clear from Eusebius, Glareanus in his chronology on Livy, and others, whereas Darius flourished in the sixty-fourth Olympiad, as we reported from Eusebius above in Book IV, chapter 14, Darius’s father must have lived many years—indeed, almost centuries—after the founding of the City. This conflicts with what Lactantius asserts here: that this Hystaspes lived long before [Col. 1008A] that Trojan people, that is, the Romans, was founded.

“From whom also the river received its name, which is now called Hydaspes.” From this you now understand why Virgil, *Georgics*, Book IV, calls Hydaspes a Mede, in these verses:

> Moreover, neither Egypt and great  
> Lydia, nor the peoples of the Parthians, nor Mede Hydaspes  
> revere their king so greatly, etc.

The interpreters of the divine poet perhaps adduced insufficiently what was relevant to the matter.

“An extraordinary dream.” Thus this passage is restored from Codex B; in the printed editions it is corruptly read, “of all things admirable.” The following words show that this is the genuine reading: “under the interpretation of the prophesying boy,” etc.

## CHAPTER XVI

“For consuming.” I have restored this in place of the corrupt reading in all editions, “for consummating.”

[Col. 1008B] “Then suddenly a most powerful enemy will arise against them from the farthest boundaries of the northern region,” etc. By the most powerful enemy who will arise against the ten kings, Lactantius does not mean Antichrist, as Francisco Ribera thought in his commentary on Revelation chapter 12, no. 13. For at the beginning of the following chapter he says that this very enemy will be destroyed with all his remnants by another king rising from Syria, the betrayer of the human race, whom he calls Antichrist in chapter 19; he explains this more clearly in chapter 11 of the *Epitome* of these books. There, after saying that ten men would seize the world and that a far more powerful and wicked man would rise against them, destroy three of their number, possess Asia, reduce the rest to his power, and enlist them, he then says that amid these evils there would arise an impious king, hostile not only to humankind but also to God, who would crush, torment, harass, and kill the remnants of that former tyrant; and he clearly shows that this man would be Antichrist.

Therefore, in that enemy who, he says, will wage war against those kings, Lactantius perhaps understood Nero [Col. 1008C]. Severus Sulpicius, *Dialogues*, Book II, at the end, reports that St Martin, bishop of Tours, held this opinion; although, as Severus writes in the same place, many others also did. St Jerome, on Daniel 2—“And his heart shall be against the holy covenant,” etc.—and St Augustine, *City of God*, Book XX, chapter 19, who rebukes those persons, believed Nero himself would be Antichrist. Lactantius is therefore mistaken here, since it is clear from the Scriptures that no king other than Antichrist himself will come upon those ten kings, subdue them, and subject them to his rule, as all interpreters teach on the end of Daniel 12, where the vision of the fourth beast is explained, and on Revelation 12, at the words, “having seven heads,” etc., and chapter 17, at the words, “and the ten horns,” etc. So also Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, Book V, chapters 25 and 26; Hippolytus the Martyr, *On the Consummation of the Age*; Theodoret, *On Daniel*, Oration 7; and Prosper of Aquitaine, in the work entitled *The Half-Time*, chapter 7. Nor is what some invent about Nero supported by the authority of St Martin; for he is not to be thought to have held it by prophetic spirit, but to have responded to questioners perhaps as he had heard it related or read by others.

## CHAPTER XVII

“A great prophet will be sent by God,” etc. Lactantius mentions only one prophet, although in Revelation chapter 11, from which he drew this, two are said to be sent. John indeed calls them prophets, but passes over their names in silence, and therefore left room for writers to speculate. All agree, however, from Malachi chapter 4, that one of them will be Elijah; but they dispute concerning the other. Some assert that he will be Moses, such as Hilary of Poitiers on Matthew 20; Ambrose, *On Cain and Abel*, chapter 2; Catharinus on Genesis; and John Arboreus, *Theosophia*, Book XI. Others say Jeremiah, as Victorinus reports and believes; Ansbert rejects this interpretation on the cited Revelation chapter 11, as does Hilary on the cited chapter 20.

Yet the view accepted by most Fathers seems to be that Enoch will be Elijah’s companion, based on Ecclesiasticus 44: “Enoch pleased God and was translated into paradise, that he might give repentance to the nations,” etc.—that is, at the end of the ages, when he will preach repentance to the nations deceived by Antichrist. So Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapter 28; St Ephrem, *Sermon on Antichrist* and *Sermon on the Consummation of the Age*; Isidore, *On the Life and Death of the Saints*, chapters 3 and 35; Hippolytus the Martyr, *Sermon on Antichrist*; Jerome, Letter 148 to Marcellus and on Psalm 20; Augustine, *Treatise on Antichrist*, *On Original Sin*, Book II, chapter 23, and *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Book IX, chapter 6; Prosper of Aquitaine, *The Half-Time*, chapter 13 and following; Gregory the Great, *Morals*, Book IX, chapter 4, and Homily 12 on Ezekiel; John Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, Book IV, chapter 27, at the end; [uncertain: “IV, likewise on the cited chapter 51”]; the Gloss; Ansbert; Aymon; Rupert; Anselm; Richard; St Thomas; Andrew; and Arethas.

“Once his deeds have been accomplished, another king will arise from Syria” [Col. 1009B], etc. The prophets will not preach before Antichrist arises, as Lactantius says, but during his persecution: for one thousand two hundred and sixty days, namely, approximately as long as Antichrist’s persecution will last. Their preaching will be given, as it were, as an antidote to that persecution, as all teach on Revelation chapter 11: “And they shall prophesy for one thousand two hundred…”

“Begotten by an evil spirit.” Not because he will be begotten by an incubus demon using another’s seed, as some have thought, but because he will be born through the working of an evil spirit, as Hippolytus the Martyr and Damascene teach. The opinion of those who assert that Antichrist will be none other than the devil must likewise be avoided; St Jerome condemns them in his commentary on Daniel 2, at “Behold, eyes like the eyes of a man,” etc.; and Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, Book IV, chapter 28.

“Of that former evil.” That is, of that former tyrant, as chapter 12 of the *Epitome* explains; above, in the preceding chapter, he had said that he would subdue the ten kings.

[Col. 1009C] “They will be marked by him like cattle.” Revelation 13 speaks of the mark of Antichrist, by which he will mark his followers; but there is uncertainty about what this mark will be. Ansbert reports from Primasius—indeed, he reports it in such a way as to suggest that it had been revealed to him by God—that the mark will be such as to contain the whole name of Christ in abbreviation, like the mark which the Emperor Constantine the Great, Leo V, and certain other emperors bore on their standards, customarily represented in two forms. Ancient coins show such a mark, and Cardinal Baronius, *Annals*, Book III, under the year of the Lord 312, as well as Stewechius on Vegetius, Book II, chapter 18, and Lipsius, *On the Cross*, chapter 15, exhibit its forms engraved in print. This seems plausible, since Antichrist will love no name more than Christ’s name, by which he will deceive Jews, Hagarenes, and many Christians as well.

## CHAPTER XVIII

“There will come also [one] of the blessed,” etc. (*Hēxei kai makarōn*, Ἥξει καὶ μακάρων, etc.). These verses occur in the fifth discourse of the Sibylline Oracles, but there the reading varies greatly.

“Of the imperishable [one]” (*Aphtitou*, Ἀφθίτου). I read thus with M. Musurus, on account of the meter, as it stands in manuscript B and the Florentine edition—not *aphthitois* (ἀφθίτοις), as in the Aldine and Plantin editions.

“And then from the sun” (*Kai tot’ ap’ hēliou*, Καὶ τότ᾽ ἀπ᾽ ἡελίου). This verse varies somewhat in the Sibylline codex, etc.

“Our slavery,” etc. (*Hēmeteras douleias*, Ἡμετέρας δουλείας, etc.). The reading varies in the Sibylline Oracles; for there it is:

> ἵνα τοι ζυγῶν ὅ περ ὑπήμειν  
> δοῦλον δυοβάστακτον ἐπ᾽ αὐχένι κείμενον ἀροῦ.

> “So that you may remove from the neck the slavish, double-bearing yoke  
> under which we had been placed.”

## CHAPTER XIX

“Whenever he comes,” etc. (*Hoppot’ an elthēi*, Ὁππότ᾽ ἂν ἔλθῃ, etc.). These lines do not occur in the Sibylline Oracles.

“And afterwards he will receive the kingdom of the world,” etc. [Col. 1010A] He speaks of the kingdom in which Lactantius falsely believed that Christ would reign on earth with the righteous for a thousand years after the judgment; of this error we shall speak below. Therefore Didacus Covarruvias was not wrong to note this passage, *Various Resolutions*, Book IV, chapter 19, no. 10. Isidore, cautiously copying almost this entire passage in *Etymologies*, Book VI, chapter 17, omitted these words.

“A sword will suddenly fall from heaven,” etc. This saying lacks the testimony of Scripture, like certain other things which Lactantius must be thought to report from traditions of his times.

“They will drink” (*Pipsousi*, Πίψουσι). This must absolutely be read thus from the Sibylline codex, as the sequence of the first letters of each verse in the acrostic indicates; not *tripsousi* (τρίψουσι), as it is commonly read here.

“But works made by hands,” etc. (*Erga de cheiropoiēta*, Ἔργα δὲ χειροποιητά, etc.). This verse too is read somewhat differently in the Sibylline Oracles.

## CHAPTER XX

“After these things the underworld will be opened and the dead will rise,” etc. [Col. 1010B] In this and the following chapters Lactantius teaches the following concerning the future final judgment and the resurrection of the dead. Souls are not judged immediately after death, but are held in a single common custody beneath the earth until the day of the universal judgment, below, chapter 21. There will be a twofold resurrection: one of the faithful—that is, of those who have lived in God’s religion—and another of the impious, that is, unbelievers.

First, therefore, he says, the souls of the faithful will be raised from the underworld—that is, from that subterranean custody—to receive their bodies, as is said here. An examination of their works will take place: if their good works are more numerous and weightier, they will be given blessed life; but if the reverse is true, they will be condemned to punishment, as is said a little below. The examination will take place through fire. For those whose sins prevail either in weight or number will be burned by fire; but those whom full righteousness and mature virtue have ripened will not feel that fire, at the end of chapter 21.

Then God will establish a holy city in the middle of the earth, where he will reign for a thousand years with those righteous persons, who will rule the living as judges. Those found then alive in their bodies will not die, but during those same thousand years will generate offspring holy and dear to God. The pagans will not be wholly destroyed, but some will be left as God’s victory, so that the righteous may triumph over them. All this is in chapter 24. Finally, after a thousand years, there will be a second resurrection, namely of the impious, who worshipped idols and either did not know or denied the true God. Without any judgment—for in this chapter he teaches from the sacred writings that the impious will not rise for judgment—they will be consigned to eternal torments with the prince of demons and his ministers. But the righteous, when the world has been renewed, will be happy and blessed, ever dwelling in the presence of the Most High in the likeness of angels and serving him forever, chapter 26.

Lactantius produced these absurdities because he did not rightly understand the prophecy of John the Apostle in Revelation 20: “And I saw thrones, and they sat upon them,” etc. But there will be only one resurrection of all. Some will go to heaven unto eternal life—namely, those who, after receiving baptism, either contracted no stain of sin or washed away and cleansed the stain they had contracted; others to the infernal eternal fire—namely, those who died in actual mortal sin [Col. 1010D]. Those, however, who died in original sin alone will be punished either in limbo, or in this world, or, as St Antoninus of Florence says in the first part of his *Summa*, title VIII, chapter 1, §4, in another place known to God alone, with the punishment of loss only, namely, deprivation of the divine vision. How the Apostle John’s words should be understood is taught by interpreters of Revelation: St Augustine, *City of God*, Book XX, chapter 7 and following; and, among more recent writers, most learnedly and clearly, Francisco Ribera on Revelation.

“Whenever he receives it,” etc. (*Hoppote kai to labēi*, Ὀππότε καὶ τὸ λάβῃ, etc.). These verses occur in the Sibylline Oracles, discourse 3, where the reading varies greatly and this verse is mutilated.

“Of a king” (*Basilēōs*, βασιλήως). The Sibylline codex and St Augustine, *City of God*, Book XVIII, chapter 23, read *basilēes* (βασιλῆες).

“That the impious will not rise for judgment,” etc. [Col. 1011A] This is to be understood with respect to the examination of merits, not to the distribution of punishments. For with respect to the distribution of rewards or punishments all will be judged, according to Romans 14: “We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ,” as St Thomas explains in *Commentary on the Sentences*, Book IV, distinction 47, single question, article 3, and as Lactantius himself says below, chapter 26.

“But of the impious,” etc. This must be read thus, since the common reading *impios vero* (“but the impious”) is corrupt; the text itself proves it. For he continues to speak of souls, of which he said a little above, “but the souls of those who were righteous [are] pure and incapable of suffering,” etc. Now he carries out the other member of this statement: “but the souls of the impious,” supplying *animas*, “have a middle nature from the contagion of the flesh, being attached to whose desires they draw in deception,” etc. Nor does *addictae* (“attached”) agree with *impios*.

“Like light winds,” etc. Do not, however, suppose that the soul is some little wind or breath.

## CHAPTER XXI
[Col. 1011B] “First, therefore, we say that God’s power is so great that it embraces even incorporeal things,” etc. He explains how the soul, though spiritual, can suffer from bodily fire. Namely, it cannot suffer by natural power, because, as he says, having in itself nothing solid or tangible, it can suffer no force from solid and bodily things; yet it can suffer by that power which our theologians call the power of obedience, by which all things are naturally fitted to obey their Creator, so that whatever he wills may be done in them. He adduces the example of the angels, who fear him and can in some ineffable manner be chastised by him; and of the demons, who are tortured and punished by him. This now asserts nothing other than what St Thomas teaches in *Sentences*, IV, distinction 44, question 2, article 3, and other theologians there also: namely, that eternal fire can act upon souls and torture them as an instrument of divine power and justice.

“For because they contracted sins in their bodies, they shall again be clothed with flesh,” etc. Lactantius thought that the whole judgment of souls was deferred until after the resurrection of bodies. Therefore, he says, although God can by his power act through fire upon souls even when stripped of their bodies, he nevertheless more fittingly wills them to suffer with the body, because they sinned in the body and shall therefore again be clothed with flesh, etc.

“And yet that flesh which God shall put upon man will not be like this earthly flesh,” etc. He does not deny that the flesh of those who shall rise will be numerically the same as that which they possessed in life—something Catholic faith teaches, as we have it in chapter 1, *On the Supreme Trinity and the Catholic Faith*, and as the Doctors demonstrate in IV, distinctions 47 and 48. Rather, he says that it will not be like this flesh; and immediately declares in what its dissimilarity will consist: namely, because our flesh melts away and is consumed at the touch of fire, whereas that flesh will be indissoluble and enduring, and will not at any time fail under those torments and that fire.

“Whose nature is different from our own,” etc. Here he takes “nature” not strictly as substance and specific form, but more broadly and improperly, saying that that fire is of a different nature—that is, that it has certain different properties and consequent operations—which he himself immediately lists here, as do others: Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 48; Minucius in the *Octavius*; Pacian, *On Penance and Confession*. Namely, it is fed by no fuel of material; it both burns and restores the wicked; and as much as it consumes from bodies, so much it replaces. Damascene too is explained in this way. In book IV of *On the Orthodox Faith*, final chapter, he says that the wicked are to be cast into eternal fire, not material fire such as ours, but such as God knows. For it is said in the addition to Part III of St Thomas, question 97, article 5, and by St Bonaventure in *Sentences*, IV, distinction 44, article 2, question 1, that Damascene does not deny that the fire of hell is simply material, but material fire such as ours, since it differs from our fire in certain properties; nor does he deny likeness in specific form, but in certain operations, as we have said. [Col. 1012A] For that the fire of hell is of the same nature and species as our fire seems more probable and is more commonly received among theologians, as is noted in the addition to Part III, cited question 97, article 6, and discussed by Soto in *Sentences*, IV, distinction 50, sole question, article 1, second conclusion.

“Nor does it have smoke mixed with it; but it is pure and clear, and fluid like water,” etc. Perhaps this is true of the fire of purgatory, for some have taught this. But all deny it of the fire of hell: Basil, on Psalm 33, on the words “Fear of the Lord”; St Gregory, *Morals*, IX.49, who says that that fire is dark and without brightness; St Thomas, *Sentences*, II, distinction 6, article 3, reply to 1, and IV, distinction 50, sole question, article 2; St Bonaventure, *Sentences*, IV, distinction 44, article 2, question 1. Yet that fire will have as much mournful light as suffices for the condemned to look upon one another, increasing their wretchedness and punishments, as St Gregory says in the place cited above.

“But when he has judged the righteous, he will also test them in fire.” [Col. 1012B] The Doctors teach approximately this concerning the fire of conflagration: St Thomas, *Sentences*, IV, distinction 47, article 4, reply to III; and St Bonaventure there, question 4, at the end; and in the *Breviloquium*, part VII, chapter 4.

“Yet let no one suppose that souls are judged immediately after death.” Lactantius held that the punishments and rewards of souls are deferred to the day of universal judgment after the resurrection of bodies, and that in the meantime souls are held in one common custody, as we said above in this same chapter. Most other ancient Fathers held the same view: Clement of Rome, *Recognitions*, I, at the end, speaking in the person of the Apostle Peter; Justin Martyr, *Questions Put by the Gentiles*, question 76; Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*; Tertullian, IV *Against Marcion* and *On the Soul*, the chapter before the last; Origen, Homily 7 on Leviticus and books II and IV of *First Principles*; Victorinus on the Apocalypse, on the words “I saw under the altar”; Prudentius in the hymn for a deceased person’s funeral and elsewhere; Ambrose, II *On Cain and Abel*, chapter 2, and *On the Good of Death*, chapter 10; Chrysostom, Homily 39 on I Corinthians; [Col. 1012C] Augustine on Psalm 36; Theodoret on chapter 11 of the Epistle to the Hebrews; Arethas on the words of the Apocalypse, “How long, Lord, do you not avenge the blood,” etc.; Oecumenius on chapter 11 of the Epistle to the Hebrews; Theophylact there and in his commentary on Luke, on the words “Today you shall be with me,” etc.; Euthymius there; St Bernard on the words of the Apocalypse, “I saw under the altar,” etc. Finally, James the Apostle is adduced for this opinion in the liturgy of the divine sacrifice; and Ockham, in the *Works of Ninety-Three Days*, reports that John, the twenty-second Roman Pontiff of that name, believed it and decreed that it should be believed; Adrian, at the end of *Sentences*, IV, in the question on the Sacrament, confirms it.

Notwithstanding these authorities, it must now be held as a certain and infallible dogma that souls are judged immediately upon leaving their bodies; and that those which possessed the use of reason are, according to the diversity of their merits, led either to the glory of paradise, or to punishment—either eternal punishment in hell or temporal punishment in purgatory. Souls, however, which died before attaining the use of reason either pass into the limbo of children, where they suffer only the punishment of loss for contracted original sin unless they received baptism; or, if washed in baptism, into paradise for the blessed life through the merit of Christ, as St Thomas, St Bonaventure, and the others teach in *Sentences*, IV, distinction 45, article 1. The contrary assertion belongs to the error of the Armenians and Anabaptists, who maintain that before the resurrection of the bodies the souls of the saints cannot enjoy the glory of the divine vision, and that the punishment both of demons and of souls is deferred until the day of judgment. That assertion concerning demons is false, as I stated above in book II, chapter 15, on the words “because they have free will,” etc. [Col. 1012D] The holy Fathers also oppose that position concerning souls: Chrysostom, Homily on the words of Wisdom 6, “The souls of the righteous,” and elsewhere; St Augustine, *Confessions*, IX.3, and *Meditations*, chapter 24; *On Spirit and Soul*, chapter 58, and *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, chapter 79; Gregory, *Morals*, IV.25; Jerome, in the epitaph of Nepotian; and all theologians in *Sentences*, IV, distinction 45; St Thomas, I–II, question [uncertain omission in source], article 3. The decretal letters also oppose it: Innocent III’s letter in chapter *Majores*, *On Baptism*, and in chapter *Apostolicam*, *On an Unbaptized Priest*; likewise Benedict XI, in a certain Extravagant, which, although not included in the *Corpus Juris*, is nevertheless authentic and of infallible authority, and which Marsilius faithfully reports in full in *Sentences*, IV, question 13, article 3, and Alphonsus de Castro in *Against Heresies*, under “Beatitude.” Even universal councils oppose it: the Council of Florence under Eugenius IV, in these words:

> We define that the souls of those who, after receiving baptism, have incurred no stain of sin whatsoever, and likewise those which, after contracting the stain of sin, have been cleansed either while in their bodies or after being stripped of those bodies, are immediately received into heaven and clearly behold the triune and one God as he is—one more perfectly than another, nevertheless, according to the diversity of merits. But the souls of those who depart in actual mortal sin, or in original sin alone, immediately descend into hell, though to be punished with unequal punishments, etc.

Likewise the Council of Trent, session V, canon 5. Finally, the oracles of Sacred Scripture oppose it: Philippians 1, “I desire to depart,” etc.; 2 Corinthians 5, “We know that if our earthly house”—a passage cited by St Thomas, *Prima Pars*, question 64, article 4, reply to 3—and in the same chapter, “We are confident, and have good will,” etc.; Luke 23, “Today you shall be with me in paradise.” To testimonies of Scripture or of the Fathers which seem to conflict, wherever blessedness or punishment is said not to be given before the day of judgment, theologians reply that this is to be understood of that consummate blessedness or punishment which will be had after the resurrection of bodies; or that it is said not because an equal recompense of merits does not befall both good and evil persons through the particular judgment of each before the day of universal judgment, but because on the day of the universal resurrection, with the whole court of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings present, each person’s deeds being publicly recounted before the tribunal of Christ the Lord, reward will be assigned to the righteous and punishment to the reprobate by a public sentence manifest to all. Thus all things will be reviewed, as though nothing had been done before that day. [Col. 1013C] Finally, it is said that this error does not detract from the learning and piety of those Fathers, since the Church had not yet established anything certain on this matter in their times. Benedict XI’s Extravagant, moreover, clears Pope John from the calumny. Whoever wishes for more against this heresy, which Vigilantius the heretic once also spread and which St Jerome refuted, and which Luther and Calvin have recently propagated, should consult St Thomas, *Opusculum against the Greeks and Armenians*, chapter 9; Ockham, *Dialogue*, part II, tract 1; Alphonsus de Castro, *Against Heresies*, in the place cited; Cardinal Bellarmine, volume I, controversy 7, *Controversies*.

## CHAPTER XXIII

“Δύσπιστον γὰρ ἅπαν μερόπων” (“For everything among mortals is hard to believe”), etc. These verses vary greatly in the Sibylline Oracles.

## CHAPTER XXIV

“He will live among humankind for a thousand years,” etc. This is Lactantius’s opinion: after that first resurrection of the faithful, the Son of God will reign on earth with the righteous for a thousand years, amid that abundance of every good thing which poets sang to have existed in the Golden Age. This error is not unreasonably attributed first to Cerinthus, as Eusebius relates, *Ecclesiastical History*, VII.23 and III.28. Papias, bishop of Hierapolis, followed him, as the same Eusebius writes in III, final chapter; Nicephorus, chapter 20; and Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under “Papias.” Then, because of the writer’s antiquity rather than the soundness of his sayings, many churchmen followed Papias, as Eusebius states in the cited final chapter, Jerome in the place cited, and in the preface to book XVIII on Isaiah. A certain Egyptian, Nepos, also defended the same error; Dionysius of Alexandria refuted him in his book *On the Promises*, as Eusebius reports, *Ecclesiastical History*, VII.22.

Yet although Jerome lists Tertullian and Victorinus among adherents of this opinion, nothing of theirs survives today containing this doctrine. Indeed Victorinus, on the Apocalypse, condemns it as a Cerinthian heresy. Tertullian, moreover, though he acknowledges a kingdom of a thousand years, nevertheless teaches at the end of book III *Against Marcion* that those delights will not be carnal but spiritual. St Augustine, *City of God*, XX.7, says that this opinion was in some way tolerable and was at one time accepted by himself. The error of these chiliasts or millenarians arose, therefore, not only from an erroneous interpretation of the words of Revelation 20, as we said on chapter 20 of this book, but also from an ancient Jewish tradition, which wrongly interpreted the prophetic oracles that often and extensively speak of Christ’s kingdom in Jerusalem, as Eusebius relates, *Ecclesiastical History*, VII.22, and Jerome under “Papias.”

Now although Jerome, commenting on Jeremiah 23, “And you shall break the flask,” etc., says that he does not dare condemn this heresy because many churchmen and martyrs held it, he nevertheless boldly and openly condemns it on Isaiah 60, as do all who have written on heresies; and not without reason. [Col. 1014B] For there will not be one resurrection first and then another, but one on the last day, when judgment shall be passed on the merits of individuals: some indeed will go into eternal life, others into eternal fire, as Matthew 25 says. This is also proved from Job 19, “For I know that my Redeemer lives,” etc. In 1 Thessalonians 4, Paul teaches that, when the Lord comes to judge, those then living will be caught up with the saints to meet Christ in the air, and so will always be with the Lord. Indeed, in the very chapter 20 of the Apocalypse from which the aforesaid persons took occasion for their error, one resurrection of all and one judgment are set forth: “And I saw the dead, great and small,” etc. From this the empty fiction is apparent of a period of a thousand years after the first resurrection, after which a second resurrection is to follow. Frederick Staphylus, in his *Epitome of Lutheran Theology*, reports that the Anabaptists, plagues of our own times, adopted the same error concerning the thousand years among their other heresies. Against it Trithemius testifies that Gennadius wrote and published writings; but they do not survive today.

“Κλῦτε δέ μου, μέροπες” (“Hear me, mortals”), etc. This verse is not found in the Sibylline codex.

“Then those who are alive in bodies will not die,” etc. These statements, and all that follows, are removed once that fiction of a thousand-year period, in which he teaches that these things will happen, has been removed.

“At that same time also the prince of demons,” etc. From Revelation 20: “And he seized the dragon, the ancient serpent,” etc.

“And when the judgment has been completed, the holy city will be established,” etc. Revelation 11: “And I, John, saw the holy city, Jerusalem,” etc. The millenarians interpreted these words of that city in which they believed the saints would reign with Christ for a thousand years. But the Apostle speaks there of the heavenly homeland, where, after judgment, the blessed will eternally enjoy the vision of God.

“And the moon will receive the brightness of the sun,” etc. These things concerning the brightness of the moon and sun, and the fruitfulness of the earth, which the prophet Isaiah mystically prophesied in chapter 30 and foretold would occur at the time of the first coming of our Savior, Firmianus falsely thought would occur in that thousand-year period of which we have spoken in this same chapter.

“Even the sailor will abandon the sea,” etc. These verses all occur in Virgil’s Fourth Eclogue; but Lactantius has remarkably disturbed their order. He also wrote, “Then too it will grow yellow softly,” etc., in place of the Poet’s “Little by little it will grow yellow softly,” etc.

“According to the poems of the Cumaean Sibyl.” I do not find them. For those which Sixtus of Siena adduces in *Bibliotheca*, II, in the chapter on the Cumaean Sibyl, from the *Collectanea* of Straton, bishop of Cumae, are the same as those which Lactantius immediately afterward reports from the Erythraean Sibyl. They are found among the Sibylline Oracles at the end of Book III, although not in the order in which they are written here.

“Οἱ δὲ λύκοι” (“But the wolves”), etc. In the Sibylline codex it is “ἐν δὲ λύκοι” (“and among them, wolves”), and the reading there varies greatly; yet it is more correct than in Lactantius. Whoever wishes may compare them.

“Εὐσεβέων δὲ μόνον” (“Of the pious alone”), etc. These verses vary somewhat in the Sibylline poem; for there it reads:

> “Ἑβραίων δὲ χθὶον ἁγία ἔστι . . . .”
>
> “But the holy land is that of the Hebrews . . . .”

## CHAPTER XXV

“Yet the entire expectation seems to be no more than two hundred years,” etc. Yet from the time when Lactantius wrote until these present times not merely two hundred but thirteen hundred years have elapsed. Since Lactantius wrote these things a little after the year of our Lord 300, as I showed on chapter 1 of book I, it is evident that he reckoned five thousand five hundred years from the beginning of the world to the Savior’s nativity. For here, and above in chapter 14, he affirms that the world will last six thousand years. St Augustine, somewhat later than Lactantius, is not far from this computation; he too writes in *City of God*, XX.7, that in his age the later portions of that sixth millennium were passing. But Eusebius, in the *Chronicle*, places the Nativity of the Lord in the 5,199th year from the beginning of the world.

“And when it has begun to be ῥύμη.” ῥύμη means “rush” or “ruin.” This is the reading of the Plantin and Aldine editions; but the Florentine Juntine edition reads: “And when it has begun to be πύρα,” as though it had entirely become a *pyra*, that is, a pile of wood to be burned by fire. Either reading seems capable of support from the Sibylline poems themselves; for in Books 3 and 8 it is said, “καὶ ῥώμη ῥύμη” (“and Rome [shall be] ruin”); and in Book 8 it is related that Rome will be consumed by fire.

## CHAPTER XXVI

“But when the thousand years,” etc. Taken from Revelation 20: “And when the thousand years are completed, Satan will be released,” etc.; these words are explained by St Augustine, *City of God*, XX.7 and at the end of chapter 11.

“Then the final wrath of God will come,” etc. The seven angels were commanded to pour the seven bowls of this wrath upon the earth, Revelation 16. See also the Sibylline poems, Book 3.

“He will shake the earth most violently,” etc. The Apocalypse says in the same passage: “And there was a great earthquake,” etc.

“And at its movement the mountains of Syria will be split,” etc. The Apocalypse says in the same passage: “And the cities of the nations fell,” etc.

“And God will cause the sun not to set for three days.” I find no Scriptural testimony confirming this statement.

“And he will set it ablaze; and excessive heat will descend,” etc. The Apocalypse: “And the fourth angel poured out his bowl upon the sun,” etc.

“And hailstones.” The Apocalypse: “And great hail, like a talent in weight, descended,” etc.

“And the mountains will be filled with corpses, and the fields will be covered with bones.” These seem to be taken both from Ezekiel 49, where all birds, every winged creature, and all beasts of the field are commanded to assemble to eat, etc.; and from Revelation 19, where John heard an angel standing in the sun and calling in a loud voice to all birds to eat the bodies of the slain. [Col. 1015D] The prophets intended to show an immense multitude of persons to be slain by Christ; for when the corpses of enemies are very numerous, they are customarily left unburied as food for birds.

“But the people of God during those three days,” etc. I have no testimony from Scripture.

“The world will be renewed by God,” etc. Revelation 21: “And I saw a new heaven and a new earth.”

“In which the wicked will be exterminated,” etc. The reading of the Florentine edition is preferable. For since above in chapter 20 he said that that first resurrection would be of the faithful, that is, of those who had lived in the religion of God, he says that this second will be of the wicked, who worshipped things made by hands, etc. The Aldine and Plantin editions read: “In which the unjust will be raised,” etc.

“But their lord also, with his servants, will be taken.” [Col. 1016A] Revelation 20: “And the Devil, who deceived them, was cast into the lake of fire,” etc.

“And he will be condemned to punishment.” Thus St Cyprian, at the end of *On the Vanity of Idols*: “He is now about to come from heaven for the punishment of the devil.” Namely, for the punishment of being cast down, as the text also makes clear; thus above also, book III, final chapter.

“They believe the things which they have invented.” After these words, the Aldine edition continues with the following address directed to Emperor Constantine. Because it is absent from both codices of St Salvator, from P., from Vatican manuscript 12, and from all other manuscripts which I have had occasion to see, and likewise from the Florentine, Plantin, and most other editions, I place it here separately from the text:

> But now, most holy Emperor, all inventions have been laid to rest, since the supreme God raised you up to restore the dwelling-place of justice and to protect the human race. Under your governance of the state of the Roman Commonwealth, worshippers of God are no longer considered criminal and impious. Now that truth has emerged and been brought to light, we who strive to perform works of justice are no longer accused as unjust. No one now reproaches us with God’s name. No one is any longer called irreligious who alone among all people is religious, because, despising images of the dead, we worship the living and true God. The providence of the supreme divinity advanced you to the imperial height, so that in true piety you might undo the evil counsels of others, correct sins, provide with paternal clemency for the safety of humankind, and finally remove wicked men themselves from the Commonwealth—men whom the same God, having cast them down in supreme piety, delivered into your hands—so that it might be clear to all what true majesty is. For those who wished, in order to defend impious religions, to abolish the worship of the heavenly and unique God lie defeated; but you, who defend and love his name, pre-eminent in courage and good fortune, enjoy the most blessed possession of your immortal glories. They both pay and have paid the penalties of their crime; you the mighty right hand of God protects from every danger and grants peaceful and tranquil rule amid the supreme rejoicing of all. Nor without reason did the Lord and ruler of all things choose you above all others, through whom he might restore his holy religion, since you alone among all proved able to furnish outstanding examples of virtue and holiness. By these you not only equal but even—what is greatest—surpass the glory of ancient rulers, though they are numbered among the good. [Col. 1016C] They perhaps were only naturally like the just. For one who does not know God, the governor of the universe, can attain a semblance of justice, but not justice itself. But you, by the inborn holiness of your character, by knowledge of truth, and by knowledge of God, accomplish works of justice in every act. It was therefore fitting that, in shaping the condition of humankind, divinity should employ you as author and minister. To it we offer daily prayers, that it may first preserve you, whom it willed to be guardian of affairs; then inspire in you the will always to persevere in love for the divine name. This is salutary for all: for you, unto happiness; for the rest, unto peace.

## CHAPTER XXVII

Let the reader attend in this chapter to Lactantius’s most splendid exhortation to live purely and innocently.

“He purified with truthful men,” etc. Lucretius: “He therefore purified with truthful men,” etc.

“And set a limit to desire,” etc. Thus the Aldine and Plantin editions, and Lucretius’s own books, read; although the Florentine Juntine edition of B. T. P. and the Venetian Tridine edition read: “And set a limit to numbness,” etc.

“By a narrow boundary.” I have followed the reading of the Lactantian manuscripts B. T. P. and of certain printed copies of Lucretius, a reading not displeasing to Lambinus. The common copies of Lucretius read “by a narrow path,” a reading which Lambinus does not particularly approve. But the manuscripts he followed read “by a sloping path,” that is, an easy and downhill one. The Venetian Tridine and Florentine Juntine editions here read “by a sloping boundary”; another reading is “by a pure boundary.”

# [EPITOME OF THE DIVINE INSTITUTES]

[Col. 1017]

## NOTICE OF O. F. FRITZSCHE

[Note: In the preface to the Leipzig edition, published by the learned man in this very year, 1844, as part II of Lactantius’s works.]

### ON THE EPITOME OF THE DIVINE INSTITUTES

[Col. 1017A] “Jerome already calls the *Epitome of the Divine Institutes* a headless book. It is entirely lacking in the Venetian editions of 1471 and 1472, the Roman edition of 1474, and the Rostock edition of 1476. The remaining editions of the fifteenth, sixteenth, and seventeenth centuries, omitting the first fifty-five chapters, contain only its final part, divided sometimes into eight and sometimes into twelve chapters. But even this fragment of the book is read in only four manuscripts: one at the Bodleian, one at Bonn, and two Royal manuscripts, one of which is the Regius-Puteanus and is also mutilated at the end: ‘Chapter 66 ends: *coming, the promised things* [promissa venientes].’

“The little book underwent a very strange fate. What one would think the author had left unfinished, or that some injury of time had mutilated, has been preserved for us almost entire—for some things have indeed been lost, such as chapters 14 and 20—in the Turin codex. From this book C. M. Pfaff first extracted the *Epitome* and published it with commentary at Paris in 1712, octavo; then Davisius again separately published it with notes at Cambridge in 1718, octavo. Thus the editors of Lactantius were able to present it not only much enlarged but also more corrected. For that latter part of the book, presented by earlier editors, derived from a thoroughly corrupt codex; but it could now easily be corrected in most places with the aid of the Turin, Bonn, and Regius-Puteanus editions.

“Moreover, that Turin codex, which besides the *Epitome* contains other books, such as a biblical genealogy—which he transcribed again together with a specimen of the history of the Manichaeans, and which Ferd., Flor., and Fleck. edited—is parchment, written in uncial letters without ligatures. The words are not separated by spaces. It was written in the sixth century, perhaps in the fifth; but the copyist erred very frequently and seems to have been almost ignorant of the Latin language. Walch alone doubted whether the *Epitome* proceeded from Lactantius himself; but the learned man advanced this opinion rashly.”

[Col. 1017]

# THE EPITOME OF THE DIVINE INSTITUTES OF LUCIUS CAECILIUS FIRMIANUS LACTANTIUS, TO HIS BROTHER PENTADIUS (C)

[Col. 1017C]

## PREFACE

[Note: Various Notes on columns 1017–1018]

**PREFACE.** This word is absent from the manuscript, as are the division into chapters, the titles, and also the summaries, which have seemed fit to be added here so that some light may be brought to this work of Lactantius.

**“To elucidate.”** In the manuscript, *inlustrandam*, according to ancient usage. Thus, in ancient texts, *vir inluster* for *vir illuster*.

**“And religion.”** In the manuscript, *religionemque*, as though it were an abbreviation for *religionemque esse*.

**“We composed.”** The manuscript has *conscribsimus*.

**“Something.”** It is absent from the printed editions, but is read in the Turin manuscript. For so the autograph reads, which the most illustrious and learned Pfaff kindly sent to us.

**“Which.”** In the manuscript, *que*, according to the practice of almost all manuscripts.

**“Into one.”** Add: “volume.”

### The design and method of the whole Epitome and of the Institutes

Although the books of the *Divine Institutes*, which we long ago composed to elucidate the truth and religion, so instruct and form the minds of readers that neither their length produces weariness nor their abundance burdens them, you desire, brother Pentadius, that an Epitome of them be made for you—presumably so that I may write something to you and your name may be celebrated in whatever work of ours it may be. I shall do what you ask, though it seems difficult to bring into one work what has been expounded in seven very large volumes. For the whole becomes less complete when so great a multitude of matters must be compressed [Col. 1019A] into a narrow space, and is rendered less clear by the very brevity, especially since very many arguments and examples—in which lies the light of proofs—must necessarily be omitted, because their abundance is so great that they could alone make a book. When these are removed, what can seem useful or clear? But I shall strive, insofar as the subject permits, to contract what is diffuse and abbreviate what is lengthy—yet in such a way that neither material appears lacking for fullness nor clarity for understanding in this work, in which truth must be brought into the light.

[Note: Various Notes on columns 1019–1019]

**“To be compressed into a narrow space.”** The manuscript has *coartanda*; perhaps this last word derives from *artus*, as the most learned Pfaff says.
