They say that the words “into a narrow space” are absent from the manuscript; nevertheless, I read them in the autograph of the most distinguished Pfaff.—“To be compressed into a narrow space.” Seneca, *On the Happy Life*, chapter 4: “An army is now spread more widely, now compressed into a narrow space.” *Natural Questions*, VII.27, end: “Not thrown and squeezed into a narrow space.” Lactantius, book VII, chapter 16: “The day will be compressed into a narrow space.” If the anonymous author in Clericus, p. 342, is to be trusted, the Turin manuscript does not contain the words “into a narrow space”; hence I enclosed them in brackets and had them printed in a different typeface, though otherwise not unworthy of Lactantius. Bunemann.

**“Brevity.”** The manuscript has *brebitate*, through the easy interchange of *v* and *b*. Thus below, where the manuscript has *brebiare*, it should read *breviare*. Likewise near the end of chapter 5.

**“To be omitted.”** In the manuscript, *preteriri*. This is common in manuscripts, where *e* is used for *ae*.

**“What can appear useful, what clear?”** Bunemann has: “What can be . . . what clear?” Thus in the manuscript. See Clericus, pp. 342–343. Pfaff supplied *utile* in the blank space and changed *poterit* to *potest*. But that empty space is too large to be adequately filled by the word *utile*. So Heumann, to whom the words “when these are removed” appear to be a gloss. Perhaps one should read: “What can appear comprehensible, what useful and clear?”

**“Is.”** Supply: “providence.”

**“That.”** It does not occur in the manuscript.

**“Since.”** This word is less suitable here; one should rather read, “And so it is certain that providence exists.” For from the creation and constant governance of the world it is proved to unbelievers that providence exists; one cannot say to the Epicurean, “Providence exists; hence all things are governed with supreme wisdom.” First one must prove to him that providence exists; this is best done from the arrangement and ordering of the universe.—“Since it is certain that providence exists.” I begin the second chapter with these words. After many years, having acquired Davisius’s edition, I see that the same pleased him. Hence there is no need, with Heumann, to read, “wherefore it is now certain.” Bunemann.

[Col. 1020D]

**“Ambiguity.”** In the manuscript, *ambiguitas*.

**“Will understand.”** In the manuscript, *intelleget*.

**“The totality of things.”** Bunemann has merely *summa*, without the word *rerum*, and provides the following note: “Pfaff had printed *rerum summa*. The word *rerum* is absent from the manuscript, according to the anonymous author in Clericus, p. 346, and the *Institutes* themselves do not contain it. Book I, chapter 3: ‘the totality cannot stand,’ where I gave more discussion. Compare *On Anger*, chapter 11.”

**“Kings.”** From Virgil, *Georgics*, IV.68.

**“Prevail.”** In the manuscript, *optineat*; likewise below the manuscript has *optineri* and *optineant*.

**“Characters.”** Davisius reads “forces.”

**“Commonwealth.”** In the manuscript, *re p.*

**“All.”** Said to be absent from the manuscript.

**“Nor indeed could it be created.”** I would prefer “nor indeed could it be created”; the *c* has been repeated from the following word. We have often corrected that *nec* in other passages of Lactantius: book II, chapter 9; book II, chapter 5. Davisius agrees.

**“That.”** In the manuscript, *illut*.

## CHAPTER I  
*(Divine Institutes, I.3.) On Divine Providence*

The first question that arises is whether there is any providence which either made or governs the world. That there is, no one doubts; for almost all philosophers, apart from the school of Epicurus, speak with one voice and hold one opinion: that the world could neither have been made without an artificer God, nor remain in being without a ruler. Epicurus is therefore refuted not only by the testimony and judgment of the most learned men but also by those of all mortals. For who can doubt providence when he sees heaven and earth so arranged, the whole universe so ordered, that they are most suitably adapted not only to marvelous beauty and adornment but also to the use of human beings and the advantage of other living creatures? Therefore, that which is manifestly ordered by reason cannot have begun without reason, since it is certain that providence exists.

## CHAPTER II  
*(Divine Institutes, I.2.) That God Is One and Cannot Be Many*

Another question follows: whether God is one or many. This indeed involves much uncertainty. For not only individuals disagree among themselves, but peoples and nations as well. But whoever follows reason will understand that there can be only one Lord and only one Father. For if the God who created all things is also Lord and also Father, he must necessarily be one, so that the same may be the head and the source of things. Nor can the totality of things otherwise stand unless all things are referred to one, unless one holds the helm, unless one guides the reins and governs all the members as though by one mind.

If there are many kings in a swarm of bees, they will perish or scatter, while

> Great discord has arisen among the kings in mighty commotion.

If there are several leaders in a herd, they will fight until [Col. 1020B] one prevails. If there are many commanders in an army, neither will the soldier be able to obey, since different commands are given, nor will unity be maintained among the commanders themselves, since each consults his own interests according to his character. Thus in this commonwealth of the world, unless there had been one governor who was also its creator, this whole structure would either have fallen apart or could not have been created at all.

Moreover, the whole could not reside in many, since each possesses his own functions and powers. Therefore none of them can be called omnipotent, which is God’s true designation; for each can do only what belongs to himself, while what belongs to others he will not dare to touch. Vulcan will not claim water for himself, nor Neptune fire; Ceres will not claim expertise in the arts, nor Minerva crops; Mercury will not claim weapons, nor Mars the lyre; Jupiter will not claim medicine, nor Asclepius the thunderbolt. He will more readily catch one hurled by another than hurl it himself. If, therefore, they cannot individually do all things, they have less strength and less power. But he must be considered God who can do the whole, not—

[Note: Various Notes on columns 1021–1022]

**“Not.”** In the manuscript, *quam*, quite rightly. Rather, supply the sense.

**“Impassible.”** In the manuscript, *inpassibilis*.

**“Prophets.”** He discusses these in book I, chapter 2.

**“And seers.”** Said to be absent from the manuscripts.

**“Unique.”** Thus Lactantius repeatedly calls God “the unique God.” See the note on chapter 5 of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*. Thus also in book II, chapter 17, near the end: “the true and unique God”; and below near the end of chapter 4.

**“The supreme God.”** You will find these words a hundred times in Lactantius.

**“Plato.”** The word “Plato” is absent from the manuscript, but it occurs near the end of chapter 5 of book I.

**“And.”** Absent in Pfaff, but restored by the anonymous author from the manuscript.

**“Antisthenes.”** Lactantius calls these same philosophers by name in the same chapter 5. In this chapter, as elsewhere, Lactantius takes no account of chronological order, but names them as they come to mind.

Of the whole. The manuscript has *utius*: the principal editor of this book rightly read *totius*; nevertheless, *hujus* might be read, which would yield an equally good sense.

“And [that] the world is governed by him alone.” These seven words, absent from Pfaff, are said to occur in the manuscript.

At. In the manuscript, *aput*.

To understand. In the manuscript, *intellegere*.

The Sibyls. On the Sibyls, see our note on book I, chapter 6.

Cimmerian. In the manuscript, *Cimmeam*, which the most learned Pfaff interprets as *Cumaean*; but J. B. le Brun thinks it is *Cimmerian*. Samian. In the manuscript, *Sammaiam*.

Albunea. Bunemann has: “*Albuneae*. Thus in the manuscript, according to the anonymous Clericus, p. 350. Pfaff printed *Albunea*. HEUMANN. The dative *Albuneae* is more elegant. Lactantius commonly uses it thus; for example, in book I, chapter 11: *Agesilao, Urano*, in the notes.”

Cumaean. In the manuscript, *Cumanae*.

Cumaean. In the manuscript, *Cymaeam*.

To be consulted again. The anonymous editor says that the manuscript reads *recurrendum est* (“one must return”).

who [says] the least about the whole [the source is a fragment].

## CHAPTER III. (Divine Institutions, book I, chapters 3 and 5.) Testimonies of the poets concerning the one God.

There is, therefore, one God: perfect, eternal, incorruptible, impassible, subject by power to no thing, himself possessing all things and governing all things—whom the human mind cannot assess by perception, nor mortal speech express. For he is loftier and greater than can be grasped either by human thought or by speech. In short, to say nothing of the prophets, proclaimers of the one God, poets also, philosophers, and seers bear testimony to the unique God. Orpheus calls him the supreme God, who created heaven and the sun with the remaining stars, the earth, and the seas. Likewise our Maro [Virgil] calls the highest God now spirit, now mind, and says that, infused as it were through the limbs, it animates the body of the entire world; likewise, that God ranges through the depths of heaven and the expanses of sea and land, and that all living creatures draw life from him. Not even Ovid was unaware that the world had been ordered by God; he calls him at times the maker of things, at times the builder of the world.

## CHAPTER IV. (Divine Institutions, book I, chapter 5.) Testimonies of philosophers that God is one.

But let us come to the philosophers, whose authority is held more certain than that of the poets. Plato asserts monarchy, declaring that there is one God by whom the world was ordered and perfected with wondrous reason. Aristotle, his pupil, acknowledges that there is one mind presiding over the world. Antisthenes says that there is one natural God, governor of the whole universe. It would take too long to recount what Thales, Pythagoras, and Anaximenes earlier, or later the Stoics—Cleanthes, Chrysippus, and Zeno—or, among our own writers, Seneca, following the Stoics, and Cicero himself, proclaimed concerning the highest God; for all these attempted both to define what God is and to affirm that the world is governed by him alone, and that he is subject to no nature, since every nature has been generated by him.

Hermes, who deserved to be called Trismegistus because of his excellence and knowledge of many arts, who preceded the philosophers in the antiquity of his teaching, and who is worshipped among the Egyptians as a god—while asserting the majesty of the unique God with limitless praises—calls him Lord and Father. He says that he is without a name, because he has no need of a proper designation, being alone; and that he has no parents, because he exists of himself and through himself. The opening of his writing to his son is as follows: “Indeed, to understand God is difficult; but to express him is impossible, even for one to whom understanding him is possible. For the perfect cannot be comprehended by the imperfect, nor the invisible by the visible.”

## CHAPTER V. (Divine Institutions, book I, chapter 6.) That the seers—that is, the Sibyls—proclaim one God.

It remains to speak of the seers. Varro reports that there were ten Sibyls: the first a Persian; the second a Libyan; the third a Delphian; the fourth a Cimmerian; the fifth an Erythraean; the sixth a Samian; the seventh a Cumaean; the eighth a Hellespontine; the ninth a Phrygian; the tenth a Tiburtine, whose name was Albunea. Of all these, he says that the Cumaean alone has three books, containing the destinies of the Romans, which are kept secret; whereas nearly all the others have one book apiece, extant and commonly available, but inscribed “Sibylline” as though under a single name—except that the Erythraean Sibyl, who is said to have lived in the time of the Trojan War, placed her true name in her book, while those of the others have been confused.

All the Sibyls of whom I have spoken, except the Cumaean—whom no one but the Fifteen Commissioners is permitted to read—testify that there is one God: ruler, creator, father, not begotten by anyone but self-generated; who both has existed from the ages and will exist through the ages, and who therefore alone ought to be worshipped, alone feared, alone honoured by all living beings. Since I could not abridge their testimonies, I have omitted them; if you desire them, you must return to the books themselves. Let us now pursue what remains.

## CHAPTER VI. (Divine Institutions, book I, chapter 8.) Since God is eternal and immortal, he has no need of sex or succession.

With. In the manuscript, *secum*; but this is an error.

He himself. In the manuscript, *ipsi*: again an error.—“The sexes,” plural number, which should not have been altered. Lactantius, book I, chapter 8: “It is clear that Hercules and Jupiter … were human beings, since they were born from two sexes”; more often in the plural, book I, chapter 6: “The two sexes were established for the sake of generation, the distinction of the sexes having been received”; and afterwards, “there are two sexes of gods.” Add book VI, chapter 23. BUNEMANN.

Pleasure. In the manuscript, *voluntas* (“will”).

And when temples and images had been erected. In the manuscript, *positique*.

The years are reckoned. Lactantius did not specify the number of years in book I, chapter 9, though here he is not far from the mark. For the expedition of the Argonauts took place eighty-three years before the destruction of Troy; from Troy’s capture to the first Olympiad there elapsed four hundred and thirty-three years; from the first Olympiad to the time when Lactantius wrote, 1,016 years are reckoned. All this makes 1,532 years.

Of Alcmena. In the manuscript, *Alcimenae*.

Born. Here and elsewhere in Lactantius’ books Hercules the Greek is under discussion; see our annotation on chapter 9 of the first book.

Megara. Lactantius had not named her in book I, chapter 9.

The garment, etc. Lactantius had not stated these details in book I, chapter 9.

And in it. It should be read *in eoque*.

Cicero. Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book III, chapter 22.

“He inscribed his groans upon the flower.” This imitates Ovid, *Metamorphoses* X.215:

> He himself inscribes his groans upon the leaves, and “Ai, Ai”  
> the flower bears inscribed.

Ariadne. In the manuscript, *Ariana*.

“The mother herself,” etc. That is, the mother of the gods, Rhea, also called Cybele. These matters through the end of the chapter refer to book I, chapter 21.

A youth. In the manuscript, *adulescentem*, as is customary in ancient manuscripts. This was Attis; see the note on page 95, volume I.

These many and great testimonies, therefore, plainly demonstrate that there is one rule in the world, one power, whose origin cannot be conceived and whose force cannot be described. Foolish, therefore, are those who think that gods are born from sexual intercourse, when sex itself and the union of bodies were given by God to mortals for this purpose: that the entire race might be preserved through succession of offspring. But what need have immortals of either sex or succession, whom neither pleasure nor destruction touches? Therefore those who are thought gods, since they are known both to have been born like human beings and to have begotten children, were certainly mortal. Yet they were believed to be gods because, being great and powerful kings, they deserved, on account of the benefits they had bestowed upon humankind, to receive divine honours after death; and, when temples and images had been set up, their memory was retained and celebrated as though they were immortal.

## CHAPTER VII. (Divine Institutions, book I, chapter 9.) The criminal life and death of Hercules.

But although nearly all nations have been persuaded that they are gods, their deeds, handed down by poets and historians alike, show that they were human beings. Who does not know in what times Hercules lived, since he both sailed with the Argonauts and, after Troy had been captured, killed Laomedon, father of Priam, for perjury? A little more than 1,500 years are reckoned from that time. Nor is he even reported to have been honourably born, but to have been begotten through Alcmena’s adultery, and himself devoted to his father’s vices. He abstained neither from women nor from men, and traversed the entire world not so much for glory as for lust, and not merely to kill beasts as to beget children. Though unconquered, he was nevertheless triumphantly mastered by a single woman, Omphale. Having handed over to her his club and the lion’s spoils, he himself put on women’s clothing, was cast at the woman’s feet, and received wool-tasks to perform. Later, carried away by a fit of madness, he slaughtered his small children and his wife Megara. Finally, after putting on the garment of his wife Deianira, when his body was dissolving in sores, unable to bear the pain, he built himself a pyre on Mount Oeta and burned himself alive upon it. Thus it follows that, even if he could have been thought a god because of his excellence, nevertheless because of these things he should be believed to have been human.

## CHAPTER VIII. (Divine Institutions, book I, chapter 10.) On Aesculapius, Apollo, Mars, Castor and Pollux, and on Mercury and Bacchus.

Tarquitius reports that Aesculapius was born of uncertain parents and for that reason exposed; that he was found by hunters, reared on the teats of dogs, and entrusted to Chiron for instruction. He lived at Epidaurus and, as Cicero says, was buried at Cynosuris after being killed by a thunderbolt. Apollo, however, his father, did not disdain to tend another man’s flock in order to receive a wife; and, having unwittingly killed the boy he loved, he inscribed his groans upon a flower. Mars, a most valiant man, did not lack the charge of adultery; indeed, bound in chains with his adulterous partner, he was put on display.

Castor and Pollux did not abduct other men’s brides with impunity; Homer testifies, not in poetic fashion but with simple credence, that they died and were buried. Mercury, who begot Androgynus (Hermaphroditus) through intercourse with Venus, deserved to be a god because he discovered the lyre and wrestling-school. Father Liber [Bacchus], conqueror after subduing India, happened to come to Crete, where he saw Ariadne on the shore, whom Theseus had both violated and abandoned. Inflamed by love, he joined her to himself in marriage and, as the poets relate, set her crown among the stars. The mother herself, after the flight and death of her husband, while living in Phrygia, a widow and old woman, kept a handsome young man as her favourite; and because he had not kept faith with her, she deprived him of his genitals and made him effeminate. For this reason she still delights in Galli priests.

## CHAPTER IX. (Divine Institutions, book I, chapters 19 and 21.) On the shameful acts of the gods.

[Variorum Notes to cols. 1025–1026]

*Regnaret* (“was ruling”). In the manuscript, *regnat* (“rules”). But *regnaret* should be read, as may be inferred from chapter 17 of book I.

*Semen* (“seed”). It is absent from the manuscript, but is read in chapter 17 of book I.

*Relegavit* (“banished”). This is certainly to be read, not indeed from the manuscripts, where there is *religavit*, but from the end of chapter 17, book I, of the *Divine Institutions*, where one reads: “Why a secret dwelling? Why banishment either so far away, or to a woman, or into solitude?” Thus Virgil too, *Aeneid* VII.775, says of Hippolytus:

> And banishes [him] to the nymph Egeria and to the grove,
> where alone, unknown, he might spend his life in the Italian woods,
> and where, his name changed, he was Virbius.

*Aetatem ageret* (“might spend his life”). Bunemann has: “*Exigeret aetatem* (‘might pass his life’). The Paris and Walch editions have *ageret*; but from the manuscript we give *exigeret*, on Pfaff’s authority, as Lactantius said from Virgil of the same Hippolytus, book I, chapter 17: ‘where alone, unknown, he might / pass his life’; and no one is ignorant of the phrase *exigere aetatem* in Terence and Cicero. Pliny used the same expression, *Natural History* VII.43: ‘in investigating these things wise men might spend their lives.’”

*Potestatis* (“power”). Bunemann, however, reads *pietatis* (“piety”) and supplies the following note on that word.—*Pietatis*. I have certainly corrected it thus, where Pfaff’s and Walch’s editions had *potestatis*. For in book I, chapter 1: “Was not Jupiter impious from his earliest youth, when he expelled and drove his father from his kingdom?” Elsewhere also I have shown that these words are confused in Lactantius. Davisius and Heumann agree with me. Compare the *Epitome*, chapter 69. BUNEMANN.

*Almenam*. This too is in the manuscript. But *Alcmenam*, the wife of Amphitryon, should be read. Leda, however, was the wife of Tyndareus, king of Laconia.

*Thetide*. In the manuscript, *Theude*; but it is a copyist’s error.

*Imbecillis ac minoris* (“weak and inferior”). In the manuscript, *imbecillis a minoris*; but this is a blemish.

*Jovem*. It is absent from the manuscript.

“Who is the bull?” These matters are set out more plainly in the *Epitome* than in book I itself, chapter 11.

*Confinxisse*. In the manuscript, *confixisse*.

*Et quaedam*. Read *sed quaedam* (“but some things”).

*Praefigurasse*. In the manuscript, *praefugurasse*; but this is an error.

*Tale*. Heumann thinks *tamen* (“nevertheless”) should be read.

*Obtinuerit*. In the manuscript, *optinuerit*.

*Poetae*. In the manuscript, *Potae*, an erroneous spelling.

By what means did Ceres beget Proserpina, if not through illicit intercourse? By what means did Latona bear the twins, if not through a transgression? Venus, exposed to the lusts of gods and men, when she ruled in Cyprus, invented the art of prostitution and ordered women to earn money, so that she would not be the sole woman infamous. And those virgin goddesses Minerva and Diana—were they chaste? Whence, then, sprang Erichthonius? Did Vulcan shed his seed upon the ground, and did a human being grow from it like a mushroom? Or why did she banish Hippolytus, whether to a secluded abode or to a woman, where he might spend his life alone amid unknown groves and, now under a changed name, be called Virbius? What do these things signify but incest, which the poets do not dare to confess?

## CHAPTER X. (Divine Institutions, book I, chapter 11.) Jupiter and his lustful life.

But Jupiter, king and father of all these gods, whom they believe holds supreme power in heaven—what power did he possess, when he expelled his father Saturn from his kingdom and pursued him in arms as he fled? What self-restraint, when he practised every form of lust? For he made Alcmena and Leda, wives of eminent men, infamous through adultery; he, captivated by a boy’s beauty, violently carried him off as he hunted and trained in manly pursuits, for feminine uses. Why should I mention the violations of virgins, whose number is shown by the number of his sons? Yet in the case of Thetis he was more restrained. For it had been foretold that the one she would bear would be greater than his father. He therefore struggled against love, lest someone greater than himself should be born. He knew, then, that he was not of perfect excellence, greatness, or power, since he feared what he himself had done to his father. Why then is he called greatest and best, when he both polluted himself with sins—which belongs to one unjust and evil—and feared one greater than himself—which belongs to one weak and inferior?

## CHAPTER XI. (Divine Institutions, book I, chapter 11.) Various emblems by which the poets veiled Jupiter’s shameful acts.

But someone will say that these things were invented by the poets. It is not poetic practice to invent in such a way that one lies about everything, but to adorn deeds that occurred with a figure and, as it were, some variegated covering. This is the limit of poetic licence: not to invent everything—which belongs to a liar and a fool—but to alter something with reason. They said that Jupiter transformed himself into a shower of gold in order to deceive Danaë. What is a shower of gold? Surely gold coins: offering a great abundance of them and pouring them into her lap, he corrupted the frailty of a virgin’s mind by this payment. Likewise, they speak of an iron shower when they mean a multitude of weapons. Ganymede was carried away in an eagle. What is the eagle? A legion, of course, since the image of this animal is the legion’s standard. Europa crossed over on a bull. What is the bull? Surely a ship whose protective emblem was fashioned in the form of a bull. Thus the daughter of Inachus did not cross the sea after literally becoming a cow; rather, she escaped Juno’s wrath in a vessel of that kind, which had the form of a cow. Finally, after she had been carried into Egypt, she became Isis, and on a fixed day her ship is celebrated in remembrance of her flight.

## CHAPTER XII. Poets do not invent everything relating to the gods.

You see, therefore, that poets have not invented everything, but have represented some things figuratively, so that, while saying what was true, they might add some semblance of divinity to those whom they called gods; as they do also concerning kingdoms. For when they say that Jupiter held the kingdom of Heaven by lot, they either mean Mount Olympus, where ancient histories report that Saturn and afterwards Jupiter lived, or the part of the East which is, as it were, higher because light arises from there; while the West is, as it were, lower, and Pluto therefore received the underworld by lot. The sea, moreover, fell to Neptune because he held the seacoast with all its islands. Poets colour many things thus; those who do not know this accuse them merely verbally of lying. In fact, however, they believe them; for they fashion images of the gods in such a way as to make some male and some female, and acknowledge some as spouses, some as parents, some as children. They therefore agree with the poets, since these things cannot exist without intercourse and generation.

## CHAPTER XIII. (Divine Institutions, book I, chapter 11.) Jupiter’s deeds recounted from the historian Euhemerus.

[Variorum Notes to cols. 1027–1028]

*Circumivisset*. In the manuscript, *circumisset*.

*Remique*. In the manuscript, *Rem. que*.

*Larentinalia*. In the manuscript, *Larentali*.—“The manuscript has not *Laurentinali* but *Larentali*, according to Pfaff’s second thoughts; from this one may more closely infer *Larentalia*. So others, and Ovid, *Fasti* III.55:

> Nor shall I pass you over, Larentia, nurse of so great a people,
> nor you, poor Faustulus, and your resources.
> Your honour will come when I speak of the Larentalia.

*Rubiginem*. In the manuscript, *robiginem*.

But let us indeed leave the poets aside. Let us come to history, which rests equally on the credibility of events and the antiquity of times. Euhemerus was a Messenian, a very ancient writer, who collected from the sacred inscriptions of ancient temples both Jupiter’s origin, deeds, and entire progeny, and likewise pursued the parents, homelands, actions, reigns, deaths, and even tombs of the other gods. Ennius translated this history into Latin. His words are these: “As these things are written, the line and kinship of Jupiter and his brothers have been handed down to us from the sacred writing in this manner.” The same Euhemerus therefore relates that Jupiter, after he had traversed the world five times, distributed dominions among his friends and relatives, gave laws to humankind, and performed many other good deeds; that, endowed with immortal glory and everlasting remembrance, he exchanged his life in Crete and went to the gods; and that his tomb is in Crete, in the town of Knossos, bearing in ancient Greek letters the inscription ΖΑΝ ΚΡΟΝΟΥ—“Jupiter of Saturn.” It is therefore established from the things I have related that he was a human being and reigned upon earth.

## CHAPTER XIV. The deeds of Saturn and Uranus drawn from historians.

Let us proceed to earlier matters, so that we may discover the origin of the whole error. Saturn is said to have been born of Heaven and Earth. This is certainly incredible. But there is a definite reason why it is so reported; anyone ignorant of it rejects it as a fable. Both Hermes and sacred history attest that Saturn’s father was called Uranus. Trismegistus, saying that there had been very few men of perfect learning, listed among them his own relatives: Uranus, Saturn, and Mercury. Euhemerus records that this same Uranus was the first to rule on earth, in these words: “At the beginning Heaven first held supreme rule on earth; he established and acquired that kingdom for himself together with his brothers.”

Here several things are missing in the manuscript codex—certainly two leaves, I think. Nor does the word *paravit* survive in full, but only *para* at the end of the page. It continues: “Divinity was attributed to the foolish goodwill and error of human beings.”

## CHAPTER XX. (Divine Institutions, book I, chapter 11.) On the Romans’ own gods.

I have spoken of religions common to all nations. I shall now speak of the gods the Romans regard as their own. Who does not know that the wife of Faustulus, nurse of Romulus and Remus, in whose honour the Larentinalia are dedicated, was of public sexual availability? For that reason she was called Lupa [“she-wolf”] and represented in the form of a wild beast. Faula also, and Flora, were prostitutes. One was Hercules’ whore, as Verrius relates; the other, having acquired great wealth by her body, made the people her heir, and for that reason the Floralia games are celebrated in her honour.

Tatius consecrated a female image found in the Cloaca Maxima and called her the goddess Cloacina. When the Romans were besieged by the Gauls, they made engines of war from women’s hair and, for this reason, established an altar and temple to Venus Calva [“the Bald Venus”]. Likewise to Jupiter Pistor [“the Baker”], because in a dream he had advised them to make bread from every kind of grain and throw it down upon the enemy. Having done so, the Gauls, despairing of subduing the Romans by famine, withdrew from the siege. Tullus Hostilius made Fear and Pallor gods. Mind too is worshipped—a thing which, I think, had they possessed it, they would never have thought should be worshipped. Marcellus invented Honour and Valour.

## CHAPTER XXI. (Divine Institutions, book I, chapter 20.) On the rites of the Roman gods.

The senate also instituted other fictitious gods of this kind: Hope, Faith, Concord, Peace, Modesty, and Filial Devotion. Although all these ought truly to exist in human minds, they placed them falsely within walls. Yet, although these have no substance whatsoever outside human beings, I would prefer them to be worshipped rather than Rust, Fever—which should not be consecrated but execrated—or the Oven, with its Fornacalian rites; or Stercutus, who first showed how to enrich the earth with dung; or the goddess Muta, who bore the Lares; or Cunina, who presides over infants’ cradles; or Caca, who reported Hercules’ theft of cattle to him, so that he killed her brother. How many other monstrosities and mockeries are there of which it is wearisome to speak! Yet I do not wish to pass over Terminus, because he is said not even to have yielded to Capitoline Jupiter, though he was a shapeless stone. They think he has guardianship of boundaries, and public supplication is made to him that he may both preserve and extend the limits of the Roman empire—the immovable rock of the Capitol.

## CHAPTER XXII. (Divine Institutions, book I, chapter 22.) On rites introduced by Faunus and Numa.

*Quam*. In the manuscript, *quae*.

*Et*. It is absent from the manuscript. “And Picus … was able.” These words do not appear in the Paris, Walch, Davis, and Heumann editions; we supplied them from the manuscript with Pfaff’s aid. BUNEMANN.—We add these words in our edition from O. F. Fritzsche, who agrees with us.

*Fatuam*. In the manuscript, *Fentan*. See *Divine Institutions* I.22 and the note there.

*Novis*. In the manuscript, *nobis*, in the manuscript’s customary spelling.

*Et*. It is absent from the manuscript.

*Ahena*. In the manuscript, *aena*.

The manuscript reads: “Even before Saturn … were thrown.” The reading of the Turin manuscript, *ante Saturno*, should not, pace the most distinguished Pfaff, have been changed to *ante Saturnum* in the Paris edition. For no one ever reported that sixty-year-old men were thrown from the bridge into the Tiber before Saturn; the words concern Saturn himself, and *ante* is adverbial in this sense: “Even earlier, men were thrown into the Tiber to Saturn as a sacrifice.” Thus Lactantius, book I, chapter 21: “Saturn was worshipped in Latium by the same kind of sacrifice: not indeed by a man being slaughtered at an altar, but by being cast from the Milvian bridge into the Tiber, a practice Varro says was performed in response to an oracle, whose final verse is this:

> Καὶ κεφαλὰς Κρονίδῃ, καὶ τῷ πατρὶ πέμπετε φῶτα.
> 
> ‘And send heads to the son of Cronus, and men/lights to the Father.’

Because this appears ambiguous, both a torch and a human being are customarily thrown. BUNEMANN.

*Prosecrabant*. Heumann reads *prosecabant*.

*Amputatis*. In the manuscript, *jamputatis*.

*Tunsisque pectoribus*. Lactantius, *Institutions* I.21: “Her priests, their bodies shaved, beat their breasts.” Lampridius, *Commodus* 9: “He observed the rites of Isis, so as to shave his head and carry Anubis. He ordered those serving Bellona actually to cut their arms, in his zeal for cruelty; but he compelled the worshippers of Isis to beat their breasts with pine-cones to the point of destruction.” BUNEMANN.

*Rhodi*. In the manuscript, *Rhodii*.

*Celebrantur*. In the manuscript, *celebratur*.

Faunus first introduced all these absurdities into Latium. He established bloody rites for Saturn, his grandfather; wished his father Picus to be worshipped as a god; and placed his wife and sister, prophetic Fauna, among the gods, calling her the Good Goddess. Then at Rome Numa burdened those rustic and uncultivated men with new superstitions, instituted priesthoods, and allotted gods to families and clans, in order to divert the minds of a fierce people from the pursuit of arms. Therefore Lucilius, mocking the absurdities of those enslaved to empty superstitions, composed these verses:

> The little terrors, the Lamiae of Faunus, which the Numases of Pompilius instituted [the transmitted wording is uncertain]—he trembles at these; here he puts down everything.  
> As little children believe that all bronze statues  
> live and are human beings, so these people think all fictions  
> true; they believe that hearts exist in bronze images—  
> a painters’ gallery: nothing true, all painted.

Cicero too, in *On the Nature of the Gods*, complains that imaginary and fictitious gods had been introduced, and that from this arose false opinions, turbulent errors, and superstitions almost fit for old women. This judgment ought to carry greater weight because it was expressed by a philosopher and a priest.

## CHAPTER XXIII. (Divine Institutions, book I, chapter 21.) On the gods and rites of the barbarians.

We have spoken of gods; now we shall speak of the rites and forms of worship. A human victim used to be sacrificed to Cyprian Jupiter, as Teucer had instituted. Likewise, strangers were sacrificed to Taurian Diana; Latiarian Jupiter too was propitiated with human blood. Even earlier, sixty-year-old men were thrown from a bridge into the Tiber for Saturn, at Apollo’s behest; and the Carthaginians not only consecrated infants to that same Saturn, but, having been defeated by the Sicilians, sacrificed two hundred sons of nobles in order to expiate their guilt. Nor are those practices more humane which are still performed for the Great Mother and Bellona, in which chief priests offer sacrifice not with another’s blood but with their own: having amputated their genitals, they pass from men without becoming women; or, their shoulders cut, they sprinkle the detestable altars with their own blood. But these are cruel rites.

Let us come to gentler ones. The rites of Isis show nothing other than how she lost and found her little son, called Osiris. At first the priests and ministers, all their limbs shaved and their breasts beaten, lament, grieve, and seek, imitating the mother’s emotion; afterwards the boy is found by a dog-headed baboon. Thus mournful rites end in joy. Similar to these is the mystery of Ceres, in which, with torches lit, Proserpina is sought through the night; when she is found, the entire rite ends in rejoicing and the brandishing of torches. The Lampsacenes sacrifice an ass to Priapus, for it seemed the more suitable victim because, by the size of its male obscenity, it could be matched to him to whom it was sacrificed.

Lindos is a city of Rhodes, where Hercules’ rites are celebrated with curses. For when Hercules had taken cattle from a farmer and sacrificed them, the man avenged the wrong done to him with abuse; and, when he himself was afterwards made priest, it was decreed that both he and the priests after him should celebrate the rites with the same curses. But the Cretan mystery of Jupiter concerns how, as an infant, he was either taken away from his father or reared. A she-goat is present, upon whose teats Amalthea fed the child. The rites of the Mother of the Gods show the same thing. For because then the Corybantes had concealed the child’s cry with the ringing of helmets and the beating of shields, the image of the event is now reproduced in the rites: cymbals are carried in place of helmets, and drums in place of shields, lest Saturn hear the crying child.

## CHAPTER XXIV. (Divine Institutions, book I, chapter 22.) On the origin of rites and religion.

[Variorum Notes to cols. 1031–1032]

*Injuriam suam conviciis ultus* (“he avenged the wrong done to himself with abuse”). In book I, chapter 21: *injuriam suam (sibi illatam) maledictis ultus est* (“he avenged the wrong done to himself with curses”). Lactantius often uses *injuria* in this passive sense: book II, chapter 9; book V, chapter 20. BUNEMANN.

*Sancitum*. In the manuscript, *sanctum*.

*Ἐξηγήσεως*. The manuscript has *ἐξητήσεως*, in Latin, “of the book of Pindaric Exposition.”

*Melissa*. In the manuscript, *Tellisa*. See book I of the *Institutions*, chapter 22. Bunemann reads *Melissea* in the same manuscript.

“And first … to Vesta.” I would prefer: “And he sacrificed to the gods, that is, to Vesta, and afterwards to the Mother of the Gods.” For thus, I think, the sense proceeds rightly and in order; otherwise it seems rather disordered. See Lactantius, *Divine Institutions* I.22. DAVISIUS.

*Historia*. In the manuscript, *storia*.

*Quemque*. Thus in the manuscript, but read *quemcumque* (“whomever”).

*Jubebat*. In the manuscript, *Juvebat*.

*Nominis*. Heumann reads *numinis* (“divinity”).

*Isti*. I think not Jupiter’s hosts, as Pfaff holds, but Jupiter himself and Melisseus are indicated. DAVISIUS.

*Isti fuerint*: that is, when, or at what time, these persons lived.

*Belum*. In the manuscript, *Bellum*, incorrectly.

*Annis*. On these years, see book I, chapter 23, page 109, volume I.

*Novis*. In the manuscript, *nobis*, since the letter *v* is almost always represented by *b*.

*Qua reddunt*. I cannot guess what these words mean, for the passage is very corrupt. Heumann thinks it should read *Quare nec intelligunt* (“wherefore they do not understand”), which seems fairly satisfactory.

*Sublati*. Perhaps *subtrahi* (“be withdrawn”) should be read.—*Furto sublati* (“taken away by theft”). Bunemann, however, reads *sublabi* (“slip away”) and supplies the following note: “*Sublabi*. This should be read at Pfaff’s wish, who wished his note in the Paris edition to be deleted; hence *sublati* appears wrongly in the Paris, Walch, and Davis editions.” BUNEMANN.

*Optimas*. Heumann reads *opimas* (“rich”).

*Uti possunt*. Read *iis uti possint* (“may be able to use them”).

These are the mysteries of the gods. Let us now also investigate the origin of religions, so that we may discover by whom and at what times they were instituted. Didymus, in the books entitled *Exegesis of Pindar* (*Ἐξηγήσεως Πινδαρικῆς*), relates that Melisseus was king of the Cretans, and that his daughters were Amalthea and Melissa, who nourished Jupiter with goat’s milk and honey. He introduced new rites and sacred processions, and first offered sacrifice to the gods—that is, to Vesta, who is called Earth. Hence the poet:

> and Earth, first of the gods;

and afterwards, “to the mother of the gods.” But Euhemerus says in his Sacred History that Jupiter himself, after he had taken power, established temples to himself in many places. For, “as he travelled around the world, whenever he came to a place, he joined the leaders of the peoples to himself in friendship and by the bond of hospitality. In order that the memory of this might be preserved, he ordered a temple to be created for himself and annual festivals to be celebrated by his hosts. Thus throughout all lands he sowed the worship of his own name.” When these persons lived may easily be inferred. Thallus writes in his history that Belus, king of the Assyrians, whom the Babylonians worship and who was Saturn’s contemporary and friend, lived 322 years before the Trojan War; and 1,470 years have passed since Ilium was captured. It is therefore apparent that no more than 1,800 years have elapsed since the human race fell into error, when new cults of gods were instituted.

## CHAPTER XXV. (Divine Institutions, book I, chapters 22 and 23.) On the golden age; on images and Prometheus, who first fashioned a human image.

Poets therefore rightly recall that the golden age was changed, since it existed during Saturn’s reign. For at that time no gods were worshipped; rather, people knew one God alone. After they subjected themselves to earthly and frail things, worshipping wood, bronze, and stones, the change of the age proceeded as far as iron. For, having lost knowledge of God and broken that one bond of human society, they began to ravage one another, plunder, and wage war. But if they were again to lift their eyes and look upon God, who aroused them to behold heaven and himself, they would never make themselves bent and lowly by venerating earthly things. Lucretius severely censures their folly, saying:

> And they make their minds lowly through fear of the gods.

And they press the downcast to the earth, where they render [something; sense uncertain in this inherited fragment]. Nor do they understand how vain it is to fear things which one has made, or to hope for any protection from things that are mute and insensible, and neither see nor hear the suppliant. What majesty or divinity, then, can things possess which were in human power either not to be made or to be made otherwise, and still are so? For they can be violated and stolen away, unless law and human guarding protect them [Col. 1032C]. Can anyone, then, seem in possession of his mind who slaughters the finest victims for such things, consecrates gifts, offers costly garments, as though they could use them—things devoid of motion? Dionysius, tyrant of Sicily, was therefore right to strip and mock the gods of Greece when, as conqueror, he had occupied it; and, after the sacrileges he had committed, he returned to Sicily under a favourable voyage and held his kingdom into old age. Nor were the violated gods able to punish him.

How much better it is, despising these vanities, to turn oneself toward God, to preserve the condition received from God, to preserve one’s name. For this reason *anthrōpos* (ἄνθρωπος) is so named: because he looks upward.

> **Note: [Col. 1033D] Variant Notes on columns 1033–1034**
>
> **Upward.** In the manuscript, *susum*; but this is an error.
>
> **Rational.** Thus the manuscript; but the Paris edition reads *irrational*, wrongly. See what precedes and follows.
>
> **And.** In the manuscript, *ad*.
>
> **Upon whom.** *In* is absent from the manuscript.
>
> **In which he had placed for him.** Davisius wishes the pronoun *ei* (“for him”) deleted. Certainly, without this pronoun, bk. II, ch. 12 reads: “in which He had placed knowledge of good and evil.” BUN.
>
> **Holy.** In the manuscript, *Sco*, which may be understood as either *sancto* (“holy”) or *sacro* (“sacred”).
>
> **To creep in.** The Anonymous reads *irrumpere* (“to break in”).
>
> **Then.** Added from the Turin manuscript.
>
> **Jealousy.** In the manuscript, *libere*.—*Livore* is rightly corrected. Compare bk. II, ch. 8: “infected by his own envy, as though with poison . . . Hence it is evident that envy is the source of all evils.” BUN.

But he looks upward who looks to the true and living God, who is in heaven; who seeks the maker and parent of his soul not only with feeling and mind, but also with uplifted face and eyes. But whoever subjects himself to earthly and low things certainly prefers what is lower to himself. For, since he himself is God’s work, whereas an image is the work of man, a human work cannot be set before a divine one; and as God is the parent of man, so man is the parent of an image. Foolish, then, and mad is he who worships what he himself has fashioned.

The detestable and foolish originator of this craft was Prometheus, son of Iapetus, Jupiter’s uncle. For when Jupiter had first gained supreme power and wished to establish himself as a god, to build temples, and sought someone able to form the human figure, Prometheus then appeared [Col. 1033B] and moulded the likeness of a man from rich clay, so realistically that the novelty and subtlety of the craft were a marvel. Accordingly, both the men of his own time and later poets represented him as the maker of the true and living man; and we too, whenever we praise skilfully wrought statues, say that they live and breathe. He, indeed, was the originator of clay images. Later descendants sculpted them from marble and cast them in bronze; then, as time progressed, ornament of gold and ivory was added, so that not only the likenesses but their very brilliance dazzled human eyes. Thus captivated by beauty and forgetful of true majesty, rational beings deemed insensible things sentient, irrational things rational, lifeless things living, and worthy of worship and veneration.

## CHAPTER XXVI. (Divine Institutes, bk. II, ch. 5.) On the worship of the elements and stars

Let us now refute also those who regard the elements of the world as gods—that is, heaven, sun, and moon. Not knowing their maker, they admire and worship the works themselves. This error belongs not only to the unlearned but also to philosophers; for the Stoics judge that all heavenly things should be counted among the gods, because they have fixed and rational motions by which they most steadfastly preserve the recurring alternations of seasons.

There is, then, no voluntary motion in them, since they obey laws laid down beforehand—not by any awareness of their own, but through the workmanship of the supreme creator, who so ordered them [Col. 1033D] that they might complete their unutterable courses and fixed intervals, through which the alternations of days and nights, summer and winter, are varied. If they admire their effects, courses, brightness, constancy, and beauty, they should have understood how much more beautiful, more glorious, and more powerful than these is God himself, their maker and artificer [Col. 1034A]. But they measured divinity by human sight, not knowing that what comes under sight cannot be eternal, nor can what is eternal be comprehended by mortal eyes.

## CHAPTER XXVII. (Divine Institutes, bk. II, ch. 13.) On the creation of man, sin and punishment; and on angels, both good and evil

One final matter remains: since it frequently happens, as we read in histories, that the gods appear to have displayed their majesty through omens, dreams, and oracles, and also through punishments inflicted upon those who committed sacrilege, I must explain what cause produced this, lest anyone [Col. 1034B] even now fall into the same snares into which those ancients fell.

When God, by the power of his majesty, had created the world out of nothing, adorned heaven with lights, and filled land and sea with animals, he breathed life into man, formed from clay in the image of his likeness. He placed him in Paradise, which he had planted with every kind of fruit-bearing tree, and commanded him not to taste from the one tree in which he had placed for him knowledge of good and evil. He threatened that he would lose his life if he did so; but, if he kept the command, he would remain immortal. Then the serpent, one of God’s ministers, envying man because he had been made immortal, deceptively enticed him to transgress God’s command and law. In this way he received knowledge indeed of good and evil, but lost the life [Col. 1034C] which God had granted as everlasting.

Therefore God expelled the sinner from the holy place and banished him into this world, that he might seek sustenance by labour and endure hardships and miseries as he deserved. He surrounded Paradise itself with a fiery barrier, so that no human being might attempt to creep into that place of perpetual blessedness before the day of judgment. Then death followed man by God’s decree; yet his life, although it had begun to be temporal, reached its end at a thousand years, and this was the span of human life until the time of the flood. After the flood, human life was gradually shortened and reduced to one hundred and twenty years.

But that serpent, who from his deeds received the name devil—that is, accuser or informer—did not cease to pursue the seed of the man whom he had deceived from the beginning. Thus, by instilling envy, he armed for the murder of his brother the man first born in this world, so that of the two first-born human beings he might destroy one and make the other a fratricide. Nor thereafter did he cease to pour the poison of wickedness into human hearts generation by generation [Col. 1035A], corrupting and depraving them, and finally overwhelming them with such great crimes that an example of justice became rare and people lived in the manner of beasts.

When God saw this, he sent his angels to cultivate human life and protect human beings from every evil. He commanded them to abstain from earthly things, lest, stained with any defilement, they be deprived of angelic rank. But that same crafty accuser, while they dwelt among human beings, enticed them into pleasures, so that they defiled themselves with women. Then, condemned by God’s judgment, cast down on account of their sins, they lost both the name and substance of angels. Thus, made attendants of the devil, they turned themselves to destroying the human beings whom they had come [Col. 1035B] to protect, so that they might have consolation for their own perdition.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On demons and their evil operations

These are the demons of whom poets often speak in their verses, whom Hesiod calls guardians of human beings. By their allurements and deceptions they so persuaded people that they believed these same beings to be gods. Thus Socrates professed that, from earliest childhood, he had a demon as guardian and ruler of his life, without whose intimation and command he could do nothing. They therefore cling to individuals and occupy homes under the name of Genii or Penates. Shrines are established for them; daily libations are poured to them as to the Lares; honour is paid them as though they drove away evils.

From the beginning, in order to turn people away [Col. 1035C] from recognition of the true God, they introduced new religions and cults of gods. They taught that memorials of dead kings should be consecrated, temples built, and images made—not in order that they might diminish God’s honour or increase their own, which they had lost through sin, but in order to take life from human beings and remove hope of the true light, lest people should attain the heavenly reward of immortality [Col. 1036A], from which those beings had fallen.

They also transmitted astrology, augury, and divination from entrails. Though these are false in themselves, yet they, the authors of evils, manage and regulate them so that they are believed true. They likewise invented the tricks of magical art to deceive the eyes. By their influence, what exists appears not to exist, and what does not exist appears to exist. They invented necromancies, lots, and oracles, in order to deceive human minds through lying divination by ambiguous outcomes. In all temples and sacrifices they are present; and, by producing certain deceptive portents to astonish those present, they so ensnare people that they believe a divine power to reside in statues and images. They also enter bodies as subtle spirits and, corrupting the limbs, bring on diseases [Col. 1036B], which they later relax when appeased by sacrifices and vows. They send dreams—or utter terrors—so that people may entreat them; or dreams whose outcomes correspond to the truth, so that they may increase reverence for themselves. Sometimes they even inflict a measure of vengeance upon sacrilegious persons, so that whoever sees it becomes more fearful and more religious. Thus by their deceits they spread darkness over the human race, so that, truth being oppressed, the name of the supreme and unique God might pass into oblivion.

## CHAPTER XXIX. (Divine Institutes, bk. II, chs. 9 and 18.) On God’s patience and providence

But someone says: “Why, then, does that true God allow these things to happen? Why does he not rather remove or destroy the wicked? [Col. 1036C] Why did he from the beginning give *archē* (ἀρχή, “power” or “authority”) to the devil himself, so that there might be one who corrupted everything and destroyed everything?”

I shall briefly state why he wished this being to be such. I ask whether virtue is good or evil. It cannot be denied that it is good. If virtue is good, then vice is, conversely, evil. If vice is evil because it attacks virtue, and virtue is good because it afflicts vice [Col. 1037A], then virtue cannot exist without vice; and if you remove vice, the merits of virtue are removed. For no victory can occur without an enemy. Thus it comes about that good cannot exist without evil.

Chrysippus, a man of keen intellect, saw this when discussing providence, and reproved as foolish those who think good was made by God but deny evil. Aulus Gellius interpreted his opinion in the books of the *Attic Nights*, saying:

> “Those to whom it does not seem that the world was established for the sake of gods and human beings, or that human affairs are governed by providence, think they employ a weighty argument when they say this: ‘If there were Providence, there would be no evils.’ For, they say, nothing is less fitting to providence than that in the world for whose sake God is said to have made human beings there should be so great a mass of troubles and evils.”
>
> To this Chrysippus, when he was discoursing in the fourth book *On Providence* (Περὶ Προνοίας), said: “Nothing at all is more foolish than those who suppose that goods could have existed if evils did not also exist with them. For since goods are contrary to evils, each must necessarily stand opposed to the other and, as it were, subsist supported by a mutual and opposing tension. No contrary exists without its other contrary. For how could there be a sense of justice unless there were injustices? Or what else is justice than the absence of injustice? Likewise, what courage is cannot be understood except from the contrast with cowardice; what self-restraint, except from intemperance? Likewise, how could prudence exist unless its contrary, imprudence, existed? Therefore,” he says, “why do foolish people not also demand this: that there should be truth and no falsehood? For likewise there are goods and evils, happiness and misfortune, pleasure and pain. For one is bound to the other, as Plato says, by their opposite extremities; if you remove one, you remove both.”

You see, therefore, that, as I have often said, good and evil are so connected with one another that neither can exist without the other. Thus, in supreme wisdom, God placed the material of virtue among evils [Col. 1038A], in order to establish for us a contest in which he might crown the victors with the reward of immortality.

## CHAPTER XXX. (Divine Institutes, bk. I, ch. 18; bk. III, chs. 2 and 3.) On false wisdom

I have shown, I think, that the worship of gods is not only impious but also vain: whether because they were human beings whose memory was consecrated after death; or because the images themselves are insensible and deaf, being fashioned from earth, and a human being who ought to look upon heavenly things should not subject himself to earthly things; or because the spirits who claim these religions for themselves are incestuous and impure, and therefore, condemned by God’s judgment, fell to earth, and it is not lawful to come under the dominion [Col. 1038B] of those over whom you are superior, if you wish to follow the true God.

It remains, since we have spoken of false religion, that we should also discuss false wisdom, which philosophers profess. They are indeed persons endowed with the highest learning and eloquence, but far removed from truth because they have known neither God nor the wisdom of God. Though they are acute and eloquent, since their wisdom is human I shall not fear to engage with them, so that it may appear that falsehood can easily be overcome by truth, earthly things by heavenly.

They define philosophy thus: philosophy is love or pursuit of wisdom. It is not, therefore, wisdom itself; for what loves must necessarily be one thing, and what is loved another. If it is the pursuit of wisdom, then not even in that sense is philosophy wisdom. For wisdom is the thing itself which is sought, while pursuit is that which seeks it. Thus the definition itself, or the meaning of the name, declares that philosophy is not wisdom itself; indeed, I would say that it is not even the pursuit of wisdom, since wisdom is not grasped by it. For who can be said to pursue a thing which he can in no way attain? One who studies medicine, grammar, or oratory can be called a student of the art he learns; once he has learned it, he is called a physician, grammarian, or orator. So students of wisdom should also have been called wise after they had learned. But since students of wisdom, so long as they live [Col. 1039A], are called such, it is apparent that this is not a pursuit which can reach the very thing sought by pursuit—unless perhaps those who strive to become wise until the end of life will be wise among the dead. Yet every pursuit has an end. Therefore a pursuit which has no end is not right.

## CHAPTER XXXI. (Divine Institutes, bk. III, chs. 3 and 4.) On knowledge and opinion

Moreover, there are two things that appear to belong to philosophy [Col. 1039B]: knowledge and opinion. If these are removed, all philosophy collapses. Yet the leading figures of philosophy themselves removed both. Socrates removed knowledge; Zeno, opinion. Let us see whether wisdom is rightly defined, as Cicero defined it, as knowledge of divine and human things. If this definition is true, wisdom does not belong to man. For which mortal could claim for himself that he professes to know divine and human things? I set human things aside. Although they are connected with divine things, nevertheless, because they are human, let us grant that a human being can know them. But he certainly cannot know divine things through himself, because he is human; whoever knows them must necessarily be divine and therefore God. But man is neither divine nor God. A human being therefore cannot fully know [Col. 1039C] divine things. No one, then, is wise except God, or at least that human being whom God has taught. But since philosophers are neither gods nor taught by God, they cannot be wise—that is, knowers of divine and human things.

Knowledge was therefore rightly removed by Socrates and the Academics. Opinion likewise does not suit a wise person. For each person holds an opinion about what he does not know. But to suppose that you know what you do not know is recklessness and folly. Opinion was therefore rightly removed by Zeno. If, then, there is no knowledge in man, and there ought not to be opinion, philosophy is cut off at the root.

## CHAPTER XXXII. (Divine Institutes, bk. III, chs. 4 and 7.) On the schools and disagreements of philosophers

> [Col. 1039D]

Moreover, philosophy is not uniform, but divided [Col. 1040A] into schools and scattered among many conflicting opinions; it has no settled condition. Since each school attacks and assails all the others, and none exists which is not condemned as folly by the judgment of the rest, the whole body of philosophy is certainly led to destruction through the discord of its members.

From this the Academy was later born. For when the leaders of that school saw that all philosophy had been overthrown by philosophers attacking one another, they undertook war against all, in order to dissolve everyone’s doctrines, asserting nothing themselves except one thing: that nothing can be known. Thus, having removed knowledge, they overthrew the old philosophy. Yet they themselves did not retain even the name of philosophers, since they confessed ignorance; for to know nothing is not the characteristic of a philosopher, nor even of a human being. Thus philosophers, [Col. 1040B] because they have no defence, destroy one another by reciprocal wounds, and philosophy itself wholly consumes and brings itself to an end by its own weapons.

But, one may say, physics alone is unsteady. What of moral philosophy? Is it supported by any firmness? Let us see whether philosophers agree even in this part, which concerns the ordering of life.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. (Divine Institutes, bk. III, chs. 7 and 8.) That the highest good must be sought in life

It is necessary to seek what is the highest good in life, so that our whole life and our actions may be directed toward it. When the highest good of man is sought, it must be defined such that, first, it belongs to man alone; second, it is proper to the soul; and finally [Col. 1040C], it is acquired by virtue. Let us see, then, whether the highest good which philosophers determine is such that neither a dumb animal nor the body can attain it, and that it cannot be acquired without virtue.

Aristippus, founder of the Cyrenaic school, who judged bodily pleasure to be the highest good, must be expelled from the number of philosophers and from the society of human beings, because he compared himself to a beast. Hieronymus’s highest good is to feel no pain; Diodorus’s, to cease feeling pain. But other living creatures flee pain, and rejoice when they do not feel pain or cease feeling it. What distinction, then, will be granted to man if his highest good is judged common to beasts? Zeno thought the highest good was living in accordance with nature. But this definition is general. For all living creatures live in accordance with nature [Col. 1040D], and each has its own nature.

Epicurus maintained pleasure of the soul. What is pleasure of the soul [Col. 1041A] except joy, by which the mind commonly luxuriates and relaxes itself, whether in play or laughter? But this good also falls to dumb animals: when filled with fodder, they dissolve into joy and frolic.

> **Note: [Col. 1041D] Variant Notes on columns 1041–1042**

>
> **Callipho.** In the manuscript, *Califfo*.
>
> **Goods of fortune.** Heumann thinks *bona* (“goods”) should be added: “goods of fortune are not.”
>
> **Are not in human power.** In the manuscript: “into human power.” We should not depart from the manuscript’s reading, for it is Cicero’s own usage, to which Gellius, *Attic Nights*, bk. I, ch. 7, bears witness: “to have been in the power of pirates.” Whoever wants more should consult Gronovius on Livy, bk. II, ch. 15, and Vorstius on Valerius Maximus, bk. I, ch. 6. BUN.
>
> **Or.** The Anonymous reads *ac* (“and”).
>
> **But.** In the manuscript, *ad*.
>
> **Could.** Read *possit* (“can”).
>
> **Small.** Heumann thinks *propria* (“proper”) should be read.
>
> **Certainly.** In the manuscript, *utiquae*.
>
> **Ethics.** In the manuscript, *Heticae*.
>
> **“Let us see,” etc.** The word order is reversed in the manuscript, which reads: “Let us now see what is the highest good; let the highest good be proposed to the wise man.” Pfaffius’s edition arranges the words more correctly.
>
> **Highest good.** These two words appear superfluous, and Heumann deletes them as unnecessary.
>
> **Understood.** In the manuscript, *intellegi*.
>
> **The same.** In the manuscript, *eamdem*. Others think *eaedem* should be read.
>
> **Presses.** In the manuscript, *urgueat*.
>
> **Sense.** That is, reason.
>
> **Wisdom.** In the manuscript, *sapientia*.
>
> **And both.** Heumann wishes to read: “But both.”
>
> **And if.** In the manuscripts, *at si* (“but if”); Pfaffius thinks *aut si* (“or if”) should be read.

Dinomachus and Callipho approved honourable pleasure; but either they said the same thing as Epicurus, namely that bodily pleasure is dishonourable, or, if they regarded some bodily pleasures as base and others as honourable, what is attributed to the body is no longer the highest good. The Peripatetics compound the highest good from goods of soul, body, and fortune. Goods of soul may be approved. But if they need assistance to complete blessedness, they are certainly weak. Goods of body and fortune, moreover, are not in human power; nor is that highest good which is assigned either to the body or to external things, since beasts too attain this twofold good, which they need in order both to be healthy and not lack food [Col. 1041B].

The Stoics are believed to have thought somewhat better, in saying that virtue is the highest good. But virtue cannot be the highest good, because, if it is endurance of evils and labours, it is not blessed in itself; rather, it ought to produce or bring forth the highest good, since one cannot attain that good without difficulty and very great labour. Aristotle, however, departed far from reason when he coupled honourableness with virtue, as though virtue could ever be separated from what is honourable or joined to baseness.

Eryllus the Pyrrhonist made knowledge the highest good. It indeed belongs both to man and to the soul alone [Col. 1041C], but it can occur without virtue. For a person should not be judged blessed merely because he has learned something by hearing or discovered it by a little reading. Nor is this a definition of the highest good, because knowledge may be of evil things or at least useless ones. Even if it is knowledge of good and useful things which you have acquired through labour, it is nevertheless not the highest good, because knowledge is sought not for its own sake but for another end. Arts are learned so that they may serve us for livelihood, glory, or even pleasure; and these certainly cannot be highest goods.

Therefore philosophers do not maintain a rule even in ethics, since in the very hinge of the matter—that is, in the discussion by which life is shaped—they fight among themselves. For their precepts cannot be equal or similar when some form people for pleasure, others for honourableness, others for nature, others for knowledge, others for seeking wealth, others for avoiding it, others for feeling no pain, and others for endurance of evils. In all these matters, as I showed above, they depart from reason because they do not know God [Col. 1042A].

## CHAPTER XXXIV. (Divine Institutes, bk. III, ch. 9.) That human beings were born for justice

Let us now see what the highest good is, what highest good is set before the wise person. Not only the sacred writings teach that human beings are born for justice; the philosophers themselves also sometimes admit it. Cicero says:

> “But of all the matters dealt with in the discussions of learned men [Col. 1042B], nothing is surely more excellent than clearly to understand that we were born for justice.”

This is most true. For we are not born for crime, since we are social and communal living beings. Wild beasts are born for savagery; otherwise they cannot live except on prey and blood. Yet even if the extremity of hunger presses them, they nevertheless spare animals of their own kind. The same is done by birds, which must feed upon the entrails of others. How much more ought a human being, joined to another human being both by commerce of speech and community of understanding, to spare and love a human being! For this is justice.

But since wisdom alone has been given to man, so that he may understand God, and since this alone distinguishes man from mute creatures [Col. 1042C], justice itself is bound by two duties. It owes one to God as to a father, the other to a human being as to a brother. For we are begotten by the same God. Therefore it has rightly and properly been said that wisdom is knowledge of divine and human matters. For we ought to know what we owe to God and what to man: religion, plainly, to God; love to man. But the former belongs to wisdom, the latter to virtue; and justice embraces both.

If, then, it is established that man is born for justice, the just person must necessarily be subject to evils, so that he may put into practice the virtue with which he is endowed. For virtue is endurance of evils. He will flee pleasures as evil; despise riches because they are fragile; and, if he has them, distribute them generously in order to save the miserable. He will not seek honours because they are brief and perishable. He will wrong no one; if he has suffered wrong, he will not repay it; and he will not pursue the person who plunders his goods. For he will judge it impious [Col. 1043A] to harm a human being; and if anyone arises who compels him to forsake God, he will refuse neither tortures nor death. Thus it will necessarily come about that he lives poor and humble, amid insults or even tortures.
