## CHAPTER XXXV. (Divine Institutes, bk. III, ch. 13.) That immortality is the highest good
What, then, will be the reward of justice and virtue, if it has nothing in life but evil? But if virtue, which despises all earthly goods, most wisely endures every evil, and even accepts death itself for the sake of duty [Col. 1043B], cannot be without reward, what remains except that its reward is immortality alone? For if the blessed life falls to man, as the philosophers maintain—being at least agreed on this one point—then immortality also falls to him. For only that is blessed which is incorruptible; only that is incorruptible which is eternal. Therefore immortality is the highest good, because it belongs alike to man, to the soul, and to virtue. Toward this alone are we directed; for attaining it we were born. For this reason God sets virtue and justice before us, so that by our labours we may attain that eternal reward. But concerning immortality itself we shall speak in its proper place. There remains logical philosophy (λογικὴ), which contributes nothing to the blessed life. For wisdom consists not in ornament of speech, but in heart and understanding. But if physics too is superfluous [Col. 1043C], so likewise is this logic; while in ethics, which alone is necessary, the philosophers went astray, since they could in no way discover the highest good. Thus all philosophy is found empty and useless: it could neither comprehend the reason of man nor fulfil its office and function.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. (Divine Institutes, Book III, chapters 17 and 18.) On the philosophers, namely Epicurus and Pythagoras.

Since I have spoken briefly about philosophy, I shall now say a few things also [Col. 1043A] about philosophers. Epicurus’ doctrine is this: first, that there is no providence. Yet he does not deny that there are gods. Both positions are contrary to reason. For if there are gods, then there is providence. Otherwise God cannot be conceived, whose characteristic property is to provide. “He cares for nothing,” he says. Therefore he cares not merely for human matters, but not even for heavenly ones. How then, or on what grounds, do you affirm that he exists? For, once divine providence and care have been excluded, it followed that you should say that God does not exist at all. You have retained him in word, but removed him in reality. Whence, then, comes the nature of things, if God cares for nothing? “There are tiny seeds,” he says, “which can neither be seen nor touched; by their chance union all things both arose and continually arise.” If they can neither be seen nor perceived by any part of the body, how could you know that they exist? [Col. 1044B] Further, if they exist, by what intelligence do they come together so as to produce anything? If they are smooth, they cannot cohere; if hooked and angular, then they are divisible. For hooks and angles protrude and can be cut off. But these things are insane and useless.

What of the fact that he likewise makes souls perishable? He is refuted not only by all philosophers and by public conviction, but also by the responses of seers, the verses of the Sibyls, and, finally, the divine utterances of the prophets themselves. Thus it is astonishing that there was one Epicurus who equated the lot of humankind with that of cattle and wild beasts.

What of Pythagoras? He was the first to be called a philosopher. Although he maintained that souls are immortal, he nevertheless held that they pass into other bodies—of cattle, birds, or beasts. Would it not have been better for them to be extinguished together with [Col. 1044C] their own bodies than thus to be condemned to alien ones? Better altogether not to exist than, after a human form, to live as a pig or a dog. And this foolish man, in order to lend credibility to his assertion, said that he himself had been Euphorbus in the Trojan war; after Euphorbus was slain, he had passed into other animal forms, and at last had become Pythagoras. O happy man, to whom alone so great a memory was granted! Or rather, unhappy man, who, when transferred into a beast, was not allowed not to know what he had been! And would that he alone had raved! He found believers too—indeed, unlearned people—to whom the inheritance of folly might pass.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. (Divine Institutes, Book III, chapters 18 and 20.) [Col. 1045A] On Socrates and his inconsistency.

After him Socrates held the first rank in philosophy. He was even declared by an oracle to be most wise, because he confessed that he knew one thing alone: that he knew nothing. By the authority of this oracle he thought it necessary to abstain from physical investigations [Col. 1045A], lest people either seek what they could not know or think that they knew what they were ignorant of. Yet let us see whether Socrates was most wise, as the Pythian oracle proclaimed. He frequently employed the proverb that what is above us is likewise nothing to us. He had now exceeded the bounds of his own judgment. For he who said that he knew one thing alone found something else which he uttered as though he knew it—but in vain. For God, who certainly is above us, must be sought; and religion must be embraced, [Col. 1045B] since it alone distinguishes us from beasts. Socrates not only rejected religion, but even mocked it, swearing by a goose and a dog—as though he could not swear by Aesculapius, to whom he had vowed a cock. Behold the sacrifice of a wise man. And because he could not himself consecrate it (*prosecrare*)—or fulfil the vow—he begged his friends, as he was dying, to discharge the vow after him, lest he be held as a debtor in the underworld. This man certainly both declared that he knew nothing and proved it.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. (Divine Institutes, Book III, chapter 21.) On Plato, whose doctrine comes nearer to truth.

His pupil Plato, whom Cicero calls the god of philosophers [Col. 1045C], alone of all philosophers pursued philosophy in such a way as to come nearer to truth. Yet because he did not know God, he erred so greatly in many matters that no one went more disastrously astray—above all because, in his political books, he wished all things to be held in common by all. Concerning property this is tolerable, though unjust. For it ought neither to harm anyone that he possesses more through his own industry, nor benefit him that he possesses less through his own fault. Yet, as I said, it can somehow be endured. But shall wives too, and children too, be common? There will be no distinction of blood, no certain lineage, no households, no kinships, no relations by marriage; but, as in herds of cattle, all things will be confused and undifferentiated. Will there be no restraint among men, no chastity among women? What marital love can exist in either sex where there is no settled or personal [Col. 1045D] affection? Who will be dutiful toward a father, not knowing from whom he was born? Who will love a son whom he thinks another’s? [Col. 1046A] Indeed, he even reserved public council for women, and allowed them military service, magistracies, and rule. How great will be the misery of that city in which women usurp the duties of men! But these matters elsewhere at greater length.

Zeno, master of the Stoics, praises virtue, yet judged that compassion—although it is the highest virtue—must be cut away as a disease of the mind. Yet compassion is dear to God and necessary to human beings. For who, being placed in any misfortune, does not wish to be pitied and desire the help of those who come to aid him? Such persons are stirred to bring assistance only by an emotion of compassion. Though he may call this humanity or kindness, he changes not the reality but the name. This is the emotion given to human beings alone, so that we might relieve our weakness through mutual assistance. Whoever removes it reduces us [Col. 1046B] to the life of beasts. For his assertion that sins are equal proceeds from the same savagery with which he attacks compassion as though it were a disease. Whoever makes no distinction among offences either judges slight faults worthy of great punishments—which is the mark of a cruel judge—or serious offences worthy of small ones—which is the mark of a lax judge. Either course is harmful to the state. For if the gravest crimes are lightly punished, the boldness of evil people will grow toward greater crimes; and if a heavier penalty is imposed for slight offences, many citizens will come into danger, since no one can be without fault, though, once corrected, they might become better.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. (Divine Institutes, Book III, chapters 18, 23, and 24.) On various philosophers and on the antipodes.

[Col. 1046C] These matters, indeed, are slight. But they arise from the same emptiness. Xenophanes said that the sphere of the moon is eighteen times larger than this earth of ours. Accordingly, another earth is contained within its hollow, inhabited by human beings and animals of every kind. Nor can anything be heard or said about the antipodes without laughter. Yet it is asserted as though it were something serious: that we should believe there are people whose footprints face in the opposite direction from ours. Anaxagoras raved more tolerably when he said that snow is black.

The sayings of some, and not merely their sayings but their deeds as well, are laughable. Democritus abandoned the field left to him by his father and allowed it to become public pasture. Diogenes, together with his troop of dogs—the Cynics—who profess that supreme and perfect virtue consists in contempt for all things, preferred to beg for his food [Col. 1046D] rather than obtain it by honourable labour or possess any household property at all. Certainly the life of a wise person [Col. 1047A] ought to be an example of living for others. If everyone imitated the wisdom of these men, how would cities stand? But perhaps these same Cynics could provide an example of modesty, since they lay openly with their wives. I do not know what virtue those who abolished shame could defend.

Aristippus was no better than these. I suppose that, in order to please his mistress Lais, he founded the Cyrenaic school, which placed the end of the highest good in bodily pleasure, so that authority might not be lacking to sins, nor doctrine to vices. Or are those stronger men more to be approved who, in order to be said to have despised death, inflicted voluntary death upon themselves? Zeno, Empedocles, Chrysippus, Cleanthes, Democritus, and Cato, who imitated them, did not know that, according to divine law and ordinance, one who kills himself is liable to the charge of homicide. For God brought us into this dwelling-place of flesh; he gave us this temporary habitation of the body, that we might dwell in it as long as he himself should will. It must therefore be regarded as a crime to wish to depart without God’s command. No force, then, must be applied to nature. He knows how to dissolve his own work. If anyone lays impious hands upon that work and breaks the bonds of the divine workmanship, he attempts to escape God, whose judgment no one, living or dead, can evade. Therefore those whom I named above are wicked and impious. They even taught the grounds which voluntary death ought to have, so that it was not crime enough that they became murderers of themselves unless they also instructed others in this wickedness.

## CHAPTER XL. (Divine Institutes, Book III, chapter 28.) [Col. 1047C] On the folly of the philosophers.

The sayings and deeds of philosophers by which their folly may be refuted are innumerable. Therefore, since we cannot enumerate them all, a few will suffice. It is enough to understand that philosophers are teachers neither of justice, which they did not know, nor of virtue, which they falsely claim. For what can those teach who frequently confess their own ignorance? I pass over Socrates, whose maxim is well known. Anaxagoras declares that all things are enveloped in darkness. Empedocles says that the paths of the senses toward discovering truth are narrow. Democritus testifies that truth lies sunk in the depths of a certain well [Col. 1048A]. Since they find it nowhere, they accordingly maintain that no wise person has yet existed. Since, therefore, there is no human wisdom—as Socrates says in Plato—let us follow divine wisdom, and give thanks to God, who has both revealed and delivered it to us. Let us congratulate ourselves that, by heavenly benefaction, we possess truth and wisdom, which philosophy, sought by so many intellects through so many ages, no one was able to find.

## CHAPTER XLI. On true religion and wisdom.

Now that we have refuted false religion, which consists in the worship of gods, and false wisdom, which is found among philosophers, let us come to true religion and wisdom [Col. 1048B]. We must indeed speak of both together, because they cohere. For to worship the true God is nothing other than wisdom. For he is the supreme God and maker of things, who made the human being as though his own image. Therefore he alone among all animals gave reason, so that the human being might render him honour as father and as lord, and might earn the reward of immortality by this piety and obedience. This is the true and divine mystery.

But among the others, because they are not true, there is no harmony. In philosophy sacred rites are not celebrated, nor is philosophy treated in sacred rites. And thus religion is false because it does not possess wisdom; wisdom is false because it does not possess religion. But where both are joined, truth must necessarily be present, so that, if one asks what truth itself is, it may rightly be called either wise religion or religious wisdom.

## CHAPTER XLII. (Divine Institutes, Book IV, chapters 3 and 7.) On religious wisdom; Christ’s name known to no one except himself and the Father.

I shall now say what either wise religion or religious wisdom is. In the beginning, before God established the world, from the fountain of his eternity and from his own divine and everlasting spirit, he himself begot for himself a Son: incorruptible, faithful, corresponding to the power and majesty of the Father. This is the power, this the reason, this the Word [*sermo*] of God [Col. 1049A], this wisdom. Through this craftsman, as Hermes says, and counsellor, as the Sibyl calls him, God fashioned the splendid and wonderful structure of this world. Finally, out of all the angels whom the same God formed from his spirits, he alone was admitted into partnership in the highest power; he alone was called God. For all things are through him, and without him nothing exists.

Finally, Plato spoke of the first and second God not altogether as a philosopher but as a prophet—perhaps here following Trismegistus—whose words, translated from Greek, I have appended: “The Lord and maker of all things, whom we have judged should be called God, made a second God, visible and perceptible. By ‘perceptible’ I mean not that he himself receives sensation, but that he sends into perception and sight. Therefore, when he had made this first, sole, and one being, he appeared excellent to him [Col. 1049B], and most full of every good.” The Sibyl likewise calls him the leader of all, made God by God; and another says, “The Son of God must be known as God,” as the examples I set forth in my books declare.

The prophets, filled with the divine spirit, proclaimed him. Solomon especially, in the Book of Wisdom, and likewise his father, a heavenly writer of hymns—both most illustrious kings, who preceded the time of the Trojan War by 180 years—testify that he was born from God. That his name is known to no one except himself and the Father, John teaches in the Revelation. Hermes says that his name cannot be uttered by a mortal mouth. Yet human beings call him by two names: Jesus, which means “Saviour,” and Christ, which means “King.” He is Saviour because he is healing and salvation for all who through him believe [Col. 1049C] in God; Christ because he himself will come from heaven at the consummation of this age, to judge the world and, once the resurrection of the dead has occurred, establish for himself an eternal kingdom.

## CHAPTER XLIII. (Divine Institutes, Book I, chapter 8; Book IV, chapters 10 and 11.) On the name of Jesus Christ and his twofold birth.

But lest you perhaps have any hesitation as to why we call Jesus Christ one who was born from God before the world, whereas he was born from a human being three hundred years ago [Col. 1050A], I shall briefly explain the reason. He is the Son both of God and of a human being. For he was born twice: first from God in the spirit before the creation of the world; afterward, in the flesh from a human being, during the reign of Augustus. This is a splendid and great mystery, in which are contained human salvation, the religion of the supreme God, and all truth.

For when the wicked and impious worship of gods first crept in through the snares of demons, the religion of God remained among the Hebrews alone. They nonetheless retained the worship handed down to them by succession in ancestral custom, not under any law, until the time when, under Moses, the first of all prophets, they departed Egypt. Through him a law was imposed upon them by God; afterward they were called Jews. Thus they served God, bound by the chains of the law. But they too, gradually wandering away to profane rites [Col. 1050B], accepted foreign gods; and, having abandoned their ancestral worship, sacrificed to senseless images.

Therefore God sent to them prophets filled with the divine Spirit, to reproach them for their sins, enjoin repentance upon them, threaten the coming vengeance, and announce that, should they persist in the same offences, he would send another bearer of a new law. He would remove the ungrateful people from the inheritance and gather for himself from foreign nations another, more faithful people. Yet they not only persisted, but even killed those very persons who were sent. Therefore he condemned them for these crimes and did not continue to send prophets to a disobedient people; rather, he sent his Son, that he might summon all nations to the grace of God.

Yet he did not exclude even them, impious and ungrateful though they were, from hope of salvation. Rather, he sent him especially to them, so that if perhaps they obeyed, they might not lose what they had received; but if they did not receive their God, then, the heirs having been disinherited, the nations might come into adoption. Therefore the supreme Father commanded him to descend to earth and put on a human body, so that, subject to the sufferings of flesh, he might teach virtue and patience not only in words but also in deeds. Thus he was born anew from a virgin without a father, as a human being; so that, just as in the first, spiritual birth he was created from God alone and became a holy Spirit, so in the second, fleshly birth, begotten from a mother alone [Col. 1051A], he might become holy flesh, so that through him flesh, which had been subject to sin, might be freed from destruction.

## CHAPTER XLIV. (Divine Institutes, Book IV, chapters 12 and 13.) Christ’s twofold birth is proved from the prophets.

The prophets had foretold that these things would occur as I have explained. In Solomon it is written thus: “The womb of a virgin was made weak, and it received a foetus; she became heavy, and in great compassion a virgin became a mother.” In Isaiah it is thus: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel,” which means “God with us.” For he was with us on earth when he put on flesh; and nevertheless God was in a human being, and a human being in God. The prophets foretold that he would be both. That he was God, [Col. 1051B] Isaiah says thus: “They shall worship you and pray in you, because God is in you, and we did not know it, O God of Israel. All who oppose you shall be confounded and ashamed, and shall fall into confusion.” Likewise Jeremiah: “This is our God, and none other shall be reckoned besides him, who discovered every way of prudence and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. Afterward he was seen on earth and conversed with human beings.” Likewise, that he was a human being, Jeremiah says: “And he is a human being, and who has known him?” Isaiah also delivers this: “And the Lord shall send them a human being who will save them; and, judging, he will heal them.” Moses himself likewise says in Numbers: “A star shall rise from Jacob, and a human being shall arise from Israel.” Therefore, since he was God, he assumed flesh, so that, having become a mediator between God and human being, he might lead the human being to God [Col. 1051C] through his teaching, death having been overcome.

## CHAPTER XLV. (Divine Institutes, Book IV, chapter 14.) Christ’s power and works are proved from the Scriptures.

We have spoken of his birth; now let us speak of his power and works. When he performed great and wonderful deeds among human beings, the Jews who saw them thought that they were done by magical power, not knowing that all the things done by him had been foretold [Col. 1052A] by the prophets. Those who were ill and weakened by various kinds of diseases he immediately strengthened not by any remedy but by the force and power of his word. He restored the infirm, raised the lame to walking, restored sight to the blind, gave speech to the mute, made the deaf hear, cleansed the defiled and leprous, restored their own minds to those maddened by demonic assault, and recalled the dead—even those already buried—to life and light. He likewise fed five thousand people with five loaves and two fish. He likewise walked upon the sea. In a storm he commanded the wind to be still, and tranquillity immediately came to pass. All these things we find foretold both in the books of the prophets and in the Sibylline verses.

Because of these miracles a great multitude flocked to him and believed him, as he was, to be the Son of God and sent by God. Filled with envy, however, the priests and leaders of the Jews were at the same time stirred by anger because he convicted them of their sins and injustice; they joined together to kill him. Solomon had foretold this, a little more than a thousand years earlier, in the Wisdom, in these words: “Let us entrap the righteous man, because he is disagreeable to us and reproaches us for sins against the law. He promises that he possesses knowledge of God and calls himself the Son of God. He has become a censure of our thoughts; he is burdensome to us even to behold, because his life is unlike that of others and his ways have been changed. We are regarded by him as trifles. He keeps himself from our ways as from impurities, and sets the latter end of the righteous before us, and boasts that God is his father. Let us therefore see whether his words are true, and test what will happen to him. Let us examine him with insults [Col. 1052C] and torments, so that we may know his reverence and prove his patience. Let us condemn him to a most shameful death.” They thought these things and went astray. For their folly blinded them, and they did not know the mysteries of God.

Therefore, forgetting these writings which they read, they stirred up the people against him as against an impious person, so that they might bring him, once seized, to judgment and demand his death with impious cries. They alleged [Col. 1053A] as the charge the very fact that he called himself the Son of God and that he dissolved the law by healing people on the Sabbath—though he said that he had come not to dissolve it but to fulfil it. When Pontius Pilate, who was then governing Syria [Col. 1053A], perceived that the case did not pertain to the office of a Roman judge, he sent him to Herod the Tetrarch and allowed the Jews themselves to be arbiters of their own law. Having received power to commit the crime, they sentenced him to the cross. But first they beat him with whips and blows, crowned him with thorns, spat upon his face, and gave him gall and vinegar for food and drink; and amid all this no cry of his was heard. Then the executioners cast lots for his tunic and cloak, suspended him on the crossbeam, and fastened him there, on the day before they were to celebrate Passover—their festival day. [Col. 1053B] Portents followed that crime, so that they might understand the wickedness they had committed. For at the very moment when he gave up his spirit, there was both a great earthquake and an eclipse of the sun, so that day was turned into night.

## CHAPTER XLVI. (Divine Institutes, Book IV, chapter 18.) It is proved from the prophets that Christ’s suffering and death had been foretold.

The prophets had foretold that all these things would happen. Isaiah says thus: “I am not rebellious, nor do I resist. I gave my back to the lashes and my cheeks to blows; I did not turn my face from the foulness of spittle.” [Col. 1053C] The same prophet says of his silence: “Like a sheep I was led to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearers, without a voice, so he did not open his mouth.” Likewise David, in Psalm XXXIV: “Lashes were gathered against me, and they did not know; they were scattered and were not pierced with remorse; they tested me, and [Col. 1054A] gnashed their teeth against me.” The same author says of food and drink in Psalm LXVIII: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.” Likewise concerning Christ’s cross: “They pierced my hands and my feet. They counted all my bones; but they looked upon me and saw me; they divided my garments among themselves, and cast lots for my clothing.” Moses says in Deuteronomy: “Your life shall hang before your eyes, and you shall fear by day and by night, and you shall not believe in your life.” Likewise in Numbers: “The Lord is not suspended like a human being, nor does he suffer threats like a son of man.” Likewise Zechariah: “They shall look upon me, whom they pierced.”

Amos says thus concerning the darkening of the sun: “On that day, says the Lord, the sun shall set at noon and the day of light shall be darkened; I shall turn your feast days into mourning [Col. 1054B] and your songs into lamentation.” Likewise Jeremiah, concerning the city of Jerusalem in which he suffered: “The sun set for her while it was still midday; she was confounded and cursed; I shall give their survivors to the sword.”

Nor were these statements made without reason. For after a short time the emperor Vespasian defeated the Jews, ravaged their lands by sword and fire, subdued those under siege by famine, destroyed Jerusalem, carried off captives in triumph, and prohibited the remaining survivors from their lands, so that at no time might they be permitted to return to their native soil. These things were done by God because of that cross of Christ, as Solomon had previously testified in their Scriptures, saying: “Israel shall be for destruction and a reproach among the people; and this house shall be deserted. Everyone who passes by it shall marvel and say: ‘For what reason has God done these evils to this land and to this house?’ And they shall say: ‘Because they forsook [Col. 1054C] the Lord their God, persecuted their king most beloved by God, and tortured him in great humiliation. For this God brought these evils upon them.’” For what would those not deserve who killed the Lord, who had come for their salvation?

*Idem et*: Pfaffius was able to add these words from the manuscript; they are absent from the Paris, Walch, Davis, and Heumann editions. We have added this word in our edition, with the agreement of O. F. Fritzsche.

*Et religio*: the manuscript has *ut religio*.

*Repudiavit*: the manuscript has *repudiabit*.

*Prosecrare*: according to the most distinguished Pfaffius in a marginal note in his manuscript, this is the same as *consecrare* (“to consecrate”). Heumann thinks that *prosecare* should be read.

*Probavit*: the manuscript has *probabit*. *Putabit*: the manuscript has *putavit*.

*Reservavit*: Heumann reads *reseravit*.

*Affectu*: the manuscript has *affectus*.

*Incommodum*: supply *est* (“is”). *Irrogetur*: the manuscript has *inrogetur*.

*Correpti*: that is, “corrected” or “chastised.”

*Itaque*: an anonymous reader cited by Heumann reads *atque*.

*De antipodis*: on this matter see above the note on chapter 24 of Book III of the *Divine Institutes*.

*Habent*: Heumann reads *habeant*.

*Canum*: he means the Cynics.

*Contemptum*: the manuscript has *contemptu*.

*Conquirere*: Heumann wishes to read *eum quaerere* (“to seek it”).

[Cols. 1047–1048.] *Iidem*: the manuscript has *idem*.

*Palam cum conjugibus suis*: afterward, however, according to Augustine, *City of God*, XIV.10, the Cynics ceased doing this, and modesty proved stronger . . . . . than error. Bunemann.

*Non*: some think that *Num* should be read.

*Ut*: the manuscript has *et*.

*Nescierunt*: the manuscript has *nec scierunt*.

*Migare*: Heumann thinks it would be better if *emigrare* were read.

*Adhibenda*: the manuscript has *at hibenda*.

*Vincula diruperit*: the manuscript has *vincla dirrumperit*.

*Sunt*: absent from the manuscript.

*Intelligi*: the manuscript has *intellegi*, as above.

*Nota*: the manuscript has *mota*.

*Humana sapientia*: the manuscript has *humanam sapientiam Deo*. Yet the scribe subsequently deleted the word *Deo*.

*Revelavit*: the manuscript has *revelabit*.

*Philosophiam*: Heumann thinks that *philosophorum* is better. *Nemo*: the manuscript has *Num*.

*Conjuncte*: the manuscript has *conjunctae*.

“*Id est, nec aliud quidquam, quam sapientiam*”: one should read, “*idem est, nec aliud quidquam, quam sapientia*” (“it is the same thing, and nothing other than wisdom”). Davis.—So indeed the anonymous Briton and Heumann: “For to worship the true God is the same thing, and nothing other than wisdom.” See Book IV, chapter 3: “To be wise is nothing other than to honour the true God with just and pious worship.” Bunemann.

*Deus*: the word added by Pfaffius should be deleted; *Deus* must be construed with *dedit*. Therefore Heumann’s *qui non fuit* should not be expelled. I was pleased when later I saw that Davis held the same view. Bunemann.

*Sapientia*: the manuscript has *sapientiam*.

*Ipse*: absent from the printed edition, though it is read in the autograph of the most distinguished Pfaffius.

[Cols. 1049–1050.] *De suis spiritibus*: read *de suo spiritu* (“from his own spirit”).—*De suis spiritibus*: Heumann says, “Read *de suo spiritu*.” But nothing should be changed here, as is clear from Book IV, chapter 8: “and he formed his other spirits into angels.” Here *spiritus* means emanations or breathings. Bunemann.

*In sensum mittat*: Heumann reads *sensum immittat*.

*In libris*: namely, *Institutes*, Book IV, chapter 6. Next, as the most distinguished Pfaffius himself corrected in several places in our new edition, so here too I think *Salomon* is to be read in the manuscript. Bunemann.

*Praecipue*: the manuscript has *praecipuae*.

*Scriptor*: the manuscript has *scribtor*.

*Antecesserunt*: Lactantius is greatly mistaken here. David and Solomon lived not before but after Troy was taken. Troy was taken in 1209 before the common era; David began to reign in 1059 before this era, and Solomon only in 1019.

*Nulli esse*: Heumann reads *nulli est*.

*Apud*: the manuscript has *aput*. *Christum*: absent from the manuscript.

*Appellemus*: the manuscript has *appellamus*.

[Cols. 1050–1051.] *Breviter*: the manuscript has *brebiter*.

*Carne*: the manuscript has *carnem*.

*Homine*: here a later hand wrote *virgine* (“virgin”) in place of *homine* (“human being”).

*Successionem*: the manuscript has *successiones*.

*Qui*: the manuscript has *hii qui*.

*Iidem*: the manuscript has *idem*.

*Insensilibus*: a later hand corrected this to *insensibilibus*. But in Lucretius, Book II, whose reading Lactantius enjoyed, *insensilibus* occurs twice.

*Iisdem*: the manuscript reads *isdem*.

*Et ingrato*: the manuscript reads *ut ingrato*.

“*Creatus ex solo Deo, sanctus*”: manuscript: “*Creatus est ex solo Deo sanctus*.” With Davis I read: “created from God alone, he became a holy Spirit.”

“*Sanctus Spiritus factus est*”: Pfaffius explains this in his preliminary dissertation, §§27–28. I add an explanation from Lactantius himself, Book IV, chapter 6: “God . . . before he began the work of the world, begot a holy, incorruptible, and irreproachable Spirit, whom he called Son.” Compare the remainder in Book IV, chapter 8, “Since he too is spirit,” and chapter 12. Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, folio 15, refers this here: “The Holy Spirit is clothed in flesh.”

[Cols. 1051–1053.] *Salomonem*: Lactantius already cites this passage in Book IV, chapter 2; but since it is not found in Solomon’s books, one may conjecture that it was taken from some writing attributed to Solomon but now lost.

*Esaiam*: the manuscript has *Eseiam*.

*Autem*: after this word the manuscript adds *Deum*.

*Eum*: in the manuscript *Deum* stands in place of *eum*. Pfaffius.—But *eum* is more correct; see Book IV, chapter 16. Bunemann. *Esaias*: see Isaiah 45:14.

*Reverebuntur*: the manuscript has *reberebuntur*.

*Confusionem*: this is the reading required by the sacred text, Isaiah 45, and by Lactantius himself, *Divine Institutes*, Book IV, chapter 13. The manuscript, however, reads *confessionem*.

*Jeremias*: the manuscript has *Hieremias*.

*Israel*: the manuscript has *Israel*.

*Medela*: the manuscript has *medella*. See Matthew 4:23; 8:16; 9:35; Mark 6:56 and 7; Luke 4:40–41; 7:10.

*Inauribat*: that is, “he made [them] hear”; certainly an obsolete and foreign word.

*Maculatos*: that is, lepers.

*Quinque millia*: see Matthew 14.

*Super mare*: earlier editors printed *supra*. With Heumann I read *super mare*, from the Vulgate translation of Matthew 14:26. Thus Hyginus, *Fabulae* 14, ed. Muncker, p. 40: “He is said to have run over the waters with dry foot.” Bunemann.

*Circumveniamus*: Lactantius also uses this word below, chapter 64, and near the end of Book V, chapter 1.

*Exprobrat*: the manuscript has *exprobat*.

*Viis*: the manuscript has *viris*.

*Praefert*: the manuscript has *praeferet*.

“*Gloriatur patrem Deum*”: this is the reading, as I have said and restored in Book IV of the *Institutes*, chapter 16. Davis held the same view here. Bunemann.

*Contumeliis et tormentis*: the manuscript has *Contumelia et tormento*, which Bunemann also has, adding: “It could more easily have been corrected from the manuscript’s *contumelia et tormento* to *contumeliis et tormentis*. I first accepted the former with Davis; the latter is Pfaffius’s, Walch’s, and Heumann’s. See what I note on Book IV of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 16.”

*Ut sciamus*: the manuscript has *et sciamus*.

*Vocibus flagitarent*: this denotes their vehemence and importunity in demanding, in the manner of Cicero and Lactantius, *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 3: “and with great cries demand their former condition”; and Book IV, chapter 18: “they began to cry out and to demand his cross with violent cries.” Bunemann.

[Cols. 1053–1054.] *Syria*: the manuscript has *Syriam*.

*Sceleris*: add *puniendi* (“of punishing”), for Latin idiom requires it.

*Addixerunt cruci*: I read *affixerunt eum cruci* (“they fastened him to the cross”). For they had already condemned him before they beat him with whips and blows. See Book IV, chapter 18. Bunemann.

*Eum*: absent from the manuscript.

*Namque*: the manuscript has *nam quae*.

*Verteretur*: the manuscript has *vertetur*.

*Quae omnia*: thus the manuscript; the Paris edition instead reads *Haec omnia*.

*Posui*: absent from the manuscript, but to be supplied from *Institutes*, Book IV, chapter 18.

*Psalmo*: absent from the manuscript.

*Minas*: the manuscript has *Minans*; see *Divine Institutes*, Book IV, chapter 18.

*Zacharias*: the manuscript has *Zaccharias*.

*Lamentationem*: the manuscript has *lamentatione*.

*Jeremias*: what follows is read differently in Book IV of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 19.

*Confusa*: this should be read, as in Book IV, chapter 19 of the *Divine Institutes*. The manuscript has *contusa*.

*Salomon*: the manuscript has *Salomoni*. But Heumann reads *Salomon*.

*Improperium*: thus the manuscript. The Paris edition has *opprobrium*. See the note on Book IV of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 18.—“*Et in improperium*”: the manuscript has *Et in improperium*, which, although less elegant, is nevertheless correct and is used elsewhere in the old translation. Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*, no. 21: “These are those whom we once had in derision and as a likeness of reproach.” The translator of Irenaeus, IV.66, fol. 364: “She suffered reproach.” Bunemann.

*Qui transiet per illam*: thus the manuscript, and here I cannot agree with the conjecture of the most distinguished Pfaffius. *Transiet* is used for *transibit*; moreover, in this very passage the Gotzian codex prefers *transiet*. I have established this form more fully in my note on Book IV, chapter 18. Lactantius and others also have *exiet* in Book IV, chapter 13, and *prodient* in Book VII, chapter 16. Bunemann.

*Domui*: the manuscript has *domi*.

*Dereliquerunt*: the manuscript has *derelinquerunt*.

*Mererentur*: thus the manuscript. Perhaps *merentur* or *merebantur* should be read.

*Salutem*: the manuscript has *salute*.

After these things, they took down his body from the cross and placed it in a tomb. But on the third day before dawn, after an earthquake had occurred and the stone with which they had closed the sepulchre had been rolled away, he rose again. Nothing was found in the tomb except the wrappings of the body. The prophets had long before foretold that he would rise on the third day. David says in Psalm XV: “You will not abandon my soul to the lower world, nor will you allow your Holy One to see corruption.” Likewise Hosea says: “This is [Col. 1055A]

“My wise son; therefore now he will not resist in the tribulation of his sons, and I shall rescue him from the hand of the lower world. Where is your judgment, O death? Where is your sting?” Again the same prophet says: [Col. 1055B] “He will make us alive after two days, on the third day.”

Therefore, after his resurrection he went into Galilee and again gathered together his disciples, whom fear had turned to flight. Having given them the commands that he wished to be observed, and arranged the preaching of the Gospel throughout the whole world, he breathed the Holy Spirit into them and gave them power to perform miracles, so that they might work for the salvation of humankind both by deeds and by words. Then at last, on the fortieth day, he returned to the Father, being taken up into a cloud. Daniel the prophet had long before shown this, saying: “I saw in a vision of the night: and behold, coming in the clouds of heaven as a son of man, he came as far as the Ancient of Days; and those standing by presented him; and there were given him kingdom, honor, and dominion; and all peoples, tribes, and tongues will serve him; and his power [Col. 1055C] is eternal, which shall never pass away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed.” Likewise David says in Psalm CIX: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet.”

## Chapter XLVIII. (Divine Institutes, Book IV, ch. 20.) On the disinheritance of the Jews and the adoption of the Gentiles.

Since, therefore, he sits at the right hand of God and will tread down his enemies—those who crucified him—when he comes to judge the world, it is evident that no hope remains for the Jews unless, converted to repentance and washed from the blood by which they defiled themselves, they begin to hope in him [Col. 1055D] whom they denied. Therefore Ezra says thus: [Col. 1056A] “This Passover is our Savior and our refuge. Consider, and let it rise into your heart that we must humble him in the sign; and after these things we hoped in him.”

That the Jews have been disinherited because they rejected Christ, and that we who are from the Gentiles have been adopted in their place, is demonstrated by the Scriptures. Jeremiah says thus: “I have forsaken my house; I have abandoned my inheritance into the hands of its enemies. My inheritance has become to me like a lion in the forest: it itself raised its voice against me; therefore I hated it.” Likewise Malachi: “I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord, and I will not accept a sacrifice from your hands, because from the rising of the sun even to its setting my name shall be glorified among the Gentiles.” Isaiah likewise says: “I come to gather all nations and tongues; and they shall come and see my splendor.” Elsewhere, speaking in the person of the Father to the Son, the same prophet says: “I, the Lord God, have called you in righteousness, and I shall hold your hand and strengthen you; I gave you as a covenant of my people, as a light of the Gentiles, to open the eyes of the blind, to bring the bound out from their chains, and those sitting in darkness out of the prison-house.”

## Chapter XLIX. (Divine Institutes, Book IV, ch. 29.) That there is but one God.

If, then, the Jews have been rejected by God, as the authority of the sacred Scriptures indicates, while the Gentiles, as we see, have been received and freed from the darkness of this secular life and from the bonds of demons, no other hope has been set before humankind unless one follows the true religion and the true wisdom that is in Christ. Whoever does not know him is always estranged from truth and from God. [Col. 1056C] Let neither Jews nor philosophers flatter themselves concerning the supreme God. Whoever has not acknowledged the Son could not acknowledge the Father either. This is wisdom, and this is the mystery of the supreme God. Through him God willed both to be known and to be worshipped. Therefore he first sent the prophets, who would preach of his coming, so that, when everything that had been foretold had come to pass in him, then both the Son of God and God might be believed by humankind.

Yet this must not be understood as though there were two Gods. For Father and Son are one. Since the Father loves the Son and grants everything to him, while the Son faithfully obeys the Father and wills nothing except what the Father wills, so great a bond cannot surely be severed [Col. 1056D] that they should be called two, in whom substance, [Col. 1057A] will, and faith are one. Therefore the Son is through the Father, and the Father through the Son.

One honor must be rendered to both as to one God; and it must thus be divided by two forms of worship, so that the division itself may be bound together by an inseparable union. Whoever separates either the Father from the Son or the Son from the Father leaves neither remaining for himself.

## Chapter L. (Divine Institutes, Book IV, ch. 25.) Why God assumed a human body and suffered death.

It remains to answer also those who think that it was unfitting and unreasonable for God to be clothed in a mortal body, to be subjected to human beings, to endure insults, and even to suffer torments and death. [Col. 1057B] I shall say what I think, and, as I can, compress a vast matter into a few words. One who teaches something ought, in my judgment, himself to do what he teaches, so that he may compel people to obey. For if he does not do so, he will deprive his precepts of authority. Examples, therefore, are necessary, so that the things commanded may have firmness; and if anyone should prove obstinate and say that they cannot be done, the teacher may refute that person by a present deed. Teaching, therefore, cannot be perfect when it is handed down only in words; but it is perfect when it is fulfilled in deeds.

Accordingly, since Christ was sent to humankind as a teacher of virtue, he certainly ought both to teach and to act, so that his teaching might be perfect. But if he had not assumed a human body, he could not have done what he taught; [Col. 1057C] that is, not to become angry, not to desire riches, not to be inflamed by lust, not to fear pain, to despise death. These indeed are virtues, but they cannot be practiced without flesh. Therefore he was embodied, so that, when he taught that the desires of the flesh must be conquered, he might himself act first, lest anyone should allege the frailty of the flesh as an excuse.

## Chapter LI. (Divine Institutes, Book IV, ch. 26.) On Christ’s death upon the cross.

I shall now speak of the mystery of the cross, lest perhaps someone [Col. 1058A] say: “If death had to be undertaken by him, it surely ought not to have been an infamous and shameful death, but one having something honorable about it.” I know indeed that many, because they shrink from the name of the cross, flee from the truth, although in it there are both great reason and power. For since he was sent for this purpose, to open the way of salvation to even the humblest persons, he made himself humble in order to free them. He therefore underwent that kind of death which is customarily inflicted on the lowly, so that all might be given the opportunity of imitation. Moreover, since he was to rise again, it was not permissible that a part of his body should be cut off or a bone broken, as happens to those who are executed by beheading. Therefore the cross was preferable, since it preserved his body with its bones intact for the resurrection.

This is further confirmed by the fact that, once he had undergone passion and death, he had to be exalted. So greatly did the cross exalt him, both in fact and in meaning, [Col. 1058B] that his majesty and power became known to all in the passion itself. For when he stretched out his hands on the cross, he surely extended his wings toward East and West, beneath which all nations from both regions of the world might gather for rest. How great is the efficacy of this sign, and what power it possesses, is evident, since every host of demons is expelled and put to flight by this sign. And just as before his passion he drove out demons by word and command, so now unclean spirits, when they have crept into human bodies, are driven out by the name and sign of that same passion, when, wrenched and tormented, confessing themselves to be demons, they yield to God who scourges them. What, then, can the Greeks have hoped from their religions and their wisdom, when they see that their gods—whom they do not deny to be those same demons—are triumphed over by the cross among humankind? [Col. 1058C]

## Chapter LII. (Divine Institutes, Book V, ch. 9.) The hope of human salvation in the acknowledgment of the true God, and the pagans’ hatred of Christians.

Therefore the one hope for humankind is life; the one harbor of salvation, the one refuge of freedom, is this: that, casting away the errors by which they were held, they open the eyes of their minds and acknowledge God, in whom alone is the dwelling-place [Col. 1059A] of truth; that they despise earthly things and things fashioned from the earth; that they regard philosophy, which is foolishness before God, as nothing; and that, having embraced true [Col. 1059A]

> [Note: [Col. 1059D] Various Notes on columns 1059–1060]
>
> “And true.” In the manuscript, “but true.”
>
> “But indeed.” In the manuscript, *Adenim*.
>

>
> “Can.” Heumann thinks it should read “may be able.”
>

>
> “Defense.” In the manuscript, the accusative.—“They defend.” Perhaps, following Heumann, one should read “they will defend.”
>

>

>

>

wisdom—that is, religion—they may become heirs of immortality.

But indeed they resist, not so much truth as their own salvation; and when they hear these things, they detest them as though they were some inexpiable crime. They do not even permit themselves to hear them; they think that their ears are violated by sacrilege if they hear them. Nor do they now refrain from abuse, but assail them with as many verbal insults as they can. And these same persons, if they obtain power, persecute them as public enemies—indeed, even more than enemies, whose penalty, when they have been defeated in war, is either death or slavery. Nor, after arms have been laid down, is any torture [inflicted], however much they may have deserved to suffer everything, upon those who wished [Col. 1059B] that piety should have a place amid swords.

Such cruelty toward innocence is unheard of; it does not deserve even the condition of enemies conquered in war. What is the cause of such great madness? Clearly, because they cannot contend by reason, they oppress by violence; and they condemn as most criminal persons those whose very innocence they have refused to establish, the cause being unknown. Nor do they think it enough if those whom they hate irrationally die a swift and simple death; instead, they tear them apart by elaborate tortures, in order to satisfy the hatred produced not by some wrongdoing but by truth. Truth is hateful to those who live badly because they cannot bear that there are some people to whom their deeds cannot be pleasing. They desire to extinguish these people by every means, so that they may be able to sin freely without a witness.

## Chapter LIII. (Divine Institutes, Book V, ch. 21.) The grounds of hatred toward Christians are examined and refuted.

But they say that they do these things in order to defend their gods. First, if the gods exist and possess any power and divinity, they do not need a human defense or patronage; they surely defend themselves. Or how can a human being hope for help from them, if they cannot avenge even their own injuries? To wish, therefore, to be defenders of the gods is foolish and vain; except that from this their distrust appears all the more clearly. For whoever undertakes the patronage of the God whom he worships confesses that he is nothing. But if he worships him because he considers him powerful, he ought not to wish to defend the one by whom he himself must be defended. [Col. 1059D]

We, therefore, act rightly. For when these defenders of false gods, rebels against the true God, persecute his name in us, we resist neither in deed nor in word; but mild, silent, and patient, we endure everything that cruelty can devise against us. For we have confidence in God, from whom we expect vengeance to follow immediately. Nor is this confidence empty: indeed, we have learned in part and see in part the miserable ends of all those who have dared this crime. No one has gone unpunished for injuring God; and whoever refused to learn by word who the true God is has learned it by his own punishment. [Col. 1060A]

[Col. 1060B] I should like to know, when they compel unwilling persons to sacrifice, what reason they have with themselves, or whom they benefit by what they do. If it is the gods, that is not worship, nor is a sacrifice acceptable that is made by the unwilling, extorted through wrong, extracted through pain. But if it is those whom they compel, it is certainly not a benefit which one would rather die than receive. If it is not good, to what do you call me? Why do you invite me to evil? Why not by words, but by blows? Why not by reason, but by bodily torments? From this it appears that the thing to which you do not entice a willing person, but drag an unwilling one, is evil. What folly it is to wish to give counsel to one unwilling! Or if someone, oppressed by evils, attempts to take refuge in death, can you, if you have snatched away his sword, broken his noose, drawn him back from a precipice, or poured out his poison, boast that you are that person’s savior, when he whom you think you have saved neither thanks you nor judges that you have acted well toward him, because [Col. 1060C] you have forbidden him the death he desired and have not allowed him to reach the end and repose of his evils? For a benefit must be assessed not by the nature of the thing but by the intention of the one who receives it. Why do you count as a benefit what is an injury to me? You want me to worship your gods, a thing that I regard as deadly to myself. If it is good, I do not begrudge it. Enjoy your good alone. There is no reason for you to wish to remedy my error, which I have adopted by judgment and choice. If it is evil, why do you drag me into a partnership in evil? Use your own lot. I prefer to die in good than to live in evil.

## Chapter LIV. On freedom of religion in the worship of God.

[Col. 1060D] These things can indeed be said justly. But who will hear them, [Col. 1061A] when frenzied and unrestrained people think that their own domination is diminished if anything in human affairs is free? Yet religion alone is that in which freedom has established its dwelling. For it is, above all things, voluntary; and no necessity can be imposed upon anyone to worship what that person does not wish. Someone may perhaps pretend, but cannot will. Finally, when some persons, through fear of tortures or overcome by torments, have consented to abominable sacrifices, they never do of their own accord what they did under compulsion. But when opportunity is again granted and freedom restored, they return to God and appease him with prayers and tears, repenting not of a will that they did not have, but of a necessity that they endured; and pardon is not denied to those who make satisfaction. What, then, does one accomplish who defiles the body [Col. 1061B] when he cannot change the will?

But people of empty minds, if they have compelled some brave person to pour a libation to their gods, exult with incredible joy and insolence, rejoicing as if they had sent an enemy beneath the yoke. But if someone, frightened neither by threats nor by tortures, has preferred faith to life, cruelty exerts its ingenuity upon that person, devising unspeakable and unbearable things. And because they know that death for God is glorious, and that this is victory for us—if, having overcome the torturers, we lay down our life for faith and religion—they too strive to conquer. They do not dispatch people by death; instead, they devise new and unheard-of tortures so that the frailty of the inward parts may yield to pain. And if it does not yield, they postpone matters and apply careful treatment to the wounds, so that repeated tortures may inflict more pain while the scars are still raw. While exercising this butchery against the innocent, they consider themselves devout, just, and religious—for their gods delight in such sacred rites—while calling the others impious and desperate. What perversity is this: that one tortured while innocent is called desperate and impious, whereas the executioner is called just and devout?

## Chapter LV. [Col. 1062A] Pagans defame as impiety the justice that consists in following God.

But they say that those who execrate the public religions handed down by their ancestors are rightly and deservedly punished. What if those ancestors were foolish in adopting vain religions, as we have already shown above? Will it be prescribed to us that we may not pursue what is true and better? Why do we take freedom away from ourselves and, as though enslaved, serve the errors of others? Let it be permitted to be wise; let it be permitted to seek truth. Yet if they wish to defend the foolishness of their ancestors, why do the Egyptians go unpunished, although they worship cattle [Col. 1062B] and beasts of every kind as gods? Why are mimes performed even about the gods themselves, and why is a person honored who has ridiculed them more wittily? Why are philosophers heard who say either that there are no gods, or that, if there are, they care for nothing and do not look upon human affairs, or who argue that there is no providence at all governing the world?

But of all people, only those who follow God and truth are judged impious. Though justice and wisdom are the same thing, these people defame them under the charge either of impiety or of foolishness; and they do not perceive what it is that deceives them, when they give evil the name of good and good the name of evil. The foremost philosophers, however—especially Plato and Aristotle—have said much about justice, asserting and exalting it as a virtue with the highest praise because it renders to each person his own, because it preserves fairness in all things; and because, whereas the other virtues are, as it were, silent and enclosed within, justice alone is neither confined to itself alone nor hidden, but wholly projects outward and is inclined to do good, so that it may benefit as many persons as possible. As though justice ought to exist only in judges and in those established in some position of authority, and not in everyone.

[Col. 1063A]

Yet there is no human being, not even among the lowest and beggars, in whom justice cannot exist. But because they did not know what justice was, from where it flowed, or what work it had, they assigned that highest virtue—that is, the common good of all—to a few persons, and said that it seeks no private advantages but is concerned only for the benefits of others. Nor without reason did Carneades arise, a man of the highest talent and acuteness, to refute their argument and overthrow justice, which had no stable foundation—not because he thought justice ought to be condemned, but in order to show that its defenders were saying nothing certain or firm about justice.

## Chapter LVI. (formerly I.) (Divine Institutes, Book V, chs. 16 and 17.) [Col. 1063B] On justice, which is the worship of the true God.

For if justice is the worship of the true God—for what is so just with respect to equity, so devout with respect to honor, so necessary with respect to salvation, as to acknowledge God as parent, venerate him as Lord, and obey his law and commands?—then the philosophers did not know justice, because they neither acknowledged God himself nor maintained his worship and law. Therefore they could be refuted by Carneades, whose argument was this: that there is no natural law; that all living beings, led by nature herself, defend their own advantages; and that justice, because it looks after the advantages of others and neglects its own, must therefore be called foolishness. But if all peoples in whose hands imperial power lies, and the Romans themselves, who have possessed the whole world, should wish to follow justice and restore to each person what they seized by force and arms, they would return to huts and poverty. But if they did this, they would indeed have to be judged just, but nevertheless foolish, because they endeavor to harm themselves in order to benefit others. [Col. 1064A]

Then, if someone finds a person who, through error, sells gold for brass or silver for lead, and necessity compels him to buy it, will he conceal the fact and buy it cheaply, or rather disclose it? If he discloses it, he will certainly be called just because he did not deceive the other; but he will at the same time be foolish, because he has produced gain for another and loss for himself. But it is easy to speak of loss. What if his life comes into danger, so that he must either kill or die: what will he do? It can happen that, after a shipwreck, he finds someone weak clinging to a plank; or that, fleeing after an army has been defeated, he finds someone wounded sitting on a horse. Will he cast the former from the plank or the latter from the horse so that he himself may escape? If he wishes to be just, he will not do so; but he will at the same time be judged foolish, because, while sparing another’s life, he betrays his own. If he does so, he will indeed seem wise because he looks after himself; but he will at the same time be evil because he harms another. [Col. 1064B]

## Chapter LVII. (Divine Institutes, Book III, chs. 17 and 18; V, chs. 15, 17, 18, and 19.) On wisdom and foolishness.

These arguments are certainly clever, but we can answer them most easily. For the similarity of the names makes this appear to be so. Justice has an appearance of foolishness, yet it is not foolishness; and wickedness has an appearance of wisdom, yet it is not wisdom. But just as this wickedness is intelligent and cunning [Col. 1065A] in preserving its own advantages,
This is [the passage], etc. I have restored this passage from the Turin and Bologna manuscripts and the two Royal manuscripts. The first Royal manuscript has: “This is the highest faith,” whence in the Bologna manuscript and Isaeus’s edition arose *fidissima* (“most faithful”). In the Regius-Puteanus manuscript *faith* is absent; in the Turin manuscript *justice* is absent. In the Revised Royal manuscript and the editions I read: “This is that most faithful [thing]”; the rest as in the text. Perhaps one should read “the summit of faith,” which approaches the *most faithful* and *most faith-filled* of the other codices.

“What they judge.” These two words are absent from the Turin manuscript.

“They judged.” The Turin manuscript alone has “they judge.”

“What it is.” Thus the three ancient manuscripts. The First Revised Royal manuscript, with the editions, has “what it may be.”

“Who is most just.” Thus the Bologna and Regius-Puteanus manuscripts. In the Turin manuscript: “who may be”; *may be* is wrongly repeated, since it immediately preceded. The First Revised Royal manuscript and editions have “who is most just.”

“Precious gifts.” Thus the three most ancient manuscripts and four editions, and Lactantius himself in Book II, chapter 4, and *On the Anger of God*, chapter 21. The Revised Royal manuscript and the other common editions have “present gifts”; wrongly.

“From whom, if hunger…” The Turin manuscript alone has “if hunger…”

“Is absent.” The Turin manuscript alone has “is present.”

[Col. 1065C] [Variorum Notes to cols. 1065–1066]

“Shrewd.” Some editions put “intelligent” in place of “and shrewd.” The following clause, “it appears to be refuted, because not …,” is textually incomplete or corrupt.

“And.” Absent from the edition and the Revised Royal manuscript, but present in the others.

“Is.” The Turin manuscript has “was.”

“Can.” Turin, Bologna, Regius-Puteanus, the First Revised Royal manuscript, and the editions have “will be able,” a reading preferred by O. F. Fritzsche.

“Thus neither …” The Turin, Bologna, and Regius-Puteanus manuscripts read as in the text. The Revised Royal manuscript and one edition read: “Therefore neither justice belongs to the foolish nor wisdom to the unjust. Therefore he is not foolish”; other editions, including Gallaeus’s, read: “Therefore neither justice can belong to the foolish nor wisdom to the unjust. Therefore the foolish person,” etc.

“They suppose.” The Turin manuscript has *aestimant* (“they judge”); the remaining manuscripts and editions, *existimant*.

“To live longer and more comfortably.” Correctly Isaeus and Spark, supported by Turin, Bologna, and five editions, which have *quod iustius* (“which [is] more just”) in place of *quo diutius* (“so that [we may live] longer”); Regius-Puteanus has *quod ius* by abbreviation; the other Revised Royal manuscript, the Paris 1525 edition, and Gryphius have *quo iustius*, an obvious error contrary to the sense. The passage should therefore be restored from Lactantius himself, *Divine Institutes* V.19: “For if after death we are nothing, it is surely the part of a most foolish person not to provide for this life, so that it may be as long as possible and full of every convenience; whoever does this must necessarily depart from the rule of justice. But if a better and longer life remains for a human being …” The Paris 1525, Gymnicus, Betuleius, Tornesius, and the margin of Plantin have *iucundius* (“more pleasantly”), as do Heumann’s manuscripts; I do not know whence this came, though it is nearly the same as *commodius*.

“Because.” Turin has “who”; the others, with the editions, have “because.”

“To prefer.” The First Revised Royal manuscript and editions have “to wish”; better, with Regius-Puteanus and Turin, “to prefer to die,” as in Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* V.

“To pour libations to the gods and depart unharmed.” Thus the Turin manuscript, the best reading; Regius-Puteanus supports it with “to free the god, but to depart unharmed.” This was mistakenly understood by a scribe hearing it as “than to pour libations to the gods and depart unharmed.” The other Revised Royal manuscript has “than he will say that a free woman departs unharmed,” with *dicet* wrongly understood for *dis et* (“to the gods, and”); editions read “although one may freely depart unharmed.” Compare above, ch. 54: “If they compel any brave person to pour libations to their gods.”

“Nevertheless.” Turin has “so”; the others and editions have “nevertheless.”

“Let them call [us] fools, provided that they themselves are the greatest fools,” etc. Thus Isaeus with Turin, Bologna, and Regius-Puteanus, except that *greatest* is absent in Turin. The Revised Royal manuscript and editions have “mark” for “call.”

“And.” The Revised Royal manuscript and editions have “from those,” corruptly; the other manuscripts have “and those.”

“Revered.” Turin has “adored.” “For worship.” Turin has “death for worship,” corruptly.

“Have not declined [tortures or death] for the worship and honour of the true God.” This is the reading of Bologna, the two Royal manuscripts, and the editions. Turin has “have not declined the God,” wrongly.

“This is,” etc. I restored this passage from the Turin, Bologna, and two Royal manuscripts. The first has “This is the highest faith,” whence *fidissima* (“most faithful”) arose in Bologna and Isaeus’s edition. *Faith* is absent in Regius-Puteanus; *justice* is absent in Turin. In the Revised Royal manuscript and the editions I read “This is that most faithful [thing]”; the remainder is as in the text. Perhaps one should read *fidei summa* (“the summit of faith”), which comes close to the *fidissima* and *fidelissima* of the other codices. [Col. 1066D]

“What the foolish judge.” These two words are absent in Turin.

“They judged.” Turin alone has “they judge.”

“What it is.” Thus the three ancient manuscripts; the First Revised Royal manuscript and editions have “what it may be.”

“Who is most just.” Thus Bologna and Regius-Puteanus. Turin has “who may be”; *may be* is wrongly repeated, having just preceded. The First Revised Royal manuscript and editions have “who is most just.”

“Precious gifts.” Thus the three most ancient manuscripts, four editions, and Lactantius himself, *Divine Institutes* II.4 and *On the Anger of God* 21. The Revised Royal manuscript and the remaining common editions have “present gifts,” wrongly.

“From whom, if hunger …” Turin alone has “if hunger …”

“Is absent.” Turin alone has “is present.”

…not wisdom, but cunning and craftiness; likewise justice ought not to be called foolishness, but innocence. For it is necessary both that the just person be wise and that one who is foolish be unjust. For neither reason nor nature itself permits one who is just not to be wise, since the just person certainly does nothing except what is right and good, and always avoids what is crooked and evil. But who can distinguish good from evil, crooked from right, unless he is wise? The foolish person acts badly because he does not know what good and evil are. Therefore he sins because he cannot distinguish crooked things from right ones. Thus neither justice can belong to the foolish person nor wisdom to the unjust person. Therefore he is not foolish who has not pushed a shipwrecked person from a plank or a wounded man from a horse, because [Col. 1065B] he has abstained from doing harm, which is a sin; but avoiding sin belongs to the wise person.

But the thing that makes him appear foolish at first sight is that they suppose the soul to perish with the body; consequently, they refer every advantage to this life. For if there is nothing after death, then surely he acts foolishly who spares another’s life at cost to his own, or who looks more to another’s profit than to his own. If death destroys the soul, effort must be made to live longer and more comfortably; but if an eternal and blessed life remains after death, the just and wise person will surely despise this bodily life together with all earthly goods, because he knows what [Col. 1065C] reward he is to receive from God.

[Col. 1066A] Let us therefore hold fast to innocence; let us hold fast to justice. Let us assume the appearance of foolishness, so that we may hold fast to true wisdom. Even though it seems absurd and foolish to men to prefer torture and death to pouring libations to the gods and departing unharmed, let us nevertheless strive, with every virtue and all patience, to show faithfulness to God. Let not death frighten us; let not pain break us, so that vigour of spirit and unshaken constancy may be preserved. Let them call us fools, provided that they themselves are the greatest fools—blind, dull, and equal to beasts—who do not understand that it is deadly, after abandoning the living God, to prostrate oneself and worship earthly things; who do not know both that eternal punishment awaits those who have revered senseless fabrications, and that those who have not declined tortures or death for the worship and honour of the true God will attain everlasting life. This is the highest faith; this [Col. 1066B] is true wisdom; this is perfect justice. It is of no concern to us what fools judge or what petty men think. We must await God’s judgment, so that afterward we may judge those who have judged us.

## CHAPTER LVIII, formerly II  
*(Divine Institutes*, Book VI, chapters 1 and 2.)  
### On the True Worship and Sacrifice of God

I have spoken of what justice is. It follows that I should show what God’s true sacrifice is, what the most just rite of worship is, lest anyone suppose that victims, fragrances, or precious gifts are desired by God—from whom, if hunger, thirst, [Col. 1066C] cold, and desire for all earthly things are absent, it follows that [Col. 1067A] he has no use for these [Col. 1065A] or for any of the things brought into temples and offered to gods made of clay. Rather, as bodily things are appropriate for bodily beings, so an incorporeal sacrifice is surely necessary for the incorporeal being.

God himself has no need of those things which he has granted for human use, since the whole earth is in his power. He has no need of a temple, whose dwelling is the world; no need of an image, since he is incomprehensible both to eyes and to mind; no need of earthly lights, since he was able to kindle the sun and the other stars for human use. What, then, does God desire from a human being except the worship of the mind, which is pure and holy? For the things made by fingers or existing outside a human being are worthless, fragile, and unacceptable. This is the true sacrifice: not that which is brought forth from a chest, but that which is brought forth from the heart; not that which is offered by hand, but that which is poured out by the mind. This is the acceptable victim which the soul sacrifices from itself.

For what do victims, incense, garments, silver, gold, and precious stones contribute if the worshipper’s mind is not pure? Therefore justice alone is what God requires. In it are sacrifice and the worship of God; and I must now discuss it and teach in what works justice must necessarily consist.

[Col. 1067C] [Variorum Notes to cols. 1067–1068]

“And to the gods.” The three ancient manuscripts have this; the Revised Royal manuscript and editions have “and to other [beings].”

“Bodily.” The Revised Royal manuscript and editions have the singular “bodily [thing].” “For the incorporeal [being].” They read “for incorporeal [beings], [an] incorporeal [thing].”

“Since the whole earth is in his power.” Thus Bologna, Regius-Puteanus, Fasitus, Isaeus, and Spark; Turin has *under* for *in*. This is much more apt and concise than “And the whole earth is under his power,” found in the Revised Royal manuscript and many editions.

“Human being.” The Revised Royal manuscript and editions have “human beings.” “For human use.” The editions from 1478–1698 and Cellarius have “for the use of human beings”; Turin, followed by editions, rightly has “for human use.” Compare *Divine Institutes* VI.2, “who gave so clear, so bright a light for human use,” and *On the Anger of God* 13, from Reimmann’s manuscripts, “made by God for human use.” (Bunemann.)

“Worthless, fragile, unacceptable.” These four words are absent from the Revised Royal manuscript and editions.

“From itself.” Turin has simply “itself.”

“Sacrifices.” The Royal manuscripts and editions have this; Turin has “will have sacrificed.”

“Both.” Turin, Bologna, Regius-Puteanus, and Isaeus have *utrique* (“both”); the First Revised Royal manuscript and many editions have *utique* (“certainly”), which follows immediately.

“Because they referred them only to the advantages of this life.” The Revised Royal manuscript and editions have “because they referred them to the advantage of this life alone”; Isaeus, with Turin and Bologna, has the text.

“One [path] of life.” Absent from Turin.

“Must be held.” The three ancient manuscripts read this; the Revised Royal manuscript and editions read “must be revered by us.”

“As a parent.” Davisius reasonably thinks these words should be deleted, though Clericus, *Bibliothèque ancienne et moderne* XI, reads “as present.”

“For he is the same one who begot us.” The Revised Royal manuscript and five editions have “He is the one who begot us”; not badly.

“And power over life and death.” In antiquity paternal power at Rome was supreme, so that a father had no less right of life and death over children than masters over slaves (Digest, book II, *On His Own and Legitimate Heirs*; final law of the Code, *On Paternal Power*; Theodosian Code, book II, *On Cases Concerning Free Persons*). Sopater on Hermogenes; Simplicius, commentary on Epictetus’s *Enchiridion*. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, II, treats this more exactly; add Dio Chrysostom, Oration 14. This paternal right passed from Attic law to Rome: Solon at Athens enacted a law *περὶ τῶν ἀκρίτων* (“concerning those not judicially tried”), permitting a parent to kill his son, as Sextus Empiricus reports, *Pyrrhonian Outlines* III. Children under paternal power differed little from slaves. Hence Libanius, *Declamations* 37: *Κύριοι τῶν παίδων οἱ γονεῖς οὐχ ἧττον ἢ τῶν οἰκετῶν*—“Parents are masters of their children no less than of their household slaves.” Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* IV.3: “That the same person is lord who is father is shown even by civil law. For who can rear children unless he has a master’s power over them?” And shortly after: “Therefore he who is a son is a slave; he who is a father is likewise a master.” Seneca the Elder, *Controversiae* III.19: “While parents live, a son in the household can be subject to no one but his father; he is free from every other servitude.” Thus, just as a slave acquired everything for his master, so under the most ancient law—that is, while the republic flourished—a son acquired everything for his father (Dionysius of Halicarnassus VIII; Philo, *On the Decalogue*). But that paternal majesty, as Valerius Maximus VII.7.5 and Quintilian, *Declamations* 375 call it, or supreme paternal power, was greatly curtailed by later legislation. To place, as it were, a curb upon parental anger, legislators fixed it a definite limit (final law, Code *On paternal power*). Thus today a father may not kill an unheard son (Digest II, *On the Cornelian law concerning assassins*; V, *On the Pompeian law concerning parricide*), except where a son plots against the safety of the state (Digest XXXV, *On religious matters and funeral expenses*). (Oiselius.)

“Both.” Bunemann reports this reading. Isaeus had already observed from Bologna that *utrique* should be read and had correctly adopted it, though Gallaeus, Spark, and Cellarius did not follow him. That *utrique* is right is clear from *Divine Institutes* VI.3. Pfaff and Walch therefore read *utique* less correctly; Davisius and Heumann rightly read *utrique*. (Bunemann.)

## CHAPTER LIX, formerly III, otherwise II  
*(Divine Institutes*, Book V, chapter 5 ff. and 19; Book VI, chapters 3, 4, 9, 10.)  
### On the Ways of Life and the Earliest Times of the World

That there are two paths of human life was unknown neither to philosophers nor to poets, but each group represented them differently. The philosophers held that one was the way of industry and the other of idleness; but this was less correct, because they referred them only to the advantages of this life. The poets did better in saying that one is the way of the just and the other the way of the impious. Yet they err in saying that these paths exist not in this life but among the dead. We speak more correctly: we say that one path is that of life and the other that of death, and that these paths are nevertheless here. But the path to the right, on which the just walk, leads not to Elysium but to heaven, for they become immortal. The more leftward path leads to Tartarus, for the unjust are condemned to eternal torments.

We must therefore hold to the path of justice, which leads to life. The first duty of justice is to acknowledge God as parent, to fear him as lord, and to love him as father. For he who begot us is the same one who gave us life by his vital spirit, nourishes us, and preserves us. Over us he has authority not only as a father but also as a master: the right to punish and power over life and death. Therefore a double honour is owed to him by humankind: love together with fear.

The second duty of justice is to acknowledge a human being as a brother. For if the same God made us and brought all people forth, on equal terms, for justice and eternal life, we are surely united by the bond of brotherhood; whoever does not acknowledge this is unjust. But the origin of this evil, by which fellowship among human beings and the bond of kinship were dissolved, arises from ignorance of the true God. For one who does not know that fountain of kindness cannot in any way be good.

Hence, from the time when many gods began to be consecrated and worshipped by human beings, justice was banished, as the poets relate. Thus every covenant was severed, and the fellowship of human law was broken apart. Then each person began to provide for himself, to reckon right by strength, to harm one another, to attack by fraud, to ensnare by deceit, to increase one’s own advantages by the disadvantages of others; to spare neither relatives, children, nor parents; to prepare poisoned drinks for the death of people, to beset roads with the sword, to infest the seas, and to give free rein to lust wherever madness might lead. In short, nothing was held sacred that accursed desire did not violate.

When these things were happening, people established laws for themselves for the common advantage, so that meanwhile they might secure themselves against injuries. But fear of the laws did not restrain crimes; it merely curtailed the freedom to commit them. For laws could punish offences, but they could not fortify conscience. Thus what had formerly been done openly began to be done secretly. Laws themselves were also circumvented, since the very guardians of the laws, corrupted by rewards and gifts, sold judgments either for the acquittal of the wicked or for the ruin of the good. To these were added dissensions, wars, mutual plundering, and a licence to rage, taken up when the laws had been overthrown.
