## CHAPTER LX  
*(Divine Institutes*, Book VI, chapter 3.)  
### On the Duties of Justice

While human affairs stood in this condition, God took pity on us, revealed himself to us, and made himself known, so that in him we might learn religion, faith, chastity, and mercy; so that, having cast off the error of our former life, we might together with God come to know ourselves, whom impiety had divided from one another; and that, as the Lord himself handed it down, we might receive the divine law—a law which joins human things with heavenly things—by which all the errors in which we had been entangled might be removed together with vain and impious superstitions.

What we owe to a human being, that same divine law prescribes; it teaches that whatever you render to a human being is rendered to God. But the root of justice and the entire foundation of equity is this: do not do to anyone what you would not wish to suffer; rather, measure another’s mind by your own. If it is bitter to endure an injury, and the person who inflicted it seems unjust, transfer to another’s person what you feel concerning yourself, and to your own person what you judge concerning another; and you will understand that you act as unjustly if you harm another as another does if he harms you.

If we turn these things over in our minds, we shall preserve innocence, in which justice stands, as it were, on its first step. For the first requirement is not to harm; the next is to help. And just as, in uncultivated fields, before you begin to sow, the land must be cleared by pulling up brambles and cutting away every root of shrubs, so first vices must be removed from our souls, and only then must virtues be planted, from which, sown through the word of God, the fruits of immortality may arise.

## CHAPTER LXI  
*(Divine Institutes*, Book VI, chapters 15, 16, 19, 24.)  
### On the Passions

There are three passions—or, so to speak, three Furies—which stir such great disturbances in human minds and sometimes compel people to sin so greatly that they permit them to have regard neither for reputation nor for their own danger: anger, which desires vengeance; avarice, which desires wealth; and lust, which seeks pleasures. Above all, these vices must be resisted; these roots must be torn out so that virtues may be planted.

The Stoics think that these passions should be cut off; the Peripatetics, that they should be moderated. Neither is correct: they cannot be wholly removed, since implanted by nature they possess a definite and important rationale; nor should they be diminished, because, if they are evil, even moderate and restrained forms must be avoided; if good, they should be used in their full strength. But we say that they should neither be removed nor diminished. For things which God has rationally implanted in human beings are not evil in themselves; rather, since they are naturally good, because they have been assigned for the preservation of life, they become evil through bad use. Just as courage is good if you fight for your country but evil if you fight against it, so also passions, if directed toward good uses, will be virtues; if toward evil, they will be called vices.

Anger, then, has been given by God for the correction of sinners—that is, for maintaining the discipline of subjects—so that fear may restrain licence and check audacity. But those who do not know its limits become angry with their equals, or even with their superiors. From this people leap forth into monstrous crimes; from this they rise to slaughter and to wars. Desire too has been granted for seeking and acquiring the necessities of life. But those who do not know its limits strive insatiably to heap up wealth. Hence come poisons, frauds, forged wills, and every kind of deception. The passion of lust, moreover, is implanted and inborn for the procreation of children; but those who do not keep its limits in mind use it solely for pleasure. Hence come illicit loves, adulteries, sexual violations, and every kind of corruption. These passions must therefore be brought back within their proper bounds and directed into the straight path, in which, however vehement they may be, they cannot incur blame.

## CHAPTER LXII, formerly V  
*(Institutes*, Book VI, chapters 12, 18, 20, 23.)  
### On Restraining the Pleasures of the Senses

Anger must be restrained when we suffer injury, both so that the evil threatening from conflict may be checked and so that we may retain the two greatest virtues, innocence and patience. Avarice must be broken when we possess what is enough. For what madness it is to labour at heaping up things which must necessarily pass to others through robbery, proscription, or death! Lust must not roam beyond the lawful marriage-bed, but must serve the begetting of children. For excessive desire for pleasure produces danger, generates disgrace, and—what must most be avoided—obtains eternal death.

Nothing is so hateful to God as an incestuous mind and an impure soul. Nor should anyone think that one must abstain only from that pleasure which is taken from union with a woman’s body, but also from the other pleasures of the remaining senses; for they too are vicious, and it belongs to the same virtue to despise them. The pleasure of the eyes is derived from the beauty of things; that of the ears, from melodious and sweet voices,

“Is poured forth in blood.” Bunemann prefers “is drenched in blood,” defending it thus: “The Latin writers do not speak in that way; therefore read with Bologna and the editions, ‘is drenched in blood.’ *Divine Institutes* VI.20: ‘Let no blood drench the conscience’; VII.1: ‘drenched in holy blood’; Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I.157, ‘the earth drenched with blood’; Tacitus, *Agricola* 45, ‘Senecio drenched us with innocent blood.’ To pour forth blood is to shed it.” (Bunemann.)
of the nostrils by a pleasant smell, of taste by sweet foods. Against all these things virtue must firmly contend, lest the mind, ensnared by these allurements, be cast down from heavenly to earthly things, from eternal to temporal things, from immortal life to everlasting punishment. In the pleasures of taste and smell there is this danger: that they can draw one into luxury. For whoever is devoted to them will either possess no household property at all, or, if he has any, will consume it and afterwards lead a detestable life. But whoever is carried away by hearing—to say nothing of songs, which so often soothe the innermost feelings that they even disturb the settled state of the mind with frenzy, by composed set speeches and rhythmic verses [Col. 1073B], or by ingenious disputations—is readily led over to impious worship. Hence it is that people do not readily believe the heavenly writings, because they appear unadorned—those, that is, who are themselves eloquent or prefer reading eloquent works. They seek not what is true but what is sweet; indeed, those things seem truest to them which flatter their ears. Thus they reject truth while being captivated by sweetness of expression.

The pleasure which concerns sight, however, has many forms. For that which is received from the beauty of precious objects incites avarice, which ought to be alien to a wise and just person; while that which is taken from the appearance of women carries one away into the other pleasure of which we have already spoken above [Col. 1074A].

## CHAPTER LXIII, formerly VI.  
*(Divine Institutions, Book VI, chapters 18 and 20.)*  
**Spectacles are exceedingly powerful in corrupting minds.**

It remains to speak of spectacles. Since these are more powerful in corrupting minds, they must be avoided and wholly shunned by the wise, because they are said to have been devised for celebrating the honors of the gods. For the presentation of gladiatorial shows belongs to the festivals of Saturn. The stage belongs to Father Liber. The Circus Games, moreover, are thought to have been dedicated to Neptune; thus anyone who attends spectacles seems, having abandoned the worship of God, to have passed over to profane rites.

But I prefer to speak of the matter rather than of its origin. What is so horrible, so dreadful, as the slaughter of a human being? For this reason our life is protected by the sternest laws; for this reason wars are detestable. Yet custom found a way in which it could commit homicide without war and without laws, and pleasure claimed for itself what was a crime. But if attendance at a homicide entails consciousness of guilt, and the spectator is bound by the same crime as its perpetrator, then in these slaughters of gladiators the man who watches is no less drenched in blood than the man who acts; nor can he be free from blood who wished it to be shed, or be regarded as not having killed when he both favored the killer [Col. 1074B] and demanded his reward.

[Col. 1075A]  
[Note: [Col. 1075C] *Various Notes on columns 1075–1076*]

**Favored (*favit*).** The printed editions have *favet*.

**Of actors (*histrionum*).** Thus the Turin and Regio-Putian manuscripts. But the recently collated Royal manuscript and the printed editions have *histrionici* (“theatrical”).

**“For mime,” etc.** Thus I have emended it from the Regio-Putian and Bolognese manuscripts and the Cambridge and Cellarius editions. In the Turin manuscript and Walch edition: “Nor less”; in the recently collated Royal manuscript: “Not less”; in the Cratander and Gryphius editions: “Or not less”—incorrectly. Six editions read: “Or is not the mime the school of corruptions?” The Juntine edition comes closer to the reading which I have restored, reading thus: “Or is not the mime the school of corruptions?” Lactantius has the same sense in Book VI, chapter 20: “What shall I say of mimes, displaying the instruction of corruptions?”

**“In which are done.”** Thus nearly all printed editions with the manuscripts, and rightly so; for it refers to *mimus* (“mime”). The new Paris edition and Walch have *in qua* (“in which [feminine]”), incorrectly.

**Shameful things (*pudenda*).** Thus the Turin and Regio-Putian manuscripts. But the printed editions, with the recently collated Royal manuscript, read: “things which are not.”

[Col. 1075D]

**Circus.** The recently collated Royal manuscript and printed editions read *non* in place of *vero*. Moreover, the circus is so called because it is built in a circle for spectacles, where games are held; and because there the procession is carried around the turning-posts and the horses run in a circuit, as Varro says in *On the Latin Language*, Book IV.

**And.** The recently collated Royal manuscript and editions read *nec non et*.

**Soothed (*deliniti*).** The Turin and Regio-Putian manuscripts have *deleniti*.

**Snares (*laqueos*).** The Turin manuscript alone has *plagas* (“traps”); the others have *laqueos*.—“May we fall into the snares of death.” The editions have *in laqueos*, as in Book II, chapter 1: “They run into the snares of death”; Book IV, chapter 26: “They run into the snares of eternal death”; Book IV, chapter 30: “Lest we should ever fall into the snares and deceits of the adversary.” In favor of the Turin reading are Book III, chapter 1: “They brought themselves into traps . . .”; and Book II, chapter 16: “They lay traps.” BUN.

**May please (*placeat*).** Thus I have restored it from the manuscripts. The editions have *placet*.

**Having overcome (*superatis*).** The recently collated Royal manuscript and editions have *suppositis*; the others agree with the text.

**“The task is easy for him who is a follower of God.”** The words *ei, qui sit* (“for him who is”) are not read in the Turin manuscript. Perhaps it should be punctuated thus: “The task is easy: the follower of God and truth will never curse” [Col. 1076B]. The Anonymous Briton, with Heumann’s approval: “the task is easy for the follower of God and truth.” BUN.

**Has hoped (*speravit*).** The recently collated Royal manuscript has *spectabit*; the editions, *expectabit*.

**“He will not swear falsely.”** Thus the Turin and Regio-Putian manuscripts. But the Bolognese manuscript has *hic pejerabit*; the recently collated Royal manuscript, *hinc jurabit*; six editions, *hinc vitabit*. Deuteronomy V; Matthew V; 1 Timothy I.

**“But he will not even swear,” etc.** I grant, rashly and vainly. Yet in a necessary matter he will swear, as St. Paul teaches in Hebrews 6:16. True oaths, necessary oaths, concerning a matter of great importance, and required by a magistrate in order that an end may be imposed upon every dispute, are altogether lawful, as is clear from many passages of Scripture and examples of saints who swore; this could be proved at length if that were now the purpose of our undertaking. See Acts 2:30, where it is said that God Himself swore to David; Revelation 10:6, where the angel swears by Him who lives for ages of ages. St. Paul also, Second Epistle to the Corinthians 1:23; Matthew V; James V.

**Had pledged (*spoponderit*).** But the Turin manuscript has *sponderit*, incorrectly.

**“Himself and his own.”** The Bolognese and recently collated Royal manuscripts and editions read *de suo* in place of *se suoque*, which is found in the Turin and Regio-Putian manuscripts.

**“Money at interest.”** Thus the Regio-Putian manuscript. The Turin manuscript has *in usu*; the recently collated Royal manuscript and editions, *in usura*. See above, Book I, chapter 15, and Book VI, chapter 18; Psalm XIV; Ezekiel XVIII.

**“From the evils of others.”** Absent from the Turin manuscript.

**To seek (*captare*).** Thus the manuscripts and editions except the Turin manuscript, which has *capere*. Deuteronomy XV; Matthew V; Luke VI.

**“If anyone.”** Thus the Regio-Putian manuscript. But the Turin manuscript has *si qui si quem*; the editions, *siquidem*.

**May be (*sit*).** Thus the recently collated Royal manuscript; but the editions have *erit* in place of *sit*, which is found in the Turin, Regio-Putian, and Bolognese manuscripts.

**Will deal (*aget*).** But the Regio-Putian and Bolognese manuscripts have *agat*. See what precedes and follows. Ecclesiasticus VII and XXXIII; Ephesians VI.

**Will wish (*volet*).** The recently collated Royal manuscript and editions have *vellet*. The Turin and Regio-Putian manuscripts have *volet*.

**Will receive (*accipiet*).** The recently collated Royal manuscript and editions have *recipiet*. The Regio-Putian and Bolognese manuscripts have *accipiat*.

**Is vindicated (*vindicatur*).** Thus the Turin and Regio-Putian manuscripts. The editions have *jubetur*; the Bolognese manuscript and editions, *vindicetur*; the recently collated Royal manuscript, *videretur*—corruptly, as is clear.

**“But by this.”** Thus I have restored it from the Bolognese manuscript and three editions; the editions have *sed nec* in place of *sed hac*. See below, “but by this precept.”

What of the stage? Is it any holier? On it comedy tells stories of seductions and loves, tragedy of incest and parricides. The shameless gestures of actors also, by which they imitate infamous women, teach the lusts which they express in dancing. For mime is a school of corruptions, in which shameful things are enacted in imitation, so that real shameful things may be done without shame. Young people watch these things, and their slippery age—which ought to be restrained and governed—is schooled by these representations in vices and sins.

The Circus is considered more innocent; but here the madness is greater. For the minds of the spectators are so carried away by frenzy that they often rise up not merely to abuse but even to quarrels, fights, and conflicts. Therefore all spectacles must be avoided, so that we may be able to maintain a tranquil state of mind [Col. 1075B]. Harmful pleasures must be renounced, lest, soothed by their deadly sweetness, we fall into the snares of death.

## CHAPTER LXIV.  
*(Institutions, Book VI, chapter 18.)*  
**The passions must be subdued, and forbidden things abstained from.**

Let virtue alone please us, whose reward is immortality when it has overcome pleasure. But once the passions have been overcome [Col. 1076A] and pleasures thoroughly subdued, the task of restraining the rest is easy for one who is a follower of God and truth. He who has hoped for blessing from God will never curse. He will not swear falsely; indeed, he will not even swear, lest at some time, through necessity or habit, he fall into perjury. He will say nothing deceitfully, nothing dissemblingly; he will neither deny what he has pledged nor promise what he cannot do. He will envy no one, being content with himself and what is his; nor will he slander another or wish another ill, upon whom perhaps God’s benefits are more lavishly bestowed. He will not steal, nor desire anything whatever belonging to another. He will not lend money at interest—for that is to seek profit from the evils of others—yet neither will he refuse a loan if someone is compelled by necessity to borrow. Let him not be harsh toward son or slave; let him remember that he too has a father and a master. Thus [Col. 1076B] he will deal with them as he would wish to be dealt with himself. He will not accept excessive gifts from the poorer, for it is not just that the estates of the rich should be enlarged through the losses of the wretched.

There is an ancient commandment: not to kill. This must not be understood as though we were commanded merely to keep our hands from homicide, which is also punished by public laws. But with this command inserted, it will not even be lawful to inflict danger by a word [Col. 1077A].

[Col. 1077A]  
[Note: [Col. 1077B] *Various Notes on columns 1077–1078*]

**To inflict (*inferre*).** I have restored from the Turin, Bolognese, Regio-Putian, and Bodleian manuscripts and four editions: “to inflict danger of death.” In the others, *mortis* is absent.—“To inflict danger.” The Turin manuscript reads: “to inflict danger of death” [Col. 1077C]; the Bolognese manuscript also has this, followed by Isaeus, Galland, Spark, and Cellarius. Heumann errs when he writes that *mortis* is omitted in the Turin manuscript. BUN.

**We are forbidden (*prohibemur*).** The Regio-Putian, Turin, and Bolognese manuscripts. The editions have *prohibetur*.

**“For if false testimony by a lie harms the person against whom it is spoken, and deceives the person before whom it is spoken.”** Thus I have restored it from the Bolognese and two Royal manuscripts. The editions read somewhat differently: “if a lie harms the person against whom it is spoken,” etc. In the Turin manuscript these words are absent: “and deceives the person before whom it is spoken.”

**“Therefore one must never lie.”** All have maintained that one must not lie where the lie is harmful or idle. But where it is serviceable, Origen, following Plato in Book III of the *Republic*, whose words Clement of Alexandria reports in *Stromata*, Book VI, thought that lying was permitted; and later Chrysostom, at the end of Book I *On the Priesthood*; Cassian, *Conferences*, Book XVII, chapter 17 and following; Jerome, in his commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians. The Catholic truth is that taught here by Lactantius and by St. Augustine in his book *On Lying*. The text in the chapter *Super eo*, title *De usuris*, the Master, and all theologians in Book III, Distinction 38, hold that one must never lie; and the doctors cited above answer the authorities of the Fathers who hold a contrary opinion. IS.—See above, note on chapter 18, Book VI of the *Divine Institutions*. Exodus XX; Deuteronomy V.

**“Therefore he is not a just man,” etc.** Thus the manuscripts, except that in the Bolognese manuscript *non est* does not occur immediately before *etiam*. The editions: “He is not a just man who, not without harm, lies in vicious speech.” Ecclesiasticus VII; Psalm V; 1 Timothy III.

**For this man (*huic*).** Thus the oldest manuscripts. But the recently collated Royal manuscript and editions have *hinc*.

**Will preserve (*custodiet*).** Thus the most ancient manuscripts. But the recently collated Royal manuscript and editions have *custodiat*.

**Unpleasant (*insuavis*).** Thus also Book V, chapter 1, and *On the Anger of God*, chapter 20.

**“Equipped for inflicting.”** Thus the recently collated Royal manuscript; but the Turin manuscript [Col. 1078B] has “for bearing,” and the Regio-Putian manuscript, “equipped for inflicting.”

**“Affection,” through “gave.”** Absent from the Turin manuscript.

**Fashioned (*ficti*).** The Royal manuscript and editions have *facti* (“made”).—*Ficti.* These words are often confused in Lactantius, as I have often noted; see, for example, Book II of the *Institutions*, chapter 10, in the note. Here, with Davisius and Heumann, I prefer *ficti*, because it is repeated from Book VI of the *Institutions*, chapter 10: “God fashioned [*finxit*] him, man”; and below, “he was fashioned by God”; *Epitome*, chapter 67: “in fashioning man.” BUN.

**Always. Therefore.** It would be better to read *semper ergo* without any separation, and to put a stop before *semper*.

**“In receiving.”** The recently collated Royal manuscript and editions have *recipiendisque*.

**“Many.”** The recently collated Royal manuscript and editions have *in multis*.

**“Our.”** It does not occur in the Turin manuscript.

**Hope (*spera*).** The editions: “Hope that what happens to another may happen to you.”

**“Your help.”** Thus the Bolognese and Regio-Putian manuscripts. But the editions have *opem tunc*; one recently collated Royal manuscript, *opem tamen*; the Turin manuscript, *operam*.

**“Let us share” (*impertiamur*).** Thus the Regio-Putian and Bolognese manuscripts and seven editions. But the Turin manuscript has *impertiamus*. Heumann considers the latter reading good, because Lactantius elsewhere reads *impertit*.—Yet Bunemann reads *impertiamus* and gives the following note.—**“Let us share” (*impertiamus*).** Davisius rightly prefers this ending from the Turin manuscript because of the elegant homoeoteleuton: *impertiamus, vestiamus, eruamus* (“let us share, clothe, rescue”). Among the editions Gymnicus alone gave it thus; afterwards Davisius and Heumann. BUN.

**“If . . . let us clothe.”** It is absent from seven editions and from the Turin and recently collated Royal manuscripts.—“If anyone is naked . . . let us clothe [him].” These words are supplied from the Bolognese manuscript. Thomas, Isaeus, Galland, Spark, and Cellarius had already added them correctly. But where the Bolognese manuscript and editions have *occurrerit* (“should encounter”), Davisius would prefer the present *occurrit*, as in *indiget . . . sustinet* (“is in need . . . suffers”). BUNEMANN.

**“If anyone.”** Absent from the Turin manuscript. Ecclesiasticus IV; Job XXXI; James I.

**“A great,” etc.** Many editions: “It is the work of a great-souled man also to visit and cherish poor sick persons.” All manuscripts and six editions agree with the text. The Turin manuscript adds *item* after *aegros*. Ecclesiasticus VII; Matthew XXV; 1 Thessalonians V.

**“Or strangers.”** Thus the old manuscripts. In place of *advenas* (“strangers”), the editions have *pauperes* (“the poor”). Tobit I.

Nor may one kill or expose an infant, nor condemn oneself by voluntary death. Likewise, one must not commit adultery. But by this command we are forbidden not only to corrupt another’s marriage, which is condemned even by the common law of nations, but are also commanded to abstain from prostituted bodies. For the law of God stands above laws; it forbids even those things which are considered lawful, in order that it may perfect justice. It likewise belongs to this law not to give false testimony, and this also extends more broadly. For if false testimony by a lie harms the person against whom it is spoken and deceives the person before whom it is spoken, one must therefore never lie, because a lie always either deceives or harms. Therefore he is not a just man who lies even without harm in idle speech. Nor is it permitted for such a man to flatter; for flattery is ruinous and deceptive [Col. 1077B]. Rather, he will preserve truth everywhere. Though it may be unpleasant for the present, nevertheless, when its fruit and usefulness have appeared, it will produce not hatred, as the poet says (*Terence, Andria*, Act I, scene 1), but gratitude.

## CHAPTER LXV, alternatively VII.  
*(Institutions, Book VI, chapter 10 and following.)*  
**Precepts concerning what is commanded, and concerning mercy.**

I have spoken of the things which are forbidden; now I shall briefly speak of those which are commanded. Mercy is next to innocence. For innocence does no evil; mercy performs good. Innocence [Col. 1078A] begins justice; mercy completes it. Since human nature is weaker than that of the other living creatures, which God fashioned both equipped to inflict force and protected to repel force, He gave us the feeling of mercy, so that we might place every safeguard of our life in mutual assistance. For if, fashioned by one God and sprung from one man, we are united by the law of blood-relationship, we ought therefore to love every human being. Thus we ought not only not to inflict injury, but not even to avenge an injury inflicted, so that innocence may be perfect within us. And therefore God commands us always to pray even for our enemies. We ought therefore to be a communal and mutually sharing creature, so that we may fortify one another by giving and receiving help. For our frailty is subject to many accidents and misfortunes. Hope [Col. 1078B] that what you see has happened to another can happen to you as well.

Only then will you be stirred to bring help, if you take on the disposition of a person who, placed amid evils, implores your aid. If anyone is in need of food, let us share with him; if anyone naked meets us, let us clothe him; if anyone suffers injury from one more powerful, let us rescue him. Let our home stand open to strangers or those in need of shelter. Let not our defense be lacking to orphans, nor our protection to widows. To redeem captives from an enemy is a great work of mercy; to visit and restore poor sick persons is likewise such a work. Let us not allow the destitute or strangers, if they die, to lie unburied [Col. 1079A]. These are the works, these the duties of mercy; whoever performs them [Col. 1079A]

[Note: [Col. 1079C] *Various Notes on columns 1079–1080*]

**Dies (*obierit*).** The editions have *perfecerit* (“has accomplished”).

**More acceptable (*litabilior*).** Two Royal manuscripts have *letabilior*, and an ancient hand thus corrected the Turin manuscript. The other manuscripts and all editions have *litabilior*. Thus, “an acceptable victim,” above in Book I of the *Divine Institutions*, chapter 21, about the middle.

**Of a beast (*pecudis*).** But the recently collated Royal manuscript and editions have *pecudum*. The old manuscripts have *pecudis*.

**“By His own law and condition,” etc.** The editions with the Turin manuscript: “by His own law and condition”; the Regio-Putian and Bolognese manuscripts, with the Isaeus edition, agree with the text.

**Of him (*ejus*).** Thus the oldest Turin and Regio-Putian manuscripts. But the recently collated Royal manuscript and editions have *ei*.

**“Where neither thief.”** Thus the manuscript codices. But the editions have: “a thief will not dig through.” Matthew VI; Luke XII; 1 Timothy VI.

**May consume (*consumat*).** The editions have *consumet*.

**May snatch away (*eripiat*).** The editions read *eripiet*.

[Col. 1079D]

**May be preserved (*servetur*).** Thus all manuscript codices; but the editions have *servabitur*.

**By religion (*religione*).** Thus all manuscripts; but the editions have *religionem*.

**Greater (*potior*).** But the recently collated Royal manuscript and editions have *potentior*.

**Than (*quam*).** Absent from the Turin manuscript.

**To apostatize (*desciscere*).** The recently collated Royal manuscript and editions have *discedere*. All the ancient witnesses have *desciscere*.

**Inner (*interno*). Eternal.** Thus an ancient hand corrected the Turin manuscript.

**Pain (*dolorem*).** But the editions have *dolor*; the manuscripts have *dolorem*.

**May overcome (*superemus*).** The editions have *superentur*; the Turin manuscript correctly has *superemus*; the Regio-Putian manuscript, *superabit*.

**“Or of burning.”** Absent from the Turin manuscript.

**All things (*universa*).** Absent from seven editions and the recently collated Royal manuscript.

**Of cruelty (*crudelitatis*).** The editions with the recently collated Royal manuscript have *dominationis* (“of domination”) in place of *crudelitatis*.

**“Since we know.”** The Regio-Putian and Turin manuscripts have *cum*; three have *sciamus*. The editions have *ut qui* in place of *cum*.

**May be (*simus*).** I follow the Turin manuscript. All editions have *sumus*. In two Royal manuscripts, the Bolognese manuscript, and the Isaeus edition: *sumus futuri* (“we shall be”). In twelve editions is found *functuri*, also in Cicero, *prospere functus fortuna*, *On Clodius* 24.

**“Having triumphed . . . coming.”** Absent from the Turin manuscript. Here the Regio-Putian manuscript ends.

**Or (*aut*).** Absent from the editions.

**Chaste (*casti*).** Thus the Turin, Bolognese, and recently collated Royal manuscripts. But the editions have “let him keep his flesh chaste.”

**Of the bedchamber (*cubilis*).** But the Turin manuscript has *cubili*. “The pledges of a chaste and inviolate bedchamber,” that is, marital fidelity.

**Adulterer, etc.** I follow the Bolognese manuscript and six editions. In most editions: “For he is an adulterer before God, just as he is incestuous.” The recently collated Royal manuscript: “For he is an adulterer before God and through incest”; the Turin manuscript: “For he is before God and incestuous.”

**“That she may not desire another.”** I follow the ancient Bolognese manuscript, the Isaeus edition, and Latinius. The Turin and recently collated Royal manuscripts and editions have *ne aliud* (“that she may not desire another thing”).

**Because (*quoniam*).** Thus the Turin manuscript. In the Royal manuscript and editions: “by which God [joined] wife to husband”; Bolognese manuscript and Isaeus and Spark editions: *quia Deus* (“because God”). Perhaps read *qua*, as in the Gymnicus edition. Genesis II; Mark X.

**Convicted (*revictam*).** Thus the Turin and Bolognese manuscripts. But *devictam* occurs in nearly all editions. “So that never” is from the Bolognese manuscript and Isaeus edition; other witnesses have *et*.

**“This also is joined to perfect chastity.”** Davisius emends to *injungitur* (“is enjoined”). But Lactantius nowhere uses *injungere* in the sense of commanding; hence I would prefer *adjungitur*, that is, “is added.” For thus in the source from which this passage was abridged, Book VI, chapter 23. From the Bolognese manuscript: “These things are added: not only that adultery must be avoided, but also the thought.” BUN.

**May be absent (*absit*).** But the Turin manuscript has *obsit*.

**“Even by an empty desire.”** Thus the editions; Pfaffius thinks that *quavis inani cupiditate* (“by any empty desire whatever”) should be read. Compare Book VI, chapter 23. BUN.

**Plain (*manifestum*).** Thus the Bolognese manuscript and six editions. But the Turin manuscript has: “thus [it is fitting] that a just man neither do nor”; the recently collated Royal manuscript and seven editions: “And thus . . . who knows himself.”

will offer to God a true and welcome sacrifice. This is a more acceptable victim before God, who is pleased not by the blood of a beast but by human piety. Because God is just, He treats a person by His own law and by that person’s own condition: He has mercy on the person whom He sees to be merciful; He is inexorable toward the person whom He sees unmerciful toward those who entreat him. Therefore, in order that we may be able to do all these things which please God, money must be despised and treasures transferred to heaven, where neither thief may dig through, nor rust consume, nor tyrant snatch away; but where, with God as guardian, they may be preserved for us unto eternal abundance.

## CHAPTER LXVI, alternatively VIII.  
*(Institutions, Book VI, chapter 23.)*  
[Col. 1079B]  
**On faith in religion and fortitude.**

Faith too is a great part of justice; it must be especially preserved by us who bear the name of faith, particularly in religion, because God is prior to and greater than man. And if it is glorious to undergo death for friends, parents, or children—that is, for a human being—and if the person who has done this attains enduring memory and praise, how much more glorious is it to do so for God, who can grant eternal life in exchange for temporal death! Therefore, when a necessity of this kind arises, that we are compelled to apostatize from God and pass over to the rites of the nations, let no fear and no terror bend us from preserving the faith handed down to us. Let God be before our eyes; let Him be in our heart. By His inward aid [Col. 1080A], let us overcome the pain of our entrails and the tortures applied to the body. Then let us think of nothing but the rewards of immortal life. Thus, even if our limbs must be torn apart or burned, we shall easily endure all that the madness of tyrannical cruelty may devise against us. Finally, let us strive to undergo death itself not unwillingly or fearfully but gladly and without fear, knowing with what glory we shall be rewarded before God, coming to the promises after triumphing over the world; and let us weigh against those goods, against such great blessedness, these brief evils of punishments and the losses of this life. But if the opportunity for this glory is lacking, faith will have its reward even in peace.

Let it therefore be maintained in every duty of life; let it be maintained in marriage. For it is not enough if you abstain from another’s bed or from a brothel. Whoever has a wife should seek nothing [Col. 1080B] outside himself, but, content with her alone, should preserve the pledges of a chaste and inviolate bedchamber. For before God, one who, having cast off the yoke, indulges in foreign pleasure with either a free woman or a slave woman is an adulterer just as much as an incestuous person. But just as a woman is bound by the bonds of chastity not to desire another, so a man is bound by the same law, because God has joined husband and wife in the compact of one body. Therefore He commanded that a wife not be dismissed unless convicted of adultery, so that the bond of the marriage covenant may never be dissolved except by that which faithlessness has broken. This also is joined to the perfection of chastity: not only must sin be absent, but even the thought of it. For it is plain that the mind is defiled even by an empty desire; and therefore a just person ought neither to do nor [Col. 1081A] to will what is contrary to this. Conscience, then, must be cleansed, for God sees through it and cannot be deceived. Let the breast be cleansed of every stain [Col. 1081A]

[Note: [Col. 1081C] *Various Notes on columns 1081–1082*]

**Let it be cleansed (*emaculetur*).** Thus the Turin and Bolognese manuscripts and Isaeus edition; but the recently collated Royal manuscript and editions have *evacuetur*.—*Emaculetur.* The editions have *evacuetur*. PFAFFIUS.—Here the Turin manuscript and Isaeus, from the Bolognese manuscript, offer the much more suitable *emaculetur*. For what follows is *labe* (“stain”). Latin writers say that a stain is *emaculare* or *eluere*, not *evacuare*. The opposite is *labe maculari*, “to be stained by a blemish.” *Epitome*, chapter 27: “Lest, stained by some blemish, they should be deprived of angelic honor”; and Book VI, chapter 23: “Although the body is stained by no blemish.” BUN.

**Of nature (*naturae*).** Absent from the Turin and Bolognese manuscripts and six editions; present in the others. 1 Kings VIII; 2 Chronicles VI; Ecclesiastes VII; Proverbs XX.

**“And us” (*ac nos*).** Thus the Turin and Royal manuscripts and the Isaeus and Cratander editions. The other editions have *aut*.

**“To those persevering” (*perseverantibus*).** Thus the Turin and Bolognese manuscripts. But the Royal manuscript and editions have *perseverabimus*.

**God (*Deo*).** Absent in the editions; but it is found in the Isaeus edition and manuscripts, as is *delictis* (“offenses”); the editions have *debitis* (“debts”).

**“For offenses” (*pro delictis*).** Several editions, including Cellarius, have *debitis*. But the Bolognese manuscript and Isaeus more elegantly have *pro delictis*, with Davisius concurring. Our author says *peccata, crimina, delicta, vulnera, errores*, etc.; but *debita*, so far as I know, nowhere.

**This (*hoc*).** The Paris edition adds *enim*, which is absent from the ancient manuscripts and six editions.

**Dear (*chara*).** The editions: “so dear.”

**“Who, since he more greatly.”** The passage is mutilated in the editions: “that he may receive with the angels the confessing sinner, whom in the heavenly kingdoms he may make to be exalted for humility.”

**Exalted (*sublimem*).** Thus the Turin and Bolognese manuscripts. The editions, with the recently collated Royal manuscript, have *sublimari*.

**Ought (*debeat*).** The editions have *debet*.

**These (*hae*).** The Turin manuscript has *haec*.

**Altar (*aram*).** The Turin manuscript has *iram* (“wrath”).—“Upon God’s altar.” Pfaffius corrected this most rightly. Thus Book VI, chapter 25: “Therefore upon the altar of God . . . justice is laid, patience, faith, innocence, chastity, abstinence.” BUN.

**Receives (*suscipit*).** The Royal manuscript and most editions have *suscipit sibi, quia*.

[Col. 1082C]

**“And grants him.”** Thus the Bolognese manuscript and Isaeus, Spark, and Turin witnesses: *idoneum praemium* (“a fitting reward”) in place of *eique donum*.

**Bestows (*impartitur*).** Thus the Bolognese and Royal manuscripts and editions; the Turin manuscript has *impertit*.

**Thought (*arbitrantur*).** Thus the Turin and Bolognese manuscripts; the Royal manuscript and editions have *putaverunt*.

**To discern (*prospicere*).** Correctly in the Turin manuscript; others have *perspicere*.

**What follows (*sequentia*).** Thus the Bolognese and Turin manuscripts. But the Royal manuscript and editions have *sapientia providere*.

**“Who did not possess the summary.”** Thus I have corrected it from the Isaeus and Spark editions and the Bolognese manuscript; the Turin manuscript has *tenebant*; the editions, “did not possess knowledge.”—It is peculiar to Lactantius to call a brief and compendious collection and knowledge of divine mysteries a *summa* (“summary”); so in Book VII of the *Divine Institutions*, chapters 6 and 7. ISAEUS.

**Of things (*rerum*).** The Royal manuscript has *eorum*. The editions: “therefore, denying providence, they denied God as well, who is its source and head.”

[Col. 1082D]

**“It cannot be said.”** Thus five editions; but ten others: “because whatever exists cannot exist without some beginning.”

**Without a begetter (*sine generante*).** Thus the Turin and Bolognese manuscripts and the Isaeus and Spark editions. The editions have *ratione*. Perhaps it would be better to read *generatione*, with the addition of one syllable. SPARK.

**“From things” (*ex rebus*).** Thus the Turin and Bolognese manuscripts, Isaeus, and Spark; the editions have *exordiis* (“beginnings”).

**Has (*habet*).** The editions have *habeat*, more correctly.

**Made (*factum*).** The Turin manuscript has *generatum* (“generated”); the others, *factum*.—“Generated by no providence.” Turin manuscript: “generated by no providence.” Elegantly so; and the following word requires *generari* or, as Isaeus wishes, *generatum* again. For *generare* is the same as creating or making, as we have shown from many passages of Lactantius in the note on Book III of the *Institutions*, chapter 14. BUN.

**Generated by reason (*ratione generatum*).** Thus the Bolognese manuscript and Isaeus and Spark editions; the others have *generari*.

**Immortal.** These words are expressed somewhat differently in the editions. In the Royal manuscript the negative particle is absent.

**The world (*mundum*).** Thus the Bolognese manuscript and six common editions. The other editions: “they thought that the world and man had been made, and that souls were immortal. But although they thought these things, these men nevertheless [were] divine.” Royal manuscript: “but though they thought these things, men of this sort nevertheless,” etc. Turin manuscript: “though they thought true things, nevertheless [they were] of this kind.”

so that it may be able to be the temple of God, which is illuminated not by the brilliance of gold or ivory but by the radiance of faith and chastity.

## CHAPTER LXVII, alternatively IX.  
*(Institutions, Book VI, chapters 24 and 25; Book VII, chapters 2 and 3.)*  
**On repentance, the immortality of the soul, and Providence.**

But all these things are difficult for a human being, and the condition of frail nature does not allow anyone to be without blemish. Therefore the final remedy is that we should have recourse to repentance, which holds no small place among the virtues, because it is self-correction: so that, if by chance we have fallen either in deed or in word, we may at once come to our senses, acknowledge that we have sinned, and pray to God for pardon. In His mercy He will not [Col. 1081B] deny it, except to those who persist in error. Great is the help of repentance, great its consolation. It is the healing of wounds and sins; it is hope, it is the harbor of salvation. Whoever removes it cuts off from himself the way of life, because no one can be so just that repentance is never necessary for him. But we, even if there is no sin, ought nevertheless to confess to God, repeatedly to entreat pardon for our offenses, and to give thanks even amid evils. Let us always render this obedience to the Lord. For humility is dear and pleasing to God; and since He receives the sinner who confesses more readily than the proud just person, how much more will He receive the just person who confesses, and make him exalted in the heavenly kingdoms because of humility.

[Col. 1082A] These are the things which a worshipper of God ought to offer; these are the victims; this is the sacrifice that wins favor; this is true worship, when a human being brings the pledges of his own mind to the altar of God. That supreme Majesty delights in this worshipper; receives him as a son; and bestows upon him the gift of immortality. Of this I must now speak, and refute the belief of those who think that souls are extinguished together with bodies. Because they knew neither God nor could discern the hidden design of the world, they did not even grasp the nature of man and of the soul. For how could those who did not possess the summary discern what follows? Therefore, denying that any providence exists, they denied God as well, who is the source and head of things. It followed that they would say that existing things had either always existed, or had arisen of their own accord [Col. 1082B], or had solidified through the aggregation of tiny seeds.

That which both exists and is subject to sight cannot be said to have always existed; for existence itself cannot be without some beginning. Nor can anything arise of its own accord, because there is no nature without a begetter. But how could primary seeds exist, when seeds arise from things and, in turn, things arise from seeds? Therefore no seed exists which has no origin. Thus it came about that, since they thought that the world had been made by no providence, they did not even think that man had been generated by any rational plan. But if no plan had been employed in fashioning man, then the soul cannot be immortal. Others, on the contrary, thought that there is one God; that the world was made by Him; that it was made for the sake of human beings [Col. 1083A]; and that souls are immortal. Yet, although they held these views, [Col. 1083A]

**Some (*aliquo*).** Absent from the editions.

**And so immense (*tamque*).** But the Turin manuscript has *tamquam*.

**Good.** Plato, at the beginning of the *Timaeus*.

**Therefore.** Absent from the Turin manuscript.

**Theodorus.** See *On the Anger of God*, chapter 9.

Therefore good things.”** This discourse through section 29, “The Stoics say,” must be understood as put forward by the impious Theodorus against Plato, whom Lactantius introduces but does not approve. He declares his own opinion in the following chapter. BUN.

**“Were contained. If evil things, then also good things, so that God either made nothing, or, if good things.”** Thus more correctly the Turin manuscript and Davisius; traces of this reading remain in corrupt ancient Venetian editions. Hence Parrhasius, Aldus, Cratander, Gymnicus, Betuleius, Tornaesius, Thomas, Cellarius, Pfaffius, and Heumann: “Therefore God made either good and evil things, or nothing. If good things.” From the Bolognese manuscript, Isaeus, Galland, and Spark: “If evil things, then also good things, so that God either made nothing, or, if only good things.” BUN.

**“They cannot even be more eternal.”** Either one should read *esse possunt*, or, preferably, “they are not even more eternal.” Davisius. But nothing must be added or changed here, as examples which I have given on Book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 16, will show. BUN.

**More fitting (*convenientius*).** Thus the Turin and Bolognese manuscripts and Isaeus edition. In the Royal manuscript and other editions, *conveniens*.

**“According to Plato’s opinion.”** Our author says this not because he thinks that it really was Plato’s opinion, but to show how Theodorus, whose role Lactantius here assumes, may reason if Plato’s hypothesis is granted, etc. DAVISIUS.

**The same (*idem*).** But the editions have *ideo*. Certainly not; for what the philosopher’s opinion is is clear from Book II of the *Republic*, near the end.

**“That the world is from God,” etc.** The editions: “that the world was made by God because the world is good, since it has embraced . . .”—“Not that the world was made by God because the world is good.” Thus I edit from the Turin manuscript with Pfaffius and Davisius. Nearest to these are the two Venetian editions of 1478, those of 1493 and 1497, Pierius, Paris, Parrhasius, Aldus, Cratander, Gymnicus, Gryphius, Tornaesius, and Betuleius: “Not that the world was made because the world is good.” But Thomas, Isaeus, Galland, Spark, and Cellarius most wrongly: “It is evident that the world was made by God because the world is good”—contrary to Lactantius’s intention, as Davisius observes, for he is here refuting Plato. they did not discern the causes, the rational grounds, or the ends of this divine work and plan, so as to bring the whole mystery of truth to completion and, as it were, to conclude it by some final end. But what they could not do, because they did not hold fast to truth continually, must be done by us, who have come to know it through God’s proclamation.

## CHAPTER LXVIII.  
*(Divine Institutions, Book VI, chapter 4.)*  
**On the world, humankind, and God’s providence.**
Let us therefore consider what purpose there was in constructing so great and so immense a work. God made the world, as Plato held; but why he made it, Plato did not show. “Because,” he says, “he is good and envies no one, he made [Col. 1083B] what is good.” But in the nature of things we see that there are both good and evil things. Therefore some perverse man might arise—such as that atheist (*ἄθεος*) Theodorus—and reply to Plato: “On the contrary, because he is evil, he made what is evil.” How will he refute him? If God made the things that are good, whence then did so many evils burst forth, evils which for the most part even prevail over good things? “They were contained in matter,” he says. God therefore made either both good and evil things, or nothing. If he made good things alone, evils, which were not made, are more eternal than goods, which had a beginning. Therefore, things which at some time began will have an end, and things which always existed will remain. [Col. 1083C] Evils, therefore, are more powerful. But if they cannot [Col. 1084A] be more powerful, neither can they be more eternal. Therefore either both always existed—and God was inactive—or both flowed from one source. For it is more fitting that God made all things than that he made nothing.

Therefore, according to Plato’s view, the same God is both good, because he made good things, and evil, because he made evil things. But if this cannot be, it is clear that the world was not made by God because the world is good. For it embraces all things, good and evil, and he made nothing for its own sake, but for something else. A house is built not merely in order that it may be a house, but that it may receive and protect an inhabitant. Likewise, a ship is constructed not merely so that it may appear to be a ship, but so that people may be able to sail in it. Vessels likewise are made not merely in order that they may be vessels, but that they may contain things necessary for use [Col. 1084B]. Thus God must necessarily have made the world for some use. The Stoics say that it was made for the sake of human beings, and rightly so. For human beings enjoy all those goods which the world contains within itself. Yet they do not explain why human beings themselves were made, or what benefit that providence—the maker of things—derives from them.

The same Plato affirms that souls are immortal (Plato, *Phaedrus*, *Phaedo*, *Gorgias*, *Laws*); but he does not comprehend why, how, when, or through whom they attain immortality; nor what, in sum, that great mystery is; why those who are to be immortal are first born mortal, and then, when the span of temporal life has run its course and the coverings of their frail bodies have been cast off, are transferred [Col. 1084C] to that eternal blessedness [Col. 1085A]. Finally, he explained neither God’s judgment nor the distinction between the just and the unjust. Rather, he thought that souls which had plunged themselves into crimes were condemned only so far as to be reborn in beasts, and thus pay the penalties of their sins until they return again to human forms; and that this happens forever, with no end to such passage. He presents to me some sort of game, like a dream, in which no reason, no divine governance, and no design appears to reside.

Compare *On Anger*, ch. 10.]

## CHAPTER LXIX, alternatively X  
*(Book VII of the Divine Institutions, chapters 5, 8, and following.)*  
**The world was made for humanity, and humanity for God.**

I shall now state what that ultimate point is which not even those who spoke true things were able to connect, after bringing together their causes and arguments [Col. 1085B]. The world was made by God in order that human beings might be born; but human beings are born in order that they may acknowledge God as Father, in whom is wisdom; they acknowledge him in order that they may worship him, in which worship is justice; they worship him in order that they may receive the reward of immortality; they receive immortality in order that they may serve God forever. Do you see how the first things are joined to the middle, and the middle to the last? Let us examine each point and see whether its rationale also holds firm.

God therefore made the world for humanity. Whoever does not see this differs little from a beast. Who looks up at heaven except a human being? Who marvels at the sun, the stars, and all God’s works, except a human being? Who cultivates [Col. 1085C] the earth? Who derives fruit from it? Who sails the sea? Who has fish, birds, and four-footed animals in his power, except a human being? Therefore God made all things for humanity, because all things have been made available for human use.

The philosophers saw this, but they did not see what follows: that God made humanity itself for himself [Col. 1086A]. For it was consequent, pious, and necessary that, since he had undertaken so great a work for humanity’s sake, and had bestowed upon humanity so much honor and so much power that humanity rules in the world, humanity should acknowledge God as the author of such great benefits—he who also made the world itself for humanity—and should render him the worship and honor due to him. Here Plato went astray; here he lost the truth which he had first grasped, when he was silent about the worship of that God whom he admitted to be the creator and father of things. Nor did he understand that humanity is bound to God by the bonds of piety, from which religion itself receives its name, and that this alone is the reason why souls are made immortal. He nevertheless perceived that they are eternal, but he did not descend to that conclusion by stages. For, having cut away the intermediate points, he fell into truth rather [Col. 1086B] as though over some sheer precipice; nor did he proceed further, because he had found the truth by chance, not by reasoning.

God, therefore, must be worshipped, so that through religion—which is also justice—humanity may receive immortality from God; nor is there any other reward for a devout mind. Since the mind is invisible, it cannot be endowed by the invisible God except with an invisible reward.

## CHAPTER LXX  
*(Book VII of the Divine Institutions, chapters 12, 13, 20, 21.)*  
**The immortality of the soul is confirmed.**

Moreover, by very many arguments it may be inferred that souls are eternal. Plato says that what always moves itself, and has no beginning of motion, likewise has no end. Now the human mind always moves itself [Col. 1086C]; and because it is capable of motion for thinking, ingenious in discovery, ready in perception, capable of learning, because it retains the past, comprehends the present, foresees the future, and embraces knowledge of many things and arts, it is immortal, since it has nothing in itself compacted by the corruption of earthly weight.

Furthermore, the eternity of the soul is understood [Col. 1087A] from virtue and pleasure. Pleasure is common to all living creatures; virtue belongs to humanity alone. The former is vicious; the latter honorable. The former accords with nature; the latter is contrary to nature—unless the soul is immortal. For virtue, for the sake of faith and justice, fears neither poverty nor exile, shudders neither at prison nor pain, and refuses not death. Since these things are contrary to nature, virtue is either folly, if it both obstructs advantages and harms life; or, if it is not folly, then the soul is immortal. It therefore despises present goods because there are other and greater goods which it will attain after the dissolution of its body.

[Variorum notes to cols. 1087–1088: “And” (*ac*): editions and manuscript have *an* for *ac*; Royal manuscript: *aut*. “Is common to all”: thus Turin and Bologna; Royal manuscript and editions: *omnis communis*. “And” (*et*) is found neither in the editions nor in the Turin manuscript. “For justice”: Heumann says that he restores *et* from the Turin codex; yet *et* is likewise absent there, having been added conjecturally by Pfaff; Davisius excludes it because asyndeton is not infrequent. All books read *qui cum Deo, et vultu et mente communis*. From Book VII of the *Divine Institutions*, ch. 15, *male* has here been restored; for it reads: “Then no one will have anything except what was either wickedly acquired or defended by force.” “And” is absent from the editions. “Will bear arms” (*tractabunt*): Turin manuscript: *tractabit*. “Devastation” (*vastitas*): thus Turin, Bologna, and Isaeus; Royal manuscript and the other editions: *vastatio*.]

This too is a most powerful argument for immortality: humanity alone acknowledges God. Among mute creatures there is no apprehension of religion, because they are earthly and prostrate upon the earth [Col. 1087B]. A human being therefore looks upright toward heaven in order to seek God. Therefore one who desires the immortal cannot fail to be immortal. One who shares with God both countenance and mind cannot be perishable. Finally, among creatures humanity alone uses the heavenly element, which is fire. For if light comes through fire, and life through light, it is evident that one who has the use of fire is not mortal, because that element is near and familiar to him, and without it neither light nor life can subsist.

But why do we gather arguments that souls are eternal when we have divine testimonies? For sacred writings and the utterances of the prophets teach this. If this seems insufficient to anyone, let him read the verses of the Sibyls and consider also the responses of Apollo of Miletus, so that [Col. 1087C] he may understand that Democritus, Epicurus, and Dicaearchus raved—these alone among all mortals denying what is evident.

With immortality established, it remains to teach by whom, to whom, how, and when it is bestowed. When the fixed and divinely appointed times begin to be fulfilled, the destruction and consummation [Col. 1088A] of the world must take place, so that the world may be renewed by God. That time, indeed, is near, so far as can be inferred from the number of years and from the signs foretold by the prophets. But since the things said concerning the end of the age and the conclusion of time are innumerable, the sayings themselves must be set forth bare, since to employ testimonies would be endless. Whoever desires them, or trusts us too little, should approach the very sanctuary of the heavenly writings. Equipped by their authority, he will recognize that the philosophers erred in thinking either that this world is eternal or that countless thousands of years have passed since it was formed. For not yet have six thousand years been completed; when that number has been fulfilled, all evil will at last be removed, so that justice alone may reign. How this is to come about [Col. 1088B], I shall explain briefly.

## CHAPTER LXXI, alternatively XI  
*(Book VII of the Divine Institutions, chapters 15, 16, 17, 19.)*  
**On the last times.**

These future things are foretold by prophets, but as seers. When the final end of the world begins to draw near, wickedness will grow strong; every kind of vice and deceit will become more frequent; justice will perish; there will be no faith, peace, mercy, modesty, or truth; force and audacity will prevail. No one will possess anything except what has been wickedly acquired and defended by force. If any good people exist, they will be regarded as prey and objects of mockery. No one will show devotion to parents; no one will pity an infant or an old person. Avarice and lust will corrupt everything. There will be slaughter and [Col. 1088C] the shedding of blood. There will be wars, not merely external and neighboring ones, but civil wars also. Cities will wage war against one another; every sex and every age will bear arms. Neither the dignity of rule nor military discipline will be preserved; rather, plunder and devastation will occur in the manner of banditry. The kingdom will be multiplied, and ten men will seize [Col. 1089A] the world, divide it, and devour it.

Then another, far more powerful and more wicked, will arise. Having destroyed three from that number, he will possess Asia; having reduced the rest to his own power and enlisted them, he will harass the whole earth. He will establish new laws and repeal the old; he will make the state his own, and alter the name and seat of empire.

But because our author and others do not usually separate these, and because all earlier editions, including Thomas and Isaeus, give *modo ferro et igni*, the conjunction *et*, in place of *modo*, was restored with Heumann. BUN. “Cold” (*frigoribus*): editions: *rigoribus*. “Bitterness” (*amaritudine*): Turin manuscript: *amaritudinem*. “For drink” (*potum*): Turin manuscript: *potu*. “Signs also will be added, etc.”: Royal manuscript and editions: “signs will happen to men for fear.” “Will be darkened by continual gloom” (*perpetuo squalore fuscabitur*): Bünemann has *pallore fuscabitur* and supplies the following note: all earlier editions substituted the more familiar word for the less familiar, *perpetuo squalore fuscabitur*. Davisius aptly cites Pliny, *Natural History* II.80: “there occur prodigious and longer eclipses of the sun … with the pallor of almost a whole year unbroken.” BUN. “The moon, etc.”: the editions read, “the color of blood will overshadow the moon.” “Restore” (*reparabit*): Turin manuscript: *reparavit*. “Confounded” (*confusis*): manuscripts: *confusi*. “Comes” (*venerit*): thus Bologna and Royal manuscripts and editions; Turin has *evenerint*. Bünemann also printed *evenerint* from that manuscript and from Davisius, and therefore gives this note: earlier editions wrongly read *venerit*; for the word relates not to the old age of the world but to the evils. Davisius rightly observed that these are Hermes’ words, quoted by Lactantius in Book VII, ch. 18: ἐπὰν δὴ ταῦτα γένηται, “whenever these things come to pass,” etc.

Col. 1090C: “When” (*quo*): Turin manuscript: *quod*. “Former” (*prioris*): Turin manuscript: *priorib*. “And” was added from Bologna and Royal. “There will be tears”: editions have *nonnisi etiam lacrymae*; Bologna and Turin: *erunt*. “To God”: thus Turin and Bologna; Royal manuscript and editions: *ad eum*. “From terror, etc.”: Royal manuscript and editions: “for terror, or sleep for quiet”; Bologna and Royal: *ad quietem*; Turin: *requiem*. “Fear” (*metum*): Turin manuscript: *tecum*; but the other manuscripts and editions have *metus* or *metum*. “Certainly to scantness [of population]” (*certe ad raritatem*) is absent from the editions. “And” is absent from the editions.

Col. 1090D: “Devoted” (*dicatos*): Turin and Bologna manuscripts; editions: *deditos*. “Christ”: editions have *Deum* for *Christum*; after *Christum* the editions add *quum sit Antichristus* (“since he is Antichrist”). “That these things may be believed”: Bünemann has *ut credi ei possit* (“that he may be believed”). “From heaven”: editions: *de coelo*. “May cease” (*desistat*): Turin manuscript and both Venice editions of 1478, Venice 1493 and 1497, and Paris 1513 have *resistat*, that is, “stand, come to a standstill.” Cicero, Terence, Seneca, and others often use it so. From Parrhasius, *desistat* entered all editions, including Pfaff’s; Davisius and Heumann read *resistat*, rightly. BUN. “His own” (*suo*) is absent from the editions. “Will entice” (*illiciet*): editions: *alliciet*. Lactantius regularly uses *illicere*. “Madman” (*vecors*): thus Turin and Bologna manuscripts and Isaeus; other editions: *protervia*. “And he will hear them”: thus Turin, Bologna, and Isaeus and Cratander; other editions: “and God will hear them and will send …”]

Then there will be an unspeakable and accursed time, in which no one will wish to live. Indeed, affairs will fall into such a condition that lamentation will attend the living and congratulation the dead. Cities and towns will perish—now by the sword, now by fire, now by frequent earthquakes, now by floods, now by pestilence and famine. The earth will produce nothing, being rendered barren either by excessive cold or by heat. All water will partly be changed into blood and partly corrupted by [Col. 1089B] bitterness, so that nothing may be useful for food or wholesome for drink. To these evils signs from heaven will also be added, lest anything be lacking to inspire fear in humankind. Comets will appear frequently. The sun will be darkened by continual gloom. The moon will be stained with blood and will not restore the loss of its light. All the stars will fall; nor will the seasons retain their proper order, winter and summer being confounded. Then year, month, and day will be shortened. Trismegistus declared that this is the old age and decline of the world. When it comes [Col. 1090A], it must be understood that the time is at hand when God will return to transform the age.

But amid these evils an impious king will arise, an enemy not only of the human race but also of God. He will crush, torture, harass, and kill the remnants of that former tyrant. Then there will be unceasing tears, perpetual mourning and groaning, and vain prayers to God: no rest from terror and no sleep for repose. Day will always increase disaster, night fear. Thus the inhabited world will be reduced almost to desolation, certainly to a scant population. Then this impious man will persecute righteous people and those devoted to God, and will command that he himself be worshipped as God. For he will say that he is Christ, whose adversary he will be. In order that these things may be believed, he will receive power to perform wonders: so that fire may descend from heaven; so that the sun may cease [Col. 1090B] from its course; so that the image which he has set up may speak. By these prodigies he will entice many to worship him and to receive his mark on hand or forehead. Whoever does not worship and receive the mark will die under exquisite tortures. Thus he will destroy nearly two parts; a third will flee to deserted wildernesses. But, raging with unappeasable anger, that madman will lead an army and besiege the mountain to which the righteous have fled. When they see themselves surrounded, they will implore God’s aid with a loud voice; he will hear them and send them a deliverer.

## CHAPTER LXXII  
*(Book VII of the Divine Institutions, chapters 20, 24, 26.)*  
**On Christ’s descent from heaven for the universal judgment, and on the thousand-year kingdom.**

Then heaven will be opened amid a storm [Col. 1091A], and Christ will descend in great power. Fiery radiance will go before him, together with the incalculable host of angels. That whole multitude of the impious will be destroyed, and torrents of blood will run. The leader himself will escape, and, repeatedly restoring his army, will wage a fourth battle. There he will be captured with all the other tyrants and handed over to burning.

But the prince of demons himself, the author and contriver of evils, bound with fiery chains, will be consigned to custody, so that the world may receive peace and the earth, harassed through so many ages, may rest. Peace having thus been won and every [Col. 1091B] evil restrained, that righteous and victorious King will hold the great judgment over the living and the dead upon earth. He will give all nations to the living righteous as servants; he will raise the dead to eternal life; and he himself will reign on earth with them, establish the holy city, and this kingdom of the righteous will last for a thousand years.

During that same time, the stars will be brighter, the sun’s radiance will increase, and the moon will suffer no diminution. Then the morning and evening rain of blessing will descend from God, and the earth will produce every crop without human labor. Honey will drip from rocks; springs of milk and wine will overflow. Beasts, having laid aside their savagery, will become tame. The wolf will wander harmlessly among the sheep; the calf will feed with the lion; the dove will gather with the hawk [Col. 1091C]; the serpent will have no poison; no [Col. 1092A] animal will live by blood. For God will provide all with abundant and harmless food.

But when the thousand years have been completed and the prince of demons released, the nations will rebel against the righteous, and an innumerable multitude will come to assault the city of the saints. Then God’s final judgment against the nations will occur. He will shake the earth from its foundations; cities will collapse; and he will rain fire, sulphur, and hail upon the impious. They will burn and slaughter one another. The righteous, however, will hide beneath the earth for a little while, until the destruction of the nations is accomplished; then they will emerge after the third day and see the plains covered with corpses. Then an earthquake will occur; mountains will split apart; valleys will sink to a profound depth; the bodies of the dead will be heaped into it; and its name [Col. 1092B] will be called Πολυάνδριον (*Polyandrion*, “place of many men”).

[Variorum notes to cols. 1091–1092: “Amid a storm” (*in tempestate*): Royal manuscript and editions: *intempesta nocte*, “in the dead of night.” “Will go before” (*anteibit*): thus Turin and Bologna; Royal manuscript and editions: *antecedet*. “Incalculable host” (*vis inaestimabilis*): editions: *virtus*. But *inaestimabilis*, in the sense of “innumerable,” is distinctive of Lactantius; see note on ch. 33 of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*. “With all the other [tyrants]”: absent from the editions. The common editions read “with the other tyrants”; Bologna, “with all tyrants.” Turin combines both readings, and rightly. BUN. “Will be handed over” (*tradetur*): Turin manuscript: *traditur*. “Fiery” (*igneis*) is absent from Turin. “And that the earth, harassed, etc.”: here the Bologna manuscript and six editions are followed. *Ut* for *et* appears in the other editions. “Harassed through so many ages”: editions before Thomas, including the Tornaesian editions, omitted *tot*, correctly added by Thomas and later editors; compare *Divine Institutions* VII.19: “the world, which has endured slavery through so many ages, will rest.” BUN. “Won” (*parta*): Turin manuscript: *parata*. “Servants” (*servitium*): Turin manuscript; Suetonius edition: *servitutem*. See Book VII, ch. 21 of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*. “Them” (*iis*): Royal manuscript and editions: *his*. On the erroneous millennial reign of Christ, see note on Book VII of the *Divine Institutions*, chs. 14 and 24. “This” (*hoc*) is absent from the editions. “And” is absent from Turin. “Will provide” (*ministrabit*): Turin and Bologna; Royal manuscript and editions: *dabit*. “Released” (*resoluto*), that is, loosed anew. Book VII, ch. 26: “He will be loosed anew and, released from custody, will go forth.” BUN. “Against the nations”: manuscript and editions read “and to destroy the nation of the saints.” “Will shake” (*concutiet*). “Will occur” (*fiet*): Royal manuscript and editions: *fient*. “Mountains will split apart”: Royal manuscript and editions: “the mountains will split themselves and sink down into the breadth of a deep valley.” “Into it” (*in eam*): Royal manuscript and editions: *ea*. “Polyandrion”: Πολυάνδριον. The pagans had *xenotaphia* (“tombs for strangers”), in which they buried strangers; these were also called *polyandria* because they were common to all. Suidas. What others call a cemetery or monument is also called a *Polyandrium*, from the two Greek words πολύς, “many,” and ἀνήρ, “man,” because many men, πολλοὶ ἄνδρες, are carried there. “Forms” (*figuras*): Royal manuscript and editions: *figuram*. “Immortality” (*immortalitatis*): Turin manuscript: *immortali*. “Forever”: after these words Turin adds, “And this will be the kingdom of God, which will have no end.” It has the flavor of a gloss and is not found in Book VII, ch. 26 of the *Divine Institutions*.

Col. 1092D: “Then the impious also will rise again, not to life but to punishment”: Bologna has *etiam*, Royal *em*, Turin *et*, and editions *enim* for *etiam*. Lactantius teaches this better than above, at Book VII, ch. 20, where he taught the contrary. “Them also” (*eos quoque*): editions: *eosque*. “Condemned to everlasting [torments] and”: editions: *damnet aeternisque*. “Penalties” (*supplicia*) is absent from the editions. “All these things are true, etc.”: Royal manuscript and editions read: “All these things are true, foretold by the harmonious administration of all”; *consona* is read in all editions and manuscripts except Turin, which has *consonanti*, and Turin and Bologna have *adnunciatione*. “Hystaspes”: thus Turin and Bologna manuscripts. “Have sung” (*cecinerint*): Turin and Bologna; editions: *concinuerint*. “That every hope” (*quin spes*): Bologna and Turin; editions: *curae spes omnes vitae*.]

After these things God will renew the world and transform the righteous into angelic forms, so that, clothed with the garment of immortality, they may serve God forever. Then the impious too will rise again, not to life but to punishment. After the second resurrection, God will raise them also, so that, condemned to everlasting torments and consigned to eternal fires, they may pay the penalties deserved for their crimes.

## CHAPTER LXXIII, alternatively XII  
*(Book VII of the Divine Institutions, final chapter.)*  
**Hope of salvation lies in the religion and worship of God.**

Therefore, since all these things are true and certain, foretold by the harmonious proclamation of all the prophets; since Trismegistus, Hystaspes, and the Sibyls have sung the same things [Col. 1092C], it cannot be doubted that every hope [Col. 1093A] of life and salvation rests in the religion of God alone.

Accordingly, unless a human being receives Christ, whom God sent and will send for deliverance; unless through him one knows the supreme God; unless one keeps his commands and law, one will fall into the punishments of which we have spoken.

[Variorum notes to cols. 1093–1094: “Rests” (*sit posita*): thus Turin and Royal manuscripts and Isaeus; other editions: *sint posita*; Bologna manuscript: *sint positae*.

Col. 1093B: “Christ” is absent from the editions. “And will send”: thus Bologna and Royal; many editions lack these words and read, “unless he knows the supreme God through him who was sent.” “And law” (*legemque*): Royal manuscript and editions: *legesque*. “May be honored” (*honoremur*): manuscript; printed editions: *oneremur*.

Col. 1094A: “May come” (*veniamus*): Turin manuscript: *fugiamus*, “may flee,” which occurred just before. “Shape” (*formet*): Bologna manuscript; Turin: *reformet*; editions: *firmet*. “Prepare for the contest” (*praeparet ad agonem*) is absent from Turin. “Torn away” (*divellatur*): Turin manuscript: *depellatur*. “Acknowledge” (*agnoscat*): Turin and Bologna manuscripts and Isaeus; other editions: *cognoscat*. “Immortality” (*immortalitatis*): Bologna manuscript: *immortalis*, incorrectly.]

Therefore fragile things must be despised, that we may attain solid things; earthly things rejected, that we may be honored with heavenly things; temporal things fled, that we may come to eternal things. Let each person train himself in justice, shape himself to self-control, prepare himself for the contest, and equip himself for virtue, so that [Col. 1094A], should the adversary perhaps declare war, he may not be torn away from what is right and good by any force, terror, or torture. Let him not prostrate himself before insensible fictions, but uprightly acknowledge the true and only God. Let him cast aside pleasures, by whose allurements the exalted soul is dragged down to earth; let him hold fast to innocence, benefit as many as possible, and acquire for himself incorruptible treasures by good works, so that, with God as judge, he may be able to attain, according to the deserts of his virtue, either the crown of faith or the reward of immortality.
